institutions.name: Rutgers College (now Rutgers University)
institutions.notes: Founded 1766 as Queen's College. Renamed Rutgers College 1825. Now Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey. Merrill Edwards Gates (HD1687) served as 9th President 1882-1890. During his tenure: built Winants Hall (first dormitory), New Jersey Hall, established Agricultural Experiment Station (Hatch Act 1887), expanded curriculum and library. Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rutgers_University

institutions.name: Amherst College
institutions.notes: Founded 1821. One of the oldest liberal arts colleges in the United States. Merrill Edwards Gates (HD1687) served as 6th President 1890-1899. Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amherst_College David Peck Todd (HD1758) was astronomy professor and observatory director 1881-1917. Millicent Todd Bingham (HD1759) received honorary LL.D. 1957.

institutions.name: Albany Academy
institutions.notes: One of the oldest secondary schools in the United States. Merrill Edwards Gates (HD1687) served as principal for 12 years (c.1870-1882), growing enrollment from 70 to 800 students and extending the curriculum from 8 to 12 years. He declined the Chancellorship of the University of Tennessee (1875) to remain at Albany. Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albany_Academy

institutions.name: University of Rochester
institutions.notes: Founded 1850. Merrill Edwards Gates (HD1687) graduated 1870 with honors in Mathematics, Latin, Greek, and the English Essay Prize. The university awarded him an honorary LL.D. in 1882. Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Rochester Asahel Clark Kendrick (I00943) was among the founding faculty (1850), served as inaugural Munro Professor of Greek 1850-1888, first librarian 1850-1866, acting president 1863 and 1877-78. His son Ryland Morris Kendrick (HD4668, class of 1889) taught Greek and Latin on the same faculty. Ryland's son Nathaniel Cooper Kendrick (HD4670) earned B.A. 1921 here before his Harvard doctorate. Nathaniel's daughter Ann Kendrick McNabb (HD4672) also received her B.A. in History here. Kendrick Hall, the first men's dormitory (1913), was named for Asahel.

institutions.name: U.S. Board of Indian Commissioners

sources.note: Merrill Edwards Gates; Board of Indian Commissioners

institutions.notes: Advisory body established 1869 to oversee federal Indian affairs and disbursement of funds. Abolished 1933. Merrill Edwards Gates (HD1687) served as Chairman 1889-1899 and Secretary 1899-1912 — 23 years total shaping federal Indian policy. He also chaired the Lake Mohonk Conferences on the Indian Question.

institutions.primary_name: Yale University (College of Connecticut / Yale College)
institutions.name: Yale University (College of Connecticut / Yale College)
institutions.notes:
Co-founded 1701 by a consortium of Congregational ministers including Rev. James Pierpont (H00116) — son of Mary Hooker Pierpont (H00034), daughter of Rev. Thomas Hooker. James Pierpont is a direct 2nd-generation Hooker descendant and one of Yale's primary founders. Yale's founding is inseparable from the Hooker-Pierpont family network. James Pierpont's daughter Sarah Pierpont (HD0418) married Rev. Jonathan Edwards; their grandson Aaron Burr Jr. (H00913) attended Princeton. The Yale connections in this database are tracked separately in the `yale_connections` array (95 entries as of v0.3.25), covering alumni, faculty, and other relationships across the Hooker tree. Primary Hooker connection: H00116 James Pierpont (co-founder), H00034 Mary Hooker Pierpont (his mother). WHITNEY PORTRAIT: The Morse portrait of Eli Whitney (1822) — accession 1827.1, among the earliest formally catalogued works — was donated by George Hoadley (B.A. 1801), husband of Hooker descendant Mary Ann Woolsey Hoadley (HD2075). Whitney had married Hooker descendant Henrietta Frances Edwards (HD2046). Yale Art Gallery: https://artgallery.yale.edu/collections/objects/31 PERCIVAL PAPERS: James Gates Percival (X01936, B.A. 1815, M.D. 1820) — papers held at Yale Beinecke Library (YCAL MSS 703), including correspondence with Emma Hart Willard (H00597) in which both Hooker descendants acknowledged their family connection. T02264 Dr. Alvan Talcott Jr. (Yale BA 1824, Yale MD 1831) endowed the Alvan Talcott Professor of Classics at Yale in 1888. Chair most recently named to Egbert Bakker (Oct 2016).
[hooker_connection] co-founded by direct Hooker descendant
[external Yale affiliations, no tree entry: EXTERNAL_DWIGHT, EXTERNAL_WHR, X01936 — detail in connections archive]

institutions.name: Princeton University (College of New Jersey)
institutions.notes:
Founded 1746 by Presbyterian New Side ministers including Rev. Aaron Burr Sr. (X00613) — who became its 2nd president, and who married Esther Edwards Burr (H00378), 4th-generation Hooker descendant. Rev. Jonathan Edwards (X00128) — father of H00378 and H00376, father-in-law of Aaron Burr Sr. — succeeded Burr Sr. as 3rd president of Princeton in 1758, dying there of smallpox inoculation complications 16 days before his daughter Esther died. NOTE: Jonathan Edwards is NOT himself a Hooker descendant — he married Sarah Pierpont (HD0418), who IS a Hooker descendant. Their children (H00376, H00378) are. Aaron Burr Jr. (H00913) — 5th-generation Hooker descendant — attended Princeton (admitted as sophomore age 13; B.A. 1772). Tapping Reeve (X00614) — founded America's first law school; married H00912 Sally Burr (Hooker descendant) — also Princeton graduate (B.A. 1763). Aaron Burr Reeve (HD1910) — Yale B.A., son of H00912. John Pierre Burr (HD1915) — Aaron Burr Jr.'s son; barred from attending Princeton because of his race, despite being grandson and great-grandson of two Princeton presidents (Burr Sr. and Edwards). The Princeton Slavery Project's essay on John Pierre Burr documents this irony in full.
[hooker_connection] president and students who are Hooker descendants or in-laws

institutions.name: Litchfield Law School
institutions.notes:
Founded 1784 by Judge Tapping Reeve (X00614) — the first law school in the United States. Tapping Reeve married Sarah "Sally" Burr Reeve (H00912), 5th-generation Hooker descendant, daughter of Esther Edwards Burr (H00378). Aaron Burr Jr. (H00913) — 5th-generation Hooker descendant — studied law here under his brother-in-law Tapping Reeve before enlisting in 1775. Among Litchfield's other notable students: John C. Calhoun (also became VP — two Vice Presidents produced by one law school). The school ran until 1833; at its peak enrolled students from across the country. Tapping Reeve House and Law School designated National Historic Landmark, 1965. In 1781, Reeve (with Theodore Sedgwick) represented Elizabeth Freeman ("Bett") in Brom & Bett v. Ashley — case that led to abolition of slavery in Massachusetts. Reeve also brought Rev. Lyman Beecher (father of Harriet Beecher Stowe) to Litchfield. The Litchfield Law School is among the most consequential institutions connected to the Hooker tree.
[hooker_connection] founded by in-law of Hooker descendant; Hooker descendant studied here

institutions.primary_name: Howard University / Freedman's Hospital School of Nursing
institutions.name: Howard University / Freedman's Hospital School of Nursing
institutions.notes:
Sara Louise Iredell Fleetwood (HD1935) — 8th-generation Hooker descendant and great-granddaughter of Aaron Burr Jr. (H00913) — enrolled in the first class admitted to Howard University's Freedman's Hospital School of Nursing in 1893, studying under Dr. Daniel Hale Williams (who had performed the first successful open-heart surgery the previous year). She graduated with Freedman's first graduating class in 1896 and in 1901 was appointed the first Black nursing superintendent at Freedman's Hospital, having outscored all national applicants on the civil service examination. Chief surgeon Dr. William A. Warfield gave her the title 'Directress of Nurses.' She organized the Freedmen's Nursing Association and served as the first Black woman on DC's nurse examining board (1907). Her husband Christian Fleetwood (Medal of Honor, Battle of Chaffin's Farm 1864) clerked at the Freedmen's Bureau after the Civil War. The Fleetwoods hosted weekly literary salons at 319 U Street NW — part of the African American Heritage Trail, Washington DC.
[hooker_connection] 8th-generation Hooker descendant served as first Black nursing superintendent

institutions.name: Philadelphia Female Anti-Slavery Society
institutions.notes:
Founded 1833 — among the earliest interracial abolitionist organizations in the US. Hester "Hetty" Elizabeth Emery Burr (X00621) — wife of John Pierre Burr (HD1915), 6th-generation Hooker descendant — was a member of the Society and participated in the Women's Anti-Slavery Conventions of 1838 and 1839. Charlotte Forten's paternal aunts (Margaretta Forten, Sarah Louisa Forten Purvis, Harriet Forten Purvis) and her grandmother Charlotte Vandine Forten were founding members of the Society. Charlotte Forten herself (connected to the Hooker tree through her aunt Annie Wood's marriage to John G. Webb HD1930) was deeply embedded in this network. Hetty Emery Burr also co-founded the Moral Reform Retreat — Philadelphia's first shelter for African American women. The Society connected the Hooker-Burr abolitionist network with the Forten-Purvis-Grimké abolitionist network that dominated Philadelphia Black civic life for three generations.
[hooker_connection] co-founded by wives and in-laws of Hooker tree members

institutions.name: Hamilton College
institutions.notes: Liberal arts college in Clinton, Oneida County NY. Sereno Edwards Dwight (HD1970) served as 3rd President 1833-1835 (his career cut short by mercury poisoning). Benjamin Woodbridge Dwight (HD1988) graduated 1835; was tutor 1839-1842. Theodore William Dwight (HD1989) graduated 1840; taught 1842-1858; Dean of Hamilton Law School 1853 before moving to Columbia. Elliott Anthony (husband of HD1991) studied law here under Theodore William Dwight. Benjamin Woolsey Dwight (HD1967) was treasurer of Hamilton College. Asahel Clark Kendrick (I00943) graduated A.B. 1831 and immediately joined the faculty as a tutor, beginning his career in classical languages before moving to Madison University (Colgate).

institutions.name: New York Law School
institutions.notes: Co-founded in 1891 by Theodore William Dwight (HD1989) after leading a faculty walkout from Columbia Law School in protest of trustees' attempt to convert to the Harvard case method. The Dwight method of instruction continues in modified form at NYLS today.

institutions.name: Chicago Law Institute
institutions.notes: Founded 1857 largely through the efforts of Judge Elliott Anthony (X00639, husband of HD1991 Mary Dwight Anthony, granddaughter of Yale president Timothy Dwight IV). Anthony drove the charter through Springfield and served as its officer for 15+ years. By 1871 the Institute held ~7,000 volumes of law books valued at ~$30,000, including a complete set of American and English reports, and many volumes from Chancellor Kent's library with his manuscript notes. GREAT CHICAGO FIRE Oct 8, 1871: The entire library was destroyed. "Smoke still rose from the ruins of the city" at the post-fire meeting, "and the deliberations were more than once interrupted by the falling of crumbling portions of the masonry of the Court-room." The Institute was immediately rebuilt and became "one of the finest law libraries in the country." Elliott Anthony's son Charles was 15 at the time of the fire.

institutions.primary_name: Bear Mountain State Park / Palisades Interstate Park
institutions.name: Bear Mountain State Park / Palisades Interstate Park
institutions.notes: Established 1909 through lobbying by a group led by Dr. Edward Lasell Partridge (X00643), husband of Gertrude Edwards Dwight Partridge (HD2001), 8th-generation Hooker descendant. After federal government rejected national park status, they secured New York State legislation establishing Bear Mountain State Park. Mary Harriman then bequeathed an additional 100,000 acres as a memorial to her husband E.H. Harriman. Partridge was appointed to the Palisades Interstate Park Commission in 1913 and served until 1930 — through three reappointments. During his tenure: Bear Mountain extended by ~50,000 acres; Storm King Highway built; Bear Mountain Bridge constructed.

institutions.name: Park Street Church, Boston
institutions.notes: Sereno Edwards Dwight (HD1970), son of Yale president Timothy Dwight IV (H00914), was ordained here Sep 3, 1817, and served as pastor 1817-1826. During his pastorate he greatly influenced young hymn writer Ray Palmer (1808-1887), author of "My Faith Looks Up to Thee." Tapping Reeve (X00614, founder of Litchfield Law School) is also connected: Dwight brought Lyman Beecher to Litchfield in 1810 to serve as Presbyterian minister, and Beecher later served at Park Street Church.

institutions.name: American Ethnological Society
institutions.notes: Founded 1842 in New York City. Theodore Dwight Jr. (HD2050) was a co-founder. The Society's founding mission was to document the languages, cultures, and histories of non-European peoples — with a particular focus, in Dwight's case, on demonstrating that African peoples had sophisticated literary and monotheistic cultures long before European colonization. The Society used this scholarship as an explicit tool of abolitionist argument. Dwight also worked through the Society to preserve and translate the Arabic-language autobiography of Omar ibn Said (1831), the only known slave narrative written in Arabic in the United States. (Wikipedia; flashbak.com 2019)

institutions.name: Wentworth Institute of Technology
institutions.notes: Founded 1904 from the $7M+ estate of Arioch Wentworth. Frederick William Atherton (HD2069) was one of three founding trustees. Opened to students 1911. (Wikipedia)

institutions.name: United States Military Academy (West Point)
institutions.notes: Founded 1802 at West Point NY. HOOKER TREE CONNECTION: Rev. George Washington Woodbridge (HD2163), son of General Jonathan Woodbridge (H00928), graduated West Point; served as 2nd Lieutenant US Army 1826-1829 before entering the Episcopal ministry. He became rector of Monumental Church Richmond VA 1843-1878 and escorted Flora Cooke Stuart to her dying husband Jeb Stuart in May 1864.

institutions.name: Jefferson Medical College, Philadelphia
institutions.notes: Founded 1824 Philadelphia PA (now Sidney Kimmel Medical College, Thomas Jefferson University). One of the leading medical schools in the US in the early 19th century. HOOKER TREE CONNECTION: Dr. Timothy Woodbridge (HD2172), first doctor born in Youngstown OH, graduated Jefferson Medical 1833. He served as Civil War surgeon at Johnson's Island POW camp and was appointed by President Hayes as surgeon at Fort Peck Montana 1879.

institutions.name: Vassar College
institutions.notes: Founded 1861 Poughkeepsie NY. One of the original Seven Sisters colleges. HOOKER TREE CONNECTION: Lucy Maria Edwards Remy (HD2224), daughter of John Stark Edwards (HD2183), granddaughter of Jonathan Edwards Jr. and great-great-great-granddaughter of Thomas Hooker, attended Vassar. Her obituary (Indianapolis newspaper, Dec 31, 1925) notes she attended the college and was "regarded as a woman of high intellectual attainments." Also: Louise Tayler-Jones (, Wellesley 1896 — though she is NOT a Hooker descendant, being from the second Tayler marriage).

institutions.primary_name: Radcliffe College (now Radcliffe Institute, Harvard University)
institutions.name: Radcliffe College (now Radcliffe Institute, Harvard University)
institutions.notes: Founded 1879, Cambridge MA. Women's coordinate college of Harvard. HOOKER TREE CONNECTION: Anne Frances Hazard Richardson (HD1587), daughter of Thomas Pierrepont Hazard (HD1579), graduated magna cum laude. She later won the Helen Homans Gilbert Award from Radcliffe for her work chairing Reading Is Fundamental 1981-1996. (HD1587 notes; Washington Post obituary Jul 28, 1999)

institutions.primary_name: University of Connecticut (founded 1881 as Storrs Agricultural School)
institutions.name: University of Connecticut (founded 1881 as Storrs Agricultural School)
institutions.notes:
Founded September 28, 1881 as the Storrs Agricultural School, Storrs, Tolland County, Connecticut. Named after brothers Charles and Augustus Storrs, who donated 170 acres of farmland, a former orphanage, $6,000, and several barns. Renamed: Storrs Agricultural College (1893, when women were officially admitted and it became Connecticut's land-grant college); Connecticut Agricultural College (1899); Connecticut State College (1933); University of Connecticut (1939). One of the top-ranked public universities in the United States. 
HOOKER TREE CONNECTION: Gov. Hobart Baldwin Bigelow (HD1438) — 50th Governor of Connecticut, 1881-1883 — signed the legislation accepting the Storrs gift and establishing the school. He was a 7th-generation descendant of Thomas Hooker through the Russell-Pierpont line: Thomas Hooker → Samuel Hooker → Mary Hooker Pierpont → Mary Pierpont Russell → Lt. Joseph Pierpont → Joseph Pierpont (Yale 1751) → Belinda Pierpont Bigelow → Gov. Hobart Baldwin Bigelow. (UConn official history; Wikipedia)

institutions.primary_name: American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions (ABCFM)
institutions.name: American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions (ABCFM)
institutions.notes: Founded 1810 at Andover Seminary, Massachusetts by prominent Congregationalists. First American foreign missionary society; first missions to China and Ceylon. Yale President Rev. Timothy Dwight IV (H00914) was among the founding figures; Dwight Mission (established 1820 in present-day Arkansas/Oklahoma for the Cherokee) was named in his honor. The board operated Brainerd Mission (Chattanooga TN, est.1817) where Harriet Ellsworth Blunt (X02121) and Ainsworth Blunt (X02122) served the Cherokee. HOOKER TREE CONNECTIONS: 1. Rev. Timothy Dwight IV (H00914) — Yale President 1795-1817; founding ABCFM figure; Dwight Mission named for him. 5th-generation Hooker descendant. 2. Elias Cornelius (X00724) — ABCFM Secretary of Domestic Correspondence 1819-1832; conducted 1817 missionary tour to Creek and Cherokee; m. Mary Ann Hooker (H01355). 3. Rev. Edward William Hooker (H01354) — corporate ABCFM member from 1840. 4. Harriet Ellsworth Blunt (X02121) — served at Brainerd Mission 1821-1837; granddaughter of Rev. Cyprian Strong (H00299). 5. Ainsworth Blunt (X02122) — Brainerd missionary 1822-1837; accompanied Cherokee on Trail of Tears 1838; first mayor of Dalton GA. 6. Dr. Mary Floyd Cushman (HD2818, gen 8) — ABCFM medical missionary in Angola 1922-1953. 7. Samuel Gelston Dwight (HD2376) — ABCFM missionary to Hawaii; children named for ABCFM colleagues Juliette Cooke and Samuel Castle. | merged from dup INST022 record: First American foreign-mission organization. Tree connections: Rev. Elias Cornelius (agent 1816, secretary 1831-32); Ainsworth and Harriet Ellsworth Blunt, missionaries to the Cherokee at Brainerd, Tennessee; Eliza Talcott, missionary to Japan; Rev. William Banfield Capron, Madura mission; Judge John Hooker, member.

institutions.name: Baldwin Home Museum (Lahaina, Maui)
institutions.description: Residence of ABCFM missionary Dwight Baldwin 1836-1868 at Lahaina, Maui. Oldest standing house in Maui County. Deeded to Lahaina Restoration Foundation 1967. Named for Dwight Baldwin, whose first name likely honored Yale President Timothy Dwight IV.

institutions.name: Auburn Button Works (Auburn Plastics)
institutions.notes: Founded 1876 by John Hermon Woodruff (Yale 1863, X00821) as "Woodruff's Button Factory" in Auburn NY. Originally in the post office on Exchange Street; moved to 1900 Washington St in 1900; larger plant on Canoga Street 1911; second plant on 24 McMaster St WWII. Products: pearl and shellac buttons, typewriter keys, butt plates for rifles, 78-rpm records, molded plastic goods. Douglas Woodruff (HD2498, Yale 1905) succeeded as president until his death 1957. Renamed Auburn Plastics 1957 when button manufacturing ceased. Connected to Hooker tree through Caroline Porter Beardsley Woodruff (HD2488), 8th-generation descendant of Thomas Hooker through Susannah Edwards (H00382).

institutions.name: Yale Sheffield Scientific School
institutions.notes: Founded 1847 as the Yale Department of Philosophy and the Arts; became the Sheffield Scientific School 1861. Merged fully into Yale College 1956. Offered 3-year programs in engineering and applied science at lower cost than Yale College. Distinct from the "Yale" of liberal arts and law — Sheffield produced engineers, industrialists, and scientists. Notable Hooker-connected alumni: Joseph Wickham Roe (HD2556, 1895) — professor of industrial engineering, NYU; author of "English and American Tool Builders" (1916). Roe family papers at Yale: MS 774.

institutions.name: Connecticut Land Company
institutions.notes: Formed 1795 by 36 Connecticut investors who purchased the entire Connecticut Western Reserve from the State of Connecticut for over $1,000,000 — land the state had 'reserved' for citizens whose property was damaged by the British in the Revolution. In April 1807, Richfield Township was acquired for $26,087 by seven men: Col. Benjamin Tallmadge (H00757), Solomon Lathrop, Jeremiah Wilcox, Uriel Holmes Jr., Pierpont Edwards (H00386), Daniel Green, and Jonathan Dwight Sr. — two of the seven being Hooker descendants. Pierpont Edwards (H00386) invested $60,000 — approximately 5% of total company holdings. His son John Stark Edwards (HD2044) served as his first agent in the Reserve, but died Feb 22, 1813 in Warren, Trumbull County OH age 35 — the year Whittlesey rode through the black swamp and nearly died at Fort Meigs. Pierpont Township, Ashtabula County, Ohio is named for Edwards. In 1811, Heman Oviatt (husband of HD2934 Eunice Newton Oviatt) bought the northwest quarter of Richfield Township from Col. Tallmadge for $1.25 an acre. John Newton (HD2925) arrived in Richfield in the early 1820s and purchased most of the east center land, building the home later owned by Homer Carter. Elisha Whittlesey (X01997) arrived in Canfield June 27, 1806 — the same summer the company was active — and became public prosecutor for the entire Western Reserve. The company was ultimately a financial failure. (Richfield Township History; Ohio History Journal; Whittlesey Genealogy #310)

institutions.name: Savannah Educational Association (SEA)
institutions.notes: Founded by Savannah's African-American community after General Sherman captured Savannah (December 21, 1864) and the U.S. government confiscated the Montmollin Warehouse (23 Barnard Street (also referenced as 21 Barnard in some sources — likely a historical street renumbering; same building)). Established Bryan School at that location. Opening day January 10, 1865: hundreds of Black children marched from First African Baptist Church to the former slave pen building. July 1865: SEA schoolchildren publicly demonstrated their learning. Absorbed by the American Missionary Association 1867. (Georgia Historical Society marker, 23 Barnard Street (also referenced as 21 Barnard in some sources — likely a historical street renumbering; same building), Savannah)

institutions.name: Beach Institute
institutions.notes: Founded 1867 by the American Missionary Association, consolidating several Savannah schools including Bryan School (formerly in the Montmollin Warehouse, 23 Barnard Street — the building whose third floor had been a slave pen belonging to John Samuel de Montmollin II, grandson of abolitionist Jonathan Edwards Jr.). (Georgia Historical Society marker, 23 Barnard Street, Savannah)

institutions.name: First African Baptist Church
institutions.notes: Founded 1788 by Andrew Bryan — oldest Black Baptist church in America. On January 10, 1865, hundreds of Black children marched FROM this church TO the Montmollin Warehouse (former slave pen of John Samuel de Montmollin II) for the opening of Bryan School. (Georgia Historical Society marker, 23 Barnard Street, Savannah)

institutions.name: Williams College
institutions.notes: Private liberal arts college founded 1793 with funds from the estate of Ephraim Williams, a colonist killed in the French and Indian War (1755). One of the original "Little Three" liberal arts colleges.

institutions.name: Case Western Reserve University
institutions.notes: Founded 1826 in Hudson, Summit County, Ohio as Western Reserve College by a group of Connecticut Congregationalist settlers, with Rev. Giles Hooker Cowles (H00443) among its founders. Called 'the Yale of the West' — same motto (Lux et Veritas), same entrance standards, same curriculum as Yale. First college in northern Ohio. H00443 (Giles Hooker Cowles, gen 5 Hooker descendant) was named 'Hooker' for both his grandfather Giles Hooker and the Hooker ancestral line. He graduated Yale 1789, moved to Austinburg, Ashtabula County OH as a missionary (Ohio Home Missionary Society), and was instrumental in establishing the college infrastructure of the Western Reserve. First college west of the Appalachians to enroll (1832) and graduate (1836) an African-American student. Hudson was a major Underground Railroad stop. Co-founder Owen Brown was the father of abolitionist John Brown. The Newton family (HD2925 John Newton, HD2927 Eben Newton) and Elisha Whittlesey (X01997) all operated in the Western Reserve contemporaneously. Whittlesey was public prosecutor for the entire Western Reserve from 1806; Eben Newton was a judge and state senator. Moved to Cleveland 1882, merged with Case Institute of Technology 1967. H00443 is the brother of H00442 (Pamelia Cowles Thompson), whose granddaughter Laura Hooker Thompson Newton (HD0532) married John Newton (HD2925) — making the founding of Western Reserve College a family affair in the deepest sense. Among the original 12-member founding board of three presbyteries that met at Warren OH 1825 to choose a college site (selecting Hudson, now Summit County): from Grand River Presbytery, Rev. Dr. Giles Hooker Cowles (H00443) and Rev. Eliphalet Austin (X01418, with Harvey Coe and A. Griswold); from Portage Presbytery, Rev. Joseph Treat, John Steward, J. H. Whittlesey, Lemuel Porter; from Huron Presbytery, A. H. Betts, L. B. Sullivan, Hon. Samuel Cowles (of San Francisco — his namesake nephew HD3710 was 2 years old in 1825), D. Betts. Charter obtained 1826.

institutions.primary_name: Peabody Museum of Natural History, Yale University
institutions.name: Peabody Museum of Natural History, Yale University
institutions.notes: Endowed by George Peabody through his nephew Othniel Charles Marsh. Dana family connection: James Dwight Dana (X00899) — curator of mineralogy; Edward Salisbury Dana (X00898) — succeeded his father as curator 1874, trustee 1885-1929, chairman after Marsh's death 1899.

institutions.name: League of Universal Brotherhood
institutions.notes: Founded by Elihu Burritt (X01932) in 1846. International peace organization. Launched at Pershore, England; supported by Joseph Sturge, James Silk Buckingham, and John Jefferson of the London Peace Society. Published Bond of Brotherhood monthly. British branch merged with London Peace Society 1857. Influenced later UK peace movement.

institutions.name: Wadsworth Atheneum Museum of Art
institutions.notes: Founded 1842 by Daniel Wadsworth (HD1330); opened 1844. Oldest continuously operating public art museum in the United States. The building was designed to house Daniel's personal art collection and establish Hartford as a cultural center. Daniel was a patron of the Hudson River School — Thomas Cole and Frederic Church both exhibited here. The museum holds ART030: John Trumbull's 1784 portrait of Daniel (age 13) and his father Jeremiah (T00387) — painted 58 years before the museum existed, now hanging in the institution Daniel built. A portrait becomes its own home. Daniel Wadsworth descends from BOTH Thomas Hooker (through his mother H00362 Mehitable Russell → H00118 Mary Pierpont → H00034 Mary Hooker Pierpont) AND from John Talcott (through his father T00387 Jeremiah → T00068 Abigail Talcott → T00045 Gov. Joseph Talcott → T00035 Lt.-Col. John Talcott Jr.). Two founding Hartford lines united in one institution.

institutions.name: Rollins College
institutions.notes: Florida's first institution of higher learning, founded by the Florida Congregational Association. Edward Payson Hooker (H02539) was its first president 1885-1892.

institutions.name: Middlebury College
institutions.notes: Liberal arts college founded 1800 in Middlebury VT.

institutions.primary_name: University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine
institutions.name: University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine
institutions.notes: HD3006 (Davenport Hooker) served as Chair of Anatomy 1919-1956.

institutions.name: The Taft School
institutions.notes:
Founded by Horace Dutton Taft, brother of President William Howard Taft. CPT building named for Charles Phelps Taft who contributed $150,000. HDT building (first permanent campus building) designed by Bertram Goodhue with landscape architecture by Frederick Law Olmsted Jr.
[former/alt detail] Founded 1890 as Mr. Taft's School; renamed 1898

institutions.name: Phillips Academy Andover
institutions.notes:
HD3067 (Charles Phelps Taft), HD3063 (Edward Swift Isham Jr.), and X02345 (Samuel Finley Brown Morse) attended Phillips Academy Andover. STAGE 6Y-174: John Adams was principal of Phillips Academy Andover for 22 years (1810-1832) — the longest principalship of the 19th century. Found Academy at 23 pupils after interregnum; grew enrollment to 100 by 1817 and held that level for 15 years. Salary $900 + house. Resigned at 60 saying no man over 60 ought to teach. Holmes referenced him in 'The School Boy' at the 1878 centennial. X02847 Rev. John Ripley Adams (Yale 1821, John Adams's son) taught at Phillips Academy briefly after Yale before entering Andover Theological Seminary 1826.
[former/alt detail] Phillips Academy, Andover MA (1778)

institutions.notes:
John Henry Colby (X00729) class of 1885; John Noyes Colby (HD2304) class of 1916. Colby family three-generation Dartmouth line (John Freeman Colby 1859, John Henry 1885, John Noyes 1916).

institutions.name: Columbia University School of Law
institutions.notes: Founded in 1858 by Theodore William Dwight (HD1989), 7th-generation Hooker descendant. Dwight accepted an invitation from Columbia College to develop a department of law. He served as dean until 1891, when he led a faculty walkout over the trustees' attempt to convert to the Harvard case method, and co-founded New York Law School. The Dwight method of legal instruction (memorization, practice drills, moot courts) competed with the Langdell case method at Harvard. A column on Columbia's College Walk is dedicated to Theodore William Dwight. institutions.notes:

Moved to Troy, NY in 1821 and renamed Troy Female Seminary. Renamed Emma Willard School in 1895. Willard resigned leadership in 1838 to her son John Willard (H01550). Almira Hart Phelps (H00598) was vice-principal; wrote Lectures on Botany (1829) during this tenure — 10,000 copies sold in three years. Twelve or more Berlin CT girls attended on Willard's invitation and expense, including Jane Porter Hart (HD2963) and Harriet Hart (HD2964). As of 2026: endowment $119M; grades 9-12 plus postgraduate; #1 private school Upstate NY 2018.

institutions.name: Hooker and Chaffee

institutions.name: Hartford Retreat for the Insane
institutions.notes:

T01062 Phineas Talcott Jr. served as steward 1828-1835; his wife I00197 Lora McLean was matron — patients called her "Good Mother Talcott." Boasted highest cure rate in the nation in its first decade. Grounds landscaped by Frederick Law Olmsted, 1860s. Became Institute of Living in 1943; incorporated into Hartford Hospital 1994. Now a comprehensive psychiatric facility at 200 Retreat Avenue, Hartford. Connecticut History Online article covers history in detail. institutions.name: Granite Mills

location.address: Just above Kelly Road, on the Hockanum River, Talcottville

institutions.notes:
Paper mill on the Hockanum River just above Kelly Road, Talcottville (Vernon) CT. GPS: 41.83210° N, 72.49648° W. Founded by T01052 Samuel Smith Talcott (1793-1882) as a linseed oil mill c.1838; converted to paper manufacturing after an 1863 fire. Manufactured albums, binders, boards, manilla and press papers — recycling old paper purchased in bales from New York, Boston, and Philadelphia. Destroyed by fire four times (1863, 1870, 1881, 1912) and rebuilt each time until the final 1912 fire. The 1881 fire article names owners as "Smith S. and Anson F. Talcott." Smith Stephen Talcott (1834-1888) — likely a son of T01052 Samuel — served as active agent from c.1864; he and T01052 ran the mill in parallel ("particularly confusing are the roles of the two S. S. Talcotts"). The Talcott Brothers (Charles Denison and Horace Wells) purchased the mill site in December 1912 primarily to acquire the water privilege. Despite the Talcott name, the Granite Mills Talcotts were from a different branch than the Talcottville mill owners. Site today: land between Tri-City Plaza and Hockanum River near Kelly Road; race exit from foundation preserved. Royal Talcott Journal, Nov 26, 1877: "young Nickols... got his foot caught in the belt" — earliest direct eyewitness account in the Royal Talcott Journal. SOURCE: Tankerhoosen Valley History, "Granite Mills (Circa 1850-1912)."
[former/alt detail] Also known as: Granite Paper Mills, Talcottville Paper Mill

institutions.primary_name: Talcott Street Congregational Church (now Faith Congregational Church)
institutions.name: Talcott Street Congregational Church (now Faith Congregational Church)
institutions.notes:
Founded 1826 by African Americans in Hartford after segregated treatment in white churches. Originally housed at Talcott Street, the congregation later took the name Faith Congregational Church. The church operated a school for African American children in its lower level — Hartford's regular school system technically accepted all children but African American parents established separate schools (1830) due to discriminatory treatment. The school met in the church's two lower rooms.

Rev. James W.C. Pennington pastored the congregation from 1840 to 1847 — writing during this period the first published history of African Americans (1841) and serving as a delegate to the Connecticut Anti-Slavery Society. It was here that John Hooker (H01626) became Pennington's friend and later, in 1851, legally purchased Pennington's freedom from his Maryland enslaver after the 1850 Fugitive Slave Law endangered him.

Other notable members of the period: Deacon James Mars (Connecticut Anti-Slavery Society executive committee); Henry Foster (state temperance society organizer); Ann Plato (teacher and author); Henry and Tamar Wilson (missionaries who accompanied the Mende return to Sierra Leone after the Amistad ruling).

Since 1912 it has occupied the James C. Flood Mansion atop Nob Hill at 1000 California Street, the only Nob Hill mansion to survive the 1906 earthquake and fire. Membership has historically included San Francisco's mercantile, banking, legal, and political elite. The Hooker family carried multi-generational membership: the 1905 Officers and Members directory lists three Hooker descendants — Charles Gay Hooker (H02703, address 967 Bush), C. Osgood Hooker (H04265, his son), and R.G. Hooker (Robert Gay Hooker, H04266, address 14 Post). A generation later, Charles Gay's grandson John Rodman Hooker (HD3243, Hooker & Fay senior partner) was also a member per his Golden Nugget Library biography. The Hooker presence at the club thus spans four generations — and is presumed to have continued with John Rodman's son Anthony Shreve 'Tony' Hooker.

institutions.notes:
San Francisco firm founded 1867 by Irwin J. Truman as a hay-press manufacturer at 1717 Front Street SF. After 15 years (~1882), the business expanded into agricultural implements, wagons, and buggies. C. Osgood Hooker (H04265, eldest son of Charles Gay Hooker H02703) joined as partner in 1885 at age 25, leaving his receiving-teller position at First National Bank. The firm relocated to 421 Market Street SF and grew to ~30 employees. Wholesale + retail business with trade extending across the Pacific Coast, to the Sandwich Islands (Hawaii), and shipments to Russia and Egypt. Osgood managed the buying and selling departments. The firm was DIFFERENT from and PRECEDED the later 'Hooker & Lent' real estate firm (LM057, founded ~1900 by Osgood's brother Robert G. Hooker H04266). Truman & Hooker reflects the earlier industrial phase of Hooker family business in SF; Hooker & Lent the later real estate phase. Irwin J. Truman: b. Oct 27, 1840 Philadelphia; Northern Irish immigrant family (1831), raised Canada; m.1860 P.J. Sage; one son I.C.J. Truman; member I.O.O.F.; Republican.

institutions.name: The Thacher School
institutions.notes:
Founded 1889 by Sherman Day Thacher (I00592) on his 160-acre Casa de Piedra ranch outside Nordhoff (now Ojai) — began as informal tutoring of a single student. The oldest private boarding school west of the Mississippi. From founding day Sherman required every boy to care for a horse, famously saying "There's something about the outside of a horse that's good for the inside of a boy." Practically, students rode five miles into downtown Ojai daily just to collect the mail. Original complex destroyed by fire June 1895; rebuilt in redwood by Sherman's architect brother Edward. Incorporated as a nonprofit in 1924; Sherman continued as headmaster until his 1931 death. Succeeded by Morgan Barnes 1931-1936 (interim five years), then by Sherman's son Anson Stiles Thacher (HD4102) 1936-1949 — the last Thacher family member to head the school. Under Anson the student body expanded from Sherman's ~60-boy cap to 94 boys. Began admitting female students in 1977. Major periods of growth in the 1960s and mid-1970s reached 189 students by 1975. The 1999-2008 $82M capital campaign funded a performing arts center, student commons, and dormitories; the 2017-launched $160M campaign grew endowment from $125M to $171M by 2018, increased financial aid budget by 50.7% by 2020, and funded a new academic building, dining hall, faculty housing, and a solar facility supplying 90%+ of the school's energy. Horse program continues — freshmen ride and care for a horse during all athletic seasons; annual gymkhana event; Western riding required with English riding elective grades 10-12. Outdoors Program offers backpacking, rock climbing, cycling, sailing, horse camping, canyoneering, backcountry skiing, kayaking. The ranch-school model influenced a wave of similar schools across California, Arizona, New Mexico, and Wyoming in the early 20th century.

narrative_blocks.header: He walked a hundred settlers to Hartford
narrative_blocks.body: In June 1636 Hooker led about a hundred men, women and children from Newtown, Mass., now Cambridge, a hundred miles to found Hartford, steering by compass and driving 160 cattle. They ate wild strawberries and arrived in a fortnight.

narrative_blocks.header: The sermon behind Connecticut's constitution
narrative_blocks.body: On 31 May 1638 Hooker told the General Court authority rests on the people's free consent; the 1639 Fundamental Orders, called the first written democratic constitution, followed. It was covenant theology; the people were church members.

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve years at the Puritan college
narrative_blocks.body: Hooker spent twelve years at the University of Cambridge, mostly at Emmanuel, the Puritan college, on a Dixie fellowship reserved for Market Bosworth's grammar-school boys. He mastered Ramist logic and the sermon; Emmanuel also formed John Cotton and his future son-in-law Thomas Shepard.

narrative_blocks.header: Silenced by Laud, he fled via Holland
narrative_blocks.body: Silenced at Chelmsford by Archbishop Laud in 1629, Hooker kept a school at Little Baddow with John Eliot. Summoned by the High Commission, he forfeited bail and fled to Holland to preach beside William Ames. In 1633 he sailed for Boston on the Griffin with John Cotton and Samuel Stone.

narrative_blocks.header: He stayed beside the despairing
narrative_blocks.body: At Cambridge Hooker knew the doctrine without feeling it, until he broke into grace. For seven years he sat with the despairing Mrs. Drake of Esher, through contrition and humiliation, and in her household met his wife, Susanna Garbrand.

narrative_blocks.header: He moderated the Hutchinson trial, then left
narrative_blocks.body: In 1637 Hooker was one of two moderators of the three-week inquiry into Anne Hutchinson's teaching, which ended in her excommunication and banishment from Massachusetts Bay. He went home to Hartford before it concluded.

narrative_blocks.header: No portrait, only his descendants' faces
narrative_blocks.body: Hooker was New England's foremost preacher, yet no portrait of him exists; the statue by the Old State House, near the First Meeting House, was modeled on his descendants' faces. Cotton Mather called him “the light of the western churches.”

narrative_blocks.header: The new curate ate at her mistress's table
narrative_blocks.body: Susanna was waiting-gentlewoman to Joane Drake at Esher, in Surrey, when the household took in a new curate, Thomas Hooker, who had his diet and lodging under the same roof from 1620. They were married the next spring.

narrative_blocks.header: About forty, she sailed on the Griffin
narrative_blocks.body: Susanna crossed to New England on the Griffin in 1633, about forty, with Thomas and their children. They lived first at Cambridge, and in 1636 went with the company through the wilderness to begin again at Hartford.

narrative_blocks.header: The overseer of Thomas's will married her
narrative_blocks.body: Elder William Goodwin, one of the overseers of Thomas's will, married Susanna about 1655 and took her to Farmington. The year before, the Particular Court had punished Walter Gray for slandering the two of them.

narrative_blocks.header: A wedding portion waited in England for Joanna
narrative_blocks.body: Susanna's eldest, Joanna, was Joane Drake's goddaughter. Francis Drake did not forget her: his will of 1634 left a portion for her wedding day to the girl by then in New England.

narrative_blocks.header: Motherless at sixteen, raised by the rector's wife
narrative_blocks.body: Susanna lost her mother in 1609, at about sixteen, and went to her childless aunt Christian Chaloner, wife of the rector of Amersham. Her uncle by marriage, Robert Chaloner, married her to Thomas in his own church on 3 April 1621.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandfather sold books to Reformation Oxford
narrative_blocks.body: Susanna descended from the Garbrands, a Calvinist family who fled the Low Countries for England. Her grandfather Garbrand Harks became the foremost Oxford bookseller of the Reformation and official stationer to the University, a post the family held for three generations.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight children, and every Hooker after them
narrative_blocks.body: Susanna died at Farmington on 17 May 1676, at about eighty-three, three years after William Goodwin and twenty-nine after Thomas. Her eight children carried the line to John Pierpont Morgan and William Howard Taft.

people.research_notes: Gentleman of Blaston, Birstall, Blaby, Countesthorpe, and Marefield. Bought house and 220 acres at Marefield Easter 1584. Father of Rev. Thomas Hooker. Hutchinson 1917 lineage: Thomas¹ of Blaston → John² → Thomas³ → Rev. Thomas⁴. [Migrated from marriage.notes (spouse X00002)]: Child is Rev. Thomas Hooker (H00001), founder of Hartford

narrative_blocks.header: He never left Marefield; his children sailed away
narrative_blocks.body: He lived out his days at Marefield in Leicestershire, where he had bought a house and land in the 1580s and where he was buried in 1635. His children carried the family far past it — a son to found Hartford, daughters across the ocean — while he never left the parish of his birth.

narrative_blocks.header: He sent his second son to grammar school
narrative_blocks.body: Of his seven children, it was the second son, Thomas, he sent some twenty-five miles away to board at the Market Bosworth grammar school. That schooling carried the boy to Cambridge, to a contested pulpit, and at last to the founding of a colony.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughters crossed to Roxbury and Hartford
narrative_blocks.body: His daughter Anne went to Roxbury with her husband George Alcock in the 1630 migration and died within months of landing, in the first hard winter. His daughter Dorothy, widowed in England, followed her brother Thomas to Hartford and became one of its original proprietors.

narrative_blocks.header: The Leicestershire will
narrative_blocks.body: Long after his death, the family was said to spring from the Devonshire Hookers — kin to Richard Hooker, the great Elizabethan divine of the English church — and even borrowed that line's coat of arms to prove it. But the local records told a plainer story: a 1558 will of John Hooker of Blaston, a yeoman, naming his son "Thomas Hocker" among working farmers, not gentry. The grand claim dissolved, leaving the founder's father among the ordinary Leicestershire farmers the documents had named all along.

narrative_blocks.header: She died in 1631 as the migration began
narrative_blocks.body: She bore at least seven children at Marefield and was buried at Tilton in the spring of 1631, just as the great Puritan migration was gathering. She did not live to see her son Thomas found Hartford — and her daughter Anne lay dying in Roxbury that very winter, an ocean away.

narrative_blocks.header: The records kept her name but little else
narrative_blocks.body: Beyond her name, her 1631 burial at Tilton, and the seven children she raised, almost nothing of her own life was set down. What she passed on surfaced only later — in a son who shaped a colony's conscience and daughters who carried the family across the sea.

narrative_blocks.header: Every Sunday she walked them to Tilton church
narrative_blocks.body: The Hookers worshipped at the parish church in Tilton, in a corner of Leicestershire then turning toward the reformed, Calvinist faith. Whatever piety her son Thomas carried into his famous pulpit, he first learned it on those Sunday walks from Marefield.

FindAGrave styles him 'Rev.' but the scholarly account (O'Brien/Flagg) describes him as a layman stationer — Rev. flag NOT applied pending Sam's review. Death Jan 1601/2 (old style).

narrative_blocks.header: Oxford stationer in his father's book trade
narrative_blocks.body: Richard Garbrand carried on the Oxford book trade as a stationer and bookseller and served as a churchwarden of St. Mary's in 1569. He was a son of Garbrand Harks, the refugee from the Low Countries who became the foremost Oxford bookseller of the Reformation.

narrative_blocks.header: Married Anne Ferrar; their daughter married Hooker
narrative_blocks.body: In 1578 Richard married Anne Ferrar, sister of the Principal of New Inn Hall, and they had eleven children. Among them was Susanna, who would marry Thomas Hooker and carry the Garbrand line to New England.

bio.notes: Maiden name uncertain, possibly Ferrar

narrative_blocks.header: Ran the Oxford bookshop as a widow
narrative_blocks.body: After Richard Garbrand died in 1601, Anne Ferrar carried on the family's Oxford bookshop until her own death in 1609. She was a sister of John Ferrar, Principal of New Inn Hall.

narrative_blocks.header: Died 26 days after her last son born
narrative_blocks.body: Her third child John was born April 2, 1646. She died April 28, 1646 — almost certainly of childbed fever, at roughly 24. Her husband Thomas Shepard had already buried his first wife Margaret weeks after arriving in New England.

narrative_blocks.header: Sailed to New England with Thomas Hooker, 1633
narrative_blocks.body: She was born in England around 1621 and crossed on the Griffin with her father in 1633, at roughly twelve. Thomas Hooker went on to found Hartford in 1636; she stayed in Cambridge and married Thomas Shepard there in 1640.

narrative_blocks.header: Named after Mrs. Drake — her mother's employer
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother Susanna Garbrand had been woman-in-waiting to Mrs. Joan Drake of Esher, Surrey — the woman whose spiritual crisis under Thomas Hooker's pastoral care became the model for his entire theology of conversion. Joanna was born in 1621, the year of her parents' marriage.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son Samuel was raised by his grandfather
narrative_blocks.body: Her firstborn Samuel Shepard was brought up in Thomas Hooker's Hartford household after her early death. The arrangement preserved Joanna's son for his Hooker grandfather while Thomas Shepard continued his Cambridge ministry.

narrative_blocks.header: A helper in the great work
narrative_blocks.body: The match joined the minister of Cambridge to the eldest daughter of the minister of Hartford, and both sides thought it highly suitable. She was remembered as a wife, a mother, and a helper in the work that was exhausting her husband.

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband outlived her by three years
narrative_blocks.body: She was buried at Cambridge. Thomas Shepard married again in September 1647 and was dead himself by August 1649, at forty-three; his widow then married Jonathan Mitchell, who had taken over his pulpit.

parents.notes: Son of William Shepard of Towcester, England

notable.notable_blurb: Harvard co-founder; key figure in Antinomian Controversy

narrative_blocks.header: Harvard came to Cambridge because of his ministry
narrative_blocks.body: A plaque at Harvard, quoting Cotton Mather, records that the college was placed at Newtowne — now Cambridge — in consideration of the salutary effect of Shepard's ministry. It was founded in 1636, the year he settled there.

narrative_blocks.header: He took Hooker's pulpit and bought his house
narrative_blocks.body: When Thomas Hooker led his congregation from Newtowne to Hartford in 1636, Shepard took the pulpit of First Church Cambridge and bought Hooker's property. He later married Hooker's daughter.

narrative_blocks.header: Born the hour Parliament was to blow up
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Towcester on the fifth of November 1605 — the day the Gunpowder Plot was found out, and by his own account at the very hour Parliament was to have been blown up.

narrative_blocks.header: Anne Hutchinson's most vocal clerical critic
narrative_blocks.body: During the Antinomian Controversy of 1637 and 1638 he sat with the colonial ministers at both of Anne Hutchinson's trials, civil and church. He was among her most vocal critics at the church trial, which ended in her excommunication.

narrative_blocks.header: Every sermon he studied cost him tears
narrative_blocks.body: At his deathbed he told the young ministers three things: that the study of every sermon cost him tears, that he got good of each one himself before preaching it, and that he entered the pulpit as if to give up his accounts.

narrative_blocks.header: Died at forty-three of a quinsy
narrative_blocks.body: He died at Cambridge on the twenty-fifth of August 1649, aged forty-three, of a peritonsillar abscess. He left an autobiography, published long after, that is one of the most personal records of Puritan spiritual life in New England.

narrative_blocks.header: Margaret died weeks after landing
narrative_blocks.body: His first wife Margaret Touteville sailed with him and their infant son on the Defence, reaching Boston on the third of October 1635. She was dead of consumption at Cambridge by that February, weeks after landing.

NOT WRITTEN, and there is a lot: his mother died when he was four and his father, a grocer, when he was ten; his stepmother disliked him and his grandparents neglected him, until an elder brother took him in — 'for him God made to be both father and mother unto me'. He entered Emmanuel College at fifteen, gambled, bowled and drank, and was converted hearing a Puritan on Romans 12, 'Be renewed in your mind'. Assistant schoolmaster at Earls Colne, Essex, 1627. Silenced for non-conformity by Archbishop Laud in 1630 and again in 1633. Sailed October 1635. Preached to the native peoples alongside John Allin and John Eliot, and published The Clear Sunshine of the Gospel Breaking out on the Indians of New England (1648); also New England's Lamentations (1645), Theses Sabbaticae (1649) and The Parables of the Ten Virgins. Three sons followed him into the ministry. Nathaniel Morton: 'By his death not only the church and people of Cambridge, but all New England, suffered a great loss.'

narrative_blocks.header: Cared for her mother on the Hartford migration
narrative_blocks.body: According to the Newton family genealogy, Mary was the daughter responsible for caring for her mother Susanna on the arduous journey from Cambridge to Hartford in 1636 — a journey in which Mrs. Hooker 'was carried on a horse litter' in poor health. Mary was roughly 13 years old.

narrative_blocks.header: Stayed in Hartford while Newton built Farmington
narrative_blocks.body: When Roger Newton went to establish the church at Farmington in the late 1640s, Mary remained in Hartford — their son Samuel's baptism on October 20, 1646 appears on the Hartford register, placing her there while her husband laid the groundwork for the congregation he would formally organize.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight children born across three Connecticut towns
narrative_blocks.body: The family's migrations are recorded in their children's birthplaces: Samuel and Roger Jr. born in Hartford; Susannah and John in Farmington; Ezekiel back in Hartford; then Sarah, Mary, and Alice in Milford — where the family finally settled and where Mary died on February 4, 1676.

narrative_blocks.header: Probably born in Esher near Hooker's curacy
narrative_blocks.body: Newton family genealogy says she was born around 1623, probably at Esher, Surrey — where Thomas Hooker had served as curate from c. 1618 to 1625. Esher was also where Hooker met her mother Susanna Garbrand.

notable.notable_blurb: Founding Farmington pastor; trained Yale's first rector

narrative_blocks.header: Hooker trained him; he founded Farmington's church
narrative_blocks.body: Roger Newton studied theology at Hartford under Thomas Hooker and, around 1645, married Hooker's eldest daughter, Mary. Ordained the first pastor of Farmington in 1652, he later served twenty-three years as the second pastor of Milford.

narrative_blocks.header: He trained Yale's first rector at his table
narrative_blocks.body: As Hooker had trained him, Newton took young men into his Milford home for theological study. One was Abraham Pierson Jr., who became the first rector of Yale College.

narrative_blocks.header: He sheltered the fugitive regicides near Milford
narrative_blocks.body: From 1661 the regicide judges Edward Whalley and William Goffe — hunted for signing the death warrant of Charles I — hid in a cellar near Newton in Milford. Their presence was kept secret through the two years they remained.

narrative_blocks.header: He brought Tunxis members into the church
narrative_blocks.body: Newton did missionary work among the Tunxis and witnessed the 1650 agreement between Connecticut and the tribe. A few Tunxis became members of his Farmington church, with the standing that membership carried.

narrative_blocks.header: He left Farmington in a year of calamity
narrative_blocks.body: Newton departed Farmington in 1657 after a season of disaster — a man named Scott was murdered, and the house of John Hart burned with most of the family inside. He waited months in Boston for passage to England before settling instead at Milford.

One of the witnesses of the 1650 agreement between the Colony of Connecticut and the Tunxis Indians.
MINISTRY: Second Pastor at Milford, Connecticut 1660-1683. Joined Milford congregational church July 29, 1660. Ordained second pastor Aug 22, 1660, succeeding Rev. Peter Prudden. Received young men into his family to train them for the ministry, including Abraham Pierson who became first President of Yale College.
PARENTAGE (uncertain; no parent entries kept): Father of Rev. Roger Newton. Said to be of the same family as Sir Isaac Newton, whose tomb is in Westminster Abbey. The name Isaac has been continued in some branches of the Newton family in every generation. GRIST (official Newton history, for reference / future CCs):
- Came from England, landed Boston ~1638; at Harvard but name not on graduate list (some early records burned).
- Drawn to Hartford by Hooker's preaching (Hooker returned to Boston/Cambridge several times; 1639 a two-hour Cambridge sermon).
- Married Mary Hooker, Thomas's eldest daughter, who as a child walked beside the litter carrying her invalid mother Susannah on the 1636 migration (scene now on the Capitol relief).
- Son Samuel bp. 20 Oct 1646 (Hartford register); Thomas Hooker's 1647 deathbed will left him £10.
- Farmington church founded 1645; Seven Pillars: Roger Newton (pastor/teacher), Stephen Hart, John Bronson, John Cole, Thomas Thompson, Thomas Judd, Robert Porter (Hart & Judd deacons).
- Decided AGAINST the Half-Way Covenant.
- Regicides Goffe & Whalley hid ~2 years from 19 Aug 1661 in a cellar near the parsonage; their presence known to Gov. Treat and Newton, who walked with them in a grove behind the house. Nicholas Camp was among those appointed to search for them.
- ~23-yr Milford pastorate; received 164 members; church ~200 at his death 7 June 1683.
- Library of 200+ volumes (octavos/quartos/folios; medical: Sibbs's Family Cordialls, Brooke's Remedies, Barrow's Method of Physicke) willed to unmarried daughters Mary & Alice; catalogue printed in Atwater's History of New Haven County (1902).
- Wife Mary Hooker ('Maria' in the record) d. 4 Feb 1676. Grave unmarked, Milford; likely Prudden's garden. 1889 250th-anniversary memorial tablet presented by descendant Henry Gleason Newton.

narrative_blocks.header: Father forbade it — he married and stayed
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas Hooker's will, written hours before his death in 1647, addressed his son's future: he could seek a wife in England, but was forbidden from marrying and tarrying there. John disobeyed on both counts — married in England, and never returned to New England.

narrative_blocks.header: Jovial parson — dissipated son of Thomas Hooker
narrative_blocks.body: Remembered as 'a jovial, rollicking, sporting Parson,' he chose Oxford over his father's Emmanuel College, Cambridge, and was ordained by the Bishop of Oxford into the Church of England in 1660.

narrative_blocks.header: Found dead in bed — buried at midnight
narrative_blocks.body: He died in 1684 — found dead in bed, then buried privately at midnight. The manner of burial suggests a death considered shameful or suspicious; possibly self-inflicted.

narrative_blocks.header: The only Hooker line that ended in England
narrative_blocks.body: He was Thomas Hooker's first son, born around 1626 at Chelmsford. His was the only Hooker line that returned to England — and it ended with him; no verified descendants survive.

narrative_blocks.header: Four daughters; two died young, two lines lost
narrative_blocks.body: John married Mary Lovell at Leckhampstead in 1659, and they had four daughters. Two died in infancy, and the lines of the surviving two cannot be traced.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father died as the wedding neared
narrative_blocks.body: Preparations were under way in the summer of 1647 when Rev. Thomas Hooker died at Hartford. She and John Wilson married soon afterward and settled at Dorchester, where he served beside Richard Mather.

narrative_blocks.header: She buried three and used the names again
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas died the year he was born in 1652, Elizabeth the same way in 1653, a second Thomas in 1662. A second John followed the first, and a second Elizabeth the first — eight children, five of them grown.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years a minister's wife at Medfield
narrative_blocks.body: Medfield was a new town when John Wilson took its first pulpit in 1651 and held it until he died in 1691. She kept that parsonage through the whole of the town's first generation.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son married her sister's daughter
narrative_blocks.body: Her son John married Sarah Newton, daughter of her sister Mary Hooker Newton. Both of Thomas Hooker's daughters raised children who married each other, and their grandchildren are the first double descent in the tree.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-four years a widow
narrative_blocks.body: She outlived him by more than three decades and died at Braintree on 20 August 1725, about ninety-five years old — born at Little Baddow in Essex before her father ever saw America.

narrative_blocks.header: A president descends from her
narrative_blocks.body: Through the Wilson children runs the ancestry of William Howard Taft, so the founder's daughter stands at the head of a presidential line.

narrative_blocks.header: He testified against the schoolmaster
narrative_blocks.body: Before Harvard existed he was a pupil at Nathaniel Eaton's school in Cambridge, and he gave evidence of the ill-treatment the scholars had from Eaton and his wife. Eaton was put out and the college began without him.

narrative_blocks.header: In the first class Harvard sent out
narrative_blocks.body: He graduated in 1642, in the first class Harvard ever sent out. His nephew by marriage Samuel Shepard took the same degree sixteen years later, and the family kept going back.

narrative_blocks.header: Taken up for dead at four storeys
narrative_blocks.body: Cotton Mather wrote that as a child he fell from a loft four storeys high into the street, and was taken up so battered and bruised and bloody that it struck horror into the beholders. His father prayed, and he lived to be seventy.

narrative_blocks.header: Minister, physician and schoolmaster at once
narrative_blocks.body: Medfield was a new town in 1651 and he was its first minister for more than forty years, doctoring and schooling it at the same time. Edward Johnson called him the gracious and godly Mr Wilson.

narrative_blocks.header: He preached twice the Sunday before
narrative_blocks.body: On the Lord's day before his death he preached both forenoon and afternoon, fervently and powerfully. He died the following Sunday, 23 August 1691, with most of his church gathered to watch him go.

narrative_blocks.header: Medfield heard thirty-two men after him
narrative_blocks.body: The town could not settle a successor for nearly six years. It heard thirty-two candidates before Joseph Baxter was ordained in April 1697.

narrative_blocks.header: An archbishop behind the family name
narrative_blocks.body: His grandfather William Wilson was a prebendary of St Paul's whose wife was niece to Edmund Grindal, Archbishop of Canterbury. The name came down the family: his daughter Susannah married Rev. Grindall Rawson in 1683.

career.notes: Also served the town as physician and schoolmaster

bio.title: Reverend
bio.bio_blurb: Harvard's first class; Medfield's first minister

burial.plot_notes: No stone survives. Well-attested tradition places the grave at the south side of Rev. Samuel Whitman's marked grave. "Mr. Whitman like Mr. Hooker, died while the minister of the town, and tradition says he was buried by the side of Mr. Hooker."

sources.notes: John Winthrop Jr., Alchemy and the Creation of New England Culture, 1606-1676 (Homer Babbidge Prize)

notable.notable_blurb: Second minister of Farmington; Harvard fellow

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-six years in Farmington's pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel preached at Plymouth from 1657, and in 1661 succeeded his brother-in-law Roger Newton as pastor at Farmington, where he stayed thirty-six years, until his death in 1697. His earnestness earned him the name the Fervent Hooker.

narrative_blocks.header: The Court thanked him and wanted it printed
narrative_blocks.body: In May 1695 the General Court appointed a committee to thank him for his great pains in preaching the Election Sermon, and to ask him for a copy to print for the people's good.

narrative_blocks.header: He talked Farmington into a free school
narrative_blocks.body: In December 1685 the town voted a year's wages for a schoolmaster and declared the result a free school for Farmington, almost certainly at his urging. It was among the earliest free public schools in the colony.

narrative_blocks.header: He sat on a tribunal that tried witches
narrative_blocks.body: In the 1660s he formed a prosecutorial tribunal with Rev. Samuel Stone of Hartford and Rev. Joseph Haynes of Wethersfield. Connecticut tried witches harder than Massachusetts that decade, three decades before Salem.

narrative_blocks.header: Ordered to the war, replaced two days later
narrative_blocks.body: On 9 March 1675/6 the Council ordered him to prepare to march with Major Treat's army toward Hadley and Northampton. Two days later it replaced him with Rev. Israel Chauncy, recording no reason.

narrative_blocks.header: His father's library came to him by default
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas Hooker's will left his printed books and manuscripts to his son John — but only if John went on with his studies and gave himself to the work of the ministry. John did neither, and the whole library passed to Samuel, who did. Through Samuel's nine sons come all of Thomas Hooker's American descendants who carry the Hooker name.

narrative_blocks.header: He got each sermon into his heart first
narrative_blocks.body: He told a friend he had three things to do with a sermon before preaching it: write it, commit it to memory, and get it into his heart. Cotton Mather wrote of “our dead Hooker, yet living in his worthy son Samuel Hooker, an able, faithful, useful minister at Farmington.”

Mary Willet — daughter of first Mayor of New York City; Willet family prominent Plymouth and New York colonists NOTE FOR MARTHA WILLET ENTRY: Mary's sister Martha Willet was the first wife of Judge Saffin. After Martha's death, Saffin married twice more, but left a record written after his third marriage that on the anniversary of Martha's death it was his custom 'to seclude himself and give way to his inconsolable grief for the irreparable loss he had sustained in the death of his beloved Martha.' The record of a man annually mourning his first wife across two subsequent marriages is one of the more striking personal documents from colonial New England.
MARRIAGE NOTE (m2): Married at age 66
M2 NOTE: After Samuel Hooker died Nov 6, 1697, Mary (then 65) married Rev. Thomas Buckingham of Saybrook CT on Aug 10, 1703 (aged 65). He died April 1, 1709. Mary then went to live with her son-in-law Rev. Stephen Buckingham at Norwalk — who was the SON of her second husband Thomas Buckingham, AND the husband of her own daughter Sarah Hooker (H00037). She died at Norwalk June 24, 1712. Her grave is in the old burying ground near East Norwalk railway station.

narrative_blocks.header: Daughter of New York City's first mayor
narrative_blocks.body: Her father Capt. Thomas Willet was appointed the first Mayor of New York City in 1665, when the English renamed the Dutch colony. He had previously succeeded Capt. Miles Standish as commander of Plymouth's militia — one of the most storied military commands in early New England. Mary carried this distinguished lineage to Farmington when she married Rev. Samuel Hooker.

narrative_blocks.header: Three generations of Willet women known for beauty
narrative_blocks.body: Mary's mother was described as possessing 'beauty and majesty almost divine.' A portrait of Mary's daughter Mary Hooker Pierpont survives, and from it contemporaries formed 'the opinion that she was a woman of uncommon beauty.' Her daughter Sarah was 'accounted the most accomplished lady that had ever come to Norwalk.'

narrative_blocks.header: Remarried at 66 — outlived two minister husbands
narrative_blocks.body: After Samuel Hooker's death in 1697, Mary married Reverend Thomas Buckingham of Saybrook at age 66. When he died in 1709 she moved to Norwalk to live with her son-in-law Reverend Stephen Buckingham, where she remained until her death in 1712 at age 74.

narrative_blocks.header: She and her daughter married father and son
narrative_blocks.body: After Rev. Samuel Hooker died, Mary Willet married Rev. Thomas Buckingham of Saybrook in 1703. Her daughter Sarah was the wife of his son, Rev. Stephen Buckingham, so a mother and daughter had married a father and his son.

notable.notable_blurb: First Mayor of New York City, 1665

narrative_blocks.header: New York's first mayor
narrative_blocks.body: When New Amsterdam became New York in 1665, Thomas was made its first mayor, with the approval of English and Dutch alike, and he served again in 1667. He had kept a house in the Dutch town for years and traded there in their language.

narrative_blocks.header: He talked Stuyvesant into surrender
narrative_blocks.body: In September 1664 Thomas went into New Amsterdam under a flag of truce to persuade Peter Stuyvesant to give up the town without a fight, and it surrendered five days later. Richard Nicolls said no Englishman knew the Dutch better.

narrative_blocks.header: Robbed twice by the French
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas came to Plymouth in 1629 with the last of the Leyden congregation and was sent to the Penobscot trading post to keep its manager honest. The French robbed the post in 1631, and in 1635 they drove him and the English out for good.

narrative_blocks.header: Captain beside Myles Standish
narrative_blocks.body: In 1648 Thomas was made captain of Plymouth's military company with Myles Standish, and he kept the post almost the rest of his life. From 1651 he sat as an Assistant to the governor.

narrative_blocks.header: A friend to Massasoit's sons
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas spoke the Native languages and was trusted by Massasoit and his sons Wamsutta and Metacom, and he bought from them the lands that became Rehoboth, Swansea and Attleboro. After he left for New York, relations soured toward war.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight enslaved people in his inventory
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas died one of the richest men in Plymouth Colony, and his inventory listed eight enslaved Black people. In 1658 he was among the magistrates who condoned the whipping of two Quakers.

narrative_blocks.header: His son Hezekiah and the war
narrative_blocks.body: His son Hezekiah was killed in King Philip's War despite the protection Philip's people had promised the family, and the news grieved Philip himself. His daughter Mary married Thomas Hooker's son Samuel in 1658.

narrative_blocks.header: Wrote Cotton Mather a eulogy for her husband
narrative_blocks.body: After Rev. Grindal Rawson died on February 6, 1715, Susanna wrote a long letter to Cotton Mather — a detailed portrait of her husband's forty-year ministry at Mendon, his Indian mission work, his character, and his final hours. His last words were "Come Lord Jesus, come quickly!" The letter was published in the Rawson Family Memorial. Cotton Mather quoted it in the sermon he preached at Rawson's funeral.

narrative_blocks.body: Her gravestone in Mendon reads: "Here lies inter'd ye Remains of Mrs. Susanna Rawson, Relict of ye late Rev. Mr. Grindal Rawson... and daughter to ye Rev. Mr. John Wilson 1st Minister of ye Gospel in Medfield." She outlived her husband by 33 years, dying July 8, 1748, age 83.

narrative_blocks.header: Ancestor of President Taft through both Taft brothers
narrative_blocks.body: Her granddaughter Mary Dorr Taft married Moses Taft, and her great-granddaughter Rhoda Rawson Taft married Aaron Taft — Moses's and Aaron's fathers were brothers. President William Howard Taft descends through the Aaron Taft line.

EASTER EGG: Rev. Grindal Rawson (1659-1715) — 33-year pastor at Mendon MA; son of Edward Rawson first Secretary of Massachusetts Bay Colony; named for Edmund Grindal Archbishop of Canterbury under Elizabeth I
b. Jan 23, 1659 Boston MA. d. Feb 6, 1715 Mendon MA. Harvard 1678. Father: X00009 Edward Rawson (Colonial Secretary of MA Bay Colony). Grindal and Susanna Wilson were second cousins: his paternal grandmother and her paternal grandfather (Rev. John Wilson Sr.) were siblings. Missionary to Indians; mastered their language in 9 months. Author: "Confession of Faith" in Indian and English; two sermons published (Artillery Election sermon 1703; Election sermon 1709). Gravestone: "Grindal Rawson... entered 6 days into ye 57th year of his age. Deceased the 35th year of his ministry."
NAME ORIGIN: Named for Edmund Grindal, Archbishop of Canterbury under Elizabeth I
MINISTRY: Pastor at Mendon, Massachusetts for 33 years. Alternate image: artistic interpretation by David Peirce (March 2026), based on the tomb portrait and portraits of his father Edward and sister Rachel. RAWSON FAMILY MEMORIAL additions: July 31 1692, the General Court ordered Revs. John Hale, Grindal Rawson, John Wise, and John Emerson to accompany the forces of the Canada expedition (Sir William Phipps); whether any sailed is unknown. 1698: with Rev. Samuel Danforth of Taunton, commissioned to visit the Indian congregations of New England; their account published in Mass. Historical Collections, 1st series, Vol. 10. Cotton Mather honored him in "Mantissa." Epitaph Latin (per the Memorial): Rev. John Wilson was his great-grandmother’s brother; Archbishop Edmund Grindal his great-great-grandmother’s brother. Algonquian translations (American Antiquarian Society holdings): Thomas Shepard’s Sincere Convert, John Cotton’s Spiritual Milk, and a Confession of Faith for Boston churches. Harvard classmate of Cotton Mather (1678), who honored him in Just Commemorations (1715): “a Master that had scarce an Equal” of the Indian language.

narrative_blocks.header: Mastered Algonquian in nine months
narrative_blocks.body: Grindal learned the Nipmuc language in nine months and preached to Nipmuc parishioners in it, translating Thomas Shepard's Sincere Convert and John Cotton's Spiritual Milk and writing a confession of faith in Indian and English. Cotton Mather, his Harvard classmate of 1678, called him a master that had scarce an equal in the language.

narrative_blocks.header: Named for Elizabeth I's Archbishop of Canterbury
narrative_blocks.body: He was named "Grindal" after Edmund Grindal, Archbishop of Canterbury under Elizabeth I — his great-great-grandmother's brother, per the Harvard commencement of 1678. At that ceremony President Urian Oakes called him "sprung from a most illustrious stock" and prayed that Rawson might "in learning, holiness and excellence of character, resemble both Wilson and Grindal."

narrative_blocks.header: Visiting the Indian churches in 1698
narrative_blocks.body: In 1698 the commissioners for propagating the gospel sent Grindal and the Rev. Samuel Danforth of Taunton to visit the Indian congregations of New England. Their account of what they found was later printed by the Massachusetts Historical Society.

narrative_blocks.header: The Artillery and the Election sermons
narrative_blocks.body: Grindal preached the sermon to the Ancient and Honorable Artillery Company in 1703 and the Election sermon before the General Court in 1709, and both were printed. When he died in February 1715 his gravestone at Mendon marked the thirty-fifth year of his ministry there.

narrative_blocks.header: Ordered to sail with the Canada invasion
narrative_blocks.body: In July 1692 the General Court ordered four ministers, Rawson among them, to accompany the forces in the expedition against Canada, “to carry on the worshipping of God.” Whether he sailed with Sir William Phipps is unknown.

narrative_blocks.header: Bay Colony secretary for thirty-six years
narrative_blocks.body: Rawson held the secretaryship of Massachusetts Bay from 1650 until the arrival of Sir Edmund Andros in 1686, even countersigning the warrant issued for the arrest of the regicides.

narrative_blocks.header: He proclaimed New England’s first Thanksgiving, 1676
narrative_blocks.body: From the steps of the Boston Council House in 1676, Edward Rawson read the proclamation now remembered as New England’s first formal day of thanksgiving.

narrative_blocks.header: He proclaimed King James II in 1685
narrative_blocks.body: On 20 April 1685, with the governor and assistants around him on horseback, thousands of people, eight foot companies, drums, trumpets, musketry and cannon, Edward read out the proclamation of James II in Boston.

narrative_blocks.header: An eloquent inditer with a careless pen
narrative_blocks.body: Edward's plain, bold hand won him the name of an eloquent inditer, yet the editor of the colony records found his e and r so alike that only the context told them apart. He wrote m for nn, making Penniman into Pemiman, and filled the books with his own contractions.

narrative_blocks.header: Relentless against the Quakers
narrative_blocks.body: Counted among the most important men in New England, Edward carried one blot on his memory: he was among the most forward and relentless of the persecutors of the Quakers.

narrative_blocks.header: Rawson's Lane, now Bromfield Street
narrative_blocks.body: In 1653 Edward bought two and a half acres between the road to Roxbury and the Common, and later cut a street through them. It was Rawson's Lane from 1670 until about 1748, when it was renamed for Edward Bromfield, and his first Newbury farm is still called Rawson's Meadow.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter became a Whittier heroine
narrative_blocks.body: His daughter Rebecca Rawson’s tale of a bigamous marriage and a shipwreck became the subject of John Greenleaf Whittier’s 1849 Leaves from Margaret Smith’s Journal.
