narrative_blocks.header: Thomas Hooker fitted him for college himself
narrative_blocks.body: His mother died when he was four and he went to Hartford, to his grandfather's house. Thomas Hooker prepared him for Harvard — which makes him one of the last men alive who had known the founder of Connecticut across a table.

narrative_blocks.header: He had the pulpit, not the teaching chair
narrative_blocks.body: Rowley ordained him its third minister in November 1665 while Samuel Phillips stayed on as teacher, the office that did the doctrine. Phillips would hold his place another twenty-eight years; Shepard had two and a half.

narrative_blocks.header: Dead at twenty-six, eight weeks after his wife
narrative_blocks.body: Dorothy was buried at Rowley on 12 February 1668 and he was dead by 7 April, buried two days later. Two young people gone from one house in one winter reads like an epidemic. Their son was eight months old.

narrative_blocks.header: His will is a list of uncles
narrative_blocks.body: Three days before he died he wrote out what he had: forty pounds still owed him from his grandfather Hooker's will, and debts among his uncles Newton, Wilson and Samuel Hooker. He left the boy to father and mother Flint.

narrative_blocks.header: A printer left him a spoon at seven
narrative_blocks.body: Matthew Day, who ran the Cambridge press, died in 1649 and left a silver spoon engraved with his name to "my old acquaintance little Samuel Shepard." The boy was seven, and the printer had thought to put him in a will.

narrative_blocks.header: A hundred acres waiting until he was twenty-one
narrative_blocks.body: The estate went to Margery Flint, his widowed mother-in-law, and her son Josiah of Beverly stood bond for it in August 1668. A hundred acres at Rowley were to come to his son at twenty-one.

MINISTRY: Pastor at First Church, Rowley 1665-1668. Third minister at Rowley. After his death, Mr. Phillips was ordained pastor and continued until his own death April 26, 1696.
WILL: Dated April 4, 1668, proved April 22, 1668. Citation: Essex County Probate file #25186; Probate Records of Essex County, Vol. 2:127; Suffolk County Probate file #488. Provisions: Named child Samuel; Left care and education of Samuel to 'father and mother Flint' (Rev. Henry and Margery Flint of Braintree); Flints to improve his estate for Samuel's upbringing; Father's 100 acres at Rowley to come to Samuel at age 21.
ANECDOTE (double_death_1668): Dorothy died February 12, 1668; Samuel died April 7, 1668 — 55 days apart, with infant son born August 1667. Almost certainly an epidemic moving through Rowley. Father's will written just three days before his death.
CHILD NOTE: Samuel Shepard (ID H00038) — Both parents dead within 8 months of his birth; raised by Flint grandparents. Birth: Aug 19, 1667.
BURIAL: Rowley Burial Ground, Rowley, Essex County, MA. Has gravestone. Plot: 4 Row, East (Marble) South front.
EDUCATION DISCREPANCY: Edward Hooker gives 1655. Gravestone inscription and church ordination records both give 1658. 1658 preferred — 1655 is likely confusion with uncle Rev. Samuel Hooker's 1653 graduation.
SIBLEY'S SOURCE: Half-brother of Thomas Shepard II (H.U. 1653, by first wife) and Jeremiah Shepard (H.U. 1669, by third wife). College charges dated 9-4-54 through 5-7-58. Affix of "Socius" suggests Fellow/Tutor but not confirmed in College Records. Admitted to full communion Cambridge church July 19, 1663; dismissed Aug 13, 1665 to Rowley church. Cotton Mather: "was one, whose Heart was a Tent in which the Lord remarkably chose to Dwell." Jonathan Mitchell quote preserved in quotes array.

narrative_blocks.header: Her uncle became president of Harvard
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother Margery was the eldest sister of Leonard Hoar, president of Harvard from 1672 to 1675. Margery was a daughter of Charles Hoare and Joanna Hincksman of Gloucester.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father held the Braintree pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: Henry Flynt came over in the Puritan migration and preached at Braintree until he died in May 1668, three months after her. Simon Bradstreet noted it in his journal: he was ancient, but in a course of nature might have lived longer.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother was widowed in Gloucester first
narrative_blocks.body: Margery Hoare married Thomas Matthewes at St Nicholas in Gloucester in December 1633 and bore him two sons. Widowed, she came to New England and married Henry Flynt by 1642; Dorothy was the eldest of their ten children.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father’s will named two of the ten
narrative_blocks.body: Henry Flynt made his will in January 1652/3 and put down only two sons by name, Josias and Seth, leaving the rest as his wife and his other young children. Dorothy was ten, and not among the names.

narrative_blocks.header: She died fifty-five days before her husband
narrative_blocks.body: She died at Rowley on 12 February 1668, twenty-five years old, and Samuel Shepard followed fifty-five days after. Their son was eight months old and went to her parents at Braintree.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandfather's will left him ten pounds
narrative_blocks.body: He was nine months old when Thomas Hooker, the founder of Hartford, died in 1647 and left him a legacy of ten pounds — a substantial bequest for an infant grandson. He grew up to carry that founder's blood into a life of soldiering and public service at Milford.

narrative_blocks.header: He fought in all the Indian wars
narrative_blocks.body: Appointed ensign in the Milford militia when King Philip's War broke out in 1675, he rose to captain and won a name as a hard fighter through that war and the frontier skirmishes that followed. The militia was no ceremonial post in a colony still hemmed by wilderness.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixteen times Milford sent him to the assembly
narrative_blocks.body: Between 1691 and 1703 Milford returned him to the Connecticut General Court for sixteen regular sessions, with four special ones besides — an unbroken run of trust from his townsmen. Soldier and legislator both, he stood among the prominent men of the colony.

narrative_blocks.header: The Fenns married into the Hookers twice
narrative_blocks.body: His wife Martha Fenn had a half-sister, Susanna, who married William Hooker — Samuel's own first cousin. In a single generation the Fenn family thus tied itself to the Hooker line twice over, by two different marriages.

narrative_blocks.header: His second wife was a slain soldier's widow
narrative_blocks.body: After Martha Fenn died, he married Sarah Welch, widow of John Fowler, who had fallen storming an Indian fort in 1693. Their son Abner carried a name found nowhere else in the Newton or Hooker lines.

narrative_blocks.header: Milford magistrate and a colonial Assistant
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin Fenn was a deacon, magistrate, and militia officer at Milford. He represented the town in the New Haven Colony and served as an Assistant of the colony from 1665 to 1672.

narrative_blocks.header: He took lot number three at Milford
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Stewkley in Buckinghamshire, Fenn came over in the Great Migration and settled at Milford. He held land on both sides of the Atlantic for the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: Two daughters married into the Hooker line
narrative_blocks.body: His daughter Martha married Samuel Newton, a grandson of Thomas Hooker; his daughter Susanna married William Hooker of Farmington. Both ties pull the Fenn family into the Hooker tree.

narrative_blocks.header: His will left each grandchild a single ewe
narrative_blocks.body: Fenn's 1672 will divided farms in Milford, New Haven, and Buckinghamshire among his sons. To every one of his grandchildren he left a single ewe sheep.

career.notes: Milford deputy 1653; magistrate 1654-1663; Commissioner of the United Colonies 1661 and 1663.

narrative_blocks.header: Father left her his three hour-glasses
narrative_blocks.body: Because Susannah had already received her portion at marriage, Roger Newton Sr.'s 1683 will left her only one cow and all three of his hour-glasses. She was living in Guilford with five children at the time. The genealogical note adds dryly: 'No one can tell why she should have all the hour-glasses.'

narrative_blocks.header: Two marriages, six children, two Connecticut towns
narrative_blocks.body: She had four children with her first husband John Stone, then married Samuel Burwell as his second wife. She was living in Guilford with five children when her father's 1683 will was written, then moved to Milford with the Burwells. She died at Milford in July 1703, age 48.

narrative_blocks.header: His father landed at Guilford with Leete
narrative_blocks.body: John Stone the elder came to New England in the summer of 1639 in the company of William Leete, afterwards governor of Connecticut, and the Rev. Henry Whitfield, and took up ground in what became Guilford. He was the eldest of the five sons Mary Simson bore him.

narrative_blocks.header: Five brothers, and only his line went on
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Simson's five sons were John, Samuel, Nathaniel, Thomas and Noah; Samuel married Sarah Taintor and Noah died unmarried in 1684. He took Susannah Newton at Guilford in 1673 and was dead by 1686 at forty-two, leaving the four children the Stone name descends through here.

narrative_blocks.header: The deputy governor married them
narrative_blocks.body: Robert Treat joined them at Milford on the fourteenth of April 1680, three years before he became governor of Connecticut and held it for fifteen. She was eighteen.

narrative_blocks.header: He left no will and four children
narrative_blocks.body: The estate was inventoried on the eighteenth of May 1699 and his widow deposed to their ages: Prudence about eighteen, Thomas about seventeen, Ezekiel about twelve, and the youngest about two. He was forty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifteen years on, still undivided
narrative_blocks.body: Distributors were appointed in March 1713/14 to settle it — dower to the widow, a double share to the eldest son and a share each to the other three. The following January his son John complained to the court that they refused and neglected to do it.

narrative_blocks.header: Built his house next to his father's
narrative_blocks.body: He built his house immediately adjacent to Roger Newton Sr.'s on the same Milford home lot. His daughter Prudence — eighteen months old — was 'just old enough to run across the yard to her grandfather's' during Roger's final illness in early 1683.

narrative_blocks.header: The youngest son went down as Joseph
narrative_blocks.body: The 1699 inventory calls the two-year-old Joseph. He was John, and he signed himself so for eighty years after; his mother left him the land and made him her executor.

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve children, and four names used twice
narrative_blocks.body: Lydia Ford bore them at Milford between 1681 and 1700. A Joseph born in 1691 died the next year and the name went to a son born in 1697; there is an Ezekiel in 1687 and another in 1700, and Sarah and Bette both repeat names already in the family.

narrative_blocks.header: She signed her deeds with a mark
narrative_blocks.body: She could not write her name, and for thirty years after her husband died the Milford land records run through her hands. In 1725 she deeded her eldest son half of five acres in the Calves-pen meadow, ground that had come to her from her brothers Thomas and John Ford.

narrative_blocks.header: She left the land to the youngest
narrative_blocks.body: Her will of March 1746 gave Thomas, the eldest, twenty shillings. The land went to John, the last-born, along with the executorship; a grandson had five pounds and two granddaughters the movables.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-eight years a widow
narrative_blocks.body: John Newton died in May 1699, leaving Lydia with five children — the youngest barely two years old. She lived as a widow in Milford until October 23, 1747, dying at roughly age eighty-five after forty-eight years on her own.

narrative_blocks.header: Granddaughter of a Mary and John voyager
narrative_blocks.body: Lydia descended from Thomas Ford, a Dorset Puritan who sailed to Massachusetts on the Mary and John in 1630 and helped found Windsor, Connecticut. Through his line — said to have left more descendants than any other Puritan immigrant — the Ford blood reached the Newton family she married into.

narrative_blocks.header: Milford's physician, who never married
narrative_blocks.body: Ezekiel Newton practiced as a physician at Milford and never married. He died there in 1734 at seventy-four, and was buried at Milford Cemetery.

narrative_blocks.header: A coat for a child he never had
narrative_blocks.body: His father’s 1683 will left him a yellow say-coat “for a child” — read as provision for a marriage that never came. He kept half the family house, the other half going to his unmarried sisters, and the Milford physician died single at seventy-four.

narrative_blocks.header: His whole estate fit on one page
narrative_blocks.body: The 1734 inventory of everything he owned was brief: clothing, a bed, a few animals and tools, and two books — one titled “Ye Felicity of Man.” A modest close for the son of Milford’s second minister.

narrative_blocks.body: Her husband John Wilson was her first cousin: her mother was Mary Hooker, his mother was Sarah Hooker — sisters, both daughters of Rev. Thomas Hooker. They married July 4, 1683 in Milford. EH and the Wilson family genealogy both confirm the cousin relationship explicitly.

narrative_blocks.header: Married 27 days after her father's death
narrative_blocks.body: Her father Roger Newton Sr. died June 7, 1683. She married John Wilson on July 4, 1683 — twenty-seven days later. The marriage had presumably been planned before his death, but she wed her cousin in the immediate shadow of her father's loss.

narrative_blocks.header: Inherited 150 Farmington acres from her father
narrative_blocks.body: Her father Roger Newton Sr.'s 1683 will left her 150 acres in 'Bohemia' Farmington. Family tradition speculates the land may have originally been given to her mother Mary Hooker by Governor Haynes — connecting it to the Hartford founding generation.

narrative_blocks.header: Left £30 for a great-nephew's Yale degree

narrative_blocks.header: He entered Yale 18 years after her death
narrative_blocks.body: She died in 1741 when her great-nephew Roger Newton was about five years old. He nonetheless fulfilled her wish — entering Yale, graduating 1758, and serving as minister at Greenfield, Massachusetts until his death. Her conditional bequest reached its purpose.

narrative_blocks.header: A regicide praised his preaching in 1682
narrative_blocks.body: In 1682 John Wilson preached in New Haven for over a year. Col. John Dixwell — one of the English regicides then living in hiding in New Haven — wrote to Rev. Increase Mather calling him "a veire hopefull yonge man of good abilities." Wilson returned to Medfield in 1684 and eventually abandoned the ministry.

narrative_blocks.header: Left Harvard — his father taught him everything
narrative_blocks.body: He left Harvard College soon after admission, but received a thorough private education from his father in divinity, medicine, and law. He settled in Braintree in 1692 and spent the rest of his life farming, practicing medicine, and performing legal services.

narrative_blocks.header: Married his first cousin — both Hooker grandchildren
narrative_blocks.body: His mother was Sarah Hooker Wilson (Thomas Hooker's daughter); his wife Sarah Newton's mother was Mary Hooker Newton (also Thomas Hooker's daughter). The two mothers were sisters. EH and the Wilson genealogy both explicitly note the cousin relationship.

narrative_blocks.header: Mother, father, grandfather — all dead by April
narrative_blocks.body: His mother Dorothy died February 12, 1668. His father wrote his will April 4 and died April 7. His grandfather Rev. Henry Flint of Braintree — appointed guardian in the will — died April 27, twenty days after.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife refused to let him be ordained
narrative_blocks.body: He served at Woodbridge in New Jersey from 1695 without ordination, his wife Alice Mason opposing any settlement there. In 1701 he told the committee there was no hope of her compliance, and advised them to look out for another man.

narrative_blocks.header: Harvard 1685, then the bench not the pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: He was the son and grandson of Harvard men. After leaving the Woodbridge ministry he stayed in New Jersey, and by a 1706 deed described himself as one of Her Majesty's Justices of the Peace in the Town of Woodbridge.

narrative_blocks.header: Three children, and the line stopped
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel came in 1700, Joanna in 1701, and a second Samuel in 1703 — the name reused, which is how the first is known to have died. None of the three reached adulthood, and Rev. Samuel Shepard's line ended with them.

narrative_blocks.header: Whole family entered the church covenant together
narrative_blocks.body: On April 1, 1711, Samuel and Phebe were admitted to full communion in the Milford church — on the very same day their two eldest children, Phebe and Samuel, were baptized. A single Sunday that sealed the whole family into the covenant at once.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Newton cousins married two Platt sisters
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel married Phebe Platt in Milford; his first cousin Fletcher Newton married Phebe's sister Hannah Platt. Two Newton cousins took two Platt sisters — the families of Milford interlacing through a single generation.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventeen when his father died
narrative_blocks.body: The 1699 inventory has him at about seventeen, the eldest son and entitled to a double share. The estate sat undivided for fifteen years, and it was his younger brother John who finally complained to the court about it.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother sold him the meadow
narrative_blocks.body: In August 1725 she deeded him half of about five acres in the Calves-pen meadow at Milford, ground that had come to her from her brothers, and he paid twenty pounds for it. She signed the deed with her mark.

narrative_blocks.header: He got twenty shillings; John got the land
narrative_blocks.body: Their mother's will of 1746 left him, the eldest, twenty shillings. The land and the executorship went to the last-born.

narrative_blocks.header: Two cousins married two half-sisters
narrative_blocks.body: He married Mary Baldwin at Milford in June 1704. His first cousin John Burwell married her half-sister Susanna, Zachariah Baldwin's daughter by his second wife, so the two Hooker cousins came into the same house from opposite sides of it.

narrative_blocks.header: No probate; the land moved by deed
narrative_blocks.body: No probate record has ever been found for him. His estate passed by deed instead, and the Milford land records carry the family's shares through three transactions between 1753 and 1775.

narrative_blocks.header: His unmarried daughter took the west end
narrative_blocks.body: In June 1753 Bettee Newton, single woman, took over her seven brothers' and sisters' rights in the westernmost part of his land, then sold them back the remainder of the ground he had dwelt on — some twenty-nine acres on the high plains. The salt meadow his uncle Ezekiel Newton Senior had given him went into the same settlement.

narrative_blocks.header: Captain Newton by his wedding in 1712
narrative_blocks.body: Harvard-educated, Roger was in his mid-twenties when he went as an officer on the expeditions of 1709 and 1710 against the French in Queen Anne's War. When he married in April 1712, the Milford clerk wrote him down as Captain Newton.

narrative_blocks.header: A judge and councillor into his eighties
narrative_blocks.body: From 1737 Roger sat as judge of the New Haven County court, and from 1738 on the colony's Council of Assistants. He held both seats until he died at Milford in January 1771.

narrative_blocks.header: Colonel of the Second Regiment at sixty
narrative_blocks.body: Roger was colonel of the colony's Second Regiment of militia for many years, and is credited with commanding Connecticut's troops in 1745 at the siege of Louisbourg, the French fortress on Cape Breton Island. He was sixty that spring.

narrative_blocks.header: Two daughters, two Whittlesey sons
narrative_blocks.body: Roger married Susannah Bryan at Milford on 10 April 1712, and their son Roger, born the next March, died the same year. Two of their daughters, Susannah and Martha, married two sons of the Wallingford minister Samuel Whittelsey, ten years apart.

narrative_blocks.header: “Newton as steel inflexible from right”
narrative_blocks.body: His Milford epitaph closes in verse: “The part the Hero left beneath the skies / Newton as steel inflexible from right / In Faith, in Law, in Equity, in Fight.” He had been thirty-three years a judge and an Assistant of the colony when he died in his eighty-seventh year.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father was dead before forty
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel Bryan of Milford married Martha Whiting in 1683 and was gone by about 1698, still a young man. Her mother remarried the magistrate Samuel Eells in 1700, a colonel of the New Haven County regiment who sat on four different benches.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Hartford founders in her great-grandfathers
narrative_blocks.body: William Pantry was one of the sixteen already living at Hartford when Hooker's company arrived in 1636, and his Cambridge home lot had adjoined Hooker's own. Major William Whiting was treasurer of the colony and the target of an assassination plot in 1646, dead the year after. She descends from both, and married into the Hooker line.

narrative_blocks.header: Rev. John Whiting was her grandfather
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother Martha was born to the Hartford minister John Whiting and Sibyl Collins; the Major was his father. On the Bryan side her grandfather Richard bought Eaton's Neck on Long Island in 1684, then one of the richest merchants in Connecticut.

narrative_blocks.header: Two of her children married two Whitings
narrative_blocks.body: Her son Jared married Hannah Whiting of New Haven in 1743 and her daughter Sarah married Hannah's brother John. A brother and sister on one side married a sister and brother on the other, which made the children of the two marriages double first cousins — sharing all four grandparents where ordinary cousins share two.

narrative_blocks.header: Her two husbands each led to a governor
narrative_blocks.body: Daniel Miles died in 1711 and she married Jonathan Ingersoll the next year. Charles Hobby Pond, the thirty-seventh governor of Connecticut, is her great-grandson by the first; Charles Roberts Ingersoll, the forty-seventh, her great-great-grandson by the second.

Abner and John were both baptized 23 October 1726 at Durham — twins.

narrative_blocks.header: Two years a miller, then a farmer
narrative_blocks.body: From 1727 to 1729 he owned and ran a corn mill at Durham. He gave it up for farming and bought land in what was still the town of Haddam, which was made part of Durham in 1773, four years after he died.

narrative_blocks.header: One son paid to keep another at Yale
narrative_blocks.body: His will of September 1754 left the larger legacy to his son Burwell on condition that Burwell furnish his youngest brother Roger, then at Yale, with suitable meat, drink, washing, lodging, apparel and all other necessarys decent for a member of that college. It also required such school books as Roger should have occasion to recite.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought Durham before selling Milford
narrative_blocks.body: On the seventeenth of June 1724 he bought a house, barn and seven-acre home lot at Durham. The next day he and Mary conveyed a quarter of a dwelling house and home lot at Milford to Susannah Burwell, widow of John Burwell — the property Mary had owned before the marriage.

narrative_blocks.header: Son Roger received Alice Newton's Yale bequest
narrative_blocks.body: Abner's son Roger Newton was the beneficiary of Alice Newton's ca.1740 conditional Yale bequest — establishing the family's Yale-funded ministerial track. Roger graduated Yale 1758 and served fifty-six years as minister at Greenfield Massachusetts until 1816 — one of the longest continuous American pastorates of the Revolutionary-Republican era.

narrative_blocks.header: Half-brother shared same first name, Abner
narrative_blocks.body: This Abner Newton was born 1699 to Samuel Newton's second wife Sarah Welch Fowler — distinguishing him from his half-brother Abner Newton baptized May 1689, who had been born to Samuel's first wife Martha Fenn ten years earlier. The repeated Abner name across both marriages was uncommon. The 1699 Abner became the documented ancestor of the Durham Newton branch — earning the 'durham_newton' tag in this entry.

narrative_blocks.body: His grave in the Milford cemetery carries a Latin reminder: "Memento Mori — Here lyes buryed the body of Lieut. Fletcher Newton." He died around 1750, about three years after drafting his will.

narrative_blocks.header: Twin daughters born 1718
narrative_blocks.body: Alice and Hannah, twins born December 1718, had different paths: Alice died unmarried in 1777; Hannah married John Prudden and carried the line forward.

narrative_blocks.header: Cousin Samuel married her sister Phebe
narrative_blocks.body: Fletcher married Hannah Platt; his first cousin Samuel Newton married Hannah's sister Phebe Platt. Two Newton cousins and two Platt sisters — all from Milford — bound the families together across a single generation.

people.research_notes:
DEATH DISCREPANCY: EH gives Feb 12 or 23, 1728. A 1930s transcription gave Dec 12, 1728 — a misreading. Probate was April 1728, making February correct. Gravestone reads "Feb'y the 12th 1728 in the 41st year of his age."
MARRIED: May 21, 1711 in Milford by Rev. Grindal Rawson of Mendon MA (husband of Susanna Wilson Rawson, H00026 — a fellow Hooker descendant). GRAVESTONE: "Here lyes the body of Mr Ezekiel Newton Deceased Febr'y the 12th 1728 in the 41st year of his age." A 1930s reading gave Dec 12, 1728 — misreading; probate was April 1728, confirming February. EH lists three additional children (Isaac, David, Mary, EH#175-177) as name-only entries; the Newton Genealogy and Milford Vital Records document only eight children and exclude these three. Per Sam (Newton Genealogy supersedes EH for this family), the three EH-only stubs were removed. Do not restore from EH. Sam's list names eight children — Eunice, Ezekiel, Abigail, Christopher, Lusiah, Avice, Sarah and John. This record also carries Isaac (H00175), David (H00176) and Mary (H00177), all undated; they are not in the list and have been left in place. The three undated extras on this record — Isaac, David and Mary — are placed here one generation too high. The printed genealogy makes all three children of his son Ezekiel No.19. Isaac has been moved; David and Mary are flagged as probable duplicates of HD0233 and HD0236 and left in place pending instruction. Isaac has been removed from this record’s children list as well as re-parented; he was briefly wired to two fathers at once. David (H00176) and Mary (H00177) deleted on Sam's instruction as duplicates of Pvt. David Newton (HD0233) and Mary Newton (HD0236), both children of his son Ezekiel No.19. This record now carries the eight children of Sam's list.

narrative_blocks.header: He was baptized at thirteen
narrative_blocks.body: The Milford record has him on the seventh of April 1700 and names his mother as widow Lydia Newton. His father had been dead not quite a year, and he was thirteen years old when he was baptized.

narrative_blocks.header: The minister was family already
narrative_blocks.body: Grindal Rawson came from Mendon in Massachusetts to marry them at Milford on the twenty-first of May 1711. His wife Susanna Wilson was a granddaughter of Thomas Hooker and first cousin to the bridegroom's father.

narrative_blocks.header: Eleven children in fifteen years
narrative_blocks.body: Abigail bore them between 1712 and 1726 and died the year of the last. He followed her two winters after, and the youngest was not yet two when both parents were gone.

narrative_blocks.header: The stone gives the forty-first year
narrative_blocks.body: Here lyes the body of Mr Ezekiel Newton Deceased Febr'y the 12th 1728 in the 41st year of his age. Probate followed in April.

narrative_blocks.header: Two years old when his father died
narrative_blocks.body: He was born about 1697 and his father was dead by May 1699. He was not baptized until the seventh of April 1700, and he lived to eighty-four.

narrative_blocks.header: He was written down as Joseph
narrative_blocks.body: The inventory of his father's estate gives the two-year-old as Joseph. Everything else he ever signed says John, and it was he who complained to the court in 1714 that the distributors would not divide the estate.

narrative_blocks.header: The record keeps the name of Jeff
narrative_blocks.body: An enslaved man in his household, Jeff, died at Milford on the eighth of May 1776. The Milford books entered the death; they did not enter a surname.

narrative_blocks.header: He buried two wives before fifty-four
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth died in July 1734 in her thirty-first year, leaving three children. He married Martha Smith four years later; she died in July 1750, and he lived on thirty-one years a widower.

narrative_blocks.body: Sarah descended from Thomas Hooker through both her parents, Dr. John Wilson of Braintree and Sarah Newton. She married John Marsh in 1701, owned the covenant at church in 1703, and named one of their twelve children Wilson.

narrative_blocks.header: The faculty moved him to the head
narrative_blocks.body: The steward placed him eighth in the class of 1705 and the faculty moved him to the head of it, which in that college meant piety among one's ancestors counted for more than money. He was great-grandson of the first minister of Boston.

narrative_blocks.header: He went after the college windows
narrative_blocks.body: He was among the least offensive boys to head a Harvard class until, just before Commencement, he joined John Rogers in a campaign against the college windows. His master's question asked whether cure by sympathetic powder was lawful.

narrative_blocks.header: He died before the church was gathered
narrative_blocks.body: He was schoolmaster at Mendon, then preached to the orthodox at Swansea who were petitioning to be set off from the Baptists as the town of Barrington. A violent fever took him in November 1713 before either town or church existed.

narrative_blocks.header: Sewall wrote that the family was deluged
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel Sewall wrote three days after: he was settleing among them to good Satisfaction; but is snatchd away by a violent Fever. By his death his Family at Braintrey was delugd with Tears. John Quincy of Braintree took his son as ward.

narrative_blocks.body: Among her four children with Samuel Low was a son named Hooker Low — an explicit tribute to her Hooker ancestry four generations on. Her grandmother was Mary Hooker Newton, daughter of Rev. Thomas Hooker. The name Hooker as a given name is a deliberate act of family memory.

narrative_blocks.header: Married Milford minister, then Middletown statesman
narrative_blocks.body: Her first husband Rev. Samuel Whittlesey served Milford for thirty-plus years until his death in 1768. She remarried Hon. Jabez Hamlin of Middletown — described as 'distinguished in civil and military life.'

narrative_blocks.header: Whittlesey genealogy: 'lady of high intellectual qualities'
narrative_blocks.body: The Whittlesey genealogy describes her as 'a lady of high intellectual and moral qualities.' This was an unusual tribute for a colonial woman, whose lives were typically invisible in family records of the era.

narrative_blocks.header: Outlived both husbands; died at 87 in Middletown
narrative_blocks.body: She outlived her first husband Rev. Samuel Whittlesey by 35 years and her second husband Jabez Hamlin as well. She died at Middletown in 1803, age 87.

narrative_blocks.header: She took a granddaughter and kept her
narrative_blocks.body: Her daughter Sarah’s third child, Susan, was carried off to Middletown and kept there so long that five more were born at New Haven whom the girl could not say she had ever seen. Susan married out of Middletown in 1805.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Newton sisters, two Whittelsey brothers
narrative_blocks.body: Her elder sister Susannah married Rev. Samuel Whittelsey the younger. Martha married his brother Chauncey in 1753. Col. Roger Newton had given two daughters to one Wallingford parsonage.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a widower with a small son
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth Whiting died in 1751 and Martha took her place two years later. Eleven more children followed between 1754 and 1773; three died in infancy.

narrative_blocks.header: Three daughters named Elizabeth
narrative_blocks.body: An Elizabeth born in 1758 died that year, and a second born in 1760 did the same. The third, born in 1773, carried the name with Susanna added, married Reuben Barnes in 1790, and lived to ninety-two.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived him by twenty-five years
narrative_blocks.body: Chauncey Whittlesey died in 1787. She kept the New Haven house until October 1812, and was buried with him in the crypt beneath Center Church.

Son of Lt. Alexander Marsh (b.1628 England; d. Mar 7, 1698 Braintree) and Mary Belcher (daughter of Gregory Belcher, prominent Puritan family). Alexander Marsh: yeoman, arrived Massachusetts 1654, worked Iron Works, became wealthy, Lieutenant in Colonial Militia. Alexander's 2nd wife was Bathsheba Lothrop Beale. Family tradition: Alexander came to the colonies with his "Uncle George" of Hingham; a Marsh diary at Quincy Historical Society suggests Marsh ancestors were executed by Cromwell and George brought the children to the colonies. m. Sarah Wilson (H00060) Aug 28, 1701. John Marsh is called "Sgt. John Marsh" in some sources.

narrative_blocks.body: John was elected Braintree's hayward, or field driver, in 1707 and a surveyor of highways in 1716, and was chosen constable in 1718 but excused. He and Sarah lived on the Wilson farm.

narrative_blocks.header: Born in the house her father built
narrative_blocks.body: She was born on 10 June 1689 at 16 Sunset Hill, three years after the house went up as her parents' wedding present. She was nineteen when they sold it to Nathaniel Paddack and took her off the island.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at twenty-four, remarried at thirty
narrative_blocks.body: She married John Wilson in May 1711 and he was dead by 1713, leaving her a son of one and a daughter born the year after. She married the Rev. Samuel Terry in October 1719.

narrative_blocks.header: Nantucket’s founder was her great-grandfather
narrative_blocks.body: Tristram Coffin, who bought the island in 1659 and was twice its chief magistrate, was her father's father's father. The Hooker line reaches this tree through her first marriage, not her second.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at sixteen, dead at thirty-two
narrative_blocks.body: Obed Hussey married her at Nantucket in 1730 when she was sixteen. She bore eight children in as many years and died in December 1746, the year the last of them was born, and lies in the Old North ground there.

narrative_blocks.header: Two of her sons' names were used twice
narrative_blocks.body: Obed died before he was two and the next boy took his name; John died the year he was born and the next John took his, and lived to thirteen. Four of the eight did not reach fourteen. Abiel reached twenty and married a Coffin.

narrative_blocks.header: She was born after her father was buried
narrative_blocks.body: John Wilson died of a fever at Swansea in November 1713 and she came the year after, posthumous. Her mother was still asking his estate for household items in 1722 to keep this child.

narrative_blocks.header: He built Nantucket's oldest surviving house
narrative_blocks.body: In 1686 Jethro Coffin raised a saltbox house on Nantucket as a wedding gift, framed with Coffin lumber on Gardner land, joining two rival founding families. It still stands as the oldest surviving house on the island.

narrative_blocks.header: He left the island his grandfather helped found
narrative_blocks.body: He was a grandson of Tristram Coffin, one of Nantucket's original proprietors. In 1708 Jethro sold the dwelling and moved to Mendon, Massachusetts, to take up inherited property.

narrative_blocks.header: She married at sixteen into the rival family
narrative_blocks.body: Her father John Gardner led the half-share men against the full-share proprietors Tristram Coffin headed. In 1686 she married Coffin's grandson Jethro at sixteen, and the wedding house went up on Gardner land with Coffin timber.

narrative_blocks.header: The first Nantucketer whose face was painted
narrative_blocks.body: She sat in Boston about 1720, during the family's years off-island, for a painter known only as the Pollard Limner. It is the earliest known portrait of a Nantucketer and the oldest painting the island's historical association holds.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty years on Sunset Hill, then Mendon
narrative_blocks.body: She bore nine children in nineteen years in the house at 16 Sunset Hill. In 1708 they sold it to Nathaniel Paddack and left for Mendon, where Jethro had inherited property; four generations of Paddacks lived in it after them.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived her husband by forty-one years
narrative_blocks.body: Jethro died in 1726 and she came back to Nantucket alone. She died there on 28 October 1767 at ninety-seven, having outlived the island's first English generation and most of her own.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the granddaughter of a rival
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas was Rev. Thomas Hooker's grandson, raised in the Hartford his ancestor founded. The woman he married was William Pynchon's granddaughter, and Pynchon had quarrelled with that ancestor and pulled Springfield out of Connecticut over it.

narrative_blocks.header: The minister's son who chose medicine
narrative_blocks.body: His grandfather founded Hartford's church and his father held the Farmington pulpit. Thomas, a second son born at Plymouth, trained as a physician instead and practised in Hartford until his death in 1720.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife was sixteen years his senior
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Smith was the widow of Richard Lord, a Hartford merchant lost at sea in November 1685. She was in her forties and Thomas in his twenties when they married, and they had no children.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran his stepson's estate until 1693
narrative_blocks.body: On marrying Mary he took charge of the Hartford estate her first husband had left. He administered it for seven years and was released from it on 8 February 1693, when it passed to his stepson, young Richard Lord.

narrative_blocks.header: His father preached; he kept a store
narrative_blocks.body: He kept a store and traded out of Hartford while living at Farmington, where his father had held the pulpit for thirty-six years. Of the minister's sons, two became physicians, two rose to the Connecticut bench, and Samuel was the merchant.

narrative_blocks.header: His bride's grandfather walked beside his own
narrative_blocks.body: In June 1687 he married Mehitabel Hamlin of Middletown, daughter of the sea captain Giles Hamlin and granddaughter of John Crow — the Hartford merchant who walked west from Newtown with Rev. Thomas Hooker in 1636. Samuel's own grandfather led that party, and fifty-one years later the two families married.

narrative_blocks.header: His house still stands under another man's name
narrative_blocks.body: His residence stood on Main Street at Farmington, next south of the old burying ground; the town came to call it the Mix house, and it stands today in the village historic district. His second son, Lt. Giles Hooker, lived directly opposite.

narrative_blocks.header: Only he and one brother were not Farmington-born
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Plymouth on 29 May 1661, in his father's last year in that pulpit; the family removed to Farmington before the year was out. Of Rev. Samuel Hooker's eleven children, only he and his elder brother Thomas were born in Massachusetts.

narrative_blocks.header: His store faced his father's front door
narrative_blocks.body: He kept a store at the junction of Farmington's main street and the road over the stone bridge across the Pequabuc, directly opposite his father's house. It was the town's most prominent corner, known long afterward as Thomas Cowles corner.

narrative_blocks.header: He left the Great Bible to his mother
narrative_blocks.body: His will, dated 8 August 1689, gave the Great Bible to his “Honoured Mother” Mary Willet Hooker and his house to his brother Thomas, the physician. Half the estate went to his wife outright, the remainder to his daughter until she turned eighteen or married.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife's sisters married Newton and Leete
narrative_blocks.body: He married Susanna Fenn of Milford, daughter of the magistrate Benjamin Fenn. Her half-sister Martha married Samuel Newton — William's first cousin — and her sister Mary married William Leete Jr., so three Fenn daughters entered three Connecticut families in a single generation.

narrative_blocks.header: His only child was born the year after
narrative_blocks.body: He died at Farmington in 1689, twenty-six years old. His daughter Susannah was born the following year and never saw him; she was the only child of the marriage.

narrative_blocks.header: His widow married into Hartford's trade
narrative_blocks.body: Susanna Fenn was twenty when he died. She married John Blackleach Jr., a noted Hartford merchant, and died in 1698 at twenty-nine.

career.notes: Store at the most prominent corner in Farmington, opposite his father's house, at the junction of main street and the road over the stone bridge.

narrative_blocks.header: He settled other towns' quarrels for the Assembly
narrative_blocks.body: He was the magistrate who did most of Farmington's business, and the Assembly sent him out repeatedly to settle difficulties in other towns and churches. In twenty-one sessions of the Lower House he was clerk twice and speaker six times.

narrative_blocks.header: He testified the land had always been Tunxis
narrative_blocks.body: In 1738 he told the Connecticut General Court that the ninety acres at Indian Neck had always belonged to the Tunxis. Five years earlier he had signed one Tunxis land deed in three capacities at once — witness, certifying assistant, and registrar.

narrative_blocks.header: The elm fell so someone could walk straight
narrative_blocks.body: His father gave him a site on the west side of Farmington's main street, where he built under a great elm. Three generations of Hookers kept house in its shade and entertained the town beneath it; a later owner cut it down because it stood between his front door and the street.

narrative_blocks.header: The bell tolled — Hooker stepped out first
narrative_blocks.body: Every Sunday the bell rang and then began to toll; at the first stroke he left his house for the Meeting House, and the minister left his at the same moment. Whoever arrived first waited at the door, and they walked the aisle together while the congregation stood.

narrative_blocks.header: The Sabbath ended when Hooker touched his gate
narrative_blocks.body: Sunday was held to end at sunset, but no child in Farmington dared stir until he gave the signal. When the sun went down he walked to his gate with his pipe and leaned on it, and the doors flew open all down the street.

narrative_blocks.header: Dark hair, dark eyes — dignity commanding respect
narrative_blocks.body: His grandson Roger remembered dark hair and dark eyes, and a dignity in his air and expression that procured profound respect. He was tall and very erect, with a prominent large nose.

OCCUPATION NOTES: Became a very prominent man at Guilford. First Probate Judge of the Guilford district. Repeatedly represented Guilford in the Colonial Assembly and was for a number of sessions its presiding officer.
DEATH DATE DISCREPANCY: EH gives "Mar. 12, 1740 or 1741." 1740 preferred.
OLD STYLE: EH's "Mar. 12, 1740 or 1741" is the dual-year form — 12 March falls before the Old Style new year of 25 March. New Style year 1741 recorded per schema §v24-6.6; corrected 2026-09-08 from 1740.

narrative_blocks.header: He was the first judge Guilford probate had
narrative_blocks.body: He was the first judge of the Guilford probate district and the town's repeated choice for the Colonial Assembly, where he presided over a number of its sessions. He had arrived from Farmington a minister's son and made himself the leading man of another town.

narrative_blocks.header: Four daughters married; the one son did not
narrative_blocks.body: His four daughters all married — into the Harts, the Bartletts and the Smiths. His only son William took a Yale degree and died at twenty-one, unmarried, so the name ended in Guilford with him.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the only Leete daughter at Guilford
narrative_blocks.body: In 1691 he married Mary Leete, the only daughter of William and Mary (Fenn) Leete of Guilford, and settled in her town rather than his own. Her grandfather was the one man who governed both New Haven Colony and Connecticut.

narrative_blocks.header: His nephew married his wife's first cousin
narrative_blocks.body: Twenty years after his own wedding, his nephew Samuel Hooker III married Mercy Leete — first cousin to Mary. Two Leete granddaughters, cousins to each other, married two Hookers a generation apart.

career.notes: First judge of the Guilford probate district; also a town magistrate.
Repeatedly represented Guilford; presiding officer for several sessions.

narrative_blocks.header: Betrothed at 29 — passed before the wedding
narrative_blocks.body: Roger Hooker was betrothed to Mary Standley of Hartford when he died on April 29, 1698, at age 29. Seven months later — December 28, 1698 — his brother Nathaniel married her instead.

naming_inspiration.description: Likely named for Rev. Roger Newton (I00003), his father's predecessor and brother-in-law at Farmington.

people.research_notes:
Son of Rev. Samuel Hooker (H00007) and Mary Willet (I00006). Brother of Hon. John Hooker (H00030) who married Abigail Standley. m. Mary Standley/Stanley (I00051), daughter of Hon. Nathaniel Stanley of Hartford. Stanley book entry 10 (MARY STANLEY): "married Nathaniel Hooker, son of Samuel and Mary (Willett) Hooker." Children (Stanley book): Mary (b. Dec 3, 1699, d. unm. Jan 2, 1765), Alice (b. Nov 12, 1701, m. D. Howard, d. 1750), Sarah (b. Nov 7, 1704, m. Hon. Daniel Edwards of Hartford), Abigail (b. 1707, m. Rev. Benjamin Lord DD of Norwich), Nathaniel (b.?, m. Eunice Talcott, Yale 1729 = H00115). His wife's father Hon. Nathaniel Stanley was of Farmington. NOTE: This is a DIFFERENT Stanley family from Capt. John Stanley (X00035, father of Abigail who married H00030 John Hooker). Two separate Stanley branches both intersecting the Hooker line. OCCUPATION NOTES: Noted merchant and prominent man at Hartford. Place of business on main street a little below present Centre Church, on property originally the building lot of his father-in-law Nathaniel Standley, who gave half his lot (extending from Second Burial Ground to the little river) to Nathaniel Hooker at marriage.
TALCOTT-EDWARDS CONVERGENCE (queued for research): His daughter Sarah Hooker (H00112) married Hon. Daniel Edwards (I00053, b.Apr 11, 1701) — whose mother was Mary Talcott Edwards (T00042), daughter of Lt.-Col. John Talcott (T00035). Daniel was also a half-brother of Richard Edwards, father of Jonathan Edwards the theologian. Their children are therefore both Hooker AND Talcott descendants. The Jonathan Edwards connection also runs through this line. See I00053 and T00042 for further research.
DISPLAY NAME NOTE: "Willett" added as middle name per Sam. Sam wrote "Rev." but EH describes him as a noted merchant — not a minister. Title left null. Verify if ministerial ordination documented.

narrative_blocks.header: A noted merchant below Centre Church
narrative_blocks.body: He kept a shop on the main street at Hartford, a little below where Centre Church stands now. The lot was his wedding present: Nathaniel Stanley gave his son-in-law half his ground, from the Second Burial Ground to the little river.

narrative_blocks.header: He died still holding his Assembly seat
narrative_blocks.body: He represented Hartford in the Connecticut Colonial Assembly for several years, and was still sitting for the town when he died in the November of 1711.

narrative_blocks.header: His bride had been promised to his brother
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Standley had been betrothed to his brother Roger, who died in the April of 1698, and before the year was out he married her himself. A third brother, John, had married an Abigail Standley of an unrelated family.

narrative_blocks.header: They gave the name Nathaniel twice
narrative_blocks.body: He and Mary lost a young son named Nathaniel and gave the name again to the boy baptized at Hartford in October 1710. That second Nathaniel lived to fifty-three and became a captain.

narrative_blocks.header: Mary outlived him by forty-two years
narrative_blocks.body: He died at forty and Mary was a widow for two years before she married John Austin, another Hartford merchant. She outlived him by forty-two years and died at Hartford in 1753.

narrative_blocks.header: Two children married into the Talcott line
narrative_blocks.body: His daughter Sarah married Daniel Edwards in 1728, bringing in the Edwards line and, through Edwards's mother Mary Talcott, the Talcott one. His son Nathaniel married Eunice Talcott, daughter of Governor Joseph Talcott.

b. ca. 1673; d. ca. 1727. Daughter of Samuel Hooker (H00007) and [mother I00006] — granddaughter of Rev. Thomas Hooker. Portrait survives (one of the few colonial-era portraits of a woman in this line). MARRIED REV. JAMES PIERPONT SR. (X00126): Together, they are the parental foundation of the entire Pierpont branch of the tree. Rev. James Pierpont Sr. was a co-founder of Yale College in 1701. His wife Mary Hooker was the granddaughter of the founder of Hartford. Their children include: James Pierpont II (H00116), Mary Pierpont Russell (H00118), Sarah Pierpont Edwards (HD0418) — wife of Jonathan Edwards — and others. Through Sarah Pierpont Edwards: the line leads to Aaron Burr, 3rd VP. Through James Pierpont II: the line leads to J.P. Morgan, Jingle Bells composer, Vermont Chief Justice, Yale mathematician, Titanic victim, Medal of Honor. Through Mary Pierpont Russell: the line leads to the Russell-Talcott convergence. EASTER EGG: Mary Hooker Pierpont — married Rev. James Pierpont, co-founder of Yale College 1701; portrait survives

narrative_blocks.header: Eight children in the house under the elms
narrative_blocks.body: Mary ran the New Haven parsonage through sixteen years of marriage and eight children, then presided over it as a widow for twenty-six more. The congregation had raised the house by voluntary subscription, and it stood for over a century.

narrative_blocks.header: Married James Pierpont the year her father died
narrative_blocks.body: Her father, the Farmington minister Samuel Hooker, died in November 1697; she married James Pierpont of New Haven the following year. The match carried her from one parsonage to the center of Connecticut’s emerging intellectual capital.

narrative_blocks.header: Her daughter’s courtship under the elms
narrative_blocks.body: It was Mary’s daughter Sarah whom Jonathan Edwards courted beneath the parsonage elms in 1726 — a match made in her widowed household that joined the Pierpont and Edwards lines and led on to college presidents and a vice president.

narrative_blocks.header: A son lost crossing the Connecticut
narrative_blocks.body: Her son Samuel — Yale 1718, newly ordained at Lyme — drowned in March 1723 crossing the Connecticut River in a canoe with an Indian guide. His body came ashore on Fishers Island six weeks later and was buried where it was found.

narrative_blocks.header: The family that named an artist
narrative_blocks.body: The unidentified colonial painter who took her portrait around 1711 is known to art history only as the Pierpont Limner — christened for this family, whose likenesses anchor his surviving work. Her husband’s companion portrait hangs at the Yale University Art Gallery.

narrative_blocks.header: A silk apron may trace to her line
narrative_blocks.body: A rare 1730s embroidered silk apron at the Connecticut Historical Society descends through three generations of Marys beginning with her. Though scholars doubt she stitched it herself, her advantageous marriage made such a luxury possible for the daughters who followed.

bio.photo_notes: Portrait of Mrs. James Pierpont (née Mary Hooker), 1711. Wikipedia Commons.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at Farmington at about age ten
narrative_blocks.body: Hezekiah Hooker was born at Farmington in 1675, one of Rev. Samuel Hooker's eleven children. He died there in 1686, about ten years old.

narrative_blocks.header: First Yale tutor, B.A. graduate in 1703
narrative_blocks.body: He was the first tutor appointed at the Collegiate School (Yale) by first rector Abraham Pierson Jr. — Yale's earliest faculty member. He received his Yale B.A. in 1703, alongside Rev. John Hart who was the first student to graduate.

narrative_blocks.header: Surgeon of the Canada expedition, 1711
narrative_blocks.body: He served as surgeon of the Massachusetts expedition against Canada in 1711 — the final major military operation of Queen Anne's War. He then returned to Wethersfield to practice medicine and law.

narrative_blocks.header: Declined his father's pulpit — chose medicine
narrative_blocks.body: After Rev. Samuel Hooker died in 1697, Farmington invited Daniel to succeed his father. He declined the pulpit and chose medicine — studying law alongside it, not to practice but to help patients make their wills.

narrative_blocks.header: First Farmington-born man with a college education
narrative_blocks.body: He graduated Harvard in 1700, then enrolled at the new Collegiate School in Saybrook to receive its B.A. in 1703. He was the first Farmington-born man to obtain a college education.

narrative_blocks.header: Inherited and divided Thomas Hooker's West Hartford farm
narrative_blocks.body: He inherited Thomas Hooker's farm in West Hartford and in 1728 deeded it to his sons. The land had been part of the original Hooker grant — passing through three generations from founder to surgeon.

narrative_blocks.header: The most accomplished lady Norwalk had ever seen
narrative_blocks.body: She was nicknamed 'Dame Buckingham' and described in family tradition as 'the most accomplished lady that had ever come to Norwalk.' She lived at Norwalk with her husband Rev. Stephen Buckingham from their 1703 marriage until her death in 1759.

narrative_blocks.header: No stone marks her grave — tradition knows
narrative_blocks.body: She died about March 26, 1759 in Norwalk, age 77. No marker survives at her grave; the location is preserved only in family tradition and her husband's burial records.

narrative_blocks.header: Her stepfather's son became her husband
narrative_blocks.body: After her father Rev. Samuel Hooker died in 1697, her mother Mary Willet married Rev. Thomas Buckingham of Saybrook. Thomas Buckingham was the father of Rev. Stephen Buckingham — whom Sarah herself married. After Thomas died in 1709, Mary came to Sarah and Stephen at Norwalk and lived with them until her death in 1712.

narrative_blocks.header: They called him an Arminian to stop him
narrative_blocks.body: A large minority of Milford objected to his ordination, alleging he was an Arminian whose preaching savoured too little of Christian experience. The council that met to ordain him split, and he went in on a compromise.

narrative_blocks.header: Fists were doubled at the ordination
narrative_blocks.body: The debate over settling him ran so hot that, by one account, fists were doubled on the occasion. The minority walked out, built a decent house for worship by 1742, and went under the presbytery of New Brunswick.

narrative_blocks.header: His father preached his ordination sermon
narrative_blocks.body: When Samuel was ordained at Milford on December 9, 1737, the sermon was preached by his father, Rev. Samuel Whittelsey of Wallingford — and then published, the elder man’s fourth and final printed work.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale at sixteen, then six years its tutor
narrative_blocks.body: He took his degree in the class of 1729 at sixteen and stayed on as a tutor of the college from 1732 to 1738. Both Yale and Harvard gave him the master's.

narrative_blocks.header: The Church of England came for his parish
narrative_blocks.body: He wrote that the Church of England was making her strongest efforts at Milford, the service read among them every Sabbath, and the neighbouring clergymen very officious in coming over to our Macedonia.

narrative_blocks.header: A Latin stone, translated for the curious
narrative_blocks.body: His Milford monument, in Latin, credits him with honors from both Yale and Harvard and “virtues, piety and good deeds” that “everywhere shone with peculiar lustre” across more than thirty years in the town’s pulpit.

narrative_blocks.header: Four Harvard and Yale men in a line
narrative_blocks.body: His mother Sarah was granddaughter to Rev. Charles Chauncy, Harvard's second president, and daughter to Nathaniel Chauncy, Harvard 1661. His father took Yale in 1705; he and his brother Chauncey followed in 1729 and 1738.

narrative_blocks.header: Her sister married her husband’s cousin
narrative_blocks.body: Hannah married Fletcher Newton; her sister Phebe married Fletcher's first cousin Samuel Newton. Two Platt sisters wed two Newton first cousins in the same generation — tightening the bonds of two old Milford families.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandfather came over with Prudden
narrative_blocks.body: Deacon Richard Platt left Ware in Hertfordshire, where Charles Chauncey had been preaching, and was among the sixty-six who founded the Milford church with Peter Prudden in 1639. He was chosen deacon of it in 1669.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father sat fourteen sessions
narrative_blocks.body: Zachariah Baldwin was auditor for Milford in 1696 and then went to the Connecticut General Assembly for fourteen sessions between 1705 and 1718. Milford styled him Sergeant all his life, though which war earned it nobody recorded.

narrative_blocks.header: Her great-grandfather founded Milford
narrative_blocks.body: Deacon Richard Platt came out of Ware in Hertfordshire with Rev. Peter Prudden and was one of the sixty-six who founded the Milford church in 1639. His name is cut on the Wepawaug memorial bridge: Deacon Richard Platt, Obit 1684 — Mary His Wife.

narrative_blocks.header: He left a Bible to each of nineteen
narrative_blocks.body: Making his will in 1683 the deacon bequeathed a Bible to every one of his nineteen grandchildren. Her mother's mother was one of the nine children who produced them.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandfather called the minister a liar
narrative_blocks.body: Luke Atkinson was charged in January 1646 with defaming Rev. John Davenport of New Haven — alleging the minister had said things he later denied, and that his own name had been darkned by it. He had come over about 1640 and signed the fundamental agreement of the colony.

bio.bio_blurb: Durham minute man who settled Greenfield

narrative_blocks.header: A minute man at forty-eight
narrative_blocks.body: He turned out for the Lexington Alarm in April 1775 with Captain Jonas Lock's company of Colonel Williams's Massachusetts regiment. He had already been commissioned at Durham to take up Tories.

narrative_blocks.header: Hemlock swamp at seven and six an acre
narrative_blocks.body: He bought wild Greenfield land at that price with his son Isaac and his brother Roger. Much of it was swamp, and much of it turned out to be worth having.

narrative_blocks.header: He was born a twin on Main Street
narrative_blocks.body: He and Abner came together on the twenty-third of October 1726 in the house on Main Street at Durham. They were named apart and lived apart, but they arrived the same hour.

narrative_blocks.header: He followed his brother north to Greenfield
narrative_blocks.body: Roger was eleven years younger and minister at Greenfield for fifty-three years. John moved up after the Revolution and took one town office after another.

narrative_blocks.header: His second wife went a fortnight before him
narrative_blocks.body: Huldah died on the fourteenth of September 1802 at sixty. He followed on the twenty-eighth, not quite seventy-six, and they were buried at High Street.

narrative_blocks.header: Born without a roof to his mouth
narrative_blocks.detail: His principal crop was rye; he spelled it 'ri.' His carefully kept account book, dated January 1, 1762, survived and was published in Caroline Newton's family history. The speech impediment was not only a social burden — it shaped his entire Revolutionary War service. Strangers could not understand him, and when he could not give the countersign intelligibly, he risked being shot by his own side. When Britain declared war with France and the colonial militia faced possible service in Canada, his Captain consulted a higher officer, who granted Burwell an exemption from duty. The document of exemption was preserved in the family. (Caroline Gaylord Newton 1914)
narrative_blocks.body: When the children in the little schoolhouse on Phillida Hill laughed at his cleft-palate speech, Burwell refused to attend. He taught himself to read, write, and keep accounts, his spelling defiantly phonetic — if he chose to spell his principal crop “ri,” that was the best way to spell it.

narrative_blocks.header: The countersign kept him out of Canada
narrative_blocks.body: He served in the town militia until Great Britain declared war on France and it looked as though the men might be sent to Canada. He was relieved of duty then, because he could not give the countersign clearly enough to be understood — the word a sentry has to hear right or shoot.

narrative_blocks.header: He was at Kingston when Congress sat there
narrative_blocks.detail: His service in both deployments was brief — not from cowardice but from the practical impossibility of the countersign problem. His unit could not rely on him for sentry duty or night patrol, since any stranger who challenged him could not understand his response. He served with what he could offer and was released. He is on the DAR lineage rolls through his descendant Miss Sarah Newton Church (NSDAR No. 99934; DAR Lineage Book 100:291). (Caroline Gaylord Newton 1914; EH 1909)
narrative_blocks.body: In 1777 Burwell was at Kingston, New York, when the Continental Congress was assembled there under threat from British troops. In 1779 he enlisted in Capt. Charles Norton's Company, Col. Thaddeus Cook's regiment, and was called to New Haven and Fairfield during the British coastal raids of July 1779.

narrative_blocks.header: His stammer nearly kept him from war
narrative_blocks.body: Born without a roof to his mouth, Burwell Newton could not give a military countersign clearly enough for strangers to understand — a danger that could get a sentry shot. When Britain’s war with France threatened to send the militia to Canada, Col. Timothy Stone authorized his discharge, writing that officers had “full Power to Relieve any Soldier… unfit for service.”

narrative_blocks.header: He never moved out of his father's house
narrative_blocks.body: He lived his whole life at Durham in the same house as Abner, the house on Main Street where he was born. Eunice Johnson came into it at nineteen and bore eight children there.

Named for grandfather Rev. Roger Newton (I00003). [Migrated from top-level anecdotes]: {"alice_newtons_bequest_fulfilled": "Alice Newton (H00018), youngest daughter of Rev. Roger Newton (I00003), died without children after 1740 and left a conditional bequest to Yale in hopes that her little grand-nephew Roger would \"follow in his grandfather's steps, and become an educated man, and a minister of the gospel.\" Roger Newton graduated Yale in 1758 and was ordained at Greenfield, Massachusetts in 1761 \u2014 fulfilling, across three generations and half a century, the dying wish of a woman he may never have met. He served as Greenfield's minister for 55 years, until his death in 1816.", "the_phillida_hill_schoolhouse": "The little schoolhouse near the Durham Newton homestead stood on a hill called Phillida \u2014 named, according to tradition, after a slave woman who had been purchased to care for an invalid master, who sold the bit of land for the money that bought her. The slave's name survived through the centuries on the hill; the master's name was forgotten. In that schoolhouse, Roger Newton received what his biographers called \"two weeks of education under Rev. Dr. Goodrich\" \u2014 though Caroline Newton's history suspects this was a significant understatement."} Yale Biographical Sketches (Dexter): b. May 12, 1737 Durham CT (baptized May 15 by Rev. Nathaniel Chauncey Y.C.1702). Theological study under Chauncey's successor Rev. Elizur Goodrich (Y.C.1752). Licensed Sep 30, 1760 by New Haven Association. Greenfield voted unanimously Aug 1761 to call him at £80 salary + 60 cords wood/year. Ordained Nov 18, 1761 (Newton genealogy gives Nov 13). DD conferred by Dartmouth College 1805 (Sprague says 1804). LOYALIST QUESTION: charged during Revolution with being 'disaffected to the popular side'; reportedly inclined to Loyalist side; exchanged pulpit with Tory Rev. Ashley of Deerfield — congregation blocked Ashley's afternoon sermon. ENSLAVED PERSON: diary entry Sep 20, 1767 records 'Tinner, my negro girl' baptized with his son Isaac. Diary extracted by Francis M. Thompson in NEH&G Register Jul 1908, 62:263-273 and in Thompson's History of Greenfield vol.1 pp.700-749. Final diary entry May 23, 1812: 'This day I am seventy five years old. I shall not and I would not live always.' Children: Roger (1763-1789, Yale 1785, tutor, consumption), Isaac (1765, d.infant), Isaac (1767-1768), Abigail (1771, m. Rev. Nathaniel Lambert Newbury VT), Susannah (1773-1777), Ozias (1775-?), Isaac (1777-1844), Susannah (1779-1855 Cambridge MA). Son Roger's death noted annually in diary. Sources: Yale Biographic Sketches; Robert S. Newton genealogy (BIB004); Thompson Greenfield history. Newton genealogy no.17 and Francis M. Thompson, History of Greenfield (1904), vol.1 pp.700-749; 'Extracts From the Diary of Rev. Roger Newton, D.D., of Greenfield, Mass.', NEH&G Register, July 1908, 62:263-273. BIRTH: born 12 May 1737 Old Style at Durham; christened 15 May; a FamilySearch extract gives 15 May at Hartford, which the book contradicts. THE CALL: Greenfield voted him 133 pounds 6s 8d as settlement and 66 pounds 3s 4d as salary, to rise 1 pound 6s 8d a year until it reached 80, and in September added sixty cords of wood yearly. ALICE BUCKINGHAM'S BEQUEST: 30 pounds toward college when he was three, conditional on his being 'likely for publick service'. DIARY, 18 Nov. 1761: 'Received The pastoral Charge of the Church of Christ in Greenfield--in the twenty fifth year of my age--being twenty four years old May 12th.' 5 Apr. 1806: complained that the parish had not raised its contributions above the 1774 amounts and that he could not afford the hospitality his late wife would have liked to keep. He noted the anniversary of his son Roger's death every year. Reportedly inclined to the Loyalist side during the Revolution. THREE SONS NAMED ISAAC AND TWO DAUGHTERS NAMED SUSANNAH. The family history sets it out as an example of the popularity of Isaac in the Newton line and of the custom, when a child died young, of giving the name to a later one. Isaac bp. 1765 died at seven weeks; Isaac b. 1767 died at fifteen months; Isaac b. 1777 lived to sixty-seven. Susannah b. 1773 died at three; Susannah b. 1779 lived to seventy-six.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-six years and no split
narrative_blocks.body: Greenfield called him unanimously in August 1761 and he was installed that November, at twenty-four. He held the pulpit until he died in 1816, and a contemporary wrote that the town's peace and union through nearly the whole fifty-six years was itself the strongest evidence of his virtue and prudence.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the call on one condition
narrative_blocks.body: The church was divided over who might come to communion, and he answered the call by naming his terms: that all persons of competent knowledge and sober lives who thought it their duty be allowed to come, provided none scandalously ignorant or immoral were admitted. On that proposal, he wrote, he accepted.

narrative_blocks.header: The parish stopped the afternoon service
narrative_blocks.body: He was thought no enthusiast for the Whigs before the Revolution and was held to be under the influence of the Rev. Ashley of Deerfield, an outspoken Tory. He swapped pulpits with Ashley one Sunday knowing the sermon would displease, and after the morning the congregation had heated words with Ashley and would not let the afternoon service be held.

narrative_blocks.header: His diary came out of a dumping barrel
narrative_blocks.body: It was rescued from a barrel with pages already gone, and Francis Thompson printed it in his History of Greenfield in 1904 and in the New England Register four years later. It is one of the primary sources for the town's published vital records.

narrative_blocks.header: He baptized his son and his slave together
narrative_blocks.body: His record of the baptisms of the twentieth of September 1767 reads: Isaac, my son, and Tinner, my negro girl. The two names stand in the same line of the same list, in his own hand.

narrative_blocks.header: I would not live always, he wrote
narrative_blocks.body: His last diary entry, on the twenty-third of May 1812, reads: This day I am seventy five years old. I shall not and I would not live always. He had moved his own birthday eleven days when the calendar changed, from the twelfth of May old style to the twenty-third new, and he lived four years more.

narrative_blocks.body: Joseph and Eunice were born at Milford in 1730 and 1732, Thomas and Jared at Wallingford in 1734 and 1738, which puts the move at about 1733. He died at Cheshire fifty years later and lies in the old graveyard there with Sarah, who had gone the September before.

Ezekiel⁴ and his wife removed from Milford to Woodbury, Litchfield County CT in 1770. On 25 March 1774 sons Isaac (HD0237 — see note below) and David Newton (HD0233) executed a deed conveying to their mother Mary Newton one-half the dwelling house in Woodbury in consideration of her giving up her right in the dwelling and lot where their honored father, Ezekiel late of Milford, had lived. Five documented children: Ezekiel⁵ (b. 1740 Milford, d. 14 Sept. 1811 Washington CT, m. Ann Smith), Lucy⁵ (b. ca. 1746 Milford, d. Dec. 1821 age 74 Milford, m. (1) Zachariah Pond 1768, (2) Capt. William Clark), Christopher⁵ (d. Feb. 1795 at sea, m. Mary Terrill), Mary⁵ (perhaps m. John Smith of Washington CT), Avis⁵ (probably m. John Herrick May 17, 1784 Washington CT). [NOTE: Existing tree IDs HD0234 Lucy, HD0235 Christopher, HD0236 Mary, HD0237 Avis — current ID HD0237 in this database is 'Avis' the daughter, not 'Isaac' the son referenced in the 1774 deed. The 1774 deed mentions David and Isaac as the deed's signatories — Isaac was likely an additional son not yet built in this database; Newton genealogy lists him separately.] Birth corrected to 1715 on Sam's list; the record had been carrying 16 Sept. 1716, which is his sister Eunice's christening date. Sam's list gives six children; Lucy (HD0234, 1748-1821) is already on this record and is not in the list — left in place, so seven are carried here. Two daughters are named Mary, born about 1734 and 1750. Newton genealogy no.19: baptized 16 Sept. 1716 at Milford, DIED BEFORE 1771. He and Mary Collins removed from Milford to Woodbury, Litchfield Co., in 1770. The book names seven children, order unknown: Ezekiel, Lucy, Christopher, Mary, Avis, Isaac and David.

narrative_blocks.header: His sons deeded their mother half the house
narrative_blocks.body: After he died his sons formally signed over half the Woodbury dwelling to their mother, in exchange for her giving up her widow’s right to the home where their father had lived. He had moved the family there from Milford only the year before his death.

narrative_blocks.header: He moved to Woodbury the year he died
narrative_blocks.body: He and Mary Collins left Milford for Woodbury in Litchfield County in 1770, and he was dead before 1771. Four years later his sons Isaac and David deeded their mother half the Woodbury house in exchange for her right in the Milford lot where he had lived.

narrative_blocks.header: Away tending stock the night his family died
narrative_blocks.body: In December 1666 a fire set to the Hart house in Farmington killed everyone inside; John, then about eleven, survived only because he had been sent that night to Nod to tend the family's stock. He grew up the sole survivor of his household.

narrative_blocks.header: Three of his sons married three sisters
narrative_blocks.body: Nathaniel, Samuel and Matthew Hart married Abigail, Mary and Sarah Hooker, the daughters of Hon. John Hooker of Farmington, in 1719, 1723 and 1726. Their father had been dead five years when the first of those weddings took place.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandfather’s will singled the orphan out
narrative_blocks.body: When Deacon Stephen Hart wrote his will in 1682, he named the fire's lone survivor directly as his eldest son's son. The boy who had lost everyone kept his place in the family record and a small legacy.

narrative_blocks.header: He began alone and died with four sons
narrative_blocks.body: The fire left him the only Hart of his household at eleven. He married Mary Moore at Farmington in 1683 and raised four sons; the eldest, John, became a Farmington deacon and sat twenty-three sessions in the General Court.

people.research_notes:
b. ~1605 Braintree, Essex, England (EH; some sources say 1603 Ipswich). d. Mar 1682/3 Farmington CT age ~77 (will Mar 16; inventory Mar 31, 1682/3). HARTFORD FOUNDER. THOMAS HOOKER'S DEACON. Came to Cambridge/Newtown ~1632 with the "Braintree Company." Admitted freeman May 14, 1634 — same session as Thomas Hooker and Samuel Stone. Had been deacon of Rev. Thomas Hooker's church at Cambridge AND Hartford. Came to Hartford with Hooker's company 1635. Original proprietor of Hartford 1639. One of 84 proprietors of Farmington 1672. One of seven pillars of Farmington church, organized Nov 1652; first deacon. Other pillars: Rev. Roger Newton (Hooker's student, married his daughter), John Cole, John Bronson, Robert Porter, Thomas Judd, Thomas Thompson. Deputy to CT General Court 1647-1655, 1660. Largest house-lot in Farmington (15 acres) granted as inducement to build mill. "Hart's Farm" in Avon still bears his name; "Hart's Ford" tradition for Hartford. LAND DESCENT: Thomas Hart (son) → Josiah Hart → daughter married Roger Hooker → Thomas Hart Hooker (only surviving child) — Hooker-Hart land connection documented. HOOKER CONNECTION: Grandson Capt. John Hart (X00031): three sons each married a daughter of John Hooker (H00030), Thomas Hooker's grandson. m.(1) [Elizabeth/Unknown] — name not recorded; d. by ~1678 Farmington. m.(2) Margaret, widow of Arthur Smith (d.1655) and Joseph Nash (d.1678); admitted church Farmington Mar 17, 1690/1; d. 1693 Farmington. (EH section on Stephen Hart; Hart Family Genealogy) EASTER EGG: Stephen Hart — deacon of Rev. Thomas Hooker's church at Newtowne (Cambridge), Massachusetts; followed Hooker to Hartford and then to Farmington; one of the Seven Pillars of the founding of Farmington church (1652); his descendants married Hooker descendants in the next generation
CC NOTE [H00001]: Hart was Hooker's deacon at Cambridge (Newtowne) and followed him in the Great Migration to Hartford in 1636, where he became an original proprietor. [Migrated from top-level anecdotes]: {"the_origin_of_hartford": "There is a tradition that Hartford was named after Stephen Hart. When the company crossed the Connecticut River, Hart discovered a ford in the river where the water was low. The settlement at that crossing became known as 'Hart's Ford' \u2014 and the transition to 'Hartford' was a simple one. This tradition, recorded in 1910, cannot be confirmed but is part of the town's founding lore. This tradition was confirmed in verse by his descendant Almira Hart Lincoln Phelps (H00598) in a poem c. 1871: 'Yes, Hartford has a charm \u2014 its name derived, / As legends say, from Stephen Hart, who lived / Where joins the \"little river\" to the \"great,\" / And Hart's-ford may be seen on ancient maps.' The poem was read publicly by Dr. Henry Barnard.", "harts_farm_and_farmington": "Stephen Hart purchased a large tract of land on the border of what is now Avon CT, known as Hart's Farm. His house lot on the west side of Main Street in Farmington was 15 acres \u2014 granted on condition he continue running the mill on the property, originally erected by the Bumsons. He was especially active in the settlement of Farmington and served as the town's first deacon. Represented Farmington at the General Court for 15 sessions 1647-1655 and once in 1660. Died March 1682 age 77."} CHILDREN REMOVED 10 Aug 2026 on Sam's instruction — both sons deleted outright: X01887 John
