narrative_blocks.header: He was at Hartford before Hooker
narrative_blocks.body: Stephen was one of the Adventurers, twenty-five men who went ahead under John Steele in October 1635 to look over the land at Hartford, and one of sixteen already living there when Hooker's company came. Two years later he fought in the Pequot War.

narrative_blocks.header: Tradition: Hartford was named for him
narrative_blocks.body: Tradition holds that when Hooker's company crossed the Connecticut River in 1636, Hart found a ford where the water was low — making 'Hart's Ford' the seed of the city's name. His descendant Almira Hart Lincoln Phelps put it in verse around 1871.

narrative_blocks.header: He found Farmington from Talcott Mountain
narrative_blocks.body: The story goes that Stephen was hunting on Talcott Mountain when he looked down on the Farmington valley, its meadows planted by the Tunxis. He led the settlement among them and bought the tract toward Avon still called Hart's Farm.

narrative_blocks.header: One of the seven pillars
narrative_blocks.body: When the Farmington church was gathered in 1652, Stephen stood with Roger Newton, John Cole, John Bronson, Robert Porter, Thomas Judd and Thomas Thompson as its seven pillars, and became its first deacon. He sat in the General Court fifteen times.

narrative_blocks.header: A Farmington house lot five times the others
narrative_blocks.body: Stephen's fifteen-acre house lot in Farmington village, opposite the meeting-house, was four or five times the size of any other, granted on condition he keep the mill turning. It passed down to his great-great-great-grandson Thomas Hart Hooker, who sold it.

narrative_blocks.header: The fire that took his son in 1666
narrative_blocks.body: In December 1666 fire destroyed his son John's house at Farmington, killing John, his wife and two of their three children; John Jr. was tending stock at Avon that night. John kept the town's records, and they burned that night too.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandchildren married three Hooker daughters
narrative_blocks.body: His grandson Capt. John Hart had three sons who each married a daughter of John Hooker — Thomas Hooker's grandson. Three Harts and three Hookers married in a single generation, knitting the families together.

people.prominent_name_reason: General Selah Hart (1732-1806) — Brigadier General, Connecticut Militia. Lt. Col. 15th Regiment under Col. Fisher Gay; captured at Battle of Long Island Aug 27, 1776. Held prisoner ~2 years while wife Ruth knew not if he lived. Promoted to Colonel in captivity after Gay's death. Appointed Brigadier General, 6th Brigade of Militia 1779. Delegate to State Convention for ratification of US Constitution, 1788. Post-war: magistrate, constable, deacon, treasurer, general of CT Militia for many years. "Patron Saint of Connecticut" per later sources. Monument in Farmington Cemetery. Slave owner: Jack and Pharaoh Hart. Pharaoh served at Germantown (1777) and Monmouth (1778); Hart demanded all of Pharaoh's army wages as compensation for freeing him. Jack freed voluntarily at 21 without payment. See: https://digitalfarmington.org/digital-farmington-project/selah-hart-saint-and-sinner/

political_offices.office: Delegate, CT State Convention for US Constitution Ratification

enslaved_persons.name: Jack
enslaved_persons.description: Taken as a very young child. Freed voluntarily at age 21 without payment. Hart told him: "The law would give me four years more of your service, but I think you have the right to be free." Received education and clothing better than average white lads in the vicinity.
enslaved_persons.source: History of New Britain; Berlin slavery article 2022

enslaved_persons.name: Pharaoh
enslaved_persons.description: Allowed to enlist in Continental Army for 3 years on condition of paying Hart a portion of wages for freedom. Fought at Battle of Germantown PA (1777) and Monmouth NJ (1778). At end of service, Hart claimed ALL wages — not just a portion — citing his own imprisonment debt. Pharaoh had no choice but to pay. 35 years later, both Pharaoh and Selah Hart received pensions. In 1777, Selah sat in a British prison while Pharaoh fought for American freedom.
enslaved_persons.source: Digital Farmington / Menapace 2022; Berlin slavery article

people.research_notes:
Only child Mary (H00556) died young. Adopted nephew Cyprian Hart (H00562, EH #562), son of his brother Nathaniel Hart No. 2 (H00274) and Martha Norton (X01029) — Cyprian's father died Oct 13, 1773 when the boy was age 4. Selah and Ruth Cole Hart raised Cyprian in their Kensington homestead and made him heir; Cyprian m. Lucy Hooker (H00537) Dec 24, 1795 and predeceased Selah by 14 weeks (Mar 1, 1806). After Selah's death the homestead passed through Cyprian's six children; his widow Lucy and Selah's widow Ruth Cole Hart kept the house together 38 years. Family farm was in area known as "Hart Quarter" in early Farmington maps. Father Nathaniel's father (John Hart Sr.) was one of first settlers in 1635, purchasing land from Tunxis Indians. See also: arw.fandom.com/wiki/Selah_Hart
BERLIN-PECK DETAILS: Captured Sep 15, 1776 retreating from NYC; held prisoner ~2 years. Freed enslaved Jack at 21: "The law would give me four years more of your service, but I think you have the right to be free." Allowed enslaved Pharaoh to enlist and earn freedom — Pharaoh fought Germantown 1777 and Monmouth 1778; both Hart and Pharaoh received federal pensions 35 years later; Pharaoh was in New Jersey in 1818. Nov 10, 1789: Washington breakfasted in Berlin; Hart greeted him as "too full for utterance." Wife Ruth Cole (1743-1844) outlived him 38 years, died ~age 101. CONTEXT: Jeremiah Wadsworth (husband of Hooker descendant Mehitable Russell) was the commissary general who coordinated supplies for both armies — his network included Connecticut officers like Hart. Washington-Rochambeau route passed through Hartford, the same theater as the Berlin/Farmington Hooker-descendant soldiers.
CC NOTE [X01936]: In 1775, Gen. Selah Hart was appointed by the General Court to manage the Kensington lead mine on the Mill River — critical to the Revolution's lead supply. Eighty years later, James Gates Percival, as Connecticut state geologist, surveyed the same mine, writing: 'I found ore there... it needs to be tested.' The mine was co-owned by Percival's father and half a mile from his childhood home. Two Hooker descendants, one vein of lead. [Migrated from marriage.spouse_notes (spouse X01027)]: b. Feb 18, 1731/2 Kensington. Daughter of Stephen Cole and Abigail Hart Cole. Died before 1763. [Migrated from marriage.spouse_notes (spouse X01028)]: b. Oct 29, 1742 Kensington; d. Jan 15, 1844 age 101 years, 2 months, 16 days — "the oldest person that ever lived in Kensington." Daughter of Matthew Cole and Mary Newell Cole. [Migrated from top-level military]: True [Stage 6Y-253 correction]: Previous research note incorrectly stated Cyprian Hart was 'son of Asahel and Ruth Hooker Strong' — that conflated Cyprian Hart (H00562, Selah's nephew via brother Nathaniel Hart No. 2) with Cyprian Strong (H00299, son of Asahel Strong Jr. and Ruth Hooker Strong). Two completely different people. EH explicitly identifies Selah's adopted nephew as the son of Nathaniel Hart No. 2. [Stage 6Y-254 correction]: Jonathan and Thomas Hart were previously listed as Selah's children — corrected. They are Selah's first cousins, sons of his uncle Dea. Ebenezer Hart and Elizabeth Lawrence. EH explicitly notes Selah's only child by Mary Cole was Mary (H00556). Reparented to X00119. (Selah Hart had no surviving issue of his own — adopted nephew Cyprian Hart H00562 carried the line.)
[Stage 6Y-264 NB#2 header trim]: 'Washington breakfasted with him — he was 'too full for utterance'' → 'Washington breakfasted with him'. REBUILD 081226. The old NB4 carried category 'moral_complexity', which is not in the enum — the block is now 'law' and every block is labelled. CAPTURE DATE CONFLICT: this card said 15 September 1776 'retreating from New York City' (Kip's Bay); the supplied accounts say 27 August 1776 at the Battle of Long Island, and a family account says he was cut off when Washington evacuated New York, which points back to September. The card now says only 'the fighting for New York in 1776'. Militia service: ensign 1762, lieutenant 1763, captain 1764; lieutenant-colonel of the 15th Regiment of Militia under Col. Fisher Gay, May 1776; colonel in Gay's place after Gay died; freed in an officer's exchange; brigadier-general of the Sixth Brigade 1779. Delegate to the state ratifying convention for the Constitution, 1788. Born 23 May 1732 at Kensington Society to Nathaniel Hart and Abigail Hooker; grandfather Stephen Hart was Farmington's first deacon and the family bought its land from the Tunxis in 1635. Married Mary Cole 4 March 1756 and Ruth Cole 22 December 1763. His uncles John and Thomas Hart and his mother's kinsman Samuel Hooker also held slaves — Farmington elites commonly did. Christopher Menapace, 'Selah Hart: Saint and Sinner' (Dr. Katherine Hermes, 2016) is the source for the Hart Quarter, the offices, and the reading of the Pharaoh bargain. OFF THE CARD FOR ROOM: Jack and Pharaoh both eventually went free, Jack without paying; both Hart and Pharaoh drew federal pensions thirty-five years later and Pharaoh was in New Jersey by 1818; his widow Ruth Cole outlived him thirty-eight years and died at about 101.

narrative_blocks.header: Farmington called him a patron saint
narrative_blocks.body: He was Farmington's man — constable, magistrate, treasurer, deacon and finally brigadier-general — from a family so old there that early maps label the southwest of town the Hart Quarter. A monument there names him an officer of the Revolution. He also owned two men, Jack and Pharaoh.

narrative_blocks.header: Promoted to colonel while in a British prison
narrative_blocks.body: He was taken in the fighting for New York in 1776 and held nearly two years, most of it with his wife not knowing whether he was alive. His own colonel died that autumn and Connecticut promoted him into the dead man's place while he sat in prison.

narrative_blocks.header: He won the captured militia their pay
narrative_blocks.body: Connecticut had no rule for paying a militia officer taken prisoner, so their families went without. In May 1777, from captivity, he petitioned the General Assembly for himself and other destitute officers, and won them the same pay as the Line.

narrative_blocks.header: He let Jack go four years early
narrative_blocks.body: The law would have given him four more years of Jack's labour. He told him so and let him go: ‘The law would give me four years more of your service, but I think you have the right to be free.’

narrative_blocks.header: Pharaoh bought his freedom with his army pay
narrative_blocks.body: Pharaoh was to earn his freedom with three years in the Continental Army, a share of his army pay going to Hart in compensation. Pharaoh fought at Germantown and Monmouth; when the term ended, Hart — in debt from his own captivity — took the whole of it.

narrative_blocks.header: The morning Washington stopped for breakfast
narrative_blocks.body: On 10 November 1789 President Washington broke his tour of Connecticut to breakfast at Berlin, and Hart greeted him. Afterwards he could only record that he had been ‘too full for utterance.’

narrative_blocks.header: A late-night trip to the cellar killed him
narrative_blocks.body: Late one October evening in 1773 he went down to his cellar — for beer, it was supposed — and was seized by a fit on the stairs, pitching forward and striking his head fatally against the edge of a board. His wife, unwell, had gone to bed early and did not know he was missing until morning, finding him only when she went down to the cellar herself. A coroner's jury ruled it accidental death.

narrative_blocks.header: Lieutenant while his brother Selah was a General
narrative_blocks.detail: The Hart family of Kensington had deep military roots: their father Nathaniel Hart (I00028) had married Abigail Hooker in 1719 in one of the three simultaneous Hart-Hooker marriages. A third brother, Rev. Asahel Hart (H00276, Yale 1764), became the first pastor of North Canaan Congregational Church — the three Hart brothers who survived to adulthood representing military service, Congregationalist ministry, and civic life respectively. Noadiah was appointed administrator of the estate of Jonathan Hurlbut Jr. in October 1761, confirming his standing in the Kensington community. (EH 1909; Hart Genealogy 1948)
narrative_blocks.body: Noadiah Hart served as a Lieutenant in the American Revolutionary War while his older brother Selah Hart rose to General in the Connecticut Militia — captured by the British in September 1776 during the New York retreat. Both were sons of Nathaniel Hart × Abigail Hooker, 4th-generation descendants of Thomas Hooker. Noadiah served through the war, became a Deacon in the Harwinton church by 1804, and died in Southington in 1817 at 80.

narrative_blocks.header: Deacon of Harwinton church; lived to 80
narrative_blocks.body: After the war, he became Deacon of the church in Harwinton in 1804, removed to Southington, and lived in his daughter Velina's household near her mill — a site later covered by the "Plant Ponds." He died in 1817 at age 80, the longest-lived of the three brothers.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale 1764 — first pastor of North Canaan
narrative_blocks.body: He graduated Yale in 1764, organized the North Canaan Congregational Church on December 5, 1769, and was installed as its first pastor on March 14, 1770. He died unmarried on June 28, 1775 — at 33 years old, just as the Revolutionary War was beginning, two of his brothers about to serve.

narrative_blocks.body: Her first husband Thomas Hollister of Kensington died 1748 leaving her a young widow. Her second husband Josiah Beckley died 1757; her third husband Capt. Ephraim Hollister was Thomas's second cousin, returning her to the same Hollister family.

narrative_blocks.header: Uncle John Hooker became guardian of her son
narrative_blocks.body: After her first husband died in 1748, her father Lieut. Samuel Hart Sr. was appointed guardian of her young son Abel Hollister. When Samuel Hart died, her uncle John Hooker assumed Abel's guardianship — bringing the boy under direct Hooker family care.

narrative_blocks.header: Third husband buried apart from his wives
narrative_blocks.body: Capt. Ephraim Hollister outlived her by four years, dying March 3, 1804 in Berlin, Connecticut, age 79. He was buried in Maple Cemetery — apart from both his wives.

CC NOTE [H00279]: Mary Hart married Dr. Joseph Welles of Wethersfield — almost certainly a descendant of Gov. Thomas Welles (1590-1660), 4th Governor of Connecticut Colony and Hartford founder. Thomas Welles arrived Hartford 1636, the same year Thomas Hooker led his congregation there. They were contemporaries and fellow architects of the Connecticut colony. Welles held land in Hartford from the February 1639/40 inventory; served as Treasurer, Secretary, Deputy Governor, and Governor. A marriage between Mary Hart (great-granddaughter of Thomas Hooker's son Samuel) and a Welles descendant unites two of Hartford's founding families in the third generation of American-born descendants. Contact: Welles Family Association, wellesfamily.org (founded 1936, published 3-volume genealogy through 2015, Barbara Jean Mathews CG FASG). Action: Submit Hooker-Welles connection to WFA when project launches. [Migrated from marriage.spouse_notes (spouse X00239)]: Physician of considerable note and extensive practice in Kensington. d. Kensington CT Nov 14, 1793. Descended from Gov. Thomas Welles (1590-1660) of Wethersfield — 4th Governor of Connecticut Colony (1655, 1658); Hartford founder; arrived New England 1635 from Tidmington, Worcestershire, England. Specific line through Thomas Welles not yet confirmed in Welles genealogy; Wethersfield geography and generation strongly suggest Gov. Thomas Welles descent.

narrative_blocks.header: Married into the Welles family of Wethersfield
narrative_blocks.body: In 1751 she married Dr. Joseph Welles of Wethersfield — a physician of considerable note and extensive practice in Kensington. His Welles family descended from Gov. Thomas Welles, 4th Governor of Connecticut Colony and a Hartford founder alongside Thomas Hooker.

narrative_blocks.header: Marriage united two Hartford founding families
narrative_blocks.body: Her marriage joined the Hooker line (through her great-grandfather Samuel Hooker) and the Welles line (through her husband's descent from Gov. Thomas Welles). Both Thomas Hooker and Thomas Welles arrived in Hartford in 1636, building the Connecticut Colony together.

narrative_blocks.header: Three brothers married three sisters
narrative_blocks.body: Three Hart brothers married three Hooker sisters at Farmington between 1719 and 1725. Every child of those three marriages, herself included, was first cousin to the rest twice over - once through a father and once through a mother.

narrative_blocks.header: Died the same day her widower remarried
narrative_blocks.body: She died on December 24, 1778 in Kensington at age forty-seven. Her husband Gideon Porter married Hannah, the widow of Avery Heath, that same day.

narrative_blocks.header: Wounded at Saratoga, September 1777
narrative_blocks.body: Serving as a lieutenant in General Wolcott's detachment, Samuel Hart was wounded at Saratoga on September 19, 1777, and two years later led the Berlin company that turned out at the New Haven alarm.

narrative_blocks.header: A thinker who could not speak unwritten

narrative_blocks.header: A posthumous son who built on Glen Street
narrative_blocks.body: Born in 1736, some weeks after his father's death, he grew up to build a house about 1759 on the corner of Sheldon and Glen Streets in Kensington — a house that still stands. He and his wife Elizabeth were admitted to the Kensington church within a few years of their marriage.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother and his daughter-in-law were both Hookers
narrative_blocks.body: His mother was Sarah Hooker, and his eldest son Matthew married Urania Hooker — so the family met the Hooker line on both sides of him. His daughter Elizabeth married Dr. James Percival and became the mother of the poet James Gates Percival.

narrative_blocks.header: Late in life he left for New York
narrative_blocks.body: Rooted in Kensington for decades, he and Elizabeth moved in old age to the New York frontier — Whitestown or De Ruyter — where he died in 1811. He left the Glen Street house behind, but it outlasted him by two centuries.

narrative_blocks.header: He cast bullets from the Kensington lead
narrative_blocks.body: He served the Revolution twice over — a private in Captain Selah Hart's company, later a corporal under Captain Stoddard — and did more for it at home, running lead from the mine near Kensington into bullets for the Continental Army.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandson bought the house he built
narrative_blocks.body: When he left for the New York frontier around 1800 he sold the Glen Street house to a neighbor. Thirteen years later it was bought by Oswin Percival — his daughter's son — and in 1824 passed to the Moores, whose family kept it for generations.

open_questions.notes: EH notes Sir John Standley was an officer in Cromwell's army and that the family was then an old one with no known connection to the famous English Stanley family. Research at Farmington Historical Society and English army records may confirm.

narrative_blocks.header: He marched against the Pequots at age thirteen
narrative_blocks.body: John Stanley came to Hartford as a boy in his uncle's care. In 1637, only thirteen, he joined the colony's expedition against the Pequots, the year after the settlers arrived.

narrative_blocks.header: He served thirty-seven years as a deputy
narrative_blocks.body: From 1659 to 1696 Stanley represented Farmington at the General Court almost without a break, one of the longest terms of service in the colony's records.

narrative_blocks.header: He built the house that became Farmington's museum
narrative_blocks.body: Around 1665 Stanley built a home on the Farmington street for his second wife. Long known as the Stanley-Whitman House, it survives today as the town's museum.

narrative_blocks.header: He rose to captain in King Philip's War
narrative_blocks.body: During King Philip's War Stanley served as a lieutenant and then captain, the rank that gave him the name by which he was always known, Capt. John Stanley.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the same day as his sister
narrative_blocks.body: On December 5, 1645, John Stanley married Sarah Scott at Hartford. The same day his sixteen-year-old sister Ruth married Isaac Moore, and both young couples settled together at Farmington.

narrative_blocks.header: Farmington militia captain his entire life
narrative_blocks.body: He held the rank of Captain in the Connecticut militia and was known by that title for the rest of his life. He spent his entire life in Farmington — born there February 15, 1704/5 and dying there December 19, 1764, in his 60th year.

narrative_blocks.header: The big chair — militia saluted him sitting
narrative_blocks.body: In later years he became so corpulent he could not attend to business. On fine days a large chair was placed in the front yard near the door, where he sat smoking his pipe and visiting with passersby. When the local militia paraded, it was customary for them to march around by his house and salute him in the big chair.

narrative_blocks.header: Heir to the famous Farmington Hooker Elm
narrative_blocks.body: He was the son of Hon. John Hooker — the Farmington judge whose famous Hooker Elm gave the town its hospitality tradition. His grandfather Rev. Samuel Hooker had ministered Farmington's church for thirty years; his great-great-grandfather Rev. Thomas Hooker founded Hartford.

narrative_blocks.header: His signature sits on a Tunxis deed
narrative_blocks.body: In November 1754 two Tunxis men sold a few acres west of Pequabuck Meadow — half an acre and six more, for thirteen pounds old tenor — and his name is signed to the deed. The Tunxis were the Native people on whose land Farmington itself had been laid out, so a Hooker's signature on their conveyance marks a quiet meeting of two histories. His father, John Hooker, had certified a similar Tunxis sale at Farmington two decades before.

narrative_blocks.body: In a single ten-day span — September 6 to 15, 1736 — three of her young children died: Lois and Ruth on the same day, then Elnathan nine days later. The cluster strongly suggests an epidemic moving through Farmington.

narrative_blocks.body: After Capt. Asahel Strong's death she married Solomon Whitman, who was Town Clerk at 92 and made a pair of shoes on his 90th birthday. He died at 93 from over-fatigue settling a fence dispute between two brothers.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept the Hooker Elm's famous hospitality alive
narrative_blocks.body: He inherited the Farmington estate and the famous Hooker Elm from his father John. He was called a thorough gentleman of the old school, and he kept up the hospitality those elm gatherings were known for.

narrative_blocks.header: Favorite son and keeper of family history
narrative_blocks.body: He accompanied his father John on official journeys around the Colony and brought his first wife home to the family house. What he knew of the family's English origins came from John, reckoned the best informed of Thomas Hooker's grandsons.

narrative_blocks.header: Three sisters married Hart brothers — knot tied
narrative_blocks.body: His sisters Abigail, Mary, and Sarah each married a son of Capt. John Hart between 1719 and 1725. Through those three marriages, Roger found himself simultaneously brother-in-law to Nathaniel, Samuel, and Matthew Hart — the Hart and Hooker families fully intertwined.

narrative_blocks.header: His granddaughter Abigail married Samuel Talcott
narrative_blocks.body: His son Thomas Hooker fathered Abigail Hooker, who married Samuel Talcott of Hartford. The marriage merged the Hooker surname into the Talcott line — a transition that defines several gen 6+ branches.

narrative_blocks.header: She opened the school in her front room
narrative_blocks.body: Her father died in 1813 leaving debts, and the next year, at twenty-six, she took girls into her own house at Middlebury and taught them in the front room. The school stayed in that room for five years.

narrative_blocks.header: Ninety girls in September, three hundred by 1831
narrative_blocks.body: Troy raised the money for a building and the seminary opened in September 1821 with ninety girls. By 1831 there were more than three hundred of them at mathematics and science, sixteen years before Mount Holyoke existed.

narrative_blocks.header: Not the satellites of men
narrative_blocks.body: The New York legislature would not answer her Plan of 1819, and some members held that a course of study for girls was contrary to God’s will. She had written: “we too are primary existencies… not the satellites of men.”

narrative_blocks.header: She read her nephew’s college books at home
narrative_blocks.body: She married John Willard at twenty-two — a Middlebury physician twenty-eight years older, with four children already. His nephew boarded with them while at the college, and going through the boy’s textbooks is where she saw the gap.

narrative_blocks.header: She schooled a dozen of her own relations
narrative_blocks.body: She brought a dozen Berlin relatives to Troy across the years and paid for their schooling out of her own pocket. Her younger sister Almira came in 1823, newly widowed, and taught at the seminary for eight years.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine months, and five years to undo it
narrative_blocks.body: Long a widow, she married Dr. Christopher Yates in 1838 and went to Boston with him. They were apart inside nine months. The decree came in 1843, and she took her first husband’s name back and kept it to the end.

narrative_blocks.header: The hymn outlasted the schoolbooks
narrative_blocks.body: Her geographies sold for decades and the atlas she made with Woodbridge was the first of its kind in the country; the profits of her travel book paid for a girls’ school in Athens. What lasted was a poem she wrote at sea in 1839.

notable.notable_blurb: Botanist, educator, Emma Willard's sister

narrative_blocks.header: Her botany textbook sold a quarter-million copies
narrative_blocks.body: Her 1829 Familiar Lectures on Botany went through nine editions in ten years and became one of the most widely used American textbooks of the century, teaching a generation their first science — many of them girls who had never been offered any. It made her one of the country's best-known science educators.

narrative_blocks.header: The book told girls to press their flowers
narrative_blocks.body: Every pupil was set the same task: gather the plants, dry them flat, and mount them in a book with their proper names — a herbarium, a bound collection of the real things rather than pictures of them. Emily Dickinson made hers at Amherst Academy and kept it the rest of her life.

narrative_blocks.header: The second woman elected to the AAAS
narrative_blocks.body: In 1859 she became the second woman ever admitted to the American Association for the Advancement of Science, after the astronomer Maria Mitchell. Her textbooks in botany, chemistry, and geology carried science to readers few schools then reached.

narrative_blocks.header: She ran a leading Maryland school for girls
narrative_blocks.body: For fifteen years she was principal of the Patapsco Female Institute at Ellicott's Mills, Maryland, one of the finest girls' schools of its day. She built the curriculum on science, mathematics and natural history, and aimed it at turning out qualified teachers.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at thirty, she published as Mrs. Lincoln
narrative_blocks.body: Simeon Lincoln, who edited the Connecticut Mirror at Hartford, died in 1823 after six years of marriage, and she went to her sister's seminary at Troy and taught there eight years — the botany book went out under the name Almira H. Lincoln. She married John Phelps in 1831, outlived him too, and was still writing in her eighties.

narrative_blocks.header: With her sister she opened science to women
narrative_blocks.body: Taught by her elder sister Emma Willard, the pioneer of American women's education, she worked at Emma's Troy Female Seminary before making her own name. Together the Hart sisters made rigorous learning respectable for American women.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran Hartford's Federalist newspaper
narrative_blocks.body: A printer by trade and a New Britain native, he and a partner acquired the Connecticut Mirror — Hartford's staunchly Federalist weekly — in 1818, and he edited it through the last years of the party's decline. He gave up the paper in 1823.

narrative_blocks.header: His early death launched his widow's career
narrative_blocks.body: He died in 1823 at only thirty-three, leaving his wife Almira Hart a young widow. Her grief turned her toward the writing and teaching that made her one of America's best-known women educators.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught at his wife's Maryland girls' school

military_service.notes: Medal of Honor, Laurel Hill, May 8, 1864 (awarded March 30, 1898).

narrative_blocks.header: Rode to the head of a breaking charge
narrative_blocks.body: At Laurel Hill on May 8, 1864, with his column faltering under close artillery fire, Phelps rode to its head and led the assault to within feet of the Confederate works — where he fell severely wounded and was captured. His citation says he placed himself conspicuously in front of the troops.

narrative_blocks.header: The Medal of Honor came thirty-four years late
narrative_blocks.body: The charge was 1864; the Medal of Honor arrived March 30, 1898, when Phelps was a sixty-four-year-old Baltimore judge. He had passed through four political parties and three careers in the interval.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother wrote the nation’s science textbooks
narrative_blocks.body: Phelps was the son of Almira Hart Lincoln Phelps, whose botany and chemistry textbooks taught a generation of American students, and the nephew of Emma Hart Willard, the pioneer of women’s education. The family’s Hart line runs back to Farmington.

narrative_blocks.header: One brother decorated, the other outlawed
narrative_blocks.body: He won his Medal of Honor leading a charge at Spotsylvania; his older half-brother, General John Wolcott Phelps, fought the same war on different ground — arming fugitive slaves at New Orleans in 1862 until the Confederacy branded him an outlaw and he resigned in protest. One brother the Union decorated; the other it was not yet ready for.

narrative_blocks.header: They waived the age limit to keep him
narrative_blocks.body: He was elected to the Baltimore supreme bench on a reform ticket in 1882 and returned to it in 1897, each time for fifteen years. In 1903 the Maryland legislature passed a special act setting aside the constitutional retirement age of seventy so that he could stay where he was.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught equity for twenty-three years
narrative_blocks.body: From 1884 to 1907 he was professor of equity at the University of Maryland law school while sitting on the bench. Princeton gave him an honorary doctorate of laws in his last year of teaching, fifty-six years after his first degree from it.

narrative_blocks.header: Captured at sea, he came home to heal
narrative_blocks.body: John Willard served on a ship’s crew at the outbreak of the Revolution, was captured by the British, and after his release became quartermaster of a Connecticut regiment. Only after the war did he train as a physician and open a practice in Middlebury, Vermont.

narrative_blocks.header: Jefferson made him a federal marshal
narrative_blocks.body: A committed Democratic-Republican, Willard backed Thomas Jefferson in 1800 and was rewarded with appointment as United States Marshal for Vermont, an office he held from 1801 to 1811. He succeeded Jabez G. Fitch and was followed by David Robinson.

narrative_blocks.header: A stolen bank key nearly ruined him
narrative_blocks.body: As a director of the Vermont State Bank, Willard was held liable when $28,000 vanished in 1812, drawing liens against his property. The money had been taken with a duplicate key; though the thief was eventually exposed and the liens lifted, his finances never recovered and he died insolvent.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the business behind a famous school
narrative_blocks.body: When the bank scandal threatened the family, his third wife Emma opened a boarding school for young women, and John became its business manager. Together they moved the seminary from Middlebury to Waterford and finally to Troy, New York, in 1822.

narrative_blocks.header: Three wives across one eventful life
narrative_blocks.body: Willard first married Esther Wilcox, who died in 1788, then Mindwell Meigs, widow of Thaddeus Frisbie. In 1809 he married Emma Hart of Middlebury, the educator whose school would carry the Willard name into history.

narrative_blocks.header: His nephew judged New York from the bench
narrative_blocks.body: Willard’s nephew and namesake, John Willard (1792–1862), became a prominent New York jurist, serving as a justice of the state Supreme Court and briefly on the Court of Appeals. The two Willards, uncle and nephew, both rose from Guilford, Connecticut, to public prominence in the North.

narrative_blocks.header: He grew up inside his mother’s seminary
narrative_blocks.body: John Hart Willard was eleven when his parents, Dr. John and Emma Willard, brought the female seminary to Troy in 1821 at the invitation of the city’s leading citizens. He had been born in Middlebury, Vermont, in 1810, the only child of his father’s marriage to Emma.

narrative_blocks.header: Schooled by the best, then West Point
narrative_blocks.body: His early education came from some of the country’s finest instructors, including the father of Bishop Huntington at Hadley, Mr. Adams of Bennington, and Capt. Partridge of Middletown. He completed his studies at the West Point military academy, which he entered in 1826.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried the school into a second generation
narrative_blocks.body: When Emma Willard remarried and stepped back in 1838, John Hart Willard and his wife took charge of the Troy Female Seminary. He remained one of the city’s best-known citizens until his death in 1883 at seventy-three.

narrative_blocks.header: His shop stood opposite the meeting house
narrative_blocks.body: He farmed at Berlin and kept a blacksmith’s shop beside his house, on what is now Berlin Street in New Britain, across from where the Methodist church was afterwards built. He sold ten acres of it to Doctor Smalley in 1788.

narrative_blocks.header: Ensign at forty-two, captain at fifty-two
narrative_blocks.body: He was made ensign of the fifteenth company of the sixth Connecticut regiment in May 1749, lieutenant in May 1752, and captain in May 1759. He was Captain John Hinsdale for the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: He moderated the meeting in the new house
narrative_blocks.body: He sat on the standing committee of the Kensington church from 1766 and was a constituent member in 1775, and when the second meeting was held in their new meeting house it was he who took the chair.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought a new farm at seventy-four
narrative_blocks.body: In March 1781 he took over John Richards’s homestead at New Britain — seventy acres with the old Skinner house on it, once the Deacon Josiah Lee farm. He was seventy-four, and he moved there and joined the First church.

narrative_blocks.header: He named two sons John
narrative_blocks.body: The first John was born in 1734 and died at nine in 1743; the second was born in 1749 and given the same name. Three daughters and four sons in all, and that first boy was the only one who did not grow up.

narrative_blocks.header: His granddaughters opened schools for women
narrative_blocks.body: Lydia married Captain Samuel Hart in 1770. Two of their daughters were Emma Hart Willard, who founded the seminary at Troy, and Almira Hart Phelps, who wrote the botany textbooks and was the second woman elected to the AAAS.

narrative_blocks.header: Three generations at the same trade
narrative_blocks.body: He was a blacksmith, his son Elijah was a blacksmith at New Britain, and his great-grandson was Elihu Burritt — the Learned Blacksmith, who taught himself thirty languages at the anvil and carried the peace movement across the Atlantic.

narrative_blocks.body: She had seven between 1734 and 1749 — John, Elizabeth, Theodore, Lucy, Elijah, Lydia, and a second John. The first John died at nine in 1743, and his name was given again to the boy born six years after him.

narrative_blocks.header: Taken into Kensington church as a bride
narrative_blocks.body: She was a daughter of Nathaniel Cole of Hartford and married John Hinsdale there in November 1733. They were received into the church at Kensington soon after, and she kept to Berlin the rest of her life.

narrative_blocks.header: Grandmother of the Willard and Phelps sisters
narrative_blocks.body: Her daughter Lydia married Captain Samuel Hart in 1770, and two of that marriage were Emma Hart Willard and Almira Hart Phelps, who between them did as much for the schooling of American women as anyone of their century.

career.notes: 47-year pastorate. Original parish embraced all of Hinsdale plus Vernon (later separated when Vermont became a state). Continued as nominal pastor and officiated weddings and funerals into old age.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter brought the Hookers to Hinsdale
narrative_blocks.body: Bunker Gay had five children with Abigail Prentice, and all but his daughter Abigail died young and unmarried. Her 1789 marriage to Seth Hooker brought Seth onto the Gay farm, known afterward as the Hooker place.

narrative_blocks.header: His Gay middle name passed down five generations
narrative_blocks.body: Through his daughter Abigail's marriage to Seth Hooker, the Gay name entered the Hooker line as a middle name. Great-grandson Charles Gay, great-great-grandson Robert Gay, and four-greats-grandson Michael Gay all carried it forward into the twentieth century.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-seven years as Hinsdale's first pastor
narrative_blocks.body: Bunker Gay came to Hinsdale in 1763 as the first settled pastor of its Congregational church, with a parish that took in the whole town and Vernon across the river. When Vermont became a state and Vernon a separate town, his church was left weak in members and property, but he stayed its pastor for life and preached until old age stopped him.

narrative_blocks.header: Published the Jemima Howe captivity narrative, 1792
narrative_blocks.body: His Hinsdale neighbor Jemima Howe had been carried off to Quebec by Abenaki raiders in 1755 and spent years in French captivity before her ransom. He recorded her oral testimony and published it as 'A Genuine and Correct Account of the Captivity, Sufferings & Deliverance of Mrs. Jemima Howe.'

narrative_blocks.header: Dedham roots in the 1636 founding wave
narrative_blocks.body: His great-grandfather John Gay was an original proprietor of Dedham, Massachusetts, in 1636, the year Thomas Hooker founded Hartford.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Raised her six children on the Gay homestead at Hinsdale; buried beside her husband on the property's cemetery.

narrative_blocks.header: Buried five of six children in fifteen years
narrative_blocks.body: Between 1773 and 1788 she lost five of her six children — Bunker Jr. at eleven, Calvin at six, John at thirteen, Henry at twenty-six, and Sally as an infant — to a series of family tragedies in frontier Hinsdale. Daughter Abigail alone survived, marrying Seth Hooker in 1789 and carrying the line forward.

people.research_notes: [Phase 8 enrichment]: Per EH 1393 + Wikipedia: b. Jul 5, 1791 Charlestown NH; m. Oct 23, 1816 Mary Daggett (X02247); d. Mar 17, 1885 Hinsdale NH age 93. Farmer at Hinsdale on the farm that had been his father Seth's and grandfather John's. 'Hale and hearty old man' — past 80 went twice to California with his children. 11 children built H02700-H02710. Most famous son: Henry Clay Hooker (H02705), Arizona cattle king. [Batch 2 enrichment]: Three of Henry Sr's sons rose to extraordinary prominence in 19th-century California, making this one of the most consequential single-family productions of the post-gold-rush American West: Charles Gay Hooker (H02703, San Francisco hardware merchant who came in spring 1851, partnered with brother John Delos in Hooker & Co. at 117-119 California Street), Henry Clay Hooker (H02705, Arizona's cattle king at Sierra Bonita Ranch from 1872), and John Daggett Hooker (H02709, donor of the 100-inch Hooker Telescope at Mount Wilson Observatory — which Hubble used to discover the expanding universe). All three began life on the Hinsdale NH family farm and made the westward migration in their twenties. [DAGGETT-PATTERN FLAG 2026]: Henry Hooker married Mary Daggett (X02247) on October 23, 1816. FOUR YEARS earlier (May 24, 1812), his distant Hooker cousin Edward Hooker (H00630, gen 6, Farmington CT branch) had married another Daggett woman — Elisabeth Daggett (X02036) daughter of Henry Daggett Esq of Attleboro MA. Two Hooker descendants from different geographic branches (Farmington CT + Hinsdale NH) marrying Daggett women within 4 years. The two Daggett brides may share common Watertown MA Daggett ancestry — see X02036 + X02247 research notes for full investigation. NOT formally a cousin_marriage (brides aren't Hooker bloodline) but a striking surname-recurrence pattern worth flagging.

narrative_blocks.header: Ninety-three, on his grandfather's farm
narrative_blocks.body: Henry spent his life on the Hinsdale farm his grandfather Rev. Bunker Gay had settled, and at ninety-three, in 1884, he was still living there, though in feeble health. He died there in March 1885.

narrative_blocks.header: Crossed to California twice in his eighties
narrative_blocks.body: After eighty Henry made two trips out to visit his sons in California, returning each time to the Hinsdale homestead.

narrative_blocks.body: Henry learned carriage making as a young man and worked at the trade alongside farming on the homestead, until he gave it up to farm full time. He married Mary Daggett of Westmoreland on 23 October 1816; she died in August 1864.

narrative_blocks.header: He followed Jonathan Edwards into a broken pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: Northampton had dismissed Jonathan Edwards in 1750 after a bitter dispute over communion; three years later Hooker was ordained over the same divided church. Where another man might have inherited only the wreckage, his even temperament held the congregation together for more than twenty years.

narrative_blocks.header: Ministers spoke of him with unqualified praise
narrative_blocks.body: Dr. Joseph Lathrop was said never to have praised any minister of the period more freely — 'unqualified praise,' in his own phrase. Peers remembered a man evangelical in his views yet catholic in spirit, and one of the most impressive and instructive preachers they had known.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughters married a governor and a senator
narrative_blocks.body: One daughter married Caleb Strong, the future governor of Massachusetts; another married Eli P. Ashmun, a United States senator; a third married Solomon Williams, Hooker's own successor in the Northampton pulpit. Through his children the parsonage tied into the political families of the young republic.

narrative_blocks.header: Smallpox reached the parsonage in 1777
narrative_blocks.body: In February 1777, with the Revolution underway, smallpox took him at Northampton, not quite forty-eight years old. He had held the pulpit for twenty-three years.

narrative_blocks.header: His son-in-law carved his epitaph in stone
narrative_blocks.body: His monument at Northampton bears an inscription thought to be the work of his son-in-law, Governor Caleb Strong. It credits him with a cultivated genius, graceful elocution, and 'the temper of the Gospel.'

military_service.notes: Enlisted Apr 21, 1777 as Private for 3 years in Capt. Caleb Bull's Company, Webb's Regiment. Promoted Sergeant May 16, 1780 for an additional 8 months. Member of the Hartford 'band of music' (eight musicians) raised 1777 and attached to the Connecticut line. Pensioned Nov 4, 1818. DAR Ancestor #A057709.

narrative_blocks.header: One of eight musicians raised in 1777
narrative_blocks.body: A band of music of eight men was raised at Hartford in 1777 and attached to Col. Webb's regiment, and he was one of them. When he died in 1826 the other seven had all been heard from within a few months, so he was reckoned the first of the band to go.

narrative_blocks.header: Private at twenty, sergeant by the end
narrative_blocks.body: He enlisted on 21 April 1777 for three years in Capt. Caleb Bull's company of Webb's regiment, served under Capt. Bulkley in the 3rd Connecticut Line, and came out a sergeant. He drew his pension at that rank.

narrative_blocks.header: Two sons named William, and one lived
narrative_blocks.body: The first William was born in 1781 and died in January 1782; a second William, born in March 1788, lived. The ninth and last child, Levi, died at six in 1808.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine children with Hannah Jones of Hartford
narrative_blocks.body: He married Hannah Jones of Hartford in 1779, a daughter of Levi and Elizabeth (Cook) Jones, and they had nine children. The family stayed at Kensington, the Berlin parish where he was born in 1756 and where he died in 1826.

burial.plot_notes: West Lane Cemetery, Kensington, Berlin CT.

people.research_notes: Father of Sarah Worthington who married Rev. John Hooker (H00264). Of Springfield, Massachusetts.

narrative_blocks.header: A Springfield street still bears his name
narrative_blocks.body: He held a large royal land grant at Springfield, and the town's first street, laid out through it, took the name Worthington Street. Under the English law of entail the land passed whole to his eldest son, and — that son leaving no sons — onward to his daughters.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandfather helped found Hartford
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Pratt's grandfather was Lieutenant William Pratt, who reached Hartford by 1637 and fought in the Pequot War before helping to settle the town. The family later removed to Saybrook.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father was a Saybrook blacksmith and deputy
narrative_blocks.body: Mary's father, Ensign John Pratt, worked as a blacksmith at Saybrook and held large landholdings there and in Hebron. A man of local standing, he represented the town several times in Connecticut's General Assembly.

narrative_blocks.header: Her daughter joined two of Hartford's founding families
narrative_blocks.body: Her daughter Sarah married Rev. John Hooker, of Thomas Hooker's line. Through the match the Pratts and the Hookers — two families present at Hartford's founding — were drawn together.

narrative_blocks.header: Father died of smallpox before her wedding
narrative_blocks.body: Her father Rev. John Hooker pastor of Northampton MA died of smallpox in February 1777 when she was 19. Caleb Strong, a lawyer who had joined her father's congregation five years earlier, married her in November 1777 — nine months after the funeral.

narrative_blocks.header: Matriarch of the Strong-Hooker-Dwight branch
narrative_blocks.body: Mother of nine children with Gov. Caleb Strong including Clarissa Strong Dwight, who married Timothy Dwight Jr. in 1809 and produced the New Haven Dwight-Lyman cluster — three sons of whom were Yale-educated and one of whom Sam's tree records as ancestor of two generations of Yale presidents.

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband's nephew married a Hooker too
narrative_blocks.body: When she married Governor Caleb Strong, she was not the only Hooker to enter his family circle: his nephew Asahel Clarke later married Abigail Hooker of Farmington, a daughter of Colonel Noadiah Hooker. The two unions tied the Hooker and Strong families together twice over.

narrative_blocks.header: A Northampton minister's son on the bench
narrative_blocks.body: John, son of Northampton's Rev. John Hooker, graduated from Yale in 1782, practised law first at Pittsfield and then at Springfield, and rose to the Court of Common Pleas. He was still Judge of Probate when he died at home on 7 March 1829.

narrative_blocks.header: A deacon on the American Board
narrative_blocks.body: John was a deacon of Springfield's First Church and a member of the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions in its first years. Sixty years after his death, the Board's president was Rev. Richard Salter Storrs, his grandson Lewis's father-in-law.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten children, four buried young
narrative_blocks.body: John and Sarah Dwight had ten children at Springfield between 1791 and 1808. They buried two as infants and two daughters in their twenties, Mary in July 1824 and Sarah the next April; their son Worthington became a Yale professor of medicine.

career.organization: American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions

career.notes: Practiced medicine at Westhampton MA per EH 1909 #529. Established the Hooker physician tradition in Westhampton continued by son Dr. Anson Hooker (H01414, 1799-1869) and through several Westhampton descendants.
Per EH 1909 #529: 'He was a physician and also a trader at West Hampton, Mass.' — supplementing physician income with a trading operation, common pattern for rural New England doctors of the period.

narrative_blocks.header: A country doctor who also kept a shop
narrative_blocks.body: Hooker came from Northampton to Westhampton as a young man and practised there the rest of his life, running a trading business alongside the medicine as rural doctors of the time generally had to. He was the first of four generations to doctor that town.

narrative_blocks.header: He took students as well as patients
narrative_blocks.body: Young men read medicine in Hooker's house before the era of medical schools, and Enoch Hale was one of them. Hale went on to Harvard, married Hooker's daughter Almira, and ended in Boston separating typhoid fever from typhus.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven children, their mother gone at forty-two
narrative_blocks.body: Anna Thompson died in April 1810 leaving him seven, from Henry at twenty-four down to Edward at eight. He married Rhoda Phelps two years later, a widow from Hartland in Connecticut, and had no more children.

narrative_blocks.header: He outlived his second wife by fourteen years
narrative_blocks.body: Hooker was born the year before the Townshend Acts and died in February 1861, six weeks before Fort Sumter, at ninety-four. His son Anson took over the Westhampton practice and kept it in the family another generation.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept an apothecary's shop in Rutland
narrative_blocks.body: He spent his life as an apothecary and grocer in Rutland, Vermont, dispensing remedies and provisions to the town — some records grant him the title "Dr." He married Sarah Brown in 1796 and raised five children before his death there in 1836.

narrative_blocks.header: The frontier pulled his children west
narrative_blocks.body: The lure of the West ran deep in the household. His son John moved to Chicago among its earliest New England settlers, and his daughter Julia Ann followed; both died there, far from the Vermont town where they were raised.

narrative_blocks.header: His twin sons took opposite roads
narrative_blocks.body: Two of his sons, John Worthington and Henry Brown, were twins whose paths split as wide as the country. John went west to settle frontier Chicago, while Henry stayed east for a life in the Congregational ministry.

narrative_blocks.header: Amiableness of the friend, gentleness of the mother
narrative_blocks.body: Her 1812 Northampton obituary described Lucy Hooker Ashmun as a woman of uncommon merits: 'the amiableness of the friend, the cheerful, mild disposition of the wife, the gentleness of the mother.' She died after a long illness at thirty-seven, leaving five children — the eldest just twelve.

narrative_blocks.header: Died four years before Eli reached the Senate
narrative_blocks.body: Lucy Hooker Ashmun died in 1812, four years before her husband Eli Porter Ashmun was elected to the United States Senate — she never saw the political career that would make his name. Their son George and son John Hooker Ashmun would go on to federal office and Harvard Law, carrying the legacy she did not live to witness.

narrative_blocks.header: Daughter of Northampton's Rev. John Hooker
narrative_blocks.body: Lucy was the daughter of Rev. John Hooker of Northampton, Massachusetts — a great-granddaughter in the line descending from Rev. Thomas Hooker who founded Hartford in 1636. She married into the Ashmun family in 1798, and her middle name Hooker would be carried by her daughter and then her granddaughter across two more generations.

narrative_blocks.body: She was only a few months old when her father, Samuel Seymour, was killed by the fall of a tree near the old fort at Kensington Parish, late in 1748. Her widowed mother was made her guardian and raised her in the parish, where she would live out the whole of her long life.

career.notes: Bought Arnold Smith hotel fall 1815. Sold to Alfred Hooker Aug 23, 1823.
General mercantile, principally Canadian trade.
First collector of port. Overseer of the poor when town organized March 27, 1821.

narrative_blocks.header: St. Lawrence River hotel owner; first port collector
narrative_blocks.body: John Hooker moved his family from Turin to Morristown in the fall of 1815 — a village of only a few houses on the St. Lawrence River — where he bought Arnold Smith's hotel and ran it until 1823. When the town was organized on March 27, 1821, he was appointed overseer of the poor and became its first collector of the port.

narrative_blocks.header: From Connecticut to Turin to the St. Lawrence
narrative_blocks.body: John Hooker left Kensington, Connecticut after his first wife Abigail Goodrich died in 1794, remarried Mary Ives in 1795, and removed the family to Turin, New York in 1802 — then in 1814 to Morristown, beautifully situated on the St. Lawrence River, where he died April 12, 1829.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at thirty-four with six young children
narrative_blocks.body: She lost her husband Cyprian Hart on March 1, 1806 and his adoptive uncle General Selah Hart fourteen weeks later on June 10. By the adoption arrangement she remained mistress of the General Hart homestead with her six children, the youngest only nine months old. She had all six baptized at Kensington church the following November.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-five years a widow, three children unmarried
narrative_blocks.body: Of her six children, three died unmarried before their forty-second year: Selah at forty-one in 1838, the physician Henry Cyprian at thirty in 1831, and Emily at twenty-nine in 1835. She herself died July 8, 1851 at Kensington aged seventy-nine — having outlived her husband by forty-five years and having shared the General Hart house with her co-widow Ruth Cole Hart for thirty-eight of them.

narrative_blocks.header: A children's book of fourteen Sabbath evenings
narrative_blocks.body: He built his Child's Book on the Sabbath as a conversation: a Mrs. Martyn and her three children, aged nine to thirteen, working through fourteen evenings on why the day mattered, to the body and to the mind. It was one of a shelf he wrote for young readers, alongside The Farmer, Prophets and Prophecy, and the Youth's Book of Natural Theology.

narrative_blocks.header: He finished the books Gallaudet left unfinished
narrative_blocks.body: With Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet he wrote The Practical Spelling Book and The School and Family Dictionary, which New England schools kept in print under both names for decades. When Gallaudet died in 1851, Hooker carried on his Scripture Biographies for Children alone.

narrative_blocks.header: His only pulpit lasted two years
narrative_blocks.body: Ordained over the Congregational church at Watertown in 1822, he was driven out by ill health within two years and never took another pastorate. He went back to Hartford and to print instead, editing the Connecticut Observer and serving as secretary of the state missionary societies from 1826 until his death.

narrative_blocks.header: Founding student of Yale's theological department
narrative_blocks.body: As a Yale tutor in 1817 he was one of twelve young men reading theology informally with Professor Eleazar Fitch, twice a week at Fitch's house. They brought in Kingsley for Hebrew and Goodrich for preaching, and the evenings hardened into Yale's first theological department.

narrative_blocks.header: Connecticut sang from his hymnbook for decades
narrative_blocks.body: With Rev. Dr. Daggett he chose and arranged the Hymns and Psalms that the General Association of Connecticut set forth for its churches. Most of the state's Congregational congregations sang from it for the next twenty years.

narrative_blocks.header: His last congregation was the Hartford Retreat
narrative_blocks.body: From 1852 he was chaplain of the Retreat for the Insane at Hartford, ministering to its patients for a decade. A stroke in August 1862 took the work from him, and he died in the city two years later.

people.research_notes: Son of William Hooker Sr. (H00533) and Hannah Jones Hooker (I00046) of Berlin/Kensington CT. Born March 10, 1788 in Berlin Hartford County CT. Named 'William' for his older brother William (H01426) who died in infancy January 10, 1782 — replacement-naming pattern. Studied medicine and migrated to Dutchess County NY. Married his cousin Amelia Stanley (H01473) on January 9, 1814 in Hartford CT — Amelia was a gen 6 Hooker descendant via both her mother Ann Hooker Stanley AND her father Seth Stanley (Hooker via Hannah Hart Stanley, gen 4). Their two children carry triple Hooker descent. Settled in South Dover Dutchess County NY where he practiced medicine and represented the town in the New York State Legislature. Two documented children: William Jr (H02791, 1819-1881) and Ann Hooker Vincent (H02792, 1825-1908). RECEIVED a now-famous 1838 letter from Mott Titus describing Ohio frontier life and the Whig sweep of New York elections — preserved by Spared & Shared archives. Died March 31, 1853 in Dover Furnace Dutchess County NY at age 65. Buried South Dover Rural Cemetery, Wingdale NY.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Hookers on one Yale faculty
narrative_blocks.body: The Yale catalogue for 1852-53 prints Charles Hooker as professor of anatomy and physiology and, directly beneath him, Worthington Hooker as professor of the theory and practice of physic. The two were second cousins, and each held his chair until he died.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped open Yale to Cortlandt Creed
narrative_blocks.body: Hooker was among the men who got Cortlandt Van Rensselaer Creed into the Yale medical school, with President Woolsey and the Reverend Leonard Bacon. Creed took his M.D. in 1857, the first African American to graduate from Yale and the first to take a medical degree at an Ivy League school.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years a surgeon, twenty-five a professor
narrative_blocks.body: His stone at Evergreen counts the years out: eminent as a physician and surgeon for forty years, professor of anatomy in Yale College for twenty-five, and dead at New Haven in the Christian faith.

narrative_blocks.header: New Haven told stories about him
narrative_blocks.body: Kensington-born and Yale 1820, Hooker was remembered as a man of great activity and influence, and the town kept a stock of stories about his eccentricities long after he was gone.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven of their nine children died small
narrative_blocks.body: Nine children were born to Charles and Eliza Hooker at New Haven between 1824 and 1841, and seven of them were dead before they were eight. Mary Phelps the second died in January 1832 and her brother Charles William twenty-five days later.

narrative_blocks.header: More than any man — Waterbury's founding father
narrative_blocks.body: Bronson wrote of him: "He was, more than any other man, with the exception of Thomas Judd senior, the ruling spirit and father of the settlement." He laid out lots, staked fences, located highways, and settled town boundaries — and as first Recorder, his was the only fully legible and business-like hand among Waterbury's earliest proprietors.

narrative_blocks.header: His manuscripts preserved Waterbury's founding records
narrative_blocks.body: His handwritten folio books — copied for preservation in 1705 by town appointment — survived into the nineteenth century and became the primary source for Waterbury's founding history. His son Nathaniel's account-book continued the family's role as the town's unofficial archivists.

narrative_blocks.header: Left Waterbury suddenly — no one knew why
narrative_blocks.body: In a time of great affliction, John Stanley quietly quit the town he had done more than any other man to build. Bronson wrote in 1858: he could not say what persuaded Stanley to leave, adding: 'It is to be hoped he had a better reason than any that can be thought of at this distant day. His loss must have been seriously felt.' He returned to Farmington and never explained himself.

narrative_blocks.header: The Farmington house he never lived in
narrative_blocks.body: Between 1709 and 1719 John had a dwelling house raised on land his father left him on Farmington's Back Lane, then sold it unfinished, with six acres, to Ebenezer Steele in December 1720. Finished by others, it survives as the Stanley-Whitman House, a National Historic Landmark and museum.

narrative_blocks.header: First lieutenant of the Waterbury train band
narrative_blocks.body: John was a sergeant in the Waterbury train band in 1682, and when the Assembly allowed the town a lieutenant in October 1689 he was the first chosen. He sat for Waterbury in the General Assembly in 1690 and 1693, and was a deacon at Farmington by 1711.

[Migrated from marriage.spouse_notes (spouse I00148)]: Of Guilford, Connecticut FindAGrave (Sam, 8 Sep 2026) (contributor 47962427, citing Hale Cemetery Inscriptions 1934 p.82, and Ancestry's 'The Descendants of Thomas Hooker'): b. 1713 Wethersfield; d. 21 May 1797 New Haven County; buried West Cemetery, Meriden. THREE THINGS THAT DO NOT AGREE AND ARE NOT RESOLVED HERE. (1) BIRTH: this record holds 1715; FindAGrave's header says 1713. Its 'aged 83-84' is computed from its own two dates, so it is not independent evidence, and Warren #82 did not record her birth at all. 1715 kept as entered. (2) DEATH: FindAGrave's header says 21 May 1797 in New Haven County, but its own narrative on the same page says 'her death at Guildford, CT., was on the 9 of May 1797' - which is what this record already held. 9 May at Guilford kept, since the page contradicts itself and the narrative matches the existing entry. (3) BURIAL: entered as supplied, West Cemetery in MERIDEN (CEM1421), but treat it as doubtful - her husband lies in the West Cemetery at MADISON (CEM038), thirty miles away, and she died at Guilford, of which Madison was then a part. Two burials called 'West Cemetery' is exactly how a FindAGrave memorial gets attached to the wrong one. DESCENT: the FindAGrave page tags her a GRANDCHILD of Thomas Hooker; its own text gives the line correctly as Thomas 1, Samuel 2, Daniel 3, Hannah - she is a great-granddaughter, generation 4, which is what this record holds. ELEVEN CHILDREN CONFIRMED: the page's count and Sam's FamilySearch list both match the eleven already built here (H00398-H00408). Two of those disagree with FamilySearch and are left as entered: Hooker Norton (H00399) b. 1741 here against 1740 there, and Azubah Norton Bartlett (H00405) d. 1815 here against 1845 there - a thirty-year gap worth settling. Arah Norton (H00398) is named on the page as the Hotchkiss ancestor.

narrative_blocks.header: Aged Maiden — died unmarried at sixty-five
narrative_blocks.body: She never married, living her entire life in Hartford. The CT Courant of January 14, 1765 noted her death simply: 'an aged Maiden, near Seventy Years old.'

narrative_blocks.header: Apoplexy in Hartford, January 1765
narrative_blocks.body: She died of apoplexy — a stroke — on Saturday, January 12, 1765, at age 65. She was baptized at the Second Church of Hartford on October 1, 1699 and lived all her years in the same town her great-grandfather had founded.

narrative_blocks.header: Two sons named Samuel, both lost
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah and Daniel had five children at Hartford, and three died young: Chloe, and two boys named Samuel, the second given his dead brother's name. Only their daughter Sarah, born in 1739, and a son Daniel are not recorded as dying young.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten years a judge's widow
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah married Daniel Edwards in 1728, when she was about twenty-four, and he rose to Connecticut's Superior Court before dying at New Haven in 1765. She outlived him by ten years and died on 31 July 1775, six weeks after Bunker Hill.

narrative_blocks.header: Captain of militia at twenty-three
narrative_blocks.body: He held a captaincy in the Connecticut militia as early as 1734, when he was twenty-three, and kept the rank and the title for the rest of his life. His trade was merchandise, in Hartford, and he left a large estate.

narrative_blocks.header: Three sessions for Hartford in the Assembly
narrative_blocks.body: He sat for the town in the Colonial Assembly across three sessions in 1757 and 1758. Dexter’s account of the Yale men calls him simply a respected and useful citizen of Hartford, which is the whole of his public character.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the Governor’s daughter
narrative_blocks.body: In 1729, the year he took his Yale degree, he married Eunice Talcott — second daughter of Joseph Talcott, Governor of the Colony from 1725 to 1741. Her brother Matthew married a Hooker in the same generation.

narrative_blocks.header: Then he married her niece
narrative_blocks.body: Eunice died and he married Eunice Wadsworth, daughter of Abigail Talcott — the first Eunice’s sister. So his second wife was his first wife’s niece, and the same Governor’s granddaughter. No children; she outlived him sixty-two years.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale 1729, and a cousin two years ahead
narrative_blocks.body: He took his degree at Yale in 1729. His mother was Mary, daughter of the Hon. Nathaniel Stanley of Hartford, which made him first cousin to the Nathaniel Stanley of the class of 1726.

narrative_blocks.header: Co-heir at the probate court, Christmas Day
narrative_blocks.body: On 25 December 1742 he and Eunice stood before the Court of Probate at Hartford and signed Governor Talcott’s estate distribution as co-heirs. It is the document that put a Hooker into a colonial governor’s property.

narrative_blocks.header: One son preached, the other traded
narrative_blocks.body: His eldest, Nathaniel, took Yale in 1755 and the West Hartford pulpit. His son James went into trade as a partner in Hooker & Chaffee, which did very well out of the Revolution.

narrative_blocks.header: Uncle, by half-blood, to a famous theologian
narrative_blocks.body: Daniel's half-brother was Rev. Timothy Edwards of East Windsor, whose son was Jonathan Edwards, the Great Awakening preacher. The judge and the theologian were one degree apart in the same Hartford family.

narrative_blocks.header: A churchman who baptized the people he enslaved
narrative_blocks.body: A devout member of Hartford's First Church, Daniel Edwards held four enslaved people, Jethro, Dick, Mina, and Betty, and saw them baptized there in 1760. Their baptism is among the few records that name them at all.

narrative_blocks.header: His father founded the Edwards family
narrative_blocks.body: Daniel's father, Richard Edwards of Hartford, was remembered as the progenitor of the celebrated Edwards family of Connecticut. From him sprang both the theologian's line and Daniel's own judicial one.

narrative_blocks.header: He rose to the colony's high court
narrative_blocks.body: Daniel Edwards read law and rose to become a judge of the Connecticut Superior Court, the colony's highest, and judge of the Hartford probate district. A Yale graduate of 1720, he gave his life to the law.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother carried the Talcott founder's blood
narrative_blocks.body: Daniel's mother, Mary Talcott, was a daughter of Lieut.-Col. John Talcott, a founder of Hartford and the colony's commander in King Philip's War. Through her the judge descended from the town's first generation.

narrative_blocks.header: His marriage first joined three founding lines
narrative_blocks.body: In 1728 Daniel married Sarah Hooker, granddaughter of Rev. Samuel Hooker. The match drew together three of Connecticut's founding families, Edwards, Talcott, and Hooker, in a single household.

b. Aug 15, 1742 Hartford CT; d. Dec 10, 1805 Windsor CT age 63. Buried Palisado Cemetery, Windsor CT. Son of Nathaniel Hooker Jr. and Eunice Talcott of Hartford. EH entry 348. Commissioned CAPTAIN. BUSINESS: Merchant of Hartford and Windsor. With his brothers succeeded to his father's Hartford business and established at Windsor. Firm became "Hooker and Chaffee" — James Hooker (silent partner), Horace Hooker (brother), and John Chaffee (brother of James's third wife). "Before the Revolutionary War this was one of the largest and most flourishing mercantile houses of New England, and transacted much business for the Colonial Government." "All the firm were devoted patriots and gave freely of their means for the assistance of the Colonial cause and at the end of the war were seriously embarrassed." Subsequently heavy losses from French and Spanish spoliations caused their FAILURE and dissolution of the firm, scattering its members. For full account see Stiles's New History of Windsor. m. (1) Hannah Allin Jan 6, 1763 — she d. Apr 19, 1765 Windsor. m. (2) Dolly Goodwin Apr 30, 1777 — she d. Feb 9, 1784 Windsor, no children. m. (3) Mary Chaffee Nov 7, 1784 — she d. Oct 7, 1846 Schenectady NY age 86. LANDMARK: Built ca. 1772 James Hooker House, 118 Palisado Avenue, Windsor CT (LM015). Part of Palisado Avenue Historic District, National Register of Historic Places. Interior later gutted for Chaffee School classrooms; exterior retains Greek Revival additions ca. 1840s over original Federal structure. SUPPLY CHAIN NOTE: The Hooker and Chaffee firm operated alongside Jeremiah Wadsworth's larger commissary operation — both Hooker descendants and Talcott descendants provisioning the Continental Army from the same Connecticut River Valley network.
MARRIAGE NOTES (migrated): No children.
OCCUPATION: Merchant, Captain
CC NOTE [I00054]: James Hooker's mother was Eunice Talcott, daughter of Gov. Joseph Talcott. Gov. Talcott's daughter Abigail Talcott married Rev. Daniel Wadsworth — and their son was Col. Jeremiah Wadsworth, commissary general for both American and French armies. James Hooker and Jeremiah Wadsworth were thus FIRST COUSINS ONCE REMOVED through the Talcott family — both grandsons/great-grandsons of Gov. Joseph Talcott. Both were supplying Continental Army troops during the Revolution: James through the Hooker and Chaffee firm as captain; Jeremiah as commissary general for the entire allied force. The Talcott family, through Gov. Joseph Talcott's children, was the connective tissue of Connecticut's Revolutionary War supply network.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty wagon teams lined up for his firm
narrative_blocks.body: Hooker and Chaffee kept West Indies ships at the Windsor wharves and six or seven coasters in the Little River, and one witness counted thirty teams in the road waiting their turn. James's influence made Windsor a port of entry.

narrative_blocks.header: The firm armed the Revolution, and paid
narrative_blocks.body: Hooker and Chaffee supplied the Continental Army and gave freely to the patriot cause, and James took a captain's commission. Peace left the partners deep in debt, and French and Spanish seizures later broke the firm.

narrative_blocks.header: The failed firm's sons rebuilt in New York
narrative_blocks.body: When the firm broke, James's sons went out into New York: Alexander to an Irondequoit farm, James to the Dutchess surrogate's court and the canal board, Horace to Carthage and nurseries, Henry to Rochester stores and Syracuse salt.

narrative_blocks.header: The bride's buckles came home to Windsor
narrative_blocks.body: Hannah Allin married James in January 1763, at nineteen, in paste-stone silver shoe buckles; she died at twenty-two, their only son at seventeen. The buckles surfaced at auction, and the Windsor Historical Society brought them home in 2012.

narrative_blocks.header: His third wife honored his first
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Chaffee, married in 1784, named their eldest daughter Hannah Allin Hooker — for the bride he had buried nineteen years before. His second wife Dolly Goodwin got a namesake daughter too.

narrative_blocks.header: His Windsor house is on the National Register
narrative_blocks.body: James built his house at 118 Palisado Avenue about 1772; it stands in the Palisado Avenue Historic District on the National Register. Gutted for Chaffee School classrooms, it keeps its Federal exterior under Greek Revival additions.

notable.notable_blurb: Treasurer of Connecticut Colony

narrative_blocks.header: Hartford's first house and first barn
narrative_blocks.body: John went ahead with the Adventurers in 1635 and had his carpenter, Nicholas Clark, build the first house any Englishman raised at Hartford that winter. The family lived first in its kitchen, and his great barn of 1636 was the first in the colony.

narrative_blocks.header: The Worshipful Mr. John Talcott
narrative_blocks.body: On May 1, 1637, John sat on the committee that weighed a war with the Pequots, and war followed. A deputy from 1637 to 1653, then treasurer and assistant through the 1650s, he was styled in the records the Worshipful Mr. John Talcott.

narrative_blocks.header: The fifth-richest man in Newtown
narrative_blocks.body: In Newtown, now Cambridge, John ranked fifth of eighty townsmen in houses and land, with four houses in the West End and marsh across the Neck, and kept thirty-six rods of the town fence in repair. The town made him a selectman and sent him to the General Court.

narrative_blocks.header: Kin to three other founders
narrative_blocks.body: John's sisters married two more Hartford founders, Rachel to John Steele and Sarah to William Wadsworth, and the founder John Skinner was his nephew. His will remembered his kinsman John Skinner and kinswoman Sara Steele, if still in his service.

narrative_blocks.header: A Latin school, if any be kept
narrative_blocks.body: John's will left his books to his son Samuel, his Martyrs book and feather bed to his son John, five pounds to his teacher Mr. Stone, and five pounds toward a Latin school at Hartford, if any be kept here.

narrative_blocks.header: He crossed on the Lyon in 1632
narrative_blocks.body: John sailed from Braintree in Essex with Hooker's company on the Lyon, twelve weeks at sea with 123 passengers, fifty of them children. The family's 1876 genealogy counts him as the first Talcott to settle here and the father of the American line.

narrative_blocks.header: Dr. Rossiter came to his sickbed
narrative_blocks.body: John fell ill that winter, and the colony later paid Dr. Bray Rossiter for coming to attend him in his sickness. He died in March 1660, and John Davenport wrote to John Winthrop Jr. that his diseases were plainly beyond curing: "no art of man could cure him."

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve weeks on the Lyon
narrative_blocks.body: Dorothy crossed with John and their small children on the Lyon in 1632, twelve weeks at sea with Hooker's company, 123 passengers and fifty of them children, who all came ashore at Boston in good health.

narrative_blocks.header: She lived first in the kitchen
narrative_blocks.body: When the family came to Hartford in 1636 they lived first in the kitchen of the house Nicholas Clark had built the winter before, the first at Hartford. The east end of the house went up in 1638 and the west end in 1645.

narrative_blocks.header: A Mott of Braintree
narrative_blocks.body: Dorothy came of the Motts of Braintree in Essex, probably a daughter of Mark Mott, whose father owned Sheme Hall. Her brother sold the family's old Braintree house in 1644, on John's order from Hartford.

narrative_blocks.header: Her only daughter married a regicides' host
narrative_blocks.body: Dorothy's only daughter, Mary, married the Rev. John Russell in 1649 and died young. Russell later hid the regicide judges in his cellar at Hadley, reached by a trap-door in the floor.

narrative_blocks.header: Her Turkey mohair coat
narrative_blocks.body: Widowed in 1660, Dorothy kept the Hartford house for life. Her will of 1669 gave Samuel her silver beer bowl, pewter flagon and three great green cushions, and John her Turkey mohair coat and all the rest.

narrative_blocks.header: The Worshipful John Talcott's only daughter
narrative_blocks.body: Mary was the eldest child and only daughter of the magistrate John Talcott of Hartford. Born in England, she came with the family in the great migration. She grew up in one of the colony's leading households.

narrative_blocks.header: She married the future Angel of Hadley
narrative_blocks.body: In June 1649 Mary wed the young minister John Russell at Hartford. She bore him a son before her early death around 1658. Her husband would later become famous as the protector of the regicides.
