notable.notable_blurb: Colonial military commander, King Philip's War

narrative_blocks.header: He led the war in the Narragansett country
narrative_blocks.body: In King Philip's War John commanded a joint force of Mohegans, Niantics, Pequots and colonists. From June 1676 into the fall they swept southern New England, pursuing Native people, Narragansett women and children among them.

narrative_blocks.header: Nipsachuck, and the captives sold away
narrative_blocks.body: At the second fight at Nipsachuck in July 1676 his men killed the Narragansett sachem Quaiapen in one of the war's few cavalry charges. Large numbers of captives were shipped out of the colonies as slaves, and the court gave him land at Hammonasset.

narrative_blocks.header: He was named guardian of the charter
narrative_blocks.body: When Connecticut's royal charter arrived from Charles II in 1662, the freemen chose John, with Samuel Wyllys and John Allyn, to keep it in their custody. A quarter-century later he would help spirit it away from Andros.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the charter as the candles died
narrative_blocks.body: By Roger Wolcott's account, when the candles were snuffed in the Hartford meeting-house in 1687, John and Nathaniel Stanley lifted the charters off the table before Andros could seize them. Wolcott names no oak; the tree came into the story later.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept the colony's purse sixteen years
narrative_blocks.body: John was treasurer of Connecticut from 1660 to 1676, taking the office from his father, and rose in the militia from ensign in 1650 to captain, major and lieutenant-colonel.

narrative_blocks.header: His father's buildings, in his own hand
narrative_blocks.body: In his parchment account book John set down when each of his father's buildings went up: the first house, raised the first winter any Englishmen built at Hartford, and the first barn in the colony. The book passed to his son-in-law Joseph Wadsworth.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter married into the Edwards line
narrative_blocks.body: His daughter Mary Talcott became the second wife of Richard Edwards of Hartford. Through that marriage the Talcott blood joined one of New England's most consequential families, the line of Jonathan Edwards.

will.summary: Will of Captain Samuel Talcott, Wethersfield CT. Bequeathed to sons: Samuel (home lot south, great meadow parcels, Westfield lot); John (home lot north, 5 acres great meadow, 12 acres Westfield); Elizur (Westfield brook land, 6 acres meadow, 50-acre lot near Farmington line); Joseph (30 acres Westfield); Benjamin (north half, east side Connecticut River, undivided Indian lands, south half 200-acre court grant); Nathaniel (south half Nawburk lot, undivided east-river land, north half 200-acre grant, one cow). Daughters: Hannah Chester £90; Rachel £80. Wife Mary: £10/yr, use of lower room, garden, one cow during widowhood. Executor: son Samuel Talcott. Overseers: Capt. Robert Wells, Ensign Samuel Butler.

Primary sketch of Rev. John Russell of Hadley: Harvard 1645, Wethersfield to Hadley, sheltering the regicides, 1693 estate inventory (incl. three enslaved people), Hopkins School fight.

notable.notable_blurb: Puritan minister; the Angel of Hadley

narrative_blocks.header: The minister who hid the king’s killers
narrative_blocks.body: For over a decade Russell secretly sheltered Edward Whalley and William Goffe — two of the judges who had condemned Charles I to death — beneath his Hadley parsonage while royal agents hunted them across the colonies. A single misstep meant death for him and his household. The historian George Sheldon later called him the “Guardian Angel of Hadley.”

narrative_blocks.header: An angel rallied Hadley, then vanished
narrative_blocks.body: During a King Philip’s War raid, an unknown gray-haired stranger appeared, took command of the panicked townspeople, drove off the attackers, and disappeared — leaving them convinced an angel had saved them. The deliverer was almost certainly the fugitive general Goffe, slipping from Russell’s house and back. The episode became New England’s enduring “Angel of Hadley” legend.

narrative_blocks.header: He led his flock out of Connecticut
narrative_blocks.body: When a bitter dispute over baptism and church membership split the Wethersfield congregation, Russell drew up a covenant and gathered the dissenting families. In 1659 they agreed to leave the jurisdiction of Connecticut for Massachusetts. They crossed the wilderness and founded the town of Hadley on a bend of the Connecticut River.

narrative_blocks.header: Bones found beneath the parsonage cellar
narrative_blocks.body: When Russell’s house was pulled down near the end of the eighteenth century, workers lifting a cellar slab uncovered large human remains. Local tradition held them to be one of the regicides, secretly buried in the minister’s own foundation. A tooth from the find was kept by a witness for decades afterward.

narrative_blocks.header: Three enslaved people in his estate
narrative_blocks.body: The inventory of Russell’s estate, taken at Hadley in January 1693, listed an enslaved man, woman, and child together valued at sixty pounds. They are recorded among the household goods, a stark line in the ledger of a celebrated minister.

narrative_blocks.header: The second wife who brought the family fortune
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Talcott, daughter of Lieut.-Col. John Talcott of Hartford, became Richard Edwards's second wife in 1692. Her prosperous Talcott connections lifted the family's standing, and her son Daniel rose to the colony's Superior Court.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son's wife was a Hooker of Norwich

narrative_blocks.header: She was buried beside Richard at Hartford

notable.notable_blurb: First Connecticut governor born within its limits

narrative_blocks.header: First Connecticut governor born within the colony
narrative_blocks.body: Born in Hartford on November 16, 1669, Joseph Talcott was the first Governor of Connecticut born within the colony rather than in England. He served from 1724 until his death on October 11, 1741 — 17 years in office, longer than any predecessor except Governor Winthrop and any successor until the modern era. His funeral expenses of £69 12s. 6d. were paid from the Colonial Treasury.

narrative_blocks.header: He presided the afternoon his wife died
narrative_blocks.body: When his wife Eunice died suddenly about noon on Thursday, May 25, 1738, the Deputy Governor was absent at Norwich. Governor Talcott did not let his private grief interfere with his official duty — he returned and presided in the upper house that same afternoon. The General Assembly appointed a committee to draw an address of condolence to the Governor.

narrative_blocks.header: He claimed his father's estate at twenty-one
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph Talcott was the fourth son of Lieutenant-Colonel John Talcott Jr. but the eldest to survive his father. In 1691, at age 21, he petitioned the General Court for his father's estate by right of primogeniture — an assertive legal claim for colonial Connecticut. He was first mentioned in public life in 1711 as a committee member to lay out the town of Coventry.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-two years with Eunice Howell
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph married Abigail Clark of Milford in 1699 and lost her five years later. In 1706 he married Eunice Howell, and they were thirty-two years together until her death in 1738.

narrative_blocks.header: A son kept the colony's treasury
narrative_blocks.body: His son Joseph followed him into the colony's service and was its Treasurer from 1755 to 1769. A grandson through his daughter Abigail, Jeremiah Wadsworth, became Washington's commissary general in the Revolution.

narrative_blocks.header: His will sent three sons to three futures
narrative_blocks.body: Richard Edwards, the only child of one of Hartford's first settlers, became the progenitor of the celebrated Edwards family of Connecticut. His will charted divergent courses for his sons — one to care for their mother, one to be educated at college and become a judge, one to be put to a trade — and through his son Timothy came his grandson Jonathan Edwards, the Great Awakening theologian.

narrative_blocks.header: Only child of two of Hartford’s first families
narrative_blocks.body: Richard was the only child of William Edwards and Agnes Spencer, each tied to Hartford's earliest settlers, and his grandmother Ann had crossed from England with his father when the boy was young. He inherited that founding stock as an only child and passed it to a large family of his own.

narrative_blocks.header: He served writs up and down colonial Hartford
narrative_blocks.body: Richard Edwards spent his life in the law at Hartford, an officer of the courts who served writs through a busy colonial town of merchants, ministers, and West India traders. He was, his descendants held, the practical root of a famous family.

narrative_blocks.header: His first marriage ended in a rare divorce
narrative_blocks.body: After twenty-four troubled years he divorced his first wife, Elizabeth Tuttle, in 1691, an outcome almost without parallel in the colony. He married Mary Talcott the next year, and her prosperous family helped make him rich.

narrative_blocks.header: From his line sprang the Edwards of Connecticut
narrative_blocks.body: Through his son Timothy by his first marriage came Rev. Jonathan Edwards, the great theologian; through his second marriage, Judge Daniel Edwards of the colony's high court. He was progenitor of the celebrated Edwards family of Connecticut.

notable.notable_blurb: Captain of the Charter Oak legend

narrative_blocks.header: He vanished into the dark with the charter
narrative_blocks.body: By tradition, when the candles went out in the Hartford meeting-house on the night of 31 October 1687, Wadsworth carried the colony's charter into the dark and hid it in a great oak on the Wyllys grounds. Historians note the evidence is thin and the duplicate may have gone to his own cellar, but the legend made his name.

narrative_blocks.header: Lieutenant in King Philip's War, captain after
narrative_blocks.body: Wadsworth served as a lieutenant during King Philip's War in the 1670s and had risen to captain by 1690. The colony long remembered him as a soldier as much as the charter's keeper.

narrative_blocks.header: Three marriages, but a single line of children
narrative_blocks.body: Wadsworth married three times: first to Elizabeth Barnard, who left no children, and last to the widow Mary Blackleach, who outlived him. All his children came through his second wife, Elizabeth Talcott, daughter of Lieutenant-Colonel John Talcott.

narrative_blocks.header: The colony quietly paid him for the deed
narrative_blocks.body: In 1715, nearly thirty years after the event, Connecticut voted Wadsworth twenty shillings for securing the duplicate charter in a very troublesome season. That grant is the closest thing to a contemporary record of his famous act.

narrative_blocks.header: His father crossed on the Lyon with Talcotts
narrative_blocks.body: Wadsworth's father William came from England aboard the ship Lyon in 1632, in the same migration as the Talcott family whose daughter Joseph would later marry. The two Hartford founding houses were thus bound twice over, by voyage and by marriage.

Her son John Hart, b. 31 Jan 1719, was a physician and died unmarried. Not built. narrative_blocks.header: Four daughters unmarried; only the son wed
narrative_blocks.body: Rev. Daniel Wadsworth, Hartford's pastor and a Yale Corporation member, was her husband from 1734 until his death at forty-three. The four daughters who survived infancy all died unmarried; only Jeremiah married and carried the family on.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought the stones meant for a church
narrative_blocks.body: When Hartford's Episcopalians began their first church in 1762, the foundation stones ended up in Samuel Talcott's house instead. He had not led the mob that wrecked the work, but he bought the stones from a man with no right to sell them. The churchmen never forgave him for it.

narrative_blocks.header: “The gates of hell shall not prevail”
narrative_blocks.body: In 1786 the Episcopalians tried again, and at the laying of the cornerstone one of their leaders rose to speak. “I lay the corner-stone of the first Episcopal Church in Hartford,” he declared, “and Sam Talcott and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” His name had become a byword for the opposition.

narrative_blocks.header: His will named only three of his children
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel and Mabel raised a houseful of children, several of whom died young. When he made his will, he named only the three who outlived him: his son Samuel, his daughter Mary Watson, and his daughter Jerusha. The document quietly records how much a colonial family could lose.

people.research_notes: b. May 3, 1717 Hartford CT; d. Sept 1805 Norwich CT. Daughter of Gov. Joseph Talcott (T00045) and Eunice Howell Wakeman Talcott. m. Dr. Daniel Lathrop of Norwich Dec 14, 1744. All three sons died before oldest reached age 4 — "three precious sons cut down like flowers of the field, almost at a single sweep of the scythe." DR. DANIEL LATHROP (b. Yale 1733; d. Norwich 1782): First druggist in Norwich, probably first in Connecticut. Went to London to study medicine; returned with large stock of medicines. Furnished stores for northern army in French and Indian War. Firm became "Bros. Lathrop" with brother Joshua (Yale 1743); then Lathrop & Coit. "Doctor Daniel, in common with others, wore a white wig and cocked hat. He rode to meeting in a yellow chaise with a red morocco top, with a negro driver in front, his dignified companion, the daughter of Gov. Talcott, sitting by his side." MRS. SIGOURNEY CONNECTION: After the deaths of her children, "Madam Lathrop" (Jerusha) raised the early childhood of Lydia Huntley Sigourney (b. Sept 1, 1791; m. Charles Sigourney of Hartford Jun 16, 1819) — the celebrated Hartford poet and author, called "the Sweet Singer of Hartford." "Having lost her own children in their infancy, she lavished all her maternal affection on this child of her heart, who repaid her tenderness with filial veneration and has embalmed her memory in hallowed verse." Source: Talcott Pedigree, entry on Jerusha Talcott. [Migrated from marriage.spouse_notes (spouse X01764)]: Of Norwich CT; Yale 1733; d. 1782

narrative_blocks.header: Three sons, none living past age four
narrative_blocks.body: Every child she bore — three boys — died before the eldest turned four, a loss her chronicler likened to flowers cut at a single sweep of the scythe. She lived on to eighty-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: The poet Sigourney was the child she raised
narrative_blocks.body: After her sons' deaths, Madam Lathrop took the young Lydia Huntley into her care — the girl who grew into Lydia Huntley Sigourney, the celebrated Sweet Singer of Hartford. The poet repaid her in verse that kept her memory.

narrative_blocks.header: To meeting in a yellow chaise
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband Daniel, Norwich's first druggist, drove to Sunday meeting in a yellow chaise with a red morocco top, wig and cocked hat in place, the governor's daughter dignified at his side.

narrative_blocks.body: Joseph Talcott served as Colonial Governor of Connecticut from 1724 to 1741. She was born to him in Hartford in 1720, his fourth-year-in-office daughter.

notable.notable_blurb: Founder of Springfield, Mass.; fur trader and theologian

narrative_blocks.header: Boston's executioner burned his book in 1650
narrative_blocks.body: On 16 October 1650 the General Court set the town executioner to burn The Meritorious Price of Our Redemption in the Boston marketplace. Pynchon had argued that Christ's obedience, not his suffering, bought atonement. Four copies survive.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded Springfield where the ships stopped
narrative_blocks.body: Scouting the valley in 1635 he settled on ground just above Enfield Falls, as far up the Connecticut as a seagoing ship could come, and equidistant from Boston and Albany. From his warehouse downriver he shipped four to six thousand beaver pelts a year and packed the first commercial pork in the New World.

narrative_blocks.header: He took Springfield out of Connecticut, 1638
narrative_blocks.body: He would not send men against the Pequots and kept trading with the Agawam and Pocumtuc, which set him against Captain John Mason and, later, Thomas Hooker at Hartford. In 1638 he took Springfield out of Connecticut and into Massachusetts, fixing that colony's southwestern line where it still runs.

narrative_blocks.header: A stolen petticoat, and a warrant forbidding force
narrative_blocks.body: A new kersey petticoat was taken from Rowland Thomas's house in 1650, and Pynchon sent his constable across the river after the thief. The warrant set a limit: persuade the man, push him forward to make him come, but if that failed, use no violence and rather leave him.

narrative_blocks.header: He recanted, then sailed for England in 1652
narrative_blocks.body: He gave the court a partial retraction in May 1651, was bound over to return in October, and did not. He signed his Springfield holdings over to his son John and sailed. That hearing had shared a day and a room with the witchcraft trial of Hugh and Mary Parsons of his own town.

narrative_blocks.header: Back in England he published the argument again
narrative_blocks.body: Out of reach of the colony's rules on lay theology, Pynchon kept publishing — The Jewish Synagogue in 1652, then a reply to John Norton's official rebuttal titled The Meritorious Price of Man's Redemption. In it he restated the arguments he had retracted in Boston.

narrative_blocks.header: His son-in-law Elizur gave Holyoke its name
narrative_blocks.body: In 1640 he renamed Agawam for Springfield in Essex, the village he had left. His daughter Mary married Elizur Holyoke that same year, and the city of Holyoke and the mountain range above it still carry his name.

will.summary: Will of Lt. Benjamin Talcott, Glastonbury CT. Wife: £80 + use of parlor, cellar, garret, ovens, gardens, one-third of orchard and land west of highway to great river — during widowhood only. Son Benjamin: lands in Bolton + 124 acres Hebron (bought of Joseph and John Phelps). Son John: 300 acres Hebron (west of Jacob Root), 50 acres Hebron (north of Richard Curtis), one yoke of steers, £10 moveable, + £15 from Elizur. Son Samuel: south half of home lot, 153 acres beyond Black Ledge River (Glastonbury/Hebron border), half undivided Glastonbury lands, smith-shop with all smithery tools, longest gun, half team. Son Elizur: north half of home lot with all buildings (except smith-shop), 60 acres Ash Swamp Glastonbury, 96 acres near bare hill Glastonbury, other half undivided lands, newest gun, half team — he to pay John £15. Daughter Sarah: £100. Daughter Hannah: £100 + decent suit of clothes or £10. Daughter Mehitabel: £100 + decent suit of clothes or £10. Executors: son-in-law Jonathan Hale and son Benjamin Talcott. Witnesses: Samuel Smith Jr., Nathaniel Talcott, Thomas Wells. Estate inventory: £2563 15s. 8d.

narrative_blocks.header: His house bore bullet marks until 1854
narrative_blocks.body: He built a fortified wooden house on Main Street, Glastonbury in 1699 — a refuge from Indian attacks for the surrounding community. The house bore bullet marks until it was taken down soon after 1854.

narrative_blocks.header: Wife Sarah died in childbed at thirty-four
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah Hollister, granddaughter of original 1636 Hartford settler John Hollister, married him in 1699 and bore him eight children. She died in childbirth at the homestead October 15, 1715.

narrative_blocks.header: Sons signed Bolton's 1731 founding patent
narrative_blocks.body: Two of his sons Benjamin and Nathaniel were listed as Bolton Proprietors in the 1731 patent, signed by their cousin Governor Joseph Talcott. A third son Elizur later chaired Glastonbury's denunciation of the Boston Port Bill.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Wright cousins married two Talcott siblings
narrative_blocks.body: His son Elizur married Ruth Wright; his daughter Mehitabel married Ruth's first cousin Hezekiah Wright. Two Wright cousins thus married two Talcott siblings, weaving the families together.

narrative_blocks.header: Farm in family from 1643 through 1876
narrative_blocks.body: His grandfather John Talcott had bought the Glastonbury farm from Samuel Sherman and Richard Gildersleeve in 1643. The land was still owned by descendant Jared G. Talcott in 1876.

narrative_blocks.body: Her first husband was lost at sea in 1701, and for years the records assumed she had died with him. In fact she lived on, married a second time, and raised three children before her death a quarter-century later.

narrative_blocks.header: First Talcott in Bolton
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin Talcott was the first of the Glastonbury Talcotts to move to Bolton, farming land his father Deacon Benjamin had willed him in 1727. As a Bolton Proprietor (1731 patent), he received one-and-a-half parts — his holdings near Bolton Road and the quarry became the base from which the entire Bolton/Vernon line descends. He had twelve children by two wives — Esther Lyman and Deborah Gillett — "from whom most of the Bolton/Vernon line of Talcotts descends."

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve children seeded the Bolton Talcotts
narrative_blocks.body: Granted land in the 1731 Bolton patent, he farmed near the quarry and gave ground to his son beside it. Five children by his first wife and seven by his second became the root of nearly the whole Bolton and Vernon line of the family.

b. Dec 31, 1709 Glastonbury CT. Father: T00135 Deacon Benjamin Talcott. m. U00049 Ruth Wright (daughter of Daniel Wright Jr and Ellen Benton) Dec 31, 1730. Ruth died Sept 12, 1791 at homestead in Glastonbury aged 80 years 3 months. "She brought a large fortune to her husband which she inherited from her father who was a man of wealth." Son T01018 George served in Revolution with father and brothers. SOURCE: Talcott Pedigree 1876; Tankerhoosen Valley History.
d. Nov 24, 1797 Glastonbury CT aged "87 years 10 months and 25 days." Wealthy landowner — held land in various places including Connecticut Susquehanna River tract (lost to defect in title). Chairman of meeting denouncing Boston Port Bill in Glastonbury. Colonel of Troop of Horse before and during Revolution. Served on Long Island; in NYC when British marched in; taken home sick on a litter. Did not rejoin Continental Army. WRIGHT FAMILY NOTE: His wife Ruth Wright (U00049) was the first cousin of U00050 Hezekiah Wright who married his sister T00460 Mehitabel Talcott. Two Wright cousins married two Talcott siblings (children of T00135 Deacon Benjamin) in the same generation. Daniel Wright (Ruth's father) and James Wright Jr. (Hezekiah's father) were BROTHERS. BOLTON PROPRIETORS: Elizur's brother T00455 Benjamin was a Bolton Proprietor (1731 patent), along with Sgt. T00437 Nathaniel. Gov. Joseph Talcott (T00045) signed the patent. SOURCE: Talcott Pedigree 1876. MILITARY SERVICE UPDATE April 2026: Battle of Long Island (Aug 27, 1776). Colonel of the Sixth Connecticut Militia 1775-1776. At age 67 — relatively aged by military standards — present at the Battle of Long Island. Became ill during the campaign and was carried back to Glastonbury CT on a litter. Resigned his commission three months later (Nov 1776). DOC013: Holograph document signed by Col. Tallcott (= Talcott — common spelling variant) at Glastonbury CT June 12, 1776 to Captain Benjamin Wright of the Fourth Company, Sixth Regiment of the Colony of Connecticut, directing the election of a new Lieutenant after the previous one's resignation. On verso: note dated June 19, 1776 from Capt. Wright in Wethersfield reporting Solomon Buckley chosen Lieutenant. Choice ratified and signed by Titus Hosmer (CT delegate to Continental Congress, Articles of Confederation signer) for the Lower House, and George Wyllys (CT Secretary of State) for the Upper House. Captain Benjamin Wright later served as a lieutenant directly under George Washington. His son (also Benjamin Wright) is considered the Father of American Civil Engineering and was Chief Engineer for the building of the Erie Canal — interesting linkage to Andrew Talcott (T01807) who served as Adjunct Chief Engineer of the New York and Erie Railroad in 1836-37 and supervised much of Andrew Talcott's later canal/railroad work in similar engineering geography. George Wyllys's family held the Connecticut Secretary of State role for 96 consecutive years.

narrative_blocks.header: Chaired Glastonbury's denunciation of the Boston Port Bill
narrative_blocks.body: As chairman of the Glastonbury town meeting he led the formal denunciation of the Boston Port Bill — one of the acts that precipitated the Revolution. He already held a commission as Colonel of a Troop of Horse and would lead that troop into the field.

narrative_blocks.header: Carried home from Long Island on a litter
narrative_blocks.body: Present at the Battle of Long Island in August 1776 at age 67, he fell so ill during the campaign that he was carried back to Glastonbury on a litter. He resigned his commission three months later and never rejoined the Continental Army.

narrative_blocks.header: Lost a Susquehanna land claim in court
narrative_blocks.body: He held substantial Connecticut Susquehanna lands in Pennsylvania — claimed under Connecticut's sea-to-sea royal charter. He lost that investment entirely when the courts ruled against the Connecticut claim.

narrative_blocks.header: Wife Ruth brought a large fortune to him
narrative_blocks.body: His wife Ruth Wright brought a substantial fortune to the marriage, inherited from her wealthy father Daniel Wright Jr. They married on his 21st birthday — December 31, 1730 — and son George later served with him in the Revolution.

narrative_blocks.header: He lost four sons to black canker
narrative_blocks.body: Of Colonel Elizur Talcott's twelve children with Ruth Wright, four young sons died of what the family record called 'black canker' between 1748 and 1750. He twice gave a dead son's name to a later child, and only a handful of the twelve lived to marry.

military_service.unit: Sixth Connecticut Militia (Sixth Regiment, Colony of Connecticut)
military_service.notes: Colonel of the Sixth Connecticut Militia 1775-1776. At age 67, present at the Battle of Long Island (Aug 27, 1776). Became ill during the campaign and was carried back to Glastonbury CT on a litter; resigned his commission three months later. Surviving documentation: a holograph order signed by Col. Elizur Talcott in Glastonbury CT June 12, 1776 to Capt. Benjamin Wright of the Fourth Company directing election of a new Lieutenant — the document was signed off by Titus Hosmer for the Lower House (Continental Congress delegate and Articles of Confederation signer) and George Wyllys for the Upper House (Connecticut Secretary of State). See DOC013.

Commanded a Troop of horses raised at Glastonbury for service in the alarm for the relief of Fort William Henry and parts adjacent, August 1757. His unit included Hooker descendant Samuel Hooker Jr (H00228) for 14 days of service. Source: Berlin-Peck Memorial Library — Berlin in the French and Indian War 1753-1763.

narrative_blocks.header: Buried in rubble at a repeal celebration
narrative_blocks.body: On 23 May 1766 he was among twenty-eight men buried when Hartford's schoolhouse exploded — gunpowder set off during the town's celebration of the Stamp Act's repeal. He survived with severe burns to his face and arms; six others did not.

narrative_blocks.header: Dead mid-war, his young sons left behind
narrative_blocks.body: A Connecticut militia colonel, he died at Glastonbury in March 1780, squarely in the middle of the Revolution he had served. His sons Samuel and Nehemiah were just fifteen and thirteen, and his gravestone still stands at the Old Eastbury Cemetery.

narrative_blocks.header: Between a Deerfield dragoon and a Manila admiral
narrative_blocks.body: His colonel's commission was one link in a long Talcott military chain — his forebear had commanded the Connecticut dragoons at Deerfield in 1690, and his great-grandson would be Admiral George Dewey, victor of Manila Bay. Three wars and two centuries ran through one family line.

FATHER: Thomas Hart Pantry of West Hartford CT. At news of the Battle of Lexington, "gave freedom to his slave" and enlisted with a company of volunteers from Farmington. Joined the Continental Army near Boston; "sickened and died the following winter and was buried at Roxbury Mass." Her father was an abolitionist and Revolutionary War patriot who died in service. Abigail born Jan 23, 1770 West Hartford; died Mar 16, 1854 West Hartford aged 84. Buried Old Center Cemetery West Hartford (with husband T01389 Samuel Talcott). SOURCE: Talcott Pedigree 1876.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father's freed slave left her his estate
narrative_blocks.body: She was five when her father, Thomas Hart Hooker, freed his slave Bristow and marched off to the Revolution, never to return. Bristow, a free man, remembered the family in his will — leaving his estate to her and her brother, the children of the man who had freed him.

narrative_blocks.header: She spent all eighty-four years in West Hartford
narrative_blocks.body: In 1795 she married Samuel Talcott, a West Hartford clothier, and lived out her long life in the town where she was born — eighty-four years in all. She lies in the Old Center Cemetery beside him.

narrative_blocks.header: Three of Hartford's founding families meet in her
narrative_blocks.body: Through her Hooker father, her Pantry grandmother, and her marriage to a Talcott, she drew together three of Hartford’s founding families in a single line. Her people had helped settle the town from its very first years.

people.research_notes: b. Sep 3, 1745 Farmington CT; d. Nov 26, 1775 Roxbury MA age 30 — pleurisy, Siege of Boston. Son of Roger Hooker (H00302's father) and Mercy Hart Hooker. Named "Thomas Hart" for Hart family (maternal). Built home 1770 (Judah Woodruff, builder); moved to Sarah Whitman Hooker Homestead 1773, corner of South Main St and New Britain Ave, West Hartford — National Register of Historic Places. Enlisting in April/May 1775, he signed a Deed of Manumission for Bristow (an African man, age 44) on May 9, 1775 — Bristow PAID £60 (equivalent to 400 days' wages; ~$25,000 in 2004). Manumission document held at Connecticut Historical Society. Deed: "do by these presents fully freely and absolutely release manumit and set at full Liberty a Certain Negro man Named Bristow... that he may go & come when & wherever he pleases without any Hindrance or molestation from me or any one claiming from by or under me." Witnesses: Salomon Whitman, Mary Root. Bristow later willed his estate to Thomas's children Abigail and Thomas Hart Jr. A West Hartford middle school was named Bristow Middle School (2005) — believed first CT school named after a formerly enslaved person. Original homestead (now owned by Miss Porter's School, Farmington) is on Connecticut Freedom Trail — later owned by abolitionist Samuel Deming who sheltered Amistad survivors 1841. Court summons document: https://www.nativenortheastportal.com/digital-heritage/summons-thomas-hart-hooker Sarah Whitman Hooker Homestead: https://www.sarahwhitmanhooker.org/

narrative_blocks.header: He freed his slave before marching to war
narrative_blocks.body: In May 1775, as he prepared to join the Revolution, he signed a deed freeing Bristow, the enslaved man in his household — he would not, he said, own property in a human being while he himself fought for freedom. Two centuries later a West Hartford school was named for Bristow, thought to be the first Connecticut school named for a formerly enslaved person.

narrative_blocks.header: First to enlist, dead by winter
narrative_blocks.body: Among the first at Farmington to answer Lexington's call, he marched to the army besieging Boston. Within months he was dead — not by a bullet but of pleurisy, an inflammation of the lining of the lungs — and was buried among the soldier dead at Roxbury in a grave that was never found again.

narrative_blocks.header: The house he built still stands
narrative_blocks.body: In 1770 he built a fine house in West Hartford and moved his young family there. It outlived him by centuries — later a stop on the Underground Railroad, and now part of Miss Porter's School, it stands on Connecticut's Freedom Trail as the Sarah Whitman Hooker House, named for the widow he left behind.

narrative_blocks.header: The homestead still carries her name
narrative_blocks.body: When her husband died at war in 1775, she was left with two young children in the West Hartford house he had built. She stayed on and raised them there, and the house — now on Connecticut's Freedom Trail — bears her name to this day, the Sarah Whitman Hooker House.

narrative_blocks.header: Her family was tied to the Hookers already
narrative_blocks.body: Even before she married a Hooker, her line was entwined with theirs — her grandfather, Rev. Samuel Whitman, had followed Rev. Samuel Hooker in the Farmington pulpit, and descended himself from Thomas Hooker's sister. She married again in 1779, to Capt. Seth Collins, and lived to ninety.

narrative_blocks.header: He rejoined two of Hartford's founding lines
narrative_blocks.body: He was a Talcott, of the line that helped found Hartford alongside Thomas Hooker; his wife Abigail was a Hooker, of the founder's own family. Their marriage in 1795 drew the two old Hartford lines back together after five generations apart.

narrative_blocks.header: His shop stood in a fallen patriot's house
narrative_blocks.body: A clothier from Glastonbury, he and Abigail made their home in the Sarah Whitman Hooker house in West Hartford — the house her father had left to march to the Revolution and die. He later sold it to her uncle and settled nearby.

narrative_blocks.header: He lived in the Sarah Whitman Hooker homestead
narrative_blocks.body: A clothier by trade, he brought his bride, Abigail — a fifth-generation descendant of Thomas Hooker — to live in the Sarah Whitman Hooker homestead in West Hartford, a house that still stands. Her father, Thomas Hart, had freed his slave before marching off to the Revolution, saying he would not fight for liberty and leave a slave at home; he sickened and died that winter.

narrative_blocks.header: His fund founded a museum of American art
narrative_blocks.body: In 1903 he gave the New Britain Institute a fund restricted to original modern oil paintings — figure, landscape and genre subjects. Advised from New York that American pictures could still be had whole and cheap, the trustees bought American, beginning with a landscape by George Inness. What grew out of that restriction is the oldest museum in the country devoted solely to American art.

narrative_blocks.header: He sat behind Frederic Church at school
narrative_blocks.body: At Hartford Public High School he sat behind Frederic Edwin Church and set down a verdict the family still repeats: “He was not a very good student. He was always looking out the window and drawing.” The boy at the window became the great painter of the Hudson River School, and Talcott spent his last years endowing the purchase of American pictures.

narrative_blocks.header: Hooks and eyes paid for the paintings
narrative_blocks.body: He came to New Britain in 1851 and went into the plainest trade a manufacturing town had — hooks and eyes, and knit underwear. He ran the New Britain Knitting Company as treasurer and general manager for fourteen years, then founded the American Hosiery Company with his brother James and took its presidency in 1885. At the St. Louis fair of 1904 its goods carried off a silver medal.

narrative_blocks.header: A free reading room for the factory hands
narrative_blocks.body: He was one of the original incorporators of the New Britain Institute, which set out to put a free reading room and a library within reach of the men who worked the city's factories and the immigrant families arriving to fill them. He served on its building and finance committees, and was its president without a break from 1882 until he died.

narrative_blocks.header: Illness kept him from play, so he read
narrative_blocks.body: A serious illness in boyhood left him unable to join the other children at their games, and he turned to books instead. He was salutatorian of the Yale class of 1846, read law in a Hartford office, and tutored at Middlebury and then at Yale. Ill health kept him from ever practicing, and he went into business instead.

narrative_blocks.header: Every party wanted him for mayor
narrative_blocks.body: He sat on the New Britain common council, served three years as alderman, and was twice elected mayor of the city. Contemporaries noted that all parties united behind his candidacy, and reckoned his administration among the most successful New Britain had had.

narrative_blocks.header: From a wheelbarrow to a Civil War fortune
narrative_blocks.body: In 1854, eighteen-year-old James Talcott arrived in New York City pushing a wheelbarrow of undergarment samples for his brother's knitting mill. By the end of the Civil War — just eleven years later — he was a millionaire, having built a factoring house whose business grew sixteen-fold in four years of wartime demand.

narrative_blocks.header: 1907 Panic: silk top hat on Wall Street
narrative_blocks.body: When the Panic of 1907 struck, the 72-year-old James arrived on Wall Street in his long-outmoded silk top hat and frock coat, carrying a list of securities and a pencil. When the market recovered, his fortunes were greatly increased — he had never speculated in his life, so he had capital ready when others were ruined.

narrative_blocks.header: He bailed Republicans out of Tammany's jails
narrative_blocks.body: An ardent Republican since the birth of the party, James took every Election Day off. After voting, he went jail to jail across New York, bailing out any Republicans who had been locked up by corrupt Tammany Hall forces after being challenged at the polls.

narrative_blocks.header: Tithed ten percent of his income, every year
narrative_blocks.body: Throughout his career James gave at least a tenth of his income to charity. He funded Talcott Hall at Oberlin College (1887), an arboretum at Mount Holyoke, a library in West Hartford, and a hospital in China, and with Dwight L. Moody helped found Northfield Seminary in Massachusetts.

narrative_blocks.header: He spoke for peace at Lake Mohonk
narrative_blocks.body: James was a frequent speaker at the Lake Mohonk Conferences on International Arbitration, the peace and Native rights gatherings convened by the Smiley brothers from 1883 onward. He died at Lake Mohonk Mountain House on August 21, 1916, age eighty-one, in the community where he had spoken on peace for decades.

narrative_blocks.header: His desk and chair kept in the office
narrative_blocks.body: The firm kept his old desk at 225 Fourth Avenue long after he was gone, with a bound volume of letters written for its eightieth anniversary lying open on it. Visitors were allowed to turn the pages, and distinguished ones were sometimes asked to sit in his chair.

narrative_blocks.header: A Bible Society home built in his memory
narrative_blocks.body: After James's death in 1916, Henrietta funded a new Gothic-style home for the New York Bible Society in his memory -- the work of architect Wilfred E. Anthony. She died in December 1921, before it opened.

narrative_blocks.header: One of eleven women who founded Barnard
narrative_blocks.body: She was one of eleven women who launched Barnard College, the women's sister to Columbia, in 1889. Her fellow founding trustees included Laura Spelman Rockefeller and suffragist Annie Nathan Meyer, and she remained a Barnard trustee for thirty-two years until her death in 1921.

narrative_blocks.header: She walked the last block to meet him
narrative_blocks.body: A shrewd judge of character, she was the one person James Talcott confided in, and she staked her own inheritance in his commission house. Each evening her carriage stopped a block short so she could walk to the office door -- to arrive in it would have been ostentatious.

narrative_blocks.header: She ran her missions with daughter and daughter-in-law
narrative_blocks.body: She founded the Bible and Fruit Mission in 1900 and led it as president, drawing in her daughter Grace as a founding member and her daughter-in-law 'Frank' as treasurer. Her faith work ran through three generations of Talcott women.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father wed a Talcott before her mother
narrative_blocks.body: Her father, the Rev. Amzi Francis of Bridgehampton, first married James Talcott’s aunt Eliza -- a Talcott who died young. He then wed Mary Hedges, Henrietta’s mother; years later Henrietta married into that same Talcott family herself.

people.research_notes: Died Falmouth, Virginia, December 3, 1862. Belonged to the 10th Regiment Connecticut Volunteers. Civil War death, generation 9 from both Thomas Hooker and John Talcott. [Migrated from top-level military]: True [Pilot106 EH 1909 entry 3199]: Born March 13, 1842 at West Hartford CT. Eldest child of Samuel Talcott's third marriage to Margaret Lewis Sage. Per EH: 'He was a soldier of the 16th Regt. Conn. Volunteers.' Died December 3, 1862 at Falmouth, Virginia. The 16th CT had been at Antietam September 17, 1862 (their first battle). Falmouth VA was the Union staging ground opposite Fredericksburg; the Battle of Fredericksburg occurred December 11-15, 1862, ten days after Arthur's death. Most likely cause of death: disease in winter encampment. The middle name 'De Neufville' is unusual — possible Huguenot family connection to be researched. [Pilot110 enrichment]: Confirmed prepared for college at Ellington High School. Entered Yale College in 1859 as Class of 1863 member; left at end of second term of Freshman year (1859-1860). Mustered into Company A of the 16th Connecticut Volunteer Infantry as Private on July 14, 1862. WOUNDED at Antietam September 17, 1862 — survived. Returned to company. Died of fever in winter camp at Falmouth VA on December 3, 1862, age twenty. Made notable with primary URL https://antietam.aotw.org/officers.php?officer_id=5320 (Federal/USV; Antietam on the Web). Yale class sketch from https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=wu.89097686612&view=1up&seq=470 (A History of the Class of 1863, Yale College, 1905). Body returned home to West Hartford for burial at North Cemetery (CEM114, FindAGrave 60254408).

military_service.unit: Company A, 16th Connecticut Volunteer Infantry Regiment
military_service.notes: Mustered into Company A of the 16th Connecticut Volunteers as a Private on July 14, 1862, having left Yale College in the second term of his Freshman year. Wounded at the Battle of Antietam on September 17, 1862 — the regiment's first engagement, where they were thrown into combat with little training and suffered roughly twenty-five percent casualties. Arthur recovered and returned to his company. The exposure of army life impaired his health, and at winter camp at Falmouth Virginia an attack of fever ended his life on December 3, 1862. He was twenty years old.

narrative_blocks.header: Wounded at Antietam in his first battle
narrative_blocks.body: Arthur was mustered into Company A of the 16th Connecticut on 14 July 1862. Two months later the untrained regiment was thrown into Antietam, its first battle, and lost a quarter of its men; Arthur was wounded there and recovered.

narrative_blocks.header: Dead of fever at Falmouth at twenty
narrative_blocks.body: The exposure of army life broke his health, and on 3 December 1862 Arthur died of fever in camp at Falmouth, Virginia, days before the battle of Fredericksburg. He was twenty.

narrative_blocks.header: He left Yale after his freshman year
narrative_blocks.body: Arthur prepared at Ellington High School and entered Yale with the Class of 1863, but left after his freshman year. He enlisted in the summer of 1862.

narrative_blocks.header: A Talcott cousin rode with Lee at Antietam
narrative_blocks.body: Arthur's distant cousin Thomas Mann Randolph Talcott, like him a descendant of Deacon Benjamin Talcott of Glastonbury, rode as an aide to Robert E. Lee through the Maryland Campaign. At Antietam on 17 September 1862 the two cousins were on opposite sides of the field.

military_service.unit: 81st New York State Volunteer Infantry Regiment (Second Oswego Regiment, after consolidation with Mohawk Rifle Regiment)
military_service.notes: Captain in the 81st New York State Volunteer Infantry Regiment, known as the Second Oswego Regiment after its February 10, 1862 consolidation with the Mohawk Rifle Regiment. The regiment left the barracks at Albany NY for the seat of war on February 21, 1862. The 81st NY served through the Peninsula Campaign and the Siege of Petersburg. Specific battles in which Capt. Francis fought are not yet documented at the individual level.

burial.plot_notes: Bridgehampton Cemetery, Bridgehampton, Suffolk County NY. FindAGrave confirms.

narrative_blocks.header: Civil War captain; mother died age 33
narrative_blocks.body: Roger A. Francis served as a Civil War captain; his Bridgehampton merchant career and Stamford Connecticut residence followed his service. Born in May 1826 at Bridgehampton Long Island, he lost his mother Eliza Talcott Francis at age three when she died at thirty-three.

narrative_blocks.header: Captained Oswego volunteers from Albany to war
narrative_blocks.body: Roger A. Francis served as a Captain in the 81st New York State Volunteer Infantry Regiment, known as the Second Oswego Regiment after its February 1862 consolidation with the Mohawk Rifle Regiment. His regiment left the Albany barracks for the seat of war on February 21, 1862, and fought through the Peninsula Campaign and the Siege of Petersburg.

narrative_blocks.header: He was wounded at Cold Harbor
narrative_blocks.body: He was on the staffs of several general officers by then, and took his wound at Cold Harbor in the June of 1864. He came back to the regiment.

narrative_blocks.header: He enlisted a private and left a captain
narrative_blocks.body: He was thirty-six and already a major in the old 16th Regiment when it disbanded at the outbreak of war. He signed on again as a private with the 81st New York — the Mohawk Rangers — in the September of 1861, and was a captain before the end.

narrative_blocks.header: A steam flour mill before the war
narrative_blocks.body: At Bridgehampton he built a large steam flouring mill and ran it for some years. Capt. David Congdon bought it afterwards and moved the whole works away.

narrative_blocks.header: Afterwards he sold dry goods in New York
narrative_blocks.body: He went to New York when it was over and took a place with James Talcott's dry goods house. Talcott was his first cousin, and from 1860 his half-sister Henrietta's husband besides. A stroke of paralysis found him in later life, and he died in the Catskills at Stamford in 1885.

[2026-07-25] DEATH PLACE CORRECTED: a newspaper correction states he died 'at Stamford, in the Catskill mountains, on the 13th inst., instead of in New-York city, his place of business' — Stamford is in Delaware County NY, not Connecticut. Canonical previously said Bridgehampton (where he is buried). MUSTER AGE: the Town of Southampton roll gives him mustering in September 1861 'at the age of 36', which implies a birth of c.1825; canonical has 17 May 1826, making him 35. Not reconciled. Before the war he built and ran a large steam flouring mill at Bridgehampton, later bought by Capt. David Congdon and moved away, and was a Major in the old 16th Regiment under Col. P. R. Jennings. Suffered an attack of paralysis in later life.

narrative_blocks.body: Samuel Talcott Francis was born July 26, 1829 in Bridgehampton. His mother Eliza Talcott Francis died exactly twenty-two days later on August 17, almost certainly from post-partum complications. Samuel survived his mother by only 18 months, dying January 29, 1831.

narrative_blocks.header: Walked to Vermont with two oxen teams
narrative_blocks.body: In February or March 1789 Mary and Zachariah moved their family from Hebron Connecticut to Berlin Vermont — traveling up the Connecticut River with two teams of oxen, then up the White River, switching from wheels to runners at Brookfield, then over a blazed trail. They arrived to find their log cabin's roof had collapsed under three to four feet of snow.

narrative_blocks.header: Lost firstborn daughter Mary in 1798
narrative_blocks.body: Mary's eldest child — also named Mary, born in Hebron — died in 1798. Four months later another daughter was born and named Mary in her sister's memory. The second Mary later married Julius Yemans Dewey and was the mother of Admiral George Dewey, hero of Manila Bay 1898.

people.research_notes: T01387 — Mary Talcott Perrin. b. June 17, 1758 Glastonbury CT to Col. Samuel Talcott (T01001) and Mary Smith. d. September 11, 1828 Berlin Corners VT age 70. Married Zachariah Perrin (X01832, 1748-1838) ca.1779/1780 in Hebron CT. Buried Berlin Corner Cemetery (CEM176) alongside Zachariah. 9 children: first 4 born Hebron CT (Mary I 1781 d.1798; Betsey 1783 m. Rev. James Hobart [TD0120 built pilot98]; Samuel; Porter — first boy born in Berlin VT, built large house at Scott Hill/Airport Road intersection 1815) and last 5 born Berlin VT including the second Mary (Elizabeth Polly Perrin Dewey, m. Julius Yemans Dewey, mother of Admiral George Dewey, hero of Manila Bay 1898). Per family lore the second Mary was 'ashamed of having been born in a log cabin' and she and a sister later went up one night and burned the original cabin to the ground. Other 8 Perrin children NOT YET BUILT into JSON: Mary I (1781-1798 died_young), Samuel, Porter (Berlin first-boy, 1815 house at Scott Hill), Elizabeth Polly Perrin Dewey (Admiral Dewey's mother — major NOTABLE pending), and others. Admiral George Dewey himself flagged for next-batch build per Sam. T01001's research_notes pre-pilot98 already had: 'NOTABLE: Descendant line leads to Adm. George Dewey... Open research: confirm Dewey connection via Talcott line.' Pilot98 confirms the chain runs T01001 → T01387 → Elizabeth Polly Perrin Dewey → Julius Dewey + George Dewey (Admiral). SOURCES: WikiTree Talcott-49; Clark Univ genealogy rr23_395; Vermont Genealogy biography of Rev. James Hobart (which preserves the family history of the Berlin migration and the second Mary's story).

narrative_blocks.header: Lived eighty-nine years across nine American presidencies
narrative_blocks.body: Hannah was born in 1759 in colonial Glastonbury Connecticut and married Epaphras Hills at twenty-one in September 1780, while the Revolution was still being fought. She bore seven children spanning twenty-four years and died in East Hartford in 1848, during the year that ended the Mexican-American War.

Mar 30, 1771 Lanesboro) Aug 10, 1790. Moved to Lanesboro MA in May 1789. Tirzah d. Lanesboro Jul 15, 1848. Father of Nehemiah Platt Talcott (T01473). CROSS-CONNECTION: His granddaughter Catharine L. Talcott (T01488) married George Lyman Ingersoll, 7th-generation Hooker descendant. Their grandson Talcott Parsons (Harvard sociologist) was named "Talcott" in honor of this Talcott ancestry.[Pilot113 enrichment]: Capt. Nehemiah Talcott — 'Captain' title from FindAGrave and family records. Born August 5, 1766 in Glastonbury CT (age 9 at the start of the Revolution). Migrated west to Lanesborough in Berkshire County MA. Married Tirzah Platt of Lanesborough on August 10, 1790 — likely in Lanesborough, where the 1790 census shows him already living. Couple had ten documented children between 1790 and 1812. Both remained in Lanesborough until their deaths in 1848 — Tirzah on July 14, Nehemiah on October 13, three months apart. Buried Talcott Cemetery, Lanesborough.

narrative_blocks.header: Migrated to Lanesborough at twenty-four
narrative_blocks.body: Capt. Nehemiah Talcott was born in Glastonbury Connecticut in 1766 and migrated to Lanesborough Massachusetts by 1790 — the year of the first US Census, which shows him already living there. He married Tirzah Platt that August in her hometown and they raised ten children in Lanesborough. He died there in 1848 at eighty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: Died three months after his wife
narrative_blocks.body: Tirzah Platt Talcott died in Lanesborough on July 14, 1848 at seventy-seven. Capt. Nehemiah followed her exactly three months later on October 13, 1848 at eighty-two. They were buried together in Talcott Cemetery — the Lanesborough burying ground that bore the family name.

narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Williamstown in the summer of 1849, daughter of the Reverend James Alexander Hazen — Yale 1834, and pastor at Hanover, Connecticut — and his second wife Fanny Lucinda Grant. She was thirteen when her father died.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a man of fifty-five at thirty
narrative_blocks.body: She married John Butler Talcott at New Britain in March of 1880, his second wife and twenty-five years his junior. Their daughter Helen would carry his museum forward, giving it a gallery and a lifetime of patronage.

narrative_blocks.body: Her brother John died in the middle of August 1877; Ella was buried beside him before the month was out. Their mother followed within the year.

narrative_blocks.header: Twice widowed, then twenty-four years alone
narrative_blocks.body: May Churchill died in 1919, leaving him four daughters, the youngest not yet ten. He married Elizabeth Norton in 1924 and buried her in 1933, and lived on at Avon another twenty-four years.

narrative_blocks.body: He was eight in the August his brother and sister died, and his mother was gone by the next spring. Of the four children of that marriage he was the only one to reach old age.

burial.plot_notes: The New Britain Museum of American Art, which she helped sustain and benefited throughout her life, is nearby.

narrative_blocks.header: Family called the museum her real love
narrative_blocks.body: She painted in watercolor herself, but it was her father's museum she gave a lifetime to. Family says it was the real love of her life.

narrative_blocks.header: She answered her father's gift with her own
narrative_blocks.body: Sixty years after her father endowed the museum, she gave it a wing of its own. It went up in the name of her husband Philip, who died in 1963 — the Helen T. and Philip B. Stanley Gallery, at the top of the stairs.

narrative_blocks.header: The founder's family never left the board
narrative_blocks.body: From the year her father endowed it, someone of the family sat on the museum's board, and she was the hinge between the founding and everything that came after. Her son Talcott served as an honorary trustee; a granddaughter-in-law was still a board member emeritus a century on.

narrative_blocks.header: She buried two daughters before the war ended
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth died in 1930, at nine years old. Jeanne, the eldest, was twenty-nine when she died in 1942. Frances and Talcott outlived their mother, and it was through Frances that the family kept its place at the museum.

narrative_blocks.header: Vassar, two years behind her sister
narrative_blocks.body: She graduated from Vassar in 1905. Her older sister Florence had gone before her.

narrative_blocks.header: Her marriage joined two old Connecticut names
narrative_blocks.body: In 1911 she married Philip Stanley of New Britain. The Talcotts had made the city's knit goods; the Stanleys made its tools, and their name is on them still.

narrative_blocks.body: His father co-founded the Stanley Rule and Level Company, and the name went out on hand tools the world over. Philip was born in New Britain, the town it built.

narrative_blocks.header: A gallery at the museum carries his name
narrative_blocks.body: He married Helen Hooker Talcott in 1911. After he died in 1963 she gave the New Britain Museum of American Art a gallery in both their names.

narrative_blocks.header: His middle name was his mother's maiden name
narrative_blocks.body: Bartholomew was his mother's family name before she married into the Stanleys, and he carried it in the middle of his own.

narrative_blocks.header: Her daffodils won national recognition
narrative_blocks.body: A lifelong member of the Garden Club of Hartford, she built a daffodil collection that drew both local and national recognition. She was a birdwatcher, a skier and a tennis player besides.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years of Gulf Stream crossings
narrative_blocks.body: She and Jack Stout began cruising to the Bahamas in 1966 in a forty-foot ketch they called Anne Bonny, and in 1972 bought a house on Man-O-War Cay in the Abacos and gave it the same name. After his death in 1994 she went on sailing there alone until 2006.

narrative_blocks.header: She went to the ball as a lobster
narrative_blocks.body: Talked into a fancy dress ball at the Misquamicut Club with nothing prepared, she pinned the shells from her own dinner party to a sheet and wore them. It was a warm evening, and her dance card stayed strangely empty.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept singing at her own parties
narrative_blocks.body: The lobster did not cost her the invitations. She went on giving musicales at Ridgecrest on Ridge Road at Watch Hill, the house first called The Arches for the porches that ran round it, and sang at them herself.

narrative_blocks.header: She had Mott Schmidt build her a house
narrative_blocks.body: In 1929 she and Walter Hope came from 123 East 80th Street into a townhouse Mott B. Schmidt put up for them at 43 East 70th. He was the architect who had just turned Sutton Place from a squalid stretch of riverfront into an enclave, for Anne Morgan and Anne Vanderbilt.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed young, remarried at twenty-eight
narrative_blocks.body: John Leete Rogers was twenty-five when he died at Englewood in December 1905, three years into the marriage. She married Walter Ewing Hope in April 1909 and stayed married to him for nearly forty.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived him by twenty-one years
narrative_blocks.body: Hope was a Milbank, Tweed partner who had been Assistant Secretary of the Treasury under Hoover; he died suddenly in 1948 on the August train up from Westerly. She sold the house to Maurice Wertheim, took an apartment at 765 Park Avenue, and died at Brooklyn in 1969.

Compiler's maternal grandmother. Born 1914 to Walter Ewing Hope (X02362) and Florence Hazen Talcott (TD0055). Vassar College student. Made her social debut 1930 at the Colony Club, hosted by her parents at 43 East 70th Street, New York. Married twice: first to David Edward Austen (X02363) at Madison Avenue Presbyterian Church 18 March 1938, with three children David Jr. (TD0106), Hope Austen Page (TD0107), and Lea Austen Hooker (TD0057, compiler's mother). After divorce from David, she married William Creighton 'Tony' Peet Jr. (X02364) and moved to San Francisco; one son with him, William Creighton Peet III (TD0108, 1957-2018). Died September 2000 as 'Helen Hope Peet'.
[NAMING NOTE]: Display name reflects her name at death (Peet, her second married surname). Maiden name Hope (her father Walter's surname). Middle name Talcott honors the maternal Talcott line per the family naming pattern.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Made her social debut here in 1930; her 1938 wedding reception followed at the house.

narrative_blocks.header: New York wedding, then a Washington household
narrative_blocks.body: She married Ned Austen at the Madison Avenue Presbyterian Church in March 1938 and went with him to Washington. Their three children came between 1939 and 1946 and were raised there. The marriage ended in divorce.

narrative_blocks.header: A fourth child eleven years after the third
narrative_blocks.body: Only after the divorce did she go out to California, where she married Creighton Peet - a vice president of Oceanic Steamship at San Francisco, and of Safeway from 1959. Their son was born in 1957, eleven years after Lea.

narrative_blocks.header: From a tea dance to a final reception
narrative_blocks.body: Her debutante season ran from late 1930 into 1931 - a tea dance at the Colony Club given by her parents, a dinner at 43 East 70th Street in January, and a last reception at the house that December. She was at Vassar.

narrative_blocks.header: Her wedding notice printed two colonial governors
narrative_blocks.body: She was married in 1938 under a New York Times notice that set out her descent from John Talcott and Thomas Hooker, which was not usual for a wedding announcement. Her middle name carries the same line.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at Sugar Bowl, with four grown children
narrative_blocks.body: She was widowed in February 1982, when Creighton Peet died of a heart attack skiing at Sugar Bowl. Her four children were by then in San Francisco, Palo Alto and New York. She lived on until September 2000.

narrative_blocks.header: Husband served under her Hooker cousin in 1777
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband Ichabod Norton was at Skenesborough, Fort Ann and Ticonderoga in 1776, and at Peekskill in the spring of 1777 under Colonel Noadiah Hooker — her first cousin once removed in the Hooker line. He rose to major.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Ruths — only one survived past four
narrative_blocks.body: Her parents' first daughter Ruth had died at age four on September 6, 1736; she was born three years later in 1739 and given the same name. Replacement naming was a common Puritan practice when an infant died young, but it left the second Ruth carrying her dead sister's identity for life.

narrative_blocks.header: Two siblings married two siblings — one ceremony
narrative_blocks.body: On November 9, 1768 in Farmington, Cyprian Strong married Sarah Bull, and his sister Elizabeth Strong married Sarah's brother Martin Bull — both weddings on the same day. Two Strong siblings and two Bull siblings, bound together in a single ceremony.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-six years keeping the town's book
narrative_blocks.body: Uxbridge's clerk for twenty-six years and a deacon of its church — an office his granddaughter Rhoda's husband Aaron Taft would hold in his turn. Grindal Rawson, Mendon's minister, was his father.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Rawson stones lost in one move
narrative_blocks.body: Buried at Uxbridge Center in 1768, he was moved to Prospect Hill a century later, and the gravestone did not survive; his son Abner's stone was lost in the same removal. Father and son lie marked only by the record.

narrative_blocks.header: His two sons each married an Allen sister
narrative_blocks.body: Both his sons Edmund and Abner married daughters of the same Allen family of Medway — Martha Allen and Mary Allen respectively. He was Deacon Edmund Rawson of Uxbridge; his sons' double Allen marriage kept the two families closely bound across a generation.

narrative_blocks.header: She gave the name Grindal twice
narrative_blocks.body: Rachel bore Edward twelve children between 1636 and 1661. Their son Grindal, born in January 1649, died young, and she gave the name again to the son born in January 1659, who became the minister of Mendon; her daughter Hannah died at two in May 1656, six days after another daughter, Rebecca, was born.

narrative_blocks.header: From Gillingham to Newbury
narrative_blocks.body: Rachel was born at Gillingham in Dorset about 1618, married Edward Rawson about 1636 when she was still very young, and went with him to Newbury in Massachusetts the next year. Her widowed mother, dying at Gillingham in 1656, left a legacy to her daughter Rachel Rawson in New England.

narrative_blocks.header: A cousin of Thomas Hooker
narrative_blocks.body: Rachel's grandfather John Hooker was an uncle of the Rev. Thomas Hooker, which made her the founder's first cousin once removed. Her son Grindal later married Susanna Wilson, of the Hooker line.

narrative_blocks.header: Her first husband died leaving her pregnant
narrative_blocks.body: William Hooker died in 1689. Susanna gave birth to their daughter Susannah in June 1690 — born into a fatherless household. She then remarried John Blackleach, a noted Hartford merchant.

narrative_blocks.header: Daughter of Deacon Benjamin Fenn of Milford
narrative_blocks.body: Susanna was a daughter of Benjamin Fenn by his second wife, Susanna Wade, and half-sister to Martha Fenn Newton. She married William Hooker of Farmington in the 1680s.

narrative_blocks.header: She remarried the merchant John Blackleach
narrative_blocks.body: Widowed when William Hooker died in 1689, Susanna married John Blackleach, a prominent Hartford merchant. She died about 1698.

narrative_blocks.header: He came of Salisbury’s tanner-grantee family
narrative_blocks.body: Paul Batt was born a twin at Salisbury in 1643, into the family of Christopher Batt — a tanner and one of the town’s twelve original grantees, who had crossed from Wiltshire on the ship Bevis in 1638, slipping out just ahead of the King’s ban on sailings.

narrative_blocks.header: His father died in a freak shooting
narrative_blocks.body: When Paul was a young man his father was accidentally shot and killed by another of his sons, who had been firing at a target in the family orchard at Boston.

narrative_blocks.header: He left his shop to his daughter
narrative_blocks.body: Paul married Sarah Wilson in 1674 and died in 1678 at about thirty-five; his will left his Boston tenement and shop to his infant daughter Sarah, charged with the support of his widowed mother.

narrative_blocks.header: The town granted him land for damning
narrative_blocks.body: Josiah and his brother Angel took a saw-mill site on School Creek at Mendon, and the town allowed them "so much land as shall be thought necessary for damning" — the old spelling of damming.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the minister's widowed daughter
narrative_blocks.body: In 1680 Josiah married Sarah Wilson at Medfield — daughter of Rev. John Wilson Jr. and Sarah Hooker, and widow of the Boston merchant Paul Batt. A year later they were keeping house in Boston.

narrative_blocks.header: He moved six times in eighty-two years
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Weymouth about 1650, Josiah lived at Boston, then Mendon from 1685, Bristol from about 1696, Barrington from 1717, and Mansfield in Connecticut from 1726, where he died in 1732.

narrative_blocks.header: Barrington made him town clerk at seventy-four
narrative_blocks.body: Josiah was assessor of Barrington in 1720, 1723 and 1724, town clerk in that last year, and constable in 1725. In 1726 the town put him on the committee to divide the ministers' lots from the school lots.

narrative_blocks.header: Mendon kept calling it the Torrey place
narrative_blocks.body: The ground Josiah and Angel settled at Mendon was known as the Capt. Bill Torrey Place long after they had gone. He sold his half to Francis Green of Woburn and never came back to live.

narrative_blocks.header: His father crossed in 1640 and stayed
narrative_blocks.body: Josiah was a son of William Torrey of Weymouth, who married Elizabeth Frye there about 1640 and died in 1690 at eighty-two. Every Torrey in this tree comes down from that house.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother Angel fathered a president’s mother
narrative_blocks.body: Angel Torrey, who bought the Mendon land and ran the sawmill with him, has a line that reaches Louise Torrey of Millbury six generations on — the mother of William Howard Taft.

narrative_blocks.header: Dunstable's first minister
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas began preaching at Dunstable on 1 May 1679, gathered its church, the fifth within the bounds of today's New Hampshire, and was ordained on 16 December 1685. The town built a larger meeting-house as the settlement grew.

narrative_blocks.header: King William's War emptied two thirds of Dunstable
narrative_blocks.body: From 1691 Indian raids in King William's War so frightened his congregation that near two thirds of Dunstable moved away, and his preaching stopped for two years or more. He stayed on at one of the most exposed frontier towns.

narrative_blocks.header: Harvard, then divinity with Danforth
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas graduated from Harvard in 1671 and studied divinity with Rev. Samuel Danforth of Roxbury. In 1681 he built his house on Dunstable's thirty-acre ministerial lot, with six hundred acres of common land besides.

narrative_blocks.header: Two infant sons, then his wife
narrative_blocks.body: In 1681 Thomas married Elizabeth Wilson, a granddaughter of Thomas Hooker. Their sons Eleazer and John died as infants in 1686, and Elizabeth died the next summer. In 1700 he married Mary Savage of Boston.

narrative_blocks.header: Thoreau stopped at his grave
narrative_blocks.body: Passing the old Dunstable graveyard in July 1858, Henry David Thoreau noted that Mr. Weld's monument was a large, thick, naturally flat rock, lying flat over the grave.

narrative_blocks.header: A man well beloved and much lamented
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas died on 7 June 1702, at forty-nine, as Queen Anne's War began; his stone says he was probably killed defending the settlement. A diarist called him “an eminent preacher of the word of god.”

career.notes: Represented Deerfield at session beginning May 23, 1689, after deposition of Sir Edmund Andros.

Began preaching 1679; ordained Dec 16, 1685. 5th church organized within limits of NH. Ministry disrupted by King William's War (Indian hostilities beginning 1691); near two thirds of inhabitants moved away. Died at beginning of Queen Anne's War, June 7, 1702.

narrative_blocks.header: His uncle handed him thirty acres in 1699
narrative_blocks.body: Rev. Samuel Torrey gave his nephew all his Weymouth real estate: the land east of North Street, running from East Street around Burying Hill to Neck Street — some thirty acres, with smaller parcels besides.

narrative_blocks.header: Deacon on the stone, husbandman in the papers
narrative_blocks.body: The town records and his gravestone both set "Deacon" before his name, as they had before his father's. The papers administering his estate call him plainly a husbandman.

narrative_blocks.header: He was buried inside his uncle's gift
narrative_blocks.body: Micajah died September 29, 1722, aged forty-nine, and he and Sarah were buried in the older half of Burying Hill — ground that lay inside the thirty acres his uncle had deeded him.

narrative_blocks.header: Guardians were set over five of his children
narrative_blocks.body: On May 30, 1726 the court placed Paul at twenty and James at thirteen with their uncle-in-law Samuel French, David at eleven and William with their uncle Joshua Torrey, and Sarah at sixteen with her stepfather.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty years crossing the ocean wide
narrative_blocks.body: His tombstone says it: near fifty years crossing the ocean wide. He commanded the Desire in 1661 and the John and James in 1679, ran the Barbados trade through Winthrop's correspondence — where an anxious 1658 letter feared him either missed at the island or foundered in the sea — and came home every time.

narrative_blocks.header: He sailed for Hooker's own companions
narrative_blocks.body: His commerce partners were men of the founding itself — John Pynchon of Springfield, Elder William Goodwin of Hartford, and his wife's father John Crow, who had walked the wilderness with Rev. Thomas Hooker in 1636 and whose name stands on the Founders Monument. Giles married into the migration.

narrative_blocks.header: His name rode down two centuries
narrative_blocks.body: Lt. Giles Hooker, his Farmington grandson, carried the name first; Rev. Giles Hooker Cowles took it to the Western Reserve; two more followed, the last falling at Petersburg in 1864. One mariner's Christian name, five bearers, nearly two hundred years.

narrative_blocks.header: A drum for the train-band
narrative_blocks.body: Middletown made him rate maker, levy-man, townsman; he gave the town a drum for its train-band in 1666, and the homestead he bought at Main and Washington in 1679 housed four generations of the family. The 1689 epidemic took him.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughters seeded two dynasties
narrative_blocks.body: Mary married Noadiah Russell, Middletown's minister and a Yale founder; Mehitabel married a son of Farmington's Rev. Samuel Hooker. When Mary's son wed the Farmington minister's granddaughter in 1719, the captain's blood stood on both sides of the altar.

narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin Fenn’s second wife, Susannah Ward, outlived him and in her 1674 will declared her intent to sail home to Worcester, England, where her aged mother was still living.

narrative_blocks.header: Land beyond the Concord, and the Training Field
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas inherited 533 acres of his father's grants lying beyond the Concord River, and sold them in 1667 to John Alcock, the Roxbury physician. At home he owned Roxbury's Training Field.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the daughter of Lynn's minister
narrative_blocks.body: In 1650 Thomas married Dorothy Whiting, daughter of Rev. Samuel Whiting, the minister for whom the town of Lynn was renamed. Their son Thomas became the first minister of Dunstable.

narrative_blocks.header: Son of Roxbury's first pastor
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas's father, Rev. Thomas Welde, was ordained pastor of Roxbury in 1632, was one of the chief inquisitors at Anne Hutchinson's trial, and in 1639 helped make the Bay Psalm Book. He went back to England in 1641.

narrative_blocks.header: His father's letter home to Terling
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas's father wrote home to Terling praising New England's corn, salt and cattle, and claimed no one had died on the crossing. The country, he wrote, was “as goodly a land as ever mine eyes beheld.”

narrative_blocks.header: The minister Lynn was named for
narrative_blocks.body: Dorothy's father, Rev. Samuel Whiting, came from King's Lynn in 1636 to be the first pastor at Saugus, which renamed itself Lynn in his honor. An Emmanuel College man, he became an overseer of Harvard in 1654.

narrative_blocks.header: Half-sister of Billerica's first minister
narrative_blocks.body: Dorothy's half-brother Samuel Whiting Jr. was Billerica's first settled minister, for fifty years. His mother, their father's second wife, was a sister of Oliver St. John, Cromwell's chief justice.

narrative_blocks.header: The only man to govern both New Haven
narrative_blocks.body: He served Guilford as town clerk from 1639, rose to Governor of New Haven Colony (1661-1664), and then Governor of the Colony of Connecticut (1676-1683) — the only person ever to hold both offices. He is buried at the Ancient Burying Ground in Hartford — the same ground as Thomas Hooker.

narrative_blocks.header: He used the Sabbath and slow horses
narrative_blocks.body: When royal agents arrived demanding the regicides Goffe and Whalley, he read the King's warrant aloud in public — alerting everyone to the agents' purpose — then furnished horses so slowly that the Sabbath intervened before they could depart. By Monday the men were hidden. Roger Newton did the same in Milford; Roger Hooker did the same in Hartford — three men in the same civic network, the same year.

narrative_blocks.header: Two granddaughters married Hookers
narrative_blocks.body: Mary, his eldest son's daughter, married Judge James Hooker of Guilford. Mercy, his son Andrew's daughter, married Samuel Hooker of the same town. The two women were first cousins and the two branches have run separately ever since.

narrative_blocks.header: One of Guilford's founding settlers
narrative_blocks.body: Leete left England in 1639 to escape the persecution of Puritans he had witnessed as a court clerk. He was among the twenty-five who signed the plantation covenant at sea and helped found Guilford, becoming one of the seven pillars of its church.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept Guilford's records for over twenty years
narrative_blocks.body: Leete served as town clerk of Guilford from 1639 until 1662, alongside terms as magistrate and deputy. The long climb through colony offices carried him eventually to the governorship.

narrative_blocks.header: Master of Arts, and dead six days later
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas took his Harvard degree in 1701 and his master's at Commencement on 15 July 1704, arguing whether a willing man can be wronged. Six days later he died at his uncle Wilson's house in Braintree, unmarried and without children.

narrative_blocks.header: A boyhood of war whoops
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas was born in the fortified parsonage at Dunstable and grew up through King William's War, until even his father's family fled to Boston. In 1702 Chelmsford hired him as its schoolmaster for half a year.

narrative_blocks.header: Judge Sewall rode to his funeral
narrative_blocks.body: Judge Samuel Sewall rode in a calash to Thomas's burial from his uncle Weld's house at Roxbury on 22 July 1704, and noted in his diary that Mr. Walter prayed in the orchard.

narrative_blocks.body: Mercy Leete, whom he married in 1711, was the granddaughter of Governor William Leete of Connecticut Colony. His uncle James Hooker had also married a Leete granddaughter — Mary Leete, Mercy's first cousin through the same Governor. narrative_blocks.header: His death at 96 killed his brother Samuel
narrative_blocks.body: On February 19, 1787, Giles Hooker died in Farmington at age 96. When the news reached his older brother Samuel — then age 98 in Kensington — Samuel "fell back in his chair and expired" on March 1, 1787. In Edward Hooker's time (1909), a flat stone in the sidewalk just below the brow of the hill still covered the old well of the Giles Hooker house. Directly opposite, his father Rev.
