narrative_blocks.header: Married Yale's first B.A. graduate
narrative_blocks.body: On December 6, 1720 she married Rev. John Hart of East Guilford as his third wife. Hart had been Yale's first B.A. graduate (1703) and second tutor — succeeding her uncle Daniel Hooker, who had been Yale's first tutor.

narrative_blocks.header: Three of her six children survived to marry
narrative_blocks.body: With John Hart she had six children — four sons and two daughters. Two sons died young and infant Mary lived only three months. Sons Thomas (1723-1813) and Benjamin (1725-1804) carried the line, while daughter Sarah married three times — twice to Yale graduates.

narrative_blocks.header: Fillis passed to her when her husband died
narrative_blocks.body: Fillis was enslaved by the Rev. John Hart at East Guilford until his death in 1731, and passed then to Mary as his widow. Mary lived another twenty-five years.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Hooker sisters married two Smith brothers
narrative_blocks.body: She married Thomas Smith; her sister Mehitable married his brother John, the physician-minister. Two daughters of Judge James Hooker of Guilford paired with two English-born Smith brothers, doubling the families' tie in one generation.

enslaved_persons.name: Peleg
enslaved_persons.description: Enslaved man. Bequeathed in Sarah's will to daughter Anna Ruggles, then to grandson Nathaniel Ruggles Jr. if unsold at Anna's death. Probate inventory lists "Negro boy Peleg, 65 pounds."
enslaved_persons.source: Sarah Hooker Bartlett probate, Guilford, Connecticut

burial.plot_notes: Old North Cemetery, Guilford CT; grave marker effaced. SOURCE: FindAGrave.

narrative_blocks.header: Her will bequeathed an enslaved man named Peleg
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah Hooker Bartlett's will, proved after her death in 1769, left to her daughter an enslaved man named Peleg, listed among the property of her Guilford estate.

narrative_blocks.header: Peleg went from her to her daughter
narrative_blocks.body: Peleg was enslaved by Sarah at Guilford and passed to her daughter Anna and her son-in-law Dr. Nathaniel Ruggles. He was still living after 1794.

burial.plot_notes: Alderbrook Cemetery, Guilford, New Haven County, Connecticut

narrative_blocks.header: Yale graduate, dead at twenty-one
narrative_blocks.body: He graduated Yale around 1722 and died March 20, 1724 in Guilford at age 21, unmarried. Edward Hooker noted he 'died unmarried, leaving no one to perpetuate his name.'

narrative_blocks.header: The last Hooker of the Guilford line
narrative_blocks.body: He was the only son of Hon. James Hooker, the Probate Judge of Guilford. With his early death, the Hooker surname disappeared from Guilford within a single generation of arriving.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandsons ran Washington's spies
narrative_blocks.body: Her daughter Susannah's son Benjamin Tallmadge ran Washington's intelligence network, and another of Susannah's sons, William, died on a British prison ship. A third daughter, Abigail, married Jacob Purdy, whose White Plains farmhouse Washington took for a headquarters.

narrative_blocks.header: Two founding lines met in her
narrative_blocks.body: Mehitable Hooker descended from Thomas Hooker, founder of Hartford, on her father's side, and from William Leete, the governor who hid the judges of Charles I, on her mother's.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Hooker sisters married two Smith brothers
narrative_blocks.body: Mehitable married Rev. Dr. John Smith of Rye in May 1724; her sister Hannah married his brother Thomas in the same years. Two daughters of James Hooker of Guilford doubled the tie between the families.

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve children across Rye and White Plains
narrative_blocks.body: She raised twelve children between Rye and White Plains while her husband kept a pulpit and a medical practice. He was called Dr. Smith as often as Reverend, and was known for treating the mentally ill when few would.

narrative_blocks.header: She buried a newborn, then Micajah, in 1722
narrative_blocks.body: A daughter was born and died on August 5, 1722. Micajah was dead seven weeks later, on September 29, leaving Sarah with five sons and a daughter still at home.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother had married her husband's uncle
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah's widowed mother, Sarah Willson Batt, married Josiah Torrey — uncle of the Micajah Torrey Jr. whom Sarah herself married about 1703. Her stepfather and her father-in-law were brothers.

narrative_blocks.header: Her new husband became her daughter's guardian
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah married Deacon Samuel White of Braintree on October 23, 1725. Seven months later the court made him guardian of her sixteen-year-old daughter Sarah, while two uncles took the four boys.

narrative_blocks.header: Her stone says eighty-five; she was ninety
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Boston in January 1673 and dead at Weymouth in May 1763, Sarah lived ninety years and three months. The stone on Burying Hill reads "in ye 85th year of her age."

narrative_blocks.header: The estate waited forty-one years for her
narrative_blocks.body: Micajah's estate was not finally divided until April 1765, when the court noted that "the widow of Micajah Torrey being dead," the shares could go to the children. She had outlived him by forty-one years.

narrative_blocks.header: Alive in 1726, alive in 1763, then nothing
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel stood first among the children in the 1726 division of his father's estate, and was still living in 1763. No record of a marriage or a death survives for the eldest of the nine.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought out his siblings’ shares
narrative_blocks.body: Paul Torrey gathered to himself the inherited shares of his brothers James and William and his sister Sarah Whitmarsh before his own death in 1763.

narrative_blocks.header: She and her daughter died nine days apart
narrative_blocks.body: Eunice Whitmarsh died at Abington on May 5, 1753, seven years old. Sarah followed on May 14, at forty-two. She left Thomas with six of their nine children still living.

narrative_blocks.header: A burial and two births in 1756
narrative_blocks.body: Micaiah Torrey died in 1756, a year old. Jacob and Jane were born the same year. James himself was dead by July 18 at Ashford in Connecticut, leaving Sarah with nine.

narrative_blocks.header: Three of their names were used twice
narrative_blocks.body: A Jacob came in 1741 and another in 1756, a James in 1743 and another in 1752, a Micajah in 1749 and a Micaiah in 1755. The first of each pair leaves no death on record.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote down a meteor, and named Groton
narrative_blocks.body: Rowing his boat to Groton in October 1665 he saw a large meteor and set it down in writing. That note is the first known written reference to the town of Groton, Connecticut.

narrative_blocks.header: He owned the ketch Hartford
narrative_blocks.body: He traded up the Connecticut rivers and along the Sound as owner and master both, and sold the brigantine Tryall out of New London in 1683. His descendants kept the Barbados run for two more generations.

narrative_blocks.header: Constable, then marshal of the county
narrative_blocks.body: New London made him constable in 1669, and he was marshal of the county — its sheriff — from 1690 until he died in 1696. He kept an inn on the side, the licence renewed in 1687.

narrative_blocks.header: He rode the dispatches in King Philip’s War
narrative_blocks.body: In January 1676 he carried dispatches from New London to the Governor at Hartford, and was granted land for the service at Voluntown and Preston. Six years earlier he had run letters between Governor Winthrop at Hartford and Governor Lovelace at New York.

narrative_blocks.header: Disinherited in Essex, he came over
narrative_blocks.body: He was disinherited by George Plumbe of Inworth in Essex and came over in his early twenties. A Hartford deposition of July 1666, in which he gave his age as about thirty-two, is what fixes his birth to 1634.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought a woman named Jenny Already
narrative_blocks.body: The New London town records have him buying an African woman called Jenny Already in 1685. Two years before that the town had given him a lot at Main and State for his work as an attorney.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept the ship-masters’ anniversary feasts
narrative_blocks.body: He hosted the anniversary feasts of the New London ship-masters, which Gurdon Saltonstall wrote about to Governor Winthrop through the 1690s. Nine children were born to him and Elizabeth Green.

career.role: Inspector of the lading of vessels

narrative_blocks.header: A Cambridge printer’s daughter
narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Cambridge in 1640 to Samuel Green, the printer who set the Eliot Indian Bible, the first Bible printed in America, and to Jane Bainbridge. She married John Plumbe in 1662 and bore nine children.

narrative_blocks.header: She joined the New London church in 1691
narrative_blocks.body: Two of her half-brothers, Jonas and Deacon Timothy Green, had settled at New London before her, which is part of why the family left Hartford. She joined the First Church there in 1691 and outlived her husband by twenty-five years.

narrative_blocks.header: The whole family entered the church covenant
narrative_blocks.body: On April 1, 1711, she and Samuel were admitted to full communion in the Milford church on the same day their two eldest children, Phebe and Samuel, were baptized. A single Sunday that sealed the whole family into the covenant at once.

narrative_blocks.header: Her sister married her husband’s cousin
narrative_blocks.body: Phebe married Samuel Newton; her sister Hannah married Samuel's first cousin Fletcher Newton. Two Platt sisters wed two Newton first cousins — the families of Milford knit together across one generation.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father took the fort at night
narrative_blocks.body: In 1671 Joseph Platt and three companions destroyed the Wepawaug fort with the utmost secrecy, at dead of night. He was lieutenant of the eldest train band at Milford by 1698 and left no will when he died.

narrative_blocks.header: The deacon's Bibles reached her father
narrative_blocks.body: Deacon Richard Platt, her grandfather, left his whole estate to her father Joseph and made him executor. He had already given a Bible to each of his nineteen grandchildren the year before.

narrative_blocks.header: Married his first cousin Phebe Platt
narrative_blocks.body: He married Phebe Platt, his first cousin: his mother was Phebe Platt and his wife was Phebe Platt, both granddaughters of Joseph Platt of Milford. The two women shared their grandfather, their first name, and their last name.

narrative_blocks.header: Died three days after his wife
narrative_blocks.body: Phebe died April 26, 1756; Jonah died three days later on April 29. Their son Jonah Jr. was about eleven years old. Edward Hooker records both dates in the same entry without comment on the coincidence.

narrative_blocks.header: Tombstone rank 'Sergt.' — daughter went to Vermont
narrative_blocks.body: His tombstone identifies him by the military rank 'Sergt.' — sergeant. His son Jonah Jr. was eleven when he died; his daughter Phebe later married Oliver Sanford and removed to Poultney, Vermont.

narrative_blocks.header: Brainerd: 'no more grace than a chair'
narrative_blocks.body: David Brainerd said it of him in 1742, and Yale expelled the student for it. Whittlesey was then a tutor of twenty-four, son of the man who led Connecticut's Old Lights — the party the revival was fighting.

narrative_blocks.header: He thought himself unfit to preach
narrative_blocks.body: Amity Parish wanted him as its candidate before he was even licensed, and he refused, writing in his diary that he was 'too little acquainted with God, the Scriptures, human nature in general, and my own heart in particular.'

narrative_blocks.header: Six years a tutor, four classes taught
narrative_blocks.body: He stayed on after his 1738 degree as a resident graduate on Bishop Berkeley's foundation, and was elected tutor when Rector Williams resigned the next year. Two of his four classes got most of their education from him.

narrative_blocks.header: He sold goods for ten years, then preached
narrative_blocks.body: He left the tutorship in 1745 and spent a decade as a New Haven merchant, sitting for the town in the General Assembly. A council declared against ordaining him; the next day it installed him over First Church, in his fortieth year.

narrative_blocks.header: He preached to the wartime Assembly
narrative_blocks.body: On May 14, 1778, with the Revolution undecided, Whittelsey gave the Election Sermon before Connecticut's General Assembly on the importance of religion in the civil ruler. The Assembly ordered it printed and sent two men with its thanks.

narrative_blocks.header: His first name came off his mother
narrative_blocks.body: His mother was Sarah Chauncy of Hatfield, and her maiden surname became her second son's given name. Through her the Whittleseys ran back to Rev. Charles Chauncy, second president of Harvard, and were still using it four generations on.

narrative_blocks.header: He wished not to exceed seventy
narrative_blocks.body: Stiles reached the room as death began and asked whether he still felt the assurance of hope — if he could not speak, to answer by pressing his hand. He rallied his strength and said it aloud instead: 'Yes.'

President Ezra Stiles (HD0346) attended Whittlesey's 1787 deathbed; per the diary record, Stiles took his hand and asked 'Do you feel now the assurance of hope?' and Chauncey rallied his dying strength to answer 'Yes.' Stiles published a eulogy describing him as 'oracular at college' for breadth of learning. Per Whittlesey Genealogy #88. [Two CCs pointed at Stiles; merged into one 081226.]

people.research_notes: Roger Newton Whittlesey (Whittlesey Genealogy entry #135). b. Feb 24, 1754 Milford Conn.; d. Mar 15, 1835 (Litchfield County). Son of Rev. Samuel Whittlesey (I00020) and Martha Newton Whittlesey (H00143). Middle name 'Newton' honors maternal grandfather Col. Roger Newton (H00044). Mother per Whittlesey Genealogy #42 child line: Susannah Newton Whittlesey Hamlin (H00142). Farmer at South Farms (now Morris) in Litchfield County. Justice of the peace many years. REVOLUTIONARY WAR: Enlisted Jan 21, 1776 Litchfield CT in Capt. Bezaleel Beebe's Company, Col. Andrew Ward Jr.'s regiment under Maj. Gen. Charles Lee, for 8-week tour defending New York City. Orders reached Capt. Beebe's Litchfield headquarters on a Sunday; the company was raised, armed, and marching toward Fairfield by Saturday. His gun (then in the hands of Breant Stoddard) appraised Jan 26, 1776. m. Apr 20, 1775 Ann Woodruff (I00075, b. Apr 5, 1756 Litchfield, d. Mar 7, 1825), dau. of Jacob Woodruff (b. 1717, m. Anne Griswold Dec 31, 1741 Litchfield; m2 Lucy Farnum May 22, 1755) and Lucy Farnum. Jacob Woodruff d. Mar 21, 1790. Ann's siblings: Jacob Jr. (Feb 2, 1746), Lydia (Aug 7, 1751), Luce (Dec 30, 1756), Ruth (Dec 7, 1761). 13 children, all Hooker descendants in tree as HD0102-HD0114 (per Whittlesey #360-#372 child list). open_questions.question: Is Elisha Whittlesey (b. Mar 8, 1783, Southbury CT; d. Jan 7, 1863) a missing child of Roger Newton Whittlesey?
open_questions.notes: Elisha Whittlesey (1783-1863) was born in Southbury CT, studied law under Tapping Reeve at Litchfield CT, moved to Canfield, Mahoning County OH in 1806, served as U.S. Congressman from Ohio and comptroller of the U.S. Treasury. His birth year (1783) falls exactly between documented children HD0105 (Chauncey, b.1781) and HD0106 (Susan, b.1784), suggesting he may be a missing child of this entry. Roger Newton Whittlesey (HD0097) lived in Litchfield County CT — where Tapping Reeve's famous law school was located. If confirmed, Elisha is a gen 6 Hooker descendant, and his 20-year law partnership with Eben Newton (HD2927) — also a gen 6 Hooker descendant — becomes a documented civic_peer cross_connection. Action: Check Whittlesey genealogy for Southbury CT branch; Litchfield County records 1783.
open_questions.resolution: Elisha Whittlesey (b. Oct 19, 1783 Washington CT) is Whittlesey book entry #310, son of John Whittlesey (#123, b.1741 Newington CT). His line descends from John Whittlesey of Saybrook through Eliphalet→Eliphalet→John→Elisha — a completely different branch from the project's Whittlesey line (which runs through Rev. Samuel Whittlesey of Wallingford/Milford). Elisha is NOT a Hooker descendant.

bio.bio_blurb: Farmer, justice of the peace, Revolutionary soldier

narrative_blocks.header: Eight-week militia tour to defend New York 1776
narrative_blocks.body: He enlisted at twenty-one in Captain Bezaleel Beebe’s company. The orders reached Beebe on a Sunday and the company was armed and marching for Fairfield by Saturday. Eight weeks defending New York, and no more service is recorded.

narrative_blocks.header: Justice of the peace, Litchfield County, many years
narrative_blocks.body: After the war he settled at South Farms in Litchfield County and was justice of the peace there for many years, which was standing in rural Connecticut. He worked his farm until he died at eighty-one in March 1835.

narrative_blocks.header: Father of thirteen children with Ann Woodruff
narrative_blocks.body: He married Ann Woodruff of Litchfield in April 1775, the month of Lexington, and they raised thirteen children. The youngest, George Washington Whittlesey, came in 1799 when Roger was forty-five. Ann was born in 1756 and died in 1825.

people.research_notes: Left no children per Whittlesey genealogy. OCCUPATION NOTES: Physician at Milford, Connecticut. [Migrated from top-level occupation]: ['Physician'] Dexter/FAG: nearly settled at Newport 1769; estate £583; no issue; gravestone: “such was the pleasure of righteous heaven he departed this life in the 31st year of his age.”

narrative_blocks.header: He came near settling at Newport
narrative_blocks.body: He read medicine after Yale and in 1769 came close to setting up at Newport in Rhode Island. He stayed instead in the town he was born in, where his father had the pulpit, and practised there the rest of his short life.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a New Haven doctor’s daughter
narrative_blocks.body: On 2 January 1771 he married Mary, daughter of Dr. Leverett Hubbard of New Haven, a Yale man like his own father. She was eighteen. They had five years together and no children.

narrative_blocks.header: His widow married a Yale tutor after
narrative_blocks.body: He died at Milford in February 1776, in his thirty-first year, and left no issue. Mary married again in March 1777 — the Rev. John Lewis, then a tutor in the college — and died herself at thirty-four.

narrative_blocks.header: The pleasure of righteous heaven
narrative_blocks.body: The stone at Milford does not say what took him. It says he was “a young Gentleman endowed with good natural abilities and furnished by education for public service, but such was the pleasure of righteous heaven.”

narrative_blocks.header: Six children, and her husband gone first
narrative_blocks.body: She married Edward Carrington, a Milford physician, in November 1771 and they had six. He died at Milford in 1795 and she in the January of 1801, in the same town, at fifty-three.

narrative_blocks.header: She was the third Elizabeth
narrative_blocks.body: Two sisters named Elizabeth had died in infancy before she was born in 1773, and Susanna was added to the name. She was the one who lived.

narrative_blocks.header: Her stone names her father, not a husband
narrative_blocks.body: She lies at Grove Street in New Haven under her maiden name, set down as the youngest daughter of the Rev. Chauncey. The Whittlesey genealogy records her the same way: she never married.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived the whole household
narrative_blocks.body: Last born of Rev. Chauncey and Martha's eleven children, she died at New Haven in March 1866 at ninety-two — seventy-nine years after her father and fifty-four after her mother.

narrative_blocks.header: A meeting-house thirty-six feet by twenty-six
narrative_blocks.body: He was ordained over New Preston in December 1807 and kept it ten years. The house he preached in was thirty-six feet by twenty-six and ten high, a hundred rods west of the one that replaced it. He added 142 members and baptised 167.

narrative_blocks.header: One post left, the next taken, same day
narrative_blocks.body: He was dismissed from New Preston on 30 April 1817 and took charge of the Deaf and Dumb Asylum at Hartford the same day. It had opened only weeks before, the first permanent school for the deaf in the country.

narrative_blocks.header: He was principal, she was matron
narrative_blocks.body: After Hartford the two of them ran large seminaries at Canandaigua and then Utica, he the principal and she the matron. It was out of the Utica house that she began the magazine that made her name.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale at twenty-seven, licensed the next June
narrative_blocks.body: He took his degree at Yale in 1803 with Phi Beta Kappa and an A.M., and was licensed to preach in June 1804. Three years passed before a church called him.

narrative_blocks.header: Gentlemanly, and equal to the variety
narrative_blocks.body: The family genealogy, which is not given to praise, stopped to record what it thought of him: “a man of gentlemanly qualities and a versality of talent to meet the variety of his employments.”

people.research_notes: Newton Whittlesey #361. Self-taught lawyer relied on by townspeople of Cornish Flats for estate settlement. Trustee of Kimball Union Academy for 26 years; secretary of the board for 4 of those. Daughter Esther Mills (HD3834) married Rev. Israel Newell (I00470), principal of the academy 1822-1835 — father-in-law and son-in-law overlapped on campus for 13 years.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-six years on the academy board
narrative_blocks.body: He was put on the board of Kimball Union Academy at Meriden, New Hampshire in 1818 and was still on it when he died in 1844 — twenty-six years, four of them as its secretary.

narrative_blocks.header: They trusted their all to him
narrative_blocks.body: He had picked up enough law that the townspeople kept asking him to settle their estates. The family book says they recognised the unapproachable character of the man, and trusted their all to him.

narrative_blocks.header: Deacon, postmaster, justice of the peace
narrative_blocks.body: He was deacon of the church at Cornish Flat in New Hampshire and the village postmaster, and a justice of the peace besides. He lived there most of his life and died over at Claremont.

narrative_blocks.header: Four by one wife, two by the next
narrative_blocks.body: Esther Robbins of Sutton died in 1818 after four children, all born at Cornish. He married Maria Mills in 1821 and had two more. She outlived him forty-nine years and died at Raleigh at ninety-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: A man of great integrity, they said

narrative_blocks.header: He kept the worship going without a minister
narrative_blocks.body: For more than two years of his deaconship the Roxbury church had no settled preacher, and the labour of keeping up the worship fell principally, and often entirely, on him. He was doing it for most of the nine months before he died.

narrative_blocks.header: Sudden removal in the midst of his usefulness
narrative_blocks.body: He joined the Roxbury church in September 1816 on a letter from Litchfield South Farms, his native place, and was elected deacon the following May. The notice of his death calls it a sudden removal in the midst of his usefulness.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandfather was a New Haven founder
narrative_blocks.body: Richard Miles was one of the forty-four church members granted the franchise as free planters at the first General Court in November 1639. A 1641 schedule of New Haven planters shows him heading a household of seven on four hundred acres, and he was a deacon of the First Church there from 1656 until his death.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandfather helped build the phantom ship
narrative_blocks.body: Governor Theophilus Eaton entrusted Richard Miles and others with constructing New Haven's great ship of 1646. It was ill-built, sailed into the Atlantic and was never seen again, and the merchant Thomas Gregson went down with it.

narrative_blocks.header: The tax his grandfather would not pay
narrative_blocks.body: The 1636 Hertfordshire arrears roll lists Richard Miles of Wormley among those who refused Charles I's ship money, with the notation gone into New England beside his name. He landed at Boston the next summer with the Rev. Peter Prudden's Hertfordshire company.

narrative_blocks.header: His father held Westfield with twenty-six men
narrative_blocks.body: In September 1675, as King Philip's War burned through the valley towns, the Council ordered Captain John Miles to stay at Westfield with twenty-six men in his charge. By November he was a lieutenant and seventh in command of all Connecticut forces, and in February 1693 he raised the hundred and fifty men for the Relief of Albany.

narrative_blocks.header: He died on Christmas Day at twenty-eight
narrative_blocks.body: He married Sarah Newton in 1707 and fathered two sons before dying on Christmas Day 1711, at twenty-eight. He was buried in New Haven's Grove Street ground.

narrative_blocks.header: His widow remarried into the Ingersolls
narrative_blocks.body: After Daniel’s early death, Sarah Newton married Jonathan Ingersoll of Milford and had five more children, knitting the Miles and Ingersoll families into the same Hooker-descended line.

parents.father_research_notes: John Ingersoll (ca.1615–Sep 3, 1684) of Westfield, MA. Descended from John Ingersoll Sr. (1626–1684), born Edworth, Bedfordshire, England.

narrative_blocks.header: His Milford gravestone still stands
narrative_blocks.body: He died at Milford in May 1760, in his eightieth year. The stone raised over him survives among those the town set before 1800, its inscription copied down and printed more than a century later.

narrative_blocks.header: Two brothers, and two Ingersoll families
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Westfield in 1681, took a Harvard degree, and settled at Milford, marrying the widow Sarah Newton Miles. His older brother Thomas never left the Massachusetts frontier. Within a generation the two Ingersoll families had lost sight of each other.

narrative_blocks.header: His father crossed the ocean at fourteen
narrative_blocks.body: His father, John Ingersoll, had come from England at fourteen in 1629, settling first at Hartford, then Northampton, and finally Westfield, where he was named one of the church's seven founding pillars. The land granted him there stayed in the family for generations as the 'Ingersoll place.'

narrative_blocks.header: The two weddings that made double cousins
narrative_blocks.body: His son Jared married Hannah Whiting in 1743 and his daughter Sarah married Hannah's brother John. A brother and sister on one side married a sister and brother on the other, which made the children of the two marriages double first cousins — sharing all four grandparents where ordinary cousins share two.

notable.notable_blurb: Colonial lawyer and stamp master

narrative_blocks.header: Five hundred horsemen met him on the road
narrative_blocks.body: Hung in effigy across Connecticut, he rode for Hartford in September 1765 to put himself under the assembly's protection. Near Wethersfield some five hundred mounted men stopped him and made him resign the stamp office, shout 'Liberty and Property' three times, and throw his hat in the air.

narrative_blocks.header: He hated the tax, took the job anyway
narrative_blocks.body: By his own account he went to London with the strongest prejudices against Parliament's right to lay stamp duties — and was persuaded there to become Connecticut's stamp distributor. He took it, he said, to make the act fall lighter than a stranger would let it fall.

narrative_blocks.header: He printed twelve letters in his defense
narrative_blocks.body: The year after the mob, he published Letters relating to the Stamp-Act at New Haven — a dozen letters, all but one his own, stitched together with a narrative defending his conduct. Timothy Dwight later judged the acceptance unwise but innocent of any design against his country.

narrative_blocks.header: The Crown repaid him with a judgeship
narrative_blocks.body: For his rough usage the Crown made him a vice-admiralty judge over the middle colonies at six hundred pounds a year, and in 1771 he moved his family to Philadelphia. The Revolution ended the court, and Pennsylvania's council sent him home to Connecticut in 1777.

narrative_blocks.header: He crossed the ocean for a war debt
narrative_blocks.body: Sent to London as the colony's agent, he pressed Connecticut's claim for reimbursement of its campaign expenses, and later contracted to ship the Navy a load of masts down the Connecticut River. He lies buried under New Haven's Center Church.

narrative_blocks.body: She was the eldest child of a New Haven magistrate, and married Jared Ingersoll at Branford in 1743. Her brother John then married one of Jared's sisters — two families bound twice over in a single generation.

narrative_blocks.header: Three of her four children died as infants
narrative_blocks.body: She bore four children and buried three of them in infancy. The one who lived, another Jared, grew up to sign the United States Constitution.

narrative_blocks.header: She followed a hated man to Philadelphia
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband was burned in effigy across Connecticut for taking the stamp office, and in 1771 the family left New Haven for Philadelphia, where the Crown had given him a court. The Revolution drove them back; she died in New Haven two years later.

notable.notable_blurb: Ridgefield pastor and army chaplain

narrative_blocks.header: One pulpit held him for forty years
narrative_blocks.body: He was ordained over Ridgefield's first church at twenty-five and preached there until he died, in the fortieth year of his ministry. The town could not replace him for eight years afterward, filling the pulpit with borrowed preachers paid in wheat and pounds.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried the gospel to Ticonderoga
narrative_blocks.body: In 1758 he went north as chaplain of the 4th Connecticut Regiment under Colonel David Wooster, to the fighting at Fort Ticonderoga. Twenty years later his gravestone still named him a chaplain of that war.

narrative_blocks.header: He swore the oath and freed a man
narrative_blocks.body: In 1777 he took the Freeman's Oath for the American cause — and in the same year, with the selectmen's approval, freed Cyphax, the twenty-year-old man he had held enslaved. It was one of the few manumissions Ridgefield ever recorded.

narrative_blocks.header: The colony's lawmakers came to hear him
narrative_blocks.body: In 1761 he was chosen to preach the Election Day sermon before the Connecticut General Assembly — the year's most public pulpit, and a mark of the standing a country pastor could reach.

notable.notable_blurb: Constitution signer and Philadelphia lawyer

narrative_blocks.header: He chose independence; his father chose the king
narrative_blocks.body: Sent to London to read law at the Middle Temple while his father administered the Stamp Act, he toured the continent in 1776 and came home having shed the family's loyalism. The father's career collapsed with the Crown's; the son's began with the republic.

narrative_blocks.header: He signed the Constitution, then argued it
narrative_blocks.body: A delegate to the Philadelphia convention of 1787, he put his name to the finished document — and spent the years after arguing what it meant. He stood before the Supreme Court in Chisholm v. Georgia, whose outcome forced the Eleventh Amendment, and in the first case ever to test an act of Congress against the Constitution.

narrative_blocks.header: His mentor handed him a practice and left
narrative_blocks.body: He read law in Joseph Reed's Philadelphia office; when Reed became governor of Pennsylvania in 1781 he asked his former student to mind the practice. From that beginning he became reckoned among the best lawyers in a city thick with the best legal minds in America.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran for vice president and lost
narrative_blocks.body: The Federalists made him their candidate for the vice presidency in 1812, on a ticket that failed. He had already served nine years as Pennsylvania's attorney general and would serve five more, and finished as United States attorney for the state's eastern district.

narrative_blocks.header: Elected to Congress, he declined to go
narrative_blocks.body: A special election in 1793 sent him to the House of Representatives. He refused the seat before the Congress convened and was never sworn in; another man was chosen in his place that November.

narrative_blocks.header: He sat out the Revolution at his desk
narrative_blocks.body: While New Haven went to war he took no part in it, keeping close to his law practice. Public life came only afterward — the assembly, the bench, and finally the lieutenant governorship.

narrative_blocks.header: He led the party that ended church rule
narrative_blocks.body: Late in life he became a leader of Connecticut's Toleration movement, which ended the Congregational establishment — a cause he served as a devout Episcopalian and longtime senior warden of his church. The Toleration party made him lieutenant governor in 1816.

narrative_blocks.header: He held the office until he died
narrative_blocks.body: Elected annually for six years and eight months, he was still lieutenant governor when he died at New Haven in January 1823. A contemporary said no citizen of Connecticut ever more entirely deserved the public's confidence.

narrative_blocks.header: A mob unseated his uncle, the stamp master
narrative_blocks.body: His uncle Jared Ingersoll took the post of stamp distributor for Connecticut in 1765 and was hanged in effigy and forced by a crowd to give it up. The family carried that taint; the nephew took no part in the Revolution, keeping close to his law practice.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept school before he kept court
narrative_blocks.body: A Berkeley Scholar at his Yale graduation, he ran a school at Middletown while reading law in the office of a brilliant young practitioner there. Only then did he settle to the New Haven bar.

narrative_blocks.header: Madison’s wartime Judiciary chairman
narrative_blocks.body: Elected to the Thirteenth Congress in 1812, Ingersoll chaired the House Judiciary Committee through the war with Britain, then spent fourteen years as Philadelphia’s federal district attorney before returning to Congress in the 1840s.

narrative_blocks.header: Anonymous in the Democratic Press
narrative_blocks.body: A writer all his life, Ingersoll published numerous anonymous contributions to the Democratic Press of Philadelphia and the National Intelligencer of Washington — the congressman arguing his causes without his name.

narrative_blocks.header: He charged Webster and lost twice
narrative_blocks.body: In 1846 Ingersoll rose in the House and accused Daniel Webster of three counts of misconduct as Secretary of State; the committee that heard the charges exonerated Webster entirely. The next year Webster led the Senate in rejecting Polk's appointment of Ingersoll as minister to France. He left politics for good and gave his last years to writing.

narrative_blocks.header: He thought Oregon was worth a war
narrative_blocks.body: In March 1846, with the northwestern boundary in dispute and the country arguing over how far to push Britain, he set out his expansionist case in a letter to an unnamed correspondent. It was printed more than a century later under the line that carried it: I consider Oregon worth a war.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother married her sister nine years later
narrative_blocks.body: He married Mary Wilcocks in 1804; in 1813 his younger brother Joseph Reed married her elder sister Ann. The double match tied the Ingersolls to the Chew and Wilcocks fortunes, including twelve thousand acres of southwestern Pennsylvania frontier.

narrative_blocks.header: He thought Napoleon looked like a midshipman
narrative_blocks.body: Fresh from the bar in 1802 he toured Europe, met Joseph Bonaparte at the American minister's house in Paris, and watched Napoleon review his troops. He wrote afterward that the First Consul was small, pale, and beardless, with nothing martial in his manner — a modest midshipman, not a colossus.

Sept 22, 1813, Ann Wilcocks (1781-1831) — sister of his brother Charles Jared’s wife Mary. Three children (James, Mary Wilcocks, +1), not built. Sidney George Fisher’s diary verdict (“mind decidedly commonplace... fluency of speech”) noted for balance.

documents.document_blurb: Du Ponceau's 1836 letter warning that killing the bank could split the states.

narrative_blocks.header: “The Cicero of the American Bar”
narrative_blocks.body: So his eulogist David Paul Brown styled him. He had argued before John Marshall as a young man, chaired the House Judiciary Committee as a Henry Clay Whig, and defended the cases arising from Philadelphia’s bloody anti-Catholic church riots of 1844.

narrative_blocks.header: Oxford gave a degree; Fillmore gave him London
narrative_blocks.body: Honored with doctorates by Lafayette, Bowdoin, and Oxford, he was sent by President Fillmore in 1852 as American minister to Great Britain. He stayed about a year, then retired, and James Buchanan took the post on his way to the presidency.

narrative_blocks.header: He called secession a folly and a crime
narrative_blocks.body: A firm Union man, he answered the Civil War with an essay bearing that title. In retirement he turned to letters, translating Latin tracts on maritime law and writing a memoir of an old Philadelphia friend.

narrative_blocks.header: A friend's letter foretold the Civil War
narrative_blocks.body: In 1836 the linguist Peter Du Ponceau — once Baron von Steuben's aide — wrote him four pages arguing that killing the national bank would set the states scrambling for capital. Fiscal wars would follow, he warned, and no national force could then prevent separation.

narrative_blocks.header: Two sons, then Ann, then his last child
narrative_blocks.body: James died at six in 1820 and Joseph at two in 1825; Ann followed in 1831, eighteen years into the marriage. Their daughter Mary died unmarried in 1842. Ingersoll lived on to 1868, a widower of thirty-seven years who had outlived every child and left no descendants.

narrative_blocks.header: Two brothers married two Wilcocks sisters
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph married Ann Wilcocks in 1813, nine years after his brother Charles Jared married her sister Mary — twin alliances binding the Ingersolls to the Chew-Wilcocks fortune. When the Panic of 1837 gutted the Wilcocks lands, both brothers’ households felt it.

narrative_blocks.header: Clerk of three courts before he was thirty
narrative_blocks.body: A Yale graduate of 1780, he became clerk of New Haven's city, county, and probate courts while still a young man — the probate seat once held by his father. He came of a line that had furnished the colony judges and deacons for four generations.

narrative_blocks.header: The scarlet fever took him at thirty-three
narrative_blocks.body: In 1794 an epidemic of scarlet fever swept New Haven, and he was among its first victims, dead at thirty-three. Those who knew him believed he would have risen as high as his forebears had he lived; instead he was buried beside them beneath Center Church.

narrative_blocks.header: A judge and deacon of old New Haven
narrative_blocks.body: A Yale graduate and tutor, he served New Haven as clerk and then judge of the probate court, sat nine sessions in the General Assembly, and judged the county court. For the last thirty years of his life he was a deacon of the First Church, his epitaph noting that most of it was given to the public service.

narrative_blocks.header: The British hauled him off without his wig
narrative_blocks.body: When the British seized New Haven in 1779, he refused to flee, pointing to an engraving of King George as proof of his loyalty. The soldiers were unmoved — he held office under the rebel government and was a Puritan deacon besides — and carried him off a prisoner so abruptly he had no time to put on his wig.

narrative_blocks.header: His line ran back to Hartford's founders
narrative_blocks.body: His father, Colonel Joseph Whiting, was a judge of the colony's high courts; his grandfather, the Reverend John Whiting, was Hartford's fourth minister; and behind them stood William Whiting, one of that town's founding settlers. Four generations of soldiers, ministers, and judges had gone before him.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother-in-law was Connecticut's hated Stamp Man
narrative_blocks.body: He married Sarah Ingersoll, and his sister Hannah married her brother — Jared Ingersoll, the colony's stamp distributor, whom a Wethersfield mob forced to resign that despised office in 1765. Two Whitings and two Ingersolls, a brother and sister from each house, married across in a single generation.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-one years in Connecticut's upper chamber
narrative_blocks.body: A New Haven man of large estate, he rose from the colony's General Court to its upper chamber, the Council, where he sat for twenty-one years. He was for many years a judge of the probate and superior courts, and Whiting Street in New Haven still carries the family name.

narrative_blocks.header: The grandfather who never came back
narrative_blocks.body: His mother's father was Thomas Gregson of New Haven, who sailed in the colony's great ship in 1646 and was never seen again. Months later the town swore the vessel had reappeared over the harbour under full sail and dissolved into smoke, and it passed into New England legend as the phantom ship.

narrative_blocks.header: Grandson of a Hartford founder
narrative_blocks.body: His grandfather William Whiting was one of Hartford's founding settlers, and his father, the Reverend John Whiting, was that town's fourth minister. He carried the family's standing into New Haven, where his children would marry into the Ingersoll line in a double match.

narrative_blocks.header: The two weddings that made double cousins
narrative_blocks.body: His daughter Hannah married Jared Ingersoll in 1743 and his son John married Jared's sister Sarah. A brother and sister on one side married a sister and brother on the other, which made the children of the two marriages double first cousins — sharing all four grandparents where ordinary cousins share two.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter's line signed the Constitution
narrative_blocks.body: Hannah's son Jared Ingersoll Jr. signed the Constitution for Pennsylvania and stood for vice-president in 1812. Jared's own sons carried it further — Charles Jared Ingersoll to Congress, and Joseph Reed Ingersoll to Congress and then to London as United States Minister to Britain.

narrative_blocks.body: A Trowbridge of New Haven, she married Colonel Joseph Whiting and shared in the large estate that made the family prominent. Whiting Street was named for the couple, whose graves lie together in the crypt of the Center Church.

narrative_blocks.header: Her two children, and their two Ingersolls
narrative_blocks.body: Her daughter Hannah married Jared Ingersoll in 1743 and her son John married Jared's sister Sarah. The children of those two marriages were double first cousins, sharing all four grandparents where ordinary cousins share two.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son's line reached the Vanderbilts
narrative_blocks.body: Her son Deacon John Whiting married Sarah Ingersoll, and their son William Joseph Whiting fathered Martha, who married Henry Collins Flagg. Out of that came the painter Jared Bradley Flagg and the architect Ernest Flagg, and Martha's daughter Rachel, whose daughter Alice Claypoole Gwynne married Cornelius Vanderbilt II.

narrative_blocks.header: His church split; he founded another
narrative_blocks.body: The half-way covenant fight broke Hartford’s First Church in 1669, and thirty-two members walked out. Whiting petitioned the Assembly “for a distinct walking in Congregational Church Order,” won, and was ordained pastor of the new Second Church — which celebrated its 350th anniversary in 2020.

narrative_blocks.header: His bride’s father sailed the phantom ship
narrative_blocks.body: His second wife Phebe was the daughter of Thomas Gregson of New Haven, lost at sea in 1646 aboard the famous “phantom ship.” Phebe outlived Whiting by forty-one years, remarrying Rev. John Russell of Hadley.

narrative_blocks.body: Widow of Rev. John Whiting of Hartford, Phebe married Rev. John Russell of Hadley in 1692. She survived him as well, then removed to New Haven. She died there in 1730, near ninety.

narrative_blocks.header: Partner of the lords in the Piscataqua patent
narrative_blocks.body: About 1633 William joined Lords Say and Brooke and George Wyllys in buying the Bristol merchants' interest in the Piscataqua patents, the Dover and Swampscott lands of New Hampshire, and they kept on Thomas Wiggin, his sister's husband, as their agent. William held his share until he died.

narrative_blocks.header: Corn shipped beyond the seas
narrative_blocks.body: William and Edward Hopkins were the two leading merchants of the colony, and after the Pequot War they began shipping corn beyond the seas. He traded to Virginia, Long Island and Piscataqua, and kept trading houses on the Delaware River and at Westfield.

narrative_blocks.header: A plot to kill him with the governors
narrative_blocks.body: In 1646 Sequassen, sachem of the Naticks, plotted to kill Governors Haynes and Hopkins and William for the protection they had given Uncas. A friendly Indian gave the plot away before it could be carried out.

narrative_blocks.header: Treasurer of the colony until his death
narrative_blocks.body: William sat with the Court of Magistrates in 1637, kept the colony's treasury from 1641 and sat as a magistrate from 1642 until he died. In 1642 he went with Major Mason to build fortifications and to collect tribute from the Indians of Long Island and the main.

narrative_blocks.header: A will written for a sea voyage
narrative_blocks.body: William wrote his will in March 1643 because he meant to go to sea, added to it in 1646 before another voyage, and made the last addition on his deathbed in July 1647. He left money to mend the highway between his house and the meetinghouse, and to the godly poor of the town.

people.research_notes: Daughter of Benjamin Johnson and Eunice Sutliff. Benjamin Johnson was great-grandson of Robert Johnson, one of first settlers of New Haven 1640 (York Street). Eunice Sutliff was daughter of Nathaniel Sutliff, first proprietor of Durham who led religious services before a pastor was settled. Nathaniel's father was burned by Indians at Deerfield, May 19, 1676. Her grandfather John Plympton came to America with John Winthrop in 1630; was burned at the stake by Indians 1675 "with great cheerfulness."

narrative_blocks.header: She left seven children and a newborn
narrative_blocks.body: Eunice Johnson married Burwell Newton at nineteen and bore eight children before dying at thirty-eight, weeks after her last son Isaac was born. With no mother and a father who never remarried, the children kept house themselves — the eldest seventeen, the youngest daughters eleven and eight.

narrative_blocks.header: Two of her forebears were burned by raiders
narrative_blocks.body: Eunice descended from a family marked by frontier violence: her great-great-grandfather Capt. John Plympton was captured and burned at the stake near Deerfield in 1675 during King Philip’s War, and her great-grandfather Nathaniel Sutliff met the same fate the following year. The orphaned Sutliff children received a grant of land for their support.

narrative_blocks.header: He marched for Ticonderoga in the snow
narrative_blocks.body: The company was raised on the twenty-fourth of February 1777 under Captain Timothy Child and he served a month and seventeen days of it. Three years later he had a captain's commission of his own in the fifth Hampshire regiment, and his final discharge came in October 1780.

narrative_blocks.header: At West Point when Benedict Arnold fled
narrative_blocks.body: Captain Isaac Newton was present at West Point when Benedict Arnold's treachery was discovered and Arnold fled to the British. He was on board the Vulture — the British warship that had carried Major André — and there saw General Washington. The 1780 episode placed him at one of the Revolutionary War's most dramatic single moments of decision.

narrative_blocks.header: Also at Fort Edward for Burgoyne's surrender
narrative_blocks.body: Isaac Newton was at Fort Edward in 1777 when General John Burgoyne surrendered — the turning-point battle that brought France into the war as a U.S. ally. Combined with his West Point presence three years later, Newton was an eyewitness participant at two of the three most consequential single events of the Revolutionary War's northern theater.

narrative_blocks.header: Captain's commission and 113 men, July 1781
narrative_blocks.body: On July 1, 1781 Captain Isaac Newton received his Captain's commission and the same day took command of 113 men at West Point. The simultaneous-day commission-and-command was unusual — most officers received their commissions days or weeks before their assigned units. The arrangement reflected the wartime pace of unit-rotation at West Point during the final years of the war.

narrative_blocks.header: The land stayed in the family a century
narrative_blocks.body: He and his brother John bought their Greenfield acres from Simon Burt, and the family still held them a hundred years later. His name is on the town tax lists from 1775.

narrative_blocks.header: Five children born over fifteen years
narrative_blocks.body: Isaac came about 1771, Sebra in 1779, Rejoice in 1782. Two more sons were born in 1784 and 1786 and neither lived out the year. Rejoice went to Dartmouth and became district attorney of Worcester County.

narrative_blocks.header: He guarded his gold with horse-pistols
narrative_blocks.body: Burwell Newton Jr. accumulated considerable property and kept his money in a great chest beside his bed, guarded by a pair of horse-pistols. When a kinsman came to borrow, several hundred dollars in gold were counted out from it.

narrative_blocks.header: He stood through every long Sabbath prayer
narrative_blocks.body: A devoted reader who made faithful use of the Durham Library — the first public library in Connecticut, founded 1733 — Burwell kept the old customs to the end. As men had done in his youth, he stood through the long meeting-house prayer each Sabbath until he was nearly ninety.

narrative_blocks.header: He commanded ships out of Milford
narrative_blocks.body: John Fowler made his living as a sea captain, sailing out of the harbor town of Milford. The title that clung to his name came from the deck rather than the parade ground.

narrative_blocks.header: A lieutenant under Captain Peck in 1775
narrative_blocks.body: When the Revolution broke out, Fowler took a lieutenant's commission in Captain Samuel Peck's company of the Connecticut militia in 1775. He was one of many Milford men who answered the first call to arms.

narrative_blocks.header: He married into a French refugee line
narrative_blocks.body: In 1767 Fowler married Mary Ann Harpin of Milford. Her family traced back to Dr. John Harpin, who had fled Rochefort in France and reached America around 1690. Their sons carried the Harpin name into the next century.

narrative_blocks.header: His stone asks if this is life's end
narrative_blocks.body: Captain Fowler died on August 17, 1787, only thirty-nine years old. His Milford gravestone carries a startled, grieving verse: “All gracious Heaven, is this the end of man, a dreadful thought, a melancholy plan.”

narrative_blocks.header: He went ahead of Hooker's party
narrative_blocks.body: In October 1635 William was one of the twenty-five men of the Adventurers Party whom John Steele led out from Cambridge to the Connecticut River. He was one of the sixteen founders already living at Hartford when Thomas Hooker's company arrived the next May.

narrative_blocks.header: Hooker's next-door neighbor in Cambridge
narrative_blocks.body: The Cambridge land records of September 1635 put William's home lot between Thomas Hooker's and James Olmstead's, and at Hartford he settled again beside Olmstead, just north of Hooker. He had been made a freeman at Cambridge that March.

narrative_blocks.header: The carpenter who built the meetinghouse gallery
narrative_blocks.body: A carpenter and joiner, William was named in 1640 to choose the site for Hartford's mill and bridge, and in 1644 to oversee the building of a gallery in the meetinghouse. The town chose him selectman in 1641 and 1646, sat him on the Particular Court jury for ten years, and made him constable in 1649.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-nine parcels of Hartford land
narrative_blocks.body: William drew ten parcels in the first division, from the Little Meadow and North Meadow to the Neck and the Venturers Field, and bought nineteen more. When his inventory was taken in November 1649 he was one of the wealthiest of Hartford's original proprietors.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter married into the Bryan merchants
narrative_blocks.body: William's daughter Mary married Richard Bryan of Milford in 1649. Their son Samuel was the father of Susannah Bryan, who married Col. Roger Newton and carried the Pantry line into the Hooker descent.

people.research_notes: His father John Fowler (d. bef.1695) was one of the "young men" of Milford who in 1671 destroyed the Indian Fort. b. Apr 5, 1691 Milford (bapt.); d. Aug 30, 1756. Son of John Fowler (d. bef.1695) and Sarah Welch Fowler — his widowed mother later m. a Newton ("Mrs. Sarah Newton, alias Fowler, d. 5th August 1723"). His grandfather William Fowler was Magistrate of the Colony of New Haven (1643), one of the "Seven Pillars" of the Milford church (1639), and built a mill near New Haven (1645) later purchased by the town — on the site where Eli Whitney erected his firearms factory. William Fowler's wife Mary Tapp was sister of Jane Tapp, wife of Gov. Robert Treat — making William Fowler's family closely connected to the Treat family. m. (1) Susannah Burwell (H00053) Feb 28, 1712; m. (2) Abigail Prince, widow of Capt. Josiah Prince. John served as Milford town clerk (inherited from his father). Will dated Aug 28, 1756 New Haven. narrative_blocks.header: Town clerk, like his father before
narrative_blocks.body: The Milford clerkship came down from the father he lost before age four — a John Fowler remembered as one of the young men who destroyed the Indian Fort in 1671. The son held the town's books to his death in 1756.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandfather's mill became Whitney's factory
narrative_blocks.body: William Fowler — a magistrate of New Haven Colony and one of Milford church's Seven Pillars — built a mill near New Haven in 1645 that the town later bought. On that same ground, a century and a half on, Eli Whitney raised his firearms factory.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-eight years as Milford's town clerk
narrative_blocks.body: He took the clerkship in 1718 and held it until he died in 1756. He captained the Milford train band from 1739 and sat as a deputy to the General Court.

narrative_blocks.header: He raised men for the march on Canada
narrative_blocks.body: The colony commissioned him to fit out troops for His Majesty's expedition against Canada, and to raise two hundred men with their officers for the frontier. He lived and died in the first William Fowler's homestead, and left it by deed to his son John.

people.research_notes:

Built a mill ca.1645 on site later occupied by Eli Whitney's cotton gin factory (~2 miles from New Haven). Town bought mill Jan 3, 1659 for £100. Chosen successively Sergeant, Lieutenant, and Captain of the Town Company. "Fowler's Cove" and "Fowler's Creek" near East Haven named for him. narrative_blocks.body: Fowler raised the colony’s first grist mill in 1645 at the falls two miles above New Haven; the town bought it from him in 1659 for a hundred pounds. A century and a half later Eli Whitney put his arms factory on the same site — today’s Whitneyville.

narrative_blocks.body: By 1645 he had married Mary Tapp, daughter of Edmund Tapp of Milford — whose sister Jane was the wife of Governor Robert Treat. His will asked that his second wife Elizabeth “continue to live with his children, to be a guide and help to them as a mother.”

DEATH NOTE: Died before 1695 — in a deed of that date Sarah Fowler is called "widow and executor." Will probated 1693; names "only son John" and "my honorable uncle, Robert Treat, Esq., the Governor."
WILL (1693): Names "only son John" (I00091). Wife to raise him in fear of God. Calls Gov. Robert Treat "my honorable uncle" — Treat was uncle by marriage through William Fowler's wife Mary Tapp. Probated 1693.
ANECDOTE (wepawaug fort): John Fowler was one of the "young men" of Milford who in 1671 destroyed the Wepawaug Indian fort — the same prank for which Joseph Platt (X00076) and friends were tried by the General Court at New Haven and fined £10 each. Both men are now X-tier ancestors in this tree through separate lines. The Wepawaug fort incident connects the Fowler and Platt families in the same act of colonial mischief, twelve years before their descendants would marry into the Newton family.

narrative_blocks.header: In his youth he wrecked an Indian fort
narrative_blocks.body: In 1671 he was among a band of young Milford men who tore down the Wepawaug Indians' fort — a piece of colonial mischief for which the New Haven court tried him, fined him £10, and bound him to good behavior.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty years later, a fort took his life
narrative_blocks.body: Two decades after wrecking one fort in mischief, he died taking another in earnest — killed storming an Indian stronghold during King William's War, around 1693. He left a will naming his only son, John, and a widow, Sarah, who would go on to marry Captain Samuel Newton.

narrative_blocks.header: He called Governor Robert Treat his uncle
narrative_blocks.body: His will named the colony's governor, Robert Treat, as his 'honorable uncle' — a tie that placed this Milford soldier among the kin of one of Connecticut's leading founders.

notable.notable_blurb: First minister of Milford

narrative_blocks.header: He came over with Davenport in 1637
narrative_blocks.body: Schooled at the Merchant Taylors' School and Emmanuel College, Cambridge, Peter landed at Boston on 26 June 1637 with John Davenport and Theophilus Eaton. Dedham offered him and fifteen of his company house lots that summer, but he declined and went on with Davenport to New Haven.

narrative_blocks.header: He named Milford for a millstream
narrative_blocks.body: In February 1639 the Herefordshire men bought the land called Wepawaug from its sachem, who handed them a twig set in a piece of turf as a sign of surrender, for six coats, ten blankets, a kettle, twelve hatchets, twelve hoes, two dozen knives and a dozen mirrors. They named it Milford for a stream that could turn a mill.

narrative_blocks.header: First of the seven pillars
narrative_blocks.body: The Milford church was gathered at New Haven on 22 August 1639, in Mr. Newman's barn, with Peter's name first among its seven pillars. That September forty-five planters and their families, some two hundred people, followed an Indian trail ten miles west to Milford, and he was ordained their pastor in April 1640.

narrative_blocks.header: Buried in his own garden
narrative_blocks.body: Peter Prudden died in August 1656 and was buried in his garden on Prospect Street alongside an infant son. The approximately seven-acre property became Milford's first graveyard. John Winthrop wrote that he "was useful in his place and of high esteem in the colony."

narrative_blocks.header: His widow married New York's first mayor
narrative_blocks.body: After Prudden's death his widow Joanna married Captain Thomas Willett, who became the first Mayor of New York City. She outlived Willett too and married a third time, to the Rev. John Bishop, in 1674.

burial.plot_notes: Cenotaph. Actual burial site is on former home lot at 55-67 Prospect Street, now marked by a 2017 roadside marker.

As a young man removed from Milford to Woodbury, Litchfield County CT. On September 11, 1773, just before his marriage, bought twenty-five acres of the Hazen home lot in Woodbury (which bordered on land he already owned). On March 25, 1774 he and his brother Isaac quitclaimed to their mother Mary Newton, during her widowhood, one-half of their dwelling houses in Woodbury, in consideration of her giving up her right in the dwelling and lot where their honored father (the late Ezekiel⁴) had lived. Sold land to Elijah Hazen of Woodbury June 2, 1775; sold part of his farm to Elnathan Mitchell April 5, 1776. Married Mary Hazen (I00101) of Norwich CT (b. September 11, 1754; d. February 4, 1823) on September 16, 1773. Migrated to Hartford VT in 1777, traveling in the dead of winter using the ice-covered Connecticut River as a highway. Revolutionary War service per pension application (rejected for lack of proof, Pension File R.7633): enlisted last day April 1775; Col. Sheldon's Regiment of Horse, Connecticut Line, Capt. Curtis, Lt. Judson, Ensign Martin; discharged Nov. 1, 1777 at Fairfield CT. Died Hartford VT December 29, 1839, age 86. Newton-line position: Roger¹ (I00003, m. Mary Hooker H00003) → John² (H00014) → Ezekiel³ (H00057) → Ezekiel⁴ (H00169) → David⁵ (HD0233). 1 Aug 2026: all sixteen children now built and wired. Five already matched FamilySearch exactly, four had names but no dates, seven were absent. The printed genealogy's '16 children who all lived' and the FamilySearch list AGREE on the count and on every date checked. Burial linked to the new Christian Street Cemetery record. NOTE the marriage PLACE is still unset: FamilySearch says Milford, but this record's own notes put the wedding at Woodbury and document a land purchase there five days before it. Left empty for Sam. Newton family chapter 35 (David^5), read from Sam's page images 1 Aug 2026; the family record quoted there is 'The Newton Family', a manuscript in the hand of Lucy Ida (Newton) Dimick, 1856-1943, kept in her Bible. Detail taken from it: he was the progenitor of all the early Newtons in the Town of Hartford; he removed from Milford to Woodbury as a young man; bought 25 acres of the Hazen home lot from Thomas Hazen 11 Sept. 1773, five days before the wedding; sold land to Elijah Hazen 2 June 1775 and part of his farm to Elnathan Mitchell 5 Apr. 1776. Thomas Hazen, his wife's uncle, had been deeded 1000 acres by the Town of Hartford on 14 May 1773 for his services in the New York negotiations, and those Hazen ties are given as the reason David chose Hartford. He made carts and was sometimes paid in land, thirty acres for one cart. He set out a tree at each child's birth; sixteen stood in the dooryard when 'The Old and The New' reported it in July 1901. Called Dea. (Deacon) David in the Dartmouth sketches of his sons, hence the deacon tag; his title field still reads Private from the military service and is left for Sam. NOT ASSERTED: the chapter says the first death in the family came 'nearly fifty-two years' after the marriage, but the wedding was Sept. 1773 and the first child to die was Jasper in 1821 or 1822 — forty-eight or forty-nine years. The source's own arithmetic does not check, so no NB uses it. The same chapter records the 25 Mar. 1774 Woodbury quitclaim by David AND HIS BROTHER ISAAC to their widowed mother. Isaac H00175 was deleted from the tree earlier today on Sam's instruction; this page is independent evidence that an Isaac was David's brother. Reported to Sam, not acted on. From the second set of page images (1 Aug 2026): David, his wife Mary and their daughter Lucy are all in the Dothan church's list of members admitted to full communion before 1820, and David was a member of the Church of Christ at Dartmouth College, Presbyterian in persuasion. CAVEAT on the deacon tag and blurb: the chapter says only that 'it is assumed that David, called Deacon as the father of two Dartmouth alumni, was a deacon in the Dothan church' — the title is attested, the office is the genealogist's inference. Sam's call whether to keep it. His registered ear mark in the Town of Hartford, where cattle ran at large and about 125 marks were recorded: 'a slanting crop at the underside of each ear.' Civic and business: with Mitchell Clark and Asa Tilden he was entrusted with the Ottauquechee bridge after the town was indicted in 1803 for neglecting it; shareholder in the White River Bridge Co. (incorporated 1815) and in the White River Turnpike Co. (incorporated 1 Nov. 1800, about twenty miles, now Highway 14). Census head of family 1790/91, 1800, 1810, 1820, 1830; in 1800 the household held eleven males and six females; by 1830 he was the only male, 70-80, with his two unmarried daughters. Died intestate; John Strong of Hartford administrator from 19 Feb. 1840; inventory filed 24 Apr. 1840 and the residue divided among twelve heirs on 5 Jan. 1842 (Hartford Probate District, Woodstock, v. 14, pp. 85-88). The family also lived through 'eighteen hundred and froze to death', the summer of 1816. Dollar figures from the inventory are deliberately kept out of all user-facing text. Career row(s) 'Cartwright' removed 1 Aug 2026 on Sam's instruction: a bare trade with no organisation and no years is not a career quick-hit, it is the blurb. The trade is carried in bio_blurb instead. TREE-WIDE NEWTON SCAN, 2 Aug 2026 (Sam asked for a full pass). Forty-six Newtons in the file carry a Vermont place. They resolve into TWO separate migrations out of Milford, Connecticut, and the two leaders are second cousins: David (b. 1753) took his family east of the Green Mountains to Hartford in Windsor County in 1777, and Lt. Charles Newton (HD8667, b. 1752, son of John Newton III) went west to Ferrisburgh in Addison County. Both descend from John Newton Sr. and Lydia Ford at +3. CC added both ways.

narrative_blocks.header: Crossed to Vermont on the frozen Connecticut River
narrative_blocks.body: David Newton moved his family from Connecticut to Hartford Vermont in 1777, traveling in the dead of winter and using the ice-covered Connecticut River as a highway according to family tradition. Just before his marriage four years earlier he had bought twenty-five acres of the Hazen home lot in Woodbury Connecticut.

narrative_blocks.header: A tree set out for every child born
narrative_blocks.body: He made carts, and was once paid thirty acres of land for a single one. Sixteen birthday trees still stood in the dooryard of his house three generations later.

narrative_blocks.header: From cart-maker to turnpike shareholder
narrative_blocks.body: The town put him in charge of replacing the Ottauquechee bridge in 1803, and he bought into the White River Bridge Company and the turnpike that ran twenty miles up the valley. He died without a will, his whole personal estate a bed, a brass clock, a box stove and those shares.

narrative_blocks.header: His children went barefoot through the winters
narrative_blocks.body: He settled at Dothan in a log house so poor that the children went without shoes all winter. Sheldon, the eldest, had none until he was eighteen.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixteen years a widower at Hartford
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Hazen died at Dothan in the February of 1823. He outlived her by sixteen years, the same number as the children they had raised, and was eighty-six when he died.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten of his sixteen children passed seventy
narrative_blocks.body: The sixteen lived more than eleven hundred years between them, and every one of them reached adulthood. Each of the sons stood over six feet.

people.research_notes: [Pilot103 enrichment]: Mary Hazen, wife of David Newton (HD0233). Born Norwich, New London County, Connecticut, September 11, 1754. Married David September 16, 1773 at Woodbury CT. Migrated with David from Connecticut to Hartford Vermont in 1777, via ice-covered Connecticut River in winter. Died February 4, 1823, age 68. Burial place not yet established. Source: Newton family genealogy. [Pilot103 data correction]: Pre-existing death.city/state values 'Dothan, Vermont' were almost certainly erroneous — Dothan is a city in Alabama, not Vermont, and the Newton genealogy bio gives no death location. Cleared to null pending source confirmation. 1 Aug 2026 — the 'Dothan' correction above was itself WRONG and is reversed. Sam's FamilySearch extract gives her death as 'Dothan, Hartford, Windsor, Vt': Dothan is a village in the town of HARTFORD, Windsor County, Vermont — the town this family migrated to in 1777 — not Dothan, Alabama. Death place restored as Hartford, Windsor County, Vermont, with the village recorded here. Burial established as Christian Street Cemetery, Hartford, coordinates from Sam. Newton family chapter 35 (David^5), read from Sam's page images 1 Aug 2026; the family record quoted there is 'The Newton Family', a manuscript in the hand of Lucy Ida (Newton) Dimick, 1856-1943, kept in her Bible. Her parentage from that chapter: daughter of Joseph^4 Hazen (Thomas^3, Thomas^2, Edward^1) and Elizabeth Durkee. Entered as names only — neither parent is built, and as parents of an in-law they are outside the Jalapeno Rule unless Sam wants them as orbit figures. Two Hazen connections worth knowing: Mary was a cousin of Capt. Joshua Hazen, and her sister Mercy Hazen was his wife — so when David served in Capt. Joshua Hazen's Hartford company in the 1780 Royalton Alarm, he was serving under his wife's cousin and brother-in-law. Joshua is not in the tree; if he is ever built that is a CC. Her uncle Thomas Hazen held 1000 acres across the north of the town, including the site of West Hartford village. She and her daughter Lucy appear with David in the Dothan church's list of members admitted to full communion before 1820. The Dothan meeting house had no steeple and no bell — locally called 'God's Barn' — and the congregation was summoned by a conch-shell blown by her uncle Thomas Hazen, which after his death no one else could sound. 1 Aug 2026: NB3 rewritten on Sam's flag. The earlier block reported the 1800 census household of eleven males and six females, which implied the full sixteen were at home; Avis had married Justin Smith in Nov. 1795 and left, and the youngest two were not yet born. The chapter's own note — fourteen at home when Sheldon turned twenty-one — is the accurate and more interesting fact.

narrative_blocks.header: Pregnant, with three under four, going north
narrative_blocks.body: She was carrying her fourth child when the family left Connecticut in the winter of 1777; Sheldon was three, Rufus two and Avis one. David was born at Hartford that March.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-four years and seven months at the last
narrative_blocks.body: Solon, the sixteenth, was born in April 1799, when she was forty-four years and seven months old. She had married five days after her nineteenth birthday.

narrative_blocks.header: Fourteen at home, and never all sixteen
narrative_blocks.body: When Sheldon turned twenty-one in 1795 there were fourteen children living at home. Avis married that November and Jasper and Solon were not yet born, so the whole sixteen were never under the roof at once.

narrative_blocks.header: Her uncle called the church with a conch
narrative_blocks.body: She and her daughter Lucy were admitted to full communion at the Dothan church before 1820. It had no steeple and no bell; her uncle Thomas Hazen summoned the congregation by blowing a conch-shell.

military_service.notes: Named in a Return of Militia dated 12 Feb. 1814. Enrolment during the war; no engagement is documented. Tag applied on Sam's instruction, 1 Aug 2026.

narrative_blocks.header: He heated a board to stand on
narrative_blocks.body: Sheldon had no shoes until he was eighteen. To keep his feet off the snow while cutting wood he would warm a board at the fire, carry it out, and stand on it until it went cold again.

narrative_blocks.header: He took in two of the town's poor
narrative_blocks.body: Putt Wilson and Charles Mattoon were placed in his keeping in March 1821 and probably stayed until 1832. Wilson had spent the four years before that confined in a cage on another man's premises.

narrative_blocks.header: Years in a log cabin, then prosperity
narrative_blocks.body: He was one of the first settlers at Hartford and kept his family in a log cabin for years. By the end he farmed well enough to afford what the chapter calls the luxuries the times would allow.

narrative_blocks.header: His father sold him a hundred acres
narrative_blocks.body: David Newton deeded him lot number twelve, north of the White River, in March 1804 — ground his father had bought from John Bennett a decade before. Philip Sprague witnessed the deed.

narrative_blocks.header: Five sons by the first wife, then daughters
narrative_blocks.body: Betsy Sanderson bore him five boys and no girls before she died in 1807. Nancy Wilder bore four daughters and one son.

narrative_blocks.header: Three brothers' farms met at Podunk
narrative_blocks.body: Rufus, Truman and Daniel held adjoining farms in Podunk, in the southwest corner of Norwich near West Hartford. Daniel died there in 1831.

narrative_blocks.header: The farm went to Nelson on one condition
narrative_blocks.body: In January 1842 he deeded the Norwich place to Nelson, and Nelson deeded it back conditionally. The paper was void unless he kept both his parents on that farm, in sickness and health, for the rest of their lives.

narrative_blocks.header: His burying ground is lost in the woods
narrative_blocks.body: He and Theda lie in the family's own plot on the Norwich homestead, behind the cellar hole. The buildings are gone, the pastures have gone back to forest, and the roads in have closed over.

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve years to the day after Orra
narrative_blocks.body: His daughter Orra died on the twenty-eighth of December 1842, thirteen months into her marriage. Rufus died on the twenty-eighth of December 1854.

burial.plot_notes: Podunk Cemetery, the family's private plot on the Norwich homestead

narrative_blocks.header: Christian Street held his birth and his grave
narrative_blocks.body: He was born on Christian Street in Hartford in the March of 1778 and lies in the cemetery on that same road. He died at Dothan of general infirmity, at eighty-six.

narrative_blocks.header: The third son to get his father's land
narrative_blocks.body: David Newton settled his sons in turn — Sheldon and Rufus by two deeds on a single day in March 1804, and David Jr. in February 1828, with a piece bought from James Culver west of the road to Rufus. He was fifty by then.

narrative_blocks.header: The first child born in Dothan
narrative_blocks.body: He was born on the first of October 1779, two years after his parents came up the river ice to Hartford, and was the first child born in the Dothan settlement. He died at Norwich in the December of 1848.

narrative_blocks.header: Chosen to raise the West Hartford meeting house
narrative_blocks.body: He and Eunice were among the sixteen who organized the West Hartford church in 1830, coming over from Dothan. Two years later he was one of five men chosen to supervise the building of the meeting house.

narrative_blocks.header: The cider mill share nobody could divide
narrative_blocks.body: The inventory of his farm counted a hundred and forty-nine sheep, four hundred and sixty-one pounds of wool and two hundred sap buckets. What could not be divided among his heirs were his pews, his horse stall at the meeting house and his share of the cider mill.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifteen days between his will and his death
narrative_blocks.body: He executed it on the fifteenth of December 1848 before Lucius Hazen, Ezra Wood and Eliza Perry, and died on the thirtieth. It was proved a fortnight after that.

narrative_blocks.header: Orson's share was a twenty-fifth of Calvin's
narrative_blocks.body: Calvin, Joseph, Laura Ann and Sarah Lucinda each took the same large legacy, and the rest fell away below them. Half the residue went to his widow for life and then to three of them; the other half went to Edward Orvis outright.

narrative_blocks.header: Three parcels bought on the turnpike in 1806
narrative_blocks.body: Erastus Chapman sold him an acre with a house west of the turnpike road, fifteen acres on the far side of it, and twenty-five more beside John Dutton's place. He farmed there on Christian Street the rest of his life and was buried across the road from his own door.

narrative_blocks.header: Equipped for the war with two brothers
narrative_blocks.body: A return of 26 June 1813 lists him among the certified equipt members of the first cavalry company in the fourth division of the state. His brothers Daniel and Sheldon were named in the militia return made at Hartford the following day, and the selectmen's book has the detached men making trips up to Burlington.

narrative_blocks.header: Wild beasts cried at him from the woods
narrative_blocks.body: Sent to the mill as a boy from his father's place at Dothan, he was frightened on the way home one evening by the noise of animals in the dark. That same road later carried the president of Dartmouth College past his farm, coming over from Hanover to the Dothan church.

narrative_blocks.header: Someone put his old white horse in verse
narrative_blocks.body: The horse took the family up to the Dothan church week after week, and an unknown hand set it down in rhyme that reached print in 1899. No Pegasus was he, the poem allows, but a good sound nag who would tug at the plow till evensong.

narrative_blocks.header: The 1860 census put him in Joseph's house
narrative_blocks.body: He had headed his own family in every Hartford census from 1810, and in 1850 was sixty-seven and farming with Catherine and their boy Joseph at home. Six years after she died the enumerator found him at seventy-nine, still called a farmer, living in that son's household.

narrative_blocks.body: Charles Pond married Martha Miles in 1767; his brother Zachariah married Lucy, and the two brides were third cousins to each other. Martha's son Charles Hobby Pond became governor of Connecticut.
