narrative_blocks.header: Second Mary — first Mary the twin died young
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Reynolds Rawson was born November 20, 1716 in Bristol Rhode Island — the second daughter named Mary, after the first Mary (twin to her sister Anne) had died young earlier in November 1716. The replacement naming worked: this second Mary lived to nearly eighty-seven, dying in 1803 after surviving two marriages and bearing children in both. Her first marriage to Dr. Samuel Morse left her widowed with three young children when he died in 1743.

narrative_blocks.header: Married her first cousin Edward Rawson in 1748
narrative_blocks.body: After widowhood in 1743, Mary remarried Deacon Edward Rawson — her first cousin through their mothers Susannah Rawson Reynolds and Wilson Rawson who were siblings, both fifth-generation Hooker descendants via the Sarah Hooker line. Their marriage was a documented Pierpont-Reynolds first-cousin union. The 'Aunt Reynolds' relationship was sometimes recorded ambiguously as grandmother rather than mother, but Mary was the daughter, not the granddaughter, of Susannah Rawson Reynolds.

narrative_blocks.header: He outlived nearly every man of ’76
narrative_blocks.body: Grindall Reynolds defended Narragansett Bay as a Revolutionary lieutenant and lived to ninety-one, dying in 1847 as one of the last surviving “real sons” of the Revolution in Massachusetts. He was named for his great-grandfather, the Rev. Grindall Rawson.

narrative_blocks.header: Three wives, seven children, fifty years apart
narrative_blocks.body: Reynolds married three times and had children by each: his first child arrived in 1780, his last in 1830, a span of half a century. His youngest son became a noted Concord minister.

narrative_blocks.body: He married Elizabeth Bradford at Duxbury in April 1784. Their son Bradford was born the next March, Elizabeth died in June a day short of twenty-six, and the boy was dead by October.

narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Bristol in Rhode Island and married there, but the children's birthplaces run from Nansemond County to Norfolk and back to Providence. He died in Nansemond County in December 1842, eighty-five years old.

military_service.notes: Enlisted 26 April 1863; served in the Army of Mississippi and Army of Tennessee; captured at Blakely, Alabama, 9 April 1865.

narrative_blocks.header: He followed a Hooker into Congress unrelated
narrative_blocks.body: Elected to the Fifty-fourth Congress in 1894, Spencer took the Mississippi seat just vacated by Charles E. Hooker, a Confederate colonel who, despite the shared surname, has no documented kinship to the Thomas Hooker line from which Spencer descended. A genuine Hooker descendant thus replaced a man merely named Hooker.

narrative_blocks.header: Captured in the war's final week
narrative_blocks.body: Spencer enlisted as a private in Cowan's Battery of the First Mississippi Light Artillery in 1863 and served through the Army of Mississippi and the Army of Tennessee. He was captured at Blakely, Alabama, on April 9, 1865, in one of the last engagements of the Civil War.

narrative_blocks.header: From cotton fields to the Capitol
narrative_blocks.body: After the war Spencer returned to Port Gibson and worked in agriculture, real estate, and insurance before entering politics. He served in the Mississippi House from 1892 to 1894 and then a single term in the United States Congress.

narrative_blocks.header: Son of a Yale-trained frontier patriarch
narrative_blocks.body: James was the sixth of ten children of Horatio Nelson Spencer, a Connecticut-born Yale graduate who became a Port Gibson banker, railroad president, and planter. The Spencers carried their Hooker descent from New England into the Mississippi cotton country.

narrative_blocks.header: His son Aman governed Argentina — smuggled pamphlets
narrative_blocks.body: His son Haman Rawson (born 1792, known in Argentina as Amán) trained as a doctor, served as a U.S. Navy surgeon, then settled in San Juan, Argentina. He governed San Juan Province for four days during a political emergency in 1831, founded the city of Caucete, and smuggled copies of Sarmiento's anti-Rosas pamphlet Facundo hidden in medicine drawers. He died in San Juan on January 12, 1847.

b. 1792 Montague MA; d. Jan 12, 1847 San Juan Argentina. Known as Amán in Argentina (born Haman). M.D. 1814; US Navy surgeon. Arrived Buenos Aires 1818; San Juan 1819. Converted to Catholicism to marry Justina Rojo. Founded Caucete city 1822. Chief physician San Juan Province; faced smallpox epidemic. Provincial deputy multiple terms. Emergency 4-day chairman 1831. Smuggled Sarmiento's Facundo in medicine drawers. (Wikipedia) [Migrated from marriage.notes (spouse X02060)]: Relationship after Justina's death 1822. Children took mother's surname Martinez except Juan de Dios who used Rawson. [Stage 6Y-264 schema cleanup]: notable_blurb trimmed from [9w] 'Founded Caucete; 4-day chairman San Juan; smuggled Sarmiento's Facundo' → '4-day chairman San Juan'.
[Stage 6Y-264 NB#1 body trim]: original body had 4 sentences, trimmed to first 3. Original body preserved here for reference: 'Amán Rawson received his medical degree in 1814 and served as a surgeon in the U.S. Navy. In 1818 — just two years after Argentina declared independence — he arrived in Buenos Aires. He spent a short time in Mendoza before settling in San Juan in early 1819. No source explains exactly why he went; the period 1817-1820 drew many American and European adventurers to the newly independent republics of South America.'

narrative_blocks.header: A navy surgeon who settled in San Juan
narrative_blocks.body: Haman Rawson of Montague, Massachusetts, took his medical degree in 1814 and served as a United States Navy surgeon. He reached Buenos Aires in 1818 and, at the invitation of his friend Colesberry, the doctor who had attended San Martín at Mendoza, settled in San Juan, Argentina, early in 1819, turning Catholic to marry Justina Rojo.

narrative_blocks.header: Four days governing San Juan, 1831
narrative_blocks.body: In April 1831, with the Federalist general Facundo Quiroga marching on San Juan, the province handed its government to a three-man emergency board of Amán, the priest José de Oro and Ignacio José Sánchez. Amán chaired it for four days, called an election and handed over to the winner.

narrative_blocks.header: Facundo in drawers marked for venereal disease
narrative_blocks.body: In his last years Amán smuggled copies of Sarmiento's Facundo, the book that damned the Rosas dictatorship, into San Juan in drawers doused with a chemical stench, under a sign saying they held remedies for venereal disease.

narrative_blocks.header: He vaccinated a province against smallpox
narrative_blocks.body: As the province's chief physician Amán met a smallpox epidemic by spreading vaccination, and for nearly thirty years he kept a drugstore in the town.

narrative_blocks.header: The American colony that became Caucete
narrative_blocks.body: In 1822 Amán planned a colony of American farmers in the province; Argentines settled it instead, and it grew into the city of Caucete, with irrigation along the left bank of the San Juan River.

narrative_blocks.header: Respected by all, but plainly a Unitarian
narrative_blocks.body: Amán sat in the provincial legislature off and on from 1822 and served Governor Martín Yanzón as minister in 1834; every faction respected him, but his sympathies were Unitarian. In 1840 he paid soldiers to overthrow the caudillo Nazario Benavídez, and when the plot failed he still kept his seat.

narrative_blocks.header: Father of a painter and a minister
narrative_blocks.body: Amán's sons by Justina were the painter Benjamín Franklin Rawson and the physician Guillermo Rawson, Mitre's minister of the interior, named for his friend Colesberry. By Mercedes Martínez he had Juan de Dios, grandfather of the general who ruled Argentina for three days in 1943.

notable.notable_blurb: Argentine interior minister and pioneer of public hygiene

people.research_notes:
b. Jun 24, 1821 San Juan Argentina; d. Jan 20, 1890 Paris France. Son of Amán Rawson (HD0277) and Justina Rojo (X01120). Jesuit education San Juan; M.D. Univ. of Buenos Aires 1844. Jailed 1853 for opposing caudillo Benavidez. Paraná Congress 1854. Interior Minister 1862 under President Mitre. Negotiated Welsh colony in Chubut — city of Rawson named for him. 1876 Centennial Exposition Philadelphia — presented Buenos Aires public health work. Elected member American Antiquarian Society 1879. Died Paris 1890 during medical treatment. (Wikipedia) [Stage 6Y-264 schema cleanup]: notable_blurb trimmed from [13w] 'Argentine Interior Minister 1862; founded Welsh colony in Patagonia; city named for him' → 'Argentine Interior Minister 1862'.
[Stage 6Y-264 NB#1 header trim]: 'He agreed to a Welsh colony in Patagonia — now the capital of Chubut bears his name' → 'He agreed to a Welsh colony in Patagonia'.
[Stage 6Y-264 NB#2 header trim]: 'Jailed for opposing the caudillo — then became the country's Interior Minister' → 'Jailed for opposing the caudillo'.

narrative_blocks.header: Telegraph, railroad and the metric system
narrative_blocks.body: Named Mitre's minister of the interior in 1862, Guillermo strung the telegraph from Buenos Aires to Rosario and Montevideo, pushed the railroad from Rosario to Córdoba, and brought in the metric system. He also studied life in the city's crowded tenements, the conventillos.

narrative_blocks.header: He agreed to a Welsh colony in Patagonia
narrative_blocks.body: As Argentine Interior Minister in 1862, Guillermo Rawson met Captain Love Jones-Parry and Lewis Jones, who were scouting Patagonia for a Welsh settlement. Rawson negotiated the agreement that resulted in the colony in the Chubut Valley. The capital of Chubut Province is still named Rawson.

narrative_blocks.header: Carrying the country while Mitre was at war
narrative_blocks.body: During the Paraguayan War, with Mitre at the front, Guillermo attended Vice President Marcos Paz through the cholera that killed him in January 1868, then carried the government himself and put down a rising in Santa Fe. When Mitre came home and overruled him, he resigned.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded the Argentine Red Cross
narrative_blocks.body: In 1873 Guillermo became the medical faculty's first professor of hygiene, and students, doctors and the public crowded his lectures; in 1877 he presented the vital statistics of Buenos Aires at Philadelphia. In 1880 he founded the Argentine Red Cross with Toribio de Ayerza.

narrative_blocks.header: The first genetics thesis in Buenos Aires
narrative_blocks.body: Guillermo took his medical degree in 1844 at twenty-three, so brilliantly that his professors asked the university to excuse him from defending his thesis; it refused, and he defended it with distinction. His subject, how physiological and pathological traits pass by heredity, made it the first thesis on genetics at the University of Buenos Aires.

narrative_blocks.header: Jailed for opposing the caudillo
narrative_blocks.body: In 1853, Rawson was imprisoned for opposing Nazario Benavidez, the strongman governor of San Juan. A decade later he was Interior Minister of Argentina under President Bartolomé Mitre, and in 1876 represented Argentina at the Centennial Exposition in Philadelphia, presenting the most developed body of work on public health in Buenos Aires at the time.

narrative_blocks.header: He paid back the city with interest
narrative_blocks.body: Losing his sight, Guillermo went to Paris in 1885 on a municipal grant to study new ideas for Buenos Aires. When his eyes kept him from the work he returned the money with the interest it would have earned; he had already turned part of his own small pension into a hygiene prize at the medical school.

narrative_blocks.header: Cepeda, Pavón and the Paraguayan war
narrative_blocks.body: Juan de Dios fought in the civil-war battles of Cepeda and Pavón, then against Paraguay in the War of the Triple Alliance, at Yatay and the siege of Uruguaiana in 1865. He rose to lieutenant colonel and served again in the Conquest of the Desert, the campaigns against the peoples of the south.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight children from Mendoza to Santa Fe
narrative_blocks.body: Juan de Dios married Elizarda Guiñazú Encinas at Godoy Cruz, Mendoza, on 28 November 1855, and their eight children were born in Mendoza, Rojas, Junín and Santa Fe. Both lie in the Recoleta cemetery in Buenos Aires.

narrative_blocks.header: He was illegitimate
narrative_blocks.body: Juan de Dios was born in 1833 to Amán Rawson and Mercedes Martínez, eleven years after the death of Amán's wife Justina, and carried both surnames, Rawson Martínez. His grandson was General Arturo Rawson, who seized the presidency of Argentina in 1943 and held it three days.

narrative_blocks.header: She left Mendon for the island at eighteen
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Mendon in Worcester County in December 1715, she married James Coffin at Nantucket on 16 January 1734, a month after turning eighteen. She spent the rest of her life on the island and died there at seventy-five.

narrative_blocks.header: The Hooker line reaches the Coffins through her
narrative_blocks.body: Her five children by James Coffin were the first of this Coffin family to carry Hooker blood, and it came through her rather than through him. Her son Joshua married his cousin Catharine Coffin.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandmother was a Gardner of Nantucket
narrative_blocks.body: Priscilla Gardner Arthur was sister to the Mary Gardner who married Jethro Coffin and sat about 1720 for the earliest known portrait of a Nantucketer. That made her a great-niece of Mary's.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father died when she was ten
narrative_blocks.body: Wilson Rawson of Mendon died in 1726 and her mother Margaret remarried a Pinkham of Nantucket. Her own daughter Susanna married Capt. John Pinkham of the island thirty-one years after that.

open_questions.question: Is Josiah Rawson (b.~1730s, m. Hannah Bass, Grafton/Warwick MA) a sibling or cousin of this entry?
open_questions.notes: The Rawson genealogy book (entry #25) documents Josiah Rawson marrying Hannah Bass of Braintree, residing in Grafton then Warwick MA. His son Lemuel (#163-4 in Rawson book) settled in Richfield, Summit County OH. Lemuel's son Dr. Secretary Rawson (b.1796) was Richfield's first physician (1824+), practiced 40 years, founded the town's first library (1825), and was active in temperance work. If Josiah is a Hooker-Rawson descendant (gen 4-5), then Dr. Secretary Rawson is a gen 6-7 Hooker descendant who settled on the same Western Reserve land as John Newton (HD2925) and Eunice Newton Oviatt (HD2934) — all Connecticut Hooker descendants converging in Richfield OH. Action: Match Josiah Rawson to Rawson genealogy entry chain in the project.

bio.title: Reverend
bio.bio_blurb: Pastor of Mendon for fifty-two years

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-two years in his father-in-law’s pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: Settled at Mendon in 1715 as successor to Rev. Grindal Rawson, Dorr then married Rawson’s daughter — keeping the pulpit in one extended family for the better part of a century. He died “in his 79th year and the 52nd of his ministry”; his epitaph reads, “His temper was mild and placid.”

narrative_blocks.header: He succeeded the father, married the daughter
narrative_blocks.body: Ordained at Mendon in 1716 to succeed the late Grindal Rawson, Dorr married Rawson’s daughter Mary eight years later — and held the pulpit fifty-two years, until his death. The son of Edward and Elizabeth Hawley Dorr of Roxbury, he was Harvard, class of 1711.

narrative_blocks.header: The Association met at his house
narrative_blocks.body: First Moderator of the Mendon Association from its 1751 founding — which gathered at his home for its first five years — he remained its standing Moderator until death, favored Jonathan Edwards’s views, and signed the ministers’ testimonial for the revival of 1740.

SIBLING OF AARON'S FATHER: Moses married H00218 Mary Dorr Taft (Hooker/Rawson, gen 4); his brother Peter's son Aaron married HD0339 Rhoda Rawson Taft (Hooker/Rawson, gen 5). Two Taft men (uncle and nephew) both married into the Hooker/Rawson line.

military_service.notes: Enlisted age 18. Reported sick in general hospital Dec 1776. Later served at Fort George.

narrative_blocks.header: Continental Line fifer at eighteen, three engagements
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph Taft enlisted on January 1, 1776 at age eighteen as a fifer in Captain Silas Wild's company of Colonel Edmund Phinney's regiment of the Continental Line. He reengaged in November 1776 under Colonel Brewer and signed a three-year term in January 1778, with later service at Fort George on Lake George. He had been reported sick in the general hospital in December 1776 — a common fate of soldiers in the smallpox-stricken winter camps of the war's second year.

narrative_blocks.header: Postwar Harvard, then physician at Weston
narrative_blocks.body: After three years in the Continental Army, Taft returned to Massachusetts and entered Harvard College — graduating in 1783, the year of the Treaty of Paris that closed the war. He practiced as a physician at Weston Massachusetts for the rest of his working life and died at Randolph Massachusetts in January 1824 at age sixty-six.

Aaron Taft Jr. — distinguished from Aaron Taft Sr. (b.1727, s. of Lieut. Joseph and Elisabeth) in Uxbridge vital records by "(Jr., c.r.i)" notation on children's entries. Aaron Taft House in Uxbridge listed on National Register of Historic Places. Moved family to Vermont 1799.

UNCLE/NEPHEW CONNECTION: His uncle Moses Taft (brother of his father Peter) married H00218 Mary Dorr Taft (Hooker/Rawson descendant, gen 4). Aaron himself married HD0339 Rhoda Rawson Taft (Hooker/Rawson descendant, gen 5). Two Taft men — uncle and nephew — each married a Hooker/Rawson woman independently.

narrative_blocks.header: He lost his property backing friends' debts
narrative_blocks.body: Aaron Taft co-signed notes for friends at Uxbridge, and when they failed, the endorsements took his property — after thirty years in town, much of it as clerk. At fifty-five he sold up and moved the family to Vermont, where his affairs recovered.

narrative_blocks.header: Nineteen yoke of oxen through the snow
narrative_blocks.body: The 1799 move to Townshend began behind two yoke of oxen; the Vermont snow lay so deep that nineteen were needed to haul the household up to the hill farm afterward called Taft Hill. His son Peter, fourteen, drove the family cow the hundred miles on foot.

narrative_blocks.header: His Vermont farmhouse is a landmark now
narrative_blocks.body: The Aaron Taft house at Townshend stands on the National Register of Historic Places — the hill farm of a man remembered for great intelligence and integrity. His grandson Alphonso founded Skull and Bones at Yale; his great-grandson reached the White House.

narrative_blocks.header: From the plow to the bench, self-taught
narrative_blocks.body: Reared a farmer with a common-school education, he taught school, worked as a surveyor, and read law on his own. The self-taught lawyer sat eight years as judge of Windham County's probate and county courts and served many years in the Vermont House.

narrative_blocks.header: The schoolteacher built a school of his own
narrative_blocks.body: He helped establish the Leland and Gray seminary in Townshend and served as its first president, with a trustee's seat from 1835 to 1841.

narrative_blocks.header: He followed his son west at fifty-six
narrative_blocks.body: He left Vermont for Cincinnati in 1841, two years after his son Alphonso settled there to practice law. The last twenty-six years of his life passed in the city where his grandson, a future president, would be born.

notable.notable_blurb: Grant's Attorney General; co-founded Skull and Bones

narrative_blocks.header: He dissented alone, and Ohio came round
narrative_blocks.body: The Cincinnati board stopped Bible reading in the schools in 1869 and his own court ordered it back. He alone dissented — the Constitution gave Protestants no right to run religion where children of every faith sat — and Ohio's Supreme Court adopted his reasoning in 1873.

narrative_blocks.header: Two cabinet chairs in a single year
narrative_blocks.body: The dissent cost him the Republican nomination for governor, which went to Rutherford Hayes. Grant made him Secretary of War in March 1876 and Attorney General three months after that.

narrative_blocks.header: Skull and Bones came out of a row
narrative_blocks.body: The Yale debating societies fell out in 1832 over who should have the Phi Beta Kappa places. He and his classmate William Huntington Russell answered by founding Skull and Bones, juniors picked for leadership as much as marks.

narrative_blocks.header: A diplomat in his seventies
narrative_blocks.body: Chester Arthur sent him to Vienna in 1882 and on to St. Petersburg in 1884 — minister to Austria-Hungary, then to Russia, past seventy.

narrative_blocks.header: He and Samuel Colt stole a cannon
narrative_blocks.body: He taught school at sixteen to pay his way to Amherst Academy; there he and young Samuel Colt, the future revolver maker, took General Ebenezer Mattoon's cannon and fired it at the school.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten children, and a President among them
narrative_blocks.body: He married Fanny Phelps in 1841 and Louisa Torrey in 1853, five children by each and four of them dead in infancy. William became President and then Chief Justice; Charles built the Cincinnati Times-Star.

b. Nov 5, 1810 Townshend VT; d. May 21, 1891 San Diego CA. Yale 1833; Yale Law School; admitted CT bar 1838. Cincinnati 1839 onwards. Co-founded Skull and Bones 1832 with William Huntington Russell. Judge Superior Court Cincinnati 1866-1872; Secretary of War Mar-May 1876; U.S. Attorney General May 1876-Mar 1877 (under Grant). U.S. Minister to Austria-Hungary 1882-1884; U.S. Minister to Russia 1884-1885 (under Chester Arthur). Father of William Howard Taft (HD0338). Buried Spring Grove Cemetery Cincinnati (CEM083). narrative_blocks.header: He turned down the Supreme Court three times
narrative_blocks.body: Theodore Roosevelt offered William Howard Taft a seat on the Supreme Court in 1902, again in 1906, and again in 1906. Each time, Taft refused — he felt his work in the Philippines or the War Department wasn't finished. The presidency he ran for in 1908 was, in his own words, 'awful to be afraid of.' The Chief Justiceship — appointed by Harding in 1921 — was what he had always wanted.

narrative_blocks.header: Two months into his presidency
narrative_blocks.body: On May 17, 1909 — just ten weeks after his inauguration — Nellie Taft suffered a severe stroke that left her partially paralyzed and unable to speak. Taft spent hours each day working with her, teaching her to speak again. It took a year.

narrative_blocks.header: 'Take Advice From Theodore,' the wits said
narrative_blocks.body: Theodore Roosevelt was so involved in Taft's 1908 campaign — pressuring delegates, issuing presidential statements, shaping the platform — that humorists coined the acronym 'TAFT': Take Advice from Theodore. Taft himself had said he needed Roosevelt's 'judgment and criticism' for his acceptance speech. Roosevelt later deeply regretted his role in making Taft president and ran against him in 1912, splitting the Republican vote and handing the presidency to Wilson.

narrative_blocks.header: He conceded cases the government had won
narrative_blocks.body: As Solicitor General in 1891 he introduced the confession of error — asking the Supreme Court to overturn a murder conviction the government had secured on inadmissible evidence. The practice continues to this day.

narrative_blocks.header: Armageddon, then an embrace at the Palmer House
narrative_blocks.body: Roosevelt made him president, then broke the party against him in 1912 — Taft carried only Utah and Vermont. They met by chance at Chicago's Palmer House in 1918 and embraced to the applause of the room; Roosevelt died the following January, and Taft wrote that he loved him always and cherished his memory.

narrative_blocks.header: A marble home he never lived to see
narrative_blocks.body: As Chief Justice he fought Congress for the Supreme Court's own building, winning the appropriation in 1927. He died in March 1930, before ground was broken; the Court moved in five years after his death.

bio.bio_blurb: North Haven pastor; Old Light controversialist

narrative_blocks.header: He left the loom for Yale at twenty
narrative_blocks.body: Bred a weaver until nearly twenty, he was tutored into Yale by Timothy Edwards, the first of his name and blood liberally educated in America. Bolton passed him over for Jonathan Edwards in 1723; North Haven called him that next January.

narrative_blocks.header: First to oppose New Light at the Election
narrative_blocks.body: Governor Law gave him the 1742 Election Sermon at Hartford, and he was the first to attack the revival from that platform. A woman screamed out in the assembly before she understood which side he was on.

narrative_blocks.header: He preached against his own melon thief
narrative_blocks.body: Seeing a parishioner in his garden during the Sunday intermission, he named him from the afternoon pulpit: I saw you, John Johnson, thou son of Belial, enter my garden and steal my melons.

narrative_blocks.header: He made his peace with his accusers first
narrative_blocks.body: Eight of his hundred and seventy families had charged him with heresy. On the Monday he walked three miles to a parishioner's funeral and called on those families to be reconciled. He was taken ill the next day.

narrative_blocks.header: Keziah died and Esther raised the boy
narrative_blocks.body: Keziah Taylor died in childbed within days of Ezra's birth in 1727. Inside the year Isaac married Esther Hooker of Farmington, who brought up his son as her own and bore him ten more children.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother's family gave him his quickness
narrative_blocks.body: His son reckoned he got his mind from his mother's side. The Stileses Ezra called dull and unambitious; the Bancrofts brisk, quick and lively, and Ruth passed that to Isaac above all her children.

narrative_blocks.header: His father died in his house at eighty-eight
narrative_blocks.body: John Stiles was a plain Windsor farmer, the first of the name to settle east of the Great River. After his second wife died he left the town for North Haven to live with his son, and died in that house in 1753.

narrative_blocks.header: Every freshman had to learn Hebrew
narrative_blocks.body: Yale made him its seventh president in 1778, and he made himself its first professor of Semitics. He gave his first commencement address in Hebrew, Aramaic and Arabic, and by 1790 admitted defeat and taught only volunteers.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-two years of daily weather and deaths
narrative_blocks.body: For thirty-two years he kept a daily record — temperatures, population counts, births, deaths and marriages, and interviews with Narragansett neighbours and Newport's Jewish families. It fills forty-two boxes at Yale, and is what historians come for.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-eight meetings with a Hebron rabbi
narrative_blocks.body: Haim Isaac Carigal spent 1773 in Newport, and Stiles recorded twenty-eight meetings with him, on everything from Kabbalah to the politics of the Holy Land. They kept writing to each other in Hebrew after he left.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-two people shocked in a row
narrative_blocks.body: With apparatus his classmate Benjamin Franklin gave the college, he charged a glass tube with static electricity, shocked fifty-two people in a row, fired spirits of wine and rum, and made counterfeit spiders crawl. His biographer says he discovered nothing new.

narrative_blocks.header: A hogshead of rum bought him a boy
narrative_blocks.body: In 1756 he sent a hogshead of rum on a voyage to Africa and was repaid with a ten-year-old boy, whom he named Newport. He also signed a letter condemning slavery's cruelty, and freed Newport in 1778.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote Brown's charter, then refused it
narrative_blocks.body: From Newport he drafted the charter of what became Brown University, banning religious tests in it while quietly packing the board with Congregationalists. The Baptists amended that, and he refused a seat, calling it a party college.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother died four days after his birth
narrative_blocks.body: Kezia Taylor died four days after bearing him at North Haven in 1727, and his father married Esther Hooker the next year — Thomas Hooker's great-granddaughter, and the only mother he knew. His daughter Emilia married Judge Jonathan Leavitt of Greenfield.

b. Dec 10, 1727 (O.S. Nov 29) North Haven CT; d. May 12, 1795 New Haven CT age 67. Son of Rev. Isaac Stiles (I00126; Yale 1722) and Kezia Taylor Stiles (d. 4 days after birth). Raised by stepmother Esther Hooker Stiles (H00092), granddaughter of Thomas Hooker. Half-brother of Isaac Stiles Jr. (H00238). Yale 1746; M.A. 1749; ordained 1749. Tutor Yale 1749-1753. Admitted New Haven bar 1753. Second Congregational Church Newport RI 1755-1776. Slaveholder: received Newport (age 10, renamed from Africa) via slave voyage 1756; freed Newport 1778 on move to New Haven; re-indentured Newport+wife for $20/yr 1782; bound Newport's son Jacob (age 2) until age 24. Also purchased Prince (age 14-15) for father Isaac. 1756: co-signed public letter with Samuel Hopkins condemning slavery. Brown University: drafted first charter 1763; revised charter adopted March 3, 1764. Yale president 1778-1795. First professor of Semitics at Yale. 1781 commencement address in Hebrew, Aramaic, Arabic. Corresponded with Jefferson, Franklin, Washington. Elected American Philosophical Society 1768; AAAS Fellow 1781. m.(1) 1757 Elizabeth Hubbard (8 children); m.(2) 1782 Mary Checkley Cranston. Daughter Mary m. Abiel Holmes (Yale 1783) → father of Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr. Daughter Emilia m. Judge Jonathan Leavitt of Greenfield MA. Portrait by Samuel King (1771), Yale Art Gallery accession 1955.3.1 (ART036). narrative_blocks.header: Her stone says her husband's heart trusted her
narrative_blocks.body: She died at thirty-seven in October 1768. The Mount Carmel stone calls her industrious, says she looked well to the ways of her own household, and asks her children to rise up and bless her memory.

narrative_blocks.header: Ezra Stiles was her half-brother
narrative_blocks.body: Rev. Isaac Stiles was father to them both. Keziah was raised beside him by her stepmother Esther Hooker Stiles, and it was their father who married her to Bazel Munson in May 1751.

military_service.notes: Per The Stiles Family in America (BIB008) entry #230: served in the Revolution and was at Horse Neck from May 1781 to March 1782. Horse Neck (Greenwich CT) was an active Revolutionary War outpost under occasional British raid throughout the war.
Served in the Revolution at Horse Neck (now Greenwich CT, on the western frontier facing British-held New York), from May 1781 to March 1782.

narrative_blocks.header: At forty-five, a soldier at Horse Neck
narrative_blocks.body: Ashbel was forty-five when he went into Revolutionary service, and he held the post at Horse Neck, now Greenwich, on the Connecticut line facing British-held New York, from May 1781 to March 1782.

narrative_blocks.header: He signed for a friend and lost everything
narrative_blocks.body: Ashbel inherited his father's house at North Haven and a comfortable property with it. He put his name to a friend's debt and lost all of it.

narrative_blocks.header: From North Haven to the Massachusetts hills
narrative_blocks.body: After the loss Ashbel took the family to Windsor, where Hannah's father lived and their daughter Ruth was born in 1778. In old age they followed Ruth, by then Mrs. Ellis, to Norwich, now Huntington, Massachusetts.

narrative_blocks.header: He married his cousin Hannah Stiles
narrative_blocks.body: In February 1759 Ashbel married his cousin Hannah, daughter of Lieut. Samuel Stiles of Windsor. They were married fifty-one years, and she died at Norwich in September 1810, a month before him.

narrative_blocks.header: His son Benjamin died in Jamaica
narrative_blocks.body: Ashbel and Hannah's son Benjamin, born in 1772, died at Jamaica in the West Indies of injuries from being thrown from a horse.

narrative_blocks.header: His half-brother Ezra Stiles ran Yale
narrative_blocks.body: Ezra Stiles, eight years older, was their father's son by his first wife, Keziah Taylor, and was raised by Ashbel's mother. He was president of Yale College from 1778 until he died in 1795.

narrative_blocks.header: She cut flowers and escutcheons from paper
narrative_blocks.body: Her son set down what he could learn of her: light complexion, grey eye, slender and rather tall, and ingenious to a great degree in needlework, in painting, and in cutting flowers and escutcheons out of paper.

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband's enemies spoke well of her
narrative_blocks.body: Keziah was remembered alike by her husband's friends and by the parishioners who turned on him thirty years later. Asked about her, neither party would name a single blemish in her character.

narrative_blocks.header: She was courted in verse
narrative_blocks.body: Isaac Stiles sent her a poetical love-letter in 1724, the year before the marriage. It survives in manuscript in the Yale College library.

narrative_blocks.header: She died in childbed at twenty-five
narrative_blocks.body: Keziah died in childbed in December 1727, twenty-five years and seven months old and two and a half years married. Ezra, the son she died bearing, was her only surviving child.

church_roles.notes: Ordained the day the church was organized; preached his own ordination sermon

people.research_notes: Taylor forbade publication of his poetry during his lifetime. His manuscript was discovered at Yale in 1937 and he is now considered the finest Puritan poet in American literature — comparable in some ways to the metaphysical poets of England. Five of his daughters by Ruth Wyllys married ministers. He is connected to the Hooker tree only through his daughter Keziah's marriage to Isaac Stiles, who then married Esther Hooker (H00092) — making Taylor's grandson Ezra Stiles the stepson of Thomas Hooker's great-granddaughter. EASTER EGG: Rev. Edward Taylor (1642-1729) — Harvard 1671; 58-year minister of Westfield MA; physician to his congregation; Puritan devotional poet who forbade publication of his work. Rediscovered 1937 and now recognized as the greatest Puritan poet in American literature. His daughter Keziah married Rev. Isaac Stiles; their son Ezra Stiles became President of Yale (1778-1795). His second wife's father Samuel Wyllys was Secretary of the Colony of Connecticut — the Wyllys family appears throughout Connecticut colonial records. bio.title: Reverend
bio.bio_blurb: Puritan poet; Westfield pastor and physician

narrative_blocks.header: He saw Christ stand pearl-like at the table
narrative_blocks.body:
Among the poems he set at the head of his meditations is one that reads as an eyewitness account of a vision at the communion table:

Once at thy Feast, I saw thee Pearle-like stand
'Tween Heaven, and Earth where Heavens Bright glory all
In streams fell on thee, as a floodgate and,
Like Sun Beams through thee on the World to Fall.

narrative_blocks.header: A hundred miles through snow, and he stayed
narrative_blocks.body: He had just been made a resident scholar at Harvard when Westfield called. He went in the dead of winter 1671, a hundred miles through deep drifts, and stayed fifty-eight years.

narrative_blocks.header: He refused to leave the frontier in 1676
narrative_blocks.body: His meetinghouse was built to serve as a fort, and a drum roll called the town to worship. Urged to withdraw to Springfield in the spring of 1676, he refused, and Westfield came through King Philip's War undamaged.

narrative_blocks.header: His remedies included powdered human flesh
narrative_blocks.body: He was the town's physician as well as its minister, a follower of Paracelsus who kept a handwritten dispensatory. Among his agents was mummia, which he glossed as 'The Deade body or flesh.'

narrative_blocks.header: He forbade his heirs ever to print him
narrative_blocks.body: He bound the poems in leather of his own making and left word that none be published; two stanzas in Cotton Mather's Right Thoughts in Sad Hours of 1689 were all that appeared while he lived. They lay unread until a Yale manuscript was opened in 1937.

narrative_blocks.header: Town clerk for thirty-seven years
narrative_blocks.body: Justice of the peace and New London’s town clerk from 1736 until his death, Coit also served as overseer of the Groton Pequots from 1741 and of the Mohegan from 1769. His second wife was Mehitable Hooker of Farmington.

narrative_blocks.header: He buried two wives and married a third
narrative_blocks.body: Lydia Christophers married him in 1721 and died in 1740; Mehitable Hooker followed in 1742 and died in 1763. In December 1764 he married the twice-widowed Elizabeth Starr, and they had no children.

narrative_blocks.header: A second Sarah for a lost first
narrative_blocks.body: Lydia's only child Sarah was born in 1726 and died at four. The daughter Mehitable bore him in 1744 was given the same name, and she lived to sixty-three.

bio.title: Captain
bio.notes: Known for wearing a scarlet cloak

narrative_blocks.header: Captain of one of America's first warships
narrative_blocks.body: Washington gave him the schooner Harrison in October 1775, one of the first vessels Congress put to sea. He took two British provision ships into Plymouth, ran her aground more than once, and later had the Oliver Cromwell out of Saybrook.

narrative_blocks.header: Made British prisoners stand on Plymouth Rock
narrative_blocks.body: He put the captured British crews ashore on Plymouth Rock, where by one account they gave three cheers and wished success to American arms. The founding myth ran backwards that day: Englishmen stood on the rock as prisoners.

narrative_blocks.header: The Great Red Dragon — scarlet cloak
narrative_blocks.body: He was tall, portly, soldierly in bearing, frank, jovial, somewhat eccentric, and very liberal. He wore a scarlet cloak that earned him the nickname 'The Great Red Dragon.'

narrative_blocks.header: First American to invert the British flag
narrative_blocks.body: He claimed to be 'the first man in the States who turned his majesty's bunting upside down' when he captured British vessels in late 1775. The symbolic act came early in the naval war.

narrative_blocks.header: “Cohorns that Noah had in the Ark”
narrative_blocks.body: He savaged his own schooner in a November 1775 letter: guns the Lords Say and Seal landed at Saybrook in 1635, a cohorn spiked so Andros could not use it, swivels not fired since 1620. Both guns of a side would split her to the keelson.

narrative_blocks.header: Arnold burned New London and took him
narrative_blocks.body: He had raised a company at New London in 1775 and paid to equip it out of his own pocket. When Benedict Arnold burned the town in September 1781 he was captured, and held a while on a prison ship off New York.

narrative_blocks.header: He went south to his daughter and stayed
narrative_blocks.body: Yale had made him a lawyer in 1761 and New London a selectman in 1771. Broken in health, he left for North Carolina in 1797 to visit his daughter Sarah, and lies in the Lillington burial ground on the Cape Fear.

narrative_blocks.header: The Christophers married into this house twice
narrative_blocks.body: Her father's first wife was Lydia Christophers, dead two years before he married her mother. When she married Robinson Mumford in 1761 she took a husband whose own mother was a Christophers of the same New London family.

narrative_blocks.header: The New London family ended in Carolina
narrative_blocks.body: Born at New London in 1744, she followed the family trade south and died at Fayetteville in 1807. Her brother William came down to Wilmington in his last years, and her eldest son died at Fayetteville too.

narrative_blocks.header: The Lillington name was made at Moore's Creek
narrative_blocks.body: George Lillington was grandson to Col. Alexander Lillington, and the family's name was made in February 1776 at Moore's Creek, where a thousand militia routed fifteen hundred Loyalists, many of them Highlanders.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a refugee of the French Revolution
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph Isadore Du Bocage came out of France in 1795 and married her at New London the next year. He bought a sugar and coffee estate on St. Lucia and grew wealthy on it before dying there in 1818.

narrative_blocks.header: She followed her grandson to Arkansas
narrative_blocks.body: Born at New London in 1780, she ended at Pine Bluff in Arkansas in 1852, where her grandson Joseph William Bocage had settled fifteen years earlier and was then judge of the county court.

narrative_blocks.header: Louis Philippe stayed a long while with them
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband was a French exile, and the future king of France paid him a lengthy visit during his own years in America. Joseph Bocage died on St. Lucia, where his estate was.

bio.notes: Called "Pretty Sally" by those who knew her

narrative_blocks.header: They called her Pretty Sally
narrative_blocks.body: She married Colonel Peter Mallett in 1780, at fifteen, and bore him thirteen children over twenty-two years at Fayetteville. She outlived him by thirty-one years and lies beside him in the burial ground that carries their name.

narrative_blocks.header: She buried four of her thirteen small
narrative_blocks.body: Charles Robinson died at three and Peter Francis at four; William Smith lived a year. Her eldest, Sarah Jane, went at nineteen. Seven of the rest reached their forties, and Edward Jones lived to eighty-six.

narrative_blocks.header: Four people held the house with guns
narrative_blocks.body: Forty men came at Council Hall in 1781 wanting provisions for Cornwallis and forced the lower floor. She, her husband, and Johnny and Hannah — two people the family held as slaves — drove them out. One shot was fired in all.

narrative_blocks.header: Her own prayer book, then her silver
narrative_blocks.body: She was one of two Episcopalians in Fayetteville when she came, and kept the occasional services in her own house. In 1817 she gave her communion goblets to be melted into the plate St. John's still uses, and a lot for the church.

narrative_blocks.header: A consul general among her sons
narrative_blocks.body: Charles Peter took Council Hall and the cotton mill, and moved the house six miles on logs to Eutaw Springs. Edward Jones went to Providence, took the consul general's post at Rome in 1858, and was made an army paymaster by Lincoln.

narrative_blocks.header: Johnny was the only man on the place
narrative_blocks.body: Every hired man was out when the raiders came, and Johnny stood with the household and fired. Hannah took a gun beside him; Mallett called them noble soldiers in his own account. Both were enslaved by the family whose house they saved.

bio.title: Colonel
bio.bio_blurb: Revolutionary commissary and Cape Fear merchant

narrative_blocks.header: Camden ruined the man who fed the army
narrative_blocks.body: Commissaries worked on commission and were paid in currency that fell as fast as it printed. He had bought on his own credit for troops who paid him in worthless paper, and the three months after Camden finished him. He resigned in 1780.

narrative_blocks.header: Named with David Fanning, then acquitted
narrative_blocks.body: Cornwallis paid him for stores the British seized, and old tent-mates from the Canada war moved him through their lines. The Assembly ordered him prosecuted for treason and left him out of the Act of Pardon. A jury cleared him in 1783.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried enslaved people from the Guinea coast
narrative_blocks.body: He bought enslaved people on the Guinea coast and sold them in the West Indies. He lost his first ship off Cape Hatteras, took a second out of Charles Town, and was fired on by the Spanish guarda costa while trading illegally at Campeche.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried a ball in his side
narrative_blocks.body: A horse was shot from under him at Halfway Brook in 1758 and a ball went through his calf at Fort George the year after. He took an ankle wound in 1777, and in 1780 a shot entered his left side and stayed there.

narrative_blocks.header: At sixteen he inherited his father’s debts
narrative_blocks.body: As executor he could not collect what was owed the estate, and having taken no legal precaution he became liable for what it owed. The insolvency sent him to sea in 1765 in a merchant ship he part-owned.

narrative_blocks.header: His father was buried the night he died
narrative_blocks.body: Smallpox took Peter Mallett the elder home from New York in January 1760, and the disease put him in the deep woods a quarter-mile from his house the same night. The slate survives, a few yards off Driftwood Lane, facing the sunrise.

narrative_blocks.header: Buried near his mill, among his children
narrative_blocks.body: His will asked to be laid near the mill at Fayetteville, among his children, in a frugal manner. The graveyard inside its brick wall stood by Council Hall on Blount's Creek, on ground the state now uses for its highway offices.

notable.notable_blurb: Chief justice, and teacher of a thousand lawyers

narrative_blocks.header: He ruled against the Confederacy on conscription
narrative_blocks.body: He read the 1862 conscription laws as exempting whole trades and letting any man send a substitute, and issued the writ again and again for those who applied. When Richmond suspended habeas corpus in 1864 he went on releasing them.

narrative_blocks.header: His former students in the legislature saved him
narrative_blocks.body: Democrats took his handling of the Kirk-Holden writs for acquiescence in the governor's war on the Klan, and impeachment came close enough that he drafted a defence. The legislature was full of men he had taught, and it never came.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded the state's first law school
narrative_blocks.body: He opened the school at Mocksville about 1836 and moved it to Richmond Hill when he bought the plantation on the Yadkin. It ran until he died, its terms alternating with the court's, and the village still carries the name.

narrative_blocks.header: Two of his students became chief justice
narrative_blocks.body: He claimed more than a thousand law students. Six reached the state supreme court, two of them the chief justiceship he had held, and three became governors of North Carolina.

narrative_blocks.header: An archbishop baptized him in Washington
narrative_blocks.body: His father died when he was thirteen and a half-brother in Congress took him to Washington. He went to a Roman Catholic school there and was baptized by Archbishop John Carroll, then came home to Statesville Academy.

narrative_blocks.header: His first wife's mind went before she did
narrative_blocks.body: Margaret Williams was afflicted with a progressive insanity that darkened the last two years at Richmond Hill, and Philadelphia did no good. She died there in 1855 at forty-two. Of their ten children, three outlived him.

narrative_blocks.header: Stricken in the buggy to Winston
narrative_blocks.body: He left home in the mail buggy for the Winston train and the January term at Raleigh. A few miles on the driver could not rouse him; he was carried into Wilson's Hotel and died at half past ten that night.

people.research_notes:
b. Jun 28, 1805 Rowan County NC; d. Jan 5, 1878 Winston-Salem NC. Son of Richmond Pearson Sr. (X01165; Revolutionary War Captain) and Elizabeth Mumford Pearson (HD0359). Middle name Mumford encodes Hooker descent: Thomas Hooker → Mehitable → Sarah Coit → Sarah Mumford → Elizabeth Mumford Pearson → Richmond. Lawyer; NC state legislator; Superior Court judge; NC Supreme Court assoc. justice 1848; Chief Justice 1859-1878. Founded Richmond Hill Law School 1848, Yadkin County NC — state's first law school; operated until his death. Pro-Union Whig; became Republican after Civil War. Elected first popularly elected Chief Justice 1868 (nominated by both Republican and Conservative parties). Nearly impeached 1870 — prevented by his former law students in the legislature. Presided over Gov. Holden's impeachment trial (only one in NC history). NOTE: FindAGrave records him as slaveholder (12 enslaved persons in 1840 census). NOTE: Reportedly had an illegitimate son John Hector Pearson by Ann Leach, a free mulatto woman — not in project. m. (1) Jun 12, 1832 Knoxville TN, Margaret McClung Williams (I00174; b.Feb 5, 1814 Knoxville; d.Dec 27, 1855 Richmond Hill NC); m. (2) ca.1858, Mary Louisa McDowell (X02086), widow of John Gray Bynum I. Buried Oakwood Cemetery Raleigh NC (CEM092). narrative_blocks.header: Three wives in five years, then fifty-nine
narrative_blocks.body: He married Susannah Hooker in 1708 and lost her in childbirth the next year, then married Mary Sands in 1710 and lost her in 1712. His third wife, Sarah Sands, he kept for fifty-nine years, until his own death at Stamford in 1772.

narrative_blocks.header: His father made him executor at twenty-three
narrative_blocks.body: He was twenty-three when his father Jonathan Selleck Jr. died at Stamford in June 1710 and left him executor of the estate. The overseers named were Rev. John Davenport of Stamford and Hon. Nathan Gold of Fairfield, his grandfather on his mother's side.

narrative_blocks.header: His last two wives were both Sands women
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Sands was a daughter of Capt. John Sands of Long Island; Sarah, whom he married the year after Mary died, was a daughter of Capt. Samuel Sands. He named two of the nine children Sands and Gold, for his wife's family and his mother's.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother died a month after her birth
narrative_blocks.body: Susannah was born at Stamford on 3 September 1709, and her mother, Hannah Hooker, died on 5 October, barely a month later, at nineteen, of the birth.

narrative_blocks.header: A son named Hooker
narrative_blocks.body: In 1742 Susannah gave her third son the name Hooker, for the mother she never knew; Hooker St. John grew up to be a Norwalk selectman and war commissioner.

narrative_blocks.header: She married the Blue Sheep
narrative_blocks.body: Susannah married Joseph St. John of Norwalk in 1733. Norwalk called him the Blue Sheep, for the tradition that he once dyed a sheep blue to start a flock of that color and the rains washed it out.

narrative_blocks.header: Five children left behind
narrative_blocks.body: When Susannah died in December 1749, at forty, she left five children between four and sixteen; her firstborn, Sarah, had died at seven. Joseph had her stone compare her to Rachel, Leah, Abigail, Lydia and Martha.

narrative_blocks.header: Three generations of slaveholding descendants
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph's 1756 inventory listed three enslaved people, Jenny, London and Peter, and her sons went on holding people after him. In 1777 her son William took half of Dover, a boy his brother Stephen had enlisted in the Continental Army, and so was spared service himself.

narrative_blocks.header: Lieutenant colonel of the 9th Connecticut
narrative_blocks.body: Stephen was commissioned captain of Norwalk's first company in 1761, major of the 9th Regiment in 1775, and its lieutenant colonel in 1777. His stone in East Norwalk Historical Cemetery gives him that command.

narrative_blocks.header: Norwalk kept sending him on its errands
narrative_blocks.body: Stephen was a Norwalk selectman on and off for twenty years. The town sent him to buy cloth for six tents in 1780, and in 1783 to press its claims for the damage the enemy had done.

narrative_blocks.header: He sent no substitute; his brother did
narrative_blocks.body: When the war came, an enslaved man named Dover was sent into the Continental Army in place of Stephen's brother, and Stephen's own household still held two people, Peter and Phyllis, when he died.

narrative_blocks.header: Two generations married Fitches
narrative_blocks.body: Stephen married Ann Fitch, daughter of Samuel Fitch, on 9 December 1757. A generation later their son Stephen married her niece, Sarah Fitch, and tied the Saint Johns to the Fitches twice.

narrative_blocks.header: Six children and a burning town
narrative_blocks.body: When the British burned Norwalk in July 1779 and the Lockwood house with it, Susannah had six living children, the youngest seven months old. A wedding dress of the 1760s, the decade she married in, was carried out of the fire and is kept at the Norwalk Museum.

narrative_blocks.header: Orphaned at thirteen
narrative_blocks.body: Susannah's mother, Susannah Selleck, died in December 1749, when she was six, and her father, Capt. Joseph St. John, in 1756, when she was thirteen.

narrative_blocks.header: Three children buried in five years
narrative_blocks.body: Between December 1793 and September 1798 Susannah buried three of her children: Susannah at twenty-two, Abigail at eighteen, and Eliphalet Hooker St. John Lockwood at sixteen.

narrative_blocks.header: The St. John-Lockwood knot
narrative_blocks.body: Susannah gave her youngest son the Hooker name that came down her mother's line, and in 1808 her son Buckingham married her brother William's daughter Polly, his first cousin, one more St. John-Lockwood match in a long run of them.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale class of 1766
narrative_blocks.body: William Saint John graduated Yale with A.B. 1766 and A.M. 1769, in the same class as Hon. Jared and Jonathan Ingersoll — two of Connecticut's most prominent legal and political figures — and served as private tutor in the wealthy Phillipse family of Phillipse, New York. He was described by contemporaries as 'a very fine looking, superior man, a person of fine address and manners, presiding handsomely at his own table.'

narrative_blocks.header: Two verdicts: DAR Patriot Ancestor and colonial Loyalist
narrative_blocks.body: One chronicler records that Saint John 'was a Loyalist and was sent to New York with the Army,' yet he is simultaneously honored as a DAR Patriot Ancestor (A099267) for Civil Service during the Revolution — a tension common among colonial Norwalk families divided by the conflict. In June 1777 he received from his brother Stephen 'the one half of his Negro boy named Dover, now inlisted into the Continental Service,' paying sixty dollars to exempt himself from actual military service.

narrative_blocks.header: Suffered heavy losses when Tryon burned Norwalk, 1779
narrative_blocks.body: William Saint John suffered significant property losses in General Tryon's burning of Norwalk in July 1779, the same raid that destroyed or damaged much of the town. He died February 1, 1800, in his fifty-sixth year — survived by his wife Mary Esther Belden, who would outlive him by fifty years, dying at ninety-seven in 1850.

narrative_blocks.header: Smallpox took his sight, not his eloquence
narrative_blocks.body: Smallpox in his twenties ruined his eyesight, and he never read print again. He studied law by having his family read the texts aloud, argued from memory what he could not see, and became one of Northampton's most eloquent advocates.

narrative_blocks.header: He shaped the Constitution but never signed it
narrative_blocks.body: At the 1787 convention he won a rule still in the Constitution — every bill raising revenue must begin in the House. A family illness called him home in August, and he left before the signing, his name absent from the document he framed.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave up the Senate for Northampton
narrative_blocks.body: He sat in the first Senate from 1789, had a leading hand in the Judiciary Act that built the federal courts, and carried the Eleventh Amendment through. He resigned in June 1796 and went home to Northampton, where he had kept the county attorney's office all along.

narrative_blocks.header: He defied a war he called unconstitutional
narrative_blocks.body: As governor in the War of 1812 he refused to give the Massachusetts militia to federal command and called the war unlawful. He went further, sounding out British officials in Nova Scotia about a separate New England peace — treason to his enemies, principle to his friends.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the daughter of his own pastor
narrative_blocks.body: In 1777 he wed Sarah Hooker, daughter of his Northampton minister and a descendant of Thomas Hooker. The marriage lasted forty years and brought nine children, four of whom outlived him. Her death in 1817 left him two quiet years.

narrative_blocks.header: He built federal power, then feared it
narrative_blocks.body: He argued for a strong union at the founding — the Constitution, the federal courts, the bank — then spent his last years shielding Massachusetts from the power he had helped create. His neighbours took him for a man of plain integrity who had gone home.

narrative_blocks.body: Ripley was a Hartford merchant and shipowner with agents at Liverpool. In 1798 the Alliance was taken by a French privateer and retaken by British warships, and her master David Jewett wrote from Liverpool to tell him so.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the banner at Fort Wayne
narrative_blocks.body: Handed his regiment’s colours at the farewell parade in September 1861, he answered: “God grant it may never trail in the dust.” He had built the skeleton regiment from nothing — drill at a quarter past five, no gambling, weapons locked.

narrative_blocks.header: A spent ball, ten minutes off the field
narrative_blocks.body: At Williamsburg on 5 May 1862 a spent ball caught him. He went off the field for ten minutes and came back, and the Fifth Michigan took heavy losses there and again at Seven Pines. His brigadier’s star ranked from July.

narrative_blocks.header: He fought most of the war sick
narrative_blocks.body: Exposure gave him rheumatism in late 1861 and he spent 1862 more or less disabled by pain in his limbs and body, with dysentery from January to April. He gave up regimental command in June and rode in an ambulance.

narrative_blocks.header: He talked his own general into retreating
narrative_blocks.body: At Baltimore Cross Roads in July 1863, within striking distance of Richmond, he fed General Keyes’s fear of Confederates massing behind them and helped persuade him to fall back. Dix and Keyes lost their field commands.

narrative_blocks.header: He disappears from the official records
narrative_blocks.body: He had a division in the Sixth Corps that autumn, gave it up twice for his health, and in January 1864 was sent to run the prison camp at Johnson’s Island. Superseded in May, he was idle until he resigned in February 1865.

narrative_blocks.header: Bright’s disease, four months’ duration
narrative_blocks.body: He went back to the law in Washington after the war and died there in June 1869 at fifty-seven, of Bright’s disease of the kidneys — four months, by the death certificate. He was carried back to Michigan.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter married his sister’s son
narrative_blocks.body: His daughter Julia married Walter Taylor Dwight at Detroit in 1876. Walter’s mother was Elizabeth Taylor Terry, his sister, so the two were first cousins — she seventeen at the wedding, he twenty-one.

narrative_blocks.header: Her great-grandfather scouted Hartford before Thomas Hooker
narrative_blocks.body: Her great-grandfather William Lewis sailed to New England aboard the Lyon in 1632 and, three years later, joined the Adventurers' Party of twenty-five who scouted the site that became Hartford — setting out in October 1635, months ahead of Rev. Thomas Hooker's own company. He served the new town as selectman and constable before helping to settle Farmington, where he died in 1683.

narrative_blocks.header: She wed into the other founding family
narrative_blocks.body: In January 1735 she married Joseph Hooker, himself a great-grandson of Rev. Thomas Hooker — so the match quietly joined the great-grandchildren of two men who had founded Hartford a century earlier. Both the Lewises and the Hookers had crossed to Connecticut in the 1630s and later settled Farmington, where the couple lie today in the same Memento Mori burying ground.

narrative_blocks.body: She married James Cowles at seventeen and bore seven children over eighteen years. She was buried at Farmington the next winter, not yet thirty-seven — and every one of the seven outlived her.

narrative_blocks.body: She and her second cousin Martha each married a Cowles brother of Farmington — Abigail to James, Martha to his elder brother Ezekiel. Their two broods grew up doubly bound: first cousins through the Cowles, distant cousins through the Hookers.

notable.notable_blurb: Revolutionary War Colonel; 40 years Justice of Peace

narrative_blocks.header: Commanded a regiment at Burgoyne's surrender
narrative_blocks.body: His Connecticut regiment fought in the Saratoga Campaign of 1777, where John Burgoyne's British army laid down its arms. The victory turned the war and brought France in on the American side.

narrative_blocks.header: First Farmington troops to reach Boston
narrative_blocks.body: He raised a hundred-man company of Farmington's elite and arrived at Roxbury three weeks before any other Connecticut soldiers. The Colonial Assembly commissioned him captain on arrival.

narrative_blocks.header: Sent an Oneida boy to mission school
narrative_blocks.body: In 1819 he paid for the education of eighteen-year-old Peter Augustus Takonotas at the Cornwall Foreign Mission School. The boy later took Hooker's surname.

narrative_blocks.header: Justice of the Peace for forty years
narrative_blocks.body: After the war he served as Farmington's Justice of the Peace from the 1780s through the 1820s. The role made him the local arbiter of debt, marriage, and civil disputes for two generations.

narrative_blocks.header: Late returning a library book in 1795
narrative_blocks.body: The Farmington Monthly Library, founded that year, recorded 'Col. Noadiah Hooker his shilling' for a late-return fine. Julius Gay's nineteenth-century history pamphlets preserved the entry.

education.school_name: No college noted — rose through militia ranks

military_service.notes: Raised the first troops enlisted at Farmington and marched in command of a company of 100+ men — the very elite of the vicinity. Arrived in Boston (Roxbury) three weeks before any other enlisted men from Connecticut. Commissioned Captain by Colonial Assembly. Commissioned Colonel by State Legislature 1776. Served in several regiments until close of War. Had command of a regiment at the capture of Burgoyne's army (Saratoga, 1777). Facebook genealogy research (2024) confirms: Samuel Woodruff (1734-1816) of Farmington CT served as private in Capt. Jesse Curtiss' company, Col. Noadiah Hooker's regiment, 1777. Also confirmed by Orderly Book of Capt. Ichabod Norton (1777, Peekskill): Norton served "under Colonel Hooker" at Peekskill 1777. Norton was husband of Ruth Strong (H00297), daughter of Ruth Hooker Strong — a Hooker descendant herself. Two branches of the Hooker tree serving together.

narrative_blocks.body: She married George Cook, a prominent citizen of St. Armand in the Eastern Townships of Lower Canada, and crossed into a district settled by Loyalist refugees from the Revolution. She lived out her life there and was buried at Frelighsburg.

narrative_blocks.header: He went south to tutor a planter's children
narrative_blocks.body: After Yale and a few years reading law in Connecticut, he moved to South Carolina in 1803 as tutor in the family of General Wade Hampton, among the wealthiest planters in the South. The connection launched his own legal career in Columbia.

narrative_blocks.header: A chancellor wrote the words on his tomb
narrative_blocks.body: He built one of the more respected practices at the Columbia bar before dying at forty-one. The epitaph on his tomb was composed by Chancellor DeSaussure, who praised his acute, logical mind and unbending integrity.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped govern South Carolina's young college
narrative_blocks.body: Two years before his death he was elected a trustee of South Carolina College, the state university founded barely a decade earlier in Columbia. He had become a settled figure in the capital's public life.

narrative_blocks.header: His widow outlived him by half a century
narrative_blocks.body: He married Mary Ann Chapman of Columbia in 1808, but the couple had no children, and he died seven years later. She remarried a South Carolina physician and lived until 1872 — more than fifty years his widow.

narrative_blocks.body: Married at nineteen to a Farmington merchant, she bore three children in six years before yellow fever reached the town. It killed her in the spring of 1808, at twenty-five, and her husband in time took a second wife.

narrative_blocks.body: He began in medicine, dispensing remedies from a Vermont drug store, and might have stayed a country physician for good. Instead a move to New Haven turned him toward finance, and he closed his life as the trusted treasurer of its savings bank.

people.research_notes: The EH entry gives a remarkably sympathetic portrait of a man caught between family loyalty and civic standing. His Ingersoll wife's family were Loyalists; Joseph remained neutral. After the war he lost the confidence of Farmington entirely while honors were heaped on his more active relatives. He rebuilt his reputation in Litchfield NY. Note: Mary Ingersoll was daughter of Rev. Jonathan Ingersoll (HD0115, Yale 1736) — himself a Hooker descendant. This is a double Hooker descent marriage. OCCUPATION NOTES: Active in Farmington town affairs before marriage. After the Revolution, found himself ostracized in Farmington — "the confidence of the town was entirely withheld from him" — while his brother and cousins who had served were honored. Removed to Litchfield, Herkimer County, NY where he rebuilt his reputation for "strict and unswerving integrity, and strong loyalty to the new born nation." Became active and trusted in public affairs in New York. [Migrated from marriage.spouse_notes (spouse X00159)]: b. Dec 20, 1748 Ridgefield CT; d. Nov 14, 1805 Litchfield NY. Daughter of Rev. Jonathan Ingersoll and Dorcas Moss Ingersoll. EH: "The Ingersoll family were strong loyalists, though never of a tricky, untrustworthy kind." Cross-connection: Rev. Jonathan Ingersoll (HD0115) is her father — Yale 1736, already in our tree as a Hooker descendant through the Ingersoll-Hooker line. This marriage unites two Hooker descendant lines. [Migrated from top-level military]: True Stage 6Y-659: wife corrected to the real Mary Ingersoll (1748-1805); death and Jerusalem Hill burial added per FindAGrave; EH #292 narrative banked in NBs.

military_service.notes: Lieutenant in the Militia pre-Revolution. Remained neutral during the war through the influence of his Loyalist wife's family.
Active in Farmington town affairs before the war; remained neutral through it (EH #292).

bio.bio_blurb: Militia lieutenant who sat out the Revolution

narrative_blocks.header: He was a militia lieutenant before he married
narrative_blocks.body: He was an active man in Farmington's affairs and a lieutenant in the militia. Then in 1771 he married Mary Ingersoll, whose family were strong loyalists — though never of a tricky or untrustworthy kind — and through her influence he stayed quietly neutral the whole war. His own sympathies were with the American patriots the entire time.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a Hooker descendant named Ingersoll
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Ingersoll was Rev. Jonathan Ingersoll's daughter, and through the Whitings a fifth-generation descendant of Thomas Hooker in her own right. He was the fifth generation on the other side and carried the name. They gave their first son the name Jared Ingersoll Hooker, and the two families went on marrying each other for two more generations.

narrative_blocks.header: He built the reputation again in New York
narrative_blocks.body: He went to Litchfield in Herkimer County and started over among people who had not watched him sit out a war. There he was trusted in public affairs, and known for strict and unswerving integrity and strong loyalty to the new nation. He died there in 1799.

narrative_blocks.header: The town gave the honors to his brother
narrative_blocks.body: When the fighting stopped he found Farmington would not have him back. Honors and public trusts went to the brother and cousins who had fought; nothing came to the man who had not. He was sensitive under it, and he left.

narrative_blocks.body: Solomon Whitman had learned shoemaking as a young man but rarely practiced the trade professionally. At 90, he made a pair of shoes — apparently for the occasion. Though never a college graduate, he was described as well-educated and deeply interested in literary matters.

narrative_blocks.body: Solomon Whitman's death at age 93 was said to have been caused by over-fatigue sustained while settling a fence boundary dispute between two brothers. He died September 13, 1803 in Farmington, Connecticut.

burial.plot_notes: Gravestone: "Rev. Cyprian Strong, D.D. Died Nov. 17th. 1811 In the 68th year of his age, And 44th of his ministry; In morals, exemplary; In doctrine, uncorrupt; In reasoning, profound; In declaring Gods counsel, Perspicuous and solemn; And in death, peaceful."

people.research_notes: b. May 26, 1743 Farmington CT; d. Nov 17, 1811 Portland (Chatham) CT age 68. Son of Asahel Strong Jr. and Ruth Hooker Strong of Farmington. Yale 1763 (confirmed: EH, Strong family book 5345-8, Yale archives). NOTE: Native Northeast Portal states Harvard — appears to be an error; all other sources agree Yale. Town Clerk Farmington CT 1764-67 (Hurlburt, Farmington Town Clerks p.68). Ordained Aug 9, 1767. Pastor Congregational Church, Chatham (now Portland) CT 1767-1811 — 44 years ministry. New Light Divinity. Opposed Half-Way Covenant. Portrait by William Jennys. Published: Discourse at Hebron, July 4, 1799. Papers at Yale: sermons (1791, 1806), correspondence Samuel Hart/Jeremiah Day, 1764 notebook. Sprague Annals of the American Pulpit vol.I pp.651-3 contains life sketch. GRANDDAUGHTER: Harriet Ellsworth (daughter of H00670 Sarah Strong) married Ainsworth Blunt at Brainerd Mission and accompanied Cherokees on Trail of Tears 1838. See X02121/X02122. [Migrated from marriage.spouse_notes (spouse X01175)]: b. Dec 18, 1748; d. Chatham CT Feb 6, 1815. Widow of Maj. Jonathan Hart of Berlin CT, killed at St. Clair's defeat Nov 4, 1791. No children with Cyprian. [Stage 6Y-253 note]: A prior CC labeled 'Gen. Hart adopted Cyprian's grandson' was removed — that was based on a misattribution conflating Cyprian Hart H00562 (Selah Hart's actual adopted nephew, son of brother Nathaniel Hart No. 2) with the Cyprian Strong line. The two Cyprians were entirely different people. The Selah Hart adoption story does not involve the Strong family.

narrative_blocks.header: His gravestone counts 44 years of ministry
narrative_blocks.body: Cyprian kept Farmington's town records as its clerk before he was ordained at Chatham, now Portland, in August 1767, and he held that pulpit until he died there in November 1811. His stone counts the 68th year of his age and the 44th of his ministry: "In morals, exemplary; In doctrine, uncorrupt; In reasoning, profound."

narrative_blocks.header: An election sermon against modern liberality
narrative_blocks.body: In May 1799 Cyprian preached the election sermon to the General Assembly at Hartford, warning the legislators to give infidelity and modern liberality no hand in government. Shun them, he said, as you would the plague that had bathed the plains of almost all Europe in blood. The Assembly thanked him and had it printed.

narrative_blocks.header: In print against the Half-Way Covenant
narrative_blocks.body: A New Light, Cyprian would baptize only the children of full church members, and he argued it in print: a Discourse on owning the covenant in 1780, an answer to John Lewis's sermons on forbearance in 1789, and two inquiries into the meaning of baptism in 1793 and 1796.

narrative_blocks.header: A double wedding with the Bulls
narrative_blocks.body: On 9 November 1768 at Farmington, Cyprian married Sarah Bull, and on the same day his sister Elizabeth Strong married Sarah's brother Martin Bull.

narrative_blocks.header: A third wife widowed at St. Clair's defeat
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah Bull died suddenly at Chatham in 1785 and Abigail White in 1795. In August 1797 Cyprian married Abigail Riley Hart, whose husband Maj. Jonathan Hart had been killed at St. Clair's defeat in 1791.

narrative_blocks.header: Four names given twice
narrative_blocks.body: Cyprian's first two wives bore him thirteen children at Chatham, and four died before they were six. Each name was given again: a second Anne in 1774, a second Florella in 1779, a second Elnathan in 1787, and a Charles in 1794 after Charles Wells.

narrative_blocks.header: His granddaughter walked the Trail of Tears
narrative_blocks.body: His daughter Sarah Strong married Judge John Ellsworth; their daughter Harriet Ellsworth married Ainsworth Blunt at Brainerd Mission, Tennessee, where they ministered to the Cherokees. When the forced removal came in 1838, Blunt accompanied the Cherokees on the Trail of Tears before illness forced him back from the Mississippi. He later became the first mayor of Dalton, Georgia.

bio.bio_blurb: Wife of a twice-dismissed frontier minister

narrative_blocks.header: She came in behind him in brocade
narrative_blocks.body: Walpole remembered her walking into the meeting-house after her husband in a full suit of brocade lutestring, no bonnet, a fan held up against the sun as was the fashion down country. She had married him that December at nineteen, and Walpole was the first parish she kept.

narrative_blocks.header: Eleven sons, and Clarissa
narrative_blocks.body: She bore twelve children across thirty years of marriage — eleven sons and a single daughter. The sons were Jonathan, Hart, Joshua, David, Roger, Erastus, Roswell, Thomas, Samuel, Horatio and Hooker; Clarissa was the only girl, and never married.

narrative_blocks.header: Clarissa handed her the wrong medicine
narrative_blocks.body: She died suddenly at Heath on 11 October 1791, forty-nine years old, after taking medicine her daughter Clarissa had given her by mistake. The funeral text was 'He hath done all things well.' Clarissa never married and was dead herself within seven years.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandsons hid Basil Dorsey five years
narrative_blocks.body: Roger Hooker Leavitt and Hart Leavitt ran Underground Railroad stations at Charlemont, the town that had turned their grandfather out of its pulpit. They sheltered the fugitive Basil Dorsey there for five years, and Roger's house is on the National Park Service Network to Freedom.

narrative_blocks.header: The astronomer came down from her
narrative_blocks.body: Down the same line came Henrietta Swan Leavitt, who found that a certain kind of star declares its true brightness by the beat of its pulse. Hubble used her yardstick to measure the distance to other galaxies and show that the universe is expanding.

bio.notes: Named for maternal grandfather Capt. Martin Kellogg

narrative_blocks.header: He and Roger bought 40 acres from Tunxis
narrative_blocks.body: In 1776, he and his brother Roger purchased 40 acres at Congee, Farmington, including a dwelling house and barn, from Tunxis men Cornelius Indian and Elijah Wampey for £150. The deed is among the documented transfers of Native land in the Farmington area, preserved at the Native Northeast Portal.

Member of the Society of the Cincinnati — Revolutionary War officers' hereditary society.

narrative_blocks.header: First from Farmington to Boston — Noadiah led
narrative_blocks.body: At the Lexington alarm he volunteered in the company of his first cousin Capt. Noadiah Hooker — 111 men, the first company from Farmington and the first from Connecticut to reach the Continental Army at Boston. He entered as a private and rose through sergeant, ensign, and 2nd lieutenant to Major of the Continental Line.

narrative_blocks.header: Flag of truce — Burgoyne's surrender delivered
narrative_blocks.body: He was sent under a flag of truce to the British commander in New York to formally announce the surrender of Burgoyne's army in October 1777. He also helped fit out fire ships at New York in 1776 under Washington's plan to attack British vessels. EH records he was "throughout the war held in high esteem by Gen. Washington, and frequently entrusted with responsible and important duties."

narrative_blocks.header: West Indies mariner — then Sheriff until 70
narrative_blocks.body: Before the Revolution he made eleven voyages to the West Indies as a merchant mariner. After the war he became Sheriff of Hartford County, served as Justice of the Peace until age 70, and was a Farmington selectman. He disposed of his estate to his brother-in-law before his death, retaining possession during his life.

narrative_blocks.header: Purchased Tunxis land with Elnathan in 1776
narrative_blocks.body: In 1776, he and his brother Elnathan purchased 40 acres at Congee, Farmington — including a dwelling house and barn — from Tunxis men Cornelius Indian and Elijah Wampey for £150. The deed is preserved at the Native Northeast Portal as one of the documented transfers of Native land in the Farmington area.

narrative_blocks.header: Cincinnati member — half-brother Thomas died in war
narrative_blocks.body: He and his brother-in-law Capt. Simeon Newell were both original members of the Society of the Cincinnati, founded 1783 by Continental officers. His half-brother Thomas Hart Hooker (different mother, Mercy Hart) died of pleurisy during the same Revolution — at Roxbury in 1775, age 30 — never seeing its end.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the future governor's sister
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Treadwell came from Ephraim's household in 1782, the year after her father's death; her brother John later rose to the governorship of Connecticut. The marriage brought no children across its forty-eight years.

military_service.unit: Company of Capt. Noadiah Hooker; Continental Line (eventually Major)
military_service.notes: Enlisted at first call (Lexington alarm) in company of his cousin Capt. Noadiah Hooker — 111 men, first from Farmington and first from Connecticut to reach the army at Boston. Rose: Private → Sergeant → Ensign → 2nd Lieutenant (under Washington) → Major. 1776: Fitted out fire ships at New York to attack British vessels (Washington's plan). As brigade major: managed correspondence for generals on whose staff he served. Sent under flag of truce to British commander in New York to announce Burgoyne's surrender. "Throughout the war held in high esteem by Gen. Washington, and frequently entrusted with responsible and important duties." Member, Society of the Cincinnati.
