narrative_blocks.body: She was fifty-nine when she died at Farmington in April 1817, four years after Isaac took the last of his commissions. He kept the homestead and outlived her by twenty years.

narrative_blocks.header: Married a Yale-educated 'quaint and erratic' preacher
narrative_blocks.body: Cynthia married Rev. Allen Olcott in 1792 — a Yale College 1768 graduate settled at the Farmington Congregational Church in 1787. After four years his preaching was deemed 'quaint and erratic' enough that he was dismissed and never settled at any other church.

narrative_blocks.header: Settled with Allen on a South Manchester farm
narrative_blocks.body: After his Farmington dismissal Allen returned to his native East Hartford and then settled with Cynthia on a farm at South Manchester, Connecticut. Family stories suggest his farming methods were as unique as his preaching had been. He died there in April 1811, leaving Cynthia a widow with five children ranging from eight to eighteen.

narrative_blocks.header: Remarried Capt. Saul Alvord at fifty-three
narrative_blocks.body: Two years after Allen's death Cynthia remarried — Capt. Saul Alvord of East Hartford, on 14 January 1813. The couple lived at East Hartford until her own death in June 1827. Through her first marriage's daughter Cynthia, her line married back into the Talcott-Hooker convergence.

Granted 25 acres by town of Guilford as settlement. "One of the first Eminence of preachers in his Day" (Rev. Thomas Ruggles Jr.). "A gentleman of eminent piety" (Rev. John Devotion). narrative_blocks.header: He alone took Yale's first degree
narrative_blocks.body: When the Collegiate School of Connecticut conferred its first bachelor's degree in 1703, he was the only student to receive it, graduating by himself at Saybrook. His diploma still survives in the Yale library.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandfather gave Hartford its name
narrative_blocks.body: His great-grandfather, Deacon Stephen Hart, came from England in 1632 and crossed the Connecticut River at a ford that took his name — Hart's ford, soon Hartford. Yale's first graduate was great-grandson to the man the capital was named for.

narrative_blocks.header: Students rebelled against 'Sir Hart,' their unpaid tutor
narrative_blocks.body: He tutored Yale's two lower classes before he held his own degree, and without pay, until the boys' discontent boiled into the college's first student revolt. The trustees backed “Sir Hart,” thanked him, and voted him fifty pounds.

narrative_blocks.header: He was East Guilford's very first minister
narrative_blocks.body: In 1707 he accepted the call to East Guilford — now Madison — and was ordained over a new church of thirteen members. He held the pulpit until his death twenty-four years later.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped spark Yale's great apostasy
narrative_blocks.body: In 1722 he joined Rector Cutler and five others in declaring before the Yale trustees that Presbyterian ordination might not be valid. The defection to the Church of England shook the young college to its foundations.

narrative_blocks.header: Greatest ingenuity and learning of all seven
narrative_blocks.body: President Ezra Stiles, looking back, called him a man of the greatest ingenuity and learning among the seven who signed the 1722 declaration. He left a substantial estate and a long pastoral memory.

narrative_blocks.header: His chair survives in a 1639 stone house
narrative_blocks.body: A roundabout chair of maple, curly maple and ash that belonged to him is kept at the Henry Whitfield State Museum in Guilford, the oldest stone house in Connecticut. Its label names him first graduate of Yale College and first pastor of East Guilford.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father took Yale first degree
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah was born at East Guilford in 1727 to the Rev. John Hart — the first man to take a degree from Yale, and the first minister of that parish — and to Mary Hooker, a great-granddaughter of Thomas Hooker. The two lines met in her.

narrative_blocks.header: Married three times — two Yale graduates
narrative_blocks.body: She married first Henry Hill, who died 1751. Her second husband Dr. Thomas Adams (Yale 1737) died only two years into the marriage, in 1753. Her third husband Rev. Amos Fowler (Yale 1753) outlived her — she died in 1789, he in 1800.

narrative_blocks.header: Children spanned three marriages and two centuries

narrative_blocks.header: He held Guilford's oldest pulpit forty years
narrative_blocks.body: Called in 1757 as colleague to the aging Rev. Thomas Ruggles, he became sole pastor of Guilford's First Church in 1770 and kept it until his death. His funeral preacher praised a “constant serenity” sustained through long, painful infirmity.

narrative_blocks.header: A talent for cooling other men down
narrative_blocks.body: The minister who preached his funeral had laboured beside him thirty-four years, and said he possessed a wonderful talent of cooling down the wrath and violence of those whose passions were tumultuous. He was cautious, Bray added, of ever speaking evil of any man.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a woman twice widowed before him
narrative_blocks.body: His wife Sarah came to him already twice widowed — first of Henry Hill, then of the physician Thomas Adams. He outlived her too, and married once more before his own death.

narrative_blocks.header: Moses was indentured to him for life
narrative_blocks.body: Moses, born enslaved to Ruth Naughty at 1 Park Street, was indentured to Fowler for life in 1762 and lived at the parsonage at number 31. He was known in Guilford as King of the Slaves. Fowler died on 10 February 1800, and his estate divided Moses among three of his children.

people.research_notes:
CC TO X03218 added 10 Aug 2026. Sam asked what their official relationship was: it is assistant
and successor, not kinship. Fowler was ordained assistant minister at Guilford First Church in
1757 while Rev. Thomas Ruggles Jr. still held it, served under him for thirteen years, took the
pulpit at Ruggles's death in 1770, and kept it until his own in 1800. No blood relationship
between them is documented and none is claimed. Note also that Fowler married Sarah Hart Fowler
(H00315) as her third husband in 1760 — daughter of the Rev. John Hart whom Ruggles Jr. praised
in his history of Guilford. ENRICHED 10 Aug 2026. Native of Guilford, Yale 1753, ordained COLLEAGUE to Rev. Thomas Ruggles Jr.
8 June 1757, sole pastor from Ruggles's death in 1770, died 10 Feb 1800 aged seventy-two in the
forty-third year of his ministry. Son of Daniel Fowler and Grace Barron. Appears in the
Connecticut Revolutionary War military lists and in the 1790 and 1800 censuses at Guilford. TWO funeral sermons were preached. Thomas Wells Bray, pastor of the Third (North Guilford) church
and his fellow-labourer for almost thirty-four years, preached "The Duty of Living and Dying to
the Lord" from Romans xiv, 8, printed 1800 at the expense of the bereaved congregation. John
Elliott, pastor of the church at East Guilford — the pulpit Fowler's father-in-law John Hart had
founded — preached from 2 Kings ii, 14, "Where is the Lord God of Elijah", and said of him that
"Mr. F. read with care the primitive fathers, but his system of faith was founded on the Bible."
Bray's character of him: placid, grave, patient and meek; remote from pride, envy and
ostentation; "a constant father to the people of his charge". ORDER: the marriage block moved to last and recategorised from character to marriage, per the doctrine that family-themed blocks sit together at the end after career and personality. MOSES, 10 Aug 2026 from Sam. b. 1741, d. 1812; son of Montros and Phillis; born enslaved to Ruth
Naughty at 1 Park Street, Guilford; indentured for life to Rev. Amos Fowler in 1762 at 31 Park
Street; called "King of the Slaves" and "Factotum". On 10 February 1800, the day Fowler died,
Moses became shared property — half to John Hart Fowler, a quarter each to Sarah and Mary Fowler,
all three Fowler's children by Sarah Hart. He died enslaved.

narrative_blocks.body: Epilepsy struck him in 1779 and never fully left him, yet his mind stayed sharp and his neighbors kept turning to him. He served some twenty years as a justice of the peace and a decade as the district's judge of probate.

narrative_blocks.body: His father was dead before his first birthday, and the stepfather who came next, Dr. Thomas Adams, within a year of the wedding. His mother's third husband, the Rev. Amos Fowler, was the one who stayed — a Guilford minister who helped raise him.

Amos Fowler (Yale 1753); b. Guilford 24 Dec 1770. Married at Westbrook, then a parish of Saybrook,
by the Rev. John Devotion, 1 July 1797. Ordained 13 Oct 1813 at Exeter Society in northwestern
Lebanon, dismissed March 1821; installed 13 Nov 1822 at Montgomery, Hampden County, Massachusetts;
died very suddenly there 12 March 1829 in his fifty-ninth year. His widow is said to have died in
1841. "A son entered the Presbyterian ministry but soon became a lawyer" — which of the seven is
not stated. THE NAMING IS RECORDED AS naming_inspiration, NOT AS A CC, and that is the schema's explicit rule
rather than a preference. Sam asked whether Rev. John Hart is the grandfather and for a CC up to
him: yes, MATERNAL grandfather — this man's mother was Sarah Hart Fowler (H00315), John Hart's
daughter. But schema F17 codifies a rollback of exactly this case: eight naming_pattern CCs
between direct lineal relatives were built and had to be removed, the rule being
"Grandfather/grandson is direct lineage -> naming_inspiration. First cousin once removed who
shares a name -> naming_pattern CC." The tree already shows the descent through his mother, so a

naming_inspiration.description: Named for his mother's father, the Rev. John Hart of East Guilford, the first man to take a degree from Yale.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried his grandfather's whole name
narrative_blocks.body: He was named for the Rev. John Hart, his mother's father — Yale's first graduate and the first minister of East Guilford. He was the only son of Rev. Amos Fowler, and took his own Yale degree in 1790.

narrative_blocks.header: He read law, then took a pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: He studied law after Yale and was probably admitted to the bar, but never practised to much extent. He was ordained instead at forty-two, on 13 October 1813, over the Exeter Society church in the northwest corner of Lebanon.

narrative_blocks.header: He died suddenly in a mountain village
narrative_blocks.body: Dismissed from Exeter in March 1821, he was installed in November 1822 over the small Congregational church at Montgomery, up in the Hampden County hills. He died there very suddenly on 12 March 1829, in his fifty-ninth year.

people.prominent_name_reason: Wife of E.L. Godkin (1831-1902), founder and first editor of The Nation magazine (1865) — one of the most influential journals in American intellectual history. 8th-generation descendant of Rev. Thomas Hooker through: Thomas Hooker → Samuel Hooker → James Hooker → Mary Hooker Hart → Sarah Hart Hill → Henry Hill (Hon.) → Catherine Hill Elliott → Elizabeth Elliott Foote → Frances Foote Godkin.

narrative_blocks.header: The Cincinnati parlors raised her
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Guilford in 1835 into the Foote family whose Cincinnati house stood at the center of the era's literary and antislavery gatherings — the world of her first cousins Harriet Beecher Stowe and Henry Ward Beecher. Moncure Conway remembered the girl who visited there for her remarkable grace and charm.

narrative_blocks.header: The elder Henry James adored her
narrative_blocks.body: Beauty, intellect, and marked social gifts, the biography credits her — and Henry James Sr. wrote that he had seen no one to compare, no one he admired, esteemed, and loved so much, while women generally were such slips of things. She had married Godkin at Trinity Church, New Haven in July 1859, two years after the young Irishman arrived with letters of introduction.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father helped build young Cincinnati
narrative_blocks.body: She grew up the daughter of one of early Cincinnati's builders — Samuel Foote, a sea captain turned civic leader who ran the young city's water company and sat on its canal board. That standing set her childhood among the city's leading families.

narrative_blocks.header: Two of her three children died in childhood
narrative_blocks.body: Only her eldest son, Lawrence, reached adulthood; her infant son Ralph died in 1868, and her daughter Lizzy in 1873, at eight. Frances herself died in 1875, before she was forty.

bio.title: Rev. Dr.
bio.bio_blurb: Physician-minister at White Plains for thirty years

career.notes: Practiced medicine alongside ministry for nearly 30 years. 'Said to have been a very successful physician... remarkably successful in cases of insanity.'
Served the White Plains church which was destroyed in the Battle of White Plains October 1776, seven years after his death.

narrative_blocks.header: He walked the Hudson with Jonathan Edwards
narrative_blocks.body: He was a close friend of Jonathan Edwards, the age's foremost theologian, from Edwards's early New York years — a friendship some credited with drawing Smith into the ministry. Walking the riverbank together, Smith once told him that separation from his friends was the bitterest trial of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: A minister who was also called Dr. Smith
narrative_blocks.body: He preached and practiced medicine at once for thirty years, and was known for treating the mentally ill — 'distracted persons,' the phrase of the day — when almost no one could. So sought-after was the skill that in his old age he publicly advertised having passed it to his son.

narrative_blocks.header: A battle was fought before his church
narrative_blocks.body: Five years after he died, the Battle of White Plains was fought in October 1776 on the ground before his Presbyterian meetinghouse, and the building was destroyed. Two more churches rose on the same spot; the last was extended out over his grave, and his headstone moved back to make room.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother helped call the first patriot congress
narrative_blocks.body: His brother William Smith was one of the New York 'Wall Street' Presbyterians — with Livingston and Scott — who helped raise the Sons of Liberty and issue an early call for a congress of the colonies. The minister at White Plains came from a family already pushing toward revolution.

burial.plot_notes: Jackson Cemetery, Tunkhannock, Wyoming County PA. SOURCE: FindAGrave; Miner's History of Wyoming.

people.research_notes: b. Mar 23, 1725 White Plains NY (FindAGrave gives Guilford CT — discrepancy unresolved); d. Jul 17, 1815 Tunkhannock, Wyoming County PA age 90. Buried Jackson Cemetery, Tunkhannock, Wyoming County PA. Named "William Hooker" for Hooker ancestry. Surgeon in the Revolutionary War. 3rd Co, 1st Regt CT / 10th Continental Regt CT. Studied medicine with his father Rev. Dr. John Smith (I00140), who was also a physician. WYOMING VALLEY: Removed to Wyoming Valley (now northeastern Pennsylvania) where he became a noted physician. BATTLE OF WYOMING (Jul 3, 1778): The Wyoming Massacre — British/Loyalist forces and Haudenosaunee warriors attacked the settlement; ~300 Patriots killed. His first wife Sarah died Jun 12, 1778 — the month after the massacre. "My wife, Sarah, died on Friday, the 12th of June, 1778, about nine o'clock at night, was buried the 14th, following, on my own land at Jacob's Plains." (Dr. Smith's family Bible, published Oxford England 1772.) FAMILY BIBLE: Dr. Smith preserved his lineage in this Bible going back to an ancestor William Smith who served as a soldier in Oliver Cromwell's army, married Elizabeth Hartley of Newport-Paquell, Buckinghamshire, after the Restoration. Source: Miner's History of Wyoming. [Birth has_discrepancy flag set]: See research notes for resolution. [Migrated from marriage.spouse_notes (spouse X00284)]: b. narrative_blocks.header: The town of Old Forge carries his nickname
narrative_blocks.body: William and his son-in-law James Sutton built an iron works in the Lackawanna Valley, and those who knew him called him Old Forge. The town that grew up around it, Old Forge, Pennsylvania, kept the name.

narrative_blocks.header: The only surgeon at Wilkes-Barre
narrative_blocks.body: William was surgeon to the 3rd Company of the 1st Connecticut Regiment and the only surgeon of the Wilkes-Barre garrison when the Wyoming Valley fell in July 1778, in a battle and massacre that killed some three hundred settlers. In the 1830s Congress passed a special act paying his heirs for the service.

narrative_blocks.header: Sarah died three weeks before the massacre
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah died at about nine on the night of Friday, 12 June 1778, as William wrote in his Oxford Bible, and two days later he buried her on his own land at Jacob's Plains. The massacre came three weeks later.

narrative_blocks.header: Ninety at Tunkhannock
narrative_blocks.body: William outlived Sarah by thirty-seven years and a second wife as well, and died at Tunkhannock, Pennsylvania, on 17 July 1815, at ninety.

people.research_notes: b. Oct 5, 1729 White Plains NY; d. Apr 21, 1768 Brookhaven (Setauket) NY age 38. Buried Setauket Presbyterian Church Cemetery. Daughter of Rev. John Smith (I00140) and Mehitable Hooker Smith (H00109). m. Rev. Benjamin Tallmadge Sr. (X00122) May 16, 1750. Mother of Major Benjamin Tallmadge Jr. (H00757) — spymaster of the Culper Ring, classmate of Nathan Hale, married daughter of a Declaration of Independence signer.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son ran Washington's spy ring
narrative_blocks.body: She married Rev. Benjamin Tallmadge of Setauket in 1750, the daughter of one prominent minister marrying another. Their second son, Benjamin, grew up to run the Culper Ring — the network that fed Washington intelligence out of British-held New York and exposed Benedict Arnold.

narrative_blocks.header: She died before the war reached her sons
narrative_blocks.body: She bore five sons at the Setauket parsonage and died in 1768, at thirty-eight. Eight years later two of them fought at the Battle of Long Island — one taken prisoner and dead within the year, one on his way to running Washington's spies. She lived to see none of it.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father treated the colony's 'distracted persons'
narrative_blocks.body: Rev. Dr. John Smith of Rye was a minister who also practiced medicine, and was known for decades of success treating the mentally ill — rare skill in colonial America. He was a personal friend of Jonathan Edwards, who is said to have helped draw him into the ministry.

bio.bio_blurb: Mistress of Washington's White Plains headquarters

narrative_blocks.header: Washington took her house in October 1776
narrative_blocks.body: Abigail Purdy was thirty, with small children in the rooms, when the general moved into the farmhouse on Purdy Hill in the days around the Battle of White Plains. Her husband was a captain of the Westchester militia and was out with it, and the war ran across their own fields.

narrative_blocks.header: He came back and stayed two months
narrative_blocks.body: In the summer of 1778 Washington returned and kept his headquarters in the house from late July to the middle of September — the stay the record actually documents. The general and his staff lived in it with her family for the better part of two months.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived her husband by seventeen years
narrative_blocks.body: Abigail Smith was eighteen when she married Jacob Purdy in 1764, and she bore ten children in the house on Purdy Hill. He died there in December 1822 and she stayed on another seventeen years, dying in November 1839 at ninety-three.

notable.notable_blurb: Westchester militia captain and Washington's host

military_service.notes: Joined Westchester Militia 1775; commissioned Captain by the Battle of White Plains (Oct 28, 1776). DAR Patriot Ancestor #A125030. His brother Gabriel Purdy was a Loyalist, fighting for the British in DeLancey's Corps.

narrative_blocks.header: The documented stay was the second one
narrative_blocks.body: The house is source-documented as Washington's headquarters from 23 July to 16 September 1778, very nearly two months of it. The 1776 use, the one the house is famous for and the one that fell in the days around Chatterton Hill, is what historians believe rather than what the record proves.

narrative_blocks.header: Captain, and also private and corporal
narrative_blocks.body: At the Revolution Purdy was living at Robbins Mills in North Castle, and he served in Colonel Thomas Thomas's Second Westchester Regiment of militia — as private, as corporal, and as lieutenant under Captain Horton. The Daughters of the American Revolution carry him on the patriot rolls as a captain of New York militia.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother fought for the other side
narrative_blocks.body: Gabriel Purdy, fifteen years the younger, took service in DeLancey's Corps and fought the British side of the same Westchester ground. He came out of the war a Loyalist under sentence of banishment and was put ashore in Nova Scotia.

narrative_blocks.header: The losing side out-bred the winning one
narrative_blocks.body: Gabriel died in Nova Scotia leaving seventeen children and a hundred and seventy grandchildren. Jacob's line, entered in the Daughters of the American Revolution rolls as patriot ancestry, is the smaller of the two Purdy descents in North America.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten children, and a widow of ninety-three
narrative_blocks.body: Purdy married Abigail Smith of White Plains in 1764, she eighteen and he twenty-four, and they raised ten children in the town both of them died in. He died there in December 1822 at eighty-three; she lived on in the same place another seventeen years, to ninety-three.

narrative_blocks.header: He raised a spy ring at his table
narrative_blocks.body: He was a minister, not a spy — but the sons he raised at the Setauket parsonage carried the Revolution. Benjamin became Washington's chief of intelligence and built the Culper Ring; William died on a British prison ship. The father's role was the raising, not the running.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale, then forty years in one pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: He took his Yale degree in 1747 and settled as minister at Brookhaven on Long Island, where he preached for the rest of his life. His first wife, a Hooker descendant, bore him the sons who carried the family into the war.

narrative_blocks.header: His parish was the spy ring's home ground
narrative_blocks.body: For forty years he preached to the Setauket congregation that his son Benjamin later drew the Culper Ring from — Abraham Woodhull, the Strongs, and the other neighbors who ran Washington's intelligence out of British-held Long Island. The network operated on the ground the minister had served his whole life.

notable.notable_blurb: Washington's chief of intelligence

narrative_blocks.header: He ran Washington's spies from his home village
narrative_blocks.detail: Appointed director of military intelligence by Washington, Tallmadge recruited Abraham Woodhull and Robert Townsend as key agents, operating under the alias "John Bolton." When Major John André was captured carrying Arnold's secret correspondence, Arnold fled to the British before he could be arrested. André was placed in Tallmadge's personal custody and executed Oct 2, 1780. Washington personally wrote of Tallmadge's intelligence operation: the Culper Ring has been called the most effective intelligence network of the American Revolution. His Yale classmate and close friend was Nathan Hale — executed as a spy by the British in 1776. Tallmadge was fighting the same war Hale died in. (Wikipedia; DAB; Society of the Cincinnati records)
narrative_blocks.body: Washington made him his chief of military intelligence, and he built the Culper Ring from the Setauket friends he'd grown up with — a farmer, a boatman, a tavern rider — passing coded reports out of British-held New York under the alias John Bolton. For most of the war it was the best window Washington had into the enemy's plans.

narrative_blocks.header: His spies caught Benedict Arnold in the act
narrative_blocks.detail: Washington personally wrote: "I have received with much pleasure the report of your successful enterprise upon Fort St. George." The raid was a textbook special operations mission — night crossing, surprise assault, clean withdrawal — conducted by the same man who was simultaneously running Washington's spy network. Tallmadge Hall at Fort Huachuca, Arizona (home of Army Intelligence) is named for him. The town of Tallmadge, Ohio bears his name. (Wikipedia; DAB)
narrative_blocks.body: When a British officer was taken carrying papers in his boot, it was Tallmadge who grasped what they meant and exposed Arnold's plot to hand West Point to the enemy. The officer, Major John André, was placed in his custody, and the two men — spymaster and captured spy — took to each other in the days before André hanged.

narrative_blocks.header: Eighty men in whaleboats, not a shot missed
narrative_blocks.detail: His father Rev. Benjamin Tallmadge officiated at the wedding. William Floyd, whose daughter he married, had been a member of the Continental Congress and signed the Declaration; Floyd also served alongside Tallmadge in the Revolutionary War as a major general of New York militia. In Congress, Tallmadge was a committed Federalist. He was a founding member of the Society of the Cincinnati (Connecticut chapter, July 1783), an organization restricted to officers who served in the Revolution. "Continues to be represented by a living descendant in the society today." (Wikipedia; DAB; Society of the Cincinnati)
narrative_blocks.body: In November 1780 he rowed eighty men across the Sound at night, marched them over Long Island, and stormed a fortified British base at Fort St. George — taking it, burning three hundred tons of hay meant for the enemy's cavalry, and losing not a man. Washington had it read aloud to the whole army.

narrative_blocks.header: A signer's daughter, then sixteen years in Congress
narrative_blocks.body: He married Mary Floyd, daughter of the Declaration signer William Floyd, in 1784, and settled at Litchfield, where he grew rich in trade and ran the local bank. Connecticut sent him to Congress for sixteen years, where he argued for the men he had once commanded.

narrative_blocks.header: He wept at Washington's farewell to his officers
narrative_blocks.body: He was in the room at Fraunces Tavern in December 1783 when Washington said goodbye to his officers, and he left the only close account of it — the general too moved to speak, embracing each man in turn. Tallmadge wrote that there was scarcely a dry eye among them.

narrative_blocks.header: His classmate Nathan Hale, hanged as a spy
narrative_blocks.body: At Yale he was close friends with Nathan Hale, class of 1773. Hale went to the gallows in 1776 for the kind of work Tallmadge would spend the war perfecting — and survive. He never forgot that his friend had been caught doing clumsily what he learned to do well.

people.research_notes:
b. Feb 25, 1754 Presbyterian parsonage, Setauket, Long Island NY; d. Mar 7, 1835 Litchfield CT age 81. Buried East Cemetery, Litchfield CT. YALE COLLEGE 1773. Classmate and close friend of Nathan Hale. Member, Brothers in Unity (Yale society). Teacher, Wethersfield High School 1773-1776. Commissioned Lieutenant Jun 20, 1776; promoted Captain Dec 1776; promoted Major. Battle of Long Island Aug 27, 1776 (same battle where brother William was captured). Battles: White Plains, Brandywine, Monmouth, Germantown, White Marsh. CULPER SPY RING: Appointed director of military intelligence by Washington. Assembled Culper Ring with Abraham Woodhull and Robert Townsend. Assumed alias "John Bolton." Instrumental in exposing Benedict Arnold's betrayal — Major André placed in Tallmadge's custody; André executed Oct 2, 1780. BATTLE OF FORT ST. GEORGE (Nov 21-22, 1780): Led 80 men in whaleboats from Fairfield CT, crossed Long Island Sound, captured and burned Fort St. George at Mastic; burned 300 tons of British hay at Coram; no American casualties. Washington personally wrote: "I have received with much pleasure the report of your successful enterprise upon Fort St. George." SOCIETY OF THE CINCINNATI: Founding member, CT chapter July 1783. Brevetted Lieutenant Colonel Sep 30, 1783. Served as CT Cincinnati Asst. Treasurer, Treasurer, VP, and President 1785-1801. "Continues to be represented by a living descendant in the society today." POST-WAR: Postmaster, Litchfield CT 1792. Merchant partner with Oliver Wolcott Jr. and Julius Deming. First president, Phoenix Branch Bank (later First National Bank of Litchfield) 1814-1826. U.S. House of Representatives (Federalist, CT at-large) Mar 4, 1801 - Mar 3, 1817. Fort Huachuca, Arizona (Army Intelligence home): Tallmadge Hall named for him. Town of Tallmadge, Ohio named for him. Talmadge, Maine owned by him in early 1800s. Benjamin Tallmadge District, Boy Scouts of America (Long Island). Portrayed in AMC series Turn: Washington's Spies by Seth Numrich. m. (1) Mary Floyd (b. ca.1764, d. Jun 3, 1805) Mar 18, 1784 — daughter of Gen. William Floyd, Signer of the Declaration of Independence. His father Rev. Tallmadge officiated. m. (2) Maria Hallett (d. 1838) 1808.
CC NOTE [X00912]: Major Ezekiel Ransom, father of Michigan Governor Epaphroditus Ransom, was present at the execution of Major André on October 2, 1780 — the execution supervised by Benjamin Tallmadge. Ransom's son later married Almira Cadwell, a 7th-generation Hooker descendant.
CC NOTE [HD2925]: Col. Benjamin Tallmadge Jr. was one of seven Connecticut investors who purchased Richfield Township, Summit County, Ohio from the Connecticut Land Company in April 1807 — paying $26,087 for the tract. John Newton arrived from Goshen CT and by the early 1820s had purchased most of the land around Richfield's east center, building the home later owned by Homer Carter. Newton likely acquired land originally held through the Tallmadge syndicate. Both men were Connecticut-born Hooker descendants who participated in the Western Reserve's transformation from wilderness to settlement — Tallmadge as original purchaser, Newton as settler. (Richfield Township History)
CC NOTE [HD2934]: Col. Benjamin Tallmadge sold the northwest quarter of Richfield Township to Heman Oviatt in 1811, making Oviatt one of Richfield's earliest settlers. Oviatt's wife Eunice Newton Oviatt was a 6th-generation Hooker descendant — sister of John Newton, who later also settled in Richfield. Tallmadge and the Newton-Oviatt family were unknowingly connected through Thomas Hooker as well as through Ohio land.
CC NOTE [X01997]: Col. Benjamin Tallmadge was one of seven investors who purchased Richfield Township in 1807. Elisha Whittlesey arrived in Canfield the year before — 1806 — and served as public prosecutor for the entire Western Reserve, then in Congress 1823-1838. Tallmadge also served in Congress (1801-1817). Their careers overlapped in both the Western Reserve land development and in Congress. Both were Connecticut-born figures instrumental in the Reserve's transition from wilderness to institutions. Tallmadge is a Hooker descendant; Whittlesey is not — but both shaped the same territory.
CC NOTE [TD0059]: Benjamin Tallmadge commanded Elijah Wadsworth in Sheldon's Horse (2nd Continental Light Dragoons) during the Revolutionary War. Decades later, both men became part of the Connecticut Land Company's transformation of the Western Reserve: Tallmadge purchasing Richfield Township in 1807, Wadsworth having already settled in Canfield in 1802 as agent for the Land Company. Wadsworth commanded Elisha Whittlesey — Eben Newton's law partner — as aide-de-camp in the War of 1812. [Migrated from top-level military]: True

military_service.notes: Participated in Battle of Trenton. "Honored with the special confidence of Washington."

narrative_blocks.header: He was at Trenton, then in Washington's office
narrative_blocks.body: He enlisted in the Revolution and was in the fight at Trenton on 26 December 1776, at twenty. He afterwards served as private secretary to Washington at Philadelphia, and his obituary said he had been honoured with the special confidence of the President.

narrative_blocks.header: His unbuilt school funded his grandson's
narrative_blocks.body: He incorporated a manual labor school and orphan asylum for Washington in 1834 and raised money for it, then died in 1843 with nothing built. Seventeen years later his grandson Edward took the directors to Congress, dissolved the corporation and moved the funds into his own school for the deaf, which became Gallaudet University.

narrative_blocks.header: Orphaned young, raised by a coin engraver
narrative_blocks.body: His father died in 1772 and his mother two years later, and before he was eighteen he had gone to live with his uncle Elisha Gallaudet. Elisha cut the die for the Continental Dollar of 1776, the first coin struck for the United States.

narrative_blocks.header: He sold copies of Washington's war accounts
narrative_blocks.body: To raise money for the school he and Michael Nourse of the Treasury sold a booklet reproducing Washington's Revolutionary expense accounts. His own 1838 pamphlet argued for an education that joined science to useful labour.

narrative_blocks.header: His ledgers burned in the Treasury fire
narrative_blocks.body: His will admits the New York book business was attended with loss, and that his account books had gone in the fire at the old Treasury before he could settle with his creditors. He asked that six boys from among their heirs be taught free at the school if it ever opened.

narrative_blocks.header: The family Bible went to his eldest son
narrative_blocks.body: The folio family Bible with the register in it went to Thomas, with his father's prayer book. To the grandson who carried his name he left Marshall's Life of Washington.

narrative_blocks.body: He founded the American School for the Deaf in Hartford on April 15, 1817 — the first permanent school for the deaf in the Western Hemisphere. He had traveled to Paris to learn French Sign Language, returning with deaf teacher Laurent Clerc to build the school together.

narrative_blocks.header: Married his own deaf student Sophia Fowler
narrative_blocks.body: Among his first students was Sophia Fowler, born deaf; he married her in 1821 after her graduation. Their son Edward Miner Gallaudet founded what became Gallaudet University in Washington, carrying the family's mission to the national stage.

narrative_blocks.header: Co-authored religious textbooks with Horace Hooker
narrative_blocks.body: In the 1830s and 1840s he collaborated with fellow Hooker descendant Rev. Horace Hooker on Scripture Biography for the Young, The Practical Spelling Book, and The School and Family Dictionary. The spelling book was reprinted under both names for years after his death in 1851.

narrative_blocks.header: He crossed the ocean to learn the method
narrative_blocks.body: In 1815 Mason Cogswell's circle sent Gallaudet to Europe to learn how the deaf were taught. At the Paris institute of the Abbé Sicard he persuaded Laurent Clerc, a brilliant deaf instructor, to sail back with him. Clerc became the first deaf teacher of the deaf in America.

narrative_blocks.header: His son's college still carries the name
narrative_blocks.body: His youngest son, Edward Miner Gallaudet, carried the family's work to Washington. There he founded the college that became Gallaudet University, the only university in the world built for deaf students. The name his father made now stands over its gates.

narrative_blocks.header: The Braidwoods wanted his silence for their method
narrative_blocks.body: In Britain the Braidwood family, who taught the deaf for high fees at London and Edinburgh, offered to take him on as an apprentice on the condition that he never pass their methods to anyone else. He refused and went to Paris instead, where the Abbe Sicard offered to teach him for nothing. American deaf education is French rather than English because of that answer.

narrative_blocks.header: A deaf woman lobbying congressmen in Washington
narrative_blocks.body: When her youngest son Edward became principal of the Columbia Institution at twenty and set out to build a college for the deaf, she took the case to Congress herself. She met repeatedly with congressmen and other men of influence, and the support she gathered helped charter and fund what was then the National Deaf-Mute College.

narrative_blocks.header: She ran the household of an entire school
narrative_blocks.body: Appointed the Columbia Institution's first matron on May 30, 1857, she held the post for nine years, until August 1, 1866. For two of them she also headed the department that taught cooking and sewing, the skills she had picked up by watching in the years before any American school taught the deaf. She gave up the post only when her health began to fail.

narrative_blocks.header: Her first day of school came at nineteen
narrative_blocks.body: Born deaf near Guilford in 1798, she reached nineteen without a classroom of any kind, since no American school yet taught the deaf, and learned to cook and sew by watching the people around her. The Hartford school opened in 1817 and she entered it that year alongside her sister Parnel, studying there until the spring of 1821.

narrative_blocks.header: Her principal proposed before she had graduated
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet was running the Hartford school when she enrolled in 1817, and by the time she finished in the spring of 1821 the two were engaged. After his death in 1851 she kept the house going for the children not yet married, on the strength of the grown ones.

narrative_blocks.header: Guilford unveiled a bronze tablet forty years on
narrative_blocks.body: Deaf America named her the Mother of the American Deaf. The bronze went up at Guilford in 1917, the work of the sculptor Eugene Hannan, in the town she was born beside.

narrative_blocks.header: Gallaudet put her name on a children's dormitory
narrative_blocks.body: Amos Kendall built it in 1858 as the Primary Department Building, a school and dormitory for the youngest deaf children, and it grew new wings in 1862 and 1866 before housing the college's first women students. Condemned as a fire risk, it came down in 1916 and went back up on the same ground, her name carried over to the new hall.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty pounds of rye bought Yale's library
narrative_blocks.body: Pierpont held John Davenport's New Haven pulpit and in 1689 bought the books Davenport had gathered for a college, paying forty pounds of rye and thirty-two bushels of corn. In 1700 he gathered ten ministers at Branford to give books for a college, and the charter followed in 1701.

narrative_blocks.header: A successor named him Yale's true founder
narrative_blocks.body: Leonard Bacon, who held Pierpont's pulpit a century later, argued in 1839 that Pierpont was Yale's true founder. No memorial to him stands on the campus, though the historian Brooks Mather Kelley wrote in 1974 that "one might, in fact, even call him its progenitor."

narrative_blocks.header: A regicide's son fetched the money for Yale
narrative_blocks.body: He had taken John Dixwell, one of the judges who sentenced Charles I, into his church under the alias James Davids. In 1710 he sent Dixwell's son to London to find Jeremiah Dummer, who returned seven hundred books and Elihu Yale's gifts.

narrative_blocks.header: He drafted Connecticut’s church constitution
narrative_blocks.body: A leader of the 1708 Saybrook Synod, Pierpont is said to have drawn up the Articles of the Saybrook Platform — the system of discipline and fellowship that governed Connecticut’s churches for more than a century.

narrative_blocks.header: Three marriages in seven years
narrative_blocks.body: Pierpont's first wife, Davenport's granddaughter Abigail, died three months after their 1691 wedding, and his second, Sarah Haynes, died in 1696 after their daughter's birth. In 1698 he married Mary Hooker, Thomas Hooker's granddaughter, and their eight children included Sarah, who married Jonathan Edwards.

narrative_blocks.header: Two elms planted at the minister’s door
narrative_blocks.body: A poor farmer with nothing else to give carried two young elms on his shoulder and planted them at the parsonage in 1686. Edwards courted Sarah Pierpont beneath them forty years on, and the last trunk was cut into blocks for the family.

narrative_blocks.header: Two enslaved men, and a Carolina plantation
narrative_blocks.body: He and his brothers held two Black men recorded as Tom and Pung, and owned a plantation with enslaved people in South Carolina. His farm at North Haven, later Clover Dairy Farm, passed to his son Joseph and stayed with Joseph's descendants for three generations.

narrative_blocks.header: Whitefield preached from his front yard
narrative_blocks.body: George Whitefield was twice his houseguest — October 1740 and again in 1745, when the revivalist preached to an immense crowd from a platform under the elm before the Pierpont house at Elm and Temple. His host had helped split New Haven's church: a leader of the separatists who raised the White Haven congregation and its blue-painted meetinghouse in 1742.

narrative_blocks.header: He chased English castles to the end
narrative_blocks.body: He revived his father's inquiries into the family's supposed English titles, engaging the agent Jeremiah Dummer and riding to Roxbury in 1724 — where a cousin, entranced by dreams of castles in Britain, raced ahead with wilder plans. The last years of his life were clouded, a chronicler wrote, by the vain pursuit of recognition as rightful heir; his son Evelyn carried the claim further still.

narrative_blocks.header: The founder's son came home to Elm Street
narrative_blocks.body: Eldest son of the Yale founder, he tutored at the college in the early 1720s, then kept an apothecary's shop in Boston through the years of his first marriage. The second marriage, in 1754, brought him home to his father's house — where five sons were born, the youngest when he was past seventy.

narrative_blocks.header: Three of his sons rode into a legend
narrative_blocks.body: Evelyn, Robert, and James — sons of the Elm Street house — became the three brothers of the Litchfield snowstorm story, each marrying a Collins sister. Through the youngest ran the line that gave America the reformer John Pierpont and, in time, the banker who carried the family name to Wall Street.

narrative_blocks.header: The apron passed through her hands
narrative_blocks.body: The embroidered silk apron at the Connecticut Historical Society — Chinese taffeta worked in eight colors of pre-dyed thread and three kinds of metal, French gold and silver that sparkled by candlelight — belonged to her maternal line: her mother Mary Hooker Pierpont, herself, her daughter Mary Russell. Made between 1730 and 1740 for formal occasions, it is the line's surviving object.

narrative_blocks.header: Mother and daughter gone in one year
narrative_blocks.body: Mary died at Middletown on 24 July 1740, at thirty-seven, and her mother Mary Hooker Pierpont followed that November: two generations gone in a single year, the year her daughter Mary married the governor's son.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine children in the ministry house
narrative_blocks.body: Married to Rev. William Russell at sixteen in 1719, she bore four sons and five daughters in the Middletown parsonage — two of the sons followed their father into Yale pulpits, and the college graduated her name's direct line for five generations. She had been born at New Haven, the Yale founder's eldest daughter.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Yale founders shared her wedding
narrative_blocks.body: Her father, Rev. James Pierpont, and her husband's father, Rev. Noadiah Russell, had stood together among the founding trustees of the College in 1701 — the 1719 marriage joined two of its first families. Her groom had himself been Yale's tutor, and would nearly be its Rector.

In autumn she traveled to Princeton to visit his grave and bring back the two orphaned Burr grandchildren — Sarah Burr (age 4) and Aaron Burr Jr. (age 2). En route, she stopped in Philadelphia where she fell ill of dysentery and died Oct 2, 1758 — exactly 6 months after her husband. She was buried beside him in President's Row, Princeton Cemetery. bio.photo_notes: Sarah Pierpont Edwards (1710-1758), wife of Jonathan Edwards.
bio.bio_blurb: Subject of Edwards’s famous meditation at thirteen

narrative_blocks.header: Nine days swallowed up in light
narrative_blocks.body: In January 1742, with Jonathan away preaching, Sarah broke down and then for nine days felt herself swallowed up with light and love. She lost her speech and strength, fainted and leapt for joy, and came out of it sure of her salvation.

narrative_blocks.header: Her raptures went into print unsigned
narrative_blocks.body: Jonathan had Sarah write the experience down and printed it, without her name, in Some Thoughts Concerning the Present Revival of Religion. An earlier draft found in 2021 shows how much of her bodily agitation he left out.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at seventeen, mother of eleven
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah married Jonathan in July 1727, at seventeen, in a boldly patterned green satin brocade. All eleven of their children survived infancy, rare in that century, and George Whitefield wrote that a sweeter couple he had not yet seen.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven years at the Stockbridge mission
narrative_blocks.body: After Northampton dismissed Jonathan in 1750, the family went to the Stockbridge mission among the Mohicans. With the French war raiding near, Sarah nursed soldiers from the barracks and sold needlework with her daughters.

narrative_blocks.header: A young lady beloved of that Great Being
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah's raptures began at about six. At thirteen she caught the eye of Jonathan Edwards, back at Yale as a tutor, who wrote on the flyleaf of his Greek grammar of a young lady in New Haven who cared for little but to meditate on God.

narrative_blocks.header: She died going to fetch the Burr orphans
narrative_blocks.body: Jonathan died in March 1758, weeks into the Princeton presidency, and their daughter Esther Burr in April. That autumn Sarah set out to bring home Esther's children, Sally and Aaron Burr, and died of dysentery at Philadelphia.

narrative_blocks.header: Her epitaph is carved on a Yale bench
narrative_blocks.body: A stone bench at Jonathan Edwards College at Yale carries the words from her tombstone: Friend, Neighbor, Mother, Wife, and Christian. Her portrait, painted about 1740 by Joseph Badger, hangs in the same college.

burial.plot_notes: Center Church on the Green Churchyard, New Haven, Connecticut

people.research_notes: Lived in the Old Pierpont Mansion, New Haven. Died age 29, leaving two young children. His widow Lydia Hemenway remarried Theophilus Morgan of Killingworth 1745 — her father disinherited her for marrying a Church of England member.

bio.bio_blurb: Root of the Brooklyn Pierrepont line

landmarks.landmark_blurb: His 1741 gravestone stands in New Haven.

narrative_blocks.header: Rev. James Pierpont's youngest son, dead at twenty-nine
narrative_blocks.body: Hezekiah was the youngest son of the Rev. James Pierpont, minister at New Haven, and his wife Mary Hooker. He lived in the old family mansion and died at just twenty-nine, in 1741, leaving his widow Lydia with two small boys — John and Jacob.

narrative_blocks.header: His short life seeded the Brooklyn Pierrepont line
narrative_blocks.body: Hezekiah barely lived, but his line did not die with him. His son John kept the family's New Haven estate, and his grandson Hezekiah Beers Pierpont went on to found the Brooklyn Pierreponts.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother raised the sons he left behind
narrative_blocks.body: Hezekiah was dead at twenty-nine, his younger boy barely fifteen months old. Their mother soon married outside the Puritan faith and was disowned for it; cut adrift, she left the children to their father's people — and John grew up in his uncle James's house on Elm Street.

people.research_notes: Daughter of Nathaniel Breck and Martha Cunnabell of Boston. No children (EH #116).

narrative_blocks.header: Her cousin's courtship filled her parlor
narrative_blocks.body: After Hannah Breck's parents died, the cousin came to live with Sarah and James in Boston — and Rev. Ebenezer Parkman's diary records an evening there in 1736, promiscuous company until nine, amid great noise of his courting Mrs. Hannah. Parkman married Hannah the next year; Sarah's parlor had hosted the match.

narrative_blocks.header: A widow brought the Sherman name in
narrative_blocks.body: Widowed of a Davenport, she married James Pierpont in 1754, twenty-six to his fifty-four, and bore five sons in the Elm Street house. Her family name traveled down the line — a grandson was christened Sherman Pierpont.

b. Mar 16, 1755 New Haven CT; d. Feb 7, 1808 New Haven CT age 52 (EH says Feb 23, 1810 — likely error). Buried Fair Haven Union Cemetery, New Haven CT. REVOLUTIONARY WAR: 2nd Lieutenant, Captain Bradley's Company, Jun 5, 1780 to Jan 1, 1781. Also Sergeant of Artillery Guards, Lt. Phineas Bradley's Company, Apr 13-31, 1778 to Jun 1, 1779. "2d Lieutenant in a company of matrosses raised for the defense of New Haven. At the time of Tryon's invasion this company was stationed partly in the town and partly in East Haven and West Haven." (Year-Book of CT Society SAR, 1891.) Friend-compatriot of Col. Noadiah Hooker (H00288). POST-WAR: Farmer at Litchfield CT; becoming reduced in circumstances found employment at Yale College (of which he was a graduate) and continued until his death. DUKE OF KINGSTON CLAIM: "Evelyn Pierpont was the legitimate heir to the titles, honors, and estates of the Duke of Kingston, England, his line of descent and hereditary right having been fully established, but being an American the English Parliament refused to recognize the family." (EH.) The name "Evelyn" was given by his father James "in a sycophantic nod to his English relations." DESCENT: Through wife Rhoda Collins, the family also descended from William Hyde, Hartford founder (proprietor by 1639), and Gov. William Leete. m. Rhoda Collins Mar 1780 (b. Oct 5, 1764; d. Jun 20, 1845 Livonia, Livingston County NY age 80). Granddaughter of Rev. Timothy Collins, 4th settled minister of Litchfield CT.

narrative_blocks.header: Parliament said no: he was American
narrative_blocks.body: His descent from the Pierreponts, Dukes of Kingston, was formally established — and Parliament refused recognition on the ground that he was an American. He had carried the dukes' own given name, Evelyn, from birth; his father chased the same inheritance to his deathbed.

narrative_blocks.header: Three brothers snowbound — three sisters married
narrative_blocks.body: The town's legend snowbound three Pierpont brothers for weeks at the Collins house in South Farms, and Evelyn's bride from the storm was Rhoda. Robert took her sister Lois, James her sister Elizabeth — and the Morris paper later credited Collins vigor, joined to Pierpont intellect, for the leaders the line produced.

narrative_blocks.header: A lieutenant when the British burned in
narrative_blocks.body: A second lieutenant of matrosses — artillerymen — raised for New Haven's defense, he stood with the company posted between the town and its harbor villages when Tryon's forces invaded the coast in 1779. Before that he had sergeanted the artillery guards through a year of the war.

narrative_blocks.header: He worked for wages at his family's college
narrative_blocks.body: The years after the war reduced his circumstances, and the Litchfield farm gave way to employment at Yale — the college his grandfather helped found, now his employer rather than his legacy. He served there until his death in 1808.

death.cause: Died while visiting daughter Laura (Mrs. Col. Anson Sperry) at Plattsburgh.

b. Jun 13, 1757 New Haven CT; d. Aug 16, 1835 Plattsburgh NY age 78. Buried Dellwood Cemetery, Manchester VT (beside his wife). Son of James Pierpont II (H00116) and Anna Sherman Pierpont. Clothier, then merchant. Lived successively at Harwinton CT and Manchester VT (removed ca.1795). SNOWBOUND STORY: Three Pierpont brothers journeying from New Haven through Litchfield County stopped overnight at the Collins home in South Farms. A great storm snowbound them for weeks. "This was Cupid's opportunity, and the three young men married three daughters of the family." (Morris, CT library: Keefer, The Town of Morris, 1937.) Robert married Lois Collins; his brother Evelyn (H00351) married her sister Rhoda; their brother James married a third sister. He and Abel Camp operated a fulling mill on Mill Brook; sold his half to brother James ca.1783. He and Lois had 5 daughters only. m. Lois Collins (b. Oct 11, 1757 Litchfield CT; d. May 5, 1826 Manchester VT) Oct 11, 1780 Harwinton CT. Daughter of Charles Collins and Anne Huntington. Sister of Rhoda Collins who married Evelyn Pierpont.
BIRTH DATE DISCREPANCY: JSON has June 13; Dwight genealogy says "June 26, 1757". June 13 source unknown — possible transcription error. Flag for verification.

narrative_blocks.header: Three brothers snowbound — three sisters married
narrative_blocks.body: The town's legend put three Pierpont brothers snowbound for weeks at the Collins house in South Farms, and Robert came out of the storm bound to Lois — married in October 1780, first of the three matches. Evelyn took her sister Rhoda, James her sister Elizabeth; the Morris paper later credited Collins vigor, joined to Pierpont intellect, for the poets and financiers the line produced.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter married a future governor
narrative_blocks.body: Frances, born at Litchfield, married Richard Skinner — the Litchfield general's son who rose to the governorship of Vermont. Robert had carried his wife and five daughters to Manchester around 1795, and the Connecticut mill was left to James.

narrative_blocks.header: He died on a visit to Plattsburgh
narrative_blocks.body: August 1835 found him away from Manchester, visiting at Plattsburgh on Lake Champlain, where he died at seventy-eight. Dellwood holds him beside Lois, gone nine years before.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughters married half of Manchester's bar
narrative_blocks.body: Frances took the future governor, Esther and Laura took state's attorneys, Nancy took the town's admired physician, and Julia's second marriage built a famous Southern school. The snowbound bride's five daughters staffed a town.

people.research_notes: b. Jan 4, 1761 (FindAGrave: Jul 27, 1761) New Haven CT; d. Apr 23, 1840 Litchfield CT age 78. Clothier, then merchant, then farmer. Settled in Litchfield/South Farms (now Morris CT). SNOWBOUND: One of three Pierpont brothers who, snowbound at the Collins home in South Farms, each married a Collins daughter. James married ELIZABETH COLLINS (sister of Rhoda and Lois). Operated a fulling mill on Mill Brook with Abel Camp; sold his half to James ca.1783. When Robert and Lois moved to Vermont, James took over the wool business. m. (1) Elizabeth Collins Sep 28, 1782 Litchfield CT (b. Sep 25, 1755; d. Jul 28, 1815). She was daughter of Charles Collins and Anne Huntington — sister of Rhoda (m. Evelyn) and Lois (m. Robert). m. (2) Lucy Strong Dec 16, 1817 Salisbury CT (widow of Rev. Crossman). She d. 1835. Family spelling: name sometimes spelled "Pierrepont" — original spelling, per EH.

narrative_blocks.header: Three brothers snowbound — three sisters married
narrative_blocks.body: Riding from New Haven, the town's legend ran, three Pierpont brothers put up at the Collins house in South Farms just as one of the worst storms in memory closed the roads for weeks — and by the thaw each had a Collins bride in view. James married Elizabeth in 1782; Robert had Lois, Evelyn had Rhoda. The Morris paper later claimed the matches made the family — Pierpont intellect, Collins vigor — and counted the poet John Pierpont and J.P. Morgan among the descendants as proof.

narrative_blocks.header: The mill ran until the year he died
narrative_blocks.body: His brother Robert and Abel Camp had raised a fulling mill on two acres of Collins land at Mill Brook; James bought half by 1783, and when Robert left for Vermont the wool business was his alone. The family held the mill until 1840, the year of his death, when it was sold and the works went dark.

narrative_blocks.header: The farmhouse that raised the reformer
narrative_blocks.body: Ten children came to him and Elizabeth Collins, and several died young — Sally at eight, a first James at four. The second-born, John, left at twenty to tutor in Carolina and became the reformer who set the family name ringing; his verse remembered this household's mother — she led me first to God, her words and prayers my young spirit's dew.

narrative_blocks.body: His three brothers Evelyn, Robert, and James were snowbound at the Collins farmhouse and each married a Collins daughter; David alone married Sarah Phelps of Litchfield, settling near his brothers but taking a different path. bio.title: Reverend
bio.bio_blurb: Minister of Middletown; Fellow of Yale

narrative_blocks.header: The son took his father's pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: Three months into a Yale tutorship his father — Middletown's minister and a founding trustee of the College — died; the town soon called the son home, and he was ordained to the same pulpit in June 1715. His tombstone would call him a man of God, eminent for wisdom, prudence, and morality.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale offered him the rectorship, second
narrative_blocks.body: When Rector Cutler's defection to the Church of England emptied the College's head office, the Trustees voted in 1724 that if Harvard's Professor Wigglesworth could not be obtained, Mr. Russell be desired to accept the place. Nothing further of the effort is recorded; he served instead as a Fellow from 1745 to his death.

narrative_blocks.header: Whitefield called him an Israelite indeed
narrative_blocks.body: The revivalist spent a night at the parsonage in 1740 and wrote in his Journal of the simplicity of his host and the order wherein his children attended family devotions — this though Russell's sympathies ran with the Old Lights, wary of the revival itself.

narrative_blocks.header: A dying man's will made the dynasty
narrative_blocks.body: His grandfather, the immigrant William Russell, directed in his will that his infant son be devoted to God in the way of learning, being likely to prove a useful instrument in the ministry — and that orphan became Middletown's minister and a Yale founder. William was the third generation of the design; his sons made it four and five.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-six years in the pulpit, to the day
narrative_blocks.body: Settled as Middletown’s pastor on June 1, 1715, William Russell died on June 1, 1761 — forty-six years in the same pulpit to the day.

people.research_notes:
b. ca. 1718 Middletown CT. Daughter of Rev. William Russell (I00144) and Mary Pierpont Russell (H00118). m. Matthew Talcott (T00070) — son of GOV. JOSEPH TALCOTT of Connecticut (1669-1741). TALCOTT DOUBLE MARRIAGE: Matthew Talcott married Mary Russell (a Hooker descendant through Pierpont), while Matthew's SISTER Eunice Talcott (I00054) married Nathaniel Hooker 2d (H00115) — a direct Hooker descendant in the EH tree. Gov. Joseph Talcott's children thus married INTO the Hooker family twice in the same generation: once through the Pierpont line, once directly through the Hooker line. This double marriage is the genealogical foundation for Sam Hooker's middle name "Talcott." Barbour Collection confirms marriage date Sep 24, 1740. Her mother Mary Pierpont Russell died Jul 24, 1740 — Mary married Matthew Talcott exactly two months later.
CC NOTE [I00054]: TALCOTT DOUBLE HOOKER MARRIAGE: Mary Russell Talcott married Matthew Talcott, son of Governor Joseph Talcott of Connecticut. Matthew's sister EUNICE TALCOTT married NATHANIEL HOOKER 2D — a direct descendant of Rev. Thomas Hooker in the EH tree. So the two Talcott siblings (Matthew and Eunice) each married into the Hooker family — Matthew through the Pierpont/Russell line, Eunice directly through the Hooker surname line. Both marriages happen in the same generation, both children of the same colonial Governor. This double Talcott-Hooker convergence is the reason "Talcott" has been carried as a middle name by Hooker family descendants (including Sam Hooker Talcott, this project's creator). Matthew TALCOTT, Sept. 24, 1740." Her mother Mary Pierpont Russell (H00118) died July 24, 1740 — Mary Russell married Matthew Talcott exactly TWO MONTHS after her mother's death. narrative_blocks.header: The minister's daughter married the governor's son
narrative_blocks.body: Mary grew up in the Middletown parsonage of Rev. William Russell. She lost her mother on 24 July 1740 and married Matthew Talcott, the governor's son, two months later, on 24 September; his sister Eunice had married her mother's cousin Nathaniel Hooker.

narrative_blocks.header: She may have stitched the family apron
narrative_blocks.body: The silk apron at the Connecticut Historical Society, Chinese taffeta worked in eight colors of silk and in French gold and silver thread, passed down three generations of Marys. Mary was the one of an age to learn such work at a finishing school in the 1730s, and may be the one who made it.

narrative_blocks.header: Jeremiah Wadsworth grew up in her house
narrative_blocks.body: When Jeremiah Wadsworth's father died in 1747, the four-year-old came to live with Mary and Matthew at Middletown. In 1764 he married her sister Mehitable, and he went on to feed Washington's army as commissary general.

narrative_blocks.header: The one Mary without a portrait
narrative_blocks.body: Her grandmother Mary Hooker Pierpont sat for the Pierpont Limner, and her mother's likeness survives too; none of Mary has ever been found. She and Matthew had no children, and the line of three Marys ended with her.

narrative_blocks.header: Much respected in all the relations of life
narrative_blocks.body: Mary died at Middletown on 16 October 1799, in her seventy-ninth year. Her stone calls her the amiable and virtuous consort of Matthew Talcott, “a character much respected by her numerous acquaintance in all the relations of life.”

Matthew Talcott thus married Mary Russell (H00356), while his sister Eunice married Mary Russell's first cousin (Nathaniel Hooker 2d). Gov. Talcott's will assigns Middletown land to Matthew specifically. Talcott Pedigree entry 70 CONFIRMS: b. 1713; no children; died Aug. 29, 1802. T00070 is a duplicate entry for this same person.
CC NOTE [H00362]: Matthew Talcott raised the orphaned Jeremiah Wadsworth from age four after Jeremiah's father died in 1747. Matthew had married Mehitable's sister Mary Russell in 1740. When Jeremiah married Mehitable Russell in 1764, Matthew's ward married his wife's sister.
CC NOTE [T00387]: Matthew Talcott raised Jeremiah Wadsworth from age four after Jeremiah's father died in 1747. Jeremiah grew up in Matthew's Middletown household, calling him uncle. The guardian became his brother-in-law when Jeremiah married Matthew's wife's sister. [Sam-provided detail]: Wife Mary Russell was daughter of William Russell + Mary Pierpont (per Sam's source: SV Talcott 1876, p. 39). By his father's will Matthew received several tracts of land including 110 acres in Middletown. He was a sea captain, MERCHANT, and SHIP OWNER. Selectman of Middletown — in 1756 on the committee that reviewed Cushoy's circumstances (elderly Wangunk sachem). Confirmed: NO CHILDREN. [Merge audit 2026-04-26]: Duplicate T00070 entry merged. Bare-bones 'Mathew' entry (Index 466, originally referenced X01762 stub for Mary Russell + U00017 mother) consolidated into this richer entry. Spelling normalized 'Mathew' → 'Matthew' per Sam (modern usage; SV's archaic single-T was confusing). Mother_id corrected I00054 (sister, wrong) → U00017 (actual mother Eunice Howell Talcott). Stale T00070 reference in I00054's children_ids removed (sister cannot be parent of brother). X01762 'Mary Russell' stub now fully orphaned (no remaining references); H00356 is the canonical Mary Russell Talcott. [Native Northeast Portal — additional Rev War detail]: Matthew was already living in Middletown when he married Mary Russell. His father Gov. Joseph Talcott died in 1741, leaving him the Middletown estate and solidifying his status as a wealthy landowner. Owned several SHIPS — Sloops HESTER, DOLPHIN, and ELIZABETH. 1773: appointed Justice of the Peace. 1776: appointed Justice of the Quorum. Nov 4, 1774: Gov. Trumbull commissioned him Major of 6th Regiment of Horse and Foot. May 11, 1775: appointed Colonel of the newly organized 23rd Regiment (Middletown + Chatham). Same month: placed on committee to procure lead from Middletown lead mine for Connecticut's military stores (budget up to £400). Aug 13, 1776: wrote to Pay Table requesting £500 advance for marching the 23rd to New York. Aug-Sept 1776: 23rd stationed along East River during the British landing at Kip's Bay. Oct 1776: resigned his colonelcy at age 63; replaced by Comfort Sage. June 1777: still active in coastal defense — borrowed three swivel guns, four dozen swivel-gun shot, wormer and ladle from the State (held at New London under Nathaniel Shaw Jr). Wife Mary Russell d. Oct 16, 1799 Middletown CT, buried Riverside Cemetery. Matthew d. Aug 29, 1802 Middletown CT, also buried Riverside Cemetery.

narrative_blocks.header: Named a nephew for him; paid his education
narrative_blocks.body: Matthew Talcott Russell, born 1761, was named by his father Rev. Noadiah Russell after Colonel Matthew Talcott — who had married his aunt Mary Russell and had no children of his own. Colonel Talcott met the expenses of his nephew's education. Matthew Talcott Russell went on to study law with Oliver Ellsworth, become State's Attorney for Middlesex County, and serve as a Yale tutor.

narrative_blocks.header: He raised his future sister-in-law's husband
narrative_blocks.body: When Rev. Daniel Wadsworth died in 1747, leaving four-year-old Jeremiah fatherless, Matthew Talcott took the boy in. Jeremiah grew up in Matthew's Middletown household calling him uncle. In 1764 Jeremiah married Mehitable Russell — the sister of Matthew's own wife Mary.

narrative_blocks.header: He weighed the Wangunk sachem's case
narrative_blocks.body: As selectman of Middletown CT, Matthew Talcott served in 1756 on a committee that reviewed the circumstances of Cushoy — an elderly and impoverished Wangunk sachem — and made recommendations to the Connecticut General Assembly. The committee's role marked one of the formal colonial-era encounters between Middletown's town leadership and the Wangunk people whose ancestral lands the town occupied.

narrative_blocks.header: He mined Middletown's lead for the war
narrative_blocks.body: The same May 1775 General Assembly that made Talcott colonel of the 23rd Regiment also placed him on a committee to procure lead for Connecticut's military stores. Middletown was the site of one of the few lead mines in colonial Connecticut, and the committee was authorized to refine the mine's ore, erect any furnace or building necessary, and draw on the State Treasurer for sums up to £400. The committee's work supplied bullet lead for Connecticut's regiments through the early years of the Revolution.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty-three, and still he took the regiment
narrative_blocks.body: A sea captain and ship owner who rose through Middletown's offices to colonel of militia, he commanded a regiment in the Revolution at sixty-three. The governor's son had married the minister's daughter in 1740 and outlived nearly everyone, dying in 1802 at eighty-nine.

burial.plot_notes: Riverside Cemetery, Middletown, Middlesex County CT (per Findagrave).

career.notes: Sea captain and merchant out of Middletown CT. Owned several ships including the Sloops Hester, Dolphin, and Elizabeth.
Elected selectman of Middletown. In 1756 served on the committee that reviewed Cushoy's circumstances (see narrative_blocks).
Appointed Justice of the Peace in 1773.
Appointed Justice of the Quorum in 1776.
Per SV Talcott 1876: judge of the Hartford County Court.

military_service.role: Regimental commander
military_service.notes: Nov 4, 1774: Gov. Jonathan Trumbull commissioned Talcott Major of the 6th Regiment of Horse and Foot. May 11, 1775: General Assembly appointed him Colonel of the newly organized 23rd Regiment (Middletown + Chatham). For most of its existence the 23rd remained in Connecticut as an administrative unit — monitoring the coast for British foraging parties, guarding public stores. Aug 1776: 23rd Regiment called to NY to reinforce Washington's Continental Army; Talcott wrote Aug 13, 1776 to the Pay Table requesting £500 advance. The regiment was stationed along the East River during the British landing at Kip's Bay (Sept 15, 1776) — resulted in precipitous American retreat. After serving through the New York crisis, Talcott (then 63) resigned his commission Oct 1776; replaced by Comfort Sage. Jun 9, 1777: still active in coastal defense, requested loan from State of three swivel guns + four dozen swivel-gun shot + wormer and ladle from New London (in care of Nathaniel Shaw Jr).

narrative_blocks.header: She stayed where the line began
narrative_blocks.body: Alone of the minister's daughters she lived out her whole seventy-four years at Middletown, marrying the merchant Samuel Johnson in April 1753 and dying in the town of her birth in 1796. Their one known son died before them both.

narrative_blocks.header: A Berkeley scholar took the Windsor pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: Yale 1745 and a Berkeley scholarship led through a tutorship to the First Church of Windsor, where he preached from 1751 until his death in 1775, at forty-nine. Palisado's burying ground — the same soil as the Hooker cousins' Windsor world — holds him and both wives.

narrative_blocks.header: Resolved a contentious meetinghouse debate at Windsor
narrative_blocks.body: He oversaw a contentious debate at Windsor about building the new meetinghouse and found resolution. His estate at his 1775 death was inventoried at £994 including 130 books — a substantial library for a colonial pastor.

narrative_blocks.header: Lost his first wife after thirteen years
narrative_blocks.body: His first wife Abigail Andrews of Milford died June 13, 1765 after thirteen years of marriage. He remarried Abigail Newberry of Wintonbury in 1770, five years before his own death.

NOTABLE DESCENDANTS: Through son John (EH 850): Samuel Russell (1789-1862) founded RUSSELL & COMPANY, the largest American trading house in China 1819-1891. Edward Augustus Russell (1797-1874) worked in the China trade, served as Mayor of Middletown 1859-1861. RUSSELL & COMPANY partner Warren Delano Jr. was the maternal grandfather of President Franklin Delano Roosevelt. [Marriage date notes (spouse X00437)]: EH says "1757" — Barbour Collection confirms 1758. EH has a one-year error. NOTE: A DIFFERENT Samuel Russell graduated Yale 1712 — son of Rev. Samuel Russell (Harv. 1681) of Branford CT, pastor of North Guilford 1725-1746, died Jan 19, 1745/6 age 52, married Dorothy Smithson 1718. He is NOT this Samuel Russell (H00359), who was born 1727 in Middletown. Future researchers should not conflate the two.

narrative_blocks.header: Ensign to captain in the train-band
narrative_blocks.body: By 1763 Barbour Collection records call him 'Ensign Samuel'; by 1773, 'Capt. Samuel.' He served as a militia officer of Middletown across the decade leading up to the Revolution.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight children, then twenty-one years alone
narrative_blocks.body: Ruth Whitmore died in April 1773 at forty-one, leaving eight children in the captain's house; he died in 1794, twenty-one years a widower. Through his son John's boys, the household's name went to Canton.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandson built the China giant
narrative_blocks.body: His grandson Samuel Russell (1789-1862) founded Russell & Company in 1819 — the largest American trading house in China through 1891. Russell & Company partner Warren Delano Jr. became the maternal grandfather of Franklin Delano Roosevelt.

MINISTRY: Licensed to preach fall 1753; preached Pomfret CT 1754; preached West Hartford and North Society in Killingly (now Thompson) 1756-57; called July 28, 1757, accepted August 30; ordained November 9, 1757. Traveled to Boston for health; died of apoplexy Oct 27, 1795 at Rev. Caleb Alexander's house in Mendon MA. MEMORIAL: Funeral sermon preached by Rev. Josiah Whitney of Brooklyn CT, published 1796. "A man of respectable talents, very strict in his attention to the order of society, and a man of great punctuality." (Rev. Daniel Dow, his successor.) CHARACTER: "His mental powers were excellent... He thought and reasoned well... His sermons were plain and serious, judicious and pungent... a steady, able advocate for religious and civil order." (Rev. Josiah Whitney funeral sermon.) m. Oct 14, 1797 Thompson CT; buried West Thompson Cemetery; daughter of Joseph Talcott Jr., Treasurer of Colony of Connecticut 1755-1769, and Esther Pratt — making Esther a GRANDDAUGHTER of Gov. Joseph Talcott T00045). NOTE: EH says "855 Noadiah, d. young" but online sources show Noadiah Jr. lived to 1817 age 57. This is a possible EH error or there may have been two children named Noadiah. narrative_blocks.header: Three pulpits, three deaths in office
narrative_blocks.body: His grandfather held Middletown's pulpit to his death; his father held the same one forty-six years to his; Noadiah held Thompson's thirty-eight years to his own — three generations of ministers, none of whom retired. His people remembered courteous manners and a serenity of temper; apoplexy took him on a Boston journey in 1795.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife's uncle married his sister
narrative_blocks.body: Esther Talcott, wed in 1758, was the governor's granddaughter — and her uncle, Col. Matthew Talcott, had married Noadiah's sister Mary eighteen years before. Two Russell-Talcott marriages in one generation sealed what the old major's 1683 recruiting letter had started; his second son carried the colonel's full name.

narrative_blocks.header: The census found slaves in the parsonage
narrative_blocks.body: The Hartford Courant's slavery accounting named good Yankee families — Alsop, Russell — and the slaveholding Noadiah Russell of the 1790 census was this one, the Thompson minister. His grandfather had willed a boy to a son; his father willed a woman and her two children, Lillian and Tom, by name.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandson co-founded Yale's Skull and Bones
narrative_blocks.body: His son Matthew Talcott Russell named a son William Huntington Russell, who at Yale in 1832 co-founded the secret senior society Skull and Bones with Alphonso Taft. The line connects this Thompson Connecticut pulpit to the most secretive of American institutions.

narrative_blocks.body: She married Eliot Rawson on June 16, 1756 in Middletown — son of Pelatiah Rawson and Hannah Hall of Dorchester. They had one child before her early death in 1764.

narrative_blocks.header: Died young leaving widower who remarried
narrative_blocks.body: She died in 1764, age thirty-two, leaving Eliot a widower with their one child. He remarried Ann Cushing of Providence and had seven more children with her.

narrative_blocks.header: Never known to be in a hurry
narrative_blocks.body: Those long intimate with her said her equanimity was so entire that she was never known to be in a hurry, and that she avoided the errors that come of impulsive speech. Through her husband's long absences the household and the raising of the children fell wholly to her.

narrative_blocks.header: Washington and Rochambeau at her table
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband's position made the Hartford house the centre of hospitality for the high command of both armies. Whether the guest was Lafayette, de Grasse, Rochambeau or Washington, she was equally self-possessed and in elegant preparation, and never spoke of it afterwards.

narrative_blocks.header: Her portrait hangs in the Atheneum
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas Sully painted her, and the canvas hangs in the gallery of the Wadsworth Atheneum with those of her husband and children. A visitor thought it a striking likeness of her character as well as her face.

narrative_blocks.header: Five of her children died as infants
narrative_blocks.body: Of nine children, five were buried in infancy between 1769 and 1779, two of them within three years of each other. Her daughter Harriet died at twenty-three in Bermuda, leaving Daniel and Catherine the only two to outlive their mother.

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband's sisters lived on with her
narrative_blocks.body: She outlived him by thirteen years, to the age of eighty-two, and kept the Hartford house going as its head. Two of his unmarried sisters lived there with her, keeping their own rooms and their father's books.

narrative_blocks.header: Her sister's husband had raised her husband
narrative_blocks.body: Her sister Mary had married Matthew Talcott of Middletown, and it was Matthew who took four-year-old Jeremiah in when his father died. She married into a household she already knew, and their children carried Russell and Hooker blood from her side, Talcott from his.

narrative_blocks.header: Founded Royalist Episcopal church at North Haven
narrative_blocks.body: He was a founder and the first senior warden of St. John's Church of England in North Haven, elected at age thirty-two in 1761. The rector and majority of members were Royalists during the Revolution but accepted the new government afterward.

narrative_blocks.header: Senior warden for fifty years until death
narrative_blocks.body: He continued as senior warden of St. John's, with few exceptions, for fifty years — until his death in 1820 at age ninety-one. He outlived his wife Elizabeth Frost by sixteen years.

narrative_blocks.header: Brick maker who served the Revolution
narrative_blocks.body: His occupation was brick maker in North Haven. Despite his Episcopal church's Royalist majority, he served in the Revolution — a fact recorded on his gravestone in the Old Cemetery.
