Gravestone: "In Memory of Joseph Pierpont Esq. who died in his 94. year. He was grandson of the Rev. James Pierpont first minister in New Haven." EH entry 366. Yale College 1751. Served in Revolution (gravestone). CHURCH: 59 years parish clerk — first Congregational, then St. John's CoE. The Congregational Church REFUSED his resignation; for 4 years he served as clerk of BOTH churches simultaneously. First Episcopalian appointed Justice of the Peace by CT Legislature. CIVIC: First town clerk when North Haven incorporated. First representative to CT General Assembly 1787; served 9 times total. First lieutenant Ninth Company Second Regt CT Militia Oct 1760; captain May 1764. OCCUPATION: Farmer, general trader, grist mill builder. LIGHTNING STRIKE 1771 (CT Journal Aug 2, 1771): On July 29, 1771, Capt. Joseph Pierpont, wife Lydia Bassett, Abel Brocket and wife, and Giles Pierpont and wife were all struck by lightning while seated on one bench in a sabbath-day-house. "Three horses and a colt...were all killed instantly upon the spot." Joseph was fixed in his seat unable to move; women were raised from seats. Blood showed "separation between the ferous and globular parts." All survived. Source: Connecticut Journal (New Haven), Aug 2, 1771, Issue 198, p.4. m. (1) Lydia Bassett Oct 21, 1756 (b. Aug 1, 1736; d. Nov 9, 1783 age 47; buried Old Cemetery NH). m. (2) Annis Warner Oct 26, 1791 (b. ca.1735; d. ca.1800). No children by second wife.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale 1751 — fifty-nine years parish clerk
narrative_blocks.body: He graduated Yale in 1751 and served as parish clerk for fifty-nine years — first at the Congregational church, then at St. John's Episcopal in North Haven. The Congregational church refused to accept his resignation, so for four years he served as clerk of both simultaneously.

narrative_blocks.header: First Episcopalian appointed Justice of the Peace
narrative_blocks.body: He was the first Episcopalian appointed Justice of the Peace by the Connecticut Legislature. He served nine times in the Connecticut General Assembly, beginning in 1787 when North Haven was first incorporated as a town.

narrative_blocks.header: Lightning struck six on a sabbath-day-house bench
narrative_blocks.body: On July 29, 1771, Capt. Pierpont, his wife Lydia, and four others were struck by lightning while seated on one bench in a sabbath-day-house. Three horses and a colt were killed instantly; all six humans survived.

narrative_blocks.header: Captain in the Connecticut Militia, served the Revolution
narrative_blocks.body: He was commissioned first lieutenant of the Ninth Company, Second Regiment Connecticut Militia in 1760, and captain in 1764. His gravestone confirms he served in the Revolution.

narrative_blocks.header: Six chimneys and one of nine silver watches
narrative_blocks.body: The 1786 lists made him the wealthiest man in North Haven: two hundred acres, one of the nine silver watches in town, and taxes on six smokes — six chimneys, which argues more than one house.

narrative_blocks.header: Lightning struck the bench he sat on
narrative_blocks.body: On 28 July 1771 lightning hit a tree five feet from the sabbath-day house and struck five people off one bench. It burnt the hair from his thigh and left the flesh red as if scalded. Three horses and a colt died where they stood.

narrative_blocks.header: Assemblyman at eighty-five
narrative_blocks.body: He served as a sergeant in the Connecticut militia during the Revolution, was selectman of North Haven in 1810 and 1811, and went to the General Assembly in 1826, at eighty-five.

narrative_blocks.header: His farm was an attorney general's birthplace
narrative_blocks.body: The tract came down from James Pierpont to his son Joseph and then to him, and on to Giles Junior, whose son Edwards Pierrepont was born on it. It ended as Clover Dairy Farm, known locally as the Patten place.

narrative_blocks.header: Five brothers, none died before seventy-eight
narrative_blocks.body: He died in January 1832 at ninety, the oldest person in town but one. His five brothers had reached ninety-three, ninety-two, eighty-four, eighty-four and seventy-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: Wife outlived him by nine months
narrative_blocks.body: He died January 16, 1832 at age 90; his wife Elizabeth Cooper Pierpont died November 1, 1832 at age 88. After 66 years of marriage, she survived him by nine months.

people.research_notes: b. Oct 5, 1703 Windsor (East Parish), Connecticut Colony; d. Mar 22, 1758 Princeton, Province of New Jersey age 54. Graduated Yale 1720 at age 16, delivering the Latin valedictory address. Master's degree 1722. Ordained at Northampton Feb 22, 1727. m. Sarah Pierrepont (HD0418) Jul 28, 1727 New Haven — she was 17, he was 23. 11 children; all born in Northampton. NORTHAMPTON MINISTRY AND DISMISSAL (1727-1750): Succeeded his grandfather Solomon Stoddard as minister of Northampton, the most important parish in Massachusetts outside Boston. The Great Awakening began under his preaching in 1735; "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God" preached Jul 8, 1741. In 1749 he insisted on "Strict Communion" — no sacrament without examination for genuine conversion. The town rose against him. Before that, church discipline over young people reading what he called "immoral books" (later identified as a midwifery textbook) had inflamed the parish. His own relatives — the Williamses and Hawleys — turned against him. Dismissed Jun 22, 1750 after a council of churches. He preached his Farewell Sermon Jul 1, 1750. Left £2,000 in debt. STOCKBRIDGE EXILE AND GREATEST WRITING (1751-1758): Went to Stockbridge (Hampshire County, now Berkshire) to minister to 12 white families and a Housatonnuck Indian mission (growing from 50 to 250+). Could not speak the Indian language; preached through an interpreter. In this period of "seclusion" he wrote his greatest philosophical works: "The Freedom of the Will," "The Nature of True Virtue," "The Doctrine of Original Sin." "Here he did his greatest writing." PRINCESTON AND DEATH: Aaron Burr Sr. (husband of his daughter Esther, H00378) died Sep 1757. Trustees elected Edwards as the next president of the College of New Jersey (now Princeton University). Inoculated for smallpox Feb 23, 1758. Died Mar 22, 1758 — president for only 35 days. PRINCETON CEMETERY EPITAPH (Latin, 41 lines): "Tall of person, but slender, worn thin by intense study, abstinence, and application; second to none among mortals in sharpness of intellect, keen judgment, and prudence...The College weeps for his loss, the Church weeps; but Heaven rejoices in receiving him." PORTRAIT: Painted in Boston 1740 (by Joseph Badger, not John Smibert as traditionally claimed) at the request of a Mr. Hogg of Scotland. Original portraits of both Jonathan and Sarah bequeathed to Yale University 1939 by Eugene Phelps Edwards; now in Jonathan Edwards College dining hall. HISTORIOGRAPHY: John Fiske estimated Edwards "the greatest intelligence of anyone yet born in America." Emerson and William James found in him "the curious, sensitive, far-ranging creative mind." Best modern biography: "Jonathan Edwards" by Ola Elizabeth Winslow (Macmillan, 1940). Yale, Princeton, and Andover-Harvard hold his manuscript collections. (Jonathan Edwards family Bible; Edwards genealogical records in The Record LXXI; F.B. Dexter, Biographical Sketches of Graduates of Yale College 1701-1745) [Migrated from death.notes]: Died 34 days after installation as President of Princeton (College of New Jersey). narrative_blocks.header: Three hundred converts, then Sinners at Enfield
narrative_blocks.body: The Northampton revival of 1734 and 1735 added three hundred members to his church in half a year, and his Faithful Narrative carried it across the Atlantic. At Enfield on 8 July 1741 he preached Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God.

narrative_blocks.header: He would not risk the Hadley measles
narrative_blocks.body: In February 1740, with measles at Hadley, Edwards declined to help keep a fast there; the distemper, he wrote, is often given in persons' breath before they fall ill. At the end of that year his whole household had it, and all lived.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandfather’s communion rule undid him
narrative_blocks.body: Solomon Stoddard had let any outwardly decent townsman take the Lord's Supper. Edwards required a profession of faith first, and Northampton dismissed him over it in 1750 — then kept him in the pulpit until a replacement was found.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten English families and two hundred Mohicans
narrative_blocks.body: Dismissed in 1750, he took the Stockbridge mission and preached to ten English families and two hundred Mohicans through an interpreter. The frontier post gave him the quiet to write his masterworks.

narrative_blocks.header: He split the will to save Calvinism
narrative_blocks.body: Freedom of the Will, in 1754, divided natural ability from moral ability: fallen people keep every faculty needed to obey God and lack only the will to use them. The distinction founded New England Theology.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale valedictorian at sixteen, in Latin
narrative_blocks.body: He entered Yale at twelve and graduated as the youngest of his class, delivering the valedictory in Latin. Bolton took him over Isaac Stiles and made him its first pastor in November 1723; a Yale tutorship drew him away six months later.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-five days into the Princeton presidency
narrative_blocks.body: He took the College of New Jersey presidency weeks after his son-in-law Aaron Burr died in office. A smallpox inoculation on 23 February 1758 killed him on 22 March. His last words: trust in God, and ye need not fear.

bio.photo_notes: Sarah Edwards Parsons (1728-1805), eldest daughter of Jonathan Edwards.

narrative_blocks.header: Born on a Sabbath afternoon in Northampton
narrative_blocks.body: She was Jonathan Edwards's first child, born August 25, 1728, and he set the hour down — between two and three on a Sabbath afternoon. She outlived him by nearly fifty years and lies in an unmarked grave at Goshen.

narrative_blocks.header: She married her father's man of business
narrative_blocks.body: Elihu Parsons handled much of Jonathan Edwards's legal and personal business, and in 1750 he married the preacher's eldest daughter. He practiced law at Northampton, then farmed at Stockbridge.

narrative_blocks.header: Warned of her temper, he married her anyway
narrative_blocks.body: When Parsons came for her hand, Edwards is said to have disclosed his daughter's difficult temper before consenting — hoping, he added, that she had grace even if she lacked ease. She bore eleven children.

narrative_blocks.header: The house filled with her orphaned siblings
narrative_blocks.body: In 1758 her father, her mother, and a brother-in-law all died within months. She and her married sister took in the younger Edwards children left behind.

narrative_blocks.header: Both her daughters married Berkshire Ingersolls
narrative_blocks.body: Two of her daughters married two Ingersoll brothers of the Berkshire hills — Sarah to David, Lydia to Aaron. Through the sisters the Edwards descent passed into a frontier farming line that reached Michigan.

people.research_notes: b. Apr 26, 1730 Northampton MA — "born on a Sabbath day, towards the conclusion of the afternoon exercise." d. Feb 14, 1748 Northampton MA age 17. Buried Bridge Street Cemetery, Northampton MA, beside David Brainerd. Edwards wrote: "...taking away by Death, the last February, my second Daughter, in the 18 year of her Age, a very pleasant and useful member of this Family, and that was generally esteemed the Flower of the Family." Betrothed to Rev. David Brainerd (1718-1747), the missionary to the Indians in New Jersey and Pennsylvania. In June 1747 she traveled to Boston — Brainerd was too ill to travel alone — and brought him to Northampton where she nursed him through his final illness. He died of tuberculosis at the Edwards home Oct 9, 1747. Unaware of the risk, she contracted the disease. "It is said Jerusha never smiled after Brainerd's death." She died five days after a final attack, four months after him. Brainerd had been expelled from Yale College for saying that one of the tutors "was devoid of grace" — so no degree was ever awarded him. Jonathan Edwards wrote Brainerd's biography, published 1749 in Boston: "An Account of the Life of the Late Reverend Mr. Brainerd." bio.bio_blurb: Edwards’s daughter; ‘the Flower of the Family’

narrative_blocks.header: Edwards called her 'the Flower of the Family'
narrative_blocks.body: She was born April 26, 1730 in Northampton — second daughter of Jonathan Edwards. After her death he wrote that she was 'generally esteemed the Flower of the Family.'

narrative_blocks.header: Brought home dying David Brainerd to nurse
narrative_blocks.body: In June 1747 she traveled to Boston to bring Rev. David Brainerd back to Northampton — the missionary to Indians in New Jersey was too ill with tuberculosis to travel alone. She nursed him at her father's home until his death October 9, 1747.

narrative_blocks.header: Contracted his TB; never smiled after
narrative_blocks.body: Unaware of the risk, she contracted tuberculosis from Brainerd. 'It is said Jerusha never smiled after Brainerd's death' — she died February 14, 1748, four months after him, age seventeen.

narrative_blocks.header: Buried beside Brainerd; Edwards wrote his biography
narrative_blocks.body: She was buried in Northampton's Bridge Street Cemetery beside David Brainerd. Her father Jonathan Edwards wrote Brainerd's biography, published in Boston in 1749 as 'An Account of the Life of the Late Reverend Mr. Brainerd.'

narrative_blocks.header: At ten, Whitefield spoke to the Edwards children
narrative_blocks.body: When George Whitefield came to Northampton in October 1740, Jerusha was ten. He paused to address the Edwards children directly, and her father wrote soon after that he believed salvation had come into his house, several of his children savingly wrought upon.

people.prominent_name_reason: Esther Edwards Burr (1732-1758) — daughter of Jonathan Edwards; wife of Aaron Burr Sr. (President of Princeton); mother of Aaron Burr Jr. (3rd U.S. Vice President, 1801-1805). Kept a journal 1754-1757, an important source for colonial women's history. Thomas Hooker's great-great-granddaughter.

notable.notable_blurb: Diarist of colonial women's daily life

narrative_blocks.header: She left colonial America’s earliest woman’s diary
narrative_blocks.body: Esther Edwards Burr’s letter-journal of 1754–1757 is the earliest known ongoing record of an American woman’s daily life. Long dismissed as the writing of merely a daughter, wife, and mother of famous men, it was not published in full until 1984 and is now prized as a landmark of early American women’s history.

narrative_blocks.header: Her diary was really a friendship in letters
narrative_blocks.body: Rather than a private record, the journal took the form of daily letters exchanged with her childhood friend Sarah Prince of Boston. The two wrote under nicknames — Burrissa and Fidelia — bundling pages into "paquets" that included secret enclosures Prince burned after reading.

narrative_blocks.header: She died at twenty-six, her children orphaned
narrative_blocks.body: Esther died in 1758 at just twenty-six, within months of her husband, her father Jonathan Edwards, and her mother — a chain of deaths that left her two small children orphaned. Her toddler son was the future Vice President Aaron Burr. The orphans were taken in and raised by Esther's sister Mary Edwards Dwight and her husband, Major Timothy Dwight.

narrative_blocks.header: She defended a woman’s right to an opinion
narrative_blocks.body: When men told her women had no business judging public affairs, Esther pushed back on paper, noting pointedly that her husband was "not of that sort." Her candid moral assessments of war, politics, and her contemporaries give the journal its living voice.

narrative_blocks.header: She was Princeton’s frontier first lady
narrative_blocks.body: As wife of Aaron Burr Sr., she managed the household of the young College of New Jersey and hosted its scholars, delighting in the religious debate around her table. She bore her son Aaron almost entirely alone, writing that with "no mother, no husband" present, "only my dear God" attended her.

narrative_blocks.header: A death chain orphaned the future Vice President
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband died of fever in 1757; her father Jonathan Edwards, his successor, died of smallpox inoculation weeks after arriving; and Esther herself died of fever in April 1758, at twenty-six. Within a year the deaths left her toddlers Aaron and Sally orphaned, sent to a maternal uncle’s crowded home.

Third child of Rev. Jonathan Edwards (X00128) and Sarah Pierpont Edwards (HD0418). Named for her great-grandmother Esther Stoddard, known for women's prayer groups. Educated at home; parents encouraged her writing. Met Aaron Burr Sr. (X00613) when he visited her father; engaged May 1752, m. Jun 29, 1752 Newark NJ (date from Wikipedia; EH says Jan 29, 1752). Lived in Newark NJ then Princeton NJ as wife of Princeton's president. DIARIST: Kept a journal Oct 1754-1757 as letter-diary to friend Sarah Prince of Boston ("Fidelia"). First published in entirety 1984 (Karlsen and Crumpacker). Now a primary source for women's lives in colonial America. DEATH: Her husband Aaron Burr Sr. died Sep 24, 1757 at Princeton. Her father Jonathan Edwards came to succeed him as Princeton president but died Mar 22, 1758 of smallpox inoculation complications. Esther died Apr 7, 1758 — 16 days after her father. Orphaned her two children Aaron (age 2) and Sally (age 4). Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esther_Edwards_Burr SLAVERY CONTEXT: Her husband Aaron Burr Sr. (X00613) purchased an enslaved man named Caesar on Sep 2, 1756 while serving as Princeton's president. people.research_notes: b. Apr 4, 1734 Northampton MA — "being Sabbath day, the sun being about an hour and a half high, in the morning." (Edwards family Bible) d. Feb 28, 1807 Northampton MA age 72. Buried Bridge Street Cemetery, Northampton MA (Dwight family plot). Daughter of Rev. Jonathan Edwards (X00128) and Sarah Pierpont Edwards (HD0418). Third daughter of Jonathan Edwards; named for his mother and grandmother Esther. Married Nov 8, 1750 Major Timothy Dwight III (X00635) — she was 16. The early marriage was allowed because the Edwards family was about to remove to Stockbridge, "now so near, were then practically far apart." Jonathan Edwards at the time wrote "I have now nothing visible to depend upon for my future usefulness, or the subsistence of my numerous family." Within two months of the marriage, Edwards went to Stockbridge "to preach to the English and the Indians." She was notably small — her husband reportedly could carry her around the room on his open palm. Mother of 13 children, all large and strong; the Dwight family source book says "the special beauty of this generation of the family came from their Edwards lineage." Description (1862 witness): "a very strong-minded woman... quick habits of observation, thorough and keen analysis of men and things... most devoted wife." WIDOWED: Her husband Major Timothy Dwight died at Natchez MS in 1777. "The fact of her husband's death at Natchez did not become known to her and her children at home, until a whole year after its occurrence." — Dwight family source book. She felt "the scorching heat of the long continued grudge of that generation against her great and godly father" — she was the only Edwards child who remained in Northampton after her family withdrew. Her son Timothy Dwight IV became 8th President of Yale (1795-1817). MADAM DWIGHT: The source describes her as "of uncommon beauty and intelligence" — very small in stature (her husband could carry her on his open palm). "Very opinionated and self-willed... of an impulsive nature, and not always in complete self-control of her temper." She "believed in the Divine Right of the Edwards dynasty." When the Rev. John Hooker — "a distant cousin" of Thomas Hooker — succeeded Jonathan Edwards as pastor at Northampton, she refused to sit in the auditorium. She had her own chair placed in the vestibule, below the belfry, opposite the pulpit. On communion Sabbaths she rode 12 miles on a pillion behind her son Cecil to take communion at another church. She used snuff and owned slaves. Her grain fields were burned and livestock stolen by Patriot rabble angered by her husband's Tory sympathies. Her young children were afraid to appear on the streets alone. (The Record LXXI; Dwight family source book)

narrative_blocks.header: Her nursery was a schoolroom
narrative_blocks.body: Widowed at forty-two with thirteen children, eleven still under age, Mary ran her nursery as a school at set hours every day and grounded each child in piety. She lived on a widow for thirty-one years.

narrative_blocks.header: Snuff and theology with her son Timothy
narrative_blocks.body: Mary and her eldest son Timothy, later president of Yale, argued theology by the hour, both taking snuff. Neither would interrupt the other, so whoever stopped for a pinch lost the floor. She always addressed him as Sir.

narrative_blocks.header: She would not sit under her father's successor
narrative_blocks.body: After Jonathan Edwards was dismissed at Northampton, Mary would not sit under his successor, John Hooker. She sat in the vestibule below the belfry, and on communion Sundays rode twelve miles on a pillion behind her son Cecil to Norwich.

narrative_blocks.header: A year before she knew, then the mobs
narrative_blocks.body: Mary learned only a year later that her husband had died at Natchez in 1777. Neighbours who hated his loyalty to the Crown burned her grain and drove off her oxen, and her son Cecil was afraid to go out alone until he was ten.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at sixteen, carried on his palm
narrative_blocks.body: Mary married Timothy Dwight in November 1750, at sixteen, two months before her father left for Stockbridge. She was so small he carried her round the room on his palm. When her sister Esther died in 1758, she took in Aaron and Sally Burr.

narrative_blocks.header: Two of her children married Woolseys
narrative_blocks.body: Mary's son Timothy married Mary Woolsey in 1777, and her daughter Elizabeth married Mary Woolsey's half-brother William Walton Woolsey in 1792, which made the two sisters-in-law twice over.

narrative_blocks.header: She carried off the Tappan baby
narrative_blocks.body: Hearing John Tappan cry so long across the street, Mary ran over, carried the baby down to his mother and asked, "Mrs. Tappan, what in the world is the matter with this child?" His mother answered, "Nothing, Madam, I am only weaning him."

people.research_notes: b. Aug 31, 1736 Northampton MA — "the last day of August, between 2 and 3 o'clock in the morning." (Edwards family Bible) d. Sep 17, 1786 Stockbridge MA age 50. Daughter of Rev. Jonathan Edwards (X00128) and Sarah Pierpont Edwards (HD0418). Granddaughter of James Pierpont and Mary Hooker Pierpont (H00034). EH entry #380. m. Jahleel Woodbridge Jun 7, 1764 Stockbridge MA. He graduated Princeton 1761; judge of Probate Court; state senator; Captain of Minute Men; Member of Provisional Congress. On July 5, 1775 the Third Provisional Congress entrusted Jahleel Woodbridge and Timothy Edwards jointly to manage wages of Stockbridge Indians enlisted in the Continental Army — preventing access to strong drink at their own petition. Lucy predeceased her husband by 10 years. Tombstone reads: "The pure in heart." Buried Stockbridge Cemetery, Stockbridge MA. (EH 1909; FindAGrave; WikiTree) GRAVESTONE (Stockbridge Burying Ground): "This Stone is erected to the Memory of Mrs. Lucy Woodbridge consort of Hon. Jahleel Woodbridge Esq. She died September 17, 1786 in the 51st year of her age." (The Record LXXI)

narrative_blocks.header: Orphaned at twenty-one, with siblings to keep
narrative_blocks.body: Lucy lost her father at Princeton in March 1758 and her mother at Philadelphia that October. With her brother Timothy and her sister Susannah she went to work to keep the younger Edwards children, with almost nothing left to them.

narrative_blocks.header: Back to Stockbridge as Jahleel Woodbridge's wife
narrative_blocks.body: Lucy spent her teens at Stockbridge, where her father preached to the Mohicans, and in June 1764, at twenty-seven, she married Jahleel Woodbridge there. He had grown up in the mission town and learned the Mahican language at its school.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine children at Stockbridge in nineteen years
narrative_blocks.body: Lucy bore nine children between 1765 and 1784 and named a daughter Sarah Edwards, for her mother. Her son Jonathan became a militia general, and her son Timothy, blind from seventeen, became a minister.

narrative_blocks.header: Her birth hour went into the family Bible
narrative_blocks.body: Lucy was born at Northampton in the years of the Great Awakening, on the last day of August 1736, between two and three in the morning, the hour her father entered in the family Bible.

narrative_blocks.header: Her stone in the Stockbridge burying ground
narrative_blocks.body: Lucy died at Stockbridge in September 1786, at fifty, the winter before Shays's insurgents broke into her husband's house at midnight and carried him off. Her gravestone reads “The pure in heart.”

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-three years the first man of Stockbridge
narrative_blocks.body: From about 1770 Timothy Edwards was the leading citizen of Stockbridge for forty-three years and probate judge of Berkshire County. For four decades the county's wills, estates, and orphans passed through his court.

narrative_blocks.header: Married into the Ogden family of New Jersey
narrative_blocks.body: His wife Rhoda Ogden was sister of Aaron Ogden (Governor of New Jersey 1812-1813) and Matthias Ogden, a lieutenant colonel who marched to Quebec with Benedict Arnold in 1775. Through her, the Edwards-Hooker line connected to early New Jersey political and military leadership.

narrative_blocks.header: The famous divine's son who chose commerce
narrative_blocks.body: Eldest son of Jonathan Edwards, Timothy was raised in the most celebrated theological household in New England, and left it. He read law, set up instead as a merchant at Elizabethtown, and never entered his father's pulpit.

narrative_blocks.header: His father died into a new presidency
narrative_blocks.body: Timothy was nineteen when his father, Jonathan Edwards, newly installed as president of Princeton, died of a smallpox inoculation in 1758, months after Timothy's own graduation from that college. Within a year he set out for New Jersey to make his own way.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife's brother marched on Quebec with Arnold
narrative_blocks.body: Timothy married into a family of Revolutionary soldiers. His wife Rhoda's brother, Col. Matthias Ogden, marched with Benedict Arnold through the Maine woods against Quebec in 1775 and was wounded in the assault. The Edwards household sat one marriage away from Arnold's own campaigns.

narrative_blocks.header: The boundary survey that renamed his son
narrative_blocks.body: Timothy served as a commissioner on a boundary-line survey into Indian country, the expedition where his son Edward was adopted by the Indians and given a name meaning the handsome man. The judge's work took the family to the literal edge of the map.

career.notes: In business as a merchant before removing to Stockbridge about 1770

narrative_blocks.header: Eighteen, and both parents gone
narrative_blocks.body: Susannah was eighteen when her father and mother both died in 1758. With her sister Lucy and her brother Timothy she went to work to keep the six younger children.

narrative_blocks.header: Stepmother to two little girls
narrative_blocks.body: In September 1761 Susannah married Eleazer Porter of Hadley, a widower whose first wife had died three years before, leaving two small daughters. Susannah raised them with the six children she had with him.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son married her sister Mary's daughter
narrative_blocks.body: In 1793 her son Jonathan Edwards Porter married his cousin Fidelia Dwight, daughter of Susannah's sister Mary.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brother married her husband's sister
narrative_blocks.body: In 1770 Susannah's brother Jonathan married her husband's sister, Mary Porter.

narrative_blocks.header: Born into the measles year of 1740
narrative_blocks.body: Susannah was born at Northampton on 20 June 1740. Her father had stayed away from a fast at Hadley that February for fear of the measles there, and at the end of that year the whole family had them; every one came through.

bio.bio_blurb: New Bern planter's wife, twice widowed

narrative_blocks.header: The house that raised her raised Burr
narrative_blocks.body: Orphaned at fifteen when Jonathan and Sarah Edwards died within months of each other, she went into her eldest brother Timothy's household at Elizabethtown. So did her sister Esther's children, and one of them was four-year-old Aaron Burr, who more than once ran away to sea to escape the strictness of the place.

narrative_blocks.header: The planter had come north for his health
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas Pollock III kept a house at Elizabethtown to get away from what he took to be the unhealthy air of his Carolina plantations, and that is how she met him. They married there in 1764 and she went south to New Bern.

narrative_blocks.header: Five Pollocks, one line of descendants
narrative_blocks.body: Of the five children she had by Thomas Pollock only Frances left any, and every one of her brothers and sisters died before her. The whole estate came to that one daughter, including from her brother George more than fifteen hundred enslaved people.

narrative_blocks.header: Her sixth child carried the line instead
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas Pollock died in 1777, in New Jersey rather than on his own land. She married Robert Hunt, another Elizabethtown man, and their one daughter Sarah married John Fanning Burgwyn and left eight children.

narrative_blocks.header: Aunt Hunt, pouring tea in November 1800
narrative_blocks.body: Her niece Susan Johnson came down to New Bern in 1800 and wrote in her diary of taking tea with my Aunt Hunt. She kept her first husband's town house there, and stayed sometimes at Runaroi on the Roanoke.

notable.notable_blurb: Abolitionist reformer and Union College president

people.research_notes:
b. May 26, 1745 Northampton MA; d. Aug 1, 1801 Schenectady NY age 56. Son of Rev. Jonathan Edwards (X00128) and Sarah Pierpont Edwards (HD0418). EH entry #384. EDUCATION: Princeton 1765. MINISTRY: Pastor, 2nd Congregational Church, New Haven CT 1769-1795. "A man of most profound talents and an eminent controversial writer. Said to have been almost as enigmatical as his father." Dismissed from New Haven church 1795 (doctrinal controversy). Settled at Colebrook CT until May 1799. UNION COLLEGE: Chosen President of Union College (Schenectady NY) May 1799; died in office Aug 1, 1801 — served only 2 years. m.(1) Mary Porter Oct 4, 1770 — daughter of Hon. Eleazer Porter Sr. and Sarah Pitkin of Hadley MA. DROWNED at New Haven CT Jun 10, 1782. CROSS-FAMILY NOTE: Mary Porter was the sister of Judge Eleazer Porter Jr., who married Susannah Edwards (H00382), Jonathan Edwards Jr.'s own sister. The two sets of siblings married each other — classic Connecticut River Valley kinship. m.(2) Mrs. Mary Sabins Dec 18, 1783 — daughter of Hezekiah and Mercy Sabins. 4 children from first marriage. (EH 1909; Princeton archives; Union College records)
ABOLITIONIST: Unlike his father (who owned at least 4 slaves), Edwards Jr. actively opposed slavery. In 1773 he published antislavery articles in the Connecticut Journal under the pseudonym "Antidoulios" (Greek: against slavery) — among the first direct antislavery writing from a New England minister. His 1791 sermon "The Injustice and Impolicy of the Slave Trade" condemned slavery from his New Haven pulpit. Princeton calls him "one of the few abolitionists Princeton ever produced." LINGUISTICS: Grew up in Stockbridge MA speaking Mohican better than English — "It became more familiar to me than my mother tongue." In 1788 published "Observations on the Language of the Muhhekaneew Indians." George Washington thanked him for a copy; James Madison sent one to Jefferson. Archive.org: https://archive.org/details/observationsonla01edwa/page/n11/mode/2up (Wikipedia; Princeton & Slavery Project) [Cause revert audit]: Earlier extraction set death.cause="drowned" but reverted: drowned — was about wife Mary Porter, not Jonathan Edwards Jr.

narrative_blocks.header: Among Princeton's only true abolitionists
narrative_blocks.body: In 1773 he published antislavery articles in the Connecticut Journal under the pseudonym 'Antidoulios' — Greek for 'against slavery.' His 1791 sermon 'The Injustice and Impolicy of the Slave Trade' delivered antislavery from his New Haven pulpit.

narrative_blocks.header: Mohican linguist, thanked by Washington
narrative_blocks.body: He grew up in Stockbridge speaking Mohican before English, writing that 'it became more familiar to me than my mother tongue.' His 1788 'Observations on the Language of the Muhhekaneew Indians' was acknowledged by George Washington and circulated through Madison to Jefferson.

narrative_blocks.header: His first wife drowned at New Haven 1782
narrative_blocks.body: His first wife Mary Porter died June 10, 1782 in New Haven by drowning, leaving four children. He remarried in December 1783 to Mary Sabins, with whom he had no further children.

narrative_blocks.header: Died as president of Union College, 1801
narrative_blocks.body: In May 1799 he was chosen President of Union College in Schenectady, New York. He served less than two years, dying in office August 1, 1801, age 56 — leaving the abolitionist Edwards line for his sons to carry.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote against slavery as “Antidoulios”
narrative_blocks.body: Ordained only four years, the twenty-eight-year-old pastor took a pen name for his 1773 newspaper attack on slavery: Antidoulios, Greek for “against slavery.” He applied the golden rule directly — why are slaveholders exempt from “whatsoever ye would that men should do to you”?

narrative_blocks.header: He blessed Benedict Arnold's marching company
narrative_blocks.body: On 22 April 1775, days after Lexington, he gave his blessing to Benedict Arnold and the Second Company of the Governor's Foot Guard as they marched from New Haven toward Boston. The minister who would soon write against slavery was sending his townsmen to war.

narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth, the youngest daughter, was eleven in 1758 when her father died at Princeton in March and her mother at Philadelphia in October. She died in 1762, at about fifteen.

notable.notable_blurb: Federal judge and Grand Master of Connecticut Masons

narrative_blocks.header: He led Connecticut's Jeffersonians
narrative_blocks.body: In 1800, in a state run by Federalists, Pierpont organized Connecticut's Jeffersonian Republicans and chaired their General Committee. In 1806 Jefferson put him on the federal bench as district judge for Connecticut, and he sat there until his death twenty years later.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years at the New Haven bar
narrative_blocks.body: Pierpont settled at New Haven about 1771 and practised law there for nearly forty years, against the best lawyers of Connecticut and the neighbouring states. His death notice remembered the brilliancy of his wit and the splendor of his eloquence, and his kindness to the younger men at the bar.

narrative_blocks.header: First Grand Master of Connecticut's Masons
narrative_blocks.body: On 14 January 1784, in bad weather and on poor roads, a special meeting at New Haven chose Pierpont Grand Master of Connecticut's Masons. When the lodges formed their own Grand Lodge on 8 July 1789, they elected him again, and its medal for distinguished members still bears his name.

narrative_blocks.header: Master Stark slept in the woods
narrative_blocks.body: In 1799 Pierpont sent his son John Stark to open Mesopotamia, his township in Ohio's Western Reserve. When the first letters reached New Haven, Pierpont wrote back that even the servants rejoiced, and that he could hear Tom calling to Eli that Master Stark had slept in the woods all night.

narrative_blocks.header: At sixty-eight he drafted a constitution
narrative_blocks.body: Pierpont was Speaker of the Connecticut House, sat in the Congress of the Confederation in 1787 and 1788, and argued for the federal Constitution at the state's ratifying convention. Thirty years later, at sixty-eight, he chaired the committee that drafted Connecticut's constitution of 1818.

narrative_blocks.header: He settled Benedict Arnold's estate
narrative_blocks.body: In 1801 Pierpont was named administrator of the estate of Benedict Arnold, once a New Haven merchant and Continental general, who had died in London that June, still reviled at home as a traitor.

narrative_blocks.header: Uncle to Burr, father-in-law to Eli Whitney
narrative_blocks.body: Pierpont's nephew Aaron Burr, the son of his sister Esther, was only six years younger than he was. His daughter Henrietta married the inventor Eli Whitney in 1817, and his son Henry W. Edwards became governor of Connecticut.

people.research_notes:
b. Apr 8, 1750 Northampton MA; d. Apr 5, 1826 Bridgeport CT age 75. Buried Grove Street Cemetery, New Haven CT. YOUNGEST CHILD of Jonathan Edwards and Sarah Pierpont Edwards (HD0418). Named "Pierpont" to honor maternal grandfather Rev. James Pierpont (co-founder of Yale). Princeton B.A. 1768. Entered private practice New Haven 1771. Connecticut House of Representatives 1777, 1784-1785, 1787-1790 (Speaker last two terms). CONTINENTAL CONGRESS DELEGATE from Connecticut 1787-1788. Member of CT convention to ratify US Constitution 1788. US DISTRICT JUDGE for the District of Connecticut: appointed by President Thomas Jefferson 1806; served until his death 1826. Member of CT State Convention that framed Connecticut's Constitution (1818). His nephew Aaron Burr Jr. (H00913) was only 6 years younger than him. m. Frances Ogden (X00654) c.1776. SON: Henry Waggaman Edwards (HD2045) — 27th and 29th Governor of Connecticut, US Senator. DAUGHTER: Henrietta Frances Edwards (HD2046) — married inventor Eli Whitney 1817. His granddaughter Henrietta Whitney Edwards (X00160) married Prof. Worthington Hooker (H01407), reuniting the Hooker and Pierpont-Edwards lines in one household.
CC NOTE [HD2925]: Pierpont Edwards, youngest son of Jonathan Edwards and himself a Hooker descendant, was one of the seven investors who purchased Richfield Township from the Connecticut Land Company in 1807. John Newton later settled that same township and became one of its major landowners in the 1820s. Neither man likely knew they both descended from Thomas Hooker — Edwards through Jonathan Edwards, Newton through the Newton-Hooker marriage of the 1640s. Two separate Hooker lines converging on the same Ohio township deed. (Richfield Township History)
CC NOTE [H00443]: Pierpont Edwards invested £60,000 in the Connecticut Land Company (1795) — 5% of the company — and sent his son John Stark Edwards as his first agent in the Western Reserve. Rev. Giles Hooker Cowles moved to Austinburg, Ashtabula County OH and co-founded Western Reserve College (1826) as 'the Yale of the West.' Both men were Hooker descendants acting as architects of the Connecticut presence in the Western Reserve — Edwards through land capital, Cowles through institutional education. Neither is documented as having known the other's Hooker descent.
CC NOTE [T00387]: In 1790 Pierpont Edwards defeated Jeremiah Wadsworth for the Connecticut Congressional seat — then declined to take it, forcing a special election which Wadsworth won. Both were from Hartford's inner circle; Edwards was a Hooker descendant through Jonathan Edwards and the Pierpont line; Wadsworth a Talcott descendant married into the Hooker line. Two men from the same ancestral Hartford network trading the same Congressional seat. (Wikipedia — Jeremiah Wadsworth)

narrative_blocks.header: Her Anglican remarriage cost her her Puritan family
narrative_blocks.body: Lydia was a daughter of the Rev. Jacob Hemenway, the Puritan minister of East Haven. Widowed young with two little boys, she married Theophilus Morgan — a member of the Church of England — and for that her father disinherited her and cut her off from her Puritan kindred.

narrative_blocks.header: The rupture left her Pierpont sons few kin
narrative_blocks.body: Her disinheritance cost her sons John and Jacob their mother's Puritan relatives. John was raised instead among his Pierpont uncles, and by his 1767 wedding — his father and brother both dead — he had, it was said, 'but few near relatives' left to attend.

narrative_blocks.body: Theophilus captained the first Killingworth company and made his name as a merchant and landholder of distinction. He settled first at Guilford, then at Killingworth, left a large estate, and is the forebear of most of the Killingworth and Clinton Morgans.

narrative_blocks.body: Jacob died in April 1761 on garrison duty at Crown Point, the Lake Champlain fort the British had just wrested from the French — most likely of camp disease, in the last stretch of the French and Indian War. people.prominent_name_reason: John Pierpont (1740-1805) — great-grandfather of J.P. Morgan (1837-1913). Chain: John Pierpont (H00388) → James Pierpont → John Pierpont the poet (1785-1866, abolitionist) → Juliet Pierpont × Junius Spencer Morgan → John Pierpont Morgan. J.P. Morgan's middle name "Pierpont" commemorates this descent from the Pierpont family of New Haven — founded by Rev. James Pierpont, who married Mary Hooker (H00034). Thomas Hooker's great-great-great-granddaughter's grandson became the most powerful financier in American history.
people.research_notes: "He was a large landholder and lived in the old family-mansion at New Haven." (Dwight) Had 10 children, only four living to adult age, only three married. Morgan's full name John PIERPONT Morgan takes the name from this line. b. May 21, 1740 New Haven CT; d. Oct 8, 1805 New Haven CT age 65. NOTE ON NAME: John was born "Pierpont" but the family later restored the French "Pierrepont" spelling — Hezekiah Beers requested this ca.1802 but didn't adopt it himself for business reasons. m. narrative_blocks.header: Generous, land-rich, and ruined by the war
narrative_blocks.body: The Revolution sank his land values for good. Generous but "neither a money-making nor a money-keeping man," as his family put it, he spent his last decades short of cash he could not pull from the land.

narrative_blocks.header: The youngest branch ended up with the heirlooms
narrative_blocks.body: By rights the founding portraits of Rev. James Pierpont and his wife Mary Hooker should have passed down the eldest line. They came to John — a youngest son of a youngest son — willed to him by a guardian making good an inheritance he had let slip.

narrative_blocks.header: He buried the valuables and fled Tryon's raid
narrative_blocks.body: When the British sacked New Haven in July 1779, John buried what he could not carry and moved his family to Hamden. The soldiers looted the house and ran a bayonet through Mary Hooker's portrait — a wound left unrepaired until the 1860s.

narrative_blocks.header: His son brought back the French 'Pierrepont'
narrative_blocks.body: John was born a plain "Pierpont." Around 1802 his son Hezekiah Beers asked the family to restore the older French "Pierrepont" — though he kept the short form himself, for business, and his descendants have been split ever since.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother married an Anglican and was disowned
narrative_blocks.body: His father died before John was two; when his widowed mother married an Anglican, her strict Puritan father disowned her outright. The boy was raised instead by his uncle, in the old family mansion on the New Haven green.

people.research_notes: FindAGrave (Sam, 8 Sep 2026): Pvt Reuben Norton, VETERAN. b. 6 Apr 1711 Guilford; d. 28 Nov 1796 at Madison, New Haven County; buried West Cemetery, Madison (CEM038). The record already said Guilford for the death and both are right - Madison was set off from Guilford as East Guilford and not incorporated under its own name until 1826. His burial had plot_notes but NO cemetery_id, so the block rendered nothing; CEM038 now set. HAND'S COMPANY - UNRESOLVED AND NOT ASSERTED: the stone credits 'Hand's Co.' Two candidates were considered. Gen. Edward Hand's Pennsylvania rifle battalion (later the 1st Continental) does not fit - wrong colony, and Reuben was a Guilford man. Capt. Daniel Hand's Company of the 7th Regiment of Connecticut Militia, the old Guilford train band, fits the geography exactly and is the likely unit, but no source Sam has supplied names Reuben in it. Note also that he turned sixty-four in 1775, so the service may belong to a son of the same name. Needs a muster roll before anything more is written. HAND'S COMPANY IDENTIFIED 8 Sep 2026 (Sam). Two sources settle which Hand. The DAR ancestor record for HAND, DANIEL (#A050936) gives a Connecticut captain born 1732 and died 1816 at East Guilford, serving under COL TALCOTT, buried at Hammonasset Cemetery, Madison. And the DAR lineage entry for Mrs. Jennie E. Coe Parmelee - who is HD3498 in this tree - records that Thomas Coe (1759-1827) of East Guilford 'was a private in Capt. Daniel Hand's company 1776'. So Capt. Daniel Hand's company was a East Guilford unit of Col. Talcott's regiment, and that is what 'Hand's Co.' on Reuben's stone means. Gen. Edward Hand's Pennsylvania rifle battalion is ruled out. Col. Matthew Talcott (T00070) is in this tree and is the likely Talcott of that regiment - NOT asserted, since the DAR record gives only the surname. ONE PROBLEM REMAINS: Reuben was sixty-four in 1775. His son Reuben Norton Jr. (H00403, b.1748) was twenty-seven and is the likelier man for active service under Hand. The service is left on the father, where the stone puts it, with the son named here as the alternative.

people.research_notes: Son of Reuben Norton (I00148) and Hannah Hooker Norton (H00126). Born 1744 in Guilford CT. Carries the Hooker family name as his given name — a tribute to his maternal Hooker line. Designated 'No. 2' in EH 1909 entry 401 because his elder brother (H00399, b. 1741) had received the same name and presumably died young; the parents reused the name in 1744. Married Sibyl Bradley (X02569), daughter of Joseph and Sibyl (Meigs) Bradley of Vergennes, Vermont. They lived at East Guilford. Eleven documented children (H01046-H01056), of whom several died young: Daniel Hooker (1764, age 9 months); Russell (1768-1774, age 6); Hannah (1779-1787, age 8); Russell (1784-1795, age 11); Zenas (1786-1795, age 9). Source: EH 1909 entry 401. [Pilot119 enrichment]: Birth full date January 15, 1744 per FamilySearch L7P9-1RY. Death July 17, 1827 in Madison CT (= former East Guilford) at age 83 per FamilySearch and WikiTree Norton-2925. Marriage to Sibyl Bradley dated 1762 in Guilford per FamilySearch (note: WikiTree records 1764). Sibyl predeceased him by 21 years, dying May 4, 1806 in Sunderland VT — meaning the family had migrated to VT by 1806, though Hooker himself returned to CT to die in Madison. Source: FamilySearch L7P9-1RY; WikiTree Norton-2925.

narrative_blocks.header: Given his deceased elder brother's name
narrative_blocks.body: Hooker Norton was the SECOND son of Reuben and Hannah Hooker Norton to be given the name Hooker. The first (, b. 1741) presumably died young. Three years later when this son was born in 1744 the parents reused the Hooker name — a common eighteenth-century replacement-naming pattern that EH itself notes by labeling him 'No. 2.'

narrative_blocks.header: Eleven children five died young
narrative_blocks.body: Hooker and Sibyl Bradley Norton had eleven documented children. Five died in infancy or childhood: Daniel Hooker at nine months in 1764; Russell at age six in 1774; Hannah at age eight in 1787; a second Russell at age eleven in 1795; and Zenas at age nine that same year. The 1795 deaths of Russell and Zenas in the same year hint at an epidemic.

narrative_blocks.header: Lived eighty-three years through three wars
narrative_blocks.body: Hooker Norton was born in colonial Connecticut on January 15, 1744 — age eleven at the start of the French and Indian War, age thirty-two when Independence was declared. He outlived the Revolutionary War, the War of 1812, and his wife Sibyl by twenty-one years. He died July 17, 1827 in Madison CT at eighty-three.

narrative_blocks.body: Eber Norton married Mabel Evarts in 1788. Mabel's brother Ezra had earlier married Eber's niece Lorain in 1783, and another brother Curtis would later marry Eber's niece Lois in 1792. people.research_notes: Son of Reuben Norton Sr. (I00148) and Hannah Hooker Norton (H00126). Born July 5, 1756 in Guilford CT — twelve days before the start of his uncle Daniel Hooker's last summer; eight years before the Stamp Act crisis. Married Mabel Evarts (X02619) — daughter of Jonathan and Lucretia Parmalee Evarts of Guilford — on November 2, 1788. They lived at Guilford. Seven documented children (H01080-H01086), of whom the eldest Lucretia died in infancy; a second daughter named Lucretia (H01083, 1799-1888) survived the replacement-naming pattern. Eber lived 87 years; died at Guilford August 13, 1843. Mabel followed him May 1, 1848. Note: Mabel Evarts was sister to two earlier Evarts marriages in this Norton tree — Ezra Evarts (X02570, husband of Eber's niece Lorain) and Curtis Evarts (X02571, husband of Eber's niece Lois). Three of Jonathan Evarts's children married into the Norton family across two generations. Source: EH 1909 entry 407.

Note: NOT to be confused with his first cousin Arah Norton (H00398, son of Hannah's brother Reuben Sr.'s namesake branch) — EH spells this one 'Anah' and the cousin 'Arah,' but the names are easily confused. bio.bio_blurb: Berlin woman who removed to Pompey

narrative_blocks.header: Berlin to the New York frontier
narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Berlin in 1736 to Andrew Hooker and Mary Lee, married Thomas Gridley in 1768, and after 1775 went west with him to Pompey in Onondaga County. She stayed there the rest of her life and outlived him by fifteen years.

narrative_blocks.header: Buried next day, and lost for eighty years
narrative_blocks.body: She died at Pompey in January 1819 and was buried the day after in a small graveyard that was later abandoned. Her great-grandson Frank Gridley Fowler came out from Bridgeport in 1898, found the grave, and had her moved.

people.research_notes: Daughter of Andrew Hooker (H00223) and Mary Lee Seymour (I00149). Born May 18, 1736 in Berlin (then part of Kensington/Farmington area), Hartford County CT. Married Thomas Gridley of Kensington on June 23, 1768 — she was his second wife. They migrated from Connecticut to Pompey, Onondaga County NY after 1775 (likely in the post-Revolutionary settlement wave that opened central New York to Connecticut migrants). Two documented sons: Giles Gridley (H01092, 1769-1866) and Thomas Hooker Gridley (H01093, 1775-1857). Thomas Sr died at Pompey NY December 22, 1804. Mary outlived him by 14 years; died at Pompey NY January 20, 1819. Buried January 21, 1819 — but her grave was lost. In 1898 her great-great-grandson Frank Gridley Fowler of Bridgeport CT searched for her grave in an old, abandoned Pompey graveyard, located it, and had her remains exhumed and reinterred. Frank Gridley Fowler is a Hooker descendant himself via this line; he is not built as a separate entry per Jalapeño Rule but his role in the exhumation story is exhibit-worthy. Source: EH 1909 entry 409; Hartford Genealogy Wiki.

people.research_notes: Born April 16, 1734 in Kensington (now Berlin) Hartford County CT per Farmington vital records and Berlin-Peck F&I War PDF — note conflict with EH 1909 entry which gives 'b. 1738.' Per Sam's source hierarchy (vital records > EH > websites), VR date adopted; EH date preserved here for audit. Berlin-Peck PDF also has internal inconsistency: it states birth April 16, 1734 (which would make him 23 at death) but elsewhere claims 'Died at age 19' (which would imply b. 1738). Father Andrew Hooker (H00223) was a brother of Samuel Hooker Jr (H00228), making Samuel Jr Martin's uncle — Samuel Jr enlisted in F&I War service two months after Martin's death (August 1757 alarm). Burial: no gravestone per Farmington VR — likely buried where he fell in service. EH preserved a family tradition (see notable_story 'martin_hooker_sentry_revenge_1757') that his death was avenged days later by a friend who shot a Native American assassin hidden in a hog skin. Source: Edward Hooker 1909 (Entry 410); Berlin-Peck Memorial Library Local History Room — Berlin in the French and Indian War 1753-1763.

narrative_blocks.header: Killed at the sentry post in June 1757
narrative_blocks.body: Martin enlisted on 8 March 1757 in Capt. Eliphalet Whittlesey's company of Col. Phineas Lyman's regiment. On 10 June he volunteered for a sentry post where several soldiers had already been picked off by a hidden Native marksman, and was killed there.

narrative_blocks.header: A friend shot the hog by the post
narrative_blocks.body: Family tradition holds that days later a close friend of Martin's took the same post and shot a hog he saw rooting nearby. Inside the hogskin was the man who had been killing the sentries, and no one else was shot at that post.

narrative_blocks.body: Giles married Abigail Smith of Newington in February 1777 at age 31. people.research_notes: Son of Andrew Hooker (H00223) and Mary Lee Hooker (I00149) of Berlin CT. Born September 19, 1759 in Berlin Hartford County CT — two years and three months after his older brother Martin (H00410) was killed in the French and Indian War on June 10, 1757 at age 19. Sam's family was therefore carrying forward the lost brother's name; entry already tagged 'replacement_naming'. Source variants: WikiTree gives birth ~September 25, 1759 (uncertain) in Farmington CT and death 1843 in Chesterfield Essex County NY; EH 1909 dates adopted here per Sam's source hierarchy (vital records > EH > websites). Married Hannah Judd (X02711) March 17, 1785; the couple removed to Tinmouth Vermont and afterward to Peru Clinton County NY. Eight documented children: Almira, Laura, Amanda, Norman, Harley, Phineas, Lucy, and Mary Lee (H01095-H01102, gen 6 — to be built in stage 5h). Hannah died July 26, 1843 in Peru NY; Martin died there two months later on September 24, 1843 at age 84. Per WikiTree he served as Private in the Revolutionary War — unit not documented.

naming_inspiration.description: Named for his older brother Martin Hooker who was killed at age 19 in the French and Indian War on June 10, 1757 — two years and three months before this Martin was born. Replacement-naming honor.

narrative_blocks.header: Named for a brother killed in 1757
narrative_blocks.body: Andrew and Mary Hooker named their son Martin in September 1759, two years after their son Martin was killed on sentry duty in the French and Indian War. This Martin served as a private in the Revolution, married Hannah Judd of New Britain in 1785, and moved to Tinmouth, Vermont, and then to Peru, New York. He died at Peru in September 1843, at eighty-four, two months after Hannah.

narrative_blocks.body: Baptized at Hartford in 1707, he kept a store at Berlin and died there in 1803, about ninety-six. He outlived his wife Elizabeth by nineteen years, and the son the Revolution killed by twenty-seven.

narrative_blocks.body: His father Ebenezer, a Hartford merchant, died in 1726 leaving an estate that set down four enslaved people by price — a man, a woman, a boy and a child. He had also helped divide Kensington into five school districts.

narrative_blocks.header: The army took him at thirty-four
narrative_blocks.body: He was killed serving in the Revolutionary army on 15 February 1776, leaving Mary Butrick at Berlin with two small children. His son Sylvanus grew up to enlist in that same army and died in it.

narrative_blocks.header: The bricks were burned on their own farm
narrative_blocks.body: The family's red brick house at Berlin went up about 1709, its bricks burned on the farm itself, where Gilbird's River now washes into the clay pit. Unusually hard and black, they shine as if enamelled; how they were made is lost.

people.research_notes: Son of Moses Gilbert (I00150) and Elizabeth Hooker Gilbert (H00224) of Berlin CT — given the maternal surname 'Hooker' as his first name. Born June 5, 1751 in Berlin/Kensington Hartford County CT (per Find-a-Grave gravestone — earlier EH 1909 entry of 1754 superseded by primary source). Lived on the ancient Gilbert farm at 551 Christian Lane in Kensington (built 1709 by Ebenezer Gilbert; sold to City of New Britain 1906). REVOLUTIONARY WAR: three enlistments — June 1776 (Capt. Gad Stanley's Co, Battle of Harlem Heights, 4 months); summer 1777 (Capt. Lankton's Co under Col. Noadiah Hooker's Regt, 3 months); July 1779 (Capt. Matthew Cole's Co, Battle of New Haven during Tryon's Raid, 10 days). Federal pension list 1838. DAR Ancestor #A045110. M1: Candace Sage (X02713) November 1, 1776 — date conflict with EH 1909 ('1796') resolved in favor of the earlier date which better fits the children timeline. Six children with Candace, all M1 — Bathsheba Jane (1785-1807), Samuel Hooker (1787-1868), David Sage (1787-1864), Chloe Sage (1789-1867), Candace (1791-1835), Moses (1793-1882). M2: Sarah Hooker (H00432, his maternal first cousin) June 30, 1807; no documented children with Sarah. Sarah died December 4, 1840 at age 77; Hooker Gilbert followed two days later on December 6, 1840 at age 89. Both buried Christian Lane Cemetery (CEM237), Kensington. Source: Edward Hooker 1909; FG memorial; Berlin-Peck Memorial Library Rev War PDF.

naming_inspiration.description: Given the surname 'Hooker' as his first name in honor of his mother Elizabeth Hooker Gilbert's family. First-name use of the maternal surname is unusual and emphatic — he later married into the Hooker line as well, his second wife Sarah Hooker (H00432) being his maternal first cousin.

military_service.unit: Multiple — Capt. Gad Stanley's Co (1776), Capt. Lankton's Co under Col. Noadiah Hooker's Regt (1777), Capt. Matthew Cole's Co (1779)
military_service.notes: Three documented enlistments: (1) June 1776 — four months in Capt. Gad Stanley's Company at the Battle of Harlem Heights; (2) summer 1777 — three months in Capt. Lankton's Company under Col. Noadiah Hooker's Regiment; (3) July 1779 — ten days in Capt. Matthew Cole's Company at the Battle of New Haven (Tryon's Raid). Placed on the federal pension list in 1838. DAR Ancestor #A045110. Source: Berlin-Peck Memorial Library.

narrative_blocks.header: Three enlistments in the Revolution
narrative_blocks.body: Hooker Gilbert served three times in the Revolution: in Capt. Gad Stanley's company at Harlem Heights in 1776, in Capt. Lankton's company of Col. Noadiah Hooker's regiment in 1777, and in Capt. Matthew Cole's company against Tryon's raid on New Haven in 1779. He drew a federal pension from 1838.

narrative_blocks.header: He married his cousin Sarah Hooker in 1807
narrative_blocks.body: Hooker Gilbert's first wife, Candace Sage, died in May 1805, and on 30 June 1807 he married Sarah Hooker, his first cousin and the daughter of his uncle Samuel Hooker.

narrative_blocks.header: He died two days after Sarah, in 1840
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah died at Kensington on 4 December 1840, at seventy-seven, and Hooker Gilbert two days later, on 6 December, at eighty-six. They had been married thirty-three years.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother's maiden name as his first
narrative_blocks.body: Hooker Gilbert carried his mother's maiden name as his first name. She was Elizabeth Hooker, a daughter of Samuel Hooker of Kensington, and he passed the name on to his son Samuel Hooker Gilbert.

narrative_blocks.header: A dozen sloops and two schooners
narrative_blocks.body: Between 1789 and 1820 Buckingham, his brother William and their father owned shares in at least a dozen sloops and two schooners, trading to Savannah, Charleston, New York, Boston and up the Hudson to Troy and Albany, and bringing rum and sugar home from the West Indies.

narrative_blocks.header: He remembered where the first church stood
narrative_blocks.body: In 1847, at seventy-three, Buckingham showed Norwalk's historian where the town's first meeting-house had stood, a spot he could still picture as open common. He had been four when the British burned his father's house in 1779.

narrative_blocks.header: A skullcap for the balding colonel
narrative_blocks.body: Buckingham sat for a pastel about 1810 with his hair combed forward, and about 1842 for an oil attributed to Ezra Bisbee, in which he wears a skullcap to hide his balding head.

narrative_blocks.header: Three names, given twice
narrative_blocks.body: In 1820 Buckingham and Polly named a son William Buckingham Eliphalet, for her father, for himself and for his father. The boy died in 1822, and the son born that December was given all three names again.

narrative_blocks.header: He married his first cousin
narrative_blocks.body: St. Johns and Lockwoods had married each other in nearly every generation since Norwalk was founded. Buckingham's mother was a St. John, and in 1808 he married her brother William's daughter Polly, his first cousin. Both were grandchildren of Joseph St. John, the Blue Sheep.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years a deacon at Holliston
narrative_blocks.body: John farmed the family land at Holliston, taught the district school for several winters, and served forty years as a deacon of the First Congregational Church, as his father Jesse had before him.

narrative_blocks.header: Uncle by marriage to Brigham Young
narrative_blocks.body: John's first wife, Betsey Howe, was a sister of the mothers of Brigham Young and Willard Richards. When the two nephews arrived from Kirtland in 1837 with the Book of Mormon and its new gospel, he received them with considerable doubt.

narrative_blocks.header: Baptized at sixty-four
narrative_blocks.body: His children joined the new church first, and on 30 June 1838 John and Judith were baptized as well. In 1841, at sixty-seven, he left the Holliston farm for Nauvoo.

narrative_blocks.header: He answered his old minister in print
narrative_blocks.body: When his former pastor at Holliston published a supposed affidavit from Solomon Spaulding's widow, naming her husband's manuscript as the source of the Book of Mormon, John's son Jesse called on the widow and heard her deny it. John then wrote a letter quoting her denial.

narrative_blocks.header: A Boston cousin's visit in 1843
narrative_blocks.body: In 1843 Charlotte Haven, a young Unitarian from Boston visiting her brother in Nauvoo, called on John and Judith, who brought out their pedigree to show that the two families shared an ancestor. She found them "a kind-hearted, honest old couple," and they asked her to call them uncle and aunt.

narrative_blocks.header: To the Salt Lake Valley at seventy-four
narrative_blocks.body: John and Judith crossed the plains in Brigham Young's company and reached the Salt Lake Valley on 23 September 1848, when he was seventy-four. He died there on 16 March 1853, at seventy-nine, among the first buried in the Salt Lake City Cemetery.

bio.title: Doctor
bio.bio_blurb: Called a father of medicine in Connecticut

narrative_blocks.header: He described the pain to the patient
narrative_blocks.body: He would sit with a case a whole day before prescribing, take the pulse again and again at different hours, and refuse to be shown where it hurt — he preferred to describe the pain to the patient. The public called him a medical oracle.

narrative_blocks.header: He was truly a self-taught man
narrative_blocks.body: He had an older brother in medicine in the same town and the run of the elder Dr. Osborn’s library, but the journals put his reputation down to his own genius. Told clergymen read scripture best, he said he had read it in as many languages.

narrative_blocks.header: A square bottle of rum a day
narrative_blocks.body: He would not look at a patient in his last years until the full bottle was in his hands and refilled daily, and he took opium in quantities to match. He was rarely drunk; when he could not stand, his judgement was unimpaired.

narrative_blocks.header: Good sense under a bundle of rags
narrative_blocks.body: An officer took his library on attachment for debt, and his bookcase was still standing in the house he had owned when they wrote him up. A patient said he had never known so much good sense covered by a bundle of rags.

narrative_blocks.header: You never half knew, he told them
narrative_blocks.body: That was what he said to anyone who admitted forgetting something. He could repeat a sermon or pamphlet nearly whole after one reading, and he read Locke, Sydenham and Boerhaave, and studied architecture well enough to instruct architects.

narrative_blocks.header: The church struck his name from the roll
narrative_blocks.body: He had been a leading man of the town and a member in close communion at Farmington, but the drink took him and the church erased him from its list. His own opinions on religion wavered all his life.

narrative_blocks.header: Buried by the north wall, no stone
narrative_blocks.body: After Abigail died in 1789 he went to Wethersfield, where old patients and the town authorities kept him. He died at a friend’s house in April 1794, seventy-seven, of a cancer in the leg, and was buried with no monument.

career.notes: Widely regarded as a founder of Connecticut medicine; often did not bill his patients.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight months on the lines at Tarrytown
narrative_blocks.body: He served in Captain Allen’s company of the 15th Connecticut Militia, Colonel Noadiah Hooker’s regiment, and from July 1779 to March 1780 was detached with Lieutenant Colonel Meade’s battalion to Tarrytown on the Hudson.

narrative_blocks.header: Three wives, the last of them at seventy
narrative_blocks.body: Esther Hooker married him in 1751 and was dead at twenty-six. Rachel Bell of Southington followed in 1761 and lived thirty-six years. In 1798, at seventy, he married Hannah Porter Henry, widow of a sergeant killed by a wound from the war.

narrative_blocks.header: His will waited thirty-three years to be proved
narrative_blocks.body: He signed it in August 1779, before he went down to Tarrytown. The witnesses did not swear to his signature until April 1812 — five years after he was buried, and thirty-three after he wrote it. The will is at Hartford still.

people.research_notes: b. Dec 21, 1752 Kensington (in town of Berlin), Conn.; d. Jan 28, 1834 Berlin/Kensington, Conn.; buried Ledge Cemetery, Berlin (CEM022). Son of Asahel Cowles (b. Kensington Jul 18, 1728) and Esther Hooker (H00230). Member of the Kensington church Oct 1783. In the 1815 plan of seating the Kensington meeting house, occupied a seat in the second row. Grand juror 1802; fence viewer several years. m. 1776 Mary Lawrence (X01214), who d. Mar 18, 1841 age 90 (tombstone, Kensington). REVOLUTIONARY WAR SERVICE (per pension affidavit Sept 19, 1832, U.S. Pension Office; claim REJECTED): (1) Jul 1776, Col. Bull of Danbury / Capt. Sloper of cavalry, marched to New York City, ~3 weeks. (2) Sept 1776, same regiment and company, marched to Peekskill and White Plains, was there when Fort Washington was taken, served ~3 weeks. (3) Oct 1777, same regiment under Capt. Sloper or his Lt. Seth Deming, marched to Peekskill and Red Hook NY, served ~2 months. (4) Oct 1779, Capt. Sloper's Co. in the New Haven Alarm, served ~1 week. Affidavit summed service to 'six months' but Pension Office calculated less than the six-month minimum required under the Act of 1832 and rejected the claim. Probate Judge Thomas Lee of Berlin certified him to the federal court as 'a worthy, honest man, a man of truth and a wealthy farmer of Berlin.' Served alongside brother Jabez Cowles (H00435), who was witness to his pension application. CHILDREN per EH 1909 entry 434 and Cowles family genealogy entry 468: +1195 James Alpheus (b. 1778, bapt. June 1784) — currently in tree as HD0508; +1196 Merritt (b. 1783, bapt. June 1784) — NOT YET IN TREE; 1197 Polly (b. 1785, d. June 15, 1808 age 23, unm., tombstone Kensington) — currently in tree as HD0509. FLAG: HD-prefix vs H-prefix mismatch on James and Polly per EH numbering convention; Merritt missing entirely. Per source: Calvin D. Cowles 1929, 'Genealogy of the Cowles Families in America' (BIB003), entry 468; EH 1909 entry 434.

quotes.text: I was born in that part of Farmington which is now Berlin, in Dec. 1752, and have lived in same place to this time.
quotes.attribution: Samuel Cowles, sworn pension affidavit, Berlin Connecticut, September 19, 1832 (U.S. Pension Office)

quotes.text: Samuel Cowles is well known to the Court as a worthy, honest man, a man of truth and a wealthy farmer of Berlin.
quotes.attribution: Probate Judge Thomas Lee of Berlin Connecticut, certifying Samuel's 1832 Revolutionary War pension application

military_service.unit: Capt. Sloper's cavalry company, Col. Bull's Connecticut regiment, Danbury
military_service.notes: Four wartime call-ups documented in his 1832 pension affidavit: (1) July 1776, marched to New York City, ~3 weeks; (2) September 1776, Peekskill and White Plains, ~3 weeks, present during the campaign that lost Fort Washington; (3) October 1777, Peekskill and Red Hook NY, ~2 months under Capt. Sloper or his Lt. Seth Deming; (4) October 1779, New Haven Alarm under Capt. Sloper, ~1 week. Pension rejected under Act of 1832 because total service fell short of the six-month minimum. Served alongside brother Jabez Cowles (H00435).

narrative_blocks.header: Four call-ups in Sloper’s troop of horse
narrative_blocks.body: He rode in Captain Sloper’s cavalry company under Colonel Bull of Danbury: New York City in the summer of 1776, Peekskill and White Plains that autumn, Red Hook in 1777, and the New Haven Alarm in 1779.

narrative_blocks.header: At White Plains when the fort fell
narrative_blocks.body: His regiment was on the ground at Peekskill and White Plains through the weeks that ended with the taking of Fort Washington. The four turns of duty came to six months, counted end to end.

narrative_blocks.header: Six months of service, and six months required
narrative_blocks.body: He filed for a pension at Berlin in 1832, setting down every call-up by date and officer. The office rejected him: his service fell short of the six months the Act of 1832 required, by no margin anyone recorded.

narrative_blocks.header: The probate judge vouched for him in court
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas Lee of Berlin certified that Samuel Cowles was known to the court as a worthy, honest man, a man of truth, and a wealthy farmer of Berlin. It did not move the Pension Office.

narrative_blocks.header: He never lived anywhere else
narrative_blocks.body: I was born in that part of Farmington which is now Berlin, he told the pension officers, and have lived in same place to this time. He was eighty-one when he died on it. His brother Jabez witnessed the affidavit.

narrative_blocks.header: Second row in the meeting house, 1815
narrative_blocks.body: When Kensington reseated its meeting house he was put in the second row, which in a Connecticut parish was a statement about a man. He was grand juror in 1802 and fence viewer several years running.

narrative_blocks.header: Tithingman 1804, grand juror by 1809
narrative_blocks.body: The tithingman kept order through services that ran for hours and reported those who broke the Sabbath. The office came out of Anglo-Saxon England, where one man answered for the conduct of ten households. He took it at twenty-six.

narrative_blocks.header: Second wife buried beside her first husband
narrative_blocks.body: He married Catherine Morris Dunham in 1842, five years after Charlotte died; Catherine had been a widow since 1832. When she died in 1889 at eighty-nine she was buried beside Dunham, not beside him.

narrative_blocks.header: Both his sons died unmarried, farming Kensington
narrative_blocks.body: James's two sons Charles Bronson and Levi A. lived their whole lives as Kensington farmers and never married, dying in 1859 and 1886. The family's surviving line ran through his daughters Mary Lawrence Botsford and Laura Woodruff Dayton.

burial.plot_notes: South Burying Ground (South Kensington Cemetery), Kensington, Berlin, Connecticut. James, his first wife Charlotte (Bronson) Cowles, and their two sons Charles and Levi all buried here per Cowles Family Genealogy.

military_service.notes: Five field tours documented in pension affidavit: (1) Jan 1776 — 3 months at Roxbury MA on Dorchester Hill, Capt. Selah Hart / Col. Wolcott (siege of Boston, occupation after British evacuation Mar 17); (2) Jul 1776 — 3 weeks to Newark NJ, Capt. Sloper / Col. Bull; (3) Oct 1776 — 3 months Peekskill and White Plains NY, same regiment (campaign during which Fort Washington fell); (4) Jan 1778 — 2 weeks Albany NY under Capt. Ichabod Norton, retrieving Gen. Burgoyne's surrendered artillery to Farmington; (5) 1779 — 1 week New Haven Alarm, Capt. Seth Deming, cavalry. PLUS express rider duty for Brig.-Gen. Selah Hart, Nov 7 and Nov 19, 1779, through Simsbury, New Hartford, Norfolk, Torrington, Canaan; paid 45 pounds 13 shillings Dec 20, 1779 (Conn. Archives Rev. War Vol. 16 p. 259). Total field service 7 months 2 weeks. Pensioned 1833. Brother Samuel Cowles (H00434) was witness to his pension application; conversely Jabez witnessed Samuel's 1832 pension application.

bio.bio_blurb: Kensington farmer and Revolutionary express rider

quotes.text: Always lived in that part of Berlin, formerly Farmington, where he now lives, and was born in Farmington, Nov. 1755.
quotes.attribution: Jabez Cowles, sworn pension affidavit (paraphrased in U.S. Pension Office record), circa 1832-1833

narrative_blocks.header: On Dorchester Hill the day Boston was lost
narrative_blocks.body: Jabez served three months at Roxbury and on Dorchester Hill in the spring of 1776 under Capt. Selah Hart of Farmington and Col. Erastus Wolcott, occupying the lines that forced the British to evacuate Boston on March 17. He was twenty years old, on his first wartime tour.

narrative_blocks.header: Pension granted 1833 — his brother's was not
narrative_blocks.body: Jabez's federal pension was approved in 1833, recognizing seven months and two weeks of Revolutionary service. His older brother Samuel had filed a year earlier and been rejected for falling short of the six-month minimum, even though both rode the same campaigns under Col. Bull.

narrative_blocks.header: Brought home the cannon Burgoyne surrendered at Saratoga
narrative_blocks.body: In January 1778 Jabez marched with Capt. Ichabod Norton to Albany to bring back artillery captured from Gen. Burgoyne after the surrender at Saratoga. The guns were carted south to Farmington across two weeks of winter hauling.

narrative_blocks.header: Five wartime tours plus express rides for Hart
narrative_blocks.body: Beyond his five field tours — Boston, Newark, White Plains, Albany, the New Haven Alarm — Jabez rode express for Brig.-Gen. Selah Hart in November 1779, carrying messages through Simsbury, New Hartford, Norfolk, Torrington, and Canaan. He was paid 45 pounds 13 shillings a month later.

narrative_blocks.header: Married a captain's widow with two stepchildren
narrative_blocks.body: Jabez married Betsey Pratt Scoville in March 1786, the widow of Capt. Daniel Scovil who had died at Colchester five years earlier. She brought two children from her first marriage — Dan and Mary — into the new Kensington household.

narrative_blocks.header: A seat in the second row, 1815
narrative_blocks.body: In 1815 the Kensington meeting house assigned him a seat in the second row. He had lived his whole life in that part of Berlin that used to be Farmington, and he died there at ninety.

narrative_blocks.header: He thought the poet had never grown up
narrative_blocks.body: Kensington argued all that summer of 1820 over why young Dr. Percival wanted to die. Cowles, sixty-five and five wartime tours behind him, put it down to a man who had never finished becoming one, and so could not meet the world.

people.research_notes: Second wife Eunecia Pardee had previously been married to his brother Luman Cowles — a levirate-style remarriage within the Cowles family. Aug 20, 1794 East Haven CT; d. Mar 19, 1869 Berlin CT. Previously married Linus's brother Luman Cowles (d.1823). After Luman's death, married his brother Linus.
