narrative_blocks.header: Farmer, Whig, and Congregational church member
narrative_blocks.body: Linus lived his entire life in Kensington, working the family farm and counting himself a Whig in politics and a member of the Kensington Congregational Church. His ten children were raised in the same parish his grandfather Asahel had joined a century before.

narrative_blocks.header: Three wives, all buried at Kensington
narrative_blocks.body: Ruth died in 1825 after thirteen years. Maria Beckwith of Berlin lasted a year and died at thirty-one in May 1828, and that November he married Eunetia, his brother’s widow. All three lie in the same ground as he does.

narrative_blocks.header: Married his brother Luman's widow in 1828
narrative_blocks.body: After Linus's first wife Ruth died in 1825, he remarried in November 1828 to Eunetia Pardee — the widow of his younger brother Luman, who had died at thirty-three in 1823. The levirate-style match kept the household and the children together within the Cowles family.

narrative_blocks.header: Father of the ecologist Henry Chandler's father
narrative_blocks.body: Linus's eighth child Henry Martyn Cowles, born to him and Eunetia in 1831, would become a Kensington farmer and deacon. His grandson — born 1869 in the same house — was Henry Chandler Cowles, the founding figure of American plant ecology.

burial.plot_notes: Ledge Cemetery, Berlin, Connecticut, per FindAGrave.

people.research_notes: b. Mar 17, 1789 Berlin Conn.; d. Jan 24, 1823 Kensington, age 33 (tombstone Kensington). m. Jan 1, 1812 East Haven Conn., Eunetia Pardee (X01219), b. Aug 20, 1794 East Haven, dau. of Chandler Pardee (Rev War vet, wounded New Haven 1779) and Lydia (Hotchkiss) Pardee. She d. Mar 19, 1869 Kensington. After Luman's death she m. (2) Nov 23, 1828 his brother Linus Cowles (HD0510). Luman lived Kensington, was a farmer, freeman 1810, town collector 1814, constable. Both Luman and his wife were Kensington Congregational Church members. Administration on his estate granted Mar 17, 1823 to Linus Cowles. Inventory $3,953.61. Children, all b. Kensington: 2884 Mary (b. Feb 27, 1813); 2885 Alonzo Smith (b. Jan 1815, d. Nov 18, 1816); 2886 Chandler (b. Dec 25, 1816); 2887 Elizabeth (b. Feb 1819, d. Feb 21, 1823); 2888 Luman Jr. (b. Jun 30, 1822). Source: Calvin D. Cowles 1929 (BIB003), entry 1199; Pardee Genealogy 1927.

bio.bio_blurb: Kensington farmer, town collector and constable

narrative_blocks.header: Freeman 1810, town collector 1814, constable
narrative_blocks.body: Luman was admitted a freeman of Kensington in 1810 at twenty-one, served as town collector in 1814, and worked as town constable. He held the standard Connecticut civic-office ladder a young man of property climbed before turning thirty.

narrative_blocks.header: His widow remarried his older brother Linus
narrative_blocks.body: Five years after Luman's death, Eunetia Pardee Cowles married Linus Cowles in November 1828 — Luman's older brother. The Cowles family kept itself intact across the gap left by Luman's early death; Eunetia outlived both husbands.

narrative_blocks.header: Dead at thirty-three in a hard winter
narrative_blocks.body: Luman died on 24 January 1823 at thirty-three, leaving Eunetia a widow with four living children. A month later the youngest girl, Elizabeth, died too. His brother Linus took out the administration on the estate in March.

people.research_notes: Farmer. m. Betsey Ann Norton Jan 7, 1838. Norton mother was Elizabeth Hooker — another Hooker connection. d. Nov 28, 1896.

bio.bio_blurb: Berlin selectman, legislator and insurance agent

narrative_blocks.header: Selectman, justice, and the board of relief
narrative_blocks.body: He was selectman of Berlin in 1855 and 1856 and again from 1861, town agent to 1870, and justice of the peace between. He sat in the legislature as a Republican and served on the board of relief in 1878.

narrative_blocks.header: Farmer, ticket agent, insurance man
narrative_blocks.body: He farmed at Kensington, sold tickets at Berlin Station, and ended as an insurance agent at New Britain, where he was still living in 1894. He and Betsey Ann joined the Congregational church in 1860 and he ran its Sunday school.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother was a Hooker of Kensington
narrative_blocks.body: He married Betsey Ann Norton at Kensington in January 1836. Her mother was Betsey Hooker, a daughter of Sergeant William Hooker of the same town, and bride and groom both stood eight generations from Thomas Hooker by separate roads.

narrative_blocks.header: One stone for him, his wife, four children
narrative_blocks.body: The Kensington burying ground holds tombstones to George, to Betsey Ann, and to four of their five children. He outlived her by thirty-one years and died at eighty-four in November 1896.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventy-six years in Kensington
narrative_blocks.body: Delia Ann joined the Kensington church in 1831 and never married. She lived nearly the whole of her life in the town she was born in, and died there in August 1890 at seventy-six.

narrative_blocks.header: She joined the church at nineteen
narrative_blocks.body: Lucy joined the Kensington church in 1835 and married Isaac William Judd of Berlin three years later. He was a carpenter and joiner at New Haven, and she was still living there in 1894, some years after his death.

bio.bio_blurb: Kensington farmer who gathered the family history

narrative_blocks.header: He gathered the family history himself
narrative_blocks.body: He took an active interest in the history of his own family and collected a great deal of it. The compilers of the Cowles genealogy set down their debt to him by name, for much valuable data that would otherwise have gone.

narrative_blocks.header: Constable, selectman, board of relief
narrative_blocks.body: He was constable of Kensington in 1852 and selectman from that year to 1854, and sat on the board of relief in 1860. He farmed and voted Republican, and joined the Congregational church at seventeen, the year he was baptised.

narrative_blocks.header: One stone for three of them at Kensington
narrative_blocks.body: He married Mary Dunham in August 1858 and outlived her by six years. The tombstone at Kensington carries him, his wife and one of their children — Elmer, who died at a year old in 1862.

career.organization: Clark and Cowles, clock trimmings and rivets, Plainville

narrative_blocks.header: Clock trimmings and rivets at Plainville
narrative_blocks.body: He was a mechanic when he married in 1850. He moved from Kensington to Plainville and founded Clark and Cowles, makers of clock trimmings and rivets, and was its president. He sat in the legislature as a Republican.

narrative_blocks.header: He died visiting his daughter at Waukegan
narrative_blocks.body: Emogene died at Plainville in August 1895. Twenty years later he went out to Waukegan in Illinois to see his daughter Helen, and died there on 24 April 1915. They brought him back to the West Cemetery at Plainville.

bio.bio_blurb: President of C. Cowles & Company, New Haven

career.organization: Russell & Cowles, coach lamps, New Haven

narrative_blocks.header: Coach lamps first, then the whole firm
narrative_blocks.body: He left Kensington for New Haven in 1845 and by 1850 was making coach lamps as Russell and Cowles. When C. Cowles and Company was organised in 1855 he came in as vice-president, and rose through secretary and treasurer to president.

narrative_blocks.header: He raised the company he then captained
narrative_blocks.body: He and two others recruited a company for the war, and he was captain of Company H of the 27th Connecticut. He enlisted in September 1862 and resigned the next May to take a commission as quartermaster of the regiment.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven years on the fire department
narrative_blocks.body: He was a director of the Mechanics Bank, seven years in the New Haven fire department, and sat in the Common Council in 1858 and 1859. He was a Grand Army man, a Son of the Revolution and a Son of Temperance.

narrative_blocks.header: Major of the Governor’s Home Guards
narrative_blocks.body: After the war he served in the Second Company of the Governor’s Home Guards, going from second lieutenant to first lieutenant to major between 1865 and 1872. He died at New Haven in June 1891.

narrative_blocks.header: The founder was his half-brother
narrative_blocks.body: Chandler Cowles, who founded the firm in 1838, was his half-brother — their mother Eunetia Pardee married Luman Cowles first and then Linus, his own father. The two of them were first cousins as well as half-brothers.

bio.bio_blurb: Founder of C. Cowles & Company, New Haven

career.organization: Conwell and Cowles, later C. Cowles & Company, New Haven

narrative_blocks.header: Conwell and Cowles, 1838
narrative_blocks.body: He and William Conwell founded a carriage-hardware firm at New Haven in 1838, making lanterns for horse-drawn carriages. From 1855 it went under his name alone, and C. Cowles and Company stamps metal for carmakers still.

narrative_blocks.header: Christmas Day at Kensington
narrative_blocks.body: Chandler was born at Kensington in Hartford County on Christmas Day 1816, a son of Luman Cowles and Eunetia Pardee. His father died when he was six, and he was in business for himself at twenty-one.

narrative_blocks.header: Susan died at thirty-six, he at forty-nine
narrative_blocks.body: He married Susan Evelina Sabin of Milford in June 1841 and they had five children at New Haven. She died in 1854 at thirty-six, their four-year-old Elizabeth having gone five years before her. He followed in 1865.

narrative_blocks.header: A daughter died at ninety-seven in Rome
narrative_blocks.body: Anne Luise, the second of the five, married a Des Granges and lived out her life in Italy. She died at Rome in January 1941, ninety-seven years old, and lies in the Campo Cestio with the other foreigners.

narrative_blocks.header: On the first telephone exchange anywhere
narrative_blocks.body: The works stood at 83 Water Street, at the corner of Chestnut. The firm was on the 1878 list of subscribers to the New Haven District Telephone Company, the first commercial telephone exchange in the world.

narrative_blocks.header: His half-brother came in as vice-president
narrative_blocks.body: Ruel Pardee Cowles was his half-brother: their mother Eunetia Pardee married his father Luman first, then Luman’s brother Linus. Ruel came into C. Cowles and Company at its organising in 1855 and ended as its president.

career.notes: Documented as Selectman of Farmington on January 10, 1816 when he co-signed the certificate of examination for the manumission of Titus, slave of Capt. narrative_blocks.header: The tribe next door took him to court
narrative_blocks.body: His Farmington farm abutted the Tunxis reservation at Indian Neck. In 1767 their spokesman James Wawowos petitioned the Assembly to recover a hundred-acre tract the town had absorbed, naming Ezekiel Cowles among the defendants.

narrative_blocks.header: Five brothers split their father's estate
narrative_blocks.body: Capt. Isaac Cowles died in 1756, a Farmington tailor turned large landholder and one of the Seven Pillars of the Kensington church. In 1763 his last five sons divided what he left between them as sole heirs.

narrative_blocks.header: He married into a very long-lived family
narrative_blocks.body: Martha Hooker's father, Lieut. Giles Hooker, died at ninety-seven in 1787, and her brother Samuel at ninety-nine the same year. She reached eighty-three herself, and Ezekiel Cowles eighty-four.

narrative_blocks.header: The farm he bought passed to his namesake
narrative_blocks.body: He bought his Farmington place in 1753 and held it for life, and his son Ezekiel and that son's heirs had it after him. His will is dated December 1792; Martha's, signed Martha Cowles, 2nd, May 1807.

narrative_blocks.header: Lost two infants then died at forty
narrative_blocks.body: Ann married Dr. Harry Wadsworth in 1807 and bore three children — Harry Jr. in 1806, Theodore in 1807 (lost as an infant the next year), and Betsey Mix in 1809 (lost at age two). Her husband died in 1813, leaving her widowed with one surviving child. She died at forty in 1824.

narrative_blocks.header: Married her second cousin through Cowles line
narrative_blocks.body: Ann's 1807 marriage to Dr. Harry Wadsworth crossed a hundred-year Cowles loop — both descended from Capt. Isaac Cowles of Farmington (1675-1756). Ann came down through Isaac's third-wife son Ezekiel; Harry came down through Isaac's first-wife son Isaac II via Mary Cowles Wadsworth. Half-blood second cousins once removed.

Aaron Austin's clerk. Reached Sergeant-Major. Pensioned under the 1832 act, paid to date of death. RECOMMENDED FOR COMMISSION: On May 20, 1782, Maj.-Gen. Samuel Holden Parsons wrote to General George Washington recommending Ezekiel for a subaltern commission. Letter preserved in the Library of Congress, Washington Papers, Correspondence with the Officers, Vol. 3 Page 2122. The commission was not granted before war's end. PUBLIC OFFICES: State Tax Collector 1794-6, '98; Deputy Sheriff 1802-14 (12 years); CT State Legislature representing Farmington 1807-10; Justice of the Peace 1809-18. TUNXIS OVERSEER 1804: The Connecticut General Assembly appointed him overseer and advisor of the Tunxis people in 1804, replacing Capt. John Porter — under whom Ezekiel had served in 1776 at the Battle of Long Island. Document on file at Native Northeast Portal (DOC018). The role made him part of the documented Hooker-family chain of Tunxis-related appointments and transactions: Hon. John Hooker (H00030, gen 2) had defended Tunxis land claims in 1738; Justice John Mix (X00263, his brother-in-law's stepfather network) signed the 1802 Sue Squa land deed and the 1816 Titus emancipation. Will dated December 29, 1849; inventory October 25, 1850 valued at $6,549.12 (on file in Connecticut State Library). Joined the church 1845. 'Lived an exemplary life and died a professed Christian' (Cowles book). Wife Rachel Woodruff (X00268, 1759-1834) predeceased him by 16 years; they had four children: Egbert (H01138, EH#1138), Alfred (H01139, EH#1139), Frederick Woodruff (H01140, EH#1140, died at 18), and Ebenezer Mix (HD0984, EH#1140a). narrative_blocks.header: From Long Island to Burgoyne's surrender
narrative_blocks.body: Ezekiel marched to New York in July 1776 under Capt. John Porter, fought on Long Island and fell back through Harlem and King's Bridge to White Plains. In 1777 he was at Saratoga for the fighting of 7 October and Burgoyne's surrender ten days later.

narrative_blocks.header: Recommended to Washington for a commission
narrative_blocks.body: By 1782 Ezekiel was a sergeant-major, and that May Maj. Gen. Samuel Holden Parsons wrote to Washington recommending him for a commission. The war ended before it came.

narrative_blocks.header: Overseer of the Tunxis, 1804
narrative_blocks.body: In 1804 the General Assembly made Ezekiel overseer of the Tunxis at Farmington, succeeding Capt. John Porter, the officer he had followed to Long Island twenty-eight years before.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-five years in Farmington's offices
narrative_blocks.body: Ezekiel collected the state's taxes in the 1790s, was deputy sheriff from 1802 to 1814, sat in the legislature from 1807 to 1810, and was a justice of the peace until 1818.

narrative_blocks.header: He joined the church at eighty-seven
narrative_blocks.body: Ezekiel joined the church in 1845, at eighty-seven, five years before he died at Farmington in August 1850, at ninety-two.

people.research_notes: [Migrated from marriage.spouse_notes (spouse X01220)]: b. Jun 8, 1760 Farmington; d. Jan 23, 1823 Hounsfield NY. Son of Stephen Dorchester Sr. and Elizabeth Gould Dorchester. Revolutionary War service 1775-1780; War of 1812 service. Moved family from Connecticut to Hounsfield, Jefferson County, NY.

narrative_blocks.header: Married in her father's house at Farmington
narrative_blocks.body: Rev. Timothy Pitkin married Anna Cowles to Alexander Dorchester on 29 May 1783 at Ezekiel Cowles's house. She was twenty-one, and within five years they had left Connecticut for the Berkshires.

narrative_blocks.header: Farmington to Richmond to Oneida to Jefferson
narrative_blocks.body: Richmond in the Berkshires came about 1788, where Hooker was born. Westmoreland in Oneida County followed, and Hounsfield in Jefferson County about 1815. She kept house in four places in one marriage.

narrative_blocks.header: Three funerals in three weeks, 1794
narrative_blocks.body: Westmoreland buried Alexander's father Stephen on 31 August 1794 and their daughter Nancy the same day. Harriot followed on 17 September, and the family had lost three in under three weeks.

narrative_blocks.header: None of her eight children outlived her
narrative_blocks.body: Only Delia and Hooker reached twenty. Delia died at twenty-four in 1810 and Hooker at forty-six in 1835, and when Anna Dorchester died in 1840 there was not one of the eight left alive.

narrative_blocks.header: A widow's pension at seventy-seven
narrative_blocks.body: Alexander had drawn his own from 1819 and died in 1823. She was inscribed on the Albany roll at eighty dollars a year from March 1836, and the certificate reached Watertown in April 1839.

narrative_blocks.header: She made her will on her birthday
narrative_blocks.body: On 18 July 1835, seventy-four that day, she left Maria the five-pail kettle and the churn, and all the rest to her granddaughter Delia Ann — the cow, four beds, the gold beads, three chests.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventy-nine, in her grandson's house
narrative_blocks.body: A neighbour wrote in 1833 that the old lady had the ague and was failing. She had seven years yet: the 1840 census found her at Cape Vincent with her grandson Alfred, and she died that September.

burial.plot_notes: Muscalunge Cemetery, Hounsfield, Jefferson, New York

bio.notes: Named "Hooker" for maternal great-grandmother Martha Hooker Cowles

military_service.notes: Assisted in the defence of Sackets Harbor 19 July 1812; served 9-20 September with his father.

narrative_blocks.header: He was named for his grandmother Hooker
narrative_blocks.body: Anna Cowles gave her son the maiden surname of her own mother, Martha Hooker Cowles of Farmington. He was born in May 1788, most likely at Richmond in the Berkshires.

narrative_blocks.header: He cut the oak for a warship
narrative_blocks.body: About 1810 he helped fell the timber that built the New Orleans at Sackets Harbor, which fought the British on Lake Ontario. He was in the village's defence when they attacked it in July 1812.

narrative_blocks.header: An accidental shot from his own gun
narrative_blocks.body: He died at Hounsfield on 6 April 1835. The Muscalunge stone gives his age as forty-seven, and Maria Dorchester told the surrogate he had left no will.

narrative_blocks.header: His three eldest chose their own guardian
narrative_blocks.body: Delia Ann, Henry and Alfred, twenty, seventeen and fifteen, petitioned the Jefferson surrogate in April 1835 for Thompson Phelps. Maria asked a fortnight later for the five younger children.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought land with his wife's people
narrative_blocks.body: In May 1816 he and John Thompson took the estate of the late John Thomson at Hounsfield, together with land over in Pultney in Vermont. Alexander Dorchester witnessed the deed.

narrative_blocks.header: The 1820 census counts five in the house
narrative_blocks.body: Hooker and Mercy Dorchester were both in their thirties then, with Delia Ann five, Henry Cowles two and Alfred one. Fifteen years later those three were choosing a guardian between them.

people.research_notes: Owned grist mill in Limerick NY. m. Margaret Carson Nelson 1840. d. Sep 13, 1881.

narrative_blocks.header: Born at East Hounsfield on New Year's Day
narrative_blocks.body: He came on 1 January 1818, eldest son of Hooker Dorchester by his first wife Mercy Thompson. He married Margaret Carson Nelson of Dexter in 1840 and settled at Limerick in Brownville.

narrative_blocks.header: Husband and wife four years apart
narrative_blocks.body: Margaret Nelson died at Limerick in December 1877 and Henry Cowles Dorchester in September 1881, and they lie together in the Dexter burying ground. All six of their children outlived them.

narrative_blocks.header: At fifteen he could teach school
narrative_blocks.body: A neighbour wrote in April 1833 that Henry's learning was now sufficient to teach school. He was fifteen, motherless since seven, and two years off choosing his own guardian.

narrative_blocks.header: Saw milling, gristmilling and pork-packing
narrative_blocks.body: He came to Bellevue in 1853 and was one of the town's leading businessmen for years, milling flour and lumber and packing dressed hogs while that was the market. Business failures retired him early.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the first governor's stepdaughter
narrative_blocks.body: Illinois Carpenter was stepdaughter to Ansel Briggs, the first governor of Iowa. They married in 1860 and had eight children, seven girls and one boy, and she died in July 1890.

narrative_blocks.header: A boy and his dog on the monument
narrative_blocks.body: The family lot in the Presbyterian cemetery at Bellevue is topped by a reclining boy with a dog, taken for Andrew Jackson Dorchester Jr., who died at two and a half in 1872 — the only son.

narrative_blocks.header: Named for Old Hickory, and called Jack
narrative_blocks.body: He was born in Jefferson County in September 1827, when Andrew Jackson was a famous general two years off the presidency. His namesake preferred A.J., or Jackson, or Jack.

narrative_blocks.header: His own gun went off on the ice
narrative_blocks.body: Pushing a sled of live decoys home from the islands above Bellevue in December 1903, he shoved at it with the butt of his shotgun. It slipped and fired, tearing his sleeve away to the elbow.

narrative_blocks.header: Well in the morning, dead by evening
narrative_blocks.body: On 9 August 1904 he was about the house at noon and seemed as usual. A pain took him in the region of the heart that afternoon, and he died at half past seven, seventy-six years old.

narrative_blocks.header: Jefferson County to Bellevue, Iowa
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Hounsfield in 1827, eldest son of Hooker Dorchester and Maria Van Schaick. He died at Bellevue in Jackson County, Iowa, in August 1904 and was buried in the Presbyterian ground.

narrative_blocks.body: Mercy Everett wrote the family dates into a book that outlasted her and is still cited for them. She married William Henry Harrison Everett at the end of 1862 and bore eight children at Limerick.

narrative_blocks.header: She proved his will and outlived him
narrative_blocks.body: William Everett died in March 1908 and letters testamentary went to her at Limerick and to their son Fred at Saranac Lake. She lived twenty-one years more and died in 1929, eighty-seven.

narrative_blocks.body: He clerked in Watertown men's shops until Nellie needed the mountain air, then bought a store at Saranac Lake in 1905 and made it known. His son Dorchester kept it going until 1975.

narrative_blocks.header: Driving home from Cornell, a tanker hit them
narrative_blocks.body: Ruth Ober and her husband had taken their daughter Dorothy to Cornell. Two miles above Pulaski on route 11 an oil tank truck met them head on. She was killed at fifty-four; Elwood survived it.

narrative_blocks.header: Secretary of the Thousand Island Park association
narrative_blocks.body: She held the post before her marriage, and was married at Thousand Island Park itself in August 1926, in her grandmother Everett's cottage. She was a Methodist and a Girl Scout councillor.

b. Aug 26, 1766 Farmington CT; d. Jul 5, 1835 Austinburg, Ashtabula County, Ohio. Son of Ezekiel Cowles (I00156) and Martha Hooker Cowles (H00232). Named "Giles Hooker" — double tribute: grandfather Giles Hooker (H00087) AND the Hooker ancestry. Yale 1789 (with honors); D.D. Williams College 1823. Studied theology with Dr. Jonathan Edwards the Younger (son of Jonathan Edwards — the same Edwards line that Worthington Hooker married into via Henrietta Whitney Edwards). Pioneer Ohio Congregational minister; built first steepled church in Ohio. "In stature he was short, thickset and very dignified in his manner, and a man of good sense and education. His sermons were logical, plain and practical." m. Feb 5, 1793 Sally White of Stamford CT (d. Jul 31, 1830 age 56). STUDIED UNDER JONATHAN EDWARDS JR.: Studied theology with Rev. Dr. Jonathan Edwards Jr. (H00384) of New Haven after Yale graduation. Licensed to preach 1791. (Yale biographical sketches of graduates) OCCUPATION NOTES: Theological studies with Dr. Jonathan Edwards the Younger, then of New Haven. Licensed to preach May 31, 1791. Ordained First Church and Society, New Cambridge (now Bristol) CT, Oct 17, 1792. Dismissed May 24, 1810; set out for New Connecticut (Ohio) May 30, 1810. Installed over United Church, Austinburg and Morgan Ohio, Sep 25, 1811. "Shortly after his arrival his congregation built the first church with a steeple in New Connecticut, and perhaps in the State of Ohio." Resigned 1830. Died Austinburg Jul 5, 1835.
CC NOTE [H00386]: Pierpont Edwards invested £60,000 in the Connecticut Land Company (1795) — 5% of the company — and sent his son John Stark Edwards as his first agent in the Western Reserve. Rev. Giles Hooker Cowles moved to Austinburg, Ashtabula County OH and co-founded Western Reserve College (1826) as 'the Yale of the West.' Both men were Hooker descendants acting as architects of the Connecticut presence in the Western Reserve — Edwards through land capital, Cowles through institutional education. Neither is documented as having known the other's Hooker descent.

narrative_blocks.header: A thirty-day wagon journey from Bristol
narrative_blocks.body: In 1811 Cowles loaded his family of nine children onto two wagons and traveled thirty to forty days over mud roads to Austinburg, Ohio — a journey so final that returning was considered nearly impossible. His congregation built the first church with a steeple in the state of Ohio, and he served it for nearly twenty-five years.

narrative_blocks.header: Drove the founding stake of Ohio's first college
narrative_blocks.body: In 1825 Cowles helped found Western Reserve College — called 'Yale of the West' for sharing Yale's motto, standards, and curriculum. He was among those who drove a stake on College Hill in Hudson, Ohio, and his name appears as an original incorporator. The college is now Case Western Reserve University.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale 1789, then theology with Edwards the Younger
narrative_blocks.body: After Yale 1789 Cowles read theology with tutor William Robinson before continuing under Rev. Dr. Jonathan Edwards Jr. at New Haven, son of the Great Awakening preacher. Edwards Jr. ordained him at Bristol's First Church on October 17, 1792.

narrative_blocks.header: 'A year never to be forgotten' — 1799
narrative_blocks.body: A revival swept his Bristol parish in 1799 and added 218 members to the church, the harvest of his early ministry. Three years later he was preaching publicly against the Bristol Baptists in defense of infant baptism, sermons that drew fierce reply.

narrative_blocks.header: His Austinburg parsonage gathered the era's reformers
narrative_blocks.body: His 320-acre Austinburg parsonage built in 1815 housed the Western Reserve's largest county library and a steady traffic of visitors — Bishop Philander Chase passing through on his Ohio diocese rounds, anti-slavery orators stopping for hospitality. The Cowles household became a way-station for the reform circuits of the Reserve.

narrative_blocks.header: Resigned the pulpit 1830, died still preaching
narrative_blocks.body: Cowles resigned his Austinburg pulpit in 1830 with a farewell sermon on 1 Samuel 12:23: 'God forbid that I should sin against the Lord in ceasing to pray for you.' Five years later, on Sunday July 5, 1835, he died at his parsonage and the Western Reserve's clergy gathered to bury him in his own churchyard.

narrative_blocks.header: Remarried at sixty-three; only daughter at sixty-six
narrative_blocks.body: William Ezekiel Root's first marriage to Harriet Leonard around 1827 produced five sons. After their separation or her departure (she 'still living' at his 1889 death and later married Orlin W. Spencer), William remarried on July 23, 1869 in Lenox Township Ohio to Paulina Monroe — and three years later, at age sixty-six, fathered his only documented daughter Mary E. Root. The late-life second-family arc was uncommon among Connecticut-Hooker-line men of his generation.

narrative_blocks.header: Catskill NY birth, EH misrecorded as Farmington
narrative_blocks.body: William Ezekiel Root was born in 1806 in Catskill New York, where his parents had settled before 1792 — though some early genealogical records mistakenly placed his birth in Farmington Connecticut. He died in Lenox Township, Ashtabula County Ohio on August 31, 1889 at age eighty-three, buried at West Lenox Cemetery. The Connecticut-to-New-York-to-Ohio migration arc spanned three states across his lifetime.

narrative_blocks.header: Five sons, four documented only by initials
narrative_blocks.body: William and Harriet's five sons were William Alonzo Root born 1832, and four others known in records only as E.L. (1859), E.W. (1860), S.L. (1860), and A.A. (1861). The use of initials for four of five sons may reflect contemporary practice or simply that fuller given names were never preserved. The 1859-1861 birth cluster of four boys came in close succession during William's middle-aged years.

people.research_notes: Son of Jay Knickerbocker (HD0544) and Florence Hillman (X01231). Born October 15, 1918 in Bangall Stanford Township Dutchess County NY. Triple Hooker descent inherited through his maternal great-grandmother Jennie Hooker Knickerbocker. Attended Duke University; began professional baseball at age 21 in 1940. In 1941 batted .406 to lead Class C Canadian-American League in hitting (Oneonta Indians: 202 hits, 135 RBI). Promoted to Triple-A Jersey City Giants 1942. Served United States Army 1943-1945 (WWII), rank Master Sergeant. Resumed pro career 1946. Made his only MLB appearances in 1947 with Philadelphia Athletics — 21 games, 48 at-bats, 12 hits as outfielder. Played 1948-1954 in minors (skipped 1952). Married Helen Gertrude Germond (X01232) in 1941; four children. Died February 18, 1997 in Clinton Corners Dutchess County NY at age 78. Buried Stanford Cemetery (CEM241), Stanfordville NY — VETERAN marker. TRIPLE DESCENT CONFIRMED Stage 6Y-677 by path analysis: three distinct ancestor-paths to Thomas Hooker (H00001), all via father HD0544, diverging at the great-grandparent level. Tag upgraded double->triple per compiler authorization; triple_hooker_ancestry is hereby canonical (schema v22 queue).

narrative_blocks.header: He hit .406 for Oneonta
narrative_blocks.body: Out of Duke, Austin turned professional at twenty-one in 1940, and the next summer hit .406 for the Oneonta Indians to lead the Class C Canadian-American League, with 202 hits and 135 runs batted in. It jumped him to the top of the minors, the 1942 Jersey City Giants.

narrative_blocks.header: His big-league debut was as a pinch runner
narrative_blocks.body: Austin reached the majors with the Philadelphia Athletics on April 19, 1947, running for another man against the Boston Red Sox. Five at-bats later, at the May cutdown, he was sent down to the Toronto Maple Leafs.

narrative_blocks.header: Called back up for September
narrative_blocks.body: After hitting .278 in 105 games at Toronto, Austin was recalled in September and started eight games, playing all three outfield spots. His big-league line was twelve hits in forty-eight at-bats, three of them doubles and two triples.

narrative_blocks.header: Master sergeant between the box scores
narrative_blocks.body: Three Army years as a master sergeant, 1943 to 1945, came between his Jersey City season and his return in the International League in 1946. He played minor-league ball until 1954, skipping 1952, then went home to Dutchess County.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a Vassar nurse
narrative_blocks.body: Austin married Helen Germond of Clinton Corners in 1941, his .406 year; she had finished at the Vassar Nursing School the year before. They were married fifty-six years, and she outlived him by twenty-seven, dying at 106.

people.research_notes: Daughter of William Hooker Jr. (H02791) and Sarah Varney Cutler Hooker (X01229). Born September 8, 1867 in Wingdale Dutchess County NY. Triple Hooker descent through her father. Married Peter Dykeman (X00958) on September 9, 1885 in Wingdale NY. Effie and Peter Dykeman were very active in the Pawling Baptist Church — a stained glass window in the church bears their names. The family held annual reunions, a tradition continued by their son Henry. Two known Dykeman children (H05308, HD0550). Died April 2, 1936 in Pawling Dutchess County NY at age 68.

narrative_blocks.header: A charter member, twice, in Pawling
narrative_blocks.body: Effie was a charter member of both the Pawling Grange and the Pawling Baptist Church — a founding presence in the town’s civic and religious life.

FamilySearch and some online trees use the Heaton variant which is a name corruption; Eaton is canonical for this family. Elizabeth Stiles Eaton. EH 1909 entry #449. b. Feb 21, 1755 North Haven (formerly Quinnipiac) Connecticut; d. 1792 North Haven CT age 37. Daughter of Isaac Stiles Jr. (H00238) and Mabel Clark Stiles (I00158). Descent line per EH: Isaac Stiles-5 / Esther Hooker-4 / Samuel-3 / Samuel-2 / Thomas-1 — gen 5 Hooker descendant. m. about 1776 New Haven CT Timothy Eaton (I00505, formerly placeholder X01367; b. 1749, d. 1808), spelled 'Eaton' in EH but 'Eaton' in modern records. Seven children all baptized at St. John's Church North Haven (no birth dates in source): Hannah (H01165 bapt 1778), Betsey (H01166 bapt 1780), Ebenezer (H01167 bapt 1782), Mabel (H01168 bapt 1783), Abigail (H01169 bapt 1786), Louisa (H01170 bapt 1789), Solomon (H01171 bapt 1791). narrative_blocks.body: Commissary at the close of the war, he had a storehouse full when the troops came back through New Haven. He called them in — now boys eat and be merry — and put the rest of the loaves to a game in the next field.

people.prominent_name_reason: Lyman Ezra Munson — Yale Law School 1851; first judge appointed by President Lincoln to the Supreme Court of the Territory of Montana, 1865; Chief Justice for three years. Great-great-great-grandson of Thomas Hooker through Kesia Stiles Munson.
people.research_notes:
b. Jan 21, 1822 Great Barrington MA. Yale Law School 1851. First judge appointed to Supreme Court of Territory of Montana by President Lincoln 1865. Chief Justice Montana Territory 3 years. d. Feb 13, 1908 New Haven. Buried Grove Street Cemetery New Haven. Wife from North Haven CT; sister of George Munson's wife. Mother was cousin of Edwin Stanton (Lincoln's Secretary of War). Arrived Helena MT Jul 9, 1865. Resigned bench 1868. Married Lucy A. Sanford Oct 6, 1846; two daughters and a son Edward Lyman Munson. (Wikipedia) DISCREPANCY: FindAGrave lists parents as 'Justus Gilbert Munson (1795-1875, Hamden CT) and Esther Stanton Munson' — different from EH which places him as child of Ebenezer Beach Munson (HD0564). EH is primary source; discrepancy flagged. Burial: Grove Street Cemetery New Haven CT (CEM009).
[Stage 6Y-264 NB#1 header trim]: 'Lincoln appointed him to Montana Territory — his mother was Edwin Stanton's cousin' → 'Lincoln appointed him to Montana Territory'.
[Stage 6Y-264 NB#1 body trim]: original body had 4 sentences, trimmed to first 3. Original body preserved here for reference: 'Lyman Ezra Munson graduated Yale Law School in 1851 and in March 1865 was appointed Associate Justice of the Montana Territorial Supreme Court by President Abraham Lincoln. He arrived in Helena on July 9, 1865. When the Territorial Supreme Court declared the second territorial legislature void in 1866, he was assigned the most remote judicial district. He resigned in 1868 and died in New Haven at 86.' [2026-07-25 BUILD-OUT] CORRECTIONS: he was an ASSOCIATE justice, not the first judge — Hezekiah L. Hosmer was appointed first Chief Justice on 30 June 1864, and Munson was appointed 11 March 1865 to replace Ammi Giddings, who declined to serve. He acted as chief justice only at times. Born to Gilbert Munson and Esther Stanton of Great Barrington. Yale Law LL.B. 1851 after Lenox Academy; admitted at New Haven 1851. Commissioner of deeds for Kentucky under Gov. Thomas E. Bramlette, sworn 18 Jan 1864. A Radical Republican, at odds with Acting Governor Thomas Francis Meagher. Presided over the territory's first formal murder trial. Wrote two autobiographical sketches and his 12 Aug 1865 grand jury charge, held by the Montana Historical Society, and 'Pioneer Life in Montana' in Contributions to the Historical Society of Montana V (1904), pp. 200-234. Sources disagree whether he resigned in 1868 or 1869.

notable.notable_blurb: Lincoln's associate justice in Montana Territory

narrative_blocks.header: Lincoln sent him to judge the Montana frontier
narrative_blocks.body: Lincoln appointed him an associate justice of Montana Territory's supreme court in March 1865, to replace a man who had declined to go, and he reached Helena that July. Hosmer was already chief justice; Munson sat in that chair at times and held the bench until he resigned.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother was Edwin Stanton's cousin
narrative_blocks.body: Munson's mother was a cousin of Edwin Stanton, Lincoln's secretary of war, a tie that set him near the administration that sent him west. A Yale Law graduate of 1851, he had trained for the bench in New Haven.

narrative_blocks.header: He came home to New Haven for good
narrative_blocks.body: After resigning the Montana bench in 1868, Munson settled back in New Haven where he had studied law. He died there in 1908 and lies in Grove Street Cemetery.

narrative_blocks.header: He sentenced a man the mob then hanged
narrative_blocks.body: He heard the territory's first formal murder trial, convicted James Daniels of manslaughter and gave him three years rather than the rope. Vigilantes took Daniels and hanged him anyway. A legislator afterwards accused Munson himself of complicity.

narrative_blocks.header: He voided a legislature and paid for it
narrative_blocks.body: The territorial supreme court declared the second legislature void in the March of 1866, and Munson was handed the most remote judicial district in Montana afterwards. A Radical Republican, he was already crosswise with the acting governor.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote down what the frontier was like
narrative_blocks.body: He gave two autobiographical sketches and his 1865 charge to the grand jury to the Montana Historical Society, and in 1904 published Pioneer Life in Montana. They are plain accounts of travel, scarcity and the slow arrival of courts, without the heroics of the dime novels.

William Huntington Russell was ALSO a Hooker descendant himself through the Pierpont-Russell line (H00360 in our tree). This means the Skull and Bones founder connected to Thomas Hooker's descendants TWICE — by his own descent AND by his son's marriage. SON of William Huntington Russell (1809-1885) — co-founder of Skull and Bones (Yale, 1832) with Alphonso Taft. BROTHER of Talcott Huntington Russell (1847-1917). This marriage connects the Hooker-Munson-Stiles line to the Russell-Skull and Bones family BY MARRIAGE — separate from the existing Hooker→Pierpont→Russell DESCENT connection through which William Huntington Russell himself was a Hooker descendant.

narrative_blocks.header: She was schooled in Europe and America
narrative_blocks.body: She had the advantage of boarding schools on both sides of the Atlantic. Her husband's family sketch credited her with perfect health, sound common sense, and a way of never tiring of doing good.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father was Lincoln's judge in Montana
narrative_blocks.body: Lyman Ezra Munson went out to Helena in 1865 as the first judge of Montana Territory's supreme court, appointed by Lincoln himself. Her brother Edward became a brigadier general and designed the shoe the American army marched in.

narrative_blocks.header: Her marriage doubled the Hooker line
narrative_blocks.body: She married Thomas Hubbard Russell in 1882 — a fifth cousin once removed, both of them down from Rev. Samuel Hooker. The Skull and Bones founder's family reached Thomas Hooker twice over after that: by his own descent, and by his son's wife.

military_service.role: Private
military_service.notes: Served in a company formed in Windsor CT during the War of 1812 with Britain. Stationed at Fort Trumbull (New London CT) in February 1813.

narrative_blocks.header: A few rods south of the Court House
narrative_blocks.body: He came up from Windsor in 1785, twenty-two years old, and opened a clock and watch shop on Shop Row at Northampton. The advertisement he put in the Springfield paper promised the work would be done with neatness and dispatch.

narrative_blocks.header: He wanted a smart active boy of thirteen
narrative_blocks.body: In November 1790 he advertised twice in the Hampshire Gazette for an apprentice to the watchmaking business — a smart active boy of thirteen or fourteen. Joel Brown and Horace Clark both served their time under him.

narrative_blocks.header: Stiles and Baldwin lasted eleven months
narrative_blocks.body: In July 1791 he took Jedidiah Baldwin in as partner, in his own shop nearly opposite the meeting house, doing clock and watch work, jewelry and every branch of the goldsmith's business. Inside a year it was finished and he left Northampton.

narrative_blocks.header: Two spoons in Deerfield carry his mark
narrative_blocks.body: Historic Deerfield holds two silver spoons struck SS. The shop itself outlasted him by a century and a half, passing to Baldwin and Storrs, then Storrs and Cook, then B. E. Cook and Son, and at last to E. J. Gare and Son on the same row.

narrative_blocks.header: Out for Shays, and again for Fort Trumbull
narrative_blocks.body: He took part in Shays' Rebellion in 1787, the year he married. Twenty-six years later, at fifty, he was a private in a Windsor company posted to Fort Trumbull at New London while the British blockaded the coast.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine children in two Massachusetts towns
narrative_blocks.body: Hannah Ellsworth married him in 1787 and bore three at Northampton between 1788 and 1791, while the shop was his, and six more at Chester between 1793 and 1802. He went back to Windsor; she died in Massachusetts.

people.research_notes: First cousin of H00459 Kezia Munson Tuttle (EH 459) via shared grandmother H00092 Esther Hooker Stiles — Samuel's father Ashbel Stiles and Kezia's mother Keziah Stiles were full siblings. Born Dec 3, 1762 Windsor CT. Parents Ashbel Stiles (H00241, 1735-1810) and Hannah Stiles Stiles (I00160, his cousin from the Lt. Samuel + Mary Phelps Stiles branch — cousin marriage in the Windsor Stiles family). Married Hannah Ellsworth (I00613, 1767-1828, daughter of Jonathan + Jerusha Ellsworth of Windsor — the Ellsworth family produced Chief Justice Oliver Ellsworth, but Hannah's specific kinship to him not established here) on October 15, 1787 at Windsor CT. Nine children born across Northampton MA (3), Chester MA (6 including twins Amelia + Julia). Life path: Northampton MA (1787-c.1793) → Chester MA (c.1793-c.1810) → Windsor CT (final). WAR OF 1812 SERVICE: Private in Windsor company, Fort Trumbull (New London) Feb 1813. Died Windsor CT Oct 15, 1826 — exactly his 39th wedding anniversary. Hannah died Chicopee MA Jan 12, 1828, fifteen months later. Multiple children died young: Samuel drowned in Lake Erie 1818 age 25, Harriet d. 1823 age 33, Ellsworth d. 1823 age 26, Amelia d. 1822 age 20 (one year after marriage to William Welch, who himself died 1822). EH 461. SILVERSMITH/CLOCKMAKER: Operated Samuel Stiles shop in Northampton MA 1785-1792. First advertised in Springfield Hampshire Herald July 27, 1785. Took apprentices Joel Brown and Horace Clark per George Barton Cutten. Partnered with Jedidiah Baldwin July 1791-July 1792 (Stiles & Baldwin firm). Two silver spoons survive in Historic Deerfield collection with 'SS' maker's mark. After dissolving the partnership, Samuel left Northampton for Chester MA where the next six children were born. This makes Samuel a documented New England silversmith trade craftsman in addition to a War of 1812 veteran.

career.organization: Samuel Stiles shop, Shop Row, Northampton MA
career.notes: Opened shop in Northampton 1785, a few rods south of the Court-House. Advertised in Springfield Hampshire Herald July 27, 1785. Made silver including spoons with maker's mark 'SS' (two examples in Historic Deerfield collection). Took apprentices Joel Brown and Horace Clark, c.1789-1793.

Partnership with Jedidiah Baldwin (1769-1849), formed July 20, 1791 in shop nearly opposite the Meeting-house in Northampton — clock and watch business, jewelry, all branches of goldsmith's business. Baldwin had served apprenticeship to Thomas Harland of Norwich CT. Partnership lasted approximately one year before Samuel left Northampton.

Family resided in Enfield CT c.1810-1821. Job died Windsor CT Apr 13, 1813 age 48 — during the Enfield period, suggesting the family had returned to Windsor briefly or that the death record location differs from primary residence. Mary survived 26 years more, dying Windsor CT Mar 14, 1839. Buried together Old Windsor Graveyard (CEM326) per 'Inscriptions on one stone' notation. EH 462.

career.notes: Shoemaker by trade (EH 462 + Stiles book). The Stiles family resided in Enfield CT for about ten years (c.1810-1821) where Job died in 1813, then his widow returned to Windsor.

narrative_blocks.header: Windsor shoemaker, brother of silversmith Samuel
narrative_blocks.body: Job Stiles was a shoemaker by trade, working in Windsor CT and later Enfield CT. His older brother Samuel Stiles was a Northampton silversmith and clockmaker — together they represent two New England craft trades within the same Stiles family generation.

narrative_blocks.header: Died at forty-eight, buried with Mary in Windsor
narrative_blocks.body: Job died at Windsor CT on April 13, 1813 at age 48, during the family's roughly decade-long Enfield CT residence (c.1810-1821). His widow Mary Drake Stiles survived him by twenty-six years, dying March 14, 1839 at age 77. They were buried together in the Old Windsor Graveyard with their names inscribed on a single stone.

burial.plot_notes: Derby Center Cemetery, Orleans County Vermont — per FindAGrave #235170328. Died a year before husband Elisha relocated the surviving family to Montreal.

people.research_notes: Died 1814 in Vermont before the family's removal to Montreal. Her children became prominent figures in Montreal business and civic life. [Migrated from marriage.spouse_notes (spouse X01250)]: b. Jan 26, 1770 Northampton MA; d. Feb 21, 1844 Champlain NY. Moved to Montreal ca.1816; his brother Lewis co-founded a drug company there. STAGE 6Y-80 ENRICHMENT: FindAGrave #235170328 confirms burial at Derby Center Cemetery, Orleans County Vermont. The family arc: born Windsor CT 1768; married Elisha Lyman Jr. in 1793 at age 24; lived at Northampton MA then Conway MA then Derby VT; died Derby VT Feb 25, 1814 age 45 — one year before husband moved family to Montreal Canada for thirteen years (1815-1828). Of her ten children, two died in infancy at Conway and Derby; three sons (William, Benjamin, Henry) became the founders of Lyman Brothers, the largest pharmaceutical wholesaler in Canada — three of Hannah's sons settled the Hooker descent line into Quebec's mercantile and professional elite. Daughter Hannah married John Easton Mills, Mayor of Montreal who died of typhus caring for Irish famine immigrants in 1847 — potentially notable spouse for separate enrichment per Sam's direction.

narrative_blocks.header: Henry was four months old
narrative_blocks.body: Hannah died at Derby, Vermont, in February 1814, at forty-five, when her youngest, Henry, was four months old. The next year Elisha took the family north to Montreal.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten children in twenty years
narrative_blocks.body: Hannah bore ten children in twenty years, at Northampton, Conway and Derby, and buried two of them as babies, Ashbel in 1796 and Horace in 1798.

narrative_blocks.header: Mother of Lyman Brothers
narrative_blocks.body: Three of her sons, William, Benjamin and Henry, built Lyman Brothers in Montreal into the largest drug wholesaler in Canada, and her daughter Hannah married John Easton Mills, the mayor who died nursing the typhus sick.

narrative_blocks.header: A grandson's insects at McGill
narrative_blocks.body: Her grandson Henry Herbert Lyman left his collection of insects to McGill University, where it became the Lyman Entomological Museum.

narrative_blocks.body: William Lyman was the eldest of Hannah Stiles and Elisha Lyman's ten children, born April 9, 1794 at Conway Massachusetts. He moved with the family to Montreal in 1815 at age twenty-one and established himself as a Montreal druggist — the first of his brothers to enter the pharmaceutical trade in Canada. He died at Champlain New York September 7, 1857 and was buried at Mount Royal Cemetery Montreal.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed by the fever
narrative_blocks.body: Hannah was the mayor's wife through the typhus summer of 1847, when John went into the fever sheds to nurse the Irish immigrants. He died of it that November, and she was a widow at forty-eight, their youngest, Alice, only two.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at St. Gabriel Street
narrative_blocks.body: A Vermonter from Derby, Hannah married the young merchant John Easton Mills at Montreal's St. Gabriel Street Presbyterian church in January 1826, and their first child, Hannah Jane, was born that November.

narrative_blocks.header: Three sons in one year
narrative_blocks.body: In 1841 Hannah lost three sons in a single year: George at six, Edwin at two, and the baby Albert.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-four years a widow
narrative_blocks.body: Hannah outlived John by thirty-four years. She died at Upper Norwood, outside London, in May 1881, at eighty-one, and was brought back to Montreal to be buried at Mount Royal.

bio.bio_blurb: Montreal drug wholesaler and pharmacy reformer

narrative_blocks.header: Partner in the family drug house at seventeen
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin joined the Montreal drug firm of his uncle Samuel Hedge and brother William in 1827, at seventeen, and from 1836 he, William and Henry ran it as William Lyman and Company. It became Lymans, Clare and Company, wholesaling drugs, paints and oils from St Paul Street, with its own works on the Lachine Canal.

narrative_blocks.header: Toronto's largest drug wholesaler
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin kept a separate Toronto house from 1832 under a succession of partners, though he went on living in Montreal. By his death in 1878 Lyman Brothers was the largest wholesale drug company in Toronto, with travellers across Ontario and Manitoba.

narrative_blocks.header: A red label for poison
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin helped found the Canadian Pharmaceutical Association in 1867 and the Canadian Pharmaceutical Journal in 1868, and was president of the Ontario College of Pharmacy from 1873. In Ontario his firm was the first to mark every dangerous preparation with a bright red label.

narrative_blocks.header: Captain of the Cold Water Company
narrative_blocks.body: When rebellion broke out again in Lower Canada in November 1838, Benjamin was made captain of the 5th Company of Montreal Rifles, known as the Cold Water Company. He signed the Annexation Manifesto of 1849, lost his commission for it in 1850, and was reinstated, retiring a major in 1862.

narrative_blocks.header: Fire captain and alderman
narrative_blocks.body: With his brother Henry, Benjamin organized Montreal's volunteer Union Fire Company in 1840 and became its captain, and he sat on the city council from 1845 to 1850. In 1875 he was elected first vice-president of the Manufacturers' Association of Ontario.

narrative_blocks.header: He laid a church corner stone in 1865
narrative_blocks.body: An elder of the American Presbyterian Church in Montreal, Benjamin laid the corner stone of its new church on Dorchester Street in 1865. He was a founder of the Mount Royal Cemetery Company and its president, and was buried there.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirteen children, four outlived him
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin married Delia Almira Wells of Waterbury, Vermont, in 1834, and they had thirteen children; only two sons and two daughters outlived him. He died of pneumonia at Toronto in December 1878, on one of his business trips.

narrative_blocks.header: Thornhill on McTavish Street
narrative_blocks.body: About 1860 Henry built Thornhill on McTavish Street, just below the McTavish mansion. His widow lived on there, then his sons Col. H. H. Lyman and A. C. Lyman and his grandson Sydney, who sold it in 1941; it was pulled down for the McTavish Apartments.

narrative_blocks.header: A druggist at fifteen
narrative_blocks.body: Henry went into the family drug firm in 1829, at fifteen, and became a partner in Lyman Brothers, the largest drug wholesaler in Canada. He was a wholesale and retail druggist all his working life.

narrative_blocks.header: Lawyer, deacon, councilman
narrative_blocks.body: Henry also took a McGill degree and studied in England, was admitted to the Quebec bar and practised with Lyman, Class & Co. He was a deacon of the Congregational Church and sat on the city council for the West Ward.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight children, five grown
narrative_blocks.body: Henry and Mary Corse had eight children in Montreal, and five lived to grow up. They lost Arthur as a baby in 1847 and Susan Alice at five in 1853; their son Henry Herbert went down with the Empress of Ireland in 1914.

narrative_blocks.header: Married in the fever summer
narrative_blocks.body: Hannah married Nathaniel Whitney in July 1847, as the Irish famine ships were bringing typhus up the St. Lawrence. Four months later her father, the mayor, died of the fever he caught nursing the immigrants in the sheds.

narrative_blocks.header: A son named for her father
narrative_blocks.body: Her first child, born the next year, was named John Easton Mills Whitney, for the father she had lost. She raised eight children in Montreal and buried a daughter, Emma, at sixteen.

narrative_blocks.header: Three brothers in one year
narrative_blocks.body: Hannah was fourteen in 1841 when three of her little brothers died, George at six, Edwin at two and the baby Albert. Sixty years later her sister Ada was shot dead in the Redpath mansion on Sherbrooke Street.

narrative_blocks.header: Buried in her father's plot
narrative_blocks.body: Hannah outlived Nathaniel by twenty-one years and died in January 1905, at seventy-eight. She was buried at Mount Royal in the plot where her father lay.

m. John James Redpath (son of sugar refinery founder) 1867 Putney England. Left estate of $179,086 (~$5M today). Both Ada and her son Clifford Redpath died Jun 13, 1901 of gunshot wounds at their home 1065 Sherbrooke Street Montreal. Clifford may have died attempting to prevent his mother from ending her life. STAGE 6Y-81 MAJOR NOTABLE BUILD: Ada Maria Mills Redpath, 1842-1901, died with son Jocelyn Clifford in the Redpath Mansion Mystery — one of Canada's most famous unsolved-cases of the Gilded Age. Born Apr 26, 1842 Montreal. Father X01251 John Easton Mills (Mayor of Montreal who died of typhus 1847; she was 5). Mother Hannah Lyman Mills (HD0581). Three sisters; three brothers dead young 1841. m. John James Redpath (I00630, son of John Redpath founder of Canada Sugar Refining Company) in 1867 at Putney England. Marriage contract gave her control of her own assets — she purchased the family villa at 1065 Sherbrooke Street Nov 1870. Five children: Amy (HD4187, 1868-1954), Peter Whiteford (HD4188, 1869-1902), John Reginald 'Regy' (HD4189, 1871-1951), Harold Mills (HD4190, 1873-1948), Jocelyn Clifford 'Cliff' (HD4191, 1876-1901). Husband John James died 1884; Ada widowed at 42. Years of documented decline: ulceration of eyes, neuralgia of jaw, painful joints (brace fitted), melancholia, partial paralysis. By 1900 seldom left her bedroom; physically and emotionally dependent on her children Amy and Clifford. Estate at death $179,086.06 (~$5M today equivalent). DEATH: June 13, 1901 at 6 PM. Two revolver shots in her bedroom at 1065 Sherbrooke. Servants found Ada dead and her 24-year-old son Clifford fatally wounded (Clifford had just graduated McGill law). Coroner's inquest June 14; both buried Mount Royal June 15. The case became known as the Redpath Mansion Mystery — coroner's narrative: Ada had suicidal intent (had asked friends if life worth living); Clifford accidentally shot trying to take revolver; mother then completed suicide. Wide newspaper publicity given Redpath sugar fortune. Dinner party guests arrived to learn 'accident' had occurred. Some historians question the official account given Clifford's head wound and bright disposition. Original body preserved here for reference: 'On June 13, 1901 at six in the evening at the Redpath Mansion 1065 Sherbrooke Street Montreal, two revolver shots were heard from Ada's bedroom. Servants found her dead and her twenty-four-year-old son Jocelyn Clifford fatally wounded. The case attracted wide publicity given the Redpaths' Canadian Sugar Refining fortune, but the coroner's inquest was perfunctory; the prevailing theory held Ada had suicidal intent and Clifford was accidentally shot trying to take the revolver from her. She was buried two days later at Mount Royal Cemetery alongside her son.'

narrative_blocks.header: The Redpath Mansion Mystery, 1901
narrative_blocks.body: At six in the evening of 13 June 1901 two revolver shots were heard from Ada's bedroom at 1065 Sherbrooke Street. The servants found her dead and her son Cliff, twenty-four and just out of McGill law, dying beside her.

narrative_blocks.header: The inquest's verdict, and the other reading
narrative_blocks.body: The inquest found the next day that Ada had meant to take her own life and that Cliff was shot trying to take the revolver from her. Cliff's head wound has led many to the other reading: that he shot his mother in a rage and then himself.

narrative_blocks.header: Seldom out of her room by 1900
narrative_blocks.body: After her husband died in 1884 Ada's health failed by degrees: ulcerated eyes, neuralgia of the jaw, joints that needed a brace, melancholia, partial paralysis. By 1900 she seldom left her bedroom and leaned on Amy and Cliff.

narrative_blocks.header: Her marriage contract kept her money hers
narrative_blocks.body: Ada married Jack Redpath, co-heir to his father's fortune, at Putney in 1867, and her marriage contract left her in control of her own property as if she had never married. The Sherbrooke Street land was bought in her name in 1870.

narrative_blocks.header: She and her sister married Redpath brothers
narrative_blocks.body: Ada's younger sister, Alice, married her husband's brother George Drummond Redpath the same year, 1867. Alice was dead within two years.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father was the mayor the fever killed
narrative_blocks.body: Ada was five when her father, Mayor John Easton Mills, died of the typhus he caught nursing Irish immigrants in the fever sheds in 1847.

Bequeathed lepidoptera collection (~20,000 specimens) and $40,000 to McGill University at his death — founding the Lyman Entomological Museum at McGill. Perished with his wife on the Empress of Ireland, May 29, 1914.

people.research_notes:
[Migrated from death.notes]: Perished with his wife Florence Holwell Kirkby Lyman when the Empress of Ireland sank in the St. Lawrence River, May 29, 1914 — one of the deadliest maritime disasters in Canadian history (1,012 dead). They were on their delayed honeymoon voyage to England. Henry had spent years caring for his ailing mother, postponing his own marriage until age 57. He married Florence in 1912 and sailed two years later. Body not recovered. [Migrated from marriage.notes (spouse X01253)]: Both died May 29, 1914 — Empress of Ireland sinking on their delayed honeymoon. STAGE 6Y-81 WIKIPEDIA ENRICHMENT: Major notable confirmed via Wikipedia. Born Dec 21, 1854 Montreal — corrected from prior 'b.1854' month/day unknown. Anglo-Protestant elite family of Montreal's Square Mile. Education: West End Academy → Montreal High School → McGill BA 1876 (Logan medal in geology + natural science) → McGill MA 1880. Military: 5th Battalion Canadian Voluntary Force 1877; retired as Major 1891. Career: joined father's Lymans Clare & Co. (Canada's largest pharmaceutical company), succeeded as senior partner and president of Lymans Limited at Toronto. Public roles: organizer of Imperial Federation League of Canada (advocacy for Britain-colonies union); director Montreal General Hospital; director British and Colonial Press Service. Scientific career: member Entomological Society of Ontario from 1875; Montreal branch VP 1877, president 1881 + 1888-1899. Published 60+ papers mainly in The Canadian Entomologist on Lepidoptera. Grew hard of hearing requiring an ear trumpet; sometimes communicated by writing. Lived single, caring for ailing mother until her death. m. Florence Holwell Kirkby (X01253) Mar 14, 1912 Manhattan NY at age 57; she was 34. Two years later embarked on delayed honeymoon May 28, 1914 — drowned with wife May 29, 1914 in Empress of Ireland sinking on St. Lawrence River (840 passengers + 172 crew lost; one of worst Canadian maritime disasters). Body not recovered. Will bequeathed ~20,000 insect specimens + entomology books + $40,000 to McGill — founded Lyman Entomological Museum and Research Laboratory (moved to Quebec 1961). Lived 1911 at 74 McTavish St Antoine Montreal with six domestic servants; Anglican Church member.

The couple finally found time to travel two years later — boarding the Empress of Ireland on May 28, 1914 for their delayed honeymoon to Europe. Early on May 29, 1914 the ship collided in the St. Lawrence River and sank in fourteen minutes; both Lymans were among the 840 passengers and 172 crew lost. Henry's body was not recovered.'

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty thousand butterflies to McGill
narrative_blocks.body: Henry left McGill nearly twenty thousand butterflies and moths, 3,249 books and money to keep them, and they became the Lyman Entomological Museum. It now holds close to three million insects, the largest university collection in Canada.

narrative_blocks.header: Summers with a net on the Atlantic coast
narrative_blocks.body: Henry joined the Entomological Society of Ontario in 1875, collected butterflies on his summer holidays along the Atlantic coast and reared them at home, and published more than sixty notes, most in The Canadian Entomologist. He led its Montreal branch in 1881 and from 1888 to 1899.

narrative_blocks.header: Fourteen minutes in the fog
narrative_blocks.body: In May 1914 Henry and Florence at last sailed for their honeymoon on the Empress of Ireland. At 1:56 on the morning of the 29th the collier Storstad rammed her in fog off Pointe-au-Père; she sank in fourteen minutes, and both Lymans were among the 1,012 dead.

narrative_blocks.header: The Logan medal, then the drug firm
narrative_blocks.body: At McGill Henry took the Logan medal in geology and natural science with his B.A. in 1876, and an M.A. in 1880. He went into the family drug firm and rose to be senior partner and president of Lymans Limited.

narrative_blocks.header: An ear trumpet
narrative_blocks.body: Henry grew hard of hearing, used an ear trumpet and sometimes had to write to be understood. He lived at home and cared for his ailing mother until she died.

narrative_blocks.header: Major, and an imperial federationist
narrative_blocks.body: Henry served in the 5th Battalion of the Canadian volunteers from 1877 and retired a major in 1891, and he helped organize the Imperial Federation League in Canada, which wanted closer union with Britain.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at fifty-seven
narrative_blocks.body: Henry married Florence Holwell Kirkby, twenty-two years younger, in Manhattan in March 1912, when he was fifty-seven. The honeymoon waited two years.

narrative_blocks.body: Brainard Hooker served in the Revolutionary War and moved his family from Wethersfield, Connecticut to Middlebury, Vermont, where he died in October 1808 at age sixty-one. He was survived by his wife Mary Deming Hooker, who outlived him by thirty-five years, dying in 1843 at age ninety.

narrative_blocks.header: Born in 1747 when David Brainerd also died
narrative_blocks.body: Brainard Hooker was born in Woodbury, Connecticut on March 4, 1747 — the same year that the renowned Presbyterian missionary David Brainerd died in Northampton, Massachusetts on October 9, 1747. The name 'Brainard' was rare in colonial Connecticut, but Brainerd was Connecticut-born (Haddam) and celebrated across New England for his missionary work among Delaware Indians; his parents almost certainly named the baby in honor of the dying missionary.

narrative_blocks.header: Outlived two husbands; died at Henrietta at eighty-seven
narrative_blocks.body: Abigail Hooker Pixley buried her first husband Isaac Pixley in 1790 when she was thirty-six — left with six children, the youngest barely two — remarried James Root in 1793, bore another child, then buried Root in 1802 when she was forty-eight, and spent the next thirty-nine years a widow in Henrietta, New York, dying on January 6, 1841 at age eighty-seven. She had migrated from Woodbury, Connecticut to the Berkshire hills of Massachusetts as a young wife, and then west again to upstate New York as an old widow, the arc of her life tracking the westward movement of her entire generation — and she outlived every chapter of it, the Puritan inheritance carried through two husbands, seven children, and eighty-seven years.

narrative_blocks.header: He saw the fighting at Bennington
narrative_blocks.body: A native of Woodbury, Connecticut, he served in the Revolution and, by one pioneer history, was with Ethan Allen and witnessed the battle at Bennington in 1777. He married at Litchfield, then pushed west with the frontier — to Greene County, then Solon, then Truxton in central New York.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept moving west his whole long life
narrative_blocks.body: He settled Truxton on lot 94 around 1798, moved on to New Jersey in 1812, and in his eighties made the journey to Illinois to visit the sons who had gone ahead. He died on the way home, at Onondaga Hollow, at eighty-three.

narrative_blocks.header: A boy soldier who saw André hang
narrative_blocks.body: He joined the Revolution as a mere lad and served, by family account, through much of the war. He was among those present in 1780 when Major John André, Benedict Arnold's British contact, was executed as a spy.

narrative_blocks.header: He turned tin into a Bristol fortune
narrative_blocks.body: After the war he settled in Bristol and became one of Connecticut's most extensive manufacturers of tinware. He and Amy raised ten children there, where he worked until his death in 1838.

orbit_connections.name: Joseph Harvey (Yale 1809) — succeeded Asahel at Goshen
orbit_connections.relationship: Harvey succeeded Asahel Hooker as pastor at Goshen CT in 1810
orbit_connections.notes: Yale Biographical Sketches (Dexter): "The Rev. Asahel Hooker (Yale 1789) was dismissed from his pastorate over the Congregational Church of Goshen, in Litchfield County, on June 12, 1810; and Mr. Harvey thereafter supplied the pulpit with such favor that he was unanimously called to the vacant place." Also: Joseph Edwards (Yale, graduated c.1806) "began the study of theology upon graduation with the Rev. Asahel Hooker (Yale 1789), of Goshen, at the same time conducting an academy there." Asahel Hooker's Goshen pastorate was evidently a center of theological training in Litchfield County during the early 19th century. (Yale Biographical Sketches of Grads 1805-1815, Dexter 1912; URL: https://www.cga.ct.gov/hco/books/Biographical_Sketches_of_Grads_of_Yale_1805-1815_1912.pdf)

people.research_notes: b. Aug 29, 1762 Woodbury, Litchfield County CT; d. Apr 19, 1813 Norwich, New London County CT age 50 (per EH; born at Bethlehem CT per some sources). Son of Asahel Hooker (H00262) and Anne Parmalee Hooker (I00166). EH #514. Yale College 1789. Congregational minister: ordained at Goshen CT September 7, 1791; 18 years beloved pastor of the church in Goshen until dismissed for ill health Jun 12, 1810. After Goshen: became pastor of Chelsea Parish, Norwich CT January 16, 1812; died there April 19, 1813. Published several occasional sermons and articles in the Connecticut Evangelical Magazine. DOUBLE HOOKER CONVERGENCE: m. June 11, 1792, Phebe Edwards (H00940), daughter of Hon. Timothy Edwards (H00381, son of Rev. Jonathan Edwards). He was gen 5 Hooker through the Hooker surname line; she was gen 5 Hooker through Mary Hooker Pierpont → Sarah Pierpont Edwards → Timothy Edwards. Their children are descended from Thomas Hooker through BOTH parents. Their son Rev. Edward William Hooker D.D. (EH #1354) later wrote "The Life of Thomas Hooker" (1849) — the foundational Hooker biography cited by Edward Hooker in the 1909 Descendants book. Buried Norwich City Cemetery, Norwich CT. (EH 1909; Yale Biographical Sketches; Sprague, Annals 2:316; FindAGrave)

narrative_blocks.header: A school for preachers in his parsonage
narrative_blocks.body: From 1803 to 1810 Asahel trained thirty-two young ministers who boarded in his Goshen parsonage, among them Noah Porter, Heman Humphrey, Bennet Tyler and Joshua Huntington. Humphrey called him an Elisha among the young prophets.

narrative_blocks.header: Inherited a divided church, left it whole
narrative_blocks.body: Asahel was ordained at Goshen in September 1791 over a divided congregation and left it united. His health failed and he left in 1810; he preached at New Haven, New York and Charleston, then settled at Norwich, where he died in 1813.

narrative_blocks.header: He married his cousin Phebe Edwards
narrative_blocks.body: In June 1792 Asahel married Phebe Edwards, a granddaughter of Jonathan Edwards and his third cousin through Rev. Samuel Hooker.

narrative_blocks.header: The son who wrote Thomas Hooker's life
narrative_blocks.body: Asahel's son Rev. Edward William Hooker, a professor at the East Windsor seminary, wrote The Life of Rev. Thomas Hooker in 1849, the standard account of the family's founder for the rest of the century.

narrative_blocks.header: A sermon that outlived him in print
narrative_blocks.body: Asahel wrote for the Connecticut Evangelical Magazine, and his 1805 sermon at John Keep's ordination in Blandford survives in print. In doctrine he counted himself at one with Joseph Bellamy.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote that the vote was past
narrative_blocks.body: As registrar of the Litchfield County Association, Asahel kept its minutes himself, and wrote, more than once, that a vote was “past.”

people.research_notes: b. Aug 5, 1764 Bristol CT; d. Jun 22, 1826 Bristol CT age 61. Son of Asahel Hooker (H00262) and Anne Parmalee Hooker (I00166). Established one of the first woolen manufacturies in Connecticut — "his fulling mill was long known as the old yellow shop, near the bridge on the corner of East and South Streets; destroyed by fire in 1903." Town Clerk of Bristol 1806 and 1811-1820. CT General Assembly representative 1812, 1813, 1814, 1817. Jul 4, 1818: appointed delegate to Hartford convention to frame the CT Constitution. "He voted on the conservative side often and was chairman of many important committees." Deacon, Congregational Church (united Sep 29, 1799). m. (1) Lydia Lewis Oct 7, 1790 Hartford — she died without issue 1804. m. (2) Nancy Lee Fuller (widow with 2 children) 1804 Bristol — 3 children: Lydia Lewis (1805), Nancy (1809), Bryan Edward (1813). narrative_blocks.header: The old yellow shop by the bridge
narrative_blocks.body: He put up one of the first woolen manufactories in Connecticut, a fulling mill at the corner of East and South Streets that Bristol called the old yellow shop for generations. Fire took it in 1903, seventy-seven years after him.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped write Connecticut a constitution
narrative_blocks.body: Bristol sent him to the General Assembly four times, and on 4 July 1818 appointed him a delegate to the Hartford convention that framed the state's constitution — the one that finally cut the church loose from the state.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the Freeman’s oath at thirty-two
narrative_blocks.body: He swore the Freeman’s oath in September 1796 and joined the Congregational church three years after, serving as its deacon for many years. He sat on the board of poor relief, and gave privately besides.

narrative_blocks.header: Fourteen childless years, then a widow
narrative_blocks.body: Lydia Lewis married him in 1790 and died in 1804 after fourteen years, leaving no children. That October he married Nancy Lee Fuller — on the seventh, the same day of the month he had married Lydia — and she brought two children.

narrative_blocks.header: “Wouldn’t you like to see your mother?”
narrative_blocks.body: His stepdaughter Rhoda Ann Fuller, nine years old, boycotted the wedding and went to her grandparents. On his own advice nobody chased her for a year — then he drove over on business, asked the question, and she came home for good.

narrative_blocks.header: She married him a year before Brooklyn
narrative_blocks.body: She married Cyrus Porter Smith in September 1826, a year before he set up in Brooklyn. He waited six months there for a first client and thirteen years for the mayoralty; she was the mayor’s wife from 1839.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine children, in two states
narrative_blocks.body: She bore nine children between 1827 and 1846, some at Brooklyn and some back at Hanover in New Hampshire, where her husband had grown up. Three of them were buried as children.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten weeks between their two funerals
narrative_blocks.body: Cyrus Porter Smith died on 13 February 1877 and she followed him on 29 April. Both lie at Green-Wood, the cemetery he had a hand in founding.

narrative_blocks.header: He left his deathbed to vote
narrative_blocks.body: Struck by illness in November 1888, he rose from his bed to go to the polls for the presidential election — and never left his house again. Pneumonia followed; he died December 10. The Courant’s obituary closed: “Hartford had no better man.”

narrative_blocks.header: He took the company nobody wanted
narrative_blocks.body: When he assumed the Broad Brook company around 1862 it was heavily in debt and its stockholders despondent. He managed it successfully for more than a quarter century, until his death.

Founded first law practice in Blandford MA. Mentored by Theodore Sedgwick. Father of George Ashmun (US Congressman, presided over 1860 Republican convention that nominated Abraham Lincoln) and John Hooker Ashmun (Harvard Law professor, first buried on Harvard Hill).

narrative_blocks.header: Sedgwick’s five-year term, done in four
narrative_blocks.body: A man became a lawyer then by reading in a practising attorney's office — five years of it for a man with no college. He had a rudimentary schooling, read with Judge Theodore Sedgwick at Stockbridge, and was admitted a year early.

narrative_blocks.header: The first law practice Blandford had
narrative_blocks.body: He opened the first legal practice the town had, at the Blandford crossroads, in a house he built at Main Street and Russell Road. It came down in the last century for a filling station.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a Hooker of Northampton
narrative_blocks.body: He married Lucy Hooker, daughter of the Rev. John Hooker of Northampton, and they had five children. In 1807 he moved his practice to her town and never left it.

narrative_blocks.header: He finished Christopher Gore’s Senate term
narrative_blocks.body: A Federalist, he climbed from the Massachusetts House to the state Senate to the Governor's Council, and in June 1816 was sent to Washington to serve out Gore's term. He gave the seat up after two years and was dead within another.

narrative_blocks.header: Story remembered him in the Senate
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph Story, who sat with him there, wrote that he filled the office with dignity, ability and public respect. He left it voluntarily, from attachment to his practice or failing health.

narrative_blocks.header: The tavern at the Blandford crossroads
narrative_blocks.body: Justus Ashmun came to Blandford in 1777, driven south when Burgoyne's army forced a village above Albany to evacuate, and took the Pease tavern by the meeting house. Eli was the eldest of his eight.

narrative_blocks.header: Three generations of Ashmun lawyers
narrative_blocks.body: He read law under a judge, his elder son held the first Royall chair at Harvard, and his second gavelled Lincoln into a nomination.

burial.plot_notes: Bridge Street Cemetery, Northampton MA. Buried next to Eli, Lucy, and Orpha.

people.research_notes: b. Dec 11, 1802 Blandford; d. Aug 27, 1820 Northampton age 17. Oldest daughter of Eli and Lucy Hooker Ashmun.

narrative_blocks.header: Died one year after her senator father, 1820
narrative_blocks.body: Sophia W. Ashmun died in 1820, one year after her father Eli Porter Ashmun died in 1819 — two deaths in rapid succession that left the four surviving Ashmun children without both parents by the time Sophia was eighteen. Her brother George, who was fifteen at her death, would go on to preside over Abraham Lincoln's 1860 presidential nomination.
