bio.notes: Named "John Hooker" honoring maternal grandfather Rev. John Hooker (H00264)

narrative_blocks.header: Latin at nine, Harvard’s junior class at sixteen
narrative_blocks.body: A Mr. Grosvenor's school at Northampton had him reckoned an extraordinary Latin scholar by nine, and his father held him back a year when he was fit for college at twelve. Three years at Williams, then Harvard's junior class and a degree in 1818 — work that cost him little effort and gave him less relish.

narrative_blocks.header: The Northampton law school became his alone
narrative_blocks.body: Judge Howe took him into the Northampton Law School in the last year of Howe's life, and when Howe died he carried it on with Elijah Hunt Mills. Mills's health failed, and the teaching fell almost entirely on him.

narrative_blocks.header: First to hold the Royall chair at Harvard
narrative_blocks.body: The Harvard Corporation voted him unanimously into the Royall Professorship of Law in 1829, unsought and unexpected. He was the first man to occupy the chair and he held it until he died.

narrative_blocks.header: But the eldest boy upon the form
narrative_blocks.body: He told his students plainly when a question beat him — I am not lawyer enough to answer that — and called himself to Joseph Story but the eldest boy upon the form. His scrutiny was severe and they loved him.

narrative_blocks.header: A feeble voice, and every important cause
narrative_blocks.body: Ill health left him without grace of person or ease of action, his voice feeble and his utterance laboured, and he was slightly deaf. In the three interior counties he was engaged on one side of every important cause.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at daybreak, before thirty-three
narrative_blocks.body: Eight years of a slow constitutional disease ended on the morning of 1 April 1833, in a childlike sleep as the first light came. A fortnight earlier he had argued a case; the day before, he had laid the next year's teaching before Story.

naming_inspiration.description: Named Lucy Hooker after her mother Lucy Hooker Ashmun — the second of three Ashmun women to carry this name (mother H00532, herself, then niece HD4946 Lucy Hooker Ashmun Hedden).

narrative_blocks.header: Named for her mother; both died young
narrative_blocks.body: Lucy Hooker Ashmun carried the same name as her mother, who had died in 1812 when Lucy was just five years old. She herself died in 1836 at twenty-nine, the second Lucy Hooker in the Ashmun family to die young — and her niece would become the third to carry the name.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at sea off Nicaragua at forty-three
narrative_blocks.body: He died aboard the sloop of war Decatur on 2 March 1852, off Nicaragua. She was then with the Home Squadron, working the Atlantic coast and the Caribbean, and reached Boston that August to be laid up for repairs.

narrative_blocks.header: Six years married, and two sons
narrative_blocks.body: He married Mary Jane Strong of Greenfield in 1846, and Lewis came the next year and George two years after that. He was dead inside six years of the wedding; she married again in 1856 and went to New Jersey.

narrative_blocks.header: The ship he died on had hunted slavers
narrative_blocks.body: He died on a vessel with a history — twice out with the African Squadron after slave ships, in 1843 and again in 1848, and landing men at Tuxpan and Tabasco in the Mexican war. Three years after his death she stood off Seattle through a battle for the town.

narrative_blocks.header: He left a five-year-old namesake
narrative_blocks.body: The boy lived until 1930 and died at Los Angeles, seventy-eight years past his father and three thousand miles west of him. The other son, George, kept to the east and died in 1908.

narrative_blocks.header: The last of the senator’s five children
narrative_blocks.body: He was the youngest of Eli Porter Ashmun's five, nine years behind the brother who took Harvard's first Royall chair in law and five behind the one who gavelled Lincoln into a nomination. Neither of them reached sixty-six; he did not reach forty-four.

narrative_blocks.header: The gold rush ran through Nicaragua
narrative_blocks.body: He died in the one stretch of water everyone was crossing. Cornelius Vanderbilt's Accessory Transit Company had opened its Nicaragua route the summer before, the shortest way from New York to the California gold, and American warships were there to watch over the traffic.

narrative_blocks.header: He gaveled Lincoln into the nomination
narrative_blocks.body: Chosen chairman of the Republican National Convention at Chicago in May 1860, he held the Wigwam through three ballots and declared Abraham Lincoln the nominee. It is the thing his name is still attached to.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried the news to Springfield
narrative_blocks.body: The convention sent him at the head of the committee that formally notified Lincoln of the nomination, and he made the address in the parlour of the house at Springfield. Lincoln accepted in writing two days later.

narrative_blocks.header: The last note Lincoln ever wrote
narrative_blocks.body: On 14 April 1865 he called at the White House, and Lincoln — already leaving for Ford's Theatre — wrote him a card: 'Allow Mr. Ashmun and friend to come in at 9 A.M. tomorrow.' The President was shot that evening, and the appointment was never kept.

narrative_blocks.header: He walked Douglas over to Lincoln
narrative_blocks.body: In April 1861, with Sumter fallen, Ashmun brought Stephen A. Douglas to the White House — the rival Lincoln had beaten five months earlier. Douglas left pledged to the Union and spent the last weeks of his life saying so in public.

narrative_blocks.header: He answered the attack on Webster
narrative_blocks.body: When Charles Jared Ingersoll rose in the House in 1846 to accuse Daniel Webster of misusing the secret service fund, the inquiry fell to Ashmun's committee, and its report cleared Webster. It fixed him in Washington as Webster's man.

narrative_blocks.header: A seat on the transcontinental board
narrative_blocks.body: After Congress he sat as a director of the Union Pacific Railroad while the line was being driven west across the plains. He died in 1870, the year after the rails met at Promontory.

narrative_blocks.header: Born at the Blandford crossroads
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Blandford on Christmas Day 1804, where his grandfather Justus kept the tavern and his father practised law there. Yale had him in 1823.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale 1817 M.D. under Dr. Eli Ives
narrative_blocks.body: After Yale College 1814 he took his medical degree from the Medical Institution of Yale College in 1817, then practiced alongside Dr. Eli Ives in New Haven. Ives — Professor of Theory and Practice of Medicine at Yale until 1852 — would later be succeeded in that chair by George's younger brother Worthington Hooker (H01407).

narrative_blocks.header: Syracuse practice, then Longmeadow homecoming
narrative_blocks.body: After his New Haven training he removed to Syracuse, New York, where he practiced medicine for some years before returning east to Longmeadow, Massachusetts. He continued practice at Longmeadow until his death there 14 March 1884 at age 91.

narrative_blocks.header: Lived ninety-one years to 1884
narrative_blocks.body: He was born 7 March 1793 to Judge John Hooker (H00527) and Sarah Dwight Hooker (X00227) at Springfield, and lived past his ninety-first birthday — dying just seven days after it on 14 March 1884 at Longmeadow. He had outlived his celebrated younger brother Dr. Worthington Hooker (H01407) by seventeen years.

narrative_blocks.header: Judge Hooker's daughter, married at Springfield
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth, daughter of Judge John Hooker, married the young lawyer and editor Frederic Adolphus Packard at Springfield in May 1822, and he soon took over the First Church's Sunday school. In 1829 his Sunday School Union editorship took the family to Philadelphia, her home for the rest of her life.

narrative_blocks.header: A son named twice for her father
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth's first son, John Hooker Packard, named for her father the judge, died on his second birthday in 1829, the year the family left Springfield. She gave the name again to a son born in 1832, who became one of Philadelphia's leading surgeons; her youngest, Lewis Richard, became Yale's professor of Greek.

narrative_blocks.header: She and her son died thirteen days apart
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth died in Philadelphia on 5 July 1862, at sixty-four, and her son Frederick followed her on the 18th. Both were carried home to Springfield Cemetery, where she lies beside her parents and where her husband joined her in 1867.

people.research_notes: EH 1407 (renamed from HD0619 Stage 6Y-147). Gen 7 Thomas Hooker descendant via direct John Hooker paternal line. His second marriage to Henrietta Whitney Edwards (X00160, also gen 7 via the Pierpont-Hooker line) is a documented double Hooker convergence — Mary Hooker (H00034) was their common ancestor, four generations back from both. They had no children together. Publications: Physician and Patient (1849); Medical Delusions (1850, prize dissertation); Homeopathy: An Examination of the Doctrines and Evidences (1852, prize dissertation); Human Physiology (1854); Rational Therapeutics (1857); Child's Book of Nature 3 volumes (1857); Science for the School and Family 3 parts (1863); plus dozen+ articles in periodical literature. Yale obit source: Obituary Record of Graduates of Yale College, Deceased During Academical Year Ending in July 1868, pp. 275-276. Naming pattern CC opportunity: his sister-in-law's son Worthington Hooker Ingersoll (born 31 October 1862) was named in his honor — not yet built in tree but flagged for future. STAGE 6Y-153 UPDATE: Per new biographical source, Worthington had 6 children total, not 5 (Yale obit's 'five' likely undercounted the unnamed 1856 infant). Six children: HD3048 John Worthington Hooker (1833-1863, Yale 1854, Amherst Professor of Hygienics/Gymnastics; followed father into medicine); HD3049 Elizabeth Martin Hooker (1835-1845); HD04869 Edward Ingersoll Hooker 1st (1838-1839); HD04870 Edward Ingersoll Hooker 2nd (1840-1841); HD04871 unnamed son with Henrietta (1856-1856); HD04872 Alfred Edwards Hooker (1857-1887, the surviving child at father's death). Per new source both Edward children were named 'Edward Ingersoll Hooker' — the 'Edward I.' in FindAGrave + Ingersoll genealogy was abbreviation. Health: chronic dyspepsia from decades of demanding practice. Death 6 November 1867 from a short but severe illness; funeral 9 November at Yale's College Chapel, officiated by Rev. Dr. Bacon of First Church, well-attended by Yale Med faculty + students + visiting physicians; buried Grove Street Cemetery. Modern scholarship: Chester R. Burns's 1972 biographical profile in Yale Journal of Biology and Medicine remains the key academic study. Tom L. Beauchamp's 1995 analysis in Beauchamp/Childress Principles of Biomedical Ethics cited Physician and Patient as foundational for modern patient autonomy. Late additions to publications: First Book in Chemistry (1865); revised editions of Human Physiology (1864) and The Child's Book of Nature (1864, 1867). Intellectual contemporaries: Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr. (whose 1842 medical-delusions address paralleled Hooker's Homœopathy 1852); Yale chemist Benjamin Silliman (his teacher); German physiologist Johannes Müller (textbook influence). Active in the Connecticut Medical Society. Hooker also served on the New Haven Board of Education — likely the institutional basis for the 1900 naming of the Worthington Hooker School in his honor. notable.notable_blurb: Physician and pioneer of medical ethics

narrative_blocks.header: The book that told doctors to stop lying
narrative_blocks.body: His 1849 Physician and Patient argued that doctors owed their patients the truth, rejecting the accepted wisdom that a physician might deceive a patient for the patient's own good. A century later, bioethicists rediscovered it as one of the earliest American arguments for what we now call patient autonomy.

narrative_blocks.header: He spent a career hunting medical quackery
narrative_blocks.body: Trained in empirical method under Yale's Benjamin Silliman, he turned that skepticism on the fashionable cures of his day — dismantling homeopathy in an 1852 treatise and cataloguing centuries of medical delusions two years earlier. In that fight he stood alongside Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr., whose parallel attacks on homeopathy he echoed and extended.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-three years in Norwich, then Yale called
narrative_blocks.body: He practiced medicine in Norwich, Connecticut, for more than two decades before Yale chose him in 1852 to fill its chair of the Theory and Practice of Medicine. He held the professorship, teaching and practicing at once, until the day he died.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the science books children read
narrative_blocks.body: Alongside his medical work he became one of America's early popularizers of science for the young, writing The Child's Book of Nature and a family of school texts built to teach observation over superstition. Historians of education credit them with shaping scientific habits of mind in a generation of American schoolchildren.

narrative_blocks.header: A New Haven school still bears his name
narrative_blocks.body: In 1900, more than thirty years after his death, New Haven named a public school for him — recognition of his Yale professorship and his service on the city's Board of Education. The Worthington Hooker School still teaches today from its original building, now on the National Register.

narrative_blocks.header: Of six children, one outlived their father
narrative_blocks.body: He married twice — first Mary Ingersoll of Springfield, then Henrietta Edwards, a Connecticut governor's daughter who, like him, descended from Thomas Hooker. Across the two marriages he buried five of his six children, several in infancy; only his youngest, Alfred, lived to see him die in 1867.

career.notes: Settled in Macon Georgia after Yale and ordination; ministered there for several decades. His son Thomas was born at Macon in 1849.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried his frail health south to preach
narrative_blocks.body: His health was never strong, and after Yale and his theology studies he settled in the South partly to improve it, ministering there while his brothers stayed north in medicine and law. It failed him early all the same — he died at forty-nine — but to the end he was known for preaching extempore, with a polish that matched his written sermons.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a Yale president's granddaughter
narrative_blocks.body: At thirty-eight Richard married Aurelia Dwight, granddaughter of Timothy Dwight of Yale and his fourth cousin once removed: both came down from Rev. Samuel Hooker of Farmington, she through his daughter Mary, he through his son John.

narrative_blocks.header: A fearless, independent mind in the pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: Those who knew him recalled a vigorous, independent mind — clear and fearless in his convictions, generous in disposition, with broad views and cultivated taste. He read widely in history, poetry, and fiction, and wrote, one memoir said, as a man whose life was rich with proofs of his faith.

narrative_blocks.header: He was the second Richard his mother named
narrative_blocks.body: An earlier Richard was born in 1801 and buried before he turned two; the name went to the boy who came seven years later. He was the youngest of five brothers who lived — John, George, Josiah, Worthington, and himself — and four of the five went to Yale, Worthington on to become a noted physician and a professor there.

narrative_blocks.header: He never met his namesake grandson
narrative_blocks.body: He had one son, Thomas, born at Macon in 1849. That son gave him three grandchildren he never saw: a girl typhoid killed at twenty-three, a boy who ran the Springfield Republican for seventeen years, and a boy who put the Hooker name on a New Haven law firm.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave up chloroform after the deaths
narrative_blocks.body: John used nothing but chloroform until 1864. After fatal accidents in his own and his colleagues' practices, he told the College of Physicians in May 1865 that he was switching to ether, given with his friend Dr. Lente's inhaler. In 1872 he was the first to describe ether's brief early stage of anesthesia.

narrative_blocks.header: The soldier's arm he photographed
narrative_blocks.body: In July 1862 a wounded soldier, Martin Keller, came by steamer from Richmond to John's ward in West Philadelphia; John sawed five pieces of bone from his shattered arm and saved it. Keller wrote that the doctor was “very proud of the operation” and had the arm photographed.

narrative_blocks.header: A surgery manual the Union Army adopted
narrative_blocks.body: John's Manual of Minor Surgery of 1863 was adopted by the United States Army, and his Handbook of Operative Surgery followed. He translated Malgaigne's treatise on fractures and was chief editor of the first American edition of Holmes's System of Surgery in 1882.

narrative_blocks.header: Paris, then forty years in Philadelphia
narrative_blocks.body: After his Penn medical degree in 1853 John spent eighteen months in the Paris hospitals and eighteen as resident at Philadelphia's University Hospital. He then operated at the Episcopal, Pennsylvania and St. Joseph's hospitals and was secretary of the College of Physicians for fifteen years.

narrative_blocks.header: A doctor's case for sea air
narrative_blocks.body: John's book Sea-Air and Sea-Bathing argued that coastal air and bathing could help particular kinds of patients. He died at the Hotel Chalfont in Atlantic City in May 1907.

narrative_blocks.header: A septic finger ended his operating
narrative_blocks.body: In 1896 a finger John infected during an operation gave him septicemia and ended his surgical career at sixty-four, after more than forty years in practice.

narrative_blocks.header: Greece turned a minister into a Hellenist
narrative_blocks.body: Lewis left Yale in 1856 meaning to enter the ministry, but after a year of study in Berlin, a tour of Greece in 1858 made him a Hellenist for life. He came back to tutor at Yale and was named professor of Greek in 1863, at twenty-seven.

narrative_blocks.header: Hillhouse Professor through a long illness
narrative_blocks.body: In 1866 Lewis became Yale's Hillhouse Professor of Greek, and he kept teaching through a chronic illness that began when he was thirty-five. He was president of the American Philological Association in 1880 and 1881.

narrative_blocks.header: Morality and Religion of the Greeks
narrative_blocks.body: His one major book, Morality and Religion of the Greeks, came out in 1881, and with John Williams White of Harvard he began the College Series of Greek Authors. His papers on Thucydides, Homer and Plato were gathered after his death as Studies in Greek Thought.

narrative_blocks.header: He went out to Athens already weak
narrative_blocks.body: Lewis helped found the American School of Classical Studies at Athens and in 1883 followed William Watson Goodwin as its second director. He went out already weakened, fell ill, and died at New Haven on 26 October 1884, at forty-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: Born in Georgia, he came home anyway
narrative_blocks.body: His father was a Presbyterian minister at Macon, Georgia, and died at New Haven when Thomas was eight. The son took his Yale degree, spent five years studying and travelling in Europe, and came back to New Haven in 1877.

narrative_blocks.header: The paper he married into passed to Richard
narrative_blocks.body: Sally Bowles was the daughter of Samuel Bowles, whose Springfield Republican was among the most powerful newspapers in America. They married in New Haven in 1874 and had three children there. In 1915 their son Richard took the paper over.

narrative_blocks.header: He lost his eldest to typhoid at twenty-three
narrative_blocks.body: Aurelia was born in 1875 and died in the January of 1899, three months short of twenty-four. His two sons both went to Yale, as he had, and his father and grandfather before him.

narrative_blocks.header: From Yale tutor to bank president
narrative_blocks.body: He came home from Europe and started, briefly, as a tutor at Yale. Then he went into New Haven money and stayed twenty-five years — vice president and then president of the New Haven Trust Company, and president of the First National Bank from 1909. He gave ten years to the city's board of education besides.

narrative_blocks.header: His uncle's paper skipped two sons to him
narrative_blocks.body: The Republican had been a Bowles paper for ninety-one years — his great-grandfather founded it, his grandfather made it, his uncle held it. When the uncle died in 1915 the paper passed over both of that man's own sons and came to Richard Hooker, son of the eldest Bowles daughter. He was thirty-seven, gave up the editorship to poor health in 1922, and kept the presidency ten years more.

narrative_blocks.header: Berlin argued with his paper, not Wilson
narrative_blocks.body: In January 1916 the Republican ran an editorial headed Britain, America and Germany, arguing that a continuing quarrel over the Lusitania served British interests. Berlin read it — apparently relayed there by the German ambassador — and on the sixth of February the Associated Press cabled out that Wilson's Kansas speech had made little impression, but the Springfield editorial had made a deeper one. Count von Reventlow answered it in print.

narrative_blocks.header: Germans counterfeited his paper to smuggle rubber
narrative_blocks.body: British postal censors published a list of things being faked to get rubber into Germany through the mails, and the Springfield Weekly Republican was on it. The trick gave itself away — the paper had at most a few score readers in all of Germany, and the censors were suddenly finding far too many copies. Somebody in Berlin had guessed its circulation from its influence.

narrative_blocks.header: He advised four presidents and took no job
narrative_blocks.body: His papers hold something under a hundred letters — Wilson on the Navy and on second-class postal rates, Taft on Frank Brandegee, Coolidge on a Cambridge subway bill, Hoover on his own candidacy, Norris on the Electoral College. Wilson offered him an assistant secretaryship and Taft had offered him the White House press office; he took neither.

narrative_blocks.header: Named for a grandfather twenty-one years dead
narrative_blocks.body: Rev. Richard Hooker went south for his health, came home to New Haven and died there in 1857, at forty-nine. His grandson was born at Augusta twenty-one years later and lived to eighty-nine.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the paper's first hundred years
narrative_blocks.body: Macmillan published his history of the Republican's century in 1924 — the flatboat that poled his great-grandfather's press up the Connecticut from Hartford, the oxen that hauled it off the bank, and everything after. He wrote the corporate histories of Massachusetts Mutual and Aetna besides.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven years hauling the army's supplies
narrative_blocks.body: He served some seven years in the Continental Army, most of it as a teamster running the supply trains that kept the army moving. His comrades called him 'Captain,' and the name stuck.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife died at home while he soldiered
narrative_blocks.body: While he was away with the army, his first wife, Sarah Hubbard, died at Wallingford, their son Agathus barely two months old. The war's cost fell on the family he had left behind.

narrative_blocks.header: At sixty-eight he pulled up for Ohio
narrative_blocks.body: After years farming in Wallingford and Salisbury, he uprooted in 1812 for the Ohio frontier, settling at Springfield, where he died a decade later. His father, the physician James Hurlbut, had spent his last years under his roof.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother had died in that country first
narrative_blocks.body: Bethuel was killed on the Wabash in November 1791 at St. Clair’s Defeat, and lies under the Fort Recovery monument in Ohio. Twenty-one years later Raphael sold up at sixty-eight and took his family out to Ohio to farm.

people.prominent_name_reason: Jessie Willcox Smith (1863-1935) — celebrated American illustrator of the Golden Age. Studied at Pennsylvania Academy of Fine Arts under Thomas Eakins; studied under Howard Pyle at Drexel University 1894. Illustrated 60+ books including Louisa May Alcott's Little Women, Robert Louis Stevenson's A Child's Garden of Verses, and Longfellow's Evangeline. Created all Good Housekeeping covers Dec 1917 to 1933. "One of the greatest pure illustrators" of the early 20th century. Lived with "The Red Rose Girls" (Elizabeth Shippen Green, Violet Oakley) — a celebrated artistic household in Villanova PA. Never married; no children. Descendant of Thomas Hooker through: Jesse Hart → Harriet Hart Willcox → Katherine Willcox Smith → Jessie Willcox Smith. Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Willcox_Smith

narrative_blocks.header: Sixteen years of Good Housekeeping covers
narrative_blocks.body: She illustrated every monthly cover of Good Housekeeping from December 1917 through April 1933 — nearly two hundred paintings of children, mothers, and seasonal moments. Those covers shaped a generation's image of American childhood.

narrative_blocks.header: Defined the look of Heidi and Mother Goose
narrative_blocks.body: Her illustrations for The Water-Babies (1916), Little Women (1915), Heidi (1922), and A Child's Garden of Verses (1905) became the definitive editions of those books for two generations of American readers. She turned down film and theater commissions to keep illustration as her sole career.

narrative_blocks.header: The Red Rose Girls, and the Cogs
narrative_blocks.body: Jessie, Violet Oakley and Elizabeth Shippen Green shared a studio apartment at 1523 Chestnut Street, and in 1902 moved to the Red Rose Inn near Villanova, which gave them their name, the Red Rose Girls. From 1906 they lived at Cogslea in Mount Airy, named for the four Cogs: Henrietta Cozens, Oakley, Green and Smith.

narrative_blocks.header: Henrietta Cozens, her companion for life
narrative_blocks.body: Henrietta Cozens, no artist herself, ran the women's household from the Red Rose Inn on, and she and Jessie, the two eldest, were closest of all; their letters to each other are tender. When Oakley took over Cogslea in 1914 they moved to a new house on the property, Cogshill, and lived there until Jessie died in 1935.

narrative_blocks.header: They called her the mint
narrative_blocks.body: The most commercially successful of the three, Jessie was known around Cogslea as the mint. She chaired the Plastic Club's committee on designs and posters for three years, and with Green drew the Bryn Mawr College calendar.

narrative_blocks.header: A kindergarten teacher at a cousin's lesson
narrative_blocks.body: Jessie was teaching kindergarten when, in 1883, she sat in on a cousin's art lesson and at twenty decided to become an artist. She went through the School of Design for Women and the Pennsylvania Academy, under Thomas Eakins and Cecilia Beaux.

narrative_blocks.header: Pyle swept away the cobwebs
narrative_blocks.body: At Drexel in 1894 Jessie studied under Howard Pyle, who counted her among his best students. His teaching, she said, swept away “all the cobwebs and confusions that so beset the path of the art-student.”

narrative_blocks.header: His whole war fit in one brutal year
narrative_blocks.body: Seth's Revolutionary service was crowded into 1776. That year he helped guard besieged Boston through the winter, stood with the army in its rout at the Battle of Long Island, and rode in the light horse covering Washington's retreat across New Jersey.

narrative_blocks.header: A second attack took him the next afternoon
narrative_blocks.body: He was carrying groceries from the garage into the house on a Wednesday morning when the first attack came. By Thursday morning he was reported improved, and by half past three that afternoon a coronary thrombosis had killed him.

narrative_blocks.header: From Moody Bible School to embalming college
narrative_blocks.body: He went from Franklin Academy at Prattsburg to the Moody Bible School in Chicago, then graduated from the Barnes College of Embalming with the class of 1909. He was a lifelong Presbyterian, a Mason and a member of the Bath Grange.

narrative_blocks.header: His son left the Navy for the business
narrative_blocks.body: For his last three years he worked beside his son Hubert, who joined him after his discharge from the United States Navy. He left three children and six grandchildren.

narrative_blocks.header: The firm carried his wife's family name
narrative_blocks.body: At Bath the business was styled the Carpenter and Waldo Funeral Home; Carpenter was the maiden name of his wife Grace, whom he married at Prattsburg in 1910.

narrative_blocks.header: He trained as a doctor, then took orders
narrative_blocks.detail: He served as agent for the Connecticut Land Company (1796-1797) surveying lands in Cleveland, Ohio. Among his boarding school students around 1809 was his nephew James Gates Percival (X01936) — son of his sister Elizabeth Hart (H00610) — who later became a noted poet, Connecticut state geologist, and Wisconsin state geologist, writing his final report from memory without notes. The Hofstra University library holds the Hart-Nichols family papers, including correspondence compiled by Seth's granddaughter Mary Amelia Hart (1838-1932). His portrait was painted by Edwin Percival (nephew James Gates's brother) around 1829. (Hart Genealogy 1948; Hofstra Hart-Nichols Family Papers)
narrative_blocks.body: He studied classics, surveying, mechanics, and medicine at Yale, and was long called 'Dr. Hart' — but his wife's family drew him toward the Episcopal Church, and he gave up medicine for the priesthood. He was ordained by Bishop Seabury, the first American bishop, and served St. George's at Hempstead for twenty-eight years.

narrative_blocks.header: His boarding school launched nephew Percival's poetry
narrative_blocks.body: He ran a boarding school at Hempstead where his nephew James Gates Percival was sent in 1807 after their father's death. Despite Percival's resentment of his uncle's 'amiable, cheerful, almost jovial' efforts to draw him out, the Hempstead years were where Percival first wrote poetry.

narrative_blocks.header: Officiated Cleveland's first baptism, marriage, and burial
narrative_blocks.body: In spring 1797 he went to the Western Reserve of Ohio as General Agent and Chaplain of the surveying party sent by the Connecticut Land Company to develop their settlement at Cleveland. He spent six months in service and officiated at the first baptism, the first marriage, and the first burial occurring in Cleveland.

narrative_blocks.header: He read Cleveland’s first burial service
narrative_blocks.body: In 1797 he led the second party of the Connecticut Land Company west to their new settlement at Cleveland. When a young man drowned crossing a river, Hart chose the ground for a graveyard and read the burial office over him — the first religious service ever held in the city.

narrative_blocks.header: Paralysis took him, and then his wife
narrative_blocks.body: A severe stroke in 1829 forced him to resign the parish he had served since 1800, and he died three years later, much lamented by his parishioners. His wife Ruth was afterward struck by paralysis herself and died in 1841.

b. Jun 24, 1763 Kensington CT (bapt. Jun 26); d. Mar 16, 1832 Hempstead, Long Island NY age 68. Son of Matthew Hart (H00286) and Elizabeth Hopkins. Yale 1784. Episcopal minister. m. Ruth Hall (X00535) Oct 7, 1788. 7 children.
CC NOTE [X01936]: James Gates Percival and his brother Edwin were sent to Rev. Seth Hart's boarding school at Hempstead after their father's death in 1807. Seth was 'amiable, cheerful, almost jovial' — in sharp contrast to his melancholy nephew. He tried to draw Percival out socially. Percival resented the effort; portions of 'The Suicide' (1816-1820) were later said to be directed toward his uncle. Despite this, the Hempstead years were when Percival first wrote poetry. Both are 5th/6th generation Hooker descendants.
CC NOTE [X01938]: Rev. Seth Hart was painted by his nephew Edwin Percival around 1829 (ART024, oil on board). Edwin was a 6th-generation Hooker descendant through his mother Elizabeth Hart, Seth's sister. A Hooker descendant painted a Hooker descendant. [Migrated from birth.notes]: Baptized June 26, 1763 (Hart genealogy). EH gives June 24 as birth date. NB1 TRIM ADDENDUM (Apr 2026): The previous NB1 body included additional details now preserved here for completeness. The Hempstead post had been vacated by Rev. John Henry Hobart, who later became Bishop of New York. At Hempstead Hart ran a private boarding school from 1801 (where his nephew James Gates Percival was sent in 1807 — see NB2). He obtained a patent for a cloth shearing machine in 1811, and by 1816 was insolvent. In 1817 the parish attempted to remove him by petition; the motion failed overwhelmingly. He oversaw construction of a new St. George's church in 1822. His wife Ruth was also struck by paralysis and died November 3, 1841. YALE BIO SKETCHES ADDENDUM (Apr 2026, Dexter Vol 4): BIRTH DATE: Yale source gives June 21, 1763 (vs Edward Hooker 1909 and Hempstead church record giving June 24; baptized June 26). DEATH DATE: Yale source gives March 14, 1832 (vs March 16 in EH and other sources). Tree retains EH dates but flags discrepancies. CLEVELAND CHAPTER: Spring 1797 sent by Connecticut Land Company as General Agent and Chaplain to surveying party developing the Cleveland settlement. Officiated at the first baptism, first marriage, and first burial occurring in Cleveland — six months of service. Energy in conducting the expedition specifically noted. EARLY MEDICAL TRAINING: Probably studied medicine after Yale graduation; began practice before marrying into Episcopal church via Ruth Hall in 1788 (her sister was married to Rev. Ambrose Hull, Harvard 1785). PATENTS: (1) Nail-making machine — patented January 1799, while serving Worthington Parish Wethersfield. (2) Cloth shearing machine — patented 1811, while at Hempstead. He preached widely while serving in Waterbury (St. James), Woodbury, Salem (now Naugatuck), Wallingford (St. Paul's), and North Haven (St. John's) before Hempstead. PUBLICATION: Sermon preached at St. George's Hempstead first Sunday after consecration of rebuilt church, September 21, 1823 (New York, 1823, 8°, 16pp). Earlier sermon preached at Worthington Parish Wethersfield 1795 printed in Shepard's History of St. Mark's Church, New Britain. PORTRAIT: Preserved in vestry-room at Hempstead; reproduced in Shepard's History of St. Mark's Church. SOURCE: Dexter, Biographical Sketches of the Graduates of Yale College, Vol IV (covering 1778-1792).

people.prominent_name_reason: Frances Livingston Hart Butler (1816-1895) married Rev. Clement Moore Butler (1810-1890) — 36th Chaplain of the United States Senate 1850-1853. Butler delivered funeral addresses for Senator John C. Calhoun (Apr 1, 1850) and Senator Henry Clay (Jul 1, 1852). He also served as chaplain at the ordination by Bishop Benjamin Treadwell Onderdonk — Onderdonk was subsequently suspended after multiple women alleged he made improper advances, including toward Mrs. Butler in a carriage the evening before her husband's ordination. Butler later served as rector in Rome, Italy 1861-1864 and professor of ecclesiastical history at the Divinity School of the Protestant Episcopal Church, Philadelphia until 1884. Frances was "a niece of Richard Channing Moore, Bishop of Virginia." Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clement_Moore_Butler

James Gates Percival's biographer Samuel G. Goodrich wrote of her: 'she seems to have imparted to her son these qualities, with a tendency to excessive mental development.' Her son James also suffered from depression. After Dr. Percival's death in 1807, she married Samuel Porter (X01935); James worked on Porter's farm before re-entering Yale. (Ward, 1866; historicbuildingsct.com) [Migrated from birth.notes]: Bapt. Dec 24, 1769 per EH. [Migrated from death.notes]: Year approximate per Hofstra; 'died c1846.' narrative_blocks.header: Widowed and bereaved in a single winter
narrative_blocks.body: In the early weeks of 1807 she lost, within five weeks of each other, her husband Dr. James Percival and her young daughter Harriet. She was left a widow with young sons, among them the boy who would become the poet James Gates Percival.

narrative_blocks.header: Her second marriage unsettled her poet son
narrative_blocks.body: Some years after her first husband's death she married the farmer Samuel Porter. Her brilliant, brooding son James, set to work his stepfather's fields, chafed at the arrangement and soon fled back to Yale and his books.

narrative_blocks.header: A Hart of Kensington who raised a poet
narrative_blocks.body: Born Elizabeth Hart in Kensington in 1769, a daughter of Matthew Hart, she married Dr. James Percival at twenty and bore him several children. She outlived her husband by nearly forty years.

people.research_notes: [Migrated from marriage.spouse_notes (spouse X01320)]: Sally Bronson — Bronson family of Hartford/Farmington. Richard Bronson baptized Jul 23, 1615 Earl's Colne, Essex, England — arrived Hartford 1636 with his brother John. John Bronson: "believed to have been one of the company who came with Mr. Hooker, in 1636, of whose church he was a member. He was a soldier in the bloody Pequot battle of 1637." One of seven pillars at organization of Farmington church 1652. Sally's exact line through Bronson family not identified — no "Sally" found in Bronson genealogy sources. Also note: Amos Bronson Alcott (1799-1888) and Louisa May Alcott (1832-1888) are from the Bronson line through Anna Bronson, daughter of Capt. Amos Bronson — a different branch.

Cowles). EIGHT CHILDREN per WikiTree (only Catharine reached adulthood with surviving descendants): - Samuel Deming (b. Mar 28, 1784) — not built - Diadema Deming (1785-1785) — died_in_infancy, not built - Catharine Deming Cowles (Feb 5, 1787 - Oct 30, 1859) — m. Only Samuel (1784) and Catharine (1787) reached adulthood; only Catharine produced surviving descendants per WikiTree. STAGE 6g ENRICHMENT — WikiTree's full child list confirmed:
Diadema and Chauncey had 8 children, of whom only Catharine reached adulthood. Per WikiTree:
1. Samuel Deming (HD3661) — died young
2. Diadema Deming (HD3662) — died young, named for mother
3. Catharine 'Katherine' Deming Cowles (H01580, EH#1580, 1787-1859) — ONLY adult survivor; m. Major Timothy Cowles (H00698)
4. Jennette Deming (HD3663) — died young
5. Unnamed infant Deming (not built — covered here in research_notes)
6. Unnamed infant Deming (not built)
7. Samuel Deming No. 2 (HD3664) — died young, replacement_naming after elder Samuel
8. Unnamed infant Deming (not built) EH 1909 records only #1580 Katherine because the others died before reaching descendant status. The replacement_naming pattern (two Samuels) and the seven infant/young deaths in a row before Catharine survived speaks to the ordinary brutal arithmetic of New England infant mortality in the 1780s-1790s.

narrative_blocks.header: Five of eight children died as infants
narrative_blocks.body: She and Chauncey Deming had eight children between 1784 and 1794 and buried seven of them small — two boys both named Samuel, two unnamed twin daughters dead at two days, and three more. Only Catharine, born in 1787, grew up.

narrative_blocks.header: Christmas Day birth in Farmington, 1756
narrative_blocks.body: She was born on Christmas Day 1756 at Farmington Hartford County CT — second child of James Cowles and Abigail Hooker Cowles. The birth occurred at the height of the French and Indian War, twenty years before Farmington would send its sons to the Revolutionary muster fields.

narrative_blocks.header: She married into the Farmington store
narrative_blocks.body: She married Chauncey Deming of Plainville at Farmington in February 1780, and he built the town’s leading mercantile house. She died at Farmington in September 1826, aged sixty-nine, six months before he did.

narrative_blocks.header: A childless second marriage
narrative_blocks.body: Amy Cowles married the widower Joseph Andrews in 1806 at age 47 and the marriage produced no children. His eight children by his deceased first wife Lydia Judd were her stepchildren, most of them already grown or buried by the time she entered the household.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a signer’s daughter
narrative_blocks.body: A merchant and sloop owner known around Rhinebeck as ‘Captain’ Cowles, he married Lydia Adams, daughter of Andrew Adams — the Connecticut chief justice who signed the Articles of Confederation. Their son Henry Booth Cowles went to Congress.

narrative_blocks.header: Four towns, and then sloops on the Hudson
narrative_blocks.body: He traded at Litchfield, then New York, then Hartford, and settled at last at Rhinebeck on the Hudson. There he owned sloops on the river, and the town called him Captain Cowles for it though he had never held the rank.

narrative_blocks.header: She married the cousin she grew up beside
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband Elijah was also her first cousin — her father James and his father Elijah were Cowles brothers, both sons of Capt. Isaac Cowles. The match kept the Farmington Cowleses marrying close.

narrative_blocks.header: She renamed two children after two she lost
narrative_blocks.body: Two of her children died young — an infant Augustus and a Harriet who reached eighteen — and each time the next child to come took the same name. The second Augustus grew up a Farmington merchant; the second Harriet outlived them all.

narrative_blocks.body: Eleazer died at Montpelier in 1831 and left her the farm and the children. She married Simeon Babbitt in 1839 and buried him in 1844, then lived another twenty-one years and died at Berlin in August 1865, aged eighty-five.

narrative_blocks.header: Her stone names her first husband
narrative_blocks.body: The marker over her grave calls her the wife of Eleazer Scovill, not of the man she married second. She had been Babbitt's widow for twenty-one years by the time it was cut.

narrative_blocks.header: She named her first son for her father
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph Langdon of Farmington was her father and Ruth Hooker her mother, and the boy born to her in October 1806 was christened Joseph Langdon Scovill. The Hooker descent she carried north came back to Connecticut in the third generation, when her grandson took Trinity Church on the New Haven Green.

narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Farmington in the March of 1772, the first child of a Hooker who had just married an Ingersoll. They gave him the name of his mother's uncle Jared Ingersoll — the man who had taken the King's stamp distributorship and been ridden off the Wethersfield road for it seven years before.

narrative_blocks.header: He went north with the family and stayed
narrative_blocks.body: His parents left Farmington after the Revolution, when the town would not have his father back, and he was young when they got to Litchfield in New York. He settled at Sangerfield in Oneida County, married there in 1800, and was a magistrate for many years.

narrative_blocks.header: Husband organized first Episcopal parish in Ohio
narrative_blocks.body: Sally's husband Rev. Roger Searle organized the first Episcopal parish in Ohio — St. Peter's at Ashtabula on February 19, 1817 — and preached the first religious service in Medina County Ohio on March 11, 1817. He went on to organize Trinity Cleveland, St. Mark's Columbia, St. James' Boardman, and St. Luke's Ravenna. Sally lived alongside this Ohio Episcopal circuit-rider mission through its founding decade.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at Ohio frontier age fifty-four
narrative_blocks.body: Sally was widowed at age fifty-four when Rev. Searle died September 6, 1826 in Ashtabula Ohio. She lived another twenty-three years and ultimately died in 1849 at Ogdensburg, Saint Lawrence County New York — having migrated from her Ohio widowhood home northeast to the Saint Lawrence River frontier. The Connecticut-to-Ohio-to-Ogdensburg migration arc spanned three frontier regions across her seventy-six years.

narrative_blocks.header: Two children: son Lucian and daughter Nancy
narrative_blocks.body: Sally and Rev. Searle had two documented children. Their son Lucian Theodoscius Searle (1808-1895) lived to age eighty-seven; their daughter Nancy Sarah Marie Searle Johnston (1817-1906) lived to age eighty-eight or eighty-nine. Both children outlived the parents by half a century and represent the surviving Searle line through Sally Pomeroy's marriage.

narrative_blocks.header: Middletown CT 1772 to Ogdensburg NY 1849
narrative_blocks.body: Sally Pomeroy was born April 21, 1772 in Middletown Connecticut, daughter of Adino Pomeroy and Lois Strong Pomeroy. She married Rev. Roger Searle on August 7, 1800 and died January 17, 1849 at Ogdensburg, Saint Lawrence County New York at age seventy-six. She is buried at Ogdensburg Cemetery.

narrative_blocks.body: The society was organised in August 1791 and he served it forty years, from 1793 until he resigned in 1833. He had been valedictorian of the Yale class of 1790.

narrative_blocks.header: Revival and abolition cost him the pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: The 1830s wanted evangelists and he was modest and scholarly. His congregation also wanted the church to lead openly against slavery. He gave it up in 1833 and farmed for twenty more years.

narrative_blocks.header: His farm is on the national register
narrative_blocks.body: He built it where Norton Road meets Washington Road outside Clinton and lived there until 1853. His brother Seth ran the Hamilton-Oneida Academy up the hill and taught at the college after it.

bio.bio_blurb: Hamilton College professor of languages and interim president

narrative_blocks.header: Principal of the Oneida Academy at twenty-seven
narrative_blocks.body: Yale gave him a degree in 1804 and kept him three years as a tutor. He went out to Clinton in 1807 to run the Oneida Academy, and stayed on when it became Hamilton College in 1812.

narrative_blocks.header: A very accurate Greek and Latin scholar
narrative_blocks.body: Gerrit Smith, a student in his time, wrote that no teacher was ever more devoted to the improvement of his pupils, and that his death was a great loss to the college.

narrative_blocks.header: Backus said he was intriguing for his shoes
narrative_blocks.body: He wanted the presidency of Hamilton and the first president knew it. When Azel Backus died of typhus in 1816, caught from a tutor he had nursed, Norton got the place and held it for a time.

narrative_blocks.header: Egyptian Revival, and no religious carving
narrative_blocks.body: He was buried in the village first and moved up to College Hill in the 1850s, where his stone is one of the handsomest in the ground. He lies beside Azel Backus, whose office he had wanted.

narrative_blocks.header: Dead at thirty-eight, in the chair
narrative_blocks.body: He held the professorship of languages six years and died at Hartford in December 1818, leaving Amanda Kellogg with a daughter born that same year. His nephew Edward Robinson had left Hamilton two years before.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight children, the first lived sixteen days
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah's first child, Maria, lived sixteen days in the autumn of 1789, and seven more followed over seventeen years, the last of them Oliver Wetmore Ellsworth in 1806. Widowed in 1816, Sarah died at Greensboro in June 1818, at forty-seven.

narrative_blocks.header: Two of her children went to the Cherokees
narrative_blocks.body: In 1821, three years after Sarah's death, her son John Clark Ellsworth and her daughter Harriet went south to Brainerd Mission in Tennessee. Harriet married the missionary Ainsworth Blunt there, and when the Cherokee removal came in 1838 he walked part of the Trail of Tears with them.

narrative_blocks.body: He was a son of Dr. Abijah Scovil, and settled his father's estate at Bristol in 1802. His Vermont descendants kept the mortar and pestle the doctor had ground his drugs with, and spoons cut from his silver knee and shoe buckles. His youngest son went into patent medicine.

narrative_blocks.header: Plymouth, then Farmington, then Vermont
narrative_blocks.body: He married Abigail Langdon at the start of 1806, and she came to him from the Farmington parish that spring. While their eldest was still an infant he moved them all back to Farmington, and by 1814 his name sat on a list of letters waiting at the Berlin post office in Vermont.

narrative_blocks.header: The first house had two rooms
narrative_blocks.body: The farm he took up at Berlin was worked out of a log house thrown together in a hurry. The better dwelling that replaced it was the best in the neighborhood for a while and ended its life as a barn.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty-two, and the stone still stands
narrative_blocks.body: He died at Montpelier on 27 September 1831 and was buried in the Elm Street ground, where his gravestone survives. Abigail was fifty-one, with six children, and did not marry again for eight years.

people.research_notes: b. Jan 11, 1731 Suffield CT; d. Sep 9, 1802 Heath MA age 71. Son of Lt. Joshua Leavitt and his 2nd wife Mary Winchell. Yale 1758. Ordained Walpole NH May 27, 1761; dismissed ca.1764 after allegedly dragging a runaway enslaved woman home by rope tied to his saddle. Installed Charlemont MA 1767; dismissed 1785 for Loyalist sentiments. Preached in schoolhouse, sued parishioners for back wages, won ~£700. Retired to Heath MA. Wore large white wig, cocked hat. "His prayers were incredibly long... his sermons dry." NOTABLE: His sister Jemima Leavitt married Capt. David Ellsworth — making him uncle of Chief Justice Oliver Ellsworth, Founding Father and first Chief Justice of the US Supreme Court. His wife Sarah died Oct 11, 1791, "as a consequence of taking wrong medicine" — the medicine given to her by their daughter Clarissa. Obituary: "inexorable death received commission, in a sudden and unexpected manner, to summon into the world of Spirits, Mrs. Sarah Leavitt... in the 49th year of her age." [Migrated from top-level anecdotes]: {"grandsons_book_1904": "Two of Rev. Jonathan Leavitt's grandsons \u2014 John Hooker Leavitt (Iowa banker) and William Hooker Leavitt (Minneapolis businessman) \u2014 published a slim volume in 1904 titled \"A Sketch of the Life and Character of Rev. Jonathan Leavitt, the first Minister of Charlemont, Mass.\" The book attempted to portray their controversial ancestor as \"a misunderstood and complicated man.\" It was published two years before John Hooker Leavitt's death in 1906.", "the_dry_sermons_and_long_prayers": "A ministerial colleague's description of Leavitt's preaching, preserved in the History of the Churches and Ministers in Franklin County, Massachusetts (Theophilus Packard Jr., 1854): \"His sermons are not fresh and beautiful by the imagination, not ardent and overflowing with love, but didactic, dry, and clean, and very long. His services were delivered in a dull monotony, and his prayers were incredibly long, in public and in family devotions.\" A separate account noted he \"would do more execution with one nod of his wig, than you or I could in talking half an hour.\" Despite this, his congregation at Walpole rose as one when he entered the meeting house to do obeisance to \"the man in black.\" His wife Sarah (Hooker) Leavitt followed him in \"full suit of brocade lutestring, without any bonnet, holding a fan to shade the sun from her face, as was the fashion 'down country'.\" Source: Wikipedia, citing Collections of the Massachusetts Historical Society, Vol. III, E.W. Metcalf & Co., Cambridge, 1833."} Stage 6Y-687: Wikipedia URL, photo, tags applied per compiler. m2 Aug 27, 1792 Tirzah (Field) Ashley, widow of his classmate (d. 1797); m3 May 20, 1798 Mary (Todd) Foote (d. 1816) — wives noted, not built. Won roughly £700 total suing his Charlemont parishioners. REBUILD 081226. The old six blocks ran 379 words and fell off the bottom of the card, the headers posed riddles, and the rope-and-saddle incident was told twice — the second time so compressed ('the minister run out of Walpole over a rope and a saddle') that it read as though he had run a MINISTER out by rope. It appears once now. FROM THE YALE OBITUARY RECORD (Dexter), supplied 081226 and the better authority where it differs: born at Suffield when Suffield was still in Massachusetts — it transferred to Connecticut in 1749. Mother Mary, daughter of Capt. Joseph Winchell of Suffield. Freegrace Leavitt (Yale 1745), who preached the ordination sermon, was his HALF-brother; the sermon was printed. Dismissed from Walpole 19 June 1764. He then meant to leave the Congregational church altogether: in May 1765 he attended the Synod at Philadelphia and was received as a member of the Presbyterian body. Installed at Charlemont October 1767. The trouble there was partly his alleged ARMINIAN doctrine and only partly his suspected lukewarmness toward the Revolution — the card's older framing, straight Loyalism, is the Wikipedia account. August 1781 the town voted him dismissed with no council held; regular dismission 15 April 1785. CONFLICT: Dexter says that, refused the meeting house, he held meetings AT HIS OWN HOUSE (used on the card); the Wikipedia account says the town schoolhouse. He recovered before the Supreme Court 500 for preaching after the meeting house was closed to him and 200 for currency depreciation. In February 1785 the part of Charlemont he lived in was set off as the separate town of HEATH — the town line moved around him rather than him moving. Married Sarah, daughter of Roger Hooker of Farmington, on 10 December 1761; eleven sons and one daughter, all of whom grew to maturity. He published A Concise View of the New Covenant, the Church's Duty, and of Divine Appointment or Decrees (Northampton, 1801), five sermons and two addresses given to the church at Heath, with eight pages of subscribers' names. His widow died at Bernardston in 1816. OFF THE CARD FOR ROOM: the congregation rising to the man in black and his full bow back; Sarah walking in behind him in brocade lutestring, no bonnet, a fan against the sun; the sermons 'didactic, dry, and clean, and very long' and the prayers 'incredibly long'; one nod of his wig doing more execution than another man in half an hour; the unproved rumour that he took the only cows of two poor parishioners for his back salary; the 'penny tax' Charlemont laid per acre; his recall to that pulpit 1 September 1769. NOT THE SAME MAN: a Rev. Jonathan Leavitt of Providence — American Seaman's Friend Society, American Colonization Society, examiner at Brown — appears in the supplied material and belongs to a later generation. Do not merge. NOTE the two Joshuas: his third son Joshua, who vanished, and his grandson Rev. Joshua Leavitt (Yale 1814), the abolitionist editor.

narrative_blocks.header: Two churches called him; both put him out
narrative_blocks.body: He was a Yale-trained Congregational minister who held the first settled pulpits of two frontier towns, Walpole in New Hampshire and Charlemont in the Berkshires. Both put him out — one for cruelty to an enslaved woman, the other for his politics.

narrative_blocks.header: He dragged a runaway woman behind his saddle
narrative_blocks.body: Walpole handed it down that he brought a runaway enslaved woman home behind his horse, on a rope tied to his saddle. Colonel Bellows said he had settled Parson Leavitt and would now unsettle him. It still took three years.

narrative_blocks.header: They locked the church; he preached at home
narrative_blocks.body: Charlemont turned on him for his doctrine and for going lukewarm on the Revolution, stopped paying him, and in 1781 voted him dismissed without a council. Shut out of the meeting house, he preached on in his own house for four years, then sued the town and won.

narrative_blocks.header: The son who vanished for eleven years
narrative_blocks.body: His third son Joshua left home secretly in 1791, at twenty-four, and the family heard nothing for eleven years. In July 1802 word came that traces of him had been found in New York, and his father set out at seventy-one. He came home worn out and died that September.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandsons ran the Underground Railroad
narrative_blocks.body: The slaveholding parson was grandfather to another Joshua Leavitt, the abolitionist editor, and to Roger and Hart Leavitt, who sheltered escaping slaves at Charlemont itself. Two descendants published a book in 1904 calling him misunderstood.

narrative_blocks.header: Uncle of the third Chief Justice
narrative_blocks.body: His sister Jemima married Capt. David Ellsworth, and their son Oliver became the third Chief Justice of the United States. Jonathan was not yet two when his father, a brother and a sister all died within three days.

people.research_notes: OCCUPATION NOTES: Judge of the Court of Common Pleas and second Judge of Probate Court, Franklin County MA. Built the "Hovey House" in Greenfield 1793. "Maintained a most attractive house about which was centered the social life of the northern portion of old Hampshire County." His wife Emilia Stiles was daughter of Ezra Stiles, President of Yale. [Migrated from death.notes]: Some sources give 1831; May 1, 1830 supported by FindAGrave. [Migrated from marriage.spouse_notes (spouse X00156)]: b. Apr 21, 1762 Newport RI; d. Nov 7, 1833 Greenfield MA. Daughter of EZRA STILES, President of Yale College (1778-1795). Cross-connection: Ezra Stiles also appears in our tree as half-brother of a Hooker descendant. [Migrated from top-level occupation]: ['Judge', 'Lawyer', 'State Senator', 'Businessman'] ENRICHED 081226 from Wikipedia and Dexter's Yale sketches. Born at Walpole the year his father was dismissed from that pulpit; raised at Charlemont. Kept a school for young ladies in New Haven with his classmate Bidwell while reading law with Judge Charles Chauncey; admitted at New Haven November 1788, settled at Greenfield 1789. State assemblyman 1802 and 1803, senator 1818. Also published 'A Letter from a Trinitarian to a Unitarian' (Greenfield, 1820, signed only J.L.) and 'Thoughts on the Gospel Message'. A miniature of him painted about 1812 is at the Yale University Art Gallery. DEATH YEAR CONFLICT: 1 May 1830 per FindAGrave and used here; Dexter says 1 May 1831 'in his 68th year'. narrative_blocks.header: The standard book on the law of paupers
narrative_blocks.body: He came to the Greenfield bar in 1789 and rose to Judge of Probate and a justice of the Court of Common Pleas. His Summary of the Laws of Massachusetts on the support and removal of paupers, printed at Greenfield in 1810, was the standard work.

narrative_blocks.header: Asher Benjamin designed him a house in 1797
narrative_blocks.body: The architect Asher Benjamin, who taught a generation of New England builders through his pattern books, designed his house on Greenfield's Main Street. It stands as the Leavitt-Hovey House, and he worked from its west wing.

narrative_blocks.header: His son died at Yale, and he resigned
narrative_blocks.body: His only surviving son Jonathan died at New Haven in May 1821, a junior at Yale, aged eighteen. He resigned both his judgeships that year, and a sister published a memoir of the boy the next.

narrative_blocks.header: First president of the county bank
narrative_blocks.body: He founded the Franklin Bank of Greenfield in 1822 and was its first president, though he gave it up within the year. He had been a deacon of the First Church since 1799 and helped form a second Congregational church in 1816.

narrative_blocks.header: The two people his wife inherited
narrative_blocks.body: He married Emilia, third daughter of Ezra Stiles, president of Yale. Three African-American servants lived in the Greenfield house, and on her father's death she inherited the two elderly people he had enslaved, Newport and Nabby.

narrative_blocks.header: The Liberty Party’s man for Lieutenant Governor
narrative_blocks.body: President of the Franklin County Anti-Slavery Society, he accepted the new Massachusetts Liberty Party’s 1840 nomination for Lieutenant Governor — the abolitionist ticket his son Joshua’s party-building made possible. His household sheltered Basil Dorsey alongside his sons’.

narrative_blocks.header: Four terms in the Massachusetts legislature
narrative_blocks.body: He was a large landowner at Heath and went four times to the General Court. In 1833 he left the family homestead for a brick mansion on the bank of the Deerfield River at Charlemont, where his sons were.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped Mary Lyon start Mount Holyoke
narrative_blocks.body: He worked with Mary Lyon at the beginning of her seminary for girls at South Hadley — the school that became Mount Holyoke, and the first of its kind in the country to endow the education of women.

narrative_blocks.header: His sons brought him over to abolition
narrative_blocks.body: He came late to the cause and his three sons brought him. After the Utica mob of 1835 he was an abolitionist for life, and the South was said to have offered a price for the head of his eldest son, Joshua.

narrative_blocks.body: Charles Jenkins died at Portland at the end of 1831, forty-five years old, and left her with three children and no pulpit. She had just turned thirty-two. She waited ten years, and married Dr. Elial Todd Foote at Greenfield in April 1841.

narrative_blocks.header: Her second marriage made her daughter a Foote
narrative_blocks.body: The 1841 marriage brought her three Jenkins children into Elial Foote's house alongside his own. Her daughter Amelia married his son Charles about eleven years later, joining the two families a second time.

narrative_blocks.header: She had a Yale president on one side
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother Emilia was a daughter of Ezra Stiles, who ran Yale College from 1778 to 1795. Her father, Hon. Jonathan Leavitt, kept the bench and the counting-house at Greenfield.

narrative_blocks.header: She gave her mother the wrong medicine
narrative_blocks.body: In October 1791 she handed her mother a dose that killed her; Sarah was forty-nine, and the death was recorded as a consequence of taking wrong medicine. Clarissa kept house for her father at Heath afterwards.

career.role: County Treasurer and Register of Deeds

narrative_blocks.header: Re-elected as long as he lived
narrative_blocks.body: He came to the bar young, and when Franklin County was organized he was elected its treasurer and register of deeds. The county returned him to both offices at every election until he died in them.

narrative_blocks.header: Mortally ill, he housed the convention anyway
narrative_blocks.body: He took the antislavery side when it was unpopular at Greenfield. A month before his death, already too ill to walk well, he made the preparations for the Liberty convention there and put the delegates up at his own house.

narrative_blocks.header: Endorsing another man cost him his property
narrative_blocks.body: A few years before the end he signed for another man's debts and lost the greater part of his property. His obituary says no creditor of his ever had to call twice, and no client ever waited for money he had collected.

narrative_blocks.header: The youngest of eleven brothers, and the last
narrative_blocks.body: He was the last of the eleven sons of Rev. Jonathan Leavitt of Charlemont, and outlived them all. He died at Greenfield on 28 October 1842, in his fifty-eighth year.

notable.notable_blurb: Abolitionist editor; founder of the Liberty Party

narrative_blocks.header: The committee that freed the Amistad Africans
narrative_blocks.body: On 4 September 1839 he formed the Amistad Committee with Lewis Tappan and Simeon Jocelyn, raising the money that defended the Africans who had seized the ship. The case reached the Supreme Court and they went free.

narrative_blocks.header: An escaped slave hidden in the family
narrative_blocks.body: Basil Dorsey escaped slavery in Maryland in 1836 and reached New York, where Leavitt sent him on to his brother Roger Hooker Leavitt at Charlemont. Dorsey and his family were hidden among the Leavitt farms there for more than five years.

narrative_blocks.header: They called him father of the Liberty Party
narrative_blocks.body: He was the prime architect of the Liberty Party, the first antislavery party to run a candidate, and put up James G. Birney for president in 1844. His Financial Power of Slavery argued the South was draining the national economy.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-four years at the editor's desk
narrative_blocks.body: He gave forty-four years to editing — the Sailors' Magazine for the Seamen's Friend Society, then the New York Evangelist, the Emancipator, and the Independent, which he ran until he was seventy.

narrative_blocks.header: Music beside every hymn, for the first time
narrative_blocks.body: His Christian Lyre of 1830 was the first American tunebook built like a modern hymnal — music for every hymn, and all the verses printed with it. The revival meetings of the 1830s sang from it.

narrative_blocks.header: Temperance, cheap postage, and free trade
narrative_blocks.body: In 1851 he helped found the American Geographical Society with Henry Evelyn Pierrepont. He was also the first secretary of the American Temperance Society, and campaigned for free trade and cheap postage.

narrative_blocks.header: His son took the pulpit at Hudson
narrative_blocks.body: He married Sarah Williams of Northampton in 1820, the youngest child of a Yale minister, and she outlived him. Of their sons, William became a Congregational minister at Hudson in New York.

people.research_notes:
b. Sep 8, 1794 Heath MA; d. Jan 16, 1873 Brooklyn NY. CAREER: Yale College 1814. Studied law Northampton MA; admitted to bar 1819. Two-year divinity course at Yale completed in one year. Ordained Congregational minister Stratford CT 1825. Moved to NYC 1828 as secretary of the Seaman's Friend Society. ABOLITIONISM: Editor of The Evangelist (founded by Arthur and Lewis Tappan) 1831. Co-founder New York Anti-Slavery Society 1833. Editor of The Emancipator (INST015) 1836 onward — the flagship abolitionist newspaper. With Lewis Tappan, broke from Garrison to form the American and Foreign Anti-Slavery Society 1840. Prime force behind the defense of the Amistad crew 1839. Key architect of the Liberty Party; ran James G. Birney for president 1844. 'Financial Power of Slavery' (1840) his most-circulated tract — called 'Father of the Liberty Party' by contemporaries. Later editor of The New York Independent 1848. Published The Monroe Doctrine 1863. Cobden Club gold medal for free trade advocacy 1869. FAMILY ABOLITIONISM: Brothers Roger Hooker (HD0868) and Hart (HD0869) operated Underground Railroad stations in Charlemont MA; Joshua in NYC coordinated their network, directing escaped slave Basil Dorsey to Roger Hooker's home 1836. Dorsey lived with the Leavitt family over five years. AGS: Co-founded American Geographical Society (INST014) 1851 alongside Henry Evelyn Pierrepont (HD1533) — two Hooker descendants through separate branches, almost certainly unaware of their shared ancestry. ANCESTRY NOTE: Wikipedia on Leavitt explicitly states 'his ancestor Rev. Thomas Hooker had left the Massachusetts Bay Colony to found the state of Connecticut' — confirming Hooker descent through grandmother Sarah Hooker (H00302). SOURCES: Wikipedia; Dictionary of American Biography; New York Times Jan 17, 1873; F.B. Dexter, Biographical Sketches of the Graduates of Yale College vol. 6.
CC NOTE [HD1533]: Joshua Leavitt co-founded the American Geographical Society (INST014) in 1851 alongside Henry Evelyn Pierrepont. Both are 6th-generation Thomas Hooker descendants through entirely separate branches — Leavitt through Sarah Hooker, Pierrepont through Mary Hooker Pierpont. Neither is known to have been aware of their shared ancestry. Stage 6Y-687: Wikipedia URL, Brady photo, Green-Wood burial applied; added to the Farmington Amistad circle story. Yale at twenty; law in Putney VT; first secretary, American Temperance Society; 44 years editing Sailors’ Magazine; Financial Power of Slavery (1841); cheap-postage campaigner. Son William a Congregational minister in Hudson NY. RESONANCE: committee co-founder Lewis Tappan was the brother of Rebecca Tappan Edwards (X01689) in this tree — Tappan himself not built per Jalapeño rule. REBUILD 081226. REMOVED, at Sam's instruction, the claim that he and Henry Evelyn Pierrepont were 'neither known to have been aware of their shared ancestry' — unknowable, and it implied both men were oblivious. Yale Obituary Record detail added 081226: prepared for college by Rev. Dr. Joseph Lyman of Hatfield; Berkeley Scholar at graduation; read law at home, admitted to the bar at Northampton 1819, practised at Putney, Vermont, and was elected deacon there; returned to New Haven in 1823 for the first class of the new Divinity School; licensed to preach August 1824; ordained at Stratford 23 February 1825; dismissed 22 October 1828 to take the Seamen's Friend Society agency. Four months as an agent of the American Temperance Society. Resigned the agency December 1831 for the New York Evangelist, which the panic of 1837 forced him to sell. Edited the Emancipator 1837-47, moving himself and the paper to Boston in 1842, and was often at odds with Garrison. Office editor of the Independent from 1848, giving up the management at seventy but working on to his death. Honorary D.D., Wabash College, 1854. Cobden Club prize essay on free trade. Died of an apoplectic stroke while visiting a son in New York. His mother Chloe was a sister of Sylvester Maxwell (Yale 1797). CCs ranked 081226 — he has eight and the card shows six. Off the card: Richard Hooker of the Springfield Republican, and Benjamin Silliman Jr., whose label ('also sat for Mathew Brady's camera') is the thinnest link on the card and a candidate for removal.

people.prominent_name_reason: Col. Roger Hooker Leavitt — Underground Railroad operator. His home in Charlemont MA is on the National Park Service's National Underground Railroad Network to Freedom. Sheltered fugitive slave Basil Dorsey (escaped Frederick County MD 1836) for over five years. Colonel in the Massachusetts militia. Member of Massachusetts legislature. Advocate for the Hoosac Tunnel. Died in Waterloo, Iowa visiting son John Hooker Leavitt, 1885. Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Hooker_Leavitt Family correspondence at Library of Congress Manuscript Division.
people.research_notes: b. Jul 21, 1805 Heath MA; d. 1885 Waterloo, Iowa. Named for grandfather Roger Hooker Leavitt (H00685). m. daughter of Col. Hugh Maxwell. Underground Railroad: sheltered Basil Dorsey 1836+; home now on NPS Underground Railroad Network to Freedom. Stage 6Y-687 full build per compiler. Died in Waterloo visiting son John Hooker Leavitt; the New York Times obituary called him “one of the prominent and leading citizens of Franklin County.” Family correspondence 1812-71 at the Library of Congress. Home now part of the Academy at Charlemont campus, NPS Network to Freedom. REBUILD 081226. NPS Network to Freedom marker, dedicated 16 July 2004 at 1351 MA-2, East Charlemont, names the safe house as sheltering Basil and Louisa Dorsey and their children, freedom seekers from Liberty, Maryland, 1838-1844. Vice-president of the Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society 1838-39. Charlemont records show the birth of Dorsey's son Charles Robert Dorsey there in 1838, and two older Dorsey children born in Maryland; 'B. Dorsey' of Charlemont gave to the Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society in 1839. Dorsey moved on to Florence about 1844. His first wife Keziah died the same year as Dorsey's first wife, and Joshua wrote him: 'I feel for Mr. Dorsey in his bereavement and trust that you will do all that Christian benevolence requires in his care.' Died at Waterloo, Iowa, visiting his son John Hooker Leavitt; the New York Times called him 'one of the prominent and leading citizens of Franklin County'. The family correspondence 1812-71 is at the Library of Congress. NOTE: he is sometimes wrongly given as Joshua's father; they were brothers, both sons of Roger Leavitt (H00685) and Chloe Maxwell (X00252), and the tree has them wired that way. FROM THE NETWORK TO FREEDOM APPLICATION (Lisa White and Bambi Miller, 11 July 2003), read 081226: he was rotten-egged for holding an antislavery meeting and would not let his wife wash the stains off, counting them a badge of honour. Married Keziah Hunt Osgood 1829, moved to Charlemont 1835; three sons, John Hooker (11 Oct 1831), William Hunt (4 Sep 1834) and Henry Jenkins (8 Aug 1836). Keziah died 11 November 1838, four days after Louisa Dorsey; he married her sister Eliza on 11 March 1839 and Basil Dorsey stayed on with them until 1844. First president of the Deerfield Valley Agricultural Society and later on the State Board of Agriculture; captain of the Heath rifles from May 1828, later colonel; deacon of the East Charlemont Congregational Church for more than fifty years; state senator 1866 and two House terms from 1868; first to shovel dirt at the Hoosac Tunnel ground-breaking. BASIL DORSEY: born Ephraim Costly at Plantation Liberty, Frederick County, Maryland; fled 14 May 1836 with three brothers, who all took the name Dorsey at Robert Purvis's farm in Bucks County; freed at Doylestown on 1 August 1837 when Judge Fox dismissed the case because the claimant's lawyer could not prove Maryland was a slave state. He had told Purvis he would cut his throat in the courthouse rather than go back. THREE SONS BY KEZIAH, built 081226: John Hooker (HD0870, b. 11 Oct 1831), William Hunt (HD10074, b. 4 Sep 1834) and Henry Jenkins (HD10075, b. 8 Aug 1836). The instruction naming them in the 081226 paste was overwritten by the Henry/Clara/Emma block, so the names were taken from the Network to Freedom application instead. No death dates for William or Henry.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: His house, and the room the Dorseys had for six years

narrative_blocks.header: The Dorseys lived in his house six years
narrative_blocks.body: Basil Dorsey escaped slavery in Maryland in 1836 and came north with his wife Louisa. Leavitt took the family into his Charlemont house and kept them there until 1844, while the 1840 census recorded no person of colour in any Leavitt household.

narrative_blocks.header: A mob at Utica turned his parents abolitionist
narrative_blocks.body: He went to the Utica antislavery convention of October 1835 with his brothers Joshua and Hart, and pro-slavery men broke it up. The violence did what argument had not: their parents came over to the cause, and within a year he led the Franklin County society.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped start the tunnel through the mountain
narrative_blocks.body: He was an original incorporator of the Troy and Greenfield Railroad, chartered in 1848 to run from Greenfield to the Vermont line, and one of the earliest promoters of the Hoosac Tunnel driven under the range to carry it.

narrative_blocks.header: His house is on the Underground Railroad map
narrative_blocks.body: The house is part of the Academy at Charlemont today, and the National Park Service lists it on the Network to Freedom beside his brother Hart's farm. He died in Iowa visiting his son, and the New York Times gave his abolition work the obituary.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept the egg stains as a badge
narrative_blocks.body: He was rotten-egged for holding an antislavery meeting, and refused to let his wife clean the stains from his coat — he counted them a badge of honour.

narrative_blocks.header: Captain of the Heath rifles, then deacon
narrative_blocks.body: He signed in as captain of the Heath rifles in 1828 and rose to colonel, was first president of the Deerfield Valley Agricultural Society and later sat on the State Board of Agriculture, and was deacon of the East Charlemont church for over fifty years.

narrative_blocks.header: Four wives, the last at seventy-six
narrative_blocks.body: Widowed of Keziah Osgood Hunt in 1838, he married her sister Eliza the next year; Olive Warriner at Chicago at seventy-one; and at seventy-six the schoolteacher Lucy Trowbridge, her first marriage, at fifty-one.

narrative_blocks.header: His store held the first post office
narrative_blocks.body: Relocating to Greenfield beside his uncle Judge Jonathan Leavitt’s law office, Hart kept the store that housed the town’s first newspaper and first post office — before returning to run his Charlemont farm as an Underground Railroad station.

narrative_blocks.header: “A sturdy abolitionist,” the historian wrote
narrative_blocks.body: Ohio State’s Wilbur Siebert catalogued him as an operator of the Franklin County underground network — “a sturdy abolitionist who did all he could to help slaves gain their freedom.” His farmhouse, like his brother Roger Hooker’s, stands on the NPS Network to Freedom.

narrative_blocks.header: The Dorseys moved between three Leavitt farms
narrative_blocks.body: His farm adjoined his brother Roger Hooker's, and Basil Dorsey's family passed between the two and their father's house in the years they were hidden at Charlemont. At the Utica convention of 1835 he was one of a handful of delegates from outside New York.

narrative_blocks.header: Selectman of Heath, then of Charlemont at war
narrative_blocks.body: He sat for Heath as selectman, went to the Massachusetts House, and served Franklin County as commissioner and justice of the peace. Charlemont made him selectman again through the Civil War.

narrative_blocks.header: His first wife died at twenty-two
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Miller, daughter of Rev. Moses Miller of Heath, died of consumption nine months after their daughter was born. He married Mary Sanderson in 1834 and had seven children with her, and at sixty married a third time.
