people.research_notes:
b. Apr 3, 1793 East Hartford (Manchester) CT; d. Mar 4, 1857 Medina, Medina County, Ohio. Buried West Cemetery, Manchester CT. YALE COLLEGE 1816 — NOTE: EH incorrectly states "Yale College, 1805" which is impossible (he was born in 1793 — would be age 12). Scholarly source (Yale Biographies and Annals, 1903) confirms the eldest Olcott son graduated Yale in 1816. Unmarried. Arrived Medina, Ohio 1820 or 1821 — one of Medina's first lawyers. County prosecutor, Medina County, 1825-1833. ABOLITIONIST: Author of "A Blow at Slavery" and "Two Lectures on the Subjects of Slavery and Abolition" (1838). "A clear, bold writer, and a great Anti-Slavery man." (EH 1909). His lectures were read aloud in Congress as evidence for the unconstitutional nature of slavery. Published in the canon of definitive abolitionist writing. Medina OH was Underground Railroad station #27 (Philadelphia was #10). Mentored Joel Tiffany (CT-born law student, later inventor of refrigerator railroad car and author of abolitionist legal theory). INVENTOR: Patented the iron (metallic) ship, Jul 13, 1835, U.S. Patent Office. "Be it known that I, Charles Alcott of Madina...have invented a new and useful improvement in ship building and naval architecture...consisting in constructing ships...wholly of iron or of any other metal." Naval board rejected it as "entirely impractical." The Navy built iron ships anyway shortly after. Olcott never received compensation. Video source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wIEun5SX-m0 (Medina County history documentary).
CC NOTE [H01148]: Charles Olcott and Betsey Mix Cowles were Hooker descendants active in the abolitionist movement in the same generation — Olcott in Medina, Ohio (1820s-1850s) and Betsey Mix Cowles at Oberlin College and with the Garrison circle (1830s-1870s). Both descended from Thomas Hooker; both were from Connecticut originally; both moved to Ohio as adults. The Hooker descendants spread the Connecticut abolitionist tradition westward.

notable.notable_blurb: Ohio abolitionist and iron-ship patentee

narrative_blocks.header: Congress heard his abolition lectures read aloud
narrative_blocks.body: He published Two Lectures on Slavery and Abolition in 1838, and it was read aloud in Congress as evidence that slavery was unconstitutional. Edward Hooker called him a clear, bold writer and a great Anti-Slavery man.

narrative_blocks.header: The Navy called his iron ship impractical
narrative_blocks.body: On 13 July 1835 he patented a way of building ships wholly of iron, worked out twenty years earlier. The naval board called it entirely impractical, then built iron ships soon after without paying him.

narrative_blocks.header: The invention made him enemies, not friends
narrative_blocks.body: It totally ruined my reputation, he wrote, and made me enemies where I ought to have none but friends. A classmate agreed it had earned him more credit than he ever got, and left him seeming visionary rather than practical.

narrative_blocks.header: Poverty, reproach, and unceasing persecution
narrative_blocks.body: Writing to his Yale classmates from Medina in 1848, he set down his whole life as resolute effort at moral, political and scientific reform. He had shared every reformer's fate before him — poverty, reproach and unceasing persecution.

narrative_blocks.header: He died in great destitution at Medina
narrative_blocks.body: Eccentricity grew on him, and drink with it, keeping him from the standing in his profession that his talents and schooling had promised. He died at Medina in 1857 with nothing, and was carried back to the Manchester ground he was born beside.

narrative_blocks.header: From farm labor into Yale’s sophomore class
narrative_blocks.body: He spent his early years on a farm in hard labour and entered the sophomore class in 1813. He was diligent and successful, strongest in Greek, and singular in his opinions and habits.

narrative_blocks.header: Mentored Joel Tiffany — refrigerator car inventor
narrative_blocks.body: He mentored Joel Tiffany, a Connecticut-born law student who went on to invent the refrigerator railroad car and to write abolitionist legal theory, in Medina's circle of Connecticut-rooted reformers.

narrative_blocks.body: At nine years old in 1806, Anna stitched a classic 'house' sampler at Miss Mary Hart's School in Farmington Connecticut — the boarding school that preceded the famous Miss Porter's. The sampler bears the verse 'Let Virtue guide and God provide' and a family record naming herself and her four siblings. Her younger sister Cynthia made matching samplers in 1810 at the same school.

narrative_blocks.header: A wife and four children lost before him
narrative_blocks.body: He knew deep loss — his first wife, Mary Meigs, died in 1809 with two of their infants, and of his six children only two lived to grow up. His youngest, born to his second wife thirty years after his eldest, was the Civil War captain William Winthrop Hart.

narrative_blocks.header: He built the pagoda-roofed house on the green
narrative_blocks.body: In the early 1830s he rebuilt the family homestead on Madison's green into an elegant Greek Revival house — soon nicknamed Hartsbourne — crowned by a flat copper roof raised like a Chinese pagoda. He also helped choose the site of the Congregational meetinghouse beside it, and the two buildings still echo each other in their columns and tall shutters.

narrative_blocks.header: He built where Yale's first graduate once lived
narrative_blocks.body: The ground he built on carried deep history: an earlier house there had belonged to his ancestor the Rev. John Hart, the first student to take a bachelor's degree from Yale and the first minister of the East Guilford church. A deacon himself, Benjamin kept the family close to that church for another generation.

narrative_blocks.body: The Yale-trained physician sat as town magistrate from 1753 until his death and in most Assembly sessions from 1754 to 1777. In 1766 the legislature sent him to investigate the Quinnipiac complaint over the sale of tribal land.

narrative_blocks.header: Born and died in Guilford, three days apart
narrative_blocks.body: Hooker Bartlett Jr. was born January 15, 1755 in Guilford Connecticut, and died January 18, 1834 in Guilford — three calendar days short of his seventy-ninth birthday and within the same town his whole life. The given name 'Hooker' had been chosen explicitly to honor his Hooker ancestry through the Bartlett line. His wife Ruth Hart outlived him by twenty-one years, dying April 9, 1855 at age ninety-four.

narrative_blocks.header: Married his Hooker cousin from the next-over family
narrative_blocks.body: Hooker Bartlett Jr. married Ruth Hart on January 7, 1784 — she was his cousin and herself a Hooker descendant. Their fathers were children of siblings: John Bartlett had married Sarah Hooker, and Reverend John Hart had married Mary Hooker. The Guilford Hooker descendants formed a tightly knit community where cousin marriages preserved the family network across multiple Hooker-line surnames.

people.research_notes:
b. Apr 26, 1835 Huntington, Luzerne County PA; d. Mar 25, 1914 Ellington, Tuscola MI. m. Catherine Elsie Kline (HD1021) Jan 8, 1857. HARTFORD FOUNDER DESCENT: Mordecai Goodwin descends from Elder William Goodwin (Hartford founder, arrived Cambridge 1632, Adventurers Party 1635). Chain: Elder William Goodwin → William Jr. (b.1629) → Nathaniel → Hezekiah → John Pantry Goodwin → Elijah Goodwin (b.1763) → Daniel Goodwin (b.1801) → Mordecai. CRUCIAL FACT: Elder William Goodwin married as his SECOND wife SUSANNAH GARBRAND, the WIDOW OF REV. THOMAS HOOKER, before Jan 1669-70 in Farmington CT. This means Mordecai's ancestor married Thomas Hooker's wife after Hooker's death — the two founding families were literally united by marriage. This makes Mordecai's marriage to a Hooker descendant (through the Smith-Baker-Kline chain) a second-order convergence of families originally joined in the 1650s-1670s.
CC NOTE [H00001]: Mordecai Goodwin descends from Elder William Goodwin of Hartford, who married Susannah Garbrand — the widow of Rev. Thomas Hooker — as his second wife ca.1669-70. Mordecai then married Catherine Elsie Kline, a descendant of Thomas Hooker through the Smith-Baker-Kline chain. Two families that were literally joined by marriage in 1669-70 (Goodwin + Hooker widow) converged again ca.1857 through their descendants.

narrative_blocks.header: Ancestor married Thomas Hooker's widow Susannah, 1669
narrative_blocks.body: His Goodwin ancestor — Hartford founder Elder William Goodwin (1591-1671) — married Susannah Garbrand, Rev Thomas Hooker's widow, as his second wife around 1669-70. Two centuries later his own January 1857 marriage to Catherine Elsie Kline reconnected the Goodwin and Hooker families across that historical gap.

narrative_blocks.body: Born at Huntington in Luzerne County Pennsylvania in April 1835, he married Catherine Elsie Kline in January 1857. The couple eventually migrated to Ellington in Tuscola County Michigan, where he died in March 1914 at age seventy-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: A signer’s daughter who married the spymaster
narrative_blocks.body: Her father, William Floyd, signed the Declaration of Independence for New York; her husband, Benjamin Tallmadge, ran Washington's spy ring. They married in 1784, the year after the war ended, in a ceremony his father performed.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven children in twenty-one years, gone at forty-one
narrative_blocks.body: She raised seven children with Tallmadge at Litchfield, where he had grown rich in trade. She died in 1805, at forty-one, thirty years before her husband — who never remarried and outlived her by three decades.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father’s house came back a ruin
narrative_blocks.body: While the British held Long Island, her family fled across the Sound to Connecticut, and the occupiers turned the Floyd estate at Mastic into a cavalry stable. Her mother died in exile at Middletown in 1781 and never saw home again.

narrative_blocks.body: William served as lieutenant colonel of the 46th United States Infantry in the War of 1812. He died unmarried at Leicester, New York, in 1822.

narrative_blocks.header: Named for an uncle who died in captivity
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin and Mary's eldest son was named for his uncle William, captured at the Battle of Long Island and starved aboard a British prison ship. He later represented the family firm, B. Tallmadge and Company, in New York.

people.research_notes: Pyne, Talmadge genealogy no.559. FamilySearch gives the marriage as 18 November 1810 and the Litchfield record as 10 November 1810. One source calls him a grocer, Pyne a merchant. Pyne calls his wife Maria C. Adams a daughter of the Hon. Andrew Adams, the signer of the Articles of Confederation; she was his granddaughter. Her father was Andrew Adams Jr. (1766-1804). Neither Adams is in the tree.

bio.bio_blurb: United States Marshal in New York

burial.plot_notes: New York Marble Cemetery, East Village

narrative_blocks.header: Marshal for the southern district
narrative_blocks.body: Tallmadge kept a store in New York and in 1851 was made United States Marshal for the southern district, the federal officer who served the courts' process in the busiest port in the country. He had married Maria Adams of Litchfield forty years earlier.

narrative_blocks.header: A carbuncle killed him at sixty-seven
narrative_blocks.body: He died on 8 July 1854 at 13 St. Mark's Place in New York, of a carbuncle — a staphylococcal abscess that in the years before antibiotics could be fatal in a man of his age.

notable.notable_blurb: Litchfield Female Academy student

narrative_blocks.header: Painted by Ralph Earl in her first year
narrative_blocks.body: In 1790, the year Maria was born, Ralph Earl painted her into a full-length portrait with her mother, Mary Floyd Tallmadge, and her brother Henry, then three. The canvas, more than six feet tall, belongs to the Litchfield Historical Society.

narrative_blocks.header: At eleven, a pupil of the Female Academy
narrative_blocks.body: Maria studied at the Litchfield Female Academy in 1801 and 1802, from the age of eleven. Three years later, in June 1805, her mother died at forty-one, and Maria at fifteen was the eldest daughter in a house of seven children.

narrative_blocks.header: Engaged first to Virgil Maxcy
narrative_blocks.body: Before John Cushman, Maria was engaged to Virgil Maxcy of the Litchfield Law School; at Christmas 1808 a friend of his still wrote of 'you & your Maria.' The match broke, and Judge Tapping Reeve wrote to console her. In 1812 she married Cushman, another of Reeve's students.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty years a congressman's widow in Troy
narrative_blocks.body: Five years after the wedding John Paine Cushman went to Congress as a Federalist, and in 1820 they built a four-story brick house at 39 First Street in Troy. He died in 1848; Maria outlived him by thirty years and died in Troy in 1878, at eighty-seven.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight children over nineteen years
narrative_blocks.body: Maria bore eight children between 1813 and 1832 and buried two of them small, Maria Hallet at four and William Henry in his first year. She gave the eldest son her father's name, Benjamin Tallmadge, and a daughter her mother's, Mary Floyd.

narrative_blocks.header: Spymaster's daughter, signer's granddaughter
narrative_blocks.body: Her father, Benjamin Tallmadge, ran Washington's Culper Ring and exposed Benedict Arnold's plot; her mother's father, William Floyd, signed the Declaration of Independence for New York. Her middle name, Jones, was her grandmother Hannah Jones Floyd's maiden name.

career.role: Clerk of the New York Court of Appeals

narrative_blocks.header: He led New York City's police force
narrative_blocks.body: After terms as a New York alderman, state senator, and city recorder, Tallmadge served as Superintendent of the Metropolitan Police from 1857 to 1862. He had earlier sat one term in Congress as a Whig.

narrative_blocks.header: From Litchfield Law School to the bar
narrative_blocks.body: A Yale graduate of 1811, Tallmadge trained at the Litchfield Law School and practiced in New York City from 1813. He closed his career as clerk of the New York Court of Appeals.

narrative_blocks.header: Son of the Revolution's master spy
narrative_blocks.body: Frederick was a son of Benjamin Tallmadge, Washington's intelligence chief, and a grandson of the Declaration signer William Floyd. He returned to his native Litchfield to die in 1869.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the Rose of Sharon in 1815
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth Hannah Canfield of Sharon was known by that name, and two Telfair brothers at the Litchfield Law School had both wanted her. Tallmadge married her on 22 May 1815 and they had five children in New York.

narrative_blocks.header: She was moved when the church came down
narrative_blocks.body: She died in July 1856 at her son Tallmadge's house in Brooklyn and was laid in her husband's vault at St. Thomas Church on Broadway. When the church was taken down she was carried up to Geneva and buried beside him.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandfather signed the Declaration
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother Mary Floyd was a daughter of Gen. William Floyd of Long Island, one of the New York signers. Her father Benjamin Tallmadge ran Washington's spy ring before he sat in Congress.

narrative_blocks.header: Five feet four, light brown hair, hazel eyes
narrative_blocks.body: The family genealogy troubled to set down what she looked like, which it did for almost no one else: slender, about five feet four inches, light brown hair and hazel eyes.

narrative_blocks.header: Named for the general his father served
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin Tallmadge ran Washington's intelligence through the Revolution and wept in the room when the general took leave of his officers in 1783. Twenty years later he named this son George Washington Tallmadge. The boy grew up at Litchfield, married Laura Pease of Ohio, and died young, at thirty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: He married on his twenty-first birthday
narrative_blocks.body: George Washington Tallmadge married Laura Pease of Warren on 13 September 1824, the day he turned twenty-one. He died eleven years later, five days short of his thirty-second birthday, and two of their three children were already dead.

bio.bio_blurb: Widow of a man lost at sea

narrative_blocks.header: Married at seventeen, the last summer of war
narrative_blocks.body: Levinah Purdy married Thomas Horton on 2 June 1783, the summer before the British gave up New York, in a town whose most famous house was her father's. She was not yet eighteen.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed with ten, and no grave to visit
narrative_blocks.body: Ten children were born between 1784 and 1800, and about 1803 Thomas Horton was lost at sea, in a place never fixed any closer than an island somewhere. Levinah was thirty-eight, and lived thirty-one more years.

COUSINRY: she was a third cousin of Esther Purdy, wife of Capt. narrative_blocks.header: She ended in the rear of the house
narrative_blocks.body: Abigail Angevine kept the house at 188 Broome Street for more than a decade after Peter died, was on Delancey Street by 1846, and was living in the rear of 188 Broome when she died in January 1853 at seventy-seven. She had been a widow thirty-five years.

narrative_blocks.header: Nobody is sure where she lies
narrative_blocks.body: The Angevines kept a burying ground at Scarsdale on the farm they had leased for a century. Whether Abigail was ever put into it is unsettled, and if she was, the grave may have gone with the others to St. Paul's at Mount Vernon or to the White Plains church her family attended.

narrative_blocks.header: She married the Loyalist brother's son
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah Purdy married Jacob Griffin Purdy on 2 January 1811. He was her first cousin — his father Gabriel had fought the British side at White Plains and been put ashore in Nova Scotia, while her father Jacob stayed and lent Washington the house.

narrative_blocks.header: She went north in 1811 and stayed
narrative_blocks.body: The Nova Scotia records call her Sally. She settled on land her husband's family had named Westchester after the county they left, died there in March 1870, and lies at Rose Cemetery.

people.research_notes: FamilySearch L5GT-7CZ. b. 26 Dec 1787 and d. 22 Sep 1870, both at Westchester Station, Cumberland County, Nova Scotia. Judge; buried Rose Cemetery, Westchester Station. Son of Sgt. Gabriel Timothy Purdy (1755-1841, LDBP-77V) and Esther Angevine (1768-1803, LCXR-V99), m. 1782 at Morrisania; eleven children. Sgt. Gabriel was a son of Samuel Purdy (1710-1796, LVJV-2H3) and Winifred Wright Griffin (1716-1783, LBXJ-3JQ), m. 17 Dec 1735 — the same couple recorded as the parents of Capt. Jacob G Purdy (X00121). Sgt. Gabriel is therefore Capt. Jacob's brother, one of the two Purdy sons who took the King's side and left Westchester for Nova Scotia in 1783 (see LM452), which makes Jacob Griffin Purdy the first cousin of his own wife Sarah Purdy (H00779). Neither generation above him is built. The McBride Loyalist account gives his death as 28 Dec 1879 against the 22 Sep 1870 recorded here, and credits him with 11 children where 12 are wired; it also has Sarah as 'Sally' and the marriage performed by Rev. Thomas G. Smith of Londonderry, Nova Scotia.

narrative_blocks.header: Born on the land they renamed Westchester
narrative_blocks.body: Jacob Griffin Purdy was born in exile: his father fled New York in June 1783 and named the Cumberland County ground he settled Westchester, after the county he had lost. He sat as a judge on it.

people.research_notes:
b. Mar 22, 1746 Berlin CT; d. Nov 4, 1791 at St. Clair's Defeat, Wabash River OH. Buried Fort Recovery Monument Park, Ohio. Son of Ebenezer Hart and Elizabeth Lawrence of Kensington CT. COUSIN of Gen. Selah Hart (H00273) — their fathers Ebenezer and Nathaniel Hart were brothers. NOT a direct Hooker descendant, but intimately connected to the Berlin Hooker-Hart community. Yale College 1768, graduated with honors. Teacher in NJ. REVOLUTIONARY WAR: Lexington Alarm; Adjutant 3rd CT Line Jan 1, 1777; Captain May 1, 1780; Brigade General (Brig-Gen) Jan 2, 1781. Siege of Yorktown 1781. Danbury attack repelled. Peekskill; West Point; White Plains; Morristown. POST-WAR: Stationed Fort Washington, Ohio; made sketch of the fort in 1791. ST. CLAIR'S DEFEAT (Battle of the Wabash), Nov 4, 1791: "He and the greater part of his command were slain attempting to cover the retreat of the shattered remains of the army when Gen. St. Clair was defeated on the banks of the Wabash." One of the worst defeats in U.S. Army history — 623 soldiers killed, ~258 wounded. m. Abigail Riley 1775. One child Alces (b.1782), who married Charlotte Overton and died childless. His widow Abigail remarried Rev. Cyprian Strong of Chatham CT, Aug 3, 1797.
HART BOOK BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCH (Connecticut Gazette, 1819): "Major Jonathan Hart was a native of this town. He was a gallant and distinguished officer, and one of the victims of the unfortunate defeat of General St. Clair, November 4th, 1791. His life and those of his command were literally offered a sacrifice for the safety of the rest of the army. When all were in confusion and dismay Major Hart was ordered to charge the enemy with the bayonet, with a view to facilitate a retreat... But the intrepid major and almost every man of his party were killed in the desperate enterprise, and their bones were left to bleach upon the borders of the waters of the Wabash, the dreary abode of wild beasts, and of savage men more wild than they." NOTE: He entered into trade with the local minister, had a serious quarrel, and was thrown into jail — where he remained until the Revolution. LAND SCOUT: While garrisoned in Ohio he wrote ~30 letters to friend Maj. William Judd of Farmington about the soil, climate, and value of Ohio lands for the Connecticut Reserve. The commissioners "wisely availed themselves of his knowledge." Letters preserved by Judd posterity in New Britain in 1875. [Migrated from top-level military]: True

bio.title: Maj. Gen.
bio.bio_blurb: Regular officer killed at St. Clair’s Defeat
bio.photo_notes: The Fort Recovery monument over the fallen of St. Clair’s Defeat.

military_service.notes: Killed 4 November 1791 at St. Clair's Defeat on the Wabash.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixteen years in the public service
narrative_blocks.body: He joined the army in 1775 and never left it, serving without a break until the day he died in 1791. He was a major of the regular establishment by the end, and had been at Yorktown along the way.

narrative_blocks.header: Ordered to charge and cover the retreat
narrative_blocks.body: At St. Clair’s Defeat he was told to take his party forward with the bayonet so the army could get away. Almost every man of them was killed. A Connecticut paper wrote that their bones were left to bleach on the Wabash.

narrative_blocks.header: A trade quarrel put him in jail
narrative_blocks.body: Back from New Jersey he went into trade with the minister at Kensington, fell out with him badly, and was thrown into prison. He was still there when the Lexington Alarm came in 1775 and the war let him out.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty letters that guided the Reserve
narrative_blocks.body: Garrisoned at Fort Washington in Ohio in 1791, he wrote some thirty letters to his Farmington friend Major William Judd on the soil, the climate and the worth of the land. The Connecticut Reserve commissioners used them.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale, then a New Jersey schoolroom
narrative_blocks.body: He was the second son of Deacon Ebenezer Hart of Kensington and Elizabeth Lawrence, and took his degree at Yale College in 1768. He went down to New Jersey afterwards and kept school there for several years.

narrative_blocks.header: His one child died childless
narrative_blocks.body: He married Abigail Riley in 1777 and they had a single child, who married and left nobody. Abigail outlived him by twenty-four years and married the minister Cyprian Strong in 1797.

narrative_blocks.body: Eunice was a year and a half old when her brother died in March 1764 and her father five weeks after him. She grew up her widowed mother's only child, and married Joseph Hart about 1780.

narrative_blocks.header: Brother John was partner in Hooker & Chaffee
narrative_blocks.body: Her older brother John Chaffee was a partner in the firm Hooker & Chaffee — the business linking her birth family directly to her husband's. The 1784 marriage to Captain James Hooker thus joined both personal and commercial lines of the Windsor Connecticut Chaffee household.

narrative_blocks.header: She named her firstborn for the first wife
narrative_blocks.body: Her first daughter, born the year after the 1784 wedding, was christened Hannah Allin Hooker — the name of the bride her husband had buried nineteen years earlier. The second daughter took Dolly Goodwin's name, the second wife's.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-one years a widow beside her sister
narrative_blocks.body: After James died in 1805 she kept house in Windsor with her unmarried sister Hepsibah, whose 1834 will divided everything between Mary and their brother John. She lived to eighty-six, dying in 1846, and lies in the Windsor ground.

narrative_blocks.header: Named for her father's first bride
narrative_blocks.body: Hannah was named for Hannah Allin, the young wife her father, Capt. James Hooker, had buried almost twenty years before she was born. Her mother, Mary Chaffee, chose the name.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine children, and six small graves
narrative_blocks.body: Hannah married the Rev. Andrew Yates in 1810 as his second wife. Of their nine children six died before they were three; Mary, James Hooker and Ann Eliza grew up.

narrative_blocks.header: A sea captain's family at 26 Front Street
narrative_blocks.body: In the early 1830s the Yateses took in the family of Captain John Dominis at 26 Front Street in Schenectady. Their son John Owen was born in the house in March 1832.

narrative_blocks.header: Her nephew rammed the Tennessee
narrative_blocks.body: Hannah's sister Dolly's son, Capt. James Hooker Strong, took the Monongahela into the Confederate ironclad Tennessee at Mobile Bay in 1864. Andrew's grandson Arthur Reed Yates was on Farragut's staff in the same fight.

narrative_blocks.header: The boy from her house married a queen
narrative_blocks.body: John Owen Dominis grew up in Honolulu, married the future Queen Liliuokalani, and died in 1891 the kingdom's last and only prince consort. His sisters who died young lie in the Yates plot at Vale Cemetery, near Hannah.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight children, and twin girls
narrative_blocks.body: Dolly bore Elisha Beebe Strong eight children between 1814 and 1828, among them the twins Martha and Bertha in 1818 and the future Rear Admiral James Hooker Strong, who carried her surname through fifty years in the Navy.

narrative_blocks.header: From Windsor to the Genesee
narrative_blocks.body: Dolly, a daughter of James Hooker of Windsor, married Elisha in June 1813 and went with him from Canandaigua to Rochester in 1816, where her brother Horace was his partner at Carthage. In 1821 Elisha became Monroe County's first judge.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Hooker women married Strongs
narrative_blocks.body: In 1729 Ruth Hooker of Farmington, first cousin of Dolly's grandfather, married Capt. Asahel Strong Jr.; eighty-four years later Dolly married a Strong. Her great-grandson Beebe Hooker Strong, born at Milwaukee in 1866, carried both names.

narrative_blocks.header: She died at Rochester in 1850
narrative_blocks.body: Dolly died at Rochester on 15 February 1850, at sixty-two, and was buried at Mount Hope. Elisha married again, moved to Detroit and died there in 1867.

Farmer Rochester NY. m.Mar 23, 1820 Lucy Case (I00901). d.Jan 2, 1849 Rochester NY. STAGE 6Y-136f. FA: b.Oct 30, 1789 Windsor Hartford Co CT; d.Jan 2, 1849 Irondequoit Monroe Co NY (age 59). Burial: Hooker Cemetery CEM454 (land he deeded to Town of Irondequoit 1840). Moved from 'Eastern States' 1824, acquired Jesse Tainter's farm. First Irondequoit Town Clerk 1839. Family plot survived 1950s accidental bulldozing of most of the cemetery. Naming: 'Alexander Allin' honors dead half-brother Alexander Allin Hooker (b.1763 d.1781 age 17; son of Capt. James Hooker H00348 by his 2nd wife Hannah Allin) per Chaffee Genealogy p.204. m. Lucy Case (I00901; b.1800; d.Jul 26, 1885; daughter of Henry Case of Putnam Co NY; burial Hooker Cemetery CEM454). 8 children H02022-H02029. STAGE 6Y-136w. ARCHIVE U of R Special Collections D.344 (Alexander Hooker Papers): Arrived Rochester area 1816 with brother H00798 Horace Hooker; opened general store 1816-1819; brothers divided assets March 1819, Alexander married Lucy Case of Bristol NY and stayed. Purchased Jesse Tainter farm 1828 for $1,700 (plus $1,700 Tainter still owed on the mortgage). Hooker Farm stretched Norton Street to Ridge Road, Portland Avenue to Goodman Street. Built red fieldstone house 1831-1833; paid mortgage 1843. First Town Clerk Irondequoit 1839. 'Burying Ground Notice' Nov 2, 1840 — made cemetery public if money raised. ~1,000 buried in 1.5 acres including Seneca Indians. Old Indian Trail from Seneca Village Boughton Hill to Genesee River passed behind the cemetery. Sister Dolly married 1812, moved Canandaigua — confirmed H00795 Dolly Goodwin Hooker Strong. NOTE: Archive says farm purchased 1828 (FA description said 1824 — FA likely conflated arrival with purchase). STAGE 6Y-136bb.

naming_inspiration.description: Named for his dead half-brother Alexander Allin Hooker (b.1763; d.1781; FAG 22532503), son of Capt. James Hooker's second wife Hannah Allin — a memorial naming that also honors the Allin family name carried through Capt. James's second wife.

military_service.unit: Unknown — service documented in son's obituary
military_service.notes: Fought at Battle of Lundy's Lane (July 25, 1814) and Battle of Queenston Heights (Oct 13, 1812). Documented in obituary of his son Capt. James Henry Hooker, Rochester newspaper, March 1907: 'His father, Alexander B. Hooker, served in the war of 1812, fighting in the battles of Lundy's Lane, Queenstown, and others.'

burial.plot_notes: Hooker Cemetery — land he deeded to Irondequoit in 1840; family plot survived 1950s accidental destruction

narrative_blocks.header: Three years of storekeeping with brother Horace
narrative_blocks.body: He and Horace came out in 1816 to visit their newly married sister Dolly at Canandaigua, and stayed to open a general store. Three years on they divided the assets; Alexander married Lucy Case of Bristol and never went back east.

narrative_blocks.header: Wolves, rattlesnakes, and the finest timber
narrative_blocks.body: The Tainter farm he bought ran from Norton Street past Ridge Road, Portland Avenue to Goodman — Hooker Farm, under some of the finest oak, white pine, and chestnut in the state, in country still worked by wolves, bears, and swamp fever. When Rochester's building boom came around 1830, millions of board feet went out of those woods.

narrative_blocks.header: He skipped mortgage payments to build it
narrative_blocks.body: With five children and a twenty-five-year-old log cabin, he arranged with his mortgage holder in 1831 to skip payments and build instead. The family moved into the red fieldstone house in 1833; the mortgage was finally cleared in 1843, two daughters later.

narrative_blocks.header: Brighton split, and he kept the books
narrative_blocks.body: When Brighton was divided in 1839 and Irondequoit came into being, the town made him its first clerk. He was also the Boudinot family's land agent for their western New York holdings, and praised for the diligence of it.

narrative_blocks.header: A thousand souls on his sandy knoll
narrative_blocks.body: By a notice of November 1840 he made the burying ground on his land public — ground crossed by the old Seneca trail from Boughton Hill to the Indian Landing, holding perhaps a thousand burials in an acre and a half, Seneca and settler, only a third ever marked. When the town accidentally bulldozed most of the cemetery in the 1950s, the Hooker family plot was among the few left standing.

narrative_blocks.header: Lundy's Lane, by his son's account
narrative_blocks.body: The 1907 obituary of his son credited him with War of 1812 service at Lundy's Lane and Queenston — two of the border war's bloodiest fields. He came west in 1816, the year after the peace.

narrative_blocks.header: The county trusted him with its dead
narrative_blocks.body: Twelve years as Surrogate of Dutchess County put the wills, estates, and guardianships of a prosperous Hudson Valley county through his hands. The Yale memorialists rated him among the safest and most conservative of counselors.

narrative_blocks.header: Litchfield trained him; Poughkeepsie kept him
narrative_blocks.body: From Yale's class of 1810 he went to Litchfield — the first law school in the country — and took the Poughkeepsie bar in 1813. Dutchess County held the whole career that followed, forty-five years to his death.

narrative_blocks.header: His bride's street runs through Manhattan
narrative_blocks.body: James married Helen Sarah Reade in January 1816. She descended from the Livingstons of the Manor and from Joseph Reade, the Trinity Church warden whose name is on Reade Street: the Windsor merchant's son had married old New York money.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-one years on one church vestry
narrative_blocks.body: Christ Church, Poughkeepsie made him a vestryman in 1817, the year after his marriage, and he was still serving at his death in 1858. A Congregationalist line had settled, quietly and permanently, into the Episcopal pew.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter married into Fifth Avenue
narrative_blocks.body: James's daughter Catherine Livingston Hooker married Col. John William Hamersley in 1840. A grandson courted Edith Carow before she chose Theodore Roosevelt, and a great-grandson was born in 1892 to headlines about his inheritance.

narrative_blocks.header: Voted in by one legislature, out by another
narrative_blocks.body: The legislature elected James a Canal Commissioner in February 1840, and a later one legislated him out, reorganizing the commission by the Act of 6 May 1844. In between he helped oversee the Erie system that had remade New York's interior.

people.research_notes: Per EH 798: b. July 5, 1794 Windsor Hartford Co CT — son of James Hooker + 3rd wife Mary (Chaffee) Hooker; d. November 3, 1865 Rochester Monroe Co NY age 71. m. Sept 3, 1822 Windsor CT Helen Wolcott (X-prefix below, 1794 Windsor CT - 1840 — daughter of Erastus + Chloe (Bissell) Wolcott of Windsor). ROCHESTER NY MIGRATION: Per EH 798: 'Like his progenitor he had the spirit of the pioneer and the glowing accounts of the Genesee Country attracted him to Western New York, where so many Hartford and Windsor families have settled.' First lived briefly at Bristol near Canandaigua in mercantile business with brother Alexander Allin Hooker; later moved to Carthage near Rochester to cooperate with brother-in-law Judge Elisha Beebe Strong (husband of his sister Dolly Goodwin Hooker Strong) in developing 'what was supposed to be the future city of Genesee.' For 20 years engaged in active commercial enterprises. Per EH: 'through all his business vicissitudes he remained a courtly gentleman of the old regime of the strictest integrity and high moral character, a power in the community in which he lived.' EIGHT CHILDREN by Helen Wolcott — only Horace B. (H02039) is fully built in this turn; others noted as stubs if listed in EH (most starred in EH). NOTE on EH 2036 ID COLLISION: EH original entry 2036 lists 'John Chaffee Hooker' (b.1830 d.1832 age 19 months Rochester NY). However, this tree has assigned H02036 to Elisabeth Daggett (X-prefix easter_egg, wife of Edward Hooker H00630). The original EH 2036 John Chaffee Hooker is INTENTIONALLY NOT BUILT to avoid ID collision — he died in infancy and has no documented descendants regardless. SOURCE UPDATE (Apr 2026): University of Rochester Special Collections (Hooker Family Papers, D.130, 1790-1963, 27 boxes) confirms Horace Hooker (1794-1865) 'came to the Rochester area from Windsor, Connecticut in 1821. He became a prominent settler in Carthage, a settlement on the east side of the Genesee River.' Legal papers deal with land and real estate in Carthage. He and partners co-founded the Rochester Commercial Nursery in 1844 — part of Rochester's emergence as the 'Flower City.' His son Horace B. Hooker (H02039) 'studied engineering under Colonel Josiah W. Bissell before joining Hooker, Farley & Company, his father's nursery business in Brighton, NY.' (ArchivesSpace, Virginia Tech, Horace B. Hooker Letters finding aid.) ARCHIVE U of R D.344 Alexander Hooker Papers: 'In 1816 Alexander and his brother Horace visited their sister and stayed to open a general store. The general store lasted three years. In March 1819 the brothers divided the asset.' Horace and Alexander came to Rochester area together 1816, ran general store 1816-1819, then separated. This H00798 Horace Hooker (b.Jul 5, 1794 Windsor CT) matches the 'brother Horace' in the archive. STAGE 6Y-136bb. [Stage 6Y-262]: Gender, residence (Rochester NY), and career array structured. Tag 'merchant' added. NBs left at 2 (existing); no forced additions.

careers.location: Bristol near Canandaigua NY → Carthage near Rochester NY
careers.notes: Per EH 798: 'He had the spirit of the pioneer and the glowing accounts of the Genesee Country attracted him to Western New York.' First lived briefly at Bristol near Canandaigua NY in mercantile business with brother Alexander Allin Hooker. Later moved to Carthage near Rochester to cooperate with brother-in-law Judge Strong (likely Elisha Beebe Strong 1788-1867, husband of Dolly Goodwin Hooker Strong) in developing 'what was supposed to be the future city of Genesee.' For 20 years engaged in active commercial enterprises.

narrative_blocks.header: The Genesee Country pulled him west
narrative_blocks.body: Glowing accounts of western New York drew him out, the family genealogy said — a man with the spirit of the pioneer. Storekeeping at Bristol with his brother Alexander came first; then Carthage on the river's east bank, developing the settlement beside his brother-in-law, Judge Elisha Beebe Strong.

narrative_blocks.header: His bet on the east bank came undone
narrative_blocks.body: Horace put his money into the east-bank landing at the Lower Falls, the head of river navigation that many expected to become the heart of Rochester, building warehouses and docks and promoting the state’s second railroad to reach them. When the Erie Canal and the Auburn railroad fixed the city’s center across the river instead, the value of it all fell away.

narrative_blocks.header: Rochester’s first murder was a robbery of him
narrative_blocks.body: The first murder in the young city of Rochester was committed to get at Horace’s money: his clerk, a man named Lyman, was shot dead by robbers after the firm’s cash. The crime was long remembered as one of the settlement’s earliest.

narrative_blocks.header: His line ran from nurseries to the Rockefellers
narrative_blocks.body: The love of growing things Horace took up late in life ran on for generations, his sons and grandsons keeping the Hooker nurseries known across the country. One grandson, Elon, carried the family’s bent into industrial chemistry at Niagara Falls, and through Elon’s daughter Blanchette the line married into the Rockefellers.

career.notes: Co-founded with partners in 1844 — part of Rochester's emergence as the 'Flower City.' Confirmed by University of Rochester Special Collections (Hooker Family Papers, D.130, 1790-1963, 27 boxes).

narrative_blocks.body: Married at twenty-one, Mary left her native Windsor for Schenectady, one of New York’s early mill towns, and made her life there. She raised her children far from the Connecticut valley where the Hooker family had begun.

narrative_blocks.header: A Hooker name carried across three generations
narrative_blocks.body: Mary was named in full for her mother, and she passed the name on again in her turn — three of her six children took Hooker as a middle name. It kept her line’s name in view in a household that had otherwise become Magoffin.

bio.photo_notes: Henry Thomas Hooker (1803-1893), Rochester merchant and Syracuse salt manufacturer

career.notes: One of the early merchants of Rochester NY.
Contributed to Syracuse's salt industry through ingenuity and practical mechanical skill. Syracuse was known as the 'Salt City' of nineteenth-century America.

narrative_blocks.header: Rochester storefronts, then Syracuse salt
narrative_blocks.body: One of Rochester's early merchants, he moved on to Syracuse and its salt works, where his obituary credited his ingenuity and practical mechanical skill with contributing not a little in the industry's earlier days. The Onondaga springs were then making Syracuse the Salt City of America.

narrative_blocks.header: At sixty he patented a better cultivator
narrative_blocks.body: From Skaneateles in December 1863 he took out patent 40935, an improvement in cultivators — a merchant's mechanical bent turned to farm machinery in the middle of the war. A great-nephew, Elon, would carry the same bent into electrochemistry.

narrative_blocks.header: Two babies lost in one year
narrative_blocks.body: Mary, not yet two, and the infant Andrew Yates both died in 1845 — half the children of the young household gone in a season. The two sons who lived carried on: Henry Cobb, and a new Thomas Hooker.

narrative_blocks.header: He died as the church bells tolled
narrative_blocks.body: Death came on a Sabbath evening at his East Fayette Street home, just as the bells rang for evening service — past ninety, still erect and firm-stepped, the old athlete's strict temperance credited for it. He never wearied, the obituary said, of the reminiscences of his early sports.

b. Jan 16, 1844 Hartford CT; d. Jul 10, 1911 Auburn, Cayuga County NY age 67. Buried Mount Hope Cemetery, Lansing, Ingham County MI. Son of James Sedgwick Hooker (HD) and Camilla Porter. SELF-IDENTIFIED as "a descendant in the eighth generation of Rev. Thomas Hooker." EDUCATION: Apprentice stonemason age 16; taught himself mathematics, history, Latin; graduated University of Michigan Law Department 1865. CAREER: Admitted bar 1865; practiced Bryan OH then Charlotte MI 1866-. Superintendent of Schools, Eaton County MI 1867-1869. Prosecuting Attorney, Eaton County MI 1873-1877 (two terms). Appointed Judge, 5th Judicial Circuit, Michigan 1878 (Gov. Charles Croswell). Elected MICHIGAN SUPREME COURT 1893; Chief Justice 1893, 1902, 1903. Served 18 years on Supreme Court; authored ~1,700 opinions across 73 volumes Michigan Reports. Participated in 8,300+ decisions. Judicial philosophy: "shortest cut, based upon reason, common sense and the experience of centuries" — described by fellow Justice Claudius B. Grant. DEATH: Died suddenly of heart disease at New York Central railroad station, Auburn NY, July 10, 1911, while en route to American Bar Association conference in Chicago. m. Emma Elizabeth Carter 1868 (b. 1844; d. Nov 24, 1909). Children: Harry Eugene Hooker (1870-1925) and Dr. Charles Eggleston Hooker (1872-1932). Chief Justice 1893, 1902, and 1903. Served 18 years on Supreme Court. Authored approximately 1,700 opinions across 73 volumes of Michigan Reports. Participated in 8,300+ decisions. Judicial philosophy described by fellow Justice Claudius B. Grant as 'shortest cut, based upon reason, common sense and the experience of centuries.'

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-three years on the bench
narrative_blocks.body: Frank sat as a judge for thirty-three years, fifteen on the Fifth Circuit and eighteen on the Michigan Supreme Court, where he wrote some seventeen hundred opinions and was chief justice in 1893, 1902 and 1903.

narrative_blocks.header: A mason taught by his sister Elma
narrative_blocks.body: At fourteen Frank learned the mason's trade and worked it through the good months; in the winters he studied higher mathematics, history and Latin under his older sister Elma, who had been schooled in New England. He entered the Michigan law department in 1863.

narrative_blocks.header: Sober, sedate, never a joker
narrative_blocks.body: At law school Frank sat at the front table under Justices Campbell and Cooley. A classmate remembered him as always in his place, sober and sedate, seldom smiling and never a joker.

narrative_blocks.header: Counsel left agape
narrative_blocks.body: As a circuit judge Frank heard both sides patiently and then decided, often so promptly that counsel on the losing side were left agape. Parties in his court rarely had cause to complain of the law's delays.

narrative_blocks.header: Beaten by the man who became his friend
narrative_blocks.body: In 1889 Frank and Claudius Grant were rivals for the Republican nomination to the Supreme Court, and Grant won. When Frank joined him on the bench in 1892 they became close friends, and their families played whist together almost every week.

narrative_blocks.header: His last letter was for someone obscure
narrative_blocks.body: Probably the last letter Frank wrote, Governor Chase Osborn said, was to him, and it was on behalf of a person weak and obscure.

narrative_blocks.header: Two years after Emma
narrative_blocks.body: Frank's wife Emma died in November 1909, and his colleagues believed the grief hastened his own death. He died suddenly at Auburn, New York, in July 1911, as he was setting out on a long-needed rest.

b. Jul 28, 1792 Litchfield CT; d. Rochester NY 1872 age 79. Buried Avon NY (former parish). Moved to Rochester 1821; ordained Presbyterian minister. Pastor Hopewell, Ontario County NY, then Avon NY. Resumed original spelling "Pierrepont." m. Mary Mulloy May 29, 1814 New Haven. She d/o Edward Mulloy of New York. 7 children; three sons — Rev. [BUILD pilot87 — Pierpont Family Genealogy]: Born Litchfield CT 28 July 1792 to Lt. Evelyn Pierpont (H00351) and his wife. Married Mary Mulloy/Malloy (X00328, daughter of Edward Mulloy of New York) at New Haven CT 29 May 1814. Moved to Rochester NY in 1821; ordained Presbyterian minister soon afterward. Pastor at Hopewell (Ontario County NY) for several years, then later at Avon (Livingston County NY). The Pierpont book observes that he consciously restored the older spelling 'Pierrepont' to the family name. The book also notes that upon Evelyn's death in 1812 at sea unmarried, Hezekiah Beers became the senior surviving male of the American branch — meaning he would have inherited the disputed English Pierrepont titles and estates if the family's claim to them had ever been recognized. Probably named for his second cousin Hezekiah Beers Pierrepont (referenced in chapter III of the Pierpont book), who at the time of Hezekiah's 1792 birth was already 'a prominent and promising member of the family that still remained at New Haven.'

narrative_blocks.header: A Rochester pastor, heir to a dukedom
narrative_blocks.body: When his elder brother Evelyn drowned at sea during the War of 1812, Hezekiah — the oldest son of an oldest son through successive generations — became heir presumptive to the English titles and estates of the Duke of Kingston. He pressed the claim for years, with conviction and no success, from a country parsonage in western New York.

narrative_blocks.header: He brought the Pierponts to Rochester
narrative_blocks.body: In 1821 Hezekiah left New Haven for the raw Genesee country, and soon after was ordained a Presbyterian minister — the first of the family to plant the Pierpont name near Rochester. He kept country pulpits at Hopewell and at Avon, where the family would bury its dead.

narrative_blocks.header: He restored the old Pierrepont spelling
narrative_blocks.body: Hezekiah deliberately went back to the ancestral spelling of the name, 'Pierrepont,' the form his English forebears had used. It was a small assertion of an old lineage by a man who believed himself heir to its titles.

narrative_blocks.body: Rebecca Lynch Purdy married Abraham Gabay Crasto at New York on 9 July 1814, four months past her seventeenth birthday. He had come from Suriname at five and been apprenticed on a farm in her own county.

narrative_blocks.header: She went into the ritual bath at twenty-three
narrative_blocks.body: At Paramaribo on 2 April 1820 Rebecca converted to Judaism and took the name Ester Ribca. The community register records that she underwent the ritual bath at the age of twenty-three years and thirteen days.

narrative_blocks.header: She had already borne two of his children
narrative_blocks.body: The Sephardic community of Paramaribo held the New York church wedding invalid, so the marriage was made again in 1820 — by which time Rachel and a second child were born. Until that day the children were illegitimate in Jewish law.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father wrote asking how to reach her
narrative_blocks.body: In June 1818, with Rebecca in Suriname, Elisha Purdy wrote to David Gabay Crasto in New York to ask how a package might be sent out to his daughter and her husband. The letter was still in the family in 1980.

narrative_blocks.header: She was buried in a Christian churchyard
narrative_blocks.body: Rebecca died at New York in April 1875 and lies at Sleepy Hollow; her husband was laid beside her within three years. Fifty-five years had passed since Paramaribo.

narrative_blocks.header: First bride of the snowbound legend
narrative_blocks.body: The town's story made her the first of the three Collins sisters won in the great storm — married to Robert Pierpont in October 1780. Five daughters followed; the family carried her to Manchester around 1795, and Dellwood took her in 1826, nine years before Robert joined her.

narrative_blocks.header: The law student found her in Litchfield
narrative_blocks.body: Richard Skinner read law at the Litchfield school in 1798, in the town where she was raised — she is believed to have attended the Litchfield Female Academy around 1796, two famous schools shaping one match. They married in 1803 and settled at Manchester, Vermont.

narrative_blocks.header: Vermont’s first lady from the snowbound house
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother Lois was one of the three Collins sisters of the snowbound legend, and her great-grandfather Rev. Timothy Collins had been Litchfield's first Congregational minister. She kept the governor's household at Manchester and outlived Richard ten years, dying in 1843; Dellwood holds the family together.

narrative_blocks.header: A snowbound bride's daughter married the doctor
narrative_blocks.body: Believed schooled at the Litchfield Female Academy around 1799, she married Dr. Ezra Isham in June 1801 and kept the Manchester household where six children were born — Pierrepont, the future judge, among them. Two years later her sister Frances married Richard Skinner; the two Pierpont sisters had claimed the town's doctor and its future governor.

narrative_blocks.header: Dunkirk with her son, then home
narrative_blocks.body: Widowed in 1835, she outlived Ezra by nearly four decades — the family record finds her at Dunkirk, New York in 1858, near her merchant son Edwin. Manchester took her back before the end; she died there in 1873, at eighty-eight, and lies at Dellwood.

narrative_blocks.header: Emma Willard sent her south to teach
narrative_blocks.body: A pupil of Mrs. Willard at Middlebury and again at the Troy Seminary in 1825, she went out under Willard's auspices to teach at Sparta, Georgia. Widowhood found her young — Henry Warne died in 1824, and their only child did not live either.

narrative_blocks.header: A women’s college rose at Barhamville
narrative_blocks.body: Beside her second husband, Dr. Elias Marks, she led the South Carolina Female Collegiate Institute near Columbia — Troy Seminary methods carried south, an ably equipped faculty, a name known through the states. Contemporaries ranked her with Emma Willard herself; the Markses retired in 1861, and fire took the buildings in 1869.

narrative_blocks.header: She taught the mother of a President
narrative_blocks.body: Barhamville's rolls carried Martha Bulloch, the future mother of Theodore Roosevelt, and Ann Pamela Cunningham, who went on to lead the rescue of Mount Vernon. The surgeon J. Marion Sims remembered it as the first and only school of its character in the South.

narrative_blocks.header: She named a daughter for his first wife
narrative_blocks.body: Joan Barham Marks carried the name of Jane Barham — the teacher-wife whose memory the school's very ground already honored. Another daughter was Fanny Skinner, for Julia's own sister; three of the five children died small, and Edward John reached Harvard by 1861.

narrative_blocks.header: He held nearly every office Vermont had
narrative_blocks.body: State's attorney, probate judge, congressman in the war Congress of 1813, Speaker of the Vermont House — then the governorship from 1820 to 1823, and the chief justiceship after, until retirement. In 1817 he had declined that same chief justice's seat; six years later he took it on his own schedule.

narrative_blocks.header: A future justice learned law at his desk
narrative_blocks.body: Among the young men who read law in his Manchester office was Pierpoint Isham, later a justice of the Vermont Supreme Court. Back in Litchfield, the schoolmaster-satirist John Pierce Brace had once put Skinner into verse — the manuscript survives at the historical society.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother shared a house with Van Buren
narrative_blocks.body: Roger Skinner — federal judge for northern New York, lifelong bachelor — kept an Albany home with the widowed Martin Van Buren, who nursed him through his final illness in 1825. Thirty-two years later Van Buren had him moved to the Van Buren family plot at Albany Rural.

narrative_blocks.header: A carriage threw him in the Green Mountains
narrative_blocks.body: Thrown from his carriage on May 10, 1833, he died of the injuries thirteen days later at Manchester, fifty-four years old. Dellwood Cemetery holds him in the same ground as his wife's parents, Robert and Lois Pierpont.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran soldier relief; his son fell anyway
narrative_blocks.body: President of the Northwestern Sanitary Commission from its founding, he organized relief for the war's sick and wounded across the whole theater — and in June 1864 his only son Richard died of wounds before Petersburg. He served the commission on, national and local, until the work disbanded.

narrative_blocks.header: He pulled Illinois out of financial chaos
narrative_blocks.body: As Finance chairman in the 1846 House he drew the bill that refunded the state debt — six or eight styles of bonds reduced to one manageable form, fraud cut off, credit restored — and carried the north's side of the convention-apportionment fight that decided whether the debt would be paid at all. A contemporary called it method and system evoked out of chaos.

narrative_blocks.header: One fight for federal office was enough
narrative_blocks.body: Tyler made him United States Attorney for all Illinois, and the Polk-era contest to keep the post — against Isaac Arnold, ended only when both men deferred to a third — showed him, he said, the descents a man must make for federal patronage; he resolved never to seek it again. With Butterfield he had won the only conviction ever obtained under the old Bankrupt Law.

narrative_blocks.header: One judge for all of Cook County
narrative_blocks.body: Elected to the Common Pleas in 1851, he sat alone — all the criminal and nine-tenths of the civil business of the county through one bench, a burden the county history called almost intolerable. Ill health made him decline re-election in 1853 and leave the law for investment work that helped raise Chicago's blocks.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Chicago schools still bear his name
narrative_blocks.body: Founder-president of the Chicago Reform School — he toured the reformatories of the East and studied European records to graft the family system onto it — an organizer of the association that became the Chicago Library, and donor of Manchester's Mark Skinner Library, which served until 2013. Skinner North and Skinner West carry the name through Chicago's school rolls today.

narrative_blocks.header: Ill health made him the valley's historian
narrative_blocks.body: Retired from the Plattsburgh bar at thirty for his health, he turned to the pen — a pioneer history of the Champlain Valley, a history of Essex County, and Men and Times of the Revolution, built from the journals of his father Elkanah, the canal projector. He lived at Port Kent in the house his father raised, now on the National Register.

narrative_blocks.header: He read law under Ambrose Spencer
narrative_blocks.body: Albany Academy and Middlebury came first, then the chambers of Chief Justice Ambrose Spencer. He was admitted to the bar in 1824 and hung out his shingle at Plattsburgh at twenty-one.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote for the society his father built
narrative_blocks.body: The New York State Agricultural Society printed The Plains of Long Island in its Transactions for 1859, and Albany issued it separately the year after — Elkanah had founded the movement those societies grew from. He argued the plains were no barren waste but land written off by hereditary opinion, so neglected it was never entered on the grand list.

narrative_blocks.header: Three conventions and an elector's vote
narrative_blocks.body: He was treasurer of Clinton County and sat in Vermont's first state senate. As a Democrat he went to the national conventions at Baltimore in 1832 and 1835 and at Cincinnati in 1856, and cast an elector's vote that year.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the governor's daughters, both
narrative_blocks.body: Frances Skinner, wed May 28, 1824 — he twenty-two, she fifteen, fresh from Sarah Pierce's Litchfield academy — died in April 1829, leaving him a son. On May 18, 1831 he married her elder sister Susan, and five more children came.

narrative_blocks.body: Elected in 1876 as a Democrat, he was the last man to hold the county judgeship and the surrogacy conjointly; Plattsburgh equity practice filled the decades after. The Sentinel's tribute said the record of his life was a better one than any that could be written.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at thirty, remarried at forty-seven
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Ann Arnold, married as he entered the bar, was dead by November 1862; seventeen years passed before Ella Barnes of Addison County, wed in September 1879. Four children came of the long-delayed second start.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years the Sun's military correspondent
narrative_blocks.body: He came to the Baltimore Sun past fifty and spent four decades as its defense and military correspondent, the man other reporters went to when they needed the Pentagon explained. He won the Pulitzer for his reporting on the war. A Pentagon officer said of him that he had keys to doors in that building even he did not know about.

narrative_blocks.header: Keys to doors even he didn't know about
narrative_blocks.body: A Pentagon officer's tribute — this man has keys to doors in this building that even he doesn't know about — capped four decades as the Sun's military correspondent, a second career begun past fifty. The 1945 Pulitzer and a place in Kennedy's first Medal of Freedom class, the only newspaperman among thirty-one, followed.

narrative_blocks.header: At fifty-six he waded ashore at Salerno
narrative_blocks.body: He went in with Fifth Army troops in September 1943 to begin nearly two years covering the fighting firsthand — this from a man whom a childhood near-drowning had left uneasy in water all his life. The dispatches blended crisp battle reporting with laments for a ruined thirteenth-century chapel.

narrative_blocks.header: A civilian's car led the column into Paris
narrative_blocks.body: Called forward so often to interpret on the August 1944 ride in, he ended up placed in a Frenchman's car leading his column up the Avenue d'Italie — the sort of thing, he wrote, a correspondent dreams of but usually meets only in the movies. Hysterical crowds clutched at the cars; he grabbed the wheel more than once.

narrative_blocks.header: Woollcott and Ross worked for him
narrative_blocks.body: As officer-in-charge of Stars and Stripes at the end of the first war, his staff included Alexander Woollcott and Harold Ross, the future New Yorker founder. Woollcott came to breakfast at the Baltimore house for decades after.

narrative_blocks.header: Three journalists under one roof
narrative_blocks.body: The Baltimore Sun's defense correspondent — one of the great figures of American military journalism — married Susan Owens, herself a journalist; their daughter Susan Barnes Watson wrote as journalist and novelist in London. He carried the name of his great-uncle, Chicago's judge.

narrative_blocks.body: A young reporter on the Baltimore Sun — the paper her family had close connections to — she flew over the city in a small plane, scattering leaflets urging women to vote. She raised two daughters strictly, and the younger carried the family trade to London.

bio.bio_blurb: Sunday Times profile writer and biographer

narrative_blocks.header: Her profiles were the era's must-reads
narrative_blocks.body: The long-form Sunday Times profiles — months of research each, deadly accurate by way of other people's quotations — took on Thorpe after the trial, Tynan, Hailsham, Kingsley Amis on the night Gaitskell died. When Tony Benn, allowed to vet his, asked her not to publish, she withdrew it at once; The Spectator ran it twenty-two years later.

narrative_blocks.header: Is it one of those pamphlets, she asked
narrative_blocks.body: Meeting the celebrated author of The Future of Socialism at a 1956 London party, she asked what exactly it was — a question that delighted him into giving her a marked copy, annotated with which chapters to skim and which to skip. Three years later she canvassed Grimsby for him in a yellow convertible while his agent despaired; he held the seat by a hundred and one votes.

narrative_blocks.header: His ashes to the sea, hers to Lake Champlain
narrative_blocks.body: Widowed at fifty, she scattered his ashes from a Grimsby trawler as they had agreed, declined his seat, and refused a life peerage — pressing it instead toward the widowed Jane Ewart-Biggs. Four years of work produced the biography hailed as a masterpiece; her own ashes were bound for the family plot above Lake Champlain.

narrative_blocks.header: The Queen taught her how to stand
narrative_blocks.body: She crossed for the 1976 Bicentennial aboard Britannia, where the Queen showed her how to stand for hours without tiring — then fell at the embassy dinner for President Ford and broke her jaw, set by the presidential surgeons. As the Foreign Secretary's wife she paid her own economy fare while Tony came back through the curtain bearing champagne.

narrative_blocks.header: She talked her way onto Fleet Street
narrative_blocks.body: Arriving with no British newspaper experience, she persuaded the Sunday Express's John Junor to take her on — the résumé, she later admitted, generously embellished — then negotiated her first contract up by eighty percent and made the Susan Barnes byline a fixture. The pen name was chosen to borrow the lustre of neither her father nor her husband.

narrative_blocks.body: Semantha, the third child of Dr. Noadiah Swift of Bennington, was sent in 1826 to Sarah Pierce's Female Academy in Litchfield. Her grandfather Rev. Job Swift, Yale 1765, had been one of the best-known divines of his day.

narrative_blocks.header: From a Bennington law office to Madison Avenue
narrative_blocks.body: Semantha married the Bennington lawyer Pierrepont Isham on 3 October 1832 and followed him to the Vermont Supreme Court. When he left the bench they moved to 112 Madison Avenue in New York, with a country place at Piermont on the Hudson.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-four years a widow, then Chicago
narrative_blocks.body: Semantha outlived her husband by twenty-four years and spent her last years in Chicago, where her son Edward had built Isham, Lincoln and Beale. She died there in January 1896, at eighty-seven; her son Henry died in Chicago the next year.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandson married a Rockefeller
narrative_blocks.body: Semantha's daughter Mary Adeline married Maj. Sartell Prentice, and their son Ezra Prentice married Alta Rockefeller, a daughter of John D. Rockefeller.

narrative_blocks.header: He made Lincoln's son his junior partner
narrative_blocks.body: In February 1872 Edward took Robert Todd Lincoln, the president's son, into his Chicago practice as junior partner. With William G. Beale's arrival the firm became Isham, Lincoln and Beale, and it kept that name until 1988.

narrative_blocks.header: With Melville Fuller before a tied court
narrative_blocks.body: In January 1876 Edward and Melville Fuller, later Chief Justice of the United States, argued that Chicago's new charter could not stretch Mayor Colvin's term. With one seat vacant the Illinois Supreme Court split three to three and decided nothing.

narrative_blocks.header: The strike injunction that became a precedent
narrative_blocks.body: In 1886 Edward won from Judge Gresham at Indianapolis a federal injunction against strikers obstructing the Lake Shore and Michigan Southern Railway. It put national law over local authority, a precedent later used to protect interstate commerce.

narrative_blocks.header: Counsel to the Newberry Library's founding
narrative_blocks.body: Edward was counsel to the trustees of Walter Newberry's estate through the litigation that founded the Newberry Library, and became its vice president. His essays for the Chicago Literary Club were its most eagerly awaited evenings.

narrative_blocks.header: At fourteen he watched the South mourn Calhoun
narrative_blocks.body: Sent to South Carolina for his health in the winter of 1849, Edward was barely fourteen when the state mourned John C. Calhoun, and read its temper with foreboding. In 1858 he set out for St. Louis or St. Paul and stopped instead at Chicago.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter died on the Titanic
narrative_blocks.body: Edward died suddenly at the Waldorf-Astoria in February 1902. Ten years later his eldest daughter, Ann Elizabeth Isham, was one of only four first-class women lost when the Titanic sank.

narrative_blocks.header: One of four first-class women lost
narrative_blocks.body: Only four women travelling first class died when the ship went down, and she was one. Her body, if it was ever picked up, was never identified, so her family raised a memorial to her in Vermont instead.

narrative_blocks.header: The dog she never owned
narrative_blocks.body: The story that she stepped out of a lifeboat rather than leave a Great Dane, and was seen days later in the water with her arms round it, has no evidence behind it at all — she kept no dog. It fastened on her because she was the one first-class woman whose movements that night nobody could account for.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine years in Paris with her sister
narrative_blocks.body: She led society in Chicago and belonged to the Friday Club and the Scribbler's Club there, but from 1903 she lived abroad, mostly in Paris with her sister Frances. She was fifty and had been gone nine years.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father practised with Lincoln’s son
narrative_blocks.body: Edward Swift Isham built the Chicago firm of Isham, Lincoln and Beale with Robert Todd Lincoln, the president's eldest son. One of the partners, Arthur Ryerson, was aboard the ship with her and died in the same sinking.

narrative_blocks.header: She was crossing to spend a summer
narrative_blocks.body: She boarded at Cherbourg on the tenth of April to go and stay with her brother Edward in New York. Her cabin was C-49, next door to Archibald Gracie, who wrote afterwards that he could not remember ever seeing her.

narrative_blocks.header: He ruined a general's career on Stanton's orders
narrative_blocks.body: After Pope's defeat at Second Bull Run, Benjamin, Pope's chief of cavalry, preferred the charges of disloyalty and misconduct against General Fitz John Porter at Secretary Stanton's prompting. His testimony at the court-martial ruined Porter's career, and Benjamin was banished to the Minnesota frontier.

narrative_blocks.header: From Valverde to Pope's staff
narrative_blocks.body: When the Civil War began Benjamin was major of the 3rd Cavalry in New Mexico, and he was brevetted colonel for the Battle of Valverde under Edward Canby. In July 1862 he was made a brigadier general and brought east as John Pope's chief of cavalry and inspector general.

narrative_blocks.header: Leading the stormers at Churubusco
narrative_blocks.body: Reappointed in 1846 as a lieutenant of Mounted Rifles, Benjamin fought at Veracruz, Cerro Gordo and Contreras, and at Churubusco was brevetted major for leading an advance party of stormers. A second brevet, to lieutenant colonel, followed for gallantry before the war ended.

narrative_blocks.header: A civil engineer in Russia first
narrative_blocks.body: Graduating fifty-third of fifty-six at West Point in 1835, Benjamin resigned four years later to build railroads, first in New York and then in Russia, on the line from Saint Petersburg to Moscow. Back home he practiced law in Iowa until the Mexican War called him into the Army again.

narrative_blocks.header: Military science at Yale, then Dellwood
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin stayed in the regular Army as lieutenant colonel of the 3rd Cavalry until 1868, then taught military science at Yale's Sheffield Scientific School until he retired in December 1870. He died in Washington in 1875 and was moved from Oak Hill Cemetery to Dellwood in his native Manchester.

narrative_blocks.header: He held the bridges as Orozco left Juárez
narrative_blocks.body: During the Orozco revolution Harris commanded at El Paso's international bridges when the rebels left Juárez in August 1912. He escorted Yaqui troops of the Mexican federal army through the United States to Agua Prieta, and arrested the revolutionists Gonzalo Enrile and Colonel Rabelo as they crossed.

narrative_blocks.header: Two troopships disabled under him
narrative_blocks.body: Harris sailed for the Philippines in 1899 on the transport Meade, wrecked leaving harbor, and came home in 1901 on the Sheridan, disabled in a storm and laid up at Nagasaki. In between he fought insurgents on Panay and commanded the west of Bohol, where he was also collector of internal revenue and captain of the port.

narrative_blocks.header: Fever at Ponce in 1898
narrative_blocks.body: Harris sailed from Tampa in July 1898 with Schwan's Independent Brigade, landed at Ponce, Puerto Rico, on 2 August, and commanded his company in camp until fever put him in hospital. He went home on the hospital ship Relief that September.

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve men at Fort Lyon
narrative_blocks.body: Out of West Point in 1880, Harris served at Fort Fetterman in Wyoming, and in October 1881 he commanded Fort Lyon, Colorado, with a detachment of twelve men. At Fort Ringgold, Texas, he sat out a yellow-fever quarantine through the summer of 1882.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter died two months before him
narrative_blocks.body: Harris retired in May 1917 after forty years, and within months was recalled to teach military science at the University of Nebraska, as his father had at Yale, and to command its Students' Army Training Corps. His daughter Elizabeth died of Spanish influenza at San Antonio that October, and Harris died at Chicago in December 1918.

people.research_notes: b. Jun 29, 1783 Litchfield CT; d. May 7, 1836 Sandusky, Erie County OH age 52. DROWNED IN LAKE ERIE. Farmer; in the family wool business. Moved to Sandusky, Ohio. His brother John wrote in a poem: "I am awakened by my weeping, to know that thou art sleeping, on Low Sandusky's shore." m. Sidney Humiston Dec 1, 1807 Litchfield CT (b. Apr 22, 1786; d. May 16, 1841 Litchfield CT). Two children: Minerva (1809-1837) and George Pierpont (1819-1884). SHERMAN PIERPONT FULL ENRICHMENT (stage 6e): Born June 29, 1783 in Plymouth Litchfield County CT — son of James Pierpont III (H00353) and Elizabeth Collins Pierpont. Married Sidney Humiston (I00369, 1786-1841) in 1807 — daughter of Jesse and Abi (Blakeslee) Humiston of Plymouth CT. Two children: Minerva Pierpont Woodward (HD1179, 1809-1837) and George Pierpont (HD1180, 1819-1884). WOOL MERCHANT: Continued the Pierpont family wool business in Litchfield County. When Sherman and Sidney moved to Sandusky Ohio (early 1830s), his younger brother James Morris Pierpont IV (H00832) took over the business per My Country (vol. 28 no. 1, winter 1994). DEATH: May 7, 1836, age 52. Sherman had been residing at Put-in-Bay on South Bass Island in Lake Erie (then also called Edwards Island). He left Put-in-Bay on a sailboat heading for Sandusky with two other men; the boat capsized in a squall and all three drowned. His body was discovered May 27, 1836 on the shore of Lake Erie and brought to Sandusky for burial at Cholera Cemetery (originally Harrison Street Cemetery — the only public burial ground in use in Sandusky at the time). POSTHUMOUS POEM by his brother Rev. John Pierpont (H00826) per Rhoda Cowles Diary vol. II: 'I am awakened by my weeping / To know that thou art sleeping / on Low Sandusky's shore.'

cross_connections.display_label: , a Hooker cousin, died a soldier at Sandusky in 1813
cross_connections.notes: Both Hooker descendants died at Sandusky, Ohio, twenty-three years apart. Norman Hart (gen 7, Marietta Hart line) died there August 1813 as a soldier of the War of 1812 aged seventeen — likely at the August 1-2 defense of Fort Stephenson. Sherman drowned in Lake Erie there May 7, 1836 aged fifty-two. Different lines of Hooker descent ending at the same Ohio frontier town a generation apart.

narrative_blocks.body: His sailboat capsized in a squall off Put-in-Bay on South Bass Island in Lake Erie on 7 May 1836; all three men aboard drowned. His body was discovered 27 May 1836 on the shore of Lake Erie — three weeks after the squall — and brought to Sandusky for burial.

narrative_blocks.body: His older brother Rev John Pierpont wrote a posthumous poem preserved in the Rhoda Cowles Diary: 'I am awakened by my weeping / To know that thou art sleeping / on Low Sandusky's shore.' The grief crossed both the family wool business and the geographic separation of Connecticut from Ohio.

people.research_notes:
b. Apr 6, 1785 Litchfield CT; d. Aug 27, 1866 Medford, Middlesex County MA age 81. Yale College 1804. Litchfield Law School. Admitted bar; lawyer in Newburyport MA. Entered Unitarian ministry; 1819-1845 Pastor of Hollis-Street Church, Boston (one of the most prominent Unitarian pulpits in America). ABOLITIONIST AND TEMPERANCE REFORMER. Published anti-slavery poems. POET: "Airs of Palestine" and other poems. Author of The National Reader (1836). "A quaint, eloquent speaker" (Rhoda Cowles diary). 1861: Chaplain. KEY DESCENDANT: His daughter Juliet Pierpont (1816-1884) married Junius Spencer Morgan I — making Rev. John Pierpont the GRANDFATHER OF J.P. MORGAN. Another son James Lord Pierpont (1822-1893) COMPOSED "JINGLE BELLS" (1857). m. (1) Mary Sheldon Lord Sep 23, 1810 Litchfield CT (his 4th cousin; b. Jan 31, 1787; d. Aug 23, 1855). Buried Mount Auburn Cemetery, Cambridge MA (removed from Oak Grove Cemetery 1871). m. (2) Harriet Louise Campbell Dec 6, 1857 (b.1811; d.1870).
CC NOTE [H00840]: Rev. John Pierpont and John D. Pierpoint were first cousins — sons of brothers James Pierpont III and David Pierpont respectively. John Pierpont became the nationally famous Boston Unitarian minister, abolitionist, temperance reformer, and grandfather of J.P. Morgan. His cousin John Pierpoint became Chief Justice of Vermont (1865-1882). "Hon. John Pierpont of Litchfield, a nephew of the poet, was chief justice of Vermont." Both bore variations of the same name; both were prominent lawyers/ministers. One went to Boston; the other stayed in Vermont. Their careers ran parallel and complementary — one in law, one in the church — until both died in the 1860s-1880s.

narrative_blocks.header: Rum in the cellar, temperance in the pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: Beneath Hollis Street Church sat storage rooms of New England rum, and much of the parish's wealth had been made in the trade — while its minister preached total abstinence. The proprietors tried to force him out; a council of Boston ministers acquitted him in 1841, and he stayed four more years on principle.

narrative_blocks.header: A chaplain at seventy-six, on one condition
narrative_blocks.body: In 1861 he volunteered for the 22nd Massachusetts on the stated condition that the regiment not march around Baltimore, and went with them to the camps defending Washington. A few weeks of army life broke even his vigor; he resigned, took a Treasury post, and spent three years compiling a digest of customs decisions.

narrative_blocks.header: He set the Fugitive Slave Law to verse
narrative_blocks.body: The Fugitive Slave's Apostrophe to the North Star carried his abolitionism into poetry; at the 1850 Springfield convention he introduced the Unitarians' resolutions against the Fugitive Slave Law itself. To see a wrong, an admirer said, was for him to attack it.

narrative_blocks.header: He failed twice before the pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: Four years tutoring in Col. William Alston's Carolina plantation household came first; then Litchfield law and a Newburyport practice that failed, and trade that failed after it. The Hollis Street pulpit found him at thirty-four, and Boston's most prominent Unitarian congregation kept its poet-reformer for twenty-six years.

narrative_blocks.header: Five words beginning with P on his stone
narrative_blocks.body: Mount Auburn's monument reads Poet, Patriot, Preacher, Philosopher, Philanthropist. The sixteen-page front-page eulogy in the Atlantic came from John Neal — the business partner of the failed dry-goods years, fifty years on, who had named a son for him.

narrative_blocks.header: His full name went to Wall Street
narrative_blocks.body: His daughter Juliet's boy, born 1837, was christened John Pierpont Morgan — the reformer's whole name on the century's great financier. The grandfather's own money years had run the other way: two failed ventures, and a contented Treasury clerkship at the end. Another son, James Lord, gave the world Jingle Bells.
