narrative_blocks.header: Invented the Russell Process for silver extraction
narrative_blocks.body: Around 1884 he invented the Russell Process — a hydro-metallurgical leaching method using sodium hyposulphite that allowed economic silver extraction from low-grade ores previously uneconomic. The process built on the older Austrian Patera method but achieved higher extraction rates and could handle ores with heavy base metals.

narrative_blocks.header: Patents across nine years, 1880-1889
narrative_blocks.body: He held US patents granted in 1880, 1883, 1884, 1885, 1886, and 1889 for separating metals from ores, leaching, purifying hyposulphites, and purifying soda ash. The process became highly lucrative for western US and Mexican silver-mining operations through the late 1880s.

narrative_blocks.header: Mining engineer at Park City, then London sociologist
narrative_blocks.body: After Yale Sheffield 1878 he worked 15-20 years as mining engineer in Park City Utah and across US + Mexico — including with the Ontario Mining Company. Gave up mining 1895 and lived in London until May 1928, devoting himself to the study of sociology + work among poorer classes.

narrative_blocks.header: Unmarried; died New Haven 1928 age seventy-two
narrative_blocks.body: He never married; on returning to New Haven May 1928 from his 33-year London period he died at the Parkhurst Sanitarium November 1928 of arteriosclerosis at age 72. Buried at Grove Street Cemetery in his birth city — alongside many of his Russell siblings.

narrative_blocks.header: In 1780 he freed five enslaved people
narrative_blocks.body: On June 30, 1780, Eliot Rawson signed a deed freeing the five Africans he held in bondage — Phillis, Duchess, Francis, Lettice, and Eve Rawson — framing the act as relief for “all those that are suffering for their country, for liberty, or for righteousness sake.” Phillis was to be freed within six months; the others at the age of twenty-four. The document, preserved in Middletown’s town records, served as a kind of moral epitaph for a man whose marble monument bore only names and dates.

narrative_blocks.header: His first wife died within a year
narrative_blocks.body: Eliot Rawson married Sarah Russell, daughter of Rev. William Russell of Middletown, who died barely a year into the marriage and was laid in Riverside Cemetery, leaving an infant daughter named Sarah to carry her name. Seven years later he married Ann Cushing of Providence, with whom he had seven more children.

narrative_blocks.header: Out on the Lexington Alarm at eighteen
narrative_blocks.body: Thaddeus went out as a minute man on the Lexington Alarm in April 1775, at eighteen, and again on the New York expedition, on which his brother Jesse Larned was killed.

narrative_blocks.header: His 1782 letter on the Huddy affair
narrative_blocks.body: In May 1782 Thaddeus wrote to Col. William Shepard at the York Huts about the Joshua Huddy affair, the hanging of a Patriot captain by Loyalists that spring, in a letter that mentions George Washington.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought Thompson from its English owners
narrative_blocks.body: In 1803 Thaddeus and Gen. Daniel Larned bought the Thompson lands from the English proprietors who had held them for a hundred and twenty years, and the speculation paid fair returns. No acre of Thompson came to its owners by confiscation.

narrative_blocks.header: He married two Russell sisters
narrative_blocks.body: Thaddeus married Abigail Russell in 1787 and, after her death in 1797, her sister Esther. A justice of the peace in Thompson, he died in January 1818, and his was the first funeral held in the new church on Thompson Common.

narrative_blocks.header: He made cotton at Larned's mill
narrative_blocks.body: George owned Larned's mill at Thompson for years and made cotton there. When he gave up business he moved to Wickford in Rhode Island, and died there in October 1874, at eighty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine children with Maria Read
narrative_blocks.body: George married Maria Cornelia Read, daughter of William Read of Thompson, on 9 January 1816, and they had nine children before she died in September 1833. Two of them, John and Henry, died as infants.

narrative_blocks.header: He married his first cousin Harriet
narrative_blocks.body: On 9 April 1835 George married his first cousin Harriet Russell of Middletown, daughter of his mother's brother Matthew Talcott Russell. They shared their grandparents, Rev. Noadiah Russell and Esther Talcott, and had five children before Harriet died in 1865.

narrative_blocks.header: His son lent the Russell sea chest
narrative_blocks.body: In April 1888 his son, Maj. George Huntington Larned, lent the sea chest of William Russell to the New Haven Colony Historical Society, on the 250th anniversary of its arrival.

Rawson genealogy entry 227. Named THOMAS HOOKER — explicitly for Rev. Thomas Hooker (1586-1647), founder of Hartford CT and ancestor of his father's first wife Sarah Russell (H00361). Elliot Rawson's first wife Sarah Russell was a 4th-generation descendant of Thomas Hooker (Thomas → Samuel → Mary Hooker Pierpont → Mary Pierpont Russell H00118 → Rev. William Russell I00144 → Sarah Russell H00361). After Sarah's death, Elliot remarried — but named his last child by his second wife for his first wife's ancestor. This is one of the most direct acknowledgments in the entire family network that the Thomas Hooker lineage was consciously honored in naming practices.
CC NOTE [H00361]: Thomas Hooker Rawson was named explicitly for Rev. Thomas Hooker (1586-1647) by his father Elliot Rawson — honoring the lineage of his first wife Sarah Russell, who was a 5th-generation descendant of Thomas Hooker. This is one of the clearest documented instances in the project of the Hooker name being consciously invoked as an ancestor two full generations after the direct connection was broken by death. Elliot Rawson himself had no Hooker blood — the name was purely an act of memorial to his deceased first wife's ancestry.

narrative_blocks.header: Daughter Louisa died thirty days after marriage
narrative_blocks.body: Theodosia's daughter Louisa Walter married Timothy Bishop on April 3, 1800 — and died on May 3, 1800, just thirty days after the marriage. Louisa was twenty. The compressed marriage-and-death cycle within a single calendar month captured the period's vulnerability to acute disease across all socioeconomic groups, even within the Pierpont-Walter household at New Haven.

narrative_blocks.header: Great-granddaughter named Theodocia Pierpont in her honor
narrative_blocks.body: A generation after Theodosia's 1806 death, her son William Walter's daughter named her daughter Theodocia Pierpont Walter Hayden (born August 20, 1817) — honoring the Pierpont great-grandmother through both first name and middle name. The naming carried the Theodosia-and-Pierpont identity forward across three generations of women in the family.

narrative_blocks.header: Grandson William Walter Hayden drowned in childhood
narrative_blocks.body: Theodosia's great-grandson William Walter Hayden — son of Theodocia Pierpont Walter Hayden — drowned on August 2, 1850 in Windsor Connecticut at age twelve. The cascading family losses — daughter at twenty in 1800, great-granddaughter at twenty in 1838, great-great-grandson at twelve in 1850 — touched four consecutive generations of the Walter-Hayden line.

narrative_blocks.header: Born North Haven 1758, died New Haven 1806
narrative_blocks.body: Theodosia Pierpont was born February 22, 1758 in North Haven Connecticut and died July 15, 1806 in New Haven Connecticut at age forty-eight. She married William Jay Walter on November 17, 1777 in North East Village, New Haven — he survived her by eighteen years, dying April 19, 1824. Her five documented children were Joel, Louisa, Lovina, Jerry, and William Jr.

narrative_blocks.header: His five-thousand-dollar bequest transformed North Haven church
narrative_blocks.body: On Ebenezer Pierpont's death in 1854, North Haven Congregational Church 'came into a legacy of five thousand dollars on the death of one of its oldest members.' The bequest was 'a munificent gift and marked the turning point in the history of the church.' His widow Lydia Blakeslee Pierpont added another thousand dollars at her own 1863 death nine years later — six thousand total, a remarkable sum for a mid-century Connecticut parish congregation.

narrative_blocks.header: Wife Lydia Blakeslee outlived him by nine years
narrative_blocks.body: Ebenezer married Lydia Blakeslee (born July 2, 1768) — daughter of Joel and Elizabeth Sackett Blakeslee. Lydia outlived him by nine years, dying July 22, 1863 in North Haven at age ninety-five, her own thousand-dollar bequest to the church supplementing his earlier five-thousand. The couple's combined legacy effectively endowed the North Haven Congregational Church mid-century operations.

narrative_blocks.header: Born and died North Haven, age eighty-three
narrative_blocks.body: Ebenezer Pierpont was born in 1771 in North Haven Connecticut and died March 4, 1854 in North Haven at approximately age eighty-three. His entire life unfolded within his birthplace town — a stability characteristic of the eighteenth-and-early-nineteenth-century New Haven County Pierpont families. His wife Lydia would live to ninety-five, an extraordinarily long life for her generation.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-four years as North Haven Town Clerk
narrative_blocks.body: Daniel Pierpont succeeded his father as Town Clerk of North Haven Connecticut and served in the role for forty-four years — from about 1807 until his death in 1851. The continuous-tenure record was one of the longer documented town-clerkships in early-Republic Connecticut, and combined with his cabinetmaking work, it positioned him as 'one of North Haven's leading citizens.'

narrative_blocks.header: Five legislative terms, Constitutional Convention delegate
narrative_blocks.body: Daniel Pierpont represented North Haven in the Connecticut General Assembly for five terms (1813, 1815, 1818, 1824, and one other), served as a Justice of the Peace for many years, and was a delegate to the Connecticut Constitutional Convention in Hartford. The combined civic portfolio — Town Clerk, JP, state representative, constitutional delegate — built one of the more complete antebellum local-leadership Connecticut careers.

narrative_blocks.header: Pierpont Homestead 1809, now local historic district
narrative_blocks.body: Around 1809 Daniel Pierpont purchased the Pierpont Homestead at 29 State Street North Haven — a Georgian Colonial built 1785 by Stephen Jacobs to which he added a rear addition in 1846. The homestead and the adjacent store run by son Rufus for over a hundred years became 'the center of life at the Pines Bridge in North Haven' and is today a local historic district. The house does not face State Street because the road originally curved to a ford across the river.

narrative_blocks.header: Born and died North Haven, age seventy-six
narrative_blocks.body: Daniel Pierpont was born May 16, 1775 in North Haven Connecticut and died there November 16, 1851 at age seventy-six, buried at Old Cemetery North Haven. He had married Esther Humiston on September 26, 1799 — she outlived him by thirteen years, dying August 17, 1864 in New Haven at age ninety. Their seven children were Bede, Elias, Esther/Stiles, Harriet, Sally, Jared, and Rufus.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son became Connecticut's 33rd governor
narrative_blocks.detail: Belinda was the daughter of Joseph Pierpont Jr. (H00873), carrying the Hooker-Pierpont line forward six generations to a sitting governor. Published biographies of her son acknowledge his descent from Rev. James Pierpont (Yale co-founder) through her, but none document the Thomas Hooker connection that runs through the same line. She is the undocumented link between Hartford's founding minister and one of Connecticut's major public institutions.
narrative_blocks.body: Belinda Pierpont Bigelow raised Hobart Baldwin Bigelow, who served as Connecticut's 33rd governor from 1881 to 1883. During his term he signed the legislation establishing the Storrs Agricultural School — today the University of Connecticut.

narrative_blocks.header: UConn opened with thirteen boys and three teachers
narrative_blocks.body: In September 1881 he signed the act accepting Charles and Augustus Storrs’ gift — a former orphanage, a hundred and seventy acres of farmland and a few barns — and chartering the Storrs Agricultural School. Classes opened on the twenty-eighth with three teachers and thirteen boys; no women were admitted until 1893.

narrative_blocks.header: Fire escapes and honest election registers
narrative_blocks.body: The same single term produced the state’s first fire-escape requirement for any firm with twelve employees or more, and a law against deceptive election registration. Assessments on mutual life insurers were cut back alongside them.

narrative_blocks.header: From a machinist’s bench to the governor’s chair
narrative_blocks.body: Born at North Haven, he quit the South Egremont Academy young for a machinist’s bench, and by 1861 owned the works that traded as H. B. Bigelow & Co., building boilers and heavy machinery. New Haven put him on its council in 1863 and kept him thirteen years, sent him to the General Assembly, then made him mayor — and the state made him governor in 1881. He stayed president of the company through all of it, and for the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: He came down from a founder of Yale
narrative_blocks.body: His mother was Belinda Pierpont, and the line runs back to the Rev. James Pierpont, who helped found Yale in 1701. The governor who signed one Connecticut college into being came down from a man who founded another.

narrative_blocks.header: Three years of parts for the Springfield rifle
narrative_blocks.body: The works took a government contract for three hundred thousand gun parts for the Springfield rifle, three years of work that put a large body of hands on his payroll. A boiler and plate-steel shop had become a supplier to the armouries.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran a bank while he was governor
narrative_blocks.body: Nathan Peck died in January 1882 and the Merchants National Bank of New Haven elected Bigelow its president — in the middle of his term as governor. He kept the post until 1889, six years after he left office.

(b) THE PIERREPONT CC was pure graph restatement — "second cousins once removed via Lt. Joseph Pierpont" — and the tree holds a thousand Pierpont cousins. The real link: BOTH WERE BORN AT NORTH HAVEN, twenty-one years apart, and that one small town sent a US Attorney General and a Connecticut governor out of the same Pierpont stock. North Haven is now in NB3 so the CC is grounded on the card.
(c) NB4 drops the double-descent genealogy — cousin-marrying-cousin paths are implicit in the tree and turn a card into a tree within a tree. It now says only that he came down from a founder of Yale, which pairs with the college he signed into being. ENRICHED 11 Aug 2026 from the biographical sketch Sam supplied. Also in it and NOT on the card: the family moved to South Egremont, Massachusetts in 1844 and he left in 1851; he learned the machinist's trade at Guilford with the Guilford Manufacturing Company and with the New Haven Manufacturing Company, then was foreman at Ives & Smith until 1861; the firm was incorporated as The Bigelow Company in 1883; councilman 1863-64, alderman 1864-65, supervisor 1871-74, fire commissioner 1875-76; a House majority of 1,638 in 1875 and a mayoral majority of 2,378 in December 1878; a director of the Derby Railroad ex officio as mayor until 1 January 1881; Church of the Redeemer; he lived on Orange Street.
DEATH DATE CONFLICT: this sketch says 13 October 1891; FindAGrave and the existing record say the 12th. The 12th is kept. TREE-WIDE CC 11 Aug 2026: Gov. Ichabod Goodwin of New Hampshire (X02381), deliberately outside Connecticut and outside the lineage. A Portsmouth merchant, ship's master and part-owner and railroad president who reached the governorship on that standing, and in May 1861 borrowed against his own credit to equip the state's regiments. Bigelow is the mirror: he kept the presidency of his boiler works through his term and was elected president of the Merchants National Bank in the middle of it. Both are men whose private business standing was the thing that made them useful in office. Runners-up considered: John Wolcott Stewart of Vermont, who left Congress to run the Middlebury bank — but after office, not during; and William Henry Vanderbilt III of Rhode Island, a bus-line founder turned governor. CLOSER-TO-THE-LINE GOVERNOR 11 Aug 2026, keeping Ichabod Goodwin alongside. narrative_blocks.header: Mother and infant buried in same casket, 1836
narrative_blocks.body: Esther Pierpont Stiles died September 26, 1836 in North Haven Connecticut at age thirty-one. Her six-month-old daughter Esther Josephine died the following day, September 27 — and per family tradition mother and infant were buried in the same casket. Her only surviving child, son Charles William Stiles born February 1833, died August 7, 1840 at age seven, ending her direct line within four years of her own death.

narrative_blocks.header: Cousin marriage; sisters wed Stiles brothers
narrative_blocks.body: Esther's 1829 marriage to Ezra Stiles was a documented Pierpont-Stiles cousin marriage — her father Daniel Pierpont and Lois Pierpont Stiles's father Benjamin Pierpont Jr. were first cousins, both grandsons of Joseph Pierpont. That made Esther and her second cousin Lois Pierpont Stiles both Hooker descendants, and the two women married brothers — Ezra and Horace Stiles. Two Hooker-Pierpont cousin marriages between siblings of two intermarried families.

narrative_blocks.header: Husband's later marriages also ended in early death
narrative_blocks.body: Ezra Stiles outlived Esther by half a century but his second marriage in 1837 also ended in his second wife's death at age forty-two in 1853. His third marriage in 1854 to Frances Elizabeth Johnson produced a third Charles, who likewise died at age six. The repeated pattern across three marriages — early-widowed wives, sons named Charles dying young — marks one of the more striking grief sequences in the Stiles branch records.

narrative_blocks.header: Marriage reunited two Hooker branches separated 170 years
narrative_blocks.body: On 9 October 1834 at North Haven CT she married Horace Stiles — both descended from Rev Thomas Hooker through different sons of his son Samuel. Levinia's line ran through Mary Hooker Pierpont; Horace's through Esther Hooker Stiles. The two branches had separated in the 1660s and converged again in this marriage 170 years later.

bio.bio_blurb: Colonial soldier and North Haven farmer

narrative_blocks.header: He fought in both the century’s wars
narrative_blocks.body: Abel Brockett went out in the French and Indian War as a young man and again in the Revolution, and the family book calls him a stalwart Colonial patriot. He was fifty when the second war began.

narrative_blocks.header: His father gave a farm per marriage
narrative_blocks.body: Moses Brockett of Wallingford held so much land that one piece ran a mile wide and two miles long, and he handed each son a farm as he married. Ezra Stiles set his name down in his manuscript notes.

narrative_blocks.header: The will left him a meadow
narrative_blocks.body: Moses gave the two-mile lot with house and barn to his eldest living son John, the homestead farm to Richard, the homestead to Stephen, four acres to a grandson — and to Abel the meadow and six acres.

narrative_blocks.header: He and his brother married two sisters
narrative_blocks.body: Abel married Hannah Pierpont in July 1755; his brother Richard married her sister Mary. By 1760 Abel and Hannah were members of the Congregational church at New Haven, and they lie together at Montowese.

narrative_blocks.header: He deeded the land to Lyman in 1802
narrative_blocks.body: A 1765 agreement on the New Haven records settled matters between Abel, his brother John and his three sisters. Nearly forty years later he deeded lands to his son Lyman, and he died in August 1815 at eighty-nine.

naming_inspiration.name_element: Pierpont (given to son Jared Pierpont Brockett)
naming_inspiration.description: Son Jared Pierpont Brockett (b. Mar 18, 1810) was given the Pierpont name as a middle name to honor Timothy's mother's family (the Pierpont line). The maternal-surname-as-middle-name was a deliberate naming convention preserving the Pierpont ancestry forward across this branch.

narrative_blocks.header: He built Saratoga's first tannery among log huts
narrative_blocks.body: Saratoga was a scatter of log huts when Timothy Brockett put up its first tannery. He had come north from Connecticut, and the works he built were the settlement's first.

narrative_blocks.header: Hudson to Albany, then the bridle path north
narrative_blocks.body: He sailed up the Hudson to Albany and crossed to Schenectady, then a small town. The rest of the way to Saratoga was a bridle path.

narrative_blocks.header: Two of his children died within one year
narrative_blocks.body: Laura was born on 19 February 1803. Her brother Abel, not quite four, died thirteen days later. Laura herself was dead before the year was out.

narrative_blocks.header: He outlived Olive Root by twenty-three years
narrative_blocks.body: Timothy married Olive Root in March 1793 and buried her at Galway in 1831. He stayed in the town another twenty-three years and was laid beside her at eighty-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: He named a son for Hannah Pierpont
narrative_blocks.body: Timothy's mother was Hannah Pierpont. His seventh child he called Jared Pierpont Brockett, sending her surname forward into a generation that would otherwise have carried only his own.

people.research_notes: b. Jul 17, 1769 North Haven CT (bapt. Aug 20, 1769); d. Sep 22, 1849 age ~80 Hamden CT. Buried Old Graveyard, Mount Carmel, Hamden CT. m. Mehitabel Candee ca.1791 (b. ca.1775; d. Nov 21, 1840 Hamden CT; daughter of Zaccheus Candee and Rebecca Smith). Resided in Hamden. WAR OF 1812: Appears in muster roll, 2nd Regiment, 7th Company, Capt. Ambrose Tuttle. SEA CAPTAIN: "He was also a sea captain engaged in West India trade. On one occasion when he did not accompany his vessel on its voyage, he had a dream that the vessel had gone down. The impression he received was so vivid that he awoke his wife and told her his dream. As a fact, the vessel was never heard from, and he always believed that it went down that night. He never went to sea again." He then engaged in the cooperage business at Mount Carmel — "one of the leading industries of the country, and an important factor in the trade between New Haven and the West Indies." narrative_blocks.header: He woke his wife about the dream
narrative_blocks.body: Hezekiah Brockett stayed ashore for one voyage of his West India vessel. That night he dreamed she had gone down, and woke Mehitabel to say so. The ship was never heard from again.

narrative_blocks.header: He never sailed again, and made barrels instead
narrative_blocks.body: He did not go back to sea. At Mount Carmel he took up cooperage, building the casks for the same New Haven and West Indies trade he had sailed in.

narrative_blocks.header: The muster roll names him of Mount Carmel
narrative_blocks.body: He appears on the 1812 muster roll of the Second Regiment, Seventh Company, under Captain Ambrose Tuttle, entered as Hezekiah Brockett of Mount Carmel. He was forty-three.

narrative_blocks.header: He buried a daughter at three weeks old
narrative_blocks.body: Julia was born on 21 October 1800 and lived twenty-one days. Hezekiah buried her in the Mount Carmel ground where he and Mehitabel would both come to lie.

NOTE: Three sons died violent maritime deaths — shark, yellow fever at sea, and death in East Indies — within the same family.

narrative_blocks.header: Three sons died violent maritime deaths
narrative_blocks.body: Three of Lyman Brockett's sons died violent maritime deaths within the same generation: Miles (born 1805) was killed by a shark while in the West Indies around 1826 at age twenty-one; Loyal (born 1811) died at sea in 1829 of yellow fever as a ship officer at age eighteen; and Lyman Goodsell (born 1823) was a ship officer who died in the East Indies. The compressed family loss across three sons in the merchant and whaling trades captured the maritime risk of mid-nineteenth-century American shipping.

narrative_blocks.header: Four or five sons in shipping and whaling
narrative_blocks.body: Beyond the three sons who died at sea, Lyman's son Lewis (born 1808) died in New Haven after returning from a three-year whaling voyage, unmarried — suggesting illness contracted on the voyage. The family was a maritime-trade family in concentration: five of nine children had ocean-going careers. The eldest son Merrick later moved inland to Peoria Illinois, where his father Lyman eventually joined him.

narrative_blocks.header: Connecticut to Illinois migration in old age
narrative_blocks.body: After his New Haven-area maritime family had been scattered or lost to the sea, Lyman Brockett moved to Rosefield Illinois in his old age and died there around 1857. He is buried at Peoria Illinois — joining his eldest son Merrick who had migrated west earlier. His wife Hannah Goodsell of Watertown Connecticut had predeceased him by about two years in 1855.

narrative_blocks.header: Born North Haven 1780, nine children with Hannah
narrative_blocks.body: Lyman Brockett was born July 25, 1780 in North Haven Connecticut (baptized September 7, 1780) and married Hannah Goodsell of Watertown Connecticut. Nine children: Merrick, Miles, Lewis, Loyal, Lucy Charlotte (married Isaac Jones and removed to Oregon; remarried William Jones), Russell (died in infancy), Harvey Russell (named for grandmother Hannah Russell Pierpont's family), Mary Ann, and Lyman Goodsell.

EDWARDS PIERREPONT BIRTH-YEAR RESOLUTION (Apr 2026): The widely circulated 1817 birth date for Edwards Pierrepont (Wikipedia, DOJ.gov, Encyclopedia.com, Wikidata, Geni) is mathematically impossible — his mother Eunice Munson Pierpont died June 23, 1814. RootsMagic Atwood Family database and WikiTree (Pierpont-470 lineage) give Nov 4, 1813, which reconciles the chronology. Tree records HD1492 with corrected birth date Nov 4, 1813. The 1817 error appears to derive from a common biographical source repeated across reference works. Edwards Pierrepont's own family genealogy (Pierpont book) gives only the month/day '4 March' — which would be 'November 4' OS rendered as 'March' by some calendar transcription error, or simply the error originated independently.

narrative_blocks.header: Three deaths in five weeks, 1842
narrative_blocks.body: Giles's son Zerah died on 30 November 1842, at twenty-five. Giles died four weeks later, on 28 December, at fifty-nine, and his daughter Laura on 3 January 1843, at sixteen.

narrative_blocks.header: His Pierpont land became Clover Dairy Farm
narrative_blocks.body: The 225 acres Giles farmed had passed from Rev. James Pierpont to his son Lt. Joseph, then to Joseph's son Giles and so to him. By 1901 D. W. Patten had made the tract Clover Dairy Farm, with hill, river and meadow and the dairy barns across it.

narrative_blocks.header: His son Edwards was Grant's attorney general
narrative_blocks.body: Giles's son by Eunice Munson, born in 1813 and named Munson Edwards Pierpont, dropped the Munson, took the spelling Pierrepont, and was President Grant's attorney general in 1875 and 1876. Eunice died in June 1814, at about twenty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: He spilled ink on Babcock's letter
narrative_blocks.body: As Grant's attorney general from 1875, Edwards prosecuted the Whiskey Ring to 110 convictions. When he caught Grant's own secretary, Orville Babcock, writing a warning to a ring member, he spilled ink over the letter.

narrative_blocks.header: "Once a President always a President"
narrative_blocks.body: As minister in London, Edwards told Lord Derby that a former president deserved a former head of state's honors, and in June 1877 he introduced Ulysses Grant to Queen Victoria at Windsor.

narrative_blocks.header: Lincoln's man, then Surratt's prosecutor
narrative_blocks.body: Lincoln put Edwards on the 1862 commission for state prisoners held by the army, and in 1867 he prosecuted John H. Surratt for Lincoln's murder. After seventy hours the jury could not agree, and Surratt went free.

narrative_blocks.header: The Committee of Seventy against Tweed
narrative_blocks.body: In 1871 Edwards sat on New York's Committee of Seventy, which went after Boss Tweed's Tammany Ring and helped put Tweed in jail.

narrative_blocks.header: A bust with a bigger head
narrative_blocks.body: Edwards believed a wide head meant a great mind, and kept telling the young Augustus Saint-Gaudens to enlarge his marble bust. Saint-Gaudens said it looked affected with some dreadful swelling disease.

narrative_blocks.header: He dropped Munson and added an r
narrative_blocks.body: Baptized Munson Edwards Pierpont, he dropped the Munson and added an r, reviving an older spelling of the family name. At Yale he graduated in 1837 with Samuel J. Tilden and William M. Evarts.

narrative_blocks.header: From Fifth Avenue to Alaska
narrative_blocks.body: At sixty-six Edwards travelled with his son Edwin to the far reaches of Alaska, and together they wrote From Fifth Avenue to Alaska. Edwin died in Rome two years later, serving as chargé d'affaires.

b. Mar 4, 1817 North Haven CT; d. Mar 6, 1892 New York City age 75. Baptized "Munson Edwards Pierpont" — dropped first name and resumed original Pierrepont spelling. Yale College 1837; Yale Law School. Tutor at Yale 1840-1841. Began practice Columbus OH (partner Phineas B. Wilcox, Yale 1821). Moved to NYC 1845 — "soon took a prominent position at the bar." 1857: elected to bench, Superior Court of New York City; resigned 1860. CIVIL WAR: Organized War Democrats 1864; advocated Lincoln re-election; supported Grant for presidency 1868. 1869: President Grant appointed him U.S. District Attorney, Southern District of NY. 1871: Leading role in OVERTHROW OF THE TWEED RING (Committee of Seventy). 1873: Appointed Minister to Russia — declined. 1875: ATTORNEY GENERAL in President Grant's cabinet. 1876: MINISTER PLENIPOTENTIARY to Court of St. James (UK). Notable case: Prosecuted John A. Surratt for complicity in Lincoln's murder. 1878: Returned from England, resumed law practice. Honorary degrees: Doctor of Laws from Columbian University (1871), Yale (1873), Doctor of Civil Laws from Oxford University (1878). m. May 27, 1846 Margaretta Willoughby (dau. of Samuel Augustus Willoughby and Margaretta Duffield, of Brooklyn). Children: Margaretta Pierrepont, Edwards Pierrepont Jr. (Pierpont Genealogy; Wikipedia; EH)
CC NOTE [HD1438]: Edwards Pierrepont (1817-1892, Attorney General) and Gov. Hobart Baldwin Bigelow (1834-1891, CT Governor) were SECOND COUSINS ONCE REMOVED. Both descend from Lt. Joseph Pierpont and Hannah Russell Sackett: Pierrepont through the Giles Pierpont branch; Bigelow through the Joseph Pierpont branch — Giles and Joseph were brothers. Pierrepont is 4 generations from Lt. Joseph; Bigelow is 5. They were active in public life simultaneously: Bigelow was Mayor of New Haven 1879-1881 and Governor 1881-1883; Pierrepont had been U.S. Attorney General 1875-1876 and U.S. Minister to Britain. Both were prominent Connecticut Republicans of the Grant era. They almost certainly knew each other — New Haven County elites were a small world, both were Yale-connected (Pierrepont Yale 1837; Bigelow's son Frank Yale 1881), and Bigelow as Mayor of New Haven overlapped with Pierrepont's active law practice in NY while he maintained his Garrison NY estate just up the Hudson. Whether they were aware of their shared Hooker ancestry is unknown. Neither's biography documents the Hooker connection.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight days in the Osawatomie asylum
narrative_blocks.body: In March 1902 the Sedgwick County probate court tried Elmon for insanity on a complaint that he was dangerous, kindling fires in the middle of the room at his home east of Wichita, where he lived with two of his children. He was admitted to the state asylum at Osawatomie on 22 March and died there of tuberculosis eight days later, at seventy-three.

narrative_blocks.header: A son buried seven miles east of Wichita
narrative_blocks.body: Elmon came to Kansas from North Haven, and by 1870 he and Caroline held land seven miles east of Wichita. Their son Elbert Wallace died there in March 1872, at twelve, and was buried on the place, where Elmon and Caroline were later laid beside him in the Pierpont Cemetery.

narrative_blocks.header: Saint-Gaudens carved her too
narrative_blocks.body: In 1874, when the young Augustus Saint-Gaudens made the marble bust of Edwards that he complained about so bitterly, he carved Margaretta's as well. The two busts are at the Smithsonian American Art Museum.

narrative_blocks.header: A Brooklyn girl on Fifth Avenue
narrative_blocks.body: Margaretta, a daughter of Samuel Willoughby of Brooklyn, married Edwards in 1846 and they began in Brooklyn. By the 1870s they lived in a brownstone on Fifth Avenue near 18th Street and spent summers at their Davis villa at Garrison.

narrative_blocks.header: Grief after Edwin
narrative_blocks.body: When their son Edwin died of a fever in Rome in 1885, Margaretta's health gave way. The next year she and Edwards went south looking for a kinder climate, and stopped at Atlanta's new Kimball House.

narrative_blocks.header: Beckwithshaw above the Stockbridge Bowl
narrative_blocks.body: In 1892 Margaretta and Leonard built Beckwithshaw, a thirty-one-room house on the west shore of the Stockbridge Bowl, with its name cut over the hall fireplace. Barely a year later, after his breakdown at the World's Fair, she and a daughter asked the court to declare him insane.

narrative_blocks.header: Her old lawn heard the first concerts
narrative_blocks.body: Widowed in 1895, Margaretta saw Beckwithshaw sit on the market until 1905. By August 1934 it was Dan Hanna's, and members of the New York Philharmonic gave three outdoor concerts there, the festival that grew into Tanglewood.

narrative_blocks.header: She inherited the house on the Hudson
narrative_blocks.body: When her mother died in 1902 Margaretta inherited Hurst-Pierrepont, the Gothic villa Alexander Jackson Davis had drawn for her parents above the Hudson at Garrison, and in 1912 she brought in Cross & Cross to add three stories of kitchen and servants' rooms.

narrative_blocks.header: A hundred years in one family
narrative_blocks.body: Hurst-Pierrepont stayed the family's country house for a century, into the 1960s. Its tall Gothic windows and the grand stair Davis set to dominate the hall survived every change Margaretta and her parents made.

narrative_blocks.header: She took in her orphaned grandchildren
narrative_blocks.body: When Rudolf Brünnow died in 1917, his and Marguerite's children went to live with their grandmother Margaretta at Philipstown, on the Hudson.

bio.bio_blurb: First American manufacturer of wagon springs

narrative_blocks.header: The first wagon springs made in America
narrative_blocks.body: Charles Brockett was the first man in the country to manufacture wagon springs. He built a handsome fortune on it at Mount Carmel, and his eldest son learned the trade beside him before going out on his own.

narrative_blocks.header: His successor resigned so he could return
narrative_blocks.body: He was a commissioner for New Haven County many years and a director of the county bank. His firm stand was said to prevent much useless litigation, and in the troubled years after the war his successor stepped down so he could be recalled.

narrative_blocks.header: He married again at fifty-eight
narrative_blocks.body: He married Amelia Bristol of Cheshire in April 1827, and she died in 1849 at forty-two, leaving him four children. In January 1862 he married Mrs. Leanor Pratt. He died at Hamden in 1884, eighty years old.

narrative_blocks.header: She perished in the Great Chicago Fire
narrative_blocks.body: Lucy Barnes Brockett died in the Great Chicago Fire of October 1871, among roughly three hundred killed as the flames took three square miles of the city. She was sixty-seven and had been a widow eleven years.

narrative_blocks.header: Three of her four children went first
narrative_blocks.body: Charles died at one, Martha at twenty-four and Mary Ann at thirty-five, all before the fire. Only Jared was still living when it took her, and he lasted another thirty-six years.

narrative_blocks.header: Named Lodeema — a name that echoed through
narrative_blocks.body: Lodeema Brockett was born in Columbia, New York in 1800, the daughter of Chauncey Brockett, who would lead his family to the Ohio frontier in 1820. She married Aaron Drake Sr. in 1823 and eventually settled in Somerset, Niagara County, New York, where she died on New Year's Day 1873 at 72. Her unusual given name was carried forward: her granddaughter was named Myra Lodeema Drake.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-six years of account books
narrative_blocks.body: Jesse, a joiner and cabinetmaker at North Haven, kept account books from 1792 to 1828, recording where he worked, for whom and for how long, with family among his customers, and what each owed him or had paid.

narrative_blocks.header: Collector of North Haven's church rates
narrative_blocks.body: In 1798 North Haven made Jesse a collector of the Ecclesiastical Society rates, the town's church tax, and residents declared their taxable property to him on lists that run through 1801 and 1802.

narrative_blocks.header: Eldest of Hezekiah Tuttle's seven children
narrative_blocks.body: Jesse was the eldest of Hezekiah and Mary Turner Tuttle's seven children, baptized at North Haven in 1780, at nine. He married Esther Pierpont, daughter of Giles Pierpont, on 30 September 1795, and when he died in 1847 their sons Dennis and Zerah administered his estate.

b. Oct 2, 1800 North Haven CT; d. Jul 22, 1884 North Haven CT age 83. Named PIERPONT for his mother's Pierpont family. m. (1) Maria Todd Apr 28, 1824 North Haven CT (b. Feb 24, 1797; d. Apr 28, 1860). m. (2) Mary Cook Oct 28, 1861 New Haven CT. Son: NEWTON TUTTLE (1825-1905) — MORMON PIONEER. Newton converted to the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints and emigrated to Utah in the William Field Company 1854. His first wife Lucinda died of cholera at Fort Leavenworth before reaching Utah; his daughter Clara (age 4) died two days into the overland journey Jun 23, 1854. Newton reached Bountiful, Davis County UT on Oct 21, 1854. Served as Utah territorial militiaman in the Utah War 1857. His diary is held in the LDS Church archives, Salt Lake City. Son Eunice Tuttle Pierpont (b.1827) was named PIERPONT for her great-grandmother's family. [Cause revert audit]: Earlier extraction set death.cause="cholera" but reverted: cholera — was about Lucinda Mix Tuttle, not Zerah Pierpont Tuttle.

narrative_blocks.header: He disinherited his son Newton
narrative_blocks.body: When Newton and his wife, Lucinda, joined the Latter-day Saints, Zerah disinherited him, and in 1854 they left North Haven for Utah against his wishes. For years neither man wrote, each waiting for the other to write first, though Newton's mother, Maria, sent him seeds.

narrative_blocks.header: Newton let in on one condition
narrative_blocks.body: When Newton came back east in 1877, Zerah did not know him at first, and Maria had been dead seventeen years. Zerah let him in on condition that he not speak of the church, and Newton went home to Utah with much of the family's genealogy.

narrative_blocks.header: Nineteen years a schoolmaster
narrative_blocks.body: Zerah taught school for nineteen years before he took up farming at North Haven, and he pressed his children to get an education and to live by it.

narrative_blocks.header: Three wives, the last at eighty-one
narrative_blocks.body: Zerah married Maria Todd on 6 April 1824, and of their five children Edgar died as a baby in 1830 and Eliza Maria in 1853. A year after Maria's death in 1860 he married Mary A. Johnson, and in 1882, at eighty-one, he married Laura Elizabeth Beecher.

notable.notable_blurb: Mormon pioneer and Bountiful water master

bio.bio_blurb: Mormon pioneer and Bountiful water master

narrative_blocks.header: Lucinda and Clara, buried on the trail
narrative_blocks.body: Newton set out for Utah in 1854 with his wife, Lucinda Mix, and their daughter Clara. Lucinda died of consumption near Fort Leavenworth on 14 May, and his diary placed her grave beside the road short of Salt Creek, in a cluster of walnut trees. Clara died on 23 June, seven weeks short of five, and Newton came on to Bountiful alone.

narrative_blocks.header: He went to break up a Mormon meeting
narrative_blocks.body: In 1844 Newton went to a Mormon meeting in North Haven with some young men who meant to break it up, and stayed to the end without a disturbance. He began going to a small branch five miles away in 1848 and was baptized on 13 October 1850.

narrative_blocks.header: Bountiful's water master, unpaid for twenty years
narrative_blocks.body: Newton was the first in Bountiful to make out water tickets and divide the irrigation water, which had caused trouble before him, and he ran it for about twenty years without pay, buying his own books and stationery. He was also ward clerk for twenty years, until his hearing failed.

narrative_blocks.header: A scout under Lot Smith in 1857
narrative_blocks.body: When Johnston's Army marched on Utah in 1857, Newton rode as a scout for the militia under Lot Smith, whose cavalry burned the army's supply trains on the plains.

narrative_blocks.header: The family records he gathered in 1877
narrative_blocks.body: Newton served a year's mission to Connecticut, and on a trip east in 1877 gathered family records that the church came to count among its most complete. He kept a diary from boyhood almost to his death, now in the church archives at Salt Lake City, and lent his large library to anyone who asked.

narrative_blocks.header: Bees he caught in the mountains
narrative_blocks.body: A blacksmith by trade, Newton raised broom corn and made brooms for years, kept large orchards, and was among the first in Bountiful to keep bees, which he caught himself in the mountains.

narrative_blocks.header: Married by Heber C. Kimball in 1855
narrative_blocks.body: Newton married Emily Amelia Stone of Middletown, Connecticut, at Salt Lake City on 7 April 1855, with Heber C. Kimball performing the ceremony. They built their home at East Bountiful and raised eleven children there.

b. Sep 11, 1727 New Haven CT; d. Feb 22, 1813 North Haven CT age 85. Buried Montowese Cemetery, North Haven CT. Brother of Abel Brockett (X00479, husband of Hannah Pierpont H00370). The two Brockett brothers married two Pierpont cousins, Mary and Hannah, both Hooker descendants — a double family link. Son of Moses Brockett and Lydia Ann Grannis. m. Mar 13, 1756 Mary Pierpont (H00371, 1738-1773) — daughter of Joseph Pierpont and Hannah Russell, granddaughter of Rev. James Pierpont (founder of Yale College and 30-year pastor of First Church New Haven), and also granddaughter of Rev. Thomas Hooker through her grandmother Mary Hooker Pierpont. The Brockett Genealogy explicitly confirms the Hooker descent. MEMBERSHIP: Richard and Mary were members of the Congregational Church in New Haven (the same First Church where Mary's grandfather James Pierpont had pastored). 1776 CURRENCY-BURNED INCIDENT: Per Connecticut Colonial Records Vol. 10: 'In 1776 Richard Brockett dropped a 20-shilling bill in the fire, and on proving that it was accidental, the General Assembly ordered the amount to be made good to him.' This is one of the few documented Connecticut General Assembly currency-replacement cases of the Revolutionary era. 1779 ALARM LIST: Per Sheldon B. Thorpe's 'North Haven Annals' historical record: 'in 1779 Col. Russell issued an order to the officers of the Alarm List and the Militia of New Haven; on its back were endorsed the names of Richard Brockett, Ebenezer Brockett, and Isaiah Brockett' — Richard and his two brothers were on the alarm list together. CHARACTER: 'a man of great integrity of character and his word was as good as his bond.' WIDOWED: Mary died Jun 21, 1773 age 34 after only 17 years of marriage. Richard outlived her by 40 years. 7 CHILDREN: Joseph (HD1527, 1757-1820, Hooker-line father of Rev. Pierpont Brockett); Mary (HD1528, 1759-? m. James Ives); Giles (H00891, 1761-1842 Rev War 3-yr enlistment); Lydia (H00892, 1763-? m. Philemon Blakeslee); Richard Jr. (H00894, 1768-1832); Jesse (H00893, 1770, died age 1 day); Jesse (H00895, 1772, died age 13 days as second-Jesse). Sources: Brockett Genealogy entry #56; Connecticut Colonial Records Vol. 10; Thorpe's 'North Haven Annals.'

military_service.source_citation: Sheldon B. Thorpe, 'North Haven Annals' — Col. Russell's 1779 order to officers of the Alarm List and Militia of New Haven endorsed names of Richard Brockett, Ebenezer Brockett, and Isaiah Brockett
military_service.role: Officer on the New Haven Alarm List — the call-up roster for civilian-soldiers expected to respond rapidly to British raids along the Connecticut coast. Three Brockett brothers appeared together on Col. Russell's 1779 endorsement.

narrative_blocks.header: He burned a banknote and got it back
narrative_blocks.body: In 1776 Richard Brockett dropped a twenty-shilling bill into the fire. He proved to the General Assembly that it had been an accident, and the Assembly ordered the money made good to him. The Connecticut colonial records carry it.

narrative_blocks.header: He and his brother married two sisters
narrative_blocks.body: Abel Brockett married Hannah Pierpont in July 1755. Richard married her sister Mary the March after. The two brothers had married two daughters of Joseph Pierpont, and both couples joined the Congregational church at New Haven.

narrative_blocks.header: Three Brocketts endorsed on one order
narrative_blocks.body: Colonel Russell sent an order to the officers of the New Haven Alarm List and Militia in 1779. Three names were written on the back of it: Richard Brockett, Ebenezer Brockett and Isaiah Brockett.

narrative_blocks.header: Two sons called Jesse, days apart
narrative_blocks.body: A Jesse was born in January 1770 and died the next day. A second Jesse came in February 1772 and lived three. Mary bore a last daughter the year she herself died, in June 1773, at thirty-four.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventeen years passed before he married again
narrative_blocks.body: Richard was forty-five when Mary died and sixty-three when he married the widow Jemima Jacobs in December 1790. She outlived him by seventeen years, dying in 1830.

narrative_blocks.header: The will made his sons pay their sister
narrative_blocks.body: Giles and Richard each took land and each owed their sister Mary Ives a payment out of it. If either neglected her, the will instructed the executor to take it from the rent of the land they had been given.

narrative_blocks.header: His word was as good as his bond
narrative_blocks.body: The North Haven annals set him down as a man of great integrity, and put it in those words. He farmed at Muddy River, held the lots his father Moses had parcelled out, and died there in February 1813 at eighty-five.

death.notes: Died on his 63rd birthday — born and died on the same calendar date Jan 17.

marriages.notes: DATE DISCREPANCY: Tree previously had 1782; Brockett Genealogy 1905 (primary family source) gives May 8, 1772. If 1772 correct, Joseph was 15 yrs 3 mos and Rebecca was 15 yrs 5 mos at marriage — extremely young but not impossible in colonial Connecticut. Counter-evidence for 1782: first child Roxanna born Nov 27, 1782 — if married 1772, 10-year gap before first surviving child is unusual but possible. Brockett family book treated as authoritative.

people.research_notes: b. Jan 17, 1757 North Haven CT; d. Jan 17, 1820 North Haven CT — DIED ON HIS 63rd BIRTHDAY (born and died on the same calendar date). Buried Montowese Cemetery, North Haven CT. Son of Richard Brockett (X00491, 1727-1813) and Mary Pierpont (H00371, 1738-1773) — through his mother the line traces back to Rev. Thomas Hooker. Per the Brockett Genealogy, Mary Pierpont was 'a grand-daughter of Rev. James Pierpont, the successor of Rev. John Davenport, as pastor of the First Church in New Haven... He was one of the founders of Yale College.' REVOLUTIONARY WAR: Service in Lieutenant Colonel Sabin's regiment per the 'Record of Conn. Men in the Revolution' at the Connecticut State Library, Hartford (Manuscripts Vol., pp. 547-548). POSTWAR: Rose to Captain in the Connecticut militia. From 1799 to 1806 represented North Haven in the Connecticut General Assembly. CAREER: 'Forehanded farmer' (Brockett Genealogy phrase) — meaning prosperous, well-to-do; in his later years also owned a shoe manufactory. Will divided estate: dwelling and personal property to wife and daughter; factory and over fifty acres of adjoining land to his two sons. RELIGION: Member with his wife of Dr. Trumbull's Church (Congregational, North Haven). CHARACTER: 'A man of excellent character and greatly esteemed in the community for his integrity and public spirit. He was administrator on the will of Capt. Gideon Todd, and on other Estates.' MARRIAGE: m. May 8, 1772 Rebecca Tuttle (X00492, b. Dec 20, 1756; d. Sep 14, 1835) — daughter of Joel Tuttle of East Haven. (Brockett book date 1772; tree previously had 1782 — flagged.) 3 CHILDREN per Brockett Genealogy: Roxanna (b. Nov 27, 1782; d. Nov 12, 1841 — eldest, not yet built in tree); Jesse (b. May 28, 1785; m. Anna Taintor — not yet built); Pierpont (HD1529, b. Oct 30, 1787 — Baptist minister, the in-tree Hooker line continuation). Sources: Brockett Genealogy 1905; Record of Conn. Men in the Revolution; Montowese Cemetery.

military_service.source_citation: Record of Conn. Men in the Revolution, State Library at Hartford, Manuscript Vol. pp. 547-548
military_service.role: Active Revolutionary War service in Sabin's regiment per the official Connecticut Men in the Revolution record; later rose to Captain in the Connecticut state militia.

narrative_blocks.header: He died on his sixty-third birthday
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph was born at North Haven on 17 January 1757 and died there on 17 January 1820, on his sixty-third birthday. He lies in the town's Montowese Cemetery.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight straight years in the General Assembly
narrative_blocks.body: A private in Lt. Col. Sabin's regiment in the Revolution, Joseph rose after the war to captain of militia. North Haven sent him to the Connecticut General Assembly every year from 1799 to 1806, eight years running.

narrative_blocks.header: Two of his sons turned Baptist in 1810
narrative_blocks.body: In 1810 the evangelist Joshua Bradley preached through North Haven, and Joseph's sons Jesse and Pierpont were converted and baptized together, leaving Rev. Benjamin Trumbull's Congregational parish for a new Baptist church. Pierpont preached for forty-one years; Jesse became its deacon.

narrative_blocks.header: His great-grandfather helped found Yale
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph's mother, Mary Pierpont, was a granddaughter of Rev. James Pierpont, pastor of New Haven's First Church and one of the founders of Yale College, and of his wife Mary Hooker, a granddaughter of Rev. Thomas Hooker.

people.research_notes: b. Mar 13, 1759 New Haven CT. m. James Ives of Great Barrington MA, Jun 16, 1779. Richard Brockett's will left her 17 pounds plus 24 pounds advanced at marriage.

narrative_blocks.header: She married into Great Barrington in 1779
narrative_blocks.body: Born at New Haven on 13 March 1759, Mary married James Ives of Great Barrington, Massachusetts, on 16 June 1779, at twenty, with the Revolution four years old. Her father's will counted what he had given her at the wedding as part of her share.

After war: 1-2 West Indies voyages as sailor, then returned to farming. m. Nov 17, 1785 Sarah Smith (b.Jul 10 1768; d.Nov 27 1841 Waterbury; dau Capt. Stephen Smith NH). Removed to Waterbury 1803. Deacon, First Congregational Church. Deputy CT General Court 1804; CT Legislature 1809. Mason. military_service.role: Enlisted as a youth in 1778, served three years through the war's later phase. Listed on the federal Pension List in 1832.

narrative_blocks.header: Three-year teen enlistment, 1832 federal pensioner
narrative_blocks.body: Giles Brockett enlisted at seventeen in 1778 in Colonel Mead's Connecticut Troop and served three full years through the Revolutionary War's later phase. His name appears on the federal Pension List in 1832 — the act that recognized aging Revolutionary veterans. After the war he tried sailing, making one or two voyages to the West Indies, then returned to North Haven to take up farming, where he lived to age eighty-one.

narrative_blocks.header: Sailor first, then deacon and Connecticut legislator
narrative_blocks.body: After his short West Indies sailing career, Giles returned to farming and married Sarah Smith in 1785. In 1803 the family removed to Waterbury Connecticut, where Giles became deacon of the First Congregational Church. He served as deputy to the Connecticut General Court in 1804 and as representative in the Connecticut Legislature in 1809, plus active membership in the Masonic Lodge — a complete local-leadership Yankee farmer profile.

narrative_blocks.header: Six children at East Farms then Dublin Street
narrative_blocks.body: Giles and Sarah's six children included Polly, Sarah, Patty, Harriet (who married Lieutenant Colonel Samuel Peck), Roswell (who died unmarried in Greenville Michigan in 1853), and Lydia (who married Smith Miller). The Waterbury farm was first at East Farms and then on what later became Dublin Street. Giles and Sarah were remembered as 'persons of a happy temperament, lovely, generous, and beloved by their family.'

narrative_blocks.header: Four Pierpont cousins married Blakeslees
narrative_blocks.body: Lydia's mother was Mary Pierpont, and her Pierpont cousins kept marrying Blakeslees. Elizabeth and Mehitable Pierpont each took a Blakeslee husband, Ezra Pierpont married Philemon's sister Mary in 1783, and on 22 February 1787, at twenty-three, Lydia married Philemon Blakeslee at North Haven.

narrative_blocks.header: Their Rimmon Road house still stood in 2000
narrative_blocks.body: Lydia and Philemon lived in the house at 222 Rimmon Road, North Haven, which was still standing in 2000. Philemon, a Revolutionary veteran and militia captain, was the town's selectman in 1803 and 1811 and sat in the General Assembly in 1814.

people.research_notes: b. Jan 16, 1770 North Haven CT; d. Jan 17, 1770. Died the day after birth.

narrative_blocks.header: Lived a single day, January 1770
narrative_blocks.body: The first Jesse Brockett was born January 16, 1770 in North Haven and died the very next day — a one-day infant life, the briefest documented in the entire Richard-Mary Brockett seven-child sibling sequence. The name 'Jesse' was attempted a second time two years later when another son was born on February 10, 1772, but that second Jesse lived only thirteen days. Two named-Jesse infant deaths in three years marked the family's mid-1770s grief.

people.research_notes: b. Jan 9, 1768 New Haven CT (EH bapt. Feb 21, 1768); d. 1832. Daughter: Tirzah (b.1792 North Haven; bapt. St. John's Episcopal Church 1792).

narrative_blocks.header: Tirzah baptized at St. John's Episcopal, 1792
narrative_blocks.body: Richard Brockett Jr. was born January 9, 1768 and died in 1832 at age sixty-four. His only documented child Tirzah Brockett was born in North Haven in 1792 and baptized that same year at St. John's Episcopal Church — a different church than his parents' Congregational membership at New Haven First Church. The shift to Episcopal practice in Tirzah's baptism marks one of the early-Republic Brockett-family denominational pivots, an era when Connecticut Episcopal congregations were growing from their post-Revolutionary 'Loyalist' status into a recognized mainstream denomination.

people.research_notes: b. Feb 10, 1772 North Haven CT; d. Feb 23, 1772 age 13 days. Second Jesse after first died.

narrative_blocks.header: Second Jesse, died age thirteen days, 1772
narrative_blocks.body: After the first Jesse Brockett died the day after his January 1770 birth, Richard and Mary Pierpont Brockett named their next son Jesse as well — this second Jesse was born February 10, 1772 and lived only thirteen days, dying February 23. The repeated-name pattern was common in colonial families honoring a deceased child's intended name, but the second Jesse's also-early death meant the name passed entirely from this sibling line. The next surviving Jesse Brockett in the family — Jesse 1785-1850, son of Joseph and grandson of Richard — would carry the name forward.

b. Oct 30, 1787 North Haven CT; d. Apr 7, 1868 Wethersfield CT age 80. Son of Captain Joseph Brockett (HD1527) and Rebecca Tuttle (X00492). Named PIERPONT for paternal grandmother Mary Pierpont (H00371) — the Hooker-descent point in this branch. EARLY MENTORSHIP: As a studious boy in North Haven Pierpont was a 'favorite' of Rev. Benjamin Trumbull DD — historian of Connecticut and Congregational pastor at North Haven — who loaned him books and encouraged his mental development. 1810 CONVERSION: Baptist preacher Rev. Joshua Bradley came to North Haven and drew crowds; Pierpont and his brother Jesse were converted, baptized, and formed the nucleus of a North Haven Baptist church. The young convert began establishing meetings in surrounding districts. Trumbull, grieved that his 'favorite boy' had left the Congregational fold and was holding meetings 'without his authority,' rebuked him strongly at first but eventually ceased opposing him. WAR OF 1812 (1812-1814): Felt called as a loyal citizen to take up arms; enlisted under Commander Abraham Hubbard; first made ensign, then promoted to lieutenant; ordered to Groton and New London to defend the Connecticut coast. THEOLOGICAL STUDY: After the war, studied under Rev. Jeremiah Chaplin DD (later president of Waterville College) at Danvers Massachusetts. CLASSMATES Coleman and Wheelock were among THE FIRST AMERICAN MISSIONARIES TO BURMA (the trail blazed by Adoniram Judson 1812+). MINISTRY (41 years, 9 successive pastorates, 6,300+ sermons preached not counting addresses/lectures): Jan 21, 1819 ordained pastor Baptist Church Canton CT. Autumn 1822 yielded to friends' urgent request to become STATE MISSIONARY FOR CONNECTICUT under the Connecticut Baptist Convention; resigned at end of one year for pastoral work. 1823-1828 pastorate Clinton CT (5 years). 1828-1835 pastorate Essex CT (7 years; 'church became strong in gifts and graces'). 1835 pastorate Agawam Church West Springfield MA. 1838-1841 pastorate North Stonington CT (3 years). 1840 First Church Saybrook CT (now Winthrop). 1843 Lyme CT. 1845-1849 Colchester CT (4 years, 'eminently successful in building up a strong united church'). 1849-1862 Wethersfield Baptist Church 'in order to be near his children' (12 years, with three-year break). CT STATE PRISON CHAPLAIN 1854-1857 — three years full-time. Per Brockett Genealogy: 'During his active ministry of 41 years he had preached more than 6,300 sermons aside from addresses, lectures, &c.' 'Possessed of a warm heart, a sympathetic nature and greatly beloved as a pastor, a counsellor and a friend.' MARRIAGE: m. Sarah Sage (X00493, 1795-1882) Sept 22, 1819, shortly after his Canton ordination. She was daughter of Col. Josiah Sage of Upper Middletown CT and Sarah Savage; she was baptized 1818 by Rev. Frederick Wightman before the marriage. 5 CHILDREN: Linus Pierpont Brockett MD (HD1530, 1820-1893, author of ~50 books); Sarah Brockett (HD5081, b/d Mar 1823 — 5 days); Henry Sage Brockett (HD5082, 1825-1826 age 10 months); Julia Helen Brockett (HD5083, 1826-1831 age 4); Edward Judson Brockett (HD1531, 1833-1919, compiled Brockett Genealogy). EDWARD JUDSON NAMING: Son Edward 'JUDSON' was almost certainly named for Adoniram Judson (1788-1850), the celebrated American Baptist missionary to Burma — given Pierpont's theological classmates Coleman and Wheelock had themselves been among the first Americans sent to Burma after Judson. Sources: The Descendants of John Brockett 1905; archive.org/details/descendantsofjoh00inbroc.

naming_inspiration.description: First name 'Pierpont' honors paternal grandmother Mary Pierpont (H00371, 1738-1773) — through whom the Hooker descent runs (her grandfather Rev. James Pierpont married Mary Hooker, granddaughter of Rev. Thomas Hooker).

military_service.role: Loyal-citizen enlistee at start of war; first made ensign, then promoted to lieutenant; served at Groton and New London to defend the Connecticut coast.

narrative_blocks.header: 6,300 sermons in forty-one years
narrative_blocks.body: Pierpont was ordained in 1819 at the Baptist church of Canton, Connecticut, and over forty-one years served nine pastorates, from Clinton, Essex and Lyme to Colchester and at last Wethersfield, to be near his children. He preached more than 6,300 sermons, besides addresses and lectures.

narrative_blocks.header: His old pastor's favorite turned Baptist
narrative_blocks.body: As a studious boy Pierpont was the favorite of Rev. Benjamin Trumbull, North Haven's Congregational pastor and the historian of Connecticut, who lent him books. When the Baptist evangelist Joshua Bradley came through in 1810, Pierpont and his brother Jesse were converted; Trumbull rebuked him, then gave up opposing him.

narrative_blocks.header: Ensign, then lieutenant, in 1812
narrative_blocks.body: In the War of 1812 Pierpont served under Commander Abraham Hubbard at Groton and New London, first as ensign and then as lieutenant. Afterwards he studied theology at Danvers under Rev. Jeremiah Chaplin, among students who included two of the first American missionaries sent to Burma after Adoniram Judson.

narrative_blocks.header: Chaplain of the state prison
narrative_blocks.body: From 1854 to 1857 the chaplaincy of the Connecticut State Prison took all of Pierpont's time, and he stepped back from his Wethersfield pulpit, returning to it until he retired in 1862.

narrative_blocks.header: A colonel's daughter and two writing sons
narrative_blocks.body: Pierpont married Sarah Sage of Middletown, daughter of Col. Josiah Sage, on 22 September 1819, the year he was ordained. Their son Linus became a doctor and the author of some fifty volumes, and Edward compiled the Brockett family genealogy.

narrative_blocks.header: Married Pierpont in his ordination year
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah Sage Brockett married Rev. Pierpont Brockett on September 22, 1819 — the same year he was ordained as Baptist pastor at Canton Connecticut — beginning a partnership in ministry that spanned forty-nine years across nine pastorates. She 'entered heartily into the work of her husband, always his faithful helper, and was the means under God of winning many to righteousness.' She had been baptized the year before the marriage by Rev. Frederick Wightman.

narrative_blocks.header: Lost three of five children before age five
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah and Pierpont's first child Linus Pierpont was born in 1820, but their next three — Sarah (1823 age five days), Henry Sage (1825-1826 age ten months), and Julia Helen (1826-1831 age four) — all died young. Only her fifth and last, Edward Judson born 1833 when she was thirty-eight, survived alongside Linus into adulthood. She lived at Edward's East Orange New Jersey home in her widowhood and died there in 1882 at age eighty-seven.

people.research_notes: b. Oct 16, 1820 Canton/Old Saybrook CT; d. Jan 13, 1893 Brooklyn NY age 72. Buried Green-Wood Cemetery, Brooklyn NY. Named PIERPONT for great-grandmother Mary Pierpont (H00371). M.D. Yale Medical College 1843. A.M. Williams College. AUTHOR OF ~50 VOLUMES. Major works: "Woman's Work in the Civil War" (1867, landmark Civil War history), "Woman: Her Rights, Wrongs, Privileges, and Responsibilities" (Hartford, 1870), "Men of Our Day" (1868). ENCYCLOPEDIAS: 2,000+ articles in Appleton's New American Cyclopedia; associate editor Johnson's Universal Cyclopedia; associate editor two foreign encyclopedias. Active in Brooklyn Baptist churches. m. Dec 22, 1846 Lucy Maria Thacher (b.Jun 25, 1823; d.Feb 26, 1907). Only child Arthur Thacher Brockett (b.Oct 6, 1847; d.Jan 31, 1854 age 6) — gravestone reads "Arthur Thacher / Only child / Until the day break." Books on archive.org. MORAL POSITION — WOMEN'S RIGHTS: "Woman's Work in the Civil War" (1867) documented women's contributions to the Union cause in sustained, systematic detail. "Woman: Her Rights, Wrongs, Privileges, and Responsibilities" (Hartford, 1870) is an explicit women's rights advocacy text. This is a sustained literary commitment across multiple major works, not a passing reference. Counterweight to documented enslavers (Dr. Hezekiah Chaffee) and opium traders (Russell & Company) elsewhere in the family network. [Stage 6Y-286 Brockett book enrichment]: Per the 1905 Brockett Genealogy (Edward Judson Brockett compiler): EDUCATION: BROWN UNIVERSITY first; then Yale Medical College graduating 1843; A.M. from Williams College. RELIGION: United with the Baptist Church in Hartford in early life; in 1860 removed to Brooklyn NY where he resided until death. Active in Hanson Place, Washington Avenue, and Emmanuel Baptist Churches of Brooklyn. MISSIONS SPECIALTY: 'especially taking an interest in the cause of Missions; in fact few laymen were ever better acquainted with the history, in detail, of Foreign Missionary work, not only in his own denomination, but of all faiths.' Foreign-missions focus (parallel to brother Edward Judson's American Baptist Home Mission Society work). DEATH: 'His patience, resignation and good cheer as he passed, by painful path, through the Valley of Death were beautiful to witness.' BIRTH-YEAR DISCREPANCY: Brockett Genealogy gives 'Oct. 16, 1829, at Canton, Conn.' — but Yale Med graduating 1843 would require age 13 at graduation, impossible. The 1820 birth date in our entry is supported by census and Yale records; the Brockett book year is a transcription error (1820 → 1829).

narrative_blocks.header: Two thousand articles for Appleton's
narrative_blocks.body: Linus took his medical degree at Yale in 1843 but chose to write rather than practise. He wrote more than two thousand articles for Appleton's New American Cyclopaedia, was some fifteen years associate editor of Appleton's Annual Cyclopaedia, and later of Johnson's Universal Cyclopaedia.

narrative_blocks.header: Books that sold a hundred thousand
narrative_blocks.body: His histories and biographies sold from 75,000 to more than 100,000 copies apiece, among them The Cross and the Crescent, on Russia and Turkey, in 1877. In all he wrote some fifty volumes, most of them on the Civil War, biography and American history.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote up women's war work
narrative_blocks.body: In 1867 Linus published Woman's Work in the Civil War, a record of the nurses, fund-raisers and Sanitary Commission workers of the Union cause, and in 1870 Woman: Her Rights, Wrongs, Privileges, and Responsibilities.

narrative_blocks.header: Until the day break
narrative_blocks.body: Linus married Lucy Thacher at Jordan, New York, on 22 December 1846. Their only child, Arthur, died at Hartford in January 1854, at six, and the family stone at Green-Wood reads Arthur Thacher, only child, until the day break.

narrative_blocks.header: Moved to Green-Wood two years on
narrative_blocks.body: Linus lived in Brooklyn from about 1865 and died there on 13 January 1893, at seventy-two. In May 1895 his remains were moved to the family lot at Green-Wood, where Lucy was buried beside him in 1907.

people.research_notes: b. Mar 7, 1833 Essex CT; d. Feb 8, 1919 East Orange NJ age 85. Buried Green-Wood Cemetery, Brooklyn NY (Lot 3874 Section 33, buried Feb 10 1919). Son of Rev. Pierpont Brockett (HD1529, 1787-1868) and Sarah Sage Brockett (X00493, b. Sept 13, 1795 Middletown CT). Younger brother of Dr. Linus Pierpont Brockett (HD1530, 1820-1893). EDUCATION: Bacon Academy, Colchester CT — one of the leading institutions of learning in New England at the time. EARLY CAREER (Hartford publishing house, late 1840s-1856): Made acquaintance of distinguished authors and literary persons. Published at his own expense: a volume of poems by Mrs. Lydia H. Sigourney; a volume of poems by Rev. Arthur Cleveland Coxe (later Bishop of Western New York); a volume on 'Formation of Character' by Rev. Thomas M. Clark (later Bishop of Rhode Island); 'Heroes and Martyrs of the Missionary Enterprise' by Rev. Lucius E. Smith DD of Boston. MID-CAREER (1856 to New York): Called to NY to take charge of the subscription book business of Messrs. Mason Brothers. Made the acquaintance (later long friendship) of Benson J. Lossing (historian of 'The Field Book of the Revolution'), James Parton (whose 'Life of Aaron Burr' gave him great celebrity), and 'Fanny Fern' (sister of N. P. Willis, whose 'Fern Leaves' had unrivaled American book sales). BUSINESS CAREER (1858-death): Entered employ of Battelle & Renwick (manufacturing white lead, importing chemicals) as bookkeeper and confidential clerk. Rose through financial positions of trust; elected treasurer and director of various corporations in which the firm was interested; appointed executor and trustee of several estates. In 1883 became a member of the firm; on its incorporation became its vice-president and treasurer. RESIDENCE: First Brooklyn (united with Hanson Place Baptist Church for twelve years); removed to East Orange NJ in 1869 — uniting with North Orange Baptist Church (elected treasurer at once; trustee 1880; president of Board for many years). Home named 'The Towers' on Prospect Street, East Orange. RELIGION: Ordained as Deacon 1881. Active in Sunday School. Member Executive Board of the American Baptist Home Mission Society (INST154) many years, chairman from June 1904. President of the New Jersey Baptist Missionary Convention ten years. Member 'Committee of Fifteen' considering the relation of National Baptist organizations to each other. Sought-after Baptist denominational counselor in State and National organizations. AUTHORSHIP: COMPILED 'THE DESCENDANTS OF JOHN BROCKETT, ONE OF THE ORIGINAL FOUNDERS OF NEW HAVEN COLONY' (1905) — one of the primary sources for this entire Hooker-Brockett project. The genealogy explicitly states Mary Pierpont H00371 was 'a grand-daughter of Rev. Thomas Hooker, one of the founders of the Connecticut Colony, at Hartford' — making this Hooker-tree explicit at a primary-source level. MARRIAGE: m. Oct 7, 1862 Mary Frances Gault (I01288, 1841-1923) — daughter of Deacon George Gault of Brooklyn (b. Dec 8, 1803 Bow NH; constituent member of Pierrepont Street, Atlantic Street, and Hanson Place Baptist Churches in Brooklyn; moved to Orange 1864) and Elizabeth Biglow Gault (m. 1831 Springfield VT). George Gault not built per Jalapeño rule. FIVE CHILDREN: George Pierpont Brockett (HD5074, 1864-1892, died 28); Francis Edward Brockett (HD5075, 1865-1929 m. Margaret Whitney 1890, took over genealogy research); Edith Agnes Brockett Quattlebaum (HD5076, 1869-1955, DAR member with seven ancestor entries); Frederick Sage Brockett (HD5077, 1872-1882, died age 10); Helen Frances Brockett Stricklett (HD5078, 1877-1962, magazine contributor). Sources: The Descendants of John Brockett (1905); FindAGrave; 1870/1910 US Census; archive.org/details/descendantsofjoh00inbroc.

notable.notable_blurb: Publisher and family genealogist

naming_inspiration.description: Middle name 'Judson' almost certainly honors Adoniram Judson (1788-1850), the celebrated American Baptist missionary to Burma — the most famous American Baptist missionary of the 19th century. Pierpont Brockett's theological-class classmates Coleman and Wheelock were 'among the first missionaries sent from this country to Burmah' after Judson, giving the family a direct line to the Judson missionary legacy.

institutions.institution_blurb: Executive Board member of the American Baptist Home Mission Society for many years; chairman from June 1904.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the Brockett genealogy
narrative_blocks.body: In 1905 Edward published The Descendants of John Brockett, One of the Original Founders of New Haven Colony, with portraits and the family arms. It traces the family to Mary Pierpont, a granddaughter of Rev. Thomas Hooker, and his son Francis spent three years on its research.

narrative_blocks.header: He published Mrs. Sigourney at his own risk
narrative_blocks.body: In his Hartford publishing years before 1856 Edward brought out, at his own expense, poems by Lydia Sigourney and by Arthur Cleveland Coxe, later Bishop of Western New York, and Thomas Clark's Formation of Character.

narrative_blocks.header: Friends with Lossing, Parton and Fanny Fern
narrative_blocks.body: From 1856 Edward sold subscription books in New York for Mason Brothers and grew close to the historian Benson Lossing, to James Parton, whose Life of Aaron Burr was a sensation, and to Fanny Fern, whose Fern Leaves outsold nearly everything. Their company turned him to historical research.

narrative_blocks.header: He chaired the Baptist home missions
narrative_blocks.body: Edward chaired the executive board of the American Baptist Home Mission Society from June 1904, was for ten years president of the New Jersey Baptist Missionary Convention, and from 1881 was a deacon and president of the trustees of the North Orange Baptist Church.

narrative_blocks.header: Bacon Academy to Battelle & Renwick
narrative_blocks.body: Educated at Bacon Academy in Colchester, Edward went into publishing and in later life was an officer of Battelle & Renwick, manufacturers and importers in New York. He lived at East Orange, New Jersey, and died there in February 1919, at eighty-five.

b. Oct 29, 1744 Stratford CT; d. Apr 15, 1835 New Haven CT age 90. Daughter of a Stratford CT family. m. John Pierpont (H00388) Dec 26, 1767 New Haven CT. 10 children; only 4 lived to adulthood; only 3 married. Had three daughters named Sarah/Sally — two died in infancy, third died age 14. Lived to 90, outliving her husband by 30 years. Sister of Capt. Nathan Beers who commanded the guard over Major André at his trial and execution 1780 (EH 388 Note). NOTE: Capt. Nathan Beers — her brother — commanded the guard over Major John André (British spy in the Benedict Arnold treason affair) at André's trial and execution on October 2, 1780. The British had raided the John Pierpont house (built by her husband) only one year earlier (1779), using it as a hospital and headquarters. EH notes this connection explicitly (EH entry 388 note).
Orbit connection: Her brother Capt. Nathan Beers commanded the guard at Major André's trial and execution Oct 2, 1780 Tappan NY. See notable_story: major_andre_execution_three_hooker_family_connections.

narrative_blocks.header: She buried seven children and lived to ninety
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah Beers married John Pierpont and bore ten children, but only four reached adulthood; she named three daughters Sarah and lost two as infants and the third at fourteen. She lived to ninety, outliving her husband by thirty years.

narrative_blocks.header: The British seized her home as a hospital
narrative_blocks.body: During the 1779 British invasion of New Haven, soldiers seized the house her husband had built and used it as a hospital for their wounded. The rooms kept the bloodstains and bayonet scars of that occupation for years after.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brother guarded the captured spy Major André
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah's brother, Captain Nathan Beers, commanded the guard over the British spy Major John André at his trial and execution in 1780. André's hanging, in the wake of Benedict Arnold's treason, was among the most talked-of events of the war.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father was shot at his own door
narrative_blocks.body: As the British marched into New Haven in 1779, they shot Sarah's father, old Nathan Beers, at the door of his house on the corner of York and Chapel. He lingered five days before dying at sixty — remembered by the town as 'an honest man and a Puritan worthy.'

people.research_notes:
b. Nov 3, 1768 New Haven CT; d. Aug 11, 1838 Brooklyn NY age 69. Buried Green-Wood Cemetery, Brooklyn (Find A Grave #58486817). CAREER: Settled New York City 1790 as Customs House clerk. Founded mercantile partnership Leffingwell & Pierpont 1793 (dissolved 1800). Moved to Brooklyn 1801; purchased Philip Livingston's brewery and converted it to ANCHOR GIN DISTILLERY — "kept the gin stored for a full year after it was made, by which it acquired the mellowness for which it was peculiarly esteemed." (Stiles, History of Brooklyn, 1869) Witnessed Robespierre beheaded in Paris during reign of terror (residing in France 7 years attending his firm's shipments). Pirates seized his ship the "Confederacy" 1797; went bankrupt. Friends with Robert Fulton. Real estate: acquired 150,000+ acres upstate NY from father-in-law's estate; "inheritor and holder of half a million of acres of land of great value in Northern New York, which were purchased originally for but eight cents an acre." (Dwight) Proposed promenade along Brooklyn Heights bluffs (precursor to today's Promenade). Distillery closed 1819; site is now part of One Brooklyn Bridge Park. m. Anna Maria Constable Jan 21, 1802 NYC (b. Mar 10, 1783 Philadelphia; d. Nov 7, 1859 Brooklyn; daughter of William Constable, one of the largest landowners in NY State). She as a child saw Washington at her father's house; Hamilton and Burr dined there 1796. Requested ca.1802 that family restore the French "Pierrepont" spelling. 12 children including Henry Evelyn Pierrepont (1808-1888). MONUMENT: Gothic Revival brownstone catafalque at Green-Wood Cemetery, designed by Richard Upjohn; designated landmark.
CC NOTE [HD0419]: Hezekiah Beers Pierrepont (Brooklyn gin distiller, city builder) was the great-grandson of Rev. James Pierpont and Mary Hooker Pierpont. His grandfather Hezekiah Pierpont was the BROTHER of Lt. Joseph Pierpont — father of all the North Haven Pierponts whose families have been documented throughout this project. So the Brooklyn Pierreponts and the North Haven Pierponts (who married into the Brockett, Ives, Eastman, and Tuttle families) are first cousins once removed from each other, all descended from the same James Pierpont/Mary Hooker household.
