narrative_blocks.header: Fifty years negotiating where troops could stand
narrative_blocks.body: He joined the Defense Department in 1949, helped negotiate the original NATO status of forces agreement, and from 1968 ran foreign military rights affairs — the basing agreements for twenty-five countries from Spain to Turkey to the Philippines. He retired in 1999.

narrative_blocks.header: He laid the groundwork for Diego Garcia
narrative_blocks.body: As politico-military attache in London from 1964 to 1966 he laid the foundations for the legal separation of Diego Garcia from Mauritius. The island became the American base used in the Gulf War of 1991 and in Iraq.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept trail miles and played the bassoon
narrative_blocks.body: Barringer hiked and maintained miles of path for the Potomac Appalachian Trail Club and served as its president. He played bassoon in a chamber music group, and was a director of the Barringer Crater Company at Flagstaff, Arizona.

people.research_notes: b. Jul 20, 1920 Boston MA; d. Dec 31, 1999 Boston MA age 79. Cerebral hemorrhage. Cremated at Mount Auburn Cemetery. Boston Brahmin family; father and grandfather both chiefs of MGH Surgical Service and Harvard Medical School professors. Park School Brookline; Milton Academy. Harvard A.B. 1941 (cum laude; Winthrop House; editor Harvard Lampoon). WWII: Combat medic, U.S. 4th Infantry Division. Participated Normandy invasion Jun 6, 1944 — crossed minefield to rescue fellow officer; among first up Causeway No. 2 from Utah Beach. Served through European campaign; Bronze Star Medal and Purple Heart with oak leaf cluster; discharged 1945 as 1st Lieutenant. Harvard Law School 1947 (president, Harvard Law Review). Clerked for Judge Learned Hand (2nd Circuit) and Justice Felix Frankfurter (SCOTUS). Joined Ropes & Gray Boston. CAREER: Asst. Secretary HEW 1957-1959; U.S. Attorney District of Massachusetts 1959-1961; Lt. Governor Massachusetts 1964; Attorney General Massachusetts 1966 (last Republican to hold that office as of 2025); Under Secretary of State 1969; Secretary HEW 1970-1973; Secretary of Defense Jan-May 1973; ATTORNEY GENERAL May 1973 — resigned Oct 20, 1973 rather than obey President Nixon's order to fire Watergate special prosecutor Archibald Cox (Saturday Night Massacre). His resignation and Deputy AG William Ruckelshaus's simultaneous resignation precipitated the constitutional crisis that led to Nixon's resignation. Ambassador to the United Kingdom 1975-1976; Secretary of Commerce 1976-1977. One of only two people in U.S. history to hold four Cabinet positions (with George Shultz). Presidential Medal of Freedom 1998. Interpol's 2018 album Marauder features his photo on the cover. Married Anne Frances Hazard (HD1587) 1952 after meeting at a dance her senior year at Radcliffe.

narrative_blocks.header: Four cabinet seats under two presidents
narrative_blocks.body: A Boston doctor's son who chose law, he served in the cabinets of Richard Nixon and Gerald Ford, and only George Shultz has also held four cabinet posts. He is still the last Republican elected attorney general of Massachusetts.

narrative_blocks.header: Nixon told him to fire the prosecutor
narrative_blocks.body: He appointed Archibald Cox to Watergate and promised Congress he would not interfere. Ordered to dismiss him on 20 October 1973 he resigned instead, and his deputy followed. He talked the solicitor general out of quitting so Justice kept a head.

narrative_blocks.header: He took down a vice-president that same autumn
narrative_blocks.body: He also ran the investigation into the kickbacks Spiro Agnew took as a Maryland official and went on taking as vice-president. Agnew resigned ten days before Richardson did.

narrative_blocks.header: A health plan and a blood-pressure campaign
narrative_blocks.body: At Health, Education and Welfare he drew up a national health plan and started the National High Blood Pressure Education Program. He later led the American delegation on the law of the sea, and took the Medal of Freedom.

narrative_blocks.header: Tax evaders had a circle of their own
narrative_blocks.body: Eisenhower made him United States attorney in Massachusetts in 1959 and he made his name on tax fraud. In his Inferno, he wrote, tax evaders had a circle to themselves; every one his office prosecuted went to jail.

narrative_blocks.header: He crossed a minefield to reach an officer
narrative_blocks.body: He landed at Utah Beach on 6 June 1944 as a combat medic and crossed a minefield to reach an officer whose foot had been blown off. He came home with the Bronze Star and the Purple Heart.

narrative_blocks.header: Frankfurter put him up for Harvard at 33
narrative_blocks.body: His father, both grandfathers, three uncles and two brothers were Harvard physicians; he chose law. He clerked for Learned Hand and then Frankfurter, who put him up for the Harvard presidency in 1953.

bio.bio_blurb: Professor of moral and political philosophy

narrative_blocks.header: Rawls supervised him, Nussbaum before that
narrative_blocks.body: He took his doctorate at Harvard in 1986 under John Rawls, with a thesis on the rational deliberation of ends. Martha Nussbaum had supervised his master's thesis at the Kennedy School, in the year he also finished law.

narrative_blocks.header: One book on thinking, one on deciding together
narrative_blocks.body: Practical Reasoning about Final Ends, in 1994, was about how a person reasons toward what to want. Democratic Autonomy, in 2002, asked how a public does it, and took both the Herbert Simon and David Easton book prizes.

narrative_blocks.header: He edited the field's journal for a decade
narrative_blocks.body: Ethics has been the central journal of moral and political philosophy since 1890, and he ran it from 2008 to 2018. He has taught at Georgetown since 1986 and sits at its Kennedy Institute of Ethics.

narrative_blocks.header: The Guggenheim year went to a vaccine paper
narrative_blocks.body: He won a Guggenheim for 2019 and began a book on the division of moral labour. The pandemic arrived, and he put it down to write, with eighteen other authors, a paper on the fair international allocation of vaccine that ran in Science that September.

narrative_blocks.header: He turned on his own teacher's ideal society
narrative_blocks.body: Rawls's just society, he has argued, is open to systematic bigoted oppression arising from inside it. A companion paper sets out how the theory might be amended to close the hole.

narrative_blocks.header: He advised UNESCO on science and ethics
narrative_blocks.body: From 2010 to 2013 he sat on the world commission advising UNESCO's director general on the ethics of science and technology. He led the Human Development and Capability Association from 2014, and wrote the normative chapter of a three-volume report on social progress.

narrative_blocks.header: A resignation and a reading programme behind him
narrative_blocks.body: His father resigned as attorney general rather than fire the Watergate prosecutor; his mother chaired the country's largest literacy programme. Their son went into moral philosophy.

narrative_blocks.header: He built the bike shop at Paragon
narrative_blocks.body: Hazard came to Telluride in 2003 and managed Paragon Ski and Sports, where he built up the bike side of the business. He met Vivian Russell there in 2008. After the store sold he spent a decade doing carpentry with Bill Ward Construction.

narrative_blocks.header: He got into mountain bikes in 1988
narrative_blocks.body: He moved to Lake Placid in 1988 to work in the young mountain-bike industry, maintaining bikes and trails, and took up road racing on the back roads there. A cycling event brought him to Dave Kirk of Serotta, who got him a job and stayed a friend.

narrative_blocks.header: Make do, do without, use it up

[Stage 6Y-264 NB#1 header trim]: 'Followed the seas, then built 'Heartsease' — one of New York's first commercial apple orchards — then took his family to Florida for Reconstruction-era citrus farming' → 'Followed the seas, then built 'Heartsease''.
[Stage 6Y-264 NB#1 body trim]: original body had 5 sentences, trimmed to first 3. Original body preserved here for reference: 'Benjamin Hall Hart (1811-1875) went to sea before settling down to marry Elizabeth Nichols of Hempstead in October 1837. He purchased a farm in LaGrange, Dutchess County, New York in 1838, establishing it as one of New York State's first commercial apple orchards. The Greek revival farmhouse was named 'Heartsease.' After the Civil War — during which his sons Walter Nichols Hart and Ambrose Burnham Hart served in the Union Army, Ambrose rising to First Lieutenant and Adjutant, wounded at Winchester, Virginia — Benjamin and his three sons purchased lands in Federal Point and Lake City, Florida during Reconstruction. There they farmed citrus, cultivated ornamental shrubs, and built a saw and ginning mill. Their plantation was named 'Three Oaks.''

narrative_blocks.header: Heartsease grew New York's early commercial apples
narrative_blocks.body: After years at sea he bought a LaGrange farm in Dutchess County in 1838 and built it into one of New York State's first commercial apple orchards. The Greek Revival farmhouse he raised there carried the name Heartsease.

narrative_blocks.header: Reconstruction drew the Harts to Florida
narrative_blocks.body: After the war — his son Ambrose came home a wounded lieutenant from Winchester — Benjamin and his three sons bought land at Federal Point and Lake City, Florida. They farmed citrus, raised ornamental shrubs, and ran a saw and ginning mill at a plantation they called Three Oaks.

narrative_blocks.header: 'Peace and plenty, always full and never empty'
narrative_blocks.body: When the house was finished in 1839 the boss carpenter blessed it with those words, and the family took them at their word — Heartsease sheltered Harts and their kin for generations. He and Elizabeth raised seven children there.

narrative_blocks.header: He raised his dead sister's orphaned daughter
narrative_blocks.body: When his sister Elizabeth died and her widower could not manage, he took in his young niece Caroline at Heartsease, where his seven children were near her age. She became the eighth child of the house, and stayed the rest of her life.

narrative_blocks.header: His apples sold wherever good apples were wanted
narrative_blocks.body: What began as a Dutchess County nursery grew into a brand: Hart apples travelled to market under their own name and were shipped abroad, and the family came to be called the best-known apple cultivators in the country. He planted the trees; three generations sold the fruit.

narrative_blocks.header: A congressman with a price on his head
narrative_blocks.body: Gates served two terms in Congress as an antislavery Whig from New York, drafting the party's protest against the annexation of Texas. His stand so angered the South that a planter offered five hundred dollars for his capture.

narrative_blocks.header: His house hid fugitives in cellar and attic
narrative_blocks.body: Gates ran a station on the Underground Railroad from his Warsaw, New York, home, concealing freedom-seekers in its cellar and attic. The house still stands and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

narrative_blocks.header: He twice ran for lieutenant governor and lost
narrative_blocks.body: After Congress, Gates twice sought the lieutenant governorship of New York on antislavery tickets, as a Free Soiler in 1848 and a Free Democrat in 1852. Both campaigns failed, but they kept him at the center of the cause.

b. Oct 16, 1800 Winfield, Herkimer County NY; d. Aug 24, 1877 Warsaw, Wyoming County NY age 76. Son of Seth Gates and Abigail (Merrill) Gates. Moved to Sheldon NY 1806; Middlebury Academy; schoolteacher; deputy sheriff Le Roy NY 1825; admitted to bar 1827; supervisor Le Roy 1830. POLITICS: Whig member NY State Assembly 1832; elected antislavery member 26th and 27th U.S. Congresses Mar 4, 1839-Mar 3, 1843. Drafted Whig protest against Texas annexation. Twice unsuccessful candidate for Lieutenant Governor of NY (1848 Barnburners/Free Soil; 1852 Free Democratic). Secretary, Wyoming County Insurance Company 1851-1865. Postmaster, Warsaw NY 1861-1870. UNDERGROUND RAILROAD: His home at Warsaw NY (built 1824, expanded c.1843) was a station on the Underground Railroad — fugitives concealed in cellar and attic. Due to his antislavery stance, a Southern planter offered $500 for his apprehension. LANDMARK: Seth M. Gates House, 15 Perry Ave., Warsaw NY — listed on National Register of Historic Places 1992. Used by Society of Village Works 1893-1924; then DAR chapter; then Warsaw Historical Society. Married three times: (1) Eliza Keyes (d. 1840); (2) Fanny Jennette Parsons (HD1673) 1841; (3) Ann Cornelia Rochester (dau. of Nathaniel Rochester) 1867. Buried Warsaw Cemetery. LANDMARK: _House

bio.bio_blurb: Marble quarrier, farmer and church deacon

military_service.notes: DAR Patriot Ancestor #A060066. Revolutionary War marker at his grave, Fairmount Cemetery, Lee.

narrative_blocks.header: The doorstep, the horseblock and the Capitol
narrative_blocks.body: The marble on his farm lay in strata near the surface, and he got it out for hearths and step stones, for his doorstep and mantels, and for the horseblock of the church built in 1800. Much of the marble in the Capitol came from that quarry.

narrative_blocks.header: He marched when Ticonderoga was given up
narrative_blocks.body: He served nineteen days in July 1777 under Colonel John Brown, in the detachment that marched from Stockbridge at the evacuation of Ticonderoga. He turned out again for four days on the Berkshire alarm of 1780.

narrative_blocks.header: The church chose him deacon in 1812
narrative_blocks.body: He helped found the Congregational church a mile and a half from his quarry, and the congregation chose him deacon in 1812; he held it until he died. The town made him selectman as well.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirteen children, two pairs of them twins
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah Parsons of Stockbridge married him in 1781 and bore thirteen children on the farm, two pairs of them twins — David and Sally in 1795, William and Alvan Hyde in 1801. Three sons became clergymen, one the first music professor at an American college.

narrative_blocks.header: He cut down his own orchard
narrative_blocks.body: His cider was pressed in white marble troughs cut from the farm, and a granddaughter remembered riding the mill beam; finding how many neighbours got drunk on it, he felled every apple tree but those the family needed. At seventy-five he made the journey out to Michigan to see the children who had gone west, and came home pleased with the country.

narrative_blocks.header: Four generations from the brother who stayed
narrative_blocks.body: His great-grandfather was Thomas Ingersoll of Westfield, whose brother Jonathan settled at Milford; that brother's son took the King's stamps and his grandson signed the Constitution. David went the other way, to a Berkshire farm and a country church.

U.S. CAPITOL MARBLE: David Ingersoll owned a marble quarry on his farm (about 1.5 miles from the Lee Congregational Church); "much of the marble in the Capitol in Washington came from this quarry." THE CIDER DECISION: Deacon Ingersoll "found so many were getting drunk from his cider that he cut down all his apple trees except those needed to supply fruit for his own family." 13 CHILDREN: All thirteen grew to maturity, married, and "mostly had large families." Over 2,000 descendants recorded. "The Ingersoll and Yale families...might well be called the founders of Lee." He was deacon of the Lee Congregational Church 1812-1839; one of its founders; selectman; held various town offices. Made a journey to Ohio and Michigan at age 75 to visit children — before railroad transportation — "in the days of rugged constitutions." Her mother Sarah Edwards Parsons lived with them for a time after her husband's death. (Jonathan Edwards Collection; Stockbridge Church records; Avery, Genealogy of the Ingersoll Family in America 1926)

narrative_blocks.header: He cast Canada's first iron ploughs, with nothing
narrative_blocks.detail: Son of Eliphalet Parsons (H00904) and Martha Young; born 1789; baptized 1791 at Stockbridge MA. Moved through Broome County NY and Wilkes-Barre PA before relocating to Canada in 1824. Married Jennett Hepburn 1815. Two children: Lewis Eliphalet Parsons (HD1672, later provisional Governor of Alabama) and Fanny Jennette Parsons (HD1673, married Underground Railroad operator Seth Gates). Died September 2, 1827 at Chippewa (Chippawa), Ontario age 38. (Hinsdale family history; FindAGrave; WikiTree)
narrative_blocks.body: He crossed into Upper Canada in 1824 with an old horse and thirty dollars, and an idea. He scoured the countryside for scrap, built a crude furnace, and cast the first iron ploughs made in Canada, three at a time — where farmers had known only wood and wrought plate. He was dead three years later, at thirty-eight; the works outlived him.

narrative_blocks.header: The horse and thirty dollars reached a statehouse

notable.notable_blurb: 19th Governor of Alabama

narrative_blocks.header: Johnson made him govern a conquered state
narrative_blocks.detail: President Andrew Johnson appointed Parsons provisional governor of Alabama on June 21, 1865. His first act was to reinstate the laws of 1861, except those pertaining to slavery. He ordered the election of delegates to a constitutional convention (Sep 12, 1865) which repealed the ordinance of secession, renounced the state's war debts, abolished slavery, and scheduled elections. He attempted to purchase the Florida panhandle for Alabama, sparking rumors he had access to unclaimed Confederate gold. Term ended Dec 13, 1865 with inauguration of Robert M. Patton. Subsequently elected to U.S. Senate but refused his seat by the Republican Party. Served as U.S. District Attorney, Northern District of Alabama 1877-78.
narrative_blocks.body: A moderate Unionist who had argued against secession, he was named provisional governor of Alabama by Andrew Johnson in June 1865. In six months he called a convention that repealed secession, abolished slavery, and repudiated the war debt, then handed off to an elected successor.

narrative_blocks.header: An iron-founder's son who reached a statehouse
narrative_blocks.detail: Lewis E. Parsons held enslaved people in Talladega, Alabama — 16 individuals recorded in the 1860 slave schedule. He served as a Confederate lieutenant at the brief Battle of Munford near Talladega in April 1865, one of the last engagements of the war. He was an Alabama House of Representatives member 1859-1865. Presidential elector 1856 and 1860. His appointment as provisional governor was intended to restore civil government under Democratic leadership in the immediate aftermath of Confederate surrender.
narrative_blocks.body: His father cast Canada's first iron ploughs and died broke at thirty-eight. The son read law in New York and Pennsylvania, went south to Talladega in 1840, and rose through the Alabama legislature to the governor's chair — the Unionist a fire-eater once called the ablest he ever faced.

narrative_blocks.header: He came to regret the lines he drew
narrative_blocks.body: He wrote later that he had made a great error in 1865, when the convention apportioned the legislature by white population alone and he did not press for limited Black suffrage. Had he, he believed, Alabama might have been readmitted at once and spared the harder Reconstruction that followed.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandson rose to major general
narrative_blocks.body: His son served as a federal attorney in Alabama; his grandson, James Kelly Parsons, became a major general, won the Distinguished Service Cross fighting blind in the Argonne, and later pressed the Army to integrate its ranks.

narrative_blocks.header: He read law before there were law schools
narrative_blocks.body: There were almost no law schools then; a young man learned by reading in a practicing attorney's office. Parsons read in Frederick Tallmadge's New York chambers and in the Philadelphia office of G.W. Woodward, a future justice of Pennsylvania's high court, before taking the bar and heading south to Talladega in 1840.

narrative_blocks.header: A Black college opened in his home town
narrative_blocks.body: Talladega is a hill town in eastern Alabama, and he practised law there from 1840. Two years after the war, freedmen and the American Missionary Association founded Talladega College in it — the oldest private college for Black students in the state.

narrative_blocks.header: He fought for the Confederacy that April
narrative_blocks.body: He was a Confederate lieutenant at the short fight at Munford, near Talladega, in April 1865. Two months later Andrew Johnson made him governor of the state he had just been fighting for.

notable.notable_blurb: College president and Indian-reform advocate

narrative_blocks.header: He led two colleges in eighteen years
narrative_blocks.detail: Merrill Edwards Gates was inaugurated President of Rutgers College on June 20, 1882. During his presidency he built Winants Hall (Rutgers' first dormitory, completed 1890, named for Garrett E. Winants) and New Jersey Hall for chemistry and biology instruction. He established the Agricultural Experiment Station under the Hatch Act (1887) and expanded funding for the scientific school under the Morrill Act (1890). He resigned in 1890 to become President of Amherst College, serving 1890-1899. Per the Rutgers biography: "His administration was marked by a large increase in the Faculty and endowments of the College. The curriculum was extended and the library greatly enlarged."
narrative_blocks.body: At thirty-four he became the ninth president of Rutgers — its first professional educator rather than a clergyman — and built its first dormitory. In 1890 he left to run Amherst, where he served nine years.

narrative_blocks.header: U.S. Board of Indian Commissioners
narrative_blocks.detail: After leaving Amherst, Gates served as Chairman of the U.S. Board of Indian Commissioners (1889-1899) and then Secretary (1899-1912) — 23 years total shaping federal Indian policy during the assimilation era. He chaired the Lake Mohonk Conferences on the Indian Question. His published works include Land and Law as Agents in Educating the Indians (1885). His work is viewed today through a complex lens: well-intentioned by the standards of his era, but deeply paternalistic and assimilationist.
narrative_blocks.body: Chairman then Secretary of the U.S. Board of Indian Commissioners; wrote on land, law, and Indian education.

narrative_blocks.header: He quadrupled a school before he was thirty
narrative_blocks.detail: Before his university presidencies, Gates served as principal of The Albany Academy for 12 years, extending its curriculum from 8 to 12 years and growing enrollment from 70 to 800 students. In 1875 he was elected Chancellor of the University of Tennessee but declined, remaining at Albany. He traveled abroad twice (1872 visiting Rugby and Oxford; 1879-80 to France, Italy, Egypt, Palestine, and Greece).
narrative_blocks.body: For twelve years he was principal of the Albany Academy, where he stretched the course of study toward a college curriculum and ran the enrollment from seventy students to three hundred. He was barely out of Rochester when he started.

narrative_blocks.header: His father hid fugitives; he reformed the agency
narrative_blocks.detail: The Rutgers College biography explicitly notes: "Through his mother he is descended from Jonathan Edwards" — Fanny Jennette Parsons (HD1673) was the great-great-granddaughter of Rev. Jonathan Edwards and Sarah Pierpont, and a great-great-great-grandchild of Rev. Thomas Hooker. His father Seth M. Gates was the antislavery U.S. Congressman whose Warsaw NY home was a station on the Underground Railroad for 15+ years. A Southern planter offered $500 for his father's apprehension.
narrative_blocks.body: He grew up in the Warsaw house where his abolitionist father sheltered escaping slaves in the cellar and attic. As chairman of the Board of Indian Commissioners he carried that reform temper into federal policy, arguing that land and law, not force, should shape the government's dealings with Native nations.

narrative_blocks.header: Rochester's best student to that day
narrative_blocks.body: He took his degree at the University of Rochester with the highest standing any student there had reached, honors in mathematics, Latin, and Greek, and the senior essay prize. Princeton, Columbia, and Williams later gave him doctorates; the American Philosophical Society elected him in 1886.

narrative_blocks.header: A friend of the Indian and the Negro
narrative_blocks.body: His gravestone names him a notable educator, a gifted orator, and a friend of the Indian and the Negro. A licensed Congregational preacher, he wrote on Indian affairs, on wealth, and on international arbitration, and spent his last years lecturing in Washington.

narrative_blocks.body: He and his brother William came together on 22 December 1801, the eleventh and twelfth of the thirteen children Deacon David Ingersoll raised on the Lee farm. Three of those sons went into the ministry.

narrative_blocks.header: One of three brothers who took a pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: He was ordained a Presbyterian minister and preached on the Western Reserve, the Connecticut tract in northern Ohio that New England families were then filling. His younger brother Elihu went from a Rhode Island pulpit to the Oberlin music chair; a third brother preached too.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at Rochester, a day past sixty-three
narrative_blocks.body: He had taken his family west from the Berkshires by way of Rochester, New York, and it was at Rochester that he died on 23 December 1864, one day past his sixty-third birthday. His daughter Sarah was teaching in that city's schools.

narrative_blocks.header: The pulpit ran back to Jonathan Edwards
narrative_blocks.body: Through his mother Sarah Parsons he descended from Jonathan Edwards, the Northampton theologian and Princeton president, whose eldest daughter Sarah married into the Parsons family of Stockbridge. The pulpit ran in the line before it reached him.

narrative_blocks.header: First music professor at any American college
narrative_blocks.body: In 1834, while still a Yale Divinity student, he was appointed Professor of Sacred Music and Principal of the Preparatory Department at Oberlin College. This was the first appointment of a professor of music at any American university.

narrative_blocks.header: Quit Rhode Island pulpit for Oberlin in 1835
narrative_blocks.body: He was ordained pastor of the Congregational Church in Woonsocket Rhode Island in December 1834. Eleven months later he resigned to take up the Oberlin music professorship, where he served almost five years.

narrative_blocks.header: Went to Kansas Territory for the anti-slavery cause
narrative_blocks.body: In April 1857 he resigned his Bloomington Illinois pulpit to go to Kansas in aid of the anti-slavery cause in the Kansas Territory. He labored at his own expense in the ministry near Burlingame until 1861.

narrative_blocks.header: First wife dead after sixteen months
narrative_blocks.body: He married Louisa Perry of Stockbridge in April 1835; she died sixteen months later in August 1836, leaving an infant son. He remarried Catharine Gillett in 1838 and had eight children with her.

narrative_blocks.header: He surveyed the county he preached in
narrative_blocks.body: After forty years of pulpits across five states he settled in Clay County, Kansas, and in 1870 the county elected him surveyor. A minister of vigorous intellect, the local paper said, who gave his life to science and theology both.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the English were a lost tribe
narrative_blocks.body: Late in life he published The Lost Tribes Found in the Anglo-Saxon Race, arguing that modern Anglo-Saxons descended from the ten lost tribes of Israel. At his death he was at work on a second book, on the Second Coming.

narrative_blocks.header: A Secret Service man in Lincoln's Washington
narrative_blocks.body: Egbert left Michigan for Washington and joined the Secret Service when General Lafayette Baker organised it, serving as a government detective through the Civil War. He had a hand in uncovering several plots against President Lincoln.

narrative_blocks.header: In the party that captured John Wilkes Booth
narrative_blocks.body: In April 1865 Egbert was one of the party that ran John Wilkes Booth to ground at the Garrett farm in Virginia, where Booth was shot on 26 April. When Egbert died in 1923 he was called the last of the war's Secret Service men.

narrative_blocks.header: Messages too important for paper
narrative_blocks.body: Egbert counted both Lincoln and Edwin M. Stanton, the Secretary of War, as friends, and carried spoken messages between the two that were judged too important to be put on paper.

narrative_blocks.header: A Delta Township settler from 1836
narrative_blocks.body: Egbert came to Delta Township, just west of where Lansing grew up, as a boy in 1836, when it was still frontier. He spent most of his long life in and around Delta and Lansing, and was counted among the earliest settlers of that country.

narrative_blocks.header: He brought Lansing its first electric power
narrative_blocks.body: Back in Michigan after the war, Egbert installed the first electric power in Lansing for E. F. Cooley, and he managed the plant for fifteen years.

narrative_blocks.header: Two months short of a hundred
narrative_blocks.body: Egbert married Mary Elizabeth Holmes in 1854, and they kept their fiftieth anniversary in 1904, three years after moving to Los Angeles. He outlived her by fifteen years and died there on 23 May 1923, two months short of his hundredth birthday.

narrative_blocks.header: The third brother in the watch firm
narrative_blocks.body: He was a partner in Robert H. Ingersoll & Bro. alongside his brothers Robert and Charles, and the father of William H. Ingersoll, who carried the family name into advertising. Three of the Michigan Ingersolls built the dollar watch between them.

narrative_blocks.header: He turned down the sheriff's badge
narrative_blocks.body: In Delta, Arthur went to Republican state conventions as a delegate and fought the Greenback Party, which is how the nomination for sheriff of Eaton County came to be offered him. He declined it, was elected justice of the peace in 1883, and took the township census in 1884.

narrative_blocks.header: Two terms on an Ontario village council
narrative_blocks.body: In 1885 Arthur left Michigan for Ontario, the province his wife Nancy was born in. He served two terms on the village council there and chaired the board of managers of its Presbyterian church for several years.

narrative_blocks.header: Three churches in eleven years
narrative_blocks.body: From that Ontario Presbyterian board, Arthur became a deacon of the Reformed Church at Greenville, New Jersey, in 1895, and moved to Brooklyn in 1896. There he taught in Plymouth Church's Sunday school, Henry Ward Beecher's old pulpit, and at times ran it as superintendent.

notable.notable_blurb: Made the first one-dollar watch

narrative_blocks.header: The watch that a dollar could buy
narrative_blocks.detail: Robert H. Ingersoll and his brother Charles Henry Ingersoll (HD1715) founded the Ingersoll Watch Company in 1892 using watches supplied by Waterbury Clock Company. In 1896 they introduced the "Yankee" at $1 — the first mass-produced dollar watch. At their peak they produced 8,000 watches a day. By end of WWI they had sold over 50 million watches worldwide. The company went bankrupt in 1921; its assets were sold to Waterbury Clock Company, which became the modern Timex Group USA. Robert was an 8th-generation descendant of Rev. Thomas Hooker.
narrative_blocks.body: He and his brother worked up from rubber stamps and patent novelties to the thing that made them: a pocket watch reassembled from a broken alarm clock and sold for a dollar in 1896. Seventy million left the factories, and Timex traces its line back through them.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten thousand watches for the catalogue
narrative_blocks.body: Robert and his brother Charles had been selling by mail from New York since about 1880 when, in 1892, they ordered ten thousand cheap clock-watches from the Waterbury Clock Company for their catalogue. At the Chicago World's Fair the next year, a version stamped with the fair's emblem sold an estimated 85,000.

narrative_blocks.header: One price in ten thousand shops
narrative_blocks.body: The brothers sold the watch at one price in every shop, and by 1901 ten thousand dealers across the United States and Canada carried it. Ingersoll built factories at Waterbury and Trenton, and bought the Trenton Watch Company in 1908 and the New England Watch Company in 1914.

narrative_blocks.header: A dollar watch, and then nothing
narrative_blocks.body: Wartime over-expansion broke the firm, and in 1921 it went into involuntary bankruptcy; the Waterbury Clock Company bought the assets for over a million dollars. He moved west and died at Denver in 1928.

narrative_blocks.header: Wife's murder-suicide at 55 Park Avenue, 1926
narrative_blocks.detail: Robert and Roberta Ingersoll were separated when the tragedy occurred Dec 19, 1926. Roberta shot Wallace M. Probasco four times in her apartment at 55 Park Avenue, then took her own life with a gunshot to the breast. Probasco survived. The incident was widely reported nationally. The couple had no children.
narrative_blocks.body: Roberta Ingersoll shot her companion Wallace Probasco then took her own life in her Park Avenue apartment, December 1926.

narrative_blocks.header: His dollar watch made the company famous
narrative_blocks.body: With his brother, Charles Ingersoll built the Ingersoll Watch Company on a one-dollar pocket watch that sold by the millions. The slogan called it the watch that made the dollar famous.

narrative_blocks.header: A day's pay bought his watch
narrative_blocks.body: The Yankee sold for a dollar in 1896 — about what a man earned in a day — and that was the whole idea. By 1899 the brothers were turning out eight thousand a day.

narrative_blocks.header: A watch you could read in the dark
narrative_blocks.body: In 1919 Charles and Robert brought out the Radiolite, an Ingersoll with a luminous radium dial, two years after their first jeweled watch, the Reliance. Within two years the post-war slump had put the company into bankruptcy.

narrative_blocks.header: After the watch failed, a dollar pen
narrative_blocks.body: When the watch firm collapsed in 1921 he started over with a one-dollar fountain pen. He also turned his thirty-room Montclair house into an inn, to the fury of the neighbors, because he thought it a sound investment.

narrative_blocks.header: He introduced Wilson to Bryan in his parlor
narrative_blocks.body: At his South Orange home he brought together Woodrow Wilson, then president of Princeton, and William Jennings Bryan. The friendship took, and it was Bryan who put Wilson's name in nomination for the presidency in 1912.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran for governor on a single tax
narrative_blocks.body: He believed land alone should be taxed — to punish speculation and reward building — and carried the argument through leagues, a monthly magazine he called Democracy, and an independent run for governor of New Jersey in 1934. He lost. A car struck him in South Orange in 1948, at eighty-two, while he was walking home.

narrative_blocks.header: She gave the world Emily Dickinson's poems
narrative_blocks.body: With Thomas Wentworth Higginson she edited the first published collections, beginning with the Poems of 1890, introducing a recluse to the reading public. A bitter feud with the Dickinson family then stalled the rest, and her daughter Millicent finished it fifty years on.

narrative_blocks.header: Her editing reshaped how Dickinson reached readers
narrative_blocks.body: Todd and Higginson smoothed Dickinson's startling punctuation, capitalization, and syntax and titled poems the poet had left untitled. Later scholars spent decades restoring the originals, but Todd's editions made the reputation.

narrative_blocks.header: She was the first Western woman up Fuji
narrative_blocks.body: Joining her astronomer husband on eclipse expeditions, Todd traveled to more than thirty countries and in 1887 became the first Western woman to climb Mount Fuji. Late in life she helped advance the creation of Everglades National Park.

narrative_blocks.header: Her affair in Amherst was an open secret
narrative_blocks.body: Todd's long affair with Austin Dickinson, the poet's brother, was widely known in Amherst and entangled her in the family's bitter feuds. It was through that connection that Emily's manuscripts came into her hands.

narrative_blocks.header: The war caught them chasing an eclipse
narrative_blocks.body: She went with him to Japan in 1887 and 1896, Tripoli in 1900 and 1905, the Dutch East Indies, Chile and Russia, and reached more than thirty countries on five continents. Russia declared war while they were between Kiev and Moscow in August 1914; they abandoned the eclipse and their instruments and got out through Sweden and Denmark.

narrative_blocks.header: Lost the suit, locked the poems away
narrative_blocks.body: Austin Dickinson left the Todds a strip of his land, and after his death Lavinia sued to take it back and won in 1898. She shut away the unpublished poems and family papers still in her hands, and the Dickinson manuscripts stayed divided between two households for half a century.

narrative_blocks.header: Two million men sat the test he built
narrative_blocks.body: Robert Yerkes pulled him into the small team that made the Army Alpha and Beta in 1917, and by the end of the war some two million men had taken them. The final forms went to press in January 1919.

narrative_blocks.header: His headstone calls him the Army's architect
narrative_blocks.body: He was the Army's chief psychologist through the second war, and by 1941 more than a million soldiers had a standardised score on file. The stone at Arlington reads: architect of the classification system of the army, 1940-1947.

narrative_blocks.header: He built the first programme of its kind
narrative_blocks.body: Carnegie Tech brought him from Dartmouth in 1915 to make a unit that would help students choose careers, and he turned it into the Division of Applied Psychology — the first academic programme working directly with industry on personnel. He founded the Personnel Journal there in 1922.

narrative_blocks.header: Popcorn money took him to the World's Fair
narrative_blocks.body: He skipped the third and fourth grades, finished high school at sixteen, and sold enough popcorn at the railway station to pay his own way to Chicago in 1893. He had already been a printer's devil and a rodman on the railway.

narrative_blocks.header: Two doctorates in the same year
narrative_blocks.body: He took one at Harvard in Münsterberg's laboratory under Edwin Holt and another at Chicago under James Angell, both in 1908, on the psychophysiology of melody. Then he went to assist Edward Thorndike at Teachers College.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a pioneering woman geographer
narrative_blocks.body: In 1920 he married Millicent Todd, who three years later became the first woman to take a Harvard doctorate in geography. She founded the memorial lectures that carry his name after he died.

notable.notable_blurb: Amherst professor of astronomy, 1881-1917

narrative_blocks.header: Maxwell wrote to him about the ether
narrative_blocks.body: The letter asking whether Jupiter's satellites might betray the solar system's motion through the luminiferous ether was addressed to him at the Nautical Almanac Office. Maxwell was dead before the Royal Society printed it, and the problem went on to Albert Michelson.

narrative_blocks.header: He said the tables were not good enough
narrative_blocks.body: He called the communication one of extraordinary importance and said in the same breath that it would be a long time before anyone had tables of Jupiter's satellites accurate enough to put it to a practical test. He was right.

narrative_blocks.header: The finest plates of the Venus transit
narrative_blocks.detail: David Peck Todd was the chief astronomer at the Lick Observatory during the transit of Venus in 1882, and created the first known photographs of the transit. The still photos were found and animated by astronomers at Lick during the 2004 transit of Venus. He led more than 11 eclipse expeditions worldwide and asteroid 511 Davida (named for him) and 510 Mabella (named for his wife) honor the pair.
narrative_blocks.body: At Mount Hamilton in 1882 he took charge of the Lick Observatory's transit of Venus work, the first important research done at that observatory. His hundred and forty-five photographs of the planet crossing the sun were the finest ever obtained, and no transit came again until 2004.

narrative_blocks.header: At twelve he found the moons of Jupiter
narrative_blocks.body: He left Lake Ridge for Auburn at five and Brooklyn at ten, and at twelve made himself a little telescope and got his first sight of the four moons of Jupiter. Columbia had no observatory, so he left it after two years for Amherst, where the old observatory was thrown open to him as an undergraduate.

narrative_blocks.header: He chased eclipses for forty years
narrative_blocks.body: He took expeditions to the Dutch East Indies in 1901, Tripoli in 1905, Chile and Peru in 1907 and Kiev in 1914. His daughter went along, and said afterwards that the travelling was what made her a geographer.

narrative_blocks.header: He knew about the affair and stayed
narrative_blocks.body: His wife's thirteen years with Austin Dickinson were an open secret in Amherst, and he seems to have accepted it. The manuscripts that came through that household are why Emily Dickinson is read at all.

people.research_notes:
b. Mar 19, 1855 Lake Ridge, Tompkins County NY; d. Jun 1, 1939 Amherst, Virginia age 84. Buried Wildwood Cemetery, Amherst MA. Son of Sereno Edwards Todd and Rhoda Peck. Studied Columbia Univ 1870-1872; Amherst College 1873-1875 (Phi Beta Kappa class of 1875); M.A. Amherst 1878; honorary Ph.D. Washington and Jefferson College 1888. US Naval Observatory 1875-1878; US Nautical Almanac Office 1878-1881. Professor of astronomy and director of observatory, Amherst College 1881-1917 (forced early retirement). Professor astronomy and higher math, Smith College 1882-1887. TRANSIT OF VENUS: Chief astronomer at Lick Observatory for 1882 transit — produced the first known photographs. Animated by Lick astronomers in 2004. ASTRONOMICAL EXPEDITIONS: Led 11+ expeditions globally including Japan (1887, 1896), West Africa (1889-90), Tripoli (1900, 1905), Dutch East Indies (1901), Andes/Peru (1907), Russia (1914). Established Standard Time in Peru 1907. Received Imperial Saké Cup from Emperor of Japan 1896. Todd crater on Phobos (moon of Mars) named after him. Asteroid 511 Davida and 510 Mabella named after him and his wife. JAMES CLERK MAXWELL LETTER: Maxwell wrote to Todd on Mar 19, 1879 asking about retardation of Jupiter satellite eclipses to detect Earth's motion through the ether — the letter caught Albert Michelson's attention and contributed to Michelson's famous speed-of-light experiments. MENTAL ILLNESS: By 1917, erratic mental behavior caused Amherst president Alexander Meiklejohn to force his early retirement; institutionalized 1922; remained in and out of care facilities until his death 1939. m. Mabel Loomis (X00568) Mar 5, 1879 Washington DC. 1 daughter: Millicent. Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Peck_Todd

notable.notable_blurb: Geographer and Emily Dickinson scholar-editor

narrative_blocks.header: She rescued Emily Dickinson's hidden poems
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother had been blocked for thirty years by the Dickinson family from publishing what was in the camphorwood chest, and made her promise to finish it. Bolts of Melody brought six hundred unseen poems out in 1945.

narrative_blocks.header: First woman with Harvard's geography doctorate
narrative_blocks.body: She took the Radcliffe master's in 1917 and the Harvard doctorate in 1923, the first woman to do either in geography and geology. The dissertation came out of her own fieldwork in Peru.

narrative_blocks.header: She learned geography chasing eclipses
narrative_blocks.body: Her father was Amherst's professor of astronomy and she went with him — the Dutch East Indies at twenty-one, then Tripoli, then Chile and Peru, then Kiev in 1914. The travelling made the geographer.

narrative_blocks.header: She gave an island to the Audubon
narrative_blocks.body: In 1935 she made the family property on Hog Island in Muscongus Bay a sanctuary in her mother's name, and Audubon put its first adult conservation camp there. She handed it over outright in 1960 and gave Amherst her mother's forest the year after.

narrative_blocks.header: A canteen at Angers, lectures at Grenoble
narrative_blocks.body: She spent 1918 pouring coffee in a YMCA canteen at a hospital in Angers and lecturing on geography to American soldiers at Grenoble for the Army Education Corps. She studied under Raoul Blanchard while she was there.

narrative_blocks.header: He invented a forerunner of the cabinet organ
narrative_blocks.body: He worked silver and built musical instruments, and invented the seraphim, an ancestor of the cabinet organ. The lead in the organ pipes poisoned him and forced him to give up the work after the family reached Michigan.

narrative_blocks.header: He knew nineteen trades and cut silhouettes

narrative_blocks.header: The city's first Cadillac arrived that week
narrative_blocks.body: The Western Automobile Company took the Cadillac agency in April 1903 with him as San Francisco representative, and the first Cadillac seen in the city arrived that week. The trade press called it a gasolene rig and a wonderful hill-climber.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the coast from San Francisco
narrative_blocks.body: He held the west coast Cadillac distributorship for eight years, with agents in California, Washington and Oregon. In January 1904 he was east for the shows at New York, Detroit and Cleveland and the race meet at Daytona.

narrative_blocks.header: He put his little brother in Portland
narrative_blocks.body: Don Lee was ten years younger and sold Cadillacs for him at Portland at twenty-three. He moved him to Los Angeles in 1905 for the new Buick — royal blue with brass trimmings and light yellow running gear — and in 1906 set him up selling Cadillacs as the Lee Motor Car Company.

narrative_blocks.header: Detroit took the line, and Don got it
narrative_blocks.body: Cadillac ended his distributorship in 1910, the Detroit management being said to dislike his running Cadillac and Packard together, and handed it to his brother the following year.

narrative_blocks.header: A showroom on Van Ness, another in Oakland
narrative_blocks.body: He built the Cadillac and Packard showroom at 2000 Van Ness in 1909, far north of every other dealer in the city. His Oakland building of 1912 was by Willis Polk in the Beaux Arts style, one of the most complete service buildings on the coast.

narrative_blocks.header: A divorce after twenty-six years
narrative_blocks.body: Erba secured her divorce on 27 June 1923 and he left San Francisco and four children behind, retiring from the motor business the next year and marrying again at fifty-five.

narrative_blocks.header: Shirley Temple lived one street over
narrative_blocks.body: The Santa Monica house was at 358 Eighteenth Street, and Shirley Temple lived round on Nineteenth between 1934 and 1936. He died in 1942 of cirrhosis.

narrative_blocks.body: She and Richard both gardened, and the showplace garden behind their Georgian Revival house on Capitol Hill was the point of the place; Lord and Schryver planted its composition in the 1930s. Their names ran in the Seattle Times society pages for two decades.

narrative_blocks.header: Mount Lee — his name above the Hollywood sign
narrative_blocks.body: The summit above the Hollywood sign is Mount Lee: Don bought it from Mack Sennett, who with the Los Angeles Times publisher Harry Chandler had put the sign up.

narrative_blocks.header: Television pioneer: W6XAO to KCBS-TV
narrative_blocks.body: In 1931 Don's W6XAO, broadcasting from a floor near his Cadillac showroom, took the first television license in Los Angeles. It is KCBS-TV today.

narrative_blocks.header: Harley Earl — the GM designer Don Lee launched
narrative_blocks.body: Don bought the Earl Automobile Works in 1919 and kept young Harley Earl on to run it. In 1927 Earl left to head General Motors' new styling department and shaped American cars for decades.

narrative_blocks.header: He put a radio station above the showroom
narrative_blocks.body: Don bought KFRC in 1926 and put it on the top floor of his San Francisco Cadillac dealership. By 1932 the Don Lee Network had twelve stations, carrying Columbia's programmes and later Mutual's.

narrative_blocks.header: From a bicycle shop to KHJ
narrative_blocks.body: Don started with a bicycle shop, learned the car trade under Earle C. Anthony, and in 1927 bought KHJ in Los Angeles from Harry Chandler.

narrative_blocks.header: He married at Riverside and told nobody
narrative_blocks.body: In April 1918 Don married Anabel Fulmer of Philadelphia at Riverside without telling even close friends, and took her to sea on his yacht Gloriana. By then he held Cadillac for all California.

narrative_blocks.header: Dead at fifty-four, the empire to his son
narrative_blocks.body: A heart attack killed Don at Los Angeles in August 1934, at fifty-four, and the car and radio business passed to his son Tommy, then twenty-eight.

people.research_notes: b. Aug 12, 1880 Lansing, Ingham County MI; d. Aug 30, 1934 Los Angeles CA age 54. Cremated; ashes given to family. WEST COAST CADILLAC DISTRIBUTOR: Exclusive west coast Cadillac distributor from 1911. Worked for brother Cuyler Lee's Cadillac distribution in Portland OR 1903-1904 age 23; transferred to Los Angeles 1905 (Buick); then Cadillac sales 1906. In 1919 purchased Earl Automobile Works of Hollywood — kept Harley Earl as manager. Renamed Don Lee Coach and Body Works; produced custom Cadillacs for the rich and famous. Harley Earl left 1927 to become head of GM styling department. BROADCASTING EMPIRE: Purchased KFRC San Francisco 1926 (relocated to top floor of his Cadillac dealership at 1000 Van Ness); KHJ Los Angeles 1927; KDB Santa Barbara and KGB San Diego by 1932. 12-station Don Lee Network affiliated with CBS 1929-1936; then Mutual Network. Don Lee Network sold to ABC Radio April 26, 1959. TELEVISION PIONEER: 1931 — granted FCC license for experimental TV station W6XAO Los Angeles. W6XAO became KTSL, then KNXT, now KCBS-TV (CBS flagship West Coast station). MOUNT LEE: The ridge above the Hollywood sign where Lee established his transmitter is still named "Mount Lee" — his permanent mark on the LA skyline. m. Etta Stewart (X00589) 1904. Son: Thomas Stewart "Tommy" Lee (HD1834). Died of sudden heart attack 1934, leaving auto and broadcasting empire to son Tommy. Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Lee_(broadcaster)

narrative_blocks.header: Gardening was the thing she pursued
narrative_blocks.body: She never worked outside the home, which her daughter put down to the days before women thought in those terms. What she pursued instead was gardening, and creating gardens rather than keeping them. The family's Bainbridge Island place is the Bloedel Reserve now, known for exactly that.

narrative_blocks.header: A children’s book on Giotto started it
narrative_blocks.body: She was interested in art without ever making it the household's primary interest, and she put a children's history of art into her daughter's hands, one that began with Giotto. Her daughter built the largest modern collection in the Pacific Northwest.

narrative_blocks.header: His library was sold for her hearing centre
narrative_blocks.body: The rare-book library her husband spent decades building was auctioned in San Francisco in November 1996, months after he died, and the proceeds went to the Virginia Merrill Bloedel Hearing Research Center at the University of Washington. The centre carries her name.

narrative_blocks.header: Their partner desk still anchors the room
narrative_blocks.body: The desk she and her husband worked at side by side still stands in the library of the Bainbridge Island residence, under the windows that look to the Cascades. The room is part of the Reserve now.

narrative_blocks.header: She gave the whole estate away
narrative_blocks.body: She went on living at Lakewold after her husband died, and in 1987 handed the entire estate to a new non-profit, the Friends of Lakewold, on the condition that an endowment be raised to keep the gardens up. They opened to the public on 7 May 1989.

narrative_blocks.header: We began in the garden, she said
narrative_blocks.body: As we become more and more city creatures, living in manmade surroundings, perhaps gardens will become even more precious to us, letting us remember that we began in the garden. That was how she explained why she had done it.

narrative_blocks.header: Landscape gardening was what she practised
narrative_blocks.body: She was a daughter of the Merrills, the Seattle lumber family, and she is remembered for what she gave to the practice of landscape gardening, of which Lakewold is the summary. She and her husband had bought the place from the Griggses in 1938.

narrative_blocks.header: Her sister made a garden too
narrative_blocks.body: Her sister Virginia married Prentice Bloedel and made the Bloedel Reserve out of the grounds of their house on Bainbridge Island. Both Merrill daughters left the state a garden that people can walk into.

people.research_notes: b. Aug 13, 1900 Bellingham, Whatcom County WA; d. Jun 15, 1996 Capitol Hill, King County WA age 95. Ashes scattered at Bloedel Preserve, Bainbridge Island WA. Leader of the timber industry. Son of Julius Bloedel, co-founder of MacMillan Bloedel Ltd. Graduated Yale (planned teaching career; joined family business 1929 at father's request). Guided MacMillan Bloedel merger — became giant MacMillan Bloedel Ltd. Created the Bloedel Reserve botanical showcase on Bainbridge Island WA. Major art patrons in Seattle with wife Virginia; tradition carried on by daughter Virginia Wright. m. Virginia Lee Merrill (HD1832) 1927.

narrative_blocks.header: He left teaching when his father asked
narrative_blocks.body: He took his Yale degree meaning to teach, and was teaching in 1929 when his father called him into Bloedel, Stewart and Welch. He ran the new Port Alberni mill, headed the firm, and took it into the MacMillan Bloedel merger.

narrative_blocks.header: He burned the sawdust to run the mill
narrative_blocks.body: The Port Alberni mill was among the first to make power from sawdust and waste, the trade's hog fuel. A pulp mill beside a sawmill, he thought, would get the most out of every stick of timber.

narrative_blocks.header: His firm was the first to plant seedlings
narrative_blocks.body: In 1938 he put the company into reforestation and it became the first to plant seedlings. Ten years on it was doing seventy per cent of all the replanting private industry did in British Columbia.

narrative_blocks.header: What are the last three books you read
narrative_blocks.body: Interviewing a man to keep his library, he asked what the last three books he had read were: the Rise and Fall of the Third Reich, Wendell Berry's essays, a life of Crazy Horse. After a pause: I believe we have found our man.

narrative_blocks.header: Paper clips in the first-edition Darwin
narrative_blocks.body: He thought of himself less a collector than a reader; rare or not, the books were to be used, and his secretary kept asking him to take the paper clips out of his first-edition Darwin.

narrative_blocks.header: The Bainbridge Island place is a park now
narrative_blocks.body: The Bainbridge Island property he and Virginia bought is the Bloedel Reserve, a showcase of gardens, pools, lawns and arbors. He died on Capitol Hill in June 1996 at ninety-five, his ashes scattered there.

narrative_blocks.header: He put money behind his daughter's eye
narrative_blocks.body: In 1969 he endowed the Virginia Wright Fund in his daughter's name to place art in public places and left the choosing to her. He had bought a Henry Moore for a Vancouver park himself.

narrative_blocks.body: In 1938 the Griggs family sold Lakewold to him and Eulalie; he was Everett Griggs's nephew, and vice-president and treasurer of the St. Paul and Tacoma Lumber Company. He also headed the C.W. Griggs Investment Company and the Wilkeson Company, which mined coal.

narrative_blocks.header: He led the west coast lumbermen
narrative_blocks.body: He was president of the West Coast Lumbermen's Association. He and Eulalie both loved being outdoors in the garden at Lakewold, and neighbours and family came out for parties there.

people.research_notes: b. May 4, 1906 Los Angeles CA; d. Jan 13, 1950 Los Angeles CA age 43. Buried Mountain View Cemetery, Altadena, Los Angeles County CA. Fell to his death from the 12th floor of a Wilshire Blvd building. Head of Thomas S. Lee Enterprises after his father Don Lee's death 1934 — inherited 9 million dollar fortune. Oversaw radio/TV empire and Cadillac distributorship. Built first LA transmitter 1931; built station atop Mt. Lee 1941 (looking down on Hollywood sign). Courts declared him mentally incompetent Aug 27, 1948. Pioneer of TV in Southern California.

narrative_blocks.header: A television empire above the Hollywood sign
narrative_blocks.body: Heir at twenty-eight to Don Lee's radio and Cadillac fortune, he built Los Angeles's first television transmitter in 1931 and later raised his station atop Mt. Lee, looking down on the Hollywood sign itself.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven Cadillac dealerships at twenty-eight
narrative_blocks.body: He came into seven Cadillac dealerships when his father died in 1934, and with them Don Lee's arrangement: a cut of every Cadillac sold in California.

narrative_blocks.header: Frank Kurtis built him a hot rod
narrative_blocks.body: Frank Kurtis had been his head body man before opening his own shop, and in 1936 he asked him for the best-looking and fastest hot rod in southern California. Kurtis built it on a 1936 Ford chassis with Cord fenders; Lee refused a Cadillac motor and insisted on a three-hundred-and-eighteen-inch Offenhauser.

narrative_blocks.header: A truck caught him at a Hollywood corner
narrative_blocks.body: Just before the war a truck hit his car broadside at a Hollywood intersection and he was badly hurt. He was in pain the rest of his life, and went on buying race cars and P-38 fighters.

narrative_blocks.header: He sponsored cars at Indianapolis and flew himself
narrative_blocks.body: He ran Thomas S. Lee Enterprises, the broadcasting system and the automobile agency his father built and the station KTSL in Hollywood, sponsored racing cars at Indianapolis, and piloted his own plane until August 1948.

narrative_blocks.header: A quiet hearing at the Pasadena Sanitarium
narrative_blocks.body: On 27 August 1948 he was declared mentally incompetent at a quiet hearing in the Pasadena Sanitarium, on the affidavit of his own physician, and gave up the broadcasting and automobile business to two court-appointed guardians. His aunt was made his personal guardian.

narrative_blocks.header: Declared incompetent, dead at forty-three
narrative_blocks.body: Courts declared him mentally incompetent in August 1948; seventeen months later he fell to his death from the twelfth floor of a Wilshire Boulevard building. He lies at Mountain View in Altadena.

narrative_blocks.body: She married a schoolteacher at Detroit in 1868 and took up the work herself, and the two of them taught for about fifteen years. She also taught music, and played the organ in the Presbyterian church at Brighton for more than thirty years.

narrative_blocks.header: They bought the Lee homestead at Brighton
narrative_blocks.body: In 1878 the Browns bought the Lee homestead at Brighton and lived there for the rest of her life. Her aunt Samantha had married into that family thirty-five years earlier, and worshipped in the same Presbyterian church.

narrative_blocks.body: She compiled The Ingersolls in America, tracing the descendants of Richard Ingersoll of Salem, and it was published in New York in 1926. She set down her father's Drake line the same way, child by child with the dates.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty years of office in one DAR chapter
narrative_blocks.body: A charter member of the General Richardson Chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution, she was its first vice-regent and then regent, registrar and historian in turn — twenty years of official service. She was State Historian of the Michigan society for three of them.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept the county's history as its secretary
narrative_blocks.body: She helped organize the Woman's Literary Club at Pontiac and was its first president from 1892 to 1894. From 1915 she served as secretary of the Oakland County Pioneer and Historical Society.

narrative_blocks.header: She taught until she married the doctor
narrative_blocks.body: She went to school at Farmington, Milford and Chelsea, where her brother-in-law was principal, and graduated there in June 1875. She taught for several years, married Dr. Aaron Avery in 1879, and moved with him from Farmington to Pontiac in November 1885.

people.research_notes: b. Aug 26, 1853 Lyndon Center, Washtenaw County MI; d. Jun 12, 1911 Pontiac, Oakland County MI age 57. Buried Oak Hill Cemetery, Pontiac MI. Graduate University of Michigan medical department. m. Lillian Drake (HD1819) Oct 22, 1879 Farmington MI.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-six years of practice at Pontiac
narrative_blocks.body: He took his medical degree at Michigan in 1878 and married Lillian Drake at Farmington the year after. In November 1885 the couple left Farmington for Pontiac, where he practised until his death in 1911.

narrative_blocks.header: A dental student took the band in 1884
narrative_blocks.body: He joined the Chequamegons as a dental student and took the leadership with Fred Weir in 1884, the year the group reached its full form. Nine or ten players who doubled on strings and winds, they could turn out as a brass band or an orchestra as the evening required.

narrative_blocks.header: A Wisconsin hotel advertised for its band
narrative_blocks.body: The players spent their summers at the Hotel Chequamegon in Ashland, Wisconsin, and took the hotel's name for their own. Ashland bought space in Michigan's 1884 commencement programme to sell itself as the place “Where the University of Michigan Band Plays!”

narrative_blocks.header: He was leading bands at fifteen
narrative_blocks.body: He began leading bands at fifteen and never stopped: his voice was in demand at political meetings for years, and in later life he went back to the cornet, taking trophies with his Masonic and other Chicago organizations. Dentistry paid for it — Marquette, then a season in Kansas, then Chicago from 1889.

narrative_blocks.header: He led the Swift and Company band
narrative_blocks.body: He practised dentistry in Chicago from 1889 and for years led the band of the Swift and Company packing house. He died in the city in March 1926, still at the cornet he had taken up as a boy.

narrative_blocks.header: He followed his brother into the same chair
narrative_blocks.body: He clerked in a store at Ann Arbor before following his brother Homer into the university's dental college, taking his degree in 1889. He took Homer's place in Dr. Jones's Marquette office for a time and then opened one of his own.

narrative_blocks.header: Woods, tennis, and Theodore Roosevelt
narrative_blocks.body: His holidays went to hunting, fishing and prospecting for minerals, and he played championship tennis as the antidote to close work at the chair. He followed Theodore Roosevelt into the Progressive ranks, and served the war as a specialist on the Medical Advisory Board.

narrative_blocks.header: Sent to Paris to run the fair's machinery
narrative_blocks.body: The United States commission sent him to Paris in 1898 to prepare the American exhibit for the exposition of 1900. He stayed in Europe for the rest of his working life — five years in Berlin with the German General Electric company, then European head of Westinghouse from Paris, and trolley systems built in Russia, Germany and Italy.

narrative_blocks.header: Every American purchase in France crossed his desk
narrative_blocks.body: He volunteered when Pershing reached Europe and was commissioned a major, serving first as chief of construction in the Quartermaster Corps and then as chairman of the technical board. As chief of the control bureau under General Dawes, every purchase the American Expeditionary Forces made in France passed through his office.

narrative_blocks.header: His commission came the evening he married
narrative_blocks.body: The Distinguished Service Medal citation credited his tact and organisation with keeping supply procurement on harmonious terms with the French government; France made him a Commandeur of the Legion of Honour and Belgium an Officier of the Order of the Crown. His lieutenant colonel's commission reached him the evening he married in Paris in September 1918.

narrative_blocks.header: He was at the Legion's first caucus
narrative_blocks.body: After the armistice he sat in the original Paris caucus that founded the American Legion, and later served as its department commander in France. He was instrumental in building Pershing Hall on the Rue Pierre Charron as the American memorial in Paris.

narrative_blocks.header: He escorted Foch across the United States
narrative_blocks.body: When Marshal Foch came to the United States in 1921 Drake was chosen to accompany him, sixty days out of Paris and more than twenty-four thousand miles. He spent the rest of his life on French-American friendship and died in New York at ninety-four.

narrative_blocks.header: He led Ann Arbor's celebrated student band
narrative_blocks.body: The Chequamegons played the opening of the city's first roller rink, its parades, its commencements and the dedication of its Masonic Temple, and the fees covered the players' college expenses. He took the leadership over from his brother Homer while finishing his dental degree.

narrative_blocks.header: He played the pit under Edwin Booth
narrative_blocks.body: At Ann Arbor's Whitney Theatre the orchestra worked the pit while Edwin Booth and Madame Modjeska held the stage. “The rottener the show,” he said long afterwards, “the more the music was needed.”

narrative_blocks.header: They bought their music and hired the halls
narrative_blocks.body: The band incorporated in 1886 and the students ran it as a business: “We had to buy our own music, hire halls and make contracts.” Summers went to hotel residencies in Wisconsin and northern Michigan.

narrative_blocks.header: A dentist who reached a hundred and one
narrative_blocks.body: He took his dental degree at Michigan in 1888 and practised in Negaunee and then Ann Arbor. He died at his Cambridge Road house in October 1970 at a hundred and one, and his family asked that gifts go to the Drake Scholarship Fund at the university.

narrative_blocks.header: He outlived a son by twenty-one years
narrative_blocks.body: He outlived his son Donald, who built the Portland construction company, by twenty-one years, and Rose by eight. The notice of his death counted three grandsons and fifteen great-grandchildren.

narrative_blocks.header: He learned telegraphy before he learned teeth
narrative_blocks.body: He went to Clyde in 1882 to learn telegraphy with his brother Ernest and worked for the Flint and Pere Marquette railroad until 1885, when he entered the dental department at Ann Arbor. The family moved back to that town in 1912, and the university took him on first as an assistant in mineralogy and then as an instructor and assistant professor in clinical dentistry.

narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Negaunee in the Michigan iron country to Samuel and Elizabeth Mitchell, both natives of England, and married the town dentist there in 1893. In 1912 the family left for Ann Arbor to give their sons better schooling.

narrative_blocks.body: He was a registered pharmacist in Pontiac, Marquette and Chicago before he tired of drug stores and went to a manufacturer's books, where he made credit man. His brother Ernest brought him to Paris in 1898 as trustee in full charge of the finances of the Vincennes Park Annex at the World's Fair.

narrative_blocks.header: He learned efficiency inside Taylor's firm
narrative_blocks.body: Back in Chicago he joined the Link Belt Manufacturing Company just as one of its own members, Mr. Taylor, was writing and introducing his methods of efficiency in business. With that tutelage he opened an office with Charles Berg selling labour- and time-saving organisation to firms as far off as Philadelphia, Kentucky and Texas.

narrative_blocks.header: Two sons who did not reach four
narrative_blocks.body: Ernest Gaston was born at Mount Vernon in December 1901 and died the following September; Gaston Clyde, born in New York a fortnight after that, died at Chicago in 1905. The couple adopted a daughter, Alice, in 1921.

narrative_blocks.header: Washington's shipping department, then Boston
narrative_blocks.body: He gave several months to the shipping department at Washington during the war, and when he was no longer needed took the comptroller's desk at the Walworth Manufacturing Company of Boston. He was afterwards made assistant to its president, and kept his home at Newton Center.

people.research_notes: b. Sep 14, 1874 Farmington, Oakland County MI; d. Oct 8, 1948 Cook County IL age 74. Buried Memorial Park Cemetery, Skokie, Cook County IL. m. William Eli Davis Aug 12, 1896 Brighton, Livingston County MI. Stub.

narrative_blocks.header: Her sister took them in at Brighton
narrative_blocks.body: Her father died when she was four, and she and her mother went to live with her older sister Imogene at Brighton, where she finished high school. She studied music at Ann Arbor and taught it until she married William Eli Davis in 1896.

narrative_blocks.header: They built at Hubbard Woods and governed it
narrative_blocks.body: Judging their children handicapped in an apartment house, the Davises built a home at Hubbard Woods, and both of them served on its common council. Her mother died in that house in 1911.

narrative_blocks.header: She supervised her children's music herself
narrative_blocks.body: She never lost interest in music and personally supervised the musical instruction of all three children; the youngest went through Northwestern's public school music course and played piano and violin. A few weeks of every summer went to the Michigan woods.

narrative_blocks.body: She took a leave of absence in 1913-14 for Europe and spent several months in Paris studying French, went back for the summer of 1920, and took her master's degree in 1925. Her holidays went principally to travel.

narrative_blocks.body: She was elected Register of Deeds for Oakland County in November 1922, the first woman to hold office there, winning by a large majority after a primary against four men. She was re-elected in 1924.

narrative_blocks.header: She went to Washington for the air service
narrative_blocks.body: When the call went out for war workers she enlisted in the personnel section of the aviation department of the Signal Service. She was in Washington from April 1918 to February 1919.

narrative_blocks.header: She organized the county's League of Women Voters
narrative_blocks.body: In 1921 she organized the Oakland Chapter of the League of Women Voters and was elected its first president. She belonged to the Pontiac Business Women's Club and the General Richardson Chapter of the D.A.R.

narrative_blocks.header: Sergeant in the water supply, then the Argonne
narrative_blocks.body: He enlisted three weeks before his engineering degree as a private in the water supply section of the Sanitary Corps, made sergeant first class inside a month, and was in France by April 1918. Transferred to Company E of the 26th Engineers in October, he was in action at Varennes in the Argonne, and finished his service studying at the University of Toulouse.

narrative_blocks.header: He visited Portland and never left
narrative_blocks.body: He took a post-graduate course at Ann Arbor and went out to Portland in 1921 on a visit. Seeing how badly the city needed houses he stayed, went into building, and in 1924 set up the general contracting firm that carried his name for seventy years.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at fifty-four with three sons out
narrative_blocks.body: He died in Oregon in June 1949, aged fifty-four, with his youngest boy nineteen. Franklin was finishing an engineering degree in Michigan, the state his father had been born in, and came home the next year to run the company with Donald and Mitchell.

narrative_blocks.header: The cabin he put up at Government Camp
narrative_blocks.body: He built a mountain cabin at Government Camp on Mount Hood with his three sons, and the family kept winter weekends there for years afterwards.

narrative_blocks.header: A summer cruise sent him to Annapolis
narrative_blocks.body: He went on a naval cruise with other Ann Arbor boys in the summer of 1916 and liked the sea enough to apply to Annapolis. The call for examinations came only after his first year at Michigan; he passed, entered the Naval Academy in June 1918, and resigned from it in August 1919.

narrative_blocks.header: He took his degree, then the power company
narrative_blocks.body: Back at Michigan he graduated in 1922, a Beta Theta Pi and a Michigan Union man, and married Eleanor Spencer at Muncie that December. They kept house a year at Barberton in Ohio before Detroit, where he went to work for the Detroit Edison company.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at forty-five, remarried at forty-eight
narrative_blocks.body: She married Donald Drake in November 1924 and was widowed in 1949, with three sons at home. In May 1952 she married Raymond Sprague of Greenwich, a member of the New York Stock Exchange, and kept houses in Portland Heights and Connecticut from then on.

narrative_blocks.header: She gave her father's name to a son
narrative_blocks.body: Her father Franklin Thomas Griffith ran Portland General Electric through the 1920s and 1930s, along with Portland Traction and Griffith Rubber Mills. She named her middle son Franklin Griffith Drake; he sat on the same electric company's board decades later.

narrative_blocks.header: Town Club, Garden Club, Colonial Dames
narrative_blocks.body: She belonged to the Town Club, the Portland Garden Club, the Colonial Dames and the Junior League. Her daughter-in-law Harriet joined the same garden club a generation later.

notable.notable_blurb: Mt. Hood Meadows founder; Portland contractor

narrative_blocks.header: He flew the chairlifts up by helicopter
narrative_blocks.body: Winning the Forest Service lease for Mount Hood's east side in the late 1960s, he used helicopters to haul concrete and steel for the first two chairlifts. Lodge, lifts, parking and every service line went up inside a year, and Mount Hood Meadows opened in 1967.

narrative_blocks.header: His company built half of Portland
narrative_blocks.body: As president from 1960 to 1995 of the company his father founded after a 1921 visit to Portland he never came back from, he built the KOIN Tower, Lloyd Center, the Stadium Freeway that became Interstate 405, the Fremont Bridge approaches and the Rose Garden Arena — and BART's underground stations in San Francisco.

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve feet a day under the West Hills
narrative_blocks.body: The Vista Ridge tunnels advanced about twelve feet a day, six hundred feet under Portland's West Hills, and he was thirty-six when he took the first contract. He had friends up on that hill, he said, and did not want to disturb them; the tunnels opened the westside to the suburbs that followed.

narrative_blocks.header: A Kingdome roof beam buckled in 1973
narrative_blocks.body: His firm took Seattle's Kingdome and lost it: a roof beam buckled in January 1973, King County fired the company the next year, and the stadium was demolished in 2000.

narrative_blocks.header: He unrolled the map on her kitchen table
narrative_blocks.body: For years he pressed for a destination resort on Mount Hood's north side, against Parkdale and Hood River residents and environmental groups. A pear grower remembered him spreading the plans on his mother's kitchen table, the last holes of the golf course sitting on their house.

narrative_blocks.header: The Government Camp cabin he built himself
narrative_blocks.body: He put up a mountain cabin at Government Camp with his father and brothers and took his children there for winter weekends. Later the family kept to the Oregon coast, first at Cannon Beach and then at Gearhart.

people.research_notes: b. Mar 22, 1928 Portland, Multnomah County OR; d. Sep 13, 2021 Portland OR age 93. Buried River View Cemetery, Portland OR. Attended Lincoln High School; Menlo Junior College; University of Michigan (Engineering) 1950. President and CEO, Donald M. Drake Company 1960-1995 — one of the Northwest's largest construction firms. Key Portland projects: Benjamin Franklin Building, KOIN Tower, Lloyd Center, Portland Towers, Stadium Freeway, Vista Ridge Tunnels, Fremont Bridge approaches, Rose Garden Arena (now Moda Center). San Francisco Bay Area: BART underground stations on Montgomery and 19th Streets; aerial links between El Cerrito and Richmond. MT. HOOD MEADOWS FOUNDER: In 1966, with brothers Donald and Mitchell, won competitive bid from U.S. Forest Service to develop Mt. Hood Meadows ski resort on the southeast face of Mt. Hood. Remained CEO developing and managing the resort until retirement in 2006; handed over to son Matthew Drake. Board member: US Bancorp, Portland General Electric, Portland Chamber of Commerce. Elected president, Multnomah Athletic Club 1963. Husband of Harriet Bouvy Drake; children Amy Drake Reeves, Matthew Bouvy Drake, Andrea Eve Hull. Private funeral at Trinity Episcopal Cathedral, Portland.
