narrative_blocks.body: Harriet Drake practised as a landscape and lighting designer and ran her own Portland firm, H.B.D. Ltd. The work put her in the Portland Garden Club and, as an emeritus member, in the Illuminating Engineering Society of North America.

narrative_blocks.header: She started the Vassar club Oregon lacked
narrative_blocks.body: A Vassar graduate of 1952, she founded both the Vassar Club of Oregon and the Alumnae Association of Oregon Episcopal School, and was president of each. She was education director of the Junior League of Portland and vice-chairman of the trustees at Lewis and Clark College.

narrative_blocks.header: They met at a Waverley dance in 1952
narrative_blocks.body: She met Franklin Drake at a Waverley dance and married him that December, settling in Raleigh Hills. The marriage ran sixty-four years, to three children and the six grandchildren who called her Boo.

notable.notable_blurb: Patron who built Seattle's modern-art scene

narrative_blocks.header: The largest modern collection in the Northwest
narrative_blocks.body: With her husband Bagley she assembled the largest collection of modern and contemporary art in the Pacific Northwest and gave it away, two hundred works and more to the Seattle Art Museum and the balance at her death.

narrative_blocks.header: She did not like contemporary art at all
narrative_blocks.body: Boarding school at Dobbs Ferry gave her the Frick, and she wrote a school story about a girl chasing popularity, stopped cold before El Greco's St. Jerome. I loved the Renaissance, and I did not like contemporary art, she said of Barnard. Then a friend talked her into Meyer Schapiro's classes: I was a total convert.

narrative_blocks.header: She bought the Rothko off the gallery wall
narrative_blocks.body: Out of Barnard she took a job at the Sidney Janis Gallery, where abstract expressionism was arriving and hardly anyone was buying it. She bought Mark Rothko's No. 10 for herself, and met a journalist named Bagley Wright on the same floor.

narrative_blocks.header: She put Barnett Newman in Red Square
narrative_blocks.body: Her father set up the Virginia Wright Fund in 1969 to put art in public places, and it has since given more than two hundred and seventy works across western Washington. She commissioned Barnett Newman's Broken Obelisk for the University of Washington.

narrative_blocks.header: The play structure was a di Suvero
narrative_blocks.body: In 1965 they asked Mark di Suvero for something the four children could climb on behind the Washington Park house, grand and thoroughly safe at once. He moved into the house while he built it. Bunyon's Chess stands in the Olympic Sculpture Park now.

narrative_blocks.header: Her daughter counted art as a fifth sibling
narrative_blocks.body: I feel as if there were five of us, her daughter Merrill said, and the fifth one was art. It lacked arms and legs but was whiny and demanding. Our friends went camping; we did not camp, we had art.

b. Jan 1, 1929 Seattle WA; d. Feb 18, 2020 Seattle WA age 91. Buried Lake View Cemetery, Seattle WA. Daughter of Prentice Bloedel (timber baron, MacMillan Bloedel) and Virginia Lee Merrill (HD1832). VIRGINIA WRIGHT FUND 1969: $1M investment from father — bought public art for Washington State, including Barnett Newman's Broken Obelisk; Western Washington University Public Sculpture Collection. WASHINGTON ART CONSORTIUM 1975-2017: Founded collective of 7 WA state art museums; 400+ works of 20th-century American art, $2.3M endowment. COLLECTION: 200+ works donated to SAM including Lichtenstein, Frank Stella, Frankenthaler, Pollock. Ran Current Editions gallery 1968-1975; Wright Exhibition Space 1999-2014. Endowed art history professorship and Virginia B. Wright Art History Prize at Barnard. Lived at Four Seasons Hotel Seattle from 2008 until death. narrative_blocks.header: The Space Needle plan was nearly dead
narrative_blocks.body: A signature tower for the 1962 World's Fair was nearly dead for lack of money when he came across the design in the architect's office and took it on. He assembled the five-man company that built the Space Needle and was its first president.

narrative_blocks.header: He quit journalism after meeting some tycoons
narrative_blocks.body: He came to New York in 1950 to write fiction and ended up editing the Sunday New York Mirror, the last of the spit-on-the-floor newspapers. Covering business at Newsweek he met tycoons and promoters, found none of them dauntingly knowledgeable or competent, and took it as a hint.

narrative_blocks.header: Do you like theater, a playgoer asked him
narrative_blocks.body: He was the Rep's founding president and guaranteed its debts in the lean years; without him, one of its actors said, the theatre would not have survived five years. Long after it named its house for him, a young playgoer asked him at intermission whether he liked theater.

narrative_blocks.header: He had his office taken apart and rebuilt
narrative_blocks.body: Leaving the forty-first floor of the Bank of California building, he could not bear to give up the office, so he had it disassembled and rebuilt on Dexter Avenue. Most people would consider that profligate, he said, but to me it was like bringing over our art.

narrative_blocks.header: The portable defibrillator was his other company
narrative_blocks.body: He backed Physio-Control of Redmond early and chaired it from 1968 until Eli Lilly bought it in 1980. It built the LIFEPAK and the first portable defibrillator that could send a patient's heart trace down a telephone line.

narrative_blocks.header: His father's mill went broke in the crash
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Marietta, Georgia, to a mill owner ruined by the 1929 crash. The family went north to Long Island, where his father became a vice-president of Cannon Mills and his mother knew Zelda Fitzgerald.

narrative_blocks.header: At seventeen he wanted the first wave
narrative_blocks.body: Taft's motto was not to be served but to serve, and at seventeen he volunteered for the 1st Marine Division rather than take the slower road through officer training: I didn't want to miss out. An expert marksman, he landed with a forward observer unit in the first wave at Peleliu and Okinawa.

narrative_blocks.header: More in common to make us friends
narrative_blocks.body: The letters he wrote his parents from the Pacific hold the appalling and the humorous together. Years later he told a Japanese veteran that we may have found ourselves on opposing sides, but in the end we have found more in common to make us friends.

narrative_blocks.header: A secret clearance at the Commerce Department
narrative_blocks.body: Discharged in 1945, he read business engineering at Yale and rowed varsity crew. In 1959 he was at the Department of Commerce in Washington with a secret clearance, helping the Defense Department work out with industry how government would carry on after a war.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the family company for twenty-two years
narrative_blocks.body: He came back to the Northwest in 1960 to the St. Paul and Tacoma Lumber Company, founded Pan Pacific and Caribou Pacific in forest products, and was chief executive of the R.D. Merrill Company from 1970 to 1992.

narrative_blocks.header: Black belt, seaplane, and the New Guinea jungle
narrative_blocks.body: He took a second-degree black belt in taekwondo, flew seaplanes, dived, skied, and went into the jungles of Papua New Guinea and Micronesia, photographing and writing it up. He sat on the boards of the Tacoma Art Museum, Tacoma General Hospital and the YWCA.

narrative_blocks.header: His sister introduced him to her classmate
narrative_blocks.body: His sister Wendy brought him together with Mary Rawlings, her classmate at Finch College, and they married in 1950 and had Mary Jane, Wendy and Richard. He married Judy in 1974, and she shared the adventures.

people.research_notes: b. Sep 13, 1927; d. Sep 11, 2014 age 86. Cremated; ashes at Bloedel Preserve, Bainbridge Island WA. narrative_blocks.header: Tacoma, then Dobbs Ferry, then Finch
narrative_blocks.body: She grew up in downtown Tacoma and on Gravelly Lake, went to Annie Wright Seminary there, then east to the Masters School at Dobbs Ferry and Finch College in New York City.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty-six years, and flowers at the end
narrative_blocks.body: She and George married in July 1948 and lived at Hamden, Longview and Eugene before settling in Tacoma in March 1957. They kept their sixty-sixth anniversary two months before she died, and she used her dwindling energies to choose flowers and arrange them for him.

narrative_blocks.header: She took a personal interest in everyone
narrative_blocks.body: She passed on her love of nature, her adventuresome spirit and her goodwill, and she wove fun into what she did. She treated all people with respect and a personal interest in who they were, and to the very end she was still thinking about how others felt.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son and her grandson went first
narrative_blocks.body: Her son George died in April 2013 and her grandson Karl Griggs in July of the following summer, two months before she did. She left fifteen grandchildren.

people.research_notes: b. Jul 8, 1926 Seattle WA; d. Jun 11, 2022 Lakewood, King County WA age 95. Cremated. Great-grandson of Frederick Weyerhaeuser, co-founder of Weyerhaeuser Company. KIDNAPPING 1935: Abducted at age 8 on a Tacoma street; held in a pit in the woods for 8 days; family paid $200,000 ransom in unmarked bills. Later advocated for release of one kidnapper and offered him a job. WWII: U.S. Navy 1944-1946. Yale B.S. Industrial Administration 1949. CEO, Weyerhaeuser Company 1966-1991 (youngest CEO at 39); board chair until 1999. Under his leadership, company pioneered "high-yield forestry" model. Board memberships: Boeing, Safeco, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, Rand, Chevron. Headstone inscription: per company press release — "an extraordinary person and leader...transformational changes to our company." m. Wendy Wagner (HD1838) Jul 10, 1948. Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Weyerhaeuser

narrative_blocks.header: He was kidnapped from the street at eight
narrative_blocks.body: In 1935 eight-year-old George Weyerhaeuser was snatched off a Tacoma street and held in a pit in the woods for over a week until his family paid a ransom. Years later he urged the release of one kidnapper and gave the man a job.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandfather's obituary set it off
narrative_blocks.body: John P. Weyerhaeuser Sr. died in May 1935, and the obituary detailing the family's timber wealth is what reportedly gave three strangers the idea. He was taken off a Tacoma street days later and left beside a forest road near Issaquah eight days on, with two blankets.

narrative_blocks.header: A boy is a pretty adaptable organism
narrative_blocks.body: A boy is a pretty adaptable organism, he told Sports Illustrated in 1969; he can adjust himself to conditions in a way no adult could. His daughter said the worst of it was being encircled by reporters with cameras and questions and microphones.

narrative_blocks.header: He became his company's youngest chief at thirty-nine
narrative_blocks.body: Great-grandson of the timber baron Frederick Weyerhaeuser, George led the Weyerhaeuser Company from 1966 to 1991, taking the helm at thirty-nine. He pushed the firm toward a high-yield forestry model.

narrative_blocks.header: He replanted every clear-cut within a year
narrative_blocks.body: The high-yield forestry he launched in 1967 was continuous logging and regeneration: clear-cuts replanted within a year, thinning, fertiliser, and seedlings bred to grow faster. By the 1990s his Pacific Northwest operations were producing twice the timber of unmanaged forest.

narrative_blocks.header: He designed the headquarters in the trees
narrative_blocks.body: He shaped the four-hundred-and-twenty-five-acre campus at Federal Way that opened in 1971, one of the first suburban corporate headquarters and acclaimed internationally. When the company sold it for Pioneer Square in 2016, he thought it was terrible.

narrative_blocks.header: Mount St. Helens flattened his timberland
narrative_blocks.body: The 1980 eruption levelled sixty-eight thousand acres of company timber and forced a salvage operation on a scale nobody had attempted.

career.notes: Believed to be the last family member in company management.

career.organization: Boeing, Safeco, RAND, Chevron and the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco

people.research_notes: b. Nov 19, 1953 Lakeview, Pierce County WA; d. Apr 15, 2013 Tacoma WA age 59. Cremated. Fatal heart attack on his boat on Commencement Bay, Tacoma. Career at Weyerhaeuser: began 1978 DeQueen AR as Contract Logging Supervisor; rose to General Manager, largest Containerboard Mill (Valliant OK); VP Manufacturing, pulp/paper; President/CEO Weyerhaeuser Canada 1993-1998; Senior VP Technology 1998-2008; then Senior Fellow, World Business Council for Sustainable Development, Geneva. Board: Foss Waterway Development Authority (President 2000-2004); Museum of Glass (Chair 2004-2007); Yale School of Environmental Studies. Co-founded two biotech start-ups for pulp/paper sustainability. His son Walker Weyerhaeuser carries the line forward. 12th-generation descendant of Rev. Thomas Hooker.

career.notes: Research and development, transportation and purchasing.

career.organization: World Business Council for Sustainable Development, Geneva

narrative_blocks.header: Fifth generation, and he started in the woods
narrative_blocks.body: Frederick Weyerhaeuser was his great-great-grandfather, and his father, grandfather and great-grandfather had each been chief executive. He began at the bottom, in the woods at Dierks, Arkansas in 1978, as a forester and contract logging administrator, and was a sawmill supervisor by 1980.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the company's Canadian operations
narrative_blocks.body: He was president and chief executive of Weyerhaeuser Canada from 1993 to 1998, and chaired the Pulp and Paper Research Institute of Canada and the Forest Alliance of British Columbia. He came back to Federal Way as senior vice-president for technology.

narrative_blocks.header: Three years in Geneva on sustainability
narrative_blocks.body: From 2006 he spent three years in Geneva as a senior fellow of the World Business Council for Sustainable Development. He revelled in getting business, government and environmental groups to negotiate their way through very complex problems.

narrative_blocks.header: Piloting his grandfather's boat with his father
narrative_blocks.body: Some of his best memories were trips on his grandfather's boat, the Wanigan, where he and his father were the pilots and the repair crew. It bonded him to his father and started his lifelong habit of working out how things worked.

narrative_blocks.header: People said exactly what they thought to him
narrative_blocks.body: People said that working for him they could say exactly what they thought and be fully heard. He never searched for the spotlight, a friend said; he wore his name well.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped found the Museum of Glass
narrative_blocks.body: He was on the Museum of Glass board from its founding in 1999 and chaired it from 2004, and as president of the Thea Foss Waterway Development Authority he worked on the revival of Tacoma's waterfront.

narrative_blocks.header: A heart attack on Commencement Bay
narrative_blocks.body: He died at fifty-nine on his boat on Tacoma’s Commencement Bay — the same waterfront he had served as president of the Foss Waterway authority and chair of the Museum of Glass.

narrative_blocks.header: He qualified as a doctor before the law
narrative_blocks.body: He taught school near Rochester for two years and at Conneaut for four more, reading medicine the whole time. He took his degree from the Western Reserve Medical College in February 1853, and that same autumn began studying law with Bolton and Kelley. He was admitted to the bar in 1855.

narrative_blocks.header: Ohio men were going untreated at Memphis
narrative_blocks.body: Word came north in 1862 that Ohio soldiers were suffering for want of proper treatment in the Memphis hospitals. He offered himself as a physician and Governor Brough gave him a special commission. He was still with the army for the siege of Petersburg in 1865.

narrative_blocks.header: He was appointed to finish another man's term
narrative_blocks.body: Judge Williamson resigned in September 1882 and Governor Foster named him to the unexpired term on the Cuyahoga bench. He served until the election of Blandin the following October, then went back to practice with Stevenson Burke.

narrative_blocks.header: Many of his clients could not pay him
narrative_blocks.body: The Cleveland bar remembered that much of his time went to people too poor to compensate him. Once he had settled that a position was right he would not recede from it, however unpopular it made him or however freely he was assailed.

narrative_blocks.header: He was given Jonathan Edwards's whole name
narrative_blocks.body: The name came down from his great-great-grandfather, the Northampton preacher, through his mother's Parsons line. He gave it to no son, but his daughter Sarah Edwards Ingersoll carried the middle name a generation further.

narrative_blocks.header: Two strokes in one week at Moosehead Lake
narrative_blocks.body: He went up to Roach River in Maine in August 1899 for his yearly vacation and had a stroke of apoplexy the Tuesday he arrived. The second one killed him on Friday the eleventh, at seventy-one. The funeral was held from the family house on Prospect Street, and the notice asked that flowers be omitted.

narrative_blocks.body: The Girls' Friendly Club was started in 1902, at an age when most of her contemporaries had stopped working. By the time she died it had a club house of its own on Prospect Avenue.

narrative_blocks.body: She was a leader in the temperance work at Cleveland, as her eldest sister Sarah had been before her. She never married, and she taught in one Cleveland classroom or another for the better part of forty years.

bio.bio_blurb: Pioneer Western Reserve editor, then Cleveland lawyer

narrative_blocks.header: At fourteen he went to make fanning mills
narrative_blocks.body: His father was a Presbyterian minister who never earned enough to send his children to college, so the boy was sent out to Ohio to learn the trade from his mother's brother. The mills were still worked by hand then.

narrative_blocks.header: He printed a paper on the Western Reserve
narrative_blocks.body: The newspaper he published at Hudson was among the first attempts at journalism in that country, and the Plain Dealer headed his obituary Pioneer Editor Called by Death. He read himself into the bar in the meantime and moved to Cleveland about 1852.

narrative_blocks.header: He traded broken railroads after the war
narrative_blocks.body: From the close of the Civil War to 1877, while short lines all over the country were failing, he bought and sold and swapped them. He had left the law once already to go into the old Cleveland Rolling Mill Company with William Bingham, and came back to it afterward.

narrative_blocks.header: Prosperous, but never after the money
narrative_blocks.body: He was comfortable and never rich, and what he wanted was not wealth but variety; the trait people fixed on was his energy. He managed farms, dealt in real estate, and was among the heaviest supporters of the old Third Presbyterian Church of Cleveland.

narrative_blocks.header: Two wives, and ten children between them
narrative_blocks.body: Kate Talcott bore him George, Edward Platt and Mary Augusta before she died at thirty-eight in 1870. He married Cornelia Saunders the next year and had seven more, Howard, Helen, Horton, Albert, Arnold, Alan and Ruth.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Hartford founders met again in Ohio
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas Hooker and John Talcott settled Hartford together in 1636, and two hundred and nineteen years later George Ingersoll married Kate Talcott out at Cleveland. He came down seven generations from the first of them and she six from the second, a thousand miles west of the river they had stopped at.

bio.bio_blurb: Coal salesman who built Ohio River barge towing

narrative_blocks.header: Out of sight is out of mind
narrative_blocks.body: The Lorain Coal and Dock Company offered him a travelling salesman's place and he hesitated, saying that out of sight was out of mind and he might miss a promotion. He was told that a successful salesman can put his feet on the boss's desk. He took the road and sold coal across Indiana, northern Michigan, Wisconsin and Illinois.

narrative_blocks.header: The twenty-below-zero hat
narrative_blocks.body: One winter selling coal in northern Michigan he bought a sealskin hat to keep his head warm. His son kept it for the rest of his own life and called it that.

narrative_blocks.header: He renamed the steamer for his son
narrative_blocks.body: He bought a steamboat in 1923 and was asked whether he meant to change her name. It came over him that the day was his boy Albert's tenth birthday, so the boat took the boy's name. She worked until fire destroyed her above Chilo in Ohio in 1940.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded the Ohio River Company in 1926
narrative_blocks.body: He had begun moving coal by barge over a tipple at Wellsburg to meet competition, and by 1926 he needed more capital for docks at Huntington and below Cincinnati. The West Virginia Coal and Coke Company came in, and the new subsidiary was the Ohio River Company with him managing it.

narrative_blocks.header: He talked Chicago into moving coal by water
narrative_blocks.body: He convinced Commonwealth-Edison in the mid-1930s that it would save by transferring coal into barges at Havana on the Illinois River rather than sending it on by rail. The service began in February 1937 and paid from the outset.

narrative_blocks.header: A surprise printed for his last birthday
narrative_blocks.body: Friends arranged for an article on his career to run in the river trade's paper for his seventy-fourth birthday in March 1953, and had copies air-mailed to California so that he could read it on the day. He died six months later, and rivermen came from considerable distances to the Cincinnati funeral.

notable.notable_blurb: Harvard sociologist; father of structural functionalism

narrative_blocks.header: He built the first general theory of action
narrative_blocks.body: The Structure of Social Action in 1937 and The Social System in 1951 set out the first broad and systematic theory of social systems attempted on either side of the Atlantic. He was the most famous sociologist in the world from the 1940s to the 1970s and the most attacked from the 1970s on.

narrative_blocks.header: He put Max Weber into English
narrative_blocks.body: He had never heard of Weber before Heidelberg, where the widow Marianne invited him to the sociological teas she held in her husband's old library. He translated the work and wrote the analyses of Weber, Durkheim and Pareto that carried all three into English-speaking sociology.

narrative_blocks.header: He made one department out of three
narrative_blocks.body: Harvard created a sociology department in 1930 and he was one of its first two instructors. In 1946 he put sociology, anthropology and psychology together as the Department of Social Relations and chaired it for ten years.

narrative_blocks.header: He traced America back to the Puritans
narrative_blocks.body: He argued that Calvinist and Puritan value patterns had been institutionalized as the American value system, and that the Puritan revolution let loose a democratic one almost by accident. The tradition he meant was Thomas Hooker's, from whom he descended, and the name he carried was Talcott's, the other family that founded Hartford.

narrative_blocks.header: He warned about the Nazis before the war
narrative_blocks.body: He was in Germany in the summer of 1930 and watched the party rise, and from the late thirties he spoke against it on Boston radio and helped start the Harvard Defense Committee. A poll of the time had ninety-one Americans in a hundred against going to war at all.

narrative_blocks.header: He was called a communist, and cleared
narrative_blocks.body: An informer told Hoover in 1952 that he led an inner group of communist sympathizers at Harvard, and a security investigation was opened on him that October. The charge kept him out of a UNESCO conference until he was cleared in the January of 1955.

STRUCTURAL FUNCTIONALISM: Best known for social action theory and structural functionalism; one of the most influential — and controversial — sociologists of the 20th century. notable.notable_blurb: Tennessee jurist and law dean

narrative_blocks.header: He lost five years over the Klan oath
narrative_blocks.detail: After establishing his law practice in Greeneville TN, Judge Ingersoll was disbarred for refusing to take the oath sworn by Ku Klux Klan members — required of lawyers in Reconstruction-era Tennessee. He lost his initial appeal and was barred from practice from 1870 to 1875. He subsequently recovered his career, was appointed to the Tennessee Supreme Court in 1879, and became Dean of the University of Tennessee Law Department 1891-1914. He was a friend and neighbor of former President Andrew Johnson in Greeneville TN.
narrative_blocks.body: Practicing law in Greeneville after the war, he refused to swear the oath Tennessee then demanded of its lawyers, disavowing the Ku Klux Klan on terms he would not accept. He was disbarred for it, appealed, and lost — barred from the courts from 1870 to 1875.

narrative_blocks.header: From Union private to the state's high bench
narrative_blocks.detail: Henry Hulbert Ingersoll attended Oberlin College and Yale University (class of 1863). He served as a private in the 7th Ohio Volunteer Infantry during the Civil War before moving south and entering law. After the KKK disbarment and reinstatement, his career accelerated: Tennessee Supreme Court 1879; LL.D. 1889; Dean of UT Law 1891-1914; Secretary of the Democratic National Convention in St. Louis 1888; President of the Tennessee Bar Association; Vice President of the American Bar Association 1907-1912; Grand Master of Tennessee Freemasons. Author of The Handbook of the Law of Public Corporations — still referenced today.
narrative_blocks.body: He enlisted at seventeen as a private in the 7th Ohio and came out of the war to read law. Tennessee put him on its Supreme Court in 1879, and for twenty-three years he was dean of the state university's law school, holding tuition at fifty dollars a year and filling the benches.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the book law students still cite
narrative_blocks.body: His Handbook of the Law of Public Corporations went into the standard hornbook series and stayed in print past his lifetime. He also served as a national vice president of the American Bar Association and grand master of the Tennessee Masons.

narrative_blocks.header: A neighbor of the president who was impeached
narrative_blocks.body: In Greeneville he was a friend and neighbor of Andrew Johnson, the tailor's apprentice who became president and was impeached. Ingersoll cast a Tennessee electoral vote for Tilden in 1876, then moved on to Knoxville.

narrative_blocks.header: He measured how sugar resists its enzyme
narrative_blocks.detail: His research engaged directly with foundational biochemistry: at concentrations above about 5 percent sucrose, the initial velocity of hydrolysis did not continue to increase as standard models predicted, but instead decreased at higher concentrations. Ingersoll investigated whether this could be explained by changes in the 'nature of the solution medium' at high sugar concentrations — where water can no longer be treated as a simple solvent. The dissertation is a window into early 20th century enzyme chemistry before molecular biology as a field existed. He was also a WW1 veteran. (Columbia University dissertation)
narrative_blocks.body: His Columbia doctorate turned on a narrow, exact question — how very high sugar concentrations slow the enzyme that breaks sugar down. A field service fellowship then sent him to study chemistry in Paris in the 1920s.

notable.notable_blurb: Mayor of Buffalo; historian; lawn-mower inventor

narrative_blocks.header: He patented the first practical American mower
narrative_blocks.body: Ketchum took out the mower patent on 10 July 1847. R. L. Howard of Buffalo built the machine to his design, and by 1864 more than twenty thousand of them were cutting grass.

narrative_blocks.header: In 1861 he patented a grenade
narrative_blocks.body: The Ketchum Grenade was patented in 1861 and carried by the Union army through the Civil War. The man who made the lawn mower made it.

narrative_blocks.header: One term as mayor, then he stopped
narrative_blocks.body: Ketchum took the Buffalo mayoralty for the Whigs in March 1844 with 1,602 votes against Oliver Steele's 1,389, and did not stand again the next year. Fillmore, a lifelong friend, made him Collector of Customs for the Buffalo Creek district in 1851.

narrative_blocks.header: Two volumes on Buffalo and the Six Nations
narrative_blocks.body: Retired from furs and hats, he gave his time to writing — a two-volume history of Buffalo in 1864 and a memoir of the Mohawk chief Joseph Brant in 1872. He was still filing 'Annals of Buffalo' to the Commercial the month he died.

narrative_blocks.header: He let the lion be the sculptor
narrative_blocks.body: Opening his history he wrote that in the fable the lion said, if lions had been sculptors the man would have been shown very differently — and that had the Indians been historians, their history would look otherwise.

narrative_blocks.header: He had never felt better, he said
narrative_blocks.body: On the Saturday he told a friend from a buggy seat that he had never felt better. Next morning the pains took him before the sermon began; he walked home to Park Place and died there while his wife was preparing the bath.

notable.notable_blurb: 2nd President of Princeton

narrative_blocks.header: He co-founded Princeton out of a revival schism
narrative_blocks.body: When the Great Awakening split the Presbyterian and Congregational churches into Old and New Lights, the pro-revival faction broke from Yale’s leadership. Aaron Burr Sr., Jonathan Edwards, and Jonathan Dickinson founded the College of New Jersey in 1746 as a New Light alternative.

narrative_blocks.header: He became Princeton’s youngest president at thirty-two
narrative_blocks.body: After Dickinson died within a year, Burr took the presidency in 1748 at age thirty-two, the youngest ever to hold it. Over his tenure the student body grew from eight to fifty, the curriculum settled, and the first commencement was held.

narrative_blocks.header: He built Nassau Hall and moved the college
narrative_blocks.body: Burr relocated the young college to its permanent home at Princeton and supervised construction of Nassau Hall, the largest building in colonial New Jersey when finished in 1756. In 1755 he was released from his Newark pastorate to give Princeton his full effort.

narrative_blocks.header: He married Jonathan Edwards’s daughter Esther
narrative_blocks.body: In 1752 Burr married Esther Edwards, daughter of the theologian who would succeed him at Princeton. Their two children were Sally, who married Litchfield’s Tapping Reeve, and Aaron Burr Jr., the future Vice President.

narrative_blocks.header: A wartime sermon blended British liberty and faith
narrative_blocks.body: As the French and Indian War opened in 1756, Burr preached a defense of "British Liberty and Property" alongside "unadulterated Christianity." Historians read it as an early fusion of secular and religious rhetoric that would echo through the Revolutionary era.

narrative_blocks.header: Overwork and a funeral sermon killed him
narrative_blocks.body: Burr died of fever in 1757 after traveling to deliver a sermon at Governor Belcher’s funeral, his end blamed on relentless overwork. His widow Esther died seven months later, orphaning three-year-old Sally and two-year-old Aaron.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought a man named Caesar in 1756
narrative_blocks.body: Though he had written against the evils of slavery, Aaron bought a man named Caesar from John Livingston in 1756 and brought him into the President's House at Princeton. When he died the next year his estate listed a second enslaved man, Harry.

people.research_notes: b. Jan 4, 1716 Fairfield CT; d. Sep 24, 1757 Princeton NJ age 41. Son of Daniel Burr (1660-1727), a wealthy farmer, and Elizabeth Pinckney (1673-1722), daughter of Capt. Philip Pinckney (1618-1689); his paternal grandfather Jehu Burr (1625-1692) was born at Lavenham, Suffolk, and settled in the Connecticut Colony as a young man. Yale B.A. 1735, then theology at New Haven, where he witnessed the First Great Awakening and came to know Jonathan Edwards and his wife Sarah, daughter of the Yale founder James Pierpont; Edwards was his mentor and later his father-in-law. Co-author of Introduction to the Latin Tongue. Founded the College of New Jersey at Elizabeth in 1746 with Edwards and Jonathan Dickinson; Dickinson was first president and died in 1747, Burr became second president 9 November 1748 after Governor Jonathan Belcher approved the charter, at thirty-two the youngest ever to hold it. The student body went from 8 in 1747 to 40-50 by 1751; among the first graduates was Richard Stockton, a signer of the Declaration, and five others became Presbyterian ministers. Released from the Newark pastorate in 1755 to work full time at Princeton. DATE PROBLEM: the Wikipedia text gives 21 December 1756 for his becoming minister at Newark, which cannot be right - he had been released from that pastorate the year before. The start year is therefore left blank here.

notable.notable_blurb: Chief Justice, founder of America's first law school

narrative_blocks.header: He founded America's first law school
narrative_blocks.body: Before Reeve, an American lawyer learned the trade by reading in a practicing attorney's office, with little system to it. In 1784 he built a small schoolhouse beside his Litchfield home and began teaching law through formal, connected lectures — the Litchfield Law School, the first in the country.

narrative_blocks.header: His students became the new nation's leaders
narrative_blocks.body: Before it closed in 1833, a school that granted no degrees had graduated more than a thousand men — among them two future Vice Presidents, three Supreme Court justices, a hundred congressmen, and dozens of senators, cabinet officers and governors.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped end slavery in Massachusetts
narrative_blocks.body: In 1781 Reeve joined Theodore Sedgwick as co-counsel for Elizabeth 'Mumbet' Freeman, an enslaved woman suing for her freedom under the new Massachusetts constitution's promise that all are born free and equal. The jury freed her, and the verdict — Brom and Bett v. Ashley — effectively ended slavery in the state.

narrative_blocks.header: He tutored the Burr orphans, then married one
narrative_blocks.body: As a young Princeton tutor, Reeve schooled the two orphaned children of the college's late president — Aaron Burr Jr. and his sister Sally. He married Sally in 1772, and two years later took his brother-in-law Aaron as the very first student of his law school.

narrative_blocks.header: Chief Justice, and author of a landmark treatise
narrative_blocks.body: Reeve sat on Connecticut's highest court for sixteen years and was made Chief Justice of its Supreme Court of Errors in 1814. His 1816 treatise, 'The Law of Baron and Femme,' was the leading American work on family law for much of the century.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran for Congress six times, never winning
narrative_blocks.body: Six times in the 1790s Reeve stood for Congress, and six times he lost — once finishing dead last in the field. The man who trained a hundred congressmen could not become one himself.

narrative_blocks.header: Indicted for libelling President Jefferson
narrative_blocks.body: After Jefferson took office, Reeve wrote in the Litchfield Monitor that the president meant to overthrow the Constitution and make himself a tyrant. A grand jury indicted Reeve and the paper's publisher for seditious libel. The case was dropped, and Reeve never apologized.

people.research_notes: b. Oct 1, 1744 Brookhaven, Long Island NY; d. Dec 13, 1823 Litchfield CT age 79. Buried East Cemetery, Litchfield CT. Son of Rev. Abner Reeve. Princeton B.A. 1763, M.A. 1766. Served as headmaster of grammar school near Princeton; tutored Aaron Burr Jr. and Sally Burr (children of Aaron Burr Sr.) — then married Sally. Studied law with Judge Jesse Root of Hartford CT 1771. (NOTE: Jesse Root was NOT a documented Hooker descendant — connection by professional tutelage only.) Moved to Litchfield CT 1772. Built house 1773. FIRST US LAW SCHOOL: In 1784 opened the Litchfield Law School — the first law school in the United States. Among his students: Aaron Burr Jr. (brother-in-law), John C. Calhoun (also became VP). Brought Rev. Lyman Beecher (father of Harriet Beecher Stowe) to Litchfield 1810. ELIZABETH FREEMAN CASE (1781): With Theodore Sedgwick, represented Elizabeth Freeman ("Bett"), an enslaved woman in Sheffield MA who asked for her freedom based on the 1780 Massachusetts Constitution's "all men are born free and equal" language. Successfully freed her on constitutional grounds — case Brom & Bett v. Ashley set precedent that led to abolition of slavery in Massachusetts. 1798: Became judge of Connecticut Superior Court. 1814: Chief Justice, Connecticut Supreme Court. Author: Law of Baron and Femme (1816) — preeminent American treatise on family law. "The first eminent lawyer of this country who worked to secure a change in the laws regulating the property of married women." (EH source) May "be classed with Kent and Story as a law commentator." His wife Sally's chronic illness prevented him from taking active part in the Revolution, "although he aided in enlistments." (EH source, The Record LXXI) NATIONAL HISTORIC LANDMARK: Tapping Reeve House and Law School, Litchfield CT (designated 1965). m. Sarah "Sally" Burr (H00912) Jun 4, 1771 (or 1772 per some sources). Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tapping_Reeve STAGE 6N MAJOR ENRICHMENT (Wikipedia, Princeton & Slavery, Litchfield Historical Society): PERSONAL: Born October 1, 1744 in Brookhaven Long Island NY, son of Rev. Abner Reeve (1708-1798). Princeton B.A. 1763, M.A. 1766. Headmaster of Princeton-affiliated grammar school in Elizabeth NJ 1763-1770, where he tutored the children of Princeton President Rev. Aaron Burr Sr. — including future VP Aaron Burr Jr. and Sarah 'Sally' Burr (his future wife). Married Sally Burr 1772 in Connecticut. They had one child Aaron Burr Reeve b.1780. Sally died 1797 (age 43); Reeve later remarried. BROM & BETT V. ASHLEY (1781): Theodore Sedgwick of Sheffield MA was approached by Elizabeth Freeman ('Mumbet'), an enslaved woman who had heard discussions of the Sheffield Declaration and the 1780 Massachusetts Constitution containing 'all men are born free and equal.' Sedgwick agreed to take her case and immediately contacted Reeve in Litchfield to be co-counsel. They won her freedom on constitutional grounds — establishing precedent that abolished slavery throughout Massachusetts. The case is now sometimes called the case that ended slavery in Massachusetts. LITCHFIELD LAW SCHOOL (1784-1833): Reeve had been teaching law since 1774 (Aaron Burr Jr. was his first student). By 1784 demand was so high he built a one-room schoolhouse adjacent to his house. The school ran 49 years and educated 1,100+ students. National-scale curriculum drew students from every state. Reeve hired former student James Gould in 1798 when he was elected to the CT Supreme Court. Famous alumni: Aaron Burr Jr. (1772, VP), John C. Calhoun (VP), Horace Mann (reformer), George Catlin (painter), Oliver Wolcott Jr. (Sec of Treasury, CT Governor), 28 U.S. Senators, 101 U.S. Representatives. TEACHING ON SLAVERY: Student Lonson Nash's 1803 notebook records Reeve's lectures: 'Until there is a Charter given from Heaven to our Sea Captains, I shall doubt their right to separate father & mother brother & sister, bear them into foreign climes, there to linger out a miserable existence in servitude & despair.' He told students that slavery was 'founded in violence and contrary to the laws of natural justice.' 1790 CT ABOLITION ATTEMPT: Reeve and six other abolitionist lawyers tried in 1790 to free all enslaved people in Connecticut through a judicial determination, but the effort did not succeed. (CT had passed a gradual abolition bill in 1784 freeing only some slaves.) BROUGHT LYMAN BEECHER TO LITCHFIELD (1810): Reeve invited Rev. Lyman Beecher to serve as Litchfield's Presbyterian minister — a 25+ year tenure. Lyman Beecher's daughter Isabella Beecher (born Litchfield 1822) later married Hooker descendant John Hooker (H01626) in 1841 — a marriage that produced the Nook Farm Hartford abolitionist circle. See CC to John Hooker. CT SUPREME COURT: Justice 1798-1814. Chief Justice 1814-1820. Retired from law school 1820, three years before his death. AUTHORED: 'The Law of Baron and Femme' (1816) — preeminent American family-law treatise of the 19th century; revised 1846, 1867, 1888. Some scholars view it as proto-feminist for its critique of common-law marriage's effect on women's property rights. Also authored 'A Treatise on the Law of Descents' (1825, posthumous). DEATH/BURIAL: Died December 13, 1823 in Litchfield CT, age 79. Buried East Cemetery Litchfield. Tapping Reeve House and Law School designated National Historic Landmark 1965. Sources: Wikipedia, Princeton & Slavery, Litchfield Historical Society, Hicks 'Litchfield Law School', Bowles 'Tapping Reeve and Mumbet'. career.title: Founder, Litchfield Law School
career.notes: Founded the first independent law school in the United States in 1784 (had been teaching law students since 1774, with Aaron Burr Jr. as first student). Built a one-room schoolhouse adjacent to his Litchfield home. Lectured on entire body of law: real estate, rights of persons, contracts, torts, evidence, pleading, crimes, equity. Taught students that slavery was illegal — 'founded in violence and contrary to the laws of natural justice' (per student Lonson Nash's 1803 notebook). Over 1,100 students attended including 2 VPs (Aaron Burr, John C. Calhoun), 28 senators, 101 representatives, 6 cabinet secretaries, 3 SCOTUS justices, 14 governors, 13 state supreme court chief justices.

notable.notable_blurb: American Revolution Patriot

cross_connections.display_label: argued at her Hermitage table with Lafayette

narrative_blocks.header: She turned her home into a Patriot haven
narrative_blocks.body: Though her husband and stepfather were British officers, Theodosia Prevost sided with the Revolution and opened her house, the Hermitage, to its leaders. Washington briefly made it his headquarters after the Battle of Monmouth.

narrative_blocks.header: Hamilton and Lafayette gathered at her table
narrative_blocks.body: The Hermitage drew the Revolution’s rising figures into salon-style debate modeled on the French style she loved. Among her guests were Alexander Hamilton and the Marquis de Lafayette, alongside generals Charles Lee and Jeremiah Wadsworth.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a British officer at seventeen
narrative_blocks.body: At seventeen she wed Jacques Marcus Prevost, a Swiss-born officer in British service, and bore five children. When he died of wounds in 1781, she was a widow with a contested estate that Patriot friends shielded from confiscation.

narrative_blocks.header: Aaron Burr courted her as an intellectual equal
narrative_blocks.body: Ten years his senior, she met Burr in 1778 and the two fell into a romance built on letters about Rousseau, Wollstonecraft, and politics. They married in 1782, modeling a partnership of "mature affection" rather than convenience.

narrative_blocks.header: She schooled her daughter as any son
narrative_blocks.body: A formidably read woman who translated French political treatises, she educated young Theodosia in Latin, Greek, and French from earliest childhood. That conviction — that a daughter deserved a son’s education — shaped the prodigy Theodosia would become.

narrative_blocks.header: Burr called her the finest woman he knew
narrative_blocks.body: She remained Burr’s sharpest political ally until cancer took her in 1794 at forty-seven, years before the Hamilton duel and the treason trial. Burr wrote that she was "the best woman and finest lady" he had ever known.

people.research_notes: b. 1775; d. 1865 age ~90. Wealthy widow. m. Aaron Burr Jr. (H00913) Jul 1, 1833 New York (he was 77, she 58). Lived at the Morris-Jumel Mansion, Washington Heights Manhattan (now National Register). Separated from Burr after 4 months when she realized her fortune was dwindling from his land speculation. bio.bio_blurb: Society scandal; Burr’s brief second wife

narrative_blocks.header: From a poorhouse to a great fortune
narrative_blocks.body: Born in a Providence poorhouse to a prostitute and a sailor, Eliza Bowen clawed her way to wealth, later inventing a story that she was born at sea to a French naval officer. Her 1804 marriage to wine merchant Stephen Jumel brought her the Morris Mansion and a fortune New York society still refused to fully accept.

narrative_blocks.header: She married Burr, then sued him for divorce
narrative_blocks.body: A year after her first husband died — amid rumors she let him bleed to death — the widow married Aaron Burr in 1833. She sued for divorce within months, calling him a fortune-hunter; the decree was finalized the very day Burr died in 1836.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived every scandal to ninety
narrative_blocks.body: Reverting to the Jumel name, she lived in style at the Morris-Jumel Mansion until her death at ninety in 1865. Furniture said to be gifts from Napoleon remains in the house, now New York’s oldest surviving residence.

narrative_blocks.header: Illegitimate daughter of a loyalist merchant
narrative_blocks.detail: William Shedden fled to England after the Revolution; his two illegitimate daughters — Annabella and Jane, born of different mothers — were raised in the new republic he had opposed. Annabella's path from loyalist's daughter to teacher at one of early America's most celebrated female academies is a quiet study in reinvention. The Litchfield Female Academy, run by Sarah Pierce, educated hundreds of women from prominent families across the early republic. Annabella's time there as both student and instructor placed her at the center of that world. (Research notes; Litchfield Historical Society)
narrative_blocks.body: Annabella was the illegitimate daughter of William Shedden, a prominent pre-Revolutionary loyalist merchant in New York. She attended the Bethlehem Female Seminary in 1798 and the Litchfield Female Academy around 1803–04, then returned to teach music there from 1805 to 1808.

narrative_blocks.header: She married the law school founder's only son
narrative_blocks.detail: The son, Tapping Burr Reeve (HD1912), was named for his paternal grandfather — Judge Tapping Reeve, the man who had opposed his parents' marriage. He died at 20 in Litchfield in 1829, the last of the Reeve line. Annabella later married David Judson Burr Sr. (X01882) in Litchfield in 1812 and moved to Richmond, Virginia, where she died in 1849. Her children from the second marriage were not Hooker descendants. (Research notes; EH 1909)
narrative_blocks.body: In November 1808 Annabella married Aaron Burr Reeve, only son of Judge Tapping Reeve — founder of the Litchfield Law School and uncle of Aaron Burr. The Reeve family initially opposed the match because of Annabella's illegitimate birth. Aaron died nine months later, leaving Annabella a widow with an infant son.

career.title: Rice planter
career.notes: One of the wealthiest rice planters in South Carolina; seat at The Oaks plantation.

narrative_blocks.header: He governed through the War of 1812
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph Alston was elected the 44th Governor of South Carolina in December 1812, taking office as the war reached the Carolina coast. A wealthy rice planter who had served as Speaker of the state House, he led the state through its most exposed wartime months.

narrative_blocks.header: He sentenced deserters, then lost in court
narrative_blocks.body: When militiamen refused to muster against a feared British landing, Alston declared that refusal would mean a death sentence. A court issued a writ of habeas corpus and freed the charged men, and an exasperated Alston briefly dismissed the entire militia — leaving the state defenseless until British troops landed and forced their recall.

narrative_blocks.header: He married Aaron Burr’s only daughter
narrative_blocks.body: In 1801 Alston married Theodosia Burr, the Vice President’s celebrated daughter; the couple honeymooned at Niagara Falls, the first recorded couple to do so. Some believed the match was partly financial, easing Burr’s chronic money troubles.

narrative_blocks.header: Burr’s conspiracy nearly pulled him under
narrative_blocks.body: Alston was implicated in the Burr conspiracy through correspondence later shown to be unreliable, a Blennerhassett journal entry, and the testimony of William Eaton. The taint shadowed his rise even as he denied wrongdoing.

narrative_blocks.header: He lost wife and son within four years
narrative_blocks.body: His only child, Aaron Burr Alston, died of fever in 1812 at age ten; months later his wife Theodosia vanished at sea aboard the Patriot. Alston died at Charleston in 1816, not yet thirty-seven, and was buried beside them at The Oaks.

burial.notes: Buried at The Oaks with wife (cenotaph) and son.

narrative_blocks.header: She was Aaron Burr's only sister
narrative_blocks.body: Sally and her toddler brother, the future Vice President, were orphaned at four when their parents and grandparents died in a single span. They were raised among their Edwards kin. The two stayed close their whole lives.

narrative_blocks.header: Her tutor became her devoted husband
narrative_blocks.body: Tapping Reeve was hired to tutor the orphaned Burr children, and in 1772 he married Sally. He took her brother Aaron as his first law student soon after. A schoolroom acquaintance became a marriage of unusual tenderness.

narrative_blocks.header: America's first law school grew in her home
narrative_blocks.body: The Litchfield Law School began in the household Sally kept, students boarding and reciting in the rooms around her. The first law school in the nation took shape under her roof. She was its founding hostess.

narrative_blocks.header: An invalid, nursed with famous devotion
narrative_blocks.body: Sally was in fragile health for much of her adult life, for years a 'delicate invalid' largely confined to her bed. Reeve's tender, unwearied care for her became a story told around Litchfield. She bore it with grace until her death in 1797.

narrative_blocks.header: She corresponded with the early Republic's leaders
narrative_blocks.body: Sally kept up a lively correspondence with prominent figures of the founding era. Her letters moved in the same world her brother and husband did. She was a woman of the new nation's lettered class.

narrative_blocks.header: She mothered an orphaned girl as her own
narrative_blocks.body: The Reeve household opened its doors to a young orphan, Amelia Ogden, who, in a contemporary's words, 'held the place of a daughter.' Childless for years but for one son, Sally mothered beyond her own. Her home gathered in the parentless, as hers once had.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brother carried the love letters
narrative_blocks.body: When Tapping Reeve courted her in 1769, a young lawyer-to-be with hardly a penny, her uncle set himself against the match. Her brother Aaron carried the letters between them, and Reeve wrote that he would never believe she would prove inconstant. They married in 1772.

people.research_notes: b. May 3, 1754 Newark, Essex County NJ; d. Mar 30, 1797 Litchfield CT age 42. Buried East Cemetery, Litchfield CT. Known as "Sally." Eldest child of Aaron Burr Sr. (X00613) and Esther Edwards Burr (H00378). After both parents died in 1757-1758, she and brother Aaron were orphaned; placed first with Shippen family in Philadelphia, then with uncle Timothy Edwards. Tutored by Tapping Reeve, who was studying at Princeton. m. Judge Tapping Reeve (X00614) Jun 4, 1771 (some sources: 1772). Often in ill health throughout her adult life. Tapping was noted for his "chivalrous devotion" and "tender watching and unwearied care" of his invalid wife (Lyman Beecher's account). 1 son: Aaron Burr Reeve (HD1910, 1780-1809). STAGE 6Q ADDITIONS: PRINCETON CONNECTION: Sally and her younger brother Aaron Burr Jr. were tutored as children by Tapping Reeve at the Princeton-affiliated grammar school in Elizabeth NJ during Reeve's headmastership 1763-1770. Their father Aaron Burr Sr. was simultaneously president of the College of New Jersey. The childhood tutoring relationship led to her marriage to Reeve in 1772 at age 18. LITCHFIELD HOME (1780): As Sally's health deteriorated, climbing stairs became difficult, and Reeve added a downstairs wing to their Litchfield house specifically for her. The same year — 1780 — she gave birth to their only child Aaron Burr Reeve (HD1910). The Tapping Reeve House (with the 1780 addition still visible) was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1965. PAPERS: Surviving correspondence preserved at Yale University Manuscripts and Archives, Litchfield Historical Society, and other repositories. Her letters provide primary-source insight into Litchfield Law School's founding decade and the Edwards-Burr family network of the early Republic. Sources: Hicks, Paul DeForest. The Litchfield Law School: Guiding the New Nation; Bowles, Suzanne Geissler. Tapping Reeve and Mumbet; Litchfield Historical Society archives. STAGE 6Q-REDO: NBs rewritten for user engagement per Sam's directive — 5 active NBs replacing 3 prior passive 'invalid wife' framings. Promoted to is_notable=true with Yale Archives primary_url. Career array rewritten with active framing. DETAILED LITCHFIELD HISTORY: In 1773 Sally and her newly-minted lawyer husband Tapping Reeve settled in Litchfield CT and built their two-story six-room house. In 1774, when Sally's eighteen-year-old brother Aaron Burr Jr. emerged from Princeton (where his late father had been president), he came to live with the couple, and Reeve began instructing him in law. This single-student arrangement grew into America's first independent law school — by 1784 Reeve had built a one-room schoolhouse next to his home to accommodate growing demand. REEVE LOVE LETTERS: After their 1772 wedding Reeve wrote to Sally, 'I am this moment enjoying the incomparable pleasure of reflecting that I have one friend in you that will be ever an unshaken friend and that I can enjoy no prosperity but what must give you satisfaction and make you the happiest.' His more playful surviving notes include the line, 'do not abuse my sweet lips with your savage little teeth' — both letters now at Yale's Beinecke Library Manuscripts and Archives. Lyman Beecher described Reeve's twenty-five years of devotion to Sally as 'chivalrous' (per Beecher's autobiography). AMELIA OGDEN: In 1797 Sally welcomed her young cousin Amelia Ogden into the Litchfield household. Amelia is believed to have been the natural daughter of Aaron Ogden and Eunice Edwards Pollock (a widow). She had earlier been placed by her mother with an African American family in Philadelphia, then a German American family in Princeton, then with her double first cousin Rev. Asahel Hooker in Goshen CT (~1792), before coming to Sally in 1797. After Sally's death Amelia remained at the Reeve house with Reeve's second wife Elizabeth Thompson Reeve, eventually inheriting the house at Elizabeth's death and living there until her own death in 1866 at age 87. HEALTH AND DEATH: By 1780 Sally's health had declined enough that climbing stairs was difficult; Reeve added a downstairs wing to accommodate her, still visible at the Tapping Reeve House. The same year she gave birth to their only child Aaron Burr Reeve. She died March 30, 1797 in Litchfield at age 42; buried East Cemetery, Litchfield CT. Reeve remarried Elizabeth 'Betsey' Thompson the following year. Sources: Princeton Alumni Weekly 'Tapping Reeve 1763: His Lawyering Had Roots in Love' (Hicks); Yale Manuscripts and Archives finding aid for Sally Burr Reeve papers; Litchfield Ledger entry #2120; Litchfield Historical Society Litchfield Law School collection; Litchfield Ledger entry #5683 (Amelia Ogden); WikiTree Burr-111.

notable.notable_blurb: Third US Vice President, lawyer and duelist

narrative_blocks.header: He killed Alexander Hamilton at Weehawken
narrative_blocks.body: On 11 July 1804 Burr shot Alexander Hamilton at Weehawken, where Hamilton's son had died in a duel three years before. Their feud dated from 1791, when Burr took the Senate seat of Hamilton's father-in-law, Philip Schuyler. He was indicted in two states and never tried.

narrative_blocks.header: Tied with Jefferson for the presidency
narrative_blocks.body: In 1800 Burr and Thomas Jefferson finished level in the electoral vote, and the House took thirty-six ballots to make Jefferson president and Burr his vice president. The deadlock produced the Twelfth Amendment, and Jefferson dropped him in 1804.

narrative_blocks.header: Tried for treason before John Marshall
narrative_blocks.body: Arrested in the Alabama backcountry in 1807, Burr stood trial at Richmond before Chief Justice John Marshall on a charge of plotting a new nation in the Southwest. He was acquitted, fled his creditors into four years' exile in Europe, and came home calling himself Edwards.

narrative_blocks.header: Mary Emmons and the children he never named
narrative_blocks.body: From about 1787 Burr kept a relationship with Mary Emmons, a woman from Calcutta who came to his household by way of Saint-Domingue. He never acknowledged their children, Louisa and John Pierre Burr, who became Philadelphia abolitionists; DNA confirmed them as his in 2018.

narrative_blocks.header: A sword stroke ended the Gulph mutiny
narrative_blocks.body: Burr went to Quebec with Benedict Arnold in 1775 and fought at Monmouth in 1778. Guarding the Gulph pass at Valley Forge, he had his men's muskets quietly unloaded, and when a mutineer fired one at him that night, Burr cut off the man's arm with his sword.

narrative_blocks.header: He believed women have souls
narrative_blocks.body: Persuaded by Mary Wollstonecraft that women have souls, Burr educated his daughter Theodosia as rigorously as any son. Their thousands of letters became one of the era's remarkable records of a father schooling a daughter as an intellectual equal.

narrative_blocks.header: An orphan at two who lost Theodosia
narrative_blocks.body: Aaron lost his father in 1757 and his mother the next year, before he turned three, and he and his sister Sally were taken in by their mother's Edwards and Dwight kin. In 1812 his grandson died of fever, and that winter his daughter Theodosia vanished at sea aboard the Patriot. At seventy-seven he married the widow Eliza Jumel, and their divorce came through the day he died, in 1836.

people.research_notes: b. Feb 6, 1756 Newark, Essex County NJ; d. Sep 14, 1836 Staten Island NY age 80. Buried near his father at Princeton Cemetery, Princeton NJ. Son of Aaron Burr Sr. (X00613, Princeton president) and Esther Edwards Burr (H00378). Orphaned at age 2 when both parents died at Princeton in 1757-1758. Reared by uncle Judge Timothy Edwards II at Elizabethtown NJ. "Burr often related that his uncle often 'licked me like a sack.'" (EH source, The Record LXXI) — a rare childhood quote preserved in the record. Princeton B.A. age 16 (1772); studied theology briefly; age 19 moved to Litchfield CT to study law with brother-in-law Tapping Reeve. CONTINENTAL ARMY: Enlisted 1775 at news of Lexington and Concord; served with Benedict Arnold's Quebec expedition; aide-de-camp to General Richard Montgomery; CARRIED MONTGOMERY'S BODY AT QUEBEC: when Montgomery was killed storming the fortifications Jan 1, 1775, Burr "carried the dead body of Major-General Richard Montgomery off the field of battle at Quebec, in the face of the enemy" (EH source, The Record LXXI); Lt. Colonel 1777; saved brigade at British Manhattan landing; endured Valley Forge; resigned due to poor health Mar 1779. 3RD VICE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: Democratic-Republican; served under Thomas Jefferson 1801-1805. Electoral College tie with Jefferson in 1800 election required House vote; Jefferson won. 12th Amendment resulted from this crisis. KILLED ALEXANDER HAMILTON IN DUEL: Jul 11, 1804 Weehawken NJ. Indicted for murder in NY and NJ; never tried; charges eventually dropped. BURR CONSPIRACY: 1805-1807 — alleged plot to form independent country from western US or Spanish territory. Arrested 1807 in Alabama; acquitted of treason. Fled to Europe briefly. Returned 1812. MANHATTAN COMPANY: Founded 1799 — ostensibly a water company, actually a bank to challenge Federalist financial monopoly. Predecessor of JPMorgan Chase. m. (1) Theodosia Bartow Prevost (X00615) Jul 2, 1782. m. (2) Eliza Jumel (X00616) Jul 1, 1833 (separated after 4 months). MILITARY REPUTATION: "To his death, Burr was far more tenacious of his military than of his professional or political reputation." (EH source, The Record LXXI) Original member of the Society of the Cincinnati (the elite Revolutionary officers' society). UNACKNOWLEDGED CHILDREN: DNA evidence confirmed in 2018 that Burr fathered Louisa Burr (c.1784-1878) and John Pierre Burr (c.1792-1864) with Mary Emmons, an East Indian servant. John Pierre Burr was an Underground Railroad agent and Underground Railroad leader — these are Hooker descendants if lineage accepted. See OR031. bio.bio_blurb: Litchfield-born attorney; only child of Judge Reeve

narrative_blocks.header: The only child of the law school's founder
narrative_blocks.body: Aaron Burr Reeve was the single child of Judge Tapping Reeve, founder of the Litchfield Law School, and his wife Sally Burr. Through his mother he was a nephew of Aaron Burr, who was running for the presidency while the boy was in college. He carried two of the most storied names in Litchfield.

narrative_blocks.header: A bright student who would not apply himself
narrative_blocks.body: Prepared for college by the Rev. Azel Backus of Bethlehem, young Reeve was well able but, by his own teachers' account, 'did not apply himself steadily.' He went on to Yale and then read law at his father's famous school. The talent was there; the discipline came harder.

narrative_blocks.header: Dead at twenty-nine, a year after marrying
narrative_blocks.body: Reeve opened a law practice in Troy, New York, with what one account called 'flattering prospects of success,' and in November 1808 he married Annabella Shedden. Within ten months he was dead, in September 1809, at twenty-nine. His only son would die at Yale twenty years later, ending the judge's direct line.

death.notes: Most likely died at sea Jan 2-3, 1813, aboard the schooner Patriot.

b. 1783 Albany NY; d. c. Jan 1813 at sea (Carolinas coast) age ~30. Only surviving child of Aaron Burr Jr. (H00913) and Theodosia Bartow Prevost (X00615). Given an unusually rigorous education by her father (classics, French, horsemanship, music) — Burr believed women deserved education equal to men. m. Joseph Alston (X00618) Feb 1801 — Governor of South Carolina 1812-1814. 1 son: Aaron Burr Alston (HD1913, 1802-1812, died of malaria age 10). LOST AT SEA: In winter 1812-1813, after her son's death, Theodosia sailed from Georgetown SC aboard the schooner Patriot toward New York to visit her father. She never arrived. The ship was never found; her fate unknown. Theories: murdered by pirates, or shipwrecked in a storm. Burr and Alston believed she died in a storm. Theodosia left no surviving descendants.

notable.notable_blurb: First Lady of South Carolina, lost at sea

narrative_blocks.header: Her father raised her like a scholar
narrative_blocks.body: Aaron Burr believed women deserved an education equal to men’s and gave his daughter a rigorous grounding in classics, French, music, and horsemanship. Theodosia became one of the most celebrated learned women of the early republic.

narrative_blocks.header: She was First Lady of South Carolina
narrative_blocks.body: Her 1801 marriage to Joseph Alston made her the state’s First Lady when he became governor in 1812. She kept up an intense correspondence with her father, numbering in the thousands of letters.

narrative_blocks.header: She lost her only child to fever
narrative_blocks.body: Her son Aaron Burr Alston died of malaria in June 1812 at age ten. The grief broke her already-fragile health and deepened her longing to reach her father in New York.

narrative_blocks.header: She vanished at sea and was never found
narrative_blocks.body: On the last day of 1812 she sailed from Georgetown aboard the schooner Patriot, bound for New York to see her father. The ship disappeared off Cape Hatteras around January 2, 1813, and no trace of Theodosia was ever found.

narrative_blocks.header: A portrait may be her only return
narrative_blocks.body: In 1869 a dying woman on the Outer Banks gave a doctor an unsigned portrait her husband had taken from a wrecked ship during the war. Some believe the "Nags Head Portrait" is Theodosia, carried as a gift to her father; the mystery endures two centuries later.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father never believed the rumors
narrative_blocks.body: For years stories surfaced that Theodosia had been taken by pirates or was living on under another name, and Aaron Burr refused every one of them. If she were alive, he said, "all the prisons in the world could not keep her from her father."

narrative_blocks.header: The first couple recorded to honeymoon at Niagara
narrative_blocks.body: She married Joseph Alston in February 1801, at seventeen, and they went north to Niagara - the first couple on record to honeymoon there. Theodore Dwight Jr.'s guidebook sent Americans after them twenty-four years later.

people.research_notes: b. Aug 16, 1809 Troy, Rensselaer County NY; d. Aug 28, 1829 Litchfield CT age 20. Buried East Cemetery, Litchfield CT. Son of Aaron Burr Reeve (HD1910) and Anabella Shedden (X00617). Only child of Aaron Burr Reeve, born the year his father died. Named for grandfather Judge Tapping Reeve. A MEMBER OF THE SENIOR CLASS, YALE COLLEGE when he died. Obituary (Litchfield Enquirer, Sep 3, 1829): "a youth of uncommon promise, of refined manners, generous sentiments, strict integrity, and honorable purposes; the budding faculties of whose mind might have produced fruits that would have done honor to the illustrious stock from which this interesting scion sprang." Headstone: "the last descendant of the late eminently learned and pious Chief Justice Reeve." The Hooker line through Sarah Burr Reeve (H00912) ends here.

narrative_blocks.header: The last of Judge Reeve's line
narrative_blocks.body: Tapping Burr Reeve, the only child of Aaron Burr Reeve, was a senior at Yale in 1829 when a sudden illness killed him at twenty. He was the only surviving descendant of his grandfather, the famous Judge Tapping Reeve. With his death the judge's direct line ended.

people.research_notes: b. 1802; d. Jun 30, 1812 Laurens County SC age 10 (malaria). Son of Governor Joseph Alston (X00618) and Theodosia Burr Alston (HD1911). Named for maternal grandfather Aaron Burr Jr. Theodosia wrote to her father on his death: "there is no more joy for me, the world is a blank. I have lost my boy. My child is gone forever." His death preceded his mother's mysterious disappearance at sea by 6 months. End of the Hooker line through Aaron Burr Jr. [6Y-787] Merged duplicate HD5985 into this record. b. 29 May 1802 Oaks Plantation; d. 30 June 1812 Georgetown SC, fever/malaria, age 10. FindAGrave #38874314, Oaks Cemetery, Murrells Inlet. Gravestone epitaph (Leiding 1921) commemorates Joseph, Theodosia, and son together.

narrative_blocks.header: A fever ended Aaron Burr’s grandson at ten
narrative_blocks.body: Aaron Burr Alston, the only child of Theodosia Burr and Governor Joseph Alston, died of fever — most likely malaria — on June 30, 1812, at age ten. His death shattered his mother’s health months before she herself vanished at sea, and he lies in the Oaks family cemetery beneath an epitaph mourning the whole lost family.

Came from Calcutta to Saint-Domingue (modern Haiti) as Eugenie Beauharnais before taking the name Mary Emmons and arriving in America. Relationship with Aaron Burr Jr. began 1787 or earlier. Mother of Louisa Burr (HD1914) and John Pierre Burr (HD1915). Burr never acknowledged this relationship during his lifetime. narrative_blocks.header: She crossed half the world into Burr’s household
narrative_blocks.body: Born in Calcutta around 1760, Mary lived in Saint-Domingue as Eugénie Beauharnais until Jacques Marcus Prevost, a British officer posted there in the early 1770s, probably brought her north to his wife Theodosia's household. When Theodosia married Aaron Burr in 1782, Mary came too.

narrative_blocks.header: Two families call her Burr’s second wife
narrative_blocks.body: Her descendants hold that Burr married Mary in Haiti after Theodosia died in 1794, which would have made her children legitimate. A descendant the family called Aunt Doll kept the marriage certificate, then destroyed it in frustration that no one cared.

narrative_blocks.header: Her children outlived Burr’s ideals in practice
narrative_blocks.body: Louisa Charlotte married Francis Webb and was the mother of the novelist Frank J. Webb. John Pierre, a barber, hid fugitives in the attic, the cellar and a backyard pit of his Philadelphia house, and helped organize the Pennsylvania Anti-Slavery Society.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son John Pierre was born at sea
narrative_blocks.body: Mary and Burr's wife Theodosia both bore him children in 1788, the year Mary's daughter Louisa Charlotte was born. Their son John Pierre followed in August 1792, born at sea as Mary sailed home from a visit to Haiti.

narrative_blocks.header: Burr kept her in Philadelphia while a senator
narrative_blocks.body: While Burr sat in the Senate in the 1790s, Mary raised their two children in Philadelphia at the house where he lodged, and his wife Theodosia stayed in New York. Burr kept this second family secret through all his political life.

narrative_blocks.header: Recognized by the Aaron Burr Association, 2018
narrative_blocks.body: On 29 September 2018 the Aaron Burr Association voted unanimously to acknowledge Mary's two children as Burr's, after her descendant Sherri Burr brought DNA evidence and a deed for land Burr bought John Pierre. A headstone went on his grave in 2019.

narrative_blocks.header: The Secret Wife of Aaron Burr, 2019
narrative_blocks.body: In 2013 the artist Camilla Huey made Mary one of nine corset portraits of the women in Burr's life, and in 2019 Susan Holloway Scott imagined her story in the novel The Secret Wife of Aaron Burr, inventing most of it for want of records.

people.research_notes: b. 1788; d. Jul 1829 Philadelphia PA age ~40. Founding member, Pennsylvania Augustine Education Society (1818). Elder in the First African Presbyterian Church and parishioner at African Episcopal Church of St. Thomas. Secretary, Haytien Emigration Society (1824) — composed of Black Americans wishing to emigrate to Haiti. Philadelphia distribution agent for Freedom's Journal 1827-1829 (first African American newspaper). Served on Board of Instruction of joint Episcopal-Presbyterian church school in Haiti 1824-1826. 1824-1826: Emigrated to Haiti with family; returned 1826 when the project failed. Died 1829, a year after his youngest son Frank was born. m. Louisa Charlotte Burr (HD1914) 1817. 5 children.

narrative_blocks.header: He built a society to educate Black Philadelphians
narrative_blocks.body: In 1818 he helped found the Pennsylvania Augustine Education Society, dedicated to schooling people of color at a time when few institutions would. He held fundraising events at Mother Bethel A.M.E. Church and beyond.

narrative_blocks.header: He spread the first Black-owned newspaper
narrative_blocks.body: He served as a distribution agent for Freedom's Journal, the first African American-owned newspaper in the country, and as secretary of the Haytien Emigration Society. The society helped Black families leave for Haiti in search of a freer life; his own family made the journey in 1824.

narrative_blocks.header: His son turned their world into a novel
narrative_blocks.body: He died young in 1829, leaving his wife Louisa to raise their four children. The youngest, Frank J. Webb, grew up to write The Garies and Their Friends, the second novel published by an African American, drawing on the family's life amid Philadelphia's race riots.

Louisa, John Pierre, and Theodosia Burr Alston had a documented relationship as half-siblings. narrative_blocks.header: Age fifteen, saved Philadelphia mansion from circus fire
narrative_blocks.body: Working as a servant for the prominent Philadelphia family of Elizabeth Powel Francis Fisher and her sister Sophia Francis Harrison, Louisa at about age fifteen helped save the Harrison mansion from a 1799 circus fire by soaking blankets and carpets to smother the flames. She later nursed Joshua Fisher, born 1807, who grew deeply attached to her. Upon his 1873 death his estate provided her an annuity and a funeral fund — recognition outside any acknowledged Burr legacy.

narrative_blocks.header: Wrote father Burr for Theodosia's portrait miniature
narrative_blocks.body: Letters from Louisa to her unacknowledged father Aaron Burr survived among his papers. In one she asked him to lend a miniature portrait of his 'beloved Theodosia' — half-sister Theodosia Burr Alston, lost at sea in 1813 — so that brother John Pierre Burr could copy it. The three unacknowledged Burr children — Louisa, John Pierre, and the recognized Theodosia — had a documented sibling relationship across the color line that Burr never publicly acknowledged.

narrative_blocks.header: She lived between abolition and the Confederacy
narrative_blocks.body: For decades Louisa was the trusted domestic of the Fisher family, Philadelphia Copperheads who sympathized with the South. By day she served a pro-Confederate household; by night she belonged to an abolitionist family, a double life that gave her a rare ground-view of the sectional crisis.

narrative_blocks.header: Born the year Burr's legitimate daughter died
narrative_blocks.body: In 1788 Aaron Burr had two daughters: a legitimate infant by his wife Theodosia, dead within the year, and an unacknowledged child by Mary Emmons who would live to ninety. The claimed daughter's life lasted months; the unclaimed one's, nine decades.

narrative_blocks.header: DNA confirmed her Burr paternity 230 years later
narrative_blocks.body: Suspected for two centuries, her descent from Aaron Burr was formally confirmed in 2018, when DNA evidence accepted by the Aaron Burr Association established his paternity beyond doubt. The finding set her at last in the family record her father had kept her out of.

notable.notable_blurb: Author and writer

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the second African American novel
narrative_blocks.detail: Frank J. Webb's novel depicts the lives of free Black and mixed-race families in antebellum Philadelphia — racial violence, anti-Black riots, middle-class aspiration, and the daily texture of life in a free Northern city. It was published in London because no American publisher would take it. Harriet Beecher Stowe, who had championed Frank's wife Mary as a dramatic reader, wrote the preface even while in mourning. Henry, Lord Brougham also wrote an introduction. The novel was dedicated to Lady Noel Byron, who had encouraged Frank during the English tour. It was not published in the United States until 1969 — 112 years after its London debut.
narrative_blocks.body: His novel The Garies and Their Friends, published in London in 1857, was the second ever written by an African American, portraying the free Black and mixed-race families of the North amid Philadelphia's racial violence. Harriet Beecher Stowe wrote its preface; the book did not appear in the United States until 1969.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife's fame carried his novel to London
narrative_blocks.detail: Mary E. Webb was born in New Bedford MA in 1828, her mother having escaped slavery in Virginia. She gained renown in Philadelphia for dramatic readings of Shakespeare and Longfellow. Harriet Beecher Stowe was so impressed that she adapted scenes from Uncle Tom's Cabin specifically for Mary's performances. In 1856, Stowe arranged an English tour for the couple. Longfellow attended a reading and wrote: "A striking scene, this Cleopatra with a white wreath in her dark hair, and a sweet, musical voice, reading to a great, unimpassioned, immovable Boston audience." In England, a London editor agreed to publish Frank's novel. Mary's health collapsed during the tour; she died in Kingston Jamaica in 1859.
narrative_blocks.body: His first wife, Mary Espartero Webb, was a celebrated dramatic reader whom Harriet Beecher Stowe took up as a patron. Their 1856 English tour opened the doors that put his novel into print there the next year.

narrative_blocks.header: From Jamaica to a Texas newspaper
narrative_blocks.body: After his first wife died in Jamaica, he stayed on as a postal clerk and planter, remarried, and around 1870 brought the family back to the States. They passed through Washington — where he clerked in the Freedmen's Bureau and wrote for Frederick Douglass's paper — before settling for good in Galveston, Texas, where he taught, wrote, and entered politics.
