narrative_blocks.header: Barber by day, Railroad conductor by night
narrative_blocks.body: John Pierre Burr ran a Philadelphia barbershop whose back rooms hid self-liberating people in the attic, the cellar, and a pit in the yard. Light-skinned, he escorted refugees through the city by claiming he was walking "his man," then moved them on toward Lucretia Mott and Canada.

narrative_blocks.header: He was Aaron Burr’s secret son of color
narrative_blocks.body: He was born in 1792 to the Vice President and Mary Emmons, a servant of Calcutta origin, while Burr’s first wife lay dying of cancer. Burr kept this family hidden through his entire political life, though he supported his son’s education and deeded him land.

narrative_blocks.header: He built a Black men’s speaking school
narrative_blocks.body: In 1837 Burr founded the Demosthenian Institute at his home, training young Black men in oratory and debate like a Toastmasters of its day. By 1841 it had forty-two members, a hundred-volume library, and its own weekly paper.

narrative_blocks.header: He organized Philadelphia’s antislavery fight
narrative_blocks.body: Burr helped organize the Pennsylvania Anti-Slavery Society and served on its Vigilance Committee, agented Garrison’s Liberator, and raised defense money for the Christiana Resistance of 1851. He protested the 1838 disfranchisement of free Black Pennsylvanians.

narrative_blocks.header: He answered Douglass’s call to arms
narrative_blocks.body: Among his last public acts, Burr signed Frederick Douglass’s "Men of Color to Arms" broadside urging Black men to join the Union army. His son John Emery Burr would muster into the U.S. Colored Troops in answer.

narrative_blocks.header: DNA restored him to the Burr name
narrative_blocks.body: For generations he was called Aaron Burr’s "natural son"; in 2018 a DNA test confirmed the paternity and the Aaron Burr Association formally acknowledged him. A 2019 headstone at Eden Cemetery names him a "Champion of justice and freedom, conductor on the Underground Railroad."

narrative_blocks.header: The son Aaron Burr fathered in exile
narrative_blocks.body: Aaron Burr fathered him in Paris around 1808, during the long European exile that followed the Hamilton duel and his treason trial. Burr brought the boy to New York in 1816 and raised him; he grew up a prominent Manhattan goldsmith and diamond importer.

narrative_blocks.header: Lobbied Lincoln on a Honduras freedmen colony
narrative_blocks.detail: In August 1860, Aaron Columbus Burr received an offer of ~150 square miles in British Honduras's Stann Creek District and conceived a plan to use it as a colony for emancipated American slaves. He enlisted political writer Anna Ella Carroll to lobby Lincoln and Secretary of State Seward, titling the plan the "Lincoln Colony." Carroll submitted memoranda arguing that minimal federal support could place freedpeople "beyond U.S. racial conflicts" under British protection. The scheme failed — undermined by the escalating war, British colonial reluctance, and freedpeople's wariness of tropical disease and unfamiliar terrain. Burr and James Grant then formed the American Honduras Company for mahogany export. In 1865 Burr helped found Linwood, Maryland — a cooperative settlement for freed Black laborers on 1,200 acres, housing over 100 families initially.
narrative_blocks.body: During the Civil War he worked with Anna Ella Carroll to propose the 'Lincoln Colony' — a settlement for freed American slaves in British Honduras (modern Belize), lobbying President Lincoln starting August 1860. Offered ~150 square miles in Stann Creek District; scheme failed due to wartime priorities and British reluctance.

narrative_blocks.header: Founded a freed Black cooperative settlement, 1865
narrative_blocks.body: With James Grant he co-founded a cooperative settlement for freed Black laborers at Linwood Maryland in 1865 on 1,200 acres — over 100 families initially housed. The successful Maryland settlement followed the earlier failed 'Lincoln Colony' Anna Ella Carroll proposal for British Honduras.

narrative_blocks.header: NYC jeweler at 167 Broadway from 1828
narrative_blocks.body: He entered the goldsmithing and silversmithing trade c.1825 and was listed in New York City directories as a jeweler from 1828 through 1870 — operating from 167 Broadway. Major importer of diamonds and fine jewelry; also traded in mahogany and tropical woods, accumulating significant wealth over four decades.

narrative_blocks.header: Midshipman, editor, the mayor's secretary
narrative_blocks.body: Schooled at Captain Partridge's military academy at Middletown, Charles held a midshipman's commission in the Navy, then worked on the Courier and Enquirer, was private secretary to Mayors Havemeyer and Wood, and deputy postmaster of New York.

narrative_blocks.header: Raised in Burr's house as an adopted son
narrative_blocks.body: Burr raised Charles in his New York home as an adopted son, and he was widely presumed to be Burr's child by an unknown mother. Charles died suddenly in September 1862, at forty-six, leaving a son serving as a master's mate in the Navy and a daughter of sixteen.

narrative_blocks.header: A Valley Forge soldier's daughter
narrative_blocks.body: Hetty was born in Philadelphia about 1796, the daughter of John Emery, a free Black private whose name appears twenty-four times on the muster rolls of Pennsylvania's Fifth Regiment, four of them at Valley Forge. A dressmaker by trade, she married John Pierre Burr at the African Episcopal Church of St. Thomas on 15 May 1817.

narrative_blocks.header: She helped found an antislavery society for women
narrative_blocks.body: In 1833, denied membership in the men's American Anti-Slavery Society, Hetty and some two dozen other women founded the Philadelphia Female Anti-Slavery Society. She sat on the business committee of the Anti-Slavery Conventions of American Women in 1838 and 1839, and counted the Grimké sisters among her friends.

narrative_blocks.header: Her home was a station on the railroad
narrative_blocks.body: Hetty and John Pierre hid self-liberating people in their house at Fifth and Locust Streets, in the attic, in a cave under the cellar and, at night, in a deep hole in the yard, until John Pierre could take them on toward Lucretia Mott and Canada. They raised ten children in the same house.

narrative_blocks.header: She helped open a refuge for Black women
narrative_blocks.body: In 1845 Hetty and Hetty Reckless, who had escaped slavery in Salem County, New Jersey, founded the Moral Reform Retreat for the most destitute Black women and girls of Philadelphia. Nearly two hundred women passed through it, staying about six weeks and leaving with schooling and a skill.

narrative_blocks.header: Food and clothes for fugitives
narrative_blocks.body: From 1838 Hetty belonged to the Female Vigilant Association, which raised money to feed, clothe and shelter fugitives passing through Philadelphia, and in 1849 she helped found the Woman's Association of Philadelphia.

narrative_blocks.header: Treasurer of the Free Produce Society
narrative_blocks.body: In 1831 Hetty was a founding member and the treasurer of the Colored Female Free Produce Society, which urged Philadelphians to buy only goods made by free labor.

narrative_blocks.header: A lyceum that let women in
narrative_blocks.body: In January 1831 Hetty was among the founders of the Gilbert Lyceum, an intellectual society unusual for taking women and men alike, with Joseph Cassey, Sarah Mapps Douglass, Grace Douglass and Harriet Purvis Jr. She also presided over one of the city's female literary societies.

narrative_blocks.header: A Philadelphia dressmaker who wrote verse
narrative_blocks.body: Well educated and independent, she ran her own dressmaking shop on Currant Alley by 1838 and later sold jams and preserves she made herself. She wrote, too: a page and a half of rhyming couplets, signed E. S. Webb, survives in a friend's keepsake album.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brother wrote an early Black novel
narrative_blocks.body: Her brother was Frank J. Webb, author of The Garies and Their Friends, among the earliest novels published by an African American. The Webb household moved in the abolitionist and literary circles of antebellum Philadelphia.

narrative_blocks.header: She worked for equal rights across three cities
narrative_blocks.body: Across a long life in Philadelphia, St. Louis, and Washington, she gave herself to the cause of equal rights for Black Americans, carrying the family's abolitionist tradition into the decades after the Civil War.

narrative_blocks.header: A freedman's son who raised a nurse pioneer
narrative_blocks.body: The son of a man born enslaved and later freed, he made his living as a barber in St. Louis and then Philadelphia. His daughter Sara grew up to become the first Black superintendent of nurses at Washington's Freedmen's Hospital.

narrative_blocks.header: He came from a North Carolina plantation town
narrative_blocks.body: His father and grandfather had been enslaved in Edenton, North Carolina, and kept working for the Johnston family after they were freed. He grew up in that plantation world, on easy terms with its planters, before heading north to Philadelphia around 1837.

narrative_blocks.header: He opened a barbershop by Joseph Cassey's
narrative_blocks.body: In Philadelphia he set up his barbershop directly across from Joseph Cassey — the wealthy Black wigmaker, hairdresser, and perfumer — and later ran one in St. Louis, where his children were born. He married Elizabeth Webb in 1838.

narrative_blocks.header: He fed his brother-in-law's famous novel
narrative_blocks.body: No one was better placed to give the city-born novelist Frank Webb — his brother-in-law — authentic details of southern plantation life. Scholars believe that firsthand knowledge of Edenton shaped the characters and settings of Webb's The Garies and Their Friends.

people.research_notes: b. 1828 New Bedford MA; d. Jun 17, 1859 Kingston Jamaica. Mother escaped slavery in Virginia; father described as a Spanish gentleman. Acclaimed dramatic reader of Shakespeare, Longfellow, and Philip Sheridan in Philadelphia. Harriet Beecher Stowe became her patron; Stowe adapted Uncle Tom's Cabin for her performances. Longfellow praised her: a "Cleopatra with a white wreath in her dark hair." Toured England 1856 with husband Frank; her acclaim helped secure publication of his novel. Health collapsed on tour; died in Kingston Jamaica 1859. m. Frank J. Webb (HD1921) c.1845. | [SOURCE MOVED] WikiTree/FamilySearch

notable.notable_blurb: Black actress and dramatic reader

cross_connections.display_label: took her up as a patron and sent her to England

narrative_blocks.header: A Black elocutionist who read for royalty
narrative_blocks.body: A free woman of color, she won international fame for her dramatic readings — Shakespeare, Longfellow, and Stowe — touring the northern states and then England for eighteen months. In London she moved in royal circles, meeting Lady Byron among others.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father may have been a Spanish regent
narrative_blocks.body: Born free in New Bedford in 1828, three weeks after her mother reached the town as a refugee from Virginia slavery, she was said to be the daughter of 'a Spanish gentleman of wealth.' Longfellow himself guessed the father was Baldomero Espartero, the Spanish general and regent whose name she carried.

narrative_blocks.header: Her stage fame got her husband's novel published
narrative_blocks.body: Harriet Beecher Stowe took her up after her 1855 Philadelphia debut, and her acclaimed English tour — reading Stowe's own The Christian Slave — persuaded a London publisher to bring out her husband Frank's novel, The Garies and Their Friends. The tour also broke her health.

narrative_blocks.header: The English tour cost her her health
narrative_blocks.body: The strain of the tour left her ill. She and Frank rested in Cannes, then sailed for Jamaica, where he had taken a post office job in hope the warm climate would help. She died there of tuberculosis in 1859, at thirty-one.

bio.bio_blurb: Civil War Medal of Honor recipient

military_service.notes: Medal of Honor, Chaffin’s Farm

narrative_blocks.header: He saved the colors at Chaffin’s Farm
narrative_blocks.body: On September 29, 1864, as color-bearer after color-bearer fell, Sergeant Major Christian Fleetwood seized the regimental flag and bore it through the fire at Chaffin’s Farm outside Richmond. For that act he received the Medal of Honor, one of the first to a Black soldier, though it arrived quietly in the mail months later.

narrative_blocks.header: A free Baltimorean raised in a merchant’s library
narrative_blocks.body: Born free in Baltimore in 1840, Fleetwood was raised in the home of a wealthy sugar merchant whose wife taught him to read and gave him the run of her library. He honed a lifelong reading habit that set him apart and shaped everything that followed.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded the Upper South’s first Black newspaper
narrative_blocks.body: In 1863, before enlisting, Fleetwood founded The Lyceum Observer, said to be the first newspaper south of the Mason-Dixon line owned and operated by African Americans. It grew out of a Baltimore literary society and his own restless pen.

narrative_blocks.header: He rose as high as law allowed
narrative_blocks.body: On enlisting in the 4th U.S. Colored Infantry he was made sergeant major — the highest rank a Black man could legally hold. Every officer of his regiment petitioned for his commission; Secretary of War Stanton refused, and Fleetwood served out the war at the ceiling set against him.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded D.C.'s first Black National Guard unit
narrative_blocks.body: After the war Fleetwood organized the Washington Cadet Corps into the 6th Battalion of the D.C. National Guard — the first African American National Guard unit — and led it as major. He later trained the high-school cadet corps whose graduates earned officer commissions in the next war.

narrative_blocks.header: A choirmaster and salon host in Black Washington
narrative_blocks.body: A trained musician, Fleetwood served as choirmaster at several Washington churches until deafness from wartime gunfire silenced him. With his wife Sara he hosted the literary and musical salons that anchored the capital’s Black elite.

narrative_blocks.header: He answered the call his father had signed
narrative_blocks.body: Eldest son of John Pierre Burr, John Emery became a barber like his father, then mustered into the U.S. Colored Troops in the Civil War — serving the cause his father had championed by signing Frederick Douglass’s "Men of Color to Arms."

narrative_blocks.header: Three generations answered three wars
narrative_blocks.body: His military service completed a striking family arc: his grandfather Aaron Burr Jr. and his great-grandfather Private John Emery both fought in the Revolution, the latter wintering at Valley Forge. John Emery Burr carried that thread into the war that ended slavery.

narrative_blocks.header: He led Connecticut's Black Freemasons
narrative_blocks.detail: Son of John Pierre Burr (HD1915, Underground Railroad conductor) and Hetty Emery Burr (X00621, co-founder of the Moral Reform Retreat), Walter Harris Burr carried forward the family's community leadership in a different state. He settled in Norwich, New London County CT around 1852 and established himself as a barber for 40+ years — the same trade as his father. He rose to Grand Master of the Prince Hall Masonic Grand Lodge of Connecticut, the historically African American Masonic order founded in the tradition of Prince Hall. He married twice: first Catherine Ann Jackson (d. Oct 5, 1882, married Oct 28, 1855 Norwich CT); then nurse Clarissa Ann Beman (married May 22, 1886 Norwich CT, who survived him by 20 years). No children from either marriage. He died Jan 6, 1913 in Norwich age 87, buried Yantic Cemetery, Norwich CT.
narrative_blocks.body: Rising through the Prince Hall order — the African American branch of Freemasonry — he became Most Worshipful Grand Master of its Grand Lodge of Connecticut. It made him one of the most prominent Black Masonic leaders of his day.

narrative_blocks.header: A Burr son barbered forty years in Norwich
narrative_blocks.body: Born into the family's Philadelphia abolitionist world, he settled around 1852 in Norwich, Connecticut, and cut hair there for more than four decades. He took up his father's barbering trade far from the city where the Burrs had worked the Underground Railroad.

notable.notable_blurb: First Black nursing superintendent at Howard's Freedman's Hospital

narrative_blocks.header: First Black nursing superintendent at Freedman's Hospital
narrative_blocks.body: In 1901 she outscored all national applicants on the civil service examination to become the first Black nursing supervisor at Howard's Freedman's Hospital. The institution had been built into a center of Black medicine by Dr. Daniel Hale Williams, who taught her in Freedman's first nursing class.

narrative_blocks.header: Wife of a Medal of Honor recipient
narrative_blocks.body: She married Sgt. Major Christian Abraham Fleetwood in 1869 — recipient of the Medal of Honor for the Battle of Chaffin's Farm in 1864. Together they hosted weekly literary salons at 319 U Street in LeDroit Park, at the center of Washington's Black professional community.

narrative_blocks.header: Great-granddaughter of Aaron Burr
narrative_blocks.body: Her great-grandfather Aaron Burr Jr. was the third Vice President; her grandmother Louisa Charlotte Burr was his unacknowledged daughter with Mary Emmons, confirmed by DNA in 2018. She grew up in Philadelphia among Webb cousins, including her uncle Frank J. Webb — author of The Garies and Their Friends.

narrative_blocks.header: Co-founded the Colored Women's League of Washington
narrative_blocks.body: In 1892 she was one of nine co-founders of the Colored Women's League of Washington. Her LeDroit Park home at 319 U Street is now a marker on the African American Heritage Trail.

narrative_blocks.header: Oberlin pupil-teacher in the late 1850s
narrative_blocks.body: She attended Oberlin College from 1856 to 1858 as a pupil-teacher — one of the few institutions then open to Black students. She went on to teach in Philadelphia, the Institute for Colored Youth, and schools in Frederick MD and Washington DC before entering nursing in 1893.

people.research_notes: b. Apr 1849 St. Louis, City of St. Louis MO; d. Feb 1, 1908 Washington DC age ~58. Originally buried Columbian Harmony Cemetery, Washington DC; reinterred National Harmony Memorial Park, Hyattsville, Prince George's County MD c.1960. Daughter of Geoffrey George Iredell (X00624) and Elizabeth Susan Webb (HD1928). Granddaughter of Louisa Charlotte Burr (HD1914) and great-granddaughter of Aaron Burr Jr. (H00913). 8th-generation descendant of Rev. Thomas Hooker. Grew up in Philadelphia, living with Webb cousins (uncle Frank J. Webb HD1921). EDUCATION: Attended Oberlin College 1856-1858 as pupil-teacher. TEACHING: Philadelphia public schools; founding member Ladies Union Association 1863 (fundraised for sick/wounded Black soldiers during Civil War); Institute for Colored Youth 1866-1867; Roberts Vaux School 1867-1868; Frederick MD public schools; then Washington DC. NURSING PIONEER: Enrolled in first class admitted to Howard University's Freedman's Hospital School of Nursing 1893; studied under Daniel Hale Williams. Graduated 1896 with Freedman's first graduating class. SUPERINTENDENT: Appointed Feb 1901 by Dr. Austin M. Curtis as replacement nursing supervisor for Freedman's Hospital training school after previous supervisor resigned. Took national civil service examination, outscoring applicants from throughout the country. FIRST POSITION: First Black supervisor to hold the post. Confirmed by chief surgeon Dr. William A. Warfield with title "Directress of Nurses." Served as director until resignation 1904. FREEDMEN'S NURSING ASSOCIATION: Organized this professional body. EXAMINING BOARD: 1907 — selected as first Black representative on DC nurse examining board by the Graduate Nurses' Association. Term expired June 1907; not reappointed despite protests from commissioners. CO-FOUNDER: Colored Women's League of Washington 1892 (one of 9 co-founders). LITERARY SALON: She and husband Christian Fleetwood hosted weekly literary gatherings at 319 U Street NW, LeDroit Park DC. RESIDENCE SITE at 319 U Street NW is part of the African American Heritage Trail, Washington DC, marked with a historic marker. m. Sgt. Major Christian Abraham Fleetwood (X00627) Nov 16/18, 1869 Washington DC. 1 surviving daughter: Edith Fleetwood (HD1960, b.1884). Died of complications of diabetes Feb 1, 1908. "In the death of Mrs. Sara Iredell Fleetwood the nursing profession sustains a distinct loss." — Lily Kanely, President, DC Nurse Examining Board, Feb 15, 1908. b. c.1831 North Carolina (Edenton area); d. May 8, 1879 Philadelphia PA age ~48. Buried Forest Lawn Cemetery (service at St. Thomas's P.E. Church, Philadelphia). Daughter of Edith "Edy" Wood (enslaved by Captain James Wood, Hertford NC) and wealthy planter James Cathcart Johnston of Hayes Plantation, Edenton NC — grandson of Governor Samuel Johnston of North Carolina. Johnston emancipated Edy and their daughters in 1832; family settled in Philadelphia 1833. Annie's sisters: Mary Virginia (m. Robert Bridges Forten), Caroline (1827-1836), Louisa (1828-1836). CHARLOTTE FORTEN: Annie's sister Mary Virginia married abolitionist Robert Bridges Forten and died of tuberculosis 1840, leaving daughter Charlotte (the future poet Charlotte Forten Grimké). Annie and young Charlotte were raised together like sisters by grandmother Edy Wood. After Edy's death in 1846, Annie was adopted by Amy Matilda and Joseph Cassey (Philadelphia); Charlotte was raised by the Forten-Purvis family. The two were essentially raised as sisters despite the aunt-niece relation. m. John G. Webb (HD1930) Apr 19, 1854 Newburyport/Salem MA. 5 documented children; daughter Charlotte Cordelia Webb named directly for Charlotte Forten. The two families — Webbs and Fortens — moved in the same Philadelphia abolitionist circles (both connected to the Philadelphia Female Anti-Slavery Society through Hetty Emery Burr, Charlotte's Forten aunts, and the First African Episcopal Church community). | [SOURCE MOVED] WikiTree/FamilySearch [Cause revert audit]: Earlier extraction set death.cause="tuberculosis" but reverted: tuberculosis — was about her sister Mary Virginia, not Annie Edith Wood Webb.

people.research_notes: b. May 27, 1726 Fort Dummer, Vermont (some sources: Northampton MA); d. June 10, 1777 Natchez, Adams County MS age 50 (in the wilderness). Unknown grave. Son of Col. Timothy Dwight (1694-1771) and Experience King. Yale B.A. 1744. Merchant in Northampton MA. Judge of common pleas 1758-1774; selectman 1760-1764; town recorder 1760-1775; Massachusetts Legislature representative. LOYALIST: Had sworn fealty to the British government as a judge; felt he could not break his oath when the Revolution came. Thorougly patriotic in feeling but could not take up arms against the Crown. NATCHEZ COLONY: In Spring 1776 set out for Natchez with sons Sereno and Jonathan, plus his widowed sister Mrs. Eleanor Lyman and her children. Purchased "nearly the whole" Crown Grant made to Gen. Lyman at Natchez — stretching 20+ miles from the mouth of the Big Black River through present-day Natchez. Paid down purchase money at the outset; also carried "a barrel of silver coin." Plan: to found "an industrial and religious colony" — to "transplant New England to the new Southwest." Near a British fort. His health, "before high and strong, gave fatally away within a year's time to the severe strain put upon it." d. June 10, 1777 in the Mississippi wilderness — his sister Eleanor had died two months previously. The new colony was broken up by sudden capture by Spaniards; settlers fled 500 miles through forest wilderness into Georgia. His title papers for the Lyman Grant were destroyed by the Spaniards. His death was not known to his family in Northampton until a full year later. Left ~3,000 acres in Northampton plus other property. Built the Dwight House in 1751 in King Street, Northampton — next south of Jonathan Edwards's house. m. Mary Edwards (H00379) Nov 8, 1750. 13 children. | [SOURCE MOVED] WikiTree/Dwight family genealogy

Judge 1758-1774. Took oath of fealty to British crown on assuming office — held this oath binding through the Revolution and refused to revoke it.

narrative_blocks.header: A Loyalist on Christian principle
narrative_blocks.body: Timothy would not practise law, thinking it too full of temptation, and sat instead as judge of common pleas from 1758. Sworn to the Crown, he would not break that oath in the Revolution, and Northampton shunned his family for it.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought a colony at Natchez
narrative_blocks.body: In May 1776 Timothy sailed from Middletown with his sons Sereno and Jonathan and his widowed sister Eleanor Lyman, having bought most of a Crown grant at Natchez, twenty miles along the river, to plant a New England colony there.

narrative_blocks.header: Dead at Natchez, the grave unknown
narrative_blocks.body: Timothy died at Natchez in June 1777, at fifty, two months after his sister Eleanor, and no grave was ever recorded. The news took a year to reach Northampton, and his son Timothy left the Continental Army to take charge of the family.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave back a winning lottery
narrative_blocks.body: Aaron Burr sent Timothy twenty Princeton lottery tickets to sell, but Massachusetts banned them. The one Timothy kept for himself drew a blank; one of the other nineteen took the top prize. He paid for the blank and gave the rest back.

narrative_blocks.header: Two stories of his strength
narrative_blocks.body: Timothy once held a farmer's cart still from behind while the man trudged on calling to his oxen. When a Worthington braggart came to try him, he finished hoeing his row, then whirled the man over his head and pitched him over the fence.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried his wife on his palm
narrative_blocks.body: Timothy stood six foot four, and Mary Edwards was so small he carried her round the room on his open palm. Their thirteen children included eight big sons; Cecil, the smallest, stood five foot eight and weighed two hundred pounds.

narrative_blocks.header: Two of his children married Woolseys
narrative_blocks.body: Two of Timothy's children married children of his Yale roommate Benjamin Woolsey: his son Timothy took Mary Woolsey in 1777, and his daughter Elizabeth married her half-brother William in 1792.

cross_connections.notes: No other family has provided three presidents of Yale. Timothy Dwight College at Yale is named for both the 8th and 12th presidents.

notable.notable_blurb: 8th President of Yale College, 1795-1817

narrative_blocks.header: He made Yale the nation's largest college
narrative_blocks.body: As Yale's eighth president from 1795 to 1817, Timothy hired Benjamin Silliman as its first chemistry professor and grew Yale into the largest college in the country. His revival sermons helped touch off the Second Great Awakening.

narrative_blocks.header: Washington took the dedication of his epic
narrative_blocks.body: Timothy began The Conquest of Canaan at nineteen, and in March 1778 Washington wrote from Valley Forge accepting its dedication. Published in 1785, it is reckoned America's first epic, and made him a Hartford Wit with Trumbull and Barlow.

narrative_blocks.header: He argued for independence a year early
narrative_blocks.body: In July 1775, at twenty-three, Timothy urged a declaration of independence, among a handful with Franklin, Samuel Adams and Patrick Henry. As an army chaplain he wrote the song Columbia, and his sermon steadied the garrison at Fort Stanwix.

narrative_blocks.header: Two thousand miles on foot to mend
narrative_blocks.body: Timothy graduated from Yale at seventeen, took seventeen guineas from his father and never needed another. When his health broke as a tutor, he walked some two thousand miles in a year and rode three thousand more to win it back.

narrative_blocks.header: Stolen pears taught him the eighth commandment
narrative_blocks.body: As a small boy Timothy took pears from a neighbour's yard with older boys; his mother told him it broke the commandment against stealing. He carried them back in tears, and when the owner sent a basket next day he would not touch one.

narrative_blocks.header: A mission in Arkansas still bears his name
narrative_blocks.body: Timothy helped found the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions in 1810, and in 1820 its Dwight Mission to the Cherokee in Arkansas was named in his honour.

narrative_blocks.header: Day took his school, then his college
narrative_blocks.body: Jeremiah Day succeeded Timothy at the Greenfield Hill academy in 1795, the year Timothy left it for New Haven. In 1817 Day succeeded him a second time, as Yale's ninth president.

Son of Major Timothy Dwight III (X00635) and Mary Edwards (H00379). Grandson of Rev. Jonathan Edwards. Yale B.A. 1769 age 17 (said to have learned the alphabet in a single lesson; could read the Bible before age 4). Principal, Hopkins Grammar School New Haven 1769-1771; Tutor at Yale 1771-1777. Pastor, Greenfield Hill Congregational Church, Fairfield CT 1783-1795. Established academy there with equal access for women. YALE PRESIDENT 1795-1817: Led Yale to become largest higher education institution in North America. Hired professors Jeremiah Day (mathematics), James Kingsley (classics), Benjamin Silliman (chemistry/geology — "patriarch of American science"). Leader of Second Great Awakening with Lyman Beecher, Nathaniel Taylor. SLAVERY: In 1788 purchased a slave named Naomi, stating intention was for her to purchase her own freedom through faithful service. Whether she achieved this is unknown. narrative_blocks.header: A surgeon in the British army
narrative_blocks.body: Sereno was a physician and a surgeon in the British army during the Revolution, while his brother Timothy served the other side as a Continental chaplain. He was lost at sea off Halifax, Nova Scotia, on 10 October 1783, at twenty-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: Three years at Natchez, then flight
narrative_blocks.body: In May 1776 Sereno and his brother Jonathan sailed from Middletown with their father to found a colony at Natchez, where their father died in 1777. The brothers stayed about three years, until the Spanish came for the settlers.

narrative_blocks.header: Through the wilderness to Georgia
narrative_blocks.body: When the Spanish turned on the Natchez settlers, Sereno, his wife Cynthia and their daughter of about two fled with the rest overland to Georgia, through forests held by hostile Indians, living on game and roots once their compass was lost.

narrative_blocks.header: The handsomest of a handsome family
narrative_blocks.body: Madam Rhoda Dwight of Northampton called Sereno the handsomest man in all that handsome family, and he was remembered for a strong, rich, musical voice.

narrative_blocks.header: Timothy named a son for him
narrative_blocks.body: Sereno was two years younger than his brother Timothy, later president of Yale, and his closest companion at home. Timothy cherished his memory, and named his son Sereno Edwards Dwight for him.

notable.notable_blurb: Federalist editor and congressman

narrative_blocks.header: He kept the minutes of a near-secession
narrative_blocks.detail: Dwight was at the center of Connecticut Federalism for two decades — as editor of the Connecticut Mirror (its primary organ), as a member of the Connecticut State Council 1809-15, and briefly as a US Congressman (Dec 1806-Mar 1807). His 1833 History of the Hartford Convention became the primary Federalist account of that controversy. The Convention's association with disloyalty during the war's victorious conclusion largely destroyed the Federalist Party, making Dwight and his cousin Aaron Burr Jr. (H00913) emblematic of two very different careers cut short by political miscalculation. (Wikipedia)
narrative_blocks.body: As secretary of the 1814 Hartford Convention, he recorded the New England Federalists' bitter protest against the War of 1812 — a gathering so close to disunion that it helped finish the Federalist Party as a national force. He later wrote its history to defend it.

narrative_blocks.header: The first American paper printed by steam
narrative_blocks.detail: He built the Advertiser into a major New York paper over nearly two decades before the Great Fire of December 1835 destroyed its offices and presses. His father's Hartford Courant and Connecticut Mirror connections gave him a journalism apprenticeship; the Advertiser represented his mature achievement. His son William Richard Dwight later co-edited the paper with him. (Wikipedia; Dwight 1874)
narrative_blocks.body: In New York he founded the Daily Advertiser in 1817 and made it the first American newspaper printed on a steam-powered cylinder press — two thousand copies an hour. The Great Fire of 1835 destroyed its offices and presses, and he retired soon after.

narrative_blocks.header: He argued the enslaved were owed reparations
narrative_blocks.detail: Using natural law philosophy, Dwight contended that Black Americans had every right to use force to defend their natural rights — a more radical position than most white abolitionists of his generation. This oration preceded his better-known journalism career and connects him, and through him his son Theodore Dwight Jr. (HD2050), to the organized abolitionist movement that would culminate in the Civil War. His son Theodore Jr. continued this tradition, working directly with the enslaved scholar Omar ibn Said. (Theodore Dwight, "An Oration... Before the Connecticut Society," published pamphlet)
narrative_blocks.body: Before a Connecticut abolition society, he made a startling natural-law case: that enslaved people, having never consented to their bondage, stood in a state of war with their enslavers, and were owed not just immediate freedom but reparations. It was a radical position for the 1790s.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote an early book naming Sally Hemings
narrative_blocks.detail: Published decades before the abolitionist press widely addressed the Hemings relationship, Dwight's 1839 work represents one of the earliest treatments of what would remain a contested historical question for more than 150 years. His anti-Jeffersonian Federalist politics gave him both motive and audience. His cousin Aaron Burr Jr. (H00913) — Jefferson's bitter political enemy — would have relished the publication had he lived to see it. (Wikipedia; The Character of Thomas Jefferson, Hartford, 1839)
narrative_blocks.body: In an 1839 book attacking Thomas Jefferson's character as duplicitous, he made public reference to Jefferson's relationship with the enslaved Sally Hemings — among the earliest such treatments in print. It was the parting shot of a lifelong Federalist foe of Jefferson.

narrative_blocks.header: He made the Connecticut Mirror a Federalist power
narrative_blocks.body: Trained as a lawyer, he found his sharper weapon in the press — editing the Hartford Courant and then the Connecticut Mirror, which he built into the Federalist organ of the state. It began a journalism career that would carry him on to Albany and New York.

narrative_blocks.header: He read law under Jonathan Edwards's son
narrative_blocks.body: He learned his profession the old way, reading law in the New Haven office of Pierpont Edwards — the youngest son of Jonathan Edwards and one of Connecticut's foremost lawyers. Admitted to the bar in 1787, he opened practice at Haddam before settling in Hartford.

narrative_blocks.header: He and Aaron Burr were briefly law partners
narrative_blocks.body: Early in his career he shared a New York law office with his first cousin Aaron Burr, but the partnership did not hold — Dwight was a staunch Federalist, Burr a Republican, and their politics pulled them apart. The cousins would spend their lives on opposite sides.

people.research_notes:
b. Dec 15, 1764 Northampton MA; d. Jun 12, 1846 New York City age 81. Son of Major Timothy Dwight (H00914's father) and Mary Edwards Dwight (H00379). Studied law under his cousin Pierpont Edwards (H00386) of New Haven; admitted to bar 1787; practiced in Haddam CT then Hartford CT from 1791. Had a brief law partnership with his cousin Aaron Burr Jr. (H00913) in New York — their political differences ended the partnership quickly. POLITICIAN: Federalist member of Congress Dec 1, 1806 to Mar 3, 1807 (filled vacancy caused by resignation of John Cotton Smith). Member of Connecticut State Council 1809-1815. Secretary of the Hartford Convention 1814-1815. JOURNALIST: Edited the Hartford Courant and Connecticut Mirror (made the Mirror the Federalist organ of Connecticut). Moved to Albany 1815 and published the Daily Advertiser. Moved to NYC 1817 and established the New York Daily Advertiser — the first American newspaper printed on a steam-powered cylinder press (1825), capable of 2,000 issues per hour. The Great Fire of December 1835 destroyed the Advertiser's offices and presses; Dwight then retired. ABOLITIONIST: Delivered "An Oration Spoken Before the Connecticut Society, for the Promotion of Freedom and the Relief of Persons Unlawfully Holden in Bondage" — argued for immediate emancipation using natural law; contended that enslaved people, having never consented to a social contract, were in a state of war with white Americans and had the right to use force; and that they were entitled not only to freedom but to reparations. AUTHOR: History of the Hartford Convention (1833). The Character of Thomas Jefferson as Exhibited in His Own Writings (1839) — argued Jefferson's duplicity and made reference to his affair with Sally Hemings (among the earliest public treatments of this subject). Honorary A.M. from Yale 1798. Buried Green-Wood Cemetery, Brooklyn. (Wikipedia; Dwight 1874; DAB)

narrative_blocks.header: Charity work for seamen in New York
narrative_blocks.body: In her last years Fidelia lived in New York with her sons and worked beside Mrs. Divie Bethune, mother of the Rev. Dr. George Bethune, in her charities, above all for seamen. She died suddenly in January 1847, at seventy-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: Through his illnesses and money troubles
narrative_blocks.body: Fidelia was often ill herself, and her husband's health and finances failed more than once. She met each setback with courage and energy.

narrative_blocks.header: She married her cousin in 1793
narrative_blocks.body: Fidelia, daughter of Major Timothy Dwight of Northampton and Mary Edwards, married her first cousin Jonathan Edwards Porter of Hadley on 16 January 1793; their mothers were sisters.

narrative_blocks.header: He first proposed the Hartford Retreat
narrative_blocks.body: In 1812 Nathaniel sent the Connecticut Medical Society a paper on a hospital for the state's insane, and a committee was named to look into it. Eleven years later the Retreat for the Insane opened at Hartford.

narrative_blocks.header: The first school geography in America
narrative_blocks.body: Nathaniel wrote the first school geography published in the country, in questions and answers, and it sold for years. He also wrote The Great Question Answered and a history of the Signers of the Declaration.

narrative_blocks.header: Doctor, then minister, then doctor again
narrative_blocks.body: Nathaniel read medicine at Hartford under Mason Fitch Cogswell, was an army surgeon on Governor's Island and practised at Westfield, New London and Wethersfield. He preached at Westchester from 1812 to 1820, then went back to medicine.

narrative_blocks.header: Lake fever at Oswego
narrative_blocks.body: Living at Norwich, Nathaniel went on a visit to Oswego, caught the lake fever there and died in June 1831, at sixty-one.

narrative_blocks.header: He rolled a 500-pound barrel up his legs
narrative_blocks.body: At Ithaca he came on two men failing to get a potash barrel up a plank into a wagon. Stand aside, he said, and rolled it up his legs into the cart — better than five hundred pounds of it.

narrative_blocks.header: Three hundred and sixty-five pounds
narrative_blocks.body: He stood over six feet, very erect, and weighed 365 pounds with a waist six feet six inches round. He had great muscular power, a rich melodious voice, and sang better than most men.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept public houses at Manlius and Ithaca
narrative_blocks.body: He had the house at Manlius in New York from 1812 to 1817 and the one at Ithaca from 1817 to 1822. He was called industrious, temperate, moral, sincere, frank and charitable.

narrative_blocks.header: The Methodist minister's hogskin purse
narrative_blocks.body: A close man once stood a long while counting out pennies to pay him a debt. You remind me, he said, of a Methodist minister who carried a hogskin purse, and every cent came out of it with a grunt.

narrative_blocks.header: One son married a South Sea chief's daughter
narrative_blocks.body: Henry Edwin the younger went to sea as an adventurer and married a daughter of one of the chiefs of the South Sea Islands. Their daughter Agnes was still living out there in 1873.

narrative_blocks.header: His widow outlived him by thirty-five years
narrative_blocks.body: He died at Cooperstown in May 1824, forty-seven years old. Electa Centre, whom he married in 1802, lived on to die at Franklin in Louisiana in 1859, a widow the whole of that time.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven sons with the Woolsey look
narrative_blocks.body: Mary's seven sons were all large men, and all but Timothy and James had the Woolsey look. Every one stood early with the antislavery men and married late or never, and by 1874 they had left only forty-three descendants.

narrative_blocks.body: She died in New Haven at ninety-one, and Grove Street Cemetery records her as widow of Rev Timothy Dwight, president of Yale College. Eight sons carried the Dwight name on.

narrative_blocks.body: Built a New York mercantile fortune as Rogers & Woolsey, then presided over the Eagle Fire Insurance Company and held a directorship at the Merchants' Bank. Helped govern the New York Hospital and the city's Chamber of Commerce besides.

narrative_blocks.header: Kept the Bible Society's accounts for free
narrative_blocks.body: Served for years as unpaid treasurer of the American Bible Society, one of a string of institutions trusted to his hands. A miniature painted on ivory survives at the New-York Historical Society.

narrative_blocks.body: He married Elizabeth Dwight in 1792, fifteen years after his half-sister Mary had married Elizabeth’s elder brother Timothy, the future president of Yale. Their father Benjamin Woolsey had roomed with the Dwights’ father at Yale a generation before.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years a New Haven hardware merchant
narrative_blocks.body: Timothy clerked in New York from the age of thirteen, 1791 to 1801, then kept a hardware business in New Haven for more than forty years. His youngest brother Henry clerked in his store after leaving Yale.

narrative_blocks.header: He published his father's works
narrative_blocks.body: After his father died in 1817, Timothy published his father's works. He died at New Haven on 13 June 1844, at sixty-six, the same evening as the architect Ithiel Town and General Nathaniel Terry of Hartford.

narrative_blocks.header: He endowed Yale's Dwight Professorship
narrative_blocks.body: Timothy gave to found Yale's Dwight Professorship of Didactic Theology, named for his father, and pledged to make up any shortfall. He was active in every New Haven revival, in 1820–21, 1827–28 and 1842–43.

narrative_blocks.header: Pen in hand, and poetry on Sunday nights
narrative_blocks.body: Timothy read standard books and the Bible with a pen in hand, and his household recited sacred poetry to one another for hours on Sunday evenings. Near-sighted and broad of frame, he was seldom if ever sick.

narrative_blocks.header: He confessed his faith at thirty-eight
narrative_blocks.body: Timothy did not publicly confess Christ until 1816, at thirty-eight, only months before his father died. He hated false shows and shams, and said what his sense of justice required.

narrative_blocks.header: He married his fourth cousin Clarissa Strong
narrative_blocks.body: Timothy married Clarissa Strong, daughter of Governor Caleb Strong, at Northampton on 24 May 1809. They were fourth cousins, both descended from Rev. Samuel Hooker of Farmington.

narrative_blocks.header: Nineteen years as Hamilton's treasurer
narrative_blocks.body: In April 1831 Benjamin settled on eighty acres at Clinton, New York, and was at once elected treasurer of Hamilton College. He ran its finances for nineteen years, and in 1833 his brother Sereno became its president.

narrative_blocks.header: The first essay on the weak stomach
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin studied medicine in Philadelphia under Benjamin Rush and Philip Physick, and made his own dyspepsia a study: his 1811 Dissertation on Chronic Debility of the Stomach was the first essay on it in any language, reprinted in England.

narrative_blocks.header: A cold basin in his cradle
narrative_blocks.body: A nurse spilled cold water on Benjamin in his cradle and left him asthmatic for life. It kept him from the ministry, night rides drove him from medicine at Catskill in 1805, and the War of 1812 ruined his crockery trade.

narrative_blocks.header: Sunday evenings with Catskill's Black families
narrative_blocks.body: A Presbyterian elder at Catskill, Benjamin gathered the town's Black residents every Sunday evening in a nearby schoolhouse, where they came in large numbers to hear him. He taught his children to care always for the poor and forsaken.

narrative_blocks.header: There are no managers in heaven
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin despised tricks and shams and liked to say there are no managers in heaven. He taught his children never to borrow, never to gossip, that manners are matter, and that it was better to be cheated sometimes than never to trust.

narrative_blocks.header: Father of Columbia Law's founding dean
narrative_blocks.body: Of Benjamin's sons, Benjamin Woodbridge Dwight became an educator and author, and Theodore William Dwight founded the Columbia Law School and was its first dean for more than thirty years.

narrative_blocks.header: His prayer against sudden death
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin dreaded sudden death, and his family prayer asked each day to be spared it: "We know not when we lie down at night that we shall rise again … and when we rise in the morning we know not that we shall lie down but in the grave."

narrative_blocks.header: He won Noah Webster's poetry prize
narrative_blocks.body: John took his Yale degree in 1802 and won the prize Noah Webster offered for the best poem written by a student at the college. He meant to enter the ministry.

narrative_blocks.header: Dead at Hadley, visiting his betrothed
narrative_blocks.body: John was at Hadley visiting Mary Kellogg, daughter of Giles Kellogg, to whom he was engaged, when consumption killed him in July 1803, at eighteen. None of his family reached Hadley in time for the funeral, and Mary died soon after him.

narrative_blocks.header: His father rarely spoke of him without tears
narrative_blocks.body: John's death was a long grief to his father, who rarely spoke of him afterward without tears. His stone at Hadley, likely his father's words, tells a gifted youth that with all his advantages he is destined to the grave and to eternity.

narrative_blocks.header: His hardware trade followed him across four states
narrative_blocks.body: James went into hardware with his brother Timothy at New Haven, carried it to Petersburg, Virginia, for ten years, set up his own firm in New York, and ended as a merchant at Columbus, Georgia. He retired to New Haven in 1854, at seventy.

narrative_blocks.header: He read the Bible through 112 times
narrative_blocks.body: James was more at home among his books than anywhere, reading history, poetry and fiction, but above all the Scriptures, which he read through a hundred and twelve times. He joined the Presbyterian church at Petersburg in 1824.

narrative_blocks.header: Lame from birth, and six feet tall
narrative_blocks.body: James was lame from birth, yet stood six feet, weighed a hundred and ninety pounds and kept almost unbroken health. He lived to seventy-eight, an age few Dwights in trade ever reached.

narrative_blocks.header: The young of the family came to him
narrative_blocks.body: James was upright, guileless and fearless in saying what he believed, and in old age his mix of earnestness and gentleness drew the younger members of the family to his side.

narrative_blocks.header: A twin, and two wives
narrative_blocks.body: James was a twin; his brother John died at nineteen, and James outlived him by sixty years. His first wife, Aurelia Darling, died of consumption in 1813, and in 1815 he married Susan Breed of Norwich.

narrative_blocks.header: His son became president of Yale
narrative_blocks.body: James's son by Susan Breed, Timothy Dwight V, followed his grandfather and namesake as president of Yale.

narrative_blocks.header: He edited Jonathan Edwards in ten volumes
narrative_blocks.body: Between 1826 and 1833 Sereno prepared the works of his great-grandfather Jonathan Edwards for the press in ten volumes, with his own long memoir of him, and wrote a memoir of the missionary David Brainerd besides.

narrative_blocks.header: Senate chaplain, then Park Street Church
narrative_blocks.body: Licensed to preach in October 1816, Sereno was at once elected chaplain of the United States Senate. On 3 September 1817 he became pastor of Park Street Church in Boston, and held it until 1826.

narrative_blocks.header: Mercury poisoned the rest of his life
narrative_blocks.body: A slow fever in 1812 was treated with so much mercury that it poisoned Sereno's blood and left him a fiery, painful eruption of the skin for life. No remedy touched it, and it broke up one post after another.

narrative_blocks.header: The New Haven Gymnasium
narrative_blocks.body: In 1828 Sereno and his brother Henry opened the New Haven Gymnasium, a boarding school for boys staffed like a college, with Ethan A. Andrews teaching Latin. It did well, but the brothers' health closed it at the end of 1831.

narrative_blocks.header: President of Hamilton College
narrative_blocks.body: In 1833 Sereno became president of Hamilton College, where his brother Benjamin Woolsey Dwight was treasurer. His illness forced him out, and he never took another post.

narrative_blocks.header: His first sermon, his father's last
narrative_blocks.body: Sereno preached his first sermon at Center Church in New Haven in 1816, and that same afternoon, from the same pulpit, his father preached what proved to be his last.

narrative_blocks.header: A widower among his books in New York
narrative_blocks.body: Susan died in 1839, and Sereno spent his last eleven years mostly in New York, among books by day and in a boarding house at night. He died at Philadelphia in 1850, where he had gone for a water cure.

people.research_notes:
b. May 18, 1786 Greenfield Hill, Fairfield CT; d. Nov 30, 1850 New Haven CT age 64. Named "Sereno Edwards" — honoring both his uncle Sereno Edwards Dwight (H00915) and great-grandfather Rev. Jonathan Edwards. Yale B.A. 1803; tutor Yale 1806-1810; practiced law New Haven 1810-1816; licensed to preach 1816. CHAPLAIN OF THE UNITED STATES SENATE: Served Dec 16, 1816 – Dec 19, 1817. Ordained Sep 3, 1817 at Park Street Church, Boston. Pastor, Park Street Church, Boston 1817-1826 (strongly influenced hymnwriter Ray Palmer). 3RD PRESIDENT OF HAMILTON COLLEGE, Clinton NY 1833-1835. Career wrecked by accidental mercury poisoning affecting his work at Boston and Hamilton College; life after 1839 "solitary and comparatively uninfluential." PUBLICATIONS: Life of David Brainerd (1822); Life and Works of Jonathan Edwards (10 volumes, 1830) — he was a great-grandson of Edwards; The Hebrew Wife (1836). His edition of Jonathan Edwards's works is still a key primary source. m. Susan Edwards Daggett (daughter of David Daggett of New Haven) Aug 1811. Only daughter did not survive infancy. narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-two years at Portland's Third Church
narrative_blocks.body: William was settled over the Third Congregational Church of Portland, Maine, in June 1832 and held it thirty-two years, through many revivals. Bangor, East Windsor and Chicago each offered him a chair of theology; he refused them all.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the antislavery side early
narrative_blocks.body: While others halted, William took strong ground for a decided antislavery policy, and his speeches on it at Providence, Brooklyn, Boston and Hartford were long remembered by those who heard them.

narrative_blocks.header: A Philadelphia lawyer turned minister
narrative_blocks.body: William read law with Charles Chauncey in Philadelphia and practised there until 1831, when he became a Christian under the preaching of Thomas H. Skinner. Within months he was licensed to preach.

narrative_blocks.header: His eyes closed his books
narrative_blocks.body: Chronic inflammation of the eyes turned William from reading law with his brother Sereno and then from his clerkship at the Eagle Bank. He spent 1816, his father's last year, at home nursing him through his final illness.

narrative_blocks.header: Moderator at Albany in 1852
narrative_blocks.body: William's grasp of parliamentary rules made him a favourite presiding officer, and he moderated the Congregational convention at Albany in 1852. He led the Maine Missionary Society for over twenty years and was an overseer of Bowdoin.

narrative_blocks.header: He published Sereno's sermons
narrative_blocks.body: Sereno had been William's first teacher in the law, before William's eyes gave out. After Sereno died in 1850, William brought out a volume of his sermons, with a memoir of his brother's life.

narrative_blocks.header: Travels in Germany made his name
narrative_blocks.body: Four years at Göttingen gave Henry his book, Travels in Germany, which literary men noticed at once. He lectured on Europe to crowds in New York and Philadelphia, and New York University offered him a chair his health made him refuse.

narrative_blocks.header: The Microscope, an American Spectator
narrative_blocks.body: Henry founded The Microscope, a New Haven weekly of essays after Addison's Spectator, with Rev. Cornelius Tuthill and Nathaniel Chauncey. The young poet James Gates Percival wrote for it, but with no money behind it the paper soon closed.

narrative_blocks.header: The New Haven Gymnasium with Sereno
narrative_blocks.body: In 1828 Henry and his brother Sereno opened the New Haven Gymnasium, a boarding school for boys run like a college, and Henry's pupils loved him. Both brothers' health gave out, and they closed it in 1831.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-two miles, noon to noon
narrative_blocks.body: In 1824, his second year at Andover seminary, Henry walked fifty-two miles home from the White Mountains in twenty-four hours. The cold he caught made his lungs bleed, ended his training for the ministry and sent him to Germany.

narrative_blocks.header: Dead before his wedding to Miss Chauncey
narrative_blocks.body: Henry was engaged to Miss Chauncey of Philadelphia when he fell ill in the summer of 1832. After two months of hard suffering he died at New Haven on 11 August, at thirty-five.

narrative_blocks.header: William Sprague knew him at Yale
narrative_blocks.body: William B. Sprague, his Yale classmate, watched an idle, popular student become a serious scholar after graduation: "I knew him as a classmate and loved him as a friend, and rarely has there been known a more generous and noble nature."

notable.notable_blurb: 10th President of Yale College 1846-1871

narrative_blocks.header: Woolsey Hall and the golden-toed statue
narrative_blocks.detail: Woolsey Hall, completed in 1901, is one of Yale's most prominent buildings. Woolsey Street in New Haven also bears his name. The statue erected in his memory on Yale's Old Campus has acquired a golden toe from being rubbed for good luck by Yale students across more than a century. Theodore Dwight Woolsey is one of only three Yale presidents from the Hooker-descended Dwight family — the others being his uncle Timothy Dwight IV and his cousin once removed Timothy Dwight V.
narrative_blocks.body: Woolsey Hall at Yale (completed 1901) is named for him, as is Woolsey Street in New Haven. A bronze statue on Yale's Old Campus has a golden toe — rubbed for good luck by generations of students.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale 1820 valedictorian, then Greek across Europe
narrative_blocks.body: He entered Yale at thirteen and graduated valedictorian in 1820, then spent a year of legal study in Philadelphia and two years of theology at Princeton. After tutoring at Yale he went abroad to study Greek at Leipzig, Bonn, and Berlin — preparation for the Greek professorship he held from 1831 to 1846.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-five years as Yale's tenth president
narrative_blocks.body: He served as the 10th President of Yale College from 1846 to 1871. Under his tenure Yale advanced in wealth and influence, and two new departments — the Sheffield Scientific School and the School of Fine Arts — were established. He personally instructed students of history, political economy, political science, and international law.

narrative_blocks.header: His family gave Yale three of its presidents
narrative_blocks.body: He was the tenth president of Yale, but hardly the only one in his family — his uncle Timothy Dwight had been the eighth, and a younger cousin, another Timothy Dwight, would become the twelfth. Only one other man's term separated Woolsey from his uncle in the line.

narrative_blocks.header: He buried three children in a single year
narrative_blocks.body: Three of his children died in 1843 alone — Edward at nine, Elizabeth at eight, and William at three — almost certainly to one of the epidemics that swept New England towns. More followed over the years: a daughter at nine in 1854, then a young son and a grown daughter in 1861. The president of Yale outlived a houseful of his children.

narrative_blocks.header: The Greek scholar who wrote the law book
narrative_blocks.body: He edited the Gorgias and four other plays of Greek out of pure scholarship, then turned and wrote the Introduction to the Study of International Law in 1860, which was reprinted for decades. Political Science followed in 1877, and Communism and Socialism in 1880.

narrative_blocks.header: Beautiful, brilliant, and the light of her home
narrative_blocks.body: Those who knew her remembered great personal beauty, a superior intellect, and a warmth that lit the household she kept. Her children carried the memory of her presence in that home long after she was gone.

narrative_blocks.header: Married in her sick gown, expecting to die
narrative_blocks.body: So ill she coughed blood at any exertion, Sophia married the physician Benjamin Woolsey Dwight in her sick gown in 1815, expecting to live only a little while. His care pulled her through, though her health never regained its old strength.

narrative_blocks.header: Her fine mind clouded in her last years
narrative_blocks.body: Sophia's health, once robust, broke the winter before her marriage and never fully returned. In her last dozen years it failed badly, and her fine mind clouded before she died on 3 December 1861, at sixty-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: She descended from the Apostle to the Indians
narrative_blocks.body: Sophia's grandfather Rev. John Woodbridge held the South Hadley pulpit for forty-one years. His grandfather was Rev. Joseph Eliot of Guilford, son of John Eliot, who translated the Bible into the Massachusett language.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the Dwight and Strong family histories
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin traced the descendants of Elder John Strong in 1871 and of John Dwight of Dedham in 1874, two volumes each, thousands of cousins in all. Two more books, on women's higher culture and on divine providence, never reached print.
narrative_blocks.detail: After building and operating three iterations of Dwight's High School (Brooklyn 1846-1858, Clinton NY 1858-1863, New York City 1863-1867), Benjamin Woodbridge Dwight returned to Clinton NY and devoted himself to writing. His school at Brooklyn in 1846 was the first American school to offer German as a regular daily subject. As genealogical compiler he produced the definitive histories of the Dwight and Strong families — still the primary sources for both lines. He contributed to Bibliotheca Sacra, The New Englander, and the NY Genealogical Record. He briefly edited The Interior, a Presbyterian weekly in Chicago, but found it financially untenable and resigned after five months.

narrative_blocks.header: German every day at his Brooklyn school
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin opened Dwight's High School in Brooklyn in 1846 and kept it twelve years, 160 boys at its largest. Latin was the great drill, and German was a daily study there, believed to be a first for an American school.

narrative_blocks.header: Dwight's Rural High School at Clinton
narrative_blocks.body: Brooklyn drew its boys into business, not college, so in 1858 Benjamin took the school home to Clinton with David Holbrook and Henry Bristol. Four buildings were joined into one, with verandas, towers and balconies on three sides.

narrative_blocks.header: The Clinton building was lost in 1865
narrative_blocks.body: In 1863 Benjamin leased the Clinton school and opened again on Broadway. The building at Clinton burned to the ground in 1865 under a second tenant, and in 1867, after ten years of boils he hoped new work would cure, he came home to write.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded Clinton's Rural Art Association
narrative_blocks.body: In 1854 Benjamin founded the Rural Art Association at Clinton, some twenty-five of the village's leading men. It met every fortnight over tea to discuss anything but politics and theology, and took up landscape gardening and tree planting.

narrative_blocks.header: Five months as owner of The Interior
narrative_blocks.body: In September 1872 Benjamin bought The Interior, a Presbyterian weekly in Chicago, and edited it with another minister as partner. Hard times drove its costs far past what he expected, and after five months he sold it without loss.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded the church at Joliet, 1844
narrative_blocks.body: After three years tutoring at Hamilton, Benjamin went west and in 1844 founded the First Congregational Church of Joliet, Illinois, and was its pastor for two years. It is now the Central Presbyterian Church.

notable.notable_blurb: Founder of Columbia Law School

narrative_blocks.header: Columbia's law school grew around him
narrative_blocks.body: Theodore came to Columbia in 1858 as professor of municipal law and warden of its new law school. It opened with thirty-five students; by 1874 it had 425 and a weekly moot court. Albert Venn Dicey called it the best in the country.

narrative_blocks.header: Hamilton diplomas that admitted men to the bar
narrative_blocks.body: Teaching law at Hamilton from 1846, Theodore got a statute passed admitting his graduates to the bar on their diploma alone. The Supreme Court struck it down; he won it back at the Court of Appeals, and Hamilton printed his argument.

narrative_blocks.header: Dwight on Charitable Uses, 1863
narrative_blocks.body: Arguing the Rose Benevolent Association case in 1863, Theodore traced the English law of charities back to its roots and showed that the courts of chancery had always enforced charitable trusts. His research came out in two volumes.

narrative_blocks.header: The prisons, the almshouses and Elmira
narrative_blocks.body: Theodore toured the prisons of New York, nearby states and Canada with Rev. Enoch Cobb Wines and wrote the first state report on almshouses. He led the Prison Association, drafted the Elmira Reformatory law and went to Stockholm in 1878.

narrative_blocks.header: The Committee of Seventy, then the bench
narrative_blocks.body: Theodore sat in the 1867 constitutional convention and shaped its judiciary article. In 1873 he chaired the legislative committee of the reform Committee of Seventy, and that December Governor Dix named him to the Commission of Appeals.

narrative_blocks.header: New York Law School, and an unfinished will
narrative_blocks.body: After thirty-three years Theodore left Columbia in 1891 and founded New York Law School with several colleagues. He died at Clinton the next year in the act of signing his will, and with the signature unfinished the will failed.

narrative_blocks.header: What James Bryce wrote home to England
narrative_blocks.body: Theodore learned under Samuel Morse and John William Draper at Hamilton and Samuel Hitchcock at Yale. James Bryce of Oxford wrote: “Better law teaching than Mr. Dwight’s it would be hardly possible to imagine.”

b. Jul 18, 1822 Catskill, Greene County NY; d. Jun 29, 1892 Clinton, Oneida County NY age 69. Buried Sunset Hill Cemetery, Clinton NY. Son of Benjamin Woolsey Dwight (HD1967) and Sophia Woodbridge Strong (X00638). Hamilton College B.A. 1840 (Alpha Delta Phi; studied physics under Samuel F.B. Morse and John William Draper). Yale Law; admitted to bar 1845. Taught at Hamilton 1842-1858: tutor, then professor of law, history, civil polity, and political economy; Dean of Hamilton Law School 1853. FOUNDED COLUMBIA LAW SCHOOL: Accepted invitation to develop law department at Columbia 1858; sole professor until 1873; built it into Columbia Law School. Dean of Columbia Law School until 1891. FOUNDED NEW YORK LAW SCHOOL 1891: After protesting Columbia trustees' attempt to convert to the Harvard "case method," led faculty walkout and co-founded New York Law School. THE DWIGHT METHOD: Emphasized memorization of treatises, practice drills, and moot courts — competed with Langdell's Harvard case method. "Where Dwight aimed to give a sound knowledge of the law to men of average ability, Harvard's case method aimed to give as much intellectual stimulation as possible to those who would become the profession's elite." (Columbia Prof. Peter Strauss) REFORMS: Prison reform activist; collaborated on Report on Prisons and Reformatories (1867); president, New York Prison Association; delegate, International Prison Congress at Stockholm 1878; helped establish Elmira Reformatory. Counsel for five Andover professors charged with heresy 1886. Non-resident professor of law at Cornell 1869-71 and Amherst 1870-72. Republican; appointed by Gov. Dix to commission of appeals 1873. A backside column on Columbia's College Walk is dedicated to Dwight. Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_William_Dwight | [SOURCE MOVED] WikiTree/Dwight family genealogy

narrative_blocks.header: A Greenback elector in 1880
narrative_blocks.body: After the war Edward gave much of his time to financial questions, and in 1880 he was a presidential elector for the Greenback Party. His brothers Theodore and Benjamin stayed Republican.

narrative_blocks.header: One term in the Wisconsin Assembly, 1860
narrative_blocks.body: Edward was a Republican and held local offices before his election to the Wisconsin Assembly in 1860. Dane County lost a seat the next year, and he did not stand for office again for two decades.

narrative_blocks.header: A whaling schooner at fifteen
narrative_blocks.body: At fifteen Edward left home for Boston, shipped on the whaling schooner Council and spent a year on the Atlantic. Then he went to Clinton to work on a farm.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-six years a Wisconsin farmer
narrative_blocks.body: Edward married Elizabeth Foote of Clinton at twenty-one and farmed at Spring Prairie in Walworth County, then from 1857 at Brooklyn in Green County. His brothers went to Yale, Hamilton and Columbia; he farmed fifty-six years.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine children, five sons lost as infants
narrative_blocks.body: Edward and Elizabeth had nine children between 1848 and 1865, and five of their sons died as infants. He was very dark, with black hair and hazel eyes; she was tall and fair, with blue eyes and brown hair.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years in three pulpits
narrative_blocks.body: Edward took Yale in 1838 and the New Haven seminary in 1843, then held pulpits at Saco, Maine, from 1844 to 1852, Amherst from 1854 to 1860, and Hadley from 1864. He was for years a trustee of Amherst College.

narrative_blocks.header: Emily Dickinson's pastor at Amherst
narrative_blocks.body: From 1854 to 1860 Edward was pastor of Amherst's First Church, where the Dickinsons worshipped. When his wife Lucy lay ill with consumption, Emily Dickinson sent flowers to the parsonage for five-year-old Ned to lay softly on his mother's pillow.

narrative_blocks.header: Emerson lectured in his meeting house
narrative_blocks.body: In 1857 Ralph Waldo Emerson lectured in Edward's meeting house at Amherst on The Beautiful in Rural Life. The same house had seen William Stearns inaugurated as president of Amherst College in 1854, the year Edward was installed.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at Gorham in 1861
narrative_blocks.body: Edward's first wife, Lucy Waterman, a Gorham doctor's daughter he married in 1849, died of consumption in September 1861, leaving Annie, ten, and Edward, five.

narrative_blocks.header: He outlived both his wives
narrative_blocks.body: Edward died at Hadley on 12 November 1890, at seventy, having outlived both his wives, and was buried at Andover. His stone gives him more than forty years as pastor at Saco, Amherst and Hadley.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a chaplain's daughter in 1864
narrative_blocks.body: In July 1864 Edward married Elizabeth McGregor Adams, whose father, Rev. John Ripley Adams, was then a chaplain with the Army of the Potomac. She died at Hadley in 1879, leaving two daughters, Marion and Julia.

b. Jun 10, 1827 Spafford, Onondaga County NY; d. Feb 24, 1898 Evanston, Cook County IL age 70. Buried Graceland Cemetery, Chicago IL. Descended from a Quaker family from Rhode Island that fought in the Revolution. Hamilton College B.A. 1850 (studied law under Theodore William Dwight HD1989). Taught at Clinton Academy where one pupil was future President Grover Cleveland. (Famous story: schoolroom out of control, five previous teachers driven out; Anthony walked to the back, grabbed the two largest boys by their collars, "knocked their heads together and sent the lads to separate corners." Perfect order thereafter.) Admitted to bar May 7, 1851, Oswego NY. Moved to Chicago 1852. CHICAGO LAW INSTITUTE: Drove charter through Springfield 1857; served as officer for 15+ years. Library of ~7,000 volumes destroyed in Great Chicago Fire Oct 8, 1871. Anthony saved ~1,500 books by burying them in his garden the night of the fire; "about one-half of which he saved by burying them in his garden, although most of his illustrated books and encyclopedias were burned." REPUBLICAN PARTY: Active from 1856; delegate, convention nominating Farnsworth for Congress. City attorney of Chicago 1858; elected Judge, Superior Court of Chicago Nov 1880. Identified with public improvements: graded streets, water works, parks, public library. President, Illinois Bar Association. Delegate to constitutional convention. Author of historical chronicle of Indian wars and struggle for independence (inherited from his father). World traveler. m. burial.plot_notes: Graceland Cemetery, Chicago IL — family plot of 12 burials he purchased

education.notes: Graduated with high honors; afterward read law under Prof. Theodore W. Dwight.

career.notes: Admitted NY bar May 1851; one year Sterling IL; returned East July 1852 to marry Mary Dwight; settled Chicago November 1852. Published a digest of the Illinois Reports within two years (with wife's aid). Elected Chicago City Attorney then Corporation Counsel.

Until consolidation with Chicago and North Western Railway 1864. Then employed by non-consenting stockholders+bondholders in litigation to break up consolidation. Argued before Justice David Davis (US Supreme Court) and Samuel Hubbel Treat Jr. (Springfield); won for his clients. Published book on railway consolidation 1865.
Under Mayor Monroe Heath; part of the great reform movement with Thomas Hoyne.
Elected November 1880 by a large majority. Identified with many of Chicago's public improvements — graded streets, waterworks, public parks, public library, cemeteries.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the Illinois party for twenty-five years
narrative_blocks.body: Raised a Quaker, Elliott was among the Chicago men who built the Republican Party in Illinois against the Kansas-Nebraska Act, and led it for a quarter century. In 1880 he helped nominate Garfield and was elected to the Superior Court.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the state's constitutions down
narrative_blocks.body: Elliott sat in the conventions of 1862 and 1869–70, chairing the committee that framed the executive article. His 1891 Constitutional History of Illinois argued that the exclusion of slavery had been deliberate from the start.

narrative_blocks.header: He sued the railroad that employed him
narrative_blocks.body: As general solicitor of the Galena and Chicago Union, Elliott argued against its own consolidation with the Chicago and North Western for stockholders who never consented. He won before Justice David Davis, and wrote the treatise in 1865.

narrative_blocks.header: He buried his books in the garden
narrative_blocks.body: Elliott drew the Chicago Law Institute's charter, carried it to Springfield and built its library. When the 1871 fire came he saved about half of his own three thousand books by burying them in the garden.

narrative_blocks.header: One of his pupils reached the White House
narrative_blocks.body: After Hamilton, Elliott taught for a year at an academy in Clinton, where a boy named Grover Cleveland sat in his classroom, and read law under Theodore Dwight.

narrative_blocks.header: Married two Dwight sisters, thirteen years apart
narrative_blocks.body: Elliott married Mary Dwight in July 1852; she died at thirty-nine, leaving four children. In January 1865 he married her younger sister Elizabeth, who raised Mary's children until her own death at thirty-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: He read his own ancestor's tablet unknowing
narrative_blocks.body: Elliott once stood reading the memorial to Dr. Francis Anthony, the London physician who sold potable gold as a cure for everything and fought the College of Physicians over it, never knowing he descended from him.

narrative_blocks.header: He went to Andover, then straight to law
narrative_blocks.body: He finished Phillips Academy Andover in 1875 and the Union College of Law in Chicago three years later, and was admitted to the Illinois bar at twenty-two. His father was already a fixture of the Chicago bar, and he practised in the same city for the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: Chicago Fire witness at fifteen
narrative_blocks.body: He was fifteen when the Great Chicago Fire swept the city 8-11 October 1871. His father Judge Elliott Anthony saved approximately 1,500 books by burying them in his garden; most of his illustrated books and encyclopedias were burned. He carried these memories into his own 60-year Chicago legal career.

narrative_blocks.header: Two of his four daughters played championship golf
narrative_blocks.body: He married Mary P. Green at Chicago in September 1879, and they had four daughters. The eldest, Bessie, took the first three Women's Western Amateur championships and then the national title in 1903; her sister Miriam played in the same tournaments.

narrative_blocks.body: Eleven months after her sister Mary died, Elizabeth married Mary's widower Elliott Anthony at New York in January 1865 and raised Mary's children. She had none of her own, and died at Chicago in June 1870, at thirty-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: Taller than her sisters
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth stood five feet seven, taller than her sisters, with blue eyes, dark brown hair, a dignified carriage and an energetic step. She had earnest convictions and a most determined will.

narrative_blocks.header: Of indifferent health, but great vivacity
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth was never strong, yet remarkable for her vivacity and energy, and gave her unmarried years to her mother's care. Her brother Benjamin wrote: “Death was to her but going home.”
