narrative_blocks.header: He kept fishing under Indian gunfire
narrative_blocks.body: On the Sevier River in Utah, fishing behind the wagon train one evening, a bullet from an Indian gun struck the ground beside him. 'That fellow can't hit me,' he remarked coolly, 'so I will stay and get this fish before I leave' — and he did.

narrative_blocks.header: Tuberculosis took his wife at twenty-nine
narrative_blocks.body: Julia Strong Dwight bore him three sons between 1848 and 1853 — Edward Huntington (d. age 4), John Chester, and Francis Hinckley — but contracted tuberculosis and died in New Haven in December 1853 at age 29. Lyman was 37 and a widower with three children, the eldest just five.

narrative_blocks.header: Married his late wife's sister, 1855
narrative_blocks.body: On 2 January 1855 he married Mary Woolsey Dwight — Julia's older sister and two years his senior — in New Haven. She bore no children but raised Julia's surviving two sons; the marriage lasted 35 years until his June 1890 death at 73 in Hadley MA. Mary outlived him by 11 months.

narrative_blocks.header: Old Spanish Trail to California, 1841
narrative_blocks.body: At twenty-five he joined the Rowland and Workman Expedition crossing from Santa Fe NM to Los Angeles via the Old Spanish Trail — a two-month overland journey through what he described as 'this valley of the Colorado of the West has no equal on this continent for barrenness... a great burial-place of former fertility.' The party arrived at LA on 5 November 1841.

narrative_blocks.header: Source for the foundational 1849 California book
narrative_blocks.body: His detailed account of the journey became the principal source material for Thomas J. Farnham's posthumous 1849 'Life, Adventures and Travels in California.' Subsequent California maps marked 'Dr. Lyman's route' — though Farnham wrote that he feared his friend would never be persuaded to write his own book, denying him the place in border literature he deserved.

narrative_blocks.header: Apache massacre letter cited by Helen Hunt Jackson
narrative_blocks.body: In a letter published in an 1871 federal Indian report he related an account of an American massacre of Apaches in the Mexican state of Sonora during his 1840-1841 travels. Helen Hunt Jackson cited Lyman's letter in her 1885 indictment of US Indian policy 'A Century of Dishonor.'

narrative_blocks.header: Northampton mansion is now Smith's Sessions House
narrative_blocks.body: In 1859 he bought the lot across Elm Street from his existing house from Samuel Hopkins and had William Fenno Pratt design and build a new house in 1860. Sold for $13,000 to Orleana Boker in 1866; the property is now Sessions House at Smith College Northampton, still standing 165 years later.

career.role: Pioneer traveler with the Rowland and Workman Expedition
career.location: Santa Fe NM → Los Angeles via Old Spanish Trail
career.notes: Traveled with John Rowland, William Workman, Benjamin D. Wilson, Albert Toomes, Wade Hampton, William Gambel, Isaac L. Given and others; arrived LA Nov 5 1841. Spent ~18 months in CA recovering at Don Abel Stearns' home. Returned East 1843 by Wilson's account (some sources 1845). His account preserved in Farnham 1849 book.

Practiced medicine for ~15 years; by 1860 census self-reported as 'gentleman' with $22,000 wealth. By 1870 census listed as attorney with $40K real estate + $250K personal property = $290K total — dramatic wealth jump possibly from law practice, inheritance, or northwestern railroad investments mentioned in obituaries.
Returned to CA during Gold Rush, leaving wife Julia in New Haven 2 yrs after their wedding. Brief return engagement with the frontier.

Moved to SF with 2nd wife Mary + son John in mid-1870s. Sold Northampton house (now Sessions House Smith College). Listed San Rafael 1879 voter reg as 'retired physician.' Sold son John some property in greater LA area 1879. Cathedral Hill SF 1882. Returned to Northampton after Mary's death mid-1880s.

narrative_blocks.header: Harvard Medical 1872, California physician
narrative_blocks.body: After two years at Yale Scientific Department he graduated Harvard Medical School in 1872 — the year his father's wealth peaked at $290,000. He followed his father to California in the mid-1870s and practiced medicine in San Francisco and across the bay at San Rafael for roughly thirty years.

narrative_blocks.header: Valvular heart disease in Chicago, 1904
narrative_blocks.body: He died at the German-American Hospital in Chicago on 29 March 1904 at age 52 — after a six-month illness of valvular heart disease. He was buried at Bridge Street Cemetery Northampton MA with his parents and brothers — the last of the Lyman family's New Haven generation to die.

narrative_blocks.header: Died of yellow fever in Brazil at eighteen
narrative_blocks.body: Francis Hinckley Lyman was born January 19, 1853 in Chicago while his family was traveling — his mother Julia died in Jamaica the same year. He died July 20, 1871 of yellow fever in Brazil at eighteen: both he and his mother died young in tropical places, each of them thousands of miles from the New Haven family home.

narrative_blocks.body: Mary's eldest, Willie, learned a fifty-line Goethe ballad from his father after two hearings, and asked why God had burned Sodom's houses when they were not wicked. Diphtheria took him at five, in August 1859.

narrative_blocks.header: Her family added an 'a' to the name
narrative_blocks.body: She was born Mary Bond Olmsted, but after the family moved to Clinton, New York, her father took to spelling the surname 'Olmstead,' with an added 'a,' to match other families in the area. Both spellings follow her through the records.

narrative_blocks.header: A Dwight before she married one
narrative_blocks.body: Mary's grandmother was Charlotte Dwight of Somers, so she carried the name before she married Theodore. On her mother's side she came down from Dr. Solomon Bond of Enfield and Sarah Hinckley.

narrative_blocks.header: She married the founder of Columbia's law school
narrative_blocks.body: In 1847 she married Theodore William Dwight, then a young Hamilton College law professor who would go on to found Columbia Law School. She bore him three children and kept his household through his decades at the head of the school.

narrative_blocks.header: A Goethe ballad after two hearings
narrative_blocks.body: Willie learned a fifty-line fairy ballad of Goethe's almost whole after his father recited it once, and perfectly after a second time. He loved horses, flowers, poetry and music.

narrative_blocks.header: Why did God burn the houses?
narrative_blocks.body: Told of the destruction of Sodom, Willie asked why God had burned the houses, which were not wicked. He would have piled up the wicked people and burned them, and left the houses standing.

narrative_blocks.header: Diphtheria at five, in August 1859
narrative_blocks.body: Willie died of diphtheria in August 1859, a little past five. His favourite lines were the close of the Goethe ballad: “They rattled and prattled for ever so long, / And then disappeared in a chorus of song.”

BEAR MOUNTAIN STATE PARK: As part-time resident of Cornwall-on-the-Hudson NY, enlisted support of Edward H. and Mary Harriman, Lyman Abbott, Henry Fairfield Osborn, George Kunz, Herbert Satterlee, and Ernest Stillman to petition for national park status for Hudson River Highlands and Palisades. Federal government rejected it; they lobbied New York State — which enacted legislation in 1909 establishing Bear Mountain State Park. narrative_blocks.header: Organized creation of Bear Mountain State Park, 1909
narrative_blocks.body: As a part-time Cornwall-on-the-Hudson resident he enlisted Edward H. and Mary Harriman, Lyman Abbott, Henry Fairfield Osborn, George Kunz, Herbert Satterlee, and Ernest Stillman to petition for federal Hudson Highlands national-park status. When that failed they shifted to New York State and won 1909 legislation creating Bear Mountain State Park.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventeen years on Palisades Park Commission
narrative_blocks.body: He was appointed to the Palisades Interstate Park Commission in 1913 and reappointed for five-year terms in 1915, 1925, and 1930. During his terms Bear Mountain was extended by nearly 50,000 acres and Storm King Highway was constructed largely from a land grant of Ernest G. Stillman.

narrative_blocks.header: Manhattan obstetrician with five hospital appointments
narrative_blocks.body: After his 1875 MD from the College of Physicians and Surgeons (now Columbia) he served more than twenty years in NYC general practice and as professor at the same school. He was visiting or consulting physician at New York Hospital, the Nursery and Child's Hospital, Sloane Maternity Hospital, and the New York Infant Asylum.

THE ACOMA (SP-1228): Designed his own wooden-hulled twin-screw motor boat and submitted the plans to the U.S. Government. The Acoma was built by Gas Engine & Power Co. & Charles L. Seabury Co., Morris Heights NY in 1917. Partridge donated the boat to the Navy on free lease Sep 25, 1917. Commissioned Oct 18, 1917; assigned to Second Naval District. Patrolled Newport RI, then New Bedford CT through end of WWI. Specs: 59'8" length, 11'8" beam, 21.9 knots cruising speed, complement 9, armed with 1 1-pounder and 1 machine gun. Returned to Partridge on Nov 25, 1918 (two weeks after the Armistice). He paid for construction of the craft; it was returned to his ownership after the Armistice. Served as Boatswains Mate First Class; eventually promoted to Ensign (Apr 1919). Later lived in Pasadena CA; died Riverside CA. narrative_blocks.header: Designed his own twin-screw motor boat, 1917
narrative_blocks.body: He designed a 59-foot wooden-hulled twin-screw motor boat himself and submitted the plans to the U. S. Government.

narrative_blocks.header: Donated his boat to Navy on free lease
narrative_blocks.body: He donated the Acoma to the Navy on free lease 25 September 1917; she was commissioned 18 October 1917 as USS Acoma SP-1228 and assigned to the Second Naval District, armed with one 1-pounder gun and one machine gun. She patrolled Newport RI and then New Bedford CT through the end of WWI.

narrative_blocks.header: Returned two weeks after Armistice, retained boat
narrative_blocks.body: The Acoma was returned to him on 25 November 1918 — two weeks after the Armistice — since he had funded her construction. He served as Boatswain's Mate First Class during the war and was promoted to Ensign in April 1919. He later lived in Pasadena CA and died in Riverside CA at eighty-six.

narrative_blocks.header: He served aboard under another man's command
narrative_blocks.body: He shipped as a boatswain's mate first class on the boat he had drawn and paid for, with Chief Boatswain's Mate Sterrett in command. He was made an ensign in April 1919, after it was over.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-nine feet, one pounder, nine men
narrative_blocks.body: The Acoma ran twenty-one knots cruising on twin screws, carried a one-pounder and a machine gun, and was worked by a crew of nine. She patrolled off Newport, then New Bedford, then Cape Cod.

narrative_blocks.header: His father organised Bear Mountain
narrative_blocks.body: Dr. Edward Lasell Partridge, a Manhattan obstetrician, spent seventeen years on the Palisades Park Commission and got Bear Mountain State Park made in 1909. The son gave the government a boat instead.

people.research_notes: b. Sep 14, 1891 Philadelphia PA; d. Mar 20, 1973 Mount Kisco, Westchester County NY age 81. Buried Hope Cemetery, Kennebunk ME. Princeton B.S. 1914; studied at U. of Freiburg; M.D. U. of Pennsylvania 1918. ROCKEFELLER UNIVERSITY: Associated since 1919; professor 1954; retired 1962. Began in laboratory of Dr. Peyton Rous; researched liver disease, gall bladder physiology, bile formation. Over 10 years studied physiology of the lymphatic system. With Dr. Stephen Hudack, demonstrated antibodies to bacteria and viruses are first formed in draining lymph nodes — foundational discovery for all subsequent antibody research. Pioneered research methods for antibody formation, chemical composition, and disease combat. WWII civilian service: Office of Scientific Research and Development; National Defense Research Committee. narrative_blocks.header: He found where the body builds its antibodies
narrative_blocks.body: With Stephen Hudack at the Rockefeller, Philip showed that antibodies to bacteria and viruses are first formed in the draining lymph nodes. Everything he studied for the rest of his career grew out of that finding.

narrative_blocks.header: Blue dye made the lymphatics visible
narrative_blocks.body: Philip injected blue dye into the skin, his own among it, and for the first time made the lymph capillaries of living people visible, rising up the limbs as blue streamers. Surgeons later used the method to trace cancer.

narrative_blocks.header: A gallbladder finding became a surgeon's test
narrative_blocks.body: In Peyton Rous's laboratory from 1919, Philip found that a healthy gallbladder concentrates the liver's bile and a diseased one does not. Surgeons built the dye test for gallstones on it.

narrative_blocks.header: To the lab in a Maine woodsman's clothes
narrative_blocks.body: Philip was small, witty and cordial, played violin and accordion for his guests, and walked to the Rockefeller in snowstorms dressed as a Maine woodsman. He met his friend Walther Goebel coming off the squash court.

narrative_blocks.header: A historian's son with a sailboat at nine
narrative_blocks.body: Philip's father was the historian John Bach McMaster. He rode out on bicycles with him and the biologist Edwin Conklin to collect specimens, spent summers at Kennebunkport, and had his first sailboat at nine.

narrative_blocks.header: Five war years on gases and burns
narrative_blocks.body: In the Second World War Philip worked for the Office of Scientific Research and Development on tests for war gases and treatments for blister burns. It kept him five years from the research he loved.

narrative_blocks.header: What his friends wired his widow
narrative_blocks.body: Philip's son and namesake carried the work on at the National Institutes of Health. When Philip died in 1973, friends wired his widow that he was “one of those few who showed that it was good to be human and alive.”

narrative_blocks.header: He scattered the asylum into cottages
narrative_blocks.body: As superintendent at Kankakee from 1879, Richard built the hospital on the cottage plan, patients housed in small homes rather than one vast asylum. The plan shaped Manteno State Hospital after it. He resigned in a political storm in 1893.

narrative_blocks.header: A German army hospital at Kassel, 1870
narrative_blocks.body: Fresh from his Michigan medical degree and a year at the Brooklyn City Hospital, Richard went into the Prussian service as a volunteer surgeon when the Franco-Prussian War began, and had charge of a military hospital at Kassel.

narrative_blocks.header: He edited the American Journal of Insanity
narrative_blocks.body: Richard edited the journal from 1894 to 1897, before it became the American Journal of Psychiatry, and ran the Milwaukee Sanitarium at Wauwatosa until 1914. His memoir of pioneering American psychiatry appeared in 1936.

narrative_blocks.header: He composed patriotic anthems
narrative_blocks.body: Richard was an accomplished musician and composed a number of patriotic anthems. He wrote verses too, and corresponded with Dorothea Dix, Jane Addams and Havelock Ellis.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-two years a widower
narrative_blocks.body: His wife Lillian died at Kankakee in November 1880, just after the birth of their fourth child, seven years into their marriage. Richard outlived her by fifty-two years.

narrative_blocks.header: A journey to El Paso at eighty-seven
narrative_blocks.body: In June 1933 Richard travelled with a daughter from La Cañada to a son's sickbed at El Paso, had a stroke, and died on 4 August. His old journal said he went “booted and spurred.”

narrative_blocks.header: She married Aaron Burr's uncle and confidant
narrative_blocks.body: Frances married Pierpont Edwards, youngest son of Jonathan Edwards and the uncle of Aaron Burr. A Yale-trained lawyer and federal judge, Pierpont was the orphaned Burr's lifelong advisor and legal associate.

narrative_blocks.header: A brother's will, addressed to the Twelve Apostles
narrative_blocks.body: Her brother David Ogden, a young law student, left a famously eccentric 1789 will, opening with an invocation to the saints and angels, directing four sturdy youth to bear his mahogany coffin, and leaving his epitaph to his brother-in-law Pierpont Edwards. Family tradition blamed his decline on a hopeless love.

narrative_blocks.header: The uncle New Jersey burned in effigy
narrative_blocks.body: Frances's uncle Robert Ogden, Speaker of the New Jersey Assembly, refused to sign the 1765 Stamp Act Congress petitions and was burned in effigy for it. Her father, Moses Ogden, was his younger brother in the same Elizabethtown family.

people.research_notes: b. Aug 23, 1777 New Haven CT; d. Feb 22, 1813 Warren, Trumbull County OH age 35. Buried Old Mahoning Cemetery, Warren, Trumbull County OH. Son of Pierpont Edwards (H00386) and Frances Ogden (X00654). Grandson of Jonathan Edwards. Died during the War of 1812 at Warren, Ohio. His burial at Old Mahoning Cemetery places him in the earliest settlement of the Western Reserve in northeast Ohio. Stub.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: His 1807 house — the oldest remaining home in Warren, Ohio, now a museum.

narrative_blocks.header: Among the first lawyers on the Western Reserve
narrative_blocks.body: Sent west in 1799 to manage his father's lands in the Connecticut Western Reserve, he settled in Trumbull County, built its first sawmill, and served as county Recorder from 1800 until his death. He was among the very first lawyers to practice on the Reserve.

narrative_blocks.header: Elected to Congress, he died en route
narrative_blocks.body: In 1812 he became the first man from the Western Reserve elected to the United States Congress. Traveling to inspect his lands that winter, he caught a fever on the road and died in February 1813, never reaching Washington.

narrative_blocks.header: He marched his regiment north after Hull's surrender
narrative_blocks.body: Commissioned a colonel of Ohio militia, he led part of his regiment to Cleveland in 1812 after General Hull's surrender at Detroit left the frontier exposed. The threat passed and he returned to Warren before his election to Congress that fall.

narrative_blocks.header: Named for the hero of Bennington
narrative_blocks.body: His father gave him the name of his old friend General John Stark, victor at the Battle of Bennington, fought just weeks before the boy was born in 1777.

narrative_blocks.header: Many county records survive in his wife's hand
narrative_blocks.body: His wife, Louisa Maria Morris, was a voracious reader who worked through his entire law library, Blackstone and all. Many of Trumbull County's earliest records are said to be in her handwriting rather than his.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a cousin from his Edwards line
narrative_blocks.body: Louisa Maria Morris was a daughter of his first cousin Mary Dwight. Both he and Mary were grandchildren of the theologian Jonathan Edwards, so in marrying Louisa he wed within his own family's Edwards branch.

notable.notable_blurb: Democratic governor of Connecticut and U.S. senator

narrative_blocks.header: Elected governor, ousted, and elected again
narrative_blocks.body: The General Assembly made Henry governor of Connecticut in 1833. He lost the office in 1834 to Samuel Foot, who had also studied law at Litchfield, won it back in 1835, and held it until 1838, when his party passed him over and he left public life.

narrative_blocks.header: He sent a poet to survey the rocks
narrative_blocks.body: In 1835 Henry's government paid for a geological survey of Connecticut, and the state geologist he chose was the poet James Gates Percival. Percival spent seven years at it, crossing the state in lines two miles apart.

narrative_blocks.header: He wanted the vote without property
narrative_blocks.body: In a message to the General Assembly, Governor Edwards called for an end to the property qualification for voting, for more government control over large business interests, and for stricter laws on joint-stock companies.

narrative_blocks.header: Lieutenant governor-elect, denied the seat
narrative_blocks.body: Henry was elected lieutenant governor of Connecticut in 1832, but a divided General Assembly kept him out of the office. A year later the same Assembly chose him for governor.

narrative_blocks.header: Clerk in 1818, senator by 1823
narrative_blocks.body: Henry went into politics in 1818 as clerk of the Connecticut House and was in Congress the next year, serving two terms. When Senator Elijah Boardman died in 1823, Governor Oliver Wolcott Jr. appointed him to the seat, and he held it until 1827.

narrative_blocks.header: Princeton at seventeen, then Litchfield
narrative_blocks.body: Henry graduated from Princeton in 1797, at seventeen, and read law at Litchfield under Tapping Reeve, the husband of his cousin Sally Burr. He married Lydia Miller of New Haven on 4 October 1801 and practised law in the town.

narrative_blocks.header: A judge, a consul and a doctor's wife
narrative_blocks.body: Of Henry and Lydia's seven children, two died as small boys. Henry Pierrepont became a justice of the New York Supreme Court, Alfred went to the Philippines as U.S. consul, and Henrietta married Dr. Worthington Hooker of the Yale medical school.

orbit_connections.name: Samuel F.B. Morse
orbit_connections.relationship: Painter of Eli Whitney's portrait (1822) — five years after Whitney's marriage to Henrietta Frances Edwards (HD2046), seven years before Morse's telegraph patent
orbit_connections.notes:
Samuel Finley Breese Morse (1791-1872) painted the definitive portrait of Eli Whitney in 1822, three years before Whitney's death. Oil on canvas, 35 7/8 × 27 3/4 in. Yale Art Gallery accession 1827.1 — accession number 1827.1 suggests this is among the very first formally catalogued works in the Yale Art Gallery collection. Yale Art Gallery: https://artgallery.yale.edu/collections/objects/31 

GIFT: Donated to Yale by George Hoadley (B.A. 1801) — the 4th Mayor of New Haven, husband of Mary Ann Woolsey Hoadley (HD2075, a Hooker descendant), and the man whose Eagle Bank presidency had nearly bankrupted Yale in 1825. The gift came in 1827 — two years after Whitney's death, two years after the bank collapse. Whether it was redemptive gesture or simply the natural action of New Haven's social elite, the Hooker family network is woven through every thread: Whitney married a Hooker descendant (HD2046); Hoadley married a Hooker descendant (HD2075); Hoadley donated the portrait to Yale, whose presidency was held by Henrietta's first cousin Timothy Dwight IV (H00914). 

Morse also taught at NYU; Theodore William Dwight (HD1989), Columbia Law School founder, studied under Morse — connecting the Hooker tree to Morse through two separate branches. (Yale Art Gallery; Wikipedia; NYC Digital Collections)

narrative_blocks.header: She gave Whitneyville its church
narrative_blocks.body: In 1834, nine years a widow, Henrietta gave land and money to found the Congregational church at Whitneyville, the armory village her husband had built on the Mill River north of New Haven.

narrative_blocks.header: Her chintz quilt survives in a museum
narrative_blocks.body: A chintz quilt she pieced around 1850 still survives, its glaze bright, at the New Haven Colony Historical Society. Quilt historians have gone back and forth over whether she copied a printed Godey's Lady's Book pattern or whether the magazine instead recorded hers.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-five years a widow
narrative_blocks.body: Henrietta was thirty-eight when her husband died in January 1825, eight years into the marriage, with three children under ten; their youngest, Susan, had died in 1823. She outlived him by forty-five years and died in New Haven in 1870.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father signed the armory's deed
narrative_blocks.body: Henrietta's father, Pierpont Edwards, the New Haven judge and congressman, signed the 1798 deed to the armory site and backed the venture. Her marriage to Eli Whitney in January 1817, at thirty, made the inventor one of New Haven's first families.

narrative_blocks.header: Aaron Burr and Timothy Dwight were her cousins
narrative_blocks.body: Henrietta was a granddaughter of Jonathan Edwards, and her first cousins included Aaron Burr, the vice president, and Timothy Dwight, president of Yale.

people.research_notes: b. Dec 8, 1765 Westborough MA; d. Jan 8, 1825 New Haven CT age 59. Buried Grove Street Cemetery, New Haven CT. Son of Eli Whitney Sr. (1741-1807) and Elizabeth Fay (1740-1777). Yale B.A. 1792, Phi Beta Kappa — graduated in three years. Technically "Eli Whitney Jr." during his lifetime (his son Eli Whitney III was known as "Eli Whitney Jr." after his death). COTTON GIN (1793): Invented at Mulberry Grove plantation, Georgia while visiting Catherine Littlefield Greene, widow of General Nathanael Greene. A single gin could clean 55 lbs of cotton daily vs. 1 lb by hand. Patent granted Mar 14, 1794. Spent years in ruinous patent litigation. INTERCHANGEABLE PARTS: Turned to US government musket contracts after gin losses. Pioneered machine manufacturing of standardized, interchangeable parts — a system that shaped the Union's industrial advantage in the Civil War. Fulfilled a contract for 10,000 musket kits. YALE CONNECTIONS: Built his arms business through Yale alumni network — Oliver Wolcott Jr. (Treasury Secretary, Yale class of 1778) and James Hillhouse (New Haven developer). Portrait painted by Samuel F.B. Morse (1822) — now at Yale. His son Eli Whitney III (1820-1895) later took over Whitney Armory and built New Haven's waterworks. Whitney Armory complex (Hamden CT) partially preserved; Eli Whitney Museum at site. m. Henrietta Frances Edwards (HD2046) Jan 6, 1817. 4 children. Died of prostate cancer; reportedly designed medical devices to ease his pain. (Wikipedia; FindAGrave)

narrative_blocks.header: Ten days in Georgia, and the cotton gin
narrative_blocks.body: When a Georgia tutoring post fell through in 1793, Eli stayed at Catherine Greene's Mulberry Grove, where planters despaired of short-staple cotton: a day's labor picked the seed from a pound. He had a model in ten days and a finished gin in six months.

narrative_blocks.header: He had never made a gun
narrative_blocks.body: Eli had never made a gun when he signed in 1798 for ten thousand muskets. He built machines before muskets at a Mill River grist mill and finished in 1809; his 1801 show for Adams and Jefferson, locks built from parts picked at random, is now thought staged.

narrative_blocks.header: A nail forge at fourteen
narrative_blocks.body: When the Revolution cut off imported nails, fourteen-year-old Eli set up a forge in his father's Westborough workshop and sold them at a profit. Later he made hatpins and walking canes to help pay his way through Yale.

narrative_blocks.header: He mended the Yale president's orrery
narrative_blocks.body: Eli taught school to save for Yale and entered at twenty-three, older than his classmates. When President Ezra Stiles's orrery arrived damaged from London, Eli spent a week making the tools and set it right; he graduated Phi Beta Kappa in 1792, meaning to read law.

narrative_blocks.header: His nephews ran the armory after him
narrative_blocks.body: In 1801 his ten-year-old nephew Philos Blake wrote home that the works had a drilling machine, a boring machine, a trip-hammer shop and five hundred guns done. Philos and his brother Eli Whitney Blake ran the Whitneyville armory from their uncle's death in 1825 until 1835.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at fifty-one, to Henrietta Edwards
narrative_blocks.body: Eli married Henrietta Edwards in January 1817, at fifty-one; her father had signed the deed to the armory site. They lost their youngest, Susan, in 1823, and Eli died of prostate cancer in 1825, after building devices to ease his pain.

narrative_blocks.header: The gin made the South rich, not him
narrative_blocks.body: Planters copied the gin faster than Eli and Phineas Miller could build it, and the 1794 patent brought years of lawsuits while the fortune went to a cotton South built on slavery. He left the South in 1804. In his words, “An invention can be so valuable as to be worthless to the inventor.”

narrative_blocks.body: Henry began practising law in New York City about 1831, and from 1847 sat for seven years as a justice of the state Supreme Court. In 1854 he served on the Court of Appeals, New York's highest court. He died in the city on 27 February 1855, at forty-six, unmarried.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventeen years in Manila
narrative_blocks.body: Alfred was trading at Manila as a young man; a passenger list has him landing at New York from Manila in March 1831, at twenty. He spent some seventeen years in the Philippines as a sugar importer and was twice U.S. consul there, the second time until he resigned in December 1853.

narrative_blocks.header: Cairo between two steamers
narrative_blocks.body: Sailing home from Manila in January 1854, Alfred told a fellow passenger, the English clergyman Thomas Bowles, that Manila was a fine town on a very beautiful island. At Cairo in February he had missed Thebes, too late in the season, but went out somewhere every day between steamers.

narrative_blocks.header: A wife for eight months
narrative_blocks.body: Back in New York, Alfred married Mary Griswold, daughter of Nathaniel and Ann Griswold, on 16 May 1856, when he was forty-five and she thirty-four. He died in Manhattan on 9 January 1857, eight months later, and Mary lived on as his widow for nearly forty years.

people.research_notes: b. Nov 2, 1760 Scarsdale, Westchester County NY; d. Dec 29, 1825 Springfield, Windsor VT. Buried Forest Hill Cemetery, Charlestown, New Hampshire (next to second wife Theoda). Son of Richard Morris (Chief Justice, NY Supreme Court 1779-1790) and Sarah Ludlow. FAMILY: Nephew of General Lewis Morris (last lord of Manor of Morrisania, Continental Congress delegate who SIGNED THE DECLARATION OF INDEPENDENCE) and nephew of Gouverneur Morris (Founding Father, "Penman of the Constitution"). REVOLUTIONARY WAR: Served as aide to General Philip Schuyler and General George Clinton (future VP). Secretary of Foreign Affairs 1781-1783. VERMONT: Moved to Springfield VT Republic 1786; established as businessman/landowner/politician. First US Marshal of the District of Vermont — appointed by President George Washington Mar 4, 1791. Windsor County court clerk 1789-1796; judge until 1801. Brigadier General, Vermont State Militia 1793; Major General First Division 1795-1817. Vermont House of Representatives 1795-1797, 1803-1808; Speaker. US REPRESENTATIVE from Vermont (Federalist) 5th-7th Congresses, May 22, 1797 to Mar 3, 1803. MARRIAGES: (1) Mary Dwight (H00921) Dec 2, 1786 — marriage proved unsuccessful; "Morris left her soon after their marriage" though daughter Louisa Maria was born. (2) Theodosia "Theoda" Olcott 1790s-1800; (3) Ellen Hunt c.1802 (five children). Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_R._Morris

narrative_blocks.header: Washington made him Vermont's first US Marshal
narrative_blocks.body: President Washington appointed Morris the first United States Marshal for the District of Vermont in 1791, soon after the republic joined the union. He went on to serve three terms in Congress as a Federalist.

narrative_blocks.header: He served Schuyler and Clinton in the Revolution
narrative_blocks.body: During the Revolutionary War, Morris was an aide to Generals Philip Schuyler and George Clinton, and worked in the office of Foreign Affairs from 1781 to 1783. He later rose to major general of the Vermont militia.

narrative_blocks.header: He was nephew to two Founding Fathers
narrative_blocks.body: Morris was a nephew of Lewis Morris, who signed the Declaration of Independence, and of Gouverneur Morris, the penman of the Constitution. His father was chief justice of New York's supreme court.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped bring Vermont into the union
narrative_blocks.body: Settling in Springfield while Vermont was still an independent republic, he served as secretary of its 1793 constitutional convention and sat in the convention that ratified the federal Constitution. He built a career there as landowner, judge, and Federalist politician.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter married her mother's first cousin
narrative_blocks.body: His wife, Mary Dwight, was a granddaughter of the theologian Jonathan Edwards. In 1807 their daughter Louisa married John Stark Edwards, Mary's first cousin.

career.notes: First U.S. Marshal for Vermont, appointed by President Washington.
Federalist; 5th-7th Congresses.

people.research_notes: b. Apr 13, 1787 Springfield, Windsor County VT; d. Dec 24, 1866 Youngstown, Mahoning County OH age 79. Daughter of Lewis Richard Morris (X00658, US Representative from Vermont, nephew of Declaration signer Lewis Morris) and Mary Dwight (H00921). 6th-generation Hooker descendant. Stub.

narrative_blocks.header: She spun, farmed, and kept the county's records
narrative_blocks.body: On the raw Ohio frontier she made the family's clothing, became an expert wool-spinner, and reared three children largely alone while her husband rode the circuit. She also read through his entire law library and wrote out many of Trumbull County's earliest records in her own hand.

narrative_blocks.header: She married her mother's first cousin
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband, John Stark Edwards, was first cousin to her mother, Mary Dwight; both families descended from Jonathan Edwards. The Edwards household welcomed her warmly, one of his sisters calling her "an inestimable jewel."

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed young, she lost her two oldest sons
narrative_blocks.body: John Stark Edwards died in 1813, and within a year she married Robert Montgomery. Soon after, her two eldest boys died, leaving only her youngest Edwards son.

narrative_blocks.header: The young of Youngstown called her Aunt Louisa
narrative_blocks.body: On a 440-acre farm near Youngstown she raised a second family, built a property worth thousands, and was said to be the first in town to make carpets. Her kindness made her widely loved, and the young called her "Aunt Louisa."

people.research_notes: b. Nov 17/18, 1765 Middletown CT; d. Apr 2, 1846 New York City age 80. Daughter of Richard Alsop (1726-1776) and Mary Wright Alsop (1740-1829). Sister of Richard Alsop (1761-1815), Connecticut author. m. Theodore Dwight Sep 9, 1792. Benjamin Woodbridge Dwight described her as "a lady of small but full figure, intelligent and sprightly... always very fond of belles lettres and poetry." Buried Green-Wood Cemetery, Brooklyn. (Dwight 1874, p.230)

narrative_blocks.header: Her brother was one of the Hartford Wits
narrative_blocks.body: Abigail's brother Richard Alsop, the Middletown poet, was one of the Hartford Wits, who mocked bad newspaper writing in the verses of the Echo. She married the editor Theodore Dwight in 1792.

narrative_blocks.header: Small in figure, sprightly, and fond of poetry
narrative_blocks.body: A family chronicler remembered her as a small but full-figured woman, intelligent and sprightly, with superior early advantages and a lasting love of belles lettres and poetry. Culture and taste ran deep in her.

notable.notable_blurb: Author, ethnologist, and reformer

narrative_blocks.header: He founded a society to prove Africa's learning
narrative_blocks.detail: The Society's founding mission aligned with abolitionist goals: if Africa could be shown to be a continent of sophisticated literate culture, the racist premises of pro-slavery ideology would collapse. Dwight worked directly with the enslaved West African scholar Omar ibn Said — one of a handful of African intellectuals whose writing survived American slavery — to gather and translate his Arabic-language autobiography. (INST033; Wikipedia; flashbak.com via FindAGrave)
narrative_blocks.body: He co-founded the American Ethnological Society in 1842 and used it to demonstrate that African peoples had deep literary and religious traditions long before European colonization. It was scholarship in the service of his abolitionism.

narrative_blocks.header: He coaxed a slave narrative written in Arabic
narrative_blocks.detail: Omar ibn Said had been brought from Futa Toro (in present-day Senegal) to South Carolina in 1807. A practicing Muslim and scholar, he wrote Arabic on the walls of his prison cell in Fayetteville NC, catching the attention of abolitionists. Dwight, as founder of the American Ethnological Society and member of the New York Colonization Society, wanted the autobiography to reach a white American audience to undermine slavery's premise. The 15-page handwritten document remains a landmark of early American literature. (Wikipedia; "The Life of Omar ibn Said," flashbak.com 2019)
narrative_blocks.body: He persuaded the enslaved West African scholar Omar ibn Said to set down his autobiography in Arabic — the only known slave narrative written in that language in America. Dwight meant it to refute the claim that the enslaved were unlettered.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote America's second travel guidebook
narrative_blocks.detail: He also compiled and published the travelogues of his uncle Timothy Dwight IV (H00914) in 1821. His work as a travel writer, like his abolitionism and his interest in foreign languages and international politics, reflected a restless engagement with the world beyond New England that contrasted sharply with his father's Federalist parochialism. He is described by the American National Biography as "undeniably one of America's foremost spokespersons for creating a national identity founded on cultural and geographical literacies." Died jumping off a departing train near Brooklyn, Oct 16, 1866. (Wikipedia; ANB)
narrative_blocks.body: His Northern Traveller (1825) was the second tourist guidebook published in the United States, steering readers to Niagara, Quebec and the Springs through six editions to 1841; he had already brought his uncle Timothy Dwight's travels to print. Theodosia Burr Alston had honeymooned at those falls in 1801, before anyone printed the way.

narrative_blocks.header: Garibaldi trusted him with his own memoirs
narrative_blocks.body: A tireless friend to Europe's political exiles, he threw himself into the cause of Italian unification — and Giuseppe Garibaldi entrusted him with his autobiography to publish in America. He founded a Philo-Italian Society to press the cause.

narrative_blocks.header: He shipped settlers west to keep Kansas free
narrative_blocks.body: As an extension of his abolitionism, he worked in the 1850s to settle the Kansas frontier with free-soilers; he and a partner persuaded some three thousand people to emigrate and hold the territory against slavery.

narrative_blocks.header: A fatal leap from a moving train
narrative_blocks.body: In 1866, after seeing his daughter onto a southbound train at Jersey City, he found the door sealed and the train already moving, and jumped — landing badly hurt. She had it stopped and found him alive; he reached home, but died that night.

narrative_blocks.header: He found the boy’s subject at last
narrative_blocks.body: He had the direction of John Pitkin Norton's studies one winter and went through the whole range of learning without catching him, until he named mineralogy. Norton took Yale's first chair in agricultural chemistry.

Published The Northern Traveller (1825) — the second tourist guidebook ever published in the United States; updated regularly through 1841. Founder of the American Ethnological Society (INST033). ABOLITIONIST: Worked with the enslaved West African scholar Omar ibn Said — persuaded him to write his autobiography in Arabic (1831), the only known extant slave autobiography written in Arabic in America. Dwight wanted the autobiography to undermine pro-slavery arguments by demonstrating Africa's deep literary and monotheistic culture. INTERNATIONAL: Passionately supported Garibaldi and Italian unification. Conversant in French, Spanish, Portuguese, Italian, German, Greek; grasp of Hebrew and Arabic. DEATH: Died of injuries sustained jumping off a departing train near Brooklyn. m. Eleanor Boyd Apr 24, 1827. 7 children. Buried Green-Wood Cemetery, Brooklyn. (Wikipedia; Yale Biographical Sketches) [Migrated from top-level primary_url]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Dwight_Jr.

people.research_notes: b. Jan 26, 1798 Hartford CT; d. Jun 8, 1864 New York City age 66. Son of Theodore Dwight Sr. (H00920) and Abigail Alsop. Merchant, banker, proprietor of the New York Daily Advertiser (co-edited with father). m. Mary Warren Fiske Mar 29, 1826. 6 children. His daughter Julia Porter Dwight (b. 1830) was painted as a toddler by miniaturist Eliza Goodridge ca. 1832 — that portrait is in the Yale University Art Gallery (accession: https://artgallery.yale.edu/collections/objects/78524). His daughter Mary Edwards Dwight Atherton (1838-1915) was the great-great-granddaughter of Jonathan Edwards and mother of Frederick William Atherton (Harvard 1886), founding trustee of Wentworth Institute of Technology. Buried Green-Wood Cemetery, Brooklyn. (Dwight 1874; FindAGrave)

narrative_blocks.header: He took over the family's New York newspaper
narrative_blocks.body: At first a merchant, William became a partner with his father, Theodore Dwight, and his brother in the New York Daily Advertiser.

narrative_blocks.header: A banker who played the flute
narrative_blocks.body: From 1839 to 1864 William was an officer of New York banks, for several years a teller at the Hanover Bank. He played the flute well, collected antiquities and art, and wrote verse for his friends.

narrative_blocks.header: One of seventy-two who founded a church
narrative_blocks.body: In 1842 William was one of seventy-two who left Brooklyn's First Presbyterian Church to found the South Presbyterian, where he was a deacon, ruling elder and clerk of the session for many years.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the daughter of an Amherst founder
narrative_blocks.body: In 1826 William married Mary Warren Fiske, whose father, the Reverend John Fiske, was among the founders of Amherst College. Their small daughter Julia was later painted by the miniaturist Eliza Goodridge.

career.organization: Hanover Bank and other New York banks

people.research_notes: b. Jun 24, 1793 Hartford CT; d. Nov 13, 1875 Flushing NY age 82. Daughter of Theodore Dwight Sr. (H00920) and Abigail Alsop. Also known as "Mary A." m. Matthew Alexander Patrick Apr 28, 1833 age 39. Matthew Alexander Patrick (1794-1834) was an officer in the 1st Artillery; he died Mar 6, 1834 at Williamsport MD while quelling a labor riot, brevet rank Captain. Congress granted Mary a pension in 1838 based on his brevet rank. A Nov 1832 letter she wrote to her fiancé Matthew is quoted in the Yale Art Gallery notes on the miniature portrait of her niece Julia Porter Dwight: "I wish you could see our parlour... my mother, aunt, cousin, brother, sister, and little niece are all talking, singing and laughing." Buried Green-Wood Cemetery, Brooklyn. (FindAGrave; Yale Art Gallery)

narrative_blocks.header: Her letter caught the Dwight parlor mid-song
narrative_blocks.body: In an 1832 letter to her fiancé she sketched the crowded Dwight parlor — mother, aunt, cousin, brother, sister, and a little niece all 'talking, singing and laughing' at once. It is a rare glimpse of the family's domestic warmth.

narrative_blocks.header: She married at thirty-nine, and was soon widowed
narrative_blocks.body: She married late, wedding the artillery officer Matthew Patrick in 1833 — with her brother Theodore and Sarah Woolsey as witnesses — but he died the very next year.

narrative_blocks.header: A widow who won her fight in Congress
narrative_blocks.body: Widowed after barely a year, she pressed Congress for years to recover the pay her husband had been denied — the gap between a captain's wages and a lieutenant's. Eighty years before women could vote, she prevailed: her bill became law in 1838.

narrative_blocks.header: Three years at Yale, then a Harvard degree
narrative_blocks.body: Jonathan spent his first three college years at Yale and took his degree at Harvard in 1786. He practised law at Hadley and sat for a time in the Massachusetts legislature.

narrative_blocks.header: Full of anecdote and wit
narrative_blocks.body: Jonathan was of middling height and full figure, with black hair and eyes, quick in mind and manner, and full of anecdote and wit in conversation.

narrative_blocks.header: Illness twice took him from the law
narrative_blocks.body: For several years illness left Jonathan unable to work at all. He recovered, moved to New Haven about 1806 and practised there until his health failed again, and died suddenly in March 1821, at fifty-four.

narrative_blocks.header: He married his cousin Fidelia
narrative_blocks.body: In January 1793 Jonathan married Fidelia Dwight of Northampton, his first cousin; their mothers were sisters.

education.dates: Three years, before transferring to Harvard

people.research_notes: b. Jul 15, 1799 Hadley MA; d. Apr 3, 1855 New York City age 55. Son of Jonathan Edwards Porter (X00660) and Fidelia Dwight Porter (H00922). Yale class of 1819. His father's death in March 1821 and his own imperfect health derailed his law studies. Devoted himself to teaching. Spent years as a private tutor in Virginia; from 1834 became a principal at the Washington Institute, a prominent boarding school for boys in NYC, which he ran with his elder brother until his death. Died unmarried, age 55. Originally buried at St. Luke's Hospital cemetery New York; reburied Grove Street Cemetery New Haven Dec 15, 1881. Named for Theodore Dwight Woolsey (HD1973), his first cousin once removed — both grandchildren of Jonathan Edwards grandchildren. (Dexter, Yale Biographical Sketches vol.VI pp.649-653)

narrative_blocks.header: Lafayette named his school
narrative_blocks.body: From 1834 Theodore ran the Washington Institute in New York with his elder brother Timothy. Lafayette had named the boys' school on his 1824 visit, the first American school to be called an Institute.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale, then the law, then Virginia
narrative_blocks.body: Theodore graduated from Yale in 1819 and read law at Philadelphia with Charles Chauncey, but his father's death in 1821 and his own health ended that. He spent some years as a private tutor in Virginia.

narrative_blocks.header: A teacher with a relish for the arts
narrative_blocks.body: Theodore was known for the finish of his dress and manners, taught Sabbath school, and loved music, painting and sculpture. He died unmarried in New York in 1855, at fifty-five.

narrative_blocks.body: Agnes Abby married a Dwight cousin trading at Franklin and died there in 1839. Mary Edwards married Dr. Joseph Warren Lyman, who practised in the same town until 1872. Electa died at Franklin in 1859.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried an infant out of Parker's Fort
narrative_blocks.body: On 19 May 1836 the fort was attacked. Malinda's father Samuel Frost and her brother Robert were killed; George, Malinda and their baby daughter Elizabeth got away with the other survivors to Fort Houston.

narrative_blocks.header: He built a water mill on Elkhart Creek
narrative_blocks.body: After the fort the family moved about a while before settling in Houston County, where he owned and worked a water mill. He had signed the 1837 petition to get the county established.

narrative_blocks.header: The baby he carried out lived to eighty-three
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth was an infant in his arms at Parker's Fort and was still telling the story of it decades later. She died at Amarillo in 1919, eighty-three years old.

narrative_blocks.header: His widow went back to Parker's Fort country
narrative_blocks.body: He died at Grapevine in February 1856. Malinda took the children up to Limestone County, near the old fort they had been driven from twenty years before, and married Eli Allen Hill there.

narrative_blocks.header: Born at Natchez, a long way from home
narrative_blocks.body: His father Henry Edwin Dwight kept public houses in New York and the family came out of Northampton in Massachusetts. He was born at Natchez on the Mississippi in 1805 and went further west still.

narrative_blocks.body: Her father, the Reverend John Fiske, preached for over sixty years at New Braintree, Massachusetts, and was among the founders of Amherst College, which gave him its doctorate of divinity in 1844. She carried that New England ministerial line into her marriage to William Richard Dwight.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandfather at André's execution
narrative_blocks.body: Mary's mother, Elizabeth Mellen, was a daughter of Colonel Mellen, the officer of the day at Major John André's execution in 1780.

narrative_blocks.header: She died at thirty-nine, never married
narrative_blocks.body: The child of the miniature never grew old; she died at thirty-nine at Roxbury, Massachusetts, unmarried. The little portrait outlived her by generations.

narrative_blocks.header: He led the mining engineers' institute
narrative_blocks.detail: He rose to the AIME presidency — the same organization his step-aunt husband Rossiter Worthington Raymond had served as secretary for 27 years (1884-1911). The Hooker-Dwight family engineering thread runs from Puritan Connecticut to the American mining frontier. (Wikipedia; FindAGrave)
narrative_blocks.body: He was president of the American Institute of Mining and Metallurgical Engineers and took its Douglas medal. He had been president of the Colorado Scientific Society at thirty-one, and served Columbia as an alumni trustee.

narrative_blocks.header: A colonel of engineers in France
narrative_blocks.detail: Eight generations from Thomas Hooker arrival in Connecticut (1636) to the Western Front (1918). (FindAGrave)
narrative_blocks.body: He came out of the war a lieutenant colonel of engineers, with the British Distinguished Service Order and a citation from General Pershing.

narrative_blocks.header: His process for fine ore went worldwide
narrative_blocks.body: With R. L. Lloyd he worked out a way of roasting and agglomerating fine ores that had been all but unusable before. The Dwight and Lloyd sintering process went into smelters the world over, and he ran the company that licensed it.

narrative_blocks.header: He turned a copper mine into an army
narrative_blocks.body: He was general manager at Cananea in Mexico in 1906, when a rising was planned to seize the mines and fund a revolt through the interior. He made a military unit of his workforce almost overnight and had the thing in hand before troops arrived.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirteen years from assayer to the top
narrative_blocks.body: He left the Columbia School of Mines in 1885 for Pueblo and started at the Colorado Smelting Company as an assayer. Thirteen years later he was its general superintendent, and had run smelters at Leadville, El Paso, Argentine and San Luis Potosi.

narrative_blocks.header: He took his mother's name for his own
narrative_blocks.body: He was born a Smith, son of Benjamin Pierce Smith, and his mother Elizabeth Fiske Dwight was dead before he was fourteen months old. He carried her surname the rest of his life, and with it a descent from Jonathan Edwards and Timothy Dwight.

narrative_blocks.body: A partner with his brothers in Atherton, Stetson and Company, a leading Boston leather house, he built the townhouse at 144 Commonwealth Avenue in 1880. He was a bank vice president and among the city's largest taxpayers.

narrative_blocks.body: He bought the lot at 144 Commonwealth from the Commonwealth of Massachusetts on 29 February 1872 and did not file a building permit on it until August 1880. Until then the family lived at 144 Warren, in the Roxbury Highlands.

narrative_blocks.body: William and Mary Atherton's eldest child and their only daughter, she was seventeen when the family left Roxbury for the new house at 144 Commonwealth Avenue. She was still living there, unmarried, at forty-four.

narrative_blocks.body: She died at the Des Brisay hospital in Boston on 23 June 1908, during an operation for an acute intestinal obstruction. She was forty-four, and was buried at Forest Hills, where her father had gone seventeen years before.

notable.notable_blurb: Founding trustee of Wentworth Institute of Technology

narrative_blocks.header: He built a college from a contested fortune
narrative_blocks.detail: The estate was contested by Wentworth daughter; after nine months of negotiation approximately $3.5M went to the Institute, which opened to students in 1911. Atherton served as Secretary and Director throughout. Harvard class of 1886 records show that when J.P. Morgan Jr. was called before a Senate committee, Atherton arrived and took his chair. (Wikipedia)
narrative_blocks.body: Named a trustee of the disputed seven-million-dollar estate of Arioch Wentworth, he helped steer half of it into founding the Wentworth Institute of Technology in 1904, then served as its secretary and director from its first plans through a quarter-century of operation.

narrative_blocks.header: Harvard named an annual lecture for him
narrative_blocks.detail: Atherton left no children. His legacy is this lecture series and his brother Percy (HD2071) $15,000 Harvard musical scholarship fund. His DC home is now the Embassy of the Ivory Coast. (Wikipedia; Harvard)
narrative_blocks.body: Since 1966 Harvard has held an annual Frederick William Atherton Lecture on ethical and social criticism; Lillian Hellman and Russell Baker are among those who have delivered it.

narrative_blocks.header: He worked Washington society for his causes
narrative_blocks.body: For more than twenty-five years he was a fixture of Washington society, entertaining diplomats and courting presidents to advance his educational philanthropies. He sat in on Senate hearings from the J. P. Morgan inquiry to the meatpacking investigation.

notable.notable_blurb: Composer and musician

narrative_blocks.header: Three European masters shaped his composing
narrative_blocks.body: After Harvard he spent years in Europe's conservatories — studying under Josef Rheinberger in Munich, Giovanni Sgambati in Rome, and Charles-Marie Widor in Paris. He came home to Boston to compose.

narrative_blocks.header: His comic operas filled Boston's concert halls
narrative_blocks.body: His comic operas — The Heir Apparent and the 'Oriental' Maharaja — and some hundred songs made him a fixture of Boston's musical life, with the Boston Pops playing his orchestral pieces. He set verses by Longfellow, Housman, and Swinburne.

narrative_blocks.header: A feminist's verses became his songs
narrative_blocks.body: He set the poems of the feminist writer Charlotte Perkins Gilman to music; their correspondence survives at Harvard. He never married, living his whole life at the family home on Commonwealth Avenue.

narrative_blocks.header: Washington put him over the nation's music
narrative_blocks.body: From 1929 to 1942 he was acting chief of the music division of the Library of Congress, where the collection swelled with manuscripts and rare instruments — including the Stradivari violins Gertrude Clarke Whittall gave in the 1930s.

narrative_blocks.header: His will funded music students at Harvard
narrative_blocks.body: His will endowed a Harvard fund for musically gifted students, with further gifts to the Library of Congress and Boston's music schools. The scholarship still carries his name.

COMPOSER: Studied under Josef Rheinberger and Ludwig Thuille (Munich); Otis Bardwell Boise (Berlin, 1896); Giovanni Sgambati (Rome, 1900); Charles Marie Widor (Paris). Composed songs, chamber music, and several comic operas. Set music to poems of Charlotte Perkins Gilman (correspondence in the Schlesinger Collection, Harvard). Friend of author Henry Gilbert (Henry Gilbert Collection, Yale). Member: Audubon Society, Longwood Cricket Club, Composers Club of Boston, Harvard Musical Association; trustee of Boston Public Library. Remained unmarried all his life at 144 Commonwealth Avenue Boston. Will: $15,000 Harvard Scholarship Fund for musically talented students; $1,000 to the music division, Library of Congress. (Wikipedia; FindAGrave)

orbit_connections.notes: Rossiter Worthington Raymond (Apr 27, 1840 Cincinnati OH - Dec 31, 1918 Brooklyn NY). Mining engineer, legal scholar, author, Civil War officer, chess player, poet. Described at his memorial as one of the most remarkable cases of versatility that our country has ever seen. Aide-de-camp to General Fremont during the Civil War; commended for gallant conduct. US Commissioner of Mining Statistics. Secretary of AIME 1884-1911 (AIME named its Rossiter W. Raymond Memorial Award after him in 1945). Raymond Peak (10,014 ft), Alpine County CA, named for him in 1865. His parents participated in the Underground Railroad in Syracuse NY. Member of the American Philosophical Society. Famous quote: Life is eternal; and love is immortal; and death is only a horizon; and a horizon is nothing save the limit of our sight. Published Western novel Brave Hearts (1873). Buried Green-Wood Cemetery, Brooklyn. (Wikipedia; FindAGrave)

narrative_blocks.header: His bank failure cost Yale its endowment
narrative_blocks.body: When his father-in-law, William Walton Woolsey, went back to his New York ventures in 1825, he handed George the presidency of New Haven's Eagle Bank. George lent out nearly all its capital on thin collateral, and when the bank failed that September it cut Yale's endowment to almost nothing and dragged the town into a depression. In 1830 he left for Cleveland in disgrace.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave Yale the Morse portrait of Whitney
narrative_blocks.body: Two years after his bank failed, he handed Yale a gift of lasting value: Samuel Morse's 1822 portrait of the inventor Eli Whitney, recorded as accession 1827.1 — among the very first works the Yale Art Gallery ever catalogued.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty thousand cases as justice of the peace
narrative_blocks.body: In Cleveland George rebuilt himself as a lawyer consulted for his learning, and from 1832 to 1846 he sat as justice of the peace. He was said to have decided more than twenty thousand cases in those fourteen years, firm but fair, with few reversed, and in 1836 he swore in the first city council.

narrative_blocks.header: Cleveland's first high school
narrative_blocks.body: Elected mayor of Cleveland in 1846, George worked with his predecessor Samuel Starkweather to open the city's first high school, a boys' school for the best of the common-school pupils. A girls' department followed in 1847, but the school's selectiveness drew enough opposition that it was eventually closed.

narrative_blocks.header: His son dropped the e and governed Ohio
narrative_blocks.body: George married the widowed Mary Ann Woolsey at New Haven in 1819, taking in her son William, and they had four children; their daughter Laura died at eighteen. Their son George dropped the e from the family name and was elected governor of Ohio in 1883.

narrative_blocks.body: Laura and William Johnson had gone out to Elliottville on Staten Island four years earlier. She joined them there and died in 1863, two years after Big Bethel took her son.

narrative_blocks.header: Father died when he was four years old
narrative_blocks.body: When the cotton gin inventor died in January 1825, his son was four. He was raised by his mother Henrietta Edwards Whitney in the Edwards family's intellectual tradition and took control of the family arms factory in his early twenties.

narrative_blocks.header: Built Whitneyville into a Civil War arsenal
narrative_blocks.body: He took over the Whitney Arms Company in 1842 and ran it for the next forty-six years. Under his management the company supplied tens of thousands of rifled muskets to the Union Army during the Civil War.

narrative_blocks.header: Founded the New Haven Water Company in 1860
narrative_blocks.body: He constructed the dam that created Lake Whitney in 1860 and founded the New Haven Water Company to supply the growing city. The company became New Haven's primary water utility and remained in family management for two generations.

narrative_blocks.header: Sold Whitney Arms to Winchester in 1888
narrative_blocks.body: In 1888 he sold the firearms business — the firm his father founded under the 1798 musket contract — to Winchester Repeating Arms. The sale ended ninety years of Whitney firearms manufacturing in Connecticut.

narrative_blocks.header: Followed Edwards tradition to Princeton in 1841

narrative_blocks.header: Tea with my Aunt Hunt, 25 November 1800

notable.notable_blurb: Lawyer

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty years on New York’s high bench
narrative_blocks.detail: A graduate of Litchfield Law School — the same institution founded by his relative Tapping Reeve (husband of his first cousin Sally Burr Reeve, H00912) — Edwards built one of the most sustained judicial careers of any Pierpont Edwards child. He also served as a Surrogate Court Judge and was a member of the New York Constitutional Convention. The Litchfield connection is direct: his father Pierpont Edwards (H00386) led Connecticut's Democratic Party; his brother Henry Waggaman Edwards (HD2045) also studied at Litchfield. The family trained three generations at the same law school. (FindAGrave; Wikipedia)
narrative_blocks.body: The Litchfield Law School graduate — trained at the school his kinsman Tapping Reeve founded — sat on the New York Supreme Court from 1821 to 1841, served as Surrogate, and joined the state constitutional convention. Jonathan Edwards was his grandfather.

narrative_blocks.header: First cousin to Aaron Burr
narrative_blocks.body: Son of Pierpont Edwards and grandson of Jonathan, the Litchfield-trained judge was first cousin to Aaron Burr — and kin through his mother Frances to the Elizabethtown Ogdens who raised Col. William Edwards to the tannery trade. He sat twenty years on New York’s Supreme Court.

narrative_blocks.header: A faction once ran him for Governor
narrative_blocks.body: Edwards earned a name as a sound and conservative statesman, a delegate to New York's 1821 Constitutional Convention and for years the city's Corporation Counsel. At the height of that standing, a faction of the Whig party put him forward as a candidate for governor. He never reached the office, but the nomination measured how far the bench and bar had carried him.

narrative_blocks.header: He died sure the Union would survive
narrative_blocks.body: An early and active member of the new Republican party, Edwards lived to watch the Civil War tear the country apart. He died in April 1862, in the thick of the fighting, holding firmly to the conviction that the Union would be preserved. He did not live to see himself proven right.

narrative_blocks.header: He gathered the pioneers' history
narrative_blocks.body: In 1874 John helped found the Mahoning Valley Historical Society, and with William Powers edited its 1876 volume of pioneer reminiscences. One of his last and favourite labours was editing the History of Trumbull and Mahoning Counties, published at Cleveland in 1882.

narrative_blocks.header: Editor of Mahoning County's first newspaper
narrative_blocks.body: When Mahoning County was organized in 1846, John moved to Canfield, its county seat, and became editor and one of the publishers of the Mahoning Index, the county's first newspaper. At Warren he had edited the Trumbull Democrat from 1840.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote as Quill Pen
narrative_blocks.body: From 1855 John sent a weekly letter to Youngstown's Mahoning Register under the pen name Quill Pen, and in 1864 he became the paper's associate editor. For fourteen years, from 1865 to 1879, he was also the Cleveland Herald's Youngstown correspondent.

narrative_blocks.header: Nominated for Congress without being asked
narrative_blocks.body: In 1842, when Joshua Giddings resigned from Congress, a Democratic convention nominated John for the seat without his knowing it was planned. His party was far in the minority and he lost, but he cut deeply into the opposition's vote.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale, then law with his great-uncle
narrative_blocks.body: John graduated from Yale in 1824 and read law at New Haven with Judge William Bristol, who had married his great-aunt Sally Edwards. He came west to Youngstown in 1832, joined the Ohio bar in 1838, and was a Youngstown justice of the peace from 1869 to 1878.

narrative_blocks.header: A wife who painted
narrative_blocks.body: John married Mary Crail at Warren, Ohio, on 14 July 1842. A talented amateur artist, she died at Youngstown on 15 May 1877, leaving three children, among them their daughter Nettie.

narrative_blocks.header: She knew exactly who she was
narrative_blocks.detail: The passage reads: "Mrs. Caspar is descended from the Rev. Solomon Stoddard, the Rev. James Pierrepont and the Rev. Thomas Hooker, who in 1636 led his band of adherents out of Newton (Cambridge) and founded the Hartford settlement." This is among the most complete contemporary acknowledgments by a living descendant of the full Hooker genealogical chain. She and her husband came to Denver in 1887 from Youngstown Ohio; she died in 1932 age 86, having led civic organizations in Montana, Ohio, and Colorado for six decades. (History of Colorado Vol. 5, 1927)
narrative_blocks.body: Her 1927 Colorado biographical entry documents the full genealogical chain: Thomas Hooker, Rev. James Pierpont, Rev. Solomon Stoddard, and Jonathan Edwards, all named as her direct ancestors.

narrative_blocks.header: Denver’s serial founder of clubs
narrative_blocks.body: She founded the Colorado Colonial Dames, the Monday Literary Club, the Homer Club of Montana, and the Twenty-second Avenue Study Club, presiding over the last for thirty years, and led Colorado’s state board of charities. Her estate went to the cathedral, the hospital, the YWCA, and the Old Ladies Home of her native Youngstown.

institutions.institution_blurb: Yale College B.A. 1895.

narrative_blocks.header: John D. Rockefeller Jr.'s longtime attorney
narrative_blocks.body: He served as the personal attorney to John D. Rockefeller Jr. for many years, advising on the philanthropist's extensive business and charitable affairs. The relationship gave the Debevoise family a direct professional tie to one of the era's most consequential American fortunes.

narrative_blocks.header: Married into the Whitney cotton-gin family
narrative_blocks.body: In the 1890s he married Anne Farnam Whitney, the eldest daughter of Eli Whitney IV and great-granddaughter of the cotton-gin inventor. Their only son, Eli Whitney Debevoise, was named for the inventor and would later co-found the law firm Debevoise & Plimpton.

narrative_blocks.header: Outlived his wife by less than two years
narrative_blocks.body: His wife Anne died in February 1957. He died December 20, 1958 in Summit, New Jersey at age eighty-four. Both are buried at Fair Mount Cemetery in Chatham, New Jersey, where their son and his second wife would later be interred as well.

narrative_blocks.header: General counsel to the Rockefeller philanthropic empire
narrative_blocks.body: Beyond his role as JDR Jr.'s personal counsel he served as general counsel to the Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research, the Rockefeller Foundation, and the General Education Board — the three pillars of John D. Rockefeller Sr.'s and Jr.'s philanthropic infrastructure. He chaired the distribution committee of the New York Community Trust from its 1923 founding and held his office at 30 Rockefeller Plaza in Manhattan.

narrative_blocks.header: The client who became his life's work
narrative_blocks.body: For nearly thirty years he built a New York practice with the firm Rounds, Hatch, Dillingham & Debevoise. In 1924 John D. Rockefeller Jr. drew him away to become the principal lawyer and spokesman for his business, civic, and personal affairs.

notable.notable_blurb: Co-founded Debevoise & Plimpton; defended Alger Hiss

narrative_blocks.header: Named for his great-grandfather the cotton-gin inventor
narrative_blocks.body: He was born in Manhattan in 1899 to Anne Farnam Whitney and Thomas McElrath Debevoise, who served as John D. Rockefeller Jr.'s longtime attorney. His mother named him for her great-grandfather, the cotton-gin inventor whose Whitney Armory had founded Whitneyville, Connecticut a century earlier.

narrative_blocks.header: Co-founded Debevoise & Plimpton with $2,366
narrative_blocks.body: In 1931, after six years at Davis Polk & Wardwell, he and fellow associate William Stevenson formed a partnership under the name Debevoise & Stevenson, with $2,366 in their account. Francis Plimpton joined them shortly after, and the firm — eventually Debevoise & Plimpton — became one of New York's most prominent international law practices.

narrative_blocks.header: Defended Alger Hiss in his perjury trials
narrative_blocks.body: He represented Alger Hiss at his 1949-1950 perjury trials stemming from the Hiss-Chambers House Un-American Activities Committee testimony, one of the highest-profile cases of the early Cold War. He also served as legal adviser to Ford Motor Company as it became a publicly traded corporation in 1956.

narrative_blocks.header: Deputy High Commissioner for occupied Germany
narrative_blocks.body: From 1951 to 1953 he served as Deputy High Commissioner for Germany and general counsel to the Allied Commission that administered Germany's affairs in the years after World War II. He returned to Debevoise & Plimpton in 1953 and remained active in international human rights work for the rest of his career.

narrative_blocks.header: Founded the International Commission of Jurists
narrative_blocks.body: After his return from Germany he co-founded the International Commission of Jurists, one of the first global human rights organizations, and chaired Governor Nelson Rockefeller's 1967-1968 Committee to Review New York Laws and Procedures on Human Rights. He retired at age 87 and died in Manhattan in 1990 at age ninety.

narrative_blocks.header: The cause he kept returning to
narrative_blocks.body: For more than twenty-five years he poured himself into the New York Association for the Blind — the Lighthouse — serving as its president from 1946 to 1951. Of all his causes, it was the one he kept returning to.

narrative_blocks.header: She read the board papers from her deathbed
narrative_blocks.body: She had helped her husband through the anxious founding years of the Vermont Law School, and after his death she served on its board herself, earning an honorary degree in 2005. Knowing she was too ill to attend the February 2024 meeting, she still asked for the board papers and read them from the hospital.

narrative_blocks.header: She met her husband crossing the Atlantic
narrative_blocks.body: A Swarthmore economics graduate, she was assisting the economist Clair Wilcox on Marshall Plan business when she crossed the Atlantic and met a young lawyer named Tom Debevoise. They married at her family's Connecticut farm on Thanksgiving Day, 1951.

narrative_blocks.header: She ran cattle and sheep in Woodstock
narrative_blocks.body: On the family's old Woodstock farm she raised Polled Hereford cattle and Polled Dorset sheep, reseeding hayfields and reclaiming worn pastureland. She served as a director of the Vermont Beef Producers Association and as a supervisor of the Ottauquechee conservation district.

narrative_blocks.header: A steward of Woodstock's library and history
narrative_blocks.body: She gave decades of trustee service to her Vermont town — among them the Norman Williams Public Library, the Woodstock Historical Society, and the Vermont Center for the Book. Years earlier, during the family's Washington seasons, she had volunteered at the Corcoran Gallery of Art.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother ran the little school she attended
narrative_blocks.body: She grew up on her family's dairy farm in Woodstock, Connecticut, and had her early schooling at The Arke School, a small independent school her mother ran out of their own house. From there she went on to Abbot Academy and Swarthmore College.

narrative_blocks.header: Helped defend Soviet spy Rudolf Abel
narrative_blocks.body: As a young Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York 1954-1956, he assisted James B. Donovan in the court-appointed defense of accused Soviet spy Col. Rudolf Abel. Donovan later used the case as leverage in the 1962 prisoner swap that returned downed U-2 pilot Francis Gary Powers in exchange for Abel's release.

narrative_blocks.header: Appointed Vermont Attorney General at thirty
narrative_blocks.body: After moving to Woodstock in 1956 and serving as Deputy Attorney General from 1959, he was appointed Vermont Attorney General in February 1960 by Governor Robert Stafford to fill a vacancy. He won a full term as a Republican that November and served until resigning in January 1962.

narrative_blocks.header: Founding-era Dean of Vermont Law School
narrative_blocks.body: He served as Dean of the Vermont Law School from 1974 to 1982, leading the institution through its formative first decade after its 1972 founding. Vermont Law School awarded him an honorary Doctor of Laws in 1984; Debevoise Hall on the South Royalton campus, renovated in 2005, was named for him and his wife Ann.

narrative_blocks.header: Led the Rockefellers' Woodstock Foundation thirteen years
narrative_blocks.body: From 1982 until his death in 1995 he served as president of the Woodstock Foundation, established by Laurance Rockefeller and Mary French Rockefeller to promote conservation and sustainable land use. He had moved to Woodstock in 1956 and made it his home for the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: Lung cancer at sixty-five at Dartmouth-Hitchcock
narrative_blocks.body: He died February 1, 1995 at the Dartmouth-Hitchcock Medical Center in Lebanon, New Hampshire of complications from surgery for lung cancer. He was survived by his wife Ann, his sister Elizabeth Debevoise Healy of Manhattan, four children, and eight grandchildren.

narrative_blocks.header: Bay of Pigs prisoners home by Christmas
narrative_blocks.body: In the fall of 1962 Attorney General Robert Kennedy asked Robert to broker a trade: Fidel Castro would free the more than a thousand exiles captured at the Bay of Pigs for food and medicine. Robert gathered the goods from private companies in six weeks, and the men were home in Florida by Christmas.

narrative_blocks.header: Eisenhower sent him down the Berlin road
narrative_blocks.body: Recruited off Wall Street in 1958 as deputy assistant secretary of defense for international security affairs, Robert took the job out of a sense of social obligation. Eisenhower sent him to drive the road into West Berlin himself, to see how the Soviets were squeezing the city, work that won him the Secretary of Defense Medal.

narrative_blocks.header: Treasury's lawyer, then a quiet errand South
narrative_blocks.body: Treasury Secretary C. Douglas Dillon made Robert his general counsel, a post that brought him the Alexander Hamilton Medal, and Paul Volcker remembered a man who exuded experience, calmness and good judgment. In 1963 Kennedy sent him quietly through Southern cities to tell bankers that civil rights legislation was coming and they should accept it.

narrative_blocks.header: Chairman of the New York Fed
narrative_blocks.body: From 1977 to 1983 Robert chaired the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, the same years he was rising to the head of his law firm. He sat as well on the boards of the Council on Foreign Relations and the Asia Foundation, and for twenty years on Intelsat's arbitration panel.

narrative_blocks.header: He took Shearman & Sterling abroad
narrative_blocks.body: Robert joined Shearman & Sterling in 1949 as an antitrust lawyer and made partner in 1955. In the 1970s and 1980s he led its expansion overseas, into the Middle East and China, and ran the firm as senior partner from 1982 to 1985.

narrative_blocks.header: The first 4.0 at Virginia Law
narrative_blocks.body: Robert came out of the war a lieutenant colonel in the Army Air Forces, earned Virginia Law's first 4.0, edited its law journal and taught there two years. From 1970 to 1990 he chaired its Law School Foundation.

narrative_blocks.header: An Eli Whitney descendant from New Haven
narrative_blocks.body: Robert was born in New Haven in 1919 to Earl Wall Knight and Frances Pierpont Whitney, a descendant of Eli Whitney, and went through Andover to Yale. He married Alice Valle in 1940 and, after their divorce, Rosemary Costikyan Gibson, called Mimi, in 1975.

b. 1738 Stockbridge MA; d. Aug 13, 1796 Stockbridge MA age 58. Son of Judge Joseph Woodbridge II and Elizabeth Merrick (widow of Joseph Barnard). Princeton 1761. Grew up in Stockbridge from age 1, attended the Indian Mission School, tutored by his uncle Timothy Woodbridge III and Jonathan Edwards; learned the Indian language. REVOLUTIONARY WAR MILITARY CAREER: 1764 — listed as member, Stockbridge company, Berkshire County Militia. 1771 — commissioned First Lieutenant. 1777 — commissioned Captain; commanded the Stockbridge company for the remainder of the war. 1777 — commanded the company on its march from Stockbridge to Ticonderoga, on the evacuation of the fort. PROVINCIAL CONGRESS: Member of the Third Provincial Congress of Massachusetts Bay Colony, meeting at Watertown May 3 - Jul 19, 1775. On military affairs and finance committees. Jul 5, 1775: Congress resolved that wages of Stockbridge Indians serving in the war be paid to Jahleel Woodbridge and Timothy Edwards — the Indians "being sensible of their want of prudence in disposing of their money, are desirous that this Congress, in their wisdom, would devise some method to prevent their getting too much strong drink." CIVIL SERVICE: Jul 6, 1774 delegate to the Stockbridge Congress against non-importation of British manufactures. Selectman; Justice of the Peace; MA State Senator 1780-84; Judge, Court of Common Pleas, Berkshire County 1781-1795; Judge, Probate Court, Berkshire County 1787-1795. SHAYS' REBELLION (1787): When insurrectionists reached Stockbridge, Woodbridge — as judge — was a primary target of the "silk stocking aristocracy." They broke into his home in the dead of night, pillaged the house, and carried him off to Great Barrington as a prisoner. A rescue party set out from Stockbridge; meanwhile Woodbridge negotiated his own release. He met the volunteers halfway between Stockbridge and Great Barrington. (Edward Bellamy's novel "The Duke of Stockbridge" draws on these events.) Second marriage: Hannah (Robbins) Keep, widow of Rev. John Keep; no issue. GRAVESTONE: "This Stone is erected to the Memory of the Hon. Jahleel Woodbridge, Esq., who died August 13, 1796 in the 59th year of his age." (The Record LXXI; FindAGrave; DAR; Autobiography of a Blind Minister)
