narrative_blocks.header: Kidnapped from home at midnight by Shays men
narrative_blocks.body: When Shays' Rebellion reached Stockbridge in 1787, the insurrectionists targeted Judge Woodbridge — symbol of the 'silk stocking aristocracy.' They broke into his home at midnight, pillaged it, and carried him off as a prisoner to Great Barrington; he negotiated his own release and met the rescue party halfway home. Edward Bellamy's 1879 novel 'The Duke of Stockbridge' drew on these events.

narrative_blocks.header: Learned the Mahican language at Mission School
narrative_blocks.body: Growing up in Stockbridge from age one, he attended the Indian Mission School and was tutored by his uncle Timothy Woodbridge and Jonathan Edwards — learning the Mahican language in the process. Princeton followed in 1761, and Berkshire County militia service by 1764.

narrative_blocks.header: Paid Stockbridge Indian soldiers to prevent strong drink
narrative_blocks.body: On 5 July 1775 the Third Provincial Congress of Massachusetts resolved that wages of Stockbridge Indians serving in the war be paid directly to Woodbridge and Timothy Edwards. The Indians had requested the arrangement themselves — 'being sensible of their want of prudence in disposing of their money, [they were] desirous that this Congress, in their wisdom, would devise some method to prevent their getting too much strong drink.'

narrative_blocks.header: Captain of the Stockbridge minutemen
narrative_blocks.body: Woodbridge commanded a company of Stockbridge minutemen — the hand-picked, fast-mustering elite drawn from the militia rolls — and contributed liberally to the commissary department of the cause. He sat in the Third Provincial Congress as the colonies turned from protest toward independence.

narrative_blocks.header: He named a son for the Apostle
narrative_blocks.body: Having learned the Mahican language himself at the Stockbridge mission school, Jahleel gave one of his sons the name John Eliot — after the Puritan missionary who first rendered scripture into a Native tongue. It was a deliberate echo of the cause his own schooling had steeped him in.

narrative_blocks.header: She married her first cousin Jonathan
narrative_blocks.body: Lucy was a daughter of Jahleel Woodbridge of Stockbridge, and the Jonathan Edwards she married was the son of her father's sister Lucy Edwards — her first cousin. Both of them descended from the theologian Jonathan Edwards, so the family's blood doubled back on itself in the match.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son married a Woodbridge cousin too
narrative_blocks.body: The pattern repeated in the next generation: her son Jonathan married a Lucy Woodbridge who was his first cousin, daughter of Lucy's own brother John Eliot Woodbridge. A Jonathan Edwards wed a cousin named Lucy Woodbridge two generations running.

people.research_notes: b. Jul 22, 1771 Stockbridge MA; d. Apr 23, 1829 Stockbridge MA age 57. EH #930. m. Louisa Hopkins (1774-1819). 3 children: Catherine Louisa Woodbridge Pitkin (1801-1863), Joseph Effingham Woodbridge (1806-1881), William Woodbridge (1814-1837). Buried Stockbridge Cemetery. NOTABLE DESCENT: Catherine Louisa × Timothy Pitkin; their daughter Katharine Louise Pitkin × Robert Henry James → Frederick Pitkin James line. Timothy Pitkin (the Congressman, 1766-1847) was a separate notable Connecticut politician from the same family. (EH 1909; FindAGrave) NOTABLE CONNECTIONS: His wife Louisa Hopkins was daughter of Colonel Mark Hopkins — a younger brother of Rev. Samuel Hopkins D.D. (the FIRST BIOGRAPHER of Jonathan Edwards, and a student in Edwards' home). Her mother Electa Sergeant was daughter of Rev. John Sergeant A.M. — the FIRST MISSIONARY to the Indian Mission at Stockbridge. So Joseph Woodbridge's marriage united the family of Edwards' biographer with the family of the first Stockbridge missionary — in a town founded by the Woodbridges themselves. (The Record LXXI; EH entry 930)

narrative_blocks.header: Marriage united Edwards biographer and missionary families
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph Woodbridge's 1798 marriage to Louisa Hopkins united two important New England religious lineages in the town his own family had founded. Louisa's father Colonel Mark Hopkins was the younger brother of Rev. Samuel Hopkins D.D. — the first biographer of Jonathan Edwards and Edwards's student in his home. Her mother Electa Sergeant was the daughter of Rev. John Sergeant, the first missionary to the Indian Mission at Stockbridge Massachusetts.

narrative_blocks.header: Wife's grandfather founded Stockbridge Indian Mission
narrative_blocks.body: Louisa Hopkins's grandfather Rev. John Sergeant A.M. had been the founding missionary to the Stockbridge Indians in the 1730s — establishing the mission that gave the town its identity and made it nationally famous as a site of early American Protestant missionary work. The Woodbridge-Sergeant-Hopkins triangle clustered three of New England's significant religious-historical surnames in a single Stockbridge household in the 1810s.

narrative_blocks.header: Daughter Catherine married into Pitkin family line
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph and Louisa's eldest daughter Catherine Louisa Woodbridge (1801-1863) married Timothy Pitkin — connecting the Woodbridge line to the wider Pitkin family, which included the Connecticut Congressman Timothy Pitkin (1766-1847), a notable politician of the same surname though distinct branch. Catherine and Timothy's daughter Katharine Louise Pitkin married Robert Henry James, opening the Frederick Pitkin James line for the next generation.

narrative_blocks.header: Born and died Stockbridge MA, age fifty-seven
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph Woodbridge was born July 22, 1771 in Stockbridge Massachusetts and died there April 23, 1829 at age fifty-seven. He is buried at Stockbridge Cemetery. He had three children with Louisa Hopkins: Catherine Louisa (1801-1863), Joseph Effingham (1806-1881), and William (1814-1837 died young at twenty-three).

b. Nov 24, 1784 Stockbridge MA; d. Dec 7, 1862 Spencertown, Columbia County NY age 77. Buried St. Peter's Presbyterian Church, Spencertown. Son of Jahleel Woodbridge (X00690) and Lucy Edwards (H00380). Educated under Rev. Stephen West D.D. at Stockbridge and Rev. Robbins at Norfolk CT. Matriculated Williams College 1799; AT AGE 17 BECAME TOTALLY BLIND — an affliction lasting until his death. Despite blindness, studied law in the office of his brother Joseph (H00930) at Stockbridge, "other students and friends acting as his eyes." In 1810 abandoned law for theology; entered Andover Theological Seminary; licensed to preach 1811 by Andover Association. Preached at First Presbyterian Church, Wall Street, New York City, 1815-16. Pastor, Presbyterian Church, Green River (now Austerlitz), Columbia County NY, installed Nov 18, 1818 — remained until 1842. Then pastor of St. Peter's Church, Spencertown — five miles distant, also Austerlitz. MARK HOPKINS AS AMANUENSIS: While at Green River and Spencertown, needed an amanuensis (reader/writer); among those who served him was MARK HOPKINS — the famous president of Williams College — his own nephew. Another amanuensis was CHARLES EDWARDS LESTER — his nephew by marriage (son of his sister Sarah Edwards, H00932), who later authored 29 books and served in the diplomatic corps. ACADEMIES FOUNDED: Green River Academy — "a famous school of the day." Spencertown Academy — founded 1846, equally famous. m. Cynthia Maria Warren (widow of Peleg Phelps) Jul 1845 Spencertown; no issue. D.D. from Williams College 1846. (The Record LXXI; Autobiography of a Blind Minister; EH entry 935)

narrative_blocks.header: Went blind at seventeen; still became a minister

narrative_blocks.header: His nephew Mark Hopkins read for him
narrative_blocks.body: While pastoring at Green River and Spencertown, he needed an amanuensis to read and write for him. One of those who served in that role was his nephew Mark Hopkins — later the famous president of Williams College.

narrative_blocks.header: Founded two 'famous' academies in Hudson Valley

narrative_blocks.header: Nine hours too late for Jeb Stuart
narrative_blocks.body: On 12 May 1864 George escorted Flora Stuart from Beaverdam to Richmond, where her husband Jeb lay dying of his Yellow Tavern wound. Past Ashland they went fifteen miles by ambulance wagon through rain, high water and the battlefield; it took over nine hours, and Stuart was dead when they arrived.

narrative_blocks.header: Nearly shot by a nervous sentinel
narrative_blocks.body: Somewhere on those fifteen miles from Ashland a jumpy sentinel drew on George, and only the driving rain may have kept the pistol from firing. He was fifty-nine and had not worn a uniform for thirty-five years.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-five years in Richmond's pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: George was rector of Monumental Church, raised over the ashes of the 1811 Richmond Theatre fire, from 1843 until his death in 1878, through secession, four years of war and the burning of the city in April 1865.

narrative_blocks.header: West Point lieutenant, then Episcopal priest
narrative_blocks.body: George graduated from West Point and served as a second lieutenant from 1826 to 1829, then resigned his commission for the ministry of the Protestant Episcopal Church.

narrative_blocks.header: First doctor born in Youngstown
narrative_blocks.detail: He barely survived the Mahoning River drowning that killed his brother John. Jefferson Medical College 1833 — the leading medical school in the US at that time. In 1847-48, David Tod (later Ohio Governor) personally chose him as family physician for his diplomatic posting in Brazil. In 1861, he was appointed surgeon at Johnson's Island on Lake Erie — the Union's prisoner-of-war camp for Confederate officers. In 1879, President Hayes appointed him surgeon at Fort Peck, Montana, where he was the medical officer for both soldiers and Native Americans. He co-founded the Mahoning County Medical Society (1872) and served as its first president for seven years. His billing eccentricities — listing "the fat woman in Brier Hill" in his day books and accepting half-fees from the poor — were celebrated in the 1882 History of Trumbull and Mahoning Counties. (Rose Melnick Medical Museum; Growing Up in Working Class Youngstown; US Army records)
narrative_blocks.body: Timothy Woodbridge was Youngstown's first native-born physician, whose career spanned from private practice in a log cabin to two separate US Army appointments — one by Lincoln's government during the Civil War, one by President Hayes in 1879.

narrative_blocks.header: Surgeon at the Johnson's Island prison
narrative_blocks.body: Timothy went into the Army as a surgeon in 1861 and served as major and surgeon of the 128th Ohio at the Johnson's Island prison camp on Lake Erie for the rest of the war. His daughter Mary was married in the camp in August 1863.

narrative_blocks.header: An Army surgeon again at sixty-nine
narrative_blocks.body: In 1879 President Hayes made Timothy an Army surgeon again, at sixty-nine, and sent him to Fort Peck in Montana, where for about three years he was medical officer to the troops and the Indians.

narrative_blocks.header: A year in Brazil with the American minister
narrative_blocks.body: From 1847 to 1848 Timothy went to Brazil as family physician to David Tod, then serving as the United States Minister there, and came home to his Youngstown practice.

narrative_blocks.header: First president of the county doctors
narrative_blocks.body: His nephew Dr. John Eliot Woodbridge joined his practice in 1871, and the next year Timothy helped found the Mahoning County Medical Society and served seven years as its first president.

narrative_blocks.header: “The fat woman in Brier Hill”
narrative_blocks.body: His ledgers listed patients by description rather than name — “the fat woman in Brier Hill” — and he routinely accepted half to three-quarters of what the poor owed him. The 1816 log cabin he moved across Youngstown in 1862 still stands.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifteen years the Treasury’s watchdog
narrative_blocks.body: Lincoln made Robert First Comptroller of the Treasury in 1863, and he held the post fifteen years under Lincoln, Johnson, Grant and Hayes, known as the watch-dog of the Treasury. His friends included Charles Sumner, William Fessenden and Salmon P. Chase, and he died in office in Washington in February 1878.

narrative_blocks.header: Youngstown's mayor, then Ohio's auditor
narrative_blocks.body: Carried to Youngstown from Harrisburg as a baby, Robert read law and spent four years as Trumbull County's prosecutor from 1839. Youngstown elected him mayor in 1851; he sat two terms in the Ohio Senate, and in 1859 beat Godwin Volney Dorsey for state auditor.

narrative_blocks.header: A widower at forty, remarried within a year
narrative_blocks.body: Robert's first wife, Louisa Woodbridge, died in February 1853, eleven weeks after their seventh child was born. Eleven months later he married Rachel Kirtland Wick, daughter of Caleb Wick, and raised a second family, among them Wick Tayler, later of the Ohio House.

notable.notable_blurb: Ohio congressman and federal judge

narrative_blocks.header: The Tayler Grant ended Cleveland's streetcar war
narrative_blocks.body: Mayor Tom L. Johnson's war to bring Cleveland's street railways under public control ended in Robert's court. His settlement, the Tayler Grant, took effect on 18 December 1909: it held the lines to six percent profit on a sliding scale and gave the city council charge of how they ran.

narrative_blocks.header: Cassie Chadwick in his courtroom
narrative_blocks.body: Theodore Roosevelt put Robert on the federal bench for northern Ohio in January 1905, with courts at Cleveland and Toledo. Among the first cases before him was the trial of Cassie Chadwick, the Cleveland swindler who had borrowed fortunes from banks by passing herself off as Andrew Carnegie's daughter.

narrative_blocks.header: He sat in judgment on contested House seats
narrative_blocks.body: Elected to Congress in 1894 for the first of four terms, Robert chaired the House Committee on Elections No. 1, which ruled on disputed seats, from 1897 until he retired. He declined to run in 1902 and went back to practice in Youngstown.

narrative_blocks.header: Superintendent of schools at twenty
narrative_blocks.body: Fresh from Western Reserve College in 1872, Robert taught a year at Lisbon High School and at twenty became the town's superintendent of schools. He then edited the Buckeye State newspaper while reading law, and in 1876 married a Lisbon girl, Helen Vance.

narrative_blocks.header: A Comptroller's son at Georgetown
narrative_blocks.body: Robert's mother died eleven weeks after he was born. His father went to Washington in 1863 as First Comptroller of the Treasury, and Robert spent three years at Georgetown University before taking his degree at Western Reserve College in 1872.

narrative_blocks.header: A cannonball killed him at Shiloh
narrative_blocks.body: Major Edwards was struck by a cannonball and instantly killed at the Battle of Shiloh on April 7, 1862, shot dead from his horse while rallying the 19th Ohio. His colonel wrote the governor that Edwards had fallen gallantly doing his duty to his regiment and his country.

narrative_blocks.header: First sergeant to major in eight months
narrative_blocks.body: Edwards enlisted as a first sergeant in the 19th Ohio Infantry in August 1861 and was discharged for promotion eight days later, rising to major on the field and staff. He held that rank for barely seven months before Shiloh, where his death opened a vacancy his colonel asked be filled at once.

narrative_blocks.header: His death at Shiloh made a future senator
narrative_blocks.body: Timothy Dwight Edwards, a major in the 19th Ohio, was killed at the Battle of Shiloh in 1862 at twenty-four. His death opened the next step on the promotion ladder for a fellow officer, Charles Manderson, who went on to serve as a United States senator from Nebraska.

narrative_blocks.header: A cenotaph waits in his Ohio hometown
narrative_blocks.body: Edwards was buried among the Union dead at Shiloh National Cemetery in Tennessee. His family raised an empty memorial stone for him at Oak Hill Cemetery in Youngstown, Ohio, the hometown he had left to enlist.

orbit_connections.name: Gov. Frederick Walker Pitkin (1837-1886)
orbit_connections.relationship: 2nd Governor of Colorado; probable Connecticut Pitkin cousin of HD2206's husband Timothy Pitkin (1792-1874)
orbit_connections.notes: Frederick Walker Pitkin (Aug 31, 1837 – Dec 18, 1886) was the 2nd Governor of Colorado 1879-1883. Born in Manchester, Hartford County CT — the same county as Timothy Pitkin the merchant (East Hartford CT, X00705, husband of HD2206). Frederick's father was Eli Pitkin (c.1799-1849, Manchester CT), son of Eleazer Strong Pitkin (1763-1822). Timothy (1792) and Eli (c.1799) were almost certainly first cousins in the Connecticut Pitkin family — same county, same generation. narrative_blocks.header: He held out for Wilson in 1912
narrative_blocks.body: He went to the National Democratic Convention of 1912 as a delegate and stayed with Woodrow Wilson's nomination to the end. He was prominent at home on public questions, women's suffrage among them.

narrative_blocks.header: The third of five generations at Brooksholm
narrative_blocks.body: He farmed the Pearl Creek place his grandfather had bought off Stephen Wilkinson in 1814 and his father had run as a station. Five generations of Brookses lived there in all.

notable.notable_blurb: Broadway playwright; McClure’s managing editor

narrative_blocks.header: Spread Eagle ran eighty nights on Broadway
narrative_blocks.body: It opened on 4 April 1927 under Jed Harris, staged by George Abbott and written with Walter Lister of the Evening Post. Raymond Massey played the Hearst-modelled Joe Cobb and directed it in London; Jamey Sheridan took the part in 1999.

narrative_blocks.header: The FCC banned it from radio
narrative_blocks.body: A titan of American business manufactures a pretext for invading Mexico to protect his holdings there, and the play was kept off the air for it. Lost for decades, it surfaced in a library basement and was recorded in 1999.

narrative_blocks.header: McClure sent for him, then Fox kept him
narrative_blocks.body: Eleven newspaper jobs and the Rochester Herald police beat brought him to S. S. McClure's notice and the managing editorship in 1925. Fox signed him for six months in 1929 and held him two years; Carole Lombard played Big News.

narrative_blocks.header: Two hundred and forty-nine soldiers at Poitiers
narrative_blocks.body: In 1919, straight off the Western Front, he was one of 249 American soldiers enrolled as full-time students at the University of Poitiers. Fifteen other French universities took soldier-students that year.

narrative_blocks.header: Deported for claiming to be Canadian
narrative_blocks.body: He tried to enlist in the Canadian Army in 1914 and was put back over the border for a false declaration of citizenship. He went instead with the 77th Division's 302nd Ammunition Train to Chateau-Thierry, the Aisne and the Meuse-Argonne.

narrative_blocks.header: His son fell in the Bulge
narrative_blocks.body: Hugh Torbert Brooks was killed on January 2, 1945, in the Battle of the Bulge — the second world war claiming the son of a man who had come through the Meuse-Argonne in the first.

narrative_blocks.header: He failed freshman English and left
narrative_blocks.body: He went up to Rochester in 1917 meaning to read law with his friend James Marshall Campbell and practise alongside him. The freshman English course beat him, he withdrew, and the practice never happened.

Birthplace: his own obituary says Brooksholm at Pearl Creek; FamilySearch says Wyoming, N.Y. Both are in Wyoming County.

narrative_blocks.body: She was professor of educational psychology at the University of Minnesota. Her husband collaborated with her on Dead or Alive in 1931, nine years after they married.

narrative_blocks.header: Taken at the Baraque de Fraiture crossroads
narrative_blocks.body: A machine gunner with D Troop of the 87th Cavalry Reconnaissance Squadron, 7th Armored Division, he was cut off as his unit pulled back from St Vith. The Germans took him at the crossroads on 23 December 1944.

narrative_blocks.header: He died a prisoner in Dulag 377
narrative_blocks.body: He died on 2 January 1945 of wounds taken in the fighting. German records say he was killed in an Allied air raid on the camp, with five other American prisoners.

narrative_blocks.header: Found in a mass grave in 1947
narrative_blocks.body: A search near Regne in March 1947 turned up nothing. His remains were recovered at Niederprum that August and buried at Ardennes in September; his final grave was given him in March 1949.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale in 1941, the army in February 1942
narrative_blocks.body: He came out of Groton High School and entered Yale in 1941. He withdrew and volunteered for the Army of the United States on 5 February 1942, at eighteen.

narrative_blocks.header: His father came home from the last war
narrative_blocks.body: George Sprague Brooks had gone out with the 77th Division in 1918 and come home to write about it. He outlived this son by sixteen years.

narrative_blocks.header: Bryn Mawr, then Cornell law, then Rochester
narrative_blocks.body: She took her degree at Bryn Mawr and her law degree at Cornell, then spent her whole professional career as an attorney for Lawyers' Co-op at Rochester.

narrative_blocks.header: She rebuilt the monuments at Arnold Park
narrative_blocks.body: She lived for years on Arnold Park in Rochester and was instrumental in financing and reconstructing the monuments at either end of it. She backed the Eastman House and the Museum and Science Center.

narrative_blocks.header: Opera houses across America and Europe
narrative_blocks.body: She and her brother David shared a passion for opera and went to hear it wherever it was sung, across the United States and Europe. At home she volunteered for the Finger Lakes Trail Conference.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brother marched to Quebec with Benedict Arnold
narrative_blocks.body: Rhoda Ogden's brother Matthias was a lieutenant colonel of the New Jersey line who marched on Quebec with Benedict Arnold in 1775 and was wounded in the assault. He later devised a daring plan to seize a visiting British prince.

narrative_blocks.header: A governor brother, a Stamp Act delegate father
narrative_blocks.body: Her father, Robert Ogden, spoke for the New Jersey Assembly and sat in the Stamp Act Congress of 1765. Her brother Aaron Ogden rose to be Governor of New Jersey. Rhoda married into the Edwards family and bore fourteen children.

narrative_blocks.header: From Elizabethtown to a Berkshire hill town
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Elizabethtown, New Jersey, in 1741, she followed her husband north to Stockbridge and outlived him by nearly a decade. She died in 1822, in her eighties.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father defied the Stamp Act Congress
narrative_blocks.body: Rhoda's father, Robert Ogden, was Speaker of the New Jersey Assembly and a delegate to the 1765 Stamp Act Congress. When he refused to sign its petitions, holding they should pass through the colonial assemblies first, New Jersey burned him in effigy, and he resigned the speakership.

Buried South Cemetery, Brooklyn, Windham County CT. (EH 1909; FindAGrave)

narrative_blocks.header: Eyes that could read your inmost soul
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah Edwards Tyler was five feet four, dark-complexioned, with piercing black eyes a granddaughter remembered as able to read one's inmost soul. Witty and vivacious, an insatiable reader who devoured Walter Scott in old age, she was called a Puritan worthy of the great Puritan divine, whose oldest granddaughter she was.

narrative_blocks.header: She married Israel Putnam's son-in-law
narrative_blocks.body: Widowed young, Sarah's second husband was Capt. Daniel Tyler, a Harvard man who had been adjutant to General Israel Putnam at Bunker Hill, and whose first wife was Putnam's own daughter. Their blended household grew so large they built a house long the wonder and admiration of the country.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son drank low, then preached crowds sober
narrative_blocks.body: Her son Rev. Jonathan Edwards Chaplin, a gifted lawyer, fell into years of ruinous drink before a dramatic 1830 conversion. He became a Methodist minister and temperance lecturer whose speeches swept all before them, dying in 1846 with the words: All is peace, all is glory.

narrative_blocks.header: Chaplin, Connecticut, was named for her in-laws
narrative_blocks.body: Her first husband, Benjamin Chaplin Jr. of Mansfield, was son of the deacon for whom the Connecticut town of Chaplin was named. A Yale student, he died about a month before their son Jonathan was born.

people.research_notes: b. Jan 20, 1763 Elizabethtown NJ; d. Feb 3, 1845 Albion, Calhoun County MI age 82. Named "Edward Hooker" — for the Hooker family heritage. m. Mary "Polly" Ballard (b.Jan 16, 1764 Hadley MA; d.Feb 12, 1824 Chenango County NY) Sep 4, 1783 Hadley MA. 11 children. Pine lumber business on Chenango and Susquehanna Rivers; ran lumber to Baltimore. NY State Legislature 1797-1798. Moved to Broome County NY c.1800, later Michigan. (EH 1909; FindAGrave; Online vital records)

narrative_blocks.header: The Indians named him the handsome man
narrative_blocks.body: Six feet three or four, slender, and uncommonly handsome, Edward went with his father to the boundary-line survey and was adopted by the Indians there, who gave him a name meaning the handsome man. His niece remembered the looks all her life.

narrative_blocks.header: He floated pine down the Susquehanna to Baltimore
narrative_blocks.body: From about 1800 Edward worked the Chenango and Susquehanna rivers, cutting pine and running lumber downstream to Baltimore. He made it pay for years, and drew his brother William into buying timberland and building sawmills alongside him.

narrative_blocks.header: A pioneer legislator who ended in Michigan
narrative_blocks.body: He lived the frontier life across new country, was elected to the New York legislature, and was much respected. Two of his children settled in Michigan, and there he followed, dying at Albion in 1845.

people.research_notes: b. Oct 16, 1764 Elizabethtown NJ; d. ~1832 Binghamton NY. EH #938. NOTE: Not the theologian Jonathan Edwards (1703-1758). m. Lucy Woodbridge (his cousin — daughter of Lucy Edwards Woodbridge H00380) — this is a double Hooker descendant marriage. The Lucy Woodbridge he married is H00929 in our tree. (EH 1909; Online vital records)

narrative_blocks.header: He married his first cousin Lucy
narrative_blocks.body: Jonathan married Lucy Woodbridge of Stockbridge, the daughter of his father's sister Lucy Edwards — his first cousin. The Edwards and Woodbridge families, already entwined at Stockbridge, were bound a generation tighter by the match.

narrative_blocks.header: He traded a farm for the town center
narrative_blocks.body: Given a Stockbridge farm by his father, Jonathan swapped it for land owned by a settler at the site of present-day Binghamton, and so came to hold property in the center of the growing town. He lived there many years, calling daily on his sister Mary Whiting nearby.

narrative_blocks.header: Remembered for his originality and wit
narrative_blocks.body: Those who knew him recalled Jonathan as a man of marked originality and sharp humor. A granddaughter remembered that he and his mother were 'mighty in prayer,' praying for their children's children to the latest generation — that they might love and honor God rather than grow rich or prominent.

narrative_blocks.header: A brilliant lawyer, gone before forty
narrative_blocks.body: He practiced law first in Albany and then in Cooperstown, where a relation remembered him as “a brilliant lawyer,” tall and fine-looking like the rest of his family. He died there in 1805, not yet forty.

narrative_blocks.header: His nephew married his daughter
narrative_blocks.body: His sister Sarah's son, Edwin Tyler, married Richard's own daughter Alla Mary — nephew and son-in-law in one man. The Edwards and Tyler families kept folding back into each other.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Her Andover home as Mrs. Farrar; later a Phillips Academy boarding house

narrative_blocks.header: Out on the snow to see Saturn
narrative_blocks.body: The winter she died, at seventy-nine, Phebe was reading new books on astronomy. When a neighbor set up a telescope one cold evening, she walked out on the snow to see the rings of Saturn; she died a few weeks later, in January 1848.

narrative_blocks.header: A reader all her life
narrative_blocks.body: Phebe grew up a reader in her father Timothy Edwards's house and stayed one. She took every new discovery and invention as a sign of progress, tending, as she saw it, toward the advancement of the Redeemer's kingdom.

narrative_blocks.header: She made Andover's seminary her household
narrative_blocks.body: Phebe's second husband, Samuel Farrar, was treasurer of the Andover Theological Seminary, and she made its concerns her own. Ministers and their families were always welcome at the treasurer's house.

narrative_blocks.header: Married to the man who trained preachers
narrative_blocks.body: Phebe's first husband, Rev. Asahel Hooker, trained young ministers who boarded in their Goshen parsonage. She was widowed in 1813, married Samuel Farrar the next year, and moved to Andover for good.

narrative_blocks.header: Two ways back to the same Hooker
narrative_blocks.body: Phebe and Asahel were third cousins, great-great-grandchildren of Rev. Samuel Hooker: she through his daughter Mary Hooker Pierpont, he down the Hooker name. Their four children had Thomas Hooker's blood from both sides.

people.research_notes: b. Nov 11, 1770 Stockbridge MA; d. 1851 Lisle, Broome County NY age ~80. m. Rebecca Tappan. (EH 1909; FindAGrave) ENRICHED Stage 6Y-686 per compiler (Beers History of Greene County; son William W. Edwards’s 1849 memorial speech). Son of Timothy Edwards (H00381) — who loaned the Continental Congress upward of $100,000 in gold, eventually lost — and Rhoda Ogden, elder sister of Gov. Aaron Ogden. Apprenticed 1784 to his uncles Col. Mathias Ogden and Col. Oliver Spencer, Elizabethtown tanners. His quarter-time tanning process and machinery transformed American leather manufacture; tannery burned 1830, rebuilt the same season. Married Rebecca Tappan on his own twenty-third birthday, Nov 11, 1793. Green-Wood Section 92, Lot 1671 — the obelisk eroded illegible except EDWARDS. DEATH-PLACE VARIANCE: EH 1909 gives d. Lisle, Broome County NY — superseded by the son’s 1849-published memorial account (last decade in New York and Brooklyn), FAG, and the Green-Wood Section 92 Lot 1671 burial record, all compiler-supplied. EH variance retained here for the record.

notable.notable_blurb: Tanner-inventor who founded Hunter, New York

career.notes: four patents before 1813: copper heater, hide mill, hot-liquor application, roller

narrative_blocks.header: He built America’s first covered tannery
narrative_blocks.body: At Hunter on the Schoharie Kill — 1,200 acres at the heart of the hemlock bark region — his New York Tannery of 1817 was believed the first modern tannery entirely under cover in the United States, built to tan 5,000 hides a year. The village that grew around it was first called Edwardsville.

narrative_blocks.header: At sixty-four he beggared himself
narrative_blocks.body: Legally discharged from his debts by the two-thirds act in 1818, he never accepted it as settlement: in 1834 he had everything he owned appraised, sold it to his three eldest sons, and distributed over $25,000 to creditors discharged sixteen years before. He spent his last decade supported by his children.

narrative_blocks.header: A childhood collision marked him for life
narrative_blocks.body: Dodging around the chimney at four years old, he collided head-on with an Indian boy at play — the blow left one side of his head permanently enlarged, a deformity that frightened children unaccustomed to him. Six feet four and of commanding presence, he was, his son said, exceedingly kind at heart.

narrative_blocks.header: He stood guard over the president-elect
narrative_blocks.body: In 1789, as Washington traveled to New York for his inauguration, he breakfasted at Elizabethtown under a guard drawn from the six tallest men of the local militia company. William Edwards, six feet three and a half, was one of them, and escorted the general to the Point to embark. In old age he called it the proudest moment of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: Not extravagant, he said, at millions
narrative_blocks.body: Edwards's patented bark mill, hide mill, heaters, and rolling machine remade American leather-making during his Northampton years. In an 1838 address, Gideon Lee enumerated three decades of progress in the trade and credited it chiefly to Edwards, rating the benefit, without extravagance, at millions.

b. Jul 12, 1774 Stockbridge MA; d. Sep 22, 1852 Jersey City NJ age 78. Sea captain — married Sarah Haigh in London England. Buried Bridge Street Cemetery, Northampton MA. (EH 1909; Wikipedia; FindAGrave)

narrative_blocks.header: Six foot three, with piercing black eyes
narrative_blocks.body: For years he was master of a sailing ship trading between Charleston, Savannah, and Liverpool, and ever after he delighted in telling the tales of that life. Dark and straight and six foot three, he was a man no room could overlook.

narrative_blocks.header: At St. Petersburg during Napoleon's invasion of Russia
narrative_blocks.body: His sea trade carried him to St. Petersburg while Napoleon's army was deep in Russia, and as far north as the White Sea port of Archangel. He liked to scoff at the old schoolbook legend of the maelstrom off Norway, having sailed those waters himself.

narrative_blocks.header: He swapped the sea for cotton, then tanning
narrative_blocks.body: After marrying an Englishwoman around 1820 he left the sea, settling first as a cotton broker in Augusta, then moving to the Catskills to take up tanning, and ending his days in Jersey City. There he served for some years as a justice of the peace.

narrative_blocks.header: Madam Dwight, a wonder and a joy
narrative_blocks.body: Northampton called Rhoda “a wonder and a joy to all who knew her, for intellectual power and brightness, to the end of her very long life,” and held her in veneration well beyond the town.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifteen children with Josiah Dwight
narrative_blocks.body: Rhoda married Josiah Dwight of Northampton on 3 March 1798, and they had fifteen children.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed about 1822 with many children
narrative_blocks.body: Josiah died about 1822, and Rhoda raised their children alone. She lived forty-one years more, and died at Northampton in 1863.

narrative_blocks.header: She made her home in Jonathan Edwards's Northampton
narrative_blocks.body: A granddaughter of Jonathan Edwards — dismissed from the Northampton pulpit in 1750 — she raised her family in that same town and died there at eighty-five.

bio.bio_blurb: Chief educator of her six daughters

narrative_blocks.header: She could match Aaron Burr for wit
narrative_blocks.body: Full of life and gaiety in her childhood, she could dance with the merriest, turn the house upside down with the girls, run away with the hearts of the young men, and match her cousin Aaron Burr in fun and wit.

narrative_blocks.header: She was the image of her grandfather
narrative_blocks.body: She was a great favourite of her father, Timothy Edwards, who once introduced her to some Scotch friends as, more than any member of the family, the image of her grandfather.

narrative_blocks.header: Two or three houses stood there then
narrative_blocks.body: At twenty-two she went with her husband, a young Berkshire lawyer, to Chenango Point where the Chenango meets the Susquehanna, now Binghamton. There were then two or three houses in the place and the county was almost a wilderness.

narrative_blocks.header: She was among the church's first members
narrative_blocks.body: The church organised at Chenango Point after she arrived counted her among its few original members. Her religion was at once a controlling principle and a ruling passion, her daily business and her constant delight.

narrative_blocks.header: She was the chief educator of her daughters
narrative_blocks.body: She taught her daughters herself and stamped her own mind, moral character and religion on them to an unusual degree. She stayed interested to the end in passing events, in her children's and grandchildren's business, in the growth of the town and the welfare of the nation.

narrative_blocks.header: The whole city crowded to her funeral
narrative_blocks.body: Her mind was as clear at fourscore and ten as it had been in the prime of life, and she died at ninety-two, the last of Timothy and Rhoda Edwards's children. All classes, all ages, all denominations and all nationalities came.

narrative_blocks.header: The town set its clocks by his prayers
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel Farrar's habits were so exact that Andover was said to time itself by him, by the hour he began family prayers, or passed on his daily walk to Indian Ridge. He was, by long repute, one of the town's leading citizens and a local character.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept the books for college and seminary
narrative_blocks.body: A Harvard-trained lawyer, Farrar became a chief founder of the Andover Theological Seminary and its first librarian, and treasurer of both the Seminary and Phillips Academy. At the secular end of the same methodical life he was the first president of the Andover National Bank, from 1826 to 1856.

narrative_blocks.header: Under his roof, America's first foreign missionary
narrative_blocks.body: As Academy treasurer he was housed at 21 Phillips Street from 1811 until his death. The same house lodged Madame Phoebe Phillips, who died there in 1812, and Adoniram Judson, the first foreign missionary sent out by the American Board, boarding at Andover before he sailed.

narrative_blocks.header: The missionary board ran in the family
narrative_blocks.body: Edward's sister Mary Ann married Elias Cornelius, who went south for the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions and died its secretary in 1832. In 1840 Edward took a seat on the Board himself, as a corporate member.

narrative_blocks.header: Thomas Hooker's life, told by a descendant
narrative_blocks.body: In 1849, the year he took the pulpit at South Windsor, a few miles up the Connecticut from Hartford, Edward published The Life of Thomas Hooker, his great-great-great-great-grandfather. The 1909 family genealogy was built on it.

narrative_blocks.header: A pastor turned temperance editor in 1829
narrative_blocks.body: Edward was ordained at Green's Farms in August 1821 and kept that pulpit eight years. In 1829 he left it to become associate general agent of the American Temperance Society and to edit its paper, the Journal of Humanity.

narrative_blocks.header: Back to Vermont, and onto Middlebury's board
narrative_blocks.body: Edward was installed at Bennington in February 1832 and preached there twelve years, and from 1834 he sat as a trustee of Middlebury, where he had graduated in 1814. In 1844 he went to East Windsor Hill to teach sacred rhetoric.

narrative_blocks.header: The son who carried the missionary's name
narrative_blocks.body: Five months after Elias Cornelius died at Hartford, Edward's son was born at Bennington, in July 1832, and Edward named him Elias Cornelius Hooker.

narrative_blocks.header: He outlived three wives
narrative_blocks.body: Edward married Faith Trumbull Huntington in 1821, and she bore all six of his children before her death in 1850. He was married six years to the widowed Elizabeth Sheldon Lyman and thirteen to Lucy Bagley, and outlived all three.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote the cookbook that fed a generation
narrative_blocks.body: Widowed young with six children, Mary Cornelius turned her domestic command into a book. The Young Housekeeper's Friend (1849) became a standard American kitchen manual, reprinted for decades.

narrative_blocks.header: Her first publication was signed A Mother
narrative_blocks.body: Before the cookbook she won a cash prize for a religious tract, Letters on Christian Education, published anonymously as A Mother. A second tract, a sailor's-conversion tale, followed.

narrative_blocks.header: Schooled at Litchfield, a century before suffrage
narrative_blocks.body: In 1810 she attended the Litchfield Female Academy, the era's foremost school for women. Her mother, father, and sister Sarah all appear in its ledgers.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a missionary, raised his six children
narrative_blocks.body: In 1818 she married Rev. Elias Cornelius, a missionary to the Cherokee and later secretary of the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions. He died in 1832; she lived another forty-eight years.

narrative_blocks.header: Cramp in one hand, so he switched
narrative_blocks.body: Decades of bookkeeping gave him writer's cramp in his right hand, so he taught himself to write with his left. He made the changeover in a few weeks and kept the books going.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped bring dial phones to Wausau
narrative_blocks.body: Among his civic ventures was the Wausau Telephone Company, an early adopter of automatic dial telephones before the technology was common. It was later folded into the system that became General Telephone of Wisconsin.

narrative_blocks.header: Made an elder for life, and he was
narrative_blocks.body: In 1893 the First Presbyterian Church of Wausau elected him Ruling Elder for life, and for fifty years he served as clerk of its session. He ran the Sunday school and its mission chapel alongside the books.

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband's fame all came after her death
narrative_blocks.body: She died at thirty-nine in the first year of his Columbia presidency. The Nobel Prize and the vice-presidential nomination that made his name were still ahead of him.

narrative_blocks.header: The same loss, one generation apart
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother died in January 1870, weeks before her seventh birthday. Thirty-three years later, she too died in January — leaving her daughter Sarah at seven, the same midwinter loss repeated.

people.research_notes: b. May 23, 1865 Jersey City NJ; d. Jan 4, 1905 Pinehurst NC age 39. Columbia 1887 (Delta Psi). NYSE member 1903; seat sold for record $82,000 at death. Named "Edwards Ogden Schuyler" for the Edwards heritage. (Wikipedia on Edwards Ogden Schuyler; FindAGrave)

narrative_blocks.header: His Exchange seat sold for a record sum
narrative_blocks.body: A Columbia-educated broker, Edwards Ogden Schuyler held a seat on the New York Stock Exchange. When he died at thirty-nine, the seat fetched a record eighty-two thousand dollars.

narrative_blocks.header: He died young at thirty-nine
narrative_blocks.body: Schuyler died at Pinehurst, North Carolina, in 1905, only thirty-nine years old. His given names carried the family's Edwards heritage.

narrative_blocks.header: A popular broker on the Stock Exchange
narrative_blocks.body: Schuyler co-founded the brokerage house that became E. O. Schuyler and Company and was elected to the New York Stock Exchange in 1903. Contemporaries knew him as one of the best-liked figures on the floor.

narrative_blocks.header: His sister married Columbia's president
narrative_blocks.body: Edwards was a son of the arms magnate Jacob Rutsen Schuyler, whose firm supplied weapons during the Civil War. His sister Susanna married Nicholas Murray Butler, the long-serving Columbia president and Nobel peace laureate.

narrative_blocks.header: He died suddenly at thirty-nine
narrative_blocks.body: After barely two years building his firm, Schuyler died of sudden intestinal complications while vacationing in 1905, at thirty-nine. He left a widow and two surviving daughters.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran Columbia for forty-three years
narrative_blocks.body: He was president of Columbia from 1902 to 1945, the longest tenure in its history, founding its schools of journalism and business and Teachers College. In 1919 he brought in admissions quotas limiting Jewish enrolment.

narrative_blocks.header: He shared the 1931 Nobel Peace Prize
narrative_blocks.body: As head of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace he pushed the Kellogg-Briand Pact outlawing aggressive war, and in 1931 shared the Nobel Peace Prize with Jane Addams. He advised seven presidents on foreign affairs.

narrative_blocks.header: Theodore Roosevelt called him Nicholas Miraculous
narrative_blocks.body: A lifelong Republican insider and a friend of Theodore Roosevelt, Butler earned the nickname for his prodigious energy and his connections. In 1912 he took the electoral votes meant for Vice President James Sherman, dead days before.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept Hemingway from the 1941 Pulitzer
narrative_blocks.body: In 1941 the fiction jury chose For Whom the Bell Tolls and the Pulitzer board agreed. Butler, its chairman by office, thought the novel offensive and talked the board out of it, so no fiction prize was given that year.

narrative_blocks.header: He chose the names carved on his library
narrative_blocks.body: Butler picked the names carved along the porticos of South Hall, Columbia's new library of 1934, and the quotations for its main rooms. In 1946, the year after he retired, it was renamed Butler Library.

narrative_blocks.header: An ex-student hid an insult in an ode
narrative_blocks.body: In 1939 Rolfe Humphries, once Butler's student, published a Draft Ode for a Phi Beta Kappa Occasion in Poetry. Read down, the first letters of its lines spelled Nicholas Murray Butler is a horses ass, and the editors apologized.

narrative_blocks.header: He welcomed Hitler's ambassador in 1933
narrative_blocks.body: On 12 December 1933 Butler gave Hans Luther, Nazi Germany's ambassador, the Columbia platform students and faculty had petitioned him to cancel, and protesters fought the police outside. Butler called their stand illiberal.

narrative_blocks.header: She organized Republican women in New York
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah was vice-chairman of the New York Republican State Committee and the party’s leading organizer of women voters in the state through the 1920s, the first decade in which American women could vote.

narrative_blocks.header: She took the state chairmanship in 1928
narrative_blocks.body: When George K. Morris died in 1928 she was called on to assume the duties of chairman and headed the Republican party in New York. She is the only woman ever to have opened a Republican convention in the state.

narrative_blocks.header: She and her father led the wet forces
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah campaigned against Prohibition alongside her father, and the two were reckoned among the leaders of the country’s sopping wet forces. Repeal came in December 1933, eight months after she married and left for England.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a Guards captain and left America
narrative_blocks.body: In April 1933 Sarah married Captain Neville Lawrence of the Coldstream Guards, son of Sir Walter Roper Lawrence, first baronet, and went to live in Surrey. She died there in February 1947 at fifty-one.

narrative_blocks.header: Schuyler and Van Rensselaer through her mother
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother Susanna Edwards Schuyler carried two of the oldest Dutch lines in New York and died in 1903, when Sarah was seven. Her father’s people were the Buchanans of Leny, at the entrance to the Scottish Highlands.

narrative_blocks.header: Roosevelt asked for her at the White House
narrative_blocks.body: Theodore Roosevelt wrote to her father to ask that he bring Sarah down for two December nights — the first at the New Willard, the second at the White House, where the Speyers and the Burgesses were being entertained.

narrative_blocks.body: Timothy Edwards Chaplin followed the sea. His voyages carried him to the far side of the continent, and he died at Acapulco, on the Pacific coast of Mexico, unmarried.

narrative_blocks.header: He drank himself low, then preached crowds sober
narrative_blocks.body: A gifted Yale-trained lawyer, Jonathan Edwards Chaplin fell into years of ruinous drink that nearly destroyed him. In 1830 he underwent a dramatic conversion, joined the Methodist church, and became a temperance lecturer whose speeches were said to sweep all before them.

narrative_blocks.header: From the Buffalo bar to an Ohio pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: Admitted to the bar in 1813, Chaplin practiced law at Buffalo, then followed the frontier west to Ohio. After his conversion he gave up the law for the ministry, preaching across Ohio and ending as principal of a university branch in Michigan.

narrative_blocks.header: His last breath: all is peace, all glory
narrative_blocks.body: Worn down by his labors as a frontier educator and preacher, Chaplin resigned his Michigan post as his health failed. He died in 1846, crying with his last breath: all is peace, all is glory.

narrative_blocks.header: A drunkard whose integrity no one doubted
narrative_blocks.body: Even at the depth of his dissipation, the account holds, he was never profane or cruel, never spoke an unkind word to his wife, and no man doubted his integrity. He gave the needy the whole of his last loaf rather than half.

narrative_blocks.header: Putnam's adjutant at Bunker Hill
narrative_blocks.body: Daniel Tyler graduated Harvard in 1771 and, when war came, served as adjutant to General Israel Putnam through many campaigns, including the field at Bunker Hill. He later raised and equipped an artillery company at his own expense.

narrative_blocks.header: A general's daughter, then a divine's granddaughter
narrative_blocks.body: His first wife was Mehitable Putnam, daughter of General Israel Putnam; his second was Sarah Edwards, granddaughter of Jonathan Edwards. The two families he married into joined Revolutionary command to Puritan theology.

narrative_blocks.header: Three sons at West Point
narrative_blocks.body: Three of Daniel's sons went to West Point: Septimus, Edwin and Daniel, the future Union general. Septimus died in 1817 aboard the frigate Congress, sailing home from Santo Domingo, where he was the U.S. commercial agent.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a widowed firebrand preacher
narrative_blocks.body: In 1817 Sarah became the second wife of Rev. Samuel Porter Williams, a blunt Calvinist already raising children from his first marriage. Nine years later she was a widow at thirty-five, and she outlived him by more than three decades.

narrative_blocks.header: She raised eight children not her own
narrative_blocks.body: When Sarah married the widowed Reverend Williams in 1817, he already had eight children from his late first wife. She took them on as her own and bore six more, running a full parsonage household until his death left her a widow at thirty-five.

military_service.notes: First lieutenant of ordnance Mar 12, 1813; captain Aug 5, 1813; retained as captain of ordnance in the peacetime army Feb 8, 1815; dismissed Aug 13, 1819.

narrative_blocks.header: His bride was also his first cousin
narrative_blocks.body: In 1821 Edwin married Alla Mary Edwards, the daughter of his mother's brother Richard — first cousins, both descended from Rev. Jonathan Edwards. The match knotted the Edwards and Tyler branches a generation tighter.

narrative_blocks.header: He died far from home in Philadelphia
narrative_blocks.body: After Alla Mary died in 1833, Edwin remarried a Harrisburg widow and moved to Pennsylvania. He died at Philadelphia in 1838, only about forty-four years old.

narrative_blocks.header: From West Point cadet to ordnance captain
narrative_blocks.body: Trained at West Point, Edwin entered the War of 1812 in the ordnance service, made first lieutenant in March 1813 and captain by that August, responsible for arming the army's 5th District across Maryland and Virginia. When the war ended he was among the few officers the shrunken peacetime army chose to keep.

narrative_blocks.header: Dismissed from the army without a reason
narrative_blocks.body: Four years into peacetime service, the War Department dismissed Captain Tyler from the ordnance corps in August 1819. No charge or explanation survives in the record — an abrupt close to a career that had risen quickly.

bio.title: Brig. Gen.

military_service.unit: 1st Connecticut Infantry; division, Army of Northeastern Virginia
military_service.notes: Commanded a division at First Bull Run; led a brigade at the Siege of Corinth; briefly commanded Camp Douglas.

narrative_blocks.header: Blamed for the Union rout at Bull Run
narrative_blocks.body: Tyler commanded a division at the First Battle of Bull Run in 1861 and absorbed much of the blame for the Union defeat, mustered out within weeks. Recommissioned in 1862, he led troops at the siege of Corinth and briefly ran the Camp Douglas prison camp.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded the Alabama city of Anniston
narrative_blocks.body: After resigning from the army in 1864, Tyler built blast furnaces and ran railroads, finding far more success in rails than in pig iron. In the 1870s he established the Woodstock Iron Company and helped found Anniston, named for his daughter-in-law Annie.

narrative_blocks.header: West Point artillerist who studied in France
narrative_blocks.body: Graduating from West Point in 1819, Tyler became an authority on artillery, studying at the French school at Metz and translating French gunnery manuals into English. His honesty inspecting private arms contractors may have stalled his promotion beyond first lieutenant.

narrative_blocks.header: First in Connecticut to volunteer, at sixty-two
narrative_blocks.body: When war came in April 1861 Daniel was sixty-two and twenty-seven years out of uniform, and he was the first man in Connecticut to volunteer. He went to the front as colonel of the 1st Connecticut Infantry and within weeks had a division under McDowell.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight thousand parolees at Camp Douglas
narrative_blocks.body: In September 1862 Daniel took over Camp Douglas in Chicago, where eight thousand Union men paroled after the surrender at Harpers Ferry waited to be exchanged, in barracks left filthy by the Confederate prisoners from Fort Donelson. He was relieved in November.

narrative_blocks.header: West Point's oldest living graduate
narrative_blocks.body: Daniel had graduated from West Point in 1819, and when he died in November 1882, at eighty-three and visiting New York, he was its oldest living graduate. He was buried at Hillside Cemetery in Anniston, the Alabama town he had founded.

narrative_blocks.header: From Bunker Hill to the White House
narrative_blocks.body: Daniel's father had been adjutant of Israel Putnam's regiment at Bunker Hill. His daughter Gertrude married Charles Carow in 1859, and her daughter Edith married Theodore Roosevelt in 1886 and was First Lady from 1901.

orbit_connections.name: Elias Boudinot (Gallegina Watie, c.1802-1839)
orbit_connections.relationship: Cornelius selected him for Foreign Mission School Cornwall CT 1818
orbit_connections.notes: Cherokee leader; editor of the Cherokee Phoenix (1828), first Native American newspaper. Signed Treaty of New Echota (1835) ceding Cherokee lands — was assassinated in 1839 by tribal opponents who saw him as a traitor. Named his son Elias Cornelius Boudinot in honor of Cornelius.

orbit_connections.name: Elias Cornelius Boudinot (1835-1890)
orbit_connections.relationship: Named for Elias Cornelius
orbit_connections.notes: Son of Elias Boudinot; Confederate colonel (2nd Cherokee Mounted Rifles); first Native American admitted to practice before the US Supreme Court; delegate to C.S. House of Representatives from Cherokee Nation 1862-1865. Called "among the great scoundrels of the Gilded Age" by historian Richard White for his railroad lobbying activities. Born in New Echota, Cherokee Nation (now Gordon County, GA); d. Fort Smith, Arkansas 1890. The name Cornelius chose for a Cherokee student rippled through four decades of Cherokee and Confederate history.

people.research_notes:
b. Jul 31, 1794 Somers, Westchester County NY; d. Feb 12, 1832 Hartford CT age 37. Father: Dr. Elias Cornelius (1758-1823) — physician, Revolutionary War surgeon, POW in New York Provost Jail 1777-1778, met Ethan Allen in prison, escaped Jan 16, 1778. Dutch ancestry; coat of arms. Yale College 1813 (entered 1810 as a 16-year-old sophomore; converted in the Yale revival winter 1812-13; "personally guided twenty classmates to profession of faith"). Studied theology under President Timothy Dwight. Also studied under Rev. Lyman Beecher at Litchfield — "became one of Beecher's closest friends and his companion on many a jaunt"; Cornelius tells the story of Beecher's squirrel-hunting with his coat off trying to climb a tree. Licensed to preach Jan 16, 1816 Litchfield CT (Litchfield South Association). ABCFM agent 1816: fundraised intensively — in one six-month stretch traveled 1,650 miles and preached 136 times. Jan 1817-Apr 1818: 19-month journey south through VA, TN, Natchez, New Orleans, visiting Cherokee/Creek/Choctaw missions; assessed Etowah Indian Mounds in Georgia (wrote the first published account by a white person visiting the mounds). Selected Gallegina Watie (Elias Boudinot) and John Ridge for Foreign Mission School in Cornwall CT — selections that shaped Cherokee political history for decades and contributed to the Trail of Tears. Ordained Jul 21, 1819 as collegiate (associate) pastor, Tabernacle Church, Salem MA. Resigned Oct 1826 → Secretary, American Education Society 1826-1831. Elected Corresponding Secretary, ABCFM Oct 1831 (succeeding Jeremiah Evarts); died less than 5 months into that role Feb 12, 1832 Hartford CT. Published: "The Little Osage Captive: An Authentic Narrative" (1824). Memoir by Bela Bates Edwards (Boston, 1834; 3rd ed. 1842). Oil portrait by Metcalf in possession of Edward G. Perry, Avon NY. m. Mary Ann Hooker (H01355) Sep 28, 1818 Somers, Westchester NY. ORBIT LEGACY: Elias Boudinot named his son "Elias Cornelius Boudinot" (1835-1890) in honor of Cornelius — who grew up to be a Confederate colonel, the first Native American admitted to practice before the US Supreme Court, and was characterized by historian Richard White as among "the great scoundrels of the Gilded Age." (Wikipedia on Elias Cornelius; Cornelius genealogy book; Sprague, Annals 2:633; Edwards, Memoir of Cornelius 1834)

narrative_blocks.header: Two Cherokee boys he sent to Connecticut
narrative_blocks.body: On his southern tour of 1817 and 1818 Elias chose two Cherokee boys, Gallegina Watie and John Ridge, for the Foreign Mission School at Cornwall, Connecticut. Both married Cornwall women, went home as leaders of the Cherokee Nation, and signed the treaty that led to the Trail of Tears.

narrative_blocks.header: Cherokee guides showed him the Etowah mounds
narrative_blocks.body: Near present-day Cartersville, Georgia, in 1817, a party of Cherokee led Elias to the great earthen mounds on the Etowah River. Neither he nor his guides knew who had raised them, or why. His journal gave the first published account of the mounds by a white visitor.

narrative_blocks.header: Eighteen months on the road south
narrative_blocks.body: Licensed to preach on 4 June 1816 and taken on as an agent of the American Board, Elias preached and raised money in Rhode Island, Connecticut and Maryland for schools among the Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw and Creek. Then he went south himself, through Virginia, Tennessee, Natchez and New Orleans.

narrative_blocks.header: A son named for the man he succeeded
narrative_blocks.body: Elias married Mary Hooker, daughter of Rev. Asahel Hooker of Goshen, in September 1818, and their sons were named Thomas Hooker and Edward Hooker. Jeremiah Evarts, his chief at the American Board, died in May 1831; Elias took his post that October, and the son born on Christmas Day was Jeremiah Evarts Cornelius.

narrative_blocks.header: Four months at the head of the Board
narrative_blocks.body: Elias became corresponding secretary of the American Board in October 1831 and soon fell ill. He died at Hartford on 12 February 1832, at thirty-seven, leaving Mary with six children, the youngest seven weeks old.

narrative_blocks.header: A Cherokee colonel carried his name
narrative_blocks.body: Gallegina Watie, by then Elias Boudinot, named his son Elias Cornelius Boudinot in 1835. That son became a Confederate colonel and the first Native American admitted to practice before the U.S. Supreme Court; the historian Richard White counted him among the great scoundrels of the Gilded Age.

narrative_blocks.header: His father was jailed with Ethan Allen
narrative_blocks.body: Elias's father, Dr. Elias Cornelius, a surgeon's mate captured at East Chester in August 1777, was thrown into New York's Provost Jail with Ethan Allen. He refused his Loyalist father's plea to take a pardon, escaped from the prison hospital in January 1778, and rowed across the Sound to rejoin the army.

narrative_blocks.header: He served on Boston Common Council
narrative_blocks.body: John Henry Colby began practice with his father in 1889, continued until his father's death in 1890, then formed the firm Colby & Bayley. He served on Boston Common Council 1893-1895, the Board of Aldermen 1897-1899, and the Massachusetts legislature in 1900. He was also clerk and trustee of the North End Savings Bank and director of the Boston City Missionary Society.

narrative_blocks.header: He died suddenly at the summer home
narrative_blocks.body: On September 11, 1909, John Henry Colby died suddenly of heart disease at the family's summer home in Hanover, New Hampshire. His son John Noyes was fifteen. Seven years later, John Noyes died in the same town — at Dartmouth's Mary Hitchcock Memorial Hospital — at age 22.

narrative_blocks.header: He died eight days before his 23rd birthday
narrative_blocks.body: John Noyes Colby graduated from Dartmouth in 1916 — class president, football letter man, Beta Theta Pi. He enrolled in a post-graduate course at the Tuck Hospital in Hanover. In early November he contracted pneumonia, recovered enough to spend Thanksgiving in Boston, returned to Hanover on December 3, relapsed, and died on December 7, 1916 at Mary Hitchcock Memorial Hospital.

narrative_blocks.header: Three generations of Dartmouth men
narrative_blocks.body: John Noyes Colby entered Dartmouth following his father John Henry Colby (class of 1885) and his grandfather John Freeman Colby (class of 1859). Three consecutive generations of the same family at the same college, each a decade and a half apart. John Noyes graduated in 1916 — the year he died.

narrative_blocks.header: Dartmouth president Hopkins called him 'a credit
narrative_blocks.body: At John Noyes Colby's funeral on December 10, 1916, Dr. Ernest Hopkins, president of Dartmouth College, represented the faculty and stated: 'a credit to mankind, to his friends and his college, a man to be remembered as a liberalizing influence, whether on the playground, in the fraternity gatherings or in the college classroom.' The church at West Newton Street was full of college students. All pallbearers were from Beta Theta Pi.

narrative_blocks.header: His editorials read like his editor's own
narrative_blocks.body: Edward Rosewater hired him to the Omaha Bee in 1879 and trained him hard. Rosewater's son recalled that Annin was soon dashing off editorials that could not be told from Rosewater's own.

narrative_blocks.header: A college geology trip left him in Omaha
narrative_blocks.body: He took his Princeton degree in 1877 and came west that summer with a college geological expedition, meaning to stay in Omaha and read law. Within two years he was on the Omaha Bee instead.

narrative_blocks.header: He left the paper for a senator's office
narrative_blocks.body: In 1887 he became private secretary to Senator Algernon Paddock of Nebraska and went east with him that autumn. He had married the daughter of the senator's cousin, which did him no harm in Washington.

narrative_blocks.header: Four Western papers read him from Washington
narrative_blocks.body: Through the 1890s he sat on the Washington staff of the Philadelphia Public Ledger and wrote as well for the Nebraska State Journal, the Salt Lake Tribune and other Western papers. His political commentary gave him a national name.

narrative_blocks.header: He led Washington's famous Gridiron Club
narrative_blocks.body: He joined the Gridiron Club in 1890 and was its president in 1896, one of the sharp men of the congressional press gallery. The club would not admit a woman for another seventy-nine years.

narrative_blocks.header: Failing health sent him to the post office
narrative_blocks.body: Declining health took him out of newspapers in 1899 and into the postal service, his last newspaper assignment being the Philadelphia Ledger. He spent his final years at Denver in the new rural free delivery division, and died at forty-six.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote no books, only thousands of columns
narrative_blocks.body: He had written no books or pamphlets, he told his college class, having been too busy with several thousand columns of newspaper dispatches and letters. For a prospective newspaper man, he held, a bachelor of arts was worth more than any technical course.

narrative_blocks.body: Born in 1820, she was named for her aunt, the novelist Catharine Maria Sedgwick. She married the Boston lawyer William Minot and made her home at Woodbourne, the family's Jamaica Plain estate.

narrative_blocks.body: Two of her sons made names in science. Charles Sedgwick Minot became a pioneering Harvard anatomist, and Henry Davis Minot — an ornithologist who befriended the young Theodore Roosevelt at Harvard — died at thirty in a railway accident.

narrative_blocks.header: She met her husband in Rome

military_service.notes: Mortally wounded rallying a broken regiment at Antietam, 17 Sept 1862; died 29 Sept 1862.

narrative_blocks.header: He fell rallying a broken regiment at Antietam
narrative_blocks.body: As assistant adjutant general to General John Sedgwick, William Dwight Sedgwick rode into the West Woods slaughter on September 17, 1862, where the division lost two thousand men in half an hour. When the line broke he spurred to the disordered 34th New York to rally it and was shot through the back, toppling from his horse.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight hours alone with no friend near
narrative_blocks.body: Left paralyzed and abandoned as the New Yorkers fled, Sedgwick lay among bursting shells for eight hours. He drew out his pocket diary and wrote that he had not uttered a groan, lying alone in the hot sun with no friend near.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother reached him before the end
narrative_blocks.body: From the field hospital at Keedysville he wrote twice to his mother, making light of his wound so she need not travel to him. She and his sister Grace came regardless and were beside him when he died on September 29.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife learned of his death abroad
narrative_blocks.body: His wife Louisa had already sailed for Germany and could not be recalled; she learned she was a widow only after landing in Europe. He left three daughters, the youngest born two months after he left for the front and never once seen by her father.

narrative_blocks.header: Comrades remembered a merry, fearless man
narrative_blocks.body: The afternoon before the battle he rode to his old regiment and talked for two hours, leaving 'merry and jolly,' Captain Robert Gould Shaw recalled. General Oliver Howard later wrote that no one's conduct was as cool and brave, and that no soldier deserved higher commendation.

narrative_blocks.header: He found his wife studying law in Germany
narrative_blocks.body: After Harvard and a year of law, he went abroad to study in Germany, and at Hanover in 1857 he married Louisa Tellkampf, a German woman he had met there. They had three daughters before the war took him.

narrative_blocks.header: She served in the war’s hospitals
narrative_blocks.body: During the Civil War she worked in the United States hospital service, tending wounded soldiers — a Sedgwick of Stockbridge doing it, in a family that had been arguing about the country since the Constitution.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a wealthy man of letters
narrative_blocks.body: In 1867 she became the second wife of Charles Astor Bristed, the classicist and grandson of John Jacob Astor, and bore him one son. She was widowed seven years later, when the boy was five.

narrative_blocks.header: A Sedgwick who went over to Rome
narrative_blocks.body: Left a widow at forty-one, she turned Catholic and took her son abroad to be brought up — winters in Rome, summers at Innsbruck, and a Jesuit college for his schooling. He grew up to serve three popes as a private chamberlain.

narrative_blocks.header: She died at St. Cloud, outside Paris
narrative_blocks.body: Twenty-three years of Europe followed the widowhood, and she never came home to Massachusetts to live. She was brought back to the Stockbridge ground her family rings, in 1897.

narrative_blocks.body: He made his home at Woodbourne, the family's Jamaica Plain estate, and named a daughter Alice Woodbourne for it. After a run of deaths there in the early 1880s — his wife, both sisters, his brother, and that daughter — he left in 1884 for a townhouse in the city.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught anatomy at Harvard for decades
narrative_blocks.body: Charles Sedgwick Minot graduated from MIT in 1872, studied in Leipzig, Paris, and Würzburg, and taught comparative anatomy at Harvard Medical School from 1880 until his death. He pioneered the study of cellular aging and assembled one of the era's great embryological collections.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped found a psychical research society
narrative_blocks.body: A rigorous empiricist, Minot was a founding member of the American Society for Psychical Research but resigned over its unscientific drift. He publicly attacked the claims of Theosophy and so-called esoteric Buddhism.

narrative_blocks.header: He asked why living things must age
narrative_blocks.body: Minot turned the microscope on mortality itself, studying how cells slow and decline with age. His 1908 book, The Problem of Age, Growth, and Death, made him a pioneer of the science of senescence.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale and Oxford honored the Roxbury anatomist
narrative_blocks.body: Honorary degrees came from Yale, Toronto, St. Andrews, and Oxford, and he presided over the American Association for the Advancement of Science. From 1912 he taught as Harvard's exchange professor in Berlin and Jena.

narrative_blocks.header: Published authoritative bird guide as a Harvard freshman
narrative_blocks.body: His 'Land Birds and Game Birds of New England' (1877) appeared when he was a seventeen-year-old college freshman. The volume remained an authoritative reference for New England ornithology for the next two decades.

narrative_blocks.header: Theodore Roosevelt's closest Harvard ornithology friend
narrative_blocks.body: He and TR met as freshman classmates at Harvard in 1877, both already serious ornithologists. They spent vacations listing birds in the Adirondacks and co-authored 'The Summer Birds of the Adirondacks' that fall — Roosevelt's first published work.

narrative_blocks.header: Left Harvard for the railroads at twenty
narrative_blocks.body: He withdrew from Harvard as a sophomore and entered railroad management — first with the Boston & Albany, then rising through several lines to assistant treasurer of the Lehigh Valley Railroad. The choice marked him as the rare Harvard man who chose practical industry over the law.

narrative_blocks.header: Killed at thirty-one in the industry he served
narrative_blocks.body: On November 14, 1890 the Day Express on the Pennsylvania Railroad's main line collided head-on with a freight train near New Florence Pennsylvania, killing him and twenty-one others. Theodore Roosevelt, by then US Civil Service Commissioner, was devastated; the friendship had defined his college years.

narrative_blocks.header: A North Dakota city bears his name
narrative_blocks.body: When the railway reached Dakota Territory in the 1880s, James J. Hill — the 'Empire Builder' whom Minot worked alongside — named the new town of Minot, North Dakota, after him. His name outlived him on the northern plains.

narrative_blocks.header: The Father of Dover
narrative_blocks.body: Around 1900 Robert bought up land at Dover, seeing it as a coming suburb, real country forty minutes from Boston. The Boston families who followed him out proved him right and gave him his name, the Father of Dover.

narrative_blocks.header: The Boston Personal Property Trust
narrative_blocks.body: Robert took his Harvard degree in 1877, went abroad in 1880 and practiced law from 1882, but within a few years gave all his time to managing trust property in his father's office with his brothers. He created the Boston Personal Property Trust and served as its actuary and trustee.

narrative_blocks.header: Winters at the Victoria
narrative_blocks.body: The Minots summered at Manchester until 1901, when Robert bought the Dover estate and made it their home. Most winters they still took rooms in a Boston hotel, the Victoria for choice.

narrative_blocks.header: Translations, roses and free trade
narrative_blocks.body: Robert published several translations and wrote often for the newspapers. He belonged to the American Free Trade League and the Massachusetts Forestry Association, and was president of the Waban Rose conservatories.

narrative_blocks.header: Quiet, serious, and gone at fifty-three
narrative_blocks.body: Robert was quiet and serious, cared little for society, and was intent on doing careful work. He died at his Dover home in May 1910, at fifty-three, after a short illness, in what looked like one of Boston's coming careers.

institutions.institution_blurb: Harvard University class of 1911. Consensus All-American halfback 1909; also earned varsity letter in baseball as outfielder. Member Institute of 1770, Delta Kappa Epsilon, Phoenix Club, Hasty Pudding.

narrative_blocks.header: Walter Camp made him All-American in 1909
narrative_blocks.body: He played halfback for Harvard, and Walter Camp — who invented the All-America team — named him to it in 1909. He took a varsity letter at baseball too, as an outfielder, and they called him Dono.

narrative_blocks.header: A battalion of 75s with the Yankee Division
narrative_blocks.body: Wayland went to France in September 1917, was made major the next June, and commanded a battalion of 75-millimeter guns in the 26th Yankee Division through all its major operations. Home in April 1919, he was back in the Guard that fall for the Boston police strike.

narrative_blocks.header: The anti-tank battalion he formed
narrative_blocks.body: Called up in June 1941, Wayland organized and trained a new anti-tank battalion, the one that became the 771st Tank Destroyer Battalion. A coronary thrombosis on the Carolina maneuvers that October ended it, and he was retired in May 1942.

narrative_blocks.header: Three sports at Nobles, then Harvard
narrative_blocks.body: He ran track and played baseball and football at Noble and Greenough before Harvard took him. There he joined the Institute of 1770, Delta Kappa Epsilon, the Phoenix and the Hasty Pudding, and left in 1911.

narrative_blocks.header: He sold bonds, then ran the parks
narrative_blocks.body: Out of Harvard he sold bonds for William A. Reed and Company. In the late twenties Cambridge made him its parks commissioner, and from 1931 he counselled investments in Boston — Wainwright, Amott Baker, Sheeline.

narrative_blocks.header: His car burned on the Charles River Dam
narrative_blocks.body: One night in January 1933 he drove into the drawbridge on the Charles River Dam. The car caught fire, and a passenger riding with him did not get out of it.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a Dublin girl at St. Leo’s
narrative_blocks.body: In April 1913 he married Anna Marie Shaughnessy, born at Dublin, in St. Leo’s church in Boston. Five children came between 1914 and 1925 — Ruth, Wayland, Anna, Elizabeth and Herbert.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the childhood friend next door
narrative_blocks.body: Roosevelt married Edith Kermit Carow in London in 1886, his second wife and a granddaughter of the Union general Daniel Tyler. Through her he entered the Tyler family, with its Edwards and Hooker roots in colonial Connecticut.

narrative_blocks.header: Harvard ornithology friendship became his first publication
narrative_blocks.body: He met Henry Davis Minot, a Boston-based naturalist, as a Harvard freshman in 1877. They spent vacations listing birds in the Adirondacks and co-authored 'The Summer Birds of the Adirondacks' that fall — his first published work.

narrative_blocks.header: Trust-busted J.P. Morgan's Northern Securities Company
narrative_blocks.body: His administration brought the antitrust suit that dissolved Morgan's Northern Securities holding company in 1904, ending the merger of the Northern Pacific and Great Northern railroads. Morgan reportedly told him 'Send your man to my man and they can fix it up' — the President refused, and the Supreme Court sided with the government.

narrative_blocks.header: He befriended Columbia's president Nicholas Butler
narrative_blocks.body: Roosevelt's circle included Nicholas Murray Butler, the long-serving Columbia president and 1931 Nobel peace laureate, whom he nicknamed Nicholas Miraculous. The two Republican allies stayed close from Roosevelt's rise through the White House years.

narrative_blocks.header: The Roosevelts borrowed a famous architect's townhouse
narrative_blocks.body: When the White House was torn up for renovation in 1902, the family decamped to a townhouse belonging to the firm of Carrère and Hastings. Its partner Thomas Hastings would go on to design the New York Public Library and Arlington's Tomb of the Unknowns.

narrative_blocks.header: The dead seal on the market slab
narrative_blocks.body: He was seven when he saw it, and he got the head. With his cousins he founded the Roosevelt Museum of Natural History in the house, taught himself taxidermy to fill it, and at nine wrote up The Natural History of Insects.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept his father’s Sunday-school habit
narrative_blocks.body: His father had led the household in prayers, and at Harvard he taught Sunday school three years at Christ Church in Cambridge. Told to turn Episcopalian if he wished to go on, he refused and took a mission class in a poor quarter instead.
