notable.notable_blurb: Nobel laureate who cured pernicious anemia

people.research_notes: b. Dec 2, 1885 Boston MA; d. Feb 25, 1950 Brookline MA age 64. Harvard BA 1908, Harvard MD 1912. Shared the 1934 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with George Hoyt Whipple and William P. Murphy for discovering liver concentrate treatment for pernicious anemia (pernicious anemia was a fatal disease at the time; liver/vitamin B12 was the cure). Was himself diagnosed with diabetes in 1921 — survived only because insulin was discovered the same year (Banting and Best). Mass General Hospital; Harvard Medical School. American Academy of Arts and Sciences 1926; APS 1935; NAS 1937. His home in Brookline is a National Historic Landmark. His father's cousin was Charles Sedgwick Minot (HD2334, 1852-1914) — the Harvard anatomist and Hooker descendant. George is NOT a Hooker descendant himself — his connection to the tree is through the Minot family line, not through Katharine Sedgwick. (Wikipedia on George Minot; Nobel Prize committee)

narrative_blocks.header: He cured pernicious anemia with liver
narrative_blocks.body: In 1926 George Minot and William Murphy showed that a diet heavy in raw liver reversed pernicious anemia, until then an almost certain death sentence. The work brought them, with George Whipple, the 1934 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

narrative_blocks.header: Insulin saved the man who saved thousands
narrative_blocks.body: Minot was diagnosed with diabetes in 1921 and survived only because insulin reached patients two years later. The reprieve let him carry out the anemia research that would earn a Nobel Prize.

narrative_blocks.header: He read the blood all his working life
narrative_blocks.body: George took up disorders of the blood as a medical student and never left them: clotting, transfusion, platelets, leukemia, the blood of workers poisoned on the job. He turned to pernicious anemia in 1914, twelve years before the liver cure.

narrative_blocks.header: He trained four hundred young physicians
narrative_blocks.body: As director of the Thorndike Memorial Laboratory at Boston City Hospital for two decades, Minot mentored more than four hundred young doctors. He shaped it into one of the nation's premier research institutions before retiring in 1948.

narrative_blocks.header: As a boy he published papers on butterflies
narrative_blocks.body: Long before medicine, young Minot poured his curiosity into natural history, publishing two scientific papers on butterflies. That same patient habit of observation later filled his notebooks with the dietary records that cracked pernicious anemia.

narrative_blocks.header: His name marked a lighthouse and a city
narrative_blocks.body: Minot came of a dynasty of Boston physicians; his great-grandfather James Jackson co-founded Massachusetts General Hospital, and an ancestor's name marked Minot's Ledge Lighthouse in the harbor. His own Brookline house is now a National Historic Landmark.

narrative_blocks.header: A great-niece wrote Monkeys
narrative_blocks.body: Minot's nephew and namesake, the Boston banker George Richards Minot, raised seven children at Manchester-by-the-Sea, and all seven became writers or artists. Susan Minot's Monkeys won the Prix Femina étranger in 1987, and her sister Eliza and brother George published novels too.

career.role: Professor of Medicine; Director, Thorndike Memorial Laboratory

career.organization: Harvard Medical School; Massachusetts General Hospital

people.research_notes: b. Oct 6, 1820 Manhattan NY; d. Jan 14 or 15, 1874 Washington DC age 53. Son of Rev. John Bristed and Magdalen Astor (daughter of John Jacob Astor, fur-trading fortune). Yale 1839; Trinity College Cambridge 1845 (foundation scholar). FIRST KNOWN USE OF "CONSPIRACY THEORY": Used this phrase in a letter to the New York Times, January 11, 1863 — referring to claims that British aristocrats were weakening the United States during the Civil War. Author: "Five Years in an English University" (1852); "The Upper Ten Thousand: Sketches of American Society" (1852); "The Interference Theory of Government" (1867). Wrote under pen name "Carl Benson." Trustee of the Astor Library. m.(1) Laura Whetten Brevoort (1823-1861). m.(2) Grace Ashburner Sedgwick (HD2333) Aug 20, 1867. (Wikipedia on Charles Astor Bristed; FindAGrave)

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve years old, and sent to Hellgate
narrative_blocks.body: Magdalena Astor, the eldest of John Jacob Astor's children, died in 1832 and the boy went up to his grandparents' seat above the East River. Washington Irving lodged there through 1836 writing Astoria, and Fitz-Greene Halleck came and went.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale, then a foundation scholar at Cambridge
narrative_blocks.body: He took his Yale degree with honours in 1839 and stayed a further year at graduate work before crossing to Trinity College, Cambridge. He came out in 1845 with a run of prizes and a foundation scholarship.

narrative_blocks.header: He explained Cambridge to the Americans
narrative_blocks.body: Five Years in an English University set down the manners of a place his countrymen barely understood. The Upper Ten Thousand did the reverse for London readers, sketching what he called the very cream of cream of New York society.

narrative_blocks.header: Carl Benson, of the Spirit of the Times
narrative_blocks.body: Under that name he turned out verse translations from the classics, a school Catullus, a defence of Americanisms — the first full-length one an American wrote — and a book against tariffs and prohibition.

narrative_blocks.header: The country seat came to him, and went
narrative_blocks.body: Astor's will left him the thirteen acres at Hellgate for life, the income to fall to his children after him. The city reached it inside twenty years: he was selling parcels by 1869, the mansion came down that year, and the courts were still dividing street awards after his death.

narrative_blocks.header: A phrase he used once, in a letter
narrative_blocks.body: Writing to the New York Times in January 1863, he dismissed the claim that British aristocrats were sabotaging the Union as a conspiracy theory. It is the earliest known use of the phrase.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a Sedgwick and lies in Stockbridge
narrative_blocks.body: Laura Brevoort died of heart disease in 1860, and in 1867 he married Grace Ashburner Sedgwick, Charles Sedgwick's daughter. An Astor grandson is buried in the Stockbridge ground the Sedgwicks ring.

career.organization: Fraser's Magazine, the Galaxy, Wilkes' Spirit of the Times

narrative_blocks.header: Chamberlain to three popes in turn
narrative_blocks.body: Brought up in Rome and Innsbruck after his father died, schooled at the Jesuits' Mondragone and then at Stonyhurst, he served in the papal household as a private chamberlain under Leo XIII, Pius X and Benedict XV.

narrative_blocks.header: He died in his box at the opera
narrative_blocks.body: At sixty-six he took a heart attack near the end of Madama Butterfly, in Box 14 of the Metropolitan — the Otto Kahn estate's box — with his daughter Symphorosa beside him. He was buried from St. Joseph's, the Roman Catholic church at Stockbridge.

narrative_blocks.header: Cambridge, then four hundred acres
narrative_blocks.body: He came out of Trinity College in 1893 as his father had, practised law a few years, and then lived on the Astor money — building his Stockbridge holdings past four hundred acres and standing as a Republican for the legislature in 1907.

narrative_blocks.header: An interpreter, because of the childhood
narrative_blocks.body: The languages the Roman winters and Austrian summers had given him put him in the Interpreters' Corps in the first war, where the record says he served with distinction.

narrative_blocks.header: Secretary of the Lenox Horse Show
narrative_blocks.body: He kept the books of the Lenox Horse Show Association for years, in a valley where the horse show was the season. His father had won a trotting race in Paris in 1852.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughters built a travel business
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Rosa Donnelly bore him Symphorosa and Katherine and died in 1931; he married again the next year. The two sisters went into business together, and the Lenox house is still in the family.

narrative_blocks.header: She sat beside him at the opera
narrative_blocks.body: At the Metropolitan in February 1936, near the end of Madama Butterfly, her father took a heart attack in the family box with her sitting next to him. She was thirty-nine, and unmarried for five years yet.

narrative_blocks.header: She ran a Madison Avenue travel agency
narrative_blocks.body: With her sister Katherine she built the Bristed-Manning Travel Agency at 625 Madison Avenue. Katherine chaired the board and Mary was a director, and the two of them were a fixture of mid-century New York business.

narrative_blocks.header: Vogue, Vanity Fair, and the Junior League
narrative_blocks.body: Before the agency she spent three years on Vogue and Vanity Fair and eleven as executive secretary of the Junior League of the City of New York. She had been working twenty years by the time she married, at forty-five.

narrative_blocks.header: Schooled in New York, Paris, Rome, and Switzerland
narrative_blocks.body: She was educated at Miss Hall's School in Pittsfield, a New York convent, and finishing schools in Paris, Rome, and Switzerland. She married late, at forty-five, to the banker George Kirchwey Livermore.

narrative_blocks.header: She lived to ninety-five in the Berkshires
narrative_blocks.body: She spent her last decades at Stockbridge, Massachusetts, near the Sedgwick family ground, and lived to ninety-five. She and her husband had no children.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a widower of the Armistice
narrative_blocks.body: George Kirchwey Livermore had lost his first wife in a motor accident the year before he married her in 1941. They had no children, and Lakeside came down to her sister's line.

Time-Life's purchase and decades-long suppression of public access to the film made Jackson's role a central element of JFK assassination history. His papers were donated to the Eisenhower Presidential Library in 1971. Served on boards of Lincoln Center and Boston Symphony Orchestra. m. Katherine Elizabeth "Grace" Bristed (1897-1989) 1931. narrative_blocks.header: Time-Life executive and Cold War propagandist
narrative_blocks.body: A senior executive at Henry Luce's Time Inc., Jackson directed Allied psychological warfare in North Africa and at Eisenhower's SHAEF during the war. He later ran the Free Europe Committee and Radio Free Europe and served as Eisenhower's Special Assistant for international affairs.

narrative_blocks.header: His magazines doubled as Cold War tools
narrative_blocks.body: As publisher of Fortune and Life, Jackson moved fluidly between journalism and intelligence work and was later described as Luce's personal liaison to the CIA. Papers opened after his death showed he had aided covert information campaigns since the late 1940s.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought the Zapruder film for Life
narrative_blocks.body: Days after President Kennedy's assassination, Jackson secured Time-Life's purchase of Abraham Zapruder's home movie of the killing. Life published individual frames but, controversially, never released the footage as a moving film during his lifetime.

narrative_blocks.header: He married into the Astor-Sedgwick Berkshire world
narrative_blocks.body: Jackson's wife, Katherine Bristed, descended from the Astor and Sedgwick families, and the couple summered at the Bristed estate near Stockbridge. He is buried within the famous Sedgwick family circle in Stockbridge Cemetery.

narrative_blocks.header: He blurred journalism and government propaganda
narrative_blocks.body: Moving fluidly between Time Inc. and Washington, Jackson embodied the Cold War alliance of media and state, drafting psychological-warfare strategy while running Henry Luce's magazines. Observers watched the line between reporting and statecraft dissolve in his career.

narrative_blocks.header: She acted on Broadway, television, and soaps
narrative_blocks.body: Anna Sedgwick Minot left Vassar already an Actors' Equity member and ushered on Broadway before replacing Jeanne Cagney in O'Neill's The Iceman Cometh. Across the 1950s and 1960s she appeared in dozens of live television dramas and daytime soap operas.

narrative_blocks.header: She strung wire for a power company
narrative_blocks.body: Between theatre engagements during the Second World War, Minot worked for a time as a lineman's helper for Florida Power and Light. She later moved to Reno to be near her son and died there in 2007.

narrative_blocks.header: She married two actors of the era
narrative_blocks.body: Minot married Arthur Franz, later a screen actor, in October 1942, while he was training as an air cadet, and had a son; the marriage did not last. In 1950 she married the actor Joseph Warren, with whom she often shared the stage.

narrative_blocks.header: A chickadee at the Buckingham School
narrative_blocks.body: Anna pointed her life at the stage from the day she played a chickadee in a kindergarten play at the Buckingham School in Cambridge. Her work there won her scholarships, and she took her Vassar A.B. in 1939 with Phi Beta Kappa.

narrative_blocks.header: Hallie Flanagan taught her at Vassar
narrative_blocks.body: She grew up at Cambridge and acted in the theatre group at the Buckingham School, then read theatre at Vassar under Hallie Flanagan. She came to New York in 1939 and took her first professional part in American Jubilee at the World’s Fair.

narrative_blocks.header: She read submitted plays for a living
narrative_blocks.body: Between engagements she was a professional reader for the Theatre Guild and the Play of the Month Guild, writing critiques of the scripts that came in. She worked with Plays for Living, which staged plays on social questions for schools.

narrative_blocks.header: The Pearl, founded at sixty-six
narrative_blocks.body: In 1984 she and Joseph Warren were founding members of the Pearl Theatre Company, and her files from Richard III, The Rivals and The Country Wife are the richest part of the papers she gave the New York Public Library.

narrative_blocks.header: He said the last deaths were needless
narrative_blocks.body: As operations officer of the 92nd Division he charged that American lives had been thrown away in unnecessary attacks on the morning of 11 November 1918, in the hours before the Armistice took hold at eleven. Pershing denied it before a House committee in January 1920.

narrative_blocks.header: France first, and the American army after
narrative_blocks.body: He was in the French Army before his own country came into the war, and served two years after that as a captain of field artillery with the American Expeditionary Forces.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale 1914, and Lenox as a private tutor
narrative_blocks.body: He came up to Lenox as a tutor the year he left Yale and never really left the valley. Harvard Law followed, then a partnership in Lawrence, Turnure & Co. and thirty years of investment banking at Brown Brothers Harriman, until 1958.

narrative_blocks.header: His first wife was killed at Pinehurst
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth Lanier Turnure Fenno — of the family whose name was on his firm — died in a motor accident at Pinehurst in May 1940. He married Symphorosa Bristed the next year and moved into Lakeside, her father's house above Stockbridge Bowl.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept the county’s best Civil War shelf
narrative_blocks.body: The war he had not fought held him: he built what was reckoned the most extensive Civil War library in the Berkshires.

narrative_blocks.header: The Tanglewood traffic did not bother him
narrative_blocks.body: He ran the Lenox Library's music committee and stood for Tanglewood when the summer people around him grumbled, cheerfully abiding the weekend cars that streamed past his door on Route 183.

narrative_blocks.header: Four parts at the Shakespeare Festival

narrative_blocks.header: Mommie Dearest, Taxi Driver, Me Natalie
narrative_blocks.body: The pictures came late and steadily: Me Natalie, Bang the Drum Slowly, Thieves, Taxi Driver and Mommie Dearest. On television he was a regular on The Jackie Gleason Show from 1967, and recurred on Dallas and All My Children.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventeen boxes of a journeyman’s career
narrative_blocks.body: He and Anna Minot both called themselves journeyman actors, and their papers went to the Billy Rose Theatre Division at the New York Public Library — seventeen boxes of headshots and resumes, the record of always auditioning again.

narrative_blocks.header: Three years in the Village Nursing Home
narrative_blocks.body: A stroke in 1990 put him into the Village Nursing Home in Manhattan, where he lived out three years and died of respiratory failure in October 1993. He left Anna, his sons Joseph and George, and his stepson Michael Minot.

people.research_notes: b. Jun 4, 1887 Milton MA; d. Mar 5, 1973 Boston MA age 85. Harvard BA 1909; Harvard Medical School MD cum laude 1912. Massachusetts General Hospital physician. NOTABLE: Founded the Allergy Clinic at Massachusetts General Hospital 1923 — the first clinic of its kind in the United States. Chief 1925-1929. Founded American Society for Asthma and Allied Conditions 1923; first president, American Association of Allergy 1934. Author of 175+ papers on allergies; redefined asthma classification (extrinsic vs intrinsic, 1918). Named for his grandfather's colleague Dr. Francis Minot (1821-1899). His dictum: "There is always something that can be done to help the asthmatic." m. Dorothy Mandell Apr 28, 1917. 4 children including Francis Jr. (who worked at Time magazine in New York — the same company that bought the Zapruder film!). (American Academy of Arts and Sciences; FindAGrave; history-of-asthma.com)

naming_inspiration.description: Named for his maternal grandfather, the physician Dr. Francis Minot.

narrative_blocks.header: Asthma has more than one cause
narrative_blocks.body: In 1918, two years out of training, Francis published a study of 150 asthma patients that treated asthma not as one disease but as a symptom with many causes, extrinsic and intrinsic. It is the paper his name is still tied to.

narrative_blocks.header: A camera for every patient
narrative_blocks.body: Francis practiced from the first floor of his house on Beacon Street and lived upstairs, and among the instruments in his consulting rooms was a camera. He made a portrait of every patient, he explained, the better to remember them.

narrative_blocks.header: Surprise visits to hunt allergens
narrative_blocks.body: Francis often turned up unannounced at patients' homes to track down the source of their allergies himself, and told them what to avoid. Along the Charles the hospital staff knew him by sight, rowing a single shell.

narrative_blocks.header: The allergy clinic he built
narrative_blocks.body: When Francis came back to Massachusetts General in 1916, Joseph Goodale was seeing asthma and hay fever patients in a room of the throat department. Out of it Francis built the hospital's Allergy Clinic, ran it until 1948, and held that something could always be done for the asthmatic.

narrative_blocks.header: Guinea pigs, then the Army camps
narrative_blocks.body: From 1914 to 1916 Francis worked under Warfield Longcope in New York on anaphylaxis in guinea pigs and on serum sickness, the work that drew him into the thirteen-man circle behind America's first asthma society. Then came the Army Medical Corps, and the influenza of 1918 in its camps.

narrative_blocks.header: A life of his cousin George Minot
narrative_blocks.body: His 1956 book The Inquisitive Physician told the life of his cousin, Harvard classmate and close friend George R. Minot, who won the Nobel Prize for his work on pernicious anemia.

narrative_blocks.header: Sneeze, Wheeze and Itch
narrative_blocks.body: For the Boston doctors taking up the new field, Francis founded the Boston Allergy Round Table, known to its members as the S.W.I.: Sneeze, Wheeze and Itch.

narrative_blocks.header: He went ashore to tend the enemy
narrative_blocks.body: George was the only medical officer aboard the USS Tacony off Fort Fisher in January 1865. On the 17th, two days after the fort fell, he went ashore to care for the Confederate wounded.

narrative_blocks.header: On the Navy's first hospital ship
narrative_blocks.body: George signed on as an acting assistant surgeon in the fall of 1862 and served with the Mississippi Squadron aboard the Red Rover, the Navy's first hospital ship. He was discharged in October 1865.

narrative_blocks.header: A sister in St. Augustine

narrative_blocks.header: He married Lucie Fornachon in 1867
narrative_blocks.body: George married Henriette Lucie Fornachon de Preux of New York in March 1867. They had seven children, and by 1870 were living at Southampton, Massachusetts.

narrative_blocks.header: His last years at the Hampton home
narrative_blocks.body: In 1890, his health broken, Lucie had George admitted to the veterans' home at Hampton, Virginia. He died there in June 1902 and is buried in the national cemetery.

narrative_blocks.header: He hid cancer surgery aboard a friend's yacht
narrative_blocks.body: In 1893, to avoid panicking a fragile economy, Cleveland had a tumor cut from his jaw in secret aboard a yacht at sea. The operation stayed hidden from the public for years.

narrative_blocks.header: His schoolteacher married into this tree
narrative_blocks.body: As a boy at Clinton Academy, Cleveland was taught by Elliott Anthony — who went on to marry Mary Dwight, a seventh-generation Hooker descendant, and to a Chicago judgeship. Teacher and pupil crossed paths long before either knew what the other would become.

narrative_blocks.header: The first to leave and come back
narrative_blocks.body: He won the popular vote in 1888 but lost the electoral college to Benjamin Harrison, went back to a New York law firm, and beat Harrison four years later. He was the first president to serve two terms that did not run together.

narrative_blocks.header: He vetoed more than every president before
narrative_blocks.body: In his first term alone he used the veto four hundred and fourteen times, more than four times any predecessor, most of them on private pension bills. Refusing seed money to drought-struck Texas farmers, he wrote that though the people support the government, the government should not support the people.

narrative_blocks.header: A letter from Savannah reached his wife
narrative_blocks.body: In 1887 Lillie Pierpont wrote to Frances Cleveland asking the President to intervene for the Seminole in a dispute at Titusville. What came back the next year made her the first woman in Florida appointed a federal agent of the Indian Bureau.

narrative_blocks.header: He put a Middletown banker on the plains
narrative_blocks.body: In 1885 he appointed Jonathan Burwell Kilbourn receiver of public moneys at the Pueblo land office, a post the Connecticut banker held for five years. Kilbourn had gone out to Colorado for his health and stayed for the work.

HOOKER-TO-HAWAII: Great-nephew of Yale president Timothy Dwight IV (H00914), great-great-grandson of Mary Edwards Dwight (H00379), and 7th-generation descendant of Thomas Hooker — Samuel Gelston Dwight settled in Hawaii as part of the missionary-connected New England diaspora. His son's name "Samuel Castle Dwight" honors Samuel Northrup Castle (co-founder of Castle & Cooke, one of Hawaii's Big Five corporations, ABCFM lay agent). m. Anna Haaheo Mahoe (X00772) — a Hawaiian woman. 3 known children: Samuel Castle Dwight (1856-1930), Juliette Cooke Dwight Lovejoy (1857-1917), Charles Bishop Dwight (1859-1904, born Molokai). (FindAGrave; WikiTree Dwight-779) DOMINIS-YATES-HOOKER ORBIT: John Owen Dominis (b.Mar 10, 1832 at Rev. Andrew Yates's home in Schenectady) was a contemporary of HD2376 Samuel Gelston Dwight in Honolulu society. Dwight's daughter HD2377 Juliette Cooke Dwight was named for Juliette Montague Cooke, co-founder of the Royal School in Honolulu — the school next to which young Dominis first met the future Queen Liliuokalani. Dwight died Honolulu Aug 20, 1880; Dominis died Honolulu Aug 27, 1891 — both lived in the same small missionary-elite Honolulu world for decades. The Yates-Dominis-Liliuokalani connection and the Dwight-Cooke-Royal School connection are two branches of the same ABCFM-Hooker-Hawaii orbit. STAGE 6Y-136n.

narrative_blocks.header: Sailor, Mobile merchant, then missionary
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel went to sea first, was a merchant in Mobile, Alabama, from 1841, then studied three years at Union Theological Seminary and sailed for Molokai in 1848 as a missionary of the American Board.

narrative_blocks.header: He married Anna and left the Mission
narrative_blocks.body: When Samuel married Anna Mahoe of Molokai about 1854, the Mission judged he could no longer keep his formal tie to it. He withdrew with its respect, and by 1873 was running a dairy farm at Pukoo.

narrative_blocks.header: Children named for the Mission
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel named his children for missionary colleagues: Juliette Cooke Dwight for Juliette Montague Cooke of the Royal School, and Samuel Castle Dwight for Samuel Northrup Castle, the Mission's lay agent.

narrative_blocks.header: Honolulu's missionary circle
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel moved in the same small missionary circle as John Owen Dominis, the future husband of Queen Liliuokalani, who first met the royal children beside the Cookes' Royal School. Samuel died in Honolulu in August 1880.

narrative_blocks.header: Named for the Mission's money man
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel was named for Samuel Northrup Castle, who came to Honolulu with the Mission in 1837 and was keeping its accounts when Samuel's father arrived in 1848. Castle founded Castle & Cooke in 1851; the Dwights farmed on Molokai.

narrative_blocks.header: He adopted two of his grandchildren
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel and Harriette adopted two of their daughter Elsie's children, Samuel Castle Miller Dwight and Harriet Kekahiliokalani, and raised them as their own; both grandchildren took the Dwight name.

narrative_blocks.header: On the first Honolulu City Council
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel sat on the first Honolulu City Council, when the city and county government began in 1909, a seat his granddaughter Harriet Ellis Oana was proud of all her life.

narrative_blocks.header: The trust that outlived its trustee
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel left his land on Oahu and Molokai in a trust that paid income to his two adopted grandchildren for more than fifty years. In 1984 the Hawaii Supreme Court surcharged its trustee, First Hawaiian Bank, for a careless purchase.

narrative_blocks.header: The only woman to clerk the Senate
narrative_blocks.body: From 1921 to 1951 Ellen took three months each year from her city post to be clerk of the Territorial Senate, the only woman ever to hold the job, steering every bill from committee to the Governor's desk.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty years a public servant
narrative_blocks.body: Ellen took a 'temporary' job in the attorney general's office in 1906 and retired in 1955 as first deputy clerk of the City and County of Honolulu. She also sat on the Hawaiian Homes Commission.

narrative_blocks.header: She tended the graves of the alii
narrative_blocks.body: For the last ten and a half years of her life Ellen was president of the Kaahumanu Society, the Hawaiian women who since 1905 have kept the graves of the alii at the Royal Mausoleum.

narrative_blocks.header: Aunty Ellen, or Ma Smythe
narrative_blocks.body: To many she was Aunty Ellen. To the boys who filled her Makiki Street house through school she was Ma Smythe, who let them turn the dining table into a ping-pong table and fed them instead of complaining.

narrative_blocks.header: Of my blood, but not of my dynasty
narrative_blocks.body: Ellen and the columnist Sammy Amalu shared a descent from the chiefess Kekauluohi. They embraced when they met and neither presumed further: she was, he wrote, 'of my blood but not of my dynasty.'

narrative_blocks.body: With his brother William he owned the China-trade ship Titan, once chartered to the French in the Crimean War. He later left the sea for New York, where he made his fortune as a merchant.

narrative_blocks.header: His father rowed back into a pirate attack
narrative_blocks.body: His father, Captain Daniel Carpenter Bacon, had been put ashore for safety when Chinese pirate junks swarmed his ship off Macao — then tore free and rowed back through the fighting to share her fate. narrative_blocks.header: A Barnstable farm his family held since 1639
narrative_blocks.body: He was born a Bacon of Barnstable, on land the family had held since the town's founding in 1639, and carried his mother Desire Gorham's name — the "Gorham" that runs on through his sons and grandsons.

narrative_blocks.header: He spent fifty years in the shipping trade
narrative_blocks.body: President of the West India Steamship Company and American agent for Liverpool's Elder Dempster Line, he spent half a century in shipping. As a boy he had apprenticed on the China-trade clipper ships his father owned.

narrative_blocks.header: His yacht Avenger won the Astor Cup
narrative_blocks.body: A keen yachtsman, he took the Astor Cup off Newport in 1911 aboard his yacht Avenger and served as commodore of the Seawanhaka-Corinthian Yacht Club. In the World War he held a naval-reserve commission as a lieutenant commander.

narrative_blocks.header: The sea had already taken two uncles
narrative_blocks.body: He died on a Cunard liner off Montevideo in 1934, in his seventy-second year. Both his Flint uncles had gone before him to the water — Edward in the burning of the Golden Gate in 1862, and young Robert swept off Vanderbilt's yacht in 1853.

narrative_blocks.header: Another of the family lost to the water
narrative_blocks.body: In the summer of 1908 he drowned in Vineyard Sound off Falmouth, at forty-two. He was the third of his family taken by the sea, after the two Flint uncles who had died on the water before he was born.

The April 5, 1939 wedding in Warrenton Virginia ended in divorce eight months later on December 11, 1939. Cookie had been described in the Depression-era press as 'one of the glamour debs.'

narrative_blocks.header: Ex-wife Cookie killed 1941 in Newport plane crash
narrative_blocks.body: Eighteen months after their December 1939 divorce, Cookie Young died July 1, 1941 in a plane crash near Matunuck Rhode Island. She was twenty-three. She had been flying in a Fairchild Model 24 monoplane in fog off Newport with Nicholas Embiricos, the Greek shipping heir. 'Cookie and her dog were thrown from the plane; Nicky died on the beach; Cookie died an hour later at South County Hospital of a fractured skull.' Her father Robert Ralph Young later died by suicide at his Palm Beach home.

narrative_blocks.header: Newport and Palm Beach social circles, four marriages
narrative_blocks.body: Robert Ogden Bacon was born May 16, 1912 in Manhattan and active in the Newport and Palm Beach social circles characteristic of mid-twentieth-century American old-money. He had four marriages total, the Cookie Young match being his second. He died August 4, 1972 in Atlanta Georgia at age sixty and is buried at Mount Hebron Cemetery, Flushing Queens New York.

narrative_blocks.header: He sat on two benches until his death
narrative_blocks.body: From a justice-of-the-peace commission in 1758 he rose to the Court of Common Pleas and the probate bench for Hampshire County, holding both offices until he died in 1797. For nearly two decades he was one of the county's principal judges.

narrative_blocks.header: His family was among the River Gods
narrative_blocks.body: Porter was one of seven family names, with Ashley, Dwight, Partridge, Pynchon, Stoddard and Williams, that held the valley's pulpits, courts and militia; people called them the River Gods. Eleazer's judgeships kept him among them.

narrative_blocks.header: He apologized in writing for hasty words
narrative_blocks.body: Rebuked in 1780 for speaking too freely against the attorney general, Robert Treat Paine, Eleazer wrote back taking his words back, thanking Paine for the rebuke, and resolving “to set a watch over my lips.”

narrative_blocks.header: His first wife was his first cousin
narrative_blocks.body: Eleazer's first wife, Anna Pitkin, was his first cousin; she died in 1758, in her twenty-fourth year, leaving two daughters. Two years later he married Susannah Edwards.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother carried the family name to war
narrative_blocks.body: His younger brother Elisha Porter commanded the Fourth Hampshire Regiment, fought at Bunker Hill, carried dispatches for Washington, and escorted the surrendered General Burgoyne to Boston after Saratoga.

narrative_blocks.header: His sister married his wife's brother
narrative_blocks.body: In 1770 Eleazer's sister Mary married Susannah's brother Jonathan Edwards, then a young minister at New Haven. She drowned there in 1782.

narrative_blocks.header: Father of the high-speed steam engine
narrative_blocks.body: Charles and the engineer John F. Allen built the Porter-Allen engine, the first steam engine made to run at high speed. In 1880 he installed one to drive a generator in Thomas Edison's laboratory at Menlo Park.

narrative_blocks.header: The fourth John Fritz Medal
narrative_blocks.body: In 1909 Charles received the John Fritz Medal for advancing steam engineering, the fourth man to win it after Lord Kelvin, Alexander Graham Bell, George Westinghouse and Thomas Edison.

narrative_blocks.header: A lawyer paid in patent rights
narrative_blocks.body: Charles practiced law at Rochester until a client paid him with a half-share of a patent for a stone-dressing machine. Fixing the faulty governor on its engine led him to invent his own, patented in 1858.

narrative_blocks.header: His engine reached London in 1862
narrative_blocks.body: Charles arrived for the London exhibition of 1862 as the Trent affair brought Britain near war, and found the American space taken away. Limited to 120 revolutions, his engine ran so smoothly that the limit was lifted.

narrative_blocks.header: Mechanics and Faith
narrative_blocks.body: Besides his books on steam engineering, Charles wrote Mechanics and Faith in 1885, on why a man of science could accept truths beyond the senses, and late in life his Engineering Reminiscences.

narrative_blocks.header: Less than two months after Harriet
narrative_blocks.body: Charles died in New York in August 1910 at the home of his son Lewis, less than two months after his wife Harriet died at their Montclair home. His family believed grief had hastened his death.

He was one of the organizers of the Oswego Starch Company 1848, secretary and treasurer 50 years; director Auburn Water Works 40 years.

bio.bio_blurb: Treasurer of the Oswego Starch Factory

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty years keeping the starch books
narrative_blocks.body: Alonzo helped organize the Oswego Starch Factory in 1848, which made starch by Thomas Kingsford's new process, and served it as secretary and then treasurer for fifty years.

narrative_blocks.header: He married his law partner's daughter
narrative_blocks.body: Alonzo read law with John Porter at Auburn, was admitted to the bar in 1842 and joined the firm of Porter & Beardsley. In 1848 he married his partner's daughter, Anna Phillips Porter.

narrative_blocks.header: Planes first made in Auburn prison
narrative_blocks.body: Alonzo formed Casey, Clarke & Co. to make carpenters' planes, a trade begun inside Auburn prison in 1823, and it became the Auburn Tool Company in 1864. He was treasurer of the Cayuga Chief mower company until 1879.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years at the water works
narrative_blocks.body: Alonzo was with the Auburn Water Works from its start, sat on its board for forty years and served as its president. He was a director of the Cayuga County National Bank and a trustee of the Young Ladies' Institute.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother was Seward's law partner
narrative_blocks.body: Alonzo's oldest brother, Nelson, was William H. Seward's law partner, and was president of the Cayuga County National Bank from 1843 until 1894, the longest tenure of any bank president in the country.

narrative_blocks.header: Two brothers in the post office
narrative_blocks.body: His brother Roswell was postmaster at North Lansing from 1828 to 1902, under twenty presidents. His brother William Clinton, postmaster at Auburn, cast an electoral vote for Franklin Pierce and helped found Fort Hill Cemetery.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven children on Genesee Street
narrative_blocks.body: Alonzo and Anna raised their family at 194 Genesee Street, where the house still stands. They had seven children and lost two as babies, George Thompson in 1856 and Nelson in 1858.

narrative_blocks.header: He built America's first state asylum at Worcester
narrative_blocks.body: In 1832 Woodward became the first superintendent of the new state lunatic hospital at Worcester, one of the country's first public asylums for the insane. Patients arrived from prisons and almshouses, some chained for years, and many improved dramatically under his care.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded and first led the future APA
narrative_blocks.body: Woodward helped found the Association of Medical Superintendents of American Institutions for the Insane and served as its first president from 1844. That body would in time become the American Psychiatric Association.

narrative_blocks.header: He crusaded for asylums in his gig
narrative_blocks.body: Before Worcester, Woodward drove his gig across Connecticut urging the founding of what became the Hartford Retreat for the Insane. He pressed the cause from a seat in the state senate and introduced sewing and spinning as therapy for his patients.

narrative_blocks.header: He was said to resemble George Washington
narrative_blocks.body: Standing well over six feet, Woodward struck contemporaries as majestic, so like George Washington in his later years that a Boston dining room reportedly fell silent as he crossed it. A public subscription paid for a portrait and a marble bust in his honor.

narrative_blocks.header: A historian consulted him on George the Third
narrative_blocks.body: George Bancroft sought Woodward's expert opinion on the madness of King George the Third for his history of the United States. Woodward also lectured for temperance and called early for asylums to treat inebriates.

narrative_blocks.header: A maniac, he held, was not to blame
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel was in demand as an expert witness on insanity. He held that a maniac was not responsible for his crime, so his testimony usually helped the defense.

narrative_blocks.header: Three asylums tried to hire him away
narrative_blocks.body: Hartford's Retreat offered Samuel its superintendency in 1834 and again in 1840, McLean courted him the same year, and in 1842 Utica offered to build its new asylum under him. He turned them all down.

narrative_blocks.header: An asylum his father never opened
narrative_blocks.body: Rufus trained at his father's Worcester hospital and spent two years in Europe studying insanity, meaning to help his father run a private asylum at Northampton. His father's sudden death in 1850 ended the plan.

narrative_blocks.header: Seeing patients the day he died
narrative_blocks.body: Rufus practised in Worcester for thirty years, as city physician, visiting surgeon at the City Hospital, and examiner of Civil War volunteers. He saw patients on the day he died, in December 1885.

narrative_blocks.header: He knew every wild flower near Worcester
narrative_blocks.body: Rufus helped found the Worcester Natural History Society and was its president for years. He spent his spare time in his garden, and a wild flower near Worcester that he did not know was rare indeed.

narrative_blocks.header: Whom have I to bury today?
narrative_blocks.body: In the 1855 yellow fever George stayed in Norfolk and buried his people nearly every day, waking to ask, “Whom have I to bury today?” By autumn it had taken his wife, Mehetable, their daughter Mary, twelve, and her sister Hatty.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote The Summer of the Pestilence
narrative_blocks.body: George set that season down in The Summer of the Pestilence in 1856. At his first service after the fever, only three families in the church were not in mourning, and some sixty orphaned children sat together.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years at one Norfolk pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: George taught chemistry and mechanics at Washington College in Lexington for thirteen years, then in 1851 took the pulpit of First Presbyterian in Norfolk, the only church he ever led, until 1891.

narrative_blocks.header: He defended slavery from the Bible
narrative_blocks.body: In 1857 George published The Christian Doctrine of Slavery, a defense of slavery from Scripture, and the next year argued it in print against Cortlandt Van Rensselaer.

narrative_blocks.header: Imprisoned under Butler, then a chaplain
narrative_blocks.body: George was imprisoned and humiliated under Gen. Benjamin Butler's occupation of Norfolk, and afterward went to the Confederate army as Presbyterian chaplain to A. P. Hill's corps.

narrative_blocks.header: A church named for him in his lifetime
narrative_blocks.body: William and Mary made George a Doctor of Divinity in 1854 and Washington and Lee a Doctor of Laws in 1886, and Berkley's Armstrong Memorial Church was built in his honor while he lived.

narrative_blocks.header: She survived the 1855 yellow fever epidemic
narrative_blocks.body: As a small child, Grace lived through the catastrophic 1855 yellow fever epidemic that swept Norfolk — the same outbreak that killed her mother and siblings. narrative_blocks.header: Her last days were at a mountain cure

narrative_blocks.header: He died Norfolk's beloved police chief
narrative_blocks.body: Dornin rose to become chief of the Norfolk police, a man the local press called able and 'particularly kind hearted.' When he died in 1898 of a long-standing heart ailment, the fire bells were tolled across the city and his passing met with 'universal sorrow.' Few men in Norfolk, the paper said, would be more sincerely mourned.

narrative_blocks.header: She was commissioned an ensign in December 1944

narrative_blocks.header: The 1938 hurricane came on her sixteenth birthday
narrative_blocks.body: The Great New England Hurricane crossed her home town of Pascoag, Rhode Island, on 21 September 1938, the day she turned sixteen. She liked a good storm for the rest of her life, and followed the weather in whichever cities her children were living.

narrative_blocks.header: She read the library out on the war
narrative_blocks.body: Her interest in the Second World War long outlasted her service in it. She was said to have read every book the Hingham library held on the subject.

narrative_blocks.header: She came back to nursing after twenty years
narrative_blocks.body: Joan left the Navy in 1946, married the following year and raised four children. She returned to the wards in 1966 and spent eighteen years at South Shore Hospital, ending as a full-time registered nurse specialising in intravenous care.

narrative_blocks.header: He took Seward's place in the firm
narrative_blocks.body: When William H. Seward left Auburn to be governor in 1839, Nelson Beardsley took John into the law firm in his place, and it became Beardsley and Porter.

narrative_blocks.header: Cayuga County's prosecutor, then its surrogate
narrative_blocks.body: John was Cayuga County's district attorney from 1821 to 1828 and its surrogate until 1836. He sat in the New York State Senate from 1843 to 1846.

narrative_blocks.header: From Hadley to Auburn
narrative_blocks.body: John was born at Hadley in 1790, graduated from Williams in 1810 and read law at Albany. Admitted to the bar in 1815, he settled at Auburn and lived there the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a congressman's niece
narrative_blocks.body: John married Abbey Phillips of Middletown, a niece of Congressman Gurdon S. Mumford, on 17 February 1825. They lost their daughter Caroline in 1847, at nine, and their son John the next year, at fourteen.

narrative_blocks.header: His son won the John Fritz Medal
narrative_blocks.body: John's son Charles Talbot Porter became an inventor of mechanical devices, and in 1909 received the John Fritz Medal.

narrative_blocks.header: A schoolhouse on top of the world
narrative_blocks.body: In July 1916 Dorothy and her Smith classmate Rosamond Underwood arrived at Hayden, Colorado, to teach at the new stone school in Elkhead. Dorothy, four feet eleven, took the younger children: ten boys and one girl.

narrative_blocks.header: Hired as teachers, eyed as brides
narrative_blocks.body: Ferry Carpenter, the rancher who hired them, meant the two teachers as prospective brides for the local bachelors, and at the Hayden Inn the cowboys only stared. Dorothy was already secretly engaged to Lem Hillman.

narrative_blocks.header: Snowshoes and a swig of whiskey
narrative_blocks.body: Riding home from the Elkhead Christmas party through a blizzard, Dorothy's horse fell in the deep snow. The teachers snowshoed it back onto its feet, and at the ranch each took a swig of Old Man Harrison's whiskey.

narrative_blocks.header: A suffragist on a soapbox
narrative_blocks.body: Before Colorado, Dorothy was president of Auburn's Young Ladies' Benevolent Association, supported Hull House, and spoke for women's suffrage from a soapbox in Owasco. The Elkhead board sent her home with a gold medal.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at forty-three, she led the Red Cross
narrative_blocks.body: Lem died in February 1930, struck by a car, and left Dorothy with four young children. She learned typing and stenography, headed the Grand Rapids Red Cross, and in the war worked at its Eastern Area headquarters.

narrative_blocks.header: She waded in when the Grand River flooded
narrative_blocks.body: When the Grand River overflowed, Dorothy went down to help the Ottawa families there, who had nothing to eat but muskrats. "She took life by the throat and dealt with it," her daughter Caroline said.

narrative_blocks.header: He proposed twice
narrative_blocks.body: Lem, a young Grand Rapids banker, proposed to Dorothy Woodruff at Auburn and was turned down, then again at Chicago as she headed west to teach in 1916, and she accepted. They married at her parents' house in July 1917.

narrative_blocks.header: Phi Beta Kappa at Colgate
narrative_blocks.body: Lem graduated from Colgate in 1909, Phi Beta Kappa, a member of Skull and Scroll and prominent in its athletics. He spent two years with United States Rubber in Philadelphia, then moved to Grand Rapids in 1911.

narrative_blocks.header: His father made rubber in New York
narrative_blocks.body: Lem's father, William Hillman, managed the Revere Rubber Company's New York branch, was vice-president of Peerless Rubber, and ran for Mount Vernon alderman as a Progressive in 1912. William died in Grand Rapids in 1927.

narrative_blocks.header: Walking to dinner on Fulton Road
narrative_blocks.body: On a February evening in 1930 Lem and Dorothy were walking to dinner at a friend's house on Fulton Road when a car struck them both. Dorothy was treated for shock and cuts; Lem died early the next morning.

narrative_blocks.header: A gravestone a century out of style
narrative_blocks.body: Lem's stone at Fort Hill in Auburn, white and narrow with rosettes and a draped urn, looks as if it were carved in the early 1800s rather than in 1930.

people.research_notes:
b. Feb 15, 1922 Grand Rapids Kent Co. MI; d. Feb 1, 2007 Muskegon MI age 84. Son of Lemuel Serrell Hillman (X00822; banker, d.1930 when Douglas was 8) and Dorothy Woodruff (HD2500). Grand Rapids Central High School. U of Michigan BA 1946; Michigan Law LL.B. 1948. WWII: U.S. Army Air Corps 1st Lt; flew B-24 Liberators, 15th Air Force, Italy; targeted Ploiești oil refineries (30% of Nazi Germany's oil) and northern Italy industrial sites. Medals. Private practice Grand Rapids 1948-1979: Lily Luyendyk & Snyder; Luyendyk Hainer Hillman Karr & Dutcher (partner 1953); Hillman Baxter & Hammond (senior partner 1965). President Grand Rapids Bar Assoc. 1965. U.S. District Judge W.D. Michigan: nominated Carter Jul 12, 1979; confirmed Sep 25, 1979; Chief Judge 1986-1991; senior status Feb 15, 1991; retired Oct 1, 2002. Notable cases: Berry v. School District Benton Harbor (desegregation, 1981-2002); Grand Traverse Band v. US (Native American gaming law); US v. Lewis 1986 (jury selection). Founded Hillman Advocacy Program 1981. ACLU Civil Liberties Award 1970. Michigan's 25 Most Respected Judges, Michigan Lawyers Weekly 1990. Co-founded World Affairs Council W. Michigan 1949 w/ Edgar Orr. Hillman-Orr Award named for him. National Inst. of Trial Advocacy faculty since 1971. Stroke 2000; hospice 2007. Memorial: Fountain Street Church, Grand Rapids, Feb 12, 2007. m. Sep 13, 1944 Sarah Adelaide 'Sally' Jones (X00826; 1923-2013). Children: Drusilla Hillman (HD3139) and Clayton Douglas 'Clay' Hillman (HD2508; 1956-1996 — predeceased father). Buried Oakhill Cemetery Grand Rapids MI (CEM099). (Wikipedia; FindAGrave) [Stage 6Y-264 schema cleanup]: notable_blurb trimmed from [10w] 'Federal judge; B-24 pilot over Ploiești oil refineries in WWII' → 'B-24 pilot over Ploiești oil refineries in WWII'.
[Stage 6Y-264 NB#1 header trim]: 'He flew B-24 bombers over the Ploiești oil refineries — the most dangerous missions in the air war' → 'He flew B-24 bombers over the Ploiești oil'.
[Stage 6Y-264 NB#1 body trim]: original body had 4 sentences, trimmed to first 3. Original body preserved here for reference: 'Douglas Hillman flew as a B-24 Liberator pilot with the Fifteenth Air Force out of Italy, targeting industrial sites in northern Italy and the Ploiești oil refineries in Romania. Ploiești supplied roughly 30 percent of Nazi Germany's petroleum. The missions were notorious: Operation Tidal Wave in August 1943 lost 54 aircraft in a single low-level run and produced five Medal of Honor recipients — the most awarded for any single action in WWII. Hillman's personal papers include detailed flight logs, photographs, and medals earned over contested European airspace.'
[Stage 6Y-264 NB#2 header trim]: 'He presided over a school desegregation case for thirty years — and was the judge who finally declared it resolved' → 'He presided over a school desegregation case'.
[Stage 6Y-264 NB#2 body trim]: original body had 5 sentences, trimmed to first 3. Original body preserved here for reference: 'Berry v. School District of the City of Benton Harbor began in the 1970s and wound through the federal courts for decades. Hillman took over the case, issued a comprehensive remedial order in 1981 mandating compensatory education, busing adjustments, and faculty diversification — rejecting inter-district mergers as too disruptive. In 2002, as a senior judge in his final year on the bench, he declared the districts 'unitary' and released Benton Harbor schools from court supervision after verifying sustained desegregation efforts. Resolution in protracted desegregation cases was, and remains, rare.'
[Stage 6Y-264 NB#3 header trim]: 'He co-founded the World Affairs Council of Western Michigan in 1949 — at age 27, two years out of law school' → 'He co-founded the World Affairs Council of Western'.

Original body preserved here for reference: 'In 1949, just two years after passing the bar, Douglas Hillman co-founded the World Affairs Council of Western Michigan alongside businessman Edgar Orr. Their mission was to heighten global awareness among Americans, with a particular focus on engaging younger generations through lectures and cultural exchange. The Hillman-Orr Award, named jointly for both founders, continues today, honoring regional contributions to international understanding. The Hillman Advocacy Program, established by him in 1981 for young trial lawyers, also bears his name.'

notable.notable_blurb: Chief judge, Western District of Michigan

institutions.institution_blurb: University of Michigan B.A. 1946; LL.B. from Michigan Law School 1948. Also a lecturer at the Institute for Continuing Legal Education, Ann Arbor, 1979-1987.

narrative_blocks.header: Chief judge in western Michigan
narrative_blocks.body: Jimmy Carter named Douglas to a new seat on the federal court for the Western District of Michigan in 1979, after thirty years in private practice at Grand Rapids. He was its chief judge from 1986 to 1991 and served until 2002.

narrative_blocks.header: He presided over a school desegregation case
narrative_blocks.body: Douglas took over Berry v. Benton Harbor, a school desegregation suit begun in the 1970s, and in 1981 ordered compensatory education, busing changes and a more diverse faculty, while rejecting a merger with neighboring districts.

narrative_blocks.header: He flew B-24 bombers over the Ploiești oil
narrative_blocks.body: In the Second World War Douglas flew B-24 Liberators with the Fifteenth Air Force from Italy, bombing targets in northern Italy and the Ploiești oil refineries in Romania.

narrative_blocks.header: He co-founded the World Affairs Council
narrative_blocks.body: In 1949 Douglas and the businessman Edgar Orr founded the World Affairs Council of Western Michigan, and its Hillman-Orr Award still carries both their names.

bio.bio_blurb: Otis Elevator executive and Harlem Savings Bank president

naming_inspiration.description: First name from his grandfather Alonzo Glover Beardsley

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-seven years at Otis Elevator
narrative_blocks.body: Glover went to the Otis Elevator Company from Yale in 1903 and stayed thirty-seven years, the last seventeen as vice president, while the city's towers climbed past anything built before.

narrative_blocks.header: From elevators to a Harlem bank
narrative_blocks.body: Glover left Otis in 1940 to become president and a trustee of the Harlem Savings Bank. He ran it for eighteen years, and in 1958 became chairman of its board, three years before his death.

narrative_blocks.header: A son lost a week short of nine
narrative_blocks.body: Glover and Daisy's son, Nelson Porter Beardsley, died in Manhattan on 7 January 1924, a week before his ninth birthday. They buried him at Woodlawn in the Bronx, where Glover followed him thirty-seven years later.

narrative_blocks.header: The Glover name went down the line
narrative_blocks.body: Glover took his first name from his grandfather, Alonzo Glover Beardsley, the Auburn lawyer who organized the Oswego Starch Company. Glover's daughter Annette gave it to her son, Glover Wagner, who settled in Bozeman, Montana.

b. Mar 4, 1918 Penns Grove, Salem County NJ; d. Jul 1, 1941 South Kingstown, Washington County RI age 23. "Cookie." Only child of Robert Ralph Young (railroad financier) and Anita Ten Eyck O'Keeffe Young (sister of artist Georgia O'Keeffe). "One of the glamour debs of the Depression era." Presented as debutante Newport RI 1936. m. Robert Ogden "Bunty" Bacon II (HD2418) Apr 5, 1939 Warrenton VA; divorced Dec 11, 1939. DEATH: Jul 1, 1941 — departed Newport RI by private aircraft with Nicholas Embiricos (Greek shipping heir), crashed near Matunuck, South Kingstown RI; fog, only basic instrumentation. Lifeguards pulled both from wreckage; Embiricos died on beach; Cookie died ~1 hour later of fractured skull, broken bones, internal injuries. Her dog's body washed up on shore. R.R. Young later died by suicide in Palm Beach when railroad plans failed. Entombed Saint Mary's Episcopal Churchyard, Portsmouth RI. (Newport society reporting; FindAGrave) [Cause revert audit]: Earlier extraction set death.cause="suicide" but reverted: suicide — was about R.R. Young (related), not Eleanor Jane Young.

narrative_blocks.header: A Depression glamour deb, dead at twenty-three
narrative_blocks.body: Eleanor 'Cookie' Young — only child of railroad financier Robert Young and a niece of the painter Georgia O'Keeffe — was presented at Newport in 1936 and called one of the glamour debutantes of the Depression. In July 1941, at twenty-three, she left Newport by private plane with a Greek shipping heir; it crashed in fog near Matunuck, Rhode Island, killing them both. Her dog's body later washed ashore.

narrative_blocks.header: Married in April, divorced by December
narrative_blocks.body: In April 1939 she married Robert Ogden Bacon at Warrenton, Virginia, but the marriage was over by December of the same year. She would die little more than a year later.

b. Oct 13, 1799 Hadley MA; d. Apr 20, 1876 Waterford, Dakota County MN age 76. Named "Moses" for his father. PHYSICIAN. Studied under Drs. Goodhue (Hadley) and Cogswell (Hartford); graduated Castleton Vermont Medical College. Practiced in Hadley MA, then Brookfield MA (where he married), returned to Hadley, then removed to Illinois 1834, then Minnesota 1855-56. Partner with Dr. Nichols in Waterford MN; practiced until 1870. Was one of the first physicians in Will County IL. Buried Red Rose Cemetery, Waterford Township, Dakota County MN. Obituary: "made a public confession of faith in Christ as his savior at the early age of sixteen...a man of mark and much influence." m. Martha Alvord Snell (1806-1886) 1827 in Brookfield MA (daughter of Rev. Dr. Snell, pastor of Congregational church in Brookfield 50+ years). (Rice County Journal obituary, May 3, 1876; EH; FindAGrave)

education.school_name: Read medicine with Dr. Goodhue of Hadley and Dr. Cogswell of Hartford

career.role: Physician, in partnership with Dr. Nichols

narrative_blocks.header: West by the Great Lakes in 1834
narrative_blocks.body: In 1834 Moses took Martha and their two small daughters west by stagecoach, the Erie Canal and sailing ship, up Lake Huron and down Lake Michigan to Fort Dearborn, since the overland road through Ohio and Indiana was too wild. He became the first practising physician of the country around Batavia and Frankfort, Illinois.

narrative_blocks.header: Trained at Hadley, Hartford and Castleton
narrative_blocks.body: Moses read medicine with Dr. Goodhue at Hadley and Dr. Cogswell at Hartford, took his degree at the medical college at Castleton, Vermont, and practised at Hadley and at Brookfield, where in 1827 he married Martha Snell, the minister's daughter.

narrative_blocks.header: Following his daughter to Minnesota
narrative_blocks.body: On 12 May 1856 Moses and Martha loaded a wagon and followed their one surviving child, Sarah, and her husband John Simpson to Waterford, Minnesota, two years before statehood. He practised there with Dr. Nichols until 1870 and broke a large farm northwest of the village.

narrative_blocks.header: A sister twice told
narrative_blocks.body: Moses's sister Lucretia married Martha's brother Thomas Snell in 1836, so that Martha, writing from Illinois, welcomed her as a sister twice told. Their son, Moses Porter Snell, carried his name.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife laid him back on his pillow
narrative_blocks.body: Consumption kept Moses unwell for his last eleven years, and he gave up practice in 1870. He died at Waterford on 20 April 1876, at seventy-six; at the end he half raised himself, and Martha gently laid him back on his pillow.

narrative_blocks.header: She married her uncle's amanuensis
narrative_blocks.body: Julia married the Rev. Joseph Dresser Wickham on 26 May 1823. He had been amanuensis to her uncle, President Timothy Dwight of Yale, and from 1828 ran the Washington Institute, the New York school her brothers later owned.

narrative_blocks.header: Small, trim and sharp-witted
narrative_blocks.body: Julia was remembered for a brilliant intellect and sparkling wit. She was small and trim, with an oval face, a high forehead and keen black eyes.

narrative_blocks.header: Her only child died at eight months
narrative_blocks.body: Julia's daughter Mary Louisa was born in November 1827 and died the next July. Julia died in New York on 23 December 1830, at thirty-seven; Joseph lived sixty years more.

narrative_blocks.header: A Hooker descendant on both sides
narrative_blocks.body: Julia descended from Thomas Hooker through both her parents, who were first cousins.

(FindAGrave; EH)

narrative_blocks.header: He left his fortune to Yale
narrative_blocks.body: In 1878 Timothy gave by far the larger part of his estate to Yale, keeping only an annuity for his family. It became the T. D. and T. W. Porter Fund, named for him and his brother Theodore.

narrative_blocks.header: The women's college he could not found
narrative_blocks.body: For years Timothy tried to give his two acres on Murray Hill, high above Kip's Bay, to found a college for young women. He could not interest others enough, and at last sold to the buyers who kept asking.

narrative_blocks.header: A medical degree he never used
narrative_blocks.body: Timothy took his medical degree at Yale in 1820 with a thesis on tests for arsenic, parts of which were published, but he never practised. He taught instead at the College of South Carolina until 1823.

narrative_blocks.header: Three New York papers in ten years
narrative_blocks.body: In New York Timothy owned the Religious Chronicle until the Observer bought it in 1826, helped edit the Albion, and founded the Atlas, a literary paper that closed about 1833 when his partner mismanaged its money.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran a school Lafayette named
narrative_blocks.body: From 1834 Timothy and his younger brother Theodore owned the Washington Institute, a New York boys' school Lafayette had named in 1824, and moved it out to Murray Hill. They gave it up when Theodore fell ill in 1855.

narrative_blocks.header: Married in 1839, two daughters
narrative_blocks.body: Timothy married Mary Eliza Hart of Utica in December 1839; she died in 1864. Of their two daughters, Julia died as a baby and Mary Louise outlived him by forty years.

b. 1826 Worcester, Worcester County MA; d. Sep 11, 1901 Portland, Multnomah County OR age ~74-75. Buried River View Cemetery, Portland OR. "Emily (Porter) Nichols was the great granddaughter of Jonathan Edwards, the first president of Princeton College." 7th-generation Hooker descendant. m. Dr. Ziba Bass Nichols (1821-1897) Mar 20, 1844 Waterford Twp., Dakota County MN. Dr. Nichols studied at Dartmouth; "oldest practicing homeopathic physician on the Pacific coast" at his death; physician and surgeon of the Minnesota state asylum for the deaf, dumb and blind for 18 years. 10 children including three Portland physicians: Dr. Ammi Sibley Nichols (1854-1931), Dr. Clarence Lincoln Nichols (1861-1911), Dr. Herbert Strong Nichols (1868-1948). Dr. Ammi Sibley Nichols was described as "son of Dr. Z.B. Nichols, preceptor of the Mayo brothers" — placing this family in proximity to the founders of the Mayo Clinic. Emily had been a resident of Portland 18 years prior to her death. (FindAGrave; Oregon Daily Journal obituary of Dr. Ziba Nichols 1897)

narrative_blocks.header: Husband oldest homeopathic physician on Pacific coast
narrative_blocks.body: Emily's husband Dr. Ziba Bass Nichols was described at his 1897 death as 'oldest practicing homeopathic physician on the Pacific coast' — a Dartmouth-trained physician who had worked the homeopathy revolution from its Minnesota mid-century days through to its Oregon-frontier late-century practice. He had served as physician and surgeon of the Minnesota state asylum for the deaf, dumb, and blind for eighteen years before the family's move to Portland.

narrative_blocks.header: Husband preceptor of the Mayo brothers
narrative_blocks.body: Dr. Nichols was described in a descendant biographical sketch as 'preceptor of the Mayo brothers' — placing the Porter-Nichols family in proximity to Charles Mayo and William Mayo, the founders of the Mayo Clinic. The preceptor-and-student relationship in nineteenth-century American medicine was a formal apprenticeship; if accurate, this placed Emily's household near the formative training of two of America's most consequential physicians.

narrative_blocks.header: Three sons became Portland physicians
narrative_blocks.body: Three of Emily and Dr. Nichols's ten children became Portland physicians in turn: Dr. Ammi Sibley Nichols (1854-1931), Dr. Clarence Lincoln Nichols (1861-1911), and Dr. Herbert Strong Nichols (1868-1948). The three-physician second generation extended the family's medical-practice continuity from 1844 marriage to mid-twentieth-century Oregon care.

narrative_blocks.header: Worcester MA 1826 to Portland OR 1901
narrative_blocks.body: Emily Porter was born in 1826 in Worcester, Worcester County Massachusetts, daughter of Benjamin Porter and Clementina Lamb. She died September 11, 1901 in Portland Oregon at about age seventy-five and is buried at River View Cemetery, Portland. She had been a resident of Portland eighteen years prior to her death.

narrative_blocks.header: A baby buried by Lake Huron
narrative_blocks.body: On the voyage west in 1834 Martha gave birth on board ship to a daughter, Mary Williams Porter, who lived a day. The captain put into shore south of St. Clair, Michigan, and Martha chose a grave under the trees looking out on Lake Huron. She never sailed again.

narrative_blocks.header: A sister twice told
narrative_blocks.body: From the Illinois log cabin in 1836 Martha wrote home to welcome her brother Thomas's bride, Lucretia Porter, who was also her husband's sister, a sister twice told.

narrative_blocks.header: Six children, one survived her
narrative_blocks.body: Martha bore six children and outlived five: Martha at three, the baby on the lake, Eleazar at nine in 1845 and Sophia at twenty-five in 1854. Only Sarah was left, and in 1856 Martha and Moses followed her to Minnesota.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brother made the family pictures
narrative_blocks.body: Martha's younger brother, William Ward Snell, later a minister, took daguerreotypes of the family, among them the portrait of her daughter Sophia. In Salem in 1856 he was publicly calling the patented ambrotype a great humbug, to the fury of a rival, Daniel Clifford.

narrative_blocks.header: A snowstorm kept hundreds from her funeral
narrative_blocks.body: Martha died on New Year's evening 1886, nearly eighty. A great snowstorm kept hundreds from the funeral, but as she had wished her grandsons carried her, and she was buried beside Moses at Waterford.

narrative_blocks.header: Her uncle made her daguerreotype
narrative_blocks.body: Sophia's likeness survives because her mother's brother, William Ward Snell, made daguerreotypes of the family. The original plate is with the Snell Family Papers at Amherst College.

narrative_blocks.header: Dead at twenty-four, the winter of 1854
narrative_blocks.body: Sophia was five when the family sailed west in 1834, and by 1850 she was the only one of the Porter children still at home in Hadley, Illinois. She died just after the new year in 1854, at twenty-four, probably at her sister Sarah's farm, and two years later her parents left for Minnesota.

people.research_notes: b. Oct 6, 1831 Hadley MA; d. Mar 26, 1891 (or 1899) Waterford, Dakota County MN. Buried Red Rose Cemetery, Waterford Township, Dakota County MN. Pioneer of Illinois and Minnesota. In 1834 moved with parents to Hadley, Will County IL. Married "neighbor" John J. Simpson (1825-1885) Nov 21, 1849 in Hadley Village, Homer Twp, Will County IL. In Mar 1856 traveled by horse and wagon, then Mississippi steamboat 400 miles, to Waterford MN. 10 children. Mentioned in Benjamin Woodbridge Dwight's 1871 "History of the Descendants of Elder John Strong of Northampton MA." (FindAGrave; FamilySearch)

narrative_blocks.header: Wagon, steamboat and wagon to Minnesota
narrative_blocks.body: In March 1856 Sarah and John took John, six, Sophia, three, and Charles, six months, two hundred miles across Illinois by wagon, up the Mississippi by steamboat to Hastings, and on by wagon to the new settlement of Waterford. Her parents set out after them in May.

narrative_blocks.header: She married the neighbors' son in 1849
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah married John Simpson at Hadley, Illinois, on 21 November 1849. His parents had come from Geneva, New York, in 1835, among the first settlers of Homer Township, and the young couple farmed across the line in Orland Township.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten children in two states
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah bore three children on the Orland Township farm and seven more at Waterford, the last two after 1871. She and John bought land in Greenvale Township, inherited her parents' farm, and divided it among their children as they married. She died at Waterford in March 1899 and lies at Red Rose Cemetery.

Eldest son of Daniel Hull Wickham Sr. of Southold NY and Mary Dresser, daughter of Capt. Jacob Dresser; uncle of William Hull Wickham, mayor of New York, and second cousin of John Wickham, Aaron Burr's counsel at the treason trial. Yale classmates included John M. Clayton and Truman Smith. He ran the Highland Gymnasium at Fishkill Landing with Charles Bartlett, and handed the Washington Institute in 1834 to his brothers-in-law Timothy Dwight Porter and Theodore Woolsey Porter. Yale holds 27 boxes of Wickham Family Papers, the gift of Marjorie Page Schauffler and Elizabeth Page.

narrative_blocks.header: He preached at Manchester for fifty-four years
narrative_blocks.body: He was licensed to preach in January 1821 and ordained at Oxford in Chenango County at the dedication of its new house of worship. He and Elizabeth then gave fifty-four years to Manchester's First Congregational Church, where he was unofficial associate pastor and taught a large Bible class.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-five years at the Burr Seminary
narrative_blocks.body: He took the Burr Seminary in December 1837 and held it twenty-five years, and under him it became Vermont's first coeducational secondary school. Its Joseph Wickham Society, named for the longest-serving headmaster, still honours staff who reach twenty-five years.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote for the president of Yale
narrative_blocks.body: Greek and Latin were his as a child; he took his Yale degree in 1815 and spent the next year as secretary to President Timothy Dwight. Then a year as rector of the Hopkins Grammar School, two as a tutor, and poems in the Microscope of New Haven.

narrative_blocks.header: Last man alive from Yale 1815
narrative_blocks.body: Five years he was the last survivor of his class, three the oldest living graduate of Yale, and the last man alive to have taken a degree under the elder President Dwight. Middlebury made him a doctor of divinity in 1861, Yale an S.T.D. the same year.

narrative_blocks.header: He was born when men lived to thirty-five
narrative_blocks.body: He died at Manchester on 12 May 1891 in his ninety-fifth year, fit and clear-minded to the last, at an age the country he was born into averaged about thirty-five.

narrative_blocks.header: Three wives, and he outlived two
narrative_blocks.body: He married Julia Ann Porter in May 1823 and she died at New York in December 1830; her first cousin Amy Porter, married a year later, died eight days after bearing Emma. Elizabeth Cooke Merwin, married in October 1834, outlived him by ten years.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Porters, and both of them Hookers
narrative_blocks.body: Julia Ann Porter was Fidelia Dwight's daughter and President Timothy Dwight's niece; Amy Porter was Col. Moses Porter's daughter, of Hadley, and her first cousin. Both carried Thomas Hooker's blood.

narrative_blocks.body: Amy Porter died at New York on 29 October 1832, eight days after bearing her. She married Alfred Cox Roe at Manchester in Vermont in October 1860 and died there herself seventy-four years later.

narrative_blocks.header: A pupil proved it with chain and transit
narrative_blocks.body: He turned to mathematics, surveying and engineering in 1852, bought a transit, and learned the work himself before he taught it. The only proof he took that a boy understood the science was to send him out with instrument and chain to measure, calculate at home, and bring back correct balanced results.

narrative_blocks.header: Willis opened Idlewild to the schoolboys
narrative_blocks.body: In 1853 he bought a mansion on fifteen acres half a mile from the Hudson, looking twenty miles upriver, and kept the school to twenty-five boys who nearly all boarded with his family. Idlewild, Nathaniel Parker Willis's house, adjoined the grounds; Willis made it free territory to the pupils and called the school in his Home Journal one of the best for boys in the country.

narrative_blocks.header: His governess got the credit for everything
narrative_blocks.body: He was taught at home by an English governess, Miss Elizabeth Woodhams, and gave her the credit for most of what he afterwards made of himself. He entered the University of the City of New York as a sophomore in 1840 and took third honour in 1843.

narrative_blocks.header: His forge iron blocked the Hudson in 1777
narrative_blocks.body: He came down from Samuel Brewster, whose four-fire forge and anchor shop on Murderer's Creek at Cornwall made the bar iron for the chevaux-de-frise laid from Pollopel's Island to Plum Point in 1777, under General James Clinton. His grandfather Jonas Williams married into the forge and later fed part of Washington's army at Morristown.

narrative_blocks.header: The British burned his grandfather out
narrative_blocks.body: His grandfather James Roe settled at Esopus, now Kingston, before the Revolution and took the patriot side; the British and Tories burned his house when they burned the town, and he barely got his family away. He was a chaplain to the New York Volunteers himself in the Civil War.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the book on American toolmakers
narrative_blocks.body: Roe's 1916 study English and American Tool Builders became the classic history of the men who built America's machine tools. A Yale-trained engineer, he later chaired industrial engineering at New York University.

narrative_blocks.header: He flew with the wartime Signal Corps
narrative_blocks.body: During the First World War Roe served as a major in the Aviation Section of the Army Signal Reserve Corps. He returned to consult for the Navy in the Second World War.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the history of machine tools
narrative_blocks.body: The first half of his book is English - Henry Maudslay and the men who made the machine tools before America had any - and he argued their creative work counted for as much as any statesman's or soldier's. He taught industrial engineering at Yale's Sheffield School and afterwards at New York University.

narrative_blocks.header: His book named the great toolmakers
narrative_blocks.body: Roe traced the lineage of American precision manufacturing through the New England armories and press-builders like the Hoe dynasty. Generations of engineers learned their craft's history from his pages.

narrative_blocks.header: He shaped early industrial-engineering education
narrative_blocks.body: Roe helped establish industrial engineering as an academic discipline, teaching at Yale's Sheffield School and later at New York University. His students carried his methods into American factories during the era of scientific management.

narrative_blocks.header: He and Mary died three months apart
narrative_blocks.body: He married Mary Augusta Sherwood of Nebraska in November 1915, at forty-four. She died at Fairfield on 30 July 1960 and he followed on 9 November, both of them eighty-nine, and they lie together at Oak Lawn.

career.notes: Pioneer of industrial-engineering education.

He ended the war as aide-de-camp to General Duncan at New Bern, North Carolina.

narrative_blocks.header: Licensed at Hartford's Black church
narrative_blocks.body: After a year as a superintendent of the Freedmen's Bureau in Washington, Moses studied at the Hartford Theological Seminary, was ordained on 8 May 1867, and in 1868 was licensed to preach at the Talcott Street Church, Hartford's Black Congregational church.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years of Washington pulpits
narrative_blocks.body: Moses was a missionary in and around Washington from 1871, an agent of the Washington City Bible Society until 1888, and then pastor at Hermon, Maryland, Clifton, Virginia, and Riverdale, Maryland. He spent his last years in government service and died at Newton, New Jersey, on the last day of 1909.

narrative_blocks.header: Grandson of an Amherst College founder
narrative_blocks.body: Moses was a grandson of Dr. Thomas Snell of North Brookfield, one of the founders of Amherst College, and a nephew of Ebenezer Snell, who taught there. He took his own Amherst degree in 1868.

narrative_blocks.header: Henderson Field ready in four days
narrative_blocks.body: Sent to Guadalcanal by Vice Admiral John S. McCain, Charles landed on 15 August 1942 with a Navy construction unit and four shiploads of aviation supplies, and under daily Japanese air raids had Henderson Field ready in four days. The first planes came in on 20 August, and the work won him the Navy Distinguished Service Medal.

narrative_blocks.header: Assistant Commandant of the Marine Corps
narrative_blocks.body: After Korea, where he ran air operations for the 1st Marine Aircraft Wing, Charles commanded that wing in Japan and the 3rd at El Toro. On 9 April 1963 he was made a lieutenant general and Assistant Commandant of the Marine Corps, and served until June 1965.

narrative_blocks.header: In Tokyo Bay on surrender day
narrative_blocks.body: As air officer to the III Amphibious Corps, Charles planned the Green Island, Emirau, Leyte and Luzon landings, and he arrived in Tokyo Bay with the first occupation forces on the day of the Japanese surrender.

narrative_blocks.header: He sailed four days before Pearl Harbor
narrative_blocks.body: In 1941 Charles helped set up the new Marine air station at Ewa, on Oahu, and sailed for San Diego just four days before the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, to become executive officer of Marine Fighter Squadron 251.

narrative_blocks.header: A railroad year before Annapolis
narrative_blocks.body: Born at San Marcial, New Mexico, Charles finished high school at Albuquerque in 1924, worked a year in the Santa Fe Railway's engineering department, tried a year at Colorado A&M, and entered the Naval Academy in 1926.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at San Diego in 1940
narrative_blocks.body: Charles married Elizabeth Rittenhouse Snell of Washington before 1935. She died at San Diego on 3 September 1940, at thirty-three, two months after he reported to the naval air station there.
