narrative_blocks.header: Among the largest slaveholders in the state
narrative_blocks.body: He was one of the wealthiest planters and merchants in North Carolina, and held more enslaved people than almost any man in it. The estate he left ran across Craven and the counties north of it.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept a New Jersey house to breathe
narrative_blocks.body: Like other Carolina planters he believed the air of his own plantations was killing him, and took a summer residence at Elizabethtown. One account has him living there the whole year round by the early 1760s.

narrative_blocks.header: He died in New Jersey, not Carolina
narrative_blocks.body: The marriage to Eunice Edwards was made at Elizabethtown in 1764 and he died there in 1777, with the Revolution running and his Carolina estates a month's travel away.

narrative_blocks.header: The Burgwyn line runs through his one daughter
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah Pierpont Hunt was born in 1789 and married John Fanning Burgwyn in 1806. Every Burgwyn in this tree descends from that marriage.

narrative_blocks.header: The largest slaveholder in the state
narrative_blocks.body: The estate his father left him ran across Craven, Bertie, Chowan and Halifax counties, and he held more enslaved people than any other man in North Carolina. He never married and left no children.

narrative_blocks.header: Devereux against Burgwyn, and others
narrative_blocks.body: His lands were distributed among his heirs between 1840 and 1843, and the fight over them went up to the state supreme court in September 1840 as Devereux v. Burgwyn and Others. His sister Frances took the bulk of what he had held.

narrative_blocks.header: The estate divided a thousand and eighty-six
narrative_blocks.body: The papers of 1839 to 1843 set out the division of one thousand and eighty-six enslaved people among his heirs, listed by family. The deeds run through Bertie, Martin, Halifax, Northampton and Franklin counties.

narrative_blocks.header: He and Aaron Burr were cousins and friends
narrative_blocks.body: His mother had been raised in the household that took in the orphaned Burr children, so he and Aaron Burr grew up in the same family. The two remained intimate friends.

Frances co-founded First Presbyterian Church, New Bern. 3 children: Thomas Pollock Devereux (1793-1869), George Pollock Devereux (1795-1837), Frances Ann Devereux Polk (1807-1875). narrative_blocks.header: New Bern called her the Spanish Galleon
narrative_blocks.body: The portion of her father's estate due her at marriage or at twenty-one was large enough that the town gave her the name. She was known besides for remarkable intellect.

narrative_blocks.header: A shipwreck brought her a husband
narrative_blocks.body: John Devereux was captain of a Charleston trading vessel when he went aground off the coast and met her at New Bern. He sold his business there and came back to marry her in 1790.

narrative_blocks.header: All three of her siblings died childless
narrative_blocks.body: George, the largest slaveholder in the state, left no children, and neither did the other two. The whole of the Pollock property came down to her and her children.

narrative_blocks.header: Her will paid a teacher for the enslaved
narrative_blocks.body: She left money to the Presbyterian church, to its schools and foreign missions, and to the Seaman's Friend Society at Norfolk. She also left a continuing annual fund to pay a teacher giving religious instruction to the people enslaved on the Roanoke River plantations.

narrative_blocks.header: A bishop, a diarist, a poet after her
narrative_blocks.body: Her daughter Frances married Leonidas Polk, who became a bishop and then a Confederate general. Her granddaughters Catherine Edmondston and Mary Bayard Clarke wrote, one a war diary and one poetry.

bio.bio_blurb: Irish-born New Bern merchant and shipowner

narrative_blocks.header: He was sent to France for the priesthood
narrative_blocks.body: A younger son of a Wexford family, he was educated at the monastery school at St Omer with orders in view, and declined to take the vows. He went into the British navy as a midshipman instead and came out of the American war a first lieutenant.

narrative_blocks.header: His family cut him off, so he sailed
narrative_blocks.body: Home in Ireland he was rejected by his relations for abandoning the priesthood, and he severed the connection. He crossed to America with nothing and went into a Charleston merchant house.

narrative_blocks.header: A shipwreck made him a Carolina merchant
narrative_blocks.body: Commanding one of the firm's trading vessels, he was wrecked off the coast near New Bern and stayed. He married the Pollock heiress in 1790 and carried on the business from her town.

narrative_blocks.header: A fleet between Boston and Barbados
narrative_blocks.body: He came to own the ships as well as the cargoes, trading north to Boston and south to the West Indies. In business circles, one account of him ran, his name was what Rothschild's was in Europe.

narrative_blocks.header: Raleigh in the twenties, both sons at Yale
narrative_blocks.body: The family moved up to Raleigh in the 1820s, and he died there in July 1844 and was buried in the City Cemetery. Thomas and George were both sent north to Yale.

bio.bio_blurb: North Carolina lawyer, Supreme Court reporter, planter

career.role: U.S. Attorney for the District of North Carolina
Reporter of the North Carolina Supreme Court
career.notes: Published four volumes of law and two of equity reports ("Devereux's Reports").

narrative_blocks.header: His law reports still bear his name
narrative_blocks.body: As reporter of the North Carolina Supreme Court from 1826, Devereux published four volumes of law and two of equity that lawyers cited for generations as Devereux's Reports. He took up law in earnest only after business reverses spent his inherited fortune.

narrative_blocks.header: He held fifteen hundred people in bondage
narrative_blocks.body: Inheriting his uncle's plantations made him one of the largest enslavers in North Carolina, holding about fifteen hundred people. He was a staunch Unionist before secession and backed the Confederacy once war came.

narrative_blocks.header: The estate cost him the law
narrative_blocks.body: He had reported the state supreme court since 1826 and left the profession when George Pollock died and the plantations came to him. The office he kept was local: justice of the peace, and presiding justice of the county court of Halifax.

narrative_blocks.header: He reported that court, then stood before it
narrative_blocks.body: Thirteen years of its decisions were printed as Devereux's Reports. In September 1840 he came before the same bench as a party, in the suit over his uncle's land.

narrative_blocks.body: Out of Yale in 1815 and the Litchfield law school after it, he practised three years alongside George Pollock and went with him on a European tour. He gave the law up for planting.

narrative_blocks.header: He married his second cousin from Connecticut
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah Elizabeth Johnson was a childhood friend as well as a cousin, and they married at Stratford in June 1827. They kept Runiroi on the Roanoke, part of his Pollock inheritance, and summered in Connecticut.

narrative_blocks.header: Delicate all his life, dead at forty
narrative_blocks.body: He was travelling north to Stratford when he died at Suffolk in Virginia in May 1837. His widow took the daughters back to her own people in Connecticut.

bio.bio_blurb: Bishop's wife, planter's daughter, war widow

narrative_blocks.header: She married the bishop who became a general
narrative_blocks.body: Frances Ann Devereux of Raleigh married Leonidas Polk in May 1830, the year he was ordained deacon. She was a bishop's wife in Louisiana for twenty years and a general's widow after a shell killed him in Georgia in 1864.

narrative_blocks.header: Her inheritance worked his sugar plantation
narrative_blocks.body: The people her family held in North Carolina were carried to Bayou Lafourche to work the cane at Leighton. The plantation was lost to debt in 1854, twelve years after he took it on.

narrative_blocks.header: She taught school to keep herself
narrative_blocks.body: Her widowhood was spent teaching at the Columbia Female Institute in Tennessee and then in New Orleans. She wrote a quarter of the six hundred letters that reached her daughter Fanny at Oxford, running on money, loneliness and the children.

narrative_blocks.header: She called the Federals the Lincolnites
narrative_blocks.body: She wrote to her husband in April 1862 that the gunboats had passed the forts and the Federals — the Lincolnites, she called them — would be up to New Orleans. Farragut anchored off the city the next day.

narrative_blocks.header: She waited out the war at Asheville
narrative_blocks.body: He was killed in June 1864 and she took a house at Asheville for what was left of the fighting. She outlived him by eleven years.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept a diary through her widowhood
narrative_blocks.body: She wrote it through 1873 and 1874, and much of her effort in those years went into recovering her husband's papers. The diary is in the Southern Historical Collection.

narrative_blocks.header: She was reinterred beside him in 1945
narrative_blocks.body: She died in 1875 and lay seventy years elsewhere. In 1945 she was moved to Christ Church Cathedral in New Orleans and laid beside Leonidas.

notable.notable_blurb: Suffragist, novelist and lobbyist

people.research_notes: Born Elizabeth Johnson Devereux at Raleigh, 12 August 1833 — the Yale obituary record gives 1835 and the NCpedia sketch says she was christened Sarah Johnson; both are variants of her mother's name, Sarah Elizabeth Johnson. Daughter of George Pollock Devereux (HD2593) and Sarah Elizabeth Johnson Devereux (HD2151); gen 8 from Thomas Hooker. Granddaughter of William Samuel Johnson (X03617), Constitution signer and president of Columbia, and great-granddaughter of the Rev. Samuel Johnson who founded King's College; both parents descended from Jonathan Edwards. First husband Frank Umsted died in 1859, an apparent suicide. In 1886 she and a party of suffragists including her daughter Katherine took a cattle barge out to the dedication of the Statue of Liberty, to say what they thought of dedicating a woman to a country where women could not vote. Answering Morgan Dix's Lenten sermons on woman's place she argued that if Eve was inferior to Adam for being created after him, then by the same logic Adam was inferior to the fishes. She held that gender roles are learned and that men and women share a common nature — the theoretical break with Anthony, who rested suffrage on women's separate moral nature. PS 6 in Manhattan is the Lillie D. Blake School. Sources: Wikipedia; NCpedia; Sophia Smith Collection, Blake Family Papers; Grace Farrell, Lillie Devereux Blake: Retracing a Life Erased (2002).

narrative_blocks.header: Named for her mother, called Lillie
narrative_blocks.body: She was named for her mother, Sarah Elizabeth Johnson Devereux, and her father called her Lillie instead for her fairness. Her diary has her at sixteen registering the position of her sex with indignation and humiliation; twenty years of watering places came between that and acting on it.

narrative_blocks.header: Five pen names paid the bills
narrative_blocks.body: Widowed at twenty-six with two daughters, she wrote for a living as Essex, Charity Floyd, Di Fairfax, Violet and Tiger Lily. Fettered for Life, printed at her own expense in 1874, sold thirteen hundred copies the day it appeared.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote the war from Washington
narrative_blocks.body: In 1861 she went to the capital on commissions from three papers and became the Evening Post's correspondent there. She described the presidential levees, and set down Lincoln's kindness and sadness of expression.

narrative_blocks.header: Her first sight of Susan B. Anthony
narrative_blocks.body: She joined the suffrage movement in 1869, and her diary registers astonishment at Miss Anthony's bloomer costume of printed dotted silk. Old friends dropped her for it, so she trained her voice, read the statutes, and went at it professionally.

narrative_blocks.header: She asked Columbia to admit her daughters
narrative_blocks.body: In October 1873 she petitioned President Barnard to open Columbia to women, arguing that the youth of the city in its charter meant daughters too. Morgan Dix had the trustees rule it inexpedient; Barnard College opened sixteen years after she asked.

narrative_blocks.header: She lobbied police matrons into existence
narrative_blocks.body: Eleven years president of the state association, she won school suffrage in 1880, women factory inspectors, women physicians in asylums, and in 1891 police matrons, over the persistent opposition of the police department. She founded the National Legislative League in 1903.

narrative_blocks.header: The histories left her out on purpose
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth Cady Stanton wanted her to succeed Anthony in 1900 and the place went to Carrie Chapman Catt instead. Anthony's official history of the movement passed over her work, and the biography that recovered it a century later is subtitled Retracing a Life Erased.

education.notes: She read the undergraduate curriculum with tutors at home; women could not matriculate.

notable.notable_blurb: Episcopal bishop and Confederate lieutenant general

people.research_notes: b. Apr 10, 1806 Raleigh NC; d. Jun 14, 1864 Pine Mountain (Cobb County) GA age 58. Killed in action by artillery shell. Buried Christ Church Cathedral, New Orleans (reinterred 1945). WEST POINT: Graduated 1827. Best friend and classmate: Jefferson Davis (future President of the Confederacy). BISHOP: Resigned military commission; entered Virginia Theological Seminary. Bishop of the Episcopal Diocese of Louisiana. One of the wealthiest slaveholding bishops in the country. Owned Leighton Plantation, Thibodaux LA — worked by slaves from wife's NC plantations. FOUNDER: University of the South, Sewanee TN (1857). CONFEDERATE GENERAL: Major General, Confederate Army; commanded corps at Shiloh, Perryville, Stones River, Chickamauga, Atlanta Campaign. DEATH: Jun 14, 1864, scouting with Generals Johnston and Hardee on Pine Mountain GA; Sherman spotted the cluster and ordered artillery. Third shell struck Polk in the left arm, went through his chest and exited, "nearly cut him in two." Three books titled "Balm for the Weary and Wounded" were found in his pocket, inscribed to Generals Johnston, Hardee, and Hood, "June 12, 1864." Military historian Woodworth: "one of the worst shots fired for the Union cause during the entire course of the war" — Polk's incompetence made him more valuable alive. Fort Polk (Louisiana) named for him until renamed Fort Johnson 2023. Second cousin of President James K. Polk. m. Frances Ann Devereux (HD2594) May 13, 1830 Raleigh NC. 7 children. institutions.institution_blurb: Principal organizing bishop and co-founder of the University of the South at Sewanee Tennessee; died June 1864 before the school opened.

military_service.notes: Commissioned 1861 despite no military service since West Point. Commanded corps at Shiloh, Perryville, Stones River, Chickamauga, Atlanta Campaign. Killed Pine Mountain GA Jun 14, 1864. Military historian Steven Woodworth called him 'one of the worst shots fired for the Union cause' — his incompetence as commander made him more valuable alive.

career.notes: One of the wealthiest slaveholding bishops in the United States. Owned Leighton Plantation, Thibodaux LA, worked by slaves brought from wife's NC plantations.
Founded the University of the South at Sewanee, Tennessee 1857 as an Episcopal university for the South. Construction interrupted by Civil War.

narrative_blocks.header: A bishop who took a general's commission
narrative_blocks.body: He was the Episcopal bishop of Louisiana when the war came, and Jefferson Davis made him a major general in 1861. He never gave up the bishopric: soldiers called him the Fighting Bishop, and he baptized two of his own commanders in camp.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded the University of the South
narrative_blocks.body: He meant it for a Harvard of the South and bought ten thousand acres on the Tennessee mountain at Sewanee. He laid the cornerstone in October 1860; the war destroyed it, and Sewanee had to be founded a second time after his death.

narrative_blocks.header: The highest-ranking Confederate killed in the war
narrative_blocks.body: Watching the Union lines from Pine Mountain in June 1864, he sent his staff off the crest and stayed for one more look. A shell killed him where he stood, and Hardee wept when he was told.

narrative_blocks.header: Six months a soldier, then a seminary
narrative_blocks.body: He roomed with Albert Sidney Johnston at West Point and was converted by the chaplain in his last year there. He graduated in 1827, resigned his commission within six months, and went to the seminary in Virginia instead.

narrative_blocks.header: Five thousand miles in six months
narrative_blocks.body: Made missionary bishop of the Southwest in 1838, he rode a territory he reckoned the size of France. In half a year he travelled five thousand miles and preached forty-four sermons.

narrative_blocks.header: Four hundred people worked his cane
narrative_blocks.body: At Leighton on Bayou Lafourche he held more than four hundred enslaved people, most of them brought from his wife's Carolina inheritance. Cholera killed a hundred of them in 1849, and the debts took the plantation in 1854.

narrative_blocks.header: Bragg wanted him court-martialled
narrative_blocks.body: He quarrelled with Braxton Bragg for two years and pressed Davis to remove him; after Chickamauga Bragg demanded a court-martial. Davis settled it by sending him to Mississippi.

people.research_notes: b. 1835 Tennessee; d. Mar 15, 1884 age 48. Daughter of Leonidas Polk × Frances Devereux. m. Peyton Horatio Skipwith Nov 13, 1866 Maury County TN. (FindAGrave)

narrative_blocks.header: She married a widower thirty years older
narrative_blocks.body: She was thirty-one when she married Peyton Horatio Skipwith in Maury County in November 1866. He was sixty, a widower with four grown children, and her father, Bishop Leonidas Polk, had been killed at Pine Mountain two years earlier.

narrative_blocks.header: She named her daughter for his first wife
narrative_blocks.body: Skipwith had already buried his first wife, Kate Anderson, sister of two Confederate officers. Their daughter was christened Catharine Anderson after her, and went by Kate for the rest of her life.

narrative_blocks.header: Her daughter was born at Sewanee in 1867
narrative_blocks.body: Kate was born in September 1867 at Sewanee, the Tennessee mountain where her grandfather, Bishop Leonidas Polk, had laid the cornerstone of the University of the South. He had been dead three years.

narrative_blocks.header: Six hundred letters came to her at Oxford
narrative_blocks.body: Between 1865 and 1884 some six hundred letters reached her at Oxford, and a quarter came from her mother, who wrote out a widowhood of debt and loneliness from New Orleans, Asheville and Nashville.

narrative_blocks.header: Skipwith hated Washington and wrote to say so
narrative_blocks.body: Peyton Skipwith travelled as a cotton broker, insurance man and debt collector, and wrote to her from Washington about the shame an ex-Confederate felt in the capital. In 1869 he was there asking Congressman James Garfield to help win legislative relief for former Confederate soldiers.

narrative_blocks.header: The Vicksburg colonel wrote to her too
narrative_blocks.body: Winchester Hall, who commanded the 26th Louisiana through the siege of Vicksburg and later wrote its history, sent her letters along with his wife Ruth. Ruth described the Union invasion of Louisiana in 1863 and a rising among the enslaved after the Confederates fell back.

people.research_notes: b. Aug 16, 1838 Ashwood Maury County TN; d. Feb 8, 1916 Nashville TN age 77 — extraordinary longevity. Daughter of Bishop Leonidas Polk and Frances Ann Devereux. Only Polk daughter married before the Civil War (m. William Dudley Gale 1858 at age 20). Nashville citizen; prominent member of Christ Church (Episcopal). Part of the intellectual Craddock circle in Nashville (Mary Noailles Murfree pen-name 'Charles Egbert Craddock'). NATIONAL PRESIDENT of the Colonial Dames of America. 5 children: Frances Polk 'Fannie' Gale Ring (1860-1937), William Dudley Gale II (1861-1959), Kate Gale (1862-1889), Leonide Polk Gale (1864-1890), Ethel Gale (1869-1870 d. infancy). Buried Mount Olivet Cemetery, Nashville. (FindAGrave obituary; Mount Olivet Cemetery records) [Stage 6Y-279 CDA context]: Colonial Dames of America (CDA) is the women's hereditary society for descendants of those who served the British North American colonies 1607-1775 in public office, military, or other approved capacity. National Headquarters: MOUNT VERNON HOTEL MUSEUM in New York City, purchased by CDA in 1924. As CDA National President, Katherine Polk Gale would have presided at this NYC headquarters. CDA is listed in the Hereditary Society Community of the United States of America. [Stage 6Y-280 Gale-Polk papers archive]: GALE AND POLK FAMILY PAPERS at the Southern Historical Collection, University of North Carolina (Chapel Hill) — contain antebellum papers of Thomas Gale (William Dudley Gale's father; Davidson TN physician with plantations in Jefferson and Yazoo counties MS); Civil War letters of Gen. Leonidas Polk (X00867) and his son-in-law William Dudley Gale (X00875); RECOLLECTIONS (1895) written by Katherine Polk Gale herself about her Civil War experiences in Nashville TN, Yazoo County MS, and Asheville NC; and the DIARY (1873-1874) of Frances Devereux Polk (HD2594) recording her activities at the Gale household near Nashville. The Civil War letters include detailed accounts of Chickamauga, the Atlanta Campaign, and Franklin/Nashville battles, plus Gale's assessments of Confederate generals Bragg, Davis, Forrest, Hood, Hardee, Johnston.

narrative_blocks.header: The only Polk daughter married before the war
narrative_blocks.body: She married William Dudley Gale at New Orleans in 1858, at twenty, the only one of the bishop’s daughters to marry before the war. She came to Nashville in 1860 and spent the next fifty-six years there.

narrative_blocks.header: She organized the Woman’s Auxiliary
narrative_blocks.body: Sixty years at Christ Church, she organized the parish Woman’s Auxiliary and was its first president, and branches of it went up across Tennessee under her. As president of the Parish Aid Society she raised the money for the new church on Broad Street.

narrative_blocks.header: The book club took a novelist’s pen name
narrative_blocks.body: She founded the Craddock Circle, the first book club in Nashville, and ran it as president. It was named for Charles Egbert Craddock, the pen name Mary Noailles Murfree wrote her Tennessee novels under.

narrative_blocks.header: She built the Colonial Dames in Tennessee
narrative_blocks.body: The national president of the Colonial Dames asked her to organize a Tennessee society, and she was its first state president and its honorary president when she died.

narrative_blocks.header: Her nephew was assistant secretary of state
narrative_blocks.body: Her brother was the New York physician William Mecklenburg Polk, and his son Frank Lyon Polk was Assistant Secretary of State by the time she died in 1916.

Joseph 'Joe' Jones MD (X00877) Jun 20, 1870 New Orleans — Confederate surgeon, Tulane medical pioneer, near-discoverer of the malarial parasite. His second marriage; her only. 1850 census: residence Lafourche Crossing LA (her family's plantation area). 3 children with Jones: Frances Devereux Jones (1871-1941), Hamilton Polk Jones (1873-1926), Laura Maxwell Jones (1876-1917) — none yet built as separate entries. Owned the c.1800 Chickasaw pipe tomahawk (ART063) acquired by her husband Joseph Jones; she sold it to George Heye in 1906, now in Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian. Sold the pipe tomahawk and her husband's papers after his 1896 death — papers relating to several generations of the Polk family now held at Yale University Library (Beinecke). (FindAGrave; FamilySearch; Smithsonian NMAI; Yale Beinecke archives)

narrative_blocks.header: She was the surgeon’s second wife
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Raleigh in 1842, the only one of the ten Polk children born in North Carolina, she married the Confederate surgeon Joseph Jones in June 1870, two years after his first wife died. They had three children at New Orleans.

narrative_blocks.header: She tried to sell his collection
narrative_blocks.body: After Joseph Jones died she set about selling the medical library and the archaeological collection he had spent a lifetime gathering, and Grace King wrote to her about it around 1901.

narrative_blocks.header: The Georgia plantations were still unsettled
narrative_blocks.body: Letters came to her and her son Hamilton from Charles Edgeworth Jones, who was handling the family estate in Liberty County, Georgia, and its Maybank, Arcadia and Montevideo plantations.

narrative_blocks.header: He was the medical school's first dean
narrative_blocks.body: When Cornell opened a medical department in New York in 1898, Polk was made its dean and professor of diseases of women, and with Lewis Stimson had the job of building it from nothing. He held the deanship until he died.

narrative_blocks.header: He built Bellevue its gynecological service
narrative_blocks.body: With W. Gill Wylie and William Lusk he made the gynecological service at Bellevue, giving up the teaching of obstetrics to concentrate on surgery. He had first come to the hospital as an interne and never really left it.

narrative_blocks.header: An iron works turned him to medicine
narrative_blocks.body: After the surrender he took charge of the outdoor department at the Brierfield iron works in Alabama, and it was there, under a local doctor named Bailey, that he began to read medicine. He took his degree in New York in 1869.

narrative_blocks.header: Drill master at sixteen under Stonewall Jackson
narrative_blocks.body: He was in his seventeenth year when the war began, and spent 1861 drilling Virginia troops at Richmond under Jackson, then Tennessee troops for Zollicoffer. He served without a break until May 1865, ending as a captain on Joseph Johnston's staff.

narrative_blocks.header: A Confederate captain, then a US lieutenant
narrative_blocks.body: In 1917, at seventy-two, he volunteered and was commissioned a first lieutenant in the Army Reserve Medical Corps, fifty-two years after he had surrendered as a Confederate captain. He still held the commission when he died the following summer.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote his father's life
narrative_blocks.body: Leonidas Polk, Bishop and General came out in 1893 and again in two volumes in 1915, built from his father's papers and from his own memory of campaigns he had served in beside him.

narrative_blocks.header: The only Polk child born in Louisiana
narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Lafourche Parish in October 1845, the only one of Bishop Polk's children born after the family moved down to the Louisiana sugar country. The rest came before it.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at thirty-seven, and forty-seven more
narrative_blocks.body: She married Edward Chapman at the start of 1870, and he was dead at thirty-five in New Orleans by 1883. She lived another forty-seven years and died at Philadelphia in 1930, at eighty-five.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote north to her sister for decades
narrative_blocks.body: She kept up a correspondence with her sister Susan Rebecca, who had married Campbell Brown, stepson of the Confederate general Richard Stoddert Ewell. One of her letters to Susan carried the news of Lucius Polk's death.

narrative_blocks.body: Arthur Middleton of South Carolina, one of the signers, was his great-grandfather on his mother’s side, and his grandfather Daniel Elliott Huger sat in the United States Senate for South Carolina. The Hugers were Huguenots who came to Carolina in the seventeenth century.

narrative_blocks.header: His father took a brigade against the Seminoles
narrative_blocks.body: Colonel John Huger was made adjutant general under General Moore in the Seminole war of 1835, kept sugar plantations on the Red River and Côte Blanche, and served as a Confederate colonel under Braxton Bragg. He had been a schoolmate and lifelong friend of Hamilton Fish.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the Marshall Plan's Paris mission
narrative_blocks.body: A New York lawyer until 1941, Labouisse spent the war and the decade after moving American money into a wrecked Europe, heading the Paris mission that delivered Marshall Plan aid to France. Dag Hammarskjold hired him away in 1954 to run UNRWA, the UN agency then responsible for 887,000 Palestinian refugees.

narrative_blocks.header: He fed both sides of Nigeria's civil war
narrative_blocks.body: Labouisse directed UNICEF for fourteen years and twice took it into a war still being fought. It supplied both the federal government and secessionist Biafra through the Nigerian civil war in 1968, and went into Cambodia in 1979 behind the Vietnamese invasion.

narrative_blocks.header: Five months in the job, and a Nobel
narrative_blocks.body: Maurice Pate, UNICEF's first director, died in office in January 1965; Labouisse took the post in June and in December accepted the Nobel Peace Prize on its behalf. It made him the fifth member of the Curie family to accept one.

narrative_blocks.header: The Curie daughter he met through NATO
narrative_blocks.body: Eve Curie had written the bestselling life of her mother and covered the war as a correspondent before joining NATO's staff in Paris, where Labouisse was running Marshall Plan aid. They met in 1951, married in New York in 1954, and she outlived him by twenty years, dying at 102.

narrative_blocks.header: A 1941 party registration cost him the job
narrative_blocks.body: Eisenhower picked him to run the government's foreign-aid agency in 1959, and the Republican national chairman blocked it because Labouisse had registered as a Democrat in 1941. Kennedy gave him the same post in January 1961, then sent him to Athens as ambassador.

narrative_blocks.header: Great-grandson of a Confederate bishop
narrative_blocks.body: His mother, Frances Devereux Huger, was a granddaughter of Leonidas Polk, the Episcopal bishop of Louisiana who took a Confederate general's commission and was killed by a shell at Pine Mountain in 1864.

b. Dec 6, 1904 Paris, France; d. Oct 22, 2007 Manhattan NY age 102. Buried Metairie Cemetery, New Orleans. Daughter of Pierre Curie and Marie Sklodowska-Curie (2x Nobel Prize). Sister: Irène Joliot-Curie (Nobel Chemistry 1935). WWII: Free French Forces; Croix de guerre; Vichy stripped her of French citizenship. Author: "Madame Curie" (1937, National Book Award winner). "Journey Among Warriors" (1943, Pulitzer nomination for correspondence). Special advisor to first NATO Secretary General Hastings Ismay 1952-1954. UNICEF: "First Lady of UNICEF" — traveled 100+ countries with husband. She joked: "There were five Nobel Prizes in my family... only I was not successful." In 1965, her husband accepted the Nobel Peace Prize for UNICEF — completing the Curie family chain of five Nobel Prize recipients. In 2004, Secretary General Kofi Annan visited her on her 100th birthday. m. Henry Richardson Labouisse Jr. (HD2603) Nov 19, 1954 NYC. No children. (Wikipedia on Ève Curie; FindAGrave)

narrative_blocks.header: A bestseller about her mother, and a silence
narrative_blocks.body: Madame Curie appeared in six countries at once in 1937, won the National Book Award and reached MGM in 1943. Written three years after her mother's death, it says nothing of the affair that had scandalized France.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty thousand miles across the war's fronts
narrative_blocks.body: As a correspondent from late 1941 she crossed North Africa, Iran, the Soviet Union, India and China, interviewing Chiang Kai-shek, the Shah and Gandhi. Journey Among Warriors came of it, and was nominated for a Pulitzer.

narrative_blocks.header: Vichy took her citizenship and her property
narrative_blocks.body: She got out of France in June 1940 on a refugee ship strafed by German aircraft, joined de Gaulle, and lost her nationality to Vichy the next year. She landed in Provence in 1944 as a lieutenant and took the Croix de guerre.

narrative_blocks.header: They called her the First Lady of UNICEF
narrative_blocks.body: She worked for UNICEF from the 1960s and went with her husband to more than a hundred countries. Kofi Annan came to her New York flat for her hundredth birthday.

narrative_blocks.header: Trained for the concert platform, not the lab
narrative_blocks.body: She took her baccalaureate at the Collège Sévigné in 1925, gave her first Paris concert that year, and played France and Belgium before writing music criticism. The American press of 1921 called her the girl with radium eyes.

narrative_blocks.header: The only Curie without a Nobel Prize
narrative_blocks.body: Her father, mother, sister and brother-in-law held four Nobel Prizes between them, and she called herself the family failure for holding none. The fifth came in 1965, when her husband accepted the Peace Prize for UNICEF.

narrative_blocks.header: The only woman in the family radium spared
narrative_blocks.body: Marie Curie died of aplastic anemia in 1934, Irène Joliot-Curie of leukemia in 1956, both from years of handling radioactive material. Ève, who never worked in a laboratory, lived to 102 and said she felt guilty for it.

narrative_blocks.body: Her father commissioned a five-story Jacobean Revival house at 46 East 70th Street in Manhattan, finished when she was three, and the family kept it until 1960. The Explorers Club has occupied it since 1964.

narrative_blocks.header: A Matisse room down the hall
narrative_blocks.body: The house she grew up in held thirteen Matisses in a room of their own by the early 1930s, when she was in her twenties. Her father's collecting went on to Yale and the Metropolitan, and his other Cooperstown project was the Baseball Hall of Fame.

narrative_blocks.header: Her great-grandfather was Singer's lawyer
narrative_blocks.body: Her great-grandfather Edward Cabot Clark was Isaac Singer's lawyer, and then his partner in the sewing-machine company. Three generations on, the Clarks were a Cooperstown family with a Manhattan house, and Elizabeth grew up in both.

narrative_blocks.header: She died at thirty-five in Washington
narrative_blocks.body: She had followed her husband to Washington when the State Department took him in 1941, and she died there in September 1945, leaving a seven-year-old daughter. She was buried at Cooperstown, where she had married ten years earlier.

narrative_blocks.header: Named for a grandmother dead eight months
narrative_blocks.body: Her grandmother Elizabeth Scriven Clark died in March 1909, while her parents were still on their honeymoon in Europe. Elizabeth was born in Manhattan that November and given the name.

narrative_blocks.header: The eldest, and the only daughter of five
narrative_blocks.body: Stephen and Susan Clark had five children and Elizabeth was the first, and the only girl. One brother died in infancy; the three who lived were all in uniform when she died.

narrative_blocks.header: Her wartime diary became a Confederate classic
narrative_blocks.body: Catherine Edmondston filled her journals with detailed, opinionated accounts of plantation life and the Civil War, later published as Journal of a Secesh Lady. She refused to let Union soldiers read it, hiding it as Sherman's men moved through North Carolina.

narrative_blocks.header: She never reconciled herself to defeat
narrative_blocks.body: An ardent secessionist who with her husband enslaved eighty-eight people, Edmondston composed Confederate poems and scrutinized leaders North and South. Years after the war she published an anonymous essay still bristling at the Union's victory.

narrative_blocks.header: She fought to keep her own land
narrative_blocks.body: When her father's bankruptcy swept the Looking Glass plantation into his creditors' hands, Edmondston battled through the state supreme court to hold it. Less than a month before her death she won it back with the highest bid at its forced sale.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father schooled his daughters like sons
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas Pollock Devereux had his daughters tutored in literature, mathematics, science, and philosophy, an education matching what his son received at Yale. Catherine finished at Belmont, a girls' school near Leesburg, Virginia.

narrative_blocks.header: Her diary outlived the world it defended
narrative_blocks.body: Childless and bitter in defeat, Edmondston left no heirs but a journal historians now mine for its unsparing view of the Confederate home front. Published in 1979, it remains one of the fullest such records from North Carolina.

narrative_blocks.body: Emily Huger was at work at Newcomb College in New Orleans between 1897 and 1902. What she painted was the Louisiana landscape — live oaks and moss and low ground — and she went on painting it for the rest of her life.

narrative_blocks.header: She was still painting the year she died

narrative_blocks.body: He was a colonel and aide-de-camp on the Confederate staff of Lieutenant-General Leonidas Polk, whose daughter Katherine he had married at New Orleans in 1858. Polk was killed at Pine Mountain six years after the wedding.

narrative_blocks.header: He lost the land and sold insurance
narrative_blocks.body: He had held large property in Mississippi and Tennessee before the war and came out of it into insurance, taking the Mutual Life agency in 1867 and keeping it until he died. He went into fire insurance with Horace Ross in 1869 and ended a partner in Gale, Thomas and Sharpe.

narrative_blocks.body: He was stricken on a Saturday morning while writing a letter in his office, was carried to his house on North Summer Street, and lay unconscious until one the next morning.

narrative_blocks.body: Of the five children who outlived him, one daughter had married a Lawrence Washington and the son, William Dudley Gale II, went into the Nashville insurance world his father had built.

b. Sep 6, 1833 Liberty County GA; d. Feb 17, 1896 New Orleans LA age 62. Sometimes listed as 'Joseph L. Jones' in Smithsonian/museum records. Education: BA + MA Princeton 1853; MD University of Pennsylvania 1855. Teaching career: Chemistry Savannah Medical College 1855; Natural Philosophy University of Georgia 1858-1860; Chemistry Medical College of Georgia 1860. Confederate Army Surgeon 1861-1865; granted authority by Surgeon General Samuel Preston Moore to inspect all Confederate hospitals. Documented HOSPITAL GANGRENE at Andersonville and other prison camps — ~2,642 cases with nearly 50% mortality. Reports compiled in Medical and Surgical Memoirs and Sanitary Memoirs of the United States Sanitary Commission (1871). Influenced post-war surgical practice; vital link to later conceptualization of necrotizing fasciitis by Frank L. Meleney (1924) and Ben J. Wilson (1951). 1868: Chair of Chemistry and Clinical Medicine, University of Louisiana (later Tulane), to 1895; Visiting Physician at Charity Hospital, New Orleans. 1870: m. Susan Rayner Polk (HD2599) Jun 20, 1870 New Orleans. Three children: Frances Devereux Jones (1871-1941), Hamilton Polk Jones (1873-1926), Laura Maxwell Jones (1876-1917). 1876-1890: Published four-volume Medical and Surgical Memoirs (war injuries, malarial pathology, yellow fever, sanitary reform). 1878 — ARRIEUX MURDER CASE: investigated bloodstains in Donaldsonville LA murder of shopkeeper Narcisse Arrieux; identified human blood and observed 'black pigment or melanaemic corpuscles' and hyaline masses now recognized as Plasmodium infection features. Published two years before Laveran's 1880 definitive parasite discovery. Asserted priority for malarial parasite at Ninth International Medical Congress (Washington, 1887). Quinine prophylaxis for Confederate troops advocated 1861 — prefigured later military prophylactic regimens. 1880-1884: President Louisiana State Board of Health — enforced quarantine laws during yellow fever epidemic; led high-profile disputes with the National Board of Health. Owned a c.1800 Chickasaw pipe tomahawk (now ART063) with provenance through Chief Kemp of Chickasaw → his son → Judge Brooks of Pontotoc MS → Rev. Edward Fontaine (1838) → Jones → widow Susan Polk Jones → George Heye 1906 → now Smithsonian NMAI. (LITFL biography; Medical and Surgical Memoirs; FamilySearch)

military_service.role: Documented hospital gangrene (~2,642 cases, ~50% mortality), tetanus, scurvy, malaria, and prison health. Foundational medical-history research compiled in Medical and Surgical Memoirs (1876-1890).
military_service.pre_war_role: Advocated quinine prophylaxis for troops 1861; investigated indigenous botanical remedies as wartime substitutes.

narrative_blocks.header: His Andersonville reports hanged the commandant
narrative_blocks.body: Authorized to inspect every Confederate hospital and prison, he spent the autumn of 1864 recording Andersonville. His reports became evidence and he was called as a witness at the trial of Henry Wirz.

narrative_blocks.header: A murder case put malaria under his lens
narrative_blocks.body: Asked whether stains on a suspect were paint or blood, he proved them human and saw dark pigment in the corpuscles, two years before Laveran named the malarial parasite. He took them for spores, and the credit went to Paris.

narrative_blocks.header: The wards, not one poison, were killing them
narrative_blocks.body: He examined the gangrene in Confederate hospitals and concluded no single agent caused it, but dead tissue and crowded filthy rooms together. He wanted wounds cut clean, the infected kept apart and the windows open.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept the fever out of New Orleans
narrative_blocks.body: Running the Louisiana board of health from 1880, he had inspectors board ten thousand ships and made the quarantine a wall. Yellow fever burned through Havana, Vera Cruz and Rio and never took the city.

narrative_blocks.header: He dosed healthy soldiers against the swamp
narrative_blocks.body: He argued that small daily doses of quinine given to well men were the best defence against southern fevers, and when it ran short he hunted for plants to replace it.

narrative_blocks.header: He dug Tennessee mounds for pipes and bones
narrative_blocks.body: He opened burial mounds on the Cumberland and the Harpeth and published his Explorations of the Aboriginal Remains of Tennessee in 1876, its plates showing the skeletons, pipes and jewelry. He said some of those bones carried syphilitic caries, evidence the disease went from America to Europe with Columbus.

narrative_blocks.header: His son-in-law curated the museum that got it
narrative_blocks.body: That collection went to the University of Pennsylvania Museum, and twenty-five years after he died his daughter Frances married its curator of general ethnology, Henry Usher Hall.

narrative_blocks.header: She took Fairntosh
narrative_blocks.body: When the Cameron lands were divided in 1947, Sally took Fairntosh, the house north of Durham where her father had lived since 1887, and her sister Isabel Van Lennep took Stagville. The Labouisses kept Fairntosh until 1972.

narrative_blocks.header: Race horses and good roads
narrative_blocks.body: Sally's father, Bennehan Cameron, turned Stagville into a stock farm of dairy cattle, goats, hogs and race horses, campaigned across North Carolina for good roads, and sat in the legislature. He died of pneumonia in 1925.

narrative_blocks.header: Four children and a lost son
narrative_blocks.body: Sally was one of four children of Bennehan Cameron and Sally Taliaferro Mayo of Richmond; their only son died as a child. She married John Witherspoon Labouisse in 1926.

narrative_blocks.body: In 1966 Bobo and her husband were among the twelve founders of the Historic Wilmington Foundation, and in 1976 they built Chandler's Wharf on the riverfront, where she opened the Brass Lantern gift shop and The Saucepan, a cookware store. narrative_blocks.header: They saved Wilmington's oldest house in 1963
narrative_blocks.body: In 1963 Bobo and her husband rescued the Mitchell-Anderson House at 102 Orange Street, built about 1738 and by then a boarding house. It is the oldest house in Wilmington that can be dated, and for years it held the offices of his Wright Chemical Corporation.

Fairntosh had been the plantation of Judge Duncan Cameron, her great-great-grandfather.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at Fairntosh in 1959
narrative_blocks.body: Bobo married Thomas Henry Wright Jr., a widower, on 9 October 1959 at Fairntosh, her parents' home in Durham County, with no attendants. His cousin the Rt. Rev. Thomas H. Wright, Episcopal bishop of East Carolina, performed the ceremony.

narrative_blocks.header: Leonidas Polk was her great-great-grandfather
narrative_blocks.body: Bobo's middle name came down four generations from Frances Devereux, wife of Leonidas Polk, the Episcopal bishop of Louisiana who became a Confederate general and was killed on Pine Mountain in 1864.

narrative_blocks.body: Graduating from Yale in 1789, he delivered the commencement's Greek oration, tutored there two years, then trained at the Litchfield Law School. He settled in Hartford in 1799 and built what contemporaries called a brilliant career as an advocate.

narrative_blocks.body: Of his four daughters, one died in infancy; the other three lived to old age, none of them ever marrying. It was a quiet contrast to his six sons, each of them a Yale graduate.

narrative_blocks.header: She and her future husband shared Litchfield
narrative_blocks.detail: Elizabeth's portrait, painted by Gerritt Schipper in 1805, now hangs at the Yale University Art Gallery. She and Jonathan had eleven children, six of whom graduated from Yale — a record that prompted the Yale obituary of one son to call them 'a family of six brothers, all graduates of this college.' She was the daughter of Moses Tryon, a family name that echoes through her children: Tryon Edwards (HD2632, the theologian) was named directly for her family. She died in 1857, the year Abraham Lincoln began his presidential campaign, having lived through the entire Early Republic. (Litchfield Historical Society; NPG Catalog of American Portraits)

notable.notable_blurb: Donor of the Edwards family portraits to Yale

narrative_blocks.header: His 1933 letter offering Yale the portraits
narrative_blocks.body: Pleased that Yale had named one of its new residential colleges for Jonathan Edwards, Eugene wrote to the university in the autumn of 1933 offering the family portraits and papers at Stone Acres, his house above Stonington. Theodore Sizer, the Yale professor sent to see him, described him as the last direct male descendant of Edwards, and on 14 October the Yale Corporation thanked him for his intention to bequeath them.

narrative_blocks.header: Five generations on the walls
narrative_blocks.body: The portraits at Stone Acres ran five generations: Jonathan Edwards and Sarah Pierpont by Joseph Badger, Jonathan Edwards Jr. by Reuben Moulthrop, Eugene's grandparents in 1805 pastels by Gerrit Schipper, and his parents, credited to George Whiting Flagg. They had come down through Jonathan Edwards Jr.'s son, his widow and his daughters to Eugene's father.

narrative_blocks.header: Lunch at Stone Acres, lemon in the dressing
narrative_blocks.body: Sizer and his wife drove down on a fine October day to Stone Acres, whose north end Charles Phelps had built in 1765, set among old trees, gardens and greenhouses. Eugene mixed the salad dressing at the table with ceremony, its secret lemon juice, then walked them back through the portraits while Sizer listed them in pencil.

narrative_blocks.header: He never wrote the codicil
narrative_blocks.body: Eugene died at Stonington on 10 June 1938, at seventy-five, and his will said nothing of the pictures or papers; he had never got round to the codicil. Stone Acres went to Dr. Frederic Paffard and his wife, the sister of Eugene's second wife, and that September they offered Yale what he had chosen.

narrative_blocks.header: Out of Stonington the day before the hurricane
narrative_blocks.body: On 20 September 1938 Sizer and Erwin Goodenough drove to Stone Acres in the rain, and when the family hesitated over which portraits were meant, the elderly Henrietta Wright settled it: "Professor Sizer is right." That night the Great Hurricane struck, and of the sixteen great trees planted round the house in 1830, two were left standing.

narrative_blocks.header: A refuge for the stranded Boston train
narrative_blocks.body: In the storm Stone Acres took in survivors of the Boston train stranded on the causeway west of Stonington, among them a mother, her injured daughter and seven schoolboys who swam some three hundred yards to its door. In the commotion Henrietta Wright, the one witness to Eugene's choice of portraits, had a heart attack and died two days later.

people.research_notes: b. Apr 1808 Savannah GA; d. Jun 9, 1859 Savannah River age 51. Buried de Montmollin Vault, Lot 1149, Laurel Grove Cemetery, Savannah GA. Son of Jean Samuel DeMontmollin I (X00887) and Maria Edwards (HD2624). Grandson of Jonathan Edwards Jr. (H00384) — America's leading abolitionist minister. 6th-generation Hooker descendant. BUSINESS: Co-partner, "Wylly & de Montmollin," general commission agents. Broker, auctioneer (elected one of 5 city auctioneers 1857). President, Mechanics' Savings Bank of Savannah (capital $250,000 in 1857). Gold and copper mines, stocks, bonds, Florida land. Built "de Montmollin's Point" plantation, Isle of Hope, Savannah 1849 — "one of the finest." Also owned rice plantations and a building with a slave pen. Mason, Solomon Lodge #1. Board of Commissioners, Savannah Waterworks. SLAVE TRADING OPERATIONS: Handled slave transactions for Charles C. Jones 1855-1858. Letter to Ziba B. Oakes (Jan 31, 1857) requesting "four Black Boys ages 18 to 21, large-size ones preferred, field hands preferred, 'buy them as cheap as possible'" (letter preserved in Boston Public Library Anti-Slavery Collection). Built the MONTMOLLIN WAREHOUSE (23 Barnard Street, City Market, Savannah) 1856-1858 — third floor was a slave pen. After Montmollin's death, ALEXANDER BRYAN leased the building and operated it as "A. Bryan's Negro Mart" — advertising in the Savannah Morning News and listed in the 1860 City Directory. Alexander Bryan was a Savannah slave trader distinct from the more famous JOSEPH BRYAN (died Dec 1863), who had a "virtual monopoly of the coastal Georgia slave trade" (historian Malcolm Bell) and who brokered the Great Slave Auction / Weeping Time at Ten Broeck Race Course (March 2-3, 1859, 436 enslaved people from the Butler plantations). NOTE: Maria Edwards de Montmollin (HD2624) was buried in the Bryan-Waters-Darby vault at Laurel Grove Cemetery — this is almost certainly the Joseph Bryan family vault, not Alexander Bryan's. The two Bryans are unrelated business associates. When General Sherman captured Savannah (December 21, 1864), the U.S. government confiscated the building and provided it to Savannah's African-American community. The Savannah Educational Association (SEA), formed by that community, established Bryan School here. On JANUARY 10, 1865 — the school's opening day — hundreds of Black children marched from First African Baptist Church (founded 1788 by Andrew Bryan, the oldest Black Baptist church in America) to the building that had been a slave pen. In July 1865 the SEA schoolchildren publicly showcased their knowledge of grammar, history, geography, arithmetic, and other subjects. The American Missionary Association absorbed the SEA in 1867 and founded Beach Institute, consolidating several schools including Bryan School. (Georgia Historical Society marker, 23 Barnard Street, Savannah) THE WANDERER (1858): Owner of the schooner Wanderer — built 1857 at Port Jefferson NY for a Boston millionaire, repurposed for slave trading. Sailed to the mouth of the Congo River; returned with 400 African captives who were deposited on the DuBignon and de Montmollin plantations in Georgia. Chased by British Men-of-War and U.S. Customs agents. GRAND JURY (April 1859): A federal court grand jury DECLINED TO INDICT Montmollin on the charge of "holding African negroes" at his plantation — he died two months later without facing legal accountability. Montmollin sold the Wanderer to C.A.L. Lamar to avoid discovery (political cover-up by officials). The resulting court case 1859-1860 "sent shock waves from the South to New York." Ship's log held at Emory University, Georgia. DEATH: Jun 9, 1859, traveling to his rice plantation 14 miles up the Savannah River. Boiler explosion on steamboat "J.G. Lawton" near Gum Swamp. Body found next day "embedded in marsh, head downwards, to the hips, some 70 or 80 yards from the spot where the explosion occurred, showing that it must have been driven very high into the air. A handkerchief, which he had in his hand at the time, was still tight in his grasp." Killed "within a short distance of the spot where his Wanderer captives had been incarcerated." WILL: Specified excellent education for children, Christian conduct, no liquor or tobacco, learn French and Spanish fluently. Requested a simple funeral. Will took 10 years to settle in court. Wife later sold 81 slaves for $88,000 (Apr 1863). m. Harriet M. de Rossignol-Belleanse Jan 20, 1842 Christ Episcopal Church Savannah. 3 children. (Wikipedia on John S. Montmollin; de Montmollin genealogy; Savannah Republican Jun 13, 1859; "The Children of Pride" ed. Myers p.1627)

narrative_blocks.header: Sent the schooner Wanderer to the Congo
narrative_blocks.body: John's family later said he organized the Wanderer's illegal voyage of 1858, which ran some four hundred captive Africans into coastal Georgia; he had owned the yacht before it passed to the Lamars. A federal grand jury declined to indict him in April 1859.

narrative_blocks.header: Four boys, as cheap as possible
narrative_blocks.body: In January 1857 John wrote to the Charleston broker Ziba Oakes for four young men of eighteen to twenty-one, large field hands preferred, to be bought as cheap as possible. In December 1858 he was asking for one or two gangs of rice-field workers.

narrative_blocks.header: His slave pen became Savannah's first Black school
narrative_blocks.body: John's three-story brick warehouse of 1856 kept enslaved people for sale on its top floor. After Sherman took Savannah in December 1864 the building went to the city's Black community, and on 10 January 1865 children marched from First African Baptist Church to open the Bryan School there.

narrative_blocks.header: Killed near where his captives were held
narrative_blocks.body: On 9 June 1859 the boiler of the Savannah River steamboat John G. Lawton exploded, killing about eleven people, close to the island where the Wanderer's captives had been held. John's body was found seventy yards away, driven head-down into the marsh, a handkerchief still in his hand.

narrative_blocks.header: His estate sold eighty-one people in 1863
narrative_blocks.body: His will told his children to live as Christians, learn French and Spanish, and keep away from liquor and tobacco, and it took ten years to settle. He left such debts that in April 1863 his widow sold eighty-one enslaved people from the estate at Savannah.

narrative_blocks.header: Aaron Burr was his mother's cousin
narrative_blocks.body: Through his mother, a daughter of Jonathan Edwards Jr., John was a first cousin once removed of Aaron Burr, who stayed at the Montmollin house in Savannah as vice president in 1802, six years before John was born.

narrative_blocks.header: Enlisted Confederate Army age seventeen, May 1861
narrative_blocks.body: John Samuel de Montmollin enlisted in the Confederate Army on May 11, 1861 at age seventeen, about a month after Fort Sumter, and served through the entire Civil War. His specific Confederate regiment is not yet documented in available sources. He returned home with his family's antebellum Savannah wealth largely dissipated by war's end.

narrative_blocks.header: Third cousin Bristol served on Union USCT side
narrative_blocks.body: John Samuel's third cousin Eugene Stuart Bristol (born 1843) served on the Union side as a First Lieutenant in the Twenty-ninth Connecticut Volunteers Colored — a United States Colored Troops regiment. Bristol was wounded at the Battle of Chaffin's Farm on September 29, 1864 in the Army of the James. Their common ancestors are Jonathan Edwards and Sarah Pierpont Edwards; their grandfathers Jonathan Edwards Jr. and Pierpont Edwards were brothers, making this one of the documented Hooker-descendant Civil-War-opposite-sides cousin pairings.

narrative_blocks.header: Two marriages, eleven children, Savannah-to-Florida arc
narrative_blocks.body: After his father's death, John Samuel de Montmollin returned from Switzerland to Savannah Georgia, and later lived in Palatka Florida with his widowed mother — the family wealth largely lost in and after the Civil War. He married twice (Sarah Ellen Hasson April 29, 1862 with seven children; Frances Eudor Hunnicutt September 15, 1892 with four children) — eleven children total. He died March 23, 1912 at age sixty-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: Three-generation Connecticut bar family of jurists
narrative_blocks.body: Louis H. Bristol came from three generations of Connecticut lawyers and jurists. His grandfather William Bristol was a judge of the Connecticut Superior Court, a member of the Connecticut Supreme Court of Errors, and a United States District Court judge for Connecticut. His father William Brooks Bristol practiced law in New Haven County for many years, and Louis himself completed the third generation in this legal dynasty.

narrative_blocks.header: Lifelong friendship with Governor Charles Ingersoll
narrative_blocks.body: Louis maintained an unusually close friendship with Charles Roberts Ingersoll, Connecticut Governor 1873-1877 — described as 'almost lifelong' in his memorial. The two were peers at the New Haven bar from the late 1860s onward, both of them descendants of prominent Connecticut legal families. The Ingersoll-Bristol friendship anchored his New Haven professional and social network for nearly half a century.

narrative_blocks.header: Counselor at law for New Haven leading interests
narrative_blocks.body: Louis became increasingly known as a counselor at law rather than a courtroom advocate — sought out by the managers of New Haven's leading financial, manufacturing, and commercial enterprises for his sound judgment and strong common sense. He worked on Leffingwell's Appeal (concerning the French Spoliation Claims Act of Congress), the Storrs School cases, the Marett will, and several New Haven Wire Company cases protecting credits extended by foreign bankers. His office-practice work outweighed his courtroom appearances in the second half of his career.

narrative_blocks.header: Founded firm 1888 succeeding father and brother's practice
narrative_blocks.body: Louis's New Haven law practice — first associated with his father William Brooks Bristol, then with his brother John Wolcott Bristol who entered the office in 1879 — was formally reformed in 1888 as Bristol, Stoddard and Bristol with Henry Stoddard. The firm later added John K. Beach and Samuel H. Fisher, becoming Bristol, Stoddard, Beach and Fisher in 1902 and merging as Bristol and White in 1913 — three years after Louis's death. The firm became one of the longest-running New Haven legal institutions of its era.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale 1859, never married, buried Grove Street
narrative_blocks.body: Louis prepared for college at General Russell's school in New Haven and graduated from Yale's Academic Department in 1859 before studying law at Yale Law School and in his father's office. He never married. He died July 20, 1910 in his hometown New Haven Connecticut at age seventy-one — buried at Grove Street Cemetery alongside his brother John Wolcott Bristol and other family members.

narrative_blocks.body: They were married in October 1883. Her husband's grandfather Silliman had held Yale's first chair of science, his father took it after him, and Edward held physics and edited the American Journal of Science for fifty-one years.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father married two Bliss sisters

narrative_blocks.header: She married into the house on Hillhouse
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband had been born at 24 Hillhouse Avenue, in the house Silliman built for his daughter on a triangle of canal fill in 1849, and he lived there most of his life. Her sons were raised in it.

narrative_blocks.header: Bar Harbor took her at fifty-nine

notable.notable_blurb: Mineralogist who held Yale's chair of physics

people.research_notes: b. Nov 16, 1849 Utica NY; d. Jun 16, 1935 New Haven CT age 85. Buried Seal Harbor, Mount Desert, Maine (summer home). Son of JAMES DWIGHT DANA (geologist/mineralogist) and Henrietta Silliman (daughter of Yale Professor Benjamin Silliman). Yale College 1870 (Scroll and Key). Sheffield Scientific School 2 years (under George J. Brush); Heidelberg and Vienna (crystal optics, crystallography); Yale M.A. and Ph.D. Professor of physics and natural philosophy at Yale 1879. Editor, American Journal of Science 1875-1926. National Academy of Sciences 1884. Trustee, Peabody Museum of Yale 1885. American Academy of Arts and Sciences 1893; American Philosophical Society 1896. Member of scientific societies in Austria, Mexico, Russia, England, Scotland. PUBLICATIONS: Textbook of Mineralogy (1877) — the standard field text; revised 6th edition of his father's System of Mineralogy (1892). The Dana Medal of the Mineralogical Society of America named for him and his father. CHARACTER: Known for "great charm, unfailing good humor, modesty"; delighted in long walks and bicycle rides around New Haven into his 80s; refused to wear an overcoat in winter. FAMILY: BROTHER of Arnold Guyot Dana (compiler of the 150-volume "New Haven Old & New" scrapbooks at the New Haven Museum). Arnold's grandson James Dana English (1932-2021) indexed the entire scrapbook collection and left $35 million to New Haven nonprofits in 2022. m. Caroline Bristol (HD2668) Oct 2, 1883. (Wikipedia; Edward Salisbury Dana memorial, American Mineralogist 1936) Father: James Dwight Dana (X00899).

narrative_blocks.header: No mineralogy chair, so he taught physics
narrative_blocks.body: His 1872 paper on the Connecticut Valley trap rocks founded petrology in America, but Yale had no opening in mineralogy and he had to earn a living. He took a tutorship in mathematics and physics instead, and ended up holding the chair of physics from 1890 until he retired.

narrative_blocks.header: He described eight Yellowstone geysers
narrative_blocks.body: In the summer of 1875 he rode with George Bird Grinnell on Captain Ludlow's reconnaissance from Carroll in Montana Territory to the Yellowstone. His forty-two pages in the Ludlow volume are one of only two geological reports he ever wrote.

narrative_blocks.header: Four generations ran the same journal
narrative_blocks.detail: Dana's greatest contribution was the 1892 sixth edition of his father's System of Mineralogy — 1,134 pages, practically the work of one man, ten years in preparation. European mineralogists kept it on their desks; the Geological Society memorial records that Waldemar Schaller wore out three copies in thirty years on the U.S. Geological Survey. 'The Bible of every mineralogical institute I have ever been in,' wrote Charles Palache. Dana refused honorary degrees even from Yale. He died at 85, having edited the American Journal of Science for 51 years. (Geological Society memorial 1936; Wikipedia)
narrative_blocks.body: Edward Salisbury Dana was the fourth in an unbroken scientific line: Benjamin Silliman founded the American Journal of Science in 1818; his son Benjamin Jr. joined him; his son-in-law James Dwight Dana joined in 1846; and Edward joined in 1875, editing it until 1926. Both the Silliman and Trumbull families traced descent from John Alden and Priscilla Mullins.

narrative_blocks.header: He defined the words for two dictionaries
narrative_blocks.body: Through the 1880s he wrote the physics, geology and mineralogy definitions for the Century and for Webster, on top of his teaching and his own papers. The strain broke his health in 1893.

narrative_blocks.header: Named for the first American Sanskrit professor
narrative_blocks.body: Edward Elbridge Salisbury was his father's Yale colleague and closest friend, and the first professor of Sanskrit in the country. The boy was born in the Hillhouse Avenue house his father built and lived in it most of his life.

narrative_blocks.body: He and Deming shared rooms every year at Yale and moved four times doing it — Pierson, Crown Street, Durfee, Vanderbilt. He ran two years on the cross-country squad, was class secretary and president of the Thacher School Club, and told the class book he expected to be a lawyer.

people.research_notes:
b. Feb 12, 1813 Utica NY; d. Apr 14, 1895 New Haven CT age 82. Pre-eminent American geologist of his time. Yale 1833; 15 months teaching mathematics on U.S. Navy ships (Mediterranean). Assistant to Professor Benjamin Silliman at Yale 1836-37. Naturalist/mineralogist with U.S. Exploring Expedition (Pacific, under Capt. Wilkes) 1838-1842. Silliman Professor of Natural History and Geology at Yale 1850-1892. PUBLICATIONS: System of Mineralogy (1837, age 24); Manual of Mineralogy (1848); Manual of Geology (1862 — standard text for 40 years). 214 published works in total. HAWAIIAN VOLCANOLOGY: Led first geological study of Hawaiian volcanics 1880-1881; theorized the two volcanic trends (Loa and Kea). Named Mount Dana and Dana Meadows (Sierra Nevada), Dana Passage (Puget Sound), Dana crater (Mars), Danalite mineral, Dana Park (Albany NY). AWARDS: Copley Medal from Royal Society 1877 — the highest British scientific honor (presented by a Yale graduate, Edwards Pierrepont, then U.S. Minister to England); Wollaston Medal (Geological Society of London) 1874; Clarke Medal 1882; President of GSA 1890; President of AAAS 1854. His portrait by Daniel Huntington (1858) is in Yale Art Gallery. FAMILY: m. Henrietta Silliman in 1844 — daughter of Yale Professor Benjamin Silliman (who had earlier married Harriet Trumbull, daughter of Connecticut Governor Jonathan Trumbull Jr. — hence the name "Katharine Trumbull Dana" for his granddaughter). Son: Edward Salisbury Dana (X00898) — distinguished mineralogist, m. Caroline Bristol (HD2668, 7th-generation Hooker descendant). Son: Arnold Guyot Dana (1862-1947) — historian of New Haven, compiler of 150-volume "New Haven Old & New" scrapbooks at the New Haven Museum. (Wikipedia; Geological Society of America history) | [SOURCE MOVED] Wikipedia; FindAGrave; FamilySearch
CC NOTE [X00904]: Dana married Henrietta Silliman in 1844 and succeeded her father as Silliman Professor of Natural History and Geology at Yale in 1850, continuing the family's dynastic influence in American science.

narrative_blocks.header: Four years reading the Pacific
narrative_blocks.body: He shipped out in 1838 as geologist and mineralogist to the Wilkes expedition and did not see home again until 1842. His notebooks came back with fifty sketches, maps and diagrams; writing them up took him thirteen years.

narrative_blocks.header: He found the two strands of Hawaii
narrative_blocks.body: He led the first geological study of the island's volcanics in 1880, and saw that the chain ran in two lines, which he called Loa and Kea. His 1890 volume stayed the definitive account for decades.

narrative_blocks.header: Written at twenty-four, still in print
narrative_blocks.body: The System of Mineralogy came out in 1837, the Manual of Mineralogy in 1848, the Manual of Geology in 1863 — 214 titles all told. Editors have revised the Manual ever since; it is on its twenty-third edition.

narrative_blocks.header: The gold rush wrote to him
narrative_blocks.body: He had said gold would likely be found all the way from the Umpqua down to the Sacramento, and after 1848 the letters would not stop. He answered in 1849 with the geology of Mount Shasta and a sketch of it — only the second view of that mountain ever published.

narrative_blocks.header: The Copley came from a fellow Yale man
narrative_blocks.body: Edwards Pierrepont, then minister to England, handed him the Royal Society's Copley Medal in 1877; the Wollaston and the Clarke came too, and he presided over the AAAS and then the Geological Society of America. A Sierra peak, a Puget Sound passage, a crater on Mars and the mineral danalite carry his name.

narrative_blocks.header: His teacher carried rocks in his trousers
narrative_blocks.body: Fay Edgerton took his Utica pupils on long tramps after minerals, plants and insects. One day they gathered more than their hands would hold, and rather than leave any the master knotted a pair of trousers into a bag and carried them home.

people.research_notes:
b. Aug 8, 1779 Trumbull CT; d. Nov 24, 1861 New Haven CT age 82. Graduated Yale 1796. Appointed Professor of Chemistry and Natural History at Yale 1804 — held the chair for 40+ years. Founded the AMERICAN JOURNAL OF SCIENCE in 1818 — the oldest scientific journal in America; maintained by him and the two Danas for 108 years (1818-1926). His daughter Henrietta Frances Silliman (1823-1892) married James Dwight Dana (X00899, the geologist) in 1844. Their son Edward Salisbury Dana (X00898) married Caroline Bristol (HD2668, 7th-generation Hooker descendant). Henrietta's mother was Harriet Trumbull (1783-1850), daughter of Connecticut Governor Jonathan Trumbull Jr. (Governor 1797-1809) — hence the family name "Trumbull" carried down to Katharine Trumbull Dana (X00900's daughter). Benjamin Silliman is therefore the great-grandfather-in-law of Caroline Bristol (HD2668) and great-great-grandfather of Mary Bristol Dana (HD2669), James Dwight Dana II (HD2670), and William Bristol Dana (HD2671). (Wikipedia on Benjamin Silliman; American Journal of Science centennial)
CC NOTE [X00899]: Silliman's daughter Henrietta Frances married James Dwight Dana in 1844. Dana had come to Yale specifically to study under Silliman, became his assistant, and was appointed his successor as Silliman Professor in 1850. The dynasty continued through their son Edward Salisbury Dana. [Migrated from marriage.spouse_notes (spouse unknown spouse)]: Harriet Trumbull (1783-1850), daughter of CT Governor Jonathan Trumbull Jr.
[Stage 6Y-264 NB#1 header trim]: 'Founded the American Journal of Science in 1818 — the oldest scientific journal in America' → 'Founded the American Journal of Science in 1818'. SIMEON BALDWIN (1761-1851), New Haven lawyer, is NOT an entry — built as X04028 and deleted 090626 at Sam's instruction. Silliman read law in his office 1798-1799 (see the education row 'Read law with Simeon Baldwin'). Two Baldwin letters to Thomas Day, 1807 and 1817, are listed in the Day family papers, MS 71, Rhode Island Historical Society. Only one verified Hooker-tree anchor (Silliman); Thomas Day is not in the tree. Search 'Simeon Baldwin' to find this again.

narrative_blocks.header: Hired to teach a science he never studied
narrative_blocks.body: Timothy Dwight gave him the chair of chemistry and natural history in 1802 rather than hire a foreigner whose manners might unsettle a Puritan college. Silliman knew no chemistry, so he went to Philadelphia and learned it from James Woodhouse, and delivered Yale's first science lecture in 1804.

narrative_blocks.header: The journal that took his own name
narrative_blocks.body: He founded the American Journal of Science in 1818 and edited it for twenty-eight years; everyone called it Silliman's Journal, and it is still the oldest scientific journal published in the country. In 1850 they named the mineral sillimanite for him.

narrative_blocks.header: A fireball over Weston, and a farmer
narrative_blocks.body: Three explosions were heard over Weston in December 1807 and stones fell in six places. His analysis was the first published scientific account of an American meteorite; the biggest stone, thirty-six pounds, its owner refused to give away and sold instead.

narrative_blocks.header: He sold soda water before anyone else
narrative_blocks.body: He bought a Nooth apparatus in 1806, analysed spring water and built an artificial version, then advertised Soda Water and Ballston Water in the New Haven papers for indigestion and for luxury. He never made money at it, and Americans have drunk it ever since.

narrative_blocks.header: He let the young women into the room
narrative_blocks.body: Every year he admitted classes of girls from the New Haven schools to his lectures, a century before Yale would enrol them. Frederick Barnard watched it as a student and carried the argument to Columbia.

narrative_blocks.header: Hear and see everything but say little
narrative_blocks.body: He called slavery an enormous evil and owned slaves himself, and when a colleague left to study the Louisiana sugar plantations that was the instruction he gave him. He sat on the board of the Connecticut Colonization Society from 1828 to 1835.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brother ran Brooklyn, Columbia, then New York
narrative_blocks.body: Her younger brother Seth Low served two terms as mayor of Brooklyn, then a decade as president of Columbia — moving the college to Morningside Heights and remaking it a university, endowing its Low Memorial Library in their father's name. He went on to win the mayoralty of consolidated New York on a reform ticket.

narrative_blocks.body: A tireless reformer, Seth Low chaired Tuskegee Institute under Booker T. Washington and led the National Civic Federation, seeking common ground between employers and unions. When he died in 1916, the honorary pallbearers at his funeral included both the financier J. P. Morgan Jr. and the labor leader Samuel Gompers.

people.research_notes: b. 1752 Dublin, Ireland; d. May 22, 1803 New York City age ~51. Emigrated from Ireland to America as child; lived in Montreal; apprenticed at a trading house in Schenectady NY. REVOLUTIONARY WAR: Traveled to Philadelphia buying goods for the Continental Army; then served as AIDE-DE-CAMP TO THE MARQUIS DE LAFAYETTE. Lafayette "remained close to the Constable family throughout his life." Married Ann White during the war. Settled in New York 1784. CLOSE FRIEND OF ALEXANDER HAMILTON — arrived in NY at the same time; also close to John Jay and Robert Morris. Colleague's description (1796): "Among the distinguished persons present were General Hamilton, Colonel Burr and Volney. Yet, even in such good company, all eyes and ears were turned to him… his most intimate associates were Jay and Hamilton, and Robert Morris, and other master spirits of the time… He lived in splendid style." CONSTABLE, RUCKER & CO.: First American firm to outfit ships for trade with China and India. After partner's death 1788, continued alone. Land speculator: partnered with Alexander Macomb in Macomb's Purchase (~4 million acres northern NY). Became one of the wealthiest people in America; detained briefly in debtor's prison 1801 after business collapse. CIVIC: Co-founded chapter of Friendly Sons of St. Patrick's, NYC 1783 (charitable aid to impoverished Irishmen); president 1789-90 and 1795. Member, NEW YORK SOCIETY FOR THE MANUMISSION OF SLAVES (with John Jay and Alexander Hamilton). GILBERT STUART PORTRAITS: His own portrait by Stuart now at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. He commissioned the duplicate Lansdowne Washington portrait (Stuart's bill receipted July 1797) — now at the Brooklyn Museum. An 1868 copy portrait of Constable by Henry Augustus Loop hangs at the Jay Heritage Center, Rye NY. Constable-Pierrepont papers (1762-1911) at Columbia University Library. (Jay Heritage Center; Wikipedia; Columbia University Library)

narrative_blocks.header: First American firm outfitting ships to China
narrative_blocks.body: Constable, Rucker and Company was the first American house to outfit ships for the China and India trade. They also owned the America, six hundred tons, one of the finest built in New York.

narrative_blocks.header: Briefly detained in debtor's prison, 1801
narrative_blocks.body: Four million acres of northern New York, bought with Alexander Macomb, made him one of the richest men in the country. When the speculation came apart he spent a short spell in debtor's prison, two years before he died.

narrative_blocks.header: Aide-de-camp to Lafayette during the war
narrative_blocks.body: He began the war buying goods in Philadelphia for the Continental Army and finished it as aide-de-camp to the Marquis de Lafayette. Lafayette stayed close to the family for the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: Washington's hand in the portrait is his
narrative_blocks.body: In 1796 he caught Gilbert Stuart painting the Lansdowne Washington and got him to work a second canvas alongside it, so both would be originals. The miniaturist Trott told the family that Stuart had only sketched the General's hand, and that Constable held out his own to be painted from.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter's marriage made Brooklyn Heights
narrative_blocks.body: Anna Maria married Hezekiah Beers Pierrepont in 1802 and they had twelve children. Pierrepont laid out the streets of Brooklyn Heights, and four of the twelve carried Constable as a middle name.

narrative_blocks.header: He dug a ditch before the Erie Canal
narrative_blocks.body: His Northern Inland Lock Navigation Company got ten-ton boats from Schenectady through to Lake Ontario, a generation before the Erie did it properly. He had come up the Mohawk himself at seventeen, apprenticed to a trading firm.

Married Mary Rutherfurd Clarkson 1807; eight children including physician-conchologist John Clarkson Jay and Anna Maria Jay Pierrepont.
