narrative_blocks.header: He argued for Black suffrage in 1821
narrative_blocks.body: As a delegate to the 1821 New York constitutional convention, Jay argued that free Black men should keep the vote, calling the notion of their inferiority completely refuted and universally exploded. He led the state Manumission Society.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded New York's oldest law library
narrative_blocks.body: Jay helped found the New York Law Institute in 1828, now the city's oldest law library, and organized its first savings bank. He served as Recorder of New York City and president of both New York Hospital and the New-York Historical Society.

narrative_blocks.header: He built the Jay mansion that still stands
narrative_blocks.body: On the family estate in Rye, Jay tore down the war-battered farmhouse and, reusing timbers from his father's boyhood home, raised the Greek Revival mansion that survives today as a National Historic Landmark.

narrative_blocks.header: The eldest son of a Founding Father
narrative_blocks.body: Peter was the eldest son of John Jay, the first Chief Justice of the United States, and at eighteen served as his father's private secretary in London during the Jay Treaty negotiations.

narrative_blocks.header: Two daughters named Eunice
narrative_blocks.body: Eunice's first child, a daughter named Eunice for her, was born and died on the same day at Hartford. When another girl came on 31 January 1797, she gave her the name again. That second Eunice lived to eighty-six.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a farmer known for his music
narrative_blocks.body: Eunice, born at Hartford on Christmas Day 1772, was eighteen when she married Joseph Hubbell of Weston, a farmer with a reputation as a musician.

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve children across twenty-four years
narrative_blocks.body: Eunice had twelve children between about 1792 and 1816, the first at nineteen and the last, William Reilly Hubbell, at forty-three. Seven were born at Hartford; the last five came after she and Joseph moved to his hometown, Weston.

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband and sisters' husbands, all soldiers
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph Hubbell was one of five men who married Dr. Daniel Hooker's daughters and served in the Revolutionary War. The others were Timothy Fisher, Roger Clark, Lemuel Rowell and Aaron Cadwell, and Eunice's brother Daniel fought too.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed twenty-two years, buried at Birmingham
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph died at Weston on 22 February 1829. Eunice outlived him by twenty-two years, died at New Haven on 9 December 1851, sixteen days before her seventy-ninth birthday, and was buried at Birmingham, Connecticut.

narrative_blocks.header: Montpelier to Bronson, 1834
narrative_blocks.body: Almira Cadwell married Epaphroditus Ransom at Montpelier in February 1827, and in 1834 went west with him by wagon and steamboat to Bronson, the village that became Kalamazoo. Two of their four children died as babies.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed in Kansas
narrative_blocks.body: After Epaphroditus took the land office at Fort Scott in 1857 and died there, Almira lived on with their daughter Antoinette, Mrs. George J. Clark, at Fort Scott, and with their son, Maj. Wyllys Ransom, at Lawrence. She died at Fort Scott in 1877, at seventy-two.

narrative_blocks.header: Home to Kalamazoo beside him
narrative_blocks.body: Almira was brought back to Kalamazoo, where she and her family had long belonged to St. Luke's church, and after the funeral there she was laid at Mountain Home beside her husband, whose body had been brought home from Kansas before her.

people.research_notes:
b. Mar 24, 1798 Shelburne Falls MA; d. Nov 11, 1859 Fort Scott, Bourbon County KS age 61. Buried Mountain Home Cemetery, Kalamazoo MI. Son of Major Ezekiel Ransom and Lucinda Fletcher. NOTE: "The André connection" — his father Major Ezekiel Ransom "was present at the execution of Major André, the British spy" Oct 2, 1780. (From obituary of his son Wyllys; also Nathan Beers, brother of X00494, commanded the guard at the same execution — two separate Hooker family connections.) 7TH GOVERNOR OF MICHIGAN 1848-1850 (first governor inaugurated in Lansing after capital moved from Detroit). Democrat; strong anti-slavery position — Democrats declined to re-nominate him for a second term because of it. CAREER: Chester Academy VT; Northampton Law School MA 1823. Practice in Townshend VT. Elected to Vermont House of Representatives. Moved to Bronson (now Kalamazoo) MI Nov 14, 1834. State legislature; first circuit court judge in the area, riding horseback through wilderness to hear cases. Associate Justice, Michigan Supreme Court 1837 (appointed by Gov. Mason); Chief Justice 1843-1848. NOTABLE RULING: 1840 — prevented removal of Catholic Potawatomi from their lands in southwestern Michigan. DURING GOVERNORSHIP: First telegraph line NYC to Detroit completed Mar 1 (first term). Dutch Reformed immigrants under Rev. Van Raalte founded Holland, Michigan (later Hope College). Mormon James Jesse Strang settled Beaver Island. First president, Michigan Agricultural Society — instrumental in creating the Michigan State Fair and Michigan State University. Regent, University of Michigan 1850-1852. Co-founder of village of Augusta, Michigan. LAST YEARS: Business ruined in Panic of 1855. Accepted appointment by President Buchanan as receiver of public monies, Osage Land Office, Fort Scott KS 1857. Died there 1859. His son Wyllys (HD2683) served as his private secretary in 1849. m. Almira Cadwell (HD2682) Feb 21, 1827 Montpelier VT. 4 children; 2 died in infancy. (Wikipedia; FamilySearch)
CC NOTE [H00757]: Major Ezekiel Ransom was present at the October 2, 1780 execution of British spy Major John André. That execution was organized and supervised by Maj. Benjamin Tallmadge, Washington's spymaster and a 5th-generation Hooker descendant. [Migrated from top-level primary_url]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epaphroditus_Ransom

narrative_blocks.header: First governor sworn in at Lansing
narrative_blocks.body: Elected governor in 1848, Epaphroditus was the first to be inaugurated at Lansing after the capital moved from Detroit, and in his term the first telegraph line from New York reached Detroit.

narrative_blocks.header: His party dropped him over slavery
narrative_blocks.body: Michigan's Democrats would not renominate Epaphroditus in 1850 because of his strong stand against slavery. Kalamazoo sent him back to the legislature in 1853 and again in 1854.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept the Potawatomi on their land
narrative_blocks.body: In 1840, as a justice of the Michigan Supreme Court, Epaphroditus issued the declaration that prevented the removal of the Catholic Potawatomi from their lands in southwestern Michigan.

narrative_blocks.header: A circuit judge on horseback
narrative_blocks.body: In Kalamazoo, still called Bronson when he arrived by wagon and steamboat in 1834, Epaphroditus became the district's first circuit judge, riding horseback through the wilderness to hear cases. Governor Mason put him on the Supreme Court in 1837; he was chief justice from 1843 to 1848.

narrative_blocks.header: The State Fair and an agricultural college
narrative_blocks.body: Ransom was the first president of the Michigan Agricultural Society, directly instrumental in establishing both the Michigan State Fair and Michigan State University. He served as regent of the University of Michigan 1850-1852 and co-founded the village of Augusta, Michigan.

narrative_blocks.header: Ruined in 1855, then a Kansas land office
narrative_blocks.body: The Panic of 1855 wrecked the business Epaphroditus ran with his son Wyllys, and in 1857, his health broken, he took President Buchanan's appointment as receiver of public monies at the Osage land office at Fort Scott, Kansas. He died there in 1859, at sixty-one.

narrative_blocks.header: His father saw André hanged
narrative_blocks.body: His father, Ezekiel Ransom, enlisted at fourteen, fought at Bennington and Saratoga, served on George Washington's non-commissioned staff and was present at the execution of Major John André. At Kalamazoo he helped found what became Kalamazoo College.

narrative_blocks.body: Mary went with Wyllys to Kansas in 1857 and lived through the border war there, and through the Civil War she was his companion in garrison and camp, nursing sick and wounded soldiers as far as her strength allowed.

narrative_blocks.header: A prairie doctor's eldest
narrative_blocks.body: Mary was the eldest child of Dr. William Mottram, who settled on Nottawa Prairie in 1833, and of Gillian Mottram of Loudoun County, Virginia. She was schooled at the university branch in Kalamazoo and the Kalamazoo Female Seminary.

narrative_blocks.header: Eleven months before him
narrative_blocks.body: Mary died at her daughter Maud's house at Holt in March 1907, with Wyllys ill in bed; he died eleven months later. She was buried in the Governor Ransom lot at Mountain Home.

people.research_notes: b. Apr 28, 1828 Townshend, Windham County VT; d. Feb 1, 1908 Grand Rapids MI age 79. Buried Mountain Home Cemetery, Kalamazoo MI (Sec E Lot 166 Grave 8). Son of Epaphroditus Ransom (Michigan Governor, X) × Almira Cadwell (HD2675). 8th-generation Hooker descendant. Great-great-grandson of Mary Hooker (H00986). EDUCATION: University of Michigan B.A. 1848 (one of oldest living graduates); A.M. 1896 (honorary). Emigrated to Michigan from Vermont with family Oct 1834. CIVIL WAR: With the fall of Fort Sumter enlisted Company E, 2nd Kansas Cavalry, elected First Lieutenant, promoted Captain. Organized and commanded 6th Kansas Cavalry (senior Major). Commands under Generals Nathaniel Lyon, Thomas Ewing Jr., Samuel R. Curtis, James G. Blunt, George Sykes. Held guerrillas in western Missouri at bay 1862 — daily skirmishes with Quantrill, Todd, Yeager, Parker. Present after the Lawrence, Kansas massacre (August 21, 1863) and participated in pursuit of Quantrill. Almost daily fights during summer 1862. Mustered out March 1865. POST-WAR ADVENTURES: As Clerk of District Court in Independence MO (1865), repelled a band of Confederate bushwhackers who attempted to free prisoners — the deputy sheriff was killed, his son shot through a window. Two weeks later attacked on Kansas City streets by five mounted armed rebels; hand-to-hand fight; "nine balls through his hat and clothing that did not strike his person"; shot and wounded one attacker before falling seriously wounded. Eventually recovered fully. RAILROAD CAREER: President, Kansas City & Cameron Railroad. Auditor/Asst. Treasurer, Leavenworth, Lawrence & Galveston RR. Auditor, Saginaw, Tuscola & Huron RR. Michigan Deputy Railroad Commissioner 1881. PUBLICATION: "Historical outline of the Ransom family of America" (1903). MICHIGAN CONNECTIONS: Secretary to his father Governor Epaphroditus Ransom 1849. President, Lawrence (KS) Board of Education 1873-1877. Beta Theta Pi fraternity; Grand Army of the Republic; Michigan Pioneer Society. m. Mary Emma Mottram (X) Mar 5, 1853 Kalamazoo MI. 7 children. Sons: Arthur (d. 1894 in railroad robbery), William E. (d. Omaha), Robert B. (Detroit), Kenneth M. (marine architect). (EH 986 line; Kalamazoo Evening Telegraph Feb 3, 1908; Ransom genealogy 1903)

narrative_blocks.header: Survived nine bullets through hat and clothing
narrative_blocks.body: Two weeks after he beat off a Confederate band trying to free prisoners at Independence, Missouri, five mounted rebels attacked Wyllys in the streets of Kansas City. Nine balls went through his hat and clothing without touching him; he shot one attacker before he fell, badly wounded.

narrative_blocks.header: Daily skirmishes with Quantrill in 1862
narrative_blocks.body: General Blunt gave Wyllys, senior major of the 6th Kansas Cavalry, a field command over western Missouri and Arkansas: three companies each of infantry and cavalry and a section of artillery. Through the summer of 1862 he fought Quantrill, George Todd and Dick Yeager almost daily.

narrative_blocks.header: Pursued Quantrill after the Lawrence massacre
narrative_blocks.body: He was present in the aftermath of Quantrill's August 1863 raid on Lawrence Kansas — where 150 unarmed men and boys were murdered — and participated in the pursuit of the Confederate guerrillas across the Kansas-Missouri border.

narrative_blocks.header: Secretary to his father the governor
narrative_blocks.body: On New Year's Day 1848, the year he took his Michigan degree, Wyllys became private secretary to his father, Epaphroditus Ransom, the new governor, as the capital moved from Detroit to Lansing. The family had come west from Vermont in 1834, when he was six.

narrative_blocks.header: He drafted Michigan's railroad laws
narrative_blocks.body: Back in Michigan from 1877, Wyllys was deputy state railroad commissioner from 1881 under four commissioners in turn, and drafted many of the railroad laws the legislature's committees passed. After the war he had been president of the Kansas City & Cameron Railroad.

narrative_blocks.header: Rose Street was named for a girl
narrative_blocks.body: At seventy-four Wyllys wrote to the Kalamazoo Gazette to correct its history of the town's streets: Main Street followed the territorial road, not the Indian trail, and Rose Street was named for Thomas Sheldon's eldest daughter, not for wild roses.

narrative_blocks.header: Historian of the Ransom family
narrative_blocks.body: In 1903 Wyllys published the Historical Outline of the Ransom Family of America, the source for his grandfather Ezekiel's march to Bennington and Saratoga and his presence at Major André's execution.

RAILROAD DETECTIVE: Connected with Union Pacific Railroad for 10 years; chief clerk to superintendent, then law and claims departments. DEATH: While investigating train robberies near Wahoo, Nebraska, confronted a thief breaking into a box car. In the scuffle, "the burglar was shot dead." narrative_blocks.header: A box-car thief near Wahoo
narrative_blocks.body: Thieves were working the Union Pacific near Wahoo, Nebraska, and William went out as its detective to find them. One evening he came on a man breaking into a box car; in the scuffle the burglar was shot dead, and William was thrown or slipped onto the end of a tie and struck his head.

narrative_blocks.header: Out of his mind to the end
narrative_blocks.body: He did not seem badly hurt, but brain fever set in and he was taken to St. Joseph's Hospital in Omaha, out of his mind from then on. He died there on 29 January 1894, at thirty-six, leaving Josephine and three children at their house on Twenty-third and Mason streets.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten years on the Union Pacific
narrative_blocks.body: William spent ten years with the Union Pacific at Omaha, as chief clerk to the superintendent and then in the law and claims departments, and was one of the best-known young railroad men in town. His father Wyllys was then auditor of the Saginaw, Tuscola & Huron at East Saginaw.

narrative_blocks.header: The Knights of Pythias met the train
narrative_blocks.body: His body came home to Kalamazoo by train, and a large delegation of the Knights of Pythias met it at the depot. At Mountain Home, Chaplain Noah Dibble read the Pythian ritual over the grave, with six Sir Knights as bearers.

narrative_blocks.header: Both brothers dead by April
narrative_blocks.body: Three months after William was buried, his older brother, Dr. Arthur Ransom, died at Kalamazoo at thirty-nine. The family laid both sons in Mountain Home that spring.

narrative_blocks.header: Born in the territorial capital
narrative_blocks.body: William was born at Lecompton, the pro-slavery capital of Kansas Territory, in October 1857, while his father was chief clerk to the surveyor general there.

narrative_blocks.header: Too young to be trusted as a doctor
narrative_blocks.body: Edward took his degree at Rush Medical College in Chicago in 1882, at twenty-one, and people then would not take a doctor so young. He went on the road instead, and for several years travelled for a maker of pharmaceuticals.

narrative_blocks.header: Holt's doctor at all hours
narrative_blocks.body: After his marriage Edward opened an office at Holt and drove the country around it at all hours and in all seasons, until the strain broke his health. His books held the births of a great many of the township's people, and the deaths of its older generation.

narrative_blocks.header: Born to Delhi's first settlers
narrative_blocks.body: Edward was born on the family farm in Delhi Township in August 1861, the son of John K. and Elizabeth Kent North, among its earliest settlers. He went from the township schools to the University of Michigan, and was buried at North Cemetery, north of Delhi.

people.research_notes: b. Feb 4, 1876 Lawrence, Douglas County KS; d. Nov 11, 1957 Pinellas County FL age 81. Buried Serenity Gardens Memorial Park, Largo FL (Indian Rocks Beach section). 9th-generation Hooker descendant. Known as "Cap" to everyone. THE VOYAGE OF THE GAZELLE (1898-1899): At age 22, built his own 30-foot yawl "Gazelle" (9-foot beam). Sailed with three companions: Lake Michigan → Chicago → Illinois Canal → Illinois River → Mississippi River (fighting ice to Baton Rouge "in the worst winter the river had ever known") → New Orleans → Gulf Coast → Pensacola → Santa Rosa Sound → Clearwater → Sarasota → Everglades → Key West → Havana → Miami → up Atlantic coast → New York → Hudson River → Albany → Erie Canal → Great Lakes → home port St. Joseph MI. 20-month trip, more than 8,000 miles. W.C. Sprague (editor, "American Boy") persuaded Ransom to write 18-month series. Doubleday, Page & Co. published "A YEAR ON A YAWL" — ran as serial in 7 newspapers. (His father Major Wyllys had sailed his father Governor Epaphroditus's name across the Trans-Mississippi theater; Cap sailed the country's inland waterways.) INDIAN ROCKS BEACH: In 1910, Cap returned to Indian Rocks FL (remembered from the Gazelle voyage). Served as BRIDGE TENDER for 25 years (retired 1933), living in a small cabin midway across the bridge. "Kids went to Cap on the bridge with their troubles and their broken toys." After Pearl Harbor, raised the American flag over the bridge every day — "buying new ones from his own pocket money as they wore out." m. Alice Grace Hamilton ("Allie") 1903. 3 children. (Tampa Bay newspapers; Indian Rocks Beach historical records; FamilySearch) | [SOURCE MOVED] FindAGrave; FamilySearch; newspaper obituaries [Migrated from birth.notes]: Year and month known; day approximate. [Migrated from death.notes]: Year and month known; day approximate.

cross_connections.display_label: wrote A Year in a Yawl, the book of his Gazelle cruise

narrative_blocks.header: Ice all the way to Baton Rouge
narrative_blocks.body: In 1898, at twenty-two, Cap took the Gazelle, the thirty-foot yawl he designed, down the Mississippi with three friends, fighting ice to Baton Rouge in the river's worst winter. By Key West, Havana and New York they came home through the Erie Canal: eight thousand miles in twenty months.

narrative_blocks.header: The cruise became A Year in a Yawl
narrative_blocks.body: W. C. Sprague of the American Boy had Cap write the voyage up as an eighteen-month serial, The Cruise of the Yacht Gazelle. Russell Doubleday turned it into A Year in a Yawl for Doubleday, Page, and seven newspapers ran the book as a serial.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-five years in the bridge house
narrative_blocks.body: In 1910 Cap came back to Indian Rocks, which he remembered from the Gazelle, and for twenty-five years, to 1933, tended its bridge from a little cabin midway across. Kids went to Cap on the bridge with their troubles and their broken toys.

narrative_blocks.header: A flag over the bridge after Pearl Harbor
narrative_blocks.body: After Pearl Harbor Cap raised an American flag over the Indian Rocks bridge and kept on raising it, buying new ones out of his own pocket as they wore out.

narrative_blocks.header: A boat factory at St. Joseph
narrative_blocks.body: In 1902 Cap headed a new boat works near the St. Joseph docks, heated by steam and lit by electricity, to build Indian canoes, sailing yachts and rowboats. His sister Agatha's husband, Ernest Smith, sat on its board.

narrative_blocks.header: Married by the marrying parson
narrative_blocks.body: Cap married Allie Hamilton at Grand Rapids in April 1903, and her father, the Rev. James Hamilton, known as the marrying parson of St. Joseph, performed the ceremony himself.

narrative_blocks.header: A Weston farmer known for his music
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph farmed at Weston, Connecticut, and had a reputation as a musician.

narrative_blocks.header: He and four brothers-in-law served
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph served as a soldier in the Revolutionary War, as did four other men who married daughters of Dr. Daniel Hooker of Hartford: Timothy Fisher, Roger Clark, Lemuel Rowell and Aaron Cadwell.

narrative_blocks.header: Hartford years, then home to Weston
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph and Eunice married in 1791 and lived at Hartford, where seven of their twelve children were born. By December 1804, when Nancy Abigail arrived, they had moved to Weston, his birthplace, where the last five were born.

narrative_blocks.header: Gave a son his mother's maiden name

narrative_blocks.header: Two brothers married two sisters
narrative_blocks.body: George Hale Morgan wed Sarah Spencer Morgan at All Saints', Ennismore Gardens in 1866; five years later, at the same London altar, his brother John Brainard married her sister Juliet. Two Hartford Morgan brothers, two of Junius's daughters — distant cousins all, and no one changed a surname.

narrative_blocks.header: Rector of the American church in Paris
narrative_blocks.body: A Union soldier of the 107th New York turned deacon in 1867, he rose to the rectorship of the American Church of the Holy Trinity in Paris and held it to his death there in 1912. Two decades on, the same cathedral would fill for the funeral of his wife's grand-nephew Junius.

narrative_blocks.header: Uncle Pierpont led her up the aisle
narrative_blocks.body: J.P. Morgan himself walked his niece to the altar of St. Mary's-in-Tuxedo in June 1908, where she married its rector, William Fitz-Simon — a man who that same year wrote his friend Mark Twain soliciting advice on the subject of marriage. The wedding breakfast filled Table Rock, her cousin Juliet Hamilton's stone mansion.

narrative_blocks.header: A cathedral porch carries her name
narrative_blocks.body: She died at Lausanne in 1916, only forty-two, and was buried at Paris. Twenty years on, her widower gave a thousand pounds to Guildford Cathedral for a porch to be known as St. Ursula's — a saint's name and his wife's, set in Edward Maufe's stone.

narrative_blocks.header: Home from Yale to doctor Kensington
narrative_blocks.body: Henry took his Yale degree in 1822, attended two courses of lectures at the Yale Medical School and received his M.D. in 1826, then went home to practise in Kensington, the parish where he was born.

narrative_blocks.header: Raised in the general's house by two widows
narrative_blocks.body: Henry was five when his father died in March 1806, and grew up in the General Hart house at Kensington with his mother Lucy and the general's widow, Ruth Cole Hart, who kept the house together for the rest of their lives.

narrative_blocks.header: A man of high promise, dead at thirty
narrative_blocks.body: Henry died at Kensington, unmarried, on 28 March 1831, in his thirty-first year and after five years of practice. He was regarded as a man of high promise.

narrative_blocks.header: She married Shepard, then his successor
narrative_blocks.body: She was his third wife, married in 1647, and he was dead two years later. Jonathan Mitchell, who had been his student, took over the church, married the pastor's widow, and took over his property.

narrative_blocks.header: Her name came from a Cumberland valley
narrative_blocks.body: She was a daughter of John Borodell; her brother John was a London merchant and her sister Ann married George Denison. The surname looks to be Borrowdale, a valley in Cumberland, worn down by use.

narrative_blocks.header: Her inheritance depended on staying a widow
narrative_blocks.body: Shepard's will left her the estate for as long as she stayed a widow, and if she did not, only the share his executors judged fit — with the gold in a box in his study. She married Mitchell, and the executors decided the rest.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son got a tankard and one share
narrative_blocks.body: Her son Jeremiah took a single portion and one of the two silver tankards. The double portion went to Thomas, eldest by an earlier marriage, with the best black suit and cloak and every book, manuscript and paper his father left.

narrative_blocks.header: Hosted the Saybrook Platform in his own house
narrative_blocks.body: On September 9, 1708, the Connecticut Synod assembled at his Saybrook home: twelve ministers, four laymen, eight of the twelve being Yale Trustees. The result was the Saybrook Platform — the document that defined Connecticut Congregationalism for the next century, a carefully negotiated middle way between Massachusetts and Presbyterian practice.

narrative_blocks.header: One of twelve original Trustees of Yale College
narrative_blocks.body: He was among the twelve ministers who signed Yale's founding documents in 1701. He died April 1, 1709 — "second in age among the Trustees, and for forty-three years pastor of Saybrook." His son Stephen received Yale's first academic degree at its first commencement.

narrative_blocks.header: His son had married his new wife's daughter
narrative_blocks.body: When Thomas Buckingham married the widow Mary Willet Hooker in 1703, his son Stephen was already the husband of her daughter Sarah. The father and son had married a mother and her daughter.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandfather came over to serve Pynchon
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel Terry the elder came from near Barnet in England in service to William Pynchon, who had to leave the country over a pamphlet he published. Springfield granted him ten acres in 1655 on condition that he stay five years.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Samuels on opposite sides of a boundary
narrative_blocks.body: His grandfather, a linen weaver, sat on Springfield's boundary committee and found his own son Samuel across the table representing Enfield. The father had been granted land at Enfield in 1664; the son settled there about 1683.

narrative_blocks.header: His father made captain at fifty-five
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel Terry of Enfield was constable, selectman and ensign of the local militia before he was made captain in 1716. The court that appointed him administrator of his father's estate styled him gentleman.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a Nantucket widow in 1719
narrative_blocks.body: Margaret Coffin was born in the oldest house on Nantucket and had been a widow six years when he married her on 25 October 1719. He was twenty-nine and she was thirty.

narrative_blocks.header: His half-brother’s line gave Hartford a mayor
narrative_blocks.body: His father married twice, and the second marriage produced Ephraim Terry of Enfield. Ephraim's son Nathaniel was a militia colonel there, and Nathaniel's son of the same name became mayor of Hartford and a congressman.

Per EH: "Mrs. Mary (Smith) Lord" — she was a widow before marrying Thomas Hooker (H00027) in 1686. Maiden name Smith, first husband surnamed Lord.
BIRTH: March 7, 1642/3, Springfield MA. Daughter of Henry Smith and Ann Pynchon (daughter of Y00004 William Pynchon). Baptized March 12, 1643 Springfield.
FIRST MARRIAGE: Richard Lord II (X02135), April 25, 1665, Springfield. He was lost at sea November 5, 1685. Son Richard Lord III born of this marriage.
SECOND MARRIAGE: Dr. Thomas Hooker (H00027), ca. 1686, Hartford. No children.
DEATH: May 17, 1702, Hartford. Buried: Ancient Burying Ground, Hartford (CEM003).
BIRTH LOCATION NOTE: Some sources give Hartford; most primary sources give Springfield. Her parents were Springfield residents. Use Springfield. [Cause revert audit]: Earlier extraction set death.cause="lost at sea" but reverted: lost at sea — was about first husband Richard Lord II, not Mary Smith Lord Hooker. REVISED 10 Aug 2026 on Sam's note that NB1 read as tabloid — the old header, "Her grandfather
founded Springfield — and was burned", implies William Pynchon was burned rather than his book,
and a reader who never expands the body is left with that. It was also 52 characters (wraps) and
its subject was her grandfather rather than her. Rewritten around her own marriage. NB2's arithmetic was wrong and is corrected: the old text had her managing the estate "alone for
seven years before marrying Thomas Hooker in 1686", which is impossible when Richard Lord was
lost at sea in November 1685. The seven years is the 1686-1693 span during which her new husband
administered the estate, which is on his entry, not hers. TWO CONFLICTS WITH SAM'S PASTE, both left as the file has them and flagged: 1. BIRTHPLACE. The entry says Springfield, Hampshire County, Massachusetts; Sam's FindAGrave paste says Hartford, Connecticut. A Springfield birth fits a Pynchon mother; Hartford fits the Smith and Lord families. Not resolved here. 2. MARRIAGE DATE. The entry says 1686; Sam's paste says May 1685. May 1685 is impossible on the file's own evidence — Richard Lord was lost at sea on 5 November 1685, so she was still his wife that May. 1686 kept. for the Smith name. She was Mary Smith, daughter of ANN PYNCHON (b. abt. 1618, William's eldest)
and HENRY SMITH of Springfield — and Henry was the son of Frances (Smith) Sandford by an earlier

narrative_blocks.header: A founders' quarrel ended at her wedding
narrative_blocks.body: William Pynchon had broken with Thomas Hooker over how to deal with the Pequots and taken Springfield out of Connecticut altogether. Two generations later his granddaughter married Hooker's grandson, a Hartford physician, and the two lines met in one household.

narrative_blocks.header: The court gave her the estate to run
narrative_blocks.body: Her first husband Richard Lord was lost at sea in November 1685. She petitioned, and in December 1686 the court granted her the personal estate, a third of the real property, and the management of all of it until her son came of age.

narrative_blocks.header: She was sixteen years older than her husband
narrative_blocks.body: Mary was born in 1643 and Thomas Hooker in 1659. She was past forty when they married, and they had no children together; her only son was Richard Lord's.

narrative_blocks.header: Her parents were stepbrother and stepsister
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother Ann was William Pynchon's daughter, and her father Henry Smith was the son of Frances, the widow Pynchon married at Dorchester in 1632. The two of them had been raised into one household before they married into it again.

Spouse of Sarah Hooker Buckingham (H00037). Name from EH/notes records. (EH 1909)
Harvard 1693 (H.U. 1693). Pastor of the Church at Norwalk, CT. Died Feb 13, 1746. Member of the Corporation of Yale College. Son of X01001 Rev. Thomas Buckingham of Saybrook (d. April 1, 1709). His father married I00006 Mary Willet (widow of Rev. Samuel Hooker H00007) in 1703. After his father died, Mary Willet moved to live with Stephen and Sarah at Norwalk until her death in 1712. Sarah Hooker was described as "the most accomplished lady that had ever come to Norwalk" — "Dame Buckingham's" stately grace was legendary in the town's traditions.
BIRTH: Sep 3 per Yale sketch, Sep 4 per FindAGrave — using Sep 4.
DEATH: EH says Feb 13, 1746. FindAGrave says "3 Feb 1745" which is likely old-style (1745/46) = Feb 3, 1746 new-style. 10-day discrepancy; keeping EH Feb 13.
Will dated Jan 1, 1745/46, proved Feb 18, 1745/46 in Fairfield. Left everything to wife Sarah.
Yale: received second academic degree at Yale's first commencement (1702). His name listed FIRST in the Triennial Catalogue of Yale College.
Ordained November 17, 1697. Served First Congregational Church Norwalk ~30 years. Resigned after long disagreement February 24, 1727.
NEPHEW: Jedidiah Buckingham (son of Thomas Buckingham Jr.) visited Stephen in Norwalk and died there March 28, 1720, age 24.
[Stage 6Y-264 NB#4 body trim]: original body had 5 sentences, trimmed to first 3. Original body preserved here for reference: 'After thirty years at Norwalk, Buckingham was charged with intemperance. A Consociation investigated and found no fault in his conduct. The town then found a letter they could construe as a resignation and accepted it before he could object. He appealed to the Assembly; the outcome is not recorded. He gave his 200-acre farm on Buckingham Ridge to his orphaned nephew, and died in 1746 — in the words of the Wilton historian — "a saddened and embittered man."'

parents.father_research_notes: X01001 married I00006 Mary Willet (widow of H00007 Samuel Hooker) in 1703. So Stephen's father became the stepfather of Stephen's wife Sarah's mother.

burial.plot_notes: East Norwalk Historical Cemetery, Norwalk, Fairfield County CT. SOURCE: FindAGrave.

narrative_blocks.header: First name in Yale's first Triennial Catalogue
narrative_blocks.body: At Yale's first commencement in 1702, Stephen received his second academic degree — the first awarded by the new Collegiate School. His name appears first in the Triennial Catalogue of Yale College, making him the college's first officially recorded graduate, despite having taken his first degree at Harvard in 1693.

narrative_blocks.header: His will left everything to his wife Sarah
narrative_blocks.body: Stephen's will, dated January 1, 1745/46 and proved February 18 in Fairfield, was simple and complete: he left everything to his wife Sarah. They had been married nearly sixty years.

narrative_blocks.header: His nephew died visiting at 24
narrative_blocks.body: Jedidiah Buckingham — Stephen's nephew — visited him in Norwalk in 1720. He had recently left his pulpit in Newark, New Jersey. He died at Stephen's house March 28, 1720, aged 24, and was buried in Norwalk.

narrative_blocks.header: Cleared of charges — then pushed out anyway
narrative_blocks.body: After thirty years at Norwalk, Buckingham was charged with intemperance. A Consociation investigated and found no fault in his conduct. The town then found a letter they could construe as a resignation and accepted it before he could object.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife's mother married his father
narrative_blocks.body: Stephen Buckingham married Sarah Hooker of Farmington. Her widowed mother, Mary Willet, later married his father, Rev. Thomas Buckingham, making his mother-in-law his stepmother as well.

research_sources.note: His stone and Find a Grave give 31 March 1784; Chapman's Pratt genealogy says 4 March, and 30 May for the birth against the stone's 31 May. The marriage to Abigail Hooker is entered as about 1728 from FamilySearch, at Sam's direction; note that it sits awkwardly with Chapman, who has Ann Taylor bearing him six children between 1722 and 1730 and a second wife after her, making Abigail his third. His first two wives, Ann Taylor of Westfield and Elizabeth, widow of Henry Tisdale of Newport, are not built.

Ann Taylor was a daughter of the Rev. Edward Taylor of Westfield and his second wife Ruth Wyllys, and so descended from Governor John Haynes and Governor George Wyllys — a possible thread if that first marriage is ever brought into the tree.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty-seven years in the one pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: Ordained over the First Church of Norwich in November 1717, he never held another charge. He was sole pastor until his eighty-fourth year, and in the course of his ministry the town divided into eight ecclesiastical societies around him.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale's highest honours, then a doctorate
narrative_blocks.body: Yale gave him its highest honours in 1714 and a doctorate of divinity afterwards, a title then conferred only on men of real learning. His stone says he was hampered all his life by much bodily infirmity and did the work anyway.

narrative_blocks.header: He swore to the new country at eighty-four
narrative_blocks.body: In 1778 he took the oath of allegiance to the United States, an old man of eighty-four who had been preaching in the same town since George II was king. The Daughters of the American Revolution count him a patriot ancestor.

narrative_blocks.header: Abigail was the third wife
narrative_blocks.body: He married Ann Taylor of Westfield in 1720 and had six children by her; a second wife died at New York soon after the wedding. Abigail Hooker, a great-granddaughter of Thomas Hooker, was his third, and she outlived him by eight years.

narrative_blocks.header: His gravestone preaches one more sermon
narrative_blocks.body: He had verses cut on his stone in the old burying ground so that the grave could go on with the work: “Thus while my Youth the solemn silence breaks, And to the eye, this cold tomb marble speaks, The dead I preach.”

military_service.notes: DAR ancestor A084787. Served in the French and Indian War before it. Captain in Col. Samuel Mott's Connecticut regiment for the Northern Department in 1776; at Peekskill under Col. Hooker in 1777. His orderly book was printed at Fort Edward in 1898.

narrative_blocks.header: Captain in July 1776, major by the end
narrative_blocks.body: He had already soldiered in the war between France and the English colonies. Colonel Mott's order of 26 July 1776 addresses him as captain of a company; he served most of the struggle and rose to major.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-three years a justice of the peace
narrative_blocks.body: He held the Hartford County commission for thirty-three years and sat several years for Farmington in the General Assembly. An orderly book he kept as captain was printed at Fort Edward in 1898.

narrative_blocks.header: Like a shock of corn fully ripe
narrative_blocks.body: He lived at Farmington until 1822 and died at Granby on the first of October 1825, in his ninetieth year — come to his grave, as the notice had it, like a shock of corn that is fully ripe, in its season.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty miles a day, in the cool
narrative_blocks.body: Mott's order sent him to Bennington with two subalterns and every equipped man. Twenty miles a day, marching in the cool and lying by through the sultry hours, no unnecessary firing, four or five balls to a man.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the fatigue party at Skenesborough
narrative_blocks.body: His company was at Skenesborough on Lake Champlain that September, and the orderly book puts him over the fatigue party. A subaltern went round the camp each day to see the men clean and their provisions well cooked.

narrative_blocks.header: The orderly book went down Elizabeth’s line
narrative_blocks.body: His eldest daughter married the Rev. William Robinson in 1790, and the manuscript descended through her — to her son Charles, to his son Arthur, and to Arthur's son Charles Mulford Robinson, who held it when it was printed.

Apr 4, 1748 New Haven CT) and Hannah Trowbridge (b. Mar 30, 1690 New Haven CT, d. Aug 9, 1748 New Haven CT). m. Sept 23, 1745 Chauncey Whittlesey. d. Oct 17, 1751 New Haven Conn. age 34. CONFIRMED NON-HOOKER DESCENDANT — Whiting/Trowbridge lines do not connect to Hooker. (Sam confirmed Stage 6Y-12 after WikiTree review.) SIBLINGS (per WikiTree, parents Joseph Whiting + Hannah Trowbridge): Hannah Whiting Ingersoll (1712-1779) — IN TREE as I00078 (married Ingersoll); Mary Alling (1715-1748); Phebe Whiting Alling (1720-1751); John Whiting (1721-1786); Elisha Whiting (1729-1766). CHILDREN with Chauncey Whittlesey (per Whittlesey #88 + WikiTree): Chauncey #146 (b. Oct 27, 1746, Yale 1764, m. Lucy Wetmore — his son Chauncey #376 was Yale 1800, War of 1812 Major from New London severely wounded, prominent New Orleans lawyer with firm Whittelsey & Henning); Samuel Joseph (b. Jul 13/14 1749, d. Aug 9 1751 infant); Elisha (b. Oct 14 1751, d. Oct 23 1751 infant). SOURCE: WikiTree Whiting-89 + Whittelsey-23; Whittlesey Genealogy #88. BURIAL of mother: Hannah Trowbridge Whiting buried Center Church on the Green Churchyard, New Haven Conn. '

narrative_blocks.header: A New Haven man who practised at Milford
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at New Haven about 1747 and married Susannah Whittlesey of Milford in November 1771, a minister’s daughter. He practised medicine at Milford and died there in September 1795.

sources.label: Whittlesey genealogy: Yale 1772; lawyer at New Haven, State Street; elected sheriff per the New Haven paper of 13 June 1786; died “the winter” before 16 Jan 1805

Find a Grave puts John, Sarah and their daughter Mary in Washington Street Cemetery, Middletown. The Whittlesey genealogy says instead "the cemetery at New Haven, near the monument of their relative, Rev. Samuel Dana, D.D." The stones are followed here. That genealogy dates his death as "the winter" before 16 Jan 1805 — which is his daughter Susan’s wedding day, five weeks after 9 December 1804

bio.bio_blurb: New Haven lawyer and city sheriff

narrative_blocks.header: His whole family went over to the King
narrative_blocks.body: When the war came his father’s family took the loyalist side and left New Haven. He alone stayed. He felt the whigs suspected him unjustly for it, and thought a share of the disloyalty would be laid at his door whatever he did.

narrative_blocks.header: At a late city meeting, elected Sheriff
narrative_blocks.body: He took his Yale degree in 1772 and practised law at New Haven, living on State Street. A newspaper there for 13 June 1786 gave the whole of his good news in one line: at a late city meeting John Chandler was elected Sheriff.

narrative_blocks.header: A grandmother took the third child away
narrative_blocks.body: His third child, Susan, was taken from the house by her mother’s mother and kept so long that five more were born at home whom she could not say she had ever seen, though they lived in the next town.

narrative_blocks.header: Pride and ambition, and neither answered
narrative_blocks.body: He had fair prospects in business before the war and little success after it. The family account calls him a man of great pride and ambition whom the breaking up of society, and of his own family, discouraged.

narrative_blocks.header: He lies in his mother-in-law’s town
narrative_blocks.body: He died on 9 December 1804 and lies at Middletown with his wife and his daughter Mary — the town his mother-in-law had taken his third child to, and out of which that daughter married five weeks after he died.

narrative_blocks.header: He buried four of them in eight years
narrative_blocks.body: His eldest son was killed at sixteen in 1796. His daughter Sarah went in 1802, his wife in 1803, his daughter Mary in July 1804. He died himself that December, five weeks before his third child married out of Middletown.

narrative_blocks.header: She died twenty days before her last child
narrative_blocks.body: Fanny Phelps Taft died on June 2, 1852. Her last child, also named Alphonso, had been born in December 1851 and died on June 22, 1852 — twenty days after his mother. Of her five children, three died in infancy.

narrative_blocks.header: She married the boy from her own town
narrative_blocks.body: Alphonso Taft had grown up at Townshend, where her father Charles Phelps sat as judge, and they married in 1841. She bore five children in nine years, buried three of them, and died at twenty-nine.

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve years writing as “three brothers”
narrative_blocks.body: With Olivia Day and Henrietta Blake she published The Yale Gallinipper anonymously from 1846 to 1858, the trio signing themselves “three brothers.” She married Alphonso Taft — her fourth cousin twice removed — and raised a president.

narrative_blocks.header: A fourth cousin, twice removed
narrative_blocks.body: She married Alphonso Taft — her fourth cousin twice removed — the day after Christmas 1853, becoming stepmother to two sons and, in time, mother of a President. Mount Holyoke, class of 1845.

narrative_blocks.header: Nothing less than success would do
narrative_blocks.body: She and Alphonso pushed William and his brothers hard, tolerating nothing short of success from any of them. Her second son reached both the White House and the Supreme Court.

narrative_blocks.header: She took on the first wife's children too
narrative_blocks.body: She came from Millbury and married him in 1853, two years after Fanny died. Five children of her own followed, one of whom did not live, and Fanny's two survivors were hers to raise.

narrative_blocks.header: A Michigan judge claimed her son as kin
narrative_blocks.body: Louise and Judge James McAllister Torrey of Flint were fifth cousins once removed, their lines parting at two sons of William Torrey of Weymouth. He wrote asking her son the president to the thirteenth Torrey reunion.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Starr brothers married two Morgan sisters
narrative_blocks.body: Her father Jonathan married Elizabeth Morgan at Groton in January 1698, four years after his brother Thomas had married her sister Mary. She was born at Groton three years on and given her mother's name.

narrative_blocks.header: Her uncle built a sloop called Sea Flower
narrative_blocks.body: She grew up on the river at Groton, where her uncle Thomas Starr held a large farm and worked as a shipwright. He was one of the patentees of New London in 1704, and the sloop he built he called the Sea Flower.

narrative_blocks.header: She was twice a widow before Daniel Coit
narrative_blocks.body: She buried Joseph Turner of Scituate and then John Jeffrey of Groton. Daniel Coit married her at Groton in December 1764, a year after his second wife died, and they had no children.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father sat on the Governor's Council
narrative_blocks.body: Jonathan Starr traded land at Groton and was elected constable at the town's first meeting in 1705. He went as deputy to the General Court from 1712 and sat on the Governor's Council, and died at Groton in 1747.

bio.title: Captain
bio.bio_blurb: Forks of the Yadkin patriot, merchant and planter

narrative_blocks.header: A fist fight decided which side they took
narrative_blocks.body: At Veach's Muster Ground in 1776 he fought the Tory captain Samuel Bryan with fists to settle which way the Forks of the Yadkin militia would go. He won; the militia went out as Patriots, and Bryan raised a Tory company of his own.

narrative_blocks.header: He fought Cornwallis across his own county
narrative_blocks.body: He was in the field against Cornwallis through the march across North Carolina in 1780 and 1781. He lived at The Shoals in Cooleemee and made his money as a merchant, mill owner and planter in the forks of the Yadkin.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten children by two wives
narrative_blocks.body: Sara Hayden married him in Virginia in 1772 and bore him four, among them Joseph, who went to Congress. Elizabeth Mumford followed in 1791 and bore him six more, the fourth of whom became chief justice of the state.

b. 1787; d. 1858. Sea captain 1805-1826. Cincinnati businessman and civic leader. Lost fortune in Panic of 1837; rebuilt as secretary Whitewater Canal Co., then Ohio Life Insurance & Trust Co. Semi-Colon Club host. Niece Harriet Beecher (Stowe) attended. Roxana Foote (1775-1816) m. Rev. Lyman Beecher — if sister of Samuel, makes Harriet his niece. Spoke French, Spanish, Italian. Made improvements in ship rigging and building. Retired New Haven 1850. Buried General Andrew Ward Cemetery (CEM012) Guilford CT. Portrait by Joseph Oriel Eaton 1855 (ART032). (Andrew Warde and His Descendants; FindAGrave) Roxanna Foote (1775-1816), Samuel's sister, married Rev. Lyman Beecher — making Harriet Beecher Stowe Samuel's niece. Confirmed: Andrew Warde and His Descendants genealogy.

Original body preserved here for reference: 'Samuel Edmund Foote was a sea captain at eighteen, self-taught, fluent in French, Spanish, and Italian, and described as one of the best-educated men of his time. He captained ships until 1826, then moved to Cincinnati where he served as director and unpaid secretary of the water company, director of the Louisville Canal, and rebuilt his fortune after losing it in the financial panic of 1837. During his Cincinnati years his home was the center of the Semi-Colon Club — a literary salon whose members included Salmon P. Chase (future Chief Justice), Judge James Hall, and his niece Harriet Beecher, who would later write Uncle Tom's Cabin. He retired to New Haven in 1850.'

burial.plot_notes: General Andrew Ward Cemetery, Guilford CT

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the city's water for free
narrative_blocks.body: In Cincinnati he served as director and unpaid secretary of the water company until the city bought it out, and sat as a director of the Ohio River canal. Contemporaries reckoned he did as much as any private citizen for the young city's growth.

narrative_blocks.header: A future Chief Justice met in his parlor
narrative_blocks.body: His Cincinnati home hosted the Semi-Colon Club, a literary salon whose regulars included the future Chief Justice Salmon P. Chase and the young professor Calvin Stowe. His niece Harriet Beecher came too — years before she became Stowe and wrote Uncle Tom's Cabin.

narrative_blocks.header: He lost a fortune and built another
narrative_blocks.body: The financial panic of 1837 swept away much of what he had made at sea and in Cincinnati. He went back to work as secretary first of the Whitewater Canal Company and then of the Ohio Life Insurance & Trust, rebuilt a second fortune, and retired to New Haven in 1850.

narrative_blocks.header: A self-taught captain at eighteen
narrative_blocks.body: He fitted himself for the sea by study and took command of ships at eighteen, sailing until 1826 and making his own improvements to ship rigging along the way. By then he read and spoke French, Spanish, and Italian, and passed for one of the best-educated men of his time.

narrative_blocks.header: He outlived both his sons
narrative_blocks.body: Both of the couple's sons died young — George Augustus at five, and Harry Ward at twenty-eight. Of their four children, only the two daughters, Frances and Katharine, would outlive him.

narrative_blocks.header: He may have drawn the Beechers to Cincinnati
narrative_blocks.body: A booster of the young city whose sister Roxana had married Lyman Beecher, he may well have helped persuade the famous preacher to move his household west. The Beecher children, Harriet among them, became fixtures of the literary salon Samuel hosted in Cincinnati.

notable.notable_blurb: editor-in-chief New York Evening Post 1883–1899

narrative_blocks.header: Abolitionists asked him to start a magazine
narrative_blocks.body: In 1865 a circle of abolitionists, led by Frederick Law Olmsted, asked him to launch a weekly of independent opinion. He became the founding editor of The Nation — still, more than a century and a half on, the oldest continuously published weekly in the country.

narrative_blocks.header: His pen helped sink a presidential candidate
narrative_blocks.body: When the Republicans nominated James G. Blaine in 1884, his editorials helped drive reform-minded "Mugwumps" out of the party and Grover Cleveland into the White House. It was the first Democratic presidential win since the Civil War, and his paper had a hand in it.

narrative_blocks.header: He fought Tammany Hall until it sued him
narrative_blocks.body: His attacks on Tammany Hall's bosses grew so relentless that in 1894 they sued him for libel, though the cases never reached trial. He was no gentler on the Spanish-American War, standing with the few against Hearst and Pulitzer when the rest of the press bayed for it.

narrative_blocks.header: He married into the Beechers' world
narrative_blocks.body: The letters of introduction he carried to New Haven in 1857 led to President Woolsey's Yale circle and to Samuel Foote's family — the household whose Cincinnati gatherings had seeded his wife's cousins' fame — and by the next summer he was engaged to Frances. The Irish journalist's American footing was laid in those parlors.

narrative_blocks.header: He reported the Crimean War from Sevastopol
narrative_blocks.body: As a young man he covered the Crimean War for a London paper, sending dispatches from the Siege of Sevastopol. He crossed to the United States in 1856 and never left journalism again.

narrative_blocks.header: He declined Harvard; Harvard kept his name
narrative_blocks.body: The chair of history was offered in 1870 and refused; Oxford's honorary doctorate came in 1897. Harvard answered with the Godkin Lectures, instituted in his memory.

narrative_blocks.header: His marriage to Frances ended in early loss
narrative_blocks.body: He married Frances Foote in 1859 and kept his home in New York, but the family met deep sorrow: two of their three children died in childhood, and Frances herself died in 1875, still in her thirties. He raised their surviving son, Lawrence, and did not remarry for nearly a decade.

people.research_notes: b. Aug 20, 1794 East Haven Conn.; d. Mar 19, 1869 Berlin Conn., aged 74. Daughter of Chandler Pardee and Lydia (Hotchkiss) Pardee of East Haven. Father Chandler Pardee was a Revolutionary War private in Capt. Bradley's Co. of Artillery raised for defense of New Haven; severely wounded July 5, 1779 at the British raid on New Haven, taken prisoner and carried to New York, pensioned. m. (1) Jan 1, 1812 East Haven, Luman Cowles (HD0511), who d. Jan 24, 1823. m. (2) Nov 23, 1828, Linus Cowles (HD0510), her deceased husband Luman's brother — a levirate-style remarriage within the Cowles family. Linus d. Jan 12, 1868; Eunetia survived him by 14 months. Both she and her first husband Luman were members of Kensington Congregational Church. Source: Calvin D. Cowles 1929, Genealogy of the Cowles Families in America (BIB003), entry 1199; Pardee Genealogy 1927.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father fell wounded defending New Haven
narrative_blocks.body: Chandler Pardee, an artillery private, was shot down and taken prisoner at the British raid on New Haven on July 5, 1779, carried to New York, and lived to draw a pension. His daughter was born fifteen years after the raid.

military_service.unit: Capt. Edward Bulkley's company, Col. Samuel B. Webb's regiment (9th Connecticut)
military_service.notes: Enlisted 1777 for three years, discharged 20 March 1780. Sick in hospital November 1778, absent without leave October 1779. Pension certificate 9755, granted 1819 at eight dollars a month.

military_service.unit: Capt. Elisha Camp's Volunteer Company, Col. Christopher Bellinger's Regiment
military_service.notes: Served 9-20 September 1812 alongside his son Hooker.

narrative_blocks.header: Three years from Peekskill to Morristown
narrative_blocks.body: He enlisted for three years in Capt. Edward Bulkley's company, under Colonel Samuel B. Webb. The regiment camped at Peekskill, served under Putnam and then Clinton, and wintered at West Point building its works.

narrative_blocks.header: He was at the battle of Rhode Island
narrative_blocks.body: The regiment went to Rhode Island with Varnum's brigade and was commended for the battle of 29 August 1778. Morristown followed in 1779, and Dorchester was discharged on 20 March 1780.

narrative_blocks.header: Farmington to Hounsfield in one lifetime
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Farmington in 1760, son of Deacon Stephen Dorchester and Elizabeth Gould. Rev. Timothy Pitkin married him to Anna Cowles at her father Ezekiel's house there on 29 May 1783.

narrative_blocks.header: Corporal again at fifty-two
narrative_blocks.body: He and his son Hooker both served as corporals in September 1812, in Elisha Camp's volunteer company of the New York militia, when the British came at Sackets Harbor.

narrative_blocks.header: A cow, twelve sheep and some kitchen iron
narrative_blocks.body: Swearing to his poverty in July 1820 to keep his pension, he listed everything he owned: the beasts, a pair of fire dogs, tongs and shovel, a trammel, three old chests, a table, two stands and five kettles.

narrative_blocks.header: Pension number 9755, eight dollars a month
narrative_blocks.body: He applied at Jefferson County in April 1818, saying his reduced circumstances left him in need of assistance from his country. The certificate came a year later, and he drew it from September 1819.

narrative_blocks.header: Sick in November, absent in October
narrative_blocks.body: The rolls have him in hospital through November 1778 and absent without leave for October 1779. His pay was two pounds a month and three pounds more for subsistence.

narrative_blocks.header: Albany-born, and a second wife within the year
narrative_blocks.body: Maria Van Schaick was born in 1809 to Michael and Caroline Truax Van Schaick at Albany. She married Hooker Dorchester in 1825, the year his first wife died, and bore him five children.

narrative_blocks.header: She asked the surrogate for her own children
narrative_blocks.body: Hooker's three eldest chose Thompson Phelps as guardian in April 1835. On 2 May she petitioned Benjamin Wright to be made guardian of Martha, Andrew Jackson, Alvira Angeneth, Catherine and Caroline.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother lived to a hundred and four
narrative_blocks.body: Maria's father Michael Van Schaick died at Cape Vincent in 1857; her mother Caroline outlived him by sixteen years and died there in 1873, aged a hundred and four.

narrative_blocks.header: She married Chauncey Smith three years after
narrative_blocks.body: Hooker Dorchester was shot by a gun in his own hands in 1835 and lived two hours. By 1838 she had married Chauncey Smith, and the 1840 census has her household next door to Anna Dorchester's.

narrative_blocks.header: Named for the president who died that day
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Orleans on 4 April 1841, the day William Henry Harrison died in office, and carried the president's three names for it. The family called him Henry.

narrative_blocks.body: He was agent for the Rome, Watertown and Ogdensburg at Limerick, taught at Dexter High School from 1877 and was twice elected school commissioner. He kept the Limerick general store with his son Edward after.

narrative_blocks.header: He hired a substitute to go instead
narrative_blocks.body: Circumstances kept Enos from enlisting for one stretch of the war, so he paid a substitute and sent him to the front in his stead. The tradition in the family is that the recruit was killed in one of the engagements around New York.

narrative_blocks.header: He brought Jacob Thorpe home by horse
narrative_blocks.body: When Tryon's men came into New Haven in 1779, Enos found the body of Jacob Thorpe, got permission to take it, laid it across his horse and carried it back to North Haven.

narrative_blocks.header: Mustered out in 1777, in again for 1812
narrative_blocks.body: He was mustered out of the Revolutionary service on 17 February 1777, and turned out again for the War of 1812 in his late fifties.

narrative_blocks.header: The will says two wives, not three
narrative_blocks.body: Hannah Jacobs died in February 1802 and Enos married the widow Eunice Lucy Tuttle in 1803. A third marriage to a Widow Mansfield is claimed, but his 1824 will leaves to his beloved wife Lucy — and two of her sisters had married Mansfields.

narrative_blocks.header: The will names seven of the eight
narrative_blocks.body: Eight children came of his first marriage, to Hannah Jacobs. The will of 1824 sets down his sons Thomas, Jarius, Justus and Levi and his daughters Hannah Butler, Sally Darrow and Patty Norton. Jesse, who never married, is not in it.

people.research_notes: Spouse of Hannah Stiles Lyman (H00463). Name from EH/notes records. (EH 1909) STAGE 6Y-80 FULL BIO BUILD: FA #251558309 confirms full vitals. Born Jan 26, 1770 Northampton MA to Elisha Lyman Sr. + Abigail Janes Lyman. Inherited family homestead but exchanged with brother Theodore upon father's death. Farmer. Settlement arc: Conway MA → Derby VT → Montreal Canada (1815-1828, 13 years) → Sunderland MA → Champlain NY. Three marriages: 1) Hannah Stiles Jan 10, 1793 (d. 1814); 2) Thankful Hunt 1814 (1770-1837); 3) Sarah Beaumont 1837. Per EH bio: 'esteemed by all who knew him as a man of sterling integrity, strictly conservative and religious.' Died Champlain NY Feb 21, 1844 age 74; buried Cimetière Mont-Royal Montreal with all three wives memorialized. X-PREFIX RETAINED per schema §2 ('do not retroactively change X→I'). Wife Thankful Hunt + Sarah Beaumont not built per Jalapeño Rule. Note marriage timing — he married each subsequent wife the same year the prior wife died.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirteen years in Montreal
narrative_blocks.body: A year after Hannah died, Elisha took the family north to Montreal in 1815 and stayed thirteen years. His sons William, Benjamin and Henry stayed on after he left and built Lyman Brothers there.

narrative_blocks.header: From Northampton to Champlain
narrative_blocks.body: Elisha traded his father's Northampton homestead to his brother Theodore and farmed in turn at Conway, at Derby in Vermont, at Montreal, at Sunderland and last at Champlain, New York, where he died in 1844 at seventy-four.

narrative_blocks.header: Three wives on one stone
narrative_blocks.body: Elisha married Hannah Stiles in 1793, Thankful Hunt in 1814, the year Hannah died, and Sarah Beaumont in 1837, the year Thankful died. A family memorial at Mount Royal in Montreal names him with all three.

narrative_blocks.header: His niece ran Vassar
narrative_blocks.body: His brother Theodore's daughter, Hannah Willard Lyman, came to Montreal in 1839, where her Lyman cousins had settled, and ran a school for young women there. In 1865 she became the first Lady Principal of Vassar College.

narrative_blocks.header: He nursed in the fever sheds
narrative_blocks.body: When typhus came up the St. Lawrence with the Irish famine ships in 1847, Mills had fever sheds built at Pointe-Saint-Charles and went into them himself, nursing sick children and comforting parents. Some six thousand died in Montreal that year.

narrative_blocks.header: He faced down the Champ de Mars
narrative_blocks.body: Angry Montrealers gathered on the Champ de Mars threatening to march on the sheds and throw them into the river, and indignation meetings at Bonsecours Market demanded the sick be moved to an island. Mills held to his plan and talked the city down.

narrative_blocks.header: The martyr mayor
narrative_blocks.body: Still working in the sheds that autumn, Mills caught the typhus and died at his house on Beaver Hall Hill on 12 November 1847. Every business in the city closed for his funeral, the largest procession Montreal had seen.

narrative_blocks.header: Ferrier voted for himself
narrative_blocks.body: The council chose Mills mayor in 1846 by ten votes to nine, but the outgoing Tory mayor, James Ferrier, voted for himself to break the majority and would not leave the chair. The Superior Court ordered a new vote, and in December Mills won it eleven to five.

narrative_blocks.header: A Presbyterian who helped build St. Patrick's
narrative_blocks.body: A member of the American Presbyterian Church, Mills put his Mills Bank behind the building of St. Patrick's, the church of Montreal's Irish Catholics, and ran the new City and District Savings Bank, founded to help the poor save.

narrative_blocks.header: Furs with his brother Cephas
narrative_blocks.body: Mills came up from Tolland, Massachusetts, as a young man and went into the fur trade with his brother Cephas as C. & J. E. Mills, then into banking. He was as much at ease in French as in English.

narrative_blocks.header: Three of his sons died in 1841
narrative_blocks.body: George at six, Edwin at two, and the infant Albert all died in 1841 — likely an epidemic year inside the household. His daughter Ada would die six decades later at the center of Montreal’s Redpath Mansion Mystery.

narrative_blocks.body: She had her mother Susan Breed's force of character and a keen intellectual bent, sharpened by wide reading. Those who knew her recalled an exhaustless humor and a frankness that made her, as one wrote, the delight of the friends she trusted.

narrative_blocks.body: Richard died in 1857, when she was forty-one, and she outlived him by seventeen years. She spent them back in her New Haven family home, where she died in 1874.

narrative_blocks.header: Her charity drank up the springs of life
narrative_blocks.body: Her last years were given over to unceasing labors for private and public charity — sympathies so generous, a memorial said, that they drank up the very springs of her life. Even her final illness was sharpened by grief for a neighbor's bereavement, to which she gave what strength she had left.

narrative_blocks.header: A Yale president wrote her memorial
narrative_blocks.body: An ardent friend and benefactor of Yale, in which her family had generations of pride, she was mourned in print by the college's own president, Noah Porter. He remembered a woman whose strength of mind left its mark on every circle she entered.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived the pastor by twenty-seven years

narrative_blocks.header: One of her two sons was not hers

narrative_blocks.header: Chaplain of the Senate for four years
narrative_blocks.body: He was chosen chaplain of the United States Senate in 1849 and held the post into 1853. He gave the funeral address for John Calhoun in the April of 1850 and for Henry Clay in the July of 1852.

narrative_blocks.header: He preached the Princeton gun disaster
narrative_blocks.body: The great gun on the warship burst on the Potomac in the February of 1844 with the president aboard, killing the Secretary of State and the Secretary of the Navy. Butler gave the address at the funeral held in the President's Mansion, and it went into print that year.

narrative_blocks.header: Rome, and the second rector of Grace Church
narrative_blocks.body: He went out in 1861 as chaplain to the United States minister at Rome and took the second rectorship of the English congregation there. The carte de visite he sat for in a Roman studio is signed in his own hand.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught church history for twenty years
narrative_blocks.body: He came home from Rome in 1864 to the chair of ecclesiastical history at his church's Philadelphia divinity school, and held it until ill health took him out in 1884. Many of the men preaching around the world at his death had sat in that room.

narrative_blocks.header: A hymn book, and the prayer book explained
narrative_blocks.body: He put out a volume of devotional verse in 1839 and a history of the Book of Common Prayer in 1845, and kept printing sermons for fifty years. Three of those printed sermons are farewells to parishes he was leaving.

narrative_blocks.header: He died in his daughter's house
narrative_blocks.body: The end came at Germantown in the March of 1890, in the rectory where Helen lived with her husband John Falkner. The service was public at the Church of the Holy Trinity and the interment at the Woodlands was private.

narrative_blocks.body: St. Peter's at Ashtabula, organized February 19, 1817, was the first Episcopal parish in Ohio — and three weeks later he preached Medina County's first religious service of any kind, in the Hamilton cabin. narrative_blocks.header: Ordained at Southington, and stayed forty-one
narrative_blocks.body: Yale gave him a degree in 1773 and licensed him to preach in 1776. He tutored there a year, took the Southington call in December 1778, was ordained in June 1780 and retired in September 1820.

narrative_blocks.header: He farmed because the living was too small
narrative_blocks.body: Dr. Stiles wrote that he had settled in 1780 worth nothing, and that by 1790 he held a two-storey house, a hundred and fifty acres, forty hives of bees and about a hundred cows let out through the parish.

narrative_blocks.header: He put clover and plaster on worn-out plains
narrative_blocks.body: He was first in the town to rotate his crops and the man who brought in clover, gathering the seed at first by a horse-drawn machine. Plaster of Paris did wonders on that soil, for corn and clover alike.

narrative_blocks.header: The large rows belong to our minister
narrative_blocks.body: A farmer refused the plaster, so they split a cornfield two rows each. His told so plainly that a passing horse dealer explained it to strangers: the large rows belong to our minister, the small ones to his people.

narrative_blocks.header: Whoever wants wheat must raise rye
narrative_blocks.body: Wheat would not thrive on the Southington plains however he tried it, and he put the lesson into a line the town went on repeating — that whoever there wished to eat wheat must raise rye.

narrative_blocks.header: Four wives, and three of them died young
narrative_blocks.body: Naomi Wolcott died of smallpox in 1782, Sophia Mosely of a quick consumption at twenty-four in 1784, and Anne Mills of measles at twenty-eight in 1789, days after a stillbirth. Elizabeth Norton outlasted them all.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Farmington boys read for Yale with him
narrative_blocks.body: Asahel Hooker and Giles Hooker Cowles prepared in his house and graduated together in 1789. Hooker came back to read theology with him, and he preached the ordination sermon at Goshen in 1791.

Spouse of George Roswell Leavitt (HD0881). Name from EH/notes records. (EH 1909) THE KENDRICK LINE, from the material supplied 081226 — no records built for these men, per Sam. Great-grandfather Capt. John Kendrick (1740-1794), born at East Harwich on Cape Cod, third of seven children of Solomon Kendrick and Elizabeth Atkins; at sea on his father's whaleboats by fourteen; the only one of the family who did not follow it to Barrington, Nova Scotia, in the 1760s. Married Huldah Pease of Martha's Vineyard in 1767; captained the whaler Lydia. Reputed to have been at the Boston Tea Party. Commissioned 26 May 1777 to the eighteen-gun privateer Fanny, also called the Boston, crew of 104, which he rebuilt as a brigantine. In 1779, with the family starving, he sailed to the Azores and was kept there two months by an American sympathiser, Arnold Henry Dohrman, before returning with the French fleet. The Columbia Expedition of 1787 ran seven years. Solomon Kendrick died when the Resolution was taken by Chief Cumshewa and all but one of her crew killed. John Kendrick died 12 December 1794 in what is now Honolulu harbour and is thought to lie in the old foreigners' burying ground near King and Pi'ikoi Streets. Biography: Scott Ridley, 2010. GRANDFATHER, DATE CONFLICT: Sam gives Capt. Alfred Lassell Kendrick born 1778; the Massachusetts birth record gives Alfred Kendrick born 20 October 1770 at Rochester, Plymouth County, and FindAGrave gives 20 October 1778 with the tombstone disagreeing again. Died 6 April 1847, buried at Rural Cemetery, New Bedford. Married Abigail 'Nabby' Hammond at Rochester; ten children between 1797 and 1824.

bio.bio_blurb: Descendant of Cape Cod sea captains

narrative_blocks.header: The king of France paid her great-grandfather
narrative_blocks.body: Her great-grandfather John Kendrick took an eighteen-gun privateer into the English Channel during the Revolution and preyed on British ships out of Jamaica, to such effect that Louis XVI rewarded him for it. He came home in 1778, bought a house and a wharf, and built a public schoolhouse.

narrative_blocks.header: Her great-grandfather opened the China trade
narrative_blocks.body: The Boston merchants who sent two ships around Cape Horn in 1787, to open trade with China and find the Northwest Passage, put her great-grandfather in command. The river he found carries his ship's name, the Columbia, and he was the first American to try to open Japan.

narrative_blocks.header: The salute that killed her great-grandfather
narrative_blocks.body: Her great-grandfather had started the Hawaiian sandalwood trade and was anchored off Honolulu in December 1794 when a British ship returned his thirteen-gun salute. One of her cannon had been left loaded with grapeshot, and it killed him and several of his men where they stood.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandfather's brother turned Spanish
narrative_blocks.body: Of her great-grandfather's sons, John stayed at Nootka Sound to join the Spanish navy — the father wept saying goodbye, and met him again as Juan Kendrick, master of a Spanish frigate. Solomon was lost when his ship was taken. Her grandfather Alfred, a captain too, raised ten children.

narrative_blocks.header: An automobile killed her father, her mother followed
narrative_blocks.body: She was twenty when a car struck her father down outside the New Haven church he had built and served as rector for twenty years. Her mother was dead inside the year, and she married six years after that.

narrative_blocks.header: She married in a church by the sea
narrative_blocks.body: She was twenty-seven when she married Thomas Hooker at St. Andrew's Church-by-the-Sea at Rye Beach, in the September of 1915. Four children came in the next nine years; she was dead at forty-nine.

narrative_blocks.header: The third Emily Malbone in three generations
narrative_blocks.body: Her grandmother was Emily Malbone Brinley. Her father's sister, the other Emily Malbone Morgan, founded the Society of the Companions of the Holy Cross and is remembered on the Episcopal calendar; she was the third to carry the name.

narrative_blocks.header: She inherited the house and died that spring
narrative_blocks.body: Her aunt bought Putnam Elms in 1906 — Colonel Daniel Putnam's farm at Brooklyn, four generations back — and ran it as a summer house for working women. When the aunt died in February 1937 she left the place to her two nieces for life. Three months later the second of them was dead.

narrative_blocks.header: He cut his own road into the forest
narrative_blocks.body: In 1828 he went down into the woods of Warren County, Pennsylvania, cutting the road as he went, and with his son Erastus built a cabin and a sawmill on the south branch of Tionesta Creek. He came back for the family the following winter; the settlement that grew there took his name.

narrative_blocks.header: Three months took his wife, child, brother, mother
narrative_blocks.body: Betsey died at Prattsburg in October 1807, his youngest child at Clinton in November, and in December his brother Erastus and his mother Eunice followed. In January his only other brother, Munson, died as well, and he was left with two small children and no brothers at all.

narrative_blocks.header: He married Betsey, then two years later Almira
narrative_blocks.body: He married Betsey Cole at Clinton in September 1802 and buried her five years later. Two years after her death he married her sister Almira; his brother Munson had already married a third sister, Amanda — three Cole daughters into one Barnes family.

narrative_blocks.header: A blacksmith before he was a miller
narrative_blocks.body: He bought part of lot six of Coxe's Patent in Paris Township, Oneida County, in November 1803, and the next spring bought the rest of it together with his brother-in-law John Gilbert. Both men are set down as blacksmiths in that deed.

narrative_blocks.header: A brief war gave him the title Captain
narrative_blocks.body: He served briefly in the War of 1812 and came out of it called Captain, a title that stayed with him for the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: He took a fourth wife at seventy
narrative_blocks.body: After Almira died in 1820 he married Ruth Taylor the following February, and thirty years after that, at seventy, he married Sylvia Gibbs, the widow of Nathan Taylor.

Spouse 1 of Helen Moore Butler Falkner Butler (HD0797). Name extracted from notes. (EH 1909) From Sam's Wikipedia, FindAGrave and newspaper extracts, 2 Aug 2026. Bachelor of arts from New York University in 1859, Phi Beta Kappa and winner of the Webster oratory prize; honorary doctor of divinity from the same university in 1881; ordained 1861. A member of the Philadelphia Academy of Political and Social Science. He took the summer services at a Maine chapel from 1901 through 1905; the Reverend Charles Henry Arndt, who took over there in 1907 and who succeeded him at Christ Church and Saint Michael's in Germantown, married his daughter Helen Moore Falkner. The Bridgeport and Germantown career years are inferred from the twenty-seven-year tenure and the 1865 sermon; neither is dated exactly in the source.

burial.plot_notes: West Laurel Hill Cemetery, Bala Cynwyd

narrative_blocks.header: He preached Lincoln twice in four days
narrative_blocks.body: On Easter Sunday 1865, the morning after the news reached Bridgeport, he preached on the death of the president at Christ Church. The citizens of the town asked him to give it again at the North Congregational Church on the day of the obsequies, then asked him for the manuscript, and it was printed.

narrative_blocks.header: He swapped his last two names around
narrative_blocks.body: The Lincoln sermon went to press in 1865 under the name John Falkner Blake, rector of Christ Church at Bridgeport. By the time he took Christ Church at Germantown he was John Blake Falkner, and he stayed so.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-seven years at Christ Church, Germantown
narrative_blocks.body: He was rector there for twenty-seven years and rector emeritus after he resigned, and was examining chaplain of the diocese of Pennsylvania from 1872. The man who followed him in that pulpit later married his daughter Helen.
