narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-nine years over Philadelphia's City Hall
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel was president of the Public Building Commission, which superintended the building of Philadelphia's City Hall at Broad and Market Streets, from 17 April 1872 until the commission was dissolved on 1 July 1901. Sir Edwin Arnold called the building the finest municipal building in the world.

narrative_blocks.header: Legal adviser to the Presbyterian Church
narrative_blocks.body: From 1878 until his death Samuel was legal adviser to the Trustees of the General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church, and from 1870 president of the Trustees of its Board of Publication.

narrative_blocks.header: A leader of the Philadelphia bar
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel read law in the office of his father, Samuel H. Perkins, and was admitted in 1851 and to the United States Supreme Court bar in 1874. An authority on old procedure, he collected early writs, briefs and arguments, and helped secure the Law Library its rooms in City Hall.

narrative_blocks.header: Grand Master as the Masonic Temple rose
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel joined the Masons at twenty-two and rose to Grand Master, and the Masonic Temple in Philadelphia was built under his direct supervision.

narrative_blocks.header: The third generation of his family at Yale
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel graduated from Yale with honor in 1848, a member of Skull and Bones and Psi Upsilon, as his father and grandfather had graduated before him. Yale later gave him an M.A. and, in 1888, an LL.D.

narrative_blocks.header: Three children, all lost in infancy
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel married Mary Hooker Packard, and their three children all died in infancy. He never quite recovered from her death in January 1900.

narrative_blocks.header: Clerk of Session at First Presbyterian
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel joined the First Presbyterian Church of Philadelphia in 1848 and was its Clerk of Session from 1870. His pastor, the Rev. George D. Baker, read out his lists of new members without checking them: “I came to consider him almost infallible in these matters, entirely incapable of an error; and in all the years I never found one.”

narrative_blocks.header: Rose of Sharon, and she was from Sharon
narrative_blocks.body: Sharon, Connecticut was her home town, and the Song of Solomon supplies the rest: “I am the rose of Sharon, and the lily of the valleys.” Litchfield used the phrase for her and it stayed on her for life.

narrative_blocks.header: He walked twenty miles to see her window
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas and Josiah Telfair, brothers at the Litchfield Law School, both fell in love with her. One offered himself and was refused, then walked the twenty miles from Litchfield to Sharon to look at the light in her window, and walked back again.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a Litchfield law student in 1815
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth Hannah Canfield married Frederick Augustus Tallmadge on 22 May 1815, a student of the Litchfield Law School and a son of Washington's spymaster, and the two of them went to New York and raised five children.

narrative_blocks.header: Twice at the Litchfield Female Academy
narrative_blocks.body: She went to Sarah Pierce's school at Litchfield in 1809 and again in 1814, as her two sisters did. Her daughter Elizabeth was sent there after her.

narrative_blocks.header: From private to lieutenant in two years
narrative_blocks.body: James French enlisted in the 100th New York Infantry as a private in August 1862 and rose through the ranks, winning a lieutenant’s commission by the spring of 1864. He was a Rochester man leading Rochester men through the Virginia campaigns of the war’s final year.

narrative_blocks.header: Wounded at Drewry’s Bluff, he died a prisoner
narrative_blocks.body: At the Battle of Drewry’s Bluff on May 16, 1864, French was struck down and taken prisoner as the Confederates broke Butler’s advance on Richmond. He was carried into Libby Prison and died of his wounds six days later, one of thousands who never left the city alive.

narrative_blocks.header: He married Frances in the war year
narrative_blocks.body: The 1917 wedding joined the young lawyer to Jack Morgan's second daughter. Locust Valley held their long married life, and its cemetery holds them both.

narrative_blocks.header: He fought at Saint-Mihiel and the Argonne
narrative_blocks.body: He crossed to France with the 305th Field Artillery, serving in artillery intelligence and as liaison to French units on the Western Front, through Saint-Mihiel and the Meuse-Argonne. After the Armistice he was aide-de-camp to the chief of artillery of the American First Army.

narrative_blocks.header: In the room where the UN began
narrative_blocks.body: A colonel on the War Department General Staff in the second war, with two tours as an observer in the China-Burma-India theater, he was sent by the State Department in 1945 to serve in the secretariat of the San Francisco conference — the meeting that created the United Nations.

narrative_blocks.header: Nineteen years running a Wall Street firm
narrative_blocks.body: He spent his career at White & Case, breaking only for a stint in investment banking, and served nineteen years as its managing partner. He ran the firm's Paris office from 1937 to 1939, and took European clients for the rest of his working life.

narrative_blocks.header: America and France both pinned medals on him
narrative_blocks.body: The Army gave him the Legion of Merit in 1945 for his General Staff work. Seventeen years later France made him a Chevalier of the Légion d'honneur — the country whose artillery he had liaised with as a young captain in 1918, and whose language and cities he had loved since boyhood in Geneva.

narrative_blocks.header: A honeymoon lake, bought nineteen years later
narrative_blocks.body: He brought his bride to Lake Tahoe on their honeymoon in 1917, touring the lake by steamer, and they vowed to return. They came back in 1936 with six children — and bought eight hundred feet of Rubicon Bay shoreline the same afternoon they first saw it, on a handshake.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother the painter was a Monuments Man
narrative_blocks.body: His elder brother, the painter Albert Sheldon Pennoyer, kept a studio shack on Paul's land at Lake Tahoe. As a Monuments Man in wartime Italy, Sheldon took the Leica photographs that are much of the record of their work. He died in a car crash near Madrid in 1957.

research_sources.note: Moffat's Pierrepont Genealogies says Henry married the adopted daughter of David Davis, the Supreme Court justice and Lincoln's 1860 campaign manager, whose home was Bloomington; Find a Grave gives her parents as George Walker and Harriett Hull of Lenox. Both can hold if the Davises raised a Walker connection of Mrs. Davis, who was herself a Walker of Lenox. Unconfirmed — the Bloomington marriage and the Lenox birth are what line up. Moffat calls Davis Vice-President; he was president pro tempore of the Senate, and so acting Vice-President, 1881-83.

The 1938 Morgan-Thatcher wedding column independently calls her daughter Sarah a great-grandniece of Senator David Davis, which corroborates Moffat's claim that Henry Villee Pierpont married Davis's adopted daughter. The same column makes Alden Kendrick Morgan a nephew of John A. Spoor, whom the 2004 Tribune obituary instead calls his father's wife's second cousin.

bio.bio_blurb: Merchant; head of Russell & Co. in Hong Kong

narrative_blocks.header: Sent to Hong Kong for the in-laws
narrative_blocks.body: The Forbes family ran much of Russell & Co., and Frances's brother Paul was a partner at Shanghai. In 1857 they sent Nelson out to Hong Kong as managing director, and in three years he won American steamers the run of China's rivers.

narrative_blocks.header: Watching Confederate raiders in France
narrative_blocks.body: When the Civil War broke out Nelson took his family to Paris and put the children in French schools. With John Bigelow, the American consul-general, he worked to keep Confederate ships from sailing out of French ports.

narrative_blocks.header: An officer of the Legion of Honor
narrative_blocks.body: Nelson ran the American exhibit at the Paris Universal Exposition of 1867. Napoleon III made him an officer of the Legion of Honor, and the Beckwiths were received at the imperial court.

narrative_blocks.header: Coffee, spices and the West Indies
narrative_blocks.body: Nelson learned the trade in Canada and Europe, set up in New York in 1835 importing coffee and spices from the West Indies and South America, and by 1852 could step away and take his family travelling through Europe.

narrative_blocks.header: The judge's son from Cazenovia
narrative_blocks.body: Nelson grew up at Cazenovia, where his father, Barak Beckwith, was a church deacon and county judge who had helped draft New York's state constitution.

narrative_blocks.header: Animals, art and the Centennial
narrative_blocks.body: Back on Fifth Avenue, Nelson was vice president of the new Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, worked for the young Metropolitan Museum of Art, and was New York's commissioner to the 1876 Centennial.

narrative_blocks.header: A daughter at Stoneleigh Abbey
narrative_blocks.body: Nelson married Frances Forbes in 1842. Their daughter Helene became Lady Leigh of Stoneleigh Abbey, and their son Leonard married Margaretta Pierrepont. After Frances died in 1885 he moved to 75 Fifth Avenue.

narrative_blocks.header: One vote saved him from disgrace
narrative_blocks.body: His friendship with an older, unmarried author at his New Haven boarding house became the scandal of the day: when he told her brother he had no intention of marrying her, the brother had him tried before an ecclesiastical court. He escaped with a reprimand by a vote of twelve to eleven — and the case was still being written about for decades.

narrative_blocks.header: He argued that the Lord's name was misspoken
narrative_blocks.body: His book Yahveh Christ set out to prove that the Hebrew name rendered 'Jehovah' had lost its true vowels to a Jewish superstition — that it was properly Yahveh, meaning not 'I am' but 'He who will be,' and that it named Christ himself. A deep Hebraist, he wrote on metaphysics and theology for the reviews.

narrative_blocks.header: He finished the article, then fell
narrative_blocks.body: Through the extreme heat of June 1880 he labored to finish an essay for the Princeton Review. He closed his work on a Thursday and was struck with apoplexy on the Friday; he was dead by Monday, at fifty-eight, leaving his wife of twenty-three years without children.

narrative_blocks.header: The university took her house for a stadium
narrative_blocks.body: The Piedmont Avenue property came to her from her father, and she and two of her sons built homes on it — until 1922, when the university condemned the land to raise Memorial Stadium. Where other faculty families raged, she had an answer ready.

narrative_blocks.header: She cut sixty acres into four
narrative_blocks.body: The family owned a hillside in Kensington, four miles north of the campus, and she divided it evenly among her four children. Two of them lived far away and sold their shares; the other two built the houses that still stand there, one now a public garden and one a Carmelite monastery.

narrative_blocks.header: A tiny, imperious matriarch and her summers
narrative_blocks.body: Widowed in 1897, she insisted her scattered family come to her every summer at the Piedmont Avenue house — the Thacher children up from Ojai, the Berkeley sons next door. Her grandson remembered a small, imperious woman presiding over children and dogs in splendid disorder.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father and brother both served Yale
narrative_blocks.body: She grew up inside the Yale faculty: her father James Luce Kingsley taught Latin, Greek and Hebrew there for forty-nine years and kept the library besides. Her brother Henry was the college’s treasurer from 1862 until a carriage threw him in 1886, and he died of it a month later.

narrative_blocks.header: She carried her mother’s maiden name
narrative_blocks.body: She was given her mother’s surname for her middle one — Lydia Coit of Norwich, who had married the Latin professor in 1811. Her brother Henry Coit Kingsley carried it too.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-five years at Bridgeport, then home
narrative_blocks.body: She married Henry Taylor Blake in May 1860, at twenty-nine, and went with him to Bridgeport, where he kept to the bar for thirty-five years. They came back about 1885 to New Haven, the town her father had taught in for half a century, and she died there in 1914.

narrative_blocks.body: She came back to Louisville in 1942 to work at the Jeffersonville Boat and Machine Company for the war effort. Lieutenant Charles Hazard was stationed at Fort Knox, and they married that October.

narrative_blocks.header: A scheme to time the world by Jerusalem
narrative_blocks.body: A good man but an impractical one, he chased one fanciful project after another — a wooden-track railroad, a numerical system drawn from scripture meant to reconcile faith and modern science, and a scheme for global timekeeping measured from Jerusalem. He sought Samuel Morse's backing for the last of these, and did not get it.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept school beside his brother the reverend
narrative_blocks.body: He served as assistant principal of Erasmus Hall Academy in Flatbush while his brother, the Rev. Timothy Clowes, was principal of the same school. He was later a vestryman of St. George's Church at Hempstead, the parish his father-in-law had led for nearly thirty years.

narrative_blocks.header: He built three sawmills where Elizabeth died
narrative_blocks.body: After Elizabeth's death he settled at Hartwood in Sullivan County, raised three water-powered sawmills there, and went into the lumber trade. He served as the village postmaster, and his mother lived out her days beside him.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughters were given away to relatives
narrative_blocks.body: Alone in the remote Sullivan County woods, he could not give his two small girls what they needed, and in 1851 the family decided the sisters should be parted — Lydia to Virginia, Caroline to her uncle's house in Dutchess County. His fanciful schemes never came to anything; his daughter became a painter.

narrative_blocks.header: She named the house for its promised ease
narrative_blocks.body: A Hempstead woman, daughter of Gideon Nichols, she married Benjamin Hall Hart in 1837 and moved to Dutchess County, where they raised seven children. They called the home they built Heartsease, hoping it would give the family comfort of both body and spirit.

narrative_blocks.header: Her women kept the house for six generations
narrative_blocks.body: She outlived her husband by twenty-two years and was buried beside him. The house passed to her eldest daughter Mary, and after her to a succession of the family's women — who have held Heartsease for more than a century and a half.

narrative_blocks.header: A studio rose beside the orchard
narrative_blocks.body: She and Benjamin raised seven children at Heartsease and took in her husband's orphaned niece Caroline besides. Her own unmarried sister, Adelia Nichols, was a talented artist and became the girl's first teacher; in 1872 a studio was built for Caroline on the grounds.

narrative_blocks.body: Milne came out of Forres in Moray as a boy of nine, to Monroe County and then Holley. He worked his way through school and through the University of Rochester, taking his degree in 1868.

narrative_blocks.body: He ran the Geneseo Normal and Training School from 1871, and when he went to Albany in 1889 his brother John succeeded him there. A library at Geneseo now carries both their names.

narrative_blocks.header: A generation learned arithmetic from him
narrative_blocks.body: His arithmetics and algebras ran through edition after edition and were authorised for schools as far off as British Columbia. Revisions were still being issued after his death.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at a White Mountain resort town
narrative_blocks.body: A heart ailment took him at Bethlehem, New Hampshire on 4 September 1914 — the year his college took the name New York State College for Teachers. He was buried at Albany.

narrative_blocks.header: A general who policed the Canadian border
narrative_blocks.body: Seth Cushman rose to brigadier general in the War of 1812, guarding the Vermont-Canada line. When a Canaan man named Beach used a cattle permit to smuggle oxen to the English, Cushman sent a squad to stop him, and in the confrontation Beach was shot dead.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran for Congress, and lost to Anti-Masonry
narrative_blocks.body: Cushman was the Jacksonian candidate in Vermont's marathon Fifth District race, where the new Anti-Masonic movement battled through eight rounds of balloting. He led early but withdrew in 1829, and the Anti-Mason William Cahoon finally won.

narrative_blocks.header: He read law at the Essex County bar
narrative_blocks.body: Admitted to the Essex County bar in 1804, Cushman built an extensive Guildhall practice, served many years in the Vermont legislature, and was state's attorney for a considerable period.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Cushman brothers, two Hooker marriages
narrative_blocks.body: Seth and his younger brother John Paine Cushman were both Litchfield-era lawyers who married into the Hooker descent within a few years of each other, Seth to Mehitable Chaplin of the Edwards line, John Paine to Maria Tallmadge. Two brothers, two branches of one family.

narrative_blocks.header: Brilliant in court, no friend to the pious
narrative_blocks.body: Handsome and gentlemanly, Cushman was not a deep student of the books yet had remarkable instinct in trying a case. A biographer's barb stuck: had his moral and religious principles equaled his natural abilities, he would have been the pride of his friends.

narrative_blocks.header: He guarded the women at Forty Fort
narrative_blocks.body: James was a Quaker and would not bear arms, but on the day of the Wyoming massacre in July 1778 he resolved to take up a musket. He was posted inside Forty Fort instead, in charge of the women, children and old men sheltering there.

narrative_blocks.header: Sutton's Creek, and the mills he lost
narrative_blocks.body: James built a saw and grist mill at Exeter on a stream that took his name, Sutton's Creek. After two years' refuge downriver he came back to find his mill burned, and the pumpkin flood of October 1786 swept away the next one.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty years of Methodist preachers at his table
narrative_blocks.body: Born to Quaker parents, James took up Methodism and led the first class formed in the Lackawanna valley. For fifty years he and Sarah lodged the itinerant preachers who rode that circuit.

narrative_blocks.header: A Westchester merchant who went to Wyoming
narrative_blocks.body: James kept a store at North Castle in Westchester County until the patriots banned British imports. He sold up and took his family, and Sarah's father, to the Wyoming Valley, and in 1808 was made a justice of the peace.

quotes.notes: Obituary excerpt for Nathaniel Stevens Whitney.

military_service.notes: Served in both winters of the Rebellions of 1837-1838 (Lower Canada Rebellion), although not of the age required by law (he was only 17 in 1837). Per the Canadian Illustrated News: 'showed himself a worthy descendant [of United Empire Loyalist stock] by serving in both winters of the rebellion, although not of the age required by law.'

burial.plot_notes: Cimetière Mont-Royal Montreal — Mr. Whitney was himself a trustee of the cemetery.

career.notes: Entered wholesale dry goods business after moving to Montreal at an early age from Frelighsburg.
Subsequently entered the leather business, in which he continued until his death.
The first meeting of the Montreal Telegraph Company at its organization was held in his office — placing him at the founding of one of the earliest Canadian telecommunications enterprises.
Largely instrumental in forming the Montreal Horticultural Society, of which he was latterly president.
Life Governor 'not in name only, but in deeds and activity, as the annual reports have testified' per the Canadian Illustrated News obituary.
Trustee of the Mount Royal Cemetery — where he himself would be buried in 1883.

career.role: Lay delegate to Synod / Governor of Diocesan College
career.organization: Church of England (Anglican Church of Canada)
career.notes: Devoted adherent of the Church of England. Lay delegate to the Synod for many years; member of the executive committee; Governor of the Diocesan College.

narrative_blocks.header: The telegraph began in his office
narrative_blocks.body: Nathaniel came to Montreal young from Frelighsburg and went into wholesale dry goods, then leather, which he kept at until he died. When the Montreal Telegraph Company was organized, its first meeting was held in his office.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded the Horticultural Society
narrative_blocks.body: Nathaniel helped found the Montreal Horticultural Society and was its president in his last years. At The Hills, his country place near Frelighsburg, he kept a large stock farm.

narrative_blocks.header: Governor of the hospital, trustee of the cemetery
narrative_blocks.body: Nathaniel was an active Life Governor of the Montreal General Hospital, and a trustee of Mount Royal Cemetery, where he was buried in 1883.

narrative_blocks.header: The Synod, not the ballot box
narrative_blocks.body: A devoted Anglican, Nathaniel sat for years as a lay delegate to the Synod and as a governor of the Diocesan College. He was asked several times to stand as the Liberal candidate for his native county, and always declined.

narrative_blocks.header: Under age for the Rebellion
narrative_blocks.body: Nathaniel was seventeen, under the age the law required, when he turned out for both winters of the Rebellions of 1837 and 1838 in Lower Canada. His family were United Empire Loyalists who had come north after the Revolution.

narrative_blocks.header: A cold caught at The Hills
narrative_blocks.body: Nathaniel caught the cold that killed him on a visit to The Hills, his farm at Frelighsburg, and died at Montreal in June 1883, at sixty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the mayor's daughter
narrative_blocks.body: Nathaniel married Hannah Mills in July 1847, the summer the Irish fever ships reached Montreal. Four months later her father, Mayor John Easton Mills, died of the typhus he caught nursing the immigrants.

He owned the office before long, by what the same man called sheer industry and economy.

narrative_blocks.header: He walked into cholera to pay the claims
narrative_blocks.body: When fire took St. Louis in May 1849 the cholera was raging there, and Howard went into the city anyway and stayed until every loss was adjusted. People trusted Hartford insurance afterward, and his companies in particular.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped start the party in Connecticut
narrative_blocks.body: An intense partisan, he was one of the organizers of the Republican Party in Connecticut and the first internal revenue collector appointed at Hartford. His brother John went west instead and became a leading lawyer in Montana.

narrative_blocks.header: The money came out of western land
narrative_blocks.body: The Ann Arbor friend who wrote his notice thought him neither brilliant nor stupid but plain, steady-going and hard-working. What he left had been made largely from land bought early in the west, not from the insurance offices he ran.

people.research_notes:
Rev. George Kemp Ward (1848-1937). Born Rochester NY 9 January 1848, son of Hon. Levi A. Ward (sometime Mayor of Rochester) and grandson of Dr. Levi Ward (pioneer of Western New York, emigrated from East Haddam CT). Cousin of Prof. Henry A. Ward (Ward's Natural Science Establishment, Rochester). Educated Rochester Collegiate Institute -> University of Rochester (Freshman year) -> Princeton 1869 (American Whig Society, Class Secretary/Historian, Iota Chapter of Delta Psi joined at Rochester) -> Princeton A.M. 1872 -> Princeton Theological Seminary 1873. Twice Moderator of the Presbytery of Rochester; editor of the Presbyterian Church Herald; member of the Livingston County Historical Society. narrative_blocks.header: Son of the mayor who built Rochester
narrative_blocks.body: George grew up the son of Levi A. Ward — a mayor of Rochester who helped found its Athenaeum and its savings bank — and the grandson of a Connecticut pioneer who had opened the western New York frontier. The Wards were among the city’s makers, and George carried the name into the pulpit and the archive rather than politics.

narrative_blocks.header: He compiled the Ward family genealogy
narrative_blocks.body: A born chronicler who had served as secretary and historian of his Princeton class, publishing its reunion volumes, George turned the same instinct on his own blood. As secretary of the Association of Descendants of Andrew Ward, he compiled the Andrew Ward Family Genealogy, a standard record of the line in America.

narrative_blocks.header: One pulpit for twenty-five years
narrative_blocks.body: George took the pastorate at the Dansville Presbyterian Church in 1873 and stayed twenty-five years — his first charge and his only one. Twice his fellow ministers elected him Moderator of the Rochester Presbytery, a settled man in a restless calling.

narrative_blocks.header: His cousin supplied the world's museums
narrative_blocks.body: George's first cousin was Henry Augustus Ward, whose Ward's Natural Science Establishment in Rochester shipped skeletons, minerals, and mounted specimens to museums and colleges across the world. The family ran to founders and collectors; the naturalist gathered specimens, and the minister gathered names.

narrative_blocks.header: Congress made him a captain after he died
narrative_blocks.body: For years the army recommended him for captain and Congress never acted, so he did a captain's work without the rank or the pay. He died of illness in Maryland in 1834 — and three months later, Congress finally confirmed the promotion he had been denied in life.

narrative_blocks.header: He died policing a canal-workers' revolt
narrative_blocks.body: In early 1834 his artillery unit was sent to Williamsport, Maryland, where federal troops had been called out against Irish laborers protesting conditions on the Chesapeake and Ohio Canal. There he took ill and died, only months after marrying Mary Alsop Dwight.

narrative_blocks.body: An Illinois-born painter trained at the Académie Julian in Paris, he made portraits of notable figures — Thomas Edison, John Muir, the singer Nellie Melba, Sam Houston, and Theodore Roosevelt among them. His Sam Houston hangs in the Texas Senate chamber.

narrative_blocks.header: He led the Allied Artists of America
narrative_blocks.body: In New York he was president of the Allied Artists of America from 1925 to 1928, and worked through the Lotos Club and the Artists' Professional League to get emerging painters exhibited.

narrative_blocks.body: He summered at Marblehead, Massachusetts, founding the Marblehead Arts Association and building himself a small Colonial Revival studio there in 1926, its tall north window pulling in the sea light.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran for governor on the anti-slavery ticket
narrative_blocks.body: The anti-slavery party put him up for governor of New York. The Liberty Party had been organised in 1839 at the Warsaw Presbyterian Church, eight miles from his own door.

narrative_blocks.header: Brooksholm was a station on the Covington line
narrative_blocks.body: His Pearl Creek house was a key stop on the Covington Connection, the route up from Pennsylvania through Friendship to Pavilion Center and east toward Le Roy. Wyoming County had the second most conductors in the state.

narrative_blocks.header: He found the famine Irish work and roofs
narrative_blocks.body: Through the Irish famine of the 1840s he helped many of the immigrants who reached Wyoming County into houses and into work. It was the decade his own house was running as a station.

narrative_blocks.header: Staunton painted him holding a temperance paper
narrative_blocks.body: Phineas Staunton painted him about 1840 with the Temperance Recorder in his hand, which dates the canvas between 1832 and 1843. The back is pencilled with his name and Middlebury.

narrative_blocks.header: Among the first children that church baptised
narrative_blocks.body: The First Congregational Church of Covington was organised in October 1817, the year he was born, and he and Phoebe Ann were the first two children it baptised. His father was one of its two first deacons.

narrative_blocks.header: His father founded the Middlebury Academy
narrative_blocks.body: Benedict Brooks came out of Cheshire in Connecticut, founded the Middlebury Academy, sat as a judge and went to the legislature. The line runs back to a Henry Brooks who had fought for Cromwell.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran Boston’s natural history museum
narrative_blocks.body: He took an A.B. in 1908, an A.M. the year after and a doctorate in 1917, taught geology, and then spent the rest of his working life as director of the Boston Society of Natural History.

narrative_blocks.header: Ninety people under him in the food office
narrative_blocks.body: The 1918 year went to the Massachusetts Food Administration, where the department he had charge of grew to ninety people. He came out of it with the title of Assistant Food Administrator.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-eight nights of fifty-five in a berth
narrative_blocks.body: He crossed Canada from Halifax to Victoria in 1913 with the International Geological Congress. Of the fifty-five nights of that trip, he counted forty-eight of them spent on the sleeping car.

narrative_blocks.header: A month spent starting a jungle laboratory
narrative_blocks.body: He went to Cuba, Jamaica and Panama in 1924 with Dr. Thomas Barbour, and in Panama the two of them spent a month getting the Barro Colorado Island laboratory started.

narrative_blocks.header: Children, Guernseys and White Plymouth Rocks
narrative_blocks.body: He kept a farm at Topsfield and lived on it most of the time. Asked what he did for recreation he answered that he had there successfully raised children, pure-bred Guernseys and White Plymouth Rock poultry.

narrative_blocks.header: Europe in 1908 with Minot and Webb Hyde
narrative_blocks.body: He went out to Europe the year he graduated with two Harvard classmates, George R. Minot and H. Webb Hyde. All three had come up through the Noble and Greenough School before Harvard.

narrative_blocks.header: Two daughters born on the same February day
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah and Jane were both born on 25 February 1923, between Mary in 1921 and Anne in 1924. With Edward in 1915 and Thomas in 1917 that made six children in ten years.

narrative_blocks.body: Born in Louisiana and educated at Yale, he ran a large cotton plantation in Claiborne County, Mississippi, worked by enslaved African Americans. He helped found Oakland College, a Presbyterian school near his lands.

narrative_blocks.header: Windsor land grants in her own name
narrative_blocks.body: As a daughter of Thomas Newberry, Rebecca received Windsor land allotments in 1640 in her own right. Her holdings ran from the Great Meadow to a tract three miles long across the Great River. She brought standing of her own into the Russell parsonage.

narrative_blocks.header: Her marriage dated by a note about apples
narrative_blocks.body: No record fixes when Rebecca married Rev. John Russell. But a 1651 ledger entry of apples sold “to brother Russell” places the wedding before 1652. She became his second wife and bore his surviving sons.

narrative_blocks.header: She raised a founder of Yale
narrative_blocks.body: Rebecca's son Samuel Russell took his Harvard degree and settled as minister at Branford. In his study there the founders of Yale College gathered to lay down their books and charter the school. Her household gave Connecticut one of its college's founders.

narrative_blocks.header: Another son shepherded Barnstable for decades
narrative_blocks.body: Her eldest son, Jonathan, held a single Barnstable pulpit for forty-seven years until his death in 1711. The colony also chose him to help treat with the Mohawk sachems at Albany in 1680. Judge Sewall remembered him simply as an “orthodox, useful man.”

narrative_blocks.header: Her Hadley monument names a mother in Israel
narrative_blocks.body: Rebecca died in November 1688, aged fifty-seven, and was buried at Hadley. Her gravestone calls her “a wise, virtuous, pious mother in Israel” and a “fellow labourer in Christ's work.” The inscription frames a life measured by faith and family.

bio.bio_blurb: Colonial divorcée; ancestress of Jonathan Edwards

narrative_blocks.header: The notorious grandmother of Jonathan Edwards
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth Tuttle was raised to be a Puritan goodwife but became one of colonial New England's most scandalous women. Centuries later she was the subject of a book, The Notorious Elizabeth Tuttle, and of long debate over the family she founded.

narrative_blocks.header: She threatened to cut her sleeping husband's throat
narrative_blocks.body: Three months after the wedding Elizabeth bore a child Richard refused to own; over the years she was repeatedly unfaithful, sold liquor to the Indians, and threatened to slit her sleeping husband's throat. In 1691 he won a divorce almost without parallel in New England.

narrative_blocks.header: Eugenicists made her the root of a family
narrative_blocks.body: In the 1920s Clarence Darrow and others counted her descendants, college presidents, senators, a vice president, and credited her with the temperament of a genius. The pseudo-science that claimed her was discredited after the Second World War.

narrative_blocks.header: Brother and sister, each killed with an axe
narrative_blocks.body: Violence ran through the Tuttle family. Her brother Benjamin murdered their sister Sarah with an axe in 1676 and was hanged; her sister Mercy killed her son the same way in 1691. Elizabeth's grief and instability amid these horrors helped end her marriage.

narrative_blocks.header: Her line: a theologian and a duelist
narrative_blocks.body: Through her son Timothy she was grandmother of Jonathan Edwards, called America's theologian; through the same blood came Aaron Burr, who killed Alexander Hamilton. Both were said to carry something of her character.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father's New Haven land is Yale's now
narrative_blocks.body: She was the eighth of the twelve children of William Tuttle, who brought the family over on the Planter in 1635 and signed the first covenant of the New Haven colony four years later. Part of the ground he took up there is Yale campus today.

narrative_blocks.header: She saw Roxbury for a single winter

Spouse of Hon. William Pynchon (Y00004). Died Wraisburgh, Buckinghamshire England Oct 10, 1657 (EH 1909) ENRICHED 10 Aug 2026 from Anderson, The Great Migration Begins, and Sam's FamilySearch
extract. She was Frances (___) (Smith) Sandford — surname at birth unknown, twice widowed
before Pynchon. William Whiteway of Dorchester, Dorsetshire recorded on 10 April 1630 that
"the beginning of this month, many of this town went to plant in New England and among the
rest, Mrs. Sandford" [Whiteway 110; NEHGR 143:109-10]. Admitted to Roxbury church in late
1632 as "Mrs. Francis Pinchon, the wife of Mr. William Pinchon", the record noting "she was
a widow, a matron of the church at Dorchester, where Mr. Pinchon married her. She came with
the first company, anno 1630" [RChR 77]. Married Pynchon by late 1632. Died Wraysbury
10 October 1657 [Hale, House 724]; buried there, CEM1542. BIRTH YEAR IS AN ESTIMATE, flagged as such. Sam's source gives a range, "from 1585 to
1590"; 1588 is the midpoint and date_precision is set to estimated, which the age validator
skips. Replace it the moment a real year appears. Sam's paste has an earlier marriage to a
Mr. Smith about 1609 in England, with at least one son. HER SON. "Henry Smith, living in New England" appears in Rev. John White's 1634 list of his
associates in the New England adventure [NEHGR 61:280]. Pynchon paid the passage of "my son
Smyth and 3 daughters and 1 maid" around Cape Cod to the Connecticut in 1636. Henry Smith is
not built; whether he married a Pynchon daughter is not established by anything in hand. Sam's paste also carries the garbled forms "Frances Stamford", "m.1632; div.1634" and
"Anna Andrews 1623-34 at Springfield Massachusetts". Anderson supersedes all three.

narrative_blocks.header: Twice widowed, she sailed in 1630
narrative_blocks.body: Frances left Dorchester in Dorsetshire for New England in the spring of 1630, twice widowed and bringing her son with her. She was a matron of the Dorchester church in Massachusetts when Pynchon, lately widowed himself, married her there about two years later.

narrative_blocks.header: She died sixteen days before her stepdaughter
narrative_blocks.body: Frances followed Pynchon back to England and died at Wraysbury on 10 October 1657. Sixteen days later, and an ocean away, her stepdaughter Mary Pynchon Holyoke died at Springfield. Pynchon buried Frances in the churchyard where he would lie five years afterward.

people.research_notes: Husband of Mary Talcott Perrin (T01387). b. March 18, 1748 Hebron CT (some sources say March 8); d. May 25, 1838 Berlin Corners VT age 90 (some sources say May 28). Source date discrepancy: WikiTree gives 18 March 1748, FindAGrave memorial 90950772 gives March 8 1749/50; Vermont Genealogy biography gives March 18, 1748 d. May 28, 1838. Defaulting to March 18, 1748 + May 25, 1838 per FindAGrave on Zachariah's own memorial. Revolutionary War veteran — 8th company of the 12th regiment Connecticut militia. Married Mary Talcott (T01387) ca.1779/1780 in Hebron CT. 9 children, first 4 born in Hebron and last 5 in Berlin VT. Berlin VT founder: removed from Hebron in May 1789 with two teams of oxen up the Connecticut River, then White River, switching to runners at Brookfield over a blazed trail. Original cabin's roof collapsed under winter snow. Permanent farm at the southeast corner of present-day East Road and Scott Hill Road. The 1300 acres in East Road School District passed through generations; some still owned by Perrins as of the modern era. Son Porter, first boy born in Berlin, built the 1815 house at Scott Hill/Airport Road still standing in greatly altered form. Notable descent: through daughter Elizabeth Polly Perrin Dewey, grandfather of Admiral George Dewey, hero of Manila Bay 1898. Through daughter Emeline Hobart Evans, great-grandfather of Ira Hobart Evans, Civil War Medal of Honor recipient. (Both Admiral Dewey and Ira Hobart Evans NOT yet built into JSON — flagged for next batch per Sam.) [Pilot101 enrichment from Berlin VT history, Hamilton Child 1888]: Zachariah Perrin came from Hebron, Connecticut, to Berlin VT in March 1789, settling in the eastern part of the town. He came with two yoke of oxen, his sled loaded with provisions and his wife and two children, traveling up the Connecticut and White rivers to Brookfield (then the end of the road), and from there along a line of blazed trees through three to four feet of snow. Elected one of Berlin's first selectmen at the inaugural town meeting March 31, 1791, alongside Capt. James Sawyer (selectman/moderator), David Nye (town clerk — later his son-in-law), Eleazer Hubbard (selectman), and Micajah Ingham (constable). Aided in the settlement and organization of the town and the support of the Congregational church. Died May 1838 aged 88.

residence.note: Settled May 1789 from Hebron CT; farmed 1300 acres at Scott Hill/East Road intersection in East Road School District.

narrative_blocks.header: Settled Berlin Vermont with collapsed-roof cabin
narrative_blocks.body: Zachariah served in the Revolutionary War with the 8th company of the 12th Connecticut militia, then in February-March 1789 led his family from Hebron Connecticut to Berlin Vermont — up the Connecticut River with two teams of oxen, switching from wheels to runners in Brookfield. They found the log cabin he had built the previous summer crushed under three or four feet of snow.

narrative_blocks.header: Founded a 1300-acre farm still in family
narrative_blocks.body: Zachariah's 1300 acres in the East Road School District of Berlin VT — at what became the southeast corner of East Road and Scott Hill Road — passed down through generations of Perrins. His son Porter, the first boy born in Berlin, built the house at Scott Hill and Airport Road in 1815 (still standing). A descendant Henry Perrin still lived in 'Perrin territory' along Scott Hill Road into the modern era.

narrative_blocks.header: A Connecticut man who soldiered in 1812
narrative_blocks.body: Born in Newtown, Connecticut, David Judson Burr served as a lieutenant in the Virginia militia during the War of 1812. He had settled south in Richmond, where he would spend the rest of his life. The Connecticut Yankee became a Virginian.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a young widow from Litchfield
narrative_blocks.body: In 1812 Burr married Annabella Shedden Reeve, the widow of Aaron Burr Reeve, in Litchfield, Connecticut. The couple raised a large family in Richmond, where Burr died of 'dyspepsia' in 1838. One of their sons, also David Judson Burr, became a founder of the Richmond Chamber of Commerce.

narrative_blocks.header: His surname invites a question about Aaron Burr
narrative_blocks.body: He shared the Burr name with the famous vice president and duelist, but the link is a distant one — both men trace back to Jehu Burr, a founder of Fairfield who crossed on the Winthrop Fleet, four or five generations before either was born. They were, at most, far-flung cousins.

narrative_blocks.header: A founding member at Farmington

narrative_blocks.header: She lost her son John in 1666

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the defense of Greek and Latin
narrative_blocks.body: With President Jeremiah Day and Benjamin Silliman he drafted the Yale Report of 1828, answering demands that the college drop the classics for practical subjects. American colleges held to the classical course for another fifty years on the strength of it.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale gave him four subjects in one chair
narrative_blocks.body: Yale made one professorship of Hebrew, Greek, Latin and ecclesiastical history in 1805 and gave the whole of it to him, its first professor of foreign languages. It shed history in 1817, Greek in 1831 and Hebrew in 1835, and he taught Latin alone until he resigned at seventy-three.

narrative_blocks.header: He published almost everything anonymously
narrative_blocks.body: He was modest to the point of disappearing: the Cicero and Tacitus he edited for his students went out unsigned, and so did most of his articles. The Latin addresses he wrote for two Yale inaugurations were never found among his papers.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale gave him its dead to write up
narrative_blocks.body: Six times the college handed him a colleague to commemorate in Latin, from President Dwight in 1817 to Osgood Johnson in 1837. His sketch of Yale’s own history, printed in 1835, is still a chief authority for the college’s early years.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Yale presidents on his Latin
narrative_blocks.body: Timothy Dwight called him the American Addison. Theodore Woolsey said he doubted any American scholar had ever surpassed him in Latin style, and a colleague reckoned Cicero his model — a surprisingly successful imitation, given that he had taught himself.

narrative_blocks.header: His students and his son-in-law carried it on
narrative_blocks.body: He put Thomas Anthony Thacher through Latin and Thacher named his eldest son for him, and Henry Cowles carried the three languages out to Oberlin. His daughter Elizabeth married Henry Taylor Blake, who wrote the history of the New Haven Green.

notable.notable_blurb: Second president of Harvard College, 1654–1672

narrative_blocks.header: England jailed him over a communion rail
narrative_blocks.body: England's Court of High Commission had him twice, in 1629 and 1634, for refusing to rail in the communion table at his Hertfordshire parish. He was imprisoned, recanted in February 1637, and sailed for America in disgrace.

narrative_blocks.header: He baptized only by full immersion
narrative_blocks.body: He held that sprinkling was no baptism at all. The Plymouth elders debated him in public, then wrote to Boston and New Haven, and every congregation answered that both forms were valid. He left for Scituate in 1641.

narrative_blocks.header: One twin fainted in the water
narrative_blocks.body: A year into Scituate he immersed his twin sons to prove the point, and one of them passed out. Another mother refused to let her child follow, took hold of him, and by Winthrop's account near pulled him in after.

narrative_blocks.header: Harvard hired him on a promise of silence
narrative_blocks.body: Passing through Boston in 1654 on his way back to England, he was offered the Harvard presidency Dunster had left. He took it on a promise to keep his baptism views to himself, and held it until he died in office at seventy-nine.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught Hebrew and Greek at Trinity
narrative_blocks.body: Westminster School sent him to Trinity College, Cambridge, where he was elected a fellow, professed Hebrew, and later lectured in Greek. His family leased Ardeley Bury, a moated manor held from the Dean and Chapter of St Paul's.

narrative_blocks.header: Six sons, six Harvard degrees, six pulpits
narrative_blocks.body: He married Catherine Eyre at Ware in 1630 and had six sons, every one a Harvard graduate bred to the ministry, and two daughters. His great-grandson Charles Chauncy led Boston's First Church for sixty years.

narrative_blocks.header: Cambridge kept a thanksgiving day for him
narrative_blocks.body: Cotton Mather wrote that the town kept a whole day of thanksgiving to God for the mercy they had enjoyed in his being there. Of Scituate, Mather said he cultivated the Lord's vineyard three years and three times three years.

narrative_blocks.header: Norwalk sent him up for twenty-two years
narrative_blocks.body: He sat for Norwalk in the Connecticut House in session after session from 1813 to 1835, the seat going out and coming back to him, and finished in the state Senate for the twelfth district in 1836. He was a merchant the whole time.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty years keeping the town's books
narrative_blocks.body: He was town clerk of Norwalk from 1814 to 1844 and parish clerk of St. Paul's on the Green from 1815 until he died. Between the two of them he wrote down most of what happened in that town for three decades.

narrative_blocks.header: Judge of probate, and of the county court
narrative_blocks.body: He held the probate bench for the Norwalk district and sat on the Connecticut county court, which is where the title on his name comes from. The Bridgeport paper called him a leading citizen when he went.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight weeks between the two of them
narrative_blocks.body: He married Fanny Bryan of Paterson, New Jersey on 18 November 1798; they were born three weeks apart in 1778 and had six children who lived. He died suddenly in July 1846 and Fanny died just as suddenly on 13 September.

narrative_blocks.body: John Isaacs was born in Norwalk, Connecticut, son of Isaac Scudder Isaacs and Susannah Saint John Isaacs (H01239, a Hooker descendant), and married Elizabeth Ann Saint John on October 7-8, 1821. His daughter Mary Etta was born in San Francisco on March 20, 1828 — when it was still called Yerba Buena under Mexican rule — placing his family among the very earliest documented New England visitors to Alta California, more than twenty years before the 1849 Gold Rush.

notable.notable_blurb: Bridgeport founder, physician, turnpike company founder

narrative_blocks.header: A saddler at Newfield before it was Bridgeport
narrative_blocks.body: John moved from Norwalk to Newfield around 1790, when the harbor village had not yet taken the name Bridgeport. With the tanner William Peet he ran the saddlery Cannon & Peet on Broad Street.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped make Newfield a borough
narrative_blocks.body: In 1796 John was among the subscribers who bought Newfield its first fire engine and organized its fire company. He helped incorporate the Borough of Bridgeport in 1800 and founded the Bridgeport & Newtown Turnpike Company the next year.

narrative_blocks.header: The Cannon store at Wilton
narrative_blocks.body: The Cannon General Store, built around 1790 in Wilton, then still a parish of Norwalk, stands at the crossroads the Wilton Historical Society calls Cannon Corner. The society restored it as one of its adaptive-use buildings, where rents from shops and offices pay for the preservation.

narrative_blocks.header: One enslaved man, Cato Cannon
narrative_blocks.body: The 1790 census counted one enslaved person in John's Norwalk household, and later Bridgeport records name him as Cato Cannon. Like many Connecticut founders of his day, the turnpike builder was a slaveholder.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter married a senator
narrative_blocks.body: John married Sarah Saint John in 1777, and they raised eight children. Their daughter Antoinette married Thaddeus Betts, later a United States senator from Connecticut.

narrative_blocks.header: U.S. Congressman, circuit judge, and rector of Troy
narrative_blocks.detail: Cushman prepared for Yale at Plainfield Academy alongside John Adams (Yale 1795) and read law under Judge Zephaniah Swift of Windham before arriving at Litchfield. At Litchfield he became close friends with William L. Marcy — who went on to serve as U.S. Senator, Governor of New York, Secretary of War, and Secretary of State. Cushman's Litchfield Law School classmate John Allen Collier gave a memorial address at the opening of the Supreme Court after his death. He was also a trustee of Union College from 1833 until his death, and a regent of New York University. His father-in-law was Colonel Benjamin Tallmadge, Washington's spymaster. (Wikipedia; Litchfield Historical Society)
narrative_blocks.body: John Paine Cushman graduated Yale in 1807, studied at the Litchfield Law School in 1808, and was admitted to the bar in 1809. He was elected to the 15th Congress (1817-1819) as a Federalist, then served as Recorder of Troy (1834-1838) and Judge of the Third Circuit Court (1838-1844). Upon his death in 1848, the U.S. Supreme Court adjourned in his honor.

narrative_blocks.header: The Cushman Mansion
narrative_blocks.detail: The mansion remained in the family's orbit through much of the 19th century. Maria's father Colonel Benjamin Tallmadge was a frequent correspondent; their social circle included the leading legal and political figures of early New York State. (Landmark; YouTube documentary)
narrative_blocks.body: The Cushman family home at 39 First Street in Troy, built in 1820, is a four-story all-brick Federal-style house. Its original owners were direct descendants of Revolutionary War heroes and Plymouth Colony settlers.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Cushman brothers, two Hooker marriages
narrative_blocks.body: John Paine and his older brother Seth Cushman were both lawyers who married into the Hooker descent within a few years of each other, John Paine to Maria Tallmadge, Seth to Mehitable Chaplin of the Edwards line. Two brothers, two branches of one family.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandfather ran Washington's spy ring
narrative_blocks.body: Harriet Cushman was a daughter of Judge John P. Cushman of the New York Supreme Court and a granddaughter of Benjamin Tallmadge, who built the Culper Ring for Washington. She married Colonel George Thacher Balch at Troy in November 1859.

narrative_blocks.header: No children in thirty-four years

parents.father_research_notes: John Theodoric Balch

notable.notable_blurb: Union ordnance chief; author of the first flag salute

narrative_blocks.header: Stanton sent him to rebuild the Ordnance Bureau
narrative_blocks.body: Balch had spent two years before the war inspecting arsenals across the country. In May 1862 Stanton, his warm friend, ordered him to Washington to reorganise the Ordnance Bureau, through which the war material of the whole Union army passed.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the flag salute before Bellamy
narrative_blocks.body: Years before Francis Bellamy's, Balch built a flag ritual and pledge for New York schoolchildren: 'We give our heads and our hearts to God and our country; one country, one language, one flag.' Bellamy thought it too childish.

narrative_blocks.header: The children voted on it themselves
narrative_blocks.body: On 1 November 1891, at one in the afternoon, the twenty-one schools of the Children's Aid Society voted on whether to adopt the salute. Of the 4,306 who voted, 44 were against. The election was repeated every November after.

narrative_blocks.header: The patriotic work was done at night
narrative_blocks.body: Balch earned his bread auditing the New York Board of Education by day. The plans and the books that carried the flag salute across the country were written at night, and Wallace Foster said he died in the harness.

narrative_blocks.header: He had no children of his own
narrative_blocks.body: The last five years of his life went to other people's children — first of all to the Aid Society's, the poorest in New York, of every colour and half the languages on earth. He and Harriet had had none of their own.

narrative_blocks.header: A year in the tenements turned him
narrative_blocks.body: A year on the New York tenement-house system sent him to Albany for emigrant statistics, and then to the Astor Library for a year on the working classes of Ireland and England.

narrative_blocks.header: He died writing an address he never gave
narrative_blocks.body: He was at work on an address to the women of the Relief Corps when the apoplexy took him, and never delivered it. He had written that he would get to the Pittsburgh meeting if he had to walk.

people.research_notes: Son of John Theodoric Balch and Elizabeth Jones Thacher; brought up in New York City, appointed to West Point from the Western Reserve district while his father lived at Akron. Fitted himself for the Academy in two years of his own study. Commanded the Charleston Arsenal after the war and briefly ran the Remington Plow Company. At the Erie Railway he found real estate the company had forgotten it owned; for Mayor Hewitt in 1886 he reported on the repaving of Fifth Avenue and other contractor frauds. Publications: General Classification of Railway Rights, Realities and Personalities (1878); The Sewage Question in Saratoga (1885); Methods of Teaching Patriotism, and Teaching Patriotism in Our Public Schools (D. Van Nostrand, 1890), from an address to the teachers of the Children's Aid Society, 28 June 1889. Obituary and biographic sketch by his co-worker Wallace Foster in The National Tribune. No connection is established between the publisher D. Van Nostrand and the Van Nostrands of this tree. Foster's sketch adds the human frame: a bread-winner through long weary days who gave his NIGHTS to the plans and the books, and who in a few months had more encouragement from the women of the Relief Corps than in the eight years he had spent trying to reach the teachers of the land. In 1888 he wrote to every State Superintendent of Public Instruction and got back a list of some five thousand county, city and town school officers — then had to abandon the plan because he could not afford to write to them all. He lived just long enough to hear that sixty San Francisco schools had formally adopted the salute, which gave him great joy. His last letter: 'I propose, under God, to give all that remains to me in life, that I may in some degree repay the inestimable gift conferred upon me by being born in the 19th century, a citizen of this grand Republic.'

narrative_blocks.body: Cushman held several pastorates in Massachusetts and lived a while in and near Troy before taking the Trinitarian Congregational church at Castine in 1885. He kept it until he died in 1901, and his widow and daughter went to a farm at West Farmington.

bio.bio_blurb: Teacher; leader of the Rainbow band

narrative_blocks.header: A seminary in Philadelphia, and music
narrative_blocks.body: The youngest daughter of Rev. John Maltby, first pastor of the Hammond Street church at Bangor, she was schooled there and at a young ladies' seminary in Philadelphia, in letters and in music, and taught for a time before she married.

narrative_blocks.header: She ran a girls' mission band called Rainbow
narrative_blocks.body: Through her husband's sixteen years at the Trinitarian church in Castine she led a women's Bible study and prayer meeting, and a band of girls she called the Rainbow band.

narrative_blocks.header: Her daughter stayed thirty years to nurse her
narrative_blocks.body: After her husband died in 1901 the two of them took a farm at West Farmington, where Mary Floyd Cushman — a physician since 1892 who wanted the mission field — kept house with her. Henriette died there in April 1921, and her daughter sailed for Angola the next year.

institution_affiliations.notes: Served in Chilesso, Angola for 20 years. Established hospital staffed by indigenous Angolan people she trained.

notable.notable_blurb: Physician; twenty years a medical missionary in Angola

narrative_blocks.header: She waited thirty years to go
narrative_blocks.body: Cushman took her medical degree in 1892 meaning to be a medical missionary, and then had the care of an invalid mother for the next thirty years. Her mother died in April 1921. She sailed for Angola the following year, aged fifty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: Grass huts and five thousand patients a year
narrative_blocks.body: The hospital she was sent to at Chilesso in Portuguese West Africa was a set of grass huts taking about five thousand patients a year. She built it into a hospital and travelled out to the far cases herself.

narrative_blocks.header: She staffed it with people she trained herself
narrative_blocks.body: Her staff was drawn wholly from the Ovimbundu she had taught, and she pressed for better schooling for their children so they could run the hospital without her. One of the girls, Vikomo, was reading for medicine in Portugal by the time she left.

narrative_blocks.header: The witch doctor inoculated before Jenner did
narrative_blocks.body: She wrote that they scarified the wrist, rubbed in a crust from a smallpox sore and bandaged it — inoculation that predated Jenner's cowpox and usually worked as well as vaccination. She opposed them anyway, for the witchcraft used when the skill failed.

narrative_blocks.header: Would you teach religion to your dog?
narrative_blocks.body: A South African Boer asked how she could think of doing missionary work among the natives — 'would you teach religion to your dog?' She put the exchange in her book, and noted that even in Angola business competition interfered with fairness to the black man.

narrative_blocks.header: Missionary Doctor, more about them than her
narrative_blocks.body: Harper published Missionary Doctor: The Story of Twenty Years in Africa in 1944. It is far more a record of the Ovimbundu than an account of herself, and she set their customs down without calling them funny or despicable.

people.research_notes: Wikipedia; Farmington obituary, September 1965; New York Times review by Calder Willingham, 26 November 1944. BIRTHPLACE UNRESOLVED: Wikipedia says Royalston, Massachusetts; FamilySearch 9VN8-NT8 says Boston; her obituary calls her a native of Farmington, Maine. Left blank rather than guessed. Resident of Castine 1885-1901 while her father held the pulpit; in general practice at Farmington when appointed the first woman on the Maine State Medical Board. Returned to the United States in 1953 at eighty-three and died in a Laconia nursing home on a Saturday, survived by her sister Margaret J. Haven. The Maine Medical Society founded the Mary Floyd Cushman Award in 2003; the Trinitarian Congregational Parish of Castine keeps the Dr. Mary Cushman Circle. Her name descends from her great-grandmother Mary Floyd Tallmadge, daughter of the signer William Floyd and wife of Benjamin Tallmadge.

parents.father_research_notes: John Delafield (1748-1824), English-American merchant and diplomat

notable.notable_blurb: Phenix Bank president and pioneer scientific farmer

narrative_blocks.header: He cut his cables and ran from Corunna
narrative_blocks.body: In January 1808 the French opened fire on the shipping at Corunna and he was ordered out instantly. He cut the cables and went to sea short of provisions, carrying a priest and a Spanish family who had come aboard in the night.

narrative_blocks.header: A prisoner of war allowed fifteen miles
narrative_blocks.body: Held in England as an American prisoner in 1812, he was given fifteen miles around Uxbridge and the City of London. The limit was lifted later so that he could study English farming, and he carried that home with him.

narrative_blocks.header: Irving called him a right worthy fellow
narrative_blocks.body: His London house was almost a home to Washington Irving, who wrote in 1820 that anyone who did not know Delafield ought to, for he is a right worthy fellow. Irving's tale The Wife came out of that friendship.

narrative_blocks.header: He resigned the bank to quiet its enemies
narrative_blocks.body: Elected cashier of the Phenix Bank in 1820 and its president in February 1838, he resigned that April rather than let the dry-goods merchants carry their quarrel against him to the legislature.

narrative_blocks.header: The Philharmonic met in his own house
narrative_blocks.body: He was first president and one of the most active founders of the New York Philharmonic Society, which met at his house for several years. He proposed the Musical Fund Society besides.

narrative_blocks.header: He revived the Historical Society himself
narrative_blocks.body: In 1828 he brought the New-York Historical Society back to life chiefly at his own expense and prepared its first catalogue with his children's help. In 1831 he pressed for a New York University free of sectarian control.

narrative_blocks.header: The agricultural college was chartered at his farm
narrative_blocks.body: Oaklands, his Geneva farm, filled twelve pages of the New York State Agricultural Society's Transactions for 1847. He was the society's first president from 1850, and the legislature sited its college at the farm in 1853.

narrative_blocks.header: She edited the Journal beside him
narrative_blocks.body: Through the last part of her husband's life she was of great assistance to him in editing the American Journal of Science — the quarterly her father had founded in 1818 and handed on.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote the street she lived on
narrative_blocks.body: Hillhouse Avenue from 1809 to 1900 came out under her name, Henrietta Silliman Dana. She died at No. 24, in the house her husband had built, in her eighty-fourth year.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son scrapbooked New Haven whole
narrative_blocks.body: Arnold Guyot Dana worked from a billiard table in his Livingston Street basement and filled about a hundred and fifty volumes he called New Haven Old and New — seven on Chapel Street alone, nine on the schools, more on the churches and railroads. He was still at it when he died in 1947.

narrative_blocks.header: She married into her father's own chair
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin Silliman held the first chair of science at Yale. In June 1844 she married James Dwight Dana, who succeeded to it, and their son Edward held the physics chair and the mineral collection after them.

narrative_blocks.header: The last of the elder Silliman's family
narrative_blocks.body: She was his third daughter, and when she died in 1907 she was the last member of his household left alive. Six children were born to her; two died in childhood.

narrative_blocks.header: That boy fell a hundred feet and lived
narrative_blocks.body: Arnold went off the head of the Sleeping Giant as a child, down the basalt to a spot later marked with a plaque. He grew up to help save the same ridge from the quarrymen and see it made a state park.

narrative_blocks.header: His 1855 report launched the oil industry
narrative_blocks.body: In 1855 the Yale chemist analyzed crude rock oil from Venango County, Pennsylvania, using fractional distillation to show it could yield kerosene and other valuable illuminants. His report convinced investors to drill at Titusville, and is credited with launching the American petroleum industry.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped found Yale's Sheffield Scientific School
narrative_blocks.body: Silliman taught chemistry and natural science at Yale and was among the founders of its scientific school, later the Sheffield Scientific School. He long co-edited the American Journal of Science, the journal his father had established.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried his father's scientific name forward
narrative_blocks.body: Son of the famous Yale professor Benjamin Silliman, he extended the family's scientific standing into a second generation. Mathew Brady's studio photographed him, and the portrait survives in the National Portrait Gallery.

narrative_blocks.header: He filed Virginia's first emancipation bill
narrative_blocks.body: In 1782 Minor introduced a bill in the Virginia legislature for the gradual emancipation of the enslaved, the first such measure in the state. He raised the cause more than once, well ahead of his planter contemporaries.

narrative_blocks.header: He became a general in 1812
narrative_blocks.body: Trained in law under George Wythe at William and Mary, Minor served as commonwealth's attorney at Fredericksburg and sat in the House of Delegates. He was commissioned a brigadier general during the War of 1812.

narrative_blocks.header: He died mid-speech before the Electoral College
narrative_blocks.body: Minor was struck down by apoplexy in 1816 while addressing the Electoral College at Richmond. His daughter Mary Berkeley Minor Blackford carried his antislavery convictions into the next generation.

narrative_blocks.header: His son healed sailors; his daughter fought slavery
narrative_blocks.body: The general's crusade against slavery carried into his children. His daughter Mary Berkeley Minor Blackford founded Fredericksburg's anti-slavery auxiliary at twenty-six and corresponded with the colonization society and Liberian missions; his son Lewis Willis served as a decorated Navy fleet surgeon, and another son, James Monroe, married into the Pierreponts.

notable.notable_blurb: Los Alamos mathematician

narrative_blocks.header: She worked missile paths by hand, Los Alamos
narrative_blocks.body: With a master's in mathematics from Michigan, Jane went out to Los Alamos in the 1950s and computed missile trajectories the hard way, by hand, before the machines took the work over.

narrative_blocks.header: She divided by hand; he built the machines
narrative_blocks.body: In 1956 Jane married James Robertson of the University of Illinois, who designed how the ORDVAC and ILLIAC computers multiply and divide. His name is on the SRT division method, the way a great many computers came to divide.

narrative_blocks.header: Long division in Roman numerals
narrative_blocks.body: Jane was sole author of a journal article working out long division entirely in Roman numerals, the kind of problem that amused a woman who had computed missile trajectories by hand.

narrative_blocks.header: Piano for the nursing homes
narrative_blocks.body: Jane played piano for shows and groups all her life, including volunteer performances in nursing homes and schools, and put her mathematics to work teaching, keeping accounts and preparing tax returns for free.

narrative_blocks.header: Precinct chair, and belly dancing
narrative_blocks.body: Jane chaired her precinct on voting days, took classes from water aerobics to belly dancing, and kept up a steady stream of letters and news clippings to the people she loved.

notable.notable_blurb: Pastor at Guilford; trustee of Yale College

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-three years in Guilford's pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: Ordained at Guilford in 1695, aged twenty-four, he held that pulpit for thirty-three unbroken years until his death. His eldest son was ordained into it on 26 March 1729, nine months after him.

narrative_blocks.header: A Yale trustee until the day he died
narrative_blocks.body: He was chosen a trustee of the college on 6 September 1710, among the first named after the ten founders. The record of his service ends on 1 June 1728 — the day he died.

narrative_blocks.header: Four Yale trustees came to Guilford that day
narrative_blocks.body: John Hart was ordained over the East Guilford church on 25 November 1706, and four of the five ministers at the service sat on the college's board — Buckingham, Pierpont and the two Russells. Hart was the college's first graduate. Ruggles joined that board four years later.

narrative_blocks.header: He left the Roxbury his family built
narrative_blocks.body: His grandfather Thomas came out of Sudbury in Suffolk and settled at Roxbury; his father Captain Samuel kept the tavern there, led the town military company, and was given custody of Joseph Dudley when Andros fell. Thomas took the Guilford pulpit in 1695 and did not go back.

narrative_blocks.header: One word on the family arms: Struggle
narrative_blocks.body: The Ruggles were long seated at Sudbury in Suffolk, and the arms they brought over carry a single word for a motto — Struggle. Two brothers carried the name to Roxbury: John in 1635, and Thomas ten years behind him.

narrative_blocks.header: He was widowed at thirty-five with five children
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah Fiske died at Guilford on 27 July 1706, thirty-one years old, in the same year their youngest was born. He kept the pulpit and did not marry again for two years.

narrative_blocks.header: He married and died on the same date
narrative_blocks.body: His second marriage, to Mary Hubbard of Boston, was on 1 June 1708. He died at Guilford on 1 June 1728, twenty years to the day.

longer rests on the disputed year. PARENTS: Capt. Samuel Ruggles of Roxbury — innkeeper, selectman, captain of the Roxbury military
company, custodian of Joseph Dudley while Andros and his associates were held, d. 15 Aug 1692
aged 63 — and Anna Bright of Watertown, his second wife, d. 5 Sept 1711 aged 67. Neither built. NOT USED, no entry to hang it on: his sister Anna Ruggles married William Heath of Roxbury, and
their grandson was Major-General William Heath of Washington's army. The 1712 settlement of his
father's estate names him "Thomas Ruggles of Guilford Conn. clerk & Mary his wife", which
independently confirms the second marriage. The Ruggles arms carry a one-word motto: Struggle. REFINED the same day: NB3's header ran to 52 characters and wrapped, and its second sentence
repeated the Yale tenure that NB4 now carries properly; replaced with the succession — his son
ordained into the same pulpit 26 March 1729. NB1 lost the editorial closer "colonial Connecticut's
tight clerical network on display". notable_blurb moved from "Fellow of Yale College 1710-1728;
Pastor First Church" to plain role nouns, and from Fellow to trustee, which is what the Yale roll
calls the office. REORDERED AND REFRAMED 10 Aug 2026 on Sam's critique — three separate faults. ORDER: two blocks had been appended without re-reading the card, leaving family material split
across NB2 and NB5 with career and Yale between them. Sam's rule: family blocks belong together
and go LAST, after career, achievement and personality. Now identity (the pulpit), distinction
(the trusteeship), the moment (the ordination), then the two family blocks together. NB1 HAD NO REASON IN IT — "Helped ordain John Hart with four other ministers", a fragment header
over a list of names. Sam: "Bill helped Bob sing at church... thanks for the facts, who cares."
The reason is in the Yale trustee roll he supplied: Thomas Buckingham, James Pierpont and Noadiah
Russell were three of the TEN FOUNDING TRUSTEES of the Collegiate School (all 1701 Oct 16);
Samuel Russell was a successor trustee from 1701 Nov 11; and John Hart, the man being ordained,
was the college's first graduate and its tutor. Ruggles joined that board 6 Sept 1710. Not five
random ministers — most of Yale's governing board, in Guilford, ordaining Yale's first alumnus. CCs: all four ordination labels read "East Guilford ordination, November 25, 1706" on BOTH ends —
a bare date, no relationship, no predicate. Rewritten to carry the trusteeship. Rev. Noadiah
Russell (X3657) was at that service and in the tree but unconnected; now linked both directions.
Samuel Russell of Branford is not in the tree. The Annie Bartlett Ruggles CC was already sound. FAMILY BROUGHT ONTO THE CARD 10 Aug 2026. Sam's point, and it was right: this material had been
filed in research_notes where no reader ever sees it — "you didn't mention his father Samuel when
I'm trying to literally have Thomas Ruggles Pynchon read my project." Two blocks now carry it, at
the end where family belongs. The full descent, for whoever needs more: Thomas Ruggles (1) of Sudbury, Suffolk, married Mary
Curtis of the parish of Nazing, Essex, 9 Nov 1620 — she was a sister of the William Curtis who
was among the first settlers of Roxbury — and died at Roxbury 16 Nov 1644/45; his widow later
married a Root and died 14 Feb 1674/75 aged eighty-six. His brother John came over in 1635, ten
years ahead of him. Their son Capt. Samuel Ruggles was born at Nasing in 1629 and came to Roxbury
in 1637 aged eight with his parents and his sister Sarah; the brother John had sailed two years
earlier in the Hopewell with Philip Elliot. Samuel kept a tavern, served fourteen years as
selectman and assessor, sat in the general court through the four years after 1689, captained the
Roxbury company, and was chosen custodian of Joseph Dudley while Andros and his associates were
held. He died 15 Aug 1692 aged 63. Wives: Hannah Fowle of Charlestown (m. 10 Jan 1654/5, d. 24
Oct 1669, eight children) and Anna Bright of Watertown (m. 26 May 1670, d. 5 Sept 1711 aged 67,
six children, of whom Thomas was the eldest). TAGS REMAPPED 10 Aug 2026. This entry carried two tags outside canonical_tags.txt, which
validate.py warns on: "yale_fellow" and "congregationalist". Neither is in the approved vocabulary
— the Yale handles are yale_connection / yale_graduate / yale_president / yale_founder /
yale_trustee / skull_and_bones, and the denominational handles are minister / clergy / deacon /
missionary / episcopal / shaker / freemason / catholic / universalist. Remapped rather than
dropped: yale_fellow -> yale_trustee (which is what the Yale roll calls the office he held from
6 Sept 1710), congregationalist -> minister + clergy. harvard_graduate added, since the Ruggles
genealogy has him a Harvard man. Was ['yale_fellow', 'congregationalist']; now ['minister', 'clergy', 'harvard_graduate', 'yale_trustee']. ARMS ADDED AS THE CARD IMAGE 10 Aug 2026. The file Sam supplied is titled for Nathaniel Ruggles
and shows the family coat rather than a portrait — appropriate here, since NB5 on this card is
about the arms and the motto. ON THE MOTTO, Sam's question — did they make the name up to fit it? Almost certainly the other
way round. "Struggle" against "Ruggles" is a CANTING motto, a heraldic pun on the surname, and the
convention is that the name comes first and the motto is built to echo it. The card asserts only
what the source says: the arms carry a single word for a motto. The canting reading is not
claimed on the card for want of a heraldic authority. NATHANIEL RUGGLES THE CONGRESSMAN (1761-1819) IS NOT IN THIS TREE, and should not be confused
with two men who are. He was born at Roxbury 11 Nov 1761, Harvard 1781, a lawyer there, judge of
the general sessions 1807, chief justice of Massachusetts 1808, Federalist member of the
Thirteenth through Fifteenth Congresses 1813-19, and died at Roxbury 19 Dec 1819. Being a Roxbury
Ruggles he is very likely a collateral descendant of Capt. Samuel Ruggles, this entry's father,
but the line is not traced here and he sits far outside the Jalapeno Rule. The two Nathaniels who
ARE in the tree: X00282 Dr. Nathaniel Ruggles of Guilford, 1713-1794, this entry's son by Mary
Hubbard; and H00726 Nathaniel Ruggles Jr., 1737-1793, that doctor's own son. Neither is the
congressman.

notable.notable_blurb: The Learned Blacksmith; founder of the peace movement

narrative_blocks.header: Founded the international peace movement
narrative_blocks.body: He launched the League of Universal Brotherhood in 1846 and convened the first International Peace Congress in Brussels two years later. Victor Hugo presided over the Paris congress that followed.

narrative_blocks.header: Taught himself thirty languages while shoeing horses
narrative_blocks.body: He worked at a New Britain forge from his teens, studying languages from Latin and Greek to Hebrew and Sanskrit. Massachusetts governor Edward Everett dubbed him 'the Learned Blacksmith,' a title Burritt disliked.

narrative_blocks.header: Lincoln appointed him U.S. Consul to Birmingham
narrative_blocks.body: He served the British industrial city from 1864 to 1868. He used the post to advocate transatlantic peace negotiations during and after the Civil War.

narrative_blocks.header: Read Emma Willard's school reform plan aloud
narrative_blocks.body: On March 18, 1840 his cousin's reform proposal was presented at Kensington Congregational Church through him, because women could not speak publicly. The crowd listened 'with deep and thrilling interest.'

narrative_blocks.header: Hinsdale family connects him to the Hooker tree
narrative_blocks.body: His grandfather Elijah Hinsdale was the brother of Lydia Hinsdale, who married into the Hart-Hooker line. Burritt was first cousin once removed of Emma Willard and Almira Hart Phelps.

John Hinsdale (X00039) is in the tree. The direct Hooker descent likely runs through Huldah Hart (H00280) but the chain is untraced. ORBIT NOTABLE: connected to the tree through the Hinsdale family.
