notable.notable_blurb: Busy country physician of Kensington, Connecticut

people.research_notes: b. Apr 20, 1767 East Haddam CT; d. Jan 22, 1807 Kensington CT age 40. Prominent physician in Kensington parish, Berlin CT. 19-year practice; 'few physicians in a country town ever performed more business in a given time.' Estate inventoried at $14,000. Made calls on horseback except in winter. Built house at 381 Percival Ave (now LMK028) ca.1784/1789. Died suddenly Jan 22, 1807 'in the midst of his usefulness.' His death and that of daughter Harriet within a month of each other in 1807 profoundly affected 11-year-old son James Gates. Left estate to three minor sons. m. Jan 1790 Elizabeth Hart Percival (H00610). Father of James Gates Percival (X01936), Oswin Percival (X01937), Edwin Percival (X01938). (Ward, Life and Letters of James Gates Percival, 1866; Historic Buildings CT) [Migrated from death.notes]: Died suddenly 'in the midst of his usefulness.' Lived just west of the meeting-house in Kensington.

narrative_blocks.header: He rode to patients across Kensington parish
narrative_blocks.body: For nineteen years Dr. Percival kept one of the busiest country practices in central Connecticut, making his calls on horseback except in deep winter. A contemporary said few country physicians ever did more business in so short a time.

narrative_blocks.header: He died suddenly at forty in 1807
narrative_blocks.body: Percival died suddenly in January 1807, and his daughter Harriet within the same month. The double loss deeply marked his eleven-year-old son, the future poet James Gates Percival.

narrative_blocks.header: His mill ground grain, then made cement
narrative_blocks.body: Besides his practice he owned half a grist and carding mill on the stream west of the Kensington church, a mill that also pressed linseed oil. After his sudden death his partner's successor, Roswell Moore, bought it whole — and the works that grew there, known as Moore's Mills, went on to make one of Connecticut's early hydraulic cements.

narrative_blocks.header: His memory shaped his brother’s biography
narrative_blocks.body: When Julius Ward wrote the 1866 life of the poet James Gates Percival, he leaned on Oswin’s recollections — including that James had tried to overdose on opium in 1820. Oswin was supplying memories gathered fifty years after the fact.

narrative_blocks.header: He died in the New Haven hospital
narrative_blocks.body: He outlived both his brothers — James by fifteen years — and died about 1871 in the New Haven hospital. A painter who knew all three of them said they never seemed to belong to this world.

narrative_blocks.header: His cousin had him declared incompetent
narrative_blocks.body: Hopeless with money, he lived near poverty despite his inheritance, until his cousin Benjamin Hart at last had him declared incompetent and took over his affairs. Like both his brothers, he never married.

narrative_blocks.header: Some thought it was about the property
narrative_blocks.body: A few in Kensington held that James was not in earnest at all in 1820, and that the talk of killing himself was got up to frighten him into parting with some of the property their father had left the three of them.

narrative_blocks.header: He painted the Harts of Kensington
narrative_blocks.body: A portrait painter of the Hart family of Kensington, Edwin painted his uncle Rev. Seth Hart and his aunt Elizabeth around 1828 and 1829.

narrative_blocks.header: His portrait of his brother still survives
narrative_blocks.body: His best-known work is the portrait of his brother, the poet James Gates Percival — the likeness by which the poet is still remembered, now held at Yale. Edwin worked as a portrait painter, chiefly among his own Connecticut kin.

narrative_blocks.header: He starved himself to death in Troy
narrative_blocks.body: Like his brothers, he was a man of painfully fine nerves who, one contemporary said, never seemed to belong to this world. He is believed to have starved himself to death at Troy, New York, in 1848.

narrative_blocks.header: He was sent with James at thirteen
narrative_blocks.body: He was thirteen when their father died and he and James were sent to their uncle Seth Hart at Hempstead on Long Island. Twenty years on he painted that uncle; the portrait of Seth Hart is his work, as is the one of his brother.

narrative_blocks.header: He braved a mob after robbing a grave
narrative_blocks.body: An Albany physician who wrote on the era's great epidemics — bilious fever, yellow fever, and cholera — he once outraged the town by exhuming a body for dissection, and faced down the furious crowd almost at the risk of his life. He also set up, less successfully, as a curer of stammering.

narrative_blocks.header: His marriage to Emma Willard lasted nine months
narrative_blocks.body: In 1838 he married the famous educator Emma Willard in the chapel of her Troy seminary — but the union collapsed within nine months, and she won a legislative divorce in 1843. A colleague's memorial judged him a man of ability whose example held 'nothing to admire, but everything to avoid.'

narrative_blocks.header: He ended his days in Nova Scotia
narrative_blocks.body: After the failed marriage he drifted north, settling at last in Parrsboro, Nova Scotia, where he died in 1848. He had lost a promising son, Winfield Scott, at eighteen some years before.

narrative_blocks.header: First husband abandoned the family, then vanished
narrative_blocks.body: Amanda's first husband Orlando Wilder — biological father of her two children Marion Eliza (born 1836) and Henry Harrison (born 1840) — last appeared in the 1840 Addison County Vermont census and then disappeared from all records. He had either abandoned the family or moved to Minnesota alone, leaving Amanda widow-like at age thirty with two young children. The disappearance was permanent.

narrative_blocks.header: Remarried Judge Joseph Hayward with three stepchildren
narrative_blocks.body: Between 1840 and 1850 Amanda remarried — to Judge Joseph Hayward of Vermont (1796-1865). Hayward already had three children from his prior marriage (Asaph, Josephine, and Benjamin); they were Amanda's stepchildren, not her own biological children. The blended Wilder-Hayward household took shape across the 1840s, with Amanda raising her two Wilder children alongside her three Hayward stepchildren.

narrative_blocks.header: Daughter Marion married into Drake family
narrative_blocks.body: Amanda's daughter Marion Eliza Wilder (born 1836) eventually married Drake — establishing the Wilder-Drake line that descended from the Hooker connection through Amanda's mother Lucinda Murray. Amanda's son Henry Harrison Wilder served as a private in the Civil War.

narrative_blocks.header: Born Addison County VT 1810, died Vermont 1887
narrative_blocks.body: Amanda Murray was born April 30, 1810 in Addison County Vermont and died December 9, 1887 in Vermont at age seventy-seven. Her two marriages with their distinct biological-vs-step parentage have been cross-checked against source records to establish the marriage order and parentage definitively.

military_service.notes: Enlisted Sept 19, 1861 in Weybridge VT as a corporal in Company F, 5th Vermont Volunteer Infantry. Wrote home about Camp Holbrook (St. Albans VT) and Camp Griffin (Virginia) where the regiment was hit hard by disease. Described the Peninsula Campaign in spring 1862, including the battles of Lee's Mill and Williamsburg. Killed in action at Battle of Savage's Station (Henrico County VA) on Jun 29, 1862, age ~22. Best friend Sergeant Merrill Samson of Weybridge wrote a letter to Henry's family describing his death.

narrative_blocks.header: Killed at Savage's Station age 22
narrative_blocks.body: Cpl. Henry Harrison Wilder of Weybridge VT enlisted in the 5th Vermont Volunteer Infantry, Company F, on Sept 19, 1861 at age 21. He survived the disease-ridden winter at Camp Griffin VA, then marched through the Peninsula Campaign — Lee's Mill and Williamsburg. On June 29, 1862, during the Seven Days Battles, his regiment was thrown into the Battle of Savage's Station in Henrico County VA.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother saved his Civil War letters
narrative_blocks.body: Henry Harrison Wilder's mother Amanda Murray Hayward saved his correspondence from the war along with Sgt. Merrill Samson's account of her son's death and the letters of condolence the family received. The collection — four folders spanning 1861-1862 — is now at the University of Vermont Special Collections (Henry Harrison Wilder Papers). Amanda is the principal correspondent in the archive.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a woman who also descended
narrative_blocks.body: Franklin Hooker married Marion Eliza Wilder Drake — and she, like him, was a descendant of Rev. Thomas Hooker of Hartford, Connecticut, making their 1853 marriage a convergence of two separate branches of the Hooker family tree across seven generations. Franklin descended through Thomas Hooker's son Samuel, while Marion descended through a different branch; the two lines had diverged in the 17th century and rejoined in Cornwall, Vermont, in 1853.

people.research_notes:
b. Apr 7, 1787 (bapt. May 20, 1787) New Britain CT; d. Mar 4, 1858 New Britain CT. Son of Ensign Levi Andrews and Chloe Welles of Newington CT. Yale B.A. 1810; practiced law New Britain 1812-22; professor ancient languages Univ. of North Carolina 1822-1828; taught New Haven and Boston. State legislator (Whig) 1851; magistrate; judge of probate. Yale LL.D. 1848 for Latin scholarship. Latin-English Lexicon (1850) → Harper's Latin Dictionary (1907). Published 'Slavery and the Domestic Slave Trade in the United States' (1836) — criticized by The Liberator as pro-slavery apologia. Co-authored Latin Grammar with Yale classmate Solomon Stoddard (1836). m. Dec 19, 1810 Lucy Hooker Cowles (H00699). is_easter_egg=True. (Wikipedia; Cowles Genealogy #644; Andrews Hist. First Church New Britain) [Migrated from death.notes]: Died 'in the midst of his literary labors.' Wikipedia gives Mar 4 (not Mar 24 as Cowles Genealogy).
[Stage 6Y-264 NB#1 header trim]: 'His Latin dictionary became Harper's Latin Dictionary — still in use today' → 'His Latin dictionary became Harper's Latin Dictionary'.
[Stage 6Y-264 NB#1 body trim]: original body had 4 sentences, trimmed to first 3. Original body preserved here for reference: 'Prof. Ethan Allen Andrews published a major Latin-English lexicon in 1850, based on Wilhelm Freund's German translation of Forcellini's 1771 dictionary. It went through many revisions and became known as Harper's Latin Dictionary (1907) — still a standard reference. He also published the first major American anti-slavery study, 'Slavery and the Domestic Slave Trade in the United States' (1836), which The Liberator nonetheless condemned as insufficiently radical. Yale conferred his LL.D. in 1848.'

narrative_blocks.header: His Latin dictionary became Harper's Latin Dictionary
narrative_blocks.body: Andrews published a Latin-English lexicon in 1850 that was revised into Harper's Latin Dictionary, a standard reference well into the twentieth century. Yale awarded him a doctorate in 1848 for his classical scholarship.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught ancient languages across the country
narrative_blocks.body: A Yale graduate of 1810, Andrews practiced law before turning to teaching, holding a professorship of ancient languages at the University of North Carolina and later running schools in New Haven and Boston. He co-wrote a widely used Latin grammar.

narrative_blocks.header: He sat as legislator, magistrate, and judge
narrative_blocks.body: Back in New Britain, Andrews served as a Whig state legislator, a magistrate, and a judge of probate. He kept at his books to the end, dying in 1858 in the midst of his literary labors.

narrative_blocks.header: His book on slavery drew abolitionist fire
narrative_blocks.body: In 1836 Andrews published a study of slavery and the domestic slave trade that The Liberator attacked as a pro-slavery apologia. The work set the scholar awkwardly against the rising antislavery tide of his native Connecticut.

narrative_blocks.header: He built schools to educate young women
narrative_blocks.body: Beyond his Latin texts he was a pioneer of women's education, founding the New Haven Young Ladies' Institute in 1829 and running the Mount Vernon Female Seminary in Boston. He edited a religious family magazine in the same years.

narrative_blocks.header: His family helped found colonial Farmington
narrative_blocks.body: The Andrews line descended from John Andrews, one of the original settlers of Farmington, Connecticut, among the founding families of that old Hooker-country town. The Latin scholar carried that deep colonial ancestry.

narrative_blocks.header: He printed the Charter Oak against slavery
narrative_blocks.body: From 1838 he edited and printed the Charter Oak at Hartford, an anti-slavery paper. He gave it up in 1843 and went home to Farmington, to the farm and to one town office after another.

narrative_blocks.header: Probate judge, notary, bank treasurer
narrative_blocks.body: Farmington gave him justice of the peace, notary public, school visitor, commissioner of deeds and of the Supreme Court, judge of probate, the Legislature, and the treasurership of its savings bank.

narrative_blocks.header: He set type at seventeen in Vermont
narrative_blocks.body: He went to learn printing at a book-publishing house at Windsor in Vermont, and by 1837 was a journeyman printer in Boston. He was back in Connecticut inside a year.

narrative_blocks.header: Her letters, a rare woman's voice on slavery
narrative_blocks.body: Between 1833 and 1846 she wrote more than ninety letters, now at the Connecticut Historical Society, setting down a young woman's first-person view of abolition — a perspective almost nothing else from the period preserves. She wrote most of them to her brother Samuel, who edited an anti-slavery paper.

narrative_blocks.header: She met the Amistad Africans and was changed
narrative_blocks.body: When the freed Mende stayed in Farmington in 1841, she befriended them, called them beautiful and elegant, and listened to the story of their capture and their revolt. She wrote that reading and talking about slavery taught her nothing next to seeing its victims face to face.

narrative_blocks.header: Married the schoolmaster, kept the cause
narrative_blocks.body: In 1843 she married Rev. Joseph Hull, a Yale man who preached and then ran a large boys' school. She had grown up in an abolitionist household at 27 Main Street and carried its convictions into her own.

career.notes: Documented Farmington abolitionist (per NPS National Historic Landmark source). Worked alongside her husband Austin F. Williams in hosting the Amistad Mende captives at the family carriagehouse during 1841 and in the family's broader Underground Railroad activity.

narrative_blocks.header: The Amistad Africans lived on her land
narrative_blocks.body: For eight months in 1841 the freed Mende stayed in the dormitory raised on the Williams property, where she and her husband saw to their keeping before they sailed home to Sierra Leone. The building became a carriage house — and a station on the Underground Railroad.

narrative_blocks.header: The trap door was in her house too
narrative_blocks.body: The Park Service records her, in her own right, as a known abolitionist. The fugitives hidden in the carriage-house cellar were sheltered by her household as much as her husband's — the work of a woman whose home was a link in the road north.

narrative_blocks.header: She buried her first two children
narrative_blocks.body: Her first two, Eliza and Horace, died in infancy in 1832 and 1835. Two daughters lived — Anna Maria and Catherine — and both grew up and married in the abolitionist Farmington she had made her home.

narrative_blocks.header: Made to confess the tea in the newspaper
narrative_blocks.body: On 23 March 1775 he and his wife Martha were made to confess in print, in the Connecticut Courant, to partaking of "that detestable and obnoxious vegetable called East India tea." All of Farmington could read the public confession over their morning paper.

narrative_blocks.header: Shamed for tea, he was feeding the siege
narrative_blocks.body: The confession made him look a loyalist, but he was nothing of the kind. In 1774 he sat on the Farmington committee gathering provisions for besieged Boston, and the next year he receipted supplies for the Rifle Battalion marching north to the camp.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave the family firm his own name
narrative_blocks.body: On Farmington's main street he kept a public inn and ran a family business under the name Solomon Cowles and Sons. The firm drew his boys — Isaac, Solomon, and Zenas — into the trade and carried the family name into the next generation.

narrative_blocks.header: He rose to captain of the Farmington trainband
narrative_blocks.body: Commissioned an ensign in the Farmington trainband in 1759, he was made captain in the colony's first regiment just two years later.

narrative_blocks.header: His sons traded care for their inheritance
narrative_blocks.body: When he set down his will in 1792, his three sons — Isaac, Solomon, and Zenas — agreed to support their aging parents in return for what they would inherit. It was an old New England bargain, tying the next generation to the last.

narrative_blocks.header: She founded a school in a rented room
narrative_blocks.body: In 1843 Sarah Porter returned to Farmington and rented an upstairs room in the stone store on Main Street to teach her first pupils. That school grew into Miss Porter's, one of the most enduring girls' schools in America.

narrative_blocks.header: Her pupils included Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis
narrative_blocks.body: Over the decades Miss Porter's School educated Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis, Gloria Vanderbilt, the architect Theodate Pope Riddle, and the physician Alice Hamilton. Porter herself, fluent in Greek, Latin, French, and German, set its demanding curriculum.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brother led Yale while she taught nearby
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah was a sister of Noah Porter, president of Yale, and a daughter of Farmington's long-serving minister. While he rose through the college, she built an institution of her own a few miles away.

narrative_blocks.header: Connecticut counts her among its great women
narrative_blocks.body: Porter ran her school for more than half a century until her death in 1900. She was later inducted into the Connecticut Women's Hall of Fame.

people.research_notes: Austin Franklin Williams (Feb 26, 1805 East Hartford CT - Dec 18, 1885 Farmington CT) — Connecticut abolitionist, Amistad Defense Committee member, Freedman's Bureau Director, and husband of Jennette Cowles Williams (H01837), a Hooker descendant. BUSINESS ARC: Began as a clerk in the drug store of Gen. George Cowles (HD0512, Hooker descendant) in Farmington, then was made partner; firm name became Cowles & Williams. Started a stone and lumber yard in Plainville CT. In 1836 organized Williams, Camp & Abbe wholesale dry-goods store in New York City. AMISTAD COMMITTEE 1839-1841: Williams was a key member of the Amistad Defense Committee. The Mende captives — 53 Sierra Leoneans who had rebelled aboard the slave-ship La Amistad in 1839 — were freed by the U.S. Supreme Court (argued by John Quincy Adams) on March 9, 1841. Williams corresponded throughout the case with Lewis Tappan of the Amistad Committee, the prominent New York abolitionist. Together with Samuel Deming and John Treadwell Norton (grandson of Gov. John Treadwell X02115), Williams arranged for the Africans to be sheltered in Farmington after their release. CARRIAGEHOUSE BARN-RAISING (May 4, 1841): The Mende men were initially housed on the second floor of Samuel Deming's store but the space was inadequate. In a communal barn-raising on May 4, 1841, Williams and his Farmington neighbors erected a temporary dormitory on his property that served as the primary home for the Mende men for the rest of their stay (until November 1841 when they sailed back to Sierra Leone). After their departure, Williams built his own house slightly southeast and converted the dormitory to a carriagehouse — both structures still stand today as National Historic Landmarks (designated 1998). UNDERGROUND RAILROAD: Oral tradition documents Williams as an Underground Railroad conductor; with neighbors Horace Cowles (H00697), Samuel Smith Cowles (HD2873), and others, Farmington became a major Underground Railroad stop sometimes called 'Grand Central Station' of the network. FREEDMAN'S BUREAU: After the Civil War, Williams was appointed Director of the Freedman's Bureau of New England and New York (formal title: Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands). He located housing and job opportunities for newly-freed African Americans across his region. FAMILY CONNECTION TO HOOKER LINE: Williams's marriage to Jennette Cowles (H01837) on September 11, 1828 made his abolitionist work one of the most consequential moral counterweights in the Hooker family arc. The Hooker-Talcott family had been deeply complicit in King Philip's War (John Talcott led the final 1676 campaign and sold surviving Wampanoag captives into Caribbean slavery) — by 1841, Hooker descendants and their spouses, the Williams-Cowles household and the Horace Cowles household and others, were leading the Amistad defense. See notable story 'farmington_amistad_circle'. BURIAL: Riverside Cemetery, Farmington — alongside his wife Jennette and their children. Tombstones to all family members at Farmington. Sources: Cowles Families in America #1617; NPS Austin F. Williams Carriagehouse and House; Connecticut Freedom Trail; Clio — Austin F. Williams Carriagehouse and House. narrative_blocks.header: He raised a house for the Amistad captives
narrative_blocks.body: When the Supreme Court freed the Mende in 1841, Williams gave them somewhere to live: in a single day that May, the town raised a dormitory on his land. After they sailed home he built his own house beside it and turned theirs into a carriage house — with a trap door to a windowless cellar where fugitives could hide.

narrative_blocks.header: A man he hid went back for others
narrative_blocks.body: Henry Davis, who had escaped slavery in Virginia, hid in the cellar of Williams's carriage house — and is believed to have gone back South, at the risk of his own freedom, to lead others out. He survived, returned to Farmington, and worked the Williams land for seventy years.

narrative_blocks.header: After the war he found freed people work
narrative_blocks.body: When the fighting ended he led the Freedmen's Bureau for New England and New York, finding housing and jobs for people just out of slavery. It was the same work he had done quietly for decades, now with a government behind it.

narrative_blocks.header: A dry-goods merchant who led the church choir
narrative_blocks.body: He built his money in a Farmington drugstore, then a New York wholesale dry-goods firm, then stone and lumber. For years he led the choir at the First Church of Christ, the Farmington congregation that was a center of the town's antislavery work.

narrative_blocks.body: The trustees of the University of Alabama elected him by unanimous vote in December 1841, to succeed the late Professor Pratt in English literature. He reached Tuscaloosa on 24 May 1842 and began his duties the next day.

narrative_blocks.body: He graduated from the University of North Carolina in 1823 and stayed on as a tutor there. He went from that to run an academy at La Grange, Alabama, and took the new college’s chair of mathematics and natural philosophy.

narrative_blocks.header: He rode with the Methodist connection
narrative_blocks.body: He spent a year or two in the travelling connection of the Methodist Episcopal Church, labouring at Nashville and about it. Then came the chair of languages at Randolph Macon College in Virginia.

narrative_blocks.header: Two years at Halle, a third in transit
narrative_blocks.body: He sailed for Europe at the beginning of 1836 and spent two years at the University of Halle perfecting his literature and science. A third year went in travel through France, Germany, Italy, Holland, Belgium and England.

narrative_blocks.header: He fell in his garden and never woke
narrative_blocks.body: On a Saturday morning in April 1845, in apparent health and superintending work in his garden, he fell insensible and was carried into the house. He died the next morning at forty, of what was supposed a ruptured blood vessel.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter was two when he died
narrative_blocks.body: He married Lucy Anne Andrews at Berlin, Connecticut, in August 1842, and their daughter Grace was born the next year. His widow afterwards married William McKinley of Georgia.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: The Gothic Revival house he built and named for his first wife, Patience Barrow.

narrative_blocks.header: He served in Georgia's legislature
narrative_blocks.body: An honor graduate of Franklin College, McKinley studied law under Judge Joseph Henry Lumpkin and won election to the Georgia legislature from Oglethorpe County in 1835. He returned to the legislature during Reconstruction at his friends' urging.

narrative_blocks.header: They called him the legislature's Chesterfield
narrative_blocks.body: McKinley was remembered for the courtesy of his manner and his wise, conservative counsel, earning the nickname the Chesterfield of the legislature. A devout Presbyterian elder, he was known as a man of broad sympathies.

narrative_blocks.header: He built Barrowville from brick he kilned himself
narrative_blocks.body: A devoted experimental farmer, McKinley built his Gothic-style house Barrowville in 1858 and 1859 from brick fired in his own yard, adapting a design from Andrew Jackson Downing's pattern book. He kept detailed records of his plantation's agriculture and weather.

narrative_blocks.header: Sherman's army camped around his house
narrative_blocks.body: During Sherman's March to the Sea, Barrowville was made the headquarters of a Federal encampment, with thousands of soldiers camped around it. The house narrowly escaped burning when the last troops marched away.

narrative_blocks.header: His son married into the Sapelo Spaldings
narrative_blocks.body: His son Archibald married a granddaughter of Thomas Spalding, whose plantation empire stood on Sapelo Island, and moved there in 1869 to farm it. He kept a journal of the seven years.

narrative_blocks.header: The longest entry eulogised a freedman
narrative_blocks.body: The entries run to weather, crops and the Darien timber trade, but also to shootings, trials, and Yankee soldiers sent to see convicts of both races treated alike. The longest is a eulogy for a freedman named Scott, whom Archibald had held as a slave.

narrative_blocks.header: A stuck drawer held it until 1969
narrative_blocks.body: Writing in 1876, Archibald left the journal to his wife, then his brother Guy, then any son a brother or sister might name for him. It surfaced in a jammed drawer in 1969, and Guy had indeed named a son for him.

narrative_blocks.header: Invalid fourteen years, one side paralyzed
narrative_blocks.body: Isaac Newton spent the last fourteen years of his life as an invalid, with one side paralyzed and 'almost helpless.' The condition is consistent with either a stroke around 1798 or progressive degenerative disease in his fifties. He died in poverty in 1812 at Goshen Connecticut at age sixty-seven, his wife Rebecca Minott saving only fifty acres at his death — and even those were sold by the town selectmen in 1816-1817 for ten dollars an acre.

narrative_blocks.header: Inherited father's property, lost it, died poor
narrative_blocks.body: Isaac came into possession of all his father Samuel Newton's property and lost it before his death — a complete inheritance-to-poverty reversal in a single lifetime. He fathered ten children with Rebecca Minott (married Jan 10, 1769) before his fourteen-year invalidism set in. The two-Isaac-Newton family network in central Connecticut — Isaac of Woodbridge born 1744 and Isaac of Durham born 1740, both Hooker descendants through Samuel and Mary Hooker Newton — were almost certainly known to each other.

narrative_blocks.body: Isaac Newton was born September 2, 1744 in Woodbridge Connecticut and was baptized the same day at the Parish of Amity. He descended from Rev. b. Oct 16, 1795 Goshen CT; d. Nov 6, 1885 Canfield, Mahoning County OH age 90. Son of Isaac Newton (HD2926) and Rebecca Minot Newton (X01995). Moved to Portage County OH 1814; studied law with Darius Lyman and John Sloane; admitted to bar 1823; practiced Canfield. Ohio Senate 1842-1851. Presiding judge court of common pleas 1844-1851. U.S. Rep. 32nd Congress (Whig) 1851-1853. Unsuccessful reelection bid 1852. Pres. Ashtabula & New Lisbon Railroad 1856-1859. Ohio Senate again 1862-1864. Resumed law and cattle farming. Presbyterian. 20-yr partnership with Elisha Whittlesey. m. May 1826 Mary Sophia Church (X01996). Died of cold caught returning from California trip. Buried Canfield Village Cemetery. 6th gen from Thomas Hooker. (Wikipedia; Bioguide Congress; Newton-Oviatt Family History 1875)
CC NOTE [X01997]: The firm Whittlesey & Newton, Canfield OH (1821-1841) partnered Eben Newton with Elisha Whittlesey for twenty years — the period during which Newton served in the Ohio Senate and as presiding judge, and Whittlesey served in Congress and as U.S. Treasury Comptroller. Whittlesey is NOT a Hooker descendant but is one of the most significant non-family figures in the Newton orbit. [Migrated from death.notes]: Made a trip to California, returned with a cold, died within a month.

narrative_blocks.header: One cited case won him Whittlesey's partnership
narrative_blocks.body: Eben was reading law in Jonathan Sloan's Ravenna office when Sloan and Elisha Whittlesey sat planning a suit. Almost a stranger to Whittlesey, Eben named the volume and page of Durnford and East holding a case in point; they won, and Whittlesey wrote offering him an equal partnership.

narrative_blocks.header: From the common pleas bench to Congress
narrative_blocks.body: A state senator from 1842, Eben was chosen presiding judge of the court of common pleas in 1844 and sat until 1851, when the Whigs sent him to Congress. He lost re-election in 1852 and came home to his practice, a railroad presidency and beef cattle on his Canfield farms.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty lawyers came out of his Canfield office
narrative_blocks.body: While Whittlesey sat in Congress, Eben carried the firm of Whittlesey & Newton across the whole Western Reserve. More than thirty young men read law in their Canfield office and went to the bar, among them Joshua R. Giddings, Edward Wade and Ralph P. Buckland.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty miles to Hudson in a single day
narrative_blocks.body: In 1814, at eighteen, Eben rode west with a man hauling a load of axes and reached Buffalo just after the British had burned it. A leaky boat got them to Conneaut, and Eben walked the fifty miles to Hudson in one day, arriving almost penniless.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother did not recognize him
narrative_blocks.body: Eben had not heard from his mother, Rebecca Minot Newton, for five years when he went back to Connecticut and found her at Woodbury with her half sister. She did not know him. He bought a cheap wagon and horse, covered the wagon himself, and drove her and her goods to Ohio.

narrative_blocks.header: His eightieth birthday fell in Milan
narrative_blocks.body: Running errands as a Goshen farm boy, Eben resolved that he would one day cross the ocean. He first went in 1851, with Mary, to the World's Fair in London, then saw Rome, Venice and Naples, and spent his eightieth birthday in Milan.

narrative_blocks.header: At ninety, California and back
narrative_blocks.body: In 1885, at ninety, Eben and Mary made a round trip of some six thousand miles to California. He came home to Canfield with a cold and died within a month, on 6 November.

open_questions.question: Was Eben Newton's 20-year law partner Elisha Whittlesey a Hooker descendant through the Whittlesey-Newton line?
open_questions.notes: Elisha Whittlesey (b.1783 Southbury CT) studied law under Tapping Reeve at Litchfield CT, then partnered with Eben Newton for 20 years in Canfield OH. Roger Newton Whittlesey (HD0097, gen 5 Hooker descendant) lived in Litchfield County and had children born 1775-1799 in Southbury CT. Elisha's birth year fits the sequence. If Elisha is HD0097's son, Newton's closest professional collaborator for 20 years was also a gen 6 Hooker descendant — neither man knowing of the shared ancestry. Note: Tapping Reeve (X00614, Litchfield law school) is already in the Hooker project through his marriage to Sally Burr. Both Newton and Whittlesey passed through his school.
open_questions.resolution: Elisha Whittlesey is NOT a Hooker descendant. He descends from John Whittlesey of Saybrook through a different branch (Whittlesey book #310, son of John #123). He did NOT study under Tapping Reeve — he studied law in his brother Matthew Beale Whittlesey's office in Danbury CT. The firm Whittlesey & Newton, Canfield OH is confirmed 1821-1841. Elisha is documented as orbit_non_descendant (X01997).

narrative_blocks.header: A 180-mile ride through the frozen Black Swamp
narrative_blocks.body: In February 1813 Maj. Whittlesey rode 180 miles in three days and nights from the Maumee Rapids to Chillicothe with a battlefield message for the Ohio legislature, traveling at night through the flooded and frozen Black Swamp to avoid Indian scouts. The War of 1812 records carry a battle entry in his name.

narrative_blocks.header: Watch dog of the treasury under three presidents
narrative_blocks.body: Taylor appointed Whittlesey first Comptroller of the U.S. Treasury in 1849; Pierce refused his resignation; Lincoln re-appointed him in 1861. Across three presidents he was known as the 'watch dog of the treasury' for refusing to approve any irregular expenditure, holding the post until his death in January 1863.

narrative_blocks.header: Closed law books on Hull's August 1812 surrender
narrative_blocks.body: When news of Hull's August 1812 surrender of Detroit reached Canfield, Whittlesey closed his law books, dismissed his clients, and was on the road to Cleveland the second day after as aide to Maj.-Gen. Wadsworth. He served the war as Brigade Major in the Army of the Northwest under Gen. William Henry Harrison.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixteen years in Congress, friend of Henry Clay
narrative_blocks.body: Whittlesey served the U.S. Congress continuously from 1822 to 1838, sixteen years, chairing the Committee of Claims. He was a founder of the Whig Party and an ardent friend of Henry Clay.

narrative_blocks.header: An eclipse darkened the road from Pittsburgh
narrative_blocks.body: On the morning after leaving Pittsburgh in June 1806, the Whittleseys were surprised to find darkness spreading over the land — the total solar eclipse of June 16, 1806. They reached Canfield Mahoning County Ohio eleven days later, his first home as the Western Reserve's public prosecutor.

narrative_blocks.header: First public prosecutor of the Western Reserve
narrative_blocks.body: Within his first year in Canfield, Whittlesey was appointed public prosecutor for the entire Western Reserve in 1807 — a region that ran the northern third of Ohio. The work paid the new family's bills and built his practice into one of the strongest legal firms in the West.

people.research_notes: Hon. Elisha Whittlesey (Whittlesey Genealogy entry #310). Lineage: Elisha → John (Whittlesey #123, b.1741 Newington CT, d.1812) → Eliphalet → Eliphalet → John Whittlesey (immigrant, of Saybrook). b. Oct 19, 1783 Washington Conn.; family removed to Salisbury Conn. 1792 when he was 9. Boyhood on a farm; during school terms went to Danbury Conn. public schools, doing chores to pay board. Studied law in office of his brother Matthew Beale Whittlesey, Danbury. Admitted Fairfield County bar; opened New Milford Conn. office 1805. m. Jan 5, 1806 Polly Mygatt (X02787, b. Jan 8, 1787 Danbury, dau. of Comfort Starr Mygatt and Polly his wife), who d. Jun 11, 1855. MIGRATION: Left Danbury Jun 3, 1806 for the West in a Jersey wagon. Arrived Canfield Mahoning Co. Ohio Jun 27, 1806. Total solar eclipse June 16, 1806 darkened the day after they left Pittsburgh. Polly's father Comfort Starr Mygatt, refusing her request for $50 for a new bonnet, silverware, and linen, told her all she would need was 'two tin cups and as many pewter spoons' — but she got the $50 anyway. OHIO CAREER: First winter taught school. 1807 appointed public prosecutor for entire Western Reserve. 1808 large house built, occupied Oct 27, 1808. Captain in militia 1808, aide-de-camp to Maj.-Gen. Wadsworth 1810. WAR OF 1812: Closed law books on news of Hull's surrender, on road to Cleveland day-after as Wadsworth's aide. Brigade Major in Army of the Northwest under Gen. Harrison. Famous 180-mile ride Feb 1813 Maumee Rapids to Chillicothe (3 days/nights through frozen Black Swamp at night to avoid Indian scouts) carrying message from Army of the Northwest after Winchester's defeat to Ohio legislature in session. Contracted camp fever at Fort Meigs; nursed by Rev. Joseph Badger and Dr. Stonard. Returned home Mar 1813. POLITICS: Ohio State House 1820-1821. U.S. Congress 1822-1838 (16 years), chairman Committee of Claims, founder of Whig Party, friend of Henry Clay. Law partner Whittlesey & Newton, Canfield, 1821-1841. Auditor for Treasury for Post-office Dept (Harrison appt 1841, resigned Sept 1843). General Agent Washington Monumental Association 1847-1849. First Comptroller U.S. Treasury (Taylor appt May 1849; Pierce refused his resignation; Lincoln re-appointed 1861). Returned Canfield 1857. Held office until death Jan 7, 1863 Washington DC. Known as 'watch dog of the treasury.' CHILDREN per Whittlesey #310 (10, none in tree as Hooker descendants — Elisha is X-prefix easter_egg): #700 Royal Frederick Lewis (b. Oct 31, 1806; m1 Mary Smith, m2 Adelia H. Clewell); #702 John (b. Nov 29, 1808; m. Eliza Alice Selby); #703 Harriet (b. Oct 13, 1810; m. Dr. Lyman Collins); #704 Anna Maria (b. Nov 7, 1812; m. Rev. William O. Stratton); #705 George Beale (b. Feb 28, 1815; m. Lois Rebecca Bostwick); #706 Lucy (b. Dec 22, 1817; m. Stephen Buckland); #707 William Wallace (b. Apr 10, 1820; m. Jerusha R. Lockwood); #708 Elisha Mygatt (b. Feb 2, 1822; m. Elizabeth Ann Jennings); #709 Comfort Starr (b. May 9, 1824; m. Virginia Hyatt); #710 Granville (b. Aug 9, 1828; m. Ellen E. Joslyn). FOOTNOTE: He was the law mentor of Frederick Whittlesey #650 (Eliza Whittlesey Cowles X02785's father), who studied 1 year at the Whittlesey & Newton Canfield office circa 1827 before opening his own Elyria practice. Source: Whittlesey Genealogy entry #310; Cothren's Hist. Ancient Woodbury; Cogswell Family of America; Appleton's Cyclopedia of Am. Biographies Vol. VI; Canfield in Early Times by Dr. Jackson Truesdale. notable.notable_blurb: Maj. Gen., War of 1812

narrative_blocks.header: Tallmadge's junior officer became Ohio's militia general
narrative_blocks.body: Elijah Wadsworth served through the Revolution under Benjamin Tallmadge, ending the war a captain. Decades later, on the Western Reserve, he was commissioned major-general of the Ohio militia. The frontier soldier had become the frontier's general.

narrative_blocks.header: The house he built became Harriet Beecher Stowe's
narrative_blocks.body: The frame house Wadsworth raised at Canfield in 1803 was the first in the township. Generations later it passed into the hands of the Beecher family. The pioneer's homestead outlived the pioneer by a long way.

narrative_blocks.header: An original signer of the Connecticut Land Company
narrative_blocks.body: In September 1795 Wadsworth was among the signers of the contract that opened the Western Reserve to settlement. He spent the summer of 1799 scouting Canfield and the surrounding towns. By 1802 he had moved his whole family west by horse and ox team.

narrative_blocks.header: He held the frontier after Hull's surrender
narrative_blocks.body: When war was declared in 1812 and General Hull surrendered Detroit, Wadsworth was called into active service as a major-general. He threw his full energy into defending the exposed Ohio frontier. Contemporaries credited him with a real service to the country.

narrative_blocks.header: A whole Ohio city now bears his name
narrative_blocks.body: Wadsworth, Ohio, in Medina County, is named for the general. He had once owned a significant portion of the land on which the city grew. His name outlasted his fortune, which the Revolution had consumed entirely.

narrative_blocks.header: He was an early mayor of Akron
narrative_blocks.body: Frederick Wadsworth helped develop frontier Ohio through wool, canal, and iron ventures before serving as mayor of Akron in 1852. He had moved west from Litchfield, Connecticut, as a boy of thirteen.

narrative_blocks.header: His father commissioned him in 1812
narrative_blocks.body: His father, General Elijah Wadsworth, appointed him a lieutenant in the Ohio militia at the outbreak of the War of 1812. The Wadsworth house he built in Edinburg Township still stands on the National Register.

narrative_blocks.header: He conquered a long battle with drink
narrative_blocks.body: For some twenty-five years Frederick Wadsworth struggled with intemperance, then gave it up entirely and never drank again. He became a fervent advocate of abstinence, saying once that five hundred dollars could not tempt him to a single drink.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped finance the rise of Akron
narrative_blocks.body: A canal commissioner and investor, Wadsworth joined Simon Perkins in the Portage Canal and Manufacturing Company that powered the new boomtown. He even lent money to the young John Brown for an Ohio farm before Brown's speculation collapsed in the Panic of 1837.

narrative_blocks.body: Rev. Daniel Wadsworth took the pulpit of Hartford's First Church in 1732 and held it until he died in November 1747, aged forty-three. His will made his widow Abigail sole executrix of a handsome estate. Eunice was eleven, Jeremiah four.

narrative_blocks.header: She married her aunt's husband

narrative_blocks.header: The last but one of six Wadsworth children
narrative_blocks.body: Daniel died at nine and Ruth at four; Abigail died in 1785. When her brother Jeremiah died in 1804, the Wadsworth genealogy records only two of the six still living: Eunice and her sister Elizabeth, who followed in 1810.

narrative_blocks.header: A private at forty in the 11th Minnesota
narrative_blocks.body: Judson enlisted on 24 August 1864, a few weeks after his fortieth birthday, as a private in Company K of the 11th Minnesota Infantry. He served out the war and was mustered out at St. Paul on 26 June 1865.

narrative_blocks.header: From Truxton to Puget Sound
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Truxton, New York, in August 1824, a son of Chellis Hooker, Judson married Susan Martin and raised four children, Challis, Ida, Arthur and Irving, born between 1855 and 1862. The family went west to Minnesota and on to Washington, where Susan died in June 1896 and was buried at Bellingham.

narrative_blocks.header: Ninety-two, at the Retsil veterans home
narrative_blocks.body: Judson outlived Susan by more than twenty years, spending his last years at the Washington Veterans Home at Retsil on Puget Sound. He died there on 13 March 1917, at ninety-two, and was buried in the home's cemetery.

bio.bio_blurb: Illinois judge and former Shakespearean actor

narrative_blocks.header: He came to Illinois as a Shakespearean actor
narrative_blocks.body: He arrived in the late 1840s with a theatrical company and left it at Nauvoo, the Mormon city on the Mississippi. There he stayed, read law, and traded the stage for the bar — an actor who became one of the oldest judges in the ninth circuit.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty years at the Carthage bar
narrative_blocks.body: He practiced law for sixty years at Carthage, Illinois, and was reckoned one of the three oldest attorneys in the ninth circuit. He was a personal friend of Stephen A. Douglas, the senator who debated Lincoln.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped drive the Mormons from Hancock County
narrative_blocks.body: He settled in Hancock County in the years when the anti-Mormon uprising was forcing Joseph Smith's followers out, and he took an active part in it. Nauvoo, where he had left his acting company, emptied as its people fled west.

(FindAGrave) U.S. Marshal for District of Connecticut, appt. by Andrew Jackson 1831, removed by Tyler June 1841. Central figure in Amistad case 1839-1841. Appointed collector of customs District of New Haven by Pres. Polk 1845. (Amistad Research Center records; Marcus Rediker, The Amistad Rebellion) [Stage 6Y-264 schema cleanup]: notable_blurb trimmed from [15w] 'U.S. Marshal for the District of Connecticut; administered custody of the Amistad captives 1839–1841' → 'U.S. Marshal for the District of Connecticut'.

Original body preserved here for reference: 'Norris Willcox was appointed U.S. Marshal for the District of Connecticut by President Andrew Jackson in 1831. When the Amistad arrived in 1839 with its cargo of kidnapped Africans, Willcox received Lt. Gedney's salvage libel, escorted the captives from New Haven to Hartford for trial, and was present at every court session. He was the officer who recorded the West African names the captives answered to — because they did not respond to the Spanish names on the Spanish planters' manifest. In March 1841, upon receiving news of the Supreme Court's decision, Willcox hurried to Westville to announce to the assembled Mende that they were free. President Tyler removed him from office two months later.'

narrative_blocks.header: Jailer to the Amistad Africans
narrative_blocks.body: Andrew Jackson made Norris United States marshal for Connecticut in 1831, and in 1839 the Africans who had seized the schooner Amistad came into his custody at New Haven. He held them for the eighteen months their case took to reach the Supreme Court.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried out the order to free them
narrative_blocks.body: When the Supreme Court ruled in March 1841 that the Africans were free, it fell to Norris to release them from federal custody. President Tyler removed him from office three months later, and President Polk brought him back in 1845 as collector of customs for New Haven.

narrative_blocks.header: Grandfather of Jessie Willcox Smith
narrative_blocks.body: Norris married Harriet Hart, and through their daughter Katharine, remembered in Berlin for her beauty, he was grandfather of the illustrator Jessie Willcox Smith. Her paintings of children filled the covers of Good Housekeeping and the pages of Little Women and Heidi.

narrative_blocks.body: Her father died when she was three and her mother in the 1880s, and Carrie went to her grandfather George Wells on Charles Street. She stayed on in that house with her uncle and her aunt Annie until she died there herself.

narrative_blocks.header: He told Olmsted to apply for Central Park
narrative_blocks.body: Elliott had studied landscape gardening under Downing and practised it at Cincinnati before the new park board took him on. At a Connecticut inn in August 1857 he told a broke, just-failed Olmsted to apply for its superintendency.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped found the Children's Aid Society
narrative_blocks.body: Elliott was one of the founders and trustees of the Children's Aid Society in 1853. He was in the iron trade in New York with his brother Henry at the time, and gave the charity his hours on top of the business.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote Toussaint L'Ouverture's life in 1855
narrative_blocks.body: Six years before Fort Sumter, Elliott published St. Domingo, its Revolution and its Hero — an American book that put the leader of a slave revolt in its title and called him the hero of it.

narrative_blocks.header: He published a novel as Mr. Thorn Whyte
narrative_blocks.body: Elliott brought out Wind and Whirlwind in 1868 under the name Mr. Thorn Whyte, and wrote several more novels he never signed at all. He had already tried the supernatural once, in Mysteries in 1852.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept a Boston shop for household art
narrative_blocks.body: Elliott managed the Household Art Company on Tremont Street. He wrote The Book of American Interiors out of houses that actually existed, illustrated by heliotype, then a guide to pottery and porcelain giving the marks.

narrative_blocks.header: Two of his three sons died small
narrative_blocks.body: Paul was two when he died in 1858, and Wyllys seven in 1865. Howard, born 1860, was the son who lived: he ran the Northern Pacific for ten years and then the New York, New Haven and Hartford.

narrative_blocks.header: New York and Boston came to Guilford
narrative_blocks.body: Elliott had moved back to the Guilford he was born in, and died there in August 1883. Richard Woodward came from New York for the funeral, Charles Clark from Boston and a judge from Washington; Calvin Leete and Henry Robinson carried him.

narrative_blocks.body: Mary outlived her husband by thirty-nine years. She kept house at 22 Garden Street in Cambridge for most of them, and was still there when she died in October 1922, in her ninety-sixth year.

narrative_blocks.header: The last of Abijah White's seven children
narrative_blocks.body: Mary was born at Watertown two days after Christmas in 1826, the daughter of Abijah White and Mary Howard. She was the last of their seven children left alive, and outlasted every one of them.

narrative_blocks.header: She buried two sons before either turned eight
narrative_blocks.body: Paul died at two in 1858 and Wyllys at seven in 1865. Howard was the one of Mary's three who grew up, and she lived to watch him run the Northern Pacific and then the New York, New Haven and Hartford.

narrative_blocks.header: Cambridge for the service, Guilford for the ground
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel McChord Crothers of the First Parish read the service at the Mount Auburn chapel. Mary's body then went down to Guilford in Connecticut, where her people had been buried for generations.

narrative_blocks.header: Her sister was the first Mrs Lowell
narrative_blocks.body: One of Mary's sisters married James Russell Lowell and was his first wife. Mary married an author too — her husband turned out histories, novels and a guide to pottery across thirty-five years.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran two great railroads in succession
narrative_blocks.body: Howard Elliott served as president of the Northern Pacific Railway from 1903 to 1913, then led the New York, New Haven and Hartford line. During the First World War he sat on the national Railroads' War Board.

narrative_blocks.header: A Harvard man who served his university
narrative_blocks.body: Trained at Harvard's Lawrence Scientific School, Elliott remained devoted to the college as one of its overseers. He died at Dennis on Cape Cod in 1928.

narrative_blocks.header: His railroad term opened with a deadly wreck
narrative_blocks.body: Days after he took over the New Haven in 1913, the Bar Harbor Express rear-ended a standing train, killing twenty-one sleeping passengers — the worst disaster the line had seen. He inherited a railroad already in crisis, and the wreck set the tone for his troubled tenure.

narrative_blocks.header: He turned down a railroad to stay east
narrative_blocks.body: When George Gould left the Missouri Pacific in 1911, its presidency was offered to him — and he declined, preferring New England to the West. He had run the Northern Pacific across the northern plains, but chose to come home.

narrative_blocks.header: He started as a rodman on summer break
narrative_blocks.body: He first entered railroad work as a teenager, holding the surveyor's rod on the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy during a college vacation. He spent the next two decades as clerk, freight agent, and manager before any title with “president” in it.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped run the railroads through a war
narrative_blocks.body: During the First World War he sat on the Railroads' War Board and advised the federal administration that took the nation's railroads under government control. The man who had run two lines now helped run them all.

career.organization: New York, New Haven & Hartford RR

narrative_blocks.header: She crossed Tibet with twenty-seven camels
narrative_blocks.body: In 1923 Janet and her husband Frederick began a nine-month National Geographic expedition with twenty-seven camels across Inner Mongolia and the Tibetan marches. She rode and photographed country few Western women had seen.

narrative_blocks.header: Her own expeditions were credited to her husband
narrative_blocks.body: The expedition's photographs and collections went out under her husband's name as naturalist of record. Only decades later were many of the pictures recognized as Janet's work.

narrative_blocks.header: She left society to nurse in wartime France
narrative_blocks.body: Before the expeditions, Janet walked out of the Boston debutante world she was bred for and crossed the Atlantic to nurse wounded soldiers in France. The drawing room never held her.

narrative_blocks.header: She and her husband died the same day
narrative_blocks.body: She and Richard Hobart, her second husband, died on the same November day in 1963, both in Cambridge. They had married late, after a first marriage and a divorce, and in the end they left the world together.

narrative_blocks.header: She read of her divorce in the papers
narrative_blocks.body: In 1929, away on a Harvard expedition to Mexico, Frederick got a surprise divorce, and Janet read in the newspapers that he would marry her closest friend, Susanne Emery. She told reporters: 'I love him and I want him back.'

narrative_blocks.header: Received by a living Buddha
narrative_blocks.body: At Kumbum in 1923 Janet was received by the monastery's living Buddha. 'It is quite a thing to be received by a Buddhist divinity,' she wrote in her diary, 'and I guess not many of the Junior League girls in New York can boast of' it.

narrative_blocks.header: Franklin Roosevelt's most enduring childhood friend
narrative_blocks.body: Rogers grew up at Crumwold Hall in Hyde Park, directly beside the Roosevelt estate, and became Franklin Delano Roosevelt's closest boyhood companion. The friendship endured into the White House years.

narrative_blocks.header: He led New York's Fulton Trust Company
narrative_blocks.body: A Yale graduate, Rogers became president of the Fulton Trust Company in New York and split his life between the city and the Hudson Valley. He kept seasonal homes from Jekyll Island to Aiken, South Carolina.

narrative_blocks.header: He brushed against the Windsor abdication drama
narrative_blocks.body: Through his brother Herman, Rogers moved in the circle of the Duke and Duchess of Windsor and advised the industrialist Charles Bedaux, at whose château the Windsors married. When Bedaux proved a Nazi collaborator, the Rogers brothers denounced him to American authorities.

narrative_blocks.header: His first wife died in childbirth at twenty-three
narrative_blocks.body: Rogers married Edith January Elliott, a Hooker descendant, in 1916, and she died in 1919 giving birth to their second son. He later married Dorothy Knox Goodyear, a prominent New York society hostess.

narrative_blocks.header: Her letters are most of what survives
narrative_blocks.body: Through the years her husband was away — at war, in Boston, abroad — she wrote to him constantly. Those letters now make up the bulk of the family's surviving papers, so that what remains of the household is largely in her hand.

narrative_blocks.header: Four children, and only one grew up
narrative_blocks.body: She and Alfred had four children between 1868 and 1873 and lost three of them young — an infant daughter, then a son at eleven and a daughter at fourteen. Only Diana lived to grow up.

narrative_blocks.header: The letters home that recorded MIT's first days
narrative_blocks.body: When the brand-new Massachusetts Institute of Technology offered her husband a professorship in 1868, he wrote to her from Boston almost daily — about the Institute's shaky finances, its curriculum, and its founders. Those letters, kept and later sold to a collector, survive as a rare close-up of MIT in its first year.

narrative_blocks.body: He went to war as captain of the 1st Connecticut Light Artillery, became chief of artillery on General Alfred Terry's staff, and ended as colonel of the 6th Connecticut. The brevet of brigadier general came in March 1865, for the Petersburg campaign of the year before.

narrative_blocks.header: He studied coal in Saxony's mining academy
narrative_blocks.body: Before the war he chased a geologist's training across Europe — the Museum of Practical Geology in London, the famous Bergakademie at Freiberg in Saxony, and a circuit of English and German collieries. He brought that home to teach mining at Yale's Sheffield School and then at the young MIT.

narrative_blocks.header: After Boston burned, they put him in charge
narrative_blocks.body: When the Great Fire of 1872 gutted downtown Boston, the city made the former general chairman of its fire commission. He later distilled what he learned into a book, Great Fires and Fire Extinction, before moving on to run the Eastern Railroad.

narrative_blocks.header: The Tory in a family of patriots
narrative_blocks.body: Eli Foote was the only Tory in a large family of Whigs during the American Revolution. His wife Roxanna was the daughter of General Andrew Ward, a renowned patriot — making for an unusual household. Bereft of professional advancement after the war, Eli turned to maritime commerce at Guilford.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter launched the Beecher dynasty
narrative_blocks.body: Eli's Foote line traced back to Wethersfield founder Nathaniel Foote 1635 through his Revolutionary War patriot father Daniel Foote of Colchester. Eli's daughter Roxanna Foote married Rev. Lyman Beecher and bore the Beecher children Harriet, Henry Ward, Catherine, and Isabella. Through Isabella's 1841 marriage to John Hooker, the Foote line reached Hartford's Nook Farm abolitionist circle.

narrative_blocks.header: He rented a man’s labour from the Pynchons
narrative_blocks.body: Between 1775 and 1777 he hired the labour of Cuff, an enslaved man held by Joseph and Sarah Pynchon, paying in goods and setting him to the grass and to a work team. The account book he kept with Pynchon is where that record survives.

narrative_blocks.header: His warehouse was robbed and it killed him
narrative_blocks.body: Thieves broke into the North Carolina warehouse he kept with his brother Justin on the night of 17 April 1791, in Murfreesboro’s first recorded crime. Prosecuting them held him south through the next summer, and yellow fever took him at Winton in September 1792.

narrative_blocks.header: He toasted King George to amuse his neighbours
narrative_blocks.body: His St. Pumpkin’s Day Ode of 1777 drank a toast to George our King and prayed that Rebels soon may swing. It was a joke his Patriot friends were willing to take from him.

b. Oct 30, 1747 Colchester CT; d. Aug 1792 Winton, Hertford County NC. Son of Daniel and Margaret Parsons Foote. Merchant; Tory loyalist and Episcopalian. m. Oct 11, 1772 Guilford CT, Roxanna Ward (X02033), dau. of Gen. Andrew Ward. 10 children incl. Samuel Edmund Foote (X01189) and Roxanna Foote (who m. Lyman Beecher). Wrote 'St. Pumpkin's Day Ode' 1777, mocking patriots. Buried Dickinson Family Cemetery Winton NC; name on monument at Foote-Ward Cemetery Guilford. (Biography in Guilford family records; Andrew Warde and His Descendants) [Migrated from death.notes]: Died in delirium at Winton NC, contracted Aug 1792. FOOTE-LINE ANCESTOR (added Stage 6P): Eli's grandfather was Nathaniel Foote of Colchester CT (m. Anne Clark; b. 6 Feb 1716/17), and his father was Daniel Foote (1717-1801) of Colchester CT, Connecticut Revolutionary War deputy to the General Court (DAR Ancestor #A040502). The Foote line traces back through Nathaniel¹ Foote, Wethersfield founder 1635 — placing Eli in the same Foote tree as Almira Mills Foote (I00396, Edwin Weed Cowles' wife) and Judge Elisha Foote Jr. (X02107, Eunice Newton Foote's husband). Through his daughter Roxanna Foote → Lyman Beecher → Isabella Beecher, Eli is the Hooker-tree connection through which the Beecher abolitionist circle reached Hartford via Isabella's marriage to John Hooker (H01626) in 1841. Source: WikiTree, Goodwin Foote Gen 1849, Abram Foote Gen 1907, NCpedia biography.

Original body preserved here for reference: 'Eli Foote was the only Tory in a large family of Whigs during the American Revolution. His wife Roxanna was the daughter of General Andrew Ward, a renowned patriot — making for an unusual household. Bereft of professional advancement after the war, Eli turned to maritime commerce at Guilford. In 1789 he partnered with his brother Justin on a trading voyage to North Carolina, where thieves broke into their Murfreesboro warehouse on April 17, 1791 — the town's first recorded crime — stealing chintz, linen, and silk. Most goods were recovered, but Eli had to remain in North Carolina to testify. In August 1792 he contracted yellow fever and died in delirium at Winton. He left behind ten children, among them Samuel Edmund, who would host a Cincinnati literary salon attended by his niece Harriet Beecher, and Roxanna, who would become the mother of Harriet Beecher Stowe.'

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed with ten children and no money
narrative_blocks.body: Eli Foote died of yellow fever in North Carolina in 1792 and left her penniless with ten children. Her father, General Andrew Ward, took the whole household in at Nut Plains and became father and educator to them.

narrative_blocks.header: Two sons, sixteen and fourteen, in two weeks
narrative_blocks.body: Two of her boys carried a coffin two miles as pall-bearers, there being no hearses in those days, and died within a fortnight of each other of the fatigue and the illness that came of it. Their grandfather laid out a burying plot on his own farm so that it could never happen again.

narrative_blocks.header: A Louisburg spoon came down to her
narrative_blocks.body: Her great-grandfather was a teetotaller among men who drew rum rations, and at the siege of Louisburg he took his in money and bought three silver spoons marked Louisburg on the back. One of them came down through her father to her.

narrative_blocks.header: Sold 300,000 copies in its first year
narrative_blocks.body: Her 1852 novel about the cruelty of slavery sold over 300,000 copies in the United States in its first twelve months — proportionally equivalent to roughly thirty million copies today. It was translated into more than sixty languages and made her the most widely read American author in the world.

narrative_blocks.header: Wrote between housework and seven children
narrative_blocks.body: She drafted Uncle Tom's Cabin at her kitchen table while raising seven children and managing the household; the novel first appeared as a serial in the National Era because she lacked time for a complete manuscript. Her sister-in-law had dared her to 'write something that will make this whole nation feel.'

narrative_blocks.header: Born into America's most famous Protestant family
narrative_blocks.body: Her father Lyman Beecher was the leading evangelical preacher of his era; brother Henry Ward Beecher would become the most famous American Protestant minister of the nineteenth century, and sister Catharine Beecher pioneered women's education. The phrase 'Beecher's Bibles' — Sharps rifles smuggled to Bleeding Kansas — referred to shipments Henry organized.

narrative_blocks.header: Founded a Florida community for newly freed people
narrative_blocks.body: After the Civil War she purchased a plantation in Mandarin, Florida and converted part of it into a school and Episcopal church for the freedmen who lived nearby. She spent half of every year in Mandarin from 1867 until her husband's death in 1886.

narrative_blocks.header: Mark Twain's neighbor for twenty-three years
narrative_blocks.body: She lived at Forest and Farmington Avenues in Hartford from 1873 until her death; her house and Mark Twain's stand a hundred yards apart in the Nook Farm literary colony. Twain visited her often and was distressed by her mental decline in old age.

narrative_blocks.header: Greensward won the 1858 park competition
narrative_blocks.body: He and the architect Calvert Vaux won a public competition in 1858 for 843 swampy acres above 59th Street. Their sunken transverse roads carried crosstown traffic beneath the park so the ground above stayed unbroken.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave the profession its name
narrative_blocks.body: Signing the Central Park drawings, he and Vaux called themselves landscape architects, a title nobody had used for the work. Yosemite, Niagara, Boston's Emerald Necklace and the Capitol grounds followed over forty years.

narrative_blocks.header: He rode the South and reported it dry
narrative_blocks.body: The New-York Daily Times sent him through the South in the 1850s, and the dispatches became The Cotton Kingdom in 1861 — an account too particular for British readers to dismiss as abolitionist heat.

narrative_blocks.header: He left the park to run army relief
narrative_blocks.body: From 1861 he was general secretary of the U.S. Sanitary Commission, directing hospital ships, supply trains and camp inspection for the whole Northern army. Mark Skinner ran its Northwestern branch out of Chicago.

narrative_blocks.header: He gathered the men who started The Nation
narrative_blocks.body: In 1865 the abolitionist circle he led asked Edwin Lawrence Godkin to edit a weekly and put up its first money. Godkin married Frances Elizabeth Foote of New Haven, which carried the editor into the family's Connecticut circle.

narrative_blocks.header: Elliott backed him before there was a plan
narrative_blocks.body: Charles Wyllys Elliott, a Wyllys-Hooker descendant who designed homewares for a living, sat among the first park commissioners and got him the superintendent's job in 1857. They worked the first decade of construction together.

narrative_blocks.header: Hartford's preacher chose his Berkeley ground
narrative_blocks.body: The College of California's trustees hired him in 1865 to lay out its campus and the town beside it — ground that Horace Bushnell, preaching in Olmsted's native Hartford, had settled on after riding round San Francisco Bay.

parents.father_research_notes: Henry Daggett Esq (b. April 9, 1741 Attleboro MA; d. Sept 24, 1830 Attleboro MA, age 89). Per WikiTree: father Elihu Daggett, mother Rebecca Stanley Daggett. Grandparents: Mayhew Daggett (~1686-1752 Tisbury Martha's Vineyard MA) + Joanna Bevin (b. Feb 10, 1687 Glastonbury Hartford Co CT). The Tisbury / Martha's Vineyard connection ties Henry's Daggett lineage to the Edgartown MA Daggett family. Henry was COUSIN (not brother) of Rev. Naphtali Daggett D.D. (1727-1780), Yale College President 1766-1777 — the FIRST Yale graduate to head the institution. Naphtali's grandparents were John Daggett (1662-1724 Edgartown) + Sarah Pease (1661-1735 Edgartown Dukes Co MA) — different grandparents from Henry but both lineages trace to the Watertown MA / Edgartown MA Daggett family of John Daggett (immigrant ~1630s, ancestor of Thomas Daggett 1630-1691 of Edgartown). Henry Daggett Esq + Naphtali Daggett were thus 2nd or 3rd cousins, both descending from the same MA Puritan Daggett family via different sons of Thomas Daggett of Edgartown.
parents.mother_research_notes: Elisabeth Prescott (b. Dec 1, 1752; d. May 11, 1813 Danvers MA, age 60). Sister of Rebecca Prescott who married Roger Sherman (Signer of the Declaration of Independence) in Danvers MA on May 12, 1763 — making Roger Sherman uncle-by-marriage to Elisabeth Daggett. Other Prescott siblings: Martha (Goodhue), James, Mercy (Gibbs), Benjamin Daggett Prescott, Mary (Barrett).

people.research_notes: b. Jul 5, 1786 New Haven CT; d. Aug 2, 1869 Hartford CT. Dau. of Henry Daggett, Esq., and Elisabeth Prescott Daggett of New Haven. Niece of Hon. Roger Sherman — Signer of the Declaration of Independence. m. May 24, 1812 Edward Hooker (H00630). (EH entry 630) [DAGGETT-PATTERN FLAG 2026]: Just FOUR YEARS after this 1812 marriage, distant Hooker cousin Henry Hooker (H01393, gen 7, Hinsdale NH branch) married another Daggett woman — Mary Daggett (X02247, 1795-1864) of Westmoreland Cheshire Co NH on October 23, 1816. Two Hooker descendants from different geographic branches (Farmington CT + Hinsdale NH) marrying Daggett women within 4 years (1812 + 1816) is a striking pattern. POSSIBLE EXPLANATIONS: (1) Coincidence — Daggett was a moderately common surname in colonial New England. (2) Shared MA Daggett ancestry — both Daggett brides MAY descend from John Daggett of Watertown MA (immigrant ~1630s) via different colonial branches: Henry Daggett Esq (Attleboro MA, b.1741) → Elisabeth (1786, this entry); and Simeon Daggett (b.1758) → Mary (1795). If both Daggett families trace to the Watertown MA founder, the two brides are themselves distant cousins (perhaps 3rd-4th degree). (3) Hooker family social network — the Hooker descendants in CT and NH may have been aware of each other's marriages and the Daggett families through shared Yale/professional networks (Henry Daggett Esq's brother Naphtali Daggett 1727-1780 was President of Yale College 1766-1777; Yale was a major node in CT Puritan-descendant social networks). RESEARCH FLAG: investigate Watertown MA Daggett genealogy to confirm or rule out shared ancestry between Henry Daggett Esq (1741) and Simeon Daggett (1758). NOTE: This is NOT formally a cousin_marriage on the Hooker bloodline (brides aren't Hooker descendants); just a striking Daggett-name-recurrence pattern across two CT-NH Hooker branches. [DAGGETT GENEALOGY EXPANSION 2026]: Henry Daggett Esq (her father, b.1741 Attleboro MA - d.1830 New Haven CT) was COUSIN (not brother as earlier noted) of Rev. Dr. Naphtali Daggett (1727-1780), YALE COLLEGE PRESIDENT pro tempore 1766-1777 — first non-Harvard graduate to head Yale. Both descended from Thomas Daggett (1630-1691) of Edgartown Martha's Vineyard MA via different sons. NAPHTALI DAGGETT'S SIGNIFICANCE: Yale 1748 (Berkeley Scholarship); first permanent pastor First Presbyterian Smithtown LI 1751; first Professor of Divinity at Yale (Livingston Chair) 1755; first pastor Yale College Church 1757; Yale President pro tempore 1766-1777. Liberalized Yale curriculum; created two new professorships; democratized student-name listing (changed from social rank to alphabetical). During July 1779 British invasion of New Haven, took up arms with shotgun in town defense; was captured, compelled to act as guide, 'repeatedly pricked with bayonets' — never fully recovered. Died Nov 25, 1780. Succeeded as Yale President by Ezra Stiles. DAGGETT-PATTERN UPDATE: With Henry now confirmed as COUSIN (not brother) of Naphtali Daggett, the Yale connection is more distant than initially flagged — but still meaningful. The Hooker family in CT (especially the Farmington branch) had multiple Yale-connected ministers, and Naphtali Daggett's tenure as Yale President 1766-1777 overlapped with the Hooker family's deep Yale connections. Edward Hooker H00630 (b.1785) was educated AT Yale (likely class of early 1800s). The marriage to Elisabeth Daggett 1812 placed Edward Hooker into a Daggett family at the Yale-faculty social periphery. (CROSS-REF: Roger Sherman the signer is now built as X02819.)

narrative_blocks.body: He graduated Yale 1805 and traveled to Columbia, South Carolina to study law with his elder brother John, also teaching briefly at Old Ninety Six. Yale appointed him tutor in 1808 — a post he held until 1812 when he returned to Farmington.

narrative_blocks.header: A sharp eyewitness to the young South
narrative_blocks.body: Visiting South Carolina in the winter of 1805–6, Edward Hooker recorded planter Wade Hampton’s scorn for New England’s clustered villages — Hampton wanted room for his barns and herds, and thought close neighbors only bred quarrels over fences. Hooker’s notebooks became a vivid first-hand contrast between Northern and Southern ideas of land and community.

people.research_notes: b. Apr 27, 1785 Farmington CT; d. May 5, 1846 Farmington CT. Son of Col. Noadiah Hooker (H00288) and Rebekah Griswold (I00133). Yale 1805. Studied law in South Carolina with brother John. Returned CT 1808 as Yale tutor. m. May 24, 1812 Elisabeth Daggett (X02036), niece of Roger Sherman (Signer, Declaration of Independence). Ran 'Old Red College' private school at Farmington — precursor to Miss Porter's School. Father of John Hooker (H01626) who married Isabella Beecher, and Edward Hooker (H01628) who compiled EH 1909. (EH entry 630) FULL BIOGRAPHY (per Edward Hooker 1909 entry 630 + WikiTree): Edward Hooker graduated Yale College 1805. After graduation he traveled to Columbia SC to study law privately under his elder brother John Hooker, an established practicing lawyer there. While in South Carolina he taught a school briefly at Cambridge SC (Old Ninety Six), then accepted a position as tutor in South Carolina College at Columbia, continuing law study under his brother. In 1808 Yale College appointed him tutor; he accepted, returned to Connecticut, and was made Clerk of the Faculty — a position he filled throughout his Yale tenure. While at Yale he met Miss Elisabeth Daggett (niece of Roger Sherman, Signer of the Declaration of Independence) and, preparatory to marrying her, resigned his Yale post in 1812. He returned to Farmington, took charge of his father's farm and business, cared for his father in declining years, built a home for his wife, and settled to farming and public duties. After his mother's death, Edward brought his father into his own house and fitted up the old Hooker family home as a collegiate-preparatory school. The 'Old Red College' (as the house was called) became quite noted — a number of men who later became prominent in public affairs were prepared for college there. This was the first formal educational movement at Farmington. The old house had been the home of a descendant of Ezekiel Cheever, the famous Colonial teacher, founder of the Boston Latin School, and author of the first school books published in America. After running the school for some years, a movement formed to establish a public Academy at Farmington. Edward proposed closing his own school in favor of the Academy and recommended Mr. Simeon Hart as principal. Hart's Academy became a famous school. The Academy was eventually relinquished, and Hart opened a private school of his own, succeeded by his nephew Edward L. Hart — both fitted many famous men for college. After 'the Old Red College' had ended its days as a school, the building did duty for a time as a tenement, then was demolished to make room for the first schoolhouse of Miss Sarah Porter — the seed of what became Miss Porter's Female School. The Memorial Building erected by Miss Porter's scholars stands a little northward and westward from the site of the Old Red College. After closing his school, Edward settled to literary work, active participation in town affairs, and scientific farming. He died at Farmington May 5, 1846, age 61. Elisabeth died at Hartford August 2, 1869, age 83. PORTRAIT: Painted c. 1840 by Jared Bradley Flagg (1820-1899), oil on canvas 30 x 24.5 inches. Provenance through great-grandson Joseph K. Hooker of Hartford CT to the Harriet Beecher Stowe Center, Hartford CT (current repository, private collection). See ART044. people.research_notes: b. Apr 19, 1816 Farmington CT; d. Feb 12, 1901 Hartford CT. Lawyer, Hartford. Reporter of the CT Supreme Court 1858-1894 (36 years); reported 38 volumes of CT Reports. m. Aug 5, 1841 Isabella Beecher (I00170), dau. of Rev. Lyman Beecher by 2nd wife Harriet Porter Beecher. Isabella was half-sister of Harriet Beecher Stowe and Henry Ward Beecher. (EH entry 1626) His own account of the manumission ran in Frederick Douglass' Paper, 26 June 1851: 'I shall defer the execution of this instrument for half an hour, till I have walked up and down the whole length of Main street, to see how it seems to be a slaveholder — especially to own a Doctor of Divinity... I have returned from my walk. The deed is executed. Jim Pembroke is merged into Rev. Dr. Pennington. The slave is free — the chattel is a man.' Tilghman had demanded five hundred dollars in 1844; the estate settled for a fraction of it. The John and Isabella Hooker House at 140 Hawthorn Street, the first built at Nook Farm and later enlarged by Octavius Jordan, went on the National Register in 1979. His 1874 letter to Mrs. J. T. Howard defending Isabella against the 'Statement by the Friends of Mr. Beecher' survives in manuscript, forty-two pages with twenty pages of addenda from January 1875. CONNECTICUT REPORTS vol. 73, 745-46, memorial by ex-Judge Dwight Loomis: entered Yale at sixteen and left within two years when his health failed; the college later granted the degree and recorded him in the class of 1837. To get his health back he shipped twice before the mast, to Spain and to China, fourteen months in all. Admitted to the bar 1841, office at Farmington, removed to Hartford 1851. Reported the decisions of seven chief justices and fifteen associate judges; resigned 2 October 1893 effective 1 January 1894. His mother Elisabeth Daggett was first cousin to the mother of Roger Sherman Baldwin, the Amistad counsel and governor, who is not in the tree. In later life he discarded much of the orthodox creed: 'It is the deed and not the creed / That serves us in the hour of need.'
