narrative_blocks.header: He owned a man for half an hour
narrative_blocks.body: Friends in Berwickshire raised the money and Hooker bought James Pennington from the Tilghman estate in 1851, taking title himself because an administrator could not free a man. Then he walked the length of Main Street to see how it felt to be a slaveholder, came back and signed the manumission.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-six years reporting the court
narrative_blocks.body: He was made Reporter of the Connecticut Supreme Court of Errors in 1858 and held it until 1894, putting out thirty-eight volumes of the Reports. Only Thomas Day served longer, and in fifty-one years he had reported twenty-six.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the bill that undid coverture
narrative_blocks.body: He and Isabella drafted A Woman's Property Bill together and she put it before the legislature every year until it passed in 1877. It let a married woman hold her own property and sue in her own name.

narrative_blocks.header: Free principles, free men, free press
narrative_blocks.body: From 1838 he published the Charter Oak for the Connecticut Anti-Slavery Society at Hartford, under that motto. He was twenty-two when he started it.

narrative_blocks.header: His office adjoined the Amistad Africans
narrative_blocks.body: He kept a law office at Deming's Store on Mill Lane, on the other side of the wall from the room the Mende used during their stay in Farmington. He was among the townspeople who saw them through the winter before they sailed.

narrative_blocks.header: Nook Farm began with his land
narrative_blocks.body: In 1853 he and his brother-in-law Francis Gillette bought the tract west of Hartford and built the first house on it. Harriet Beecher Stowe came, and in 1871 Mark Twain rented from him before building next door.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-two pages in his wife's defence
narrative_blocks.body: When the Beecher-Tilton scandal broke over Isabella in 1874 he wrote a forty-two page letter answering the charges against her point by point, and added twenty pages more the next January. The family never closed the breach.

people.research_notes: b. Feb 22, 1822 Litchfield CT; d. Jan 25, 1907 Hartford CT. Dau. of Rev. Lyman Beecher by 2nd wife Harriet Porter Beecher. Half-sister of Harriet Beecher Stowe (X02034) and Henry Ward Beecher — different mothers. Prominent women's suffrage advocate; organized first women's rights convention in CT. m. Aug 5, 1841 John Hooker (H01626), 6th-generation descendant of Rev. Thomas Hooker. Lived Hartford CT entire adult life. (Wikipedia) Inducted Connecticut Women's Hall of Fame. INGERSOLL CONNECTION: Harriet Jencks Ingersoll (Ingersoll genealogy entry 238) attended Hartford Female Seminary under Catharine Beecher (Isabella's sister). The Ingersoll family and the Beecher orbit overlapped through this educational connection. Catharine Beecher is a candidate for an orbit entry when this thread is developed further. Born at Litchfield, not Cincinnati — Lyman Beecher did not go west to Cincinnati until 1832. Her mother was Harriet Porter, Lyman's second wife, who died when Isabella was a teenager; she was raised largely by her half-sister Mary Beecher Perkins at Hartford, where she met John Hooker. She reintroduced the married women's property bill every year from 1870 until it passed in 1877, and organised the 1871 Washington convention at her own expense. She corresponded with Lucy Stone across the 1869 split and after it: Stone wrote to her in 1869 debating the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments — 'I believe that just so far as we withhold or deny a human right to any human being, we establish a basis for the denial and withholding of our own rights' — and Hooker wrote to Stone from Hartford on 11 July 1878 about a letter of Olympia Brown's to the state executive committee. Susan B. Anthony wrote to her on the same amendments in 1878. National American Woman Suffrage Association Records, General Correspondence.

narrative_blocks.header: She founded the state association in 1869
narrative_blocks.body: Isabella founded the Connecticut Woman Suffrage Association in 1869, the state's first organized suffrage body. Two years later she paid out of her own pocket for a national suffrage convention in Washington, D.C.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven years to win married women property
narrative_blocks.body: Beginning in 1870 Isabella shepherded a married women's property bill through the Connecticut legislature year after year, defeated and reintroduced. It finally passed in 1877, ending the doctrine that a wife's earnings and property automatically belonged to her husband.

narrative_blocks.header: Read Blackstone — spent decades undoing it
narrative_blocks.body: At nineteen she married John Hooker and became a regular visitor to his Hartford law office, where she read Blackstone's Commentaries and found that marriage suspended a woman's legal standing entirely. She spent the rest of her life undoing it.

narrative_blocks.header: She did not want to marry at all
narrative_blocks.body: She knew the marriage contract was the last legal document a woman ever signed, and she wanted none of it. John Hooker courted her two years, mostly by letter, before she agreed.

narrative_blocks.header: One of the famous Beecher children
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother Harriet Porter kept to her bedroom for most of Isabella's childhood and died when she was a teenager, and the girl was passed among older half-siblings until she settled in Hartford with her sister Mary Beecher Perkins. It was in that house that John Hooker noticed her.

narrative_blocks.header: She broke with her family over a scandal
narrative_blocks.body: When her brother Henry Ward Beecher was accused of adultery the Beechers closed ranks behind him, and Isabella said publicly that she believed the charge. Relatives put it about that she was unfit of mind, and the rift with Harriet never healed.

narrative_blocks.header: Her last years were spent awaiting the dead
narrative_blocks.body: A committed spiritualist, she believed the veil between the living and the dead was thin. After John died in 1901 she withdrew to her room waiting for word from him, and lent her name to the suffrage cause until a stroke took her in 1907.

notable.notable_blurb: Civil War naval commander and Hooker genealogist
notable.primary_url_label: Naval History and Heritage Command — Manuscript Collection

narrative_blocks.header: A merchant captain who went to war
narrative_blocks.body: He was bred to the sea and had command of a merchant vessel by twenty-three. When the war came in 1861 he left the merchant service and entered the Navy as an acting master — the volunteer's rank, not the career officer's road — and never went back to trade.

narrative_blocks.header: The first acting master wounded in the war
narrative_blocks.body: He was the first officer of his rank wounded in the Civil War, hit severely in October 1861, and wounded twice more before it ended. Twice he was promoted on the field for gallantry, and at the war's close he was taken from the volunteer service into the regular Navy.

narrative_blocks.header: He held the Rappahannock with a flotilla
narrative_blocks.body: From 1863 he commanded a division of the Potomac Flotilla on the Rappahannock River, running the gunboats Currituck, Yankee, and Commodore Read against Confederate shore batteries and blockade-runners. He served through the Burnside Expedition and all its engagements.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the code his ships signaled by
narrative_blocks.body: Around 1863 he compiled a handwritten code of naval signals — an alphabetical index of some twelve hundred entries for maneuvers, shipboard orders, compass headings, and the recognition of ships under foreign flags. The volume survives at the Naval Academy's library at Annapolis.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandmother's uncle signed the Declaration
narrative_blocks.body: His mother, Elizabeth Daggett, was a niece of Roger Sherman — the only man to sign the Declaration of Independence, the Articles of Confederation, and the Constitution. On his father's side he descended from Col. Noadiah Hooker of the Revolution and, beyond him, from Rev. Thomas Hooker himself.

narrative_blocks.header: Blind, he still finished the family's genealogy
narrative_blocks.body: In retirement he gave years to compiling the history of his family, gathering the records that became the 1909 Descendants of Rev. Thomas Hooker — the standard genealogy of the whole line, and the source this project is built on. He worked until his eyesight failed and died in 1903, six years before it saw print.

[CC web context — writing ancestries] Cmdr. Edward Hooker U.S.N. (1822-1903) compiled the foundational 'Descendants of Rev. Thomas Hooker, Hartford Connecticut, 1586-1908' (1909) — going blind in the process. Brig. Gen. Sebastian Visscher Talcott (1812-1888) had earlier compiled the parallel 'Talcott Pedigree in England and America, 1558-1876' (1876). The two men were distant cousins through the founding generation of Hartford, CT (Rev. Thomas Hooker and John Talcott both arrived 1636). These two volumes are the foundational primary sources for this entire genealogy project. narrative_blocks.header: Huck Finn's bad grammar was the whole point
narrative_blocks.body: Huckleberry Finn (1885) is told start to finish in the speech of an unschooled Missouri boy, in an age when novels were written in the language of books. American fiction has sounded like that since.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept a clergyman to sharpen his appetite
narrative_blocks.body: The fashionable Asylum Hill congregation he named the Church of the Holy Speculators, then took its minister Joseph Twichell as his closest friend. His account: “I keep a clergyman to remonstrate against my drinking — it gives zest and increase of appetite.”

narrative_blocks.header: He married into an Underground Railroad station
narrative_blocks.body: A Missouri boyhood taught him that slaveholding was ordinary; he married into an Elmira family that had quit its church over the question and hidden fugitives moving north. Their minister was Thomas K. Beecher, brother to Stowe and to the abolitionist Henry Ward Beecher, and Huckleberry Finn was written on that family's hill.

narrative_blocks.header: He let King Leopold answer for the Congo
narrative_blocks.body: King Leopold's Soliloquy (1905) let the Belgian king defend his Congo atrocities in his own voice. Told to stop cussing and shout Glory, he said a pessimist before forty-eight knows too much, an optimist after it too little.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventeen Hartford years he called his happiest
narrative_blocks.body: He built the house on Farmington Avenue in 1874 and raised three daughters there, the happiest years of his life by his account. Harriet Beecher Stowe lived a hundred yards up the street, and after Susy died in 1896 none of them lived there again.

narrative_blocks.header: The Gilded Age also made an actor
narrative_blocks.body: The Gilded Age (1873), written with his walking companion Charles Dudley Warner, named the post-war era — and its stage version gave William Hooker Gillette his first part.

narrative_blocks.header: He called Bushnell a theological giant
narrative_blocks.body: Twain admired the Hartford divine Horace Bushnell, who was twice tried for heresy and twice cleared. His own pastor Joseph Twichell had been Bushnell's protege and preached his eulogies at Asylum Hill in the spring of 1876, the season before Twain began Huckleberry Finn.

notable.notable_blurb: founded the Stowe-Day Foundation

narrative_blocks.header: She turned her family's houses into museums
narrative_blocks.body: In 1924 Katharine Day bought the Hartford house of her great-grandaunt Harriet Beecher Stowe, and spent the rest of her life preserving it and the homes around it. She organized the rescue of Mark Twain's neighboring house from demolition and founded what became the Harriet Beecher Stowe Center. She made a family's memory into a place the public could visit.

narrative_blocks.header: Granddaughter and grandniece of famous Beechers
narrative_blocks.body: Katharine was the granddaughter of the suffragist Isabella Beecher Hooker and a grandniece of the novelist Harriet Beecher Stowe. She grew up on Nook Farm, the Hartford colony where her family's reformers and writers lived side by side. The Beecher sense of mission ran straight through her.

narrative_blocks.header: She trained as a painter in Paris
narrative_blocks.body: As a young woman in Europe, Day studied the new Pointillist and Neo-Impressionist styles in Paris and exhibited there. Back in New York she painted under William Merritt Chase before returning to the Académie Julian. Art was her first vocation, long before preservation became her life's work.

narrative_blocks.header: She earned graduate degrees past fifty
narrative_blocks.body: Having left high school when her family moved to Europe, Day went back to college as a freshman at forty-seven and took a master's in psychology from Radcliffe. At sixty-six she earned a second graduate degree, in history, from Trinity College. She treated learning as something to pursue at any age.

narrative_blocks.header: She marched, and took on Tammany Hall
narrative_blocks.body: Like her Beecher forebears, Day spoke out where it was unpopular — marching for suffrage in New York and London when women were arrested for it, and helping the Women's Municipal League fight the corruption of Tammany Hall. In Hartford she crusaded for public health and against the open burning of garbage. Reform was the family trade, and she kept at it.

notable.notable_blurb: Anatomist and pioneer of fetal-development research

narrative_blocks.header: Youngest anatomy department chair in the country
narrative_blocks.body: Davenport Hooker arrived at the University of Pittsburgh in 1914 as assistant professor of histology and neurology — Yale alumnus, World War I artillery officer. By 1919, at 32, he was the youngest chair of any anatomy department in the country. He would sit on the lab balcony watching students dissect below, and bellow offenders' last names across the room if he spotted a mistake.

narrative_blocks.header: He filmed human fetuses moving
narrative_blocks.body: Hooker's life work was studying fetal reflex development. He filmed embryonic movement at Pittsburgh, producing research cited in over 40 scholarly publications and covered in TIME magazine. His findings occupied three full pages of the 1947 Encyclopedia Britannica.

narrative_blocks.header: The methods behind the films trouble historians now
narrative_blocks.body: His filming depended on previable human fetuses, and the record shows the specimens were obtained through surgeries on women, in at least a hundred and forty-nine cases. Later scholars have placed him among the century's serious research-ethics failures, alongside better-known names. The findings shaped embryology; the means are not defensible by modern standards.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept his alumni linked through the war
narrative_blocks.body: From 1943 to 1949 he wrote and mailed a newsletter, the Pitt Anatomy Snooze, to former medical students scattered across the armed forces — fifty-nine issues of news, poems, and campus humor sent to Europe and the Pacific. It began as a single v-mail sheet and ran until the men came home.

narrative_blocks.header: He went from valedictorian to the Senate
narrative_blocks.body: Gillette was elected valedictorian of Yale's class of 1829, then served in the Connecticut legislature before reaching Washington. He filled a United States Senate vacancy as a Free Soil man in 1854, in the thick of the slavery fight.

narrative_blocks.header: His farmhouse sheltered the Underground Railroad
narrative_blocks.body: Gillette ran an Underground Railroad station at his Bloomfield farm and helped found Connecticut's Republican Party. He was a silent partner in the Evening Press, the state's first Republican newspaper.

narrative_blocks.header: He built Nook Farm with John Hooker
narrative_blocks.body: In 1853 Gillette and his brother-in-law John Hooker founded Nook Farm, the Hartford enclave that would draw Mark Twain and Harriet Beecher Stowe. His wife was Elisabeth Daggett Hooker.

narrative_blocks.header: His son became Sherlock Holmes on stage
narrative_blocks.body: Gillette's son William Hooker Gillette grew into the celebrated actor who defined Sherlock Holmes for American audiences. Another son, Edward, went to Congress.

notable.notable_blurb: Greenback congressman, Populist editor, Iowa Humane Society officer

narrative_blocks.header: Ten-cent papers paid for his campaign
narrative_blocks.body: In 1878 Edward ran for Congress as a Greenbacker in a district that had gone Republican by six thousand votes. He had no campaign money, sold papers from the platform at ten cents each, and won by about a thousand.

narrative_blocks.header: In court for children and drunkards' wives
narrative_blocks.body: For more than twenty-seven years Edward was an officer of the Iowa Humane Society. He appeared in court for mistreated animals, children and the wives of drunkards, and missed almost no board meeting until his last years.

narrative_blocks.header: He married his fallen brother's fiancée
narrative_blocks.body: Sophia Stoddard had been engaged to Edward's brother Robert, killed at Fort Fisher on 16 January 1865, the morning after the fort fell. Edward married her at Milford on 26 June 1866 and took her home to Iowa.

narrative_blocks.header: He left college to run the Iowa land
narrative_blocks.body: In 1863 Edward left the agricultural college at Ovid to look after Iowa land his father, Senator Francis Gillette, and his uncle John Hooker had bought. Outside Des Moines he raised high-bred stock and sheep, built, and made brick.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten years editing the Populists' paper
narrative_blocks.body: Edward was a delegate to the 1876 Indianapolis convention that formed the Greenback Party and later chaired its national committee. For ten years he edited the Iowa Tribune, and in 1893 he lost a run for Iowa secretary of state.

narrative_blocks.header: In 1880 the Democrats ran their own man
narrative_blocks.body: Edward sat in the 46th Congress beside Iowa's other Greenbacker, James B. Weaver. In 1880 the Democrats put up their own candidate, the vote split, and the Republican John A. Kasson took the seat back.

narrative_blocks.header: A library building beside his farmhouse
narrative_blocks.body: Edward gathered one of the most valuable libraries in Iowa and put up a building for it near the house at Clover Hills, his farm by Valley Junction. He died there in 1918, the one Gillette not buried at Farmington.

b. Aug 1, 1842 Bloomfield CT; d. Jan 16, 1865 Fort Fisher NC age 22. Son of Sen. Francis Gillette (I00173) and Elisabeth Daggett Hooker (H01625). Traveled to China and California before age 18. Capt., Company K, 14th CT Infantry (enlisted Dec 20, 1862); resigned after fever at Harpers Ferry. Appointed asst. paymaster US Navy 1863; served blockade ships NC coast; rose to Paymaster. Paymaster aboard USS Gettysburg during both assaults on Fort Fisher. narrative_blocks.header: Glory forever, hours before the blast
narrative_blocks.body: Robert wrote 'Glory forever' to his parents the night Fort Fisher fell. At daylight on 16 January 1865 he went ashore to see the damage; as he stood on the parapet the magazine blew, and flying timber killed him at twenty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: A blast set off by the victors
narrative_blocks.body: An inquiry found that drunken Union soldiers, sailors and marines, firing weapons and carrying torches inside the fort's magazine, set off the explosion that killed Robert and perhaps two hundred others.

narrative_blocks.header: He would rather fight in the ranks
narrative_blocks.body: Commissioned captain of Company K, 14th Connecticut, Robert caught up with his regiment at Antietam and wrote home that he would sooner fight in the ranks as a private than lead men he had not yet met.

narrative_blocks.header: Fever, then the Navy
narrative_blocks.body: A fever caught at Harpers Ferry broke his health and he resigned, but in 1863 he was back as an assistant paymaster blockading the North Carolina coast, and rose to paymaster of the Gettysburg for both assaults on Fort Fisher.

narrative_blocks.header: Around the world before eighteen
narrative_blocks.body: Before eighteen Robert had sailed a merchant ship to China and gone to California to see his brother Frank, who died of consumption before he arrived; Robert brought him home. He later helped raise two companies for the war.

narrative_blocks.header: His own words are on his stone
narrative_blocks.body: His captain, Roswell Lamson, wrote that Robert was loved throughout the fleet. His stone at Farmington carries his own words: 'I shall go into battle trusting in God that he will do by me what is best for us.'

narrative_blocks.header: Engaged to the girl his brother married
narrative_blocks.body: Robert was engaged to Sophia Stoddard when he died. The next year she married his brother Edward.

NB1: 'William Hooker Gillette grew up at Nook Farm, where Mark Twain was his parents' neighbor. At 20, after leaving a New Orleans stock company unpaid, he returned to Hartford. Twain encouraged him and secured him an engagement at the Globe Theatre in Boston; he made his debut on September 15, 1875.' NB2: detailed history of calabash pipe origin in 1898 rewrite of Conan Doyle play, replacing Sidney Paget's straight pipe. NB3: '24-room fieldstone castle above the Connecticut River in East Haddam between 1914 and 1919, designing every detail himself — 47 unique doors with trick locks, secret passages, mirrors above the great hall to spy on arriving guests, a spring-loaded bar that appeared and disappeared.'

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Built Gillette Castle 1914-1919 as his home; designed it himself including 47 unique locks, secret passages, and a miniature railway.

institutions.institution_blurb: No formal Yale degree; educated Hartford High School, College of the City of New York, and Boston University.

narrative_blocks.header: He wired Doyle: may I marry Holmes?
narrative_blocks.body: Adapting the stories in 1899, he cabled Arthur Conan Doyle: “May I marry Holmes?” Back came: “You may marry him, or murder or do what you like with him.” He played the part more than 1,300 times.

narrative_blocks.header: The deerstalker and curved pipe were stage fixes
narrative_blocks.body: Sidney Paget's straight pipe would not stay put while he spoke, so he curved it and took the deerstalker from the same illustrations. He named Holmes's pageboy Billy — played in London by the young Charlie Chaplin.

narrative_blocks.header: His only Holmes script burned in San Francisco
narrative_blocks.body: His secretary crossed San Francisco to wake him at half past three with the news of the Baldwin Hotel fire of November 1898. He asked whether his own hotel was on fire, was told no, said to come back in the morning — and rewrote the play in a month.

narrative_blocks.header: He patented the sound of a galloping horse
narrative_blocks.body: Coconut shells knocked on marble did not convince him, so in 1888 he patented a method for hoof-beats — clappers struck on stone, brick, gravel or bridge planking. He called his doctrine the Illusion of the First Time.

narrative_blocks.header: His will warned against a blithering saphead
narrative_blocks.body: He designed the fieldstone castle above the Connecticut River himself: forty-seven trick locks, mirrors set to watch guests arrive, a three-mile railroad. His will forbade the place passing to “some blithering saphead.”

narrative_blocks.header: A neighbour's parlour, then Boston's Globe Theatre
narrative_blocks.body: Mark Twain, a Nook Farm neighbour, had him perform in his own living room, then recommended him to Boston's Globe. He debuted there in 1875 in the stage version of Twain's The Gilded Age.

narrative_blocks.header: His father had driven two sons there before
narrative_blocks.body: Francis Gillette thought the theatre no life, and drove his twenty-year-old son to the station anyway — he had taken two sons to that platform who never came back, Frank to consumption in California, Robert to the Fort Fisher magazine.

notable.notable_blurb: Designed the Munson Last G.I. shoe 1912

narrative_blocks.header: He designed the G.I. shoe
narrative_blocks.body: Munson spent four years studying the feet of 2,000 soldiers, then designed a shoe last — snug in heel and arch, with a roomy upturned toe. The Munson Last became U.S. military footwear from 1912 onward: the hobnail brogan of WWI and the G.I. shoe of WWII.

narrative_blocks.header: He was at McKinley's side in Buffalo
narrative_blocks.body: He was one of the physicians who attended President McKinley at Buffalo after he was shot on the sixth of September, 1901. The president lived eight days.

narrative_blocks.header: He halved the sick rate at his fort
narrative_blocks.body: His first post was Fort Assinniboine in Montana, where in his first year the five hundred and thirteen men went to hospital at a rate of eleven hundred a thousand. By 1897 he had it down to five hundred and forty. His father had been Lincoln's judge in the same territory thirty years before.

narrative_blocks.header: Manila's health officer, until it made him ill
narrative_blocks.body: He went to the Philippines in 1903 as health officer for Manila under Governor William Howard Taft. Tuberculosis took hold, and in 1904 he was sent home to the Army's own tuberculosis hospital at Fort Bayard in New Mexico, where his son was born that August. He went back to the islands twice more.

narrative_blocks.header: A hospital at Leavenworth carries his name
narrative_blocks.body: The Munson Army Hospital at Fort Leavenworth is named for him. He had commanded the American medical relief sent to Japan after the Great Kanto earthquake of 1923, and finished at the Medical Field Service School at Carlisle Barracks.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the Army's book on morale
narrative_blocks.body: As chief of the training division under the Surgeon General he was made a brigadier general late in 1918, and afterwards ran the Morale Branch. His 1921 handbook on the systematic development of morale and the control of human behaviour came out of that work.

[2026-07-25 REBUILD] From the Military Medicine (Vol. 164, Jan 1999) biographical study: the MUNSON ARMY HOSPITAL at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas is named for him. Yale College, then M.D. Yale Medical 1892; internship at the Connecticut State Hospital, a then-rare privilege. Accepted a US Navy commission in April 1893, resigned it, and took a 1st Lieutenant's commission in the Army in May 1893 — missing the first class of George Sternberg's new Army Medical School and learning on the job. FIRST POST FORT ASSINNIBOINE, MONTANA: 513 troops; first-year hospital admission rate 1,182 per 1,000 per year (33 of them for alcohol), non-effective rate 31 per 1,000. By 1897: admissions 540 per 1,000, non-effective 18 per 1,000. In 1895 he diagnosed and surgically managed an appendicitis case and the report went into the Surgeon General's annual report to the Secretary of War. On 15 June 1897 he wrote the Surgeon General describing a field splint improvised from the cavalry carbine boot. DATE ERROR IN WIKIPEDIA: it gives 'In 1889 he received a new assignment to Fort Adams' — impossible, since he joined in 1893; the Military Medicine study says he went to Fort Adams after four years, i.e. 1897. His son Edward Lyman Munson Jr. (HD3016) was born at Fort Bayard, New Mexico on 26 Aug 1904 — the Army tuberculosis hospital George Ensign Bushnell (HD7244) commanded from that year, and where Munson was sent to recover from the tuberculosis he caught in the Philippines.

notable.notable_blurb: Armed Forces Radio founder and NBC television chief

narrative_blocks.header: He founded Armed Forces Radio Service
narrative_blocks.body: As chief of the Army Information Branch from 1941, Munson created Armed Forces Radio, Yank the Army Weekly, and the Army Pictorial Service — the voice, the paper, and the pictures of the GI war.

narrative_blocks.header: Zanuck hired him off the Pictorial Service
narrative_blocks.body: He was still running the Army's film service in the October of 1945 when Darryl Zanuck wrote offering him work at Twentieth Century-Fox. Three weeks later Zanuck announced that the chief of the Army Pictorial Service would join the studio as a production executive.

narrative_blocks.header: He built the Army's research branch
narrative_blocks.body: He organized and ran the Research Branch of the War Department, the unit that set out to find what American soldiers actually thought. What it learned shaped how the Army informed and led them.

narrative_blocks.header: West Point to brigadier in nineteen years
narrative_blocks.body: He came out of the Military Academy in 1926 a second lieutenant and was a brigadier general by the June of 1945, at forty-one. In between he ran the Army's information branch and then its pictorial service.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the book his father had written
narrative_blocks.body: His father had published a handbook on the systematic development of morale in 1921, out of the Army's Morale Branch. The son put out Leadership for American Army Leaders through the Infantry Journal in the September of 1941.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran NBC television, and foresaw robot cameras
narrative_blocks.body: Running NBC's television network operations, he told the affiliates what was coming: a flying boxcar that could carry a mobile broadcasting unit to any event of public interest, and a remote-control camera worked like a robot plane.

narrative_blocks.header: He was born on a tuberculosis post
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Fort Bayard in New Mexico in the August of 1904 — the Army's tuberculosis hospital, where his father had been sent home from the Philippines to recover. He grew up on posts from California to Hawaii to Georgia.

Organized the Army Research Branch of the War Department. Served in Europe, North Africa, the Middle East and the Pacific. Darryl Zanuck announced on 20 Nov 1945 that he would join Twentieth Century-Fox as a production executive; he supervised production of all Army motion pictures during the war except Air Force technical training films, and the distribution of Army films and Hollywood entertainment pictures to the troops. His papers, including WWI and WWII propaganda posters, phonograph records and 16mm film from the War Department Pictorial Unit, are held as a collection. [081226] AUTHORSHIP OF THE BOOK, asked and answered: 'Leadership for American Army Leaders' (The Infantry Journal, Fighting Forces Series, copyrights 1941/1942/1944, first edition September 1941) is bylined 'Colonel Edward Lyman Munson, Jr.' — it is HIS, not his father's. The father, Brig. Gen. Edward Lyman Munson Sr. (HD3015), wrote the 1921 morale handbook the son worked from, and has his own card. NB5 previously gave the son's title as 'Leadership for the American Soldier', which is wrong; corrected here.
ZANUCK: Darryl F. Zanuck to Lyman Munson Jr., 29 October 1945, Lyman Munson Papers Box 9, American Heritage Center, University of Wyoming — Zanuck hired him as a Twentieth Century-Fox consultant, and mentions his 'marvelous' personal relationship with Gen. Marshall in the same letter. Reproduced in Culbert 1990 vol. III, 146-147; cited in David L. Robb, 'Zanuck Caught in D.C. Gunsights', Variety, 31 Oct 1989. The source article is Sklar/'Adjuncts of Government': Darryl F. Zanuck and 20th Century-Fox in Service to the Executive Branch, 1935-1971 — its frame is Fulbright's 'adjuncts of government' and Nye's 1941 'gigantic engines of propaganda'. NOT written into the card: that argument is about Zanuck and the studio, not about Munson, and putting it on his card would be editorial.
NBC, from the trade-press clippings: as Director of Television Network Operations he announced the appointment of Ernest Theiss as Manager of Production Operations, and Anthony M. Hennig returned from ABC to manage television studio and building operations reporting to him. He spoke on the television session of an NBC affiliates convention alongside Joseph H. McConnell, Edward D. Madden, George H. Frey and Fred Shawn — the source of the flying-boxcar and robot-camera forecast in NB7.
CC CANDIDATE REJECTED: Lyman Ezra Munson (HD0570), Lincoln's Montana territorial justice, is his GRANDFATHER — a family relationship, so the structural link carries it and no CC was written. The Lyman in his name comes down from him.

notable.notable_blurb: Portrait and history painter; founder of Argentine art

narrative_blocks.header: The murder of Maza, painted in 1860
narrative_blocks.body: His most important historical canvas, the Murder of Manuel Vicente Maza of 1860, shows the killing of the former governor of Buenos Aires Province. The same year he painted the Flight of the Malón, a father, mother and son riding away from their burning house after a raid.

narrative_blocks.header: Sarmiento's pupil, then his fellow exile
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamín first studied under Domingo Faustino Sarmiento, his lifelong friend, and in 1842 San Juan's feuds and that friendship drove him into exile in Chile. There he shared Sarmiento's house, studied under the French painter Raymond Monvoisin alongside Sarmiento's sister Procesa, and painted the young Sarmiento; Sarmiento put those years into his Recuerdos de provincia.

narrative_blocks.header: A rescue Sarmiento never made
narrative_blocks.body: His Rescue in the Cordillera of 1855 shows Sarmiento handing out bread to Unitarian soldiers caught in a snowstorm after their defeat at Rodeo del Medio, a heroic episode in which Sarmiento had in fact played no part.

narrative_blocks.header: Sent to Buenos Aires at eighteen
narrative_blocks.body: After lessons in San Juan from Amadeo Gras and Pierre Douet, Benjamín was sent by his father at eighteen to Buenos Aires, where Fernando García del Molino taught him portraits and miniatures. He painted his self-portrait there in 1838 and his brother Guillermo the next year.

narrative_blocks.header: A true painter, then the daguerreotype
narrative_blocks.body: Portraits and miniatures were most of his work, because the wealthy paid well for them. At his 1856 show in Buenos Aires the French painter Jean-Léon Pallière called the drawing correct, the nature perfectly understood and the color that of a true painter, but the daguerreotype soon began taking his sitters.

narrative_blocks.header: Deputy for a year, then back to painting
narrative_blocks.body: In March 1847 Benjamín married Manuela de la Paz Mendieta in San Juan, and that year he was elected a provincial deputy. He resigned and went back to Buenos Aires to study under Martín Boneo.

narrative_blocks.header: Yellow fever took him in 1871
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamín died in Buenos Aires on 14 March 1871 in the yellow fever epidemic, which his brother Guillermo caught fighting beside him and survived. Since 1938 the fine arts museum of San Juan has carried his name.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the book that Amán Rawson smuggled
narrative_blocks.body: Domingo Faustino Sarmiento wrote Facundo in 1845 while in Chilean exile — a devastating attack on the Rosas dictatorship that was banned inside Argentina. He and Benjamín Franklin Rawson shared a house during that exile. It was Amán Rawson — the Hooker descendant from Massachusetts — who smuggled copies of Facundo back into San Juan hidden in drawers reeking of chemical stench, labeled as remedies for venereal diseases.

narrative_blocks.header: He rose from teacher to president of Argentina
narrative_blocks.body: Sarmiento served as president of Argentina from 1868 to 1874, championing public education on a national scale. He had begun as a provincial schoolteacher in San Juan.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught the Hooker line's Benjamin Rawson
narrative_blocks.body: Sarmiento's very first pupil was Benjamin Franklin Rawson, the San Juan boy of Massachusetts Hooker descent. The two shared a house in Chilean exile and stayed friends for life.

narrative_blocks.header: His Facundo became a Latin American classic
narrative_blocks.body: Written in Chilean exile, Sarmiento's Facundo attacked the dictator Rosas through the life of a gaucho strongman, framing a struggle between civilization and barbarism. It is often called the single most important book of nineteenth-century Spanish America.

narrative_blocks.header: He studied schools across Europe and America
narrative_blocks.body: Chile sent Sarmiento abroad in 1845 to examine education systems, and he returned convinced the United States offered Latin America its model. As president he founded teachers' colleges, libraries, and museums for a largely illiterate country.

narrative_blocks.header: From brevet major to Chicago real estate
narrative_blocks.body: Sartell was a captain in the regular 12th U.S. Infantry during the Civil War, and came out of it a brevet major. He settled in Chicago, where he managed real estate for the firm of Isham and Prentice.

narrative_blocks.header: A fur-trade family out of Albany
narrative_blocks.body: Sartell's parents were Ezra Parmalee Prentice and Philena Cheney; his father was a wholesale fur merchant and railroad president who lived at Mount Hope in Albany, and his grandfather Sartell Prentice, whose name he carried, had been an Albany fur-trade merchant.

narrative_blocks.header: An uncle who kept the Brooklyn Bridge's accounts
narrative_blocks.body: Sartell's uncle John Hill Prentice, whose mansion stood on Grace Court in Brooklyn Heights, was treasurer of the New York and Brooklyn Bridge Company. He was an incorporator of Green-Wood Cemetery in 1838, a founder of what became Packer Collegiate Institute, and a Prospect Park commissioner.

narrative_blocks.header: He chose electric light over the law
narrative_blocks.body: Edward broke the family habit of the law. After a start at Marshall Field & Co. in Chicago he became secretary and a director of the General Incandescent Arc Light Company and the New York Electrical Equipment Company, and made his career as an electrical engineer.

narrative_blocks.header: Class president and Skull and Bones
narrative_blocks.body: At Yale, class of 1891, Edward joined Eta Phi as a sophomore, Delta Kappa Epsilon as a junior and Skull and Bones as a senior, and was president of his class. He had prepared at Phillips Andover and the King's School in Stamford.

narrative_blocks.header: First schools in Berlin and Paris
narrative_blocks.body: The family went abroad in the winter of 1871, and Edward, not yet four, had his first schooling in Berlin and Paris; his sister Frances was born in Berlin that January. Chicago schools came after.

narrative_blocks.header: Summers at Ormsby Hill
narrative_blocks.body: Edward married Laura Miller in New York on 14 November 1900, and their three children spent their summers at Ormsby Hill, the family house at Manchester, Vermont. He died in New York in May 1927, at fifty-nine.

narrative_blocks.header: The only Lincoln son to reach thirty
narrative_blocks.body: Eddie died at three, Willie at eleven in the White House, and Tad at eighteen. Robert alone came through, and outlived them all by more than half a century, dying in his sleep at Manchester at eighty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: At Appomattox, then Ford's five days later
narrative_blocks.body: Commissioned a captain in February 1865, he spent the last weeks of the war on Grant's immediate staff — a place that kept him well clear of any fighting. He stood at Appomattox Court House on 9 April when Lee surrendered. His father was shot five days after that.

narrative_blocks.header: The firm carried his name for a century
narrative_blocks.body: He finished his law studies in Chicago after the assassination and came to the bar in 1867, joining Edward Swift Isham's practice as junior partner in 1872. The firm kept the name for a hundred and sixteen years.

narrative_blocks.header: He turned down one post and took another
narrative_blocks.body: He refused Hayes's offer of the assistant secretaryship of state in 1877, then served as Garfield's Secretary of War and stayed on under Arthur until 1885. narrative_blocks.header: He stockpiled pig-iron before the Civil War
narrative_blocks.body: Sinton saw the Civil War coming and bought pig iron to hold rather than sell. When the war drove prices up, he unloaded the stockpile at wartime rates, and that one bet made much of the fortune that left him among the wealthiest men in America.

narrative_blocks.header: Cincinnati mansion became the Taft Museum of Art
narrative_blocks.body: Sinton lived in the old Longworth mansion on Pike Street, built by Martin Baum in 1820 and the oldest wooden house in downtown Cincinnati. His daughter Anna and her husband Charles Phelps Taft stayed on there, and in 1927 they gave the house and 690 works of art to the city. It opened as the Taft Museum in 1932.

narrative_blocks.header: Four dollars a month at thirteen
narrative_blocks.body: David was three when his family left County Armagh for Pittsburgh in 1811; his Quaker father had made linen. At thirteen he went out as a salesman on four dollars a month. By the 1830s he was managing the ironworks at Hanging Rock, Ohio, and in 1846 he owned them.

narrative_blocks.header: Cincinnati money for Alabama coke iron
narrative_blocks.body: Alabama had yet to prove that coke iron could turn a profit when Colonel Sloss and James Thomas went looking for backers. Sinton came in with the Cincinnati investors, took a majority of the Eureka Company, and by the time Oxmoor merged into the DeBardeleben Coal and Iron Company he practically owned old Oxmoor.

narrative_blocks.header: A Texas town named Sinton
narrative_blocks.body: The town of Sinton, Texas, carries his name, and it came from grazing land, not iron. David was the majority stockholder in the Coleman-Fulton Pasture Company, and the town was named in his honor.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed with two children under six
narrative_blocks.body: David married Jane Ellison at Union Landing, Ohio; she was eighteen years younger. Jane died in 1853, leaving a son, Edward, and a daughter, Anna, both under six. Edward died in 1869, about twenty-one, and Anna was his only surviving child.

narrative_blocks.header: Ohio's richest man, and a president's campaign
narrative_blocks.body: When David died in 1900, at ninety-two, he was the richest man in Ohio, and the whole fortune went to Anna. Her husband, Charles Phelps Taft, was William Howard Taft's older brother, and Sinton money was said to have paid for the campaign that made him president in 1908.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought two papers and built an empire
narrative_blocks.body: In 1879 the lawyer-congressman bought the Times and the Star, merged them into the Cincinnati Times-Star, and installed his brother Peter as publisher — the seed of what grew, through his nephew's radio purchases, into Taft Broadcasting. The paper's loyalty to Boss Cox ran on, to the lasting embarrassment of his half-brother the President.

narrative_blocks.header: Heidelberg, the bar, then one term in Congress
narrative_blocks.body: Columbia law and a Heidelberg degree led home to Cincinnati practice — first at Sage, Haacke and Taft, then beside Gen. Edward Noyes, the future governor — the Ohio legislature, and a single term in the U.S. House from 1895. The family's public life he mostly financed rather than lived.

narrative_blocks.header: His half-brother accepted the presidential nomination
narrative_blocks.body: William Howard Taft accepted the 1908 Republican presidential nomination standing on the portico of Charles Phelps Taft's Cincinnati home at 316 Pike Street — the house their father-in-law David Sinton had purchased and that Charles and Anna later bequeathed to the public as the Taft Museum of Art. The nomination scene on that portico is one of the moments that cement the house's place in American political history.

narrative_blocks.header: The most valuable collection in the West
narrative_blocks.body: By 1908 his pictures were called the West's most valuable — a Rembrandt portrait, Gainsborough's Tompkinson Boys, Goya, Hals, van Dyck, and Duveneck's Cobbler's Apprentice among them, with cases of fine Chinese porcelain besides. His widow's five million to the University of Cincinnati endowed the fund that bears his name.

narrative_blocks.header: He owned the Cubs and the Phillies
narrative_blocks.body: Charles Phelps Taft became a minority owner of the Chicago Cubs in 1905 and helped fund the purchase of the Philadelphia Phillies in 1909 — publicly denying the connection until it became untenable. After serving one term as a congressman and building the Cincinnati Times-Star into the foundation of a media empire, his greatest business legacy was baseball. He sold the Cubs after the 1915 season and his estate, the Taft Museum of Art, is now open to the public.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten boys at Pelham Manor started it
narrative_blocks.body: He left a Yale Latin tutorship in 1890 to open a school with about ten students; three years later he moved them into a Civil War-era hotel at Watertown, and in 1898 gave the school his name. It grew into one of the leading preparatory schools in America.

narrative_blocks.header: The law lasted a year
narrative_blocks.body: Yale 1883 — the Commencement speech, the Townsend Prize for speaking, the Porter Prize for a thesis on municipal government — then Cincinnati Law and a year in his father's firm before he admitted the profession did not appeal to him. Latin tutoring at Yale showed him where his life actually was.

narrative_blocks.header: A visit to Ojai settled everything
narrative_blocks.body: In 1889 he traveled to Sherman Thacher's new boys' school in California's Ojai Valley — a Yale friendship carried into lifelong correspondence — and came home resolved. Within the year he had a school of his own, and the two founders exchanged letters the rest of their lives.

narrative_blocks.header: Schoolmaster; no other experience
narrative_blocks.body: Connecticut's 1917 military questionnaire asked the fifty-five-year-old what he could offer the war effort; the six-foot-four headmaster answered that he was a schoolmaster and had no other experience. He taught his civics course until the year he died, and published Memories and Opinions the year before.

narrative_blocks.header: As a boy he met Sherman and Grant
narrative_blocks.body: Horace Dutton Taft's 1942 memoir Memories and Opinions records a childhood trip to Washington where his mother introduced him to General Sherman and President Grant. Sherman was 'spry and chatty and joked with his father, who was then Secretary of War.' Grant 'was about as cheerful and communicative as a tombstone.' On the way home at the 1876 Philadelphia Centennial, he saw an early telephone demonstration. Some people, he was told, foolishly believed 'we should soon be able to talk all over town.'

narrative_blocks.header: Seventeen years, then the school alone
narrative_blocks.body: Winifred Thompson, a Buffalo-born art teacher at a New Haven high school, married him in 1892 and died of cancer in December 1909; there were no children. The school became the family.

narrative_blocks.body: As superintendent of the Big Four's Cleveland division he skipped the parlor car and rode a handcar down his own line -- chilled and travel-stained, taking his turn at the pumps. He would stop to climb under trestles and walk the ties for a mile, learning every section crew and every inch of roadbed.

narrative_blocks.header: His father ran the Big Four before him
narrative_blocks.body: His father, Melville Ezra Ingalls, was president of the Big Four and Cornelius Vanderbilt's Midwest man on the New York Central. Asked if he was truly his father's son, Albert shot back 'You bet I am' -- then climbed the same roads to a vice-presidency of his own.

narrative_blocks.body: Dying in 1961, she left the University of Cincinnati a dedicated Classics endowment in her husband's honor — the largest gift in the university's history to that time — with bequests besides to the Taft Museum, the Art Museum, Christ Church, and Children's Hospital. notable.notable_blurb: The Navy's only World War I ace

narrative_blocks.header: The Navy's only First World War ace
narrative_blocks.body: Leaving Yale at eighteen with the First Yale Unit, David flew Sopwith Camels with the RAF's 213 Squadron over Flanders, sixty-three missions in all, and was credited with six victories, the only ace the Navy produced in that war.

narrative_blocks.header: A pipe-smoking woman in a Flanders field
narrative_blocks.body: In September 1918, his engine dead, David glided toward a field where a woman sat smoking a pipe, a sight he had never seen. The engine caught again behind the German lines, and coming at them from the rear he shot down a Fokker D.VII.

narrative_blocks.header: He tripled the Navy's aircraft for Hoover
narrative_blocks.body: After Harvard Law and two terms in the Ohio House, where he co-wrote the state's aviation code, David became Hoover's Assistant Secretary of the Navy for Aeronautics in 1929. He tripled the Navy's aircraft and pressed for carrier task forces.

narrative_blocks.header: Back in uniform for the Pacific war
narrative_blocks.body: In 1941 David was running Pan American's air ferries; after Pearl Harbor he went back into the Navy, served at Guadalcanal and commanded the air station at Pearl Harbor, retiring a rear admiral. He had helped his friend Lindbergh chart Pan Am's routes to the Orient.

narrative_blocks.header: Taft's campaign, then the Times-Star
narrative_blocks.body: David managed his cousin Robert A. Taft's 1952 run for the Republican nomination, then became president and publisher of the Cincinnati Times-Star and vice chairman of Taft Broadcasting, before going back to the law in 1958.

narrative_blocks.header: Fourteen thousand hours in the air
narrative_blocks.body: David logged more than fourteen thousand hours and in his last years still flew himself from the Chagrin River airfield in a Beechcraft King Air. Yale's Ingalls Rink carries his name and his son's, and he entered the National Aviation Hall of Fame in 1983.

narrative_blocks.header: President Taft's grandnephew
narrative_blocks.body: His mother, Jane Taft, was a niece of President William Howard Taft, and he was named for his great-grandfather, the industrialist David Sinton. In 1922 he married Louise Hale Harkness, of the Standard Oil fortune.

notable.notable_blurb: First Lady who planted D.C.'s cherry blossoms

narrative_blocks.header: She visited the White House at 17
narrative_blocks.body: Helen Herron visited the White House at age 17 as the guest of President Hayes, an intimate friend of her parents. The visit set an ambition. When her husband was repeatedly offered the Supreme Court seat he actually wanted more than the presidency, it was Nellie who pushed him toward Washington.

narrative_blocks.header: She ordered the cherry trees planted around
narrative_blocks.body: Nellie Taft requested the Japanese cherry trees that were planted along the Tidal Basin in 1912 — they are among Washington's most lasting landmarks. She did not get to enjoy them fully: on May 17, 1909, just ten weeks after the inauguration, she suffered a severe stroke on the presidential yacht. Taft spent hours each day teaching her to speak again.

narrative_blocks.header: A half hour that changed the Court
narrative_blocks.body: When Roosevelt weighed her husband for a Supreme Court seat in 1906, she went to the President herself and talked him out of it in a half-hour meeting. The White House, not the bench, was the ambition — and it was hers first.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten weeks in, a stroke took her voice
narrative_blocks.body: On a Potomac cruise in May 1909 she collapsed, losing her speech and the use of her right side. The President spent hours each day teaching her to speak again; by the silver anniversary gala of 1911, five thousand guests saw her fully returned.

narrative_blocks.header: First to ride beside him from the Capitol
narrative_blocks.body: On inauguration day 1909 she rode with her husband in the parade from the Capitol to the White House — the first presidential wife ever to do so.

notable.notable_blurb: 'Mr. Republican' — three-time presidential candidate

narrative_blocks.header: He was first in his class
narrative_blocks.body: Robert Alphonso Taft graduated first in his class from The Taft School — run by his uncle Horace Dutton Taft. He then finished first at Yale (class of 1910) and first at Harvard Law School (1913), where he edited the Harvard Law Review. He scored the highest mark in Ohio on the bar exam.

narrative_blocks.header: He condemned the Nuremberg trials
narrative_blocks.body: In 1946, Robert Taft condemned the Nuremberg trials as 'victor's justice' under ex post facto law: 'About this whole judgment there is the spirit of vengeance, and vengeance is seldom justice.' His own party turned on him. The condemnation is widely credited with costing him the 1948 Republican presidential nomination. Senator John F.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran for president three times and lost
narrative_blocks.body: Robert Taft sought the Republican presidential nomination in 1940, 1948, and 1952 — the front-runner each time, denied each time. In 1952, with Dewey no longer a candidate, Taft appeared certain to win. Then the moderates convinced Dwight Eisenhower to enter.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife suffered a stroke in 1950
narrative_blocks.body: Martha Taft suffered a severe stroke in May 1950 that left her unable to walk or care for herself. His biographer called it 'the deepest personal blow of his life.' Taft called her every night he was away, read to her at home, pushed her wheelchair at public functions and helped feed her. His public image was cold and intellectually distant; what he did privately for Martha belied every bit of it.

narrative_blocks.header: Named one of the Senate's five greatest
narrative_blocks.body: From 1939 until his death he anchored the Senate's conservative wing so completely that the press simply called him 'Mr. Republican,' and he led the coalition that blocked the New Deal's expansion. In 1957 a Senate committee named him one of the five greatest senators in the body's history, beside Clay, Webster, Calhoun, and La Follette.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the law that reined in unions
narrative_blocks.body: After the strike wave of 1945 and 1946 he co-authored the Taft-Hartley Act, which banned the closed shop, opened the way to state right-to-work laws and tightened federal limits on organized labor; Congress passed it over Truman's veto. A generation earlier Talcott Huntington Russell had drafted Connecticut's workmen's compensation act, which ran the other way — the first pulling protection toward labor, the second pulling power back from it.

notable.notable_blurb: Dean and acting president of Bryn Mawr

narrative_blocks.header: A dean at twenty-six
narrative_blocks.body: Two years after finishing her Bryn Mawr degree she was its dean — at twenty-six — and the college’s acting president by 1919. A suffragist who stumped the country for the vote, she ran the deanship until 1941 and the history department until 1957.

narrative_blocks.header: A year away to nurse the First Lady
narrative_blocks.body: She left college for 1909-1910 to stand in for her mother at the White House after Nellie Taft’s stroke — then went back, finished, and became a history professor at Bryn Mawr. She lived to ninety-five.

narrative_blocks.header: Katharine Hepburn met her first love here
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband's closest friend, the poet Phelps Putnam, was so fixed in the household that it was likely here the young Katharine Hepburn first met him. Hepburn later called Putnam her first male lover, writing that she 'flew up onto a pink cloud' the moment she saw him.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept publishing history into old age
narrative_blocks.body: After stepping down as dean she taught history at Bryn Mawr until 1957 and went on researching and publishing for decades beyond retirement. The scholarship outlasted the administration; she remained a working historian into her later years.

narrative_blocks.header: On the morning his mother had her stroke
narrative_blocks.body: May 17, 1909: On the same morning that First Lady Nellie Taft suffered her severe stroke on the presidential yacht, eleven-year-old Charles Phelps Taft II was undergoing what his biographers noted as a 'bloody adenoid operation.' The president's household absorbed two medical crises simultaneously. Charles was not told about his mother's stroke until he recovered.

narrative_blocks.header: Fortune called his Cincinnati the best-managed big city
narrative_blocks.body: Charles Phelps Taft II served as Mayor of Cincinnati from 1955 to 1957, during which Fortune magazine ranked Cincinnati the best-managed large city in the United States. He was known as 'Mr. Cincinnati.' He was also known for keeping a canoe tied to his car at all times, in anticipation of his next trip. When he died in 1983, his family had 'Gone fishing' inscribed on his grave at Spring Grove Cemetery.

narrative_blocks.header: He and his brother Robert founded the law
narrative_blocks.body: In 1924, Charles Phelps Taft II and his brother Robert A. Taft co-founded Taft Stettinius & Hollister in Cincinnati — a firm that continues to carry the Taft name. He had been youngest-ever president of the International YMCA, served as Hamilton County Prosecutor, and helped introduce the city manager form of government that Cincinnati — the first major city to adopt it — still uses today.

narrative_blocks.header: Polio at fourteen; a Yale PhD anyway
narrative_blocks.body: As a teenager Cynthia and her younger sister Rosalyn both caught polio; Rosalyn died at eleven, and Cynthia was left paralyzed from the waist down. She went on to Vassar, a master's at the London School of Economics, and a Yale doctorate in 1959 under the labor economist Lloyd Reynolds.

narrative_blocks.header: Three books with Irma Adelman
narrative_blocks.body: With Irma Adelman, Cynthia pioneered quantitative studies of what drives economic development, arguing that no economy could be explained without its politics and institutions. Their work ran from Society, Politics, and Economic Development in 1967 to Comparative Patterns of Economic Development, 1850 to 1914, in 1988.

narrative_blocks.header: She out-sang a polka band
narrative_blocks.body: Elected president of the Economic History Association in 1994, Cynthia gave her presidential address on which capitalist institutions spread capitalism's benefits widely, while a polka band with a tuba played in the next room. She raised her voice again and again, then sang her conclusion over the tuba, and the room stood to applaud.

narrative_blocks.header: Did the Marshall Plan raise wages?
narrative_blocks.body: Working for the Marshall Plan in Paris, Cynthia gathered wage data from the capitals of Western Europe to answer one question: had the Plan raised the workers' standard of living? She later joined the World Bank as Hollis Chenery was building its research department.

narrative_blocks.header: A causal diagram every week
narrative_blocks.body: Cynthia held a chair at Smith for fifteen years, one of the few women senior economists in the country, and taught eighteen years at American University, where her students drew a causal diagram every week. Retired at seventy, she came back to American as its Distinguished Economist in Residence.

narrative_blocks.header: He interviewed Mussolini and Trotsky
narrative_blocks.body: As editor and publisher of the Cincinnati Times-Star, Hulbert Taft secured interviews with Benito Mussolini in 1929 and Leon Trotsky. The journalist John Gunther, in his book Inside U.S.A., described Taft as 'the most conservative man I met in forty-eight states.' Political candidates in Cincinnati viewed his endorsements as 'tantamount to election.'

narrative_blocks.header: The employees outbid him for the Enquirer
narrative_blocks.body: Publisher after his uncle Charles's death in 1929, he tried in 1952 to buy the rival Cincinnati Enquirer — and lost the bidding war to the Enquirer's own employees, who pooled their assets to top him. When the Times-Star itself sold to Scripps-Howard in 1958, he was reportedly the only family member opposed.

narrative_blocks.header: The paper became Taft Broadcasting
narrative_blocks.body: The 1939 purchase of WKRC radio from CBS seeded Radio Cincinnati, and when the paper sold, the broadcast side reorganized as Taft Broadcasting — the family name carried from an afternoon daily onto television screens nationwide.

narrative_blocks.header: He married his late wife's niece
narrative_blocks.body: When his first wife, Nellie Leaman, died in 1927, he married her niece Virginia Kittredge the following year. His third wife, Eleanor Gholson, whom he wed in 1946, was in turn a distant relative of Virginia's.

narrative_blocks.header: He grew Taft Broadcasting into a national power
narrative_blocks.body: As president and then chairman he pushed the family's Cincinnati newspaper and radio holdings into a national broadcasting company, buying television stations across the country. narrative_blocks.header: He bought the studio behind the Flintstones
narrative_blocks.body: In 1966 his company bought Hanna-Barbera, the cartoon studio behind the Flintstones and Yogi Bear. A Cincinnati broadcasting family suddenly owned one of the biggest names in American animation.

narrative_blocks.header: He died in a bomb shelter he built
narrative_blocks.body: In November 1967 a liquid-propane explosion demolished the bomb shelter he had built on his Indian Hill estate, and killed him. His son Dudley took his seat on the company board days later and eventually led it.

narrative_blocks.header: His old school named its library for him
narrative_blocks.body: A major patron of the arts in Cincinnati, he was remembered at his old school two years after his death, when the Taft School dedicated its new library in his name. It still anchors the campus his great-uncle Horace Dutton Taft had founded.

narrative_blocks.header: She helped found Cincinnati's preservation
narrative_blocks.body: In 1964 Margot and two other women founded the Miami Purchase Association to save Fort Miami. It widened to buildings across the region and, renamed the Cincinnati Preservation Association, shaped the city's historic districts and law.

narrative_blocks.header: She sat on the museum's founding committee
narrative_blocks.body: When Indian Hill debated what to do with its vacated Little Red Schoolhouse in 1973, she joined the steering committee that turned the building into a historical museum. The effort grew into the Indian Hill Historical Society.

narrative_blocks.header: A classics fellowship still carries her name
narrative_blocks.body: The Margo Taft Tytus Visiting Fellowship in the University of Cincinnati's classics department brings scholars there to research and write. Its fellows have worked on everything from the Parthenon frieze to childhood in ancient Greece.

narrative_blocks.header: He lost the seat and took it anyway
narrative_blocks.body: He was declared beaten by William Crawford in 1898 and contested it. The House turned Crawford out in May 1900 and seated him for the last ten months of the term, the third of the three Congresses he sat in.

narrative_blocks.header: Roosevelt sent him to Persia
narrative_blocks.body: Theodore Roosevelt made him consul at Genoa in 1901, minister to Persia the year after, and minister to Greece and Montenegro in 1907. He had begun at twenty-two as consul at Verviers and Liège in Belgium.

narrative_blocks.header: He built a Richmond Hill of his own
narrative_blocks.body: His father's house on the Yadkin was called Richmond Hill, and the Victorian manor he and Gabrielle raised near Asheville took the same name. He died in it in 1923.

narrative_blocks.header: The house became a museum, then an inn
narrative_blocks.body: His daughter kept it after him and it opened as a museum in the fifties. The Preservation Society of Asheville moved the whole building to save it from demolition, and it burned on a night in March 2009.

narrative_blocks.header: Two of their four children grew up
narrative_blocks.body: The first Richmond died at one and the second at fifteen. Marjorie and Thomas both lived into old age at Asheville, and neither of them married.

narrative_blocks.header: Horner Military Academy, then Princeton
narrative_blocks.body: He went from Horner Military Academy to Princeton, read law, and was admitted to the bar in 1874. He sat a single term in the North Carolina House in the middle eighties before Congress.

narrative_blocks.header: His nephew made major general
narrative_blocks.body: Richmond P. Davis, son of his sister Mary Williams, rose to major general in the United States Army and died at Washington in 1937.

notable.notable_blurb: Governor of North Carolina, 1889 to 1891

narrative_blocks.header: He governed from an unfinished mansion
narrative_blocks.body: Daniel was the first governor to live in the present Executive Mansion at Raleigh, moving into the unfinished house with his own furniture and filing a careful list of it with the state treasurer so no one would mistake whose was whose. He died there on 7 April 1891, and his ghost is said to walk it still.

narrative_blocks.header: Railroads, schools and college for women
narrative_blocks.body: As governor Daniel created and chaired a railroad commission to guard the people and the railroads alike against abuse of power, urged a tax levy where counties could not keep a four-month school year, and gave part of his 1891 message to higher education for women.

narrative_blocks.header: Off the bench rather than obey the army
narrative_blocks.body: Appointed a superior court judge in 1865 and then elected for life by the legislature, Daniel stepped down in 1867 rather than carry out the orders of the military commander of the Carolinas under Reconstruction.

narrative_blocks.header: He opposed secession and enlisted anyway
narrative_blocks.body: Against secession, Daniel volunteered as a private in the Raleigh Rifles once the state had gone, helped raise the 31st North Carolina, and was captured with it on Roanoke Island in February 1862. Paroled a fortnight later, he was made adjutant general by Governor Vance in 1863 and resigned after a quarrel.

narrative_blocks.header: He married his law teacher's daughter
narrative_blocks.body: Daniel finished first in his class at William Bingham's school, graduated from Princeton in 1851, and read law at Richmond Hill under Judge Richmond Mumford Pearson. In 1856 he married Pearson's daughter Ellen Brent, who died in 1862 at twenty-three.

narrative_blocks.header: Sworn in at a warehouse in the rain
narrative_blocks.body: Rain on 17 January 1889 drove Daniel's inauguration indoors to Stronach's Warehouse. Soon after, his reception for the legislators at the mansion began a tradition of welcome that later governors kept.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter served as first lady
narrative_blocks.body: Of Daniel's children by his second wife, Mary Haywood, Helen acted as first lady at the mansion, Fabius was killed as a boy in a hunting accident, and Daniel Jr. served in the Spanish-American War, the Philippines and the First World War.

narrative_blocks.header: On the day he was born
narrative_blocks.body: When Alfred Wild Gardner was born on December 17, 1929, his father Henry Burchell Gardner — himself St. Paul's Form of 1909 and Harvard All-American — immediately sent a Western Union telegram to St. Paul's requesting that Alfred be added to the admissions list. Alfred enrolled in 1943 as a Second Former, lettered in football, hockey, and crew. His grandfather Junius Morgan had been St. Paul's Form of 1884 — three consecutive generations at the same school.

narrative_blocks.header: He built a ranch on the Fryingpan River
narrative_blocks.body: A fanatical fly-fisherman, he bought and developed Otto Creek Ranch along the Fryingpan River near Aspen in 1969, and three years later left banking and the East for good. He started a real-estate firm in Basalt and spent the rest of his life within reach of the water.

narrative_blocks.header: Eighteen years at the bank, then Colorado
narrative_blocks.body: He spent eighteen years with First National City Bank — the Personal Banking Division, then vice president in Commodities — with a Harvard management program along the way. In 1972 he traded all of it for a house he built on a Colorado river.

narrative_blocks.header: He outlived his wife and his son
narrative_blocks.body: His son Burchell died in 1977, and his first wife Sandra in 1996; he retired the year after losing her. In 1998 he married Katharine Wert, also widowed, and they divided their years between Colorado, the New Jersey shore, and the California desert.

narrative_blocks.header: He faced the North across the Panmunjom table
narrative_blocks.body: Three decades of sea duty crested at Korea — commander of U.S. naval forces and the U.N. Command's naval component, and in 1974 senior member of the Armistice Commission, sitting opposite the North Koreans at Panmunjom. The Legion of Merit capped the 1975 retirement.

narrative_blocks.header: Four submarines, then ships of his own
narrative_blocks.body: Commissioned in October 1944 out of an accelerated wartime Harvard, he served aboard four submarines and rose to command the USS Tusk, the tender Fulton, and the missile cruiser Providence. The banker's great-grandson chose the wardroom over the boardroom.

narrative_blocks.header: An admiral married the admirals' daughter
narrative_blocks.body: His second marriage, in 1973, joined him to Sandy McCain — daughter and granddaughter of four-star admirals, sister of the senator and Navy flier John McCain. His grandfather had run the Navy as Hoover's secretary; the wardroom ran on both sides of the family.

narrative_blocks.header: The admiral went back to school
narrative_blocks.body: Retirement at fifty came with a George Washington law degree and twelve years of admiralty practice at Houston with Vinson and Elkins — the sea from the other side of the docket. Gibson Island and Annapolis held the last decades.

narrative_blocks.header: His sixteenth Bermuda Race at eighty-five
narrative_blocks.body: Sailing since 1930, when he was six, he crossed to Bermuda for the sixteenth time in 2010 — and was still coaching the Naval Academy's offshore sailing team and racing Wednesday nights until the week before his death in May 2011. Arlington took the admiral; the Severn kept the sailor.

narrative_blocks.header: Trained in Rome under Franco Ferrara
narrative_blocks.body: After Harvard and two years in the Army, Miles studied conducting in Rome with Franco Ferrara at the Accademia di Santa Cecilia, then assisted Dean Dixon at the Frankfurt Radio Orchestra. He went on to direct the Associazione Musicale Romana and, from 1976, the Bangor Symphony Orchestra in Maine.

narrative_blocks.header: The last living witness to Anne Morgan
narrative_blocks.body: Miles's great-aunt Anne Morgan ran the relief of devastated France from the Château de Blérancourt after the First World War, and the museum's friends called him the last living witness to her. He toured an exhibition on her 350 women volunteers through eighteen American cities, and in 2019 brought the film Anne Morgan's War to 951 PBS markets.

narrative_blocks.header: A surprise visit for Blérancourt's centennial
narrative_blocks.body: In July 2024, six weeks before he died at ninety-five, Miles turned up unannounced at the Château de Blérancourt for the museum's hundredth year and studied the new gallery of photographs of his great-aunt. He had sat on its scientific committee when it was rebuilt and reopened in 2016.

narrative_blocks.header: France's gold medal on his ninety-fifth birthday
narrative_blocks.body: France made Miles a member of the Légion d'Honneur and an Officier of the Ordre des Arts et des Lettres, and on his ninety-fifth birthday La Renaissance Française gave him its gold medal at the ambassador's residence in Washington. He spoke the language fluently.

narrative_blocks.header: A Janus Films director, 1956 to 1963
narrative_blocks.body: From 1956 to 1963 Miles was a director of Janus Films, the company that brought Ingmar Bergman and Akira Kurosawa to American art-house audiences. He had been one of its original officers.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-three years at the Bamboo Organ Festival
narrative_blocks.body: An early-music man, Miles sat on the boards of the Boston Early Music Festival and the Venice Music Festival. From 1982 to 2005 he was a regular at the Bamboo Organ Festival at Las Piñas in the Philippines, and from 2000 to 2017 an artistic director of the Tropical Baroque Festival in Miami.

narrative_blocks.header: Life partner of Richard de Combray
narrative_blocks.body: Miles was the third of the five sons of Henry Sturgis Morgan, a founder of Morgan Stanley, and his life partner was the writer Richard de Combray, who died in 2013. Over the years he made his homes in New York, Rome, Paris, Venice and Miami.

narrative_blocks.header: He won Olympic gold in sailing at Helsinki
narrative_blocks.body: John Adams Morgan competed at the 1952 Summer Olympics in Helsinki in the 6 Metre class, winning gold with the boat Llanoria as part of a six-person crew. He was 21 years old. He graduated from Yale the following year, in 1953.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded the boutique bank Morgan Joseph
narrative_blocks.body: After careers at Dominick & Dominick and Smith Barney (VP and vice chairman of M&A), Morgan told the New York Times in 1986: 'The physical and mental pressures of investment banking are tremendous. Here the atmosphere is more pleasant and the pace is survivable.' The Times noted that in banking 'pedigree opens doors' — his Morgan name built 'the network of relationships, alliances and directorships that has made his small house among the most profitable of the new investment boutiques.' He co-founded Morgan Joseph in 2002 and chaired it until 2016.

narrative_blocks.header: He owned a 3.5-acre private island off Stamford
narrative_blocks.body: John Adams Morgan owned Caritas Island, a 3.5-acre private island compound off the coast of Stamford, Connecticut, with a 26-room, 14,000-square-foot home originally built in 1906. He listed it for sale in 2011 for $18.9 million.

narrative_blocks.header: He served on the Morgan Library board
narrative_blocks.body: He sat on the board of the Morgan Library and Museum for thirty-five years, until his death in January 2025. He was the great-grandson of J.P. Morgan, who founded it, and the son of Henry Sturgis Morgan, who long presided over it.

narrative_blocks.header: He held the Navy together through the slump
narrative_blocks.body: Hoover made him Secretary of the Navy in March 1929, seven months before the crash. He spent four years arguing the fleet's case in public and keeping its strength and efficiency intact on Depression money.

narrative_blocks.header: At London he would not go below Britain
narrative_blocks.body: At the London naval conference of 1930 he held out for parity with the Royal Navy and got it. Hoover wrote later that had he known Adams at the start of his term as he did at the end, he would have made him Secretary of State.

narrative_blocks.header: He steered Resolute past Lipton's challenger
narrative_blocks.body: He took the helm of Resolute in the 1920 America's Cup against Sir Thomas Lipton's Shamrock IV and won it after losing the first two races. They called him the Dean of American Helmsmen, and the Cup's hall of fame took him in 1993.

narrative_blocks.header: Three cups nobody had taken in one year
narrative_blocks.body: In 1939 he won the King's Cup, the Astor Cup and the Puritan Cup — the three most coveted American yachting trophies — in a single season. He was seventy-three that summer.

narrative_blocks.header: He saved two famous ships from the breakers
narrative_blocks.body: Presiding over the Massachusetts Historical Society in 1903, he asked Congress to restore the frigate Constitution; she was opened to the public in 1907. In 1939 he led the committee that kept the whaler Charles W. Morgan.

narrative_blocks.header: Mayor of Quincy, then forty-three boards
narrative_blocks.body: Quincy elected him mayor in 1896 and turned him out a year later. He had read law at Harvard, and was at one point an officer of forty-three corporations — the New Haven and the Union Pacific among them, and Harvard itself.

narrative_blocks.header: Two presidents behind him, and an uncle
narrative_blocks.body: He was a great-grandson of John Quincy Adams and a great-great-grandson of John Adams. The Charles Francis Adams he was named for was his uncle, not his father; his father was John Quincy Adams II, whose brother had daughters first.

narrative_blocks.header: She saved her ancestor John Jay's childhood home
narrative_blocks.body: Jane-Kerin Moffat was a direct descendant of John Jay, first Chief Justice of the United States. In the 1980s, the 23-acre Jay Estate in Rye, New York — where Jay had spent his childhood — was slated for development. She spent thirteen years rallying 65 environmental, historic, and government groups into the Jay Coalition.

narrative_blocks.header: She organized 180 groups for Long Island Sound
narrative_blocks.body: As coordinator of the National Audubon Society's Long Island Sound Watershed Alliance, Jane-Kerin brought together more than 180 organizations. She held hearings along the Connecticut and New York coasts to document the Sound's decline, and co-authored the report that followed.

narrative_blocks.header: The Audubon called her its 'One Sound Lady'
narrative_blocks.body: She convened a Citizens Summit that drew 200 environmentalists and legislators from both states to plan the Sound's recovery. The National Audubon Society honored her with its Activist Award and profiled her in 2000 as 'One Sound Lady.'

narrative_blocks.header: Continental Army veteran and DAR Patriot Ancestor
narrative_blocks.body: Jotham Tuttle served as a Private in the American Revolution under Captain Stephen Goodyear and later with the 2nd Connecticut Regiment. He is documented as a Daughters of the American Revolution Patriot Ancestor (A131826), meaning his Revolutionary War service has been verified by the DAR. He married Kezia Munson in New Haven in 1780, four days after she turned 17.

narrative_blocks.header: Remarried four months after his first wife's death
narrative_blocks.body: Jotham Tuttle's first wife Kezia Munson died August 2, 1799 at age 36, leaving him with five children ranging from infancy to 17 years old. He married his second wife, Elizabeth Perkins, on December 2, 1799 — exactly four months and a day after Kezia's death. Quick widowhood remarriage was common in early American farming families with young children needing maternal care.
