narrative_blocks.header: Seven documented children with Thankful Asenath Perkins
narrative_blocks.body: Eli Tuttle and his wife Thankful Asenath Perkins Tuttle had seven documented children between 1807 and the late 1820s. Five of the seven were Lucius (1807-1885 who stayed in Hamden), Leonard (1810-1875 Ohio migration), Lauren (1815-1860 two wives), Mehitable Tuttle Cooper (1819-1868 two husbands), and Lucy (died 1827). Two more — Louisa and Asahel — died young.

narrative_blocks.header: Daughter Louisa died as an infant in 1822
narrative_blocks.body: Eli and Thankful's daughter Louisa Tuttle was born in 1821 and died in 1822 — an infant death within her first year. The early death was one of three children Eli outlived: Louisa as infant; Lucy who died in 1827 as a young child; and Asahel by 1850 in his adulthood. The cumulative loss across both childhood and adult-child mortality was typical of nineteenth-century rural Connecticut family experience.

narrative_blocks.header: Born and died in Hamden, Connecticut
narrative_blocks.body: Eli Tuttle was born December 28, 1781 in Hamden, New Haven County Connecticut, son of Jotham Tuttle and Kezia Munson Tuttle. He died April 21, 1844 in Hamden at age sixty-two and is buried at Mount Carmel Burying Ground, Hamden. The lifelong-Hamden residence pattern was common among the Tuttle-Munson cluster of north New Haven County families.

b. Aug 1, 1809 Lee Berkshire Co. MA; d. Oct 22, 1883 St. Louis MO at daughter Mary's home. Son of Elisha Foote Sr. (d. Apr 8, 1846) and Delia (née Battle) Foote. NOTE ON NAME: 'Elisha Foote Jr.' means his FATHER was also named Elisha — NOT that he was Eunice's son. Cousin of U.S. Senator Solomon Foot of Vermont. His grandfather/great-uncle Samuel A. Foot served as CT state rep, U.S. Rep., U.S. Senator, and Governor of CT. Albany Institute education. Read law under Judge Daniel Cady (father of Elizabeth Cady Stanton) in Johnstown NY. Admitted to bar; District Attorney then Judge of Court of Common Pleas, Seneca County NY; resigned 1846. Patent law specialist. Stove patent (on wife Eunice's invention) litigated to US Supreme Court 3x as Foote v. Silsby. Board of Examiners-in-Chief US Patent Office 1865-1868. 11th Commissioner of Patents Jul 25, 1868-Apr 25, 1869 — exposed $80,000+ fraud. Founding member National Institute of Applied Sciences 1870. Mathematician: wrote calculus treatise. m. Aug 12, 1841 East Bloomfield NY, Eunice Newton (HD3148). (Wikipedia — Elisha Foote; Patent and Trademark Office Society biography) FOOTE-LINE ANCESTOR (added Stage 6P): Per Abram Foote's 1907 Foote Family genealogy, Elisha Jr.'s line traces back to Nathaniel¹ Foote, Wethersfield founder 1635: Elisha Jr. (1809-1883) → Elisha Foote Sr. (1775-1846, Lee MA) → Jonathan Foote + Deliverance Gibbs → ... → Nathaniel¹. This places Elisha Jr. in the same Foote tree as Almira Mills Foote (I00396) and Eli Foote (X02032). Three Foote-line in-law marriages into the Hooker tree — Almira Mills Foote → Edwin Weed Cowles, Eli Foote → Beecher → Isabella Hooker, and Elisha → Eunice Newton Foote — all share Nathaniel¹ as common ancestor. Source: Foote, Abram. Foote Family: Comprising the Genealogy and History of Nathaniel Foote of Wethersfield, Conn. and his Descendants (1907) Vol. 1, pp. 224-225 + 352-354. institutions.institution_blurb: His wife Eunice Newton Foote attended Troy Female Seminary 1836-1838; Elisha's work as Patent Commissioner and her scientific papers were published in parallel.

narrative_blocks.header: The last commissioner of the old regime
narrative_blocks.body: He was put in on the twenty-fifth of July 1868 to finish the term of a man forced to resign, and was out by the following April — the last before the patent laws were rewritten in 1870. Everyone expected him to be kept on. He would not campaign for it.

narrative_blocks.header: He audited the office and found a hole
narrative_blocks.body: Supplies were over-ordered and under-delivered, prices were exorbitant, and the contracts had been made on handshakes where the law required paper. He also found patents that had been granted for money rather than on merit, complained to the Secretary of the Interior, and got an investigation.

narrative_blocks.header: He argued his own patent three times up
narrative_blocks.body: The automatic draft regulator for stoves — the stove his wife had actually invented — went to the Supreme Court as Foote v. Silsby and was decided there three separate times. It is still cited on publications and disclaimers. He appeared on his own behalf in every one of them.

narrative_blocks.header: A skate, a drying machine, a reaper
narrative_blocks.body: He patented all three, wrote a treatise on the calculus, and read original papers before the scientific societies. In 1870 he was among the founders of the National Institute of Applied Sciences.

narrative_blocks.header: Henry read her paper for her
narrative_blocks.body: He had known Joseph Henry since Albany, and it was Henry who read Eunice's greenhouse paper to the AAAS in 1856, women not being permitted to present. That August the two of them stood together at the dedication of the Dudley Observatory; the one woman in the back row of the painting of it may be her.

narrative_blocks.header: He read law in Cady's Johnstown office
narrative_blocks.body: Judge Daniel Cady took him as a reader while he kept himself by teaching and surveying. Cady's daughter Elizabeth married Henry Stanton, who had read in the same office, and the two couples were friends at Seneca Falls.

notable.notable_blurb: First to describe the greenhouse effect, 1856

narrative_blocks.header: First paper on the greenhouse effect, 1856
narrative_blocks.body: In 1856, Eunice Newton Foote submitted a paper to the AAAS demonstrating that carbon dioxide absorbs significantly more heat than air or hydrogen, and theorizing that higher CO2 levels would raise the Earth's temperature. This was the first known scientific paper to identify the greenhouse effect. Her paper predated John Tyndall's 1859 work by three years.

narrative_blocks.header: She signed the Declaration of Sentiments
narrative_blocks.body: Foote and her husband Elisha were both signatories of the Declaration of Sentiments at the 1848 Seneca Falls Convention, the first gathering focused solely on women's rights. She was one of five women who prepared the proceedings for publication. Elizabeth Cady Stanton was her neighbor; Elisha had purchased the house that the Stanton family moved into in 1847.

narrative_blocks.header: Studied at Troy alongside cousin Almira Phelps
narrative_blocks.body: Eunice Newton attended Troy Female Seminary from 1836 to 1838. During her attendance, Almira Hart Lincoln Phelps — Emma Willard's sister and another Thomas Hooker descendant — was assistant principal, teaching science and writing the botany textbooks used in class. Eunice also studied at the adjacent Rensselaer School under Amos Eaton, learning laboratory methods.

narrative_blocks.header: Her inventions patented in her husband's name
narrative_blocks.body: Eunice Foote was a prolific inventor: a thermostatically controlled cooking stove (1842), a rubber boot insert (1860), and a paper-making machine (1864). She told Elizabeth Cady Stanton in 1868 that half of all patents filed were on women's inventions — but men took out the patents because women couldn't defend them in court. Her husband Elisha collected a substantial infringement settlement on the stove patent.

narrative_blocks.header: Married into the Wethersfield Foote line
narrative_blocks.body: Eunice's 1841 marriage to Elisha Foote folded her into the Foote family that had founded Wethersfield Connecticut in 1635. Her own Hooker descent ran through Mary Hooker and Roger Newton — but her husband's line ran back to Nathaniel Foote, shared with Almira Mills Foote and Eli Foote as the three Foote-line in-laws of the Hooker tree.

narrative_blocks.header: A man had to read her paper aloud
narrative_blocks.body: Women were not permitted to present at the AAAS, so Joseph Henry read Circumstances Affecting the Heat of the Sun's Rays for her in 1856. He had known her husband since their Albany days. No verified likeness of her survives; she was kept out of the frame.

notable.notable_blurb: 'Empress of Sixteenth Street'

narrative_blocks.header: Single-handed and alone, and she won
narrative_blocks.body: For four decades she went before committees of Congress herself to get Meridian Hill developed, and sold the land for the park when they agreed. The Commission of Fine Arts wrote after her death that she won.

narrative_blocks.header: She built a dozen houses and sold embassies
narrative_blocks.body: She bought blocks of Meridian Hill and had the architect George Oakley Totten Jr. design nearly a dozen mansions along 15th and 16th Streets, then sold them to foreign governments. The first was the Pink Palace.

narrative_blocks.header: She got 16th Street renamed for a year
narrative_blocks.body: She wanted 16th Street called the Avenue of the Presidents and lined with busts of every President and Vice-President. The law passed in 1913, the busts were refused, and the old name came back a year later.

narrative_blocks.header: She emptied his wine cellar into the street
narrative_blocks.body: She was a temperance woman married to a man with a thirty-year cellar. When it went, the bottles went into the gutter on Sixteenth Street, with a crowd gathered at the bottom of the hill to watch.

narrative_blocks.header: She led Missouri's suffragists and taught design
narrative_blocks.body: In St. Louis she was president of the Missouri State Suffrage Association, founded the St. Louis School of Design and the Women's Exchange, and studied art at Washington University. She painted and carved wood.

narrative_blocks.header: Three books and a creed of clean living
narrative_blocks.body: She published Practical Cooking and Dinner Giving in 1877, Diet for the Sick in 1885 and The Aristocracy of Health in 1904. At ninety she was still driven to the Lincoln Memorial to walk twice round the reflecting pool.

narrative_blocks.header: At ninety she disinherited her granddaughter
narrative_blocks.body: When her granddaughter Beatrice had her declared mentally incompetent, she answered by making public that Beatrice was not her son's natural daughter. She left most of her estate to her secretary Jesse Shima.

notable.notable_blurb: U.S. senator from Missouri; special prosecutor

narrative_blocks.header: A slave-state senator wrote the slavery ban
narrative_blocks.body: He put a proposal to abolish slavery to the Senate on 11 January 1864, representing Missouri, which was a slave state. The Judiciary Committee folded his draft in with Charles Sumner's and two others, and Congress passed it a year later.

narrative_blocks.header: He voted to acquit and knew the cost
narrative_blocks.body: In May 1868 he broke with his party and voted against convicting Andrew Johnson, one of ten Republicans who did. He did not stand again that autumn, and he never won another election.

narrative_blocks.header: The first special prosecutor, fired by Grant
narrative_blocks.body: Grant named him in 1875 to prosecute the Whiskey Ring at St. Louis, the first special prosecutor the country had had. When the trail reached Grant's own private secretary, Grant dismissed him for impertinence to a grand jury.

narrative_blocks.header: Four parties in five years
narrative_blocks.body: He went into the war a Democrat, took his Senate seat as a Unionist, was nominated in 1863 by the Emancipation party on gradual abolition, and was returned that November as a Radical Unionist. Missouri moved and he moved with it.

narrative_blocks.header: A brigadier general in a state that split
narrative_blocks.body: Commissioned brigadier general of the Missouri State Militia in 1861, he commanded federal forces in the northeast of the state. He went to the Senate that January, into the seat the expelled Trusten Polk had left.

narrative_blocks.header: A farm hand who read himself into law
narrative_blocks.body: Born near Danville in Virginia and taken as a boy to Lincoln County, Missouri, he studied on his own while working as a farm hand and teaching school. He was admitted to the bar in 1844.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a month after the acquittal vote
narrative_blocks.body: He married Mary Foote in June 1868, weeks after the Johnson vote and months before he left the Senate. They built Henderson Castle on Sixteenth Street in Washington and he died there in 1913.

The firing became a scandal; Grant was forced to appoint a replacement prosecutor. [] He voted to acquit Andrew Johnson at impeachment — knowing it would end his Senate career

notable.notable_blurb: Diplomat, malacologist, Smithsonian Regent

narrative_blocks.header: He paid for the expeditions himself
narrative_blocks.body: Shells were a boyhood hobby that turned into thirty years at the National Museum, where he kept his own desk and paid an assistant out of his own pocket. He financed his collecting trips and bought other men's collections outright — Jamaica, Haiti, Cuba, the Lesser Antilles, Hawaii, Japan, China — and published forty-three papers, most of them in The Nautilus. Nearly all the specimens went to the Smithsonian.

narrative_blocks.header: A West Indies lizard carries his name
narrative_blocks.body: Anolis hendersoni, native to the West Indies, was named for him, and he compiled the first index volume of The Nautilus. He wrote American Diplomatic Questions in 1901 and The Cruise of the Tomas Barrera in 1916, the second out of his expedition to Cuba.

narrative_blocks.header: Regent of the Smithsonian, as his father
narrative_blocks.body: In 1911 he was made a citizen member of the Smithsonian Board of Regents and held the seat until he died. His father, the senator who wrote the Thirteenth Amendment, had sat on the same board before him.

narrative_blocks.header: He watched the great powers drill
narrative_blocks.body: Out of Harvard and Columbian law he went to China in 1896 as private secretary to John W. Foster, then advising the Chinese government. The next year he crossed Europe and the Ottoman Empire with General Nelson Miles as a civilian observer of the great powers' armies.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife died after an operation
narrative_blocks.body: Angelica Crosby married him in 1903; in July 1907 she died in a Portland hospital after an operation, while the family was summering at Kennebunkport, leaving their adopted daughter Beatrice at one year old. In 1931 Beatrice tried to have her grandmother Mary Foote Henderson declared incompetent, and Mary answered by making the adoption public and cutting her out of the will.

narrative_blocks.header: Arthur sent him to govern Montana
narrative_blocks.body: Chester Arthur made him fifth governor of Montana Territory in 1883, and he antagonised a Democratic legislature with his veto pen for two years before resigning to take the postmastership. He blocked the cattle interests from getting hold of Yellowstone, and organised one of the largest big-game hunts ever held in the country - the party included the President, his own Secretary of War, and a senator.

narrative_blocks.header: Lincoln thanked him for the dispatches
narrative_blocks.body: During the Red River campaign he carried dispatches through Confederate country to Admiral Farragut, and Lincoln wrote him a letter of thanks for it. He was brevetted four times for gallantry and left the army in 1871 a lieutenant colonel.

narrative_blocks.header: Congress struck him a medal for the wreck
narrative_blocks.body: A squall capsized the yacht Mohawk in New York harbour in July 1876. He got Miss Edith May out alive and went back for the others; Congress voted him a life-saving medal the following year for what it called extreme and heroic daring.

narrative_blocks.header: A band of forgers, and a crown
narrative_blocks.body: As consul at Florence he helped the Italian authorities take and prosecute a band forging public securities. On 29 June 1881 the government thanked him with the Order of the Crown of Italy.

narrative_blocks.header: The valet came at him with a knife
narrative_blocks.body: In January 1913 the Japanese valet who had served him seven years went suddenly insane, took a short knife from Crosby's own collection of old weapons, and came at him in his sickbed. At seventy-three he got up and wrestled the man down until the household came. His obituary said he never recovered from the strain.

narrative_blocks.header: He shot buffalo with Sheridan and Cody
narrative_blocks.body: He helped found the Westchester Polo Club and took the international pigeon-shooting cup at Newport in 1875 against a field that included two Lorillards and Perry Belmont. On buffalo and bear hunts in Wyoming and Montana his companions were Sheridan, Custer, and Buffalo Bill Cody.

narrative_blocks.header: His father gave him one week to decide
narrative_blocks.body: His father Ephraim — a stern Puritan militia captain — told him at sixteen that he had one week to decide whether to receive a college education. John accepted before the week expired. He prepared under the Rev. Timothy Pitkin, then entered Yale in 1763.

narrative_blocks.header: Assumed the governorship when the sitting governor died
narrative_blocks.body: He served as Lieutenant Governor for eleven years under Gov. Jonathan Trumbull Jr. On August 7, 1809, Trumbull died in office, and Treadwell assumed the governorship. He was elected in his own right in 1810, receiving 10,265 votes to 7,185 for the Republican candidate.

narrative_blocks.header: "Father of common school education"
narrative_blocks.body: He negotiated the $1,200,000 sale of northeastern Ohio land to endow the Connecticut School Fund — the permanent foundation for public education in the state. He was appointed to the Board of Managers to administer the Fund and is remembered as "the father of common school education." He also co-founded the Connecticut Academy of Arts and Sciences (incorporated 1799).

narrative_blocks.header: The last Puritan governor
narrative_blocks.body: He is considered the last Puritan governor of Connecticut — in him, wrote his obituary, "we see blended for the last time the theologian and statesman." He was a founding member and President (1798-1822) of the Connecticut Missionary Society, the oldest missionary society in the United States, sending Congregational ministers to new settlements in Vermont, New Hampshire, and western New York.

narrative_blocks.header: Failed as a merchant — recovered by manufacturing nitre
narrative_blocks.body: After Yale he rejected a law career to work the family farm, then ventured into mercantile trade and failed badly. He recovered by manufacturing nitre (saltpetre), extricating himself from the financial loss. He went on to serve as Farmington's Probate Judge for 26 years, which he treasured for the chance to help widows, orphans, and the less fortunate through wills and estates.

narrative_blocks.header: A sister and a daughter married Hooker men
narrative_blocks.body: His sister Mary wed Maj. Roger Hooker of the Continental Line in 1782; a generation on, his daughter Dorothy married Romanta Norton of the same descent. The governor's family joined the Farmington Hookers twice.

narrative_blocks.header: Arrived at Brainerd first — met Ainsworth there
narrative_blocks.body: Harriet came south from Greensboro, Vermont, with her brother John Clark Ellsworth in November 1821 to teach at Brainerd Mission. Ainsworth Blunt arrived the next April, and on 17 November 1822 they married there, in one of the first white weddings in the Cherokee country south of the Tennessee.

narrative_blocks.header: She stayed at the mission in 1838
narrative_blocks.body: When the Cherokees were driven west in 1838, Harriet stayed at the mission while Ainsworth rode with them in a wagon as far as the Mississippi, where ice held the crossing shut for a month and illness sent him home.

narrative_blocks.header: Two daughters buried at Brainerd
narrative_blocks.body: Of the five children Harriet bore at Brainerd, two daughters died young: Harriet Eliza at two in December 1825, and Sarah Elizabeth at eleven days in October 1834.

narrative_blocks.header: The Dalton house she did not see finished
narrative_blocks.body: In 1843 the family moved to Cross Plains, soon to be Dalton, Georgia, where Ainsworth began building the two-story house that still stands on Thornton Avenue. Harriet died in June 1847, before it was finished.

narrative_blocks.header: Carried home to the mission cemetery
narrative_blocks.body: Harriet died at Dalton on 10 June 1847. Her family remembered that her husband carried her to the old mission cemetery at Brainerd on a travois behind one of his horses, to lie beside their two small daughters.

narrative_blocks.header: A woman of rare intelligence
narrative_blocks.body: Those who knew her described Harriet as "a woman of rare intelligence and great piety," with unusual executive ability.

narrative_blocks.header: He sailed south to teach the Cherokee
narrative_blocks.body: In 1822 the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions sent Ainsworth Blunt from Boston to the Brainerd Mission in the Cherokee Nation, where he taught literacy, Christianity, carpentry, and farming. He ran a ferry across Chickamauga Creek and oversaw the mission’s wild oxen, reporting that “much good” was being done.

narrative_blocks.header: A mission wedding among the Cherokee
narrative_blocks.body: On November 17, 1822, Blunt married fellow teacher Harriet Ellsworth at Brainerd Mission Church — one of the earliest recorded white weddings in Cherokee territory south of the Tennessee River. The couple raised their family at the mission station until illness forced a move in 1837.

narrative_blocks.header: He walked part of the Trail of Tears
narrative_blocks.body: When the Cherokee were forced west in 1838, Blunt accompanied them on the Trail of Tears as far as the Mississippi before illness turned him back. He afterward bought part of the former mission property to protect the cemetery where converts and missionaries lay buried.

narrative_blocks.header: From mission farmer to a town’s first mayor
narrative_blocks.body: Resettling at Cross Plains, Georgia, Blunt became its first postmaster and, when the town was incorporated as Dalton in 1847, its first mayor. He helped found the First Presbyterian Church there and built, in 1848, the town’s first two-story house.

narrative_blocks.header: His house became a Union hospital
narrative_blocks.body: The 1848 Blunt House sheltered Confederate General Joseph E. Johnston and his staff in 1863–64, then served as a Union field hospital after the army pushed toward Atlanta. The family refugeed to Illinois in 1864 and returned after the war; Blunt died the following December.

narrative_blocks.header: One bed and one whole chair
narrative_blocks.body: In 1823 Ainsworth wrote home that he and Harriet lived in a log cabin fourteen feet square, daubed with mud, furnished with one bed, one whole chair and one with no back. Their utensils ran to three spoons, three tin cups and four plates, and he was, he said, contented.

narrative_blocks.header: He sailed with Prudden and Eaton in 1637
narrative_blocks.body: Vicar of Saint Stephen's, Coleman Street, Davenport left the Church of England in 1633 for Holland, where his son John was born at The Hague in 1635. In the spring of 1637 he sailed from London with Theophilus Eaton, Peter Prudden and their followers, landing at Boston that June.

narrative_blocks.header: He sat at Anne Hutchinson's trial
narrative_blocks.body: Staying with John Cotton in Boston in March 1638, Davenport sat through the church trial that cast out Anne Hutchinson. That spring he and Eaton led their company to Quinnipiac and founded the New Haven Colony, with Eaton as its governor.

narrative_blocks.header: He hid the regicides Goffe and Whalley
narrative_blocks.body: When the regicides William Goffe and Edward Whalley fled in 1660, Davenport sheltered them in his New Haven home for over a month. He preached a sermon urging his congregation to hide the fugitives.

narrative_blocks.header: A doctored letter and a split church
narrative_blocks.body: Boston's First Church called Davenport in 1667, and he came the next year bearing excerpts of a letter from New Haven that seemed to release him; it was later found to have been cut to mislead. Opponents of his hard line on the Half-Way Covenant left to found the Old South Church, and he died of apoplexy in March 1670 and was laid in John Cotton's tomb.

narrative_blocks.header: He imagined a college before Yale
narrative_blocks.body: Davenport proposed a college for New Haven decades before one existed and helped found its Hopkins School in 1660. Yale was chartered some thirty years after his death, and Davenport College bears his name.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale's first class met in his parsonage
narrative_blocks.body: Chosen first rector of the Collegiate School on 11 November 1701, Abraham would not leave his Killingworth congregation, so the college came to him and its students were taught in his parsonage, where Jacob Hemingway of East Haven was for half a year the whole college.

narrative_blocks.header: The chair Yale's presidents sit in once
narrative_blocks.body: Abraham's great chair of white oak, made at Branford about 1650 with lathe-turned Doric columns for legs and arms, has belonged to the Yale University Art Gallery since 1841. Each new president of Yale sits in it at the installation, and only then.

narrative_blocks.header: He hired Thomas Hooker's grandson to teach
narrative_blocks.body: The first tutor Abraham hired for the college was Daniel Hooker, a grandson of Rev. Thomas Hooker of Hartford. In 1702, at the college's first commencement, Stephen Buckingham of Saybrook took the first degree it ever awarded.

narrative_blocks.header: Trained by Roger Newton at Milford
narrative_blocks.body: After Harvard, class of 1668, Abraham studied theology at Milford under Rev. Roger Newton, Farmington's first pastor, who had trained under Thomas Hooker. At Milford he also came to know Thomas Buckingham, later a fellow founding trustee of the college.

narrative_blocks.header: Newark, Greenwich, then Killingworth
narrative_blocks.body: Abraham assisted his father at Newark and succeeded him there, then preached at Greenwich from 1692 and at Killingworth, now Clinton, from 1694 until he died in office as rector on 5 March 1707. A statue of him stands in the yard of the Morgan School at Clinton.

narrative_blocks.header: Born where his father would not bend
narrative_blocks.body: Abraham was born at Southampton on Long Island in 1646, in a town his father, Rev. Abraham Pierson, had helped found. The elder Pierson moved the family to Branford and, after New Haven was absorbed into Connecticut, to Newark in 1666, each time because he would not compromise on church membership.

narrative_blocks.header: His sister married Davenport's son
narrative_blocks.body: Abraham's sister Abigail married John Davenport Jr., son of the founder of New Haven, who had hoped for a college in the town decades before Yale was chartered and who, like the elder Pierson, rejected the Half-Way Covenant.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight terms, but never two in a row
narrative_blocks.body: The Fundamental Orders that Haynes drafted with Thomas Hooker and Roger Ludlow barred a governor from serving consecutive years. Elected Connecticut's first governor on 11 April 1639, Haynes simply traded chairs with his deputy, holding the top office eight times before he died.

narrative_blocks.header: He beat Roger Ludlow for governor
narrative_blocks.body: Massachusetts Bay expected Roger Ludlow to be its governor in 1635, but Haynes, campaigning to lower taxes, won instead. Ludlow, not even returned as an assistant, charged that deputies had made private deals before the vote, and soon left for the Connecticut River.

narrative_blocks.header: He banished Roger Williams, then regretted it
narrative_blocks.body: Haynes presided in 1635 over the trial that drove Roger Williams out of Massachusetts. Williams later wrote that Haynes came to regret the sentence. The same year Haynes's court banned smoking tobacco and outlawed showy clothes.

narrative_blocks.header: A sin to leave rich land unplowed
narrative_blocks.body: When a Dutch trader protested that Englishmen had seized land he claimed on the Connecticut River, Haynes answered that the Dutchman had never worked it, and that leaving such rich land idle was a sin. The quarrel ran on until the Treaty of Hartford in 1650.

narrative_blocks.header: Two English manors, sunk into Connecticut
narrative_blocks.body: Before sailing Haynes was lord of Gurney's Manor at Hingham in Norfolk and owner of Copford Hall near Colchester. He poured most of that wealth into Connecticut, and his son Hezekiah, an officer in the English Civil War, wrote that it ruined the family in England.

narrative_blocks.header: He crossed on the Griffin with Thomas Hooker
narrative_blocks.body: Haynes and Thomas Hooker were close friends in Puritan Essex, and in 1633 they crossed together on the Griffin, Haynes leaving the young children of his first marriage behind. At Newtowne, now Cambridge, he lodged with Thomas Dudley until his own house was built.

narrative_blocks.header: His granddaughter married a Yale founder
narrative_blocks.body: His son Joseph, born at Hartford in 1642, took the First Church pulpit that Thomas Hooker had founded and held it until he died at thirty-seven in 1679. Joseph's daughter Sarah married James Pierpont in 1694, seven years before Pierpont won Yale its charter.

narrative_blocks.header: She crossed on the Defense at twenty
narrative_blocks.body: Mabel Harlakenden sailed for Massachusetts on the Defense in July 1635, at twenty, with her brother Roger. Her portrait was painted in England just before she left.

narrative_blocks.header: At twenty-one she married the governor
narrative_blocks.body: Within a year of landing, Mabel married John Haynes, a widower twenty years older who had just served as governor of Massachusetts Bay. That same year her brother Roger rode as lieutenant colonel of the militia regiment Haynes commanded.

narrative_blocks.header: Remarried in November, dead by June
narrative_blocks.body: John Haynes died at Hartford in January 1654, and that November Mabel married Rev. Samuel Eaton. An epidemic swept Hartford the next summer and took them both, Mabel in June 1655, at forty.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son Joseph held Hooker's pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: Mabel and John had five children, Ruth, John, Roger, Joseph and Mabel. Joseph, born at Hartford in 1642, became pastor of the First Church that Thomas Hooker had founded, and died there in 1679 at thirty-seven.

narrative_blocks.header: He excommunicated Anne Hutchinson from the pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: At the close of her church trial in March 1638 Wilson pronounced the sentence: "I doe cast you out and deliver you up to Sathan... as a Leper to withdraw your selfe out of the Congregation." She left the colony within the week.

narrative_blocks.header: Mary Dyer: nay, I repent not
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Dyer climbed the Boston gallows on June 1, 1660, having come back to the colony against orders. Wilson called out, "Mary Dyer, O repent, O repent." She answered, "Nay, man, I am not now to repent."

narrative_blocks.header: Hoisted into a tree at the 1637 election
narrative_blocks.body: The Cambridge election of May 1637 turned into a shoving match between the men backing Henry Vane and those backing John Winthrop. Wilson climbed onto the bough of a tree above the crowd and shouted at the freemen to look to their charter.

narrative_blocks.header: He brought up a sagamore's orphaned son
narrative_blocks.body: Wilson was among the first English ministers in New England to preach to the Massachusett, and he took the orphaned son of a sagamore into his household and raised the boy there.

narrative_blocks.header: He would not let anyone paint him
narrative_blocks.body: Wilson refused ever to sit for a portrait — "such a poor vile creature as I am," he said, and the thing was never done. When his house burned he told the neighbours God had meant to give him a better one.

narrative_blocks.header: His father sent him to law school
narrative_blocks.body: Alarmed at his Puritanism, Wilson's father packed him off to the Inns of Court to make a lawyer of him; he went back to Cambridge instead. Dying, the old man told him to keep a good conscience and walk by his own light.

narrative_blocks.header: He and Thomas Hooker overlapped at Emmanuel
narrative_blocks.body: Wilson took his M.A. at Emmanuel College in 1613, where Thomas Hooker was then a fellow. A generation later, in Hartford, Hooker's daughter Sarah married Wilson's son John.

narrative_blocks.header: One of Milford's fifteen founding families
narrative_blocks.body: He arrived in Boston on July 31, 1637 from England as an infant with his family, part of the company that included Rev. John Davenport and Rev. Peter Prudden. On August 22, 1639, the First Church of Christ in Milford was organized, and Thomas was among the founding fifteen families and one of the church's first pillars. He died in 1657 when his son Daniel was twenty-one.

narrative_blocks.header: Son Daniel served as church elder 45 years
narrative_blocks.body: His son Daniel Buckingham was named ruling elder of the First Church of Milford in 1667, ten years after Thomas's death, and held that position until his own death in 1712 — the last person ever to serve in that role. Daniel's second wife was Alice Newton, granddaughter of Rev. Thomas Hooker.

narrative_blocks.header: Thomas Hooker trusted him above all others
narrative_blocks.body: In his 1647 will, Rev. Thomas Hooker named his "beloved friend William Goodwin" as overseer of his estate — the man he trusted to protect his widow and children. After Hooker's death, Goodwin married that widow, Susanna Garbrand Hooker, sometime after 1654.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the widow of his pastor

narrative_blocks.header: A silver medal, and not for sport
narrative_blocks.body: He took a silver medal at the Louisiana Purchase Exposition of 1904 for four landscapes, The Pasture Oaks among them. The Saint Louis fair shared its grounds and its summer with that year's Olympic games. His work hung regularly at the National Academy and the Pennsylvania Academy besides.

narrative_blocks.header: No one his peer in painting trees
narrative_blocks.body: Charles Vezin, a fellow painter at Old Lyme, said no one was his peer in knowing trees and how to paint them. To get the bark he would turn the brush around and drag the handle through the wet paint.

narrative_blocks.header: One summer at Old Lyme, 130 sketches
narrative_blocks.body: His first summer at Florence Griswold's boarding house in 1901 was one of the most delightful he had ever had, he wrote, and he came home with a hundred and thirty sketches; his enthusiasm brought Frank DuMond after him. Henry Ward Ranger had meant the colony as an American Barbizon, but Childe Hassam turned it Impressionist after 1903, and from 1902 it hung its own summer show in the draped-over town library.

narrative_blocks.header: His father opposed France; his mother paid
narrative_blocks.body: Seth Talcott wanted a successor for his drug house, not a painter, and set himself against the trip. The family remembered that his mother Sarah found the money. She went with him to Europe, and later kept her own room at the Griswold house in Old Lyme.

narrative_blocks.header: He knew his son for a hundred days
narrative_blocks.body: Agnew was born in Manhattan that February. A heart attack took his father at the Old Lyme house on the first of June, aged forty-one.

narrative_blocks.header: He rented Van Gogh's house at Arles
narrative_blocks.body: Three years at the Académie Julian put his work in the Paris Salons of 1893 and 1894. In 1897 he was living in Arles, renting the house where Van Gogh had worked, with the painter Frank DuMond.

The award was an exposition medal, not an Olympic one — the Olympic art competitions did not begin until 1912 — but the 1904 games were run on the exposition grounds at Saint Louis through that same summer, which is why the two sit side by side here and why the cross-connection to Herbert Jamison's Athens silver is worth keeping. narrative_blocks.header: Four volumes of Hartford, 1896 to 1919
narrative_blocks.body: She kept the diaries for twenty-three years, the third volume thick with the First World War. Her daughter Alice edited the four of them and put them into print in 1990, fifty-one years after her death.

narrative_blocks.header: She worked against the vote
narrative_blocks.body: Her papers sit in the Hartford collection filed under Women's Suffrage, on the opposing side of it: she took part in the anti-suffrage campaign in the same city and the same years that Isabella Beecher Hooker was running the state association.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a Talcott at Winsted in 1895
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Dudley Vaill married Charles Hooker Talcott of Hartford on 20 June 1895 and had four children by him — Seth, Dudley, Charles and Alice. Her husband carried the Hooker name down his own line, and Isabella Beecher Hooker had married into it too.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father wrote the regiment's history
narrative_blocks.body: Mary's father, Theodore Vaill, was adjutant of the 2nd Connecticut Heavy Artillery and was wounded near the end of the war. He wrote the regiment's history, edited the Winsted Herald, and died when she was six.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father was a cousin of the Gunns
narrative_blocks.body: Mary's grandmother Flora Gold Vaill was a sister of Mary Wakeman Gold Brinsmade, so her father was a first cousin of Abigail Brinsmade Gunn, who with her husband Frederick founded the Gunnery at Washington.

narrative_blocks.header: New Yorker said America had found its sculptor
narrative_blocks.body: At Dudley Talcott's 1927 debut at Valentine Dudensing Galleries, The New Yorker wrote: "We heard recently that if America ever produced a sculptor it was in the person of Dudley Talcott... Talcott has departed and has still clung to the thing that gives power and beauty." Three years later five of his pieces were shown at MoMA alongside Alexander Calder and Isamu Noguchi.

narrative_blocks.header: Six years in Norwegian fjords
narrative_blocks.body: From 1925 to 1931 Talcott spent six years in Norway, canoeing fjords and working on North Sea fishing boats, then co-owned the vessel Norkap II for four pack-ice voyages to Greenland with scientists and sportsmen. The expeditions produced three illustrated books and directly shaped his figurative sculptures of fishermen and Nordic figures.

narrative_blocks.header: Olympic art entrant — honorable mention, 1932
narrative_blocks.body: In 1932, sculpture was still an Olympic competition. Talcott entered The Wrestler in the Los Angeles Games art category and received an honorable mention — among the few American sculptors to compete in the Olympic arts.

narrative_blocks.header: Kopernik still stands on the Parkway
narrative_blocks.body: His last major commission was Kopernik, a sixteen-foot stainless steel orbital circle given to Philadelphia for the five hundredth anniversary of Copernicus. It stands on the Benjamin Franklin Parkway still.

narrative_blocks.header: She published her mother's diaries of Hartford life
narrative_blocks.body: Alice edited and published the diaries of her mother Mary Dudley Vaill Talcott, which depicted daily life in Hartford in the early twentieth century. She was a trustee of the Hartford Symphony Orchestra in the 1950s and a founding parent of Renbrook School in West Hartford.

narrative_blocks.header: Pianist, watercolorist, avid Connecticut hiker
narrative_blocks.body: Alice studied piano with Yale professor Bruce Simon and performed at the Roulade Club as soloist and in chamber music groups for years. She also painted in watercolor and pastel, and was an avid walker of Connecticut hiking trails.

narrative_blocks.header: She hired her brothers to build Northington
narrative_blocks.body: She and Ostrom Enders named their fifty-seven-acre Avon farm Northington, after an old name for the place. They commissioned her brothers Charles and Seth to build the house in the International Style then arriving from Europe.

narrative_blocks.header: Three generations of Enders in Hartford money
narrative_blocks.body: His grandfather Thomas O. Enders founded Aetna Life and was its second president. His father John Ostrom headed the United States Security Trust Company, and Ostrom went into his father's bank out of Yale in 1925.

narrative_blocks.header: A Nobel brother, and sixty-four years with Alice
narrative_blocks.body: John F. Enders won the prize for medicine in 1954, for the cell-culture research the vaccine came out of. Ostrom married Alice Talcott in 1928, and they had sixty-four years before she died in 1992.

narrative_blocks.header: Polo in the valley, and a pilot's licence
narrative_blocks.body: He helped start the Farmington Valley Polo Club in the thirties and rode on its team for years. He flew his own aircraft, shot, and fished for trout and salmon wherever his travels took him.

narrative_blocks.header: Murmansk convoys, then a Pacific carrier
narrative_blocks.body: He was a lieutenant in the Navy from 1942. The escort carrier Bogue took him on convoy duty to the British Isles and to Murmansk; later he was squadron air combat intelligence officer aboard the Antietam.

narrative_blocks.header: He opened the bank's training to all comers
narrative_blocks.body: In his first years as president after the war he pressed to take the racial barriers out of the bank's career training programmes. He also drove Connecticut's move to branch banking.

narrative_blocks.header: Careful with money, early to computers
narrative_blocks.body: Robert Newell, who followed him as chairman, said he felt personally responsible for every dollar deposited — and that the bank was among the first to get computers, because he saw the industry changing.

narrative_blocks.header: Swans on the lawn, and rare bird books
narrative_blocks.body: He bred rare North American waterfowl at Avon after retiring in 1967, for release where the species had gone; descendants are still at the National Zoo. His bird books went to Trinity's Watkinson Library.

narrative_blocks.header: She built refugee camps in Cambodia
narrative_blocks.body: In Cambodia during the war, from 1970 to 1974, Gaetana set up refugee camps while Thomas was deputy chief of mission, and stayed on at the embassy after the other wives left. President Ford then named her to his refugee panel.

narrative_blocks.header: She found homes for 400 refugees
narrative_blocks.body: Back in Washington in 1975, the only woman among the seventeen on President Ford's refugee committee, Gaetana rallied her friends to sponsor Cambodian and Vietnamese families and found homes for 350 to 400 people.

narrative_blocks.header: Gorbachev, Rostropovich, two queens
narrative_blocks.body: When Thomas left the Foreign Service in 1986 Gaetana turned journalist; in twenty-seven years as international editor of Hola and Hello she interviewed Gorbachev, the first Bush, Rostropovich, Bloomberg and the queens of Norway and Sweden.

narrative_blocks.header: Tangier in 1953, married two years after
narrative_blocks.body: Gaetana was the youngest of four daughters of Giuseppe Marchegiano, who ran judicial affairs for the International Zone of Tangier. There in 1953 she met Thomas Enders, a tall young Yale man at work on his master's thesis.

narrative_blocks.header: Six postings, and work made in each
narrative_blocks.body: Gaetana followed Thomas to Sweden, Yugoslavia, Cambodia, the European Community, Canada and Spain, and worked at humanitarian and cultural ties at every post.

narrative_blocks.header: The music programme she began at seventy-six
narrative_blocks.body: Gaetana joined the board of the Casita Maria Center for Arts and Education in 2007 and founded its music programme in 2010. She sat on the boards of the Mexican Cultural Institute and the Salzburg Festival Society too.

narrative_blocks.header: A Dame of Malta and of Savoy

narrative_blocks.header: Terse calls from Admiral Rickover
narrative_blocks.body: At the Atomic Energy Commission Wallace was assistant to the director of reactor development, and took many terse telephone calls from Admiral Hyman Rickover. He moved on to nuclear safety and retired from the Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board.

narrative_blocks.header: Technology policy as the Cold War ended
narrative_blocks.body: The work Wallace liked best came in Reagan's second term, at the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, travelling widely for American technology policy as the Cold War ended.

narrative_blocks.header: He counted orchids beside her for eight years
narrative_blocks.body: From 1993 to 2000 Wallace and March censused the showy lady's slippers at Abe Run, a limestone seep in Tucker County, West Virginia, tagging and measuring every stem weeks after bloom. A third of the plants turned out to sit whole years underground, some for four.

narrative_blocks.header: A Rock Creek birder before dawn
narrative_blocks.body: In retirement Wallace took Latin and ornithology at the University of Maryland, and joined the birders of Rock Creek Park before dawn in the migration seasons, keeping a record of the species that ran for decades.

narrative_blocks.header: From Chelsea to a Yale engineering degree
narrative_blocks.body: The son of George and Jennie Kornack of Chelsea, Massachusetts, Wallace went from Northeastern to a Yale master's in engineering, where he met March Enders, then studying medicine, and served in the Army as a bridge engineer.

narrative_blocks.header: A bomb in his car at Phnom Penh
narrative_blocks.body: In September 1972, while Thomas was deputy chief of mission at Phnom Penh, a bomb exploded in his car. Two others were killed, and he escaped unhurt.

narrative_blocks.header: He built the International Energy Agency
narrative_blocks.body: After the 1973 oil crisis, as Assistant Secretary for Economic Affairs, Thomas led the creation of the International Energy Agency, which still coordinates the energy policy of the Western nations.

narrative_blocks.header: Free trade with Canada
narrative_blocks.body: As ambassador to Canada from 1976 to 1979, Thomas made free trade the heart of his mission and travelled fifty thousand miles a year across the country. The free trade agreement his work prepared came into force in 1989.

narrative_blocks.header: He sought peace with the Sandinistas
narrative_blocks.body: In August 1981 Thomas flew to Managua for two days of talks with Daniel Ortega and reached a tentative agreement to end the conflict. His ambassador there believed it could have spared Nicaragua the contra war.

narrative_blocks.header: Phi Beta Kappa as a Yale junior
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas was elected to Phi Beta Kappa in his junior year at Yale, took master's degrees at the University of Paris and at Harvard, and joined the State Department in 1958.

narrative_blocks.header: Mountains and rare books
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas climbed widely in the Canadian Rockies and the Alps, and collected rare books on travel and exploration.

narrative_blocks.header: His uncle won the Nobel Prize
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas's uncle was John F. Enders, the virologist who shared the Nobel Prize for growing the polio virus in the laboratory.

narrative_blocks.header: Physiatrist, and an associate professor
narrative_blocks.body: She came out of Yale medicine into rehabilitation, taught it as a fellow at Tufts-New England, and became associate professor of rehabilitation medicine at George Washington. She was board certified in it.

narrative_blocks.header: Her only son came when she was forty-seven
narrative_blocks.body: She married Wallace Kornack in June 1973, a year after the engagement was given out at Avon, and Thomas was born three years later. She gave herself to bringing him up.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty years back to the same Swiss valleys
narrative_blocks.body: A summer's travelling from college took her to Switzerland, where she found hiking and alpine life. She went back to those same valleys nearly every year for more than sixty, later with her husband and son.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight years counting orchids at Abe Run
narrative_blocks.body: She and Wallace Kornack censused the West Virginia site from 1993 to 2000, and the demographic study that came of it thanks them by name. They hunted rare orchids and alpine plants together.

narrative_blocks.header: Wiecor, and the music for other riders
narrative_blocks.body: She rode dressage and brought her horse Wiecor up to the top level. When she could no longer ride she chose the music and set the choreography for the young riders she sponsored.

narrative_blocks.header: Hundreds of watercolours, shown several times
narrative_blocks.body: She painted landscapes mostly and exhibited more than once. Intellectual and European history held her all her life — it was what she had read at Oberlin — and archaeology after it.

narrative_blocks.header: Three days short of eighty-six
narrative_blocks.body: She died at her Georgetown house on 26 March 2015. The memorial was kept for Waterford in Connecticut, where the family had long summered on Long Island Sound.

narrative_blocks.header: Moved to Paris — to bring Yoplait to America
narrative_blocks.body: In 1972 Bennet moved his family to Paris for a year of intensive immersion in the yogurt business, then used his Michigan dairy company to develop Yoplait USA, introducing it to the American market in 1974. He sold both companies to General Mills in 1975.

narrative_blocks.header: Amherst's most alive alumnus — "a rage to live"
narrative_blocks.body: His Amherst classmate wrote that Bennet had "a presence I can only describe as 'a rage to live'... a force that transformed each setting, venue or place." He danced, competed, built businesses and pioneered platform tennis across the Midwest — "his glass was always much more than half full."

narrative_blocks.header: From selling soap to owning a dairy
narrative_blocks.body: Bill sold for Procter & Gamble out of Amherst, then advertising for Look in Chicago, and rose at the Jewel Companies to director of marketing for its food stores while earning a Chicago M.B.A. at night. In 1968 he led the investors who bought Michigan Cottage Cheese of Otsego.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixteen paddle courts by force of personality
narrative_blocks.body: In 1970 Bill built the first platform tennis court in western Michigan, then talked the local country clubs into building sixteen more, and started a regional tournament that became a draw of its own.

narrative_blocks.header: He said he lived his life backward
narrative_blocks.body: For his fiftieth reunion Bill wrote that a friend said he had lived his life backward, rich fast and the family made by his late thirties. “I thought I was invincible. The next 40 years weren't always so kind, but I have few regrets.”

narrative_blocks.header: Lacrosse champion, then Episcopal minister
narrative_blocks.body: J. Frederick Talcott graduated Princeton in 1888 as a champion lacrosse player, then studied theology at Oxford, traveled Egypt and Palestine, took an eleven-day horseback caravan into Syria, and returned to be ordained an Episcopal minister in 1893.

narrative_blocks.header: He grew the firm without owing the banks
narrative_blocks.body: After joining his father's factoring house in 1897, J. Frederick led its shift from a merchandise-handling firm into a capital-lending institution. Through the boom of the 1920s and the Depression he simply expanded sales and made more loans, never owing the banks.

narrative_blocks.header: He funded America's first Black college
narrative_blocks.body: As a trustee of Lincoln University -- the nation's first degree-granting historically Black college -- Talcott led its 1934 building campaign for a new library, dining hall, gymnasium, and assembly hall. He also lent his name to the J. Frederick Talcott Award, once the country's highest honor for etching.

narrative_blocks.header: Two officers to an account, one always in
narrative_blocks.body: The house factored about four hundred concerns under him, most of them small manufacturers nobody outside the trade had heard of. Each account was assigned two officers with authority to decide, and the standing rule was that one of the two was always to be at his desk.

narrative_blocks.header: The first voting shares sold outside the family
narrative_blocks.body: The house went to the public for the first time in his presidency, selling preferred stock one spring and common stock the year after. It was the first voting stock ever offered to anyone who was not a Talcott or a friend of the Talcotts.

narrative_blocks.header: Sailed to Japan at 37
narrative_blocks.body: In March 1873, thirty-seven-year-old Eliza Talcott arrived in Kobe, Japan, considered "relatively old by missionary standards." Within two years she had co-founded Kobe Girls' School with Julia Dudley, which became Kobe College in 1894. It remains open today, one hundred and fifty years later.

narrative_blocks.header: Known in Japan as "Eliza Tarukatto"
narrative_blocks.body: Talcott was dubbed the "Florence Nightingale of Japan" for her nursing work during the First Sino-Japanese War in Hiroshima in 1894. She learned Japanese quickly and was known in Japan by her transliterated name, Eliza Tarukatto. She died in Kobe on November 1, 1911, having spent nearly four decades in Japan.

narrative_blocks.header: Both parents died before she was eighteen
narrative_blocks.body: Ralph Talcott died in 1847 when Eliza was eleven; her mother Susan died in 1854 when she was eighteen. Orphaned, she was educated at the Sarah Porter School in Farmington, then returned to teach there before choosing a life of missionary service.

narrative_blocks.header: 'Good Mother Talcott' — beloved matron at Retreat
narrative_blocks.body: From 1828 to 1835 she served as matron of the Hartford Retreat for the Insane — described as 'a small-sized, delicate woman of fine fastidious tastes, yet very efficient.' The inmates called her 'Good Mother Talcott.'

narrative_blocks.header: Husband mourned her for thirty-one years
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband Phineas — later a Connecticut state senator, probate judge, and founder of the American Mills — never remarried after her death in 1835. He was buried at her side in Elmwood Cemetery thirty-one years later.

narrative_blocks.header: Educated at Catherine Beecher's Hartford Female Seminary
narrative_blocks.body: She studied at Miss Catherine Beecher's Hartford Female Seminary in the 1820s — among the earliest experiments in women's higher learning in America. Her education there equipped her for the demanding role of matron when her husband became steward in 1828.

narrative_blocks.header: Her gravestone now stands on Cliff Street
narrative_blocks.body: Her original gravestone was moved from Elmwood Cemetery to Phineas's farm above Rockville when a consolidated family monument was built. The stone now stands on private property on Cliff Street — broken but still legible.

narrative_blocks.header: Steward of America's pioneering psychiatric hospital
narrative_blocks.body: From 1828 to 1835, Phineas Talcott Jr. served as steward of the Hartford Retreat for the Insane, one of only four such facilities in the country. He worked alongside Dr. Eli Todd, the first superintendent, helping develop a program of moral care that achieved the highest cure rate in the nation. His wife Lora was the beloved matron; she died at the Retreat in 1835.

narrative_blocks.header: Senator, judge, and mill president at once
narrative_blocks.body: Phineas served as Rockville's judge of probate for sixteen years across four terms, Connecticut State Senator in 1851, and president of the Rockville Railroad Company — while simultaneously running the American Mills, the Savings Bank of Rockville, the Aqueduct Company, and two mill interests. His home's left wing was his courtroom.

narrative_blocks.header: Rode west on horseback after losing Lora
narrative_blocks.body: After Lora's death in January 1835, he and his brother Ralph rode west on horseback in November — Buffalo to Sandusky, then on to Quincy, Illinois, prospecting for land. He bought no property and returned to Rockville, where within fifteen months he had become agent of the Rock Manufacturing Company under his father-in-law Francis McLean.

narrative_blocks.header: Died of a fall, buried beside Lora
narrative_blocks.body: Phineas Talcott Jr. died June 6, 1863 when a fall on the street caused a concussion of the brain. He was described as 'a man of heavy weight and commanding figure.' He was buried at the side of his wife Lora in Elmwood Cemetery — she had died 31 years earlier, and he had never remarried.

TANKERHOOSEN.INFO ADDENDUM (Apr 2026): Father Deacon Phineas Talcott Sr. (T01031, 1758-1835); mother Hannah Kellogg (I00195, 1768-1836) — daughter of Rev. Ebenezer Kellogg, first minister of Vernon (North Bolton). TEACHING CAREER (pre-Retreat): 1820 Colchester (1 year); 1821-1822 Glastonbury; 1822-1827 Hartford 'Stone School House' supervising 600 pupils + 10 teachers. WESTERN TRIP: After Lora's death May 1835 returned to parents' Bolton Road home with two small sons; Nov 1835 he and brother Ralph went West via Buffalo→Sandusky OH→horse and saddle→Quincy IL→back to Rockville. Trip may have been cut short by father Deacon Phineas's death Dec 1837, mother's death Jan 1838. ROCK MFG CO (1837-1842): Worked as agent for father-in-law Francis McLean's Rock Manufacturing Company for 5 years before resigning to farm. Bought Hinkley farm 1842 north of Prospect Street — 'choicest residential section of Rockville.' Built 68-70 Prospect Street home 1846; left wing of house was probate courtroom. AMERICAN MILLS: Lumber for construction came from son Frederick's lumber mill in Fulton NY. PROBATE JUDGE 1844-1858 Ellington Court district. Gravesite: Elmwood Cemetery (consecrated 1835 — Talcott family among earliest burials, plot near entrance). Source: Tankerhoosen Phineas Talcott Jr. page; Cogswell 'History of Rockville from 1823 to 1871'; Brooks 'Cascades and Courage' (1955); Cole 'History of Tolland County' (1888); Abbott 'Building the Loom City - Rockville CT 1821-1908.'

narrative_blocks.header: Mayflower descendant — her ancestor founded Plymouth Colony
narrative_blocks.body: Vienna Bradford was the great-great-great-granddaughter of Governor William Bradford, who arrived on the Mayflower in 1620 and governed Plymouth Colony for thirty years. She died in Glastonbury on August 17, 1785, at age 27, leaving behind her husband George Talcott and several children — including Harriet, Fanny, and Rebecca.

narrative_blocks.header: Married a Bradford of the Mayflower
narrative_blocks.body: George Talcott's first wife, Vienna Bradford, was a direct descendant of Governor William Bradford of the Mayflower. She died in 1785 at age 27. George remarried the following year, had six more children, and lived on the family homestead in Glastonbury — land his family had farmed since his grandfather's 1699 deed.

narrative_blocks.header: At the Long Island retreat with his father
narrative_blocks.body: He served in the Revolution alongside his father Col. Elizur and his brothers, present at the army’s night escape from Long Island. A Glastonbury farmer, he held the homestead that came down through his father.

narrative_blocks.header: His first wife traced to the Mayflower
narrative_blocks.body: He married Vienna Bradford in 1777 — of the Plymouth Bradford line — and lost her at twenty-seven. His second marriage, to Abigail Goodrich, lasted until his death from “inflammation of the brain” in 1813.

narrative_blocks.body: Elijah Talcott married Rebecca Olmstead on November 17, 1779. Three years later his brother Benjamin married Rebecca's sister Jerusha Olmstead. Two Talcott brothers married two Olmstead sisters — a pattern the family repeated in the generation above, when two Wright cousins married two of their father's children.

narrative_blocks.header: Died at 56, leaving children still in diapers
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel Talcott died May 26, 1813 at age 56 — two years after his father Deacon Benjamin. At his death his oldest son was 20 and his youngest son James had just been born. He left an estate valued at $5,215, including a home lot and buildings worth $1,650.

narrative_blocks.header: Named replacement children after two he lost
narrative_blocks.body: Their first daughter Sarah died at ten days old in March 1796, and the next daughter, born fourteen months later, was given the same name. The pattern repeated with James Tudor — when the first one died at three months in 1811, they gave the name to their final son, born two years later in 1813.

narrative_blocks.header: Built the Granite Mills
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel Smith Talcott founded the Granite Mills on the lower Hockanum River in Talcottville, establishing a linseed oil operation around 1838 that was converted to paper manufacturing after an 1863 fire. The mill purchased old paper in bales from New York, Boston, and Philadelphia, recycling it into binder boards, album covers, and press paper — running day and night, producing up to 25 tons a week. His middle name "Smith" honored his mother Sarah Smith; his mills neighbored, but were entirely separate from, the Talcottville mill of his distant cousins.

narrative_blocks.header: The mill burned four times
narrative_blocks.body: The Granite Mills burned in 1863, 1870 and 1881 and were rebuilt each time; after the second fire the Tolland County Journal remarked that there was enterprise enough remaining there to rebuild. The fourth came on 1 August 1912, started by spontaneous combustion in seventy-five tons of waste paper. That time it was not rebuilt.

A pottery collection under her name is held here.

narrative_blocks.header: Designed the system that saved the Athenian Agora
narrative_blocks.body: Lucy Talcott joined the Athenian Agora excavations in 1931 as recording secretary. She designed a system for organizing, recording, storing, and cross-referencing the thousands of objects recovered from the ancient marketplace — a system considered critical to the project's final success and a model for all subsequent excavations. She published it in Archaeology magazine.

narrative_blocks.header: Decorated by the King of Greece
narrative_blocks.body: After the war closed the dig she went back to Athens in 1947, stayed eleven more years, and managed the local museum as well. She held a Fulbright, and in 1956 King Paul decorated her for her work on the excavations.

narrative_blocks.header: She preferred the storeroom to the trench
narrative_blocks.body: She went out to Corinth in 1930 for her first season of digging and found she cared more for what became of the objects afterwards. The next year she was made recording secretary of the Agora excavations and held the post for the rest of the decade.

narrative_blocks.header: The blue book they still reach for
narrative_blocks.body: With Brian Sparkes she wrote the two-volume Agora XII on black and plain pottery of the sixth to fourth centuries, published the year she died. It became the standard reference for household pottery at sites across the Mediterranean.

narrative_blocks.header: No doctorate, few papers, enormous reach
narrative_blocks.body: She never took a doctorate and published relatively little, and is still counted among the most influential archaeologists of her century. A later director of the Agora said she had a mind like a computer before computers were invented, and that a doctoral oral was child's play beside a session reviewing records with her. The American School named a room in Loring Hall for her in 2024.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandfather founded a museum too
narrative_blocks.body: The New Britain Museum of American Art was founded in 1903 by her grandfather John Butler Talcott, and her first cousin Talcott Stanley later sat on it as honorary trustee. A pottery collection under her name is held at Miss Porter's School in Farmington, where it drew a lecture in 1991.

narrative_blocks.header: From London to the Morningside Meeting
narrative_blocks.body: Born in London in 1935, he made his life in New York as a dedicated Quaker — serving the Morningside Meeting, the Friends Fiduciary investment committee, and the board of Friends Seminary. He helped arrange the financing that built Kendal-on-Hudson at Sleepy Hollow.

narrative_blocks.header: He provided for the museum in his estate
narrative_blocks.body: He and his wife Caryl joined the Heritage Society of the New Britain Museum of American Art, the roll of those who provide for it through their estate plans.

narrative_blocks.header: Codebreaking for the Army in the war
narrative_blocks.body: He enlisted at Hartford in July 1942 and served as a first lieutenant in the Signal Intelligence Service, the Army's cryptanalysis arm and the ancestor of the NSA. He came home, married, and took his Yale law degree in 1947.

narrative_blocks.header: He retired at fifty-four to volunteer
narrative_blocks.body: He practiced law in West Hartford six years, then twenty in the trust department of Connecticut Bank & Trust. Retiring early in 1973, he gave the next thirty-five years to the Hartford Symphony, the Hartt School and other boards.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty years at the Wadsworth Atheneum
narrative_blocks.body: He gave the Wadsworth Atheneum fifty years and rose to president of its board, as he did at Newington Children's Hospital where his father had held the chair. In 1988 it gave him its Goodwin Medal, only the fourth ever made.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandfather's museum, and a Calder
narrative_blocks.body: The New Britain Museum of American Art was founded by his grandfather in 1903, and Talcott served it as honorary trustee. He and the Charles F. Smith Fund gave it Alexander Calder's mobile The Red Candle.

narrative_blocks.header: He outlived two of his three wives
narrative_blocks.body: He married Nina Brower Hewitt in December 1945 and they had four children, the eldest born while he was still at New Haven. Nina died in 1990, his second wife Marjorie Scott Trotter before him; his third, Marguerite Sundheim, survived him.

narrative_blocks.header: He found the family fund a bigger home
narrative_blocks.body: He sat on the board of the Alix W. Stanley Foundation for forty-five years, and was the one who steered it into the Community Foundation of Greater New Britain. The family's giving became the region's, and reached further for it.

narrative_blocks.header: A sloop called Bagheera and a good table
narrative_blocks.body: He raced a sloop called Bagheera, skied, and was good for a golf tall tale. He kept a table of friends going over the art and politics of the day, and did not seek the limelight; the number who called him a mentor would have surprised him.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-five years at Allen, Russell & Allen
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas went into Hartford insurance out of Harvard, with the Standard Fire Insurance Company from 1924. He joined Allen, Russell & Allen in 1931, was a partner from 1936, and became its president when the firm incorporated in 1965, the year before he died.

narrative_blocks.header: Private to major in the Second World War
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas served in the Army of the United States in the Second World War, going in as a private in his forties and coming out a major.

narrative_blocks.header: Pomfret's graduate, then its treasurer
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas finished at Pomfret School in 1919 and at Harvard in 1923, and in later life he went back to Pomfret as a trustee and its treasurer.

narrative_blocks.header: He married Jeanne Stanley in 1935
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas married Jeanne Stanley on 31 May 1935; they were divorced by 1940, and she died in New York two years later. On 9 August 1946 he married Elinor Righter, and he had two children, Leslie Taylor and Elinor Foster Oakes.

narrative_blocks.header: His father ran steamships out of Seattle
narrative_blocks.body: Walter Oakes went west after Harvard and co-founded the Puget Sound & Alaska Steamship Company with Charles E. Peabody, the line that became the Alaska Steamship Company, and ran the Roslyn Fuel Company besides. He was dead at forty-six, when his son was ten.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandfather ran the Northern Pacific
narrative_blocks.body: His grandfather and namesake, Thomas Fletcher Oakes, started on the Kansas Pacific in 1863 and rose to the presidency of the Northern Pacific, running the line from the Great Lakes to Puget Sound from 1888 to 1893.

narrative_blocks.header: Princeton 1933, then two law degrees
narrative_blocks.body: He went from the Pingry School to Princeton in the class of 1933, where he belonged to the Quadrangle Club, and afterwards took law degrees at Connecticut and New York University. He spent many years as vice president and trust officer at the Hartford National Bank and Trust Company.

narrative_blocks.header: A house at Man-o-War Cay
narrative_blocks.body: He belonged to the Cruising Club of America and kept a house at Man-o-War Cay in the Abacos, sailing there from New England for many years.

narrative_blocks.header: In 1962 he went into development
narrative_blocks.body: In 1962 he formed a real estate development company and put up retail properties across southern New England.

narrative_blocks.header: He chaired the Community Chest in 1953
narrative_blocks.body: He chaired the Community Chest, now the United Way, in 1953. He was a life trustee of the Greater Hartford Boys and Girls Club and a corporator of Hartford Hospital.

narrative_blocks.header: Two years old on the ox cart west
narrative_blocks.body: Her parents Ziba and Sally Hurd left Tinmouth, Vermont on July 19, 1816 with three children aboard an ox cart — Eliza nine, Norman eight, Hannah two. They settled four hundred acres of what became Castile, New York.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother named the town Castile
narrative_blocks.body: It was her mother Sally who chose the village's name in 1821, reaching for the old Spanish kingdom. Her father Ziba was Castile's first postmaster and, by the county history's account, its first town supervisor.

narrative_blocks.header: Raised by the town's temperance man
narrative_blocks.body: Her father built Castile's first potash works and made maple sugar, but refused the settlement's demand that he distill whiskey — an early temperance man who read from Watts's sermons at the town's first religious meeting.

narrative_blocks.header: Their first winter, the father went back
narrative_blocks.body: That first fall Ziba returned to Vermont for supplies, leaving Sally and the three children alone in the raw Genesee Country. He came back in the spring of 1817 with two yoke of oxen, two cows, two potash kettles, and his mother.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother died; the family scattered
narrative_blocks.body: Sally Gilbert Hurd died in January 1841, fifty-five years old, in the first frame house built in Castile. Within the year her father had remarried and her brother Norman had left town — he stayed away twenty years.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father's last years under her roof
narrative_blocks.body: Years of failing health brought her father at last into the home she kept with Anson Howard, and there, in April 1854, he chose his own ending. The family was hurt enough that most scattered west; she stayed in Castile the rest of her days.

burial.plot_notes: Grace Cemetery, Castile, Wyoming County NY.

narrative_blocks.header: Born the day his mother died
narrative_blocks.body: Anson Howard was born September 24, 1805, in Bolton, Connecticut. His mother Rachel Talcott Howard died that same day, aged 39.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the founder's daughter
narrative_blocks.body: His wife Hannah was a daughter of Ziba Hurd, who had brought his family to the Genesee country by ox cart in 1816 and served as Castile's first postmaster.

narrative_blocks.header: His father brought him west at twenty-four
narrative_blocks.body: Born in Bolton, Connecticut, he came to the young Genesee settlement when his father located there in 1829. He stayed nearly sixty years, dying in Castile at eighty-one.

narrative_blocks.header: His boy became the town's animal doctor
narrative_blocks.body: His son Riley trained at the Ontario Veterinary College in Toronto and came home to practice veterinary medicine in Castile for forty-five years.

Original body preserved here for reference: 'Lory Sr's son Thomas Brace married Electa Alling Deming in 1823, and his daughter Eliza Ann Brace married Walter Deming in 1827. Hartford May 30, 1828. 9 children EH 2124-2132 — high infant mortality (3 of first 4 children died young: Mahala age 5, first Lucy age 1 month, first Fanny age 5). [Stage 6Y-264 NB#1 body trim]: original body had 5 sentences, trimmed to first 3. Original body preserved here for reference: 'Manning Brace and Lucy Webster lost three of their first four children: Mahala (b.1796) died age 5 in 1802; their first Lucy (b. Jan 1798) lived only 30 days; their first Fanny (b.1799) died age 5 in 1804. The fourth, Lucy Mahala (b.1801), lived to 1865 — given a name combining her two lost sisters' names. When a second daughter was born in 1804, she was named Fanny No. 2, after the lately-buried first Fanny. Replacement-naming was a New England convention — a way of keeping the names of dead children in family use.'

narrative_blocks.body: Henry was made lieutenant of the 4th Company of Hartford's train band in October 1743 and its captain in May 1760. When his son Henry marched for New York in August 1776, he was sixty-three, long past the militia's age limit of fifty.

narrative_blocks.header: Noah Webster proved his will
narrative_blocks.body: Henry signed his will on 28 December 1781. When it was proved on 27 September 1787, the witnesses were sworn before the justice of the peace, Noah Webster, then twenty-eight, whose speller had come out four years before.

narrative_blocks.header: The grist mill went to his son Henry
narrative_blocks.body: The will left his son Henry half the house and lands, the grist mill and all his carpenter's tools, on condition that Henry keep him for life and pay his debts. Moses had the other half and the stock; most of the rest had five shillings apiece.

narrative_blocks.header: Two wives and ten children
narrative_blocks.body: Henry married Elizabeth Cadwell, daughter of Samuel Cadwell, in July 1740, and she died in 1766 at fifty-three. That December he married the widow Dinah Merry, who died in 1775. Of the ten children, the younger Henry married Abigail Hooker.

notable.notable_blurb: Author of the 1828 American Dictionary

narrative_blocks.header: He played the flute for Washington
narrative_blocks.body: When George Washington passed through New Haven in June 1775 on his way to take command at Boston, the Yale students turned out to serenade him, and Noah, sixteen and in his first year, played the flute.

narrative_blocks.header: New York's first daily newspaper
narrative_blocks.body: Alexander Hamilton lent Noah the money to move to New York in 1793 and edit a Federalist paper. That December Noah founded the American Minerva, the city's first daily, and wrote the first known newspaper editorial in its first issue.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty million Blue-Backed Spellers
narrative_blocks.body: Noah's speller of 1783 went through 385 editions in his lifetime and sold some sixty million copies by 1890, teaching most American children of the century to read. Its half-cent royalty carried him through the long years on his dictionary.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventy thousand words, 2,500 copies sold
narrative_blocks.body: Noah finished his dictionary in a Cambridge boarding house in January 1825 and published it in 1828, at sixty-nine: seventy thousand words, twelve thousand of them, skunk among them, never before in a dictionary. It sold only 2,500 copies, and he mortgaged his house for the second edition.

narrative_blocks.header: From the Brace will to Percival's proofs
narrative_blocks.body: On 27 September 1787, at twenty-eight, Noah swore the witnesses to Henry Brace's will as a Hartford justice of the peace. Forty-one years later his American Dictionary went to press with James Gates Percival, a sixth-generation Hooker descendant, as its principal assistant.

narrative_blocks.header: Recruited a Hooker descendant for his Dictionary
narrative_blocks.body: Noah Webster recruited James Gates Percival to edit the 1828 American Dictionary. Percival — poet, geologist, Yale graduate, fluent in over twenty languages — corrected Webster's errors in scientific and European language terms. "I feel like the living tied to the dead," Percival wrote of the collaboration.
