people.research_notes: b. Apr 20, 1718 Haddam CT; d. Oct 9, 1747 Northampton MA age 29 of tuberculosis. Father Hezekiah Brainerd (Connecticut legislator); mother Dorothy Hobart. Orphaned by age 14. Yale 1739-1742, expelled for saying a tutor 'has no more grace than a chair.' A recent Connecticut law forbade ordination without a Harvard, Yale, or European degree, so his expulsion blocked normal ministry; the College of New Jersey (Princeton) was founded 1746 partly in response. Licensed to preach July 29, 1742 by New Lights. Called by Society in Scotland for Propagating Christian Knowledge. MISSIONS: Kaunameek (Mahican, NY) 1743-44; Forks of the Delaware (PA) 1744-45; Crossweeksung (Delaware, NJ) 1745-46 with 77 baptisms in less than a year; Cranberry NJ 1746. Reached Jonathan Edwards's home in Northampton May 28, 1747. Nursed by Jerusha Edwards (H00377). Bidding Jerusha goodbye on his deathbed: 'Dear Jerusha, are you willing to part with me? ... we shall spend a happy eternity together!' Buried Bridge Street Cemetery, Northampton MA, beside Jerusha (who was buried beside him four months later when she died of TB contracted from him). Jonathan Edwards published his diary 1749 as 'An Account of the Life of the Late Reverend Mr. David Brainerd' — bestselling religious book of 19th-century America, with 30+ editions, inspiring William Carey, Henry Martyn, Jim Elliot, Adoniram Judson, John Wesley, McCheyne, John Piper, others. Brother John Brainerd continued his work. Cousin James Brainerd Taylor was a Second Great Awakening evangelist. ENTRY CLASSIFICATION NOTE: Brainerd is added per compiler's directive as an 'orbit' connection — tied to the Hooker tree by life events (engaged to and nursed by Jerusha Edwards H00377; lived/died in Jonathan Edwards X00128's home; subject of Edwards's published Life). The compiler has distinguished 'orbit' (deep life-event connection) from 'easter egg' (genealogical surprise via spouse parentage), but the v13 schema currently uses `is_easter_egg: true` for both categories. Flagged for future schema evolution to separate the two. narrative_blocks.body: He took his Yale degree in 1785 with distinguished scholarship and read history, the law of nations and English municipal law, meaning to practise in Massachusetts. His strength was in the deeper mathematics and philosophy, and the family history says he was such an adept in them as to be no dishonor to the illustrious name of Newton.

narrative_blocks.header: Elected tutor in the autumn, dead by summer
narrative_blocks.body: Yale made him a tutor at the commencement of 1788 and he entered on the office that October. Consumption took him the next August, in his twenty-sixth year, and his classmate and fellow-tutor Mr. Bidwell gave the funeral oration in the college chapel on the second of September.

narrative_blocks.header: His father kept the day every year
narrative_blocks.body: Rev. Roger noted the anniversary of this son's death in his diary each year for the rest of his life. The printed oration is bound with other matter in the Yale College library.

narrative_blocks.header: Bought Nantucket in 1659 with two beaver hats
narrative_blocks.body: On 2 July 1659 he led a group of Salisbury investors who bought the island from Thomas Mayhew, part of the price being two beaver hats his son Tristram made. He took first choice of land and settled near Capaum pond.

narrative_blocks.header: Chief magistrate of Nantucket twice appointed
narrative_blocks.body: He was appointed chief magistrate on 29 June 1671 and again in 1677 for a four-year term. That first year he and Thomas Macy went to New York to secure the settlers' claim from Governor Lovelace.

narrative_blocks.header: He broke Haverhill with a plow he made
narrative_blocks.body: Church warden at Brixton in 1639 and constable in 1641, he sailed in 1642, and his name is on the November deed for the Pentucket land. He is said to have been the first there to turn ground with a plow of his own making.

narrative_blocks.header: A ferry, a tavern, and a commissioner’s title
narrative_blocks.body: From 1648 he ran a ferry across the Merrimack at Newbury and kept an ordinary there with Dionis. He sold both about 1654 for Salisbury, where he signed himself Tristram Coffyn, Commissioner of Salisbury.

narrative_blocks.header: Peter, Tristram Jr. and James took island land
narrative_blocks.body: All three sons took Nantucket land beside him, and he bought the thousand acres of Tuckernuck on his own account. His grandson Jethro built the house that still stands on Sunset Hill.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty grandchildren, and a count made in 1728
narrative_blocks.body: He died on 2 October 1681 leaving seven children and sixty grandchildren, most of his property already given away to them. A grandson counted the descendants in 1728 and reached 1,582, of whom 1,128 were living.

narrative_blocks.header: Most notable Nantucket Americans descend from him
narrative_blocks.body: His descendants ran to whalers, Loyalists who fled to Canada, and Quaker abolitionists. Almost every notable American with Nantucket roots descends from him; Benjamin Franklin was the exception.

people.research_notes: Born Tristram Coffyn 11 March 1609/10 in Brixton, Devon, England. Son of Peter Coffin and Joanna Kember. Married Dionis Stevens 1630; nine children, first five born in England. Came to Massachusetts 1642 with wife, children, two sisters and mother. Operated tavern at Newbury (wife Dionis 'presented' for selling beer above legal price 1653, acquitted because her beer was stronger than ordinary). Moved to Salisbury, MA — signed himself 'Tristram Coffyn, Commissioner of Salisbury.' Bought Nantucket from Thomas Mayhew July 2, 1659 with Salisbury investors. Bought Tuckernuck Island. Built corn mill employing local Native Americans. Chief magistrate Nantucket 1671 and 1677. Died Nantucket Oct 2, 1681. Sources: Wikipedia 'Tristram Coffin (settler)'; Coffin family genealogies. notable.notable_blurb: 4th Governor of Connecticut Colony; Hartford founder

narrative_blocks.header: Twice Governor of Connecticut Colony in the 1650s
narrative_blocks.body: He served as Governor of Connecticut Colony in 1655 and 1658, and as Deputy Governor in 1654, 1656, 1657, and 1659. He had been Treasurer of the Colony four years and Secretary five — one of the most important and influential men in early Connecticut.

narrative_blocks.header: Arrived Hartford 1636 — same year as Hooker
narrative_blocks.body: He emigrated from Burmington, Worcester, England in 1635, first holding a house in Cambridge, Massachusetts. He removed to Hartford in 1636 — the same year Thomas Hooker led his congregation there — and was immediately made a magistrate of the colony.

narrative_blocks.header: Hartford land grant: seven acres of meadow
narrative_blocks.body: In the February 1639/40 land inventory of Hartford he held seven acres and two roods on which his dwelling house stood, plus a 90-acre parcel, twelve acres at Hockanum, and three acres in the swamp by the Great River. He moved to Wethersfield in 1646.

notable.notable_blurb: Governor of Connecticut; 2nd Speaker of US House

narrative_blocks.header: He took Hamilton's place beside Washington
narrative_blocks.body: When Alexander Hamilton walked off the staff in February 1781, Trumbull was made lieutenant colonel and secretary to the commander in chief in his room. Every letter out of headquarters was his until the war ended in December 1783.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the dispatch from Yorktown
narrative_blocks.body: He stood at the surrender of Cornwallis and drafted Washington's victory dispatch to Congress. The reports on the army's whereabouts and wants had been going out over his pen for two years by then.

narrative_blocks.header: First Comptroller of the United States
narrative_blocks.body: Congress made him Paymaster General of the northern department in 1775, and in 1778 elected him the first Comptroller of the Treasury. He gave the office up inside a year.

narrative_blocks.header: He was the second Speaker of the House
narrative_blocks.body: He took the chair of the United States House in 1791, in the Second Congress, between two terms of Frederick Muhlenberg. He had been Speaker of Connecticut's own House three years before that.

narrative_blocks.header: Eleven re-elections, then he died in office
narrative_blocks.body: He became governor of Connecticut in 1797 and was returned every year until his death in 1809, the longest tenure any governor has had since the Revolution. He sat as chief justice of the state's high court at the same time.

narrative_blocks.header: He came from Connecticut's first patriot family
narrative_blocks.body: He was a son of Jonathan Trumbull Sr., the only colonial governor to back the Revolution from start to finish, and a brother of John Trumbull, who painted the Declaration of Independence. The family seat at Lebanon, Connecticut, was a hub of wartime government.

narrative_blocks.header: His three daughters married Hartford and Yale
narrative_blocks.body: Faith married Daniel Wadsworth, who founded America's oldest public art museum; Harriet married Benjamin Silliman, the father of American science. The third, Maria, published her girlhood letters from New York and died at twenty.

notable.notable_blurb: Farragut's officer; Commandant of Cadets at Annapolis

narrative_blocks.header: He met the first Confederate ram
narrative_blocks.body: He was twenty-two, and six months a lieutenant, when the ram Manassas came at the Richmond in the dark at the Head of Passes on 12 October 1861. It was the first Confederate ram the navy had faced.

narrative_blocks.header: One ship carried him through the whole war
narrative_blocks.body: He joined the steam sloop Richmond in 1861 and never left her — the batteries in Pensacola Bay, the forts below New Orleans, the gauntlet at Vicksburg, the guns at Port Hudson, Mobile Bay. Four years, one deck.

narrative_blocks.header: Mobile Bay shut the Gulf
narrative_blocks.body: On 5 August 1864 he was in Farragut’s line going into Mobile Bay, the day that closed the last Confederate port on the Gulf. It was the last big action of his war, and he was twenty-five.

narrative_blocks.header: The navy took him at fourteen
narrative_blocks.body: He was made acting midshipman on 21 September 1853, eight months short of fifteen, and came out of Annapolis in 1857. His first cruise was the sloop Germantown, with the East India Squadron off China.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the midshipmen for three years
narrative_blocks.body: He had the gunboat Saco with the Asiatic Fleet from 1870 and made commander at thirty-two. In 1875 Annapolis gave him the whole corps of cadets as commandant, and he kept it three years.

narrative_blocks.header: He went to Colorado for the air
narrative_blocks.body: Consumption took him off duty in 1881. He went out to Manitou Springs, where the tubercular went for the mountain air, and died there on 1 June 1882, at forty-three. He and Marion had no children.

narrative_blocks.header: His stone is a column snapped off
narrative_blocks.body: Two destroyers have carried his name. He lies at Annapolis under a granite column seven feet high, cut to look broken off at a jagged angle; the inscription names Mobile Bay, Vicksburg and New Orleans.

people.research_notes: b. Jan 24, 1839 Hartford CT; d. Jun 1, 1882 Manitou Springs CO age 43. Buried United States Naval Academy Cemetery, Annapolis MD. Son of Dr. Edward Pomeroy Terry (HD1346) and Sophia Hamilton Ross Pollock (I00299). NAVAL ACADEMY: Appointed acting midshipman Sep 21, 1853 at age 14; commissioned midshipman Jun 10, 1857; promoted passed midshipman Jun 25, 1860, master Oct 24, 1860, lieutenant Apr 3, 1861. EARLY SERVICE: USS Germantown, East India Squadron, 1857-1859. CIVIL WAR (1861-1865): USS Richmond, Western Gulf Blockading Squadron throughout the war. Engagements: (1) Battle of the Head of Passes — Confederate ram CSS Manassas attack, Oct 12, 1861; (2) Artillery duel with Fort McRee and Pensacola Bay shore batteries, Nov 22, 1861; (3) Passage of Forts Jackson and St. Philip and capture of New Orleans, Apr 18-29, 1862; (4) Vicksburg gauntlet summer 1862 — joined Charles Henry Davis's riverine fleet; promoted lieutenant commander Jan 4, 1863; (5) Bombardment at Port Hudson Mar 14, 1863 — cutting Red River supply line; (6) Battle of Mobile Bay Aug 5, 1864 — last major Confederate Gulf port. POST-WAR: Pacific Squadron USS Powhatan 1866-67. First USNA tour 1868-69. First command USS Saco (gunboat) with Asiatic Fleet 1870-72; promoted commander Oct 30, 1871. Returned USNA 1873; appointed Commandant of Midshipmen 1875-1878. Then Pacific Squadron Flag Captain on USS Pensacola — to Rear Adm C. R. Perry Rodgers, then 1880-81 to Rear Adm Thomas H. Stevens. Took leave due to illness 1881; died at Manitou Springs CO Jun 1, 1882. NAMESAKES: Two USS Terry destroyers — DD-25 (1910-1930, WWI) and DD-513. m. Dec 25, 1867 Detroit MI Marion Stuart (I00300, b.1845 Detroit; d.1906 Dresden Germany; daughter of explorer Robert Stuart). No children. narrative_blocks.body: When her husband, a Navy commander, died in 1882, her trips abroad grew longer and longer until in 1900 she simply stayed — settling in Dresden, where she died six years later. A nephew who traveled with her was said to be like the son she never had.

narrative_blocks.header: A congressman's daughter, then a general's
narrative_blocks.body: Her father David Stuart sat in Congress for Michigan and rose to brigadier general in the Civil War, dying in 1868, the year after her Christmas-Day wedding. His father was Robert Stuart of Astor's Astoria fur venture.

notable.notable_blurb: 19th-century Americana book collector; bequeathed Yale 12,000 volumes
notable.primary_url_label: William L. Clements Library — George Brinley Papers

narrative_blocks.header: He kept buyers wherever books were sold
narrative_blocks.body: He was a Hartford banker with an inherited fortune, and he had started collecting Americana while he was still a student. He bought through agents posted wherever books came up, and the Tribune called him a bold, shrewd, and determined buyer in the auction room. He had better than twelve thousand rare volumes when he died.

narrative_blocks.header: Five libraries got to bid without paying
narrative_blocks.body: He left a memorandum: when the library was sold at auction, five institutions should be allowed to bid up to fixed amounts and take the books free — Yale ten thousand dollars' worth, the Watkinson and the American Antiquarian Society five thousand each, New York and Pennsylvania less. It was never put into the will. His children carried it out anyway.

narrative_blocks.header: Harvard's librarian called it a new device
narrative_blocks.body: Justin Winsor, the Librarian of Harvard, attacked the arrangement in print twice — a scheme, he said, that stimulated the bidding, spared the estate the cost of its own generosity, and inflated Americana prices for every buyer who came after. The charge was answered at length, and is argued over still.

narrative_blocks.header: The book money came from a drug store
narrative_blocks.body: His father stood many years at the head of a large Boston drug store and laid a fortune there. His son said he had taken from that father a love of books, an interest in American history, a delicate constitution, and an anxiety about his health. A Brinley two centuries earlier, in Newport, had collected books too.

narrative_blocks.header: Florida gave him the fever that killed him
narrative_blocks.body: He went to Florida in the winter of 1874 for his health and caught a malarial fever there that broke his constitution. In the spring he sailed for Bermuda hoping the change would help, and died at Hamilton in May.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought the books for another man's library
narrative_blocks.body: He was president of the board of the Watkinson Library of Reference in Hartford and took a large share of the work of choosing and buying its books; the collection is reckoned among the best in the country. He was also a trustee of the Wadsworth Atheneum, the museum his wife's uncle had founded.

bio.bio_blurb: Midvale Steel superintendent; pioneer survey photographer

narrative_blocks.header: Four years to make Midvale pay
narrative_blocks.body: William Sellers put him over the Midvale Steel Works in 1872 — a trained chemist with a gift for organization, set on a business that was not working. He took the steel formulas apart with applied chemistry, brought in a fellow Yale chemist as his assistant, and inside four years Midvale was prosperous.

narrative_blocks.header: At eighteen he photographed Arizona for the Army
narrative_blocks.body: In 1865, before he had been to college, he got himself onto an Army expedition surveying wagon roads through Arizona and California, and was handed the job of photographing the terrain — among the first men to do that work. Hualapai and Yavapai harried the surveyors across Skull Valley and Indian Pass, and the expedition broke up when the escort's enlistments ran out.

narrative_blocks.header: Arizona hired him to write up its riches
narrative_blocks.body: Five years after the survey broke up, the Arizona Territorial Legislature commissioned him and two others to prepare a pamphlet on the territory's resources — pastoral, mineral, and agricultural. He had a new doctorate in metallurgy and chemistry by then, and he had already walked the ground.

narrative_blocks.header: A valentine arrived three weeks before he died
narrative_blocks.body: His wife died in 1911 and his daughter Katharine stayed on to keep him. In February 1919 an unsigned valentine reached his Sixteenth Street house — somehow things don't seem the same, when you are not along — and with it a note from the head of his granddaughter's school, glad to hear he was better. He was dead by the second of March.

narrative_blocks.header: His nephew offered to copy the book
narrative_blocks.body: Like Brinleys before him he was drawn to the family's own records, and in his last years he was putting a book of them together. His nephew, who kept the library of the Harvard Law School, wrote offering to have it typewritten with several carbons so that all of them could have copies.

bio.bio_blurb: Colorado Springs photographer and YWCA president

narrative_blocks.header: The pictures of that neighborhood are hers
narrative_blocks.body: She was a photographer. Working out of her sister's household in Colorado Springs through the 1880s, she made the pictures of the Adams family and of the streets around them that the Pikes Peak Library District holds today, and that local historians still work from.

narrative_blocks.header: The building she raised became a flu hospital
narrative_blocks.body: She had led the fundraising that put up the Kiowa Street YWCA building; when influenza swept Colorado Springs in the winter of 1918 she got it turned over free of charge as an emergency hospital. Hundreds were nursed there.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept the presidency until her health broke
narrative_blocks.body: She sat on the board of the Colorado Springs YWCA before taking its presidency in 1908, and held it thirteen years, through the war and the influenza winter. Ill health forced her to give it up in December 1922; she lived another nine years and died of pneumonia.

narrative_blocks.header: Her society existed to build one dormitory
narrative_blocks.body: She organized the Woman's Educational Society of Colorado College with two other women of the town for a single purpose — to put up a residence for the college's women students — and served as its president. In the same years she founded St. Stephens Episcopal parish.

narrative_blocks.header: She lived in her sister's house twenty years
narrative_blocks.body: She came out to Colorado Springs in the early 1880s with her sister and the brother-in-law whose lungs had brought them, and stayed in their household until her sister died in 1905. In 1910 she built her own house on the same street and took in her niece, who was still with her when she died in 1931.

narrative_blocks.header: Skirts, hats, and a banjo in the hills
narrative_blocks.body: She turns up in photographs of hiking parties and picnics in the hills above Colorado Springs, the women in long skirts and hats and somebody carrying a banjo along. A portrait from 1915 shows her with her dog.

notable.notable_blurb: Waltham physician; Colorado College trustee; civic leader

narrative_blocks.header: At twenty-seven he inherited a whole town's practice
narrative_blocks.body: His father, Dr. Horatio Adams, had been the general family physician of Waltham for many years, and when the son came home from London and Paris in 1866 the whole of it fell to him — a large and responsible practice such as rarely fell to a man so young. He worked it for a year before it broke him.

narrative_blocks.header: A year of it sent him to Minnesota
narrative_blocks.body: Overwork drove him out of Waltham in 1867 and he spent two years in St. Paul. He came back and carried his father's practice thirteen more years, long enough to be counted one of the leading physicians of the state, and then his lungs gave out and he was finished at forty-three.

narrative_blocks.header: In Colorado he was apparently a private citizen
narrative_blocks.body: He came to Colorado Springs in 1882 and never took up medicine again; to most of the town he was simply a quiet man who lived there. To the few who knew him he was its wisest counsellor, and there was scarcely a public enterprise in the place that had not been shaped by his opinion.

narrative_blocks.header: Elected a trustee, often too ill to attend
narrative_blocks.body: Colorado College put him on its board of trustees in 1887 and kept him there until he died, though his health frequently prevented him from reaching the meetings. The board counted him among its most valued members anyway.

narrative_blocks.header: His sister-in-law photographed the house he built
narrative_blocks.body: In 1886, four years after his health brought him west, he built a family house at 410 North Cascade Avenue in downtown Colorado Springs. The photographs of it and of the neighborhood around it are held today by the Pikes Peak Library District, attributed to his wife's younger sister — who was living with the family and gave her occupation to the 1885 Colorado census as photographer.

notable.notable_blurb: Harvard Law School librarian; Boston attorney

narrative_blocks.header: He died in office, keeping the school's books
narrative_blocks.body: He came to the Harvard Law School library from the Social Law Library in Boston, and his colleagues thought his devotion to the place complete. A stroke took him at fifty, nine years into the work.

narrative_blocks.header: Someone had strung cattle wire across the gate
narrative_blocks.body: Vacationing in Colorado Springs in the summer of 1894, he galloped through the Country Club gate where a careless steward had stretched cattle wire across the entrance. His horse went down with him; he lay unconscious for nearly a month and was an invalid for close to a year. He never got back the quick, forcible speech his friends had known him for.

narrative_blocks.header: The class he entered with graduated without him
narrative_blocks.body: He led his first year at the Harvard Law School in scholarship and was made an editor of the Law Review, a man his classmates marked for brilliant ability. Then he lost two years, and did not come back until the fall of 1896 — taking his degree with the class of 1897, two years behind the men he had started with.

narrative_blocks.header: He was only there because of his father
narrative_blocks.body: His father's lungs failed in 1882 and drove the family from Waltham to Colorado Springs; twelve years later he was there on a visit when his horse went down. The elder Adams had taken his Harvard medical degree with the highest honors and built a large practice, only to have overwork end it at forty-three — he never resumed it, and gave the rest of his life to a college board instead. His son tried the Colorado bar before coming home to Boston.

notable.notable_blurb: Sculptor and painter of animals and flowers

narrative_blocks.header: She did not begin until she was widowed
narrative_blocks.body: She married at twenty-five and was a widow at thirty; three years later she went to Munich and apprenticed herself to the sculptor Hans Stangl. She stayed eight years, working among a circle that took in the cartoonist Otto Nückel and the painter Karl Zerbe. She showed at the Günther Galerie in 1933 and was back in Cambridge by the end of that year.

narrative_blocks.header: Rivera told her to paint and she painted
narrative_blocks.body: She had been a sculptor for a dozen years when she first went to Mexico in 1935, and she kept going back. In 1937 she met Diego Rivera, who pushed her toward oil; she was forty-five, and she moved to Mexico City for good fifteen years after that.

narrative_blocks.header: Animals, flowers, and open-heart surgery
narrative_blocks.body: Animals were her subject and she used them in most of her work, with flowers after them. She also made a series on open-heart surgery. Her late sculpture ran to Archaic Greek busts and portraits, worked under the influence of pre-Columbian art.

narrative_blocks.header: The autobiography stayed in her notes
narrative_blocks.body: She wrote poetry and children's stories, and left notes for an autobiography she never wrote. Her daughter kept all of it — four linear feet, most of it the letters the two of them exchanged — and it went to the Smithsonian's Archives of American Art after the daughter's own death.

narrative_blocks.header: Mexico sent a retrospective touring after she died
narrative_blocks.body: She had lived in Mexico City twenty-six years when she died there in 1978, and a national arts fund put a travelling homage exhibition of her work on the road for the next two years. Her sculpture and painting are held by the Philadelphia Museum of Art, the Harvard Art Museums, and the Museo de la Solidaridad Salvador Allende in Santiago.

narrative_blocks.header: He worked full time for no pay
narrative_blocks.body: From 1990 he was president of the American Chess Foundation, and in 1996 he renamed it for the thing it actually did — Chess-in-the-Schools. By the year he died it was in a hundred and sixty New York schools, reaching better than thirty-two thousand children, and had been copied in seventeen other cities. He took nothing for it.

narrative_blocks.header: Italy and Japan both decorated him
narrative_blocks.body: He gave twenty-eight years to Mobil, running its affiliates in Italy and in Japan, and Mobil South at home. Italy gave him its Order of Merit; Japan gave him the Third Order of the Sacred Treasure and the Third Order of the Rising Sun.

narrative_blocks.header: He resigned in Moscow rather than turn
narrative_blocks.body: He is credited with a leading part in reforming the United States Chess Federation and hauling its finances back from the edge of bankruptcy. At the 1994 congress in Moscow its board leaned on him to reverse his position and back the world body's leadership; he resigned his seat on the spot instead, and inside a year the membership elected him back onto it.

narrative_blocks.header: A first lieutenant in the parachute infantry, twice
narrative_blocks.body: He served as a first lieutenant in the Parachute Infantry in the Second World War and went back in for Korea. He came out with a Bronze Star.

narrative_blocks.header: He was born the day his mother died
narrative_blocks.body: His mother, Rose Bradley, was twenty-three. She bore him in Boston on the twentieth of July, 1923, and died the same day; he was named for his father and buried beside her seventy-six years later.

narrative_blocks.header: He denied the Adams ancestry to an opponent
narrative_blocks.body: His obituary called him a direct descendant of Samuel Adams, of a brother of President John Adams, and of Peter Faneuil, who built Faneuil Hall. Four years earlier a man who had just played him at a team tournament asked him about it, and he denied the whole thing — his people, he said, were Dutch settlers of New York, and the name Faneuil misled everyone.

quotes.text: Fan Adams was a man of integrity. When he was the delegate of the United States Chess Federation to the infamous 1994 FIDE Congress at Moscow his integrity shone through. At that Congress, Fan led the battle against the heavy handed and illegal tactics employed by the World Chess Federation's leadership in order for them to stay in power. Rather than go against his principles, Fan resigned on the spot from a job he cherished.
quotes.attribution: Don Schultz, eulogy for Faneuil Adams Jr., NYC, April 1, 1999

narrative_blocks.header: Wounded in the shoulder at Battle of Shiloh
narrative_blocks.body: Commanding a brigade in Sherman's division on April 6, 1862, his men were attacked at dawn in their isolated camp near Pittsburg Landing. He rallied two of his three regiments before taking a shoulder wound and turning over command to Colonel Thomas Kilby Smith.

narrative_blocks.header: Father was Astoria expedition fur trader Robert Stuart
narrative_blocks.body: His father Robert Stuart was a key figure in John Jacob Astor's Pacific Fur Company — leader of the 1812-13 overland expedition that established the Astoria fur post on the Columbia River. He inherited the family appetite for distance and risk, moving West to Detroit before the war.

narrative_blocks.header: Senate rejected his Brigadier General promotion 1863
narrative_blocks.body: Provisionally appointed Brig. Gen. November 29, 1862, his promotion was rejected by the US Senate on March 11, 1863, for reasons that were never published. Sherman removed him from command and he resigned April 3, 1863.

narrative_blocks.header: Reputation destroyed by 1860 divorce-case scandal
narrative_blocks.body: As a Chicago attorney for the Illinois Central, his reputation was destroyed when banker Isaac Burch accused his wife Mary of adultery with him in 1860. The Illinois governor refused to let him raise Civil War regiments; he appealed directly to the federal government and equipped two regiments with his own funds.

people.research_notes: b. Mar 12, 1816 Brooklyn NY; d. Sep 11, 1868 Detroit MI age 52, of paralysis. Buried Elmwood Cemetery, Detroit MI. Father of Marion Stuart Terry (I00300, wife of HD3335 Cmdr. Edward A. Terry). FATHER: Fur trader Robert Stuart (1785-1848) — key figure in John Jacob Astor's Pacific Fur Company / Astoria expedition. EDUCATION: Phillips Academy; Oberlin College; Amherst College (grad. 1838). LAW: Admitted to bar 1842, practiced Detroit; city attorney for Detroit; Wayne County prosecuting attorney 1844. POLITICS: Elected 1852 to US House (Michigan 1st District), Democrat, served 1853-1855. Chaired Committee on Expenditures, Treasury Department. Defeated for re-election by William A. Howard. Reputed 'one of the most effective stump speakers in Michigan' per 1907 Michigan Pioneer & Historical Society work. 1855 moved to Chicago — solicitor for Illinois Central Railroad, befriended Stephen Douglas. 1860 SCANDAL: divorce case where Chicago banker Isaac Burch accused his wife Mary of adultery with Stuart; Mary denied affair and counter-accused. Reputation ruined. CIVIL WAR: 1861 raised 42nd Illinois Infantry (Lt. Col. Jul 22, 1861) and 55th Illinois Infantry (Col. Oct 31, 1861) — denied permission by IL governor due to public outcry, appealed to federal government, equipped both regiments at own expense. Brigade command in Sherman's division Feb 27, 1862. BATTLE OF SHILOH Apr 6, 1862: brigade attacked at dawn near Pittsburg Landing, isolated from Sherman's main division; rallied two of three regiments, took shoulder wound, turned over command to Col. Thomas Kilby Smith. Lt. Col. Oscar Malmborg (whom Stuart had let conduct all training) made the tactical error of forming 55th IL into a square. Recovered for Siege of Corinth. Brigade commands District of Memphis Oct-Dec 1862. Brig. Gen. provisional Nov 29, 1862. Battle of Chickasaw Bayou Dec 28, 1862 — took divisional command after Morgan L. Smith was wounded. Battle of Arkansas Post Jan 1863 (under McClernand's Army of the Mississippi). Steele's Bayou Expedition March 1863. PROMOTION REJECTED by Senate Mar 11, 1863 — reason never published (Warner). Sherman removed from command. Resigned Apr 3, 1863. POSTWAR: Returned to Detroit law practice; brief move to New Orleans LA; back to Detroit 1868 where he died Sep 11. m. 1842 Sarah Lawrence Benson (X02359, 1820-1895). Daughter Marion (b. May 29, 1845, m. Cmdr. Edward A. Terry HD3335) is the connection to the Hooker tree. SOURCES: Wikipedia; Biographical Directory of US Congress; Ezra J. Warner; Larry Tagg; Victor Hicken; 1907 Michigan Pioneer and Historical Society work.

narrative_blocks.header: The view from his veranda became a poem
narrative_blocks.body: His stucco house on Torrington Avenue was not large or imposing, but it had a superb view. His sister-in-law Rose Terry Cooke took the prospect for The Two Villages, setting the mill town along the river against the graveyard on the hill.

narrative_blocks.header: He took his father’s seat on the board
narrative_blocks.body: He went into the Collins Company sales department and its Water Street store in Manhattan, came home to Collinsville, and on his father’s death in 1871 took a seat on the board. He held it forty-three years, the oldest man on it.

narrative_blocks.header: His bank failed two years after him
narrative_blocks.body: He had been treasurer of the Collinsville Savings Society, and in 1872 he organised a private commercial bank of his own. It became the Canton Trust Company in 1899. It failed in 1916, two years after he died.

narrative_blocks.header: Cattle in Canton, and a love of birds
narrative_blocks.body: He kept a farm in Canton and raised cattle on it, and late in life he went into shipping. He was fond of outdoor sports and of nature, and of flowers and birds above everything.

narrative_blocks.header: His widow paid for the Canton library
narrative_blocks.body: Alice died in 1877 and he married Helen Raymond the next year. After his own death she gave the money for the first Canton Public Library building on Center Street, put up in his memory.

narrative_blocks.header: The truth on his lips, spoken in love
narrative_blocks.body: Rockwell Potter of the Hartford church called him a man of true nobility and spiritual strength. His observations upon life, Potter said, were always wise and just, and the truth upon his lips was always spoken in love.

narrative_blocks.header: Collins Company directors carried him
narrative_blocks.body: His last years left him largely confined to the Hartford house or the cottage at Watch Hill. The funeral was in Hartford and the burial at Collinsville, and the directors of the Collins Company served as his pallbearers.

narrative_blocks.body: Through the war she was treasurer of the Western Reserve branch of the United States Sanitary Commission, the body that supplied and nursed the Union armies. Afterwards she was secretary of the New York State Charities Aid Association.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a fourth cousin at forty-five
narrative_blocks.body: Charles Frederick Johnson of Trinity College married her in 1883, and they were fourth cousins. Her line ran back through the Wadsworths to Mary Pierpont; his through the Dwights to Mary's sister Sarah, who married Jonathan Edwards.

narrative_blocks.header: A general cousin, a colonel brother-in-law
narrative_blocks.body: Her obituary traced her to Nathaniel Terry and Jeremiah Wadsworth, and named Major General Alfred Terry as her cousin. Her sister had married Colonel Henry W. Closson of the army.

narrative_blocks.header: Started as Erie Canal cook at sixteen
narrative_blocks.body: Born to a Scipio NY farm family, he hired on as a camp cook on the Erie Canal in 1820 at age sixteen. The construction superintendent Benjamin Wright noticed his self-taught mathematics and made him a surveyor; within seven years he was construction superintendent of the New Haven and Northampton Canal.

narrative_blocks.header: Built first railroad bridge across the Mississippi
narrative_blocks.body: His Chicago, Rock Island and Pacific Railroad opened the first railroad bridge across the Mississippi River in 1856, opposed by St. Louis steamboat operators who sued. Abraham Lincoln, then a railroad lawyer, defended the company in the bridge case — for years the only Mississippi crossing south of St. Paul.

narrative_blocks.header: His son bought Yale's women a lavatory
narrative_blocks.body: The medical faculty would admit women only if they were college graduates and only if someone paid to put in a suitable lavatory. Henry Walcott Farnam wrote to President Hadley offering to meet the expense, and the Corporation voted women in on 16 June 1916. Two of the three admitted took their degrees in 1920, and one of them was Louise Whitman Farnam, his granddaughter.

narrative_blocks.header: Sons led Yale's economics and finance
narrative_blocks.body: Son Henry Walcott Farnam was an economist and President of the American Economic Association in 1911. Son William Whitman Farnam served as Treasurer of Yale University. Daughter Sarah Sheffield Farnam Whitney married Eli Whitney IV.

Elected February 1921; served nearly 30 years until death. Built up the bird collections; spearheaded the Brewster-Sanford, Whitney South Seas, and Blossom Expeditions, and the 1932 Rothschild Collection acquisition.

narrative_blocks.header: Surgery paid for the birds
narrative_blocks.body: Leonard was a New Haven surgeon, trained at Yale College and Yale's medical school, and his practice at New Haven Hospital paid for his ornithology. For half a century he traveled, collected and backed museum bird research without ever holding a salaried scientific post.

narrative_blocks.header: He talked Gertrude Whitney into Rothschild's birds
narrative_blocks.body: His greatest coup came in 1932, when he persuaded Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney, two years a widow, to buy Lord Rothschild's bird museum at Tring, England, for the American Museum of Natural History. Its 280,000 specimens made the museum's bird collection the world's finest.

narrative_blocks.header: Fuertes painted the plates for his duck book
narrative_blocks.body: He had come to the museums as an ornithologist in his own right: in 1903 he wrote The Water-Fowl Family with Louis Bishop and Theodore Van Dyke, a standard work on ducks, geese and swans, illustrated by Louis Agassiz Fuertes.

narrative_blocks.header: The seabirds behind Oceanic Birds of South America
narrative_blocks.body: His first expedition sent Rollo Beck down both coasts of South America from 1912 to 1917 for some eight thousand seabirds, the collection behind Robert Cushman Murphy's Oceanic Birds of South America. In the 1920s the schooner Blossom gathered thirteen thousand more for the Cleveland Museum.

narrative_blocks.header: Eleven years in the Pacific on the France
narrative_blocks.body: A museum trustee from 1921, Leonard then put Harry Payne Whitney's money behind the Whitney South Seas Expedition. Its schooner France worked the Pacific islands from 1921 to 1932 and brought home some forty thousand birds.

narrative_blocks.header: A sea-eagle, a bowerbird and a lemur
narrative_blocks.body: Sanford's sea-eagle, Sanford's bowerbird, Sanford's brown lemur and Sanford's emo skink all carry his name, and the American Museum of Natural History named its Hall of the Biology of Birds for him.

narrative_blocks.header: He married Eli Whitney's great-granddaughters
narrative_blocks.body: Leonard married Sarah Tracy Whitney in 1900, and she died within the year, at twenty-three. In 1904 he married her sister Henrietta, and they were married forty-six years, until his death in Florida in 1950. Both sisters were great-granddaughters of the inventor of the cotton gin.

people.research_notes: b. Sep 19, 1868 New Haven CT; d. Dec 7, 1950 Stuart (Port Sewall), Martin County FL age 82 at his winter home (extraordinary longevity). Buried Grove Street Cemetery, New Haven CT. PARENTS: Leonard Jacob Sanford (educator) and Anna Maria Cutler. Father descended from Thomas Sanford, an early English settler arriving New England ca. 1632-1634. EDUCATION: Yale College B.A. 1890; Yale Medical School M.D. 1893; intern Presbyterian Hospital NYC 1896. CAREER: New Haven Hospital attending surgeon and Yale School of Medicine instructor in operative surgery. Member New Haven County Medical Society. ORNITHOLOGY: AOU Associate 1902, Life Associate 1919. AMNH trustee Feb 1921 to 1950. Co-authored 'The Water-Fowl Family' (1903) with L.B. Bishop and T.S. Van Dyke (illustrated by Louis Agassiz Fuertes), a major work in Anatidae taxonomy. EXPEDITIONS: (a) Brewster-Sanford Expedition 1912-1917 (Rollo H. Beck field leader, ~8000 specimens, basis of Robert Cushman Murphy's 'Oceanic Birds of South America' 1936); (b) Whitney South Seas Expedition 1921-1932 (~40,000 Pacific specimens, schooner France, rediscovery of Procellaria munda 1926); (c) Blossom Expedition 1923-1926 (Cleveland Museum, schooner Blossom, ~13,000 specimens). ROTHSCHILD ACQUISITION 1932: Persuaded Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney (after husband Harry Payne Whitney's 1930 death) to fund $225,000 purchase of Lord Walter Rothschild's Tring Museum bird collection (~280,000 specimens). Cataloged by newly hired Associate Curator Ernst Mayr. AMNH later named the Leonard C. Sanford Hall of the Biology of Birds for him. EPONYMOUS TAXA: Sanford's sea-eagle (Haliaeetus sanfordi); Sanford's bowerbird (Archboldia sanfordi); Sanford's brown lemur (Eulemur sanfordi); Sanford's emo skink (Emoia sanfordi). MARRIAGES: SOROTORIAL — m1. Sarah Tracy Whitney (HD2107, 1877-1901) on unknown date 1900, ended by her death at age 23 within a year of the wedding; m2. her sister Henrietta Edwards Whitney (HD2106, 1876-1963) 1904, ended by his own death 1950. CHILDREN: One documented son William F. Sanford (Yale 1928, intercollegiate 440-yard swim record holder, New York Trust Company official) — flagged not built per scope. William's wife Janet Holliday Wear Sanford fell to her death from their 9th-floor apartment window in January 1937 at age 25 (per NYT) — also flagged not built. SOURCES: Wikipedia (two articles, with minor birth-year discrepancy: infobox 1869 vs body text 1868; FindAGrave gives 1868); FindAGrave.

narrative_blocks.header: He married into New Haven's water dynasty
narrative_blocks.body: He came north from Charleston in 1908 to marry Louise Whitney, whose grandfather had founded the New Haven Water Company. In time he chaired that company and the Milford Water Company both.

narrative_blocks.header: Director of First New Haven National Bank
narrative_blocks.body: Beyond the water utilities he served as a director of the First New Haven National Bank, one of the city's principal banks of the period. South-Carolina-born and trained in Charleston, he had moved north by his marriage in 1908 and integrated into the Whitney family's New Haven civic and financial circle.

narrative_blocks.header: Two terms in the Connecticut General Assembly
narrative_blocks.body: He served two non-consecutive terms in the Connecticut General Assembly, in 1917 and 1921. The tenure straddled the World War I home-front session and the immediate postwar reconstruction-era session.

His New Haven Water Company chairmanship continues a Whitney family chain — founded by HD2082 (Eli Whitney III, 1860), run as president by HD2085 (Eli Whitney IV), and now chaired by him via marriage to HD2109. career.notes: Early 1950s.

narrative_blocks.header: She carried on her family's Babylonian patronage
narrative_blocks.body: She continued the benefaction her mother had begun, giving the grant that carried forward Yale's Texts from the Babylonian Collection — the series publishing the ancient tablets her grandfather, the Assyriologist Albert T. Clay, had studied. Three generations of her family sustained the same corner of Mesopotamian scholarship.

narrative_blocks.header: Fresh from Vassar, she taught in the city
narrative_blocks.body: After graduating from Vassar in 1949 she taught in the early 1950s at the Nightingale-Bamford School, one of Manhattan's established girls' schools. She had herself been schooled nearby, at Brearley.

narrative_blocks.header: A Paris year, then travels far afield
narrative_blocks.body: The mid-1960s took her to live in Paris, and from there she and her husband ranged widely — Greece and Scandinavia, Russia and Egypt, on to Israel, India, and Morocco. Travel became a through-line of her long life.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept old New York's society traditions
narrative_blocks.body: She belonged to the Colony Club and to two lineage societies of old New York, the Colonial Dames of America and the Society of Daughters of Holland Dames. Between the city and her New Jersey home she kept to flowers, fresh vegetables, and long nature walks.

narrative_blocks.header: First American to lead the oldest bar federation
narrative_blocks.body: He was the first United States lawyer elected president of the Union Internationale des Avocats, the world's oldest international federation of bar associations. He had earlier helped persuade the American Bar Association and other American bars to join it.

narrative_blocks.header: He opened New York to foreign lawyers
narrative_blocks.body: He was among those whose work produced the 1974 New York rules that let foreign lawyers practice as legal consultants without becoming citizens or sitting for the bar exam. The reform matched the internationalizing of the profession he spent his career advancing.

narrative_blocks.header: He opened his firm's first office abroad
narrative_blocks.body: In 1964 he established Debevoise & Plimpton's Paris office, the first the firm had ever opened outside New York, and lived there through the mid-1960s. It became the base for the international practice that shaped the rest of his career.

narrative_blocks.header: France awarded him the Legion of Honor
narrative_blocks.body: In 1984 France named him to the Legion of Honor for his support of the international practice of law, built over nearly four decades at Debevoise & Plimpton. He retired from the firm in 1992.

narrative_blocks.header: He served two U.S. Attorneys General
narrative_blocks.body: In 1957 he left private practice to become executive assistant to Attorney General Herbert Brownell and then to his successor, William P. Rogers. He returned to Debevoise & Plimpton two years later and was made a partner.

narrative_blocks.header: From Casper, Wyoming to the Yale Law Journal
narrative_blocks.body: Born in Denver and raised there and in Casper, Wyoming, he took his undergraduate and law degrees at Yale, where he rose to executive editor of the Yale Law Journal. He joined Debevoise & Plimpton in 1949, after Army service in the Second World War.

career.notes: Rural advocacy group; a $9,000-a-year post.

narrative_blocks.header: A dare at the grain elevator changed everything
narrative_blocks.body: A lawyer's daughter bound for law school herself, she took a year to work out West as an organizer for a Montana ranchers' group. Cowboys at the local grain elevator dared her to drive sixteen miles of back roads and introduce herself to a rancher named Andy Ostby — and within two years she was his ranch wife instead.

narrative_blocks.header: She fought the state oil board and won
narrative_blocks.body: In 2012 Montana's Board of Oil and Gas Conservation imposed drilling-spacing units across Bakken shale country that reached the Ostbys' land, and she and her husband petitioned for judicial review. A district court threw the case out, but in 2014 the Montana Supreme Court reversed and reinstated their challenge.

narrative_blocks.header: She traded torts for branding irons and calving
narrative_blocks.body: Instead of torts and statutes she learned to brand a calf, midwife a cow, and load a pack horse. There was no season off — cattle to feed in winter, calves in spring, crops in summer — and she counted herself lucky to stay home and learn the life.

career.notes: Photography, iris prints, and text-based imagery.

career.role: Teacher of art and computer applications

narrative_blocks.header: His work Edge hangs in the Brooklyn Museum
narrative_blocks.body: His 1997 photographic series Edge entered the permanent collection of the Brooklyn Museum. Working in fine-art photography and iris prints, he pushed his images toward computer-generated effects and text until, in the end, words themselves became his imagery.

narrative_blocks.header: From a literature degree to Warhol's studio
narrative_blocks.body: He took a literature degree at Trinity College in 1975, then moved to New York in 1989 to work at the Warhol studio and earn an MFA at the School of Visual Arts. Poetry had entered his art early — his first poem came at nine, prompted by the Kennedy assassination — and it never left it.

narrative_blocks.header: He drove west to California and its curators
narrative_blocks.body: In 1997 he drove across the country to San Francisco, stopping to meet the museum curators who had taken an interest in his work. In northern California he taught art and computer applications, built some of the early web, and finished an online book of photographs and poems called Home.

narrative_blocks.header: A gift camera at nine set his course
narrative_blocks.body: His life in art began with a present — an instamatic camera given to him in Vermont in 1963, when he was nine. The boy who pointed it at the world grew into a photographer whose images reached museum walls.

narrative_blocks.header: Played jazz piano at Paris Les Deux Magots
narrative_blocks.body: After graduating from Princeton he spent a year in Paris playing jazz piano at Les Deux Magots, the Left-Bank cafe of Sartre, de Beauvoir, and Hemingway. He remained a gifted pianist for the rest of his life and brought the music of that year home to Richmond.

narrative_blocks.header: Three-year Army enlistment ended in Philippines
narrative_blocks.body: His Princeton education was interrupted by a three-year US Army enlistment during World War II, service ending in the Philippines. He returned to Princeton afterward and graduated, then took the year in Paris before settling into a New York business career.

narrative_blocks.header: Sold his financial firm at seventy-five
narrative_blocks.body: After founding Cecil-Waller Company in 1965 and earning his Certified Financial Planner credential in 1977, he ran Cecil Financial Planning Corporation (later Cecil, Walke & Company) until selling it at age seventy-five in 1998. He then joined Trend Line Capital Management and managed accounts of old friends for many years more.

narrative_blocks.header: Died peacefully at one hundred
narrative_blocks.body: He died peacefully in his sleep on May 24, 2024, two months shy of what would have been his 101st birthday. He was predeceased by his wife of nearly 69 years Suzan Knight Cecil and his sister Jane Abert Cecil; survived by sister Patricia Cecil Hass of Princeton, three children, four grandchildren, and a great-grandchild.

people.research_notes:
Born Bristol PA September 15, 1879; died 1948. New York attorney; Princeton 1901 valedictorian; New York Law School 1903; admitted NY bar 1903. Wartime US Fuel Administration director of State organizations 1917, then chair of presidential commission investigating fuel conditions in Allied Europe October 1918. 1928 Hoover campaign Eastern vice treasurer. Asst Secretary of Treasury 1929-1931 in charge of fiscal offices. Founding partner Milbank, Tweed, Hope & Webb 1931 (the firm long associated with the Rockefeller family and Chase Manhattan Bank). Princeton life trustee, chairman of the Graduate Council 1914-1917, president Princeton Club of NY 1924-1927. President of the Institute for the Crippled and Disabled, the Watch Hill Chapel Society. Trustee Presbyterian Hospital and Madison Avenue Presbyterian Church. Member American Bar Association, NY State Bar Association, Bar Association of NYC. Clubs: University, Century, Downtown, Racquet and Tennis, Riding. Son of the American Revolution. (See NB on the 1949 1,800-acre Suffolk County wildlife refuge donation.)
MARRIAGE: Married Florence Hazen Talcott Rogers (TD0055) in 1909 — her second marriage, his first. Two daughters: Marian Talcott Hope (TD0105, 1912-1976) and Helen Talcott Hope (TD0056, 1914-2000), the compiler's grandmother.
[NAMESAKE pilot82, kinship corrected pilot90]: His surname Hope was passed forward as a middle name to his granddaughter Florence Hope 'Hopey' Austen Norris (TD0107, b.1941) — the compiler's maternal aunt. See cross_connections.

notable.notable_blurb: Hoover's Asst Treasury Secretary; Princeton life trustee

narrative_blocks.header: His own name went into the firm
narrative_blocks.body: He joined Masten & Nichols at 49 Wall Street in 1901 and became a partner in 1909. After the Treasury years the merger that followed carried his name in it — Milbank, Tweed, Hope, Hadley & McCloy, counsel to the Rockefellers.

narrative_blocks.header: Hoover walked up Park Avenue to breakfast
narrative_blocks.body: Hoover made him Assistant Secretary of the Treasury in October 1929, over the revenue bureau, the mint, the engravers and the Secret Service. Three weeks after leaving the White House in 1933 the ex-president walked the length of Park Avenue to his house for breakfast, with only his son and an aide.

narrative_blocks.header: Wilson sent him to see the Allies' coal
narrative_blocks.body: He ran forty-eight state fuel organisations for the war administration without taking a salary, and in October 1918 Wilson made him chairman of the commission that went to Britain, France and Italy to look at fuel conditions.

narrative_blocks.header: Eighteen hundred acres for a refuge
narrative_blocks.body: The year after he died his estate carried out a wish of his and gave eighteen hundred acres of Suffolk County, Long Island, as a permanent wildlife refuge. A great-grandson does the same work today at river scale.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-four years for the disabled
narrative_blocks.body: He was president of the Institute for the Crippled and Disabled from 1924 until his death — the oldest rehabilitation centre in the country working on modern lines. Bruce Barton took the chair after him.

narrative_blocks.header: Princeton valedictorian and life trustee
narrative_blocks.body: He led the class of 1901 out of Princeton and never left it alone afterwards: graduate council chairman, president of the Princeton Club of New York, library committee chairman, and a life trustee. He died on the August train up from Westerly in 1948.

narrative_blocks.header: Played running back at Yale 1929 to 1931
narrative_blocks.body: Austen played running back for Yale's football team across three seasons from 1929 through 1931 during the heyday of Ivy League football. He married Helen Talcott Hope at Madison Avenue Presbyterian Church in 1938.

narrative_blocks.header: His father was sixty when he was born
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Charlottesville on 21 October 1909, thirteen months after his brother George. His father was sixty by then and his mother thirty, and the two boys were the whole of that late marriage.

narrative_blocks.header: From New York to Washington in eleven years
narrative_blocks.body: He was living in New York when his father died in 1938 and in Washington by the time his mother died in 1949. In between he went down to Charlottesville to stay at her house on Rugby Road.

narrative_blocks.header: A lawyer for Kaiser Aluminum in Washington
narrative_blocks.body: He went from Yale to the law school at the University of Virginia, and practised in Washington as a lawyer for the Kaiser Aluminum company. The family took its summers on Martha's Vineyard.

narrative_blocks.header: He left for Europe, came back to Stonington
narrative_blocks.body: The marriage to Helen Hope ended in divorce, and in 1958 he left the country for Europe. He came back across the Atlantic in the end to Stonington, and died there.

narrative_blocks.header: He was secretary of the wartime merchant fleet
narrative_blocks.body: He spent the war in Washington as secretary of the U.S. Maritime Commission, the agency that built and manned the American merchant fleet. He held a lieutenant commander's commission in the Navy while he did it.

narrative_blocks.header: A Navy officer at a desert air station
narrative_blocks.body: He wore Navy blue at a Marine Corps air station in the California desert, attached to the Headquarters Squadron at Mojave. It was an odd berth for an officer whose war was otherwise ships and Washington.

narrative_blocks.header: From steamships to the grocery business
narrative_blocks.body: After Washington he was named a vice president of the Oceanic Steamship Company at San Francisco. In 1959 he left shipping altogether and became a vice president of Safeway, which is where he finished.

narrative_blocks.header: A heart attack on Mount Lincoln at seventy-four
narrative_blocks.body: He died on Saturday 13 February 1982 of a heart attack, skiing Mount Lincoln at Sugar Bowl. At his own request there were no formal services, and the burial was private and for the family only.

bio.bio_blurb: Developer and compiler of this family history

narrative_blocks.header: Why build this project?
narrative_blocks.body: Born and raised in Northern California, and a student of American Civilization at Boston College, I grew up hearing that my family went far back in American history, but I could never figure out exactly who I was descended from: was my great-grandfather, Samuel F. B. Morse, a direct descendant of the inventor of the telegraph? I heard different things; the answer is that he was a distant cousin, and the name was more of an inspiration. I also assumed I was directly related to Joseph Hooker, the famed general of the Army of the Potomac, and I got a lot of credit in high school for it, until some digging showed he had no children, which left me needing to find out more.

narrative_blocks.header: How can you reach me?
narrative_blocks.body: Click [here](contact) to give feedback, ask questions, correct any genealogical or technical errors, or just to say hello!

narrative_blocks.header: What was your main source material?
narrative_blocks.body: My family had a copy of Edward Hooker's epic genealogy of the descendants of Rev. Thomas Hooker, published in 1909 and completed by Margaret Huntington Hooker after Edward died. The book answered a lot of questions and is the backbone of research for this project. Each of the major founding Hartford families has its own genealogy, and I used those along with online resources like FamilySearch and Ancestry.

narrative_blocks.header: How are you connected to the founders?
narrative_blocks.body: My father's great-grandfather Charles Hooker moved to California in 1851, one of three brothers who went west, and started a hardware business; my mother's mother moved west in the 1950s to get a divorce in Reno and start fresh in San Francisco. I grew up thinking that the connection to Thomas Hooker came through my father and the John Talcott connection came through my mother, then found out my mother also descends directly from Thomas, and the Hooker name runs through a lot of her close family. Through this project I discovered I'm connected to 22 of the original Hartford founders through 27 direct lines, including three to John Stanley and two to Stephen Hart.

narrative_blocks.header: Rounds for a refugee camp, from Sharon
narrative_blocks.body: From home in Sharon in the winter of 2020, James ran the COVID response for the Rohingya refugee camp at Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, where clinics were built of bamboo. He held case rounds by computer in the snow, to the camp's tropical birds and evening call to prayer.

narrative_blocks.header: A fogged visor in the COVID wards
narrative_blocks.body: In March 2020 James went into Yale New Haven's isolation rooms in a puffy blue-and-yellow outbreak suit and an air-fed helmet. The visor fogged at once and the rushing air drowned every word, so he gestured at terrified patients with rubber-gloved hands.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped trace TB through Botswana
narrative_blocks.body: In Gaborone James directed the CDC's tuberculosis and HIV research program, and helped design the Kopanyo study, which used the bacteria's genetic fingerprints to trace how TB spread where HIV was common.

narrative_blocks.header: Botswana on the eve of the pandemic
narrative_blocks.body: On 2 February 2020 James and his wife flew from Johannesburg to Gaborone on a plane full of Chinese travelers coming home from the New Year, ten days after Wuhan locked down.

narrative_blocks.header: A farm to keep Sharon land open
narrative_blocks.body: To keep open land in agriculture, James started Smokedown Farm on Sharon Mountain at the western edge of the Housatonic valley. As owner and manager he runs its American Aberdeen cattle, Katahdin sheep and experimental orchard.

narrative_blocks.header: She bought a tractor and left the law
narrative_blocks.body: She took her law degree at Maine in 1976 and practised for a few years. In 1979 she bought her first tractor and started an organic farm at Harpswell instead.

narrative_blocks.header: First certified organic seller at Brunswick
narrative_blocks.body: At Mill Cove Farm she raised sheep and grew mixed vegetables and flowers, and was the first certified organic farmer to sell produce at the Brunswick Farmers Market. She sat on the board of the Natural Resources Council of Maine.

narrative_blocks.header: She helped save two Harpswell shorelines
narrative_blocks.body: She became a trustee of the Harpswell Heritage Land Trust in 2001 and co-chaired its Special Places Campaign until 2003. The campaign preserved Skolfield Shores and Johnson Field for the public in perpetuity.

narrative_blocks.header: She gave away her own land in 2021
narrative_blocks.body: She and Charlie worked their Monmouth land into flower beds, fruit trees and vegetable gardens, then gave a piece of it away for good. The Jacobs-Stanley Conservation Area went to the Kennebec Land Trust in 2021.

narrative_blocks.header: The Canadian Rockies, then South America
narrative_blocks.body: Between Smith in 1970 and law school in 1976 she worked in Washington and went backpacking in the Canadian Rockies. She travelled around South America with her friend Lucia.

narrative_blocks.header: A 1958 Farmall Cub and the Sunrise
narrative_blocks.body: She mowed her fields with a 1958 Farmall Cub tractor and went round Penobscot Bay with Charlie in a boat called Sunrise. Late on she learned the cello and sang in the community chorus with what she called a so-so voice.

narrative_blocks.header: Chaired the Richard King Mellon Foundation through 2010
narrative_blocks.body: Richard served as board president and later chairman of the Richard King Mellon Foundation — named for his father, the General who built the Mellon banking interests in the postwar era — until his 2010 retirement, remaining an active emeritus member thereafter. The foundation is one of Pennsylvania's largest private grantmakers and anchors the Mellon family's contemporary philanthropic legacy.

narrative_blocks.header: A lifetime within sight of Rolling Rock
narrative_blocks.body: The eldest son of the postwar Mellon patriarch never really left Ligonier — Valley School as a boy, longtime governor of the Rolling Rock Club as a man — while hunting Alaska and boating the Maine coast in season. He was a devoted stepfather to Kitty’s daughter Shrevie Hooker Shepherd, and died on Cousins Island, Maine, on a summer visit.

narrative_blocks.header: The Pahsimeroi reconnected after 125 years
narrative_blocks.body: With his brother Michael, Tom helped reconnect the Pahsimeroi River to its tributaries for the first time in 125 years, working with a coalition of agencies and conservation groups on endangered-fish mitigation money from the Bonneville Power Administration.

narrative_blocks.header: A feedlot turned back into a creek
narrative_blocks.body: When Tom bought one piece of Big Creek Ranch in 2014, the ground by the creek was a feedlot, a foot deep in mud and manure. By 2021, after he moved irrigation water back into the stream and rebuilt its banks, the creek wandered through willow and grass.

narrative_blocks.header: Cattle beside Chinook and steelhead
narrative_blocks.body: At Big Creek Ranch, at the foot of the Lemhi Mountains, Tom grazes cattle on 8,000 acres of his own and holds the grazing permit on 112,000 acres of public land, managing it for endangered Chinook and steelhead.

narrative_blocks.header: Writing the restoration into law
narrative_blocks.body: Tom knows that water put back in a stream and wildlife-friendly fencing could be undone by the next owner. As policy chair of the Western Landowners Alliance, and on the board of the Idaho Conservation League, he works to make that kind of restoration stick.

narrative_blocks.header: From an Eagle County land trust
narrative_blocks.body: Before Idaho, Tom worked in land conservation, water quality, river recreation and access planning for a land trust in Eagle County, Colorado, and for the Eagle River Watershed Council. Settled at Hailey, he sat on Blaine County's land advisory board from 2009 to 2015.

narrative_blocks.header: His father's Madison Valley ranch
narrative_blocks.body: Tom's first restoration was the Madison Valley ranch in Montana that his father Harry Page bought in the late 1990s and rebuilt with him. His great-grandfather Walter Ewing Hope had given 1,800 Long Island acres as a refuge in 1949.

narrative_blocks.header: Public lands as a huge asset
narrative_blocks.body: Tom has spent his working life on land he does not own outright. "I look at the public lands as a huge asset, assuming you take the time to understand how they work and get to know the people involved."

people.research_notes:
Co-owner of Big Creek Ranch in Idaho's Pahsimeroi Valley with brother Michael (TD0115). Splits time between Hailey ID and the Pahsimeroi. Worked for non-profit land-and-natural-resource management organizations as a young adult. First restoration project was the Madison Valley Montana ranch his father Harry Page (X02366) acquired in the late 1990s; after Harry's 2004 death Tom and Mike acquired several connected ranches in Idaho's Upper Salmon River Basin (~5,500 deeded acres, 13,000 acres state leases, 7 BLM permits totaling 120,000 acres) and named them Big Creek Ranch. Three endangered fish species (bull trout, steelhead, Chinook salmon) on the property; reconnected the Pahsimeroi River for the first time in 125 years through a coalition of nearly a dozen agencies and conservation orgs. President of the Idaho Wildlife Federation Board; member of the Central Idaho Rangelands Network (CIRN); former member of the Blaine County Land, Water and Wildlife Levy Advisory Board. Married Molly Page (I00337, Bowdoin grad, finance background, settled in Wood River Valley with him in 2007). Two children Henry (TD0116) and Lilia (TD0117). Tom enjoys hunting in Central Idaho and fly fishing for native trout with family.
[GENERATIONAL THROUGH-LINE]: Four-generation conservation thread Walter Hope (1949 Suffolk wildlife refuge) → Harry Page (Madison Valley restoration) → Tom (Big Creek Ranch) — see NB.

narrative_blocks.header: He invests alongside his clients
narrative_blocks.body: Michael founded Alpine Investment Group in Sun Valley in 2009 and, as managing partner, puts money into each deal beside his investors: office buildings, shopping centers, industrial projects and apartments across the Northwest.

narrative_blocks.header: Four ranches in the Pahsimeroi with Tom
narrative_blocks.body: From 2009 to 2013 Michael and his brother Tom bought four ranches in Idaho's Pahsimeroi Valley and made them Big Creek Ranch. They graze cattle in rotation and gave up building rights on nearly six thousand acres for sage grouse and salmon.

narrative_blocks.header: Conservation as the better business
narrative_blocks.body: As Tom's partner, Michael backed piped irrigation that left water in the Pahsimeroi, and grazing changes that brought back sage grouse and elk. “The value of the property doing what we’re doing is increasing far faster,” he said.

career.organization: Big Creek Ranch, Pahsimeroi Valley, Idaho

narrative_blocks.header: Rescuing potatoes at Picabo
narrative_blocks.body: In the spring of 2020, as farmers dumped crops they could no longer sell, Molly led about two dozen volunteers to a farm at Picabo, loaded seven pickups, two SUVs and a small dump truck with potatoes, and piled them on the lawn of the Hailey police station. They were gone within two days.

narrative_blocks.header: A calling after 2016
narrative_blocks.body: Molly moved her family from Vail to Blaine County about 2008. After the 2016 election she and a group of women founded Indivisible Blaine County, for education, women's rights, civil rights and the environment.

narrative_blocks.header: Medicaid on the Idaho ballot
narrative_blocks.body: For Reclaim Idaho's Medicaid expansion initiative, Molly planned a campaign tour across southern Idaho, from Pocatello and Driggs to Mountain Home and Twin Falls, then led the signature drive in Blaine County.

narrative_blocks.header: The conduit, not the cause
narrative_blocks.body: Molly chaired the Conservation Voters for Idaho Education Fund and was nominated as the Wood River Valley's Woman of the Year. "I feel like I am the conduit to direct people to an outlet for their activism."

narrative_blocks.header: Born of Rochester's Ward and Pierpont families
narrative_blocks.body: Ruth was born into two of the families that built Rochester — the Wards, who gave it a mayor, an Athenaeum, and a savings bank, and the Pierponts, who came from Connecticut to fill its Presbyterian pulpits. Her parents' marriage had already joined the two lines a generation before her own.

narrative_blocks.header: Her marriage rejoined two Hooker branches
narrative_blocks.body: Ruth descended from Thomas Hooker through her mother's Pierpont line; Horace Willard Hooker, whom she married in 1906, descended from him directly. Two branches that had parted in colonial Connecticut came together again in a single Rochester marriage.

narrative_blocks.header: Wartime France service then Wall Street partner
narrative_blocks.body: Kenneth shipped to France with the American Expeditionary Forces in WWI, then returned to Manhattan in 1919 and joined Hemphill Noyes & Co. — the investment banking partnership at 15 Broad Street that he served as partner for the rest of his life. The arc from young Guaranty Trust clerk through the trenches to Wall Street partnership took just over five years.

narrative_blocks.header: Held the 1921 St. Andrew's Golf Club championship
narrative_blocks.body: Kenneth held the club championship at St. Andrew's Golf Club in Hastings-on-Hudson NY in 1921, three years after returning from France. He chaired the club's golf committee from 1922 to 1923 and remained on the board of governors as a 25-year member of the club — one of the country's oldest, founded 1888.

narrative_blocks.header: Heart attack at Shelter Island at fifty-one
narrative_blocks.body: Kenneth died suddenly of a heart attack on Shelter Island NY on 2 April 1939, age 51, just over three years into his marriage to Florence McAndrews. He left no children. Buried Ferncliff Cemetery and Mausoleum in Hartsdale NY, away from his Rochester family.

notable.notable_blurb: Turfgrass pioneer; introduced zoysiagrass to America

narrative_blocks.header: Sailed for the Gold Rush at age eighteen
narrative_blocks.body: In 1849 James B. sailed from Connecticut to San Francisco aboard the Henry Lee as part of the California Gold Rush, age eighteen. He worked for an import company specializing in exotic Pacific plants, ran a tavern in Sacramento, then sailed around the world collecting grass specimens — visiting Hawaii, Korea, Britain, France, and Germany.

narrative_blocks.header: Introduced zoysiagrass to the United States
narrative_blocks.body: From 1889 under the auspices of the Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station, James B. began an obsessive turfgrass research project at his Manchester farm 'The Ranch.' One acre held more than 1,500 distinct grass specimens in five-square-foot plots, which he mowed and maintained using tools of his own invention. He traveled to Europe, Australia, and New Zealand collecting samples, and was the first to introduce zoysiagrass to America.

narrative_blocks.header: Advised Olmsted on Central Park and Bushnell lawns
narrative_blocks.body: Frederick Law Olmsted consulted James B. Olcott on the lawns of his most famous landscape designs — New York's Central Park and Hartford's Bushnell Park. Olcott's reputation as 'the Grass Man' brought him into the inner circle of the most influential landscape architect of the era.

narrative_blocks.header: Founding trustee of the Storrs Agricultural School
narrative_blocks.body: In 1880 James B. served on a three-person Connecticut General Assembly committee — with William Henry Brewer of Yale and George A. Bowen — that reviewed Charles and Augustus Storrs's offer to donate land and money for a state agricultural school. He was appointed to the school's first board of trustees in 1881 and stepped down in 1888 after advocating Yale retain its land-grant status.

narrative_blocks.header: Worked for Cheney Brothers and the Connecticut Grange
narrative_blocks.body: Between his farm and his turfgrass work, James B. oversaw outdoor work — landscaping and road construction — for the Cheney Brothers silk-manufacturer company town in South Manchester. He co-founded the Manchester chapter of the Connecticut State Grange in 1885; some peers thought him 'something of a crank.'

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty years writing for the Courant
narrative_blocks.body: He had set type at a Hartford paper at sixteen and came back to print as a writer, publishing in the Courant from 1869 to 1889. Most of the State Board of Agriculture reports across those same years were written by him as well.

narrative_blocks.header: Berlin Vermont's first settled minister thirty-one years
narrative_blocks.body: Ordained November 7, 1798 as Berlin Congregational's first settled minister, James drafted the church's confession of faith, covenant, and articles of discipline himself. His 31-year pastorate ran to May 1829, when a mutual council dismissed him. He then spent twelve years preaching in New Hampshire and twenty more itinerating around Worcester, Berlin, and West Berlin Vermont.

narrative_blocks.header: Walked six miles and preached at ninety-five
narrative_blocks.body: Per his obituary, 'in the very last year of his life, his 96th, he was able to preach a pretty well connected discourse, and could walk 6 or 8 miles in a day.' Below ordinary height with erect carriage, great memory, and a strong distinct voice, James was described as 'self-denying, laborious and persevering, having quite a missionary spirit.'

narrative_blocks.header: Three daughters married Congregational ministers
narrative_blocks.body: Three of James and Betsey's daughters married Congregational ministers across New England: Pamelia married Rev. Rufus Child (Gilmanton NH then Berlin), Julia married Rev. Pliny Fisk Barnard (Richmond ME then Williamstown VT then Westminster VT), and Hannah married Rev. George Craven (Methodist, Danville VT). The Berlin pulpit's reach extended through the next generation.

narrative_blocks.header: Walked six miles a day preaching at ninety-six
narrative_blocks.body: In the ninety-sixth year of his life Rev. Hobart preached well-connected discourses and was able to walk six or eight miles in a day. Below average height, he stood erect and was blessed with a retentive memory, strong voice, and good delivery.

Education: Dartmouth A.B. 1794 (B.A.); studied theology with Rev. Asa Burton of Thetford VT 1794-95. Approbated to preach Spring 1795. Married Betsey Perrin (Aug 30, 1804) age 38. 12 children — 7 sons, 5 daughters. BERLIN VT FIRST SETTLED MINISTER: ordained Nov 7, 1798 at Berlin Congregational. Ordination sermon by Rev. Asa Burton; participants Edw. Bourroughs, Martin Fuller, Stephen Fuller, E. Lyman, D. H. Williston. Drafted the church's confession of faith, covenant, and articles of discipline. 31-year pastorate to May 1829. Dismissed by mutual council. Then 12 years preaching in NH (Plymouth, Wentworth, Enfield, Alexandria, Bridgewater, near Portsmouth), then 20 years in Worcester/Berlin/West Berlin VT 'preaching most of the time somewhere.' Per his obituary: 'In the very last year of his life, his 96th, he was able to preach a pretty well connected discourse, and could walk 6 or 8 miles in a day.' Below ordinary height, erect carriage, great memory, clearness of mind, good eyesight, strong distinct voice. 'Self-denying, laborious and persevering, having quite a missionary spirit.' His usual Sabbath practice at Berlin was to preach a third discourse in a distant part of the town or border of a neighboring town. Two daughters married Congregational ministers: Pamelia (m. Rev. Rufus Child, minister at Gilmanton NH then Berlin) and Julia (TD0128 m. Rev. Pliny Fisk Barnard X02369, minister Richmond ME then Williamstown VT). Daughter Emeline m. Doct. narrative_blocks.header: Mother of Civil War Medal of Honor recipient
narrative_blocks.body: Emeline Hobart Evans was mother of Ira Hobart Evans — Civil War Medal of Honor recipient and later Speaker of the Texas House — and of three other surviving children. Of her seven total children, only three reached middle age: Mary Emeline who married Captain Thomas Blossom Yale, Edward P. (1842-1913 Civil War 10th Vermont Infantry severely wounded Cold Harbor), and Ira Hobart Evans (1844-1922). The two Civil War sons gave the family a doubled Vermont-regiment combat record from the same Berlin Vermont household.

narrative_blocks.header: Lost four of seven children before adulthood
narrative_blocks.body: Emeline and Dr. Ira Evans's seven children included four childhood deaths: Mary E. (1834-1837, age 3); Ira (1836-1838, age 2 — the first attempt at the Ira name that her later son would carry); J. Annette (1840-1842, age 2); and William Dwight (1849-1861, age 12). All four were buried at Berlin Corner Cemetery in Vermont alongside their parents — a sequential-grief family burial cluster.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed 1852, moved family to Barre Vermont
narrative_blocks.body: After her husband Dr. Ira Evans died in 1852 at age forty-nine in Piermont New Hampshire, Emeline moved the family to Barre Vermont so her surviving sons could complete their education at Barre Academy — the pivot positioned both Edward and Ira Hobart Evans for their Civil War service paths. Emeline lived another forty-two years as widow, dying in 1894 around age eighty-three. She was born in 1811 in Berlin Vermont.

A week later they started for Richmond ME (arrived November 14); Pliny ordained as Richmond pastor January 14, 1847. Settled Westminster 1890 and remained active in church work through his death. 7 children: Ellen Amelia 'Nellie' (1849 Richmond ME, m. Hall, Greenville NH); Alice Theresa (1851 Richmond ME, d.
