Meeker, Manistee MI); William D. (December 22, 1865 Williamstown VT, d.1910 Manistee MI). Children NOT yet built per pilot98 MID scope. Lyman branch + Pierce branch + Hall branch + Meeker branch all flagged. NAMESAKE NOTE: Named for Rev. Pliny Fisk (1792-1825), the Andover-trained ABCFM (INST041) missionary who served the Palestine Mission 1819-25. Pliny Barnard was 5 years old when his namesake died in Beirut. The missionary Pliny Fisk himself is NOT in the Hooker tree — his mother was Sarah (Barnard) Fisk; he may share Barnard ancestry with Pliny Barnard, but the connection has not been verified and would be too many in-law steps to qualify for orbit easter-egg per Jalapeño Rule. narrative_blocks.body: Pampa was founded in 1902 with Timothy as a leading figure. Twenty-five years later, in 1927, the town elected him mayor. narrative_blocks.body: From 1932 Timothy served as sole administrator of the JA Ranch — Charles Goodnight's pioneering 1876 cattle enterprise. He had served as executor of the Cornelia Adair estate since 1921. Twice president of the Texas and Southwestern Cattle Raisers Association, his Vermont schoolteacher beginnings ended in stewardship of one of the most storied ranches in the American West.

Berlin VT schools superintendent before moving to Texas in 1882. Worked for the New York and Texas Land Company under surveyor E. A. Giraud 1882-86, learning the soils, climate, vegetation, and wildlife of Texas. Headquarters Mobeetie 1886; in charge of 1 million Panhandle acres on open range. President of Panhandle-Plains Historical Society for six years late 1920s/early 1930s; helped secure funds for the first unit of the Panhandle-Plains Historical Museum dedicated April 14, 1933 (Canyon TX). Twice president of the Texas and Southwestern Cattle Raisers Association. Major road and park in Pampa named after him. narrative_blocks.header: Burned the log cabin where she was born
narrative_blocks.body: Per family lore, Mary Polly was 'ashamed of having been born in a log cabin' — she and a sister later went up one night and burned the original Perrin cabin to the ground. Her father Zachariah's permanent farm at Scott Hill in Berlin Vermont stood on the same land, but the dirt-floor structure of her birth was gone by her own hand.

narrative_blocks.header: Mother of Manila Bay's Admiral, died at forty-four
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Polly bore Admiral George Dewey on December 26, 1837 — her third child. He was five years old when she died at age 44 in September 1843 Montpelier Vermont. Her husband Julius later married twice more, but Mary Polly was the mother of all his children.

naming_inspiration.description: Named for her elder sister Mary Perrin (1781-1798), born Hebron CT, who died at age seventeen — four months before her parents named the second baby Mary in her memory. The second Mary was sometimes called Polly to distinguish from her dead namesake.

notable.notable_blurb: Vermont physician; founded National Life Insurance

narrative_blocks.header: Founded Vermont's largest life insurance company
narrative_blocks.body: Julius founded the National Life Insurance Company at Montpelier in 1850 and served as its president until his death twenty-seven years later. He personally delivered the remittance for the company's first claim, prompting a public thank-you from the surviving family. NLI remains one of the ten oldest insurance companies in the United States.

narrative_blocks.header: Married three Susans and one Mary Perrin
narrative_blocks.body: After his Berlin sweetheart Mary Polly Perrin died in 1843 leaving four young children, Julius married twice more — both wives named Susan, neither bore him children. His third wife Susan Elizabeth Griggs Lilley had a daughter from a prior marriage who later married Julius's own son Edward — making Edward and his stepsister-in-law husband and wife.

narrative_blocks.header: Backed his son's beating from Pangborn the teacher
narrative_blocks.body: When eleven-year-old George Dewey led an attack on his Montpelier schoolteacher Z.K. Pangborn — and Pangborn flogged the boys into submission with a stick of stove fuel and walked the bruised George home to explain — Julius listened gravely, then thanked the teacher and asked him to repeat the punishment whenever necessary. George later credited the discipline with saving him from prison.

people.research_notes: X-prefix non-Hooker, non-Talcott spouse. NOTABLE Vermont physician and businessman. Husband of Mary Polly Perrin Dewey (TD0138, Talcott descendant). b. August 22, 1801 Berlin VT to Capt. Simeon Dewey (1770-1863, Hebron CT-born settler of Berlin VT) and Prudence Yemans Dewey. d. May 29, 1877 Montpelier VT age 75. Buried Green Mount Cemetery Montpelier (CEM180). Three marriages, all to women named Susan or Mary: (1) Mary Polly Perrin June 9, 1825 Berlin VT — four children, all his children; (2) Susan Edson Tarbox August 4, 1845 Randolph VT — no issue; she d.1854; (3) Susan Elizabeth Griggs Lilley March 9, 1855 Montpelier VT — no issue. Susan Lilley's daughter from a prior marriage was Susan Griggs Lilley (X02375) who later married Julius's son Edward. Education: Washington County Grammar School Montpelier, Norwich Military School (then American Literary Scientific and Military Academy), and University of Vermont Medical Department class of 1824. Practiced medicine in Montpelier 1824-1851 as 'most prominent practitioner and one of the leading citizens of the capital of Vermont' (W.J. Lawrence 1899). Founded the National Life Insurance Company in 1850 (some sources 1848) and served as its first president to his death; he personally delivered the remittance for the company's first claim. Other roles: Trustee of Norwich University; founder of Christ Episcopal Church Montpelier; surgeon for the First Regiment, Vermont State Militia. The Sunday evening home singing tradition led by Julius — 'fond of all music, possessed an excellent voice' — became part of the Dewey family pattern. Favorite poets Burns and Cowper. Famously firm parent: when teacher Z.K. Pangborn complained about 11-year-old George Dewey's behavior at school, Julius replied: 'If you can't manage that eleven-year-old boy you'd better resign your position.' Pangborn returned to school and beat the rebellious students into submission with a stove-fueling stick, then escorted the bruised George home. Julius listened gravely, then thanked the teacher and asked him to repeat the punishment whenever necessary. George later credited the chastisement with saving him from 'ending my career in the penitentiary.' Vermont Historical Society holds an oil portrait c.1860 (1989.23.2, 35¾" × 28¼" unframed) gift of Susan Howland estate (ART052). NLI is still active 21st century — 250,000+ policyholders, 3,500 brokers in all 50 states, one of the 10 oldest US insurance companies, one of Montpelier's largest private employers.

narrative_blocks.header: Quartermaster at Cedar Creek and Opequon
narrative_blocks.body: Edward joined the 8th Vermont Volunteer Infantry as Lieutenant Quartermaster in Louisiana January 1864, accompanied the regiment to Virginia in July, and saw action at Opequon and Cedar Creek. He was promoted Captain in February 1865, resigned three months later, and returned home. His quartermaster invoices for 1864 survive at the Vermont Historical Society.

narrative_blocks.header: Built the 1889 Queen Anne State Street mansion
narrative_blocks.body: Edward commissioned a Queen Anne brick house at 120 State Street Montpelier in 1889 — designed by city mayor and architect George Guernsey on the site of his family's earlier home. The old house was moved to 144 State Street where it stood until 1969. Edward's 1889 house was moved to 128 State Street in 1948 to make way for the Vermont State Office Building.

notable.notable_blurb: Vermont Speaker; US District Judge 1906-1915

narrative_blocks.header: Law clerkship at fourteen; federal bench at sixty
narrative_blocks.body: James paid his own tuition at age fourteen by working in a chair factory, producing maple sugar, and clearing land. He read law with Hoyt Henry Wheeler — and forty years later succeeded that same Wheeler on the federal bench when Theodore Roosevelt appointed him United States District Judge for Vermont in 1906.

narrative_blocks.header: Speaker of Vermont House for four straight years
narrative_blocks.body: James served in the Vermont House of Representatives 1874-1882 and was elected Speaker 1878-1882 — four consecutive years presiding over the chamber. Subsequent service: State Tax Commissioner three terms, US Attorney for Vermont 1898-1906, and Federal District Judge from 1906 to his death in 1915.

narrative_blocks.header: Lost three children of first marriage by 1882
narrative_blocks.body: James's first marriage in 1869 to Delia Howard ended with her death in 1881 and the loss of all three of their children — Jimmie who lived 1873 to 1880, an unnamed infant who lived only days in 1877, and a second Delia who lived from 1881 to 1882. None survived to adulthood, and James remarried in 1884 to Jessie Dewey — with whom he had three daughters who all reached adulthood.

notable.notable_blurb: Admiral of the Navy; Manila Bay 1898 hero

narrative_blocks.header: Mother dead at five; Norwich expelled him
narrative_blocks.body: George was five when his mother Mary Polly Perrin Dewey died in 1843. His father remarried twice and George was raised under stern discipline — at eleven, after George led a schoolyard rebellion, his father backed the teacher's beating of him with a stick of stove fuel. At fifteen George went to Norwich Military School; at seventeen Norwich expelled him for drunkenness and herding sheep into the barracks.

narrative_blocks.header: Steered the Mississippi past Forts Jackson and Philip
narrative_blocks.body: As Executive Lieutenant of USS Mississippi at the start of the Civil War, George was at the helm when David Farragut's first division ran past the Confederate defenses on April 24-25, 1862. He maneuvered Mississippi through shallows, evaded a ramming attack by the ironclad CSS Manassas, then ran the ironclad down — Manassas ran aground, was abandoned, and a boat from Mississippi set her on fire.

narrative_blocks.header: Six hours sank the Spanish Pacific fleet
narrative_blocks.body: 'You may fire when you are ready, Gridley' — Dewey opened the Battle of Manila Bay at first light May 1, 1898, and in six hours his Asiatic Squadron sank or captured the entire Spanish Pacific fleet under Adm. Patricio Montojo y Pasarón, with one American casualty (heart attack). He was promoted rear admiral that May, full admiral the next year, and Admiral of the Navy by Act of Congress 1903 — the only person ever to hold the rank.

narrative_blocks.header: Wore his Manila Bay medal reversed for modesty
narrative_blocks.body: The Battle of Manila Bay Medal — designed by Daniel Chester French and produced by Tiffany & Co. — bore Dewey's profile on the obverse, so he wore his medal reversed out of modesty. He was one of only four Americans (with Sampson, Byrd, and Pershing) ever entitled to wear a US government medal carrying their own image.

narrative_blocks.header: Briefly Democratic presidential candidate, then withdrew
narrative_blocks.body: In 1900 Dewey explored the Democratic presidential nomination and made a string of public missteps — calling the presidency easy, admitting he had never voted in a presidential election, and prophetically predicting 'Our next war will be with Germany.' Critics also attacked his Catholic marriage to Mildred Hazen and his transferring his $50,000 public-gift mansion to her. He withdrew in mid-May and endorsed William McKinley.

people.research_notes: TD0141 — Admiral of the Navy George Dewey, the only person in United States history to hold that rank (Special Rank, Act of Congress 1903 retroactive to 1899). Hero of the Battle of Manila Bay, May 1, 1898. b. December 26, 1837 Montpelier VT directly opposite the Vermont State House to Dr. Julius Yemans Dewey (X02373) and Mary Polly Perrin Dewey (TD0138). Mother died when George was 5. Two older brothers (Charles, Edward) and a younger sister (Mary Perrin Dewey TD0142). Episcopal — baptized at his father's Christ Episcopal Montpelier. EDUCATION: Public schools in Johnson VT. Norwich Military School age 15 (1852-1854) — expelled 1854 'for drunkenness and herding sheep into the barracks' per Wikipedia. United States Naval Academy 1854-1858; graduated fifth of fourteen who completed the program. CIVIL WAR: Executive Lieutenant USS Mississippi at the Battles of Forts Jackson and St. Philip April 24-25, 1862 (Dewey at the helm). Steered ship through CSS Manassas ramming attack. Battle of Port Hudson March 14, 1863 — Mississippi ran aground, was abandoned; Dewey among last to leave the wreck. Promoted to Executive Officer USS Agawam under Farragut. After James River service, Executive Officer USS Colorado. Second Battle of Fort Fisher January 1865 — Dewey saw the tactical opportunity that took the position in fifteen minutes; New York Times called it 'the most beautiful duel of the war.' Promoted Lieutenant Commander. POSTWAR: USS Kearsarge European station 1866; Naval Academy duty 1867-1870 commanding USS Constitution as training ship; instructor 1868-1870; USS Narragansett Pacific Coast Survey 1873-1877; Lighthouse Board secretary 1880; promoted Commander; USS Juniata Asiatic 1882 (hospitalized Malta with liver abscess and typhoid 1882-1884); promoted Captain 1884; USS Dolphin (one of original 'white squadron'); USS Pensacola European 1885-88; promoted Commodore 1896; Asiatic Squadron commander 1897 (Theodore Roosevelt secured him over more senior officers). MANILA BAY: Olympia flagship. April 27, 1898 sailed from China. May 1, 1898 attack at first light: 'You may fire when you are ready, Gridley.' Six-hour battle sank or captured entire Spanish Pacific fleet under Adm. Patricio Montojo y Pasarón; one American died (heart attack). August 13, 1898 cooperated with Gen. Wesley Merritt taking Manila. Returning Sept 27, 1899 — two-day NYC parade. Battle of Manila Bay Medal (Dewey Medal) struck by Tiffany & Co. designed by Daniel Chester French; Dewey wore his REVERSED out of modesty since his image was on obverse. POLITICS 1900: Withdrew from Democratic presidential nomination after PR missteps ('our next war will be with Germany'; admitted never voting in presidential election; transferred public-gift mansion to Mildred). Endorsed McKinley. MARRIAGES: (1) October 24, 1867 Portsmouth NH to Susan Boardman Goodwin (X02379, daughter of NH Civil War Gov. Ichabod Goodwin X02381); she died December 28, 1872 Newport RI five days after birth of son George Goodwin Dewey (TD0157). (2) November 9, 1899 Washington DC to Mildred McLean Hazen (X02380, widow of Civil War Maj. Gen. William Babcock Hazen — Hazen NOT built per Jalapeño). Mildred Catholic, Dewey not — they married in St. Paul's rectory rather than the Catholic church; some anti-Catholic criticism plus anger over Dewey transferring his $50,000 public-gift mansion to her. DEATH: Washington DC January 16, 1917 age 79 after 62 years US Navy active service (one less than Adm. Hyman Rickover). Lay in state at US Capitol rotunda. Originally Arlington National Cemetery; mausoleum built; remains transferred 1925 by Mildred to Bethlehem Chapel crypt Washington National Cathedral. MEMBERSHIPS: Honorary New York Society of the Cincinnati 1901 (INST115). Metropolitan Club Washington DC. 'Dewey' was 19th most popular boys' name 1898 (jumped from 111th the year before). MAJOR NAMESAKES: Dewey-Humboldt AZ; Dewey OK; Dewey County OK; Dewey Beach DE; multiple ships USS Dewey including Arleigh Burke-class destroyer DDG-105 commissioned 2010; Dewey Hall Norwich University 1899; Dewey Hall and Field US Naval Academy; Dewey Field Naval Station Newport; Dewey Square Boston 1898; Roxas Blvd Manila (formerly Dewey Blvd); Dewey Monument San Francisco Union Square. DESCENT: Sole 'son' line carries through George Goodwin Dewey (TD0157, b.1872 d.1963) — bachelor — so direct Dewey-line ended with him. Other Dewey descendants alive today come through Charles's seven children (TD0143-TD0149) and Edward's children TD0150-TD0153 lines.

narrative_blocks.header: Borrowed against himself to equip Civil War regiments
narrative_blocks.body: In May 1861 as the Civil War began, Goodwin responded to the first calls for soldiers by borrowing funds against his own personal credit to equip two New Hampshire regiments. The legislature ratified his action when it convened the following month. His pre-war business interests had been heavily interlinked with cotton produced by enslaved labor in the South.

narrative_blocks.header: Last Whig governor candidate; first NH Republican
narrative_blocks.body: Goodwin lost as the last Whig candidate for Governor of New Hampshire in 1856, switched parties to Republican, and won the office in 1859. He had served at the Whig national conventions that nominated Henry Clay, Zachary Taylor, and Winfield Scott — vice-president of the first two bodies.

narrative_blocks.header: Daughter married Admiral Dewey at the Goodwin Mansion
narrative_blocks.body: Goodwin's daughter Susan married Lt. Cmdr. George Dewey at the family Portsmouth NH mansion on October 24, 1867 — five years before her death in childbirth. The Goodwin Mansion has been preserved and is now part of the Strawbery Banke Museum complex in Portsmouth.

narrative_blocks.header: Mother dead five days after his birth
narrative_blocks.body: George was born December 24, 1872 at the Naval Training Station Newport Rhode Island. His mother Susan Goodwin Dewey died five days later on December 28 of childbirth complications, age 28. His father — heartbroken Lt. Cmdr.

narrative_blocks.header: Bachelor stockbroker died alone in Chicago mansion
narrative_blocks.body: Educated at St. Paul's School Concord and Princeton, George went into the New York Stock Exchange and reportedly accumulated more than a million dollars in the market. He never married. The last 13 years of his life he was confined to a wheelchair after a 1960 hip fracture; he died of a stroke at his 20-room mansion on Chicago's Near North Side in 1963 age 90, the last direct descendant of the Admiral.

narrative_blocks.header: Estate sent Dewey relics to Naval Academy
narrative_blocks.body: Per his obituaries, George Goodwin Dewey's will disposed of many relics and documents linked to his father Admiral George Dewey, most of which were already on loan to museums. The principal beneficiaries were the United States Naval Academy at Annapolis and the Library of Congress.

notable.notable_blurb: Civil War Medal of Honor; Texas House Speaker

narrative_blocks.header: Walked alone into the no-man's-land at Hatcher's Run
narrative_blocks.body: On April 2, 1865, when Gen. William Birney needed deserters questioned before a planned afternoon assault on Confederate works at Hatcher's Run, Captain Evans was the only staff officer to volunteer. He dismounted, passed alone over the ridge — the only Union soldier in view from Confederate lines — drew a sharp musketry fire, made the rifle pit, questioned the deserters, and returned through another shower of bullets to report.

narrative_blocks.header: Honor guard at Lincoln's funeral
narrative_blocks.body: Two weeks after his Hatcher's Run heroism, Evans was selected as one of the officers in President Abraham Lincoln's funeral cortège honor guard on April 17, 1865. He was twenty-one years old. He had risen from private to brevet major in three years.

narrative_blocks.header: Speaker of the Texas House at twenty-six
narrative_blocks.body: Elected Speaker of the Texas House of Representatives in 1870 — the youngest person ever to hold the office. Months later he opposed an August 1870 election law that postponed the next election from 1871 to 1872 in violation of the 1869 Constitution; the Republican caucus denounced him and voted to remove him from the speakership the following morning.

narrative_blocks.header: Funded a Black college's industrial-training building
narrative_blocks.body: Trustee of Tillotson College (now Huston-Tillotson University) 1881-1920 and board president 1909-1920, Evans donated $10,000 to construct the 1912 Evans Industrial Building — which trained Black students in construction skills and bears his name. The building stands today as a Texas Historical Site. He bequeathed an additional $10,000 for the college president's residence.

narrative_blocks.header: First cousin of Pampa Texas's Timothy Dwight Hobart
narrative_blocks.body: Wikipedia confirms what the Berlin Vermont genealogy shows — Ira's mother Emeline Hobart Evans and Timothy Dwight Hobart's father David Hobart were full siblings, children of Rev. James Hobart of Berlin Vermont. Two Berlin Vermont-born first cousins, both Texas pioneers, both buried back home. Timothy at Pampa Fairview, Ira at Berlin Corner.

people.research_notes: TD0163 — Ira Hobart Evans, Civil War Medal of Honor recipient, Texas House Speaker (youngest in state history), and major Austin civic and business figure. Sixth child of Dr. Ira Evans (X02383) and Emeline Hobart Evans (TD0124). b. April 11, 1844 Piermont NH. Father died 1852 when Ira was 8; mother moved family to Barre VT where Ira completed Barre Academy. CIVIL WAR: Enlisted Private Co. B 10th Vermont Volunteer Infantry July 28, 1862 (same regiment as older brother Edward P. Evans). Commissioned 1st Lieutenant 9th US Colored Troops December 18, 1863. Promoted Captain commanding Co. B 116th US Colored Troops January 27, 1865. MEDAL OF HONOR ACTION April 2, 1865 at Hatcher's Run VA — per Gen. William Birney's account: my division held a portion of the Union line; rifle pits and open ground swept by Confederate fire; newly arrived deserters needed interviewing for an afternoon assault. Birney called for a volunteer; Captain Evans was the only one who responded. Dismounted, passed rapidly over the ridge in front of the division — only Union soldier in view from Confederate line — drew sharp fire of musketry, disappeared into rifle pit, questioned deserters, returned through another shower of bullets to report. Citation (presented March 24, 1892): 'For extraordinary heroism on 2 April 1865, while serving with Company B, 116th Colored Infantry, in action at Hatcher's Run, Virginia. Captain Evans voluntarily passed between the lines, under a heavy fire from the enemy, and obtained important information.' Brevetted Major March 13, 1865 'for gallant and meritorious service'; assigned acting assistant adjutant general of XXV Army Corps, Army of the James. April 17, 1865 — officer in honor guard of Lincoln's funeral cortège (six days after Lincoln's assassination). Sheridan occupation force in Texas; provost marshal Brownsville. Discharged Louisville KY February 7 (or January 31), 1867. TEXAS POLITICS: 1867 settled north of Corpus Christi to ranch — lost investment through dishonest partner. Joined Freedmen's Bureau Wharton TX; resigned January 31, 1868 angered by incompetent superiors. Internal Revenue Service Eagle Pass then Corpus Christi. 1869 ran for Texas House of Representatives at urging of Republican gubernatorial candidate Edmund Jackson Davis; won Western District seat. SPEAKER OF THE TEXAS HOUSE 1870 at age 26 (Wikipedia gives 25; primary sources give 26) — youngest person ever to hold the office. August 1870 election-law dispute: a measure to postpone the next election from 1871 to 1872 violated the 1869 Constitution; Evans opposed it (with all Democrats and a few Republicans) and was called before a Republican caucus, denounced, and removed from the speakership the following morning. Completed his House term; left political life when 12th Legislature adjourned December 2, 1871. TEXAS BUSINESS CAREER: General Manager Texas Land Company of Houston 1872; Secretary Houston and Great Northern Railroad 1873; Secretary then Director International-Great Northern Railroad 1874-1908; PRESIDENT NEW YORK AND TEXAS LAND COMPANY (INST117) 1880-1906 — same firm where his first cousin Timothy Dwight Hobart (TD0133) worked as surveyor 1882-86 and as Mobeetie HQ manager of 1 million Panhandle acres 1886-1903. Co-founder and director Austin National Bank 1890-1922; Receiver Austin Rapid Transit Railway 1897-1902; President Austin Electric Railway 1902-03; Founder and President Texas Life Insurance Company. PHILANTHROPY AND CIVIC LIFE: Lifelong supporter of educational advancement for African Americans. Trustee of Tillotson College (now Huston-Tillotson University, INST116) 1881-1920; board president 1909-1920. Donated $10,000 for the construction of the Evans Industrial Building (1912, LM064, named for him, Texas Historical Site) which trained students in construction skills; $10,000 bequest for the college president's residence. President of the American Home Missionary Society. Trustee First Presbyterian Austin (22 years); board president First Congregational Austin (5 years); cofounder First Congregational Palestine TX (1881). Founder and first president Texas Society Sons of the American Revolution (1896 Vermont SAR member; national #2751, VT Society #51). Member Society of Colonial Wars and MOLLUS. His Austin home (North-Evans Chateau, LM063, now Austin Woman's Club, Austin Historic Landmark) was the meeting place for the Texas State Historical Association. FAMILY: First marriage July 1871 to Francese Abi 'Fannie' Hurlbut (X02385, 1838-1924) of Upper Alton IL — three sons: Wilber Leslie (TD0165), Hobart Yale (TD0166), Francis Hurlbut (TD0167). DIVORCED 1917 after 46 years. Second marriage 1920 to Jessie M. Stewart (X02386). NO biological children with Jessie. CARTOGRAPHIC NOTE on cousin connection: Per Wikipedia infobox 'He and Texas businessman Timothy Dwight Hobart were cousins.' Their mothers Emeline Hobart Evans (TD0124) and David Hobart (TD0129) were full siblings — children of Rev. James Hobart (X02368) and Betsey Perrin Hobart (TD0120) of Berlin VT. Therefore Ira Hobart Evans and Timothy Dwight Hobart of Pampa TX (TD0133) were FIRST COUSINS. Both Berlin Vermont-born Texas pioneers; both deceased in 1930s; Timothy buried Pampa, Ira buried Berlin Corner. CC linked in pilot100. RETIREMENT: Retired to San Diego CA 1921. d. April 19, 1922 San Diego CA age 78. Buried Berlin Corner Cemetery (CEM176) Berlin VT per his wishes — same cemetery as parents and most siblings. The Ira Hobart Evans Papers held at University of Tulsa McFarlin Library.

sources.label: FindAGrave — Rev Truman 'Freeman' Perrin

narrative_blocks.header: Berlin Vermont son who took the gospel south
narrative_blocks.body: Truman was born in Berlin Vermont in 1796 to the Perrin family's newly-cleared 1300-acre Scott Hill farm. He took the Presbyterian ministry as his calling and migrated south through Alabama and Mississippi where his three children grew up — but he died in Massachusetts in 1869, and was returned to Vermont for burial near the family land where he had been born.

narrative_blocks.header: Southern bank failures ruined him by 1850
narrative_blocks.body: After years preaching and accumulating merchant property in Alabama and Georgia, the failure of several Southern banks around 1850 wiped out most of his fortune. He returned to Vermont and spent his remaining nineteen years 'preaching in various places, and in the employ of the American Tract Society.'

narrative_blocks.header: Wife stayed in Aberdeen Mississippi when he returned
narrative_blocks.body: His wife Pronecy Tindall remained in Aberdeen Mississippi when he moved back north around 1850. He died at Washington Massachusetts in November 1869; she lived another fifteen years in Aberdeen, dying there in 1884.

narrative_blocks.header: Buried Vermont family land though died Massachusetts
narrative_blocks.body: Despite dying at Washington Berkshire County Massachusetts in November 1869, he was buried at East Road Cemetery in Berlin Vermont — adjacent to the 1300-acre Perrin family land his father Zachariah had established in 1789. His parents had chosen a different Berlin cemetery; Truman's plot lay closer to the farm.

career.notes: Per Pronecy's 1884 obituary 'the late Presbyterian minister.' Migration history: Berlin VT (b.1796) → Alabama (children born early 1830s) → Mississippi (raised William in Aberdeen) → Massachusetts (d.1869 Washington Berkshire County).

people.research_notes: TD-prefix Talcott blood descendant. Son of Zachariah Perrin (X01832) and Mary Talcott Perrin (T01387). b. April 24, 1796 Berlin VT — among the first generation of Perrin children born in Vermont after the family's 1789 migration from Hebron CT (his older sister Mary Perrin I was born Hebron, died young 1798). d. November 19, 1869 Washington, Berkshire County MA age 73. Presbyterian minister — per his estranged wife Pronecy's 1884 obituary, 'the late Presbyterian minister.' Migration: Berlin VT → Alabama (where his son William Alexander Perrin was born 1838 to Pronecy in Henry County AL) → Aberdeen Mississippi (where William was raised) → Washington Berkshire County MA (where Truman died 1869). Wife Pronecy remained in Aberdeen MS until her 1884 death. MARRIAGE: 1835 to Pronecy B. Tindall (X02389, 1808-1884), daughter of Dr. John Lewis Tindall Sr. and Mary Ritchey Tindall of Smithland KY. Three children: Mary Caroline Perrin Pollard (TD0171, 1837-1866 d.young 29), William Alexander Perrin (TD0172, 1838-1903, attorney + Confederate Civil War vet), Amanda Perrin (TD0173, 1839-1912 unmarried lifelong schoolteacher). Buried East Road Cemetery, Berlin VT — adjacent to the Perrin family land at East Road / Scott Hill intersection in Berlin VT (the 1300-acre farm his father Zachariah established 1789). Family-graveyard burial even though he died in Massachusetts. His mother Mary Talcott Perrin (T01387 — buried Berlin Corner Cemetery CEM176) and father Zachariah Perrin (X01832 — Berlin Corner) chose a different Berlin VT cemetery; Truman's East Road Cemetery is closer to Perrin family land. Solo Hooker-tree connection in East Road Cemetery — no CEM entry built per §0.4 threshold (need 2+); flag for future research if other Perrins are identified there. FACTUAL FLAG: A William Alexander Perrin biographical source incorrectly states 'His sister, Mary Perrin, was the mother of Admiral George Dewey.' Mary Polly Perrin Dewey (TD0138, 1799-1843) was William's AUNT (Truman's sister, both children of Zachariah and Mary Talcott Perrin), NOT his sister. Document this as source error, not factual claim. [Pilot101 enrichment from Berlin VT history, Hamilton Child 1888, and Talcott Pedigree (1876) entry 1397]: Birth date discrepancy: Talcott Pedigree gives April 24, 1796; Berlin VT history gives April 28, 1796. Graduated Dartmouth College 1817. Ordained 1822. Preached in various places in Vermont, New Hampshire, and New York. Spent several years in Indiana, Georgia, and Alabama before returning to Vermont in 1850. Died Washington, Massachusetts, November 19, 1869, aged 73 years. [Pilot103 enrichment from Hemenway, Vermont Historical Gazetteer (1881 Berlin chapter)]: After returning North in 1850 (following the failure of several Southern banks that wiped out most of the merchant property he had accumulated in Alabama and Georgia), spent his remaining years 'preaching in various places, and in the employ of the American Tract Society.' Birth date discrepancy noted across sources: Talcott Pedigree (1876) entry 1397: April 24, 1796. Berlin VT history (Hamilton Child, Gazetteer of Washington County VT, 1888): April 28, 1796. The Hemenway 1881 source uses 'Apr. 28, 1796.' Wife's name spelling variant: Pronecy B. Tindall (Talcott book) or Pronecey B. Tyndall (Hemenway). Hemenway also confirms 'one son and two daughters' from this marriage — three children documented in this database (TD0171, TD0172, TD0173).

sources.label: FindAGrave — William Alexander Perrin

narrative_blocks.header: LL.B. four months before the Civil War
narrative_blocks.body: William graduated with his Bachelor of Laws from the Law Department of the University of Louisiana — what is now Tulane University — on Saturday March 30, 1861. Four months later he married Clara Niven on the eve of his 28th birthday at Osyka Mississippi; less than a year after that he enlisted in the Confederate Washington Artillery Battalion at New Orleans.

narrative_blocks.header: Married his daughter's wedding host nine days later
narrative_blocks.body: After his first wife Clara died Waxahachie Texas in January 1886, William moved east to Thornton Calhoun County Arkansas. His daughter Louise married Dr. Daniel Frizzell at Camden Arkansas on October 8, 1889 — nine days later October 17, 1889 William himself married Mrs. Sarah Bullard at Thornton.

narrative_blocks.header: First cousin to Admiral Dewey and Speaker Evans
narrative_blocks.body: Through his grandmother Mary Talcott Perrin and grandfather Zachariah Perrin, William was first cousin to Admiral George Dewey of Manila Bay (whose mother Mary Polly was William's aunt) and a cousin twice removed of Civil War Medal of Honor recipient Ira Hobart Evans of Texas and of Pampa Texas's Timothy Dwight Hobart. The Vermont Perrin matriarch's grandchildren scattered across Confederate Mississippi, Union Vermont, Texas frontiers, and the Spanish-American War Pacific.

EDUCATION: Bachelor of Laws (LL.B.) from the Law Department of the University of Louisiana (now Tulane University), graduated Saturday March 30, 1861 — just before the Civil War broke out. CIVIL WAR (Confederate): Enlisted Private March 7, 1862 New Orleans LA in the 2nd Company, Washington Artillery Battalion of Louisiana. Service record present through October 1863; absent with leave late 1863; absent without leave early 1864; returned active duty March 1864; served until February 1865. Occupation recorded 'lawyer'; residence Osyka MS. FIRST MARRIAGE: Two days before his 28th birthday on Thursday, July 18, 1861 at the Church of Our Saviour in Osyka, Pike County MS, married Clarentine 'Clara' Cowling Niven (X02390, 1839-1886). Ceremony by Rev. Dr. Spencer (believed to be Capt. John Thomas Spencer, teacher at Floridian Academy in Greensburg, St. Helens Parish, LA). Clara was daughter of New Orleans businessman James Neil Niven and Maria Sophia Clarentina 'Clara' Cowling. Her maternal grandparents John Granberry Cowling and Louisa Marie Anne Martha Georgette of Savannah, GA. Five children — see TD0174-TD0178. POST-WAR CAREER: Attorney at Law in Greensburg, Amite, and New Orleans LA. Cotton Broker in Amite, Tangipahoa Parish LA. Schoolteacher at the Smithville Male and Female Normal Institute in Smithville Monroe County MS — alongside his wife Clara (who taught French and music there), Mrs. Clay Elliott, Professor William Saville, and Dr. John T. M. Gregory. Note: Smithville Normal Institute NOT built as INST per Sam pilot100 directive. Later: Fire Insurance Agent. 1900 U.S. Census Enumerator for Midland County TX. Member Rising Glory Masonic Lodge No. 215, F. & A.M., Osyka MS. WIDOWED 1886: Clara died January 28, 1886 Waxahachie TX. William relocated east to Thornton, Calhoun County AR (near Fordyce). Daughter Louise Frizzell married Dr. Daniel Frizzell at Camden, Ouachita County AR October 8, 1889. Nine days later October 17, 1889, William married Mrs. Sarah Bullard at Thornton (officiated by Rev. David Edwin Gambrell, Baptist). Sarah Bullard NOT BUILT as X-prefix per Jalapeño Rule (limited information; 2nd-marriage spouse with no documented children). LEGAL CASEWORK FOOTNOTE: Represented Wolf Silverstein/Silverstone (Polish-born naturalized US citizen Tangipahoa LA businessman) before the United States Southern Claims Commission, claim #16155 for $2,994 in clothing/stores confiscated by Union forces under Brig. Gen. John Wynn Davidson during 1864 Baton Rouge → Mobile expedition. Case continued July 21, 1877 (Silverstein had moved to Weatherford, Parker County TX). Claim eventually denied. Brig. Gen. Davidson NOT BUILT (non-tree). FACTUAL FLAG: William Alexander Perrin biographical source incorrectly states 'His sister, Mary Perrin, was the mother of Admiral George Dewey.' Mary Polly Perrin Dewey (TD0138, 1799-1843) was William's AUNT, not sister — both children of Zachariah Perrin and Mary Talcott Perrin (T01387) one generation above William (whose father Truman was Mary Polly's brother). Documented as source error; actual genealogy: Ira Hobart Evans (TD0163), William Alexander Perrin (TD0172), and Admiral George Dewey (TD0141) are all genealogical cousins of varying distances through the same Mary Talcott Perrin / Zachariah Perrin matriarch and patriarch.

sources.label: FindAGrave — Louise Matilda 'Lula' Perrin Frizzell

narrative_blocks.header: Father remarried nine days after her wedding
narrative_blocks.body: Louise married Dr. Daniel Harrison Frizzell on October 8, 1889 at Camden Arkansas. Just nine days later, her widowed father William Alexander Perrin remarried — to Sarah Bullard at Thornton Arkansas. The compressed nine-day father-and-daughter wedding sequence in October 1889 marked the end of their three-year shared widowhood-and-grief after the mother's 1886 Waxahachie Texas death.

narrative_blocks.header: Christmas Eve 1925 pneumonia death at sixty-three
narrative_blocks.body: Louise died of pneumonia on Christmas Eve, December 24, 1925 at Banks Arkansas at age sixty-three. She is buried at Williams Cemetery in Warren Arkansas. She was survived by her husband, three sons, and two daughters per the Arkansas Gazette obituary published December 27, 1925.

narrative_blocks.header: Arkansas schoolteacher across multiple county towns
narrative_blocks.body: Louise was a schoolteacher in addition to mothering five children. The Frizzell family moved across Arkansas towns — Princeton and Bucksnort in Dallas County, then Kingsland in Cleveland County, then finally Banks in Bradley County. Five children all named with Hooker-Talcott family-tradition names: Clara Amanda, Francis Niven, Lillie Irene, Garland, and James Austin.

narrative_blocks.header: Born Amite LA 1862, eldest of Perrin daughters
narrative_blocks.body: Louise Matilda 'Lula' Perrin was born April 19, 1862 in Amite, Tangipahoa Parish Louisiana — eldest daughter of William Alexander Perrin and Clarentine 'Clara' Niven Perrin. After her mother's 1886 death in Waxahachie Texas, Louise and her widowed father moved east to Thornton in Calhoun County Arkansas, where she met her future husband Dr. Daniel Harrison Frizzell.

narrative_blocks.header: First male child born in Berlin Vermont
narrative_blocks.body: Porter was born February 1, 1790, less than a year after his parents Zachariah Perrin and Mary Talcott Perrin migrated by ox-sled from Hebron, Connecticut, to settle the eastern frontier of Berlin. He married Lucy Kinney of Plainfield in November 1815, lived his entire life in Berlin, and died there in May 1871 at age eighty-one.

narrative_blocks.header: Distributed his fortune to charity and his children
narrative_blocks.body: Porter accumulated more property in farming than any other man before him in Berlin, according to the 1881 Vermont Historical Gazetteer. He gave a large share to charitable and religious purposes during his lifetime, distributed much of the rest among his many children, and left enough for his widow's support to her death.

people.research_notes: Fifth child and second-surviving son of Zachariah Perrin Esq. and Mary Talcott Perrin. Born Berlin VT February 1, 1790 — the first male child born in Berlin. Married Lucy Kinney (X02394, daughter of Rev. Jonathan Kinney of Plainfield VT) on November 2, 1815, at Plainfield. Their son MAJ Porter Kendrick Perrin (TD0184) served as a Civil War Major. Porter died May 17, 1871, age 81. Source: Talcott Pedigree (1876) entry 1395; biographical detail from Berlin VT history (Hamilton Child, Gazetteer of Washington County VT, 1888).

death.cause: died at age thirty-one. Berlin VT history (Child 1888) attributes death to alcoholism that began as a medical prescription: his attending physician prescribed brandy as treatment for the ill health he developed in South Carolina, and the resulting addiction killed him. Talcott Pedigree (1876) silent on cause. Source-discrepancy preserved as historical record.

education.notes: Class of 1812 per Talcott Pedigree (1876); Berlin VT history (Child 1888) gives 1813. Discrepancy unresolved.

career.notes: Preached in various places in Vermont, New York, and Pennsylvania.
Three-year pastorate in South Carolina taken for health reasons; did not recover; returned to Berlin.

institutions.institution_blurb: Graduated Middlebury College Class of 1812.

narrative_blocks.header: Pastor in South Carolina sent home to die
narrative_blocks.body: Poor health led Rev. Perrin to accept a three-year pastorate in South Carolina, hoping a warmer climate would restore him. He did not recover and returned to Berlin Vermont, where he died in February 1824 at age thirty-one.

narrative_blocks.header: Wrote two volumes of poetry before age thirty-one
narrative_blocks.body: Rev. Perrin published two volumes of poetry as a Congregational minister preaching in Vermont, New York, and Pennsylvania. A third volume titled Eloida is rumored but no extant copy has been found.

narrative_blocks.header: Brandy prescribed as medicine became fatal addiction
narrative_blocks.body: Per the 1888 Berlin Vermont history, Rev. Perrin's attending physician prescribed brandy as a medical treatment for the ill health that drove him from his South Carolina pastorate back to Berlin. The prescription created an addiction that the source frankly attributes as the cause of his death at thirty-one.

people.research_notes: Sixth child and third son of Zachariah Perrin Esq. and Mary Talcott Perrin. Born Berlin VT April 25, 1792 (Talcott Pedigree 1876); some later sources give 1793 — discrepancy unresolved, primary defaults to Talcott Pedigree per project rule. Graduated Middlebury College Class of 1812 (Talcott book) or 1813 (Berlin VT history). Married Fanny Thompson of Montpelier VT (X02395, daughter of Capt. Daniel Thompson) about 1812. Ordained Congregational minister; preached in Vermont, New York, and Pennsylvania. Took a three-year pastorate in South Carolina for his health, did not recover, returned to Berlin and died February 9, 1824, age 31. Buried East Road Cemetery, Berlin VT (FindAGrave memorial 103993). Published two volumes of poetry; a rumored third volume Eloida has no recorded extant copy. NOT to be confused with the Irish Rev. William Perrin (1792-1824) to whom Hebrew Canticles is sometimes wrongly attributed. Source: Talcott Pedigree (1876) entry 1396; Berlin VT history (Child 1888); Marcus Davis Gilman, The Bibliography of Vermont (1897); Catalogue of the Graduates of Middlebury College (1853). [Pilot103 enrichment from Hemenway, Vermont Historical Gazetteer (1881 Berlin chapter)]: Death cause discrepancy. Talcott Pedigree (1876) entry 1396 records death and place but no cause. Berlin VT history (Hamilton Child, Gazetteer of Washington County VT, 1888) is explicit: 'a victim to the immoderate use of ardent spirits. His attending physician prescribed brandy for a medicine, the use of which created an appetite which' [text continues but is the cause]. Iatrogenic alcoholism following a South Carolina pastorate undertaken for failing health. The Berlin source also adds: preached in New York State 1 year, then near Charleston SC for 2-3 years before failing health drove him north. Married Fanny Thompson 1815 (Berlin source) — Talcott book and WikiTree both give 'about 1812' so a date discrepancy of about 3 years exists across sources.

narrative_blocks.header: Brother lawyers and Clinton County judges in Michigan
narrative_blocks.body: After the Civil War, Major Porter Kendrick joined his older brother Henry in Saint Johns Michigan to practice law. Both Perrin brothers served as Clinton County judges of probate; Henry also served as a Michigan state senator. Their niece Harriet Eliza later joined them in Saint Johns.

narrative_blocks.header: Two years' war service made him a Major
narrative_blocks.body: He went out with the 27th Michigan Infantry and transferred to the staff of the 2nd Michigan, the major's rank a wartime promotion rather than a starting commission.

Sessions (X02397, b. 1846). Children: Archer M. Perrin (TD0185, 1863-1927) and Paul Rex Perrin (TD0186, 1869-1869, died in infancy). Lived adult life in Saint Johns, Clinton County, Michigan. Died March 20, 1903, age 69. Buried Mount Rest Cemetery, Saint Johns MI alongside wife and son. Source: FindAGrave Mount Rest Cemetery memorial. [Pilot103 enrichment from Hemenway, Vermont Historical Gazetteer (1881 Berlin chapter)]: Fifth son of Porter Perrin. Graduated Albany Law School. Practiced law in Saint Johns MI in partnership with his older brother Henry M. Perrin (TD0209). Served as Clinton County MI judge of probate. Civil War service: 'served 2 years or more in the war of the secession, and was promoted to the office of major' — confirms Major rank promotion was a wartime advancement, not a starting commission. Saint Johns Perrin cluster now wires to four people in this database: Porter Kendrick (TD0184), his wife Ella Sessions (X02397), their sons Archer (TD0185) and Paul Rex (TD0186), brother Henry M. (TD0209), and niece Harriet Eliza (TD0202).

narrative_blocks.header: Served Berlin schools twenty years and legislature twice
narrative_blocks.body: Justus Newton Perrin served as Berlin Vermont's superintendent of schools for more than twenty years and represented the town twice in the Vermont state legislature. He balanced public service with running the family dairy farm, where his fifteen-year-old son Porter Elisha documented the operation in an 1874 diary now held by the Vermont Historical Society.

narrative_blocks.header: Outlived two wives and reached ninety-one
narrative_blocks.body: Justus's first wife Arethusa Hosford died in 1855 at age thirty, leaving him with two young daughters. He remarried in 1858 to Mary Wild and had five more children. He lived to ninety-one and is buried at Berlin Corner Cemetery alongside generations of his Perrin and Talcott ancestors.

people.research_notes: Eldest son of Porter Perrin (T01395) and Lucy Kinney Perrin (X02394). Born Berlin VT November 21, 1822. Married Arethusa Rosette Hosford (X02409) December 22, 1847; she died March 27, 1855. Two daughters from this marriage: Lucy Helen Perrin (TD0201) and Harriet Eliza Perrin (TD0202). Married second wife Mary Wild (X02410) January 13, 1858; five children: Elisha Newton (TD0203), Porter Elisha (TD0204), Mary Newton (TD0205), and Rev. Justus Newton Jr. (TD0206). Berlin VT superintendent of schools for over 20 years; twice elected to Vermont state legislature (sessions including October-November 1874 per his son Porter Elisha's diary). Died Berlin VT January 29, 1914, age 91. Buried Berlin Corner Cemetery. NOTE: Possibility of Newton-line connection through wife Mary Wild's mother's family was considered (his middle name 'Newton' and several children's names with 'Newton' echo this), but no direct genealogical link to David Newton's Hartford VT Newton line has been established. Naming may reflect family friendship or fashion rather than descent. Source: WikiTree Perrin-2939; Berlin VT history (Hamilton Child, Gazetteer of Washington County VT, 1888); Vermont History Explorer (vermonthistoryexplorer.org).

narrative_blocks.header: Motherless at four, she followed the uncles
narrative_blocks.body: Arethusa died in 1855 when her daughter was four. Grown, Harriet left Berlin, Vermont for Saint Johns, Michigan, where her uncles Porter and Henry Perrin had built law practices together — and there she stayed to the end, in 1926.

Perrin (TD0209) in Saint Johns at some point — both her uncles emigrated to Michigan as lawyers. The Saint Johns Perrin cluster constitutes a distinct second-generation Vermont-to-Michigan migration off the original Hebron-CT-to-Berlin-VT migration of her great-grandfather Zachariah Perrin. Marital status, burial place, and date of migration to Michigan not yet established. Source: WikiTree Perrin-2945.

narrative_blocks.header: Kept a 1874 farm diary at age fifteen
narrative_blocks.body: Porter Elisha and his twin brother Elisha Newton spent their teenage years working the family dairy farm in Berlin Vermont. At fifteen Porter began a diary that documents thirty-six head of cattle, six hundred and twelve maple trees tapped for sugar, his own twenty-cents-per-week wage, and his father's October legislative service in Montpelier.

people.research_notes: Twin son of Justus Newton Perrin (TD0200) and Mary Wild Perrin (X02410). Born Berlin VT November 1, 1858 — twin brother of Elisha Newton Perrin (TD0203). Lived and worked his entire life on the family dairy farm at Scott Hill Road and Airport Road, Berlin (LM065 Porter Perrin Farm). At age fifteen kept a daily diary in 1874 documenting farm operations: cattle (36 head, some Jerseys), maple sugaring (612 trees tapped), butter production (Father churned), seasonal work (haying finished August 17), personal pay (20 cents/week), schoolwork (only attended school in winter when farm work was lighter), and his father's October-November service in the Vermont legislature. The diary has been transcribed and published by vermonthistoryexplorer.org. Died Berlin VT December 24, 1946, age 88. Burial place not yet established. Source: WikiTree Perrin-2941; Vermont History Explorer (vermonthistoryexplorer.org); The Bridge VT, History Corner: Diary of a Vermont Farm Boy in 1874 by Carla Occaso (September 30, 2024).

career.notes: Elected as a Democrat to the 38th Congress March 4, 1863 to March 3, 1865. First Washington Territorial Delegate to Congress to hail from the East side of the state. Last Democrat to represent the Washington Territory in Congress until 1885. Did not seek renomination in 1864.
6th Governor of Washington Territory. Appointed by President Andrew Johnson November 1866; served January 8 to March 4, 1867. Preceded by William Pickering, succeeded by Marshall F. Moore.
Helped oversee construction of railroad line from Portland to Roseburg.

Two terms as Spokane County Treasurer after 1889 move to Spokane.

narrative_blocks.header: Governed Washington Territory for two months
narrative_blocks.body: Appointed 6th Governor of Washington Territory by President Andrew Johnson in November 1866, George Edward Cole served just under two months — from January 8 to March 4, 1867. He was the last Democrat to represent the Washington Territory in Congress until 1885 and helped draft the 1853 memorial that created the Territory itself.

narrative_blocks.header: Followed gold rush from Illinois to Oregon
narrative_blocks.body: George moved from his birthplace in Trenton New York to Illinois, then joined the 1849 California gold rush, and reached the Oregon Territory in 1850. Within two years he was a member of the Oregon territorial legislature; within thirteen he was Washington Territory's Delegate to Congress.

narrative_blocks.header: Switched parties between Democrat and Republican
narrative_blocks.body: Elected as a Democrat to Congress in 1862 and appointed Governor by Democrat Andrew Johnson, George Edward Cole switched his allegiance to the Republican Party during the 1870s. He held postmaster appointments under Republican Presidents Grant and Hayes and served as Spokane County treasurer in the 1890s.

people.research_notes: George Edward Cole, 6th Governor of Washington Territory and 5th Delegate from Washington Territory to the U.S. Congress. Son of Nathan Cole (X02398) and Laura Hills Cole (TD0189). Born December 23, 1826 in Trenton (now Trenton Falls), Oneida County, New York. Educated at public schools and Hobart Hall Institute; employed as a country store clerk before moving to Illinois, then joining the 1849 gold rush to California, and reaching the Oregon Territory in 1850. Career timeline: Oregon House of Representatives (1852-1853, helped draft the memorial calling for the establishment of Washington Territory); mercantile and Willamette River steamboat business; clerk of the U.S. District Court of Oregon (1859-1860); relocated to Walla Walla WA 1860; Delegate to the 38th Congress as a Democrat (1863-1865, first delegate from the eastern side of the state); appointed 6th Governor of Washington Territory by President Andrew Johnson November 1866, served January 8 to March 4, 1867; returned to Portland Oregon and worked on the Oregon & California Railroad (1867-1872); switched to the Republican Party in the 1870s; appointed Postmaster of Portland by President Grant 1873, reappointed by President Hayes 1877; Northern Pacific Railroad official through 1882; relocated to Spokane WA 1889; Spokane County Treasurer two terms 1890-1892; extensive interests in mining, manufacturing, and farming through retirement. Married first wife Mary E. Cardwell (X02418) in 1853; she died 1875. Two children from this marriage: Cecella 'Ella' (TD0212) and George Frederick 'Fred' (TD0213). Married second wife Annie Augusta King (X02419, b. 1836 Maine, d. 1913). Died Portland OR December 3, 1906, age 79. Buried Lone Fir Pioneer Cemetery, Portland. Source: Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Edward_Cole); BDUSC; Hines, Illustrated History of the State of Oregon (1893) p. 349; Richards, A Brief History of Politics in Washington Territory. William Joseph Lehigh, first husband of Cecella 'Ella' Cole (TD0212). Born 1848 in Portland, Multnomah County, Oregon. Married Cecella 1882 in Multnomah County. Per the period news report, the cause was attributed to 'financial reverses and despondency.' Survived by his widow Cecella, identified in the report as 'daughter of Ex-Governor George A. Cole of Spokane, Wash.' (newspaper misnaming of George E. Cole). Buried River View Cemetery, Portland. Source: FindAGrave memorial 195810434; period news report.
[Stage 6Y-264 NB#1 body trim]: original body had 4 sentences, trimmed to first 3. On November 11, 1897 he committed suicide by gunshot in his office, age forty-nine. The contemporary news report attributed his death to financial reverses and despondency. His wife Cecella outlived him by eleven years.'

burial.plot_notes: Los Angeles County Crematorium Cemetery, Boyle Heights, Los Angeles County, California.

narrative_blocks.header: Outlived his fifteen-month marriage by three decades
narrative_blocks.body: Alden married the widowed Cecella Cole Lehigh in Portland Oregon in August 1907; she died in November 1908, fifteen months later. Alden lived until September 1937 — outliving the marriage by nearly twenty-nine years and dying in Los Angeles at eighty-one.

people.research_notes: Alden Ensign 'Al' DeVere, second husband of Cecella 'Ella' Cole (TD0212). Born November 9, 1855 in Iowa. Married Cecella August 3, 1907 in Portland OR — she died approximately 15 months later in November 1908. Alden survived nearly three more decades after her death; died Los Angeles September 23, 1937, age 81. Buried Los Angeles County Crematorium Cemetery, Boyle Heights. Any subsequent marriages or descendants not yet established. Source: FindAGrave memorial 162482768.

narrative_blocks.header: Lived ninety years across the nineteenth century
narrative_blocks.body: Sophia was born in 1816 just after the War of 1812 and died in 1906 — ninety years spanning the canal era, the Civil War, the Gilded Age, and the early automobile age. Two of her sons established the Risley line in Madison County New York.

people.research_notes: Daughter of David I. Brewer (X02399) and Fanny Hills Brewer (TD0190). Born July 11, 1816. Married Chauncey Risley (X02422). Two known sons: Edwin Hills Risley (TD0215, 1842-1921) and Sylvester Risley (TD0216, 1846-1920). Died November 6, 1906, age 90. Birth and death places, burial place not yet established. Source: WikiTree Reynolds-22849 (tree owner of the Hills/Brewer/Risley line; flagged for outreach contact list).

Chauncey Risley, husband of Sophia Brewer Risley (TD0214). Born February 9, 1815 in Glastonbury, Hartford County, Connecticut — same town as the early Talcott family seat. Died April 11, 1893 in Clinton, Clinton County, New York, age 78. Two known sons through Sophia. Burial place and parentage not yet established. Source: WikiTree Risley-827.

narrative_blocks.header: Risley name died with him in Utica
narrative_blocks.body: Edwin took his maternal grandmother's surname Hills as his middle name. He died in Utica New York in November 1921 at seventy-nine, leaving no documented descendants — the Risley name on this branch passed to the next generation only through his younger brother Sylvester.

people.research_notes: Elder son of Chauncey Risley (X02422) and Sophia Brewer Risley (TD0214). Given his maternal grandmother Hills's surname as middle name. Born Brookfield, Madison County, New York, February 5, 1842. Died Utica, Oneida County, New York, November 1, 1921, age 79. Marital status, descendants, and burial place not yet established. Source: WikiTree Risley-1188.

burial.plot_notes: Graham Cemetery, Hubbardsville, Madison County, New York.

narrative_blocks.header: Born at a place called Talcott Hill
narrative_blocks.body: Sylvester was born at Talcott Hill in Madison County New York in 1846 — a place name suggesting the Talcott family had settled the area generations earlier. He married Mary Ann Nower and was the only one of Sophia Brewer Risley's two sons to produce documented descendants.

people.research_notes: Younger son of Chauncey Risley (X02422) and Sophia Brewer Risley (TD0214). Born March 2, 1846 at Talcott Hill, Madison County, New York — a place name that suggests Talcott family settlement in the area. Married Mary Ann Nower (X02423). Daughter Florence Mabel Risley Wratten (TD0217, 1873-1923) is the documented descendant of this marriage. Sylvester died Hamilton, Madison County, New York, October 21, 1920, age 74. Buried Graham Cemetery, Hubbardsville. Source: WikiTree Risley-826; FindAGrave Graham Cemetery memorial.

narrative_blocks.header: Single daughter carried the Risley line forward
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Ann's only documented child Florence Mabel Risley Wratten was born in 1873 — Mary Ann's twenty-seventh year. Mary Ann died at forty-seven in 1893, when Florence was twenty. The entire continuing Risley-Wratten-Stapleton chain that runs to the twenty-first century passes through this single daughter.

people.research_notes: Mary Ann Nower, wife of Sylvester Risley (TD0216). Born 1846 in New York. Died April 1893 at approximately age 47. Daughter Florence Mabel (TD0217) documented. Birth place, death place, parentage, and burial not yet established. Source: WikiTree Nower-17.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at fifteen and bore nine children
narrative_blocks.body: Florence Mabel Risley married the English-born James Sims Wratten in 1888 when she was fifteen and he was twenty-three. She bore nine children between 1890 and 1919, then died in Hamilton New York in 1923 at fifty.

people.research_notes: Only documented child of Sylvester Risley (TD0216) and Mary Ann Nower Risley (X02423). Born June 3, 1873 in Hamilton, Madison County, New York. Married James Sims Wratten (X02424) in 1888 — she was approximately 15 years old at marriage. Nine documented children spanning 1890-1919. Died Hamilton, NY December 23, 1923, age 50. Burial place not yet established. Source: WikiTree Risley-825.

burial.plot_notes: Graham Cemetery, Hubbardsville, Madison County, New York. FindAGrave memorial 98431389.

narrative_blocks.header: Came from Cranbrook Kent to Madison County
narrative_blocks.body: James Sims Wratten was born in Cranbrook in the Tunbridge Wells Borough of Kent, England in September 1865. He emigrated to Madison County New York and married the fifteen-year-old Florence Mabel Risley there in 1888. He died in Brookfield New York at seventy-three.

people.research_notes: James Sims Wratten, husband of Florence Mabel Risley Wratten (TD0217). Born September 7, 1865 in Cranbrook, Tunbridge Wells Borough, Kent, England — the only England-born spouse in this Hooker-line branch documented to date. Married Florence in 1888 in the United States. Nine documented children spanning 1890-1919. Died Brookfield, Madison County, New York, November 6, 1938, age 73. Buried Graham Cemetery, Hubbardsville. Source: FindAGrave memorial 98431389.

narrative_blocks.header: Lived ninety-four years across two centuries
narrative_blocks.body: Minnie Blanche was born in 1898 to Florence Risley Wratten and the English-born James Sims Wratten of Madison County New York. She lived ninety-four years and died in 1992 — outliving all eight of her siblings except Ruth Ellen, the youngest.

narrative_blocks.body: Sylvester Risley Wratten was given his maternal grandfather's full name — first and middle — when born in 1902. He died in 1934 at thirty-two without documented marriage or descendants. He was the Risley line's namesake but not its continuator.

narrative_blocks.body: Alice Marie was the sixth child of the English-born James Sims Wratten and Florence Risley Wratten of Madison County New York. She married Richard P. Stapleton in 1924 at eighteen and bore four children.

narrative_blocks.header: Air Force veteran and Lockheed-Martin technician
narrative_blocks.body: Howard graduated Hamilton High School in 1956 and served in the United States Air Force. He worked for many years with G.E. and Lockheed-Martin as an electronic technician before retirement. He died at home in Frankfort New York in December 2020 at eighty-two with his family beside him.

people.research_notes: Howard W. Stapleton, son of Richard P. Stapleton (X02425) and Alice Marie Wratten Stapleton (TD0223). Born November 28, 1938 in Hubbardsville, Madison County, New York. 1956 graduate of Hamilton High School. Served in the United States Air Force. Married Elizabeth Horgan (X02426) on November 9, 1968 at St. Francis DeSales Church in Utica NY. Two daughters: Jennifer (TD0230, m. Lorne Smith of Richfield Springs) and Bethany (TD0231, m. Randy [last name unknown]). Five grandchildren (Sheila m. Dan, Alexis, Shaine, Jeffrey, Dillon) and two great-grandchildren (Hailey, Brantley) per his obituary. Career: Electronic Technician with G.E./Lockheed-Martin for many years before retirement. Predeceased by his three sisters Beverly Larkin (TD0227), Barbara Fisk (TD0226), and Cecille Eisenhut (TD0228). Died at home in Frankfort, Herkimer County, New York, December 14, 2020, age 82, with his family at his side. Services were private via Smith Funeral Home. Burial place not specified in obituary. Source: FindAGrave memorial 219891918; published obituary 2020.

narrative_blocks.header: West Hartford son built an Iowa farming family
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel was the eldest surviving son of John Whitman and Elizabeth Talcott Whitman of West Hartford Connecticut. He migrated west to Iowa in his teens or twenties, married Iowa-born Barbara Ellen Rodgers in Audubon in 1882, and raised ten children in Panora, Guthrie County. He carried his mother's Talcott surname west and gave it to one of his sons.

people.research_notes: Second child of John Whitman (X01829) and Elizabeth Talcott Whitman (H03194). Born May 16, 1855 — given his mother's maiden surname Talcott as middle name. Migrated west to Iowa as a young man. Married Barbara Ellen Rodgers (X02437) in Audubon Iowa on January 21, 1882. They raised ten children in Panora, Guthrie County Iowa. Barbara died in 1900; Samuel survived her by thirty-five years. Died March 14, 1935 in Panora at seventy-nine. Buried Brethren Cemetery, Panora. The Iowa anchor of the West Hartford Whitman line. Source: FindAGrave memorial 10952211; FamilySearch M2JJ-LT9.

The Iowa-born child died at seven in 1895.

narrative_blocks.header: Born in Iowa carrying the Hartford founder's name
narrative_blocks.body: Nine generations after Rev. Thomas Hooker founded Hartford Connecticut in 1636 and four generations after his namesake descendants began carrying his surname as a middle name, Mabel Hooker Whitman was born in Panora Iowa in 1896. The Hooker name had traveled from Hartford CT through West Hartford to the prairies.

Thomas Hooker founded Hartford in 1636, his name still travels in this Iowa-born child. Lived eighty-one or eighty-two years to 1978. Source: FamilySearch LX9L-577.

narrative_blocks.body: Edward Cone Talcott was the only child of George Talcott and Laura Wright Cone Talcott of Hartford. He was born in 1863 and died in infancy that same year — and his mother Laura died on April 1, 1863. He is buried at Cedar Hill Cemetery alongside his parents.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed thirteen days after her wedding
narrative_blocks.body: Eleanor married George Talcott on May 16, 1871 in Hartford at twenty-six. While on their bridal tour at Niagara Falls, George contracted pneumonia and died thirteen days later on May 29, 1871. Eleanor lived another thirty-one years and remarried a man named Hillyer.

people.research_notes: Eleanor Stone Hurd, daughter of William S. Hurd of Hartford CT. Born 1845. Married George Talcott (H03206) on May 16, 1871 at age 26. George died of pneumonia thirteen days later on May 29, 1871, while they were on their bridal tour at Niagara Falls. Eleanor later remarried a man surnamed Hillyer (her FindAGrave-recorded final last name); details of the second marriage not yet established. She died in 1902 at approximately 56 or 57. Source: FindAGrave 14236128. Per Jalapeño Rule, William S. Hurd not built as easter egg — single-event tree connection (his daughter's brief marriage) does not meet the orbit-entry threshold.

narrative_blocks.body: Emma Amelia Hall married Francis Wayland Talcott of West Hartford on October 16, 1877 when she was twenty-five. She bore him two children: Herbert Wayland (1879) and Mabel Hall (1884). Francis died in 1893; Emma's death date and burial place are not yet documented.

narrative_blocks.body: Herbert Wayland Talcott was born in West Hartford in October 1879 — the elder of two children. His father Francis Wayland Talcott was forty-two when Herbert was born and farmed in West Hartford until his death in 1893, when Herbert was fourteen and his sister Mabel was eight.

narrative_blocks.header: Atlanta widower married a Hartford widow
narrative_blocks.body: Henry Hilyer of Atlanta Georgia married Eleanor Stone Hurd in 1879 — eight years after she had been widowed by George Talcott's death on their honeymoon. Eleanor outlived this second marriage as well, eventually dying in 1902 with the Hilyer surname.

people.research_notes: Henry Hilyer of Atlanta GA. narrative_blocks.body: Pamela Talcott Butler outlived five of her seven children. Two died in infancy; three more died as young adults from various causes. Only her surviving daughters carried the line forward through their own descendants.

narrative_blocks.header: Replacement-named for older sister who died
narrative_blocks.body: Tirzah Ophelia Sherman was named for her elder sister Tirzah, who had died in infancy in 1819. The naming was a common nineteenth-century replacement pattern — keeping a lost child's name alive in the next-born of the same sex.

people.research_notes: Child of Capt. Nehemiah Talcott (T01390) and Tirzah Platt Talcott (X01834) of Lanesborough, Berkshire County MA. Married Joel Bradley Sherman (X02444) in 1830 in Lanesborough. narrative_blocks.header: Continued Capt. Nehemiah's line through Caroline
narrative_blocks.body: William Augustus Talcott was Capt. Nehemiah's youngest son. Through his daughter Caroline's marriage to Manton Wood the Talcott line extended into the Wood-Sherman families and ultimately west to Utah and California.

narrative_blocks.header: Lived ninety-two years in Lanesborough
narrative_blocks.body: George Bradley Sherman was born in Lanesborough in 1836 to Tirzah Ophelia Talcott Sherman and Joel Bradley Sherman. He spent the entire ninety-two years of his life in Lanesborough — never leaving the Berkshire County town his grandparents had founded as a family seat. He died there in 1929.

narrative_blocks.header: Massachusetts boy who built Utah life
narrative_blocks.body: Allen Talcott Wood was born in Massachusetts but moved west during young adulthood. He spent his working life in Ogden Utah, where he raised his son Chuck and is buried at Aultorest Memorial Park.

people.research_notes: Son of Manton Augustus Wood (X02447) and Caroline L. Talcott Wood (T01484). Born March 27, 1870 in Massachusetts. Carries his mother's maiden surname Talcott as middle name. Migrated west to Ogden, Weber County, Utah, where he married Charlotte Elizabeth Chase (X02449) — Utah native. Allen died in Ogden August 22, 1952 at 82. Buried Aultorest Memorial Park, Ogden. One documented son Charles Lawrence 'Chuck' Wood (T01492) who later migrated again to California. Source: FindAGrave 64360515.

narrative_blocks.header: Six generations from Glastonbury to Vallejo
narrative_blocks.body: Chuck Wood was born in 1898 in Vallejo California — six generations removed from his Glastonbury Connecticut ancestor Capt. Nehemiah Talcott. He died in Vallejo in 1980 at eighty-two, marking the West Coast terminus of one branch of the Talcott line.

people.research_notes: Son of Allen Talcott Wood (T01490) and Charlotte Elizabeth Chase Wood (X02449). Born November 16, 1898 in Ogden Utah. Married Harriet Maud 'Peggy' Wilson Wood (X02450) of Huntsville UT. Migrated to California with Peggy. Died January 3, 1980 in Vallejo, Solano County, California at 81. Buried Skyview Memorial Lawn, Vallejo. Through Chuck and Peggy this Capt. Nehemiah → William Augustus → Caroline → Manton Wood line ends in mid-twentieth-century California — six generations from Glastonbury Connecticut. Source: FindAGrave 100184395.

She returned east to marry William Bradley Sherman, also a Connecticut man, continuing the New England diaspora pattern of the mid-1800s.

narrative_blocks.header: Returned to Guilford in widowhood
narrative_blocks.body: Hannah Norton Hotchkiss married Amos Hotchkiss in East Guilford on December 12, 1791, and they raised their family in Wallingford CT. Amos died in 1808 at forty-three; Hannah lived another forty-three years and died in Guilford — her natal town — in 1851.

people.research_notes: Child of Arah Norton (H00398) and Phebe Scranton Norton (X02452) of Madison CT. Born February 3, 1769. Married Amos Hotchkiss (X02453) of Guilford CT. Three documented Hotchkiss children: Amos Cornwall (H02143, b. 1794), Horace (H02144, 1796-1830), Betsey (H02145, b. 1798). Lived at Wallingford CT where Amos died 1808; she outlived him by 43 years, dying April 12, 1851. Source: EH 1909 entry 1040. [Pilot115 corrections]: Death city Wallingford → Guilford per FamilySearch G4BK-Y85 (she may have returned to her natal Guilford in widowhood after Amos's 1808 death; the Wallingford residence per EH refers to where the couple lived). Marriage date December 12, 1791 in East Guilford added per FamilySearch. Added fourth documented child Ezekiel Hotchkiss (HD3458, b. 1801) per FamilySearch — not named in EH 1909 entry 1040, which records only three children.

narrative_blocks.header: Two daughters married the same Dowd
narrative_blocks.body: Mabel Norton's daughters Adelia and Phebe both married Harvey H. Dowd — a sororate marriage in which Phebe married her sister's widower after Adelia's death. The pattern was common in nineteenth-century New England when widowers needed help with young children.

people.research_notes: Child of Arah Norton (H00398) and Phebe Scranton Norton (X02452) of Madison CT. Born December 17, 1773. They lived at Guilford CT where Justus died December 3, 1857; Mabel predeceased him on February 17, 1846. Source: EH 1909 entry 1042.

career.notes: Self-made farmer. Cleared land and built a log cabin upon arrival in Addison County VT about 1800. Owned 500 acres at the time of his death in 1833. The homestead was inherited by his son Hiram Norton.

narrative_blocks.header: Cleared Vermont homestead at age twenty-three
narrative_blocks.body: Abel Norton was born in Connecticut in 1777 and migrated to Addison County, Vermont about 1800. He cleared land, built a log cabin, and farmed there the rest of his life. By his 1833 death he owned five hundred acres and was called in the local history 'a self-made man.' His son Hiram inherited the homestead.

narrative_blocks.header: Raised ten children eight survived to adulthood
narrative_blocks.body: Abel and Mehitable raised ten children at the Vermont homestead. Per the 19th-century Addison County local history, eight of the ten survived to adulthood — a high rate for the early-1800s frontier. Two children are presently identified: Calvin and Hiram.

people.research_notes: Child of Arah Norton (H00398) and Phebe Scranton Norton (X02452) of Madison CT. Born October 3, 1777. Married Mehitable Norton per EH; wife not built per Jalapeño. Death date and descendants not given by EH. Source: EH 1909 entry 1043. [Pilot117 enrichment]: Per WikiTree Norton-4165 and a 19th-century Addison County local history, Abel Norton migrated from Connecticut to Addison County, Vermont about 1800 — at age 23. He cleared a homestead, built a log cabin, and raised a family of ten children with his wife Mehitable Norton (X02553). Eight of the ten children survived to adulthood per the local history (which was written after Abel's 1833 death). At his death he owned 500 acres and was described as 'a self-made man.' His son Hiram Norton (HD3481) inherited the homestead. Two children are presently identified in WikiTree records: Calvin Norton (HD3479, b. 1811 Weybridge) and Hiram Norton (HD3481, dates unknown). Eight remaining siblings are documented as a group but not individually named in extant sources. Sources: WikiTree Norton-4165; Addison County, Vermont history (19th c.).

narrative_blocks.header: Died at fifty-one in Guilford
narrative_blocks.body: Diadema Norton Murray died July 10, 1837 in Guilford CT at age fifty-one — twenty-seven years after the death of her husband Calvin Murray. She had been widowed at twenty-five with three young children all under five, of whom her youngest Beulah Maria was born just six weeks before Calvin's 1810 death.

people.research_notes: Child of Arah Norton (H00398) and Phebe Scranton Norton (X02452) of Madison CT. Born November 17, 1785. Married Calvin Murray (X02455) of East Guilford. Three documented Murray children (H02156-H02158). Calvin died at East Guilford November 14, 1810 — Diadema was widowed at age 24 with three young children. Diadema's death date not given by EH. Source: EH 1909 entry 1044. [Pilot117 enrichment]: Death date added per WikiTree Norton-4166 — died July 10, 1837 in Guilford CT at age 51. WikiTree CONFUSION FLAG: WikiTree's Murray-8112 record incorrectly identifies 'Calvin Murray (1808-1889) of Madison CT' as Diadema's husband. That is wrong — that 1808-1889 person is actually Diadema's SON Calvin Nelson Murray (H02157), born July 14, 1808 to Diadema and her actual husband Calvin Murray Sr. (X02455, 1781-1810). EH 1909 entry 1044 is unambiguous: 'b. Sept. 14, 1781, at East Guilford... He died at East Guilford, Conn., Nov. 14, 1810.' Diadema was widowed at 25 with three children all under five.

narrative_blocks.header: Eldest daughter omitted from EH's record
narrative_blocks.body: Rhoda Norton was born in 1763 — three years before her brother Josiah, the eldest child whom Edward Hooker named in his 1909 genealogy. WikiTree documents Rhoda's marriage to Zebul Norton in Waterbury in 1782 and four children. The reason for her omission from EH is not established; she may have been overlooked as a daughter who married out of Connecticut documentation.

people.research_notes: Daughter of Arah Norton (H00398) and Phebe Scranton Norton (X02452) of Madison CT. Born 1763 in Guilford CT — NOT named in EH 1909 entry 398's six-child list; documented in WikiTree (Norton-3439) as the eldest daughter. Married Zebul Norton (X02456) on June 12, 1782 in Waterbury CT at age 19. Four documented children: Sabrina (HD3442), Friend Congress (HD3443), Augustus (HD3444), Osmynd (HD3445). Widowed about 1803 when Zebul died. Lived to about 1840, age approximately 77. Per WikiTree she predates Josiah (the eldest EH-named child, 1766) by three years. Reason for omission from EH not established. Source: WikiTree Norton-3439.

military_service.unit: 3rd Battalion, Col. Roger Enos, Wooster's Brigade, Connecticut State Troops
military_service.notes: Private Zebul Norton served with Capt. James Peck's Company in the 3rd Battalion, Col. Roger Enos, Wooster's Brigade, Connecticut State Troops, during the American Revolution. Documented enlistment as Minute Men and volunteers, September 17, 1777.

narrative_blocks.header: Mustered as Private at age sixteen
narrative_blocks.body: Zebul Norton enlisted as a Private in Captain James Peck's Company, 3rd Battalion under Colonel Roger Enos in Wooster's Brigade of the Connecticut State Troops on September 17, 1777 — at age sixteen. He served the Revolutionary cause and returned home to Connecticut, where he married Rhoda Norton in 1782 and fathered four children before dying about 1803.

people.research_notes: Husband of Rhoda Norton (HD3441). Born September 20, 1761 in Guilford CT — son of David Norton and Susa Bristol. Served as Private in Capt. James Peck's Company, 3rd Battalion under Col. Roger Enos in Wooster's Brigade, Connecticut State Troops, Revolutionary War (mustered September 17, 1777, age 16). Married Rhoda Norton on June 12, 1782 in Waterbury CT — both Nortons but apparently unrelated branches of the Connecticut Norton families. Four documented children. Died about 1803, age 41 — location unknown. Source: WikiTree Norton-3155.

Daughter of Zebul Norton (X02456) and Rhoda Norton (HD3441). Birth and death dates, marital status, descendants not yet established. Per WikiTree the eldest of Rhoda's four documented children. Source: WikiTree.

narrative_blocks.header: War of 1812 veteran moved family to Onondaga
narrative_blocks.body: Augustus Norton was born in Connecticut in 1785, the son of a Revolutionary veteran. He served in the War of 1812 and moved his young family to Onondaga County, New York, where he farmed and raised at least one documented son. He died at Onondaga Hill in 1859.

One documented son Augustus Jr. (HD3446). Died March 7, 1859 in Onondaga Hill at age 73. Source: WikiTree Norton-?.

narrative_blocks.header: Married Truman Benedict on Independence Day
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth Hotchkiss married Truman Benedict on July 4, 1819 in Connecticut — an Independence Day wedding. Across twenty years they had ten children, including three sons all named Truman who each died in infancy or at age two. Elizabeth died in 1867; Truman outlived her by thirteen years.

narrative_blocks.header: Three sons named Truman all died young
narrative_blocks.body: The Benedict household lost three sons in succession all named Truman: the first (born 1821) died at age two in 1823; the second (born 1828) died the same year; the third (born 1831) also died the same year. Elizabeth and Truman tried three times to give their family the father's name and three times lost the child.
