narrative_blocks.header: Hotel landlord ended life as state pauper
narrative_blocks.body: Augustus Norton Jr. ran a hotel and tavern in Onondaga County NY for decades. He died in 1887 at the Onondaga County Poor House — the local indigent-relief institution — having lost his standing in the years before his death.

people.research_notes: Son of Augustus Norton Sr. (HD3444) and Nancy Riggs Norton (X02457). Born March 15, 1812 in Syracuse NY. Worked successive careers across his lifetime: hotel landlord, NY State Canal assistant weighmaster, NYC Railroad watchman. Married first Juliett M. Spencer Norton (X02458, 1815-1852); after her death married second Lucinda Wells Norton (daughter of Margaret Wells; not built per Jalapeño). One documented son in 1864 American Civil War records died at Fort Monroe Virginia: Mott Norton (relation: brother or son, unclear from extant sources). Another son Joseph Norton committed suicide in 1879. Augustus Jr. himself died September 8, 1887 in the Onondaga County Poor House after 303 days residency, listed as State Pauper with boarding paid at $2/week, cause: debility. Three documented children with Juliett: Mortimer (HD3447), Emma (HD3448), Florence Alzina Spencer (HD3449). Source: WikiTree Norton-3096; 1850, 1870, 1880 US Census records.

narrative_blocks.header: Career arc from bookkeeper to IRS agent
narrative_blocks.body: George Burton 'Bertie' Spencer was born in Onondaga in 1873 and built a varied career across his lifetime: office bookkeeper through 1910, manufacturing accountant, US Post Office Inspector from 1917, and US Treasury Internal Revenue Agent by 1930. He raised three children in Rochester NY at 255 Lark Street.

narrative_blocks.header: Silver plated on Artizan Street
narrative_blocks.body: Edward and John Spencer Bromley plated silver as J. S. & E. Bromley at 6 Artizan Street in New Haven from about 1844, and in 1859 the firm opened a branch in New York City. Edward kept a shop of his own on Chapel Street after 1860, and was still an electroplater in Detroit in 1880.

narrative_blocks.header: New Haven boy buried in Detroit
narrative_blocks.body: Edward A. Bromley was born in New Haven Connecticut in 1823 and married Elizabeth Benedict there in 1846. After Elizabeth's 1865 death he migrated to Detroit Michigan, where he died in 1891 at sixty-seven and was buried at Woodmere Cemetery.

narrative_blocks.header: America's first staff news photographer
narrative_blocks.body: Edward came to Minnesota with his parents in 1867 and joined the St. Paul Pioneer Press as a reporter who also made pictures. At the Minneapolis Journal from 1894 he became what is counted the first regular newspaper staff photographer in the country, pressing editors to tell the news in photographs.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven thousand glass plates from his rivals
narrative_blocks.body: After giving up on coins, Edward collected negatives instead: five hundred from Benjamin Upton of St. Anthony in 1878, when Upton left for Florida, sixteen hundred from William Illingworth's St. Paul gallery, and within ten years the plates of some thirty others, about seven thousand in all.

narrative_blocks.header: He put early Minneapolis in one album
narrative_blocks.body: In 1900 Edward published Minneapolis Album, a photographic history of the city's growth from its first settlement to 1880, with portraits of the pioneers. In 1914 he sold some two hundred lantern slides and seventeen hundred glass plates to the Minneapolis Public Library.

narrative_blocks.header: His camera went out among the tribes
narrative_blocks.body: At the Pioneer Press Edward took up Minnesota's Indian history, and he would carry a camera out among the tribes looking for feature stories. In 1897 he photographed the Lower Sioux Agency, which the Dakota attacked on the first morning of the 1862 war.

narrative_blocks.header: With the Minnesota troops in 1898
narrative_blocks.body: When war with Spain came in 1898, the Minneapolis Times sent Edward out as its correspondent with the Minnesota troops, to report and photograph at once.

sources.label: Edward A. Bromley Photographs collection — Hennepin County Library Special Collections (M/A 0323)

people.research_notes: Child of Edward A. Bromley (X02467) and Elizabeth Benedict Bromley (HD3468). Pioneering Minnesota newspaper photographer. Considered the first regular newspaper staff photographer in the United States — established the staff photographer role at the Minneapolis Times and the Minneapolis Journal. Born September 24, 1849 in New Haven CT to Edward A. Bromley (X02467) and Elizabeth Benedict Bromley (HD3468). Arrived in Minnesota with his parents in 1867 — first St. Paul, then Minneapolis. Worked as news reporter and photographer for the St. Paul Pioneer Press; transferred to Minneapolis edition 1877; began at the Minneapolis Journal 1894. Lifetime collector — purchased over 7,000 negatives from 30+ photographers including B.F. Upton (500 in 1878 when Upton moved to Florida), W.H. Illingworth (1,600 from his St. Paul gallery), Pepper, Jacoby, Rugg, Harvey. War correspondent in the Spanish-American War 1898 with the Minneapolis Times, embedded with Minnesota troops. Published 1900 'Minneapolis Album: A Photographic History of the Early Days in Minneapolis'. Special interest in photographing Indigenous peoples — would take cameras out among the tribes for feature stories. Hennepin County Library Special Collections holds his Edward A. Bromley Photographs collection (M/A 0323) — nearly 1,400 photographs (1849-1917), primarily glass-plate negatives. Died June 21, 1925 in Minneapolis at age 75. Buried Lakewood Cemetery, Minneapolis. Source: FindAGrave; Hennepin County Library; FamilySearch K64W-6TX.

narrative_blocks.header: She gave West Hartford her whole calendar
narrative_blocks.body: She came east from Illinois in 1963 and volunteered at nearly everything within reach — the Wadsworth, the Hartford Hospital women's auxiliary, the Noah Webster House, the Mark Twain House, the Bushnell, and Literacy Volunteers. She later married Talcott Stanley, who had given the Wadsworth fifty years of his own.

narrative_blocks.header: She buried three of her sons
narrative_blocks.body: Two of her sons, Robert and Scott Hennessy, died before her, and an infant son, William, before them. Her daughter Joan and her son John survived her, with two grandchildren.

narrative_blocks.header: Class officer and sorority president at Denison
narrative_blocks.body: She graduated from Denison University, where she was vice president of her senior class and president of Kappa Kappa Gamma. She kept up the sorority's Hartford alumnae group for the rest of her life.

narrative_blocks.header: Two lakes and an island of summers
narrative_blocks.body: She was a camper and then a counselor at Camp Kamaji in Bemidji, Minnesota, and spent summers at Williams Bay on Lake Geneva. The later ones she spent with Talcott on Fishers Island.

narrative_blocks.header: Bridge, duck pins, and a practical joke
narrative_blocks.body: She played bridge, tennis and golf, skied, and bowled duck pins. She had a green thumb and a flair for practical jokes.

people.research_notes: Third wife of TD0074 Talcott Stanley. Per her obituary: born 21 Aug 1923 Chicago IL, one of three children of George M. and Bertha K. Sundheim; raised in La Grange IL; Denison University (VP senior class, president Kappa Kappa Gamma); lived Hinsdale IL until moving to West Hartford 1963; died 26 Mar 2010 after a brief illness. Volunteered at the Wadsworth, Hartford Hospital Women's Auxiliary, Noah Webster House, Literacy Volunteers, Mark Twain House, the Bushnell Memorial and the Kappa Kappa Gamma alumnae group. Member Hartford Golf Club, Town and County Club, Seed & Weed Garden Club. Survived by sister Dorothy S. Webber of Hinsdale IL; daughter Joan 'Joanie' Hennessy Wright (husband Arthur W.) of New Canaan; son John D. Hennessy (wife Rhonda) of Winter Garden FL; grandchildren Nicholas and Jennifer; nieces and nephews Duf, Dave, Siouxzy, Barb. Predeceased by brother George M. Sundheim Jr. and by sons Robert D., Scott D. and infant William D. Hennessy. None of the Hennessy or Sundheim relatives are built - they are her family, not Talcott's line.

narrative_blocks.header: Lived to ninety-five in Connecticut
narrative_blocks.body: Mehitable Norton was born in Guilford CT in 1765 and married Abel Norton — twelve years her junior. They migrated together to Addison County Vermont about 1800, where she bore ten children. After Abel's 1833 death she returned to her natal Guilford and lived there twenty-seven more years, dying January 8, 1860 at age approximately ninety-five.

Bore him ten children, eight of whom survived to adulthood. Note: the local history of Calvin Norton (HD3479) refers to the mother as 'Mabel' — this is either a transcription or memory error for 'Mehitable' (the WikiTree-confirmed name) or an alternate family-use form. After Abel's 1833 death she returned to Guilford CT — where she died January 8, 1860 at age approximately 95. Source: WikiTree Norton-4167.

American poet (1830-1886). Easter Egg / orbit entry — not a Hooker descendant. Connected to the Hooker tree via close friendship with Samuel Bowles III (X02841), father of Sally Bowles Hooker (X01276), grandfather of Richard + Thomas Hooker Jr. Bowles received approx 40 poems and 50 letters from Dickinson, mostly 1861-62. He was the only non-family member she spoke to at her father Edward Dickinson's 1874 funeral. Scholarly debate continues about whether Bowles was Dickinson's 'Master' figure or simply a close confidant — see Richard Sewall vs John McDermott interpretations. Per Emily Dickinson Museum source provided by Sam: Bowles described as 'a creator of endless perspectives' by Susan Dickinson. Burial: West Cemetery Amherst MA (not in tree as CEM). career.notes: Purchased a farm in Essex County NY where he remained twelve years.
Returned to Addison County VT in 1847 and purchased the Goodale farm — 166 acres with a residence built by Jared Goodale at an early date.
Moved to Weybridge VT in 1854 and bought the Lawrence place — 50 acres. Owned multiple farms in Addison County aggregating more than 500 acres.

narrative_blocks.header: Owned five hundred acres across Addison County
narrative_blocks.body: Calvin Norton spent his life consolidating Vermont farmland. He bought a farm in Essex County NY for twelve years; in 1847 bought the 166-acre Goodale farm in Addison County; in 1854 moved to Weybridge and bought the 50-acre Lawrence place. At peak he owned over five hundred acres across multiple Addison County farms — matching the size of his father Abel's original homestead.

narrative_blocks.header: Remarried at seventy-three to Jane's birthday
narrative_blocks.body: Calvin's first wife Sarah Sargeant died November 1884 after forty-nine years of marriage. Four months later, on March 19, 1885 — Jane Sargent's forty-third birthday — Calvin married her, daughter of Samuel Sargent of Middlebury. Calvin was seventy-three; Jane was thirty years his junior.

narrative_blocks.header: Three children only Calvin Jr survived
narrative_blocks.body: Calvin and Sarah Sargeant had three children — one daughter and two sons. Only the youngest son, Calvin Junior, survived to adulthood. The local history does not name the two children who died young.

people.research_notes: Son of Abel Norton (H01043) and Mehitable Norton (X02553). Born March 10, 1811 in Weybridge, Addison County, Vermont — eleven years after his father's 1800 migration from Connecticut. Educated in the common schools and brought up to farming until age 24. Married Sarah Sargeant — a native of Addison County, surname also given as Sargent — on October 8, 1835 (when Calvin was 24, matching the local history's 'till he reached the age of twenty-four years'). They had three children (one daughter and two sons per the local history); only one — Calvin Jr. (HD3480) — survived to adulthood. Calvin then purchased a farm in Essex County NY and remained twelve years; in 1847 returned to Addison and bought the Goodale farm (166 acres); in 1854 moved to Weybridge VT and bought the Lawrence place (50 acres). At peak owned over 500 acres across multiple Addison County farms. Sarah died November 1884; on March 19, 1885 Calvin remarried Jane Sargent (X02567) — daughter of Samuel Sargent of Middlebury VT. Calvin's death date not given in available sources (the local history was written while he was still living at the Lawrence place). Source: WikiTree Norton-13237; Addison County VT local history (19th c.). Note: An earlier WikiTree summary gave the marriage to Sarah as 1853, which contradicts the 'age 24' passage from the more detailed local history; 1835 is preferred.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at twenty-two had four children
narrative_blocks.body: Darling Dudley — recorded as 'Darlington' by Edward Hooker in 1909 but as 'Darling' by FamilySearch — married Artemisia Stannard on February 1, 1796 in Guilford CT at age twenty-two. They had four children spanning twenty years: Fannie (1796), Mary Ann (1798), Horace Sherman (1803), and Charles M. (1816). EH records his removal to Vermont, but the FamilySearch-documented Connecticut births of all four children show this migration was late.

narrative_blocks.header: Family migrated to Vermont before her death
narrative_blocks.body: Sibyl Bradley Norton was born in Guilford CT in 1745 and married Hooker Norton there in 1762 at seventeen. By her 1806 death the family had migrated to Sunderland, Bennington County, Vermont — establishing that the Hooker Norton household made the New England westward move sometime between 1786 (when her youngest son Zenas was born in CT) and 1806. Her husband Hooker returned to Madison CT to die in 1827.

people.research_notes: Wife of Hooker Norton (H00401). Born March 1745 in Vergennes, Addison County, Vermont — daughter of Joseph Bradley and Sibyl Meigs Bradley. Carries her mother's first name 'Sibyl'. Eleven documented children with Hooker. Death date not given by EH. Source: EH 1909 entry 401. [Pilot119 enrichment]: Birth full date March 29, 1745 per WikiTree. Birth place Guilford CT per WikiTree (EH gives Vergennes VT — possibly her father's later residence; WikiTree's CT origin preferred). Death May 4, 1806 in Sunderland, Bennington County, Vermont — establishing that the family had migrated from CT to VT by 1806. Source: WikiTree.

narrative_blocks.header: Two sisters married Evarts brothers
narrative_blocks.body: Lorain Norton married Ezra Evarts of Guilford in 1783; nine years later her younger sister Lois married Ezra's brother Curtis. Both Evarts brothers were sons of Jonathan and Lucretia Parmalee Evarts. Lorain and Ezra removed to Vermont; Lois and Curtis stayed in Connecticut.

narrative_blocks.header: Three Evarts siblings married three Nortons
narrative_blocks.body: Lorain Norton married Ezra Evarts in 1783. Years later Ezra's brother Curtis married Lorain's sister Lois, and their sister Mabel Evarts married Lorain's uncle Eber Norton. Three Evarts siblings married three Nortons across two generations — an unusually dense intermarriage between the two Guilford families.

narrative_blocks.header: Wife died three days after twins born
narrative_blocks.body: Bela Norton's first wife Lydia Bushnell gave birth to unnamed twins on March 17, 1813. She died three days later on March 20 — strongly suggesting complications from the birth. Bela went on to marry Mary Paine and then Mary Ann Mulliken.

narrative_blocks.header: Migrated west to Mexico New York
narrative_blocks.body: Bela Norton was born in East Guilford CT in 1772 but ended his life two thousand miles away — in Mexico, Oswego County, New York, where he died in June 1845 at age seventy-two. The migration date is not documented; he had spent his early married years in Connecticut.

narrative_blocks.header: Migrated four states across his lifetime
narrative_blocks.body: Bela Norton's life traced the New England westward migration in four stages: born in Connecticut in 1772; married Lydia Bushnell in Cheshire, Massachusetts in 1794; raised his children in Addison, Vermont where Lydia died 1813; ultimately died in Mexico, Oswego County, New York in 1845. His remains appear to have been returned to Vermont — buried Hindes Cemetery, Addison.

people.research_notes: Child of Hooker Norton (H00401) and Sibyl Bradley Norton (X02569) of East Guilford CT. Born November 15, 1772. Three marriages: (M1) Lydia Bushnell (X02572), who died March 20, 1813; (M2) Mary Paine (X02573); (M3) Widow Mary Ann (___) Mulliken (X02574). Twelve+ documented children, of whom the unnamed twins (HD3482, HD3483) were born March 17, 1813 — three days before Lydia's death, suggesting Lydia died in childbirth. Migrated west to Mexico, Oswego County, New York, where he died June 1845. Source: EH 1909 entry 1050. AUTO-NOTE: child wiring assigns all children to M1 (Lydia) by default — some may belong to M2 or M3 and this is open for research. [Pilot119 enrichment]: Marriage to Lydia Bushnell on March 18, 1794 in Cheshire, Berkshire County, Massachusetts at age 21 per WikiTree Norton-11678. The couple's documented children include Diantha Amelia (H02164, b. April 10, 1795) — implying Diantha was born within a year of the marriage. The migration sequence: Connecticut (birth) → Massachusetts (marriage 1794) → Vermont (Addison, where Lydia died 1813) → New York (Mexico, where Bela died 1845). FindAGrave records his burial at Hindes Cemetery, Addison VT (CEM203) — most likely body returned to be buried alongside Lydia. Source: WikiTree Norton-11678; FindAGrave. [Pilot121 research-note]: FamilySearch (LZK2-CD4) records 9 children with Lydia Bushnell — Lydia 1793-1799, Diantha Amelia 1796 (note: FS gives different death year 1858 vs FindAGrave 1868), Zenas 1798-1883, Polly 1801-?, Phineas Bushnell 1803-1887 (note: FS 'Phineas Bushnell' vs EH 'Phineas'), Anson 1805-1817, Amasa Decker 1806 (NOT in EH), unnamed son 1813-1813 (one twin), Lydia A. 1813-1901 (the other twin? — and possibly the same as EH's '2168a Twins'). Compared to EH's 12-child list (2163-2171a + 2 letter-suffix entries), several discrepancies: (1) FS adds 'Amasa Decker Norton' not in EH; (2) FS only documents one of the unnamed twins as Lydia A.; (3) FS dates one twin's survival to 1901; (4) FS death years for Diantha, Zenas, Phineas, Anson differ from currently-built entries. Open research question — current build retains EH structure; reconciliation pending.

narrative_blocks.header: Came to Kansas during territorial period
narrative_blocks.body: Henry E. Norton was born in Connecticut in 1831 and migrated to Kansas in 1855 at age twenty-four — during the territorial period that became known as 'Bleeding Kansas.' He returned east to New York in 1858, then back to Kansas in 1864 — straddling the Civil War. He worked in real estate in Emporia until his 1892 death.

people.research_notes: Son of Henry H. Norton (X02579) and Diantha Amelia Norton (H02164) of Madison CT. Born June 22, 1831 in New Haven County CT. Married Helen Rebecca Wilson (X02593) of Topeka in 1875 (she was 31; he was 44). Three documented children: Lucy (HD3491, 1873-1896 — born BEFORE the marriage, suggesting either an earlier marriage Sam's source did not record or that 1875 is the marriage to Helen specifically rather than Henry's first marriage), Harry (HD3492, the Santa Fe RR clerk), and Minnie (HD3493, the Normal student). Died July 7, 1892 in Emporia KS at age 61. Buried Topeka Cemetery (CEM204). Source: FindAGrave; family history in Sam's notes. AUTO-NOTE: Marriage year 1875 vs Lucy's 1873 birth needs reconciliation — possibly an earlier marriage of Henry E.

narrative_blocks.header: Died of consumption in Colorado at twenty-two
narrative_blocks.body: Lucy Norton was stricken with consumption in August 1895 and went to Colorado the next month seeking the climate cure that was a common nineteenth-century treatment. She died at her aunt's home in Wolcott, Colorado on January 15, 1896 at age twenty-two. In the three years before her death she had lost her father, her mother, and a grandmother.

narrative_blocks.header: Newspaper obituary praised her courage
narrative_blocks.body: The Emporia local newspaper obituary singled out the responsibilities Lucy had borne after her father's 1892 death and her mother's 1893 death: 'She has been called upon to fight the hard battle of life and to assume its responsibilities single handed and alone. She has made a good fight.' She left a brother Harry and a fifteen-year-old sister Minnie.

quotes.quote: She has shirked no duty, however hard, and as a reward she passes out of life, aged 22 with sincere love, sympathy and respect of every person with whom she has been brought in contact.
quotes.speaker: Anonymous obituary writer

people.research_notes: Eldest daughter of Henry E. Norton (HD3490) and Helen Rebecca Wilson Norton (X02593). Born May 11, 1873 in Emporia, Lyon County, Kansas. Stricken with consumption in August 1895 and went to Colorado in September seeking the climate cure. Died January 15, 1896 at the home of her aunt Mrs. R. J. Wilson (also given as Mrs. J. L. Woston in another newspaper) at Wolcott, Eagle County, Colorado at age 22. Buried Topeka Cemetery (CEM204). She had lost her father (1892), mother (1893), and a grandmother in the three years before her own death — left with siblings Harry and fifteen-year-old Minnie. The local newspaper obituary praised her: 'She has shirked no duty, however hard, and as a reward she passes out of life, aged 22 with sincere love, sympathy and respect of every person with whom she has been brought in contact.' Source: FindAGrave 235877611; Emporia local newspaper obituary.

narrative_blocks.header: Three Evarts siblings married three Nortons
narrative_blocks.body: The 1788 marriage to Eber Norton made a second thread — her brother Ezra had wed Eber’s niece Lorain in 1783, and brother Curtis followed with Lorain’s sister Lois in 1792. Three Evarts siblings, three Nortons, one Guilford family across two generations.

Outlived Eber (d. August 1843) by less than a year; died at Guilford May 1, 1848 at age 84. Source: EH 1909 entry 407. [Pilot124 update]: Burial confirmed at West Cemetery (CEM038) per FindAGrave memorial 61367318. Both her parents died the same year (1795) when Mabel was 31. parents.father_research_notes: Roswell Evarts (1771-1815) of Guilford CT. Per FamilySearch KF5K-8YW. parents.mother_research_notes: Ruth Cruttenden Evarts (1771-1856) of East Guilford CT. Per FamilySearch KHVK-HQ5. Note: SAME maiden surname Cruttenden as Lois Cruttenden Norton (X02598, b. 1758, wife of Reuben Norton Jr H00403). Ruth was 13 years younger than Lois — possible cousin, niece, or sister. The Cruttenden surname appearing in two Norton-Evarts marriages across the same East Guilford community suggests another tightly-clustered intermarriage pattern alongside the three Evarts siblings.

narrative_blocks.header: Mother shared maiden name with Norton in-laws
narrative_blocks.body: Austin Evarts's mother was Ruth Cruttenden — same maiden surname as Lois Cruttenden Norton, wife of Reuben Norton Jr. The two Cruttenden women, born thirteen years apart in East Guilford, suggest a kinship: sisters, cousins, or aunt-niece. The Norton-Cruttenden-Evarts tangle in this small coastal town ran deep across two generations.

narrative_blocks.header: Five children orphaned inside a year
narrative_blocks.body: He died in August 1843, forty-three years old; Amanda followed the next April. Their five children lost both parents inside nine months.

people.research_notes: Husband of Amanda Norton Evarts (H01082). Born February 1800 in East Guilford CT. Surname Evarts — almost certainly a cousin of Amanda's mother Mabel Evarts Norton (X02619) given the East Guilford location and shared surname, though the exact kinship is not yet established. Married Amanda May 15, 1822. Five documented children. Died August 5, 1843 at 43; Amanda followed him in April 1844. Source: EH 1909 entry 1082. [Pilot124 update]: FamilySearch KH4C-NXN confirms Austin's parents as Roswell Evarts (1771-1815) and Ruth Cruttenden (1771-1856). Austin had 7 siblings (NOT BUILT per Jalapeño): Russell Evarts (1797-1864), Harry Evarts (1799-1849), Caroline Evarts (1802-1836), Lyman Evarts (1804-1850), Eliza Evarts (1808-1835), Marvin Evarts (1809-1868), and Austin himself born 1800. Austin married Amanda Norton in 1822 — so Austin's mother Ruth (Cruttenden surname) carries the same maiden name as Lois Cruttenden Norton, wife of Reuben Norton Jr, raising the question of additional Norton-Cruttenden-Evarts kinship density in the East Guilford area.

narrative_blocks.body: Samuel Newell Coe married Sarah Elizabeth Whedon in September 1846 and they had eight children across nineteen years, from Clark Wilson in 1848 to Harvey Whedon in 1867. He lies at Madison under a stone cut Newell, though the family genealogy set his middle name down as Norton, his mother's maiden surname.

'Newell' has no obvious immediate-family precedent and may honor a more distant ancestor or family friend. Death January 16, 1891 NEW from FG (NOT in EH). Buried West Cemetery (CEM038). BLOCK REWRITTEN 8 Sep 2026 on Sam's note that it broke the fourth wall - it had made Edward Hooker's 1909 genealogy and the gravestone the subjects of the sentence and drew a conclusion about the book ('the published genealogy got his name wrong'). The disagreement is still on the card but he is the subject of it, and no verdict is passed on either source. narrative_blocks.header: Lost two sons to the Civil War
narrative_blocks.body: Stephen Bidwell Norton died July 16, 1856 at age 53 — eight years before the Civil War took his son Francis M. on February 6, 1864 and six years after the war had taken his son William Erastus on December 13, 1862 at Fredericksburg. He was spared the news; Roxanna lived to see both deaths.

people.research_notes: Child of Anah Norton (H00408) and Mary Bidwell Norton (X02623). Born August 1, 1802. Carries his mother's maiden name 'Bidwell' as middle name. Two marriages, both to Wilcox women — possibly sisters: M1 Achsah Wilcox (X02627) had five children before her death October 22, 1834; M2 Roxanna Wilcox (X02628, b. February 2, 1792 — ten years older than Stephen) had one child. The pattern of marrying two women of the same surname is sororate-style and frequently meant the second wife was the first wife's sister. Stephen lost two sons to the Civil War — Francis M. (H02222) February 6, 1864 and William Erastus (H02227) December 13, 1862 (likely Battle of Fredericksburg). Stephen died at Madison July 16, 1856 at age 53 — eight years before the war losses. Source: EH 1909 entry 1091.

First wife of Stephen Bidwell Norton (H01091). Birth date unknown. Five documented children. Died October 22, 1834. Stephen later married Roxanna Wilcox (X02628) — likely Achsah's sister given the shared surname. Source: EH 1909 entry 1091.

narrative_blocks.header: Likely sister of her sister-in-law-and-predecessor
narrative_blocks.body: Roxanna Wilcox married Stephen Bidwell Norton after his first wife Achsah Wilcox died October 22, 1834. The shared surname strongly suggests Roxanna and Achsah were sisters — a sororate marriage in which a widower married his deceased wife's sister, common when young children needed mothering.

people.research_notes: Second wife of Stephen Bidwell Norton (H01091). Born February 2, 1792 — ten years older than Stephen. One documented son William Erastus (H02227) — killed in the Civil War December 13, 1862. Roxanna outlived Stephen (d. 1856) by 14 years; died at Madison May 14, 1870 at age 78. Source: EH 1909 entry 1091.

narrative_blocks.header: Killed at Fredericksburg on December thirteenth
narrative_blocks.body: William Erastus Norton was killed in action December 13, 1862 — the date of the Battle of Fredericksburg, one of the bloodiest single days of the war with approximately 12,600 Union casualties. Connecticut sent the 14th, 21st, and 27th Infantry to Fredericksburg; the 27th alone lost 198 men assaulting Marye's Heights. His specific regiment is not yet confirmed.

people.research_notes: Child of Stephen Bidwell Norton (H01091). Born February 16, 1838 — only child of Stephen and his second wife Roxanna Wilcox. KILLED IN ACTION in the Civil War on December 13, 1862 at age 24. December 13, 1862 was the date of the Battle of Fredericksburg — one of the bloodiest single days of the war with approximately 12,600 Union casualties. William's death on that specific date strongly suggests he fell at Fredericksburg, though the regiment is not confirmed. Connecticut sent multiple regiments to Fredericksburg including the 14th, 21st, and 27th Connecticut Infantry — the 27th in particular suffered devastating losses at Marye's Heights. narrative_blocks.header: Twenty to thirty sweaters a year
narrative_blocks.body: Priscilla Doane Morse kept the books at the Guilford Forge for more than twenty-five years and was treasurer of her Congregational church through the nineteen-eighties. YES, THIS IS HER (Sam's question, 8 Sep 2026): the Guilford Funeral Home obituary for MORSE, PRISCILLA DOANE, 14 Apr 2010, gives b. 23 Nov 1911 Jacksonville FL and d. 19 Mar 2010 at Guilford - both matching this record exactly. From it: daughter of Adelbert Franklin Doane Jr. and Mary Bartlett Doane; early years at Beaufort, North Carolina, summering in North Guilford with the Bartlett cousins; her mother died when she was eleven and she went to an aunt in Florida; Northfield Academy and the Katharine Gibbs School of Business; secretary in Boston, two years in Illinois with her sister Annis, then Texas with her father; financial accountant at the Guilford Forge for over twenty-five years, retiring 1976; Congregational Church Alpha Club and church treasurer in the 1980s; buried Alderbrook. She goes by PRISCILLA throughout, now set as bio.chip_first_name. MARRIAGE YEAR CONFLICT: the obituary says she moved back to Guilford to marry Whitney Lester Morse in 1936; this record and FamilySearch both give 6 Dec 1937. Left at 1937, unresolved. Her parents and her sister Annis are named but not built - an in-law's ancestors are terminal.

narrative_blocks.body: Morse began as a draftsman at Kevin Roche and Dinkeloo in Hamden, went to the State of Connecticut in 1970 - the health department first, then public works - and retired after twenty-seven years in 1997. He put in seven more behind the counter at Page's Hardware in Guilford.

narrative_blocks.body: Morse served in the United States Navy from 1958 to 1962, at the opening of the Vietnam conflict, and mustered out as a Draftsman Second Class, petty officer. He carried the trade straight into his working life.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine Guilford founders on his mother's side
narrative_blocks.body: Morse descended from nine of the 1639 founders of Guilford through his mother, and from John Moss, one of the original planters of Wallingford, through his father. He kept the family's genealogy himself, belonged to the Doane Family Association, and was buried at Alder Brook with military honours.

narrative_blocks.header: Dartmouth surgeon stationed at Sackets Harbor
narrative_blocks.body: Giles Gridley graduated Dartmouth and practiced medicine before serving as surgeon of the 21st New York during the War of 1812. He was stationed at Sackets Harbor, the American naval base on Lake Ontario where Commodore Chauncey's fleet faced repeated British attacks 1812-1814.

narrative_blocks.header: Practiced medicine across three states
narrative_blocks.body: Giles practiced in Boston Massachusetts, then across upstate New York (Albany, Durham, Pompey, Monticello), and finally settled in northern Pennsylvania (Liberty, Candor, Ulysses). Few physicians of his era moved that many times — possibly tied to the receding frontier of medical practice as settlements matured.

people.research_notes: Son of Thomas Gridley (X02647) and Mary Hooker Gridley (H00409). Born November 27, 1769 in Kensington CT. Graduated Dartmouth College and became a practicing physician. Married Ruth George of Concord NH on February 21, 1803. Eleven documented children. The family resided across Massachusetts (Boston), New York (Albany, Durham, Pompey, Monticello), and Pennsylvania (Liberty, Candor, Ulysses) — an unusually itinerant family pattern likely tied to his medical practice. Died at Ulysses PA May 12, 1866 at age 96. Lived 96-97 years — qualifies for `extraordinary_longevity` (≥91). narrative_blocks.body: Thomas Hooker Gridley was given the full name of his great-great-great-grandfather Rev. Thomas Hooker, founder of Hartford. The naming honored a preacher five generations removed who had died in 1647 — a 1775 echo of the Puritan founding.

narrative_blocks.body: Thomas Hooker Gridley served as a soldier at Oswego NY during the War of 1812. The Lake Ontario port was captured by the British in May 1814 and the fort burned. His specific role and fate during the engagement are not documented in EH 1909.

people.research_notes: Son of Thomas Gridley (X02647) and Mary Hooker Gridley (H00409). Born January 31, 1775 in Kensington CT. Named 'Thomas Hooker' in honor of his great-great-great-grandfather Rev. Thomas Hooker, founder of Hartford. Married Lucilla Kirtland of Saybrook CT (later Durham NY) on February 23, 1800. Six documented children. Family lived at Kensington CT until 1790, then Durham NY (where he married), then in 1809 to Pompey NY (joining his parents who had migrated there), and in 1824 to North Chili NY (Monroe County) where he remained until his death. Soldier of the War of 1812, stationed at Oswego NY — a Lake Ontario frontier port captured by the British in May 1814. Lucilla died at North Chili June 24, 1826; Thomas Hooker outlived her by 31 years and died there August 4, 1857 at age 82. Source: EH 1909 entry 1093.

narrative_blocks.header: Pioneer Hooker line into Michigan
narrative_blocks.body: Harriet Louisa Gridley and Anson Fowler married at Ogden NY in 1831 and later migrated to Wheatland Township in Hillsdale County Michigan — among the first Hooker-descended families to settle west of New York. Four of their five children were born in Michigan; Anson is buried at Churches Corners Cemetery there.

narrative_blocks.header: Charter member of frontier Free-Will Baptist Church
narrative_blocks.body: Harriet was an early member of the First Free-Will Baptist Church of Wheatland Michigan, organized February 19, 1838 in Eli Eastman's home shortly after the Fowlers arrived. The church gathered at Church's Corners just a few miles from her farm; local accounts noted that before the congregation organized, 'there was more rifle-shooting done on Sunday than any other day.'

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at forty-five, managed her own land deals
narrative_blocks.body: When Anson died in 1855 Harriet was forty-five, with five surviving children. Hillsdale County records show her buying and selling acreage within a few miles of the original 1835 patent for the next two decades — alone or jointly with relatives. She remained financially comfortable through the 1870 and 1880 censuses, outlived Anson by forty-three years, and died in Wheatland Township in 1898.

narrative_blocks.header: Origin of the name Anson remains uncertain
narrative_blocks.body: Anson was born in Fairfield Herkimer County NY in 1809 to Abel and Mary Eddy Fowler — but the Fowler line shows no documented earlier Anson. Genealogists have suggested the name may trace to Mary's possible Eddy or Ross matrilineal kin: a William Anson Eddy and an Anson Ross were both born around 1809, and three Ross sisters had married three Eddy brothers in that family network. Whether the name came from those collateral relatives or from a popular contemporary figure named Anson is unresolved.

narrative_blocks.header: Frontier child became Michigan land-patent pioneer
narrative_blocks.body: Anson was about seven when his parents moved the family west from Herkimer County NY to Genesee County NY around 1816. After marrying Harriet Louisa Gridley in Ogden NY in 1831, the couple bought land in Wheatland Township Hillsdale County Michigan from a federal land office in 1835 — second-wave New England migration into the Old Northwest. Three of their five surviving children were born in Wheatland on that patent.

career.organization: Professor O. S. Fowler (phrenologist and lecturer)
career.notes: Joined the noted phrenologist Orson Squire Fowler in spring 1857 in Cincinnati and traveled with him visiting principal cities of the United States and Canada. Recommended for the post by shorthand instructor Andrew J. Graham. Whether Frank and O. S. Fowler were related is undocumented despite the shared surname.

career.organization: Public schools of Springfield Illinois and vicinity
career.notes: Awarded a lifetime teaching diploma by the Illinois Department of Public Instruction after rigid examination by the state superintendent. Originally moved to Springfield intending to take up legislative reporting; appropriation failed and he accepted a tutoring position instead.

Constructed a novel windmill at the request of a country friend, then realized the device was also a propellor and could be used for vessel propulsion and steering. Secured patents and exhibited the invention in Chicago, Buffalo, and New York City; awarded a medal by the American Institute and a diploma by the Centennial Commission. The work brought him to Bridgeport CT, but he later discovered he had no pecuniary interest in the enterprise and abandoned the field.

Returned to shorthand work after the windmill enterprise collapsed; within three years built an extensive practice. Author of two works on shorthand and developer of a high-speed shorthand process. Connecticut's general stenographic law of 1884 was passed largely through his patrons' efforts; appointed to an official position with the application signed by nearly every attorney in the county. First in his region to produce a daily transcript on the typewriter; reported the 1864 patriotic speeches of Generals Sherman, Logan, and Sickles, President Andrew Johnson, Senator Wilkinson, and Governors Yates and Oglesby.

narrative_blocks.header: He went looking for a lost grave
narrative_blocks.body: In 1898 he searched out an abandoned graveyard at Pompey in New York for the grave of his great-grandmother, Mary Hooker Gridley, buried there in 1819. He found it, had her taken up and reinterred, and wrote down how he did it.

narrative_blocks.header: His middle name was the errand
narrative_blocks.body: Gridley came from his mother, Harriet Louisa, and ran back through Giles Gridley to Mary Hooker. Sixty-two years after he was christened with it he went to Pompey and made the name do something.

narrative_blocks.header: Phrenologist’s assistant, then court stenographer
narrative_blocks.body: He travelled as secretary to the phrenologist O. S. Fowler, taught school around Springfield in Illinois, worked as a mechanical engineer and inventor, and from 1880 held an official stenographer’s post in the Connecticut courts.

narrative_blocks.header: He found a grave and lost his own
narrative_blocks.body: He died at Bridgeport in 1907 and was buried at Mountain Grove beside his son Frederick. In 1932 his remains were taken up and cremated, and nobody wrote down where the ashes went. The Michigan stone is a cenotaph.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at sixty-four, remarried in Florida
narrative_blocks.body: After his wife Dora died in 1959 he wintered in Florida like many in his family. In Largo, Pinellas County, on February 3, 1960, he married Winifred Brooks Vroman — a Michigan-born widow herself who carried the same maiden surname as his mother Nellie Pearl Brooks. He lived another 33 years after Dora's death, reaching ninety-eight.

None of the four died young: Luella reached 77, Lois 71, Lillian 85, and Edith herself 87 — the kind of generational survival pattern unusual in Michigan working-class families of their era. narrative_blocks.header: Watched Rock Island grow from log cabins
narrative_blocks.body: At age four her family settled in Rock Island Illinois — then called Stephenson — making the trip from Pennsylvania by wagon and water. She grew up watching the trading village of a few log cabins become a city of nearly forty thousand people. She died at age 86 at her daughter LuLu's home in Blue Island Illinois.

narrative_blocks.body: The partnership he formed with W. L. Sweeney in 1860 built wagons at Rock Island for twenty-four years, until his failing health dissolved it in 1884. Consumption took him at home two years later, at fifty-nine, with his wife and all nine children around him.

career.title: Farmer — Dykeman Farm, Pawling NY
career.notes: Known as 'Farmer Hank.' Famous for best sweet corn and freshest vegetables. Ran hayrides in the pumpkin patch; known for stories about Indian corn and spoon gourds. narrative_blocks.header: Farmer Hank ran Pawling hayrides for generations
narrative_blocks.body: Henry Dykeman — 'Farmer Hank' — was known for the best sweet corn in Pawling and for hayrides through the pumpkin patch that generations of local children remember. He was a Trustee and Deacon at Central Baptist Church and wintered in Jensen Beach Florida, where he surf fished for pompano on the beach. He and Jean celebrated seventy years of marriage before his death in 2017.

people.research_notes: Son of Henry Dykeman (HD0550) and Velma Mary Ellis Dykeman (X00959). Born March 9, 1928; died July 30, 2017 at age 89 — 'Farmer Hank.' Ran Dykeman Farm in Pawling: famous sweet corn, hayrides in pumpkin patch, 'never-ending stories about Indian corn and spoon gourds.' Lifted his eyes to surrounding mountains each day. Triple Hooker descent through his mother H04404 Effie Keziah Hooker. Life member Central Baptist Church of Pawling; affiliate Dover First Baptist Church Wingdale; Trustee and Deacon. Wintered in Jensen Beach FL with Jean — surf fished for pompano. Son Wright and grandson Henry carry the farm into third and fourth generation (living, not built per Jalapeño rule). narrative_blocks.header: Lost his father as an infant of one
narrative_blocks.body: Cyprian was Esther's eighth and youngest child, born April 5, 1797 in Glastonbury Connecticut. His father John House IV died on November 14, 1798 when Cyprian was only nineteen months old. Cyprian later migrated north to Turin Lewis County New York, married Sophia Risley in 1819, raised four children there, and lived to age eighty-six.

narrative_blocks.header: Wisconsin pioneer taught school twenty-five years
narrative_blocks.body: Henry settled on a farm in Calamus Dodge County Wisconsin in the fall of 1857 and raised nine children there. He went to Nashville in 1864 to serve in the Civil War Quartermaster Department until going home on sick leave. Trained as both teacher and farmer, he taught school for twenty-five years and held several town offices.

narrative_blocks.header: Lifelong Turin farmer died where he was born
narrative_blocks.body: Chester was born in Turin and lived there all seventy-one years of his life, dying on the same spot where he had been born. His obituary called him 'a man of strict integrity, an honored citizen and farmer' who would be greatly missed in the community. He was survived by his wife Olive Mickel and two of their children.

people.research_notes: Third child of Cyprian House (HD3619) and Sophia Risley House (X02754). Born September 29, 1825 in Turin Lewis County NY — and died April 28, 1896 at age 70 'on the spot where he laid down the armor last Tuesday morning' per his obituary. Lived his entire life in Turin. Married Olive Jane Mickel (X02757, 1833-1897) of Schodack Center. Two surviving children at his death: Eugene M. (HD3643) and Mrs. Emmitt J. Johnson (HD3642). Obituary: 'Chester House merits more than a passing notice. Mr House was born in Turin 71 years ago and his entire life was spent in this county, most of it on the spot where he laid down the armor last Tuesday morning. Truly it can be said of him, to know him was to respect and trust him... a man of strict integrity, an honored citizen and farmer, and will be greatly missed in the community.' Buried Turin Cemetery (CEM248).

narrative_blocks.header: Elijah Cowles and Company led Connecticut trade
narrative_blocks.body: He stood at the head of Elijah Cowles & Co., which at the close of the eighteenth century was one of the leading mercantile houses in the state. He traded in company with his four brothers.

narrative_blocks.header: A shoemaker once, and close with money
narrative_blocks.body: He had been a shoemaker before the trade, and the family record sets down that he was very close and saving. He lived on the north corner opposite his father's house and sat as a director of the Hartford Bank.

narrative_blocks.header: His uncles married Hookers before he did
narrative_blocks.body: He married Elizabeth, a granddaughter of Capt. Joseph Hooker, and he was not the first Cowles to do so — his uncles Ezekiel and James had each married a Hooker woman a generation earlier. Within two generations the Cowleses had tied themselves to the Hooker line three times over.

narrative_blocks.body: Late in life he moved into the house his father had built for Gen. George Cowles and gave himself to his Unionville holdings, and above all to the water-power. His will was proved in the January after he died.

career.title: Pastor of the Congregational Church
career.notes: Ordained and instituted at Southampton LI on May 25, 1785. Salary £70/year plus 40 cords of wood delivered yearly. Resigned April 1, 1789. Local history records he received 486 members into the church during his Southampton tenure.

career.title: Pastor of the Harwinton Congregational Church
career.notes: Installed March 3, 1790. The present (1808) church was erected at a cost of $8,000. Recorded in his memorandum that 'for seven years his salary of $350 was sufficient; but that then the expense of living was nearly doubled.' Worn down by labors of a revival in November 1820, attacked by disease that confined him 77 days. Petitioned for release; in May 1822 the people gave him $1,000 and he was dismissed in June 1822.

narrative_blocks.header: Two pulpits, hundreds of conversions, seventy-seven days down
narrative_blocks.body: Joshua served the Southampton Long Island church for four years (1785-1789), receiving 486 members into communion before resigning. He was installed at Harwinton Connecticut in 1790 and stayed thirty-two years. In November 1820, exhausted by a revival, he was confined to the house seventy-seven days; the people of Harwinton gave him a thousand-dollar gift in 1822 and he was released.

narrative_blocks.header: He outlived son and grandson by years
narrative_blocks.body: Removing to Bethlehem to live with his youngest son in 1822, the son died in 1831 having graduated Yale and practiced medicine. Joshua then went to the Upper Houses to be with his eldest son Joshua Lewis — who died December 29, 1832, the day before his son also died at Yale. Father and grandson were buried in one grave January 1, 1833.

people.research_notes:
Father of Rev. Joshua Lewis Williams (X00266). Born February 3, 1761 — son of Capt. Elias Williams (not built). Yale 1780. Licensed October 1782 by the Hartford South Association to preach as a candidate. MARRIAGE: October 24, 1781 to Mary Webb (X02771, b. Sept 2, 1760, daughter of David Webb and Mary Williams) — note the wife's mother was a Williams. TWO PULPITS:
- Southampton Long Island NY: ordained May 25, 1785; salary £70/yr + 40 cords wood delivered yearly; resigned April 1, 1789. Received 486 members.
- Harwinton Litchfield County CT: installed March 3, 1790. Built present church 1808 ($8,000). His memorandum: 'for seven years his salary of $350 was sufficient; but that then the expense of living was nearly doubled.' November 1820 disease confined him 77 days; people gave him $1,000 in May 1822; dismissed June 1822. EARLY ADOPTER OF MISSIONS PRAYER: Harwinton Church record Feb 7, 1815 — 'conversed on the subject of a monthly prayer meeting for missions.' Williams told a grandson he and neighboring ministers were 'about the first in the world' to establish the monthly concert of prayer for missions. FINAL TRAGEDIES: Removed to Bethlehem to pass remainder of days with youngest son (died Sept 28, 1831 age 31, Yale + medicine). Returned to Harwinton, then Upper Houses to be with eldest son Joshua Lewis (X00266) — who died Dec 29, 1832; grandson at Yale aged 17 died next day; both buried same grave Jan 1, 1833. In 1830, husband of his youngest daughter Dr. Conant Catlin had died and been interred in Bethlehem. Williams reported having had 24 grandchildren and 17 great-grandchildren by his old age. TWO CHILDREN per Williams Genealogy: Orinda Williams (b. Feb 25, 1783, m. Abijah Catlin — not built per Jalapeño, sister of an X-spouse) and Joshua Lewis Williams (X00266, BUILT). DEATH: February 8, 1836 at age 75 (gravestone). Wife Mary Webb Williams died May 16, 1838 at age 77 (gravestone). Burial location not specified in Williams Genealogy. OBITUARY by Rev. Noah Porter of Farmington (Connecticut Observer March 5, 1836): 'Of a stature not above the medium he was in neither body or mind, but in both agile. Confessedly a man not perfect in piety, his religion was sincere and like his temperament, ardent. As a minister of Christ, both in South Hampton and in Harwinton, he had been wise to win souls. Though not distinguished either as a scholar or an orator, he was more than either, for he was a good man and full of faith and of the Holy Ghost and much people were added to the Lord.'

narrative_blocks.header: Held specie reserves to save Hartford Bank
narrative_blocks.body: During the War of 1812, all Connecticut banks except the Hartford Bank suspended specie payments. Chauncey held large reserves of hard currency in Farmington and produced them as needed to keep the Hartford Bank's credit intact. He served as a director of banks in both Hartford and Middletown.

narrative_blocks.header: Powdered queue, blue coat, gilt buttons
narrative_blocks.body: Chauncey Deming was a strong rider and dressed for it. He galloped along Farmington Street on a 'strong and elegant horse,' and sat in church in a powdered queue, bright blue coat, and gilt buttons — a sartorial holdover from the eighteenth century preserved into the 1820s.

narrative_blocks.header: Foremost in enterprise, and his own vessels
narrative_blocks.body: He bought at Hartford and New York and brought West India cargoes into Farmington in vessels of his own. Among that town’s merchants he was reckoned first for strength and positiveness of character, and foremost in enterprise.

narrative_blocks.header: He soldiered before he kept a store
narrative_blocks.body: He served the Revolution as a soldier in Captain James Stoddard's company of Colonel Mosley's regiment. He was in his twenties then, and married Diadema Cowles at Farmington in February 1780, the year after the New Haven Alarm.

people.research_notes: Husband of Diadema Cowles Deming (H00614). Born July 19, 1757 in Plainville Hartford County CT. Married Diadema February 28, 1780. Eight children together — five died as infants or young children, only Catharine Deming Cowles (1787-1859, m. Timothy Cowles) produced surviving descendants (see H00614 research_notes for full child list). FARMINGTON MERCHANT KING (per Trumbull's Memorial History of Hartford County, 1886, Unionville chapter by James L. Cowles): 'Mr. Chauncey Deming was first among these merchants for strength and positiveness of character and for business ability. He was foremost in enterprise, and was an active and influential director in one of the banks of both Hartford and Middletown.' WAR OF 1812 SPECIE STORY: 'During the War of 1812, all the banks of the State except the Hartford Bank suspended payments in specie, and it is confidently asserted that Mr. Deming held large specie reserves in Farmington, which he produced from time to time to save its credit.' CONTEMPORARY DESCRIPTION: 'No one who ever saw him in his vigorous old age as he galloped along the street upon his strong and elegant horse, or as he sat in church, with his powdered queue and his bright blue coat and gilt buttons, will forget the impression.' Active in the Farmington mercantile trade 1780-1825 — period of greatest Farmington commercial wealth. Per Governor Treadwell (1802): 'a greater capital is employed in [Farmington trade] than in any inland town in the State.' Trade declined after the Litchfield + Albany turnpikes were extended over Talcott Mountain, making Hartford more accessible to both Farmington merchants AND their customers. Died March 26, 1827 in Farmington at age 69 — five months after Diadema's September 1826 death. Burial location not yet documented; Memento Mori Cemetery (CEM254) is plausible given his Farmington residence and extended Cowles family connections there. STAGE 6g ENRICHMENT: Parents identified per EH #614 + WikiTree — Samuel and Anna Deming of Plainville Hartford County CT. Birth in Plainville confirmed by WikiTree. Eight children with Diadema (1781-c.1797 birthdays); only Catharine 'Katherine' (H01580, EH#1580) reached adulthood. The seven other births include named infants Samuel, Diadema, Jennette, replacement Samuel No. 2 plus three unnamed infants. narrative_blocks.header: Senior warden, selectman, state representative
narrative_blocks.body: Sherman Woodward gave a quarter-century to Christ Church as senior warden and served his town as Litchfield selectman and in the Connecticut state legislature. Widowed at thirty by Minerva Pierpont's death, he remarried Hannah Eliza Russell in 1838 and they lived together in Watertown for nearly sixty years until his death in 1896 at eighty-nine.

Married Hannah Eliza Russell (X02772, 1808-1899) — no documented children. CIVIC CAREER: 25 years senior warden of Christ Church (Episcopal); Selectman of Litchfield CT; member of the Connecticut state legislature. Died March 27, 1896 in Connecticut at age 89. Hannah Eliza outlived him by 3 years (died 1899 age 91). Buried Evergreen Cemetery (CEM260) in Watertown CT. FIRST-NAME DOUBLE: Sherman Pierpont and Sherman Prindle Woodward were father-in-law and son-in-law sharing an unusual first name — Sherman Pierpont was named for his ancestor Rev. John Pierpont's family connections; Sherman Woodward was independently named. Coincidence rather than naming inspiration.

narrative_blocks.header: She raised another mother's daughters
narrative_blocks.body: Minerva Pierpont Woodward died in 1837 leaving girls of five and three; the second wife stepped into the Watertown household and raised Rachael and Minerva as her own, bearing no children herself. She outlived nearly everyone, dying at ninety-one in the last week of the century.

No documented biological children, but raised her stepdaughters Rachael (HD3653, age 5 at remarriage) and Minerva (HD3654, age 3 at remarriage). Died December 22, 1899 in CT at age 91 — extraordinary longevity. Buried Evergreen Cemetery (CEM260) Watertown CT. POSSIBLE HOOKER-RUSSELL CONNECTION (UNVERIFIED): The Hooker tree includes a documented Russell-Hooker connection through H00118 Mary Pierpont Russell (1703-1740) — daughter of Mary Hooker Pierpont (H00034) — who married a Russell. Hannah Eliza Russell (b.1808) would need to descend from H00118's Russell line 4-5 generations down to qualify as a Hooker descendant herself. No documentary chain established at this time. Flagged parentage_unverified pending compiler research. Her marriage to Sherman Prindle Woodward — himself an I-spouse of Hooker descendant — places her in the extended family network regardless of her own descent. Sam noted family lore about the Hooker-Pierpont-Russell-Talcott Family Apron in the Connecticut Historical Society, suggesting the Russell-Hooker connection is real and traceable, but not yet to this specific Russell.

MIGRATION ARC: Lived in New Brunswick NJ until 1877, then moved to Richmond Virginia where he lived until 1892, then to Waterbury CT where he resided the rest of his life. The 1877 move took the family south during the Reconstruction era; the 1892 move back to CT followed Caroline's 1888 death. TOBACCO MANUFACTURER: Spent 'the greater part of his life in the manufacture of tobacco and cigars.' Obituary called him 'a connoisseur on tobacco' and 'a fine scholar.' Died January 20, 1904 in Waterbury CT after a short illness, age 70. Survived by 7 children: William L., Arthur V., Mrs. Julia C. Loucks, Mrs. Mary T. Rhodes (Waterbury CT); Dr. Royal E. (Tottenville); Herbert S. (Naugatuck); Mrs. Minnie V. Adams (Syracuse). Also survived by two sisters Mrs. Mary A. Brokaw (Dunellen) and Mrs. T. Walker Jones (Bedminster).

Alfred's path: Isaac → Ezekiel Sr. (I00156) → Ezekiel Jr. (H00439) → Alfred. The two grandfathers Solomon and Ezekiel Sr. were brothers — both sons of Capt. Isaac Cowles by his third wife Elizabeth Smith. NOTE: This is a Cowles-Cowles cousin marriage; Alfred alone carries Hooker descent (via his paternal grandmother Martha Hooker Cowles H00232). narrative_blocks.header: Third Edgar in family — first two died young
narrative_blocks.body: Edgar Philip Cowles was the third son of Egbert and Sophia Cowles to bear the name Edgar — the first Edgar had died in infancy in 1817 and the second died in 1833 at age twelve to fourteen. This third Edgar survived to age sixty-five, dying June 29, 1896 in Farmington Connecticut. The replacement-naming pattern was common in early-Republic families memorializing children lost in epidemics, but rare to find three documented attempts before a name-bearer survived.

narrative_blocks.header: Name recorded three different ways across sources
narrative_blocks.body: His name appears in three different forms across the historical record: 'Edgar Philip,' 'Philip Edgar,' and 'Philip Egbert.' The 'Philip Egbert' variant may indicate that his father's patronymic Egbert was transcribed as Edgar by some sources; the Civil War service note similarly hedges 'perhaps he served as a private Company A, Twenty-fifth Connecticut Volunteer Infantry, September 1862 to August 1863.' The three-name puzzle remains unresolved.

people.research_notes: Wife of John Egbert Cowles (HD3683). Born April 8, 1826 in Cambridge Middlesex County Massachusetts. Daughter of Thomas Whittemore (X02773) — the prominent Universalist minister, author, and Massachusetts state legislator who chaired the 1834 disestablishment committee — and Lovice Corbett Whittemore Sr. (1801-1882). Married John Egbert April 15, 1851 in Boston Suffolk County MA. Died 1897 at age 70-71. Buried Mount Auburn Cemetery Cambridge MA. RELIGIOUS-FAMILY CONTEXT: Her marriage to John Egbert created a fascinating multi-religious family arc. John Egbert's father Egbert Cowles (H01138) was an 80-year Connecticut Congregationalist who supported the ABCFM (American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions, the Congregational/Trinitarian missionary body) and carved an axe helve for its Morning Star steamer. Lovice's father Thomas Whittemore was a Universalist who actively opposed the established status of Congregational and Unitarian churches in Massachusetts, championing their disestablishment in the 1834 referendum. The two families (in-laws by 1851) represented opposing sides of the New England religious-political settlement of the early 19th century. See notable story 'cowles_whittemore_religious_inversion'.

narrative_blocks.header: He preached that hell does not exist
narrative_blocks.body: Universalists held that every soul is finally saved. Whittemore went further, to what was called ultra-universalism: no punishment after death at all. The final holiness and joy of all men, he wrote, is the central sun of Universalism.

narrative_blocks.header: He unseated the state church of Massachusetts
narrative_blocks.body: Cambridge sent him to the legislature in 1831 and he chaired the committee on disestablishment. No civil government, he held, may compel citizens to support any system of religion. The vote of 1833 ended the establishment.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran one paper for thirty-three years
narrative_blocks.body: In 1828 he bought the Universalist Magazine and made it The Trumpet and Universalist Magazine. He was its editor, owner and chief clerk for thirty-three years, and by 1836 it had five thousand subscribers.

narrative_blocks.header: A bass viol seat converted him
narrative_blocks.body: He was singing in a Baptist choir in Boston in 1820 when the Second Universalist Society hired him to play the bass viol. Hosea Ballou's preaching converted him from the gallery, and Ballou trained him for the ministry.

narrative_blocks.header: He printed the names of debtors
narrative_blocks.body: He named the writers he thought long-winded and published the list of subscribers who had not paid their bill. Unitarian clergy he called clerical dandies, who preach as near nothing as a man can who preaches at all.

narrative_blocks.header: A bank president who saved a railroad
narrative_blocks.body: He was president of the Cambridge Bank and then of the Vermont and Massachusetts Railroad, and used the one office to keep the other out of bankruptcy. He served Cambridge as selectman and then alderman.

narrative_blocks.header: Tufts gave him its first honorary degree
narrative_blocks.body: He was a founding member of Tufts College and sat on its board from 1852 until he died. The college gave him the first honorary doctorate it ever conferred.

people.research_notes:
Christian Universalist minister, magazine editor, author, and Massachusetts state legislator. Born January 1, 1800; died March 21, 1861 in Cambridge Middlesex County MA. Buried Mount Auburn Cemetery Cambridge. PERSONAL CONNECTION TO THIS TREE: Thomas Whittemore is parent-of-an-in-law to a Hooker descendant. His daughter Lovice Corbett Whittemore (I00388, 1826-1897) married John Egbert Cowles (HD3683, 1824-1905) on April 15, 1851 in Boston. Through this marriage, Thomas is the father-in-law of John Egbert and (by extension) the unrelated in-law of John Egbert's father Egbert Cowles (H01138) — the lifelong Connecticut Congregationalist whose religion Thomas Whittemore actively worked to disestablish in Massachusetts. RELIGIOUS-POLITICAL POSITION: Christian Universalist (ultra-universalist view: no punishment in afterlife). Editor of The Trumpet and Universalist magazine from 1828 (succeeding Hosea Ballou). Co-founded Universalist Historical Society 1834. Like Hosea Ballou and Hosea Ballou II (first president of Tufts College), contributed to Universalist historiography by identifying precedents in early Christianity for Universalist beliefs. MASSACHUSETTS LEGISLATURE 1831-1836: Cambridge's representative. Chaired the committee overseeing the disestablishment of the Congregational and Unitarian Churches — to whose constitutionally privileged position Whittemore was opposed — from the Massachusetts Constitution. Held that 'no civil government has a right to compel the citizens to support any system of religion whatsoever.' Supported the 1834 popular referendum on separation of church and state; the results brought Massachusetts into accord with the First Amendment. PAPERS: Personal papers at Harvard Divinity School Library (Cambridge MA). Family papers at Tufts University Digital Collections and Archives. QUOTE: 'The glory of God, and of His Son Jesus Christ, as manifested in the final holiness and happiness of all men, is the central sun of Universalism.' EASTER EGG STATUS: Built per project rule — non-Hooker-descendant notable parent of a Hooker descendant's spouse. Wikipedia subject; documented religious-political contrast with the Hooker-line Congregational tradition embodied by his in-laws. is_easter_egg=true; is_thomas_descendant=false.

Original body preserved here for reference: 'Whittemore founded The Trumpet and Universalist magazine in 1828, succeeding Hosea Ballou's earlier Universalist magazine. With Thomas J. Sawyer of New York, he co-founded the Universalist Historical Society in 1834. His historiography identified precedents for Universalist beliefs in early Christianity, influencing many readers to regard early Christians as Universalists.'

narrative_blocks.header: He inherited the spring shade-roller empire
narrative_blocks.body: His father, Stewart Hartshorn, patented the spring-operated window shade in 1864 and built it into a company that crowded every rival off the American market. In 1925 the father handed him the reins, and he ran the business his family's name was stamped on.

narrative_blocks.header: His father built a town for the fortune
narrative_blocks.body: The shade money bought more than fifteen hundred acres in New Jersey, which the elder Hartshorn laid out as Short Hills — a planned community for people who, he said, appreciated nature, with some of the first water and sewer systems in the state. Stewart Henry was born and raised in it.

narrative_blocks.header: Her great-grandfather fought at the Falls Fight
narrative_blocks.body: Three generations back, her ancestor Nathaniel Foote stood in the Falls Fight at Turner’s Falls — the brutal 1676 dawn raid of King Philip’s War. She married a doctor, bore six children, and carried that Wethersfield-founding line west to Cleveland, where she died in 1846.

narrative_blocks.header: A Cowles twice over, by two marriages
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother Sarah had been the widow of Joseph Cowles of Norfolk before marrying Asa Foote; Almira then married a Cowles herself — Dr. Edwin Weed Cowles — and died in Cleveland, where her half-brother Samuel had settled.

narrative_blocks.header: She pushed her husband into medicine
narrative_blocks.body: Edwin Weed Cowles began on his father’s farm, but he had a taste for study and a hand with the sick, and she urged him to read medicine with Dr. O. K. Hawley. When the diploma came they left the bend of the river for Mantua, where he practised.

narrative_blocks.header: Her youngest son was born at Mantua
narrative_blocks.body: That move gave her a last child at Mantua in 1832 — Alfred, who went to Chicago and made the Tribune. Her husband afterwards practised at Cleveland.

narrative_blocks.header: Her granddaughter quoted her quaint sayings
narrative_blocks.body: A granddaughter, Ellen M. Phelps, remembered her as a noble pioneer grandmother whose quaint sayings the family went on repeating. She was several years older than the husband she married in 1815.

narrative_blocks.header: Journaled a call on General Harrison, future president
narrative_blocks.body: In 1839-40 Giles kept a journal of a trip by boat from Cleveland to New Orleans — buying and selling goods at New Orleans and towns up and down the Mississippi and Red Rivers. Among his stops he called on General William Henry Harrison, who would win the presidency the following year and die thirty-one days into his term.

narrative_blocks.header: Died of consumption at twenty-three, journal unfinished
narrative_blocks.body: His 1839-40 journal — documenting the New Orleans voyage and the call on future President Harrison — is his primary historical legacy, preserved in family records. He died April 2, 1842 of consumption in Cleveland, unmarried at twenty-three; his first cousin of the same name, Giles Hooker Cowles, would be killed before Petersburg twenty-two years later.

narrative_blocks.body: After Markham died she went back to Cleveland, studied anatomy and physiology, and stood up before large audiences of women to lecture on both. The lecturing stopped when she married Buel Goodsell Wheeler in 1853 and went out to Sterling, Illinois.

narrative_blocks.body: She went to Oberlin with the class of 1843 and married Dr. Franklin Markham in January 1845. He was dead by September 1850, and in June 1853 she married Buel Goodsell Wheeler.

narrative_blocks.header: Carried from Virginia to the Cowles plot
narrative_blocks.body: She died at Charlottesville in January 1892 and her body was taken to her brother's widow at Cleveland, where it lay in the receiving vault at Lake View until the family ground could be opened.

narrative_blocks.header: Her three brothers ran three newspapers
narrative_blocks.body: Edwin kept the Cleveland Leader and Alfred the Chicago Tribune, and Samuel went to California and the bench. She was Dr. Edwin W. Cowles's only daughter, and she outlived all three of them.

narrative_blocks.header: San Francisco police then county judge 1860-1868
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel was elected San Francisco Police Judge in 1860 — also one of three commissioners selecting the SF police force — and served the County Court bench from 1863 to 1868. His recorded decisions form a significant chapter in California jurisprudence during the state's formative years.

narrative_blocks.header: Member of San Francisco's 1856 Vigilance Committee
narrative_blocks.body: An earnest and efficient worker in 'the great social purification' of San Francisco, Samuel served the 1856 Vigilance Committee — one of the largest extralegal civic movements in 19th-century US history. He gloried in those days and rehearsed the story in later life.

narrative_blocks.header: His Cleveland diary documents the 1849 cholera epidemic
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel kept a clear daily diary from July 1849 through July 1850 in Cleveland, recording the cholera epidemic that he himself contracted and survived; an hour-by-hour account of President Zachary Taylor's death; steamboat-fire disasters; and his own self-recorded depression. The diary survives as an important primary source for early Cleveland history.

narrative_blocks.header: Migrated to California with childhood friend Mastick
narrative_blocks.body: Struck with 'California fever,' Samuel left Cleveland in 1852 with his childhood friend and law partner Edwin P. Mastick. He had been preceded by his brother Edwin Cowles' departure for Chicago — both sons of Dr. Edwin Weed Cowles fanning out from Austinburg Ohio in the same gold-rush decade.

narrative_blocks.header: The committee he prized, Sherman called mob rule
narrative_blocks.body: The 1856 committee Samuel served so proudly was no small affair — six thousand strong, it seized state armaments and tried a California Supreme Court justice. General William T. Sherman resigned his militia command rather than support it, condemning the movement as dangerous mob rule.

people.research_notes: Fourth child of Dr. Edwin Weed Cowles (H01141) and Almira Mills Foote Cowles (I00396). Born March 21, 1823 Austinburg Ohio. Died November 17, 1880. Boyhood in Mantua, Austinburg, Detroit, and Cleveland. Education at Grand River Institute and Western Reserve College. LAW STUDIES: 1844 Cleveland with Andrews, Foot & Hoyt; 1846 with Prentiss brothers; admitted to bar 1846. Partnered Loren Prentiss to 1850, then Edwin B. Mastick to March 1852. CALIFORNIA: Both partners 'concluded they would emigrate to the New Eldorado and try their fortune there' in 1852. SF POLITICS: 1856 elected SF police judge by Law and Order Party. Member of famous 1856 SF Committee of Vigilance. 1860 elected Republican judge of the Court of Common Pleas; re-elected 1863; served until January 1, 1868. Only three of his decisions reversed on appeal during his six-year judicial career. 1877: Member of Committee of Safety of 25 principal citizens during railroad strikes. MARRIAGE (Mar 28, 1849 Cleveland): Anna L. Wooster — great-granddaughter of Gen. David Wooster, Revolutionary War general who d. May 2, 1777 of wounds received April 27, 1777 at the Battle of Ridgefield CT. Seven children gen 8 (not built this stage; all but eldest born CA, prob. SF): Samuel Wadsworth (1850 Cleveland - 1912 SF, m. Margaret A. Powers 1893, no children, d. diabetes + heart failure), Edwin Wooster (1855-1886 unm.), Myra Augusta (1857, m. Joseph D. Redding 1881; her daughter Josephine d.1915 age 22 nursing in French Croix-Rouge — Médaille de Guerre + Croix-Rouge diploma), Helen Cornelia (1859-1868 d.young), Anna Elizabeth 'Anita' (1861, m1 Timothy H. Rearden 1 dau, m2 1904 Janie Lacy SF), Charlotte Mary (1864-1880 d.young), Sarah Frances (1867, m. Alpheus Shreve Badger Chicago). STAGE 6W-3 ADDITION: Diary of Samuel Cowles 1849-1850 (DOC021) preserved with Cleveland bookseller M. C. Younglove; viewable via Carpe Librum Books listing — also now serving as Samuel's primary URL anchor. Bancroft Library photograph 1870s. CAREER CORRECTION: Police Judge 1860-1863 (NOT 1856 as earlier project notes had it); County Judge 1863-1868. Death Nov 17, 1880; obituary in San Francisco Examiner Nov 19, 1880. DIARY HIGHLIGHTS (per Carpe Librum description): clients accused of rape, arson, insanity; joined a posse to recapture 1850 jail escapees; secretary-treasurer of the Cataract Fire Company No. V; eyewitness to steamboat fires (encountered a man in the streets crazy with grief over having lost his wife and children the day before in a steamboat fire); hour-by-hour record of President Zachary Taylor's death; met Henry Clay; LocoFoco/Whig/Free-Soil disputes; partner's marriage and his own son's birth; departure of his brother Edwin for Chicago; bouts of depression and 'fears of failure' — 'Business stagnated, and the door of the poor house opens in the distance.' These details inform NBs 3 + 4.

narrative_blocks.header: The Republican Party began in his rooms
narrative_blocks.body: In the winter of 1854 a meeting in the Leader’s editorial rooms called the Pittsburgh convention that fused Know-Nothings, Whigs and Free-Soilers into the Republican Party. Joseph Medill was there, and left afterwards for Chicago and the Tribune.

narrative_blocks.header: Lincoln would not remove him for it
narrative_blocks.body: After Bull Run he ran an editorial headed Now is the time to abolish slavery, and friends of the administration pressed Lincoln to take his Cleveland postmastership away to placate the South. Lincoln refused, saying he knew of no law forbidding postmasters a free expression of opinion.

narrative_blocks.header: A doctor’s son apprenticed to the press
narrative_blocks.body: The son of a Cleveland physician, he went into a printing office at fourteen and was in partnership by 1844. He took the Forest City Democrat outright in 1854 and renamed it the Leader.

narrative_blocks.header: He built the free delivery system there
narrative_blocks.body: He held the Cleveland post office five years from 1861 and established free mail delivery in the city. Andrew Johnson replaced him with the editor of the more moderate Herald.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran an anti-Catholic order from that room
narrative_blocks.body: He headed the Cleveland chapter of the Order of the American Union, whose object was to keep Catholics out of public office, and warred in print with the Catholic Universe. In 1877 a whole Republican city ticket was framed up in his back room.

narrative_blocks.header: He never heard a bird sing
narrative_blocks.body: A defect of hearing kept the hissing sounds of speech from him, and the fife, and birdsong, which he took for poetical fiction until an elocutionist shut him in a room with twenty canaries.

narrative_blocks.header: The rival paper mourned him anyway
narrative_blocks.body: He died at half past two on a March morning in 1890. The Plain Dealer’s man, antagonistic to him for a third of a century, wrote that whenever the two met their relations were invariably pleasant.

people.research_notes: Fifth child of Dr. Edwin Weed Cowles (H01141) and Almira Mills Foote Cowles (I00396). Born September 1825 Austinburg Ohio. Died March 4, 1890 Cleveland. BOYHOOD: Austinburg, Mantua, Cleveland Ohio; Ann Arbor and Detroit Michigan. Lived as boy in East Cleveland west of Adelbert College. Later lower Prospect St, then Prospect/Erie corner, then 656 Prospect St homestead built 1889. PRINTING: Age 14 in 1839 began printer's trade, mostly with Cleveland Herald. Grand River Institute 1843 brief. Age 19 in 1845 firm Smead & Cowles. CLEVELAND LEADER: 1853 firm Medill, Cowles & Co. publishers of Forest City Democrat. 1854 renamed Cleveland Leader. 1855 Vaugh + Medill sold their interests to Edwin and moved Chicago to buy Tribune (where brother Alfred HD3712 became business manager). Edwin sole proprietor + editor of the Leader to death. REPUBLICAN PARTY ORIGINS CLAIM: Per Cowles book #1719: 'It is said that the Republican Party had its origin in the editorial rooms of the Cleveland Leader during the winter of 1854-5, and that a number of gentlemen connected therewith agreed upon the call for the first national convention of the party which met at Pittsburgh in 1855.' (Note: one of several competing GOP origin stories — others place founding in Wisconsin and Michigan.) POLITICAL EVOLUTION: Liberty (1841) → Free-Soil (1848) → Republican (1855), tracking his father Edwin Weed's evolution. BULL RUN EDITORIAL (July 1861): 'Now's the time to abolish slavery as a war, as well as a moral measure.' Severely denounced by Administration friends who urged Lincoln to remove him from Cleveland Postmastership. Lincoln declined: 'he knew of no law which forbade postmasters a free expression of opinion.' Edwin held Postmaster role 1861-1866. EDITORIAL CHARACTER: 'A vigorous writer and very bold in his political utterances.' 'Outspoken, partisan, but possessed vigor, ability and honesty, secured it the respect of its strongest opponents who pronounced it a perpetual monument to his memory.' MARRIAGE (May 15, 1849): Elizabeth Caroline Hutchinson (b. May 10, 1827 Cayuga NY) — SISTER of his brother Alfred Cowles' wife Sarah Frances Hutchinson. Daughter of Hon. Mosely Hutchinson (b. 1795 Ithaca NY; lawyer, associate judge, NY assembly member; d. 1861) and Elizabeth Boardman (Hall-Davis) Hutchinson. SIX CHILDREN gen 8 (not built this stage, all prob. Cleveland): Almira Foote Cowles (1850), Helen Hutchinson Cowles (1851), Eugene Hutchinson Cowles (1855), Alfred Hutchinson Cowles (1858), Lewis Hutchinson Cowles (1861), Edwin Samuel Cowles (1868-1870 d.young). ORIGINAL NOTABLE_BLURB (moved here from notable.notable_blurb in Stage 6Y-4 to comply with schema's 8-word ceiling — content preserved): Cleveland Leader editor and proprietor 1854-1890 — one of the most influential Republican newspaper editors of the founding era. The Republican Party 'is said to have had its origin in the editorial rooms of the Cleveland Leader during the winter of 1854-5.' Cleveland Postmaster 1861-66; Lincoln declined to remove him after his post-Bull Run editorial advocating abolition as a war measure. Adherent of Liberty Party + Free-Soil until 1855 when he became identified with the Republican Party. Brother of Chicago Tribune business manager Alfred Cowles. FINDAGRAVE ENRICHMENT: FGA says birth Sept 19, 1825 Cleveland OH; current JSON has Austinburg Ashtabula County OH per EH — discrepancy noted, EH retained per §0.8. Death March 4, 1890 Cleveland OH confirmed. Cause of death: heart failure. CLEVELAND LEADER FOUNDING: True Democrat anti-slavery Whig paper started in Olmsted Falls 1847, moved to Cleveland and converted to daily same year. In 1854 Cowles merged several abolitionist and pre-Republican titles to create the Cleveland Leader. UNBUILT ENTRY: Giles Hooker Cowles (b. June 12, 1843 Austinburg OH, d. June 17, 1864 Petersburg VA, buried Poplar Grove National Cemetery Dinwiddie County VA) is likely a child of this family, named in honor of HD3708 Giles Hooker Cowles who died 1842. Civil War death during Siege of Petersburg — pending build.
