narrative_blocks.header: Rescued the Chicago Tribune at twenty-three
narrative_blocks.body: In 1855 the paper’s new owners handed its “deplorable” finances to a twenty-three-year-old clerk from his brother’s Cleveland print shop. Over twenty-eight years he turned it into one of the foremost journals in the land and took a controlling share.

narrative_blocks.header: A printer’s boy who became a Chicago power
narrative_blocks.body: He picked up the trade in his brother Edwin’s newspaper office and rose to wealth among Chicago’s capitalists, remembered for “strict integrity… shrewd judgment and tireless industry.”

narrative_blocks.header: His children built him a monument at Yale
narrative_blocks.body: Forty years after he steadied the Tribune, his three surviving children gave Yale $350,000 to found a research foundation in his name — the seed of today’s Cowles Foundation for Research in Economics.

narrative_blocks.header: A childless judge’s fortune launched him
narrative_blocks.body: When his great-uncle Samuel Cowles — a Cleveland judge and early antislavery man — died childless, he left his estate to the family; Alfred was only five, but the inheritance set the family’s course.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Cowles brothers married two sisters
narrative_blocks.body: He married Sarah Frances Hutchinson the same year his elder brother Edwin married her sister Elizabeth — two brothers wedding two sisters of one Cayuga family.

people.research_notes: Sixth and youngest child of Dr. Edwin Weed Cowles (H01141) and Almira Mills Foote Cowles (I00396). Born May 13, 1832 Mantua Portage County Ohio. Died December 20, 1889. EARLY DAYS: Cleveland, Detroit, Austinburg. Grand River Institute several years. Picked up printer's trade in elder brother Edwin's Leader office. Finished education University of Michigan. TRIBUNE 1853-1889: 1853 entered Leader as bookkeeper. 1855 Vaugh + Medill sold out interests in Leader to Edwin Cowles, moved Chicago, bought Chicago Tribune. They offered 23-year-old Alfred inducements to take charge of Tribune's business department, then 'in a deplorable condition.' He accepted. 'The result of the swarming out of the Leader office of these three gentlemen was the resuscitation of the Tribune, then considered on its last legs, and the making of that paper what it has been since, one of the foremost journals in the land, both editorially and financially.' CHARACTER: 'Strict integrity and fair dealing, shrewd judgment and tireless industry... taking a position among the wealthy capitalists of Chicago.' (History of Ashtabula Co., Ohio, 1878.) 'A man of strong character with a genial and brilliant mind. He accumulated a large fortune.' CHICAGO RESIDENCE: 1805 Michigan Ave Chicago in later years. MARRIAGE (Jan 31, 1860): Sarah Frances Hutchinson — SISTER of his elder brother Edwin's wife Elizabeth Caroline Hutchinson, the same Hutchinson family of Cayuga NY. The two Cowles brothers married two Hutchinson sisters. FOUR CHILDREN (gen 8, not built this stage): Edwin (b.1861 d.infancy 1861), Sarah Frances Cowles Stewart (b.1862 Chicago), Alfred Cowles (b.1865 Yale Class of 1886), William Hutchinson Cowles (b.1866 Evanston IL Yale Class of 1887). ALFRED COWLES FOUNDATION FOR STUDY OF GOVERNMENT, YALE (1928): At 1928 Yale Commencement, President Angell announced $350,000 joint gift from Mrs. Sarah Frances [Cowles] Stewart and brothers Alfred Cowles (Yale 1886) + William H. Cowles (Yale 1887) — to establish the 'Alfred Cowles Foundation for the Study of Government' at Yale in memory of their father. Foundation continues today as the Cowles Foundation for Research in Economics — among Yale's most important social-science investments. ORIGINAL NOTABLE_BLURB (moved here from notable.notable_blurb in Stage 6Y-4 to comply with schema's 8-word ceiling — content preserved): Chicago Tribune business manager 1855-1889 (controlling owner until ~1883) — credited with rescuing the Tribune from near-failure and making it 'one of the foremost journals in the land, both editorially and financially.' Joined the Tribune at age 23 from his brother Edwin's Cleveland Leader. His three surviving children Sarah Frances Cowles Stewart, Alfred Cowles (Yale 1886), and William Hutchinson Cowles (Yale 1887) jointly endowed the Alfred Cowles Foundation for the Study of Government at Yale University in 1928 in his memory ($350,000).

Her ninety-five years spanned the entire arc of American industrial history.

narrative_blocks.header: Enlisted from school
narrative_blocks.body: Giles Hooker Cowles was a student at Grand River Institute when the Civil War broke out and enlisted in the Ashtabula regiment; at his term's end he returned home and resumed his studies. He re-enlisted February 24, 1864 — four months before he was killed before Petersburg, promoted sergeant-major, recommended for first lieutenancy, at twenty-one.

quotes.quote: As to the young hero for whose death we are all in mourning to-day what can I say that shall do justice to the feelings of our hearts; a personal enumeration of his virtues would be a mockery. Gentle, upright, tender and true, who ever saw him without feeling attracted to him? His memory is enshrined in our hearts. If we were proud of him while living, much more are we proud of his heroic death. A braver man it would not be easy to find. In the presence of danger he was without fear; calm on the battlefield as in the hour of quiet repose. Though in the service but a few months, he had been advanced to the post of Sergeant-Major, and had been recommended for promotion to a first lieutenancy. But at the tender age of 21, the angels took him and advanced him to a higher post and a nobler service. 'All honor to the patriot dead. May they rest in peace, in peace forever rest.'

narrative_blocks.header: Argued landmark Indian-law case at twenty-seven
narrative_blocks.body: In 1886, at twenty-seven, Joseph argued United States v. Kagama before the Supreme Court for Kagama, a Yurok accused of murder. Justice Samuel Miller's opinion upheld the 1885 Major Crimes Act, a founding ruling of federal Indian law still cited today.

narrative_blocks.header: Wrote America's first opera produced in France
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph wrote the libretto for Victor Herbert's Natoma, sung by Mary Garden in 1911 and toured to more than thirty American cities. His own opera, Fay Yen Fah, opened at Monte Carlo in 1925, the first grand opera by an American to premiere in Europe.

narrative_blocks.header: France awarded him the Legion of Honour
narrative_blocks.body: France gave Joseph the Legion of Honour for Fay Yen Fah, and in 1919 he was elected to the Société académique d'histoire internationale. His daughter Josephine had earned the Légion d'honneur herself, nursing for the French Red Cross in the war.

narrative_blocks.header: Co-founded the San Francisco Symphony in 1911
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph sat on the founding board of the 1909 Musical Association, which launched the San Francisco Symphony in 1911, and pressed for his friend Henry Kimball Hadley as its first music director and the Dutch violinist Eduard Tak as concertmaster.

narrative_blocks.header: Pacific Coast chess champion in 1888
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph beat the master Johannes Zukertort twice in 1884, won the 1888 San Francisco tournament and with it the Pacific Coast title, beat George H. D. Gossip, and in 1889 took on the whole Sacramento Chess Club by telegraph and won.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the Cremation of Care
narrative_blocks.body: President of the Bohemian Club and of the San Francisco Arts Administration, Joseph wrote The Cremation of Care, the Druid spectacle that has opened the club's summer encampment at Bohemian Grove since 1893, and in 1902 The Man of the Forest, the first Grove play.

narrative_blocks.header: Ambrose Bierce made fun of his fish
narrative_blocks.body: As a California Fish Commissioner Joseph shipped a refrigerator car of Maine lobsters west and pressed carp on Californians as a food fish. Ambrose Bierce answered with mock epitaphs and a Devil's Dictionary entry: Ichthyologist, n. A Jo Redding.

narrative_blocks.header: San Francisco judge in the gilded age
narrative_blocks.body: Born Wooster Ohio 1839, Timothy graduated Kenyon College in 1859 and came to San Francisco in 1863 after brief Civil War service. He clerked at the U.S. Mint while studying law, opened practice around 1872, and served as a San Francisco judge until his death May 10, 1892.

narrative_blocks.header: Bret Harte and Ambrose Bierce literary circle
narrative_blocks.body: Timothy was a serious student of languages and literature, a member of the Chit-Chat Club, and part of San Francisco's golden-age literary scene including Ambrose Bierce, Bret Harte, Fanny Osbourne (later Stevenson), and Ina Coolbrith. His book 'Petrarch and Other Essays' was published after his death.

narrative_blocks.header: Married his friend Judge Cowles's daughter Anita
narrative_blocks.body: Timothy married Anita Cowles in 1888 — the daughter of his friend Hon. Samuel Cowles, San Francisco judge of the Court of Common Pleas. Their daughter Anna Rearden Baeck (1888-1970) became the first woman to write the 'Partheneia' pageant at UC Berkeley Class of 1912, and her papers along with Timothy's are preserved in the Baeck Family Papers at the Online Archive of California.

Eventually became a San Francisco judge. LITERARY: Member of the Chit-Chat Club; serious student of languages and literature; part of SF's literary scene with Ambrose Bierce, Bret Harte, Fanny Osbourne (later Stevenson, wife of Robert Louis Stevenson), Ina Coolbrith, and Porter Garnett. His book 'Petrarch and Other Essays' published posthumously. MARRIAGE: Married 1888 Anita Cowles (HD3729) — daughter of his friend Hon. Samuel Cowles (HD3710). Their daughter Anna Wooster Rearden (1888 SF - 1970 Berkeley) graduated UC Berkeley Class of 1912 (Prytanean Society member); wrote the FIRST 'Partheneia' performed by women students at Berkeley; married John Eric Baeck 1917; lived in Berkeley until 1970. (Anna is gen-9 Hooker descendant — flagged for future stage.) narrative_blocks.body: She married Edwin Cowles in 1849 and her sister Sarah married his brother Alfred, so that two Hutchinson sisters carried the name into two newspapers. She bore Edwin three sons and two daughters.

narrative_blocks.header: Two of her sons built the aluminum furnace
narrative_blocks.body: Eugene and Alfred worked out the electric smelting process, and their father spent his last strength promoting the company they formed on it. Her surviving daughter Almira married Charles Whitney Chase of Cleveland.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty years a widow in Cleveland
narrative_blocks.body: Edwin died in 1890 and she outlived him by twenty years, dying at Cleveland in July 1910. She lies with him at Lake View.

people.research_notes: Wife of Edwin Cowles, Cleveland Leader publisher (HD3711). Married May 15, 1849. SISTER of Sarah Frances Hutchinson Cowles (I00414, wife of Edwin's brother Alfred Cowles HD3712) — two Cowles brothers married two Hutchinson sisters from Cayuga NY. Daughter of Hon. Mosely Hutchinson (1795-1861, lawyer/judge/NY assembly) and Elizabeth Boardman (Hall-Davis) Hutchinson. Six children built Stage 6T (HD3732-HD3737).

Eldest child of Edwin Cowles (HD3711, Cleveland Leader publisher) and Elizabeth Caroline Hutchinson Cowles (I00413). Born 1850. Named for her paternal grandmother Almira Mills Foote Cowles (I00396). Per Cowles book.

narrative_blocks.header: She sailed to Italy against her father's pleading
narrative_blocks.body: Bedridden three and a half years, she had spent two of them in her father's Cleveland house and four fruitless months at Clifton Springs. Then she conceived an irresistible wish to join her husband in Europe, and went despite the earnest remonstrances of both parents.

narrative_blocks.header: Two hours between the cable and the news
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother had sailed three months earlier to nurse her at Florence. At two o'clock one afternoon a cable reached her father in Cleveland saying the patient was worse; two hours later came a second, of two words — Helen dead.

narrative_blocks.header: Vassar, and several languages after it
narrative_blocks.body: She was educated at Vassar College and added to it a wide range of reading and a thorough knowledge of several literatures. Foreign travel and the years abroad did the rest; she was married at Paris in 1880.

people.research_notes: Her husband's obituary gives her death as April 1883; her own obituary and FindAGrave give April 1884, which fits the three-and-a-half-year illness dated from November 1880. Entry follows 1884.

bio.bio_blurb: Co-inventor of the electric smelting furnace

notable.notable_blurb: Co-inventor of the electric smelting furnace

career.organization: Brush Electric Light and Power Company, Cleveland
Cowles Electric Smelting and Aluminum Company

cross_connections.display_label: went to Niagara for the same cheap power, nineteen years later
patented electric-furnace metallurgy in the field he opened

narrative_blocks.header: A reporter sent to see the electric light
narrative_blocks.body: He was covering an early exhibit of Brush lighting for his father’s paper when he began to study electricity and what it might do for smelting. In 1880 he left the news business to organise and run the Brush Electric Light and Power Company.

narrative_blocks.header: Consumption sent him to the New Mexico mines
narrative_blocks.body: Tuberculosis took him west to the copper-zinc mine the family bought on the Pecos in 1883, and that year he designed a furnace to draw the zinc out of its ores. He and his brother Alfred came back to Cleveland for the equipment to carry it further.

narrative_blocks.header: Four furnaces on Brush dynamos, then Niagara
narrative_blocks.body: They built their first furnace at the Brush works and filed for a patent, organising the company in 1885 with four furnaces each run off a Brush dynamo. Their father’s capital moved them to Lockport, where Niagara gave cheaper power.

narrative_blocks.header: He took his daughter off a platform
narrative_blocks.body: A few years after his father died he carried his little girl away from her aunt in Cleveland and swung aboard a moving Lake Shore train heading west. The sheriff went after him with a writ of habeas corpus.

narrative_blocks.header: Dead at thirty-seven in El Paso
narrative_blocks.body: He married Alice Hale in 1879 and Claire Luneschloss in 1891, and died the next spring at El Paso, a long way from Cleveland. He was thirty-seven, and was brought home to Lake View.

people.research_notes: Third child of Edwin Cowles (HD3711) and Elizabeth Caroline Hutchinson Cowles (I00413). Born 1855. Per Cowles book.

notable.notable_blurb: Metallurgist; electric-furnace and aluminum pioneer

cross_connections.display_label: , his first cousin, captained Yale’s crew to a Thames record
ran the chemistry at his brother’s electrochemical works

narrative_blocks.header: The first electric furnace in the world
narrative_blocks.body: He and his brother Eugene built it at Lockport in 1886, on power drawn off a Niagara tailrace, their father having put up the capital. A sister works rose at Stoke-upon-Trent in England, and the company was the first to make aluminum in quantity.

narrative_blocks.header: They let Alcoa walk out of the plant
narrative_blocks.body: Charles Martin Hall worked a year at Lockport and they declined his electrolytic patent; he left in 1888 to found the Pittsburgh Reduction Company, afterwards Alcoa. It sued them, shut the works by court order in 1893, and the aluminum business never recovered.

narrative_blocks.header: The furnace threw off carbide and phosphorus
narrative_blocks.body: The same furnace gave calcium carbide, cheaper carbon bisulphide and cheaper phosphorus, and later silicon carbide and graphite. The litigation left him credited with the modern method of producing aluminum.

narrative_blocks.header: He rowed at Henley, Putney and Vienna
narrative_blocks.body: He went from the Ohio agricultural college to Cornell in 1877 and made the crew there. In 1881 he was one of a four that rowed at Henley, at Putney and at Vienna.

narrative_blocks.header: He urged aluminum guns on the Navy
narrative_blocks.body: At Annapolis in 1887 he read a paper to the Naval Institute arguing that aluminum alloys would give heavy guns longer life and greater power at less weight. A long table of officers and engineers rose to argue it with him.

narrative_blocks.header: At sixty-four he turned to detergent
narrative_blocks.body: In 1923 he found what sodium metasilicate would do as a washing agent, and founded the Cowles Detergent Company on it.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Franklin medals and a Paris gold
narrative_blocks.body: The Franklin Institute gave him the Elliott Cresson and John Scott Legacy medals in 1886, and the Paris Exposition a gold medal in 1889. He was vice-president of the American Electrochemical Society.

people.research_notes: Fourth child of Edwin Cowles (HD3711) and Elizabeth Caroline Hutchinson Cowles (I00413). Born 1858. Per Cowles book.

narrative_blocks.header: He married again at sixty, after thirty years
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah Hutchison married him in 1891 and they lost their only child Isabell at four. Sarah died at Cincinnati in 1927; six years earlier he had already married Ellen Clendon, who outlived him by nineteen years. All four lie at Lake View.

people.research_notes: Fifth child of Edwin Cowles (HD3711) and Elizabeth Caroline Hutchinson Cowles (I00413). Born 1861. Per Cowles book.
Sixth and youngest child of Edwin Cowles (HD3711). Born 1868, died 1870 age 2. Per Cowles book.

parents.mother_research_notes: Built as easter_egg X02778 in Stage 6X-6.

cross_connections.display_label: was her sister, and married her husband’s brother Edwin

narrative_blocks.header: Why does Vassar still carry her name?
narrative_blocks.body: Long after her death a scholarship at Vassar College and a fellowship at the University of Chicago carried her name, endowed in her memory — a quiet legacy for a woman the records otherwise kept thin.

narrative_blocks.header: She and her sister married two brothers
narrative_blocks.body: She married Alfred Cowles of the Chicago Tribune the same season her sister Elizabeth married his elder brother Edwin — two Hutchinson sisters of Cayuga wedding two Cowles brothers of Ohio.

people.research_notes: Wife of Alfred Cowles, Chicago Tribune business manager (HD3712). Married Jan 31, 1860. SISTER of Elizabeth Caroline Hutchinson Cowles (I00413, wife of Alfred's brother Edwin Cowles HD3711). Daughter of Hon. Mosely Hutchinson (1795-1861) and Elizabeth Boardman (Hall-Davis) Hutchinson. Four children built Stage 6T (HD3738-HD3741).
First child of Alfred Cowles (HD3712, Chicago Tribune). Born 1861, died 1861 in infancy. Per Cowles book.

notable.notable_blurb: Yale Cowles Foundation co-founder, 1928

cross_connections.display_label: was her father-in-law, the Vermont governor

narrative_blocks.header: Her gift to Yale became an economics powerhouse
narrative_blocks.body: With her two brothers she gave Yale $350,000 in 1928 to honor their father — a foundation that grew into the Cowles Foundation for Research in Economics, a force in the field to this day.

narrative_blocks.header: A newspaper fortune wed a governor’s son
narrative_blocks.body: Daughter of the Chicago Tribune’s Alfred Cowles, she married Philip Battell Stewart, a Vermont governor’s son, and built a home with him in Colorado Springs.

people.research_notes: Second child and eldest daughter of Alfred Cowles (HD3712, Chicago Tribune) and Sarah Frances Hutchinson Cowles (I00414). Born 1862 Chicago. Married (surname Stewart). Co-founder with her brothers Alfred Cowles (HD3740, Yale 1886) and William Hutchinson Cowles (HD3741, Yale 1887) of the Alfred Cowles Foundation for the Study of Government at Yale University, established at 1928 Yale Commencement with $350,000 joint gift in memory of their father. Foundation continues today as the Cowles Foundation for Research in Economics — among Yale's most important social-science institutions.

notable.notable_blurb: Chicago Tribune director for 48 years

career.notes: 48 years, from 1891

career.organization: Civic Federation; Bureau of Public Efficiency

cross_connections.display_label: printed one of the Western Reserve's first newspapers
captained the 1845 boat that founded the Yale Navy he later led
coached the Yale crew he came back to advise in 1899
, his first cousin, rowed for Cornell at Henley and Vienna
coached his 1886 Yale crew to the Thames record
was a vice-president of the Continental Illinois Bank

narrative_blocks.header: His crew record stood for 37 years
narrative_blocks.body: In his senior year at Yale he captained the champion varsity crew to an upstream record on the Thames that no one broke until 1923. He was tapped for Skull and Bones the same year.

narrative_blocks.header: Admitted to the bar, he barely used it
narrative_blocks.body: Yale Law School took him from 1887 to 1888 and Northwestern the year after, and he was admitted to the Illinois bar in 1889. He practised in Chicago only a few years before the paper claimed him.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave the Tribune forty-eight years
narrative_blocks.body: Two years after his father died he joined the Chicago Tribune’s board and served as a director for forty-eight years. He sat besides on the boards of the Continental Illinois Bank and Trust and the American Radiator Company.

narrative_blocks.header: He waged war on government waste
narrative_blocks.body: A campaigner against public extravagance, he led the Civic Federation and the Bureau of Public Efficiency from 1932 to 1935, pressing Chicago and Illinois to spend the public’s money carefully.

narrative_blocks.header: He raised four sons alone
narrative_blocks.body: His wife Elizabeth Cheney died of lung disease in 1898, leaving him to bring up their four boys — among them Alfred III, the future economist, and the architect Knight — on his own.

narrative_blocks.header: Three Cowleses endowed Yale for their father
narrative_blocks.body: At the 1928 Commencement he, his brother William and his sister Sarah endowed a foundation at Yale for the study of government and public affairs, named for their father. It survives today as the Cowles Foundation for Research in Economics.

narrative_blocks.header: Pneumonia took him on Lake Shore Drive
narrative_blocks.body: Heart disease and pneumonia took him at 1130 Lake Shore Drive in January 1939, ten days after his seventy-fourth birthday. He had played golf and shot game for pleasure.

people.research_notes: Third child of Alfred Cowles (HD3712, Chicago Tribune). Born 1865. Yale College Class of 1886. Co-founder with siblings Sarah Frances Cowles Stewart (HD3739) and William Hutchinson Cowles (HD3741, Yale 1887) of the Alfred Cowles Foundation for the Study of Government at Yale (1928, $350,000 gift). Stage 6Y-721: enriched as notable (Chicago Tribune director 48 yrs); married Elizabeth Cheney (X03368, d.1898 lung disease); four sons Alfred III (HD6396), Knight Cheney (HD6397), John Cheney (HD6398), Thomas Hooker (HD6399) wired. Yale crew captain 1886 (upstream Thames record unbroken to 1923); Skull and Bones; estate ~$985,000.

notable.notable_blurb: Spokesman-Review founder; Yale Cowles Foundation co-founder

education.notes: Yale Law School graduate; concluded journalism rather than law was his future.

career.title: Police reporter, Chicago Tribune
career.notes: Worked for his father Alfred Cowles' paper, on duty 7pm-4am while attending business school in the afternoon.

career.title: Co-owner and business manager, The Spokesman
career.notes: Came to Spokane WA in 1891 to protect his investment in The Spokesman. After 1893 consolidation became one-fourth owner of The Spokane Review.
career.role: Co-owner and business manager, The Spokesman

career.title: Sole owner and publisher, The Spokesman-Review
career.notes: In 1894 became sole owner and publisher; renamed paper The Spokesman-Review. Built it into Spokane's dominant daily over 52 years. Founded the Cowles family newspaper empire that continues to today (4th generation). Later acquired the Spokane Chronicle as the paper's afternoon companion.
career.role: Sole owner and publisher, The Spokesman-Review

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Whitworth University, Spokane

cross_connections.display_label: ran the rival Chronicle, and reached Spokane two years before him

narrative_blocks.header: He went west to save an investment
narrative_blocks.body: He came to Spokane in 1891 to protect his stake in The Spokesman, a paper then losing a circulation war. He took sole ownership after the 1893 consolidation, renamed it The Spokesman-Review, and in 1897 bought the rival evening Chronicle that Thomas Hooker had come west to run.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-two years running one paper
narrative_blocks.body: He published the Spokesman-Review from 1894 until his death in 1946, fifty-two years at the head of Spokane’s dominant daily. The family newspaper company he founded is in business still.

narrative_blocks.header: He took a law degree and never practised
narrative_blocks.body: He read law at Yale, took his degree there in 1889, was admitted to the bar, and never practised. He had already worked the overnight police beat at his father’s Chicago Tribune while sitting in business classes in the afternoons.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the Yale News and joined Bones
narrative_blocks.body: At Yale he was chairman of the News and belonged to the University and Bicycle clubs, to Delta Kappa Epsilon and to Skull and Bones. His elder brother Alfred had been tapped for Bones the year before him.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a Cheney, as his brother had
narrative_blocks.body: In February 1896 at South Manchester he married Harriet Bowen Cheney, a daughter of the silk manufacturer Knight Dexter Cheney. His brother Alfred had married her sister Elizabeth seven years earlier.

narrative_blocks.header: The three of them endowed Yale in 1928
narrative_blocks.body: At the 1928 Commencement he, his brother Alfred and his sister Sarah endowed a foundation at Yale for the study of government, named for their father. It survives as the Cowles Foundation for Research in Economics.

narrative_blocks.header: He died on his brother’s date
narrative_blocks.body: Death took him at Spokane on 15 January 1946 — the same day of the year on which Alfred had died at Chicago seven years before. He was seventy-nine.

people.research_notes: Fourth child of Alfred Cowles (HD3712, Chicago Tribune). Born 1866 Evanston IL; died 1946 Spokane WA. Yale College 1887 + Yale Law School (LL.B.). After two years at Chicago Tribune as a police reporter, came to Spokane 1891 as part-owner/business manager of The Spokesman. After 1893 consolidation he became one-fourth owner of The Spokane Review; in 1894 bought out his partners to become sole owner and publisher, renaming the paper The Spokesman-Review. Published the paper for 52 years until his death in 1946. Founded the Cowles family newspaper empire that continues to today (great-grandson William Stacey Cowles is current publisher 4th generation). Sons William H. Cowles Jr. (1902-1970) and Cheney Cowles (1908-1943, KIA Army plane crash Alabama) both Yale graduates worked at the paper. Co-founder with siblings of Yale's Cowles Foundation 1928. Sources: HistoryLink.org; Spokane Historical.

notable.notable_blurb: Buckhorn Furnace pig-iron manufacturer

parents.father_research_notes: Uriah Seeley of Painesville (b. 25 May 1791, Weston, Conn.)
parents.mother_research_notes: Abbie Turney Seeley of Weston, Conn.

cross_connections.display_label: left the army in 1864 for blast furnaces, and founded Anniston in 1873

narrative_blocks.header: Pig iron at Buckhorn before Carnegie
narrative_blocks.body: He went south to Lawrence County and made charcoal and pig iron at Buckhorn Furnace, shipping it down the Ohio to St Louis. He retired out of the trade with a fortune in 1869.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept company with Giddings and Wade
narrative_blocks.body: Before and during the war he was active in politics and counted Joshua Giddings, Benjamin Wade, Salmon P. Chase and Gideon Welles among his friends and associates.

narrative_blocks.header: His father ran a station for a thousand
narrative_blocks.body: Uriah Seeley of Painesville was sheriff of Geauga County, an anti-Jackson state senator and an abolitionist who kept an Underground Railroad station and helped more than a thousand people reach Canada.

narrative_blocks.header: Portland at the end, after a golden wedding
narrative_blocks.body: He and Charlotte kept their golden wedding at Flavel in Oregon in 1898 with all six children present. She died at Portland in 1904 and he in 1910, eighty-eight, of heart failure.

narrative_blocks.header: Home to his father's farm in 1873
narrative_blocks.body: In 1873 Boudinot brought his family back to the Painesville farm his father Uriah had cleared in 1815, because Uriah was old and the children needed schooling. He farmed its three hundred acres until he moved to Oregon in 1893.

people.research_notes: Birth year contested: the 1893 county biography gives 23 March 1823 and has him at Hanging Rock from nineteen; his 1910 obituary gives 1822 and the move south in 1848, and the Oregonian 1843. It also has him back at Painesville in 1873 and at Portland in 1893, against the obituary’s 1898.

bio.bio_blurb: Vassar alumnae president; D.A.R. vice-president general

cross_connections.display_label: gave Vassar's Alumnae House to the association Kate led

narrative_blocks.header: She led the Vassar alumnae for three years
narrative_blocks.body: Vassar gave her a B.A. in 1870 after two years at Lake Erie Seminary, and she was president of its alumnae association from 1904 to 1907 and of the Virginia collegiate alumnae for several terms.

narrative_blocks.header: Vice-president general of the D.A.R.
narrative_blocks.body: She joined in 1892, was twice regent of the Albemarle chapter and vice-president general of the national society from 1900 to 1902. Her Who's Who entry records that she favoured woman suffrage.

narrative_blocks.header: Charities and corrections for the state
narrative_blocks.body: She presided over the Charlottesville Benevolent Society, was vice-president of its public health association, and sat on the executive committee of Virginia's State Board of Charities and Corrections.

narrative_blocks.header: She was married at Paris in 1873
narrative_blocks.body: Albert Tuttle was travelling in Europe after his two years at Harvard, and the wedding was there on 7 August. She had grown up at Austinburg, in a family whose house had been an Underground Railroad station.

narrative_blocks.header: Her body was brought east to join his
narrative_blocks.body: She died at Berkeley in 1920 and he in 1927. He was buried in the university cemetery at Charlottesville and she was brought there that spring, so the two would lie side by side where they had lived twenty-five years.

people.research_notes: Eldest child of Charlotte Cowles Austin Seeley (HD3714) and Boudinot Seeley (I00411). Born 1849 Austinburg OH; died 1920 Berkeley CA. Three children including Anna Seeley Tuttle b.1877 (gen 9 — not built this stage).

narrative_blocks.header: Miller Chair of Biology for twenty-five years
narrative_blocks.body: He took the chair at Virginia in 1888 and held it until he retired in 1913, turning down the presidency of Ohio State to stay. A dormitory on the grounds carries his name.

narrative_blocks.header: A private guarding prisoners, not an officer
narrative_blocks.body: He enlisted at nineteen, telling recruiters he was twenty, and served sixty days as a private of the 8th Ohio Independent Battery guarding captured Confederate officers on Johnson's Island.

narrative_blocks.header: One of Agassiz's last students at Harvard
narrative_blocks.body: He took a B.Sc. at Pennsylvania State in 1870 and spent two years at Harvard under Louis Agassiz and Jeffries Wyman, as instructor in microscopy. He then taught at Ohio State for fifteen years.

narrative_blocks.header: The Ohioan they called a genuine old Virginian
narrative_blocks.body: Recommending him in 1888, R. D. Bohannon wrote that one does not feel he is a Yankee or a Westerner but a genuine old Virginian. He lived twenty-five years among Confederate veterans and lies among them.

narrative_blocks.header: He married Kate Seeley in Paris
narrative_blocks.body: The wedding was at Paris on 7 August 1873, while he was travelling in Europe. Their three children were born at Austinburg and Columbus before the family went south in 1888.

narrative_blocks.header: He published on charophytes days before dying
narrative_blocks.body: At eighty-two he was still a guest worker in the Berkeley laboratories. He addressed the American Association for the Advancement of Science weeks before his death and put out a paper on charophytes days before it.

people.research_notes: Private, 8th Independent Battery Ohio National Guard; mustered in 15 Aug 1864, out 17 Oct 1864 at Johnson’s Island. Rank in and out: private. Berkeley obituary: "one of the few surviving pupils of Agassiz". Retired on the Carnegie foundation in 1913.

bio.bio_blurb: Oswego iron founder and steamboat owner

career.organization: Columbia River and Puget Sound Navigation Company
Ohio, Fleetwood, Telephone and Flyer, with U. B. Scott and E. W. Crichton
Brown, Seeley, Crichton and Donohoe, owners of the Oswego iron furnace

cross_connections.display_label: made his fortune in West Coast iron at Los Angeles's Baker Iron Works

narrative_blocks.header: The first iron furnace in the West
narrative_blocks.body: L.B. came to Oregon in 1873, at twenty-two, to run the iron furnace at Oswego, the first west of the Mississippi. His syndicate raised its stone stack from thirty-two feet to forty-two and laid a narrow-gauge railroad to the Prosser mine.

narrative_blocks.header: Steamers on the Columbia and Puget Sound
narrative_blocks.body: With Captain U. B. Scott and E. W. Crichton, L.B. built the steamers Ohio, Fleetwood, Telephone and Flyer. He organized the Columbia River and Puget Sound Navigation Company, whose Flyer and Bailey Gatzert were known across the Northwest.

narrative_blocks.header: A cane from Washington's tomb
narrative_blocks.body: About 1871 L.B. cut a small evergreen at George Washington's tomb at Mount Vernon and made a cane of it for his father, Boudinot. By 1926 it had passed to the fourth generation, his grandson Tyler Woodward Seeley.

narrative_blocks.header: At seventy-five, a poem for Oregon
narrative_blocks.body: On his seventy-fifth birthday in 1926 L.B. wrote a poem to Oregon and proposed that the old furnace stack at Oswego, forty-two feet of hewn stone, carry a statue of Sam Simpson, the poet of the Willamette.

narrative_blocks.header: Bought at a sheriff's auction in 1877
narrative_blocks.body: In 1877 L.B. and Ernest W. Crichton led a group of Ohio iron makers who bought the bankrupt Oregon Iron Company at a sheriff's auction. They borrowed heavily from Simeon G. Reed for their improvements, and four years later sold him the company.

narrative_blocks.header: His new steamer rolled over at her launch
narrative_blocks.body: When the Flyer was launched into the Willamette in 1891 with no boilers or engines aboard, she flopped over in the water, and L.B.'s partner Capt. U. B. Scott, riding her down the ways, had to climb out through a window.

people.research_notes: Second child of Charlotte (HD3714) and Boudinot Seeley (I00411). Born 1851 Lawrence County OH. Married 1876 Amelia C. Carpenter (I00406); 4 children (gen 9, not built). Resided San Francisco and Austinburg OH. Per Cowles book.

narrative_blocks.header: San Francisco, then Portland
narrative_blocks.body: Married at West Andover in 1876, Minnie went with L.B. to San Francisco, where he represented the Oregon Iron Company, and in 1892 they settled in Portland. She died at Redlands, California, in 1926, where she had gone for the winter.

people.research_notes: Married 1876 Lamar Boudinot Seeley (HD3743). 4 children. Per Cowles book.

narrative_blocks.body: Two of Anna's brothers named children for her and her husband, Ceylon Bernard: Edward's daughter Anna Bernard Seeley, born in 1890, and Orville's son Ceylon Bernard Seeley, born in 1903.

narrative_blocks.header: He managed the steamer Flyer on Puget Sound
narrative_blocks.body: Uri spent most of his life in Seattle as manager of the steamship Flyer, which ran between Tacoma and Seattle. His brother, L.B. Seeley, was one of the men who built her.

narrative_blocks.header: Died suddenly at the ironworks
narrative_blocks.body: Uri died suddenly on the night of 22 April 1921 while at work in the Willamette Iron & Steel plant in Portland.

narrative_blocks.header: The Flyer outran the steel Indianapolis
narrative_blocks.body: On 28 July 1910 the Flyer and the Puget Sound Navigation Company's steel steamer Indianapolis left the Seattle dock together, and the Flyer was unloading at Tacoma before her rival arrived. The company bought the Flyer the next June.

narrative_blocks.header: The Flyer's boiler, built where he died
narrative_blocks.body: The Flyer's original steel boiler was built by Willamette Iron and Steel Works of Portland, the plant where Uri died at work in April 1921.

narrative_blocks.body: Alma's father, Rev. Alden Walker, known in Saybrook as Uncle Alden, preached ten years as a Methodist circuit minister, then spent thirty as the railroad's station agent. He had come to the township as a boy of seven, when it was still wilderness.

narrative_blocks.body: Edward's eldest child, Charlotte Selby Seeley, died at Portland at about four, around 1888. His daughter Alma Walker Seeley died in 1897, at about ten.

notable.notable_blurb: California Secretary of State; Sacramento mayor

narrative_blocks.header: Redding, California is one letter off Reading
narrative_blocks.body: He bought ground at Poverty Flats in 1868 for the Central Pacific, inside Major Pierson B. Reading's grant of twenty-seven thousand acres. The town took Redding's name in 1872, one letter off the landowner's, and the two are confused still.

narrative_blocks.header: Assembly, then the mayoralty, then the state
narrative_blocks.body: Redding sat for Yuba and Sierra in the Assembly from 1853, was elected mayor of Sacramento in 1856, and held the secretary of state's office from 1863 to 1867 under Leland Stanford and Frederick Low. He was the first elected to it.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote his way out of the diggings
narrative_blocks.body: After the Yuba River and the Pittsburg bar, Redding took the associate editorship of the Shasta Journal, drew up papers for the sale of claims and arbitrated disputes. He later owned and edited Sacramento's Democratic State Journal.

narrative_blocks.header: He chartered a ship and went for gold
narrative_blocks.body: A Yarmouth boy who had clerked in Boston since sixteen, Redding got up a company of young men in 1849 and sailed from Nova Scotia. They made San Francisco on May 12, 1850, and he went straight to the Yuba diggings as a labourer.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave his relic collection to the Academy
narrative_blocks.body: Redding belonged to the California Academy of Sciences and the Geographical Society of the Pacific, followed the paleontology of the coast closely, and handed his collection of prehistoric and aboriginal relics to the Academy museum.

narrative_blocks.header: A regent of the University of California
narrative_blocks.body: He was appointed in 1880 to serve out Frank M. Pixley's unexpired term as a regent of the University of California under president John LeConte, and was reappointed in 1882. He was Fish Commissioner when he died.

narrative_blocks.header: Three institutions sent men to his funeral
narrative_blocks.body: Redding died of apoplexy at San Francisco in August 1882, fifty-eight years old. The service at the First Congregational Church drew delegations from the Central Pacific, the Academy of Sciences and the university regents.

sources.short: Exploring Shasta County History (Jeremy M. Tuggle 2019)

people.research_notes: Born January 17, 1824 Yarmouth Nova Scotia, son of Fitz W. Redding and his wife Mary; died August 21, 1882 San Francisco of apoplexy at age 58. EDUCATION: Yarmouth Academy. EARLY LIFE: 1840 emigrated alone to Boston at age 16 as a clerk. 1843 entered retail grocery and ship chandlery business. In 1840s married Mary Prescott Putnam (b.1820 Boston). CALIFORNIA GOLD RUSH: Joined the California Gold Rush in 1850; mined the Yuba River diggings and Pittsburg bar in Yuba/Sierra counties. Family joined him in California after his initial mining work. JOURNALISM: Associate editor of the Shasta Journal; while in Assembly wrote for the San Joaquin Republican; 1854 became editor and proprietor of Sacramento's Democratic State Journal. POLITICS: 1853-1854 California State Assembly (Yuba/Sierra counties); 1856 elected mayor of Sacramento; 1863-1867 Secretary of State of California (appointed by Governor Frederick Low); left state government 1868 with administration change. RAILROAD: 1868 became first land agent for the Central Pacific Railroad. Bought property in Poverty Flats for the railroad's northern terminus. When the line reached Shasta County in summer 1872, the railroad NAMED THE NEW TOWN REDDING CA IN HIS HONOR (incorporated Oct 4, 1887). The naming was disputed in 1874 in favor of Pierson B. Reading but officially changed back to Redding by 1880. UC REGENT: Appointed 1880 to fill Pixley unexpired term; reappointed 1882. SCIENCE: Member California Academy of Sciences; member Geographical Society of the Pacific. Coastal paleontologist; collected and donated prehistoric and aboriginal relics to the Academy museum. Also California Fish Commissioner at time of death. CHILDREN with Mary Prescott Putnam Redding: William (b.~1848 MA), J. Albert (b.~1850 MA), George H. (b.~1856 CA), Joseph Deighn (b.1859 Sacramento - d.1932 SF; Bohemian Club president, Natoma opera librettist; built in this project as I00401, married Myra Augusta Cowles HD3727 = Hooker descendant via Edwin Weed Cowles → Hon. Samuel Cowles SF). DEATH: August 21, 1882 SF at 58 of apoplexy. Funeral Aug 23 First Congregational Church; Central Pacific Railroad delegation, California Academy of Sciences delegation, and UC Regents present. Buried Sacramento Historic City Cemetery. EASTER EGG ROLE: X-prefix non-descendant per Jalapeño Rule §5 criterion #1 — notable parent of I-prefix Hooker-tree spouse Joseph D. Redding (I00401, who married Myra Augusta Cowles HD3727). Sources: Wikipedia 'Benjamin B. Redding'; Find a Grave Memorial 110607551; Sacramento Historic City Cemetery; Sacramento Daily Union obituary Aug 22, 1882; Shasta Courier obituary Aug 26, 1882; Jeremy M. Tuggle 'Exploring Shasta County History' blog (2019); Familypedia Redding California; Rails-to-Trails Conservancy Sacramento River Rail Trail Hall of Fame article; HistoryLink (Spokesman-Review article references his railroad role).

narrative_blocks.header: Two daughters married two Cowles brothers
narrative_blocks.body: Mosley's daughters Elizabeth Caroline (born 1827) and Sarah Frances (born 1837) both married Cowles brothers from the Hooker family line — Edwin Cowles, the Cleveland Leader publisher, and Alfred Cowles, the Chicago Tribune business manager. The double sister-brother exchange tied the Cayuga County Hutchinsons into both branches of the Cowles newspaper empire.

narrative_blocks.header: Married a widow with two hundred Cayuga acres
narrative_blocks.body: Mosley married Elizabeth Boardman Hall in October 1822. She was a young widow — her first husband John Davis had drowned falling off the Cayuga Lake bridge in 1819 — and came to the marriage with two hundred acres of lake-front land, on which Mosley built what local historians call the Hutchinson Homestead. A historical marker stands on the site today.

narrative_blocks.header: Mayflower descent through his mother Betsy Buell
narrative_blocks.body: Mosley's mother Elizabeth 'Betsy' Buell (1774-1825) was a documented Mayflower descendant. This ancestry passed through Mosley to his daughters Elizabeth Caroline and Sarah Frances Hutchinson, and from them to their children by Edwin Cowles and Alfred Cowles — adding a Plymouth Colony thread to the broader Hooker-Cowles lineage.

narrative_blocks.header: Chicago Society of Artists president in 1942
narrative_blocks.body: An indispensable presence in Chicago's interwar art community, Frances served as president of the Chicago Society of Artists in 1942. She was an active member of the Arts Club of Chicago and shared studio space at the Tree Studios in the mid 1930s with Rue Wintherbotham Shaw, the Arts Club's president.

narrative_blocks.header: WPA muralist after the family fortune collapsed
narrative_blocks.body: After the Great Depression wiped out the Badger family's fortune, Frances qualified for the WPA Illinois Art Project despite her socially prominent background. She painted murals for libraries, schools, hospitals, and field houses across Chicago, Oak Park, and Joliet — including the 1933 Century of Progress Hall of Science and a Treasure Island series at the Audy Home.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventeen exhibitions at the Art Institute of Chicago
narrative_blocks.body: Frances exhibited at the Art Institute of Chicago seventeen times between 1927 and 1943. Her most celebrated canvas, 'Celery Pickers No. 1' — a luminous oil depicting Black agricultural workers — appeared at the 1941 Chicago and Vicinity Exhibition. A gouache sequel followed in the 1943 International Watercolor Exhibition.

narrative_blocks.header: Studied and taught at the Art Institute herself
narrative_blocks.body: Frances began at the SAIC junior branch in Winnetka at age six and earned her studio art degree there in 1925 under Matilda Vanderpoel and John Warner Norton. She returned to teach in the 1940s alongside Ethel Spears and Kathleen Blackshear, and completed a formal B.F.A. there in 1949.

narrative_blocks.header: She painted her way into the Whitney
narrative_blocks.body: Flora Schofield built a four-decade career as a painter and printmaker across Chicago, Provincetown, and Paris, moving from academic training to bold modernist abstraction. Her paintings entered the permanent collection of the Whitney Museum of American Art — a New York honor for an artist who made her life in Chicago.

narrative_blocks.header: Her paintings split a Chicago art society apart
narrative_blocks.body: In 1923 a radical faction seized the Art Institute's jury and voted three of Flora's abstract paintings into the annual show. The old guard was so enraged that the Chicago Society of Artists tore in two, and a critic dubbed her the "storm petrel" of the city's modernists.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father paid for art school in secret
narrative_blocks.body: Flora's mother demanded seven years of piano and forbade art, so her father quietly paid her Art Institute tuition without telling his wife. She studied in hiding until she landed a teaching job at the school and simply stopped pretending.

narrative_blocks.header: A wharf shanty made her a modernist
narrative_blocks.body: Bored by the conventional teacher she'd paid to study under in Provincetown, Flora spotted a shanty on the wharf painted violent yellow and blue — a "Modern Art School" run by two radicals. Not daring to tell her traditionalist friends, she enrolled to learn the new painting, took up the Provincetown printers' white-line woodblock method, and never looked back.

narrative_blocks.header: Paris made her a citizen of two continents
narrative_blocks.body: Through the 1920s Flora spent more time in Paris than at home, studying cubism under Albert Gleizes and Fernand Léger until she felt herself a citizen of two continents. Art, she insisted, was universal and never local — a painting's worth lay in its construction, and that was contribution enough.

people.research_notes: Born 1873 Lanark, Illinois (per Wikipedia primary record); died October 5, 1960 Chicago. Note birth-year DISCREPANCY: Find a Grave gives 1871. Her work is in the permanent collections of the Whitney Museum of American Art and the Provincetown Art Association and Museum. narrative_blocks.header: Iwo Jima on the fifth day of battle
narrative_blocks.body: A US Army Air Corps officer, Edwin Jr. spent twenty-two months in the Western Pacific combat area during World War II. He landed on Iwo Jima on the fifth day of the battle — one of the bloodiest engagements of the Pacific Theater — and retired in 1946 with the rank of Major.

narrative_blocks.header: Episcopal priest at St. Giles Northbrook 1950-1966
narrative_blocks.body: After Seabury-Western Theological Seminary in 1950, Edwin Jr. was ordained as an Episcopal priest in the Diocese of Chicago. He served as Priest-in-Charge then Rector at St. Giles Church in Northbrook IL from 1950 through 1966 — sixteen years at one parish — and on numerous diocesan committees and councils.

narrative_blocks.header: Dean of Ohio University Chillicothe 1969-1981
narrative_blocks.body: After three Indiana University degrees in adult education and political science, culminating in a 1969 doctorate, Edwin Jr. headed Ohio University's Chillicothe regional campus as Dean for twelve years. He continued as a supply priest in the Diocese of Southern Ohio after retiring.

narrative_blocks.header: Eagle Scout and Silver Beaver Award honoree
narrative_blocks.body: A lifelong Boy Scouts of America supporter, Edwin Jr. attained the rank of Eagle Scout and was later presented with the Silver Beaver Award for his service to the Chief Logan Council. He was also a Paul Harris Fellow of Rotary International through the Chillicothe Rotary Club.

EDUCATION: New Trier High School Winnetka; University of Chicago B.A. 1940 (Delta Kappa Epsilon); U.S. Army Air Corps WWII service 1942-1946 retiring as Major (22 mo Western Pacific, landed Iwo Jima day 5 of battle); Seabury-Western Theological Seminary B.D. 1950; Indiana University M.A. Adult Education 1967, M.A. Political Science 1968, Ed.D./Ph.D. Education and Political Science 1969. MINISTRY: Ordained Episcopal priest 1950 in Diocese of Chicago. Priest-in-Charge then Rector at St. Giles Episcopal Church, Northbrook IL 1950-1966. Continued on multiple diocesan committees, boards, and councils. After retiring, supply priest at St. Paul's Episcopal Church Chillicothe and other parishes in Diocese of Southern Ohio. ACADEMIC LEADERSHIP: Dean of Ohio University Chillicothe Campus 1969-1981 (12 years). SCOUTING: Lifelong supporter of the Boy Scouts of America. Eagle Scout rank achieved. Silver Beaver Award for service to Chief Logan Council. ROTARY: Strong member of Chillicothe Rotary Club + Rotary International. Paul Harris Fellow. INTERESTS: British history, travel, wildlife preservation (special focus on wolf restoration), environmental studies, classical music, railroads. MARRIAGES: m1 1946 Mary Todd 'Polly' Heaslett (b. Jan 10 1918 Birmingham AL — d. Mar 29 2012 Northbrook IL; WWII Red Cross Pacific Theater) — children Thomas Michael Badger + Mary Janet Beladi; divorced ~1967. m2 Virginia Ann Curtis Badger (stepdaughters Leslye Winslow + Nancy Winslow). Both wives to be built in Stage 6X-4. CHILDREN (with Polly): Thomas Michael Badger; Mary Janet Beladi (m. Beladi family — grandchildren Cyrus, Bijan, Aram Beladi). narrative_blocks.header: Young widow with two hundred Cayuga Lake acres
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth married Dr. John Davis in February 1818, but he drowned falling off the Cayuga Lake bridge in 1819 — leaving her a widow before twenty, owning two hundred acres of lake-front land. Three years later she married attorney Mosley Hutchinson, and together they built the Hutchinson Homestead that remained a Cayuga landmark until it burned in 1910.

narrative_blocks.header: Both daughters married prominent Cowles brothers
narrative_blocks.body: Two of Elizabeth and Mosley's daughters — Elizabeth Caroline (born 1827) and Sarah Frances (born 1837) — married the Cowles brothers Edwin and Alfred, who ran the Cleveland Leader and the Chicago Tribune respectively. Elizabeth outlived her husband Mosley by sixteen years, running the homestead until her death at age seventy-six in 1877.

people.research_notes: Born April 15, 1801 Cayuga Cayuga County NY; died May 28, 1877 Cayuga at age 76. Buried Lakeview Cemetery Cayuga (per Find a Grave Memorial 92032994) with husband Mosley Hutchinson (X02775) and several of their children. FIRST MARRIAGE: Dr. John Harvard Davis (Feb 4, 1818). Davis fell off the Cayuga Lake bridge and drowned in 1819. Elizabeth was widowed before age 20 and owner of 200 acres of Cayuga Lake front land previously owned by Davis. SECOND MARRIAGE: Attorney Mosley Hutchinson (Oct 22, 1822). 8 children together (see X02775 research_notes for full list). Survived Mosley by 16 years, running the Hutchinson Homestead until her death. LOCAL HISTORY: The History of Cayuga village (date unknown) contains a passage about Elizabeth on the Academy's lawn in 1817 — she was observed by John Davis, who 'fell in love with her at first sight.' The original house Mosley and Elizabeth built burned in 1910; a historical marker identifies the site. EASTER_EGG ROLE: X-prefix non-descendant per Jalapeño Rule §5 criterion #1 — notable parent (mother) of I00413 + I00414, the two Hutchinson sisters who married the Cowles brothers. (Mosley X02775 is the father; both parents qualify.) Sources: Find a Grave Memorial 92032994; Spared & Shared 4 blog; Baker Family Tree blog Ch. 14; History of Cayuga village (via Baker blog).

narrative_blocks.body: She belonged to the Prytanean Society and in her graduating year of 1912 wrote the first Partheneia staged at Berkeley by the women students. The pageant became a university tradition that ran into the 1930s.

NAME RESOLUTION: OAC Baeck Family Papers finding aid (Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley) uses 'Anna Wooster Rearden Baeck' as the formal archival name. Find a Grave Memorial 75874428 and Wikitree (Reardon-1094) both use 'Nancy Reardon Back/Baeck.' Per project source hierarchy (institutional archive > Find a Grave; Wikitree is downstream of FG), OAC adopted as primary. 'Nancy' likely informal family usage — possibly to distinguish her from her grandmother Anna Louise Wooster Cowles (I00412), who was still living when she was a child. VITAL DATES: Born 1888 San Francisco (per OAC). Find a Grave gives Dec 13, 1888 California. Combining: born Dec 13, 1888 San Francisco. Died Feb 20, 1970 Alameda County CA at age 81. EDUCATION: California and Illinois public schools (per OAC); UC Berkeley A.B. 1912; member Prytanean Society (UC Berkeley women's honor society); WROTE THE FIRST 'PARTHENEIA' to be staged at UC Berkeley by women students, performed her graduation year 1912. The Partheneia was a Berkeley tradition that ran through the 1930s. CAREER: Taught school for several years before 1917 marriage. Per OAC. MARRIAGE: John Erik Baeck (I00422) in 1917 per OAC. Resided Berkeley almost continuously until her death. CHILD: Anne Charlotta Baeck (HD3758, 1920-1996). PAPERS: Her papers and her father's papers (Judge Timothy Rearden) form the bulk of the Baeck Family Papers, BANC MSS 74/101 c, Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley. Includes papers of her uncle Joseph D. Redding (I00401) and his wife Myra C. Redding (HD3727), plus papers of her mother Anita C. Rearden (HD3729), grandfather Samuel Cowles (HD3710), grandfather-in-law Benjamin B. Redding (X02774). Correspondents include Ambrose Bierce, Ina Coolbrith, and Porter Garnett. BURIAL: Cypress Lawn Memorial Park, Colma CA (CEM267) with husband and daughter.

narrative_blocks.body: Samuel was given the Cowles surname as his middle name from his great-grandmother Sarah Frances Cowles Badger of the San Francisco Cowles judicial family. He passed it to his son Samuel Cowles Badger Jr., extending the Cowles thread that began with their great-great-grandfather Dr. Edwin Weed Cowles of Austinburg, Ohio.

career.title: Pioneer Atlanta citizen + railroad agent
career.organization: Macon & Western Railroad; later Georgia Railroad
career.notes: Arrived Atlanta 1845 at age 10. Originally with Macon & Western Railroad as chief clerk; remained through the Civil War. Later served as agent for the Georgia Railroad for many years. Said to be the first man to record a legal paper on the books of the City of Atlanta. 'Saw Atlanta build up from a little village.' At his 1896 death was one of Atlanta's oldest citizens.

landmarks.notes: Built Werner home on Washington Street, Atlanta 1870s; home demolished 1912.

narrative_blocks.header: A boy of ten when Atlanta was a village
narrative_blocks.body: He came to Atlanta in 1845, a ten-year-old in a place barely a village, and stayed through the war and fifty-one years — chief clerk for the Macon and Western, then the Georgia Railroad's agent. He was said to be the first man to record a legal paper in the city's books.

people.research_notes: Born January 15, 1835 South Carolina; died June 10, 1896 Georgia at age 61. Buried Oakland Cemetery Atlanta. German descent, son of William Werner of Pendleton SC. 'A most respected citizen and agent of the Georgia Railroad for many years; a Democrat and Presbyterian' (EH, entry 1698). Arrived Atlanta 1845. With Macon & Western Railroad originally (chief clerk, remained through Civil War); later Georgia Railroad agent. LANDMARK: Built Werner home on Washington Street near Mitchell Street intersection, Atlanta, 1870s (LM101). Home torn down 1912. A group photo of Georgia Railroad Freight Depot employees from the Alabama/Loyd Street depot shows Werner as 6th of 14 men. MARRIAGE: Married Florence Woodruff Cowles (HD3774) December 18-19, 1872 at Madison or Huntsville, Alabama (EH says 'Dec. 19, 1872, at Huntsville'; FamilySearch says 'December 18, 1872 Madison Alabama'). Per EH, he was 'born about 1834 in South Carolina' but FG/FamilySearch gives birth Jan 15, 1835 SC. Source: EH entry 1698; FamilySearch MBGM-Q4Q (Edward Alphonso Werner 1835-1896); Find a Grave; Atlanta city history sources cited in landmark notes.

narrative_blocks.header: Born in Georgia's capital, educated in Alabama
narrative_blocks.body: Florence was born March 6, 1843 in Milledgeville — Georgia's state capital — and educated at the Huntsville Female Seminary, a Presbyterian institution then foremost in educating young Southern women. She married Georgia Railroad agent Edward Werner in Huntsville in December 1872 and settled permanently in Atlanta.

narrative_blocks.header: Her estate sparked a Georgia Supreme Court battle
narrative_blocks.body: Florence died November 29, 1911, never having distributed her late husband Edward's estate to their four children. Her son Lynn assumed management without court authority; by 1943 the estate dispute reached the Georgia Supreme Court, where Edward Jr. sued Lynn, Florence, and Ray over property mismanagement and a disputed sale of 528 West Peachtree Street Atlanta.

sources.short: Werner v. Werner, 195 Ga. 868 (Ga. Sup. Ct. May 6, 1943, Reid CJ)

people.research_notes: Born March 6, 1843 Milledgeville, Baldwin County, Georgia; died November 29, 1911 Georgia at age 68. Buried Oakland Cemetery Atlanta (CEM270). PARENTS: Ebenezer Mix Cowles (HD0984, b.1801 Farmington CT; moved south by 1843) and Frances M. Atwood Cowles (I00385, Mayflower descent via Atwood line). EDUCATION: Huntsville Female Seminary, Huntsville Alabama — 'foremost in educating young ladies; a Presbyterian institution' (EH entry 1698). MARRIAGE: Married Edward Alphonso Werner Sr (I00425) December 18-19, 1872 at Huntsville/Madison Alabama. He was described by EH as 'a most respected citizen and agent of the Georgia Railroad for many years; a Democrat and Presbyterian; son of William Werner of Pendleton, S.C.' Werner died June 10, 1896. Florence did not distribute the estate. ESTATE LITIGATION: After Florence died 1911, her estate was never administered. Son Lynn W. Werner (HD3776) managed it without court authority. In 1943 the Georgia Supreme Court adjudicated Werner v. Werner (No. 14530) — an equitable partition proceeding initiated by Edward Jr (HD3775) against Lynn, Florence Brine (HD3777), and Ray Cowles (HD3778). Issues included accounts between parties, deed cancellation, receiver appointment, and disputed profits from the 528 West Peachtree Street Atlanta property. Future build: DOC023. Source: EH entry 1698; FamilySearch KD7Q-YNP; Find a Grave Memorial 97125562; Georgia Supreme Court, Werner v. Werner, No. 14530 (May 6, 1943, Reid CJ).

narrative_blocks.header: Plaintiff in 1943 Georgia Supreme Court estate suit
narrative_blocks.body: Edward Werner Jr. was named plaintiff in the Georgia Supreme Court 1943 estate case Werner versus Werner — number 14530 — in which he sued his brothers Lynn and Ray and sister Florence Brine over their parents' estate. Edward alleged that brother Lynn had mismanaged the estate and appropriated profits from the sale of 528 West Peachtree Street Atlanta. The reported case became part of the published record of mid-twentieth-century Georgia probate law.

narrative_blocks.header: Two marriages and three documented children
narrative_blocks.body: Edward had two marriages with three documented children. His wife Elizabeth Weakley bore daughters Elisabeth Werner born 1908 and Harriette Werner born 1915; his wife Ethel Margaret Cook of Atlanta bore daughter Elizabeth C. Werner born 1907. The chronological ordering of the two marriages remains unsettled across descendant records.

narrative_blocks.header: Huntsville Alabama 1874 to Atlanta Georgia 1955
narrative_blocks.body: Edward Werner Jr. was born September 5, 1874 in Huntsville, Madison County Alabama and died May 24, 1955 in Atlanta, Fulton County Georgia at age eighty. He is buried at Oakland Cemetery Atlanta — one of the most prominent nineteenth-century Southern garden cemeteries, holding the graves of Margaret Mitchell, Bobby Jones, and many of Atlanta's founding families.

narrative_blocks.header: Hooker descent through mother Florence Cowles Werner
narrative_blocks.body: Edward inherited Hooker descent through his mother Florence Woodruff Cowles Werner — the Connecticut Cowles family being one of the major mid-nineteenth-century New England-to-Deep South migration lines that brought Connecticut Yankees south of the Mason-Dixon. His father Edward Alphonso Werner Sr. was a non-Hooker line spouse.

narrative_blocks.header: A messenger boy at thirteen
narrative_blocks.body: Clifford's father lost everything in the Civil War and died, leaving his widow to support herself, so Clifford had only a common-school education. In 1874, at thirteen, his sister's husband Edward Werner took him on as messenger boy in his office, where he learned telegraphy and shorthand.

narrative_blocks.header: He moved his widowed mother to Decatur
narrative_blocks.body: While still a clerk in Werner's office, Clifford moved his widowed mother out to Decatur, six miles from Atlanta. In January 1888 he married a Decatur girl, Florence Candler, whose father Milton had sat in Congress.

narrative_blocks.header: Three cities in his first year of marriage
narrative_blocks.body: Clifford married while he was the East Tennessee, Virginia and Georgia's contracting freight agent at Chattanooga. That August the post moved him to Jacksonville and in November to Atlanta, where in 1889 he became General Southern Traveling Agent.

narrative_blocks.header: Two congressmen from one Georgia district
narrative_blocks.body: Florence grew up in Decatur, the daughter of Milton Candler, who represented Georgia's Fifth District in Congress from 1875 to 1879. Her mother's father, Charles Murphey, had held the district's seat in the early 1850s.

narrative_blocks.header: A daughter at twenty-seven, a grandson at nine
narrative_blocks.body: Florence's daughter Florence Hardisty died in February 1920 at twenty-seven, and her grandson John Hardisty in December 1927 at nine. Both were buried at Westview Cemetery in Atlanta, where Florence was laid beside them in 1940.

narrative_blocks.header: Her uncle Asa built Coca-Cola
narrative_blocks.body: Florence was one of twelve children of Milton Candler, the eldest of thirteen. His younger brothers were her uncles Asa Griggs Candler, who built the Coca-Cola Company, and the Rev. Warren Akin Candler, who became president of Emory University.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped expel thirty-three Black legislators
narrative_blocks.body: In 1868, sitting in the Georgia Senate, Milton was instrumental in the illegal expulsion of thirty-three newly elected Black members of the legislature. They were reinstated in 1870, with the help of President Grant and Frederick Douglass.

narrative_blocks.header: He quit Congress over free silver
narrative_blocks.body: Georgia's Fifth District sent Milton to Congress in 1874 and again in 1876. In 1878 the district convention adopted a free-silver plank, and rather than run on it he withdrew and went back to his law practice in Decatur.

narrative_blocks.header: A cavalry captain west of the Chattahoochee
narrative_blocks.body: When his father-in-law, former Congressman Charles Murphey, died in January 1861, the Candler family outfitted a DeKalb County company of Confederate troops named the Murphey Guards. In 1863 Milton took a captain's commission in the 10th Georgia Cavalry, State Guards, mounted infantry defending the country west of the Chattahoochee.

narrative_blocks.header: Eldest of thirteen, raised at Villa Rica
narrative_blocks.body: Milton was the first of thirteen children of Samuel Charles Candler, who moved the family to Villa Rica after the Creek were driven out and by 1860 held seventeen enslaved people and leased nineteen more. Milton, a slaveholder himself, was educated privately and graduated from the University of Georgia in 1854, at seventeen.

narrative_blocks.header: Older brother of Coca-Cola's Asa Candler
narrative_blocks.body: Milton's younger brothers included Asa Griggs Candler, who built the Coca-Cola Company, Warren Akin Candler, president of Emory University, and John Slaughter Candler of the Georgia Supreme Court. A street in Decatur is named for Milton.

people.research_notes:
Born January 11, 1837 Campbellton, Campbell County (now Fulton County since 1932), Georgia. Died August 8, 1909 Decatur, DeKalb County, Georgia at age 72. PARENTS: Samuel Charles Candler (1809-1873) of Columbia County GA, served both houses of Georgia legislature; slaveholder per 1860 census (17 owned + 19 leased). Mother Martha Bernetta Beall (1819-1897) of Bartow County GA. Grandfather Col. William Candler (1730-1784) led Georgia troops in American Revolution. EDUCATION: Private education in Campbellton/Villa Rica. UGA Athens A.B. 1854 (age 17). LEGAL CAREER: Admitted to Georgia bar 1856. Started practice Cassville, Bartow County (where his mother's family + Congressman Cooper lived). Moved to Decatur, DeKalb County 1857; practiced there most of remaining life. MILITARY SERVICE: Captain, 10th Regiment Georgia Cavalry, State Guards (Murphey Guards), August 1863. Confederate mounted infantry serving six months as local defense west of Chattahoochee River. The Murphey Guards were named for Eliza's late father Charles Murphey, former US Representative who died January 1861. POLITICAL CAREER:
- Georgia State House of Representatives (DeKalb County) 1861-1863
- Delegate, Georgia State Constitutional Convention 1865 (Reconstruction)
- Georgia State Senate 1868-1872
- Delegate, Democratic National Convention 1872, 1876
- US House of Representatives 44th-45th Congresses (1875-1879), Democrat from Georgia
- Withdrew from 1878 re-nomination after district adopted free-silver plank — late-1870s Bourbon Democrat / Greenback fracture in Southern politics
- Resumed Decatur law practice until death 1909 MARRIAGE: Married Elizabeth Caroline 'Eliza' Murphey (X02781) 1857. Twelve children including Florence Candler Cowles (I00429, b. Oct 23, 1867, d. narrative_blocks.header: A congressman's daughter, married at seventeen
narrative_blocks.body: Eliza was the daughter of Charles Murphey of Decatur, who sat in Congress for Georgia's Fifth District in the early 1850s. She married Milton Candler in 1857, at seventeen, and bore him twelve children, among them Florence, who married Clifford Cowles.

narrative_blocks.header: Three children buried before her
narrative_blocks.body: Eliza lost her daughter Laura in 1880 and her son Maury Lee in 1889, both in their teens, and her son Milton Jr. in 1893. Widowed in 1909, she died at her house in Decatur in January 1917, at seventy-seven.

narrative_blocks.header: Founder of Austinburg Township, Ohio Western Reserve
narrative_blocks.body: A Connecticut Land Company partner, Eliphalet purchased wide tracts across the Connecticut Western Reserve in the late 1790s and settled at present-day Austinburg in 1799 — the township still bears his name. He carried the mail across the region, operated a cattle-dealing business, and served in the Ohio Senate 1829-1831.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife rode horseback to recruit a minister
narrative_blocks.body: In spring 1810, his wife Sybil Dudley Austin rode six hundred miles by horseback to Bristol Connecticut — alone, with her wardrobe in a portmanteau — to recruit Rev. Giles Hooker Cowles to settle Ashtabula County's first Congregational minister. Giles, his wife Sally, and their eight children arrived in Austinburg the following summer 1811. The Austin-Cowles partnership defined Austinburg's pioneer era.

narrative_blocks.header: His Austinburg house is on the National Register
narrative_blocks.body: Eliphalet built the brick house at 1879 State Route 45 Austinburg in 1811 (or 1815 per Wikipedia). His grandson Louis B. Austin remodelled it in the Italianate style during the 1860s.

people.research_notes:
Born 1761 Litchfield County Connecticut. Died January 28, 1838 Austinburg Ohio at age 76-77. CONNECTICUT LAND COMPANY: Joined the Connecticut Land Company (formed late 18th century to settle and develop the Western Connecticut Reserve in Ohio). Purchased wide tracts across the region including present-day Austinburg Township, which is named for him. Settled at present-day Austinburg 1799. AUSTINBURG ROLE: 'As northeastern Ohio developed, he became regionally prominent: his land holdings were located in multiple counties, he was responsible for carrying the mails, he operated a cattle-dealing operation, and he was a state senator from 1829 to 1831' (Wikipedia, citing Owen 2003). WIFE'S RECRUITMENT RIDE: His wife Sybil Dudley Austin (X02783) determined in spring 1810 that Austinburg needed a settled minister. She rode horseback alone 600 miles back to Connecticut, met Mrs. Sally Cowles, persuaded her, and through her Rev. Giles Hooker Cowles (H00443) — the result being the Cowles family's 1811 migration to Austinburg, where Giles served as Ashtabula County's first settled minister until his 1830 retirement. The 1878 Williams Brothers History records this episode in dramatic detail. HOUSE: Built the present brick house at 1879 State Route 45 Austinburg c.1811-1815. His grandson Louis B. Austin remodelled it in the Italianate style during the 1860s. NRHP listed February 24, 1975 (reference 75001313). One of three NRHP-listed properties in Austinburg Township along with the Congregational Church of Austinburg and the L.W. Peck House in Eagleville. FAMILY: Married Sybil Dudley (X02783, b.1761 Conway CT - d. April 2, 1844 Austinburg OH). Multiple children, including Rev. Eliphalet Austin Jr (X01418, 1793-1837, who married Sally Berrien Cowles H01142 — establishing the Austin-Cowles connection in the Hooker tree) and several daughters who attended Litchfield Female Academy (Sybil Webb 1818, plus Chloe, Florilla, and Sophia per Litchfield Historical Society Ledger). EASTER_EGG ROLE: X-prefix per schema §5 — notable parent of I-prefix Hooker spouse (X01418 Rev. Eliphalet Austin Jr, husband of H01142 Sally Berrien Cowles). Substantive Wikipedia URL for the Austin House anchors his historical significance. Source: Wikipedia 'Eliphalet Austin House'; Williams Brothers 'History of Ashtabula County' (1878); NRHP reference 75001313.

narrative_blocks.header: Rode 600 miles alone to recruit a minister
narrative_blocks.body: In spring 1810 Sybil concluded that the new settlement of Austinburg needed a settled Congregational minister. She rode alone by horseback over six hundred miles to Bristol Connecticut — clothing in a portmanteau, thirty-day journey through unsettled forest — to persuade Sally and Rev. Giles Hooker Cowles to migrate to the Western Reserve. Her ride succeeded; the Cowles family arrived in Austinburg in 1811.

narrative_blocks.header: Daughters all attended Litchfield Female Academy
narrative_blocks.body: Four of her daughters attended the Litchfield Female Academy — Sybil Webb in 1818, Chloe, Florilla, and Sophia. The Academy founded by Sarah Pierce in 1792 was among the earliest formal secondary schools for women in the United States.

people.research_notes: Born 1761 Conway, Connecticut. Died April 2, 1844 Austinburg Ohio at age 82-83. Buried Austinburg Center Cemetery (CEM035). Married Judge Eliphalet Austin (X02782). DUDLEY LINEAGE (per EH 688): Daniel, Daniel, Caleb, Joseph, William Dudley line. William Dudley emigrated from Richmond (formerly Sheen) in Surrey England, arrived in Guilford CT from Guilford Surrey, married Jane Lutman by Rev. Henry Whitfield (rector of Ockley Surrey) August 24, 1636. Source: Dudley Genealogy 1892. HISTORIC SIGNIFICANCE — RECRUITMENT RIDE: In spring 1810 Sybil concluded that Austinburg needed a settled minister and notified her husband she would ride back to Connecticut to find one. She rode alone on horseback approximately 600 miles, clothing in a single portmanteau, over 30+ days through largely unsettled forest. She arrived at Bristol CT, met with Sally Cowles, persuaded her to support the relocation, and through her brought Rev. Giles Hooker Cowles (H00443) to consider the call. Giles made an exploratory trip, agreed, and the Cowles family migrated to Austinburg in 1811. The 1878 Williams Brothers History records this episode in dramatic detail and contrasts Sybil's portmanteau with the 'enormous Saratoga trunks' of her great-granddaughters in the 1870s — a passage often quoted to illustrate pioneer Ohio settler grit. DAUGHTERS AT LITCHFIELD FEMALE ACADEMY: Per Litchfield Historical Society Ledger — Sybil Webb (LFA 1818), Chloe, Florilla, Sophia. Chloe married John Henderson (Wikitree). EASTER_EGG ROLE: X-prefix wife of X02782 + mother of X01418 Rev. Eliphalet Austin Jr (Hooker tree spouse). Her recruitment ride is the foundational act of the entire Austin-Cowles connection in this tree. Source: Williams Brothers 'History of Ashtabula County' (1878); EH 1909 entry #688; Litchfield Historical Society Ledger; Dudley Genealogy 1892.

narrative_blocks.header: Served the War of 1812 under Capt. Deming
narrative_blocks.body: Merritt served as a private in the Connecticut militia during the War of 1812 under Capt. Deming, three decades after his father Samuel and uncle Jabez had ridden the Revolution under Capt. Sloper. The Cowles family carried two American wars across two generations.

narrative_blocks.header: Outlived his wife by twenty-nine years
narrative_blocks.body: Merritt married Rosetta Peck of Berlin in December 1813. She died in 1843 at fifty-three; Merritt lived on at Kensington until 1872, twenty-nine years a widower. Both lie in South Kensington Cemetery.

narrative_blocks.header: His son Samuel Brainard kept the country store
narrative_blocks.body: Merritt's son Samuel Brainard Cowles served as Kensington's postmaster, kept the country store, and rose to colonel of militia — all before consumption killed him at thirty-two in 1851. The store passed out of family hands; the militia rank lived on.

narrative_blocks.header: He lost two sons in four days
narrative_blocks.body: George Gridley died on Christmas Day 1851 at twenty-seven, unmarried. Four days later consumption took Samuel Brainard at thirty-two, leaving a widow and a small son. Both were buried at South Kensington.

bio.photo_notes: Connecticut farmer and deacon, father of botanist Henry Chandler Cowles.

burial.plot_notes: Oak Hill Cemetery, Southington, Hartford County, Connecticut.

career.notes: The family had worked the same Connecticut land since the 1750s.

narrative_blocks.header: Ninth generation on the same ground
narrative_blocks.body: He farmed the Kensington land the Cowleses had worked since the 1750s and gardened it for market, the ninth generation of the family in Connecticut. He held it until some time after 1894, then moved to Southington, where he died in 1915.

narrative_blocks.header: Constable, assessor, and the General Assembly
narrative_blocks.body: The town gave him nearly every office it had: constable, assessor, justice of the peace, selectman, and a seat on the board of relief. Berlin sent him up to the General Assembly, and in politics he stood a Prohibitionist.

narrative_blocks.header: Deacon, and over the Sunday school
narrative_blocks.body: He was a deacon of the Kensington Congregational Church and superintendent of its Sunday school, the two offices a New England farming town handed the man it trusted most with its children and its accounts.

narrative_blocks.header: Eighth of Linus Cowles’s ten children
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Kensington in April 1831 and baptised there the following June, the eighth of Linus Cowles’s ten. His mother Eunetia Pardee had been married first to Luman, his father’s brother, so his half-brothers were also cousins.

narrative_blocks.header: Eliza Whittlesey, of a militia lieutenant’s line
narrative_blocks.body: Eliza Whittlesey of Cleveland married him in May 1866, joined the Kensington church in 1877, and died there in 1888 at forty-nine; her great-grandfather Lemuel had been commissioned lieutenant of Connecticut militia in 1779.

narrative_blocks.header: He married again, and raised an ecologist
narrative_blocks.body: Widowed seven years, he married Mrs. Emma Sutliffe of Southington at Berlin in January 1895, her second marriage as well as his. His son Henry Chandler, born at Kensington in 1869, became the central figure of American plant ecology.
