parents.father_research_notes: Hon. Frederick Whittlesey (X02788, Whittlesey Genealogy #650, Cleveland OH judge/legislator). Built as easter_egg in Stage 6Y-11. Frederick Whittlesey, Whittlesey Genealogy entry #650, b. Dec 13, 1801 Southington Conn., d. Nov 13, 1854 Cleveland OH. Yale College 1822, Phi Beta Kappa. Lineage: Frederick (650) → Roger → Lemuel → Eliphalet → Eliphalet → John Whittlesey (immigrant). Different Whittlesey branch from the one already in the Hooker tree (HD0097 Roger Newton Whittlesey, whose father was Rev. Samuel Whittlesey via I00020/X01900). Both branches share John Whittlesey of Saybrook (the immigrant) as a common ancestor, but diverge generations earlier. Career: studied law in CT, then one year (1827?) in the Canfield OH law office of Hon. Elisha Whittlesey (X01997, Whittlesey Gen #310, already in tree). Removed to Lorain Co. 1827, opened law office at Elyria. Ohio state legislature both chambers; served as Speaker. Editor of Ohio Atlas (Whig organ of Lorain Co.). Removed to Cleveland 1834. With Col. Charles Whittlesey (#693) bought Cleveland Herald 1836; principal editor ~2 years. Associate judge of Cuyahoga County for several years; effectively presiding judge. Appointed Clerk of Cuyahoga Court of Common Pleas; served full 7-year term despite paralysis. Suffered paralysis 14 years before death; deathbed quote: 'Tell him that I bear evidence of the supporting realities of the Christian religion.' Source: Cleveland Herald obituary Nov 22, 1854; Whittlesey Genealogy #650. PROPOSED for build as X-prefix easter_egg pending Sam's notability decision.

narrative_blocks.header: A judge's daughter, orphaned of him at fifteen
narrative_blocks.body: Fourth of the eight children of Frederick Whittlesey, a Cleveland judge and legislator, she lost him in 1854, at fifteen. Marriage carried her back east to Kensington, Connecticut — the reverse of her family's westward road.

narrative_blocks.header: Her great-grandfather raised militia in 1779
narrative_blocks.body: Lemuel Whittlesey was commissioned by the General Assembly in May 1779 as lieutenant of the 5th Company, 6th Connecticut Militia. She joined the Kensington Congregational Church in 1877, eleven years after marrying its deacon.

narrative_blocks.header: His dissertation founded American plant ecology
narrative_blocks.body: Cowles's 1898 PhD thesis on the Indiana Dunes — 'The Ecological Relations of the Vegetation on the Sand Dunes of Lake Michigan' — established his reputation overnight and became one of the most influential studies in American botany. It used the dunes' geological gradient to show how plant communities succeed each other over time.

narrative_blocks.header: Learned Danish to read Eugen Warming in original
narrative_blocks.body: Cowles's intellectual debt was to the Danish botanist Eugen Warming and his 1895 book Plantesamfund. He taught himself Danish to read it, visited Warming in Copenhagen in 1905, and became the primary American popularizer of Warming's term 'oecology' — the word ecology itself.

narrative_blocks.header: Cowles Bog and the Indiana Dunes preserved
narrative_blocks.body: His decades of conservation work helped save the Indiana Dunes — first as Cook County forest preserves and Starved Rock State Park, eventually as the Indiana Dunes National Lakeshore. One of his Indiana field sites is now Cowles Bog, named in his honor; the broader park became a national park in February 2019.

narrative_blocks.header: His students founded what came after
narrative_blocks.body: Victor Shelford, who sat in his classes, went on to found the Nature Conservancy; May Theilgaard Watts started the Illinois Prairie Path, the first rails-to-trails project in the country. He was at his best out of doors, lecturing as he walked them through bogs and dunes.

narrative_blocks.header: Met his wife in his own botany course
narrative_blocks.body: Cowles met Elizabeth Lucretia Waller, a Louisville schoolteacher, when she enrolled in nine undergraduate botany courses at Chicago. They married in 1900 in Louisville. Their daughter Harriet was born in 1912.

narrative_blocks.header: Parkinson's disease ended his teaching in 1932
narrative_blocks.body: Cowles was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease in the late 1920s, stopped teaching in 1932, and retired in 1934. He died in Chicago in September 1939 at seventy.

people.research_notes: Henry Chandler Cowles, founding figure of American plant ecology. b. Feb 27, 1869 Berlin Conn. (Whittlesey Genealogy #2357 has Feb 29, 1869 but 1869 was not a leap year; Wikipedia and FindAGrave both have Feb 27, 1869). d. Sept 12, 1939 Chicago Cook County IL, age 70, of Parkinson's disease. Son of Henry Martyn Cowles (HD3786) and Eliza Whittlesey Cowles (X02785). Educated Oberlin College (undergraduate, INST077) then University of Chicago (PhD 1898, INST119), doctoral advisor John Merle Coulter. Thesis: 'The Ecological Relations of the Vegetation on the Sand Dunes of Lake Michigan.' Taught at University of Chicago 1898-1934. Founding member of Ecological Society of America 1915. Editor of Botanical Gazette. President of Ecological Society of America, Association of American Geographers, Botanical Society of America, Phytogeography and Ecology section of International Botanical Congress. Special field assistant of USGS. MARRIAGE: m. 1900 Louisville KY, Elizabeth Lucretia Waller (X02786), b. Jan 6, 1873 Louisville KY, d. Jul 31, 1963 St. Louis MO, dau. of William A. and Mary Arabella Senteny Waller. Elizabeth was a Louisville schoolteacher who took nine undergraduate botany courses at Chicago where she met Henry. CHILD: Harriet Cowles Waller (HD3788, b. 1912). BURIAL (RECONCILED Stage 6Y-9): Originally interred Oak Woods Cemetery Chicago Sept 14, 1939 (per Illinois Deaths and Stillbirths Index 1916-1947). Remains transferred to Cave Hill Cemetery, Louisville KY (CEM275) in 1982 to rest beside wife Elizabeth (per Victor M. Cassidy, 'Henry Chandler Cowles, Pioneer Ecologist,' 2007, p. 346). WORKS: 'Ecological Relations of the Vegetation on the Sand Dunes of Lake Michigan' (1899); 'Plant Societies of Chicago and Vicinity' (1901); 'Text-Book of Botany Vol. II: Ecology' (1910, with John Merle Coulter and Charles Reid Barnes). STANDARD AUTHOR ABBREVIATION 'Cowles' in botanical taxonomy. STUDENTS who advanced ecology: Victor E. Shelford, William Skinner Cooper, Paul B. Sears, George Damon Fuller, Walter P. Cottam, Arthur G. Vestal, May Theilgaard Watts, O. D. Frank. LEGACY: Cowles Bog (Indiana Dunes National Lakeshore, west of Mineral Springs Road, Town of Dune Acres IN) named in his honor. His conservation work led to Cook County forest preserves, Starved Rock State Park, Indiana Dunes National Lakeshore (national park as of Feb 2019). Photo: https://res.cloudinary.com/dc5clrqtw/image/upload/v1778346190/PSM_V84_D208_Henry_C_Cowles_nt6b9d.jpg Sources: Wikipedia article on Henry Chandler Cowles; University of Chicago Henry C. Cowles Collection (Hanna Holborn Gray Special Collections Research Center, 25.75 linear feet, 21 boxes, circa 1860s-1985); FindAGrave 112930967; Illinois Deaths and Stillbirths Index 1916-1947; Whittlesey Genealogy #2357; Victor M. Cassidy, 'Henry Chandler Cowles, Plant Ecologist' (2007). [2026-07-25] Career array was keyed 'title'/'dates' — neither of which the card reads (it needs role/organization/start_year/end_year), so his positions rendered without titles or years. Rewritten. Education notes shortened; the Oberlin note had repeated the school's own name. FACTS HELD BACK FROM THE CARD: left Chicago for 1894-95 to teach sciences at Gates College, Neligh, Nebraska; named the final stage of succession the CLIMAX, the term that dominated American plant ecology for fifty years; organized and led the 1913 International Phytogeographical Excursion across the United States for European botanists after joining Tansley's 1911 British excursion; testified in the Texas-Oklahoma Red River oil boundary case, pitted indirectly against Frederic Clements; helped found the Prairie Club of Chicago in 1911 with Jens Jensen and Thomas W. Allinson; filled in as botany department chair 1923-24 and held it 1925-28. Students included Victor Shelford (later founder of the Nature Conservancy), May Theilgaard Watts (who began the Illinois Prairie Path, the first rails-to-trails project), William S. Cooper, Arthur Vestal, Paul Sears and Stanley Cain. NPS page added as a source; Wikipedia kept as primary_url.

narrative_blocks.header: Speaker of the Ohio House and county judge
narrative_blocks.body: After his Yale 1822 degree and a year studying at Hon. Elisha Whittlesey's Canfield law office, Frederick rose fast in Ohio — state legislator both chambers, then Speaker, then associate judge of Cuyahoga County who served as de facto presiding judge. He moved his practice from Elyria to Cleveland in 1834.

narrative_blocks.header: Cleveland Herald editor for two years before paralysis
narrative_blocks.body: In 1836 Frederick partnered with Col. Charles Whittlesey to buy the Cleveland Herald and serve as principal editor for two years. Then paralysis withdrew him from public life for the next fourteen.

narrative_blocks.header: Fourteen years a paralytic, dying at fifty-two
narrative_blocks.body: Frederick suffered paralysis the last fourteen years of his life, withdrawn from active practice though he served the constitutional seven-year term as Clerk of the Cuyahoga Court of Common Pleas. His deathbed message for an absent friend: 'Tell him that I bear evidence of the supporting realities of the Christian religion.'

narrative_blocks.header: From Elyria attorney to Cleveland Whig editor
narrative_blocks.body: Frederick was admitted to the Connecticut bar after Yale 1822, then spent a year at Whittlesey & Newton in Canfield Ohio with his cousin Elisha. He removed to Lorain County 1827, opened an Elyria practice, edited the Ohio Atlas Whig newspaper there, and removed to Cleveland in 1834.

narrative_blocks.header: Married a Suffield Ohio neighbor in 1830
narrative_blocks.body: Frederick married Eliza Burrall in September 1830 — daughter of Jabez and Mary Robbins Burrall of Suffield Ohio. Eight children followed, including Eliza Whittlesey Cowles, mother of botanist Henry Chandler Cowles.

narrative_blocks.header: He counted the city’s liquor sellers
narrative_blocks.body: Five reformers met at the Old Stone Church in March 1836 and made him president of the Cleveland City Temperance Society, which sent a committee to count the trade. Its Statistics of Intemperance found ninety-nine places selling drink; by 1843 the society had fifteen hundred members and counted eight.

narrative_blocks.body: On 27 October 1837, at sixty-six, Stephen was run over by a carriage and his foot and leg were crushed. He went through the amputation without being held or tied to the table, and died two days later.

narrative_blocks.body: Stephen farmed at New Preston, kept a mill there and captained the town's militia company, and was remembered as a strong and courageous man.

narrative_blocks.body: Stephen married Anna Camp in May 1791 and had six children before her death in 1810. Susan Whittlesey married him in December 1811, a widower of forty, and bore three more before she died in 1823; Rachel Seymour gave him a last son, George, in 1825.

narrative_blocks.body: His eldest daughter, Sarah, married Philo Mills Wooster in September 1817, and in April 1820 her sister Ruth Ann married him too.

notable.notable_blurb: Founder of the Mother's Magazine

narrative_blocks.header: She started it in the Utica seminary house
narrative_blocks.body: She joined the new Maternal Association at Utica and offered to edit its magazine. The Mother’s Magazine came out from the winter of 1832 and went with her to New York; by 1837 it was printing ten thousand copies.

narrative_blocks.header: Pages for orphans and the poor
narrative_blocks.body: It was among the first periodicals of its kind in America — discipline, schooling, the care of small children — and it gave its own pages to orphans and to the children of the poor. Maternal Associations followed it into Europe.

narrative_blocks.header: She resigned rather than go commercial
narrative_blocks.body: In 1848 the association merged her magazine with a rival and wanted a more commercial tone. She resigned instead, and two years later started her own again with her son Henry, and kept it two years more.

narrative_blocks.header: A country schoolhouse, then Sarah Pierce’s
narrative_blocks.body: She went to the West Lane schoolhouse at Ridgefield as far as the eighth grade and then to Sarah Pierce’s academy at Litchfield. She taught school out in the Finger Lakes of New York, and that is where she met her husband.

narrative_blocks.header: Six of the seven came before Canandaigua
narrative_blocks.body: Six of her seven children were born while her husband had New Preston and then the Hartford asylum. Two she buried small — a son at birth in 1811 and Charles Chauncey at six in 1818. Emily, the last, came at Canandaigua.

narrative_blocks.header: A son washed overboard, bound for California
narrative_blocks.body: Charles Augustus, a navigator, was swept from the deck of the William G. Hackstaff on February 7, 1849, on the passage to California. He was in his mid-twenties.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brother was Peter Parley
narrative_blocks.body: The Goodriches left Ridgefield for Berlin, where her father took the church and she was chiefly schooled. Her brother Samuel wrote as Peter Parley; her sister Mary Ann was the one James Gates Percival read his verses to.

bio.title: Colonel
bio.extra_names: Brevet Brigadier General, U.S. Volunteers
bio.photo_notes: Civil War portrait; Brevet Brigadier General U.S. Volunteers (Mar 13, 1865); Chief Quartermaster Army of Georgia under Sherman.
bio.bio_blurb: Chief quartermaster of the Army of Georgia

death.cause: Died at Saint Elizabeth Hospital near Washington DC. (Findagrave gives Aug 8, 1873; Whittlesey Genealogy #824 records Aug 10, 1873 — minor 2-day source discrepancy.)

burial.plot_notes: Evergreen Cemetery, Owego Tioga County NY (his wife Maria Louise's family region). Buried beside wife Maria Louise Sweet Whittlesey (d. 1878).

notable.notable_blurb: Army of Georgia quartermaster; family genealogist

education.dates: read law; admitted to the bar 19 July 1845

military_service.unit: Volunteer Michigan Regiments → 1st Division 20th Army Corps (Sherman's Army of the Cumberland / Army of Georgia)
military_service.notes: Instructor to volunteer Michigan regiments at Fort Wayne Oct 31, 1861. Captain and assistant quartermaster (1861). Division quartermaster, 1st Div 20th Army Corps under Gen. A. S. Williams. Brevet Brigadier General appointment Mar 13, 1865. Chief Quartermaster Army of Georgia (Col. rank, Aug 5, 1865). Chief Quartermaster Dept. of Mississippi (Sept 13, 1866). Chief Quartermaster Freedman's Bureau (through 1870). Mustered out July 17, 1867 with rank of brigadier by brevet.

institutions.institution_blurb: Studied law at Yale; bar admission Jul 19, 1845.

cross_connections.display_label: compiled the Talcott Pedigree in 1876, twenty-one years later
wrote the 1849 Life of Thomas Hooker six years before his own Whittlesey genealogy
took the Fifth Michigan out of Fort Wayne six weeks before him
was North Carolina's Confederate chief quartermaster in 1865

narrative_blocks.header: He held millions and nobody ever asked
narrative_blocks.body: Through every year of the war he was the custodian of millions of dollars of public money and property passing through his own department. His corps commander wrote that his fidelity in that branch of the service was unsurpassed.

narrative_blocks.header: A county desk to the Army of Georgia
narrative_blocks.body: In the summer of 1861 he left the Register of Deeds office at Wayne County to take a captaincy. By August 1865 he was chief quartermaster of the Army of Georgia with a colonel’s rank, and a brevet brigadier before he was done.

narrative_blocks.header: From army supply to the city’s books
narrative_blocks.body: His last army work was supplying the Freedmen’s Bureau, and he went on doing it three years after he was mustered out. In 1870 Washington made him comptroller of the city — the District’s accounts, not the army’s.

narrative_blocks.header: Detroit knew him before the war did
narrative_blocks.body: He went out to Detroit in 1854 and was, his commander said, among the foremost young men of the place — the Young Men’s Society, the fire department, the militia companies, the schools. Few were more esteemed there.

narrative_blocks.header: A magazine for mothers, and one child
narrative_blocks.body: Before Detroit he published his mother’s magazines — Abigail Whittelsey’s Mother’s Magazine, the first American periodical for mothers. He married a widow in 1866. They had one child and it died in infancy.

narrative_blocks.header: He put the family in order himself
narrative_blocks.body: He gathered the material and wrote up the Whittlesey family history that was published in 1855. The man who did the later book said it had proved invaluable to him, and that only someone who had tried it knew what it cost.

narrative_blocks.header: None knew him but to love him
narrative_blocks.body: He died at the military hospital near Washington in August 1873, at fifty-one. The Detroit Post printed his corps commander’s notice of it, which closed on an old line: “None knew him but to love him. None named him but to praise.”

quotes.text: None knew him but to love him; none named him but to praise.
quotes.context: Eulogy by his corps commander, Gen. A. S. Williams, published in the Detroit Post upon Henry Martyn's death August 1873.

sources.label: Whittlesey Genealogy #824: studied law at Yale, admitted to the bar 19 July 1845; published his mother’s magazines; assistant secretary of the Whittlesey Association; to Detroit 1854; instructor to the volunteer Michigan regiments at Fort Wayne 31 Oct 1861; chief quartermaster, Army of Georgia, 5 Aug 1865; Department of Mississippi 13 Sept 1866; Freedmen’s Bureau; mustered out 17 July 1867; comptroller of Washington 1870. One child, died in infancy

people.research_notes:
Col. Henry Martyn Whittlesey (Whittlesey Genealogy entry #824, son of HD0102 Samuel Whittlesey + I00434 Abigail Goodrich Whittlesey). b. Aug 12, 1821 Hartford Conn.; d. Aug 8, 1873 (Findagrave) or Aug 10, 1873 (Whittlesey #824) at Saint Elizabeth Hospital near Washington DC, age 51. DIFFERENT person from HD3786 Henry Martyn Cowles (b. 1840s, Sam's father of botanist Henry Chandler) — same first/middle name, common 19th-century naming. HOOKER LINEAGE (gen 8): Thomas Hooker → Mary Hooker → Rev. Roger Newton (m. 1644) → Samuel Newton (b. 1646 Hartford) → Roger Newton (b. 1685 Milford, H00044) → Susannah Newton (b. 1716, H00142) → Roger Newton Whittlesey (b. 1754, HD0097) → Samuel Whittlesey (b. 1775, HD0102) → Henry Martyn (HD3790). EDUCATION: Yale College (studied law); admitted to the bar July 19, 1845. EARLY CAREER: Published his mother's Mother's Magazine (and later Magazine for Mothers — see I00434 Abigail). Assistant secretary of the Whittlesey Association. Removed to Detroit Mich. 1854. CIVIL WAR: Instructor to volunteer Michigan regiments at Fort Wayne Oct 31, 1861. Captain and assistant quartermaster. Division quartermaster, 1st Division, 20th Army Corps (Sherman's Army of the Cumberland → Army of Georgia) under Gen. A. S. Williams. Brevet Brigadier General USV appointment Mar 13, 1865 — for faithful and meritorious service. Aug 5, 1865 Chief Quartermaster Army of Georgia with rank of Colonel. Sept 13, 1866 Chief Quartermaster Department of Mississippi. Chief Quartermaster Freedman's Bureau through 1870. Mustered out July 17, 1867 with rank of brigadier by brevet. POST-WAR: 1870 appointed Comptroller of the city of Washington — held until death Aug 8, 1873. GENEALOGICAL WORK: 'devoted much of his leisure time during several years next prior to his decease in collecting information and writing up the family history, published in 1855, which has proved invaluable to the compiler' (Whittlesey #824). His 1855 family history became foundational for Charles B. Whittelsey's 1898 expanded Whittlesey Genealogy. MARRIAGE: m. July 12, 1866 Maria Louisa Johnson née Sweet (I00446) — widow of Benjamin Johnson Esq. of Oswego NY. She was b. Mar 5, 1822 Salem NY (Washington Co.), dau. of Ezra Smith Sweet (b. New Bedford Mass. Jun 3, 1796, d. Oswego NY Oct 16, 1869) and Janet McLaren Clow (b. Shaghticoke NY Mar 13, 1798, d. Nov 22, 1881). ONE CHILD died in infancy. BURIAL: Evergreen Cemetery Owego Tioga Co. NY (CEM276). His wife Maria Louise died 1878 and was buried beside him. EULOGY by Gen. A. S. Williams in Detroit Post Aug 12, 1873: 'To those who lived in Detroit twelve years ago, General Whittelsey was well known as among the foremost young men in most public enterprises... so conscientious in the discharge of even minor duties of office; so punctilious in the discharge of all social courtesies; a friend so loving, generous, and noble, a man so full of the attributes of honor and honesty... None knew him but to love him; none named him but to praise.' Photo: https://res.cloudinary.com/dc5clrqtw/image/upload/v1778353213/colhenrywhittlesey_irllvb.jpg Sources: Whittlesey Genealogy #824; FindAGrave 82189268; Adjutant-General's Report 1896; Detroit Post Aug 12, 1873 (eulogy).

narrative_blocks.header: From this hour, he is risen
narrative_blocks.body: He was five and a half when he died at New Preston in April 1818. The family book keeps what somebody wrote afterwards: “when my fond heart would inquire, Where have you laid him? — from within and without proclaims, He is risen.”

quotes.text: Till now my thoughts had too often found a lodgment in the cold grave; but from this hour, when my fond heart would inquire, 'Where have you laid him?' from within and without proclaims: 'He is risen.'

narrative_blocks.header: She was eighteen and went west
narrative_blocks.body: She married James William Tillman in 1833 and went out to Detroit with him, where he kept a store. She was the fourth of her father’s seven children, and the first of them to leave Connecticut for good.

narrative_blocks.header: Dead at thirty-two in Detroit
narrative_blocks.body: She died on 26 January 1848 and lies at Elmwood in Detroit. Her husband outlived her nineteen years and is buried beside her; her son William was thirteen when she died.

death.cause: Washed overboard from the William G. Hackstaff (California-bound) during a storm while serving as navigator. Per Whittlesey Genealogy #825: 'The guards of the ship were low, and, in giving some order to furl in sail in a storm, he himself was washed overboard, Feb. 7, 1849.'

narrative_blocks.header: He left his studies when his father died
narrative_blocks.body: His father died suddenly in 1842 and he judged it best to give up his studies for an active life. A berth on one of the great New York merchant ships was reckoned a favour to be granted, and he got one.

narrative_blocks.header: Calcutta, China, and Rotterdam
narrative_blocks.body: He made several voyages out of New York before he was twenty-five — one to Calcutta, two or three to China, and one to Rotterdam. Then he was appointed navigator of the William G. Hackstaff, bound for California.

narrative_blocks.header: The guards of the ship were low
narrative_blocks.body: In a storm he gave an order to furl sail, and went over the side. The family book blames the low guards of the ship and gives the date, 7 February 1849. He was twenty-five, and his mother outlived him nine years.

people.research_notes: Charles Augustus Whittlesey (Whittlesey #825). b. Oct 20, 1823 Hartford Conn.; d. Feb 7, 1849 at sea — washed overboard from the William G. Hackstaff during a storm en route to California (Gold Rush era). Sixth child of HD0102 Samuel Whittlesey + I00434 Abigail Goodrich. Per Whittlesey #825: 'At the time of his father's sudden death (1842) he thought it best to leave his studies and follow a more active life. At that time to obtain a position on one of the great merchant ships of New York was considered a great favor. He went on several voyages — one to Calcutta, two or three to China, and one to Rotterdam. He was appointed navigator of the William G. Hackstaff, bound for California. The guards of the ship were low, and, in giving some order to furl in sail in a storm, he himself was washed overboard, Feb. 7, 1849.' Hooker descent gen 8. Source: Whittlesey Genealogy #825.

narrative_blocks.header: A soul of fidelity with few equals
narrative_blocks.body: The Whittlesey book, which is sparing with people, stopped over her: a soul of fidelity, courage, religious strength and devotion that has few equals. She was the last of her father’s seven children.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-three years, and no children
narrative_blocks.body: She married Lucius Curtis in June 1848 and they had no children. She followed him through Woodbury, Colchester, Wisconsin and Iowa, and home to Hartford; he died in 1901 and she in 1907, in the town they were both born near.

bio.title: Colonel
bio.bio_blurb: Detroit merchant; first furniture store in Michigan

parents.father_research_notes: Family of Tillman (vitals not given in Whittlesey #823).

narrative_blocks.header: The first furniture store in Michigan
narrative_blocks.body: He was a Detroit merchant more than thirty years and had started the first furniture store ever opened in the state. By the end he had outlived nearly every man who was in business in Detroit when he began.

narrative_blocks.header: Two in the morning, after a few days
narrative_blocks.body: He was ill only a few days. He died at two o’clock in the morning of 7 March 1867 at his own house, and the Detroit paper called him one of the oldest and most prominent citizens of the city.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a minister’s daughter east
narrative_blocks.body: He married Elizabeth Ely Whittelsey in 1833, daughter of the man who had run the Hartford asylum for the deaf, and took her west to Detroit. She died there at thirty-two, and he lived nineteen years after her.

people.research_notes: Col. James William Tillman. Two marriages: m1 Elizabeth Whittlesey Tillman (HD3794) — son Maj. William Tillman (HD3849) + daughter Katherine Whittelsey Tillman Bull (HD3850). m2 Martha Ann Conant (b.1823, d.1903; later remarried surname Williams after James's 1867 death) — son Harry Conant Tillman (b.1851 Detroit, d.1895 Detroit) not built as separate entry, non-Hooker.

parents.father_research_notes: Eleazier Curtis, descended from Thomas Curtis of Wethersfield Conn. through grandfather Zebulon Curtis (son of Thomas Curtis of Farmington, captain under Col. Wolcott, m. Mary Goodrich 1703). Father of Daniel B. Oviatt of Milford Conn. line per Whittlesey #826.
parents.mother_research_notes: Amanda Steele of New Hartford Conn., descended from John Steele of Hartford and Governor William Bradford of Plymouth Mass. Per Whittlesey Genealogy #826.

career.notes: Eight-year pastorate.
Twelve-year pastorate; 'his health failing, he made a short tour abroad — in England, Scotland, and the continent.'
Seven years as acting pastor.
Resided in Hartford Conn. and engaged in preaching and literary work.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept a school at Rochester first
narrative_blocks.body: Out of Williams in 1835 he went to Rochester in New York and taught a private school there for several years before he settled on the ministry at all. Andover came after that, not before.

narrative_blocks.header: He followed a fifty-year pastorate
narrative_blocks.body: His first pastorate was Woodbury, where he took the pulpit from Dr. Andrew, who had kept it half a century. His health broke and he resigned it. Eleven years at Colchester went the same way, closing in 1868.

narrative_blocks.header: Ripon offered; he would not take it
narrative_blocks.body: He went west for his health and preached at the Ripon College church in Wisconsin, which offered him the permanent pastorate. He declined it, took Lyons in Iowa for five years, and gave that up for the same reason.

narrative_blocks.header: He finished the book and then died
narrative_blocks.body: He stopped preaching about 1895 and turned to writing. He had just finished the manuscript of The Immortal Life, argued from the scientific side, and sent it to a New York house, when he died at the Hartford hospital at eighty-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: The last of a large family
narrative_blocks.body: He outlived every one of his brothers and sisters. One of them, Fanny, had married the Rev. Dr. John P. Gulliver, who preached at Norwich and afterwards at Chicago and was a name in his denomination.

narrative_blocks.header: Governor Bradford on his mother’s side
narrative_blocks.body: Through his mother, Amanda Steele of New Hartford, he came down from John Steele of Hartford and from Governor Bradford of Plymouth. His father’s line went back to Thomas Curtis of Wethersfield.

people.research_notes:
Rev. Lucius Curtis. b. Nov 16, 1812 Torrington Conn.; d. unknown. Son of Eleazier Curtis (descended from Thomas Curtis of Wethersfield Conn. through grandfather Zebulon Curtis, son of Capt. Thomas Curtis of Farmington who served under Col. Wolcott, m. Mary Goodrich 1703) and Amanda Steele of New Hartford Conn. (descended from John Steele of Hartford and Governor William Bradford of Plymouth Mass.). EDUCATION: Williams College 1835; theology 2 years Andover Mass.; 1 year New Haven Seminary. MINISTRY ARC: Pastor First Congregational Church Woodbury Conn. 8 years (~1838-1846). Pastor 'long church' in Colchester Conn. 12 years (~1846-1858); health failing, took 'a short tour abroad — in England, Scotland, and the continent.' Acting pastor Ripon Wis. and Lyons Iowa 7 years (~1858-1865). Returned to Hartford Conn. and engaged in preaching and literary work. MARRIAGE: m. Jun 28, 1848 Emily Chauncey Whittlesey (HD3796). No children. Note: Curtis is NOT a Hooker descendant (Bradford/Steele line, not Hooker). His ancestry includes Mayflower (William Bradford) and early Hartford (John Steele) connections. Charles Egbert Whittlesey (Whittlesey Genealogy #384). b. Mar 1, 1802 New Jersey; d. Sept 4, 1824 (location not specified) age 22. BOOK CONFLICT: per Whittlesey #384, 'After his father had moved to the West, the son entered the army; he served in the Crimean War, with much valor and distinction. He died Sept. 4, 1824.' This is anachronistic — the Crimean War was 1853-1856, almost thirty years after his death. Possible reconciliations: (1) book conflates with another Charles Whittlesey of similar name; (2) book misnames the conflict (could have been local Indian conflict on the Indiana frontier); (3) date is wrong. Recorded as the book has it, with the discrepancy noted. Hooker descent gen 7. Source: Whittlesey Genealogy #384.

narrative_blocks.body: She married at thirty-eight and went out to Illinois. She died at Bunker Hill in Macoupin County in November 1845, three years after her sister Lucy Ann died in that same small town. They had one child and it died in infancy.

narrative_blocks.header: She married the principal at nineteen
narrative_blocks.body: Israel Newell was running Kimball Union when he married her at Cornish Flat in August 1824. She was nineteen and he twenty-nine. His health took the school from him eleven years later and they went home to his farm in Maine.

narrative_blocks.header: A widow for twenty-seven years
narrative_blocks.body: He died at Durham in 1846 and she lived on until 1873, dying out at Minneapolis. She was brought back to Rochester and buried at Mount Hope, in the same ground as her sister Caroline.

narrative_blocks.header: Six winters teaching before he came of age
narrative_blocks.body: He worked his father’s farm at Durham through the summers and taught school six winters running before he came of age, and fitted himself for college in the middle of it. He entered Bowdoin as a sophomore.

narrative_blocks.header: Confessedly the foremost man of his class
narrative_blocks.body: That is the phrase the account uses. He took his degree in 1819, spent two years at Andover, and had charge of an academy on Nantucket for a year before New Hampshire sent for him.

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve hundred pupils in thirteen years
narrative_blocks.body: He was made principal of Kimball Union at Plainfield in 1822 and gave it thirteen years. Twelve hundred young people passed through his hands there and he fitted about two hundred of them for college.

narrative_blocks.header: A sermon a week through all of it
narrative_blocks.body: He preached the whole time he was teaching and the whole time he was farming, about a sermon a week by the reckoning — well studied, well arranged, clear, instructive and affecting, said the man who wrote him up.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave up the work he loved
narrative_blocks.body: His health broke and he had to give up the school in 1835, the employment he was fitted for and loved. He went home to Durham and farmed until he died there in 1846, at fifty. He had been feeble most of his life.

bio.title: Major
bio.bio_blurb: Army paymaster, then a Louisville banker

military_service.notes: Per Whittlesey Genealogy #1781 and Courier-Journal obituary 1918. Branch: United States Army; Role: Paymaster.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixteen hundred days of army payrolls
narrative_blocks.body: From September 1861 to January 1866 he carried Union payrolls — better than sixteen hundred days of soldiers’ wages, counted out and signed for. He was twenty-seven when the war began and thirty-one when he finished.

narrative_blocks.header: He married into Louisville in wartime
narrative_blocks.body: He married Mary Steele at Louisville in June 1863, out of a family well known in the city, while the war was still on and Kentucky was still deciding what it was. He stayed connected to the place for the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: Wife’s sisters married a financier and a soldier
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Steele’s sisters married Charles H. Petit, who headed the Robinson-Petit Company, and Col. Sanford C. Kellogg of the United States army. The three husbands were a banker, a merchant and a regular officer.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-five years a Louisville man
narrative_blocks.body: He came to Louisville about 1873 and was a prominent banker of the city for a score of years. He died there at eighty-three in his apartment on South Fourth Street, after an illness of only a few days.

narrative_blocks.header: Four daughters came from four cities
narrative_blocks.body: Four daughters survived him, and the paper gave where each was living — Cincinnati, Montclair in New Jersey, Larchmont in New York, Dallas in Texas. One reached Louisville the day after he died.

narrative_blocks.header: He was thirteen when his mother died
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth Ely died at Detroit in January 1848 and he was thirteen. His father lived another nineteen years; the Tillman children born after her death were not hers.

Half-brother of Harry Conant Tillman (b.1851 Detroit, d.1895 Detroit, not built — non-Hooker m2 son of father I00448 + Martha Ann Conant). NOTE: a different William Tillman (c.1834 Milford Delaware) was the Black mariner who recaptured the schooner S.J. Waring July 1861 — coincidence of name only.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at Santa Barbara at twenty-one
narrative_blocks.body: She married James Henry Bull at Santa Barbara in March 1878, a naval officer who had gone through Annapolis at seventeen. She was born at Detroit and died at Santa Barbara sixty years after the wedding.

narrative_blocks.header: She lies at Arlington, not at Elmwood
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother and grandfather are at Elmwood in Detroit and her father’s people in Connecticut. She was buried at Arlington, on her husband’s commission, four thousand miles from where she was born.

narrative_blocks.header: Six women in engineering, studying alone
narrative_blocks.body: When Carolyn went to work at Northwestern Engineering in the early 1960s, as an associate dean's secretary, the school had six women students, each studying alone and some sure they were failing physics because they were women. She put them in the same class so they had someone to work with.

narrative_blocks.header: Career Day for Girls, from 1971
narrative_blocks.body: In 1971 Carolyn started an open house for grade-school girls, now Career Day for Girls. Twenty came the first year, and the only trouble was that no woman administrator or professor could be found for the panel; by 2020 it drew 139.

narrative_blocks.header: Women in Tech, then a SWE chapter
narrative_blocks.body: With too few women at first for a Society of Women Engineers chapter, Carolyn started a group called Women in Tech, and by 1976 there were enough for a chapter. She also built a course introducing younger students to computers and helped design the EXCEL program.

narrative_blocks.header: Her children ask if she can say no
narrative_blocks.body: Carolyn's children ask whether she knows how to say no; sometimes she does not. She has led the Evanston Woman's Board of the Northwestern Settlement House, tutored readers, written an anti-bullying program for an Evanston school, and in 2013 won Northwestern's Alumni Service Award.

narrative_blocks.header: She meant to go into the ministry
narrative_blocks.body: Carolyn first wanted to study for the ministry, less for the sermons than to work with people. She took a religion degree at Mount Holyoke and, working full time while raising a daughter, a master's in counseling at Northwestern in 1969.

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve strangers for dinner
narrative_blocks.body: When the Northwestern Alumni Association began its Dinner with 12 Strangers, Carolyn and Gil opened their Evanston home to students, who talked journalism and politics and left trading contact details. Meeting as strangers and leaving as friends, she said, really worked.

notable.notable_blurb: Founder of computer science at Northwestern

career.notes: First academic posting after MIT Ph.D.

career.organization: Case Institute of Technology (later Case Western Reserve)

career.role: Professor of Industrial Engineering, then founding chair Department of Computer Science
career.notes: Joined industrial engineering 1960; proposed and chaired the new Department of Computer Science from 1971; director of the Artificial Intelligence Laboratory; also appointments in linguistics and psychology in Weinberg College. Retired 2000.

cross_connections.display_label: built the arithmetic of the ORDVAC and ILLIAC computers at Illinois

narrative_blocks.header: He started computer science at Northwestern
narrative_blocks.body: When Gil came to Northwestern in 1960, computers filled whole rooms and the university had no computer science department, so he and a few colleagues taught the first computer courses out of industrial engineering. He proposed the department, saw it founded in 1971, chaired it, and hired its first faculty.

narrative_blocks.header: Teaching a computer to read
narrative_blocks.body: Gil directed Northwestern's Artificial Intelligence Laboratory and held appointments in linguistics and psychology, the fields that shaped his work on how a machine might understand language. It became his book, Computer Processing of Natural Language.

narrative_blocks.header: Navy officer, chemist, psychologist, engineer
narrative_blocks.body: Gil served as a Navy engineering officer from 1943 to 1946, took his MIT degree in chemical engineering in 1944, a master's in psychology at Springfield College in 1948 and an MIT doctorate in 1950, then taught at Michigan, Tufts and Case before Northwestern, where he stayed until 2000.

narrative_blocks.header: He raised Sarah alone, then met Carolyn
narrative_blocks.body: Gil's first wife, Dorsey Parker, whom he married at Cleveland, died while their daughter Sarah was small, and he raised her alone until he met Carolyn Hall. They married in 1970, added Catherine and Margaret to the family, and were together more than forty-six years.

narrative_blocks.header: A trombone, after his father's trumpet
narrative_blocks.body: Gil's father was a successful trumpet player around Boston, and Gil was a musician all his life, in his later years playing trombone with the North Shore Concert Band and the New Horizons Band.

narrative_blocks.header: Summers on the water at Hingham
narrative_blocks.body: Gil grew up with his brother Robert in Belmont, Massachusetts, and spent his boyhood summers on the ocean at Hingham. In Evanston he served on the City Mental Health Board and with the United Way of the North Shore.

sources.short: Northwestern McCormick obituary Jan 26 2017; Daily Northwestern Jan 26 2017

people.research_notes: Gilbert 'Gil' Krulee. b. circa 1924 (age 92 at death Jan 18, 2017). Professor emeritus of electrical engineering and computer science at Northwestern University. U.S. Navy engineering officer 1943-1946 during WWII. MIT B.S. chemical engineering; Springfield College M.S. psychology 1948; MIT Ph.D. industrial engineering 1950. Briefly assistant professor University of Michigan, then assistant professor psychology at Tufts, then associate professor Case Institute of Technology (INST044). Joined Northwestern in 1960 in industrial engineering. Attended the 1969 First International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence in Washington. Proposed creating Northwestern's Department of Computer Science (INST124); department established 1971 with him as chair, hiring its founding faculty. Also director of the Northwestern Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. Appointments in linguistics and psychology in Weinberg College. Author of Computer Processing of Natural Language (1991). Retired 2000. Fellow at Lindgren Hall (science and engineering residential college, predecessor of Slivka Residential College). Played trombone in community ensembles; served on City Mental Health Board and United Way of the North Shore. m. Carolyn Hall (HD3877) — 'beloved wife of 46 years' at his death. Three daughters: Catherine (HD3878), Sarah Krulee Harms (HD3879), Margaret (HD3880). Four grandchildren named in obituary: Rebekah Carlyn Krulee, Max Charles Harms, Douglas Edward Harms, Myron Paul Jackson. Memorial service Alice Millar Chapel Jan 29, 2017. Source: Northwestern McCormick News Jan 23 2017; Daily Northwestern Jan 26 2017.

narrative_blocks.header: Three children with Margaret Catharine Fern
narrative_blocks.body: William Alonzo Root married Margaret Catharine Fern about 1882; she was born August 1852 in New York. Their three documented children were Edgar Francis Root (1883-1941, born Buffalo New York and died Bluefield West Virginia), Ethel M. Root (born 1885), and Margaret E. Root. Edgar Francis's career took him from Buffalo to West Virginia — a substantial geographic move from the family's Ashtabula County Ohio center.

narrative_blocks.header: Ohio birth, Ontario death; eldest of five
narrative_blocks.body: William Alonzo Root was the eldest of his father William Ezekiel Root's five sons born in Austinburg, Ashtabula County Ohio in the late 1850s and early 1860s. The five brothers — William Alonzo, E.L., E.W., S.L., and A.A. — formed an unusually compressed 1859-1861 birth cluster. William Alonzo eventually moved north into Ontario Canada, dying in Wentworth at age about seventy-one in 1930.

narrative_blocks.body: Of the six Blakeslee children born after her 1810 marriage, Sophronia wed her second cousin Isaac Lorenzo Stiles, and a grandson, Anson Blakeslee Clinton, took a third cousin from the same Stiles line. The North Haven families kept folding back into one another.

narrative_blocks.header: Descended from New Haven Colony's first governor
narrative_blocks.body: Mabel Eaton descended from Theophilus Eaton (about 1590-1658) — co-founder of New Haven Colony in 1638 and its first governor for two decades. The Eaton lineage placed her among the small group of Connecticut Hooker descendants who carried New Haven Colony founding-family ancestry alongside their Hartford-Hooker line. The combined Eaton-Hooker descent represented the merger of the two principal seventeenth-century Connecticut colonial-founder lineages.

narrative_blocks.header: Named for aunt Mabel Stiles Frost
narrative_blocks.body: Mabel was given the same first name as her maternal aunt Mabel Stiles Frost — the 'father of music at North Haven' Titus Frost's wife — preserving the family name across the Stiles-Eaton lines of the late-eighteenth-century North Haven community. Her grandmother Mabel Clark Stiles had been the original Mabel; the name passed through three generations of the family.

narrative_blocks.header: Baptized 1783 at St. John's Church North Haven
narrative_blocks.body: Mabel was baptized in 1783 at St. John's Episcopal Church North Haven Connecticut. No birth date was recorded for her or for her siblings — the North Haven family's documentation for this generation depends on baptismal records rather than birth registers. Her death date is not documented in available sources.

narrative_blocks.header: Mother died the year after his birth
narrative_blocks.body: Solomon Eaton was the youngest of his mother Elizabeth Stiles Eaton's seven children; she died in 1792, the year after Solomon's 1791 baptism. He grew up motherless from his earliest infancy — a common eighteenth-century late-childbearing fate for women bearing seven children across two decades of their reproductive years. His father Timothy Eaton was left widowed with the seven young children.

narrative_blocks.header: Descended from New Haven Colony's first governor
narrative_blocks.body: Solomon descended from Theophilus Eaton (about 1590-1658) — co-founder of New Haven Colony in 1638 and its first governor for two decades. The Eaton lineage placed him alongside his elder sister Mabel Eaton among Connecticut Hooker descendants carrying both Hartford-Hooker and New Haven Colony founding-family ancestry. The two principal seventeenth-century Connecticut colonial-founder lineages merged in this branch of the family.

narrative_blocks.header: She brought the Apostle Eliot into the line
narrative_blocks.body: Charlotte Frost descended through her mother from John Eliot, who preached to the Indians, and from the Wyllys family of Hartford. Her eldest son was christened William Eliot Goodyear.

narrative_blocks.header: Tuttle, Hooker, Stiles and Willett on one side
narrative_blocks.body: Her father Samuel Frost's line carried all four of them. Her mother was Ruth Merriman, her grandparents Titus and Mabel Stiles Frost, and she married William Bradley Goodyear in May 1830.

narrative_blocks.header: She died at her son-in-law's Brooklyn house
narrative_blocks.body: Charlotte Goodyear was widowed in 1889 and died on 9 February 1891 at Colonel Crafts's home in Brooklyn. Her daughter Lizzie died on that same date forty-two years afterwards.

bio.bio_blurb: New Haven merchant and family genealogist

narrative_blocks.header: He raised the family monument at Hamden
narrative_blocks.body: William Bradley Goodyear put it up some years before he died, and had an inscription to Governor Stephen Goodyear cut on it. He set another tablet to the governor in Center Church at New Haven.

narrative_blocks.header: The family genealogy rests on his notes
narrative_blocks.body: He worked the life of Governor Stephen Goodyear out of the Colonial Records, and the documents he gathered carried the compilers of the family history through. He belonged to the New Haven Historical Society.

narrative_blocks.header: Cortland trade, then New Haven property
narrative_blocks.body: He left Hamden for Cortland in New York soon after marrying and traded there successfully for years. In middle life he came back to New Haven and put his money into real estate. He crossed to California in 1850 and again in 1875.

career.organization: Federal boundary survey, California and Mexico

military_service.unit: Second Regiment, Connecticut Volunteers ('the Grays'), company of Maj. C. E. Walter Osborn
military_service.notes: Served with the Grays in General Terry's Second Regiment. Later attempted Navy enlistment but rejected (lost portion of one finger). Sutler at Grapevine Point conscript camp.

cross_connections.display_label: crossed the plains a year later with an ox team, bound for Oregon
commanded the Connecticut regiment he scouted for in 1861

narrative_blocks.header: He rode Atlantic to Pacific in 1852
narrative_blocks.body: Twenty-one years old, he started overland for California in 1852 and rode the whole way from Atlantic to Pacific. He stayed eight years through the gold rush, among the old emigrants, mountaineers and scouts.

narrative_blocks.header: Lost finger barred him from Navy enlistment
narrative_blocks.body: Back from California he went out in 1861 with the New Haven Greys under Major Walter Osborn, scouting for General Alfred Terry. The Navy later refused him: he had lost part of a finger along the way.

narrative_blocks.header: He sang thirty years in the choir
narrative_blocks.body: He sang in the choir of the Second Congregational Church at Fair Haven for nearly thirty years, and left it only weeks before he died of Bright's disease in June 1881, at fifty.

narrative_blocks.header: He surveyed the Mexican boundary
narrative_blocks.body: He studied for an engineer's profession during his eight California years, and was employed by the federal government on the boundary line between California and Mexico.

narrative_blocks.header: The largest majority the town had given
narrative_blocks.body: He held offices at New Haven and East Haven and carried real weight in both. The Assembly seat came on the biggest majority the town had ever returned, and he was a devoted Knight Templar.

narrative_blocks.header: He died with the book unfinished
narrative_blocks.body: His accounts of encounters with Indians were published with J. S. C. Abbott's works. At the end he was gathering the anecdotes of camp and mining life he had told his friends into a book of his own.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter married a Goodyear cousin
narrative_blocks.body: Two years after he died, Charlotte married Arthur Smith, grandson of Eliza Goodyear Smith. Both were great-grandchildren of Andrew Goodyear, so Goodyear blood reached their children twice.

Jun 17, 1881 Fair Haven CT age 50 of Bright's disease per New Haven obituary June 18, 1881. Buried Central Burying Grounds (CEM289), Hamden CT — interment in Centerville. Eldest son of Charlotte Lorraine Frost Goodyear (HD3913) and William Bradley Goodyear (I00514). Started overland for California in 1852, making the entire trip from Atlantic to Pacific on horseback through 'the wild and trackless West' per obituary. Stayed eight years in CA through the gold rush, becoming familiar with mining camps and emigrants; studied engineering and surveyed the California-Mexico boundary for the federal government. Returned to CT and served the Civil War with General Terry's Second Regiment (the 'Grays') under Maj. C. E. Walter Osborn. Later tried Navy enlistment, rejected for losing part of one finger. Sutler at Grapevine Point conscript camp Fair Haven; after the war briefly in the oyster business. Prominent in East Haven politics, represented the town in the Connecticut General Assembly. Member Second Congregational Church (sang in the choir for nearly 30 years, retiring weeks before death); prominent Free Mason of Adelphi Lodge F. & A. M. Per obituary: 'He had a checkered life, and in his composition there was an element of the adventurous... He was pre-eminently a good story teller and always found prompt and responsive listeners. He was ever free handed.' m. 1864 Nellie Luranda Murray (I00515, 1845-1877). Per 1881 obituary: 'his wife died a few years ago, and two daughters survive.' Only one documented daughter — Elizabeth Abbott Goodyear Dockendorff Levey (HD3917). The second daughter's name and dates are not in available source; entry not built pending further research. Gen 8 Hooker descendant via mother. Sources: New Haven obituary 1881; FindAGrave 16981280.

narrative_blocks.header: Brickmaker, postmaster, JP, state representative
narrative_blocks.body: Isaac Stiles built a multi-role public life in North Haven Connecticut — farmer and brick manufacturer, Justice of the Peace and Postmaster for many years, warden of St. John's Episcopal Church, and representative of North Haven in the Lower House of the Connecticut General Assembly in 1831. He 'held all important town offices' per the Stiles family book — typical of the local-elite figure who structured pre-Civil-War Connecticut town life.

narrative_blocks.header: Two young sons died 1832, probable epidemic
narrative_blocks.body: Two of Isaac Stiles's documented six children — Edward C. and William H. — both died in 1832. The shared death year strongly suggests an epidemic; 1832 was the year of the first North American cholera pandemic that reached Connecticut. Isaac himself died February 4, 1842 at age forty-nine, leaving widow Lois Cooper Stiles to live until 1872 — thirty years past him.

bio.title: Captain
bio.bio_blurb: North Haven brickmaker and Civil War captain

notable.notable_blurb: North Haven brickmaker and Civil War captain

career.notes: Per Stiles book #953: 'when eighteen years old went to Haddam, Conn., to take charge of a brick yard.'
Brick manufacturing business with his brother Isaac Lorenzo Stiles (Stiles book #950).
Independent militia company; the source of the title he carried for life. Chosen about the time of his 1845 marriage (Stiles book #953).
Three terms from 1855.
Resigned in August 1862 to enlist in Civil War.
Republican campaign marching company; drilled the men who volunteered in 1862.

military_service.rank: Captain (Co. K 15th CT Vol Inf, then Co. B 21st Veteran Reserve Corps)
military_service.unit: 15th Connecticut Volunteer Infantry, Co. K (commission dated Aug 1, 1862); then 21st Veteran Reserve Corps, Co. B (Dec 1863)
military_service.notes: Enlisted Aug 9, 1862 New Haven CT; elected Captain of Co. K, 15th Connecticut Volunteers (commission Aug 1, 1862). Engaged at the Battle of Fredericksburg (December 1862, BTL026), at Edenton Road, Providence Church, and skirmishes near Norfolk Virginia. Honorable discharge for ill health Aug 17, 1863. Returned to service December 1863 as Captain of Co. B, 21st Regiment Veteran Reserve Corps, assigned to Providence Rhode Island as Post Commandant. In March 1864 removed with his company to Albany New York where he commanded the Rendezvous Camp. While there he organized, armed, and equipped the 192nd New York State Volunteers. Acting Post Commissary, Quartermaster, and command of two companies — these arduous duties broke his health again, and he resigned his commission Aug 1, 1865. On separation, his commands presented him with an inscribed sword, a heavy gold-headed cane, a costly jewelled watch and chain, field-glasses, and revolvers.

cross_connections.display_label: held a brigade at Suffolk through the same 1863 siege
marched with the Exeter Wide-Awakes in the same 1860 campaign
served in his regiment at Fredericksburg and was killed at Wyse Fork

narrative_blocks.header: His neighbours would not enlist without him
narrative_blocks.body: He held human life too dear to see it spent in war, and thought himself no leader. The young men of North Haven made it a condition of volunteering in 1862 that Hobart Stiles command them, and he gave way.

narrative_blocks.header: Captain of the Wide-Awakes in 1860
narrative_blocks.body: In 1860 he was made captain of the Wide-Awakes, the marching clubs got up for that year's political campaign. The men who learned to drill with him were the ones who volunteered two years later.

narrative_blocks.header: The Blackberry Raid finished his health
narrative_blocks.body: After Fredericksburg the regiment went to Newport News, then to the siege of Suffolk, then out on the Blackberry Raid, which disabled a great many men and accomplished nothing else. He asked to be relieved.

narrative_blocks.header: He went back in the invalid corps
narrative_blocks.body: Discharged for disability in 1863, he took a captaincy in the Veteran Reserve Corps, where men no longer fit to fight still served. At Albany he raised the 192nd New York; his commands gave him an inscribed sword when he left.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran a brick yard at eighteen
narrative_blocks.body: At eighteen he went to Haddam to take charge of a brick yard. He came home to join his brother Isaac Lorenzo in the business that became I. L. Stiles & Son, and stayed in it as far as his health allowed.

narrative_blocks.header: The town sent him to Hartford three times
narrative_blocks.body: Between 1845 and 1855 North Haven gave him most of its minor offices, then returned him to the Connecticut legislature for three terms. He was Selectman and Town Agent until he resigned in August 1862.

narrative_blocks.header: He put his affairs in order in 1877
narrative_blocks.body: He understood in the fall of 1877 that he was dying and put his business in order. He lived another eighteen months, and died at North Haven on 2 April 1879, aged fifty-four.

sources.label: The Stiles Family in America (BIB008) entry #953

people.research_notes: Capt. Henry Hobart Stiles. b. Oct 4, 1824 North Haven CT; d. April 1878 (day of month obscured by OCR in source as 'il of April'; could be 1st, 4th, 8th, or 11th — left as null pending verification) presumed at North Haven. Common school education. At age 18 (~1842) went to Haddam CT to take charge of a brick yard. Per Stiles book #953: 'The position developed the character that he afterwards sustained through life.' Returned home and associated with his brother Isaac Lorenzo Stiles (b. 1819) in business — the association becoming I. L. Stiles & Son, brickmakers. Lover of music and musician himself; home open to social entertainments. Chosen Captain of the North Haven Rifles — from which command the title 'Captain' (by which he was ever afterwards designated) derives, predating his Civil War commission. Held many minor town offices 1845-1855. Elected to the Connecticut Legislature 1855 and served three terms; then Selectman and Town Agent of North Haven until August 1862. CIVIL WAR: enlisted Aug 9, 1862 New Haven, elected Captain Co. K 15th CT Vol Inf (commission Aug 1, 1862); engaged at Fredericksburg (Dec 1862, BTL026), Edenton Road, Providence Church, and skirmishes near Norfolk Virginia. Honorable discharge for ill health Aug 17, 1863. December 1863: Captain Co. B, 21st Regiment Veteran Reserve Corps, assigned Providence Rhode Island as Post Commandant. March 1864 to Albany New York commanding the Rendezvous Camp, where he organized, armed, and equipped the 192nd New York State Volunteers. Resigned commission Aug 1, 1865 from arduous duties (Post Commissary, Quartermaster, command of two companies). His commands presented him on separation with an inscribed sword, heavy gold-headed cane, jewelled watch and chain, field-glasses, and revolvers. people.research_notes: Mabel Stiles Warner. b. Oct 26, 1878 N. Haven CT; d. Jan 6, 1925 Tucson Pima County AZ age 46 at her home 109 South Scott Street (her Tucson residence of the past 11 months). Body shipped back to New Haven by the Reilly Undertaking Company for burial at New Center Cemetery (CEM293) N. Haven. At her death survived by husband Charles Bennet Warner (I00530) and her sister Mrs. Edward Stiles ('E. I. Stiles' of Hartford from her father's 1907 obit — sibling not yet built pending identification); Mrs. Stiles was with Mabel at her Tucson death and accompanied the body home. Daughter of Dr. Isaac Wadsworth Stiles DDS (HD3938) and his first wife Margaret Ella Dickerman Stiles (I00527). m. 1899 at the home of her father Dr. I. W. Stiles in West Haven, Charles Bennet Warner (I00530). Wedding described contemporaneously: 'pretty home wedding' at 6 PM, bride in rich white satin with rare lace trimmings and tulle veil fastened with lilies of the valley (her bridal bouquet), Bertha Warner (groom's sister) as maid of honor in blue mousseline de soie over silk lining, Fichtl's orchestra playing bridal music, Rev. naming_inspiration.description: Middle name 'Lorenzo' carries his grandfather Isaac Lorenzo Stiles's middle name through three generations (Isaac Lorenzo Stiles → Dr. Isaac Wadsworth Stiles → Stanley Lorenzo Stiles). His uncle Frank Lorenzo Stiles (HD3939) also shares the same middle name.

narrative_blocks.header: Mother died about a year after his birth
narrative_blocks.body: Stanley Lorenzo Stiles was born in 1888 to Dr. Isaac Wadsworth Stiles DDS and his first wife Margaret Ella Dickerman Stiles. His mother died on October 21, 1889 — approximately one year after his birth — and the death may have been childbirth-related, though the cause is not specified in available records. He was raised by his father, who eventually remarried.

narrative_blocks.header: Lorenzo middle name carried through three generations
narrative_blocks.body: Stanley's middle name 'Lorenzo' was a family tradition carried across three generations: his grandfather Isaac Lorenzo Stiles, his uncle Frank Lorenzo Stiles, and Stanley himself all bore it. The repeated-middle-name pattern was characteristic of the late-nineteenth-century Stiles branch's deliberate genealogical naming conventions, preserving a distinctive ancestor's mark forward across the line.

narrative_blocks.header: Dual Hooker descent through both Stiles lines
narrative_blocks.body: Stanley Lorenzo Stiles inherited dual Hooker descent paths from his father Dr. Isaac Wadsworth Stiles — who himself was double-descended through both his father (Isaac Clark Stiles branch) and his mother (Mabel Stiles Frost branch). Both lines converge at Isaac Stiles born 1729 — making Stanley a doubly-rooted Hooker descendant on his paternal side alone, with the non-Hooker maternal side adding no additional paths.

narrative_blocks.header: Lived to about sixty-one, marriage not documented
narrative_blocks.body: Stanley Lorenzo Stiles died in 1949 at about age sixty-one. He was listed as 'Stanley L. Stiles surviving' in his father's February 1907 obituary at about age nineteen. Marriage and any descendants are not documented in available records.

bio.title: Colonel
bio.bio_blurb: Connecticut Militia colonel at North Haven

career.notes: Per Goodyear book #6852-1: 'Colonel Blakeslee was for many years an active and enthusiastic member of the Connecticut Militia.' Title 'Colonel' used throughout.

narrative_blocks.header: The militia title followed him all his life
narrative_blocks.body: He was an active member of the Connecticut Militia for many years and was known as Colonel in North Haven ever after. In his eighties he was still leading an energetic life in the town.

narrative_blocks.header: Three wives, and two of them cousins
narrative_blocks.body: Charlotte Pierpont married him in May 1835 and was dead by September 1836. Polly Goodyear followed a year later and lasted thirty-nine years. His third wife Cornelia was Polly's cousin, both great-granddaughters of Titus Bradley.

narrative_blocks.header: Charlotte was his fourth cousin once removed
narrative_blocks.body: Both descend from Rev. Samuel Hooker of Farmington - he through the son Samuel and the Stileses of North Haven, she through the daughter Mary and the Pierponts. Six generations on his side, five on hers.

narrative_blocks.header: Harriet at eighteen, Polly thirteen days later
narrative_blocks.body: Harriet was eighteen when she died on 12 September 1876. Polly followed her on the twenty-fifth, and the family set it down to grief. She had the lines of an Isaac Watts hymn on her lips at the end.

narrative_blocks.header: Ninety-four years, and born out of town
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Plymouth in August 1814 while the family was briefly away from North Haven, where every one of his brothers and sisters was born. He died there in February 1909 and lies in New Center Cemetery.

bio.bio_blurb: New Haven mother who died of grief

parents.father_research_notes: Daughter of Andrew Goodyear (1784-1819) and Patty Bradley (1782-1821), both of Hamden CT (Goodyear book #6852). Andrew d. when Polly was age 4; Patty d. when Polly was age 6. After parents' deaths, Polly lived with her grandmother Bradley in North Haven. Mother Patty's line traces through Titus + Lydia (Todd) Bradley of N. Haven; same Bradley line as HMB's second wife Cornelia Bronson Andrews (I00534), so Polly and Cornelia are Bradley cousins. Goodyear line also produced significant Hooker connections elsewhere — Polly's brother William Bradley Goodyear m. Charlotte Frost (Hooker descendant via H00448 Mabel Stiles Frost). NOTE: This Goodyear line does NOT directly descend from Thomas Hooker; Polly is non-Hooker spouse to HMB.

narrative_blocks.header: She died of grief days after her daughter
narrative_blocks.body: When her eighteen-year-old daughter Harriet died in September 1876, she followed less than two weeks later; her family laid her death to grief. They lie together in the New Haven cemetery.

narrative_blocks.header: Orphaned at six, raised by her grandmother
narrative_blocks.body: Both her parents were dead before she turned six, and her Bradley grandmother in New Haven raised her. A family chronicle remembered her as firm and gentle at once, with an unshakable faith.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brother founded Ogden, Utah
narrative_blocks.body: One of her brothers, Miles Goodyear, became a Western trapper who founded what is now Ogden, Utah, and married a daughter of a Ute chief — a far cry from the New Haven world she kept to all her life.

quotes.text: Jesus can make a dying bed feel soft as downy pillows are, while on His breast I'll lean my head, and breathe my life out sweetly there.
quotes.source: Reported as Polly Goodyear Blakeslee's last words in the Goodyear book #6852-1, drawn from Isaac Watts hymn 'Why should we start, and fear to die?'

people.research_notes: Polly Goodyear Blakeslee. b. Nov 20, 1815 Hamden CT; d. Sep 25, 1876 Connecticut age 60 — less than two weeks after her youngest daughter Harriet's Sep 12, 1876 death age 18; family attributed her death to grief. Buried New Center Cemetery (CEM293), N. Haven. Daughter of Andrew Goodyear (1784-1819) + Patty Bradley (1782-1821) of Hamden CT; orphaned by age 6 (father d. 1819, mother d. 1821), raised by grandmother Bradley in N. Haven. m. Sep 17, 1837 N. Haven (officiant Rev. Mr. Griggs) Col. Henry Merwin Blakeslee (HD3944). Goodyear book describes her as 'a woman of most beautiful character, in which were blended the best traits of the Goodyears and the Bradleys. With strength and firmness of purpose and speech, she was yet gentle and tender, and possessed an absolutely perfect faith in her Creator, and in the wisdom of His ways.' Four children all gen 8 Hooker (via HMB father): Theodore M. (HD3950, 1839-1901), Charlotte/Lottie (HD3951, 1844-1902), George (HD3952, b. 1850), Harriet (HD3953, 1857-1876 age 18 — preceded mother in death by 13 days). Her brother William Bradley Goodyear (1807-1889) m. Charlotte Frost (Hooker descendant via H00448 Mabel Stiles Frost) — so Polly herself is non-Hooker but Goodyear-Frost cross-marriages in next generation produced Hooker-descended Goodyear children (Eliza, William Eliot, Miles Herschel — all flagged for future Goodyear branch stages). Polly's miles-traveling brother Miles Morris Goodyear (1817-1849) founded Ogden Utah and married Pomona, daughter of Chief Pah-tete-nete of the Utahs. Sources: Goodyear book #6852-1; FindAGrave; CT vital records.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at forty-five, fathered twin sons at fifty-six
narrative_blocks.body: Theodore M. Blakeslee did not marry until February 9, 1885, age forty-five, when he wed Susan Anne 'Susie' Drake (1859-1933) at Middleborough Massachusetts. Their first daughter Hattie May was born ten months later in November 1885 but died age five in 1891. After their daughter Lottie was born in 1889, Theodore and Susan had twin sons Merwin Theodore Blakeslee and Miles Edwin Blakeslee on the same day, July 23, 1896 — Theodore was fifty-six.

narrative_blocks.header: Civil War veteran; body returned to North Haven
narrative_blocks.body: Theodore Blakeslee served as a Civil War veteran — specific unit and rank are not documented in surviving records, but his veteran status is confirmed. He died January 5, 1901 in New York City at age sixty-one. His body was returned to his Connecticut hometown of North Haven for burial at New Center Cemetery, where the Blakeslee-Stiles family clustered four generations of graves around the Stiles-Hooker line center.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at eighteen, to his second cousin
narrative_blocks.body: The wedding came three days past his eighteenth birthday, in August 1883, and the bride was kin — his grandmother and Charlotte's grandfather had been Goodyear siblings. Two branches of one family folded back together.

narrative_blocks.header: Leverett followed her within three days
narrative_blocks.body: She died December 20, 1868, in Illinois; her husband Leverett was gone by the twenty-third, and Princeville Township Cemetery took them side by side. The road there had run from New Haven through Schoharie County to the prairie.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine children scattered across the West
narrative_blocks.body: The children born between 1808 and 1826 spread with the country — Eliza to Elgin, Henry to Peoria, John to McHenry County, Sarah Angeline to Michigan, Edward to Princeville. The parents followed the migration they had raised.

narrative_blocks.header: Died by suicide on New Year's Day, 1904
narrative_blocks.body: Edward Mansfield of Princeville Illinois died on January 1, 1904 by swallowing London purple, an arsenic-based pesticide widely available to farmers of the era. The Brimfield News January 7 1904 obituary attributed his death to declining health following a runaway accident two years earlier from which he had never fully recovered.

narrative_blocks.header: Returned from California Gold Rush after four years
narrative_blocks.body: In 1849 — at age twenty-two — he left Illinois for the California Gold Rush. He returned to Illinois in 1853 to enter Knox College at Galesburg; the gold years did not make him wealthy but they made him a man who had crossed the continent twice before settling into farming.

narrative_blocks.header: Born in NY during family's CT-to-IL migration
narrative_blocks.body: He was born August 1826 in Schenectady County NY — a temporary stop on the family's migration from Connecticut to Illinois. His parents were on the move; he and his eight older siblings together trace the path of a Connecticut Yankee family relocating westward in the second quarter of the nineteenth century.

narrative_blocks.header: Three of nine children died in infancy
narrative_blocks.body: He and his wife Rebecca Fulton had nine children between 1858 and 1876. Three — George 1862, Richard 1869, and Josephine 1869 — died in infancy or as twin to a sibling who survived. The fifty-percent surviving rate of his infants reflected the brutal mortality of mid-century Illinois prairie childhood.

people.research_notes: Edward Mansfield Sr. b. Aug 8, 1826 Schenectady County NY (during family's NY residency between CT and IL migration); d. Jan 1, 1904 Princeville Peoria County IL age 77 yrs 4 mo 23 days. Cause of death: suicide by swallowing London purple (an arsenic-based pesticide). The Brimfield News obit cited declining health following a runaway accident two years earlier as a contributing factor. Ninth and youngest child of HD3919 + I00544. Buried Princeville Township Cemetery (CEM296) alongside parents and most of his own family. EARLY LIFE per obit: first located Kane County IL upon arriving in Illinois (same county sister Eliza Kelley settled in). In 1849 went to California Gold Rush — returned IL 1853 to enter Knox College Galesburg. Teacher for some years, then home farm. m. 1857 Rebecca Fulton (1833-1898, daughter of Josiah Fulton) — DEFERRED full marriage + 9 children build to Stage 6Y-52. The 9 children: Leverett (1858-1934), Albert (1859-1913), George (1862-1862 infant), Edward Jr 'Eddie' (1865-1915), Sanford (1866-1921), Richard (1868-1869 infant), Joseph (1869-1959 TWIN of Josephine, never married), Josephine (1869-1869 infant TWIN of Joseph), Charles (1876-1958). Edward owned 'some five or six hundred acres of land, a part of which is in Jubilee Township' — substantial Illinois farmer. Obit notes the family's origin: 'one Richard Mansfield, who located near North Haven, Conn., in the 17th century, coming to this country from Exeter, Devonshire, England, in 1639' — Mary Stiles Mansfield's husband Richard Mansfield Sr's grandfather. Gen 7 Hooker descendant. Sources: FindAGrave 22076145; Brimfield News Jan 7, 1904 obit; undated obit at Princeville Heritage Museum #163.2019.123.

people.research_notes: Laura Stiles Mansfield. b. 1787 Connecticut; d. 1879 age 91-92. ELDEST documented daughter of H00454 Capt. Isaac Clark Stiles (1767-1834) + X01370 Eunice Blakeslee Stiles (1767-1853). Older sister of HD3922 Isaac Stiles (1792-1842). Per FamilySearch LZGF-FGR, her father H00454 had NINE documented children — Laura is one of two currently built (HD3922 + HD3996); SEVEN GEN-6 STILES SIBLINGS REMAIN UNBUILT and warrant their own stage when source data is available. m. Dec 26, 1814 North East Village (now part of N. Haven) CT Ebenezer Mansfield (I00546, 1791-1865). Anomaly: their first child Mary Mansfield (HD3997) is recorded as b. 1813 — BEFORE the 1814 marriage date — possible date error in source, premarital birth, or earlier undocumented marriage. Seven Mansfield children all gen 7 Hooker. The branch through their second son Isaac Mansfield (HD3998, 1815-1895) leads to NOTABLE descendant ARCHIBALD ROMAINE MANSFIELD (gen 9, 1871-1934, Episcopal clergyman who founded the Seamen's Church Institute of New York and had a WWII Liberty ship named after him in 1944) — to be built in Stage 6Y-54. Laura's daughter Laura Mansfield (HD4003, 1826-1828) is buried at New Center Cemetery (CEM293) N. Haven, the same cemetery as Sam's HD3922 family — confirming the Stiles-Mansfield N. Haven neighborhood and likely close-cousin ties. Gen 6 Hooker descendant. Source: FamilySearch LZGF-NQY. COUSIN MARRIAGE 6Y-58: Laura's marriage to Ebenezer Mansfield (I00546) confirmed as FIRST COUSIN MARRIAGE. Laura's father H00454 Capt. Isaac Clark Stiles and Ebenezer's mother H00452 Mary A. Stiles are siblings (both children of H00238 Isaac Stiles Jr + I00158). Tag 'cousin_marriage' applied. Implications: All 36 of Laura+Ebenezer's documented descendants inherit DOUBLE Hooker descent (via Laura AND via Ebenezer's mother), so descent_paths_to_thomas updated to 2 for them all in this stage. ROLLBACK 6Y-58-ROLLBACK: cousin_marriage tag REMOVED. Stage 6Y-58 attributed Ebenezer as Laura's first cousin (via H00452 Mary Stiles) — this was based on FamilySearch K679-HW6 which contradicts EH 1909 entry 452 (Mary Stiles has only 3 sons: Leverett, Richard, Stiles — NO Ebenezer). Laura's marriage to Ebenezer is therefore NOT a cousin marriage based on current evidence. Ebenezer's parentage UNKNOWN pending NEHGS research. Date discrepancy: EH 454 gives death as Mar 19, 1879; Pierpont genealogy entry 370 gives May 19, 1879. Using May 19 per Pierpont genealogy. EH 1181 Lucina also lists 'd. Mar. 19, 1879' which is almost certainly a transcription confusion between the two sisters; FindAGrave confirms Lucina died June 10, 1858.

parents.father_research_notes: Parents UNKNOWN — EH 1909 entry 452 (Mary Stiles + Richard Mansfield) lists only 3 sons: Leverett, Richard, Stiles. NO Ebenezer. Earlier attribution to I00519+H00452 was based on FamilySearch user-tree (K679-HW6) which contradicts EH and should not be trusted. Ebenezer's actual parentage requires NEHGS or Connecticut vital records research.

narrative_blocks.header: He held four offices in one small town
narrative_blocks.body: At Morris in Otsego County he was town assessor, then supervisor, then justice of the peace, and he sat on the board of the Morris Union School.

narrative_blocks.header: A Whig until the party broke apart
narrative_blocks.body: Mansfield came up a Whig and crossed to the Republicans after the party came apart in the 1850s.

narrative_blocks.header: He left Hamden before he was twenty-seven
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Hamden in 1815, he was in New York State before his marriage to Maria Hitchcock in May 1842, and he died at Morris fifty-three years after that.

notable.notable_blurb: Seamen's Church Institute founder, Liberty ship namesake

education.notes: Annandale-on-Hudson, New York. St. Stephen's later renamed Bard College.

career.employer: Seamen's Church Institute of New York
career.title: Reverend
career.notes: First Superintendent. Recruited by Benoni Lockwood in 1895. With Edmund Lincoln Baylies helped establish the Institute at 25 South Street. Created MEDICO radio medical service for ships.

institutions.notes: 38 years of service. After his death, a $100,000 memorial campaign was led by Rear Admiral Reginald R. Belknap.

naming_inspiration.name: SS Archibald R. Mansfield
naming_inspiration.notes: WWII Liberty ship built by the New England Shipbuilding Corporation 1944, named in Mansfield's honor 10 years after his death.

cross_connections.display_label: put the Seaport Museum on that same South Street seventy years later

narrative_blocks.header: He led the Seamen's Church Institute for decades
narrative_blocks.body: An Episcopal priest, Mansfield served as the first superintendent of the Seamen's Church Institute of New York for thirty-eight years. He helped build its great headquarters on South Street, a haven for sailors in the port.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave ships medical advice by radio
narrative_blocks.body: Mansfield created MEDICO, a pioneering radio service that relayed medical advice to ships at sea. It carried the Institute's care to sailors far beyond the harbor.

narrative_blocks.header: A wartime Liberty ship carried his name
narrative_blocks.body: A memorial fund was raised after his death for his thirty-eight years with the Institute, the committee headed by Rear Admiral Reginald Belknap. In 1944 a Liberty ship was launched as the SS Archibald R. Mansfield.

people.research_notes: Rev. Archibald Romaine Mansfield. b. Jan 3, 1871 Spring Valley Rockland Co NY; d. Feb 10, 1934 Manhattan NY age 63 (Wikipedia: Feb 11; FindAGrave: Feb 10 — using FAG). Cause: heart disease per news obituary headline 'SEAMEN'S LEADER DIES.' Bur Moravian Cemetery (CEM301) Staten Island. Eldest child of Rev. Romaine Stiles Mansfield (HD4004) + Emelia A Moore (I00548). EDUCATION: St. John's School Ossining NY (graduated 1888); St. Stephen's (now Bard College) Annandale-on-Hudson NY BA 1892; seminary 1896. Ordained Episcopal deacon 1896, priest 1897.
