narrative_blocks.header: Died of cholera Montreal 1832, age twenty-six
narrative_blocks.body: Edwin Stiles Lyman died of cholera at Montreal September 22, 1832 at age twenty-six — during the first major North American cholera pandemic, which killed roughly four thousand Montrealers, or six percent of the city's population, in a single summer. He was unmarried. His death came seventeen years after the Lyman family had settled in Montreal in 1815 and four years after their 1828 departure for Sunderland Massachusetts — Edwin may have remained in Montreal when his father moved south.

people.research_notes: EH 1216. Born May 3, 1806. Died of cholera at Montreal Canada September 22, 1832 at age 26. The 1832 cholera pandemic was the first major cholera outbreak in North America, devastating Montreal especially — approximately 4,000 deaths in Montreal alone, about 6% of the city's population. Edwin's death came four years after his father Elisha had moved the family from Montreal to Sunderland MA in 1828, suggesting Edwin remained in Montreal as a young adult (age 22 at the family departure). Unmarried. Middle name Stiles for maternal grandfather Ashbel Stiles (H00241).

narrative_blocks.header: Eldest son in the Montreal drug trade
narrative_blocks.body: Frederick, eldest son of Henry and Mary Corse Lyman, followed his father into the drug trade, which Henry had entered at fifteen in 1829, and became a partner in Lyman, Sons & Co., wholesale druggists of Montreal.

narrative_blocks.header: Two daughters, one lost at twenty
narrative_blocks.body: Frederick and Louisa had two daughters eight years apart. Edith died at twenty in November 1892; Evelyn married an English officer, Maj. Alfred Dixon, and died at Bournemouth in 1938, thirty years after her father.

narrative_blocks.body: Walter was a partner in Rolland, Lyman and Burnett and a vice-president and director of Lymans Limited, the family drug house, and commanded the 7th Siege Battery of the Canadian Garrison Artillery in the militia, retiring a lieutenant-colonel. He died at Montreal in August 1950, at eighty-eight.

narrative_blocks.body: Edith Mary Louise Lyman was born in Montreal on 28 July 1872 and died there on 19 November 1892, at twenty, when her sister Evelyn was twelve. Frederick buried her at Mount Royal Cemetery and outlived her by sixteen years.

parents.mother_research_notes: Janet McPhee (1791 Stormont Glengarry Upper Canada - Jul 26, 1834 Montreal age 43). John Redpath Sr.'s first wife. Died the year John James was born — likely childbirth-related complications. Not built as separate entry per Jalapeño Rule.

career.organization: John Redpath and Son (later Canada Sugar Refining Company)
career.notes: Made partner alongside brother George Drummond Redpath by contract registered July 4, 1862 when their father John withdrew from the business. Partnership ended December 31, 1867; Peter Redpath + Drummond continued alone, joined by Francis Robert Redpath in 1872.

naming_inspiration.description: First name John honors his father John Redpath Sr., the Scottish-born founder of Canada Sugar Refining Company.

cross_connections.display_label: was arming the Union when he helped raise the Victoria Rifles in 1862

narrative_blocks.header: He helped found the Victoria Rifles
narrative_blocks.body: In 1862 Jack Redpath and his brother George were made partners in their father's sugar refinery, but the partnership ended with 1867. Jack chose soldiering instead, helped found the Victoria Rifles, and rose to be its major.

narrative_blocks.header: He built 1065 Sherbrooke Street in 1870
narrative_blocks.body: In 1870 Jack had the architect John James Browne build him a mansion at 1065 Sherbrooke Street, on the corner of Redpath Street, on land his father had bought on the slope of Mount Royal.

narrative_blocks.header: He married Ada Mills at Putney in 1867
narrative_blocks.body: Jack married Ada Maria Mills, the late mayor's daughter, at Putney in 1867, the same year his brother George married her sister Alice. They had five children, and he died at Montreal in June 1884, at fifty.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother died when he was a baby
narrative_blocks.body: Jack was born in 1834, and his mother, Janet McPhee, died that July. His father married Jane Drummond the next year.

narrative_blocks.header: Ada and Cliff, shot in 1901
narrative_blocks.body: Seventeen years after Jack's death, Ada and their youngest son, Cliff, were shot dead in the Sherbrooke Street house. The inquest found that Ada had meant to take her own life; many have since read it that Cliff shot his mother in a rage and then himself.

people.research_notes: Son of John Redpath (founder of Canada Sugar Refining Company 1854). Born Jan 13, 1834 Canada. Made partner in family firm John Redpath and Son alongside brother George Drummond July 4, 1862 when father withdrew. Brother George Drummond Redpath (X01592) married John James's wife Ada's sister Alice Stiles Mills (HD0586) the same year 1867 — dual Mills/Redpath family alliance. Five children: Amy (HD4187), Peter Whiteford (HD4188), John Reginald 'Regy' (HD4189), Harold Mills (HD4190), Jocelyn Clifford 'Cliff' (HD4191). Died Jun 4, 1884 Montreal age 50. Wife Ada widowed at 42, would die in the Redpath Mansion shooting June 13, 1901. STAGE 6Y-85 PARENTAGE WIRED: Father John Redpath Sr. now X02825 in tree (easter egg notable). Mother Janet McPhee (1791-1834) named but not built per Jalapeño Rule. John James was born 1834 — the same year his mother died age 43, possibly in childbirth. After her death his father remarried Jane Drummond 1835, who became John James's stepmother.

bio.photo_notes: Portrait of Amy Linda Redpath Roddick (1868-1954).
bio.bio_blurb: Poet; donor of McGill's Roddick Gates

burial.plot_notes: Cimetière Mont-Royal Montreal — Redpath family grave.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Holds the Roddick Gates architect's work
Her gift to McGill, 1924

cross_connections.display_label: designed the Roddick Gates she paid for in 1924

narrative_blocks.header: She gave McGill the Roddick Gates
narrative_blocks.body: Amy's husband had often said McGill needed a clock tower, and in 1924 she paid for the Roddick Gates on Sherbrooke Street in his memory, their bell tower ringing the quarter-hours. Her niece Betty's husband, Grattan Thompson, designed them.

narrative_blocks.header: A small book of verse nearly every year
narrative_blocks.body: Poetry was Amy's great occupation. For years a small volume of her lyrics came out almost annually, mostly short poems drawn from close watching of nature, and she wrote a mystery play with an Indigenous setting and two other plays.

narrative_blocks.header: She stopped his exhumation in court
narrative_blocks.body: Four days after Sir Thomas was buried in 1923, his will turned out to ask for cremation, and his executors moved to exhume him. Amy said he had changed his mind before he died, fought them in the Quebec Superior Court, and won.

narrative_blocks.header: A library fund for her two brothers
narrative_blocks.body: In 1911 Amy set up the Peter Whiteford and Jocelyn Clifford Redpath Library Fund for the brothers she lost in 1901 and 1902, had Robert Harris paint Peter in his graduation robes, and wrote a poem for each of them.

narrative_blocks.header: She took up the people of Caughnawaga
narrative_blocks.body: In her later years Amy turned to the Indigenous community at Caughnawaga, studying its life and paying to keep some of its older traditions and practices going.

narrative_blocks.header: She ran the house on Sherbrooke Street
narrative_blocks.body: As her mother failed, Amy ran 1065 Sherbrooke Street: she hired the servants, the gardener and her mother's nurse, paid the bills, went with Ada to her doctors, and rewrote Cliff's law lectures so he could study them.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at thirty-eight, at Chislehurst
narrative_blocks.body: Amy's diaries mention no suitors, and she was thirty-eight when she married Thomas Roddick, sixty and a widower, at Chislehurst in Kent in September 1906. Her mother's will had kept her inheritance hers, as though she were single.

people.research_notes: Per FA #167273833. Born 1868 Montreal, died 1954 age ~86. Eldest daughter of John James Redpath and Ada Maria Mills Redpath. Her mother's will stipulated Amy would have complete control over her inheritance 'as though single' if married — a protective provision echoing Ada's own 1867 marriage contract. Married name Roddick. STAGE 6Y-82 ENRICHMENT: Born May 16, 1868. Spent infancy in Europe. Family matriarch role from Ada's decline through Clifford's law studies. Hired household staff (live-in servants, handyman, gardener, charwoman, sewing girl, nurse for Ada). Close to maid Mary Rose Shallow. Rewrote brother Clifford's law lectures to facilitate his studying. Accompanied mother to medical/dental appointments; kept vigil through difficult days. m. Sir Thomas George Roddick (I00634) Sept 3, 1906 at age 38 — her diaries reveal no prior suitors or expressed interest in marriage. Never had children. Major philanthropist: 1911 established Peter Whiteford and Jocelyn Clifford Redpath Library Fund in memory of brothers; commissioned Robert Harris painting of Peter in graduation robes (hangs to this day in Rare Books division of McLennan Library at McGill); 1924 commissioned and donated the famous Roddick Gates at McGill (designed by sister Elizabeth Grace's husband Lt. Grattan Dalrymple Thompson, I00640) to commemorate her late husband; $120,000 bequest to Redpath Library on her death 1954. Wrote poems 'Because he Lived' and 'On the Tablets of Memory P.W.R.' to commemorate Peter. Buried Mount Royal in Redpath family grave. Photo applied.

education.notes: Studied sciences at McGill University. Was too ill to work for any length of time due to chronic illness.

narrative_blocks.header: Witness to mother's death, dead within a year
narrative_blocks.body: Peter Whiteford Redpath was the eldest son of Ada Maria Mills Redpath and John James Redpath. He told the story of his mother's death — he heard the shots from his mother's bedroom on June 13, 1901, dashed in, and found her and his younger brother Clifford on the floor. Peter himself died the following year, 1902, at age thirty-two or thirty-three.

narrative_blocks.header: Tuberculosis cure across continents, died California
narrative_blocks.body: Peter Whiteford Redpath studied sciences at McGill but was too ill to work, declining a position his uncle offered at the family sugar mill. He spent long periods pursuing rest cures for tuberculosis in Ste-Agathe-des-Monts in the Laurentians, upper New York State, Colorado, and finally California. After his mother's death in June 1901 his health rapidly deteriorated; his sister Amy accompanied him by train to Redlands California where he died of tuberculosis May 18, 1902, his body returned to Montreal for burial at Mount Royal.

people.research_notes: Per FA #109005550. Born 1869 Montreal, died 1902 age 32-33. Was the family witness who first reached his mother's room after the June 13, 1901 shooting. He gave the family account to investigators. Died less than a year after his mother and brother — cause undocumented but the proximity to the family tragedy is notable. STAGE 6Y-82 ENRICHMENT: Born Jul 17, 1869 — fourteen months after sister Amy. Studied sciences at McGill but too ill to work; rejected uncle Peter Redpath's offer of a sugar mill position. Pursued European medical treatment for sciatica and rest cures for TB in Ste-Agathe-des-Monts, upper New York State, Colorado, and California. Following the June 1901 Redpath Mansion mother+brother shooting, his health rapidly deteriorated. Amy traveled with him to Ste-Agathe and then to Redlands CA where he died of TB May 18, 1902 age 32. Amy accompanied his body back to Montreal by train; buried Mount Royal family plot. Died intestate and childless — share of Redpath estate reverted to surviving siblings. Sister Amy established the Peter Whiteford and Jocelyn Clifford Redpath Library Fund in 1911; commissioned Robert Harris painting of Peter in graduation robes — hangs in Rare Books division of McLennan Library at McGill to this day. Amy wrote poems 'Because he Lived' and 'On the Tablets of Memory P.W.R.' to commemorate him.

burial.plot_notes: Ross Bay Cemetery Victoria BC — moved west from Montreal in later life.

narrative_blocks.header: Moved west to British Columbia in later life
narrative_blocks.body: John Reginald 'Regy' Redpath married Florence Amelia Botterell in 1907 and had three sons born in Alberta and Quebec. He eventually moved west to Oak Bay near Victoria British Columbia where he died at age eighty in November 1951. He was buried at Ross Bay Cemetery Victoria — outside the Mount Royal family burial pattern that held for his siblings and parents.

people.research_notes: Per FA #121311516. Born 1871 Montreal, died 1951 age ~80. Known as 'Regy'. Middle child of John James Redpath and Ada Maria Mills Redpath. STAGE 6Y-82 ENRICHMENT: Born Jan 16, 1871 Montreal. m. Florence Amelia Botterell (I00635) 1907. Three sons: James Bailey (HD4196, 1908-1940 d. age 31), James Botterell (HD4197, 1908-1992, also 8 Jun 1908 — likely twins, evidence supports both as real per FA + family records though one researcher Alan Gorman in 2025 suggested only two sons total), Huntly Roddick (HD4198, 1911-1972). Moved to Oak Bay BC in later life. Died Nov 27, 1951 age 80. Buried Ross Bay Cemetery Victoria BC (NOT Mount Royal — westward migration broke the family burial pattern).

naming_inspiration.description: Middle name Mills carries the maternal grandfather's surname — John Easton Mills, the Mayor of Montreal who died of typhus 1847. Naming honors the Mills civic legacy across the Redpath generation.

narrative_blocks.header: Bonnie Brae summer farm, two marriages, four children
narrative_blocks.body: Harold Mills Redpath married Alice Graham Watson in July 1897 and moved with her to 355 Olivier Avenue Westmount; in 1901 he purchased the Merriman farm in Georgetown Quebec and renamed it Bonnie Brae, where the family summered regularly through 1910. He and Alice had four children — Elizabeth Grace, John, Peter Harold, and Hugh — before separating; he later married Marie Adele Prendiville. He died at Saanich near Victoria British Columbia on December 26, 1948 at age seventy-five.

people.research_notes: Per FA #109005541. Born 1873 Montreal, died 1948 age ~75. Middle name Mills carries his mother's maiden name + grandfather John Easton Mills's surname. STAGE 6Y-82 ENRICHMENT: Born Nov 9, 1873 Montreal — fourth child of Ada Maria Mills Redpath + John James Redpath. Unlike Peter and Clifford did NOT attend McGill (career unclear). m. Alice Graham Watson (I00638) Jul 22, 1897; moved to 355 Olivier Ave Westmount. burial.plot_notes: Cimetière Mont-Royal Montreal — Redpath family grave; buried with his mother June 15, 1901.

notable.notable_blurb: McGill law graduate; Redpath Mansion shooting victim

narrative_blocks.header: He had just earned his law degree
narrative_blocks.body: Cliff went into Arts at McGill in 1896, moved into Law the next year and graduated in 1900, apprenticing all the while at Campbell, Meredith, Allan & Hague. Days before he died he sent in his application to sit the bar examination.

narrative_blocks.header: The son at home ran the family money
narrative_blocks.body: As the youngest, and the only son still living at 1065 Sherbrooke Street, Cliff managed the family fortune, writing to his eldest brother, Peter, for advice. He lived in that house his whole life.

narrative_blocks.header: He read to his mother through her illness
narrative_blocks.body: Cliff took his mother to upstate New York in the summers, kept her company, read to her when her health gave way, and saw to her care whenever his sister Amy was away.

narrative_blocks.header: Walking the mountain with Amy
narrative_blocks.body: Cliff and his sister Amy went to the same parties, and her diary has them walking or riding on Mount Royal together several times a week. At eight she had stood as one of his godparents.

narrative_blocks.header: Shot in his mother's bedroom, 1901
narrative_blocks.body: At six on the evening of 13 June 1901 Cliff and his mother were found shot in her bedroom. He was taken unconscious to the Royal Victoria Hospital and died there at ten to midnight. The family never called the police, and the two were buried together two days later.

narrative_blocks.header: The verdict: shot trying to save her
narrative_blocks.body: The inquest sat the next day and found that Cliff was shot trying to take the revolver from his mother, who then turned it on herself. The papers called him bright and cheerful; others have since suspected he fired both shots.

narrative_blocks.header: Amy wrote two poems for him
narrative_blocks.body: His sister Amy wrote “Perfect in Thy Promise” and “On the Tablets of Memory” for him, and in 1911 set up the Peter Whiteford and Jocelyn Clifford Redpath Library Fund in the names of her two lost brothers.

people.research_notes:
Born Nov 17, 1876 Canada — youngest of John James Redpath + Ada Maria Mills Redpath's five children. Just graduated McGill University in law when he died June 13, 1901 at the Redpath Mansion shooting at age 24. Per newspaper accounts of the day: 'Mr. Clifford Redpath was a bright, intelligent, cheerful youth... in perfect health. They were deeply attached to each other, and any cause in the shape of a quarrel must be dismissed.' The official coroner's verdict held Ada had suicidal intent and Clifford was accidentally shot trying to take the revolver from her, then his mother carried out her intention. Buried with his mother at Mount Royal Cemetery June 15, 1901. Per FA #108233534. Photo applied. Newspaper accounts described him as 'a bright, intelligent, cheerful youth' in 'perfect health,' deeply attached to his mother. He was taken unconscious to the Royal Victoria Hospital where he died; he and his mother were buried together at Mount Royal Cemetery two days later.'

people.research_notes: Per FA #108930155. Wife of Walter Ernest Lyman (HD4182), m.1901. Two daughters Beatrice Mary Tudor + Faith Dorothy Roswell. Buried Cimetière Mont-Royal.

bio.bio_blurb: Historian of the Canadian animal-welfare society

career.organization: Canadian Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals

narrative_blocks.header: For Those Who Cannot Speak, 1970
narrative_blocks.body: Beatrice Johnston wrote the hundred-year history of the Canadian Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, 1869 to 1969, and published it in 1970. She had given the society years of her own.

narrative_blocks.header: Twins in 1932, and no other children
narrative_blocks.body: Walter Tudor and Ursula Wyatt were born on 17 January, three years after she married Henry Wyatt Johnston at Montreal, and she had no more after them. He became a plasma physicist and she a painter.

narrative_blocks.header: Northglint, at the end of the cape
narrative_blocks.body: Her father Walter Ernest Lyman kept the house at Cap à l'Orignal, in what is now the Parc National du Bic. Her son learned to sail there in the cold water, and the family called it the Cape.

narrative_blocks.header: Eighty-two, and twelve days past her birthday
narrative_blocks.body: She was the eldest daughter of Walter Ernest Lyman and Anna Scrimger, born at Montreal in December 1905. She died on 30 December 1987 and lies in the Cimetière Mont-Royal.

people.research_notes: Per FA #108176965. b. Dec 18, 1905 Montreal — eldest daughter of Walter Ernest Lyman + Anna Mark Scrimger Lyman. m. Henry Wyatt Johnston (I00632, Lt Col Canadian Engineers) 1929; two children — twins Walter Tudor and Ursula Wyatt born 1932. d. Dec 30, 1987 age 82. Buried Cimetière Mont-Royal.

career.organization: Montreal General Hospital and the Allan Memorial Institute

naming_inspiration.description: Middle name Roswell carries the name of her uncle Roswell Corse Lyman (1850-1892), who had died at age 42 before Faith was born — and his middle name Corse came from his mother Mary Corse Lyman.

narrative_blocks.header: Head Girl at Traf, 1936 to 1937
narrative_blocks.body: Faith moved from The Study in Westmount to the Trafalgar School for Girls, where she fell for sport, basketball above all, and was Head Girl for 1936 to 1937, a title she was proud of to the end.

narrative_blocks.header: Refused by the Navy, hired on the spot
narrative_blocks.body: Faith trained as a nurse at Kingston during the war and came home in 1943 to enlist at the Naval Recruitment Centre, which turned her down. She walked into the Montreal Neurological Institute instead, was hired on the spot, and there met Bill Feindel, a neurosurgical resident she married in 1945.

narrative_blocks.header: She painted Bic over and over
narrative_blocks.body: Faith began painting in oils and watercolours in Saskatoon in her mid-thirties and later studied with Yehouda Chaki in Montreal. For decades her subject was Bic, the Lyman summer place on the lower St. Lawrence near Rimouski, where she sailed her 13-foot Freia alone and swam every morning in the river.

narrative_blocks.header: A psychiatric nurse until ninety
narrative_blocks.body: Once her six children were grown Faith went back to nursing, trained as a psychiatric nurse, and worked at the Montreal General and then the Allan Memorial Institute until she resigned, reluctantly, at ninety. She died at home in Montreal in June 2016, at ninety-six.

people.research_notes: Per FA #241844871. Born 1920 — fifteen years after sister Beatrice; lived to 2016, age 95-96. Younger daughter of Walter Ernest + Anna Mark Scrimger Lyman. Middle name Roswell honors her uncle Roswell Corse Lyman (HD4181, 1850-1892). Married name Feindel.

career.organization: Partnership with M. E. A. Charlton

military_service.unit: 17th Duke of York Royal Canadian Hussars
military_service.notes: Joined 1922; commanded the regiment 1932-1936; colonel 1936 with the third cavalry brigade to 1940; non-combatant personnel in the war; honorary colonel of the Royal Canadian Hussars from 1971.

narrative_blocks.header: He commanded the Hussars while the barracks rose
narrative_blocks.body: Henry Wyatt Johnston joined the 17th Duke of York Royal Canadian Hussars in 1922 and had the regiment from 1932 to 1936, the years the Côte-des-Neiges barracks was built.

narrative_blocks.header: Colonel at forty, honorary colonel at last
narrative_blocks.body: He took the third cavalry brigade in 1936 and held it to 1940, then spent the war among the army's non-combatant personnel. The Royal Canadian Hussars made him their honorary colonel in 1971.

narrative_blocks.header: Oxford under Julian Huxley, then McGill
narrative_blocks.body: He went from Lower Canada College to Oxford and read under Sir Julian Huxley, and finished at McGill with a doctorate in chemical engineering in 1929. He married Beatrice Lyman that same year.

narrative_blocks.header: Refining, then a firm of his own
narrative_blocks.body: After the war he worked for Sutherland Refiners Limited and then went into partnership with M. E. A. Charlton as consulting engineers. He died at Knowlton in Quebec at seventy-seven.

people.research_notes: Per FA #108925336. b. Oct 18, 1896 Montreal; d. Aug 14, 1974 Knowlton Estrie Region QC age 77. McGill civil engineer with PhD. Lt Colonel Canadian Engineers, active duty from 1940 in WWII. m. Beatrice Mary Tudor Lyman (HD4192) 1929. Two twin children born Jan 17, 1932: Walter Tudor Wyatt (HD4194) and Ursula Wyatt (HD4195, m. Dr. Francis Berger Trudeau Jr.).

bio.photo_notes: Portrait of Walter Tudor Wyatt Johnston (1932-2016).

career.notes: NASA projects simulating plasmas in space.

narrative_blocks.header: A benchmark book on plasma kinetics
narrative_blocks.body: The Particle Kinetics of Plasma, which he co-wrote in 1966, set the mark in the field. He published more than a hundred and fifty times, and co-wrote Survival Skills for Scientists off fifty years of it.

narrative_blocks.header: He simulated space plasmas for NASA
narrative_blocks.body: Four years at Houston from 1969 went on that. He came back to Quebec in 1973 for the new INRS energy centre at Varennes and stayed there the rest of his working life.

narrative_blocks.header: Six years editing Physical Review Letters
narrative_blocks.body: He was an associate editor from 2000 and a referee after, and twenty-three of his own papers had appeared in it. The American Physical Society made him a Fellow, and INRS emeritus in 2012.

narrative_blocks.header: A knife, pliers and pens on a lanyard
narrative_blocks.body: He carried them in case anything needed fixing or writing down. Bridge, chess, crosswords and three-dimensional puzzles held him — anything with a findable path to an answer.

narrative_blocks.header: A hand on the tiller cured his seasickness
narrative_blocks.body: He learned to sail off his father and uncle at his grandfather Lyman's house, Northglint, in the cold water at the end of Cap à l'Orignal. Dinghy, catamaran or keel boat, it was all one to him.

narrative_blocks.header: He would read anything but organic chemistry
narrative_blocks.body: That was too messy, and North American history too short. He would grant any thesis as plausible so long as it was properly defended, which made him hard work to argue with.

people.research_notes: Per FA #294921762. Born Jan 17, 1932 Montreal — twin of Ursula Wyatt Johnston Trudeau (HD4195). Died Aug 24, 2016 Knowlton QC age 84. Buried Cimetière Mont-Royal. Photo applied.

bio.bio_blurb: Montreal painter and Adirondack Artists Guild member

burial.plot_notes: Saint Johns In The Wilderness Episcopal Cemetery, Brighton NY — same as husband Dr. Francis Berger Trudeau Jr.

education.school_name: Studied painting under Hans Hofmann, Stanley Cosgrove and Alfred Pellan

narrative_blocks.header: Billboards painted by hand, and window displays
narrative_blocks.body: Out of the Beaux-Arts at Montreal she took freelance commercial work: fashion illustration, billboards painted by hand, costume and set design for theatre and television, textiles, child portraiture.

narrative_blocks.header: Hofmann, Cosgrove and Pellan taught her
narrative_blocks.body: She learned painting from all three and kept at it for sixty years, showing at Montreal, Lake Placid, Saranac Lake and the Virgin Islands. The Adirondacks and the Caribbean were her two subjects.

narrative_blocks.header: Two years in Paris, and then Saranac Lake
narrative_blocks.body: She was working there when she met Francis Trudeau. They married in 1960, she moved to his town, and she became stepmother to his three children by his first marriage.

narrative_blocks.header: Grand Marshal of the Winter Carnival
narrative_blocks.body: Saranac Lake gave her that in 2014. She had worked for the Adirondack Antiques Show and the Pendragon Theatre, and sat on the board of the Trudeau Institute.

narrative_blocks.header: She recruited for the Lake Placid Games
narrative_blocks.body: Ursula Trudeau was recruitment officer for the 1980 Winter Olympics while her husband ran the medical side of the Nordic events. She went on to Sarajevo and Lillehammer as a spectator.

narrative_blocks.header: Ski patrol on Whiteface, and the hats
narrative_blocks.body: She skied, kayaked, rode, cooked and kept dogs, and patrolled Whiteface Mountain. The hats she collected from around the world made her impossible to miss in the town.

narrative_blocks.header: Twin to a plasma physicist
narrative_blocks.body: Ursula and Walter Tudor Wyatt Johnston were born on the same January day in 1932 at Montreal to Colonel Henry Wyatt Johnston and Beatrice Lyman. He went before her by three years.

people.research_notes: Per FA #233241961. Born Jan 17, 1932 Montreal — twin of Walter Tudor Wyatt Johnston (HD4194). Married Dr. Francis Berger Trudeau Jr. (I00633) in 1961 — second wife. Francis's first marriage to Jean Moore Amory produced three children including the Doonesbury cartoonist Garry Trudeau. Ursula's children with Francis (if any) not documented. Moved to Saranac Lake Franklin County NY; died there Dec 5, 2019 age 87. Buried Saint Johns In The Wilderness Episcopal Cemetery Brighton NY with husband. Photo applied. narrative_blocks.header: Third Trudeau doctor in the same town
narrative_blocks.body: His grandfather Edward Livingston Trudeau opened the sanatorium that made Saranac Lake a cure town, and his father carried the practice on. He came home to it in 1954 and stayed thirty-one years.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the institute his grandfather began
narrative_blocks.body: When the sanatorium closed in 1954, he sold its grounds in 1957 and put the money into a new laboratory on Lower Saranac Lake, opened in 1964 as the Trudeau Institute. He was its president until shortly before he died, and chairman emeritus at the end.

narrative_blocks.header: Naval Reserve at Yale, and a destroyer
narrative_blocks.body: In May 1941 he was finishing the reserve course alongside his degree, with a fortnight's cruise in a destroyer coming. The family hoped he would get his last Yale year before active duty.

narrative_blocks.header: He jumped for Yale in the thirties
narrative_blocks.body: He ski-jumped for the college and competed nationally, and he never stopped. In 1982, on a new hip, he won a fifteen-kilometre masters race at the Empire State Games.

narrative_blocks.header: Senior medical officer at Lake Placid
narrative_blocks.body: He had the Nordic events at the 1980 Winter Olympics and was physician to the United States Nordic team. He looked after the Saranac Lake schools as well.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventeen years chief of medicine
narrative_blocks.body: He held that post at the General Hospital in Saranac Lake from 1960, and practised internal medicine in the town until he retired in 1985.

narrative_blocks.header: Put on the park agency, then off it
narrative_blocks.body: Governor Carey named him to the new Adirondack Park Agency in the mid-seventies as a second Essex County commissioner. He stepped down when the legality of that under the one-county rule was disputed.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Trudeau Institute

people.research_notes: Per Adirondack Daily Enterprise obituary April 25, 1995. Born Jul 21, 1919 Saranac Lake NY. Three-generation Trudeau physician dynasty: grandfather Dr. Edward Livingston Trudeau founded the Trudeau Sanatorium (TB pioneer), father Dr. Francis Berger Trudeau Sr. continued the medical practice. Yale 1942 (BA, ski jumping team in 1930s, also national ski jump competitions); WWII Navy; Columbia P&S MD 1950; intern/resident Bellevue + NYU; fellowship Royal Victoria Hospital Montreal (connection to his future wife Ursula's family city). Practiced internal medicine Saranac Lake 1954-1985 (31 years). Chief of medicine General Hospital 1960-1977 (17 years). Trudeau Institute founding president from 1954; chairman emeritus shortly before death. 1980 Winter Olympics senior medical officer for Nordic events + US Nordic Ski Team physician + Saranac Lake school district physician. Mid-1970s appointed by Gov. Hugh Carey as Adirondack Park Agency commissioner; stepped down following dispute over single-county-commissioner rule (he was second Essex County member). 1985 Winter Carnival grand marshal. 1982: after hip replacement, won 15km masters nordic ski race Empire State Games. January 1995: received key to Saranac Lake. August 1994: son Garry presented him with bronze bust for the institute's library. April 26, 1995: died at Adirondack Medical Center age 75. TWO MARRIAGES: 1st Jean Moore Amory (three children including Garry Trudeau, Doonesbury cartoonist — NOT a Hooker descendant since mother was Jean not Ursula); 2nd m. Ursula Wyatt Johnston (HD4195) 1961 — no documented children. Photo applied. Buried Saint Johns In The Wilderness Episcopal Cemetery Brighton NY (CEM329) with Ursula. bio.title: Sir
bio.photo_notes: Portrait of Sir Thomas George Roddick (1846-1923), McGill professor of surgery and pioneer of antisepsis in Canada.

burial.plot_notes: Cimetière Mont-Royal Montreal — family monument designed to resemble the Roddick Gates of McGill.

notable.notable_blurb: Surgeon; founder of the Medical Council of Canada

education.notes: M.D., first in his class, Holmes Medal

career.role: Member of Parliament for St. Antoine

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Keeps him as an officer of the regiment
Raised in his memory

narrative_blocks.header: He learned antisepsis from Lister himself
narrative_blocks.body: Alarmed by the infections killing patients at the Montreal General, Thomas went to Edinburgh to study with Joseph Lister in 1872 and again in 1877. Within two years his deaths from infection fell from more than half to about three in a hundred.

narrative_blocks.header: The Roddick Bill took eighteen years
narrative_blocks.body: Elected to Parliament for St. Antoine in 1896, Thomas carried the Canada Medical Act, the Roddick Bill, in 1902 and spent until 1912 bringing every province round. The Medical Council of Canada gave him its first certificate of registration, and he was knighted in 1914.

narrative_blocks.header: Allergic to the antiseptic, he became dean
narrative_blocks.body: By 1901 Thomas could no longer operate: he had become allergic to iodoform, the antiseptic that replaced his carbolic spray. McGill made him dean of medicine, and in 1907 he saw the faculty through a fire that destroyed half its building.

narrative_blocks.header: Surgeon general in the North-West, 1885
narrative_blocks.body: In the 1885 rebellion Thomas was deputy surgeon general to the field force. He gathered its doctors, nurses and supplies, followed the fighting, cared for wounded Métis as well, and saw the casualties out by barge and rail until late August.

narrative_blocks.header: A train wreck kept him in Montreal
narrative_blocks.body: Bound for medical school in Edinburgh in 1864, Thomas stopped in Montreal just as a train with 458 passengers ran through an open drawbridge into the Richelieu. Dr. George Fenwick took him to the wreck, and was so struck by his skill that he talked him into McGill instead.

narrative_blocks.header: He married Amy Redpath at Chislehurst
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas's first wife, Urelia McKinnon of Pointe-Claire, died in 1890 after ten years of marriage. In September 1906, at sixty, he married Amy Redpath, thirty-eight, at Chislehurst in Kent. Neither marriage had children.

narrative_blocks.header: The clock tower he wanted for McGill
narrative_blocks.body: A punctual man, Thomas had often told his wife that McGill needed a clock tower. In 1924, the year after he died, she gave the university the Roddick Gates on Sherbrooke Street, whose bell tower rings the quarter-hours.

people.research_notes: Major medical pioneer notable. Born Jul 31, 1846 Harbour Grace Newfoundland (at the time the first and oldest British Crown Colony; Newfoundland did not join Canadian Confederation until 1949). Studied surgery in Britain under Joseph Lister; 1877 introduced Lister's antiseptic methods to Montreal — major moment in Canadian surgical history. Professor of surgery at McGill University. 1885 Deputy Surgeon General of the force sent to subdue the Northwest Rebellion. KNIGHTED for medical service. m. Urelia M. McKinnon 1880 (d.1890); m. Amy Linda Redpath (HD4187) Sept 3, 1906 — Amy was 38, Thomas was 60. Died Feb 20, 1923 Montreal age 76. Buried Cimetière Mont-Royal — family monument designed to resemble the Roddick Gates of McGill (which Amy donated in his memory in 1924). Photo applied. X-... actually I-PREFIX as direct spouse of HD4187.

bio.photo_notes: Portrait of James Botterell Redpath (1908-1992), President of Dome Mines Limited.

career.notes: President of Dome Mines Limited 1959-1977. Dome Mines was a major Canadian gold mining company.

narrative_blocks.header: From surveyor to president of Dome Mines
narrative_blocks.body: James started at Dome Mines in 1931 as a surveyor at South Porcupine and rose to be its president, from 1959 to 1977. He led the Canadian Mining Association in 1957 and 1958.

narrative_blocks.header: His children grew up on the Sigma mine
narrative_blocks.body: In 1935 James went to Val-d'Or as general superintendent of Dome's Sigma mine, and he was its general manager from 1946. His three children grew up on the mine site until the family moved to Toronto in 1954.

narrative_blocks.header: He married Margaret Stockton in 1932
narrative_blocks.body: In November 1932, a year after he started at Dome, James married Margaret Stockton, daughter of H. C. Stockton. They had two sons, Jim and John, and a daughter, Anne.

narrative_blocks.header: Born in Alberta to Montreal parents
narrative_blocks.body: James was born at Lethbridge, Alberta, in 1908 to Montreal parents, Regy and Florence Botterell Redpath, and went from Brentwood College to McGill, where he trained as a mining engineer.

people.research_notes: Per FA #154927827. Born Jun 8, 1908 Lethbridge Alberta. President of Dome Mines Limited 1959-1977 (Canadian gold mining giant). m. Margaret Isobel Stockton (I00636) 1932. Raised family at Val-d'Or Quebec around mining operations. Three children: James Stockton 'Jim' (HD4203, founded J.S. Redpath Ltd. mining contractor, Order of Ontario), Florence Anne (HD4204, World Bank), John Huntly (HD4205, Stanford anesthesiologist). Died Mar 2, 1992 Toronto age 83. Buried Mount Pleasant Cemetery Toronto. Photo applied.

naming_inspiration.description: Middle name Roddick honors his aunt Amy Linda Redpath's husband Sir Thomas George Roddick — McGill surgery professor and namesake of the Roddick Gates. Born in 1911 between Amy and Sir Thomas's 1906 marriage and Sir Thomas's death in 1923.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote a dog story, Happiness Land
narrative_blocks.body: In 1960 Huntly published Happiness Land at Montreal, a dog story with bits of verse whose characters include a Newfoundland dog named Sport, Mayor Alsatian and Alderman Charlie Chow.

narrative_blocks.header: His aunt's will named him an adviser
narrative_blocks.body: When his aunt, Lady Amy Roddick, died in 1954, her handwritten will asked her trustees to take counsel with Huntly, then a Montreal realtor, and his brother James. Quebec later passed a private act to spell out what the trustees could do.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifteen years at Fort Macleod
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Pincher Creek, Alberta, in 1911, Huntly went to New York in 1933, spent about fifteen years at Fort Macleod, Alberta, and then settled in Montreal, where he sold real estate.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried Sir Thomas Roddick's name
narrative_blocks.body: Huntly's middle name was the surname of his aunt Amy's husband, the surgeon Sir Thomas Roddick, who died in 1923.

people.research_notes: Per FA #109005542. Born 1911 Pincher Creek MD of Pincher Creek No. 9 Alberta — father John Reginald was 40 and mother Florence Amelia was 39 at his birth. Immigrated to New York City 1933. Lived ~15 years at Fort Macleod Alberta. m. Margaret Edna Heal (I00637, 1913-1985). At least four children: Lawrence Andrew (HD4206, 1935-1993), Phoebe Winona (HD4207, 1938-2021), and (per Phoebe's 2021 obituary) surviving siblings 'Amy Linda Redpath of Flat River Prince Edward Island' (HD4208) and 'Peter Mills Redpath of Victoria British Columbia' (HD4209). Died Dec 21, 1972 Montreal age 61. Buried Cimetière Mont-Royal.

narrative_blocks.body: Betty, the eldest of Harold Mills Redpath's four children, was born at 355 Olivier Avenue in Westmount in 1898. She married Grattan Thompson, the architect of McGill's Roddick Gates, which her aunt Amy gave in 1924 in memory of Sir Thomas Roddick.

military_service.notes: Pilot for Air Transport Command WWII.

narrative_blocks.header: Knighted by three Scandinavian kings for aviation
narrative_blocks.body: Peter Harold Redpath flew as TWA co-pilot, served as Air Transport Command pilot in World War II, directed Canadair Limited in Montreal, and spent five years in Sweden organizing the Scandinavian Air Industry as Vice President of Scandinavian Airlines. He was knighted by the kings of Denmark, Norway, and Sweden for his contributions to aviation and SAS — three royal knighthoods earned in a single career.

narrative_blocks.header: Died in mid-flight emergency landing Chicago 1977
narrative_blocks.body: Peter Harold Redpath died November 8, 1977 of a heart attack aboard a Northwest Airlines flight from Minneapolis to New York. The pilot diverted to O'Hare International after a flight attendant noticed him slumped in his seat; he died at a Chicago hospital. He was a Bellingham Washington resident since 1961, a director of the Whatcom County Museum Foundation Board, and active in the Bellingham Yacht Club and Rotary Club.

career.notes: Founded J.S. Redpath Ltd. at age 26 — mining contracting company specializing in shaft sinking. Built it into a global leader in mining services before stepping away at age 50.
Led the Capitol Arts Centre North Bay for several years after leaving mining; supported local artists and cultural growth.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded J.S. Redpath at twenty-six
narrative_blocks.body: Jim took his McGill degree in mining engineering and at twenty-six founded J.S. Redpath Ltd. at North Bay, a contractor that sank mine shafts and grew into a world leader in mining services. He stepped away from it at fifty.

narrative_blocks.header: From shaft sinking to the Capitol Arts Centre
narrative_blocks.body: After mining, Jim studied art curation at Sotheby's in New York and came back to run North Bay's Capitol Arts Centre for several years. Later he and his wife, Bobbi, threw themselves into the arts of St. John's.

narrative_blocks.header: Nipissing's first chancellor, 1994 to 2002
narrative_blocks.body: Jim was Nipissing University's first chancellor, from 1994 to 2002, and gave to its buildings, scholarships, awards and bursaries. McGill and Nipissing both made him an honorary doctor, and he held the Order of Ontario and both Jubilee Medals.

narrative_blocks.header: Two summers on a Hudson Bay boat
narrative_blocks.body: Jim grew up on the Sigma mine site at Val-d'Or, the eldest of three, and spent two teenage summers on a small exploration boat in Hudson Bay, which gave him his lifelong love of the Canadian North.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty years with Parkinson's
narrative_blocks.body: Jim and Bobbi were married more than fifty years and settled in St. John's, where he died on 2 August 2025, at eighty-eight, after twenty years with Parkinson's disease.

narrative_blocks.header: His great-uncle was born at Harbour Grace
narrative_blocks.body: Jim's great-aunt Amy Redpath married Sir Thomas Roddick, born at Harbour Grace, Newfoundland, in 1846. Jim ended his life in the province where Sir Thomas began his.

narrative_blocks.header: Among the first women with a York MBA
narrative_blocks.body: Anne grew up at Val-d'Or, graduated from McGill, and was one of the first women to take an MBA at York University. She started at the World Bank in Washington, worked on research projects, and then advised small, growing companies.

narrative_blocks.header: On the board of Canadian Woman Studies
narrative_blocks.body: Anne backed York's School of Women's Studies and sat for many years on the advisory board of Inanna Publications and its journal, Canadian Woman Studies. She was an activist when it was needed.

notable.notable_blurb: Anesthesiologist and Interplast volunteer

career.notes: Partner at Palo Alto Medical Foundation 1977 until retirement 1998. Also served on Medical Board of Stanford Hospital. Active in Interplast (international plastic surgery charity).
Internship Toronto then opened family practice. Changed course in 1975 to anesthesia.

narrative_blocks.header: From family doctor to anesthesiologist
narrative_blocks.body: John took his McGill M.D. in 1968 and practised family medicine in Toronto for seven years. In 1975 he started over as an anesthesia resident in Calgary, finished at Stanford, and was a partner at the Palo Alto Medical Foundation from 1977 to 1998.

narrative_blocks.header: Interplast took him to three continents
narrative_blocks.body: John was long active with Interplast, the surgical charity, and went with it to countries in Central America, South America and Asia. He also sat on Stanford Hospital's medical board.

narrative_blocks.header: Head prefect, then Princeton
narrative_blocks.body: John was born at Val-d'Or, where his father ran Dome's Sigma mine, and moved to Toronto with the family in 1954. He was head prefect at Bishop's College School and graduated from Princeton in 1964.

narrative_blocks.header: Two marriages, and three children
narrative_blocks.body: John married Barbara Zieman after Princeton, and they had Peter, Scott and Julia before the marriage ended. In 1988 he married Kathy Smith, a nurse he knew from Stanford, and they retired together to Angels Camp in 1998.

Died Mar 3, 2024 Palo Alto age 81 — long fight with aggressive cancer + treatment complications. Survived by wife + children + brother Jim/Bobbi. Photo applied. Children not built per Jalapeño Rule.

institutions.institution_blurb: Harvard Graduate School of Education, Ed.M. elementary education 1961.

narrative_blocks.header: The Discovery of Canada and Other Animals
narrative_blocks.body: In 1990 Phoebe published The Discovery of Canada and Other Animals, poems for children and some adults, illustrated with her own drawings.

narrative_blocks.header: The defender of the office against chaos
narrative_blocks.body: For fifteen years she kept the editorial machinery of Dionysius running — the Dalhousie classics journal whose editor crowned her its principal defender against chaos. She had come back to Halifax in 1976 and never left the university's orbit.

narrative_blocks.header: Ontario refused her Harvard degree
narrative_blocks.body: The province's education authorities would not recognize the Ed.M. she had taken at Harvard in 1961, so the London years went instead to the Kiwanis Senior Citizens' Centre. Halifax, six years later, took her back — degree and all.

narrative_blocks.header: A Golden Apple for her reading help
narrative_blocks.body: Phoebe volunteered with children who had trouble reading at Halifax's Sir Charles Tupper School, and the Halifax Regional Municipality gave her its Golden Apple award for the work.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father wrote a dog story too
narrative_blocks.body: Her father, Huntly Redpath, had published his own animal book at Montreal in 1960, Happiness Land, a dog story with bits of verse, thirty years before hers.

people.research_notes: Per family obituary. Born May 18, 1938 Montreal. Elder daughter of Huntly Roddick + Margaret 'Margot' Redpath. The Study Montreal (Head Girl 1955-56). Dalhousie 1960. Met future husband Henry Roper at Dalhousie. Harvard Ed.M. 1961 (elementary education). Married Henry Roper 1961. Cambridge England elementary teacher. 1967-68 Halifax Ladies College (now Armbrae Academy). 1970 moved London ON — Ontario education refused to recognize Harvard degree; worked London Kiwanis Senior Citizens' Centre. 1976 returned Halifax. 15 years assistant editorial board Dionysius (Dalhousie Classics journal). Volunteer reading tutor Sir Charles Tupper School — received Golden Apple award from Halifax Regional Municipality. Wrote poetry; 1990 published 'The Discovery of Canada and Other Animals' (children's poems she illustrated). Recorder player with 'Hemiolas' women's group 30+ years. Dalhousie Chorale (Bach, Mozart, Handel). Quilter + crewel-work + gardener (birds + flowers themes). Died Apr 2, 2021 Halifax age 82. Buried Fairview Lawn Cemetery Halifax. Survived by husband Henry Roper, sister Amy Linda Redpath (HD4208, Flat River PEI), brother Peter Mills Redpath (HD4209, Victoria BC); predeceased by brother Lawrence Andrew Redpath (HD4206) and wife Louise 1993.

narrative_blocks.body: A Montrealer all her life, June became a physical education teacher. She crossed Canada in a Suburban with a canoe on the roof and a tent trailer behind, and rode on horseback into the Rockies.

narrative_blocks.body: June and her husband Eric built a country house at Austin, Quebec, on Lake Memphremagog, and for more than forty-five years filled it with their five children, the grandchildren, the boats and the water-skiing she loved.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father designed the Roddick Gates
narrative_blocks.body: June's father, Grattan Thompson, designed the Roddick Gates at McGill, given in 1924 by her great-aunt Amy Redpath Roddick in memory of her husband, Sir Thomas Roddick.

narrative_blocks.header: He drew McGill’s Roddick Gates
narrative_blocks.body: Commissioned in 1924 by his wife’s aunt Amy Redpath Roddick in memory of her husband Sir Thomas, the Grenadier Guards veteran designed the iconic gates that front McGill — alongside hospitals, industrial plants, and private homes across Montreal.

narrative_blocks.header: From the Guards to the drafting table
narrative_blocks.body: Home from the war, he took a McGill architecture degree in 1919 and spent three years at Ross & MacDonald before opening his own Montreal practice. The work ran from the Film Trades Building on Monkland Avenue to extensions of the Cadbury chocolate factory, in drawings that explored the young Art Deco style.

narrative_blocks.header: His church became a house for the dying
narrative_blocks.body: St. Raphael the Archangel in Outremont, commissioned in 1932, was his church of concrete and steel clad in fieldstone masonry. Decades later it became Maison St-Raphaël, Montreal's first palliative-care residence.

narrative_blocks.header: An OBE earned across two wars
narrative_blocks.body: The Order of the British Empire recognized his two wars: Great War service with the Canadian Grenadier Guards, then administration of the Montreal War Services Council through the Second.

narrative_blocks.header: The draftsman was a painter too
narrative_blocks.body: He exhibited both paintings and architectural renderings at the Montreal Museum of Fine Arts. His 1930 rendering of the Montreal Boys' Association club house is recorded by the Canadian Grenadier Guards Museum.

narrative_blocks.header: A biplane on floats, built in his garage
narrative_blocks.body: With his brother Bud, Eric spent years riveting together a Durand Mark V biplane, reworking it with its designer, William Durand, to fly on floats. Registered C-FECH, it made its first flight in May 1990 from the beach below his house on Lake Memphremagog.

narrative_blocks.header: A snow plane to race the frozen lake
narrative_blocks.body: A Montreal dentist by trade and an engineer at heart, Eric built his lake boat rather than buy one, then a snow plane, a swamp boat on skis, to race the frozen lake, a catamaran and an ice boat. He learned to fly and built a Coot amphibian before the biplane.

narrative_blocks.header: His plane flies on in Wisconsin
narrative_blocks.body: Eric fell ill with cancer while the biplane's flaps were being reworked and died at Austin in July 2003. C-FECH later went to a new owner in Wisconsin, Jim Swatosh, to be made airworthy again.

narrative_blocks.header: The first comic strip to win a Pulitzer
narrative_blocks.body: He drew Bull Tales for the Yale Daily News in 1968, about the quarterback Brian Dowling. Universal Press syndicated it as Doonesbury the month after he graduated, and in 1975 it took the Pulitzer — the first to a strip.

narrative_blocks.header: The Yale girlfriend behind Joanie Caucus
narrative_blocks.body: Garry came to Yale from an all-male prep school, and his first strips showed it. Dating a woman from three generations of feminists changed him, and out of that crash course came Joanie Caucus, who leaves her husband for law school. Yale's Beinecke Library holds over ten thousand of his papers.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave his page over to deployed soldiers
narrative_blocks.body: After sending his character B.D. home wounded from Iraq he ran The Sandbox for nine years, posting more than eight hundred essays by soldiers, veterans and their families. The Army gave him its Commander's Award.

narrative_blocks.header: Altman filmed his fake campaign for HBO
narrative_blocks.body: He wrote Tanner '88 with Robert Altman, a satire of that year's presidential race that won an Emmy and a gold medal at Cannes. He also wrote a Broadway musical, an Oscar-nominated cartoon, and Alpha House for Amazon.

narrative_blocks.header: One panelist in three guessed who he was
narrative_blocks.body: He kept out of sight. His rare 1971 turn on To Tell the Truth fooled two of the three panelists, and when Newsweek put him on the cover in 1990 it was his first interview in seventeen years.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother left when he was ten
narrative_blocks.body: Garry grew up in Saranac Lake, a town built around the sanatorium his great-grandfather Edward Livingston Trudeau founded, where Robert Louis Stevenson was an early patient. Garry was ten when his mother left; in 1961 his father married Ursula Wyatt Johnston, a Hooker descendant.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the woman on the morning news
narrative_blocks.body: He married the broadcaster Jane Pauley in 1980 and they had three children.

people.research_notes: ORBIT CONNECTION — not Hooker bloodline. Per Sam's direction: 'he's an orbit connection similar to Mark Twain' (not easter_egg). Born Jul 21, 1948 New York City as Garretson Beekman Trudeau. Display name uses common publishing name 'Garry Trudeau'. Biological son of Dr. Francis Berger Trudeau Jr. (I00633, Trudeau Institute founding president) and Jean Moore Amory (his father's first wife). When his father remarried Ursula Wyatt Johnston (HD4195, Hooker descendant) in 1961, Garry was 13 — making the Hooker connection through stepmother rather than biological mother. Yale BA 1970, Yale MFA 1973. Doonesbury debut: Yale Daily News 1968 as 'Bull Tales'; nationally syndicated by Universal Press Syndicate October 26, 1970. 1975 PULITZER PRIZE for Editorial Cartooning — first comic strip to win the prize. Married Jane Pauley (NBC anchor) June 14, 1980; three children: twins Ross + Rickie (b.1983), Tommy (b.1986) — not built per Jalapeño Rule + not Hooker descendants. DOCUMENTED DIRECT INTERACTION WITH HOOKER LINE: August 1994 presented father Francis Jr. with a bronze bust at Trudeau Institute library ceremony (per Francis Jr.'s 1995 obituary). Multiple Saranac Lake visits throughout father's life through 1995. Stepmother Ursula (HD4195) lived Saranac Lake until 2019. CLASSIFICATION: is_thomas_descendant=false, is_easter_egg=false, include_in_path_calculation=false. X-PREFIX. Note: Pierre Trudeau (Canadian PM 1968-1979 + 1980-1984) and Justin Trudeau (Canadian PM 2015-2025) are NOT related to this Trudeau line — they descend from Charles-Émile Trudeau, an entirely separate French-Canadian Trudeau lineage. WIRING CORRECTED 081226: Ursula Wyatt Johnston (HD4195), a tenth-generation Hooker, was recorded as his MOTHER and he was listed among the children of her 1961 marriage to his father. She was his stepmother — her own obituary lists him among 'her stepchildren, Michelle Trudeau, Jeanie Fenn and Garry Trudeau'. His mother was Jean Douglas Moore (1921-2014), his father's first wife, married 1942 and not built. He now hangs from his father alone, with the relational label 'Stepson of a Tenth Generation Hooker'. FamilySearch shows him as '1948-1995', which is wrong — he is living. Full name Garretson Beekman Trudeau; married Jane Pauley 14 June 1980; three children including Ross, a crossword constructor. REBUILT 081226 and flagged an easter egg; display name set to his full Garretson Beekman Trudeau with 'Garry' as the chip name. The two earlier blocks ran 71 and 81 words. Off the card: Hitler Moves East, made with David Levinthal; Rap Master Ronnie; 37 honorary degrees; the Starbucks and Ben & Jerry's literacy tie-ins; the 2015 Polk Award speech on Charlie Hebdo; and the bronze bust he gave his father at the Trudeau Institute in August 1994. [081226] CC to Col. George Bushnell (HD7244) — the better Trudeau link by far, and both halves were already sitting on the two cards. Bushnell's NB2 says the Army handed him its tuberculosis hospital at Fort Bayard and 'he brought Trudeau's system to it'; Garry's own NB5 says his great-grandfather Edward Livingston Trudeau founded the Saranac Lake sanatorium. Nothing new was asserted — the two records were simply never joined.

narrative_blocks.header: Named for grandfather mayor dead a year before
narrative_blocks.body: John Easton Mills Whitney was born July 14, 1848 in Montreal — exactly one year and eight months after his maternal grandfather John Easton Mills died of typhus while serving as Mayor of Montreal during the 1847 Irish famine immigrant crisis. He carried his grandfather's full name forward, married Adele Sherlock, and worked as a leather agent in Montreal continuing his father Nathaniel's leather trade. He died in 1906 at age fifty-seven and was buried at Mount Royal Cemetery.

narrative_blocks.header: Scandalous Montreal society marriage and separation
narrative_blocks.body: Arthur Stevens Whitney married Susan Mary O'Brien October 6, 1892 in Montreal — a wedding that caused a stir because the Protestant groom and Catholic bride crossed Montreal's sharp religious lines. The marriage was short-lived; Susan filed for separation in fall 1895 alleging mistreatment and adultery with the singer Maude Burdette, charges Burdette denied. He later partnered with Emma Maude Dunlop and had a daughter Lucy who died of diphtheria in 1914 at age six; he died in Toronto in 1920 at the Royal Cecil Hotel.

awards.citation: The names of the undermentioned Officers, Warrant Officers, Non-Commissioned Officers and Men have been brought to the notice of the Secretary of State for War, in accordance with the terms of Army Order 193 of 1919, for gallant conduct and determination displayed in escaping or attempting to escape from captivity. Dated 5th May, 1919.

military_service.notes: Reported missing April 28, 1915 — captured by enemy at Staden Belgium during Second Battle of Ypres (when German forces first deployed chlorine gas on Western Front). GSW 3rd finger left hand at capture. POW journey through seven German camps over 3.5 years: Reserve Lazarett Hofgeismar (field hospital, Jun 1915) → Munden (Jul 1915) → Wesel (Nov 1916) → Crefeld (May 1917) → Schwarmstedt (Jul 1917) → Holzminden (Nov 1917). Transferred to neutral Holland for internment via Anglo-German prisoner exchange Mar 18, 1918. Arrived Prince of Wales Hospital London Nov 2, 1918 admitted for effects of gas poisoning. Died of influenza pneumonia Nov 23, 1918 — 12 days post-Armistice — age 26. Buried Family Plot L 8 Range 24 St Jude's Cemetery Oakville. Commemorated at Oakville War Memorial. Mentioned in Despatches 'A' List awarded Jan 30, 1920 (London Gazette Issue 31759) for gallant conduct and determination in escape attempts. Service file B0507-S008 available at LAC. CWGC ID 425227.

cross_connections.display_label: took gas in France and lingered eleven years with it

narrative_blocks.header: Captured Second Ypres 1915, three camps later
narrative_blocks.body: Captain Edward Osler 'Tod' Bath embarked for France April 1, 1915 with the 15th Battalion Canadian Infantry. He was reported missing April 28, 1915 — captured at Staden Belgium during the Second Battle of Ypres, the same campaign in which German forces first deployed chlorine gas on the Western Front. He arrived at his first German camp with a gunshot wound to the third finger of his left hand.

narrative_blocks.header: Mentioned in Despatches for escape attempts
narrative_blocks.body: After Tod Bath's death the British government Mentioned him in Despatches on the 'A' List — published in the London Gazette Issue 31759, January 30, 1920 — for gallant conduct and determination displayed in escaping or attempting to escape from captivity during his three years in German custody. The award placed him among the small group of Canadian officers formally recognized for escape activity in WWI prisoner camps.

narrative_blocks.header: Gas poisoning and flu killed him post-Armistice
narrative_blocks.body: Released to Holland for internment March 18, 1918 and repatriated to England aboard a hospital ship arriving November 2, 1918, he was admitted to Prince of Wales Hospital London for the effects of gas poisoning. He died of influenza and pneumonia at Endsleigh Palace Hospital London on November 23, 1918 — twelve days after the Armistice — at age 26. He was buried in his family plot at St Jude's Cemetery Oakville and is commemorated on the Oakville War Memorial.

people.research_notes:
MAJOR NOTABLE WWI VETERAN — Canadian Great War Project profile. Born Mar 23, 1892 Toronto Ontario; height 66.5 inches (5'6.5"); Church of England; single; pre-war occupation Mortgage Broker. Educated at Upper Canada College and St. Andrew's College Aurora. Captain in 15th Battalion (Canadian Infantry, Central Ontario Regiment), CEF — recruited via the 48th Highlanders of Toronto militia regiment. Embarked France Apr 1, 1915. CAPTURED Staden Belgium Apr 28, 1915 during Second Battle of Ypres (same campaign as first German chlorine gas attacks on Western Front). GSW 3rd finger left hand at capture. POW journey: Hofgeismar (Jun 22, 1915, Reserve Lazarett field hospital) → Munden (Jul 17, 1915) → Wesel (Nov 8, 1916) → Crefeld (May 28, 1917) → Schwarmstedt (Jul 11, 1917) → Holzminden (Nov 2, 1917). Transferred to neutral Holland for internment Mar 18, 1918 via Anglo-German prisoner exchange. Repatriated to England Nov 2, 1918; admitted Prince of Wales Hospital London for gas poisoning effects. Died of influenza pneumonia Nov 23, 1918 at Endsleigh Palace Hospital London age 26 — 12 days post-Armistice. Body returned to Canada; buried St Jude's Cemetery Oakville Family Plot L 8 Range 24. Father Percy A. Bath listed as next of kin. MENTIONED IN DESPATCHES 'A' List awarded Jan 30, 1920 (London Gazette Issue 31759) for 'gallant conduct and determination displayed in escaping or attempting to escape from captivity.' Per Cox & Cos. POW list. Service file B0507-S008 available at LAC; CWGC ID 425227; LAC ID 29046. Memorials: St. Andrew's College, Upper Canada College, St Jude's Anglican Church Memorial, George's Square Town of Oakville Memorial Roll. Photo applied. STAGE 6Y-84 MAJOR ENRICHMENT.

He was reported missing April 28, 1915 — captured at Staden Belgium during the Second Battle of Ypres, the same campaign in which German forces first deployed chlorine gas on the Western Front. He arrived at his first German camp with a gunshot wound to the third finger of his left hand. narrative_blocks.header: He took Montreal's Black Watch to France
narrative_blocks.body: In 1914 George raised the 42nd Battalion of the Royal Highlanders of Canada, Montreal's Black Watch, and took it to France as its first commanding officer. He led it until the end of 1916 and won the Distinguished Service Order that December.

narrative_blocks.header: What the Black Watch of Canada was
narrative_blocks.body: The Black Watch of Canada was Montreal's Highland regiment, raised in 1862 by six of the city's Scottish chieftains when the American Civil War made Canada fear for its border. Its men wore the dark Government tartan and a red hackle, and some twelve thousand of them served in the First World War.

narrative_blocks.header: Pressed flowers for his baby daughter
narrative_blocks.body: Through 1915 and 1916 George pressed flowers from the fields where his men camped into letters to his daughter Celia, not yet two when he sailed, so she would have something of him if he did not come back. Ten of his Somme letters, with their daisies, poppies and heather, became the Canadian War Museum's War Flowers exhibition.

narrative_blocks.header: Sent home worn out in 1918
narrative_blocks.body: After the Somme George organized the 20th Reserve Battalion and commanded it until 1918, when battle fatigue sent him home to Montreal.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventy years in uniform, honoured at eighty-eight
narrative_blocks.body: He joined the Royal Highlanders of Canada in 1885 and was made lieutenant-colonel in 1906. He was the regiment's honorary colonel when it marked his seventy years of service in 1955, and he died the next year.

narrative_blocks.header: Beatrice Campbell and five children
narrative_blocks.body: He married the daughter of the seigneur du Bic, and they had one son and four daughters at 502 Sherbrooke Street West in Montreal. She died in 1923 and he outlived her by thirty-three years.

narrative_blocks.header: His son inherited the regiment and lost it
narrative_blocks.body: Stephen Douglas Cantlie took the Black Watch in January 1942 and was relieved fifteen months later as short of tactical knowledge. A regimental history calls him le Dauphin, carrying a double yoke.

people.research_notes: EASTER EGG: per Sam — 'easter egg parent of non hooker spouse notable'. Notable URL: americanaristocracy.com/people/george-stephen-cantlie. WWI: Original commanding officer of 42nd Battalion (Royal Highlanders of Canada / Black Watch), CEF 1914-1916. Distinguished Service Order awarded Dec 29, 1916/Jan 1, 1917 (London Gazette). Then organized + commanded 20th Reserve Battalion 1916-1918. Sent home 1917 with 'battle fatigue.' Service file: B1473-S056. Five children including Giana (his daughter who married into the Hooker tree) and Celia (the 1913-born baby of the war flowers letters). The 'Dear Wee Celia' War Flowers letters: 300+ written 1915-1916; ten to Celia with pressed daisies, poppies, yellow roses, heather form the basis of the touring Canadian War Museum exhibition curated by Viveka Melki with Reford Gardens. Cantlie survived war. Died 1956 age 89. Photo applied. is_easter_egg=true. career.notes: Apprenticed as stonemason in Edinburgh under George Drummond — expert stone mason, successful building contractor, Edinburgh City Council member. Fellow apprentice was Drummond's brother Robert.

Came to Canada 1816 under British Government's emigration scheme to employ returning veterans from the Napoleonic Wars. Worked as a mason on the Lachine Canal (Montreal) and the Rideau Canal (Ottawa) — two of British North America's most important early infrastructure projects.

Built Canada's first sugar refinery in 1854, importing sugar cane from the West Indies on his own ships. The company became Redpath Sugar — still operating today, now owned by American Sugar Refining.

narrative_blocks.header: Canada's first sugar refinery, 1854
narrative_blocks.body: In his late fifties, already rich from contracting, John began Canada's first sugar refinery on the Lachine Canal in 1854. His ships, the Helen Drummond and the Grace Redpath, named for his daughters, brought the raw sugar in from the West Indies.

narrative_blocks.header: He built the locks of the Lachine Canal
narrative_blocks.body: With Thomas McKay, John supplied the stone for the new Notre-Dame Church and built the locks of the Lachine Canal, opened in 1825. In 1827 and 1828 the two built the locks at Jones Falls on the Rideau Canal, the largest works anywhere on that line.

narrative_blocks.header: He wanted Canada to join the United States
narrative_blocks.body: A director of the Bank of Montreal from 1833 until he died, John was president in 1849 of the Montreal Annexation Association, which asked that Canada join the United States. He warned its members that thousands of skilled Canadian artisans were leaving for the States.

narrative_blocks.header: He took on the trade in immigrant women
narrative_blocks.body: A Free Church Presbyterian, John led a small group that pressed the government to act against the traffic in poor immigrant women, working through Montreal's Magdalen Asylum. He helped found the Protestant House of Industry and Refuge.

narrative_blocks.header: He walked barefoot from Quebec City
narrative_blocks.body: John trained as a stonemason under George Drummond in Edinburgh and left Scotland in 1816, at twenty, with only enough for his passage as far as Quebec City. He walked the rest of the way to Montreal, barefoot.

narrative_blocks.header: Terrace Bank, on the slope of Mount Royal
narrative_blocks.body: In 1836 John bought 235 acres on the mountain from the Desrivières heirs of James McGill's wife. He gave the old house to his daughter Elizabeth Dougall and built Terrace Bank for himself. Rue Redpath and Place Redpath still cross the ground.

narrative_blocks.header: Two sons married the Mills sisters
narrative_blocks.body: John had seventeen children by his two wives. Two of the sons, John James and George, married Ada and Alice Mills, daughters of the late mayor John Easton Mills, in England in 1867.

career.notes: Came to Meadville 1826 (then a comparatively new and unsettled region) due to delicate health requiring a change of climate. For many years had to ride on horseback to all parts of Crawford County, largely through forests where 'blazed' trees (marked by the axe) were the only guides. Practiced for nearly 60 years until his death. The oldest practicing physician in Meadville at his death.
Organized the Crawford County Medical Society at Meadville PA in 1832 and served as its first President for many years.

narrative_blocks.header: Blazed trees were his only guides
narrative_blocks.body: Edward came to Meadville in 1826, at twenty-two, because his health was delicate and he needed a change of climate. For years he rode on horseback to every corner of Crawford County, often through forest where trees blazed with an axe were his only guides.

narrative_blocks.header: Still practicing at eighty-one
narrative_blocks.body: Edward practiced in Meadville for nearly sixty years, and at eighty-one he was still seeing patients, his strength remarkable and his health unimpaired. He died in May 1885 after a short bout of pneumonia, the oldest practicing physician in town.

narrative_blocks.header: A fortune lost on Meadville's factories
narrative_blocks.body: Edward put a large fortune into Meadville manufacturing and other ventures that promised to make the town prosper, and lost all of it. He had already helped many young men through school and set others up in business, and the losses never soured his cheerful temper.

narrative_blocks.header: Twice widowed by forty
narrative_blocks.body: Edward married a widow, Mary Kennedy, in April 1832, and she died in 1840. In March 1842 he married Sarah Buchanan of Meadville, who died in March 1844, a year after the birth of their daughter Elizabeth, and he never married again.

narrative_blocks.header: Five brothers, each six feet tall
narrative_blocks.body: Edward was one of nine children of Ebenezer Ellis, a Chester farmer whose five sons all stood six feet or more. Edward's grandfather Samuel Ellis had fought in the French and Indian War and the Revolution.

Aided many young men obtain education + established others in business. Largely interested in manufacturing + other Meadville enterprises that turned out unfortunate — total loss of his large property. Losses 'neither lessened the cheerfulness of his temper nor his kindness of heart.' Died Saturday May 2, 1885 Meadville age 81 of short illness of pneumonia. Sincerely regretted by large circle. Burial cemetery not specified in available sources. STAGE 6Y-86 CORRECTIONS: Birthplace corrected to Cheshire Berkshire Co MA per Salisbury 1885 family bio (not Chester Hampshire). Attended school at Windsor CT in 1818 (mother's hometown). Graduated Berkshire Medical College Dec 16, 1829. FIRST PRESIDENT Crawford County Medical Society organized 1832 at Meadville PA; held office many years. Horseback practice through 'blazed' tree forests — extraordinary frontier medical practice.
[Stage 6Y-264 NB#1 body trim]: original body had 4 sentences, trimmed to first 3. Original body preserved here for reference: 'Dr. Edward Ellis came west to Meadville Pennsylvania in 1826 at age twenty-two — then a comparatively new and unsettled region — because of delicate health requiring a change of climate. For many years he rode on horseback to all parts of Crawford County, often through forests where blazed trees marked by the axe were his only guides. He practiced medicine there for nearly sixty years and was the oldest practicing physician in Meadville at his death in 1885. In 1832 he organized the Crawford County Medical Society and served as its first President for many years.'
[Stage 6Y-264 NB#2 body trim]: original body had 4 sentences, trimmed to first 3. Original body preserved here for reference: 'Edward Ellis was twice widowed — his first wife Mary M. Kennedy died in 1840 after eight years of marriage, and his second wife Sarah Buchanan died in 1844 after only two years. From his second marriage came one daughter Elizabeth Ruth, who in 1864 married Rev. Marison Byllesby — then Rector of Christ Church Meadville, the same parish where Edward Ellis served as Warden and Vestryman. He lost his large property in unsuccessful manufacturing investments but his losses 'neither lessened the cheerfulness of his temper nor his kindness of heart.''

narrative_blocks.header: Wounded at Spotsylvania, dead at Fredericksburg
narrative_blocks.body: He went into the Overland Campaign with Company K of the 1st Massachusetts Heavy Artillery, a garrison regiment sent to the field that spring. He was wounded at Spotsylvania Court House and died in the hospital depot at Fredericksburg on the twenty-second of May, 1864.

narrative_blocks.header: Two children left with no one
narrative_blocks.body: Their eldest, Elbert, had died in his first year in 1851. So when Luthena went in 1861 and he went in Virginia in 1864, the two left were Asahel at eleven and Katie at five.

narrative_blocks.header: His body came home to Norwich Hill
narrative_blocks.body: They brought him back to the burying ground at Huntington, where he had been born on the last days of 1825. Luthena was already there, and Katie would follow at thirteen in 1872.

narrative_blocks.body: His mother died at Northampton when he was eight. His father was killed at Fredericksburg in May 1864, and he was raised out from under both of them.

narrative_blocks.body: He came to Manistee as a salesman in another man's drug store and by 1879 owned it. He bought up four rival shops, moved twice into bigger rooms on River Street, and in 1894 incorporated the whole thing as the A. H. Lyman Company.

narrative_blocks.body: He fell ill in the first week of January 1896, pneumonia set in, and he was dead on the sixteenth at forty-two. His minister told the funeral he had been leaned on heavily and loved by all.

Julia is Talcott descendant via her mother Julia Hobart Barnard (TD0128) + grandmother Betsey Perrin Hobart (TD0120). No children documented for Asahel + Julia in current sources. Migrated to Manistee MI. Died 1896 Manistee Township Manistee Co MI age 42-43. Buried Oak Grove Cemetery Manistee — same cemetery as uncle Dr. Lathrop Stiles Ellis (HD4244) who would die 1900 + aunt Sarah Weston Harmon Ellis (I00657) who would die 1906. CONFLICT, 2026-07-29, from the Manistee County history of A. H. Lyman: it states plainly that 'The Lymans and their two daughters lived at 453 Third Street in Manistee.' This record and Julia's both said she was left a CHILDLESS widow and both marriages carry an empty children_ids. Two daughters are unnamed and unbuilt. The childless claim is removed from the prose pending a name for either girl.
AGE CORRECTED: born 17 Apr 1853, died 16 Jan 1896 = FORTY-TWO, not the forty-three both blocks carried.
Same source: Massachusetts Agricultural College 1873; College of Physicians and Surgeons, New York; salesman for Carleton & Company, sole owner by 1879 at 401 River Street, 427 River Street from 1885, later also 425; incorporated 1894; deacon of the Congregational church and a Mason; married Julia Barnard at Westminster, Vermont, in 1878; funeral sermon by Rev. A. M. Brodie.
NOT HIS FATHER: the Sheboygan County, Wisconsin biography of ASAHEL P. LYMAN (b. 1814 Brookfield NY, son of another Asahel and Dolly Blair, Great Lakes shipowner) is an unrelated man. This Asahel's father was John Burt Lyman Jr. (I00663, 1825-1864), killed at Fredericksburg. The two daughters are built: Alice L Lyman (HD8456) and Carrie Lyman (HD8457). The childless-widow claim on both cards was wrong and has been removed.

narrative_blocks.header: She went back east and stayed thirty-three years
narrative_blocks.body: Asahel Lyman died at Manistee in January 1896 and she left Michigan for good. She lived another thirty-three years and died at Greenville, New Hampshire, in 1929, buried at Pleasant Street Cemetery a long way from his grave at Oak Grove.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father was named for a missionary
narrative_blocks.body: Pliny Fisk was one of the first two American missionaries sent to Palestine, and his mother was a Barnard. He sailed in 1819 and died at Beirut in 1825; the Barnard boy born in 1820 carried his whole name into a Congregational pulpit of his own.

people.research_notes: Per FA #168075415. Born 1853 Vermont — youngest of Rev. Pliny Fisk Barnard (X02369, 1820-1908) + Julia Hobart Barnard (TD0128, 1819-1908)'s three daughters. Talcott descendant via mother TD0128 (who descended from Betsey Perrin Hobart TD0120 — Talcott line via Perrin family). m. Asahel Hubert Lyman (HD4267, Hooker descendant via Luthena Ellis Lyman HD4245) — FIRST DOCUMENTED HOOKER-TALCOTT CROSS-LINE MARRIAGE in the project. No children documented. Widowed 1896. Returned east after husband's Michigan death. Died 1929 Greenville Hillsborough Co NH age 75-76. Buried Pleasant Street Cemetery Greenville. Same first name as her mother — common Victorian-era naming continuation. See HD4267 research_notes: the Manistee source names TWO DAUGHTERS of this marriage, against the childless-widow claim this card carried. Both girls unnamed and unbuilt. Her husband was 42 at death, not 43. RESOLVED 2026-07-29: the two daughters the Manistee history referred to are Alice L Lyman (HD8456, 1884-1943) and Carrie Lyman (HD8457, b.1886), both born at Manistee. Alice is buried at Pleasant Street Cemetery, Greenville NH, the same ground as her mother — Julia took the girls east with her after 1896. Carrie married Ernest Fremont Robinson at 24 Aug 1916; no children recorded for either daughter.

narrative_blocks.header: Twin daughters lost in 1851
narrative_blocks.body: Noah married Hannah Ellis of Norwich at Huntington in January 1839 and spent his life in Chester. Their twin daughters, Mary and Martha, both died in 1851, and their daughter Sarah at twenty-four in 1871; Hannah died in 1876, and Noah lived on at Chester until January 1881.

people.research_notes: Per FA #49595886 (cross-referenced with FA #49596323 for father Noah Sr.). Born 1811 Chester Hampden Co MA. Father Noah Ellis Sr. (1769-1828); grandfather Samuel Ellis (1739-1826) of Chester, French and Indian + Revolutionary War veteran. m. Hannah Ellis (HD4239) Jan 14, 1839 Huntington MA — both grandchildren of Samuel Ellis. Per Vital Records of Chester MA, separate listing shows them marrying at Chester Feb 20, 1839 (likely a second civil/church recording). Four children: HD4269 John C. (1840-1915), HD4270 Sarah (1846-1871 age 24 unmarried), HD4271 Mary + HD4272 Martha E. (twins, both died 1851). Lived Chester all his married life. Died Jan 10, 1881 Chester age 69-70. Buried Eastman Cemetery Chester. Within-Ellis-family cousin marriages were a recurring pattern in the close-knit Hampden-Hampshire Co MA hill towns.
