narrative_blocks.header: From the Pithole oil boom to Meadville
narrative_blocks.body: John was living in Venango County when the Frazier Well struck oil in January 1865 and turned the neighborhood into Pithole City. When the boomtown died he moved on to Meadville, where his uncle Dr. Edward Ellis had practiced medicine since 1826, and lived there the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: Two wives dead before thirty
narrative_blocks.body: John's first wife, Lois Hibbard, died at twenty-four in 1871, five days before their daughter Florence turned seven; his second, Elsie Ann Jolly, died at twenty-six in 1885, a year after their son John Clarence was born. In 1900, at sixty, he married a widow, Mrs. Florence Ellis.

people.research_notes: Per FA #122971127. Born Jul 5, 1840 Chester Hampden Co MA — only son of Hannah Ellis Ellis (HD4239) + her first cousin Noah Ellis (I00664). PITHOLE CITY ERA: Living in the forested farmland of Venango Co PA when daughter Florence Hannah was born Jul 12, 1864 — six months before the Jan 1865 Frazier Well oil strike that turned the area into Pithole City. Pithole became one of Pennsylvania's most spectacular oil-boom towns: at peak ~15,000 residents, 50+ hotels, 3 churches, daily newspaper, and the 3rd-busiest post office in PA. By 1870 the wells had run dry and the town collapsed — sold for $4.50 in 1878 versus millions at peak. The Ellis family was there before the boom and left during the bust. Migrated to Meadville Crawford Co PA — where his maternal great-uncle Dr. Edward Ellis MD (HD4235) had been practicing medicine for ~40 years (1826-1885). Edward's two deceased wives Mary Kennedy (d.1840) + Sarah Buchanan (d.1844) were buried at Greendale Cemetery Meadville — establishing the family burial ground that John and his daughter Florence Hannah would also be buried in. Three marriages, all ending in widowhood for him: m1 Lois Olive Hibbard (I00665, 1846-1871 died age 24) — one daughter HD4273 Florence Hannah Ellis McFarland (1864-1933, born Pithole City). m2 Elsie Ann Jolly (I00666, 1859-1885 died age 25-26) — one son HD4274 John Clarence Ellis (1884-1977 age 93). m3 Mrs. Florence Ellis (I00667, unknown-1930) m. 1900 when John was 60. Died Sep 28, 1915 Meadville Crawford Co PA age 75. Buried Greendale Cemetery Meadville with first wife Lois Olive Hibbard.

Per FA #49595886. Born 1846 Chester MA — second of Hannah + Noah Ellis's four children. Died unmarried 1871 age 24. Cause of death undocumented; burial undocumented. Coincidence with sister-in-law Lois Olive Hibbard's death the same year suggests possible epidemic or shared cause — not confirmable from available sources.

Per FA #49596395. Born and died 1851 Chester MA — twin sister of Martha E. Ellis (HD4272). Both twin girls died as infants in 1851. Twin loss is rare and devastating; the Ellis family's grief that year compounded by Hannah's also losing access to the support of her aging father Ebenezer Ellis (then 78).
Per FA #49596467. Born and died 1851 Chester MA — twin sister of Mary Ellis (HD4271). Both twin girls died as infants in 1851.

burial.plot_notes: Greendale Cemetery, Meadville Crawford County PA.

narrative_blocks.header: Died at twenty-four, daughter not yet seven
narrative_blocks.body: Lois Olive Hibbard died on July 7, 1871 at age twenty-four — five days before her only daughter Florence Hannah would have turned seven. The same year her sister-in-law Sarah Ellis also died unmarried at twenty-four in Massachusetts, suggesting possible epidemic conditions. Lois left her husband John Ellis a widower with their young daughter, who would grow up in Meadville visiting her mother's grave at Greendale Cemetery.

people.research_notes: Per FA #155960517. Born Aug 2, 1846; died Jul 7, 1871 age 24 — FIVE DAYS before only daughter Florence Hannah's 7th birthday (Florence b. Jul 12, 1864 at Pithole City PA). Buried Greendale Cemetery Meadville. m. John C. Ellis (HD4269) sometime ~1863. Coincidence with sister-in-law Sarah Ellis (HD4270) dying same year at same age 24 — possible epidemic or shared cause; not confirmable from current sources. Cause of death undocumented.

burial.plot_notes: McDowell Cemetery, Dicksonburg Crawford County PA.

narrative_blocks.header: Died young like first wife, leaving infant son
narrative_blocks.body: Elsie Ann Jolly Ellis died February 26, 1885 at twenty-six — almost the same young age at which John Ellis's first wife Lois Olive Hibbard had died fourteen years earlier. She left their only child John Clarence at just over a year old. Both of John's young wives are buried in Crawford County Pennsylvania but in separate cemeteries — Elsie at McDowell Dicksonburg, Lois at Greendale Meadville.

people.research_notes: Per FA #176242862. Born 1859; died Feb 26, 1885 age 25-26. Second wife of John C. Ellis (HD4269); m. ~1883. One son: John Clarence Ellis (HD4274, 1884-1977 age 93) — born ~1 year before her death. Buried McDowell Cemetery Dicksonburg Crawford Co PA — separate from her husband's first wife at Greendale Meadville. Cause of death undocumented. The parallel of John C.'s two young wives dying at 24 and 26 respectively (separated by 14 years) is biographically striking.

narrative_blocks.header: Third wife, married John when he was sixty
narrative_blocks.body: Mrs. Florence Ellis married John Ellis in 1900 — his third marriage after twice being widowed of young wives, and his first marriage after the age of forty. Her courtesy title 'Mrs.' with the Ellis surname suggests she was already a widow before this marriage, possibly carrying the surname from a prior Ellis husband. She outlived John by fifteen years, dying in 1930.

people.research_notes: Per FA #122971137. Birth year unknown; died 1930. m. John C. Ellis (HD4269) in 1900 when he was 60 — his third marriage. The fact that she was already 'Mrs. Florence Ellis' before marrying John C. Ellis is striking — likely a widow of a prior Ellis husband (possibly a more distant cousin in the extensive Crawford Co PA Ellis network). No children documented with John C. Outlived him by 15 years. Burial location undocumented.

marriages.spouse_research_notes: Harmon Demmington Unger (I00668, 1857 MN - 1894 PA) — four children born to this marriage: Rush John Unger (1882), Bertha Mae Unger Young (1884), Ransom Andrew Unger (1888), Irvin Clarence Unger (1889). Children to be built Stage 6Y-91.

naming_inspiration.description: Middle name Hannah honors her paternal grandmother Hannah Ellis Ellis (1812-1876), who was alive at her birth and likely her godmother.

narrative_blocks.header: Born where Pithole boomed and died
narrative_blocks.body: Florence was born on 12 July 1864 at what became Pithole City, six months before the Frazier Well struck oil in January 1865. Within months the place had fifteen thousand people, fifty hotels and the third-busiest post office in Pennsylvania; by 1870 the wells had run dry.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at seventeen, widowed at twenty-nine
narrative_blocks.body: Florence lost her mother five days before her seventh birthday, married Harmon Unger in 1881 at seventeen and had four children by him. Harmon died in January 1894 at thirty-six, and the next year she married Reuben Bishop McFarland, who outlived her by five years.

people.research_notes: Per FA #122739545. Born Jul 12, 1864 PITHOLE CITY Venango Co PA — six months before the January 1865 Frazier Well oil strike that turned the area into one of Pennsylvania's most spectacular boomtowns. By the time Florence was a small child, Pithole had boomed to ~15,000 residents and collapsed back to ghost-town status. Only daughter of John C. Ellis (HD4269) + Lois Olive Hibbard (I00665). Mother died Jul 7, 1871 age 24 — five days before Florence's 7th birthday. Father remarried Elsie Ann Jolly (1883) who died Feb 26, 1885 — Florence had a half-brother John Clarence Ellis (HD4274) at this point. m1 Harmon Demmington Unger (I00668, 1857 MN - 1894 PA) 1881 age 17. Four Unger children born 1882-1889: Rush John, Bertha Mae, Ransom Andrew, Irvin Clarence (children built Stage 6Y-91). Widowed at 30 when Harmon died Jan 29, 1894 age 36. m2 Reuben Bishop McFarland (I00669, 1845-1938) 1895 — no documented McFarland children. Died Nov 20, 1933 Meadville Crawford Co PA age 69. Buried Greendale Cemetery Meadville — with father John Ellis and first husband Harmon Unger. Middle name Hannah honored her paternal grandmother Hannah Ellis Ellis (HD4239).

burial.plot_notes: Greendale Cemetery, Meadville Crawford County PA — with father-in-law John Ellis and wife Florence Hannah Ellis Unger McFarland.

narrative_blocks.header: Minnesota-born settler died Pennsylvania at thirty-six
narrative_blocks.body: Harmon Demmington Unger was born March 24, 1857 in Minnesota — far from his eventual Pennsylvania home — and migrated east to Crawford County, where he married Florence Hannah Ellis in 1881. They had four children between 1882 and 1889. He died in Pennsylvania on January 29, 1894 at thirty-six, leaving Florence widowed with four children aged five to twelve.

people.research_notes: Per FA #122331045. Born Mar 24, 1857 Minnesota — unusual Minnesota birth for the era (Minnesota became a state only in 1858, the year after his birth). Migrated to Crawford Co PA at some point and married Florence Hannah Ellis (HD4273) in 1881. Four children born 1882-1889: Rush John Unger, Bertha Mae Unger Young, Ransom Andrew Unger, Irvin Clarence Unger (to be built Stage 6Y-91). Died Jan 29, 1894 Pennsylvania age 36. Cause of death undocumented. Buried Greendale Cemetery Meadville with father-in-law John Ellis.

narrative_blocks.header: Outlived wife by five years, died ninety-three
narrative_blocks.body: Reuben Bishop McFarland married Florence Hannah Ellis Unger in 1895, the year after her first husband Harmon Unger had died — he was fifty at the marriage and she was thirty with four small Unger children. They had no children together. He outlived her by five years, dying in 1938 at age ninety-three.

people.research_notes: Per FA #79550617. Born 1845; died 1938 age 92-93 — extraordinary_longevity tag applies. Second husband of Florence Hannah Ellis McFarland (HD4273); m. 1895 the year after her first husband Harmon Unger died. He was 50 at marriage, she was 30 with four small Unger children. No documented McFarland children. Burial location undocumented. Florence's children kept the Unger surname rather than taking McFarland — consistent with their being old enough to have established Unger identities by the time of the second marriage.

narrative_blocks.header: Lost mother at one, lived to ninety-three
narrative_blocks.body: John Clarence Ellis was born October 5, 1884 at Meadville Pennsylvania to John Ellis's second wife Elsie Ann Jolly, who died of unknown causes when he was just over a year old. Despite this early loss he lived to ninety-three, dying December 15, 1977 at Conneautville Crawford County Pennsylvania — sixty-two years after his father.

narrative_blocks.header: Married Gertha Walton in 1904, sixty-nine years
narrative_blocks.body: John Clarence married Gertha Walton in 1904 when both were young — they would remain married for sixty-nine years until her death in 1973. Their only known son Carmen served in World War II. The family is buried at Conneautville Cemetery north of Meadville rather than at Greendale where his father, half-sister, and step-grandfather lie.

people.research_notes: Per FA #124173755. Born Oct 5, 1884 Meadville Crawford Co PA — only son of John C. Ellis (HD4269) + 2nd wife Elsie Ann Jolly (I00666). Mother died Feb 26, 1885 when he was just over 1 year old. Raised at Meadville by widowed father (with half-sister Florence Hannah Ellis Unger McFarland 20 years older, married out by 1881). m. Gertha E. Walton Ellis (b. Feb 22, 1885 Summerhill Twp Crawford Co - d. Nov 25, 1973 Meadville age 88) 1904. 69-year marriage. Son Carmen A. Ellis (1920-1997, WWII veteran). Died Dec 15, 1977 Conneautville Crawford Co PA age 93. extraordinary_longevity tag applies. Buried Conneautville Cemetery — north of Meadville, distinct from the Greendale Cemetery Meadville family plot. Wife + son + downstream descendants to be built Stage 6Y-91+.

marriages.spouse_research_notes: Mary Elizabeth Curry Unger (I00670, 1884-1981 age 96). Sons Robert Harmon Unger (1910-2011 age 101) + Harold Alison 'Tubby' Unger (1916-2002 WWII vet) to be built later.

narrative_blocks.header: Eldest child, twelve when father died young
narrative_blocks.body: Rush John Unger was born June 1, 1882 in Geneva Crawford County Pennsylvania to seventeen-year-old Florence Hannah Ellis and her young Minnesota-born husband Harmon Demmington Unger. He was twelve when his father died at thirty-six in 1894, leaving him the eldest of four siblings — the youngest just five — in his widowed mother's household. Florence remarried Reuben McFarland the following year.

narrative_blocks.header: Both spouses lived past eighty in Meadville
narrative_blocks.body: Rush married Mary Elizabeth Curry of Meadville in 1906 — they would be married for sixty years until his death in 1966. Mary outlived him by fifteen years and reached ninety-six. Their two sons would also live extraordinarily long: Robert reached one hundred and one, Harold reached eighty-five.

people.research_notes: Per FA #179441695. Born Jun 1, 1882 Geneva Crawford Co PA — eldest of Florence Hannah Ellis (HD4273) + Harmon Demmington Unger (I00668)'s four children. Father died at 36 in 1894 when Rush was 12. m. Mary Elizabeth Curry of Meadville 1906 (I00670, 1884-1981 age 96 extraordinary_longevity). Two sons: Robert Harmon Unger (1910-2011 age 101 extraordinary_longevity, Talon engineering dept 40 yrs, owned Unger's Antique Shop Kerrtown PA), Harold Alison 'Tubby' Unger (1916-2002 WWII veteran S Sgt US Army). Died Dec 15, 1966 Meadville age 84. Buried Roselawn Memorial Gardens Meadville. STRIKING DETAIL: Rush died Dec 15, 1966 — his younger sister Bertha Mae's birthday (Dec 15, 1884). She had predeceased him by 7 years.

burial.plot_notes: Greendale Cemetery, Meadville Crawford County PA — body returned from Florida.

marriages.spouse_research_notes: Freeman Delbert Lybarger (I00671, 1874 MN - 1913 PA). Two confirmed sons: Freeman Wilbur Lybarger (1906-1988, WWII vet), Irvin Clarence Lybarger (1908-1973). Per Gertrude Winger's 2014 obit there may have been additional siblings: 'Chester, Irvin, and Wilbur Lybarger' — Chester (and possibly others) to be researched. Children built later stages.

Silas Howard Young (I00672, 1873-1953). Multiple children — confirmed Gertrude Virginia Young Winger (1926-2014); per Gertrude's obit also Joseph, Noble, Leah, Austin, Reno, David Young, Lois Stanley, Paul Young, Dortha Free. Children to be built later stages.

narrative_blocks.header: Twice widowed, ended life far from home
narrative_blocks.body: Bertha Mae Unger was widowed twice — first when Freeman Delbert Lybarger died in 1913 at thirty-nine, then when second husband Silas Howard Young died in 1953 after twenty-eight years of marriage. She moved south to Florida in her later years and died in Hollywood Broward County in 1959 at seventy-four. Her body was returned to Meadville and buried at Greendale Cemetery.

narrative_blocks.header: Two husbands, many children across both marriages
narrative_blocks.body: Bertha's first marriage to Freeman Lybarger produced at least two confirmed sons before his 1913 death — Freeman Wilbur (1906) and Irvin Clarence (1908). Her second marriage to Silas Young in 1925 produced multiple Young children including Gertrude Virginia born 1926. Per a later family obituary at least ten siblings spanned the two marriages — many remain unbuilt pending research.

people.research_notes: Per FA #122304456. Born Dec 15, 1884 Meadville Crawford Co PA. m1 Freeman Delbert Lybarger (I00671, 1874-1913) 1902 — at least 2 confirmed sons: Freeman Wilbur Lybarger (1906-1988 WWII vet), Irvin Clarence Lybarger (1908-1973). Widowed 1913. m2 Silas Howard Young (I00672, 1873-1953) 1925 — multiple Young children; confirmed daughter Gertrude Virginia Young Winger (1926-2014). marriages.spouse_research_notes: Matilda E Shadley Unger (I00673, 1889-1978). Four children: Florence F Unger McGraw (1915-2013 age 97), Elvira M Unger (1916-1918 toddler death in 1918 pandemic), Viola M Unger (1921-2011), Rita M Unger Minnis (1923-2011). Children to be built later stages.

narrative_blocks.header: Lost two-year-old daughter Elvira to 1918 pandemic
narrative_blocks.body: Ransom Unger and his wife Matilda lost their second daughter Elvira at age two in 1918 — the year of the global influenza pandemic that killed more Americans than World War I. Their three other daughters all lived into their eighties or nineties: Florence to ninety-seven, Viola to ninety, Rita to eighty-eight. The pandemic was particularly devastating for healthy young adults and children.

narrative_blocks.header: Left Meadville for Erie, died there at eighty-eight
narrative_blocks.body: Ransom was born in Vernon Township Crawford County in 1888, three years before his father Harmon's death. Sometime after marrying Matilda Shadley he moved north to Erie Pennsylvania, where their later daughters were born and where the couple lived until death. He died October 9, 1976 at Erie at eighty-eight.

people.research_notes: Per FA #102376331. Born Feb 14, 1888 Vernon Twp Crawford Co PA (Valentine's Day) — third of Florence Hannah Ellis (HD4273) + Harmon Demmington Unger (I00668)'s four children. m. Matilda E Shadley (I00673, 1889 Meadville - 1978 Erie). Four children: Florence F McGraw (1915-2013 age 97), Elvira M (1916-1918 died age 2 during 1918 INFLUENZA PANDEMIC), Viola M (1921-2011), Rita M Minnis (1923-2011). Family migrated from Meadville to Erie at some point. Died Oct 9, 1976 Erie Erie Co PA age 88. Buried Trinity Cemetery Erie.

narrative_blocks.header: Youngest brother outlived all siblings to ninety-eight
narrative_blocks.body: Irvin Clarence Unger was the youngest of Florence Hannah's four Unger children — only five years old when his father Harmon died at thirty-six in 1894. He outlived all three older siblings to die in 1987 at ninety-eight. The Unger-Curry generation produced extraordinary longevity across the family: nephew Robert Unger reached one hundred and one, sister-in-law Mary Curry Unger reached ninety-six.

people.research_notes: Per FA #179441597. Born 1889 Crawford Co PA — youngest of Florence Hannah Ellis (HD4273) + Harmon Demmington Unger (I00668)'s four children. Father died in 1894 when Irvin was just 5 years old. Died 1987 age 97-98. extraordinary_longevity. Outlived all three siblings: Rush d.1966, Bertha d.1959, Ransom d.1976. Marriage status and children undocumented in current sources. Burial location undocumented.

burial.plot_notes: Roselawn Memorial Gardens, Meadville Crawford County PA.

narrative_blocks.header: Ninety-six years in a single Pennsylvania county
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Elizabeth Curry was born February 5, 1884 in Meadville Pennsylvania and died there January 24, 1981 — ninety-six years in a single Pennsylvania county. She married Rush John Unger in 1906 and they were married for sixty years until his death in 1966. She outlived her husband by fifteen years.

people.research_notes: Per FA #179441719. Born Feb 5, 1884 Meadville; died Jan 24, 1981 Meadville age 96. extraordinary_longevity. m. Rush John Unger (HD4275) 1906 — 60-year marriage. Two sons: Robert Harmon (1910-2011 age 101), Harold Alison 'Tubby' (1916-2002 WWII vet). Buried Roselawn Memorial Gardens Meadville with husband. Lived her entire 96-year life in Crawford County PA.

burial.plot_notes: Greendale Cemetery, Meadville Crawford County PA — with father-in-law Harmon Unger's Greendale-buried Ellis-Unger family.

narrative_blocks.header: Minnesota-born like his wife's late father Harmon
narrative_blocks.body: Freeman Delbert Lybarger was born April 14, 1874 in Fairfield Swift County Minnesota — by uncanny coincidence the same state where his wife Bertha's father Harmon Demmington Unger had been born seventeen years earlier. Both Minnesota-born men migrated east to Crawford County Pennsylvania, married into the Ellis-Unger family, and died young in Pennsylvania. Freeman died at thirty-nine in Warren PA on September 20, 1913.

people.research_notes: Per FA #122781802. Born Apr 14, 1874 Fairfield Swift Co MN. STRIKING COINCIDENCE: Both Bertha Mae's father (Harmon Demmington Unger, b.1857 MN) and her first husband (Freeman Delbert Lybarger, b.1874 MN) were Minnesota-born men who migrated east to Crawford Co PA, married into the Ellis-Unger family, and died young in Pennsylvania (Harmon at 36 in 1894, Freeman at 39 in 1913). m. Bertha Mae Unger 1902. Two sons (possibly more): Freeman Wilbur Lybarger (1906-1988 WWII vet), Irvin Clarence Lybarger (1908-1973). Per Gertrude Winger's obit possibly also a Chester Lybarger. Died Sep 20, 1913 Warren Warren Co PA age 39. Buried Greendale Cemetery Meadville. Cause of death undocumented.

narrative_blocks.header: Born Lancaster Pennsylvania, far from family base
narrative_blocks.body: Rita was born April 27, 1923 in Lancaster County Pennsylvania — surprising given her family's deep roots in Crawford and Venango counties on the western side of the state. Her parents Ransom and Matilda may have been traveling or temporarily living in Lancaster around her birth. She would eventually return there after her 1946 marriage to Donald Minnis.

narrative_blocks.header: Married Armistice Day 1946, six children spread cross-country
narrative_blocks.body: Rita married Donald M. Minnis on November 11, 1946 — Armistice Day, which would be renamed Veterans Day eight years later in 1954. They had six children: three sons and three daughters spread between Pennsylvania, Ohio, Montana, and Illinois.

narrative_blocks.header: Vietnam Navy veteran, thirty-six years at Eriez Magnetics
narrative_blocks.body: Donald McGraw served in the U.S. Navy during the Vietnam War as a young man. He returned home to work at Eriez Magnetics in Erie Pennsylvania for thirty-six years, retiring in 2008. He died seven years later in Erie at sixty-nine, survived by his wife Judith of thirty-six years and three adult children.

narrative_blocks.header: Postwar Erie birth, father dead at fifty-six
narrative_blocks.body: Donald was born February 15, 1946 in Erie Pennsylvania — during the surge of postwar births that followed World War II. His father Dudley died in 1975 when Donald was twenty-nine and only recently returned from Vietnam. He outlived his ninety-seven-year-old mother Florence by only two years.

He also tutored young people at Family Services and helped at the Jamestown Food Pantry.

narrative_blocks.header: Built New York's first million-dollar hotel
narrative_blocks.body: Treadwell co-owned the St. Nicholas Hotel when it opened on January 6, 1853 — a 600-room luxury hotel that was the first New York City building to cost over $1 million. By year's end it had expanded to 1,000 rooms, setting a new standard for lavish appointments in American hospitality.

narrative_blocks.header: Hotel ended the Astor House's fifty-year reign
narrative_blocks.body: When the St. Nicholas opened, it directly challenged the Astor House — Manhattan's preeminent hotel since 1836 — and within months had displaced it as the city's premier destination. Treadwell had helped engineer a decisive shift in Manhattan's hotel hierarchy.

narrative_blocks.header: Built New Milford estate same year hotel opened
narrative_blocks.body: In 1853, the same year the St. Nicholas launched in New York, Treadwell built the Homestead Inn at 5 Elm Street in New Milford as his private residence. The house sheltered three generations of Treadwells until 1915 and still operates today as a bed and breakfast.

narrative_blocks.header: Railroad president, and a wealthy man
narrative_blocks.body: Frederick ran the Fairfield County National Bank at Norwalk from 1868 to 1890 and the Danbury and Norwalk Railroad from 1882 until he died, and he sat on the board of the Norwalk Savings Society for more than forty years. He died one of the wealthiest men in Connecticut.

narrative_blocks.header: The Augusta, first boat of the Yale Navy
narrative_blocks.body: In August 1845 Frederick captained the Augusta, an eight-oared cedar shell his classmates clubbed together to buy, later counted the first boat of the Yale Navy. He graduated in 1849 with Timothy Dwight, the future twelfth president of Yale.

narrative_blocks.header: Two generals' staffs, three Assemblies
narrative_blocks.body: From 1859 to 1862 Frederick served on the staffs of Generals King and Russell, and he sat for Norwalk in the Connecticut General Assembly in 1865, 1866 and 1872.

narrative_blocks.header: The British had burned his grandfather out
narrative_blocks.body: A century after the British burned his grandfather Eliphalet's house, Frederick joined the Connecticut Society of the Sons of the American Revolution. He was a Knight Templar and a Grand Army man, and kept up the Norwalk Club to the end.

narrative_blocks.header: He dropped dead before bed
narrative_blocks.body: At eighty-two Frederick was in robust health, and his friends were surprised when he dropped dead in his room at Cedarhurst, his house on East Avenue, just before retiring on the night of 12 October 1907.

narrative_blocks.header: Cedarhurst on East Avenue
narrative_blocks.body: Frederick married Caroline Ayres of Troy in February 1866, and they raised Elizabeth, Frederick and Julia at Cedarhurst, their house on East Avenue in Norwalk.

narrative_blocks.header: A sampler at ten and a half
narrative_blocks.body: In August 1868 Manice finished a cross-stitch sampler of alphabets and numerals in bright commercially dyed wools, white, dark green, yellow, pale blue, lavender and black, and signed it with his full name and his age, ten years and six months.

narrative_blocks.header: Three brothers before the camera
narrative_blocks.body: About 1868 Whitney & Beckwith photographed the three Lockwood boys together: Manice in the center, Buckingham at the left, and little William perched on a footstool at the right.

narrative_blocks.header: A mansion behind the 1784 farmhouse
narrative_blocks.body: Between 1914 and 1916 Manice built a mansion on the old Lockwood farm, just behind the farmhouse his great-grandfather Eliphalet had raised in 1784. It later became a convent, and St. Philip's Church stands on the old farmhouse's foundation.

narrative_blocks.header: At home on North Avenue
narrative_blocks.body: Manice married Annie Lawrence of New York in November 1880, and they lived at 23 North Avenue in Norwalk. He died at Norwalk Hospital in August 1946, at eighty-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: She and Manice paid for the museum
narrative_blocks.body: Julia and her cousin Manice deForest Lockwood Jr. paid to build Lockwood House on East Avenue in Norwalk, raised from 1971 to 1973 to hold the family's antiques and papers. It opened in 1978, two years after her death, with the portraits of her great-grandfather Capt. Eliphalet Lockwood.

narrative_blocks.header: A thousand fruit trees at Blithefield
narrative_blocks.body: In 1915 Julia and Mayone Lewis bought Blithefield Farm at Norwalk and planted orchards of more than a thousand fruit trees, running it as a commercial peach farm. Through the war they sold tomatoes, onions, melons and lima beans. She had studied farming at Storrs and Amherst.

narrative_blocks.header: Unbeatable at tennis
narrative_blocks.body: At Vassar, class of 1901, Julia was president of the Athletic Association and ran track and played basketball and tennis, unbeatable at tennis and winner of the hurdle race. Afterwards she took prizes in golf and sailing and rode with the Oxbridge Hunt Club in Darien.

narrative_blocks.header: Flintridge's golfer
narrative_blocks.body: Julia led a women's handicap tournament at the Hollywood Country Club in January 1924 with a net 71, and played for the Flintridge Country Club at Pasadena: on its winning team in 1926, its women's tournament chairman in 1927 and a finalist for its championship.

narrative_blocks.header: Pasadena's giver
narrative_blocks.body: At Pasadena Julia gave to the Huntington Library, Descanso Gardens, the Pasadena Boys' Club, the YWCA and YMCA and the Sierra Club, and was active in the College Woman's Club.

narrative_blocks.header: Through the Rockies to California
narrative_blocks.body: Julia and Mayone Lewis rode through the Canadian Rockies on horseback and made California their home, building a Norwegian farmhouse in 1925. From there Julia traveled the world, keeping journals, riding an elephant, and made her last circumnavigation of the globe in 1938.

narrative_blocks.header: Contentment on the farm
narrative_blocks.body: 'If one has a love for animals and for outdoor life generally,' Julia wrote of Blithefield in the Vassar Quarterly in 1918, 'she can certainly find contentment and happiness on the farm.'

narrative_blocks.header: His recruits were the first 'Yankee Doodles'
narrative_blocks.body: In 1755, British surgeon Dr. Richard Shuckburgh wrote mocking verses about Captain Fitch's Connecticut recruits — wearing chicken feathers in their hats for lack of uniforms — dubbing them 'Yankee Doodle.' Colonial soldiers turned the insult into a rallying cry, playing it triumphantly at British troops after Burgoyne's surrender at Saratoga in 1777.

narrative_blocks.header: Senior Colonel of sixteen regiments at Ticonderoga, 1759
narrative_blocks.body: By the end of his service in the French and Indian War, Fitch held the rank of Senior Colonel in command of sixteen regiments — the highest-ranking Norwalk officer in the conflict. His Connecticut troops suffered disproportionate casualties in the attacks on Ticonderoga and Crown Point in 1759, with the campaign ultimately ending in British victory.

narrative_blocks.header: Helped rebuild Norwalk after British burned it, 1779
narrative_blocks.body: After British forces burned Norwalk in July 1779, Fitch — who had already represented the town fourteen terms in the Connecticut House of Representatives — helped lead the reconstruction effort. He had served in the first Norwalk delegation to the General Assembly after the Revolution began, and continued as a civic pillar until his death in 1795.

narrative_blocks.header: Son of the colony's most learned governor
narrative_blocks.body: His father was Thomas Fitch, Connecticut's longest-serving colonial governor and a chief justice whom Yale's president judged the most learned lawyer the colony had produced. Raised in that household of law and office, the son turned instead to soldiering and to the same General Assembly his father had led, representing Norwalk for fourteen terms.

narrative_blocks.header: The household enslaved Dover, Elrania, Naomi, and Eleanor
narrative_blocks.body: Like his father the governor, Fitch held people in bondage at Norwalk; the family's records name four of them — Dover, Elrania, Naomi, and Eleanor. Their presence is part of the documented record of a family long remembered for its public offices.

bio.bio_blurb: Richmond banker and Masonic Grand Secretary

narrative_blocks.header: He took his father-in-law's chair in 1876
narrative_blocks.body: Dr. John Dove was Grand Secretary of the Masonic grand bodies of Virginia; Isaacs married his daughter Julia in 1844 and spent years helping him do the work. When Dove died in 1876 the lodges chose him, and he held it until he died.

narrative_blocks.header: Known to more Masons than any man alive
narrative_blocks.body: He was also Grand Recorder of the Grand Encampment of Knights Templar, and the notices written when he died say he was personally known to more Masons than any other man in the country. Nineteen years in the one office did it.

narrative_blocks.header: Richmond knew him as a banker first
narrative_blocks.body: The notices printed when his son died called him a prominent banker and a widely known business man of the city. The Masonic offices came later and lasted longer, but the money came first and the Norwalk boy made it in Virginia.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried the wounded, not a rifle
narrative_blocks.body: His war service was with the Confederate Ambulance Corps at Richmond. What he did there was the same thing he did afterward for nineteen years — keep track of men, and be the one everybody knew.

narrative_blocks.header: A Norwalk boy who died a Virginian
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Norwalk in 1818, son of the man who kept that town's books for thirty years, and went south to Richmond young. He died there in June 1895 and lies in Hollywood Cemetery; Julia outlived him fourteen years.

narrative_blocks.header: Four children, and the name reached a third
narrative_blocks.body: Julia Lee Dove gave him John Dove, William Bryan Jr., Francis Benjamin and Anne Elizabeth, between 1848 and 1856. William Bryan Jr. named a son William Bryan Isaacs III, and John Dove named one John Dove Isaacs Jr.

narrative_blocks.body: He died at his home in Fresno in March 1918, a native of Richmond who had been gone twenty years. They brought him back for a funeral at St. Stephen's and buried him in the family section at Hollywood.

narrative_blocks.header: Into his father's firm while still a boy
narrative_blocks.body: John L. Williams and Sons took him in young, and he was one of nine children. He was born at Paxton in Powhatan County, his mother's family seat, and gave the name to the house he built at Richmond.

narrative_blocks.header: President of a railroad at thirty-four
narrative_blocks.body: He began pulling smaller lines into the Seaboard Air Line in 1895, a short road from New York to Florida, and finished the merger in 1900. Thomas Fortune Ryan and the New York men forced him out in 1903.

narrative_blocks.header: He drew the Federal Reserve districts
narrative_blocks.body: As one of three men on the Reserve Bank Organization Committee he settled how many reserve banks there would be, where they would sit, and where the lines between the districts would run.

narrative_blocks.header: He segregated the Bureau of Engraving
narrative_blocks.body: One of his first acts at the Treasury in 1913 was to order the work areas divided by race, and he ended promotion for Black employees. The policy went with him into the comptrollership.

narrative_blocks.header: Riggs convicted, then a month of hearings
narrative_blocks.body: He said the national banks lent at usury, and the Riggs officials at Washington were convicted after the suits he brought. When Wilson reappointed him in 1919, Louis McFadden fought it for a month.

narrative_blocks.header: He published how call money was rigged
narrative_blocks.body: His report of 31 July 1920 showed the rates worked to suit insiders while borrowers paid more. Out of office the year after, he charged the Board's deflation had broken farm prices, and Congress sustained part of it.

narrative_blocks.header: Lila wrote to the sons, and made speeches
narrative_blocks.body: He married Lila Lefebvre Isaacs in 1895 and they had John and Hubert. Most of the family letters he kept are hers to the boys, and the papers hold speeches she gave as well as his own.

narrative_blocks.header: Art teacher who braided rugs
narrative_blocks.body: Sally Jane was an art teacher who brought her craft into every corner of her life — sewing her own clothing, creating stained glass windows, braiding wool rugs, growing celebrated gardens, and painting throughout her ninety-three years in Colorado. She traveled the world with friends, collected early American antiques and vintage clothing, and was an active member of Fellowship Community Church.

narrative_blocks.body: Matthew served as a soldier in the Revolution, and lived out his life at Pimpawaug in Wilton, on the homesite his great-grandfather had chosen about 1730 by following an Indian trail up from Norwalk.

narrative_blocks.body: Four generations of Marvins held that same land and served the Wilton Congregational Church. His grandson Matthew Marvin and great-grandson Charles Marvin were both deacons there.

narrative_blocks.body: Charlotte Marvin Storm was born in 1913 in Hopewell Junction and lived until 2009 in Wilmington, Delaware — ninety-five years spanning two World Wars, the Depression, the Space Age, and the digital revolution. She married Ernest Homer Dodge, a Phillips Andover and MIT-trained electrical engineer, connecting the colonial Hooker-Marvin-Underhill line to the engineering culture of early-twentieth-century Cambridge.

narrative_blocks.header: WAVE in World War II
narrative_blocks.body: Jean Rapelje Storm graduated from Hood College in 1940 and joined the U.S. Navy as a WAVE at the outbreak of World War II — a service she remained proud of all her life. It was in the Navy that she met Jack Fairley, whom she married in 1945, and together they retired to Southport, North Carolina in 1972.

narrative_blocks.header: Founded hospital volunteers; designed logo still in use
narrative_blocks.body: When Jean Fairley arrived in Southport in 1972, she became a founding member of the Dosher Hospital Volunteers, served for over forty years, and designed the logo still used today by Dosher Memorial Hospital. She also created and edited the first issue of St. Philip's Episcopal Church's newsletter, the Philippian, and was active in the choir, altar guild, flower guild, and Bible study for decades.

narrative_blocks.header: Three terms as lieutenant governor
narrative_blocks.body: Thaddeus served three terms as Connecticut's lieutenant governor, under John Samuel Peters from 1831 to 1833 and under Samuel A. Foot in 1834 and 1835. The Whigs sent him to the United States Senate in 1839.

narrative_blocks.header: President Van Buren came to his funeral
narrative_blocks.body: Thaddeus died in Washington on 7 April 1840, just over a year into his Senate term. His funeral was held in the Capitol with President Martin Van Buren present, and he has a cenotaph in the Congressional Cemetery.

narrative_blocks.header: A Norwalk lawyer from 1810
narrative_blocks.body: Thaddeus graduated from Yale in 1807 and was admitted to the bar in 1810, then went home to practice in Norwalk. In 1815 he sat in the Connecticut House beside Benjamin Isaacs, a cousin of his future wife, Antoinette Cannon.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a lung specialist
narrative_blocks.body: Mary married Dr. Edward Newman Packard in New York in November 1919. He became one of the leading lung specialists at Saranac Lake, the tuberculosis town, and later ran 6,500-bed Army hospitals in the Second World War.

parents.father_research_notes: Father: Rev. Edward Newman Packard D.D. (b.c.1840s, New England minister). Family lived in Evanston IL c.1872-1876, then Dorchester MA. Siblings: Charlotte Mellen Packard (b.1872, d.1954); Elizabeth Ford Packard Quereau (b.1876, d.1948), whose son Edmund Packard Quereau lived to 98; Agnes Kent Packard Cooper (b.1881, d.1963), who served as president of New York Women's Board of Missions 1921-22 and was a twenty-year member of American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions. Agnes's son Lawrence Carleton Cooper (Michigan Phi Beta Kappa MBA 1932) was a Bankers Trust VP for utility investments. Lawrence's daughter Carol Packard Cooper (b.1941, d.2016) was one of the country's first open heart surgery patients, operated on by Dr. Denton Cooley in 1959 aged 17. Agnes's husband Dr. Hermon Charles Cooper earned a chemistry PhD at Heidelberg 1900 and co-authored an inorganic chemistry textbook with Dutch chemist Arnold Holleman in 1901; he was also a research associate at MIT.

narrative_blocks.header: Commanded 6,500-bed WWII hospitals; received Legion of Merit
narrative_blocks.body: Edward Packard served as a physician in WWI and then from 1941 to 1946 as lieutenant colonel and then colonel commanding 6,500 combined beds at Fort Dix and Holloran General Hospitals — for which he received the Legion of Merit. He married Mary Bissell Betts, 'one of the earliest occupational therapists,' and after her 1926 death continued his medical career, practicing internal medicine and cardiology in Pensacola until 1968.

narrative_blocks.header: Minister's son; sister led American missions board
narrative_blocks.body: Edward Packard came from a distinguished New England clerical family — his father was a D.D. minister and his sister Agnes Cooper served as president of the New York branch of the Women's Board of Missions and held a twenty-year membership on the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions. A niece, Carol Packard Cooper, was among the country's first open heart surgery patients, operated on by Dr. Denton Cooley in 1959 at age seventeen.

narrative_blocks.header: Christy Mathewson's doctor
narrative_blocks.body: At Saranac Lake Edward was one of the leading specialists in lung disease, and personal physician to Christy Mathewson, the Giants pitcher, who died there of tuberculosis in 1925.

people.research_notes: Rev. Edward Newman Packard, D.D. Father of Col. Edward Newman Packard Jr. (I00747), direct spouse of HD4419 Mary Bissell Betts Packard (Hooker descendant, gen 10). Congregationalist minister — the ABCFM (American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions, INST041) was the primary missionary arm of the Congregationalist church. Rev. Packard's daughter Agnes Kent Packard Cooper was a corporate member of ABCFM from 1926 and honorary member from 1946, and served as president of the New York branch of the Women's Board of Missions (1921-22). Rev. Packard himself may have had ABCFM affiliations as a D.D. minister in the Congregationalist tradition, but personal membership not documented. Family lived in Evanston IL c.1872-1876, then Dorchester MA area by 1881. Note: the ABCFM connection is far more strongly documented in the tree through the Dwight line (H00914 Timothy Dwight, HD2376 Samuel Gelston Dwight `hawaii_mission_era`, HD2379 Charles Bishop Dwight), Elias Cornelius (X00724, ABCFM secretary who married a double Hooker descendant), Eliza Talcott (T01213, ABCFM missionary), and Dr. Mary Floyd Cushman (HD2818, Hooker descendant, ABCFM physician in Angola). STAGE 6Y-119.

narrative_blocks.header: Died childless; her sister Diantha married her widower
narrative_blocks.body: Lucy Strong Phelps died on February 22, 1866 at age forty-five — without children — and just eight months later her sister Diantha married her widower Franklin Hope, repeating the very pattern that had brought their parents together: their mother Mary Deming Hooker had married Burnham Phelps after Burnham's first wife Louisa Hooker died in 1812. The Hooker-Phelps family repeated this pattern across two generations.

narrative_blocks.header: Twin of Americus Vespucius
narrative_blocks.body: Christopher Columbus Phelps was born as a twin with Americus Vespucius Phelps in 1823 — both named for the explorers most closely associated with the Americas: Christopher Columbus, who first reached the New World, and Amerigo Vespucci, whose name became America itself. Americus Vespucius died in 1826 at age three; Christopher went on to settle in Bureau County, Illinois and have two children who would leave documented descendants into the twenty-first century.

narrative_blocks.header: Born San Francisco 1828 — before the Gold Rush
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Etta Isaacs was born on March 20, 1828 in San Francisco — then a tiny settlement called Yerba Buena in Mexican Alta California — placing her family among the very earliest documented New England visitors to what would become California, more than twenty years before the 1849 Gold Rush. Her father John Isaacs, a Hooker descendant through the Norwalk Saint John and Isaacs families, was likely engaged in the Pacific hide-and-tallow trade that drew New England merchant ships around Cape Horn to California ports throughout the 1820s.

narrative_blocks.body: Winfield Scott Hanford was born on October 1, 1814 — just three months after General Winfield Scott's celebrated stand at the Battle of Lundy's Lane in July 1814, one of the most intense engagements of the War of 1812 — placing him among many children named for the war hero in those immediate postwar years. He was born sixteen months before his mother Charlotte Saint John Hanford died at age thirty, and was raised thereafter by his father Joseph Piatt Hanford.

narrative_blocks.header: He cast the first plow made in Michigan
narrative_blocks.body: Alby learned the machinist's trade at Auburn and came to Michigan in 1836, spending six months at Marshall building and running a furnace, where he ran the first iron and cast the first plow made in the state. At Allegan he started another furnace, made the first sled in the county, and ran his furnace and machine shop for twenty-nine years.

narrative_blocks.header: Allegan's water works, built under him
narrative_blocks.body: Alby was Allegan's justice of the peace for five years, and its alderman, village marshal and superintendent of the water works, which were built under his supervision. He laid out fifteen acres of his farm in village lots, called the Rossman Addition.

narrative_blocks.header: From Andrew Jackson to Grover Cleveland
narrative_blocks.body: The youngest of sixteen children, Alby was a Democrat from his first ballot, cast for Andrew Jackson, to his last, for Grover Cleveland.

career.organization: Fond du Lac Journal, Fond du Lac Wisconsin
career.notes: Co-founded with J.O. Henning. First newspaper established in Fond du Lac County. Sold within six months.

career.organization: Fond du Lac Whig, Fond du Lac Wisconsin
career.notes: Bought half interest with J.M. Gellett after selling Journal. Sold interest January 1848 and moved to Waupun.

Read law in Waupun from 1848. Admitted to bar Aug 6, 1850 per personal diary (USBD says Apr 17, 1854 — discrepancy). Practiced ~40 years. Traveled on horseback across Dodge County to court in Juneau; sometimes stayed overnight at inn between Minnesota Junction and Juneau.
Active as lobbyist in 1850s per Waupun city history records.
Published Republican paper 1866; sold personal interest 1867 but remained corresponding editor. Firm Hooker, Bell & Hooker continued until paper was sold in 1894.
Operated printing press alongside law practice; with son Culver ran printing business for many years.
With others formed oil company 1866; sold oil by the barrel from West Virginia well.

cross_connections.display_label: sat for Connecticut at the 1860 convention that nominated Lincoln

narrative_blocks.header: He printed Fond du Lac's first newspaper
narrative_blocks.body: Arriving in Wisconsin in 1846, he co-founded the Fond du Lac Journal, the county's first paper, then a second, before selling out in 1848 to read law at Waupun. The bar came after, and with son Culver and a grandson the practice grew into Wisconsin's longest-running family law firm.

narrative_blocks.header: Horseback to court, and Chicago for Lincoln
narrative_blocks.body: Court at Juneau meant a ride across Dodge County, with a night at the inn between Minnesota Junction and Juneau when the distance demanded. In 1860 he sat in the Chicago convention that nominated Lincoln.

narrative_blocks.header: Catherine followed him by a month
narrative_blocks.body: He died at Waupun on December 10, 1889; his wife of thirty-eight years, Catherine, died the following January 10. They had come to Wisconsin young and left it together.

narrative_blocks.header: Wounded at Trevilian Station, 1864
narrative_blocks.body: Nelson enlisted at Independence in August 1862 in the 130th New York, which became the 1st New York Dragoons, and was wounded at Trevilian Station on 12 June 1864, the largest all-cavalry battle of the war. He was mustered out from Mower Hospital, Philadelphia, in May 1865.

narrative_blocks.header: Burned out, then peddling buttermilk
narrative_blocks.body: In 1888 fire destroyed the farmhouse Nelson lived in at Barton, taking his furniture and his money with it. In his last years he peddled buttermilk from F. A. Schuyler's creamery there, and he died at Waverly in February 1892, at sixty.

narrative_blocks.header: Fatherless at five; the name Armeanest
narrative_blocks.body: Nelson was five when his father, a Dryden shoemaker, died in 1837. He married twice, the second time to Sarah Masterson, and passed his unusual middle name, Armeanest, to his son Ernest, born in 1887.

narrative_blocks.header: Four deaths in forty days
narrative_blocks.body: His father Eli died December 10, 1889; his mother followed January 10, his infant daughter Laura Belle on the thirteenth, and his wife Josephine — likely of childbirth's complications — on the eighteenth. He was thirty-four, with the Waupun Times and the family law office suddenly in his hands.

narrative_blocks.header: Mayor the year everything fell apart
narrative_blocks.body: Waupun made him mayor in 1889, months before the forty days that emptied his house. The town kept him: editor of its Times, head of Hooker, Bell and Hooker, and from 1919 president of its National Bank.

narrative_blocks.header: A Red Hook freight fortune raised her
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah's father, John Reade, ran a freighting business from his Red Hook storehouses on the Hudson, and her mother, Catherine, was a Livingston of the Manor. The youngest daughter, Sarah married the Poughkeepsie lawyer James Hooker in 1816.

narrative_blocks.header: The Reade daughters married across New York
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah kept to Poughkeepsie while her sister Catherine married Nicholas William Stuyvesant. Their sister Anne married Robert Kearney and was grandmother of Anna Morton, born at Poughkeepsie in 1846, Second Lady of the United States in 1889.

narrative_blocks.header: Reade Street carries her family name
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph Reade, Trinity Church's warden for fifty years, gave Lower Manhattan's Reade Street its name. As a councillor he urged delay on the Stamp Act, and sat on the 1741 grand jury that sent thirty-four people to their deaths.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-one years a widow at Poughkeepsie
narrative_blocks.body: James died in 1858; she stayed on at Poughkeepsie another twenty-one years, dying at eighty-eight in January 1879. They lie together at Poughkeepsie Rural — a granddaughter named Helen Reade carrying her names into the next century.

narrative_blocks.header: A century on, the Reades came back
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah married a Hooker in 1816. Her sister Anne's great-granddaughter Alice Morton married Winthrop Rutherfurd in 1902, and their son married Alice Polk, a Hooker descendant, in 1940, bringing the Reade blood into the family again.

narrative_blocks.header: He met the Pasha of Egypt in 1834
narrative_blocks.body: Few Americans had crossed the Atlantic at all when he went through the Middle East in 1834 and was received by Muhammad Ali Pasha, the Albanian-born ruler remaking Egypt. The Court of Saint James had already received him; the traveling never really stopped.

narrative_blocks.header: A New York banquet reached Mexico City
narrative_blocks.body: With James William Beekman he staged the famous New York banquet whose speeches for the Mexican Republic — against Napoleon's puppet emperor — helped move Congress toward recognition. He extracted a promise from Minister Romero that Maximilian's life would be spared; Mexican popular fury made it impossible to keep.

narrative_blocks.header: A novelist made him the hero
narrative_blocks.body: Captain Mayne Reid, the British adventure writer and an intimate friend, put him at the center of The Lone Ranche. His own pen produced several works and a translation of Abbadie from the French.

narrative_blocks.header: Friday nights at 255 Fifth Avenue
narrative_blocks.body: His receptions drew the eminent writers and artists of the city to the house, alongside a rare library collected across Europe. Public office he always declined — otium cum dignitate, retirement with dignity, was the phrase he lived by.

narrative_blocks.header: His children answered with a brass lectern
narrative_blocks.body: A Grace Church member for many years, he gave amply and without show; after his death the children set a massive brass lectern there in his memory. His son built a Children's Aid library at Bath Beach in his name.

narrative_blocks.header: He was the squire of Clermont Manor
narrative_blocks.body: John Henry was a Livingston of Clermont, the Hudson River manor, and a great-grandson of Chancellor Robert R. Livingston, who swore in George Washington. He presided over the Order of Colonial Lords of Manors in America.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought his ancestral manor for one dollar
narrative_blocks.body: When his father died in 1895, Clermont passed not to him but to his young daughter Katherine — the old man had disliked John Henry's second wife. He later bought the manor back from his daughter, reportedly for a single dollar.

narrative_blocks.header: He outlived two wives before a third marriage
narrative_blocks.body: His first wife, Catherine Hamersley, died in childbirth in 1873; his second, Emily Evans, died suddenly in 1894. At fifty-eight he married a third time, to Alice Delafield Clarkson, and had two more daughters.

narrative_blocks.header: Rare abilities and sterling worth, they wrote
narrative_blocks.body: The Poughkeepsie Surrogate's daughter married the Manhattan lawyer John William Hamersley in 1840 and made her life in his Fifth Avenue world. The memorial that outlived her settled on a phrase: a lady of rare abilities and sterling worth. She died at forty-nine, in 1867, and went home to Poughkeepsie Rural ground.

narrative_blocks.header: She folded the family into the Manor twice
narrative_blocks.body: She carried Livingston as a middle name from her mother's line; her daughter Catherine married John Henry Livingston, great-grandson of the Chancellor, folding the family into the Manor blood twice over. Another daughter, Helen Reade, carried her grandmother's names.

narrative_blocks.header: Five children, and one courted Edith Carow
narrative_blocks.body: She had five children by Colonel Hamersley between 1841 and 1857, in the Fifth Avenue house. James Hooker Hamersley, the elder son, courted Edith Carow before she chose Theodore Roosevelt.

narrative_blocks.header: The seven-million-dollar baby was her grandson
narrative_blocks.body: She had been dead twenty-five years when Louis Gordon Hamersley was born in 1892 and the newspapers counted his inheritance at seven million. Another grandchild, Catherine, carried the Hamersleys into the Astor orbit.

narrative_blocks.header: Courted Edith Roosevelt before she chose Theodore
narrative_blocks.body: In the early 1880s he was among the suitors of Edith Kermit Carow, who in 1886 married Theodore Roosevelt instead. The courtship set him squarely in the young New York world the future president moved through.

narrative_blocks.header: His son's birth in 1892 made international headlines
narrative_blocks.body: His son Louis's birth in 1892 unlocked a $7 million inheritance that had hinged on his producing a male heir — a fortune bound up with a cousin's estate and the former Duchess of Marlborough. His coachman reportedly tore through Newport crowing about the 'seven million dollar baby.'

narrative_blocks.header: He stepped aside for William Waldorf Astor
narrative_blocks.body: Nominated for the New York State Assembly in 1877 by the Independent Republicans, he withdrew in favor of his friend William Waldorf Astor and then campaigned to elect him. He turned his own energy to law and real estate.

narrative_blocks.header: He donated the Children's Aid Society's main building
narrative_blocks.body: A steady patron of the Children's Aid Society and its Newsboys' Lodging House, he gave the main building of the Society's new summer home for poor city children at Bath Beach, Brooklyn, in 1895. The Astors furnished the surrounding cottages.

narrative_blocks.header: The lawyer was also a published poet
narrative_blocks.body: Alongside the law he wrote verse, publishing a collection called The Seven Voices in 1898. It fit the literary, moneyed New York world he moved through.

narrative_blocks.body: In 1871 she married John Henry Livingston of Clermont, joining the Hooker line to one of colonial New York's great dynasties. She died in April 1873, nine days after giving birth to her daughter Katherine.

narrative_blocks.header: Once reported engaged to Vincent Astor
narrative_blocks.body: Before her marriages she was rumored engaged to Vincent Astor, and instead wed his first cousin Henry Coleman Drayton in 1922. Three marriages and three divorces later, she outlived all her siblings, dying in 1977 as the last of J. Hooker Hamersley's children.

narrative_blocks.header: Her second husband's family defined the Four Hundred
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband Henry Coleman Drayton was a grandson of Caroline Astor, whose ballroom held the four hundred guests that named New York's social aristocracy. His uncle was John Jacob Astor IV, who died on the Titanic; his sister married an FDR ambassador to Italy.

narrative_blocks.header: New York called her the Million Dollar Cinderella
narrative_blocks.body: By her father's will she grew up on a twenty-five-cent monthly allowance, ignorant of the million-plus fortune waiting at twenty-one. A novelist built his 1906 bestseller The Danger Mark on her; told in Central Park that she was the richest child in New York, she called it an awful fairy tale.

narrative_blocks.header: First American woman inside Riyadh
narrative_blocks.body: In January 1939 she crossed Syria, Iraq, and central Arabia to reach the closed capital of Riyadh — the first American woman received there. She stayed in King Abdulaziz's palace, rode out on a royal falcon hunt no Western woman had joined, and came home to a Royal Geographical Society fellowship.

narrative_blocks.header: Her camera caught the King at home
narrative_blocks.body: Her photographs from that 1939 journey — King Abdulaziz, the falcon camp, herself in Najdi dress — survive at the Litchfield Historical Society, a rare glimpse of pre-war Saudi Arabia. Timbuktu and an erupting volcano had filled her earlier albums.

narrative_blocks.header: The seven-million-dollar baby who collected it
narrative_blocks.body: At his 1892 birth the family coachman reportedly raced through Newport shouting about a 'seven million dollar baby' — for he stood to inherit a contested fortune. He won it in 1913 after suing off more than a hundred rival claimants, then spent it on speedboats, estates, and a twenty-three-room penthouse.

narrative_blocks.header: Coolidge presented him the President's Cup in 1926
narrative_blocks.body: In 1926 he raced his all-duralumin speedboat Cigarette IV to victory in three straight heats at the first national speedboat regatta on the Potomac, and President Coolidge handed him the trophy in person. He had already set a Hudson River speed record and raced ocean schooners.

narrative_blocks.header: He demolished the family mansion; built a penthouse
narrative_blocks.body: In 1923 he tore down the family's Fifth Avenue mansion — where his mother had died and where he and his sister were raised in deliberate ignorance of their fortune — and put up a twelve-story building crowned by a twenty-three-room penthouse for himself. Real estate became his empire.

narrative_blocks.header: From ambulance driver to First Division artillery officer
narrative_blocks.body: Before America entered the First World War he drove ambulances at the French front with the American Field Service. Commissioned in 1917, he fought as a First Division artillery officer through four major offensives — Soissons, St. Mihiel, and the Meuse-Argonne among them — and came home a major.

narrative_blocks.header: He boated twelve hundred veterans up the Hudson
narrative_blocks.body: In 1921 he brought twelve hundred wounded veterans by steamer up the Hudson to his Dutchess County estate for a three-day outing — 'one glorious old outing for the boys who came back from the war.' He hosted his First Division comrades again the next summer, quiet charity from an heir to millions.

naming_inspiration.description: Named Livingston for her father's family, the Livingstons of Clermont — and also her mother's Livingston middle name.

narrative_blocks.header: She was born as her mother lay dying
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother died nine days after her birth in 1873, and she was raised at Clermont by her Hamersley aunts before rejoining her father. Christened Catherine, she later changed the spelling to Katherine to set herself apart from the mother she never knew.

narrative_blocks.header: The Clermont daughter made her home in England
narrative_blocks.body: She grew up on the Hudson at Clermont, briefly inherited the manor, then sold it back to her father. After marrying Lawrence Timpson in 1900 she moved to England, settling at Appleton Manor, where she is buried.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son married a duchess
narrative_blocks.body: She raised five children, including twins born in 1915. Her son Robert Timpson married Louise Campbell, Duchess of Argyll, in 1954, and was later expelled from the New York Stock Exchange.

narrative_blocks.header: A three-year world tour ended before the Queen
narrative_blocks.body: After sudden deaths in the family, her father took her on a three-year world tour, from Japan across Asia and the Middle East to Europe. It ended in England, where she was presented to Queen Victoria.

narrative_blocks.header: She poured her fortune into a medieval manor
narrative_blocks.body: In 1924 she bought Appleton Manor, a moated twelfth-century house in Oxfordshire, and spent the rest of her life and much of her mother's inheritance restoring it. It became the family's English seat and the place she died.

narrative_blocks.header: A sea captain's family under his roof
narrative_blocks.body: Around 1831 Andrew and his wife Hannah took in the family of Captain John Dominis at 26 Front Street, Schenectady. There, in March 1832, John Owen Dominis was born, the boy who would marry Hawaii's last queen.

narrative_blocks.header: Latin and Greek at the new Union College
narrative_blocks.body: Andrew taught Latin and Greek at Union College from 1797 to 1801, two years after its charter; his cousin Joseph C. Yates, later governor of New York, was among its founders. He came back in 1814 to teach moral philosophy.

narrative_blocks.header: Two of his family at Mobile Bay
narrative_blocks.body: Two men of Andrew's family fought at Mobile Bay in August 1864: his grandson Arthur Reed Yates, on Farragut's staff, and Hannah's nephew James Hooker Strong, whose Monongahela rammed the ironclad Tennessee.

narrative_blocks.header: His first wife was an Austin
narrative_blocks.body: Andrew's first wife, Mary Austin, who died in 1806, was said to be kin to Stephen F. Austin of Texas. He gave her name to his first daughter by Hannah, and it came down to a granddaughter, Mary Austin Yates Stuyvesant.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirteen years in the East Hartford pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: Between his two terms at Union, Andrew was pastor of the East Hartford Congregational church from 1801 to 1814. Without great eloquence, it was said, he was a sound divine who preached with great power.

narrative_blocks.header: He read Holland Dutch
narrative_blocks.body: Andrew took his Yale degree in the 1790s, studied theology under John H. Livingston, and was among the most learned men upstate, Holland Dutch among his languages. From 1825 to 1836 he ran the Polytechnic at Chittenango.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty ministers, and an epitaph on a bell
narrative_blocks.body: Andrew taught theology to young men at East Hartford and Schenectady, and thirty went into the ministry, Francis Wayland of Brown among them. He died ten days before his last mission church was dedicated; his epitaph is on its bell.

narrative_blocks.header: Monroe County's first judge
narrative_blocks.body: When Monroe County was set up in 1821, Governor DeWitt Clinton made Elisha its first judge, ten days after the county was organized, and he held the bench for several years. He had sat in the Assembly for Ontario County in 1819–20.

narrative_blocks.header: A thousand acres by the Genesee falls
narrative_blocks.body: In 1816 Elisha left his Canandaigua law practice for Rochester, where he and Elisha Beach bought a thousand acres on the east bank of the Genesee, taking in all of Carthage. With Herman Norton he drove its settlement.

narrative_blocks.header: An inclined railway down the gorge
narrative_blocks.body: At Carthage Elisha and his partner built storehouses, a railway on an inclined plane to carry freight between the boats below and the bank above, and a bridge in one immense arch over the chasm north of the lower falls.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale, then Litchfield Law School
narrative_blocks.body: Prepared for college by Nathan Johnson, Elisha graduated from Yale in 1809, attended Litchfield Law School in 1810 and read law at Canandaigua, where he was admitted to the bar in 1812. A presidential electorship came later.

narrative_blocks.header: A Catholic at the end
narrative_blocks.body: After many reverses Elisha moved to Detroit in 1861. His second wife, Ellen O'Keefe of Detroit, was a Catholic, and he took her faith; he died in its communion in October 1867, at seventy-eight, and was buried at Rochester.

narrative_blocks.header: He married Dolly Goodwin Hooker
narrative_blocks.body: Elisha married Dolly Goodwin Hooker of Windsor on 24 June 1813, and she bore him eight children, among them Rear Admiral James Hooker Strong. Dolly died at Rochester in 1850.

bio.title: Rear Admiral

notable.notable_blurb: Rear Admiral; Battle of Mobile Bay hero, 1864

education.notes: Interrupted studies Feb 2, 1829 to accept naval appointment as midshipman.

career.notes: Full career: Midshipman Feb 2, 1829; Passed Midshipman Jun 4, 1836; Lieutenant Sep 1841; Commander Apr 24, 1861; Captain Aug 5, 1865; Commodore Mar 21, 1870; Rear Admiral Sep 1873; retired Apr 25, 1876 after 47 years service.

military_service.unit: USS Mohawk, USS Flag (South Atlantic Blockading Squadron); USS Monongahela (West Gulf Blockading Squadron)
military_service.notes: May 8, 1862: captured schooner Amelia off Charleston aboard USS Flag (blockade runner with cotton). Aug 5, 1864: Battle of Mobile Bay — commanding USS Monongahela, rammed Confederate ironclad CSS Tennessee to shield Farragut flagship USS Hartford; promoted to Captain for this action. Commanded USS Canandaigua in Mediterranean 1869-70. Commanded South Atlantic Squadron as Rear Admiral 1873-75. Retired Apr 25, 1876.

naming_inspiration.description: Middle name 'Hooker' honors the maternal Hooker lineage.

narrative_blocks.header: He rammed the ironclad and others followed
narrative_blocks.body: Tennessee was steering to ram Farragut's flagship when he drove Monongahela into her at full steam. It tore off his own iron cutwater and he took her guns point-blank going past; the other ships followed, and Buchanan surrendered.

narrative_blocks.header: The Confederate admiral was Farragut's old friend
narrative_blocks.body: Franklin Buchanan had CSS Tennessee, the most powerful ironclad the Confederacy built, and meant to fight to the end. He gave her up ninety minutes after Monongahela struck him, and Strong was made captain for it.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty years passed before his first command
narrative_blocks.body: He was made midshipman at fourteen, in February 1829, breaking off his studies at the Polytechnic College at Chittenango. His first cruise was Lexington off Brazil, and his first command the store ship Relief, thirty years on.

narrative_blocks.header: He took a cotton runner out of Charleston
narrative_blocks.body: Commanding Flag in the South Atlantic Blockading Squadron, he caught the schooner Amelia on the night of 8 May 1862, running cotton out of Charleston. A storm opened her seams a week later and she was abandoned under tow.

narrative_blocks.header: He commanded a ship named for his birthplace
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Canandaigua in the Finger Lakes, he took the sloop-of-war Canandaigua into the Mediterranean Squadron in 1869. He made rear admiral in 1873 and had the South Atlantic Squadron two years before retiring.

narrative_blocks.header: Two destroyers bore his name, both lost
narrative_blocks.body: USS Strong DD-467 was sunk by Japanese aircraft off Bougainville in 1943, months after she was commissioned. DD-758 served Korea and Vietnam, went to Brazil in 1973, and foundered off Durban under tow to the scrapyard.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother's surname went to sea with him
narrative_blocks.body: Dolly Goodwin Hooker gave him the middle name he carried through fifty years of the Navy. Captain Arthur Reed Yates, grandson of the man who married her sister, stood on Farragut's staff at Mobile Bay the same day.

narrative_blocks.header: A founder of Detroit's Protestant Orphan Asylum
narrative_blocks.body: Martha helped found Detroit's Protestant Orphan Asylum and was its first directress from 1852 to 1860. In her last years she was the only one of its first board still living.

narrative_blocks.header: The only house on Woodward above Grand Circus
narrative_blocks.body: About 1843 Martha and John built the house at Woodward and High where both of them would die. When it went up it was the only building on Woodward Avenue north of Grand Circus Park, and all around it was forest.

narrative_blocks.header: Born a twin
narrative_blocks.body: Martha was born at Rochester on 13 April 1818, a twin to her sister Bertha Rosabella. Bertha died at Chicago in 1845, at twenty-seven; Martha lived to eighty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: He followed her home to Rochester
narrative_blocks.body: Martha met John Winder on a girlhood visit to Detroit. He followed her home, they married at Rochester in September 1836, and in Detroit they lived at first in the only inn. John was clerk of Michigan's federal courts for thirty years.

narrative_blocks.header: He found the ground for Forest Home
narrative_blocks.body: Robert helped secure the land for Forest Home Cemetery in Milwaukee and persuaded St. Paul's Episcopal Church to lay it out there. He was buried in it in 1892, and his son Beebe and granddaughter Marian after him.

narrative_blocks.body: Robert came west while Wisconsin was still a territory, and in the winter of 1839-40, at nineteen, he clerked for its legislature.

narrative_blocks.body: In Milwaukee Robert was a partner in Kellogg and Strong, steamboat owners and warehousemen, and later managed the Newberry Furnace Company.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at thirty-seven with three children

narrative_blocks.header: Artistic, poetic, and a scholar of German
narrative_blocks.body: She was artistic and poetic, read German, and wrote with wit and elegance; those who knew her called her a critic of unusual acuteness. Her husband had published his own translations of the German poets two years before he married her.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father took the Hooker name to Rochester
narrative_blocks.body: Alexander Allin Hooker farmed at Irondequoit and was counted among Rochester's first settlers. He was a son of Capt. James Hooker of Windsor, so the Connecticut line reached the Genesee in her father's generation and she was born into it.

narrative_blocks.header: Her children were sixteen and thirteen
narrative_blocks.body: Josephine was sixteen and Ryland thirteen when she died. Josephine married Dr. Emory Hunt and was gone herself by 1890, leaving a daughter named Helen. Ryland took his father's Greek chair at Rochester and bought back the Hooker homestead.

narrative_blocks.header: Eighteen years younger than her professor
narrative_blocks.body: She married Asahel Clark Kendrick in 1857, Rochester's founding professor of Greek and eighteen years her senior. She died at fifty-three; he taught on another fifteen years and was laid beside her at Mount Hope.

narrative_blocks.header: Two hundred thousand dollars, Roosevelt as executor
narrative_blocks.body: His 1904 will left the sum to the United States to found a military school of high ethical standards, naming President Roosevelt executor; when he died in 1907 it made the front page of the Times. The courts declared the will illegal — the school was never built, and Roosevelt never served.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine months a captain in Illinois blue
narrative_blocks.body: He went to Illinois as a young man, and when the war came he raised a company, mustering as captain in the 39th Illinois Volunteers in August 1861. His discharge came the following May, and Irondequoit had him back for the rest of a long civilian life.

narrative_blocks.header: He sold the family chapel for a dollar
narrative_blocks.body: In 1793 Peter sold the Stuyvesant family chapel to the Episcopal Church for one dollar, on condition that a new church rise there for Bowery Village. St. Mark's in-the-Bowery was consecrated in 1799, over his great-grandfather's vault.

narrative_blocks.header: He laid out the East Village streets
narrative_blocks.body: Peter drew the first street plan for the family land between Fourth Avenue and the East River, from 5th Street to 20th, running true east and west. The 1811 grid swallowed it; Stuyvesant Street still follows his line.

narrative_blocks.header: A house for his daughter Elizabeth
narrative_blocks.body: When his daughter Elizabeth married Nicholas Fish in 1803, Peter built them the house at 21 Stuyvesant Street, which still stands. Their son Hamilton Fish became governor of New York and Secretary of State.

narrative_blocks.header: Two great New York families
narrative_blocks.body: Peter married Margaret Livingston, granddaughter of the first lord of Livingston Manor, in 1764. Their son Nicholas William built what is now Greenwich Village's oldest house; Peter Gerard helped found the New-York Historical Society.

narrative_blocks.header: Painted by Gilbert Stuart
narrative_blocks.body: Gilbert Stuart painted Peter's portrait in the 1790s. It stayed in the family more than a century, down to his great-great-grandson Winthrop Astor Chanler.

narrative_blocks.header: Six days short of seventy-eight
narrative_blocks.body: Peter died on 7 October 1805, six days short of seventy-eight, and was laid in the vault of his ancestors within the walls of St. Mark's: 'the kind father, the faithful friend, the honest citizen.'

narrative_blocks.header: Namesake of the last Dutch governor
narrative_blocks.body: Peter was the great-grandson and namesake of Peter Stuyvesant, the last Dutch director-general of New Netherland, who surrendered New Amsterdam to the English in 1664. Peter inherited his old farm, the Bouwerie.

narrative_blocks.header: He built the Village's oldest house
narrative_blocks.body: In 1795, the year he married Catherine Reade, Nicholas built the Federal-style house at 44 Stuyvesant Street. It stands today as the oldest house in Greenwich Village.

narrative_blocks.header: His street became St. Mark's Place
narrative_blocks.body: Nicholas inherited the family mansion near 8th Street on his father's death in 1805. In 1829 he ceded that stretch of 8th Street to the city; rowhouses and a new name, St. Mark's Place, followed within two years.

narrative_blocks.header: Schooled in Scotland through the Revolution
narrative_blocks.body: Nicholas was sent to Scotland for his schooling. The letters that reached his father between 1781 and 1787 reported his progress, and how Britain saw the closing years of the war.

narrative_blocks.header: The Reade sisters and the Hookers
narrative_blocks.body: Nicholas and Catherine had nine children. Her sister Helen married Judge James Hooker of Poughkeepsie, and in 1840 their son John married Mary Austin Yates, the judge's niece.

narrative_blocks.header: His nephew became Secretary of State
narrative_blocks.body: His sister Elizabeth married Adjutant General Nicholas Fish, and their son Hamilton Fish rose to New York's governorship, the U.S. Senate, and the State Department under Grant.

narrative_blocks.header: He died in the family mansion
narrative_blocks.body: Nicholas died in the Stuyvesant mansion in March 1833. Catherine lived more than thirty years longer, but the family sold the house within the year, and it came down.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran for vice president in 1824
narrative_blocks.body: Twice a senator from New York and then Chancellor of the state, its highest judge, Nathan drew thirty electoral votes for vice president in 1824, a distant second to John C. Calhoun.

narrative_blocks.header: He struck property from the vote
narrative_blocks.body: At New York's constitutional convention of 1821 Nathan introduced the amendment that ended owning property as a qualification for voting.

narrative_blocks.header: He argued the case of the fox
narrative_blocks.body: Nathan was the appellate lawyer for Jesse Pierson in Pierson v. Post, the landmark case over a fox and who owns a wild animal.

narrative_blocks.header: Three wives, and a son at fifty-four
narrative_blocks.body: Nathan married three times. His third wife, Mary Buchanan, a granddaughter of the signer Thomas McKean, bore him Robert in 1831, when Nathan was fifty-four; he died seven years later.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter married Melville's uncle
narrative_blocks.body: Nathan's daughter Mary, of his second marriage, married Peter Gansevoort, Herman Melville's uncle; their son Henry Sanford Gansevoort became a Civil War general. Sanford Hall, his Flushing house, became an asylum in 1845.

narrative_blocks.header: Signed by Jefferson, and by a Yates
narrative_blocks.body: Nathan's 1802 commission as general commissioner of bankruptcy bears Thomas Jefferson's signature. His 1823 appointment as Chancellor was signed by Governor Joseph C. Yates, a cousin of the Rev. Andrew Yates.

narrative_blocks.body: John's aunt Helen Reade had married Judge James Hooker, so their daughter Helen Mary was John's first cousin as well as Mary's. When she died at eighteen, John and Mary gave her name to their first child, in 1841.

narrative_blocks.header: His land had been Peter Stuyvesant's farm
narrative_blocks.body: John, son of Nicholas William Stuyvesant and Catherine Reade, inherited Manhattan land that had once been part of Peter Stuyvesant's farms, and kept a country house at Hyde Park.

narrative_blocks.header: A widower who married again
narrative_blocks.body: John's first wife, Catharine Ackerly, a doctor's daughter, died in 1837 without children. In 1840 he married Mary Austin Yates, and they had three daughters before his death in 1853.

narrative_blocks.header: A stable on East Ninth Street
narrative_blocks.body: By the 1850s a two-story brick stable stood on John's land at 231 East 9th Street. His heirs leased it out and sold it in 1891; since then it has been a mattress works, a theater, a garage and a restaurant.
