narrative_blocks.header: The senator's youngest son
narrative_blocks.body: Robert was born at Albany in December 1831, the only child of Senator Nathan Sanford's third marriage, months after his father left the Senate. He was six when his father died at Flushing.

narrative_blocks.header: He raised his mother a church of stone
narrative_blocks.body: When his mother died in 1879, Robert set up her gravestone at Poughkeepsie in the shape of a small church, carved with her husband's offices and her descent from the signer Thomas McKean.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a Stuyvesant at Poughkeepsie
narrative_blocks.body: Robert married Helen Mary Hooker Stuyvesant in May 1867, and they raised six children at Poughkeepsie. Their son Stuyvesant died at thirteen, and a daughter, Desiree, carried McKean as her middle name.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept a journal like his mother
narrative_blocks.body: Robert kept a journal of his life, as his mother had. His and hers are among the Sanford Family Papers at the New York State Library.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty cents in his pocket
narrative_blocks.body: John had clerked in the Uniontown prothonotary's office from sixteen, and reached Detroit on 3 October 1824, at nineteen, with fifty cents in his pocket, sent with Major Thomas Rowland to gather statistics on the Indians of Michigan Territory.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-four years in Michigan's courts
narrative_blocks.body: John was clerk of the territorial supreme court from 1826, of the state supreme court until 1841, of the federal circuit and district courts from 1837, and of the circuit court until 1870. Forty years before he died he bought land that became the heart of Detroit.

narrative_blocks.header: A colonel on two governors' staffs
narrative_blocks.body: John took his title from the staffs of Governors Mason and Porter, and was president of the Brady Guard, Detroit's militia company.

narrative_blocks.header: He read the papers, then slept away
narrative_blocks.body: At nearly ninety-three John breakfasted with his family, read the morning papers and talked over the news, then lay down on a couch at three. His son found him twenty minutes later, dead in his sleep.

narrative_blocks.header: Married first to a general's daughter
narrative_blocks.body: John married first a daughter of General John R. Williams, and in 1836 Martha Cornelia Strong, daughter of Judge Elisha Beebe Strong of Rochester. He died in 1897, three years before her.

narrative_blocks.header: He climbed the fence to meet a princess
narrative_blocks.body: In Honolulu John's day school backed onto the Royal School, and he climbed the fence to watch the royal children. In 1843 the Cookes admitted him; one classmate was Lydia Kamakaʻeha, the future Queen Liliʻuokalani.

narrative_blocks.header: He married his schoolmate
narrative_blocks.body: In 1862 John married Lydia Kamakaʻeha, his old Royal School classmate, and brought her home to Washington Place, his mother's house. She became queen in January 1891; he did not live to see her overthrow.

narrative_blocks.header: Prince consort for seven months
narrative_blocks.body: John died at Washington Place in August 1891, seven months after his wife became queen: the kingdom's only prince consort, and its last.

narrative_blocks.header: Governor of Oahu under five sovereigns
narrative_blocks.body: Kamehameha V made John governor of Oahu in 1864, and he held it through every reign after, adding Maui, Lanai and Molokai in 1878. He was the contemporary of five sovereigns, and a strong influence on each.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother's boardinghouse became Washington Place
narrative_blocks.body: After his father was lost at sea in 1846, John's mother took in boarders; one, the American minister, named the house Washington Place. It passed to John, then to Liliʻuokalani, and is now the governor's residence.

narrative_blocks.header: Born in a minister's house in Schenectady
narrative_blocks.body: John was born in March 1832 at 26 Front Street, Schenectady, where his parents boarded with the Rev. Andrew Yates and his wife, Hannah Allin Hooker. His Italian-American father was a sea captain in the Pacific trade.

narrative_blocks.header: The Cookes also named a Dwight
narrative_blocks.body: Juliette Cooke, who taught John at the Royal School, gave her name to a Hooker child in the islands: the missionary Samuel Gelston Dwight named his daughter Juliette Cooke Dwight for her.

quotes.text: The lamented Prince was the contemporary of five reigning sovereigns, with every one of whom he exercised a strong influence. His counsels were born of an excellent judgment and he had rare tact in impressing others with his views.
quotes.attribution: Daily Bulletin, Honolulu, August 28, 1891 (obituary)

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the history of the Trenton crossing
narrative_blocks.body: Henry was one of the historians of Congress, and wrote and lectured on the Battle of Trenton. Governor Sproul named him to the Washington's Crossing Commission, and the ground where Washington crossed the Delaware lay in his district.

narrative_blocks.header: A Quaker against Prohibition
narrative_blocks.body: Henry belonged to the Society of Friends and spoke in Congress for world peace. He opposed the Eighteenth Amendment and the Volstead Act, and in twelve years on Ways and Means stood with Joseph Grundy for the protective tariff.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought a railroad in 1909
narrative_blocks.body: In 1909 Henry bought the Washington, Potomac and Chesapeake Railway and was its president for twenty years. At home in Langhorne he helped organize the Peoples National Bank and an electric railway to Bristol.

narrative_blocks.header: Pennsylvania's oldest member of Congress
narrative_blocks.body: Henry was seventy-seven and just re-elected to a tenth term when he died at Beechwood, his Langhorne home, in August 1933. That February the state's Republican members had made him chairman of their delegation.

narrative_blocks.header: A second marriage on Armistice Day 1922
narrative_blocks.body: Henry married Annie Masden Vaughan of Wilmington in 1897; she died in 1914. On 11 November 1922 he married Cornelia Winder Ball, a Navy widow from Detroit, and she and her daughter Janet were at his bedside in 1933.

bio.title: Doctor
bio.photo_notes: Dr. Oscar Wilhelm Carlson, Milwaukee physician (1843-1920)
bio.bio_blurb: Homeopathic physician and Civil War veteran

burial.plot_notes: Valhalla Memorial Park Milwaukee per FA

education.notes: Graduated MD 1872. Medical preceptor: uncle Dr. Charles Leuthstrom.

career.notes: Partner with Dr. Leuthstrom, then Dr. William Danforth (1879-1885), then solo. President Wisconsin Homeopathic Society; President Milwaukee Academy of Medicine; 18 years gratuitous service to Milwaukee Protestant Orphan Asylum.

military_service.notes: Enlisted Waukesha 9 Aug 1862; first action at the Port Washington draft riot; sunstroke carrying dispatches for Gen. Salomon at Helena, 4 July 1863; special mail agent Memphis-Little Rock under Gen. Steele; Mount Elba, Saline River, Spanish Fort, relief of Fort Blakely; mustered out Brownsville, discharged Madison 23 Sept 1865. Later Junior Vice Commander, E. B. Wolcott Post No. 1, GAR, and Medical Director, Department of Wisconsin, GAR.

cross_connections.display_label: , a Union hospital steward turned homeopath, was Livy Clemens's doctor
, his wife's half-brother, also took a Hahnemann medical degree

narrative_blocks.header: Shipwrecked at ten, alone
narrative_blocks.body: Oscar left Sweden alone on his tenth birthday, 1 August 1853, to be raised by an uncle in America. The ship was dismasted and drifted for months, short of water, before it reached Londonderry. He reached New York in January 1854.

narrative_blocks.header: His first action was a draft riot
narrative_blocks.body: Oscar enlisted in the 28th Wisconsin at Waukesha in August 1862, and saw his first action before the regiment left the state, when it was sent to put down the draft riot at Port Washington.

narrative_blocks.header: Sunstroke carrying dispatches at Helena
narrative_blocks.body: At Helena on 4 July 1863, when the Union garrison was attacked by three times its number, Oscar was carrying dispatches for General Salomon and went down with sunstroke. He was in the hospital there until November.

narrative_blocks.header: Mail rider between Memphis and Little Rock
narrative_blocks.body: General Steele made Oscar a special mail agent between Memphis and Little Rock. He later laid pontoon bridges on the Saline River, lay in the trenches at Spanish Fort outside Mobile, and was mustered out in Texas in 1865.

narrative_blocks.header: Milwaukee's homeopath, free to the orphans
narrative_blocks.body: Oscar trained at Hahnemann College in Chicago and practised in Milwaukee from 1872. He led the state's homeopathic society and the city's Academy of Medicine, and for eighteen years treated the Protestant Orphan Asylum's children free.

narrative_blocks.header: A father who never left the Swedish army
narrative_blocks.body: Oscar's father, Carl Johan Carlson, spent his whole life in the Swedish army and was still attached to it at eighty. His mother's family had come to Sweden from France with Bernadotte.

Came to Waukesha WI 1853/54 (age 10, alone). Enlisted Co. A 28th Wisconsin Infantry Aug 1862 Waukesha; served 3 years (honorably discharged Sept 22, 1865). Battles: Battle of Helena AR (4,000 Union vs 18,000 Confederate), Siege of Mobile, before Spanish Fort (Mar 27-Apr 8). Detailed to special assignments by General Steele. Medical preceptor: uncle Dr. Charles Leuthstrom (first homeopathic physician in Columbus OH). Hahnemann Medical College of Chicago, graduated 1872. Practice: Milwaukee; partner with Dr. Leuthstrom then Dr. William Danforth (died 1885); then solo. President Wisconsin Homeopathic Society; President Milwaukee Academy of Medicine; Supreme Medical Director for US for Royal Adelphia; Commander E.B. Wolcott GAR Post No.1; staffs of Generals Fairchild, Veasy, Warner (GAR commanders-in-chief). Gratuitous services Milwaukee Protestant Orphan Asylum 18 years. Mother's family: Leuthstrom, descendants of French family who followed Bernadotte into Sweden (supporters after Bernadotte became King Charles XIV John 1818). m. narrative_blocks.header: Roosevelt wrote him: "You are still young"
narrative_blocks.body: When the Senate balked at Tom's nomination to the Interstate Commerce Commission in 1939, Roosevelt wrote that he too had once been called a wild-eyed radical: "You are still young and I hope that you will continue."

narrative_blocks.header: A Republican who said capitalism was dying
narrative_blocks.body: Tom went to Congress in 1931 as a Republican from a Wisconsin farm district and by 1933 was saying openly that capitalism was dying. Few members ever elected as Republicans have voted further to the left.

narrative_blocks.header: Talked of for president on a third ticket
narrative_blocks.body: As chairman of the American Commonwealth Political Federation, Tom said on a 1935 national broadcast that there was "nothing in the Roosevelt program save charity capitalism." In 1936 he was mentioned for president on its ticket.

narrative_blocks.header: He graded Congress on its votes
narrative_blocks.body: In 1942 Tom became Washington director of the new Union for Democratic Action, which barred Communists and became Americans for Democratic Action. In 1944 he graded members of Congress on labor votes for the CIO.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother fought in Spain
narrative_blocks.body: Two days after Tom voted in 1937 to ban arms to both sides in Spain, his brother Hans was reported to have joined the International Brigades. Hans rose to command the Lincoln Battalion, and Tom later helped bring wounded volunteers home.

narrative_blocks.header: Two marriages, five children
narrative_blocks.body: Tom married Marian Strong in 1925; she died in 1930, and in 1932 he married Gehrta Farkasch Beyer. He had four sons and a daughter, and in later years kept a small law practice and rooming houses near the university in Madison.

quotes.text: A quarter of a century ago I, too, was called a Communist and a wild-eyed radical because I fought for factory inspection, for a fifty-four-hour-a-week bill for women and children in industry and similar measures. You are still young and I hope that you will continue to work for the improvement of social and economic legislation under our framework of Government.

people.research_notes: Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Ryum_Amlie. b.Apr 17, 1897 Binford Griggs Co ND; d.Aug 22, 1973 Madison Dane Co WI (age 76). Cremated; remains interred Forest Hill Cemetery Madison WI (cenotaph) CEM453. Education: Cooperstown ND High School; Univ of North Dakota 1916-18; Univ of Minnesota (1 year); Univ of Wisconsin Law School JD 1923. Bar 1923. Assistant clerk Dane County Superior Court 2 years; legal examiner State Dept of Markets 1 year. District chairman La Follette presidential campaign 1924. Practiced law Beloit WI (firm Fiedler, Garrigan, and Amlie); then Elkhorn WI (permanent residence). Congressional career: 72nd Congress 1931-33 (Republican, WI 1st district; filled vacancy from death of Henry Allen Cooper); lost renomination 1932; returned 74th-75th Congresses 1935-39 (Wisconsin Progressive Party). DW-Nominate score -0.322. Voted: aid to agriculture, public works, TVA (Muscle Shoals), veterans bonuses, tariff reduction. FDR nominated him Interstate Commerce Commission 1939 — withdrew under fire (Wisconsin Assembly resolution calling him Communist sympathizer; WI Speaker Vernon Thomson opposed). FDR wrote him personally on withdrawal. Roosevelt appointed him special assistant US attorney Federal Land Commission Milwaukee. Helped found Farmer-Labor-Progressive League (1933), Farmer-Labor Progressive Federation (1935). Founding member and director, Union for Democratic Action 1941 (became Americans for Democratic Action 1946 — Amlie's congressional scorecard methodology foundational). Joined Democratic Party 1941. Ran WI Supreme Court 1949 (lost); ran Congress again 1958 (lost); practiced law Madison until health issues 1962; owned properties until death. m.1: 1925 HD4648 Marian Caldwell Strong Amlie (d.May 4, 1930). m.2: 1932 Gehrta Farkasch Beyer Amlie (b.1898 d.1984 buried Forest Hill Cemetery Madison CEM453). 5 children total. Brother Hans Amlie: XV International Brigade Spanish Civil War (Lincoln Battalion commander). STAGE 6Y-136v.

bio.title: Doctor
bio.photo_notes: Doctor Robert Morris (1809-1904), surgeon of the 91st NY Infantry

education.notes: One of the preeminent medical schools in New York.

career.notes: Retired at age 94. Most of professional life in Ogdensburg, but practiced partnership periods.

military_service.notes: Severely injured at Key West FL when thrown from horse while stationed there.

narrative_blocks.header: Translating Latin from memory at age ninety-five
narrative_blocks.body: Two months before his death in November 1904, confined to his bed in Ogdensburg, Dr. Robert Morris sent for a volume from his library and read from it aloud, translating the classical Latin text 'with a readiness and correctness that were most remarkable in one so old,' according to the 1905 tribute published in the Albany Medical Annals. His mind held perfectly at the end of a life that had crossed from Scotland to America, from a Hamilton County farm to a medical college, and from a Civil War field hospital to six decades of practice in the same St. Lawrence River city.

narrative_blocks.header: Thrown from his horse while serving as surgeon
narrative_blocks.body: As surgeon of the 91st New York Infantry, Dr. Robert Morris was 'quite severely injured while stationed at Key West, Florida, by being thrown from his horse' — a wound that did not curtail his career but rather introduced a note of battlefield contingency into an otherwise steady civilian practice. He had trained at Albany Medical College, graduating in 1846, and the Civil War interruption was the one major departure from the Ogdensburg practice he would otherwise sustain for nearly sixty years.

narrative_blocks.header: Retired at ninety-four; his practice never left Ogdensburg
narrative_blocks.body: Dr. Robert Morris retired from his Ogdensburg practice in 1903 at the age of ninety-four — one of the longest documented medical careers in northern New York — and died the following year, having spent the better part of six decades within a single city on the St. Lawrence River. His wife Lucy Case Hooker Morris died in 1856 at thirty-five; he outlived her for forty-eight years, longer than she had lived.

narrative_blocks.header: Named Hooker eight generations from the founder
narrative_blocks.body: Homer Hooker Benjamin was born on September 4, 1893 in Monroe County — the same landscape where his great-great-grandmother's family had deeded land for Hooker Cemetery fifty years earlier — and his middle name 'Hooker' traced back through Mary C. Hooker Benjamin, through her father Alexander Allin Hooker of Irondequoit, through Captain James Hooker of Windsor, to the Rev. Thomas Hooker who founded Hartford in 1636. That the name survived eight generations into a family that had long since become 'Benjamin' is one of the quieter acts of genealogical memory in the Hooker tree.

narrative_blocks.header: Rochester's first Greek chair was made for him
narrative_blocks.body: The University of Rochester opened in 1850 with a handful of professors, and Greek was his. He held the Monroe chair thirty-five years, and ran the place himself as executive officer while the trustees went looking for a president.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped America rewrite the King James
narrative_blocks.body: From 1872 to 1880 he sat on the American committee revising the New Testament — the first reworking of that English text in two hundred and seventy years. He had taught Hebrew and New Testament interpretation at the Rochester seminary.

narrative_blocks.header: At sixteen he had barely been to school
narrative_blocks.body: His father Clark Kendrick was a Baptist missionary in Poultney, Vermont, and the boy read what the house and the neighbours could lend him. At sixteen he took his studies up in earnest. Hamilton College graduated him in 1831, one of nine.

narrative_blocks.header: He crossed an ocean to hear Greek spoken
narrative_blocks.body: In 1852 he sailed for Greece and sat in the lecture rooms of the University of Athens, among the first American professors to do it, then went on to Italy and Germany. He came home in 1854 and taught the language another thirty years.

narrative_blocks.header: He woke laughing at a poem he dreamt
narrative_blocks.body: He had dreamt two lines and was pleased with them, and told the story on himself for years. His Greek grammars sat on desks across the country, but he also published translations of the German poets and an anthology of English verse.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter wrote the book about him
narrative_blocks.body: Florence Kendrick Cooper published An American Scholar in 1913, eighteen years after he died — a daughter of his first marriage writing about a house his second wife Helen had kept. Rochester opened Kendrick Hall the same year.

naming_inspiration.description: Third consecutive generation to carry 'Hooker' as a middle name in the Magoffin family — following grandfather James Cole Magoffin's wife Mary Chaffee Hooker and father Rev. James Hooker Magoffin.

narrative_blocks.header: Named Hooker; he married on his own birthday
narrative_blocks.body: Frank Hooker Magoffin carried the 'Hooker' middle name his father had established in the family, and married Mary Josephine Scott on June 27, 1881 in Jasper, Iowa — his own twenty-second birthday, a choice that suggests the date was deliberate — before eventually settling in San Bernardino, California, completing the Magoffin family's three-generation migration from New York through Wisconsin through Michigan through Iowa to the Pacific coast. He was the third consecutive Magoffin to bear 'Hooker' as a given name: a thread from his grandmother Mary Chaffee Hooker of Windsor, Connecticut, carried four thousand miles and sixty years to a California desert city.

narrative_blocks.header: College-educated when almost no women were
narrative_blocks.body: Born on the Wisconsin frontier in 1861, Caroline took an education few women of her generation could — graduating from Helmuth College in Ontario and then studying at the University of Michigan. At a time when barely one woman in fifty went to college at all, she carried her learning into the family she raised.

narrative_blocks.header: She raised a Secretary of the Treasury
narrative_blocks.body: Caroline's eldest son, George Magoffin Humphrey, carried her family's name into public life, serving as Secretary of the Treasury under President Eisenhower. The Magoffin name reached back through her to the frontier Episcopal priest who was her father.

narrative_blocks.header: Horse shot at the Wilderness; wounded at Trevilian
narrative_blocks.body: Watts rode with the 1st Michigan Cavalry through the Overland Campaign's worst fighting — his horse was shot from under him at the Wilderness in 1864, and weeks later he was wounded at Trevilian Station. He came home to study law and start again.

narrative_blocks.header: He wired northern Michigan's mines and railroads together
narrative_blocks.body: From a Cheboygan law practice founded in 1869, Watts became one of northern Michigan’s most powerful attorneys, counsel to sugar and railroad interests and a director of the copper giant Phelps Dodge. He served as county treasurer and, in 1890, ran as the Republican candidate for Congress.

narrative_blocks.header: Married a third time on his birthday
narrative_blocks.body: Watts married Emma Fisher at Perry in 1870 and lost her in 1883, and his second wife, Melvina Smart, died about 1887. On 3 January 1888, his forty-fourth birthday, he married Caroline Magoffin at Hegewisch, outside Chicago.

narrative_blocks.header: His son ran the Treasury a generation later
narrative_blocks.body: The corporate world Watts moved in shaped his son George Magoffin Humphrey, who ran the M. A. Hanna Company before serving as Secretary of the Treasury under Eisenhower. Two generations of Humphreys managed the sinews of American industry before turning to public life.

narrative_blocks.header: Eisenhower's Secretary of the Treasury
narrative_blocks.body: George ran the Treasury for Eisenhower from January 1953 to July 1957, fighting for a balanced budget, tight money and the 1954 tax cuts. In fiscal 1956 he produced the first federal surplus in five years.

narrative_blocks.header: From counsel to president of M. A. Hanna
narrative_blocks.body: George left his father's Saginaw law firm in 1917 to be general counsel of the M. A. Hanna Company in Cleveland, and was its president from 1929, pulling it out of deficit and into banking, copper, plastics and natural gas. After the Treasury he chaired National Steel.

narrative_blocks.header: He surveyed Germany's war industry
narrative_blocks.body: After the Second World War George led the committee that advised the Allies on dismantling German industry. The work brought him to General Lucius Clay, who recommended him to Eisenhower for the Treasury in 1952.

narrative_blocks.header: Magoffin, from his mother’s Hooker line
narrative_blocks.body: George's middle name was his mother's: Caroline Magoffin, whose father, the Rev. James Hooker Magoffin, carried the Hooker name west from Connecticut. The Hooker line runs through the Magoffins back to Mary Chaffee Hooker of Windsor.

narrative_blocks.header: Eisenhower came to Milestone for quail
narrative_blocks.body: George built a house at Milestone Plantation outside Thomasville, Georgia, and Eisenhower came there to shoot quail over his pointers and play golf. For one visit Mamie had a knotty-pine guest cottage painted white, with pink curtains, as she had asked.

narrative_blocks.header: When George speaks, we all listen
narrative_blocks.body: He took a pay cut of more than nine-tenths to join the cabinet, and became one of its most influential voices. In 1957 he warned that without spending cuts the country would have “a depression that will curl your hair,” and Eisenhower said, “When George speaks, we all listen.”

narrative_blocks.header: A flier in 1918, then Ecuador’s mines
narrative_blocks.body: Watts enlisted in the New Jersey National Guard in 1916, was commissioned in the Aviation Section in February 1918 and discharged a year later. In the 1920s he worked in Ecuador as a mining engineer.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped plan the bombing of Germany
narrative_blocks.body: Back in uniform as a major in 1942, Watts served on the staffs of the 306th Bomb Group, VIII Bomber Command and Eighth Air Force headquarters, then on the Combined Operational Planning Committee and the Strategic Bombing Survey, and taught at the Air War College.

narrative_blocks.header: The CIA’s man in Chicago
narrative_blocks.body: From 1947 to 1950 Watts directed the Central Intelligence Agency's Chicago field office, then spent sixteen years as a private investment officer. He died at Princeton in 1968.

narrative_blocks.header: A Legion of Merit for reading the Luftwaffe
narrative_blocks.body: As chief of intelligence for the Combined Operational Planning Committee in 1943, Lt. Col. Watts Humphrey worked out how to estimate the German fighter response to each planned British and American bombing mission, and was given the Legion of Merit for it.

narrative_blocks.header: His son became the father of software quality
narrative_blocks.body: His son Watts became the father of software quality: founder of Carnegie Mellon's Software Process Program, maker of the Capability Maturity Model and winner of the National Medal of Technology. His brother George, meanwhile, was Eisenhower's Secretary of the Treasury.

narrative_blocks.body: Bud joined the M. A. Hanna Company his father had headed from 1929 to 1952, was its president in 1960 and chairman from 1961. narrative_blocks.header: Yale football and hockey, then the Navy
narrative_blocks.body: Bud played varsity football and hockey at Yale, graduated in 1939 and took his law degree there three years later. He served in the Navy through the war, then came home to practise law in Cleveland with Jones, Day, Cockley & Reavis.

narrative_blocks.header: He married into the Hanna family
narrative_blocks.body: In December 1939 Bud married Louise Ireland, a great-granddaughter of Howard Melville Hanna, the brother of Senator Mark Hanna. Four years earlier his sister Pamela had married a Hanna too.

narrative_blocks.header: A round of golf, then surgery
narrative_blocks.body: In June 1979 Bud played a round of golf at Carmel and had lunch, and then the pains in his abdomen began. He had exploratory surgery that Saturday and died the next day, at sixty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: The Treasury Secretary’s only son
narrative_blocks.body: Bud was the only son of George Humphrey, who ran the M. A. Hanna Company from 1929 and left its chairmanship for Eisenhower's Treasury in 1953.

narrative_blocks.header: He took apart a Labrador Duck
narrative_blocks.body: At Michigan, Phil took apart, for a time, one of the few surviving specimens of the extinct Labrador Duck to study its anatomy and feather tracts. The sea-ducks had been his doctoral subject in 1955, and waterfowl stayed his study for life.

narrative_blocks.header: The paper that named every plumage
narrative_blocks.body: In 1959 Phil and Kenneth Parkes published the terminology of molts and plumages that ornithologists still use, built on new feather growth as the start of a molt. The same year he co-edited The Darwin Reader with Marston Bates.

narrative_blocks.header: A survey of four million square miles
narrative_blocks.body: At the Smithsonian from 1962 Phil was curator of birds, moving the 1,400-case collection into the new East Wing, then chairman of vertebrate zoology. He led the Pacific Ocean Biological Survey across some 4.3 million square miles of ocean.

narrative_blocks.header: Patagonia with Roger Tory Peterson
narrative_blocks.body: A Guggenheim year in Argentina put Phil in Patagonia for three months of 1960 with Roger Tory Peterson. It began a lifelong interest in the steamer-ducks, and in 1981 he and Max Thompson described a new species, Tachyeres leucocephalus.

narrative_blocks.header: Director of the museum at Dyche Hall
narrative_blocks.body: In 1967 Phil became director of the University of Kansas Natural History Museum and chairman of zoology. He began its summer programmes for children and a book series on the vertebrates of Kansas, and stayed until he retired in 1995.

narrative_blocks.header: Birds from boyhood in Litchfield
narrative_blocks.body: Phil grew up in Litchfield, where his interest in birds began before he could remember, encouraged by S. Dillon Ripley and his childhood friend Duryea Morton. After three years in the Army Air Forces, Ernst Mayr steered him to Amherst.

narrative_blocks.header: He graded software on five levels
narrative_blocks.body: In a 1987 report Watts set out five levels of process maturity, from Initial to Optimizing, and his 1989 book showed a company how to climb them. The Capability Maturity Model grew from it in 1991, and the Defense Department soon required level 3 of anyone writing its software.

narrative_blocks.header: He failed first grade in Battle Creek
narrative_blocks.body: Watts failed first grade because he was dyslexic. His father moved the family to Connecticut for a school that could teach him and commuted to Wall Street in his own seaplane, and Watts graduated valedictorian, then enlisted in the Navy at seventeen, too late for the war.

narrative_blocks.header: Four thousand engineers under him at IBM
narrative_blocks.body: Watts joined IBM from Sylvania in 1959 and rose to vice-president of technical development, running software work in fifteen laboratories in seven countries. In the late 1960s his team introduced the first software license, the start of software sold as a product in its own right.

narrative_blocks.header: A second career at sixty
narrative_blocks.body: At sixty he began again at Carnegie Mellon, founding the Software Engineering Institute's Software Process Program for a Defense Department whose software kept arriving defective, late and over budget. After it came his personal and team software processes, and eleven books in all.

narrative_blocks.header: The President hung the medal on him
narrative_blocks.body: The National Medal of Technology, awarded in 2003, was presented by President George W. Bush in the East Room on 14 March 2005. By then a software quality institute in Chennai carried his name, and Embry-Riddle had made him an honorary doctor of software engineering.

narrative_blocks.header: His parents were third cousins
narrative_blocks.body: Watts came into the Hooker line twice over. His parents, Watts Sherman Humphrey Jr. and Katherine Strong, were third cousins, both great-great-grandchildren of Captain James Hooker of Windsor.

narrative_blocks.header: His uncle signed the nation’s money
narrative_blocks.body: His father's brother, George Magoffin Humphrey, was Eisenhower's Secretary of the Treasury from 1953 to 1957, and his signature went onto some four and a half billion banknotes.

narrative_blocks.header: Born in 1830; outlived all her children
narrative_blocks.body: Henrietta Theresa Parsons Strong was born in Michigan in 1830 and died in Kansas City, Missouri in November 1924 at age ninety-three — surviving her husband George Parish Strong by thirty-seven years, the Civil War, two children who predeceased her, and the first World War, her life spanning virtually the entire arc of American expansion from the frontier Michigan of Andrew Jackson's presidency to the Model T era. She was buried at Crown Hill Cemetery in Indianapolis — the same cemetery that holds the tomb of President Benjamin Harrison — a woman who had watched three American generations unfold from a Michigan farm to a Missouri city, buried in a cemetery more famous for a president she had outlived.

naming_inspiration.description: Middle name 'Hooker' honors the family's Hooker ancestry — his grandmother Dolly Goodwin Hooker Strong brought the Hooker name into the Strong family when she married Elisha Beebe Strong in 1813.

narrative_blocks.header: Named Hooker; his daughter married her Hooker cousin
narrative_blocks.body: George Hooker Strong was named for his grandmother Dolly Goodwin Hooker Strong, who had brought the Hooker name into the Strong family through her 1813 marriage to Elisha Beebe Strong — and he carried that name west from Kansas, where he was born in 1871, to Pennsylvania, where he worked as an accountant connected to Lukens Steel in Coatesville and served on the board of deacons of the Presbyterian Church. He died in Altoona, Pennsylvania in 1938, outlived by a daughter and a grandson who carried the Hooker name into the Vietnam War.

narrative_blocks.header: An accountant connected with Lukens Steel in Pennsylvania
narrative_blocks.body: George Hooker Strong settled in Chester County, Pennsylvania, where he worked as an expert accountant connected with Lukens Steel — the Coatesville ironworks that had been rolling armor plate since the Civil War and would become one of the nation's most storied steel producers, known for the plates that built American warships and later for pioneering stainless steel production. He was an active member of the Presbyterian Church and served on the board of deacons, maintaining the denominational tradition of his grandfather George Parish Strong and the broader Hooker family's Congregationalist and Presbyterian roots.

narrative_blocks.header: His son Henry also bore the name Hooker
narrative_blocks.body: George Hooker Strong named his son Henry Hooker Strong (born 1901), carrying the name into yet another generation of the Strong family, four generations removed from Dolly Goodwin Hooker Strong who first brought it into the Strongs through her 1813 marriage to Elisha Beebe Strong. Henry Hooker Strong's own son, Captain Henry Hooker Strong Jr., also bore the name — making it five consecutive generations of Hooker-named Strongs, ending with a Navy Skyhawk pilot shot down over North Vietnam in 1972.

death.cause: Heart failure on Monon train outside Indianapolis

narrative_blocks.header: Died of heart failure on the Monon train
narrative_blocks.body: John Winder Strong, a newspaper man, died on January 3, 1904 when his heart failed on the Monon Railroad train outside Indianapolis at age fifty-two. He left behind a wife and two sons who would serve in two World Wars: Major General George Veazey Strong, who became the Army's intelligence chief in World War II, and Captain William Robert Strong, who fought at Chateau-Thierry and was killed in a hunting accident in 1919.

narrative_blocks.header: His sons fought in two separate World Wars
narrative_blocks.body: John Winder Strong had two sons who served in different American wars: his elder son George Veazey Strong became the Army's intelligence chief in World War II as a major general, and his younger son William Robert Strong fought at Chateau-Thierry in World War I as a captain before being killed in a Montana hunting accident in 1919, leaving a daughter born two months after his death. The newspaper man who died on the Monon train in 1904 left a military legacy that spanned two world wars.

narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth Veazey Strong was widowed at forty-eight when her newspaper husband John Winder Strong died on the Monon Railroad train in 1904, and spent the remaining twenty-seven years of her life as the mother of two sons who would fight in two different World Wars — the elder becoming the Army's intelligence chief, the younger dying in a hunting accident in Montana in 1919. She was buried at Fort Leavenworth National Cemetery in Kansas — a military burial ground reserved for veterans and their dependents — following her son Major General George Veazey Strong's military star long after she had outlived the newspaper man who had been her husband.

narrative_blocks.header: Buried at Crown Hill alongside his mother
narrative_blocks.body: Robert Hunter Strong died in Indianapolis on January 31, 1921, and was buried at Crown Hill Cemetery in Indianapolis — the same cemetery where his mother Henrietta Theresa Parsons Strong (who outlived him by three years, dying in 1924 at age ninety-three) was also interred, two members of the same family converging on the same Indiana cemetery after lives that had begun in Wisconsin and New York. He had been born on January 4, 1854 in Fond du Lac, Wisconsin — when his father George Parish Strong was still moving the family through the Midwest — and his wife Mary Elizabeth Johnson Strong died in Lafayette, Indiana in August 1915 at age forty-three, predeceasing him by nearly six years.

narrative_blocks.header: Half a million men to St. Mihiel
narrative_blocks.body: In the First World War, St. Mihiel took over 500,000 men to assemble in September 1918 and the Meuse-Argonne 1.2 million that autumn, and he moved them all. The citation called it tireless energy and sound judgment.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran Ultra from Sherman’s old desk
narrative_blocks.body: Through the Second World War he ran Military Intelligence, from 1942 to 1944: Ultra left Bletchley unbetrayed, Fortitude covered Normandy, counterintelligence reached Oak Ridge and Los Alamos. He worked at Sherman's old desk, its whiskey compartment empty.

narrative_blocks.header: His report on the Blitz quieted the country
narrative_blocks.body: The Chief of Staff sent him to London at the worst of the bombing. He reported that the city could not be wiped out by those means, and that the British loss figures were honest.

narrative_blocks.header: Ute country, Moro country, then Tokyo
narrative_blocks.body: He began as a cavalryman against the Ute and the Moros in the Philippines. Picked in 1908 as one of two officers sent to learn Japanese, he spent three years on dictionaries and married Gerda Loenholm at Tokyo, where their son was born.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten years arguing arms limits at Geneva
narrative_blocks.body: He advised the American delegation at the Geneva disarmament conferences from 1925 to 1935, fought the move to ban experiments in gas defence, and later opposed selling arms to any nation the Axis threatened.

narrative_blocks.header: He advised the conference that drafted the UN
narrative_blocks.body: Retired in February 1944 and kept on by the War Department, he sat at Dumbarton Oaks that autumn while four powers drafted the UN Charter, and at Mexico City the year after.

narrative_blocks.header: Stilwell and McNair sat in his class
narrative_blocks.body: He came to West Point from the Michigan Military Academy, where he was adjutant and a prize-winning fencer. Joseph Stilwell of his class took China-Burma-India; Lesley McNair took the Army Ground Forces and died under American bombs.

narrative_blocks.header: Daughter of a Danish professor
narrative_blocks.body: Gerda Elfrieda Loenholm's father taught law at the Imperial Japanese College in Tokyo — one of the foreign professors Japan recruited in the Meiji era to build its modern university system — and it was in that scholarly expatriate world that she met and married George Veazey Strong, one of the first two U.S. Army officers sent to Japan to study the language, at Tsukiji Cathedral on June 2, 1909. She outlived her husband by twenty years, remaining in Washington until her death in 1966, and was buried beside him at West Point — where their son George Loenholm Strong, born in Tokyo, had once imagined his father lecturing on law during his brief academic assignment at the Academy.

military_service.notes: Secretary Helena Rifle Club before war. Carried Colt automatic pistol at Chateau-Thierry. Killed in hunting accident Oct 19, 1919 near Ovando MT, witnessed by gunwriter Elmer Keith.

narrative_blocks.header: Killed hunting; daughter born two months later
narrative_blocks.body: Captain William Robert Strong served at the Battle of Chateau-Thierry in World War I carrying the Colt automatic pistol he had bought as Secretary of the Helena Rifle Club, and was shot and killed in a hunting accident north of Ovando, Montana on October 19, 1919 — gunwriter Elmer Keith, standing six feet away, recalled the fatal slug missed him by inches. His daughter Billie Louise was born on December 16, 1919, two months after his death, and died in 1925 at age five.

narrative_blocks.header: At Chateau-Thierry he did not miss a shot
narrative_blocks.body: Captain William Robert Strong fought at the Battle of Chateau-Thierry in 1918 carrying the .30-06 Colt automatic pistol he had purchased for $14.25 through the DCM and NRA as Secretary of the Helena Rifle Club before the war — and told gunwriter Elmer Keith that he 'used several clips in one engagement and did not think he missed a shot,' a soldier's account that Keith found credible enough to preserve in his book Sixguns. Keith was standing six feet away from Strong on the morning the hunting accident took his life in 1919 — 'the 150 grain .30-06 slug that took his life missed me by inches' — making him the last witness to a man who had carried the same gun through a World War.

He died in Hagerstown, Maryland in November 1961 at fifty-one after a long illness, survived by a son in California — the Tokyo-born son of one of the Army's most significant intelligence officers ending his days as a quiet civilian aerospace engineer.

military_service.notes: Participated in strike mission near Vinh City, North Vietnam, May 25, 1972. Aircraft shot down by enemy fire. Declared Missing in Action. Promoted to Captain during period maintained as missing. Awards: Distinguished Flying Cross, Bronze Star Medal, Air Medal (Gold Star), Navy Commendation Medal with V4GS.

naming_inspiration.description: Fifth consecutive generation to carry 'Hooker' as a middle name in the Strong family, descending from Dolly Goodwin Hooker Strong (H00795) through four generations to this Navy pilot who carried the name into Vietnam.

narrative_blocks.header: He called Rolling in, and then nothing
narrative_blocks.body: Weather closed the primary target, so he took his thirty-plane strike to a road bridge south of Vinh instead. He called 'Rolling in', led the attack, and was hit by flak. No parachute, no beeper, no wreckage.

narrative_blocks.header: Not among the 591 who came home
narrative_blocks.body: He was declared missing in action, and promoted to Captain while he was still listed that way. When the prisoners were released in 1973 he was not among them, and the Vietnamese denied all knowledge of him.

narrative_blocks.header: He led the squadron he was flying with
narrative_blocks.body: He was commanding officer of Attack Squadron 212 aboard the Hancock when he was lost. Ten years before, as a lieutenant, he had been the Navy's A-4 project officer at Albuquerque.

narrative_blocks.header: Two memorials, and no grave
narrative_blocks.body: He is carried on the Courts of the Missing at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific, and on Panel 01W, Line 33 of the Wall in Washington. He has never been accounted for.

narrative_blocks.header: His two children were left asking
narrative_blocks.body: He left two children, who stayed a military family and spent years trying to get answers about what happened to him. Nobody has ever been able to give them one.

Struck target near Vinh City North Vietnam May 25, 1972; aircraft shot down by enemy fire; declared MIA; promoted to Captain while maintained as missing. Awards: Distinguished Flying Cross; Bronze Star Medal; Air Medal (Gold Star); Navy Commendation Medal with V4GS. Son of HD4707 Henry Hooker Strong and I00965 Agnes Dugan Strong. Named 'Hooker' — fifth consecutive generation of Hooker-named Strongs in this line. Gen 9 Hooker descendant. STAGE 6Y-136jj. [Stage 6Y-264 schema cleanup]: notable_blurb trimmed from [9w] 'Navy Skyhawk pilot shot down over North Vietnam, 1972' → 'Navy Skyhawk pilot shot down over North Vietnam'. [081226] Rebuilt from the POW Network, DPAA, honorstates and Skyhawk Association material. Death city set to VINH per Sam; the exact loss point was the Ben Thuy road bridge about three miles south of the city, coordinates 48Q WF 733 607, aircraft A-4F BuNo 155045, side number NP-301. TWO CONFLICTS ON RECORD: (1) honorstates gives the incident location as QUANG TRI PROVINCE, which cannot be right for a target at Vinh — Vinh is in Nghe An. (2) THE BURIAL HERE IS ARLINGTON (CEM044) but every source says he was never recovered and is memorialised on the Courts of the Missing at the Honolulu Memorial; the Arlington burial was NOT removed, because removing it was not asked for, but it is probably wrong. Rank at loss was Commander (O-5); Captain came while he was missing. Some pilots thought they heard him call 'feet wet' crossing the coast. Decorations: Distinguished Flying Cross, Bronze Star, Air Medal, five Navy Commendation Medals. Home of record North Wales, PA. Service 1956-1972. [081226] Wife Christina Cordaire Heiberger (I03334) built, married 27 July 1957. CC to his great-granduncle Rear Admiral James Hooker Strong added — the Navy runs from Mobile Bay in 1864 to a Skyhawk over Vinh in 1972 in the same family.

narrative_blocks.header: She built the Navy's budget counseling
narrative_blocks.body: Judy spent twelve years with the Navy-Marine Corps Relief Society, as a volunteer and then on its staff, and developed its Budget Counselor Service, writing the guidance and making films for the Society and the Department of Defense. In retirement at Lynchburg she was twice president of the Hill City Master Gardener Association.

narrative_blocks.header: Panhellenic president at Penn
narrative_blocks.body: Judy studied interior design at Penn's School of Architecture and graduated in 1960, having been president of the Panhellenic Council and a member of the President's Student Advisory Board.

narrative_blocks.header: She married her brother's fellow cadet
narrative_blocks.body: She married Herb Kinney in the July of 1960 at Virginia Beach. He had gone into Navy flight training alongside her brother Henry, and flew the same Skyhawks.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brother and father died in one year
narrative_blocks.body: Her brother went missing over North Vietnam in the May of 1972 and was never found. Her father died eight weeks after that.

narrative_blocks.header: Buried at Arlington, and he followed her
narrative_blocks.body: She died at Lynchburg in Virginia in the June of 2008, sixty-nine years old, and was buried at Arlington that July. Her husband was laid there three years after her.

military_service.notes: Flew A-6 Intruders. Deployed USS Independence Vietnam 1965. Commanded VA-52 Oct 1972. Saigon evacuation April 1975; Mayaguez repatriation May 1975. Commanded USS Cleveland (LPD-7) 1978-80. JCS J-5 staff 1975.

narrative_blocks.header: Among the first A-6 Intruder pilots
narrative_blocks.body: Herb was among the first pilots trained on the all-weather A-6 Intruder, joining VA-75, its first fleet squadron, in 1963 and flying it to Vietnam off the Independence in 1965. He took command of VA-52 aboard the Kitty Hawk on 3 October 1972 and flew his last combat mission a month later.

narrative_blocks.header: He was off Saigon when the city fell
narrative_blocks.body: In April 1975 Herb was operations officer aboard the Coral Sea for the evacuation of Americans from Saigon. The next month he was there for the retaking of the Mayaguez.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven Distinguished Flying Crosses
narrative_blocks.body: Herb flew 4,200 hours in thirty-one years of naval service and made 659 carrier landings, 173 of them at night. He was awarded the Legion of Merit, seven Distinguished Flying Crosses and eighteen Air Medals.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-one years, and two commands
narrative_blocks.body: Herb commanded the amphibious transport dock Cleveland from December 1978 to July 1980, served on the Joint Chiefs' staff for the Far East and South Asia, and retired a captain in 1986.

narrative_blocks.header: He learned to fly at a college airfield
narrative_blocks.body: Herb was an engineering student at Maryland when he found flying at College Park, and held a commercial licence by 1955. He was designated a Naval Aviator on 20 September 1956, his twenty-second birthday, and finished a political science degree at night while at the Naval War College.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the sister of his fellow cadet
narrative_blocks.body: Herb married Judith Ann Strong in July 1960 — the sister of Henry Hooker Strong Jr., who had gone through flight training with him. They bought a house at Virginia Beach.

narrative_blocks.body: Doctor Arthur Kimball Northrop practiced medicine in Great Falls, Montana, where his wife Joanne devoted her years as treasurer for the Women's Medical Auxiliary for both Cascade County and the Montana State Association — an intimate domestic partnership between a physician's work and its institutional support, sustained through decades of Montana winters, golf trips to California and Hawaii, and summers at their Whitefish condo. narrative_blocks.header: Typhoid Mary cooked for them that summer
narrative_blocks.body: He was nineteen the summer the family took a house at Dark Harbor in Maine and most of the household came down with typhoid. The cook that season was Mary Mallon, whom the country would know a few years later as Typhoid Mary.

narrative_blocks.header: At thirteen he stayed with his father
narrative_blocks.body: His parents' marriage came apart in public: his mother was seen too much in London with another New Yorker, and his father challenged the man to a duel in Paris. The divorce went through in 1896, the fault was hers, and the children stayed with their father while she went to England and married again.

narrative_blocks.header: Two marriages, both got quietly
narrative_blocks.body: A first marriage to Mary Constance Knower was ended by a decree granted in secret at White Plains in 1907; she later married a French count. In February 1922 he married Catherine Hamersly Hinckley at West Palm Beach, days after her own Reno decree, with two friends standing up and no one else there.

narrative_blocks.header: The darling of the Newport set
narrative_blocks.body: He kept a house at Newport called Fair Oak and another in New York, and that was what the society columns called him.

narrative_blocks.header: The papers placed him by his grandmother
narrative_blocks.body: Notices called him a grandson of the late Mrs. William Astor, whose ballroom held the four hundred. His uncle John Jacob Astor went down with the Titanic in 1912.

career.notes: Relocated to Gallipolis Ohio in 1818, then to a farm near New Albany Indiana where he died in 1852.

military_service.unit: Captain James Watson's Company, Third Connecticut Regiment (Colonel Samuel B. Webb)
military_service.notes: Enlisted June 20, 1777 at age 10 — one of the youngest soldiers in the Revolutionary War. Served as fifer; participated in each march and engagement of his unit. Met both George and Martha Washington and General Lafayette. Served full 3-year term; discharged June 20, 1780. Gravestone: 'A musician in the Army of the Revolution' / 'Ten Year Old Fifer'.

narrative_blocks.header: His tombstone reads: 'Ten Year Old Fifer'
narrative_blocks.body: Richard Lord Jones enlisted in June 1777 in Colonel Samuel B. Webb's Regiment and was put under the Master of the Band to learn fife; arriving at Morristown in January 1780, he would later write: 'The Inhabitants remarked that it was the coldest winter ever known by the oldest inhabitants. The troops drew no rations of meat for two days (hungry times.)' His gravestone at Fairview Cemetery in New Albany, Indiana carries two inscriptions — the original reads 'A musician in the Army of the Revolution,' and a government-issued stone beside it reads 'Ten Year Old Fifer,' for a man who was ten when he shouldered a fife into the Continental Army.

narrative_blocks.header: He sang God Save America for Martha Washington
narrative_blocks.body: Colonel Webb directed Jones to go to Colonel Jackson's hut, where Martha Washington and some ladies were, and sing her a song; Jones later wrote: 'I did so sing the song when she presented me with a bill of three dollars, Continental Currency. The bill has been kept, folded as she gave it to me.' The three-dollar Continental bill — kept folded precisely as Martha Washington handed it to a ten-year-old fifer in a New Jersey officer's hut in 1780 — is one of the most extraordinary artifacts in this entire family's history, passed from Washington's hands to a child soldier who would live to farm in Indiana and die at eighty-five in 1852.

narrative_blocks.header: Walked 150 miles home to Hartford at thirteen
narrative_blocks.body: When Jones received his discharge on June 20, 1780 — having served his full three-year term from age ten to thirteen — he left Jockey Hollow with two other discharged men and walked 150 miles north to Hartford, Connecticut, recording in his memoir that he arrived home 'without any accident.' That phrase — 'without any accident,' after a 150-mile walk home from a war entered at ten — is a small window into what it meant to be a child soldier in the Continental Army, and into the plainspoken Yankee temperament with which Jones recorded his entire service in the memoir he would write decades later in Indiana.

narrative_blocks.header: Innkeeper of Great Barrington
narrative_blocks.body: Isaac Pixley kept a tavern at Great Barrington, Massachusetts, that burned in 1787 — the Pixley genealogy notes the fire 'is said to have been incendiary,' suggesting arson — and after losing the building he built the old red house that David Humphrey would later occupy for many years; his wife's sister Anna Hooker, present at the fire, fractured her leg badly jumping from the second-story window to frozen ground. He died three years later, on May 11, 1790, at Great Barrington, age forty — leaving Abigail with six children under seventeen — and she would outlive him by fifty-one years, eventually dying in Henrietta, New York in 1841 at eighty-seven.

narrative_blocks.header: His great-grandson won the Nobel Peace Prize
narrative_blocks.body: James Root's first wife was Lydia Anna Robb (1749-1788 of Westfield, Massachusetts), and their son Elihu Root Sr. (born 1772) began a family line that produced Oren Root (born 1803) and then Elihu Root (born 1845) — Secretary of War under President McKinley, Secretary of State under Theodore Roosevelt, and winner of the Nobel Peace Prize in 1912 for his work in international arbitration. When James Root then married Abigail Hooker as his second wife in 1793, he connected his family to the descendants of Rev. Thomas Hooker — meaning the Pixley-Hooker family and the Elihu Root line share a common progenitor in James Root, though the Nobel laureate descended from Lydia Robb's branch and carries no Hooker blood.

narrative_blocks.header: One of the early settlers of East Bloomfield
narrative_blocks.body: Ira Pixley was born at Great Barrington, Massachusetts in 1783 — in the same Berkshire hills where his parents' tavern burned in 1787 and his father died in 1790 — and by 1809 had moved his family west to East Bloomfield, Ontario County, New York, where he and Sarah Adams married that August and where he would spend the rest of his life. His gravestone at East Bloomfield Cemetery calls him simply 'one of the early settlers of East Bloomfield, Ontario County, New York' — the son of an innkeeper who died young, become himself a founding farmer of an upstate New York township, eighty years old when he died there in 1863.

engagements: Battle of Swan's Quarter, NC (April 30, 1863) — coastal sound operation where Sperry was wounded

narrative_blocks.header: Discharged from the Civil War at Swan's Quarter
narrative_blocks.body: Dr. Moses Sperry served in the medical department of the Third New York Cavalry under Colonel Mix, treating wounded men through the campaigns of 1862-1863, until injuries he received at the Battle of Swan's Quarter, North Carolina forced his discharge in 1863 — a small, overlooked engagement in the coastal war, but the one that ended his service. He returned to Rochester, where he became a practicing physician and eventually health officer of the city, the same skill set he had deployed under fire in the Carolina sounds now directed at the public health of a peacetime industrial city on the Erie Canal.

narrative_blocks.header: Returned wounded; became Rochester city health officer
narrative_blocks.body: Discharged in 1863 from injuries at Swan's Quarter, Sperry returned to Rochester New York and resumed civilian medical practice. He served as Health Officer of the city — directing Rochester's public-health response to the cholera, smallpox, and tuberculosis threats of the Gilded Age industrial city on the Erie Canal. His wartime cavalry-medicine training carried directly into peacetime municipal sanitation work.

narrative_blocks.header: Born Henrietta, died Rochester, both Monroe County
narrative_blocks.body: Sperry's life arc traced a tight twelve-mile orbit within Monroe County New York. He was born April 1, 1830 in Henrietta and died September 24, 1902 in Rochester — the same county where he had practiced medicine for nearly forty postwar years. He married Olive Canfield of Bennington NY on January 8, 1857, five years before he marched south with the Third New York Cavalry.

STAGE 6Y-136ww. [Stage 6Y-283 deepening]: military_service array built (was empty). 3rd New York Cavalry medical department under Colonel Simon H. Mix. Battle of Swan's Quarter NC April 30, 1863 was part of the Federal sound-and-river operations on the North Carolina coast; Mix's cavalry harassed Confederate supply lines in Tyrrell and Hyde counties. Sperry's injury and discharge ended his combat service but enabled his Rochester health officer career — a notable transfer of wartime medical skills to municipal public health. Postwar Rochester health officer thread: Sperry is one of multiple Hooker-line Civil War surgeons who transitioned to municipal or state public-health work — alongside Hamilton Polk Jones (Louisiana State Analyst/Food Commissioner) and Joseph Jones (Louisiana State Board of Health President). The Civil War → municipal sanitation pipeline.

narrative_blocks.header: Killed by a powder explosion at Battle Creek
narrative_blocks.body: Edward Sperry died December 10, 1892 at Battle Creek, Michigan — killed instantly by a powder explosion, according to EH, though the Pixley genealogy places the event in Joliet, Illinois in 1881, a discrepancy that has never been resolved. He had married Clarissa Delano Colvin in 1858, but she predeceased him by twenty-one years, dying in 1871 also at Battle Creek; by the time the explosion killed him, he had been a widower for two decades and left behind five children who ranged in age from twenty-three to thirty-three.

narrative_blocks.header: Settled Lyons township in 1840
narrative_blocks.body: John Amos Root moved with his family to Lyons township, Ionia County, Michigan in 1840 when he was about eight or nine years old — the family having come west from Moscow, New York — and spent the next sixty-one years there, farming the same land where he died, serving as director of the Farmers' Mutual Fire Insurance Company of Ionia County and officer of his school district. He married Sarah March on June 4, 1856, and his obituary in the Lyons paper noted that 'by his kindly nature and pleasant ways he had endeared himself to all with whom he came in contact,' closing with the motto he had followed: 'Do Unto Others as ye would that they should do unto you.'

narrative_blocks.header: Entered the jewelry trade at twenty
narrative_blocks.body: William Pixley went into the jewelry trade in Detroit at age twenty, then moved to Columbus, Ohio after his marriage to Hattie Fleming, and continued in the jewelry business as the family settled eventually in Reedsburg, Wisconsin, where he died on May 17, 1912 at seventy-eight. His birth city was Milford, Michigan — in the Oakland County countryside where his father Isaac Chauncey Pixley had settled after moving west from New York — and his whole arc tracked the same westward drift: Michigan to Ohio to Wisconsin, jeweler to jeweler, town to town across the Great Lakes tier.

narrative_blocks.header: Berkshire Medical School graduate; died at twenty-five, unmarried
narrative_blocks.body: George Burling Pixley graduated from Berkshire Medical School — one of the New England proprietary medical schools of the antebellum era, operating in Pittsfield, Massachusetts from 1823 to 1867 — and died December 11, 1846 at Henrietta, New York, unmarried, at approximately twenty-five. His middle name Burling honored his mother Mary Burling Pixley's Quaker family, the same family from which Burling Slip in lower Manhattan took its name; he was the only one of John Hooker Pixley's children by Mary Burling to pursue a medical degree.

career.organization: Troy Tow-Boat Line; Troy and Whitehall Towing Company; Northern Transportation Line; Pattison & Hart
career.notes: Started as business clerk at Pattison & Hart after moving to Troy ~1820. Built extensive freight operation on Erie, Oswego, and Champlain Canals, Lake Champlain, and Hudson River. By 1851: 11 barges (5,100 tons), 120 canal boats to Buffalo/Rochester/Oswego/Whitehall, 11 sail vessels and steam propeller 'James H. Hooker' on Lake Champlain, 6 steamboats + 5 propellers on Buffalo Canal Line, 800 horses on Erie Canal, 50 agents throughout NY state. Never married.

narrative_blocks.header: A steamship on Lake Champlain bore his name
narrative_blocks.body: By 1850, Colonel James H. Hooker operated one of the most extensive freight transportation networks in the American northeast — 50 canal boats to Buffalo, 29 to Rochester, 16 to Oswego, 25 to Whitehall, eleven barges totaling 5,100 tons, six steamboats and five propellers on the Buffalo Canal Line, eleven sail vessels on Lake Champlain, and a steam propeller named the 'James H. Hooker' carrying 300 tons between Albany and Montreal.

narrative_blocks.header: Violent in his speech; fair with his workers
narrative_blocks.body: James Harvey Hooker never married — his extended family knew him as 'Uncle James' while 20th century descendants called him 'the Fat Man' for his portly girth — and contemporaries described him as 'a passionate eccentric, violent in his speech and action, but ultimately fair and just with his workers and associates.' His portrait, painted by Nelson Cook in the period 1845-1848 when Cook was at his mature peak, survived in a California private collection and was cleaned and restored in February 2026 by Susan Brown-Madorsky of SB Conservation in Laguna Beach — 175 years after its subject died in Troy on December 28, 1851.

Hooker' carrying 300 tons between Albany and Montreal. The Troy Daily Whig described him in February 1850 as 'a self-made man' who kept 'himself well posted in all details of his immense business,' noting that his 800 horses on the Erie Canal — managed by 90 men and 400 boys — moved the industrial output of an expanding republic westward, while his 200 horses on Lake Champlain moved agricultural bounty east.'

narrative_blocks.header: Died at thirty; infant Joseph eight months old
narrative_blocks.body: Ann Hooker Congdon married Joseph Congdon on October 2, 1823 and bore six children in eleven years; her youngest, Joseph, was born April 17, 1834, and she died December 17 that same year at Freedom, New York, at thirty years old — leaving an eight-month-old infant among her surviving children. Her husband Joseph Congdon outlived her by thirty-eight years, dying at Elmira in 1872; the eldest child she had named 'James Hooker' had himself died nine months before that, in May 1865, leaving her family's history as a study in how early death cascades through a generation.

narrative_blocks.header: Died at thirty-one; widow renamed herself Whitton
narrative_blocks.body: Henry Hooker died March 25, 1866 in Indianapolis at thirty-one — leaving Clementine Russell Hooker with four children under eight, the youngest, Henry Samuel, barely a year old — and within a few years she had remarried, becoming Clementine Russell Hooker Whitton, a name that preserved and then buried her first husband's in the same breath. She outlived him by eleven years, dying in 1877; their son James Harvey survived to 1931, their daughter Margaret to 1952, meaning Henry Hooker's children outlasted him by decades in the same Indianapolis streets where he had died young.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the widow of his company's Private
narrative_blocks.body: Sergeant Major John 'Jack' Hooker served in Company H of the 12th Indiana Volunteer Infantry during the Civil War; Private John Brooks served in the same company and died April 22, 1864 at Scottsboro, Alabama, buried at Chattanooga National Cemetery. After the war ended, Jack Hooker married Brooks's widow, Louisa Vanzant — a connection that collapsed the distance between survival and loss into a single family, the sergeant major and the dead private joined permanently through the woman who had belonged to both.

narrative_blocks.header: Named Hooker; died at Fort Plain at forty
narrative_blocks.body: James Hooker Congdon — his middle name preserving his mother Ann Hooker's birth family — married Jane Augusta Wagner on February 9, 1852, lived at Troy and Fort Plain, New York, and died there on May 25, 1865 at forty years old, his wife surviving him by forty-two years until her own death in 1907 at Johnstown, New York. He was the eldest child of Ann Hooker Congdon, who herself died at thirty at Freedom, New York in 1834 — and his surname Congdon rather than Hooker was the reason his 'Hooker' name migrated to the middle position, a naming pattern repeated throughout the Hooker family tree when daughters married out.

narrative_blocks.header: Died of a skull fracture
narrative_blocks.body: Marquis R. Hooker died March 20, 1934 in Indianapolis at fifty-three, killed by a skull fracture suffered in a fall from scaffolding to a cement floor — possibly at Tomlinson Hall, Indianapolis's famous civic and market venue, though the specific work site is unconfirmed. His death by industrial accident at the height of the Depression ended a life that had begun in the city his grandfather Azel Hooker and great-grandfather Gilbert Hooker had never seen, but which had become home to three generations of the family over sixty years of Indiana settlement.

military_service.notes: Enlisted Aug 17, 1862. Mustered into Company H, 12th Indiana Volunteer Infantry, Aug 17, 1862. Died April 22, 1864 at Scottsboro, Alabama. Buried Chattanooga National Cemetery. Same company (Company H, 12th Indiana) as Sgt. Major John 'Jack' Hooker, who later married his widow Louisa Vanzant.

narrative_blocks.header: Died in the same company whose sergeant major
narrative_blocks.body: PVT John Brooks enlisted August 17, 1862 in Company H, 12th Regiment, Indiana Volunteer Infantry — the same company in which John 'Jack' Hooker served as Sergeant Major — and died April 22, 1864 at Scottsboro, Alabama, at approximately twenty-five years old, buried at Chattanooga National Cemetery. After the war ended, his widow Louisa Vanzant Brooks married the man who had commanded his company as its senior non-commissioned officer — Jack Hooker — a connection that made the Civil War's death and survival into an intimate family story.

narrative_blocks.header: Vermont to Illinois to Iowa in three generations
narrative_blocks.body: Martial Edson Crossett's parents Jacob Royal and Abigail Perkins Crossett had migrated west from Washington County, New York and Rutland, Vermont through Illinois — settling in Cortland Township, DeKalb County in 1846 — and Martial was born there in 1844, then moved further west himself to Iowa, where he married Orphany Louisa Cheaseboro in Cortland in 1866 and died in Wellman in 1931 at eighty-seven. He left five children and outlived his wife Orphany by eighteen years, the generation that completed the family's migration from New England through the Midwest.

narrative_blocks.header: Enlisted after WWII; still serving when Vietnam ended
narrative_blocks.body: Donald Carl Crossett was born June 21, 1925 in Washington, Iowa — the same day as his twin brother Richard Earl, who served in the Navy in World War II — and Donald went into the Army after the war, serving for twenty-six years through Korea and Vietnam before retiring as a Master Sergeant in 1973. The two twins' combined service spanned both branches of the military, two theaters of war, and nearly three decades; Richard was buried in Illinois, Donald in Purdy, Virginia, neither of them returning to the Iowa county where they were born.

narrative_blocks.header: First woman rural route carrier in Washington County
narrative_blocks.body: Barbara Joan Henderson worked for the United States Postal Service as a clerk for seventeen years and then as a rural route carrier for thirteen years — becoming the first woman rural route carrier in Washington County, Iowa — after teaching school for five years following her marriage to Eury Henderson in 1947. Her obituary notes that she 'enjoyed to travel, watching wildlife, and flower gardens,' and that she was a member of the Order of Eastern Star, Past Worthy Matron and Instructor; she died November 28, 2014 at Parkview Manor in Wellman at eighty-seven, survived by her husband of sixty-seven years.

narrative_blocks.body: James Russell Crossett, a Senior Chief Petty Officer in the Navy, died in Fairfax, Virginia on March 26, 1988 at fifty-seven; his wife Marjorie Ann Bull, who had grown up in the same Washington County, Iowa farming community, was buried beside him at Arlington twenty-three years later when she died in 2011. narrative_blocks.header: Orphaned at two, brought to Hinsdale at twelve
narrative_blocks.body: His father Cyrus Jones died when he was about two years old and his mother Sally Bowker moved the family to Athol, Massachusetts. At twelve he was sent to Hinsdale to live with his uncle Windsor Bowker; he never left.

narrative_blocks.header: Married Julia Worthington Hooker, December 1842
narrative_blocks.body: He married Julia W., daughter of Henry Hooker of the Hinsdale homestead, on 7 December 1842. They raised three children, two of whom became mechanics in Keene.

narrative_blocks.header: Built a Canal Street doors-and-sash factory
narrative_blocks.body: After three years running a Kilbourn brook sawmill in the mid-1830s, he bought a shop on Canal Street in Hinsdale village and manufactured doors, sash, blinds, and dressed lumber for many years. The shop was a fixture of the manufacturing village.

narrative_blocks.header: Constitutional convention delegate, 1876
narrative_blocks.body: He served three terms as selectman, represented Hinsdale in the state legislature in 1876–77, and sat as a delegate to the 1876 New Hampshire constitutional convention. Earlier he had been captain of the Ashuelot Guards, a Hinsdale militia company.

narrative_blocks.header: Born in Gerry, Massachusetts — renamed Phillipston, 1814
narrative_blocks.body: His birthplace was named for Elbridge Gerry, fifth vice-president of the United States, but the town was renamed Phillipston in 1814 after Gerry's political fall from grace. He was thus born in Gerry but always identified as a Phillipston native.

narrative_blocks.body: Elihu married Sally Gay Hooker, daughter of Seth Hooker and granddaughter of Rev. Bunker Gay, on 11 November 1824. Their three children, John Mills, Sarah H. and Edward, were born on the Stebbins homestead.

narrative_blocks.header: Selectman and Hinsdale legislator
narrative_blocks.body: Elihu farmed his father's homestead until his death at seventy-seven, served as selectman, and repeatedly represented Hinsdale in the New Hampshire legislature.

narrative_blocks.header: Stebbins line traces to Ipswich, England, 1634
narrative_blocks.body: He descended from Rowland Stebbins, born 1594 in Ipswich, England, who sailed on the Francis in 1634 and went up the Connecticut River with William Pynchon to help found Springfield. His father Elihu Sr. brought the family to Hinsdale in 1786.

narrative_blocks.header: Life with Lucy Sturdevant
narrative_blocks.body: By 1900 Elizabeth and Lucy Huston Sturdevant, daughter of Gen. Ebenezer Warren Sturdevant of Wilkes-Barre, were keeping house at Asheville, North Carolina, where the census listed Lucy as head and Elizabeth as her partner. They moved between Asheville, Wilkes-Barre and Nantucket for the rest of Elizabeth's life.

narrative_blocks.header: Lucy wrote for the Atlantic
narrative_blocks.body: Lucy wrote short stories for the Atlantic Monthly, among them A North-West End in 1909, and had one chosen for the Best Short Stories of 1915, the year Elizabeth died. She wrote about untrained nurses, the waterfront and Quaker teachers.

narrative_blocks.header: She left almost everything to Lucy
narrative_blocks.body: When Elizabeth died at Wilkes-Barre on 31 March 1915 she left nearly her whole estate to Lucy, with a small bequest to her brother Francis, and named Lucy her executor. Lucy lived on in Wilkes-Barre until 1940.

sources.label: Wilkes-Barre Record, 7 Apr 1915, on the Packard will

people.research_notes: EH 4333. Per Sam's research and 1900 census: Elizabeth was the partner of Lucy Huston Sturdevant, who was the daughter of General Ebenezer Warren Sturdevant and Lucy Huston of Wilkes-Barre PA. The 1900 census in Buncombe County NC explicitly lists Lucy as head and Elizabeth as 'partner' with South Carolinian cook Lena Brooks and maid Martha Mook. Elizabeth's residence shifted between Wilkes-Barre, Asheville, and Nantucket; she hosted tea parties with her sister and traveled. Her death certificate lists her as single; same for Lucy. Lucy died 1940 having always insisted Wilkes-Barre was her real home. Lucy was an Atlantic Monthly short-story writer (e.g. 'A North-West End' 1909; included in Best Short Stories of 1915). She lived at the Hotel Sterling in Wilkes-Barre, a hotel managed by Robert Mills — a side-thread of personal interest to Sam (his Mills ancestor). See Christine E. Sleeter's 2020 Genealogy journal piece on tracing LGBTQ family members.

narrative_blocks.header: Auditor to president in seven years
narrative_blocks.body: Charles joined the Pennsylvania Company for Insurance on Lives and Granting Annuities as its auditor in 1892 and was its president by 1899. He ran it for thirty-five years, keeping it in the front rank of Philadelphia's banks.

narrative_blocks.header: He merged failing banks into his own
narrative_blocks.body: A conservative banker and a steadying influence through difficult years, Charles was credited with saving the depositors of more than one failing bank by merging it into the Pennsylvania Company.

narrative_blocks.header: Railroads, a ferry and the telephone
narrative_blocks.body: Charles sat on a score of boards, from the Lehigh & New England and Catawissa railroads and the Elizabethport and New York Ferry to Bell Telephone of Pennsylvania and the Insurance Company of North America.

narrative_blocks.header: Penn at twenty, then its trustee
narrative_blocks.body: After Rugby Academy, Charles graduated from the University of Pennsylvania in 1880, at twenty, and later served it for eight years as a trustee and as treasurer of its Athletic Association.

narrative_blocks.header: Quiet gifts to clergy widows
narrative_blocks.body: Charles gave widely and seldom publicly. He was for many years a trustee of the Episcopal Hospital and of a fund for the widows of Episcopal clergymen, and a vestryman of St. James the Less, where he is buried.

narrative_blocks.header: Golf until he was seventy
narrative_blocks.body: Golf was Charles's hobby for years, and he gave it up only at seventy. He belonged to the Philadelphia, Racquet, St. Anthony and Rittenhouse clubs and the Philadelphia Country Club, and lived on Rittenhouse Square.

narrative_blocks.header: A daughter lost in her first summer
narrative_blocks.body: Charles married Eliza Gilpin McLean of Virginia in 1882. Their daughter Elizabeth was born the next March and died that July, and their son John grew up to be a vice president of his father's company.

narrative_blocks.header: Charity, at eighteen
narrative_blocks.body: In 1810, at eighteen, at the Misses Patten's school in Hartford, Rachel stitched a silk picture of Charity from a mezzotint by P. Stampa: a woman handing bread to a small child outside her door. It has been in the Smithsonian since 1951.

narrative_blocks.header: The sampler she made at eleven
narrative_blocks.body: About 1803, at eleven, Rachel worked a sampler at Northampton with its whole ground covered in long satin stitches. It turned up near Philadelphia in 2011, and the Smithsonian bought it, reuniting it with her Charity as its first pair of a girl's early sampler and her later silk work.

narrative_blocks.header: A date settled by the sampler
narrative_blocks.body: The back of Charity's frame says 1810, in her eighteenth year, and someone later penciled in 1803 and eleven. The rediscovered sampler settled it: both were right, the sampler at eleven and the silk picture at eighteen.

narrative_blocks.header: Latin, Greek and embroidery
narrative_blocks.body: Rachel went to Deerfield Academy for three twelve-week sessions from April 1806, and at eighteen to the Misses Patten's school in Hartford, which taught Latin, Greek, French, bookkeeping, astronomy and embroidery.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight children, four grown
narrative_blocks.body: Rachel married Dr. George Hooker in January 1819 and bore eight children in thirteen years. She lost Sarah at five, Lucy and George as babies and Josiah at twenty-nine, and gave her next daughter the name Sarah Dwight again.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father died when she was nine
narrative_blocks.body: Her father, Joseph Hunt Breck of Northampton, died in 1801 at thirty-five, when she was nine. Her mother, Abigail Kingsley Breck, never remarried and lived another forty-five years.

narrative_blocks.header: She prized education above all but religion
narrative_blocks.body: She made her children feel that a liberal education was, next to personal religion, the greatest blessing of life, and she would go anywhere or do anything to secure it for them. One of those children, Timothy Dwight V, grew up to be president of Yale.

narrative_blocks.header: She never let those who trusted her waver
narrative_blocks.body: Full of energy and a persuading power that convinced others her plans were always wisest, she led by never letting anyone who trusted her see her own resolve falter. Obstacles, a family memoir said, only raised her resolution to meet them.

narrative_blocks.header: A son's death began her final illness
narrative_blocks.body: The disease that ended her life was traced, her family believed, to the sudden loss of her eldest son eight years before — a blow that struck at her ancestral home in Norwich. She never fully recovered from it.
