At age 15 went to Hebron CT to assist in his uncle's business. Yale College B.A. 1817 'with high honor.' Law apprenticeship under Judge William Bristol of New Haven CT 1817-1819. Litchfield Law School (INST024) 1819. Admitted to New Haven bar. PENNSYLVANIA MIGRATION: Family crisis prompted relocation. Conducted an academy at Wilkes-Barre PA for 1½ years starting 1822. Removed to Easton PA where he practiced law for many years. Lafayette College board secretary 1826-1835 and trustee through 1852. 1830 CIVIL CODE COMMISSIONER: Appointed by Governor George Wolf as one of three commissioners (with William Rawle and Thomas I. Wharton) to revise the civil code of Pennsylvania. The team's 1836 PA Senate report produced enduring statutory compilations. 1834 to Philadelphia. 1835 Associate Judge Philadelphia District Court → 1845 Presiding Judge (resigned 1847 to accept Girard College presidency). Notable Delaware River fisheries ruling. GIRARD COLLEGE 1847-1849: First president of Girard College — Stephen Girard's 1831 endowed institution for poor white male orphans, with controversial Vidal v. Girard's Executors 1844 SCOTUS clergy-ban precedent. Resigned 1849 for mayor's race. PHILADELPHIA MAYOR 1849-1850: Elected Oct 9, 1849 narrow Independent defeat of Whig Charles Gilpin. Inaugurated Oct 16, 1849. Lost 1850 reelection to same Gilpin Oct 15, 1850. One-year term under pre-1854 city charter. 1849 cholera epidemic + Board of Health sanitation drives. Some sources call him Democratic, others Independent; he won 6,429 votes (50.19%) per Wikipedia. AMERICAN PHILOSOPHICAL SOCIETY 1848 member. PRINCETON honorary doctorate 1848 per Litchfield Law School records. ART: Auguste Edouart 1842 silhouette of Joel Jones with George Stroud — ink wash, chalk + cut paper on paper, Smithsonian Institution National Portrait Gallery (Gift of Robert L. McNeil Jr., Object ID JJGS1884) — catalogued as ART061 in tree. MARRIAGE: Married Eliza Perkins Sparhawk (I01136, 1801-1882, daughter of Dr John Sparhawk X02863 of London Book Store Philadelphia) June 14, 1831 Philadelphia. 6 children per Wikipedia (5 named on FindAGrave): Rev John Sparhawk Jones (TD0240, 1841-1910 — only survivor to adulthood; deferred to next stage); Elizabeth Jones (d.1837 young); Joel Jones (d.1837 young); Mary Jones (d.1844 young); Sarah Jones (d.1849 young); sixth child unnamed in sources. THEOLOGICAL WRITINGS:
- Notes on Scripture (1860 posthumous Martien; published by widow)
- Story of Joseph, or Patriarchal Age (Girard College student use)
- The Knowledge of One Another in the Future State
- A Manual of Pennsylvania Land Law
- A Syllabus of the Law of Land Office Titles in Pennsylvania (1834)
- Edited The Literalist (5 vols 8vo English works on prophecy, with extensive original additions)
- Translated Outlines of a History of the Court of Rome and of the Temporal Power of the Popes (from French, with original notes) Ruling elder Presbyterian Church. Pennsylvania Historical Society longtime member. Earnest advocate of literal interpretation of Second Coming prophecy. Died February 3, 1860 Philadelphia age 64. Buried Laurel Hill East Cemetery, Philadelphia. INSTs NOT BUILT this stage (deferred to Stage 6Y-206 Kirkpatrick line which adds 4+ connections each): Lafayette College, American Philosophical Society, Girard College, Pennsylvania Historical Society. Smithsonian National Portrait Gallery referenced in ART061 but not built as separate INST. CLASSIFICATION: TD-prefix Talcott descendant gen 7. is_notable=True. Wikipedia URL primary. Notable_blurb 'Mayor of Philadelphia 1849, Girard College first president' = 8 words.
[Stage 6Y-264 NB#3 body trim]: original body had 4 sentences, trimmed to first 3. Original body preserved here for reference: 'Appointed by Governor George Wolf in 1830 as one of three commissioners — alongside William Rawle and Thomas I. Wharton — to revise the Commonwealth's civil code. The team's report to the Pennsylvania Senate January 15, 1836 produced enduring statutory compilations. His 1834 'A Syllabus of the Law of Land Office Titles in Pennsylvania' became a standard practitioner's guide.'

narrative_blocks.header: Founding minister of Baltimore's Brown Memorial Presbyterian
narrative_blocks.body: Pastored Brown Memorial Presbyterian Church Baltimore — the Bolton Hill congregation built around the memorial endowment for George Brown, the Baltimore-Ohio Railroad co-founder. Taught history and was an early advocate for women's higher education before being called to Calvary Church Philadelphia.

narrative_blocks.header: The only child of five to survive
narrative_blocks.body: Mayor Joel Jones of Philadelphia lost four children young in the 1830s and ‘40s; this son alone survived to adulthood, and became a minister. He founded Baltimore’s Brown Memorial Presbyterian, endowed for a B&O Railroad founder.

narrative_blocks.header: He preached women’s higher education
narrative_blocks.body: Beyond the pulpit he taught history and argued for women’s right to it — a Presbyterian minister advocating their higher education when few did. His daughter Elizabeth became a noted painter.

His four siblings — Elizabeth, Joel Jr, Mary, Sarah — all died young in the 1830s-40s. CAREER: Founding minister of Brown Memorial Presbyterian Church Baltimore (Bolton Hill; the church endowed in memory of George Brown, Baltimore-Ohio Railroad co-founder). Later called to Calvary Church Philadelphia. Author of numerous religious books and publications. Taught history and advocated women's higher education. Married Harriet Sterett Winchester (I01137, 1858-1946) — direct descendant of Charles Carroll of Carrollton, Maryland's Catholic Declaration signer and last surviving signer. Two daughters: Elizabeth Sparhawk-Jones (TD0241, 1885-1968 painter — to be built Stage 6Y-203b) and Margaret Carroll Jones Turnbull (TD0242, 1887-1981 — to be built Stage 6Y-204). Died August 20, 1910 Philadelphia age 69. Buried Immanuel Episcopal Church Cemetery, Sparks MD — family burial ground. His sudden 1910 death profoundly affected his elder daughter Elizabeth, contributing to the mental breakdown that interrupted her painting career. narrative_blocks.body: The verdict came from her elder daughter Elizabeth Sparhawk-Jones, the painter — domineering, but a mother who pushed her children toward their creative pursuits. She outlived her minister husband by thirty-six years.

narrative_blocks.header: New York Times' 'find of the year', 1908
narrative_blocks.body: Won the only American honorable mention at the 1908 Carnegie Institute international exhibition in Pittsburgh — the only woman to take any honor that year. The New York Times reviewer called her painting 'The Porch' the 'most unforgettable canvas' and dubbed her 'the find of the year.'

narrative_blocks.header: Mary Smith Prize at PAFA, 1908 and 1912
narrative_blocks.body: Won the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts' Mary Smith Prize twice — 1908 for 'Roller Skates' and 1912 for 'In the Spring,' her Paris flower shop noted for radiant colors. Her 1912 canvas 'Shop Girls' was the first painting by a woman purchased by the Friends of American Art at the Art Institute of Chicago.

narrative_blocks.header: Works at MoMA, Met, Art Institute Chicago
narrative_blocks.body: Her paintings are held by the Art Institute of Chicago, Metropolitan Museum of Art, Museum of Modern Art, Whitney Museum of American Art, Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts, Delaware Art Museum, and Wichita Art Museum. The actor Claude Rains became a notable private collector of her work.

narrative_blocks.header: Father's 1910 death broke her painting career
narrative_blocks.body: Her father's sudden 1910 death contributed to a mental breakdown that interrupted her early Impressionist career; she was institutionalized in 1913, with her output effectively silent for fifteen years. Returned later to a second career as a modern watercolorist, with residencies at the MacDowell Colony, Yaddo, and the Maitland Research Studio in Florida.

- Other early works: Shoe Shop, The Dreamer, Caryatides, Startled Woman, The Sea Claims Its Own, The Generations BREAK IN CAREER: Father's sudden Aug 20, 1910 death precipitated a mental breakdown. Institutionalized 1913. Career effectively silent for ~15 years. SECOND CAREER as a modern watercolorist:
- 1928 MacDowell Colony resident (Peterborough NH)

Gilpin Fund) — catalogued as ART062. Never married. Died Aug 5, 1968 Hopewell NJ age 83. Buried Immanuel Episcopal Church Cemetery Sparks MD — family plot. Smith studied 1885-1888 under Eakins; Sparhawk-Jones studied c.1899-1907 after Eakins forced out. They did not overlap at PAFA but shared the institution, the city, and the era of breakthrough for American women painters. narrative_blocks.body: Organized the Graeme Turnbull lecture series at La Paix — named for her husband's brother who died young — bringing T.S. Eliot, W.H. Auden, Robert Frost, Archibald MacLeish, and Marianne Moore to the Towson estate to lecture. The poets visited the same grounds where F. narrative_blocks.header: Bryn Mawr graduate seven years before women voted
narrative_blocks.body: Graduated Bryn Mawr more than a decade before the Nineteenth Amendment, then took a master's degree in history at the University of Pennsylvania. Taught history at Miss Irwin's School in Philadelphia and served on the board of the Prisoners Aid Society — all credentials uncommon for women of her generation.

narrative_blocks.header: Outlived her painter sister, her son, her husband
narrative_blocks.body: Lived to age 94 — outliving her elder sister Elizabeth the painter by thirteen years, her husband Bayard by twenty-seven, and her son Andrew the Fitzgerald biographer by eleven. The longevity preserved the La Paix tradition until the property was razed in 1962, after which she lived quietly in Maryland.

narrative_blocks.header: Three-state migration before age five, Connecticut to Indiana
narrative_blocks.body: Henry Augustus Huntington was born August 26, 1816 in Coventry Connecticut, three years before his parents' 1819 westward move. The family went first to Lebanon Ohio, then about a year later to Connersville Indiana, and in 1821 finally settled 'in the wilds of Sugar Creek township' in Shelby County Indiana, where Henry grew up. The whole multi-step journey unfolded before he reached his fifth birthday.

narrative_blocks.header: Died exactly one month after wife Sarah
narrative_blocks.body: Henry and his wife Sarah Ann Edwards Huntington lived on the same Sugar Creek farm from 1852 until both died in 1895. Sarah died October 26, 1895; Henry died November 26, 1895 of paralysis — exactly one month later, to the day. They had been married forty-five years.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirteen-year Sugar Creek Township trustee
narrative_blocks.body: Henry served as Sugar Creek Township trustee for thirteen years — the longest single elected term in his community's documented late-nineteenth-century record. He was a Democrat and described in his 1895 obituary simply as 'an honest' man. The trustee role oversaw township roads, poor-relief, and school funding through the years of the agrarian populist movement that reshaped Indiana politics.

career.notes: Elected 1840 as Democrat from Johnson County. Two years in House. Chairman of Educational Affairs Committee. First to make a report favorable to the Insane Hospital at Indianapolis.

narrative_blocks.body: As Chairman of Educational Affairs in the Indiana House 1840-42, he 'was the first to make a report favorable to the Insane Hospital at Indianapolis' — the institution now known as Central State Hospital, Indiana's first state mental-health facility (opened 1848).

bio.bio_blurb: Long-lived last survivor of her family

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived every one of her siblings
narrative_blocks.body: Of the family she was born into she lived longest by far — five of her siblings died in childhood, and she outlasted the last of the survivors by more than thirty years, reaching ninety-three.

narrative_blocks.header: One year took her father and two sisters
narrative_blocks.body: She was eleven in 1794 when Rev. Joseph Huntington died and her sisters Hannah and Mercy Penelope died with him — possibly one epidemic sweeping the Coventry parsonage. She would outlive that year by eighty-two more.

narrative_blocks.header: Both of them were seventeen in 1803
narrative_blocks.body: Henry married Sylvia Wales at Westhampton in 1803, when each of them was seventeen and a New England man ordinarily waited until his middle twenties. Their first child Emily arrived the following December, before either parent turned nineteen. Four more followed over the next sixteen years.

narrative_blocks.header: The only one of seven who stayed home
narrative_blocks.body: His brothers left for Westfield, Cambridge and Cleveland, and his sister Almira died at Gardiner in Maine; Henry was born, married, farmed, and was buried inside the same Hampshire County town. He was the eldest of the seven and the only one who never took up his father's medicine either.

narrative_blocks.header: He named his last child for Almira
narrative_blocks.body: Almira Hooker Hale died at Gardiner in December 1816, twenty-four years old and three years married to the physician who had trained in her father's house. Henry gave her name to the last of his children, born in 1819, who in turn died at thirty.

naming_inspiration.description: Middle name Thompson honors maternal grandfather Hugh Thompson of East Windsor CT, father of Anna Thompson Hooker.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept the shop, not the medicine
narrative_blocks.body: His father doctored Westhampton and ran a trading business on the side; of the seven children, Anson took the medicine and Hugh took the trade. He kept shop and farmed in the same town for the whole of his life and died there in April 1856.

narrative_blocks.header: He buried both children and had no more
narrative_blocks.body: Worthington died in August 1843 at twenty and Sarah Judd in February 1848 at twenty-two, the only two born of a marriage made when Hugh was twenty-nine. He lived another eight years after the second grave and Sarah lived fifteen, with nobody left to take the farm.

narrative_blocks.header: His dead son's name went to his nephews
narrative_blocks.body: Worthington Hooker was twenty when he died in 1843. Hugh's brother Festus called a son Worthington in April 1846 and buried him at eight months, then gave the name a third time to the boy born in November 1848, who carried it to sixty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: She married her father's medical student
narrative_blocks.body: Almira's father, Dr. William Hooker, was the physician of Westhampton, and Enoch Hale read medicine with him there before going to Boston and Harvard. Almira married him in September 1813, three months after he took his degree.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Hookers married two Hales in two years
narrative_blocks.body: Her brother William married Octavia Hale in 1811 and Almira married Octavia's brother Enoch in 1813, tying two Hooker children to two children of the Westhampton minister. Both couples began in the same small hill town.

narrative_blocks.header: Dead at twenty-four in a Maine winter
narrative_blocks.body: Almira followed Enoch to Gardiner in Maine, where he had gone to practise, and died there on 5 December 1816 at twenty-four. Her daughter Almira, born in 1814, had not lived either.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-seven years in one East Cambridge practice
narrative_blocks.body: Hooker took his Harvard medical degree in 1822 and practised at East Cambridge until he died in 1869. His son came into the practice after his own Harvard degree, and his grandson after that.

narrative_blocks.header: From the council to the state house
narrative_blocks.body: The practice was only half of it. He sat on the East Cambridge Common Council, then as alderman, and then in the Massachusetts legislature.

narrative_blocks.header: A birth and a death in one spring
narrative_blocks.body: His youngest son Edward Dwight was born in the East Cambridge house on 17 March 1858. Six weeks later his nephew Edward, who had come to read medicine with him, died there of a fever caught in hospital service.

career.notes: His first practice, opened after Williams College.
Returned to Massachusetts and practised here; married Mary Ann Dwight at South Hadley in 1834.
Soda manufacture. He removed from Rochester to Cleveland in 1835 and stayed until his death in August 1841.

institutions.institution_blurb: Graduated Williams College 1820.

narrative_blocks.header: He went west, came back, then went again
narrative_blocks.body: Out of Williams at eighteen, Hooker opened a law office at Ravenna in the Ohio backcountry, then gave it up and returned to Massachusetts to practise at South Hadley. He married a doctor's daughter there in 1834 and within a year had turned round for the west again, to Rochester and then to Cleveland.

narrative_blocks.header: He left the bar for a soda works
narrative_blocks.body: At Cleveland he stopped practising law and went into manufacturing soda with D. H. Lamb and Company, in a lake town barely a decade old. He was dead six years later, on the first of August 1841, at thirty-nine.

narrative_blocks.header: The obituary spent its space on his praying
narrative_blocks.body: A man of thirty-nine with a business and two small children might have been remembered for either. What his obituary chose instead was that he had lately joined the Congregational church at Ohio City, and that those who knew him called him a man of prayer.

narrative_blocks.header: Six hundred miles between the two graves
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Ann Dwight was thirty when he died, with a boy of six and a girl of three. She took them back to her father's town of South Hadley, never married again, and lies in Evergreen Cemetery there; Hooker is still at Cleveland, where nobody of his went with him.

narrative_blocks.header: The Boston child they adopted, dead at three
narrative_blocks.body: Louisa W. Kingsley was born at Boston in November 1844 under the surname Somerby and was brought out to Westhampton as a small child. She was dead by 1847 and buried among the Kingsleys, the eighth name on a family stone she had been part of for barely three years.

narrative_blocks.header: Two daughters, two family names, in one year
narrative_blocks.body: The first, born February 1827, she called Julia Ann Rust for Orrin's mother Miriam Rust Kingsley; the second, born the following January, she called Sarah Henry for her father Capt. Henry Hooker. The third she named Emily, for herself.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brother became the historian of Hadley
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah Judd was born at Westhampton in May 1791 to Sylvester and Hannah Burt Judd. Her brother Sylvester, two years the elder, became the antiquarian who gathered up the records of the Connecticut valley towns and gave Hadley its history.

narrative_blocks.header: She died at seventy-two with nobody left
narrative_blocks.body: She married Hugh Thompson Hooker in November 1818 at twenty-seven and had two children, and both were dead before their father — Worthington at twenty in 1843, Sarah Judd at twenty-two in 1848. She outlived her husband by seven years and died at Westhampton in December 1863.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped separate typhoid from typhus
narrative_blocks.body: In 1839 Hale gave the Massachusetts Medical Society's annual oration and published it as Observations on the Typhoid Fever of New England. With papers by Shattuck, Gerhard and Bartlett it drew the line between two fevers that physicians had long treated as one.

narrative_blocks.header: A student thesis that London answered back
narrative_blocks.body: Hale took his Harvard medical degree in 1813 with a dissertation on the production of animal heat by respiration, and it was printed. Sir Benjamin Brodie replied to it in the columns of the London Medical and Physical Journal.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Boylston prizes and the Dispensary
narrative_blocks.body: Hale became district physician to the Boston Dispensary in 1819 and took the Boylston prize at Harvard that year and again in 1821. He was among the early visiting physicians at the Massachusetts General and was elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 1823.

narrative_blocks.header: A bad chest sent him to chemistry first
narrative_blocks.body: Hale's health was poor as a young man, with a cough and blood in it, and he went to New Haven rather than into practice, sitting Professor Silliman's lectures and giving himself to chemistry. He came to medicine afterwards.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave a dead daughter's name to another
narrative_blocks.body: His wife Almira Hooker died at Gardiner in Maine in December 1816, and their daughter Almira, born in 1814, did not live either. He used the name again for a daughter born in 1820, and she died at two.

narrative_blocks.header: Bright's disease, and he worked through it
narrative_blocks.body: Hale spent his last years with Bright's disease and practised in great pain. He died at Boston in November 1848, remembered as honest, frank, and somewhat intolerant of unfairness in others.

military_service.notes: Commissioned surgeon September 10, 1861. Served in Department of the Gulf (Ship Island, Mississippi, then New Orleans area following its capture April 1862). Resigned June 18, 1862 due to disability from exhausting tropical diseases. First of young surgeons to offer services to Governor John Andrew at the start of the war per NEJM obituary January 8, 1874. Returned to state service in charge of military camps, May 1863. Tribute from Surgeon General Dale at his passing.

narrative_blocks.header: First of the surgeons to offer himself
narrative_blocks.body: When the war began Hooker was the first of the young Massachusetts surgeons to put himself in front of Governor John Andrew. He was commissioned to the 26th Massachusetts in September 1861 and sent to Ship Island and then to New Orleans after the city fell.

narrative_blocks.header: The Gulf broke him in nine months
narrative_blocks.body: Tropical fever took hold of him in the Department of the Gulf and he resigned his commission in June 1862, disabled. He came back to state service the next spring to run the Massachusetts military camps, but he never got his health back.

narrative_blocks.header: He held his father's practice five years
narrative_blocks.body: Hooker joined his father in the East Cambridge practice after Harvard, and took the whole of it when his father died in 1869. He died on New Year's Eve 1873 at forty-four, with the Surgeon General of the state paying him tribute.

narrative_blocks.header: One twin lived four days, the other ninety
narrative_blocks.body: Twin daughters were born on 15 March 1866 and Mary Marshall died four days later. Elizabeth Mather lived, and was identified in the 1909 family genealogy as the last surviving descendant of Cotton Mather.

narrative_blocks.header: The best-known doctor in two towns
narrative_blocks.body: Hooker took his Harvard degrees in 1880 and 1884 and trained at a New York state hospital before coming home to practise. He became one of the best-known physicians in Cambridge and in Arlington, where he lived.

narrative_blocks.header: Born into a house full of doctors
narrative_blocks.body: His father Anson had practised at East Cambridge since 1822 and was fifty-eight when this son was born, and his half-brother Anson Parker, twenty-nine years older, was already in the practice. Six weeks after the birth their cousin Edward, reading medicine in the same house, died of a hospital fever.

narrative_blocks.header: Septicemia, at fifty-three
narrative_blocks.body: Hooker died at Arlington on 27 October 1911 of blood poisoning, aged fifty-three. He left Ida and four daughters, the youngest of them three years old.

narrative_blocks.body: He graduated Williams in 1855 and came to East Cambridge to read medicine under his uncle, Dr. Anson Hooker. He died there in 1858, at twenty-two, of a disease he contracted doing hospital service — before he could finish his training.

narrative_blocks.header: The stone calls him Doctor anyway
narrative_blocks.body: He never finished the training, but the marker set over him in Evergreen Cemetery at South Hadley reads Dr Edward Hooker. He lies beside the mother who outlived him by thirty-three years.

people.research_notes: Son of H01415 Edward Hooker and I01162 Mary Ann Dwight Hooker. Born February 14, 1835 South Hadley MA. Williams College 1855 (INST043). Died April 26, 1858 East Cambridge MA age 23 — of disease contracted in hospital service per EH 1909: 'studied medicine with his uncle, Dr. Anson Hooker, and died from disease contracted in hospital service.' NOTE: 'hospital service' likely civilian hospital work, not military. Disease etiology unknown — possibly tuberculosis or typhus common in hospital environments. [CORRECTION] Birth year changed from 1835 (Edward Hooker 1909 #2763) to 1836 per FindAGrave Memorial #125223879, whose stone gives 14 Feb 1836 and an age of 22 at death. Burial Evergreen Cemetery, South Hadley (CEM1713); the stone is inscribed 'Dr Edward Hooker'.

narrative_blocks.header: Husband died of yellow fever in Indiana, 1873
narrative_blocks.body: Henry Walworth Smith had been a merchant at St. Thomas in the West Indies before settling at Cincinnati and operating a wrecking business on the Ohio River. He died of yellow fever December 2, 1873 at Evansville Indiana, leaving Mary a widow at thirty-five with two young sons.

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband milled at Puget Sound
narrative_blocks.body: Maryett's husband Edward Webster Kingsley made a remarkable career arc — millwright at Puget Sound in Washington Territory, then lumber manufacturer at Coos New Hampshire, before settling back at Westhampton as a mechanic. The couple had one documented child, Edward Anson Kingsley, born 1878.

narrative_blocks.header: Outlived her husband by ten years; nearly ninety
narrative_blocks.body: Maryett Chapman Kingsley outlived her husband Edward Webster Kingsley by ten years — he died at Westhampton July 6, 1913, she on April 29, 1923 at age eighty-nine. Her life ran from the Jackson presidency to the early 1920s, rooted in the same Westhampton community for over half a century.

narrative_blocks.header: A claim about ancestry, made in 1909
narrative_blocks.body: Edward Hooker's family genealogy of 1909 named Elizabeth the last living descendant of Cotton Mather, and her middle name carried the claim from birth. Nothing in her recorded ancestry shows the path, and the line she was said to end has had a century to be disproved.

naming_inspiration.description: Middle name Mather signals descent from Cotton Mather (1663-1728), Puritan minister and author; lineage not yet fully traced in project sources.

people.research_notes: Daughter of H02760 Anson Parker Hooker and I01166 Rebecca Pitman Boies Hooker. Born March 15, 1866 East Cambridge MA — twin of H04368 Mary Marshall Hooker (who died March 19, 1866, four days after birth). Alive as of EH 1909 writing. COTTON MATHER CLAIM: EH 1909 explicitly states 'She is the last living descendant from Cotton Mather.' Cotton Mather (1663-1728) was the Boston Puritan minister, author of Magnalia Christi Americana (1702) which celebrated Thomas Hooker. The descent path through which Elizabeth connects to Mather is not documented in the EH entry — likely runs through the Boies or another maternal line. RESEARCH NEEDED: trace the Mather descent line. Verify against published Mather genealogies. This claim connects the Hooker and Mather Puritan networks directly. TWIN: Born same day as H04368 Mary Marshall (both March 15, 1866). Her twin died four days later; Elizabeth survived. No EH asterisk — no documented descendants per 1909 record.

notable.notable_blurb: Poet, librettist, and translator of Cyrano de Bergerac

education.notes: He wrote for, edited and managed the campus humour magazine, The Yale Record.

career.notes: June Love, Marjolaine, The Vagabond King, White Eagle, Through the Years and The O'Flynn.
Mona, Fairyland, Morven and the Grail, and the ode A.D. 1919.
He co-edited the collection Yale Fun in 1901.

cross_connections.display_label: put his Cyrano translation into the Post's Second Readings
taught English at Yale in the years he taught rhetoric there
wrote the first American opera staged in France, as he wrote Mona
writes opera librettos a century later, one the Met would not stage

narrative_blocks.header: A friend ordered him to go translate Cyrano
narrative_blocks.body: Clayton Hamilton told Hooker to drop whatever he was doing, retire to the country for two months, and make an English Cyrano de Bergerac that Walter Hampden could actually speak. It opened at the National Theatre in October 1923 and ran 232 performances.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote it by ear, for the ear
narrative_blocks.body: Hooker chose blank verse over Rostand's Alexandrine couplets, which would have sounded outlandish from an American stage, and he cut nothing and added nothing. Where Cyrano invoked Celadon he put Sir Launcelot, and into the speech about the nose he slipped a phrase of Marlowe's, so an audience would catch it without a footnote.

narrative_blocks.header: Ferrer was reviving it the month he died
narrative_blocks.body: For decades Hooker's blank verse was the standard English Cyrano, and Walter Hampden played it for years before Jose Ferrer took it back to Broadway in October 1946. Hooker died that December, with the revival still running.

narrative_blocks.header: Only a Rose came out of his pen
narrative_blocks.body: Hooker wrote the lyrics for Rudolf Friml's 1925 operetta The Vagabond King, among them Only a Rose and Song of the Vagabonds, and co-wrote its book. Earlier he had taken the Metropolitan Opera's prize for a new American opera with Mona, written to Horatio Parker's music, and the American Opera Association's prize for Fairyland.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught rhetoric, then quit to write
narrative_blocks.body: Hooker taught rhetoric at Columbia and at Yale and lectured in Columbia's extension school before leaving the profession in 1909 to live by his pen. He sold essays, a novel called The Right Man and a mystery written with Wells Hastings, and Yale published his Poems in 1915.

narrative_blocks.body: On her birthday in March 1846 the former President — seventy-eight, and serving out his last years in the House beside her father — wrote six lines headed 'To Miss Lucy Hooker Ashmun.' narrative_blocks.header: Third generation named Lucy Hooker in this family

narrative_blocks.header: His pen reached further than any pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: Beyond his churches he was a writer of religious tracts — the American Tract Society printed eight of them, and he added Sunday-school books with titles like "Plea for the Heathen." Such tracts traveled where he could not, pressed into hands across the country.

narrative_blocks.header: He spent his last decades sending others out
narrative_blocks.body: After thirty years in parish pulpits, he became secretary of the Massachusetts Home Missionary Society in 1858 and held the post until 1873. From a Boston desk he helped place and support the ministers fanning out across a growing nation.

narrative_blocks.header: He served the board his daughter sailed for
narrative_blocks.body: From 1845 he sat as a corporate member of the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions. Years later his daughter Sarah and her husband carried that same board's work to South India — the mission cause running straight through the family.

narrative_blocks.header: His twin went west; he took the pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: He chose the Congregational ministry while his twin brother John struck out for the Chicago frontier in 1836. Forty years of pastorates and mission work followed — in South Carolina, the Berkshires, and on Cape Cod.

narrative_blocks.header: She ran a girls' school a world away
narrative_blocks.body: Arriving at Madura in 1857 she was handed charge of the Girls' Boarding School while her husband preached and built. Teaching Tamil girls became her life's work, and the school she built carries her name today.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at the mission, she would not leave
narrative_blocks.body: William died of heart disease at Madura in 1876. Her daughters were already back in Massachusetts with her sister, and she stayed on alone another ten years before she would come home.

narrative_blocks.header: She trained at a hospital to heal women
narrative_blocks.body: She spent six weeks in a Madras government hospital in 1875 learning what medicine she could, then gave two hours each morning to prescriptions. The dispensary she opened became the Madura Hospital for Women and Children.

narrative_blocks.header: A famous revivalist called her to Chicago
narrative_blocks.body: In 1889 Dwight Moody asked her to lead the women's department of his new Bible Institute in Chicago. When she doubted her fitness he answered that it was the experience of life he wanted. She stayed five years.

narrative_blocks.header: The city was sorry to lose its teacher
narrative_blocks.body: Before India she was a celebrated schoolteacher. When she left the Oliver High School at Lawrence in 1852 the committee lamented losing someone of such peculiar aptness in teaching.

narrative_blocks.header: They called her the Mother of the City
narrative_blocks.body: She went about Madura in an American carriage drawn by two white bullocks, and people in the street would say, that is the Mother of the City.

narrative_blocks.header: A Brahmin met her train with a wreath
narrative_blocks.body: Leaving India in 1886 she was called to the platform at Madura station by a Brahmin gentleman whose servant carried a brass tray. He laid a wreath of white jasmine on her shoulders for what she had done for the women of the city.

ADDITIONAL BIOGRAPHY DATA: Set sail for India November 21, 1856; arrived ~100 days later. In charge of Madura Girls' Boarding School from arrival. Moved to Manamadurai 1864. Returned to U.S. on furlough 1872. 1874 sailed back to India (daughters Annie and Laura left with H02771 Anne Tufts). Sarah took medical lessons after returning to Madurai 1874. William died Oct 6, 1876; Sarah remained, reassigned to Madurai. Stayed in India until 1886. Returned U.S., Women's Board of Missions 1886-1889. 1889 superintendent Women's Dept, Bible Institute for Home and Foreign Missions Chicago (later Moody Bible Institute). Retired 1894. Lived with sister H02771 Anne Tufts in Boston. Both moved to Poughkeepsie to live with daughter Laura Keith. d. December 15, 1918 Poughkeepsie NY, age 90. WIKIPEDIA NOTE: Wikipedia birth year listed as 1824 — incorrect; confirmed birth April 24, 1828 from multiple family and genealogical sources. Capron Hall School cornerstone laid 1902 by Governor Lord Ampthill of India. She founded Madura Hospital for Women and Children (grew from her dispensary work). During Great Famine 1876-1878 (~5M died in Madras Presidency/Deccan) received monthly grant from Mansion House fund London for famine relief. Education: 'trained as assistant teacher under Horace Mann' per contemporary biography. Graduated State Normal School West Newton, November 1850. Taught Hartford High School until April 1854. Moody quote: 'It is the experience of life that I want.' Described as descending from 'pioneer spirit of her ancestor Rev. Thomas Hooker who led his flock into the Connecticut wilderness.' They moved to Monte Vista, Colorado, then eventually to Los Angeles, where Sarah died January 23, 1915, and where Joseph was buried after his death in 1895.

Rose to Colonel. Key roles at Fort Ticonderoga (1775), Canadian campaign (1775-76), Saratoga campaign (1777), Stone Arabia (1780).

military_service.notes: Participated in capture of Fort Ticonderoga May 10, 1775. Selected by Ethan Allen to carry Ticonderoga news to Continental Congress. Canadian campaign 1775-76; Battle of Chambly Oct 19, 1775 (key to fall of Fort St. John). Saratoga campaign 1777 — raid on Ticonderoga and nearby outposts. Killed at Battle of Stone Arabia, Mohawk Valley, October 19, 1780 (his birthday). First to formally bring charges against Benedict Arnold.

narrative_blocks.header: Killed in an ambush at Stone Arabia
narrative_blocks.body: In 1780 John took a Massachusetts regiment to defend the Mohawk Valley, and on 19 October he was drawn into an ambush of Indians and regulars at Stone Arabia, where he and forty of his men were killed. It was his thirty-sixth birthday.

narrative_blocks.header: He first proposed taking Ticonderoga
narrative_blocks.body: Sent to Montreal in March 1775 to sound out merchants angry at the Quebec Act, John wrote back on 29 March with the first proposal to seize Fort Ticonderoga. He went with the expedition that took it in May, and was sent to carry the news to the Continental Congress.

narrative_blocks.header: He took Fort Chambly with 300 Canadians
narrative_blocks.body: On 18 October 1775 John and James Livingston, with fifty Americans and three hundred Canadians, took the British fort at Chambly. Its fall ended the siege of Saint-Jean and opened the road to Montreal.

narrative_blocks.header: Arnold accused him; he foresaw Arnold's treason
narrative_blocks.body: John distrusted Benedict Arnold, whom he had first met at Yale, and predicted his treason. In the Quebec campaign Arnold charged him with plundering the baggage of captured British officers. The charge was false, but Congress would not clear him, and in February 1777 he resigned his commission.

narrative_blocks.header: A ghost's confession to Mother Ann Lee
narrative_blocks.body: A Shaker tale has it that John called on Mother Ann Lee near Albany shortly before his death and promised to join her people once the army released him, and that a fortnight later, already dead, he appeared to her in spirit to confess his sins.

narrative_blocks.header: He read law under an Arnold
narrative_blocks.body: After Yale, John read law at Providence with Oliver Arnold, Benedict's first cousin, who had married John's sister. He served briefly as King's Attorney at Caughnawaga, New York, then settled at Pittsfield in 1773, and in 1779 became a judge of the county court.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter never knew him
narrative_blocks.body: John was killed when his daughter Sarah was barely a year old. His widow, Huldah, later married Capt. Jared Ingersoll of Pittsfield, and in 1796 Sarah married Thomas Hooker of Northampton.

burial.plot_notes: Killed at Stone Arabia NY, October 19, 1780. Burial location not documented.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave up a Hartford classroom for India
narrative_blocks.body: Trained at Yale and Andover and ordained an evangelist, he had led the Hopkins Grammar School in Hartford for six years. When the American Board called in 1856, he traded the schoolroom for the mission field, sailing for Madura in South India weeks after his wedding.

narrative_blocks.header: He built a mission bungalow in the field
narrative_blocks.body: His early years at Madura mixed preaching with construction — he supervised the building of a new bungalow at the Mana Madura outstation, where the family settled in 1864. The work of those years was evangelical, medical, and educational, spread across the villages south of the city.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother followed him, then died young
narrative_blocks.body: When he left Hartford for the mission field, his younger brother Samuel Mills Capron took his place at the head of the Hopkins Grammar School. Samuel died in 1874 at forty-two, and William — home on furlough — helped prepare the memorial volume for the brother who had followed in his footsteps.

narrative_blocks.header: His heart failed him at the mission, 1876
narrative_blocks.body: He died suddenly at Madura in October 1876, his heart giving out after nearly two decades in the field. His widow Sarah, certain her work was unfinished, chose to stay on in India another ten years rather than sail home.

narrative_blocks.header: He was a Whig until 1860
narrative_blocks.body: Tufts came up a Whig and went over to the Republicans in 1860. He sat three years in the Massachusetts house and two in the senate, and was a presidential elector in 1884.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped nominate Benjamin Harrison
narrative_blocks.body: In 1888 he went to the Chicago convention as a delegate, and it nominated Benjamin Harrison. The next year he took a seat on the governor's council and held it three years.

narrative_blocks.header: A lumber merchant who ran a savings bank
narrative_blocks.body: He was a partner in Flint & Tufts, wholesale lumber dealers of Boston, and president of the Institution for Savings in Roxbury. He sat as a director of the Commonwealth Insurance Company.

narrative_blocks.header: His house took in his wife's nieces
narrative_blocks.body: He married Annie Hooker in 1853, into a family deep in the foreign missions. When her sister sailed back to South India in 1874, the two Capron girls were left to grow up in the Tufts household.

narrative_blocks.header: A Boston lawyer who kept Wellesley's books
narrative_blocks.body: He practiced law in Boston and for years served as treasurer of Wellesley College, a steward of its finances as much as a courtroom advocate. Summers drew him to the family house on Main Street in Boxford, where three generations gathered.

narrative_blocks.header: His bride was born at an India mission
narrative_blocks.body: In 1897 he married Annie Hooker Capron, who had come into the world at Madura in South India, where her parents served as missionaries. She died young in 1909, leaving him with two small children.

narrative_blocks.header: A playground rose where his summers had been
narrative_blocks.body: After his death in 1930, his widow Ednah gave his Boxford land to the town for a children's playground beside the village school. A stone marker placed by local volunteers still carries the Morse name.

narrative_blocks.header: He searched the world's far corners for oil
narrative_blocks.body: After a Harvard doctorate in geology, he joined Standard Oil in 1920 and spent sixteen years as a chief geologist abroad, prospecting across Europe, the Middle East, Asia, and Africa. He inspected old fields and hunted new ones, mailing weekly diaries home and amassing thousands of photographs of the places the work carried him.

narrative_blocks.header: He photographed the Western Front from the air
narrative_blocks.body: Commissioned in 1918, he commanded the Second Army's Thirteenth Photographic Section in France, directing aerial reconnaissance over the trenches in the war's last months. Among the images his unit produced were German camps printed from captured enemy film.

narrative_blocks.header: At twenty-one he sailed for Brazil
narrative_blocks.body: Still a Harvard student, he joined the 1908 Shaler Memorial Expedition to Brazil — the first of a lifetime of journeys. Summer field trips to Montana, Colorado, and Quebec followed, training him for the global wandering geology would demand.

narrative_blocks.header: A Boston wedding, then a life in Paris
narrative_blocks.body: In 1925 he married Anna Hooker Morse at the First Church in Boxford and took her home to Paris, where their two sons were born at Neuilly. The family lived abroad through his Standard Oil years before settling back in Massachusetts.

narrative_blocks.header: Harvard claimed him at the start and end
narrative_blocks.body: He took three Harvard degrees by 1914 and returned decades later as a visiting lecturer, then sat on the university's Board of Overseers. His papers — diaries, field notes, and more than five thousand photographs — now rest at the University of Wyoming.

narrative_blocks.header: Mother died when she was ten
narrative_blocks.body: Anna Hooker Morse's mother Annie Hooker Capron died in October 1909 when Anna was just ten years old — born in India to missionaries, her mother died in her prime at forty-nine. Anna herself lived to ninety-three, dying May 10, 1992 in Boxford, Massachusetts.

narrative_blocks.header: Both sons born in France
narrative_blocks.body: Anna married Winthrop Perrin Haynes — who had served as a 2nd Lieutenant in World War I — in Boxford on August 10, 1925. Both their sons, Lewis Rogerson (1926) and Edward Hamilton (1928), were born in Neuilly-sur-Seine, France, where the family was then living.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father's playground is still a Boxford landmark
narrative_blocks.body: The Lewis Kennedy Morse Playground, donated posthumously by her stepmother Ednah Rich Morse and dedicated October 31, 1930, commemorated Anna's father on the grounds of what is now Cole School in Boxford. The Haynes family estate on Main Street — the Pearson-Morse-Haynes house — was named Elmlea and became the Elmlea Tree Farm.

narrative_blocks.header: The schoolhouse she gave the town's children
narrative_blocks.body: A former pupil of Boxford's one-room District No. 2 school, she deeded it to the town's children in 1931. The last of five such schools, it outlived the Lewis Morse playground beside it and stands today on the National Register, brought back by local volunteers.

narrative_blocks.header: Died over Rabaul; Boyington captured the same day
narrative_blocks.body: Captain George Malcolm Ashmun was shot down over Rabaul on January 3, 1944, flying with VMF-214 — the Black Sheep Squadron — when his Corsair burst into flames and crashed into the ocean. His wingman, Major Gregory 'Pappy' Boyington, was himself shot down minutes later and spent the rest of the war as a Japanese prisoner of war.

narrative_blocks.header: First kill; last flight over Rabaul, 1944
narrative_blocks.body: George Ashmun flew 67 combat missions over two tours with the Black Sheep without shooting down a single enemy aircraft — nearly 150 combat hours, scoreless. On January 3, 1944, flying as Boyington's wingman on a sweep of Rabaul, he finally scored his first aerial victory — and was killed in the same engagement.

narrative_blocks.header: Boyington's wingman on his squadron's last combat day
narrative_blocks.body: Boyington chose Ashmun as his wingman knowing he was eager to get on the scoreboard. Ashmun had told him: 'Go ahead and shoot all you want, Gramps. All I'll do is keep them off your tail.' As Ashmun's plane trailed smoke toward the water, Boyington screamed at him to dive — but George's plane burst into flames before he could answer.

narrative_blocks.header: Crewmates mourned him as 'a real nice guy'
narrative_blocks.body: Fellow VMF-211 pilot Wallace Thompson said that 'a real shock wave went through the pilots' camp' at the loss of Ashmun and Boyington. Ed Olander, Ashmun's closest companion — who had trained with him in Jacksonville, crossed the country with him on the Santa Fe Chief, and bunked with him in the Pacific — said George's death troubled him more than any other loss in the war.

people.research_notes: FGA #56786683. b. April 21, 1919 Newark NJ. Killed in action January 3, 1944, Rabaul, East New Britain. Listed on Tablets of the Missing, Manila American Cemetery CEM558 — no known grave. Officially declared dead January 15, 1946. Education: Newark Academy (1937), Hobart College (1941, enlisted June 24, 1941). Service: enlisted June 24, 1941; commissioned July 17, 1942 as Marine officer. Training at Naval Air Station Jacksonville. Earned pilot's wings; Marine Corps commission. Reached rank of Captain by mid-1943. Joined VMF-214 Black Sheep summer 1943. Campaigns: Solomon Islands (two tours). 150 combat hours, 67 missions. Individual decorations: Distinguished Flying Cross, Purple Heart. One aerial victory (January 3, 1944 — his first and last). Primary unit: VMF-214 Black Sheep Squadron under Major Gregory 'Pappy' Boyington. Boyington himself was shot down and captured in the same engagement. narrative_blocks.header: Navy WWII veteran; forty-two years at Buckeye Pipeline
narrative_blocks.body: Charles 'Charlie' Ashmun Jr. served in the U.S. Navy from 1942 to 1945, then spent forty-two years at Buckeye Pipe Line Company in New York City — starting by digging ditches and retiring in 1979 as vice president managing all product traffic through the system. He lived to ninety-five.

narrative_blocks.header: Brother George was shot down flying
narrative_blocks.body: Charlie's younger brother Captain George Malcolm Ashmun flew with VMF-214 — the Black Sheep Squadron — as a Marine fighter pilot and was shot down over Rabaul on January 3, 1944, the same day Pappy Boyington was captured. George was officially declared dead January 15, 1946; he was twenty-four years old.

narrative_blocks.header: Retired Rear Admiral from the U.S. Navy
narrative_blocks.body: Theodore Strong Thompson served in the Civil War with the 45th Massachusetts Regiment, then spent forty years in the United States Navy's Pay Corps — rising from Assistant Paymaster in 1863 to Pay Director in 1901, retiring December 26, 1903 as a Rear Admiral. His official accounts across four decades are recorded as among the most complete and accurate ever received by the Naval Department.

narrative_blocks.header: Served on the Polaris expedition to the Arctic
narrative_blocks.body: Thompson sailed on the Polaris Search Expedition to the Arctic and later brought survivors of the Virginius massacre from Santiago de Cuba to New York aboard a Navy vessel. He also served on the battleship Massachusetts to the close of the Spanish-American War.

narrative_blocks.header: Son of a minister; grandson of the Governor
narrative_blocks.body: Theodore Strong Thompson was the son of Rev. Augustus Thompson, fifty-nine-year pastor of Eliot Congregational Church in Roxbury, and the grandson of Governor Caleb Strong of Massachusetts — one of the most prominent Federalist politicians of the early republic. The Rear Admiral thus carried both pastoral and gubernatorial lineage.

narrative_blocks.header: Plane irons, coach lace, then paper
narrative_blocks.body: Timothy kept a hardware store at New Haven, made plane irons, drawing knives and augers at Humphreysville, now Seymour, then made coach lace, and later railway cars at Chicago. From 1869 he manufactured paper there.

narrative_blocks.header: Beloit, then South Evanston

narrative_blocks.header: He married Lucy Starr Olmstead

narrative_blocks.header: Pastor of Roxbury's Eliot Church for fifty-nine years
narrative_blocks.body: Rev. Augustus Thompson began his pastorate at Eliot Congregational Church, Roxbury, Massachusetts in 1842 and remained senior pastor until his death on September 26, 1901 — fifty-nine unbroken years. In that time he published more than fifteen devotional books, outlived two wives and three children, and became one of the most prolific Congregationalist authors of the mid-Victorian era.

narrative_blocks.header: Led ABCFM deputation to India in 1854
narrative_blocks.body: In 1854-5, Thompson accompanied Rev. Dr. Rufus Anderson as the ABCFM's deputation to its missions in India and Sri Lanka — visiting stations to resolve disputes over educational policy at a time when British colonial grants were pressuring missionaries toward English-language instruction. The same visit brought him to the Madura mission in South India where William Banfield Capron — husband of Hooker descendant Sarah Brown Hooker Capron — was then serving.

narrative_blocks.header: He landed the first steel at New London
narrative_blocks.body: He left a Salem farm at seventeen to clerk in a small country store, and within a few years had his own grocery in New London. He pushed it into hardware, tools and farm implements, and became the first man to import steel into the port.

narrative_blocks.header: A painkiller paid for all of it
narrative_blocks.body: He took the agency for Davis' Pain Killer and in 1848 opened J. N. Harris & Company in Cincinnati to sell it west. Travelling agents worked Ohio and Indiana on his account, and it was the patent medicine, not the hardware, that made the fortune.

narrative_blocks.header: A grocer's name on a Kyoto school
narrative_blocks.body: He endowed the Harris School of Science at Doshisha University in Kyoto, the Christian college founded by Joseph Hardy Neesima under the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions. The money came out of rents: he had put up the Harris Building on State Street in 1885, five storeys of offices, apartments and a dry-goods store, and gave away what it earned.

narrative_blocks.header: A bank president who ran a boys' school
narrative_blocks.body: In 1892 he settled a permanent endowment on a hospital in New London, after years as president of the city's national bank. He was also president of the Mount Hermon School for Boys at Northfield, Massachusetts.

narrative_blocks.header: His house became a school, then a church
narrative_blocks.body: He built at 130 Broad Street in 1859-60, an Italian Villa in brick by Leopold Eidlitz, the architect of P. T. Barnum's Iranistan and New York's Tweed Courthouse. It was cut into classrooms for the Williams Memorial Institute in 1891, and is now New London's United Methodist Church.

narrative_blocks.header: He buried six of his eight children
narrative_blocks.body: His first wife, Jane M. Brown, daughter of Benjamin Brown, bore him eight children. Five of them died as small children, and a sixth at twenty-two.

narrative_blocks.body: Martha Bodine Strong was among the first psychiatric social workers in the United States, in the nineteen-twenties and thirties, when the work was only beginning to have training or standards of its own. narrative_blocks.header: He went out preaching the small house
narrative_blocks.body: As the housing administration's chief architect Smith spent 1937 on the road telling builders and realtors that the shortage would be answered by many houses at moderate prices rather than a few large ones. At Jamaica he told them a plan lives or dies on closet space, on wall room for the furniture, and on doors that do not waste the floor they swing across.

narrative_blocks.header: He drew in Cass Gilbert's office
narrative_blocks.body: Smith came into the office of Cass Gilbert, then among the most sought-after architects in the country, and had charge of design work there in the early twenties while the New York Life and the Supreme Court were on the boards. He was afterwards consultant architect on the George Washington Bridge, and ran his own Manhattan firm, Smith and Ward.

narrative_blocks.header: He left Washington to build air bases abroad
narrative_blocks.body: Smith retired from government in 1953 and went to Paris as director of overseas operations for Cutting and Associates, which designed Air Force and Navy air bases across Europe and North Africa. He had first come to Paris thirty years before, straight out of the Army, to study at the École des Beaux-Arts.

people.research_notes: NYT Obituary, March 21, 1974. b. Jan 27, 1894 Avoca, Steuben County NY. d. March 19, 1974 Canandaigua, Ontario County NY (age 80). Buried Newton Cemetery CEM564. Education: A.B./A.M. Carnegie Institute of Technology 1916/1917; Ecole des Beaux Arts Paris. Career: Associate of Cass Gilbert; design charge: Woolworth Building, NY Life Building, US Supreme Court. NOTABLE RECOMMENDATION for consideration: NYT obituary; Woolworth/Supreme Court/GWB architectural connection. REBUILT 8 Sep 2026 on Sam's note that the blocks read as wiki headers and data dumps. Every thread was kept except one. THE WOOLWORTH CLAIM IS OFF THE CARD: the obituary says that in the early nineteen-twenties, as an associate of Cass Gilbert, he 'was in charge of design for the Woolworth, New York Life and Supreme Court buildings in Manhattan'. The Woolworth Building was finished in 1913, when Smith was nineteen and three years from his first degree, so he cannot have designed it; the obituary has compressed Gilbert's famous works into a list. The New York Life (1928) and the Supreme Court (1932-35) do fall in or after his years there - and the Supreme Court is in Washington, not Manhattan, another slip in the same sentence. The card now says he had charge of design work in Gilbert's office in the early twenties, which the source supports, and names only the two buildings that fit. ADDED from the Times of 7 and 14 Feb 1937 (Sam, 8 Sep 2026): as FHA chief architect he addressed a builders' and realtors' conference at the Essex House, Newark, arguing for numerous moderately priced small houses and pointing to five FHA-standard demonstration houses at Bethesda; and told the Small Home Planning Conference at Jamaica, Long Island, that a square or rectangular house lives on a simple floor plan, closet space, wall space for furniture, door placement and orientation to the sun. YES, THAT IS HIM - the by-line 'chief architect of the Federal Housing Administration' in Feb 1937 sits inside his 1935-1950 FHA tenure. Education notes were shortened; they were repeating the school name, which the row already prints.

narrative_blocks.header: He joined the social-work school's overseers

Alfred died three years before his mother Melinda and eighteen years before his father.

narrative_blocks.header: A childless general took him in at four
narrative_blocks.body: When Cyprian's father Nathaniel Hart died at Kensington in October 1773, the boy was four. His uncle General Selah Hart, whose only daughter had died young, took him in and raised him on the Hart homestead as his heir.

narrative_blocks.header: Died before the General who had raised him
narrative_blocks.body: Cyprian died at Kensington on 1 March 1806, at thirty-seven, leaving his youngest daughter Emily nine months old. General Selah Hart followed him fourteen weeks later, on 10 June, in the same house, and the Hart estate passed to Cyprian's six children.

narrative_blocks.header: Two widows shared the house thirty-eight years
narrative_blocks.body: After both husbands died in the spring of 1806, his widow Lucy Hooker Hart and his adoptive aunt Ruth Cole Hart kept the Kensington homestead together for the rest of their lives. Ruth died in the house in January 1844 at one hundred and one. Lucy lived another seven years alone, dying there in July 1851.

narrative_blocks.header: He married his second cousin Lucy Hooker
narrative_blocks.body: On 24 December 1795 Cyprian married Lucy Hooker of the same Kensington parish, his second cousin through their great-grandfather the Hon. John Hooker of Farmington. Six children followed in nine years, all born in the general's house.

narrative_blocks.header: A Hart of the Hartford founder's line
narrative_blocks.body: Through the Kensington Harts Cyprian descended from Deacon Stephen Hart, a founder of Hartford, and the general who raised him came of the same line, so the founder's name came down to him twice, by blood and by the house that brought him up.

sources.label: FindAGrave — Cyprian Hart

people.research_notes: Baptized Feb 5, 1769 Kensington CT by Rev. Samuel Clark of Kensington Congregational Church. Birth date Feb 6, 1769 per FindAGrave #61935571. Sixth son of Nathaniel Hart No. 2 (H00274) and Martha Norton (X01029). Father died October 13, 1773 when Cyprian was age 4; widow Martha removed to Hartford. Adopted by uncle General Selah Hart (H00273) and raised on the General Hart homestead in Kensington — Selah's only natural daughter Mary (H00556) had died young, leaving him childless. Married December 24, 1795 to Lucy Hooker (H00537), daughter of Elijah Hooker (H00267) of Kensington and Susannah Judd (I00045). COUSIN MARRIAGE: Cyprian and Lucy were second cousins — both descended from H00030 Hon. John Hooker through different children (Cyprian via paternal grandmother H00099 Abigail Hooker; Lucy via paternal grandfather H00098 John Hooker — siblings, both children of H00030). Resided on Gen. Selah Hart's homestead in Kensington until his early death March 1, 1806 aged 37. Died fourteen weeks before his uncle Selah (who died June 10, 1806). EH #537 records: 'his widow and the widow of his uncle Gen. Selah Hart occupied the General Hart house and property together as long as they lived.' Buried Ledge Cemetery, Berlin, Hartford County CT (CEM022). Six children EH #1444-1449: Selah, Ruth, Abigail, Henry Cyprian (Yale Med 1826), Lucy Hooker, Emily. Sources: EH 1909 #274 (under father's record) and #562 ('For his record look under his wife's name'); Hart Genealogy entry #106; FindAGrave Memorial #61935571. Stage 6Y-253.

He was nine when both his father and the general died in the spring of 1806, and he died at Berlin, unmarried, in May 1838.

cross_connections.notes: The General Hart homestead at Kensington descended through three generations: built and lived in by Gen. Selah Hart (d. 1806); held by his adopted nephew Cyprian Hart (Abigail's father) and his cohabiting widows Lucy Hooker and Ruth Cole Hart for thirty-eight years; passed to Abigail and her husband Oliver Moore upon her mother's death in 1851. Hart Genealogy explicitly identifies the property: 'where the late Oliver Moore lived.'

narrative_blocks.header: Inherited the General Hart homestead through marriage
narrative_blocks.body: On March 25, 1829 at Kensington she married Oliver Moore. The General Hart house at Kensington — built by her great-uncle General Selah Hart, held by her adopted-heir father Cyprian Hart from 1773 to 1806, then by her widowed mother and great-aunt Ruth Cole Hart together for thirty-eight years — became the Moore residence by the time of her own death in 1850. Three generations of Hart property descent ended at her household.

narrative_blocks.header: Died at Meriden four months after her husband
narrative_blocks.body: Late in life Sheldon grew infirm and the couple removed from Kensington to Meriden, where he died July 31, 1872 aged seventy-eight. She survived him by three months and twelve days, dying at Meriden on November 12, 1872 aged sixty-nine. Both were buried at Walnut Grove Cemetery in Meriden, alongside her husband and the children who survived them.

narrative_blocks.header: Married Bradley & Hubbard co-founder, 1859 Meriden
narrative_blocks.body: On her twenty-fifth birthday year, 1859, she married Nathaniel Lyman Bradley of Meriden — co-founder, treasurer, and later president of the Bradley & Hubbard Manufacturing Company, the kerosene-lamp and metal-goods firm that grew to seven acres and 1,500 employees. Their only son Clarence Peck Bradley would succeed Nathaniel as president in 1915 and leave the firm's Meriden homestead and over a million dollars for the Bradley Home for the Elderly. She survived her husband by five years.

narrative_blocks.header: A Vermont detour, then back to Farmington
narrative_blocks.body: After marrying, Gideon moved his growing family north to Castleton, Vermont, only to turn back and resettle in Farmington. So thoroughly did the household uproot and return that even the birthplaces of his children were later left in doubt.

narrative_blocks.header: Fatherless young, the family left Kensington
narrative_blocks.body: When Gideon was still a boy, his father died and his widowed mother moved the household from Kensington to Hartford. He came of age in the shadow of that early loss before building a restless, much-relocated life of his own.

narrative_blocks.header: Settled at Marietta on the Ohio frontier
narrative_blocks.body: Fifth son of Nathaniel Hart No. 2, named for his uncle General Selah Hart of Kensington who had adopted his brother Cyprian. Migrated from Connecticut to the Ohio frontier — among the early settlers at Marietta, Washington County, in the Ohio Company's territory. EH #561 records his Ohio descendants at numbers 1494-1503.

narrative_blocks.header: Killed by a falling tree in Ohio, 1836
narrative_blocks.body: He died in Ohio in 1836, killed by a falling tree. One son Norman had been killed earlier at Sandusky in 1813 during the War of 1812. EH numbers ten Ohio-born descendants in the next generation.

narrative_blocks.header: Fourteen years a magistrate of excellent judgment
narrative_blocks.body: He served as a magistrate at Marion, Morgan County, Ohio for about fourteen years, and was generally accounted of good judgment and local influence. Both he and his wife Sarah were active church members from early life. The Hart Genealogy of 1875 records that the place was greatly missed and mourned over at his death, so great was the loss.

people.research_notes: b. Jan 30, 1767 Kensington CT; baptized Feb 8, 1767. d. Jan 6, 1836 Marion (Morgan Co.) OH age 68, killed by fall of a tree (or fall of a limb per Hart Genealogy). Fifth son of Nathaniel Hart No. 2 (H00274) and Martha Norton (X01029). Named for his uncle Gen. Selah Hart (H00273). m. Oct 30, 1793 Sarah Walter (I01254, b. Mar 5, 1766). Both 'members of the church from early life' per Hart Genealogy. MIGRATION TIMELINE: 1789 — Removed from Kensington CT to Marietta, Washington Co. OH (among the original Ohio Company settlers of Marietta, founded 1788). 1796 — Removed to Watertown, Washington Co. OH. 1821 — Removed to Marion, Morgan Co. OH (where he was killed by tree fall 15 years later). CAREER: Farmer all his life. Magistrate at Marion ~14 years; 'generally accounted of good judgment and local influence.' 10 children H01494-H01503 per EH #561: Norman (d. Sandusky War of 1812 1813), Walter, Selah Jr., Seth, Sally, William (d. 1847), Hiram, Cynthia, Mary, Betsey (d. 1817 age 6). Sources: EH #561; Hart Genealogy of 1875. Sources differ on EH vs Hart book on (a) Selah Jr. birth date Nov 29 vs Mar 29, 1797; (b) Seth's marriage year 1835 (EH typo) vs 1825 (Hart book — chronologically correct since first child b. 1826). Stage 6Y-256 reconciles in favor of chronological feasibility. Stage 6Y-254 (built) + 6Y-256 (enriched: marriage, baptism, 3rd NB, full migration timeline).

cross_connections.display_label: drowned on Lake Erie in 1836, and his brother John put him in a poem
cross_connections.notes: Both Hooker descendants drowned in lakes — Sherman Pierpont in Lake Erie at Sandusky Ohio on May 7, 1836, his body washed ashore three weeks later. Albert Norton Butler in Lake Garfield at Monterey Massachusetts on September 28, 1915, when his rowboat capsized. Seventy-nine years and two generations apart, both Connecticut-origin Hooker descendants ended their lives in lake waters away from their home parishes.

narrative_blocks.header: He cut and built the north end
narrative_blocks.body: Albert went from Yale into real estate, coal and lumber in Meriden. He was president of the Butler & Klein Lumber Company, which cut timber at the north end of the city, and of the Butler & Lyman Land Company, which developed it.

narrative_blocks.header: He could not swim
narrative_blocks.body: Albert was visiting his brother-in-law, Dr. Charles Engelke, at Lake Garfield in the Berkshires when his rowboat capsized in rough water on 28 September 1915. He could not swim, and searchers dragged the lake for two days.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale, like his uncle before him
narrative_blocks.body: Albert graduated from Yale in 1900. His uncle, Dr. Henry Cyprian Hart, had taken his medical degree there in 1872.

career.role: Portrait painter (Native American subjects) and illustrator
career.notes: From 1935 onward, occupied with a pictorial survey in oils of the Indian tribes commissioned by the National Geographic Society — a project that took him from the Atlantic to the Pacific and from Mexico to the Arctic. Also illustrated books including Marius Barbeau's 'Indian Days in the Canadian Rockies' (1923), Frances Carpenter's 'Pocahontas and Her World' (1961), and the children's story 'Flat Tail' by Alice Gall and Fleming Crew (1935). Painted Nathan Hale murals at Hale-Ray High School in Moodus (East Haddam).

narrative_blocks.header: The Blackfeet named him Chase Enemy in Water
narrative_blocks.body: In 1919 Langdon followed his teacher Winold Reiss to the Blackfeet in Montana and painted his first portraits. In 1920 the tribe adopted him as Zoi-och-ka-tsai-ya, Chase Enemy in Water, and its pictogram often sat by his signature.

narrative_blocks.header: Portraits without sentiment
narrative_blocks.body: Railroad commissions carried Langdon through the West and northwest Canada in the 1920s, painting tribes he believed were vanishing. A Brooklyn Museum show toured some forty institutions; the Times found his portraits free of sentiment.

narrative_blocks.header: Atlantic to Pacific, Mexico to the Arctic
narrative_blocks.body: From 1935 Langdon painted the tribes for the National Geographic Society, from the Atlantic to the Pacific and from Mexico to the Arctic. Twenty years on, in 1955, the work became the book Indians of the Americas.

narrative_blocks.header: A pupil of Winold Reiss
narrative_blocks.body: Langdon, son of Alfred and Carrie Peck Kihn, was singled out for his drawing at Boys' High in Brooklyn. At the Art Students League in 1916 and 1917 he studied under Homer Boss and Winold Reiss, whose Indian portraits set his course.

narrative_blocks.header: Alice murals for his daughter
narrative_blocks.body: Langdon married Helen Butler of Meriden in 1920 and settled at Hadlyme. In 1934 he painted Alice in Wonderland murals, after Tenniel, on the walls of their daughter Phyllis's bedroom, inscribed 'A ma chère Phyllis.'

narrative_blocks.header: Nathan Hale in five scenes
narrative_blocks.body: In 1935 Langdon painted Nathan Hale's life in five scenes, a federal relief project, in East Haddam's old town hall; the panels went onto the Hale-Ray School's walls. He also illustrated books for Marius Barbeau and Frances Carpenter.

narrative_blocks.header: A run for the Connecticut House in 1948
narrative_blocks.body: In November 1948 Langdon and the writer Donald Barr Chidsey stood as Democratic candidates for the Connecticut House from Lyme. He died at Lawrence Memorial Hospital in New London in December 1957, at fifty-nine.

b. Sep 5, 1898 Brooklyn NY; d. Dec 12, 1957 New London CT age 59. Buried Cove Cemetery, Hadlyme CT (FindAGrave #135411069). Parents: Alfred Charles Kihn and Carrie Lowe (Peck) Kihn. Education: Boys' High School Brooklyn; Art Students League of NY 1916-17 under Homer Boss and Winold Reiss. 1920 admitted to Blackfeet tribe of Montana, given name 'Zoi-och-ka-tsai-ya' (Chase Enemy in Water). Painted pictogram of this name alongside his signature on portraits. From 1935 onward: principal work was pictorial survey in oils of American Indian tribes commissioned by the National Geographic Society — covered Atlantic to Pacific and Mexico to the Arctic. Painted Nathan Hale murals at Hale-Ray High School in Moodus (East Haddam). Painted Tenniel-style 'Alice in Wonderland' murals on his daughter Phyllis Kihn's bedroom walls in Hadlyme home, 1934. Inscription: 'A ma chere Phyllis, with fond affection these walls are respectfully inscribed. W. Langdon Kihn 1934.' (Note: per Peggy Bragdon Shepley's 2019 obituary, Kihn also painted Alice in Wonderland murals in Peggy's bedroom at her grandmother's 1688 East Haddam house — possibly a separate commission, possibly Peggy's obit conflating with Phyllis's documented murals.) Illustrated books: Marius Barbeau 'Indian Days in the Canadian Rockies' (1923); Frances Carpenter 'Pocahontas and Her World' (1961); Alice Gall + Fleming Crew 'Flat Tail' (1935). 1948: Democratic candidate for Connecticut House of Representatives from Lyme (alongside writer Donald Barr Chidsey). m. 1920 Helen Van Tine Butler (HD4970, 1899-1975). Daughter Phyllis Kihn (HD4978, 1924-2004). Collections: McCord Museum (Montreal), Davison Art Center (Wesleyan), Vancouver Art Gallery, National Geographic Society. narrative_blocks.header: Get A Move On
narrative_blocks.body: For more than four decades Peggy was one of St. Louis's top residential real estate agents. Her slogan was “Get A Move On,” her car wore a brass bumblebee, and her Jack Russell terriers told clients she was on the scene.

narrative_blocks.header: Alice in Wonderland on her bedroom walls
narrative_blocks.body: Peggy spent her early childhood in her grandmother's 1688 farmhouse at East Haddam, where her uncle, W. Langdon Kihn, painted Alice in Wonderland murals on her bedroom walls. National Geographic later profiled them.

narrative_blocks.header: She wanted art school and got Wheaton
narrative_blocks.body: Peggy wanted the Rhode Island School of Design; her father insisted on Wheaton, and she transferred to Washington University. She later created and hosted a television review of St. Louis attractions.

narrative_blocks.header: A hurricane, then St. Louis
narrative_blocks.body: The Bragdons came through the 1938 hurricane when Peggy was three, then moved to St. Louis, where her grandfather was a founding executive of D'Arcy Advertising and her father went to Carter Carburetor.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-one years of laughter with Ethan
narrative_blocks.body: Peggy married Dr. John Meyer in 1954, and they raised their three children together even after their 1969 divorce. In 1970 she married Ethan Shepley, who steered her into real estate, and they had twenty-one years of laughter.

narrative_blocks.header: She and Ethan were distant cousins
narrative_blocks.body: Peggy and her second husband, Ethan Shepley, were distant cousins: both descended from Thomas Hooker, she through the Butlers and he through the Dwights.

Family 1688 East Haddam farmhouse with W. Langdon Kihn murals later profiled in National Geographic. Survived 1938 New England hurricane. Family moved CT → St. Louis after hurricane. Stage 6Y-254.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded Copper Exchange in 1973
narrative_blocks.body: Dudley worked for Chase Brass and Copper and Hubbell Metals before he founded the Copper Exchange Company at Ballwin in 1973. He ran it until he died, after heart surgery, in November 2002.

narrative_blocks.header: A collector of clocks and watches
narrative_blocks.body: Dudley collected clocks and watches, and belonged to both the National Association of Watch and Clock Collectors and the American Watchmakers-Clockmakers Institute.

military_service.notes: 334th Bomb Squadron, 95th Bomb Group (Heavy), 8th AAF. Radio Operator on B-17G Flying Fortress. Completed 34 combat missions over Germany — beyond the standard 25-mission tour, completing a full extended tour. The 95th Bomb Group was based at Horham, Suffolk, England.

cross_connections.display_label: , his wife's cousin, forecast weather for the Army Air Corps
cross_connections.notes: Two WWII Army Air Corps men in the same Butler-Bragdon family circle. Ethan Shepley Jr. flew thirty-four combat missions over Germany as B-17G radio operator with the 95th Bomb Group (Heavy), 8th AAF. His wife Peggy Bragdon Shepley's first cousin Wesley W. Yando Jr. served in the Army Air Corps Meteorology Division — the discipline that fed weather forecasts to bomber crews like Shepley's. They never met as fellow servicemen but the family connection ties their war service together.

cross_connections.display_label: , his wife's cousin, was shot down in a 94th Bomb Group B-17 in 1944

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-four missions as a radio operator
narrative_blocks.body: Ethan was radio operator on a B-17G in the 95th Bomb Group at Horham in Suffolk, the only group to win three Distinguished Unit Citations. He flew thirty-four missions over Germany, nine past the standard tour.

narrative_blocks.header: He turned Peggy toward real estate
narrative_blocks.body: Ethan married Peggy Bragdon Meyer in 1970 and encouraged her to put her eye for houses into a residential real estate career. They had twenty-one years together, until his death in December 1991.

narrative_blocks.header: His father ran Washington University
narrative_blocks.body: Ethan's father, Ethan A. H. Shepley, a St. Louis lawyer, chaired Washington University's board and was its chancellor from 1955 to 1961.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran Boatmen's and chaired MasterCard
narrative_blocks.body: Ethan was president of Boatmen's Bancshares from 1969 to 1985 and retired as vice chairman in 1988. He also chaired the Missouri Bankers Association and MasterCard International.

narrative_blocks.header: The United Way's fund-raising system
narrative_blocks.body: As chairman of the United Way in St. Louis Ethan built a fund-raising system still in use when he died, and led drives for the Arts and Education Council and Webster College. Downtown St. Louis gave him its Levee Stone award in 1975.

narrative_blocks.header: He and Peggy were distant cousins
narrative_blocks.body: Ethan and Peggy were distant cousins: both descended from Thomas Hooker, he through the Dwights and she through the Butlers.

narrative_blocks.header: Editor, then archivist
narrative_blocks.body: Fifi worked as an editor for the Connecticut Historical Society, and after she retired became archivist of the East Haddam Historical Society.

narrative_blocks.header: Keeping her father's portraits in view
narrative_blocks.body: After her father died in 1957, Fifi kept his work before the public, and spoke for it at length in Wesleyan's 1987 Davison Art Center exhibition of his Native American portraits.

narrative_blocks.header: Only child of a painter and a designer
narrative_blocks.body: Fifi was the only child of W. Langdon Kihn, the painter of American Indians, and Helen Butler Kihn, an interior designer, and lived most of her life around Hartford and East Haddam.

narrative_blocks.header: Her portrait came home to East Haddam
narrative_blocks.body: Her father's oil portrait of Fifi went to the East Haddam Historical Society as the gift of her cousin Cliff Bragdon and his wife Sarah, who wanted it back in the town at the center of both their lives.

cross_connections.notes: Two WWII Army Air Corps men in the same Butler-Bragdon family circle. Wesley Yando Jr. served in the Army Air Corps Meteorology Division — interrupting his Brown University degree — while his first cousin Margaret 'Peggy' Bragdon Shepley's second husband Ethan Shepley Jr. flew thirty-four combat missions over Germany as a B-17G radio operator with the 95th Bomb Group (Heavy), 8th AAF, based at Horham, Suffolk. narrative_blocks.header: Forecasting weather for the Army Air Corps
narrative_blocks.body: Wes left Brown for the Army Air Corps' Meteorology Division in the Second World War, then came back to finish with the class of 1945.

narrative_blocks.header: Braided rugs with his father in Pawtucket
narrative_blocks.body: Wes went to work beside his father at the Braided Rug and Specialties Co. in Pawtucket, worked with him there for many years, and in time became its owner.

narrative_blocks.header: A deacon at Central Congregational
narrative_blocks.body: Wes belonged to Central Congregational Church in Providence for more than fifty years and served it as a deacon. He sang with the University Glee Club for nearly thirty years, and later with the Jamestown Men's Chorus.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-one years with Lorri
narrative_blocks.body: After his wife Betsey died, Wes spent his last twenty-one years with Lorri Spooner, a painter who had studied at the Rhode Island School of Design. They travelled the world together.
