narrative_blocks.header: Co-founded the Meriden lamp works in 1852
narrative_blocks.body: He started the firm with his brother William, Walter Hubbard and the Hatch brothers. The Hatches were gone inside two years; in 1862 he and Hubbard bought William out, and the lamps that began in 1859 carried the name worldwide.

narrative_blocks.header: Two hundred patents on how a lamp burns
narrative_blocks.body: Between 1856 and 1934 the firm took out more than two hundred patents — wick-raising gears, oil-level gauges, metal ridges to stop spillage, flame spreaders. The engineering was the product as much as the brass was.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven acres, and fifteen hundred hands
narrative_blocks.body: The works covered seven acres and employed about fifteen hundred people, with salesrooms in New York, Boston, Chicago and Philadelphia. Marshall Field, Sears and Montgomery Ward carried the lamps across the country.

narrative_blocks.header: A legislator father, a fertilizer brother
narrative_blocks.body: Levi Bradley of Cheshire sat in the Connecticut legislature and found the town's first barytes mine, running it two years. Brother William Lambert founded Bradley Fertilizer; his only son Clarence took the presidency in 1915.

narrative_blocks.header: What the Irish servant kept saying
narrative_blocks.body: The servant said he came to her room at night. His wife Hattie confronted him, the girl repeated it in front of the household, and he settled money on her and sent her off — she never took it back. A soldier's letter carries the account.

narrative_blocks.header: President of the B & H lamp works
narrative_blocks.body: Bradley & Hubbard, begun as a partnership by Clarence's father Nathaniel Bradley and Walter Hubbard in 1854, made gas and electric light fixtures, fireplace furniture and the celebrated B & H lamps, sold from showrooms in the leading cities. Clarence joined as a clerk, became assistant treasurer in 1885, and succeeded his father as president in 1915.

narrative_blocks.header: Europe instead of college
narrative_blocks.body: After the Russell Military School in New Haven, Clarence was offered the choice between college and a long tour of Europe, and took Europe. His father then kept him a clerk at the works until he had proved himself.

narrative_blocks.header: His house became the Bradley Home
narrative_blocks.body: Clarence left his Meriden homestead and most of his fortune to found the Bradley Home for the Elderly, which ran through the twentieth century; earlier he had paid for the Meriden Hospital's new nurses' home. The Meriden Hall of Fame inducted him in 1982.

narrative_blocks.header: Clubhouse builder and collector
narrative_blocks.body: In 1905 Clarence became president of Meriden's Home Club and drove the building of its new clubhouse, and he collected rare objects from all over the world. He never married, and died at home in March 1934, a year after a cerebral hemorrhage.

military_service.notes: Per EH #1494 and Hart Genealogy of 1875: 'soldier of the War of 1812, died in the army' at Sandusky, Ohio in August 1813 aged seventeen. Specific unit and circumstances not yet researched. The Battle of Fort Stephenson at Sandusky was fought August 1-2, 1813 — Norman's August death is consistent with that engagement, though could also reflect typical disease casualties at frontier garrisons.

cross_connections.display_label: , a Hooker cousin, drowned off Sandusky in 1836
cross_connections.notes: Both Hooker descendants died at Sandusky, Ohio, twenty-three years apart. Norman Hart (a great-grandson of Nathaniel Hart through the Marietta line) died there August 1813 as a soldier of the War of 1812, aged seventeen. Sherman Pierpont (descended through the James Pierpont III line) drowned in Lake Erie at Sandusky on May 7, 1836, aged fifty-two — his body washed ashore three weeks later. Sandusky was an early Connecticut-frontier convergence point and both men ended their lives at it through different paths.

narrative_blocks.header: Eldest son killed at Sandusky, summer 1813
narrative_blocks.body: Born August 29, 1795 at the family's Marietta home in Ohio, eldest of Selah Hart and Sarah Walter's ten children. He enlisted as a soldier in the War of 1812 and died at Sandusky, Ohio in August 1813, aged seventeen. The August timing aligns with the defense of Fort Stephenson on August 1-2, 1813 under Major George Croghan — Sandusky's most notable engagement of the war.

narrative_blocks.header: Married Mary Thompson by Justice Corner, 1826
narrative_blocks.body: He removed from the family's Watertown home to Marion, Morgan County, Ohio with his parents in 1821, then married Mary Thompson, daughter of Hugh, on February 23, 1826 at Marion. The ceremony was performed by George Corner, Justice of the Peace. He farmed at Marion for the rest of his life and had eight children.

narrative_blocks.header: Migrated Ohio to Wisconsin, died Vernon County 1865
narrative_blocks.body: Born December 6, 1799 at Watertown, Ohio, fourth son of Selah Hart and Sarah Walter. He married Sally Rush of Morgan County, Ohio on October 27, 1825 and remained in Morgan County through his ten children. Late in life the family moved to Vernon County, Wisconsin, where Seth died September 3, 1865 aged sixty-five — his widow later removing to Muscatine County, Iowa, where she was living in 1874.

narrative_blocks.header: Outlived husband by seventeen years
narrative_blocks.body: Married Walter Hart on May 30, 1818 at age seventeen — twelve children together over more than two decades. Walter died September 5, 1872 at age seventy-five. b. May 15, 1859 Paris; d. Apr 19, 1906 Paris age 46 — run over by a horse-drawn cart in Rue Dauphine. Son of Dr. Eugène Curie, physician. Co-discovered piezoelectricity with brother Jacques Curie in 1880. m. Marie Skłodowska Jul 26, 1895. Daughters Irène (b. 1897, Nobel Chemistry 1935) and Ève (b. 1904, X00870). Shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with Marie and Antoine Henri Becquerel for the discovery and study of radioactivity. Reinterred at the Panthéon, Paris, in 1995. Easter-egg orbit entry: father-in-law of HD2606 Henry Richardson Labouisse Jr. via daughter Ève Curie (X00870).

notable.notable_blurb: Physicist; co-discoverer of radium and polonium

cross_connections.display_label: was the UNICEF chief who married his daughter Ève

narrative_blocks.header: He and Jacques discovered piezoelectricity
narrative_blocks.body: He and his brother Jacques showed in 1880 that crystals under stress throw off an electric charge, and a year later that the effect runs backwards. Almost every digital circuit now keeps time on a quartz crystal doing that.

narrative_blocks.header: Curie’s law, and the Curie temperature
narrative_blocks.body: He found in his doctoral work that magnetic pull falls away as a substance warms, and that above one critical point a ferromagnet stops being one. Those are Curie's law and the Curie temperature.

narrative_blocks.header: A tonne of pitchblende, two new elements
narrative_blocks.body: He put down his own crystal work in 1898 to join the search his wife had started, and by December they had announced radium as well as polonium. The measurements ran on an electrometer he and Jacques had built.

narrative_blocks.header: He and a student found nuclear energy
narrative_blocks.body: With his student Albert Laborde he showed that radium gives off heat continuously with nothing feeding it — the first sight of nuclear energy. Bending the emissions through a magnetic field, he found some positive, some negative, some neutral.

narrative_blocks.header: He investigated séances as physics experiments
narrative_blocks.body: He read through the spiritualist literature and sat at Eusapia Palladino's séances in 1905 with instruments, noting every observation. He had written to Marie that these were questions of physics; he was an atheist.

narrative_blocks.header: The Royal Society let him speak, not Marie
narrative_blocks.body: The Royal Society asked him to present their work in London in 1903 but would not let Marie speak. Lord Kelvin sat beside her while he spoke; they took the Davy Medal, and the Nobel with Becquerel that December.

narrative_blocks.header: Killed by a cart on the Rue Dauphine
narrative_blocks.body: He slipped crossing the Rue Dauphine in heavy rain on 19 April 1906 and went under a horse-drawn cart. A wheel passed over his head and killed him at once, at forty-six. The Panthéon took him in 1995.

career.organization: Faculty of Sciences, University of Paris

people.research_notes: b. Nov 7, 1867 Warsaw, Russian-controlled Poland; d. Jul 4, 1934 Passy (Haute-Savoie), France age 66 — aplastic anemia from sustained radiation exposure. Born Marie Salomea Skłodowska. Emigrated to Paris 1891 to study at the Sorbonne. m. Pierre Curie Jul 26, 1895. 1903 Nobel Physics (shared with Pierre and Becquerel) — first woman Nobel laureate. 1911 Nobel Chemistry (sole) for discovery, isolation, and study of radium and polonium — first person to win Nobels in two sciences. Director of the Curie Laboratory at the Radium Institute, University of Paris, founded 1914. Developed portable X-ray vehicles ('Little Curies') for WWI field hospitals. Daughters: Irène Joliot-Curie (1897-1956, Nobel Chemistry 1935) and Ève Curie (1904-2007, X00870). 1995: first woman buried under the Panthéon dome by Republic of France honors. Easter-egg orbit entry: mother-in-law of HD2606 Henry Richardson Labouisse Jr.

notable.notable_blurb: Physicist and chemist; only Nobel laureate in two sciences

was the woman whose physics publishing she followed decades later

narrative_blocks.header: She named radioactivity, working in a shed
narrative_blocks.body: She worked in a converted dissecting shed beside ESPCI, neither ventilated nor waterproof, measuring pitchblende at four times the activity of the uranium in it. She concluded the radiation had to come from the atom itself, and gave it a name: radioactivity.

narrative_blocks.header: She isolated radium from a tonne of ore
narrative_blocks.body: By 1902 she had separated a tenth of a gram of radium chloride from a tonne of pitchblende, and pure radium metal took her until 1910.

narrative_blocks.header: The Flying University met in secret
narrative_blocks.body: Shut out of Warsaw's universities because she was a woman, she took her first lectures at the clandestine Flying University and worked as a governess to pay her sister's studies in Paris. Her sister paid her way in turn.

narrative_blocks.header: She took Pierre’s Sorbonne chair, the first woman
narrative_blocks.body: She was given the chair created for Pierre on 13 May 1906, twenty-four days after the cart killed him, and took it to build the laboratory he never got. She was the first woman to hold a professorship in France.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty vans of X-rays at the front
narrative_blocks.body: She learned radiology, anatomy and motor mechanics in a hurry and had twenty mobile X-ray vans in the field hospitals within a year of the war starting. Over a million wounded men passed through them, and France never thanked her.

narrative_blocks.header: A second Nobel, through the Langevin scandal
narrative_blocks.body: She took the 1911 chemistry prize while the papers printed her affair with Paul Langevin. The Nobel chairman asked her to stay away; she answered that the prize was for polonium and radium, not her private life.

narrative_blocks.header: Her notebooks are still radioactive
narrative_blocks.body: She left papers from the 1890s that sit in lead-lined boxes at the national library, where readers sign a waiver and put on protective clothing. The radium in them has some fifteen centuries left to run.

notable.notable_blurb: President of Wright Chemical Corporation

landmarks.landmark_blurb: The Wrights' 1976 riverfront restoration

narrative_blocks.header: A founder of the Historic Wilmington Foundation
narrative_blocks.body: In 1966 Thomas and his wife, Bobo, were among the twelve founders of the Historic Wilmington Foundation, as urban renewal was clearing downtown Wilmington. In 1976 they built Chandler's Wharf on the riverfront, and the two shared the Ruth Coltrane Cannon Award for Historic Preservation.

narrative_blocks.header: He saved Wilmington's oldest house in 1963
narrative_blocks.body: In 1963 Thomas and Bobo rescued the Mitchell-Anderson House at 102 Orange Street, built about 1738 for Edward Mitchell and by then a boarding house. It is the oldest house in Wilmington that can be dated, and Wright Chemical Corporation, which he ran as president, kept its offices there.

narrative_blocks.header: Woodberry Forest, the Navy, Wright Chemical
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas went to Woodberry Forest School and the University of North Carolina, served four and a half years in the Navy, leaving as a lieutenant, and became president of Wright Chemical Corporation in Wilmington.

narrative_blocks.header: Married by his cousin the bishop
narrative_blocks.body: A widower, Thomas married Bobo Labouisse on 9 October 1959 at Fairntosh, her parents' home in Durham County, with no attendants. His cousin the Rt. Rev. Thomas H. Wright, Episcopal bishop of East Carolina, performed the ceremony.

narrative_blocks.header: She married Tim Self and stayed in Asheboro
narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Asheboro in 1953 and married Timothy Cecil Self there in 1980, and they raised three children in the town she had grown up in.

narrative_blocks.header: She went to East Carolina and cheered Carolina
narrative_blocks.body: She attended East Carolina University and kept her allegiance to the North Carolina Tar Heels regardless, and raised her three children to do the same.

narrative_blocks.header: Child support work came after the children
narrative_blocks.body: She spent her early adulthood as a full-time mother and a volunteer in Asheboro, and later went to work for Randolph County Child Support Services.

narrative_blocks.body: In place of flowers her family asked for gifts to the Southern Poverty Law Center.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at forty with a nine-year-old
narrative_blocks.body: Louise Woeste married John Middleton Huger in New Orleans in 1900 and he died there in 1912, at forty-four. She did not marry again, and outlived him by forty-seven years.

narrative_blocks.header: A New Orleans family in a Virginia churchyard
narrative_blocks.body: She died in the Bronx in 1959, at eighty-seven, and was buried at Union Cemetery in Leesburg rather than in the Metairie ground that holds her husband and his Huger and Polk kin. Her daughter and son-in-law lie there with her.

narrative_blocks.body: The Werleins published sheet music and kept Werlein's for Music on Canal Street, an institution in the city for generations. Betty married into the Hugers in 1913, and was buried in their ground at Metairie.

narrative_blocks.body: Hardie married Jessie Edson Hendrick on a Friday in 1932 and the announcement came the day after, without a word of where or by whom the ceremony had been performed. He was a Yale man of the class of 1926, living at his mother's house on East Forty-eighth Street.

narrative_blocks.header: Two of their four children died as infants
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph Hardie III was born and died in 1936, and Edson Hendrick Hardie in 1943. The two who lived were William Huger Hardie Jr., born in 1938, and Robin, born in New York in 1942.

narrative_blocks.body: Jessie Hendrick took degrees at Bryn Mawr and at Oxford and was practicing law by the time she married in 1932. Her father Frank Hendrick was an attorney too, with offices at 120 Broadway.

narrative_blocks.header: Married in secret on a Friday
narrative_blocks.body: Her marriage to William Huger Hardie was announced the day after it took place in 1932, and no account was given of where or by whom it was performed. She was twenty-five and already at the bar.

Yale engineering degree (in deference to his engineer father), University of Virginia LLB (in deference to his lawyer mother). Three years at Davis Polk in New York; moved to Mobile AL 1966; worked at Johnstone Adams (law firm) until death. Published many articles of legal research; voted best lawyer in his field many times. St. Paul's Episcopal Church, Mobile: 5th grade Sunday school teacher; vestry; vestry clerk for 20 years; completed 4-year EFM course. Wife: Alix Winter Hardie (X02873). Four children: Frank Winter Hardie (HD5039, 1979-2007 died of cancer), William Huger Hardie III 'Tuck' (m. Jennifer; not yet built), Edward Thomas Lingham Hardie 'Ted' (m. Chris O'Hare; not yet built), Rebecca Hardie Tait (m. Chip; not yet built). Grandsons: Gabriel Alexander O'Hare-Hardie, Charles Lucas Tait, Frank Hardie Tait, Jasper Edward Hardie. Polymath interests per obituary: religion, geography, physics, philosophy, history, sailing, scuba, underwater photography, amateur flying, classical and jazz music, theater, baseball, crossword puzzles, computer programming, sewing, toilet repair, genealogy, travel, wine. Buried Thornhill Cemetery, Talladega County AL. (Bill Hardie obituary)

narrative_blocks.header: Both degrees taken in deference
narrative_blocks.body: He took an engineering degree at Yale and a law degree at Virginia, and said he had chosen both in deference to his parents. Three years at Davis Polk in New York were enough; in 1966 he moved to Mobile and stayed at Johnstone, Adams for the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: Toilet repair sat beside physics
narrative_blocks.body: The things he taught himself ran from religion, physics and the study of time to sailing, amateur flying, crossword puzzles, computer programming, sewing and toilet repair. He bragged shamelessly about his children.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty years keeping the vestry minutes
narrative_blocks.body: He taught fifth-grade Sunday school at St Paul's Episcopal in Mobile, sat on the vestry and kept its minutes for twenty years, and finished the four-year Education for Ministry course.

narrative_blocks.header: He buried a son and followed him
narrative_blocks.body: Frank Winter Hardie died of neuroendocrine cancer in December 2007, at twenty-eight. His father was buried beside him at Thornhill twelve years later, in the family ground at Talladega.

narrative_blocks.header: A year in Hong Kong before the handover
narrative_blocks.body: For his 1992 Stanford dissertation, Ted Hardie spent September 1990 to September 1991 in Hong Kong, interviewing would-be emigrants and migration advisers about leaving before the territory passed to China in 1997.

people.research_notes: b. Sep 13, 1871 NYC; d. Feb 7, 1943 NYC age 71. Son of William Mecklenburg Polk (HD2601) and X01884 (his Polk wife). Yale College B.A. 1894 (Scroll and Key Society); Columbia Law School LL.B. 1897. Spanish-American War service as Captain, Trooper Squadron A. Law practice NYC from 1897. New York Civil Service Commission 1907-1909. NYC Board of Education 1907, 1910. Corporation Counsel NYC 24 Jan 1914 (appointed by Mayor John Purroy Mitchel). Wounded by gunfire Apr 17, 1914 in attempted assassination of Mayor Mitchel by a former city employee. Appointed Counselor to U.S. Department of State 16 Sep 1915 (Senate confirmed 17 Dec 1915), serving through 1919 (4th Counselor). FIRST U.S. UNDER SECRETARY OF STATE — Jul 1, 1919 to Jun 15, 1920 (office created; first to hold the title; succeeded by Norman Davis). Acting Secretary of State Feb 14, 1920 to Mar 12, 1920 (between Robert Lansing and Bainbridge Colby). Headed American Commission to Negotiate Peace 1919; represented U.S. at Paris Peace Conference after Wilson and Lansing departed. Managed John W. Davis's 1924 Democratic presidential campaign. President of New York Public Library Apr 13, 1932 until death. NC Society of the Cincinnati 1919; Grand Officer French Legion of Honor. Portrait painted by Sir Oswald Birley 1923. Davis Polk & Wardwell — NAME PARTNER (still the firm's name today). m. Elizabeth Sturgis Potter Jan 27, 1908 Philadelphia. 5 children. Buried Woodlawn Cemetery Bronx NY. (Wikipedia; FindAGrave) [Stage 6Y-277 from Yale Obituary Record]: Education: Groton (Mass.) School, then Yale 1894. Yale activities: Freshman Football Team, Freshman Crew, Class crew 3 years, substitute University Football Team freshman year, Class cup committee, member University Club, Hé Boulé, Psi Upsilon, and Scroll and Key. Mother: Ida Ashe Lyon Polk (X01884) of Demopolis, AL. Brother: John Metcalfe Polk Sr (HD5055), Yale Sheffield 1896, died 1904 age 28. Legal career detail: Clerk Evarts, Choate & Beaman 1897-1900; Partner Watriss & Polk (later Alexander, Watriss & Polk) 1900-1914; Stetson, Jennings & Russell 1914-1943 (firm evolved into Davis Polk & Wardwell). Acting Secretary of State dates per Yale obit slightly differ: Dec 4, 1918 - Jul 18, 1919. Honors: M.A. Hon. Yale 1918; D.C.L. University of the South 1928; LL.D. Rollins 1930 and NYU 1935. Grand Officer Order of Leopold (Belgium) 1920; Légion d'Honneur (France) 1926; Grand Cross Order of Crown of Roumania; Order of Polonia Restituta 1st class; Heraldic Order of Cristóbal Colón (Dominican Republic) 1940. Civic: National Municipal League president 1924-1927. NY Public Library trustee 1921-1943 (president 1932-1943, where he died of coronary occlusion). Cathedral of St. John the Divine trustee 1929-1943. Met Museum trustee 1931-1937. Pan-American Society president 1936-1943. Survived by 8 grandchildren at his 1943 death.

military_service.role: Captain, Squadron A, New York cavalry.

narrative_blocks.header: First in an office that had not existed
narrative_blocks.body: The post of Under Secretary of State was created in 1919 and Polk was the first to hold it. He was Acting Secretary for a month in 1920, and when Wilson and Lansing left Paris he stayed to head the American commission there.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the letter that made the firm
narrative_blocks.body: Allen Wardwell brought him into the old Stetson firm in 1920, and Polk wrote to John W. Davis, then quitting the London embassy, to argue him into joining. The door read Davis Polk from 1921, and in 1924 Polk ran his presidential campaign.

narrative_blocks.header: He was shot at instead of the mayor
narrative_blocks.body: In April 1914, while he was the city's corporation counsel, a discharged municipal employee tried to shoot Mayor John Purroy Mitchel. It was Polk who was hit, and Polk who recovered from the wound.

narrative_blocks.header: His papers keep the wiretap transcripts
narrative_blocks.body: The twenty-two feet of papers he left run from 1915 to 1920 and hold his own diaries of conversations with foreign envoys, together with transcripts of telephone calls the government tapped between 1915 and 1917.

narrative_blocks.header: Eleven years begging for the library
narrative_blocks.body: From 1932 until his death he was president of the trustees of the New York Public Library, and spent the years trying to wring more money from the city.

narrative_blocks.header: Boy Scouts, Salvation Army, and Yugoslavia
narrative_blocks.body: He worked for the Boy Scouts, the Salvation Army, the Church Pension Fund and the Citizens Crime Commission, and presided over the Knickerbocker Club and the American Friends of Yugoslavia. The Yugoslav government sent flowers to his funeral.

narrative_blocks.header: He rode with Squadron A
narrative_blocks.body: He served in the Spanish-American War as a captain in Squadron A, New York's cavalry troop. France made him a Grand Officer of the Legion of Honor, and the Society of the Cincinnati took him in 1919.

Frank Lyon Polk Jan 27, 1908 Philadelphia. 5 children (HD5048-HD5052). Residences: 6 East 68th Street NYC; Syosset (Long Island); Boca Grande FL. Buried Woodlawn Cemetery, Bronx NY. (FindAGrave; Frank Polk Wikipedia)

cross_connections.display_label: bought the Phillies from her father in 1904

narrative_blocks.header: Her father had the Phillies for two seasons
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth Potter grew up in a Philadelphia house that owned a baseball club: her father James led the syndicate that bought the Phillies in 1903, kept them two seasons and sold out to Charles Phelps Taft, then spent the rest of his working life as Cunard's general agent.

narrative_blocks.header: She chose the psalms and kept it plain
narrative_blocks.body: Twelve hundred people came to her husband's funeral in 1943, and the Roosevelts sent flowers, but at her asking the service was the plain Order for the Burial of the Dead. She picked the first and fifteenth psalms herself, and gave his papers to Yale that year.

cross_connections.display_label: was his uncle, dead at twenty-eight, and gave him his name

naming_inspiration.note: Named for his late paternal uncle John Metcalfe Polk Sr. (HD5055, 1875-1904) who died of autopsy-acquired pneumonia at 28, four years before HD5048's 1908 birth.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried a name the family had lost
narrative_blocks.body: The first John Metcalfe Polk was teaching medicine at Cornell and studying the pneumonias that follow influenza when a chill caught at an autopsy killed him in March 1904, twenty-eight years old. His brother's son, born four years later, was given the name.

narrative_blocks.header: He married an English banker’s daughter in 1939
narrative_blocks.body: In December 1939, three months into the war, he married Virginia Brand of Eydon in Northamptonshire. He was thirty-one and she was twenty-one; he died nine years later and she went home to England.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at thirty-nine in Polk County
narrative_blocks.body: He died in January 1948 at Tryon, in the North Carolina county that carries his own surname, and was brought back to Woodlawn.

people.research_notes: b. Jul 31, 1910 Cedarhurst, Nassau County NY; d. Mar 23, 1990 Manhattan NY age 79 (some sources say b. Jul 21). Daughter of Frank Lyon Polk (HD5047) and Elizabeth Sturgis Potter (X02878). Attended what is now the Juilliard School of Music. m. Raymond Richard Guest 1935 (X02879); divorced 1953. Settled on farms in Middleburg VA, then Front Royal VA during WWII. Later divided time among Front Royal VA, Washington DC, and Islesboro ME. Boards/trustee positions: Washington Opera Society, Boston Opera Co., Ellington Fund, DC Youth Orchestra. Supported Dance Theater of Harlem, Joffrey Ballet, NY String Seminars for Young People. Founder Musicians Emergency Fund; member Metropolitan Opera Association; member Middleburg Hunt. Godmother of violinist Pinchas Zukerman; gave him his first violin. 1 child: Raymond R 'Andy' Guest Jr (HD5053). (FindAGrave; obituary)

narrative_blocks.header: She gave Pinchas Zukerman his first violin
narrative_blocks.body: She was godmother to Pinchas Zukerman and put the first violin in his hands. She spent her life paying for young musicians, and sat on the boards of the Washington Opera Society, the Boston Opera Company and the D.C. Youth Orchestra.

narrative_blocks.header: She founded a fund for broke musicians
narrative_blocks.body: The Musicians Emergency Fund was set up to carry players through the stretches when the work stops, and she was among its founders. She backed the Dance Theatre of Harlem, the Joffrey and the New York String Seminars for Young People the same way.

narrative_blocks.header: She co-founded the Kennedy Center’s Friends
narrative_blocks.body: She was a co-founder of the Friends of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts and a founding member of the District of Columbia Arts Council, and sat as trustee of the Powhatan and Foxcroft schools and of Warren Memorial Hospital.

narrative_blocks.header: Eighteen years, Middleburg then Front Royal
narrative_blocks.body: She married Raymond Guest in June 1935 and they kept house in Virginia's hunt country, first at Middleburg and then at Front Royal. They divorced early in 1953, and she divided the rest of her life between Front Royal and Islesboro in Maine.

narrative_blocks.header: Partner for two years, then dead at forty
narrative_blocks.body: He was admitted to the bar in 1940 and went straight onto the staff of Davis Polk & Wardwell, the Broad Street firm his father had helped build and still gave its name to. He made partner in 1950 and died in 1952, after a week's illness, at forty.

narrative_blocks.header: A first son born at law school
narrative_blocks.body: Groton, then Yale in 1934, then the University of Virginia law school, where he finished in 1937. Charlottesville is where the eldest of the three boys was born, in the spring of 1935, while the degree was still two years off.

narrative_blocks.header: A Navy lieutenant guarding the Canal Zone
narrative_blocks.body: From 1942 to 1945 he was a lieutenant and a Navy security officer, posted to New York and to the Panama Canal Zone. It was the only stretch of twelve years he spent away from the firm.

narrative_blocks.header: Three Franks, and he was the middle one
narrative_blocks.body: His father took the Yale class of 1894 and he took the class of 1934, and his own eldest was born the next year to carry the name a third time. He was also a great-grandnephew of President James Knox Polk.

narrative_blocks.header: A widow and three boys under twenty
narrative_blocks.body: He married Katharine Hoppin Salvage in 1934 and they had Frank, Samuel and William in 1935, 1938 and 1940. When he died the youngest was twelve and the eldest seventeen.

cross_connections.display_label: was his wife's elder sister, and married his brother Frank

narrative_blocks.header: Two Polk brothers married two Salvage sisters
narrative_blocks.body: He married Margaret Smith Salvage in 1933, the middle of three sisters, a year before his elder brother Frank married the eldest of them. The two households shared both sets of parents.

narrative_blocks.header: He outlived his brother by thirty-five years
narrative_blocks.body: Frank was dead at forty in 1952, in the same city where both of them had been born. James Potter Polk was born in Manhattan in 1914 and died there in 1987, at seventy-two.

narrative_blocks.header: A Jesuit married her in the drawing room
narrative_blocks.body: She was married in 1940 in her parents' house at 6 East Sixty-eighth Street, and the Rev. John La Farge performed the ceremony. Her sister, by then Mrs. Raymond Guest, was matron of honour, and her brother James was one of the ushers.

narrative_blocks.header: Born in Washington while her father ran State
narrative_blocks.body: She was born in Washington in October 1917, six months after the country entered the war and while her father was counselor of the State Department. By the time she was three he had been Acting Secretary of State and the household was back in New York.

narrative_blocks.header: Ninety-one years, and twelve great-grandchildren
narrative_blocks.body: She died in New York in 2009 at ninety-one, twenty-one years after Winthrop, leaving ten grandchildren and twelve great-grandchildren. Of her five children, Lewis went out to Hong Kong and made a career in venture capital. White roses were laid on her casket at the Church of the Heavenly Rest.

narrative_blocks.header: A president and a fighting bishop behind her
narrative_blocks.body: She was a great-grandniece of James Knox Polk, the eleventh President, and a great-granddaughter of Leonidas Polk, the bishop who took a general's commission and was killed in Georgia. Both descents reached her through her father.

people.research_notes: b. Nov 25, 1907 Manhattan NYC; d. Dec 31, 1991 Fredericksburg VA age 84 of pneumonia. Son of the Right Honorable Frederick E. Guest (English) and Amy Phipps (American steel heiress). St. George's School RI; Phillips Academy Andover; Yale 1931. Horse racing: 1962 Epsom Derby winner (Larkspur); 1965 Preakness winner (Tom Rolfe); 1968 Epsom Derby winner (Sir Ivor, also took DC International same year); 1975 Grand National winner at Aintree (L'Escargot — two-time Cheltenham Cup winner). WWII: U.S. Navy in Atlantic, minesweepers, Europe; briefly aide to U.S. Ambassador John Gilbert Winant at Court of St. James. Decorated Legion of Merit and Bronze Star (both with combat V) plus decorations from Britain, France, Denmark, Norway. Director of Bessemer Securities NYC. Virginia State Senate 1947-1953 (Democrat). Virginia Fish and Game Commission 1959-1965. U.S. Ambassador to Ireland 1965-1969 (appointed by LBJ). Trustee Virginia Museum of Fine Arts Richmond. Donated Amy Guest wing to Mary Washington Hospital Fredericksburg. Brother of Winston Guest (top US polo player together in 1930s). 3 marriages: Elizabeth Sturgis Polk (HD5049, 1935-1953 div); Ellen Tuck French Guest (Astor, 1953-1974 d.); Princess Caroline Murat (1960-?). Powhatan Plantation King George VA — horse-breeding operations late in life. (Washington Post obit; FindAGrave)

narrative_blocks.header: Two Epsom Derbys out of one Virginia farm
narrative_blocks.body: Larkspur took the Derby for him in 1962 and Sir Ivor in 1968, along with the Two Thousand Guineas and the Washington International. Vincent O'Brien trained his flat horses and Dan Moore his jumpers, in chocolate silks with pale blue hoops.

narrative_blocks.header: He won the Grand National as well
narrative_blocks.body: L'Escargot was steeplechase horse of the year in America in 1969, took the Cheltenham Gold Cup in 1970 and again in 1971, and won the Grand National in 1975. Almost nobody has ever won both that race and the Epsom Derby.

narrative_blocks.header: Two U.S. Opens with the Templeton team
narrative_blocks.body: Raymond and his brother Winston both played polo, and Raymond won the U.S. Open twice with the Templeton team. The Museum of Polo and Hall of Fame inducted him posthumously in 2006.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the OSS navy section in London
narrative_blocks.body: He joined the naval reserve in 1940 and served on minesweepers before taking charge of the Navy Section of the Office of Strategic Services in London under Ambassador Winant. He came out a commander with the Legion of Merit, the Bronze Star and the Croix de guerre.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave back part of an ambassador’s pay
narrative_blocks.body: Johnson sent him to Dublin in 1965, and he returned a good share of the salary to the State Department to pay for training Foreign Service officers.

narrative_blocks.header: He named a hospital wing for his mother
narrative_blocks.body: He bought Powhatan Plantation in King George County in 1952 and built the stable there that carried his colours. At Mary Washington Hospital in Fredericksburg he paid for the Amy Guest Wing, after the mother whose Phipps money had built the family.

narrative_blocks.header: Churchill was his first cousin once removed
narrative_blocks.body: The Guests came down from the seventh Duke of Marlborough through the first Baron Wimborne, which put Winston Churchill one step sideways in the family. His mother's father was Henry Phipps, Carnegie's steel partner.

parents.mother_research_notes: Mother: Alice Kearny Morton Rutherfurd (1879-1917) — daughter of Levi P. Morton, VP under Harrison; died of appendicitis age 38 leaving 6 young children. Not built as separate entry.

marriages.notes: Also fathered Winthrop III, Alice, James, Linda Rutherfurd — not yet built.

people.research_notes: b. Dec 5, 1904 New York County NY; d. Feb 25, 1988 age 83. Son of Winthrop Chanler Rutherfurd Sr. (X02881, easter-egg entry) and Alice Kearny Morton (1879-1917; daughter of Levi P. Morton — U.S. Vice President under Benjamin Harrison and Governor of New York). His mother died of appendicitis when he was 12, leaving six young children. Through Levi P. Morton he descended from prominent NYC society. Through father from astronomer Lewis Morris Rutherfurd (Rutherfurd Crater on the Moon named for him) and the Stuyvesant fortune (via grandmother Margaret Chanler Stuyvesant). Stepmother Lucy Page Mercer Rutherfurd — President Franklin D. Roosevelt's confidante (the FDR affair that nearly ended his marriage to Eleanor and his political career). Former president of Coast Metals (manufacturer of hard-surface metals, Little Ferry NJ). m. Alice Potter Polk (HD5052) 1940. 5 children including Lewis Polk Rutherfurd (HD5054). Buried Rutherfurd family plot Tranquility Cemetery NJ. (FindAGrave; Wikipedia chain)

narrative_blocks.header: He was twelve when his mother died
narrative_blocks.body: He was twelve when Alice Morton Rutherfurd died of appendicitis in 1917 and left six young children. The stepmother who came into the house was Lucy Mercer, whose place in Franklin Roosevelt's life nearly ended a marriage and a career.

narrative_blocks.header: He rowed at Princeton and kept three clubs
narrative_blocks.body: He was graduated from Princeton in 1928, where he was a prominent oarsman and belonged to the Ivy Club. In New York he kept up the Knickerbocker and the Racquet and Tennis.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran a hard-surface metals works
narrative_blocks.body: He was president of Coast Metals at Little Ferry in New Jersey, which made hard-surfacing alloys. It was an unshowy business for a man whose wedding guests filled a society column.

narrative_blocks.header: A Vice President for a grandfather
narrative_blocks.body: He was a grandson of Levi P. Morton, governor of New York and Vice President under Benjamin Harrison. He grew up between the Rutherfurd houses at Allamuchy in New Jersey and Aiken in South Carolina.

career.notes: hard-surface metals manufacturer

people.research_notes: b. Feb 4, 1862 New York County; d. Mar 19, 1944 Aiken SC age 82. Father of Winthrop Chanler Rutherfurd Jr. (X02880) — making him paternal grandfather-in-law to HD5052 Alice Potter Polk Rutherfurd and great-grandfather of HD5054 Lewis Polk Rutherfurd. EASTER-EGG entry per project rule (notable parent of Hooker spouse). Son of astronomer Lewis Morris Rutherfurd (1816-1892, 'Rutherfurd Crater' on the Moon named for him) and Margaret Chanler Stuyvesant (1820-1890, niece+adopted daughter of Peter Gerard Stuyvesant). Brother of Stuyvesant Rutherfurd who changed name to Rutherfurd Stuyvesant per Peter Gerard Stuyvesant's 1847 will to transmit the Stuyvesant fortune. Columbia College 1884. m1. Alice Morton (1902-1917 d.; 6 children); m2. Lucy Page Mercer (1920-1944 d.; 1 daughter Barbara). WESTMINSTER KENNEL CLUB: His champion fox terrier 'Warren Remedy' won Best in Show 3 consecutive years 1907, 1908, 1909 — a feat that has NEVER been duplicated in the show's history. Favorite fox terrier named 'Brass Tacks.' Romance: In 1895 secretly engaged to railroad heiress Consuelo Vanderbilt before her forced marriage to the Duke of Marlborough (later annulled by the Sacred Rota of the Roman Catholic Church on the grounds that she had loved Winthrop). Allamuchy Farms NJ (18,000 sf brick home commissioned 1903-1905) and Ridgeley Hall Aiken SC. Wife #2 Lucy Mercer was Eleanor Roosevelt's social secretary 1914 and had romantic affair with Franklin D. Roosevelt — the affair that could have ended FDR's marriage and political career. Stroke 1941, recuperated until 1944 death with Lucy at his side. Buried Rutherfurd family plot Tranquility Cemetery NJ. (Wikipedia; FindAGrave) [Stage 6Y-276 sibling context from Find A Grave / Rutherfurd family record]: Siblings of Winthrop Rutherfurd Sr: (1) Stuyvesant Rutherfurd (1842-1907) — changed his name to 'Rutherfurd Stuyvesant' per Peter Gerard Stuyvesant's 1847 will to transmit the Stuyvesant fortune; (2) Louisa Morris Rutherfurd (1855-1892) — died age 37; (3) Margaret Rutherfurd White (1854-1916) — m. Henry White, U.S. diplomat (ambassador to France and Italy); (4) Lewis Morris Rutherfurd Jr. (1859-1901) — co-owner of Rutherfurd Kennels and fellow fox-terrier breeder. Family seat 'Tranquility Farms' in Allamuchy NJ predated Winthrop Sr's 18,000 sf 'Allamuchy Farms' commission of 1903-1905.

narrative_blocks.header: Warren Remedy won Westminster three years running
narrative_blocks.body: He bred Warren Remedy, the smooth fox terrier who took Best in Show at Westminster in 1907, 1908 and 1909. No dog has managed three since, and his own favourite was a terrier called Brass Tacks.

narrative_blocks.header: Rome annulled a duchess over him
narrative_blocks.body: In 1895 he was secretly engaged to Consuelo Vanderbilt, until her mother forced her into the ninth Duke of Marlborough instead. Rome annulled that marriage thirty-one years later, finding she had loved an American named Rutherfurd and been made to give him up.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the governess, who was Roosevelt’s
narrative_blocks.body: He married Lucy Page Mercer in February 1920, weeks after his eldest boy died of pneumonia at sixteen. She had been Eleanor Roosevelt's social secretary and Franklin's lover, and had come to Allamuchy as governess to his six motherless children.

narrative_blocks.header: Edith Wharton wrote her first novels off him
narrative_blocks.body: He was, Edith Wharton said, the prototype of her first novels, and Ward McAllister had already counted him among the four hundred. He stayed a bachelor until he was forty.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-eight rooms beside his brother’s land
narrative_blocks.body: He set Whitney Warren to build a thirty-eight-room Tudor house at Allamuchy in 1902, next to his brother's place, with a boathouse, a powerhouse, nine holes of golf and kennels. The thousand acres ran Holstein cows and Dorset sheep.

narrative_blocks.header: Kidnappers threatened to take his two sons
narrative_blocks.body: A threat in 1907 to carry off two of his boys from the Allamuchy estate caused a sensation in New York. Guards went onto the children, and nobody ever came.

narrative_blocks.header: A moon crater carries his father's name
narrative_blocks.body: He was the youngest of seven born to Lewis Morris Rutherfurd, who left the law in 1849 for astronomical photography and built the spectroscope. A crater on the moon carries that name. The boys got up dog fights in the stable yard while their father read the dog stars.

people.research_notes: b. Sep 29, 1939 NYC; d. Apr 2, 2001 Front Royal VA age 61 of cancer at Rock Hill Farm. Son of Elizabeth Sturgis Polk Guest (HD5049) and Raymond Richard Guest Sr. (X02879). Spent childhood at Carter's Grove Plantation (1755). Yale 1964 (took year off to serve in Marines Corps Reserves; entered Class of 1963, returned to graduate with Class of 1964). Proud Marine tattoo on upper arm. Banker and farmer by profession. m1. Patricia Hazard Donovan 1962-1971 div. m2. Mary Scott Derrick (X02882). Virginia House of Delegates 1972-2000 (28 years, 7 terms): Republican. Districts: 17th (1972-82), 18th (1982-83), 31st (1983-92), 15th (1992-2000). House Minority Leader Dec 3, 1985 - Nov 19, 1991. Co-chairman Conservation and Natural Resources Committee in final 1999 session. Champion of pari-mutuel betting (1988 bill led to Colonial Downs horse track New Kent + four parlors). Cancer: non-Hodgkin lymphoma diagnosed 1996 with 6-month prognosis; took up polo again in VA and FL; stem-cell transplant extended life ~5 years per his own assessment. During isolation in 1994 chemo, the VA legislature set up an absentee voting system so he could vote — testament to his stature on both sides of the aisle. SHENANDOAH RIVER RAYMOND R. 'ANDY' GUEST JR. STATE PARK (south fork Shenandoah River, Warren County VA) named for him in 1995 — only person in history to have a national/state park named after them while still living per his Yale '64 classmate remembrance. He and Mary Scott put easements on Rock Hill Farm (3.5 miles riverfront) and bequeathed it to State of Virginia. Helped establish free medical coverage for underprivileged immigrants at St. Luke's free medical clinic. Survivors: wife Mary Scott Derrick Guest (X02882); daughter Mary Elizabeth Looney (Middleburg); sons Raymond R. Guest III (Bradenton FL), William G. Yarborough III (Asheville NC); 3 sisters incl Virginia Guest Valentine, Laetitia Guest Oppenheim, Elizabeth Guest Stevens; brother Achille Murat Guest (Fredericksburg). (Yale '64 In Memoriam; Richmond Times-Dispatch obit 2001; Wikipedia) [Stage 6Y-276 from Yale '64 In Memoriam, Chris Getman remembrance]: Yale '64 classmate Chris Getman noted Andy 'devoted his life to conservation and the environment.' Getman's characterization: 'A fighter all his life.' Getman quote: 'Andy is the only person in history to have a national park named after him while still living.' Note: Getman calls it 'National Park' but the official designation is Virginia STATE Park (Shenandoah River Raymond R. Andy Guest Jr. State Park). Getman gives 26 years in legislature; Wikipedia/Times-Dispatch obit give 28 years (1972-2000, 7 terms) — using 28. Quote from his retirement floor speech: 'I don't know how to say goodbye and I'm not going to' — both sides of the aisle wept openly.

notable.notable_blurb: Virginia delegate and House minority leader

death.cause: cancer (non-Hodgkin lymphoma); died at Rock Hill Farm

landmarks.landmark_blurb: South fork of the Shenandoah, Warren County

military_service.note: Took year off from Yale to serve in Marine Corps Reserves between Yale Class of 1963 and Class of 1964 (graduated with latter). Cold War era; no specific war. Proudly sported Marine Corps tattoo on upper arm.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-eight years, and six leading
narrative_blocks.body: He sat for Warren County in the Virginia House of Delegates for seven terms, from 1972 to 2000, and led the Republican minority from 1985 to 1991, when it still held few seats in Richmond.

narrative_blocks.header: He voted from chemotherapy isolation
narrative_blocks.body: He lost thirty-five days of the 1994 session to chemotherapy, so the legislature rigged a way for him to watch the floor and vote from his hospital bed. He sponsored four bills and budget amendments from isolation.

narrative_blocks.header: A state park named for him, still living
narrative_blocks.body: Virginia named a state park for him in 1995 — the Shenandoah River Andy Guest Jr. State Park, on the south fork near his Rock Hill Farm. He and Mary Scott left three and a half miles of its riverfront to the state under easement.

narrative_blocks.header: His 1988 bill built Colonial Downs
narrative_blocks.body: He carried the pari-mutuel betting bill of 1988 that brought thoroughbred racing back to Virginia and built Colonial Downs. The paddock there carries his name, with a bronze figure of him beside it.

narrative_blocks.header: A Bessemer board seat, and a farm
narrative_blocks.body: He sat on the boards of Bessemer Trust and Bessemer Securities, the firms his great-grandfather Henry Phipps founded, and farmed at Rock Hill otherwise. He had grown up at Carter's Grove, the 1755 plantation on the James.

narrative_blocks.header: He got a clinic built in Warren County
narrative_blocks.body: He sat on the board of Warren Memorial Hospital and was the moving force behind St. Luke's Community Clinic. The Ruritan Club, the Izaak Walton League and the Elks all had him on their rolls.

narrative_blocks.header: Six months given, and five years taken
narrative_blocks.body: He was told in 1996 that non-Hodgkin lymphoma left him six months, and took a stem-cell transplant he reckoned bought five more years. He died at Rock Hill Farm in April 2001, at sixty-one, still carrying his Marine Corps tattoo.

people.research_notes: b. Apr 18, 1941 Worcester MA; d. May 23, 2019 Greenville SC age 78 (at the Woodlands at Furman). Daughter of Butler Carson Derrick Sr. and Mary Scott Derrick. Grew up in Johnston SC. Queens College (music); University of South Carolina (English and Law). Boards: Piccolo Spoleto Festival; College of the Building Arts. President Sea Pines Corporation. One of the earliest female stockbrokers at Harris, Upham & Co. m. Raymond R. 'Andy' Guest Jr. (HD5053). Son William G. Yarborough (Greenville SC); 3 grandchildren Evelyn 'Ellie', William 'Will', Mary Carson 'Casey' (all of Asheville NC). After Andy's 2001 death, moved Charleston SC → Palm Beach FL → Greenville SC. Sister: Ambassador Rita Derrick Hayes (Sullivan's Island SC). (Obituary 2019)

narrative_blocks.header: One of the first women on that floor
narrative_blocks.body: She was among the earliest women taken on as a stockbroker by Harris, Upham and Company, and later ran the Sea Pines Corporation as its president. In between she ran political campaigns and lobbied for the causes she cared about.

narrative_blocks.header: Music at Queens, then law at Carolina
narrative_blocks.body: She read music at Queens College and went on to English and law at the University of South Carolina. She sat on the boards of the Piccolo Spoleto Festival and the American College of the Building Arts.

narrative_blocks.header: A brother in Congress, a sister an ambassador
narrative_blocks.body: Her father Butler Carson Derrick ran an insurance agency at Johnston and chaired the university's scholarship foundation after commanding as a lieutenant commander in the war. Her brother Butler went to Congress and her sister Rita became an ambassador.

people.research_notes: b. Aug 3, 1944. Son of Alice Potter Polk Rutherfurd (HD5052) and Winthrop Chanler Rutherfurd Jr. (X02880). Grandfathers: Winthrop Chanler Rutherfurd Sr. (X02881, easter-egg) and Frank Lyon Polk (HD5047, first U.S. Under Secretary of State). Great-grandfather Levi P. Morton, U.S. Vice President under Benjamin Harrison and Governor of New York. Princeton 1966 (BA East Asian Studies). Harvard MBA (with distinction, Graduate School of Business). Set up Inter-Asia Venture Management Ltd in Hong Kong 1972 — first fund raised $1 million, completed 15 investments. 1974: expanded McDonald's into Hong Kong. 1989: Managing Director Royal Trust Enterprise Capital Hong Kong. As of March 2016: Co-founder + Managing Director Inter-Asia Venture Management. Former Governor + Vice President American Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong. Advisory Board Princeton in Asia. Former trustee Berkshire School. Past Co-Chairman + executive committee Hong Kong Venture Capital Association. Trustee Mary Wood Foundation. m1. Janet Jennings Auchincloss (X02883) Jul 30, 1966 — daughter of Hugh Dudley Auchincloss Jr. and Janet Norton Lee. Janet was the HALF-SISTER of Jacqueline Lee Bouvier Kennedy Onassis (and Lee Radziwill). Through marriage, Lewis was brother-in-law to former First Lady Jackie Kennedy. Janet died of cancer Mar 13, 1985. They had three children — Lewis Stuyvesant, Andrew Hugh Auchincloss, Alexandra. m2. Katharine duPont Sanger (X02884) Jun 10, 1989 — granddaughter of Lammot du Pont II. Divorced 1994. (Wikipedia; American Aristocracy) [Stage 6Y-277 from Grokipedia & expanded sources]: Second of FIVE children (siblings Winthrop III, Alice, Linda, James). Inter-Asia Venture Management Ltd in Hong Kong founded 1972 with co-founder/partner CYRIL FUNG. Initial fund $1M; firm now oversees FIVE private equity funds focused on China, India, Thailand, Singapore, Indonesia. 2015: At age 70 completed DOCTOR OF BUSINESS ADMINISTRATION from City University of Hong Kong; doctoral thesis on pre-deal processes in Asian venture capital funds 1980-2000. Maintains ties to US but resides primarily in Hong Kong. Advisory roles and trusteeships including Mary Wood Foundation. Wedding venue refined: married Janet Auchincloss Jul 30, 1966 at St. Mary's Roman Catholic Church in Newport RI — same church where Jackie Bouvier married JFK in 1953. Reception for 600 at family estate. NBs rebuilt 081126. Two came out: 'Founded Inter-Asia Venture Management, Hong Kong 1972' (absorbed into the new NB1) and 'Married Jackie Kennedy's half-sister Janet Auchincloss', which restated the marriage array. Superseded text: [career] Founded Inter-Asia Venture Management, Hong Kong 1972 — Lewis Polk Rutherfurd moved to Hong Kong after his 1966 marriage and founded Inter-Asia Venture Management Ltd in 1972 — raising $1 million for his first fund and completing fifteen investments. In 1974 he led the expansion of McDonald's into Hong Kong. He has remained co-founder and Managing Director of the firm for over fifty years, serving also as Vice President of the American Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong. | [marriage] Married Jackie Kennedy's half-sister Janet Auchincloss — On July 30, 1966 Lewis married Janet Jennings Auchincloss — the half-sister of First Lady Jacqueline Lee Bouvier Kennedy Onassis. They had three children before Janet's death from cancer in 1985 at age forty. The marriage made him brother-in-law to Jackie Kennedy through her mother Janet Lee Auchincloss Bouvier's second marriage to Hugh Auchincloss. | [achievement] Earned Doctor of Business Administration at age 70 — In 2015 at age 70, Lewis Polk Rutherfurd completed a Doctor of Business Administration at City University of Hong Kong. His thesis examined pre-deal processes in Asian venture capital funds from 1980 to 2000 — drawing on his own four decades pioneering the field. Inter-Asia Venture Management now oversees five private equity funds focused on China, India, Thailand, Singapore, and Indonesia. His father Winthrop Rutherfurd Jr. was president of Coast Metals, Little Ferry, New Jersey. Advisory board of Princeton in Asia; former trustee of Berkshire School; trustee of the Mary Wood Foundation.

narrative_blocks.header: He took McDonald's into Hong Kong in 1974
narrative_blocks.body: He set up Inter-Asia Venture Management in Hong Kong in 1972 and it went on to complete fifteen investments. Two years in, it brought McDonald's to the colony.

narrative_blocks.header: East Asian Studies at Princeton, then Hong Kong
narrative_blocks.body: He read East Asian Studies at Princeton, took an MBA with distinction from Harvard, and went to Hong Kong and stayed. He was a governor and vice-president of the American Chamber of Commerce there, and co-chaired the Hong Kong Venture Capital Association.

narrative_blocks.header: A doctorate in business at seventy
narrative_blocks.body: In 2015, at seventy, he completed a Doctor of Business Administration at City University of Hong Kong — forty-nine years after the Princeton degree.

narrative_blocks.header: Two grandfathers and a Vice President
narrative_blocks.body: He was the grandson, on his mother's side, of Frank L. Polk, Wilson's Under Secretary of State and the named founder of Davis Polk & Wardwell, and on his father's side of Winthrop Rutherfurd. Levi P. Morton, governor of New York and Vice President under Benjamin Harrison, was his great-grandfather.

narrative_blocks.header: She left Newport for Hong Kong at twenty-one
narrative_blocks.body: She married in July 1966 and was in Hong Kong within months, teaching French at the Chinese University there until 1968. She stayed nineteen years, adviser and shareholder in the venture-capital firm her husband built, and came home only when the cancer was found.

narrative_blocks.header: She founded the League's first chapter abroad
narrative_blocks.body: In 1979 she helped start what was then the first overseas chapter of the League of Women Voters, in Hong Kong. She was still its honorary president when she died six years later.

narrative_blocks.header: She married at Jackie's altar, thirteen years on
narrative_blocks.body: On 30 July 1966 she married Lewis Polk Rutherfurd at St. Mary's in Newport — the church where her half-sister Jacqueline Bouvier had married Senator John F. Kennedy thirteen years before. John F. Kennedy Jr. was a page and Caroline a flower girl, and five thousand people came to look.

narrative_blocks.header: A thousand guests, and Newport dressed as Venice
narrative_blocks.body: For her coming-out at Hammersmith Farm in August 1963 the lawns were dressed as a Venetian garden: pink marquees on gondola poles, the band in gondolier costume behind a thirty-foot gondola. More than a thousand came, seven ambassadors and two senators among them, and the Kennedys sent the bouquet she carried.

narrative_blocks.header: Jackie was at the bedside at the end
narrative_blocks.body: Lung cancer was found in August 1984 and moved to her brain and pancreas. She died at Dana-Farber in Boston at thirty-nine with her half-sister beside her, and after the funeral at Trinity Church, Newport, Jacqueline Onassis rode to the grave with Lee Radziwill.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven children, four marriages, one household
narrative_blocks.body: A Christmas photograph from about 1950 shows the whole blended house: Lee and Jackie from her mother's first marriage, Nina, Hugh and Tommy from her father's earlier two, and Janet and Jamie from the marriage that joined them. She was named for her mother and called Janet Jr.

narrative_blocks.header: A duPont granddaughter who sold sailboards
narrative_blocks.body: She was a granddaughter of Lammot duPont, president and chairman of E. I. du Pont de Nemours, and a daughter of Reynolds duPont, a Delaware state senator and president pro tem. She ran Windsurfing of Sanibel, a Florida sailboard and sportswear shop.

narrative_blocks.header: Janet's sons were his best men
narrative_blocks.body: When she married Lewis Rutherfurd on Fishers Island in June 1989, his sons by Janet Auchincloss served as his best men and his daughter Alexandra was flower girl for her stepmother. Her own two sons escorted her up the aisle.

people.research_notes: b. May 6, 1875 Demopolis, Marengo County, AL (mother Ida Lyon's hometown); d. Mar 29, 1904 NYC age 28. YOUNGER son of William Mecklenburg Polk (HD2601) and Ida Ashe Lyon (X01884); younger brother of Frank Lyon Polk (HD5047). Grandson of Bishop Leonidas Polk. Yale Sheffield Scientific School class of 1896 — Vice-President University Club, Class Committee member at graduation. Cornell University Medical School MD 1899. Intern at Bellevue Hospital (Medical Side) 1899-1901. Studied pathology and medical diagnosis in Vienna 1902. January 1903: Instructor in Medicine and Physical Diagnosis at Cornell Medical College (his father's institution); also Adjunct Assistant Visiting Physician to Bellevue Hospital. Research focus: blood changes from infectious diseases, particularly influenza and the pneumonias associated with influenza. Death circumstances: while performing an autopsy he became chilled; acute pneumonia developed within hours; died March 29, 1904 at age 28. Buried Woodlawn Cemetery, Bronx NY (same cemetery as elder brother Frank Lyon Polk later). DISTINCT FROM HD5048 John Metcalfe Polk (1908-1948), who is the nephew of this John, named for him — son of Frank Lyon Polk (HD5047). Two John Metcalfe Polks, uncle and nephew, in the same Hooker line. (Yale University Obituary Record for John Metcalfe Polk; FindAGrave)

birth.notes: The Yale class record gives Demopolis; FamilySearch gives New York City.

death.cause: acute pneumonia developed within hours of becoming chilled while performing an autopsy

cross_connections.display_label: was his nephew, born four years after he died and given his name

narrative_blocks.header: The pneumonia he studied is what killed him
narrative_blocks.body: He had come back from Vienna interested in what influenza does to the blood, and in the pneumonias that follow it, and had a paper on the subject in the medical school's annual volume. He caught a chill at an autopsy in March 1904, acute pneumonia came on within hours, and he was dead in days.

narrative_blocks.header: He took his degree at his father’s school
narrative_blocks.body: He went from the Sheffield Scientific School to the medical college his father had opened in New York four years earlier, and took the M.D. there in 1899. Two years as an interne at Bellevue followed, then a year in Vienna reading pathology.

narrative_blocks.header: Fourteen months of teaching, and no more
narrative_blocks.body: He began as instructor in medicine and physical diagnosis at Cornell in January 1903, with a visiting appointment at Bellevue alongside it. He was dead the following March, in his twenty-ninth year.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother gave the name to a son
narrative_blocks.body: Four years after he died, Frank Lyon Polk named a first son John Metcalfe Polk. That nephew, who never knew him, carried the name until 1948.

career.role: Instructor in medicine and physical diagnosis

marriages.notes: Second wife of Wm M Polk (after Ida Lyon's 1912 death). No children. Maria outlived husband by 23 years.

people.research_notes: b. Sep 29, 1857 Flushing, Queens County NY; d. Feb 8, 1941 Manhattan NY age 83 — extraordinary longevity. Married Dr. William Mecklenburg Polk (HD2601) as his SECOND wife after the 1912 death of his first wife Ida Ashe Lyon Polk (X01884). No children with William. Widowed 1918 at age 60-61. Buried Mount Auburn Cemetery, Cambridge MA — strikingly NOT in the Polk family Woodlawn Cemetery plot in the Bronx (where Wm Mecklenburg, Ida, and the deceased Polk sons are buried). The separate burial suggests she had her own family ties to the Boston/Cambridge area through the Dehon family. Dehon family was a prominent New York/Boston family — likely connected to the Boston Episcopal Bishop Theodore Dehon line. (FindAGrave)

narrative_blocks.header: Leon died young

b. Oct 26, 1873 (some sources 1872) New Orleans LA; d. Dec 6, 1926 New Orleans age 53. Son of Confederate surgeon Joseph Jones (X00877) and Susan Rayner Polk (HD2599). Tulane University academic course; Tulane Medical Department MD 1894. Career on Tulane medical faculty: assistant to Professor of Chemistry and Medical Jurisprudence (before grad), Assistant Demonstrator in Chemistry, Demonstrator in Chemistry, Instructor in Clinical Medicine. Charity Hospital New Orleans visiting physician and surgeon from 1894. 1897: Resident physician at the Isolation Hospital, old Beauregard School, New Orleans. SPANISH-AMERICAN WAR 1898: Acting Assistant Surgeon U.S.A. at field hospital Santiago Cuba; after yellow fever outbreak placed in charge of 'JONES' YELLOW FEVER HOSPITAL' (named for him) for all soldiers outside Santiago to Sept 1898. Executive officer First Division Hospital Montauk Point Sept-Oct 1898. Served May-Oct 1898. Recommended to Congress for brevet. 1905: In charge of yellow fever emergency hospital at New Orleans as physician-in-chief. 1910-11: Louisiana State Analyst; then 1 year as Food Commissioner. U.S. government expert on blood/blood pressure and authority on nutrition (significant bleached flour case). Chemical and bacteriological expert in important private litigation. Publications: 'Reports on Yellow Fever Hospitals'; 'Medical and Surgical Notes on the Spanish-American War'; 'Reports on Chemical and Microscopical studies of water of Lake Pontchartrain'; similar Bayou Teche studies; 'Medical Aspects of Exophthalmic Goitre.' Member Orleans Parish, Louisiana State, American, and Southern Medical Associations. Secretary Orleans Parish Medical Association. Democrat. m. Caroline Elizabeth Merrick (X02886) Jun 25, 1901. 1 son: Joseph Merrick Jones Sr (HD5062, 1903-1963, notable Tulane Board president). Buried Lafayette Cemetery #1, New Orleans. [Stage 6Y-280]: Notable status confirmed by Sam. Tulane Med faculty, eponym of 'Jones' Yellow Fever Hospital' Santiago Cuba 1898, recommended to Congress for brevet, LA State Analyst/Food Commissioner.

narrative_blocks.header: The fever hospital at Santiago took his name
narrative_blocks.body: When yellow fever broke out among the American troops outside Santiago in 1898, he was put in charge of every fever case beyond the city, and the place was known as the Jones Yellow Fever Hospital. He was recommended to Congress for brevet.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the fever hospital at home too
narrative_blocks.body: In 1905 he was physician-in-chief of the yellow fever emergency hospital at New Orleans, eight years after serving as resident physician at the isolation hospital in the old Beauregard school.

narrative_blocks.header: He never left Tulane or Charity Hospital
narrative_blocks.body: He entered the Tulane medical department in 1894 and was a visiting physician and surgeon at Charity Hospital from the day he graduated, working up from assistant demonstrator of chemistry to instructor of clinical medicine.

narrative_blocks.header: He testified on bleached flour and blood
narrative_blocks.body: The federal government used him as an expert on blood and blood pressure and on nutrition in the case over bleached flour, and private litigants hired him as a chemical and bacteriological witness.

narrative_blocks.header: He was asked why the fish were dying
narrative_blocks.body: As state analyst from 1910 and food commissioner after it, he studied the water of Lake Pontchartrain and Bayou Teche to find what was killing the fish in numbers, and published what he found.

David Thomas Merrick — Confederate Civil War officer; struck by minié ball entering side of head from right ear, passing over cavity of mouth, exiting lobe of left ear; recovered with near loss of hearing. Paternal grandfather: Chief Justice Edwin Thomas Merrick Sr. (1809-1897) — Louisiana Supreme Court Chief Justice for 10 years before the Civil War, re-elected under the Confederacy. Paternal grandmother: CAROLINE ELIZABETH THOMAS MERRICK (1825-1908) — prominent suffragist, temperance leader, author; President of Louisiana Women's Christian Temperance Union; organized first women's suffrage association in Louisiana (Portia Club, 1892, 9 charter members); President of Louisiana State Woman Suffrage Association 1896; first woman of Louisiana to speak publicly in behalf of her sex (1879 State convention); helped secure article in Louisiana Constitution making women over 21 eligible for public school office. Represented Louisiana at Woman's International Council Washington DC 1888 and at Woman's Suffrage Association convention same year. Great-grandfather: Capt. David Thomas of Cottage Hall Plantation East Feliciana Parish — Battle of New Orleans veteran, trustee of Centenary College (later Centenary College of the Methodist Episcopal Church South). narrative_blocks.header: She was named for a Louisiana suffragist
narrative_blocks.body: Her grandmother Caroline Elizabeth Merrick was the first woman in Louisiana to speak publicly on behalf of women, addressed the state convention in 1879, and helped win the article making women over twenty-one eligible for school office.

narrative_blocks.header: The grandmother married at fifteen
narrative_blocks.body: Caroline Merrick was fifteen when she married Edwin Thomas Merrick, a jurist of thirty-seven who became chief justice of the Louisiana supreme court, and she gave the first twenty years of that marriage to her children before taking up temperance and suffrage.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at forty-eight, she lasted to ninety-four
narrative_blocks.body: Hamilton Polk Jones died in 1926 and she did not marry again, living another forty-seven years at New Orleans and outliving her only son by ten.

narrative_blocks.body: She trained at Sophie Newcomb College in New Orleans, then under Howard Pyle in Delaware, whose other pupils included Maxfield Parrish and Jessie Willcox Smith, and finished at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts.

narrative_blocks.body: By 1907 she was in Philadelphia and teaching. She worked in sculpture, crafts and decoration and exhibited with the Philadelphia Art Alliance, the National Association of Women Artists and the Pennsylvania Academy.

narrative_blocks.body: She married Henry Usher Hall at Philadelphia in 1921, at fifty, and was known in the art world afterward as Mrs Harry Usher Hall.

narrative_blocks.header: She nursed the bush and he thanked her
narrative_blocks.body: She went with her husband to Sierra Leone in 1936 and spent six months tending the sick and maimed, managing the supplies, and collecting stories from the Sherbro women. He credited her in print with winning the expedition its trust.

narrative_blocks.header: Her Shenge watercolor came out of that trip
narrative_blocks.body: The watercolor of palm oil being prepared at Shenge dates from 1937, the year she spent in the chiefdom, and hangs now at the Delaware Art Museum. She kept a diary of the journey and copied down four Sherbro recipes.

narrative_blocks.header: He went down the Yenisei in 1914
narrative_blocks.body: He joined Maria Czaplicka on her 1914 expedition down the Yenisei River to the Kara Sea, the first anthropological expedition a woman ever led. The ornithologist Maud Haviland and the artist Dora Curtis went with them.

narrative_blocks.header: He built the museum’s African section
narrative_blocks.body: He was assistant curator and then curator of general ethnology at the University of Pennsylvania Museum from 1915 to 1935, and it was he who established its African collections.

narrative_blocks.header: He dug in the Dordogne in 1923
narrative_blocks.body: He had a standing interest in prehistoric archaeology and excavated in the Dordogne in the summer of 1923 as a student of the American School of Prehistoric Research, following it with special work in London ten years later.

narrative_blocks.header: The museum laid him off and rehired him
narrative_blocks.body: Museum finances cost him his post in 1935, and the next year it re-employed him to lead an expedition to West Africa, paid for in part by selling off African objects it held as duplicates.

narrative_blocks.header: He and Frances lived among the Sherbro
narrative_blocks.body: From December 1936 to May 1937 the two of them lived on Sherbro Island and in the Shenge chiefdom, he gathering ethnography and objects while she nursed the sick and took down stories from the women.

narrative_blocks.header: His report opened the Poro society
narrative_blocks.body: He published The Sherbro of Sierra Leone in 1938, a report on the expedition that carried an account of the Poro, the secret society of the Sherbro men.

Mar 11, 1963 Metairie LA age 59 of apparent heart attack at Ochsner Foundation Hospital — upon learning of his wife's death by asphyxiation in pre-dawn house fire that destroyed their Metairie home that morning. ARSON SUSPECTED BUT NEVER PROVEN. Son of Dr. Hamilton Polk Jones (HD5059) and Caroline Elizabeth Merrick Jones (X02886). Maternal great-grandson of Louisiana suffragist Caroline E. Thomas Merrick. Maternal great-great-grandson of Battle of New Orleans veteran Capt. David Thomas. Paternal grandson of Confederate surgeon Joseph Jones and Susan Polk Jones. Paternal great-grandson of Bishop Leonidas Polk. TULANE graduate; admitted to LA bar. Senior partner Jones, Flanders & Waechter (founded); reorganized 1937 → eventually JONES, WALKER, WAECHTER, POITEVENT, CARRÈRE & DENÈGRE L.L.P. (still one of the South's leading law firms). WWII: Too old to enlist (was 38 at Pearl Harbor). Joined State Department 1942. Wrote speech sections for Dean Acheson, Secretary of State George C. Marshall, and President Harry S. Truman in support of the Marshall Plan. 1946: ASSISTANT SECRETARY OF STATE FOR PUBLIC AFFAIRS (closing months of WWII). Active supporter of Marshall Plan. 1948: Returned to Louisiana law practice. Fellow of Yale University Department of Political Science; editor of Fortune magazine; special consultant to the United Nations. 1947: Joined Board of Administrators of Tulane Educational Fund. Became its president, served until death. EARLY 1963: ANNOUNCED TULANE WOULD ADMIT BLACK STUDENTS beginning the spring semester. The house fire that killed him and his wife occurred soon after. Arson was suspected but never proven. Garden District residence, New Orleans. m. Eugenie Elizabeth Penick (X02888) Nov 27, 1928 New Orleans. Both died March 11, 1963 in the same fire. 3 children: Joseph Merrick Jones Jr (Canal Barge Lines vice president, thoroughbred horse owner of notable horses including Chou Croute; not yet built); Eugenie Penick Jones Huger (HD5063, b.1932 d.2011, m. Killian Loew Huger Jr); Susan Jones (m. H. Merritt Lane Jr; not yet built). (Wikipedia; Grokipedia; FindAGrave) [Stage 6Y-280 additional context per NY Times 1963 obituary]: FOUNDED CANAL BARGE COMPANY 1933 in New Orleans with other investors, starting with one barge. (Company by 1990s grew to 26 vessels including 800-7200hp towboats, offshore supply vessel, two 7,500-ton tankships, ~525 barges.) President of CANAL BARGE LINES at his death. President of the NATIONAL WATERWAYS CONFERENCE — organization set up by the towboat industry to fight Federal user charges on the waterways. Past president of the Bureau of Governmental Research of New Orleans. Past president of the New Orleans Bar Association. FORMER KING OF CARNIVAL (Mardi Gras Rex). Jones Walker law firm 1933 founding paralleled Canal Barge Company 1933 founding — same year. His son Joseph Merrick Jones Jr (HD5064) succeeded him as Canal Barge Company president 1963 and served as Chairman 40 years; inducted into National Rivers Hall of Fame.

HUGER SURNAME MARRIAGE: Killian Huger Jr.'s parents Arthur Middleton Huger (1877-1924) and Jeanne Nathalie Charbonnet Huger (1879-1945) are NOT in our Hooker tree. They likely descend from the broader Charleston Huger family (the 'Middleton' middle name suggests common ancestry with Col. John Middleton Huger — father of Wm Elliott Huger who married HD2600 Elizabeth Polk Huger). If Arthur Middleton Huger and Wm Elliott Huger were cousins, Eugenie's marriage to Killian put her into the SAME Huger family that her great-great-aunt Elizabeth Polk Huger (HD2600) had married into 89 years earlier. This is a Hooker-tree-orbit Huger re-marriage rather than a Hooker-line cousin marriage. b. ~1935 (age 66 at 2001 death); d. Sep 13, 2001 New Orleans LA of lengthy battle with heart and kidney disease. Son of Joseph Merrick Jones Sr (HD5062) and Eugenie Penick Jones (X02888). Parents both died March 11, 1963 in suspected-arson Metairie house fire when he was ~28. CANAL BARGE COMPANY: 40 years active service in the marine transportation business. Joined the company 1957 (founded 1933 by his father). Took the reins 1963 (after parents' deaths). Chairman of the Board. Under his leadership Canal Barge grew to one of the most successful product movers on the river including 'project' cargoes. Company milestones included industry's first all-welded steel tank barge (1933), the revolutionary m/v Bull Calf (1939) that became model for WWII landing craft, the industry's first integrated tank barge tow (1947), and first high-speed integrated tow and towboat dedicated to liquid chemicals (1957). INDUCTED into the NATIONAL RIVERS HALL OF FAME (River Museum, Dubuque IA) — Achievement Award winner. HORSE RACING: Started mid-1960s. Co-owned with E.V. (Tony) Benjamin III, Isidore Newman II, and Sam Israel Jr. the 1972 champion sprinter CHOU CROUTE. She beat the speedy Icecapade in the Fall Highweight Handicap at Belmont Park 1972 (same year Secretariat was Horse of the Year as a 2-year-old). She won 5 other stakes + placed in 4 others that year. Career: 18 wins of 28 starts. INDUCTED INTO THE FAIR GROUNDS RACING HALL OF FAME 2000. Also co-owned millionaire MANNDAR — won 2000 Manhattan Handicap (gr. IT) and Woodford Reserve Turf Classic Stakes (gr. IT); ran second in Arlington Million (gr. IT). Trainer Albert Stall Jr. quote: 'He was the easiest guy to train for, a good man who always put the horses first. I had horses from him since Day One I started training in 1991.' Siblings: Eugenie Penick Jones Huger (HD5063, m. Killian Loew Huger Jr); Susan Jones m. H. Merritt Lane Jr (not built). (National Rivers Hall of Fame; Bloodhorse obituary Sept 13 2001; NY Times 1963 fire coverage)

narrative_blocks.body: He joined his father’s Canal Barge Company in 1957 and was running it by 1963, the year the Metairie fire killed both his parents. He chaired the board for the next thirty-eight years.

people.research_notes: b. Dec 6, 1805 Coates GA; d. Mar 11, 1898 Oxford MS age 92 — extraordinary longevity. Son of Peyton Skipwith Sr. and Cornelia Greene. MATERNAL GRANDSON of Major General Nathanael Greene (1742-1786) — Revolutionary War hero, second in command to George Washington, commander of the Southern Department who turned the tide against Cornwallis. Pre-Civil War: rice plantation on Crooked River, Georgia; cotton thread business; commission merchant in New Orleans until the war. 1860 census (New Orleans Ward 2, Orleans LA): SLAVEHOLDER of 18 enslaved persons per the U.S. Slave Schedule. Post-war: moved to Oxford, Mississippi as a mercantile merchant. m. Frances Devereux Polk (HD2596) Nov 13, 1866 Maury County TN — her first marriage, his second (his first wife had died). 2 children with Frances: Katherine Anderson 'Kate' Skipwith (HD5065, 1867-1961), Francis Polk 'Frank' Skipwith (HD5066, 1872-1926). Widowed 1884 (Frances d. age 48); Peyton outlived her by 14 years. Buried Oxford Memorial Cemetery, Oxford MS. [LIBERIA SKIPWITH PARALLEL — significant context]: A separate Peyton Skipwith (1800-?) — a Black man emancipated by Virginia planter John Hartwell Cocke in 1833 and sent to Monrovia, Liberia with his wife and six children — wrote a celebrated series of letters to Cocke (1834-1846+ at University of Virginia Library) that are foundational documents in African American emigration history. That enslaved Peyton Skipwith likely took his master's family name as was the practice; he is unrelated by blood to our Peyton Horatio Skipwith but the surname connection traces both to the broader Virginia Skipwith planter network that both employed and named enslaved persons after themselves. Our Peyton Horatio (white) owned 18 enslaved persons in 1860; the parallel Peyton Skipwith (Black) was emancipated and emigrated to Liberia — these two threads embody very different sides of the antebellum Skipwith story. (FindAGrave; WikiTree; 1860 Slave Schedule)

narrative_blocks.header: Born on a rice plantation, grandson to Greene
narrative_blocks.body: He was born in December 1805 on a rice plantation on the Crooked River in Georgia, grandson of Major General Nathanael Greene through his mother Cornelia and great-grandson of Sir Peyton Skipwith of Virginia.

narrative_blocks.header: Skipwith Hall kept a room for the coffins
narrative_blocks.body: His mother Cornelia Greene and her second husband built Skipwith Hall in Maury County in 1815, the first house in the county with a piano and with a room where the family coffins were kept on show. He and his brother George inherited it in 1836.

narrative_blocks.header: The bank took Skipwith Hall, then the plantation
narrative_blocks.body: In Tennessee he and George manufactured cotton thread, and by 1849 George had signed Skipwith Hall over to the Planters Bank. The next spring their Mississippi cotton plantation at Skipwith’s Landing was advertised for sale as well.

narrative_blocks.header: In 1860 he held eighteen enslaved people
narrative_blocks.body: By then he was a commission merchant in New Orleans, and the slave schedule of 1860 records eighteen enslaved people held by him in the second ward.

narrative_blocks.header: Another Peyton Skipwith wrote from Monrovia
narrative_blocks.body: A Black man of the same name, enslaved by the Virginia planter John Hartwell Cocke and freed to Liberia in 1833, wrote a celebrated series of letters home from Monrovia. He carried the name because the Virginia Skipwiths gave their surname to the people they held.

narrative_blocks.header: The carriage step killed him at ninety-two
narrative_blocks.body: He helped form the first Episcopal congregation in Tennessee, at Nashville, and was the last of its nine members alive. The oldest citizen of Oxford, he died in March 1898 of a fall taken getting out of his carriage the evening before.
