narrative_blocks.header: Pierpont name reached fifth generation, died at twenty-eight
narrative_blocks.body: George Pierpont Brockett carried the Pierpont name into the fifth generation of the Brockett-Hooker line — honoring great-great-great-grandmother Mary Pierpont, the granddaughter of Rev. Thomas Hooker through whom the family's Hooker descent runs. He died September 3, 1892 at age twenty-eight. The line did not continue through him.

people.research_notes: b. Jun 11, 1865 East Orange NJ; d. 1929. Second child of Edward Judson Brockett (HD1531) and Mary Frances Gault (I01288). EDUCATION: East Orange High School + Eastman Business College Poughkeepsie NY. CAREER: Brown Brothers & Co. (banking, NYC) 3 years → National Lead Trust (in which his father was interested) 12 years rising to positions of responsibility. Health impaired; spent time in travel; then devoted himself to church work and literary labor. GENEALOGY RESEARCH: 'During the last three years he has spent much of his time in research for the preparation of this volume' [The Brockett Genealogy] — he was the on-the-ground research partner for father Edward Judson's 1905 magnum opus. RELIGION: Vestryman of St. Paul's Church East Orange NJ for many years (Episcopal — note shift from father's Baptist). m. Oct 8, 1890 in Grace Church by Rev. Alex. Allen to Margaret Whitney (I01289), daughter of James A. and Eliza Crear Whitney of St. John NB Canada. Two daughters: Alice Whitney Brockett (HD5079, 1891) and Elisabeth Gault Brockett (HD5080, 1894). Sources: The Descendants of John Brockett 1905; 1910 Census East Orange NJ.

narrative_blocks.header: Brown Brothers banker, then National Lead executive
narrative_blocks.body: Francis Edward Brockett began at the Banking House of Brown Brothers & Company in New York City for three years after Eastman Business College, then moved to the National Lead Trust in which his father held interests — staying twelve years and filling positions of growing responsibility. When his health failed he traveled, then returned to East Orange to devote himself to church work and literary labor. He shifted denominations to Episcopal, becoming a vestryman of St. Paul's Church East Orange for many years.

narrative_blocks.header: Spent three years researching father's Brockett Genealogy
narrative_blocks.body: In the early 1900s Francis Edward devoted three years specifically to genealogical research for his father Edward Judson Brockett's 1905 family genealogy — serving as the on-the-ground research partner for the magnum opus that documents the Hooker-Brockett descent line. Known as 'of a genial disposition, winning the friendship of those with whom he becomes acquainted,' he outlived his father by ten years.

people.research_notes: b. Jul 2, 1869 New Jersey; d. 1955 age ~85. Third child of Edward Judson Brockett (HD1531) and Mary Frances Gault (I01288). narrative_blocks.header: DAR member entered on records of seven ancestors
narrative_blocks.body: By 1905, when Edith was thirty-six and still unmarried, she was an active member of the Daughters of the American Revolution 'having entered on the records of seven ancestors' — an unusually high number. She had received a liberal education, traveled abroad, and was 'fond of historical research,' the genealogy-research instinct her father exemplified passed along in her own scholarly direction. She married a Quattlebaum later, lived to about eighty-five, and died in 1955.

narrative_blocks.header: Baptized with his brother Pierpont in 1810
narrative_blocks.body: In 1810 the Baptist evangelist Joshua Bradley came through North Haven, and Jesse and his younger brother Pierpont were converted and baptized together. They became the core of the town's new Baptist church; Pierpont went into the ministry for forty-one years, and Jesse stayed on as its deacon.

narrative_blocks.header: A lieutenant in 1812, captain in 1815
narrative_blocks.body: Jesse held a lieutenant's commission in the Connecticut militia when war with Britain broke out in 1812, and was made captain in 1815. Pierpont served too, as ensign and then lieutenant at Groton and New London.

narrative_blocks.header: Deacon, justice and three-term legislator
narrative_blocks.body: For many years Jesse was North Haven's justice of the peace, and the town sent him to the General Assembly in 1829 and 1830, and again in 1839.

narrative_blocks.header: Died of paralysis in November 1881, unmarried
narrative_blocks.body: Antoinette Brockett never married. She died in November 1881 at age sixty-six of paralysis — likely a stroke given the era's medical terminology, where 'paralysis' covered both stroke aftermath and progressive nerve disease. Born in 1815 just as her father Jesse was being promoted from War of 1812 Lieutenant to postwar Captain in the Connecticut militia, she lived the full sixty-six-year arc of antebellum-through-Reconstruction Connecticut, dying as the Gilded Age began.

people.research_notes: b. Aug 3, 1817; d. Apr 7, 1892 Yaphank Long Island NY age 74. Son of Jesse Brockett (HD5085) and Anna Taintor (I01290). MARRIAGE: m. narrative_blocks.header: From farm papers to his own garden
narrative_blocks.body: William wrote for Hearth and Home and other agricultural papers in New York. Around 1880 he left the city for Orient, at the far end of Long Island's North Fork, and took up gardening himself.

narrative_blocks.header: Three children lost in six years
narrative_blocks.body: William married Helen Brewer on 17 October 1846, while living at Chicopee, Massachusetts, and they soon moved to New York. There they lost three of their four children: Helen Josephine at five and Emma at eight days, both in 1854, and Ada at eleven months in 1860. Only Clarence grew up.

narrative_blocks.header: No Baptist church at Orient
narrative_blocks.body: A member of a Baptist church in New York, William found none at Orient and worshipped with the Congregationalists there. He died on 7 April 1892, at seventy-four, at Yaphank, where his son Clarence was living.

Buried at the Adrian Dominican Sisters Cemetery, Adrian Michigan. CHRONOLOGY FLAG: Father Merwin (1863-1921) and his documented wife Minnie Gilbert Andrews (1851-1909). Either Merwin remarried 1910-1913 (second wife not yet documented), or Priscilla was an out-of-wedlock daughter; without further source this is left as 'mother unknown.' birth.notes: Sound Beach, now Old Greenwich

narrative_blocks.header: A minister's granddaughter in a Dominican habit
narrative_blocks.body: Priscilla's grandfather Moses Porter Snell was a Protestant minister, and her father Merwin converted to Catholicism in 1895. Priscilla entered the Adrian Dominican Sisters in Michigan, took the name Sister Marie Virginia, and lies in the sisters' cemetery at Adrian.

narrative_blocks.header: At fifteen she wrote on educating women
narrative_blocks.body: Priscilla and her sister Margaret went to St. Joseph's Academy at Adrian, and in May 1929, at fifteen, she wrote to Charles Stimming of Loyola University Chicago on women's own engagement with religion and the need to educate women.

narrative_blocks.header: A convent in Puerto Rico
narrative_blocks.body: In 1947 and 1948 Sister Marie Virginia wrote home from a convent in Puerto Rico about her fellow nuns, her travels on the island and the life of the order. She died at Adrian on 11 February 2002, at eighty-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: Buffalo NY birth, Bluefield West Virginia death
narrative_blocks.body: Edgar Francis Root was born May 1, 1883 in Buffalo, Erie County New York — and died April 2, 1941 in Bluefield, Mercer County West Virginia at age fifty-seven. The Buffalo-to-Bluefield migration spanned a thousand miles and crossed two distinct American regions: the late-Gilded-Age industrial Northeast where his father William Alonzo had settled, and the early-twentieth-century Appalachian coal-and-rail South where he ended his life.

narrative_blocks.header: Died thirty days after her April marriage
narrative_blocks.body: Louisa Walter married Timothy Bishop on April 3, 1800 and died on May 3, 1800 at age nineteen — about thirty days after the marriage, with no children. The compressed marriage-and-death cycle within a single calendar month was striking even by the period's standards of vulnerability to acute disease. Her husband Timothy lived another seventy-three years and remarried twice.

narrative_blocks.header: Buried Grove Street Cemetery, New Haven
narrative_blocks.body: Louisa is buried at Grove Street Cemetery in New Haven, Plot 11 Cypress Avenue East. The cemetery — one of America's first planned burial grounds and a National Historic Landmark — became the family-burial cluster for the Walter-Pierpont line, with her parents William Jay Walter and Theodosia and several siblings later joining her there.

people.research_notes: Timothy Bishop. b. October 29, 1777 New Haven CT; d. March 6, 1873 New Haven CT age 95. Son of Captain Daniel Bishop. Member of Cong. Ch.; a successful merchant; director in the bank at age 91. Three marriages: m1 Louisa Walter (HD5099) April 3, 1800 — Louisa died May 3, 1800 about 30 days later with no children; m2 Esther Huggins (1778-1845) before 1845; m3 Elizabeth Beers (1790-1854) 1846. Two daughters survived to be named in records: Louisa W. Bishop (born May 24, 1804; m. Enos B. M. Hughes; d. Oct 6, 1872) and Mary H. Bishop (b. Sep 1, 1805; m. Louis Xavier Huder; d. 1859) — both apparently from m2 to Esther Huggins. Source: FindAGrave 131910709, FamilySearch.

narrative_blocks.header: First wife died thirty days after wedding
narrative_blocks.body: Timothy Bishop's first wife Louisa Walter married him on April 3, 1800 and died on May 3, 1800 — about thirty days later, at age nineteen. Timothy was twenty-three at the time. He went on to remarry twice and live another seventy-three years, dying at age ninety-five.

narrative_blocks.header: Bank director at age ninety-one
narrative_blocks.body: Timothy Bishop was a successful New Haven merchant and member of the Congregational Church. He served as a bank director at age ninety-one — still active in business governance four years before his death. The late-life professional engagement was characteristic of a Connecticut merchant patriarch who outlived three wives.

Walter (HD5103, 1812-1831), Lavinia Walter (HD5104, 1814-1815 died_in_infancy), and Theodocia Pierpoint Walter Hayden (HD5105, 1817-1838). Died in Charleston SC age 30 — body returned to New Haven for Grove Street burial. Source: FindAGrave 139004903 William Walter Jr.

narrative_blocks.header: Died Charleston South Carolina age thirty
narrative_blocks.body: William Walter Jr. died October 6, 1817 in Charleston, South Carolina at age thirty — four days short of his thirty-first birthday. His body was returned to New Haven Connecticut for burial at Grove Street Cemetery. The Charleston-to-New Haven body return tracks the established New England merchant-and-professional travel patterns of the period, when business interests took young New Englanders to southern coastal cities.

narrative_blocks.header: Three young children at his death
narrative_blocks.body: William Jr. left three young children at his 1817 death: Ann K. (age 5), Lavinia (already deceased as an infant in 1815), and Theodocia Pierpoint (born about a year before his death). His wife Nancy Kirby continued raising the surviving children before her own death in 1830 at age thirty-nine.

people.research_notes: Nancy Kirby Walter. b. 1791; d. February 10, 1830 New Haven CT age 39. Buried Grove Street Cemetery New Haven. m. William Walter Jr. (HD5102). Three children. Survived her husband by 13 years and died age 39. Source: FindAGrave 139004955.

Theodocia Pierpoint Walter Hayden. b. August 20, 1817; d. August 19, 1838 New Haven CT age 20 — one day before her twenty-first birthday. Daughter of William Walter Jr. (HD5102) and Nancy Kirby Walter (I01295). m. July 6, 1837 Nathaniel Hayden (I01296, 1805-1875) — silversmith, partner in Gale & Hayden silver firm. One son: William Walter Hayden (HD5106, 1838-1850, drowned). Named for her paternal great-grandmother Theodosia Pierpont Walter (H00868). Buried Grove Street Cemetery New Haven. Source: FindAGrave 139005053.

naming_inspiration.description: Named for her paternal great-grandmother Theodosia Pierpont Walter (H00868) — preserving the Pierpont-Walter great-grandmother's name across three generations into a Hayden-line granddaughter.

narrative_blocks.header: Died one day before twenty-first birthday
narrative_blocks.body: Theodocia Pierpoint Walter Hayden was born August 20, 1817 and died August 19, 1838 — one day before her twenty-first birthday, in New Haven Connecticut. She had married Nathaniel Hayden about thirteen months earlier on July 6, 1837. The compressed marriage-motherhood-death cycle across thirteen months captured the period's vulnerability of young women in the postpartum period.

narrative_blocks.header: Named for great-grandmother Theodosia Pierpont
narrative_blocks.body: Theodocia Pierpoint Walter Hayden was named for her paternal great-grandmother Theodosia Pierpont Walter — preserving the great-grandmother's name across three generations of women. The Pierpont-Walter-Hayden name chain carried family memory of the eighteenth-century North Haven Pierpont line into a nineteenth-century Hartford-County Hayden household.

narrative_blocks.header: One son who would die at twelve
narrative_blocks.body: Theodocia's only documented child William Walter Hayden was born August 7, 1838 — twelve days before her death. The son would live only twelve years before drowning in the Connecticut River in 1850. The Walter-Hayden line through Theodocia thus produced no surviving direct descendants past 1850.

people.research_notes: Nathaniel Hayden. b. November 28, 1805 Hayden, Hartford County CT; d. February 23, 1875 Hayden CT age 69. Buried Palisado Cemetery, Windsor CT. SILVERSMITH/JEWELER: Prominent jeweler in Charleston SC in partnership with William Gregg 1838-43. Then left for New York to become partner of important silversmith William Gale (1799-1867) — the firm 'Gale & Hayden' 1846-50. His brother H. Sidney Hayden replaced him in partnership with William Gregg in Charleston 1846-52 at 232 King Street. Gale & Hayden silver in many important public and private collections including Winterthur Museum (Wilmington DE) — the Gale & Hayden presentation ewer at Winterthur was won by Henry F. Du Pont's grandfather as an agricultural award in 1849. m. July 6, 1837 Theodocia Pierpoint Walter (HD5105, 1817-1838) — she died one day before her 21st birthday, about a year after marriage. One son: William Walter Hayden (HD5106, 1838-1850, drowned). NOTE: The William Gale in this partnership is the NYC silversmith (1799-1867), NOT the Hooker-tree X00875 William Dudley Gale (Confederate officer, 1819-1888) — different people. Sources: American Silver at Winterthur by Ian Quimby; South Carolina Silversmiths by E. Milby Burton and Warren Ripley; Don Soeffing in Charles Venable's Silver In America.

narrative_blocks.header: Gale & Hayden silver firm partner, NYC 1846-50
narrative_blocks.body: Nathaniel Hayden was partner with William Gale in the New York City silversmith firm Gale & Hayden from 1846 to 1850. Gale & Hayden silver appears in many important public and private collections including the Winterthur Museum in Wilmington Delaware. The Gale & Hayden presentation ewer at Winterthur was won by Henry F. Du Pont's grandfather as an agricultural award in 1849 — making it a known piece in American silver history.

narrative_blocks.header: Earlier Charleston SC partner with William Gregg
narrative_blocks.body: Before the NYC partnership, Nathaniel Hayden was a prominent jeweler in Charleston South Carolina in partnership with William Gregg from 1838 to 1843. After he left for New York, his brother H. Sidney Hayden replaced him in the Charleston partnership 1846-52, with the shop at 232 King Street. The career arc moved Hayden between two of the most important American silver-and-jewelry centers of the era.

narrative_blocks.header: Lost wife and only child to early death
narrative_blocks.body: Nathaniel married Theodocia Pierpoint Walter on July 6, 1837 — she died August 19, 1838 at age twenty, one day before her twenty-first birthday, about thirteen months after the marriage. Their only son William Walter Hayden drowned in 1850 at age twelve. Nathaniel outlived his wife by thirty-seven years and his son by twenty-five — he died February 23, 1875 in Hayden, Hartford County Connecticut at age sixty-nine.

people.research_notes: William Walter Hayden. b. August 7, 1838 — twelve days before his mother Theodocia Pierpoint Walter Hayden (HD5105) died at age 20. d. August 23, 1850 Windsor, Hartford County CT — drowned while bathing in the Connecticut River, age 12 years and 16 days. Buried Palisado Cemetery, Windsor CT. Son of Nathaniel Hayden (I01296) and Theodocia Pierpoint Walter Hayden (HD5105). The Walter-Hayden line through Theodocia ended with his death — no documented descendants. Source: FindAGrave 8979039.

narrative_blocks.header: Drowned bathing in Connecticut River at twelve
narrative_blocks.body: William Walter Hayden drowned on August 23, 1850 while bathing in the Connecticut River near Windsor, Hartford County Connecticut — age twelve years and sixteen days. The summertime drowning ended the Walter-Hayden direct descent line: his mother Theodocia had died at twenty just twelve days after his birth in 1838; his father Nathaniel survived him by twenty-five years but had no further marriages or children documented.

narrative_blocks.header: Born twelve days before his mother died
narrative_blocks.body: William Walter Hayden was born August 7, 1838 — twelve days before his mother Theodocia Pierpoint Walter Hayden died on August 19, 1838 at age twenty. The compressed birth-and-maternal-death sequence reflected the period's postpartum mortality risk for young first-time mothers. William was raised by his father Nathaniel and Hayden grandparents in the Hayden Hartford-County household.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father scored a symphony for a Ford
narrative_blocks.body: Her father was the composer Frederick Shepherd Converse, whose Pipe of Desire was the first American opera staged at the Metropolitan — and who, in 1927, wrote Flivver Ten Million, a full-orchestra epic for the ten-millionth Ford leaving Detroit. Through her mother the Tudor 'Ice King' fortune ran in the line as well.

narrative_blocks.header: The composer's daughter who kept Salutation
narrative_blocks.body: A daughter of the Boston composer Frederick Converse, she married Junius Spencer Morgan III in 1915 and became mistress of Salutation, the family's Long Island estate. She raised three children into the Morgan and Pierpont world.

narrative_blocks.header: Twice she gave a dead son's name again
narrative_blocks.body: Of her ten children, two boys died as infants — a Charles in 1795 and an Edward in 1809. To each of the next sons born, she gave the lost child's name again. Both grew up: one to the federal bench, the other to a Buffalo pulpit.

narrative_blocks.header: Napoleon's court called her a beauty
narrative_blocks.body: A New Haven judge's daughter, she married into the French nobility and was reckoned one of the beauties of the court of Napoleon I. She died at Paris in 1816, twenty-nine years old.

narrative_blocks.header: He turned down a seat in the Senate
narrative_blocks.body: In 1835 the governor offered him the Senate seat left vacant by Nathan Smith's death, and the legislature would almost certainly have confirmed him. He declined it flatly and went back to his law practice.

narrative_blocks.header: Polk sent him to the czar's court
narrative_blocks.body: President Polk appointed him the sixteenth American minister to the Russian Empire in 1846. He presented his credentials at St. Petersburg the following spring and resigned the post after little more than a year.

narrative_blocks.header: He entered Congress an Adams man
narrative_blocks.body: Four straight terms in the House began with his election as an Adams candidate and ended with him reelected as an Anti-Jacksonian — the parties reshuffling around him. He chose not to run again in 1832.

narrative_blocks.header: His voice was almost musical
narrative_blocks.body: A contemporary of wide experience called him the best public speaker he ever knew: a pleasant, nearly musical voice of unusual compass, distinct in its lowest tones. He carried it from the bar into the House.

narrative_blocks.header: He led the state house, then the city
narrative_blocks.body: He sat five years in the Connecticut house, the last two as its speaker, and later served as state's attorney for New Haven County. In 1851 the city elected him its mayor.

narrative_blocks.header: He clerked that court for thirty-three years
narrative_blocks.body: From 1820 he kept the records of the federal district and circuit courts in Connecticut — and in 1853 President Pierce nominated him to the bench of the very court he had clerked. The Senate confirmed him two days later.

narrative_blocks.header: He never studied law in a classroom
narrative_blocks.body: He read law in an office rather than a lecture hall, as most lawyers then did, and came to Yale only for a master's degree in 1827. By then he had been a court clerk for seven years.

narrative_blocks.header: He judged wills for a quarter century
narrative_blocks.body: Alongside the clerkship he sat as New Haven's probate judge from 1829, settling the estates of the city's dead for twenty-four years, and served four years as state's attorney before the federal appointment came.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty years in one Buffalo pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: After Yale in 1831 Edward served churches at Westport, Troy and Genesee. In 1844 Trinity Church in Buffalo, eight years old and housed at Washington and Mohawk Streets, installed him as its second rector, after Cicero Hawks, later Bishop of Missouri.

narrative_blocks.header: Trinity split over moving, and he resigned
narrative_blocks.body: By 1874 Trinity was divided over leaving Washington and Mohawk Streets, after some members bought land from the estate of Dr. Ebenezer Johnson, Buffalo's first mayor, to push the parish into moving. Edward resigned that year, after thirty years as rector.

narrative_blocks.header: A Tiffany window burns purple for him
narrative_blocks.body: Five years after his death, a Buffalo church dedicated a memorial chapel bearing his name, and with it a Tiffany window of purple fleurs-de-lis given by a wealthy parishioner. Both still stand on Jewett Parkway.

narrative_blocks.header: The law bored him; he ran a paper
narrative_blocks.body: He studied law and hung out a shingle in Ravenna, Ohio, but the practice kept losing him — first to several years as secretary of an Indian Commission, then to editing a political newspaper.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten months in a Wisconsin land office
narrative_blocks.body: Appointed register of the land office at Mineral Point in October 1840, he gave it up in under a year and went back to his newspaper. Only in 1845 did he return to the law, at Sandusky.

narrative_blocks.header: A fishing trip on Lake Erie killed him
narrative_blocks.body: In June 1846 he went out to Scott's Point, past Sandusky Bay, on a fishing excursion. He drowned there on the fifth of the month, in his thirty-second year.

narrative_blocks.header: At twenty-eight he ran the Russian legation
narrative_blocks.body: Sent to St. Petersburg as secretary of the American legation while his father held the ministry, he was left as acting chargé d'affaires in 1848 — the young man holding the post between two ministers.

narrative_blocks.header: Two terms in the House, then the law
narrative_blocks.body: Elected a Democrat in 1850, he served four years in Congress representing his New Haven district, then went back to his practice at the New Haven bar.

narrative_blocks.header: He took an office twice, lost it twice
narrative_blocks.body: Connecticut made him adjutant general in 1867, replaced him with Samuel Merwin in 1868, gave him the post again in 1870, and handed it back to Merwin the next year. The two men traded the office between them.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded a secret society at Trinity
narrative_blocks.body: As an undergraduate he was a founding member of Trinity College's Phi Kappa Society, a secret club that eventually became the college's chapter of Alpha Delta Phi.

narrative_blocks.header: Hartford won the capital on his watch
narrative_blocks.body: Four years as governor spanned a depression that took the state six years to shake off, and settled a long rivalry: Hartford, until then co-capital with New Haven, became Connecticut's sole seat of government. A constitutional amendment doubled the governor's term to two years.

narrative_blocks.header: Three generations held Connecticut's high offices
narrative_blocks.body: His grandfather sat as lieutenant governor and supreme court judge; his father served four terms in Congress and went to Russia as American minister. He made the third generation, and the one who reached the governorship.

narrative_blocks.header: Two years at sea before he read law
narrative_blocks.body: Yale gave him a degree at nineteen, and instead of going straight to the bar he shipped out aboard the frigate Preble, commanded by his uncle, cruising Europe for two years. Only then did he return for law school.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried cases to the Supreme Court
narrative_blocks.body: Out of office he went back to the bar, arguing cases at the state and federal levels and before the United States Supreme Court. He helped organize the Connecticut State Bar Association and served as its vice president.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale's counsel was his closest friend
narrative_blocks.body: His friendship with the New Haven attorney Louis Bristol — founder of his own firm and senior counsel to Yale — was remembered as one of special closeness. They were fixtures of the same New Haven bar.

narrative_blocks.header: Two governors from one woman's marriages
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah Newton of Milford married twice: Daniel Miles in 1707, and after his death Jonathan Ingersoll in 1712. Charles Hobby Pond comes down from the first marriage in three generations and Charles Roberts Ingersoll from the second in four, so the two men are half second cousins once removed. Two governors of Connecticut out of one woman's two husbands.

narrative_blocks.header: A district judge by Governor Robinson
narrative_blocks.body: Charles practised law in New York City from 1865. Governor Lucius Robinson made him a justice of the Seventh District Court, and he was twice appointed a state commissioner for loaning United States moneys.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the family law south to Manhattan
narrative_blocks.body: Where three generations of Ingersolls had held Connecticut's benches, he crossed to the New York bar and sat as a judge in Manhattan. He was buried at Green-Wood in Brooklyn rather than the family ground at New Haven.

narrative_blocks.header: Two months at Yale Law, then Albany

narrative_blocks.header: CNN, NPR, and the Times before breakfast

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the book on Portland's power
narrative_blocks.body: Three volumes traced how a sleepy Oregon backwater became a city, and who ran it: the business and politics of 1885 to 1915, power from 1915 to 1950, and the merchants and money behind the establishment. He was the first to treat the twentieth-century city seriously.

narrative_blocks.header: He refused to strip people out of history
narrative_blocks.body: Against a scholarly fashion for impersonal forces, he defended writing history through personalities, and said so plainly in a 1979 preface. In tweed and pipe smoke, he looked the part he had left behind.

narrative_blocks.header: He went west to escape his own class

narrative_blocks.header: He built himself a château in New Haven
narrative_blocks.body: In 1896 he commissioned the Bridgeport architect Joseph Northrup to design him a Chateauesque mansion on Whitney Avenue — bold colors, a tall hip roof, a prominent tower, and French medieval fleurs-de-lis. It still stands, now given over to offices.

narrative_blocks.header: At forty-two he ran a railroad's engineering

narrative_blocks.header: New York paid him ten thousand for bridges
narrative_blocks.body: In 1906 the city appointed him chief engineer of its Department of Bridges at a salary of ten thousand dollars — a considerable sum then — succeeding the engineer who stayed on as his consultant.

narrative_blocks.header: Nineteen years to the top of one road
narrative_blocks.body: He took his Yale degree in 1880, spent a year on the Missouri Pacific, and joined the New York, New Haven and Hartford in 1881 as an assistant in the engineer department. He was still there nineteen years later when they elected him chief engineer.

narrative_blocks.header: He spent his vacations in Geneva
narrative_blocks.body: Several of his college vacations were passed studying in Europe, chiefly at Geneva. His nephew George Pratt Ingersoll was schooled there too, a generation on.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten months as minister to Siam
narrative_blocks.body: Wilson named him envoy extraordinary and minister plenipotentiary on the eighth of August 1917; he presented his credentials at Bangkok that November and left the post the following June. Siam had entered the war on the Allied side three weeks before his appointment.

narrative_blocks.header: Three generations sent to two courts
narrative_blocks.body: His grandfather Ralph Isaacs Ingersoll went to St. Petersburg as Polk's minister to the czar, and his father Colin Macrae Ingersoll was there as secretary of legation and left acting chargé d'affaires. He made the third, at Bangkok, seventy years after.

narrative_blocks.header: He lost the House and refused the Senate
narrative_blocks.body: He ran at large for Congress as a Democrat in 1910 and was beaten, and afterwards declined to stand for the United States Senate. In 1914 he was made vice chairman of the national Democratic committee and prosecuting attorney for Fairfield County in the same year.

narrative_blocks.header: His speciality was other people's trusts
narrative_blocks.body: The circuit court made him United States Commissioner for Connecticut at twenty-eight, and Governor Morris put him in as counsel to the state board of health four years later. Through three firms in two states he kept to trust estates, and retired from practice in 1917 to go to Siam.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped incorporate his own graveyard
narrative_blocks.body: On the thirtieth of October 1908 he was one of four men who incorporated Fairlawn Cemetery at Ridgefield. Nineteen years later he was buried in it.

narrative_blocks.header: A prince of Siam came to the house
narrative_blocks.body: The summer place on West Lane at Ridgefield was called Ingleside, and he once entertained a Siamese prince there. It stood directly across the road from the First Congregational Church, where his great-great-grandfather Jonathan Ingersoll had been the second minister — and he was an Episcopalian.

people.research_notes: George Pratt Ingersoll. b. Apr 24, 1861 New Haven CT; d. Feb 24, 1927 Stamford Hospital Stamford CT age 65 after two-month illness. Buried Fairlawn Cemetery Ridgefield CT (one of four incorporators of the cemetery Oct 30, 1908). Son of Colin M. Ingersoll and Julia Harriet Pratt. Maternal grandfather US Rep Zadock Pratt of NY. Maternal great-grandfather Jonathan Ingersoll Jr. Lt Gov of CT. Hopkins Grammar School (INST001). Studied Geneva Switzerland. Trinity College BA 1883 (Delta Psi fraternity, faculty selected commencement speaker). Yale Law School LLB 1885. Trinity College MA 1885. Admitted CT + NY bars 1885. Legal specialty trust estates. Member Murray Ingersoll Hodge & Humphrey 22 William Street NYC. Partner Tyler Ingersoll & Morgan New Haven. Associate counsel then consulting counsel Cummings & Lockwood Stamford from Oct 1914. US Commissioner for Connecticut 1889 (US circuit court appointment). Legal representative CT Board of Health 1893 (Gov Luzon B. Morris appointment). Democratic nominee Probate Judge Ridgefield 1903+. 1900 Democratic Convention delegate. CT representative to International Peace Conference Washington 1910 (Gov Frank B. Weeks appointment). Unsuccessful US House candidate (Democrat CT) 1910. Declined Senate run. Vice Chair National Democratic Committee 1914. Prosecuting Attorney Fairfield Co CT 1914. VP First National Bank of Ridgefield. Retired law practice 1917. ENVOY EXTRAORDINARY AND MINISTER PLENIPOTENTIARY TO SIAM (Thailand) Aug 8, 1917 - Jun 23, 1918 (Wilson appointment). m. Nov 3, 1891 Trinity Church New Haven Alice Witherspoon (daughter of Rev. Orlando Witherspoon of Buffalo NY; descendant of founding father John Witherspoon). 2 children Collin M. Ingersoll + Gertrude M. Ingersoll. Residence: 67 Glenbrook Road Stamford CT + summer home Ingleside in Ridgefield CT. Berkeley Divinity School Yale trustee. CT School for Boys trustee. Metropolitan Club NYC + Suburban Club Stamford. President Stamford Historical Society. Episcopalian. Source: Wikipedia. DISCREPANCIES: FindAGrave gives the death as 23 Feb. 1927 and the New York Times dateline is Feb. 23; Wikipedia and the Political Graveyard give 24 Feb. 1927 at 'age 65 years, 306 days', which computes exactly from a 24 April 1861 birth — 24 Feb. retained. The NYT also gives the Trinity M.A. as 1889 and the Siam mission ending 27 Aug. 1918; the State Department register gives credentials presented 24 Nov. 1917 and post left 23 June 1918, taken here. Delta Psi at Trinity; chosen by the faculty as a commencement speaker. Delegate to the 1900 Democratic national convention. Connecticut's representative to the International Peace Conference at Washington, 1910. Vice president, First National Bank of Ridgefield. Trustee of the Berkeley Divinity School and of the Connecticut School for Boys. President of the Stamford Historical Society. Metropolitan Club of New York, Suburban Club of Stamford. Episcopalian. Lived at 67 Glenbrook Road, Stamford.

narrative_blocks.body: He took his Yale law degree in 1917 and signed for the war in the 102nd Infantry that same day. He went overseas with the Yankee Division and served nineteen months, coming home a first lieutenant.

narrative_blocks.header: The gas took eleven years to finish
narrative_blocks.body: He came through a gas attack in France and was practically an invalid for the last six years of his life. He died at his mother's house on Glenbrook Road in February 1929, four days short of thirty-six, and the Stamford paper said plainly that the gas had done it.

narrative_blocks.body: Colin Macrae Ingersoll the elder sat two terms in Congress and was twice Connecticut's adjutant general. The name skipped past his uncle Colin Macrae Jr. and came to him with a middle name of his own.

narrative_blocks.header: He walked the Catskills with a dog, looking
narrative_blocks.body: Widowed twice and holding fourteen thousand dollars, he spent the summer of 1824 tramping the mountains alone but for his dog, hunting a site with hemlock and water. He bought a meadow for thirteen hundred dollars, dammed the creek, and raised a tannery five hundred and fifty feet long — the largest in the world, sixty thousand hides a year.

narrative_blocks.header: He built a town that took his name
narrative_blocks.body: Around the tannery rose a village he stocked with churches, an academy he half-paid for, a newspaper, and a bank he capitalized himself. In 1833 the legislature carved it out of Windham, and it has been Prattsville ever since.

narrative_blocks.header: His gravestone brags about cheaper postage
narrative_blocks.body: In Congress he pushed the 1838 bill slashing postage rates, arguing that costly mail was a tax on intelligence that fell hardest on the poor, and in 1844 moved the first survey for a railroad to the Pacific. Both are carved on his tombstone.

narrative_blocks.header: He backed young Jay Gould, then backed out
narrative_blocks.body: In 1856 he took a partnership with an unknown Delaware County surveyor named Jay Gould, financing a tannery that became the town of Gouldsboro. Three years later, uneasy about his partner's appetite for risk, he sold out — just before Gould's next quarrel ended in an armed fight at the tannery.

narrative_blocks.header: Two sisters, married in turn, both consumptive
narrative_blocks.body: His first wife died of tuberculosis within a year, so he married her sister, who died of it too. He buried four wives in all, and lost a third to complications of childbirth; the deaths pushed him toward the tannery that made his name.

narrative_blocks.header: He governed a Dutch sugar colony at twenty-two
narrative_blocks.body: Appointed commander of Demerara on the South American coast in 1765, he ruled the colony for five years and owned two plantations there, worked by enslaved people. The territory is now part of Guyana.

narrative_blocks.header: A Maastricht baron turned New York merchant
narrative_blocks.body: Born to a noble family in the Dutch province of Limburg, he left the colonies for New York, trading as a merchant with the Dutch West India Company. He died in the city at eighty-three.

narrative_blocks.header: Yellow fever drove him to New York
narrative_blocks.body: He left the colonies in 1790 and set up at 87 Liberty Street as a merchant with the Dutch West India Company. In 1800 he moved to the corner of Broadway and Barclay.

narrative_blocks.header: The Woolworth Building stands on his corner
narrative_blocks.body: The house he took in 1800 at Broadway and Barclay sat on the ground the tower went up on a century afterwards. He was made a director of the United States Branch Bank in 1801.

narrative_blocks.header: Three wives, and children by all three
narrative_blocks.body: Maria Storm van 's Gravesande died in 1771 and Frederica van Baerle in 1793, and he married Charlotte Apthorp the year after that. Margaret was Frederica's; Maria Eliza was Charlotte's.

narrative_blocks.header: Four hundred acres at Bloomingdale
narrative_blocks.body: Frederica van Baerle bought them off James McEvers in 1792, a year before she died, in what was then open country above the city. The farm and mansion stood there until 1827.

narrative_blocks.header: He willed the farm to a dead widow
narrative_blocks.body: His will of 1822 gave Charlotte the use of the Bloomingdale house so long as she stayed his widow. She died three years before he did, and the children sold the whole of it to Francis Price.

career.organization: Dutch West India Company, New York

people.research_notes: Baron Jan Cornelis Van den Heuvel. b. Dec 23, 1742 Maastricht Limburg Dutch Republic; d. May 6, 1826 New York City age 83. GOVERNOR OF THE DUTCH PROVINCE OF DEMERARA 1765-1770 (preceded Laurens Lodewijk van Bercheijk, succeeded Paulus van Schuylenburgh). Later moved to New York City and became merchant with the Dutch West India Company. 3 marriages: (1) Maria Catharina Storm van 's Gravesande (d. 1771); (2) Frederica Henrietta Justina van Baerle (d. 1793); (3) 1794 Charlotte Augusta Apthorp (d. 1823, daughter of prominent NY landowner Charles Ward Apthorp). Henry Wager Halleck 1855). Also grandfather (through daughter Susan) of Charlotte Augusta Gibbes (1825-1887 m. John Jacob Astor III 1822-1890). Source: Wikipedia.

narrative_blocks.header: Mayflower Elder Brewster descent on father's side
narrative_blocks.body: Justine Arnold was a documented descendant of Elder William Brewster — the senior elder of the Plymouth Colony Pilgrims who arrived on the Mayflower in 1620. The Brewster line came through her father Dr. Harold Sears Arnold's family. The Mayflower connection placed her in two of the most documented founding-era American ancestral lines: Brewster (Mayflower 1620) and Hooker (Hartford 1636) through her mother.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale Fine Arts student married fellow student
narrative_blocks.body: Justine attended Mrs. Day's School in New Haven and the Yale School of Fine Arts. On June 19, 1937 at Christ Church New Haven, she married Edward Mortimer Linforth — also a Yale School of Fine Arts student and son of Professor Ivan M. Linforth of Berkeley California. Her cousin Leeanne Gwynne (the Portland piano teacher) was a flower girl at the wedding and her brother Ingersoll 'Ingy' Arnold served as an usher.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-six years in uniform, three wars
narrative_blocks.body: Jefferson commissioned him in 1809, and he was still serving when the Civil War ended — through the War of 1812, the Mexican blockade, and finally as the officer superintending the private yards building the Union's ironclads. Two destroyers were later named for him.

narrative_blocks.header: The Royal Navy pressed him; he got away
narrative_blocks.body: Sailing in the American merchant marine, he was seized by the Royal Navy on suspicion of being a British deserter and forced into its service. He escaped — and months later President Jefferson made him a midshipman.

narrative_blocks.header: He wheeled the boundary stone to dinner
narrative_blocks.body: Held in England after his 1814 capture, he was let out on a gentleman's agreement, his limits fixed by a large marker stone. Accused of breaking the terms to attend a dinner party, he led his accusers outside to a wheelbarrow parked at the corner — the marker stone sitting in it.

narrative_blocks.header: At twenty-one he was hunting pirates
narrative_blocks.body: In a single month of 1811, commanding a gunboat in the Gulf, he crippled one pirate schooner off Pensacola, captured another off Mobile, and took a pirate ship and two more schooners near Barataria.

narrative_blocks.header: He sailed Greece its first flagship
narrative_blocks.body: In 1826 he took a sixty-four-gun frigate built on New York's East Side across the Atlantic to the Greek revolutionary government; it became the Greek navy's first flagship against the Ottomans. Two years earlier he had fitted out the frigate that carried Lafayette home to France.

narrative_blocks.header: His ship took a brig carrying captives
narrative_blocks.body: Commanding the Raritan, he seized the Porpoise, a brig employed in transporting enslaved people. He later commanded the squadron patrolling the African coast, where the navy worked to suppress the slave trade.

military_service.unit: US Navy (USS Revenge under Oliver Hazard Perry, USS Vesuvius/Gun Boat 162, Lake Ontario under Isaac Chauncey)
military_service.notes: Appointed midshipman Jan 16, 1809 by Jefferson. Served USS Revenge (Oliver Hazard Perry). Capt anti-pirate actions 1810-1811 off Pensacola/Mobile/Brassa-Barataria captured La Franchise, Santa Maria, La Divina, La Sophie, Le Vengeance, La Pandrita, Diomede, Alexandria. Lake Ontario under Isaac Chauncey — attacks on Toronto, Kingston, Fort George. Promoted lieutenant Jan 28, 1814. Captured by British Aug 1814, refused parole, sent to England held until June 1815 (months after war ended). FAMOUS STORY: under house arrest with stone marker boundary; arrived at dinner party past boundary, then revealed he had wheeled the entire marker stone in a wheelbarrow.

military_service.unit: USS Raritan (blockade squadron off coast of Mexico)
military_service.notes: Commanded blockade squadron off Mexican coast 1846-1847 aboard USS Raritan.

military_service.unit: Union Navy (Superintendent of Private Shipyards, iron-clad construction)
military_service.notes: Returned to naval service to superintend construction and fitting-out of naval vessels in private shipyards, including iron-clad vessels. Promoted to Rear Admiral July 16, 1862.

career.role: Rear Admiral, superintendent of ironclad construction

people.research_notes: Rear Admiral Francis Hoyt Gregory USN. b. Oct 9, 1789 Norwalk CT; d. Oct 4, 1866 Brooklyn NY age 76. Buried Grove Street Cemetery New Haven CT. Son of Moses Gregory + Esther Hoyt. Third great-grandson of John Gregory (founding settler of Norwalk). Impressed into Royal Navy as American merchant marine; after escape, appointed midshipman Jan 16, 1809 by Jefferson. Career US Navy 1809-1865 (56 years). War of 1812: served USS Revenge under Oliver Hazard Perry; Lake Ontario under Commodore Isaac Chauncey at attacks on Toronto, Kingston, Fort George; captured by British Aug 1814, held in England until June 1815 (FAMOUS WHEELBARROW-STONE INCIDENT during house arrest). Mexican-American War: commanded USS Raritan blockade squadron off Mexico 1846-1847. African squadron commander 1849-1852. Boston Navy Yard commandant; retired Feb 1856. Civil War: returned to service as superintendent of private shipyards for iron-clad construction; promoted REAR ADMIRAL Jul 16, 1862; served through end of war then retired. TWO US NAVY DESTROYERS named USS Gregory (DD-82 + DD-802) in his honor. m. Elizabeth Shaw (1801-1873, X02897, daughter of Capt John Shaw — early naval commander, hero of 1st Barbary Coast campaign + War of 1812). FATHER OF VIRGINIA GREGORY INGERSOLL I01301 (wife of Governor Charles R. Ingersoll HD5120). Source: Wikipedia (Francis Gregory); Findagrave.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father chased pirates off Tripoli
narrative_blocks.body: Captain John Shaw, born in Ireland and come to America at seventeen, made his name in the Quasi-War with France and the Barbary campaigns, commanding a succession of United States warships. She was his eldest daughter.

narrative_blocks.header: Her letters followed a warship to Brazil
narrative_blocks.body: Her correspondence with her husband survives — New Haven gossip and family affairs answered by his impressions of Brazil and the business of the navy, including the day his ship seized a brig carrying enslaved people.

narrative_blocks.header: At eighteen he wrote up the Rockies
narrative_blocks.body: In the summer of 1871, still a teenager, he crossed Colorado's mountains and parks with a companion and published a detailed account of the month-long journey — the vistas, the towns, the encounters along the way. It was printed in Wilmington that same year.

narrative_blocks.header: He chronicled the shipyard he would run
narrative_blocks.body: In 1886 he privately printed a semi-centennial memoir of the Harlan & Hollingsworth Company, the Wilmington shipbuilder whose iron steamships supplied the great coastal lines. He later served as the company's president.

narrative_blocks.header: She published two volumes of her own verse
narrative_blocks.body: Wife of the critic Henry Seidel Canby, she was a poet in her own right, publishing two volumes — High Mowings in 1932 and On My Way in 1937. A Times reviewer called the latter well-ordered thought expressed in poetry.

narrative_blocks.header: Willa Cather leaned on her in grief
narrative_blocks.body: She was a close friend of the novelist Willa Cather, who wrote her warm letters over many years — one thanking her for verses that came 'like the hand of real friendship' after Cather's mother died. Their correspondence survives at Yale's Beinecke library.

narrative_blocks.header: She helped found a colony for writers
narrative_blocks.body: In 1922 she and her husband joined a handful of literary families in founding the Yelping Hill Association, a summer colony in the Connecticut hills. It became a working retreat for editors, poets, and novelists for decades.

narrative_blocks.header: His weekly told America what to read
narrative_blocks.body: A Yale English professor, he founded and edited the Saturday Review of Literature, one of the most influential book-review weeklies of its day. He also wrote critical biographies of Thoreau, Whitman, and Mark Twain.

narrative_blocks.header: He picked the nation's books of the month
narrative_blocks.body: As the first editor-in-chief of the Book of the Month Club, he helped choose the novels that millions of American households read through the 1920s and 1930s. He chaired its board of judges for over two decades.

narrative_blocks.header: Twice he led American writers against censorship
narrative_blocks.body: Twice president of the American branch of P.E.N., the writers' free-expression league, he attended its 1933 congress in Dubrovnik just after the Nazi book-burnings — where an exiled German-Jewish playwright's protest became the meeting's most charged moment.

narrative_blocks.header: A hilltop colony was his editorial headquarters
narrative_blocks.body: Much of his work for the Saturday Review and the Book of the Month Club was done at Yelping Hill, a summer writers' colony he co-founded in the Connecticut hills. He once wrote that for some years a book's fate hung more on those hills than on anything but its own merits.

Marion Gause (HD-MARION). 2 sons: Edward Tatnall Canby (1912-1998 notable choral director/WNYC host) and Courtlandt Canby (1914-2004). Source: Findagrave; obituary.

narrative_blocks.header: His Renaissance choir still sings under his name
narrative_blocks.body: In the early 1950s he founded the Canby Singers, a New York chamber choir devoted to Monteverdi, Byrd, and Josquin. It has kept performing under his name since his retirement.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped make the first Jean Ritchie recordings
narrative_blocks.body: Fresh out of Harvard, he joined the folklorist Alan Lomax on 1930s expeditions into Appalachia, where they made the first recordings of the singer Jean Ritchie — later called the mother of American folk.

narrative_blocks.header: His audio column ran forty-eight years
narrative_blocks.body: A charter member of the Audio Engineering Society, he wrote a column for Audio magazine for forty-eight years, from 1948 to 1996. An exacting audiophile, he engineered and mastered his own radio tapes at a home studio.

narrative_blocks.header: His radio show debuted Stockhausen and Moog
narrative_blocks.body: For over twenty years his WNYC program 'Recordings, E.T.C.' made him one of the most widely heard American music critics — and an early champion of electronic music, giving listeners their first hearing of Stockhausen, Robert Moog, and Tod Dockstader.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the Beach Boys seriously first
narrative_blocks.body: A classical critic of vast erudition, he startled his field in the mid-1960s by insisting the Beach Boys deserved serious attention, pointing to the sophistication of their vocal harmonies.

people.research_notes: Edward Tatnall Canby. b. 1912 New Haven CT; d. Feb 21, 1998 Cornwall Litchfield Co CT age 85. Son of Marion Gause Canby and Henry Seidel Canby. Harvard 1934 (music degree). Taught at Finch College NY 1950s. WNYC HOST 1946-mid-1970s — show 'The New Recordings' / 'Recordings, E.T.C.' Harper's record reviewer 1952-1959. Audio magazine columnist 1948-1996 (48 YEARS). Nonesuch label annotator. Album notes for dozens of recordings. Early advocate of electronic music. Asserted Beach Boys' vocal harmonies should be taken seriously. Author 'The Saturday Review Home Book of Recorded Music and Sound Reproduction' (1952). Source: NYTimes obituary; WNYC archive.

narrative_blocks.header: An OSS captain who became a book editor
narrative_blocks.body: Harvard-trained and a captain in the OSS during the Second World War, he followed his father into letters — writing and editing for Time-Life Books and other publishers in New York, Switzerland, and England. Among his own books was A History of Flight.

people.research_notes: Courtlandt Canby. b. Mar 11, 1914 New Haven CT; d. Jan 20, 2004 Leeds Hampshire Co MA age 89. Buried Wilmington and Brandywine Cemetery DE. Son of Marion Gause Canby and Henry Seidel Canby. m. 1948 Natalie Green (1919-2022, d. age 102). Source: Findagrave.

narrative_blocks.header: A wartime veteran who lived to 102
narrative_blocks.body: A veteran of the Second World War, she married Courtlandt Canby in 1948. She outlived him by eighteen years, reaching the age of 102.

narrative_blocks.header: A Navy captain's daughter who joined the WAVES
narrative_blocks.body: Daughter of a US Navy captain, she grew up a 'Navy brat' on both coasts and served as a WAVE during the Second World War. Her brother was a decorated submarine veteran; her sister, an MIT graduate, worked for the CIA in the Cold War.

narrative_blocks.header: They bought a haunted 1763 farmhouse
narrative_blocks.body: In the early 1950s she and her editor husband, Courtlandt Canby, left Manhattan for the suburbs, buying an old farmhouse dated 1763 — said to be haunted — in Ossining. She kept lifelong friendships with a circle of Westchester 'coffee girls.'

narrative_blocks.header: Her family scattered across Europe and beyond
narrative_blocks.body: In 1961 the family moved to Geneva, then to London and Oxford for a decade; her sons came home to America, but her daughters stayed on in Europe. She took pride in a family spread across six countries.

narrative_blocks.header: She smoked, dodged doctors, and reached 102
narrative_blocks.body: A lover of books, gardens, and good conversation, she smoked and avoided doctors well into her nineties. She lived to the age of 102, prized by friends for her wit and vitality.

people.research_notes: Natalie Green Canby. b. Jun 10, 1919 New York NY; d. Jan 21, 2022 Hadley Hampshire Co MA age 102 (extraordinary longevity). Veteran. m. 1948 Courtlandt Canby. Source: Findagrave.

narrative_blocks.header: A Wall Street financier across opera and railroads
narrative_blocks.body: From a Yale tap into Skull and Bones he built a financier’s life: senior partner in a Stock Exchange house, president of the Metropolitan Opera’s real-estate company, and director of western railroads and a sugar concern.

narrative_blocks.header: A breakdown ended his life at fifty-nine
narrative_blocks.body: After a year and a half of illness following a nervous breakdown, he took his own life in 1925 and was buried at Green-Wood. He had given time to the Foundling Hospital and the society for children’s welfare.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the opera chair his father filled
narrative_blocks.body: His father had run the Metropolitan Opera's real-estate company for years, digging into his own pocket when the house neared ruin, and leading the charge that got Salome pulled from its stage. Eleven years after the old man died, the son was elected to the same presidency.

narrative_blocks.header: At twenty-two he built a Berkshire house
narrative_blocks.body: Fresh out of Yale, he built Sunnycroft at Lenox, Massachusetts, in 1888, a country seat in the Berkshire colony where New York money summered. Newport and Manhattan houses came with the family besides.

narrative_blocks.header: Coal, then railroads, then the Exchange
narrative_blocks.body: He started at a Wilkes-Barre coal company, moved into railroads as secretary and treasurer of two lines and general manager of one, and in 1896 joined the Stock Exchange firm he would eventually lead.

narrative_blocks.body: Out of Yale in 1916, he joined the American Field Ambulance Service in France, then took a commission as a second lieutenant in the Seventeenth Field Artillery of the Second Division.

narrative_blocks.header: A seat on the Exchange cost him $105,000
narrative_blocks.body: In 1925 he paid a hundred and five thousand dollars for a seat on the New York Stock Exchange, trading with a brokerage house and belonging to the Racquet Club. He sold the seat a few years later.

narrative_blocks.header: He spent his last years in Surrey
narrative_blocks.body: After a divorce he married again in London in 1935 and settled in England for good, returning to America only once. He died at Surbiton in Surrey in 1944, at fifty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: A conscientious objector who vanished into Indonesia
narrative_blocks.body: Facing a low draft number in the Vietnam War, he declared himself a conscientious objector and left to teach English in Indonesia for three years. His draft board never ruled on his status — nor ever found him.

narrative_blocks.header: Shamans, remote peaks, and a near-drowning
narrative_blocks.body: In Sulawesi and Bali he threw himself into local life — studying with village shamans, climbing remote mountains where a fellow climber once died, and nearly drowning in a boating accident in the Makassar Strait. He came home fluent in Indonesian.

narrative_blocks.header: His spiritual path led him to counseling
narrative_blocks.body: Back in Massachusetts he earned a master's in education and became a licensed mental-health counselor, working mostly with children and families at Brightside. He saw the work as the natural outcome of his years of spiritual searching.

narrative_blocks.header: He drove a Mercedes on vegetable oil
narrative_blocks.body: A committed environmentalist, he heated his house with a wood-pellet furnace, adopted solar panels early, and for years drove a rusty 1980s Mercedes converted to run on vegetable oil. He played saxophone in a local brass band besides.

narrative_blocks.header: His last work was a Stonehenge trilogy
narrative_blocks.body: Drawn to prehistoric peoples and the movement of the stars, he wrote a trilogy of historical fiction set in and around Stonehenge. A natural storyteller, he finished it in the years before his death.

narrative_blocks.header: He built a museum students could touch
narrative_blocks.body: He founded the St. Mary’s College of Maryland collection in 1971 and meant it to be handled rather than roped off. Fifteen hundred study works hang through the college’s forty-seven academic buildings, with five hundred more in storage.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty works of the college’s own scenery
narrative_blocks.body: The core collection turns on twentieth-century America, strongest in the New York painters of the sixties and seventies he had come up with. More than sixty of its works are of the college’s own riverside grounds.

narrative_blocks.header: The sixth Jonathan Ingersoll of New Haven
narrative_blocks.body: He was the sixth Jonathan Ingersoll of his line, after a lieutenant-governor of Connecticut and a federal judge who broke the run of the name. He taught art in Maryland, and was carried back to Grove Street in New Haven.

narrative_blocks.header: Weaving and silverwork at Wohelo
narrative_blocks.body: Jonathan was a camper at Camp Timanous from 1941 to 1943 and a boats helper at Sebago Wohelo through 1947, then came back in 1963 to run weaving and later silverwork. Karine joined him there in 1966.

people.research_notes: Jonathan 'Ing' Ingersoll Jr. b. Apr 7, 1929 New York NY; d. Dec 22, 2002 Washington DC age 73. Buried Grove Street Cemetery New Haven CT. Resided Leonardtown St. Mary's County Maryland. Son of Jonathan Ingersoll (HD5187, Yale '96 S) and Helen Scott Ingersoll. Carries his father's name and great-grandfather Judge Charles Anthony Ingersoll's son's name pattern. PROFESSOR OF ART AT ST. MARY'S COLLEGE OF MARYLAND. FOUNDING DIRECTOR of the SMCM Boyden Gallery study collection 1971 — built it as a hands-on teaching collection for the campus community. Today the SMCM collection consists of 1,500+ works in the College's 47 academic buildings + ~500-work core collection housed in Collections Storage. Current focus: works illuminating the story of 20th-century America and its art, particularly strong in mid-century American art (especially New York 1960s-70s artists). m. Sep 5, 1964 Karine Beata Robson (1939-2019 Stockholm-born). 2 daughters: Annmari Ingersoll, Christina Ingersoll Mulqueen (m. Thomas Mulqueen). 1 grandson Jonathan 'Jack' Mulqueen. Memorial service Jan 4, 2003 at The Commons in Montgomery Hall at SMCM St. Mary's City. Source: SMCM obituary; Findagrave (memorial 102013349); SMCM Boyden Gallery history. Invalid “notable” tag removed Stage 6Y-674 (notability lives in the notable object).

narrative_blocks.header: She ski-commuted to school in Sweden
narrative_blocks.body: Stockholm-born to a Danish mother and Swedish father, she grew up with Denmark summers and winters skiing to school. America came after college — and a 1964 marriage to Jonathan Ingersoll made it permanent.

narrative_blocks.header: Maryland named her Teacher of the Year
narrative_blocks.body: She taught sailing at St. Mary's College of Maryland through the seventies, then thirty more years in the county public schools — Teacher of the Year in 2000, seven years before retirement.

narrative_blocks.header: More than fifty summers at Camp Wohelo
narrative_blocks.body: Karine came to Camp Wohelo on Sebago Lake in 1966 and spent more than fifty summers there, teaching paddle painting from 1968, then crafts, and directing sailing at Little Wohelo. Her last summer, 2019, she ran Paddle Painting.

narrative_blocks.header: An American citizen at sixty-four
narrative_blocks.body: The papers came in 2003, thirty-nine years after the marriage that brought her over. Grove Street at New Haven — the Ingersoll ground — holds her.

narrative_blocks.header: Love, security and fun
narrative_blocks.body: A camper who became a counselor under Karine remembered what she taught: that there is a reason behind all behavior, that everyone can learn and has something to offer, and that “kids need love, security and fun.”

narrative_blocks.header: Great-grandson of two pulpit giants
narrative_blocks.body: Williams descended on both sides from celebrated New England divines: Solomon Stoddard, who held Northampton before Jonathan Edwards, was his mother's grandfather, and the William Williams whose name appears in the controversial pages of Edwards was his father's. His memorialist wrote that the family seemed almost to hold a hereditary claim on the pulpit.

narrative_blocks.header: At thirteen he entered Yale, and wasted it
narrative_blocks.body: Pushed into Yale at just thirteen, Williams later judged the four years badly wasted — 'time, expectation, money, all squandered,' he wrote, vowing to redeem what was lost. He graduated in 1796 and drifted into trade before religion took hold.

narrative_blocks.header: He failed at business by being honest
narrative_blocks.body: Out of Yale, Williams tried his hand at trade and got nowhere; he hated dissembling, his eulogist wrote, more than he cared for profit. The frankness that ruined a merchant would later arm a fearless preacher.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept silent for two years
narrative_blocks.body: Called to a Mansfield congregation split between orthodox and Unitarian factions, Williams — by nature anything but quiet — held his tongue on the disputed doctrines for two years to keep the peace. When he finally preached the divinity of Christ, it reopened the quarrel and cost him the parish in 1817.

narrative_blocks.header: A reprover, never a comforter
narrative_blocks.body: His own funeral preacher admitted Williams was 'more formed for a reprover than a consoler,' poorly suited to the sickroom because he would not soften a hard truth. He held that repentance had to precede comfort, and scorned the sentimental piety of the age.

narrative_blocks.header: His final sermon was on life's value
narrative_blocks.body: Worn down by years of stomach illness, Williams preached his last sermon on Thanksgiving Day 1826, on the value of life itself. He died a month later, leaving Sarah a widow with a houseful of children from his two marriages.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son painted her portrait
narrative_blocks.body: Polly Sutton Catlin sat for a portrait by her son, the painter George Catlin; the picture is now held by the Smithsonian American Art Museum.

narrative_blocks.header: Mother of fourteen, including a famous painter
narrative_blocks.body: Raised in the Wyoming Valley by pioneer settlers, Polly married the lawyer Putnam Catlin in 1789 and raised fourteen children — the fifth of whom was the artist George Catlin.

narrative_blocks.header: Detained by Iroquois in the 1778 massacre
narrative_blocks.body: During the Wyoming Massacre of July 1778, Polly and her mother Sarah were taken captive by Iroquois raiders near Forty Fort and held for weeks before being released unharmed. She grew up telling her fourteen children fireside stories of the frontier and of the Indians she remembered as self-reliant and free — tales that helped turn her son George into the painter of Native America.

narrative_blocks.header: He painted hundreds of Native American portraits
narrative_blocks.body: In the 1830s George Catlin journeyed across the American West, painting more than five hundred portraits and scenes of Native life among dozens of tribes.

narrative_blocks.header: His Indian Gallery toured America and Europe
narrative_blocks.body: Catlin gathered his works into a traveling "Indian Gallery" shown across the United States and in London and Paris, while he argued for the preservation of Native cultures.

narrative_blocks.header: His paintings anchor the Smithsonian
narrative_blocks.body: A large body of Catlin's work is held today by the Smithsonian American Art Museum, among the fullest visual records of Plains peoples before mid-century.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother survived an Indian captivity
narrative_blocks.body: George's mother, Polly Sutton, had been taken captive as a girl during the 1778 Battle of Wyoming in Pennsylvania. He grew up on her stories and among the trappers, hunters, and Native delegations who passed through the family home on their way west.

narrative_blocks.header: Consumption took his wife in Paris
narrative_blocks.body: Clara Bartlett Gregory married him in 1828, at nineteen, and followed him on his journeys west. In 1845, while the family was living in Paris, she and their youngest son both died of consumption.

narrative_blocks.header: He told the world to shut its mouth
narrative_blocks.body: Late in life Catlin turned his Plains observations into a health crusade, publishing Shut Your Mouth and Save Your Life in 1862. He credited the nose-breathing he had seen among Native families for their strength and straight teeth, and urged readers to keep their own mouths closed.

narrative_blocks.header: She went west with her painter husband
narrative_blocks.body: Despite frail health, Clara Gregory accompanied her husband George Catlin on one of his western journeys to record Native American life.

narrative_blocks.header: She died of consumption in Paris
narrative_blocks.body: Clara died of consumption in 1845 while the family was in Paris; the couple's youngest son died the same year, losses that deeply affected the artist.

narrative_blocks.header: She met him over a governor's portrait
narrative_blocks.body: Clara Bartlett Gregory met George Catlin in her hometown of Albany while he was there painting Governor DeWitt Clinton, and married him in 1828 at twenty-one. Despite frail health she followed him west, supporting his work among Native nations until her death in Paris.

narrative_blocks.header: Putnam Catlin's eldest son joined the bar
narrative_blocks.body: Charles, the eldest of Putnam Catlin's sons, was admitted to the bar of Luzerne County, Pennsylvania, on March 28, 1814. He was an elder brother of the painter George Catlin.

narrative_blocks.header: Buried, or lost at sea
narrative_blocks.body: The record of Charles's death is unsettled — family tradition holds he was either buried or lost at sea, leaving no certain grave.

bio.bio_blurb: Ripon, Wisconsin banker and land developer

narrative_blocks.header: He founded the first Bank of Ripon
narrative_blocks.body: Richard came to Ripon in the 1840s at his sister Eliza Catlin Dart's urging, bought 110 acres, and platted it as "Catlin's Addition." He founded the town's first bank with partner Edward Payson Brockway, selling lots and lending buyers the money to build on them.

narrative_blocks.header: Ripon called him its wealthiest citizen
narrative_blocks.body: At his death in 1874 the local papers named Richard the wealthiest man in Ripon, his fortune estimated at $300,000 to $500,000. He served as a trustee of Ripon College and built two houses that still stand in the town.

narrative_blocks.header: Two marriages, no children, a tangled will
narrative_blocks.body: His first wife Darwina died of typhoid in 1870; he remarried Phoebe Burling, then died of a stroke in 1874, leaving no children. His hand-written will named eighteen relatives and took nine years and five lawsuits to settle.

narrative_blocks.header: President Taylor made him a land-office register
narrative_blocks.body: Frank came to Wisconsin in 1845 and was appointed by President Zachary Taylor as the first register of the Willow River land office at Hudson. He later served as register of deeds for St. Croix County.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed young, he raised his sons alone
narrative_blocks.body: His wife Elizabeth died in 1851 at thirty-four, leaving Frank a widower with young children on the Wisconsin frontier. He remained a widower for many years afterward.

narrative_blocks.header: Called the last survivor of the Wyoming Massacre
narrative_blocks.body: She was three years old and in Forty Fort with her father when the valley was overrun in July 1778, and went down the Susquehanna with him. At her death in 1856, at eighty, she was said to be the last living survivor of that day.

people.research_notes: Family note (S.P.S.M.): Sarah was with her father in Forty Fort at the time of the Wyoming massacre, 1778; married 24 May 1792 Rev. Nathaniel Randolph Snowden. Her seven children are all built. Two grandsons carried the name further - Col. A. Loudon Snowden, son of Dr. Isaac Wayne Snowden (HD5218), and Maj. Gen. George Randolph Snowden (HD8418), son of Dr. Nathaniel Duffield Snowden (HD5223). THE LAST-SURVIVOR CLAIM DOES NOT HOLD against this tree's own records. Deborah Sutton Bedford (H01927), a child at the same settlement that day, lived to ninety-six and died in 1869, thirteen years after Sarah. Her sister Mary Sutton Catlin (H05316), taken captive by Iroquois near Forty Fort with their mother Sarah Smith (H00746), died in 1844. All three were grandchildren or daughters of Dr. William Hooker Smith (H00320), the Continental Army surgeon at Wyoming; Sarah Smith was Sarah Gustine's aunt and the two Sutton girls her first cousins. The NB keeps the claim as something she was said to be, which is what the 1898 notice says, not as fact.

Witness to the Treaty/capitulation of Forty Fort, 1778. Took part in Sullivan's Expedition. Remarried Rebecca Parker at Carlisle c.1780; prospered as a physician. The family house at 5 South Hanover Street, Carlisle, is the one President Washington stayed in during his 1794 visit to organise troops against the Whiskey Rebellion; they kept a Herwick clock on the stairwell landing. BIRTH YEAR CONFLICT: canonical has 26 July 1747 at Old Saybrook; the Gustin family note in the press gives 1749 at Saybrook. LINEAGE per that note: John Gustin (1647-1720, d. Falmouth), m. Watertown 1678 Elizabeth Brown; their eldest Samuel Gustin m. 1712 Abigail Shaw of Stonington; their son Lemuel b. 1724; his son this Lemuel. Siblings: Joel, who married a daughter of General Thomas Greene of Maryland; Hannah, who married Archibald Loudon of Carlisle; and a daughter who married William Templeton. The same note gives Lemuel and Susannah only two children, Sarah (1775-1856) and Susan (b. and d. 1778), against the three wired here. SOURCE: Jordan, Colonial and Revolutionary Families of PA (1911) p.1650; FindAGrave; S.P.S.M. family note.

narrative_blocks.header: He followed his father-in-law to Wyoming
narrative_blocks.body: Lemuel Gustine learned medicine from Dr. William Hooker Smith, married Smith's daughter Susannah, and removed with his father-in-law to the Wyoming Valley, serving alongside him as an assistant surgeon in the Continental army.

narrative_blocks.header: He escaped the Wyoming Massacre by the Susquehanna
narrative_blocks.body: Present at the surrender of Forty Fort, Gustine signed the capitulation and — having buried his wife only weeks earlier — fled the July 1778 massacre by floating down the Susquehanna with his infant daughter Sarah, reaching Carlisle.

narrative_blocks.header: Washington slept in his Carlisle house in 1794
narrative_blocks.body: The Gustines lived at 5 South Hanover Street in Carlisle, and set their Herwick clock on the stairwell landing where every visitor to the house would see it. President Washington lodged there in 1794, while he was assembling the troops that put down the Whiskey Rebellion.

burial.plot_notes: Laurel Hill East Cemetery, Philadelphia PA. SOURCE: FindAGrave; Wikipedia.

narrative_blocks.header: He paid for the coin cabinet by restriking
narrative_blocks.body: As Director of the Mint from 1853 to 1861 he had older dies brought out and restruck - half cents of the forties and fifties, the 1827 quarter, the 1856 Flying Eagle cent, the Gobrecht dollars - and sold the results to collectors. The money went into the Mint's own cabinet, which he built into a national collection.

narrative_blocks.header: Twice Speaker of the Pennsylvania House
narrative_blocks.body: Admitted to the Venango County bar at nineteen, he sat for Venango and Clarion from 1838 and was elected Speaker on 4 January 1842 and again on 2 January 1844. The bills he signed from the chair covered the state debt, the incorporation of insurance companies, the drawing of election districts, and money for the education of the poor.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the book on Washington's medals
narrative_blocks.body: He came to numismatics through the Mint and became one of the noted collectors of his day, publishing on the Mint's own cabinet, on the medals of Washington, and on the coins of the Bible and its money terms. He wrote for Bouvier's Law Dictionary besides.

narrative_blocks.header: Three presidents put him near the money
narrative_blocks.body: Pennsylvania made him State Treasurer in 1845; Polk made him Treasurer of the United States Mint in 1847; Pierce made him its Director in 1853. He left the Mint in May 1861 and was appointed prothonotary of the state supreme court that year.

narrative_blocks.header: He named the smallest coin America ever struck
narrative_blocks.body: The silver three-cent piece of 1851 was fourteen millimetres across, smaller than a modern dime, and it took its nickname from him: the trime. It was cheap enough that nobody troubled to melt it and small enough to pay for a stamp without carrying a handful of large cents.

narrative_blocks.header: A colonel whose regiment was never called
narrative_blocks.body: He was elected colonel of a volunteer regiment while still in the legislature and presided at the state military convention of 1845. In the Civil War he was lieutenant-colonel of the Philadelphia First Regiment of Home Guards, which offered its services and was never ordered to the field.

people.research_notes: Son of Rev. Nathaniel Randolph Snowden and Sarah Gustine. Dickinson College, where his father had been a professor and was curator from 1794 to 1827; M.A. Jefferson College 1845; honorary LL.D. Washington and Jefferson 1875. Admitted to the Venango County bar in 1828 at nineteen and settled at Franklin; deputy attorney general. Pennsylvania House for Venango and Clarion 1838-43 and for Venango, Jefferson and Clarion in 1844; elected 67th Speaker 4 January 1842 and again 2 January 1844. Act 79 establishing Wyoming County passed under his first speakership; he signed legislation on state debts, on regulating and incorporating insurance companies, on election districts, and appropriating money for the education of the poor. Colonel of a volunteer regiment and president of the State Military Convention in 1845. State Treasurer 1845-47. Treasurer of the United States Mint 1847-50 by appointment of President Polk; solicitor of the Pennsylvania Railroad from 1850; Director of the Mint June 1853 to May 1861 by appointment of President Pierce; prothonotary of the Pennsylvania Supreme Court from 1861. Oversaw the reconstruction and fireproofing of the Mint building. Contributed to Bouvier's Law Dictionary. His great-grandfather Nathanael Fitz Randolph, known as Fighting Nat, was given a sword by the New Jersey legislature for his Revolutionary service. CHILD COUNT CONFLICT: Wikipedia says five children; the Pennsylvania House biography names nine - Sara Patterson (Mitchell), Louise Hortense, Frank Patterson, Gertrude, Charles Gustine, Llewellyn Randolph, Mary Thompson (Stansfield), James Ross and Robert Patterson. All nine are now built.

Son of Isaac Snowden of Philadelphia, one of five sons of whom four became ministers, and descended from a long line of Presbyterians including the first Elder ordained in Pennsylvania and perhaps the first in the United States. He was the first minister at Derry Church born on American soil. Graduated Princeton 1787; studied theology under Rev. Dr. Charles Nesbit at Dickinson; licensed 1792. Called on 9 April 1793 by the united congregations of Harrisburg, Paxton and Derry at 50 pounds a year from each, and installed 2 October 1793 - following Rev. John Elder's fifty-plus years. Derry pew records then show about 40 contributing families out of a congregation of at least 70, living six to ten miles off. He asked to be released from Derry after about a year, saying the work was too much for his health, with the city and country churches also falling out; the ministry to the three lasted two years and six months. The older generation spoke of his vast learning and strong piety and his knowledge of the Greek scriptures, which he read as constantly as his English Testament. Later pastorates at Williamsport, Chester, Pittsburgh and Kittanning. Chaplain of the United States Army in 1812, and at his death the oldest living graduate of Princeton. Diary and Remembrances at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania, call no. Phi.Am156-1568, covering his youth to 1846; it records the Isaac Potts account of the Valley Forge prayer taken from Potts directly, a visit to President Washington with some seventy other clergymen on 22 February 1792, and a Morristown communion at which Washington came forward at the head of his officers. DEATH DATE CONFLICT: 2 November 1850 here, against 12 November 1851 in the Valley Forge Historical Society account. CAVEAT on the prayer: the story traces to Weems 1816 and the Valley Forge Park Commission refused a monument in 1918 after reviewing the manuscript record; Snowden's diary is the nearest thing to authentication, not proof.
