narrative_blocks.header: Pastor of the founding Harrisburg congregation
narrative_blocks.body: Ordained in 1793, Snowden served the united churches of Harrisburg, Paxtang, and Derry, becoming first pastor of the English-speaking congregation now known as Market Square Presbyterian, and taught classics to support his salary.

narrative_blocks.header: He recorded Washington praying at Valley Forge
narrative_blocks.body: He knew the Quaker miller Isaac Potts and took the account from him directly - I got it from the man myself, he wrote in his diary - Potts coming on Washington kneeling alone in the woods, his sword on one side and his cocked hat on the other. Historians have never corroborated it, and in 1918 the Valley Forge Park Commission refused a monument on the claimed spot; Snowden's diary remains the nearest thing to an authentication there is.

narrative_blocks.header: Five brothers at Princeton, four in the pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: He was the fourth of Isaac Snowden's five sons, and all five took their degrees at the College of New Jersey, where their father sat as president of the board of trustees. Four of the five went into the Presbyterian ministry.

narrative_blocks.header: His grand-uncle gave Princeton its ground
narrative_blocks.body: Nathaniel Fitz Randolph, his mother's uncle, started the first subscription paper to found the college and gave the ground on which Nassau Hall was built. Snowden was baptised in his name and took his own degree in that building in 1787.

narrative_blocks.header: He died the oldest living Princeton graduate
narrative_blocks.body: He took his Princeton degree in 1787 and outlived every man who had graduated before him. In 1812 he served as a chaplain of the United States Army.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventy clergymen called on Washington in 1792
narrative_blocks.body: On Washington's birthday in February 1792 he went with some seventy other ministers to pay their respects to the President. He wrote afterwards that he felt much impressed in his presence, and that Washington always retired before a battle for prayer and direction.

narrative_blocks.body: Isaac Snowden served as President of the Board of Trustees of the College of New Jersey (Princeton), where his five sons took degrees and four became Presbyterian ministers.

narrative_blocks.header: His signature is on Continental currency
narrative_blocks.body: A quartermaster of the Fourth Pennsylvania Battalion and a Commissioner for the Issue of Continental Currency, Snowden signed notes now displayed at Independence Hall, and served as treasurer of Philadelphia County.

people.research_notes: Son of John Snowden and Ruth (Fitz Randolph) (Harrison) Snowden; born Philadelphia 14 April 1732, died near Chester 16 December 1809 and buried in the old Middletown graveyard in Delaware County while his son Nathaniel was pastor there. Joined one of the Associated Companies of Philadelphia at their first organisation in 1775; when they were reorganised into the Fourth Battalion under Col. Thomas McKean he was commissioned its quartermaster and served until the fall of 1777, and is named in the Journal of Congress that year as quartermaster of Pennsylvania militia. One of the commissioners appointed by Congress to sign the Continental currency 1777-79 - notes bearing his signature are at Independence Hall, Harvard and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania. Treasurer of Philadelphia county 1780-82. Sent his family to Princeton for safety during the war. President of the board of trustees of the College of New Jersey, where all five of his sons graduated and four became Presbyterian ministers. Charter member and elder of the Second Presbyterian Church of Philadelphia, and a member of the committee to draft the form of government of the Presbyterian Church. ANCESTRY CONFLICT: one account makes him the son of John Snowden and Ruth Fitz Randolph; another, written by his descendant Maj. Gen. George R. Snowden, makes Nathaniel R. Snowden's grandfather an Isaac Snowden the first, a ruling elder of the Second Presbyterian Church, with John Snowden the great-grandfather and the first elder ordained in Pennsylvania. The two cannot both be right. DEATH DATE: 16 December 1809 in one account, 26 December in the FindAGrave memorial, which may be the burial.

narrative_blocks.body: Susan Engle Patterson, daughter of Maj. Gen. Robert Patterson, married James Ross Snowden in 1848 at Market Square Presbyterian in Harrisburg and raised their large family in Philadelphia.

narrative_blocks.header: Winfield Scott's second-in-command in Mexico
narrative_blocks.body: A major general in the Mexican-American War, Patterson served as Winfield Scott's second-in-command, fighting at Veracruz and Cerro Gordo on the march toward Mexico City.

narrative_blocks.header: Blamed for the Union rout at Bull Run
narrative_blocks.body: Recalled as a major general in 1861, Patterson failed to pin down Confederate general Joseph Johnston in the Shenandoah; Johnston slipped away to reinforce Bull Run, and Patterson was widely blamed for the Union's first major defeat.

narrative_blocks.header: An immigrant's son who built a cotton empire
narrative_blocks.body: Patterson came to America as a boy after his father was banished for joining the 1798 Irish Rebellion; he grew wealthy in Philadelphia manufacturing, eventually owning some thirty cotton mills.

narrative_blocks.header: His Louisiana sugar plantation rested on enslaved labor
narrative_blocks.body: Among Patterson's many enterprises was a sugar plantation in Louisiana — an operation, like all antebellum Louisiana sugar estates, worked by enslaved people.

narrative_blocks.header: Grant and Sherman bore his coffin
narrative_blocks.body: When Patterson died at eighty-nine in 1881, his pallbearers included Ulysses S. Grant and William Tecumseh Sherman; his sons Francis and Robert had both served as Union generals.

narrative_blocks.header: Militia against the 1844 church burners
narrative_blocks.body: Sent by the governor in 1844 to guard Philadelphia's Irish Catholic churches from nativist mobs, Patterson led the state militia into the streets. St. Michael's and St. Augustine's burned anyway, and men died on both sides.

narrative_blocks.header: Grant's envoy in the disputed election
narrative_blocks.body: When the 1876 presidential count was disputed, President Grant asked Patterson to go to Washington and talk with Southern members of Congress. Hayes later made him president of West Point's board of visitors, as Jackson had in 1835.

institutions.institution_blurb: One of the first two women to earn a B.S. (biology) from Penn, 1898; first Dean of Women, 1920-1925.
Studied history and literature at the Sorbonne in Paris.

narrative_blocks.header: A friend who is their very own
narrative_blocks.body: Penn created the office of Advisor of Women in 1920 and gave it to her, the first administrator the university ever had for the lives of its women students; she held it, later titled Dean of Women, until 1925. The Women's Undergraduate Record wrote of her in 1921 that the girls feel they have a friend who is their very own.

narrative_blocks.header: The first two women to take a B.S.
narrative_blocks.body: In 1898 she and the zoologist Caroline Burling Thompson became the first two women to take a Bachelor of Science at the University of Pennsylvania; hers was in biology, with honours. She studied afterwards at the Sorbonne and taught medieval history at Wellesley.

narrative_blocks.header: The French army made her a lieutenant
narrative_blocks.body: She went out as a relief worker with the French army before her own country was in the war, then ran hospitality sites for the American forces in France and Belgium. The French gave her the honorary rank of lieutenant, and in 1930 the Medaille de la Reconnaissance Francaise.

narrative_blocks.header: Five women, and she was one of them
narrative_blocks.body: The undergraduate women of 1929 founded a hall of fame at Pennsylvania and put five names in it; hers was one, alongside a chemist, a law librarian, and the first secretary of the graduate department for women. She had been president of the Women's Overseas Service League since 1923.

narrative_blocks.header: She planted a grove for the war dead
narrative_blocks.body: She took the chair of the World War Memorial Grove Committee in 1926 and dedicated a grove of trees in Philadelphia that year. She died of breast cancer at sixty-six, and a portrait miniature of her painted in 1925 hangs in the Cincinnati Museum of Art.

narrative_blocks.header: Gertrude Snowden, dead at fifteen
narrative_blocks.body: She was born on 14 August 1858 and died on 20 January 1874, five months short of sixteen. She lies at Laurel Hill with her father and four of her brothers and sisters.

narrative_blocks.header: Her family name outlasted her by five generations
narrative_blocks.body: She was born a Loudon and gave the name to her son. It travelled down through his daughter to Loudon Wainwright Jr. of Life magazine, and then to the folk singer Loudon Wainwright III, born a hundred and thirty-eight years after her.

narrative_blocks.header: Her parents died five days apart, in 1832
narrative_blocks.body: Archibald Loudon died on his Juniata farm on March 22, 1832, and her mother followed him five days later. Margery married Isaac Wayne Snowden that same year.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father traded the farm for the Juniata
narrative_blocks.body: She grew up on the ridge northeast of New Kingstown, on land near where her grandfather had settled when the Loudons first came into the Cumberland Valley. About 1820 her father traded it for a farm on the Juniata opposite Newport, and moved the family there.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father tried iron, and lost heavily
narrative_blocks.body: In 1800 he and a neighbor, John Walker, went into iron manufacture at Mount Holly. The partnership failed within two years and both men lost heavily.

people.research_notes: FATHER — Archibald Loudon, b. 18 Mar 1763, d. 22 Mar 1832, buried Silver Spring Presbyterian Church Cemetery, Cumberland County, Pennsylvania. Farmer on the ridge northeast of present New Kingstown, near where his own father settled on coming into the Cumberland Valley. With a neighbour, John Walker, manufactured iron at Mount Holly 1800-1801; the venture failed and both lost heavily. About 1820 exchanged the New Kingstown farm for one on the Juniata opposite Newport, Perry County, and removed there with his family; died there 22 Mar 1832. His wife died five days after him. FindAGrave flags him Veteran but the entry carries NO service particulars, so no military NB was written — see the collision note below for why that matters. NAME COLLISION — DO NOT MERGE THESE TWO MEN. A second Archibald Loudon (b. 14 Aug 1754 aboard ship in the Gulf Stream, eldest son of the immigrants James and Christiana Loudon of Raccoon Valley) was the Carlisle PRINTER and publisher: postmaster of Carlisle under Jefferson, publisher of Loudon's Indian Narratives, the Cumberland Register, Thompson's Travels and Riley's Narrative, a militia ensign and Whiskey Rebellion marcher, and a partner in a failed 1815 paper mill at Mount Holly with John McClure and William Barber. He is NOT established as Margery's father and the identification should not be made without proof: his daughters by Mary Carson (d. 1795) were Margaret, Christina, Mary, Catharine and Sarah, and his only child by his second wife Hannah Holcomb was a son, James, b. 9 Mar 1799 — no Margery, and a daughter born 1808 does not fit that family. The two men share a surname, a county, a death year (1832) and a failed Mount Holly venture, which is precisely how they get conflated. The printer's material — the Logan visit of 1765, the Indian Narratives, the postmastership — is recorded here UNUSED, and no NB draws on it. Margery married Isaac Wayne Snowden in 1832, the year both her parents died. The exact marriage date is not established, so the NB deliberately does not claim whether it fell before or after her father's death on 22 March. CORROBORATION for the farmer over the printer: Margery herself is buried at Silver Spring Presbyterian Church Cemetery, Mechanicsburg, the same ground as the Archibald Loudon of the FindAGrave block. Circumstantial, not proof, but it points the same way. BIRTH DATE — set to 29 Sept 1808 per Sam, 29 July 2026, with birthplace Carlisle, Cumberland County, Pennsylvania. The record previously carried 30 Sept 1808; the day is the only point of difference and the earlier value is noted here in case a source is ever produced for it. Death 25 Jan 1888 in Cumberland County already matched.

narrative_blocks.header: The gold fever of 1849 took him west
narrative_blocks.body: He was educated in the best schools of Virginia to be a statesman and a diplomat, as his brother became. Instead he shipped for California in the rush, and the home ties he severed were never reknit; his obituary said he became alien to his family and friends.

narrative_blocks.header: Old Ralph, the Shakespearean Scholar
narrative_blocks.body: He first tried the stage, then cried jewellery as an auctioneer in the mining towns, and ended his life hunting and fishing out of Watsonville. Shakespeare and Byron were his authors, and having a retentive memory he would entertain his few friends with long stretches of both.

narrative_blocks.header: He knew Edwin Booth in his youth
narrative_blocks.body: While he was still at his studies he came to know the Booth family closely, and to the day of he died he cherished the memory of Edwin Booth, the great actor he had known as a young man.

narrative_blocks.header: Alone in a fishing smack off the Salinas
narrative_blocks.body: Nobody saw it. His boat was overturned somewhere off the mouth of the Salinas and his body was found floating in Monterey Bay on the Saturday morning, 19 August 1900, in his seventieth year.

people.research_notes: San Francisco Call, 19 and 20 August 1900: Scholar, argonaut, actor, auctioneer, hunter, fisherman, philosopher - that is the life history of Randolph N. Snowden, Old Ralph, who at three score and ten perished in the sea. Baptised 7 April 1834 at Silver Spring Presbyterian Church, Mechanicsburg, Cumberland County, the record naming his father as J W Snowden, almost certainly a misreading of I. W. for Isaac Wayne, and his mother as Margery. 1870 census, San Francisco Ward 4, occupation miner; 1880 census, Pajaro, Monterey County, occupation hunter, single, and noted sick with a cut foot. His only known relatives at his death were his brother A. Loudon Snowden of Philadelphia and his sister Miss Maud L. Snowden of Churchill, Ohio.

narrative_blocks.header: He represented the United States to four nations
narrative_blocks.body: Archibald Loudon Snowden served simultaneously as U.S. Minister to Greece, Romania, and Serbia from 1889 to 1892, and then as Minister to Spain from 1892 to 1893.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the Philadelphia Mint
narrative_blocks.body: Snowden rose through the Philadelphia Mint from chief coiner to superintendent (1879-1885), and twice declined appointment as Director of the United States Mint.

narrative_blocks.header: He raised a regiment for the Union
narrative_blocks.body: At the outbreak of the Civil War he helped raise a Pennsylvania infantry regiment, serving as lieutenant-colonel during its training, and was afterward captain of Philadelphia's First City Troop.

narrative_blocks.header: Marshal of the Constitution's centennial
narrative_blocks.body: In 1887 Snowden served as Marshal of the Philadelphia celebration marking the centennial of the United States Constitution.

narrative_blocks.header: He read law and never took the bar
narrative_blocks.body: He graduated from Jefferson College in 1856 and studied law afterwards without ever entering the bar. He was made register of the United States Mint in May 1857, at twenty-one, and the Mint had him on and off for the next thirty years.

narrative_blocks.header: The Loudon name went four generations down
narrative_blocks.body: His daughter Caroline married Stuyvesant Wainwright in 1889 and the name travelled with the blood. His grandson was Loudon Snowden Wainwright, his great-grandson Loudon Wainwright Jr., and his great-great-grandson Loudon Wainwright III.

people.research_notes: Jefferson College 1856; studied law but never entered the bar. Register of the United States Mint 7 May 1857. A Democrat until 1860, when he turned Republican believing Democratic policy hurt the country's manufacturing interests. Helped raise a regiment of Pennsylvania volunteer infantry in 1861 and was commissioned lieutenant-colonel; when the regiment was taken into United States service it was divided among several Pennsylvania regiments and he was not voted one of their officers, so he went back to the Mint, and was afterwards elected captain of the First City Troop of Philadelphia. Chief coiner at the Philadelphia Mint from 1 October 1866; vice president of the Fire Association 1873 and its president from 1878; postmaster of Philadelphia 1877-79; superintendent of the Mint 1879-85; twice declined the directorship of the United States Mint offered by President Hayes in 1878. Elected to the American Philosophical Society 1873. Made improvements and inventions in coining machinery and wrote on coinage and on the great seal of the United States. Marshal of the Constitution centennial, Philadelphia, 1887. President of the Fairmount Park Commission. In 1903 he was accused, with Charles A. Porter, C. Kennedy Crossan and Ludwig S. Filbert, of making illegal profits through the Danville Bessemer Company. Died after a nine-month illness. SOURCE CONFLICT: the Wikipedia lead gives him as chief coiner 1877-79, which contradicts its own body text of 1 October 1866 and the postmastership in those years; the body is followed here. It also says the 1879 superintendency was an appointment by Grant, who had left office in 1877.

narrative_blocks.header: Margaretta Bines Snowden, dead at sixteen
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Lancaster on 10 January 1838, she carried her mother Margery's middle name, Bines. She died on 25 March 1854, two months past her sixteenth birthday, and was buried at Mechanicsburg.

narrative_blocks.header: He painted across Europe with George Catlin
narrative_blocks.body: As a young man Theodore Burr Catlin worked as a portrait painter and traveled for years through Europe in the company of his uncle, the celebrated Indian painter George Catlin. He married Margaret Dowd in London before the couple settled briefly in New York and then moved west to Wisconsin.

narrative_blocks.header: He led the 5th Wisconsin up Marye's Heights
narrative_blocks.body: Commissioned captain of Company D, 5th Wisconsin Infantry in 1861 and later its lieutenant-colonel, Catlin commanded the regiment's left wing in the charge up Marye's Heights at Fredericksburg. Burnside had failed against those same heights at a cost of ten thousand men, and though Catlin's assault carried the slope, half his regiment fell.

narrative_blocks.header: He fought from Williamsburg to Petersburg
narrative_blocks.body: His regiment saw heavy action from Williamsburg and the Peninsula through Antietam, Chancellorsville, and Gettysburg. He led it through the first three days of the Wilderness before sickness sent him to the hospital, returning in time for the siege of Petersburg and muster-out in 1864.

narrative_blocks.header: He raised a company the week Sumter fell
narrative_blocks.body: As soon as word of Fort Sumter reached Beaver Dam, Catlin began enrolling volunteers, and his men were mustered as Company D of the 5th Wisconsin. Comrades remembered him as a brave, kindly captain, popular though no strict disciplinarian.

narrative_blocks.header: He died on the sidewalk walking home
narrative_blocks.body: The day after attending an old comrade's funeral, the seventy-one-year-old colonel walked several blocks on an errand, refusing to rest because he was tired and almost dead. He sat down on the sidewalk a short way on and was found dead minutes later.

narrative_blocks.header: The Marquette prison warden, stabbed by an inmate
narrative_blocks.body: As warden of the Marquette Branch Prison, Theodore Burr Catlin II was stabbed by a convict during a Sunday film showing in December 1921 — the first time employees of a Michigan prison were killed by inmates.

narrative_blocks.header: He lived six weeks after the attack
narrative_blocks.body: His deputy warden died at the scene; Catlin lingered six weeks before dying of his wounds in January 1922. The attacker was said to be angered by privileges the new warden had withdrawn.

narrative_blocks.body: Charles William Catlin fought for the Union in Company H of the 20th Wisconsin Infantry and Company B of the 41st Wisconsin Infantry, and was buried with military honors.

narrative_blocks.header: He clerked the rates for the Wabash line
narrative_blocks.body: Charles Catlin spent his working life as chief rate clerk for the Wabash Railway, the man who set what the road charged to move freight. A Union veteran in his youth, he belonged to the Royal Arcanum's Kirkwood lodge.

narrative_blocks.header: She and her sister married Miner brothers
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Darwina and her sister Ellen — Minnie and Nellie — both married into the Miner family of Rome, New York: Minnie to Herbert Isaac Miner and Nellie to his brother Payson. The Miner brothers were sons of the merchant Isaac T. Miner and partners in the family dry-goods firm.

narrative_blocks.body: A graduate of Westminster College and McCormick Seminary, James Darrah Catlin was ordained in 1897 by the Presbytery of Choctaw and is remembered as among the first ordained Presbyterian pastors in the Indian Territory, serving charges at Atoka and Oklahoma City.

narrative_blocks.header: He married into a Choctaw Nation family
narrative_blocks.body: Catlin married Claude Money Standley, daughter of a Confederate officer who had taken Choctaw Nation citizenship; their children were raised within the Choctaw community of Atoka.

military_service.notes: Elected first lieutenant of the Carrolton Rifles, which left Carrollton on 29 April 1861 and became Company K of the 11th Mississippi, organized at Corinth. Acting assistant adjutant general in turn on the staffs of Gen. Barnard Bee, Gen. W. H. C. Whiting and Gen. Dorsey Pender. narrative_blocks.header: First honors, then a lieutenancy at twenty
narrative_blocks.body: He took first honors of his class at the Kentucky Military Institute in June 1860 and began reading law that October in a Carrollton office. The following April he was elected first lieutenant of the company his town had raised, and left Mississippi with it for Virginia. He was twenty.

narrative_blocks.header: On General Bee's staff at First Manassas
narrative_blocks.body: Elected first lieutenant of the Carrolton Rifles — Company K of the 11th Mississippi — Standley was detailed as acting assistant adjutant general on General Barnard Bee's staff and fought at the First Battle of Manassas in July 1861.

narrative_blocks.header: A wound at Seven Pines ended his war
narrative_blocks.body: Shot in the right arm at the Battle of Seven Pines on the last day of May 1862, Standley was left permanently disabled and, having risen to captain, resigned his commission the following year.

narrative_blocks.header: He represented the Choctaw Nation in Washington
narrative_blocks.body: After the war Standley practiced law, secured his family's Choctaw Nation citizenship in 1874, and for years pressed the Nation's "Leased District" claims as its delegate in Washington City.

bio.bio_blurb: Mayor of Rome, New York and leading local lawyer

burial.plot_notes: Rome Cemetery, Rome NY. SOURCE: FindAGrave.

narrative_blocks.header: Rome's last village president and early mayor
narrative_blocks.body: Edward Livingston Stevens served as the last president of the village of Rome in 1869 and, after the city was incorporated, as its mayor in 1877-78, having built one of the strongest law practices in Oneida County.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped found a school for the deaf
narrative_blocks.body: A four-decade Mason and onetime master of his lodge, Stevens sat on the founding board of the Central New York Institution for Deaf Mutes and served on Rome's board of education.

narrative_blocks.header: A Cornell engineer who built across Pennsylvania
narrative_blocks.body: Harold Burr Stevens graduated in civil engineering from Cornell in 1902 and spent his career in engineering work across Pennsylvania, settling at Masontown.

burial.plot_notes: Fort Rosecrans National Cemetery, San Diego CA.

narrative_blocks.header: He went down with his Navy plane
narrative_blocks.body: A U.S. Navy commander from the First World War, Melville Stuart Brown served as executive officer of the aircraft carrier USS Lexington and was killed in a plane crash in 1936.

narrative_blocks.header: The eldest sister who looked after everyone
narrative_blocks.body: Susan Schrader spent her life as a caregiver in northwoods nursing homes and, as the eldest of four, was remembered for watching over her younger siblings.

people.research_notes: Native of Lodi, Seneca Co., NY; a Methodist marble dealer and cutter at Hornellsville.

narrative_blocks.header: A marble cutter from Penn Yan
narrative_blocks.body: John cut and dealt in marble for his living. He spent twenty-one years at Penn Yan, where his son William grew up, and in 1853 moved to Hornellsville, where he kept at the trade for the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty years a Methodist
narrative_blocks.body: John was an earnest Methodist for fifty years. He married twice, the second time after Catherine's death in 1873, and his second wife outlived him when he died at his house on Washington Street in August 1886.

bio.bio_blurb: University of Michigan graduate and hotel manager

bio.bio_blurb: General manager of the Hal Roach film studios

narrative_blocks.header: He ran Hal Roach's comedy studio for decades
narrative_blocks.body: Sidney Sutton Van Keuren was general manager of the Hal Roach Studios from 1919 into the 1950s, overseeing the Culver City lot behind the Our Gang shorts and the Laurel and Hardy comedies.

bio.bio_blurb: Syracuse architecture professor and Civil Air Patrol officer

narrative_blocks.header: He planned facilities for the 1980 Winter Olympics
narrative_blocks.body: A professor of architecture at Syracuse, Robert Van Keuren prepared the master plan and renderings for the 1980 Lake Placid Winter Olympics and commanded the Syracuse group of the Civil Air Patrol as a lieutenant colonel.

education.school_name: graduate study: Indiana University, University of Wisconsin

notable.notable_blurb: Pioneer photographer of Steuben County

cross_connections.display_label: was running New York's largest gallery when William opened his in 1857

bio.bio_blurb: Whaler turned career photographer at Hornellsville

narrative_blocks.header: The panic of 1857 made him a photographer
narrative_blocks.body: William was a machinist at Hornellsville until the panic of 1857, and then bought George S. Young's photograph gallery. For a time he was the only man making photographs between Elmira and Buffalo.

narrative_blocks.header: Four years on the whaler Columbia
narrative_blocks.body: Restless at home, William went to Nantucket at eighteen and shipped on the whaler Columbia under Capt. Joseph C. Chase. The voyage lasted four years, touched Samoa and Java, and took him around the world.

narrative_blocks.header: 100,000 negatives on Main Street
narrative_blocks.body: By 1899 the Sutton Gallery at 131 and 133 Main Street held more than 100,000 negatives, and copies were still constantly ordered from them. William also kept branch galleries at Andover, Wayland and Cohocton.

narrative_blocks.header: Wilson Marlatt traded his camera for a brush
narrative_blocks.body: William employed Wilson Marlatt as a photographer at the Hornellsville studio. Marlatt painted so well that he gave up photography for landscape painting, and by 1884 had his own studio in Buffalo.

narrative_blocks.header: Village trustee and alderman at Hornellsville
narrative_blocks.body: A Republican, William served two years as a Hornellsville village trustee and two as an alderman. He was a Mason of Hornellsville Lodge No. 331 and an Odd Fellow.

narrative_blocks.header: He handed the gallery to his son Charles
narrative_blocks.body: William brought his son Charles into the gallery at seventeen, and handed it over to him about a year before he died. He died suddenly of heart failure at Charles's house on Main Street on 17 May 1899.

career.notes: Four-year voyage out of Nantucket, around the world
Branch galleries at Andover, Wayland and Cohocton

narrative_blocks.header: She died on her eightieth birthday
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Louisa died at her daughter Jennie's house in Onarga, Illinois, on 22 April 1904, her eightieth birthday. She had not been able to walk for ten years, and was brought home to Hornellsville to be buried.

narrative_blocks.header: In his father's gallery from seventeen
narrative_blocks.body: Charles went into his father's gallery at seventeen and stayed, apart from four years at Paynesville and Minneapolis, Minnesota, where his son Francis was born in 1890. The gallery was his by 1898.

narrative_blocks.header: Five views of a face at one sitting
narrative_blocks.body: Charles had the only multiplying mirror in the district, which caught a sitter's face from five angles at one sitting. The gallery also made crayon and watercolour portraits, flashlight pictures, and prints of 18 by 22 inches.

narrative_blocks.header: He and Lillie ran the gallery together
narrative_blocks.body: Charles married Lillie Comstock of Andover on 4 September 1883. The two of them managed the Sutton Gallery together, and both gave the business their undivided attention.

narrative_blocks.header: From Gibson City to South Miami
narrative_blocks.body: Jennie and her husband were among the pioneer settlers of Gibson City. They moved to Le Roy in 1922 and to Florida in 1924, where she belonged to the Methodist church and the Coco-Plum Woman's Club in Miami.

narrative_blocks.header: A Christmas fall at South Miami
narrative_blocks.body: Jennie fell at home in South Miami on 28 December 1935 and broke her hip. Her daughter Mary had come down for Christmas and was with her when she died in hospital two weeks later. She was buried at Gibson City.

cross_connections.display_label: chaired anatomy at Pittsburgh when he took his Ph.D. there in 1923

military_service.unit: 307th Field Artillery Regiment; 153rd Field Artillery Brigade
military_service.notes: Inducted at Hornell 26 Sep 1917. 307th Field Artillery to 17 Nov 1917, then 153rd Field Artillery Brigade to discharge. Private first class (machinist) Apr 1918; corporal 1 May 1918. Overseas 7 May 1918 to 18 Jul 1919; honorably discharged 25 Jul 1919.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventeen years teaching science at Foochow
narrative_blocks.body: Willard chaired the science department of Fukien Christian University at Foochow from 1924 to 1941, while his wife Ellen practised there as a medical missionary. Their daughter Margaret was born in China in 1924.

narrative_blocks.header: He brought ceramics to Bandung
narrative_blocks.body: A graduate of Alfred's School of Ceramics, Willard taught ceramic engineering there from 1941 to 1961. The United Nations sent him to Bandung in 1953 to establish ceramics at the university, and he went back to Indonesia in 1962.

narrative_blocks.header: A corporal of field artillery in France
narrative_blocks.body: Willard was inducted at Hornell in September 1917, a few months out of Alfred, and made corporal in the 153rd Field Artillery Brigade on 1 May 1918. He was overseas from that month until July 1919.

narrative_blocks.header: Deacon and president of the Alfred church
narrative_blocks.body: Willard joined the Alfred Seventh Day Baptist Church in June 1943 and served in nearly every office, as deacon from 1960. He was its president when he died after a seizure at home in Alfred on 9 March 1970.

gave thirty-five years to the Hankow mission and died in China

bio.title: Dr.
bio.bio_blurb: Medical missionary and physician in China

narrative_blocks.header: Fourteen years a doctor at Foochow
narrative_blocks.body: Ellen took her B.A. at Alfred in 1917 and her M.D. at the Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania. She then practised fourteen years as a medical missionary at Foochow, where her husband was teaching science.

narrative_blocks.header: Alfred's school doctor, 1938 to 1952
narrative_blocks.body: Ellen was the public school physician at Alfred from 1938 to 1952, and then went with her husband to Indonesia. After his death in 1970 she went to live with her children.

narrative_blocks.header: Born in China to Presbyterian missionaries
narrative_blocks.body: Ellen was born in China, a daughter of Presbyterian missionaries. At Alfred she and her husband were pillars of the Seventh Day Baptist church, and both were known for their gentleness with the young.

career.notes: About fourteen years

narrative_blocks.header: Nearly forty years in country schools
narrative_blocks.body: Judson taught his first school at seventeen in New York and soon went west to Illinois. For nearly forty years he taught its country schools, most of them in Ford County, and went back to the Brethorst school three times.

narrative_blocks.header: His pupils paid his way into the pension
narrative_blocks.body: When Illinois began pensioning teachers in 1915, Judson could not raise the back payments he needed to enrol. People he had taught organized a fund to raise the money for him.

narrative_blocks.header: His father died of wounds from Antietam
narrative_blocks.body: Judson's father died of wounds received at Antietam, and left the boy to fend for himself young. He was one of eleven children, and outlived all ten of his brothers and sisters.

career.notes: Nearly forty years across Ford, McLean, and Ogle counties

narrative_blocks.header: She raised her brother's son at Le Roy
narrative_blocks.body: Mary and her husband Lester Reeder raised her nephew Judson at Le Roy after her brother's sudden death in 1918. She spent Christmas 1935 with her parents at South Miami, and was with her mother when she died there.

military_service.notes: U.S. Army sergeant, World War I (grave marker).

narrative_blocks.header: An Army sergeant in the First World War
narrative_blocks.body: Karl served as a sergeant in the U.S. Army in the First World War. He died at San Diego in January 1953 and lies in Fort Rosecrans National Cemetery there.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years at St. Anne with Clyde
narrative_blocks.body: Kathleen was a telephone operator for Illinois Bell for many years. She married three times, and spent her last forty years with Clyde Slifer at St. Anne, in the Presbyterian church and the American Legion Auxiliary.

bio.title: LTC
bio.bio_blurb: Bronze Star soldier of the Pacific and Korean wars

military_service.notes: Field aide to Brig. Gen. Julius Cunningham; 18 months combat in New Britain, New Guinea, the Philippines, and the occupation of Japan. Awarded the Bronze Star Medal.
Recalled to active duty; stationed at Ft. Lewis and West Coast bases. Retired from the Illinois National Guard 1964.

narrative_blocks.header: Aide to a general across the Pacific
narrative_blocks.body: Judson enlisted in 1941 and served as field aide to Brig. Gen. Julius Cunningham of the 112th Cavalry Regimental Combat Team, through eighteen months of combat in New Britain, New Guinea and the Philippines. He won the Bronze Star.

narrative_blocks.header: He raised Le Roy's own Guard battery
narrative_blocks.body: In 1948 Judson formed a Le Roy National Guard unit that became Battery C of the 144th AAA Battalion, 44th Infantry Division. He was recalled for the Korean War, and retired from the Guard in 1964 as a lieutenant colonel.

narrative_blocks.header: Feed mill, furniture barn and a hog machine
narrative_blocks.body: Trained at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago, Judson came home to Le Roy and ran the 3Q Feed Mill and QVO Feed Store, refinished furniture at Jud's Barn, and invented the Pork-a-Matic hog-raising system.

narrative_blocks.header: He started Le Roy's ambulance service
narrative_blocks.body: Judson sat on the Le Roy school board, was a charter member of its historical society, started the Explorer Scout post and the talent contest, chaired the Bicentennial, and founded the Le Roy Emergency Ambulance Service.

narrative_blocks.header: His father died before he was born
narrative_blocks.body: Judson's father died suddenly in October 1918, seven months before Judson was born. He was raised at Le Roy by his aunt and uncle, Mary Chubbuck Reeder and Lester Reeder.

education.school_name: School of the Art Institute of Chicago

narrative_blocks.header: She married a husband seven years younger
narrative_blocks.body: Alice was born in March 1856 and married Frank Hastings Bardeen of Fremont around 1881, when he was about seventeen. They lived at Big Creek, near Hornell, and she was buried from the Big Creek Church in December 1934.

bio.title: Dr.
bio.bio_blurb: Physician and Civil War militia private

military_service.notes: Served 1862.

narrative_blocks.header: A corporation lawyer who soldiered in 1863
narrative_blocks.body: Trained at Albany Law School and admitted to the bar in 1862, George R. Bedford practiced corporation law at Wilkes-Barre for over sixty years, briefly taking the field as a soldier in the 1863 emergency call of Governor Curtin.

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve years a Master in Chancery
narrative_blocks.body: George stood for the Democratic nomination for judge in 1874 and never ran for office again, though he chaired the party's Twelfth Congressional District committee in 1882. For the twelve years before 1899 he was Master in Chancery, and he sat on the boards of the Wilkes-Barre Hospital and the Female Institute.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father went to Congress twice
narrative_blocks.body: Emily's father, Henry Mills Fuller, was a Wilkes-Barre lawyer who sat in the Pennsylvania House in 1848 and 1849 and went to Congress twice, as a Whig in 1851 and for the Opposition Party in 1855. He died in 1860, when Emily was thirteen.

narrative_blocks.header: A month apart, after fifty-three years
narrative_blocks.body: Emily died at Wilkes-Barre on 8 May 1927, fifty-three years after her marriage, and George followed her exactly a month later, on 8 June. Both were buried at Hollenback Cemetery.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father went back to his own school
narrative_blocks.body: Hugh Henderson Hamill left Lawrenceville in the class of 1868 and Princeton in 1871, then returned to the school as instructor, vice-principal, superintendent of grounds and buildings, and finally trustee. He read law with his cousin Caleb S. Green, was admitted to the New Jersey bar in 1877 and made a counselor in 1888.

narrative_blocks.header: He left the law for the Trenton bank
narrative_blocks.body: He practiced until 1890, when he was made president of the Trenton Trust and Safe Deposit Company, and he held the office until he died in 1909. He was president of the Real Estate Title Company as well, and the family lived at 231 West State Street.

narrative_blocks.header: The brother who lived one year
narrative_blocks.body: She was the second of four. Barker came in 1880 and married Page Aylett Royall in 1910, Hugh Jr. came in 1885, and Samuel McClintock Hamill, named for their grandfather, was born in 1888 and died the next year. She outlived all three, dying at ninety-nine.

narrative_blocks.header: He died a week after his son
narrative_blocks.body: Fred's son Frederick Jr. died unexpectedly at the family home on 5 March 2021. Fred died a week later at St. Mary's in Langhorne, at eighty-two, and father and son were buried together after one funeral at Our Lady of Mount Carmel in Doylestown.

people.research_notes: Farmer, miller and lumberman of Exeter Township; drowned crossing the Susquehanna near Exeter, 24 March 1842. A sixth child, Benjamin D., died young and is not entered for lack of data.

narrative_blocks.header: He drowned crossing the Susquehanna in 1842
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel Sutton farmed, milled and lumbered the family homestead at Exeter until 1842, when the skiff he was crossing the Susquehanna in went down and he and a companion were lost.

people.research_notes: Daughter of Stephen Buckingham (1763-1814, Revolutionary War veteran, selectman of Columbia CT) and granddaughter of Col. George Dorrance, killed at the Wyoming Massacre. Lumber-company clerk who enlisted 29 Apr 1861 in Co. E, 1st Minnesota Infantry; wounded at First Bull Run; mustered out 1864. Later a Minneapolis merchant. Never married.

bio.bio_blurb: Union private wounded at First Bull Run

military_service.notes: Enlisted 29 Apr 1861; wounded at the First Battle of Bull Run, July 1861; mustered out 3 May 1864.

narrative_blocks.header: He took a wound at First Bull Run
narrative_blocks.body: A lumber clerk who enlisted with the 1st Minnesota in 1861, Stephen Sutton was wounded at the First Battle of Bull Run and served until 1864, later settling as a Minneapolis merchant.

narrative_blocks.header: The Exeter farm boy who became mayor
narrative_blocks.body: One of twin sons raised on the Exeter homestead, Charles B. Sutton went into business in Wilkes-Barre and was elected mayor of the city.

people.research_notes: Twin of Charles B. Sutton; some twenty-five years in the New York City rubber trade (Car Spring Rubber Co.). Never married.
Daughter of John Dorrance Sutton; mother of June by Edward Ross Adams (1899-1981, veteran); later married a Brady.

bio.bio_blurb: Accountant and World War I veteran

people.research_notes: Daughter of Ruth Darling Sutton and Edward Ross Adams.

narrative_blocks.header: He saw Illinois when it was wilderness
narrative_blocks.body: He visited the new state soon after it entered the Union, when most of it was still literal wilderness. Twenty years on he came back with his son for the Rock River contracts, and died near the mouth of the river of malarial fever with the work unfinished.

narrative_blocks.header: A hotel, a store, and a farm
narrative_blocks.body: In Luzerne County he was a public man in several capacities at once, keeping a hotel, selling goods and farming. His son James carried the same trade and the same courtesy title of Major out to Illinois.

career.notes: State contracts for canals and locks on the Rock River

bio.title: Major
bio.bio_blurb: Canal contractor; namesake of Sterling, Illinois

narrative_blocks.header: A Pennsylvanian put his name to the vote
narrative_blocks.body: He was running the state's canal and lock work on the Rock River in 1836 when the settlers met to name their village. Several names were proposed before a Mr. Worthington, a fellow Pennsylvanian, put up Sterling and spoke warmly of the family as he had known it back east. The meeting took it, and the city stands there still.

narrative_blocks.header: He befriended Lincoln and lived to elect him
narrative_blocks.body: Sterling struck up a lasting friendship with Abraham Lincoln, and counted among the last satisfactions of his life voting for Lincoln and living to see him elected president in 1860.

narrative_blocks.header: The state went broke and ruined him
narrative_blocks.body: His contracts were with Illinois, and when the state failed he was ruined by it. He worked where he could across the West and back in Pennsylvania, and in 1847 brought his family to Dixon, where he built canals and bridges, kept a store, milled, and cut lumber.

narrative_blocks.header: The title was not a military one
narrative_blocks.body: He was called Major, as his father had been before him, and in neither case did the rank mean anything martial. Both men were contractors on public works, and the courtesy travelled with them.

narrative_blocks.header: Quick consumption took him at Dixon
narrative_blocks.body: He had retired to a farm three miles west of Dixon while the state's insolvency ground on through the courts. He died there on 15 November 1860, at fifty-five, of what the record calls quick consumption.

career.notes: Canals, bridges, milling, lumbering, merchandising

people.research_notes: Birth year conflict: FindAGrave gives 1800; the FamilySearch sibling list gives 1807, which also separates him from the elder Lewis (HD5378, 1803-1806) who died in infancy. Entry follows 1807.

narrative_blocks.header: Dead at twenty-six, three children behind
narrative_blocks.body: She married James Sterling in Luzerne County in May 1824 and bore three children in six years — Amanda, and the twins Edward and Edwin. She died in August 1830, in the prime of life, and lies at Black Walnut.

narrative_blocks.header: She died at her youngest son's house
narrative_blocks.body: She came out to Illinois with her husband when he moved to locate, and helped make the home at Dixon where she raised five children. A steady Methodist to the last, she died in the autumn of 1889 at the house of her youngest son, John Milton, at eighty.

people.research_notes: Twin of Edward; went to California in 1849 as a miner, later resident of San Francisco.

Daughter of John Mansfield; baptized Henley-on-Thames 3 Dec 1592; married Rev. John Wilson c.1617.

cross_connections.display_label: came to Boston in 1668 when her husband took John Wilson's pulpit

narrative_blocks.header: Margaret Winthrop marveled at her refusal
narrative_blocks.body: Wilson crossed in 1630 and sailed back to fetch her; she would not go. "I marvel what mettle she is made on," Margaret Winthrop wrote in May 1631. "Sure she will yield at last, or else we shall want him exceedingly in New England."

narrative_blocks.header: Her father was Queen Elizabeth's Surveyor
narrative_blocks.body: John Mansfield, Esq., was Master of the Minories and Surveyor to Queen Elizabeth. Elizabeth was baptized at Henley-on-Thames on December 3, 1592, and married Wilson about 1617, at twenty-four.

narrative_blocks.header: Her sister married Capt. Robert Keayne
narrative_blocks.body: Anne Mansfield married Capt. Robert Keayne, who founded the Ancient and Honorable Artillery Company of Boston in 1638 — and who was hauled before the General Court for overcharging on a bag of nails.

narrative_blocks.header: She and Wilson lie in one tomb
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth died in Boston in January 1658, nine years before her husband. They were laid in a single tomb in King's Chapel Burying Ground, the oldest graveyard in Boston.

bio.title: Rev.
bio.bio_blurb: Minister at Tisbury on Martha’s Vineyard

narrative_blocks.header: The son who became Tisbury’s minister
narrative_blocks.body: Where his father was a clothier and militia captain, Josiah Torrey Jr. took the pulpit, serving as minister at Tisbury on Martha’s Vineyard until his death at forty-two.

bio.title: Rev.
bio.bio_blurb: Tisbury minister who followed his father-in-law

narrative_blocks.header: He took his father-in-law’s Tisbury pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: Rev. Nathaniel Hancock married Sarah Torrey and succeeded her father, Rev. Josiah Torrey Jr., as minister of the church at Tisbury.

career.notes: Succeeded his father-in-law Rev. Josiah Torrey Jr.

bio.bio_blurb: Mother of fifteen on Martha’s Vineyard

narrative_blocks.header: She bore fifteen children at Tisbury
narrative_blocks.body: Tabitha Hancock married Cornelius Dunham at Tisbury in 1766 and bore fifteen children there before the family removed to Windsor in the Berkshires.

people.research_notes: Tisbury yeoman and mariner; corporal in the Sea Coast Defense (Capt. Benjamin Smith’s company) 1775; voted yea to ratify the U.S. Constitution at the 1788 Massachusetts convention.

narrative_blocks.header: He stood seacoast guard on the Vineyard
narrative_blocks.body: In 1775 Cornelius served as a corporal in Capt. Benjamin Smith’s company, posted on Martha’s Vineyard for the defense of the seacoast.

narrative_blocks.header: He voted to ratify the Constitution
narrative_blocks.body: As a Tisbury delegate he cast a yea vote for ratification of the federal Constitution at the Massachusetts convention of 1788.

narrative_blocks.header: He named two Mississippi towns after himself
narrative_blocks.body: J.S. Butterfield built a sawmill town in south Mississippi and named it Norfield for himself and his partner Norwood; a second community, Jayess, spelled out his initials.

narrative_blocks.header: One of the South’s great pine lumber barons
narrative_blocks.body: Through the Butterfield Lumber Company and Railroad he became one of the largest yellow-pine lumber barons in the country, his mills cutting some thirty-five thousand acres of timber.

narrative_blocks.header: Out of Washington County
narrative_blocks.body: J. S. was born in Washington County, New York, in November 1833, the fifth of six children of John Butterfield and Sarah Ann Jacques, who took the family west to Columbus, Wisconsin.

narrative_blocks.header: A widower with three under seven
narrative_blocks.body: His first wife, Mary Elizabeth Westgate, died at Chicago in June 1870, a month after their son William was born, leaving him Charles, Sadie and the baby.

narrative_blocks.header: He married his late wife's sister
narrative_blocks.body: In March 1876 J. S. married Emma Westgate, his late wife's younger sister, and they had Ralph that December and Mary Edith in 1884. Emma died in 1909, and he followed at Chicago in May 1912; he lies at Graceland.

career.notes: Yellow-pine lumber; founded Norfield and Jayess, Mississippi.

bio.bio_blurb: Teacher who trekked the Himalayas blind

narrative_blocks.header: Blindness never kept her off the trail
narrative_blocks.body: Diagnosed with retinitis pigmentosa as a teenager, Julie trekked the Himalayas in 1994 — joking that blindness was an asset on the swaying bridges — and took up skiing at sixty in a blind-skier vest.

narrative_blocks.header: She talked her way past the eye test
narrative_blocks.body: As her sight failed, Julie talked her doctor into waiving the vision part of her driving test, having found a route to work with no busy roads and no left turns. With assistive technology she built a second career in the 1990s as a medical office manager.

narrative_blocks.header: Running rats at Michigan
narrative_blocks.body: Julie met Bob Crowder at a freshman mixer at Michigan; they ran rats through mazes in the psychology lab and finished in three years, and she always said her grades were better than his. After a Yale master's she taught at Madison High School and the University of Hartford.

narrative_blocks.header: By freighter to Morocco
narrative_blocks.body: In 1976 the Crowders sailed by freighter to Morocco with their two small boys, and in 1978 they went round the world to Australia, where Bob was a visiting professor at the University of Melbourne.

narrative_blocks.header: A California girl on her father's trains
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Pasadena in 1939, Julie always counted herself a California girl, and remembered crossing the West by train with her father, a railroad attorney. At thirteen she moved to Wilmette and took top honors at New Trier.

narrative_blocks.header: Eloped at Ann Arbor
narrative_blocks.body: After a spell of study together in Paris, Julie and Bob eloped at Ann Arbor in April 1962, with a few friends for witnesses. She nursed him through his last illness until he died in July 2000.

bio.bio_blurb: Yale psychologist and authority on memory

narrative_blocks.header: A Yale psychologist who mapped memory’s echoes
narrative_blocks.body: Robert Crowder spent his career at Yale, where with John Morton he proposed the theory of precategorical acoustic storage — echoic memory — and wrote the standard text Principles of Learning and Memory.

narrative_blocks.header: He went looking for evidence against himself
narrative_blocks.body: When evidence began to tell against his own precategorical acoustic store, Bob went looking for more of it. His department chair, Peter Salovey, called his willingness to bow to evidence among his most remarkable qualities.

narrative_blocks.header: Memory, reading, and the sense of smell
narrative_blocks.body: Bob's 1976 textbook Principles of Learning and Memory was still in print when he died. He wrote The Psychology of Reading with Richard K. Wagner, edited Memory for Odors with Frank Schab, and edited the journal Memory and Cognition.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-three years at Yale
narrative_blocks.body: Bob came to Yale as a lecturer in 1965, was a full professor by 1976, and for sixteen years ran its graduate and undergraduate studies in psychology. He retired in 1998 as his health failed, and his students held a Festschrift for him in 1999.

narrative_blocks.header: Melton's student at Michigan
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Waterloo, Iowa, and raised in Evanston, Bob took his B.A. at Michigan in 1960 and his doctorate in 1965 under Arthur Melton, in a line that ran back through James Rowland Angell and John Dewey to William James.

career.notes: Lecturer 1965, full professor 1976; an authority on human memory.

bio.title: S/Sgt.
bio.bio_blurb: Bulge veteran turned Wisconsin bank president

military_service.notes: Battle of the Bulge; among the first across the Rhine at Remagen. Bronze Star and Purple Heart.

narrative_blocks.header: Bronze Star in the Bulge’s frozen foxholes
narrative_blocks.body: With the 309th Infantry of the 78th Lightning Division, Dar spent the winter of 1944-45 in the foxholes of the Bulge and was among the first across the Rhine at Remagen, earning the Bronze Star and Purple Heart. For fifty years he would not speak of it.

narrative_blocks.header: A decade nursing Betty
narrative_blocks.body: Dar married Betty Jones of Brookhaven, Mississippi, in July 1949, and through the last ten of their fifty-nine years he nursed her himself through Alzheimer's disease. She died in June 2008; he died three years later.

narrative_blocks.header: He grew his bank fivefold as president
narrative_blocks.body: Dar joined the First National Bank of Wisconsin Rapids as its auditor in 1955 and was its president from 1969 to 1986; its assets grew more than fivefold under him. As a banker he financed the first business in the city's industrial park.

narrative_blocks.header: A banker who ended up growing potatoes
narrative_blocks.body: Before he retired, Dar and his partner Pat Daly began buying Juneau County land to turn into irrigated farmland, and found themselves farmers. Thirty years on, their B & D Farms and Central Wisconsin Farms were harvesting nine hundred truckloads of potatoes a year.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty years at Bank-A-Count, and the Has Beens
narrative_blocks.body: For fifty years Dar was a director and officer of the Bank-A-Count Corporation at Rudolph, and he chaired the Wisconsin Rapids Industrial Development Commission. In retirement his favourite gathering was a lunch of old business leaders who called themselves the Has Beens.

narrative_blocks.header: Eighty acres on the Yellow River
narrative_blocks.body: Dar went duck hunting in Saskatchewan every autumn for forty-five years running, and late in life he bought eighty acres of wetland and prairie on the Yellow River in Juneau County and tended it as a family nature preserve.

narrative_blocks.body: Bob came home to Brookhaven in 1956 to practise law and drill for oil and gas, and ran the town's Chamber of Commerce and its Industrial Development Foundation. He was also, for one season, King of the Krewe of Ceres Harvest Ball.

bio.title: Brig. Gen.
bio.bio_blurb: Union brigadier general of the Vermont Brigade

military_service.unit: 11th Vermont Infantry; 1st Brigade, 2nd Division, VI Corps
military_service.notes: USMA 1860 (40th of 41). Wounded at Spotsylvania; brevetted for Spotsylvania, Winchester, Fisher’s Hill, Cedar Creek.

narrative_blocks.header: Wounded, he refused to leave the field
narrative_blocks.body: James's 11th Vermont came out of the Washington forts in May 1864 with more than 2,000 men, more than the rest of the battered Vermont Brigade together. In its first fight, at Spotsylvania on 18 May, he was shot in the neck walking the earthworks to steady his men, and would not leave the field until the day was done.

narrative_blocks.header: Cited for gallantry in the Shenandoah Valley
narrative_blocks.body: Back in command of a Sixth Corps brigade under Sheridan, James won his brevet as brigadier general for Spotsylvania, Winchester, Fisher's Hill and Cedar Creek. At Cedar Creek his was one of the few Union brigades still holding an organized line before Sheridan's ride rallied the army.

narrative_blocks.header: Fort Wise, with Sedgwick and Jeb Stuart
narrative_blocks.body: Out of West Point in 1860, fortieth in a class of forty-one, James served at Fort Wise in Colorado Territory among officers who included John Sedgwick, future commander of the Sixth Corps, and Jeb Stuart, who went south. He stayed on the frontier until the summer of 1862, more than a year into the war.

narrative_blocks.header: From general to Albany papermaker
narrative_blocks.body: After the war James settled in Albany, New York, as president of the Albany Card and Paper Company, and in December 1889 Benjamin Harrison's administration made him the city's postmaster.

narrative_blocks.header: He died in his seat at Daly's Theatre
narrative_blocks.body: On 16 March 1897 James dined in New York with his son James Allen Warner, who then took him to Daly's Theatre. They had only just sat down when he was struck by apoplexy and died almost at once, at sixty-one, and he was carried home to Middlebury for burial.

narrative_blocks.header: Great-uncle of the generals' cataloguer
narrative_blocks.body: James was a great-uncle of Ezra J. Warner, whose Generals in Blue and Generals in Gray became the standard reference on the Civil War's general officers, the Union volume with James in it.

narrative_blocks.header: He led Connecticut’s highest court
narrative_blocks.body: John rose from a Norwich law practice to the Connecticut Supreme Court in 1864 and became its chief justice in 1874. He sat thirty-five years on the bench in all, fifteen of them as chief, until the law retired him at seventy in 1889.

narrative_blocks.header: A judge who trusted equity over technicality
narrative_blocks.body: Remembered for sound judgment rather than book-learning, he was known to set aside a technical rule when the justice of a case seemed to demand it, as in his vigorous dissent in Dickerson’s Appeal from Probate.

narrative_blocks.header: The legislature made a post just for him

narrative_blocks.header: From Lafayette Foster's office to the bench
narrative_blocks.body: John read law in Lafayette Foster's Norwich office in 1845, opened his own practice there in 1847, and in 1854 was chosen by the General Assembly as judge of the New London County court. Yale gave him an honorary master's degree in 1861 and a doctorate of laws in 1878.

narrative_blocks.header: A murder trial adjourned for his wife
narrative_blocks.body: Emma had been very ill with diphtheria the autumn before and never recovered her strength. When she died suddenly at their Norwich home in September 1884, John adjourned the Conant murder trial he was hearing until the Monday.

narrative_blocks.body: Stuyvesant took up yacht racing in the early 1880s and sailed the Caramia, the Mimosa and the Butterfly to many prizes, winning the Brooklyn Ocean Yacht trophy for the race around Long Island four years in a row.

people.research_notes: New York Sun, 4 November 1930: died at his home on Milton Point, Rye, aged 67; funeral at Christ Church, Rye. Retired from the building and real estate business; educated in the New York public schools and in France and Germany; descended in the seventh generation from Peter Stuyvesant. Took up yacht racing in the early eighties - the Caramia, the Mimosa and the Butterfly won many prizes - and won the Brooklyn Ocean Yacht trophy for the sail around Long Island four years running. Commissioned a lieutenant in the navy in the world war, most of his service on the Leviathan carrying troops. Senior warden of the Church of St. John the Evangelist, raised as a memorial to his grandfather Bishop Wainwright. Member of the New York Yacht Club and the Union Club and a founder of the Apawamis Club of Rye. The obituary names his wife as Mrs. Mary Hughes Wainwright - a later wife, after his marriage to Caroline Smith Snowden ended; she is not built. WIDOW NAME CONFLICT: the New York Times (4 Nov 1930) calls his surviving widow 'the former Miss Sarah Hughes'; the New York Sun the same day calls her 'Mrs. Mary Hughes Wainwright'. She is not built either way. OCCUPATION CONFLICT: the Times says he was 'in the metal business, retiring many years ago'; the Sun says he retired from 'the building and real estate business'. Both recorded; the metal trade is carried in the career array as the earlier and more specific claim. His brother Col. J. Mayhew Wainwright (1864-1945) and brother Richard Tighe Wainwright are named in the obituary; neither is built.

Widowed when Charles Randolph Snowden died in a 1913 auto accident; married John Converse (a passenger in the same car) in 1917. Her child by Converse, John Heman Converse (1920–1999), is non-Hooker and not built. Merged 2026-07-28: HD8367 'Bertha Dep. Snowden' (b. Feb 1880 PA) was the same woman, mis-filed as a DAUGHTER of A. Loudon Snowden and Elizabeth Robinson Smith Snowden when she was their daughter-in-law. Deleted on Sam's explicit instruction; she had no marriages, children, NBs or CCs of her own, and was unlinked from both parents' children_ids first. Birth year differs between the two records (1878 FindAGrave vs Feb 1880 FamilySearch) -- 1878 retained.

military_service.role: Third Naval District, New York
military_service.notes: Commissioned Sept 29, 1917; U.S. Navy service in the Third Naval District (New York) through the war, released March 1919. Recognized on the Rye, NY World War I Memorial.

narrative_blocks.header: An early devotee of competitive contract bridge
narrative_blocks.body: After serving as a Navy lieutenant in New York’s Third Naval District during the First World War, Stuyvesant Wainwright Jr. settled into a long career as a Manhattan stockbroker. He became a familiar figure in the early world of competitive contract bridge, in the years the modern game was taking shape.

narrative_blocks.header: Born in Philadelphia, his mother's city
narrative_blocks.body: The eldest of five, he was born at Philadelphia in 1891 to Caroline Smith Snowden, daughter of the mint superintendent A. Loudon Snowden. By 1900 the family had settled at Rye, where he grew up and where his name was later cut into the town's World War I memorial.

people.research_notes: Born 30 January 1891 at Philadelphia, his mother's city; eldest of the five children of Stuyvesant Wainwright and Caroline Smith Snowden. Living with the family at Rye by 1900. Commissioned Lieutenant (jg) 29 September 1917, U.S. Navy, Third Naval District (New York) - the command responsible for port security, logistics and the movement of men and materiel through the Port of New York - released March 1919; named on the Rye, N.Y. World War I memorial plaques. Afterwards a stockbroker in New York City, with houses in Manhattan and on Long Island, and a figure in early competitive contract bridge. Died 4 February 1975 at Naples, Collier County, Florida, aged 84; buried Cedar Lawn Cemetery, East Hampton. DATE CONFLICT, UNRESOLVED: FamilySearch gives his marriage to Clara Louise Flinn as 14 June 1934 but places all three of their children before it (1925, 1927, 1931). Either the marriage date is wrong or the children belong to an earlier, unrecorded marriage. Recorded as FamilySearch has it and FLAGGED - do not build an NB on the 1934 date until this is settled.

military_service.role: U.S. Naval Reserve Force, Third Naval District
military_service.notes: Enrolled at the New York Recruiting Station on 17 July 1918 and served stateside in the Third Naval District through the Armistice, released to inactive duty on 10 February 1919. He never went overseas.

narrative_blocks.header: A Western Electric clerk who joined the Navy
narrative_blocks.body: He was clerking for the Western Electric Company in New York when he enrolled as a seaman at the recruiting station in July 1918. The Third Naval District he was sent to ran the Port of New York, and his eldest brother Stuyvesant had been commissioned into the same command the year before. He was released to inactive duty four months after the Armistice, having never gone overseas.

narrative_blocks.header: His second wife was buried among du Ponts
narrative_blocks.body: His first wife, Caroline Seymour, died at Manhattan in 1929, thirty-two years old. He then married Aimee du Pont Andrews, named for her mother Julia Sophia du Pont, and she was buried in the du Pont family cemetery at Wilmington.

people.research_notes: Third son of Stuyvesant Wainwright and Caroline Smith Snowden, named for his grandfather John Howard Wainwright (X03790). Born 9 February 1896 in New York City; died 9 May 1968 at East Hampton. Married (1) Caroline Seymour, 22 June 1917, who died at Manhattan 30 November 1929 aged 32; (2) Aimee du Pont Andrews (1909-1980), daughter of James Newman Andrews (1866-1953) and Julia Sophia du Pont (1887-1952) - no marriage date recorded. Aimee is buried in the Du Pont de Nemours Cemetery, Wilmington, Delaware. Her parents are NOT built. The Julia Sophia du Pont Shubrick (1805-1882) who was a daughter of Victor Marie du Pont de Nemours is the elder namesake, not Aimee's mother. VETERAN RECORD: worked as a clerk for the Western Electric Company in New York City before the war; enrolled at the New York Recruiting Station 17 July 1918 as a Seaman in the U.S. Naval Reserve Force, assigned to the Third Naval District, stateside only, released to inactive duty 10 February 1919. Address of record at death, 56 East 65th Street, New York; he and Aimee kept houses in the city and at East Hampton. BIRTHPLACE CONFLICT: the veteran record says he was born at RYE, New York, on 9 February 1896; FamilySearch says New York City. Rye is where the family lived, so it is plausible; New York City is kept for now. At his death in 1968 he was survived by his wife Aimee and by his brother Stuyvesant; of the five sons only those two were still living.

narrative_blocks.header: He trained as an Army pilot, never deployed

He went on to become a senior partner in the New York insurance firm Wainwright & Page.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at forty-three, recuperating at the shore
narrative_blocks.body: He was senior partner of the insurance firm Wainwright and Page on East Forty-second Street and lived out at Hewlett on Long Island. He died at Atlantic City in January 1942, where he had gone to get over an illness, leaving a widow and a son of seventeen.

people.research_notes: New York Times obituary, 24 January 1942: senior partner of the insurance firm Wainwright & Page, Inc., 60 East Forty-second Street; died 23 January 1942 at Atlantic City, N.J., where he had been recuperating from a recent illness, aged 43; lived at Hewlett, Long Island. Attended Pawling School and was a member of the class of 1920 at Princeton; served as a pilot in the Army air service in the World War. BIRTHPLACE CONFLICT: the obituary says he was born in Philadelphia; FamilySearch gives 5 April 1898 in New York City. His eldest brother was born at Philadelphia in 1891 but the two next were born in New York in 1893 and 1896, so the family had already moved; New York is recorded here and Philadelphia flagged. The obituary calls his mother 'Mrs. Carl F. Wolff' and his father 'the late Stuyvesant Wainwright of Rye' - she had remarried after the divorce. OPEN QUESTION: it names 'four brothers, Stuyvesant W., Carroll, John Howard and Livingston Wainwright'. Only four sons besides him are known, one of whom is Carroll LIVINGSTON Wainwright - the obituary has very likely split one man's name into two. Caroline's own 1960 obituary names only three surviving sons and no Livingston. No sixth son built. A second published sketch agrees with the obituary that he was born in PHILADELPHIA and confirms Pawling School, Princeton 1920, the Army air service, the Wainwright & Page partnership at 60 East Forty-second Street, the Hewlett house and the single son. Two sources now say Philadelphia against FamilySearch's New York City; New York is still recorded because FamilySearch carries nine sources for the birth, but Philadelphia is the stronger narrative claim and this should be resolved.

narrative_blocks.header: He left Wall Street to paint miniatures
narrative_blocks.body: Briefly a Wall Street broker after his 1920 elopement with Gould heiress Edith Catherine Gould, Carroll Wainwright abandoned finance in 1923 to devote himself to painting, specializing in miniature portraits.

narrative_blocks.header: His brothers had him committed at thirty-one
narrative_blocks.body: In February 1931 his three brothers put him into Bloomingdale Hospital and petitioned to have him declared incompetent, testifying to hallucinations going back to a 1916 pneumonia and to breakdowns brought on by overwork and the strenuous demands of society. Three psychiatrists agreed with them. He came to court without a lawyer, said he had been taken there by a ruse and held prisoner, and after six hours a jury of sixteen men found him competent.

narrative_blocks.header: They eloped to Elkton, for thrift
narrative_blocks.body: He was twenty-one and she was eighteen, and they married in a Maryland rectory hours after she left Miss Spence's, the engagement kept from both families. His father, asked that night, said he had never met a Gould. Asked why they had run, he said: why should we have a big church wedding, with a whole lot of fuss and flowers and needless expense forced upon us.

people.research_notes: Born 2 December 1899 at Philadelphia; died 6 July 1967 at East Hampton after a long illness - the Times obituary calls him 68, he was 67. Pawling School, left 1917 to enlist. Eloped with the eighteen-year-old Edith Catherine Gould to Elkton, Maryland on 27 May 1920, married in the rectory of the Elkton Presbyterian Church a few hours after her graduation from Miss Spence's, the engagement kept secret from both families; his own father, asked about it that night, said he had never met a Gould and did not know his son was engaged. Asked why, he told a reporter: why shouldn't we practise what we preach and be thrifty, why should we have a big church wedding with a whole lot of fuss and flowers and needless expense forced on us. A Wall Street broker after the marriage; in 1923 he left it to paint, and painted miniatures for most of the rest of his life. Built Gulf Crest at East Hampton in 1927. Divorced 1932. Nephew of Gen. Jonathan Mayhew Wainwright, the hero of Bataan. THE COMPETENCY CASE: on 21 February 1931 his brothers Stuyvesant, J. Howard and Loudon had him committed to Bloomingdale Hospital at White Plains and petitioned to have him declared incompetent and a commission appointed over his affairs. They testified he had been subject to hallucinations since a 1916 pneumonia and appendicitis, with breakdowns in 1916, 1923 and 1929 brought on by overwork and the strenuous demands of society. Three psychiatrists testified to his instability, one that he was completely incompetent. He came to court without a lawyer, took the stand, said he had been taken to Bloomingdale by a ruse and held prisoner since, and laid his troubles to his mother and stepfather. On 20 May 1931, after a six-hour hearing, a jury of sixteen men disregarded all three doctors and found him competent.

notable.notable_blurb: Life magazine writer and editor

cross_connections.display_label: helped launch Life, then founded his own newspaper
went to the war he brought home in photographs, a generation earlier
