, his ancestor nine generations back, surrendered New Amsterdam in 1664

military_service.role: U.S. Marine Corps
military_service.notes: Enlisted at seventeen straight out of St. Andrew's School and served to the end of the war; he never saw combat. His letters home to his mother survive, some of them scorched in the 1966 family fire, and became the spine of his son's stage piece Surviving Twin.

narrative_blocks.header: He walked into Life as an office boy
narrative_blocks.body: He joined the magazine in 1949 fetching and carrying, and by the 1950s was its reporter, correspondent and bureau chief. In 1964 he started The View From Here, the first personal column Life ever ran, and he was still writing it the week he died.

narrative_blocks.header: He printed the week's dead, face by face
narrative_blocks.body: In 1969 he and Philip Kunhardt put to Life the idea of publishing the photograph, name and home town of every American killed in Vietnam in a single week. The magazine had always played it down the middle; the issue cost it subscriptions and drew the angriest and the most grateful mail it had had.

narrative_blocks.header: He rode with the Mercury astronauts for Life
narrative_blocks.body: As a Life correspondent, Loudon Wainwright Jr. covered the Project Mercury astronauts — once sitting in John Glenn’s car as the two listened to John F. Kennedy’s 1961 inaugural — then wrote the long-running column “The View From Here” and, finally, an inside history of the magazine itself.

narrative_blocks.header: His column ran in Life for twenty-four years
narrative_blocks.body: Loudon Wainwright Jr. launched “The View from Here” in 1964 and wrote it until his death in 1988, turning his father, his children, and ordinary family life into its recurring subject. The columns later supplied passages his son recited from the stage between songs.

narrative_blocks.header: At fifty-seven he wrote about a new daughter
narrative_blocks.body: The column that had carried the Mercury astronauts and the week of Vietnam dead turned, in his last decade, to a man in his fifties raising a small child. That was Anna, his daughter with Martha Fay. He wrote about his own cancer in it too, and was still writing it the week he died.

narrative_blocks.header: His son knew none of the mourners
narrative_blocks.body: He was a functioning alcoholic, and his son grew up unable to reach him. At the gathering after his death, people from his therapy and his AA groups came up one after another to say he had been the warmest man they knew and had helped them. His son stood there thinking: who are you all talking about?

people.research_notes: Born 16 December 1924 in Manhattan; died there 12 December 1988 of colon cancer, aged 63, after two years of illness; buried Cedar Lawn Cemetery, East Hampton. St. Andrew's School, Middletown, Delaware, 1942; U.S. Marine Corps 1942-45; University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Phi Beta Kappa and St. Anthony Hall. Joined Life in 1949 as an OFFICE BOY (AP obituary, 13 December 1988), then reporter, correspondent, bureau chief and staff writer through the 1950s; covered the Project Mercury astronauts and counted John Glenn and Scott Carpenter as friends; with Philip Kunhardt conceived Life's 1969 issue printing the faces, names and home towns of every American killed in Vietnam in a single week. Began 'The View From Here', the magazine's first personal column, in 1964 and wrote it until his death - over 200 columns. Assistant managing editor from 1969 until the weekly folded at the end of 1972; rejoined the staff when Life revived as a monthly in 1978, retiring from the editorship in 1985. The Great American Magazine (Knopf, 1986) is his inside history of it. MARTHA FAY IS NOT A WIFE: he married Martha Harriet Taylor on 13 September 1945 and never divorced her, though they were separated for the last decade or more of his life. Martha Fay lived with him for his last twelve years and is the mother of his daughter Anna Fay Wainwright (b. 1982). The record is wired as a marriage entry because that is the only way the child links, but it carries relationship_type=partner and is_marriage=false; the card has no partner label yet. UPI, 13 December 1988: joined Life in 1949 as a copy boy (the AP the same week says office boy) and spent his entire career at the one publication. In his last decade the column turned to a man in his fifties fathering and raising a small child - his life with Martha Fay and their daughter Anna Fay Wainwright, who was six when he died - and he wrote about his own colon cancer in it as well, continuing until his death.

military_service.role: U.S. Marine Corps Women's Reserve
military_service.notes: A private first class in the Marine Corps Women's Reserve at the time of her wedding in September 1945.

narrative_blocks.header: She was a Marine private when she married
narrative_blocks.body: Martha Harriet Taylor of Tifton, Georgia was a private first class in the Marine Corps Women's Reserve when she married a fellow recruit eleven days after Japan signed the surrender. They had four children and were separated for the last decade of his life, without ever divorcing.

narrative_blocks.header: Inch by inch, life's a cinch
narrative_blocks.body: Her daughter Sloan remembers her as a slogan sayer. Inch by inch, life is a cinch; yard by yard, life is hard; want a loan - it is good to want things. And if you want to be happy, keep your mind off your thoughts.

narrative_blocks.header: A turntable in every room of the house
narrative_blocks.body: Everyone had their own turntable in their own bedroom and there was a stereo in the living room besides, so Glenn Gould, Carole King, the Monkees, the Beatles, Janis Joplin and the Incredible String Band all blended in the hallways at once. Two of her four children became working musicians, and three of her grandchildren after them.

narrative_blocks.header: Her death stopped her son writing for years
narrative_blocks.body: She died in Georgia in 1997. Her son Loudon sank into a depression deep enough that he believed he would never write again, went to her cabin in the woods, and came out of it with a record called Last Man on Earth. Her daughter Sloan made her second album in her memory.

people.research_notes: Daughter of Walter Taylor of Atlanta, Georgia; born 4 April 1922 at Tifton, Tift County, Georgia; died 25 March 1997 in Georgia; buried St. Matthew's Episcopal Churchyard, Bedford, Westchester County, New York. BURIAL CORRECTED: this record previously carried Cedar Lawn, East Hampton, where her husband and his parents lie; the sourced burial is St. Matthew's at Bedford. She and Loudon Snowden Wainwright Jr. were separated for the last decade of his life but never divorced. She taught yoga. Her daughter Sloan remembers her as a slogan sayer - inch by inch, life's a cinch; yard by yard, life is hard; want a loan? it's good to want things; if you want to be happy, keep your mind off your thoughts - and remembers a house where everyone had a turntable in their own room and a stereo in the living room besides, with Glenn Gould, Carole King, the Monkees, the Beatles, Janis Joplin and the Incredible String Band blending in the hallways. Sloan's second album, From Where You Are (1998), was made in her memory. Her son Loudon III fell into a depression after her death in 1997, believed he would never write again, retreated to her cabin in the woods, and came out of it with Last Man on Earth. NAME FIELD: 'Martha Harriet' still sits in first_name; splitting Harriet out would move her slug a second time this week, so it is flagged rather than done.

NOT A WIFE - a partner. Loudon Snowden Wainwright Jr. married Martha Harriet Taylor in 1945 and never divorced her. Martha Fay lived with him for the last twelve years of his life and is the mother of their daughter Anna Fay Wainwright (b. 1982). She lent his son the collection of his wartime letters home that became the source for Surviving Twin. Her record is wired through a marriage entry because that is the only way the child links; it carries relationship_type=partner and is_marriage=false.

narrative_blocks.header: She handed him the box of letters
narrative_blocks.body: She kept the letters Loudon Snowden Wainwright Jr. wrote his mother from the Marine Corps between 1942 and 1945, some typed, most in pencil, many still blackened and singed from a house fire. She gave them to his son, who built the stage piece Surviving Twin out of them. In the last of them his father works up the nerve to mention a fellow recruit from south Georgia called Martha Taylor.

notable.notable_blurb: Folk singer-songwriter

cross_connections.display_label: his grandmother, who found him the boatyard job behind his first song
walked out of the Taft dynasty into a Seattle grunge band
was his great-great-great-grandmother, and the Loudon in his name

narrative_blocks.header: Dead Skunk, then songs about his children
narrative_blocks.body: A confessional folk singer-songwriter who scored an unlikely hit with Dead Skunk, he turned his marriages and his children into song, and raised a houseful of musicians who would answer him back in records of their own.

narrative_blocks.header: A lobsterman named Edgar got his first song
narrative_blocks.body: Jailed five days in Oklahoma at twenty-one and bailed out by his father, he took a boatyard job in Rhode Island to earn the money back. An old lobsterman there moved him enough to borrow a friend's guitar and write his first song about him. Within a year he had twenty more.

narrative_blocks.header: He overslept the day he was to enlist
narrative_blocks.body: Just turned twenty, he signed up for the army's airborne division and then slept through the morning he was due to enrol. He woke up, decided the military was not for him, and never went back. Vietnam was dodged later on a letter from his father's psychiatrist calling him a sociopath, which he says he acted his way into for forty-five minutes.

narrative_blocks.header: He played the singing surgeon on M*A*S*H
narrative_blocks.body: Beyond his recording career, Loudon Wainwright III acted on screen for decades, recurring as a guitar-strumming Army surgeon on M*A*S*H and appearing in films and series from the 1970s onward. The split between musician and actor became a thread running through his one-man shows.

narrative_blocks.header: His father's Life column, found in a cabin
narrative_blocks.body: Put up in a Maine cabin before a show, he pulled a 1971 Life out of the magazine rack and found his father's essay on having the family dog put down. He was laughing by the first paragraph and sobbing by the last, and went home to read all two hundred columns.

narrative_blocks.header: Surviving Twin, made from his father's columns
narrative_blocks.body: It sets his own songs against his father's columns and the letters he wrote his mother from the Marine Corps at seventeen, some of them still scorched from a house fire. It premiered in 2013 at Chapel Hill, where his father had gone to college seventy years before.

people.research_notes: Born 5 September 1946 at Chapel Hill, North Carolina, where his father was at university on the GI Bill; raised at Bedford, Westchester County, and sent to St. Andrew's School in Middletown, Delaware, the same boarding school his father had been miserable at. Dropped out of drama school; at twenty-one was jailed five days in Oklahoma on a marijuana charge and bailed out by his father, then worked as a cinema janitor, a boatyard labourer and a cook to pay him back. His grandmother Eleanor Painter Sloan got him the boatyard job in Rhode Island, where an old lobsterman named Edgar moved him to borrow a friend's guitar and write his first song, 'Edgar'. Signed to Atlantic in 1969; debut album 1970; 'Dead Skunk' 1972; Captain Calvin Spalding in three third-season episodes of M*A*S*H, 1974-75. Grammy for Best Traditional Folk Album, January 2010, for High Wide & Handsome: The Charlie Poole Project. Memoir Liner Notes, 2017. After his mother died in 1997 he fell into a depression and believed he would never write again; he retreated to her cabin in the woods, had therapy, and came out of it with Last Man on Earth (2001). MARRIAGE RECORD: married Kate McGarrigle (the Wikipedia article says 1971, his own book jacket says 1973) and divorced her in 1976; SUZZY ROCHE WAS NEVER A WIFE - in his own words, 'Suzzy and I were never actually married... we lived in sin for nine years'; their daughter is Lucy Wainwright Roche. His second marriage was to Ritamarie Kelly, mother of Alexandra. Since 2015 he has lived with Susan Morrison, an editor at The New Yorker; she is not built. GUARDIAN INTERVIEW, 5 September 2022 (age 76): partner since about 2015 is SUSAN MORRISON, articles editor of The New Yorker; they live on Long Island and the album Lifetime Achievement is dedicated to her - the biggest prize, the great surprise, is I managed to win you. Married twice, four children by three women, and only Lexie is not a musician. On the family money: his great-grandfather's people were investment bankers, and the story in the family is of his grandparents in a European hotel in 1929 being told to get the boat home because a fortune had just gone; none of it reached his father or him, though they belonged to the golf club and a Rhode Island yacht club on a journalist's salary. Went to acting school in Pittsburgh and did not finish; at twenty he enlisted for the army's airborne division and OVERSLEPT the morning he was to enrol, then decided against it; later kept out of Vietnam by a letter from his father's psychiatrist calling him a sociopath, which he says he acted his way into for forty-five minutes. On being called the new Dylan: he stopped listening to Dylan because it would be like being in a horse race and looking over at the other jockey. On the drinking: he would order a shot of Jack Daniel's and a beer and pour half the shot away when nobody was looking, because he wanted to LOOK like he drank more than he did. On the first marriage: they split in Copenhagen days after the wedding; he found her again in London; they separated five years on. I was promiscuous, and that of course is murder on any marriage. I was a shit. DELIBERATELY NOT WRITTEN INTO ANY NB: the song he says he regrets, That Hospital, and what it references about Kate's pregnancy with Martha. It is published and he volunteered it, but it is too personal to a living person to put on a family card.

notable.notable_blurb: Contralto singer-songwriter and songwriting teacher

cross_connections.display_label: was her sister-in-law, who gave her a banjo for her sixteenth birthday

narrative_blocks.header: An open mic win, at thirty-two
narrative_blocks.body: In 1989 she won the Open Mic Finals at the Towne Crier Cafe in Pawling, which got her a first professional booking opening for Shawn Colvin. She was thirty-two, and had co-owned the Bakers Cafe on Katonah Avenue since 1982. She sold her share of the cafe in 2000 and made eleven albums.

narrative_blocks.header: Kate McGarrigle gave her a banjo at sixteen
narrative_blocks.body: Her brother's wife brought traditional music into the family and gave her the instrument for her sixteenth birthday. She took clawhammer lessons from the family friend Jay Ungar and played piano in a string band, then left the banjo alone for thirty years. She found her way back to it in her sixties and started writing songs on it again.

narrative_blocks.header: Her nephew Rufus calls her the Voice
narrative_blocks.body: Loudon Wainwright III is her brother, Kate McGarrigle was her sister-in-law, and Rufus, Martha and Lucy are her nephew and nieces. Her nephew Rufus says that in a family where everyone gets dubbed something, Sloan is most always crowned the Voice. Her second album, From Where You Are, was made in memory of her mother.

people.research_notes: Born 1957, fourth child of Loudon Snowden Wainwright Jr. and Martha Harriet Taylor; younger sister of Loudon Wainwright III; aunt of Rufus, Martha and Lucy Wainwright Roche. Married George McTavey, who died in December 2008 after a long illness; two sons, Sam and Gabe. Contralto; a hybrid of pop, folk, jazz and blues developed in the Greenwich Village clubs. Kate McGarrigle brought traditional music into the family and gave her a banjo for her sixteenth birthday; she took clawhammer lessons from the family friend Jay Ungar and played piano in a string band, moved away from the instrument for decades, and came back to it in her sixties. Co-owner of the Baker's Cafe on Katonah Avenue from 1982; sold her share in 2000 to her business partner and sister, Teddy Wainwright. Won the Open Mic Finals at the Towne Crier Cafe in Pawling in 1989, which produced a first professional booking opening for Shawn Colvin. Eleven albums between the mid-1990s and 2021, ten of them with the guitarist Stephen Murphy; venues include Carnegie Hall, Royal Albert Hall and the Newport Folk Festival. Teaching from 1994: the Swannanoa Gathering, the SummerSongs camps from 1999, and master classes in songwriting at SUNY Purchase from 2017. Rufus Wainwright: in a family where everyone is dubbed something, Sloan is most always crowned The Voice. DEBUT DATE CONFLICT: Wikipedia says the self-titled debut was 1996, the New York Times says 1995, her own biography says 1993 - recorded here as the mid-1990s. SLUG MOVED when Sloan was split out of first_name into the middle name, per Sam; eleanor-sloan-wainwright-1957 becomes eleanor-wainwright-1957, which is worse for a performer billed as Sloan Wainwright. Flagged.

notable.notable_blurb: Canadian folk singer-songwriter, Order of Canada

cross_connections.display_label: is her sister-in-law, who took up the banjo she gave her at sixteen
was a concert pianist who soloed on the same Carnegie Hall stage

bio.bio_blurb: Canadian folk musician of the McGarrigle sisters

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Outremont square named for her, 2013

narrative_blocks.header: She sang for decades with her sister Anna
narrative_blocks.body: Kate McGarrigle performed for more than thirty years alongside her sister Anna as the McGarrigle Sisters, Montreal songwriters whose harmony-laden albums drew a devoted following on both sides of the border. Their songs were covered widely across the folk world.

narrative_blocks.header: She read engineering at McGill
narrative_blocks.body: Behind the bohemian image was a woman who took an engineering course and came out of McGill with a science degree, which almost no woman there did in the 1960s. Her son liked to point it out afterwards, on the way to calling her a genius musician.

narrative_blocks.header: Six weeks before the end, Royal Albert Hall
narrative_blocks.body: Diagnosed in 2006, she set up a fund at the McGill University Health Centre in 2008 to make people aware of sarcoma, the rare cancer she had. Her last public appearance was on the Royal Albert Hall stage with Rufus and Martha, six weeks before she died, raising money for it. Her sister wrote that she departed in a haze of song and love, surrounded by family and good friends.

narrative_blocks.header: The song she wrote when he left
narrative_blocks.body: He went to Europe with another woman while she was carrying what would have been their third child. She followed him from Canada to England, lost the baby, and was told there that he was leaving. She put all of it into Go Leave, and her daughter Martha says you can hear a tear land on a guitar string at the end.

narrative_blocks.header: They split up on the Copenhagen honeymoon
narrative_blocks.body: They married in 1971 and came apart in Denmark days later, after he told her, in what he calls his overly honest and stupid way, how conflicted he felt about having just married her. She walked out; he found her again in London and they went on another five years.

narrative_blocks.header: Rufus called his father to Montreal
narrative_blocks.body: When she was dying in 2010 their son telephoned the husband she had separated from thirty-four years before and asked him to come. He got on a plane and was in the house with the rest of the family when she went. She was past conversation by then, but their son wanted him there.

people.research_notes: Born Catherine Frances McGarrigle. Born 6 February 1946 in Montreal, died there 18 January 2010 of clear-cell sarcoma, aged 63. Youngest of three sisters - Jane, Anna, Kate - raised at Saint-Sauveur-des-Monts north of Montreal by the Irish pianist Francis McGarrigle and Gabrielle Latremouille, French Canadian; first piano lessons from the village nuns. Mountain City Four, 1963-67, with Jack Nissenson and Peter Weldon. Read ENGINEERING at McGill and took a science degree - rare for a woman there in the 1960s - while Anna studied painting at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts. The 1976 self-titled debut with Anna was Melody Maker's record of the year; Junos for Matapedia (1996) and The McGarrigle Hour (1998); Women of Originality award 1999; SOCAN Lifetime Achievement 2006; Member of the Order of Canada 1993. Diagnosed with cancer in 2006 and set up the Kate McGarrigle Fund at the McGill University Health Centre in 2008 to raise awareness of sarcoma. Last public appearance with Rufus and Martha at the Royal Albert Hall six weeks before she died, a benefit for the fund. Anna's notice: she departed in a haze of song and love surrounded by family and good friends. Jane remembers her as wild, wilful and fearless from her earliest days, and not too fine a point on it, a holy terror as a child. Emmylou Harris wrote Darlin Kate for her. Place Kate-McGarrigle was inaugurated in Outremont on 7 August 2013, by where she lived; it holds Robert Wilson's double-chair sculpture Kate and Nora, given by her family - Nora was her more sedate alter ego as a child. She urged Rufus to accept Lorca Cohen's offer that he father her child, and regretted not living to see Viva born.

notable.notable_blurb: Singer-songwriter of the folk trio The Roches

bio.bio_blurb: Singer of the folk trio The Roches

narrative_blocks.header: A Roche sister who also writes novels
narrative_blocks.body: Suzzy Roche sang with her sisters Maggie and Terre as The Roches, a wry, close-harmony trio of the downtown New York folk scene. She later turned to fiction, publishing novels and a children’s book.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine years together, and never married
narrative_blocks.body: She and Loudon Wainwright III were together nine years - in his words they lived in sin and never tied the knot - and had a daughter, Lucy. Long after it ended he called her his best friend, and the two of them still appear on stage together, sometimes with Lucy between them.

people.research_notes: Partner of Loudon Wainwright III for nine years, never married - in his own words, they lived in sin and never tied the knot. Mother of Lucy Wainwright Roche. Long after the relationship ended he called her his best friend; they still appear on stage together, sometimes with Lucy. Photographed with the family in 2012 alongside Martha, Rufus, Lucy and Loudon.

bio.bio_blurb: Craftsman who restored Katonah's old houses

narrative_blocks.header: He put the old houses of Katonah back
narrative_blocks.body: He took a fine arts degree from the School of Visual Arts and turned it into a building trade, founding Katonah Homewrights and restoring a good many of the older houses in the village. He died at fifty-two of complications from a stem cell transplant, twenty-six years married.

people.research_notes: Born 9 July 1956 at Mount Kisco; died 27 December 2008 at Boston under the care of Dana Farber, aged 52, of complications from an earlier stem cell transplant. Fox Lane High School 1974; B.F.A., School of Visual Arts, 1978. Founded Katonah Homewrights and restored many of the older houses in Katonah. Survived by his wife of twenty-six years, Sloan Wainwright McTavey, and sons Samuel George and Gabriel Taylor McTavey; sisters Victoria Marwell and Melanie Grogan, neither built. The twenty-six years dates the marriage to 1982, the same year Sloan took her share of the Bakers Cafe.

marriages.notes: Children-only link: Viva, by parenting partnership with Lorca Cohen, not a marriage.

people.research_notes: Rufus McGarrigle Wainwright, born 22 July 1973 at Rhinebeck, New York; dual US and Canadian citizenship. His parents divorced when he was three and he grew up with his mother in Montreal. Millbrook School - which got its own song - and a short spell studying piano at McGill. Piano from six; touring at thirteen with the McGarrigle Sisters and Family alongside his mother, his aunt Anna and his sister; a Genie nomination at fourteen for I'm a-Runnin' from Tommy Tricker and the Stamp Traveller, and a Juno nomination for most promising male vocalist in 1990. Demo tapes cut in Montreal with Pierre Marchand reached Van Dyke Parks through his father, and Parks passed them to Lenny Waronker at DreamWorks, who signed him in 1996; the debut took 56 songs across 62 rolls of tape. Wrote most of Poses while living six months in the Chelsea Hotel. Eleven studio albums; the operas Prima Donna (2009), Hadrian (Canadian Opera Company, 2018) and Dream Requiem (2024, with Meryl Streep); nine Shakespeare sonnets set for a Robert Wilson theatre piece. Married Jorn Weisbrodt at Montauk on 23 August 2012, Justin Vivian Bond officiating. Sang the Canadian anthem before game five of the 2025 World Series and altered a line of it as a protest against American annexation talk. NOT WRITTEN INTO AN NB, DELIBERATELY, AND SAM SHOULD DECIDE: he has said in several interviews that he was raped in Hyde Park at fourteen by a man he had met in a bar, robbed and half strangled afterwards, and survived by faking an epileptic seizure. It is on the public record and he has told it himself more than once, so it is not a secret - but it is the single most serious thing in this file and it belongs to a living man, so I have not put it on a card without being asked.

notable.notable_blurb: Baroque-pop singer, songwriter, and composer

cross_connections.display_label: wrote the first Broadway comic opera by a woman, in 1904
had two sons by surrogate, a decade after Wainwright had his daughter
won the Metropolitan Opera's prize for his libretto to Mona
, his ancestor eight generations back, laid out the East Village streets

narrative_blocks.header: Pop wasn’t enough, so he composed operas
narrative_blocks.body: Son of Loudon III and Kate McGarrigle, Rufus Wainwright built a career of lush, baroque pop, wrote full-length operas, and re-staged Judy Garland’s legendary Carnegie Hall concert note for note.

narrative_blocks.header: He sang Judy Garland's Carnegie Hall, entire
narrative_blocks.body: In June 2006 he stood on the Carnegie Hall stage and performed the whole of the 1961 Judy Garland concert album recorded there, song for song, to two sold-out houses. He took it on to the London Palladium, the Paris Olympia and the Hollywood Bowl. Garland's daughter Lorna Luft said afterwards that she approved.

narrative_blocks.header: The Met balked at a French libretto
narrative_blocks.body: Peter Gelb commissioned his first opera for the Metropolitan, and the two sides then fell out over his decision to write the libretto in French and over finding it a slot. Prima Donna opened at the Manchester International Festival in 2009 instead. It took a Dora Award two years later.

narrative_blocks.header: Crystal meth took his sight for a while
narrative_blocks.body: The addiction cost him his vision for a time and peaked in a week of 2002 he called the most surreal of his life, hallucinating his father all through it. He decided afterwards that it was rehab or moving in with the real one: I knew I needed an asshole to yell at me, and I felt he fitted the bill. He went to Minnesota for a month.

narrative_blocks.header: A Rolling Stone piece set father against son
narrative_blocks.body: He needled his father about being written up in Rolling Stone for the first time in decades, and only on the back of his son's success. His father went off like a rocket. He put the evening into Dinner at Eight, and his father, asked years later, allowed that he liked that song rather better than the one his sister wrote.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter’s other grandfather is Leonard Cohen
narrative_blocks.body: In a parenting partnership with his friend Lorca Cohen, Rufus Wainwright has a daughter, Viva — a child whose two grandfathers are folk songwriter Loudon Wainwright III and the late Leonard Cohen, joining two of music’s most storied families in one girl.

notable.notable_blurb: Singer-songwriter; owner of Ursa in Montreal

cross_connections.display_label: also a daughter who wrote the book on a famous parent

narrative_blocks.header: The song everyone read as being about him
narrative_blocks.body: Bloody Mother Fucking Asshole arrived in 2005 as the title of an EP and was taken at once as an answer to a father who wrote songs about his family instead of tending to it. She has always refused the reading: the song is not about my dad, she says, he was just the springboard. A year before it she had sung a duet with him on one of his own records.

narrative_blocks.header: A bar in Montreal, a studio downstairs
narrative_blocks.body: She opened Ursa on Parc Avenue in 2019 - a cafe, a bar, a room to play in and a room to record in. When the city shut down she ran sing-alongs off its balconies, and made Love Will Be Reborn downstairs.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote the memoir and named it honestly
narrative_blocks.body: Stories I Might Regret Telling You came out in 2022, in English and in French. She is hardest on herself in it, calling herself average across the board, but she also sets down on the second page that her father had pressed her mother to end the pregnancy, and that knowing she had only just made the cut never quite left her.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother wrote the song that opens it
narrative_blocks.body: Come Home to Mama came out of two years in which she lost her mother and had a son born too early, and it opens with Proserpina, which Kate McGarrigle wrote not long before she died. She has said she stopped hearing it as a sad song and started hearing it as something her mother left behind.

narrative_blocks.header: She learned mid-show that the song was hers
narrative_blocks.body: She had always assumed I'd Rather Be Lonely was about some old girlfriend, and had felt sorry for the woman. Then, waiting to go on at a show she was touring with him, she heard her father tell the audience he had written it about his daughter. She wrote later that part of her wanted to jump from her seat, and that instead she dried her eyes and walked down to the stage.

people.research_notes: Born 8 May 1976 in New York City; moved to Montreal with her mother and brother at one and was raised there. Seven studio albums. Ground Floor, a self-released cassette, 1997; the EPs Bloody Mother Fucking Asshole and I Will Internalize, 2005; the self-titled debut 2005, a Juno nomination for New Artist of the Year. Sang Set the Fire to the Third Bar with Snow Patrol in 2006 - Gary Lightbody wrote it with her voice in mind. I Know You're Married But I've Got Feelings Too (2008) had Donald Fagen on synthesizers and Pete Townshend on guitar. A Piaf record recorded live at Dixon Place in 2009. Come Home to Mama (2012), cut at Sean Lennon's home studio and produced by Yuka Honda, opens with Proserpina, written by her mother shortly before she died. Songs in the Dark (2015) with her half-sister Lucy, as the Wainwright Sisters - the lullabies Kate McGarrigle and Suzzy Roche had sung to them. Goodnight City (2016). Love Will Be Reborn (2021), written after the separation and recorded in the basement of her own bar. Opened URSA on Parc Avenue in Montreal in 2019 - cafe, bar, concert hall and recording room - and ran balcony sing-alongs across the city during the pandemic with POP Montreal. Memoir: Stories I Might Regret Telling You, 2022. Acted in The Aviator and in the HBO series Olive Kitteridge. Married Brad Albetta in September 2007, divorced 2018; two sons, Arcangelo and Francis. SHE DENIES THE OBVIOUS READING of her most famous song: the song is not about my dad, he was just the springboard. Her existing NB1 header has been softened accordingly. REVERSAL WORTH SAM'S DECISION: I earlier kept the abortion her father wrote about out of the NBs because it belonged to a living person who had not spoken of it. She has since put it on the SECOND PAGE of her own memoir, in her own words - that she had only just barely made the cut, and that knowing it did not help. It is now self-published and therefore arguably fair for an NB. Still not written into one; Sam decides.

notable.notable_blurb: Folk singer-songwriter

narrative_blocks.header: She taught grade school before turning to music
narrative_blocks.body: Lucy Wainwright Roche spent years as an elementary-school teacher before stepping fully into the family trade, releasing a string of folk records and touring with her half-siblings. The teaching came first; the songwriting followed.

narrative_blocks.header: Her first solo show was a disaster
narrative_blocks.body: Her own words for it: terrible, awkward, horrible. Halfway through the second one she decided to talk to the room the way she would talk to one person, and that fixed it. I am not much of a mystique builder, she says.

narrative_blocks.header: A song about her came out in 1985
narrative_blocks.body: Her father and her aunt Terre Roche wrote Screaming Issue that year, a lullaby about her as a squalling baby. She spent her childhood disliking it, because people sang it at her wherever she went. She likes it now.

narrative_blocks.header: Her parents still share a stage with her
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother and father were together nine years and never married, and it ended - but they stayed friendly enough that the three of them still turn up on the same bill. Her father calls her mother his best friend.

narrative_blocks.header: They made up the years on the road
narrative_blocks.body: Her parents separated when she was two and her father spent much of her childhood in England, so they saw very little of each other. As an adult she has toured with him a great deal. Most people who miss a parent as a child never get to make it up, she says, and they have.

people.research_notes: Daughter of Suzzy Roche and Loudon Wainwright III, who separated when she was two; he spent much of her childhood in England and they saw little of each other, which she says they have since made up on the road as adults - most people who miss a parent as a child never get to. Half-sister of Rufus and Martha Wainwright. Taught elementary school in New York City and had no intention of performing - I had no interest in being a musician because I was surrounded by them, it seemed like a terrible plan - until Rufus asked her to sing backup on tour. EPs 8 Songs and 8 More; the album There's a Last Time for Everything, made deliberately with no family on it, in a little bubble away from them, and carrying a stripped-down cover of Robyn's Call Your Girlfriend. Songs in the Dark (2015) with Martha, as the Wainwright Sisters - the lullabies Kate McGarrigle and Suzzy Roche had sung to them as children. She first reached listeners in 1985 as the subject of Screaming Issue, a lullaby her father wrote with her aunt Terre Roche about her as a squalling baby, which she disliked as a child because everyone sang it at her. MAGGIE IS NOT BUILT: Sam asked for the Runs in the Family video to go on 'maggie and Lucy'. There is no Maggie Roche in this tree and no other Maggie who fits; she would be Suzzy's sister and Lucy's aunt, and she sits outside the easter-egg rule as the sister of an unmarried partner. The video is on Lucy alone until Sam says whether to build her. CORROBORATION, incidental: a Guardian review of 11 November 2015 describes Martha's son Arc as five years old, which fits the 16 November 2009 birth date the fan wiki gives and this project had only recorded as approximate. The same review calls Lucy Martha's stepsister; they are half-sisters, same father.

narrative_blocks.header: Three chords on his father's old guitar
narrative_blocks.body: He played jazz saxophone at Fox Lane, then found his father's old guitar in high school, learned three chords and wrote a song called God, I Wish I Could Sing. Years later, at a folk-song week his mother was teaching in North Carolina, he stood up and sang in front of her for the first time. She had to hold herself together, because she was the one running the class.

people.research_notes: Elder son of George Edward McTavey and Eleanor Sloan Wainwright. Twenty-five in August 2008, so born about 1983 - no exact date sourced. Jazz saxophonist at the Fox Lane school; found his father's old guitar in high school, learned three chords and wrote a first song called God, I Wish I Could Sing. Sang in front of his mother for the first time during Contemporary Folk Song Week at the Swannanoa Gathering in Asheville, in his third year of college, while she was teaching it. Living in Brooklyn in 2008, working as a geologist, with a five-song CD called The Sampler; opened for his mother five or six times by then.

Younger son of George Edward McTavey and Eleanor Sloan Wainwright. Twenty-one in August 2008, so born about 1987 - no exact date sourced. Taking college classes that year and helping care for his father through the bone marrow transplant.

narrative_blocks.header: An enabler of artists, by his own choice
narrative_blocks.body: He studied opera direction in Berlin under Ruth Berghaus, Heiner Muller and Peter Stein, and became Robert Wilson's personal assistant. Interning at Wilson's laboratory on Long Island settled it: I realized that I wasn't an artist, I was an enabler of artists. He was running the place by 2006.

narrative_blocks.header: Four years running Toronto's Luminato
narrative_blocks.body: He took the city's arts festival in 2012 and held it to 2016, on the principle that a festival should not simply buy in productions from the touring circuit but get artists to make something that did not exist yet. Joni Mitchell's seventieth birthday concert and the North American premiere of Robert Wilson's Marina Abramovic piece both happened on his watch.

people.research_notes: Born 26 January 1973 in Hamburg. Studied opera direction at the Hanns Eisler Music Conservatory in Berlin, graduating in 2000, working as a student under Ruth Berghaus, Heiner Muller, Peter Stein, Peter Konwitschny and Robert Wilson, and becoming Wilson's personal assistant. Interned at the Watermill Center, Wilson's laboratory on Long Island, where he concluded he would rather enable art than make it. Afterwards McKinsey & Company, assistant director at the Deutsches Theater, co-founder of Zwischenpalastnutzung, and artistic production director at the Berlin State Opera. Moved to the United States in 2006 as executive director of RW Work Ltd and director of the Watermill Center, building partnerships with the Guggenheim, the Baryshnikov Arts Center, the Moscow Biennale, MASS MoCA and Columbia among others. Artistic director of Toronto's Luminato Festival from January 2012 to July 2016; artistic director of ALL ARTS, WNET's streaming channel, from 2018. NOTHING ABOUT HIM WAS EVER HIDDEN: the living-person rule suppresses DATES only. His card looked bare because he had no NBs at all - now he has two.

bio.bio_blurb: Bassist and record producer, Monkey Boy Studios

narrative_blocks.header: He produced what he played on
narrative_blocks.body: A bassist and co-owner of Monkey Boy Studios in Tribeca, Brad Albetta produced much of Martha Wainwright's catalogue and played bass in her band at the same time, and co-produced Willie Nile's Beautiful Wreck of the World. They married in 2007 and divorced in 2018, and the record she made next was written out of it.

people.research_notes: Bassist and producer; co-owner of Monkey Boy Studios in Tribeca, where much of Martha Wainwright's work was recorded, and co-producer of Willie Nile's Beautiful Wreck of the World. Produced and played on his wife's records and toured in her band. Married Martha Wainwright in September 2007; divorced 2018; two sons, Arcangelo and Francis.

narrative_blocks.header: Her two grandfathers wrote the songs
narrative_blocks.body: Her father is Rufus Wainwright; her mother is the photographer Lorca Cohen, whose father was Leonard Cohen. The two of them were childhood friends who never married, and she lives with her mother under an arrangement the three of them made between them. Her grandmother Kate McGarrigle had urged the whole thing on, and died thirteen months before she was born.

narrative_blocks.header: Three parents, and a Deputy Dad
narrative_blocks.body: Her father announced her birth as being to proud parents Lorca Cohen, Rufus Wainwright and Deputy Dad Jorn Weisbrodt, signing himself daddy number one. All three of them were to raise her, and she lives with her mother. Her name is for her grandmother Kate McGarrigle, who had died thirteen months before.

people.research_notes: Born 2 February 2011 in Los Angeles. Named for her grandmother, the singer Kate McGarrigle, who died thirteen months before. Her father announced her on his website as born to proud parents Lorca Cohen, Rufus Wainwright and Deputy Dad Jorn Weisbrodt, calling himself daddy number one and welcoming her with a line from A La Claire Fontaine - il y a longtemps que je t aime, jamais je ne t oublierai. He publicly corrected the press that called her mother a surrogate. She is a granddaughter of Leonard Cohen and of Loudon Wainwright III, and a niece of Martha Wainwright.

notable.notable_blurb: Gould heiress, writer, and socialite

bio.bio_blurb: Gould heiress and writer; later Lady MacNeal

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Her grandfather's estate on the Hudson, a Gould house all her life.

narrative_blocks.header: Born on a yacht into the Gould fortune
narrative_blocks.body: A granddaughter of robber baron Jay Gould, Edith was born aboard her father’s yacht and eloped at eighteen — hours after graduating from Miss Spence’s — with the artist Carroll Wainwright. She later wrote a candid memoir of growing up a Gould.

narrative_blocks.header: At twenty-four she published the family
narrative_blocks.body: Her 1925 autobiography told at length what it was like to be a millionaire's granddaughter, and set down the inner secrets of Gould family life as she had known them as a child. She was the sixth of seven, and twenty-four when it appeared.

narrative_blocks.header: Divorced and remarried the same afternoon
narrative_blocks.body: She got her decree at Reno in 1932 and married Sir Hector MacNeal, a Scottish shipowner she had met there, within hours of it, and there was no property settlement. Born under a British flag on her father's yacht, she died a British knight's wife five years later. She was thirty-six, and it was a liver ailment, not the pneumonia often given.

people.research_notes: Born 3 August 1901 aboard her father's yacht Sybarite, anchored off Cold Spring Harbor and flying the British flag - she would die the wife of a British knight. Sixth of the seven children of George Jay Gould I and the actress Edith Kingdon; granddaughter of Jay Gould. Miss Spence's School. Married Carroll Livingston Wainwright at Elkton hours after graduating, 27 May 1920. In 1925 she published her autobiography, telling at length how it felt to be a millionaire's granddaughter and setting down the inner secrets of Gould family life as she had known them as a child. Divorced at Reno in 1932 and married Sir Hector MacNeal, the Scottish shipowner and Cunard director, within hours of the decree; she had met him in Reno. There was no property settlement. Died at Gulf Crest, East Hampton, on 10 September 1937, aged thirty-six, of a liver ailment, after two years of poor health; buried in the Gould mausoleum at Woodlawn. Her daughter Caroline, thirteen, was told by radio to the Normandie, on which she was coming home from school in England.

bio.bio_blurb: Jay Gould’s eldest son and railroad heir

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Grew up on the estate; his father bought it when he was sixteen.

narrative_blocks.header: He inherited an empire and slowly lost it
narrative_blocks.body: Eldest son and chief heir of Jay Gould, George ran the family’s transcontinental railroad system at the turn of the century, only to see rivals led by E. H. Harriman dismantle much of it.

narrative_blocks.header: He saw Tutankhamun and was dead in months
narrative_blocks.body: He went to Egypt in 1923 and visited the newly opened tomb, took a fever there, and died of pneumonia on the French Riviera that May at fifty-nine. The papers made what they liked of the timing. He is at Woodlawn with his father.

narrative_blocks.header: He hid his own name from Harriman
narrative_blocks.body: To push the Denver and Rio Grande through to San Francisco he sent surveyors down the Feather River canyon, and had to run the work through third-party companies because E. H. Harriman held both the Union Pacific and the Southern Pacific and would have stopped him. The route they staked became the Western Pacific main line.

people.research_notes: Eldest of the six; took the largest single share of his father's estate and his railroad holdings. Ran the Denver and Rio Grande Western, the Western Pacific and the Manhattan Railway. Sent surveyors through the Feather River canyon to reach San Francisco and had to hide his hand behind third-party companies because E. H. Harriman held both the Union Pacific and the Southern Pacific; the line they staked became the Western Pacific main. His mother strongly disapproved of his marrying an actress. He kept a second household with Guinevere Jeanne Sinclair and three children, and married her on 1 May 1922 once Edith was dead. Died on the French Riviera on 16 May 1923 of pneumonia, after taking a fever in Egypt where he had gone to see the tomb of Tutankhamun. MARRIAGE YEAR CONFLICT: this record says 1886, Wikipedia says 1885.

notable.notable_blurb: Gilded Age railroad magnate and robber baron

cross_connections.display_label: financed his first tannery, then quit over his risk-taking
called him the mightiest disaster ever to befall the country
inherited Hurst-Pierrepont, the Davis villa at Garrison, in 1902

bio.bio_blurb: Gilded Age railroad financier and speculator

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Bought the estate in 1880 and lived there until his death in 1892.

narrative_blocks.header: Wall Street’s most hated robber baron
narrative_blocks.body: A self-made speculator in railroads and telegraphs, he built one of the Gilded Age's great fortunes. Mark Twain thought the lesson the country drew from it worse than the fortune: get money quickly, get it in abundance, dishonestly if you can and honestly if you must.

narrative_blocks.header: He tried to corner the entire gold market
narrative_blocks.body: In 1869 he and James Fisk schemed to corner the nation's gold supply; when the Treasury released gold on September 24 the crash became known as Black Friday and ruined scores of speculators.

narrative_blocks.header: He invented a forest to get a partner
narrative_blocks.body: Hired in 1856 to survey Zadock Pratt's land, he proposed a partnership instead and told the tanner of a hemlock stand he had not yet found. He went into the Pennsylvania woods, found one, and they built the tannery; he broke with Pratt once the hides fetched more in New York.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty cents and a sack of clothes
narrative_blocks.body: Told the boy wanted nothing to do with farming, his father drove him to a school and left him with fifty cents and a sack of clothes. He kept a blacksmith's books to pay his way, and was twenty when he published a history of the county.

narrative_blocks.header: He commuted by steam yacht, behind armed guards
narrative_blocks.body: He bought Lyndhurst at Tarrytown in 1880 for the greenhouse, filled it with orchids, and had the grounds patrolled by armed men. He went down to Manhattan by steam yacht, and took a certain pride in being the most hated man in America.

narrative_blocks.header: He changed the name and little else
narrative_blocks.body: Lyndenhurst was named for the linden trees; he cut it to Lyndhurst and altered almost nothing of Alexander Jackson Davis's 1838 house. Fifty pieces of the architect's furniture still stand in it.

narrative_blocks.header: Lord and Burnham built him a glass house
narrative_blocks.body: The greenhouse that drew him to the place burned, and in 1881 he replaced it with an iron-framed, onion-domed conservatory three hundred and ninety feet long.

people.relational_label_override: Grandfather-in-law of an Eleventh Generation Hooker
people.research_notes: Born Jason Gould at Roxbury, Delaware County, 27 May 1836; died in New York 2 December 1892 and buried at Woodlawn. Married Helen Day Miller on 22 January 1863 at the South Dutch Church in New York; six children. He is here as the grandfather-in-law of an eleventh-generation descendant, through his granddaughter Edith, who eloped with Carroll Livingston Wainwright in 1920. Born Jason Gould at Roxbury to John Burr Gould (1792-1866) and Mary More (1798-1841) and raised poor on a small dairy farm; his father, told the boy wanted nothing to do with farming, dropped him at a nearby school with fifty cents and a sack of clothes. Hobart Academy, paid for by keeping the books at a blacksmith's, who then offered him a half-interest in the shop. Surveyed Ulster County in 1854 and published a History of Delaware County and Border Wars of New York in 1856, at twenty, having shortened Jason to Jay by then. Tanning at Gouldsboro with Zadock Pratt; ice harvested off Gouldsboro Lake and railed to New York for the summer trade. The Erie War with Fisk and Drew; Tammany, with Boss Tweed made a director of the Erie; the gold corner of Black Friday, 1869. By 1882 he controlled about a ninth of American railway mileage and Western Union besides. Bought Lyndhurst at Tarrytown in 1880, drawn by the greenhouse, kept Ferdinand Mangold on as master gardener and filled it with orchids, patrolled the grounds with armed guards round the clock, and commuted to Manhattan on his steam yacht Atalanta. Took a certain pride in being called the most hated man in America. Died of tuberculosis on 2 December 1892 and lies at Woodlawn. His daughter Helen completed the Roxbury church he was funding and endowed the Gould Memorial Library at New York University.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Married into the household that summered at Lyndhurst.

narrative_blocks.header: She died on her own private golf course
narrative_blocks.body: A Broadway actress before her marriage, Edith Kingdon Gould left the stage for the Gould fortune and the vast Georgian Court estate in New Jersey. She died suddenly of a heart attack there in 1921 while playing a round of golf on the family links.

narrative_blocks.header: One afternoon, back on a stage
narrative_blocks.body: Twenty-three years after leaving the theatre to marry a Gould, she played the lead in a one-act comedy in the ballroom of the Plaza, with the furniture carried over from her own apartments and her sons ushering. The boxes held Vanderbilts, Fishes and Mackays. An old friend from Daly's said her acting was like mahogany when first hewn and when seasoned.

people.research_notes: Daughter of Charles Dennis Kingdon and Mary Carter of Toronto; educated in England; a working stage actress at Daly's until she married. She and George hired Bruce Price to build Georgian Court at Lakewood, now Georgian Court University, and she died on its golf course on 13 November 1921. Buried in the Jay Gould mausoleum at Woodlawn. In January 1908 she went back on a stage for one afternoon, playing the lead in Mrs. Van Vechten's Divorce Dance in the ballroom of the Plaza with Frederick Townsend Martin: the furniture came from her own apartments, her sons Kingdon and George ushered and paged, and the boxes held Vanderbilts, Fishes, Mills, Drexels and Mackays. An old friend from Daly's said her acting reminded him of mahogany when first hewn and when seasoned with a few years of care and confidence.

notable.notable_blurb: U.S. Congressman from New York, 1953–1961

cross_connections.display_label: planned Allied deception one echelon above his own OSS post
, his great-great-great-great-grandfather, gave St. Mark's its land
was chief engineer of the First Army whose OSS units he led in France

bio.bio_blurb: New York congressman and OSS officer
bio.title: Lt. Col.

military_service.role: Commanding officer, First Army OSS units in France
military_service.notes: Enlisted as a private immediately after Pearl Harbor and rose through the ranks; commanded the First Army OSS units in France, then worked on intelligence coordination in the War Department at Washington. Discharged as a captain; held the rank of major in the Active Army Reserve while in Congress and retired a lieutenant colonel in 1960. In 1956 he became the first member of Congress and the first reservist to take the combat parachute training course with the 82d Airborne Division.

narrative_blocks.header: From OSS spy to the U.S. Congress
narrative_blocks.body: Stuyvesant Wainwright II left Yale to serve with the Office of Strategic Services in wartime Europe, then won four terms in Congress — where he authored the bill that created the Fire Island National Seashore.

narrative_blocks.header: A Marine under him was a film star
narrative_blocks.body: Wainwright's OSS detachment in First Army intelligence included a “Captain John Hamilton,” really the actor Sterling Hayden, fresh from running guns to Tito. Wainwright, a rich young conservative of twenty-four, baited him about politics.

narrative_blocks.header: The first congressman to jump with the 82nd
narrative_blocks.body: In 1956, while in the House, Wainwright took the 82nd Airborne's combat parachute course, the first congressman and first reservist to do it. He had enlisted as a private after Pearl Harbor and served in the reserve fifteen years.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the bill that saved Fire Island
narrative_blocks.body: Wainwright authored the legislation establishing the Fire Island National Seashore, shielding the barrier island from development. Though he introduced it while in Congress, it became law in 1964, after he had left office.

narrative_blocks.header: He backed both Eisenhower-era Civil Rights Acts
narrative_blocks.body: Across four terms representing eastern Long Island, Stuyvesant Wainwright II sat on the Armed Services and Foreign Affairs committees and voted for the Civil Rights Acts of 1957 and 1960. He narrowly lost his seat in the 1960 election.

narrative_blocks.header: Thanksgiving at Georgica Pond, every year
narrative_blocks.body: Every November generations of Wainwrights gathered for Thanksgiving at his house on Georgica Pond, his favourite day of the year. He raced his boats as Wainscott Wind, and hunted, golfed, played squash and sailed into old age.

people.research_notes: Congressional Directory / CIA release: born New York 16 March 1921; Yale University and Yale Law School; married Janet Parsons; four children, Stuyvesant 3d, Jonathan Mayhew, Snowden and Laura Livingston; of Wainscott, N.Y. Enlisted as a private immediately after Pearl Harbor, rose through the ranks, commanded First Army OSS units in France, then intelligence coordination in the War Department; discharged as captain, later a major in the Active Army Reserve. First Member of Congress and first reservist to take the combat parachute training course with the 82d Airborne Division (1956). Member of the law firm Wainwright & Matthews; vestryman of St. Luke's Episcopal Church; University Club of New York, Union Club, Masonic Lodge, Chi Psi, Phi Delta Phi. Elected to the 83d Congress 4 November 1952 and reelected 2 November 1954, 6 November 1956 and to the 86th; member of the University Club of New York, the Union Club of New York City, a Masonic lodge, Chi Psi and Phi Delta Phi. CORRECTION TO MY OWN CC, 2026-07-28: I first wrote the Ingersoll link as though Wainwright ran OSS units 'under the deceptions Ingersoll planned'. That overstates it and is not documented. What IS documented, in a history of Marines in the OSS, is that First Army's G-2 wanted as little to do with Donovan's people as he could manage, that after August 1944 only a token OSS force was attached to the command, and that the 24-year-old Wainwright headed it inside the G-2's political section. Ingersoll's deception work sat at 12th Army Group, the formation above First Army. Both men were in Allied intelligence in the same theatre in the same months; neither source puts one under the other's orders, and the CC now says only what is on the record. THE MARINE UNDER HIM WAS STERLING HAYDEN, serving as Captain John Hamilton - the film actor, who had run guns to Tito's partisans in the Adriatic. The same account has Wainwright, a wealthy young conservative, delighting in taunting Hayden about his support for Tito and his left-wing politics, and Hayden answering with a clenched-fist communist salute. Hayden later named names to HUAC and spent the rest of his life ashamed of it. FOUR MARRIAGES, ALL ENDED IN DIVORCE, three wives predeceasing him, per his 2010 obituary; only Janet Isabel Parsons is built and the other three are unnamed in the sources here. Also: Westminster School, Simsbury; a year at Lawrenceville 1936-37 on the tennis team in Dickinson House; enlisted as a private 30 January 1942 at twenty, commissioned 1943, overseas 30 December 1943, home 10 June 1945, discharged a captain 13 December 1945. Partner in Walker, Beale, Wainwright & Wolf and later Battle, Fowler, Lidstone, Jaffin, Pierce & Kheel; opened his own Wainscott office in 1975. Director and general counsel of Potter Instrument; first president of Miltope. Diplomatic missions to Korea and Vietnam. Raced under the name WAINSCOTT WIND - Newport to Bermuda, Annapolis to Newport, Marblehead to Halifax, and at least thirty-five Block Island races. Thanksgiving was his favourite day; the family gathered at Georgica Pond for it every year. MARRIAGE COUNT, ON ONE SOURCE ONLY: the East Hampton Star obituary says all four of his marriages ended in divorce and three wives predeceased him. NOTHING ELSE HERE CORROBORATES IT - FamilySearch and every other record show only the 1941 marriage to Janet Isabel Parsons. The claim has been taken back out of the NB and left here until a second source turns up.

bio.bio_blurb: Gould granddaughter raised between two continents

institutions.institution_blurb: Attended Miss Porter's School in Farmington, Connecticut.

narrative_blocks.header: She wore her grandmother's veil to St. Thomas
narrative_blocks.body: She married an ensign at St. Thomas Church three days before Christmas 1945, in a veil of tulle and duchesse lace that had belonged to her grandmother, Caroline Snowden. Her two brothers ushered, one of them a Marine sergeant. The reception filled the Plaza ballroom.

narrative_blocks.header: A childhood measured in Atlantic crossings
narrative_blocks.body: Her parents divorced when she was eight and she grew up going back and forth: the Aurania out of Southampton in 1931, the President Harding out of Le Havre in 1934, and at fourteen a school in Berkshire with Claridge's given as her address. She came home on the Normandie.

people.research_notes: Middle child of Carroll Livingston Wainwright and Edith Catherine Gould, and eight when they divorced. A childhood of Atlantic crossings: the Aurania out of Southampton in August 1931, the President Harding out of Le Havre in April 1934, and in 1938, at fourteen, over to school at Wallingford in Berkshire, with Claridge's given as her English address, home again on the Normandie that August. Miss Porter's at Farmington; Pine Manor Junior College, 1943; the Junior Assembly the same year. Married Ensign Edward Townsend Shean at St. Thomas Church, New York, on 22 December 1945, the Rev. Dr. Roelif H. Brooks officiating, in a veil of tulle and duchesse lace that had been her grandmother's - Mrs. Carl F. Wolff, who was Caroline Smith Snowden. Her brothers Carroll Jr. and Stuyvesant 2d ushered. Five children: Townsend, Edith, Margo, Clair and Caroline. Divorced 1963. Died at East Hampton at forty-five; the Times obituary said forty-six. BIRTHPLACE CONFLICT: FindAGrave says New York City, a family association record says Rye.

notable.notable_blurb: Rockefeller-family lawyer at Milbank, Tweed

cross_connections.display_label: put his own name into Milbank, Tweed before the war
was the Rockefellers' lawyer a generation before him
served the Rockefellers from Milbank Tweed too
gave the American Museum of Natural History thirty years
built Rockefeller Center, which he sold out of the family in 1989

institutions.institution_blurb: Attended St. Paul's School in Concord, New Hampshire.

military_service.role: U.S. Marine Corps aviation
military_service.notes: Lied about his age to enlist at seventeen in 1942 and trained on the Grumman F4U Corsair; the war ended before he saw combat. Discharged a first lieutenant.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty years at Milbank, Tweed, one firm
narrative_blocks.body: He made partner in 1963 and stayed until he retired, doing trusts, estates and not-for-profits, and was deep enough in Rockefeller business to handle the sale of Rockefeller Center in 1989. His clients were the institutions themselves: the American Museum of Natural History, Cooper Union, Vassar, the Episcopal Church Pension Group.

narrative_blocks.header: He lied about his age to fly Corsairs
narrative_blocks.body: He was seventeen in 1942 and told the Marine Corps otherwise. They trained him on the Grumman F4U and the war ended before he got to use it. He came out a first lieutenant and married Nina Walker at East Hampton three years later.

narrative_blocks.header: He put wolves back, and he ran cattle
narrative_blocks.body: He sat on the board of the Greater Yellowstone Coalition and was instrumental in returning wolves to the region, which is not what a man with a cattle ranch in the Centennial Valley of Montana is expected to do. He kept the ranch and visited it often.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-four floors, on foot, for practice
narrative_blocks.body: He kept himself in hard condition into old age at squash, fishing and duck shooting, and when a hiking or climbing holiday was coming he would walk up the forty-four floors to his office at Chase Manhattan Plaza rather than take the lift.

narrative_blocks.header: At eight, he stowed away to sail home
narrative_blocks.body: Homesick in Bermuda, eight-year-old “Sonny” Wainwright stowed away on a New York-bound liner and made headlines worldwide as “the silk-stockinged stowaway.” He grew up to spend his career as a Rockefeller-family lawyer at Milbank, Tweed.

narrative_blocks.header: He sold Rockefeller Center to Mitsubishi
narrative_blocks.body: He was the lead lawyer when the Rockefeller Group sold Rockefeller Center to Mitsubishi Estate in 1989. His clients were mostly the city's institutions — the Museum of Natural History, Cooper Union, Vassar — whose boards he also sat on.

people.research_notes: Known all his life as Sonny. Born 28 December 1925; grew up in New York and on West End Road at East Hampton in the house his parents built - the family obituary calls it Gullcrest, the 1937 press called it Gulf Crest, and both spellings are on the record. Malcolm Gordon School at Garrison, then St. Paul's at Concord. Lied about his age to join the Marine Corps in 1942 at seventeen and trained on Grumman F4U Corsairs; the war ended first. Married Nina Walker at East Hampton on 2 July 1948; Yale College 1949; Harvard Law 1952. Assistant general counsel to Governor Nelson Rockefeller 1959-60, and otherwise his whole career at Milbank, Tweed, Hadley & McCloy, a partner from 1963, in trusts, estates and not-for-profits; deep in Rockefeller family business, including the Rockefeller Group's sale of Rockefeller Center in 1989. Clients included the American Museum of Natural History, Cooper Union, Vassar, the New York Community Trust and the Episcopal Church Pension Group. Trustee of the Boys' Club of New York for fifty years from 1966, president 1986-94, honorary trustee from 2000, and the man who got the first women elected to its board; trustee of the AMNH 1968-94, Cooper Union 1970-95, US Trust 1981-98. Boards of the Edward John Noble Foundation, the Yale University Council and the Greater Yellowstone Coalition. Vestryman of Trinity Church Wall Street and St. Luke's East Hampton; treasurer and vice-president of the New York City Bar; adjunct professor at Washington and Lee law school; New York State Commission on Judicial Conduct 1974-83. President of the Down Town Association 1985-92 and of the Maidstone Club 1970-73. A colleague said his service was characterised by the sense of decency he brought to it.

institutions.institution_blurb: Attended Miss Porter's School in Farmington, Connecticut.

narrative_blocks.header: Married in her parents' Texas garden
narrative_blocks.body: A Rochester broker's daughter, out of Miss Porter's at Farmington, she married him in her parents' house at Jourdanton, Texas in June 1941, six months before he enlisted. There was a garden reception and they drove off to Canada. She was twenty-one.

people.research_notes: Second and last child of Thomas Crouse Parsons, a broker, and Janet Blanchard Mowry; raised at 975 University Avenue, Rochester. The Columbia School in Texas, then Miss Porter's at Farmington. Married Stuyvesant Wainwright II on 12 June 1941 in her parents' house at Jourdanton, Texas, the Rev. Samuel Capers of Christ Church, San Antonio, officiating; a garden reception followed and they left by motor car for Canada. Living at 1350 Madison Avenue in 1950 while he practised law. narrative_blocks.header: He fought to save his beloved Georgica Pond
narrative_blocks.body: A Yale- and NYU-trained lawyer who spent his whole career at Cadwalader, Wickersham & Taft, Jonathan Wainwright co-founded the Friends of Georgica Pond to battle the algal blooms threatening the East Hampton pond he loved.

narrative_blocks.header: Proudest of the one-room schoolhouse
narrative_blocks.body: St. Bernard's, Landon, St. Paul's, Yale and a law degree from New York University, and his family said the schooling he was proudest of was the Wainscott one-room schoolhouse and Mrs. Mansir, who taught him in it.

people.research_notes: Called Jon. Born at Baltimore 4 April 1944 to Stuyvesant Wainwright II and Janet Parsons; raised mostly at Wainscott and lived between there and New York all his life. St. Bernard's in Manhattan, the Landon School near Washington, St. Paul's at Concord, then Yale and a law degree from New York University in 1968 - but his family said he was proudest of the Wainscott one-room schoolhouse and Mrs. Mansir who taught him in it. His whole legal career, 1968 until his death, at Cadwalader, Wickersham & Taft, where he was among the profession's foremost hands on investment management, alternative investment products and family offices, and senior counsel at the end. Federal Bar Council; boards of a national trust company, investment managers, family offices and closely held companies. Secretary and treasurer of the B. Robert Williamson Jr. Foundation from 2012; director of Lighthouse Guild International 2005-18 and its vice chairman 2010-18. Board of the Nature Conservancy on Long Island 2013-20. Founded the Friends of Georgica Pond Foundation in 2015 over the blue-green algal blooms, was its treasurer 2015-23 and president from 2023; under him it hired Dr. Christopher Gobler as science adviser, put an aquatic weed harvester on the pond and set the first round-the-clock telemetry buoy on Long Island. His house on the pond was called Home Again and he kept a cottage at the Long Point Company, a duck-hunting club in Canada. A squash player young, an upland and duck hunter always, a gardener and a New York Times puzzle whiz; Maidstone Club. Died of esophageal cancer at home on Park Avenue after five years ill, aged 80; buried at Wainscott. First married Patricia Gilchrest, two sons; married Candace Drake 29 January 1993, with two stepdaughters, Kate Olmsted Grossman and Lexi Olmsted Tran. Married Patsy Gilchrist at St. Luke's Episcopal Church, East Hampton, on 26 June 1966, the Rev. Samuel Davis officiating, with the reception at the Maidstone Club.

narrative_blocks.body: Dave joined The Daily Pantagraph in 1953, the Bloomington paper his great-great-grandfather Jesse Weldon Fell had acquired in 1846, and published it from 1968 to 1980 while running Evergreen Communications. narrative_blocks.body: Dave shipped to Japan in 1951 and then to Korea as a second lieutenant of Marines, where he led a rifle platoon for eight months. narrative_blocks.header: Salmon rivers from Iceland to Russia
narrative_blocks.body: Dave was a trustee of the Illinois Nature Conservancy and a lifelong conservationist, fishing for Atlantic salmon in Iceland, Norway, Canada, Alaska and Russia and releasing what he caught.

narrative_blocks.header: He raised Nancy's son as his own
narrative_blocks.body: Dave married Nancy Snowden Smith of Philadelphia on 14 November 1958 and raised her two-year-old son, James Bogert Tailer IV, as his own. Nancy died at Tucson in 1995 after thirty-seven years of marriage, and in 1998 he married Sharon Adkins Todd.

Married John Howard Wainwright at Stuyvesant Square on 25 April 1861 and, after his death, William Huggins Catlin (1845-1911) on 5 July 1880 - which is why the 1902 portrait of her by Marie Constantin, at the Cincinnati Art Museum, is titled Mrs. William Huggins Catlin. OBITUARY (1928): died Sunday night at her home in Rye; funeral at Christ Church, Rye, where she had been a parishioner for eighty years, by the Rev. Richard Townsend Henshaw; burial Greenwood Union Cemetery. Her father Nicholas W. Stuyvesant was a descendant of Peter Stuyvesant in the fifth generation. Her son Col. J. narrative_blocks.body: She was a parishioner of Christ Church, Rye, for eighty years, and her funeral was read there in March 1928. Two of her sons were buried out of the same church, and all three lie in Greenwood Union nearby.

narrative_blocks.body: Margaret's son Col. J. Mayhew Wainwright rose from the New York Assembly and Senate to four terms in Congress, with a turn as Harding's Assistant Secretary of War. He built Wainwright House on Milton Point, bought by his father in 1864.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandfather's sister-in-law married a Hooker
narrative_blocks.body: Helen Reade married Judge James Hooker in 1816, and her sister married Margaret's grandfather, Nicholas William Stuyvesant. His son John married Mary Austin Yates, a Hooker; Margaret's son made it three, marrying Caroline Snowden in 1889.

narrative_blocks.header: Peter Stuyvesant runs down to a folk singer
narrative_blocks.body: Her father descended in the fifth generation from Peter Stuyvesant, the last Dutch governor of New York. Four generations the other way from Margaret, the same line reaches the singer-songwriter Loudon Wainwright III.

narrative_blocks.header: He sold Northern carriages South, then his own
narrative_blocks.body: He started out in 1830 by opening a repository in a Southern city to sell Northern-built carriages, then came home to New Haven to make his own. Through a run of partnerships that ended as Henry Hooker & Company, incorporated in 1868, he built one of the largest carriage works in the country.

narrative_blocks.header: His carriages sold as far as France
narrative_blocks.body: The firm built to a high standard for the carriage trade of the cities, and its reputation carried well beyond New Haven — it kept a New York sales agency and shipped work abroad, even to the carriage houses of France. One of its phaetons survives today, the Henry Hooker maker stencil still preserved beneath the seat cushion.

narrative_blocks.header: He remade the house his grandfather built
narrative_blocks.body: The old Hooker homestead at Kensington had stood since about 1769, raised by his grandfather Elijah. As the carriage money came in he modernized it — a bracketed roof and dormer gable, a new entry portico, the central chimney torn out to open a hall three stories high — and kept it as a summer home until he died there in 1873.

narrative_blocks.header: He left the works to two sons
narrative_blocks.body: At his death in 1873 the company passed to two of his sons — Frank Henry as treasurer and manager, Norman Albert as secretary — who kept the Hooker name in the carriage trade for another generation.

narrative_blocks.body: He headed Henry Hooker & Company, the New Haven carriage house his father had built into one of the largest in the country, and served for years as secretary-treasurer of the national carriage manufacturers' association. narrative_blocks.body: In 1878, under his management, Henry Hooker & Company put its name among the original subscribers to the New Haven District Telephone Company — the first commercial telephone exchange in the world. narrative_blocks.header: A graduated shock restarted the heart
narrative_blocks.body: At Johns Hopkins in the early 1930s he showed that a correctly measured electric shock could restore the rhythm of a fibrillating heart. Modern defibrillation rests on that work.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave up teaching at thirty-eight
narrative_blocks.body: Before Hopkins made him an instructor he had spent several years in Europe watching the famous physiological laboratories work. In 1914 he left teaching for research and editing, and never went back.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-two years editing, much of it unpaid
narrative_blocks.body: He was managing editor of the American Journal of Physiology from 1914 until he died, made it pay for itself, and in 1921 helped found its companion, Physiological Reviews.

narrative_blocks.header: Secretary to the biologists' federation
narrative_blocks.body: The Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology made him its first permanent secretary in 1935, and he held the post alongside both editorships.

narrative_blocks.header: The recreation centre he built with Edith
narrative_blocks.body: Roosevelt Park opened at Baltimore around 1916 with the two of them behind it. In 1941 they made a further gift to the city, towards a recreation centre for its Black residents.

narrative_blocks.header: The guild that named their street
narrative_blocks.body: He and Edith founded the Guild of St George in 1907. Building at Roland Park a few years later, they named the new lane St George's Road and the house on it Uplands.

narrative_blocks.header: He died where he had spent his career
narrative_blocks.body: Several months' illness ended at Johns Hopkins Hospital on 1 August 1946, when he was seventy. He was cremated, and his ashes went to Evergreen Cemetery at New Haven, where he was born.

narrative_blocks.body: His mother, Anna Louisa Newton Hooker, died July 6, 1926; he followed barely five weeks later, on August 15, at the family seat in Kensington, aged fifty-four.

narrative_blocks.header: Took suffrage to the streets by automobile
narrative_blocks.body: She founded Maryland's Just Government League in 1909 and its weekly Maryland Suffrage News in 1912, then carried the cause across the state in open-air meetings held from an automobile. In 1917 she became editor of The Suffragist, the National Woman's Party paper.

narrative_blocks.header: Her sister was Katharine Hepburn's mother
narrative_blocks.body: Edith and her older sister Katharine Houghton Hepburn were both prominent leaders of the woman-suffrage movement; that sister's daughter was the actress Katharine Hepburn, making Edith the actress's aunt. The Houghton sisters were raised by freethinking parents who championed women's education.

narrative_blocks.header: Left Johns Hopkins medicine for a reformer's life
narrative_blocks.body: One of the first women admitted to the Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, she left without finishing to marry her classmate Donald Hooker. With him she founded the Guild of St. George, a Baltimore home for unwed mothers and their children.

people.research_notes: Wife of Dr. Donald Russell Hooker (H04422); m. June 14 1905 Baltimore. Of the Houghton family (Corning glass); daughter of Alfred Augustus Houghton and Caroline Garlinghouse. Suffragist and social reformer: founded the Just Government League (1909) and Maryland Suffrage News (1912), editor of The Suffragist (1917, National Woman's Party). Co-founded Guild of St George and Planned Parenthood Association of Baltimore. Maryland Women's Hall of Fame (inducted 1999). Sister of Katharine Houghton Hepburn (suffrage leader, mother of actress Katharine Hepburn) — Edith was the actress's aunt. Birth Dec 29 1879 per Wikipedia; FamilySearch gives Dec 22 1879. 5 children + 3 adopted. PROPOSED TAG womens_hall_of_fame pending Sam's canonicalization (not applied).

narrative_blocks.header: He operated on Japanese wounded too
narrative_blocks.body: At a field hospital in the Philippines and New Guinea he treated enemy soldiers alongside wounded Americans. His son put it plainly: his profession was to save lives.

narrative_blocks.header: Four years in the Pacific with Unit 118
narrative_blocks.body: He joined the Johns Hopkins Hospital unit of the Army Medical Corps in 1942 and served in Australia, New Zealand, the Philippines and New Guinea, coming home a major in 1946.

narrative_blocks.header: Sound and meticulous, never flamboyant
narrative_blocks.body: A surgeon who served beside him said he was a marvellous example of what a real doctor should be, and the kind who could never say no to anyone. He was a Fellow of the American College of Surgeons.

narrative_blocks.header: President of the Princeton student body
narrative_blocks.body: He captained an undefeated wrestling team and was vice-president of the senior class, belonging to the Triangle and Ivy clubs, before his chemistry degree in 1932 and his Hopkins medical degree in 1936.

narrative_blocks.header: First cousin of the actress Katharine Hepburn
narrative_blocks.body: His mother, Edith Houghton Hooker, was the eldest of the Houghton sisters; the youngest, Katharine, was the mother of the actress Katharine Hepburn, making him the actress's first cousin.

narrative_blocks.header: Boca Grande for the last eighteen years
narrative_blocks.body: He gave up the thoracic surgery post at the Baltimore veterans' hospital in 1978 and went to Florida with Greenie. He died there in 1996, eight years after their eldest daughter Elizabeth.
