narrative_blocks.header: An abdominal surgeon at Mount Kisco
narrative_blocks.body: Gilman, Princeton and Johns Hopkins made him a surgeon. After a New York Hospital residency he practised at Pleasantville, then joined the Mount Kisco Medical Group, and retired from it at fifty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: A captain who patched up a German plane
narrative_blocks.body: He went out in July 1942, when his son was six weeks old, and served three years with the Army Air Corps in North Africa, Sicily, India, England and China. In Sicily he dragged a downed German aircraft back to camp and tried to fly it.

narrative_blocks.header: He threw stones at her window, then flew
narrative_blocks.body: He had learned at fifteen or sixteen, and in his early twenties would wake Margaret Creighton before light and take her up. A cork bobbing in a tube of petrol was the fuel gauge in those machines.

narrative_blocks.header: He researched reversible male sterilisation
narrative_blocks.body: After retiring he did the work pro bono at a Worcester facility, looking for a surgical method that could be undone. At Bolton he was also the school doctor, and farmed cattle, sheep and ducks.

narrative_blocks.header: He moved to a town his ancestors founded
narrative_blocks.body: His second wife, Anita Norseen, farmed Misty Meadows at Bolton in Massachusetts. The town had been settled in the sixteen hundreds by the Houghtons his mother Edith came from, and he did not know that when he went there.

narrative_blocks.header: Agnostics' son, baptised at thirty-eight
narrative_blocks.body: His parents kept no religion. He was baptised Presbyterian at Pleasantville in 1949 with three of his children, took up Moral Rearmament, and by 1951 was an Episcopalian and a deacon at Chappaqua.

narrative_blocks.header: A New Yorker cover with no words
narrative_blocks.body: Prostate cancer came back into his spine at seventy. He refused chemotherapy, saying he would not be an experiment, and spent that year reaching his children. The last thing he sent showed hearts falling as weather.

narrative_blocks.header: She test-flew fighters for Grumman at Bethpage
narrative_blocks.body: She took her pilot's licence at the University of Baltimore in 1940, out of the summer civil air-training course, and was flying new fighters off the Grumman line at twenty-seven. Smith had her before that.

narrative_blocks.header: She rode a burning fighter down before jumping
narrative_blocks.body: The plane caught fire eight thousand feet over Long Island Sound in June 1943. She stayed with it to about fifteen hundred, trying to put it into the water, and got out with singed eyebrows. It missed a house.

narrative_blocks.header: She answered Mrs. Roosevelt on equal rights
narrative_blocks.body: Writing to the Baltimore Sun that August, she asked why two people doing the same work should be paid differently, one having blue eyes and the other brown. She was arguing for the Equal Rights Amendment.

narrative_blocks.header: Three husbands, and a twin in Baltimore
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Baltimore in May 1916, twin to Edith, she married Peter Gring in 1944, Paul Fagan in 1963 and Charles Storke in 1988. She died at Santa Barbara in 2010, eight days short of ninety-four.

narrative_blocks.header: A helicopter took her first husband
narrative_blocks.body: Peter Gring was killed in the mountains near Fresno in March 1958, leaving her with four children under ten. She stayed on at Santa Barbara and buried two more husbands after him.

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband made a house of a barn
narrative_blocks.body: Johannes Ilmanen converted a barn on what had been a farm at North Baltimore, and they lived in it. After the divorce in the sixties she went to New Haven, which was her father's town, and gardened there.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept the Baltimore land she left
narrative_blocks.body: She kept the Baltimore land after she left it - four parcels, one of them eight and a half acres of stream and steep wooded slope that the neighbourhood still worried over two years after her death.

narrative_blocks.header: She fought to keep Assateague from the builders
narrative_blocks.body: She joined Judith Johnson's Committee to Preserve Assateague, founded in 1970, and her hundred-acre Mobjack Farm nearby was its headquarters through two decades. She did not want another Ocean City.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept a menagerie and took in orphans
narrative_blocks.body: Ruxton called her the wild animal lady. Two spider monkeys, a tropical stork, raccoons, a mynah bird, five dogs and the horses and ponies, and seven greyhounds retired off the track.

narrative_blocks.header: A bird journal kept for decades
narrative_blocks.body: She recorded what she saw in Antarctica, New Zealand, South America, Mexico, Puerto Rico and Alaska, where she hiked and camped six weeks. At home she walked children round Cylburn and Oregon Ridge.

narrative_blocks.header: The Office of Strategic Services in the war
narrative_blocks.body: She took a zoology degree at Smith in 1940, married a Marine fighter pilot in October 1942, and worked in Washington for the OSS while he was in the Pacific. He was lost there the following June.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother pushed the cousin onto the stage
narrative_blocks.body: Edith Houghton Hooker and Katharine Houghton Hepburn were sisters, and it was Edith who urged her niece to act. Edith had wanted the stage herself and been told it was not proper for a woman.

narrative_blocks.header: Hepburn arrived with Howard Hughes
narrative_blocks.body: Her cousin drove down to St. George's Road in the thirties with the aviator beside her, and once let the girls try on the Paris trunks. Kath just looked better in them than we did, she said.

narrative_blocks.header: She buried three husbands
narrative_blocks.body: Westerlind was lost in 1943, Louis Huppman died in 1958 and Kenneth Marty in 1995. She outlived the last of them by twelve years, and died of heart failure at her Belfast Road farm in January 2007.

narrative_blocks.body: James D. Harrison came up from Danville in Virginia, started as a bank cashier in 1908, and was senior vice-president when the First National was formed by merger in 1928. He was its president from 1945.

narrative_blocks.header: Chairman until 1959, and her son after him
narrative_blocks.body: He took the chairmanship in 1957 and held it to his retirement, sitting on the Patapsco and Back River Railroad board among others. Her son Donald came to the same bank as a vice-president.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father forbade the design career she won
narrative_blocks.body: At Wellesley she took first place in a national design competition for Marshall Field's and was told such work was not appropriate for a woman in the 1930s. She put the artistry into gardens instead.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty years of gardens at Misty Meadows
narrative_blocks.body: She came back to Massachusetts in 1954, widowed at thirty-nine, and spent the next half-century laying out the forty-acre place at Bolton. The Smithsonian holds photographs of what she made there.

narrative_blocks.header: She helped build Tower Hill Botanic Garden
narrative_blocks.body: As trustee and then vice-president of the Worcester County Horticultural Society she was behind its development at Boylston. She had presided over the Worcester Garden Club and took prizes at the Boston Flower Show.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandson showed her his Tony model
narrative_blocks.body: Beowulf Boritt spent his summers in her garden and said it gave him design as a way of life. After he won the Tony he brought her the set model for Act One; she died that year, at a hundred.

narrative_blocks.header: Her daughter married a Lincoln historian
narrative_blocks.body: Gabor Boritt came out of Budapest, survived the Holocaust and the rising of 1956, and reached America a refugee. He directed the Civil War Institute at Gettysburg and took the National Humanities Medal in 2008.

narrative_blocks.header: She married her late husband's doctor
narrative_blocks.body: Russell Hooker had been Wilbur Norseen's surgeon, and she had known him at the church at Chappaqua years before. They married in 1964 and farmed Misty Meadows together until he died there in 1984.

narrative_blocks.header: He was vice-president of his grandfather's bank
narrative_blocks.body: James D. Harrison ran First National in Baltimore as president from 1945 and chairman from 1957. His daughter's son came to the same bank as a vice-president, and went on to lead First Maryland LeaseCorp.

narrative_blocks.header: His thesis was on the Lost Generation
narrative_blocks.body: He read English at Princeton and wrote on American prose fiction of the 1920s, calling it The Myth of the Lost Generation. He threw the javelin for the varsity track team in his last two years.

narrative_blocks.header: Five years teaching physics in California
narrative_blocks.body: After Beirut he married Betsey Norris in 1965 and went out to the Webb School at Claremont, where he taught, coached and lived until Baltimore and banking took him back.

narrative_blocks.header: Heart trouble took him in West Virginia
narrative_blocks.body: He died suddenly in February 2024 at his vacation house in Shepherdstown. He had sponsored the Contemporary American Theater Festival there with Mary Bradshaw, his partner of sixteen years.

narrative_blocks.body: He found a six-person operation in a trailer at Perryville in Arizona in 1995 and took it over. Televerde works two hundred and fifty inmates there, selling software for Cisco, SAP and Hitachi.

narrative_blocks.header: Eleven per cent go back, against forty
narrative_blocks.body: That is the return rate among the women who worked for him, set against the national figure for female felons. They leave prison with savings behind them, and he hires a quarter of them outright.

narrative_blocks.header: The world has it upside down on prisoners
narrative_blocks.body: He said so plainly: they are kicked in, treated like savages, kicked out, and expected not to come back. He had flunked out of Washington and Lee as a senior before the Army and an American University degree.

narrative_blocks.header: He made his life in New York City
narrative_blocks.body: Of Seth's children, Lucius left Connecticut for New York City, where he married Hannah Robinson. He made his life there until his death in 1871, far from the Rocky Hill of his childhood.

narrative_blocks.header: Half the pewter firm Boardman & Hart
narrative_blocks.body: For two decades Hart was the New York partner in Boardman & Hart, one of the country's leading makers of Britannia and pewter ware. The firm's wares sold across the country from its Manhattan showrooms.

narrative_blocks.header: His pewter survives in museum collections
narrative_blocks.body: Tea sets, urns, and beakers stamped Boardman & Hart and Lucius Hart & Co. survive today in collections of early American pewter. Examples are held by museums documenting the nineteenth-century metalware trade.

narrative_blocks.header: He drove a wagon six weeks to Illinois
narrative_blocks.body: In 1834 Norman Hart and his wife Marcia drove from Connecticut to Adams County, Illinois, six weeks on the road, settling finally in Otho, Iowa, by 1854.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped found the Otho Congregational Church
narrative_blocks.body: With his wife and grown children, Hart was a charter member of the Otho Congregational Church when it organized in 1855.

narrative_blocks.header: A tailor's granddaughter who married a commodore
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah was the youngest daughter of Lucius Hart and the granddaughter of a Rocky Hill tailor. She married the banker and yachtsman E.C. Benedict in 1859 and presided over Indian Harbor, his estate on the Greenwich shore.

narrative_blocks.header: A lost son broke her health for good
narrative_blocks.body: When her only son Frederick was killed in a 1901 automobile accident, Sarah's health collapsed and she never recovered. She died of heart disease at Indian Harbor in the September of 1907, and the funeral was private.

narrative_blocks.body: Margery lived only a single day. She lies with her mother Jennie in the memorial church Henry Flagler built, the infant cradled in her mother's arms.

cross_connections.display_label: had his secret 1893 cancer surgery aboard the Oneida

narrative_blocks.header: A president's secret surgery on his yacht
narrative_blocks.body: In 1893 Benedict lent his yacht Oneida to his friend President Grover Cleveland for a secret operation to remove a cancerous growth from the president's jaw.

narrative_blocks.header: The dish eggs Benedict may bear his name
narrative_blocks.body: One enduring origin story credits the Commodore with the first eggs Benedict, a recipe said to have surfaced decades later in a letter to a newspaper food editor.

narrative_blocks.header: Robert Peary named a Greenland fjord for him
narrative_blocks.body: A restless yachtsman who loved strange waters, Benedict had Benedict Fjord in Greenland named in his honor by the explorer Robert Peary.

narrative_blocks.header: He fished with a president and an actor
narrative_blocks.body: Days at a time he drifted off Buzzards Bay with Grover Cleveland and the actor Joseph Jefferson, three lines trailing. Jefferson yanked at every nibble and came up with an empty hook; told to stop, he said the fish had yanked first.

narrative_blocks.header: He warned people away from Wall Street
narrative_blocks.body: Sixty-four years on the Street, he said late in life, and he had never once invited anybody into it — he had invited many to stay away. Asked whether he meant to retire, he said it was better to bust out than to rust out.

narrative_blocks.header: His architect married his daughter
narrative_blocks.body: He hired Carrere and Hastings to raise Indian Harbor on eighty acres of Greenwich waterfront, with the Olmsted firm laying out the grounds. Thomas Hastings later married his daughter Helen.

notable.notable_blurb: Beaux-Arts architect of the New York Public Library

institutions.institution_blurb: Co-founder and partner of the Beaux-Arts firm Carrère & Hastings.
Designed Woolsey Hall and the Hewitt Quadrangle (1901).

cross_connections.display_label: , his brother-in-law's father-in-law, gave his firm its first hotels
commissioned building designs from his firm
lived with his family in the firm's townhouse during repairs
drew 501 Fifth Avenue to match his library across the street
worked on the Chicago Public Library straight from the Beaux-Arts

narrative_blocks.header: He designed the New York Public Library
narrative_blocks.body: With his partner John Carrère, Hastings designed the New York Public Library, regarded as a high point of American Beaux-Arts architecture.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandfather wrote the hymn 'Rock of Ages'
narrative_blocks.body: His grandfather, also named Thomas Hastings, composed the hymn 'Rock of Ages.' The architect carried the name into a different art.

narrative_blocks.header: He fought the rise of the skyscraper
narrative_blocks.body: Hastings denounced tall buildings as ruinous to the human-scaled city, urging that none be allowed to rise above eight stories, as in Paris.

narrative_blocks.header: He built the Indian Harbor estate at Greenwich
narrative_blocks.body: Hastings's firm designed Indian Harbor, the waterfront estate of Commodore E.C. Benedict on Long Island Sound. Benedict was the father of his wife, Helen.

narrative_blocks.header: He designed Arlington's Tomb of the Unknowns
narrative_blocks.body: After Carrère's death, Hastings designed the Arlington Memorial Amphitheater and the Tomb of the Unknowns, the marble sarcophagus honoring America's unidentified war dead.

bio.bio_blurb: Henry Flagler's daughter, lost at sea

narrative_blocks.header: She died at sea off the Carolina coast
narrative_blocks.body: She never recovered from the birth of her daughter in February, and died aboard the Oneida off the South Carolina coast on March 25, 1889. She was thirty-four, a week past her birthday.

narrative_blocks.header: Her daughter Margery lived a few hours
narrative_blocks.body: Margery was born on February 9, 1889, and was dead before the day was out. Her mother's health never came back, and the voyage south was meant to be her convalescence.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father's train waited at Charleston
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband borrowed his father's yacht and put out to sea with a physician and a staff of nurses aboard. Her father ordered a special train to Charleston to meet her, and she died off the coast before it could.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father built a church over her grave
narrative_blocks.body: In her memory Henry Flagler raised the Memorial Presbyterian Church in St. Augustine. Jennie lies there with the infant daughter she lost the same year.

narrative_blocks.header: Her doctor gave the Bible on the lectern
narrative_blocks.body: George Shelton, the New York physician who attended her through her last illness, gave the great silver-mounted Bible that rests on the eagle lectern of the memorial church. It was finished, furnished and dedicated within a year of her death.

notable.notable_blurb: Aviation pioneer and founder of the Harmon Trophy

cross_connections.display_label: died at his controls in 1929, a commercial-aviation pioneer
held Aero Club licence 32 and built seaplanes for the Navy
wrote the story of the pilots he flew among, Jennys to jets

narrative_blocks.header: First to fly across Long Island Sound
narrative_blocks.body: In 1910 Harmon became the first man to fly across Long Island Sound, from Garden City to Greenwich. He aimed for his father-in-law E.C. Benedict's estate but came down nearby in the fading light.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded aviation's Harmon Trophy
narrative_blocks.body: Harmon created and funded the Harmon Trophy for the world's outstanding aviators; its recipients included Lindbergh, Earhart, and Howard Hughes.

narrative_blocks.header: A railroad station still bears his name
narrative_blocks.body: His development of Harmon-on-Hudson, later folded into Croton-on-Hudson, survives in the Croton-Harmon station and school district that carry his name.

narrative_blocks.header: His father-in-law cut him out of the will
narrative_blocks.body: After Harmon left Louise Benedict in 1916 following a quarrel with her father over money, the Commodore excluded him from his will; the couple divorced in 1925.

notable.notable_blurb: Standard Oil co-founder who built Gilded Age Florida

cross_connections.display_label: married his daughter Jennie, who died at sea in 1889
, his son-in-law's brother-in-law, built Whitehall and his hotels
ran the Northern Pacific while Flagler built the Florida East Coast
co-founded Standard Oil with him in 1870

narrative_blocks.header: He left Standard Oil to build Florida
narrative_blocks.body: A co-founder of Standard Oil, Flagler turned in his sixties to Florida, laying a railroad down the east coast and raising grand hotels as far as Key West.

narrative_blocks.header: He named the village he reached 'Miami'
narrative_blocks.body: When his railroad arrived at a fishing village near the Everglades, grateful residents wished to name the town for him. He urged them to use the local river's name instead.

narrative_blocks.header: His overseas railroad was called Flagler's Folly
narrative_blocks.body: Dismissed as folly, his railroad leapt across the sea to Key West, reaching it in 1912 with the old man aboard the first train to arrive.

narrative_blocks.header: He died falling down his own marble staircase
narrative_blocks.body: In 1913 the eighty-three-year-old Flagler fell down the marble steps of Whitehall, the Palm Beach mansion built for him. He died of his injuries days later.

narrative_blocks.header: His monument stands on a man-made island
narrative_blocks.body: Seven years after his death Carl Fisher raised an obelisk a hundred and ten feet high on a man-made island in Biscayne Bay, four allegorical figures at its base. The island is a boaters' picnic ground now, and the monument has spent decades in disrepair.

narrative_blocks.header: Students sleep in his old hotel
narrative_blocks.body: The Ponce de Leon, the grand St. Augustine hotel he opened in 1888, was an instant success and set off his idea of an American Riviera. Since 1968 undergraduates have lived in it, as the centerpiece of Flagler College.

notable.notable_blurb: President of Union Theological Seminary

cross_connections.display_label: married his son Thomas in 1900
held the biblical-literature chair through his Union years

narrative_blocks.header: He led the seminary through a heresy trial
narrative_blocks.body: As president of Union Theological Seminary, Hastings presided over the trial of professor Charles Briggs, charged with heresy for questioning scripture's literal authority.

narrative_blocks.header: He admitted the seminary's first women students
narrative_blocks.body: During his presidency the seminary opened its curriculum to electives and admitted its first female students.

narrative_blocks.header: His father composed the hymn 'Rock of Ages'
narrative_blocks.body: His father, also named Thomas Hastings, was the church musician who wrote the melody for the hymn 'Rock of Ages.'

narrative_blocks.header: He married and was ordained in one week
narrative_blocks.body: He married Fanny de Groot of Brooklyn on 1 July 1852 and was ordained in the Fourth Presbytery of New York six days after that. Inside the month he had his first pastorate, at Mendham in New Jersey.

narrative_blocks.header: He lectured on to the year he died
narrative_blocks.body: He gave up the presidency in 1897 and retired in 1904, but stayed professor emeritus and went on lecturing in pastoral theology until 1911. He died suddenly that April at his New York house, aged 83.

narrative_blocks.header: She was president of the Virginia Day Nursery
narrative_blocks.body: Katherine was elected president of the Virginia Day Nursery in New York the winter before she died, after years as an official of the charity's summer place at Bernardsville.

narrative_blocks.header: She died in Brussels visiting her son
narrative_blocks.body: Katherine went out to Brussels in 1949 to be with her son Chalmers, secretary at the American embassy there. She died in the city that November, five weeks short of fifty-five.

narrative_blocks.header: The groom's brother read the service
narrative_blocks.body: Katherine married Chalmers Wood at St. Bernard's in Bernardsville on the last Saturday of September 1916. The groom's own brother, William Lawrence Wood, performed it, their uncle Rowland Cotton Smith assisting.

military_service.notes: Argonne offensive, 1918; Judge Advocate with the army at Paris, 1919.
Came out of retirement.

cross_connections.display_label: was a major in the Argonne as well, and a judge advocate after

narrative_blocks.header: He left the law for the Argonne
narrative_blocks.body: Gardiner gave up his New York practice when the First World War began, went out as a major in the 77th Infantry Division and was in the Argonne offensive of 1918. He was still with the army in Paris the next spring.

narrative_blocks.header: He came out of retirement a second time
narrative_blocks.body: Gardiner had been retired for years when the second war came, and took work in military censorship in New York City. He was in his sixties by then.

narrative_blocks.header: Born at West Point, where his father taught
narrative_blocks.body: Gardiner was born at the Military Academy in February 1877, in the middle of his father's four years as its first professor of law. He went to St. Paul's at Garden City and then to Columbia.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at thirty-eight, remarried at forty-seven
narrative_blocks.body: Gardiner's first wife Evelyn Poor died in 1915. He married Helen Ramsey Turnbull in 1924 and settled at Bernardsville, where her sister had married eight years before. Helen outlived him by forty-three years.

narrative_blocks.header: His father's Medal of Honor was taken back
narrative_blocks.body: Asa Bird Gardiner had held the medal forty-five years when a board under Nelson Miles found nothing to support it and the War Department asked for it back in 1917. He refused to return it.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Little Ipswich, Syosset

narrative_blocks.header: A stockbroker in the Knickerbocker Club
narrative_blocks.body: Wood came out of Columbia in 1905 and went into stockbroking. He belonged to the Knickerbocker, the Racquet and Tennis and the Essex Fox Hounds, and kept a Long Island house called Little Ipswich on the Syosset-Woodbury Road.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother read the service
narrative_blocks.body: Wood married Katherine Benedict Turnbull at St. Bernard's in Bernardsville on the last Saturday of September 1916. His brother, the Rev. William Lawrence Wood, performed it, with their uncle Rowland Cotton Smith assisting.

notable.notable_blurb: Cold War diplomat in Vietnam and the Pacific

career.role: Officer in Charge of Vietnamese Affairs

cross_connections.display_label: was killed in the province Wood was senior adviser for

narrative_blocks.header: From the Vietnam desk into the province
narrative_blocks.body: Wood ran Vietnamese affairs out of Washington from 1959 to 1963. Four years on he went to the country itself as senior adviser for Binh Dinh province, and stayed from 1967 to 1969.

narrative_blocks.header: One envoy to Fiji, New Zealand, Samoa, Tonga
narrative_blocks.body: From November 1972 Wood was chargé d'affaires to four countries at once, resident at Wellington, where he was deputy chief of mission as well. He held all of it until April 1974.

narrative_blocks.header: Five years in the Army Air Force first
narrative_blocks.body: Wood took his Harvard degree in 1940 and went into the Army Air Force for the length of the war. He joined the Foreign Service in 1947, and the first postings were Brussels and Manila.

narrative_blocks.header: Greece, then Vietnam, then Cyprus
narrative_blocks.body: Wood was the State Department's officer for Greece before Vietnam, and directed its Cyprus office in 1967. He was first secretary in London for the two years between them.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at Princeton in 1991
narrative_blocks.body: Wood left the Foreign Service in 1974 and consulted on energy research afterwards. He died of a brain hemorrhage at Princeton in June 1991, leaving four children: Ramsay, Chalmers, Felicity and Penelope.

people.research_notes: FindAGrave lists birth 1843, impossible given 1850 marriage; FamilySearch birth 1830 adopted.

bio.bio_blurb: President of the Presbyterian women’s foreign missions board

career.organization: Woman’s Foreign Missionary Society of the Presbyterian Church, New York State branch

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty years at the head of the board
narrative_blocks.body: She was president of the New York state branch of the Woman’s Foreign Missionary Society of the Presbyterian Church for twenty years, from its rooms at 156 Fifth Avenue, and was prominent in many other women’s societies.

narrative_blocks.header: A hymn of hers reached the Golden Censer
narrative_blocks.body: Her hymn Jesus Died for Me was printed over the name Mrs. H. N. Beers in William Bradbury’s Golden Censer in 1864. She had written it for a Presbyterian church in New York.

narrative_blocks.header: She gave her son her father’s name
narrative_blocks.body: Martha was a daughter of Lucius Robert Hart of New York. She married Henry Newell Beers in October 1853, and when their second son was born in 1859 they called him Lucius Hart Beers.

narrative_blocks.header: Dropsy took her at her son’s Quogue house
narrative_blocks.body: She died of dropsy on the night of 26 June 1909 at the summer house of her son Lucius at Quogue. A short service was read there by the Reverend Thomas Coyle, and the funeral was at Lucius’s house on East Thirty-ninth Street.

people.research_notes: A hymnary source speculates she may be the 'Mrs. H. N. Beers' credited with the 1864 hymn 'Jesus Died for Me'; unconfirmed.

career.notes: Continued his father’s firm with Charles E. Huntington after 1871.

narrative_blocks.header: He lost all four of his children young
narrative_blocks.body: Lucius Hart Jr. and his wife buried all four of their children, none living to carry on the family name. The losses left him without direct heirs at his death in New York in 1898.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried on his father's metalware firm
narrative_blocks.body: Lucius Hart Jr. learned the silverplating trade in his father's New York house, and on the elder Hart's death in 1871 he and Charles E. Huntington kept the business alive. They renamed it the Lucius Hart Manufacturing Company, continuing the Britannia and metalware line the firm was known for.

narrative_blocks.header: His firm's wares survive in museum collections
narrative_blocks.body: The Hart workshops turned out Britannia, pewter, and silverplated goods for the American household trade through the middle of the century. Pieces bearing the Hart marks are preserved today in collections such as the Winterthur Library.

bio.bio_blurb: New York glass manufacturer and municipal reformer

education.institution_name: University of the City of New-York
education.school_name: University of the City of New-York

narrative_blocks.header: He hunted municipal abuses for twenty years
narrative_blocks.body: Beers spent years exposing abuses in the city government and pressing economy on it. His work before the Board of Estimate and Apportionment and at Albany drew heavy criticism from politicians, and was generally reckoned beneficial.

narrative_blocks.header: One of the organizers of the Seventy
narrative_blocks.body: He was one of the organizers of the Committee of Seventy, and of the Council of Political Reform that grew out of it. He was a member of the Council until the day he died.

narrative_blocks.header: He got the Park Commissioners investigated
narrative_blocks.body: In 1884 he was instrumental in having the Park Commissioners investigated by the Supreme Court, and the inquiry exposed a good many abuses in the running of the city.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years in New York, fifteen retired
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Lexington in Greene County in 1819, he took his degree at the University of the City of New-York and came down to the city, where he lived the last forty years of his life. He made glass until about 1872.

bio.bio_blurb: New York lawyer at Lord, Day & Lord

cross_connections.display_label: had Beers draw up the guardianship papers for his children
, his mother’s father, gave him the name he carried

narrative_blocks.header: A senior partner at Lord, Day & Lord
narrative_blocks.body: Beers practiced law in New York for decades as a senior member of the old firm Lord, Day & Lord and sat on corporate boards.

narrative_blocks.header: He handled legal affairs for the Roosevelt family
narrative_blocks.body: Beers prepared the papers naming Edith Roosevelt guardian of two of Theodore Roosevelt's children, Kermit and Ethel.

narrative_blocks.header: Quogue, and then Westhampton Beach
narrative_blocks.body: The family summered at the eastern end of Long Island for sixty years. His mother died at his Quogue house in 1909 and he died at Westhampton in 1948, and his widow kept the Westhampton Beach place until her own death.

bio.bio_blurb: New York clubwoman and suffrage-era organizer

narrative_blocks.header: Smith, then the Fifteenth Assembly District
narrative_blocks.body: She took her degree at Smith in 1899 and married Lucius Hart Beers in 1903. In New York she worked the Fifteenth Assembly District for the League of Women Voters, and gave her time to the American Farm School.

narrative_blocks.header: The Colony Club and the Colonial Dames
narrative_blocks.body: She belonged to the Colony Club and to the National Association of Colonial Dames, and was reckoned a prominent clubwoman in the city. The Beers kept 131 East Sixty-second Street and a summer house at Westhampton Beach.

narrative_blocks.header: She died at Winchester, near her daughter
narrative_blocks.body: She outlived her husband by four years and went down to Virginia, where her daughter Mary had married a Dillard of Millwood. A short illness took her at Winchester Memorial Hospital in February 1952, leaving seven grandchildren.

bio.bio_blurb: Partner in N. Howard & Son, financial advisers

career.organization: N. Howard & Son Inc., financial advisers

narrative_blocks.header: DuPuy of Pittsburgh, Atkins of Indianapolis
narrative_blocks.body: She was a daughter of Charles Meredith DuPuy of Pittsburgh, and her mother married again, to William Avery Atkins of Indianapolis. She kept houses in New York, at Remsenburg on Long Island and at Fort Lauderdale.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at Trinity, down on Broadway
narrative_blocks.body: She was married to John Doerschuck at Trinity Church in New York on 14 January 1956, her father giving her away and her brother Richard among the ushers. Her half-sister Helen Culver was maid of honour.

people.research_notes: Identified as brother of Eunice Dupuy Beers in a 1940s wedding notice; minimal detail.

bio.bio_blurb: Wall Street banker and namesake of Coppell, Texas

notable.notable_blurb: Wall Street banker and namesake of Coppell, Texas

cross_connections.display_label: , his son-in-law, married Mary in 1899 and died five years later
took control of the Denver and Rio Grande he had chaired
was a director of the Denver and Rio Grande he chaired

narrative_blocks.header: A Texas town took his name
narrative_blocks.body: The St. Louis Southwestern opened its line through a Texas town called Gibbs in 1888 and named the depot Coppell, for the Wall Street banker who had sat on the bondholders' committee that reorganized the railroad. In 1892 the town took the depot's name; George probably never saw it.

narrative_blocks.header: Britain's consul in wartime New Orleans
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Liverpool, George came to America about 1859 and was acting British consul at New Orleans through the Civil War. He married Helen Hoffman Gillingham of New Orleans there on 14 March 1862, six weeks before the city fell to Union forces.

narrative_blocks.header: He reorganized America's troubled railroads
narrative_blocks.body: Senior partner from 1886 of Maitland, Phelps & Co., a Wall Street house founded in 1796, George renamed it Maitland, Coppell & Co. in 1896 and chaired the reorganizations of the Denver & Rio Grande, the Norfolk & Western and the Wisconsin Central.

narrative_blocks.header: The Pooh-Bah of Western railroads
narrative_blocks.body: In 1891 the New York Herald called George the Pooh-Bah of Western railroads, after a shouting match in which he fired one of his managers. In 1898, as chairman of the Rio Grande, he spoke bitterly against the coming war with Spain.

narrative_blocks.header: Two mansions on Engle Street
narrative_blocks.body: In the late 1870s George built Birchwood Knole on forty-five acres at Tenafly, New Jersey; he later gave it to his son Herbert and in 1883 moved a block north into The Towers. The family's Engle Street estates kept gardeners, maids, butlers and drivers who lived on the grounds.

narrative_blocks.header: He may have invented his own surname
narrative_blocks.body: One study argues the English-born financier took the Coppell name from a half-brother and was born a Chilcott, leaving humble origins behind.

cross_connections.display_label: , his father-in-law, gave Mary a house at Tenafly when they married

narrative_blocks.header: Married and buried from Grace Church
narrative_blocks.body: Edgar married Mary Coppell at Grace Church on 28 November 1899, while her father lay ill at 40 Fifth Avenue. He died at their house at 144 East 35th Street on 6 March 1904, at forty-two, and his funeral was held at Grace Church two days later.

narrative_blocks.header: Robert died young
narrative_blocks.body: Robert died in 1867, in his first year.

narrative_blocks.header: Alice died young
narrative_blocks.body: Alice died in 1869, aged about one.

narrative_blocks.header: Her dog came to the wedding
narrative_blocks.body: When Mary married Oliver DeLancey Coster, her black dog Pommie came to the wedding in a white satin bow, carried into the church by one of the chauffeurs. At her first wedding, to Edgar Booth in 1899, her father had given her a house at Tenafly.

narrative_blocks.header: Carrie died young
narrative_blocks.body: Carrie died in 1869, aged about two.

narrative_blocks.header: Henry died young
narrative_blocks.body: Henry died in 1882, aged about eleven.

narrative_blocks.header: Florence died young
narrative_blocks.body: Florence died in 1873, aged about two.

narrative_blocks.header: Lucius died young
narrative_blocks.body: Lucius died in 1881, aged about two.

narrative_blocks.header: Married on her twenty-first birthday
narrative_blocks.body: She was born on the tenth of July and married Charles Ames at Plainville on the tenth of July 1876, the day she turned twenty-one. Their only child was born in 1881 and did not live out the year.

bio.bio_blurb: Principal of a Hartford public school

narrative_blocks.header: Bertie died young
narrative_blocks.body: Bertie died in 1881, in his first year.

bio.bio_blurb: Keeper of a general store at Plainville

narrative_blocks.header: A general store at Plainville
narrative_blocks.body: He kept a general store at Plainville in 1894 and had a hand in his father’s clock-trimming works. By 1915 he was living at Springfield in Massachusetts, and he finished in California.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine years a resident of Pasadena
narrative_blocks.body: He was a native of Connecticut and had been in Pasadena nine years when he died there in May 1937, at 125 Club Road. Three daughters survived him, in Pasadena, in South Orange and in Springfield, and a sister at Waukegan.

narrative_blocks.header: She buried two of her three children
narrative_blocks.body: Katherine married James David Hale at Springfield in September 1924. David died at three in 1929 and Nancy at one in 1931; only Alan came through. She outlived her husband by thirty-six years and died at ninety-one.

narrative_blocks.header: A travel author, and ninety-eight years
narrative_blocks.body: She married Edward Tiffany Van Deusen in 1922 and George Gellhorn Jr. in 1935, and wrote travel books. Her husband’s work took the family to Pasadena, Longmeadow, New York, St. Louis, South Orange and Bahia in Brazil.

narrative_blocks.header: The town clerk wrote her Lena May
narrative_blocks.body: She was entered in the birth record as Lena May and lived her life as Helen May. She married Keith Fitch of Waukegan in Illinois, was still living there in 1915, and died there in 1941, the town her father had come out to visit.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried the family west to Michigan
narrative_blocks.body: Noah Hart left Connecticut for Massachusetts and New York and finally settled in Bronson, Michigan, where he died in 1852.

narrative_blocks.header: He married two Carr sisters in turn
narrative_blocks.body: After his first wife Dinah Carr died young, Noah married her sister Mary, and most of their children scattered across New York and Michigan.

people.research_notes: Documented as a son of Seth and Anna (Goodrich) Hart; absent from Edward Hooker's 1909 genealogy, which under-recorded the Michigan migrants.

narrative_blocks.header: He was wounded storming Kennesaw Mountain
narrative_blocks.body: Urbane Hart served with the 11th Michigan Infantry and was wounded at Kennesaw Mountain in 1864 before mustering out the next year.

narrative_blocks.header: Milo died young
narrative_blocks.body: Milo died young in 1864.

people.research_notes: Died at 2 months 18 days, son of U. & H. A. Hart.

narrative_blocks.header: She was named Nebraska Mother of the Year
narrative_blocks.body: A Falls City music supervisor and state PEO president, Maude Weaver was chosen Nebraska Mother of the Year in her later life.

notable.notable_blurb: 22nd Governor of Nebraska, 1929–1931

education.school_name: University of Nebraska College of Law

cross_connections.display_label: helped draft North Dakota's first constitution at its 1889 convention

narrative_blocks.header: He governed Nebraska as the Depression hit
narrative_blocks.body: Weaver won the governorship in 1928 and served from 1929 to 1931, the years of the Wall Street crash. His administration wound up Nebraska's failed state bank guarantee system and began a biennial state budget, and in 1930 he lost to Charles W. Bryan, William Jennings Bryan's brother.

narrative_blocks.header: President of the 1919 constitutional convention
narrative_blocks.body: Weaver was elected president of the Nebraska Constitutional Convention that sat in 1919 and 1920, then served as a presidential elector and chaired the state's Electoral College in 1920. Four years later he presided over the Republican state convention.

narrative_blocks.header: Lawyer, fruit grower, mayor of Falls City
narrative_blocks.body: Weaver opened a law practice in his home town of Falls City in 1896, sat in the state house at twenty-five, and served as city and county attorney. In 1904 he set the law aside for farming, stock-raising and fruit growing, and in 1915 he was elected mayor.

narrative_blocks.header: The Missouri River and the first parks board
narrative_blocks.body: Out of office, Weaver led the Missouri River Navigation Association and sat on Nebraska's first State Parks Board. He was president of the Native Sons and Daughters of Nebraska in 1933 and 1934 and of the Nebraska State Historical Society from 1936 to 1940, and ran for the Senate in 1940.

narrative_blocks.header: Two wives, six children
narrative_blocks.body: His first wife, Persa Morris of Humboldt, died young, and on 2 September 1908 he married Maude Hart of White Pigeon, Michigan; they had two sons and four daughters. He died at home in Falls City in October 1945, soon after a stroke.

notable.notable_blurb: U.S. Representative from Nebraska, 1883–1887

cross_connections.display_label: married his son, Governor Arthur Weaver of Nebraska
, his grandson, held Nebraska's first district seat from 1955 to 1963
represented Connecticut in Congress from 1883 to 1887
took his Harvard law degree in 1869 as well

narrative_blocks.header: He went from Harvard Law to Congress
narrative_blocks.body: Archibald took his law degree at Harvard in 1869, was admitted in Boston and went straight out to Falls City to practise. When Nebraska was given a first congressional district in 1883 he was its first congressman, and after two terms he lost a bid for the Senate in 1887.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded a Nebraska political dynasty
narrative_blocks.body: His son Arthur presided over Nebraska's 1919 constitutional convention and was governor from 1929 to 1931. His grandson Phillip Hart Weaver won Archibald's old first district in 1954 and held it for four terms.

narrative_blocks.header: Two constitutional conventions, then the bench
narrative_blocks.body: Archibald sat in Nebraska's constitutional conventions of 1871 and 1875 and was district attorney for the first district in 1872. Elected judge of the first judicial district in 1875 and again in 1879, he resigned in 1883 to go to Congress, and forty-four years after his second convention his son Arthur presided over the next.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught at the seminary he finished
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Dundaff in Susquehanna County, Pennsylvania, Archibald graduated from Wyoming Seminary at Kingston and stayed on its faculty from 1864 to 1867 before going to Harvard. His son Arthur was later sent back east to the same school.

narrative_blocks.header: Dead at forty-four, weeks out of Congress
narrative_blocks.body: Archibald left Congress on 3 March 1887, lost the Senate race and went back to the law, and on 18 April he died at Falls City, three days after his forty-fourth birthday. His wife Martha outlived him by thirty-five years and lies beside him in Steele Cemetery.

narrative_blocks.header: Four terms in Congress from Falls City
narrative_blocks.body: Phil Weaver, a Falls City car dealer, won Nebraska's first district in 1954 and served four terms. He voted for the Civil Rights Acts of 1957 and 1960 and for the amendment banning the poll tax in federal elections, and lost his bid for renomination in 1962.

narrative_blocks.header: Glider wings and a Bronze Star
narrative_blocks.body: Phil went into the Army on 1 June 1942 and served on command, staff and liaison duties with the 17th Airborne Division and the First Allied Airborne Army. He came out of it with the Combat Infantryman Badge, glider wings and a Bronze Star with oak leaf cluster.

narrative_blocks.header: He ended the war in occupied Berlin
narrative_blocks.body: Phil's last posting was headquarters of the Berlin District, in the occupied city. He was discharged a captain in March 1946, married within weeks, and stayed on in the Army Reserve until he retired a lieutenant colonel.

narrative_blocks.header: A radio announcer at nineteen
narrative_blocks.body: Phil was a staff announcer for radio stations from 1938, the spring he turned nineteen, until 1940, while he studied at St. Benedict's College in Atchison, Kansas. He finished at the University of Nebraska and took his A.B. in 1942, the year he went into the Army.

narrative_blocks.header: Insurance first, then an automobile agency
narrative_blocks.body: Back in Falls City in 1946, Phil went into insurance and finance and joined the board of Falls City Wholesale & Supply. After 1949 and 1950 in Chicago as a civilian aide to the Fifth Army's personnel staff, he came home and opened an automobile agency.

narrative_blocks.header: A decade on rural towns at Agriculture
narrative_blocks.body: Turned out of Congress in 1962, Phil spent ten years at the Department of Agriculture on rural development, as acting administrator of its Rural Community Development Service in 1969 and deputy assistant to the Secretary until 1973. In 1974 he went home to Falls City.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandfather held the same House seat
narrative_blocks.body: Phil was the son of Arthur J. Weaver, governor of Nebraska from 1929 to 1931, and the grandson of Archibald Jerard Weaver, the first district's first congressman. He won Archibald's seat in 1954, sixty-seven years after his grandfather left it.

narrative_blocks.header: War work in Topeka and New York
narrative_blocks.body: Betty worked in Topeka and then in New York during the war. On 6 April 1946, a few weeks after Phillip Hart Weaver came out of the Army a captain, she married him at Sabetha.

narrative_blocks.header: A member of the 84th Congressional Club
narrative_blocks.body: Betty was a long-time member of the 84th Congressional Club, named for the Congress her husband entered in January 1955. At home in Falls City she belonged to P.E.O. and Sorosis and volunteered at the First Presbyterian Church.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-three years a widow in Falls City
narrative_blocks.body: Widowed in April 1989, Betty lived on in Falls City for twenty-three years, and in her seventies she took up painting. She survived cancer for more than thirty-five years and died on 3 June 2012, ten months after a stroke.

narrative_blocks.header: He won Amherst its founding charter
narrative_blocks.body: As Amherst College's second president, Humphrey secured a state charter in 1825 over the opposition of Williams and Harvard, giving the young college its legal footing.

narrative_blocks.header: No class graduated without a revival
narrative_blocks.body: Stepping down in 1845, he recited the dates of the seven revivals the college had seen since its founding: 1823, 1827, 1828, 1831, 1835, 1839 and 1842. By comparing these dates, he told them, it will be seen that no class has ever yet graduated without passing through at least one season of spiritual refreshing.

narrative_blocks.header: He preached temperance before it was popular
narrative_blocks.body: From about 1810 Humphrey campaigned for temperance, wrote early tracts against intemperance, and founded a college society whose members abstained from alcohol, tobacco, and narcotics.

narrative_blocks.header: The student who wrote his presidency down
narrative_blocks.body: William Seymour Tyler took his degree in the class of 1830, in the middle of those revivals, and came back six years later to a chair he held for fifty-six years. Tyler wrote the college's first history, and Humphrey's twenty-two years are set down in it, revival dates and all.

narrative_blocks.body: A Yale student during the Revolution, George Welles commanded a band of fellow students who volunteered to oppose the British invasion of New Haven in 1779. He graduated in the class of 1779.

narrative_blocks.header: Land agent and innkeeper on the Pennsylvania frontier
narrative_blocks.body: After Yale, Welles settled at Athens on the Pennsylvania frontier as agent for the Carroll lands and proprietor of the Athens Hotel. He grew rich in valuable lands and served as a justice of the peace.

narrative_blocks.header: He died in the Sheshequin fever epidemic
narrative_blocks.body: In 1813 a deadly epidemic the settlers called the 'Sheshequin fever' swept Tioga Point, striking only adults and sparing no one under fifteen. George Welles was among its victims, buried in late June at the height of the outbreak.

narrative_blocks.body: Feeling unwell, Jerusha Welles was advised to take a small dose of variolated tartar. A wrong label led her to swallow corrosive sublimate of mercury instead, and she died within days in 1778, leaving five children and a reputation for piety and charity.

narrative_blocks.header: The general who wrote Pennsylvania's Academy Bill
narrative_blocks.body: Elected to the Pennsylvania House in 1809 and the state Senate from 1815 to 1819, Henry Welles authored the 1813 Academy Bill to expand schooling across the commonwealth. Governor Simon Snyder named him an aide with the rank of general, the title by which everyone afterward knew him.

narrative_blocks.header: A township was named in his honor
narrative_blocks.body: A fluent orator said to charm any room or legislature he entered, Welles became one of the foremost makers of Athens, Pennsylvania. Wells Township was named for him.

narrative_blocks.header: His first wife died weeks after the wedding
narrative_blocks.body: Henry married Phoebe Patrick in February 1809, but she died only weeks later, leaving him a young widower. Three years on he married Sarah 'Sally' Spalding, who would outlive him by forty-four years.

narrative_blocks.body: Susan Welles married John Hollenback in 1805, and her brother Charles Fisher Welles later married John's sister Ellen, joining two of Judge Matthias Hollenback's children to two of George Welles's. Susan and John had no children of their own.

narrative_blocks.header: Bradford County's first clerk of courts
narrative_blocks.body: At twenty-three Charles Fisher Welles was appointed the first prothonotary and clerk of the courts of Bradford County, holding the offices six years. His court records were long admired as models of neatness and accuracy.

narrative_blocks.header: A diffident poet with a trenchant pen
narrative_blocks.body: A lifelong lover of poetry who studied law but was too shy to practice it, Welles instead wielded a busy pen for the press. His political essays were said to carry conviction to the reader and scathing rebuke to the corrupt politician.

narrative_blocks.header: A fall from his wagon killed him
narrative_blocks.body: Welles kept a hand in public affairs for half a century and rarely missed a term of court at Towanda. In 1866, getting down from his wagon, he was thrown heavily and died of his injuries.

narrative_blocks.header: Raphael Pumpelly's brother who settled in Massachusetts
narrative_blocks.body: John Hollenbeck Pumpelly, an elder brother of the geologist Raphael Pumpelly, was born at Owego, New York, in 1826. He married Mary Ann Foote in 1868 and died at Waltham, Massachusetts, in 1907.

notable.notable_blurb: Geologist and explorer of Asia's interior

narrative_blocks.header: He mapped Asia's deserts for American science
narrative_blocks.body: Trained as a mining engineer, Raphael Pumpelly surveyed mineral country across Japan, China, and Mongolia in the 1860s and crossed the Gobi Desert. His later expeditions into Russian Central Asia searched for the origins of agriculture and early civilization.

narrative_blocks.header: He tied windblown dust to climate history
narrative_blocks.body: Pumpelly's studies of loess, the fine wind-laid soil of northern China, helped show how such deposits record ancient climate. At home he directed the northern transcontinental railroad survey and led major government geological surveys.

narrative_blocks.header: He held Harvard's first chair in mining
narrative_blocks.body: From 1866 to 1875 Pumpelly served as Harvard's first professor of mining, between expeditions that carried him around the world. He later organized the economic-geology division of the new U.S. Geological Survey and directed its New England branch.

narrative_blocks.header: His Anau dig pushed Central Asian history back
narrative_blocks.body: In 1903 Pumpelly led a Carnegie-funded expedition to the Anau mounds in Turkmenistan, uncovering a settlement he dated to about 4500 BCE. The mineral pumpellyite, found in Michigan's copper country, was later named in his honor.

narrative_blocks.header: He blazed the Pumpelly Trail up Monadnock
narrative_blocks.body: From his summer place at Dublin, New Hampshire, Pumpelly cut a ridge trail to the summit of Mount Monadnock that still carries his name. He spent his last decades at Newport and presided over the Geological Society of America in 1905.

narrative_blocks.body: At fourteen John Spalding fifed for his father's company on the 1779 Sullivan Expedition against the Iroquois, encamped at Fort Sullivan in present-day Athens. He was the eldest son of General Simon Spalding, who founded the first settlement at Sheshequin.

narrative_blocks.body: The boy who had piped his father's men into the wilderness was later commissioned colonel of the Pennsylvania state militia. He settled at Sheshequin on the Susquehanna, where he and Wealthy Ann Gore raised fourteen children.

narrative_blocks.header: Three terms in Congress for the Whigs
narrative_blocks.body: A Whig elected to three Congresses from New York's sixteenth district between 1845 and 1851, Hugh White chaired the House Committee on Agriculture. He had trained in law but never practiced, turning instead to business.

narrative_blocks.header: He made America's first waterproof cement
narrative_blocks.body: With his brother Canvass White, the Erie Canal engineer who patented American hydraulic cement, Hugh ran the Rosendale Cement Works, whose product was the first water-proof cement made in the country and was used on the Croton Aqueduct. He also built mills, ran a bank, and helped build the Michigan Southern and Northern Indiana Railroad.

narrative_blocks.header: Townsfolk saved his mansion from the wreckers
narrative_blocks.body: Hugh White's 1830 Waterford homestead, built of brick and timber shipped down the Erie Canal, was marked for demolition in 1964. Within weeks a group of residents raised the money to buy it and moved it to a new site, where it became the Waterford Historical Museum.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandfather founded Whitestown, New York
narrative_blocks.body: Hugh descended from Judge Hugh White, the Revolutionary quartermaster who founded and gave his name to Whitestown. His father and grandfather both served in the war before the family built up central New York.

narrative_blocks.header: He harnessed the Mohawk at Cohoes
narrative_blocks.body: Moving to Cohoes in 1830, Hugh helped develop water power from the Mohawk River and built up the Rosendale cement works. It made him a fortune before he ever entered Congress.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped invent American dermatology
narrative_blocks.body: Home in 1870 after five years in Europe, he founded the Boston Dispensary for Skin Diseases in 1872, headed skin diseases at the Boston City Hospital, and chaired the 1876 Philadelphia meeting that organised the national association.

narrative_blocks.header: American dermatology was a desert, he said
narrative_blocks.body: Presiding ten years after he had called that first meeting to order, he told the association that before the last quarter-century the American field had been a desert, worked by pioneers each fighting for his own hand.

narrative_blocks.header: Skin patients were shut out of beds
narrative_blocks.body: Hospitals gave a fever and a fracture the best nursing and the most eminent attention, he said, while a disease of the skin was debarred from both. There was neither reason nor justice in it.

narrative_blocks.header: He built the library Boston’s doctors still use
narrative_blocks.body: He gave the first impetus to the Boston Medical Library Association, compiled the Boston Medical Register, and pressed the law that made physicians register in Massachusetts.

narrative_blocks.header: A surgeon’s war before a surgeon’s peace
narrative_blocks.body: He was medical assistant to the Sanitary Commission before Richmond in June 1862, enlisted that September as a private in the Forty-fifth Massachusetts, and was its hospital steward within a month, at Kingston, Whitehall and Goldsboro.

narrative_blocks.header: A chair and a hall carry the name
narrative_blocks.body: Harvard's chair of dermatology carries his name for the Baretta models he gave the medical school. Wigglesworth Hall in the Yard carries his family's, built where his great-great-grandfather's house stood, on ground Thomas Shepard held.

narrative_blocks.header: A hill, green apples and a hornets nest
narrative_blocks.body: He wrote to a classmate in 1895 of making a summer home at Jackson in New Hampshire out of compost and grass seed heaped on granite, and offered him board, lodging and gratitude, a hill, green apples and a hornets nest.

narrative_blocks.header: He took YMS-390 through the Pacific
narrative_blocks.body: Edward Wigglesworth went into the Navy as an ensign in 1942, commanded the minesweeper in the Pacific and came out a lieutenant. Harvard had given him an A.B. and he went back to chemistry after.

narrative_blocks.header: Born on her parents’ dairy farm
narrative_blocks.body: Meredith Farm at Topsfield was where she started, with winters on Chestnut Street in Boston. She went to Beaver School and then to the Brownmoor School in Santa Fe, and came home to the American Women's Voluntary Services.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived her grandson by eleven months
narrative_blocks.body: Prescott Wright disappeared in Maine in December 2012 and she died at Hyannis Port the November after. She had volunteered years at the Dedham Women's Exchange, and was happiest on the Cape.

narrative_blocks.header: He drowned rowing out to a sloop
narrative_blocks.body: He was seventeen, and had been through two operations for brain tumours in the two years before. He fell from a dinghy off the Manchester Yacht Club; a Coast Guard helicopter spotted him and a skindiver brought him up from eight feet.

narrative_blocks.header: She is in the Ski Hall of Fame
narrative_blocks.body: Marian McKean was elected to the United States National Ski Hall of Fame in 1966. She was one of a dozen American women sent to Europe in the late 1930s to race against the best in the world.

narrative_blocks.header: In 1938 she beat her own team captain
narrative_blocks.body: That winter she won a slalom in Europe, took second in a downhill, a slalom and the combined, and third in another slalom. She finished in the top ten thirteen times, ahead more often than not of her captain, Betty Woolsey.

narrative_blocks.header: Ninth down a course that broke five men
narrative_blocks.body: The 1936 downhill at Innsbruck was run with almost no snow, and the first five men down it had to be carried off. The women were sent down the same course anyway, and McKean, new to international racing, came ninth.

narrative_blocks.header: She never got to start an Olympics
narrative_blocks.body: She was an alternate on the 1936 team and did not race. Named to the United States team for 1940, she never started there either — those Games were cancelled once the war began.

narrative_blocks.header: She taught skiing, then guided in Wyoming
narrative_blocks.body: She passed the Austrian state examination for ski instructors and joined the ski school staff at Sun Valley. She came to Betty Woolsey's Trail Creek Ranch in 1952, took guests down the slopes each winter, and stayed thirty years.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son drowned at seventeen
narrative_blocks.body: Edward Wigglesworth III drowned in a boating accident on the East Coast in 1960. His mother left Massachusetts for Wyoming that year and took her daughter Sally with her.

narrative_blocks.header: She won prizes for her lettuce
narrative_blocks.body: Her father taught her to garden when she was small and she never stopped. Her vegetables fed the whole ranch through the summer, and her lettuce took the county fair ribbon year after year.

notable.notable_blurb: Boston physician and Harvard's third Hersey Professor

narrative_blocks.header: He built 65 Marlborough as home and office
narrative_blocks.body: Dr. Francis Minot, a widowed Boston physician, built 65 Marlborough Street in 1876 as both his home and his medical office. His daughter Julia lived there with him and, after marrying Felix Rackemann in 1886, raised her young family there.

narrative_blocks.header: He joined the Massachusetts General staff in 1859
narrative_blocks.body: After Harvard College in 1841 and the medical school in 1844, Francis Minot opened a practice on Charles Street and joined the surgical staff of Massachusetts General Hospital in 1859. He served the hospital for four decades, until his death in 1899.

narrative_blocks.header: He held Harvard's third Hersey Professorship
narrative_blocks.body: Minot became the third Hersey Professor of the Theory and Practice of Physic, a chair the family held across generations of Boston medicine. Contemporaries remembered him as a leading physician and a brilliant intellect.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at his daughter's Milton home
narrative_blocks.body: In his final years Minot left the Back Bay for Milton, dying in 1899 at the home of his daughter, Mrs. Felix Rackemann. He was buried at Forest Hills, in the wooded hills his family had long summered near.

notable.notable_blurb: Judge and founder of the Massachusetts Historical Society

narrative_blocks.header: He recorded the vote that ratified the Constitution
narrative_blocks.body: As secretary of the 1788 Massachusetts convention, George Richards Minot kept the record of the close vote, 187 to 168, that ratified the federal Constitution. He went on to serve as a probate judge and chief justice of the court of common pleas.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded the Massachusetts Historical Society
narrative_blocks.body: In 1791 George was among the ten incorporators of the Massachusetts Historical Society, said to have gathered in his Court Street law office.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote Shays's Rebellion as it ended
narrative_blocks.body: George published The History of the Insurrections in Massachusetts in 1788, an account of Shays's Rebellion written while the rising was still fresh. That August he wrote to George Washington, and he went on to continue Thomas Hutchinson's history of the province.

narrative_blocks.header: Boston's first municipal judge
narrative_blocks.body: When Boston set up its Municipal Court in 1800, George became its first judge, and he held the seat until he died in January 1802, at forty-three. He had clerked the Massachusetts House for ten years, from 1782.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife's father was scalped at Ticonderoga
narrative_blocks.body: Minot married Mary Speakman, whose father Captain Thomas Speakman was scalped alive after a 1757 ambush near Ticonderoga in the French and Indian War. The relief party later found the captain's severed head fixed upon a pole.

narrative_blocks.header: A Nobel laureate carried his name
narrative_blocks.body: His great-great-grandson and namesake, George Richards Minot, shared the 1934 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for treating pernicious anemia with liver.

narrative_blocks.header: He grew Franklin's fund for sixty years
narrative_blocks.body: William managed Boston trusts and wills for more than sixty years, among them the bequest Benjamin Franklin left the city. Under his hand the Franklin Fund grew some twenty-five-fold between 1804 and 1868.

narrative_blocks.header: His Beacon Street house survived a great fire
narrative_blocks.body: In 1817 Minot built a fashionable Beacon Street townhouse opposite the Common, with tall wooden columns in the High Regency manner of London. A fire gutted six neighboring buildings in 1824, but his stood, and he lived there sixty years.

narrative_blocks.header: Son of the judge, father of a doctor
narrative_blocks.body: William was eighteen when his father, the judge, died in January 1802, the year he took his Harvard degree. Of his own sons, William managed a fiftieth of all Boston's property and Francis became Harvard's Hersey Professor of physic.

narrative_blocks.header: He died rich; his grandfather died bankrupt
narrative_blocks.body: William died in 1873 at eighty-nine, a rich man, where his grandfather Stephen, a founder of King's Chapel, had died bankrupt.

narrative_blocks.header: She painted Niagara before the canal
narrative_blocks.body: Louisa, a writer and art teacher, saw Niagara Falls with her sister in 1815, ten years before the Erie Canal turned it into a tourist stop. In 1818 she painted a pair of canvases of the gorge, the only works known from her hand.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven when her father built on Congress Street
narrative_blocks.body: Louisa was seven when her father, Daniel Davis, United States Attorney for Maine, built the family's house on Congress Street in Portland in 1794. He later became Solicitor-General of Massachusetts and moved them to Cambridge.

narrative_blocks.header: Mother of a lawyer and a professor
narrative_blocks.body: Louisa married William Minot in 1810. Their son William came to manage a fiftieth of all the property in Boston, and their son Francis became Harvard's Hersey Professor of physic.

They settled in Grass Valley, California, where the family ran a grocery and she was keeping its books by the age of nine.

narrative_blocks.header: Junior League president through the war
narrative_blocks.body: Dorothy led the Junior League of Boston from 1941 to 1944, through the war years, and went on to sit as a director and vice president of the Association of Junior Leagues of America. She later presided over the Vincent Club of Boston.

narrative_blocks.header: The Lenox Rackemanns' youngest went to California
narrative_blocks.body: Wilfred Henry was the youngest child of the musician Friedrich Rackemann and Elizabeth Sedgwick of Lenox. He married Hattie Stevens at Fitchburg in 1899 and later carried the family west to California, where he died about 1920.

narrative_blocks.header: Three marriages across the Midwest
narrative_blocks.body: Stella Olive Green married three times across the Midwest, ending with Wilfred Rackemann and then Stanley Moore. She is buried at Mount Pleasant Cemetery in Johnson County, Indiana, beside her children and husbands.

narrative_blocks.header: An Indianapolis artist who built his own guitar
narrative_blocks.body: Bill Rackemann spent his whole life on the south side of Indianapolis, far from the family's New England and Bremen beginnings. He worked as an artist and musician and even built his own guitar.

narrative_blocks.header: John Singer Sargent painted her portrait
narrative_blocks.body: In 1887 John Singer Sargent painted a waist-length portrait of Eliza Shepard Pumpelly, now held by the Berkshire Museum. She had married the geologist Raphael Pumpelly in 1869 and shared his homes at Newport and in the New Hampshire hills.

narrative_blocks.header: An exhibited portrait painter and Bahá'í
narrative_blocks.body: Margarita 'Daisy' Pumpelly Smyth painted portraits shown in New York exhibitions, among them a likeness of the architect Rose Standish Nichols. She joined the Bahá'í Faith after hearing 'Abdu'l-Bahá speak at her parents' New Hampshire home in 1912.

narrative_blocks.header: Her Greenwich Village home drew many faiths
narrative_blocks.body: In the 1940s Daisy shared a house at 48 West 10th Street with the Bahá'í artist Juliet Thompson, making it a gathering place for people of many races and religions. Visitors came for fireside meetings that ran almost continually.

narrative_blocks.header: Wife and husband lived largely apart
narrative_blocks.body: Daisy married the Harvard geology professor Henry Lloyd Smyth in England in 1894. Though never divorced, the two kept separate households for much of their long marriage.

narrative_blocks.header: He lost his fortune, then rebuilt it
narrative_blocks.body: After an extravagant life and a bitter 1925 divorce left him penniless, Raphael Welles briefly took his children to live in a cave on Mount Monadnock. Within a year he had rebuilt the family's finances as a New York stockbroker.

narrative_blocks.header: He built 'Samarkand,' a vast Carolina farm
narrative_blocks.body: Naming it for the Asian city his father had visited, Raphael Welles built Samarkand, a two-thousand-acre showplace in the North Carolina sandhills. He set out twenty-four thousand peach trees and bred horses before failed crops forced him to sell.

narrative_blocks.header: A Bahá'í who spoke for the faith
narrative_blocks.body: From 1938 Raphael Welles lectured on the Bahá'í Faith across New York and as far as Idaho, and in 1948 served as a Bahá'í delegate to a United Nations religious conference. His parents had hosted 'Abdu'l-Bahá in 1912.

narrative_blocks.header: A Harvard professor of mining and geology
narrative_blocks.body: Born in Ontario and raised in Pennsylvania, Henry Lloyd Smyth graduated from Harvard in 1883 and became a professor of mining and geology there. He married Daisy Pumpelly in England in 1894.

narrative_blocks.header: Husband and wife kept separate houses
narrative_blocks.body: Though married for half a century, Smyth and Daisy lived largely apart, he in Cambridge and Plainfield, she in New York. Census takers sometimes recorded him as a widower while his wife was living elsewhere.

narrative_blocks.body: A New York socialite by birth, Amelie married the African-American boxer and cabinetmaker John Henry Bates in 1935, when such unions were illegal in many states. As Bahá'ís, the couple held to the faith's teaching of the oneness of humankind.

narrative_blocks.body: Born to wealth, Amelie became a painter who made graphic designs and posters for a labor union. She and John moved among the Black artists and writers of the late Harlem Renaissance.

narrative_blocks.body: The family kept an ancestral farm at Fayston, Vermont, where their friend Ralph Ellison stayed during the war. Ellison later credited the visits as a direct spark for his novel Invisible Man.

narrative_blocks.header: She died on a Bahá'í mission abroad
narrative_blocks.body: After teaching the Bahá'í Faith in Haiti, Amelie moved with her family toward Mexico City. She died there suddenly of a coronary embolism in 1951, at the age of forty-one.

narrative_blocks.body: As a boy Raphael III spent about a year with his father and siblings in a cave on Mount Monadnock after the 1925 divorce. He later settled in California, where his second wife went on to marry a film composer.

narrative_blocks.header: A one-armed engineer after the war

narrative_blocks.body: The son of a Virginia-born porter, John Henry Bates boxed as 'Brooklyn Johnny Bates' until a car wreck ended his ring career. He then built fine furniture with his brothers, one of them a figure of the Harlem Renaissance.

narrative_blocks.header: He modeled for Gordon Parks's 'Invisible Man'
narrative_blocks.body: Bates and his wife counted Ralph Ellison among their friends, and their Vermont farm helped inspire his novel. For a 1952 Life magazine essay on Invisible Man, Gordon Parks photographed Bates as the model for the unnamed narrator.

narrative_blocks.header: His family had been enslaved in Virginia
narrative_blocks.body: The Bates family had been enslaved at Dinwiddie, Virginia, before John's father came north to work as a porter. From that beginning John boxed professionally and married into an old New England family.

narrative_blocks.header: A Bahá'í who taught the faith in Haiti
narrative_blocks.body: Bates embraced the Bahá'í Faith and its teaching of the oneness of humankind. In 1947 he and his family moved to Port-au-Prince to support the Bahá'í community there.

narrative_blocks.header: A Vermont soul singer and caseworker
narrative_blocks.body: Clyde 'Jay' Burr fronted the Vermont band Pure Pressure, his voice crossing jazz, funk, reggae, and blues. Away from music he worked as a residential caseworker in community mental health, which he called his most fulfilling work.

narrative_blocks.header: From Washington activist to Vermont's valley
narrative_blocks.body: Raised in northeast Washington, Burr helped start one of the first student-run high schools before settling in Vermont's Mad River Valley in 1974. He married Bess Bates and her three young sons and had a son with her in 1981.

narrative_blocks.header: A guitarist who loved the Vermont woods
narrative_blocks.body: Solomon Foster grew up between California and Vermont and was known for playing electric guitar and for fishing, hunting, and camping with his son. He died unexpectedly at forty-one in 2018 and was buried beside his mother at South Fayston.

narrative_blocks.body: George died in 1850, aged about one.

notable.notable_blurb: Richest man in old Hampshire County

narrative_blocks.header: He ran potash works and an iron foundry
narrative_blocks.body: A Yale graduate and Hatfield-born merchant, Josiah Dwight built his fortune at Westfield and Springfield through trade, a potash manufactory, and an iron foundry. He was reckoned the richest man in the old County of Hampshire at his death in 1768.

narrative_blocks.header: He judged the county court for eighteen years
narrative_blocks.body: From 1750 until his death Dwight sat as a judge of the Court of Common Pleas for Hampshire County and held the rank of lieutenant-colonel in the militia. His estate was inventoried at more than nine thousand pounds.

narrative_blocks.header: A Yale man of the old Dedham Dwights
narrative_blocks.body: Dwight graduated from Yale in 1736 and came of the Dedham Dwights, a first cousin of the grandfather of Yale's president Timothy Dwight. He kept shop at Westfield before establishing himself at Springfield.

narrative_blocks.header: His two daughters married into prominent families
narrative_blocks.body: By his second wife, Elizabeth Buckminster, he had five children who lived to maturity. Sarah married Judge John Hooker and Clarissa married Major Abel Whitney, while his son Josiah carried on the Springfield line.

narrative_blocks.header: She left no children by Josiah Dwight
narrative_blocks.body: She married him at Springfield on 5 September 1741 and died there in August 1755, leaving no children. The two of his who married Hookers were born in 1764 and 1767, to the wife who followed her.

narrative_blocks.header: The Deerfield house was hers for twelve years
narrative_blocks.body: Josiah bought the Springfield house two years after their marriage and gave it the broken-scroll doorway and gambrel roof in the 1750s, while she was mistress of it. It stands now at Historic Deerfield.

narrative_blocks.header: Mother of the Springfield Dwight line
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth Buckminster of Brookfield became Josiah Dwight's second wife in 1757 and bore the five children who survived him. She outlived him by thirty years, dying at Springfield in 1798.

narrative_blocks.header: Her eldest went to Congress for one term
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas, born in 1758, graduated from Harvard in 1778 and practised law at Springfield. He sat in both houses of the Massachusetts legislature, served a single Federalist term in Congress from 1803, and was a selectman of the town.

narrative_blocks.header: Clarissa bore eleven, then married again
narrative_blocks.body: Her daughter Clarissa married Major Abel Whitney in 1783 and had eleven children by him, two of them dead in infancy. Whitney had been aide to General Shepard at Springfield during Shays' Rebellion; widowed, Clarissa married Calvin Waldo of Dalton.
