narrative_blocks.header: She later married a Star Trek composer
narrative_blocks.body: Shirley Bonesteel married Raphael Pumpelly III in 1949 and had four children before their 1980 divorce. She then married the composer Alexander Courage, with whom she is buried in Los Angeles.

notable.notable_blurb: Composer of the Star Trek theme

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the Star Trek fanfare
narrative_blocks.body: Hired at Jerry Goldsmith's suggestion, Alexander 'Sandy' Courage composed the soaring theme for the original Star Trek and several of its episode scores. The opening fanfare became one of the franchise's most enduring musical signatures.

narrative_blocks.header: He made the Enterprise 'whoosh' himself
narrative_blocks.body: When sound editors could not find the right effect, Courage produced the famous 'whoosh' of the Enterprise crossing the screen himself. He later fell out with Gene Roddenberry, who claimed half the theme's royalties by writing lyrics never meant to be sung.

narrative_blocks.header: He orchestrated for Williams, Previn, and Goldsmith
narrative_blocks.body: At MGM and beyond, Courage orchestrated scores for André Previn, John Williams, and Jerry Goldsmith, on films from My Fair Lady to Superman. He arranged celebrated dance numbers in Seven Brides for Seven Brothers and Gigi.

narrative_blocks.header: A boyhood tune that foretold his career
narrative_blocks.body: As a boy Courage taught himself to pick out songs from a show called The Band Wagon, with no idea what lay ahead. Years later he was writing arrangements for Fred Astaire in the film version of that very show.

narrative_blocks.header: An Emmy, a camera, and fast cars
narrative_blocks.body: Courage won a 1988 Emmy for music direction on a Julie Andrews Christmas special. A keen photographer and racing enthusiast, he counted the drivers Phil Hill and Stirling Moss among his friends.

notable.notable_blurb: Founder of the Henry Holt publishing house

narrative_blocks.header: He built a great American publishing house
narrative_blocks.body: Henry Holt joined Frederick Leypoldt's firm in 1866, and by 1873 it bore his own name. Henry Holt and Company published serious literature and, by his choice, sold no books at retail.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote novels and an octogenarian's memoir
narrative_blocks.body: Holt issued the novels Calmire and Sturmsee anonymously before reprinting them under his name, and capped his career with Garrulities of an Octogenarian Editor in 1923. He also founded and edited the Unpopular Review.

narrative_blocks.header: Carnegie called his board the most useless
narrative_blocks.body: As president of the Simplified Spelling Board, Holt received Andrew Carnegie's blunt 1915 letter complaining that no more useless body of men had ever assembled. His daughters Edith and Winifred founded the New York Association for the Blind.

narrative_blocks.header: The publisher's son, an artist in Vermont
narrative_blocks.body: Henry Holt Jr., son of the publisher Henry Holt, was a Harvard-educated artist who made his home in Stowe, Vermont. His 1922 marriage to Elizabeth Cabot produced two children before ending in a difficult divorce.

narrative_blocks.header: He died flying a wartime Thunderbolt
narrative_blocks.body: Second Lieutenant Henry Holt III, a Groton schoolboy turned Army Air Corps pilot, was lost over the water off Venice, Florida, in November 1943. He was twenty years old and had married only months before.

notable.notable_blurb: Publisher of the Providence Journal

narrative_blocks.header: He led the Providence Journal for decades
narrative_blocks.body: George Pierce Metcalf served as president of the Providence Journal Company, the newspaper his family had guided for generations. He had earlier run the family's Wanskuck woolen mills, reorganizing the firm through the textile industry's hard postwar years.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave RISD prints and a Monet
narrative_blocks.body: Through his wife, Raphael Pumpelly's granddaughter, Metcalf held a rare album of Japanese surimono prints the geologist had carried home in 1863, which he gave to the Rhode Island School of Design in 1956. He also gave the museum a Monet landscape, Honfleur.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: His father built this house, now the RISD president’s house.

narrative_blocks.header: A devoted patron of RISD's museum
narrative_blocks.body: Esther Metcalf Mauran, a Sarah Lawrence graduate, gave decades to the Rhode Island School of Design as a docent and chair of its Fine Arts Committee. The museum granted her an honorary degree.

narrative_blocks.header: He published the Providence Journal like his forebears
narrative_blocks.body: Michael Pierce Metcalf served as publisher, chief executive, and chairman of the Providence Journal Company, continuing a family tradition reaching back generations. The paper was known for hard-edged investigative reporting on organized crime in Rhode Island.

narrative_blocks.header: His own paper sought a death inquiry
narrative_blocks.body: Metcalf died in September 1987, a week after a freak bicycle accident near his Westport summer home left him with severe head injuries. His own company asked prosecutors to examine the unusual circumstances, though no foul play was ever established.

narrative_blocks.header: He left trusts for his young children
narrative_blocks.body: Metcalf died with three children still in their early teens, leaving a web of family trusts to provide for them. Decades later those trusts became the subject of litigation among his heirs.

narrative_blocks.header: Lawyer, tugboat man, and preservationist
narrative_blocks.body: Frank Mauran III left the law and Governor Chafee's staff to run the family's Providence Steamboat Company. A wartime paratrooper and Yale and Harvard Law graduate, he restored the Sullivan Dorr house and led the Providence Preservation Society.

narrative_blocks.header: He led the Society of the Cincinnati
narrative_blocks.body: Long active in the Rhode Island Society of the Cincinnati, Mauran served as its national President General from 1989 to 1992. An avid collector of rare books, he gave himself to building the Society's library.

narrative_blocks.header: Navy veteran, publisher, and Cincinnati officer
narrative_blocks.body: Frank Mauran IV, a Navy veteran of the Reagan years, has run ventures from a Rhode Island humor magazine to a money-management firm and a Providence parcel store. Like his father, he is an officer of the Society of the Cincinnati.

narrative_blocks.header: She leads Rhode Island's Mount Vernon Ladies
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth Rollins Mauran serves as Rhode Island's Vice Regent to the Mount Vernon Ladies' Association, which preserves George Washington's estate. A great-granddaughter of New Hampshire governor Frank West Rollins, she has long led her family's Maine timber company.

notable.notable_blurb: Providence Journal president and RISD benefactor

narrative_blocks.header: He led the Providence Journal thirty-six years
narrative_blocks.body: Stephen Olney Metcalf became a director of the Providence Journal Company in 1890 and its president from 1905 until 1941. He guided the paper for thirty-six years while running the family's Wanskuck woolen mills.

narrative_blocks.header: Eighth-generation heir to a textile fortune
narrative_blocks.body: Metcalf was the eldest son of the eighth American generation of his line, descended from a settler at Dedham in 1637. He led the Wanskuck Company, one of the nation's foremost woolen-fabric makers, and held directorships across banking and insurance.

narrative_blocks.header: At twenty-seven he became RISD's treasurer
narrative_blocks.body: Elected treasurer of the Rhode Island School of Design at twenty-seven, Metcalf began a lifetime of giving to the school his family had helped found. He left his Colonial Revival mansion to RISD as its president's house.

narrative_blocks.header: A Brown man who served as trustee
narrative_blocks.body: A graduate of Brown University in 1878, Metcalf served the school as a longtime trustee and benefactor. His brother Jesse Metcalf sat twelve years in the United States Senate.

notable.notable_blurb: Painter of Connecticut's fabled Charter Oak
notable.primary_url_label: Rhode Island Heritage Hall of Fame

narrative_blocks.header: He painted the Charter Oak after it fell
narrative_blocks.body: Brownell lived opposite Hartford's Charter Oak and painted it in 1857, the year after the historic tree came down in a storm. His canvas became the tree's definitive likeness and hangs today at the Wadsworth Atheneum.

narrative_blocks.header: He left the law for landscape painting
narrative_blocks.body: Admitted to the Connecticut bar in 1843, Brownell abandoned law after a decade when illness and a love of sketching drew him to art. He studied in Hartford and kept a studio there before moving to New York in 1860.

narrative_blocks.header: He became America's painter of Cuba
narrative_blocks.body: Brownell spent seven winters on the Cuban sugar plantations of his mother's family, the De Wolfs of Bristol, becoming perhaps the mid-century American artist most associated with the island. He befriended the Hudson River School painter Frederic Church, a fellow son of Hartford.

narrative_blocks.header: He married into the Metcalf family's orbit
narrative_blocks.body: In 1865 Brownell married Henrietta Knowlton Angell Pierce of Bristol and became stepfather to her daughter Esther, the future wife of Providence Journal publisher Stephen Olney Metcalf. He settled in Bristol, where the couple raised four sons.

narrative_blocks.header: His diary was written in Greek letters
narrative_blocks.body: For years the restless Brownell kept a curious diary, English words spelled out in the Greek alphabet. He traveled almost ceaselessly, from the White Mountains and Cuba to Egypt and South America, until a broken hip slowed him near the end.

narrative_blocks.header: He painted what Andros never got
narrative_blocks.body: The tree he painted was the one Connecticut's charter went into in 1687, the night Governor Andros came to Hartford to take it and the candles in the meeting-house went out. Brownell had the oak from his own window.

narrative_blocks.header: She died six days after her son came
narrative_blocks.body: She married the Rev. George Goetchius in 1875 and bore a son, William, on 9 April 1876. She was dead by the fifteenth, at twenty-six, and lies in the Memory Hill ground at Milledgeville.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brother married her husband’s sister
narrative_blocks.body: Her brother Guy McKinley married Mary Goetchius, her husband’s younger sister, so that two McKinleys took two Goetchiuses. Mary was dead herself by 1882, at twenty-five.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at twenty-one of fever
narrative_blocks.body: Andrew McKinley, known in the family as Arny, died in 1875 at twenty-one after a two-week bout of fever. He was buried with military honors by his company, the Baldwin Blues.

narrative_blocks.header: His son Lee lived past a hundred
narrative_blocks.body: Guy married twice, to Mary Goetchius and then to Forrest Lee Carrington, raising children of both marriages near Milledgeville. His son Lee Carrington McKinley lived from 1898 to 2001, past the age of a hundred.

narrative_blocks.header: At seventy-two he wrote down the war
narrative_blocks.body: In 1930 he set down what he remembered of his childhood on his parents’ plantation across the Oconee from Milledgeville, when Sherman’s march engulfed the place in 1864. Two Union generals were quartered on the McKinley land.

narrative_blocks.header: He buried one wife and married again
narrative_blocks.body: His first wife Mamie Goetchius died in 1882 leaving him two small children, the younger a few weeks old. In December 1885 he married Forrest Lee Carrington at her father’s house near Milledgeville, and she outlived him by seventeen years.

narrative_blocks.header: She married the founder of Chandler, Arizona
narrative_blocks.body: Julia first married Dr. Alexander Chandler, the developer who founded the Arizona city that bears his name. She later married William Loftus and settled in California.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried his Georgia family west
narrative_blocks.body: Pope, a University of Georgia man, married Grace Sims and moved the family from Georgia to Missouri in 1872. His children scattered west to Arizona, Montana, and California.

notable.notable_blurb: Veterinarian, rancher and founder of Chandler, Arizona

narrative_blocks.header: Three hundred buyers, three wooden shacks
narrative_blocks.body: On 17 May 1912 Chandler opened his townsite office, and excursion trains on the new Arizona Eastern Railroad brought three hundred speculators who bought lots that day, each bound to build within a year. The town was then three wooden shacks; he laid it out around a landscaped square with covered walkways.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty days as Arizona's first veterinarian
narrative_blocks.body: Hired in 1887 by Governor C. Meyer Zulick and the new Livestock Sanitary Commission to fight cattle disease, Chandler came from Detroit to Prescott as Arizona Territory's first veterinary surgeon. He ordered checks on every herd driven in from Texas and was disturbed by how many arrived starving. Thirty days in, he resigned and set up practice in Phoenix.

narrative_blocks.header: Eighty desert acres, then eighteen thousand
narrative_blocks.body: In 1891 Chandler bought eighty acres of federal land south of Mesa, studied the new science of irrigation engineering, and built canals across the desert. He ran Mesa's canal under contract and in time united every canal south of the Salt River; by 1900 his ranch covered eighteen thousand acres.

narrative_blocks.header: Fourteen Wright buildings the Depression stopped
narrative_blocks.body: Chandler and his friend Frank Lloyd Wright planned some fourteen buildings for the town, and the Depression stopped every one. The Bank of Chandler failed, he lost his San Marcos Hotel to creditors, and he spent his last years in a small cottage on its grounds. An eight-foot bronze of the two men stands downtown.

narrative_blocks.header: He once staged an ostrich drive
narrative_blocks.body: In 1910 Chandler bought the Pan American Ostrich Company's whole flock and drove the birds like cattle some twenty-seven miles from Avondale to his ranch. In 1899 he had planted Egyptian long-staple cotton seed sent by the USDA's David Fairchild, then plowed it under when no pickers could be found.

narrative_blocks.header: Dummy owners beat the 160-acre water cap
narrative_blocks.body: The Salt River Project's charter gave each landowner water for only 160 acres. Chandler got around it with dummy owners who took up land and mortgaged it to him, backed by the money of Dexter Ferry, his old employer from Detroit.

narrative_blocks.header: First mayor of the town named for him
narrative_blocks.body: During World War I the Goodyear Tire Company leased eight thousand acres south of town from Chandler's Improvement Company and built the town of Goodyear. When the townspeople voted to incorporate in May 1920, Chandler served as its first mayor until one could be elected.

narrative_blocks.header: He moderated the assembly in its jubilee year
narrative_blocks.body: He was moderator of the general assembly of the Presbyterian church in 1897, when it met at Charlotte to mark two hundred and fifty years since the Westminster assembly. That session was reckoned the most historic in the life of the southern church.

narrative_blocks.header: The academy enlisted and he went with it
narrative_blocks.body: He was sixteen and at the Georgia Military Academy at Marietta when its students enlisted, and he joined the Confederate army with them a year or two after. He served without intermission until the Confederacy fell.

narrative_blocks.header: Clarkesville, Albany, Milledgeville, Augusta, Rome
narrative_blocks.body: He took the University of Georgia in 1868 and the seminary at Columbia, and began preaching in 1870 around Clarkesville. Albany, Milledgeville and Augusta followed, and in 1884 the First Presbyterian church at Rome called him for the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: Every other church closed for his funeral
narrative_blocks.body: His own church at Rome was crowded past its capacity and many could not get in. Services in every other church in the town were abandoned for the occasion.

narrative_blocks.header: He was widowed the week his son came
narrative_blocks.body: Julia McKinley bore their son William on 9 April 1876 and was dead on the fifteenth, at twenty-six. The boy lived to seventeen and died at Davidson College.

narrative_blocks.header: He came of a long line of ministers
narrative_blocks.body: He was descended from a line of ministers famous in the history of the Dutch Reformed church in America. He was clerk of the synod of Georgia for years and its moderator in 1883.

narrative_blocks.header: His first son was raised by the Scudders
narrative_blocks.body: Julia Scudder died in 1873, months after bearing him a son, and the boy Julian was reared at Athens by her parents. Julian managed the alkali works at Saltville and was that town’s mayor from 1909 to 1920.

narrative_blocks.body: She died on her husband’s farm near Milledgeville in the spring of 1882, at twenty-five, leaving two little children of whom the younger was a few weeks old. She had been born and reared at Columbus.

narrative_blocks.header: She came by letter from her brother’s church
narrative_blocks.body: The Milledgeville session received her in May 1881 by letter from the Second Presbyterian Church of Augusta, where her brother George was the pastor. Two of her other brothers, Henry and Charles, stayed at Columbus.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at her father’s house at night
narrative_blocks.body: The Reverend Donald McQueen married her to Guy Cummins McKinley on a Thursday night in December 1885, at her father Lafayette Carrington’s house near Milledgeville. Her brother was Major Frank de Launay Carrington, whose name her eldest daughter carried.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at twenty-six, full of promise
narrative_blocks.body: Guy's only son by his first marriage, William trained as a physician but died in 1906 at twenty-six after a long illness. His gravestone called him gentle in manner and gifted in mind, taken at the threshold of a life of promise.

narrative_blocks.header: The historic Goetchius house passed to her
narrative_blocks.body: Mary married Samuel Marshall Wellborn of Columbus, Georgia, and through her the historic Goetchius family house descended another generation. Her son Sam carried the line into the twentieth century.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty years an agent for the railroad
narrative_blocks.body: He was agent for the Georgia Railroad at Milledgeville for more than fifty years, and an officer of the First Presbyterian Church there. He died in a local hospital on a Friday morning in 1951.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried the name his uncle willed
narrative_blocks.body: His uncle Archibald, who kept the Sapelo journal, had directed in 1876 that the book pass to any son a brother or sister might name for him. His father Guy named this one twelve years later.

narrative_blocks.header: She died of the child that went first
narrative_blocks.body: Her illness ran some weeks and she made a hard struggle before she died at Milledgeville in September 1916, at twenty-five. The infant had gone to the grave ahead of her.

narrative_blocks.header: He retired a colonel and went to Sarasota
narrative_blocks.body: He made his career in the United States Army and retired a colonel. By 1951 he was living at Sarasota in Florida, while his brothers held Milledgeville and St. Louis.

narrative_blocks.header: He lived from 1898 to 2001
narrative_blocks.body: Lee Carrington McKinley lived past a hundred and three, from 1898 to 2001. He married late, taking Amy Jones Boyd as his wife in 1989, and died in St. Louis.

narrative_blocks.header: He was a Georgia accountant and Bulldog
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel Marshall Wellborn Jr attended the University of Georgia, graduating in 1930, and became a certified public accountant. He lived in Columbus with his wife Betty Gardiner.

narrative_blocks.header: She finished the Milledgeville college at eighteen
narrative_blocks.body: She graduated from the Georgia Normal and Industrial College in 1910, and her senior photograph is in that year’s Brown Book. She married Archibald Carlisle McKinley five years afterwards.

narrative_blocks.header: She played tournament tennis to eighty-six
narrative_blocks.body: She kept at the game until she was eighty-six and took trophies at St. Louis, at Mason’s Island in Connecticut and at Manasota Key in Florida. She died on the eve of her hundred and first birthday.

narrative_blocks.header: She married again at eighty, to a McKinley
narrative_blocks.body: She came out of Columbia in 1929 and worked several years on Wall Street before marrying Shapleigh Boyd in 1935 and going to St. Louis. Widowed in 1981, she married Lee Carrington McKinley there in 1989.

narrative_blocks.header: Worcester called him Doctor Lem
narrative_blocks.body: Woodward took his degree from Harvard Medical School in 1881 and practised in Worcester as a surgeon and city physician, the third generation of his family to doctor the town. Patients and neighbours knew him as Doctor Lem.

narrative_blocks.header: His ambition was the year's first mourning dove
narrative_blocks.body: Woodward kept a nature calendar and a record of bird migration, logging the red-winged blackbirds and swallows as they came north and the nighthawks that nested on the roofs around his house. His standing ambition was to be the first man each spring to report the mourning dove's return.

narrative_blocks.header: A trip to California was the prescription
narrative_blocks.body: In 1884 the Worcester physician Thomas Hovey Gage was treating John Washburn's recurring mental illness with long journeys, and sent Woodward, three years out of medical school, to take him to California. Woodward wrote back through the spring on how his patient was standing the trip.

narrative_blocks.header: Elected to the bird club at nineteen
narrative_blocks.body: Woodward was made a resident member of the Nuttall Ornithological Club in 1876, among its early members, resigned three years later, and came back in 1880 as a corresponding member. He joined the American Ornithologists' Union in 1917 and led the Worcester Natural History Society as president and then trustee until his death.

narrative_blocks.header: He stroked Harvard's crew and hung bird boxes
narrative_blocks.body: At Harvard he stroked the varsity crew; at home he rowed with the Quinsigamond boat club and ran swimming classes for the boys of Worcester on the lake. He put up bird boxes on the club's grounds.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty years of Amherst catchers began with him
narrative_blocks.body: In 1935 Amherst picked the outstanding player at each position from its previous fifty years of baseball, and five men made the roll at catcher. Woodward, class of 1881, was the earliest of the five.

notable.notable_blurb: Hall of Fame newspaper sports editor and columnist

narrative_blocks.header: He made a sports page worth reading
narrative_blocks.body: Woodward ran the New York Herald Tribune's sports section from 1938, and again from 1959. Told the Times had twice his staff, he answered that they could not outwrite him, and he refused to let athletes be godded up. The sportswriters' hall of fame took him in 1974.

narrative_blocks.header: He named the Ivy League to needle Harvard
narrative_blocks.body: Writing on 14 October 1933 about nine eastern football colleges, Woodward called them the ivy colleges, the first use of the phrase that became the Ivy League. He meant it as needling, a colleague said, Harvard above all.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine eye operations, and he still played tackle
narrative_blocks.body: Cataracts took his sight from boyhood and he was cut for them nine times, the first at seventeen. He played the Amherst line nearly blind until a helmet was contrived to hold his glasses.

narrative_blocks.header: He printed the strike and it collapsed
narrative_blocks.body: On 9 May 1947 Woodward reported that Cardinals players were canvassing the National League to strike against Jackie Robinson, and that its president would suspend every man who joined. The strike never came.

narrative_blocks.header: Asked to name two men, he named himself
narrative_blocks.body: Ordered in 1948 to put two of his staff up for dismissal, Woodward sent his own name and Red Smith's — the columnist he had found in Philadelphia. He was fired that year, and came back eleven years later.

narrative_blocks.header: He went into Arnhem with a scout knife
narrative_blocks.body: Woodward set the sports page aside to report the war, riding a glider into the Netherlands with the 101st Airborne in 1944 carrying a Boy Scout knife and a sheaf of pencils.

narrative_blocks.header: He pitched to the Yankees in Gehrig's shirt
narrative_blocks.body: Woodward once threw batting practice for the Yankees in a uniform borrowed from Lou Gehrig. Away from the desk he sailed a battered ketch alone on the Sound, played the violin hard, and walked the woods after birds.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Caldecott Honors for another woman's stories
narrative_blocks.body: Woodward's watercolours for Lavinia Riker Davis's Roger and the Fox took a Caldecott Honor in 1948, and The Wild Birthday Cake a second in 1950. She illustrated some two dozen children's books, and wrote several of her own.

narrative_blocks.header: Blind, she painted with twigs and waxed paper
narrative_blocks.body: Diabetes took her sight in the late 1960s and she went on working, feeling her way with twigs, tree branches and wads of waxed paper. She turned to black and white until a friend began mixing her colours into numbered pots she could count by touch.

narrative_blocks.header: Find the dragonfly, she called from the scaffold
narrative_blocks.body: In 1953 she painted the full length of one cafeteria wall at the Center School in Brookfield, Connecticut, while the children ate below her. One of them remembered her calling down to ask who could find the dragonfly. The mural is still there.

narrative_blocks.header: Her work hung well beyond the nursery shelf
narrative_blocks.body: Woodward showed at the Worcester Art Museum, the Metropolitan Museum of Art and Hartford's Wadsworth Atheneum, and had a solo exhibition at the Marie Sterner Gallery in New York in 1932. She drew adult humour and fiction too, and left studio sketches of George Bernard Shaw.

narrative_blocks.header: A stranger in Boston handed her a trade
narrative_blocks.body: Trained at the Museum of Fine Arts School in Boston and then in Paris, Woodward came home about 1930 and met the illustrator Marguerite Davis, who showed her book illustration as a field. Her first commission followed in 1931.

narrative_blocks.header: Her orchard house was always full of children
narrative_blocks.body: She moved to Brookfield in 1942 and stayed the rest of her life in a low white house standing in an apple orchard. A neighbour wrote that a visitor might find her painting, digging in the garden, canning vegetables, or giving children a thoroughly good time. She never married.

narrative_blocks.header: His obituaries named him for his wife
narrative_blocks.body: In a rare reversal for the era, Grinfill Blake's 1896 death notices identified him chiefly as the husband of the suffragist Lillie Devereux Blake. The New York merchant and his wife had lived apart for his final thirteen years.

narrative_blocks.header: His funeral banished all religious ceremony
narrative_blocks.body: A rationalist and philosophical anarchist, he asked that his 1923 memorial avoid anything funereal or churchly. Seventy-five friends met at the Artists' Guild Hall, and where the casket would have stood there was a chair with a pillow of yellow chrysanthemums spelling his name in purple flowers.

narrative_blocks.header: He designed buildings and fought building law
narrative_blocks.body: A partner in the New York firm Thayer and Robinson, he went on to oversee the city's school buildings for the Board of Education and to write Principles of Architectural Composition in 1908.

narrative_blocks.header: He put Proudhon into English
narrative_blocks.body: He translated the General Idea of the Revolution in the Nineteenth Century, which Freedom Press brought out in London in the year he died. His own essays carried European libertarian argument to American readers.

narrative_blocks.header: They rose one by one and said why
narrative_blocks.body: Nobody introduced the speakers; Clark McAdams asked each in turn to stand and say why they had honoured him. The librarian quoted the Psalms anyway, and said he believed Robinson had a soul whether Robinson had thought so or not.

narrative_blocks.header: The chimes were across the street
narrative_blocks.body: Bells rang out at two o'clock and the room took them for a knell, but they were the church opposite telling the hour. The body was never in the hall at all, and he was cremated privately.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten years teaching architecture in St. Louis
narrative_blocks.body: He was head of the school of architecture at Washington University, having come out from New York in 1910. He died at seventy in the house on West Pine Boulevard.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter married at her own bedside
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth fell seriously ill two weeks before her 1911 wedding and the couple refused to put it off. Rev. Charles Scovil, a cousin of the bride, married her to Dr. William McKim Marriott where she lay, and there was no reception.

narrative_blocks.header: He decoded the chemistry of sick infants
narrative_blocks.body: Marriott's research into acidosis and infant feeding reshaped pediatric care in the early twentieth century. He served as dean of Washington University's medical school and, just before his death, of the University of California's.

narrative_blocks.header: He led two medical schools as dean
narrative_blocks.body: Marriott served for years as dean of Washington University's medical school and in 1936 took the deanship at the University of California, only to die months later. He was twice president of the American College of Physicians.

narrative_blocks.header: She chose the art world over activism
narrative_blocks.body: Unlike her suffragist mother and educator sister, Elizabeth Robinson was known not for reform but for the art circles of St. Louis, where her husband John Beverly Robinson led Washington University's school of architecture. The family's intellectual energy resurfaced two generations later in anthropology.

notable.notable_blurb: Educator, suffragist, and peace activist

narrative_blocks.header: She led one school for thirty-four years
narrative_blocks.body: Katherine Blake became principal of the girls' department of Public School 6 in 1894 and held the post for thirty-four years. In 1916 the school was renamed for her mother, the suffragist Lillie Devereux Blake.

narrative_blocks.header: She marshaled fifteen thousand teachers for suffrage
narrative_blocks.body: Blake organized New York's teachers behind the vote and each summer from 1911 to 1919 was sent by the national suffrage association to campaign in states weighing the question. She marched at the head of the teachers' contingent in the 1915 New York parade.

narrative_blocks.header: She was the board's first woman treasurer
narrative_blocks.body: Blake became the first female treasurer of the New York Board of Education and rose to the presidency of the National Education Association. She founded the city's first evening high school for women in 1897.

narrative_blocks.header: She carried seven million names against war
narrative_blocks.body: As a leader of the Women's International League for Peace and Freedom, Blake was chief spokesperson for the Disarmament Caravan that brought a petition of nearly seven million signatures to President Hoover in 1931 and to Geneva in 1932. In 1928 she was among nineteen educators chosen to accompany John Dewey to Russia.

narrative_blocks.header: Her activism doubled her famous mother's
narrative_blocks.body: Both Katherine and her widowed mother took the surname Blake when Lillie remarried in 1866, and both became suffragists. Katherine later co-wrote her mother's biography, Champion of Women.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote the book that saved her mother
narrative_blocks.body: Champion of Women, written with Margaret Louise Wallace in 1943, was built out of her mother's own papers. Lillie had been left out of the movement's official histories, and this answered them.

narrative_blocks.header: She taught, and argued for teaching girls better
narrative_blocks.body: She spent her working life in the schools and pressed for a progressive education for girls rather than an ornamental one. She took the suffrage cause from her mother and the pacifism was her own.

narrative_blocks.header: She set out to prove Carolina's literary worth
narrative_blocks.body: Writing as Tenella, Mary Bayard Clarke compiled Wood Notes, the first anthology of North Carolina poetry, then filled magazines North and South with her own verse and prose. The Raleigh News and Observer later mourned her as one of the state's most gifted daughters.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote to keep her family afloat
narrative_blocks.body: After her husband returned from Confederate prison broken in health and income, Clarke turned her pen into the household's support, editing journals and selling hymns at five dollars apiece. She translated Victor Hugo's poems so ably that the work drew notice in France.

narrative_blocks.header: Her gifts passed to daughter and granddaughter
narrative_blocks.body: Clarke's daughter Mary married the photographer Rufus Morgan, and her granddaughter Bayard Wootten became one of the South's pioneering photographers. The family's creative streak ran from Mary Bayard's verse to the camera lens within two generations.

narrative_blocks.header: She hid behind a string of pen names
narrative_blocks.body: Clarke published as Tenella and Betsey Bittersweet, names that let a Southern woman write freely for a press that frowned on it. Her satirical political pieces during Reconstruction drew particular notice.

narrative_blocks.header: One family's women wrote for both sides
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Bayard Clarke's verse and her sister Catherine's war diary spoke for the Confederacy, while their first cousin Lillie Devereux Blake became a leading Northern suffragist. The Devereux women left a literary record spanning the divide of the Civil War.

narrative_blocks.body: Francis entered the Confederate Navy as a midshipman in 1863, at fourteen, and served aboard the Patrick Henry, the ironclad Tennessee, the Chicora, the Raleigh, the Richmond and a torpedo boat. narrative_blocks.body: After years at the New York Institution for the Deaf, Clarke directed the Arkansas school and then, from 1892, the Michigan School for the Deaf at Flint. He published his Methods Used in the Michigan School for the Deaf in 1908.

narrative_blocks.header: Engineering degrees came between his teaching posts
narrative_blocks.body: Between stints at the New York deaf institution Clarke took a master's degree and a civil-engineering degree from Columbia and briefly practiced as an engineer. He kept returning to deaf education, the calling he found through a boyhood tutor.

narrative_blocks.header: He died a grand master of Masons
narrative_blocks.body: Clarke joined the Masons after moving to Michigan and was serving as grand master of the state's Grand Lodge when he died in 1913. His funeral was among the largest the city of Flint had ever seen.

narrative_blocks.body: Mai Clarke's first husband, Rufus Morgan, was a traveling photographer who died young in California. Their daughter, Bayard Wootten, would carry the camera much further, becoming one of the South's photographic pioneers.

narrative_blocks.body: Caleb Bradham mixed a soda in his basement next door, and Wootten drew its first trademark. Her family told a second story too: told the drink had pepsin in it, she made Pepsi-Cola of the word.

narrative_blocks.header: Over a cliff and up a water tower
narrative_blocks.body: Wootten had herself lowered by rope over Linville Falls to get the angle, flew over New Bern for some of the first aerial photographs made by a woman, and late in life climbed a water tower to shoot a mill.

narrative_blocks.header: She sewed her own National Guard uniform
narrative_blocks.body: Hired as photographer and publicity director at the Camp Glenn station, Wootten became the first woman in the North Carolina National Guard. She was photographed in a uniform she had made herself.

narrative_blocks.header: In 1910 she wrote against her own trade
narrative_blocks.body: Wootten published a protest at the treatment of women in a photographic journal in 1910, and afterwards marched in suffrage demonstrations, and lent her standing to women's groups across the South.

narrative_blocks.header: She bought her own camera and competed
narrative_blocks.body: When the photographer who had lent her a camera said she would never make the grade and took it back, she bought her own. From a shack beside her house she built the firm her half-brother and half-sister joined, the Wootten-Moulton Studio.

narrative_blocks.header: Her lens preserved a vanishing South
narrative_blocks.body: From back roads few outsiders entered she photographed sharecroppers, former slaves and mountain families, and her pictures carried books such as Cabins in the Laurel. A forestry association prized her live oaks in 1934.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother's letter got her into college
narrative_blocks.body: She reached the state's new college for women in 1892 on a letter her mother sent its founder: the girl meant to fit herself for a teacher, as she had her own way to make in the world. She left two years later, unable to pay.

narrative_blocks.body: Wootten joined the Merchant Marine at fifteen during the Second World War, enlisted in the Army afterwards and took his commission in 1951. He served through five wars and conflicts and retired a lieutenant colonel in 1967.

narrative_blocks.body: He was born in January 1929 at Hankow, one of the three towns later merged into Wuhan, while his father was serving with the United States Navy in China. He grew up in Hyattsville, Maryland.

narrative_blocks.body: Out of the Army in 1967, Wootten owned Brokenstraw Oil in Pennsylvania before founding House of David ministries with his wife Batya, and a publishing house after it. His own titles were Take Two Tablets Daily and Restoring Israel's Kingdom.

narrative_blocks.body: Angus Jr., John and Michael all went ahead of their father. He was ninety-one when he followed them, at Kissimmee in Florida, and was buried at Arlington.

narrative_blocks.header: He won over twelve hundred high-school games
narrative_blocks.body: In forty-six seasons at DeMatha Catholic High School, Wootten went 1,274-192 and never had a losing year. He took five national titles and thirty-three conference ones, and twice, in 1977-78 and 1990-91, his teams did not lose at all.

narrative_blocks.header: He reached the Hall without coaching college
narrative_blocks.body: In 2000 Wootten became the third high-school coach in the Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame, and the first admitted for schoolboy work alone. John Wooden said he knew of no finer coach at any level and stood in awe of him.

narrative_blocks.header: In 1965 his team toppled a dynasty
narrative_blocks.body: Wootten's DeMatha side ended the seventy-one-game winning streak of Lew Alcindor's Power Memorial in 1965. Half a century later Kareem Abdul-Jabbar still placed a DeMatha man by it: you are from that school.

narrative_blocks.header: He turned down every college that called
narrative_blocks.body: North Carolina State, Georgetown and American offered him jobs, and Duke, Wake Forest and Virginia enquired. He wanted only Maryland, two miles from DeMatha, and that offer never came — so he stayed where he was for forty-six years.

narrative_blocks.header: He started at an orphanage, coaching three sports
narrative_blocks.body: Wootten began in 1951 at St. Joseph's Home and School for Boys, an orphanage in northeast Washington, taking baseball, football and basketball at once. He finished a Maryland degree and reached DeMatha in 1956.

narrative_blocks.header: What his players remembered was not the winning
narrative_blocks.body: He sent more than a dozen boys to the NBA, among them Adrian Dantley and Danny Ferry. What they recalled was a coach who never once obsessed over winning a game, only over what each of them might become.

narrative_blocks.header: A coaching giant from a photographer's line
narrative_blocks.body: Wootten was born at Duke Hospital while his parents were visiting his grandmother, the photographer Bayard Wootten, in Chapel Hill. The New Bern family behind him had made its name in pictures rather than in sport.

notable.notable_blurb: Anthropologist who reframed the study of caste

narrative_blocks.header: He revolutionized how scholars study caste
narrative_blocks.body: At the University of Chicago, McKim Marriott built the leading center for South Asian anthropology and reframed the study of caste around Indian categories rather than Western ones. His 1955 volume Village India became a founding text of the field.

narrative_blocks.header: A wartime posting to India shaped him
narrative_blocks.body: Drafted as an army private who knew Japanese, Marriott was sent to India to translate radio transmissions and spent his days exploring villages near Delhi. The experience drew him from Harvard to a Chicago doctorate on rural Indian life.

narrative_blocks.header: He turned Hindu cosmology into a game
narrative_blocks.body: Marriott invented Samsara, a cube-based board game in which players took on caste statuses and occupations to inhabit traditional Hindu society. Students recalled the delight of stepping into the lives of the people they studied.

narrative_blocks.header: He reached one hundred, teaching to the end
narrative_blocks.body: Remembered as a spritely presence leaping up Haskell Hall's steps, Marriott trained generations of South Asia scholars across half a century at Chicago. He turned one hundred in February 2024 and died five months later.

narrative_blocks.header: Banker and railroad builder of Port Gibson

narrative_blocks.header: His upside-down movement put the gears on top
narrative_blocks.body: Hoadley designed shelf-clock movements of his own, including an unusual 'upside down' works with the great wheels mounted at the top. He is also credited with introducing ivory bushings that let his clocks run with little or no oil.

narrative_blocks.header: A clockmaker who reached the state senate
narrative_blocks.body: Hoadley ran the Greystone district of Plymouth, served three terms in the Connecticut assembly, and won a state senate seat in 1844. He retired a wealthy man in 1849 beside his rival Eli Terry.

narrative_blocks.header: His monument bears the Masonic square and compass
narrative_blocks.body: A Freemason of high standing in Harmony Lodge No. 42, Hoadley was eulogized as an honest man, the noblest work of God. His Plymouth gravestone was carved with a large outward-facing square and compass.

narrative_blocks.header: He learned carpentry from an uncle in Ohio
narrative_blocks.body: Hoadley was apprenticed as a carpenter to his uncle Calvin Hoadley before coming to Plymouth. It was Calvin who had built the gristmill at the Greystone falls where his nephew would later make clocks.

narrative_blocks.header: He asked the railroad to move its track
narrative_blocks.body: In March 1853 Hoadley wrote to the president of the railroad asking that the line be shifted to the east bank, because the road it would destroy was the one his clocks went out on. The road was moved.

narrative_blocks.header: He drew with the smoke of a candle
narrative_blocks.body: Hoadley is the earliest documented practitioner of fumage, in which an image is made from the soot of a candle or lamp. One of his, from about 1810, is in the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston.

notable.notable_blurb: First City Engineer of San Francisco

narrative_blocks.header: First City Engineer of San Francisco
narrative_blocks.body: Arriving in 1849, Milo Hoadley served as deputy to the city's first surveyor and became San Francisco's City Engineer in 1854. He laid out the street grades of the booming Gold Rush city.

narrative_blocks.header: His grades would have leveled the city's hills
narrative_blocks.body: Hoadley's 1854 plan would have flattened Telegraph, Russian, and Nob Hills to fill the bay, but public outcry defeated the so-called Hoadley Grades. He had better success surveying Hayes Valley, Bernal Heights, and his own Hoadley Tract in the Western Addition.

narrative_blocks.header: He proposed the Crystal Springs reservoir
narrative_blocks.body: Around 1870 Hoadley proposed damming a valley in San Mateo County to hold water for San Francisco. The reservoir was built as Crystal Springs — by Spring Valley, the monopoly his own water company had failed to displace.

narrative_blocks.header: A clockmaker's son who surveyed the frontier
narrative_blocks.body: Milo was the eldest son of the Connecticut clockmaker Silas Hoadley and left the family trade for engineering in Gold Rush California. He died in 1887 after being thrown from his buggy near Sonora.

narrative_blocks.header: He sold Sonoma wine with his two sons
narrative_blocks.body: In 1864 Hoadley formed Hoadley & Co., Dealers in Native Sonoma Wines, with his sons Silas and James. The firm lasted about four years, and Silas was killed in Mexico in the middle of it.

narrative_blocks.header: He fought the water monopoly and lost
narrative_blocks.body: In 1867 he organised the San Francisco Water Company with James T. Boyd and John H. Turney, and spent the next decade attacking the Spring Valley Water Company in print. Spring Valley kept the city.

narrative_blocks.header: The house outlasted the plans
narrative_blocks.body: His Bush Street house survives as a designated San Francisco landmark. The street grades he drew were thrown out by public outcry, and the reservoir he proposed was built by the rival that beat him.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: The Bush Street house he built in 1858, now a city landmark.

bio.bio_blurb: First City Engineer of San Francisco

narrative_blocks.header: He was his father's assistant city engineer
narrative_blocks.body: James Hoadley assisted his father Milo through the years Milo held the city engineer's post at San Francisco. A notebook of his survives from about 1862, with detailed plans and measurements of the city's streets.

narrative_blocks.header: He sold Sonoma wine with his family
narrative_blocks.body: In 1864 he joined Hoadley & Co., Dealers in Native Sonoma Wines, alongside his father Milo and his brother Silas. The firm ran about four years.

narrative_blocks.header: He married three times and died in Arizona
narrative_blocks.body: He married Lucy Wills and then Maria Webster, divorcing both, and last Frances Kinsella Beddy. He spent his working life surveying out of San Francisco and was living at Bisbee in Arizona Territory at the end.

narrative_blocks.header: He drew the map of Hunter's Point
narrative_blocks.body: In February 1867 Hoadley hand-drew the plan of the South San Francisco Homestead and Railroad Association tract at Hunter's Point, for the engineer William H. Bryan. The grid he laid down still shapes Bayview-Hunters Point.

narrative_blocks.header: He married at twenty-nine and had two sons
narrative_blocks.body: Hoadley married Lucy Wills of New York in June 1861. Their sons Milo and Charles Henry were born at San Francisco in 1862 and 1864; the marriage ended in divorce, and Lucy outlived him by forty-one years.

narrative_blocks.body: Mary died in 1836, aged about two.

narrative_blocks.header: He rode into the mountains and never returned
narrative_blocks.body: Hoadley went into Mexico in 1865 to value mining properties for investors, reached the mines hundreds of miles inland, and wrote home that he was safe. On the ride back he was pursued and killed by robbers for the money he carried.

narrative_blocks.header: His family waited four years for the news
narrative_blocks.body: He was twenty-eight, and his body was never recovered. For nearly four years his wife and parents did not know what had become of him.

narrative_blocks.header: The daughter he never saw
narrative_blocks.body: He sailed from New York in September 1865 expecting to be away a few months. His infant son Charles had died that August, and his daughter Sadie was born at Brooklyn the following March.

narrative_blocks.header: He was selling California wine when he detoured
narrative_blocks.body: In 1865 he joined a New York company formed to carry California wines and liquors into eastern and southern markets, and travelled for it as its representative. The Mexican mining survey was an unexpected offer taken up along the way.

narrative_blocks.header: He died of brain fever off Gibraltar
narrative_blocks.body: A lieutenant in the United States Navy, Tallmadge died of brain fever aboard the frigate Brandywine near Gibraltar in 1831, still unmarried. He had received an honorary master's degree from Yale only the year before.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale gave him a degree he never collected
narrative_blocks.body: Yale made the naval lieutenant an honorary member of the class of 1830 and gave him a master's degree that year. He was at sea, and dead off Gibraltar the following June, unmarried, at thirty-eight.

notable.notable_blurb: Connecticut judge; Western Reserve land proprietor

narrative_blocks.header: Canfield, Ohio bears his name
narrative_blocks.body: He bought 6,171 of the 16,324 acres of Township No. 1, Range 3 from the Connecticut Land Company, the largest share. On 15 April 1800 the settlers voted to call the place Canfield instead of Campfield.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife would not live in the town
narrative_blocks.body: The two of them came out to the township meaning to settle, but the surroundings were not congenial to Mrs. Canfield. She did not stay long and went back east, and soon after her husband followed her.

narrative_blocks.header: Sharon's noted horticulturist and sheep breeder
narrative_blocks.body: He improved the horned cattle, went extensively into sheep and their breeding, and manufactured woollen goods. His fruit made Sharon known for its apples, pears, peaches, grapes, strawberries, raspberries and currants.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven years on the Litchfield County bench
narrative_blocks.body: Canfield sat in the Connecticut General Assembly from 1802, took the county bench at Litchfield in 1808 and a seat in the state senate in 1810, and held both until 1815. He had practised law at Sharon since the year he married.

narrative_blocks.header: He lost the farm that made his name
narrative_blocks.body: The years given to public business ruined him. He sold the Sharon house and the cultivated farm that had made his reputation, and a contemporary found him hardly able to be other than depressed.

narrative_blocks.header: He spent the Revolution as his father's clerk
narrative_blocks.body: Canfield was at West Point through the war as clerk to his father, Colonel Samuel Canfield, and the Connecticut rolls carry him as a private of militia at the Danbury alarm. The colonel was sent to Sharon at Shays' Rebellion, to put down the agitation in his son's own town.

narrative_blocks.header: Six feet, and elastic in his step
narrative_blocks.body: He was six feet or more, symmetrically proportioned, straight and elastic, and a gentleman of the old school in politeness and suavity of manners.

notable.notable_blurb: Signer of the Declaration of Independence

narrative_blocks.header: A New York signer of the Declaration
narrative_blocks.body: Floyd was the first of New York's four delegates to sign the Declaration, and the youngest of them — the only signer from Suffolk County on Long Island. A plain plantation man rather than a lawyer or orator, he sat through the debates saying little and did his work on the committees instead.

narrative_blocks.header: His militia met the British on Long Island
narrative_blocks.body: A major general of the Suffolk County militia, Floyd resisted an early British landing before the island fell. His family fled across the Sound to Connecticut and lived as refugees until the war's end.

narrative_blocks.header: First Congressman, then a frontier pioneer
narrative_blocks.body: Floyd served in the first United States Congress from 1789 to 1791 and twice sat as a presidential elector. At sixty-nine he moved to the Mohawk frontier, where Oneida County's town of Floyd bears his name.

narrative_blocks.header: At eighteen, a plantation and six children
narrative_blocks.body: His father died when he was eighteen, and William took over the family's Mastic plantation on Long Island and the raising of his six younger siblings. He had little formal schooling; what he learned came from running the estate and from the educated men who passed through his manor house.

narrative_blocks.header: He came home to his house a stable
narrative_blocks.body: The British occupied Long Island for seven years, and when the war ended and he finally returned to Mastic, the enemy cavalry had used his home as a stable and left it wrecked. His wife had died in exile in Connecticut two years earlier and never saw it. He rebuilt, and married again.

narrative_blocks.header: A future president courted his daughter
narrative_blocks.body: James Madison sat with Floyd in the Continental Congress, and there the young Virginian met Floyd's daughter Catharine. The two became engaged in 1783 and traded miniature portraits — Madison's painted by Charles Willson Peale, set with a lock of his hair. Then sixteen-year-old Kitty broke it off by letter to marry a clergyman instead, and the future president stayed a bachelor for a decade more.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: His Long Island home, the Old Mastic House, now a National Park Service site.

bio.bio_blurb: Signer of the Declaration of Independence

narrative_blocks.header: She ran Mastic while he signed the Declaration
narrative_blocks.body: From the moment William Floyd entered public life, the Mastic plantation was hers to manage. A Southampton girl married to him in 1760, she bore three children and held the estate together through his years in Congress.

narrative_blocks.header: She died in exile and never saw home
narrative_blocks.body: When the British took Long Island, fishermen carried her and the children across the Sound to safety in Connecticut. She spent the rest of the war hiding at Middletown and died there in 1781, two years before the peace let the family go home.

narrative_blocks.header: The second wife who came after the war
narrative_blocks.body: William Floyd married her in 1784, the year after he returned to a Mastic home the British had ruined and rebuilt. A Setauket woman, she was his companion through his last decades — the frontier move upstate, the state senate years — and outlived him by five years.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a Philadelphia merchant
narrative_blocks.body: John Parker White was born in Delaware and traded in Philadelphia. He married Elizabeth Canfield Tallmadge in 1836, when she was nineteen, and the two of them had eight children.

narrative_blocks.header: Third in her family at Sarah Pierce's
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother had gone to the Litchfield Female Academy and her father to the Law School across the green. Elizabeth, living in the town, was almost certainly sent to Pierce's in her turn, about 1832.

people.research_notes: Litchfield Ledger: she is believed to have attended the Litchfield Female Academy c.1832, inferred from residence and her parents' schooling, not from a roll. Eight children are recorded; five are in the tree.

narrative_blocks.header: She ran the Litchfield Historical Society
narrative_blocks.body: An amateur historian in a town full of history, she led the Litchfield Historical Society for years after its founding in 1856. Two years after she died her grandson put up a building for it and the town library, and named it for her.

narrative_blocks.header: A pupil of Sarah Pierce, and a subject
narrative_blocks.body: She was taught at Sarah Pierce's Litchfield Female Academy, the school that took girls seriously before almost anyone else did. Her daughter Emily later wrote its history in two volumes.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept her grandfather’s house
narrative_blocks.body: With her husband, the New York lawyer William Curtis Noyes, she held the Litchfield house of her grandfather Benjamin Tallmadge. It passed to Emily after them.

narrative_blocks.header: She was the lawyer's second wife
narrative_blocks.body: William Curtis Noyes came to the marriage a widower with one surviving child by Anne Tracy of Utica. Julia Tallmadge married him in New York on 7 October 1841 and bore him three more.

notable.notable_blurb: Sons of the Revolution president; saved Fraunces Tavern

narrative_blocks.header: His gift saved Fraunces Tavern
narrative_blocks.body: As the Sons of the Revolution's second president, Tallmadge set his sights on the decaying Fraunces Tavern, where Washington had bidden his officers farewell. He signed the purchase contract on his deathbed in 1904, and his estate cleared the debt.

narrative_blocks.header: Great-grandson of two Revolutionary patriots
narrative_blocks.body: Tallmadge descended from the Declaration signer William Floyd and from Benjamin Tallmadge of the Culper Spy Ring. A New York lawyer, he belonged to the Union Club, the New-York Historical Society, and the Society of the Cincinnati.

narrative_blocks.header: He left the society his library and relics
narrative_blocks.body: In his will Tallmadge gave the Sons of the Revolution his library and Revolutionary relics, among them Benjamin Tallmadge's handwritten memoir. A bronze tablet by Victor Brenner marks Fraunces Tavern as his memorial.

narrative_blocks.header: He owned Napoleon's gift to an actor
narrative_blocks.body: Among his relics were a gold repeating watch Napoleon gave the tragedian Talma, the original death mask of Cromwell, and George Clinton's sword. A Sharples portrait of Washington hung with them.

narrative_blocks.header: He left his house to be a museum
narrative_blocks.body: His will gave No. 23 Gramercy Park South to the Sons of the Revolution, to be made as nearly fireproof as possible and filled with Revolutionary relics. The society sold it instead and put the money into Fraunces Tavern.

narrative_blocks.body: Mary Floyd Tallmadge married Edward Woodruff Seymour in New York on 12 May 1864. Both families had been Litchfield names for three generations, and two daughters were born to the couple.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived him by a quarter century
narrative_blocks.body: Edward Seymour died of cerebral meningitis in 1892, still sitting on the Connecticut supreme court. Mary kept on at Litchfield another twenty-five years and was buried beside him five days short of eighty-six.

notable.notable_blurb: Eminent New York lawyer and legal codifier

narrative_blocks.header: One of the New York bar's giants
narrative_blocks.body: Noyes rose from district attorney of Oneida County to the front rank of the New York bar, prized for his cross-examination and equity practice. In 1857 he was named a commissioner to codify the laws of the state.

narrative_blocks.header: He left Hamilton College his law library
narrative_blocks.body: Noyes assembled one of the finest law libraries in the country and bequeathed its five thousand volumes to Hamilton College, which had granted him an honorary LL.D. He had no college education himself.

narrative_blocks.header: A Union man courted for the Senate
narrative_blocks.body: A founder of the Union League and a peace-conference delegate in 1861, Noyes was a leading candidate that winter for a United States Senate seat. He declined politics for the law until his sudden death in 1864.

narrative_blocks.header: The Tallmadge house was his in Litchfield
narrative_blocks.body: He married Julia Tallmadge and with her held the Litchfield house of her grandfather Benjamin Tallmadge, a New York practice notwithstanding. The house went to their daughter Emily.

notable.notable_blurb: Painter, author, and Litchfield historian

narrative_blocks.header: A hundred squares of an Egyptian mummy
narrative_blocks.body: She ruled a ten-by-ten grid and filled it with the colours of one object — a cup and saucer, a Japanese vase, the case of an Egyptian mummy — each shade given as many squares as its share of the whole.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty years before Albers, and unattributed
narrative_blocks.body: Color Problems ran to 400 pages and 116 plates in 1902, one of the first books on colour written and published by a woman. It went unread for decades, then turned up prefiguring Klee, Albers and Rothko — whose own Interaction of Color credits her nowhere.

narrative_blocks.header: Bronze at the Woman’s Building, 1893
narrative_blocks.body: She studied under Robert Swain Gifford and William Sartain and took a bronze medal at the Woman's Building of the Chicago exposition. The book was written for dressmakers, florists, milliners and decorators — the trades then open to women.

narrative_blocks.header: She remade Litchfield in Colonial Revival
narrative_blocks.body: As curator of the Litchfield Historical Society she drove the town's Colonial Revival, behind the business district and the restorations of the Congregational Church and the Litchfield Law School. She founded the local DAR chapter, named for her great-grandmother Mary Floyd Tallmadge.

narrative_blocks.header: Chronicles of a pioneer school
narrative_blocks.body: The Chronicles of a Pioneer School, her two-volume history of the Litchfield Female Academy her mother had attended, put a girls' school of 1792 into the record. She left her art pottery to the Historical Society and her Japanese collection to the Norwich museum.

narrative_blocks.header: She finished her son’s gift to Litchfield
narrative_blocks.body: When John Arent died with his library building unfinished, she completed it and set a memorial tablet to him beneath its Palladian window. The building honoured her mother, Julia Tallmadge Noyes.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at twenty-three, and stayed so
narrative_blocks.body: John Aaron Vanderpoel died in April 1866, a year after the wedding and seven weeks before their son was born. She never married again, and had seventy-three years to spend.

narrative_blocks.body: The building went up at South and East Streets in 1901 and was enlarged within six years. The library left for a house of its own in the 1960s, and the Litchfield Historical Society, founded in 1856, took the whole of it.

narrative_blocks.body: Trumbull-Vanderpoel was incorporated in 1912 and he helped start it, then left the presidency in 1926, in his middle thirties. He had twenty-two years of Litchfield left.

narrative_blocks.header: A T above a V, stamped in slate
narrative_blocks.body: The works marked its switches with a triangle a quarter-inch wide — a T above a V, and CONN USA — registered at the patent office in 1919. One of them still throws the current in Old Main at Colorado, the logo readable only under a raking light.

narrative_blocks.header: Ninety hands on the Bantam River
narrative_blocks.body: The 1914 catalogue offered knife switches, switchboards, panel boards and steel and wood cabinets, and by 1922 ninety people worked the brick building on the river. Electrical makers held it for eighty years after him; it opened as an arts factory in 2018.

narrative_blocks.header: A charter member of the Cinema League
narrative_blocks.body: Amateur film and amateur radio held him for the rest of his life: a charter member of the American Cinema League, and active for many years in the American Radio League.

narrative_blocks.header: Three days in the Torrington hospital
narrative_blocks.body: He went into the Charlotte Hungerford Hospital on a Tuesday and was dead of a cerebral hemorrhage by Thursday afternoon, at fifty-seven. Only one of his two sons was left to bury him.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at St. Michael’s, Litchfield, 1914
narrative_blocks.body: She was married to Floyd Lewis Vanderpoel there on an August afternoon in 1914, before three hundred guests, with the reception after at Forked Chimney, her father's house.

narrative_blocks.header: Seymour Cunningham drowned on his walk
narrative_blocks.body: Seymour Cunningham, a civil engineer of about eighty, went out one afternoon in May 1944 as he always did and fell from the private footbridge over the Bantam River on his own land. A man working the estate found him that evening, half a mile from the house.

narrative_blocks.header: The flower girl married a du Pont
narrative_blocks.body: Pamela Cunningham, her youngest sister and the flower girl at her wedding, married Lammot du Pont Copeland of Wilmington, afterwards president of the DuPont company. A third sister, Alexis, stayed at Litchfield, and their brother Macklin farmed at Goshen.

narrative_blocks.header: Ninety-three letters to the mothers
narrative_blocks.body: He commanded the 424th Bomb Squadron — 750 men — and flew B-24s from the Admiralty Islands toward the Philippines. Ninety-three of his letters went to the mothers of dead pilots.

narrative_blocks.header: Tokyo Rose said his plane had gone down
narrative_blocks.body: He took the first plane over Palau, photographing targets before the Navy invasion, and cloud drove him from 22,000 feet to 9,000. Zeros came up after him; Tokyo Rose reported the lone B-24 lost, and they listened to her show for the music.

narrative_blocks.header: They took helmets to the evening film
narrative_blocks.body: The evening movie started at a quarter past six and the men brought their helmets, because the Japanese cut their engines and glided in under the radar. One night a bomb hit an aircraft loaded for the morning and took two more with it, his own among them.

narrative_blocks.header: Lindbergh flew escort once, and scored
narrative_blocks.body: They flew without fighter escort, close enough to see the faces of the pilots coming through the formation. The one exception was Charles Lindbergh, out selling airplanes, who taught them to lean their engines and shot down a Japanese fighter that trip.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-three, and teaching men to fly
narrative_blocks.body: Called up from the MIT reserve early in 1941, he was kept instructing when he wanted the war, and worked through sixty or seventy engine failures on the poor fuel training units drew.

narrative_blocks.header: The island loudspeaker announced his son
narrative_blocks.body: He married in September 1941 and named the first boy Eric, for the brother buried the year before. The microphone cut into the evening film on the island to tell him the second son had been born.

narrative_blocks.header: High-wheel bicycles and racing wheelchairs
narrative_blocks.body: After the Air Force he restored high-wheel bicycles and the boneshakers before them, rode centuries in two countries, crossed the continent alone more than once, and put 200,000 miles on his road bike. Hall's Wheels, his company with the athlete Bob Hall, made more than a sport wheelchair a day.

military_service.notes: Commanding officer of a B-24 squadron in the Pacific theater; retired from the U.S. Air Force in 1967.

career.organization: Hanscom Air Force Base and the Pentagon

narrative_blocks.header: Trinity’s freshman class came in a body
narrative_blocks.body: A freshman at Trinity College, dead at nineteen, he was carried by his Alpha Delta Phi brothers of the class of 1944 in the college chapel, the president of Trinity officiating. The whole freshman class attended together, and he went home to Litchfield to be buried.

narrative_blocks.header: A nephew took his name in 1942
narrative_blocks.body: John married ten months after the funeral, and the first boy born to him in August 1942 was called Eric.

narrative_blocks.header: Married the day after he got his wings
narrative_blocks.body: John Arent Vanderpoel was commissioned in the Army Air Corps on 26 September 1941 and they were married the next day. It lasted sixty-six years, to his death.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-eight years of other people’s postings
narrative_blocks.body: Through his service she sat on the boards of spouse support groups and kept the books as secretary of the officers' wives club in Washington. Settled at Concord afterwards, she gave her time to the Red Cross, Emerson Hospital, and Trinity Church.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived a husband and a son
narrative_blocks.body: John Jr. died at Acton in 2002 and her husband at Concord six years after. She had five years more, and one son left — Eric, a Navy captain at Alexandria.

notable.notable_blurb: U.S. Congressman; the 'Kinderhook Roarer'

narrative_blocks.header: The ‘Kinderhook Roarer’ of Congress
narrative_blocks.body: He went to Washington as a Jacksonian in 1833, lost the seat in 1836, and took it back in 1838. The carrying power of his voice earned him the name the Kinderhook Roarer.

narrative_blocks.header: He settled Benjamin Franklin’s grandson’s estate
narrative_blocks.body: William Temple Franklin had been his grandfather's secretary in Paris and had edited his papers, and left land in five states when he died in 1823. Vanderpoel took on the administration and did not lay it down until 1866.

narrative_blocks.header: The King’s side cost his father everything
narrative_blocks.body: Isaac Vanderpoel was made adjutant of a Kinderhook militia regiment in 1775, removed for disaffection, and went over to command a company of refugees on Staten Island. The state took his estate after the war and left him a small farm at Chatham.

narrative_blocks.header: His niece married the President’s son
narrative_blocks.body: He was close to Andrew Jackson and closer to Martin Van Buren, his neighbour at Kinderhook. In 1841 his brother James's daughter Elizabeth married John Van Buren, the President's second son.

narrative_blocks.header: From Van Schaack’s office to the bench
narrative_blocks.body: He read law with Peter Van Schaack, the blind Loyalist lawyer of Kinderhook, finished with his brother James, and was admitted in 1820. After Congress he sat seven years as a justice of New York's superior court, from the house he built on East Sixteenth Street.

narrative_blocks.header: Brady’s plate, scratched ‘Judge Vanderpool’
narrative_blocks.body: Mathew Brady's studio took him in a gold-toned half-plate daguerreotype, side whiskers and all, some time between 1844 and 1860. Whoever put the plate away scratched the name on the back and spelled it wrong.

narrative_blocks.header: She married the Kinderhook Roarer
narrative_blocks.body: Judge Aaron Vanderpoel had been a widower two years when she married him in April 1839, and she was sixteen years younger. They lived in the house he built at 114 East Sixteenth Street.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father held half New York’s Irish trade
narrative_blocks.body: James McBride came out of County Armagh in 1795 and built a merchant house on the Ireland trade, with ships of his own — the Erin, and the old Dublin Packet that carried emigrants as well as goods. He was the last New York merchant in direct trade with Dublin.

narrative_blocks.header: Take me to my own room, he said
narrative_blocks.body: Near the end he had himself helped downstairs, and asked his daughter Ann where the fire was. Told the bright one was in his own room above, he looked round and said: take me to my own room, where I have slept and where I will shortly be laid out.

narrative_blocks.header: Irish clients, and land on the Erie Canal
narrative_blocks.body: James McBride practised law besides, acting for clients in Ireland who held property in New York, and dealing in western New York land with the Holland Land Company. His partners bought the Walton tract at Syracuse in 1824, where the new canal ended.

narrative_blocks.header: She married the spymaster's son in 1810
narrative_blocks.body: Maria Adams of Litchfield married Henry Floyd Tallmadge there on 18 November 1810, when she was twenty-two, and had six children by him. They went to New York, where he kept a store and was made United States Marshal for the southern district.

narrative_blocks.header: Dropsy took her father at thirty-eight
narrative_blocks.body: Her father, Andrew Adams Jr., collected Litchfield's taxes and died there of dropsy at three on a Sunday morning in December 1804, his going as sudden as a flitting meteor. Maria was sixteen, one of the two children he left.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandfather signed the Articles
narrative_blocks.body: Maria was a month short of ten when her grandfather died at Litchfield in 1797. Andrew Adams had signed the Articles of Confederation at Philadelphia in 1778 and was chief justice of Connecticut for his last four years.

burial.plot_notes: New York Marble Cemetery, East Village

people.research_notes: Her father was Andrew Adams Jr. (1766-1804) of Litchfield, tax collector, who married Annis Canfield (1769-1814) on 25 April 1785; the Litchfield Monitor of 12 December 1804 carried the death notice quoted in NB2. Her grandfather was the Hon. Andrew Adams (1736-1797), Yale 1760, king's attorney for Litchfield County 1772, colonel of Connecticut militia, speaker of the state house 1779-80, delegate to the Second Continental Congress and a signer of the Articles of Confederation in 1778, chief justice of Connecticut 1793 until his death; buried in what the congressional biography calls East Cemetery, Litchfield, now officially West Cemetery. Pyne calls Maria a daughter of the Hon. Andrew Adams; she was his granddaughter. Neither Adams is in the tree.

narrative_blocks.body: Laura died in 1816, aged about two.

narrative_blocks.header: He drowned boating off Staten Island
narrative_blocks.body: Henry Adams Tallmadge was the youngest of Henry Floyd Tallmadge's six children and the only one to die by accident. He went out boating off Staten Island and drowned, not yet twenty.

notable.notable_blurb: Broker of A. G. Norwood & Co.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years on the Stock Exchange floor
narrative_blocks.body: He started as a broker on his own account in 1833 and was among the oldest members of the Exchange when he died. His father had been a New York merchant before him, of one of the older families in the city.

narrative_blocks.header: The name outlasted every partner
narrative_blocks.body: He founded Norwood & Robinson in 1846; when Robinson retired his son came in and it became A. G. Norwood & Co. The firm was dissolved in 1857 and he took Lawrence R. Jerome in, keeping the title, and retired in 1865.

narrative_blocks.header: The Exchange flew its flag at half-mast
narrative_blocks.body: President Ives announced his death at the opening of business and a committee was named to draw up resolutions and attend the funeral. It was held from his house at 236 West Fourteenth Street; heart disease had troubled him for some time.

narrative_blocks.header: He gathered the papers for a spy's life
narrative_blocks.body: He and Emily Wilkins collected the family letters that became Washington's Secret Agent Benjamin Tallmadge, the book about his wife's grandfather. The Tallmadge-Norwood-Wilkins collection runs from 1769 to 1962.

notable.notable_blurb: Wall Street financier who built Glenview Mansion

narrative_blocks.header: A Wall Street financier and Colgate's partner
narrative_blocks.body: Trevor came to New York in 1849 and joined the Stock Exchange in 1850, partnering with James Boorman Colgate in the brokerage that became James B. Colgate & Company. He remained a partner until his death in 1890.

narrative_blocks.header: He built Glenview on the Hudson
narrative_blocks.body: In 1877 Trevor built Glenview, a greystone country house in Yonkers, commuting from there to Wall Street by rail. The mansion survives today as part of the Hudson River Museum.

narrative_blocks.header: Trotting horses and horticulture
narrative_blocks.body: At Glenview, where the family lived from April through December, John drove his trotting horses and gave his leisure to horticulture, his chief hobby, commuting to Wall Street by rail.

narrative_blocks.header: A church and a hospital in Yonkers
narrative_blocks.body: John helped build the Warburton Avenue Baptist Church in Yonkers and helped found what became St. John's Riverside Hospital. He also supported the Yonkers Free Reading Room and the local YMCA.
