notable.notable_blurb: Lawyer; architect of the 1924 immigration quotas

narrative_blocks.header: A Legion of Honor from France
narrative_blocks.body: John served in the First World War and was made a chevalier of the French Legion of Honor. After the armistice the Army put him in charge of its military intelligence branch in New York, which watched the city's immigrants, Jews above all, and he left the service in 1919 a captain.

narrative_blocks.header: A founder of Paul Smith's College
narrative_blocks.body: John was a founding trustee and later vice president of Paul Smith's College in the Adirondacks, near his family's summers on the St. Regis lakes, where he was commodore of the yacht club. He was also a trustee of New York University and of the American Museum of Natural History.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the national origins formula
narrative_blocks.body: John devised the national origins formula of the Immigration Act of 1924, which sharply cut immigration from southern and eastern Europe and barred Asian immigrants altogether. The quotas stood forty years, until 1964, and he spent the rest of his life defending them.

narrative_blocks.header: Counsel to the Lusk Committee
narrative_blocks.body: In 1919 John became special deputy attorney general of New York for the Lusk Committee, whose raids on suspected radicals arrested some five hundred and deported 246. In 1920 he was associate counsel to the Senate inquiry that saw the Soviet agent Ludwig Martens deported.

narrative_blocks.header: Keep America American
narrative_blocks.body: In 1927 John founded what became the American Coalition of Patriotic Societies, over a hundred groups under the slogan Keep America American, and led it until 1950. It fought the admission of Jewish refugees from Nazi Germany, and Louis Adamic called him America's alien-baiter No. 1.

narrative_blocks.header: His office was next to Madison Grant's
narrative_blocks.body: In the Financial District John's office was next door to Madison Grant's, and he moved in Grant's eugenics circle as a member of the Eugenics Research Association and the American Eugenics Society. The Sons of the American Revolution gave him its gold medal for Americanism in 1951.

narrative_blocks.header: He married Eleanor Roosevelt's friend
narrative_blocks.body: John married Caroline Murray Wilmerding, one of Eleanor Roosevelt's oldest friends, at her parents' house on June 25, 1908, with Robert Walton Goelet as best man, and the couple went abroad for a year or more. Their sons were John B. Trevor Jr. and Bronson.

notable.notable_blurb: Art collector; bequeathed his collection to Harvard

narrative_blocks.header: He gave Harvard one of America's great collections
narrative_blocks.body: Winthrop amassed some four thousand works, including the largest holdings of Ingres and Blake, Pre-Raphaelite paintings, French drawings, and Chinese jades. He bequeathed the entire collection to Harvard's Fogg Art Museum, having never lent a piece in his lifetime.

narrative_blocks.header: He posed as the butler for visitors
narrative_blocks.body: Shy and reticent, Winthrop guarded his Fifth Avenue collection closely and pretended to be the butler when guiding guests through it. The critic Richard Dorment likened him to a figure out of Henry James.

narrative_blocks.header: He restored the old village of Lenox
narrative_blocks.body: From his estate Groton Place, Winthrop restored Lenox's Congregational church, academy, and colonial courthouse, the last becoming the Lenox Library. He served as the library's president for the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: Both his daughters eloped with the help
narrative_blocks.body: They married in a single ceremony at Stockbridge in September 1924, got up to keep clear of him — Kate to a twenty-one-year-old electrician, Emily to the chauffeur he had lately dismissed for it. He was said to be readier to forgive Kate.

narrative_blocks.header: He never lent a picture in his life
narrative_blocks.body: His will let the Fogg lend his pictures only if Harvard first made a gift to the New York Foundling Hospital. Sixty years on the university paid, and the collection went to Lyon, to London, to the Metropolitan and to Washington.

narrative_blocks.header: Five hundred peacocks at Groton Place
narrative_blocks.body: His Lenox estate ran a hundred and fifty acres over Baldhead Mountain, the house by Carrère and Hastings and the grounds laid out to his own designs. Peacocks and pheasants walked the lawns, and the Massachusetts Horticultural Society gave him awards for it.

notable.notable_blurb: New York banker; founded Robert Winthrop & Co.

narrative_blocks.header: He put his own name up in 1871
narrative_blocks.body: The Drexels wanted to move into European investing and he did not, so Drexel, Winthrop was dissolved and Robert Winthrop & Company took its place. It stayed in the family for more than a hundred years; his son Beekman ran it from 1913 to 1939.

narrative_blocks.header: Cotton and sugar before he ever banked
narrative_blocks.body: He began with J. & A. Dennistoun Wood in the cotton and sugar trade, turned to banking with Read & Drexel in 1859, and was admitted to the New York Stock Exchange three years later.

narrative_blocks.header: An original Real Estate Exchange man
narrative_blocks.body: When the Real Estate Exchange and Auction Room was got up in New York in 1883 he took a share of the founding subscription. John Jacob Astor III, William Astor and Lloyd Aspinwall came in beside him.

narrative_blocks.header: The Roosevelts lived next door
narrative_blocks.body: He was a friend, neighbour and business associate of Theodore Roosevelt the elder, and the two families stayed close into the next generation. He was a vestryman at St. George's from 1876, and died at 38 East 37th Street in 1892.

narrative_blocks.header: He married Moses Taylor's daughter
narrative_blocks.body: Kate Wilson Taylor came to him in June 1859. Her father ran the National City Bank for twenty-seven years and financed railroads, iron and coal, and Winthrop became one of his closest associates.

narrative_blocks.header: He descended from the Winthrop colonial governors
narrative_blocks.body: Robert Winthrop descended from John Winthrop, founding governor of Massachusetts Bay, and his son John Winthrop Jr. of Connecticut. His wife Kate was a daughter of the financier Moses Taylor.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-three years a widow
narrative_blocks.body: Robert died in 1892 and she lived on to 1925, outlasting him by more than half her marriage again. Six of her children reached adulthood and she buried two of them.

narrative_blocks.header: Third largest at National City Bank
narrative_blocks.body: The Taft administration's 1913 survey of banking control, drawn up for the Pujo inquiry, listed her as the third largest shareholder of the National City Bank of New York. Her husband's firm was the sixth largest in the National Bank of Commerce.

narrative_blocks.header: Her children scattered wide
narrative_blocks.body: Robert Dudley banked and never married, Grenville collected the pictures that went to Harvard, Katharine married a United States senator, Albertina a Dutch diplomat, and Beekman governed Puerto Rico.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father's bank is Citibank now
narrative_blocks.body: Moses Taylor took the presidency of the City Bank in 1855 and held it for twenty-seven years, financing railroads, iron and coal, among them the Delaware and Hudson. The bank he ran carries the name Citibank today.

notable.notable_blurb: Sculptor, collector, and Audubon Sharon benefactor

narrative_blocks.header: Sculptor who studied with Daniel Chester French
narrative_blocks.body: Miles trained under Daniel Chester French and leading women sculptors of the day, and worked also as a painter, poet, and photographer. Her sculpture entered the Metropolitan, Montclair, and Harvard's Fogg collections.

narrative_blocks.header: She eloped with her father's chauffeur
narrative_blocks.body: In 1924 the heiress eloped with Corey Miles, the widowed estate chauffeur, in a double wedding alongside her sister Kate. Their father Grenville was reportedly bitter for years over the matches.

narrative_blocks.header: Her glass and ceramics went to Brooklyn
narrative_blocks.body: An avid collector, Miles left some 948 pieces of eighteenth-century Wedgwood, glass, and ceramics to the Brooklyn Museum. She also endowed the Emily Winthrop Miles wildlife sanctuary at Audubon Sharon.

narrative_blocks.header: She hung her photographs in the Berkshires
narrative_blocks.body: She showed at the Berkshire Museum and at the Lenox Library, in the village her father had rebuilt. She kept a studio in New York and lived latterly at Sharon, Connecticut.

narrative_blocks.header: She died on Christmas morning
narrative_blocks.body: A long illness took her at Roosevelt Hospital in 1962, at sixty-nine, her husband two years gone. The family asked that flowers be left off and money go to the Cancer Fund or the Audubon Society instead.

narrative_blocks.header: She married her father's electrician
narrative_blocks.body: Darwin Morse was twenty-one and wired the houses on the Lenox place; she was twenty-five and a Winthrop. Her father had spent his life buying pictures and she married the man who ran the wires past them.

narrative_blocks.header: Two sisters married in one ceremony
narrative_blocks.body: They went to Stockbridge in September 1924 to keep clear of their father, she at twenty-five and Emily at thirty-one. Reporters ran the couples down in a Burlington hotel; the men were her father's electrician and his chauffeur.

narrative_blocks.header: She was her sister's only survivor
narrative_blocks.body: When Emily died on Christmas Day 1962 the notice named one immediate survivor, Mrs. Darwin S. Morse of Richmond. She kept the Berkshire house another ten years.

narrative_blocks.header: The chauffeur his employer had just fired
narrative_blocks.body: Winthrop caught them together and dismissed him from the Lenox place, and in September 1924 they married at Stockbridge in a double wedding with her sister. He was middle-aged and lately widowed; she was thirty-one.

narrative_blocks.header: He ended a flier of some note
narrative_blocks.body: The Arizona paper called him a retired aviator of note when he died. He had been six weeks a guest at the Diamond P Ranch at Wickenburg when a heart attack took him, in February 1960.

narrative_blocks.header: His ashes went home to Neverland
narrative_blocks.body: He was cremated at Phoenix and the remains sent east to Sharon, to be scattered on the Miles family place in Connecticut, which they called Neverland. There were no children.

narrative_blocks.body: He married a Winthrop heiress four years his senior at Stockbridge in September 1924, in a double wedding run to avoid her father. Reporters found them in a Burlington hotel and he told them he deplored the notoriety, had no plans, and did not know where they would live.

narrative_blocks.header: He farmed the Berkshires for sixty years
narrative_blocks.body: The 1930 census found him a farmer at Richmond township, and he stayed. He and Kate lie together in the Burghardt burying ground there.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father was expected to forgive him
narrative_blocks.body: Insiders told the papers the old financier would likely soften toward him and put Kate's choice down to a youthful indiscretion. It was the other daughter's marriage he could not forgive.

narrative_blocks.header: A friend of Eleanor Roosevelt's
narrative_blocks.body: Caroline was the only daughter of Lucius and Caroline Wilmerding, and one of Eleanor Roosevelt's oldest friends. Franklin and Eleanor, married three years, were among the guests when she married John B. Trevor at her parents' house on June 25, 1908.

notable.notable_blurb: Linen merchant and Union Club president

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-four years in linen
narrative_blocks.body: Lucius was a partner in Wilmerding & Bisset, importers of linen, from 1874 to 1904, and a special partner for fourteen years more. In 1919, at seventy, he became a special partner in the Stock Exchange house of Gray & Wilmerding.

narrative_blocks.header: President of the Union Club
narrative_blocks.body: Lucius was president of the Union Club, at Fifth Avenue and Fifty-first Street, when he died. He was also a trustee of the Greenwich Savings Bank, a member of the Metropolitan Club in New York and Washington, and summered at East Islip.

narrative_blocks.header: Columbia, then Europe
narrative_blocks.body: Lucius took his degree at Columbia in 1868 and his master's in 1871. In between he spent 1868 and 1869 traveling in Europe, writing home as he went.

narrative_blocks.header: An auctioneer's son
narrative_blocks.body: His father, Henry Augustus Wilmerding, founded the New York auction house of Wilmerding, Hoguet & Co., and Lucius started there in 1870. His grandfather Christian had come to America from Brunswick, in Prussia.

narrative_blocks.header: He fell ill at his Stock Exchange desk
narrative_blocks.body: Lucius was taken ill at his desk at Gray & Wilmerding, 5 Nassau Street, on a Tuesday in December 1922, and died of heart disease that Friday at his house on East Seventy-seventh Street, in his seventy-fifth year.

narrative_blocks.header: Anti-aircraft control for the Navy
narrative_blocks.body: In the Second World War John was the project engineer in charge of developing and testing shipborne anti-aircraft control systems at the Naval Research Laboratory, and wrote classified manuals for the services. The Navy gave him its Meritorious Civilian Service Award in October 1945.

narrative_blocks.header: Commodore on St. Regis three times
narrative_blocks.body: John was commodore of the St. Regis Yacht Club in 1938-39, again in 1962-64 and again in 1979-80, forty-two years apart end to end. In 1936 he had co-written Wind and Tide in Yacht Racing with H. A. Calahan.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-two years at the Trudeau Institute
narrative_blocks.body: John was a trustee of the Trudeau Institute at Saranac Lake for twenty-two years and an honorary trustee at his death. The institute grew out of the tuberculosis sanatorium Dr. Edward Livingston Trudeau opened there in 1884.

narrative_blocks.header: President of the genealogists
narrative_blocks.body: John was a president of the New York Genealogical and Biographical Society and a trustee of the Cooper-Hewitt Museum. When he died, at ninety-seven, he was the oldest member of the Union Club, the club his grandfather Lucius Wilmerding had led.

narrative_blocks.header: He directed the Pioneer Fund for decades
narrative_blocks.body: Trevor spent decades as a director and treasurer of the Pioneer Fund, a backer of race science, and carried on his father's immigration-restriction work. Testifying in 1965, he warned that mixing racial and ethnic groups would bring cultural decline.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at St. James in 1938
narrative_blocks.body: Evelyn made her debut in the 1933-34 season and married John B. Trevor Jr. at St. James Church in New York on November 18, 1938. They were married sixty-two years, until her death at Palm Beach in 2001.

narrative_blocks.header: John Jay's great-great-granddaughter
narrative_blocks.body: Evelyn was the youngest of the four children of Alexander Jay Bruen and Constance Fiedler Bruen, and through her father a great-great-granddaughter of John Jay, the first Chief Justice of the United States.

narrative_blocks.header: Three primaries for the county party
narrative_blocks.body: From 1937 to 1939 Bronson sat on the Republican County Committee of New York County, and led the primary campaigns of those three years to free the local organization from what he called its leftwing affiliations.

narrative_blocks.header: The Saranac Lake hospital's finances
narrative_blocks.body: Bronson was a director of the General Hospital of Saranac Lake and chaired its finance committee. He also belonged to the American Forestry Association and the Council for Agricultural and Chemurgic Research.

narrative_blocks.header: Best man, then a groom
narrative_blocks.body: Bronson was best man at his brother John's wedding in 1938. He married Eleanor Darlington Fisher on November 8, 1946, and they were married fifty-six years, until his death in 2002.

narrative_blocks.header: A hundred and fifty ascents in the Alps
narrative_blocks.body: Over fifty-seven years Ellis made more than a hundred and fifty major ascents in the Alps, the first the Schilthorn in 1906, when he was fourteen. The last came in July 1965, at seventy-three, for the hundredth anniversary of the first ascent of the Matterhorn.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the American Alpine Club
narrative_blocks.body: Ellis joined the American Alpine Club in 1921 and became its workhorse: treasurer from 1924 to 1934 and again from 1939 to 1949, and president from 1935 to 1937. Young climbers who could not afford a hotel stayed at his house for the club's New York meetings.

narrative_blocks.header: Mount Sir Donald by the northwest arête
narrative_blocks.body: In 1914 Ellis climbed Mount Sir Donald in the Selkirks by its northwest arête. Year after year he went back to the Riffelhorn above Zermatt, always by the Matterhorn Couloir.

narrative_blocks.header: Glaciers, long after the climbing
narrative_blocks.body: Glaciology held Ellis long after his hardest climbing was done, and he wrote learned papers on Forbes banding and the structure of ice. He also compiled exhaustive bibliographies of American and Canadian mountaineering.

narrative_blocks.header: At seventeen he paid for two volcanoes
narrative_blocks.body: In the summer of 1909 Ellis paid for Dr. William G. Anderson, director of the Yale Gymnasium, to take an expedition to Mexico and climb two volcanoes, to learn what altitude does to an athlete's heart. Ellis was seventeen.

narrative_blocks.header: He died on the way to the board
narrative_blocks.body: Ellis sat thirty-one years on the board of the Melville Shoe Corporation and was a director of the Babson Gravity Research Foundation. In January 1966 he died of a heart attack in his car, on his way to a Melville board meeting.

narrative_blocks.header: A boy killed on the road at Stratford
narrative_blocks.body: On June 1, 1909, driving back to Yale with a classmate, Ellis struck and killed thirteen-year-old John Christianson on the road at Stratford, Connecticut. He was tried for manslaughter and acquitted; the boy's father sued, and settled that August.

narrative_blocks.body: Spence collapsed of a heart attack at the attorneys' table while making oral arguments before the Wisconsin Supreme Court. One of the state's best-known lawyers, he was a name partner in the leading Milwaukee firm Quarles, Spence & Quarles.

narrative_blocks.header: Irish famine immigrant turned Wisconsin assemblyman
narrative_blocks.body: Spence came from County Tyrone during the Great Famine and rose through Fond du Lac law and politics to two terms in the Wisconsin Assembly. A Cornell valedictorian, he chaired the 1884 Republican State Convention.

notable.notable_blurb: The Clockwork Historian of New England

narrative_blocks.header: He was known as the Clockwork Historian
narrative_blocks.body: He was known as the Clockwork Historian and wrote under it. His subject was the early clockmakers of New England, above all the men who built tower clocks, and his lists covered every known American installation from 1717 on.

narrative_blocks.header: Two dozen articles over twenty-one years
narrative_blocks.body: He wrote for the NAWCC Bulletin from 1994 to 2015 on Stephen Hasham, John Osgood, Jedidiah Baldwin, Daniel Burnap and Thomas Harland, and Vermont's Nathan Hale. He also edited the second edition of Frederick Shelley's book on tower clocks.

narrative_blocks.header: He put the Pittsfield clock back together
narrative_blocks.body: Stephen Hasham's 1822 tower clock came out of the Congregational Church at Pittsfield in hundreds of pieces. He helped reassemble it before it went into the Berkshire Museum, a block south of the steeple it had run for a century.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the women back into the trade
narrative_blocks.body: One 2001 article recovered four of them — Candace Roberts the dial painter, Emeline Loomis paid two and a half cents a dial, Clara Stephenson the watchmaker, and two English nuns who made watchcases. He listed six hundred years of others.

narrative_blocks.header: A Navy rating, and a veteran's grave
narrative_blocks.body: He served in the United States Navy as a TD2 and is buried at the Vermont Veterans Memorial Cemetery at Randolph Center, site D-163B. He died at Lyndonville in August 2017, three days after his seventy-ninth birthday.

narrative_blocks.header: Maybe it'll happen by 3000
narrative_blocks.body: He proposed that the association document every tower clock installation in the country before the year 2000 and could not get it done. What he wrote about it afterward was: “But, it didn't happen. Maybe it'll happen by 3000.”

narrative_blocks.header: She married her own Hooker cousin
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Floyd Cushman descended from Thomas Hooker through the Tallmadge line, and the man she married, Edwards C. Williams, descended from the same founder through the Edwards family. Their marriage doubled their daughters' descent from Hartford's Puritan minister.

narrative_blocks.header: She named a daughter for a Declaration signer
narrative_blocks.body: Through her own family Mary carried the blood of William Floyd, a New York signer of the Declaration of Independence. She passed the Floyd name to her daughter, the historian Mary Floyd Williams.

notable.notable_blurb: Founder of the Mendocino Lumber Company

narrative_blocks.header: He founded the Mendocino Lumber Company
narrative_blocks.body: Williams surveyed Big River for its redwoods in 1852 and crossed Panama to buy milling machinery shipped around Cape Horn. He founded and long led the Mendocino Lumber Company, the redwood mill that built the coastal town.

narrative_blocks.header: A New York Volunteer in the Mexican War
narrative_blocks.body: Williams served with the 1st New York Volunteers in the Mexican-American War and reached California in 1847, on the eve of the Gold Rush. He lived to witness the 1906 San Francisco earthquake from his lumber company's ruined offices.

narrative_blocks.header: He and his wife were Hooker cousins
narrative_blocks.body: Williams married Mary Floyd Cushman, who shared his own descent from Thomas Hooker — the two were cousins, his line running through the Edwards family and hers through the Tallmadges. Their daughters were born to a double descent from Hartford's Puritan founder.

narrative_blocks.header: He died one day short of ninety-three
narrative_blocks.body: Edwards Williams was born at Northampton on 2 March 1820 and died at Oakland on 1 March 1913. He had buried his first wife fifty-seven years before, and his second three years earlier.

narrative_blocks.header: His shipyards reached as far as Chile
narrative_blocks.body: Williams built ships and ran steamship lines, carrying his trade into South American ventures centered on Valparaíso, Chile, where his son was born in 1858. The family moved with the business between Connecticut, New York, and the Pacific coast of South America.

narrative_blocks.header: The census named what killed him
narrative_blocks.body: When Williams died at Stratford in 1870, at forty-seven, the federal census mortality schedule recorded the cause without euphemism: delirium tremens. The shipbuilder's life ended in the grip of drink.

notable.notable_blurb: First woman history PhD at UC Berkeley

narrative_blocks.header: First woman to earn a Berkeley history doctorate
narrative_blocks.body: At fifty-two Williams became the first woman to complete a history doctorate at the University of California, with a landmark study of San Francisco's 1851 Vigilance Committee. The dissertation was published by the University of California Press in 1921.

narrative_blocks.header: Librarian and historian of Gold Rush California
narrative_blocks.body: Williams helped found California library science and was among the first readers admitted to the new Huntington Library. She lectured on California history and traveled widely across Asia, illustrating her talks with her own photographs.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote the definitive history of the Vigilantes
narrative_blocks.body: Williams spent years in the archives reconstructing the 1851 San Francisco Committee of Vigilance, publishing both a documentary collection and a full scholarly history through the University of California Press. Hers was the first authoritative account of that violent chapter of Gold Rush justice, and it remains a standard source.

narrative_blocks.header: She lectured on Tibet from her own photographs
narrative_blocks.body: In her sixties and seventies Williams traveled across Asia — Tibet, Burma, Cambodia, Bali, India, China, Japan — and came home to lecture on what she had seen, illustrating her talks with lantern slides she had shot herself. Late in life she also published a historical novel set in the 1850s San Francisco she knew so well.

narrative_blocks.header: She died on her ninety-third birthday
narrative_blocks.body: Williams died in 1959 at her Palo Alto home, on the exact day she turned ninety-three. Her lantern slides and papers were kept at the University of California, the institution that had made her its first woman history doctorate four decades earlier.

narrative_blocks.body: Alfred ran the Anniston Manufacturing Company in the Alabama iron town his father helped found. The new city took its name from his wife, Annie Scott Tyler, originally 'Annie's Town.'

narrative_blocks.header: The handsomest girl in the room
narrative_blocks.body: She and Charles Carow are supposed to have met at the New York Hotel, the caravansary New Englanders used. Promenading the corridor after dinner, he asked her to look at the handsomest girl in the parade and led her to a mirror.

narrative_blocks.header: Will you give me her hand?
narrative_blocks.body: Carow wrote to Captain Daniel Tyler at Philadelphia on 7 March 1859, marked it Private, and came to the point: “I have won Gertrude’s heart. Will you give me her hand?”

narrative_blocks.header: Six brides at her wedding, the groom said
narrative_blocks.body: She was married at Norwich on a June evening in 1859, the service put off until half past eight so the church could be lit. Several of the married women came in their own wedding dresses, and Carow said he had six brides at his wedding.

narrative_blocks.header: From Paris polish to genteel poverty
narrative_blocks.body: Educated in Paris during her father the general’s European years, Gertrude married the shipping heir Charles Carow in 1859 — and watched his drinking dissolve the family fortune. Widowed in 1883, she eventually moved to Italy, where living was cheaper.

narrative_blocks.header: Her daughter grew up with the Roosevelts
narrative_blocks.body: The Carows were intimates of the East 20th Street Roosevelts, and her daughter Edith was raised in and out of Theodore’s nursery — becoming First Lady in 1901, six years after Gertrude died at Turin.

narrative_blocks.header: First in French, far from it in drawing
narrative_blocks.body: At West Point he stood first in French and Spanish “without having to work very hard” and was far from distinguished in drawing, his classmate Dorst remembered. Five frontier years with the 4th Cavalry followed — scouting from Fort Clark’s armed camps, where no one walked two hundred yards unarmed.

narrative_blocks.header: Snow-blind on Mackenzie’s winter expedition
narrative_blocks.body: A volunteer on Crook’s Powder River Expedition after the Custer disaster, he rode in Mackenzie’s November 1876 destruction of the Cheyenne village — and left on sick leave, his eyes burned by glare off the snow. He resigned in 1878, “regretted, loved and respected.”

narrative_blocks.header: Seven thousand acres of American tea
narrative_blocks.body: Commanding the 3rd Connecticut Volunteers in South Carolina in 1898, the colonel saw commercial promise in southern tea and bought four Colleton County plantations — Holly Grove, Rutledge Island, Mowbray, Turkey Hill — whose flourishing gardens and factory his son Frederick managed.

narrative_blocks.header: The Russian ambassador took his house
narrative_blocks.body: The stately residence he built at 1634 I Street, facing Farragut Square in Washington, later housed the Russian ambassador. He was president of New London’s Pequot Casino Association at his death, a clubman to the last afternoon.

narrative_blocks.header: Born on his brother’s thirteenth birthday
narrative_blocks.body: May 2, 1851 — thirteen years to the day after his brother Edmund, born May 2, 1838. The Tyler brothers shared a birthday a generation apart.

narrative_blocks.header: A lop-eared pony from Palo Duro Canyon
narrative_blocks.body: In September 1874 Augustus rode with Mackenzie into Palo Duro Canyon, charging seven miles up through the Cheyenne, Comanche and Kiowa camps after twenty-seven hours in the saddle. From the captured ponies he kept a lop-eared brute he still could barely mount a year later.

narrative_blocks.header: Adjutant at Mackenzie's dawn charge
narrative_blocks.body: At the Cheyenne village in the Big Horn Mountains on 25 November 1876, Augustus was adjutant of Mackenzie's larger battalion, smoking his pipe through the all-day fight. His close friend Lt. John McKinney was killed leading his troop into the village at dawn.

notable.notable_blurb: New York merchant and Liverpool packet shipowner

narrative_blocks.header: He owned the packet ship West Point
narrative_blocks.body: Carow took over the Kermit and Carow line from Robert Kermit, his father’s partner, and owned the Liverpool packet West Point through the 1860s. The Civil War broke American shipping and the house never recovered from it.

narrative_blocks.header: Both his children were given the name Kermit
narrative_blocks.body: Robert Kermit, his father’s partner, had no children and treated Charles almost as a son. He named his first son Robert Kermit Carow and his elder daughter Edith Kermit, and she in turn gave the name to a son of hers.

narrative_blocks.header: The money was gone when he died
narrative_blocks.body: Carow died in New York in March 1883 at fifty-seven, and the shipping fortune his father had built was spent. His widow Gertrude and their younger daughter Emily left for Italy, where what remained went further.

narrative_blocks.header: Columbia, class of 1844, and no degree
narrative_blocks.body: He was at Columbia College with the class of 1844, belonged to the Peithologian Society and left without a degree. When his father died in 1850 he was taken straight into partnership with Robert Kermit.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter became a president's wife
narrative_blocks.body: The Carows lived beside the Roosevelts in New York, and his daughter Edith grew up alongside young Theodore. She married him in 1886 and became First Lady fifteen years later.

notable.notable_blurb: New York merchant and Chamber of Commerce president

narrative_blocks.header: In 1797 he stopped being a Quereau
narrative_blocks.body: He was born Isaac Quantine Quereau, of a Huguenot family that left France after the Edict of Nantes was revoked. On 1 January 1797, to make the spelling match the way the name was said, he began writing it Carow.

narrative_blocks.header: He led New York's Chamber of Commerce
narrative_blocks.body: Carow built his fortune in the Kermit and Carow shipping line and presided over New York's Chamber of Commerce from 1840 to 1842. He was an original incorporator of the Bank of Commerce, a forerunner of today's Morgan banking house.

narrative_blocks.header: The St. Andrew beat the news from Liverpool
narrative_blocks.body: Kermit and Carow ran a Liverpool service whose ships were each named for a saint. In 1834 the St. Andrew made a crossing fast enough that her owners knew cotton had jumped before the news reached anyone else in New York.

narrative_blocks.header: Smallpox in the forecastle, and a medicine chest
narrative_blocks.body: Sailing for Liverpool in the packet Silas Richards in April 1827, he found a sailor down with smallpox and four of the crew who had never had it. He dosed the man out of a book in the medicine chest, and the mate inoculated the four.

narrative_blocks.header: The little girl left behind in England
narrative_blocks.body: When the Quereaus at last got a ship out of England, a small daughter was staying with English friends and was to follow on the next sailing. She never came, and no trace of her was found. The family called her the Broken Branch.

notable.notable_blurb: First Lady; wife of Theodore Roosevelt

narrative_blocks.header: She built the modern First Lady's office
narrative_blocks.body: Edith hired the first salaried social secretary for a First Lady and directed the 1902 White House renovation that created the West Wing. Historians credit her with shaping the modern institution of the role.

narrative_blocks.header: She burned a lifetime of love letters
narrative_blocks.body: After Theodore died, the intensely private Edith destroyed the letters he had written her across their courtship and marriage. It is part of why her inner life stayed, by her own design, almost unknowable.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote her own Connecticut ancestors' history
narrative_blocks.body: Late in life Edith researched her mother's Tyler family and co-wrote a history of their colonial Connecticut roots. She bought the family's ancestral home in Brooklyn, Connecticut, returning there each summer.

narrative_blocks.header: She stumped for Hoover to disown Franklin
narrative_blocks.body: Edith kept out of politics for decades, then made a rare appearance for Herbert Hoover in 1932. Part of her motive was to remind voters that the Democratic nominee, Franklin Roosevelt, was only a distant cousin and not her son.

narrative_blocks.header: Theodore regretted overruling her judgment
narrative_blocks.body: A childhood neighbor whom Theodore Roosevelt married in 1886, Edith ran Sagamore Hill and raised six children while quietly advising him on people and politics. Roosevelt admitted he was worse off whenever he ignored her counsel.

narrative_blocks.header: Italy was cheap, and she wanted to paint
narrative_blocks.body: Charles Carow died in 1883 having run through the family money, and Emily and her mother left for Italy, where what was left of it went much further. She wanted to paint. They were settled at Porto Maurizio by the end of 1886.

narrative_blocks.header: She ran hospital work for soldiers in Italy
narrative_blocks.body: Through the First World War she led hospital work among the soldiers in Italy, and she stayed with the hospitals after the armistice. The children of a Porto Maurizio orphanage were her particular charge to the end of her life.

narrative_blocks.header: The aunt who stayed in Italy
narrative_blocks.body: Emily never married, and Porto Maurizio on the Italian Riviera was her address for the rest of her life. She crossed the Atlantic for family occasions and was a frequent caller at the White House while her sister was First Lady.

narrative_blocks.header: A Rough Rider pin for her birthday
narrative_blocks.body: Theodore Roosevelt, then governor of New York, sent her a small Rough Rider pin for her birthday with a letter on how the children were doing: Kermit holding his own, Ethel motherly, Archie mischievous, Quentin cuter every day.

narrative_blocks.header: She stayed in Italy when the war came
narrative_blocks.body: When Europe went to war in 1914 she chose to stay, and her brother-in-law wrote that he would not try to influence her while the danger seemed distant. Belgium, he told her, was enough to wring a man’s soul.

narrative_blocks.header: Alice Roosevelt named her snake Aunt Emily
narrative_blocks.body: Her niece Alice kept a pet snake at the White House and called it Aunt Emily. The reason Alice gave was that Emily looked like a snake and the snake looked like Emily.

narrative_blocks.header: Pneumonia took her at Porto Maurizio
narrative_blocks.body: She died of pneumonia in March 1939 after a three-week illness, seventy-three years old. She was cremated, and her ashes were placed in niche 389 at the Campo Santo di Ponente at Imperia.

narrative_blocks.header: They called her Sunshine
narrative_blocks.body: She stood five foot six, with blue-grey eyes and long wavy fair hair, and her family called her Sunshine for the temper she kept. She played the piano and went in for tennis, archery and boating.

narrative_blocks.header: She took eight months to say yes
narrative_blocks.body: They met at the Saltonstalls’ next door in October 1878, and Roosevelt said he never forgot how prettily she greeted him. He proposed in June 1879, she waited eight months, and they were engaged on 14 February 1880.

narrative_blocks.header: She learned state politics in a boardinghouse
narrative_blocks.body: They toured Europe for five months in 1881, and in the autumn of 1882 she moved into his Albany boardinghouse and learned New York politics at first hand. Expecting a large family, they bought land at Oyster Bay.

narrative_blocks.header: The baby came two days early
narrative_blocks.body: The daughter was born at half past eight on 12 February 1884 in his mother’s house in New York. Roosevelt was on the Assembly floor at Albany, sure the child would come on Valentine’s Day, four years to the day from their engagement.

narrative_blocks.header: She died two days after giving birth
narrative_blocks.body: The pregnancy had masked Bright’s disease and it went undiagnosed. He reached her near midnight and held her until she died on Valentine’s Day afternoon, eleven hours after his mother died of typhoid in the same house.

narrative_blocks.header: The light has gone out of my life
narrative_blocks.body: He marked that day in his diary with a large black cross and one line: the light has gone out of my life. He gave away her photographs, tore the pages about her out of the diary, and burned nearly all their letters.

narrative_blocks.header: He never spoke of her to their daughter
narrative_blocks.body: He handed the newborn to his sister Bamie and went west to Dakota. Their daughter learned of her mother from Bamie and from the Lees, and her father never spoke of her. Her stone reads: for joy or for sorrow, my life has now been lived out.

narrative_blocks.header: He banked at Boston's Lee, Higginson firm
narrative_blocks.body: Lee was a partner in the Boston investment bank Lee, Higginson and Company, co-founded by his father John Clarke Lee. His daughter Alice married the young Theodore Roosevelt.

narrative_blocks.header: His sister’s house was next door
narrative_blocks.body: His sister was the mother of the Saltonstalls, who lived beside them at Chestnut Hill. It was in their drawing room in October 1878 that his daughter Alice met a Harvard classmate of her cousin Dick’s named Theodore Roosevelt.

narrative_blocks.header: Four daughters married, and Alice gone
narrative_blocks.body: Four of his daughters married — Mrs Fessenden and Mrs Mumford of Chestnut Hill, Mrs Hammond of California and Mrs Reginald Gray — and his son George carried on at Lee, Higginson. Alice had been dead twenty-six years.

narrative_blocks.header: He died on his eightieth birthday
narrative_blocks.body: Lee was born at Boston on 21 March 1830 and died at Brookline on 21 March 1910, eighty years to the day. The funeral was at the Arlington Street church, with Saltonstalls and a Peabody among the ushers.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother’s name went to her daughter
narrative_blocks.body: Caroline was a daughter of Elisha Haskell and Alice Russell Hathaway of Boston. Both of her mother’s names went to the child born in 1861 — Alice Hathaway Lee, who married Theodore Roosevelt at nineteen.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived her daughter by thirty years
narrative_blocks.body: Alice died in 1884 at twenty-two and Caroline lived thirty years past her. The granddaughter learned about her mother from the Lees, because Roosevelt would not speak of Alice to the child at all.

notable.notable_blurb: Theodore Roosevelt's daughter; Washington wit

narrative_blocks.header: Washington's sharpest tongue for seventy years
narrative_blocks.body: Longworth reigned over Washington society for decades from her Massachusetts Avenue salon, feared for her wit and her feuds with both Roosevelt cousins. A pillow on her sofa read, 'If you can't say something good, sit here by me.'

narrative_blocks.header: If you can't say anything nice, sit here
narrative_blocks.body: She kept a sofa cushion embroidered with that line and lived by it, skewering presidents for six decades. She dismissed Thomas Dewey as the little man on the wedding cake and would not call her cousin anything but Franklin.

narrative_blocks.header: Pet snake, cigarettes, the White House roof
narrative_blocks.body: The president's irreverent eldest daughter smoked on the White House roof when forbidden to below and carried a pet snake to receptions. Her father said he could run the country or control Alice, but not both.

narrative_blocks.header: Princess Alice toured Asia for her father
narrative_blocks.body: At twenty-one she joined the 1905 Taft mission to Japan, China, and the Philippines as the president's envoy-celebrity, mobbed everywhere as Princess Alice. Her favorite blue-gray set off a national craze called Alice blue, even a hit song.

narrative_blocks.header: The 1906 White House wedding of the year
narrative_blocks.body: In February 1906 she married Ohio congressman Nicholas Longworth in the East Room before all of official Washington, the most watched wedding of its day. The match cooled after he backed Taft over her father, and she outlived him by nearly fifty years.

notable.notable_blurb: Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives

narrative_blocks.header: A House office building still bears his name
narrative_blocks.body: The first lawmaker to move straight from Majority Leader to Speaker, he ran the House for three terms with charm and a tight hand on procedure. In 1962 Congress named one of its office buildings the Longworth Building in his memory.

narrative_blocks.header: He backed Taft over his father-in-law
narrative_blocks.body: When Theodore Roosevelt bolted the Republican Party in 1912, Longworth stayed with the regulars and stood by Taft, straining his marriage to Alice. The split cost him his seat for a term before he returned and climbed to the top of the House.

narrative_blocks.header: A violin virtuoso holding the Speaker's gavel
narrative_blocks.body: Efrem Zimbalist and other professionals counted him among the finest amateur violinists in America. Legend says Alice burned his Stradivarius in a temper, but the instrument was only a fine copy and came through unharmed.

narrative_blocks.header: He doted on a daughter not his own
narrative_blocks.body: In 1925 Alice gave birth to her only child, Paulina, whose father was almost certainly Senator William Borah; friends called the baby Aurora Borah Alice. Nick, who almost surely knew, was delighted with her and doted on her.

narrative_blocks.header: He felt his own head and agreed
narrative_blocks.body: Lounging in a chair at the Capitol, Nick felt another member run a hand over his bald head and remark that it was nice and smooth, just like his wife's bottom. Nick felt his own head and said, so it does.

notable.notable_blurb: Medal of Honor general; eldest Roosevelt son

narrative_blocks.header: Only general in D-Day's first wave
narrative_blocks.body: At fifty-six, with a heart condition and walking with a cane, Roosevelt was the only general to land with the first wave at Utah Beach on June 6, 1944. He died of a heart attack five weeks later and received the Medal of Honor posthumously.

narrative_blocks.header: He turned a landing error into a foothold
narrative_blocks.body: When the first craft drifted a mile south of their mark, he walked the fire-swept beach, met each arriving regiment, and improvised the attack from where they actually stood. Bradley later called it the bravest thing he saw in the war.

narrative_blocks.header: A father-son Medal of Honor, a century apart
narrative_blocks.body: His posthumous Medal of Honor and his father's, awarded at last in 2001 for San Juan Hill, made the Roosevelts only the second father and son both to earn it. The other pair were the two MacArthurs.

narrative_blocks.header: Father and son both hit the beaches
narrative_blocks.body: He was the only father to land with a son on D-Day; his boy Quentin came ashore at Omaha while he led at Utah. The family's soldiering instinct had carried into a second world war.

narrative_blocks.header: Dead of a heart attack five weeks later
narrative_blocks.body: He never saw the medal coming; a heart attack killed him in Normandy about five weeks after the landing. He was buried near the front and later moved to lie beside his brother Quentin, lost flying in the first war.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped call the Legion into being
narrative_blocks.body: In March 1919 he was among the officers who convened the Paris caucus of the American Expeditionary Forces that founded the American Legion. The organisation he helped start became the largest veterans' body in the country.

people.research_notes: Born Theodore Roosevelt III, Sept 13 1887, Oyster Bay NY; eldest son of President Theodore Roosevelt and Edith Kermit Carow. Educated at Groton School and Harvard College (A.B. 1909). Entered business (carpet/wool trade and investment banking) before WWI. WWI: 26th Inf Regt, 1st Division; wounded at Soissons and gassed at Cantigny; Distinguished Service Cross and French Croix de Guerre. Co-founded the American Legion, 1919. NY State Assembly 1920-21 (Nassau, 2nd district); opposed the 1920 expulsion of five Socialist assemblymen. Assistant Secretary of the Navy 1921-24 (Harding/Coolidge); 1924 Republican nominee for Governor of New York, lost to Al Smith. Governor of Puerto Rico 1929-32 (first U.S. governor to study Spanish; known as 'El Jibaro de La Fortaleza'); Governor-General of the Philippines 1932-33. Chairman of the Board, American Express; vice-president, Doubleday, Doran. WWII: Brig. Gen., Asst Division Commander, 4th Infantry Division; Operation Torch, Tunisia, Sicily; only general in the D-Day first wave at Utah Beach at age 56, walking with a cane. Died of a heart attack at Meautis, France, July 12 1944, five weeks after D-Day. Medal of Honor awarded posthumously September 1944 (his father TR Sr received the MoH for San Juan Hill, awarded in 2001). Buried Normandy American Cemetery beside brother Quentin. Sources: Wikipedia; Theodore Roosevelt Center (Dickinson State); ABMC; Find A Grave.

notable.notable_blurb: Explorer and author; son of Theodore Roosevelt

narrative_blocks.header: He tore through Harvard in record time
narrative_blocks.body: A voracious reader, he compressed the four-year Harvard course into about two and a half years, breaking off after his freshman year to join his father's African safari. He took his degree in 1912.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept his father alive on the Amazon
narrative_blocks.body: On the 1914 expedition down Brazil's River of Doubt, Kermit rationed his own quinine to his malarial father and was credited with saving the former President's life. He nearly died of the fever himself.

narrative_blocks.header: He won the Military Cross in Mesopotamia
narrative_blocks.body: In 1917 he took an honorary captaincy in the British Army and fought under General Maude in the Mesopotamian campaign, where he earned the Military Cross. He crossed to the American artillery in France for the war's last offensive.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped found a transatlantic steamship line
narrative_blocks.body: An explorer and writer, Roosevelt co-founded the Roosevelt Steamship Company, which became part of the United States Lines. He published books on hunting and travel.

narrative_blocks.header: A hard ending to an adventurer's life
narrative_blocks.body: Kermit lived boldly — his father's African safari and the near-fatal Amazon descent, then soldiering in both World Wars. Long troubled in his later years, he died in Alaska in 1943 while on military duty, his struggles finally overtaking him.

people.research_notes: Born Oct 10 1889 at Sagamore Hill, Oyster Bay NY; second son of President Theodore Roosevelt and Edith Carow. Groton School; Harvard College (A.B. 1912, completed in about two and a half years). Accompanied his father on the 1909-10 African safari and the 1913-14 Brazilian River of Doubt expedition, on which he rationed his own quinine to keep his malarial father alive; the river's main branch was renamed Rio Roosevelt and a tributary Rio Kermit. Assistant manager, National City Bank of Buenos Aires, 1914-16. Married Belle Wyatt Willard, Madrid, 1914; four children (Kermit 'Kim' Jr., Joseph Willard, Belle Wyatt, Dirck). WWI: honorary captain, British Army (from Aug 1917), 14th Light Armored Motor Battery, Machine Gun Corps, under Gen. Maude in Mesopotamia; awarded the Military Cross. Transferred April 1918 to the AEF as a captain, Battery C, 7th Field Artillery, 1st Division (Meuse-Argonne). Author of 'War in the Garden of Eden' (1920). Founded the Roosevelt Steamship Company and the United States Lines (merchant marine). VP, New York Zoological Society, 1937-39. WWII: commissioned a major by his cousin President Franklin Roosevelt and posted as an intelligence officer to Fort Richardson, Alaska. Fought lifelong depression and alcoholism. Died at Fort Richardson, June 4 1943, by suicide; his death was reported to his aged mother Edith as a heart attack to spare her. Buried Fort Richardson National Cemetery. Sources: Wikipedia; Find A Grave; Naval History and Heritage Command; VA News; WikiTree.

narrative_blocks.header: She nursed the wounded in wartime France
narrative_blocks.body: Early in the First World War she went to Paris with her husband and worked at the American Ambulance Hospital while he operated on men brought in from the front. She came home to decades of civic and hospital work on Long Island.

narrative_blocks.header: She made Sagamore Hill a national shrine
narrative_blocks.body: More than anyone she pushed to preserve her father's home, Sagamore Hill, as a public historic site, and guarded the Roosevelt papers given to Harvard. In Oyster Bay, where she fought for low-income housing, neighbors called her the Queen of Oyster Bay.

narrative_blocks.header: One of the museum's first women trustees
narrative_blocks.body: She became one of the first two women on the board of the American Museum of Natural History, the institution her grandfather had helped found. She also chaired the Nassau County Nursing Service and led the county's Red Cross.

narrative_blocks.header: Painted in her Red Cross uniform
narrative_blocks.body: For her formal family portrait she chose to sit in her Red Cross uniform rather than evening dress and jewels. She gave the organization some sixty years and chaired its Nassau County work.

narrative_blocks.header: The Roosevelt child who stayed close to home
narrative_blocks.body: Of all the president's children she was the steady one, anchoring the family at Oyster Bay long after her brothers scattered to wars and far places. She married the surgeon who would tend the wounded beside her in France.

bio.bio_blurb: TR's only surviving daughter by Edith Carow

people.research_notes: Born Aug 13 1891, Oyster Bay NY; youngest daughter and fourth child of President Theodore Roosevelt and Edith Carow. Educated at the National Cathedral School (Cathedral School for Girls), Washington, graduating 1906; White House debut 1908. Married Dr. Richard Derby (Harvard 1903; Columbia M.D. 1907), 1913, Oyster Bay; four children (Richard Jr., Edith, Sarah Alden, Judith). WWI: the first of TR's children to serve - joined her surgeon husband in France in 1915 and worked as a volunteer nurse at the American Ambulance Hospital, Paris; chose to sit for her family portrait in her Red Cross uniform. Active in the American Red Cross for some sixty years (Nassau County chairman) and chaired the Nassau County Nursing Service. One of the first two female trustees of the American Museum of Natural History (founded in part by her grandfather Theodore Roosevelt Sr., 1869). Leading family proponent of preserving Sagamore Hill as a National Historic Site; active in the Theodore Roosevelt Association and the Theodore Roosevelt Collection established at Harvard, 1943; assisted the National Audubon Society's Theodore Roosevelt Sanctuary (1975). Worked to secure low-income housing in Oyster Bay against local discrimination; civic leader at Christ Episcopal Church, nicknamed 'Queen of Oyster Bay.' Amateur botanist and ornithologist; hiker into her 80s. Died Oyster Bay, Dec 10 1977. NOTABLE CANDIDATE (awaiting Sam's approval): NPS biographical profile at https://www.nps.gov/people/ethel-roosevelt-derby.htm. Sources: NPS; Theodore Roosevelt Center; trgravesite.org; Wikipedia.

notable.notable_blurb: TR's son; wounded and decorated in two wars

narrative_blocks.header: The only man twice ruined by one wound
narrative_blocks.body: A grenade in New Guinea in 1943 shattered the same knee German fire had wrecked in France in 1918, leaving him the only American ever rated totally disabled for one wound in two wars. He came home with four Silver Stars.

narrative_blocks.header: The old lion is dead
narrative_blocks.body: When Theodore Roosevelt died in January 1919, Archibald wired the news to his scattered brothers and sister in five blunt words. He was still recovering from his French wounds at the time.

narrative_blocks.header: From Teapot Dome to a bond house
narrative_blocks.body: He resigned from Sinclair Oil during the Teapot Dome inquiry and, though never implicated, gave testimony damaging to his former employer. After the second war he founded the municipal-bond firm Roosevelt and Cross, which still trades today.

narrative_blocks.header: A hard turn to the far right
narrative_blocks.body: In his later years he joined the John Birch Society and founded the Veritas Foundation to root out what he called socialist influence at Harvard. In 1954 he published a pamphlet attacking the award of a Theodore Roosevelt medal to the diplomat Ralph Bunche.

narrative_blocks.header: The last of Edith's sons
narrative_blocks.body: He outlived every brother, the only son of Theodore and Edith to come through both World Wars alive. His stone at Oyster Bay reads, the old fighting man home from the wars.

people.research_notes: Born Apr 9 1894, Washington D.C.; fifth child of President Theodore Roosevelt and Edith Carow. Attended Groton (expelled), then Phillips Academy Andover, the Evans School for Boys (Mesa, Arizona), and Harvard (1917). WWI: captain, 1st Infantry Division, in France; severely wounded and discharged with full disability; two Silver Star citations and the French Croix de Guerre. Business between the wars: executive at Sinclair Consolidated Oil and VP of its subsidiary Union Petroleum; resigned during the 1922 Teapot Dome inquiry (never implicated, gave damaging testimony); then the family firm Roosevelt & Son. WWII: petitioned FDR to return; Lt. Col., 3rd Battalion, 162nd Infantry Regiment, 41st Division, in New Guinea (Salamaua campaign); a contested ridge was named Roosevelt Ridge in his honor. August 1943: a grenade shattered the same knee wounded in 1918, making him the only American rated 100% disabled twice for one wound in two wars; four Silver Stars in all. Founded the municipal-bond house Roosevelt and Cross after the war. In later life joined the John Birch Society and founded the Veritas Foundation; in 1954 published a pamphlet opposing the Theodore Roosevelt medal to diplomat Ralph Bunche (positions recorded here factually). Died Stuart, Florida, Oct 13 1979, the last surviving son of Theodore and Edith. Buried Youngs Memorial Cemetery, Oyster Bay. Sources: Wikipedia; Find A Grave; Sam-provided biographical paste.

notable.notable_blurb: Roosevelt's aviator son, killed in action 1918

narrative_blocks.header: Shot down behind enemy lines at twenty
narrative_blocks.body: On July 14, 1918, his patrol met German fighters over Chamery and his plane went down behind enemy lines. German troops buried the president's son with full military honors, and the grave became a shrine that thousands of American soldiers came to see.

narrative_blocks.header: The White House's most incorrigible small boy
narrative_blocks.body: He shot spitballs at the official presidential portraits, flung snowballs from the roof at passersby, and once gouged a baseball diamond into the South Lawn. His father, who quietly counted him the favorite, mostly delighted in it.

narrative_blocks.header: He left Harvard for the cockpit
narrative_blocks.body: Admitted to Harvard like his father and brothers, he dropped out in 1917 at his father's urging to train as a pursuit pilot. He shipped to France and eventually flew with the Ninety-fifth Aero Squadron.

narrative_blocks.header: Reinterred beside the brother he idolized
narrative_blocks.body: In 1955 his remains were moved to the Normandy American Cemetery to lie beside Ted, who had died after leading men ashore on D-Day. A Long Island airfield, and much later a shopping center, carried his name.

narrative_blocks.header: His death benefits went to a small nephew
narrative_blocks.body: He left what he had to his sister Ethel's young son, a boy who had taken to pointing at passing planes and calling them Uncle Quentin. The child would die only four years after Quentin himself.

narrative_blocks.header: Engaged to a Whitney heiress before he fell
narrative_blocks.body: Before he shipped out to fly over France, he became engaged to Flora Whitney, daughter of the sculptor Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney. They wrote each other constantly and even tried to marry in France; he was shot down in July 1918, weeks before the armistice, and they never wed.

narrative_blocks.header: A poem came from Painted Post
narrative_blocks.body: A visitor who had gone home to Painted Post sent her verses in May 1824. He apologised for not writing prose: her husband, he said, had a taste so sublime that he could not endure even good sense in mere rhyme.

narrative_blocks.header: She is in the mausoleum at Trinity
narrative_blocks.body: Eliza died in New York in May 1837, eight days after her fifty-fourth birthday. She lies in the westerly division of the mausoleum at Trinity Church Cemetery, with Isaac, who outlived her by thirteen years.

notable.notable_blurb: Wartime relief organizer and photographer

narrative_blocks.header: Red Cross and YMCA work across two wars
narrative_blocks.body: Eleanor ran YMCA canteens in France in the First World War and directed the American Red Cross Club in England in the Second. She organized the first American women's committee for China relief in 1937.

narrative_blocks.header: She left five thousand photographs to the nation
narrative_blocks.body: A serious photographer, she developed her own film and made her own prints with a Voigtländer camera, capturing presidents, dignitaries, and her travels across Europe, Mexico, and Asia. Her daughter later gave some five thousand of her photographs and albums to the Library of Congress.

narrative_blocks.header: A wartime anniversary letter from her soldier husband
narrative_blocks.body: She married Theodore Roosevelt Jr. in 1910 and followed his soldiering life across the world. On their thirty-third anniversary in 1943 he wrote to her from the front — 'we never thought our thirty-third anniversary would find us deep in our second war and me again at the front' — a year before he died in Normandy.

narrative_blocks.header: From French canteens to Puerto Rico to China
narrative_blocks.body: Her causes spanned the globe and the decades — a YMCA canteen in France in the Great War, better conditions for Puerto Rican women during her husband's governorship, the first American women's committee for China Relief in 1937, and a Red Cross club in wartime England. France, General Pershing, and the War Department all decorated her for it.

narrative_blocks.header: A Roosevelt who ran the CIA's gadget shop
narrative_blocks.body: Cornelius headed the CIA's Technical Services Division, the branch that built espionage devices and guarded against electronic eavesdropping. A mining engineer and Navy veteran, he gave the National Gallery a major collection of Escher prints.

narrative_blocks.header: The spymaster who collected Escher
narrative_blocks.body: The same mind that ran the CIA's technical shop built one of the great private hoards of M. C. Escher prints, alongside Japanese netsuke and Andean finds. He later gave more than fifty of the Escher works to the National Gallery of Art.

narrative_blocks.header: His division's secret work touched MKULTRA and Castro
narrative_blocks.body: As chief of the CIA's Technical Services Division he oversaw Sidney Gottlieb and the agency's darkest experiments — the MKULTRA mind-control program, a scheme to poison Fidel Castro, and LSD trials in which he served as a subject himself. To family he described his work more modestly, as building devices to find hidden microphones.

narrative_blocks.header: His plane went down off Hong Kong
narrative_blocks.body: Named for his uncle the fallen WWI aviator, Quentin landed at Omaha Beach on D-Day while his father landed at Utah. He became a China aviation executive and died at twenty-nine in a Hong Kong plane crash, an end echoing his namesake's.

narrative_blocks.header: At fourteen he found a new fossil species
narrative_blocks.body: As a boy Quentin explored an Arizona cave and unearthed an extinct pronghorn, described as a new species in a museum paper. At nineteen he traveled alone into western China and brought back a thousand rare Naxi manuscripts for the Library of Congress.

narrative_blocks.header: His Harvard thesis on a vanishing script
narrative_blocks.body: As a student he traveled to the Tibetan borderlands of western China and brought back rare Naxi manuscripts, whose pictographs faintly recall Egyptian hieroglyphs. He made them the subject of his Harvard senior thesis before the Army claimed him.

military_service.notes: Artillery officer; wounded at Kasserine Pass; landed in the first wave at Omaha Beach. Silver Star, Purple Heart, Croix de Guerre.

people.research_notes: Killed in the CNAC Basalt Island air crash near Hong Kong, 1948; remains believed unrecovered. Cenotaph at Youngs Memorial Cemetery.

narrative_blocks.header: A Kentucky bride for a Roosevelt heir
narrative_blocks.body: The daughter of a Louisville family, she married Theodore Roosevelt III in 1940 in a grand Second Presbyterian wedding, his brothers Cornelius and Quentin among the party. She left Kentucky for the Roosevelt world of Oyster Bay and beyond.

narrative_blocks.header: In death she asked for the wilderness
narrative_blocks.body: She lived her last years at Bryn Mawr, Pennsylvania, and died in 2001. In place of flowers she asked that gifts be made to the Wilderness Society — a nod to the conservation cause that ran deep in the family she had married into.

narrative_blocks.header: She sketched the Alger Hiss trial
narrative_blocks.body: A Red Cross worker who married Quentin Roosevelt two months before D-Day, Frances became a portrait artist at Oyster Bay. She also worked as a courtroom sketch artist, covering the perjury trial of Alger Hiss.

narrative_blocks.header: A portrait painter at Sagamore Hill
narrative_blocks.body: After the war she settled her family at Sagamore Hill, the old Roosevelt estate, and made her name as a portrait artist in Oyster Bay. She taught art at C.W. Post College and represented the Roosevelt family at events for decades.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed by a plane crash near Hong Kong
narrative_blocks.body: After the war she and Quentin moved to Shanghai, where he worked for a Chinese airline. In 1948 he died in a plane crash near Hong Kong, leaving her a widow at thirty-one with three young daughters to raise.

narrative_blocks.header: Her three daughters made remarkable lives
narrative_blocks.body: Her three daughters carried the family forward in striking directions — Anna became an Amazon archaeologist and a MacArthur Fellow, Alexandra a photographer, and Susan a Harvard scholar of Chinese law who became First Lady of Massachusetts. Her son-in-law, Governor William Weld, gave the eulogy at her funeral.

career.notes: Taught at C.W. Post College; courtroom sketch artist who covered the Alger Hiss trial.

narrative_blocks.header: She rescued books from the Florence flood
narrative_blocks.body: The Smithsonian's first paper conservator, McMillan was sent to Florence in 1969 to help save books and prints drowned by the Arno's catastrophic flood. She rose to chief conservator and helped found the Washington Conservation Guild.

narrative_blocks.header: She gave her blue Mustang to the Smithsonian
narrative_blocks.body: McMillan donated her iconic powder-blue 1965 Ford Mustang to the Smithsonian in 2004. Legend held she was once ticketed for riding the express lanes with an inflatable man propped in the passenger seat.

narrative_blocks.header: From Navy SEAL to Wall Street banker
narrative_blocks.body: After Harvard he served two years in Vietnam as a Navy SEAL, then built a long career in investment banking, rising to managing director at Lehman Brothers and later Barclays. He carried his great-grandfather's name, Theodore Roosevelt, and something of his restlessness.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried the family's conservation torch
narrative_blocks.body: Like his great-grandfather, he made conservation his cause — chairing climate and energy groups, serving the Wilderness Society, and speaking on the environment at the 2000 Republican Convention. A lifelong Republican, he broke with his party over climate and in 2016 backed John Kasich.

notable.notable_blurb: Amazon archaeologist; MacArthur Fellow

narrative_blocks.header: She doubled the known age of Amazon settlement
narrative_blocks.body: From 1990 to 1992 Anna excavated the Painted Rock Cave near Monte Alegre and found people living there 10,000 to 11,000 years ago, beside some of the oldest rock paintings in the Western Hemisphere.

narrative_blocks.header: Mound builders on Marajó Island
narrative_blocks.body: Through the 1980s Anna surveyed the mounds of Marajó Island at the Amazon's mouth, and in 1991 argued that the Marajoara were among the great indigenous achievements, a dense society the rainforest was long thought unable to feed.

narrative_blocks.header: The earliest pottery in the Americas
narrative_blocks.body: Digging with University of Illinois students on Fulbright grants, Anna found the earliest pottery yet known from the Americas, in settled fishing villages on the lower Amazon.

narrative_blocks.header: The Heye collection was hers for ten years
narrative_blocks.body: She was curator at the Museum of the American Indian from 1975 to 1985, the collection George Heye had built — including the Chickasaw pipe tomahawk he bought from Joseph Jones’s widow in 1906.

narrative_blocks.header: Lumumba's assassination and the CIA
narrative_blocks.body: Turning to the Congo basin, Anna has written on the crisis of 1960 to 1965, on covert NATO action in the former Belgian Congo, and on the CIA's part in the assassination of Patrice Lumumba.

narrative_blocks.header: Mesa Verde at nine, Latin at East Woods
narrative_blocks.body: Anna was nine when her mother, her reading and a trip to Mesa Verde made her want to be an archaeologist. At East Woods School on Long Island her headmaster, Langdon Rankin, taught her the Latin that led her into the classics.

narrative_blocks.header: A MacArthur Fellow in 1988
narrative_blocks.body: The MacArthur Foundation gave Anna a five-year fellowship in 1988. She holds the Explorers Medal, the Society of Woman Geographers' Gold Medal and Brazil's Order of Rio Branco, and is a fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences.

narrative_blocks.header: Scholar of China's ancient covenants
narrative_blocks.body: Susan took a Radcliffe degree in 1970, a Harvard law degree in 1974 and a Harvard doctorate in 1990 on the covenant texts dug up at Houma and Wenxian. She taught Chinese history and law at Harvard, Northeastern, Boston College and SAIS.

narrative_blocks.header: General counsel on China's legal reforms
narrative_blocks.body: From 2002 to 2005 Susan was general counsel to the Congressional-Executive Commission on China, traveling there to watch legal reform, women's rights, HIV in Xinjiang and rural land law. She then led Georgetown Law's Law Asia program.

narrative_blocks.header: First Lady, and a delegate to Beijing
narrative_blocks.body: Susan was First Lady of Massachusetts from 1991 to 1997, married to Governor William Weld. She co-founded MassAction for Women and went as a U.S. delegate to the United Nations' Fourth World Conference on Women in Beijing in 1995.

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband ran against her cousin
narrative_blocks.body: In 1994 her husband, Governor Weld, was re-elected against the Democrat Mark Roosevelt, her second cousin and, like her, a great-grandchild of Theodore Roosevelt. The Oyster Bay family sat on both sides of the race.

narrative_blocks.header: A photographer among the Roosevelt sisters
narrative_blocks.body: The youngest of Frances Roosevelt's three daughters, she trained at Stanford and made her career as a photographer, keeping her own name professionally. In 1988 she married the anesthesiologist and writer Ronald Dworkin.

notable.notable_blurb: Republican governor of Massachusetts, 1991-1997

narrative_blocks.header: Governor of Massachusetts by one frank answer
narrative_blocks.body: Bill Weld was the Republican governor of Massachusetts from 1991 to 1997. Trailing John Silber in 1990, he told Boston television his greatest flaw was laziness; his campaign ran the clip to Election Day, and he won, 51 to 49.

narrative_blocks.header: Tax cuts and a balanced budget
narrative_blocks.body: Facing a Democratic legislature, Bill cut taxes again and again and balanced the budget in his first year. In 1994 Massachusetts re-elected him with 71 percent, the second of his two terms.

narrative_blocks.header: Boston's corruption-hunting U.S. Attorney
narrative_blocks.body: As U.S. Attorney in Boston from 1981, Bill indicted forty-eight public officials and convicted forty-six. In 1986 he took over the Justice Department's Criminal Division, and in 1988 quit in protest over Attorney General Edwin Meese.

narrative_blocks.header: Into the Charles in his clothes
narrative_blocks.body: In 1996 Bill dove fully clothed into the Charles River to show off its cleanup. The river, he admitted later, was not as clean as he had thought; he had an earache for three weeks.

narrative_blocks.header: The ring he would not kiss
narrative_blocks.body: In 1997 Bill resigned as governor to be President Clinton's ambassador to Mexico. He would not court Jesse Helms, who had never forgiven his break with Meese, and Helms denied him a hearing. The nomination was withdrawn.

narrative_blocks.header: From Republican to Libertarian and back
narrative_blocks.body: Bill ran for vice president on the Libertarian ticket with Gary Johnson in 2016, drawing the most votes in that party's history, then challenged President Trump in the 2020 Republican primary before endorsing Joe Biden.

narrative_blocks.header: A Declaration signer, and Oyster Bay
narrative_blocks.body: Bill descends on his mother's side from William Floyd, a signer of the Declaration of Independence. His 1975 marriage to Susan Roosevelt joined Oyster Bay; their daughter Ethel Derby Weld carries the name of Susan's great-aunt.

narrative_blocks.header: An anesthesiologist who writes political philosophy
narrative_blocks.body: By day a practicing anesthesiologist in Baltimore for decades, he built a second life as a writer and thinker — a Johns Hopkins doctorate in political philosophy, a Hudson Institute fellowship, and books on medicine and American culture. His works range from The Rise of the Imperial Self to Medical Catastrophe, a confessional memoir of his own field.

career.notes: Writes on medicine and American culture; teaches political philosophy at George Washington University.

notable.notable_blurb: Plate-glass importer and New York philanthropist

narrative_blocks.header: A museum chartered in his front parlour
narrative_blocks.body: He helped found the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the American Museum of Natural History, and the charter of the second was accepted in his own front parlour at 28 East Twentieth Street. He was a director of both.

narrative_blocks.header: They called him Great Heart
narrative_blocks.body: He set aside time every week for the poor, the poorhouses and a mission school, and his children went with him on Sunday evenings to the Newsboys’ Lodging House. New York called him Great Heart.

narrative_blocks.header: He filled a party with children in braces
narrative_blocks.body: Bamie was born with a curved spine. He invited rich New York to what it took for a party and showed it a room of small children in new braces, and enough was raised that day to start the Orthopedic Hospital.

narrative_blocks.header: He sold Lincoln on a soldiers’ pay plan
narrative_blocks.body: His wife’s brothers fought for the Confederacy, so he hired a substitute rather than take the field. Instead he drew up a plan letting soldiers send their pay home, got it through Washington with Lincoln’s help, and toured the army signing men up.

narrative_blocks.header: He told the boy to make his body
narrative_blocks.body: He walked the floor for hours at a time with his asthmatic son in his arms, and then refused to coddle him. Make your body, he told the boy, who took up hard exercise and, after a beating from bullies, boxing lessons.

narrative_blocks.header: The Senate rejected him, and it broke him
narrative_blocks.body: Hayes named him Collector of the Port of New York in October 1877, partly to embarrass Roscoe Conkling. Conkling stalled the confirmation for months, the Senate threw it out twenty-five to thirty-one, and he collapsed two days later.

narrative_blocks.header: His son came from Cambridge and missed him
narrative_blocks.body: The tumour in his stomach was taken for peritonitis, and he kept the worst of it from the boy at Harvard until February. Nineteen-year-old Theodore took a train down from Cambridge and reached the house a few hours too late.

narrative_blocks.header: A Georgia belle who inspired Scarlett O'Hara
narrative_blocks.body: She was a celebrated Southern beauty, and Margaret Mitchell is thought to have drawn on her for Scarlett O’Hara. Mitchell had interviewed Evelyn King, Mittie’s closest childhood friend and a bridesmaid at her wedding.

narrative_blocks.header: Born at Hartford, raised in Georgia
narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Hartford in July 1835 and was three when Major Bulloch moved the family from Savannah up to the new village of Roswell. The house he built there, Bulloch Hall, was finished in 1839.

narrative_blocks.header: A girl named Lavinia was her shadow
narrative_blocks.body: The Bullochs held thirty-one enslaved people in 1850, most of them in the cotton fields. Like each of her siblings Mittie was given an enslaved child as a companion — Lavinia, who waited outside her classroom and slept beside her bed.

narrative_blocks.header: Married in front of the dining-room doors
narrative_blocks.body: She married Theodore Roosevelt at Bulloch Hall on 22 December 1853, in front of the pocket doors of the formal dining room. They went north to 28 East Twentieth Street, a wedding present from her father-in-law.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brothers fired for the Confederacy
narrative_blocks.body: Her brother Irvine was the youngest officer on the Alabama and fired the last gun before she went down off Cherbourg, and her half-brother James was a Confederate agent in Britain. She stayed unreconstructed to the day she died.

narrative_blocks.header: Two deaths in one house on Valentine's Day
narrative_blocks.body: On Saint Valentine's Day in 1884 Mittie died of typhoid in the family home as her son Theodore kept vigil. One floor above, his first wife was dying the same day, hours after bearing his daughter.

narrative_blocks.header: A perfect trump, said Theodore Roosevelt
narrative_blocks.body: When she was about to marry Kermit in 1914 his father delivered his verdict on her: Belle is a perfect trump. Thirty years later his distant cousin in the White House, whose fourth term she had just campaigned for, saluted her as my favourite Oyster Bay Roosevelt.

narrative_blocks.header: She crossed party lines for FDR
narrative_blocks.body: She walked unannounced into Democratic headquarters in 1944 and asked to be allowed to address envelopes and lick stamps from nine to five; within days the speakers bureau had her on the platform at Carnegie Hall. The rest of the Oyster Bay Roosevelts were for Dewey and the argument went into print, her sister-in-law publishing Why the Oyster Bay Roosevelts are for Dewey and Belle answering with Why I Am Going to Vote for Roosevelt.

narrative_blocks.header: She built a school for disabled children
narrative_blocks.body: In memory of her mother, Belle donated family land to create the Belle Willard School, the first Fairfax County school built for special-needs children. It opened in 1957 with wheelchair ramps and therapy rooms.

narrative_blocks.header: She asked only that it not be monotonous
narrative_blocks.body: They married in Madrid in 1914 and spent their first two years at Buenos Aires, where Kermit was assistant manager of the National City Bank; she waited out the war in Madrid while he served with the British army in the Middle East. The one thing I asked in life was that it shouldn't be monotonous, she told a friend, and dear knows it hasn't been that.

narrative_blocks.header: She gave his papers to the nation
narrative_blocks.body: Kermit died on active duty in the Aleutians in 1943, a major in the army. She handed the twenty-five thousand items of his letters and papers to the Library of Congress.

narrative_blocks.header: She put the children to work on relief
narrative_blocks.body: For ten years before the war she worked with the Lenox Hill Neighborhood Association and its hospital. When war came in 1941 she organised Young America Wants to Help, the junior division of British War Relief.
