notable.notable_blurb: CIA officer who ran the 1953 Iran coup

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the CIA's 1953 Iran coup
narrative_blocks.body: He ran Operation Ajax on the ground - the CIA and British plot that overthrew Iran's prime minister and put the Shah back on his throne in August 1953. It became the Agency's model elsewhere in the Cold War.

narrative_blocks.header: He refused to repeat the trick in Guatemala
narrative_blocks.body: Asked to engineer a second coup in Guatemala in 1954, Roosevelt declined, judging that Iran had worked only because so many Iranians shared its aims. He left the Agency a few years later for the oil and defense industries.

narrative_blocks.header: His father shot himself in Alaska
narrative_blocks.body: He was twenty-seven and in the Office of Strategic Services when his father, posted to Fort Richardson in Alaska, took his own life on 4 June 1943. Born at Buenos Aires in 1916, where Kermit Sr. ran a bank branch, he grew up at Oyster Bay near Sagamore Hill.

narrative_blocks.header: He crossed into Iran as James Lochridge
narrative_blocks.body: He crossed the border under that cover name on 19 July 1953 and set about getting the Shah to sign the decrees dismissing Mossadegh. The first attempt failed on 15 August and headquarters told him to get out; he stayed and ran a second that held.

narrative_blocks.header: Eisenhower gave him the medal in secret
narrative_blocks.body: The director cabled Tehran on 20 August 1953 that his persistence, extreme competence and courage should be commended most highly. Eisenhower pinned the National Security Medal on him at a closed ceremony on 26 March 1956.

narrative_blocks.header: He built a pro-Arab lobby for the Agency
narrative_blocks.body: He was executive director of the Committee for Justice and Peace in the Holy Land from 1948 and helped found the American Friends of the Middle East in 1951, to argue that America should back Arab nationalism as the European empires withdrew. Historians have since shown it was secretly CIA-funded.

narrative_blocks.header: The Agency called his own memoir fiction
narrative_blocks.body: He submitted Countercoup to the CIA for clearance in 1979 and took the changes it asked for; a reviewer noted the book had therefore become essentially a work of fiction. Historians have said much the same - that he inflated his own part, and America's, in what happened.

narrative_blocks.header: He captained a warship into southern France
narrative_blocks.body: Commissioned in the Naval Reserve in 1940, he served in the Pacific and rose to command the USS Greene. His ship supported the Allied landings in southern France in August 1944, then returned to escort duty in the Pacific.

narrative_blocks.header: He lectured on music at three universities
narrative_blocks.body: Beyond his own compositions, Joseph earned diplomas and degrees from several conservatories. He lectured on music at Columbia, Fairleigh Dickinson, and the New York College of Music.

narrative_blocks.header: A Roosevelt granddaughter with her own convictions
narrative_blocks.body: A granddaughter of Theodore Roosevelt and daughter of the explorer Kermit Roosevelt, she was educated at Barnard and in Europe and gave her energies to causes she believed in, among them the International Rescue Committee. She married the future Columbia dean John Gorham Palfrey.

narrative_blocks.header: She crossed party lines for a wartime president
narrative_blocks.body: Her Oyster Bay Roosevelts were staunch Republicans, but as the Second World War raged she broke from them to support her Hyde Park cousin Franklin's re-election, joining the Service Wives to Re-elect Roosevelt. She judged the wartime president worth keeping over party loyalty.

narrative_blocks.header: He drove ambulances for the British Eighth Army
narrative_blocks.body: Discharged from the Army for illness soon after enlisting at eighteen in 1943, he joined the American Field Service instead. He drove an ambulance with the British Eighth Army up through Italy until the fighting ended.

narrative_blocks.header: Oxford honors in history after the war
narrative_blocks.body: With the war over he read history at Oxford for three years and took his degree with high honors. He had prepared at Buckley, Groton, and Brooks before everything was interrupted.

narrative_blocks.header: Dead at twenty-eight in his Sutton Place bed
narrative_blocks.body: He was found dead one January morning in 1953 at his home on Sutton Place, the exact cause never established. He had lately come through surgery in England, where he was a postgraduate student at the University of London.

military_service.notes: Enlisted in the U.S. Army in 1943, discharged for illness, then drove an ambulance with the British Eighth Army in Italy.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught a book group inside prisons
narrative_blocks.body: A Harvard-trained lawyer who once taught school in Tanzania, Jonathan found his calling in the Massachusetts prison system. For ten years he ran a revered book-discussion group for incarcerated men.

narrative_blocks.header: Washington, Kinshasa, Accra, Washington again
narrative_blocks.body: The family moved to Washington in 1966, where his three children were born, and in 1969 on to Kinshasa in the then-Congo. He worked for the United States government from there and from Accra in Ghana, and came back to Washington in 1973.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught in Tanganyika between degrees
narrative_blocks.body: He left Groton in 1958 and Harvard in 1962, then went with his first wife Jae to teach school at Moshi in Tanganyika for a year. They returned to Cambridge in 1963 and he took his Harvard law degree in 1965.

narrative_blocks.header: A part of his heart stayed in Africa
narrative_blocks.body: He died at home in Sudbury in June 2013, seventy-three years old, after a long illness, with his wife Laine Gifford beside him. The service was at the First Parish Unitarian Universalist meeting house there.

narrative_blocks.header: Killed at nineteen, weeks into fatherhood
narrative_blocks.body: Simon died in a car accident at nineteen, only weeks after becoming a father. He left a wife and a ten-month-old child.

narrative_blocks.header: Lost at nineteen in a car accident
narrative_blocks.body: A student at Simon's Rock College, he died in a car accident at nineteen. His younger brother David would be lost the same way four years later.

narrative_blocks.header: Lost at twenty-one on a Berkshire road
narrative_blocks.body: He died in a car accident in the Berkshires, at twenty-one. His older brother Caleb had been killed the same way four years earlier.

narrative_blocks.header: A Boston pediatrician who led a Harvard house
narrative_blocks.body: In 1999 Sean and his wife Judy, both pediatricians, took over Adams House at Harvard as its masters, a title later changed to faculty deans. They lived with its undergraduates for twenty-two years and stepped down in 2021.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years against lead poisoning
narrative_blocks.body: Sean directed lead poisoning prevention programs in Boston for forty years, latterly at Boston Medical Center. He warned that clean water would be among the gravest questions of the coming centuries, and that wars would be fought over it.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-two years at Boston City Hospital
narrative_blocks.body: Sean spent thirty-two years on the staff of Boston City Hospital, which became Boston Medical Center, as professor of pediatrics and public health, many of his patients from low-income homes. He won the Jack B. McConnell Award for volunteer work beyond the clinic.

narrative_blocks.header: From neurophysiology to pediatrics
narrative_blocks.body: Sean took a Harvard biology degree in 1967 and started in neurophysiology at Rockefeller University before moving to Columbia's medical scientist program, finishing in 1974. After a Tufts residency he ran pediatrics at St. Vincent Hospital in Worcester for ten years.

narrative_blocks.header: TR's great-grandson, working for his daughter
narrative_blocks.body: Sean counted Theodore Roosevelt as his great-grandfather and credited the family genes for his conservation work. In retirement he works for Conservation Centers for Species Survival, the wildlife alliance his daughter Katy runs.

narrative_blocks.header: Poet and painter named for a Confederate spy
narrative_blocks.body: Antonia was a poet, photographer, and painter who took her name from her ancestress Antonia Ford, a Civil War Confederate agent. She made her life in the arts in central Massachusetts.

narrative_blocks.header: She farmed, painted, and taught the land
narrative_blocks.body: She poured her many talents into a rural life — working as a landscaper, raising animals and vegetables on her own farm, and teaching children to ride and to love the natural world. Her heart was in horses, the American West, and its ranches and wilderness.

narrative_blocks.header: From Washington childhood to a Massachusetts farm
narrative_blocks.body: Born in New York in 1954, she grew up between the city, Washington, and Cambridge as her father, the Columbia dean John Gorham Palfrey, moved between the university and government. She turned from that world toward the land, making her home among the hills of central Massachusetts.

notable.notable_blurb: President of the MacArthur Foundation

narrative_blocks.header: He runs the MacArthur Foundation
narrative_blocks.body: John became the sixth president of the MacArthur Foundation on 1 September 2019, after seven years as head of Phillips Academy, where admissions stayed need-blind, the number of faculty of color doubled, and he founded the Tang Institute to spread good teaching.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the book on digital natives
narrative_blocks.body: With Urs Gasser, John wrote Born Digital in 2008, on the first generation to grow up online, and Library Journal named it a top science and technology book of the year. That year he also chaired the national Internet Safety Technical Task Force on keeping children from unwanted contact online.

narrative_blocks.header: Iran named him a conspirator
narrative_blocks.body: John's work on the internet and democracy, through the OpenNet Initiative, was cited by dissidents in Iran's Green Movement, and at the show trials of 2009 and 2010 the Iranian government named him and his colleague Ethan Zuckerman as conspirators.

narrative_blocks.header: Undefeated on the squash court
narrative_blocks.body: John graduated magna cum laude from Harvard in 1994 as co-captain of the undefeated squash team that won the school's fourth straight national title, then read history at Pembroke College, Cambridge, as a Rotary Scholar.

narrative_blocks.header: A love letter to libraries
narrative_blocks.body: As vice dean John ran the Harvard Law School library, and he was founding chair of the Digital Public Library of America until 2015. His 2015 book BiblioTech, which he called a love letter to libraries, argued that they matter more than ever in the age of Google.

narrative_blocks.header: He defended Shepard Fairey's Hope poster
narrative_blocks.body: John was on the pro bono legal team that defended the street artist Shepard Fairey when the Associated Press claimed his Obama Hope poster had taken its photograph without fair use.

narrative_blocks.header: Theodore Roosevelt's great-great-grandson
narrative_blocks.body: John's grandmother Belle Wyatt Roosevelt Palfrey was a daughter of Kermit Roosevelt, which makes him a great-great-grandson of Theodore Roosevelt. He married his college sweetheart, Catherine Carter, in 1998.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran for Massachusetts lieutenant governor
narrative_blocks.body: A Harvard-trained lawyer, Quentin Palfrey was the 2018 Democratic nominee for lieutenant governor of Massachusetts. He has held senior posts in federal economic and infrastructure policy.

career.organization: White House Office of Science & Technology Policy

narrative_blocks.header: She leads a coalition saving endangered species
narrative_blocks.body: Katy Palfrey heads the Conservation Centers for Species Survival, an alliance of institutions working to breed and reintroduce endangered wildlife. The network spans some hundred thousand acres.

narrative_blocks.header: Daughter of a famous poet, married a Roosevelt
narrative_blocks.body: Nancy was the daughter of the poet E.E. Cummings, raised amid the literary world of Greenwich Village. She married Joseph Willard Roosevelt, and the marriage ended in divorce.

birth.notes: Greenwich Village

narrative_blocks.header: She met Mr. Death with wit and indignation
narrative_blocks.body: Ill for a long time, she faced her own end with humor and the occasional flash of indignation at the mixed signals sent by 'Mr. Death.' She was, she said, surrounded by beauty — and she died at home in Orient, among her family and caregivers.

narrative_blocks.header: Her long marriage was shadowed by tragedy
narrative_blocks.body: Born on Staten Island in 1935, she married the composer Joseph Willard Roosevelt and built a home with him at Orient on the North Fork, designed by a local architect. Their life together was long and loving, but darkened by the loss of both their sons.

bio.bio_blurb: Gardener and passionate advocate for justice

notable.notable_blurb: Columbia dean and Atomic Energy commissioner

narrative_blocks.header: Dean of Columbia who policed the atom
narrative_blocks.body: Palfrey became dean of Columbia College at thirty-nine, then served on the Atomic Energy Commission under Kennedy and Johnson. A law professor, he pressed for control of the nuclear arms race.

narrative_blocks.header: He shared a Harvard class with John Kennedy
narrative_blocks.body: Palfrey graduated from Harvard in 1940 alongside the future President Kennedy. His five older sisters were all national junior tennis champions, one a two-time U.S. singles winner.

narrative_blocks.header: FDR came to his wedding to a Roosevelt
narrative_blocks.body: In 1942 he married Belle 'Clochette' Roosevelt, a granddaughter of Theodore Roosevelt — a wedding that drew Franklin and Eleanor Roosevelt among the guests. Their daughter Antonia grew up to be an artist of the Massachusetts hills.

narrative_blocks.header: Heir to a Boston line of scholar-soldiers
narrative_blocks.body: He came of an old Boston family thick with distinction — great-grandson of John Gorham Palfrey, a congressman and the first dean of Harvard's Divinity School, and grandson of Francis Winthrop Palfrey, a Civil War officer and historian. He carried the family name into law and public service.

narrative_blocks.header: A sister in the Tennis Hall of Fame
narrative_blocks.body: John's sister Sarah Palfrey Cooke won the U.S. singles title in 1941 and again in 1945, by then a mother, with eleven major doubles titles besides. In 1950 she pressed the national tennis association to admit Althea Gibson to its whites-only championships.

narrative_blocks.header: She led the nation's pediatricians
narrative_blocks.body: A Harvard pediatrician, Palfrey championed community child health and care for children with special needs. She served as president of the American Academy of Pediatrics and ran Michelle Obama's Let's Move initiative.

narrative_blocks.header: Pediatrics after the disasters
narrative_blocks.body: Judy and her husband Sean went to Indonesia, Chile, Haiti and New Orleans after natural disasters to help restore children's medical services there, and she helped found the global health program at Boston Children's Hospital.

narrative_blocks.header: A date that began with Under Milk Wood
narrative_blocks.body: Sean Palfrey was dating one of Judy's Radcliffe roommates when he asked whether any of them would see Dylan Thomas's Under Milk Wood with him, and Judy said yes. They married in Baltimore in September 1967, two days after he came home from a Glee Club world tour, and two days later she started medical school.

narrative_blocks.header: A kazoo at the head of the parade
narrative_blocks.body: Judy and Sean were faculty deans of Adams House at Harvard for twenty-two years. At the house's seventy-fifth anniversary festival she marched at the front of the parade with the Harvard band, playing the kazoo.

narrative_blocks.header: The Olympic torch, half run, half danced
narrative_blocks.body: Judy was one of twenty Americans invited to Canada to carry the Olympic torch, and covered her stretch half running and half dancing while the crowds along the road cheered.

notable.notable_blurb: Modernist American poet

narrative_blocks.header: He made poems by breaking every rule
narrative_blocks.body: Cummings reinvented American poetry with shattered syntax, lowercase lines, and typography that danced across the page. By his death he was among the most widely read poets in the country.

narrative_blocks.header: A French prison gave him his first novel
narrative_blocks.body: Volunteering as an ambulance driver in the First World War, Cummings was jailed by French authorities on suspicion of being a spy. The ordeal became his book The Enormous Room.

narrative_blocks.header: The Crosbys were his crowd in Paris
narrative_blocks.body: He and Harry Crosby had both driven ambulances in France before either published a line, and through the twenties they belonged to the same expatriate circle around the Black Sun Press. Crosby counted him a friend alongside Hart Crane and Archibald MacLeish. When Crane threw the Crosbys a farewell party in Brooklyn in December 1929, cummings was in the room.

narrative_blocks.header: Thayer's Dial made his name
narrative_blocks.body: Scofield Thayer, his Harvard friend, paid Cummings to write an epithalamion for his 1916 wedding, and in January 1920 opened the new Dial with seven of his poems. Cummings told his father it was like having his own printing press.

narrative_blocks.header: Muse and wife to a circle of artists
narrative_blocks.body: Elaine moved through the literary avant-garde of the 1910s and 1920s, marrying in turn an art-magazine editor and the poet E.E. Cummings. She spent her later years abroad.

notable.notable_blurb: Editor of The Dial; modern-art collector

narrative_blocks.header: Seven Cummings poems in his first Dial
narrative_blocks.body: Scofield and James Sibley Watson bought The Dial at the end of 1919, and their first issue, in January 1920, carried seven poems and four drawings by his Harvard friend E. E. Cummings. Amy Lowell bet him that Cummings would never reach the pantheon of American poets.

narrative_blocks.header: First in America with The Waste Land
narrative_blocks.body: Scofield brought out T. S. Eliot's The Waste Land before any other American publisher, saw that Mann's Death in Venice was a masterpiece before it was translated, and wrote the first survey of all of Joyce's work. Under him The Dial printed Yeats, Proust, Lawrence and Picasso.

narrative_blocks.header: A wedding poem that foretold the end
narrative_blocks.body: For his marriage to Elaine Orr in June 1916 Scofield paid Cummings to write an epithalamion, and the marriage came apart on the honeymoon. By 1919 Elaine was with Cummings, and when their daughter Nancy was born that December, Scofield was named on her birth certificate.

narrative_blocks.header: Freud's patient in Vienna
narrative_blocks.body: Scofield sailed for Europe in July 1921 and ran The Dial from Vienna, where Sigmund Freud analysed him. Breakdowns forced him out as editor in June 1926; he was certified insane in 1937 and lived out his life among servants in Bermuda, Florida, Boston and Martha's Vineyard.

narrative_blocks.header: Four hundred works for the Met
narrative_blocks.body: Scofield died at Edgartown on Martha's Vineyard in July 1982, at ninety-two, and left four hundred works from his collection to the Metropolitan Museum and his Aubrey Beardsley drawings to the Fogg. Picasso's Erotic Scene turned up among his stored papers in Worcester.

narrative_blocks.header: His uncle wrote Casey at the Bat
narrative_blocks.body: Scofield was the only child of Edward D. Thayer, a Worcester woollen-mill owner who died when the boy was seventeen and left him most of the fortune. His uncle Ernest Thayer had written Casey at the Bat.

notable.notable_blurb: Irish senator, banker, and journalist

narrative_blocks.header: He gave Fine Gael its name
narrative_blocks.body: In 1933 Frank founded the National Centre Party with James Dillon and led it into a merger with Cumann na nGaedheal and the Blueshirts that same year. He became a vice-president of the new party, Fine Gael, and is said to have devised its name.

narrative_blocks.header: He quit over Mussolini's war
narrative_blocks.body: Frank rebuked Eoin O'Duffy when the Blueshirt leader questioned democracy in 1934, and resigned from Fine Gael himself in 1935, when party members attacked de Valera for condemning Italy's invasion of Ethiopia at the League of Nations.

narrative_blocks.header: De Valera put his critic in the Senate
narrative_blocks.body: Frank fought the 1937 constitution over the Catholic Church's special position and Irish as first language, and did not stand again in 1938. De Valera, whom he had opposed for years, then named him to the Senate, where he urged Ireland to join the Allies in the war.

narrative_blocks.header: A major, then a New York banker
narrative_blocks.body: Educated at Downside and Oxford and called to the bar at King's Inns, Frank ended the First World War a major in the Royal Army Service Corps. He banked in New York from 1919 to 1927, then won Roscommon for the Dáil in 1932 as an Independent.

narrative_blocks.header: Cummings thought of killing him
narrative_blocks.body: Elaine Orr left E. E. Cummings for Frank within months of her 1924 marriage to the poet, and Cummings considered killing him. Frank and Elaine married, fought Cummings for custody of her daughter Nancy, and had a son of their own, Brian.

narrative_blocks.header: The life of Wolfe Tone
narrative_blocks.body: Frank's Theobald Wolfe Tone and His Times came out in 1939 and stood as the standard life of Tone for fifty years, until Marianne Elliott's in 1989. He later wrote from America and Paris for The Irish Times.

narrative_blocks.header: Youngest son of the Prince of Coolavin
narrative_blocks.body: Frank was born in Dublin in 1886, the seventh and youngest son of Hugh Hyacinth O'Rorke MacDermot, Prince of Coolavin.

notable.notable_blurb: Fashion model, photographer, and Cummings's companion

narrative_blocks.header: The greatest model Steichen ever shot
narrative_blocks.body: Edward Steichen photographed Marion through the 1920s and 1930s for Vogue and Vanity Fair, and called her the greatest fashion model he ever shot. When she put on the clothes, he wrote, she became a woman who really would wear that gown or that riding habit.

narrative_blocks.header: Five foot nine, too tall for the stage
narrative_blocks.body: Schooled in Hartford at St. Anne's Academy, Marion came to New York in the 1920s to act. At five feet nine she found parts hard to get; in front of a camera, her height became an asset.

narrative_blocks.header: Her camera, his lowercase captions
narrative_blocks.body: Marion took up the camera herself, and after her husband died in 1962 she published Adventures in Value, her photographs of nature, still lifes and friends such as Marianne Moore, with his captions in lowercase. One reviewer called her a fine and sensitive photographer.

narrative_blocks.header: Three decades on Patchin Place
narrative_blocks.body: Marion and her husband lived on Patchin Place in Greenwich Village for nearly thirty years, and many of his books of poems were dedicated to her; he also painted her portrait. She died in 1969, at sixty-three, planning a book of her portraits of him and their friends.

narrative_blocks.header: A famed model who became Cummings's muse
narrative_blocks.body: One of the most photographed fashion models of her era, Morehouse later took up photography herself. She was E.E. Cummings's companion for the last decades of his life and collaborated with him on a book.

narrative_blocks.header: She campaigned to end Prohibition
narrative_blocks.body: A prominent figure in Boston's Back Bay, she threw herself in the 1930s into the fight to repeal Prohibition, founding the Women's Organization for National Reform. It was reform work of a wet, not a dry — she wanted the noble experiment ended.

narrative_blocks.header: Willa Cather declined her invitation, then apologized
narrative_blocks.body: In 1932 she invited the novelist Willa Cather to speak before an organization her husband had co-founded. Cather declined — she had mistaken the letter for advertising and left it unopened — and sent a rueful apology for the delay.

narrative_blocks.header: A fatal crash near their Long Island home
narrative_blocks.body: In 1971 she was killed in an automobile crash near the couple's old house on Long Island, her husband Archibald at the wheel. They had been married fifty-four years, since a wartime wedding in Boston in 1917.

notable.notable_blurb: CIA station chief in Istanbul, Madrid and London

narrative_blocks.header: He ran three CIA stations
narrative_blocks.body: He joined the Central Intelligence Group in 1947 and served at Beirut, ran the Near East section of the Voice of America from New York, and was station chief at Istanbul from 1951, Madrid from 1958 and London from 1962 to 1966. He retired in 1974 after twenty-seven years and joined Chase Manhattan the next year.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixteen languages, and jokes in each Arabic
narrative_blocks.body: He spoke sixteen languages, Edmund Morris said, so fluently that he could joke in different versions of Arabic - the only one of Theodore Roosevelt's many descendants, Morris thought, with the encyclopedic intelligence of his grandfather. Among them were Hebrew, Turkish, Russian, Swahili and Uzbek, and he had been a Latin and Greek scholar as a boy.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote a memoir that names no country
narrative_blocks.body: For Lust of Knowing came out in 1988, and he kept his oath so strictly in it that he would not identify a single country he had served in. He told interviewers they could work it out from his Who's Who entry, and that he would not break the oath even if the government told him to.

narrative_blocks.header: He went ashore in North Africa in 1942
narrative_blocks.body: He landed with American troops as an Army intelligence officer, and what he saw of French colonial administration and the first stirrings of Arab nationalism set the direction of his working life. He served five years, rose to captain, and finished as military attache in the Middle East.

narrative_blocks.header: He would not be a Le Carre character
narrative_blocks.body: An intelligence officer, he wrote, must swim in foreign seas like Mao's guerrillas and then pull himself to shore and look back calmly at the waters that immersed him. He must know whose side he is on and believe it the right one, and not imitate the cynical protagonists of Le Carre's novels.

narrative_blocks.header: His son would steward the family name
narrative_blocks.body: His son Tweed, born in 1942, grew up to chair the Theodore Roosevelt Association and carry the family's public legacy forward. The line of the president's soldier sons did not end on the battlefield.

people.research_notes: Washington Post obituary by J. Y. Smith, 7 June 1990, entered in the Congressional Record by Rep. Mary Rose Oakar. Son of Archibald Roosevelt and Grace Lockwood; first job on a Seattle newspaper. He described himself as the product of a conventional, Waspish, preppy world who escaped a Wall Street career because he lived in another world of his imagination. New York Times obituary by Eric Pace, 1 June 1990: died in his sleep at his Georgetown house, with a history of heart trouble; Harvard 1939 there against the Post's class of 1940; sixteen languages on Edmund Morris's count against the Post's twenty; Army 1942-47, rising to captain; joined Chase Manhattan in 1975. Mother Grace Stackpole Lockwood. Three sisters survived him - Nancy Roosevelt Jackson, Edith Roosevelt and Theodora Roosevelt Rauchfuss. Richard Helms said Archie made a significant contribution to the national security of his beloved country.

notable.notable_blurb: Roosevelt granddaughter; lesbian pulp-fiction novelist

narrative_blocks.header: Nine dark novels, then silence
narrative_blocks.body: Between 1950 and 1962 she published nine novels of psychological menace, full of characters with hidden and dangerous second selves, then stopped writing for good. Patricia Highsmith, who almost never reviewed anyone, praised her first book.

narrative_blocks.header: An early voice of lesbian pulp fiction
narrative_blocks.body: Her frank treatment of gay and lesbian lives made her one of the daring postwar writers who opened American fiction to those themes. Long forgotten, her books were rediscovered and reissued in the early two-thousands.

narrative_blocks.header: A debutante who danced in South America
narrative_blocks.body: She came out in New York society in 1937, then made her living as a professional dancer in South America and Canada. She gave it up in 1945 to marry an artist and move to Paris.

narrative_blocks.header: She played down the Roosevelt name
narrative_blocks.body: She wrote under her first husband's surname and downplayed her famous lineage, wanting the work judged on its own merits. She married three times and spent her last years alone in the North Carolina woods with cats and chickens.

narrative_blocks.header: The one woman writer Highsmith praised in print
narrative_blocks.body: Patricia Highsmith, famously grudging toward other women writers, gave Keogh’s first novel a heated, admiring review — the only woman she ever praised in print. Its willful heroine, a knife-carrying twelve-year-old, was modeled on Theodora’s own childhood.

narrative_blocks.header: A wildcat in her Hotel Chelsea apartment
narrative_blocks.body: During her second marriage she kept a margay — a small South American wildcat — in her apartment at the Hotel Chelsea. Legend said it bit off her ear one night; in truth it took a few nips at an earlobe, after which she simply restyled her hair.

cross_connections.display_label: was a fellow novelist who chronicled the fading American gentry
came out in print at sixty-four with Lily Briscoe: A Self-Portrait

narrative_blocks.header: The quiet sister among soldiers and writers
narrative_blocks.body: Born between her decorated father's two wars, she lived more privately than her siblings and married into the Jackson family. She outlived all but the youngest of them.

narrative_blocks.header: Her daughter married America's most elusive novelist
narrative_blocks.body: Her daughter Melanie, a literary agent, married the famously reclusive novelist Thomas Pynchon — making Nancy the mother-in-law of a writer almost no one has ever photographed. The Roosevelt line thus brushed against one of American letters' great enigmas.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brief marriage to a Soviet defector
narrative_blocks.body: A Barnard graduate, she was married for four years to Alexander Barmine, a former Red Army general who had defected and become an American broadcaster. Their daughter Margot carried the Roosevelt name forward.

narrative_blocks.header: She hunted Soviet influence in her own column
narrative_blocks.body: After her marriage ended she made her name as a journalist, writing a syndicated column, Between the Lines, that tracked Soviet and communist influence operations inside American government and media. She and her former husband, though divorced, had shared those convictions.

narrative_blocks.header: Division surgeon under fire in France
narrative_blocks.body: He served fourteen months as surgeon of the Second Infantry Division, wounded in the field and decorated by France with the Croix de Guerre and the Legion of Honor. The American army added its Distinguished Service Medal.

narrative_blocks.header: He rebuilt hospital care across Long Island
narrative_blocks.body: For some thirty years after the war he led surgery at the Glen Cove hospital and drove the founding of a new laboratory there, later named in his honor. Friends raised a quarter of a million dollars to build it.

narrative_blocks.header: A hunter in his father-in-law's mold
narrative_blocks.body: Like Theodore Roosevelt he loved big game, stalking Kodiak bear in Alaska and filming moose on long northern trips. He titled his own war memoir Wade in, Sanitary.

narrative_blocks.header: The nephew Quentin left everything to
narrative_blocks.body: He was the small boy who pointed at passing planes and called them Uncle Quentin, and the aviator left him his death benefits. He died at eight, four years after the uncle he adored.

notable.notable_blurb: Historian, conservationist, and Republican committeewoman

narrative_blocks.header: She seconded Nixon's nomination in 1960
narrative_blocks.body: A granddaughter of Theodore Roosevelt, she addressed the Republican convention and served for forty years as her state's Republican committeewoman. Washington's governor later named her a trustee of the state university.

narrative_blocks.header: Founder of an island health center
narrative_blocks.body: On Vashon Island she founded a community health center and pressed for cleaner air and water across the Northwest. The Roosevelt conservation streak ran strong in her.

narrative_blocks.header: Her Seattle house held a president's china
narrative_blocks.body: The home a celebrated architect built for her family held White House china from her grandfather's table, some of it now in the Smithsonian. She kept the Roosevelt past close at hand.

narrative_blocks.header: Half of Brattleboro's club-champion couple
narrative_blocks.body: She and her husband became the only pair to hold both the men's and women's golf championships at their Vermont country club. She had come a long way from the Oyster Bay of her grandfather.

narrative_blocks.header: A president's granddaughter turned Vermonter
narrative_blocks.body: She raised her family in Brattleboro while her husband built a long career in law and the statehouse. Both of them took honorary degrees from the state university.

bio.bio_blurb: TR's granddaughter; married Vermont senator Gannett

narrative_blocks.header: Named for the uncle lost over France
narrative_blocks.body: Quentin Roosevelt, the president's youngest son, was shot down over France in 1918. Five years later this niece was born and given his name to keep — Judith Quentin Derby.

narrative_blocks.header: She married into a dynasty of scientists
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband and his father both made their names studying the brain and the eye, a rare scientific lineage. She died in 1973, in her forties, the mother of three.

narrative_blocks.header: Her wedding invitations were recalled
narrative_blocks.body: She was to marry Adelbert Ames 3d at Christ Church in Oyster Bay on the sixteenth of October 1948. Her grandmother Edith Roosevelt died that morning; the invitations were called back and they married quietly, with only the families there.

notable.notable_blurb: Harvard neuroscientist; created the Ames medium

narrative_blocks.header: The fluid that keeps brain tissue alive
narrative_blocks.body: He devised an artificial cerebrospinal fluid, the Ames medium, that lets scientists keep nervous-system tissue working for days outside the body. It remains the standard solution for the purpose today.

narrative_blocks.header: The no-reflow phenomenon
narrative_blocks.body: Working with rabbit brains, he showed that after enough minutes without blood the smallest vessels clamp shut and will not refill, the first irreversible injury of a stroke. The finding later proved true in the heart and other organs.

narrative_blocks.header: Skiing competitively into his late eighties
narrative_blocks.body: Class valedictorian at Exeter and Phi Beta Kappa at Harvard, he kept racing in masters ski events until almost ninety. He was last seen on cross-country skis at ninety-six.

led the largest NINDS trial on preventing a second stroke

bio.bio_blurb: Harvard neuroscientist; created the Ames medium

notable.notable_blurb: Vermont legislator and Brattleboro lawyer

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years in the Vermont legislature
narrative_blocks.body: He served four terms in the Vermont House and ten in the state Senate, working across party lines on budgets, taxes, and the shape of town government. He helped write Brattleboro's unusual representative town meeting into law.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty-four years at the Vermont bar
narrative_blocks.body: He practiced tax and estate law in Brattleboro for more than six decades, at his retirement the senior member of the state bar. An early law partner became Vermont's attorney general and a federal judge.

narrative_blocks.header: He waited eighty-seven years for the Red Sox
narrative_blocks.body: Born eleven months before the 1918 title, he followed the team through generations of broadcasters before they won again just after his birthday in 2004. He chased a golf ball with the same patience into his nineties.

military_service.notes: Field artillery, combat service in Europe 1944-1945.

narrative_blocks.header: He brought a president's granddaughter west
narrative_blocks.body: After the war he settled his family in the Seattle area, in a house a noted architect designed for them. He and Edith raised three children on the far side of the country from Oyster Bay.

narrative_blocks.header: He turned twelve lawyers into four hundred
narrative_blocks.body: Over a thirty-five-year career at the Seattle firm now called Perkins Coie, he served as managing partner and personally welcomed each young lawyer to his Vashon Island home. Under his steady hand the firm grew from about a dozen lawyers to hundreds; his clients included Boeing and the Seattle Pilots.

narrative_blocks.header: A chicken on his head, and he laughed
narrative_blocks.body: A man of warm, self-deprecating humor, he loved the joke to be on himself — once sitting through a family dinner with a chicken his grandchildren had perched on his head, delighted. He spent his weekends working around his Vashon Island farm.

career.notes: Thirty-five-year career; Navy service in World War II.

narrative_blocks.header: A Marine corporal in Vietnam
narrative_blocks.body: He joined the Marine Corps in 1964 and served through the war in Vietnam. He died in Alaska and was buried near Fairbanks.

narrative_blocks.header: She married the Discovery Institute's founder
narrative_blocks.body: Bruce Chapman had been Secretary of State of Washington and Reagan's census director before founding Discovery Institute at Seattle in 1990. They married in 1976 and have two sons.

narrative_blocks.header: Theodore Roosevelt was her great-grandfather
narrative_blocks.body: The line runs from Roosevelt and Edith Carow through their daughter Ethel Derby to her mother, Edith Roosevelt Derby Williams. She is his great-granddaughter, not the second remove some accounts give her.

notable.notable_blurb: Discovery Institute founder; Reagan-era official

narrative_blocks.header: He founded Discovery Institute in Seattle
narrative_blocks.body: Bruce founded Discovery Institute at Seattle in 1991 with his Harvard roommate George Gilder, after a Hudson Institute fellowship. He has chaired it since 2011; it works on economics, transportation and technology, and its Chapman Center on Citizen Leadership bears his name.

narrative_blocks.header: Headquarters of the intelligent design movement
narrative_blocks.body: The institute's Center for Science and Culture made it the hub of the intelligent design movement, which holds that features of life are best explained by an intelligent cause. A federal court ruled in 2005 that intelligent design is religion rather than science.

narrative_blocks.header: Reagan picked a Ripon Republican for the census
narrative_blocks.body: Bruce's 1966 book had mocked Reagan's class-B movie world, and Lyn Nofziger said he had never recommended a Ripon Society Republican for anything. Reagan made him census director anyway in 1981, and Bruce set out to keep the bureau professional.

narrative_blocks.header: Reagan's ambassador to the UN at Vienna
narrative_blocks.body: Bruce went from the census to the White House as a deputy assistant to the President, then from 1985 to 1988 served as ambassador to the United Nations organizations at Vienna, where his brief ran from nuclear proliferation and refugees to narcotics control.

narrative_blocks.header: He attacked Goldwater, then the draft
narrative_blocks.body: At Harvard Bruce and George Gilder started Advance, a Republican journal; their 1966 book The Party That Lost Its Head charged the Goldwater campaign with abandoning civil rights. A Herald Tribune editorial writer, he next argued against the draft in The Wrong Man in Uniform.

narrative_blocks.header: He talked the governor into taking refugees
narrative_blocks.body: As Secretary of State he persuaded Governor Dan Evans to open Washington to Vietnamese refugees, most of whom faced death if they were sent back. He also ran the state's Bicentennial committee and pushed the teaching of civics.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped save Pike Place Market
narrative_blocks.body: Elected to the Seattle City Council in 1971, he made his name in historic preservation — the fight to keep Pike Place Market among it — and in building out the city's parks.

military_service.notes: Air Force Reserve, 1965-1969.

narrative_blocks.header: A pioneer of New York eye surgery
narrative_blocks.body: Trained in Berlin under the great von Graefe, he became a leading ophthalmic surgeon in New York and an officer of the national eye-surgeons' society. He held posts at the New York Eye and Ear Infirmary and other hospitals.

narrative_blocks.header: He fought contagious blindness in the schools
narrative_blocks.body: As a public-health investigator he traced contagious eye disease through New York's tenements and institutions, then pushed a law through the legislature to protect children in residential schools. Hospitals for such cases followed his reports.

notable.notable_blurb: Scientist behind the Ames room illusion

narrative_blocks.header: He built rooms that fool the eye
narrative_blocks.body: His distorted Ames room and tilting Ames window became among the most famous demonstrations in the science of perception. They showed how much the mind supplies what the eye merely seems to see.

narrative_blocks.header: From law and painting to the eye itself
narrative_blocks.body: He took a law degree at Harvard and tried painting before deciding to study vision scientifically, meaning to return to art once he understood it. The study mastered him instead, and optics became his life's work.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the Dartmouth Eye Institute
narrative_blocks.body: He founded a department of physiological optics at Dartmouth and became research director of its eye institute, recruiting designers and clinicians to study binocular vision. Rockefeller money and the optical industry sustained the work.

narrative_blocks.header: Son of a Reconstruction general and governor
narrative_blocks.body: His father had been a Union general and a Reconstruction governor and senator in Mississippi, a defender of Black suffrage in the bitter years after the war. His mother was the daughter of the controversial general Benjamin Butler.

narrative_blocks.header: His ideas reached far beyond the lab
narrative_blocks.body: His transactional theory of perception drew him into correspondence with the philosopher John Dewey and shaped a school of psychology after him. He was honored late with the optical society's highest medal.

narrative_blocks.body: For a few brilliant years around 1950 his drawings lit up French Vogue, all citrus yellow and shocking pink under a draughtsman's easy line. He designed for ballet, theater, and films, including a Judy Garland musical.

narrative_blocks.header: He drew the covers of his wife's novels
narrative_blocks.body: Even after their tempestuous marriage ended he illustrated the jackets of Theodora's books, and she called him her estranged but still beloved Tom. His career, crowded with talent, never quite cohered before his early death.

narrative_blocks.body: Before Vogue he apprenticed under the great ballet costumier Karinska, helping build the gowns Marlene Dietrich wore in Kismet, and earned a single solo screen credit designing costumes for Minnelli’s The Pirate. narrative_blocks.body: On Martha's Vineyard she started the Tashmoo Press and brought out two dozen books by and about Islanders, mentoring a generation of local writers. She had been an art editor at Viking Press, producing coffee-table picture books.

narrative_blocks.header: A free spirit in overalls and pearls
narrative_blocks.body: Outspoken and unconventional, she photographed Vineyard children and Wampanoag elders and founded an animal-spaying charity on the island. A first marriage to a Roosevelt grandson had not suited her taste for diplomatic life.

narrative_blocks.body: He led the long campaign that finally brought Theodore Roosevelt the Medal of Honor for San Juan Hill, awarded in 2001 more than a century late. It hangs now in the White House room that bears the family name.

narrative_blocks.body: On his fiftieth birthday in 1992 he rafted a thousand miles down the Brazilian river his great-grandfather had charted in 1914, finding that nothing and everything had changed. He has long carried the family's public memory as head of the Theodore Roosevelt Association.

narrative_blocks.header: From anti-war marcher to China investor
narrative_blocks.body: He marched on the Pentagon in 1967 and stood among the crowds at Woodstock before a career in finance and consulting. He came to chair a family investment firm spanning Boston and Shanghai.

notable.notable_blurb: Supreme Court justice; chief Nuremberg prosecutor

narrative_blocks.header: The only man to hold all three offices
narrative_blocks.body: He served as solicitor general, attorney general, and Supreme Court justice, the only American ever to hold all three. He reached the bench having never earned a law degree, admitted instead by reading law.

narrative_blocks.header: Chief American prosecutor at Nuremberg
narrative_blocks.body: He took leave from the Court to lead the prosecution of the Nazi leadership before the international tribunal in 1945 and 1946. His opening and closing statements there are still studied as landmarks of the rule of law.

narrative_blocks.header: A stylist who defended individual liberty
narrative_blocks.body: Widely held the finest writer on the Court, he wrote the flag-salute opinion shielding schoolchildren's conscience and a framework for presidential power still cited today. He dissented when the Court upheld the wartime internment of Japanese Americans.

narrative_blocks.header: He read law instead of attending it
narrative_blocks.body: The son of Pennsylvania farmers, he apprenticed under a Jamestown lawyer and spent a single year at Albany Law School, never taking a degree. Justice Scalia later called him the best legal stylist of the twentieth century.

narrative_blocks.header: His three-zone map still governs presidential power
narrative_blocks.body: In his 1952 concurrence in the Steel Seizure Case, Jackson sorted presidential power into three zones — strongest with Congress's backing, weakest against its will. It became the most-cited separation-of-powers opinion in American law.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought the house that became the Kennedys'
narrative_blocks.body: In 1941, on the eve of his Supreme Court appointment, he bought Hickory Hill, an antebellum estate in McLean, Virginia, and made it his family home. After his death his widow sold it to Senator John F. Kennedy — later the home of Robert Kennedy's large family.

narrative_blocks.body: A passionate horsewoman, she gave her wartime years to service — as a Red Cross Gray Lady comforting wounded soldiers, and as an air-raid warden. She had met her husband, the future Justice Robert Jackson, in Albany when she was a state secretary and he a law student.

narrative_blocks.header: He was his father's right hand at Nuremberg
narrative_blocks.body: Fresh from Harvard Law and the Navy, he served as personal assistant to his father, the chief American prosecutor of the Nazi leadership. That trial was the first case of his career.

narrative_blocks.header: A lifetime at one great firm
narrative_blocks.body: He spent his whole career at Milbank, Tweed, rising to chair the firm and head its litigation. His clients ranged from Nelson Rockefeller to Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis and the New York Stock Exchange.

narrative_blocks.header: He argued for a permanent war-crimes court
narrative_blocks.body: He edited the published record of the Nuremberg evidence and pressed in print for a standing international criminal court decades before one existed. He twice argued before the Supreme Court.

narrative_blocks.header: He counseled Rockefeller, Onassis, and a king
narrative_blocks.body: His client list read like a century’s who’s-who — he advised Nelson Rockefeller through his 1974 vice-presidential confirmation, represented Jacqueline Onassis over her husband’s estate, and counseled the King of Morocco and the collector Baron Thyssen. He also argued and won two landmark Supreme Court cases for the New York Stock Exchange.

narrative_blocks.header: He questioned Göring, Hess, and Speer
narrative_blocks.body: As his father’s law clerk and private secretary at Nuremberg, he took part in interrogating Hermann Göring, Rudolf Hess, and Albert Speer. He then co-edited the eight government volumes of the trial’s printed evidence.

narrative_blocks.header: A Supreme Court justice was his best man
narrative_blocks.body: When he married Nancy Roosevelt in 1944, his father, Justice Robert H. Jackson, stood as best man — the only time the justice ever officially filled that role. Months later, father and son left together for Nuremberg.

narrative_blocks.body: He served two years as a Peace Corps volunteer in Liberia before joining a New York advertising agency. He married a great-granddaughter of Theodore Roosevelt.

narrative_blocks.body: At Gettysburg he commanded the Army of the Potomac's Artillery Reserve, whose massed guns helped repel the Confederate assault on the third day. Two horses were shot from under him during the fighting.

narrative_blocks.body: His uncle Daniel Tyler also wore a Union general's star and later founded the Alabama city of Anniston. Both men descended from the theologian Jonathan Edwards through their Connecticut family.

narrative_blocks.body: A bullet shattered his ankle at Cold Harbor in 1864, ending his field command. He was brevetted major general for gallantry and served out the war at a desk.

narrative_blocks.body: His war injuries wore at his health, and he died young. He had just completed an autobiography, published in 1878 and still in print.

narrative_blocks.header: He soldiered the frontier before the war
narrative_blocks.body: Before the Civil War he campaigned in the Yakima War in the Pacific Northwest and the Utah War, crossing the young frontier as an artillery officer. Gettysburg lay years ahead.

narrative_blocks.header: His boycott ruling defined a workingman's rights
narrative_blocks.body: Carpenter wrote a celebrated opinion fixing the limits of labor boycotts so clearly that the question stayed settled for decades. From the same bench he upheld the property rights of married women.

narrative_blocks.header: Passed over for chief justice, he never recovered
narrative_blocks.body: When the chief justiceship opened in 1889, the entire state bar expected the senior justice Carpenter to rise to it; the governor chose another man. Carpenter felt the slight as a deep injustice and carried it the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: Self-taught farm boy who reached the high court
narrative_blocks.body: Denied the college education he wanted, Carpenter taught district school for seven years while reading law on his own. He was admitted to the bar at twenty-two and climbed to the state's highest court.

narrative_blocks.header: He married into the Hooker and Edwards line
narrative_blocks.body: His second wife, Sophia Tyler Cowen, descended from both Thomas Hooker and the theologian Jonathan Edwards. Through her, his Hartford household joined two of New England's founding ministerial lines.

narrative_blocks.body: George Frederick Tyler became the first president of the Norfolk and Western Railroad. He spent his career and fortune in Philadelphia, far from the family's Connecticut roots.

narrative_blocks.header: He built a bank, then sat on everything
narrative_blocks.body: He came home from Providence to organise the Fourth Street National Bank and became its president, and it was later folded into the Philadelphia National. Baldwin Locomotive, Standard Steel, Midvale, two Philadelphia electric companies and two Susquehanna ones all had him on the board.

narrative_blocks.header: He took a broken railroad out of receivership
narrative_blocks.body: He was sole receiver of the Shenandoah Valley Railroad and then ran it as president for several years afterwards. He was president of the Asphalt Company of America besides.

narrative_blocks.body: He married Mary Woodrow Binney of Providence in 1880 and she died four years later, leaving two children. In 1888 he married Ida Elkins, and it was the first pair who survived him — Charlotte at Ithan and George at Newtown.

narrative_blocks.header: Three years in Europe, then the bar
narrative_blocks.body: Out of Episcopal Academy and Harvard in 1872 he spent three years abroad before reading law with George W. Biddle, and was admitted in 1878. He went almost straight into insurance instead.

narrative_blocks.body: Heir to a Philadelphia banking family, George Tyler spent his leisure on big-game safaris, mountain climbing, and yacht racing. After the First World War he turned increasingly toward farming and philanthropy.

narrative_blocks.header: His country estate is now a state park
narrative_blocks.body: He built a French-Norman house called Indian Council Rock on a sprawling Bucks County farm. The land today forms Tyler State Park and the campus of Bucks County Community College.

narrative_blocks.header: The war pulled him out of his cocoon
narrative_blocks.body: By his grandson's account, the First World War and surviving the 1918 pandemic transformed him from an insular Philadelphia aristocrat into a public-minded benefactor.

narrative_blocks.header: A late-blooming sculptor who founded a school
narrative_blocks.body: Stella Elkins took up sculpture at forty-nine under Boris Blai. In 1935 the two founded the art school at Temple University that still carries her name.

narrative_blocks.header: Her debut show was sixty bronzes at once
narrative_blocks.body: Two years after her first lesson, her 1935 debut at New York's Grand Central Galleries filled the room with sixty works, all cast in bronze. The late starter had become a working sculptor.

narrative_blocks.header: Her country house became a college
narrative_blocks.body: In 1963, the year she died, Stella gave Temple her Bucks County estate, Indian Council Rock at Newtown, a French Norman manor of 1930 hung with tapestries she had made herself. Bucks County Community College was founded on it, and the house is its Tyler Hall.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty years a Temple trustee
narrative_blocks.body: Stella sat on Temple University's board of trustees from 1940 to 1960. Temple gave her an honorary doctorate of humane letters in 1940 and its Russell Conwell Award in 1947, the year George died.

narrative_blocks.header: She played Beethoven long before she ever sculpted
narrative_blocks.body: Music came first: she studied piano in France and in 1927 represented the Philadelphia Orchestra at Vienna's centennial of Beethoven's death. Sculpture would not claim her until her late forties.

narrative_blocks.header: She married the stepson of her aunt
narrative_blocks.body: Stella's aunt Ida Elkins had married George Tyler's widowed father. Seventeen years later Stella married George himself, joining the Tyler and Elkins fortunes.

narrative_blocks.header: Horace Binney's great-grandchildren married
narrative_blocks.body: Charlotte Tyler and Robert Montgomery were both great-grandchildren of the Philadelphia lawyer Horace Binney, which made them second cousins. They married in 1902, and their home, Ardrossan, became a Main Line legend.

narrative_blocks.header: Tea in the library at four
narrative_blocks.body: Charlotte's sitting room at Ardrossan was the library, where she did the needlepoint that covered the dining-room chairs. On Mondays at four anyone in the family could come for tea, and on Sunday nights there were suppers with guests.

narrative_blocks.header: Her daughter became Tracy Lord
narrative_blocks.body: Her eldest daughter, Hope, said to have had four proposals on the night of her 1922 debut, became Philip Barry's model for Tracy Lord in The Philadelphia Story.

narrative_blocks.header: Thrown from his horse, he bought the view
narrative_blocks.body: Fox hunting near Villanova, Robert was thrown from his horse and knocked out; coming to, he saw rolling hills, old woods and streams, and bought them. In 1911 he had Horace Trumbauer design a fifty-room Georgian Revival house there, and named the estate Ardrossan after the Scottish town his family came from.

narrative_blocks.header: Founder of Janney Montgomery Scott
narrative_blocks.body: Home from the Spanish-American War, Robert set out to refill the family coffers in finance and co-founded the investment firm now called Janney Montgomery Scott. Financing the Baldwin Locomotive Works made the fortune that built Ardrossan.

narrative_blocks.header: Ayrshires from Scotland, mares from Ireland
narrative_blocks.body: Below the house Robert set up a dairy with nine Ayrshire cows imported from Scotland and a broodmare stable with seven mares and a stallion from Ireland, and ran the estate's eight hundred acres as a working farm. He kept a pack of foxhounds and hunted with the Radnor Hunt.

narrative_blocks.header: Late in life, the autogyro
narrative_blocks.body: In later life Robert took up aviation and helped pioneer the autogyro, the rotor-winged forerunner of the helicopter. He died at Georgetown, South Carolina, where the family kept the Mansfield plantation, in January 1949.

narrative_blocks.header: The house Philip Barry put on stage
narrative_blocks.body: The playwright Philip Barry was a regular guest at Ardrossan, and its household became The Philadelphia Story, with Robert's daughter Hope the model for Tracy Lord. After the play's success Katharine Hepburn stayed there as a houseguest.

narrative_blocks.body: Philip Barry modeled Tracy Lord, the heroine of his 1939 hit The Philadelphia Story, on Hope Scott. Katharine Hepburn played her on stage and screen, and Grace Kelly in the musical remake.

narrative_blocks.header: The one debutante who defended bobbed hair
narrative_blocks.body: Hope came out in 1922 as the one Philadelphia debutante who would defend bobbed hair, and the papers reported that her husband must be tall, good-looking, good-natured and worth a million. She had four proposals on the night of her debut and turned them all down.

narrative_blocks.header: She seated her dog at a dinner party
narrative_blocks.body: Known for her nerve and wit, she once placed her dog as a guest at a formal dinner. She danced the Charleston with Josephine Baker in Paris and the foxtrot with the Duke of Windsor.

narrative_blocks.header: Augustus John's portrait, and his advances
narrative_blocks.body: A size eight all her life, Hope stayed on the couture best-dressed lists and was admired by Cecil Beaton and Augustus John. John's portrait of her hung in the Ardrossan ballroom, and she said she had had to fight off his advances.

narrative_blocks.header: Decades as queen of the Devon Horse Show
narrative_blocks.body: A lifelong horsewoman, she chaired and directed the Devon Horse Show for decades, turning its galas into fundraisers for Bryn Mawr Hospital. She rode and showed well into old age.

narrative_blocks.header: She reigned over the 800-acre Ardrossan
narrative_blocks.body: She grew up and presided at Ardrossan, the Georgian manor her father raised in Villanova. After his death she ran its dairy farm and threw open the great house for her charities.

narrative_blocks.body: She performed as a concert pianist and dancer, soloing at Carnegie Hall and recording Saint-Saens with the Philadelphia Orchestra. In 1932 she founded the Montgomery Ballet and ran it as director and choreographer.

narrative_blocks.header: Her last travel lecture, the day she died
narrative_blocks.body: Widowed in 1964, she made fourteen journeys through South Asia and photographed thousands of scenes. She gave travel lectures for decades, delivering her final one on the day she died in 1995.

military_service.notes: Merchant Marine procurement in Philadelphia; senior watch officer aboard USS General E. T. Collins in the Pacific.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: He lived his whole life on the Ardrossan estate, hosting Presidents Ford and Bush.

narrative_blocks.header: A Navy officer in the wartime Pacific
narrative_blocks.body: He volunteered for the Naval Reserve in the Second World War, handling Merchant Marine procurement and serving as a watch officer aboard a transport in the Pacific. He came home to the family brokerage.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped found the family brokerage at Ardrossan
narrative_blocks.body: With his father he helped build Montgomery Scott & Co., staying a partner until 1989. He spent his whole life on the Ardrossan estate.

narrative_blocks.header: He hosted two presidents at Ardrossan
narrative_blocks.body: A Republican and a Radnor township commissioner, Robert welcomed Presidents Gerald Ford and George Bush to Ardrossan, the 650-acre estate where he lived his whole life.

narrative_blocks.header: His guns went to Valley Forge and Aberdeen
narrative_blocks.body: Robert collected firearms, and gave pieces to the Valley Forge Military Academy and to the Army's Aberdeen Proving Ground in Maryland. From several trips to Africa he filled a room at Murray House, his home on the estate, with African memorabilia, and he died there on 14 March 1997.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Born just as the family moved in, she returned to her childhood bedroom at Ardrossan.

narrative_blocks.header: A debutante who flew her own plane
narrative_blocks.body: Fearless and funny, Charlotte Ives earned a pilot's license and flew her own WACO biplane while her peers went to dances. She was a nationally ranked horsewoman with a gift for animals.

narrative_blocks.header: She chose her childhood bedroom at Ardrossan
narrative_blocks.body: Late in life she sold her Carolina home and returned to Ardrossan, taking her old third-floor bedroom over any other. She brought her dogs and cats with her.

cross_connections.display_label: drove a volunteer ambulance in France and was jailed there as a spy

narrative_blocks.header: Two years around the world on the Sagamore
narrative_blocks.body: Edgar left Harvard without a degree, and at twenty-two his mother bought him a 185-foot schooner, the Sagamore. With a crew of thirty, his mother, and a party of friends and cousins, he spent two years sailing around the world and kept a diary of the voyage.

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve dates, then a nine-month wait
narrative_blocks.body: Edgar met Hope Montgomery at a Main Line dinner party, and after a dozen dates they decided to marry, but her parents made them wait nine months more. Her father gave them Orchard Lodge, a fieldstone house of about 1720 on the Ardrossan estate, and they were married seventy-one years.

narrative_blocks.header: Paris-born, at an ambulance wheel at seventeen
narrative_blocks.body: Edgar was born in Paris in 1899 while his father was at the American embassy, and was schooled in England until he came home for Groton at fourteen. In 1916, at seventeen, he was back in France as a volunteer driver for the Norton-Harjes ambulance service.

narrative_blocks.header: Philip Barry was his friend from Harvard
narrative_blocks.body: Edgar and Philip Barry became friends in George Pierce Baker's playwriting workshop at Harvard. Barry went to Broadway; Edgar tried writing, then bought a seat on the Stock Exchange and joined his father-in-law's firm. Barry drew Tracy Lord in The Philadelphia Story from Hope.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: He and Hope lived at Orchard Lodge on the Ardrossan estate.

people.research_notes: Listed by FindAGrave as 'Edgar Scott Jr.' though generationally Edgar Scott III; his own son is Edgar Scott III of Centerville, DE.

narrative_blocks.header: A hundred-year life atop a brokerage
narrative_blocks.body: Edgar left Groton early to enlist in the Marines and served in Japan, then finished Harvard in 1949 and joined Montgomery, Scott & Co. He was senior partner at the 1971 merger that made Janney Montgomery Scott, and as co-chairman grew it by mergers into one of the largest regional brokerages in the country.

narrative_blocks.header: Foxhunting with the Cheshire into his eighties
narrative_blocks.body: Edgar and Lindsay passed over Ardrossan for a farm at Unionville, where they raised their two children among horses and dogs and hunted with Mr. Stewart's Cheshire Foxhounds. He still rode out with the hunt well into his eighties.

cross_connections.display_label: resigned from the Philadelphia Club under wartime public pressure

landmarks.landmark_blurb: He grew up at Ardrossan, his grandfather's estate.

bio.bio_blurb: President of the Philadelphia Museum of Art

narrative_blocks.header: He led Philadelphia's great art institutions
narrative_blocks.body: Bob ran the Academy of Music until 1980, then became the Philadelphia Museum of Art's first full-time president in 1982. In fourteen years attendance rose from 400,000 to 950,000 a year, and he brought in the Barnes Foundation's French paintings in 1995 and Cézanne the year after.

narrative_blocks.header: He sent Rocky's statue back down the steps
narrative_blocks.body: After Rocky III was filmed on the museum's steps in 1982, the museum paid to have the eight-hundred-pound statue of Sylvester Stallone hauled away. When it came back in 1990 for Rocky V, Bob, who deplored it politely in public, saw that the producers collected it as soon as filming ended.

narrative_blocks.header: A French horn packed with sweets
narrative_blocks.body: From 1969 to 1973 Bob was special assistant to Walter Annenberg, the ambassador in London. He would put his bicycle on the train and ride out to his daughter Janny's English boarding school with forbidden treats, and once slipped into the music wing and packed her French horn with them like a cornucopia.

narrative_blocks.header: Ardrossan's host asked to be called Bob
narrative_blocks.body: Bob gave the tours of Ardrossan himself, met every guest at the door and asked to be called Bob, not Mr. Scott. He lent the house to community groups, and after his mother died he hosted the Devon Horse Show's sponsors there every spring for ten years.

narrative_blocks.header: Sundays behind the beagles
narrative_blocks.body: Every Sunday in fall and winter Bob took out the beagles and horses for a ramble through the Chester County fields and woods, and called his children along, though they could rarely keep up. Years later Janny rode bicycle tours of New England and Europe with him and had to pedal hard to keep pace.

narrative_blocks.header: An inspector-general who died in France
narrative_blocks.body: In his mid-forties Edgar went to France as a major in the Inspector General's office at the American Expeditionary Force's headquarters in Chaumont. He died there on duty on 20 October 1918, three days after his forty-seventh birthday and three weeks before the Armistice.

narrative_blocks.header: Second Secretary at the Paris embassy
narrative_blocks.body: After Groton, Harvard in 1893 and two years of law at the University of Pennsylvania, Edgar went to Paris in 1898 as Second Secretary of the American Embassy. His son Edgar was born there in January 1899.

narrative_blocks.header: Trumbauer built him Woodburne in 1906
narrative_blocks.body: Edgar had Horace Trumbauer design Woodburne, a summer house built in 1906 on Springfield Road in Darby, on land his father had bought. Trumbauer went on to draw Ardrossan for Robert Montgomery, whose daughter Hope would marry Edgar's son.

narrative_blocks.body: Three years after her husband died in France, Mary bought their son Edgar a 185-foot schooner, the Sagamore, and hired a crew of thirty. She sailed with him and a party of friends and cousins on a two-year voyage around the world, while he kept a diary.

narrative_blocks.header: A sea merchant's daughter, fatherless at four
narrative_blocks.body: Mary's father, Robert Shaw Sturgis, was a Boston export merchant who in 1861 kept a house at Bonchurch in England with six servants. He retired to Philadelphia and died there in April 1876, when Mary was four.

narrative_blocks.header: The railroad king who ran the Union's trains
narrative_blocks.body: In 1861 Tom took charge of the railroads and telegraphs serving the Union armies, and as Assistant Secretary of War he ran the department between Cameron and Stanton. In 1863 Stanton called him back to move two army corps by rail to relieve Rosecrans at Chattanooga.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave young Andrew Carnegie his start
narrative_blocks.body: Tom, a tavern-keeper's son who had left school at ten, hired a teenage telegraph clerk named Andrew Carnegie as his secretary in Pittsburgh. Carnegie later introduced him, on a train to Philadelphia, to his neighbor Anna Riddle, who became Tom's wife.

narrative_blocks.header: He told Lincoln to slip into Washington
narrative_blocks.body: Before the 1861 inauguration Tom was one of the railroad men who arranged Abraham Lincoln's special train through the North. He urged the president-elect to make the run into Washington covertly, out of reach of Confederate spies and assassins.

narrative_blocks.header: A rifle diet for the strikers of 1877
narrative_blocks.body: When Pennsylvania Railroad pay cuts set off the Great Railroad Strike of 1877, Pittsburgh saw the worst rioting in the country and the company's depot was burned. Tom said the strikers should be given a rifle diet for a few days, to see how they liked that kind of bread.

narrative_blocks.header: His railroad and the Compromise of 1877
narrative_blocks.body: Tom wanted federal money for his Texas and Pacific line to California, and courted Southern Democrats in Congress to get it. His plan was folded into the Compromise of 1877, which settled the disputed presidency for Rutherford Hayes and ended Reconstruction, but the subsidy never came.

narrative_blocks.header: His nephew struck California's first gusher
narrative_blocks.body: Tom put money into the oil seeps around Ojai, California, that Benjamin Silliman had noted, and sent his nephew Thomas Bard out to drill them. In 1867 Bard brought in the state's first gusher.

narrative_blocks.header: Andrew Carnegie introduced them on a train
narrative_blocks.body: Anna Riddle met Tom Scott about 1860 on a train between Pittsburgh and Philadelphia, and Andrew Carnegie made the introduction. She was Carnegie's neighbor in Pittsburgh, and Tom was his boss.

narrative_blocks.header: A Penn chair of mathematics in his name
narrative_blocks.body: After her husband died in 1881, Anna endowed a professorship of mathematics and a fellowship in hygiene at the University of Pennsylvania in his name, with beds for the chronically ill at its hospital.

narrative_blocks.body: A Wharton graduate and Army engineer, O'Malley joined Montgomery Scott in 1967 and became senior vice president of the merged Janney Montgomery Scott. From 1971 until his death he was a trustee of Ardrossan.

narrative_blocks.header: A cyclist and Shakespearean in equal measure
narrative_blocks.body: Beyond finance he was a literary man and treasurer of the Shakespeare Society, an avid cyclist who toured Morocco and Vietnam. He served on the boards of the Magee and Episcopal hospitals.

marriages.notes: Old St. David's Church

narrative_blocks.header: The 503rd, from Panama to Corregidor
narrative_blocks.body: Sidney went into the Army at Camp Croft, South Carolina, five days after Pearl Harbor, at thirty. He served a year in Panama, then fought with H Company of the 503rd Parachute Regimental Combat Team, and was wounded on Corregidor.

narrative_blocks.header: Silver Star, then killed on Negros
narrative_blocks.body: Sidney won the Silver Star, and a Purple Heart for wounds taken at Silay, on Negros, on 12 April 1945. He was killed on Negros on 11 May 1945, at thirty-three, and lies in the Manila American Cemetery.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at Old St. David's in 1943
narrative_blocks.body: Sidney married Sophia Morris at Old St. David's Church in Radnor on 21 October 1943. Nineteen months later he was dead.

narrative_blocks.header: His father was a West Point gunner
narrative_blocks.body: His father, Capt. Sidney Frederick Tyler Brock, West Point 1906, served as a captain in the 310th Field Artillery in France in the First World War.

narrative_blocks.header: She went to Tito for the World Bank
narrative_blocks.body: In 1948 Sophia, assistant to a vice-president of the World Bank, went to Yugoslavia with the survey team that opened talks with Tito on loans to rebuild his shattered economy, one of the first women to negotiate for it in the Eastern Bloc.

narrative_blocks.header: She opened Turkey's first development bank
narrative_blocks.body: After her first husband, Lt. Sidney Brock, was killed on Negros in 1945, Sophia went to Washington as an aide in the U.S. Senate, then took a similar post at the World Bank. In 1949 it sent her to Turkey to open the country's first development bank.

narrative_blocks.header: Married and buried at Old St. David's
narrative_blocks.body: Sophia married Sidney Brock at Old St. David's Church in Radnor in October 1943, and was buried in its churchyard forty-one years later.

narrative_blocks.header: Paris, Rome and Florence with Edward Bayne
narrative_blocks.body: In 1951 Sophia married Edward Ashley Bayne, then an economist rebuilding Europe's industries under the Marshall Plan. They lived in Paris, then twelve years in Rome and Florence, and divorced in 1965.

narrative_blocks.header: Craig Koelle, her third husband
narrative_blocks.body: Her third husband, Craig G. Koelle, headed an international firm of architects and engineers. He died in 1975, and she kept his name for her last nine years.

narrative_blocks.header: Her daughter married a Boorstin
narrative_blocks.body: Sophia's daughter, Josephine Bayne, married David Boorstin, son of the Librarian of Congress Daniel J. Boorstin, in October 1984, six months after Sophia died.

narrative_blocks.header: Dead at thirty-one, her widower died in London
narrative_blocks.body: She died at thirty-one in Philadelphia, far from the Hartford family she was born into. Her husband Cyprian Beach outlived her by twenty-seven years and died in London.

narrative_blocks.header: Repairing flood-wrecked track, he worked himself to death
narrative_blocks.body: As supervisor of the Erie Railroad's Tioga division, Bryan led crews repairing track after a cloudburst, laboring long in the water. Weeks later his strained heart gave out and he died suddenly at forty-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: He sold a produce business for oil
narrative_blocks.body: William started as a Philadelphia grocery clerk, failed in lumber, and in 1853 went into produce with Peter Sayboldt, soon buying him out. At the outbreak of the Civil War he sold up, and in 1863 he went to the Pennsylvania oil regions to sink wells.

narrative_blocks.header: Gasoline before the world wanted it
narrative_blocks.body: William built refineries in Philadelphia until he controlled the city's oil refining, and his Monument Oil Works was one of the first to make gasoline, turning out twenty thousand barrels a month. He sold half the business to Standard Oil in 1876 and the rest in 1880, and stayed a major shareholder.

narrative_blocks.header: Streetcars in six cities with Peter Widener
narrative_blocks.body: From 1873 William and his friend Peter Widener bought up Philadelphia's street railways and merged them, company by company, into the Philadelphia Rapid Transit Company, then did the same in New York, Chicago, Baltimore, Saint Louis and Pittsburgh. His United Gas Improvement Company lit Philadelphia and some sixty other cities.

narrative_blocks.header: Elstowe Manor and its 132 paintings
narrative_blocks.body: In 1898 Horace Trumbauer built him the 45-room Elstowe Manor at Elkins Park, with Chelten House beside it for his son George. William hung it with 132 paintings, from Raphael and Rembrandt to Monet and Manet, and left the collection to Philadelphia after the death of his last heir.

narrative_blocks.header: Council, colonel and two world fairs
narrative_blocks.body: William sat one year on the Philadelphia city council, in 1876, served Governor John Hartranft as aide-de-camp with the rank of colonel, and represented the city at the expositions of Vienna in 1873 and Paris in 1900.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Tyler marriages in the family
narrative_blocks.body: In 1888 his daughter Ida married Sidney Frederick Tyler, a widowed banker. Seventeen years later his granddaughter Stella married Sidney's son George, tying the Elkins and Tyler fortunes together twice.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter gave Harvard its library
narrative_blocks.body: His daughter Eleanor married George Widener, son of his streetcar partner, and lost her husband and her son Harry when the Titanic sank in 1912. In Harry's memory she gave Harvard the Widener Library.

narrative_blocks.header: From his father's office to coal tar
narrative_blocks.body: George went to work in his father's firm at eighteen, was treasurer of the Elkins Manufacturing and Gas Company by 1880, and in 1883 joined the Ehret firm of coal-tar makers. He became president of its successor, the Barrett Manufacturing Company, and retired from business in 1904, at forty-six.

narrative_blocks.header: Chelten House at Elkins Park
narrative_blocks.body: George raised his family at Chelten House, the manor Horace Trumbauer built for him in 1898 beside his father's Elstowe Manor at Elkins Park. He married Stella McIntire of Dayton in 1881, and after her death married Allethaire Ludlow in 1917.

narrative_blocks.header: Stricken after eleven holes
narrative_blocks.body: On 22 October 1919, playing a foursome at the Philadelphia Country Club, George had played eleven holes and was raising his club when he fell with an apoplectic seizure. He died the next day, too ill to be moved to Folly Farm, the Abington country place where he had spent most of his time since his second marriage.
