narrative_blocks.header: Orphaned young, raised by a childless uncle
narrative_blocks.body: His father Leonard died when Henry was a boy, and his uncle David King — childless himself — adopted Henry and his brother. The King name passed sideways through the family.

narrative_blocks.header: From college treasurer to a frontier Indian agency
narrative_blocks.body: He kept the books for Hillsdale College and a Michigan bank, then took a federal post as Indian agent at Leech Lake, Minnesota. He served on that northern frontier until the family settled in Oberlin in 1884.

narrative_blocks.body: Widowed young when her first husband died at thirty, Myra married twice more and followed the frontier from Michigan to Denver to Pasadena. Two of her three husbands were Civil War veterans.

narrative_blocks.header: No one has led Oberlin longer
narrative_blocks.body: From 1902 to 1927 King served as Oberlin's president, a twenty-five-year tenure no successor has matched. He had risen there from mathematics tutor to dean.

narrative_blocks.header: Wilson sent him to redraw the Ottoman map
narrative_blocks.body: In June 1919 Wilson sent King and Charles Crane to ask the people of Syria and Palestine what they wanted, and from Jaffa to Aleppo they met 442 delegations and gathered 1,863 petitions. Their report warned against the mandates, and it was kept secret until 1922, after the Treaty of Sèvres had divided the region anyway; France made King a chevalier of the Legion of Honor for the work.

narrative_blocks.header: A mathematician who became a national churchman
narrative_blocks.body: Trained first in mathematics, King turned to theology and philosophy and wrote widely read books on rational faith. He moderated the National Council of Congregational Churches and chaired its education foundation.

narrative_blocks.header: His Oberlin home was the college's social heart
narrative_blocks.body: He bought the old Burrell house on East College Street and made it the center of his presidency. From public readings to New Year's open houses, the Kings drew students and town into their home.

narrative_blocks.body: Ordained a Congregational minister, Philip served as a Navy chaplain aboard the USS Pittsburgh through the end of the First World War. A decade of pulpits later, he became president of Washburn College in Kansas.

narrative_blocks.header: The president's son took three Oberlin degrees
narrative_blocks.body: Son of Oberlin's president, Philip earned three degrees at his father's college before studying theology in New York. His career ran through Congregational pulpits and college administration.

narrative_blocks.header: Miami's books doubled under his thirty-four years
narrative_blocks.body: Edgar King ran Miami University's library from 1922 until 1956, the longest tenure in its history. The collection doubled under his care, and the campus library now bears his name.

narrative_blocks.body: He was born in Berlin in 1893, where his father was pursuing theology before the Oberlin presidency. The family soon returned to Ohio, where Edgar built his life in libraries.

narrative_blocks.header: From North Lyme to frontier Arizona medicine
narrative_blocks.body: George left Connecticut for territorial Arizona and became one of its pioneer physicians, for many years heading the staff of St. Joseph’s Hospital in Phoenix. ANCESTRY RESOLVED (FindAGrave chain): son of Grindal Rawson Sr. (1762-1788, b. Milford MA, died when Grindall Jr. was an infant) < Nathaniel Rawson Jr. (1716-1803, Braintree-born, Rev. War veteran, d. West Stockbridge) < Nathaniel Rawson I (1689-1731, b. Mendon) < William Rawson (1651-1726) and Anne Glover. William was the BROTHER of Rev. Grindal Rawson of Mendon — so Grindall Jr. descends from Colonial Secretary Edward Rawson through William’s line, NOT through Rev. Grindal’s marriage to Susanna Wilson. No Hooker blood; classification stands. The given name came down a collateral line honoring the Mendon pastor. Sister Rhoda Rawson Prince (1785-1856) noted, not built (sibling of spouse).

narrative_blocks.header: Six guns, twelve men, one British prize
narrative_blocks.body: Commissioned in May 1781, Timothy captained the privateer sloop Hamlin — six guns and twelve men, several of them Starr kin — for its owner, a colonel in the family’s Middletown merchant network. That July he took the British brigantine Agnes.

narrative_blocks.header: Five-seven, slender, dark, wears a wig
narrative_blocks.body: His privateer commission describes him: about fifty years old, five feet seven inches, dark complexion, rather slender, and wears a wig. A captain from his youth, he left the sea for the merchant’s counter after his first wife died while he was away on a voyage.

people.research_notes: Starr family history: “remarkably neat and particular in his habits and personal appearance.” His second wife Abigail was the widow of Capt. Christopher Hamlin — the privateer he later commanded bore the Hamlin name (origin of the name undocumented). A 1762 diary of a Starr voyage to Cuba aboard a British man-of-war (Journal of American History, vol. 3, 1909, pp. 113ff) may be his — unverified. Crew of the Hamlin included John, Justus (his son), Elihu, and Nathaniel Starr. Sources: A History of the Starr Family of New England (Burgis Pratt Starr); Maritime CT during the Revolution, Vol. 2, pp. 104-105; 1970s Middletown kinship thesis.

people.research_notes: EASTER EGG: father of James Pierpont, Yale’s principal founder, who married Mary Hooker. b. 1617 or 1619, London (gravestone "Aetatis suae 65" supports ~1617). Settled c. 1640; 1648 deed of Roxbury land from father-in-law John Stow; bought the Prichard fifty acres 1657; licensed a fulling-mill 1658. Family-book claim that his 1656 Dorchester purchase was named for his cousin the Marquis of Dorchester is chronologically doubtful (the town predates the 1645 marquisate) — recorded as tradition only. Gravestone at Eliot Burying Ground still legible. Children NOT built per easter-egg rule.

narrative_blocks.header: He fortified his mills in Philip’s War
narrative_blocks.body: During King Philip’s War in 1675-6, John fortified his Roxbury homestead, “where were malting and mills for grinding and fulling, God having blessed him with a considerable estate.” The tide-mill’s foundation timbers were still visible two centuries later.

narrative_blocks.header: A son who carried Roxbury to Carolina
narrative_blocks.body: His son Benjamin led a company from Roxbury in 1691 to found an independent church in South Carolina, and died in the ministry at Charleston — while James, the son who stayed, founded a college in Connecticut.

people.research_notes: Youngest child of John Whittelsey of Saybrook. Declined two war chaplaincies (Port Royal 1710; Canada 1711). Leader of the Old Light party after the Great Awakening; prominent in the discipline of Rev. Philemon Robbins of Branford. Published four sermons. Probate inventory: ~£22,000 estate, about £100 in books and fourteen times that amount in enslaved servants.

narrative_blocks.header: Wallingford built a house to get him
narrative_blocks.body: The town's 1709 offer ran to land, firewood, and a two-story house forty-two feet long, at a salary climbing to a hundred pounds a year — paid in wheat, rye, Indian corn and pork. He supplied the glass and nails.

narrative_blocks.header: He preached the sermon at his ordination
narrative_blocks.body: Installed as colleague pastor at Wallingford in May 1710, he took 2 Corinthians iv:7 as his text and preached the ordination sermon himself. He never held another pulpit.

narrative_blocks.header: Connecticut sent him to Nova Scotia
narrative_blocks.body: Three months after his installation the General Assembly named him chaplain of the colony's forces on the expedition against Port Royal. Offered the post a second time in 1711, he declined it.

narrative_blocks.header: He led the Old Lights against the revival
narrative_blocks.body: When the Great Awakening split Connecticut's churches he headed the party opposing it. He gave the 1731 election sermon, preached that year at Boston's First Church, and preached at his son Samuel's ordination in 1737.

narrative_blocks.header: "One of the greatest men in Connecticut"
narrative_blocks.body: So Dr. Charles Chauncy of Boston judged him. Ezra Stiles, who wrote the obituary, praised an engaging elocution and a reserve that let him take an insult without returning one.

narrative_blocks.header: A hundred pounds in books, more in people
narrative_blocks.body: His probate inventory showed an estate near twenty-two thousand pounds — a scant hundred of it in books, and fourteen times that in enslaved and mulatto servants.

narrative_blocks.header: A mortification in his legs took him slowly
narrative_blocks.body: A mortification in his legs and feet wore him down through a long final illness. He died on 15 April 1752, a month short of completing the forty-second year of his ministry at Wallingford.

narrative_blocks.header: The governor's horse knew her door
narrative_blocks.body: The governor dined at the parsonage so often on his way to the New Haven legislature that his horse would not pass it unwhipped. After her husband died he rode by without stopping, and she never forgave it.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept the store the whole town used
narrative_blocks.body: She kept a store of goods for the benefit of the parish, which in Wallingford then meant every inhabitant of the town. Her house stayed the local seat of hospitality for fifteen years after she was widowed.

narrative_blocks.header: Her hospitality ran on enslaved labor
narrative_blocks.body: The estate her husband left in 1752 held fourteen times more value in enslaved and mulatto servants than in books. She kept the parsonage open to the colony's governors for fifteen years after, on that labor.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father was dead before she turned three
narrative_blocks.body: Rev. Nathaniel Chauncy of Hatfield died in November 1685. Her childhood was spent with her mother in Deacon Medad Pomroy's household at Northampton, and part of her girlhood with her uncle, Rev. Israel Chauncy of Stratford.

narrative_blocks.header: She named two daughters Sarah and buried both
narrative_blocks.body: The first Sarah was born in 1720 and died at five. The second, born in 1726, lived to fifteen. Six of her eight children outlived her.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandson entered Yale at eleven
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel Whittlesey Dana, son of her daughter Katherine, matriculated at eleven and graduated at fifteen. He sat in Congress from 1797, and as senator was one of thirteen who voted against war with Britain in 1812.

people.research_notes: USNA appointed 1885, commissioned Ensign 1891; Rear Admiral Dec 31, 1921; retired July 1, 1933 after 48 years. Executive Officer of USS Mayflower (the presidential yacht) 1905-06; aboard USS Delaware at George V’s coronation 1911; commanded USS Arizona briefly 1921. Court-martialed 1917 after USS Louisiana struck a submerged wreck — found “guilty but without culpability,” read as acquittal by Secretary Daniels. Decorated by Japan: Order of the Sacred Treasure, Third Class. Governor, Army and Navy Club. Interment May 14, 1938; burial location not in source set.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried an army past the U-boats
narrative_blocks.body: Commanding the giant transports Great Northern and Leviathan through waters “infested with enemy submarines and mines,” Phelps ferried troops to Europe and home again, and was awarded the Navy Cross for it.

narrative_blocks.header: “Guilty but without culpability”
narrative_blocks.body: When the cruiser Louisiana struck a submerged wreck under his command in early 1917, Phelps was tried for culpable negligence and lost ten numbers — but the court’s odd verdict, “guilty but without culpability,” was treated by Navy Secretary Daniels as tantamount to acquittal. It was the only serious mark in forty-eight years of service.

narrative_blocks.header: From the President’s yacht to the Yangtze
narrative_blocks.body: His forty-eight Navy years ran from executive officer of Theodore Roosevelt’s yacht Mayflower to command of the Yangtze Patrol in China, where Japan decorated him with the Order of the Sacred Treasure.

narrative_blocks.header: Winthrop Ames came to Cape Cod for her
narrative_blocks.body: In 1928 Eleanor played summer stock on Cape Cod with the University Players, Henry Fonda and Joshua Logan among them. Winthrop Ames came up to watch her rehearse and hired her for George Arliss's Merchant of Venice tour.

narrative_blocks.header: From Baltimore to the Count’s island
narrative_blocks.body: The judge’s granddaughter played Princess Haydee opposite Robert Donat in the 1934 Count of Monte Cristo — the role she would be best remembered for, in a stage and screen career that ran nearly five decades.

narrative_blocks.header: Her last bow was Mrs. Higgins
narrative_blocks.body: Forty-seven years after her 1929 Broadway debut, Eleanor closed her stage career in the 1976-77 revival of My Fair Lady, playing both Mrs. Eynsford-Hill and Mrs. Higgins.

narrative_blocks.header: Radio's Dr. Susan, and The Secret Storm
narrative_blocks.body: Eleanor thought some of the best acting was in soap operas. She starred in CBS radio's Life and Love of Dr. Susan from 1939, and played the rich Grace Tyrrell on The Secret Storm from 1970 to 1973.

narrative_blocks.header: George Arliss tried to discourage her
narrative_blocks.body: Eleanor's father opposed the stage. Her mother took her to meet George Arliss at Beekman Place, and he tried to discourage her too. She went to Vassar instead and studied theatre under Hallie Flanagan.

narrative_blocks.header: A Hershey commercial with a cow
narrative_blocks.body: Eleanor once made a Hershey commercial as an elegant lady stepping into an elevator with a cow. She loved Latin America and wore its bright colors and Aztec designs.

narrative_blocks.header: Two marriages and one daughter
narrative_blocks.body: Eleanor's marriage to the actor Alden Chase was annulled in 1935. With her second husband, the Danish chemical engineer Halfdan Hebo, she had one daughter, Lisa, born in 1940.

narrative_blocks.header: Highpockets of the 1st Battalion, 5th Marines
narrative_blocks.body: From November 1966 to September 1967 Peter commanded the 1st Battalion, 5th Marines, one of the longest battalion commands of the Vietnam War. Six foot six, he was Highpockets to his Marines and the Dragon to his officers.

narrative_blocks.header: A Silver Star for Operation Swift
narrative_blocks.body: Peter won the Silver Star for gallantry in Operation Swift, and his battalion took two Presidential Unit Citations. In Korea he had won a Bronze Star as an artillery forward observer.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote Highpocket's War Stories
narrative_blocks.body: Peter wrote an autobiography, Highpocket's War Stories, and a cowboy story, Buckshot and the Boy. His article on Sergeant Hillous York won the Marine Corps Gazette's combat initiative award in 2004.

narrative_blocks.header: The memorial at Great Falls
narrative_blocks.body: After September 2001 Peter led the committee that built the Great Falls Memorial beside the town library, now the center of the town's patriotic events.

narrative_blocks.header: Annapolis, then Legg Mason
narrative_blocks.body: Peter enlisted in the Marines out of St. George's School in 1945, took a fleet appointment to Annapolis and graduated in 1951. He retired a colonel in 1972 and became a vice president at Legg Mason.

narrative_blocks.header: Uncle Pete to his brother's children
narrative_blocks.body: Peter was uncle, and something like a grandfather, to the five children of his brother Fielding, who died in 1980.

narrative_blocks.header: He took Jacqueline Bouvier to a dance
narrative_blocks.body: At St. George's, Peter asked a friend's sister, Jacqueline Bouvier, to a dance, and did not try to kiss her in the cab home: “she might rebuff me, and with the taxi driver as witness, my humiliation would be complete.”

narrative_blocks.header: An insurance man who ran City Hall
narrative_blocks.body: Hooker built a fire-and-liability insurance agency, Hooker & Penrose, before politics pulled him in. He chaired the banking committee in the state House, then won the mayor's office in 1908, respected across party lines for an alertness and shrewd sense that colleagues remarked on.

narrative_blocks.header: He died suddenly at his summer place
narrative_blocks.body: After two years as mayor and a defeat at the next election, Hooker went on to the state senate. He died without warning of chest pain one September afternoon in 1915, at his summer home on Eastern Point, only forty-nine, and was entombed at Cedar Hill in Hartford.

narrative_blocks.header: Major of the veteran battalion, Foot Guard quartermaster
narrative_blocks.body: Beyond business and politics, Hooker kept a long militia life — a major of the Veteran Battalion by 1905, and captain and quartermaster in Connecticut's ceremonial Governor's Foot Guard. He had come up through the Hartford City Guards as a young man.

notable.notable_blurb: One of the first women in Connecticut's legislature

narrative_blocks.header: Her first House speech was about smoking
narrative_blocks.body: On the first day of the 1921 session she became the first woman to speak on the Connecticut House floor, and she used it to tell the men to keep smoking as if no women were present. The chamber had been agonizing over whether to ban tobacco now that women had seats.

narrative_blocks.header: She arrived the first year women could
narrative_blocks.body: Elected in 1920, the first year Connecticut women could run for state office, she was one of just five women in the entire General Assembly. She took her seat in the first session held after the Nineteenth Amendment.

narrative_blocks.header: The suffrage opponent who changed her mind
narrative_blocks.body: She had opposed votes for women until a seat on the Hartford Board of Education changed her thinking. To go on opposing the ballot, she decided, would be not only inconsistent but wrong.

narrative_blocks.header: She finished the term her husband left
narrative_blocks.body: When her husband died in 1915 she was named to complete his unexpired term on the Hartford Board of Education, the one office Connecticut women could already hold. Three years later she won the seat in her own right, and her political life began.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife’s mother gave it to the Atheneum
narrative_blocks.body: He painted The Leaning Tree at Point Lobos during his California years. Mrs Edward W. Hooker — Mary Mather Turner Hooker, his wife's mother — gave it to the Wadsworth Atheneum in 1917, two years after her husband died.

narrative_blocks.header: Best man at her wedding, then her husband
narrative_blocks.body: Rosalie Hooker married his cousin William Welling in 1911 with Dixon standing as best man. Four years later she divorced, and married Dixon at Salinas in August 1915.

narrative_blocks.header: He studied under Robert Henri
narrative_blocks.body: Training came under Frank DuMond, Robert Henri, and Charles Hawthorne — the Ashcan master among his teachers. A senator's grandson, he painted landscapes instead of politics.

narrative_blocks.header: The War Department hired him to sing
narrative_blocks.body: Through the First World War he worked out of New York as an Army and Navy song leader for the War Department. He went on singing for the painters at the Salmagundi Club for fifty years.

narrative_blocks.header: He drew motorcars before he painted coasts
narrative_blocks.body: In 1902 he was one of three draftsmen illustrating James Homans's treatise on self-propelled vehicles, a practical manual on the construction and management of every form of automobile.

narrative_blocks.header: A Paris divorce, then a prince
narrative_blocks.body: Rosalie won a Paris divorce in 1925 on the ground of abandonment. The next year she married Prince Levan Melikov de Somhetie, whose family had once ruled in Georgia; Dixon married Emilie McMillan in 1929.

narrative_blocks.header: A Silver Star over the Pacific
narrative_blocks.body: Edward left Yale in 1942 for the Navy and flew fighters in the Pacific, coming home a lieutenant junior grade in the Naval Reserve with the Silver Star.

narrative_blocks.header: A seat on the Stock Exchange
narrative_blocks.body: After the war Edward became a stockbroker with E. F. Hutton & Co. and held a seat on the New York Stock Exchange. He had just sold it when he died of a heart attack at home on Park Avenue in March 1967, at forty-three.

narrative_blocks.header: The FBI asked him about George
narrative_blocks.body: His mother’s remarriage made Edward stepson to Dmitri von Mohrenschildt — and step-nephew to Dmitri’s brother George, later famous as Lee Harvey Oswald’s closest friend. Vetted by investigators in 1957, Edward judged George “normal mentally and physically” but unable to respect a confidence, and declined to recommend him for work touching national security.

narrative_blocks.header: He priced the Great War’s risks
narrative_blocks.body: In 1917 the Secretary of the Treasury named Woodward to the committee of actuaries advising on war risk insurance — the mathematics behind insuring two million soldiers. He had been president of the Casualty Actuarial Society before he was thirty-seven.

narrative_blocks.header: Actuary to two states, then his own firm
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph left Harvard Law after a year for actuarial work: the Travelers, then the Connecticut and New York insurance departments, then in 1922 his own consulting firm, Woodward, Fondiller & Ryan. In 1927 he joined the board of the Union Labor Life Insurance Company, founded by the labor movement.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother died seven months after his birth
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph was born in Hartford in March 1882, and his mother, Mary Williams Hooker Woodward, died that October at thirty. He died of pneumonia in New York in 1928, at forty-six, leaving four children.

narrative_blocks.body: At forty-five Elspeth joined the first class of Yale's new Department of Drama, in 1927, and the next spring was widowed with four children. She raised them while becoming a published novelist and playwright.

narrative_blocks.body: Joseph took his medical degree at Columbia's College of Physicians and Surgeons in 1935, interned at Lawrence and Memorial Hospitals in New London and rose to senior surgeon there. He was a diplomate of the National Board of Medical Examiners.

narrative_blocks.header: Navy Medical Corps, then the Cancer Society
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph served in the Navy Medical Corps from 1943 to 1946, and afterward led the New London branch of the Connecticut Cancer Society. He died in 1976 at Edge Lea, his house in the South Lyme section of Old Lyme.

narrative_blocks.header: Two thousand children a year on skis
narrative_blocks.body: Hooker directed the Otis Ridge Junior Ski Camp in the Berkshires, the first overnight ski camp for juniors, teaching skills and etiquette to about two thousand children a year; it won national recognition. She was still winning giant slalom trophies in her late seventies, and skiing at ninety.

narrative_blocks.header: A honeymoon skiing in Chile
narrative_blocks.body: Hooker married the writer William David Judson Jr. in January 1936, and they sailed by banana boat to Chile for two months of skiing, among the first Americans to ski there. At Old Lyme they later edited and published a regional paper, The Connecticut Shore.

narrative_blocks.header: Nose Dive before the lifts
narrative_blocks.body: In the 1930s Hooker and Dave climbed Mt. Mansfield to ski the Nose Dive, before there were lifts, and about 1950 they built the first cabin at the base of Mad River Glen. Summers they sailed a Herreshoff H28 on Long Island Sound and Buzzards Bay.

narrative_blocks.header: She went by Hooker
narrative_blocks.body: All her adult life Mary went by Hooker Judson, for her ancestor Thomas Hooker. After Rosemary Hall and Vassar she worked in NBC Music's copyright division by day, wrote plays by night, and was invited to the Yale Drama School.

narrative_blocks.body: Susie started in public relations at the Miami Herald, supervised at Lizette Food Service in Danbury for five years, then spent more than fifteen as chef and food-service manager at Mystic River Homes, helping her staff send out fifty meals a day until she retired in 2007.

narrative_blocks.body: Susie gave tours of the Eolia mansion as a docent at Harkness Memorial State Park. After Ted died of cancer in 2015 she greeted patients at the Smilow Cancer Hospital care center in Waterford in his honor.

narrative_blocks.body: An Air Force veteran, Ted managed facilities at Heublein in Hartford before starting his own property-management firm on the shore, and was elected Commodore of the Westerly Yacht Club. He fished, clammed, kayaked and golfed.

narrative_blocks.header: Kicking up sand at Esker Point
narrative_blocks.body: Summers, Ted and Susie could be found at the concerts on the beach at Esker Point, kicking up the sand to the music. He died at home in Noank in December 2015, with Susie beside him, and was buried at sea.

narrative_blocks.body: Her daughter Elizabeth married Sidney George Fisher, whose Philadelphia diary was published a century later as an unsparing record of the city's gentry. narrative_blocks.header: The younger sister married first, at twenty
narrative_blocks.body: Her 1804 marriage to Charles Jared Ingersoll was the first of two matches between the families; nine years later her elder sister Ann married his younger brother Joseph Reed. Both women were granddaughters of Pennsylvania's colonial chief justice.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived her husband by fifteen weeks
narrative_blocks.body: They married in October 1804 and were still married when he died in May 1862. She followed him that August, in the same city. Nine children came between.

Son of Rev. Thomas Ruggles Sr. (X01929); son of Sarah Fisk (first wife). Pastor of Guilford’s First Church; first known owner of Cuff. Had no sons; his daughter Sarah carried the line to the Pynchons. Wife identified Stage 6Y-671: Rebecca Hart (X01906), daughter of Rev. John Hart by his FIRST wife Rebecca Hubbard — born before Hart married Mary Hooker Hart (H00105). The Pynchon chain therefore descends from Mary Hooker’s stepdaughter: family network, not Hooker blood. Verdict settled. Second daughter Mary Ruggles (1737-1756) noted, not built. He is not an optional entry: his daughter Sarah (X03219) married Joseph, and Sarah's mother is
Rebecca Hart — the stepdaughter of Mary Hooker Hart through whom the whole Pynchon line reaches
this tree. Deleting him would orphan Sarah and cut the documented path. Yale 1723, ordained March 1729, succeeded his father in the Guilford First Church pulpit and
held it until his death in 1770; an Old Light in the New Light years. He wrote a manuscript
history of Guilford, published in 1795 in the Collections of the Massachusetts Historical Society
as "A Sketch of a History of Guilford, in Connecticut". m. Rebecca Hart 25 Sept 1734 at Guilford. ENRICHED 10 Aug 2026 from the material Sam supplied earlier and which had gone unused. Yale 1723;
ordained March 1729; succeeded his father Rev. Thomas Ruggles Sr. as pastor of Guilford First
Church and held it until his death in 1770; an Old Light. His manuscript history of Guilford was
published in 1795 as "A Sketch of a History of Guilford, in Connecticut, from a Manuscript of the
Rev. Thomas Ruggles", Collections of the Massachusetts Historical Society (Samuel Hall, 1795),
182-188. Sources: Dexter, Yale Biographical Sketches; Guilford, Conn. First Congregational Church
records 1717-1843. In that history he wrote of "the Rev. and Learned Mr. John Hart" that he "proved one of the first
Eminence of preachers in his Day" — now carried as a reciprocal CC with I00137. The Guilford pulpit in order: Henry Whitfield 1643, John Higginson 1650-59, Joseph Eliot 1664-94,
Thomas Ruggles Sr. 1695-1728, Thomas Ruggles Jr. 1729-70, Amos Fowler 1757 (assistant) to 1800. ENRICHED FURTHER 10 Aug 2026 from Sam's Guilford church history — Sam's note that these were
"tiny pellet NBs". Ordained 26 March 1729; died 19 Nov 1770 aged sixty-five; fellow of Yale during
the last twenty-four years of his life, so from about 1746. His funeral sermon was preached by
Jonathan Todd, pastor of the Second Church in Guilford, on the Lord's day after his death, from
Numbers xx, 28-29 — "Judgment and Mercy, or Aaron dead and lamented, and Eleazer in his Office" —
and described him as a man of sound understanding, solid judgment, penetrating genius and a very
strong and tenacious memory. THE SCHISM: "Upon the settlement of Mr. Ruggles the younger, an unhappy separation took place
which, only after the lapse of nearly a century, was healed." The seceders took Edmund Ward, a
Guilford native and Yale 1727 then newly licensed, as their candidate and built a meeting house.
After councils and legislative committees failed, they were incorporated as the Fourth Society in
Guilford — with the same territorial limits as the First — by act of the general assembly, May
session 1733. The pulpit succession was surfaced from these notes onto the card 10 Aug 2026, on Sam's point that research_notes is the circular file.

narrative_blocks.header: He followed his father into the same pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: Ordained in March 1729, a year after his father died, he took the Guilford church his father had held since 1695. Between the two of them the Ruggles kept that pulpit for seventy-five years.

narrative_blocks.header: The fifth man in that pulpit since 1643
narrative_blocks.body: The church at Guilford had had four ministers in the eighty-six years before him — Henry Whitfield who gathered it in 1643, John Higginson, Joseph Eliot, and his father. Amos Fowler came in as his colleague in 1757 and carried it on to 1800.

narrative_blocks.header: His settlement split the church for a century
narrative_blocks.body: When he was settled at Guilford in 1729 a large part of the church would not receive him, withdrew, and built their own meeting house under Edmund Ward. Councils and committees of the legislature failed to reconcile them, and in May 1733 they were made the Fourth Society in Guilford. The breach was not healed for nearly a hundred years.

narrative_blocks.header: An Old Light through the Great Awakening
narrative_blocks.body: He held Guilford for forty-one years, across the revivals that split New England, and stood with the Old Lights against them. Rev. Amos Fowler was ordained his assistant in 1757 and took the pulpit at his death.

narrative_blocks.header: A Yale fellow for his last twenty-four years
narrative_blocks.body: He sat on the Yale corporation for the final twenty-four years of his life, as his father had for the last eighteen of his. Between them the Ruggles of Guilford held a seat on that board for forty-two years.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the history of his own town
narrative_blocks.body: He left a manuscript history of Guilford, printed in 1795 — twenty-five years after his death — in the Collections of the Massachusetts Historical Society as A Sketch of a History of Guilford, in Connecticut.

narrative_blocks.header: His funeral sermon called him Aaron
narrative_blocks.body: Jonathan Todd of the Second Church preached over him on the Lord day after his death in November 1770, taking Aaron dead and lamented, and Eleazer in his office for his text. Todd called him a man of penetrating genius and tenacious memory.

narrative_blocks.header: Her maiden name became the family's first name
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah Ruggles married Joseph Pynchon at Guilford in 1759. Their son was christened Thomas Ruggles Pynchon, and the name carried down five generations — to the novelist's father, and to the novelist.

narrative_blocks.header: Cuff appears beside him in the census
narrative_blocks.body: At eighteen Doc Pynchon inherited Cuff under the will’s comfort clause, and the 1790 census of Guilford records them together. Cuff’s own dates were never written down anywhere — the Alderbrook charts and that census line are nearly all that remember him.

narrative_blocks.header: Three of the family gone in three years
narrative_blocks.body: His wife Rebecca died in 1794, he in September 1796 at thirty-six, and their daughter Mira Monimia the same year at four. All three were buried on the Guilford Green, and their stones were moved to Alder Brook in the next century.

people.research_notes: Died in the 1790s per Alderbrook charts. One source gives her given name as Mary rather than Rebecca. Buried on the Guilford Green with her husband and their daughter Mira Monimia; the stones were moved to Alder Brook Cemetery in the 1800s.

narrative_blocks.body: Mary Murdoch was born at Schenectady in 1801, her father out of Stirling in Scotland, and they married in 1819. She outlived him by forty-nine years and died at Hartford.

notable.notable_blurb: President of Trinity College, 1874-1882

people.research_notes: Great-grand-uncle of the novelist Thomas Pynchon (his brother William Lyon’s great-grandson). Resigned the presidency Oct 1882 amid faculty and alumni friction but stayed on at Trinity. Bio years 1823-1904 held year-only pending the Trinity encyclopedia full dates. ADDED 081226: Boston Latin School, then Washington (now Trinity) College from 1837, graduating 1841; tutor in Classics and lecturer in chemistry to 1847; deacon 1848, priest 1849; rector at Stockbridge and Lenox 1849-54; inaugural Scovill Professor of Chemistry from October 1854; college librarian in name 1857-82; Acting Chaplain through much of the Civil War and chaplain of the student Missionary Society; D.D. from St. Stephen's; took public offence at Abner Jackson's election to the presidency in 1867, which Jackson noted in his diary; Brownell Professor from 1888; Acting President again for six months in spring 1896; Professor Emeritus 1902. The sabbatical took him to Paris and Cambridge and on a geological tour of southern France, Italy and Sicily that may have included a night climb of Etna; he brought chemical apparatus home and the Trinity laboratory was remodelled around it. Introduction to Chemical Physics, 1881. Memorial: 'A teacher of science, morals and religion. In his life he exemplified devotion to all, knowing that each revealed the one true God.' Of Hawthorne's Pyncheons he wrote that the family circle was 'an exceedingly small one — probably there are not more than 20 persons in the whole country bearing the name'. Pynchon Family papers 1840-1904 at the Watkinson Library, Trinity College. GRAVITY'S RAINBOW: the novelist Thomas Ruggles Pynchon Jr. is his great-grandnephew through his brother William Lyon; the Slothrops come from their shared ancestor William Pynchon, in America from 1630. [080926] is_notable set false on Sam's instruction; the Trinity encyclopedia URL and notable_blurb are left in place rather than stripped, and the card falls back to bio_blurb 'Ninth president of Trinity College'. His purple Pynchon title line comes from TITLE_ONLY in derive-pynchon-line.mjs and is unaffected.

narrative_blocks.header: He took America’s first sabbatical
narrative_blocks.body: Teaching chemistry at Trinity, Pynchon took one of the first sabbatical leaves in American higher education, studying at Paris and Cambridge — and shipped chemical equipment home from France, forcing a major remodel of the college’s laboratory.

narrative_blocks.header: He broke ground on the new campus
narrative_blocks.body: Elected president in November 1874, Pynchon pushed William Burges’s architectural plan forward incrementally, breaking ground at the Summit Campus on July 1, 1875. The move succeeded; his relationships with faculty and alumni did not, and he resigned in October 1882.

narrative_blocks.header: Hawthorne got two letters of protest
narrative_blocks.body: When The House of the Seven Gables (1851) put a fictional Pyncheon family before the nation, Hawthorne — who “knew of no extant Pynchons” — was surprised to receive two letters of protest. One came from this Pynchon.

narrative_blocks.header: Fanny Kemble judged his music execrable
narrative_blocks.body: At Lenox the actress Fanny Kemble stopped him on the church steps, shook a finger and said his music was execrable — then offered to pay to have the organ sent to Pittsfield and tuned. She became a regular attender, a liberal giver, and his friend.

narrative_blocks.header: The students called him Old Pynch
narrative_blocks.body: He was no favourite. Classes lit large bonfires against him and held votes to record their disagreement with his administration, and in October 1882 he resigned the presidency amid calls that he should. He stayed on as a professor for twenty more years.

narrative_blocks.header: Valedictorian, and second in his class
narrative_blocks.body: He came from Rogers High School at Newport to Trinity, and left in 1890 second in class standing and valedictorian. A Harvard master's followed in 1893, and then several years teaching geology back at Trinity.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave up geology to survey Oyster Bay
narrative_blocks.body: He left the college for Oyster Bay, where he worked as the town's civil engineer and surveyor until he died there in January 1910, forty-two years old. His son Thomas was two.

people.research_notes: Recorded here until 081226 as Caroline Moyses Pynchon; the sources give Carrie Susan Moyses, daughter of Joseph L. Moyses, banker, and Elizabeth A. Woodworth. Married at Oyster Bay 5 September 1896. She outlived her husband by less than eight months, leaving their son Thomas orphaned at three.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote down her husband's life
narrative_blocks.body: Four months after he died she filled in a form about him for a Trinity College biographical directory — his schools, his standing, his work as the town's surveyor. The directory was never published, and her page is most of what is known about him.

narrative_blocks.header: She followed him inside eight months
narrative_blocks.body: She died at Liberty in Sullivan County in August 1910, away from Oyster Bay, less than eight months after her husband. Their son Thomas was three, and lost both parents in one year.

people.research_notes: Industrial surveyor, town supervisor, and local Republican Party official; family moved to Oyster Bay c. 1941.

education.notes: Engineering physics, then English; attended Nabokov’s classes

people.research_notes:

NOT Hooker or Talcott blood — settled Stage 6Y-671: his ancestress Rebecca Hart was Rev. John Hart’s daughter by his first wife, born before Hart married Mary Hooker (H00105). narrative_blocks.header: Two years in the Navy, then V.
narrative_blocks.body: Out of Oyster Bay High School in 1953, Pynchon went to Cornell, served two years in the Navy from 1955, and published his first novel, V., in 1963 — the beginning of one of American fiction’s most private and most celebrated careers.

narrative_blocks.header: Gravity’s Rainbow, then the genius grant
narrative_blocks.body: Gravity’s Rainbow took the National Book Award for Fiction in 1974, and the MacArthur Fellowship followed in 1988. The encyclopedic novelist descends in a straight line from the Guilford Ruggles parsonage — and from the Springfield Pynchons Hawthorne fictionalized.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote manuals for nuclear missiles
narrative_blocks.body: From 1960 to 1962 Pynchon worked at Boeing as a technical writer on the Bomarc and Minuteman nuclear missile programs — then quit, finished V., and never held an ordinary job again. Gravity’s Rainbow’s rockets had a paper trail.

narrative_blocks.header: A paper bag for his son’s sake
narrative_blocks.body: Only about ten public images of Pynchon exist — “‘Recluse’ is a code word generated by journalists,” he said, “meaning ‘doesn’t like to talk to reporters.’” But when his son Jackson loved The Simpsons, Pynchon voiced his own cameo, animated with a paper bag over his head.

narrative_blocks.header: He put the burned book in the novel
narrative_blocks.body: Gravity's Rainbow gives Tyrone Slothrop an ancestor, William Slothrop, who wrote a heretical tract that was condemned and burned in Boston. Pynchon's own earliest American ancestor founded Springfield and had his book burned there in 1650.

Jackson. Wife of the novelist Thomas Pynchon; mother of Jackson Pynchon. Clients include Pynchon, Ron Chernow, Steve Coll, Wole Soyinka, Percival Everett, Lorrie Moore, Richard Powers. notable.notable_blurb: Literary agent to Pynchon and DeLillo

narrative_blocks.header: She represents the author no one can find
narrative_blocks.body: Melanie Jackson founded the Melanie Jackson Agency, representing a distinguished roster of authors including Nobel laureate Wole Soyinka, Pulitzer winners Ron Chernow and Steve Coll, and novelist Percival Everett. Her most famous client is the reclusive Thomas Pynchon.

narrative_blocks.header: Her most elusive client became her husband
narrative_blocks.body: Jackson began representing Thomas Pynchon in the 1980s, after the famously private novelist left his longtime agent. The two married in 1990 and have guarded their privacy ever since.

people.research_notes: LIVING — limited public bio per compiler. Son of Thomas Pynchon and Melanie Jackson; Hooker descendant through his mother’s Roosevelt line (Edith Kermit Carow). Paternal Hooker-blood question settled (Stage 6Y-671): the Pynchon line runs through Mary Hooker’s stepdaughter Rebecca Hart — network, not blood. His sole Hooker descent is maternal, through the Roosevelt-Carow line.

narrative_blocks.header: He found his father’s archive a home
narrative_blocks.body: Jackson compiled and represented the Pynchon archive in its placement at The Huntington — drawn, he said, to its aerospace and mathematics holdings and “extraordinary map collection.” The famously private novelist’s papers now sit beside rocket history.

people.research_notes: Sister of Mary Chew Wilcocks Ingersoll (X03217). Also a daughter of Alexander Wilcocks and Mary Chew Wilcocks — parentage noted, not wired, per compiler single-connection-to-Mary rule.

narrative_blocks.header: Her sister Mary married first, by nine years
narrative_blocks.body: Mary married Charles Jared Ingersoll in 1804. Ann, three years older, married his younger brother Joseph Reed in September 1813, at thirty-two. Two Wilcocks daughters and two Ingersoll sons, paired across a decade and crossed by age.

narrative_blocks.header: At twenty she inherited frontier acres
narrative_blocks.body: When Alexander Wilcocks died in 1801, six thousand acres in Somerset and Fayette Counties passed to five of his children, Ann among them — land he and her grandfather Benjamin Chew, chief justice of colonial Pennsylvania, had acquired from the Penn family during the Revolution. She never saw any of it. Her heirs sold it in the Panic of 1837, six years after her death.

narrative_blocks.header: None of her three children reached thirty
narrative_blocks.body: She and Joseph Reed Ingersoll had two sons and a daughter. James died at six and Joseph at two; the daughter, Mary Wilcocks Ingersoll, died unmarried in 1842, eleven years after her mother. He outlived them all and left no descendants.

bio.bio_blurb: Philadelphia lawyer, judge, and city recorder

people.research_notes: m. May 18, 1768, Mary Chew, daughter of Benjamin Chew (1722-1810), Chief Justice of Pennsylvania. Children include Benjamin Chew Wilcocks (1776-1845, US Consul at Canton, China), Elizabeth, Samuel, Ann (m. Joseph Reed Ingersoll), and Mary (m. Charles Jared Ingersoll) — siblings mentioned per compiler rule, not built. Buried St. Peter’s Episcopal Churchyard, Philadelphia.

narrative_blocks.header: Both his daughters married Ingersoll brothers
narrative_blocks.body: In 1768 he married Mary Chew, whose father was chief justice of the colony and lawyer to the Penns. Two of their daughters married two sons of Jared Ingersoll, who signed the Constitution. The Chew name and money went with them.

narrative_blocks.header: Patriot committeeman, then city recorder
narrative_blocks.body: He sat on Philadelphia's Committee of Safety while the Revolution was still a hanging offense. Afterward the city made him Recorder, keeper of the deed books everyone's property rested on.

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve thousand acres he never saw
narrative_blocks.body: Forty-three frontier tracts, held with his father-in-law — Death of the Fawn, White's Little Mill Seat, Hunting Lot. Agents worked them, two hundred and forty miles from his door. He may never have laid eyes on one.

narrative_blocks.header: Chew was arrested for treason; Wilcocks was not
narrative_blocks.body: In 1777 Wilcocks sat on the Committee of Safety for the Revolution. That same year his father-in-law and law partner was seized for treason, paroled to a New Jersey ironworks, and shelled out of his Germantown house.

narrative_blocks.header: Elected to govern the college that taught him
narrative_blocks.body: He took his degree from the College of Philadelphia in 1761 and was elected one of its trustees eighteen years later. The Philosophical Society had already taken him in at twenty-seven.

narrative_blocks.header: His son rang bells from Canton
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin Chew Wilcocks went out to China and came home rich enough to hang eight great bells in St. Peter's. His parents lie in the churchyard beneath them.

bio.bio_blurb: Daughter of Pennsylvania's colonial chief justice

people.research_notes: Daughter of Benjamin Chew (1722-1810), Chief Justice of the Pennsylvania Supreme Court (mentioned per compiler sibling/ancestor rule, not built). Of his daughters’ social standing it was said it was “social suicide” not to know them. Ruled out as a cross-connection: Benjamin Chew Wilcocks (son of X03237/X03238, not a tree entry) pioneered the American opium trade from Turkey and British India and left Canton in 1827; Samuel Russell (HD1371) reached Canton 1819 and led the trade by the 1830s. Real documented parallel, but it runs through a non-entry, so no CC is legal. Do not re-investigate.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father helped draw the Mason-Dixon line
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin Chew spent eighteen years arguing the Penns' boundary against the Baltimores. The line was finally run in 1768 — the year she married. He was chief justice of the colony, and later arrested for treason.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father sold the boy Richard Allen
narrative_blocks.body: Richard Allen was born enslaved on Chew's Delaware estate in 1760. In 1768 Chew sold the eight-year-old and his whole family to a neighbor. Allen went on to found the first Black denomination in America.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son was called the high devil
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin Chew Wilcocks was very tall, and the Chinese named him for it. He spent thirty years at Canton, selling silk, porcelain, and opium.

narrative_blocks.header: A forgiven debt unsettled her son's mind
narrative_blocks.body: He owed the Hong merchant Houqua seventy-two thousand dollars. Houqua tore up the debt so he could sail home rich, and his partner said the kindness broke something in him. He spent twelve years indoors.

narrative_blocks.header: She saw neither daughter marry an Ingersoll
narrative_blocks.body: She died in 1794, at forty-seven. Ten years later Mary married Charles Jared Ingersoll; nine years after that, Ann married his brother Joseph.

people.research_notes: Grandson of Anna Elsie (Outhouse) Smith Caldwell; buried Norfolk County, Ontario; parentage not yet traced. Stub per compiler.

narrative_blocks.header: She spun the first communion linen
narrative_blocks.body: The first communion linen of St. Paul’s, spun and woven by Sarah Marshall’s own hands, is still kept at the Marshall home in Woodbury — beside the chair in which, tradition says, every Bishop of Connecticut from Seabury down has sat.

career.organization: Society for the Propagation of the Gospel

people.research_notes: NOTABLE per compiler ruling (Litchfield Magazine URL). Birth June 22 (FAG) vs. June 14 (correspondent note) — FAG retained. Five children noted (Susannah built; Rukard Burke, Anna Maria Susanna Moseley, John Panet, Elsie Rutgers Phelps not built). Raised Dutch Reformed in New York; prepared for ministry under Dr. Johnson; ordained Deacon by the Bishop of London July 25, 1771, and Priest July 28 — the last but one Connecticut candidate to cross the ocean for Holy Orders. NINE children (per Glebe House Museum; earlier FAG note of five corrected) — Susannah and Hermanus built. The Glebe House household 1771-1786 included THREE ENSLAVED PEOPLE whose names the records do not preserve — remembered here per the Cuff precedent; compiler may wish a notable_story. Died January 1789: “he laid down his armor and went to his rest.”

narrative_blocks.header: Ten priests met in profound secret
narrative_blocks.body: On March 25, 1783 — weeks after independence was secure — ten of Connecticut’s fourteen clergy gathered at Marshall’s Glebe House, the meeting “kept a profound secret even from their most intimate friends of the laity,” and no records were made. From it came the election of Samuel Seabury, first Bishop of the Church in America.

narrative_blocks.header: A sliding panel hid the rector
narrative_blocks.body: Twice beaten in the road and left for dead, Marshall could finally leave his house only on Sundays, when the old Puritan law forbade arrest on the Sabbath. The Committee of Patriots searched the glebe again and again — never finding the sliding closet panel that dropped him into the cellar.

narrative_blocks.header: He furnished the glass and nails
narrative_blocks.body: When the Society withdrew its aid at the war’s outbreak, Marshall labored on from Milford to Great Barrington, and when St. Paul’s finally raised its church in 1785 he supplied the glass and nails himself. The Prayer Book he marked up in his own hand anticipated the revised American text he did not live to see adopted.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine children and three enslaved people
narrative_blocks.body: From 1771 to 1786 the Marshalls lived at the Glebe House in Woodbury with their nine children and three enslaved people.

narrative_blocks.header: Four sons swallowed by the sea
narrative_blocks.body: Of her sons, Capt. William went down with the brig Henry & Isabella in 1810, Robert was lost the same year, Capt. Charles in 1820, and Francis in 1825 — four sailors the ocean never returned. Only George the privateer, of all her seafaring boys, died ashore in old age.

people.research_notes:
“The Worshipful” John Pynchon, the magistrate. Bridge entry (Stage 6Y-674) completing the line from Hon. William Pynchon (Y00004) to the Guilford Pynchons and the novelist; year-level dates per Notabledoc2 — compiler to supply richer sources for enrichment. Mother assigned as Ann Andrew (William’s first wife) per standard genealogies. REBUILT 10 Aug 2026 from Sam's chronology of John Pynchon and Indian affairs in western
New England. BIRTH moved 1621 -> ca. 1626, at Springfield in the parish of Chelmsford, Essex. The old slug
/person/john-pynchon-1621 is preserved in former_ids. DEATH DATE — OLD STYLE / NEW STYLE, not a conflict. Sam's header gives "1626-17 January 1702";
the chronology places the death under 1703. Both are right: under the Old Style calendar the
year began 25 March, so 17 January 1702 O.S. is 17 January 1703 N.S. Recorded as 1703, which
is what the existing entry already carried and what modern reckoning gives. Properly written
17 January 1702/3. TITLES. Made captain of the train band and major of the troop of horse in 1657, sergeant-major
for western Massachusetts 1669, and colonel by Andros in 1687; reverted to captain after the
1689 revolution and was a colonel again from 1691. "Major" is used as the display title per
Sam. OFFICES not carried as career rows (the card renders only three): selectman and town treasurer
of Springfield from November 1650, freeman 13 April 1648, commissioner to administer justice
1652, magistrate and lieutenant of the trainband 1653, deputy to the General Court 1662,
presided over the first Hampshire County Court in March 1663, one of the commissioners who
received Stuyvesant's capitulation of New Netherland in 1664, Dudley's Council and then the
Andros Council 1686, and re-elected to the Council annually from 1693 until his death. CHILDREN. Five, all of whom married into gentry families. Only X03298 is built. Named but
unbuilt: Joseph (boarded at Cambridge with Goodman Beale, Harvard 1664), John Jr. (established
as a Boston merchant 1669, deeded the Boston, New London and Antigua holdings in 1680), and
Mary (b. ca. 1650, probably stricken with poliomyelitis). DETAIL NOT USED. Educated by his father and the Rev. George Moxon, and learned an Algonkian
dialect. Interested in a graphite mine at Tantiusque (Sturbridge) 1657-59. Erected the first
sawmill at Springfield 1667 and a vertical-log house in 1678. In 1677 borrowed saved pinetree
shillings at Hadley to send to Antigua. Petitioned in 1696 for expenses four and a half years
in arrears. In 1697 referred to a victory over hostile Indians "otherwise unknown to history".
Visited England 1656-57, living in London or at Wraysbury where his exiled father was, and
again 1663-64 to settle that father's estate as principal beneficiary. FURTHER MATERIAL 10 Aug 2026 from Sam's two new sources, held here rather than forced into a
card already at the seven-block ceiling. "BROTHER PYNCHON" — the name the region's native communities used for him. He kept the peace with
regular visits to their villages, carrying gunpowder, cloth and tools against furs bound for
England. This is the strongest unused fact on the entry and is the standing proposal to replace
NB6 (the Dutch privateers). OFFICES: styled "The Worshipful" from 1652 to 1660; Chief Justice of the Court of Common Pleas
for Hampshire County 1692-1702; Commissioner of the United Colonies; confirmed lieutenant 1653,
captain 1657, sergeant-major 1671. INDUSTRY: cider and turpentine mills, flour and corn mills, a lumber mill and an iron foundry —
between them employing much of Springfield's population. Land at Northampton, Hadley and
Deerfield. With James Rogers he bought 2,400 acres at New London. Interests in at least five
vessels between 1652 and 1689, a turpentine distilling plant in 1692, and mining ventures. He
advanced his own money to buy Northampton, Hadley, Westfield, Deerfield, Enfield and Suffield
from the native owners and was repaid by the settlers later. HIS OWN VIEW OF THE COMMAND: he thought himself unfit for it, and held that Connecticut's refusal
to take his advice led to the destruction of Springfield and the outlying towns. His reputation
suffered for the burning and was restored before his death. ESTATE: settled only in 1737 at 8,446 pounds, of which barely 166 was personal property. DATE CONFLICTS, none resolved: birth given variously as "abt. 1620", "1624 or 1625", and ca. 1626
(this entry, from the chronology); death as 17 January 1702-3 at about seventy-seven, which is the
Old Style dual year already recorded as 1703. NB6 REPLACED 10 Aug 2026 on Sam's instruction — the Dutch-privateer block gave way to "Brother
Pynchon". The privateer facts are kept: a privateer seized six hogsheads of his furs in October
1653, and in July 1666 the Dutch took another shipment of beaver with John Plumb's vessel. SWAP 10 Aug 2026, Sam approving: the brick-mansion block gave way to the mills, the Worshipful
style and the Chief Justiceship — three facts that had been stranded in these notes. The house
itself still appears on the card as landmark LM373, so nothing is lost from the visible surface
except the fifty-thousand-brick order, which is recorded above. BLOCKS REORDERED after the swap — the new block had simply appended to the end. Career and distinction first, paired themes adjacent, family and death last.

narrative_blocks.header: The Mohawks renamed Massachusetts after him
narrative_blocks.body: At Albany in April 1677 he and James Richards of Hartford brought the Mohawks to a covenant of peace with the North Indians. By then the Mohawks were calling Massachusetts itself Pinshon, after him. It was the first conference the Dutch and English let New Englanders hold directly with the Iroquois.

narrative_blocks.header: At twenty-six he inherited the valley trade
narrative_blocks.body: When his father sailed for England in 1652 rather than face the heresy court, John took over every account and every property in New England. He was twenty-six, and within a few years was reckoned the greatest man in all the west.

narrative_blocks.header: His mills employed much of Springfield
narrative_blocks.body: He ran cider and turpentine mills, flour and corn mills, a lumber mill and an iron foundry, and between them they employed much of the town. Men had addressed him as The Worshipful since 1652, and from 1692 he sat as Chief Justice of the Common Pleas for Hampshire County.

narrative_blocks.header: They called him Brother Pynchon
narrative_blocks.body: He kept the peace with the valley's native communities by going to their villages himself, carrying gunpowder, cloth and tools against furs bound for England. They called him Brother Pynchon, and he was still the man both sides sent for when a treaty was wanted.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded four towns up the Connecticut
narrative_blocks.body: He advanced the purchase money for Northampton in 1653, then founded Brookfield in 1667, Enfield in 1671, and helped found Northfield in 1672. He also negotiated the Massachusetts boundary with the Connecticut his father had walked out of.

narrative_blocks.header: He marched to Springfield while it burned
narrative_blocks.body: On 5 October 1675 he brought his men down from Hadley to a Springfield already almost burned out. His own buildings, mills and tenants went with it. He gave up command of the western forces the following year, for family reasons.

narrative_blocks.header: Stoddard preached his funeral sermon
narrative_blocks.body: John Pynchon died on 17 January 1703. Solomon Stoddard came down from Northampton to preach over him, and printed the sermon at Boston that year as Gods Frown in the Death of Usefull Men.

narrative_blocks.header: The last surviving founder of Enfield
narrative_blocks.body: Enfield was the township granted in 1683 on the Connecticut below Springfield, at the falls where his father had put up the first sawmill twenty years before. He was one of the men who founded it, and Suffield beside it, and outlived every other one of them.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife was born two days after him
narrative_blocks.body: John was born at Springfield on 15 October 1647 and Margaret Hubbard at Ipswich on the seventeenth. They had at least three children and lie in the same Springfield ground; he outlived her by four and a half years.

career.role: Clerk of the Courts and Register of Deeds

narrative_blocks.header: She came from Ipswich to the river towns
narrative_blocks.body: She was a Hubbard of Ipswich on the coast, daughter of the Rev. William Hubbard and Mary Rogers, who were twenty-six and nineteen when she was born. She married into the Pynchons of Springfield and is buried there.

narrative_blocks.header: Two days younger than the man she married
narrative_blocks.body: Margaret was born at Ipswich on 17 October 1647; John Pynchon had been born upriver at Springfield on the fifteenth. They had at least two sons and a daughter, and she died at Springfield sixty-nine years old.

narrative_blocks.header: Father and son sat in the House together
narrative_blocks.body: He was Springfield's town clerk for many years and its representative to the General Court. For a time he and his son William, who carried the same name, sat in that House at once.

narrative_blocks.header: Her will named six children
narrative_blocks.body: Katherine Brewer married William Pynchon at Springfield on 15 May 1721 and outlived him by six years. Her will names six children — William, Margaret, Sarah, Daniel, John and Joseph — of whom Joseph carried the line down to Guilford.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father fed Washington's army
narrative_blocks.body: Charles Pettit, her father, was a Philadelphia merchant who served as assistant quartermaster general to the Continental Army and later sat in the Continental Congress. She married Jared Ingersoll in 1781, the year the fighting ended.

narrative_blocks.header: He claimed twelve million Florida acres
narrative_blocks.body: Deeded the tract by the Duke of Alagon in 1819, Jefferson’s former consul at Cadiz asserted ownership of a Florida the size of a small state. The Supreme Court finally extinguished the claim in 1908 — sixty-five years after his death, one of the longest-running land cases in American law.

narrative_blocks.header: A grave marked only R.S.H.
narrative_blocks.body: His large vault-stone in Norfolk’s Cedar Grove Cemetery bears nothing but initials and a year — “R.S.H., 1843” — in an otherwise empty family plot, leaving a modern cemetery researcher to rediscover the consul who once claimed Florida.

people.research_notes: Daughter of Col. Thomas Mann Randolph Sr. (1741-1793) and Anne Cary Randolph of Tuckahoe — parents noted, not built per compiler. Her brother Thomas Mann Randolph Jr. (1768-1828) married Martha Jefferson and became Governor of Virginia.

narrative_blocks.header: Dolley Madison’s best friend from Tuckahoe
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Tuckahoe plantation to Col. Thomas Mann Randolph, she counted Dolley Madison among her closest friends. Her brother married Martha Jefferson — making her sister-in-law to the President’s daughter — and rose to the governorship of Virginia.

narrative_blocks.header: A schoolboy’s elegy for Hancock’s son
narrative_blocks.body: At thirteen, from Boston’s South School, he painted a watercolor elegy for John George Washington Hancock — the Governor’s only child, dead at eight after a fall on his new skates. The piece hung in the Metropolitan Museum’s American art exhibition of 1963.

narrative_blocks.header: Reinterred beside both wives at Mount Auburn
narrative_blocks.body: First buried in the Granary Burying Ground, the Boston merchant was moved to Mount Auburn in 1845 along with Lucy Fox and Susan Brown, his two wives. His grandson George Bucknam Dorr became the father of Acadia National Park.

Daughter of Joseph Lasinby Brown (1753-1804) and Susanna Adams. Two children, Susan Elizabeth and Charles Hazen Dorr.

narrative_blocks.header: Four children, none reached twenty-one
narrative_blocks.body: Henry Dorr died in infancy, Lucy Jane at two, Emily Elizabeth at seventeen, Henry Augustus at eighteen — Martha outlived her last child by three decades. She rests at Mount Auburn beside her parents.

narrative_blocks.header: He raised the money for Amherst science
narrative_blocks.body: As an Amherst College trustee he signed appeals with Alpheus Hardy to match a $20,000 gift conditioned on placing the Scientific Department “on a complete and thorough basis.” He outlived his wife and all four of his children.

narrative_blocks.header: A Boston merchant who governed a hospital
narrative_blocks.body: Edwards made his fortune as a Boston merchant and turned it toward public institutions rather than display. In his own city he served as a trustee of Massachusetts General Hospital, one of the country's oldest teaching hospitals. He was the kind of merchant-trustee whose quiet wealth underwrote nineteenth-century New England's colleges and hospitals.

narrative_blocks.header: For forty years he never left Amherst's board
narrative_blocks.body: A Boston man of affairs — city government, the Massachusetts House, the board of the Massachusetts General Hospital — he held one post longest of all: four decades as a trustee of Amherst College.

Son of Benjamin and Elizabeth (Marsh) Tappan — the elder Benjamin also a DAR-recognized patriot. Sons Arthur and Lewis Tappan were the abolitionist financiers; Lewis co-formed the Amistad Committee.

narrative_blocks.header: Gilbert Stuart painted them both
narrative_blocks.body: The Northampton silversmith-turned-merchant and his wife Sarah sat for Gilbert Stuart in 1814; the pair of portraits now hangs in the National Gallery of Art. He had learned his trade under William Holmes — his future father-in-law, a nephew of Benjamin Franklin.

narrative_blocks.header: His sons remade American reform
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin Jr. became a US Senator from Ohio and Edwin Stanton’s law partner; Arthur and Lewis Tappan bankrolled the abolitionist movement, Lewis forming the Amistad defense committee. Their father had marched toward Saratoga as a twenty-eight-day private in 1777.

narrative_blocks.header: A revival at Falmouth turned her
narrative_blocks.body: She came back from a revival at Falmouth convinced she could not be regenerated by her own effort — only by the Holy Spirit, and only by bending her own will into submission to Providence.

narrative_blocks.header: The last son they sent to a college
narrative_blocks.body: Her eldest, Benjamin, came away from college in 1793 with Voltaire for his theologian and Paine's Rights of Man for his creed. He was the last son the Tappans offered to any institution of higher education.

narrative_blocks.header: She raised the brothers who funded abolition
narrative_blocks.body: Two of her eleven children, Arthur and Lewis Tappan, became the money and the organisation behind American abolition, and she was reckoned the source of it.

narrative_blocks.header: Married by Dr. Cooper, eleven children
narrative_blocks.body: Rev. Dr. Cooper married her to Benjamin Tappan at Boston on the twenty-second of October 1770, and they had eleven children. Benjamin Jr. was born at Northampton in the May of 1773, Rebecca in the July of 1775.

narrative_blocks.header: She married her sister’s widower
narrative_blocks.body: A year after Keziah’s death, Eliza married Roger Hooker and raised her sister’s three boys; she had no children of her own.

people.research_notes: Second wife (m. March 29, 1839); sister of Keziah Osgood Hunt Leavitt. NOT notable.

narrative_blocks.header: Her books, and the world outside the room
narrative_blocks.body: She was an invalid for months and in severe pain, and bore it, her obituary said, with an uncomplaining and even cheerful spirit — keeping to the last an interest in those about her, in her books, and in the great world outside her quiet chamber.

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband handed his business to others
narrative_blocks.body: Col. Leavitt married her in 1876, four years before she died. When she began to fail he gave the running of his affairs over to other men so that he could nurse her himself.

narrative_blocks.header: Buried at Deerfield beside her first husband
narrative_blocks.body: She lies in the old Deerfield cemetery next to H. Ryland Warriner, who had been preceptor of Deerfield academy before practising law at Philadelphia. She spent the best years of her life in that city, in Dr. Furness's congregation.

narrative_blocks.header: She followed Lucretia Mott in three weeks
narrative_blocks.body: An invalid through her last year, she grieved deeply at the November 1880 death of her “venerable and beloved friend” Lucretia Mott — and, as she had foreseen, followed her within three weeks. Her best years had been spent in Philadelphia as Mrs. H. Ryland Warriner.

people.research_notes: Third wife (m. Chicago, Feb 28, 1877). NOT notable per compiler; NOT a Hooker — spouse only, no Hooker children. Daughter of Capt. narrative_blocks.header: A bride for the first time at fifty-one
narrative_blocks.body: The Buckland schoolteacher — who had started school herself at two and a half — taught from South Deerfield to seven years in the far West before marrying the widowed colonel in 1882, her first marriage.

people.research_notes: Fourth wife. NOT notable. Marriage date Jan 28, 1882 (Charlemont VR) vs. Feb 16, 1882 (Buckland VR) — both recorded, possibly Boston JP per Charlemont record. Franklin Academy 1848; Conway high school. No children.

narrative_blocks.header: He stumped Pennsylvania for Lincoln
narrative_blocks.body: He filled the Deerfield town hall on a wet night in 1860, then canvassed Pennsylvania for Lincoln. Of pro-slavery men joining the Democrats he said he felt like the Irishman whose horse got a foot in the stirrup: if you're getting on, I'll get off.

narrative_blocks.header: A silver fork, and one for his wife
narrative_blocks.body: His Deerfield pupils gave him a bible and a silver fork at the close of the winter term in 1855, and gave his wife a matching fork. He left that spring to run the Boys' High School in Philadelphia.

narrative_blocks.header: Loyal to his convictions of right
narrative_blocks.body: He practised law in Philadelphia from 1855 until he died there in January 1873. His obituary called him an earnest, hard-working lawyer of rare amiability, yet loyal to his convictions of right.

narrative_blocks.header: His pupils raised him a monument
narrative_blocks.body: Within a month of his death his old Deerfield scholars proposed a monument, and in November 1875 a shaft of Tennessee marble arrived, paid for by subscription among them — eighteen years after he had left the school.

narrative_blocks.header: General Hooker gave him orders
narrative_blocks.body: At Antietam on September 17, 1862, he rode the field as Hooker’s aide-de-camp, carrying the First Corps’ attack orders under fire until the general was carried off wounded — service the brevets later honored as “gallant and meritorious.” From Fredericksburg through Chancellorsville he bore the orders of a corps, a grand division, and finally the Army of the Potomac itself.

narrative_blocks.header: He married into the real Hooker line
narrative_blocks.body: The Hooker whose orders he carried was “Fighting Joe” — a different Hooker line entirely, no relation to the Rev. Thomas Hooker family of this tree. Moore’s true tie came in 1875, when he married Gen. Daniel Tyler’s daughter Mary Law, a Hooker descendant.

narrative_blocks.header: In the Peach Orchard when Sickles fell
narrative_blocks.body: On Daniel Sickles’s staff during the Gettysburg campaign, Moore was present in the Peach Orchard on July 2, 1863, when a Confederate shell took the general’s right leg. Brevets for gallantry followed — major, lieutenant colonel, and colonel.

narrative_blocks.header: Court-martialed at Powder River, then remitted
narrative_blocks.body: Commanding the 5th Battalion at the Battle of Powder River in March 1876 — the strike on Crazy Horse’s village — he was court-martialed for failing to support the attack; the President remitted the sentence, and Moore resigned in 1879 to ranch in Guadalupe County, Texas.

narrative_blocks.header: Nicknamed for a fictional Irish dragoon
narrative_blocks.body: Hooker’s staff called the Ballymoney-born aide “the Charley O’Malley of the army” — after the dashing Irish cavalry hero of Charles Lever’s bestselling 1841 novel. Hooker thought the name apt “except in one respect: I doubt if your prototype ever possessed the confidence of his commander to the degree you had mine.”

narrative_blocks.header: He founded the Army’s artillery school
narrative_blocks.body: In 1911 Moore became founder and first commandant of the US Army School of Fire at Fort Sill, Oklahoma — today’s Field Artillery School. He had served as White House military aide to Theodore Roosevelt, husband of his first cousin Edith.

narrative_blocks.header: Married in Lucerne between White House seasons
narrative_blocks.body: Washington society followed the aide’s November 1906 wedding to Luvie Butler in Lucerne, Switzerland — two months’ leave, returning “just at the opening of the social season.” She died in 1915, leaving him three children under ten.

narrative_blocks.header: He blinded Roosevelt in a sparring bout
narrative_blocks.body: As the President's sparring partner he landed a blow that cost Roosevelt the sight of an eye. He learned of it only in 1917, from a newspaper: Roosevelt had described a boxing aide from the artillery and never named him.

narrative_blocks.header: He finished Zurich two classes ahead of Einstein
narrative_blocks.body: Raised at Hanover and schooled in Switzerland, he took his degree from the Eidgenössische Polytechnische Schule at Zurich in 1898, two classes ahead of Albert Einstein.

narrative_blocks.header: First foreigner at the Kaiser's artillery school
narrative_blocks.body: Only Germany had a working system of indirect fire, so Roosevelt wrote to Kaiser Wilhelm II calling him his young cousin and got him admitted, the first foreigner ever. He spent 1909 and 1910 there playing the amiable idler while learning everything.

narrative_blocks.header: A spy ring ran out of his house
narrative_blocks.body: At the Army War College he put up Franz von Papen, his old room-mate from Germany and a future Chancellor. Von Papen was running a spy ring from the house and was expelled for it; Moore knew nothing.

narrative_blocks.header: He loafed six weeks to beat the customs
narrative_blocks.body: Coming home in 1910 he stayed on in Holland until he had been abroad two full years, which let him re-enter as a non-resident and land his German household goods duty-free.

people.research_notes: Wife of Col. Augustus Cleveland Tyler (m. Jan 3, 1878, Norwich). Birth year 1854 (FAG) vs 1856 (FamilySearch) — FAG retained. “Lady Bountiful” of New London; her summer home The Elm anchored the Pequot colony’s society. NOT notable per standing rule (no compiler ruling) despite the Broadway first — flagged as a strong notability candidate for compiler review. A VENETIAN ROMANCE IS NOW DATED: Knickerbocker Theatre, 2 May to 28 May 1904, 28 performances. Book by her, music and lyrics by Frederic Coit Wright, directed by Al Holbrook, produced by Frank L. Perley - it was Richard Mansfield, a frequent guest at the Tyler house, who pushed them from amusement to serious effort and brought Perley to it. Carroll McComas and Walter Percival both made their Broadway debuts in it. OBITUARY (New London): widow of Col. Augustus Cleveland Tyler, who held his rank in the Third Connecticut National Guard, served in the Spanish-American War and died 27 November 1906. She married him on 3 January 1878 when he was a lieutenant in the Fourth United States Cavalry; they went first to Fort Clark, Texas, and came to New London for a summer home when he resigned from the army soon after. The original family house at Gardner and Pequot avenues burned about 1896 and was replaced by the mansion that is now the Memorial Hospital; when the mansion and part of the grounds were sold the family kept the cottage, the flower garden and the name The Elm. Her garden hosted the meetings and teas of the New London League of Women Voters, of which she was a member, as she was of the American Red Cross and the parish of St. James'. She was a lover of good music. Survived by her daughters Edna Leighton Tyler and Sarah Tyler Marshall of Abington, Pennsylvania, and her son Frederick Osgood Tyler of Anniston, Alabama. BIRTH YEAR UNSETTLED: FindAGrave gives 31 August 1854 (aged 77 at death), which this record follows; the Osgood family account says 1856, and the obituary headline calls her 75, which fits 1856. Two sources against one.

narrative_blocks.body: In 1913 Edward organized the American Manganese Company, the first to turn out ferro-manganese commercially in the United States. Through the First World War he ran six plants making it and spiegeleisen for steel, until cheap imports undercut the trade after the Armistice.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale football in its bone-breaking years
narrative_blocks.body: At Yale Edward played football when the game was at its roughest, so brutal that its survival as a college sport was in doubt. In 1898 he enlisted in the Yale Battery, Battery A of Connecticut, which never got near the fighting in the Spanish-American War.

narrative_blocks.header: Tin plate and a rolling mill at Marshallton

narrative_blocks.header: A patent medicine built the fortune
narrative_blocks.body: “Dr. Osgood’s India Cholagogue,” his remedy for fever and ague formulated on the Michigan frontier, sold in impressive quantities for fifty years — funding the Norwich drug house, the Shetucket Bank, a railroad presidency, and a founder’s share of the Norwich Free Academy.

narrative_blocks.header: Five hundred stampless letters survive him
narrative_blocks.body: Grand Valley State University holds more than nine hundred of his papers — including over five hundred stampless folded letters from his Michigan land-speculation years, among them seven bearing the six-month-lived Havre post office’s cancellations. Philatelists prize the collection.

narrative_blocks.header: Three Osgood mayors of Norwich
narrative_blocks.body: Ill health forced him from the mayoralty in 1876 — his cousin Hugh Henry Osgood held the office before him and resumed it after, and his son Frederic took it in 1896. The India Cholagogue fortune stood behind them all.

people.research_notes: EASTER EGG per compiler Stage 6Y-690: father of Cornelia Osgood Tyler (X03328), wife of Col. Augustus Cleveland Tyler (HD6079). Son of Dr. Erastus Osgood. Mayor of Norwich 1876, resigned in ill health — preceded AND succeeded by cousin Hugh Henry Osgood; son Frederic L. Osgood also mayor, 1896-1900. Home on Washington Street beside the present Congregation Brothers of Joseph Synagogue. Compiler asked for further CC candidates: the natural one is Brig. Gen. Daniel Tyler (HD2280) — Norwich contemporaries and co-fathers-in-law of the 1878 marriage — but no documented interaction is in hand, so per the documented-overlap rule no CC was added; flagged for compiler ruling. Son of Erastus Osgood, M.D. (1780-1867) and Martha Morgan Osgood (1787-1876), eldest of seven. Bacon Academy at Colchester, then medicine under his father, then the Yale medical school, 1833. Practised at Monroe, Michigan Territory from September 1835, speculating in land and holding stock in the Havre Company, a town-founding venture that the Panic of 1837 undid, and acting as an agent for the Aetna. Around 1840 he compounded a remedy for bilious fevers and ague called Dr. Osgood's India Cholagogue, and its success is probably what brought him back to Connecticut in 1841. At Norwich he built the pharmaceutical business, founded the Shetucket Bank, and was prominent in the Norwich Savings Society and the New London Mutual Fire Insurance Company.

narrative_blocks.body: The figure had stood over her for more than a century and was among the most photographed things in Norwich when it vanished one February. A local runner who used to clean the cobwebs off it noticed first. It was recovered and the city restored it.
