narrative_blocks.body: The President offered the White House for his birth; his mother declined, and Roosevelt — his father’s commander and his cousin Edith’s husband — stood godfather instead.

narrative_blocks.header: Cairo’s spymaster with two jobs
narrative_blocks.body: A civilian major in Donovan’s OSS, he sat overtly as deputy to the Middle East economic mission while covertly running the region’s counterintelligence — choking Germany’s industrial-diamond supply, foiling an assassination plot against King George II of Greece, and inventing a hoist for airlifting spies.

narrative_blocks.header: His pulp novel became Gymkata
narrative_blocks.body: The Terrible Game (1957), grown from a Saturday Evening Post story, became the 1985 cult film Gymkata; the Navy put his Cloak and Cipher on every warship. He launched a trade firm with Eliot Ness and grew the International Platform Association past ten thousand members.

narrative_blocks.header: His treaty gave the OSS half the world
narrative_blocks.body: Moore hammered out the treaty between Donovan and his arch-rival J. Edgar Hoover that handed the OSS the eastern hemisphere and the FBI the western. Thirty years on, CIA Director William Colby accepted his lecture invitation, “interested in clarifying the real nature of modern American intelligence.”

narrative_blocks.body: A Philadelphia lawyer, he published a volume called Fears for Democracy. Frank Polk remarked that it contained more fears than democracy.

narrative_blocks.header: The Constitution their grandfather signed was their bible
narrative_blocks.body: Charles and his brother Edward were called Copperheads — Northerners opposed to the war. They held, on constitutional grounds, that the South had a right to secede, and Philadelphia, long the commercial gateway to the South, held families who felt the same. They suffered for it.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventy-five thousand stoves a year
narrative_blocks.body: Hired by the Rathbone stove works at seventeen and a partner at twenty-five, the tailor's son built Rathbone, Sard & Company into one of Albany's largest plants, turning out about 75,000 stoves a year by 1886. For seventeen years he sat on the board of Washington Park.

They also summered at Dark Harbor, Maine, and Grange belonged to the Jekyll Island Club.

narrative_blocks.body: In Colorado he became a hunting and camping companion of Theodore Roosevelt, close enough that the president twice tried to pull him into the federal government.

narrative_blocks.header: Roosevelt wanted him to run the land office
narrative_blocks.body: The president pressed him to become Commissioner of the General Land Office, promising he’d work beside Gifford Pinchot in a housecleaning of the Interior Department. Stewart was in no hurry — and Roosevelt invited him and his wife to stay at the White House.

narrative_blocks.header: A marble bust outlived the man
narrative_blocks.body: In 1884 the sculptor Charles Calverley cut his likeness in marble; a century later a museum paired the bust with images of anonymous women, asking why privileged men so dominate what we keep.

career.notes: 1870-1872; first two-year term

narrative_blocks.header: First governor Vermont let serve two years
narrative_blocks.body: When Vermont changed its governor’s term from one year to two, he was the first man elected to the longer term, taking office in 1870 after years as Speaker of the state house.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped swing Vermont from Seward to Lincoln
narrative_blocks.body: As a delegate to the 1860 Republican national convention he played a part in moving the Vermont delegation from Seward to Lincoln — a small hinge in the nomination that made Lincoln president.

narrative_blocks.header: At eighty-two he filled a dead senator’s seat
narrative_blocks.body: When Senator Redfield Proctor died in 1908, the governor appointed the eighty-two-year-old Stewart to hold the seat until a successor was chosen — a capstone to a career begun before the Civil War.

narrative_blocks.header: Speaker twice, a decade apart
narrative_blocks.body: John was Speaker of the Vermont House from 1865 to 1868 and was chosen again when he returned to the house in 1876, after his governorship. He went on to four terms in Congress, from 1883 to 1891.

narrative_blocks.header: He left Congress to run a bank
narrative_blocks.body: Declining renomination in 1890, he went home to run the Middlebury bank as its president — a quieter second career after decades in public life.

narrative_blocks.header: He read law with his wife's grandfather
narrative_blocks.body: John studied law in the office of former Senator Horatio Seymour, whose granddaughter Emma Battell he married in 1860, and was admitted to the bar in 1850. He was state's attorney for Addison County from 1851 to 1854, while his brother Dugald rose toward state auditor.

narrative_blocks.header: His house is now the Swift House Inn
narrative_blocks.body: John retired to his house at 25 Stewart Lane in Middlebury, built by Judge Samuel Swift, the grandfather of Charles Swift. It is now the Swift House Inn.

narrative_blocks.body: Emma married John Wolcott Stewart on 21 November 1860, a lawyer who had read law with her grandfather Horatio Seymour. They had six children, among them twins Jessica and Robert, and she died in Boston in 1900, fifteen years before him.

narrative_blocks.header: Her parents met at a commencement ball
narrative_blocks.body: Her father, Philip Battell, took his Middlebury degree in 1826, the year of the commencement ball remembered for him and Emma Hart Seymour; they married in 1836. narrative_blocks.header: Her brother built the Bread Loaf Inn
narrative_blocks.body: Her brother Joseph Battell founded the Bread Loaf Inn at Ripton and became one of Middlebury College's great benefactors. Through their mother the two were grandchildren of Senator Horatio Seymour.

narrative_blocks.header: He left Vermont but returned to rest
narrative_blocks.body: He spent his life far from the family seat — born in Boston, dying in California at eighty — yet was carried back to the Middlebury ground where the Stewarts gather, generation after generation.

narrative_blocks.header: He married twice, thirty-six years apart
narrative_blocks.body: His first marriage came in 1920, his second not until 1956 — a span of thirty-six years between the two women who shared his long life.

narrative_blocks.body: Sibyl Collins married Rev. John Whiting around 1654 and bore his earliest children before her death in 1672. Daughter of Edward Collins and sister of Rev. John Collins, she connected two ministerial families of early New England.

narrative_blocks.header: Her sons commanded armies and pulpits
narrative_blocks.body: Two of Sibyl's sons rose to prominence: Col. William Whiting led Connecticut troops against French and Indian forces and later served as High Sheriff of Hartford County, while Rev. Samuel Whiting became the first minister of Windham, preaching his first sermon there on New Year's Day 1693.

bio.title: Rev.
bio.bio_blurb: Yale-educated minister of wandering Connecticut pulpits

narrative_blocks.header: A Yale minister with a wandering pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: Ebenezer Martin graduated from Yale College in 1756 and was ordained in 1759 as the first pastor of the church at Becket, Massachusetts. His career proved restless: he was dismissed in 1764 amid disputes over land ownership and unspecified personal indiscretions.

narrative_blocks.header: Debt chased him from parish to parish
narrative_blocks.body: After Becket he preached at Groton, then Ashford, where by 1772 his debts grew so deep he petitioned the Colony assembly to escape imprisonment. He continued moving through New York and Pennsylvania pulpits for the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: He sent his son to a famous grandfather
narrative_blocks.body: Ebenezer and Susanna Plumb married around 1758 and had several children. Their son Joseph, raised partly by affluent Milford grandparents, would become one of the most quoted common soldiers of the Revolution.

notable.notable_blurb: Revolutionary War memoirist, Sappers and Miners sergeant

narrative_blocks.header: A teenager who vowed to run to war
narrative_blocks.body: Fifteen and eager after Lexington and Concord, Joseph Plumb Martin won his grandparents’ consent to enlist only by threatening to run off as a privateer. He joined the Connecticut Militia in June 1776 and reached New York just as the British Long Island campaign opened.

narrative_blocks.header: He cleared the way for Hamilton at Yorktown
narrative_blocks.body: Promoted to sergeant in Washington’s new Corps of Sappers and Miners, Martin dug the entrenchments before Yorktown. During the siege his corps cleared the abatis so Alexander Hamilton’s regiment could storm Redoubt #10.

narrative_blocks.header: His memoir became history’s common soldier
narrative_blocks.body: Published anonymously in 1830 and lost for over a century, his narrative resurfaced in the 1950s to become one of the finest primary accounts of the Revolution. Historians prize it precisely because Martin was no general but an ordinary private.

narrative_blocks.header: A war hero who died owning nothing
narrative_blocks.body: Settling Maine’s frontier, Martin lost a bitter land dispute to Henry Knox and was insolvent by 1818, when a $96 annual pension finally came. He served his town of Prospect as clerk for twenty-five years.

narrative_blocks.header: Hollywood and a marching salute remembered him
narrative_blocks.body: In 1836 a passing platoon of Light Infantry fired a salute outside his home. He has since been portrayed by Philip Seymour Hoffman among others, and a trail around Valley Forge bears his name.

people.research_notes: DAR Patriot Ancestor #A074384 (Sergeant, Connecticut). Sapper/Miner in Corps of Engineers, Continental Army.

military_service.unit: 8th Connecticut Regiment; Corps of Sappers and Miners
military_service.notes: Enlisted Connecticut Militia 1776 at age 15; Continental Army 1777. Corporal in Light Infantry 1778; Sergeant in Sappers & Miners 1780. Present at Yorktown clearing abatis ahead of Hamilton’s assault on Redoubt #10.

Sarah Content Ward, aged 87 at the time of writing, is the source for 'Aunt Mitty'. Sally Chamberlain, whose mother was Martha Newton, married a Mr. Babcock of New Haven; their daughter Harriet married Edward Pickett Camp. None of the four wards is built here.

narrative_blocks.header: They raised other people's children instead
narrative_blocks.body: They had none of their own, so they took relatives' children into the Hartford house to give them a city education. Delight Camp, who married her nephew Horace Newton, was one; Samuel Johnson, afterwards president of Columbia College, was another; and so were Sally Chamberlain and Emma Coe.

narrative_blocks.header: Aunt Mitty wore her own hair
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah Content Ward, at eighty-seven, remembered her cutting it short across her forehead when every other woman in the town bought a false front to wear under a cap as soon as her own began to grey.

narrative_blocks.header: Named for the aunt she never mentions
narrative_blocks.body: She was called Submit for her mother's sister, Submit Johnson. After Samuel died she made her home with Horace and Delight Newton and lived another seventeen years.

people.research_notes: No children by Submit Newton.

narrative_blocks.header: The gout took his tavern from him
narrative_blocks.body: He kept a hotel at Hartford until the gout made the work impossible. They moved to Middletown, to a house standing where the insane hospital was afterwards built, and finally back to Durham.

narrative_blocks.header: He left the lot to a public institution
narrative_blocks.body: They had accumulated considerable property and his will gave it to a public institution rather than to kin. Some of the furniture, china and silver stayed in the family, the spoons marked S. C. — the S standing for Samuel and Submit both, as the fashion then was.

people.research_notes: Twin of Abner; died age 2. Twin, born 29 December 1764 at Durham. The printed genealogy names Abner and Roger as twins; a FamilySearch extract dates Abner to 1765.

bio.title: Dea.
bio.bio_blurb: Boy soldier of 1779, later a Durham deacon

narrative_blocks.header: He marched to New Haven at fourteen
narrative_blocks.body: Abner Newton enlisted before he was fifteen and marched with his company to New Haven in July 1779 when the British invaded under General Tryon. The heavy flintlock musket he carried was kept until his death in 1852, when his grandsons destroyed it.

narrative_blocks.header: “Their guns shone like silver”
narrative_blocks.body: In extreme old age Abner relived his war years, pointing to a hill near his home and saying he had watched the British come over it, their guns shining like silver — and that he was glad to see them go. He had stood guard the night Arnold burned New London.

narrative_blocks.header: He refused a pension on principle
narrative_blocks.body: Though his comrades applied for pensions, Abner would not, saying he did not wish his townsmen to remark when he died, “Another old pensioner gone.” He was ordained deacon some twenty-five years after his boyhood service.

narrative_blocks.header: His twin died and the name came back
narrative_blocks.body: Roger died at two years and five months and Abner, six months older than the memory should allow, kept it: running hand in hand with him over the hill to Uncle John's, and his grandfather the first Abner lifting him to look at the dead face by the light of a candle. A son born in May 1768 was given the name again.

narrative_blocks.header: A knock in the jaw at daybreak
narrative_blocks.body: Fowler's history of Durham records Capt. Charles Norton meeting him one morning after a night on guard in the cold: you have had a cold time, you must now come in and take a knock in the jaw. That is, a glass of bitters. He was fifteen or sixteen, and would not be ordained deacon for another twenty-five years.

narrative_blocks.header: Hartford sent men out to dig them through
narrative_blocks.body: They left Hartland for Durham in March 1804 so as to be in the new place for the spring work, and a heavy snow came down after they started. The cattle could not be moved; word was sent ahead to his sister Submit Camp at Hartford and men came out from the city to dig a path. The crust afterwards bore them anywhere over the tops of the fences.

cross_connections.display_label: rode with the horse at the same alarm, at forty-six

people.research_notes: Twin, born 29 December 1764 at Durham. The printed genealogy names Abner and Roger as twins; a FamilySearch extract dates Abner to 1765. Caroline Gaylord Newton's family history. His first service was July 1779 when Tryon landed 3,000 men off West Haven from about forty-eight vessels; Abner was fourteen years and six months old, tall and strong for his age. He served at Stratford several times, at Guilford when Arnold burned New London, and at West Haven, sometimes under Capt. Bunnel of Cheshire but usually under Capt. Norton of Durham, and never left the state. Burwell gave him 300 dollars at twenty-one; thirteen years at Hartland turned it into 3,000, and on 23 Feb. 1804 he bought the Curtis Bates homestead at Durham for 1,600. He left Hartland partly to escape the militia captaincy he had taken by commission from Gov. Oliver Wolcott on 23 May 1796 — it carried no pay, and the captain had to feed his whole company on training days, so his wife baked through the night before a parade. Elected deacon 1 Sept. 1808, at the meeting after the church voted to discipline any member who attended balls.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father died saving smallpox prisoners
narrative_blocks.body: Abigail Fairchild’s father Elisha drove his team to Milford in January 1777 to carry home Continental soldiers released sick and dying from British prison ships. He caught smallpox from those he rescued and died within three weeks, leaving his widow with five young children.

narrative_blocks.header: Her wedding dress was fine linen chintz
narrative_blocks.body: Abigail Fairchild married Abner Newton in 1788 in a wedding dress of fine linen chintz, having survived a hard childhood after her father’s death left her mother a widow at thirty-one with five small children. The couple lived thirteen years in Hartland before returning to Durham.

narrative_blocks.header: His head swelled up like a bushel basket
narrative_blocks.body: She was ten years old and helped nurse her father through the smallpox he had caught bringing prisoners home from Milford. That is what she said of it afterwards. He died on the twenty-fifth of January 1777, three weeks after the rescue.

narrative_blocks.header: The Mayflower comes in through her grandmother
narrative_blocks.body: Her father's mother was Abigail Crowell, and the line runs back through the Crowells and Knowleses to Major John Freeman and Mercy Prence, and from Mercy to Thomas Prence and Patience Brewster, daughter of Elder William Brewster. The Fairchilds themselves were Fairbairns in Scotland before they were Fairchilds in England.

narrative_blocks.header: Two years a helpless invalid
narrative_blocks.body: What they called rheumatic consumption took her use of herself for the last two years, and her eldest daughter Content nursed her while Parnel came when she could leave her own family. She died in November 1825, and two years later Abner married her cousin Huldah Crowell Hubbard.

people.research_notes: Caroline Gaylord Newton's family history. Elisha Fairchild drove his own team to Milford after a British flag-of-truce ship landed two hundred sick and dying Continental prisoners on the ice in the harbour on 2 Jan. 1777; twenty had died on the passage up the Sound and forty-six more within the month, buried in a long line in the Milford graveyard. William Butler is the only man he is known to have brought home; Butler recovered and drew a pension. Her mother was widowed at thirty-one with five children and lived on more than half a century, dying at Hartland 19 Jan. 1828. Thomas Fairchild, her great-great-grandfather, was one of the first settlers of Stratford and died there in 1670.
Ordained Deacon, First Congregational Church Durham 1827; Representative to General Assembly 1856.

narrative_blocks.header: He prosecuted neighbors over the Sabbath
narrative_blocks.body: Ordained deacon of Durham’s First Congregational Church in 1827, Samuel Newton was appointed the officer charged with prosecuting Seventh-day Baptists for not observing the Christian Sabbath. He led the Durham Sunday School Association until his death and sat in the General Assembly in 1856.

narrative_blocks.header: His birthday verses warned of the grave
narrative_blocks.body: A writer of verses, Samuel marked his daughter Eliza’s eighth birthday with a poem warning that before eight more years passed, her “head may lie low in the dust.” She lived instead to seventy, teaching school and remembering the church in her will.

narrative_blocks.header: He praised five brothers who never quarreled
narrative_blocks.body: A merchant in the South, Durham, and Middletown who ended his days in Jersey City, John Newton wrote admiringly of his father’s generation — the five brothers Abiathar, Burwell, Abner, Roger, and Isaac — saying he never knew so upright a band of brothers, among whom no word of censure ever passed.

people.research_notes: Teacher at Johnson Lane School; died unmarried; remembered church and Sunday School in her will.

narrative_blocks.header: A fine bass voice and a salesman’s road
narrative_blocks.body: John Burwell Newton became an agent for the S. S. Scranton publishing firm at about twenty, traveling the American South and the West Indies selling their books. He had a notably fine bass voice and was much in demand in musical circles.

narrative_blocks.header: Rejected for war, undone by his spine
narrative_blocks.body: He enlisted in the 14th Connecticut Regiment in 1862 and was surprised to be rejected for physical disability — a judgment soon justified when a worsening spinal condition forced him to give up farming. He died after long suffering at thirty-eight, having represented Durham in the 1868 Assembly.

narrative_blocks.header: His father guarded New York in 1776
narrative_blocks.body: Joel Ensign’s father, Lieutenant Eleazer Ensign, served with the 18th Regiment of Connecticut Militia under Col. Jonathan Pettibone, in Capt. Abel Brace’s company, guarding New York from August to September 1776.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight cents to collect a farewell
narrative_blocks.body: She was engaged young to a Mr. Pearce, whose health failed; the engagement was broken in August 1813 when she was twenty-four, and he recovered and married another woman. His last letter closed with a verse about shrouding his humble head among the dead, and she had to pay eight cents postage to the postmaster before she could read it.

narrative_blocks.header: She went to the ball anyway
narrative_blocks.body: Her father forbade it, so she arranged to meet a friend at a neighbour's house and went from there. Two months later the church voted that any professor of religion who attended balls should be disciplined, and at the next meeting Abner Newton was elected deacon. The family said her life never seemed prosperous after that one act of disobedience.

narrative_blocks.header: A broken leg she carried for life
narrative_blocks.body: In 1831 the horse ran on the steep hill near Daniel Southmayd's, she jumped from the carriage, and the compound fracture never came right. Dr. Chauncey Andrews made seventy visits for it. She never married and was buried in 1859 in an imitation black walnut coffin with an engraved plate.

narrative_blocks.header: Linen woven for a house she never had
narrative_blocks.body: Flax was sown and broken and spun and woven year by year, and everything beyond daily use was laid up as sheets and table-cloths and pillowcases for the setting-out of the two daughters. Content did much of the weaving herself, sitting at the loom whole days. Hers was never used in a family of her own.

narrative_blocks.header: The only one who never joined
narrative_blocks.body: Twenty-eight were admitted to the Durham church at the communion service following her father's election as deacon in September 1808, and she was not among them. She never united with the church — alone of the whole family — and the account of her says she would have done it in later life but for her invalidism.

narrative_blocks.header: A niece carried her name instead
narrative_blocks.body: She had no children of her own. Her sister Parnell's youngest, born in 1825, was christened Sara Content Ward, and that niece outlived all three of her brothers and sisters and lived to 1914.

people.research_notes: Caroline Gaylord Newton's family history. Dr. Andrews's bill for the seventy visits, medicines included, was 50 dollars and 12 cents. The 1859 funeral bills survive: 10 dollars to J. B. Southmayd for the coffin, plate and trimmings, and 2 dollars 8 cents to Sophronia Camp for shrouding, muslin and the making of shroud, cap and handkerchief. She did much of the family weaving, sitting at the loom whole days; the household saying was that when you begin to patch home-made linen it is only half worn out.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son married her brother's daughter
narrative_blocks.body: Henry Ward, born at Middletown in November 1818, married Abigail Maria Newton in May 1852. She was the daughter of Parnell's brother Elisha, so the two were first cousins and the marriage folded two branches of Abner Newton's family back into one household.

narrative_blocks.header: The house her great-grandfather lived in
narrative_blocks.body: By 1831 she was keeping house on Main Street in Durham, near Mill Bridge, in the same house where her great-grandfather had lived in 1724. Her sister Content was driving down to visit her when the horse ran away on the steep hill and she jumped, and broke her leg for life.

narrative_blocks.header: Eighty-nine years, the longest of the eight
narrative_blocks.body: Born on West Mountain at Hartland in July 1791, she died in July 1880 at eighty-nine — the longest life of Abner and Abigail's eight children, in a family that averaged eighty years. Through the two years her mother lay helpless she came to help Content nurse her as often as she could leave her own family.

bio.research_notes: Death 26 Oct 1868 per the Newton family history (aged 75); FamilySearch (LH5R-87G, 0 sources) gives 8 Oct 1868 — the printed date is kept.

narrative_blocks.header: The first son got the sick-room's name
narrative_blocks.body: Abigail Fairchild's first two children were daughters. When a son came in August 1793 she gave him her father's name entire — Elisha Fairchild — for the man she had nursed at ten through the smallpox he caught bringing prisoners home off the Milford ice.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten years old and driving the cattle
narrative_blocks.body: He was the eldest son and ten years old when the family left Hartland for Durham in March 1804, and he went with his uncle Isaac to drive the stock. A heavy snow came down after they started and the cattle could not be got along; word was sent ahead and men came out from Hartford to dig a path.

narrative_blocks.header: His small son sat with the dying woman
narrative_blocks.body: He married Sally Camp in 1820 and settled near the homestead. Through the last two years of his mother's life, when she lay a helpless invalid with what they called rheumatic consumption, his little boy Israel was her comfort and company; she died in November 1825, when the child was three.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter married his sister's son
narrative_blocks.body: Abigail Maria, born in 1825, married Henry Ward of Middletown in May 1852. Henry was the son of Elisha's elder sister Parnell, which made the couple first cousins.

bio.bio_blurb: Founder and editor of the Middletown Constitution

cross_connections.display_label: wrote the theology his New Haven firm was the first to reprint
founded his own town's paper and edited it thirty years

narrative_blocks.header: Apprenticed at fourteen to the Courant
narrative_blocks.body: Hudson & Goodwin, who published the Hartford Courant, took his indenture at fourteen and held it until he was twenty-one. He set type afterward in Philadelphia, and in New York for the Commercial Advertiser.

narrative_blocks.header: The first power press in Connecticut
narrative_blocks.body: Peck & Newton of New Haven put a wooden-frame Adams press to work in 1831, the first in the state. Theirs was also the first printing office in Connecticut to employ girls.

narrative_blocks.header: They reprinted the London Quarterlies first
narrative_blocks.body: The firm ran three papers at once and reprinted standard editions, Dwight's Theology among them. They were the first house in the country to bring out the London quarterly reviews.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-three years on one newspaper
narrative_blocks.body: Middletown Whigs asked him in December 1837 to start a paper for them, and the first number of the Constitution appeared in January 1838. He conducted it for thirty-three years and was rarely out of his office in business hours.

narrative_blocks.header: Cautious in judgment, firm in opinion
narrative_blocks.body: He kept the respect of the men who disagreed with him, and a quiet humor went with it. He professed religion young at Center Church in Hartford under Dr. Strong, and was an influential man at North Church in Middletown afterward.

narrative_blocks.header: He was seven when they crossed the snow
narrative_blocks.body: He was born on West Mountain at Hartland in April 1796, the fourth surviving child, and was seven years old when the family made the hard March journey back to Durham in 1804. He died at Durham in May 1871 at seventy-five, the same age his elder brother Elisha reached.

people.research_notes: Farmer, district-school teacher, militia captain, selectman, assessor; deacon of First Congregational Church Durham for 40 years.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years a deacon, a winter schoolmaster
narrative_blocks.body: Gaylord Newton farmed, taught the district school in winters, served as militia captain, selectman, and assessor, and was for forty years a deacon of Durham’s First Congregational Church. His son Henry Gleason would carry the family name into Connecticut law.

narrative_blocks.header: He learned his book like a gentleman
narrative_blocks.body: A certificate from the Durham district school survives: Gaylord Newton behaves himself handsomely in school, and learns his book like a little gentleman, signed by his instructress Esther Maria Lyman.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-five winter terms of school
narrative_blocks.body: He began teaching at sixteen and kept at it for thirty-five winters, in district and select schools. George Atwell of Durham said he had been Gaylord's pupil, and so had every one of his nine children.

narrative_blocks.header: Delirious, his head was in the mill
narrative_blocks.body: Pneumonia nearly killed him in the spring of 1828 and his younger brother Roger Watson nursed him through it. He raved that his head was under the wheel of the grist-mill their grandfather had owned, which the brothers had tended as boys.

narrative_blocks.header: Captain before twenty, and refused major
narrative_blocks.body: He was captain of the eighth company of Connecticut militia before he was twenty, was chosen major and would not take it, and resigned after his illness in September 1828.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter married his brother's son
narrative_blocks.body: Caroline Gaylord Newton married Henry Huntington Newton in December 1864, and the two brothers' households became one family. Gaylord and Roger Watson had been raised in the same Durham house and were deacons of the same church.

narrative_blocks.header: He once left a day’s clams behind
narrative_blocks.body: A cousin’s fond letter recalled Gaylord spending a whole day gathering clams at Long Pond, only to drive home and realize — on seeing the water — that he had left every clam behind. It was offered as a gentle emblem of how memory fades with age.

bio.title: Deacon
bio.bio_blurb: Durham farmer and deacon of the First Church

narrative_blocks.header: The youngest son ended the homespun
narrative_blocks.body: Flax was sown and broken and spun and woven at the homestead, and nearly every kind of cloth the family wore was made there. That held for forty years after the move to Durham, until he — the youngest of the eight — changed it.

narrative_blocks.header: He added field to field at home
narrative_blocks.body: He never left the place, living in the house with his father Abner and his sister Content, and as his four sons grew he bought the neighbouring land until it was one of the largest farms in Durham. His uncle Burwell Newton's house on the hill that carries the name he bought and deeded to his eldest son, and it is in ruins now.

narrative_blocks.header: Photographed at eighty-five with three of them
narrative_blocks.body: The picture taken at eighty-five has Charlie and Katharine at his side and his namesake Roger Rossiter in his arms. His eyes were bright and his hair as black as a young man's; he was ready to die at eighty-seven, and life was pleasant to him to the last.

narrative_blocks.header: His son married his brother's daughter
narrative_blocks.body: Henry Huntington Newton married Caroline Gaylord Newton, Gaylord's youngest, in December 1864. Both fathers were deacons of the First Church in Durham, as their father Abner had been before them.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept the bills for her funeral
narrative_blocks.body: When his sister Content died in January 1859 it was he who settled with J. B. Southmayd for the imitation black walnut coffin with its engraved plate and plated trimmings, and with Sophronia Camp for three and a quarter yards of shrouding, a yard of book muslin, and the making of the shroud and cap. Both receipts, made out to R. W. Newton, survive.

narrative_blocks.header: She married the man who had taught her
narrative_blocks.body: She taught at the Durham district school before her marriage, and Gaylord Newton, whom she married in December 1838, had been her own schoolmaster. He was six years older than she was.

narrative_blocks.header: She met death as if taking a journey
narrative_blocks.body: Those who knew her said she watched the slow approach of certain death as calmly as a woman about to travel into a neighbouring state. To the last hour she was thoughtful for the husband and three children she was leaving.

people.research_notes: Second wife of Gaylord Newton; no children.

narrative_blocks.header: She had the household at fourteen
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother's long illness put the household into her hands at fourteen. She had an unusually fine ear and was the church organist at Durham while she was still a girl.

narrative_blocks.header: Her strength failed at the last letter
narrative_blocks.body: Dying at twenty-two, she set out to write to every scholar in her Sunday-school class. She got through all of them but the last.

narrative_blocks.header: A valedictorian who wrote for Britannica
narrative_blocks.body: Henry Gleason Newton graduated valedictorian of Yale Law’s class of 1872, taking prizes for the best common-law and civil-law essays. He went on to author the Encyclopedia Britannica’s article on bankruptcy and the probate-law chapter of Townsend’s edition of the Civil Officer.

narrative_blocks.header: He had himself unseated from office
narrative_blocks.body: Re-elected to the General Assembly in 1886 by a single vote, Newton discovered the count was in error — and, acting as attorney for his own opponent, contested the result and had himself unseated on the second day of the session, the shortest tenure on record.

narrative_blocks.header: He argued through insomnia and a speech defect
narrative_blocks.body: Like his ancestor Burwell Newton, Henry struggled to make himself understood, and suffered lifelong insomnia from boyhood. An indomitable persistence carried him over both, and he became one of the foremost lawyers in Connecticut.

narrative_blocks.header: Counsel to a bank and a presidential candidate
narrative_blocks.body: His clients included the Yale National Bank, Brown Brothers of New York, and William Jennings Bryan in the matter of the Bennett will. He argued many causes before the courts of last resort and was much consulted by the public and the bar alike.

narrative_blocks.header: Wesleyan took him three tries
narrative_blocks.body: Ill health drove him out of Wesleyan in 1861 and again in 1863. He taught school between attempts and finally graduated in 1870, Phi Beta Kappa.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught in his great-uncle's schoolroom
narrative_blocks.body: The South school at Northford, where he taught in 1865 and 1866, was the building Burwell Newton had taught in years before, and Burwell had left it a fund.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the History of Durham
narrative_blocks.body: His chapter on the town went into Beers's History of Middlesex County, and he was president of the day at Durham's bicentennial on the fourth of July 1899.

bio.bio_blurb: Genealogist of the Newtons and the Merwins

people.research_notes: Educated Durham Academy; taught school in Durham and Wallingford; active in Durham Historical Society. Both she and her husband were 7th-generation descendants of Miles Merwin (cousin marriage).

narrative_blocks.header: She published two family genealogies
narrative_blocks.body: Miles Merwin, 1623-1697, and One Branch of His Descendants came out under her name in 1909, and Rev. Roger Newton, Deceased 1683, and One Line of His Descendants followed. She wrote the Newton sketch that most of what is known of this family rests on.

narrative_blocks.header: She took the organ bench from her sister
narrative_blocks.body: Ellen Maria had been church organist at Durham until her death in 1863, and Caroline took the bench and kept it for years. She had taught school at Durham and Wallingford before her marriage at nineteen.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed, she went to Baalbek and Egypt
narrative_blocks.body: Henry Huntington Newton died in October 1907 after nearly forty-three years of marriage, and she travelled hard afterward. Europe in 1908, and in 1910 the Holy Land, Baalbek, Damascus and Egypt.

narrative_blocks.header: Her house was hung with Benjamin Coe's pictures
narrative_blocks.body: Henry Huntington Newton bought the old home of Benjamin H. Coe, the artist, in 1866, and they lived in it ever after. Several pictures Coe had painted seventy-five years earlier were still on its walls.

narrative_blocks.header: She never missed a meeting of the Society
narrative_blocks.body: The Durham Historical Society was formed at the town's bicentennial in 1899 and she was at every meeting of it. She was a Daughter of the American Revolution in the Mary Clapp Wooster Chapter, on her grandfather Abner's service.

people.research_notes: Schooled at Durham Academy; enlisted Co. B, 14th CT Regiment 1862 but rejected for disability after one night. Farmer; Board of Education; Republican; represented Durham in General Assembly 1902. Owner of the historic Curtis-Coe House.

narrative_blocks.header: One night in camp ended his soldiering
narrative_blocks.body: Henry Huntington Newton joined Company B of Connecticut’s 14th Regiment in 1862 but, after a single day and night of tent life, was rejected for physical disability. He returned to farming and represented Durham in the 1902 General Assembly.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept one of Durham’s oldest houses
narrative_blocks.body: With his wife Caroline, Henry owned the historic Curtis-Coe House — among the earliest structures still standing in Durham — long associated with the Curtis, Coe, Merwin, and Newton families. The house has remained in the Newton family since.

narrative_blocks.header: He surveyed land, then gave it up
narrative_blocks.body: He practised as a civil engineer and land surveyor before leaving the profession behind. He took the Horace Newton place at Durham, one of the four brothers who all settled in the same town.

narrative_blocks.header: He farmed the land bought in 1731
narrative_blocks.body: The homestead the first Abner Newton purchased in May 1731 came to him, and he kept it under excellent cultivation. He was a Republican like all his family and went to the General Assembly in 1907.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave a piano in his son's name
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth Imogene Foote died in 1889 after ten years of marriage, leaving him a boy of three, and her mother Selina Bunnell Foote stayed in the house until she died in 1911. After an accident killed Charlie at eighteen his father gave a fine piano for church use, with the boy's name engraved on a silver plate above the keyboard.

bio.bio_blurb: Durham farmer on the home place

narrative_blocks.header: Named for the rum that lost a ship
narrative_blocks.body: Selden Huntington of Haddam, a favourite uncle of his mother's, was a wealthy shipowner and a hard temperance man. Caught in a great storm at sea, he refused his crew the extra allowance of rum they demanded; they refused their orders in return, and the ship was lost.

narrative_blocks.header: The youngest son stayed on the farm
narrative_blocks.body: His three brothers took places of their own about Durham and he remained on the home farm with his father. Two of his four children were dead before they were twenty-two.

bio.bio_blurb: Connecticut banker turned Pueblo, Colorado financier

narrative_blocks.header: A presidential appointment in the West
narrative_blocks.body: After two decades in Middletown banking, Jonathan Burwell Kilbourn followed his health to Colorado in 1880 and rose through Pueblo’s First National Bank. In 1885 President Grover Cleveland appointed him receiver of public moneys at the Pueblo Land Office, a post he held until 1890.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a famous inventor’s granddaughter
narrative_blocks.body: In 1873 Kilbourn married Mary Adeline Douglas, granddaughter of the noted inventor William Douglas of Middletown, whose “Douglas Pump” was sold worldwide. Ironically, it was as a traveling salesman for the Douglas Pump company that Kilbourn first came west.

narrative_blocks.header: He saw a savings bank swell by millions
narrative_blocks.body: Before going west, Kilbourn rose from teller to treasurer of the Middletown Savings Bank across the 1870s, a period in which its deposits increased by several millions. He had begun his working life as purser aboard the steamship Liberty, running between New York and Havana.

narrative_blocks.header: A churchman who built a mansion out West
narrative_blocks.body: An elder and former treasurer of Pueblo’s First Presbyterian Church, Kilbourn built a prominent 1896 mansion where the family lived with domestic staff. His business reach extended to mining ventures across Nevada, California, and Colorado and a real-estate and loan agency.

career.organization: U.S. Land Office, Pueblo (appt. Pres. Cleveland)

narrative_blocks.header: A promising life cut short at nineteen
narrative_blocks.body: Jonathan Douglas Kilbourn graduated from Pueblo High School in 1893 and entered Chicago’s Armour Institute to study electrical engineering. A sudden illness took him the next summer, before his family could reach him; the institute’s president conducted his funeral.

narrative_blocks.header: He patented his own construction strips
narrative_blocks.body: A graduate of the Colorado School of Mines, William Douglas Kilbourn inherited his great-great-grandfather’s inventive streak, patenting “Kilbourn’s Construction Strips” at home and abroad. He worked as a chemist in steel plants and rose to superintend a large smelting plant at Murray, Utah.

narrative_blocks.header: A children’s librarian married to a colonel
narrative_blocks.body: Sancha Kilbourn spent many years as a children’s librarian in New London, New Hampshire. Her marriage to Col. Dale Garvey lasted sixty-four years, ending only when both died within months of each other in 2002.

bio.title: Rev.
bio.bio_blurb: Osage and Cherokee missionary; San Antonio pioneer

narrative_blocks.header: He buried a wife and child mid-journey
narrative_blocks.body: In 1821 he set out from New York with his wife Betsey and their children for Harmony Mission among the Osage. Their newborn died near Louisville and Betsey died near Shawneetown in Illinois, both before the mission was reached.

narrative_blocks.header: He married two missionary widows in turn
narrative_blocks.body: Widowed on the trail, he married Mary Hunt McCarty at Harmony Mission in 1822, the widow of the missionary John Seeley. After Mary died in 1835 he married a third missionary widow, Sophia Palmer Joslyn.

narrative_blocks.header: The first Protestant to settle San Antonio
narrative_blocks.body: He brought his family to San Antonio in 1848, when the town had scarcely a shingled roof among its adobe houses. Family record holds he was the first Protestant to settle there; he opened a school and helped found its First Presbyterian.

narrative_blocks.header: Six generations of Samuels before him
narrative_blocks.body: He was the sixth Samuel Newton in unbroken succession, back to the immigrant minister Roger Newton, and he carried that Connecticut line from a Woodbridge parsonage out to the Texas frontier.

narrative_blocks.header: She died in transit to the mission field
narrative_blocks.body: Betsey Baldwin married Samuel Newton in 1813 and bore him three children before the family set out for Harmony Mission in 1821. She died near Shawneetown, Illinois, following childbirth on the journey, her newborn having died days earlier; she was later memorialized at Woodbridge beside her parents.

people.research_notes: Widow of missionary John Seeley (d.1821). m. Samuel Newton at Harmony Mission 1822; mother of 7 of his children; died at the Forks of the Illinois mission station.

Daughter of John Hampden Palmer (d. War of 1812) and Lydia Loomis. Widow of missionary Matthias Joslyn. m. Samuel Newton 1835 as his 3rd wife; co-founder of First Presbyterian Church San Antonio 1851; survived him by 34 years.

narrative_blocks.header: At twenty-one she went to the Osage
narrative_blocks.body: Sophia Palmer, youngest of four sisters whose father died serving in the War of 1812, became a missionary at twenty-one — first to the Osage, then the Cherokee in Indian Territory. She married two missionaries in turn, burying the first at Dwight Mission in 1833.

narrative_blocks.header: She helped found a frontier church
narrative_blocks.body: After reaching San Antonio in 1848, Sophia taught school — many old San Antonians recalled being her pupils — and was a founder of the city’s First Presbyterian Church, organized in 1851. She outlived Samuel by thirty-four years, dying in 1899.

people.research_notes: Born at Harmony Mission. Lawyer, Civil War officer, mayor of San Antonio. His former home (the "Newton House") was uncovered in 2025 archaeology at Fox Tech campus.

narrative_blocks.header: A mission-born baby became San Antonio’s mayor
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Harmony Mission among the Osage in 1823 and took the name of a Russian prince the mission family admired. He read law, served as an officer through the Civil War, and was elected mayor of San Antonio.

narrative_blocks.header: His lost house surfaced in a school dig
narrative_blocks.body: Construction at San Antonio's Fox Tech High School turned up the remnants of his house in the south parking lot in 2025, along with the 1700s San Pedro acequia. The district filmed the dig and will set a plaque there.

narrative_blocks.body: He was born in the Cherokee Nation in Indian Territory in December 1834, where his father was at mission work, as his brother the Colonel had been born among the Osage. He married at San Antonio in 1867 and died there in 1918.

narrative_blocks.header: Four generations carried the name Galitzin
narrative_blocks.body: His father the Colonel was the first Samuel Galitzin Newton, born at Harmony Mission in 1823; he was the second, his son the third and his grandson the fourth. The name came from a Russian prince the mission family admired.

narrative_blocks.header: He died a week short of seventy-five
narrative_blocks.body: Born at San Antonio on 9 November 1856, he died there on 2 November 1931, seven days before his seventy-fifth birthday. He had outlived Bettie by eleven years, and their son Wallace by the same eleven.

people.research_notes: "Sadie"; m. William Woodworth Bogel 1882; 8 children; Marfa-area ranch family.

narrative_blocks.header: Her children were raised on burro milk
narrative_blocks.body: She could not nurse her eight children out on the ranch and raised them on burro milk, telling them the burro colts were their brothers. They were not weaned until ten or twelve, and the family lived a while in the cave at La Tinaja.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight children on the ranching country at Marfa
narrative_blocks.body: She was called Sadie, and married William Woodworth Bogel in 1882. They raised eight children out in the ranch country around Marfa, and her sister Jessie later gave the same name to a daughter of her own.

people.research_notes: m. Samuel Moore Gaines; mother of the TCU physicist Newton Gaines.

narrative_blocks.header: Her maiden name went into her son's
narrative_blocks.body: She was born a Newton at San Antonio in 1862 and married Samuel Moore Gaines in 1889. Their son was christened Samuel Newton Gaines and went through life as Newton, carrying her family name as his own.

people.research_notes: m. William Cassin 1885 (Irish immigrant farmer); the town of Cassin and Cassin Lake named for the family.

narrative_blocks.header: A town and a lake took her name
narrative_blocks.body: She married William Cassin in 1885, an Irish immigrant who farmed south of San Antonio. The settlement of Cassin and Cassin Lake in Bexar County both carry the family's name.

people.research_notes: Irish immigrant (County Kilkenny); prominent San Antonio farmer; built Cassin Lake Dam 1907; town of Cassin named for family.

narrative_blocks.header: A lake and a town bear his name
narrative_blocks.body: William Cassin, an Irish immigrant from County Kilkenny, became a prominent farmer south of San Antonio after marrying Charlotte Newton in 1885. He built the Cassin Lake Dam in 1907 to irrigate his land, and the flag-stop town of Cassin was named in the family’s honor.

bio.bio_blurb: West Texas sheep rancher and judge

narrative_blocks.header: Sheep, then cattle, and they called him Judge
narrative_blocks.body: He came out of a Shreveport drug-store family by way of the Louisiana State cadet corps and a year in Germany, took tuberculosis, and went west to mend. He ran ten thousand sheep south of Marfa, then cattle, and was Judge Bogel after.

narrative_blocks.header: Born in Ohio by mistake, called a Yankee
narrative_blocks.body: His mother was up in Ohio on a visit from Shreveport when he was born in 1855. Friends after the war would call him a Yankee for it, which he did not find funny, and he would lead with his left.

narrative_blocks.header: He practiced speeches naked on a table
narrative_blocks.body: Cadets at the Louisiana State military school steadied their nerves by standing on a barracks table stripped bare and delivering the next day's oration over the taunts of the rest. The president followed the noise and caught him at it.

narrative_blocks.header: His class refused carpetbagger diplomas
narrative_blocks.body: Louisiana diplomas had to carry the governor's signature, and in 1874 that was William Pitt Kellogg, whom the class held a carpetbagger. All of them refused theirs. Fifty years on he went looking for his and found the capitol had burned.

narrative_blocks.header: Fourteen consumptives, and two came out
narrative_blocks.body: He took a room in a San Antonio boarding house with thirteen other young men dying of tuberculosis. One of them, a doctor, meant to fight it with a toddy twice a day. At the end of the year only those two were alive.

narrative_blocks.header: Cattlemen roped his tent and dragged it away
narrative_blocks.body: He put ten thousand sheep on grass the cattlemen had run free for years. While the family was in Marfa for groceries they roped his tent and hauled it off, and the Bogels lived in a cave called La Tinaja until the house was up.

narrative_blocks.header: Free-list wool made a Republican of him
narrative_blocks.body: Wool went on the free list under Cleveland and the price fell to a tenth of what it had been. It did not break him but it bent him badly. He sold the sheep for cattle, and never again voted Democrat or looked a sheep in the face.

people.research_notes: b. Monterrey, Mexico; m. Morris P. Kirk; kept the family ranch brand.

narrative_blocks.header: Born in Monterrey, widowed at thirty-one
narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Monterrey in 1882 while her father was running sheep in Mexico. Harry Hubbard died aboard ship off Mazatlan in 1914, leaving her two small boys, and she brought them home to her parents at Marfa.

people.research_notes: "Gus".

narrative_blocks.header: He outlived the sale by four months
narrative_blocks.body: He and his brothers ran the Sauceda, the hundred-section spread south of Marfa that their father had leased and stocked. The Bogel Brothers ranch was sold in May 1934, and he was dead in a San Antonio hospital by the end of September.

narrative_blocks.header: The Sauceda is inside a state park now
narrative_blocks.body: The hundred sections he and his brothers ran south of Marfa lie inside Big Bend Ranch State Park today. He was photographed out there in a cowboy hat and a gun belt, in front of a brick building with a tin roof.

narrative_blocks.header: A son died at five; the name survived
narrative_blocks.body: Augustus Julius Bogel Jr. was born in 1921 and died at five in June 1927. A later son took the name again as the third, alongside Tom and their sister Margaret.

education.school_name: Agricultural and Mechanical College of Texas

narrative_blocks.header: He sang the gol-darned wheel to John Lomax
narrative_blocks.body: He was a student at the Agricultural and Mechanical College of Texas, taking electrical engineering in 1908, when he sang That Gol-Darned Wheel to the folklorist John Lomax. Zebra Dun came from him too.

narrative_blocks.header: A horse kicked him; he died next day
narrative_blocks.body: He was kicked in the head by a horse on the country south of Marfa, taken to hospital, and died the day after, in February 1919. He was thirty-three, and left a widow and a son of six.

people.research_notes: Storyteller whose 1953 ranch reminiscences (told to daughter Barclay Bogel Green) preserved the family’s West Texas history.

narrative_blocks.header: He preserved a ranching family’s tall tales
narrative_blocks.body: In 1953 he told his daughter Barclay the stories of his father's West Texas sheep and cattle country - the burro-milk childhood, the cave at La Tinaja they lived in, and Geraldo the foreman who shot two herders.

narrative_blocks.header: A lieutenant in the new Air Service
narrative_blocks.body: He took a commission as a second lieutenant of the Air Service in the First World War. He had married Sarah Barclay at Marfa in April 1916, and the two of them finished their lives at Brownsville on the lower Rio Grande.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-five years of trade in Mexico City
narrative_blocks.body: He spent thirty-five years in Mexico City in the import and export business, and came back to Brownsville only for his last two. His brother Galitzin, who outlived him by five months, was the one survivor his notice named.

narrative_blocks.header: A Texas cavalry private in the first war
narrative_blocks.body: He went to the First World War a private of Texas cavalry. Born at Marfa in 1889, he died at El Paso in 1938 at forty-eight, and was carried back to be buried at Marfa with his family.

people.research_notes: "Hennie".

narrative_blocks.header: From a Marfa ranch to the Philippines
narrative_blocks.body: She married Everett Collins, an ordnance officer out of Norwich, and left the ranch country for a life of army posts, the Philippines among them in the 1930s. A photograph of about 1916 has her beside her mother, both in long white dresses.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the mail that travelled by rail
narrative_blocks.body: He was superintendent of the Railway Mail Service at Fort Worth, the branch whose clerks sorted the post in moving cars between stations. Born in Tennessee in 1859, he died at Fort Worth in 1940.

narrative_blocks.header: His father left West Point for smallpox
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel Moore Gaines the elder entered West Point in 1834 and was called home by a smallpox epidemic. He took his degree at the University of Tennessee instead, and was teaching at Madisonville when his son was born there in 1859.

narrative_blocks.header: He outlived his father by thirty-four years
narrative_blocks.body: His father lived to ninety and died in 1906, styled by then the Hon. Samuel W. Gaines of Bowling Green in Kentucky. He himself died at Fort Worth in 1940, thirty-four years after him.

narrative_blocks.header: He killed bacteria with a terrific squeak
narrative_blocks.body: As TCU’s founding physics chairman, Newton Gaines pioneered using ultrasound to sterilize milk, holding patents for the method. A 1931 Science News report described his “terrific squeak” of high-pitched sound waves used to kill bacteria.

narrative_blocks.header: A kilted professor who threw boomerangs
narrative_blocks.body: He led the Texas Folklore Society and was an authority on working cowboy songs, cutting cylinders for the Library of Congress under John Lomax. Each spring he put on a kilt and a coloured cap to throw boomerangs from a campus hilltop.

narrative_blocks.header: He stenciled “stolen from TCU” on everything
narrative_blocks.body: He marked every piece of his laboratory apparatus, much of it homemade through the Depression, 'Stolen from TCU.' At his retirement luncheon his colleagues gave him a new pocketknife stencilled with the same words.

narrative_blocks.header: He sang as Jim New, signed as arranger
narrative_blocks.body: He cut four cowboy songs in one Dallas session for Victor on 12 October 1929. Two came out in 1931 on the budget label Timely Tunes, credited to a Jim New who did not exist, with his own name on both sides as arranger.

narrative_blocks.header: A rail wreck one side, whiskey the other
narrative_blocks.body: He sang Wreck of the Six Wheeler on one face, a railroad disaster ballad close kin to Ben Dewberry's Final Run. The reverse was For Work I'm Too Lazy, the Texas song also sung as Rye Whiskey or Jack o' Diamonds.

narrative_blocks.header: The label he appeared on lasted three months
narrative_blocks.body: Victor started Timely Tunes in April 1931 as a cheap line to ride out the downturn, and dropped it three months later after some forty records. Two of his sides were among the last things it issued.

narrative_blocks.body: Born at Fort Worth in 1892, she married James Foster Jackson and raised three sons in New York - Richard, Ralph and Willis. She died at Wilmington in Delaware in 1978, a long way from Texas.

narrative_blocks.header: A woman named Charlie, widowed at seventy
narrative_blocks.body: She was born Charlie Helen Jones at New York, in Henderson County, Texas, and went by Helen all her life. She married Newton Gaines at Fort Worth in 1922, was widowed in 1963, and died in California fifteen years after him.

people.research_notes: "Betty"; TCU geology degree 1948; worked for Shell Oil as a computer/programmer; later high-school math teacher; m. Robert K. Stanton 1957.

narrative_blocks.header: A geologist who became a “computer”
narrative_blocks.body: She worked for Shell Oil at Midland as a computer in the geophysics department, doing by hand the arithmetic the surveys ran on, and then as a programmer once the machines arrived.

narrative_blocks.header: Geology, then mathematics, then the welfare rolls
narrative_blocks.body: After three children she went back to college and taught high-school mathematics until 1978. She then joined the Orange County welfare department in California and retired from it in 1991 as an eligibility worker.

narrative_blocks.header: Her memorials went to her father's physics fund
narrative_blocks.body: She took her geology degree from TCU in 1948 and stayed a devoted alumna of a family that counted itself a TCU legacy. Gifts in her memory were asked for the Professor Newton Gaines Endowed Scholarship in Physics.

narrative_blocks.header: She was born on the Wallace plantation
narrative_blocks.body: She was born on 11 August 1862 on the Wallace plantation, which then stood on the Cibolo River in Bexar County, to Julian Devereaux Holcombe and Mary Ann Wallace Holcombe. She was schooled privately in San Antonio.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son died, and she went into decline
narrative_blocks.body: She had been ill for months, but the collapse came a few weeks after her son Wallace died in 1920. She died at 4:15 in the morning at the family home on Main Avenue, and was buried at Alamo Masonic.

narrative_blocks.header: Six nephews carried her to the grave
narrative_blocks.body: Her pallbearers were her husband's sisters' sons - E. W. and D. S. Cassin, Terrell Bartlett, T. J. Newton Jr., and Graves and Gallitzin Newton Bogel. The Cassin, Bogel and Newton households had all come out of one San Antonio family.

bio.bio_blurb: Assistant district attorney of San Antonio

narrative_blocks.header: The third Samuel, and the county's prosecutor
narrative_blocks.body: He was assistant district attorney of San Antonio, the office he held when his mother died in 1920. He had married May Ellen Tobin Bell in December 1905, and they had six children inside eleven years.

narrative_blocks.header: Her second name came from her mother
narrative_blocks.body: Deveraux was her mother's middle name before it was hers - Bettie Devereaux Holcombe, born on the Wallace plantation. She married Clinton Padgitt and was living at Waco when her mother died in 1920.

narrative_blocks.header: Named for a grandmother and a plantation
narrative_blocks.body: He was called Wallace for his mother's mother, Mary Ann Wallace Holcombe, and for the plantation on the Cibolo where his mother was born. He died in 1920, and his mother went into decline and followed him inside a few weeks.

people.research_notes: Second wife of Ainsworth Blunt (m. 1849). One daughter, Lillie.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at sixteen to a railroad builder
narrative_blocks.body: Martha married Benjamin Clark Morse, a Vermonter building the Western and Atlantic Railroad, at Cross Plains, Georgia, on 2 September 1842, when she was sixteen. Her first child, Harriet, was born at Chattanooga the next July.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed with seven children by 1864
narrative_blocks.body: Martha bore seven children over twenty years, and two of the boys, a Benjamin and the youngest, Lucian, died as small children. Benjamin died in February 1864, and Martha lived on until June 1898, when she died at Omaha, where her son John had settled.

bio.bio_blurb: Chicago and North Western chief engineer

people.research_notes: Lived to 94. Removed to the Chicago area; founder of the Blunt banking line.

narrative_blocks.header: A Dakota town bears his name
narrative_blocks.body: John was chief engineer of the Chicago and North Western Railway when it laid out a station in Hughes County, Dakota Territory, and the town of Blunt was named for him. Years before, he had been an officer of the Galena and Chicago Union, the first railroad out of Chicago.

narrative_blocks.header: An engineer on Chicago's railroads
narrative_blocks.body: John engineered railroads in the South before the Civil War, then went north to the Chicago lines and settled at Wheaton, Illinois. During the war his father and stepmother left Dalton, Georgia, to sit out the fighting with him in Illinois.

narrative_blocks.header: Born at the mission on Christmas Day
narrative_blocks.body: John was born at Brainerd Mission on Christmas Day 1828, the third of Ainsworth and Harriet Blunt's five children, and was nine when the Cherokees were driven west.

bio.title: Capt.
bio.bio_blurb: Union cavalry captain and wheat breeder

people.research_notes: Maintained family prominence in Dalton, Georgia.

cross_connections.display_label: spent forty years on the proteins of seeds at a Connecticut station

narrative_blocks.header: Four hundred kinds of wheat
narrative_blocks.body: Ainsworth was Bradley County's first scientific farmer, and he hybridized grains until he had bred more than four hundred strains of wheat, most of which he could name at a glance without reading the label.

narrative_blocks.header: Colorado, then New Mexico
narrative_blocks.body: Ainsworth went on to teach agriculture as a professor at the Colorado State Agricultural College, and in 1890 set up a new agricultural station in New Mexico.

narrative_blocks.header: A Union captain from East Tennessee
narrative_blocks.body: Ainsworth left the principalship of the Masonic Female Institute at Cleveland, Tennessee, in 1861 to serve with the Union's First Tennessee Cavalry, and rose to captain of Company F before he left the army in 1864.

narrative_blocks.header: Cleveland's school, then the county's
narrative_blocks.body: Home again in January 1865, Ainsworth reopened the girls' school at Cleveland and was the town's postmaster for eight years. In 1868 he became the first superintendent of Bradley County's schools.

narrative_blocks.header: He watched the Trail of Tears at seven
narrative_blocks.body: As a boy of seven Ainsworth stood by the road at Brainerd and watched the Cherokees file past on their way west, and the sight stayed with him all his life. Years later he could still talk and sing in the Cherokee language.

people.research_notes: Vice-president of Continental Illinois National Bank & Trust.

cross_connections.display_label: was a director of the Continental Illinois Bank and Trust

narrative_blocks.header: Vice-president of Continental Illinois
narrative_blocks.body: John was a vice-president of the Continental Illinois National Bank and Trust Company in Chicago. He married Carlene Curtis of Ilion, New York, in June 1898, and they raised four children at Evanston.

bio.bio_blurb: Chicago and North Western civil engineer

people.research_notes: Civil engineer for the Chicago & North Western Railway for 45 years.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-five years on the North Western
narrative_blocks.body: Frank followed his father, the road's chief engineer, onto the Chicago and North Western Railway and spent forty-five years there as a civil engineer. He and Nellie made their home in Madison for decades, on South Broom Street.

people.research_notes: Smith College graduate.

bio.bio_blurb: Co-founder, Blunt Ellis & Simmons investment bank

people.research_notes: Co-founder of Blunt Ellis & Simmons investment bank; trustee of Hull House and the Hadley School for the Blind.

narrative_blocks.header: From Lee Higginson to his own firm
narrative_blocks.body: Out of Dartmouth Jack went into investment banking with Lee Higginson in Chicago, and became a vice president and director of the Lee Higginson Corporation in 1939. In 1948 he founded Blunt Ellis & Simmons and was its senior partner until he died in December 1965.

narrative_blocks.header: A governor of the Investment Bankers
narrative_blocks.body: Jack chaired the Central States Group of the Investment Bankers Association and served as a governor of both that association and the Association of Stock Exchange Firms.

narrative_blocks.header: He banked, then gave his time away
narrative_blocks.body: Jack was a vice president and trustee of Jane Addams's Hull House in Chicago and a trustee of the Hadley School for the Blind in Winnetka.

narrative_blocks.header: Phi Beta Kappa and the Junior Prom
narrative_blocks.body: At Dartmouth Jack won Phi Beta Kappa, chaired the Junior Prom Committee and acted with Footlights.

bio.bio_blurb: Chicago lawyer and Evans Scholars Foundation chairman

cross_connections.display_label: won the first three women's western golf championships, from 1901
, his son-in-law, sat on Northwestern's board and founded Golden Apple
gave Northwestern's medical campus the Prentice Women's Hospital

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty years for caddie scholarships
narrative_blocks.body: Carleton was a founding member of the Evans Scholars Foundation, the college scholarships for caddies begun by his old friend the golfer Chick Evans, and chaired its trustees for more than fifty years. In his time 5,815 former caddies went to college on them.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-five years at Bell, Boyd & Lloyd
narrative_blocks.body: Carleton grew up in Evanston, took his law degree at Northwestern, and was a partner in the Chicago firm of Bell, Boyd & Lloyd for thirty-five years. In 1949 he was general chairman of Chicago's Community Fund campaign.

narrative_blocks.header: New England diving champion at Dartmouth
narrative_blocks.body: At Dartmouth Carleton was Phi Beta Kappa and New England diving champion on the swimming team, class of 1926. He went on to preside over its General Association of Alumni, and the college named the Blunt Alumni Center for him and made him a Doctor of Laws in 1978.

narrative_blocks.header: A life trustee of Northwestern
narrative_blocks.body: Carleton sat on Northwestern University's board of trustees for decades, died a life trustee, and raised much of the money for its Evans Scholars House. He was also president of the Western Golf Association, and his memorial service was held in the university's Alice Millar Chapel.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded the Country Club of Florida
narrative_blocks.body: Carleton founded the Country Club of Florida at the Village of Golf, where he lived and served as mayor, and the Ocean Club of Florida at Delray Beach. His nephew John Thorp Blunt was later the club's president.

narrative_blocks.header: He remarried at seventy-eight
narrative_blocks.body: Two years after Rebecca died, Carle married Helen Tobey in 1984. She was the widow of Newton Tobey of the Dartmouth class of 1925, a year ahead of his own, and his classmates welcomed her into the 1926 family.

people.research_notes: Northwestern B.S. Psychology; m. John Noble 1954; avid swimmer; co-founded "The Cat House" gift shop.

narrative_blocks.header: Five miles from Excelsior to Wayzata
narrative_blocks.body: Estelle swam a mile without stopping three times a week for decades, and many times swam the five miles across Lake Minnetonka from Excelsior to Wayzata. She golfed, canoed, kayaked and rode as well, and raised her four sons in Minnesota on the Vikings and the Twins.

narrative_blocks.header: The Cat House, with her best friend
narrative_blocks.body: With her sister-in-law and best friend, Sally Partridge Noble Kahn, Estelle founded The Cat House, a gift shop for cat lovers.

narrative_blocks.header: A minister for a second husband
narrative_blocks.body: In 1990 Estelle married the Rev. Harold King, who had been senior minister of the Wayzata Community Church for twenty years. They were married until his death in 2002.

bio.bio_blurb: Northern Trust executive and investment adviser

people.research_notes: Dartmouth A.B. 1958, Tuck & Thayer Schools 1959; 30-year career at Northern Trust, retired as President of Northern Investment Management; founded Blunt Associates.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-five years in trusts and finance
narrative_blocks.body: John Thorp Blunt joined Northern Trust in 1960 and spent thirty years there, retiring as president of its asset-management arm before founding his own advisory firm. He sat on the boards of companies including Schwinn Bicycle, carrying on the family’s long Chicago finance tradition.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty years with Susan Fencl
narrative_blocks.body: At Dartmouth John met Susan Fencl of Evanston, and they married on 11 January 1960, the year he joined Northern Trust. They were married sixty years.

narrative_blocks.header: Chairman of the Allendale trustees
narrative_blocks.body: John chaired the board of trustees of the Allendale Association and served the Northfield Community Fund and United Christian Community Services. In Florida he was president of The Country Club of Florida.

career.role: Various roles to President, Northern Investment Management

cross_connections.display_label: was a vice-president of Northern Trust after the Bank of San Francisco

people.research_notes: "Nellie".

narrative_blocks.header: President of the North Western Woman's Club
narrative_blocks.body: Nellie, a native of New York State, lived in Madison for more than fifty years and was a past president of the Chicago and North Western Woman's Club there. She belonged to St. Raphael's Cathedral parish and the Catholic Woman's Club.

bio.bio_blurb: Beloit trial lawyer and city attorney

people.research_notes: Beloit attorney and trial lawyer; Beloit city attorney; UW Law graduate.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-eight years at the Beloit bar
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph grew up near Afton, took his law degree at the University of Wisconsin and practised in Beloit for twenty-eight years, first with Woolsey and Arnold, soon Woolsey, Arnold and Johnston, and on his own from 1938. A skilled trial lawyer, he was at one time city attorney of both Beloit and South Beloit.

people.research_notes: WWII U.S. Navy; 30 years U.S. Postal Service.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty years at the Madison Post Office
narrative_blocks.body: Joe finished Beloit Memorial High School in 1945 and went into the Navy in the last months of the war. After ten years with General Telephone he moved to Madison and worked thirty years for the Postal Service, retiring in 1989.

people.research_notes: "Patti"; m. Arthur C. Davis 1948; civil-rights activist at St. Peter Claver House in the 1950s.

narrative_blocks.header: Civil rights from the St. Peter Claver House
narrative_blocks.body: In the 1950s Patti worked for civil rights and against poverty as an active member of the St. Peter Claver House. Widowed at twenty-six when Art died in July 1955, she raised their two daughters and worked as a draftsman for Fairbanks Morse and in banking, insurance and the law.

people.research_notes: "Art"; m. Patti Johnston 1948.

narrative_blocks.header: A voice in St. Jude's Laetare choir
narrative_blocks.body: Art finished Beloit High School in 1939, sang in St. Jude's Laetare choir and worked at George Brothers, and before that at the Dunnick Clothing store. He died after a long illness in July 1955, at thirty-four.

people.research_notes: Shreveport druggist (store est. 1885) and trained physician; superintendent of Allen’s Infirmary; plantation owner; Louisiana State Pharmaceutical Association; Master Mason and Knight of Pythias.

narrative_blocks.header: A trained doctor who chose the drugstore
narrative_blocks.body: John Little Hodges studied medicine, served a year as superintendent of Allen’s Infirmary, then opened a Shreveport drugstore in 1885 that quickly won local favor. At the Louisiana State Fair he took two diplomas — one for the best display of drugs, another for perfumes.

narrative_blocks.header: Druggist, planter, and Master Mason
narrative_blocks.body: Beyond his drugstore, Hodges owned and farmed a fertile plantation across Bossier and Webster Parishes that yielded handsomely each year. A Master Mason and Knight of Pythias, he was counted among the leading druggists of Shreveport while still a young man.

cross_connections.display_label: founded the order he was knighted in, in 1864

people.research_notes: LCDR, U.S. Naval Reserve; served in both World Wars.
Harcum School graduate; DAR State Regent; member Colonial Daughters of the 17th Century and Order of the Crown of Charlemagne.

narrative_blocks.header: A Texas daughter who ran with horses
narrative_blocks.body: Charlotte Newton left San Antonio to marry into Pennsylvania’s Hanover Shoe Farms, the standardbred-breeding dynasty. A DAR State Regent and member of the Colonial Daughters of the 17th Century, she bridged a frontier Texas lineage and Eastern society.

people.research_notes: President of Hanover Shoe Farms (standardbred horse breeding).

narrative_blocks.header: He bred champions at Hanover Shoe Farms
narrative_blocks.body: Lawrence Baker Sheppard led Hanover Shoe Farms, one of the foremost standardbred horse-breeding operations in the country. His wife and daughter Charlotte would both remain active in the farm’s direction for decades.

people.research_notes: Harcum Junior College; DAR State Regent; Colonial Daughters of the 17th Century; Order of the Crown of Charlemagne; bred standardbred horses; Hanover Shoe Farms board.

narrative_blocks.header: Regent, horsewoman, and farm director
narrative_blocks.body: Charlotte Sheppard DeVan served as a DAR State Regent and belonged to the Order of the Crown of Charlemagne, tracing deep colonial and medieval lineages. She bred standardbred horses and sat on the board of Hanover Shoe Farms, the family business.

people.research_notes: "Sonny"; died in a plane crash at 26.
of Orlando, FL.

Lt. Col., U.S. Army surgeon; commanded the 42nd Field Hospital in the European Theater (WWII) and was Chief of Surgery, 8054th Evacuation Hospital (Korea); awarded Croix de Guerre, Bronze Star, five campaign stars; W&L and Penn Medicine.

narrative_blocks.header: A battlefield surgeon in two wars
narrative_blocks.body: William Todd DeVan commanded the 42nd Field Hospital in the European Theater during World War II and served as Chief of Surgery of an evacuation hospital in Korea. He was decorated with the Croix de Guerre, the Bronze Star with Oak Leaf Cluster, and five campaign stars.

bio.title: Col.
bio.bio_blurb: U.S. Army colonel and political science professor

people.research_notes: Kansas State 1936, Emporia State M.A. 1960; U.S. Army 1936–1959, retired colonel; Bronze Star & Army Commendation Medal; professor of political science at Emporia State for 16 years; co-founder of the Ausbon Sargent Land Preservation Trust.

narrative_blocks.header: From the Army to the lecture hall
narrative_blocks.body: Dale Garvey served in the U.S. Army from 1936 to 1959, retiring as a colonel with the Bronze Star after World War II and Korea. He then taught political science at Emporia State University for sixteen years and helped found a New Hampshire land-preservation trust.

bio.bio_blurb: Naturalist and cookbook author; "The Sea-Beach at Ebb-Tide"

people.research_notes: 2nd daughter of Eunice Newton Foote and Elisha Foote; writer; m. Francis Benjamin Arnold, a New York coffee importer, 1869. Author of "The Sea-Beach at Ebb-Tide" (1901), a long-used guide to shore life.

narrative_blocks.header: Her tide-pool guide shaped Rachel Carson
narrative_blocks.body: Augusta Foote Arnold’s 1901 "The Sea-Beach at Ebb-Tide" was the first popular guide to American intertidal life, cited later by both Rachel Carson and Ed Ricketts. Promoted in the children’s magazine St. Nicholas, it may have steered a generation toward marine biology.

narrative_blocks.header: A scientist who moonlighted as Mary Ronald
narrative_blocks.body: To keep her cookery writing separate from her natural-history work, Augusta published two best-selling cookbooks — The Century Cook Book and Luncheons — under the pen name Mary Ronald. Only her seashore guide carried her own name.

narrative_blocks.header: A leaping blenny may bear her name
narrative_blocks.body: The Pacific leaping blenny, Alticus arnoldorum, is thought to honor Augusta: the naturalist who named it had read her book and gave several species similar epithets. A member of the Torrey Botanical Club and the AAAS, she counted herself a serious scientist.

notable.notable_blurb: Tide-pool naturalist; wrote a seminal intertidal guide

education.institution_name: Private schools, Saratoga Springs, New York
education.school_name: Private schools, Saratoga Springs, New York

career.organization: The Century Co. (The Century Cook Book, 1895; Luncheons, 1905)

collected the shells her tide-pool book taught readers to find
signed her zoology and hid her poems behind Richard De Veaux
