people.research_notes: New York coffee importer; son of Benjamin Green Arnold (founding president of the Coffee Exchange). m. Augusta Foote 1869.
Died at 25.

bio.bio_blurb: Assistant Attorney General under President Taft

people.research_notes: Harvard College & Columbia Law; Assistant Attorney General under George W. Wickersham in the Taft administration; practiced law in Reno, NV.

narrative_blocks.header: A grandson of Eunice Foote in Taft’s cabinet
narrative_blocks.body: Henry Newton Arnold, son of the naturalist Augusta Foote Arnold, served as Assistant Attorney General under George W. Wickersham in the Taft administration. He had earlier practiced law as far west as Reno, Nevada.

people.research_notes: Lived to ~101; residing in NYC 1907.

bio.bio_blurb: Founding president of the New York Coffee Exchange

notable.notable_blurb: Founding president of the New York Coffee Exchange

narrative_blocks.header: He opened the floor of the Coffee Exchange
narrative_blocks.body: The New York Coffee Exchange elected him founding president at its 1882 establishment, and he presided over the new futures market for a trade he had spent decades in. His son married the naturalist daughter of Eunice Newton Foote — the scientist who first tied carbon dioxide to a warming sky.

narrative_blocks.header: He printed the Arnold family tree
narrative_blocks.body: A New York merchant, Benjamin compiled and printed the Arnold family tree with his cousin George C. Arnold. He had the gravestones of his ancestor Stephen Arnold, who died in 1699, and Stephen's wife Sarah brought from the old home at Pawtuxet and set in a family lot at Swan Point Cemetery in Providence.

narrative_blocks.header: A distant cousin of Benedict Arnold
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin descended from William Arnold, who sailed from Dartmouth in 1635 and helped Roger Williams found Providence. The traitor Benedict Arnold came down the same tree through William's son Benedict, Rhode Island's governor, and his wounded leg has a monument at Saratoga that leaves out his name.

people.research_notes: Founding president, New York Coffee Exchange (1882). Father of Francis Benjamin Arnold (I01816), who married Augusta Foote Arnold (HD6528).

cross_connections.display_label: was his daughter-in-law, the naturalist who married his son Francis

Mother-in-law of a Ninth Generation Hooker

bio.title: Brig. Gen.
bio.bio_blurb: Buffalo Soldier officer; survivor of the 1877 Staked Plains ordeal

notable.notable_blurb: 10th Cavalry officer who led men out of the Staked Plains

narrative_blocks.header: He found the way out of the desert
narrative_blocks.body: A white officer of the all-Black 10th Cavalry, he survived the 1877 Nolan expedition, when his troop ran out of water on the Llano Estacado and men drank horses' blood to live. He found the old wagon trail at night that led them back.

narrative_blocks.header: He took a commission in a Colored regiment
narrative_blocks.body: He enlisted as a private of the 71st New York Militia at seventeen, and in September 1864 took a second lieutenancy in Company A of the 127th United States Colored Infantry. He was nineteen.

narrative_blocks.header: Private in 1862, brigadier general in 1910
narrative_blocks.body: He went in as a militia private in May 1862 and came out a brigadier general at Philadelphia in 1910, by way of the 39th Infantry, twenty-seven years with the 10th Cavalry, and the 5th, 14th and 15th after that.

narrative_blocks.header: The Tribune called him Roosevelt's friend
narrative_blocks.body: He died in 1919 and was buried at Arlington, where Flora joined him ten years later in the same plot. The New York Tribune ran his notice under the line: Brig. Gen. Cooper, Roosevelt's Friend, Dead.

people.research_notes: Father of Forrestine Cooper Hooker. Rose from Civil War private to Brigadier General; buried Arlington. Wife Flora Green Cooper also buried Arlington.

cross_connections.display_label: was his son-in-law, heir to the Sierra Bonita ranch
rode across the Staked Plains with Mackenzie in the 1874 campaign

career.notes: Buffalo Soldier regiment

bio.bio_blurb: Western novelist; "Child of the Fighting Tenth"

notable.notable_blurb: Western novelist raised among the Buffalo Soldiers

narrative_blocks.header: A child of the fighting Tenth Cavalry
narrative_blocks.body: Forrestine Cooper grew up on frontier army posts as daughter of an officer in the all-Black 10th Cavalry, the Buffalo Soldiers. She later turned those childhood crossings of the plains into the memoir "Child of the Fighting Tenth."

narrative_blocks.header: She once set off a cavalry alarm
narrative_blocks.body: Sent at twelve to drive a borrowed milk cow three miles to camp, she chased it up a canyon wall. A soldier who saw her raised the alarm that Apaches had the girl, and the whole troop saddled up armed to fetch her back.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine books, and one told by a pony
narrative_blocks.body: She wrote nine novels for young readers out of her army childhood and her years as a ranch woman in southern Arizona. In Star, the Story of an Indian Pony, a Comanche chief's mare and her foal talk their way through the frontier war.

narrative_blocks.header: Wyatt Earp told her his life himself
narrative_blocks.body: Her account of Wyatt Earp came from Earp's own telling, and it is read now with an eye on how much of it he invented. Her frontier memoir, Child of the Fighting Tenth, was published after her death.

narrative_blocks.header: A cattle baron's son, and then a divorce
narrative_blocks.body: In 1885 she married Edwin Rockwell Hooker, son of the Arizona cattle baron Henry Clay Hooker. The marriage ended in divorce, and she brought up a daughter, Forrestine, and a son, Harry Edwin.

cross_connections.display_label: won custody of her son in an 1895 divorce, and lived by her pen
raised animals on her farm and taught children to ride
retold Schoolcraft's legends as American Indian Fairy Tales

narrative_blocks.header: She bore a daughter in Indian Territory
narrative_blocks.body: She followed the Tenth Cavalry from post to post, and her youngest was born out in Indian Territory in November 1872. She outlived Charles by ten years and was buried beside him at Arlington.

narrative_blocks.header: Her second marriage ended in tragedy
narrative_blocks.body: Forrestine Hooker, daughter of the western novelist, married first J. Thomas Froelich and then Jesse Lee Gatlin. In February 1935 she was fatally shot in Ajo, Arizona; her husband died of self-inflicted wounds the same day.

people.research_notes: Dau. of Edwin R. & Forrestine Cooper Hooker. m1 J. Thomas Froelich (son Forrest Hooker Froelich b.1913), m2 Jesse Lee Gatlin.

bio.bio_blurb: Sierra Bonita rancher; built the ranch feed mill

people.research_notes: Reinstated Sierra Bonita farming operation and built a feed mill. m. Jessie G. Peck. After his 1952 death, son-in-law William Hughes managed the ranch.

narrative_blocks.header: He brought the plow back to Sierra Bonita
narrative_blocks.body: Grandson of the ranch’s founder, Harry Edwin Hooker reinstated the farming operation at Sierra Bonita and built a feed mill. The ranch passed through his daughter’s family after his death in 1952.

bio.bio_blurb: Fourth-generation steward of Sierra Bonita Ranch

people.research_notes: Known as "Rinki." m. Charles Steelman Davis 1942; later m. William A. Hughes, who helped manage Sierra Bonita.

narrative_blocks.header: Rinki kept the ranch for fifty-six years
narrative_blocks.body: After her father, Harry, died in 1952, Rinki and her second husband, Bill Hughes, moved onto the Sierra Bonita to run it for her mother, Jessie. Rinki held the ranch until her death in 2008, when her grandson Jesse took full charge of it.

narrative_blocks.header: He won his summers back in court
narrative_blocks.body: Charles and Jacqueline Hooker divorced in Arizona on 19 September 1949, and he kept their son, Chuck, for July and August at his house in Manhattan Beach, California, where he worked as a metallurgist. When a court cut that to two weeks in 1953, Charles appealed, and in November 1954 the Arizona Supreme Court reversed it.

people.research_notes: Fifth generation at Sierra Bonita; owned the Lightning Ranch. Father of Jesse Hooker Davis.

narrative_blocks.header: Sole owner of the Lightning Ranch
narrative_blocks.body: Chuck was part owner and manager of the Sierra Bonita, the fifth Hooker generation there, before going out on his own as sole proprietor of the Lightning Ranch near Willcox and Bonita. He ranched it until his death on 28 September 2010, at sixty-six.

narrative_blocks.header: A Pinkerton watched him at the beach
narrative_blocks.body: After his parents divorced in 1949, Chuck spent his summers with his father at Manhattan Beach. In 1953, when he was nine, his mother had a Pinkerton agent watch him fish off the pier and surf; the agent found him an intelligent boy who did nothing foolish, and in 1954 the Arizona Supreme Court gave his father back the summers.

narrative_blocks.header: An engineer at Hughes, then law school
narrative_blocks.body: After Bonita Elementary School, the Judson boarding school in Scottsdale and a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, Chuck worked as an engineer at Hughes Aircraft in California, took courses at USC, and went on to graduate from Southwestern Law School.

narrative_blocks.header: Met in 1978, married in 1990
narrative_blocks.body: Chuck met Mary Combs in 1978 and married her twelve years later, in 1990; she stayed on at the Lightning Ranch after him. He had been born at Albany, Georgia, on 13 March 1944, to Charles Davis and Jacqueline Hooker.

bio.bio_blurb: Arizona Farm and Ranch Hall of Fame inductee

people.research_notes: Sixth-generation Hooker steward of Sierra Bonita, Arizona’s oldest ranch (est. 1872). Raises Hereford cattle; purchased his late father’s Lightning Ranch to keep the original holdings intact. Inducted Sierra Bonita into the Arizona Farm & Ranch Hall of Fame.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixth generation on Arizona's oldest ranch
narrative_blocks.body: Jesse runs the Sierra Bonita, which his great-great-great-grandfather Henry Clay Hooker founded in 1872 and which marked 150 years in the family in 2022. The ranch is bigger than him, Jesse has said; it is just his turn to take care of it.

narrative_blocks.header: Six hundred head, gathered on horseback
narrative_blocks.body: Jesse runs about six hundred cattle on the ranch's sixty thousand acres, a Hereford base herd crossed with Red and Black Angus bulls. Trucks and four-wheelers are for chores and checking water; the cattle are gathered on horseback, because vehicles leave tracks that damage the grass.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixteen miles of pipe for the wildlife
narrative_blocks.body: Jesse drilled a well and laid about sixteen miles of underground pipeline to carry water into country where wildlife could not otherwise live, and the Arizona Association of Natural Resource Conservation Districts named the Sierra Bonita its Conservation Ranch of the Year.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought his father's Lightning Ranch
narrative_blocks.body: Jesse took full charge of the Sierra Bonita when his grandmother Rinki died in 2008. When his father, Chuck, died two years later, Jesse bought Chuck's Lightning Ranch and kept the original Hooker holdings whole.

narrative_blocks.header: He led the Cochise-Graham Cattle Growers
narrative_blocks.body: Jesse has been president of the Cochise-Graham Cattle Growers and represented Graham County on the board of the Arizona Cattle Growers' Association. In 2025 he was inducted into the Arizona Farm and Ranch Hall of Fame.

narrative_blocks.header: Raised in San Diego, back for roundups
narrative_blocks.body: Born in Arizona, Jesse grew up in San Diego and came out to the Sierra Bonita for the roundups. He went east to Cornell University, where he played football.

narrative_blocks.header: No burn-and-turn on the Sierra Bonita
narrative_blocks.body: Jesse has no use for what he calls burn-and-turn ranches, bought, overstocked and sold off. His family has been on the Sierra Bonita long enough, he says, to know what numbers the land will hold and still flourish.

notable.notable_blurb: Connecticut Congressman and state constitution framer

narrative_blocks.header: A farmer who helped write the state’s charter
narrative_blocks.body: Orange Merwin sat on the committee of twenty-four that drafted Connecticut’s 1818 constitution before winning two terms in Congress. Between sessions he returned, by his own preference, to agricultural pursuits in New Milford.

narrative_blocks.header: He watched Congress argue over a slave’s injury
narrative_blocks.body: In an 1828 letter, Merwin described ten days of House debate over whether to compensate for a man enslaved and injured at the Battle of New Orleans — a debate that dissolved into speeches for and against Andrew Jackson. He noted the man himself was forgotten for hours at a time.

narrative_blocks.header: Millers kept complaining about tramp iron
narrative_blocks.body: Selling milling equipment in 1941 he heard the same grievance everywhere: wire, nails, bolts, horseshoes and hammers riding down the chute with the grain, wrecking the machinery and threatening a fire in the dust.

narrative_blocks.header: He built the first one in his basement
narrative_blocks.body: Alnico — aluminium, nickel, cobalt and iron — held up to thirty times the magnetic strength of cobalt steel. In the basement of his Erie house he made a permanent magnetic plate separator from it, sold it to a grain miller in 1942, and had a company.

narrative_blocks.header: He was seventy-one when he started it
narrative_blocks.body: Most of a working life had gone by before the separator. He ran Eriez for the decade he had left, and his son Bob and daughter-in-law Betty took it into foreign markets in the 1950s; his grandson Richard is its chairman now.

narrative_blocks.header: Erie's basement firm reached six continents
narrative_blocks.body: Eriez makes magnetic separation, flotation, metal detection and material-handling equipment from twelve wholly owned subsidiaries on six continents, with something near a thousand employees. Guinness recognised its electromagnet as the largest ever built in 1997; it still hangs in a Chilean copper mine.

narrative_blocks.header: Erie's hall of fame, fifty-nine years late
narrative_blocks.body: WQLN-TV named him to the city's hall of fame fifty-nine years after his death, in a class that included the railroad man William L. Scott and the Juilliard president Peter Mennin.

narrative_blocks.body: Garwood enlisted on 11 September 1862 in Company H of the 19th Connecticut Volunteers and was promoted sergeant after the regiment reached Virginia. That winter it stood picket duty around Alexandria.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at twenty in the Alexandria hospital
narrative_blocks.body: Garwood died of typhoid fever at the regimental hospital in Alexandria on 23 January 1863, four months after he enlisted. His regiment, renamed the 2nd Connecticut Heavy Artillery that November, saw its first heavy fighting at Cold Harbor in 1864.

bio.title: Dr.
bio.bio_blurb: Co-founder of the Massachusetts Eye and Ear Infirmary

notable.notable_blurb: Founded the Massachusetts Eye and Ear Infirmary, 1824

education.school_name: Studied under Dr. John Collins Warren

narrative_blocks.header: He brought European eye surgery home to Boston
narrative_blocks.body: After training under John Collins Warren, Reynolds crossed to London to study the eye under William Lawrence and surgery under Astley Cooper and Abernethy, then to Paris under Bichat and Dupuytren. He returned among the first Americans equipped to practice the new ophthalmic surgery.

narrative_blocks.header: His infirmary still runs two centuries on
narrative_blocks.body: In 1824 Reynolds and John Jeffries opened a charity eye clinic that became the Massachusetts Eye and Ear Infirmary, the first of its kind in the country and now past its bicentennial. It made the diseases of the eye and ear a recognized American specialty.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventy years of practice, one cased portrait
narrative_blocks.body: Reynolds practiced for more than seventy years, long enough that the colleagues of his prime had nearly all died before him. He survives in a single daguerreotype of the Society for Medical Improvement, the twelve Boston physicians who met to dissect each other’s hardest cases.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the first Boston mayor’s daughter
narrative_blocks.body: In 1825 Reynolds wed Margaret Wendell Phillips, daughter of John Phillips, Boston’s first mayor. Her younger brother Wendell Phillips would become the era’s most famous abolitionist orator, a connection Reynolds married into at the height of his surgical fame.

narrative_blocks.header: He operated on his father's blindness
narrative_blocks.body: His father told him one morning that he was at last totally blind. Reynolds found a cataract and, knowing of no such operation ever performed in America, went into his closet to pray, took a glass of sherry and operated. His father saw again.

narrative_blocks.header: He prescribed ninety minutes of manual labour
narrative_blocks.body: Lecturing in 1835 on physical culture for literary men and especially clergymen, he urged an hour and a half of manual labour and an hour out of doors every day. The eye he called the channel of most of our knowledge of nature.

narrative_blocks.body: Margaret married into the Reynolds medical family, but her younger brother Wendell Phillips became the most celebrated abolitionist orator in America. Their father, John Phillips, was the first mayor of Boston.

narrative_blocks.header: She linked a mayor’s house to a surgeon’s
narrative_blocks.body: Daughter of Boston’s first mayor, Margaret married the founding surgeon of the Massachusetts Eye and Ear Infirmary. Their son carried both legacies into a Harvard professorship in obstetrics.

bio.title: Dr.
bio.bio_blurb: Harvard professor of obstetrics for over twenty years

notable.notable_blurb: Harvard professor of obstetrics; physician in Boston

narrative_blocks.header: A classicist pressed into the family trade
narrative_blocks.body: Reynolds excelled in the classics at Boston Latin and taught there two years before his father pressed him into Harvard Medical School. He took to obstetrics, and held the Harvard chair in the subject for more than two decades until 1885.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a granddaughter of Paul Revere
narrative_blocks.body: In 1859 Reynolds married Jane Minot Revere, granddaughter of the Revolutionary silversmith. The match folded the Revere line into a family already two generations deep in Boston medicine, with his father the founding surgeon of the eye-and-ear infirmary.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandson couldn’t name his colleagues
narrative_blocks.body: A book of his medical correspondence passed to a grandson who, in 1913, wrote the hospital librarian that he could not vouch for the handwritten list of names inside or recognize the hand. The doctor’s working world had grown unreadable within two generations.

narrative_blocks.header: He was better at delivering than at billing
narrative_blocks.body: Reynolds cared more for bringing his patients safely through childbirth than for collecting from them, and his frequent failure to send a bill at all was the despair of his wife. He served as president of the American Gynecological Association.

narrative_blocks.header: He advised eight or ten, and had eight
narrative_blocks.body: In an address he recommended that healthy and well-to-do couples have sons and daughters eight or ten, or thereabouts, and he raised four of each. A Nahant paper wondered how he packed sixty-five feet of family into so small a cottage.

bio.bio_blurb: Granddaughter of Paul Revere; Boston matriarch

people.research_notes: Daughter of Joseph Warren Revere and Mary Robbins; granddaughter of Paul Revere.

narrative_blocks.header: The Revere name entered Boston medicine
narrative_blocks.body: Jane Minot Revere was a granddaughter of Paul Revere and daughter of the copper magnate Joseph Warren Revere. Her 1859 marriage to Dr. John Phillips Reynolds braided the Revere line into three generations of Boston physicians.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son bought back the Revere house
narrative_blocks.body: Among Jane’s eight children was John Phillips Reynolds Jr., who in 1902 purchased and preserved her grandfather’s house in Boston’s North End. The Revere ancestry she carried became the cause that defined his life.

narrative_blocks.header: Her name carried two Boston dynasties
narrative_blocks.body: Jane Minot Revere bore the names of two old Boston families, the Minots and the Reveres, at the moment they joined the medical Reynoldses. Her children’s names, Paul Revere Reynolds and Mary Robbins Reynolds among them, kept the ancestry deliberately visible.

narrative_blocks.header: She left no room for argument
narrative_blocks.body: Right was right to Jennie Revere and wrong was wrong, and she laid the law down early enough that all eight children grew up sure of the fundamentals. An observer of the household called them an appallingly righteous family.

bio.bio_blurb: Financier who saved the Paul Revere House, 1902

notable.notable_blurb: Saved the Paul Revere House in 1902

career.organization: Walter M. Lowney Company, chocolate manufacturers
Suncook Mills, Submarine Signal Co., Peter Bent Brigham Hospital, and others

narrative_blocks.header: He bought his ancestor’s house to save it
narrative_blocks.body: In 1902 Reynolds, a great-grandson of Paul Revere, purchased the decaying Revere house in the North End and formed an association to restore it as a museum. It survives as the oldest building in downtown Boston.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept the letters of the abolitionists
narrative_blocks.body: As grandnephew of Wendell Phillips, Reynolds preserved Phillips’s collection of letters from the leading abolitionists, Susan B. Anthony, Garrison, Emerson, Lydia Maria Child, and others. The correspondence is now catalogued at the Harvard Library.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried Revere money to a Union spy
narrative_blocks.body: In the 1880s and ’90s Reynolds traveled to Richmond to deliver money from the Revere family to the aging Union spy Elizabeth Van Lew, who had cared for two imprisoned Revere cousins. After her death he marked her grave with a boulder from the Massachusetts State House.

narrative_blocks.header: He raced a Kaiser and built a galleon
narrative_blocks.body: A passionate yachtsman, Reynolds raced the German Kaiser at Kiel and the young King of Spain at Bilbao in 1907, then published his account anonymously as "The Cruise of the Golden Eagle." His Maine vacation house, designed to resemble a Spanish galleon, still stands as a coastal landmark.

narrative_blocks.header: He moved a museum and shunned the credit
narrative_blocks.body: Among the financiers who relocated the Museum of Fine Arts to Huntington Avenue and built the Copley Plaza on its old site, Reynolds preferred to organize ventures without taking visible charge. He disliked being photographed, and pictures of him are scarce.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Wilson sisters, two lines, one wedding
narrative_blocks.body: Reynolds descended from Susanna Wilson Rawson. Lucretia Munroe, whom he married in 1884, descended from Susanna's sister Sarah Wilson Torrey. Both women were granddaughters of Thomas Hooker; the bride stood one generation further down.

people.research_notes: m. Lucretia Revere Munroe 1884; children Priscilla and John Phillips Reynolds III. Great-great-grandson of Paul Revere; grandnephew of abolitionist Wendell Phillips. Published "The Cruise of the Golden Eagle" anonymously.

narrative_blocks.header: Her middle name came from an aunt
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother's sister, Lucretia Watson Lunt, married Paul Joseph Revere, and the baby was named for that aunt — Revere and all. She had no Revere blood of her own. The husband she took in 1884 did: he was Paul Revere's great-grandson.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at twenty, a mother at twenty-one
narrative_blocks.body: They married in 1884, he being twenty-one himself. Priscilla came the next year and John Phillips the third in 1887.

narrative_blocks.header: The Marlborough house was put in her name
narrative_blocks.body: He bought 79 Marlborough in April 1907 and by the January following had transferred it to a trustee for her sole use and her heirs. She kept it after he died and sold it in the summer of 1922.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived him by twenty-seven years
narrative_blocks.body: He died in December 1920 and she and their son stayed on at Marlborough Street through 1921 before moving. She died at Milton in 1948 and lies beside him.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a sixth cousin once removed
narrative_blocks.body: John Phillips Reynolds Jr. came down from Susanna Wilson Rawson; Lucretia came down from Susanna's sister Sarah Wilson Torrey. The two women were daughters of Rev. John Wilson Jr. and Sarah Hooker, and the lines had parted in the 1680s.

bio.bio_blurb: Son of Paul Revere; president of Revere Copper

notable.notable_blurb: Ran Revere Copper; pioneered rolled-copper sheets

narrative_blocks.header: He turned his father’s mill into an empire
narrative_blocks.body: Named for the Bunker Hill martyr who sent his father on the midnight ride, Joseph Warren Revere took over the Canton copper works in 1811 and built Revere Copper into a major industrial concern. He perfected the rolling of copper into large sheets for sheathing ships.

narrative_blocks.header: His sons fell at Antietam and Gettysburg
narrative_blocks.body: Two of his children died in the Civil War — assistant surgeon Edward at Antietam and Colonel Paul Joseph Revere of wounds after Gettysburg. His daughter Jane married into the Boston Reynolds family of physicians.

narrative_blocks.header: He commissioned matching portraits of father and son
narrative_blocks.body: In 1813 Joseph commissioned Gilbert Stuart to paint his 78-year-old father Paul Revere, and sat for a companion portrait in the same pose. The pair of paintings, now at the Museum of Fine Arts, attests to the bond between them.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a lieutenant governor’s daughter
narrative_blocks.body: In 1821 Joseph married Mary Robbins, daughter of Edward Hutchinson Robbins, a former lieutenant governor of Massachusetts. The match tied the self-made Revere copper fortune to one of the colony’s old governing families.

people.research_notes: Third of eight children of Paul Revere by Rachel Walker. Father of Jane Minot Revere (married Dr. John Phillips Reynolds).

bio.bio_blurb: Revolutionary patriot and silversmith of the midnight ride

notable.notable_blurb: Silversmith whose 1775 midnight ride became legend

narrative_blocks.header: His midnight ride became American legend
narrative_blocks.body: On the night of April 18, 1775, the Boston silversmith rode to warn the militia that British troops were marching on Lexington and Concord, a feat immortalized in Longfellow’s poem. He was also a Son of Liberty and engraver of the famous Boston Massacre print.

narrative_blocks.header: He rolled the first American copper sheets
narrative_blocks.body: After the war Revere turned silversmith’s skill into industry, casting bells and cannon and, in 1801, opening the first copper-rolling mill in North America. His firm became Revere Copper and Brass; his son Joseph ran it into a great-granddaughter’s Boston marriage.

narrative_blocks.header: The worst naval defeat before Pearl Harbor
narrative_blocks.body: Massachusetts sent forty-four ships and more than a thousand men up the Penobscot in July 1779 to drive the British out of the coast they had renamed New Ireland, and Revere went as lieutenant colonel commanding the artillery. Three weeks of siege failed, a British relief fleet came up from New York in August, and the whole American fleet was driven up the river and burned. It stood as the country's worst naval defeat until Pearl Harbor.

narrative_blocks.header: A court-martial nearly shadowed his name
narrative_blocks.body: Revere’s militia service ended in disgrace after the disastrous 1779 Penobscot Expedition, and he pushed for years to clear his name. A 1782 court-martial finally exonerated him, and the midnight ride later eclipsed the episode entirely.

narrative_blocks.header: He identified a hero by dental work
narrative_blocks.body: Revere practiced dentistry to support his family, wiring in false teeth of walrus ivory and gold. When Joseph Warren fell at Bunker Hill and was buried in a mass grave, Revere later identified the body by a dental bridge he had made, an early forensic identification.

bio.bio_blurb: First mayor of Boston; Massachusetts Senate president

notable.notable_blurb: First mayor of Boston, 1822

narrative_blocks.header: Boston’s first mayor was a compromise choice
narrative_blocks.body: When Boston incorporated as a city in 1822, rivals Harrison Gray Otis and Josiah Quincy deadlocked, and their supporters settled on John Phillips. Ill health led him to decline a second term, and he died twenty-eight days after leaving office.

narrative_blocks.header: A daughter to medicine, a son to abolition
narrative_blocks.body: Through his daughter Margaret, Phillips became grandfather to the Boston Reynolds physicians; his son Wendell Phillips grew into the most famous abolitionist orator of the age. He had eight children with Sally Walley.

narrative_blocks.header: A mayor who sat on Harvard’s governing board
narrative_blocks.body: Before the mayoralty, Phillips was elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and the American Antiquarian Society, and joined the Harvard Corporation in 1812. He gave the city’s Fourth of July oration in 1794, at twenty-three.

narrative_blocks.header: The town meeting had become a farce
narrative_blocks.body: Boston had governed itself by town meeting since its founding, and by 1820, with forty-three thousand people, fewer than fifty voters turned out to one. Phillips chaired the committee of twelve that wrote the charter making the town a city.

narrative_blocks.header: They nearly called the office Intendant
narrative_blocks.body: The charter's first draft called the head of the city an Intendant, and the French word was put aside for Mayor before the voters approved it. Phillips was inaugurated on 1 May 1822 and gave the office a single year.

narrative_blocks.header: He aimed to allure, not to repel
narrative_blocks.body: Quincy said his administration laid the foundation of the city's prosperity deep and on right principles. Otis said his aim was to allure, not to repel, to reconcile by gentle reforms, not to revolt by startling innovations.

people.research_notes: First mayor of Boston (1822-23); president of the Massachusetts Senate. Father of Margaret Wendell Phillips (m. Dr. Edward Reynolds) and abolitionist Wendell Phillips.

notable.notable_blurb: Preeminent abolitionist orator of his era

narrative_blocks.header: One speech made him abolition’s golden trumpet
narrative_blocks.body: In December 1837, the 26-year-old lawyer leapt to the stage at Faneuil Hall to denounce the men who excused the murder of abolitionist editor Elijah Lovejoy. The extemporaneous speech catapulted Phillips into the front rank of the antislavery movement, where he stayed for decades.

narrative_blocks.header: Abolition cost him his practice and his society
narrative_blocks.body: His marriage to abolitionist Ann Terry Greene and his embrace of the cause exiled Phillips from Boston’s elite and ended his law practice; his own family considered committing him as mad. He gave away over forty thousand dollars to those in need across his life.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept fighting long after emancipation
narrative_blocks.body: Unlike many allies, Phillips insisted that the vote and land were as vital as freedom, and he carried the fight into women’s suffrage, labor reform, temperance, and Native American rights. He ran, unsuccessfully, for governor of Massachusetts on a labor ticket in 1870.

narrative_blocks.header: He fought to seat women in London
narrative_blocks.body: At the 1840 World Anti-Slavery Convention in London, Phillips pressed, unsuccessfully, to seat the American women delegates whom the organizers had refused. Stanton and Mott later dated the birth of the women’s rights movement to that rebuff.

bio.bio_blurb: Founded the first literary agency in America

notable.notable_blurb: America’s first literary agent

narrative_blocks.header: He invented the American literary agent
narrative_blocks.body: Reynolds came to New York in 1891 selling books for Cassell of London, and in 1893 opened the first literary agency in the United States — a trade that did not exist here. He held the agencies of Heinemann, Sampson Low and Constable besides.

narrative_blocks.header: The month he opened, the market blew up
narrative_blocks.body: McClure's appeared in May 1893 at fifteen cents, Cosmopolitan cut to twelve and a half in July and Munsey's to ten in September, against Harper's thirty-five. Serial rights soon mattered more to his office than book rights.

narrative_blocks.header: He made an author write frail for loose
narrative_blocks.body: The great magazines printed only what could be read aloud to a whole family, and Reynolds had to say so. He got Albert Bigelow Paine to change a loose woman in a Century story to a frail one.

narrative_blocks.header: A syllabus of a client list
narrative_blocks.body: He represented Stephen Crane, Conrad, Shaw, Wells, Galsworthy, Tolstoy, Leacock, Wodehouse and Richard Wright. Walter Hines Page, later ambassador to London, said he would have been a credit to the diplomatic service.

narrative_blocks.header: Harvard clubs, and the one he actually liked
narrative_blocks.body: Out of Boston Latin and Adams Academy he took his Harvard degree in 1887. He joined the Institute of 1770, the Hasty Pudding and Delta Phi, but the club he cared for was the Philosophical.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Fords, no radio, and baggy tweed
narrative_blocks.body: Tall, spare and awkward among the groomed commuters, he wore tweed that bagged at the knees. He would leave the train at Crestwood or Hartsdale, short of Scarsdale, and walk home to a house of books and open fires with no radio in it.

narrative_blocks.header: Revere on one side, Phillips on the other
narrative_blocks.body: A great-grandson of Paul Revere and a great-nephew of Wendell Phillips, he carried the midnight rider's name and the abolitionist's blood into the business of letters.

narrative_blocks.body: Grindall Reynolds held Concord’s Unitarian pulpit from 1858 to 1894, the decades when Emerson, Thoreau, and the Alcotts made the town a capital of American letters. He is buried among them in Sleepy Hollow’s Authors’ Ridge.

narrative_blocks.body: Susan left him William Fairfield and Richmond Peters Burr; Priscilla bore Benjamin Munroe Burr in 1922. He died at Dobbs Ferry in March 1971 and Priscilla seven months later.

burial.plot_notes: Sleepy Hollow Cemetery, Westchester County NY; interred 5 May 2012.

narrative_blocks.header: The Pacific, then Parris Island for Korea
narrative_blocks.body: He fought with the Marine Corps in the Pacific during the Second World War, and was recalled afterwards to Parris Island to train Marines for combat in Korea. He took his Harvard degree with the class of 1945.

narrative_blocks.header: He sold chemicals for DuPont and Hercules
narrative_blocks.body: His working life went in marketing for DuPont and the Hercules Chemical Company. He and Ginny kept a place at Georgetown in Maine from 1974 and retired to St Augustine in 2005; she died six weeks before him in 2012.

people.research_notes: Son of George Lindsley Burr and Priscilla Munroe Reynolds. VP at Guaranty Trust; later marketing executive at DuPont and Hercules Chemical. m. Virginia Monks.

bio.bio_blurb: Painter, blues guitarist, and family historian

burial.plot_notes: Sleepy Hollow Cemetery, Westchester County NY.

narrative_blocks.header: He painted landscapes and old buildings
narrative_blocks.body: He painted landscapes and historical architecture, played blues guitar, and wrote local and family histories. As a docent for the Society for the Preservation of New England Antiquities he took visitors through the Moffatt-Ladd House at Portsmouth.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixteen years helping people stop drinking
narrative_blocks.body: He was a member of Alcoholics Anonymous for more than sixteen years and helped many people in Portland and southern Maine through recovery. He took a summa cum laude degree from the University of Southern Maine and died of pancreatic cancer at fifty-one.

narrative_blocks.header: Georgetown remembered her for forty years
narrative_blocks.body: From 1974 she and Ben spent most of each year at Georgetown in Maine, twice wintering there, and she gave her time to the Georgetown Quilting League, the Georgetown Historical Society and Bath Memorial Hospital. She outlived one son and died six weeks before her husband.

people.research_notes: Descendant of Roger Williams. President of the Children’s Association in the 1920s, a forerunner to the Department of Child Welfare.

narrative_blocks.header: Three posts at twenty-two, and a boys club
narrative_blocks.body: At twenty-two Stead was secretary of the Consumers' League in the mornings, librarian of the Brearley School in the afternoons, and in the evenings ran a boys' club for the Nurses' Settlement in the Henry Street district. The club held her till half past ten on weeknights and from two till half past ten on Sundays.

narrative_blocks.header: They met arguing about the Consumers' League
narrative_blocks.body: Mrs. Charles Russell Lowell, who had founded the league, brought her to the Social Reform Club on Second Avenue for an evening on whether its principles could be made to work. Reynolds was the club's secretary. They married in September 1899 at her mother's house in Plainfield, Connecticut.

narrative_blocks.header: A doctor's advice moved them to the country
narrative_blocks.body: Emmett Holt, the children's physician, urged country air for a delicate second child, and in 1906 the Reynoldses built at Scarsdale, twenty miles north of New York. They took the house that December, when Mary was four, Revere two and Wendell five months old.

bio.bio_blurb: Literary agent who ran the family agency

narrative_blocks.header: He inherited America’s first literary agency
narrative_blocks.body: Paul joined his father's pioneering agency when he graduated from Williams in 1926 and later became its president, representing leading British and American authors until 1978. The agency's records now fill nearly three hundred boxes at Columbia.

narrative_blocks.header: Alex Haley, Malcolm X, and the James estate
narrative_blocks.body: Across half a century Reynolds represented Alex Haley, Malcolm X, Richard Wright, William Shirer, Howard Fast and Morris West, and the estate of Henry and William James. He wrote five books of his own, among them The Middle Man: Adventures of a Literary Agent.

narrative_blocks.header: They said every hmmm raised the price
narrative_blocks.body: An author called him the late George Apley for his slow New England manner and swore the price went up every time he said hmmm in a negotiation. A Doubleday editor in chief called him an old-time agent, tough but fair, who unlike most read every book he sold.

narrative_blocks.header: He called some of his rivals predatory sharks
narrative_blocks.body: Reynolds founded the Society of Author's Representatives, the country's oldest body of literary agents, and led it for years. A number of the people listed as agents, he wrote in 1966, are not really agents but predatory sharks.

narrative_blocks.header: More beautiful than the Black Forest?
narrative_blocks.body: Paul's house at Chappaqua filled with editors and authors, and with the books they had dedicated to him at his urging. One fall evening he marched a noted author from Vienna through the woods, asking again and again whether it was not more beautiful than the Black Forest; the author kept nodding, and never told him he was colorblind.

people.research_notes: Son of Paul Revere Reynolds and Amelia Stead. President of the Paul R. Reynolds Agency.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the Army’s medical supply in WWII
narrative_blocks.body: As a brigadier general, Reynolds served as chief of the Army Medical Supply Service in the Office of the Surgeon General from 1942 to 1945. He had charge of medical supplies across the wartime force.

narrative_blocks.header: From utility president to Harvard’s back office
narrative_blocks.body: After the war and a stint as president of Columbia Gas and Electric, Reynolds became administrative vice president of Harvard from 1946 to 1960. He brought a general’s logistics to the running of the university.

people.research_notes: Son of Dr. Edward Reynolds and Harriet Wolcott Parker. m. Dorothea Curtis Jordan.

narrative_blocks.header: A Harvard gunner lost just after the armistice
narrative_blocks.body: Charles Parker Reynolds, Harvard class of 1918, served as an operations officer with the 101st Field Artillery in the 26th “Yankee” Division. He died in Lorraine in January 1919, after the armistice, and lies in the Saint-Mihiel American Cemetery.

people.research_notes: Son of Dr. Edward Reynolds and Harriet Wolcott Parker. Captain, 101st Field Artillery, 26th Division. Recorded in Memoirs of the Harvard Dead. Died Jan 10 1919, after the armistice (likely illness during the occupation), not in combat.

narrative_blocks.body: George married Ruth Sears Cheney in 1931, and they were distant cousins. Their nearest shared ancestor was Thomas Hooker himself: George came down from his daughter Sarah, born in 1630, and Ruth from his son Samuel, born in 1633. The two branches had run apart for three centuries.

narrative_blocks.header: She died three days after her second son
narrative_blocks.body: Richmond Peters Burr was born at Boston on 23 September 1918 and she died there on the twenty-sixth, twenty-nine years old. Her husband married her first cousin Priscilla fifteen months afterward.

narrative_blocks.header: The portrait hung in the family eighty years
narrative_blocks.body: Her parents had Frank Benson paint her about 1909. The picture passed to her and her husband at Massachusetts and St Michael's in Maryland, then by his 1983 bequest to a cousin of his, and came to the National Gallery of Art in 1992.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a captain in April 1915
narrative_blocks.body: She married Clarke Withers of New York on 14 April 1915, two days after her twenty-first birthday. He outlived her by ten years and kept the Benson portrait until he died.

bio.bio_blurb: Episcopal rector at Malden and Brockton

career.organization: Christ Church, Broadway and 71st Street, New York

narrative_blocks.header: He started a mission in a rented block
narrative_blocks.body: In Lent 1897, rector of St Paul's at Brockton, he began holding Episcopal services in private houses at Whitman. The first regular service was held in Jenkins' Block on the Sunday before All Saints' Day, and the date gave the mission its name.

narrative_blocks.header: He paid Frank Benson to paint his daughter
narrative_blocks.body: He and his wife commissioned the portrait of their daughter Margaret from Frank Benson, the American impressionist, about 1909. It stayed in the family for eighty years and reached the National Gallery of Art in 1992.

people.research_notes: Son of John Woolfolk Burke of the Alexandria banking firm Burke and Herbert. University of Virginia. Alexandria alderman 1887-1897 and 1901-1907.

bio.bio_blurb: Harvard mathematician; first master of Lowell House

notable.notable_blurb: Harvard geometer; first master of Lowell House

narrative_blocks.header: He taught a future president at Groton
narrative_blocks.body: Before joining Harvard, Coolidge taught at Groton, where one of his pupils was Franklin Delano Roosevelt; the two remained friends for life. He went on to spend his whole career at Harvard, chairing its mathematics department.

narrative_blocks.header: He held Oxford’s first science degree
narrative_blocks.body: After Harvard, Coolidge took the very first Bachelor of Science ever awarded by Oxford, in 1897, then a doctorate at Bonn under Eduard Study. His treatises on the circle, the sphere, and non-Euclidean geometry became standards.

narrative_blocks.header: He built Lowell House from raw brick
narrative_blocks.body: Named the first master of Lowell House in 1930, Coolidge had to invent the residential culture of a building “new and raw from the builders’ hands.” His vision shaped Harvard’s house system for generations.

narrative_blocks.header: A geometer who commanded two thousand men
narrative_blocks.body: During the First World War, Coolidge served as a major and liaison officer to the French General Staff, with two thousand American men under his command in Paris. France made him a chevalier of the Legion of Honor in 1919.

narrative_blocks.header: In retirement he wrote mathematics’ history
narrative_blocks.body: After retiring in 1940, Coolidge turned to the history of his field, publishing studies of geometrical methods and "The Mathematics of Great Amateurs." He was a record-setting miler in his Oxford days and a lifelong oarsman.

people.research_notes: m. Theresa Reynolds 1901; seven children. President of the Mathematical Association of America (1925); VP of the American Mathematical Society. Descendant connection to Thomas Jefferson via the Coolidge family.

narrative_blocks.header: She gave the portrait to the nation
narrative_blocks.body: After her husband died she gave Janet Gregg Schroeder's 1977 bust of him to the National Portrait Gallery. He had run the Boston Athenaeum for twenty-seven years.

narrative_blocks.header: A Coolidge buried at Monticello
narrative_blocks.body: Her father was the Harvard geometer Julian Lowell Coolidge and her mother a Reynolds, and the Coolidge line runs back to Jefferson. She lies in his burying ground, as her daughter and son-in-law would.

people.research_notes: Died age 3½ of scarlet fever, 1907.

Son of Julian Lowell Coolidge and Theresa Reynolds. Educator at Hotchkiss School; m.(1) Susan Thistle Jennings 1927, m.(2) author Olivia Ensor 1946. NOT to be confused with his great-uncle Archibald Cary Coolidge (1866-1928), the Harvard historian and first library director.

narrative_blocks.header: He shared a name with a famous uncle
narrative_blocks.body: A Hotchkiss schoolmaster for twenty years and a Navy officer in the Second World War, Archibald Cary Coolidge lived to ninety-nine. His second wife was the children’s author Olivia Coolidge, and he carried the name of his great-uncle, Harvard’s first library director.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty years at Hotchkiss
narrative_blocks.body: He took his Harvard degree in 1927 and an Oxford B.Litt. in 1929, taught English at Harvard for a year, and then went to the Hotchkiss School at Lakeville and stayed until 1950. The Navy had him for three of those years as a lieutenant commander, and Trinity College, Dublin gave him his doctorate in 1937.

narrative_blocks.header: From headmaster to Steuben Glass
narrative_blocks.body: After Hotchkiss he was headmaster of the Manlius School in upstate New York for two years, executive director of the English-Speaking Union in Manhattan from 1952 to 1958, and an executive of Steuben Glass, then taught at the Landon School in Bethesda until he retired. Summers he spent at his camp on Squam Lake.

narrative_blocks.header: He died three months short of a hundred
narrative_blocks.body: He was ninety-nine when he died in his apartment at Essex, Connecticut, leaving his wife Olivia, two daughters and two sons. There were fourteen grandchildren and fifteen great-grandchildren.

bio.bio_blurb: Director of Harvard’s Fogg Museum for twenty years

notable.notable_blurb: Fogg Museum director; MFA Boston president

narrative_blocks.header: He gave up architecture for its history
narrative_blocks.body: The 1932 International Style show that Hitchcock and Philip Johnson put on had fired him for modern architecture, so he went to Columbia to build it. He decided within a year that he had no talent for design, and crossed to New York University to study its history instead.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty years steering the Fogg
narrative_blocks.body: Named director of Harvard’s Fogg Art Museum at thirty-four, Coolidge ran it for two decades, strengthening its Islamic and modern holdings and adding the museum’s first modernist works. He treated the museum as a laboratory for training future curators.

narrative_blocks.header: He roller-skated between his train commutes
narrative_blocks.body: A co-founder of the Society of Architectural Historians, Coolidge later presided over the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston. He was known to roller-skate between stations on his Princeton-to-New-York commute.

narrative_blocks.header: He studied under the scholars Hitler drove out
narrative_blocks.body: New York University had just taken on Erwin Panofsky and Karl Lehmann, both lately out of Nazi Germany, and he enrolled in 1936 to work with them. Walter Friedlaender took his dissertation.

people.research_notes: Son of Julian Lowell Coolidge and Theresa Reynolds. m. Mary Elizabeth “Polly” Welch 1935.

bio.bio_blurb: Director of the Boston Athenaeum; “leading cultural figure”

notable.notable_blurb: Boston historian and Athenaeum librarian

narrative_blocks.header: Boston’s leading cultural figure for a generation
narrative_blocks.body: From the Boston Athenaeum, which he directed from 1946 to 1973, Whitehill led nearly every New England cultural institution and wrote more than a dozen books, including the standard topographical history of Boston. The New York Times called him the city’s leading cultural figure.

narrative_blocks.header: He transcribed a medieval codex in Spain
narrative_blocks.body: Trained as a medievalist, Whitehill earned a London doctorate on the Romanesque architecture of eleventh-century Spain and made the first full transcription of the Codex Calixtinus at Santiago de Compostela. The Spanish Civil War sent him home to American maritime history.

narrative_blocks.header: He addressed a queen at the Bicentennial
narrative_blocks.body: For the 1976 Bicentennial, Whitehill delivered a televised address on Boston’s history at the Old State House before Queen Elizabeth II. An Episcopalian Republican who kept a fifteen-thousand-volume library in a converted barn, he founded the journal The American Neptune.

narrative_blocks.header: His papers run to a wartime admiral
narrative_blocks.body: What he left is mostly institutional — the Massachusetts Historical Society, the bodies he catalogued in Independent Historical Societies, libraries, his own books. Among it are his journals and his correspondence with Admiral Ernest J. King.

narrative_blocks.header: His widow gave his head to the nation
narrative_blocks.body: Janet Gregg Schroeder modelled him in 1977, the year before he died, beard and moustache and all. Jane Revere Coolidge Whitehill gave the sculpture to the National Portrait Gallery.

people.research_notes: m. Jane Revere Coolidge 1930, a great-granddaughter of Dr. John Phillips Reynolds and (via the Coolidges) a descendant of Thomas Jefferson. Recording secretary of the Massachusetts Historical Society; editor for the Colonial Society of Massachusetts.

bio.bio_blurb: Author of classical retellings and biographies for youth

notable.notable_blurb: Newbery Honor author and classicist

career.role: Teacher of Greek, Latin and English
career.organization: Schools in Germany and England, then the Low-Heywood and Winsor Schools

narrative_blocks.header: She made the ancient world speak to children
narrative_blocks.body: Daughter of the British historian Sir Robert Ensor, Olivia Coolidge taught classics before publishing twenty-seven books, beginning with "Greek Myths" in 1949. Her retellings brought Homer and the Greek legends to generations of young readers.

narrative_blocks.header: A Newbery honor and a shelf of lives
narrative_blocks.body: Her "Men of Athens" was a 1963 Newbery Honor book, and she wrote young-adult biographies of Churchill, Gandhi, Edith Wharton, Eugene O’Neill, and Tom Paine. Critics praised her objective scholarship that credited genius without hiding its flaws.

narrative_blocks.header: She married into a Harvard dynasty at thirty-eight
narrative_blocks.body: In 1946 the London-born classicist married Archibald Cary Coolidge of Connecticut, a widower with four children, and became a naturalized American. She wrote on into her nineties, living to ninety-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: She taught Greek in Germany, England and America
narrative_blocks.body: After Oxford Olivia taught Greek, Latin and English in Germany and in England, then crossed to America, where she taught at the Low-Heywood School in Stamford and the Winsor School in Boston before her marriage.

narrative_blocks.header: From the Persian court to Socrates condemned
narrative_blocks.body: Men of Athens framed the Golden Age in short stories: the Persian court at Sardis, the battle of Salamis, an athlete at the Olympic games, a potter in the marketplace, and at the close the day Socrates was condemned to death.

people.research_notes: m. Archibald Cary Coolidge 1946 (his 2nd marriage). Papers held at the University of Minnesota Children’s Literature Research Collections.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty years in the same choir
narrative_blocks.body: She sang at St. Paul's Memorial Church in Charlottesville for almost sixty years, and served on its vestry and as senior warden. She had come down from Massachusetts in 1959 when her husband joined the Darden faculty.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept the graveyard at Monticello
narrative_blocks.body: She was a custodian of Jefferson's burying ground, read for Recording for the Blind, and volunteered at the university library. She was buried in the graveyard she had looked after.

narrative_blocks.header: Her daffodils took prizes
narrative_blocks.body: She gardened her own ground and belonged to the Garden Club of Virginia, and her daffodils won. Summers went to the family house at South Dartmouth and sailing on Buzzards Bay.

narrative_blocks.header: Born in Barcelona, like her father's chronicles
narrative_blocks.body: She was born in Spain in 1931, where her father was working on a medieval codex, and she kept detailed accounts of her own travels the way he had. She outlived her husband, her sister Diana and her daughter Joy.

career.organization: Darden Graduate School of Business, University of Virginia

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-three years at Darden
narrative_blocks.body: He joined the faculty of the University of Virginia's Darden Graduate School of Business in 1959 and stayed to emeritus. He died at Charlottesville in December 2002, at seventy-three.

narrative_blocks.header: He lies in the Jefferson graveyard
narrative_blocks.body: He was buried at Monticello, in the family burying ground his wife had spent years looking after. Her Coolidge line ran back to Jefferson.

career.organization: Weldon Cooper Center for Public Service, University of Virginia

narrative_blocks.header: She went where the conflict was
narrative_blocks.body: For nine years she ran the Center for the Study of Mind and Human Interaction and edited its journal, travelling to Estonia, Greece and Turkey for its work on ethnic conflict. Then she went to global health, and to South Africa, Brazil and Tanzania.

narrative_blocks.header: The University's highest award for an employee
narrative_blocks.body: Twenty years of service brought her the Leonard Sandridge Award. The letters her colleagues wrote to nominate her spoke less about her competence than about her kindness.

narrative_blocks.header: Her degree came nine months before the end
narrative_blocks.body: Her master's in public health came through in January 2011 and she died in October, at fifty-one, at home in Esmont. Her son was a first-year at Williams, the college she had gone to herself.

narrative_blocks.header: Married the year he left Harvard
narrative_blocks.body: Polly Welch, daughter of Ralph Waldo and Mary B. Welch, married John Coolidge in 1935, the year he graduated from Harvard. Their daughter, Penny, went to Westover and Radcliffe and married William Bradford Warren in 1955, while John was director of the Fogg.

narrative_blocks.header: Remembered in the church he had studied
narrative_blocks.body: Polly died in April 2003, at ninety-one, and her memorial service was held at Christ Church, Cambridge, the 1760 building her husband had studied and written about. The family asked that gifts go to the John Coolidge Objects Laboratory at Harvard or to the Arnold Arboretum.

bio.bio_blurb: New York attorney general and advocate
bio.photo_notes: Portrait of Samuel Austin Talcott. Cloudinary.

notable.notable_blurb: Attorney General of New York

narrative_blocks.header: He beat Daniel Webster at the Supreme Court
narrative_blocks.body: Arguing a landmark trusts-and-perpetuities case before the U.S. Supreme Court, Talcott prevailed against Daniel Webster himself. The dispute, over the Sailors' Snug Harbor estate, was a stage few country-trained lawyers ever reached. The victory sealed his standing among the era's great advocates.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight years as New York's attorney general
narrative_blocks.body: Appointed attorney general of New York in 1821, Talcott held the office for eight years. He was a leading member of the Albany Regency, the machine that ran the state for the Van Buren faction. Few lawyers argued more often before its highest courts.

narrative_blocks.header: From a country office to the front rank
narrative_blocks.body: Talcott studied law in the office of Gold and Sill and was admitted to the bar in 1812. He built his practice outward from Lowville to Utica before reaching New York City. Within a decade he stood among the most respected advocates in the state.

narrative_blocks.header: Forced out for “irregular habits”
narrative_blocks.body: In 1829 Talcott resigned the attorney generalship under the phrase “irregular habits.” It was the period's polite euphemism for a drinking problem. The brilliance of his public career ran alongside that private struggle.

narrative_blocks.header: The bar said his learning was never surpassed
narrative_blocks.body: At his death the New York Bar gathered to mourn him in the Supreme Court chamber. Its resolution praised talent and scholarship “rarely equaled and never surpassed” at the bar of the state. He was forty-six.

bio.bio_blurb: Founder of the Cowles Commission for economics

people.research_notes: Alfred Cowles III (1891-1984), "Bob." Yale 1913, Skull and Bones. Founder/president of the Cowles Commission for Research in Economics (1932, Colorado Springs; to Chicago 1939; to Yale 1955 as Cowles Foundation). Underwrote Econometrica + Econometric Society. Investment counselor who left markets before the 1929 crash; tested whether forecasters could forecast (they could not). Typhoid 1914, tuberculosis ~1916 (Cragmor Sanatorium). m1 Betsy Strong 1924 (div 1939, adopted son 1925 + daughter 1928); m2 Louise Lamb Phelps 1949. d. Lake Forest IL 1984, buried Graceland (CEM268). Built Stage 6Y-722. THREE CROSS-CONNECTIONS Added 2 Aug 2026 on Sam's question about further connections for Alfred Cowles III. Talcott Parsons was born at Colorado Springs in 1902, the town a tuberculosis sanatorium brought Cowles to and where the commission was founded thirty years later, and both men turned a social science quantitative. Charles Lancelot Minor pioneered the sanatorium treatment of tuberculosis at Asheville and helped found a society of its physicians, which is the other end of the year that rerouted Cowles's life. Frederick Cecil Mills is the contemporary economist Sam asked about, and the link is the trade itself: Cowles paid for Econometrica, Mills led the American Economic Association in 1940.

notable.notable_blurb: Economist; founded the Cowles Commission

career.organization: Cowles Commission for Research in Economics
career.notes: founded 1932

narrative_blocks.header: Could the stock forecasters actually forecast?
narrative_blocks.body: Convinced after the 1929 crash that he didn’t understand markets, he set out to test whether investment advisers beat random chance — and found they did not. To run the numbers he founded the Cowles Commission in 1932, bankrolling a brain trust that helped turn economics into a quantitative science.

narrative_blocks.header: He bankrolled the journal that built a field
narrative_blocks.body: He offered to underwrite a new journal, Econometrica, and the fledgling Econometric Society, in exchange for assembling leading scholars around his commission. The journal debuted in 1933 with Cowles himself as its circulation manager and treasurer.

narrative_blocks.header: He left the market just before it crashed
narrative_blocks.body: A Colorado Springs investment counselor, he pulled out of the financial markets before the Wall Street Crash of 1929. Growing skeptical of the advisers he’d once relied on, he closed his own forecasting newsletter in 1931, telling subscribers he simply did not know enough yet.

narrative_blocks.header: Tuberculosis sent him west to the mountains
narrative_blocks.body: Within two years of starting his own railroad-investment firm in Chicago he contracted tuberculosis and entered a Colorado Springs sanatorium for a year. The illness rerouted his whole life to Colorado, where the commission that bears his name was born.

narrative_blocks.header: A name three generations deep he set aside
narrative_blocks.body: He was the third Alfred Cowles in a row — grandfather, father, and son all tied to the Chicago Tribune — but he preferred to be known simply as Alfred, or “Bob” to his family. He and his wife Betsy adopted two children before their 1939 divorce.

people.research_notes: Knight Cheney Cowles (1892-1970), Chicago architect. Second son of Alfred Cowles Jr. (HD3740). Yale, Harvard, École des Beaux-Arts. Holabird & Root 1925-28, then own firm Cowles & Colean. m. Alice Winslow Farnsworth (X03370) 1919; daughters Edith (HD6400) and Elizabeth (HD6401). Built Stage 6Y-723.

narrative_blocks.header: His own album sits in the Art Institute
narrative_blocks.body: He gave the Art Institute of Chicago a leather-bound portfolio of photographs of his buildings, made about 1929 to 1931. It holds a Chicago restaurant, a laboratory at Dayton, and houses at Lake Forest, Louisville and Glenview.

narrative_blocks.header: Holabird & Root, then his own office
narrative_blocks.body: He worked in the Chicago office of Holabird & Root from 1925 to 1928, then opened Cowles & Colean under his own name. The firm’s work ran through Illinois and the Midwest.

narrative_blocks.header: He trained for architecture in three countries
narrative_blocks.body: He studied at Yale, at Harvard, and at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris before he ever took a drawing board in Chicago. The Beaux-Arts training shows in the houses he built afterwards.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter was born during his Paris studies
narrative_blocks.body: He was still studying architecture in Paris when his daughter Elizabeth was born there in 1923. The family came back to Chicago and then settled at Lake Forest, Illinois.

narrative_blocks.header: One of four boys raised by their father
narrative_blocks.body: He was five when his mother Elizabeth Cheney died of lung disease, leaving his father to bring up the four of them alone. His eldest brother Alfred founded the Cowles Commission for economic research.

people.research_notes: John Cheney Cowles, son of Alfred Cowles Jr. (HD3740) and Elizabeth Cheney (X03368); gen-10 Hooker descendant. Full build in a later stage. Stage 6Y-725: m. Elizabeth R. Cowles (X03374, 1910-1971); buried Naples Memorial Gardens (CEM888).

narrative_blocks.header: One of four brothers raised by a widower
narrative_blocks.body: Third of the four Cowles boys left motherless in 1898, he grew up under his father’s sole care alongside his brothers — the economist Alfred and the architect Knight — and lived to seventy-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: Andover at twenty, Glee Club and wrestling
narrative_blocks.body: He came to Andover in 1914 at twenty, out of the family house at 1130 Lake Shore Drive in Chicago, and went on from there to Yale. He sang in the Glee Club, wrestled, and made the second football team.

people.research_notes: Thomas Hooker Cowles, son of Alfred Cowles Jr. (HD3740) and Elizabeth Cheney (X03368); gen-10 Hooker descendant. Full build in a later stage. Stage 6Y-725: m. Barbara Granger (X03375) 1921; WWI infantry captain in France; Chicago real-estate broker; d. spinal meningitis Denver 1927; buried Graceland (CEM268). Wife was granddaughter of railroad president Marvin Hughitt; her father architect Alfred Hoyt Granger (X03376, easter egg).

narrative_blocks.header: Meningitis killed him on a Colorado vacation
narrative_blocks.body: A Chicago real-estate broker who had been an infantry captain in France during the war, he was vacationing in Colorado Springs with his wife when spinal meningitis struck. He died in Denver at thirty-two, leaving a widow and two small children.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried the founding ancestor’s name
narrative_blocks.body: Named Thomas Hooker Cowles for the family’s Hartford-founding forefather, he was the youngest of the four Cowles brothers — and the first to die, in 1927.

bio.bio_blurb: Diplomat’s wife of the Cowles family

narrative_blocks.header: She married a diplomat, then an engineer
narrative_blocks.body: Her first husband, Joseph Greene, gave thirty-two years to the Foreign Service; her second, Charles Poor, helped build America’s first supersonic wind tunnel. She lived to ninety, dying in Washington in 2010.

people.research_notes: Edith Farnsworth Cowles (1920-2010), elder daughter of Knight Cheney Cowles (HD6397) and Alice Farnsworth (X03370); gen-11 Hooker descendant. m1 Joseph Nathaniel Greene Jr. (X03371, Foreign Service); m2 Charles Lane Poor III (X03372, aeronautical engineer). Built Stage 6Y-723.

narrative_blocks.header: A ranch life, then a lifetime of service
narrative_blocks.body: Bessie married Lester Armour Jr. during the Second World War, and they raised cattle at Dragoon and Sonoita in Arizona and at Canal Point in Florida. From 1959, at Delray Beach, she gave decades to the Soup Kitchen at Boynton Beach and to migrant families, and in 2000 the Bethesda Hospital Foundation named her one of its Women of Grace.

narrative_blocks.header: A school field and award named for her
narrative_blocks.body: Bessie was a trustee of the Gulf Stream School, worked for years in its library, and in 2000 gave it Armour House, now the headmaster's house. The school named its playing field for her, and each year gives the Bessie C. Armour Award for Community Service to a pupil carrying on her work.

narrative_blocks.header: Caps for wheelchairs until ninety-four
narrative_blocks.body: Bessie volunteered until she was ninety-four, her eyesight failing, collecting, sorting and selling plastic caps for Caps of Love to buy wheelchairs for children. Her daughter Susan said the group's end was the beginning of her decline, and Bessie died at home on 7 February 2020, three days short of ninety-seven.

narrative_blocks.header: Born in Paris to an architecture student
narrative_blocks.body: Bessie was born in Paris in February 1923, while her father Knight Cowles was studying architecture there, and grew up in Chicago and Lake Forest with her sister Edith. She finished at the Ethel Walker School and went on to Sarah Lawrence College.

people.research_notes: Elizabeth "Bessie" Cheney Cowles Armour (1923-2020), younger daughter of Knight Cheney Cowles (HD6397); gen-11 Hooker descendant. Born Paris. m. Lester Armour Jr. (X03373). Ethel Walker School, Sarah Lawrence. Decades of FL community service; Gulf Stream School Bessie C. Armour Award. Built Stage 6Y-723.

narrative_blocks.body: Taken ill with consumption in December 1897, Elizabeth went to Colorado Springs, and her parents brought out her four small boys. She died at the Antlers Hotel in April 1898, at thirty-two, the first of Knight Cheney's eleven children to go, and was carried home to Manchester.

sources.label: ADST oral history, 1993; Office of the Historian; obituary, 2010

notable.notable_blurb: US diplomat; principal officer in Cairo, 1972–73

narrative_blocks.header: America's man in Cairo, 1972 to 1973
narrative_blocks.body: With no diplomatic relations between Washington and Cairo, Jerry ran the American interests section inside the Spanish embassy from February 1972 to July 1973, and carried the secret channel between Henry Kissinger and Sadat's adviser Hafez Ismail before the October War.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote Trieste’s constitution at twenty-six
narrative_blocks.body: In 1946 Jerry spent a month in Paris drafting the Statute of the Free Territory of Trieste, which went into the Italian Peace Treaty. Around 1969 a State Department Italian exam handed him a passage to translate: the statute. He told the examiner he had written it.

narrative_blocks.header: His memo spared Monte Cassino, for a time
narrative_blocks.body: As a junior political officer in Naples in 1944, Jerry was asked what to do about the Benedictine abbey at Monte Cassino, and wrote the advice that spared it, at least at first. Allied bombers destroyed it later, and the Germans turned out never to have used it.

narrative_blocks.header: From Navy boot camp to the OSS
narrative_blocks.body: Drafted while posted to Rome in 1944, Jerry went home through Navy boot camp and came out an ensign for the OSS. By June 1945 he was political adviser to the Allied commanders at Trieste, out of uniform so that an ensign could sit with generals.

narrative_blocks.header: Deputy to Chester Bowles and Walter Annenberg
narrative_blocks.body: Jerry was deputy chief of mission to Chester Bowles in New Delhi from 1963 to 1968 and to Walter Annenberg in London in 1970. After thirty-two years he left State to direct the Seven Springs Conference Center and help found a Connecticut foreign-relations committee.

narrative_blocks.header: Dean Acheson taught him for the exam
narrative_blocks.body: Out of Yale in 1941, Jerry crammed for the Foreign Service exam at a Washington school where Dean Acheson taught economics, his best paper. His first job, after Pearl Harbor, was deciding the cases of refugees from Nazi Europe who wanted to stay in America.

bio.bio_blurb: Aeronautical engineer; built a supersonic tunnel

narrative_blocks.header: He built America’s first supersonic wind tunnel
narrative_blocks.body: A Harvard-trained aeronautical engineer and Navy man of the Second World War, he was instrumental in establishing the country’s first supersonic wind tunnel at the Aberdeen Proving Grounds. He later served as Assistant Secretary of the Army for Research and Development.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped write the rules of ocean racing
narrative_blocks.body: An avid offshore sailor on the Chesapeake and beyond, he gave years to U.S. Sailing’s measurement committee and chaired the international technical committee of the Ocean Racing Congress — shaping how yacht races worldwide were judged.

narrative_blocks.header: He sang in a group: Bach and Beer
narrative_blocks.body: A lover of choral music, he was an active member of a Washington men’s singing group named Bach and Beer, and chaired the Citizens Association of his Georgetown neighborhood.

narrative_blocks.header: A B-24 bombardier in the war
narrative_blocks.body: Les flew the Second World War as a B-24 bombardier and came out a captain in the Army Air Forces. Afterwards he took his degree at the University of Arizona and began a life of cattle ranching in Arizona, New Mexico and Florida.

narrative_blocks.header: A four-goal amateur polo player
narrative_blocks.body: For most of his life Les played polo as an amateur and reached a four-goal rating. He bred, raised and trained polo ponies that were played in the United States, England and Argentina.

narrative_blocks.header: Great-grandson of Philip Danforth Armour
narrative_blocks.body: Les was a great-grandson of Philip Danforth Armour, who built Armour and Company at Chicago, through his grandfather Philip Danforth Armour II, who died in 1900. He died of cancer at his home at Sonoita, Arizona, in November 2008, at eighty-seven.

people.research_notes: Barbara Granger (1899-1995), daughter of architect Alfred Hoyt Granger (X03376) and Belle Hughitt (X03377); granddaughter of railroad president Marvin Hughitt. m1 Thomas Hooker Cowles (HD6399) 1921; m2 Chester D. Shepard. Built Stage 6Y-725.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at twenty-eight with two small girls
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas Hooker Cowles died at Denver in August 1927, leaving her with their daughters Sarah and Mary. In October 1929 she married Chester D. Shepard, a stockbroker, and left Lake Forest for Neenah, Wisconsin.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father drew the house she lived in
narrative_blocks.body: The Shepards built on Lake Road in Neenah between 1932 and 1933, a long brick house with four hipped dormers over a four-car garage. Her father, the architect Alfred Hoyt Granger, designed it.

narrative_blocks.header: Her sister married Arthur Krock
narrative_blocks.body: Barbara was one of Alfred and Belle Granger's three daughters. Her sister Elizabeth married Charles E. Brown Jr., and her sister Martha married first William Mitchell Blair and then the columnist Arthur Krock.

sources.label: New York Times obituary, 4 Dec 1939; Wikipedia; FreshWater Cleveland, 23 Feb 2023

notable.notable_blurb: Architect of railroad stations and homes

narrative_blocks.header: He drew for the 1893 World's Fair
narrative_blocks.body: Straight from the École des Beaux-Arts, Alfred went to Chicago in 1891 with Shepley, Rutan and Coolidge to work on the Art Institute built for the World's Columbian Exposition, and on the Chicago Public Library.

narrative_blocks.header: He laid out Euclid Heights
narrative_blocks.body: In 1893 Alfred opened Granger & Meade in Cleveland and laid out Euclid Heights, putting up twenty-two buildings in four years. His own house on Overlook Road, drawn that first year, was the first in the development and still stands.

narrative_blocks.header: Stations for his father-in-law's railroad
narrative_blocks.body: With his brother-in-law Charles Sumner Frost, Alfred ran Frost & Granger in Chicago from 1898 to 1910, designing LaSalle Street Station, the Chicago and North Western terminal and depots all along the line their father-in-law, Marvin Hughitt, ran.

narrative_blocks.header: A captain of engineers, out a major
narrative_blocks.body: In the First World War Alfred chaired the emergency construction committee of the War Industries Board, commanded Company C of the 78th Engineers at Camp Humphreys, and headed the War Department's public works section. He came out a major.

narrative_blocks.header: A guidebook for the Century of Progress
narrative_blocks.body: Alfred wrote a study of Charles Follen McKim's life and work in 1913, England's World Empire in 1916, Chicago Welcomes You, the guidebook for the 1933 Century of Progress fair, and The Spirit of Vienna in 1935.

narrative_blocks.header: His father fought at Cedar Creek
narrative_blocks.body: His father, Judge Moses Moorhead Granger, was brevetted colonel as of October 19, 1864, the day of Cedar Creek, and later wrote The Battle of Cedar Creek. He later sat as chief judge of the Ohio Supreme Court Commission, from 1883 to 1885.

narrative_blocks.header: General Sherman's great-nephew
narrative_blocks.body: His mother was a niece of General William T. Sherman and Senator John Sherman, and as a boy Alfred spent long stretches in their company and in that of the historian Henry Adams.

narrative_blocks.body: Belle's father, Marvin Hughitt, started as a telegrapher on the Illinois Central and ran the Chicago and North Western for more than forty years. Her sister Mary married Charles Sumner Frost, so her husband and her brother-in-law both built stations for his line.

narrative_blocks.header: The house he drew at Lake Forest
narrative_blocks.body: After a short spell in Cleveland, Belle and Alfred settled at Lake Forest in Woodleigh, the house he designed for the family at 907 North Sheridan Road. She died at Lake Forest in 1963, at ninety-six, twenty-three years after him.

narrative_blocks.header: He baptized 452 souls in one parish
narrative_blocks.body: Rev. Jonathan Russell led the Barnstable church for twenty-eight years, from 1683 until his death in 1711. Contemporaries remembered him as a pious and learned divine; during his pastorate 171 members joined the church and 452 were baptized.

narrative_blocks.header: His estate held a surgeon's instruments
narrative_blocks.body: When his estate was inventoried in 1711, it listed drugs and a set of surgeon's instruments alongside his books. Like many frontier ministers of his era, he seems to have tended his congregation's bodies as well as their souls.

narrative_blocks.body: George Adams Richardson spent his career as a guardian of the Marshall Field fortune, serving the estate as executor and then trustee from 1921 through 1943 and later as assistant to Marshall Field III. The Auburn, New York furniture-maker’s son had met the Field family while at Yale.

narrative_blocks.header: A soldier in two world wars
narrative_blocks.body: He was a field-artillery captain in World War I, having also served in the Mexican Border campaign, and rose to lieutenant colonel of air transport in World War II.

narrative_blocks.header: He raised another man’s children
narrative_blocks.body: In 1918 he married Anne Camden Thompson, recently parted from Samuel F. B. Morse, and helped raise her three young children in Lake Forest, Illinois. The household later moved west to Rancho Santa Fe.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran an inn beside the Pacific
narrative_blocks.body: In 1943 he bought the Rancho Santa Fe Inn, and the Richardson family operated it until his death in 1958.

narrative_blocks.header: A painter who ran Pebble Beach
narrative_blocks.body: John Boit Morse was remembered as a well-known painter and a former president of Del Monte Properties, the company his father built around Pebble Beach. The artistic streak ran in the family.

narrative_blocks.header: He served in the wartime Navy
narrative_blocks.body: He served in the U.S. Navy from June 1941 to November 1945, then settled into real-estate development on the Monterey Peninsula.

narrative_blocks.header: Raised under a stepfather’s roof
narrative_blocks.body: After his parents separated, he grew up with his mother Anne and stepfather George Richardson in Lake Forest, Illinois. He married Margaret McLennan in 1934.
