narrative_blocks.body: Born in Boston in 1840, Elizabeth married Rev. Isaac Newton Stanger in 1869 and settled in Philadelphia. She lived to ninety-one, dying in 1931.

narrative_blocks.header: She taught at her father's freedmen's school
narrative_blocks.body: In 1864 Sarah joined the Beaufort school her father opened on the Sea Islands, teaching the formerly enslaved. She served there until 1865, the second of the Peck women to take up the work.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father married her to a USCT major
narrative_blocks.body: In 1870 she married Ira Winans, a Union major of the U.S. Colored Troops, with her father Rev. Solomon Peck officiating. They settled in Rochester, where both are buried at Mount Hope.

narrative_blocks.header: A diary for the son she lost
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah kept a diary of her children's lives. Its most piercing pages trace her son Edwin, his smiles, his love of the Sabbath, his death from scarlet fever at three in 1875, a mother's record of a child she could not keep.

cross_connections.display_label: supplied the Port Royal freedmen’s schools, and drowned off Edisto

landmarks.landmark_blurb: taught freedpeople at Beaufort during the wartime Port Royal Experiment

narrative_blocks.header: A Roundhead soldier turned minister
narrative_blocks.body: Stanger served as a private in Company A of the 100th Pennsylvania Infantry, the Roundhead Regiment, during the Civil War. He later entered the ministry and settled in Philadelphia.

narrative_blocks.header: A Delaware rectory, then Kenyon's board
narrative_blocks.body: Called from Germantown in 1870, Stanger served as rector of Christ Church, Christiana Hundred, in Delaware, where the congregation grew through his tenure. He later sat as a trustee of Kenyon College in Ohio.

narrative_blocks.header: He rose to major in the Colored Troops
narrative_blocks.body: Winans enlisted in 1861, was a captain by 1862, and in March 1864 was promoted to major of the 26th U.S. Colored Troops. He mustered out at Hilton Head at the war's close.

narrative_blocks.header: His last years went to 2,600 Winanses
narrative_blocks.body: In retirement he turned genealogist, compiling The Winans Family in America from some 2,600 records. His manuscript notes survive in the Rochester library.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife's diary mourned their son Edwin
narrative_blocks.body: Ira's wife Sarah kept a diary of their children. Its tenderest pages follow their son Edwin, his first smiles, his love of the Sabbath, until scarlet fever took him at three in 1875. He was buried near his grandfather Solomon Peck at Mount Hope.

narrative_blocks.header: A Hartford cooper who unseated the colony secretary
narrative_blocks.body: William Edwards made barrels for a living, but in 1663 he charged Connecticut's colony secretary with breaching his oath. The accusation stuck, and the secretary lost his post at the next court.

narrative_blocks.header: Fined for street tobacco and a funeral's wine
narrative_blocks.body: The records catch him plainly: cited in 1656 for smoking in the street against the law, and in 1661 fined for drunkenness at a neighbor's funeral. A man, his biographer wrote, not averse to tobacco and wine.

narrative_blocks.header: From his line came Jonathan Edwards
narrative_blocks.body: A London cooper's son who came to Hartford with his widowed mother, he was the immigrant root of the family. Through his son Richard and grandson Timothy descended the theologian Jonathan Edwards.

cross_connections.display_label: was his only child, who served writs up and down colonial Hartford

narrative_blocks.header: Twice widowed at the founding of Hartford
narrative_blocks.body: Agnes Harris came from Barnstaple in Devon and married two of Hartford's founders in turn: William Spencer, who died in 1640, then William Edwards in 1645. She outlived the town's first generation.

narrative_blocks.header: Two husbands, two famous American lines
narrative_blocks.body: Through her first marriage she was ancestress of Lyman Beecher and Harriet Beecher Stowe; through her second, great-grandmother of Jonathan Edwards. Two of New England's defining families trace to one Devon woman.

cross_connections.display_label: was her only child by her second husband, a Hartford court officer

narrative_blocks.header: He clerked Cambridge before Hooker arrived
narrative_blocks.body: William Spencer was town clerk of Cambridge in the early 1630s and a deputy to the Massachusetts General Court, settled there before Thomas Hooker's company came. When Hooker moved west, Spencer followed to help found Hartford.

narrative_blocks.header: A founder of the Ancient and Honorable Artillery
narrative_blocks.body: He was one of four founders of the Military Company of Massachusetts, today the Ancient and Honorable Artillery Company, the oldest in the nation, holding the rank of lieutenant. He died at Hartford in 1640, not yet forty.

narrative_blocks.header: A lifelong bachelor merchant at Union
narrative_blocks.body: The eldest of the Edwards sons, John King Edwards kept a merchant's trade in the village of Union, New York, and never married. He outlived most of his ten siblings, dying there in 1866 at eighty-one.

narrative_blocks.header: From shop clerk to county sheriff
narrative_blocks.body: Robert Ogden Edwards began as a clerk to a Mr. Whitney and rose over the years to merchant, Justice of the Peace, and Sheriff at Chenango Forks, where he spent his whole adult life. He and his wife Caroline raised ten children before her early death in 1828.

career.role: Justice of the Peace and Sheriff

bio.bio_blurb: County judge of Steuben County, New York

narrative_blocks.header: A county judge who wrote the justices' handbook
narrative_blocks.body: George Cunningham Edwards sat as judge of the Court of Common Pleas for Steuben County, New York, from 1825 until his death. In 1830 he published 'Powers and Duties of Justices of the Peace,' a working manual for the local magistrates of his day, before a brief and painful illness took him at fifty.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed, she married a revival preacher
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Edwards married James McKinney in 1832 and was widowed within five years. In 1838 she married the Reverend John Ercanbrack, a Methodist circuit preacher of western Michigan known for setting his charges 'in a blaze of revival,' and lived out her life at Sturgis.

narrative_blocks.header: He made lumber and scythes at Lisle
narrative_blocks.body: William Edwards built a manufacturing trade in lumber and scythes at Lisle, New York, where he and his wife Betsy Fay raised twelve children. He lived there to eighty-one.

narrative_blocks.header: Dead at Ithaca before he turned thirty
narrative_blocks.body: Timothy Edwards never married and died young at Ithaca, New York, in 1825, at twenty-eight. Two of his brothers, Alexander and the next Timothy, also died as young men far from Stockbridge.

narrative_blocks.header: Three wives across the Michigan frontier
narrative_blocks.body: Edwin Edwards married three times in frontier Michigan — first Nancy Williams, who bore one child before her death in 1836; then Hannah Lewis, mother of nine more; and finally Celestia Chamberlain. He left ten children between his first two marriages.

narrative_blocks.header: Daughter of Old Put, the Revolution's folk hero
narrative_blocks.body: Mehitable Putnam was a daughter of General Israel Putnam, Old Put, the Connecticut farmer-soldier famed for leaving his plow at the news of Lexington. She married Capt. Daniel Tyler in 1771 and bore him seven children before her death at forty.

narrative_blocks.header: A general's daughter who married a Tyler
narrative_blocks.body: Mehitable was born to Israel and Hannah Putnam in 1749 and in 1771 married Daniel Tyler, carrying the Putnam blood into the Tyler line. She grew up in the household of Connecticut's most celebrated soldier.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother's diary kept his short life
narrative_blocks.body: Born in Rochester in 1871, Edwin loved the Sabbath and hymns; his mother recorded his first smiles and his question, Why don't they have church in heaven? Scarlet fever took him at three, and she wrote down every day of him.

narrative_blocks.header: From Dutch Staten Island to pioneer Rochester
narrative_blocks.body: The Winans came from the early Dutch settlers of Staten Island; Henry's grandparents were among the first families of Chili in Monroe County. Henry was born at Rochester in 1873 and lived there his whole life, dying in 1946.

narrative_blocks.header: A Rochester physician of the Winans line
narrative_blocks.body: William Wallace Winans trained as a physician and practiced in Rochester, where he was born in 1874. He was one of the six children of Major Ira Winans and Sarah Edwards Peck, and lived his life in the city, dying there in 1938.

narrative_blocks.header: West Point dropout turned Maine county attorney
narrative_blocks.body: Charles entered West Point in 1823 but resigned three years later. He read law at the Litchfield Law School, was admitted to the bar at Bangor, Maine, in 1832, and served as Penobscot County Attorney.

narrative_blocks.header: A smallpox scare that traveled by handshake
narrative_blocks.body: In February 1846 a Bangor neighbor wrote a friend in alarm: Charles Cushman had broken out with varioloid smallpox, and anyone who had shaken his hand should be revaccinated at once. Charles survived that bout, only to die three years later.

narrative_blocks.header: He followed the country west to Milwaukee
narrative_blocks.body: Like many of his generation, Charles moved his family westward, settling at last in Wisconsin. He died at Milwaukee in 1849.

narrative_blocks.header: Two of his daughters married sea captains
narrative_blocks.body: Charles Chaplin Cushman's daughters wed into the seafaring life: Mary married Capt. Arthur Child, and Sarah Maria married Capt. Howard Higgins. From a Vermont legislator's son, the family scattered toward the coasts and the West.

narrative_blocks.header: She married the captain Lincoln defended
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah Cushman married Capt. John McNab in 1844. Years later her husband would be dismissed from the army for disloyalty at Fort Laramie, and become the subject of a personal intervention by President Lincoln, who argued he deserved a hearing.

narrative_blocks.header: From Vermont to Wisconsin and home again
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Guildhall in 1809, Maria married Russell Hopkinson in 1834 and followed the westward tide as far as Sheboygan, Wisconsin, by 1850. In the end she returned east, dying at Derby, Vermont, in 1876.

narrative_blocks.header: She buried two of her three children young
narrative_blocks.body: Betsey Cushman married John Nichols and settled in Wisconsin. Of their three children, two died in infancy, only Helen lived to marry. Betsey herself died at thirty, in 1852.

narrative_blocks.header: The traitor captain Lincoln still wanted heard
narrative_blocks.body: Commanding Fort Laramie in 1861, McNab was dismissed from the army for disloyalty, accused of tampering with his own enlisted men toward the Confederate cause. Yet Lincoln himself intervened, writing that an officer dismissed on suspicion who does not go over to the enemy entitles himself to a hearing. No record shows he was ever restored.

documents.document_blurb: Lincoln's 1861 endorsement asking that he receive a hearing.

narrative_blocks.header: A Williams lawyer who carried the family west
narrative_blocks.body: John Nichols graduated Williams College in 1839 and practiced law. In 1844 he married Betsey Cushman and settled at Janesville, Wisconsin, part of the family's broad migration into the new West. Betsey died young at thirty, and Nichols lived to 1898.

narrative_blocks.header: She died weeks after her last child's birth
narrative_blocks.body: Harriet Hoisington married Jonathan Edwards Chaplin in Ohio in 1820 and followed his restless path west. She died at Tiffin in 1840, when her youngest son, William, was just four weeks old.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed, she married a reformed preacher
narrative_blocks.body: After Snelling's death she was left a widow with young children. In 1841 she married Rev. Jonathan Edwards Chaplin, the reformed lawyer turned Methodist temperance preacher, becoming his second wife in his last years in Ohio and Michigan.

narrative_blocks.header: The colonel who built and named Fort Snelling
narrative_blocks.body: Josiah Snelling led the charge that helped win Tippecanoe in 1811 and was brevetted major for bravery in the War of 1812. In 1820 he designed and built the diamond-shaped limestone fort above the Minnesota-Mississippi junction; the War Department renamed it Fort Snelling in his honor.

narrative_blocks.header: He turned a frontier fort into a farm
narrative_blocks.body: Cut off from reliable supply, Snelling set his soldiers to farming and milling, cultivating two hundred acres and grinding their own flour at St. Anthony Falls. His men spent more time behind plows than at drill.

narrative_blocks.header: Dysentery, brandy, and a death under a cloud
narrative_blocks.body: Chronic illness from the war, treated with opium and brandy, deepened a drinking problem that frayed his command. Summoned to Washington to answer for army expenditures, he died there in 1828 before the charges could be heard.

cross_connections.display_label: built the fort Terry later expanded

narrative_blocks.header: He traded an Illinois farm for Nebraska
narrative_blocks.body: Edwards Hastings Chaplin farmed in Warren County, Illinois, through the early 1850s. In 1856 he sold the land and moved his family west to Nebraska, settling near Omaha on ground that is now a city park. He and his wife died within a year of each other in the early 1870s.

narrative_blocks.header: His children scattered across the frontier West
narrative_blocks.body: From a Nebraska farm, the Chaplin children fanned out into the new West. His sons Benjamin and Harvey became Union Pacific railroad men, each marked by terrible injuries on the line; another son, William, rose to be Wyoming's Secretary of State and a noted newspaper publisher.

narrative_blocks.header: Raised by an aunt after his mother died
narrative_blocks.body: William Rapier Chaplin was four weeks old when his mother, Harriet, died at Tiffin. He was raised from infancy by his aunt, Eleanor Hoisington Thomas, who carried him west to Illinois, where he grew up far from his father's frontier pulpits.

narrative_blocks.header: Captured with his regiment at Lexington
narrative_blocks.body: Chaplin enlisted in the First Illinois Cavalry under Captain Palmer and rode in the early Western campaigns. He was taken prisoner with his whole regiment at Lexington, Missouri, in 1861, paroled, and afterward turned from soldiering to the law.

narrative_blocks.header: From a prairie college to the Kansas bar
narrative_blocks.body: Educated at Lombard University in Galesburg, Chaplin studied law and was admitted to the bar by 1864. He settled at last in Louisburg, Kansas, where he practiced until his death in 1886.

narrative_blocks.header: From Bunker Hill to Fallen Timbers
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas Hunt marched as a minuteman to Lexington in 1775 and fought at Bunker Hill, was wounded at Stony Point and again at Yorktown, then carried on into the western Indian wars, surviving St. Clair's Defeat and fighting at Fallen Timbers. He rose at last to colonel of the First Infantry.

narrative_blocks.header: An original member of the Cincinnati
narrative_blocks.body: When the officers of the Revolution founded the Society of the Cincinnati in 1783, Hunt was admitted an original member for Massachusetts. The Society bound the men who had won independence, and their eldest descendants after them.

narrative_blocks.header: His blood ran to a Gettysburg general
narrative_blocks.body: Hunt's daughter Abigail married Col. Josiah Snelling, builder of the fort that bears his name. His grandson, Henry Jackson Hunt, commanded the Union artillery at Gettysburg, the guns that broke Pickett's Charge.

cross_connections.display_label: co-founded the Society of the Cincinnati with him in 1783
married his daughter Abigail as her second husband
turned out for the same alarm at forty-eight

narrative_blocks.header: A railroad engineer felled by an old wreck
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin Asel Chaplin fired and then drove locomotives for the Union Pacific out of Laramie. A head-on collision at Carbon broke his health, and though young and strong he never fully recovered, dying at thirty-four in 1887.

narrative_blocks.header: He always sheltered his firemen from blame
narrative_blocks.body: Quiet and uncomplaining, Chaplin was known on the line for taking trouble onto himself, shielding his firemen and assuming responsibility in any accident. His brother engineers held him in a regard stronger than ordinary friendship.

cross_connections.display_label: sat on the Union Pacific board while he was firing its engines
was a Union Pacific detective who died at thirty-six of a fall on duty

narrative_blocks.header: He lost a foot between two railcars
narrative_blocks.body: Harvey Stillman Chaplin came to Wyoming in 1875 and worked as a fireman and engineer for the Union Pacific. In 1888, crossing a train in the Cheyenne yards, his foot was crushed between two cars and had to be amputated.

narrative_blocks.header: From the rails to the Globe Hotel
narrative_blocks.body: After the injury he was given a passenger run on the Cheyenne and Northern, then left railroading to buy the Globe Hotel at Wheatland, which he kept for the rest of his life. He outlived two wives before dying in 1912.

narrative_blocks.header: His second wife's father was a murderer
narrative_blocks.body: Harvey Chaplin's second wife, Maggie Ryan, was the daughter of Posey Ryan, a Wyoming pioneer who in 1909 shot his other wife and her daughter dead in a Cheyenne restaurant. Through Maggie, the Chaplin line brushed up against one of frontier Wyoming's most sensational crimes.

cross_connections.display_label: father of his second wife Maggie; murdered his own other wife in 1909
mother of his second wife Maggie; girl in Gardner's 1868 photograph
married Sophie Mousseau, mother of his wife Maggie

landmarks.landmark_blurb: managed the Globe Hotel in Wheatland, Wyoming

narrative_blocks.header: She married into a frontier trading family
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Anne Chaplin, called Mamie, married John Calhoun Marley of North Carolina in 1890 and raised her family at Louisburg, Kansas. Widowed young, she later married again, her life spanning the settling of the Kansas-Missouri border country.

bio.bio_blurb: Wyoming Secretary of State; Laramie newspaper publisher

narrative_blocks.header: An orphan who rose to print frontier Wyoming
narrative_blocks.body: William Chaplin reached Laramie in 1873 as a thirteen-year-old orphan from Nebraska and went straight to work in a newspaper plant. He apprenticed under the territory's pioneer editors, became a founding stockholder of the Laramie Boomerang in 1881, and by 1886 was president of its publishing company.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded the Laramie Republican
narrative_blocks.body: When the Boomerang was sold in 1890, Chaplin founded the Laramie Republican and edited it for the next thirty years. For half a century he knew nearly every editor and publisher in frontier Wyoming, and his recollections became a primary record of the territory's newspaper days.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped write Wyoming into a state
narrative_blocks.body: Chaplin was a delegate to the 1889 convention that drafted Wyoming's constitution, served on the Laramie City Council and as mayor in 1894, and was register of the U.S. Land Office at Cheyenne. He capped his public life as Wyoming's Secretary of State from 1919 to 1923.

cross_connections.display_label: founded Middletown's paper in 1838 and ran it thirty-three years

bio.bio_blurb: Half-Oglala daughter of a Wyoming frontier family

narrative_blocks.header: Her father became a notorious murderer
narrative_blocks.body: Four years after Maggie married Harvey Chaplin, her father Posey Ryan shot his second wife and stepdaughter dead in a Cheyenne restaurant in 1909. It was among frontier Wyoming's most sensational crimes, and Maggie did not live to see her father pardoned a decade later.

narrative_blocks.header: She was half Lakota and half French Canadian
narrative_blocks.body: Maggie Ryan was the daughter of Sophie Mousseau, an Oglala Lakota woman, and the Irish settler Posey Ryan; her grandfather was the French-Canadian fur trader Alexis Mousseau. When she married Harvey Chaplin, she carried Lakota and frontier-trader blood into the Hooker descent.

narrative_blocks.header: The hotel keeper's wife at Wheatland
narrative_blocks.body: Maggie married Harvey Chaplin in 1905 and helped him run the Globe Hotel at Wheatland, Wyoming. She had come from a hard frontier childhood to a settled life as an innkeeper's wife, though it would prove brief.

narrative_blocks.header: She died young after an operation
narrative_blocks.body: In June 1910, only five years into her marriage, Maggie underwent surgery for appendicitis and seemed to be recovering when complications set in. She died at thirty-three, leaving two young children from a prior marriage.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: managed the Globe Hotel in Wheatland, Wyoming

bio.bio_blurb: Wyoming pioneer, teamster, and convicted murderer

narrative_blocks.header: He shot his second wife in Cheyenne
narrative_blocks.body: In 1909, while Posey was away hauling freight, his second wife sold their Guernsey hotel and fled with the money. He found her at a Sunday lunch in Cheyenne, shot her and her daughter dead, and surrendered, saying he expected to hang.

narrative_blocks.header: A teamster on the Bozeman Trail at eighteen
narrative_blocks.body: Irish-born and a Civil War veteran, Posey came west in 1865 as an army teamster building the Bozeman Trail forts, and skirmished with Oglala warriors at Fort Phil Kearny in Red Cloud's War.

narrative_blocks.header: Pardoned after saving lives in a prison fire
narrative_blocks.body: In the 1912 uprising at the Rawlins penitentiary, Posey helped get convicts out of the burning broom factory. Wyoming citizens petitioned for him, the governor pardoned him in 1919, and he died ten years later at the soldiers' home.

narrative_blocks.header: One of Wyoming's earliest settlers
narrative_blocks.body: Posey homesteaded north of Fort Laramie in 1867, two years before Wyoming became a territory, and helped found the town of Guernsey. Despite the murder, he was remembered as a well-liked pioneer who helped build the state.

narrative_blocks.header: He won Sophie in Fort Laramie's shadow
narrative_blocks.body: Discharged at Fort Laramie, Posey settled among the French-speaking traders and their Lakota families. Around 1882 he took Sophie Mousseau, daughter of a trader and an Oglala mother, as his common-law wife; Maggie was their eldest.

narrative_blocks.header: A sensational trial and a long sentence
narrative_blocks.body: Ryan's August 1909 trial in Cheyenne drew crowds. Found guilty of second-degree murder, he was sentenced to thirty to ninety-nine years in the new state penitentiary at Rawlins, where he would later help save lives in a prison fire.

was the first husband of Mary, his murdered second wife

narrative_blocks.header: The unnamed girl in an 1868 treaty photograph
narrative_blocks.body: At about eight, Sophie Mousseau stood beside six U.S. generals in Alexander Gardner's famous photograph of the 1868 Fort Laramie treaty. The men were all named on the print; she was labeled only Arapaho or Dakota, her identity lost for over a century until a historian recovered it.

narrative_blocks.header: A child translator between two warring worlds
narrative_blocks.body: Daughter of an Oglala Lakota mother, Yellow Woman, and a French-Canadian trader, Sophie served as an interpreter during the treaty negotiations as a girl. She lived a hard life of displacement and violence and died at Pine Ridge in 1936, her name long forgotten by the record.

narrative_blocks.header: Her children were raised across a racial divide
narrative_blocks.body: Sophie Mousseau's children grew up split between worlds, some raised as white, some as Lakota, in the fluid racial landscape of the frontier. After Posey Ryan she married John Monroe, an Oglala Lakota man, and raised a large family on the Pine Ridge Reservation.

narrative_blocks.header: Better documented than most born in 1859
narrative_blocks.body: Because she stood in a famous photograph and lived among record-keeping institutions, more is known of Sophie Mousseau than of almost any other girl born on the northern plains in her time. A historian's book, The Girl in the Middle, finally told her story in full.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father was a Fort Laramie fur trader
narrative_blocks.body: Sophie's father, Alexis Magloire Mousseau, trapped furs for the American Fur Company and ran a sutler's store near Fort Laramie. Her mother was Ellen Yellow Woman, an Oglala Lakota; Sophie was born of their union around 1859 in that frontier trading world.

bio.bio_blurb: Oglala Lakota head of family, Pine Ridge

narrative_blocks.header: An Oglala Lakota man of Pine Ridge
narrative_blocks.body: John Monroe, known as Long Time Sleep, was the son of T.B. Monroe and Spotted Horse Woman. He married Sophie Mousseau around 1893 and headed a large family recorded on the Pine Ridge Indian Census rolls through the 1890s and 1900s.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the name Monroe off a sign
narrative_blocks.body: Long Time Sleep travelled to Europe with a Wild West show as one of Buffalo Bill's Show Indians. Somewhere on that tour he saw the name Monroe, took it for his own, and carried it home to Pine Ridge.

narrative_blocks.header: Head of the household, four times counted
narrative_blocks.body: The Indian census rolls list him head of the household at Pine Ridge in 1894, at Medicine Root in 1895, again in 1896 and at Pass Creek in 1904. Alloysius was born the first of those years and Zoye four years after.

people.relational_label_override: Stepfather-in-law of a Ninth Generation Hooker
people.research_notes: Mark Monroe, An Indian in White America (Temple University Press, 1994), 16: his grandfather Long Time Sleep was a Show Indian for Buffalo Bill, saw the name Monroe while in Europe and adopted it, then married an Oglala Lakota woman from Pine Ridge. That memoir calls him Cheyenne while the census rolls and the Stevens genealogy call him Oglala Lakota; FamilySearch gives his birthplace as the Cheyenne Nation, Dakota Territory. Birth given as 1869 by one source and April 1870 by another. Son of T.B. Monroe and Spotted Horse Woman. Children recorded with Sophie: Lena (about 1880, so probably Sophie's by an earlier union), Alloysius (1894) and Zoye (1898); none has an entry. NOT the Nick Lassa of the Blackfeet Nation who used the same name Long Time Sleep and played for the Oorang Indians in the NFL in 1922-23 — a different man entirely.

bio.bio_blurb: Wyoming hotelkeeper killed by her husband

narrative_blocks.header: She sold the hotel and vanished
narrative_blocks.body: While her husband was away on a long freight haul in 1909, Mary sold the Guernsey hotel the couple had run together for fifteen thousand dollars and fled to Cheyenne to live in style. Thirteen thousand dollars was later found hidden on her body.

narrative_blocks.header: Killed at a Sunday restaurant lunch
narrative_blocks.body: Ryan found Mary and her daughter Nellie at a Cheyenne restaurant in March 1909. After harsh words he drew a revolver and shot them both dead, then surrendered to a lawman eating nearby, saying they had bled him of all he had.

narrative_blocks.header: The killing that filled a Cheyenne courtroom
narrative_blocks.body: Mary's death made a sensation. Her husband was tried in Cheyenne in August 1909, convicted of second-degree murder, and sentenced to thirty to ninety-nine years; she was buried at Lakeview Cemetery beside her first husband and her daughter.

narrative_blocks.header: The first man in America called librarian
narrative_blocks.body: Harvard chose him Library keeper on 27 March 1667, and the orders drawn up with the post required him to keep the library duly swept and the books clean and orderly. He is the first American known to history by that title.

narrative_blocks.header: The Pope of the Connecticut Valley
narrative_blocks.body: For nearly sixty years Stoddard ruled the Northampton church and much of the western frontier with such authority that rivals called him the 'Pope of the Connecticut Valley.' He threw open the communion table to any upright baptized resident, treating the sacrament itself as a tool of conversion — and infuriating the Mathers in Boston.

narrative_blocks.header: He proposed hunting Indians with dogs in 1703
narrative_blocks.body: In 1703 he proposed that dogs be used to hunt Indians as they hunted bears, and Massachusetts passed an act for raising them three years later. By 1723 he had reversed himself and become their most outspoken defender, urging their conversion instead.

narrative_blocks.header: Raiders twice spared his life
narrative_blocks.body: According to Timothy Dwight, a later president of Yale, Native war parties twice held their fire and spared Stoddard's life out of respect for his reputation for holiness.

narrative_blocks.header: He railed against long hair and petticoats
narrative_blocks.body: In a 1722 pamphlet of cases of conscience he ruled that long hair was 'Effeminacy and a vast Expence' and that hooped petticoats had 'something of Nakedness'. The satire that answered him, Hoop-Petticoats Arraigned and Condemned, is attributed to Benjamin Franklin.

narrative_blocks.header: His father went to prison over a book
narrative_blocks.body: Anthony Stoddard was jailed in Boston for standing by William Pynchon's The Meritorious Price of Our Redemption after the General Court had it burned in 1650. His son spent the next sixty years widening who was allowed to come to the communion table.

narrative_blocks.header: His famous grandson undid his life's work
narrative_blocks.body: Stoddard groomed his grandson Jonathan Edwards as assistant and successor at Northampton. A generation later Edwards repudiated the open-communion practice Stoddard had built — and the same congregation that revered the grandfather drove the grandson from that pulpit.

sermon he preached and printed. HARVARD'S FIRST LIBRARIAN — surfaced onto the card 10 Aug 2026, the best unused fact in Sam's
material. Harvard BA 1662; Fellow and Tutor of the Corporation; chosen "Library keeper" 27 March
1667 under sixteen orders "for the rectifying of ye Library" — keep it "duly swept", the books
"clean and orderly", and no scholar under a senior to borrow at all. First American librarian
known to history by that title; served to 1674. His Common Place Book and Sermon Notes, 1660-64,
survive at the Burke Library, Union Theological Seminary, MS 104. THREE LIBRARIANS FOUND AND CONNECTED, on Sam's hunch that there were others: HD1554 Edward
Claudius Herrick, YALE's first librarian 1843-58 — the exact parallel; HD4107 Robert Pierpont
Blake, Director of the Widener; HD3347 Edward Brinley Adams, Harvard Law School librarian
1913-22, dead in office. NOT ON THE CARD, worth blocks if room is made: his mother Mary Downing was sister to Sir George
Downing — of Downing Street — and niece of Gov. John Winthrop, and died when he was an infant.
Chaplain to Governor Daniel Searle at Barbados 1667-69. He married Eleazar Mather's widow Esther,
daughter of Rev. John Warham, moved into his house and took his pulpit; thirteen children. In
1703 he proposed dogs be used "to hunt Indians as they do Bears" and Massachusetts passed an act
for raising them three years later; by 1723 he had reversed entirely and become their most
outspoken defender. His 1722 pamphlet against hoop petticoats drew a satire attributed to
BENJAMIN FRANKLIN, "Hoop-Petticoats Arraigned and Condemned". SWAP 10 Aug 2026, Sam approving: "He preached in Barbados to recover" gave way to the 1703
proposal and its reversal. Sam's instruction on the framing — "being real about dogs and indians
is approved, nothing tabloidy or nasty just direct, no subtle commentary" — so the block states
the proposal, the act that followed, and the reversal, and stops. Tagged moral_complexity. The Barbados facts are kept: he wrecked his health with study and sailed as chaplain to Governor
Daniel Searle 1667-69, returning to take the late Eleazar Mather's pulpit and marry his widow
Esther, daughter of Rev. John Warham. The petticoat block gained the Benjamin Franklin
attribution rather than being replaced. BLOCKS REORDERED after the swap — the new block had simply appended to the end. Career and distinction first, paired themes adjacent, family and death last.

bio.bio_blurb: Solomon Stoddard's wife; Jonathan Edwards's grandmother

narrative_blocks.header: She married two Northampton ministers in turn
narrative_blocks.body: Widowed young by Rev. Eleazer Mather, Esther married his successor in the Northampton pulpit, Solomon Stoddard, around 1670. Over the following decades she bore some fourteen children, among them the mother of Jonathan Edwards.

cross_connections.display_label: was at the siege of Knoxville too, on Burnside's staff

narrative_blocks.header: He raised his own artillery battery
narrative_blocks.body: Edward Henshaw raised and led an Illinois light-artillery company that carried his name — Henshaw's Battery — through the Civil War. He stayed in uniform afterward, taking a Regular Army commission in the 24th Infantry.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at a lonely Texas fort
narrative_blocks.body: Lieutenant Henshaw died on duty in 1872 at Fort McKavett, an isolated post on the west Texas frontier. His remains were later disinterred and carried to the San Antonio National Cemetery for permanent burial.

military_service.notes: Raised and commanded the Illinois volunteer light-artillery company that bore his name.
Took a Regular Army commission after the war; died on frontier duty in 1872 at Fort McKavett, Texas, and was reburied at San Antonio National Cemetery.

narrative_blocks.header: She carried the family to Gold Rush California
narrative_blocks.body: Born in Connecticut and married in Illinois, Sarah followed her husband's army career west and ended her life in Oakland, where she died in 1894. Her sons rose with the new state — one of them onto its Supreme Court.

narrative_blocks.header: She managed Civil War relief in Chicago
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah served as one of the associate managers of the Chicago branch of the U.S. Sanitary Commission during the Civil War, organizing relief for Union soldiers far from the front. She afterward wrote the published history of the commission's Northwestern Branch.

narrative_blocks.header: From express agent to lumber and machinery
narrative_blocks.body: The eldest of the Henshaw sons, Edward left Illinois young and by twenty was an express agent in Placer County, California. He settled into Oakland trade — a partner in the lumber firm Taylor & Co. and later a wholesale machinery merchant — as his mother and younger brothers followed him west.

narrative_blocks.header: The brother who drew the family to California
narrative_blocks.body: Edward went west first, and the others came after: by 1880 his widowed mother Sarah and brothers Frederick, William, and Edwin were all living under one Oakland roof on Myrtle Street. The pioneer Bay Area family that produced a Supreme Court justice and two bankers gathered first around its eldest son.

narrative_blocks.header: A Victorian still bears his name
narrative_blocks.body: The Henshaws lived at 974 16th Street, a Victorian built in 1879 that the city later designated Oakland Historical Landmark #72. Restored and still standing, it carries his name to this day as the Reed-Henshaw House.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: lived in the Victorian later named the Reed-Henshaw House

notable.notable_blurb: California Supreme Court justice

cross_connections.display_label: was a second cousin who also studied at Berkeley
was his father-in-law, the Oakland hotelier and cemetery founder
was a fellow Ottawa, Illinois native and Hall of Fame coach

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-three years on California's highest bench
narrative_blocks.body: Elected to the Supreme Court of California in 1894 at thirty-six, Henshaw sat for nearly twenty-three years — among the longest tenures in the court's history. He won re-election to a second twelve-year term in 1906 before stepping down in 1918.

narrative_blocks.header: Accused of selling a vote for cash
narrative_blocks.body: In 1918 Henshaw publicly denied charges that he had taken a bribe, while still on the bench, to swing his vote in the contested estate of silver senator James G. Fair. The accusation trailed him out of office and was never fully laid to rest.

narrative_blocks.header: A photograph tied him to a crooked boss
narrative_blocks.body: A 1908 newspaper printed a convention photo placing Henshaw beside Abe Ruef, boss of San Francisco's notorious graft machine, hinting that he belonged to it. Three years later an attorney moved to impeach him over how he had handled a rehearing in Ruef's own case.

narrative_blocks.header: A police judge at twenty-five who wouldn't leave
narrative_blocks.body: Henshaw won a police-court judgeship in Oakland at twenty-five, then was cited for contempt in 1889 when he refused to surrender the office to the man elected to replace him. He moved up to the county bench that same year.

narrative_blocks.header: He followed his brothers west to Berkeley
narrative_blocks.body: Born in Ottawa, Illinois, Henshaw trailed his older brothers Edward and William to California, took a degree from the young University of California in 1879, and read law into the bar a year later. From a police-court seat he reached the state's highest court within fifteen years.

narrative_blocks.header: He promised Wilson a year that never came
narrative_blocks.body: Leaving the bench, Henshaw pledged to serve President Wilson in Washington as a 'dollar-a-year' efficiency man — but no record shows he ever went. He returned instead to private practice in Oakland.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran Oakland's Union Savings Bank
narrative_blocks.body: Henshaw rose to the presidency of Oakland's Union Savings Bank around the turn of the century — the bank where his nephew Fritz would later work under him. He had begun in real estate and newspaper publishing, and closed his career in construction and water ventures down in San Diego.

narrative_blocks.header: A fatal accident with the family car
narrative_blocks.body: In 1910 the Henshaw family car, carrying his wife and daughters and driven by their chauffeur, struck and killed a young boy in the street. The driver faced a manslaughter charge in the aftermath.

narrative_blocks.header: Two brothers married two Tubbs sisters
narrative_blocks.body: Henshaw married Hetty Tubbs in 1886; his brother Frederick married her sister Grace — paired alliances that raised two 'Tubbs-Henshaw' households in East Oakland, near the Tubbs Hotel. His own was the 1887 Queen Anne house that still carries the name.

narrative_blocks.header: He built a lake that bears his name
narrative_blocks.body: Beyond the Oakland bank, Henshaw founded the San Diego Water Company and drove the great water projects of early southern California — building Lake Henshaw, which carries his name, and standing as the main force behind Lake Hodges. His company bought the sprawling Warner Land Grant from Henry Huntington to secure the water rights.

narrative_blocks.header: A Montecito estate that played a movie set
narrative_blocks.body: Henshaw's home was Mira Vista, a grand house with vast gardens at Montecito, near Santa Barbara. Its grounds were borrowed as a location for the unreleased 1940s film 'Brazil.'

landmarks.landmark_blurb: raised his family in the 1887 Queen Anne Tubbs-Henshaw House

cross_connections.display_label: stroked and captained Yale's crew, a class ahead of him

narrative_blocks.header: A thirty-year partnership with one classmate
narrative_blocks.body: Out of Yale and Columbia law, Williams went into New York practice and in 1881 formed a partnership with his college classmate Frederick Julian Stimson that lasted three decades. He advised major industrial corporations and served as vice-president of a railway in the Chesapeake & Ohio system.

narrative_blocks.header: An American lawyer born in Valparaíso
narrative_blocks.body: Williams was born in 1858 in Valparaíso, Chile, where his father's steamship and trading ventures had taken the family. Carried north as a small child, he grew up between Norwich, New York, and Stratford before entering Yale as the youngest member of his class.

narrative_blocks.header: He sat on tennis's national committee
narrative_blocks.body: A standout athlete, Williams played two seasons on Yale's varsity baseball nine. In later years he ranked among the country's strong lawn-tennis players and sat on the executive committee of the National Lawn Tennis Association.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale men and a senator behind him
narrative_blocks.body: Williams carried a Yale and Lanman pedigree: grandson of the Rev. Samuel Porter Williams, Yale 1796, and great-grandson of United States Senator James Lanman, Yale 1788. He took his own Yale degree in 1877.

narrative_blocks.header: A year's illness pulled him from work
narrative_blocks.body: Serious illness forced Williams to give up his practice entirely in the fall of 1911. He died of cancer in New York in July 1912, after more than a year's decline, and was buried back at Norwich.

career.organization: Virginia & Portland Railway Co. (Chesapeake & Ohio system)

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived her husband by fifty-five years
narrative_blocks.body: Katherine married Williams in 1907, already once widowed, and lost him just five years later. She lived on to ninety-eight, dying in 1967 — fifty-five years a widow — and was buried with the family at Norwich.

cross_connections.display_label: married his daughter Grace

narrative_blocks.header: Rope that rigged ships from Peru to Japan
narrative_blocks.body: With his brother Alfred, Tubbs built the Tubbs Cordage Company into a San Francisco institution, making marine rope sold to ship riggers and mining firms across the western United States, Mexico, Peru, China, and Japan. The Dogpatch plant outlived him by decades, running until 1962.

narrative_blocks.header: The grand hotel that never turned a profit
narrative_blocks.body: In 1871 Tubbs raised a 200-room luxury hotel east of Lake Merritt, hoping to draw an affluent crowd; the young Gertrude Stein lived there a year and Robert Louis Stevenson lodged there to court Fanny Osbourne. It burned in 1893 having reportedly not made money in years, by then down to twenty guests.

narrative_blocks.header: He built the first vault to coax others
narrative_blocks.body: Tubbs sat at the 1863 meeting where Mountain View Cemetery was conceived and became the founding board's first treasurer, the most engaged of the original trustees. In 1865 he and a partner built the cemetery's first family vaults, hoping the example would persuade others to follow.

narrative_blocks.header: His streetcars were East Oakland's only link
narrative_blocks.body: Tubbs founded the Oakland, Brooklyn and Fruitvale Railroad, a horse-drawn line running up 12th Street to 13th Avenue on four cars and twenty-two horses. For two decades it was East Oakland's only connection to the city apart from 7th Street, before the tracks passed to the Southern Pacific.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave it away rather than will it
narrative_blocks.body: Tubbs rejected the old practice of hoarding wealth until death, instead handing his children and grandchildren their shares as soon as they proved able to manage them. A liberal giver to the poor, his memorial filled the house with flowers and ringed his portrait in sweet peas.

career.organization: Oakland, Brooklyn and Fruitvale Railroad (the "Tubbs Line")

landmarks.landmark_blurb: built and owned the 200-room Tubbs Hotel

narrative_blocks.header: She waded ashore from a shipwreck
narrative_blocks.body: Sailing for California in 1853 aboard the steamer Tennessee, Susan and Hiram were wrecked just outside the Golden Gate. No lives were lost — the passengers walked ashore at low tide, and the Tubbses began their California life soaked but intact.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine children, and only five grew up
narrative_blocks.body: Susan bore nine children across San Francisco and Oakland, but only five lived to adulthood — among them Grace and Hetty, who married the Henshaw brothers. She outlived her husband by eight years, dying in Oakland in 1905.

narrative_blocks.header: Music was banned at her husband's funeral
narrative_blocks.body: When Hiram died in 1897 the family forbade music at the memorial, fearing Susan would be too overcome to bear it. Her only grown son, Herman, had been killed in a Sausalito accident not long before.

narrative_blocks.header: Typhoid took him six weeks after his wedding
narrative_blocks.body: Tyler had just married Irene O'Connor in August 1913 when typhoid fever killed him that September, barely six weeks later, at twenty-three. He was only beginning his life as a young Oakland attorney.

narrative_blocks.header: He walked away from a near-fatal wreck
narrative_blocks.body: In June 1915 Stanley, a justice's son of twenty-four, survived an early-morning auto wreck in Oakland that badly injured a fellow passenger. He married Mooney Berlin years later, in 1929, and had no children.

narrative_blocks.header: He jilted one girl and eloped with another
narrative_blocks.body: Fritz had been all but engaged to Pauline Painter when, within weeks, he eloped instead with Mary Gwendolyn Henderson in July 1913. She slipped away under cover of visiting his mother at Ben Lomond, met him at San Jose for a hasty Catholic wedding, and the pair sailed for a Honolulu honeymoon before her guardian even knew.

narrative_blocks.header: A bond broker who banked for his uncle
narrative_blocks.body: Fritz worked at the Union Savings Bank under his uncle William G. Henshaw before making his career as an investment-bond broker. He and Mary kept a summer home at Ben Lomond and later a Piedmont house, and traveled as far as Yokohama.

narrative_blocks.header: Two marriages and a daughter lost at nine
narrative_blocks.body: Stuart married Edith Emmons in 1918 and they had a daughter, Sally Midge, who died at nine in 1936. He married again in 1937, to Pauline Adams, and died two years later at forty-one.

narrative_blocks.header: One of two sisters who married two brothers
narrative_blocks.body: Hetty Tubbs married William G. Henshaw in 1886; her sister Grace married his brother Frederick — twinned alliances that bound the Tubbs and Henshaw fortunes and raised two 'Tubbs-Henshaw' households in East Oakland. She was famously inconsistent about her own birth year, giving 1863, 1867, 1870, and 1872 to different ship manifests over the years.

narrative_blocks.header: A fatal accident with the family car
narrative_blocks.body: In 1910 Hetty, her daughters, and a niece were riding in the family car when their chauffeur struck and killed a young boy in the street. The driver was charged with manslaughter.

was her sister-in-law, and put the same Europe into a book

narrative_blocks.header: Three husbands, ending with an Italian prince
narrative_blocks.body: Alla married three times: first to mining engineer Harry Chickering in 1907, then — after a 1915 divorce — to Brent Tanner in Paris in 1922, and finally, widowed again, to Prince Jean Capece Zurlo of Italy in 1927. She spent her later life abroad and died at the Hotel Metropole in Monte Carlo.

narrative_blocks.header: She carried her great-grandmother's name
narrative_blocks.body: Alla was named down the line from Alla Mary Edwards, the Connecticut wife of Capt. Edwin Tyler two generations before her. The unusual name traveled from a New England parsonage family to a princess's villa on the Riviera.

naming_inspiration.description: Named down the line for her great-grandmother Alla Mary Edwards (HD2305), the Connecticut wife of Capt. Edwin Tyler.

narrative_blocks.header: The middle child of the water baron
narrative_blocks.body: Florence was the middle of William and Hetty Henshaw's three children, born in Oakland in 1890 and raised between the family's Adams Street house and its later San Francisco homes. She married Charles Clarke Keeney and raised three sons of her own.

cross_connections.display_label: was an uncle who passed his Ibis Club duck marsh down to him

narrative_blocks.header: He kept a duck club on Grizzly Island
narrative_blocks.body: From the 1930s into the 1950s, Henshaw owned a private rod-and-gun club on the marshes near Grizzly Island, in Solano County northeast of Benicia. It was likely the old Ibis Club, partly owned by his uncle, the Supreme Court justice Frederick Henshaw, and passed down to him.

narrative_blocks.header: A colonel's daughter from Portland
narrative_blocks.body: Ida was a daughter of Col. S. R. Harrington and his wife Marguerite, a prominent Portland, Oregon family. She married the Oakland businessman Tyler Henshaw in 1894 and bore three children before her death twelve years later.

narrative_blocks.header: Buried among her parents and four sisters
narrative_blocks.body: Ida died in 1906 after a long illness, only thirty-three. She was laid to rest in the Harrington family plot in Portland, alongside her parents and four of her sisters — her children carried on in California.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-five years moving other people's money
narrative_blocks.body: Henshaw spent his career as an investment banker, rising to vice president at the San Francisco firm of Davis, Skaggs & Co. and holding a seat on the New York Stock Exchange. He worked the markets for forty-five years, the fourth generation of a pioneer Bay Area family to make its living in California finance.

narrative_blocks.header: He retired a major in the Air Force
narrative_blocks.body: Beyond the trading floor, Henshaw served in the U.S. Air Force and retired with the rank of major — the title carved on his stone. The wartime interruption sat in the middle of a long banking life on either side of it.

narrative_blocks.header: An opera board seat and three private clubs
narrative_blocks.body: Henshaw gave his civic energy to the San Francisco Opera, sitting on its board of directors. He moved through the city's old institutions — the Pacific Union Club, the Cercle de l'Union, and the San Francisco Bond Club.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried his Civil War grandfather's name
narrative_blocks.body: Edward Carrington Henshaw bore the full name of his grandfather, the Union artillery captain who raised Henshaw's Battery and died on the Texas frontier. The soldier's name came down three generations to a Marin County banker who married late and left no children of his own.

naming_inspiration.description: Bears the full name of his grandfather Edward Carrington Henshaw (I01892), the Union artillery captain who raised Henshaw's Battery and died on the Texas frontier.

narrative_blocks.header: A two-year marriage at the Henshaw home
narrative_blocks.body: Harry married Alla in 1907 at her parents' Oakland house, the first marriage for them both. By 1915 it had ended in divorce, and Alla went on to two further marriages in Europe while Harry, a mining engineer, faded from her story.

cross_connections.display_label: was his sister, and came to Fernwood sixty years after him
was his father-in-law, the St. Mary's football coach

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the family's cement and water empire
narrative_blocks.body: Trained as an electrical engineer at Berkeley, Henshaw began at PG&E before taking the helm of the family enterprises his grandfather had built — president of the Henshaw Investment Co. and the Warner Resort Company behind Lake Henshaw, and chairman at Riverside Cement. He held the threads of the Tubbs and Henshaw fortunes, down to secretary-treasurer of the Hiram Tubbs Estate.

narrative_blocks.header: He lived by the Webb honor code
narrative_blocks.body: Henshaw served more than twenty years on the board of the Webb School that shaped him, and friends said he carried its honor code into every part of his life. A voracious reader with a mechanical mind, he kept a lifelong passion for railroad history.

narrative_blocks.header: Riding the rails with his railroad grandfather
narrative_blocks.body: Among Henshaw's fondest memories was time spent with his grandfather, the Western District Supervisor of the Central Pacific, riding the line in his private car. A fourth-generation Californian, he was a fifty-year member of the Pacific Union Club.

bio.bio_blurb: Stanford graduate; San Francisco arts patron

narrative_blocks.header: A world traveler who never stopped gardening
narrative_blocks.body: Mary-Tom took her Stanford degree in 1950 and spent a life between two passions — wide travel abroad and the soil at home, where she was a devoted gardener. She gave her patronage to the San Francisco Opera, Symphony, Ballet, and the Merola Foundation.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a classmate for forty-seven years
narrative_blocks.body: At Stanford she met Robert Leefeldt, '49, and married him the year she graduated; the marriage lasted forty-seven years until her death. Together they raised four children and shared a life in Piedmont steeped in the Bay Area's cultural life.

cross_connections.display_label: sat on the de Young board and ran the 1945 UN welcome

narrative_blocks.header: The football coach's daughter who married a Henshaw
narrative_blocks.body: Patricia was the daughter of the famous Saint Mary's coach Slip Madigan; in 1950 she married William G. Henshaw III and settled in Piedmont to raise three children. The marriage lasted sixty years, until his death just short of their anniversary.

narrative_blocks.header: A flower-show judge who golfed as a Paiute
narrative_blocks.body: A devout Catholic and skilled gardener, Patricia was a sought-after flower-show judge and a fixture of Piedmont and Bay Area society. She played tennis for the Claremont Country Club for years and golfed at Lake Tahoe as a member of the Paiute club.

was a fellow Ottawa, Illinois native whose family he married into
wrote the eastern college game Madigan came east to crash
coached VPI to a conference title five years before he started

narrative_blocks.header: He turned a 127-to-0 loss into a power
narrative_blocks.body: Madigan took over a Saint Mary's program fresh off a 127–0 defeat to California in 1920, recruited sixty men, and drilled them in Knute Rockne's Notre Dame plays plus tricks of his own like the 'forward fumble.' Within a few years his 'Galloping Gaels' were beating USC, UCLA, California, and Stanford.

narrative_blocks.header: The night he partied with Babe Ruth
narrative_blocks.body: For a 1930 showdown at Fordham, Madigan rode east with 150 fans on a train billed as 'the world's longest bar,' and threw a pre-game party for sportswriters and celebrities including Babe Ruth and Mayor Jimmy Walker. His underdog Gaels came back from 12–0 down to win, 20–12.

narrative_blocks.header: A small Catholic college's national football name
narrative_blocks.body: Though Saint Mary's enrollment rarely topped 500, Madigan built it into a nationally known power over nineteen seasons before his controversial 1939 firing. He entered the College Football Hall of Fame in 1974.

narrative_blocks.header: He never overlooked a silver dollar
narrative_blocks.body: Madigan lived by the creed that 'it doesn't cost any more to go first class,' and spent freely enough that a 1939 profile joked he'd pry up any silver dollar not nailed down. By the end his business ventures seemed to interest him more than his team, and the lavishness helped cost him the job he'd held for nineteen years.

bio.bio_blurb: Advertising executive; San Francisco arts patron

narrative_blocks.header: He rebuilt Piedmont's parks for twenty-five years
narrative_blocks.body: An advertising man at Foote, Cone & Belding, Leefeldt founded the Piedmont Parks and Art Festival and the Piedmont Parks Improvement Fund, driving the city's award-winning park restoration for a quarter century. He gave the same energy to the San Francisco Opera, chairing its 50th-anniversary celebration.

narrative_blocks.header: Ashes scattered together off the Carmel cliffs
narrative_blocks.body: Leefeldt married his Stanford classmate Mary-Tom Henshaw in 1950 and outlived her by six years. At his death his ashes were scattered into the sea below the Carmel Highlands cliffs, joined with hers in a private family ceremony.

career.role: Account executive, head of business development

notable.notable_blurb: Continental Army major general, "Old Put"

cross_connections.display_label: , his son-in-law, was his aide-de-camp at Bunker Hill

narrative_blocks.header: He crawled into a wolf's den alone
narrative_blocks.body: A young Connecticut farmer plagued by a wolf killing his sheep, Putnam tied a rope to his feet, took a torch and a musket, and crawled alone into the narrow den when his dogs and neighbors would not. He shot the wolf in the dark and was dragged out a local legend — 'Old Wolf Put,' a name that followed him for decades.

narrative_blocks.header: 'The whites of their eyes' at Bunker Hill
narrative_blocks.body: At Bunker Hill in June 1775 Putnam helped plan the fortification and fought in the thick of it, and the war's most famous order — to hold fire until the enemy was close enough to waste no powder — is among those attributed to him that day. The Americans inflicted over a thousand casualties before being forced back for want of ammunition.

narrative_blocks.header: He left his plow for the war
narrative_blocks.body: Plowing with his son when news of Lexington and Concord reached him in April 1775, Putnam rode a hundred miles in eight hours to reach Cambridge and offer his services. Weeks later Congress made him a major general — one of only two officers, with Washington, elected unanimously.

narrative_blocks.header: Half-shaved, he outran the British dragoons
narrative_blocks.body: Surprised by British regulars at Greenwich in 1779 while shaving, Putnam dropped the razor, roused his hundred and fifty men, and spurred his horse straight down a steep flight of stone steps no dragoon dared follow. He escaped under fire, rallied the militia at Stamford, and captured forty of the men who had chased him.

narrative_blocks.header: He threatened to level a governor's house
narrative_blocks.body: As a founder of Connecticut's Sons of Liberty, Putnam confronted Governor Thomas Fitch over the Stamp Act, warning that Fitch's house would be 'leveled with the dust in five minutes' if he did not surrender the stamped paper. The repeal came months later, and the hated tax was never enforced in the colony.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight counties carry his name
narrative_blocks.body: One of the Revolution's most beloved officers, 'Old Put' lent his name to eight American counties and to towns, parks, and his own preserved Connecticut farm. His remains rest in a sarcophagus beneath a mounted monument at Brooklyn, moved there in 1888 after souvenir hunters chipped away his original tomb.

narrative_blocks.header: Buried while her husband stayed at his post
narrative_blocks.body: Hannah, Putnam's wife of twenty-six years and mother of his children, died in 1765. News of a later loss reached him on duty in 1777; true to form, he took only a short absence to see his wife buried before returning to the war.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father was Benjamin Franklin's cousin
narrative_blocks.body: Hannah's father, Joseph Pope, a farmer in Salem Village, was a first cousin of Benjamin Franklin. Her mother, Mehetable, was a Putnam, so in marrying Israel in 1739 Hannah married back into her mother's family.

people.relational_label_override: First Mother-in-law of the Husband of a Sixth Generation Hooker

narrative_blocks.header: Her household held four people in bondage
narrative_blocks.body: The Norwalk household she shared with her husband, Colonel Thomas Fitch, held four people in slavery — Dover, Elrania, Naomi, and Eleanor. Naming them keeps the enslaved among the documented lives of a family long remembered for its public offices.

narrative_blocks.header: She bore eight children, then died young
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Hanford Webb married the Reverend Williams in 1801 and bore him eight children in fourteen years before dying in 1815, at thirty-five. Her widower soon married Sarah Pierpont Tyler, who took the young Williams children as her own and raised a second family alongside them.

bio.bio_blurb: Congregational minister at Sunnyvale and Palo Alto

narrative_blocks.header: He set his circuits ablaze with revival
narrative_blocks.body: A Methodist Episcopal minister from 1817, Ercanbrack rode the circuits of western Michigan and was remembered for seldom failing to leave a charge 'in a blaze of revival.' He served four years as Presiding Elder of the Kalamazoo District before dying at Bronson in 1852, eulogized as a beloved 'Father in Israel.'

narrative_blocks.header: A Princeton tutor turned frontier minister
narrative_blocks.body: Jesse Edwards took his degree at Princeton in 1839, finished its theological seminary, and stayed on as a college tutor before going west into the ministry. He died at Plover, Wisconsin, in 1866, far from the New York valley where he was raised.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived a Bath probate family
narrative_blocks.body: Clarissa married James Rowe Dudley at Bath, New York, in 1844 and raised four children there. Widowed in 1873, she long outlived her husband in the Steuben County town where her father had sat as judge.

narrative_blocks.header: He settled at Dansville and stayed
narrative_blocks.body: Alexander married Elizabeth Gray McCurdy at Dansville, New York, in 1849 and made his life there until his death in 1900. The family took deep root in the Genesee Valley town, where his descendants would return for generations.

cross_connections.display_label: carried the gospel to the Choctaw, as Catlin did a generation on
did for the Choctaw what John Eliot, this cousin's namesake, did

narrative_blocks.header: He put the Bible into the Choctaw tongue
narrative_blocks.body: Ordained by the Indian Presbytery at Wheelock in 1853, John Edwards spent his life as a missionary in the Choctaw Nation, where he translated portions of scripture into Choctaw and worked on a revision of the Choctaw New Testament — doing for the Choctaw what John Eliot had done for the Algonquian two centuries before. He died at San Jose, California, in 1903.

narrative_blocks.header: Two wives, thirty years apart
narrative_blocks.body: Edwards married Rose Hill Murphy of Philadelphia in 1851 and had three children before her death in 1881. Five years later, at Huntsville, Ohio, he married Constance Lucretia Hunter, who bore him one more.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years a pastor to the Choctaw
narrative_blocks.body: John Edwards gave his life to the Choctaw mission at Wheelock in Indian Territory — preacher, pastor, and superintendent of its academy for girls. He retired once at the Civil War's outbreak and again about 1895 to California, a great-great-grandson of Jonathan Edwards carrying the family's faith to the frontier.

narrative_blocks.header: He refused to take up the Confederate cause
narrative_blocks.body: In 1861 Texas troops and Confederate Choctaws searched his mission for Union men and demanded he pledge to fight for the South. He answered that they might as well ask him to strike his mother — he would do nothing against them, but would not take up arms, and held to it though it nearly cost his life.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifteen minutes to flee the hanging party
narrative_blocks.body: Three weeks after that refusal, a neighbor warned that men were riding to hang him that day. Edwards handed his keys to his assistant, changed into warm clothes, took the house money and a prayer with his wife, and was in the saddle within fifteen minutes — gone from Indian Territory until the war was over.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: the Choctaw mission and girls' academy in Indian Territory where he served as superintendent and she taught

narrative_blocks.header: He married into a Revolutionary general's line
narrative_blocks.body: Hamilton married Martha Ann Hanford at Barry, New York, in 1862. Her family ran back through the Hanfords of New Canaan to Brigadier General John Mead of Greenwich, a Connecticut officer of the Revolution.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed young by a frontier doctor's death
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Ann married Dr. Sidney Sheldon of Kingston, Ontario, in 1829 and was left a widow when he died in 1838, only nine years later. She outlived him by nearly sixty years, dying in 1897 at eighty-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a Dutch-descended engineer
narrative_blocks.body: Caroline married William Bunker Vedder, a civil engineer whose family had come from Holland, and they raised six children. She died at Palatine Bridge in 1865, two years before her husband.

bio.bio_blurb: Surrogate and judge of Broome County

narrative_blocks.header: Eighteen years on the Broome County bench
narrative_blocks.body: Educated at the Homer and Binghamton academies, William Burr Edwards was admitted to the bar in 1853 and went on to serve as Surrogate and Judge of Broome County for eighteen years. He practiced and judged in Binghamton until his death there in 1893.

narrative_blocks.header: Four years in the Civil War quartermaster's service
narrative_blocks.body: Charles Henry Edwards spent four years of the Civil War in the quartermaster's service, supplying the Union armies rather than fighting in their lines. He settled afterward at Addison, New York, where he raised six children and died in 1900.

narrative_blocks.header: Iron, locks, and a detour to Iowa
narrative_blocks.body: After fourteen years in dry goods he turned to manufacturing iron and nails with the Wood and McKnight firm, then locks, latches, and platform scales, before pulling up stakes in 1856 for the hardware trade in Dubuque. He came back to Pittsburgh in 1862 and built his last house, R. Edwards & Son, in insurance with his boy Ogden.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter married the cemetery's maker
narrative_blocks.body: Richard's daughter Margaret married Frederick Chislett, the Englishman who built Crown Hill — tying the Edwardses to the Chislett line of cemetery architects. His own portrait was engraved for a history of Allegheny County's prominent men.

narrative_blocks.header: His portrait hangs in a county history
narrative_blocks.body: Richard's likeness was steel-engraved for Cushing's history of Allegheny County's prominent men. His daughter Margaret married the cemetery-builder Frederick Chislett, and his son Maurice wrote the family's published genealogy.

narrative_blocks.header: The elder elected before there was a pastor
narrative_blocks.body: When Pittsburgh's Third Presbyterian Church organized in 1833, Richard was made its first ruling elder — chosen to office before the congregation had even called a minister. For decades he ran its Sunday school and carried much of its support, and it was said no one but the pastor did more to make the church a power in the city.

narrative_blocks.header: Father and son sold insurance together
narrative_blocks.body: Back in Pittsburgh in 1862 after the Iowa years, Richard built his last firm — an insurance agency, R. Edwards & Son, that held the agencies of several of the largest companies in the country. He ran it with his son Ogden until his death in 1884.

narrative_blocks.header: His ship burned on Lake Superior
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph Edwards was aboard the propeller St. Clair when it burned on Lake Superior in July 1876. He and his wife had settled at Marquette, Michigan, on the lake where the disaster struck.

narrative_blocks.header: A sea captain's daughter who went to Pittsburgh
narrative_blocks.body: Catharine was a daughter of Captain John May of Haddam, the Connecticut sea officer and USS Connecticut lieutenant. She married Richard Edwards and raised eleven children in Pittsburgh, where the Edwards name took root in iron, cemeteries, and the church.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son made her a book's subject
narrative_blocks.body: Late in life Catharine became the matriarch of a documented dynasty: her son Maurice, a minister, wrote a full genealogy of her and her husband Richard, their ancestors and descendants. Through her the Haddam May line joined the Pittsburgh Edwardses.

narrative_blocks.header: Two sisters married two business partners
narrative_blocks.body: Catharine's sister was the wife of William Bell, the Pittsburgh dry-goods merchant whose house Richard Edwards clerked in and then joined as partner. The two May sisters thus married the two partners — and it was a Bell kinswoman who first drew Richard into the firm.

narrative_blocks.header: He rode as Lew Wallace's chief of staff
narrative_blocks.body: Elston went to war as an officer of the 11th Indiana and rose to colonel, serving as chief of staff to General Lew Wallace — the future author of Ben-Hur, and his brother-in-law. He came home to run the family bank his father had founded on the Crawfordsville frontier.

narrative_blocks.header: His father's bank, the town they made
narrative_blocks.body: The Elstons more or less built Crawfordsville: his father platted Michigan City, helped lay out Lafayette, and ran the first store and bank. Isaac took the banking firm into the national system and presided over the Elston National Bank, a line that eventually folded into the institutions of a later century.

narrative_blocks.header: A senator and a novelist for brothers-in-law
narrative_blocks.body: His sisters married well into Indiana's first rank — one to U.S. Senator Henry S. Lane, another to General Lew Wallace. Their grand houses stood near his own in the wooded Elston Grove, a family enclave at the edge of town.

military_service.notes: Captain, Co. I, 11th Indiana, April 1861; major September 1861; lieutenant colonel and aide-de-camp July 1862 on General Wool's staff; chief of staff to Gen. Lew Wallace with the rank of colonel; resigned June 1863.

bio.bio_blurb: Merchant captain and USS Connecticut lieutenant

narrative_blocks.header: He chased French privateers off St. Kitts
narrative_blocks.body: Commissioned a lieutenant in the young United States Navy in 1799, May served as second officer aboard the sloop-of-war Connecticut, hunting French privateers through the Caribbean during the Quasi-War. He was the man sent aboard captured ships to check their papers, and was promoted to first lieutenant on the quarterdeck before the cruise was done.

narrative_blocks.header: The sea captain who rescued sinking crews
narrative_blocks.body: Back in the merchant trade, May twice came upon vessels in distress on the open ocean — once provisioning a starving schooner, once taking aboard the entire crew of the foundering Sea-Horse as she rolled onto her beam-ends. He delivered the rescued men safely to New Bedford.

narrative_blocks.header: He went down, no grave but the sea
narrative_blocks.body: May died in July 1811 on the return passage from Cuba to New York and was buried at sea. The stone that bears his name in Haddam marks only his memory; his body lies somewhere beneath the water he sailed all his life.

narrative_blocks.header: A parson's son who went to Yale
narrative_blocks.body: John May was a son of the Reverend Eleazar May of Haddam, who baptized him days after his birth in 1758. He took his degree at Yale in the class of 1777 before going to sea, a minister's son turned merchant captain.

narrative_blocks.header: Master of sloops to the sugar islands
narrative_blocks.body: Before the Navy, May commanded merchant vessels out of Connecticut and Hartford — the Ranger, the Betsey, the Pearl, the Hiram — carrying New England goods to the Caribbean and bringing home molasses and sugar from Martinique and St. Martin. He sailed the Connecticut River trade for years.

narrative_blocks.header: Tryon picked him to be number two
narrative_blocks.body: It was Moses Tryon of Wethersfield who recommended May for a navy commission, and aboard the USS Connecticut Tryon administered his oath and made him second officer. When Tryon took sick leave near the cruise's end, command passed to Captain Richard Derby, and May stayed at his post until the ship was sold off at the war's close.

narrative_blocks.header: A bill of sale in her hand survives
narrative_blocks.body: In 1796, newly widowed, Margaret Dwight sold an enslaved woman named Flora — about nineteen years old — to a Stratford man for twenty-five pounds, her brother witnessing the deed. The document survives in the Smithsonian's museum of African American history, a record of her name on the wrong side of a human sale.

narrative_blocks.header: Her two marriages knotted the Edwards line
narrative_blocks.body: Margaret first married Maurice Dwight, a grandson of Jonathan Edwards; widowed, she married Capt. John May. Her daughter by May, Catharine Pond, then married Richard Edwards — a great-grandson of the same Jonathan Edwards — making Margaret mother-in-law to a man of the very family her first husband had come from.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave Pittsburgh its first real architecture
narrative_blocks.body: Trained at Bath and arriving in Pittsburgh in the early 1830s, Chislett became the first architect of whom the city really knows anything — a master of the Greek Revival whose Bank of Pittsburgh and 1841 courthouse set the standard. Little of his building work survives, but Burke's Building on Fourth Avenue still stands.

narrative_blocks.header: He designed a cemetery like a garden
narrative_blocks.body: Caught up in the rural-cemetery movement, Chislett designed and built Allegheny Cemetery in 1844 — modeled on Mount Auburn — and ran it as superintendent for over twenty years. He laid out sinuous drives, ponds, and naturalistic groves, a style he carried to cemeteries across several states.

narrative_blocks.header: Blind at the last, a sculptor at first
narrative_blocks.body: Before architecture he had been a sculptor, painter, and organist in England, and he kept painting through his Pittsburgh years. Washington College gave him an honorary master's in 1847; he spent his final years blind, and was buried in the cemetery he had made.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: the 1865 Lawrenceville home he built near the Allegheny Cemetery he designed and superintended

cross_connections.display_label: was her father-in-law, architect of Allegheny Cemetery

narrative_blocks.header: She led Indiana's Colonial Dames
narrative_blocks.body: Margaret served as president of the Society of Colonial Dames in Indiana, presiding over the patriotic-heritage women of Indianapolis society. She had come west from Pittsburgh as the bride of the man building the city's grand cemetery.

narrative_blocks.header: Her name rides one stone with her husband's
narrative_blocks.body: Margaret outlived Frederick by eleven years and shares his monument at Crown Hill, the cemetery he spent thirty-six years shaping. She wrote the tribute carved on its back, crediting him with laying the foundations of his life's work.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: the Indianapolis cemetery her husband built and ran, where she lies buried beside him

narrative_blocks.header: He married the magnate's daughter, then his railroad
narrative_blocks.body: He spent his career inside the rail empire of William Thaw, whose eldest daughter he had married — running the Star Union freight line, then as a Pennsylvania Railroad freight agent. The match set him at the center of a great Pittsburgh fortune.

narrative_blocks.header: A Pittsburgh man, he soldiered for Iowa
narrative_blocks.body: Though a Pittsburgh man through and through, he served the Civil War as adjutant of the 5th Iowa Volunteer Cavalry. He was afterward an original companion of the Loyal Legion's Pennsylvania commandery.

narrative_blocks.header: Partner in his father's insurance house
narrative_blocks.body: Ogden went into business with his father Richard as R. Edwards & Son, a Pittsburgh agency representing several of the nation's largest insurance companies. He had joined the firm at its founding in 1862 and carried it on after his father died in 1884.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave his time to the city's sick
narrative_blocks.body: Beyond the insurance trade he sat as a director of three of Pittsburgh's institutions of care — its Western Pennsylvania Hospital, its asylum at Dixmount, and its school for the blind. Civic duty ran alongside business in his ledger.

narrative_blocks.header: He backed a settlement house and his church
narrative_blocks.body: He managed the Kingsley Association, one of Pittsburgh's settlement houses, and served as a trustee of Shadyside Presbyterian Church. The same Presbyterian conscience showed up across his charities.

narrative_blocks.header: She died in Beirut, an ocean from home
narrative_blocks.body: Born in upstate New York and raised in Pittsburgh, she died at sixty-two in Beirut, then part of Ottoman Syria, in the spring of 1908. Her family marked her not at her grave abroad but with a cenotaph in the Allegheny Cemetery at home.

burial.plot_notes: Cenotaph; died and buried at Beirut

narrative_blocks.header: The historian of Minnesota's Presbyterians
narrative_blocks.body: Maurice, a Presbyterian minister with a doctorate from Hamilton, wrote the History of the Synod of Minnesota of the Presbyterian Church in the U.S.A., and put his preaching into print as The Value of Life, and Other Parish Sermons, and Fifty Years of Progress.

narrative_blocks.header: One son to China, one to the hymnal
narrative_blocks.body: Of Maurice's four children, all born at St. Paul, Dwight Woodbridge Edwards gave forty-three years to the YMCA in China and Japan and Deane Edwards became president of the Hymn Society of America. Maurice lived to ninety-three, four years past his wife Annie.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the book on his parents
narrative_blocks.body: Maurice compiled the genealogy of his parents, Richard Edwards and Catharine Pond May, tracing their ancestors, lives and descendants through 240 pages. He opened it with Ben Jonson: "It is the highest of earthly honors to be descended from the great and the good."
