bio.bio_blurb: First superintendent of Crown Hill Cemetery

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-six winters making a cemetery beautiful
narrative_blocks.body: Frederick arrived at the raw Crown Hill grounds on a rainy New Year's Eve in 1863 and woke the next morning to twenty-seven below zero. He spent the next thirty-six years building its drives, draining its marshes, and planting the trees that made it a park — Indianapolis's grand cemetery, realized from his father's design.

narrative_blocks.header: The designer who lived hidden in his grounds
narrative_blocks.body: In 1869 the family moved from their cabin into a house so screened by trees that few realized the man selling cemetery lots also lived among them. An ardent churchman remembered for his integrity, he was buried down Crown Hill's eastern slope, near where that first cabin had stood.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: the great Indianapolis rural cemetery he built and ran for thirty-six years as its first superintendent

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-five years at Renshaw's
narrative_blocks.body: Richard spent his early life in Indianapolis and in 1893 came to Pittsburgh as a member of the grocery firm of John A. Renshaw & Co., staying until it was dissolved in 1928. Then he retired to La Jolla, California, where he died on 1 June 1938.

narrative_blocks.header: One wife for two brothers
narrative_blocks.body: Richard married Mary Bailey Renshaw of Pittsburgh on 26 October 1880, and she was his wife until her death in 1922; she was also married to his brother John. The two brothers died near San Diego in 1938, John in February and Richard four months later.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandfather built a court house
narrative_blocks.body: Richard's grandfather John Chislett was the architect of Pittsburgh's old Court House.

narrative_blocks.header: He and his brother married the same woman
narrative_blocks.body: John was married to Mary Bailey Renshaw of Pittsburgh, who was also the wife of his older brother Richard from 1880 until her death in 1922. John died at San Diego in February 1938, and Richard died at La Jolla four months later.

cross_connections.display_label: was his father-in-law, the Crawfordsville banker and colonel

narrative_blocks.header: Ataxia, and the cure he sought abroad
narrative_blocks.body: Stricken with locomotor ataxia, Fred tried travel in America and Europe, and spent a winter abroad with his wife at the baths said to help the disease. He came home no better and died at his father's house near Crown Hill on 8 March 1897, at thirty-six.

narrative_blocks.header: Weak eyes sent him into business
narrative_blocks.body: Weak eyesight cut short Fred's schooling at Indianapolis and South Williamstown, Massachusetts, so he went into business, first with Hildebrand & Fugate and from 1883 for six years with one of Chicago's largest hardware firms. After marrying Katharine Elston in 1892 he ran the Kurtz & Crossland storage business in Indianapolis.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: The Elston family home in Crawfordsville.

narrative_blocks.header: She married two Chislett brothers
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Bailey Renshaw of Pittsburgh married two Chislett brothers, John and Richard. She was Richard's wife from 26 October 1880 and the mother of his four children, died at Pittsburgh in December 1922, and lies at Crown Hill in Indianapolis.

bio.bio_blurb: Naval architect and VMI New Market cadet

narrative_blocks.header: A teenage cadet in the New Market charge
narrative_blocks.body: In May 1864, not yet twenty, Woodbridge marched out with the Virginia Military Institute cadets at the Battle of New Market and helped drive back a Union advance up the Shenandoah Valley. He had risen to cadet sergeant major, and was made adjutant of the corps after the fight.

narrative_blocks.header: Called to hold Richmond's trenches at the end
narrative_blocks.body: In April 1865 Woodbridge was among the VMI cadets summoned to man the Richmond trenches left open as Lee's army withdrew. He returned to the institute that July and graduated tenth in his class, the war over and the cause lost.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years drafting ships for the Navy
narrative_blocks.body: Woodbridge went north to the Chester shipyards, rising to superintending engineer at John Roach's works, then spent four decades as a naval architect building vessels for the merchant marine and the U.S. Navy. The Virginia cadet became one of the men who designed the new American steel fleet.

narrative_blocks.header: He built her a manor named 'The Louise'
narrative_blocks.body: In 1888 Woodbridge designed and built an English-style manor house in Chester as a wedding gift to his wife Louise, naming it 'The Louise' and laying it up in handmade brick. The house outlived them both and stands today on the Widener University campus.

career.organization: John Roach shipyard / U.S. government, Chester & Philadelphia PA

military_service.role: VMI Corps of Cadets, Confederate Army

landmarks.landmark_blurb: the English-manor-style house he designed and built in 1888 as a wedding gift to his wife, now a Widener University residence

narrative_blocks.header: A society wife who took up the camera
narrative_blocks.body: Louise took up photography in 1884, and within nine years her landscapes hung in Philadelphia's Sixth Joint Annual Exhibition and at Chicago's World's Columbian Exposition. She photographed until about 1915 and left her collection to the Delaware County Historical Society.

narrative_blocks.header: Her seascapes chased light over fact
narrative_blocks.body: Her 1884 view of Edwin Booth's boathouse near Newport sets the small building against a vast rocky beach and a cloud-filled sky, reaching for mood over record. Critics noted how she married factual detail to broad tonal effect, prizing light and atmosphere.

narrative_blocks.header: Gold medal for scholarship at Brooke Hall
narrative_blocks.body: Louise graduated from Brooke Hall at Media on 24 June 1865 and took the gold medal for scholarship, given by the principal, Maria Eastman.

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband named their manor The Louise
narrative_blocks.body: Louise married Jonathan Edwards Woodbridge, a naval architect at the Chester shipyards, at St. Paul's Church, Chester, on 23 May 1876. The English-style manor he designed for her there was called The Louise, and it stands today on the Widener University campus.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brother gave Chester a park and gallery
narrative_blocks.body: Louise descended from Pierre Deshong, who came over from France early in the eighteenth century. Her eldest brother, Alfred Deshong, gave the family land around their Chester mansion to the city as a park, with a gallery for his paintings, bronzes and ivories.

narrative_blocks.header: Governor for a year, then the Senate
narrative_blocks.body: Iredell was elected North Carolina's governor in 1827 and gave up the office within a year to finish Nathaniel Macon's term in the U.S. Senate. His brief tenure left little mark, though he pressed for roads, schools, and one of the state's first experimental railroads.

narrative_blocks.header: He digested seventy years of state law
narrative_blocks.body: After politics Iredell returned to Raleigh and the law, reporting the decisions of the North Carolina Supreme Court for a dozen years. He compiled a three-volume digest of every reported case in the state from 1778 to 1845, a standard reference for the bar.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten times Speaker of the Commons
narrative_blocks.body: Before the governorship Iredell sat for Edenton in the North Carolina House of Commons across more than a decade, elected Speaker again and again as men like Ruffin and Stanly stepped aside. He had come to it young, admitted to the bar at twenty and a militia captain in the War of 1812.

narrative_blocks.header: Raised by an uncle who was governor
narrative_blocks.body: Iredell was ten when his father, a justice of the first U.S. Supreme Court, died; his uncle, Governor Samuel Johnston, took him in and sponsored his Princeton education. He grew up at the center of North Carolina's founding gentry, at Edenton and the Hayes plantation.

career.role: Speaker of the House of Commons

military_service.notes: Commanded volunteers in the defense of Norfolk; brigadier general 1815

narrative_blocks.header: A cavalry captain who wrote home from war
narrative_blocks.body: Cadwallader rode as a captain in the 1st North Carolina Cavalry through the Virginia campaigns, and his wartime letters to his fiancee survive — camp life, marches, and the great names of the war passing through his account. He married twice, the second time late in life to Roberta Edmond.

narrative_blocks.header: Three Dansville generations under one stone
narrative_blocks.body: James lived his whole life in Dansville, the Genesee Valley town his father had settled, and was buried at Green Mount alongside three generations of the family. His daughter Helen carried the line west to Wisconsin and a dynasty of judges.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a judge and raised another
narrative_blocks.body: Helen left the Genesee Valley for Milwaukee as the wife of Edward T. Fairchild, who rose to chief justice of the Wisconsin Supreme Court. Their son Thomas became a justice of the same court and then a federal judge — two generations on one bench. When she died in 1962, her body was brought home to Dansville.

bio.bio_blurb: Chief Justice of the Wisconsin Supreme Court

narrative_blocks.header: He swore in his son as justice
narrative_blocks.body: When Edward retired as chief justice in January 1957, after twenty-seven years on the Wisconsin Supreme Court, the man the voters had chosen for his seat was his son Thomas. Edward gave him the oath of office himself.

narrative_blocks.header: Father of the continuation school
narrative_blocks.body: In the state Senate from 1907 Edward sat on the committee that framed Wisconsin's workmen's compensation act, the first in the country, and he carried so many school bills that the legislative reference librarian Charles McCarthy called him the father of the Continuation School Movement in America.

narrative_blocks.header: Beaten for governor by the Progressives
narrative_blocks.body: A conservative Republican, Edward ran for governor in 1910 and was beaten by the Progressive Francis McGovern. He went back to practice, won his Senate seat again in 1914, and in 1916 Governor Emanuel Philipp made him a Milwaukee circuit judge, the start of forty-one years on the bench.

narrative_blocks.header: A Dansville farm boy who read law
narrative_blocks.body: Edward was five when his family, farmers of modest means, moved from Towanda to Dansville, New York. He worked on a newspaper, read law for three years in Charles H. Rowe's office, passed the bar at twenty-one and in 1894 left for Milwaukee; later he bought a Dansville farm for his vacations.

narrative_blocks.header: His chambers were the court's living room
narrative_blocks.body: Fairchild's chambers became the social center of the court, where the justices came for tea and stories. A good teller of them, he filled the room with accounts of the political and legal fights of his turn-of-the-century youth.

bio.bio_blurb: Federal appeals judge and Wisconsin attorney general

narrative_blocks.header: He ran at Joseph McCarthy and lost
narrative_blocks.body: In July 1952 Tom gave up his post as U.S. attorney to run against Senator Joseph McCarthy, a decision his friends the Feingolds said he made sitting on their living-room couch in Janesville. Soft-spoken where McCarthy roared, he said the senator's wrecking of men's characters revolts us, and he lost in November.

narrative_blocks.header: 22,000 pages of the Chicago Seven
narrative_blocks.body: Tom joined the Seventh Circuit panel on the Chicago Seven appeal as a substitute after Judge Otto Kerner stepped aside under indictment, and read all 22,000 pages of the trial record. In 1972 he wrote the panel's opinion vacating the convictions and ordering a new trial, which the government never held.

narrative_blocks.header: He outlawed Stop the Music before an election
narrative_blocks.body: Elected attorney general in 1948, the only Democrat to win statewide that year, Tom let his office rule the radio giveaway show Stop the Music illegal gambling just before his 1950 Senate race. Voters scrawled insults on their ballots, and the professionals concluded he was too honest for politics.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the clients no lawyer wanted
narrative_blocks.body: In 1956, while preparing to run for the state supreme court, Tom agreed to represent Wisconsin Communists subpoenaed by the House Un-American Activities Committee who could not find lawyers, and recruited others at the bar to join him.

narrative_blocks.header: His father swore him onto the same court
narrative_blocks.body: Tom won his father's seat on the Wisconsin Supreme Court in 1956 with over 77 percent of the vote, and his father swore him in. Roger Traynor, chief justice of California, told a new colleague that Tom and George Currie were the two best appellate judges in the country.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years on the federal appeals bench
narrative_blocks.body: Lyndon Johnson put Tom on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit in 1966. He was its chief judge from 1975 to 1981, kept hearing cases as a senior judge until he died at ninety-four, and since 1988 the University of Wisconsin Law School has held a lecture in his name.

narrative_blocks.header: She taught Choctaw girls at Wheelock
narrative_blocks.body: Constance taught at the Wheelock Academy for Choctaw girls in Indian Territory, where she married the mission's pastor John Edwards as his second wife. After his death she lived with her only daughter, mostly in Oregon.

narrative_blocks.header: From a Choctaw mission to Stanford 1910
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Constance spent her first seven years at the Wheelock mission where her father preached and her mother taught, then came west when the family retired to California. She was at San Jose High when the 1906 earthquake wrecked the school, and graduated from Stanford in 1910.

narrative_blocks.header: He chaired Oregon physics for fifteen years
narrative_blocks.body: Caswell took a Stanford doctorate under Fernando Sanford in 1911, studying the Peltier effect in metals, then built his life at the University of Oregon, chairing its physics department from 1934 to 1949. He wrote a general-physics textbook used across the country.

narrative_blocks.header: His radar handbooks went to war
narrative_blocks.body: During the Second World War Caswell joined the staff of the MIT Radiation Laboratory, leading a section that wrote the instruction handbooks for prototype radar sets. The Oregon professor spent the war teaching the Allied fleet how to use its newest eyes.

narrative_blocks.header: A research fellow's year at Princeton
narrative_blocks.body: In 1919 a National Research Council fellowship took Caswell to the Palmer Physical Laboratory at Princeton to study the properties of metals, the subject that occupied his research life. He carried the work back to Oregon and a thirty-five-year teaching career.

narrative_blocks.header: His sheep and cattle swept the state fairs
narrative_blocks.body: Jonathan Ogden Edwards built a national reputation breeding merino sheep and shorthorn cattle at Youngstown, his herd carrying off prize after prize at the Ohio state fairs. He raised sheep until 1879, then bred shorthorns in partnership with his sons Ogden and Allen.

career.role: Breeder of merino sheep and shorthorn cattle

narrative_blocks.header: Second wife to a Pittsburgh merchant
narrative_blocks.body: Orra married Robert Dickey of Pittsburgh in 1867, his second wife — a grocery and commission merchant whose firm had clawed back from a total fire loss in 1845 to outlast half a century. She had no children and died seven years into the marriage, in 1874.

bio.bio_blurb: President of the Pennsylvania Bar Association

narrative_blocks.header: He led the Pennsylvania bar
narrative_blocks.body: George Breed Gordon built a leading Pittsburgh law practice with the firm of Gordon, Smith, Buchanan & Scott and rose to president of the Pennsylvania Bar Association. He was a trustee of the University of Pittsburgh, a fixture of the city's legal establishment.

narrative_blocks.header: He owned the chairs Washington gave away
narrative_blocks.body: Gordon inherited a set of Chippendale chairs that George Washington had presented to a Major John Clark of York — handed down through his father's family to him. His estate left them, with a collection of art, to Pittsburgh's Carnegie Museum.

narrative_blocks.header: His widow endowed a prize given in Rome
narrative_blocks.body: After their daughter Katherine died young, Gordon and his wife endowed a fellowship in her name at the American Academy in Rome. The Katherine Edwards Gordon Rome Prize in Architecture is still awarded today, a century on.

narrative_blocks.header: Daisy and Lily flour out of Troy
narrative_blocks.body: Ogden gave up breeding shorthorns at Youngstown in 1890 and moved to Troy, founding the flour-and-grain house of Edwards Brothers with his brother Allen. Their mill and two elevators shipped Daisy Patent and Lily Patent flour across Ohio.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the onion marsh and the bank
narrative_blocks.body: Allen P. Edwards managed the Scioto Land Company's twenty-five hundred acres, the largest holding in the onion-marsh country of northwest Ohio, and presided over the Alger Savings Bank besides. He had come to McGuffey in 1889, the year the company was founded, and was known across the region.

career.organization: Edwards Brothers (flour and grain), Troy, Ohio
Scioto Land & Improvement Company, McGuffey, Ohio

narrative_blocks.header: She married her first cousin Alexander
narrative_blocks.body: Catherine's husband, Alexander J. Gordon, was the son of her aunt Katherine — her father Jonathan and his mother were brother and sister, both children of Matthias Ogden Edwards. The two grandchildren of Matthias married in 1892, keeping the line doubled back on itself.

narrative_blocks.header: A Western Reserve daughter, DAR and clubwoman
narrative_blocks.body: Kate King came of early settlers of the Western Reserve and was educated in Warren before marrying Ogden Edwards three days before the couple left for Troy. A member of the DAR and the Altrurian Club, she kept those ties through failing health to the end.

narrative_blocks.header: He married his first cousin Catherine
narrative_blocks.body: Alexander's wife, Catherine G. Edwards, was the daughter of his uncle Jonathan — his mother Katherine and her father were sister and brother, both children of Matthias Ogden Edwards. Two of Matthias's grandchildren wed, a generation after the family's earlier cousin matches.

bio.bio_blurb: Physician and Walnut Hall horse breeder

narrative_blocks.header: A doctor who took over a horse farm
narrative_blocks.body: He trained as a physician and taught medicine, but when his father-in-law died in 1915 he inherited the reins of Walnut Hall, Kentucky's great trotting nursery. For twenty-five years he traded the lecture hall for the breeding shed, refining its bloodlines mare by mare.

narrative_blocks.header: He married into a Standard Oil fortune
narrative_blocks.body: His wife, Lela Harkness, was a Standard Oil heiress — daughter of Lamon Harkness, who had turned a Kentucky farm into the nation's foremost trotting nursery. The match tied a Pittsburgh doctor to one of the Gilded Age's great fortunes.

bio.bio_blurb: Walnut Hall Farm owner and Standardbred breeder

narrative_blocks.header: An oil heiress who bred trotting horses
narrative_blocks.body: She was a Standard Oil heiress who, on her father's death in 1915, inherited Walnut Hall and ran the great Kentucky trotting farm beside her physician husband for the next thirty years. The breeding shed, not the ballroom, was where she spent her life.

narrative_blocks.header: The farm stayed in her family for generations
narrative_blocks.body: Walnut Hall had come from her father, Lamon Harkness, who built it into the country's foremost trotting nursery; it passed in turn to her daughter Katherine and on to a granddaughter's stud. Four generations kept its horses running.

narrative_blocks.header: She was born in a Kansas cow town
narrative_blocks.body: She was born in a Kansas ranching town in 1873, while her father was still running cattle and years before Standard Oil made the family rich. By the time she grew up the Harknesses had moved east, into the former Rockefeller estate in Greenwich.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowhood left her sole mistress of the farm
narrative_blocks.body: When her husband died in 1940 she became the sole owner of Walnut Hall, by then some 3,600 acres and the foremost trotting nursery in the country. She ran it on her own until failing health forced her to slow.

bio.bio_blurb: Standard Oil heir and Standardbred horse breeder

narrative_blocks.header: His fortune came from a Standard Oil bet
narrative_blocks.body: His father, Stephen Harkness, quietly backed John D. Rockefeller's young oil company as a silent partner — and that bet made the family one of the richest in America. Lamon inherited a major stake in Standard Oil, and with it the means to do almost anything he pleased.

narrative_blocks.header: He built a Kentucky horse-breeding empire
narrative_blocks.body: A trip to Kentucky in 1892 to buy a few carriage horses ended with him buying a four-hundred-acre farm called Walnut Hall instead. He grew it to five thousand acres and fourteen hundred trotting horses — the best-known Standardbred nursery in the world.

narrative_blocks.header: His barn ran longer than a city block
narrative_blocks.body: In 1897 he raised a barn at Walnut Hall that stretched four hundred and seventy-six feet, with fifty-two stalls and its own auction ring. More than a century later the “Big Barn” still stood, the centerpiece of Kentucky's horse park.

narrative_blocks.header: His farm still runs in the family today
narrative_blocks.body: He died in 1915 leaving an estate of roughly a hundred million dollars, but his lasting mark was Walnut Hall, handed down through his daughters and their heirs. The sport later voted him into its Hall of Fame, and his descendants were still breeding horses on the land generations on.

narrative_blocks.header: His yacht went to war with the Navy
narrative_blocks.body: Among the trappings of his fortune was a steam yacht, the Wakiva. After his death it was taken into the United States Navy and saw service in the First World War.

narrative_blocks.header: His father's money came with a condition
narrative_blocks.body: The Harkness stake went into Rockefeller's refinery on one term: that Henry Flagler be made a partner in it. Flagler was his father's stepbrother, and had married Mary Harkness, Lamon's own first cousin once removed.

narrative_blocks.header: He rose to lead a Pittsburgh bank
narrative_blocks.body: A Princeton man and Phi Beta Kappa, he climbed to the presidency of a Pittsburgh bank that would one day fold into National City. His brother bred racehorses in Kentucky; he kept the family's feet in Pennsylvania finance.

narrative_blocks.header: For decades he was his church's treasurer
narrative_blocks.body: For twenty-five years he served as treasurer of the Pittsburgh Presbytery, tending the finances of the church as carefully as those of his bank. Faith and ledger were of a piece for him.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried the Harkness name and died young
narrative_blocks.body: The only son of the Walnut Hall family, he was given the Harkness surname as his own first name and lived among the Kentucky horse farms. He died at forty-one in Lexington, leaving a young son to carry it on.

notable.notable_blurb: Hall of Fame harness-racing horsewoman

cross_connections.display_label: built the Walnut Hall farm his granddaughter would run and drive

narrative_blocks.header: She drove trotters faster than two minutes
narrative_blocks.body: In 1936 and 1937 she ranked among the country's leading women reinsmen, driving the mare Margaret Castleton to three miles under two minutes — a real mark of speed in harness racing. Long after, she was voted into the sport's Hall of Fame as an “Immortal.”

narrative_blocks.header: She inherited the country's oldest trotting farm
narrative_blocks.body: Walnut Hall, the Standardbred nursery her grandfather Lamon Harkness built in the Kentucky bluegrass, came in time to her — the oldest such breeding farm in America. She kept it running and bred its trotters until her death.

bio.bio_blurb: Long Island justice of the peace

narrative_blocks.header: He kept the peace at Dosoris
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin Woolsey served as a justice in the commission of the peace on the Long Island estate of Dosoris, which he inherited from his father. He married twice and raised ten children there.

narrative_blocks.header: His father named the estate for a dowry
narrative_blocks.body: The Dosoris land had come to Benjamin's father, the Rev. Benjamin Woolsey of Southold, through marriage — the name a contraction of the Latin for 'wife's dowry.' Benjamin held his share until it was sold off after his death.

narrative_blocks.header: Four generations of Woolsey ministers behind him
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin's father was the Rev. Benjamin Woolsey, pastor at Southold, and the name traced back through Long Island merchants to a Rev. Benjamin Woolsey who had preached at Rotterdam. The pulpit ran in the family for generations before it reached him.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father was Connecticut's King's Attorney
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah was the daughter of Charles Chauncey of New Haven, the King's Attorney for Connecticut in 1776 and a judge of the state's Superior Court from 1785. She raised the children of her husband's first marriage as her own, though she had none herself.

notable.notable_blurb: Biblical scholar and public-education pioneer

bio.bio_blurb: Biblical scholar; literary agent; public-education advocate

narrative_blocks.header: A baker's son who taught himself Latin
narrative_blocks.body: His father, a village baker, died in an accident in 1808, leaving an impoverished widow and two boys; at twelve he was apprenticed to a papermaker. Craving books he couldn't afford, he picked up Latin in stolen moments at the mill and saved for a single year at Bradford Academy.

narrative_blocks.header: Why Ohio copied Prussia's schoolhouses
narrative_blocks.body: Ohio's legislature sent him to Europe in 1836 to study how the German states ran their schools. His Report on Elementary Education in Europe urged Ohio to build a state-backed system on the Prussian model — and the legislature thought enough of it to put a copy in every school district.

narrative_blocks.header: A future president sat beside him in exams
narrative_blocks.body: At Bowdoin he was the brightest in a remarkable room — Longfellow and Hawthorne were a class behind, and the future president Franklin Pierce, a classmate, freely admitted he did better on examinations by sitting next to him. The college made him its paid librarian before he had even finished his degree.

narrative_blocks.header: He hid runaways yet was no abolitionist
narrative_blocks.body: The Cincinnati household he shared took in freedom seekers bound north on the Underground Railroad. Yet he was no abolitionist himself — he held that scripture tolerated slavery and favored resettling free Blacks in Liberia, and softened only after a novel written under his own roof changed the nation's mind.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten thousand volumes on the Ohio frontier
narrative_blocks.body: As Lane Seminary's librarian he built a collection that reached ten thousand volumes by 1837, some of it gathered on a book-buying voyage to Europe. By an 1840 survey it was the largest academic library anywhere west of the Alleghenies.

notable.notable_blurb: Whig congressman who founded the Court of Claims

cross_connections.display_label: drafted the Whigs' protest against the annexation of Texas

narrative_blocks.header: He built the court for suing the government
narrative_blocks.body: As a Connecticut congressman he chaired the House Committee on Claims, and in 1855 became the chief founder of the U.S. Court of Claims — the tribunal created so citizens could finally bring suit against the federal government. He argued before it himself until his death.

narrative_blocks.header: Connecticut's case against Texas, 1845
narrative_blocks.body: In December 1845, weeks after taking his seat, John presented Connecticut's resolutions against admitting Texas as a slave state, and when members objected even to printing them he took the floor. The resolutions called annexation a deliberate assault upon the compromises of the Constitution; he called the House's refusal to print them a preposterous doctrine.

narrative_blocks.header: A Whig who tried to hold the Union
narrative_blocks.body: He served two terms in Congress as a Whig before losing his seat in 1849. A decade later, as the country split, he joined the call for the Constitutional Union Party — the last-ditch coalition that ran on simply preserving the nation. In May 1860 he went to its convention as a Connecticut delegate and was named to its national committee.

narrative_blocks.header: A colony in Illinois called Rockwell
narrative_blocks.body: In 1836 John and his brother Charles William Rockwell founded the Rockwell Land Company to settle La Salle County, Illinois, and laid out a colony called Rockwell there. The brothers went on into western land, canals, railroads and banking.

narrative_blocks.header: Cut in black paper at Norwich, 1840
narrative_blocks.body: In 1840 the French silhouettist Auguste Edouart cut John's profile in black paper at Norwich, top hat and all, and set it against a lithographed porch and trees. The silhouette is now in the National Portrait Gallery.

cross_connections.display_label: ran the Northern Pacific and the New Haven, a railroad cousin

narrative_blocks.header: From Altoona apprentice to the railroad's machine shops
narrative_blocks.body: He started at the bottom of the Pennsylvania Railroad, an apprentice in the Altoona machine shops, and rose to assistant general superintendent of motive power for the whole Eastern Region. He ran its locomotives and shops until he retired in 1937.

narrative_blocks.header: The sociologist's son who chose locomotives
narrative_blocks.body: His father was William Graham Sumner, Yale's famous and combative professor of social science. Eliot edited the Yale Record and graduated in 1896, then turned from the academy his father ruled and gave his life to railroads instead.

narrative_blocks.header: He married his second cousin
narrative_blocks.body: Eliot married Diana Ward Rockwell, his second cousin: her grandmother Elizabeth and his grandfather Henry Hill Elliott were sister and brother, both children of Andrew and Catherine Elliott. The marriage folded one branch of the Elliott line back onto itself.

career.role: Assistant General Superintendent of Motive Power

narrative_blocks.header: He taught America's first sociology course
narrative_blocks.body: In 1876 he became the first person in the English-speaking world to teach a course called 'sociology,' built on Spencer and Comte. For nearly four decades at Yale his lectures drew students by the hundreds — among them the economist Irving Fisher and the maverick Thorstein Veblen.

narrative_blocks.header: His 1906 book named folkways and mores
narrative_blocks.body: Folkways argued that the customs a people live by are not chosen but grown - assembled without anyone deciding, one habit at a time, until they harden into what everybody calls right and wrong. He named the ordinary ones folkways and the weightier ones mores. Both words went straight into the language and are still in it.

narrative_blocks.header: Ethnocentrism, and the Forgotten Man
narrative_blocks.body: He coined ethnocentrism for the habit of judging other peoples by the standards of your own. And he popularized the Forgotten Man - the ordinary taxpayer who, in his telling, quietly foots the bill for every scheme dreamed up to improve somebody else.

narrative_blocks.header: He defied Yale's president and won
narrative_blocks.body: When Yale's president Noah Porter ordered him to drop Herbert Spencer's text from his classroom, he flatly refused, and the faculty split into camps over it. He held his ground — one of the first real fights for academic freedom at an American university.

narrative_blocks.header: He called America's empire a conquest by Spain
narrative_blocks.body: When the United States seized the Philippines after beating Spain, he was disgusted, and titled his most famous lecture 'The Conquest of the United States by Spain.' His point: in taking colonies, America had adopted the very empire it claimed to have defeated.

narrative_blocks.header: An ordained priest who quietly lost God
narrative_blocks.body: He was an Episcopal clergyman before he was a professor — ordained, and preaching twice every Sunday. His faith then slipped away without a struggle; he said he had left his beliefs in a drawer and, opening it long after, found 'nothing there at all.'

narrative_blocks.header: The social Darwinist label came after his death
narrative_blocks.body: Sumner was among America's most widely read intellectuals in his lifetime and was largely forgotten within a generation of his death. Richard Hofstadter's Social Darwinism in American Thought fixed that label on him in 1944, and it is now most of what he is remembered by.

career.role: Professor of Political and Social Science

notable.notable_blurb: Anthropologist and explorer

cross_connections.display_label: painted the Indian tribes for National Geographic from 1935

narrative_blocks.header: He led a camel caravan across the Alashan
narrative_blocks.body: In 1923 the National Geographic Society sent Frederick into China's northwest for nine months: twenty-seven camels, fifteen miles a day, from Baotou across the Alashan. He brought back over two thousand specimens and a photographic record.

narrative_blocks.header: An engineer by training, he chose to wander
narrative_blocks.body: Frederick took an engineering degree at Harvard, then went to sea instead of building anything, and was collecting animals in East Africa before he had even graduated.

narrative_blocks.header: His expeditions reached from the Congo to Persia
narrative_blocks.body: Beyond China, Frederick collected in the Belgian Congo and French Equatorial Africa, and in the deserts of northeast Persia he excavated the ancient mound of Tureng Tepe.

narrative_blocks.header: He came late to the lecture hall
narrative_blocks.body: Only after two decades in the field did he settle into teaching, taking a Harvard doctorate in anthropology at thirty-eight and a long professorship at Tufts. He held the chair there until he retired in 1957.

narrative_blocks.header: He and Janet explored China together
narrative_blocks.body: His wife, Janet, rode the camel caravans at his side and kept the diaries that recorded them, though the expeditions went out under his name alone. They divorced in 1929, not long after the China years that had bound them.

cross_connections.display_label: wrote a history of the Chinese porcelain Hobart collected
built a rival collection of Tang and Song ceramics, left to Boston

narrative_blocks.header: His Chinese ceramics ended up at Harvard
narrative_blocks.body: A Boston investment banker by trade, he spent his life assembling a discerning collection of ancient Chinese ceramics and painting. Pieces he gathered — a Ming blue-and-white bottle, a Song-era celadon bowl — later passed through his daughter to the Harvard Art Museums.

narrative_blocks.header: He died a day before turning twenty-two
narrative_blocks.body: He married in early 1946 and died that same year in Mexico City, one day short of his twenty-second birthday. Whatever he might have become went with him.

narrative_blocks.header: A diplomat's wife who died at forty
narrative_blocks.body: A Radcliffe graduate, she married a young Foreign Service officer in 1949 and raised six children through his postings abroad. She died at forty, years before his ambassadorship in Nepal.

cross_connections.display_label: saved Fraunces Tavern as a fellow Son of the Revolution

narrative_blocks.header: He rode with the 1st New York Cavalry
narrative_blocks.body: He served as a commissioned officer in the 1st New York Cavalry through the hardest years of the war, from 1861 to 1864. The regiment spent much of it in the Shenandoah Valley and the running cavalry fight across northern Virginia.

narrative_blocks.header: A patriotic order gathered to bury him
narrative_blocks.body: He belonged to the Sons of the Revolution, the hereditary society of men descended from those who won American independence. When he died, his brethren in the order turned out to bury him — the same society that, led by Frederick Tallmadge, had bought and saved Fraunces Tavern as its New York home.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept the books for the Hawkins Zouaves
narrative_blocks.body: He went to war as quartermaster of the 9th New York Infantry — the flamboyant “Hawkins Zouaves,” known for their red-trimmed uniforms and hard fighting on the Carolina coast and at Antietam. His was the unglamorous work of feeding and supplying them.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught geography from the air
narrative_blocks.body: A Navy navigator in the Pacific during the war, he turned that view from above into a career — a doctorate in geography, a professorship at San Francisco State, and summer “airborne geography” courses that flew students to Africa and Latin America. He believed a place was best understood by going to it.

narrative_blocks.header: He brought the world to Bay Area television
narrative_blocks.body: In the late 1950s he hosted a Bay Area program called “People, Places, and Politics,” bringing a geographer's eye to the new medium of television. He was a teacher who never confined himself to a classroom.

narrative_blocks.header: He navigated Navy planes across the Pacific war
narrative_blocks.body: When the country went to war he served as a Navy navigator, flying out of the air station at Alameda to scattered points across the Pacific. He was past thirty when he mustered out, with a young family and no settled career yet behind him.

cross_connections.display_label: crossed Tibet by camel, a generation before his airborne geography
earned the first woman's Harvard doctorate in geography, his own field

narrative_blocks.header: She did her fieldwork among the Zapotec
narrative_blocks.body: Late in life, after retiring from teaching, she went to live in the Zapotec villages of Oaxaca, studying why some communities turned to violence and others did not. The work, done among the people themselves, wore down her health in her final years.

narrative_blocks.header: She became an anthropologist in middle age
narrative_blocks.body: Her degrees were in English, and she spent her thirties in California raising two children. Only after that did she turn to anthropology — studying at Stanford under Felix Keesing, and finding her direction after a seminar with the famous Gregory Bateson.

narrative_blocks.header: She studied conversion among Mexican Americans
narrative_blocks.body: Her doctoral research asked why some Mexican American families in San Jose left the Catholic Church for Protestant ones while their neighbors stayed. She did the work up close, living among and learning from the people whose choices she was trying to understand.

left Bryn Mawr in 1939 and published her first book at sixty-four
earned an anthropology doctorate at fifty-six, after library school

narrative_blocks.header: A hospital ward still carried her name
narrative_blocks.body: Out of the family's Standard Oil fortune she endowed a ward at Good Samaritan Hospital that bore the Harkness name. It was an early thread in what became a long family tradition of medical giving.

narrative_blocks.header: He published the bible of harness racing
narrative_blocks.body: From Lexington he ran the company that published Horseman and Fair World, the trade paper of the trotting world, and chaired the Grand Circuit that governed its biggest races. He had married into Walnut Hall, and gave his life to the sport it served.

narrative_blocks.header: He built a resort on a Caribbean island
narrative_blocks.body: Beyond the racetrack he helped develop Petit St. Vincent, a private-island resort in the Grenadines. A Harvard man and an Air Force colonel, he ranged well past the Kentucky bluegrass.

career.organization: Horseman Publishing Co. (Horseman and Fair World)

narrative_blocks.header: She bred the family's trotters a generation on
narrative_blocks.body: She ran her own Standardbred operation, Dunroven Stud in the Kentucky bluegrass, breeding and racing trotters as her mother and great-grandfather had before her. In 2009 the state's harness horsemen voted her into their Hall of Fame.

narrative_blocks.header: She bred French cattle and backed the theater
narrative_blocks.body: Horses were not her only herd — she raised Charolais cattle and sat on their breed associations in two states. Off the farm she gave her time to children's theater and the arts in Kentucky and beyond.

narrative_blocks.header: Her broodmares produced trotting champions
narrative_blocks.body: From her broodmare band came My MVP, the 2012 Kentucky Futurity winner, and Must Be Victory, who took the Hambletonian Oaks — names that still echo on the trotting circuit. The bloodlines reached back to the Walnut Hall stock her family had tended for a century.

narrative_blocks.header: She taught school before the horses
narrative_blocks.body: Before settling into the breeding business she taught — at the Indian Hill School near Cincinnati and at Sayre School in Lexington. Vassar had trained her for a life of more than the barn.

narrative_blocks.header: She married the man who ran Walnut Hall
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband, Steve Brown, managed Walnut Hall in the years it foaled the great Abercrombie, then took over Dunroven Stud at her side. For fifty-one years the farm and the marriage were the same enterprise.

cross_connections.display_label: breeds Thoroughbreds at Gunston Hall, on the next pike over

narrative_blocks.header: He grew up among Pittsburgh's famous names
narrative_blocks.body: He was born into a genteel Pittsburgh — a house with a clay tennis court in the yard, summers and dinners among the Fricks, the Carnegies, and the Hunts. The bank president's son grew up inside the city's Gilded Age aristocracy.

narrative_blocks.header: His ship sank a U-boat off Nova Scotia
narrative_blocks.body: As communications and anti-submarine officer aboard the destroyer escort USS Baker, he helped send the German submarine U-233 to the bottom off Nova Scotia in July 1944. He had rushed an accelerated Princeton degree to reach the war in time.

narrative_blocks.header: He turned $9,000 into a fortune for charity
narrative_blocks.body: With two others in the Charleston Rotary he founded a community foundation in the 1970s and served as its first and longest-serving president. The $9,000 it started with grew, in time, past $185 million for the Lowcountry's good.

narrative_blocks.header: He was a fifth-generation Princeton man
narrative_blocks.body: He was the fifth generation of his family to graduate from Princeton — a college whose second president, Jonathan Edwards, was his own seventh-great-grandfather. The line had kept faith with the school for more than a century.

cross_connections.display_label: was a cousin whose ship a U-boat torpedoed off that same coast

narrative_blocks.header: Orphaned at thirteen, she found a new family
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother died when she was thirteen, and she was sent from her engineer father's wandering job sites to live with Charleston relatives. The week she graduated from college she married Howard Edwards and came home to that city for good.

bio.bio_blurb: Walnut Hall manager and Standardbred breeder

narrative_blocks.header: He managed the farm that raised a champion
narrative_blocks.body: He ran Walnut Hall during the years its mare Bergdorf foaled Abercrombie, the trotter voted Horse of the Year in 1978. In 1985 he took over Dunroven Stud, the old farm's offshoot, and bred champions of his own.

narrative_blocks.header: He climbed the ranks of the horse business
narrative_blocks.body: After an Air Force hitch and a Kentucky degree he learned the trade from the ground up — at the Stallion Station, then the Lexington Trots Breeders — before Walnut Hall handed him its barns. He married into the family that owned the farm and never left the bluegrass.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the medicine at Pearl Harbor
narrative_blocks.body: A Pittsburgh internist in civilian life, he joined the Navy as a commander in 1942 and served as chief of medicine at Pearl Harbor. The base he oversaw was the one the war had opened with.

narrative_blocks.header: He practiced medicine for fifty years
narrative_blocks.body: He cared for Pittsburgh patients in internal medicine and cardiology for half a century, from 1928 until he retired in 1978. Two hospitals kept him on as a doctor emeritus to the end.

narrative_blocks.header: He fought through France with the First Division
narrative_blocks.body: Commissioned out of the Plattsburg officers' camp in 1917, he shipped to France with the 5th Field Artillery of the 1st Division and saw heavy combat. He came home a captain, having risen through two promotions under fire.

narrative_blocks.header: He led a New York watch-case company
narrative_blocks.body: He served as president and a director of the Fahys Watch Case Company and held a seat on the New York Stock Exchange. Business kept him in the city he had been born in.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the family's century-old art house
narrative_blocks.body: He led A.B. Closson Jr. Co., the downtown Cincinnati interior-design and fine-arts firm his grandfather had founded in 1866. For most of a century it stayed in the family and on the same block.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded the club behind the debutante ball
narrative_blocks.body: He founded and first led the Bachelors, the Cincinnati club whose annual ball introduced each season's debutantes, and sat as a trustee of the city's art museum and the Taft Museum. Civic art was the cause of his long life.

narrative_blocks.header: She bred trotting horses and show dogs
narrative_blocks.body: A noted breeder twice over, she raised both Standardbred trotting horses and prize show dogs from her Kentucky base. She had married into the Walnut Hall family young, and stayed in horse country the rest of her life.

narrative_blocks.header: A Democrat running Nancy Reagan's parties
narrative_blocks.body: A lifelong Democrat and friend of the Kennedys, Muffie became social secretary in 1981 to her fellow Smith alumna Nancy Reagan, and ran the state dinners of the Reagan White House until 1985.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother's lost expedition, found at Harvard
narrative_blocks.body: In 1975 Muffie found her mother's archive at Harvard: nineteen hundred photographs from the China, Mongolia and Tibet expeditions of 1921 to 1925, which had gone out under her mother's first husband's name.

narrative_blocks.header: Across the Gobi with her mother's letters
narrative_blocks.body: Muffie spent five years transcribing her mother's letters at the Houghton Library. 'If my mother could cross the Gobi on a camel for forty days,' she said, 'I can write this book.' Vanished Kingdoms came out in 2003.

narrative_blocks.header: Jackie read the first draft
narrative_blocks.body: Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis, a friend of many years, urged Muffie on with Vanished Kingdoms and read a first draft of it before she died in 1994.

narrative_blocks.header: Three husbands, from Embassy Row to Cambridge
narrative_blocks.body: Muffie married Eric Wentworth of the Washington Post, then in 1970 Henry Brandon of the Sunday Times, whose parties ruled Washington. Widowed in 1993, she married Louis Cabot in 1997 and went home to Cambridge.

narrative_blocks.header: Givenchy in the closet, Goodwill beside it
narrative_blocks.body: For all the Givenchy gowns, Muffie bought boxed wine at Costco and evening jackets at Goodwill. Under stress she checked into the Four Seasons, and on September 11 she told her daughter Ali to book a suite at once.

narrative_blocks.header: He made Bradlee's leftover beats his own
narrative_blocks.body: Recruited to the Washington Post by Ben Bradlee in 1966, he took the beats Bradlee cared least about — science, medicine, education, religion — and found his calling in them. The education beat put him at the center of 1968's campus revolts, from Harvard to the Paris barricades.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandfather gave Chicago its Grande Jatte
narrative_blocks.body: Born a Bartlett of Chicago before he was adopted into the Wentworth name, he descended from the collector Frederick Clay Bartlett, who gave the Art Institute its Helen Birch Bartlett Memorial Collection — Seurat's Grande Jatte among it. The eye for art was inherited.

narrative_blocks.header: He left the newsroom for the easel
narrative_blocks.body: He gave up journalism in 1977 to paint, returning again and again to watercolor — the towpath, the Eastern Shore, Maine, even Bhutan. He showed with the Washington watercolor circle and kept winning its small prizes to the end.

career.organization: Council for Advancement and Support of Education

narrative_blocks.header: He was Washington's best-connected foreign reporter
narrative_blocks.body: For more than thirty years he was the London Sunday Times's man in Washington and, by reputation, the most powerful foreign correspondent in America. He turned Georgetown dinner gossip and after-tennis confidences into the coin of insider knowledge, often writing on “the highest authority.”

narrative_blocks.header: His friend Kissinger had his phone tapped
narrative_blocks.body: Henry Kissinger spent Sundays at his swimming pool, yet it was Kissinger's office that handed his name to the FBI for one of the Nixon wiretaps in 1969. When he confronted his friend, Kissinger denied it.

narrative_blocks.header: He fled the Nazis; his mother did not
narrative_blocks.body: A Czech Jew, he left Bratislava for London the day the Germans seized the rest of Czechoslovakia in 1939, parting from his mother at his father's grave with a promise to meet again. She died in a concentration camp in 1942; he was buried beside her name half a century later.

bio.bio_blurb: Cabot Corporation chairman and civic leader

narrative_blocks.header: He rose from the carbon-black plant to chairman
narrative_blocks.body: He started in the family's carbon-black business as a laborer in a Texas plant, then opened Europe's first such plant in England under the Marshall Plan. By the time he retired as chairman in 1986, Cabot Corporation's sales had grown from twenty-seven million dollars to one and a half billion.

narrative_blocks.header: He thought making money a poor goal
narrative_blocks.body: He chaired the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston and, in retirement, the Brookings Institution, and told a business audience that “making money as an end in itself is a fault, not a virtue.” He measured a life by more than its balance sheet.

narrative_blocks.header: A Navy engineer who never left the sea
narrative_blocks.body: He spent the war as a Navy aeronautical engineer repairing aircraft from the Pacific, and a lifetime as a sailor “nobody could touch.” He chaired the America's Cup Foundation and served the Woods Hole Oceanographic trustees out of a lifelong love of the ocean.

chaired the New York Federal Reserve Bank; Cabot had Boston

notable.notable_blurb: Cabot Corporation chairman and civic leader

narrative_blocks.header: She broke in doing impressions on sketch TV
narrative_blocks.body: She made her name on Fox's In Living Color in the early 1990s, doing impressions of everyone from Hillary Clinton to Princess Diana. A run of sitcom turns followed — most memorably as Jerry Seinfeld's “Schmoopie” in the Soup Nazi episode.

narrative_blocks.header: She made comedy out of her own pedigree
narrative_blocks.body: Her first book was a tongue-in-cheek WASP Cookbook; later memoirs mined the same blue-blooded world for laughs. The daughter of a Reagan social secretary turned her inheritance of finger bowls and nicknames into material.

narrative_blocks.header: A blind date led her to an anchor
narrative_blocks.body: A mutual friend set her up with George Stephanopoulos in 2001; they were engaged within two months and married before the year was out. Her father-in-law, a Greek Orthodox priest, performed the ceremony.

narrative_blocks.header: She built her own shows and a podcast
narrative_blocks.body: Past her sketch-comedy years she created and starred in series like Nightcap, launched the Go Ask Ali podcast, and co-founded a production company with her husband. Its first project followed Brooke Shields.

cross_connections.display_label: led The Good Wife through the season she guested in

notable.notable_blurb: Actress, comedian, and author

narrative_blocks.header: He helped win Clinton the White House
narrative_blocks.body: As communications director of Bill Clinton's 1992 campaign — a role caught on film in The War Room — he was one of the young strategists who put a little-known Arkansas governor in the White House. He went in with him as a senior advisor, the inner circle's most public face.

narrative_blocks.header: He went from the West Wing to anchoring
narrative_blocks.body: After leaving the White House in 1996 he reinvented himself at ABC News, rising to host This Week and to co-anchor Good Morning America. The operative who once spun the press became the man asking the questions.

narrative_blocks.header: His memoir confessed the cost of the job
narrative_blocks.body: His 1999 memoir, All Too Human, topped the bestseller lists and laid bare the toll of the work — the depression and the hives that came with carrying a president's message. Clinton later wrote that he regretted the pressure he'd put on so young a staffer.

narrative_blocks.header: A priest's son who studied theology at Oxford
narrative_blocks.body: The son of a Greek Orthodox dean, he was a Columbia salutatorian and a Rhodes Scholar who took a master's in theology at Oxford before turning to politics. Faith and discipline shaped the household he came from.

cross_connections.display_label: ran Wilson's State Department, a Democratic insider before his time
anchors CNN's nights, reporting from wars, hurricanes and disasters
co-hosted Today, its NBC rival, for thirteen years until 1989

notable.notable_blurb: Clinton White House aide turned ABC News anchor

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at twenty-three, she lived to ninety-two
narrative_blocks.body: Her marriage lasted only months before her young husband died in Mexico in 1946. She outlived him by nearly seventy years.

bio.bio_blurb: U.S. Foreign Service officer and ambassador

narrative_blocks.header: He spent his life in the Foreign Service
narrative_blocks.body: Born in France and Harvard-trained, he gave thirty-six years to the U.S. Foreign Service, capped by an ambassadorship to Nepal in the early 1980s. Diplomacy took him across the postwar world.

narrative_blocks.header: Carried to Morocco, born near Paris
narrative_blocks.body: Carleton's parents were on an expedition in Morocco's Rif mountains while his mother was carrying him, and he was born at Neuilly, outside Paris, on the way home in 1927.

narrative_blocks.header: A county of his own in Hesse
narrative_blocks.body: As Kreis Resident Officer at Büdingen from 1950 to 1952, Carleton ran film shows in over a hundred villages, signed every pass for a visit to the East Zone, and debated the local Communist deputy.

narrative_blocks.header: Two ambassadors in neighboring capitals
narrative_blocks.body: In 1968 Carleton married Jane Abell, a Foreign Service officer whom the rules of the day forced to resign; she raised his six children. In 1981 he was ambassador to Nepal and she to Bangladesh, two hours apart by air.

bio.bio_blurb: YMCA secretary and China relief director

narrative_blocks.header: He gave forty-three years to China's YMCA
narrative_blocks.body: A Princeton man, he sailed for Asia in 1906 and spent the next forty-three years as the YMCA's senior secretary in China and Japan. He married in Peking and raised his children in the country he served.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran American relief for war-torn China
narrative_blocks.body: When the Sino-Japanese War tore through China, he became field director of United China Relief, the largest American aid effort for the Chinese. His wife was interned in a Japanese prison camp; they did not see each other for four years.

bio.bio_blurb: President of the Hymn Society of America

narrative_blocks.header: He wanted hymns a child could sing
narrative_blocks.body: Edwards led the Hymn Society of America and was its president emeritus when he died. What he pushed for there was hymns fit for children to sing.

narrative_blocks.header: The Depression broke the town he preached to
narrative_blocks.body: He was pastor of the Dutch Reformed church at Bronxville and then of the interdenominational church at Radburn in New Jersey, built to serve a planned community. The Depression undid the town, and the family moved on to Englewood.

narrative_blocks.header: He fought to keep Prohibition
narrative_blocks.body: As president of the Westchester Council of Churches in 1928 he called on public-spirited citizens to hold the Eighteenth Amendment, and to put the public welfare above personal indulgence.

narrative_blocks.header: An island on Lake Superior carries his name
narrative_blocks.body: Edwards Island on Isle Royale took the family's name, and the cabin they raised there in 1912 still stands on the National Register. He courted Margaret Dulles on it.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifteen years in Riverside's junior school
narrative_blocks.body: She ran the junior department of the school division at Riverside Church from 1935 to 1950, and did ecumenical work either side of it. At Rye she was president of the United Church Women.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote a pharaoh for children
narrative_blocks.body: Child of the Sun set an Egyptian pharaoh down for young readers. Opening the Old Testament followed, along with a long run of articles on religious education.

narrative_blocks.header: The children took notes on the sermon
narrative_blocks.body: The five of them went to church each Sunday with pencils and notebooks, and the sermon was gone over at dinner afterwards. She called it a very serious business — they felt they were reporters on their father.

narrative_blocks.header: An island courtship on Lake Superior
narrative_blocks.body: She was on Isle Royale in the summer of 1912, chaperoned by her mother, and came to an understanding there with Deane Edwards on the island his family had given its name to. They married the next year.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son turned from empire to art
narrative_blocks.body: From a family of statesmen and spies she raised a son who went entirely the other way — Richard, a conscientious objector who became one of the first American scholars of Chinese painting. The Dulles drive went into art instead of power.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brothers took the other road
narrative_blocks.body: John Foster Dulles became Secretary of State and Allen ran the Central Intelligence Agency. She stayed in the church the three of them had been raised in.

residence.notes: Holly Lane.

narrative_blocks.header: He led a seminary against biblical literalism
narrative_blocks.body: A Presbyterian theologian, he headed the Auburn Theological Seminary and helped found the American Theological Society, taking the liberal, ecumenical side against biblical literalism in the age of the Scopes trial. Faith, for him, was meant to think.

narrative_blocks.header: His children ran America's foreign policy
narrative_blocks.body: His children carried the family far past the pulpit: John Foster became Eisenhower's Secretary of State, Allen the director of the CIA, and Eleanor a diplomat. A grandson, Avery, became the first American theologian named a cardinal.

narrative_blocks.header: Three Secretaries of State stood in his family
narrative_blocks.body: He married Edith Foster, daughter of John W. Foster, Benjamin Harrison's Secretary of State; his sister married Robert Lansing, Woodrow Wilson's; and his son John Foster Dulles would hold the same office under Eisenhower. The cabinet post ran through three sides of the house.

narrative_blocks.header: His father preached to the Hindus of Madras
narrative_blocks.body: His father, John Welsh Dulles, sailed from Boston in 1848 as a missionary in South India until the loss of his voice forced him home to edit Presbyterian books and periodicals. The family's devotion to the church ran generations deep before it turned to statecraft.

narrative_blocks.header: Archaeology in Sinai before the pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: Fresh from Princeton Seminary and a spell at Leipzig and Gottingen, he spent 1881 on archaeological work in the Sinai peninsula in the company of Henry Clay Trumbull, who came home convinced he had located Kadesh Barnea. Dulles took the pulpit of the Trumbull Avenue Presbyterian Church in Detroit the same year.

His father John Welsh Dulles sailed for South India in 1848 and was invalided home when he lost his voice, ending the family's field work; she was BORN on the China field to Presbyterian missionaries, took her medical degree at the Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania and went back for fourteen years at Foochow. Both facts are already on the two cards — nothing was asserted that the records do not carry.
TWO CANDIDATES REJECTED, and why. Rev. John Edwards (HD6752) is the better ERA match and carries an explicit 'Presbyterian missionary, Choctaw Nation, Indian Territory, 1853' career row — but that is a domestic mission, not the round-the-world work Sam asked for. Rev. Frank Alphonso Wood (I02067, 1845-1878, 'Missionary in Syria') is the tempting one, since Dulles did archaeological work in Sinai and Judea in 1881 and the Syria Mission passed to the Presbyterian Board in 1870 — but HIS RECORD IS A BARE BLURB with no career rows, no blocks, no notes and no dates on the field, so the exact claim could not be made without inventing it. If his record is ever filled in, he is the sharper link and should replace or join this one.

narrative_blocks.header: He pioneered the study of Chinese painting
narrative_blocks.body: He was among the very first American scholars to specialize in Chinese painting, building his work on close study of single masters — Shen Zhou, Tao-chi, Wen Cheng-ming. His final book, on the Song painter Ma Yuan, appeared when he was ninety-four.

narrative_blocks.header: A pacifist, he drove ambulances through the war
narrative_blocks.body: A conscientious objector who still wanted to serve, he carried stretchers with the American Field Service in North Africa and drove medical-supply trucks over the Burma Road into China. “The guy you're fighting against is just like you,” he liked to say — to him the enemy was only a man in a different uniform.

narrative_blocks.header: A torpedo sank his ship bound for Africa
narrative_blocks.body: On his way to serve in North Africa his ship was torpedoed by a German U-boat; everyone reached the lifeboats and was picked up off Nova Scotia. He noted that the submarine's captain had waited until all had jumped before firing the final salvo — even there he found the enemy's humanity.

narrative_blocks.header: He fell for his Chinese teacher
narrative_blocks.body: Sent to Yale to learn Chinese for his new field, he fell for his teacher, Vee Tsung Ling; on their first date at the Metropolitan Museum, he later admitted, he was too taken with her to notice the art. They married in 1947 and became an inseparable scholarly couple.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught his students by making them look
narrative_blocks.body: He would put a slide on the screen and make a room of students stare in silence until they truly saw it, refusing to hand over his own conclusions. His second word as a baby, his journal recorded, had been “see.”

narrative_blocks.header: She interpreted for ping-pong diplomacy
narrative_blocks.body: In 1972 she served as interpreter for the first Chinese table-tennis team to visit the United States — the “ping-pong diplomacy” that cracked open relations between the two countries. Three years later China invited her and her husband back in thanks.

narrative_blocks.header: She left an island in China for Yale
narrative_blocks.body: Raised on the island of Gulangyu off Xiamen, she came to America at eighteen to study piano and stayed to teach Chinese at Yale. She missed her homeland much of her life, her son later said.

narrative_blocks.header: He dates Chinese caves to read past climates
narrative_blocks.body: He helped develop uranium-thorium dating into a precise tool and turned it on the mineral deposits of Chinese caves, reading 600,000 years of monsoon and climate history layer by layer. His ages have caught ice ages and the fall of the Tang dynasty in the rock.

narrative_blocks.header: He followed his parents back to China
narrative_blocks.body: Seventy years after his father drove medical trucks along China's wartime border, he was received in the Great Hall of the People as a member of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. The cave records he reads lie in the country both his parents loved.

narrative_blocks.header: He took his ministry to the city's poor
narrative_blocks.body: As Cincinnati's minister-at-large he set out to pull the poor and their children away from what he called evil associations and to find them work. He named the enemies plainly: pauperism, poverty, infidelity, vice, and crime.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped found Cincinnati's Semi-Colon Club
narrative_blocks.body: He was a founder of the Semi-Colon Club, the literary circle that met at Samuel Foote's house and counted Harriet Beecher among its members before she became Stowe. Writers read their work aloud there and argued it out.

narrative_blocks.header: He chronicled the American West from Cincinnati
narrative_blocks.body: Trained as a lawyer, he bought a Cincinnati newspaper instead, then left journalism for the Unitarian pulpit and a ministry to the city's poor. His essays on life in what was then America's far frontier made him an early historian of the West.

narrative_blocks.header: He drowned in the Ohio River at thirty-nine
narrative_blocks.body: He struggled for years with his health and his spirits, and in December 1849 he drowned in the Ohio River, by his own hand. His body was never recovered.

narrative_blocks.header: His father trafficked enslaved people in the Caribbean
narrative_blocks.body: His father, Samuel Gardiner Perkins, made his money as a slave trader at Saint-Domingue and a partner in the Boston house of S. Higginson & Company. The Unitarian who preached to Cincinnati's poor was a son of that trade.

narrative_blocks.header: His orphaned son built a railroad empire
narrative_blocks.body: His eldest boy, Charles, was nine when he died, yet grew up to run the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy for a quarter-century. The Cincinnati minister's line ran straight into the age of the great railroads.

narrative_blocks.header: She linked two Secretaries of State by name
narrative_blocks.body: Her father, John W. Foster, was Benjamin Harrison's Secretary of State; her eldest son, named John Foster Dulles in his honor, would hold the same office under Eisenhower. The name passed from one cabinet to another through her.

narrative_blocks.header: A third Secretary of State married her sister
narrative_blocks.body: Her sister married Robert Lansing, Woodrow Wilson's Secretary of State — the third holder of that office to stand beside her. Her grandson set her down as a woman of gracious charm, marked executive ability, and a wisdom born of long experience.

narrative_blocks.header: She left a poem with the dishcloth
narrative_blocks.body: Chaperoning her daughter Margaret on Isle Royale in August 1912, she went to the housewarming of the new Edwards cabin and left the campers a scrubbing rag and a verse to find. 'When far from your island I am living,' it ended, 'my thoughts to that table will fly, and the fresh air again I'll feel blowing.'

narrative_blocks.header: She clocked the fastest flower on Earth
narrative_blocks.body: On a field trip to Isle Royale she and a student found that the bunchberry dogwood fires its pollen into the air faster than a bullet leaves a rifle — a discovery that ran in Nature and the Guinness Book of World Records. A flower on the forest floor opened a whole new line of research.

narrative_blocks.header: She still sends Williams students into the woods
narrative_blocks.body: For five decades she has taught field botany and conservation at Williams, sending generation after generation of students out to look closely at the living world. They carry her habit of attention into their own science.

narrative_blocks.header: Arabic, Ottoman Turkish and Persian
narrative_blocks.body: He took his doctorate at Chicago in 1979 on the workings of the Ottoman army under Murad IV, and held fellowships in Cairo, Istanbul and Damascus. He works primarily in Arabic, Ottoman Turkish and Persian.

narrative_blocks.header: Columbia, Istanbul, then Birmingham
narrative_blocks.body: He taught at Chicago and Michigan State, then a decade at Columbia from 1982 with a visiting professorship at Istanbul University in between. Birmingham took him in 1992, where he became Reader in Ottoman Studies.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the book on Ottoman warfare
narrative_blocks.body: Ottoman Warfare, 1500-1700 came out in 1999 and was translated into Turkish in 2006. Exploring Ottoman Sovereignty followed in 2008, and he has co-edited Archivum Ottomanicum since 1988.

narrative_blocks.header: Pine Rest, and the rehabilitation programme
narrative_blocks.body: She read art at Washtenaw and Eastern Michigan, spent two years at Spring Lake Ranch in Vermont, and went to Grand Rapids in 1984. She worked at Pine Rest in housekeeping and the cafeteria, and volunteered in a rehabilitation programme.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-seven, after a long illness named plainly
narrative_blocks.body: She died suddenly on 15 July 2004, after what her family called in print a long battle with schizophrenia. They asked for gifts to the National Alliance for the Mentally Ill rather than flowers, in two Michigan counties.

narrative_blocks.header: He drove medical trucks across wartime China
narrative_blocks.body: A conscientious objector who believed killing solved nothing, he spent the war driving charcoal-powered trucks of medical supplies across southwest China with the British Friends Ambulance Unit. Along the way he met both Chiang Kai-shek and Mao.

narrative_blocks.header: He became a leading historian of Asia
narrative_blocks.body: He turned those wartime years into a scholarly life, writing more than eighty works on the history and cities of China and South Asia and leading the field's main professional association. His “Shanghai: Key to Modern China” became a standard text.

narrative_blocks.header: For a quarter-century, he was the Burlington
narrative_blocks.body: He rose from a fruit-store clerk to president of the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy, building it across the plains to Denver, St. Paul, and Montana until it spanned eight thousand miles. A historian wrote that for twenty-five years he simply was the Burlington.

narrative_blocks.header: He left a Colorado wonderland to the public
narrative_blocks.body: Urged by General Palmer to run his railroad to Colorado Springs, he instead bought hundreds of acres in the Garden of the Gods and left the red-rock formations untouched for anyone to enjoy. After his death his children gave the land to the city, and it became a public park.

narrative_blocks.header: His railroad halted the day he was buried
narrative_blocks.body: On the day of his funeral the entire Burlington system came to a standstill in his memory, every train stopping where it stood. He had shunned publicity all his life and was buried quietly near Boston.

narrative_blocks.header: His cousin gave him his railroad start
narrative_blocks.body: He owed his start to his cousin John Murray Forbes, the Boston financier who controlled the Burlington and gave the nineteen-year-old clerk his first place on the line. Family connections ran the railroad as much as track did.

narrative_blocks.header: He broke the great railroad strike of 1888
narrative_blocks.body: He fired union members on sight, and when his engineers walked out in 1888 he hired strikebreakers and won a sweeping federal injunction that crushed the boycott. A unionized worker, he held, owed loyalty to the union, not to the railroad that paid him.

narrative_blocks.header: His fortune stood on opium and slavery
narrative_blocks.body: The Perkins and Forbes families he was born and married into had built their wealth in the Caribbean slave trade and the China opium traffic. The railroad fortune he made rested on an older one his descendants rarely named.

narrative_blocks.header: She died in the Santa Barbara earthquake
narrative_blocks.body: On a June morning in 1925 the earth heaved under Santa Barbara and the Arlington Hotel came down with her inside it. She was eighty-two and had outlived her husband by eighteen years.

narrative_blocks.header: She may have inspired a Willa Cather heroine
narrative_blocks.body: Willa Cather knew her in Boston and admired her, and scholars suspect she and her husband sat for the railroad magnate and his wife in Cather's “A Lost Lady.” The two women exchanged warm letters.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father was the opium captain turned humanitarian
narrative_blocks.body: She was the daughter of Captain Robert Bennet Forbes, who made his name in the Canton opium trade and then sailed America's first famine-relief ship to Ireland. The contradictions of that fortune sat behind her Boston respectability.

documents.document_blurb: Willa Cather wrote to her, 1915.

narrative_blocks.header: He was a captain for Russell & Company
narrative_blocks.body: He went to sea for his Perkins uncles at thirteen, took his first command before twenty, and rose to head Russell & Company, the largest American trading house in Canton. China made the Forbes fortune.

narrative_blocks.header: He commanded a floating opium warehouse
narrative_blocks.body: His first command in the East was the Lintin, a storeship anchored off the China coast that held opium for sale into a country that had outlawed it. The drug was the foundation of his wealth and the firm's.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped bring on the Opium War
narrative_blocks.body: Back in Canton as head of Russell & Company at the end of the 1830s, he was among the American merchants whose opium dealing helped push Britain and China into war. He defended the trade as the conflict came.

narrative_blocks.header: He sailed America's first famine-relief ship to Ireland
narrative_blocks.body: In 1847 he turned from opium to command the navy sloop Jamestown, packed it with eight thousand barrels of food, and crossed to famine-struck Cork in fifteen days. It was the first time the United States sent a warship on an errand of pure mercy.

narrative_blocks.header: He jumped overboard to save the drowning
narrative_blocks.body: When his steamer ran down an emigrant ship in 1849, he threw himself from the rail into the sea and pulled out a woman, a child, and a man. The Liverpool Shipwreck and Humane Society gave him its medal for gallantry.

narrative_blocks.header: The house he built is now a museum
narrative_blocks.body: The Greek Revival mansion he raised in Milton became a National Historic Landmark and a museum to his seafaring family. He told his own story in a memoir, “Personal Reminiscences.”

narrative_blocks.header: She died on her ninety-second birthday
narrative_blocks.body: Born on the eighth of July in 1876, she died on the eighth of July in 1968 — ninety-two years to the day. Twice married, she outlived both her husbands by decades.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the railroad his father had built
narrative_blocks.body: He served as president of the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy from 1918 to 1921, the railroad his father had run for a quarter-century before him. He held a board seat until 1929, then left the East for California.

narrative_blocks.header: He and Franklin Roosevelt were Harvard classmates
narrative_blocks.body: He went through Harvard alongside Franklin Roosevelt and kept the tie in later life. When Roosevelt built his foundation to fight infantile paralysis, Perkins served as one of its trustees.

narrative_blocks.header: He bred a Kentucky Derby winner in California
narrative_blocks.body: He bought the Alisal Ranch near Santa Barbara in the late 1920s and turned to thoroughbreds, breeding Flying Ebony, who won the Kentucky Derby in 1925. The railroad heir ended his life a California horseman.

cross_connections.display_label: was the era's dominant breeder, twice a Derby winner

narrative_blocks.header: She chased the ghosts of Custer's last stand
narrative_blocks.body: She turned amateur historian of the American West, gathering letters, clippings, and articles on George Custer and the Battle of the Little Bighorn. One prize was an 1874 letter written to Major Reno; the collection she built outlived her by decades.

narrative_blocks.header: A broken marriage sent her to wartime Europe
narrative_blocks.body: She married a Wyoming rancher in 1911, but within a few years the match had come apart. She sailed for Europe to work for the Red Cross through the war, and was divorced soon after she came home.

narrative_blocks.header: She co-owned the ranch behind a Derby winner
narrative_blocks.body: She and her brother Charles held the Alisal Ranch together from the late 1920s — ten thousand acres of cattle and Thoroughbreds in the Santa Ynez valley. She spent her last years nearby, in Montecito.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran Russell & Company's business in Shanghai
narrative_blocks.body: A partner in Russell & Company, the largest American house in the China trade, he served as US vice-consul in Shanghai and chaired the foreign-run Shanghai Municipal Council. He helped found China's first steam navigation line on the Yangtze.

narrative_blocks.header: His Milton estate became a public park
narrative_blocks.body: The large estate he kept in Milton between his years in China later became Cunningham Park. His wife, Fanny, spent much of their married life beside him in Shanghai.
