narrative_blocks.header: She taught a legendary producer to fly
narrative_blocks.body: A Texas socialite and pilot, she married the Hollywood and Broadway producer Leland Hayward in 1921 and taught him to fly, planting the aviation passion that ran through his life. They married twice and divorced twice; before and between, she was briefly wed to Frederic Sayles.

narrative_blocks.header: He was a Navy aviator in the Pacific
narrative_blocks.body: A Navy lieutenant commander, he trained as an aviator during the Second World War and met his future wife in San Francisco before they married in 1942. They raised five children on the Massachusetts North Shore.

narrative_blocks.header: She helped save islands and build hospital gardens
narrative_blocks.body: A Vassar woman who married a Navy aviator, she led the Women's Educational and Industrial Union and the Chilton Club in Boston and worked through the Trustees of Reservations to protect Misery Island off the North Shore. She founded gardens at Beverly Hospital and backed Mass Audubon for decades.

narrative_blocks.header: He was counsel to his brother's railroad
narrative_blocks.body: A Boston lawyer and cotton buyer for the New England mills, he served as counsel to the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy — the railroad his brother Charles ran. He had learned his law in the office of the financier John Murray Forbes.

narrative_blocks.header: He rowed Yale on Lake Quinsigamond
narrative_blocks.body: Exeter first, then Harvard and the law school. He pulled an oar for Harvard against Yale at Worcester, on the lake that held the race for a dozen years before it moved down to New London.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought cotton for the New England mills
narrative_blocks.body: Besides the law he bought raw cotton for the mills of New England and opened up mining properties. His brother Charles ran the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy and Edward was its counsel, so the family had law, rails and cotton between them.

narrative_blocks.header: His father preached in Cincinnati
narrative_blocks.body: James Handasyd Perkins was a Unitarian minister and newspaper editor at Cincinnati, and Sarah H. Elliott his mother. Edward was born there in 1844, grew up in Connecticut, and settled at Milton with Jane Sedgwick Watson in 1869.

narrative_blocks.header: Her twin sister died before she was one
narrative_blocks.body: She and Louisa were born at New Bedford on 16 May 1838 and Louisa was dead within the year. Jane lived to seventy-three at Milton, where she raised four sons with Edward Cranch Perkins.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother's twin married John M. Forbes
narrative_blocks.body: Mary and Sarah Hathaway were twins, daughters of Stephen Hathaway of New Bedford. Mary married Robert Sedgwick Watson and Sarah married John M. Forbes, and Jane named her fourth son John Forbes Perkins.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Mayflower passengers, through her mother
narrative_blocks.body: The Hathaways of Dartmouth came from Arthur Hathaway, who married Sarah Cooke. Her father John Cooke crossed on the Mayflower with his own father Francis, and her mother was Sarah Warren, Richard Warren's daughter.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandmother was a Sedgwick of Stockbridge
narrative_blocks.body: Frances Pamela Sedgwick, third child of Theodore Sedgwick and Pamela Dwight, married Ebenezer Watson in 1801, and their fourth child Robert was Jane's father. That makes Jane a great-granddaughter of the Speaker of the House.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father went out to California in 1849
narrative_blocks.body: Robert Sedgwick Watson was born at Stockbridge in 1809 and married her mother in 1833 at the New Bedford mansion of her uncle, Governor Swain. In 1849 he went to California and set up Captain McCondry's bank before coming back east.

narrative_blocks.header: He built one of Boston's great law firms
narrative_blocks.body: He joined Ropes, Gray & Loring in 1897 and helped grow it from six lawyers to nearly sixty, until the firm carried his name as Ropes, Gray, Boyden & Perkins. Out of that office he moved into war supply, reparations and Harvard.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped run the War Department in 1918
narrative_blocks.body: During the First World War he served as chief counsel of the War Industries Board and assistant to the Secretary of War, marshalling American industry. He crossed to Paris on the American commission to the Inter-Allied War Conference.

narrative_blocks.header: He held a deciding vote on German reparations
narrative_blocks.body: When the Dawes Plan reset German war reparations in 1924, he was placed on the Reparations Commission holding the swing vote among the five nations. He served as an alternate to J.P. Morgan on the American side.

narrative_blocks.header: He welcomed a freshman class as acting head
narrative_blocks.body: In 1936 he was Senior Fellow and acting president of Harvard, and stood up to welcome the entering class — the first substitute president in the college's history to do it. He had sat on the Corporation twenty years by then.

narrative_blocks.header: A room at Harvard still bears his name
narrative_blocks.body: He sat as a Fellow of the Harvard Corporation for thirty years, the youngest ever elected to it. After his death the university named the Perkins Room in Massachusetts Hall for him, where its presidents still meet.

narrative_blocks.header: An old fortune built on slaves and opium
narrative_blocks.body: The Perkins money began generations before him in the St. Domingue slave trade and grew in the China opium traffic that followed. His great-grand-uncle Thomas Handasyd Perkins built the Granite Railway, the first in America.

narrative_blocks.header: He captained the crew that beat Yale
narrative_blocks.body: In 1891 he captained the Harvard crew to victory over Yale, a feat that made him famous in his college days. The oarsman went on to direct the Boston & Maine, AT&T, the Southern Pacific, and a dozen other companies.

narrative_blocks.body: She descended directly from John Quincy Adams, the sixth president — his great-granddaughter, born in the Adams family town of Quincy. Through her the Adams line ran into the Perkins family.

narrative_blocks.header: He steered a great bank through the Depression
narrative_blocks.body: He rose to head the National City Bank of New York — today's Citibank — and carried it through the depths of the Depression, cutting the par value of its stock and selling preferred shares to the federal government to keep it standing.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the Red Cross across Europe
narrative_blocks.body: In 1918 he was given complete charge of the American Red Cross organisation across Europe. He had crossed to France while still a vice-president of the bank in New York, and the army commissioned him that September.

narrative_blocks.header: He moved an army to Coblenz
narrative_blocks.body: As a lieutenant colonel he was assistant chief of staff of the Second Army at Chaumont and then of the Third, the Army of Occupation, with charge of the supplies that shifted it to Coblenz. France, Belgium and his own country decorated him.

narrative_blocks.header: He began in a chocolate factory
narrative_blocks.body: His first job was with Walter Baker & Company, the chocolate makers of his own town, and he stayed until 1905 and left an executive. Banking took him from Boston to Albany to New York and the largest trust company in the country.

narrative_blocks.header: Class president four years, and crew captain
narrative_blocks.body: Milton Academy, then Harvard, where his class elected him president all four years and he captained the crew in 1898. He came back as an overseer for eight years and chaired the visiting committee on economics.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept the natural history museum's books
narrative_blocks.body: He was treasurer and a trustee of the American Museum of Natural History, a trustee of Smith, of Sarah Lawrence and of the Berkshire School, and from 1935 a director of the New York Philharmonic Symphony Society.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at dinner at a friend's house
narrative_blocks.body: He had toured South America the year before, visiting the bank's branches and broadcasting from Buenos Aires and Lima. On 12 July 1940 he died at Mount Kisco, dining at a friend's house, aged sixty-four.

narrative_blocks.header: She took her degree the month she married
narrative_blocks.body: Edgewood at Greenwich, then Milton Academy, then a year at a small school in France, and her Sarah Lawrence degree in June 1936 — the same month she married. She was twenty-three and had been schooled on two continents.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a salesman who ran Mobil later
narrative_blocks.body: Albert Nickerson was selling for Socony when they married in June 1936, three years off the forecourt of a filling station. He was president of the company by 1955 and chairman of Mobil by 1961. They raised the four children at Lincoln.

narrative_blocks.header: One of them counted seabirds for a living
narrative_blocks.body: Christine came in 1938 and Albert Winslow in 1939, then Elizabeth and Victoria. Albert Winslow took a Harvard M.B.A., left banking, and spent years at the Manomet Bird Observatory counting seabirds and marine mammals off the coast.

bio.bio_blurb: Harvard historian; Master of Lowell House

narrative_blocks.header: He presided over a Harvard house for decades
narrative_blocks.body: A historian, he was Master of Lowell House at Harvard for decades, presiding over one of its residential colleges and the undergraduates who came through it. His second marriage, in London, joined him to the English Baker-Wilbraham family.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirteen years to get out of Harvard
narrative_blocks.body: He took his A.B. in 1923, read law two years, went into the graduate school for three more and took his master's, and had no doctorate until 1936. Then he taught history in the place that had schooled him.

narrative_blocks.header: Divorced at thirty-four, remarried in London
narrative_blocks.body: Josephine Choate of Southborough married him in June 1927 and they were divorced in 1935. Two years later, on the first of April in London, he married Frances Baker Wilbraham, daughter of Sir Philip Baker Wilbraham.

narrative_blocks.header: He walked into his father's firm
narrative_blocks.body: Milton Academy, then Harvard in 1927 and the law school after it, and then Ropes, Gray, Boyden & Perkins — the Boston firm his father had joined in 1897 and whose name he was still carrying when he died in 1937.

narrative_blocks.header: Three children, and the old names again
narrative_blocks.body: He married Marian Hungerford Gibbs of Baltimore at Sugar Hill in New Hampshire in June 1930. Their three were born at Boston and named for the family on both sides: Louisa Catherine, James Handasyd, and Rufus MacQueen Gibbs.

narrative_blocks.body: Noble & Greenough and then Harvard, B.S. in 1931, and a Boston banking house rather than the family law firm his brother walked into. He ran the Bowen Corporation later on.

narrative_blocks.header: Two daughters on Grove Street
narrative_blocks.body: Anne Bissell Houghton of Milton married him in June 1939 and they settled on Grove Street at Westwood, in the town his father had lived and died in. Mary Laughlin came in 1940 and Anne in 1941, both born at Boston.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Houghton brothers out of Bolton
narrative_blocks.body: Rufus Houghton of Bolton had thirteen children, and two of them matter here. Amory founded the glass works that became Corning; Francis, her grandfather, superintended glass at Somerville and appears in an 1850 census beside him.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father sold White Star Line passages
narrative_blocks.body: Frederick Oakes Houghton was a steamship passenger agent for the White Star and the other great lines serving New England. The family kept 133 Beacon Street in Boston until about 1923 and a house on Adams Street in Milton.

narrative_blocks.header: Katharine Hepburn was her cousin's daughter
narrative_blocks.body: Edith Houghton married a Hooker and led the Maryland suffragists; her sister Katharine married Thomas Hepburn and bore the actress. Edith and Anne were second cousins, which puts Katharine Hepburn one further step out.

June 1860) was a steamship passenger agent for the White Star Line, of 133 Beacon Street and Milton; his father Francis Houghton (1821-1879) of Bolton, Massachusetts superintended glass works at Somerville and appears in the 1850 Cambridge census beside Amory, 33, manufacturer; Francis's father was Rufus Houghton (1769-1853).

Rufus Houghton (1769-1853) of Bolton, Worcester County, married Abigail Barnard there on 7 February 1796. Two of their thirteen children carry these lines: Amory Houghton Sr. (1812-1882), who founded the glass works, and Francis Houghton (1821-1879), the glass superintendent at Somerville. Amory Sr. → Alfred Augustus Houghton (1851-1892) → Edith Houghton Hooker (I01359). Francis → Frederick Oakes Houghton (b. 1860) → Anne Bissell Houghton Perkins (X03546). The two women are therefore second cousins, and neither intervening generation is built in this file.

narrative_blocks.header: They dropped a T out of his name
narrative_blocks.body: The family spelled itself Elliott. The number of L's and T's was thought rather a burden for a first name, so one T came out, and he was Elliot all eleven years of his life. His grandmother was a Sarah H. Elliott of Connecticut.

narrative_blocks.header: He got as far as the Milton schoolroom
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Milton in October 1873, the second of Jane and Edward Cranch Perkins's four sons, he went to preparatory school in the same town and died there at eleven. His three brothers all lived past sixty.

bio.bio_blurb: Boston juvenile court judge and banker

narrative_blocks.header: He ended on the juvenile court bench
narrative_blocks.body: He was counsel to Boston's board of police almost as soon as he began practising, then went into Storey, Thorndike, Palmer and Thayer, and at the end of a long career was appointed judge of the Boston Juvenile Court.

narrative_blocks.header: Sound underwater, then copper, then bonds
narrative_blocks.body: He was vice-president of the Submarine Signal Company from 1909 and crossed to Europe ten times on its business, then treasurer of Calumet & Hecla Mining from 1915. Later came J. M. Forbes & Company and Tucker, Anthony.

narrative_blocks.header: He rationed the country's copper
narrative_blocks.body: In the First World War he sat on the Copper Committee, which decided how the metal was distributed among the industries, and on the War Labor Board. He had been treasurer of a copper company for two years by then.

narrative_blocks.header: Trustee of his own school for sixty years
narrative_blocks.body: Milton Academy took him as a boy, and he joined its board of trustees in 1903, the year he left the Harvard Law School, and stayed. He had spent the year after Harvard travelling round the world.

narrative_blocks.header: Two brothers married two Coolidge sisters
narrative_blocks.body: He married Mary Coolidge at Portsmouth in September 1905, and his brother James Handasyd married her sister Katrine the year after. Both were daughters of J. Templeman Coolidge and Katharine Scolley Parkman.

narrative_blocks.header: He took his own life on the ranch
narrative_blocks.body: He grew up among his father's thoroughbreds and made his own life in the Santa Ynez valley. In 1965, at forty-seven, he died by his own hand on the ranch.

narrative_blocks.header: He guarded prisoners in the war with Spain
narrative_blocks.body: English-born but Boston-bred, he served with the 33rd Michigan and stood guard over prisoners at Siboney in the Spanish-American War. In civilian life he was a stockbroker on the Boston exchange.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran two of Massachusetts's state agencies
narrative_blocks.body: He gave more than thirty years to Massachusetts public service as the state's Commissioner of Correction and later its Commissioner of Conservation. The work made him a fixture of Boston's civic life.

narrative_blocks.header: She crossed oceans under sail with her husband
narrative_blocks.body: With her husband Henry she sailed across the Atlantic, up the Seine, down the coast of Africa and up the River Gambia, and across the Pacific to Japan and China. The voyages were ambitious and sometimes harrowing — a gale at one inlet, a forced landing that had her throwing luggage from an overloaded plane.

narrative_blocks.header: She gave decades to caring for the sick
narrative_blocks.body: She worked for years with the elderly and the ill, first as a volunteer at Norwood Hospital and then on staff at Boston's Deaconess. She backed the Southern Poverty Law Center and Native American causes.

narrative_blocks.header: A champion dog breeder, murdered at home
narrative_blocks.body: He bred and showed German shorthaired pointers, taking his first champion after he transitioned and began living as Cam. In 1987 he was murdered at his Rhode Island home; his remains were not found for a decade, and a court fixed his death at that July.

narrative_blocks.header: Her junior year was spent in Hamburg
narrative_blocks.body: The Winsor School in Boston, then Smith, with her third year at the University of Hamburg. She took her degree in 1963 and went to work for International Business Machines in New York.

narrative_blocks.header: Two IBM families married in 1967
narrative_blocks.body: She was at IBM in New York and William Wallace McDowell Jr.'s father was a vice-president of the company when they married at Dedham in June 1967. Her own father had died two years earlier and her mother gave the announcement.

narrative_blocks.header: Her sister stood up for her at Dedham
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Laughlin Perkins, a year older, was her matron of honour by then Mrs. John H. Bauhan. Their brother Thomas Nelson Perkins III had been born in 1944, three years after Anne.

narrative_blocks.header: Harvard medicine, Tucson, then Chicago
narrative_blocks.body: Milton Academy, the Thatcher School in California, Harvard with the class of 1932 and the medical school in 1936, then two years interning at the Massachusetts General. He practised at Tucson and taught at Harvard before the move west.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a Dover girl in 1938
narrative_blocks.body: Frances Williams, daughter of Ralph B. and Susan Jackson Williams of Dover, married him there on the first of July in 1938, the year after he began at the Massachusetts General. He taught at the medical school as an instructor.

narrative_blocks.header: He made his name on the lungs
narrative_blocks.body: He went to the University of Chicago Medical School in 1947 and built an international reputation as a respiratory physiologist there. He died at Chicago in August 1966, at fifty-seven, with his wife and three children surviving him.

bio.bio_blurb: Founder of Friends of Handicapped Riders

narrative_blocks.header: She taught disabled people to ride
narrative_blocks.body: She founded Friends of Handicapped Riders in 1970 so that disabled people could gain strength, agility and self-esteem by learning to control a horse. She insisted it serve a city, and kept its offices on North Wabash Avenue.

narrative_blocks.header: She skippered a national win at seventeen
narrative_blocks.body: She crewed in the women's national sailing championships three times and skippered her first victory at seventeen. She took up windsurfing in her late sixties and went on sailing alone into her mid-seventies.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-three years of Chicago, then the coast
narrative_blocks.body: She came out with her husband when the University of Chicago took him, worked in the Hyde Park Neighborhood Club, and went back east in 1980 to Bedford and Cohasset. She died at the Cohasset summer house in May 1993.

bio.bio_blurb: Boston lawyer and wartime ferry pilot

narrative_blocks.header: He ferried planes over the Southern Route
narrative_blocks.body: He joined the Air Transport Command at Miami in November 1942 and flew as a ferry pilot to Persia, India and Scotland, then on the Burma flight. His last six months were as safety officer and he came out a captain in December 1945.

narrative_blocks.header: He left New York for a pilot's licence
narrative_blocks.body: Harvard magna cum laude in 1936 and the law school in 1939, then two years at Parker & Duryee in New York — the firm of his cousin's husband. In 1941 he took a commercial aviator's licence meaning to instruct or to fly for the Air Corps.

narrative_blocks.header: He married at Miami during the war
narrative_blocks.body: Sheila Redmond, daughter of Roland L. and Sarah Delano Redmond of New York, married him at Miami on 1 February 1944 while he flew for the Air Transport Command. Their son was born there in October 1945, two months before his discharge.

military_service.notes: Air Transport Command; ferry pilot on the Southern Route and the Burma flight; safety officer at Miami.

sources.label: Sedgwick family genealogy, B43,444 — the children of John Forbes Perkins

narrative_blocks.header: Liberating Buchenwald turned a pilot into a doctor
narrative_blocks.body: He flew fifty combat missions in P-51 Mustangs over France and Germany, and was among the troops who reached Buchenwald at its liberation in 1945. What he saw there sent him into medicine.

narrative_blocks.header: He led two Southern medical schools
narrative_blocks.body: A pathologist trained at Massachusetts General, he became Dean of the Medical College of Georgia and then of the Bowman Gray School of Medicine. He helped pioneer a problem-based way of teaching doctors.

narrative_blocks.header: He animated medicine and played rugby for life
narrative_blocks.body: He founded Animation Technologies, building animations that explained complex medical and legal ideas, and produced media for medical education. A lifelong rugby man, he played into his later years with the Boston Brahmins Old Boys.

narrative_blocks.header: He owned the poems he first published unsigned
narrative_blocks.body: He brought out a volume of his verse under his own name in 1839, eight years after the same poems had appeared anonymously. Poetry was the thread that ran through a life otherwise spent in government offices.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught mathematics to a Mediterranean fleet
narrative_blocks.body: The Navy made him a teacher of mathematics, and he sailed with the Mediterranean squadron for four years. Land office, State Department library, a consul's post in Turkey — the rest of his working life was Washington desks.

narrative_blocks.header: He drowned in Brazil at twenty-five
narrative_blocks.body: He followed his brother Henry to Brazil, where Henry served as American consul at Bahia. There, in 1814, he drowned at twenty-five.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept one pulpit for fifty-three years
narrative_blocks.body: Ordained over the Congregational church at Milford in 1796, he held that one pulpit for fifty-three years until his death. His headstone tallies the ministry: seven revivals, 716 members admitted, 1,117 baptized, and 1,126 of his flock buried.

narrative_blocks.header: His family had fled France for their faith
narrative_blocks.body: The Pinneos descended from Huguenots who left France when the Edict of Nantes was revoked and Protestant worship outlawed. Two centuries later he stood in a Connecticut pulpit, a Protestant minister himself.

cross_connections.display_label: founded the Milford church where he became seventh pastor

narrative_blocks.header: He started over on the Oklahoma frontier
narrative_blocks.body: Past fifty, he moved his family from Iowa to the new town of Altus, Oklahoma, going into real estate and then a wholesale produce concern. He died there suddenly one night in 1917, of a heart attack at home.

narrative_blocks.header: Two wives, no children, two he chose
narrative_blocks.body: Two marriages brought him no children of his own, so he and Hannah raised two adopted daughters as Hookers. One died small; the other, Martha, lived to ninety and carried the name into Ohio.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed in Ohio, she married again
narrative_blocks.body: Her first husband, Norman Bird, died in 1837, leaving her with two sons in Cincinnati. She married Charles Valentine and lived on there to ninety, the matriarch of a large Ohio family.

narrative_blocks.header: A Connecticut tinsmith's son ran Montgomery
narrative_blocks.body: Born in Bristol, he went south and served as mayor of Montgomery, Alabama. He died in Texas in 1840 at forty-four, his three children all lost in infancy.

narrative_blocks.header: A Yankee who died a Southern official mid-war
narrative_blocks.body: As a young man he left Connecticut for Montgomery, Alabama, where he built a merchant's business and rose to clerk of the county court. He died there in 1863 — a Northern-born official in the city that had just been the Confederacy's first capital.

people.research_notes: Daughter of Lewis Catlin of Harwinton.

narrative_blocks.header: The adopted daughter who died small
narrative_blocks.body: Taken into Asahel and Hannah Hooker's home as an adopted daughter, she died at Bristol in the winter of 1842. The family counted her among their own Hookers.

narrative_blocks.header: Adopted by one Hooker, she married another
narrative_blocks.body: Born a Griswold, she was adopted as a daughter by Asahel Hooker and grew up inside the family. At sixteen she married Henry Norman Bird — her adoptive father's nephew — folding two Hooker branches back together.

people.research_notes: Birth daughter of Ozias Griswold & Sally Ann Rich of Wethersfield; adopted by Asahel Hooker.

narrative_blocks.header: He married his uncle's adopted daughter
narrative_blocks.body: His mother Anna's brother Asahel had adopted a daughter, Martha Griswold, raising her as a Hooker. In 1851 Henry married her, and the cousins by adoption raised four children in Cincinnati.

narrative_blocks.header: Outlived him by fifty-six years
narrative_blocks.body: Widowed in 1840 when Moseley died in Texas, she lived on another fifty-six years, into the 1890s. To the family that remembered her she was simply “Grandma Hooker.”

people.research_notes: Sgt., Co. H, 131st Infantry, A.E.F. (WWI).

narrative_blocks.header: He died on his own birthday
narrative_blocks.body: Born in Plainville on the twentieth of May, he died seventy-three years later to the day, out in Grand Junction, Iowa. The Connecticut boy had carried the family west to the prairie.

people.research_notes: Of Southington CT.

narrative_blocks.header: He enlisted twice for the Union
narrative_blocks.body: He served first with the 24th Ohio Infantry at the war's outbreak, then re-enlisted with the 9th Ohio Cavalry and rode through to the surrender in 1865. Two enlistments bracketed the whole of the war.

narrative_blocks.header: From a Terryville hardware store to California
narrative_blocks.body: He sold hardware in Terryville and served as a sergeant through the Civil War. In later life he carried his family west to California and became a deacon of a Congregational church at San Bernardino.

narrative_blocks.header: He took a wound at Cold Harbor
narrative_blocks.body: He enlisted in 1862 and served with the 17th Connecticut and the 2nd Connecticut Heavy Artillery. He was wounded at Cold Harbor, one of the war's costliest assaults, and mustered out in 1865.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years over the bank's books
narrative_blocks.body: For more than forty years he was treasurer of the Thomaston Savings Bank, and he served two years in the state legislature on its banking committee. His Stoughton line traced back to an early colonial governor of Massachusetts.

narrative_blocks.header: She founded a guild of hooking artists
narrative_blocks.body: After a Smith degree, WAVES service in the war, and a late master's in library science, she founded the Association of Traditional Hooking Artists in 1979. The rug-hooking guild she started now numbers in the thousands worldwide.

narrative_blocks.header: He designed for Yosemite and the Seabees
narrative_blocks.body: A Stanford-trained architect, he served with the Navy Seabees in Japan during the Korean War, then spent thirty-three years designing schools, homes, and resorts around San Francisco Bay. He took particular pleasure in his Yosemite work, laying out campgrounds and resort buildings.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote and edited for the Sunday schools
narrative_blocks.body: A Yale-trained minister, he left the pulpit for the desk, editing papers and writing books for the American Sunday School Union in Philadelphia. He had a hand in Schaff's Dictionary of the Bible and a popular commentary on the Gospels.

bio.bio_blurb: World War II Navy pharmacist's mate

narrative_blocks.header: He fought the patent wars, then ran them
narrative_blocks.body: A self-made authority on patent law, he argued most of the great patent cases of his day — until President Harrison put him over the whole system as Commissioner of Patents in 1889. He ran the office through the Patent Centennial of 1891, then went back to the courtroom.

narrative_blocks.header: A freshman lawmaker rewrote the whole code
narrative_blocks.body: In his very first term in the assembly, in 1880, he chaired the corporations committee and redrafted the corporation laws of the entire state. Offered a seat in the state senate, he turned it down.

narrative_blocks.header: He retired from law to make Stanley's tools
narrative_blocks.body: Leaving the law in 1902, he took the presidency of the Stanley Rule and Level Company, the famous New Britain toolmaker, and ran it until his death in 1911.

narrative_blocks.header: Five hardware firms, one small village
narrative_blocks.body: New Britain threw up five hardware firms inside fifteen years — Stanley Works and Landers, Frary & Clark in 1842, P. & F. Corbin in 1848, Stanley Rule and Level in 1854 — in a village of a few thousand. He practised patent law there.

narrative_blocks.header: In a clock town, they remembered his music
narrative_blocks.body: He worked in the great Welch clock factory at Forestville — the firm his father-in-law headed. Yet in that town of clockmakers, it was his music that people remembered.

career.organization: E.N. Welch clock company, Forestville CT

narrative_blocks.header: He died young; his widow married his cousin
narrative_blocks.body: He died at twenty-nine, a dry-goods merchant, leaving his second wife Harriet Barbour a young widow. She married again — to Ira Hooker Stoughton of Terryville, a cousin of her late husband.

people.research_notes: Widow Martha (Mayes) Millard.

narrative_blocks.header: His father judged patents; he guarded the city's
narrative_blocks.body: Yale and Columbia trained, he made his career as a patent lawyer in New York — the very field his father had ruled over as Commissioner of Patents. For a dozen years he served as patent counsel to the City of New York.

career.organization: Law Dept., City of New York

narrative_blocks.header: He died cleaning a pistol at his table
narrative_blocks.body: A Hartford dentist for half a century, he had his fishing tackle and two pistols spread on the dining table one night in 1934 when one slipped from his hand as he cleaned it and fired. The medical examiner ruled the death an accident; he had just turned seventy-seven.

narrative_blocks.header: She was raised on a clothing-store fortune
narrative_blocks.body: She grew up in Springfield's McKnight district, daughter of Lyman Waterman Besse, whose "Besse System" chain of clothing stores stretched across the Northeast. A Wellesley graduate, she married into the Mitchell family in 1918.

narrative_blocks.header: The magnate's eldest, she long outlived her husband
narrative_blocks.body: She was the firstborn of William Thaw, the Pittsburgh transport magnate who built the Star Union line and helped run the Pennsylvania Railroad. She outlived her railroad-man husband, George Breed Edwards, by twenty-five years.

narrative_blocks.header: He built a bank to hold workingmen's dimes
narrative_blocks.body: After years as a New York merchant and a stint in his father's tannery town of Hunter, he helped found Brooklyn's Dime Savings Bank — meant for small savers — and served as its treasurer. He worshipped under Henry Ward Beecher at Plymouth Church.

narrative_blocks.header: He and his wife buried five infants
narrative_blocks.body: Of their nine children, five died before the age of three, and his wife followed at thirty-six. The losses are recorded together on the family stone at Northampton.

burial.plot_notes: Cenotaph also at New York Marble Cemetery

narrative_blocks.header: First in New York to sell silk alone
narrative_blocks.body: Alfred Edwards was the first New York merchant to carry silk to the exclusion of all other goods, and for years no one competed in the line. While still young he was the acknowledged leader of the city's dry-goods trade, one of its merchant princes.

narrative_blocks.header: He moved his store uptown to Park Place
narrative_blocks.body: The firm stood at Pearl and Hanover streets, then the centre of New York trade, but Hanover Square was not to Alfred's taste. About 1852 he went as far toward Harlem as Park Place, into a store running through to Murray Street, and the trade followed him uptown.

narrative_blocks.header: Apprenticed at sixteen to his uncle Arthur Tappan
narrative_blocks.body: In 1820 Alfred went to work for his uncle Arthur Tappan, whose abolitionism later put a slaveholders' bounty on his head. Within a few years Alfred rose from clerk to partner, and the dry-goods house became Alfred Edwards and Company.

narrative_blocks.header: He paid for New York's sparrow houses
narrative_blocks.body: Alfred was among the first to urge bringing the English sparrow to New York to rid the city of the measuring-worm. Much of the money for the thousands of birdhouses put up in its streets and parks came out of his pocket.

narrative_blocks.header: A manager of the American Bible Society
narrative_blocks.body: For years Alfred sat on the board of managers of the American Bible Society. He taught Sunday school with Harlan Page from 1825, and his love for children was said to be almost a passion: for twenty-five years he spent part of every Sunday teaching at the Home for the Friendless.

narrative_blocks.header: Pacific Mutual's president until 1867
narrative_blocks.body: When the Pacific Mutual Marine Insurance Company was formed, Alfred was persuaded to take its presidency. About 1867 he put all business aside and spent his last fifteen years in retirement, seldom seen in business circles.

narrative_blocks.header: He married Zechariah Lewis's eldest daughter
narrative_blocks.body: On 21 June 1831 Alfred married Sophia Matilda Lewis, eldest daughter of Zechariah Lewis, for seventeen years editor of the New York Commercial Advertiser. They had six children; Eliza died at sixteen in 1854, and the other five outlived their father.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father tutored in George Washington's family
narrative_blocks.body: Sophia's father, Zechariah Lewis, was a Yale tutor, then studied theology at Philadelphia while tutoring in George Washington's family. He was licensed to preach, but delicate health kept him from ever taking a pulpit.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father followed Noah Webster as editor
narrative_blocks.body: Sophia was born three years after her father, Zechariah Lewis, succeeded Noah Webster as editor of the New York Commercial Advertiser. He kept the chair for seventeen years, until she was thirteen.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father's tract society went national
narrative_blocks.body: From 1814 to 1820 Sophia's father was corresponding secretary of the New York Religious Tract Society, from which the American Tract Society grew. Zechariah Lewis then started the American Missionary Register, and after 1825 gave his time to charity.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandfather preached sixty years at Greenwich
narrative_blocks.body: Sophia lost her grandfather and her father in 1840. Rev. Isaac Lewis, pastor at Greenwich, Connecticut, for sixty years, died at ninety-six, and Zechariah Lewis followed him that November at Brooklyn Heights.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother's father came from Dresden
narrative_blocks.body: Sophia's mother, Sophia Nitchie, was the daughter of John George Nitchie, who came over from Dresden in Saxony about 1750, and Elizabeth Slidell. She married Zechariah Lewis in New York on 11 January 1804 and was buried at Green-Wood in January 1846.

narrative_blocks.header: She married the silk merchant Alfred Edwards
narrative_blocks.body: Sophia married Alfred Edwards on 21 June 1831, and they had six children between 1833 and 1848. Their daughter Eliza died at sixteen in 1854; the other five outlived both their parents.

cross_connections.display_label: edited the Commercial Advertiser until her father took it over in 1803

narrative_blocks.header: She married in Paris and died at sea
narrative_blocks.body: She was wed to the New York merchant Benjamin Curtis in Paris in 1830. Fourteen years later she died of a heart ailment aboard the packet ship Oneida near Le Havre, and was brought home to be buried in Connecticut.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a theologian already named Edwards
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband, Edwards Amasa Park, bore the name of the family he was marrying into — and earned it, as professor at Andover and the last great voice of the theology descended from Jonathan Edwards. They raised three children there.

bio.bio_blurb: Abbott Professor of Christian Theology at Andover

narrative_blocks.header: He held Edwards's line into the Jacksonian age
narrative_blocks.body: He set divine sovereignty beside what he called the theology of the heart, where Charles Hodge fused Edwards to Scottish philosophy instead. Lyman Abbott called him the last man to try it.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty volumes of the Bibliotheca Sacra
narrative_blocks.body: He founded the quarterly with Bela Bates Edwards in 1844 and was its chief editor from 1851 to 1884. With Austin Phelps and Lowell Mason he also made a hymn book that sold a hundred and twenty thousand.

narrative_blocks.header: An original trustee of Smith College
narrative_blocks.body: He was one of its first trustees, and president of the Abbott Academy board for more than thirty years. Abbott was the girls' school in his own town, and Smith opened to women in 1875.

narrative_blocks.header: Heretical meetings were held in his parlor
narrative_blocks.body: In his brick house on Andover's Main Street, gatherings were held that helped break a wing of New England Congregationalism from orthodoxy. He lived in that house for sixty-four years.

narrative_blocks.header: Providence, Brown, Braintree, Amherst, Andover
narrative_blocks.body: Brown gave him a degree in 1826 and Andover in 1831. He preached a while at Braintree, taught moral and intellectual philosophy at Amherst two years, and came back to Andover in 1836 to stay.

narrative_blocks.header: His own student called him an anachronism
narrative_blocks.body: Frank Hugh Foster said he had become one by 1881, the year he gave up the chair. He stayed on at Andover as emeritus professor of sacred rhetoric and died there in 1900, at ninety-one.

narrative_blocks.header: From a Catskill tannery to Buenos Aires
narrative_blocks.body: A world away from the family's Catskill tannery, he served several years as United States consul at Buenos Aires. He married only at forty, and died at Elizabeth, New Jersey.

narrative_blocks.header: Her daughter married back into the Edwards clan
narrative_blocks.body: One of the eleven children of the Catskill tanner Colonel William Edwards, she watched her daughter Rebecca marry a Forbes who was himself an Edwards cousin. The tannery family's branches kept circling back to one another.

cross_connections.display_label: Edwards kinswoman whose son William married daughter Rebecca

narrative_blocks.header: A coal baron who chased butterflies
narrative_blocks.body: He opened some of West Virginia's first coal mines and built a fortune in the Kanawha coalfields — and across those same decades became the foremost butterfly scientist in America. The two lives ran in parallel for forty years.

narrative_blocks.header: His travel book sent Wallace to the Amazon
narrative_blocks.body: At twenty-four he went up the Amazon by sailing bark and native galliota, a thousand miles to Manaus, and wrote A Voyage Up the River Amazon. Reading it, Alfred Russel Wallace and Henry Walter Bates chose the Amazon for the expedition that would shape the theory of evolution.

narrative_blocks.header: He raised butterflies and shipped them by rail
narrative_blocks.body: In a garden laboratory at his Coalburg home he bred butterflies through their full life cycles — confining females over host plants, rearing the larvae, and shipping live eggs and caterpillars by railroad to his Philadelphia illustrators. He kept one alpine colony going for nearly thirty years.

narrative_blocks.header: To fund his masterwork, he sold his butterflies
narrative_blocks.body: His three-volume Butterflies of North America took thirty years and 152 hand-colored plates, rivaling Audubon for beauty. To pay for it he sold off his own specimen collection, financing the very book that made his name.

narrative_blocks.header: At seventy-five he turned on Shakespeare
narrative_blocks.body: Setting butterflies aside, he wrote Shaksper Not Shakespeare in 1900, arguing the man from Stratford was not the true author of the plays. The title drew the distinction he meant: "Shaksper" the actor was not "Shakespeare" the writer.

narrative_blocks.header: His last book traced his own family
narrative_blocks.body: In 1903, at eighty-one, he published a genealogy of the Edwards family of Stockbridge — the line reaching back to his great-great-grandfather, the theologian Jonathan Edwards. It was the final project of a restless mind.

narrative_blocks.header: Her marriage knotted Tappans and Edwardses twice
narrative_blocks.body: Her father, the abolitionist Arthur Tappan, was brother to Rebecca Tappan, who had married Colonel William Edwards a generation earlier. So when Katherine wed William Henry Edwards — Rebecca's grandson, and her cousin — she knotted the two families together a second time.

narrative_blocks.header: She grew up in a house mobs attacked
narrative_blocks.body: Born in New Haven to the hunted abolitionist Arthur Tappan, she came of age in a household that anti-abolition mobs twice assaulted. She spent the second half of her life far from that storm, in the West Virginia coal town of Coalburg.

narrative_blocks.header: Her children carried the line into West Virginia
narrative_blocks.body: Her son William Seymour Edwards became a coal developer, author, and Speaker of the West Virginia House of Delegates. Her daughter Edith married the entomologist Theodore Mead, her father's protégé.

narrative_blocks.header: A butterfly was named for her before marriage
narrative_blocks.body: Years before she married the naturalist Theodore Mead, he named a butterfly he had collected — Gaeides editha, "Edith's Copper" — for her. They wed in 1882 and built a horticultural life together in Florida.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote travel books from Yukon to Moscow
narrative_blocks.body: A Coalburg coal man and West Virginia politician, he spun his journeys into popular travel books — Into the Yukon, On the Mexican Highlands, Through Scandinavia to Moscow. His West Virginia home stands on the National Register.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the book on Kanawha coal
narrative_blocks.body: He literally authored the handbook on the coals and cokes of the Great Kanawha and New River fields — the reference for a generation of operators. His fortune, like his subject, came straight out of the West Virginia seams.

narrative_blocks.header: He held the gavel in West Virginia's House
narrative_blocks.body: A Democrat when the state leaned the other way, he sat in the West Virginia House of Delegates and rose to Speaker. He ran, without success, for both governor and Congress.

narrative_blocks.header: She left New York for the coal country
narrative_blocks.body: A daughter of the butterfly scientist William Henry Edwards, she married Webster Smith and moved to the West Virginia coalfields at Coalburg. She became a prominent Charleston clubwoman, and died there in 1930.

narrative_blocks.header: She married her first cousin, a Manila merchant
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband, Ogden Ellery Edwards, was her first cousin — the son of her father's brother — and a merchant out in Manila in the Philippines. She joined him there, and their daughter was born in Manila in 1862.

narrative_blocks.header: She and her husband gave their sanitarium away
narrative_blocks.body: In 1872 she married Dr. Henry Foster, whose Clifton Springs Sanitarium in upstate New York drew patients from around the world. In 1881 the couple signed it over by deed of trust to a self-perpetuating board, so that its profits would always return to patient care.

narrative_blocks.header: She buried four of her seven children young
narrative_blocks.body: Of her seven children with Anthony Gilkison, four died in infancy, childhood, or young adulthood. The survivors scattered — one to a Philadelphia banker, one as far as Italy.

narrative_blocks.header: A midnight vision set his life's work
narrative_blocks.body: Arriving at the Finger Lakes sulphur springs in 1849, he had a vision he likened to St. Paul's: "the Heavens seemed to open and the Glory of God filled my whole being." He bought the land and built a water-cure house on the spot.

narrative_blocks.header: His water cure grew into a famous sanitarium
narrative_blocks.body: From a crude wooden water-cure house opened in 1850, he built and rebuilt for fifty years until the Clifton Springs Sanitarium filled a five-story brick building with a rooftop solarium. He treated body and soul alike, setting a chapel at its heart.

narrative_blocks.header: A village grew up around his cure
narrative_blocks.body: As patients flocked to his springs, shops, churches, and schools rose to serve them, and the crossroads settlement became the village of Clifton Springs. He had founded a town almost by accident.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran a model farm of four silos
narrative_blocks.body: To feed his patients, he bought and drained a marshy farm north of the village and turned it into a 300-acre showplace — four silos when the whole state had perhaps one, the first alfalfa in the area, and a 225-cow dairy. A milk inspector reported in 1893 that it could not, in any respect, be improved.

education.notes: M.D.; medical department later part of Case Western Reserve

narrative_blocks.header: He left the Gold Rush for Manila
narrative_blocks.body: After heading a small company of miners on California's Yuba River, he sailed on to Hong Kong and then Manila in 1852, starting there as a customs-house clerk. Within a few years he was a partner, and then United States Consul.

narrative_blocks.header: He followed his cousin into the Manila consulate
narrative_blocks.body: His cousin Alfred Henry Pierpont Edwards had been U.S. Consul at Manila into 1854; Ogden held the same post from 1854 to 1860. Two great-grandsons of Jonathan Edwards filled the office back to back.

narrative_blocks.header: A Manila merchant who became a Carolina 'Colonel'
narrative_blocks.body: After his trading years he settled in North Carolina, summering at Blowing Rock and wintering in Charlotte for nearly forty years, known there as "Colonel Edwards." His family papers, now held at Michigan and Notre Dame, trace a life that ran from the California Gold Rush to the Spanish Philippines.

documents.document_blurb: His Manila letters to his younger brother Robert.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a Confederate judge's daughter
narrative_blocks.body: A New York lawyer, he married Harriet Patton, daughter of Judge James French Patton of West Virginia — and thus a kinswoman of the future General George S. Patton. Their eldest son carried the name into a fourth Ogden Ellery Edwards.

bio.bio_blurb: New York silk-merchant prince and abolitionist

narrative_blocks.header: He made his fortune importing silk
narrative_blocks.body: Arthur left Northampton at fifteen for a Boston dry-goods house, then ran his own firms at Portland and at Montreal and struggled on through the War of 1812. In 1826 he and his brother Lewis opened a silk-importing house in New York that made them both rich.

narrative_blocks.header: His dry-goods house trained his nephew Alfred
narrative_blocks.body: He ran one of New York's great silk and dry-goods houses, Arthur Tappan & Company, and took his nephew Alfred Edwards in as an apprentice. When Arthur left the trade, Alfred carried the firm on under his own name as Alfred Edwards & Company.

narrative_blocks.header: His sister and his daughter both married Edwardses
narrative_blocks.body: His sister Rebecca had married Colonel William Edwards, the Catskill tanner, first binding the Tappans to that family. A generation later his daughter Katherine married William Henry Edwards — Rebecca's grandson — knotting the two lines a second time.

narrative_blocks.header: The South put a price on his head
narrative_blocks.body: A wealthy merchant, he poured his fortune into abolition as founding president of the American Anti-Slavery Society. Southern states posted a a bounty reward — a fortune — for his capture and delivery to New Orleans.

narrative_blocks.header: He bankrolled the Amistad captives' freedom
narrative_blocks.body: He led the funding of the fight that freed the Africans of the slave ship Amistad, then helped build the American Missionary Association out of the cause. He also financed Oberlin, Lane Seminary, and an antislavery paper founded with Samuel Morse.

narrative_blocks.header: A mob burned his house for an idea
narrative_blocks.body: After he backed a proposed college for African Americans, a New Haven mob destroyed his summer home in 1831, and rioters struck again in 1834. The crash of 1837 wiped out his silk fortune, yet he kept giving for the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.body: Her father, Colonel Edward Antill, served as chief engineer under General Montgomery at the 1775 assault on Quebec and as Benedict Arnold's adjutant general in Canada. When Antill died, his friend Alexander Hamilton became godfather and then guardian to his infant daughter.

narrative_blocks.header: Her daughter married into the Edwards line
narrative_blocks.body: She and Arthur Tappan raised their children between New York and New Haven. Their daughter Katherine married the naturalist William Henry Edwards — her cousin, and a grandson of Arthur's sister Rebecca.

bio.bio_blurb: First Lieutenant killed at Fort Wagner

narrative_blocks.header: He carried the flag up Wagner's wall
narrative_blocks.body: When the color sergeant fell in the July 1863 assault on Fort Wagner, he seized the national flag and rushed the parapet, calling "Come on Company C — follow this Flag." He reached the rampart and was shot through the chest, falling back into the flooded ditch.

narrative_blocks.header: On the morning he died, he wrote this
narrative_blocks.body: Hours before the attack he was writing to his sister Annie: "I shall never find a better use for my life, than to give it up in this War." He was killed that evening; the unfinished letter was found in his baggage.

narrative_blocks.header: His men called him 'every inch a Soldier'
narrative_blocks.body: A corporal who watched him die wrote the family that the whole company "felt that he was every inch a Soldier." The same letter cursed the assault as a slaughter the men had been "decoyed into."

narrative_blocks.header: He cut a relic from Fort Pulaski's flag
narrative_blocks.body: Before Wagner he soldiered along the Carolina coast, sketching maps of his regiment at Port Royal and Fort Pulaski. When Pulaski surrendered in 1862 he cut a fragment from its captured flag and mailed it home to Brooklyn.

narrative_blocks.header: Five Tappan great-grandsons died in that war
narrative_blocks.body: His Northampton gravestone names him among five great-grandsons of Benjamin and Sarah Tappan killed for the Union — a colonel, a major, a captain, a chaplain, and a lieutenant. The same Tappan line gave the country the abolitionist brothers Arthur and Lewis.

narrative_blocks.header: Her children kept marrying back into the family
narrative_blocks.body: Her son Joseph married his first cousin Helen Edwards, and her granddaughter Dorothy married a third cousin, Ogden Edwards IV. The Edwards and Rogers families kept folding back into each other across three generations.

narrative_blocks.header: She spent her life at her brother's side
narrative_blocks.body: Unmarried, she followed her brother Ogden — the Manila merchant who represented American export houses — through years in Europe and the Philippines. In old age she summered with him at Blowing Rock and wintered in Charlotte, dying there in the household where he lived.

narrative_blocks.body: Her husband, Dr. William Beale Lewis, was her second cousin — both descended from the Tappan merchants of Northampton — and a Navy surgeon who had served at Mobile Bay. Widowed at thirty after five years of marriage, she outlived him by sixty-two years.

narrative_blocks.header: A confirmed bachelor who finally married his cousin
narrative_blocks.body: A civil engineer, he stayed single into his fifties before marrying his first cousin Helen Edwards in 1911. Both were grandchildren of the New York merchant Ogden Edwards.

narrative_blocks.header: He and his wife died the same summer
narrative_blocks.body: He married Grace Howard Stevens, and they had one daughter, Dorothy. He died at twenty-eight in June 1896; his wife followed barely a month later, leaving the child an orphan.

narrative_blocks.header: His first name was his mother's surname
narrative_blocks.body: Spencer was christened Edwards for Sophia Matilda Lewis Edwards, and the name carried a place with it: her line ran back to Hon. Timothy Edwards, the first man of Stockbridge for forty-three years and probate judge of Berkshire.

narrative_blocks.header: He married at thirty-nine in Paris
narrative_blocks.body: Spencer was thirty-nine and Emily Meredith Read thirty-one when they married at the American Cathedral in Paris in June 1894. She came to him a widow; her first husband, Francis Aquila Stout, had run the Nicaragua Canal Company.

narrative_blocks.header: He reached the Berkshires and died that year
narrative_blocks.body: Spencer wanted Lenox because his mother's people were Berkshire people. He and Emily bought the Nowood cottage in 1911 and began doubling it into Shipton Court, and he was dead by 30 December of the same year, at fifty-seven.

narrative_blocks.header: Brooklyn born, and buried back in Brooklyn
narrative_blocks.body: Spencer was born at Brooklyn in 1854, as his mother had been in 1833, and lies at Green-Wood with both parents, both brothers and the one sister who never married.

narrative_blocks.body: She married late, at forty-two, to Dr. Donald Cammann, a New York specialist in diseases of the heart and lungs. His father had invented the binaural stethoscope that made such listening possible.

narrative_blocks.body: Of her three children with Maurice Heckscher, two died young — Eleanor as an infant, Constance at fifteen. Only Gertrude lived to marry, into the Philadelphia Biddles.

narrative_blocks.header: He was a Navy surgeon at Mobile Bay
narrative_blocks.body: Leaving Yale for the war, he joined the Navy as an assistant surgeon and served under Farragut aboard the Monongahela and the doomed Tecumseh. He was present at the Battle of Mobile Bay in 1864, where the Tecumseh struck a mine and went down.

narrative_blocks.header: He pioneered kidney science, then died of consumption
narrative_blocks.body: He built a career around diseases of the kidney, lecturing on renal science and joining the medical faculty of the University of the City of New York. Tuberculosis killed him at thirty-two, six years after his marriage.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandfather bankrolled the abolitionist cause
narrative_blocks.body: He was a grandson of Arthur Tappan, the silk magnate who poured a fortune into the antislavery movement and swore he would be hanged before he gave it up. The doctor carried that Tappan descent into a New York medical life cut short at thirty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: Her sister married her husband's brother
narrative_blocks.body: She and her sister Arabella, daughters of the coal magnate Duncan S. Magee, married the Edwards brothers Lewis and Alfred within three years of each other. The two New York households were bound twice over.

cross_connections.display_label: was her husband Lewis's brother, who married her sister Arabella

narrative_blocks.header: She left a count to marry a general
narrative_blocks.body: Engaged in 1901 to the Hungarian Count Franz Wenckheim, she never went through with it; the reason is lost. Eight years later she married Brigadier-General Douglas MacEwen of the British Army and spent decades crossing the Atlantic at his side.

narrative_blocks.header: She taught school, then married the Colonel
narrative_blocks.body: Before her marriage she taught at the old Charlotte Female Academy, and former pupils later clustered near her. She became Ogden Edwards's second wife in 1888 and outlived him by ten years.

narrative_blocks.header: He was a Civil War assistant surgeon
narrative_blocks.body: Trained at Amherst and in medicine, he served as an assistant surgeon during the Civil War. He married late, at forty, taking a widow as his wife; they had no children.

narrative_blocks.header: He built a church out in Los Angeles
narrative_blocks.body: After Amherst and Union Seminary he held New York pastorates, then went west and built the Church of the Redeemer in Los Angeles. He came home to lead the old Dutch Reformed church at Tappan, the same village where his sister-in-law later died.

narrative_blocks.header: His Lewis line had tutored a president's household
narrative_blocks.body: He came of a long line of clergymen; his great-grandfather, the Rev. Zachariah Lewis, had tutored George Washington's stepchildren. One of his own daughters married the pastor of the American Church in Paris.

narrative_blocks.header: Two of his children outshone their preacher father
narrative_blocks.body: A Gloversville pastor like his forebears, he married a daughter of the Andover Edwardses and raised a remarkable pair: a daughter who became a college president and a son who reshaped American pediatrics.

narrative_blocks.header: He went south to teach freed slaves
narrative_blocks.body: In 1862, months into the war, he sailed to St. Helena Island off South Carolina with the first northern party sent to educate freed slaves — the Port Royal experiment. He taught there before the guns had settled the question of their freedom.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave a mill town a public library
narrative_blocks.body: Settled over the Gloversville church in New York for nearly thirty years, he pushed his congregation toward education and founded the town's public library. An unusual number of its young men went on to Yale.

narrative_blocks.header: He edited the journal his father had edited
narrative_blocks.body: In his last years at Oberlin he became associate editor of Bibliotheca Sacra, the religious quarterly his father Edwards Amasa Park had run for forty years. The Park name ran through New England theology for two generations.

narrative_blocks.header: He crossed the ocean seven times
narrative_blocks.body: Beyond the pulpit he served as a Christian Commission delegate at Nashville during the war and made seven long journeys abroad. For twenty-five years he sat on the board that sent American missionaries overseas.

narrative_blocks.header: Her aunt and her daughter both led colleges
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth Storrs Billings Mead, her mother's sister, was president of Mount Holyoke from 1890 to 1901. Her own daughter Marion took Bryn Mawr in 1922 and held it for twenty years.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father and her husband were Andover men
narrative_blocks.body: Bela Bates Edwards founded the Bibliotheca Sacra with her husband's father in 1844, and her mother Jerusha Billings kept a school for girls at Andover. She married William Park there in March 1874.

narrative_blocks.header: She led Bryn Mawr through depression and war
narrative_blocks.body: From 1922 to 1942 she was the third president of Bryn Mawr College, holding it steady through the Great Depression and the opening of the Second World War. She joined other colleges in placing refugee scholars who had fled European universities.

narrative_blocks.header: A classicist who deaned Radcliffe before Bryn Mawr
narrative_blocks.body: Trained in Greek and Latin, she took all three of her degrees at Bryn Mawr and studied at the American School in Athens. She was Dean of Radcliffe the year before Bryn Mawr called her back to lead it.

narrative_blocks.header: She told students the world would be unrecognizable
narrative_blocks.body: Opening the college year in 1933, as fascism spread, she warned her students they were being schooled for a world "different from anything of which we have now had experience."

narrative_blocks.header: He proved vitamin D could stop rickets
narrative_blocks.body: Running the Harriet Lane Home at Johns Hopkins, he showed through bone studies that vitamin D prevents rickets, then a crippler of infants. He built the nation's model children's hospital around deep research into a few diseases.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran a Belgian orphanage during the war
narrative_blocks.body: When the First World War broke out, the Red Cross sent him to Le Havre to run an orphanage for Belgian children with three doctors and a nurse. There he saw what hunger and poverty did to disease, and never forgot it.

narrative_blocks.header: He designed the 'Park fly' for salmon
narrative_blocks.body: At his summer place on Cape Breton's Margaree River he kept fishing for salmon and tied his own fly — the "Park fly" — to catch them better. He died and was buried there in his ninety-second year.

narrative_blocks.header: She married her sixth cousin at home
narrative_blocks.body: She was born in the Rowland homestead at Fairfield and married Arthur Whiting Talcott in the same rooms. Their common ancestor was Rev. Samuel Hooker, the founder's son, seven generations above them both.

narrative_blocks.header: The Harris name came from her second marriage
narrative_blocks.body: Widowed at thirty-one, she married Edward Wykoff Harris of Rye and carried his name the rest of her life. When she died in 1949 her granddaughter's wedding that season was cut back to family only.

narrative_blocks.header: She married her second cousin
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband, William Jehiel Forbes, was her second cousin — the two shared Edwards descent, their mothers first cousins from the Edwards brothers Timothy and William. She carried the Tappan and Edwards names down from that side.

narrative_blocks.header: He married his second cousin
narrative_blocks.body: His mother, Hannah Maria Edwards, and Rebecca's mother were first cousins — daughters of the Edwards brothers Timothy and William — which made him and Rebecca second cousins. Both lines ran back to the theologian Jonathan Edwards, and their one daughter carried the doubled descent.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the family export trade to Australia
narrative_blocks.body: He spent his career in the overseas firm of R.W. Forbes & Son, living nearly two years across New Zealand, Australia, and South Africa. Later he joined exploration work in little-mapped corners of Mexico and Lower California.

narrative_blocks.header: He standardized supplies for fifteen hospitals
narrative_blocks.body: In 1910 he became purchasing agent for a new bureau that centrally bought and standardized hospital supplies. It grew to serve fifteen New York hospitals, Yale's mission in China, and Grenfell's Labrador expeditions.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at eighteen, far out in Colorado
narrative_blocks.body: He died at eighteen in Colorado, almost certainly sent west to the mountains for his health, as many young Easterners were in those years. His body was brought home to be buried at Grove Street in New Haven.

narrative_blocks.header: A dozen Atlantic crossings
narrative_blocks.body: Forbes was an expert ocean sailor who crossed the Atlantic a dozen times, and belonged to the Cruising Club of America, the Corinthians and the Norwalk Yacht Club, where his friends gathered to remember him.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight months aboard Blithe Spirit
narrative_blocks.body: In 1990 Forbes and Emily left Darien with three friends aboard their Swan 43, Blithe Spirit, for eight months: Cork, the Channel, France, Spain, Portugal and Madeira, back across to Barbados, then down through the Caribbean to the Bahamas.

narrative_blocks.header: His own electrical company
narrative_blocks.body: Forbes made his living from Electro-Mec Laboratories, the company he owned in Watertown, Connecticut, which built electrical equipment. He was married three times; his daughter Adele was born to his first wife, Elizabeth.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a fellow ocean sailor
narrative_blocks.body: Forbes married Emily Potter in 1986, at sixty-nine; she was a Rear Commodore of the Ocean Cruising Club. In his last years she cared for him at their house in Pound Ridge, and she died nine months after him.

narrative_blocks.header: Three butterflies still carry his name
narrative_blocks.body: Apprenticed under his father-in-law, the lepidopterist William Henry Edwards, he went to the Colorado Rockies at nineteen and brought back over twenty butterfly species new to science. Three still bear his name — Mead's Sulphur, Mead's Silverspot, and Mead's Wood-Nymph.

narrative_blocks.header: He found a petrified forest on horseback
narrative_blocks.body: Hearing of a strange petrified forest at Florissant, Colorado, he rode out to investigate and hauled away twenty-five pounds of fossil-bearing shale. His specimens first alerted science to the site now preserved as Florissant Fossil Beds National Monument.

narrative_blocks.header: His patience cracked the orchid-growing problem
narrative_blocks.body: He spent decades hybridizing orchids — once waiting seventeen years for one cross to bloom — and his sterile-germination insights and donated seed helped Cornell's Lewis Knudson solve reproducible orchid growing. That breakthrough launched the modern orchid industry.

narrative_blocks.header: He saved oranges by freezing them in ice
narrative_blocks.body: After the Great Freeze of 1894 ruined central Florida's groves, his engineer's mind reasoned that an ice cocoon from overhead irrigation would hold fruit at thirty-two degrees however cold the air fell. He proved it on an acre of oranges — the first description of a method still used today.

narrative_blocks.header: He took Darwin's side against his evangelical mother
narrative_blocks.body: From his own studies of butterfly variation he sided with Darwin in the storm after On the Origin of Species, setting himself against his devout mother. He pursued science as rigorously as any professional, yet sought no fame for it.

narrative_blocks.header: A Stanford flier who crashed crossing the country
narrative_blocks.body: A Stanford student and pilot, he was flying coast-to-coast toward New York — planning to sail on to Europe with his mother and sisters — when his plane went down in 1930. He was twenty-four.

narrative_blocks.header: He painted and chronicled old Charleston
narrative_blocks.body: A Charleston historian, illustrator, and West Virginia legislator, he wrote The Kanawha Spectator and other histories of the valley. His paintings of early Charleston hang in state collections.

narrative_blocks.body: Her husband, Joseph Warren Rogers Jr., was her first cousin — the son of her father's sister Fanny. They married late, in 1911, and divided their later years between Brooklyn and Blowing Rock.

narrative_blocks.header: He was the nation's youngest high-court judge
narrative_blocks.body: Appointed to the West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals in 1881, he was the youngest man then holding such a seat anywhere in the country. He died of heart failure less than a year later, at thirty-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: A Cold Harbor wound he bore until death
narrative_blocks.body: At eighteen he joined the 22nd Virginia under his brother's command and served as adjutant through the war, taking a terrible wound at Cold Harbor. Three of his brothers, all Confederate colonels, were killed — two at Gettysburg.

narrative_blocks.header: He was General Patton's great-uncle
narrative_blocks.body: His brother George commanded the 22nd Virginia, and that brother's grandson was George S. Patton, the famous general of the Second World War. The judge was himself a great-grandson of the Revolutionary general Hugh Mercer.

narrative_blocks.header: He married his third cousin, a Rogers
narrative_blocks.body: His wife, Dorothy Howard Rogers, descended from Ogden Edwards's sister Fanny — making the couple third cousins, both great-grandchildren of the same New York merchant. She gave decades of service to the New York City Mission Society.

narrative_blocks.header: Orphaned at six, she married an Edwards cousin
narrative_blocks.body: Both her parents died within a month in the summer of 1896, when she was six. Grown, she took as her second husband her third cousin, Ogden Edwards IV — another Rogers married back into the Edwards line.

narrative_blocks.header: She gave her years to the city's poor
narrative_blocks.body: A director of the New York City Mission Society, she chaired its Good Neighbor committee and served families in need across the city. An earlier marriage, to Frank Sprague, had given her a daughter.

narrative_blocks.header: He led the nation's oldest savings bank
narrative_blocks.body: A Philadelphia lawyer of Scotch, Swedish, and Huguenot descent, he became president of the Philadelphia Saving Fund Society — the oldest savings bank in the country — in 1903. William Merritt Chase painted his portrait.

cross_connections.display_label: ran the Pennsylvania Company and was a manager of the Saving Fund

narrative_blocks.header: His father electrified the American streetcar
narrative_blocks.body: His father, Frank Julian Sprague, built the first successful electric trolley line and won the name "father of electric traction." The Sprague Electric Works was later absorbed into General Electric.

narrative_blocks.header: Too old at forty-eight to build fresh
narrative_blocks.body: Emily wanted a Lenox cottage of her own design, then reckoned that at forty-eight she might not live to see one finished. She and Edwards Spencer bought Robert Spencer's 1885 house Nowood instead, doubled it, and renamed it Shipton Court.

narrative_blocks.header: A staircase from England, columns from France
narrative_blocks.body: Emily collected rooms out of other people's buildings. She shipped an English staircase into Shipton Court, set French columns around a bay window and worked Italian pieces through the rest; the house still carries them.

narrative_blocks.header: Isadora Duncan and a piglet named Rosie
narrative_blocks.body: Emily entertained hard once Shipton Court was hers, and the dancer Isadora Duncan was among the guests. Her pet piglet Rosie had the run of the parlor while she did it.

narrative_blocks.header: Her initials are still over the door
narrative_blocks.body: Emily's monogram is cut above the main door at Lenox to this day. Larry and Sophie Howitt bought Shipton Court in 1951, renamed it Seven Hills and opened it to Tanglewood audiences; her renovation blueprint hangs in the hall.

narrative_blocks.header: Edwards Spencer died the year they bought Nowood
narrative_blocks.body: Emily had hesitated over building because she doubted she would live to see it done. Edwards Spencer died on 30 December 1911, inside the year the two of them bought the Lenox house, and she kept Shipton Court without him.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed young, she married again in Paris
narrative_blocks.body: Emily married Francis Aquila Stout, head of the Nicaragua Canal Company, in 1884. Two years after his death she married Edwards Spencer at the American Cathedral in Paris.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Shipton Court, Lenox, MA

narrative_blocks.header: He chased the dream of a Nicaragua canal
narrative_blocks.body: Trained as an engineer in Paris, Stout led the Nicaragua Canal Company's bid to cut a waterway across Central America, decades before Panama. He also helped drive New York's triangulation survey and the American Geographical Society.

narrative_blocks.header: Marble House stands where his garden was
narrative_blocks.body: Stout made the family's Newport place on the cliffs into gardens, raising tropical fruit under glass and orchids good enough to matter to the trade. After his father died the heirs sold Ferncliff to Alva Vanderbilt, who pulled it down.

narrative_blocks.header: A special policeman in the draft riots
narrative_blocks.body: Stout was sworn in as a special police officer during the New York draft riots of 1863. He had turned down the family counting house for public work, and this was the least comfortable form it ever took.

narrative_blocks.header: His hours went to the blind and old
narrative_blocks.body: Stout carried a long list of New York institutions — libraries, schooling, charities for blind people and for the elderly. What he gave them was not only money but his own time, which was the scarcer of the two.

narrative_blocks.header: The Newport room where North met South
narrative_blocks.body: Stout helped found the old Newport Reading-room, where in the years before the war representative men of North and South still met and talked. Most of the historic names of the country passed through its rooms.

narrative_blocks.header: His father-in-law helped write his memorial
narrative_blocks.body: Stout died at Alexandria Bay in July 1892, fifty-eight years old. Two years on, Ehrman Syme Nadal, Henry Clay Taylor and his wife's father John Meredith Read put out a volume on his life and what he had done with it.

narrative_blocks.header: He paid for the Greek legation himself
narrative_blocks.body: Congress cut the Athens appropriation in 1879 and Read judged the crisis too sharp to leave. He ran it out of his own pocket until he resigned that September. King George, by then a close friend, made him Knight Grand Cross of the Redeemer.

narrative_blocks.header: Adjutant general of New York at twenty-three
narrative_blocks.body: He had led a cadet company at Brown and been aide-de-camp to Rhode Island's governor at twenty. When Fort Sumter fell, Read chaired the committee of three that drafted New York's bill to buy arms, and the War Department thanked him.

narrative_blocks.header: A cannon ball through his room in Paris
narrative_blocks.body: Read was the first American consul general for France, and took Germany's interests on as well once the Franco-Prussian War began. He stayed at his post through the whole siege of Paris, and stayed after a cannon ball pierced his room.

narrative_blocks.header: His tip sent a grain fleet to Russia
narrative_blocks.body: During the Russo-Turkish War, Read worked out that one Russian port was still open and told Secretary of State William Evarts what a New York grain fleet could do there. American cereal exports multiplied inside a year.

narrative_blocks.header: He went hunting Henry Hudson's origins
narrative_blocks.body: Read published a Historical Enquiry concerning Henry Hudson at Albany in 1866, arguing where the navigator came from and what ideas steered him. The Archaeological Society of Athens later elected him president.

narrative_blocks.header: Priscilla Read died when he was four
narrative_blocks.body: Read was four when his mother Priscilla died in 1841, and eighteen when his father remarried. Chief Justice John Meredith Read fought the spread of slavery from the Pennsylvania bench, and southern senators kept him off the Supreme Court.

narrative_blocks.header: His great-grandfather signed the Declaration
narrative_blocks.body: George Read of Delaware was one of two men to sign the 1774 Petition to the King, the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution. Read's grandfather stayed in Philadelphia through the yellow fever of 1793 and later ran its bank.

narrative_blocks.header: He refined the stethoscope his father invented
narrative_blocks.body: A New York heart-and-lung physician, he published a modification of the binaural stethoscope his father George had introduced a generation earlier. His textbook on diagnosing diseases of the chest carried the family's listening art forward.

narrative_blocks.header: Oxford, then the College of Physicians
narrative_blocks.body: Donald took a B.A. at Oxford in 1876 and his medical degree at the College of Physicians and Surgeons in New York in 1879. He married Sophia Edwards Spencer in November 1901, at forty-nine, and died at Clifton Springs in October 1928, at seventy-six.

career.role: Physician, diseases of the heart and lungs

artworks.artwork_blurb: National Museum of Amer. History, DC

narrative_blocks.header: His binaural stethoscope, never patented
narrative_blocks.body: In 1852 George unveiled the first commercially made binaural stethoscope, built for him by the New York instrument maker George Tiemann, with gutta-percha ear tips on steel tubes joined at a hinge. He never patented it, believing the design should belong freely to every physician.

narrative_blocks.header: He learned to listen in the Paris wards
narrative_blocks.body: In the Paris hospitals from 1828 to 1830 George attended the lectures of Pierre-Charles-Alexandre Louis, a friend and colleague of Laennec's, and caught the new art of auscultation. Back in New York he practised largely among the working poor, where he felt the need for a better instrument.

narrative_blocks.header: Listening while he tapped the chest
narrative_blocks.body: George also worked out auscultatory percussion, listening through the stethoscope while tapping the chest to judge the size and borders of the organs beneath, and published his results to sharpen physical diagnosis. Textbooks and journals taught the technique through the middle of the century.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a Lorillard in 1833
narrative_blocks.body: In 1833 George married Anna Catharine Lorillard, a granddaughter of the founder of Lorillard Tobacco. Their son Donald, born in April 1852, the year the binaural stethoscope appeared, became a chest physician too and published his own refinement of it.
