narrative_blocks.header: She married into the old Philadelphia Biddles
narrative_blocks.body: In 1922 she married Alfred Alexander Biddle, a partner in the Biddle, Whelen & Co. brokerage and a son of the Philadelphia bar. A long illness took her at Bryn Mawr in 1942.

narrative_blocks.header: His brokerage traced its roots to 1764
narrative_blocks.body: He was a general partner in Biddle, Whelen & Co., the Philadelphia investment house whose Biddle half went back to a firm founded in 1764. He outlived his wife by twenty-five years.

narrative_blocks.header: His father wrote the lawyers' standard treatises
narrative_blocks.body: His father, Arthur Biddle, was a Philadelphia attorney who authored standard treatises on the law of stockbrokers, of warranties, and of insurance. Yale gave the elder Biddle an honorary degree for the warranties work in 1893.

bio.bio_blurb: Fall Brook coal and railroad magnate

narrative_blocks.header: He built the Fall Brook coal trade
narrative_blocks.body: As superintendent and then president of the Fall Brook Coal Company, he shipped Pennsylvania bituminous coal down to Corning and beyond. Miners remembered him as a man who heard their complaints and shared their misfortunes.

narrative_blocks.header: He named the coal town for Irish Antrim
narrative_blocks.body: Dipping a glass at a spring among his mines, he christened the place Antrim, after the county in northern Ireland his family came from. He took the company presidency in 1868 and was dead within the year.

narrative_blocks.header: A rugby blue who rose to brigadier-general
narrative_blocks.body: Commissioned in the Cameron Highlanders in 1889, he served through the South African War and commanded an infantry brigade in the Great War, ending as a brigadier-general with the C.B. and the Legion of Honour. At Trinity, Cambridge he had earned a rugby blue.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at forty-five with eleven children
narrative_blocks.body: A New Haven merchant, he married Charlotte Root — daughter of the world-voyaging supercargo Joel Root — and died at forty-five, leaving her with eleven children. One of them married the Yale chemist Benjamin Silliman Jr.

cross_connections.display_label: , his great-great-grandson, carried the Forbes name as his first name

narrative_blocks.header: Her father sailed around the world for sealskins
narrative_blocks.body: Her father, Joel Root, spent four years as supercargo of the sealing brig Huron — rounding Cape Horn, sealing on the island that inspired Robinson Crusoe, and trading the skins in Canton, Hamburg, and St. Petersburg. He came home with a small fortune and never went to sea again.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven daughters survived smallpox while he sailed
narrative_blocks.body: While Joel Root was four years at sea, his wife and seven daughters came through a New Haven smallpox epidemic alive. Charlotte was among them; he brought each daughter fabric for her trousseau and a set of China tea cups.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed with eleven children, she married again
narrative_blocks.body: Forbes left her at forty-one with eleven children; she later remarried, to a man named L'Aignoux, and lived to ninety. One of her daughters married the Yale chemist Benjamin Silliman Jr.

narrative_blocks.header: He joined his cousins' export firm
narrative_blocks.body: A Princeton man, he became a partner in R.W. Forbes & Son — the export house his Forbes first cousins ran, sons of his aunt Hannah Maria Edwards. The Edwards and Forbes branches did business as well as marriage.

narrative_blocks.header: He chaired Lloyd’s as its great crisis loomed
narrative_blocks.body: Lawrence succeeded Peter Miller as chairman of Lloyd's of London on New Year's Day 1988 and held it to 1990, as the market went into the asbestos and pollution losses that ruined thousands of its Names. He was fifty-two when he was chosen.

narrative_blocks.header: The agency in the market carried his name
narrative_blocks.body: He was senior partner of Murray Lawrence & Partners, the fourth-largest underwriting agency at Lloyd's, and went to the chairmanship from it. The name the market knew him by was his third, not his first.

narrative_blocks.header: Three first-class matches, two runs in all
narrative_blocks.body: He opened for Oxford University against Middlesex in 1954, played Hampshire, and turned out once for the Free Foresters against his own university. His top score was one and his average 0.66. He took three catches.

narrative_blocks.header: His middle names are a whole other name
narrative_blocks.body: His mother was Sarah Schuyler Butler, daughter of Nicholas Murray Butler — president of Columbia for forty-three years and a Nobel peace laureate. The boy was christened Walter Nicholas Murray Lawrence and went by Murray all his life.

narrative_blocks.header: A baronet on the other side
narrative_blocks.body: His father Henry Walter Neville Lawrence was a son of Sir Walter Roper Lawrence, first baronet, private secretary to the Viceroy of India. Lawrence was born at Marylebone and raised wholly English.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at home, sixty years married
narrative_blocks.body: Lawrence married Sally Louise O'Dwyer, daughter of an Irish Guards colonel, in April 1961, and she went first. He died at home in November 2021 at eighty-six, and they buried him from St Nicholas Church at Sandhurst in Kent.

narrative_blocks.header: From country lawyer to Speaker of the House
narrative_blocks.body: A Stockbridge Federalist, he sat in the Continental Congress, both houses of Congress, and from 1802 on the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court. He took the Speaker's chair in 1799, the first to hold it having already been a senator.

narrative_blocks.header: He argued the case that freed Mum Bett
narrative_blocks.body: In 1781 Elizabeth “Mum Bett” Freeman walked four miles from the Ashley house to his Sheffield office and asked him to sue for her freedom. He and Tapping Reeve won, and slavery in Massachusetts ended.

narrative_blocks.header: He argued for freedom while owning a slave
narrative_blocks.body: A bill of sale from 1777 has him buying an enslaved woman named Ton — four years before Mum Bett's case. It drew little comment in his own day.

narrative_blocks.header: The clerkship that made Eli Ashmun a lawyer
narrative_blocks.body: There were no law schools: a man read for years in a practising attorney's office, five of them without a college degree. Eli Porter Ashmun read in his and was admitted after four, then followed him to the Senate.

narrative_blocks.header: The carriage ride home with John Adams
narrative_blocks.body: He worked for Adams's election and thought the inauguration sublime, then wrote of a mind ruled by caprice alone when Adams sent envoys to France. They rode home in one carriage on his last day in office.

narrative_blocks.header: He remarried eight months after Pamela died
narrative_blocks.body: Smallpox he brought home in 1771 killed his first wife, eight months pregnant. Pamela Dwight bore him ten children and took poison in 1807; eight months later he married Penelope Russell, telling none of them.

narrative_blocks.header: A ring of graves circles him at Stockbridge
narrative_blocks.body: At Stockbridge his descendants lie in rings around him and Pamela — the “Sedgwick Pie” — each generation as near the founders as its standing allowed. Elizabeth Freeman lies in the circle beside his daughter Catharine Maria.

narrative_blocks.header: A year each at three colleges
narrative_blocks.body: Robert spent a year each at Williams, MIT and Harvard, and illness kept him from finishing at any of them. It kept him, too, from settling into any lasting place in business.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote for the Manitoba Free Press
narrative_blocks.body: Robert made his living as a commercial and real estate salesman and as a journalist, writing for the Manitoba Free Press in Winnipeg and for several Long Island newspapers.

narrative_blocks.header: Nice, Bordighera, St. Augustine, Tucson
narrative_blocks.body: Robert and Rose lived in New York, in Paris and Nice, at Bordighera on the Italian Riviera, and at St. Augustine, Miami, Tucson and St. Petersburg. Through all of it their permanent address stayed the family firm, Minot, Williams & Bangs, on Federal Street in Boston.

narrative_blocks.header: A Mayflower boy raised by strangers
narrative_blocks.body: Her line runs to Henry Sampson, who came over on the Mayflower at sixteen in the care of relatives named Tilley — though his parents were alive in England and nobody knows why. Edward and Agnes Tilley were dead by the end of that first winter. The boy lived, was constable of Duxbury forty years on, and spelled the name Samson; the p crept in generations later, in America.

narrative_blocks.header: Her cousin Deborah soldiered disguised as a man
narrative_blocks.body: From a collateral branch of the Sampsons came Deborah Sampson, who enlisted in the Continental Army disguised as a man and served until a wound exposed her — among the first American women to soldier in battle.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived him by fifty-five years
narrative_blocks.body: She married an army surgeon at twenty and was a widow at twenty-five, with a girl of four and a boy of two. She never remarried, and did not die until 1875 — she had been a widow her whole adult life.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother is the one nobody can find
narrative_blocks.body: Her father was Dr. Caleb Sampson of New Hartford; her mother is given as Jane Plant and nothing about her holds up. There are stories of an Irish girl and a runaway to New York, and there were two Caleb Sampsons in the same places at the same time. The early Duxbury records burned before 1666, and the Sampson genealogist gave some questions of descent up in despair.

narrative_blocks.header: Her great-grandmother was Standish's granddaughter
narrative_blocks.body: Caleb Sampson, the first of three of that name in her line, married Mercy Standish in the 1670s — a granddaughter of Miles Standish, the Plymouth soldier. Her grandfather Paul Sampson took a license to sell liquor at Duxbury in 1784.

narrative_blocks.header: The 1871 fire took even her family's papers
narrative_blocks.body: She and her husband were living in Chicago when the Great Fire of 1871 swept the city, and they lost a great deal of property — among it all the family's records and papers. They afterward settled at Buffalo.

narrative_blocks.header: He was two when his father died
narrative_blocks.body: Dr. Joseph Hooker died at Oswego in the October of 1820, five years married. Charles was two and his sister four. Their mother took them west and did not remarry in the fifty-five years she had left.

narrative_blocks.header: He added Benjamin to his own name
narrative_blocks.body: He was baptised Franklin Sherman at Rome, New York. He put the Benjamin on the front himself, and practiced law under it at Oswego, then in New York, then Chicago, and at last Buffalo.

narrative_blocks.header: The fire took the family's papers
narrative_blocks.body: He was practicing law in Chicago when the fire went through the city in 1871. He and his wife lost a great deal of property, and among it every record and paper the family had. They moved to Buffalo afterward.

career.location: Oswego, New York City, Chicago, and Buffalo

narrative_blocks.header: She and her sister married two Day brothers
narrative_blocks.body: She married Daniel Day, a Lima farmer, in 1828; her sister Mary married his brother Levi. The two Hooker sisters became sisters-in-law twice over.

narrative_blocks.header: He became the country's authority on plums
narrative_blocks.body: From a nursery at Geneva, New York, he grew into one of the nation's leading authorities on plums, importing new varieties from Europe and, with Liberty Hyde Bailey, writing Cornell's 1897 bulletin describing seventy of them.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran horticulture at the 1901 Pan-American fair
narrative_blocks.body: For decades he led the horticultural department of New York's state fair, and in 1901 he directed horticulture at the Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo.

burial.plot_notes: laid beside his brother Dr. Edward T. Hooker (H01694); no stone located

narrative_blocks.header: Her only child lived less than four months
narrative_blocks.body: Married at thirty to Abel Kittredge of the Hinsdale woolen family, she bore one son, Benjamin, in the spring of 1855; he died that August, not four months old. She had no other children and died at fifty-six.

narrative_blocks.header: He didn't expect to see the sun set
narrative_blocks.body: An aide-de-camp to Colonel Thomas Smyth, he came through the carnage of Gettysburg and wrote his father the next day that he had had "no expectations of seeing the sun set" the night before. He sent home the regiment's casualty list himself.

narrative_blocks.header: He held the dying general as he passed
narrative_blocks.body: He rose from quartermaster-sergeant to captain and assistant adjutant general on Smyth's staff. When Smyth was shot near Farmville days before Appomattox — the last Union general killed in the war — Parsons was at his side as he briefly came to.

cross_connections.display_label: marched as a private in that same 1864 campaign and died of it

narrative_blocks.header: A Union officer's son settled in Mexico
narrative_blocks.body: He married Camerina Peralta of Veracruz and lived between Manhattan, San Antonio, and Mexico City, where he died in 1952. Their three children grew up Mexican.

narrative_blocks.header: His Kittredge kin reached the Vermont statehouse
narrative_blocks.body: A woolen manufacturer at Hinsdale, he came from a Berkshire family of some local weight. His Kittredge kinsmen included Charles J. Kittredge, the town's leading mill owner and a Massachusetts legislator, and William Cullen Kittredge, who rose to lieutenant governor of Vermont.

narrative_blocks.header: Two of his children died within one month
narrative_blocks.body: In the spring of 1878 he and his wife Sophia lost two of their three children within a single month — Nettie at eight months in May, and Frederick at seven years in June. Only their daughter Lorena lived to grow up.

narrative_blocks.header: He lies at Antietam, where he never fought
narrative_blocks.body: He served in the 2nd Connecticut Heavy Artillery through the hard campaign of 1864, then, worn out and sick, was sent to an army hospital at Frederick, Maryland, where he died at nineteen. His remains were later moved to the new National Cemetery at Antietam — a field he had never fought on — and his name was cut into the soldiers' monument back home in Farmington.

narrative_blocks.header: He outlived his twin by eighteen years
narrative_blocks.body: He and his brother Franklin were born twins in December 1845; Franklin lived only four months. Frederick survived to enlist at eighteen and died a year later in the war, the second of the pair lost young.

cross_connections.display_label: served on the staff of the same Army of the Potomac in 1864

burial.plot_notes: grave 71, lot B, section 16; reinterred when the national cemetery opened; named on the Farmington soldiers' monument

narrative_blocks.header: A patrolman killed on duty in a crash
narrative_blocks.body: He went into police work and was killed on duty in a motor-vehicle crash at Vero Beach, Florida, in 1929, only thirty-six. His widow, a nurse, brought him home to be buried at Natick.

narrative_blocks.header: A trained nurse who outlived her young husband
narrative_blocks.body: A graduate nurse, she was widowed at forty-three when her husband was killed on duty in Florida. She kept nursing — by 1940 she was posted to the U.S. Marine Hospital on Martha's Vineyard — and died at Baltimore in 1944.

narrative_blocks.header: At seventy-five he pulled up roots for Illinois
narrative_blocks.body: After a lifetime in Connecticut, he moved his household west to Peoria, Illinois, about 1851 — roughly his seventy-fifth year. The family took firm hold there: his children and grandchildren married into prominent Peoria houses and prospered for generations.

narrative_blocks.header: An accident ended his law career for good
narrative_blocks.body: He graduated from Yale and read law under Judge Gilbert of Hebron, was admitted to the bar in 1800, and practiced in his native Columbia until a severe accident around 1815 left him unfit for hard mental labor. He turned to farming and worked the land until he went west.

narrative_blocks.header: His uncle the governor also married a Hooker
narrative_blocks.body: His mother was a sister of Caleb Strong, the Federalist governor of Massachusetts — who had himself married Sarah Hooker. In wedding Abigail Hooker, Asahel made the second Hooker match between two closely tied families.

narrative_blocks.header: A Charleston importer who resettled in Peoria
narrative_blocks.body: For years a merchant and importer at Charleston, South Carolina, he left the South and rebuilt his trade as a dry-goods dealer in Peoria, Illinois. He raised six children there.

narrative_blocks.header: His store stood for nearly ninety years
narrative_blocks.body: In 1863 he opened Clarke & Company in a small frame building at 14 South Adams in downtown Peoria. The dry-goods house he founded served the city's families for eighty-eight years.

narrative_blocks.header: Eighteen prosperous years in Charleston first
narrative_blocks.body: Before Peoria he tried the South, running a dry-goods business in Charleston for eighteen prosperous years. Only in 1854 did he move west to Illinois, where he planted the store that carried his name for generations.

narrative_blocks.header: A turned faucet cost him his life
narrative_blocks.body: In old age a simple misstep undid him: reaching to turn a faucet, he lost his balance and fell the full length of the stairs. The fall left him paralyzed, and from it he never recovered.

narrative_blocks.header: Lindbergh flew its first air express package
narrative_blocks.body: The frame shop at 14 South Adams became a four-storey building in 1910 and an eight-storey one, dedicated in 1923, with carpets and furniture on the upper floors. When air mail first reached Peoria, Charles Lindbergh carried in the first air express package and Clarke's received it. The store closed in 1951 and the building, by then the Citizens Building, came down in 1980.

opened Rochester's Boston Store, later Sibley's, in 1868

narrative_blocks.header: A fall in the back hallway widowed her
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband went into the hallway at the head of the back stairs one Friday afternoon in November 1892 to turn a water faucet, lost his balance and fell the length of them. He was paralysed from the waist down and speechless for two days before he died in their house on Seventh Avenue.

narrative_blocks.header: Her six were grown and scattered by then
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel Mortimer and Edward were keeping the Peoria store, Robert was at Flagstaff in Arizona and Herbert at Pittsburgh. Ella had married T. A. Grier and Belle was still at home, so both daughters were in the city with her. She lived on seventeen years after him.

narrative_blocks.header: He inherited his father's department store
narrative_blocks.body: Born in New York City, he came up in the family business and took over from his father as head of Clarke & Company, the dry-goods house that anchored Peoria's main commercial corner. He kept it running into the new century.

career.organization: Clarke & Company (wholesale and retail dry goods)
career.notes: Peoria, Illinois; succeeded his father Samuel Strong Clarke.

narrative_blocks.header: Her name traveled down to a niece
narrative_blocks.body: A generation on, her sister Ella's daughter — born into the Grier grain fortune at Peoria — was christened Isabel Hooker, the name carried into the next century. That niece grew up to marry William A. Jack and take her own place in the city's society.

narrative_blocks.header: She lived her whole life inside the family
narrative_blocks.body: She never married, moving among the households of her own people — her parents' home, then her bachelor brother Edward's, then her sister Ella's. The Clarke family circle was the whole shape of her life.

narrative_blocks.header: A merchant who never left the family hearth
narrative_blocks.body: He spent his life as a Peoria merchant and never married, despite a stray 1880 record that names a wife. By 1910 he was keeping house with his unmarried sister Isabel, the two of them anchored to the family they came from.

bio.bio_blurb: Arizona sheep rancher and California mining man

narrative_blocks.header: Born in Peoria, he died East, lies West
narrative_blocks.body: His life ranged far from the Peoria he was born into: he died at Newport, Vermont, in 1950, an old man of eighty-eight, and was laid to rest clear across the country at El Cerrito, California, beside his wife Grace.

narrative_blocks.header: From Peoria to Arizona sheep to California silver
narrative_blocks.body: Schooled at Peoria, he struck out for Arizona Territory in 1887 to raise sheep, then crossed to California in 1891 and threw in with the Silver King Mining Company. An Illinois dry-goods family had produced a Western mining man.

career.notes: California

narrative_blocks.header: He built the world's largest gas retorts
narrative_blocks.body: Trained in engineering at Cornell and the University of Illinois, he went south in 1911 to the oil country of Tampico, Mexico, as a construction engineer for the Huasteca Petroleum Company. There he was credited with the largest gas retorts in the world, and stayed with the work into the 1920s.

narrative_blocks.header: A lifelong bachelor at a Manhattan hotel
narrative_blocks.body: Born at the old Clarke homestead in Peoria, he never married, and after his engineering years he roamed Europe through the 1920s. He spent his later decades a resident of the Prince George Hotel in Manhattan, far from where he began.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a Peoria grain magnate
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband, Thomas Atherton Grier, built a small grain elevator into a business that helped remake the city of Peoria. The couple raised five children there.

bio.bio_blurb: Peoria grain merchant and grain-elevator magnate

narrative_blocks.header: Carried west to Peoria before he could walk
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Wilkes-Barre in 1850, he was a year old when his parents gave up Pennsylvania for Illinois and put down roots at Peoria. There the infant grew into the city's foremost grain merchant, his name known across the country as a byword for the Peoria market.

narrative_blocks.header: He left school at sixteen for a bank
narrative_blocks.body: At sixteen he closed his books for a clerk's stool at the Mechanic's National Bank, then crossed into the grain trade under his older brothers, even keeping their eastern accounts from Boston. In 1886 he struck out alone, and the house he founded became the largest grain firm in the city.

narrative_blocks.header: A small grain elevator that remade a city
narrative_blocks.body: His brothers Robert and David had thrown up Peoria's first grain elevator — a modest thing, but the nucleus of an immense trade. It was that swelling family enterprise he came up through, the one that helped lift Peoria into the front rank of the nation's grain markets.

narrative_blocks.header: He set out to make Peoria sing
narrative_blocks.body: Past the elevators and the board of trade, he poured himself into building a public taste for music, until the city counted him among its leading patrons of the art. The passion was no civic pose; by his own nature it ran deep in him.

narrative_blocks.header: Two governors called him from his counting-house
narrative_blocks.body: Office held no charm for him, yet the statehouse reached for him twice. Yates sent him to Buffalo as Illinois's commissioner to the 1901 Pan-American Exposition, and Deneen later named him a trustee of the state hospital at South Bartonville.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter married a man with a medal
narrative_blocks.body: His eldest daughter took her degree at Smith and then, in 1901, married Herbert Jamison of Peoria. Her husband had run for the United States at the first modern Olympic Games in Athens, carrying home a silver medal in the quarter-mile.

cross_connections.display_label: was the Olympic sprinter who married his daughter

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty years at one Callender Street address
narrative_blocks.body: From her marriage in 1909 she kept the same Callender Street house in Peoria to the end of her life, more than sixty years in one place. Her husband, a hardware-company officer, died in 1940, and she lived on there three decades a widow.

narrative_blocks.header: He won silver at the first modern Olympics
narrative_blocks.body: One of four Princeton men chosen for the United States team at the 1896 Athens Games — the first modern Olympics — he took silver in the 400 meters, finishing behind the American champion Tom Burke. His favorite race, the 200 meters, was not yet on the program.

narrative_blocks.header: He was born into a Peoria business dynasty
narrative_blocks.body: His father, Charles A. Jamison, was a Peoria magnate — vice-president of the Kingman plow and farm-implement company, with interests in sugar, cordage, banking, and a 6,000-acre Hereford cattle ranch. Herbert left the family business after a few years to build his own insurance agency.

narrative_blocks.header: His last years were shadowed by loss
narrative_blocks.body: He settled into the insurance trade in Peoria, but his last years were heavy ones: his son Thomas was killed in a shooting accident in 1933, and financial reverses pressed hard. Worn down by grief and worry, he took his own life in the summer of 1938.

career.notes: Peoria, IL

narrative_blocks.header: A rifle-cleaning accident killed him in the Guard
narrative_blocks.body: At eighteen, stationed with a National Guard unit at Taylorville, Illinois, he was killed when a comrade's rifle discharged during cleaning. His father, the Olympian Herbert Jamison, never recovered from the loss.

narrative_blocks.header: Only the second woman on her bank's board
narrative_blocks.body: She was the second woman ever appointed to the board of the First National Bank of Peoria — the first had been Lydia Moss Bradley, the city's great benefactor. A Northwestern graduate, she gave decades to Peoria's civic and charitable life before retiring to Florida.

narrative_blocks.header: From an Army shop company to Caterpillar
narrative_blocks.body: Trained as an engineer at Purdue, he served with the 497th Engineer Heavy Shop Company during the war. He came home to research engineering at Caterpillar Tractor, the great Peoria firm, where the rest of his working life unfolded.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a future president of the economists
narrative_blocks.body: Born in Los Angeles, she married Frederick Cecil Mills at Berkeley in 1919, just as he joined the Columbia faculty. He rose to lead the nation's economists, and from their household came children who carried the family into the front rank of American academic life.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years an economist at Columbia
narrative_blocks.body: From 1919 he taught economics at Columbia for forty years and held the Barton Hepburn chair, and in 1940 he led the American Economic Association as its president; he had headed the American Statistical Association six years before. An authority on prices and business cycles, he spent nearly three decades with the National Bureau of Economic Research.

narrative_blocks.header: He dressed as a hobo to study labor
narrative_blocks.body: Long before the professorship, the twenty-two-year-old took a strange first assignment: clad deliberately in rags, he joined California's itinerant work force in 1914 to investigate labor unrest for a state commission. What he saw among that 'floating army' of migrant men appalled him, shaped his conscience, and became the thesis that won him his Columbia doctorate.

narrative_blocks.header: He went to France with the A.E.F.
narrative_blocks.body: Between his Berkeley years and his Columbia chair he served overseas with the American Expeditionary Forces in the First World War. He came home to spend his life measuring the booms and busts of the peacetime economy.

paid for the journal that made their trade a quantitative one

bio.bio_blurb: Theoretical physicist, co-author of Yang–Mills theory

narrative_blocks.header: A 1954 office-share that reshaped physics
narrative_blocks.body: Sharing an office at Brookhaven National Laboratory, he and the physicist C. N. Yang worked out a theory of how subatomic particles interact, published in 1954. Known ever since as Yang–Mills theory, it became a cornerstone of the modern Standard Model and reshaped both physics and mathematics.

narrative_blocks.header: The Nobel for his idea went to others
narrative_blocks.body: The 1954 paper was slow to be understood for what it was. Only in 1980 did the American Academy of Arts and Sciences give him and Yang its Rumford Premium, and when the 1999 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded, it went to other men for work built directly on the framework he had helped create.

narrative_blocks.header: From the Merchant Marine to a Cambridge first
narrative_blocks.body: A Quaker-school graduate who served in the Merchant Marine through the war's end, he was named a Putnam Fellow in 1948 and took first-class honors in the Cambridge Tripos. He earned his physics doctorate at Columbia in 1955 and spent a year at the Institute for Advanced Study before heading west to teach.

narrative_blocks.header: Famous for one theory, devoted to the classroom
narrative_blocks.body: Though his name rides on a single breakthrough, his thirty-nine years at Ohio State were given to teaching quantum mechanics and to later work on alloys and many-body theory. He wrote two books, earned a faculty award for his devotion to students, and taught a Fulbright year in Ireland after retiring in 1995.

narrative_blocks.header: His last months were on a Vermont lake
narrative_blocks.body: Away from physics he was a church elder in Columbus and, with his wife, a friend to a generation of international students. The family kept a place on Echo Lake in Charleston, Vermont, and it was there, in the Northeast Kingdom woods, that he spent his final months in 1999.

bio.bio_blurb: Teacher of English to international students

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty years teaching English to the world's students
narrative_blocks.body: For three decades she taught English to a stream of international students at Ohio State, writing the materials herself, and many kept up with her for the rest of her life. With her husband she helped build the programs that drew foreign scholars into local homes, work the university honored in 1991.

narrative_blocks.header: Eleven cities and six homes abroad
narrative_blocks.body: A Smith graduate of 1946, she married the young physicist in 1948 and began a roving life that carried the family through eleven cities, abroad on six occasions, as his career advanced. She outlived him by nearly two decades, reaching the age of ninety-two.

narrative_blocks.header: He outlived his first wife by thirty-six years
narrative_blocks.body: A Farmington merchant and farmer, he lost his young wife Nancy to yellow fever in 1808 and married again. He lived on at Farmington until 1844, dying at seventy, long outlasting the wife of his youth.

narrative_blocks.header: The only one of three to grow old
narrative_blocks.body: Of her mother's three children she alone reached adulthood, her brothers lost as a baby and as a boy. She lived out sixty-six years in Farmington, never marrying, and was buried among her father's people.

narrative_blocks.header: A Middlebury graduate gone at twenty-five
narrative_blocks.body: He took his degree at Middlebury College and turned to the study of medicine, the path his father had walked before him. He died at New Haven in 1835, only twenty-five, before he could ever practice it.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed twice before she was forty
narrative_blocks.body: She married the Binghamton physician Horatio Baldwin in 1840 and was a widow at twenty-five when he died at twenty-six, and two years later she married his third cousin Samuel Hooker. Samuel died in 1852, and she followed in 1858, leaving three children under thirteen.

narrative_blocks.header: He married his third cousin’s widow
narrative_blocks.body: Lydia had been married to Dr. Horatio Baldwin of Binghamton, a physician who was Samuel’s third cousin, and was widowed at twenty-five. She and Samuel married two years later and lived at New Haven.

narrative_blocks.header: He never saw what his two sons became
narrative_blocks.body: He left two small boys and a daughter of two behind at New Haven. One son came out of Antietam and Andersonville to keep a shop at Meriden, and the other carried the family west to run a Spokane newspaper.

narrative_blocks.header: He died in Michigan and was carried home
narrative_blocks.body: He died at White Pigeon in Michigan in July 1852, at thirty-five, and was buried in Grove Street Cemetery at New Haven, where Lydia followed him six years later.

narrative_blocks.header: Her line ran back to Rhode Island's founder
narrative_blocks.body: Born in New York and married into the Hooker descent, she brought a famous lineage of her own — a direct line back to Roger Williams, founder of Rhode Island and an apostle of religious liberty. In her children the blood of two dissenting founders, Hooker and Williams, ran together.

narrative_blocks.header: From business manager to the paper's president
narrative_blocks.body: He came to the Spokane Chronicle as its business manager and ran that side of the paper for several years before taking the presidency, which he held until he died.

narrative_blocks.header: At nineteen he farmed with a future congressman
narrative_blocks.body: Out of public school at nineteen, he went west to Des Moines and joined his cousin Edward Hooker Gillette in opening one of Iowa's largest grain and stock farms. He served four years as a deputy internal revenue collector before turning to the Spokane newspaper trade.

narrative_blocks.header: A daily golfer felled by appendicitis
narrative_blocks.body: Into his seventies he played golf every day. It was not age but acute appendicitis that took him, at Spokane, in the first days of 1923.

narrative_blocks.header: He reached Spokane the month after it burned
narrative_blocks.body: He came to Spokane in 1889, arriving the very month after the great fire that leveled its downtown. Into that raw, rebuilding city he brought his family and, in time, took the helm of its Chronicle.

narrative_blocks.header: The Chronicle became a family business
narrative_blocks.body: The paper drew in his children too: his son Arthur worked its advertising desk, and the Hooker name ran through the Chronicle offices as much as its columns.

narrative_blocks.header: He inherited a libel suit with the paper
narrative_blocks.body: When the Chronicle Publishing Company was sued for printing the wrong woman’s name in a breach-of-promise story, he and Henry Rising had already succeeded to all the company’s property and franchises. They asked the court to make them defendants in its place, and were refused.

career.notes: Managing editor after the family reached Spokane; rose to president.

narrative_blocks.header: He sold Spokane on its own home-made goods
narrative_blocks.body: As managing secretary of Spokane's Home Industry Bureau, he made it his work to push the city's locally made merchandise — good quality, made at home, was the bureau's whole creed. He died at forty-seven in 1925, the newspaper family's son who sold the city to itself.

narrative_blocks.header: Before Spokane, he hauled chain through the wilderness
narrative_blocks.body: As a young man he worked the field end of his older brother Edward's survey crews — the chainman who stretched and dragged the surveyor's heavy measuring chain across raw Washington townships in 1895 and 1896. It was hard outdoor labor, brush and distance and a long count, well before he ever settled into Spokane's offices.

bio.bio_blurb: Publisher of the Daily Racing Form

narrative_blocks.header: Annenberg made him a racing-paper publisher
narrative_blocks.body: He spent some thirty years with Triangle Publications, handling personnel and labor relations for the Philadelphia Inquirer and its sister divisions. In 1966 Walter Annenberg named him publisher of the Daily Racing Form and the Morning Telegraph — and within a decade he would marry Annenberg's sister.

narrative_blocks.header: Late in life he married an Annenberg
narrative_blocks.body: Newly retired in 1974, he married Janet Annenberg Neff — sister of his old chief Walter and a philanthropist in her own right. The marriage lasted barely two years before cancer took him at Palm Beach in 1976; but his Hooker name outlived him, fixed to her great Smithsonian gifts.

narrative_blocks.header: A journalism degree led him into labor peace
narrative_blocks.body: He studied journalism at Michigan but made his name off the page, in the back rooms where newspapers and their unions hammered out terms. For some thirty years he kept that peace for Triangle Publications and the Philadelphia Inquirer.

narrative_blocks.header: His own paper died in a strike
narrative_blocks.body: He had spent a career as a labor-relations man, smoothing disputes between newspaper management and its unions. Then in 1972 one of the very papers he published, the Morning Telegraph, was shut down for good by a strike of its own.

narrative_blocks.header: A Smithsonian gem hall carries her name
narrative_blocks.body: She gave the Smithsonian a 75-carat emerald once worn by an Ottoman sultan, a suite of rare yellow starburst diamonds, and five million dollars toward a new gem gallery. When the Janet Annenberg Hooker Hall opened in 1997, it held her gifts alongside the Hope Diamond.

narrative_blocks.header: She was born into a publishing dynasty
narrative_blocks.body: Her father Moses Annenberg built an empire on the Daily Racing Form and the Philadelphia Inquirer, and her brother Walter became a billionaire publisher and ambassador to Britain. One of eight children, she turned the family fortune toward museums, music, and historic rooms.

narrative_blocks.header: She helped redecorate the White House
narrative_blocks.body: Her taste for the decorative arts reached into the nation's grandest rooms. She backed the costly renovation of the State Department's diplomatic reception rooms in the 1980s and gave toward the White House Blue Room, work that spanned several administrations.

narrative_blocks.header: Her third husband gave the gems their name
narrative_blocks.body: She married three times; her last husband, the publisher Stewart Hooker, died in 1976, only two years after their wedding. It was his Hooker name — a New England line older than the country — that she fixed to the emerald, the diamonds, and the Smithsonian hall.

narrative_blocks.header: She owned grand homes she barely used
narrative_blocks.body: Her life moved among great houses — a seventeen-room Sutton Place penthouse, an Italianate Palm Beach villa running ocean to waterway, and, in 1992, the Newport mansion Fairholme, which she bought but never lived in as her health failed. She died in Manhattan in 1997, at ninety-three.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brother befriended a queen
narrative_blocks.body: Her only brother Walter became Nixon's ambassador to Britain and a confidant of Queen Elizabeth II — a publishing billionaire who gave away two billion dollars. At his desert estate, Sunnylands, she mixed with presidents and royalty.

bio.bio_blurb: Frontier land surveyor and engineering salesman

narrative_blocks.header: At nineteen he won a federal survey contract
narrative_blocks.body: At nineteen, fresh from carrying chain for John Ashley at Ruby, he was awarded a government contract to survey raw townships in the Washington wilderness — the Salmon Creek country of Okanogan County and the land east of Deer Lake. His younger brother Harold carried chain for him on the later surveys.

narrative_blocks.header: Five years to be paid, minus a penalty
narrative_blocks.body: One of his townships was rejected and suspended, sending him back into the field to resurvey and then to fix his ties to the mineral monuments. The work dragged from 1892 to 1897, and when the government finally paid him it docked five percent for being late.

narrative_blocks.header: He crossed to France again and again
narrative_blocks.body: His surveying years behind him, he settled into New York as an engineering salesman and through the 1920s and ’30s sailed back and forth to France with his wife Marion — 1926, 1928, 1929, 1939. She made the crossing alone in 1933.

narrative_blocks.header: His father edited, then ran, the Chronicle
narrative_blocks.body: He was the eldest child of Thomas Hooker and Mary Denison, born in Iowa in 1873. The family came west to Spokane, where his father became managing editor of the Chronicle and in time its president.

narrative_blocks.header: The Northern Pacific paid for one township
narrative_blocks.body: A second contract in 1893 covered land east of Deer Park that lay inside the railroad grants, so the Northern Pacific put up the money for the survey. He ran it in the summer of 1894 and waited to February 1896 to see it accepted.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept asking Washington for more time
narrative_blocks.body: He asked for an extension the moment his first contract was approved, then another in May, then another in July with a doctor’s certificate attached. Half the work he finally turned in was sent back to be done again.

career.notes: Ruby, Washington
Okanogan, Stevens & Spokane Counties, WA; first contract at 19; brother Harold carried chain 1895-96.

narrative_blocks.header: He sold ad space for his father's paper
narrative_blocks.body: He took a place at the Spokane Chronicle his father had risen to lead, working as its assistant advertising manager. The newspaper that had carried the family west gave more than one of them their living.

narrative_blocks.header: A family lost on a single spring day
narrative_blocks.body: A long depression overtook him in the spring of 1934 — he had been brooding for some time, unable to bear watching his daughter suffer. On the thirtieth of May he took the lives of his wife Mabel and their two girls, Marjorie and Virginia, and his own. The four were laid to rest together at Fairmount.

narrative_blocks.header: He married into the clothing firm he served
narrative_blocks.body: As treasurer of the Wentworth Clothing Company he kept its books — and in 1917 he married Winnifred Wentworth, of the very family the firm was named for. He lived to ninety-two, dying in Pittsburgh in 1975.

bio.bio_blurb: Meriden printer and Civil War veteran

narrative_blocks.header: He enlisted at sixteen and bled at Antietam
narrative_blocks.body: A Hartford boy of sixteen, he joined Company A of the 16th Connecticut in July 1862 — and was shot through the right shoulder at Antietam that September, in the bloodiest single day of the war. He lived; thousands around him did not.

narrative_blocks.header: Captured at Plymouth, he survived Andersonville
narrative_blocks.body: Two years after Antietam he was taken prisoner at Plymouth, North Carolina, and sent to Andersonville, the Confederate camp whose starvation and disease killed thousands. He was paroled at the end of November 1864 and mustered out the next summer, still only nineteen.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped found his town's veterans' post
narrative_blocks.body: Back in civilian life he set type for a living, in time owning a printing shop in Meriden. In 1887 he helped found the town's Grand Army of the Republic post and served that year as its adjutant, keeping the old soldiers' fellowship alive.

narrative_blocks.header: A Connecticut printer chased Arizona gold
narrative_blocks.body: Late in life he reached for a fortune far from his press: in 1901 he became a director of the Relief Gold Mining Company, working claims near Phoenix in Arizona Territory. The mine did strike gold, and was still producing in 1909.

narrative_blocks.header: Her great-grandfather soldiered in the Revolution
narrative_blocks.body: She brought a Revolutionary pedigree to the marriage: her great-grandfather Robert Denison had served under Colonel Parsons in 1775 and stood sergeant at Fort Trumbull the next year. A soldier's blood ran down to the wife of a soldier.

bio.bio_blurb: Daily Racing Form and Inquirer publisher

narrative_blocks.header: From hawking papers to owning them
narrative_blocks.body: He came from East Prussia as a boy of eight, steerage class, and started out hawking newspapers on Chicago's streets in the rough circulation wars. From that beginning he built an empire — the Daily Racing Form, then the Philadelphia Inquirer.

narrative_blocks.header: Al Capone's judge sent him to prison too
narrative_blocks.body: In 1939 the government charged him with evading millions in taxes. He pleaded guilty, and the same federal judge who had sentenced Al Capone gave him three years and a record eight-million-dollar fine. He was released in June 1942 and died weeks later.

narrative_blocks.header: His empire became his children's fortune
narrative_blocks.body: The papers he built passed to his only son Walter, who spun them into Triangle Publications and TV Guide. His daughters' inheritances — Janet's among them — went on to fund museums, schools, and the redecoration of the White House.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter made the Hooker name shine
narrative_blocks.body: Of his eight children it was Janet who married into an old New England family called Hooker — and made that borrowed name famous. As Janet Annenberg Hooker she gave the Smithsonian its great emerald, its rare yellow diamonds, and a gem hall that carries the Hooker name to this day.

narrative_blocks.header: She anchored a household of eight children
narrative_blocks.body: Between 1900 and 1914 she bore eight children — seven daughters and the son Walter — and was the steady center of the household through her husband's rise, disgrace, and imprisonment. The family name she helped hold together.

narrative_blocks.header: Her children pledged millions in her honor
narrative_blocks.body: Her own giving ran to medicine and learning — a pediatrics department, a school of communication, an irrigation institute in Israel. On her eighty-sixth birthday her children pledged eight million dollars toward a Mount Sinai medical school in her name.

narrative_blocks.header: A young doctor dead at twenty-six
narrative_blocks.body: A Litchfield-born physician, he settled at Binghamton, New York, and married there into the Strong family of Vermont. He died at twenty-six in 1842, and his only child, an infant daughter, followed him to the grave within the year.

narrative_blocks.header: His widow later married his cousin
narrative_blocks.body: His young widow Elizabeth did not stay alone. Two years on she married Samuel Hooker — a man said to be Baldwin's own third cousin — and bore the sons who would carry the Hooker line to a Meriden printing shop and a Spokane newsroom.

narrative_blocks.header: His firm's ships ran to the West Indies
narrative_blocks.body: With his brother Chauncey he kept the Farmington mercantile house of John and Chauncey Deming, whose ships sailed between New London and the West Indies. The store stocked everything from pepper and chocolate to calico and beaver hats, bought by the crate from New York merchants.

narrative_blocks.header: He and his brother married two sisters
narrative_blocks.body: He married Susannah Cowles in 1775; his brother and partner Chauncey married her sister Diadema five years later. The two Deming brothers and the two Cowles sisters bound the families twice over, in the counting-house and at the altar.

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband descended from the same Hooker forebear
narrative_blocks.body: She and Captain Richard Cowles both came down from Hon. John Hooker, the founder's grandson — her line through his son Joseph, Richard's through his son Roger. Two brothers' branches, parted for three generations, rejoined the day these distant cousins married.

narrative_blocks.header: Cornet to major, then a lieutenant again
narrative_blocks.body: He went up the Connecticut cavalry in eleven years - cornet of the 7th in 1798, second lieutenant of the 4th in 1800, captain in 1804, major in 1807. In 1811 he took a lieutenancy in the 18th Infantry and dropped four ranks.

narrative_blocks.header: He traded with all four of his brothers
narrative_blocks.body: He lived in the house next north of the Farmington meeting-house and traded in company with his four brothers. He sat as a director of the Hartford Bank from 1818 and of the Farmington Canal Company from 1827.

narrative_blocks.header: Three of nine died in their birth year
narrative_blocks.body: Julia Ann in 1803, John Deming in 1806 and Jane Eliza in 1820 each died in the year they were born, and a second Julia Ann was given the first one's name. Henry Augustus reached twenty-one and no further.

narrative_blocks.header: Farmington, Sandusky, Syracuse, Cleveland
narrative_blocks.body: Yale gave him a degree in 1826 and the rest of it was trade. He kept a business at Farmington, went out to Sandusky in Ohio, came back, set up at Syracuse about 1849, and made a last move to Cleveland in November 1856.

narrative_blocks.header: He lost his wife and the baby together
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Lewis died in the September of 1848 and their son Gad, seven months old, died within days of her. Both are at Riverside in Farmington. He married Evelina Robinson of Syracuse two years after.

narrative_blocks.header: His aorta gave way without warning
narrative_blocks.body: He died suddenly at Cleveland in the May of 1859, fifty-one years old, of a ruptured aorta, two and a half years after moving there. They carried him back to Farmington to bury him.

narrative_blocks.body: He entered Norwich Academy in Vermont in 1825 and graduated three years later, but lost his eyesight in early life and could never enter the active business his family was known for. He and his wife had no children, and he lived to eighty-three in the Farmington house the Cowleses had built.

narrative_blocks.header: He lost the house his father gave him
narrative_blocks.body: When he married in 1803, his father built him a fine brick house on Main Street in Farmington as a wedding gift. George never had a head for business, and in time the house slipped from him in foreclosure, passing to a wealthier relative.

narrative_blocks.header: His sign read Drugs and Medicines
narrative_blocks.body: The store stood where the D. R. Hawley house was later built, and the sign across its front read George Cowles, Drugs and Medicines. He kept it going a great many years.

narrative_blocks.header: He was his father's aide, then his equal
narrative_blocks.body: From 1807 to 1812 he was major and aide-de-camp to Maj. Gen. Solomon Cowles, his father. In 1824 he took the 1st Division himself, the command his father had held until 1815.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight ranks in fifteen years
narrative_blocks.body: Second major of the 15th Connecticut in 1810, first major in 1813, lieutenant-colonel commanding in 1815, colonel of the 14th in 1816, brigadier in 1820, major general in 1824, adjutant general from 1825.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife's mother was a Cowles too
narrative_blocks.body: Abigail Deming was the daughter of John Deming and Susannah Cowles of Farmington. They married on 3 December 1803 and joined the church together in 1821.

narrative_blocks.header: She left Farmington for the Illinois frontier
narrative_blocks.body: Married in 1849, she traveled west with her missionary husband by river and canal boat to Ottawa, Illinois — and as their belongings were unloaded, her trousseau tumbled into the water and was hauled out soaked. She spent the rest of her long life on the prairie, far from the Connecticut town her Cowles and Deming forebears had helped settle.

narrative_blocks.header: Meant to stay months, he stayed decades
narrative_blocks.body: A missionary society sent him to the struggling church at Ottawa, Illinois in 1849, expecting only a brief supply of the pulpit. The congregation refused to let him leave; he served as their pastor for twenty-one years and made Ottawa his home for the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: He became a church statesman of the prairie
narrative_blocks.body: After his long Ottawa pastorate he ran the Home Missionary Society for central and southern Illinois, planting and shoring up frontier congregations. For more than forty years he held office in the Congregational General Assembly, ending as its state registrar.

narrative_blocks.header: Postmaster for thirty-one years
narrative_blocks.body: He held the Farmington post office from 1841 until he died in 1872, sat on the school board in 1854, and ran the drug business his father had built on Main Street.

narrative_blocks.header: Aide-de-camp to the division his father led
narrative_blocks.body: Quartermaster of the 4th Connecticut Cavalry in 1827, he was major and aide-de-camp to the 1st Division from 1830 to 1833 — the division his father George had taken command of in 1824.

narrative_blocks.header: He went to Norwich Academy at seventeen
narrative_blocks.body: After the schools of Farmington he entered the Norwich Academy in Vermont, now Norwich University, in 1825 and graduated in 1827. He came home to Farmington and stayed.

narrative_blocks.body: Noah Loomis Phelps and Jemima Stedman of Simsbury were her parents. She went to Sarah Pierce's school at Litchfield in 1825, married six years after it, and joined the church in 1838.

narrative_blocks.header: Assessor, then collector, then burgess
narrative_blocks.body: He left Farmington for Wallingford when he married in 1855 and served the borough through the nineties: town assessor in 1894 and 1895, collector from 1896 to 1899, burgess in 1900 and 1901.

parents.father_research_notes: Martin Kellogg Sr. (1658–1750), early Deerfield settler; redeemed after the 1704 raid.

narrative_blocks.header: Taken at seventeen in the Deerfield raid
narrative_blocks.body: He was seventeen when French and Native raiders destroyed Deerfield in 1704 and marched him some three hundred miles to Kahnawake near Montreal. He escaped home within a year, only to be seized again on a 1708 scouting mission and held several more years among the Mohawk.

narrative_blocks.header: Captivity made him the colony's Mohawk go-between
narrative_blocks.body: The years he lost to the Mohawk left him fluent in their language and at home in their country. Connecticut put that to use, sending him in 1740 as a guide for the British fleet on the St. Lawrence and the next year as its agent to clothe the Mohawk.

narrative_blocks.header: His Indian school ended in complaint and disgrace
narrative_blocks.body: From 1748 he ran a boarding school for Mohawk and Oneida boys at Stockbridge, but drew complaints that he underfed them and set them to work on his own farm. Jonathan Edwards judged him unfit for it and the mission society sent a replacement, yet Kellogg refused to surrender the post.

narrative_blocks.header: His sisters chose the Mohawk over home
narrative_blocks.body: His half-sister Joanna, taken as a girl in the same raid, refused every chance to come home and lived out her life married into a Kahnawake family. His half-sister Rebecca did return, serving as an interpreter at the Stockbridge mission, where the Mohawk named her "the bridge."

narrative_blocks.header: She descended from a founding Connecticut governor
narrative_blocks.body: Through her mother Sarah, she came down from Thomas Welles, one of Connecticut's earliest governors and the only man to hold all four of the colony's highest offices. The captive interpreter's wife carried that founding blood into the Kellogg line.

narrative_blocks.header: He drifted west while his sister stayed
narrative_blocks.body: Born in the Ottawa parsonage, he did not settle in Illinois like his sister but kept moving west — to Grand Island, Nebraska, and at last to San Diego, where he died at eighty-seven. The minister's son ended his days on the Pacific, a continent from the Connecticut town his mother had left as a bride.

narrative_blocks.header: She taught music and had a fine voice
narrative_blocks.body: Trained at Shurtleff College, she taught music at the Monticello Seminary and was admired for a fine singing voice. It was at the dedication of a memorial chapel there that a widowed Chicago banker, William Reid, first met her.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a banker, then a doctor
narrative_blocks.body: Her first husband, William Reid, left her a wealthy widow in 1910; her second, Dr. Henry Reynolds, had helped found a medical school. Through both marriages she kept her father's house on the Ottawa bluff — Whittlesey Place — as a summer home.

narrative_blocks.header: He told Chicago's richest man no
narrative_blocks.body: As a bank vice-president he once refused Philip Armour — then perhaps the most powerful financier in Chicago — a million-dollar loan, judging the collateral too thin. Armour was furious, slept on it, then went about town praising the bank's nerve, and the gamble made its name.

narrative_blocks.header: He started at fifteen and built a fortune
narrative_blocks.body: Sent off with a country storekeeper at fifteen after a schoolyard dispute, he learned trade by swapping goods for farmers' butter and eggs. He worked up through riverboat packet lines and a wholesale grocery before Chicago banking made him rich.

narrative_blocks.header: He never spoke of his first wife again
narrative_blocks.body: When his first wife, Eleanor, died in 1888, he came home to Ohio, told his family every detail, then asked that the subject be closed forever. A reticent, intense man, he carried her memory quietly the rest of his life, even after he married again.

narrative_blocks.header: A memorial chapel brought him a second wife
narrative_blocks.body: Grieving his first wife, he paid to rebuild the fire-gutted Monticello Seminary in downstate Illinois and gave it a memorial chapel. At its dedication he met Caroline Whittlesey, a music teacher there and a country minister's daughter, and within the year he had married her.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at his wife's bluff-top home
narrative_blocks.body: Though his steel-framed mansion stood on Chicago's Prairie Avenue among the Armours and Fields, he kept his wife's family home — Whittlesey Place, on the Ottawa bluff — as a country retreat. It was there, a month back from his last trip to Europe, that he died in 1910.

narrative_blocks.header: The only one that stayed a single home
narrative_blocks.body: Beers, Clay & Dutton finished his house on Prairie Avenue in 1894, with a large Palladian window across the third floor. Of all the mansions on that street it is the only one that has never been anything but one family’s home.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped raise a medical school in Chicago
narrative_blocks.body: A Canadian-trained physician, he was among the early faculty of the University of Illinois College of Medicine and a professor of dermatology there. He went on to found the American Medical Association's first section devoted to diseases of the skin.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the banker's widow late in life
narrative_blocks.body: In 1911, a year after William Reid's death, the dermatologist married Reid's widow, Caroline Whittlesey, at Ottawa. He outlived her too, dying in Chicago at ninety-six.

narrative_blocks.header: His degree came with a New York prize
narrative_blocks.body: He trained in Toronto and earned his medical degree at Bellevue Hospital Medical College in New York in 1875, carrying off the Mott prize. He practiced in Michigan before settling in Chicago and turning to the young specialty of skin disease.

narrative_blocks.header: He pushed Michigan to regulate its doctors
narrative_blocks.body: Before leaving Michigan he helped establish the state's first regulation of medical practice and its compulsory public-sanitation rules in 1881. It was early, contested work in an age when almost anyone could hang out a shingle and call himself a physician.

narrative_blocks.header: The dermatologist ended his days a broker
narrative_blocks.body: Late in life he stepped away from medicine to head a Chicago merchandise brokerage. He lived to ninety-six, outliving two wives and most of the colleagues who had founded his specialty alongside him.

narrative_blocks.header: He alone stayed in Leicestershire while others left
narrative_blocks.body: As the firstborn, he remained in Leicestershire all his life, dying at Tilton in 1655. While his brother Thomas and three sisters crossed to New England, John kept to the family's home ground — the last of the Hookers to hold it.

narrative_blocks.header: A widow, she crossed to found Hartford
narrative_blocks.body: Left a widow in Leicestershire in 1628, she followed her brother Thomas to New England, reaching Cambridge by 1634 and removing with him to Hartford two years later. She was numbered among the town's original proprietors, holding five parcels of its first land in her own name.

narrative_blocks.header: She may have sailed the Griffin beside Thomas
narrative_blocks.body: Tradition holds she boarded the ship Griffin in 1633 with her famous brother, though the first certain trace of her is a 1634 grant of four acres at Cambridge. However she came, she ended a landholder in her own right in the wilderness town he led.

narrative_blocks.header: Few women held Hartford land in their name
narrative_blocks.body: In a colony where land and standing ran through husbands and sons, the widow held her Hartford home lot and meadows herself. When she died about 1662, her estate passed not to a husband but through an administrator and her son Leonard, who had settled at Wethersfield.

narrative_blocks.header: She married at fifteen and bore eight children
narrative_blocks.body: She married John Tarleton at Marefield in 1607, around the age of fifteen, and over the decades that followed bore him eight children — the largest family of all Rev. Thomas Hooker's siblings.

people.relational_label_override: Sister of Thomas Hooker

narrative_blocks.header: She died in Roxbury within months of landing
narrative_blocks.body: She crossed in the great 1630 migration with her husband George Alcock, among the first English families to settle Roxbury. The new world undid her quickly: she died that first brutal winter, leaving a young son, while George stayed on to become a deacon of the church.

narrative_blocks.header: The infant she left became a Boston doctor
narrative_blocks.body: The young son she died leaving behind, John, was raised across the ocean after his father sailed back to fetch him. He grew up to practice medicine in Roxbury and Boston, marrying into the Palgrave family and raising eleven children of his own.

people.relational_label_override: Sister of Thomas Hooker

narrative_blocks.header: She too crossed the sea, died in Hartford
narrative_blocks.body: Married to Robert Milner at Birstall in 1622, she joined the family's migration and ended her life in Hartford in 1668. Three of Thomas Hooker's siblings — Dorothy, Anne, and Elizabeth — followed him across the ocean, though only two lived to grow old there.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at thirteen, before the family scattered
narrative_blocks.body: The last of Thomas Hooker I's children, he died at Marefield before he turned fourteen, in 1616. He never saw the migration that would carry his brother and sisters across the world.

narrative_blocks.header: He died in Leicester before Dorothy ever sailed
narrative_blocks.body: He married Dorothy Hooker at Birstall in 1609 and died at Leicester in 1628, never crossing to New England. It was as his widow that Dorothy carried the Chester name to Hartford, where their son Leonard also settled.

narrative_blocks.header: He sailed back to England for his son
narrative_blocks.body: After Anne died in Roxbury's first winter, the widowed deacon made two voyages back to England — once for the young son the couple had left behind, once for a second wife. The minister John Eliot remembered him as a man who "lived in a good godly sort."

narrative_blocks.header: The country girl's husband became a London brewer
narrative_blocks.body: Born in a Leicestershire village, he married Frances Hooker at Marefield in 1607 and later rose to citizen and brewer of the City of London, settling across the Thames in Southwark. He was still listed at the trade in 1653, near seventy, having raised eight children far from the parish where he wed.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the name of a dead brother
narrative_blocks.body: His parents had given the name Edward Huntington to a first son who died the day he was born in 1853; when he arrived two years later, they gave it to him again. He grew up to take orders, serving as an Episcopal rector at parishes in Minnesota and Illinois.

parents.mother_research_notes: Mary Ann (Kendall) Greene of Washington, D.C.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at twenty-two, far west in Utah
narrative_blocks.body: Unmarried, he died at twenty-two in Salt Lake City in 1881 — a long way from the Wisconsin towns where the family had settled. What carried him to Utah the record does not say.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-five years a missionary in the East
narrative_blocks.body: He gave his life to the American Board in Ceylon and then Madras, compiling a monumental Tamil–English dictionary and helping build the mission's schools. After more than four decades abroad, he died in 1864 at the Cape of Good Hope, traveling for his health.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a fellow missionary's widow
narrative_blocks.body: His later wife was Mary Billings Williams, who had come to India as the wife of Robert Ogden Dwight. After Dwight died at Madura, she married Winslow — binding two American Board households into one. She died at Madras in 1852.

narrative_blocks.header: One of three brothers, all eminent divines
narrative_blocks.body: He and his brothers Hubbard and Gordon were all noted clergymen, and all three died in 1864. A single marble monument in Williston, Vermont, honors the three together — "Their works do follow them."

narrative_blocks.header: Born in Venezuela, he came home to Boxford
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Caracas in 1955, during the family's years in Venezuela — a generation after his grandfather Winthrop had spent his life prospecting oil across the globe. The Hayneses were a family at home abroad, yet he came back to Boxford, their New England seat, where he died in 2016.

narrative_blocks.header: Born on Venezuela's great oil lake
narrative_blocks.body: She came into the world at Maracaibo in 1958, in the heart of Venezuela's oil country, the second of Edward's children born abroad. Like her brother she found her way back to Boxford, dying there in 2013 — the family's long wandering ending where it had begun.

narrative_blocks.header: She died twelve days after her last child
narrative_blocks.body: Theodore Salisbury Woolsey was born on the twenty-second of October 1852 and she was dead by the third of November. She had borne nine children in nineteen years and buried four of them already.

narrative_blocks.header: Scarlet fever took three in one day
narrative_blocks.body: In December 1843 the epidemic reached the president's house at Yale and Edward, Elizabeth and William Walton all died on the seventeenth. Edward was nine, Elizabeth eight, William three.

narrative_blocks.header: Two sisters died two days apart
narrative_blocks.body: Martha died on the sixth of December 1870 at twenty-three and Helen on the eighth, at twenty-one. Of the nine children of their father's first marriage, only Agnes and Theodore were left.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived Denver by thirty years
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband died in Colorado in 1901 and she came back to New Haven, the town she was born in while her father ran Yale. She died there in 1931 and was buried in Grove Street with the Woolseys.

narrative_blocks.header: She buried a daughter at seven
narrative_blocks.body: Georgeanna was born in 1887 and died in 1894. The three who lived — Roger, Alfred, and Agnes — all reached their eighties or better.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote for magazines while raising a family
narrative_blocks.body: While her husband built his architecture practice, she raised their children and wrote for the New Republic and the Atlantic Monthly. She had grown up in the household of the Yale theologian Benjamin Wisner Bacon, and carried that literary cast into her own home.

narrative_blocks.header: She taught convicts to write for magazines
narrative_blocks.body: After her years on the staff of the New Republic, she spent part of her later life inside Connecticut's prisons, teaching inmates how to write and sell articles to magazines.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-one years dissecting the Gospels at Yale
narrative_blocks.body: As Yale's Buckingham Professor of New Testament Criticism he spent three decades applying the era's higher criticism to the Gospels, arguing over the sources behind Mark and the authorship of John. His many books made him one of America's most cited biblical scholars.

narrative_blocks.header: The Yale fullback who became a Bible critic
narrative_blocks.body: Before the pulpit and the lectern he spent four seasons as a fullback on the Yale football team. The man who once anchored the line went on to anchor the nation's debates over how the Gospels came to be written.

narrative_blocks.header: He sent a fourth straight generation to Yale
narrative_blocks.body: When his son entered Yale, he joined a direct male line running back through Bacon, his father Leonard Woolsey Bacon, and his grandfather — four generations, plus two uncles and a cousin. For this family the college class lists read almost like a genealogy.

narrative_blocks.header: His father told Savannah he wanted mixed schools
narrative_blocks.body: Leonard Woolsey Bacon was pastor of the Independent Presbyterian Church in Savannah in 1887 when he said publicly that he favoured schools open to Black and white children together, and would not object if his daughter married a Black man. It caused a sensation in Georgia. He wrote A History of American Christianity, held pulpits from Litchfield and Brooklyn to Geneva, and was buried at Grove Street beside his son.

narrative_blocks.header: A general's daughter who married the theologian
narrative_blocks.body: A daughter of General William Appleton Aiken of Norwich, she married the young pastor Benjamin Wisner Bacon in 1884, just as his Yale career was taking shape. Their daughter Dorothy would marry into the Woolsey line.

narrative_blocks.header: Born in Paris to a wandering American architect
narrative_blocks.body: She and her younger brother were both born in Paris while their father studied and practiced architecture abroad. She came home to Connecticut, attended Sarah Lawrence, and spent most of her long life in Kent.

narrative_blocks.header: The Yale president's name, four generations on
narrative_blocks.body: He was named for his great-great-grandfather, the tenth president of Yale — the latest Woolsey to carry the name down the line. Born in Paris, he was buried in the family ground at Glen Cove.

narrative_blocks.header: His hand shaped the Constitution's final wording
narrative_blocks.body: At the 1787 Convention he chaired the Committee of Style, the group that turned the delegates' resolutions into the final text of the Constitution. He backed the compromise that gave every state an equal Senate.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped write the colonies' first joint protest
narrative_blocks.body: At the 1765 Stamp Act Congress he drafted the Declaration of Rights and Grievances — the colonies' first united argument that they alone could tax themselves. The final version survives in his own hand.

narrative_blocks.header: Torn between two countries, he trusted neither side
narrative_blocks.body: Sent to London as Connecticut's agent, he spent five years defending the colony's charter and came home half-English in sympathy, doubtful that independence was wise. In 1779 patriots arrested him for "communicating with the enemy," though the charge was soon dropped.

narrative_blocks.header: He resigned the Senate to lead Columbia
narrative_blocks.body: Elected one of Connecticut's first United States senators in 1789, he gave up the seat two years later to become the third president of Columbia College. He led the school until retiring in 1800.

narrative_blocks.header: The famous Dr. Johnson envied his company
narrative_blocks.body: The English writer Samuel Johnson told this American namesake that there was scarcely anyone whose acquaintance he had more wished to cultivate. The two shared a name and a learning that reached across the Atlantic.

narrative_blocks.header: She died young in a German spa town
narrative_blocks.body: First wife of Charles Astor Bristed, she died at thirty-six at Baden-Baden after a short illness. The town turned out for her funeral, with diplomats and members of society following her to the grave.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded and led Adelphi College
narrative_blocks.body: He built Adelphi from a Brooklyn academy into a college in 1896 and served as its first president until 1912. Its main building and its global-scholars program still carry his name.

narrative_blocks.header: The prize his peace plan won
narrative_blocks.body: In 1924 he won the American Peace Award for the best workable plan to bring the United States into cooperation with other nations. His scheme would have entered the country into the League of Nations on special terms.

narrative_blocks.header: His glee club included a future president
narrative_blocks.body: As a graduate student at Johns Hopkins he befriended a young Woodrow Wilson, the two of them fellow members of the glee club. Decades later he campaigned for the League of Nations that Wilson had championed.

narrative_blocks.header: He aimed the plan at one senator
narrative_blocks.body: He wrote with the speeches of George Wharton Pepper open in front of him — the senator who led the anti-League organisation — and said he had visualised Pepper as a target. The middle of the road was what he was after, not the irreconcilables and not the enthusiasts.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept a deflation department
narrative_blocks.body: Congratulations poured in once his name was published, and he set the sour letters aside in what he called his deflation department, to be looked at whenever his head showed a tendency to swell.

narrative_blocks.header: The referendum that kept being extended
narrative_blocks.body: Half a million ballots came in and seven in eight were favourable, but the closing date moved and moved again while the rest of the award waited on a sufficient popular response. A Republican paper counted his votes against Eugene Debs's and found them wanting.

narrative_blocks.header: The first iron works in Trumbull County
narrative_blocks.body: Robert came west to Trumbull County in 1806 and built the Hopewell furnace on Yellow Creek, a mile below Poland, the first iron works in the county. Remnants of it can still be seen along the creek's west bank.

narrative_blocks.header: Taught surveying by a Continental Congressman
narrative_blocks.body: Robert learned surveying from his father, who had served in the Revolutionary army and sat in the Continental Congress. A widower with one child, he married Louisa Morris Edwards in 1814 and moved the family to Coitsville two years later.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped win the nation's wool tariff
narrative_blocks.body: A successful farmer and wool-grower near Youngstown, he became so expert on the subject that in 1867 he traveled to Washington and helped secure a federal tariff on wool. He sat in the Ohio House in 1862 and 1863.

narrative_blocks.header: An old Jackson man who turned against slavery
narrative_blocks.body: He cast his first presidential vote for Andrew Jackson but grew into a bold and aggressive opponent of slavery, holding to the Union cause through the war.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother's uncle signed the Declaration
narrative_blocks.body: Through his mother, Louisa Morris, he descended from the Morris family of New York. Lewis Morris, a signer of the Declaration of Independence, was her great-uncle.

narrative_blocks.header: A doctor's wife who worked as a missionary
narrative_blocks.body: She was active as a missionary and church worker in the First Presbyterian Church. Her husband, the physician Moses Haseltine, moved the family west to Pittsburgh and then Northville before his death in 1862.

narrative_blocks.header: She took a doctorate and taught inside Bellevue
narrative_blocks.body: A graduate of Vassar and the Columbia journalism school, she earned a doctorate at New York University and taught English and literature for years — at the Emma Willard School and, unusually, at the public school inside Bellevue Hospital.

narrative_blocks.header: She lost husband and son in one week
narrative_blocks.body: Her first husband, the New York Times editorial writer Wellington Wales, died of a heart attack at forty-eight, days after their nineteen-year-old son Samuel was struck and killed by a train in Boston. Father and son were buried together.

narrative_blocks.header: Journalist, soldier, and Caribbean bulldozer man
narrative_blocks.body: He wrote editorials for the New York Times and edited newspapers in three states, but between newsrooms he ran a road-building outfit in the Virgin Islands, sold liquor, and taught water-skiing. A wartime combat photographer, he was discharged a captain.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine children, five buried small
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Ann and Thomas had nine children between 1841 and 1849. Four sons died as newborns, unnamed, and Theodore before he was two; George died at twenty-four and Sarah at twenty-six. Only Mary and Emma lived past thirty.

narrative_blocks.body: He trained for medicine, then abandoned it for fourteen years as a Cleveland merchant before reading law for a year. In his late thirties he came back to medicine as a convert to homeopathy, took his degree, and practiced in Utica and Detroit.

narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth and Joshua Bates made their home at Woodburn, outside Cincinnati, where her half-brother W.W. Scarborough also lived. They named their third son William Scarborough Bates.
