narrative_blocks.header: Fifteen Ohio regiments in one summer
narrative_blocks.body: Named one of Ohio's three militia brigadier generals in April 1861, Joshua commanded Camp Harrison, helped build Camp Dennison and organized fifteen infantry regiments. At forty-four, too old for combat, he resigned that August.

narrative_blocks.header: Bates Battery, on the Kentucky hills
narrative_blocks.body: When Kirby Smith's Confederates threatened Cincinnati in 1862, Joshua, president of the city's Committee of Public Safety, commanded a division. An earthwork in northern Kentucky defending the city was named Bates Battery.

narrative_blocks.header: Andrew Jackson sent him to West Point
narrative_blocks.body: Joshua's father, the Boston physician George Bates, was a friend of Andrew Jackson, who appointed the boy to West Point. He graduated in 1837, fought the Seminoles in Florida and guarded the Canadian border, reading law on the side.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty-six years at the Ohio bar
narrative_blocks.body: Joshua read law with Bellamy Storer, was admitted in 1842 and practised at Cincinnati until 1905, latterly as Bates & Kaufman. He sat twice in the Ohio Senate, was a presidential elector in 1872 and led the Cincinnati Bar Association.

narrative_blocks.header: A Democrat until the war came
narrative_blocks.body: A Democrat before the Civil War, Joshua became a Republican when it began and stayed one. On wartime visits to Washington he met Lincoln, and kept the memories. He died at the Burnet House in 1908, at ninety-one.

narrative_blocks.header: He ended his days on a Washington farm
narrative_blocks.body: Trained as an electrical engineer, he married Kate Stevens in 1913 and from 1925 lived at Cloverfield Farms near Olympia, Washington — far from the Cincinnati of his birth.

narrative_blocks.header: Governor of Ohio, 1884 to 1886
narrative_blocks.body: George left the Democrats over slavery and the Union in the Civil War and came back in the 1870s, presiding over their 1880 convention. In 1883 he won the governorship of Ohio, beating Joseph Foraker, and lost it in 1885.

narrative_blocks.header: A mob burned the courthouse on his watch
narrative_blocks.body: In 1884 a lenient Cincinnati verdict set off three days of rioting; a crowd burned the courthouse and dozens died before the militia restored order. His use of troops in the Hocking Valley coal strike angered both sides.

narrative_blocks.header: He argued before the 1877 Electoral Commission
narrative_blocks.body: George argued the Oregon and Florida cases before the commission that decided the 1876 presidential election. Rutherford Hayes, whose presidency hung on it, had been his classmate at Harvard Law.

narrative_blocks.header: Salmon Chase made him a partner
narrative_blocks.body: George read law in Salmon Chase's Cincinnati office and rose to partner in Chase, Ball & Hoadly. After the governorship he moved his practice to New York in 1887.

narrative_blocks.header: He twice declined Ohio's Supreme Court
narrative_blocks.body: George sat on the Superior Court of Cincinnati from 1851 to 1853 and again from 1859 to 1866, and was city solicitor between. He turned down seats on Ohio's Supreme Court in 1856 and 1862.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty years teaching law
narrative_blocks.body: George taught for twenty years at the Cincinnati Law School, sat as a trustee of the University of Cincinnati and later of Barnard College, and took honorary doctorates from Western Reserve, Yale and Dartmouth.

narrative_blocks.header: He dropped the e from Hoadley
narrative_blocks.body: Born George Hoadley, son of the New Haven and Cleveland mayor, he dropped the e. His mother was a niece of Yale's President Timothy Dwight and the eldest sister of Yale's President Woolsey.

narrative_blocks.header: She christened the first floating bridge
narrative_blocks.body: In 1940 Kate christened the first Lake Washington floating bridge, smashing an urn of water from fifty-eight of the state's lakes, streams and bays against a pylon at its west end. She was eighty-seven.

narrative_blocks.header: Save the first governor's house
narrative_blocks.body: In 1928 Kate urged Olympia, in the Washington Historian, to keep her father's 1856 house, the territory's first executive mansion, as a museum and park. Her diaries, 1880 to 1936, are at the University of Oregon.

narrative_blocks.header: A Portland writer and society figure
narrative_blocks.body: Her first marriage took her to Portland, Oregon, where she wrote for newspapers and magazines and joined the Unitarian society. After that husband's horseshoe-manufacturing venture failed and he later died, she married James Bates and moved east.

narrative_blocks.header: Daughter of Washington's first governor
narrative_blocks.body: Kate was a daughter of Isaac Stevens, Washington Territory's first governor, killed as a Union general in 1862. She reached Olympia by canoe and wagon in 1854, grew up in Newport and Dorchester, and died the state's best-known pioneer.

narrative_blocks.body: A wool-grower and brick manufacturer who supplied brick for Youngstown's buildings, he enlisted as a private in Company F of the 155th Ohio Volunteers and served three months for the Union.

narrative_blocks.header: She died on her fiftieth birthday
narrative_blocks.body: Mary died at the family house on Wilson Avenue in Youngstown on 20 November 1893, her fiftieth birthday, after a year of failing health. She was buried in the Montgomery plot at Oak Hill, where Theron joined her in 1905.

death.notes: At his daughter's house on Wilson Avenue; he had been living at Linesville, Pennsylvania

narrative_blocks.header: A quarry on the Montgomery farm
narrative_blocks.body: Theron grew up near Brier Hill, schooled in a log schoolhouse on the Girard-Warren road, and learned the stonemason's trade. For many years he ran a stone quarry on the Montgomery farm at Haselton, and gave up the work about 1895.

narrative_blocks.header: Three months in the 19th, then the 105th
narrative_blocks.body: When the war came Theron volunteered for three months with the 19th Ohio, then enlisted again in the 105th Ohio Volunteer Infantry and served to the close of the war. He lies as a veteran in the Montgomery plot at Oak Hill.

narrative_blocks.header: A kinsman of President McKinley
narrative_blocks.body: Theron, son of the pioneer settlers Matthew R. McKinley and his wife, was counted a relative of President William McKinley, born four years after him at Niles, a few miles from Theron's birthplace near Brier Hill.

narrative_blocks.header: A fortune in Poland land
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel left the college at Hudson without a degree and went into trade at Brookfield as Henry Wick's partner, then at Hubbard from 1836, before settling at Poland to manage the land that made him a fortune. He sat on the Farmers' Bank board.

narrative_blocks.header: A sunstroke, then a fall on the walk
narrative_blocks.body: About 1887 Samuel was struck down by a severe sunstroke and never fully recovered. In December 1892 he slipped on the walk at his house in Poland and broke his hip, and he faded through the spring and died in May 1893, at seventy-seven.

career.role: Merchant, in partnership with Henry Wick

narrative_blocks.header: He chose the ground for a steel giant
narrative_blocks.body: As the valley's leading corporate lawyer he was central to founding the Youngstown Sheet and Tube Company. When surveys showed the first proposed site lacked water, it was his judgment that secured the 300-acre plant site at Campbell, fronting both the river and the railroads.

narrative_blocks.header: His law partner went to the Supreme Court
narrative_blocks.body: For eleven years his partner was John H. Clarke, who later sat as a justice of the United States Supreme Court. Clarke called him the most trusted legal adviser behind the great enterprises of the Mahoning Valley.

narrative_blocks.header: The corporate lawyer had been a ballplayer
narrative_blocks.body: Before the law he played catcher for the Poland Resolutes and first base for the Mahoning Baseball Club, one of the area's first semi-professional teams. Friends found the reserved, stern-seeming man warm and generous underneath.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped found the valley's historical society
narrative_blocks.body: In 1909 he was one of the incorporators of the Mahoning Valley Historical Society and wrote its articles of incorporation himself.

narrative_blocks.header: Sheet and Tube closed its offices for him
narrative_blocks.body: Cecil died of a heart attack at Pasadena in February 1920, wintering with his daughter as he had for years. On the day of his Youngstown funeral Sheet and Tube closed its general offices, and the county bar attended in a body.

narrative_blocks.header: He hated trickery and sham
narrative_blocks.body: L. A. Manchester, later counsel to Sheet and Tube, said Cecil had the greatest analytical mind he ever met: he went straight to his point, and he hated trickery, underhanded methods, dishonesty and sham.

narrative_blocks.header: Dropped dead in Yellowstone Park
narrative_blocks.body: In September 1905 Robert was touring the West with Charles A. Bowers, once of Youngstown, in perfect health as far as anyone at home knew, when he dropped dead in Yellowstone Park. The telegram reached his brother Edwin that afternoon.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirteen years inspecting Ohio's mines
narrative_blocks.body: Robert practised twenty years as a mining engineer before Governor Joseph Foraker made him Ohio's chief inspector of mines in 1888. He served thirteen years as a state mine inspector, and moved from Youngstown to Columbus the next year.

narrative_blocks.header: Born in the quarter named for his family
narrative_blocks.body: Robert was born in 1846 in Haselton, the Youngstown East Side quarter around Wilson Avenue and Center Street that took its name from the Haseltines, among the Mahoning Valley's earliest settlers.

narrative_blocks.header: Four of seven children lost as babies
narrative_blocks.body: Robert married Orre Ann Barnes in 1870, and four of their seven children died as babies between 1876 and 1881. Orre died in 1885, weeks after their daughter Orre was born, and his second wife, Marietta Lesher, died a year after their 1889 wedding.

narrative_blocks.body: Edwin was a Youngstown civil engineer and at one time or another Mahoning County surveyor, city councilman, school board member and president of the valley's society of professional engineers. In 1897 he took his cousin's son George Montgomery into partnership.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept the Bible Society's desk
narrative_blocks.body: After years of pulpits in New York, Maine and Connecticut he became secretary of the American Bible Society and stayed in the work until he died. The parishioners' letters followed him from every place he had served.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother opened Johns Hopkins
narrative_blocks.body: Daniel Coit Gilman helped raise the Sheffield Scientific School at Yale, ran the University of California, then opened Johns Hopkins in 1876 — an inauguration since called the beginning of postgraduate education in America.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote to his daughter for fifty years
narrative_blocks.body: The letters run from 1847 to 1899, most of them between him and his eldest, Caroline. They went to Yale out of Julia's estate with the Gilman and Coit family photographs.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the professor's youngest daughter
narrative_blocks.body: Julia Silliman was the last of the nine children born on Hillhouse Avenue, and they married in 1850. Five children followed: Caroline, Julia, Louise, Arthur and Henry.

narrative_blocks.header: Of all the children, she lasted longest
narrative_blocks.body: Born in Manhattan in 1884, she outlived her siblings and nearly everyone of her generation, reaching the age of one hundred and three.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped run America's great silk house
narrative_blocks.body: A director of Cheney Brothers, the Manchester silk manufacturer his family built, he graduated from Yale's Sheffield Scientific School in 1889.

narrative_blocks.header: He crossed the Pacific to grade world silk
narrative_blocks.body: In 1923 he went to Japan and China as vice chairman of a silk commission, and the next year helped draft the first international system for grading raw silk.

narrative_blocks.header: He soldiered in two wars, decades apart
narrative_blocks.body: He served with the Yale battalion in the Spanish-American War, then rode with Troop B of the First Connecticut Cavalry in the First World War.

narrative_blocks.header: His father came back from Antietam shot
narrative_blocks.body: Frank Woodbridge Cheney took a bullet through the elbow at the Lower Bridge in 1862 and spent the next forty years as the company's treasurer. Austin went into the same house and ran it on into the next century.

cross_connections.display_label: was his second cousin, of the same Cheney Brothers silk family

narrative_blocks.header: Pierponts on her side, Reynoldses on his
narrative_blocks.body: Ruth and her husband George were distant cousins, both descended from Thomas Hooker. Her line ran from his son Samuel through the Pierponts, Edwardses, Dwights and Bacons; George's ran from Samuel's sister Sarah through the Rawsons and a line of Boston physicians. Ruth stood ten generations from Hooker, George nine.

narrative_blocks.header: He and his father-in-law shared an infirmary
narrative_blocks.body: A Williams College physician, he served on the staff of the New York Eye and Ear Infirmary — the same hospital where his wife's father, Dr. Gorham Bacon, was a leading surgeon.

notable.notable_blurb: Author of The Chocolate Touch

narrative_blocks.header: He gave the world the Chocolate Touch
narrative_blocks.body: The 1952 classic — a boy whose lips turn everything to chocolate — became a children's perennial and grew into the John Midas series across four decades. His father, a Reuters man, had advised that writing was better than working; the memoir took the phrase for its title.

narrative_blocks.header: He married his editor's daughter
narrative_blocks.body: A Royal Canadian Air Force navigator turned Baltimore Sun reporter, he wed Susan Barnes Watson — daughter of the Sun's own Mark Watson — and the 1956 London posting changed both their lives. The marriage ended in 1960; along the way he interviewed Louis Armstrong and James Baldwin and befriended P.G. Wodehouse.

narrative_blocks.header: A hundred years, ending in west Cork
narrative_blocks.body: Ireland claimed him from 1971 — Castle Leslie first, then west Cork on his friend Wolf Mankowitz's advice — and he reviewed for the Irish Times into his nineties. He died at Bantry in January 2026, one hundred years old, survived by his partner of fifty years and four children of two marriages.

narrative_blocks.header: He rewrote what socialism was for
narrative_blocks.body: The Future of Socialism, written after losing his seat in 1955, argued the left should stop equating socialism with nationalization and aim instead at ending poverty and widening life's pleasures — total abstinence and a good filing system, he wrote, are not now the right signposts to utopia. It dominated Labour thinking for a generation.

narrative_blocks.header: A Plymouth Brethren boy jumped into Italy
narrative_blocks.body: Raised in the Exclusive Brethren — a faith he rejected and hated being reminded of — he went from Oxford into the Parachute Brigade, landing at Taranto in 1943 and gathering front-line intelligence at Monte Cassino. He came back a captain, took a First in twelve months, and won the Oxford Union presidency.

narrative_blocks.header: He took Kissinger to watch Grimsby Town
narrative_blocks.body: Education Secretary, Board of Trade, Environment, and at the last the Foreign Office — where he marked his first meeting with Henry Kissinger by taking him to Blundell Park for Grimsby against Gillingham. On his heart, he told his wife, they would find engraved fish and Rhodesia.

narrative_blocks.header: The most exciting friend of my life
narrative_blocks.body: Roy Jenkins's memoir gave him that title, remembering the camel-hair coat and the MG called the Red Menace; their Oxford intimacy — an exceedingly close and intense friendship, Crosland later called it — fills letters that still read warm nearly a century on. The two rose, rivaled, and cooled together across four decades of Labour politics.

narrative_blocks.header: He died with the Rhodesia paper unfinished
narrative_blocks.body: The stroke came at the Adderbury mill on a February Sunday in 1977, a détente speech half-drafted on his desk; six days of coma ended at Oxford, fifty-eight years old. His ashes went into the sea off Grimsby, from a trawler, as he and Susan had agreed.

narrative_blocks.body: Watertown-born, he went out with the Navy's construction battalions at twenty, building the Pacific war's bases. Home again, Nichols College and the Maryland Casualty Company led to an insurance agency of his own, which he ran for many years.

narrative_blocks.header: A lifetime measured in boats
narrative_blocks.body: It began on Lake Ontario, summers at the family cottage at Henderson Harbor, and carried through decades of exploring the Chesapeake's coves with Ellen and bareboating the Caribbean together. Fifty-nine years married, fifty of them in Cleveland Park, and years volunteering with Washington's auxiliary police.

narrative_blocks.header: He named the school for his dead wife
narrative_blocks.body: Jane Barham — the teacher-wife who shared his cause and died in 1827 — gave her name to the ground at Barhamville where his South Carolina Female Institute opened the next year. The four-year classical curriculum drew more than a hundred and twenty students by the 1850s.

narrative_blocks.header: His enslaved nurse shaped his faith
narrative_blocks.body: Born to a South Carolina family in 1790, he converted to Christianity early in life, influenced by the Methodist faith of the enslaved woman who nursed him. Medicine came at New York's College of Physicians and Surgeons, and practice beside the famous surgeon Valentine Mott.

narrative_blocks.header: Ninety-five years, ending at Oak Hill
narrative_blocks.body: Retired from Barhamville in 1861, he weathered the war and brought Julia and their daughter Edwina to Washington, publishing verse translations in the long evening of his life. He outlived Julia by eight years, dying in 1886 at ninety-five; Oak Hill holds them both.

narrative_blocks.header: France cited her to the nation
narrative_blocks.body: After her death the Council of Ministers ordered her name cited to the nation in the Journal Officiel — fifteen months under fire, two evacuations of women and children managed during retreats, then six years restoring 175,000 acres, two towns, and a hundred and twenty villages. She was the first woman ever elected to the French Academy of Agriculture.

narrative_blocks.header: A doctor remade a hundred villages
narrative_blocks.body: Edinburgh-born, briefly married to an MIT instructor and divorced by 1914, she joined Anne Morgan's committee as its working chair — dispensaries, milk stations, traveling canteens, a nurses' school, the whole framework of social life rebuilt and then handed to local committees to keep. The Croix de Guerre and the Legion of Honor followed; the Blérancourt museum opened the year after she died.

narrative_blocks.header: Two future in-laws raced for the Cup
narrative_blocks.body: In 1920 he skippered Vanitie against Charles Francis Adams's Resolute for the right to defend the America's Cup — Adams won the honor, and three years later Adams's daughter married the brother of Nichols's wife, folding the rival skippers into one family. In 1930 he tried again with Weetamoe, the Morgan syndicate sloop, beaten late by Vanderbilt's Enterprise.

narrative_blocks.header: The Goose swept three countries
narrative_blocks.body: His most famous boat took the Scandinavian Gold Cup in 1938, cleaned up in Finland and then Bermuda — and won the Gold Cup twice more in 1947 and 1948 under Briggs Cunningham's hand, still Nichols's boat. He had been Commodore of the New York Yacht Club, succeeding Vanderbilt, and chaired its racing-appeals committee for decades.

narrative_blocks.header: The swordsmith's daughter of Gion
narrative_blocks.body: Daughter of a samurai swordsmith, she trained as a Gion geisha and was called Kokyū no Sekka for performances on the bowed kokyū remembered as sublime. George Morgan saw her perform at the Miyako Odori in 1902 and courted her for two years.

narrative_blocks.header: Rejected in Newport, at home in Paris
narrative_blocks.body: Reported to the family as a bride of excellent lineage, she met rejection in America — the Newport visit cut short — and the couple made their life between Yokohama and Europe's capitals instead. Widowed at Seville in 1915, she spent two decades on the Riviera before returning to Japan in 1938.

narrative_blocks.header: Japan turned her scorn into a musical
narrative_blocks.body: The nationalist press of 1938 sneered at the Japanese who doesn't speak Japanese, and wartime police watched her — but a serial of her life ran an unprecedented two hundred sixty newspaper installments, a musical followed in 1951, and the Morgan family sought her out after the war to support her. Baptized Theresa in 1953 for her favorite saint, she died at Kyoto in 1963.

narrative_blocks.body: Nineteen years at the New York Federal Reserve — his 1927 Reserve Banks and the Money Market became the standard text — led to National City Bank's chairmanships, the presidency of the American Bankers Association, and Eisenhower's Treasury as undersecretary. In 1957 the President sent him to Paris as ambassador to NATO.

narrative_blocks.body: While Randolph sat at Treasury and then NATO, his elder brother Robert directed the United States Census Bureau — two schoolteacher's sons running federal institutions through the same administration.

narrative_blocks.body: The Columbia dissertation of 1920 was Trends of School Costs — an education statistician who became the money market's great explainer. His first wife, Dr. May Ayres, was a statistician too; his second, a Morgan granddaughter and Army lieutenant colonel.

bio.title: Rev.
bio.bio_blurb: Minister of Middletown; founding trustee of Yale

people.research_notes: Solo/orbit entry (father of I00144 Rev. William Russell). Orphaned at one; his New Haven house sold by order of the General Court to fund his Harvard education; published an Almanack 1684; Ipswich schoolmaster; 37 years minister at Middletown; a founding trustee of Yale (1701). NBs pending Fable draft.

narrative_blocks.header: Pulpit power in a merchant's town
narrative_blocks.body: Middletown's minister for twenty-five years, a framer of the Saybrook Platform that governed Connecticut's churches for a century, and a founder of Yale — he stood where the colony's clerical power concentrated, and married where its merchant power did, taking Capt. Giles Hamlin's daughter Mary in 1690. His son's marriage to a Pierpont a generation later joined the College's two founding houses.

narrative_blocks.header: The Court sold his house for Harvard
narrative_blocks.body: Orphaned at about a year old, he was devoted to God in the way of learning by his dying father's will — and in 1677 the Connecticut General Court ordered his New Haven house and land sold to keep him at college, judging him likely to prove a useful instrument in the work of God. The Widow Osborn paid in hides, thirty-two a year, shipped to Boston.

narrative_blocks.header: He printed an almanack at twenty-four
narrative_blocks.body: His Cambridge years left a diary — cataloguing the College Library's double books, carrying his Almanack to the press in January 1684 — and an Ipswich schoolmastership before Middletown ordained him in October 1688. Maj. Talcott of Hartford had tried first, recruiting him for Waterbury; he answered negatively.

narrative_blocks.header: The disease he caught became his whole subject
narrative_blocks.body: He was interning at a New York hospital when the first signs of pulmonary tuberculosis appeared. They faded, and in the February of 1881 he took a commission in the Army Medical Corps and went to Fort Yates in Dakota; seventeen years of frontier posts and outdoor work held it latent. Then the Spanish war put him behind a desk in Washington and it came back for good.

narrative_blocks.header: He learned the cure as a patient
narrative_blocks.body: Invalided out in 1898, he went to Asheville and put himself under Charles Minor — and learned from his own physician how the disease was treated. Six years later the Army handed him its tuberculosis hospital at Fort Bayard in New Mexico and he brought Trudeau's system to it. He commanded there nearly fourteen years.

narrative_blocks.header: He staffed his lab with fellow patients
narrative_blocks.body: The Army rotated its officers, which kept Fort Bayard from ever becoming a research centre. So he built his team out of men who had the disease themselves — officers the service could not send anywhere else — and taught them the work.

narrative_blocks.header: He argued everyone caught it as a child
narrative_blocks.body: He was among the first to hold that the primary infection came in infancy or childhood, that everything after was reinfection from within, and that a healthy adult practically never took it from outside. He fought the use of tuberculin as a diagnostic test and got it stopped in Army practice.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight hospitals and a standard chest examination
narrative_blocks.body: With the war coming in 1917 he saw the Army would have to examine enormous numbers of men fast, and worked out a standard method of chest examination for it. Eight hospitals went up on his plan, with room for eight thousand patients. He passed retirement age that September and they kept him on anyway.

narrative_blocks.body: In 1947 Elizabeth and Rush Sturges handed 55 Power Street to Brown University in memory of her father, a Brown graduate. Since 1949 it has been the official residence of the university's president, and every one of them has lived there.

narrative_blocks.header: She hired a senator's son to build it
narrative_blocks.body: The 1922 house on Power Street was designed by William T. Aldrich, son of Senator Nelson Aldrich and brother of Abby Aldrich Rockefeller, who had trained at the Beaux-Arts in Paris. Beatrix Farrand laid out the walled garden on its east and south sides.

narrative_blocks.header: Her sister-in-law's brother built the summer house
narrative_blocks.body: For the 1933 stone manor at Wakefield the Sturgeses hired the Philadelphia architect Thomas Pym Cope, whose sister Anne had married Elizabeth's brother Thomas Pierrepont Hazard. Farrand designed those gardens too, and they retired there in 1942.

narrative_blocks.header: Five generations of Hazards spun the family wool
narrative_blocks.body: Her great-great-grandfather Rowland Hazard bought half a fulling mill on the Saugatucket in 1802, and the family turned it into the Peace Dale Manufacturing Company. Her great-grandfather ran the looms by day and wrote philosophy by night, trading letters with John Stuart Mill.

narrative_blocks.header: Her cook stayed with the family for years
narrative_blocks.body: The Sturges household at 55 Power Street ran on domestic servants, most of them women who had emigrated from Ireland. Their cook, Margaret Sullivan, stayed with the family many years.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped find a predicted antimatter particle
narrative_blocks.body: In 1962 he was among the physicists who discovered the anti-XI-minus, one of the last antimatter particles theory had predicted but no one had yet seen. The finding helped confirm the deep symmetry between matter and its mirror-image antimatter.

narrative_blocks.header: He learned physics from Enrico Fermi
narrative_blocks.body: He took his doctorate at Chicago under Enrico Fermi, and early on he built one of the first systems to let computers read the tangled particle tracks in bubble-chamber photographs. It was pioneering work in handing raw physics data over to machines.

narrative_blocks.header: He steered Yale College through hard years
narrative_blocks.body: Beyond the lab he served as master of Davenport College and then, from 1971 to 1979, as dean of Yale College through a period of real institutional strain. Colleagues credited him with steady, far-sighted leadership when the university most needed it.

narrative_blocks.header: A heart attack took him at his desk
narrative_blocks.body: At fifty-seven he suffered a fatal heart attack while working in his office at Yale's Josiah Willard Gibbs physics laboratory. He was still teaching and still chasing a particle called the tau-neutrino at the time.

narrative_blocks.header: For two months he ran the Pentagon
narrative_blocks.body: He spent the 1980s as the Defense Department's top lawyer and then its deputy secretary, and when the Senate rejected George H. W. Bush's first nominee, he served as acting Secretary of Defense for two months in early 1989. He was the third in his family to head a military department as a civilian, after his great-grandfather the president and his great-great-grandfather Alphonso Taft.

narrative_blocks.header: He began as one of Nader's Raiders
narrative_blocks.body: Fresh from Harvard Law, he joined Ralph Nader's team probing the Federal Trade Commission, and his work so impressed the incoming FTC chairman, Caspar Weinberger, that Weinberger hired him. It began a decades-long partnership; he followed Weinberger through the budget office, the welfare department, and finally the Pentagon.

narrative_blocks.header: He warned against suspending the Geneva Conventions
narrative_blocks.body: As the State Department's legal adviser after the September 11 attacks, he argued in a 2002 memo that the president could not suspend U.S. obligations under the Geneva Conventions and called the contrary case legally flawed and impossible. He and Secretary Colin Powell lost the internal fight, but he later co-signed a warning that redefining the conventions endangered American troops.

narrative_blocks.header: A lifelong Republican who broke with his party
narrative_blocks.body: From a dynasty of Republican leaders — a senator father, a president grandfather — he served Republican administrations for four decades. In 2016 and again in 2020 he publicly refused to back Donald Trump, joining scores of former Republican national-security officials to endorse the Democratic nominee instead.

narrative_blocks.body: However far her missions carried her — Ethiopia, Bangladesh, Armenia — she made it home for Christmas without fail, and asked her children to give their toys to children caught in the disasters she worked. The relief work and the family ran together, not apart.

narrative_blocks.header: The fourth Taft generation to hold high office
narrative_blocks.body: He was elected the 67th governor of Ohio in 1998, extending a dynasty that ran back through a senator father, a senate-leader grandfather, and a president great-grandfather. His two terms in Columbus made him the fourth straight Taft generation to hold major office.

narrative_blocks.header: He bet a billion on Ohio's high-tech future
narrative_blocks.body: His signature Third Frontier program poured hundreds of millions into biomedical, alternative-energy, and advanced research to modernize the state's aging industrial economy. By 2008 it was credited with billions of dollars in economic impact and tens of thousands of jobs.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught in Tanzania before he entered politics
narrative_blocks.body: Between college and law school he spent two years as a Peace Corps volunteer teaching in Tanzania. Four decades later, as a former governor, he returned and found the buildings where he had taught and lived still standing.

narrative_blocks.header: A gift-disclosure scandal shadowed his second term
narrative_blocks.body: In 2005, as the Coingate investment scandal engulfed his administration, he was charged with four misdemeanors for failing to report golf outings and gifts from lobbyists. He pleaded no contest and apologized to the state, closing an otherwise unblemished thirty-year public career — the first Ohio governor charged while in office, though for lapses in disclosure rather than corruption.

narrative_blocks.header: He later turned against the executions he oversaw
narrative_blocks.body: As governor he presided over the return of the death penalty to Ohio, and twenty-four people were executed during his terms. Years later, out of office, he co-wrote an op-ed with two former state attorneys general urging Ohio to abolish capital punishment.

cross_connections.display_label: served as Ohio's 36th governor

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the family's broadcasting empire
narrative_blocks.body: After his father died in 1967 he rose to run Taft Broadcasting, steering it through its theme-park era — the years it opened Kings Island — and its Hollywood holdings around Hanna-Barbera. He led the company as president and chief executive.

narrative_blocks.header: He bid to keep the company in Cincinnati
narrative_blocks.body: Pushed out of the CEO's chair in 1986 as outside investors moved to break up Taft Broadcasting, he answered in 1987 with a $1.34 billion cash bid to buy the firm and keep it rooted in Cincinnati. The bid failed, and he was the last Taft to run the family company.

narrative_blocks.header: His boardrooms ran from newspapers to power companies
narrative_blocks.body: Beyond broadcasting he became one of Cincinnati's most connected corporate directors, sitting on the boards of the Tribune Company, Duke Energy, Fifth Third Bancorp, and Cinergy. Trained in law at Yale and Virginia, he made his mark in boardrooms rather than courtrooms.

narrative_blocks.header: The Taft who chose blues rock over politics
narrative_blocks.body: Born into the political and broadcasting dynasty, he ran hard the other way — into a guitar. After stints in the Seattle grunge bands Sweet Water and Second Coming, he built a solo career in blues rock, touring Europe and drawing a 2017 nomination for best guitarist at the European Blues Awards.

narrative_blocks.header: His prep-school band held two future Phish members
narrative_blocks.body: At the Taft School he started his first band, Space Antelope, alongside two classmates who would go on to found Phish — guitarist Trey Anastasio and drummer Jon Fishman. The three even busked together through Europe.

narrative_blocks.header: His song surfaced in a horror blockbuster
narrative_blocks.body: A song he co-wrote for Second Coming, 'Unknown Rider,' landed in M. Night Shyamalan's 1999 thriller The Sixth Sense, playing under a pivotal scene. The soundtrack credit reached a wider audience than the band's own records had.

narrative_blocks.header: He came home and bought Frampton's old studio
narrative_blocks.body: In 2013 he returned to Cincinnati a self-styled prodigal son, buying a home and recording studio that had once belonged to Peter Frampton. There he now cuts his blues-rock records and plays low-key hometown shows, close to the family roots he had once fled.

narrative_blocks.header: He built a home for the aged poor
narrative_blocks.body: In 1887 he founded and endowed the Field Home for the aged and infirm at Cortlandt Manor, in his mother's memory, and gave the town of Peekskill its public library as another tribute to her. Both still carry the family's name.

narrative_blocks.header: He turned his home into a Christian center
narrative_blocks.body: Deeply religious, he and his wife Virginia — known as 'Nina and Cort' — made their home a center of Christian life, hosting conferences, Bible studies, and fellowship and backing her Hephzibah House ministry. He founded St. Catharine's Church in 1888.

narrative_blocks.header: His father led the New-York Historical Society
narrative_blocks.body: He inherited both a fortune and a calling from his father, Benjamin Hazard Field — a merchant who presided over the New-York Historical Society, drove the building of its fireproof home, and served as a trustee of the American Museum of Natural History. Charity ran deep in the family.

narrative_blocks.header: At eighteen he became his uncle's partner
narrative_blocks.body: He joined his uncle Hickson Field's Manhattan importing house as a partner at eighteen, took over the whole business when his uncle retired in 1838, and won 'both fortune and fame' before retiring himself in 1875. His son Cortlandt carried the firm on under a new name.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded a hospital and led two societies
narrative_blocks.body: In retirement he gave himself to charity, founding the Home for Incurables in the Bronx in 1866 as its first president, and later presiding over both the Saint Nicholas Society and the New-York Historical Society. He drove the building of the Historical Society's fireproof home.

narrative_blocks.header: He put Farragut's statue in Madison Square
narrative_blocks.body: He was largely responsible for the Admiral Farragut monument in Madison Square Park — the bronze by Augustus Saint-Gaudens on a pedestal designed by Stanford White, a landmark of American public sculpture.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandson became a pioneer balloonist
narrative_blocks.body: He married Catherine de Peyster, of an old Knickerbocker family, in 1838; their son Cortlandt inherited both the business and the charitable habit. Through their daughter Florence came a grandson, Cortlandt Field Bishop, a pioneer aviator and balloonist.

narrative_blocks.header: She joined two of old New York's dynasties
narrative_blocks.body: She was born a de Peyster and a Van Cortlandt, two of the oldest Dutch families of colonial New York, the daughter of Frederic de Peyster. In 1838 she married the merchant Benjamin Hazard Field.

narrative_blocks.header: She raised a family on Madison Square
narrative_blocks.body: She and Benjamin lived on the northern edge of Madison Square Park and raised two children — Cortlandt, who carried on the family firm and charities, and Florence, who married into the Wolfe fortune. Her son later built the Field Home for the aged in her memory.

narrative_blocks.header: A New York lawyer who fought for Britain
narrative_blocks.body: Columbia-trained and admitted to the New York bar in 1891, he began as a captain in New York's own First Regiment. Drawn to England, he took a commission with the Hampshire Carabiniers and served with the British Expeditionary Force through the First World War.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother's gift set him up at Maizefield
narrative_blocks.body: When he married Katharine Livingston in 1900, his mother gave the couple Maizefield, the Dutchess County manor she had bought for them. By 1924 he had moved the family for good to Appleton Manor in Oxfordshire, a life lived on both sides of the Atlantic.

narrative_blocks.header: He watched the British army for Washington
narrative_blocks.body: In 1903 the United States sent him as a military attaché to observe the British army's maneuvers — a role that suited a New Yorker already at home in England. It was a foretaste of the British soldiering he would take up in earnest a decade later.

bio.bio_blurb: British Army officer who held Calais

narrative_blocks.header: The eldest son soldiered across the Empire
narrative_blocks.body: Sent from New York to England as a boy, he trained at Eton and Sandhurst and spent two decades as a British Army officer — in Ireland, India, and Palestine. By 1940 he was a major, second-in-command of the Queen Victoria's Rifles.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped hold Calais to save Dunkirk
narrative_blocks.body: In May 1940 his outgunned battalion was thrown into the defense of Calais against a German armored assault. They held the town for days — buying time for the Dunkirk evacuation — until it fell and he was taken prisoner; he was later mentioned in dispatches for gallantry there.

narrative_blocks.header: He spent five years in German captivity
narrative_blocks.body: The next five years passed in German prison and reprisal camps, his rank frozen while Sandhurst classmates rose to general; he retired in 1948 an honorary lieutenant colonel. His report on the siege of Calais, lost to the Russian archives, came back to the family only in 1997.

narrative_blocks.header: He drowned visiting his brother in South Africa
narrative_blocks.body: In March 1965, on a trip to South Africa to see his brother Robert, he drowned at Knysna at the age of sixty-four. He had survived Calais and five years a prisoner, only to die on a family visit.

narrative_blocks.header: She chose the stage over a duke's son
narrative_blocks.body: Groomed to marry the Duke of Marlborough's heir and presented at court at nineteen, she wanted none of it. She trained instead as an actress and performed at the Oxford Playhouse under the name Katherine Livingston.

narrative_blocks.header: Her fluent Russian drew Cold War surveillance
narrative_blocks.body: In Paris she learned Russian from the White émigrés who had fled the Revolution — so fluently that decades later, during the Cold War, the police kept her under watch. She spoke French too, and roamed between Paris, Florence, and London.

narrative_blocks.header: She watched Hitler speak and thought him deluded
narrative_blocks.body: Living in Mussolini's Italy she admired his drive to modernize; visiting a cousin in Germany, she heard Adolf Hitler give a speech and came away thinking him somewhat deluded. She had a front-row view of the dictators of her age.

narrative_blocks.header: She lectured the House of Lords in person
narrative_blocks.body: Confident and outspoken, she would turn up at the House of Lords to tell the peers when she thought politics had gone wrong. She was also a published poet, with verse in print by twenty-seven, and lived her long life unmarried.

narrative_blocks.header: An Eton physics prize, then Wall Street
narrative_blocks.body: Raised in England on the grounds of Blenheim Palace, he won the Eton physics prize and graduated Harvard Phi Beta Kappa in physics. Then he turned from science to Wall Street, rising to managing partner of a brokerage and founding his own investment bank.

narrative_blocks.header: He married an heiress, then a duchess
narrative_blocks.body: His first wife was a brokerage heiress; his second, Louise Clews, was the former Duchess of Argyll, who gave up the title to marry him and kept their Hudson River estate when they parted. His third wife, Hilles Morris, was the widow of his cousin Louis Hamersley.

narrative_blocks.header: He flew as a wartime radar officer
narrative_blocks.body: In the Second World War he served as a major in the Army Air Corps, a radar officer with the First Fighter Command who joined a Joint Chiefs mission to the Southwest Pacific. Physics found a use after all.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother drowned as they swam together
narrative_blocks.body: In 1964 his brother Theodore, visiting from England, drowned while the two were swimming together — a tragedy that shadowed his later years. He ended his days at Southampton on Long Island and lies buried near Clermont, beside his father and grandfather.

narrative_blocks.header: Her Red Cross post found her captured brother
narrative_blocks.body: In the war she worked for the Red Cross at the office that tracked wounded, missing, and captured British soldiers. When her brother Theodore was feared killed at Calais, she used her post to discover he had been taken prisoner, and carried the news to the family.

narrative_blocks.header: She ran a tea plantation in Kenya
narrative_blocks.body: After marrying a Swiss Huguenot she met in a wartime hospital, she moved to Kenya and ran a tea plantation in the White Highlands. She and her daughter learned Kiswahili and grew devoted to the land and its people.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept a pistol in the soap dish
narrative_blocks.body: Through the Mau Mau uprising of the 1950s she kept a loaded pistol always within reach — even setting it in the soap dish while she bathed. She held her nerve through years of danger on the farm.

narrative_blocks.header: Three countries forced her to start over
narrative_blocks.body: Kenyan independence cost her the plantation, then a cattle farm; upheaval in Rhodesia drove her on again, until she settled at last in South Africa. Each time she rebuilt — a market garden, then a share in a Victorian hotel she helped run near Cape Town.

narrative_blocks.header: Unqualified, she served as the chapel's pastor
narrative_blocks.body: In her Karoo village she stepped in, untrained, as pastor of the local chapel, and kept up her passions for gardening, world affairs, and cricket to the end. Every year she mailed the family Christmas cards bright with African landscapes and wildlife.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran 106 miles on a bet
narrative_blocks.body: At Cambridge in 1936 he ran from the university to London and back — 106 miles in twenty-three hours and two minutes — winning bets worth some £250. His last refreshment along the way was an iced orange squash.

narrative_blocks.header: He raided behind Rommel's lines in the desert
narrative_blocks.body: A Scots Guards captain, he volunteered for the Long Range Desert Group, whose small patrols ranged hundreds of miles behind German and Italian lines to watch and raid. He fractured his skull when his jeep dropped off a dune, and his soldier-servant was left paralyzed.

narrative_blocks.header: He posed as a German officer to escape
narrative_blocks.body: Caught in a camp of Bedouin allied to the Germans, he used the fluent German his childhood nurse had given him to pass himself off as a German officer and avoid capture. Another night, spotted by a German column, he slipped away through a wadi and returned the next day to rescue a separated comrade.

narrative_blocks.header: Twice wounded, he wrote the desert war down
narrative_blocks.body: Back with the Scots Guards he was wounded at Salerno and again at Monte Camino, where a shell left his right arm nearly useless and sent him to six months in hospital. For his service he received the Military Cross, and later set his desert war down in a memoir, In Rommel's Backyard.

narrative_blocks.header: An American artist's daughter became a duchess
narrative_blocks.body: Born in Paris to the American sculptor Henry Clews Jr. and a descendant of James Madison, she married into the Scottish peerage. As the wife of the eleventh Duke of Argyll she reigned at Inveraray Castle until their 1954 divorce.

narrative_blocks.header: She ran wartime relief flights from Lisbon
narrative_blocks.body: While her husband the future duke sat in a German prison camp, she based herself in neutral Lisbon and organized relief flights, enlisting civilian pilot friends to fly supplies. It was the boldest chapter of a well-connected life.

narrative_blocks.header: Three marriages, and a title given up
narrative_blocks.body: After a first marriage at eighteen ended in divorce, she wed the Duke of Argyll, then in 1954 married the American banker Robert Timpson — surrendering her ducal title to do so. She kept their Hudson River estate, Grasmere, when that marriage too came apart.

narrative_blocks.body: Known for a gay and charming manner, she married Theodore in 1928 and raised two children with him. When he came home worn from five years in German captivity, she nursed him back to health on an English farm.

narrative_blocks.body: Harvard-trained with an MBA, he spent two decades climbing the ranks at the First National Bank of Boston, from investment officer to senior vice president, and in 1984 became head of treasury at the Bank of Boston. Marquis Who's Who named him a noteworthy banker.

narrative_blocks.header: He flew for the RAF before banking
narrative_blocks.body: Born in London, Theodore's son served as a pilot officer in the Royal Air Force in the early 1950s before crossing to America for Harvard and a Boston banking career. Like his father, he kept a foot on each side of the Atlantic.

narrative_blocks.body: She was the daughter of Sir George Houstoun-Boswall, fourth baronet of Blackadder, a Grenadier Guards officer who fought in the Boer War and was killed in action in 1915, months after her birth. She grew up a Scottish baronet's fatherless daughter.

narrative_blocks.header: A Montreal shipping fortune ran in her blood
narrative_blocks.body: Through her mother she was a great-granddaughter of Sir Hugh Allan, the Montreal magnate who built one of the great Atlantic steamship lines of the Victorian age. She married John Alastair Timpson in 1940, joining two transatlantic families.

notable.notable_blurb: Zoologist, marine biologist, and poet

narrative_blocks.header: Her memoir on living matter won worldwide fame
narrative_blocks.body: A Bryn Mawr-trained zoologist, she published in 1897 a classic memoir, The Living Substance as Such and as Organism, exploring the structure and behavior of protoplasm. It drew admiration from biologists around the world and was later called a work of genius.

narrative_blocks.header: She studied biology from Bryn Mawr to Roscoff
narrative_blocks.body: The daughter of a Philadelphia lawyer and paleontologist, she trained at Bryn Mawr, the University of Pennsylvania, and the marine laboratories of Woods Hole and Roscoff in France. She was a gracious figure in the Woods Hole scientific circle of the early 1890s.

narrative_blocks.header: She published her poems under a man's name
narrative_blocks.body: The zoologist was also a poet, writing under the male pseudonym Richard De Veaux. After her death her husband gathered her verse into a two-volume set published under that name.

narrative_blocks.header: Her comic ode to Theodore Rooster-velt
narrative_blocks.body: In October 1912, in the Bull Moose campaign, Gwendolen signed and dated every page of a fourteen-stanza carbon-copy poem about Theodore Roosevelt, hailing him as great at magnification and prone to amplification. She wrote on its title page that the original had been stolen from her papers more than once, she believed to keep it from counting in an election.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father dug up America's first dinosaur
narrative_blocks.body: She grew up the daughter of William Parker Foulke, the Philadelphia scholar who in 1858 unearthed the Hadrosaurus at Haddonfield — the first nearly complete dinosaur skeleton found in North America. Science ran in the family before she made it her own.

narrative_blocks.header: His father studied ants; he chose bees
narrative_blocks.body: Raised in a zoologist's household, he became a naturalist like his father — but where the elder Andrews made ants his subject, the son became an authority on bees. Natural history ran in the family.

narrative_blocks.header: He cleared a wasp swarm blocking TV reception
narrative_blocks.body: In one memorable job he removed a great swarm of wasps that had settled atop the bat-wing television antenna of Baltimore's Mathieson building, where they had been interfering with reception. Insects were both his study and his trade.

narrative_blocks.header: His hobbies were birds and photography
narrative_blocks.body: Away from bees and wasps he was a keen birdwatcher, a member of the Maryland Ornithological Society, and one of the first members of the Baltimore Camera Club. The naturalist's eye followed him into his leisure.

notable.notable_blurb: Abolitionist Union general

narrative_blocks.header: He raised Black troops before the Union would
narrative_blocks.body: In 1862, commanding a camp near New Orleans crowded with fugitive slaves, he organized the first Black soldiers in Union service — a year before the government would arm them. When his superior refused them weapons, he resigned in protest, and the Confederacy declared him an outlaw for arming enslaved men against their masters.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran for president on an anti-Masonic ticket
narrative_blocks.body: After the war he took up two crusades — against slavery's legacy and against the Masonic order — and in 1880 ran for president as the Anti-Masonic Party's candidate. The ticket drew barely a thousand votes, but it fit a life of stubborn, unpopular conviction.

narrative_blocks.header: A West Point soldier through four wars
narrative_blocks.body: West Point trained him, and for over two decades he soldiered through the Seminole wars, the Mexican War, and the Utah expedition against the Mormons before the Civil War made him a brigadier general. The army became, for him, a tool for the moral causes he championed.

narrative_blocks.header: He married at sixty-nine and turned to letters
narrative_blocks.body: He did not marry until he was sixty-nine, wedding a widow half his age in 1883. In retirement at Guilford, Vermont, he became a scholar and linguist, translating French histories and helping lead the state's historical society.

narrative_blocks.body: Her father, Frederic W. Tilton, was for a time principal of Phillips Academy in Andover — where her future husband, Frederick Atherton, had been a schoolboy. They married in 1911 and made their life in Washington society.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a Navy captain in 1860
narrative_blocks.body: Ellen married Capt. Charles Kennedy of North Carolina on 18 February 1860, as his second wife. Their only child, Theodore, was born at Norfolk, Virginia, in 1866, where Charles had become a merchant after the war.

narrative_blocks.header: A tea house in a general's home
narrative_blocks.body: After retiring early from the law he and his wife ran a tea house at East Haddam, in the old home of General Champion of the Revolution. Dainty lunches and afternoon teas drew a steady clientele.

burial.plot_notes: Grove Street Cemetery, New Haven CT

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve of four thousand pictures won first
narrative_blocks.body: At the 1896 Paris Salon, four thousand works were entered and twelve took first place — three of the twelve were her miniatures. The Salon made her an associate soon after, an honor most painters wait until middle age for, if it comes at all.

narrative_blocks.header: Among four women to earn Yale's art degree
narrative_blocks.body: Of the twenty-eight bachelor of fine arts degrees Yale awarded between 1891 and 1913, only four went to women. Hers came in 1903, more than twenty years after she first studied there.

narrative_blocks.header: She painted a future president's mother
narrative_blocks.body: Among her early miniatures was a portrait of Sara Roosevelt, whose son Franklin would enter the White House three decades later. A critic called her 'our American Kauffman,' after the great neoclassical painter.

narrative_blocks.header: Her studio sat above Carnegie Hall
narrative_blocks.body: From 1898 she worked in the Carnegie Hall Studios, among the first artists in the skylit warren built above the concert hall. Before that a Paris chalet near the Rue de Vaugirard held her studio, hung with old silks and antique silver.

narrative_blocks.header: She loved a sculptor's Berkshire studio
narrative_blocks.body: A horticulturalist by devotion, she gave her affection to Chesterwood — the Massachusetts studio and gardens of Daniel Chester French, who carved the seated Lincoln. Her son later sat on the council that preserved it.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran The New Yorker, then invented Fortune
narrative_blocks.body: He trained as a mining engineer and worked in California, Arizona and Mexico before going to New York at twenty-two to write. Within three years he was managing editor of the young New Yorker, and within ten he had devised the formula for Fortune and was running Henry Luce's whole company.

narrative_blocks.header: He turned down Luce's million to start PM
narrative_blocks.body: Henry Luce offered him a million dollars in stock to stay five more years at Time. He refused, raised his own money, and in 1940 launched PM, a New York daily that carried no advertising so that it would answer to no one.

narrative_blocks.header: He walked out when PM took ads
narrative_blocks.body: In November 1946 Marshall Field, who had bought out PM's other backers to keep the paper alive, announced that it would start carrying advertising. Ralph quit. Two years later PM was folded into a succession of other papers, all of which eventually died.

narrative_blocks.header: Harold Ross spilled an inkwell on his suit
narrative_blocks.body: Interviewing at the young New Yorker, he watched Harold Ross tip an inkwell over his new pale suit; embarrassed, Ross hired him. On the way out he heard Ross mutter to his secretary, I hire anybody. He held the magazine together through its first five years.

narrative_blocks.header: He dreamed up the Ghost Army
narrative_blocks.body: Working on strategic deception in London before the invasion, he proposed a unit that could impersonate whole divisions with inflatable tanks and sound trucks. He called the men his con artists, and the idea his only original contribution to his country's armed forces.

narrative_blocks.header: Hemingway started calling him Ingersnake
narrative_blocks.body: He fished and drank with Ernest Hemingway in Key West and was hugged for landing his first sailfish. A quarrel over a film soured it, and Hemingway took to calling him Ingersnake behind his back.

narrative_blocks.header: His son bought his papers and stopped speaking
narrative_blocks.body: The newspaper chain he founded in 1957 grew profitable enough that in 1982 his son purchased it out from under him, in a deal bitter enough that the two never spoke again.

narrative_blocks.header: She died weeks after her last child's birth
narrative_blocks.body: She bore the tanner Zadock Pratt three children, the last a daughter born in January 1834. Two weeks later she was dead of the birth, at twenty-eight, and the infant girl followed her within months.

narrative_blocks.header: The only wife to give Zadock Pratt children
narrative_blocks.body: Pratt married five times, twice to pairs of sisters — two Dickermans lost to consumption, then Abigail and her sister Mary Watson. Of all five wives, only Abigail bore him children, the three who carried his line on.

narrative_blocks.header: She died giving birth to Ian
narrative_blocks.body: Elaine married Ralph Ingersoll in 1945, and their two sons came in quick succession. She died in 1948 giving birth to the second, Ian, while her husband's newspaper PM was failing.

narrative_blocks.header: He took his boy along on hospital rounds
narrative_blocks.body: A noted Boston surgeon, he brought his youngest son with him on rounds — an education in purpose and responsibility that the boy carried into a long life of service.

narrative_blocks.header: He listed 'volunteer' as his occupation
narrative_blocks.body: Retiring at seventy-five from four decades in Boston banking, he gave the rest of his life to the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and called volunteering there one of the most rewarding experiences of his life. He was privileged, he said, to listen to patients' stories.

narrative_blocks.header: He offered his house to a stranger
narrative_blocks.body: On impulse he told a patient in a clinical trial to come stay with them, then explained it to his wife over dinner. For years afterward their home took in patients, fellows, and researchers; he later helped found Boston's Hope Lodge for the same purpose.

narrative_blocks.header: He sailed The 7 C's to national titles
narrative_blocks.body: An accomplished sailor on Buzzards Bay, he captained a boat named The 7 C's to several Bullseye national championships in the late 1960s. Summers at Wareham ran on sailing, clamming, and Winnie-the-Pooh.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother turned Quaker and preached the world
narrative_blocks.body: The Revolution stripped his father's estates from an old noble family of Limoges. He rose to serve Napoleon as a treasurer of France; his younger brother Etienne fled to America, became a Quaker, and preached across two continents as Stephen Grellet.

narrative_blocks.header: Cholera took him; the sea took his body
narrative_blocks.body: Sailing from New York for Portland aboard the schooner Advance, he fell ill with cholera near Brookhaven on the Sound and died. He was buried at sea.

burial.plot_notes: Center Church on the Green Churchyard, New Haven CT

narrative_blocks.header: Her uncle sold the King's stamps
narrative_blocks.body: Jared Ingersoll took Connecticut's stamp distributorship, and five hundred horsemen on the Wethersfield road made him give it up. Her father, a chaplain, swore the Freeman's Oath for the American side. Her husband stayed neutral between them, and Farmington never trusted him again.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brother became lieutenant governor
narrative_blocks.body: Her uncle Jared took the King's stamp distributorship and five hundred horsemen ran him off the Wethersfield road for it; his son signed the Constitution at Philadelphia. Her brother Jonathan sat as lieutenant governor of Connecticut. His son went to Congress and on to Russia as minister, and his grandson took the governorship.

narrative_blocks.header: The last of Joseph Reed Ingersoll's children
narrative_blocks.body: Her brothers James and Joseph died in early childhood, in 1820 and 1825; she alone reached adulthood. She never married, and died in 1842, eleven years after her mother. Her father outlived her by twenty-six years, and the line ended with her.

narrative_blocks.header: He entered the asylum in 1859 and stayed
narrative_blocks.body: In November 1859 he was admitted to the Pennsylvania Hospital for the Insane. He was still there thirty years later, when he died at eighty-two. The family remembered only that he spent most of a long life inside.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried his grandfather's whole name
narrative_blocks.body: Alexander Wilcocks was a Philadelphia lawyer and the city's Recorder, six years dead before this grandson was born. The name went to the second son.

cross_connections.display_label: was his grandfather, Philadelphia's Recorder, whose name he carried

naming_inspiration.description: Named for his maternal grandfather Alexander Wilcocks (X03237), Philadelphia lawyer and city Recorder, six years dead before the boy was born.

narrative_blocks.header: He left Philadelphia for the cotton trade
narrative_blocks.body: In the 1830s he set up as a commission merchant and cotton broker in New Orleans and Natchez. By the late 1840s he had assembled Ingleside, two thousand acres on the Yazoo River. The papers called him a scientific planter.

narrative_blocks.header: He enslaved ninety-four people at Ingleside
narrative_blocks.body: The 1860 slave schedule lists ninety-four people held on the Ingersoll estate — forty male, fifty-four female, from one year old to fifty-eight. None of them are named. The census valued them at a hundred and ten thousand dollars, more than it valued the land.

narrative_blocks.header: The railroad crossed his land, named it Eden
narrative_blocks.body: In the 1880s the Yazoo & Mississippi Valley ran its line straight across the old Ingersoll estate. The right-of-way came so easily, the story went, that the railroad men decided they had found paradise. Eden, Mississippi was incorporated in 1890.

narrative_blocks.header: His son served the Confederacy as a surgeon
narrative_blocks.body: Charles Jared Ingersoll took his medical degree at Jefferson in 1858 and passed the Confederate army's board of examination five years later. He served as an assistant surgeon across Mississippi, Alabama, Tennessee, and Georgia. The Philadelphia cousins kept a photograph of him in uniform.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Yazoo County, Mississippi

narrative_blocks.header: His father brought the body home from Rome
narrative_blocks.body: He died in Italy, unmarried and prosperous. Charles Jared Ingersoll wrote out in his own hand the account of fetching his son's body back across the Atlantic and burying it at the Woodlands.

narrative_blocks.header: On Sundays she went to church without him
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband stayed home. Not irreligious, the diary insists — simply not a churchgoer. She took their son every Sunday.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept the house on her family's charity
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband's money went into a Maryland plantation and never came back. By the end they were living at Forest Hill on what the Ingersolls gave them.

narrative_blocks.header: She married and died on May 28
narrative_blocks.body: She married Sidney George Fisher on May 28, 1851. She died on May 28, 1872 — twenty-one years to the day, and ten months after him.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Earleville, MD

narrative_blocks.header: He passed the bar and never practiced
narrative_blocks.body: Penn in 1835, the bar in 1838, and then no practice at all. He wrote about the law instead — habeas corpus, grand juries, and other men's treatises edited for the American trade.

narrative_blocks.header: In the war his sympathies ran south
narrative_blocks.body: Philadelphia lampooned him as a Copperhead. In 1862, with the city at war, he published Personal Liberty and Martial Law against the suspension of habeas corpus.

narrative_blocks.header: Three brothers took the South's side
narrative_blocks.body: Edward, Charles, and Harry were all counted Copperheads, and Harry removed himself to London until the fighting stopped. A fourth brother, John, was planting cotton on the Yazoo with ninety-four people held on his land.

narrative_blocks.header: A mob came for him after Lincoln died
narrative_blocks.body: In the days after the assassination he made anti-administration speeches in the street. The Philadelphia police pulled him out of the crowd and locked him up overnight. He was released the next morning.

narrative_blocks.header: The Supreme Court cited the book he wrote
narrative_blocks.body: His History and Law of Habeas Corpus appeared in 1849, thirteen years before he argued against Lincoln's suspension of it. The Court was still citing it as authority generations afterward.

narrative_blocks.header: He resigned the club and left the law
narrative_blocks.body: The Union League was founded in his brother-in-law's parlor on Walnut Street, and Philadelphia was choosing sides. Under public pressure Edward resigned from the Philadelphia Club and gave up practice, retiring to Germantown — his large family, a few friends, wide reading, and old legal treatises to edit. The war was never mentioned in that house.

narrative_blocks.header: She married the doctor and died at thirty-four
narrative_blocks.body: John Forsyth Meigs was a Philadelphia physician who helped make pediatrics a field. She died in 1856 — six years before Union men gathered in his parlor to found the Union League.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventy volumes, kept for thirty-seven years
narrative_blocks.body: He filled seventy volumes with Philadelphia — dinners, funerals, street talk, treason arrests. He judged everyone, his own family included, and the diary outlived them all.

narrative_blocks.header: He called the Weeping Time a monstrous thing
narrative_blocks.body: In 1859 his friend Pierce Mease Butler sold four hundred and twenty-nine enslaved people at a Savannah racetrack. Fisher called it monstrous in his diary, then wrote that the South must keep slavery all the same.

narrative_blocks.header: He defended slavery until the war changed him
narrative_blocks.body: He thought slavery evil and necessary both, and published a book arguing it. Four years of war changed his mind; by 1863 he wanted it destroyed.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the war's only Constitution book
narrative_blocks.body: The Trial of the Constitution appeared in 1862 — the only full-length book on the Constitution written and printed during the war. No president, he argued, could suspend habeas corpus alone.

narrative_blocks.header: The Maryland plantation that ate his fortune
narrative_blocks.body: Mount Harmon came down from his grandfather and namesake, and he would not let it go. It bled him for thirty years. He died living on his relatives' charity.

narrative_blocks.header: He read law with one Ingersoll, married another
narrative_blocks.body: He read law under Joseph Reed Ingersoll, then quit the bar — a profession, he thought, was beneath a gentleman. In 1851 he married Joseph's niece Elizabeth and never worked much again.

narrative_blocks.header: Three books beginning with the word True
narrative_blocks.body: He wrote The True Benjamin Franklin, The True William Penn, and The True History of the American Revolution — each against the received story. Readers kept buying them, edition after edition.

narrative_blocks.header: He woke his father with news of Lincoln
narrative_blocks.body: He was eight, and he knocked on the bedroom door one April morning in 1865. His father, the diarist, wrote the calamitous news down.

narrative_blocks.header: Suspended for a Washington's Birthday song
narrative_blocks.body: Trinity's faculty wanted the students' birthday songs vetted first. Fisher, senior class president, took the singing into town instead — and the whole college walked out until the suspensions were lifted.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifteen when both parents died within a year
narrative_blocks.body: His father died in July 1871, his mother the following May. The only child of an inward household, he was sent away to boarding school and needed an extra year to finish.

narrative_blocks.header: He fought his college president over land
narrative_blocks.body: A Trinity trustee for thirty-two years, he blocked the president from giving away a piece of the campus in 1923. He also complained that the chapel bell sounded worse than a cow bell.

narrative_blocks.header: The plantation and its people passed to her
narrative_blocks.body: John Ingersoll died in 1859, and Ingleside — two thousand acres on the Yazoo — went to his widow and their children. The 1860 slave schedule counted ninety-four people held on the estate, not one of them named. Emancipation was five years off.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived him by thirty-seven years
narrative_blocks.body: The Philadelphia Ingersolls lost touch with the Mississippi branch. Sarah stayed in Yazoo City until 1896, and was buried at Glenwood near her husband.

narrative_blocks.header: Jefferson trained him; the Confederacy commissioned him
narrative_blocks.body: He took his degree from Jefferson Medical College in 1858. Five years later he passed the Confederate States Army board of medical examination and went to the field as an assistant surgeon under Stephen D. Lee, then W. H. Jackson.

narrative_blocks.header: His Philadelphia uncles opposed the war too
narrative_blocks.body: His father had left Philadelphia for a Mississippi cotton plantation. Three uncles — Edward, Charles, and Harry Ingersoll — opposed the Union from inside it, while their nephew wore the other uniform.

narrative_blocks.header: He waited five years to marry, then farmed
narrative_blocks.body: He married five years after the surrender and took up farming in Missouri. By 1900 he was working land in the Rivanna country of Albemarle County, Virginia.

narrative_blocks.header: Her money came down the Hudson to Philadelphia
narrative_blocks.body: Anna Warren of Troy brought means from a substantial Hudson Valley family. Her husband had, as his son said of him, not a commercial nerve in his body.

narrative_blocks.header: A train at Wayne Junction killed her husband
narrative_blocks.body: She married Harry Wilcocks McCall in 1878. About ten years later a railroad train struck him down at Wayne Junction station.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years an invalid, and undimmed
narrative_blocks.body: A fall from a horse ruined her back, and asthma finished the work; she spent the last forty years of her life an invalid. Her nephew wrote that pages would be needed to set down what she gave them all.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought a bankrupt railroad and got rich
narrative_blocks.body: With Francis Gowen he reopened the Choctaw, Oklahoma and Gulf, then sold it to the Rock Island in 1901. The money built a Montgomery County house he called Forest Hill, staffed with a butler, a chauffeur, and a pageboy known as Buttons.

narrative_blocks.header: The drives were raked after every car
narrative_blocks.body: Forest Hill's gravel was freshened each time a vehicle passed down it. When the market turned in the twenties he economized by dismissing Buttons, packed the family off to White Sulphur Springs, and hired another one.

narrative_blocks.header: He lost Congress by two thousand votes
narrative_blocks.body: He worked Harrity's 1892 campaign for Cleveland and was made Appraiser of the Port of Philadelphia after losing a run for City Solicitor. In 1896 he sat at Bryan's feet through the Cross of Gold speech, then walked out of the convention with the other Gold Democrats. He ran for Congress himself in 1902 and lost by 2,609 votes.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried the failure alone for twenty years
narrative_blocks.body: The Midland Valley Railroad took most of his fortune and returned nothing for two decades. From 1905 into the twenties he lived with acute financial anxiety and a private sense of failure, and never let it show at home. Oil traffic after the war saved the road, and he paid every debt before he died.

narrative_blocks.header: Railroading was in his blood, not law
narrative_blocks.body: He read law under Francis Rawle and partnered with Francis Gowen and James Hood, but the practice never took. He was better read in American history than in statutes, and he went out to Oklahoma summer and winter because he loved the work.

narrative_blocks.header: The Union League was founded in his parlor
narrative_blocks.body: On December 27, 1862, pro-Union Philadelphians met at his house on Walnut Street and adopted articles of association for the Union League. Membership asked one thing: unqualified loyalty to the government and support for putting down the rebellion.

narrative_blocks.header: He took up medicine after his father
narrative_blocks.body: Charles Delucena Meigs pioneered American obstetrics. His son published A Practical Treatise on the Diseases of Children in 1848, two years ahead of his father's own book on the subject, and helped turn the care of children into a field. His son Arthur followed him onto the ward.

narrative_blocks.header: He put his juniors' names on his research
narrative_blocks.body: In 1866 he studied the blood of malarial fever patients shipped up from Southern seaports, and established facts about the disease not yet proven in this country. When the work was published he insisted the resident physicians who had helped him be named as its authors.

narrative_blocks.header: He treated the seamstress like the heiress
narrative_blocks.body: For twenty-two years he attended the Pennsylvania Hospital, giving up his summers so he could spend more hours daily on the ward. A colleague wrote that his manner with a poor servant girl was exactly his manner in the chamber of his wealthiest patient.

narrative_blocks.header: He paid an assistant to record every case
narrative_blocks.body: Dr. Meigs hired an assistant out of his own pocket, and paid him liberally, to keep full records of every patient on his wards at the Pennsylvania Hospital. William Pepper, who knew those records well, called them admirable specimens of clinical work.

narrative_blocks.header: His lectures sounded like conversation
narrative_blocks.body: He took his full share of the hospital's public clinical teaching, a tradition by then 107 years old. William Pepper said his lectures were unlike any he had heard: no oratory, only a natural, candid talk that ranged well beyond the case at hand.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother was Lincoln's quartermaster general
narrative_blocks.body: Montgomery C. Meigs supplied the Union armies for the length of the war. His wife's brothers — Edward, Charles, and Harry Ingersoll — were being called Copperheads a mile away.

narrative_blocks.header: The illumination left out her dead son
narrative_blocks.body: When she died in 1944, Violet Oakley set down her descendants in gold leaf and ink. Harry, killed in France in 1918, was not among the names.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father came home from China at thirty-four
narrative_blocks.body: Robert Shaw Sturgis was the youngest of fourteen and spent sixteen years in the China trade before he came back to marry. He brought weak lungs home with him, and died while she was still a girl.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought the house she grew up in
narrative_blocks.body: Her father had moved the family to 1815 Walnut Street. After her mother died, Charles Edward Ingersoll bought the house, and Henrietta lived in it until the end.

narrative_blocks.header: A lost Goya hung on her wall
narrative_blocks.body: Goya painted The See-Saw around 1791, a cartoon for the royal tapestry works. It vanished from the palace cellars in Madrid and stayed lost for a century — until it turned up at Forest Hill, her house at Penllyn. She gave it to the Philadelphia Museum of Art in 1975, where her brother had been president.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandfather's cabinets went to the museum
narrative_blocks.body: Daniel Pabst built a pair of cabinets for Edward Ingersoll at Fernhill. A century later his granddaughter left them to the Philadelphia Museum of Art, where they hang in American Art.

narrative_blocks.header: Her letters ended up in her brother's file
narrative_blocks.body: She corresponded with the painter Henry McCarter for years. After his death her brother Robert gathered letters for a biography of him that never got written, and hers were among the papers he collected.

narrative_blocks.header: Machine guns at Montfaucon, the first morning
narrative_blocks.body: He led Company H of the 313th Infantry into the Argonne on September 26, 1918, the opening day of the offensive. Machine gun fire cut him down short of the wire the Germans had strung around Montfaucon since 1914. The town fell the next day.

narrative_blocks.header: A church tower in Philadelphia stands for him
narrative_blocks.body: He was twenty-eight, second of six children, and his brother called his death the only break in their parents' married life. The tower of the Church of the Messiah is his memorial. He lies at Meuse-Argonne, in Romagne.
