bio.bio_blurb: President of the Philadelphia Museum of Art

narrative_blocks.header: Sixteen years running the Philadelphia Museum of Art
narrative_blocks.body: He was the museum's president from 1948 to 1964, and had built its Board of Governors first, chairing it from 1947. He was also the fifth Ingersoll lawyer in a line that began with a signer of the Constitution.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother was killed in France
narrative_blocks.body: Captain Harry Ingersoll died in action in 1918. Robert named his own youngest son for him — and a generation later his nephew, Sergeant Charles Jared Ingersoll Jr., was killed in Italy.

narrative_blocks.header: Boards for the zoo, the orchestra, the railroads
narrative_blocks.body: He sat for the Philadelphia Savings Fund Society, the zoological society, the orchestra association, the Fairmount Park Art Association, and several railroads. The American Philosophical Society elected him in 1950.

narrative_blocks.header: The painter's life he never wrote
narrative_blocks.body: He spent years gathering letters for a biography of the painter Henry McCarter, writing to Cecilia Beaux, Albert Barnes, and the Biddles for material, and mounted McCarter's memorial exhibition in 1943. The book never came.

narrative_blocks.header: A lost Šíma hung in his house
narrative_blocks.body: In 1952 he bought a 1927 canvas called Europa from the collector Bernard Davis. The art world believed the only version of it hung in Brno; seventy years later, tests in Prague authenticated his — and a Czech historian called it the rediscovery of the century.

narrative_blocks.header: A monocle, a waxed mustache, and Picassos
narrative_blocks.body: He collected Picasso, Modigliani, and Brancusi, and hung them where the family could see them. A great-granddaughter remembered a very tall man with a waxed mustache and a monocle, and an intensity you could feel across a room.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the railroads his father nearly lost
narrative_blocks.body: When Charles Edward died in 1932, Jared took over the Midland Valley and the KO&G and ran them well. The family sold the roads to the Texas & Pacific in 1962.

narrative_blocks.header: His son was killed in Italy
narrative_blocks.body: Sergeant Charles Jared Ingersoll Jr. died in action in 1944, at twenty-one. His father lived another forty-four years.

narrative_blocks.header: He photographed the houses before they came down
narrative_blocks.body: He assembled two albums of the family's homes: 1815 Walnut Street facing Rittenhouse Square, where his mother grew up, and Fern Hill. Twenty-one images, each with a long typewritten caption. The Walnut Street house was dismantled in 1945.

narrative_blocks.header: Three houses on one Penllyn hillside
narrative_blocks.body: Forest Hill Lodge belonged to his brother Sturgis, Forest Hill to his sister Anna, and Hillfield to him — all on the ground their father had summered on. Fifty houses have gone up between them since.

narrative_blocks.header: He sat out the war in London
narrative_blocks.body: A Copperhead like his brothers Edward and Charles, Harry left Philadelphia when the Civil War began. He did not come back until it ended.

narrative_blocks.header: His son George died at nineteen
narrative_blocks.body: George Roberts Ingersoll was born in 1836 and died in 1855. His father outlived him by thirty-one years.

narrative_blocks.header: He took his father's ward at the hospital
narrative_blocks.body: John Forsyth Meigs resigned from the Pennsylvania Hospital in 1881, and the board appointed his son in his place. Arthur Vincent had taken his Penn medical degree ten years before, and he would go on to preside over the College of Physicians.

narrative_blocks.header: Three Meigs, three books on children
narrative_blocks.body: His grandfather Charles Delucena wrote on the diseases of young children, his father wrote the American treatise on them, and Arthur Vincent carried the work into infant feeding. Historians of pediatrics count all three.

bio.bio_blurb: Philadelphia architect of country houses and war memorials

narrative_blocks.header: Country houses for the Philadelphia gentry
narrative_blocks.body: With Walter Mellor he built a practice on Pennsylvania farmhouse, Cotswold, and Norman styles, and his own family connections brought the clients in. George Howe joined in 1916 and left in 1928, taking the savings-fund account with him and turning modernist.

narrative_blocks.header: A captain who came home to build memorials
narrative_blocks.body: He served as an artillery captain in the First World War. In 1925 the Commission of Fine Arts chose his firm to design the Coast Guard's memorial at Arlington — a twelve-foot marble pyramid on pink granite, with a bronze seagull by Gaston Lachaise at its foot. It was dedicated on a spring afternoon in 1928, before two thousand people.

narrative_blocks.header: A chapel at the Somme, a Kemmel monument
narrative_blocks.body: The American Battle Monuments Commission gave his firm two of its First World War commissions: the chapel at the Somme American Cemetery near Bony, and the monument to the 27th and 30th Divisions between Ypres and Mount Kemmel.

narrative_blocks.header: Goodhart Hall and the zoo's bird house
narrative_blocks.body: Beyond the country houses, his firm built Goodhart Hall at Bryn Mawr, the science laboratory at Haverford and the bird house at the Philadelphia Zoo. The Philadelphia chapter of the AIA gave Arthur its medal in 1922, and the Architectural League of New York its gold medal in 1925.

narrative_blocks.header: He told students to find an apprenticeship instead
narrative_blocks.body: Asked in 1935 how architectural training might be bettered, he answered that nothing could substitute for the apprentice system. He had learned that way himself, under Theophilus Chandler and then Edgar Seeler, before he was twenty-four.

narrative_blocks.header: He warned that specialization in art was dangerous
narrative_blocks.body: Writing in 1930 about Robert McCracken's small stone house in Germantown, Arthur praised the way house and garden fused, because owner and architect had cared about every part of it together. It was an age of specialists, he wrote, and specialization in art was dangerous.

narrative_blocks.header: The first race at Land Hope was his
narrative_blocks.body: In April 1936 his horse El Rey Keno won the first steeplechase ever run on his Unionville estate, before several thousand people. Three years later Red Ned took Broad Axe by eight lengths, on a day when another of his horses fell and broke its back.

bio.title: Lt.
bio.bio_blurb: Ordnance manager at the Bethlehem Iron Company

narrative_blocks.header: Ordnance manager at Bethlehem Iron
narrative_blocks.body: Lieutenant Meigs managed ordnance for the Bethlehem Iron Company, the works that became Bethlehem Steel. He and Jane made their home in the Dunglison house at the corner of Delaware Avenue and Freytag Street in Fountain Hill.

narrative_blocks.header: He left a widow and a ten-month-old
narrative_blocks.body: Typhoid fever killed him in November 1884, at thirty-three. Adelaide Bond wore black or white through the sixty years of widowhood that followed, and outlived him by sixty-three.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandfather's portrait hangs at Hill Field
narrative_blocks.body: He was named for Stephen Warren of Troy, his mother's father. The portrait is still with the family.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at thirty-eight, dead at fifty-three
narrative_blocks.body: James Logan Fisher took her to Fernrock, on the four-hundred-acre Fisher farm, where a generation of nieces and nephews spent their holidays. She was always delicate, and an operation for appendicitis killed her in 1905.

narrative_blocks.header: He graduated from Penn and never worked
narrative_blocks.body: Frail as a young man, he took his degree and then simply never took a job. He wintered in Paris, sang in the church choir, kept his garden, and served the Penllyn Club as its secretary and treasurer.

narrative_blocks.header: His sister kept house for him fifty years
narrative_blocks.body: After their parents died the two of them moved to Annandale Farm in Horsham Township and never left. Jennie nursed him to the end, in 1943.

narrative_blocks.header: She nursed her brother for fifty years
narrative_blocks.body: From about 1893 she and Henry lived together at Annandale Farm, and she cared for him until he died in 1943. She inherited the farm, kept it eight more years, and left it to a grandniece.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty years in black or white
narrative_blocks.body: Typhoid took her husband in 1884, ten months after their son was born. She dressed in black or in white for the rest of her life, and outlived him by sixty-three years.

narrative_blocks.header: She taught them Sunday School without piety
narrative_blocks.body: The Ingersoll children were constantly in and out of her house by the Forest Hill barn. She never missed church, and her nephew wrote that there was not the least touch of sanctimony in her.

narrative_blocks.header: She built her own house and stayed
narrative_blocks.body: In 1909 she left the house by the barn and built at Spring House, where she lived alone for thirty-eight years. She buried her only son in 1918 and died there in 1947.

narrative_blocks.header: A headache on the train home
narrative_blocks.body: He had just taken his discharge from the Air Service in Washington, in December 1918. The influenza that had emptied Philadelphia's streets that autumn killed him at home within three days — three months after his cousin Harry fell in the Argonne. He left Emily and four children.

narrative_blocks.header: A stockbroker who lived for horses
narrative_blocks.body: He kept an office in the old Drexel Building on Fifth Street and a house at Spring House, a gift from his uncle. The cousins who lunched with him remembered the man, not the ledgers.

cross_connections.display_label: his cousin, killed at Montfaucon three months before him

narrative_blocks.header: His Christmas presents were donkeys and ponies
narrative_blocks.body: He and Mary had no children of their own. To her nieces and nephews he gave donkeys, ponies, sleds, and bronzes, and he stayed their close friend for the twenty years he outlived her.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty years of collecting with Mimi
narrative_blocks.body: Paul married Mimi Koehler of St. Louis on 6 October 1951, a year after she was crowned Veiled Prophet Queen, and the two collected antiques together through sixty years of marriage.

narrative_blocks.header: Born the day the market crashed
narrative_blocks.body: October 29, 1929. He spent his working life in the brokerage business — the Philadelphia National Bank, then Merrill Lynch, then thirty years at Smith Barney.

narrative_blocks.header: The high jump record stood thirty years
narrative_blocks.body: He captained track at St. Paul's and jumped higher than anyone there for three decades afterward. At his fiftieth reunion he handed his medal for all-round excellence in track to the boy who had won it that year.

narrative_blocks.header: He captained the First City Troop
narrative_blocks.body: He served in Germany during the Korean War with the 28th Reconnaissance Company. Years later he commanded the First Troop Philadelphia City Cavalry, and after he retired he ran its capital campaign.

narrative_blocks.header: A volunteer on the postoperative floor
narrative_blocks.body: For many years Henry volunteered at Bryn Mawr Hospital, working its postoperative floor.

was elected captain of the First City Troop after the Civil War

military_service.notes: Served in Germany

narrative_blocks.header: She married four months after her brother died
narrative_blocks.body: Sergeant Charles Jared Ingersoll Jr. was killed clearing mines near Minturno in May 1944. That September she married Brooke Roberts, a surgeon she had met at a party at Princeton. They had fifty-eight years.

narrative_blocks.header: Four years of antiques built a hospital fund
narrative_blocks.body: She co-chaired the Philadelphia Antiques Show through the 1960s and drew dealers to it from across the country. Under her the show became a serious source of money for the University of Pennsylvania's hospital, where her husband operated.

narrative_blocks.header: History at Vassar, then the War Labor Board
narrative_blocks.body: She led the class of 1943 as its president and took her degree in history. She worked at the War Labor Board in Philadelphia until she married.

bio.bio_blurb: Army combat engineer, killed in action

narrative_blocks.header: He turned down officer school to stay
narrative_blocks.body: He enlisted as a private and landed in an engineer battalion made largely of coal miners. He liked them enough to refuse Officers' Training School more than once, rather than risk being moved out of the outfit. They called him Slim.

narrative_blocks.header: Two months in North Africa, learning mines
narrative_blocks.body: Charles went overseas in December 1943 and spent a couple of months in North Africa, where he became expert in handling enemy mines. It was the work his squad was doing on the day he was killed.

narrative_blocks.header: Eighteen days from the front to the grave
narrative_blocks.body: His division reached the line near Minturno on April 26, 1944, and he took a platoon that day as acting sergeant, under artillery fire for the first time. He was dead eighteen days later, at twenty. The Purple Heart came afterward.

narrative_blocks.header: Four men, three tanks, one mule trail
narrative_blocks.body: On May 14 his squad was ordered to clear mines around three disabled American tanks at the foot of Hill 85, west of Minturno. Under heavy artillery and mortar fire he sent most of the squad back and finished the work with four men. Walking out along a mule trail, a shell caught them; he was in the lead and died instantly.

narrative_blocks.header: The only son, with three sisters
narrative_blocks.body: Charles was the only son of Charles Jared Ingersoll Sr., with sisters Anna, Sally and Gainor. His mother, Marian, died in 1939, when he was fifteen.

cross_connections.display_label: , his uncle, was killed at Montfaucon in the Argonne in 1918
covered the Fifth Army's Italian campaign, in which he was killed

military_service.unit: Company B, 310th Engineer Combat Battalion, 85th Infantry Division
battles: Italian Campaign — Minturno and the Gustav Line
military_service.notes: Enlisted as a private; corporal February 1943, sergeant September 1943; overseas December 1943. Two months in North Africa, where he became expert in handling enemy mines. Division entered the line near Minturno 26 April 1944. Killed in action 14 May 1944 at twenty, clearing mines around three disabled American tanks at the foot of Hill 85, west of Minturno. Purple Heart, posthumous.

narrative_blocks.header: He joined his father's firm and the Troop
narrative_blocks.body: He practiced at Ballard, Spahr, Andrews & Ingersoll, where his father was a name partner. He commanded the First Troop Philadelphia City Cavalry, as his cousin would after him.

cross_connections.display_label: was his cousin, who captained the First City Troop after him

narrative_blocks.header: Two years in the wartime OSS
narrative_blocks.body: George served with the Office of Strategic Services, America's wartime intelligence agency, from 1942 to 1944.

bio.photo_notes: Class book, Class 43-C advanced pilots, Ellington Field, Texas, 1943

narrative_blocks.header: Railroads by day, the children's hospital besides
narrative_blocks.body: He was a vice president of the Pennsylvania Railroad, the fourth generation of his family in the business. He also served as president of the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia.

narrative_blocks.header: Class 43-C at Ellington Field, Texas
narrative_blocks.body: In 1943 Charles went through advanced pilot training with Class 43-C at Ellington Field, the Army Air Forces flying school outside Houston.

cross_connections.display_label: was consulting physician to the children's hospital he later led
ran the Pennsylvania Railroad as its president from 1874 to 1880

military_service.unit: Class 43-C, advanced pilot training, Ellington Field, Texas

narrative_blocks.header: Veiled Prophet Queen of St. Louis, 1950
narrative_blocks.body: Mimi was crowned Veiled Prophet Queen in St. Louis in October 1950, the city's premier debutante honor. When her reign ended she married Paul Ingersoll, on 6 October 1951.

narrative_blocks.header: A collector who became an antiques dealer
narrative_blocks.body: Mimi and her husband collected together through sixty years of marriage, and the collecting became her career as an antiques dealer.

narrative_blocks.header: She taught English to Southeast Asian immigrants
narrative_blocks.body: For years Mimi taught English as a second language to Southeast Asian immigrants in Philadelphia. She also worked for Mothers Against Drunk Driving and Planned Parenthood of Southeastern Pennsylvania.

narrative_blocks.header: A story for every painting but one
narrative_blocks.body: Meticulous about the collection he inherited, he set down the history of each piece for his children. About Europa, the canvas hanging in his office, there was nothing at all — and it was the only lost one in the house.

narrative_blocks.header: He sent it all to auction, for fairness
narrative_blocks.body: Rather than have his four children choose among the pictures, he told them to sell everything. An auction, he said, was the only fair way to divide what he loved.

Children: Harriet Newel (1815-1907), Timothy Dwight (1817-1910). Birthplace and death place not given on the stone record. | Avery, Ingersoll genealogy #133 (screenshots, Sam 7 Sep 2026): 'Theodore Sedgwick(6) Ingersoll (David,5 William,4 David,3 Thomas,2 John1), born April 26, 1786 at Lee, Mass.; died Apr. 3, 1873 at Berea, O.; married, June 10, 1812, his cousin, Lydia Brewer, born Oct. 19, 1792; died June 25, 1893: daughter of Joseph and Elizabeth (Ingersoll) Brewer, of Tyringham, Mass. She lived to be nearly 101 years old. A public celebration was made for her at the Armory on her 100th birthday by the town of Berea.' Quoting Oberlin News, Apr. 2, 1907: 'Theodore Ingersoll was among the first pioneers of Oberlin, coming there in 1833. He was the fourth to sign the Oberlin Covenant. He was the first postmaster and carried the mail for a number of years twice a week from Elyria to Oberlin, also keeping the first store, on the corner where O. M. Harter has his drug store.' And: 'The first Anti-Slavery Convention was held at the home of Theodore Ingersoll.' CONFLICT (unresolved): the genealogy gives his death as Apr. 3, 1873 and hers as June 25, 1893; FindAGrave and FamilySearch both give 3 Aug 1873 and 25 Jul 1893. The FindAGrave/FamilySearch dates are used here. AMBIGUITY: the genealogy does not say which body's first anti-slavery convention met at his house, or whether it sat at Oberlin or later at Berea; the Oberlin context is assumed and not proven. LYDIA WAS HIS COUSIN through her mother Elizabeth Ingersoll — the connecting generation is not established and no entries are to be built for the Brewers. | 7 Sep 2026: FamilySearch places three of his sons' births at Ogden, Monroe County NY — William Brewer 1819, Luman Church 1823, Charles Freeman 1831 — with Timothy born in Massachusetts in 1817. The family therefore went Berkshires → western New York by 1819 → Oberlin 1833.

naming_inspiration.description: Born at Lee in 1786 and given the full name of Theodore Sedgwick, then the Berkshire County lawyer at Sheffield and Stockbridge who had argued the Mum Bett freedom suit five years earlier. No blood or marriage tie between the families has been found.

narrative_blocks.header: The first anti-slavery convention met in his house
narrative_blocks.body: He was among the first pioneers of Oberlin, reaching the new colony in 1833, and was the fourth man to sign the Oberlin Covenant that bound the settlers to plain living and the cause. The first anti-slavery convention there was held at his house.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried the mail and kept the store
narrative_blocks.body: He served as Oberlin's first postmaster and for a number of years carried the mail himself, twice a week, over the road from Elyria. He also kept the first store in the place, on the corner where the town druggist stood by 1907.

narrative_blocks.header: He married his cousin, who reached a hundred
narrative_blocks.body: In June 1812 at Tyringham he married Lydia Brewer, his cousin, a daughter of Joseph Brewer and Elizabeth Ingersoll. She outlived him by twenty years, and the town of Berea held a public celebration for her at the Armory on her hundredth birthday.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the Berkshire family west to Ohio
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Lee in Berkshire County, one of Deacon David Ingersoll's thirteen children, and by 1819 had moved his own family to Ogden in western New York, where three of his sons were born. He went on to Ohio in the year Oberlin was founded; his brother William followed, his brother Elihu took the college's music chair in 1835, and two nieces came out to study.

narrative_blocks.header: Six sons, a daughter, a plot at Oberlin
narrative_blocks.body: He died at Berea in Cuyahoga County in 1873, the same year as his brother William, and was carried back to Westwood Cemetery at Oberlin. His wife, his eldest daughter and his son Timothy were buried in the same ground.

narrative_blocks.header: He built the arithmetic inside early computers
narrative_blocks.body: At Illinois he designed the multiplication and division for the ORDVAC and ILLIAC machines and was chief engineer of ILLIAC II. His name is on the SRT division method and on a patent for signed-digit arithmetic, the way a great many computers came to divide.

narrative_blocks.header: Built for the Army's ballistics lab
narrative_blocks.body: The ORDVAC, whose multiplication, division and much of whose control circuitry James designed, was built at Illinois for the Army's Ballistic Research Laboratory at Aberdeen; its twin, the ILLIAC, stayed at Urbana.

narrative_blocks.header: Run by telephone from Urbana
narrative_blocks.body: After the ORDVAC passed its tests at Aberdeen in March 1952, Illinois ran it by telephone up to eight hours a night, one of the first computers used from a distance. The multiplier James designed for it took 732 microseconds.

narrative_blocks.header: Soviet computer centers, 1958
narrative_blocks.body: In 1958, the year after Sputnik, James went to the Soviet Union to visit its computer centers, and kept his notes of the trip with the rest of his papers.

narrative_blocks.header: A Fulbright year in Sydney
narrative_blocks.body: In 1962 and 1963 James spent a Fulbright year researching computers at the University of Sydney, whose SILLIAC had been built from the Illinois design.

narrative_blocks.header: A Cherokee minister’s son from Oklahoma
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Fairfax, Oklahoma, son of Albion Lorenzo Robertson, a Cherokee Presbyterian minister, and came up through Oklahoma A&M and the Army Signal Corps before Illinois. He went to every Computer Arithmetic Symposium from its first in 1969.

narrative_blocks.body: Erastus Ingersoll settled the land in 1836; it passed son to son to daughter to him. He took it over from his mother Lela and worked it as the fifth generation on the same soil. The family held it until 1974.

narrative_blocks.header: The one son who left the land
narrative_blocks.body: Youngest of twelve children on a Delta farm, he took a common-school education and a clerk's job at eighteen, then bought into the store where he clerked. Among a whole generation of Ingersoll farmers, he was the one who chose the counter over the field.

narrative_blocks.header: He built Lansing's finest dry-goods house
narrative_blocks.body: He bought out his partner after two years, moved into a brick building in Lansing, and ran it wholesale and retail — dry goods and millinery, the finest in the city. He wore old clothes doing it.

narrative_blocks.header: Her hymns outlived her by decades
narrative_blocks.body: A collection of her verse, Hymns of Nature and Songs of the Spirit, appeared three years after she died and carried her work to congregations she never saw. Two of her hymns had already entered the standard books. She wrote for The Atlantic, The Independent, and The Youth's Companion.

narrative_blocks.header: She taught before she married the president
narrative_blocks.body: Before she married Merrill Gates in 1873 she taught at the Le Roy Female Seminary in New York. She came from a Rochester family of lawyers and legislators and counted Roger Williams, the founder of Rhode Island, among her forebears.

narrative_blocks.header: A missions board, and a Japanese war song
narrative_blocks.body: She gave years to the Reformed Church's Women's Board of Foreign Missions, and her range was wider than hymns: she once versified a Japanese war song into fierce English rhyme. A contemporary said her true home was with the Nazarene.

narrative_blocks.header: Gassed blind, he would not leave the field
narrative_blocks.body: In the Argonne in the fall of 1918 he took over a battalion whose commander had fallen, was knocked down by shellfire, and rallied the men anyway. The next day he assumed command of the whole regiment and led it in the attack — refusing evacuation after gas had blinded him. The Distinguished Service Cross followed.

narrative_blocks.header: He tried to desegregate the Army, and lost
narrative_blocks.body: In the 1920s he proposed opening positions across the Army to Black soldiers, who were then confined largely to labor and infantry. The Army rejected it. He held the progressive view, decades early, that the service should be mechanized and integrated both.

narrative_blocks.header: Four wars, from Cuba to a world war
narrative_blocks.body: He enlisted for the Spanish-American War in an Alabama volunteer regiment, took a commission for the Philippines, won his cross in France, and served through the opening of the Second World War before retiring a major general in 1941. He commanded the tank school and helped shape the Army's first mechanized doctrine.

narrative_blocks.header: Dead in a harbor he sailed to see
narrative_blocks.body: Retired and traveling, he died in November 1960 aboard the liner Caronia as she lay in port at Venice. He was eighty-three, and lies with Volinda at Arlington.

narrative_blocks.body: Phebe died at Marshall in 1839, when Laura was fifteen. Frances Fowler Tallmadge, her younger sister and the wife of Rev. John Marsh, took the girl into their Brooklyn house and kept her there for years.

bio.bio_blurb: Black Rock customs officer; New York merchant

narrative_blocks.header: Deputy Collector of Customs at Black Rock
narrative_blocks.body: He clerked at Utica and Oswego as a young man, then spent twenty years at Black Rock on the Niagara from 1834, most of them collecting customs under George W. Clinton.

narrative_blocks.header: Gas-works, coal, and goods going west
narrative_blocks.body: At New York afterwards he forwarded goods westward, put up gas-works and dealt in coal, and acted as a special agent of the Treasury. By 1873 he was collecting claims against the United States.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife's father fled Ireland with Emmet
narrative_blocks.body: Catharine Edmondston's father John was a Trinity College Dublin man who came over as an Irish refugee of 1798. He was a lawyer, then a merchant at Troy and Watertown, and died at Kingston in Canada.

narrative_blocks.header: Three sons named George Payson Barker
narrative_blocks.body: The first was born in 1835 and died at eighteen months, the second in 1838 and died at six. They gave the name a third time in 1843, and that boy carried it to 1905.

narrative_blocks.header: He wintered in Washington, they lived at Harlem
narrative_blocks.body: His family kept house at Harlem while he spent every winter in Washington on the claims business. He died in the city in January 1875.

sources.label: Dwight, The History of the Descendants of John Dwight of Dedham (1874)

narrative_blocks.header: A bride lost to consumption in seven months
narrative_blocks.body: She married Zadock Pratt in 1818, the first of his five wives. Consumption took her within seven months, before the marriage had well begun.

narrative_blocks.header: Her dead sister's widower married her next
narrative_blocks.body: Three years after her sister Beda died, Pratt married Esther in her place. Consumption claimed her too, within two and a half years — the second Dickerman sister lost to the same disease.

narrative_blocks.header: The Watson sister whose marriage finally lasted
narrative_blocks.body: After his third wife Abigail Watson died in childbirth, Pratt married her sister Mary. Unlike the marriages around it, this one endured — until Mary's death in 1868, more than thirty years on.

narrative_blocks.header: Married in the Prattsville church he had built
narrative_blocks.body: Pratt's fifth and last wife, she married him in 1869 in the Prattsville church he had given the land and half the money to build. They stayed together until his death two years later.

bio.bio_blurb: New York merchant and prison reformer

narrative_blocks.header: He gave years to prison and child reform
narrative_blocks.body: A merchant who had traded in Pittsburgh and New York, he turned much of his energy to reform, laboring for years on behalf of prisoners and of neglected and delinquent children. Later in life he took an interest in the silver mines of Nevada.

narrative_blocks.header: His father shipped the world from Chambers Street
narrative_blocks.body: His father, also named Rensselaer Havens, was a New York shipping merchant of the firm Jenkins & Havens, at 100 Chambers Street. The son grew up in that mercantile world before making his own way in trade and reform.

narrative_blocks.header: A cabinet maker who became a theology professor
narrative_blocks.body: He began life as a cabinet maker, working the trade in Connecticut and New York towns before turning to the ministry in his twenties. He rose to become the first professor of theology at the Auburn Seminary and one of the leading Presbyterian divines of his day.

narrative_blocks.header: Priced out of Yale, taught by Timothy Dwight
narrative_blocks.body: He entered Yale in 1789 but had to leave after a single year, unable to bear the cost. He finished his preparation for the ministry instead under Timothy Dwight at Greenfield Hill — the man who would later become president of Yale.

narrative_blocks.header: Moderator at thirty-seven, wary of revival excess
narrative_blocks.body: At just thirty-seven he was chosen moderator of the Presbyterian General Assembly. A measured Calvinist, he was later cited as a voice against the excesses of the revivalists who imitated Charles Finney.

narrative_blocks.header: His great work was published after his death
narrative_blocks.body: Though he published sermons and addresses in his lifetime, he is best remembered for his Lectures on Mental Philosophy and Theology, drawn from his Auburn teaching and issued three years after his death. A sketch of his life was printed with it.

narrative_blocks.body: She married Anthony Dey of Preakness in February 1820, a Jersey City and New York attorney twenty-two years her senior and a widower. Seven children followed between 1821 and 1834. She outlived him by twelve years.

narrative_blocks.header: First in his class at Nassau Hall, 1823
narrative_blocks.body: He took his degree at Nassau Hall in 1823 with the highest honors of his class, then went to Litchfield to read law under Judge James Gould, who was president of the law school. He was admitted to the New York bar in 1827.

narrative_blocks.header: His second wife was his first wife's niece
narrative_blocks.body: Margaret Smith Evertson died at Auburn in July 1833, leaving him two small sons. Four years later he married Mary Howe Givan of Dutchess County, who was seventeen, and who was his first wife's niece.

narrative_blocks.header: The Hudson took his twelve-year-old son
narrative_blocks.body: He lost the younger boy of his first marriage on 22 April 1843, when Henry Evertson Richards drowned in the Hudson River a month short of thirteen. He outlived him by three years and died at Poughkeepsie at forty-three.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife died in his father's seminary town
narrative_blocks.body: Margaret died at Auburn in 1833, where his father Rev. James Richards had been the first professor of theology at the seminary since 1823. Six of his eight children came after her, most born at Poughkeepsie.

narrative_blocks.header: He entered his father's calling, not his fortune
narrative_blocks.body: The son of the eminent theologian James Richards, he followed his father into the Presbyterian ministry but never found his father's steadiness. Struggles with drink and with what would now be recognized as manic-depressive illness moved him from pulpit to pulpit, each pastorate ending in difficulty.

narrative_blocks.header: A ministers' association warned churches against him
narrative_blocks.body: By 1860 his conduct had brought repeated ecclesiastical trials, and a Connecticut association printed a pamphlet of documents cautioning congregations against employing him. Deposed from the Presbyterian ministry, he spent his last years abroad and died in 1875 from a fall in Scotland.

narrative_blocks.header: His children rose above the shadow he cast
narrative_blocks.body: Unable to raise them, he left his children to their grandparents in Canandaigua, and they made names his own life never did — his daughter Caroline for a beloved diary of village life, his son John Morgan Richards for his memoirs, and his granddaughter Pearl Craigie as a celebrated English novelist.

narrative_blocks.header: An LL.D. from a Mississippi planters' college
narrative_blocks.body: He prepared at the polytechnic school at Chittenango, spent two years at Union College and took his degree at Hamilton in 1834. Lafayette later made him a D.D., and in 1853 Planters College in Mississippi gave him an LL.D.

narrative_blocks.header: Three wives, the first dead at Penn Yan
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth Beals of Canandaigua married him in August 1836 and died at Penn Yan in June 1846. He married Sarah Wisner of Penn Yan the next year, and in 1857 a third wife, Mrs. Helen L. Franklin, by whom he had no children.

career.notes: Pastorates at Aurora, Penn Yan, Morristown, New Orleans, and Charleston.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father landed with 168 coppers
narrative_blocks.body: David Kennedy came ashore at New Castle in Pennsylvania on 18 May 1760, and his Bible records that all he owned that day was two English shillings and a hundred and sixty-eight old coppers. Margaret was the daughter of his third wife, Margaret Lewis.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed twice, and buried in Devon
narrative_blocks.body: She had already lost a husband named Archer when she married Major Tallmadge in 1827, and was a widow again by the end of 1832. She died on 7 December 1862 in Devonshire, at the house of her daughter Julia.

people.research_notes: Transcription of the David Kennedy Bible. David Kennedy born 17 March 1741; married Agnes White 1774 (died 1777), Susannah Pugh 1783 (died 1785) and Margaret Lewis 12 November 1788, born 16 April 1765. None of the Kennedys are in the tree.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother died in her house that year
narrative_blocks.body: Julia Tallmadge married an English clergyman in 1850 and never came home. She and her mother both died in 1862, the mother in Devonshire at Julia's own house in December.

narrative_blocks.header: Dead at thirty-two, she became a paragon
narrative_blocks.body: She died of tuberculosis at thirty-two, and her memory settled over her children as a standard they could never quite reach — 'she hoped we would be as good as our mother was,' an old friend told her daughter Caroline. The girl, tired of the comparison, once wrote that children in the old days were surely not as bad as now.

narrative_blocks.header: Her memorial stone wandered for fifty years
narrative_blocks.body: The stone tablet raised to her in Penn Yan wandered for half a century — moved out for renovations, sent to the Beals family home, laid in a cemetery lot — until her son John at last brought it back to the Penn Yan church at his own expense.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave Britain the cigarette habit
narrative_blocks.body: In 1877 he took the British agency for Virginia-made cigarettes and, through aggressive American-style advertising, turned a niche product into a national habit. He paid chemists to stock them and dressed a Piccadilly shop window with a Quaker trademark until 'Richmond Gems' caught on across the country.

narrative_blocks.header: He made a fortune on patent medicines
narrative_blocks.body: His larger fortune came from patent medicines, marketed to Britain with the same flair — Carter's Little Liver Pills and Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People among them. He built one of the great transatlantic advertising businesses of his day.

narrative_blocks.header: An American who kept his citizenship in London
narrative_blocks.body: He settled permanently in London in 1867 but never gave up his American citizenship, calling himself an 'unnaturalised alien.' A chairman of the American Society in London, he bought Steephill Castle on the Isle of Wight, where he spent his last years.

narrative_blocks.header: His children carried the family into letters
narrative_blocks.body: A memoirist himself, he raised a literary family: his daughter Pearl became the novelist John Oliver Hobbes, and his son Grant founded a London publishing house. After Pearl's early death he compiled a volume of her letters as a tribute.

narrative_blocks.header: His obituary called him a doubtful benefit
narrative_blocks.body: The Times remembered him as 'the pioneer of a doubtful benefit,' crediting his work for Anglo-American trade while noting the cigarette habit he had done so much to spread. It was a mixed verdict on a life of restless salesmanship.

narrative_blocks.header: A schoolgirl's diary became a beloved book
narrative_blocks.body: She began a diary at ten and kept it for twenty years — a record of small-town life in Canandaigua through the Civil War, laced with a sly wit. Published long after as Village Life in America, it became a cherished window on nineteenth-century America.

narrative_blocks.header: She heard Dickens, Barnum, and Susan B. Anthony
narrative_blocks.body: Her pages caught the great voices that passed through her Finger Lakes town — Charles Dickens, P.T. Barnum, and the suffragist Susan B. Anthony. When war came she watched Canandaigua's young men march off, and even wrote a letter of support to General McClellan.

narrative_blocks.header: Raised by strict grandparents after her mother died
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother died when she was small and her father proved unable to raise her, so she and her sister Anna grew up in Canandaigua under devout, old-fashioned grandparents. She married the Civil War veteran Edmund Clarke in 1866.

notable.notable_blurb: Diarist of nineteenth-century village life

bio.bio_blurb: Civil War veteran and pension agent

narrative_blocks.header: He enlisted, was disabled, and came home
narrative_blocks.body: He enlisted in the Union Army in the spring of 1863 and served until September 1864, when he was discharged for disability, unable to do manual labor for years afterward. He kept his soldier's tie for life, commanding the local Grand Army of the Republic post.

narrative_blocks.header: He won pensions for a thousand old soldiers
narrative_blocks.body: After the war he took up pension work and, over the years, secured nearly a thousand pensions for those legally entitled to them. He was a village fixture besides — a schoolteacher, a notary for thirty years, and for decades the local newspaper correspondent.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventy-five years at his village church
narrative_blocks.body: From boyhood he gave seventy-five years to the Naples Presbyterian Church — as Sunday school superintendent, choir leader, elder, and delegate to the wider assemblies. His grandfather, a Revolutionary officer, had been among the town's first settlers.

career.notes: Taught many terms over the years.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the Winthrop schools for two decades
narrative_blocks.body: A Williams College graduate, he spent his career in the schools of Winthrop, Massachusetts — principal of the senior high school from 1915, then superintendent of the town's schools from 1927 until 1938.

narrative_blocks.header: She telegraphed advice to the world's leaders
narrative_blocks.body: One of Ventnor's most colourful characters, she came to consider herself an emissary of God and would fire off curt telegrams directing world leaders in their affairs of state. They often carried strange postscripts — 'have faith in onions!' one advised, or a remark on the daffodils.

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband's headstone reads 'My Laurie'
narrative_blocks.body: For all her eccentricity, she and John Morgan Richards were married more than fifty years, and he called her Laurie to the end. When she died in 1914, he had her Ventnor headstone engraved simply, 'My Laurie.'

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Ventnor, Isle of Wight

narrative_blocks.header: Her first novel was an instant sensation
narrative_blocks.body: Writing as John Oliver Hobbes, she made her name at twenty-four with Some Emotions and a Moral, an epigrammatic first book that sold eighty thousand copies in a few weeks. A dozen novels and a string of West End plays followed, witty and serious by turns, on ill-matched marriages and disillusioned love.

narrative_blocks.header: A literary star of 1890s London
narrative_blocks.body: She was a fixture of literary London, admired by Thomas Hardy and befriended by Yeats and Beardsley, and in 1895 became president of the Society of Women Journalists. She lectured on both sides of the Atlantic and was received everywhere from Mayfair drawing rooms to the Viceroy's court in India.

narrative_blocks.header: Against the vote, for women journalists
narrative_blocks.body: Pearl earned her living by her pen, presided over the Society of Women Journalists and won custody of her son after a public trial, yet she sided with the anti-suffragists against votes for women. Her last novel, The Dream and the Business, of 1906, turned obliquely on the clever woman's predicament.

narrative_blocks.header: She converted, and her fiction turned to faith
narrative_blocks.body: Raised in a strict Nonconformist family, she was received into the Roman Catholic Church in 1892 and remained a devout, serious member for life. The religious cast of her thought deepened her later novels, reaching its height in The School for Saints and its sequel, Robert Orange.

narrative_blocks.header: She won her son in a public divorce
narrative_blocks.body: At nineteen she married Reginald Walpole Craigie; the marriage soon failed, and she obtained a separation and then, in 1895, a divorce, keeping custody of their young son. She never remarried, and wrote often, with a knowing eye, of marriages gone wrong.

narrative_blocks.header: Her first stories were in print at nine
narrative_blocks.body: Pearl was born at her grandmother's house in Chelsea, Massachusetts, in November 1867, and had her first stories in print at nine. She was schooled in Berkshire and Paris, and after her marriage wrote regular drama and art columns.

narrative_blocks.header: She died suddenly at thirty-eight
narrative_blocks.body: In August 1906, on her way to a Scottish holiday, she died in her sleep in London of heart failure, at thirty-eight, at the height of her fame. Queen Alexandra wrote to her parents in sympathy. Lord Curzon unveiled a memorial to her at University College London two years later.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father signed the Articles of Confederation
narrative_blocks.body: She was a daughter of Andrew Adams of Litchfield — a Yale-trained lawyer, colonel of Connecticut militia, and chief justice of the state, who sat in the Continental Congress and signed the Articles of Confederation. She carried that Revolutionary pedigree into the Cowles family.

bio.bio_blurb: Decorated Grenadier Guards officer of the Great War

narrative_blocks.header: The Military Cross for a night bombing raid
narrative_blocks.body: As the bombing officer of his Grenadier Guards company, he led a grenade attack on a German observation post in October 1915, taking a stretch of enemy trench but a wound to his leg and foot. For it he was awarded the Military Cross.

narrative_blocks.header: Wounded four times in a single year
narrative_blocks.body: In the first ten months of 1915 he was wounded four times, staying with his battalion after the first three. Service in the Grenadier Guards was brutal work — one study reckoned an officer’s odds of becoming a casualty at better than eight in ten.

narrative_blocks.header: His novelist mother’s estate sent him to Eton
narrative_blocks.body: Raised at his grandfather’s castle on the Isle of Wight, he was sent to Eton and Oxford on the estate his novelist mother left when she died. At Oxford he befriended the future king, through whom he took his commission in the Grenadier Guards.

narrative_blocks.header: France decorated him; he lived to eighty-five
narrative_blocks.body: The French awarded him the Croix de Guerre in 1917, and he ended the war a captain. He stayed in the reserves for the rest of his life, took a major’s commission again in the Second World War, and died in 1975 at eighty-five.

narrative_blocks.header: Litchfield born, Rhinebeck ever after
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Litchfield in March 1796, the second of Elias Cowles’s sons, he kept a store at Rhinebeck as his father and his brother James did. He died there in November 1867, twenty-four years a widower.

narrative_blocks.header: He voted against Indian Removal in Congress
narrative_blocks.body: Elected to Congress in 1828 as an Anti-Jacksonian from the Hudson Valley, he served a single term opposing President Jackson’s policies. In 1830 he cast his vote against the Indian Removal Act, siding with those who called the forced displacement of the southeastern tribes unjust.

narrative_blocks.header: He trained at Litchfield and practiced for decades
narrative_blocks.body: He read law at the famous Litchfield Law School under Tapping Reeve and James Gould, then built a career that ran from rural Putnam County to New York City. After his single term in Congress he practiced in the city for nearly four decades, until his death.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandfather signed the Articles of Confederation
narrative_blocks.body: He came of a prominent Farmington family, and through his mother he was a grandson of Andrew Adams — a Connecticut chief justice and delegate to the Continental Congress who signed the Articles of Confederation. The lawyer’s calling ran in the blood.

narrative_blocks.header: Eleven years old when the family moved west
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Hartford in March 1798 and went with his father to Dutchess County in 1809. He took his degree at Union College in Schenectady in 1816, read law, and opened a practice in Putnam County.

narrative_blocks.header: He never married, and the line stopped
narrative_blocks.body: He died at New York in May 1873, at seventy-five, unmarried — the Cowles genealogy and the Congressional Directory agree on it. He was carried up to Rhinebeck and buried there among the family he had come to as a boy.

narrative_blocks.header: A Rhinebeck girl who married to New York
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Rhinebeck the year after her parents married, she wed Henry Adams Blyth of New York about 1862 and went down to the city with him. They had no children. She died in Manhattan in December 1914 and he outlived her by four months.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven children over nineteen years
narrative_blocks.body: She married George Esselstyn at Rhinebeck in June 1868 and bore seven children there — Louise, Catherine, Florence, Henry, Clara, Mabel and Robert, the last nineteen years after the first. She lived to eighty-two and died in 1924.

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband practised law in Dutchess thirty years
narrative_blocks.body: George Esselstyn was born at Rhinebeck a fortnight before her and died there. He practised law across Dutchess County for more than thirty years and served a term as supervisor of the town.

narrative_blocks.header: He catalogued Yale’s Greek and Roman coins
narrative_blocks.body: A physician who barely practiced, he gave his energy instead to Yale’s collection of ancient coins — tending and enlarging it, and editing at his own expense the 1880 catalogue of its Greek and Roman coins. He left his own valuable collection to the college.

narrative_blocks.header: He and his father gathered the family’s history
narrative_blocks.body: Alongside his father, he spent years collecting material for a genealogy of the Edwards family, which he had expected to publish. He also served faithfully as secretary of his Yale class.

narrative_blocks.header: Roman fever abroad broke his health for good
narrative_blocks.body: The year after his marriage he and his wife spent a year in Europe, and he came home with his constitution undermined by Roman fever, the old name for malaria. He passed the rest of his life in increasing weakness, and died at forty-four without children.

narrative_blocks.header: She followed her mother into Cincinnati's art world
narrative_blocks.body: Daughter of the ceramic artist Jane Porter Hart Dodd, she began as a teenager at her mother's side in the Women's Art Museum shows, then trained at Drexel and the Pennsylvania Academy under Howard Pyle. narrative_blocks.header: Thirty years of books, then the rainforest

narrative_blocks.header: Of four who fled Stalin, only he survived
narrative_blocks.body: A Red Army general by twenty-two, he fled his post as Soviet chargé d'affaires in Athens in 1937 as Stalin's purges swallowed his colleagues one by one. Whittaker Chambers wrote that of four Soviet agents who bolted that year, hunted by assassins, only Barmine outran them.

narrative_blocks.header: His son's school letter told him to run
narrative_blocks.body: The warning came in a letter from his fourteen-year-old son, who wrote that the family was going 'far, far away' and named the generals just executed — one of whom had lived in their building. Followed by NKVD agents, Barmine chose exile, and never saw his mother or sons again.

narrative_blocks.header: From Red Army general to American private
narrative_blocks.body: In America the former general enlisted as a forty-two-year-old private in an anti-aircraft unit, then served in the wartime OSS. He went on to run the Russian branch of Voice of America for sixteen years and to advise the U.S. Information Agency on Soviet affairs.

narrative_blocks.header: He testified that a US professor was Soviet
narrative_blocks.body: Before a Senate subcommittee in 1952 he testified that Soviet intelligence had described the scholar Owen Lattimore as 'one of our men.' His revelations made him a witness in the era's fiercest fights over communist infiltration.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote as if walking in a graveyard
narrative_blocks.body: His memoir One Who Survived opened with the confession that writing it felt like walking in a graveyard, all his friends and associates shot. He believed going public was itself a shield — that Stalin could not so easily silence a man the world was reading.

narrative_blocks.body: His great-grandfather founded Hornblower & Weeks, and his grandfather and father were partners there in turn. The old firm is gone, but the right to the Hornblower name passed down the line to him — and he heads an investment firm that carries it still.

narrative_blocks.body: At nine he was tossing a ball with his mother on the back lawn when she waved it and told him to run at her. He drove his head into her stomach and knocked her back a yard; she beamed and told him he really hit. From then on he ran the football with total abandon.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept a French painter's signed card

The two women, born thirteen days and sixteen years apart on opposite sides of the Atlantic, both made their names painting livestock, and neither ever married.

narrative_blocks.header: Her cows bought her freedom
narrative_blocks.body: The income from her paintings let her stay comfortably self-sufficient and unmarried all her life — with a studio built for her at Heartsease in 1872 and another beside an orange grove she bought in Florida. She died at Heartsease in 1904, at sixty-four.

narrative_blocks.body: Born at Heartsease, she married Edwin Smith Hubbard in 1882 and made her life at Federal Point, Florida, where she raised two children and worked in the Episcopal church and Sunday school. She belonged to the state horticultural society and the local literary club.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son carried the orchard home again
narrative_blocks.body: She brought her children back north for their schooling, and her son E. Stuart Hubbard returned each autumn to help with the LaGrange apples. He settled at Heartsease for good in 1917 and took over the apple business his grandfather had begun.

narrative_blocks.header: Hart apples went wherever good apples went
narrative_blocks.body: He took over the family business at his father's death and made the Hart orchards famous — the apples sold wherever good apples were wanted, and shipped abroad. He was the last of his generation of what was called the best-known family of apple cultivators in the country.

narrative_blocks.header: Born and died in the same house
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Heartsease and died there eighty-one years later, in a house his family had held since 1838. A graduate of Riverview Military Academy and Dartmouth, elected to Phi Beta Kappa, he never missed a class reunion.

narrative_blocks.header: Princeton's star fullback married a Morgan
narrative_blocks.body: A star fullback for Princeton, he married Sarah Morgan Gardner in 1935 at her stepfather's house in Santa Fe — a match announced only after her earlier engagement, to an assistant Navy secretary's son, was quietly broken. The marriage later ended in divorce.

narrative_blocks.header: From Madison Avenue to the Carolina sandhills
narrative_blocks.body: A Navy lieutenant in the Pacific in the war, he spent years as an account executive at a Manhattan advertising agency, left in 1960 to sell insurance, and finally set up his own consulting firm in Pinehurst. He was president of the Princeton Club of New York in the 1970s.

narrative_blocks.header: His name ran in the alumni magazine
narrative_blocks.body: He founded his own insurance firm in New York in 1962, and his advertisements became a familiar fixture in the Princeton alumni weekly for the rest of his life. He never fully retired.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirteen marathons and a selectman's seat
narrative_blocks.body: An art major and varsity hockey player at Princeton, he was a sportsman all his life — thirteen marathons, racquet sports, skiing, kayaking. He had just been elected a selectman of Mount Desert, Maine, when he died in 2011.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave his life to his old school
narrative_blocks.body: Proctor Academy set the course of his life, and he repaid it — chairing its board through several terms and difficult times. He served the American School of Tangier and the Skowhegan School of Painting and Sculpture the same way.

education.notes: Art major; varsity hockey; Ivy Club.

narrative_blocks.header: He moved Wall Street to a Connecticut Victorian
narrative_blocks.body: Chairman of his own international securities firm, he moved its headquarters off Wall Street to a quaint Victorian building on the main street of Falls Village, Connecticut — betting that technology would let business decentralize and let him escape the pressure. Two years before he died he moved it back to New York, homesick.

narrative_blocks.header: He clothed the Union Army
narrative_blocks.body: Through the entire Civil War he ran the Bureau of Clothing and Equipage in the Quartermaster-General's office — the office that put uniforms, shoes, and blankets on a million men. He never commanded in the field, and was brevetted brigadier general in 1865 for it anyway.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-one years in uniform, Seminoles to San Francisco
narrative_blocks.body: Commissioned out of West Point in 1851, he fought the Seminoles in Florida, taught mathematics and drawing at the Academy, chased Chippewa on the Minnesota frontier, and served as chief quartermaster of the Platte, of Texas, of the East, and at last of the Pacific — retiring in 1892 after forty-one years.

narrative_blocks.header: The soldier in a family of sailors
narrative_blocks.body: He came of the Perrys of New London — his grandfather a Revolutionary naval officer, his kinsman Oliver Hazard Perry the victor of Lake Erie, another kinsman the commodore who opened Japan. He alone took the Army's road, and made his war in a Washington office instead of on a deck.

narrative_blocks.header: A general who sat as a church delegate
narrative_blocks.body: In 1874 he went as a lay delegate from Nebraska to the general convention of the Episcopal Church in New York — a quartermaster on the frontier finding time for the business of the diocese. He lies at Arlington.

narrative_blocks.header: Buried between her husband and her son
narrative_blocks.body: A daughter of Augusta, Georgia, she left it only when she married General Perry, and kept his home in Washington after his retirement. Her son, a retired Army captain, lived with her and died the week before she did; she was laid at Arlington between the two of them.

narrative_blocks.header: At home with young and old alike
narrative_blocks.body: An indigestion attack turned to pneumonia and killed her in her eightieth year. Those who knew her in Augusta and Washington remembered a gifted and cultured woman, prominent in society, and as easy in the company of young people as of her own generation.

people.research_notes: Formal first name Relief; known as Lefee.

narrative_blocks.header: Her parents deeded her half a paradise
narrative_blocks.body: In 1957 her parents divided their Rubicon Bay land between their two daughters, both married to native Californians. She received the southern half — fourteen acres and its outbuildings — of the Tahoe shore her father had bought on a handshake in 1936.

narrative_blocks.header: Two months' courtship, sixty-seven years
narrative_blocks.body: She married a Californian in wartime after a courtship of only two months, and traded a childhood of Paris, skiing in Europe, and a beloved horse for the open spaces of the West. She hiked, rode, and explored the Sierra with him, and was happiest serving others.

narrative_blocks.header: A private woman married to a public man
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband's career as Reagan's natural-resources secretary drew her into an arena she never wanted. She preferred quiet walks at the family's Napa ranch, her uncle Sheldon's California landscapes, birdsong, and chocolate — though she gave her name to school boards when asked.

narrative_blocks.header: Three carrier hits, then home in the dark
narrative_blocks.body: At the Battle of the Philippine Sea in June 1944 he pressed his torpedo bomber through intense anti-aircraft fire from the Japanese fleet, scoring three hits and a near miss on an enemy carrier. He then flew three hundred miles after dark, through foul weather, and landed safely on his own ship. The Navy gave him its Cross for it.

narrative_blocks.header: A supply ship, a lifelong friend
narrative_blocks.body: He spent a month aboard a supply ship in the Pacific with a young officer named John F. Kennedy, and the two remained friends for life. He finished the war a lieutenant junior grade with a Navy Cross, an Air Medal, and three Gold Stars.

narrative_blocks.header: He built an aviation practice from nothing
narrative_blocks.body: Out of the Navy and through Harvard Law, he was hired to start a law firm's aviation department from scratch. He spent thirty more years as a litigator in antitrust and securities work, and in 1976 argued Piper v. Chris-Craft Industries before the Supreme Court.

narrative_blocks.header: 'A Descendant, But Not an Heir'
narrative_blocks.body: That was the title he gave the memoir he published near the end of his life — a Morgan grandson's plain statement of where he stood. What he wanted to leave his children, he wrote, was the law's clear view of what makes a society work, and of human nature in all its shadings of good and bad.

narrative_blocks.header: She opened the house each spring for decades
narrative_blocks.body: Given the northern half of the Tahoe property in 1957 — the house, the pier, the original seven acres — she adored the place and ran it with good humor and a firm grasp of what it took to feed an army, opening it every spring and closing it every fall for her siblings and her own growing family.

narrative_blocks.header: It left the family in 2012
narrative_blocks.body: When her health failed in 1976 her daughter took over the running of the place, and stayed at it until the land was sold out of the family in 2012. They hoped a buyer would respect the old house, but set no conditions — and expected it would be modernized or torn down.

narrative_blocks.header: She judged flowers for the whole country
narrative_blocks.body: Joining a garden club in 1951, she rose to become a nationally respected horticulturist and flower judge, taking a Garden Club of America achievement award in 1988. She served her Woodside schools and library, guided visitors at Filoli, and recorded books for the blind.

narrative_blocks.header: Born in the house that became a museum
narrative_blocks.body: He was born in 1925 in his grandfather J.P. Morgan's house on Madison Avenue — the building that is now part of the Morgan Library. He served the library as a trustee for more than fifty years, and the Metropolitan Museum for as long.

narrative_blocks.header: First American ashore on Hokkaido
narrative_blocks.body: After Pearl Harbor he went through Harvard in eighteen months and joined the Navy at nineteen, on the cruiser Pensacola — badly hit at Iwo Jima, then through the kamikazes at Okinawa. His unit occupied Hokkaido, and he was first ashore.

narrative_blocks.header: He defended the Army against Joe McCarthy
narrative_blocks.body: In the Office of the Secretary of Defense in the mid-fifties he helped defend the Army through the Army-McCarthy hearings, defying the senator across the subcommittee table. He had come there from the U.S. Attorney's office in New York.

narrative_blocks.header: He opened a halfway house in East Harlem
narrative_blocks.body: In the 1960s he founded Exodus House, a halfway house in East Harlem for men coming out of prison and out of addiction, and gave it years as a trustee. He backed human-rights lawyers and women's rights, and became a Democrat.

narrative_blocks.header: At ninety he wrote it all down
narrative_blocks.body: He titled the memoir As It Was, and published it at ninety — a century's worth of one man's view, from the Morgan house on Madison Avenue to the deck of a burning cruiser to sixty years at the same law firm. He died at ninety-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty-five years at one law firm
narrative_blocks.body: Patterson Belknap took him as an associate in 1958 and he was a partner from 1962 to 1995 and of counsel long after, still walking the halls in his nineties. The American Lawyer gave him its lifetime achievement award in 2006.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty-five years married, and eleven grandchildren
narrative_blocks.body: Victoria Lee Parsons married him at Orange in June 1948 and died in 2013. Christy, Russell, Tracy and Peter were their four, and eleven grandchildren and eight great-grandchildren came after them.

narrative_blocks.header: In the lab when DNA was young
narrative_blocks.body: She took a biology degree from Vassar in 1947 and went to work as a research assistant at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory in the earliest years of DNA research, later moving to the American Museum of Natural History. It was uncommon work for a woman of her circle and her moment.

narrative_blocks.header: She wore out her walker's bearings twice
narrative_blocks.body: 'Count your blessings and keep moving,' she liked to say, and she meant it — an afternoon walk was the best part of her day, and when a walker became necessary she wore the bearings out of it twice. She lived to ninety-one.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine months across the Pacific
narrative_blocks.body: She sailed with her husband on many oceans, culminating in a nine-month passage across the Pacific in 1991, and the two were among the founding families of the Stratton Mountain ski area. For fifty-three years they lived in a Colonial farmhouse in Greenwich that they restored themselves.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept a highway out of the Sierra
narrative_blocks.body: As Reagan's natural-resources secretary — the only cabinet member to serve all eight years — he talked the governor out of the Mammoth Pass Highway, which would have cut the Sierra wilderness in two, and out of the road to a proposed Disney ski resort at Mineral King. Redwood National Park was established on his watch, and the Dos Rios Dam was not built.

narrative_blocks.header: He crossed all fifty high passes, both ways
narrative_blocks.body: He started a mule-packing outfit in the southern Sierra in 1929 and ran it more than a decade, taking Sierra Club members into the mountains. He took pride in having crossed every one of the fifty highest Sierra passes — in both directions.

narrative_blocks.header: He played baseball at the Berlin Olympics
narrative_blocks.body: Captain of the Stanford baseball team, he played for the United States exhibition side at the 1936 Berlin Games. In the war he was a Navy lieutenant in the landings at Sicily, Iwo Jima, Okinawa, and Palau; he married in 1943 after a courtship of two months.

narrative_blocks.header: Twice decorated for naval intelligence
narrative_blocks.body: An MIT graduate of 1937, he was twice decorated as a naval intelligence officer during the war, and came home to the Bay Area in 1946. He served as president of the family's estate company, founded on his grandfather's spice business, and of Leslie Salt.

narrative_blocks.header: She cast garden pots from estate originals
narrative_blocks.body: In 1989 Cecily founded the company now called Pennoyer Newman, casting weatherproof garden planters in resin mixed with crushed marble and rock. She began in an old squash court at Locust Valley, making molds of her in-laws' garden pots; Martha Stewart's gardens use them now.

narrative_blocks.header: Wall Hall urns and Nile River jars
narrative_blocks.body: Her first models came from her husband's grandfather, J. P. Morgan Jr.: the Nile River jars he brought back from Egypt, the urns from his rose garden at Wall Hall in Aldenham, and a Della Robbia planter the family once lent to the Metropolitan Museum.

narrative_blocks.header: A master's in art history, and Artworld
narrative_blocks.body: Cecily took a master's in art history at C.W. Post, wrote for the journal Artworld, and worked with the International Foundation for Art Research in New York and Blunden Associates of London.

narrative_blocks.header: On Nassau County's arts board
narrative_blocks.body: Once her children were grown, Cecily sat on the board of the Nassau County Office of Cultural Development and worked with the Long Island Community Trust and the Hutton House Lectures at C.W. Post.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty years in the Locust Valley stables
narrative_blocks.body: Cecily married Paul Pennoyer Jr. in 1949, and they moved into the former stables of his childhood home at Locust Valley. They lived there more than sixty years and raised five children among horses, dogs, crows and raccoons.

narrative_blocks.header: Summers riding on Naushon Island
narrative_blocks.body: Cecily spent her summers walking and riding horses on Naushon Island and sailing the Arabella off the New England coast. In 1989 her daughter Jennifer married Raymond Emerson, whose parents kept a house on Naushon.

birth.note: Birth year calculated from age 83 at death (June 2006); approximate.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-five Bermuda races and one Pacific
narrative_blocks.body: An accomplished sailor who owned a series of yachts mostly named Chasseur, he raced across the Northeast, Europe, and the Caribbean, including twenty-five Bermuda races. In 1991 he sailed from New York through the Panama Canal and across the Pacific to New Zealand.

narrative_blocks.header: He built a ski mountain for families
narrative_blocks.body: He was among the founders of Stratton Mountain, which opened in 1961, and served as its president and chairman. His vision made it one of the first family-oriented ski resorts in the industry, and he later led the national ski-area association.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave the yacht club a home
narrative_blocks.body: As commodore of the New York Yacht Club he was instrumental in establishing Harbour Court at Newport as the club's home. His love of the sea ran deeper still — he chaired the board of the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution and sat on Mystic Seaport's.

narrative_blocks.header: He collected other men's sailing letters
narrative_blocks.body: He gathered and annotated an anthology of sailing manuscripts, published in 1964 as Life Under Sail, and in his last years was writing a historical novel set in the Civil War. He sang in his church choir, fished, and painted.

narrative_blocks.header: At seventeen he came west with letters
narrative_blocks.body: A Cambridge boy, he arrived in 1945 to meet the California uncles he'd only heard of, carrying letters of introduction to his late father's friends. His uncle Anson took him in hand — checked which letters he'd delivered, walked him through the museums and clubs, and set him among the old family friends who had known his grandmother.

narrative_blocks.header: Asked to write the house's history down
narrative_blocks.body: When the university's president moved into his uncle's old house, he and his wife wanted to know whose house it had been. What the nephew wrote for them, Notes on the Blakes in England and America, became the foundation of nearly everything since known about the family — and he later placed their circulating letters with a historical society, where anyone can read them.

narrative_blocks.header: She opened her own firm in 1952
narrative_blocks.body: A fine-arts graduate of Berkeley's wartime class of '47, she founded Elizabeth Denton Interiors in 1952 and was listed in the first edition of Who's Who in American Women. She held her profession's accreditation for nearly forty years.

narrative_blocks.header: Yemen, Burma, and a New Hampshire farm
narrative_blocks.body: She and her husband spent nearly forty-nine years traveling — Yemen, Iran, Papua New Guinea, Burma, India — always returning to their farm in New Hampshire. Between trips she took blue ribbons for flower arranging in national garden-club shows.

narrative_blocks.header: He medaled at the Olympic Stadium in wartime
narrative_blocks.body: In September 1944, in the last months of Finland's war, he took a medal in the pole vault at the national championships, held in the Helsinki Olympic Stadium. He was the only vaulter from his club to medal at those games in the whole decade.

narrative_blocks.header: He came with a Helsinki law degree
narrative_blocks.body: He held a law degree from the University of Helsinki, then studied at MIT, where in 1954 he published a study of cooperative apartments in Sweden. He spent his American career planning Boston, on the staff of its Redevelopment Authority.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote for the Finns of Massachusetts
narrative_blocks.body: He stayed close to the Finnish-American community after emigrating, writing for Raivaaja, the Finnish-language newspaper published in Fitchburg.

career.notes: Documented on the staff from 1957.

narrative_blocks.header: He took over steam just as steam died
narrative_blocks.body: In December 1938 he was elected president of the Baldwin Locomotive Works, which had built more steam locomotives than any concern on earth — better than seventy thousand of them. The market was already turning to diesel, and Baldwin never took the share of it that it needed.

narrative_blocks.header: Same school, same steel works, same pulley company
narrative_blocks.body: His father had come out of Yale's Sheffield Scientific School to run Midvale Steel and then to preside over the American Pulley Company. The son took his own Sheffield degree in 1901, went to Midvale as a chemist, and was president of American Pulley by 1919 — the same three steps in the same order.

narrative_blocks.header: The name Roosevelt could set him off
narrative_blocks.body: The mention of Franklin Roosevelt was enough to start him on a tirade, which his grandson thought typical of the conservative businessmen of the day. In the summer of 1952 the two of them sat in the North Haven living room with the radio on, counting delegates at the Republican convention until Eisenhower had the number he needed.

narrative_blocks.header: His job got lumber to a wartime island
narrative_blocks.body: The family took a house on North Haven, off the Maine coast, during the Second World War. Building materials were nearly impossible to come by, but his place at Baldwin let him arrange to have what he wanted shipped out to the island.

narrative_blocks.header: He put his grandson on a new locomotive
narrative_blocks.body: Around 1949 he walked his grandson through the Baldwin plant, showed him the office, and put him up on a locomotive fresh off the floor. He gave the boy a rowboat for the Maine summers and paid for sailing lessons; the boy was grateful, and disappointed there was no outboard motor.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at the wartime island house
narrative_blocks.body: He had been through a heart attack, poor circulation in his legs, and cancer of the tongue; the family counted six heart attacks in all. The last took him in the summer of 1963 at North Haven, and at the funeral one of his sisters told his grandson how fond of him the old man had been.

narrative_blocks.header: She held the baby and the dementia lifted
narrative_blocks.body: Days before she died, her chauffeur drove her from the convalescent home to a house in Gwynedd Valley to meet her great-grandson, five weeks old and named for her husband and her son. She stayed in the back seat; they brought him out and put him in her arms, and while she held him the dementia went. Then she said it was time to go home, and that was the last they saw of her alive.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother threw her a dance at eighteen
narrative_blocks.body: She came out in Philadelphia in the spring of 1901, at a dance her mother gave for her at the Natatorium Hall. Seven years later she married in the Episcopal church at Rydal, and the reception was held at Avila, her father's summer place nearby, which is gone now.

narrative_blocks.header: They made a house from a horse shed
narrative_blocks.body: Her summers ran first to Northeast and Southwest Harbors and then out to North Haven, on the Maine coast. There they built a house from a horse shed near the ferry landing, looking down the Fox Island Thoroughfare.

narrative_blocks.header: A picnic lunch in a parked car, weekly
narrative_blocks.body: Near the end her daughter Polly came once a week for a lunch eaten in the car — the chauffeur collected her from the Frigate Book Store, and then found somewhere different to park each time. Her grandchildren called her Ducky, and remembered playing Go Fish with her at the writing desk on Gravers Lane.

narrative_blocks.header: He married four months out of Yale
narrative_blocks.body: He took his degree in the June of 1938 and married Isabel Kearny Day that October at Christ Church in New Haven — the church his mother's father had built the east end of and served twenty years as rector. Her father had clerked at the law firm his father would make partner in.

narrative_blocks.header: He married her sister after she died
narrative_blocks.body: Isabel died in 1966 at forty-seven. The next year he married Jane, her younger sister — who had stood as maid of honor at their wedding twenty-nine years earlier, and whose own marriage to a naval ensign had ended. She outlived him by eleven years and is buried a Hooker.

narrative_blocks.header: The third Thomas Hooker had no son
narrative_blocks.body: There had been a Thomas Hooker in this New Haven family for three generations — his grandfather in the banks, his father in the law, and himself. Neither of his marriages produced a child, and the name stopped with him in 1994.

narrative_blocks.header: Five days to get out of Munich
narrative_blocks.body: She had read German at Vassar and was twenty-one, in Germany on a student exchange, when the Wehrmacht crossed into Poland. It took her five days to get out of Munich; she went north through Scandinavia and came home from Denmark on a Swedish liner.

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband was dead at forty-seven
narrative_blocks.body: She married Hamp Barclay in the September of 1943 and they raised four children in New Haven. He died in 1958 at forty-seven; she was forty, and she did not marry again in the fifty-seven years she had left.

narrative_blocks.header: The garden center, the seamen's society, the hospital
narrative_blocks.body: She gave New Haven half a century of board work — president of the Edgerton Garden Center, president of the Woman's Seamen's Friend Society of Connecticut, president of the Gaylord Hospital auxiliary and a trustee of the hospital besides. She sat on the board of the Grove Street Cemetery, where her family lies.

narrative_blocks.header: She finished the crossword into her nineties
narrative_blocks.body: Well into her nineties she kept a monthly book group, played bridge every week, and finished the New York Times crossword daily. In her last months she worked them with her children and grandchildren, who thought her remarkable at it and themselves rather less so.
