narrative_blocks.header: They lay on the bathroom floor until quiet
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband ran the political section of the American embassy in Beirut, and in the Lebanese revolution of 1958 their apartment house came under fire. They spent several hours on the bathroom floor waiting for the shooting to end, and were posted back to Washington soon after.

narrative_blocks.header: Lucky in her work, and she said so
narrative_blocks.body: Out of Vassar she went to the British Information Service in New York, and in 1952 to the State Department's Office of Public Opinion Studies in Washington, where she met her husband. She said often how lucky she had been to have jobs she enjoyed that much, with colleagues she liked that well.

narrative_blocks.header: She was not outdoorsy until she was widowed
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband died at sixty-one in 1976, and as a widow she took up walking trips — Britain mostly, and France and Italy. She had never thought herself an outdoor person; she wrote in her fiftieth reunion notes that some of her happiest hours were spent hiking up and down five-thousand-year-old footpaths and clambering over countless muddy stiles. She was still going into her eighties.

narrative_blocks.header: She took up acting at eighty-six
narrative_blocks.body: At eighty-six she left Washington to be near her daughter and moved into a retirement community outside Boston. She joined a poetry group and a walking program — and decided it was time to start acting, and performed in several plays for the place.

narrative_blocks.header: Cousin to the Adirondack Murray
narrative_blocks.body: Nellie Murray was born at Madison in 1845 and married William Eliot Goodyear in March 1864. Rev. Jos. Murray, whose Adirondack writing made the name, was her cousin.

narrative_blocks.header: She died at thirty-two with the girls small
narrative_blocks.body: Nellie Goodyear died in June 1877, thirteen years married. Charlotte was twelve and Lizzie ten, and their father outlived her by only four years.

notable.notable_blurb: American poet (1830-1886) of Amherst MA

burial.plot_notes: West Cemetery, Amherst — the Dickinson family plot

narrative_blocks.header: Seven poems printed, seventeen hundred kept
narrative_blocks.body: Only seven of her poems appeared in her lifetime, all of them unsigned, one in A Masque of Poets — the 1878 anthology that printed every contributor anonymously. She said one of the seven had been stolen from her, and her sister found nearly eighteen hundred more sewn into little books after she died.

narrative_blocks.header: Eleven editions in under two years
narrative_blocks.body: The first volume came out in 1890, four years after her death, and went through eleven printings before it was two years old. A complete edition did not appear until 1955.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept the herbarium her textbook set
narrative_blocks.body: The botany she learned at Amherst Academy came out of Almira Lincoln's Familiar Lectures, the book that told her to make a herbarium. She kept hers for the rest of her life, and the pressed flowers turn up all through the poems.

narrative_blocks.header: Her school sent her to college lectures
narrative_blocks.body: Amherst Academy had grown out of Amherst College and sent its pupils to hear the college lecture on astronomy, botany, chemistry and geology. Heman Humphrey was president through her first years there, and had won the college its charter.

narrative_blocks.header: Sent forty poems and fifty letters to Bowles
narrative_blocks.body: She met Samuel Bowles III at her brother Austin’s home about 1858 and over the next decade sent him some forty poems and fifty letters, most of them in 1861 and 1862, her most prolific years. He printed a handful anonymously in the Springfield Republican but never any from the letters she sent him directly.

narrative_blocks.header: The breach healed at her father's funeral
narrative_blocks.body: She and Bowles had a falling-out in 1863 that lasted eleven years, despite his continued visits to her brother Austin next door at The Evergreens. The breach ended when her father Edward died in 1874 — Bowles was the only non-family member she spoke to at the funeral, and she wrote thanking him for his kindness shortly after.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran embassy politics when the shooting started
narrative_blocks.body: He was head of the political section at the American embassy in Beirut from 1956, and in the Lebanese revolution of 1958 the apartment house he lived in came under fire. He and his wife spent hours on the bathroom floor waiting for it to stop; Washington pulled them home soon after. He was dead at sixty-one, in 1976.

narrative_blocks.header: He turned down Harvard and a university presidency
narrative_blocks.body: Harvard offered him the head of its philosophy department and California offered him its presidency. He said he was too fond of Yale and of New Haven to leave, and held the chair there twenty-eight years.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave up the chair for Congress
narrative_blocks.body: He retired from Yale in 1933 to take Connecticut's at-large seat in the House, and spent his single term a bitter critic of Roosevelt's New Deal. He lost two bids to get back.

narrative_blocks.header: He was the Red Cross's Italian historian
narrative_blocks.body: In the war he served under the American Red Cross's Italian Commission as inspector and historian, with the rank of major and deputy commissioner. He wrote the story of it in 1920, and gave Yale sixteen albums of the photographs he had taken among Italy's refugees.

narrative_blocks.header: His Nietzsche review brought seven letters back
narrative_blocks.body: In the May of 1926 he reviewed the complete works of Nietzsche, and seven letters came back to him about it from the Yale community and beyond. He kept them nineteen years and then gave them to the university.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught at Bryn Mawr before her birth
narrative_blocks.body: He was an associate professor at Bryn Mawr for two years at the turn of the century, seventeen years before his daughter was born. She took her own degree there in 1938.

narrative_blocks.header: She studied art while her husband taught nearby
narrative_blocks.body: In 1904 she was living in Berkeley and studying at the Mark Hopkins Art Institute, while her husband was a professor at the university across the bay. The year after, they went east to New Haven and did not come back.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brother gave the state two thousand acres
narrative_blocks.body: She bought a house on Beacon Street in Boston in 1909 and her brother Bradley Palmer, an attorney, moved into it; she sold it to him eleven years later. He never married, and when he died in 1946 the rest of his Topsfield land went to Massachusetts for a park.

narrative_blocks.header: Only relatives came to the chapel
narrative_blocks.body: She married at St. Elizabeth's Chapel near Tuxedo Park in the June of 1930 — her sister the only attendant, his brother the best man, and nobody present but family. Five years later she took up residence in Reno and had the decree on the twenty-sixth of December, 1935.

narrative_blocks.header: Two more husbands after the Reno decree
narrative_blocks.body: She married James Bogart Tailer the year after the divorce, and when that ended she married George Townsend Adee in 1946. She had no children by any of the three, and died in 1975.

narrative_blocks.header: She married her first husband's cousin
narrative_blocks.body: She married Edgerton Warburton in the May of 1923, at eighteen. When that ended she married his cousin — Captain John Wanamaker, whose grandfather had built the department store — in the August of 1932, and was a widow inside two years. Her third husband married her on the day his own divorce came through.

narrative_blocks.header: He crossed the Channel at fifty feet
narrative_blocks.body: He was one of the original C-47 pilots trained as a Pathfinder — the crews sent ahead of D-Day to drop teams who would set radio beacons for the paratroopers behind them. On the sixth of June 1944 he flew in the first wave, twenty aircraft carrying two thousand men, low over the water to stay under German radar, then climbing for the drop. Hundreds more C-47s and thirteen thousand paratroopers came in behind him.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-one bomber missions, then Smirnoff
narrative_blocks.body: In Korea he flew B-25s — fifty-one combat missions across three large operations, and a Distinguished Flying Cross out of it. Then he went to work for Smirnoff Vodka, and was their chief pilot for eighteen years.

narrative_blocks.header: Duxford honored him seventy-five years later
narrative_blocks.body: He went back to England in the June of 2019, to Duxford, for the seventy-fifth anniversary of the invasion he had flown the first aircraft of. The place turned out for him.

narrative_blocks.header: Anina married his cousin first
narrative_blocks.body: Anina Paepcke had been married to Leonard Woods since 1948 — a first cousin of his, the son of his father's sister. She married him in 1963 and was buried a Hamilton; her daughter by Woods became his stepdaughter.

narrative_blocks.header: Her sons ran Yale's money and its magazine
narrative_blocks.body: Henry Coit Kingsley was elected treasurer of Yale in July 1862 and held the office until his death in 1886. William Lathrop Kingsley edited the New Englander for thirty-five years. She died seven months before Henry took the post.

narrative_blocks.header: Her eldest drowned off a Sandusky wharf
narrative_blocks.body: George Theodore Kingsley went to Sandusky on business and stepped onto the wharf at midnight on 9 June 1842 to catch the Cleveland steamboat. The night was dark and the bay rough; he fell, tangled in the cloak over his arm, and drowned. He was twenty-nine and unmarried.

narrative_blocks.header: She married the Latin professor in 1811
narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Norwich in 1789 and married James Luce Kingsley that September, ten years into a Yale career that would run half a century. Her maiden name went to two of her children, Henry Coit Kingsley and Elizabeth Coit Kingsley Blake.

narrative_blocks.header: Tuxedo Park, Dolphin Cove, Lighthouse Point
narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Tuxedo Park in 1922 and married David Blair Hamilton there in 1945. Later she kept house at Dolphin Cove in Stamford, and she died at Lighthouse Point in Florida, the widow of a second husband, Frederick Norman.

narrative_blocks.header: Gifts in her memory went to Mashomack
narrative_blocks.body: Her memorial service was private. Gifts in her memory went to the Nature Conservancy for the Mashomack Preserve on Shelter Island. She was survived by a daughter and a son, Lanier and Pierson Hamilton, and a grandson.

narrative_blocks.header: He was the governor's executive secretary at twenty-four
narrative_blocks.body: He came out of Yale Law and was admitted to the bar in the June of 1884. Seven months later Governor Harrison made him his executive secretary, for a two-year term. He went back to New Haven in 1887 and practiced law there the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: Father and son, secretaries of their classes
narrative_blocks.body: He kept the records of the Yale class of 1882 and compiled its sexennial book. His father had been secretary of the class of 1848 from 1873 until the day he died, and had published the Osborne family genealogy besides.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brother shot the college clock
narrative_blocks.body: She came to New Haven with her aunt and her brother Ogden Rood, who put an arrow into the face of the college clock in his sophomore year and stopped its hands. Nobody saw him do it, but the arrow carried his initials and Yale rusticated him. He was so furious he refused to go back and finished at Princeton instead.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a man four years younger
narrative_blocks.body: She was twenty-seven and he was twenty-three. She had come into the Blake household as a friend of the sisters and married out of it, and his work interested her the whole of their nine years — she was his supporter as much as his wife.

narrative_blocks.header: She spent her life fighting the vote
narrative_blocks.body: She wrote The Blakes of 77 Elm Street in 1924, the book most of her family's history comes down through. She was also, in her later years, a leading woman opponent of women's suffrage, and an anti-vice campaigner.

bio.bio_blurb: Hampton Institute teacher; Providence charity manager

career.notes: Greek and geometry; The Southern Workman.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother died before his second birthday
narrative_blocks.body: He was born in New Haven in the February of 1867, the year his father left Vermont to cover Ogden Rood's chair at Columbia. The next year the family went to Cornell, and the cold at Ithaca broke his mother's health; she went back to her sister's house at Providence and died there days before he turned two.

narrative_blocks.header: Never physically very strong, and always thinking
narrative_blocks.body: His sister wrote that he was never physically very strong — tall but very slight, and his active brain was always too much for his body. It did not keep him out of the freshman-sophomore football game his first year at Brown, where he edited the Brunonian and was, she said, very active in all dramatic affairs of the college.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the law degree and taught Greek
narrative_blocks.body: He came out of Harvard Law and decided not to practice it — he preferred the theory — and went to the Hampton Institute in Virginia instead, the school built to teach freed slaves, where Booker T. Washington had been a student. Hampton had been taking Native American boys since 1878, and he was assistant disciplinarian over them. He taught Greek and geometry and wrote for the school's magazine.

narrative_blocks.header: His sister bought a museum in his name
narrative_blocks.body: He was at Hampton one year, and dead at thirty-five. A year after, his sister gave the school five thousand dollars to found an Indian museum in his memory; it opened in 1905 and grew to thousands of objects. It is part of the Hampton University Museum now — the oldest African American museum in the country.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran Providence charity at twenty-five
narrative_blocks.body: He came back to Providence in the June of 1892 and took over as general manager of the Providence Society for Organizing Charity. The society is still going.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote a comic opera for Brown
narrative_blocks.body: In 1894 he helped write a comic opera and the college put it on. Priscilla, or, a Maid of Brown had the daughter of Brown's first president courted by a run of suitors in 1776. It went over very well.

narrative_blocks.header: She was in the Atlantic boats with children
narrative_blocks.body: She went with her daughter and her two granddaughters on the Republic in the January of 1909, bound for Europe, and was put into a lifeboat twice in the dark and a heavy sea off Nantucket. She had been a widow since 1877, when her husband died at thirty-one in Chicago, leaving her one child. She had moved to Buffalo in 1887 to live with his sister.

bio.bio_blurb: Pianist trained at the Brussels Conservatory

career.notes: Trained at the Brussels Conservatory.

narrative_blocks.header: Her ship was struck in fog off Nantucket
narrative_blocks.body: In the January of 1909 she sailed for Europe with her mother and her two small girls. Before dawn on the first night out the Italian liner Florida came out of the fog and struck the Republic amidships, and they were put into lifeboats twice in a heavy Atlantic sea before another ship took them off. Six people died in the collision; about fifteen hundred were saved.

narrative_blocks.header: The first ship saved by wireless
narrative_blocks.body: The Republic carried the new Marconi set and sent the first distress call in the history of the sea. Ships came out of the fog for it all day, and she went down the next afternoon — the largest vessel ever lost to that point. The industry decided lifeboats for everyone were unnecessary, and held that view until the Titanic.

narrative_blocks.header: She trained for the concert stage at Brussels
narrative_blocks.body: She prepared for a career as a pianist at the Brussels Conservatory of Music. She never stopped crossing the Atlantic after the Republic — many times over, and once the whole way round the world.

career.notes: Cancer research and therapy to retirement.

narrative_blocks.header: He brought hypnosis back from Paris
narrative_blocks.body: In the summer of 1892 he sat in on clinics in psychiatry and hypnosis in Paris and was elected to the Société de Psychologie et Hypnologie; in September he joined the International Congress of Experimental Psychology at University College London. He was among the first in America to use hypnosis therapeutically. He had gone over to study the heart under Theodor Schott at Bad Nauheim.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote a novel under another name
narrative_blocks.body: He put out better than thirty medical monographs under his own name — The Metabolic Theory of Cancer, The Psychoneurosis of the War. Then, as Prescott Locke, he published a fictionalised case history of the pathology of religious evangelism, and called it The Conversion of Hamilton Wheeler.

narrative_blocks.header: His father left the manuscript unfinished
narrative_blocks.body: Dr. Cyrenius Wakefield spent his life on the family's genealogy and died with it in manuscript. His son took it up, went to England in 1892 to work out the family's English origin, and published The Wakefield Memorial in 1897 after twelve years. He opened it with Daniel Webster: those who do not look upon themselves as a link connecting the Past with the Future do not perform their duty to the world.

narrative_blocks.header: He was thirteen on his first Atlantic crossing
narrative_blocks.body: He crossed for the Paris exposition of 1878 and never afterward passed a summer without travelling somewhere — the States, Canada, Britain, the continent. He was a Republican in politics and, he said, a liberal in sentiment but a non-sectarian independent.

narrative_blocks.header: She was a small girl in the lifeboat
narrative_blocks.body: She was one of the two little girls her mother took aboard the Republic in the January of 1909, bound for Europe. The ship was struck in fog before dawn on the first night out, and they were handed twice between boats in a heavy sea before they were safe.

narrative_blocks.header: He was a marine for one day
narrative_blocks.body: The Corps accepted him on the thirtieth of April, 1918, and posted him from New York to Parris Island on the first of May. That night the French cruiser La Gloire came out of dense fog off the Delaware coast and cut through the steamer carrying him like paper. Sixty-seven were lost and he was one of them, in his twenty-second year.

narrative_blocks.header: They married on the day the ship sailed
narrative_blocks.body: He had come out of Yale and trained at Plattsburg. He married Elizabeth Wakefield the day the ship sailed that took him off to the service, and he was dead inside two days.

narrative_blocks.header: The tallest pillar in the whole yard
narrative_blocks.body: His mother's people put up a monument for him in the Westerly District at Trinity Church Cemetery — the tallest thing standing in it. His wife lies near him under a simple marker. She died in 1964, forty-six years after the two days they had.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother left Williams a million dollars
narrative_blocks.body: His father and his grandfather had both gone to Williams. In 1942 his mother's estate gave the college one million four hundred thousand dollars — everything she had, plus the surplus of her trusts — to found a fund for needy students, named for her husband and her son.

narrative_blocks.header: The Kemps came out of County Cavan
narrative_blocks.body: His mother's father George Kemp came over from County Cavan in 1834 with a widowed mother and five brothers and sisters, and went into a New York drug house founded in 1808. He and his brothers ended up owning it — Lanman and Kemp, which is still selling Florida Water out of New Jersey. The fortune bought 720 Fifth Avenue, where Abercrombie and Fitch stands now, and the Buckingham Hotel, which came down for Saks.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandfather was tried for preaching Methodist
narrative_blocks.body: The Rev. Stephen Tyng organized the Church of the Holy Trinity at Madison and Forty-second in 1865 and was chaplain of the Twelfth New York in the war. The church put him on trial for preaching in a Methodist pulpit. He left the ministry in 1881, went to Paris to run Equitable's office there, and died president of the American Chamber of Commerce.

narrative_blocks.header: He rode an ox to Illinois
narrative_blocks.body: He left Watertown in the May of 1837 and went west by Chicago, LaSalle, and a boat down the Illinois River to Pekin. There was no stagecoach to Bloomington, so an ox team carried his trunk the rest of the way and he walked beside it. He worked his brother's farm until November and then taught school.

narrative_blocks.header: He called himself a doctor without training
narrative_blocks.body: His brother Zera was a real physician, riding fifty miles to treat the fevers, and people who could not get an appointment came to Cyrenius instead. He made them patent medicines and took the title. He had not a day of medical training in his life.

narrative_blocks.header: A rat poison ad between two cake recipes
narrative_blocks.body: He published almanacs to sell the medicines — moon phases, farming advice, short stories that always ended with somebody needing a Wakefield product. In the 1879 domestic recipes section an advertisement for Browen's Rat Killer sits between two cakes.

narrative_blocks.header: The balsam had potassium carbonate in it
narrative_blocks.body: Blackberry Balsam was twelve per cent alcohol, blackberry root, oak bark, camphor — and potassium carbonate, which is what wood ash and soft soap are made of, and which is poison. Another ingredient, culvers root, causes vomiting and violent diarrhoea. He sold it for dysentery and for teething children, and a New York firm was still selling it in the 1990s.

narrative_blocks.header: Two fires took the business in three years
narrative_blocks.body: His house burned in the February of 1852 and he carried no insurance on it. In the October of 1855 eight buildings went up on the Phoenix Block, two of them his; the new fire department had buckets, ladders, and hooks, and the insurance covered two thousand dollars of seventeen. He rebuilt both times, and put a fourth storey on the second one.

narrative_blocks.header: He died of what had killed his brother
narrative_blocks.body: Zera's lungs filled from thirty years of other people's fevers, and he was dead thirty-six hours after he took ill in 1848. Thirty-seven years later a congestive chill and pleuro-pneumonia took Cyrenius the same way, a week from first symptom to grave.

narrative_blocks.header: She married her neighbour and schoolmate
narrative_blocks.body: They had grown up next door to each other at Watertown and sat in the same schoolroom. He came back from Illinois to marry her in the August of 1843 and they made the month-long trip west two weeks after the wedding, to eighty acres in DeWitt County. She bore him seven children there and in Bloomington.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty hours a week selling sewing machines
narrative_blocks.body: In 1940 he was a district salesman for a retail sewing machine agency at McMinnville, Oregon, working sixty hours a week, fifty-two weeks a year. He and Lucille rented a house for twenty-five dollars a month and had a two-year-old. Ten years later he had his own real estate office at Glendale.

narrative_blocks.header: The draft board wrote down brown hair
narrative_blocks.body: His 1940 registration puts him at five feet ten, a hundred and seventy-five pounds, light complexion, brown hair, blue eyes. His son says the blue was more than that — it was intense.

narrative_blocks.header: She went to Pontiac and met a Hooker
narrative_blocks.body: She was a coal miner's daughter, one of six children in Ira and Cordelia Neal's house. After high school she went up to Pontiac to stay with her sister Idabelle, and there she met Howard Hooker. They married in 1936, when she was twenty.

narrative_blocks.header: A soldier's daughter widowed by the epidemic
narrative_blocks.body: Her father, Medad Lyman, had fought at Louisburg in the old French war before keeping an ill-fated New Haven inn that left his estate insolvent. She married William Joseph Whiting in 1784 and lost him to the scarlet fever ten years later, then raised their children through thirty-five years of widowhood.

narrative_blocks.header: The Whiting mother of an artistic dynasty
narrative_blocks.body: A New Haven Whiting, she married the young Henry Flagg while he was still a Yale undergraduate and followed him between Connecticut and South Carolina for decades. She bore seven children, among them three painters and the mother of the Vanderbilt matriarch, and through her ran the old Connecticut blood.

narrative_blocks.header: A Carolina aristocrat who became New Haven's mayor
narrative_blocks.body: Born near Charleston and aristocratic to the bone, he moved between South Carolina and New Haven all his life, yet always called himself a South Carolinian. He served five years as mayor of New Haven and a term in the state senate, and kept up his daily fencing practice into old age, ready at any moment for a duel.

narrative_blocks.header: He fought the Commodore's steamships for New Haven
narrative_blocks.body: When Cornelius Vanderbilt's steamships began cutting fares and squeezing New Haven's trade, Flagg helped found the Citizen's Line to fight back and keep the city's commerce its own. Two generations later his granddaughter Alice would marry the Commodore's grandson.

narrative_blocks.header: A Southerner who stood for the Union
narrative_blocks.body: Though a proud South Carolinian, his devotion to the Union ran deeper. In 1832 he stood beside his friend James Petigru against the Nullifiers who would have had the state defy Washington, and he held that line to the last.

narrative_blocks.header: His half-brother was the painter Washington Allston
narrative_blocks.body: His mother's first marriage made him the younger half-brother of Washington Allston, the great Romantic painter. It was Allston who taught the next generation of Flaggs to paint, seeding an artistic streak that ran for a century through the family.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: His gravestone at Jamestown, New York, recording that he fell serving the nation.

narrative_blocks.header: He chose the sea over the family studio
narrative_blocks.body: While his brothers painted and preached, he went to sea, marrying Olivia Sherman and raising five children between voyages. He had reached the rank of commander and retired before the war called him back for the last time.

narrative_blocks.header: He died for the Union in 1862
narrative_blocks.body: When the Civil War came he was recalled to service, and in 1862 he died of a disease contracted in the Union cause. His gravestone records that he fell 'while serving the nation' — a commander of the United States Navy to the end.

narrative_blocks.header: Her sons became New York bankers and cashiers
narrative_blocks.body: A daughter of the Flagg family, she married the merchant George Sherman and raised a line of New York financial men — sons who became bank cashiers and Produce Exchange officers. Like several of her kin, she carried the middle name Allston, for the painter uncle the family revered.

narrative_blocks.header: A child prodigy trained by Washington Allston
narrative_blocks.body: He drew likenesses of his schoolmates for fifty cents apiece, and won over his doubtful parents only when his portrait of a Charleston bishop astonished the city. At fifteen he went to Boston to study under his uncle, the great Romantic painter Washington Allston.

narrative_blocks.header: A New York patron sent him to Europe
narrative_blocks.body: At eighteen his history paintings at the National Academy caught the eye of Luman Reed, New York's most generous art patron, who bought them and financed a season of study in England, France, and Italy. Eleven of the young man's 'ideal' pictures hung in Reed's gallery beside works by Cole and Durand.

narrative_blocks.header: He swapped queens to paint 'Lady Jane Grey'
narrative_blocks.body: His best-known picture, 'Lady Jane Grey Preparing for Execution,' began as a portrait of Mary, Queen of Scots — until he changed the subject midway, writing to his patron that Mary 'was too old at the time of her execution to make an interesting picture.' It made him famous young, though his renown faded as history painting fell from fashion.

narrative_blocks.header: A Northern painter of the Southern gentry
narrative_blocks.body: Though New Haven–born, he made his best living in the 1850s painting the planters and politicians of Charleston — among them a governor's wife in a life-size, six-by-nine-foot portrait that still hangs in her old drawing room. Many of his sitters were old friends of his father, who had stood against the nullifiers of South Carolina.

narrative_blocks.header: The Civil War sent him to London
narrative_blocks.body: His loyalties split between the North of his birth and the South of his living, he left the country as war came and spent five years painting in London. There he made portraits and literary subjects — a Hester Prynne, a 'Columbus and the Egg' — before returning home to New Haven in 1866.

narrative_blocks.header: He took Holy Orders, then returned to paint
narrative_blocks.body: Late in life he studied theology and entered the ministry, like his brothers, before returning to his brushes in his final years. He retired to Nantucket at sixty-three and painted on until his death at eighty, a motto above his fireplace: that he who makes haste to be rich shall not be innocent.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: His hand-cut stone wine cellar (1859) on Lower Twin Creek at Buena Vista, Ohio.

cross_connections.display_label: was his nephew, who inherited his vast Ohio estate

narrative_blocks.header: The Flagg who wrote instead of painted
narrative_blocks.body: Where his brothers took up the brush, he took up the pen. Trained as a lawyer in New Haven, he made his name as a writer, scholar, and man of affairs — and as the family’s rare example of financial stability.

narrative_blocks.header: His sister married him to a wine heiress
narrative_blocks.body: His sister, a Cincinnati matchmaker who had already steered her daughter toward a Vanderbilt, arranged his match with Eliza Longworth, a daughter of the wine millionaire Nicholas Longworth and nearly a decade his senior. The marriage brought no children but a great fortune, and drew him into his father-in-law's vineyards.

narrative_blocks.header: He grew wine on ten thousand Ohio acres
narrative_blocks.body: He threw himself into his father-in-law's wine business, building a hand-cut stone cellar on Lower Twin Creek in 1859 and assembling an estate of some ten thousand acres above the Ohio River. When phylloxera ravaged the vines, he spent three years in Europe hunting a cure, and wrote 'Three Seasons in European Vineyards.'

narrative_blocks.header: His last book appeared the day he died
narrative_blocks.body: He wrote fiction set around his beloved Ohio cabin, served in the state legislature, and turned in old age to finance and philosophy. His final work, 'Youga,' a fifteen-year study of the world's religions, was published on the very day he died — which was also his eightieth birthday.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped make Nantucket's Siasconset a resort
narrative_blocks.body: Among his many ventures, he helped develop Siasconset on Nantucket into a summer resort. At his death his vast Ohio lands passed to his nephew, the architect Ernest Flagg, who held them for another half-century before much of the estate became part of a state forest.

narrative_blocks.header: He learned to paint from Washington Allston
narrative_blocks.body: Trained by his brother and their uncle, the great Romantic painter Washington Allston, he exhibited a portrait of his father at the National Academy at sixteen. He grew into one of the leading portrait painters of his day, elected an academician for an ideal picture, 'Angelo and Isabella.'

narrative_blocks.header: He painted the Commodore many times over
narrative_blocks.body: Among his many sitters he painted Commodore Vanderbilt again and again; one of those portraits still hangs in the directors' room at Grand Central. He also painted the Commodore's son William Henry, years before his niece Alice would marry into the family.

narrative_blocks.header: He left the easel for the pulpit awhile
narrative_blocks.body: After his young first wife died, he turned to theology and was ordained an Episcopal priest, serving eight years as rector of Grace Church in Brooklyn. Then he set down the collar and took up the brush again, painting for the rest of his long life.

narrative_blocks.header: His book on Allston outlived his paintings
narrative_blocks.body: In 1892 he published 'The Life and Letters of Washington Allston,' a biography of the uncle who had first set him painting. Celebrated as a portraitist in his own day, it is for this book that he is best remembered now.

narrative_blocks.header: His children scattered into art, scandal, and letters
narrative_blocks.body: His children carried the family's artistic streak in every direction: Charles Noel became a painter, Ernest a celebrated architect, and Louise married the publisher Charles Scribner. One son, Jared Jr., took a darker path, convicted of running a Ponzi scheme.

narrative_blocks.header: A New Haven mayor's daughter, twice wed
narrative_blocks.body: Daughter of Henry Collins Flagg, the longtime mayor of New Haven, she married a Cincinnati lawyer, Abraham Gwynne, and bore the future Vanderbilt matriarch Alice. Widowed young, she married again, to the author Albert Mathews; through her New England line the old Connecticut blood entered the Vanderbilt family.

narrative_blocks.header: A gold-medal scholar turned priest and poet
narrative_blocks.body: A gold medalist as a schoolboy in New Haven, he studied engineering and law and entered Trinity College, but financial hardship forced him to leave before he could graduate. He turned to theology instead, took Holy Orders, and served as an Episcopal rector in Connecticut, Baltimore, New Orleans, and New Jersey.

narrative_blocks.header: Ill health made him a poet and lecturer
narrative_blocks.body: When ill health drove him from parish work, he took to the lecture circuit across the Northeast, speaking on history, logic, and literature. He wrote poetry late in life, some of it set to music, and published a collection, 'Poems and Later Poems,' in 1890.

narrative_blocks.header: The second Mrs. Whiting, and a second Trowbridge
narrative_blocks.body: After his first wife, Sarah Ingersoll, died in 1769, Deacon John Whiting married Sarah Trowbridge — of the same New Haven family as his mother, Hannah Trowbridge. She was his second wife and outlived him by seven years.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a New Jersey lawyer
narrative_blocks.body: A granddaughter of Martha Whiting Flagg, for whom she was named, she married the Orange, New Jersey lawyer Benjamin Potts in 1868 and raised a large family in Millburn. Several of her seven children did not survive childhood.

narrative_blocks.header: A merchant, coal man, and vestryman
narrative_blocks.body: He was a hardware merchant in New Haven and New York before joining the Empire Stone Dressing Company and serving as secretary of an American coal company. He was a vestryman at the Little Church Around the Corner in Manhattan.

narrative_blocks.header: His first wife, gone within three years
narrative_blocks.body: Jared Flagg's first wife, she died in 1844, only two years into the marriage, leaving an infant son, Montague, who grew up to be a portrait painter like his father.

narrative_blocks.header: She mothered a houseful of Flagg talent
narrative_blocks.body: A New Britain doctor's daughter, she married the painter-minister Jared Flagg and bore him six children in twenty years. From that household came an architect, a painter, and a publisher's wife, though she did not live to see their fame, dying at thirty-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: Her letter mourned Lincoln's murder to a sister
narrative_blocks.body: The day after Lincoln's assassination, she wrote her sister a stricken letter, faint and sick at heart, wondering who could steer the country with his justice and prudence. She hoped, even then, that the calamity might soften the bitterness of the times and bring some reconciliation.

narrative_blocks.header: She was the New Britain doctor's daughter
narrative_blocks.body: Her father, Dr. Samuel Hart of New Britain, practised medicine there from early manhood until age forced him to stop, and died in June 1863 at seventy-seven. He treated by long observation rather than theory, and would not try hazardous experiments.

narrative_blocks.header: The parish knew her two years and mourned
narrative_blocks.body: She came to Westville a stranger in 1865, when her husband took St. James Church as acting rector, and died there on the night of 18 January 1867. The vestry set down that the church's improvements owed no little of their success to her suggestions.

narrative_blocks.header: A judge's daughter, his third and last wife
narrative_blocks.body: The daughter of an Ohio judge and congressman, she became Jared Flagg's third wife in 1869 and his companion through his final decades of painting. She outlived him by twelve years.

narrative_blocks.header: He tried business, even Australia, before art won
narrative_blocks.body: Though born into a family of painters, he resisted the calling, chasing a business career as far as Australia. Only at twenty-six, at his father's urging, did he take up the brush — and then went to Paris for a full decade of study.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten years in Paris, from the Commune's ashes
narrative_blocks.body: He reached Paris in 1872 with his half-brother Charles Noel and two other Hartford painters, when the streets still smoked from the Commune. He worked in a French master's atelier and then the École des Beaux-Arts, staying a full ten years before coming home to New York.

narrative_blocks.header: Eakins painted him and called it 'The Wanderer'
narrative_blocks.body: So well-traveled was he — Australia, Paris, and beyond — that Thomas Eakins, the great American realist, painted his portrait and titled it 'The Wanderer.' It is as a subject of that famous brush, as much as for his own careful canvases, that he is remembered.

narrative_blocks.header: He worked so slowly he was never prolific
narrative_blocks.body: A modest, exacting man, he painted so slowly and revised so carefully that he never let a canvas leave his studio until it was as good as he could make it. He was never noted for volume, but his portraits — of Charles Scribner, of the Vanderbilts, of Charles Foster hung in the Paris salon — were prized.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught the girls of Miss Porter's School
narrative_blocks.body: For many years he was the drawing master at Miss Porter's celebrated school for girls in Farmington, and later taught at St. Margaret's in Waterbury. Teaching steadied a career that his own slow, exacting hand kept from ever being lucrative.

narrative_blocks.header: She sailed to Paris with the young painters
narrative_blocks.body: A Frenchwoman by birth, she married Montague Flagg and crossed to Paris with his band of Hartford painters in 1872. Her husband painted her as 'Portrait of My Wife,' shown at the National Academy in 1909; the childless couple died within a year of each other.

artworks.artwork_blurb: Mark Twain, painted from life in Hartford

cross_connections.display_label: sat for his portrait in Hartford in 1890

narrative_blocks.header: Hartford's leading portrait painter for a generation
narrative_blocks.body: Trained by his painter father and in the ateliers of Paris, he settled in Hartford in 1887 and became the portraitist of choice for the city's leaders. He painted most of Connecticut's late-century governors and, in 1890, Mark Twain.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded a free night school for workingmen
narrative_blocks.body: In 1888 he opened a free night drawing school in his Hartford studio, teaching a dentist, a saloonkeeper, and any workingman who wished to learn — one of the country's first cooperative art schools. It grew into the Connecticut League of Art Students, which he led for the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: His school asked no man's race or religion
narrative_blocks.body: He held that art should be open to all, refusing to bar any student on grounds of character, race, or religion — a striking creed for his day. His school required only 'an avowed desire to study.'

narrative_blocks.header: He helped save the state capitol from demolition
narrative_blocks.body: As first president of Hartford's Municipal Arts Society, he led the successful fight to keep the Connecticut state capitol from being torn down. He gave much of his energy to the civic and cultural life of the city, founding its society of artists and its academy of fine arts.

narrative_blocks.header: His students paraded a skeleton through the streets
narrative_blocks.body: When his art school outgrew its quarters, his students dismembered their classroom skeleton and carried it bone by bone through the streets to the new building, the first man bearing the skull. A policeman spotted the parade, recognized Flagg, and let the strange procession pass.

narrative_blocks.header: Her portrait was her brother-in-law's masterwork
narrative_blocks.body: She married the painter Charles Noel Flagg in 1874. Her brother-in-law Montague painted her portrait, remembered as one of his finest canvases.

narrative_blocks.header: Before Charles Ponzi, there was Jared Flagg
narrative_blocks.body: A decade before Charles Ponzi lent his name to the fraud, Flagg was running the same scheme in New York — paying old investors with new deposits and promising one percent a week. When postal inspectors raided his office in 1911, he had taken in more than a million dollars from some eight hundred and fifty clients.

narrative_blocks.header: He built an empire on no money down
narrative_blocks.body: He got his start as a furniture salesman with a simple idea: let a young couple furnish an apartment with nothing down and pay it off over time. The 'Flagg Flats' plan spread across New York, and by the eighteen-nineties he had parlayed it into a furnished-apartment business of some four hundred and eighty flats.

narrative_blocks.header: He died mid-interrogation, protesting his innocence
narrative_blocks.body: His fraud conviction was overturned in 1920 after a court ruled his records had been seized without a proper warrant. Six years later he collapsed and died of a heart attack in the state's fraud bureau while being questioned over a suspect mortgage deal — the investigators at first suspecting he was faking to escape them.

narrative_blocks.header: He built the tallest tower in the world
narrative_blocks.body: A Beaux-Arts architect who practiced in New York, he designed the Singer Building in lower Manhattan — for one year, in 1908, the tallest building in the world, and when it fell in 1968 the tallest ever demolished. His Corcoran Gallery in Washington and his campus for the U.S. Naval Academy at Annapolis secured his place among America's leading architects.

narrative_blocks.header: A Vanderbilt cousin paid for his training
narrative_blocks.body: His cousin by marriage, Cornelius Vanderbilt II, was so struck by his early work that he paid to send him to the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris. Flagg earned its highest honor but, having passed thirty, was denied the formal prize — then came home in 1891 to build a practice on French classicism.

narrative_blocks.header: He fought for light, air, and cheap homes
narrative_blocks.body: Beyond his towers he was an urban reformer, shaping New York's first zoning laws in 1916 to keep light and air on the streets below and building model tenements for the working poor. He also devised a modular stone-building system meant to put sturdy, handsome houses within reach of ordinary families. A darker note fell in 1912, when his own car struck and killed a boy who had skated into its path.

narrative_blocks.header: He traced his line to New England's founders
narrative_blocks.body: Late in life the architect turned genealogist, publishing in 1926 a painstaking study that traced his own descent from a hundred and seventy-two families who settled New England between 1635 and 1640. Ranging from Massachusetts to South Carolina, it stands as a model of deep and careful family research.

narrative_blocks.header: He won St. Luke's over eighty rival architects
narrative_blocks.body: One of his first major commissions came by open competition, his design for St. Luke's Hospital in Manhattan besting some eighty rival architects and rising at a cost of three million dollars. Before the century was out he had also drawn the plans for the Washington State Capitol at Olympia.

narrative_blocks.header: The one Flagg who chose money over art
narrative_blocks.body: Born into a family of painters, he broke with the artistic line and went to Wall Street. There he cofounded the brokerage of Post & Flagg and served as a governor of the New York Stock Exchange.

narrative_blocks.header: His name came from a celebrated painter kinsman
narrative_blocks.body: He was named for Washington Allston, the South Carolina painter and poet who was himself among the first Americans named for George Washington. The name went on to his son and grandson — three Washington Allston Flaggs on Wall Street.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at forty-three, leaving young children
narrative_blocks.body: He died in 1903 at just forty-three, leaving a young widow and three small children. When their daughter Josephine married four years later, it was her widowed mother who stepped forward to give the bride away.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: The Scribner family house (1910) at Cornwall, New York.

narrative_blocks.header: Her marriage made her brother the family architect
narrative_blocks.body: When she married the publisher Charles Scribner in 1882, she drew her brother, the architect Ernest Flagg, into the family's orbit — and Scribner went on to give the young man some of his first great commissions. Ernest designed six buildings for the Scribners, from their Fifth Avenue store to the townhouse where Louisa lived.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty years in the same Morristown house
narrative_blocks.body: For sixty years she made her home in Morristown, New Jersey, outliving her husband by eighteen. Her son and grandson would carry the Scribner publishing house through most of the twentieth century.

narrative_blocks.header: One of Mrs. Astor's fabled Four Hundred
narrative_blocks.body: An eccentric society figure, she was counted among Mrs. Astor's 'Four Hundred' — the pillars of old New York said to be all who could fit in the great hostess's ballroom. She and her husband divided their years between Manhattan and a quieter life on Nantucket.

narrative_blocks.header: Motherless as an infant, raised by kin
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother, Louisa Hart Flagg, died only ten weeks after Rosalie was born, and she was raised in part by an uncle and aunt between New York and Nantucket. She and her husband, the broker William Jaffray, had no children, and both died on the island in 1949.

narrative_blocks.header: A bluestocking who restored her family's paintings
narrative_blocks.body: Intelligent, well-traveled, and fiercely proud of her ancestry, she was a bluestocking of the old school — an amateur actress, a stalwart of the Colonial Dames, and a skilled restorer of paintings, especially those by her father and grandfather. She never married, and as the eldest daughter she stayed on in the family home.

narrative_blocks.header: She let the ancestral house be torn down
narrative_blocks.body: For all her pride in the past, it was she who ended it: unable to keep up the crumbling eighteenth-century family house, she sold it not to the historical society that wanted it but to Standard Oil, which had outbid them. The house and its ancient walnut tree were razed for a filling station.

narrative_blocks.header: She moved to a mansion facing Nook Farm
narrative_blocks.body: She took a twenty-room house on Forest Street, directly across from Nook Farm — the literary colony that had been home to Harriet Beecher Stowe and, next door, Mark Twain. There she lived out her days, dying in 1939.

bio.bio_blurb: Founder of C. N. Flagg & Company

narrative_blocks.header: The painter's son who built a company instead
narrative_blocks.body: Born in Paris while his father studied painting there, he grew up among artists but made his own way in business, founding the successful C. N. Flagg & Company. He and his wife, Julia, raised six children between Meriden and the Connecticut shore at Fenwick.

narrative_blocks.header: His company built Connecticut's pipes and power
narrative_blocks.body: The firm he founded in 1910 grew into one of Connecticut's substantial contractors, laying the pipelines, sewers, and heavy mechanical works of the greater Hartford region. It stayed in the family's hands for three generations, run in turn by his sons and grandson.

narrative_blocks.header: The draft board found him tall and hazel-eyed
narrative_blocks.body: When he registered for the draft in 1918, the clerk set him down as a tall man of medium build, brown-haired and hazel-eyed — a passing snapshot of a Meriden businessman then in his prime.

narrative_blocks.header: He designed the tower at Fifth and Forty-second
narrative_blocks.body: He made his name on banks and commercial towers in New York. The largest was 501 Fifth Avenue, put up by the Oceanic Investing Company and named for the Astor Trust Company, which took the lower three floors on a twenty-one-year lease.

narrative_blocks.header: A Navy officer who collected fine antiques
narrative_blocks.body: He served as a Navy officer in the First World War, commanding a yacht lent by the Dodge family, and was known besides as a discerning collector and dealer of antiques. He died at his Hartford home in 1924, only forty years old.

narrative_blocks.header: He won a portrait prize, then quit
narrative_blocks.body: Flagg trained as a painter, studying for years in France and at the École des Beaux-Arts, and took the Proctor Prize for portraiture at the National Academy in 1909. He had left that work behind by the time he drew 501 Fifth Avenue.

narrative_blocks.header: He matched it to the library opposite
narrative_blocks.body: The design answers the New York Public Library across Fifth Avenue: limestone throughout, semi-classical, with three tall arched windows above the banking floor. A refacing in black granite broke the resemblance, and a restoration undid that in 2014.

narrative_blocks.header: The bank was gone before the building opened
narrative_blocks.body: Astor Trust merged into Bankers Trust in April 1917, months before the building carrying its name was finished. Flagg's own drawing of the entrance already read Bankers' Trust, with the Astor name pushed onto the bases of the signs.

narrative_blocks.header: His uncle was the architect Ernest Flagg
narrative_blocks.body: Ernest Flagg was his father's brother, and the first Montague Flagg was another of them. He came to the family trade late, and out of painting rather than out of building.

narrative_blocks.header: She followed a football hero to Texas
narrative_blocks.body: A daughter of the painter Charles Noel Flagg, she married Harry Maxson, a football star from nearby Trinity College, and left Connecticut for Dallas. She carried the family's Hartford roots to Texas, where her descendants still keep its portraits and stories.

narrative_blocks.header: A promising lawyer dead at thirty-three
narrative_blocks.body: A Cincinnati lawyer who studied briefly at Yale, he won a high reputation at the bar before dying suddenly, at thirty-three, of apoplexy. He left his widow Rachel with five young children, among them the future Vanderbilt matriarch Alice.

education.notes: Class of 1842; edited the Yale Literary Magazine

narrative_blocks.header: A lawyer who wrote as Paul Siegvolk
narrative_blocks.body: A New York lawyer for forty-five years, he led a second life in letters under the pen name Paul Siegvolk, contributing essays and a novel to the magazines of literary New York. He had edited the Yale Literary Magazine as a student and moved easily among the city's authors' clubs.

narrative_blocks.header: He was stepfather to a Vanderbilt matriarch
narrative_blocks.body: In 1861 he married Rachel Flagg, the widowed mother of young Alice Gwynne. When Alice grew up to marry Cornelius Vanderbilt II and reign over Newport, the quiet man of letters found himself stepfather to one of the Gilded Age's great matriarchs.

narrative_blocks.header: The grandfather of scandal and letters
narrative_blocks.body: Little survives of his own life, but his descendants left a vivid mark. His son Edward Erskine Gwynne fathered three memorable children: Kiki Preston, the 'girl with the silver syringe'; Erskine Gwynne, who founded a Paris magazine and lent his name to a cocktail; and Edward Claypool Gwynne, an airman lost in the First World War.

narrative_blocks.header: For sixty years she ruled as family matriarch
narrative_blocks.body: Small in stature but exacting in every detail, she reigned as matriarch of the Vanderbilts for more than sixty years, known to all as 'Alice of the Breakers.' She ran her households by rigid rule and worshipped as devoutly as her husband.

narrative_blocks.header: She shaped The Breakers from its ashes
narrative_blocks.body: After the family's wooden Newport cottage burned in 1892, she took charge of the rebuilding, working with Richard Morris Hunt on the seventy-room stone palace that became The Breakers and shaping its design down to the cloud-painted sky on the great hall's ceiling. It remains the most visited of Newport's Gilded Age mansions.

narrative_blocks.header: She came to the ball as electric light
narrative_blocks.body: At the most fabled costume ball of the age, in 1883, she appeared as 'the Electric Light,' in a gown of white satin and diamonds with a torch raised in her hand, inspired by Edison's new illumination of Manhattan. The photograph became one of the enduring images of the Gilded Age.

narrative_blocks.header: Her daughters had a cottage of their own
narrative_blocks.body: At The Breakers she kept a separate cottage for her daughters Gertrude and Gladys, staffed with its own butler and French chef. A portrait of the era shows the three of them at tea in the mansion's great library.

narrative_blocks.header: She mourned him for thirty-five years
narrative_blocks.body: Widowed in 1899 after thirty-two years of marriage, she never set aside her mourning. Through the later loss of two grown sons she wore black to the end, living on another thirty-five years as the family's grieving matriarch.

narrative_blocks.header: Her nickname came from a French town
narrative_blocks.body: Born in Cincinnati, she was christened with the real name 'Cettie,' after the town of Cette in southern France. With her sister she built Sunnymead, a shingled summer cottage at Narragansett Pier that stayed in the Gwynne family for nearly ninety years.

narrative_blocks.header: A daughter of old Cincinnati and older Philadelphia
narrative_blocks.body: Through the Flaggs she descended from the Claypooles of colonial Philadelphia and from officers of the Revolution. A member of the Colonial Dames and the Daughters of the Cincinnati, she summered at Narragansett until her death in 1931.

narrative_blocks.header: One of the Gwynne sisters of Cincinnati
narrative_blocks.body: A daughter of the Cincinnati Gwynnes, she married the Boston publisher William Fearing Gill — Edgar Allan Poe’s first biographer. With her sister she had bought and built the summer cottage Sunnymead at Narragansett Pier, later signing over her share to the Shepherds.

narrative_blocks.header: The favorite grandson who earned it by working
narrative_blocks.body: Alone among the Commodore's grandchildren, he won the old man's favor not by charm but by industry, clerking in a bank at sixteen. He rose to lead the New York Central and its forty-nine allied railroads, and carried the weight of heading the family so gravely that friends said he never seemed quite happy.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave away wealth faster than it grew
narrative_blocks.body: Deeply religious, he poured his fortune into the YMCA, the Red Cross, the Salvation Army, and his churches, and gave so freely that, almost alone among the Gilded Age titans, he died no richer than his father had left him.

narrative_blocks.header: The houses he and Alice raised together
narrative_blocks.body: With Alice he raised two of the most spectacular houses of the age: a Fifth Avenue mansion that filled a city block, the largest New York ever saw, and The Breakers at Newport, a seventy-room palace above the Atlantic. He supplied the fortune and she much of the vision; he himself rarely had time to enjoy either. The mansion later gave way to Bergdorf Goodman; The Breakers still stands.

narrative_blocks.header: A father's grief hardened into a pointed will
narrative_blocks.body: He buried a daughter at five and his namesake son at twenty-one, dead of typhoid at Yale. When his eldest surviving son eloped against his wishes, he rewrote his will to disinherit him, pointedly dating the new document to the very day the wedding had been set. His health broke soon after, and he never fully recovered.

narrative_blocks.header: He met his wife teaching Sunday school
narrative_blocks.body: He was a devout young man teaching Sunday school at St. Bartholomew's when he met Alice Gwynne, who taught there too. They married in 1867 and shared their faith, their charity, and their griefs across thirty-two years, a genuinely close partnership among the Gilded Age's great couples.

narrative_blocks.header: The firstborn, and the first they lost
narrative_blocks.body: The first of Cornelius and Alice's seven children, she died of a childhood illness in 1873, at the age of five. She was laid to rest in the family mausoleum on Staten Island, the earliest of the losses that shadowed her parents' long lives.

narrative_blocks.header: The head of the family he never became
narrative_blocks.body: Cornelius Vanderbilt II's eldest son, he stood first in line to lead the family — a standout at St. Paul's and Yale, stroke of the crew, one of the most popular men in his class. Had he lived, the leadership of the Vanderbilts would have fallen to him.

narrative_blocks.header: He was twenty-one when typhoid took him
narrative_blocks.body: Typhoid fever caught him during his years at Yale, and he died at twenty-one, weeks before his class would graduate. His grieving parents raised Vanderbilt Hall on the campus in his memory, where it still stands.

narrative_blocks.header: His marriage cost him the Vanderbilt fortune
narrative_blocks.body: His 1896 elopement with Grace Wilson so enraged his father that the two came to blows, and he was largely cut out of the will, left a fraction of what his brothers received. Days after the quarrel his father suffered a stroke, and his mother did not speak to him for twenty-seven years.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped build New York's first subway
narrative_blocks.body: A trained mechanical engineer, he patented more than thirty improvements to locomotives and freight cars. In 1904 he partnered with August Belmont to found the Interborough Rapid Transit Company, which built New York City's first subway line.

narrative_blocks.header: He rose to brigadier general in the Guard
narrative_blocks.body: Commissioned in the New York National Guard in 1901, he rose to brigadier general by 1918 and won the Distinguished Service Medal, though his war was spent training troops rather than in the field. He was 'General Vanderbilt' for the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: He captained one of yachting's great defenders
narrative_blocks.body: A passionate yachtsman and Commodore of the New York Yacht Club, he backed the syndicate that built Reliance, the largest racing yacht ever made, which defended the America's Cup in 1903. He himself skippered the Aurora to win the King Edward VII Cup.

narrative_blocks.header: At first she sculpted under a false name
narrative_blocks.body: Born to one of America's greatest fortunes, she became a serious sculptor — and at first signed her work with a false name, fearing 'Vanderbilt' would get it dismissed as a rich woman's hobby. Neither her family nor her husband took the ambition seriously; she worked, she said, for the pure joy of it.

narrative_blocks.header: The Met's refusal gave America the Whitney
narrative_blocks.body: In 1929 she offered the Metropolitan Museum her collection of nearly seven hundred American artworks, plus money to house them — and was refused, because the Met would not take American art. So she built her own: the Whitney Museum of American Art, which she opened in 1931 and endowed at her death.

narrative_blocks.header: A refuge for artists the establishment ignored
narrative_blocks.body: From her Greenwich Village studio she opened galleries and a club where young, unknown American artists could show their work, backing the Ashcan painters and buying at the 1913 Armory Show. She pushed especially for women artists in a field that shut them out, championing the likes of Georgia O'Keeffe.

narrative_blocks.header: The poor little rich girl became her ward
narrative_blocks.body: When her brother Reggie's ten-year-old daughter, Gloria, fled to her studio saying her mother meant to harm her, Gertrude took the child in — and fought Gloria's mother for custody in the sensational 1934 'trial of the century.' She won, and raised the girl at her Long Island estate, though the two were never close.

narrative_blocks.header: In wartime France she built a soldiers' hospital
narrative_blocks.body: During the First World War she founded and paid for a full military hospital outside Paris, sketching the wounded soldiers there for the war memorials she would later sculpt. In the middle of it, in 1915, her brother Alfred drowned in the sinking of the Lusitania.

narrative_blocks.header: In her youth, a love her mother forbade
narrative_blocks.body: As a young woman she loved Esther Hunt, daughter of the architect who had built her family's mansions — a bond their surviving letters show ran to open desire. Her mother, alarmed, forbade the friendship; Gertrude called Esther's kiss one of the thrills of her life, then married Harry Whitney.

notable.notable_blurb: Sportsman and Vanderbilt railroad heir

cross_connections.display_label: went down with the Titanic after handing his wife into a lifeboat
drowned on the Empress of Ireland a year before the Lusitania sank

narrative_blocks.header: His father skipped the eldest son for him
narrative_blocks.body: When Cornelius Vanderbilt II died in 1899, he disinherited his eldest surviving son over an unwelcome marriage and made Alfred his principal heir instead — more than forty million dollars, over half the family fortune. Alfred also received the Congressional gold medal that had come to mark headship of the Vanderbilts.

narrative_blocks.header: He drove four-in-hand coaches for sport
narrative_blocks.body: A devoted sportsman who fox-hunted and belonged to the Coaching Club, he kept a custom four-in-hand named Venture, built for him by Brewster in 1903. He loved the old English coaching runs best, driving London to Brighton himself and stopping along the way for lunch and telegrams.

narrative_blocks.header: He built the Vanderbilt Hotel and ran railroads
narrative_blocks.body: For all his sporting life he took up his inheritance in earnest — clerking and then directing at the New York Central, and sitting on a string of railroad and Pullman boards. On the site of the old family mansion he raised the Vanderbilt Hotel and made it his home in the city.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave his life jacket and couldn't swim
narrative_blocks.body: When a torpedo sank the Lusitania off Ireland in May 1915, he gave his lifebelt to a young mother and tied it on for her — though he could not swim and knew there were no boats left for him. Witnesses saw him carry children to the boats two at a time, telling his valet to 'find all the kiddies you can.' His body was never recovered; he left two small sons, Alfred Jr. and George, aged two and not yet one.

notable.notable_blurb: Equestrian and horse-show founder

cross_connections.display_label: ran the Lenox horse show while he ran the national association
ran the Devon horse show he once dodged a subpoena to reach
helped found the American Grand Prix Association of show jumping

narrative_blocks.header: Horses were the one thing he took seriously
narrative_blocks.body: Horses were the one pursuit he gave himself to entirely. He led the Association of American Horse Shows and the Hackney Horse Society, bred and judged and exhibited, and during the war pressed the country's wealthy to raise more horses — a campaign that caught on.

narrative_blocks.header: New Haven knew his car by its roar
narrative_blocks.body: As a Yale man, his enormous foreign motorcar told the whole town his schedule — roaring out into the night, roaring home at dawn. Classmates who watched this dashing whip and polo player voted him the one most likely to succeed.

narrative_blocks.header: A fortune raced away at the card table
narrative_blocks.body: Cards and fast company drew him far more than any ledger. He gambled through most of his inheritance, and once, subpoenaed to answer for his losses, slipped past a houseful of detectives in disguise — the more urgent business being a horse show in Philadelphia.

narrative_blocks.header: The daughter he never lived to know
narrative_blocks.body: Cirrhosis took him at forty-five, when his younger daughter, Gloria, was not yet two. He never lived to see her become the designer Gloria Vanderbilt, nor to know his grandson would be the journalist Anderson Cooper.

narrative_blocks.header: The youngest Vanderbilt became a Hungarian countess
narrative_blocks.body: The youngest of Cornelius Vanderbilt II's children, she married the Hungarian Count László Széchenyi in 1908 in the most celebrated international wedding since her cousin Consuelo's to the Duke of Marlborough. She spent much of her marriage in Hungary, raising five daughters who married into European aristocracy.

narrative_blocks.header: She gave The Breakers a second life
narrative_blocks.body: She inherited The Breakers, the grandest of the Newport cottages, at a moment when many assumed she would let it be sold and turned into a hotel. Instead she leased it to the Preservation Society for a dollar a year, kept a private apartment on its third floor, and made it the public treasure that is now Rhode Island's most-visited house.

narrative_blocks.header: Cut off by war, she fed Hungary's children
narrative_blocks.body: The First World War trapped her in a Hungarian hunting lodge for four years, without gas or electricity, as the Russian advance came within five miles. She came home to America and threw herself into raising money to feed starving Hungarian children, telling audiences that a nickel bought a child a meal.

narrative_blocks.header: A marriage that outlasted financial ruin
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband lost much of her great dowry in stock and land speculations, and by 1913 the newspapers were predicting divorce. She stayed married to him for twenty-five years, until his death, and served as his hostess when he represented Hungary as its minister in Washington.

narrative_blocks.header: The scholarship carries her father’s name
narrative_blocks.body: She endowed the Edward Octavius Flagg Scholarship at Trinity College in Hartford, where her father had taken his degree, and it has carried students through the college for close to a century.

narrative_blocks.header: She left her sister the Flushing building
narrative_blocks.body: Her will left a Flushing apartment house to her sister Elizabeth, furniture and antiques and silver to friends and relatives, and a bequest to Saint Luke’s Home for Aged Women.

narrative_blocks.header: The Staten Island land came from her family
narrative_blocks.body: She married the architect Ernest Flagg in 1899, and it was on her family's land at Dongan Hills, Staten Island, that he built their estate, 209 Flagg Place, and tested his ideas for affordable stone houses. Their only child, Betsy, became a noted painter of portrait miniatures.

notable.notable_blurb: Miniature portrait painter

cross_connections.display_label: was an earlier family miniaturist, shown at the Paris Salon
published Samuel Eliot Morison, whom she painted in miniature

narrative_blocks.header: A master of the portrait in miniature
narrative_blocks.body: She specialized in miniature portraits — watercolor on ivory only a few inches high — and rose to lead the American Society of Miniature Painters as its president. Her work reached the Smithsonian and the National Gallery, and in 1942 took the society's Levantia White Boardman prize.

narrative_blocks.header: She trained under the painter Cecilia Beaux
narrative_blocks.body: After the Spence School she studied in the early 1920s under Cecilia Beaux, among the foremost American portraitists of the day. Her own sitters came to include the writer Marguerite Yourcenar, Brooke Astor, and Admiral Samuel Eliot Morison.

narrative_blocks.header: She painted her father in miniature
narrative_blocks.body: Among her finest works is a small 1935 portrait on ivory of her father, the architect Ernest Flagg, his name and profession inscribed beneath. First given to the Corcoran Gallery that he had designed, it hangs today in the National Gallery of Art.

narrative_blocks.header: A Harvard banker who served in France
narrative_blocks.body: A Harvard man of the class of 1917, he drove for the American Field Service in France and then served as an infantry lieutenant, before making his career on Wall Street as an investment banker. Through his mother he was a great-grandson of Paran Stevens, the hotelier of the old Fifth Avenue Hotel.

narrative_blocks.header: Nationally known as a poet, she also painted
narrative_blocks.body: She won national recognition as a poet and held a one-woman show of her paintings in New York, a fourth generation of the family to make art. She belonged to the National Women Painters Society and worked from her home on Mount Desert Island.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept the books for her architect grandfather
narrative_blocks.body: Though poetry and painting were her true calling, she studied accounting at Columbia and spent several years as bookkeeper to her grandfather, the architect Ernest Flagg. As a girl she had spent time at his Staten Island estate, 209 Flagg Place.

narrative_blocks.header: She spent her adult life with Lyman King
narrative_blocks.body: She made her home with her partner, Lyman Spire King, on Mount Desert Island in Maine, sustained by a deep Episcopal faith. She died there in 2005 and is buried near her mother at Northeast Harbor.

narrative_blocks.header: A widow who gave her daughter away
narrative_blocks.body: Widowed young when the broker W. Allston Flagg died in 1903, she stepped from the front pew to give her daughter Josephine away herself. Five years on she married another New York broker, John Turner Atterbury.

narrative_blocks.header: His two daughters married two brothers
narrative_blocks.body: A New York broker and yachtsman with a summer cottage at Islesboro, Maine, he married the widowed Anna Flagg in 1908, uniting two long-intimate families. Two of his own daughters had married a pair of Potter brothers — sisters wedding brothers.

cross_connections.display_label: became her stepfather by marrying her widowed mother

narrative_blocks.header: A society bride turned interior decorator
narrative_blocks.body: Astors, Vanderbilts and Morgans were among the throng at her 1907 wedding at St. Thomas's. She worked later as an interior decorator, and in 1939 helped compile a cookbook of low-carbohydrate Hay diet menus.

narrative_blocks.header: She founded a craft guild for Maine women
narrative_blocks.body: At her summer colony of Dark Harbor on Islesboro, Maine, she helped found and led the Islesboro Industries, which gave the island's women paid handicraft work. She served as its president, binding her name to the community she summered in for decades.

education.notes: Harvard College, studies interrupted by war

narrative_blocks.header: He chased submarines in two world wars
narrative_blocks.body: His Harvard studies were cut short by the First World War, when he commanded a submarine chaser, and he returned to uniform in the Second as a lieutenant commander. In between and after, he was an investment banker and a governor of the New York Stock Exchange.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried on his father's brokerage house
narrative_blocks.body: He succeeded his father as a partner in the Wall Street firm of Post & Flagg, staying on when it merged into Harris, Upham & Company. He led the Piping Rock Club and sat as a governor of the Racquet and Tennis Club.

narrative_blocks.header: He built Scribner's into a literary powerhouse
narrative_blocks.body: For half a century he led Charles Scribner's Sons, the house his father had founded, grooming its list until it stood as a 'blue ribbon' for American authors. He took the reins after his Princeton graduation in 1875 and relaunched Scribner's Magazine in 1886 to lasting success.

narrative_blocks.header: He was Theodore Roosevelt's friend and publisher
narrative_blocks.body: A close friend of Theodore Roosevelt, he published the former president's writings — Roosevelt's 1909 account of his African safari became the most widely circulated work in the company's history. It was Roosevelt, too, who talked the firm into publishing 'The Wind in the Willows.'

narrative_blocks.header: He gave Princeton its university press
narrative_blocks.body: A devoted Princetonian, he gave the building that housed the Princeton University Press in 1912 and became its first president. He held that the press would do best affiliated with the university but not directly run by it.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife's brother became his architect
narrative_blocks.body: His 1882 marriage to Louisa Flagg brought him a gifted brother-in-law, the young architect Ernest Flagg, whom he launched with early commissions. Flagg designed six Scribner buildings, including the Fifth Avenue store and the family's Beaux-Arts townhouse on East Sixty-sixth Street.

narrative_blocks.header: His firm's checks paid for Churchill's Chartwell
narrative_blocks.body: His house published Winston Churchill's sweeping history of the Great War, 'The World Crisis,' across five volumes in the 1920s. The income from it helped Churchill buy Chartwell, the country home that anchored him through his 'wilderness years.'

landmarks.landmark_blurb: The Scribner family house (1910) at Cornwall, New York.

narrative_blocks.header: The season's first great Easter wedding
narrative_blocks.body: Her 1904 marriage to the lawyer George Schieffelin was the first grand Easter wedding of the New York season, held at St. Bartholomew's before a church full of Vanderbilts and Roosevelts. Her father's wedding gift was a house in Morristown, near the family's country place, where she would live out her life.

narrative_blocks.header: The first divorce in the Scribner family
narrative_blocks.body: When her husband deserted her in 1935, she waited years before seeking a divorce — there had never been one in the Scribner family, and she was loath to be the first. The decree finally came in 1941, uncontested.

notable.notable_blurb: President of Charles Scribner’s Sons, 1932–1952

landmarks.landmark_blurb: The Scribner family house (1910) at Cornwall, New York.
Charles Scribner II gave the building (1911) and became the Press’s first president.
155 Fifth Avenue (1893) — Ernest Flagg's Scribner store.
