narrative_blocks.header: The third Scribner to run the family house
narrative_blocks.body: He was the third generation to lead Charles Scribner’s Sons, taking the presidency in 1932 after seven years as vice-president and holding it until his death twenty years later. Under him the house carried its great authors through the Depression and the war years.

narrative_blocks.header: He grew up in his uncle's masterpiece
narrative_blocks.body: The East Sixty-sixth Street townhouse where he was raised was designed by his uncle, the architect Ernest Flagg — a Beaux-Arts house so glassy in its facade that critics said it presaged the curtain wall by half a century. It stands today as one of Flagg's finest surviving buildings.

narrative_blocks.header: An eccentric broker of Manhattan and Nantucket
narrative_blocks.body: A New York broker by trade, he married Rosalie Flagg in 1890, and the childless couple lived, by family lore, as mild eccentrics. They divided their days between Manhattan and Nantucket, where both died in 1949.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: His hand-cut stone wine cellar (1859) on Lower Twin Creek at Buena Vista, Ohio.

narrative_blocks.header: A wine millionaire's daughter who married late
narrative_blocks.body: A daughter of Nicholas Longworth, the Cincinnati millionaire who fathered American grape culture, she was in her forties and nearly a decade older than William Flagg when they wed in 1852. The marriage was childless but companionable, and her fortune let him live as a gentleman-scholar.

narrative_blocks.header: A hidden son later sued for the fortune
narrative_blocks.body: As a young woman she had borne a son out of wedlock and was quietly kept from society by her mother. Decades later, in 1894, that son sued the Longworth estate for a share of the family fortune — a case that drew national attention, with her husband testifying against the claim.

narrative_blocks.header: He spent a fortune he did not have
narrative_blocks.body: A nephew of the Vanderbilts with extravagant tastes and little profession, he ran up enormous debts — including a $50,000 bill for diamonds from a Paris jeweler — and filed for bankruptcy in 1902, listing liabilities of more than $56,000 against assets of just $57. Two years later he died of kidney disease at thirty-five, on the very day his creditors' suit was set to be heard.

narrative_blocks.header: Descended from a signer and a commodore
narrative_blocks.body: She was a great-granddaughter of Samuel Chase, a signer of the Declaration of Independence, and a granddaughter of Commodore Joshua Barney, a naval hero of the Revolution and the War of 1812. Widowed young when her spendthrift husband died, she raised their three children largely in Europe.

notable.notable_blurb: Jazz Age socialite

narrative_blocks.header: The girl with the silver syringe
narrative_blocks.body: Among the hard-living British and American expatriates of Kenya's Happy Valley set in the 1920s and 1930s, she was one of the most talked-about — known as 'the girl with the silver syringe' for the syringe she used to inject morphine, often in company. Beautiful and quick-witted, she made little effort to hide an addiction that would shadow the rest of her life.

narrative_blocks.header: Not a Vanderbilt, but a Gwynne by blood
narrative_blocks.body: The newspapers loved to call her a Vanderbilt, but her blood was Gwynne and Flagg: her great-aunt Alice Gwynne — the sister of her grandfather David — had married Cornelius Vanderbilt II. The famous name opened doors, even though her own branch had lost most of its money when her father went bankrupt.

narrative_blocks.header: Prince George’s family forced her out of Britain
narrative_blocks.body: Her affair with Prince George, Duke of Kent — a younger son of King George V — alarmed the royal family, who blamed her for the prince’s drug use and, in 1929, pressed her to leave Britain. It was long rumored, though never proven, that she had borne him a son.

narrative_blocks.header: A life shadowed by loss, ending in 1946
narrative_blocks.body: Her later years were marked by grief — her second husband died in 1934, and her son Ethan was killed in the Normandy landings in 1944. Long troubled and in failing health, she died by suicide in New York in 1946.

narrative_blocks.header: Kiki's first husband, a soldier turned executive
narrative_blocks.body: He married Alice 'Kiki' Gwynne in Paris in 1919, after his service in the Great War, and they had a son and a daughter before she divorced him in 1924 on grounds of desertion. He later became an executive in a plastics company and died in the Bahamas.

narrative_blocks.header: The 'untamed' banker who took her to Kenya
narrative_blocks.body: A Harvard-educated investment banker from Colorado, described by one acquaintance as 'a creature of instincts,' he married Kiki Gwynne in 1925. The couple built a house on Lake Naivasha and threw themselves into the hard-drinking life of Kenya's Happy Valley, until his death in 1934 left her a widow.

cross_connections.display_label: was killed flying in France six months before him

narrative_blocks.header: He died in uniform in 1918, at twenty-two
narrative_blocks.body: Twin brother of Erskine, he became a second lieutenant in the Army Air Service during the First World War. He died in uniform in October 1918, at just twenty-two, as the war drew to its close.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded Paris's Boulevardier — and its cocktail
narrative_blocks.body: In 1927 he founded 'The Boulevardier,' an English-language literary magazine for the expatriates of interwar Paris, and wrote for the European edition of the Herald Tribune. His name survives in the whiskey cocktail called the Boulevardier, which he is said to have inspired and which is still poured a century later.

narrative_blocks.header: He survived the crash that killed his cousin
narrative_blocks.body: In November 1933 he was a passenger in the automobile accident in South Carolina that killed his cousin, the sportsman William Kissam Vanderbilt Jr. Gwynne escaped with minor injuries and helped summon aid. It was one of the most reported episodes of his later life.

narrative_blocks.header: A colorful figure of expatriate Paris
narrative_blocks.body: Energetic and sociable, he was one of the recognizable characters of American Paris between the wars, at home in literary salons, cafés, and the resorts of the Normandy coast. In 1936 he published 'Paris Adventure,' a guide to the city he knew so well.

narrative_blocks.header: A Patou model who married the boulevardier
narrative_blocks.body: An American model for the great Paris couturier Jean Patou, she married Erskine Gwynne in 1926 after a courtship the newspapers loved — including a tale of Gwynne defending her honor at a Paris ball. The marriage ended in divorce in 1932, without children.

narrative_blocks.header: He was lost over the Atlantic in 1944
narrative_blocks.body: Kiki's son flew with the Royal Canadian Air Force, and on the night of 7 June 1944 — the day after the Normandy landings — his Liberator failed to return from an anti-submarine patrol over the Atlantic. He was twenty-five, and is commemorated on the Runnymede Memorial among the airmen with no known grave.

narrative_blocks.header: From selling rare books to flying Liberators
narrative_blocks.body: Born in Biarritz and schooled in London, Kenya, Switzerland, and Rhode Island, he had been selling rare books in California when he crossed to Montreal in 1941 to enlist in the Royal Canadian Air Force. He was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross before his final patrol.

narrative_blocks.header: Kiki's daughter, who married an airman
narrative_blocks.body: Born in 1921, she was Kiki Preston’s only daughter and outlived both her mother and her brother Ethan. She married Geoffrey Borden Russell, a pilot officer, and lived to 2003.

narrative_blocks.header: She was New York's last great society hostess
narrative_blocks.body: For half a century she reigned as one of the last true 'heads of society,' entertaining on a scale that recalled the Gilded Age even as that world faded around her. Kings and kaisers were her guests; she counted every British monarch since Victoria among her friends.

narrative_blocks.header: One of the socially ambitious 'marrying Wilsons'
narrative_blocks.body: She came from a family the papers dubbed the 'marrying Wilsons' for their brilliant matches into the Astor, Goelet, and Pembroke families. Her own 1896 elopement with Neily Vanderbilt, made against his father's fierce objection, fractured the Vanderbilt family for a generation.

narrative_blocks.header: She called her Fifth Avenue mansion a cottage
narrative_blocks.body: After her husband's death she was forced from their vast Fifth Avenue mansion into a merely grand house at 1048 Fifth, which she wryly called 'the Gardener's Cottage.' The building survives today as the Neue Galerie.

was sent to prison by the judge who had sentenced Al Capone

narrative_blocks.header: He fled his fortune to chase headlines
narrative_blocks.body: Against his family's furious wishes, he turned his back on Fifth Avenue to become a newspaperman, founding a string of tabloids that lost nearly six million dollars. He spent his life trying to convince the world that a rich man's son could be in earnest.

narrative_blocks.header: He interviewed Capone, Mussolini, and Hitler
narrative_blocks.body: His press card opened doors to the century's most notorious figures. He interviewed Al Capone, who told him the real graft went to the bankers, and he rode in Mussolini's car when it struck and killed a child, the dictator shrugging, 'What is one life in the affairs of a state?'

narrative_blocks.header: He made the first anti-Nazi film
narrative_blocks.body: In 1934 he released 'Hitler's Reign of Terror,' covertly filmed in Nazi Germany and regarded as the first anti-Nazi film, an exposé of the regime's persecution of Jews. It was banned in New York and dismissed by critics who scoffed at its warning that Hitler threatened world peace.

narrative_blocks.header: His memoir got him struck from society
narrative_blocks.body: His 1935 memoir, 'Farewell to Fifth Avenue,' exposed the artifice of the society he was born into and got his name stricken from the Social Register. He called it a game of people 'building high fences and beating their heads against a stone wall.'

narrative_blocks.header: His seven marriages, and one landmark divorce
narrative_blocks.body: He married seven times but had no children, and made his home in Reno, the nation's divorce capital, where he ended several of the marriages himself. One split reached the United States Supreme Court, which ruled in 1957 that even a Reno divorce could not cut off the support rights a spouse held in another state.

marriages.place: Ridgewood, Bergen County, New Jersey, United States

narrative_blocks.header: The press linked her to a future king
narrative_blocks.body: Presented at the British court, she was publicly courted in the papers as a possible match for Prince George, the future King George VI, and other European nobles. She married none of them, choosing to live independently in New York, for a time working as a shop girl.

narrative_blocks.header: She married against her parents' wishes
narrative_blocks.body: In 1927 she married Henry Gassaway Davis in a quiet civil ceremony at the Marriage License Bureau, without her parents' consent; when the marriage faltered, her mother whisked her to Europe at midnight to avoid scandal. She later married Robert Livingston Stevens, of the family that founded Stevens Institute.

narrative_blocks.header: One of thoroughbred racing's greatest owners
narrative_blocks.body: Few names in American thoroughbred racing stood higher — leading owner in the country eight times over, breeder of nearly two hundred stakes winners, and in 1915 the man whose filly Regret became the first of her sex to win the Kentucky Derby. The Hall of Fame later named him a Pillar of the Turf.

narrative_blocks.header: A ten-goal polo player who beat England
narrative_blocks.body: Beyond the track he was a champion sportsman — a rare ten-goal polo player who captained the American team that took back the international cup from England in 1909. He also raced his yacht Vanitie in trials for the America's Cup.

narrative_blocks.header: The sculptor across the street became his wife
narrative_blocks.body: Heir to an oil-and-tobacco fortune, he married Gertrude Vanderbilt in 1896 — she had lived just across Fifth Avenue from his family. He never much valued her sculpting, but his wealth underwrote a life of horses, polo, and, through her, the beginnings of a great museum.

narrative_blocks.header: A Pacific expedition bore his name
narrative_blocks.body: In 1920 he financed the Whitney South Seas Expedition for the American Museum of Natural History — a years-long scientific voyage that surveyed the birds of thousands of Pacific islands. His name still rides on the venture.

narrative_blocks.header: For thirty years she led her mother's museum
narrative_blocks.body: When Gertrude Whitney died in 1942, Flora took over the museum her mother had founded — serving as its president and then chairman for more than thirty years. Under her, the family gallery grew into a national institution with outside trustees and a countrywide program.

narrative_blocks.header: A president's son, killed before they could wed
narrative_blocks.body: At twenty she became engaged to Quentin Roosevelt, the youngest son of President Theodore Roosevelt, who left Harvard to fly for the Army Air Service. He was shot down over France in July 1918, weeks before the armistice; their wartime love letters were later published, and Flora grew close to the grieving Roosevelts for years, standing godmother to the nephew named in Quentin's memory.

narrative_blocks.header: Two marriages: one unhappy, one long and happy
narrative_blocks.body: She married twice after Quentin — first the aviator and stockbroker Roderick Tower, a union undone by his drinking and infidelity, and then the artist-architect George 'Cully' Miller, in a Cairo wedding that began a long, happy marriage. Four children came from the two.

narrative_blocks.header: A family Turner set an auction record
narrative_blocks.body: In 1980 she sold a J.M.W. Turner painting her family had owned since 1901, 'Juliet and Her Nurse,' at auction for $6.4 million — then the highest price ever paid for a work of art at auction. A Gilded Age heirloom passed, very publicly, into a new era.

career.role: Assistant Secretary of the Air Force

narrative_blocks.header: He turned inherited millions into real achievement
narrative_blocks.body: Born into both the Vanderbilt and Whitney fortunes, he could have simply spent — instead he ranged across a dozen serious careers, from aviation and mining to film, government, and horse racing. Few heirs of his class ever converted so much privilege into so much actual accomplishment.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped launch Pan American Airways
narrative_blocks.body: In 1927 he put his money behind a young Yale acquaintance named Juan Trippe, backing the airline that became Pan American Airways. As chairman he steered its bold push across the Pacific, and flew some of its pioneering routes to Asia himself.

narrative_blocks.header: A Hollywood producer behind Gone with the Wind
narrative_blocks.body: An early Hollywood financier and Technicolor investor, he helped bankroll Gone with the Wind and Rebecca. Later, through his own C.V. Whitney Pictures, he produced John Ford's Western classic The Searchers.

narrative_blocks.header: The third Whitney generation at the racetrack
narrative_blocks.body: Taking over his father Harry's famous stable in 1930, he carried the Whitney silks for another sixty years — breeding scores of champions, though the Kentucky Derby always eluded him. In 1950 he founded the National Museum of Racing at Saratoga.

narrative_blocks.header: A colonel who served two world wars
narrative_blocks.body: A flight instructor in the First World War, he volunteered again in the Second and rose to colonel in the Army Air Forces, earning the Distinguished Service Medal. He then served President Truman as the first Assistant Secretary of the Air Force.

narrative_blocks.header: Five marriages, and a scandal before them
narrative_blocks.body: As a young Yale man he fathered a son with the dancer Evan-Burrows Fontaine, denied it, and beat her breach-of-promise suit in a sensational trial — the first sign of what one biographer called 'the true aristocrat's disdain of fidelity.' He went on to marry five times: his first wife, Marie Norton, became First Lady of New York, and his last, the actress Marylou, reigned for decades as Saratoga's 'Queen.'

narrative_blocks.header: She founded a museum for jewels and design
narrative_blocks.body: Raised among the art and horses of the Whitney and Vanderbilt worlds, the youngest of Gertrude and Harry's three children made collecting her life's work. With her third husband she founded the Headley-Whitney Museum near Lexington, Kentucky, devoted to jewelry, bibelots, and the decorative arts.

narrative_blocks.header: Three marriages, ending with a jeweler
narrative_blocks.body: She married three times — first the banker-turned-reformer Barklie Henry, then Samuel Peck, and finally the jewelry designer George Headley, her partner in the museum. Each marriage carried her further from Long Island society toward a life in art.

narrative_blocks.header: She married her close friend's brother
narrative_blocks.body: She was a close friend of Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney — the sculptor who would found the Whitney Museum — and in 1901 she married Gertrude's brother Alfred at Newport. Their only son, William, born that year, later became Governor of Rhode Island.

narrative_blocks.header: Her 1908 divorce became a public scandal
narrative_blocks.body: In 1908 she left Alfred Vanderbilt and filed for divorce, naming another woman — the wife of a Cuban diplomat in Washington. The case filled the newspapers, and the woman named in it took her own life the next year.

narrative_blocks.header: The Lusitania made her a young widow
narrative_blocks.body: Alfred was her second husband — she had earlier been married to a Baltimore physician — and the Lusitania left her a widow in 1915 with two small sons. She married again in 1918, to the politician Raymond Baker, and had a daughter, Gloria.

cross_connections.display_label: was his stepson and later Governor of Rhode Island

narrative_blocks.header: He married the former Mrs. Alfred Vanderbilt
narrative_blocks.body: A Navy officer from Newport, he married Elsie French in 1919 — the divorced first wife of Alfred Vanderbilt Sr., who had gone down with the Lusitania four years before. Eastern society was taken by surprise at the match.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Navy men in one Newport family
narrative_blocks.body: He was a Newport Navy man, and so was his stepson. William Vanderbilt had enlisted at fifteen in the last war, and would grow up to become Governor of Rhode Island.

notable.notable_blurb: 59th Governor of Rhode Island

cross_connections.display_label: married his mother in 1919, becoming his stepfather

narrative_blocks.header: The reform governor who lost for it
narrative_blocks.body: Elected Governor of Rhode Island in 1938, he pushed merit hiring over patronage and cut hundreds of state jobs. His refusal to reward loyal Republicans — and a wiretapping scandal from an election-fraud probe he had funded himself — cost him a second term.

narrative_blocks.header: He left prep school at fifteen to enlist
narrative_blocks.body: In 1917 he dropped out of boarding school to take a midshipman's commission in the Naval Coast Defense Reserve, one of the youngest Americans to serve in the First World War. He tested torpedoes off Newport and crossed to Europe on a destroyer, and was discharged before he turned eighteen.

narrative_blocks.header: He built a bus line, not a railroad
narrative_blocks.body: The Vanderbilts had built a railroad empire; in 1925 he started something smaller and more modern — The Short Line, running motor coaches between Newport and Providence. He grew it across New England, and it outlived him as Bonanza Bus Lines.

narrative_blocks.header: From the governor's chair to Donovan's OSS
narrative_blocks.body: Called back to the Navy in 1941, he rose to captain and served as an executive officer in the Special Operations Branch of the OSS under 'Wild Bill' Donovan. He finished the war on Admiral Nimitz's Pacific staff at Pearl Harbor.

narrative_blocks.header: He ended far from the family mausoleum
narrative_blocks.body: When the wars and the governorship were behind him, he retired not to a Newport cottage but to a working farm in the Berkshire hills. He is one of the few of his line not buried in the Vanderbilt mausoleum on Staten Island.

narrative_blocks.header: The heir who chose the racetrack over business
narrative_blocks.body: Heir to the Vanderbilt fortune, he skipped conventional business for the racetrack — president of Pimlico at twenty, and at twenty-four the youngest man ever elected to the Jockey Club. He pushed the sport toward the mechanical starting gate and the photo finish, and turf writers four times voted him the man who did the most for racing.

narrative_blocks.header: His gray colt lost only once in twenty-two
narrative_blocks.body: At Sagamore Farm in Maryland — six hundred acres his mother gave him at twenty-one — he bred seventy-seven stakes winners over seven decades, none greater than the gray colt Native Dancer. Native Dancer won twenty-one of his twenty-two starts and took the 1953 Preakness and Belmont, and his bloodline still runs through much of American racing.

narrative_blocks.header: He staged the 1938 Match of the Century
narrative_blocks.body: As owner of Pimlico he arranged the 1938 match race between Seabiscuit and War Admiral, talking the reluctant owner of the reigning Triple Crown winner into running. More than forty thousand packed the track and millions listened by radio as Seabiscuit won by four lengths — a jolt of drama for a country still shaking off the Depression.

narrative_blocks.header: He shot lions with Hemingway
narrative_blocks.body: His close friends came from the theater and film — George Abbott, Hal Prince, Fred Astaire — and he once hunted big game with Ernest Hemingway. On a 1950s trip to Moscow, his Soviet hosts put the American capitalist up in their hotel's Lenin suite.

narrative_blocks.header: He won the Silver Star in the Pacific
narrative_blocks.body: He set racing aside in 1942 to enlist, and went on to command a patrol torpedo boat in the Southwest Pacific. He earned the Silver Star for a March 1944 night action in which his boat helped shoot down an attacking Japanese floatplane.

narrative_blocks.header: Orphaned at two by the Lusitania
narrative_blocks.body: He was two years old when his father, Alfred Vanderbilt Sr., went down with the Lusitania in 1915 — remembered for giving his life jacket away as the ship sank. The boy grew up a posthumous heir, raised largely by his mother in New York.

notable.notable_blurb: Yachtsman and scientific explorer

education.notes: Saranac Lake, New York and Miami, Florida

career.notes: World War II; awarded the Legion of Merit

landmarks.landmark_blurb: His Sands Point, New York estate, built 1937

cross_connections.display_label: was his uncle, who funded the Whitney South Seas Expedition

narrative_blocks.header: He turned his yachts into research vessels
narrative_blocks.body: Though he never went to college, he became a self-taught naturalist, sailing to Panama, Africa, the Galápagos, and the South Pacific. He brought back tens of thousands of fish, birds, and reptiles for scientific study.

narrative_blocks.header: His serious science stayed in the family's shadow
narrative_blocks.body: Aboard the schooners Cressida and Pioneer he catalogued more than ten thousand fish specimens across hundreds of species, and founded the George Vanderbilt Foundation to fund marine research. His work was respected by scientists but overshadowed, always, by the Vanderbilt name.

narrative_blocks.header: He revived the family's famous auto races
narrative_blocks.body: In 1936 and 1937 he brought back the Vanderbilt Cup, the pioneering auto race his uncle had founded decades earlier. It drew enormous crowds to a new speedway on Long Island.

narrative_blocks.header: Not yet one when the Lusitania orphaned him
narrative_blocks.body: He was less than a year old when his father, Alfred Vanderbilt Sr., gave away his life jacket and went down with the Lusitania. Raised by his mother, he grew up the posthumous son of the ship's most famous hero.

narrative_blocks.header: His last years were overshadowed by trouble
narrative_blocks.body: For all his wealth and discovery, his final years were troubled — failing business ventures, heavy drinking, and a fourth marriage that lasted only months. Despondent, he took his own life in San Francisco in 1961, at forty-six.

narrative_blocks.header: Pittsburgh newspaper heiress, three times married
narrative_blocks.body: A granddaughter of the owner of the Pittsburgh Dispatch, she married the future governor in 1923 and had a daughter before their divorce five years later. She married twice more, the last time not long before her death at thirty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept a bookshop before she married
narrative_blocks.body: Before her 1929 marriage she ran a New York bookshop with a friend, Peggy Phipps. She had come out into society only two years earlier and been presented at the British court.

narrative_blocks.header: She campaigned for her husband in French
narrative_blocks.body: As First Lady of Rhode Island she stumped for the governor in both English and French, and was honored for it as an 'achievement guest' of the Women's National Press Club. During the war she helped found a Ships Service Committee for the Navy.

narrative_blocks.header: Politics was in her blood before Rhode Island
narrative_blocks.body: Her father, Everett Colby, was a well-known New Jersey reform politician, so public life was familiar long before she became a governor's wife. The instinct carried on: her daughter Anne would give her life to Democratic campaigns.

narrative_blocks.header: She founded a philanthropy for Harlem and prisons
narrative_blocks.body: With her husband, the former governor, she founded the South Forty Corporation, which backed storefront academies in Harlem, prison reform, and affordable housing. It was the heart of her public life.

narrative_blocks.header: She worked for Central American peace and Cuba
narrative_blocks.body: She took up Central American peace work through Witness for Peace and pushed to reopen trade with Cuba. A trustee of Fisk University and Bennington, she gave her later years to civil rights and reconciliation.

narrative_blocks.header: Married to a playboy, then left alone
narrative_blocks.body: At eighteen she married Reginald Vanderbilt — and found herself wed to the family's most restless playboy. Within a few years he had drifted off to his horses and his card tables; in 1920 she divorced him for desertion and raised their daughter herself.

narrative_blocks.header: A real-estate heiress who died young in Paris
narrative_blocks.body: Her own fortune traced to Thomas Davis, the New York real-estate baron ranked in his day just behind the Astors. Remarried and wintering in Paris beside her ailing mother, she collapsed of heart failure at forty — only days after dancing at a society ball.

notable.notable_blurb: Socialite

cross_connections.display_label: won custody of her daughter from her in 1934

narrative_blocks.header: She and her twin dazzled 1920s society
narrative_blocks.body: She and her identical twin, Thelma, were celebrated beauties known as 'the Magnificent Morgans' — daughters of an American diplomat, at home in New York and European society. Cecil Beaton photographed them; Thelma became a mistress of the Prince of Wales.

narrative_blocks.header: At eighteen she married a man of forty-two
narrative_blocks.body: At eighteen she married Reginald Vanderbilt, twenty-four years her senior, and had a daughter, Gloria. Two years later he was dead, leaving her a widow at twenty-one with a small child and a contested fortune.

narrative_blocks.header: She lost her daughter in a famous trial
narrative_blocks.body: In 1934 she fought her wealthy sister-in-law, Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney, for custody of 'Little Gloria' in one of the most sensational trials of the century. Amid a storm of tabloid coverage and hearsay about her private life, she lost.

narrative_blocks.header: She spent her last years beside her twin
narrative_blocks.body: From the 1940s she lived with her twin, Thelma, in New York and Los Angeles, and the two wrote a joint autobiography, 'Double Exposure.' She is the grandmother of the journalist Anderson Cooper.

narrative_blocks.header: To her daughter she was a magical stranger
narrative_blocks.body: In Paris she lived on a separate floor from her small daughter, going out most nights and spending much of the child's trust-fund allowance on her own social whirl. Her daughter would remember her only as a 'magical stranger' glimpsed disappearing down the hallway.

notable.notable_blurb: Heiress and socialite

narrative_blocks.header: A New York heiress who died in Havana
narrative_blocks.body: Married and divorced three times, she followed her third husband — a Havana newspaper publisher — into Cuban society, dividing her last years between New York and Havana. She died there in 1944, two days after her fortieth birthday, and was buried in a Havana cemetery, far from the Vanderbilt vaults.

narrative_blocks.header: A fortune divided between two half-sisters
narrative_blocks.body: When her father, Reginald Vanderbilt, died in 1925, she was twenty-one; she and her half-sister — the young Gloria Vanderbilt — divided the bulk of his estate and a five-million-dollar family trust. The money framed her life more than any occupation ever did.

notable.notable_blurb: Fashion designer and artist

education.school_name: Art Students League of New York

cross_connections.display_label: was her aunt, who won custody and raised her

narrative_blocks.header: The poor little rich girl of the Depression
narrative_blocks.body: At ten, a millionaire since she was a toddler, she became the prize in the 1934 'trial of the century' — her mother and her aunt Gertrude Whitney battling for her and her fortune before a ravenous press. The ordeal cost her the bond with her mother and left a wound she carried the rest of her long life.

narrative_blocks.header: The first designer jeans carried her signature
narrative_blocks.body: In 1976 she stitched her name and a small swan onto a snug-fitting jean and created the first designer denim — an overnight sensation that put her name on millions of backsides. The heiress born to a fortune had gone out and built one of her own.

narrative_blocks.header: The father she never knew
narrative_blocks.body: Her father, Reggie Vanderbilt, died of drink when she was eighteen months old — having run through his own share of the family fortune, though a trust her grandfather had locked safely away still made the baby an heiress. She built her life around a line she loved from the writer Mary Gordon: that a fatherless girl 'thinks all things possible but nothing safe.'

narrative_blocks.header: Four husbands, and a search for belonging
narrative_blocks.body: The girl who never had a stable home married four times looking for one — an abusive agent at seventeen, then the conductor Leopold Stokowski, then the director Sidney Lumet. Only with her fourth husband, the writer Wyatt Cooper, and their two sons did she say she finally found the family she'd wanted.

narrative_blocks.header: Actress, painter, author — she kept remaking herself
narrative_blocks.body: Determined not to be defined by the trial that made her famous, she remade herself again and again — a stage and television actress, a painter with real gallery shows, the author of memoirs and novels. Each new career was another way to make something of a life that had begun as a public spectacle.

narrative_blocks.header: One son she lost; one the world knows
narrative_blocks.body: Of her two sons with Wyatt Cooper, she lost the elder, Carter, to suicide at twenty-three in 1988 — a grief she chose to speak of openly, she said, to keep him alive. The younger, Anderson Cooper, became one of the country's best-known journalists and her closest companion to the end.

narrative_blocks.header: A violent first marriage at seventeen
narrative_blocks.body: A Hollywood agent rumored to have mob ties, he married the seventeen-year-old Gloria Vanderbilt in 1941, weeks after she arrived in California. The marriage was brief and brutal — she later said he beat her and mocked her cruelly — and they divorced within four years.

narrative_blocks.header: An alleged mobster who named a Bond producer
narrative_blocks.body: A Hollywood agent and producer, he was long rumored to run errands for the crime boss Lucky Luciano — a reputation that clung to him more than any film credit. He was also a cousin of Albert Broccoli, and the man who saddled him with the nickname 'Cubby,' under which Broccoli went on to produce the James Bond pictures.

narrative_blocks.header: A world-famous conductor, forty years her senior
narrative_blocks.body: One of the most celebrated conductors of his age — the maestro who shook Mickey Mouse's hand in Disney's 'Fantasia' — he married Gloria Vanderbilt in 1945, forty-two years her senior. Their ten-year marriage gave her two sons before ending in divorce.

narrative_blocks.header: He shook hands with Mickey Mouse on screen
narrative_blocks.body: His collaboration with Walt Disney on the 1940 film 'Fantasia' made him a household name, conducting Bach and Mussorgsky for animation — and sharing a famous on-screen handshake with Mickey Mouse. He liked to say it was really Mickey who got to shake hands with him.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave America its first Rite of Spring
narrative_blocks.body: For sixty years he championed living composers, leading the American premieres of Stravinsky's 'Rite of Spring,' Mahler's Eighth Symphony, Berg's 'Wozzeck,' and Schoenberg's 'Gurre-Lieder.' No major conductor of his day was more adventurous or more eclectic.

narrative_blocks.header: He conducted without a baton, a born showman
narrative_blocks.body: Over a quarter-century with the Philadelphia Orchestra he shaped the lush, unmistakable 'Philadelphia Sound,' and grew famous for conducting with his bare hands after throwing the baton away. Critics dismissed him as a showman; admirers heard an original.

narrative_blocks.header: New York's grit became his signature on film
narrative_blocks.body: Across half a century he became one of America's finest directors, famous for gritty, morally charged New York dramas and for drawing career-best work from his actors. Nominated five times for the Academy Award without a competitive win, he received an honorary Oscar in 2004 for a body of work few could rival.

narrative_blocks.header: Her third husband, a rising film director
narrative_blocks.body: Her third husband was Sidney Lumet, then early in a directing career that would produce '12 Angry Men,' 'Serpico,' and 'Network.' They married in 1956 and divorced seven years later, with no children between them.

narrative_blocks.header: A poor Mississippi boy who became a writer
narrative_blocks.body: Raised in a poor family with deep Southern roots near Quitman, Mississippi, he made himself into a writer — screenplays, a friendship with Dorothy Parker, and in 1975 a memoir titled 'Families.' Its subject was the one thing his crowded Southern boyhood had given him richly, and the thing he would bring to his own marriage.

narrative_blocks.header: The husband who taught her what family meant
narrative_blocks.body: A Mississippi-born author and screenwriter, he became Gloria Vanderbilt's fourth husband in 1963 — and the first, she said, to show her what a family could be. Their fifteen years together, and their two sons, gave the poor little rich girl the stable home she had always wanted.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifteen years, ended on a surgeon's table
narrative_blocks.body: In 1978, at fifty-one, he died during open-heart surgery, ending the marriage Gloria called the happiest of her life. Their younger son, Anderson, was ten — young enough that the loss taught him to always brace for the next catastrophe.

narrative_blocks.header: A Hungarian count who married a Vanderbilt
narrative_blocks.body: Scion of one of Hungary's great noble families, he married the Vanderbilt heiress Gladys in 1908 and later represented his country as its minister in Washington and London. He was once offered the throne of the new Albania — an idea his wife flatly refused to entertain.

narrative_blocks.header: He tried to be the Vanderbilt of Hungary
narrative_blocks.body: Ambitious to become 'the Vanderbilt of Hungary,' he plunged his wife's dowry into stock and land speculations on the Budapest exchange, and lost much of it after the Balkan war. The losses fueled divorce rumors in 1913, but the marriage held for another quarter-century.

narrative_blocks.header: The first of five aristocratic daughters
narrative_blocks.body: The eldest of the five Széchenyi daughters, born at the family's Hungarian castle in 1908, she alone among them married an American — Eugene Bowie Roberts, of an old colonial Maryland family. She died in 1958, seven years before her mother, who left her share of The Breakers to Cornelia's three children.

narrative_blocks.header: A countess who founded a New Hampshire college
narrative_blocks.body: Raised between Hungary and Newport as the second Széchenyi daughter, she lived as a Hungarian countess until the war drove her family to America in 1946. In New Hampshire she helped found White Pines College, turning an aristocrat's exile into a second act.

narrative_blocks.header: A thousand guests saw her Washington wedding
narrative_blocks.body: Her 1931 marriage to Count Béla Hadik drew a thousand guests to a Washington church, a papal blessing read by cable, and a diamond necklace once given by the Empress Maria Theresa. She wore her mother's wedding gown and veil.

narrative_blocks.header: She loaned the family's art to Newport
narrative_blocks.body: A keen horticulturalist, she kept the family's ties to The Breakers alive by lending its artwork to the Preservation Society of Newport. She and her husband settled in Chester, New Hampshire, in a house that had belonged to a Vanderbilt cousin.

narrative_blocks.header: She was Countess of Winchilsea for a decade
narrative_blocks.body: Her 1935 marriage to the Earl of Winchilsea made her an English countess, dividing her life between Hungary's transplanted aristocracy and rural Britain. The marriage ended in divorce a decade later.

narrative_blocks.header: She left a title to marry an American
narrative_blocks.body: Nearly a decade after her divorce, she married Arthur Talbot Peterson, an American banker, in a quiet 1954 ceremony at London's Caxton Hall. Both had been married before, and she traded a countess's title for a life back in America.

narrative_blocks.header: She lived her life inside The Breakers
narrative_blocks.body: For most of her life she kept the family's presence in The Breakers, living in an apartment on the third floor of the seventy-room mansion long after it opened to the public. She insisted that the tourists always be called 'guests.'

narrative_blocks.header: She rode a silver tray down the staircase
narrative_blocks.body: A lively woman with an impish humor, she tobogganed down the Breakers' grand staircase on a silver tray as a child and raced her bicycle around the great hall — traditions younger Vanderbilts took up after her. In later years she would slip into the public tours in plain clothes, unrecognized, and correct the guides.

narrative_blocks.header: She built a model railroad for the centennial
narrative_blocks.body: For the Breakers' 1995 centennial she built, in the estate's stables, a working model of the New York Central Lines that the Commodore had founded, using her own trains. She turned up to the opening in an engineer's cap and a bandaged foot, which she claimed to have hurt bungee jumping.

narrative_blocks.header: She led Newport's arts and preservation world
narrative_blocks.body: Beyond the mansion she was a force in Newport, serving as president of the Rhode Island Arts Foundation and working closely with the Preservation Society, organizing its coaching weekends and aiding its charities. An avid amateur photographer, she was rarely without a small camera at a party.

narrative_blocks.header: To her, the tourists were always 'guests'
narrative_blocks.body: Even as paying visitors filled The Breakers, Sylvie refused to call them tourists — they were 'guests,' a quiet insistence that the palace was still, first, a home. Her daughter Gladys kept the word.

narrative_blocks.header: An American heiress marries into medieval Germany
narrative_blocks.body: In 1946 she married Count Alexander von und zu Eltz, joining a Vanderbilt granddaughter to one of Germany's oldest noble houses. Her brother-in-law Béla Hadik gave her away at the Washington wedding.

narrative_blocks.header: An Albany gentleman devoted to music
narrative_blocks.body: From a family long prominent in Albany, he was a devoted patron of music and served as a director of the New York Symphony Society. He and his wife divided their years between New York, Narragansett, and travels abroad.

narrative_blocks.header: A Vanderbilt goddaughter married at Sunnymead
narrative_blocks.body: A prominent debutante and a goddaughter of Cornelius Vanderbilt, she was married in 1918 at Sunnymead, her family's shingled cottage at Narragansett Pier. She lived afterward at Mount Kisco, north of the city.

narrative_blocks.header: A cavalry trooper who became a decorated colonel
narrative_blocks.body: He rode the Mexican border with Squadron A in 1916, then went to France as a field-artillery officer, rising to lieutenant colonel and chief of staff of the Fifth Army Corps. He came home with the Distinguished Service Medal, two Silver Stars, the Croix de Guerre, and the Legion of Honor — and served again in the Second World War.

narrative_blocks.header: A Beaux-Arts architect who built a museum
narrative_blocks.body: Trained at Harvard and the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris, he practiced in New York and Chicago and, with his partner, designed the Washington County Museum of Fine Arts in Hagerstown, Maryland. He died in a car accident in South Carolina in 1971.

notable.notable_blurb: Poe's first biographer

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Poe’s Fordham cottage, which Gill bought at auction in 1889 to preserve it.

cross_connections.display_label: wrote the life of his father-in-law, Henry Ward Beecher, in 1888

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote Poe's first full-length biography
narrative_blocks.body: A Boston publisher, he wrote 'The Life of Edgar Allan Poe' in 1877 — the first book-length biography of the writer. His aim was to clear Poe's name of the slanders that Poe's rival Rufus Griswold had spread after the poet's death, and he gathered his account from those who had known Poe firsthand.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept Mrs. Poe's bones under his bed
narrative_blocks.body: When the Fordham cemetery holding Poe's wife Virginia was razed, he rescued her bones just as they were about to be discarded, and kept them in a box beneath his bed for two years. In 1885 he arranged for her to be reburied beside Poe in Baltimore, on the anniversary of the poet's birth.

narrative_blocks.header: He saved Poe's cottage for posterity
narrative_blocks.body: In 1889 he bought at auction, for seven hundred and seventy-five dollars, the Fordham cottage where Poe had written 'The Raven,' preserving the poet's last New York home. It stands today as a Poe museum.

narrative_blocks.header: A polyglot war hero, generous and amusing
narrative_blocks.body: He drove ambulances for the French army, then served as a Marine translator, winning Silver Stars at Belleau Wood and Château-Thierry. A generous, amusing man who spoke French, Arabic, Spanish, and Italian, he married three times, once to Cathleen Neilson, Reginald Vanderbilt's former wife.

narrative_blocks.header: Mistress of a famous Newport cottage
narrative_blocks.body: She entertained lavishly at Clarendon Court, the Newport villa her family owned, during her marriage to the war hero Sidney Colford. The daughter of a spendthrift railroad heir, she left the marriage in 1920 and later remarried.

cross_connections.display_label: edited the Civil War Book Review in a life nearly as brief

narrative_blocks.header: Books and history were his first loves
narrative_blocks.body: From boyhood he was the reader of the family, the one drawn to history — smart, thoughtful, and kind. After Princeton he took a job editing a history magazine in New York and writing book reviews, and those who knew him imagined a writer's life ahead of him.

narrative_blocks.header: Two brothers, two years and one wall apart
narrative_blocks.body: Growing up, he and his younger brother, Anderson, lived in rooms next to each other for eighteen years, playing Dungeons & Dragons together to escape the grief of losing their father young. Two years the elder, Carter was the quieter, more scholarly of the two.

narrative_blocks.header: A loss that shaped the brother he left
narrative_blocks.body: In July 1988, a year out of Princeton, he took his own life at twenty-three — an act his mother believed was set off by a sudden psychotic episode. The loss helped turn his younger brother, Anderson, toward journalism and a lifelong reckoning with grief.

notable.notable_blurb: Broadcast journalist

cross_connections.display_label: anchors ABC's mornings, after running Clinton's White House press
had a daughter with a friend nine years before Cooper had his sons

narrative_blocks.header: One of America's best-known broadcast journalists
narrative_blocks.body: For more than two decades he has anchored CNN's 'Anderson Cooper 360°,' reporting from hurricanes, wars, and disasters, while also serving as a correspondent for '60 Minutes.' His unflinching coverage of Hurricane Katrina made him one of the most recognized faces in American news, and he has won eighteen Emmy Awards.

narrative_blocks.header: The family losses that shaped his life's work
narrative_blocks.body: Ten when his father died and twenty-one when his brother, Carter, took his own life, he has said those losses drew him toward journalism and the world's most grief-stricken places. Decades later he turned grief itself into the subject of an acclaimed podcast, 'All There Is.'

narrative_blocks.header: The most prominent gay journalist on television
narrative_blocks.body: In 2012 he confirmed publicly that he is gay, and was soon described as the most prominent openly gay journalist on American television. Four years later he became the first openly LGBT person to moderate a general-election presidential debate.

narrative_blocks.header: A son named for the father he lost
narrative_blocks.body: In 2020 he became a father to a son, Wyatt — named for the father he had lost at ten, with his grandmother Gloria Morgan's maiden name as the middle name. The next year he published 'Vanderbilt,' a history of the family he called a letter to his son.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Her seaside cafe and nightclub

narrative_blocks.header: A comedienne in the Marx Brothers' orbit
narrative_blocks.body: One of the busiest comic actresses of the early sound era, she appeared in scores of films — sparring with the Marx Brothers in 'Monkey Business' and 'Horse Feathers,' and clowning alongside Laurel and Hardy. She made the leap from silents to talkies with an ease that eluded many of her peers.

narrative_blocks.header: Her seaside café caught the wrong attention
narrative_blocks.body: In 1933 she opened Thelma Todd's Sidewalk Café on the Pacific Coast Highway, a fashionable spot with a nightclub above it. Its success, by some accounts, drew overtures from organized crime that she turned down.

narrative_blocks.header: Her death remains an unsolved Hollywood mystery
narrative_blocks.body: One December morning in 1935 she was found dead in her car in a garage above the café, at twenty-nine. Ruled first suicide and then accidental, her death has been whispered about as murder ever since — with her ex-husband among the names that surface.

notable.notable_blurb: Film actress

narrative_blocks.header: Discovered in a hotel lobby by Hughes' scout
narrative_blocks.body: A Portland beauty-queen, she was spotted in a Phoenix hotel lobby by a talent scout for Howard Hughes and briefly became the Western-picture actress Linda Douglas. She gave up acting for good after marrying Pat DiCicco in 1952.

narrative_blocks.header: After DiCicco came a baseball Hall of Famer
narrative_blocks.body: Once her marriage to DiCicco ended, she married the baseball Hall of Famer Hank Greenberg in 1966 and took his name. Widowed twenty years later, she spent her final decades running an animal-welfare foundation she had set up in their names.

people.research_notes: Born Mary Joanne Tarola.

narrative_blocks.header: Cathleen's first husband, from an old Boston family
narrative_blocks.body: A financial adviser descended from an old Boston family — and a nephew of the illustrator Otho Cushing — he married Cathleen Vanderbilt in 1923 in the gardens of the Ambassador Hotel. The marriage lasted nine years and produced a son before ending in divorce.

cross_connections.link_text: Brig. Gen. Edward Lyman Munson Jr.
cross_connections.display_label: ran the Army's pictorial service, then built NBC television
ran CBS's Pacific Coast network while he was a CBS vice president
was an executive producer of public affairs programs at CBS

narrative_blocks.header: Cathleen's second husband helped build television
narrative_blocks.body: Cathleen's second husband was a pioneer of American broadcasting — a vice president of CBS in the early days of radio and television, when the networks were still inventing themselves. They married in 1932 and divorced eight years later.

narrative_blocks.header: In the war he directed OSS communications
narrative_blocks.body: During the Second World War he served as a colonel directing communications for the Office of Strategic Services, forerunner of the CIA. He came back to broadcasting afterward, helping launch CBS's postwar television division.

narrative_blocks.header: Cathleen's third husband, a Havana publisher
narrative_blocks.body: Her third and final husband was a Cuban newspaperman — publisher of PM, Havana's English-language afternoon paper — and the son of a Cuban marquesa. He married Cathleen in 1940 and drew her into Havana society for the last four years of her life.

cross_connections.display_label: reached a nine-goal rating and polo's Hall of Fame in 1999

narrative_blocks.header: For polo, he spent thirty years in Rome
narrative_blocks.body: Polo organized his whole life: he settled in Rome for thirty years because there, he wrote, a Vanderbilt could afford to keep his own team. He fielded squads that won across Europe and played with royalty from Jordan to Egypt.

narrative_blocks.header: A wartime codebreaker at the Pentagon
narrative_blocks.body: Before the polo years, he left Cornell to join the Army after Pearl Harbor and spent the war as a cryptographer, handling codes at the Pentagon and in the South Pacific. Then he turned to the game that would define the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: His memoir cast him as a modern knight-errant
narrative_blocks.body: Late in life he wrote a candid memoir, Vanderbilt Scion: Memoirs of a Modern Knight-Errant, unabashed about his taste for beautiful women and the good life his name afforded. It is the self-portrait of a man who chose pleasure and sport over enterprise.

narrative_blocks.header: He built subdivisions across Prince George's County
narrative_blocks.body: A lifelong Marylander and husband of Cornelia Széchenyi, he sold Washington real estate through the 1920s and '30s before developing apartments and communities of his own across Prince George's County. He also ran the family's Fairwood Farm, which passed to their son.

cross_connections.display_label: was his grandmother, who leased The Breakers to the society he served
was his aunt, who led Newport society from within The Breakers
sat on the board of the Newport Historical Society in the same town

narrative_blocks.header: He kept Angus cattle from age seven
narrative_blocks.body: He grew up on Fairwood, the Maryland farm he called the most beautiful place on earth, and kept a herd of Angus cattle from the age of seven into his sixties. He liked to joke that he got his degree at Yale but his education in the beef barns of Penn State.

narrative_blocks.header: He turned the family farm into a town
narrative_blocks.body: After the Peace Corps in Colombia and an MBA in Chicago, he spent years planning a diversified holding company before coming home to farm turfgrass at Fairwood. Foreseeing Washington's sprawl, he partnered with the Rouse Company to turn the old farm into the mixed-use Fairwood community.

narrative_blocks.header: He loved genealogy as much as cattle breeding
narrative_blocks.body: Family history was his great passion — a cousin called his the most interesting lineage he had ever met, running back to Lord Baltimore, Thomas Hooker, Roger Williams, and the Commodore. He served the Preservation Society of Newport as a trustee for thirty years, and found his joy in bringing kin together.

marriages.place: Washington, District of Columbia, United States

landmarks.landmark_blurb: The Chester, New Hampshire college, opened 1965.

cross_connections.display_label: was given away by him at her 1946 wedding

narrative_blocks.header: He descended from a Berlin-capturing hussar general
narrative_blocks.body: He descended from András Hadik, the hussar general who briefly seized Berlin during the Seven Years' War, and carried the family's honors as a Knight of the Golden Fleece and a member of Hungary's House of Magnates. He served as a cavalry lieutenant in the war.

narrative_blocks.header: War cost him his ancestral Hungarian estate
narrative_blocks.body: He took over his family's grand estate at Seregélyes after his marriage, but the war ended that world — German and then Soviet troops occupied the palace, the family's possessions were lost, and in 1948 they began again in New Hampshire.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped bring back the Vizsla
narrative_blocks.body: In America he took up breeding Vizslas, the Hungarian pointing dog, at his Futaki Kennels — part of the effort that revived the breed, producing champions like Futaki Darócz. It was a piece of Hungary carried into New Hampshire exile.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: The Chester, New Hampshire college, opened 1965.

narrative_blocks.header: He rebuilt the Hadik name in New Hampshire
narrative_blocks.body: He married a German countess, Vita Strachwitz, in Munich in 1956 and settled in Chester, New Hampshire, where his exiled parents had rebuilt their lives. He was killed in a plane crash in the summer of 1973, at forty-one.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: The Chester, New Hampshire college, opened 1965.

narrative_blocks.header: A count descended from Vanderbilts and Hungarian ministers
narrative_blocks.body: He was born a Hungarian count — grandson of Count László Széchenyi, Hungary's minister to Washington, and of Count János Hadik, a Hungarian cabinet minister. Through his grandmother Gladys Vanderbilt he also descended from Commodore Cornelius Vanderbilt.

narrative_blocks.header: Harvard, the Army in Germany, then Chase
narrative_blocks.body: Raised in New Hampshire, he went to Brooks School and Harvard, then served two years with the Fourth Armored Division in occupied Germany. He settled into a banking career at Chase Manhattan in New York, married Edith Gaillet in 1962, and raised three sons.

narrative_blocks.header: An English earl with an American fortune
narrative_blocks.body: Half-American through his mother, a Drexel of Philadelphia, he inherited the ancient earldoms of Winchilsea and Nottingham in 1939. His short life bridged two great American fortunes, the Drexels and the Vanderbilts, before he died at thirty-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: His uncle inspired 'Out of Africa'
narrative_blocks.body: His family tree held remarkable figures: his uncle was Denys Finch-Hatton, the big-game hunter and lover of the writer Isak Dinesen, later played by Robert Redford in 'Out of Africa.' His great-grandfather Anthony Drexel had co-founded the banking house of Drexel, Morgan & Co.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a countess at Caxton Hall
narrative_blocks.body: An American banker in his fifties, he married the former Countess of Winchilsea in a quiet 1954 ceremony at London's Caxton Hall. Both had been married before, and the match drew her back into American life.

cross_connections.display_label: was his uncle by marriage, who saved refugees of an earlier war

narrative_blocks.header: He wore his ancient title like a burden
narrative_blocks.body: He inherited two ancient earldoms at thirteen and spent much of his life regarding them as a burden he could not justify. A grassroots Liberal at heart, he was happiest delivering leaflets and canvassing on doorsteps, and only reluctantly took his seat in the House of Lords.

narrative_blocks.header: He drove rainbow convoys across the Sahara
narrative_blocks.body: His deepest cause was the displaced Sahrawi people, stranded in Algerian desert camps since 1975. He organized ten 'Rainbow Rover' convoys of rainbow-painted Land Rovers carrying food and medicine to the camps, and drew Jimmy Carter and James Baker into the search for a settlement.

narrative_blocks.header: He championed taxi-drivers and policemen in Parliament
narrative_blocks.body: In the Lords he made himself the voice of two unglamorous groups, licensed taxi-drivers and the police. Grateful cabbies presented him with a London taxi, and to understand the policeman's lot he spent a stretch walking a beat in Hackney.

narrative_blocks.header: He loved jazz, America, and Coca-Cola
narrative_blocks.body: His enthusiasms ran wide: a love of jazz that earned him his own series on Jazz FM, a lasting affection for America from his years living there, and a patronage of the Terrence Higgins Trust after a friend fell ill with AIDS. Even a heart attack couldn't part him from his beloved Coca-Cola.

narrative_blocks.header: She won a council seat of her own
narrative_blocks.body: Elected a county councillor in her own right, she campaigned for better resources in Britain's comprehensive schools and insisted her children attend the local state schools. She was the steadying force in a formidable political partnership.

narrative_blocks.header: He sheltered 300,000 refugees during the war
narrative_blocks.body: As an officer of the Hungarian Red Cross, he served as liaison to the International Red Cross and helped some 300,000 Polish refugees who had fled into Hungary. It was work that would nearly cost him his life.

narrative_blocks.header: Condemned at Mauthausen, a king saved him
narrative_blocks.body: In 1944 the occupying Germans arrested him and imprisoned him for nine months at Mauthausen, where he was condemned to die. He was released only through the personal intervention of the King of Sweden.

narrative_blocks.header: He fought for stateless athletes at the Olympics
narrative_blocks.body: In America he led the Union of Free Eastern European Sportsmen, which pressed — without success — for refugee athletes to compete at the 1952 Helsinki Olympics. He had helped found the Hungarian National Sports Federation before the war.

narrative_blocks.header: His family's castle has stood 850 years
narrative_blocks.body: He belonged to the House of Eltz, an ancient German family of imperial knights whose ancestral seat, Burg Eltz on the Moselle, has remained in the family for over eight centuries, never once destroyed. It is among the oldest continuously held estates in Europe.

parents.mother_name: Fernandine Széchényi von und zu Eltz

narrative_blocks.header: He lived among the old Austrian nobility
narrative_blocks.body: Raised in the Eltz family's Austrian world, he married Michèle Landry in 1976 and spent his life among the old nobility of Styria. He died at sixty-one and was buried at Altaussee.

narrative_blocks.header: His ancestral castle graced the 500-mark note
narrative_blocks.body: Through his father he belonged to the House of Eltz, whose fairy-tale castle on the Moselle is among the most famous in Germany. For thirty years it was pictured on the 500-Deutsche-Mark banknote.

His father's yacht, on the 1853 grand tour

painted his portrait as well as his father's
gained a Vanderbilt stepmother when his father remarried in 1920
decided who sat at the old opera house, and would not seat him
sang at the Metropolitan Opera for thirty seasons from 1970

narrative_blocks.header: The 'blockhead' son who doubled the fortune
narrative_blocks.body: His father the Commodore scorned him as a 'blatherskite' and a blockhead and packed him off to a Staten Island farm. Given the family railroads at last, he doubled the greatest fortune in America in barely eight years, dying worth some two hundred million dollars.

narrative_blocks.header: Four words made him the era's villain
narrative_blocks.body: Asked whether he ran an unprofitable express train for the public's sake, he snapped, 'The public be damned!' The line, splashed across the papers, came to stand for the arrogance of Gilded Age wealth for the rest of the century.

narrative_blocks.header: He returned a fallen general's sword
narrative_blocks.body: When a Wall Street swindle ruined Ulysses S. Grant, the old general repaid a debt to Vanderbilt with his Civil War swords and mementos. Vanderbilt took them, cleared the debt, and after Grant's death quietly returned every piece to his widow.

narrative_blocks.header: Refused a box, he built a bigger house
narrative_blocks.body: The Academy of Music kept eighteen boxes and the old families kept them among themselves; Vanderbilt offered for one and was turned down. He and the other rejected men put up the Metropolitan Opera House on Broadway instead, three tiers of boxes deep, and the Academy never recovered.

narrative_blocks.header: The family waited to be let in
narrative_blocks.body: The Vanderbilts were swells, not nobs — money without the generations behind it — and no hostess in New York would take them on until Mrs Astor said she was ready. So they waited, and spent, and waited.

narrative_blocks.header: A parson's daughter at the fortune's center
narrative_blocks.body: A country parson's daughter, she married Billy Vanderbilt when he was a struggling clerk and steadied him through the hard farm years before the railroad fortune came, encouragement he later credited for his rise. She never took to the display the money brought, keeping an early-rising, church-going life and giving to charity on the condition her name be left off.

narrative_blocks.header: He quit school at eleven for the harbor
narrative_blocks.body: He left school at eleven to work his father's Staten Island ferry, and at sixteen borrowed a hundred dollars for a boat of his own. From that he built the greatest shipping and railroad empire of the age, dying the richest man in America.

narrative_blocks.header: Any man can make a fortune, he said
narrative_blocks.body: Ruthless in the steamship and railroad wars, he crushed rivals from Nicaragua to the Erie board and drove his lines into the heart of Manhattan at Grand Central. 'Any man can make a fortune,' he said; 'it takes brains to hold onto it.'

narrative_blocks.header: His will pitted his children against each other
narrative_blocks.body: A hard father who scorned most of his thirteen children, he left ninety-five percent of his fortune to a single son, Billy. The others contested the will, claiming a spiritualist medium had swayed him; Billy settled to spare the family further scandal.

narrative_blocks.header: His fortune founded a university in the South
narrative_blocks.body: Late in life, with almost no history of giving, he was persuaded by his young second wife to found a Methodist university in Nashville, endowing it with a million dollars, the largest charitable gift in America to that time. It still bears his name, and its teams are called the Commodores after his own.

narrative_blocks.header: Grief for a lost son pierced even him
narrative_blocks.body: For all his hardness, the war broke something in him: his youngest and favorite son, George, a West Point graduate and his intended heir, fell ill and died in 1862 before ever seeing battle. The Commodore, who had given a warship to the Union and won a Gold Medal for it, never fully recovered.

narrative_blocks.header: He sailed a floating palace to Europe
narrative_blocks.body: In 1853 he built the North Star, over two hundred and fifty feet of paddle-wheel steam yacht with marble and gold below decks, and took the family on a grand tour — England in eleven days, then St. Petersburg, Denmark, France, Malta and Constantinople. A boy of nineteen went overboard off Portugal on that voyage. From 1854 she carried mail and passengers like any other ship he owned.

narrative_blocks.header: She bore thirteen children to a ruthless man
narrative_blocks.body: A cousin the Commodore married at eighteen, she bore him thirteen children and ran a profitable New Jersey inn that fed and schooled them through the lean early years. When she resisted his plans late in the marriage, he briefly had her committed to an asylum.

narrative_blocks.header: Her parents named her for a man
narrative_blocks.body: Her parents named her Frank, after a beloved friend, before she was born and before they knew she would be a girl. A Mobile belle and zealous Methodist, she married the seventy-five-year-old Commodore Vanderbilt in 1869, when she was thirty.

narrative_blocks.header: She founded a university to heal a rift
narrative_blocks.body: Her cousin's husband was the Methodist bishop Holland McTyeire, who dreamed of a Southern university; in 1873 she steered a million dollars of her husband's fortune to found it in Nashville. The Commodore, who had helped defeat the Confederacy at sea, gave it as a gesture of reconciliation to the South, though he never once visited.

narrative_blocks.header: An unrepentant Confederate to the end
narrative_blocks.body: An unrepentant Confederate through the Civil War and after, she counted Generals Braxton and Thomas Bragg among her wedding guests. The university she helped found long kept her Southern loyalties out of its official story, a silence its own students later noted.

people.relational_label_override: Second Wife of Grandfather-in-law of a Ninth Generation Hooker

narrative_blocks.header: His first wife, wed before 3,000 guests
narrative_blocks.body: She was Cornelius Vanderbilt IV's first wife, married in 1920 in an elaborate ceremony for more than three thousand guests. The marriage ended in divorce a few years later, after his tabloid ventures collapsed.

narrative_blocks.header: She divorced one husband to marry another
narrative_blocks.body: She obtained a divorce from her first husband barely half an hour before marrying Cornelius Vanderbilt IV in 1928. That marriage ended three years later.

narrative_blocks.header: She met him sketching in New Mexico
narrative_blocks.body: A doctor's daughter from West Virginia, she was sketching in Albuquerque when she met Cornelius Vanderbilt IV, and married him in 1935. After their divorce she married Jack Frye, the founder and president of TWA, at the dawn of commercial aviation.

narrative_blocks.header: A Mexican cattle heiress and a president's kin
narrative_blocks.body: Heiress to a vast cattle estate in Mexico, she was a grandniece of President Porfirio Díaz and a granddaughter of Mexico's ambassador to Washington. Her 1946 marriage to Cornelius Vanderbilt IV lasted two years.

narrative_blocks.header: Their divorce reached the Supreme Court
narrative_blocks.body: Her 1948 marriage to Cornelius Vanderbilt IV ended in a Nevada divorce she refused to accept. She fought it to the United States Supreme Court, which ruled in her favor in 1957, a landmark holding that a Nevada divorce could not cut off the support rights she held in New York.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandfather ran for vice president at eighty
narrative_blocks.body: He was a grandson of Senator Henry Gassaway Davis, the West Virginia coal-and-railroad baron who, at eighty, became the Democrats' 1904 nominee for vice president, the oldest man ever placed on a major national ticket. Towns, a college, and mountains across West Virginia still bear the family name.

narrative_blocks.header: He married into the Vanderbilts twice
narrative_blocks.body: He married Grace Vanderbilt in 1927, and after their divorce married another Vanderbilt, Consuelo Vanderbilt Earl. He lived out his later years quietly in New York and Connecticut.

marriages.place: Ridgewood, Bergen County, New Jersey, United States

cross_connections.display_label: was his father-in-law, a Commodore of the New York Yacht Club

narrative_blocks.header: He descended from America's first family of engineers
narrative_blocks.body: He was a grandson of Edwin A. Stevens, who founded the Stevens Institute of Technology, and a descendant of Col. John Stevens, a steamboat and railroad pioneer. His forebear John Cox Stevens was the first Commodore of the New York Yacht Club, whose schooner America gave the America's Cup its name.

narrative_blocks.header: She traded Fifth Avenue for the Idaho mountains
narrative_blocks.body: She married the Marine and oilman Charles McCain in 1949 and raised three children, making her home at last in Sun Valley, Idaho, far from the Fifth Avenue world of her Vanderbilt grandmother.

narrative_blocks.header: A Marine who served in two wars
narrative_blocks.body: He enlisted in the Marine Corps in 1942 and served two and a half years in the Second World War, then was recalled for the Korean War, retiring as a first lieutenant.

narrative_blocks.header: He struck out in the Louisiana oil fields
narrative_blocks.body: He learned the oil business from the ground up at Texaco, then joined H.L. Hunt's Placid Oil before helping to found Winwell Petroleum. His firms helped discover Louisiana's Fairway Field, and he ran his own McCain Oil Company until his death at ninety-seven.

narrative_blocks.header: Engaged at twenty-seven, announced from Water Mill
narrative_blocks.body: Grace Stevens was engaged to Edmund Hollis Sutton in December 1967, the announcement made by her father Robert Livingston Stevens from the houses he kept in New York and at Water Mill on Long Island.

narrative_blocks.header: She hit her first hole-in-one at sixteen
narrative_blocks.body: An exceptional golfer, she made the first of ten career holes-in-one at sixteen. She was a serious skier too, spending her later years on the slopes of Vail and Klosters.

narrative_blocks.header: A self-taught painter who lived to a hundred
narrative_blocks.body: She was a talented primitive painter, known for three-dimensional works depicting the Caribbean and New England. Widowed after forty-four years with her second husband, a champion skier, she lived to one hundred.

narrative_blocks.header: Preserving Arcadia became her life's work
narrative_blocks.body: Arcadia, the South Carolina plantation her family had held for generations, passed to her from her father — and preserving it became her life's work. A committed conservationist, she spent decades as its careful steward, and gave herself to philanthropy under a creed that to whom much is given, much is required.

narrative_blocks.header: A painter, photographer, and family genealogist
narrative_blocks.body: Away from the land, she painted, photographed, and took up genealogy, tracing her own family's history. She had grown up between Palm Beach, her father's nature expeditions across the Pacific, and summers with her grandmother Margaret Emerson at Camp Sagamore in the Adirondacks.

narrative_blocks.header: A senior year that never began
narrative_blocks.body: Lulu Pate's son was seventeen, just starting his senior year of high school, when a drunk driver struck the car he was riding in near Georgetown, South Carolina. He and a schoolmate were killed in the crash.

cross_connections.display_label: gave the Smithsonian the gem hall where the Hope Diamond is shown

narrative_blocks.header: She married the man who staged Seabiscuit's race
narrative_blocks.body: She was a niece of Charles S. Howard, the California car dealer who owned Seabiscuit. In June 1938 she married Alfred Vanderbilt — months before he staged Seabiscuit's celebrated match race against War Admiral.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother-in-law owned the Hope Diamond
narrative_blocks.body: Her Vanderbilt marriage ended in 1942, and she later married into the McLean family. That made her mother-in-law Evalyn Walsh McLean, the mining heiress and last private owner of the Hope Diamond.

narrative_blocks.header: A publicity agent at the Stork Club
narrative_blocks.body: Before her marriage she worked as a publicity agent at the Stork Club, and during it as a production assistant on the David Frost Show — working jobs unusual for a Murray heiress. The Murrays were a wealthy Irish Catholic family of New York and Southampton.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandfather held 462 patents
narrative_blocks.body: She was a granddaughter of Thomas E. Murray, the New York power-plant engineer often called the most prolific American inventor after Edison. His four hundred and sixty-two patents included the dimmer switch and the screw-in fuse.

narrative_blocks.header: She eloped by private plane to Philadelphia
narrative_blocks.body: In 1945 she married Alfred Vanderbilt at Philadelphia City Hall, having eloped from New York by private plane. They had two children, Heidi and Alfred III, before divorcing a decade later.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Grew up on the family Maryland horse farm

cross_connections.display_label: runs her own studio, blending clay sculpture with painting

narrative_blocks.header: She chose the studio over society
narrative_blocks.body: Born into the Vanderbilt name and photographed for one of Lilly Pulitzer's first campaigns, she turned away from the social circuit for a life in the studio. Working in wood, aluminum, acrylic, and watercolor, she built a modernist career that ran six decades.

narrative_blocks.header: Georgia O'Keeffe helped shape her modernism
narrative_blocks.body: Her sense of clean, disciplined form was shaped by two mentors — the painter Georgia O'Keeffe and O'Keeffe's sister, Anita Young. In 2008 her work entered museums nationwide through the Vogel Collection's 'Fifty Works for Fifty States,' including the National Gallery of Art.

narrative_blocks.header: A near-tragedy turned her into a safety crusader
narrative_blocks.body: After she watched a driver run a red light and nearly kill a friend's child, she helped found STOP — the Stop Traffic Offenses Program. It was practical civic work, not ceremonial philanthropy.

narrative_blocks.header: She made light dimmers from margarine tubs
narrative_blocks.body: A natural tinkerer, she once built her friends light dimmers out of margarine containers as Christmas gifts. She was just as known for a vast, high-powered email list where she posted everything from political commentary to dirty jokes.

notable.notable_blurb: New York State Parks Commissioner

career.organization: New York State Office of Parks, Recreation and Historic Preservation

narrative_blocks.header: He followed Robert Moses and stayed eighteen years
narrative_blocks.body: Appointed in 1975 to run New York's state parks, he took over from the legendary Robert Moses — 'a tough act to follow' — and served eighteen years, the longest tenure the office has known. He spent them shielding the state's parks from budget cuts rather than building new ones.

narrative_blocks.header: An Army pilot, badly wounded at the Bulge
narrative_blocks.body: Flying as a spotter for the field artillery, he was badly wounded in Germany during the Battle of the Bulge, losing one leg and much of the use of the other. He was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross and the Purple Heart, and used crutches for the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: His injuries turned him toward the disabled
narrative_blocks.body: His own wounds gave him a lifelong cause. In 1947 he helped Eleanor Roosevelt and Bernard Baruch found Just One Break, the country's oldest employment service for people with disabilities, and chaired it for more than fifty years.

narrative_blocks.header: He walked away from Lehman Brothers
narrative_blocks.body: A great-grandson of a Lehman Brothers founder and great-nephew of Governor Herbert Lehman, he spent five years at the family bank and left, saying only that he 'didn't want to devote my life to making money.'

narrative_blocks.header: He even produced a Pulitzer-winning play
narrative_blocks.body: His life ran well beyond parks. He produced the off-Broadway play that won the 1971 Pulitzer for drama, and in later years kept company with the comedian Joan Rivers.

notable.notable_blurb: Writer, actress, and horsewoman

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Grew up on the family Maryland horse farm

narrative_blocks.header: Onstage at seventeen in Ruth Gordon's play
narrative_blocks.body: At seventeen she made her Broadway debut, as Heidi Murray, in a play written by and starring the actress Ruth Gordon. Six years later she married Gordon's son, Jones Harris, trading the stage for a life of photography and writing.

narrative_blocks.header: The stage lost her to the writer's desk
narrative_blocks.body: Giving up acting, she built a career as a photographer, poet, and author. Her fiction and nonfiction won her a 1983 Edgar Award from the Mystery Writers of America, and her first novel, 'The Scar Rule,' drew on the horse world she had made her home.

narrative_blocks.header: A hundred-mile ride she finished three times
narrative_blocks.body: An accomplished horsewoman, she finished the grueling hundred-mile Tevis Cup endurance ride three times. She spent her later years on an Arizona ranch, raising horses, donkeys, goats, pigs, and dogs, in love with the Southwest desert and its animals.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Grew up on the family Maryland horse farm

narrative_blocks.header: Five to eight hours a day writing
narrative_blocks.body: He spent five to eight hours a day at the typewriter, working to break into freelance writing from Austin. He had just begun to break through — a first national piece in Vogue, an advance from Sports Illustrated, and Above the Dawn, a half-finished screenplay about the camaraderie and rivalries of a group of climbers.

narrative_blocks.header: He served stew to Austin's street people
narrative_blocks.body: A convert to Catholicism, he gave two mornings a month to an Austin soup kitchen called Angels House, cooking and serving stew to the city's poor.
