narrative_blocks.header: A great-granddaughter married a Hooker
narrative_blocks.body: Clement Treat was born at Milford in 1743 to his grandson Joseph, and married David Ingersoll there in March 1768. Ingersoll's descent ran back to Thomas Hooker through the Newtons, so two of the colony's founding lines closed on one household.

narrative_blocks.header: An architectural historian who kept the family's story
narrative_blocks.body: An architectural historian by profession, he became the keeper of his family's long memory, writing its history and gathering seven generations of ancestral portraits into his Austin home. It was two of those painted faces — a Flagg and a Maxson, both Trinity men — that drew him east to the same college in 1965.

narrative_blocks.header: He devoted himself to Trinity's Long Walk
narrative_blocks.body: At Trinity College he fell in love with the Gothic Long Walk buildings, a passion that shaped his career as an architectural historian. Decades later he and his partner made a major gift to help restore them, so the Long Walk would stand at the heart of the campus for generations to come.

narrative_blocks.header: He was drafted into a long family tradition
narrative_blocks.body: Inducted into the Army weeks after graduating in 1969, he entered a family tradition of service that ran back three centuries — to Flagg sons killed in King Philip's War and the Revolution. He chronicled that ancestry himself, an architectural historian who was also his family's genealogist.

narrative_blocks.header: A Princeton man who ranched the Nevada desert
narrative_blocks.body: A Princeton graduate of an old Nevada family, he trained thoroughbred horses and ran the vast Grass Valley Ranch northeast of Austin. The purebred Hereford herd he built there became the foundation of the ranch his wife Molly would later make famous.

parents.father_research_notes: Bernard Shirley and Louise Hope (Thacher) Carter of Paris, France.

cross_connections.display_label: was a fellow president of the Museum of Modern Art
guarded the museum she gave seventy years to, before he painted

narrative_blocks.header: Seventy years shaping the Museum of Modern Art
narrative_blocks.body: Known as Eliza Parkinson, she was at the Museum of Modern Art for nearly seventy years and its president from 1965 to 1968. Niece of the founder Lillie Bliss, she treated the whole collection as her own.

narrative_blocks.header: She carried modern American art to the world
narrative_blocks.body: As president of the museum's International Council from 1957 to 1966 she was credited with an almost ambassadorial gift for carrying postwar American painting abroad, in the years the Modern was called the parent of them all.

narrative_blocks.header: She began as a fox-hunting fundraiser
narrative_blocks.body: She came to the museum young, more taken with fox-hunting than with art, and started as a fundraiser before ripening into a real connoisseur and collector. In time she kept a great Rothko glowing on her own bedroom wall.

narrative_blocks.header: He married into the Modern's founding circle
narrative_blocks.body: In 1932 he married Eliza Bliss Parkinson, niece of a founder of the Museum of Modern Art, and the couple settled at Westbury on Long Island. During the Second World War he served in the Navy.

bio.bio_blurb: Baroque art historian and Scribner publisher

narrative_blocks.header: He went undercover in Miami Beach
narrative_blocks.body: In 1991 he worked undercover with United States Customs agents in Miami Beach to trap art thieves and recover a Rubens oil sketch stolen from a museum in Spain. The Treasury Department gave him its Yorktown Certificate, and a documentary told the story twelve years later.

narrative_blocks.header: He signs his books the third
narrative_blocks.body: The family reset its numbering at his grandfather, so the fifth Charles Scribner signs his books Charles Scribner III. He is the fifth generation in a house founded in 1846.

narrative_blocks.header: A Princeton doctorate in Baroque art
narrative_blocks.body: He came up through Buckley, St. Paul’s and Princeton, where he took a doctorate in art history in 1977 and taught Baroque art. His monographs on Rubens and Bernini appeared in the Masters of Art series.

narrative_blocks.header: He outlasted three changes of owner
narrative_blocks.body: He joined his father at Scribner’s in 1975 and rose to executive vice-president, then went to Macmillan as vice-president for special projects until 2004. Talleyrand, he said, was his model for surviving the successive owners.

narrative_blocks.header: Art carried him into the Catholic Church
narrative_blocks.body: The Shadow of God, written as a journal, traces the journey through art and memory that led him to convert to Roman Catholicism. He returned to the subject in Home by Another Route and in Sacred Muse.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote his own family’s five generations
narrative_blocks.body: Scribners: Five Generations in Publishing appeared in 2023, and Artists & Authors followed in 2026. He had spoken before for documentaries on Edith Wharton and on Fitzgerald and Hemingway.

narrative_blocks.header: His skater mother read him Hans Brinker
narrative_blocks.body: His mother was a professional figure skater, and the Scribner book he remembers her reading him is Hans Brinker, or the Silver Skates. His father had written one of the house’s children’s books himself.

people.research_notes: Publishes as Charles Scribner III; Princeton graduate, art historian and author.

bio.bio_blurb: Sculptor of assemblage and found objects

cross_connections.display_label: builds his sculpture from studio sweepings and scrap in Brooklyn

narrative_blocks.header: Bones, fake food, and old toys
narrative_blocks.body: He reconstitutes anatomical prints, soil and sand, fake food, bones and old toys into sculpture, working in collage and assemblage. The disjointed narratives that result reach after history, science, literature and the arts.

narrative_blocks.header: The National Arts Club gave him a show
narrative_blocks.body: Embracing Chance: The Art of John Scribner opened at the National Arts Club in New York in 2024. He exhibits there as an artist member and with the Woodstock Artists Association and Museum.

narrative_blocks.header: He works the Hudson Valley galleries
narrative_blocks.body: His work has hung at the Limner Gallery in Hudson, at Emerge Gallery and the Jane Street Art Center in Saugerties, at the Woodstock Byrdcliffe Guild, and at the Olive Free Library in West Shokan.

people.research_notes: Columbia University graduate and visual artist.

bio.bio_blurb: Director of the Buckley School’s middle school

narrative_blocks.header: He directs the middle school at Buckley
narrative_blocks.body: He is director of the middle school at the Buckley School on East 73rd Street, a boys’ school of some four hundred founded in 1913. Its motto is Honor et Veritas — honour and truth.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother was schooled where he now works
narrative_blocks.body: His elder brother Charles came up through Buckley before going on to St. Paul’s and Princeton. Blair directs its middle school.

people.research_notes: Director of the Buckley School's Middle School.

education.school_name: Hazelden Graduate School of Addiction Studies

narrative_blocks.header: A Vanderbilt who counsels young addicts
narrative_blocks.body: He works at the Hazelden Betty Ford Foundation's treatment centre for youth and young adults at Plymouth, Minnesota, as a chemical-dependency counsellor. He took his master's in addiction studies at Hazelden's own graduate school.

narrative_blocks.header: Married in a county park by a friend
narrative_blocks.body: He married Meghan Marie Knutson of Burnsville on 27 September 2014 at Albert A. Kordiak Park in Columbia Heights, Minnesota. A friend of theirs, Jordan Hansen, ordained through the Universal Life Church, performed it.

narrative_blocks.header: Connecticut behind him, Minnesota in front
narrative_blocks.body: He grew up in Norwalk, where his father Alfred works at Rowayton as a public relations consultant to New York nonprofits and his mother Alison was a database specialist for a charity serving chronically ill children.

sources.label: 'Meghan Knutson, Travis Vanderbilt', The New York Times Vows, 28 September 2014

narrative_blocks.header: She met her count at a Plaza ball
narrative_blocks.body: Born in France, the youngest of six, she came to America with her family after the war and settled in Larchmont, New York. It was at a ball at the Plaza Hotel that she met Count John Hadik, whom she married in 1962.

narrative_blocks.header: Competitive, funny, and always the center of attention
narrative_blocks.body: Known to all as 'Didi,' she was competitive and quick to laugh, loved games and singing, and delighted in being the center of any room. She and her count raised three sons and lived in several countries before her death in New Hampshire at eighty-four.

military_service.notes: Nine months of service.

narrative_blocks.header: He designed lamps on Fifth Avenue
narrative_blocks.body: He was a draftsman and designer for the Schroeder Lamp Company on Fifth Avenue, and was living on East Ninety-fifth Street when the war took him.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine months in the Army, then Great Neck
narrative_blocks.body: He served nine months in the United States Army in 1918, and afterward moved out to Great Neck and then to Jackson Heights, where he was still living in 1940.

narrative_blocks.header: She married her painter on Valentine's Day
narrative_blocks.body: She married the painter George Whiting Flagg on Valentine's Day, 1849, and bore him four children. She followed his restless career from New Haven to Charleston and London, and at last to his studio on Nantucket.

narrative_blocks.header: Coleridge called him the first Western genius
narrative_blocks.body: Coleridge, a friend for life, called him the first genius the Western world produced, and for his colour, the American Titian. In 1827 the Boston Athenaeum hung twelve of his pictures, the first American show given to one artist.

narrative_blocks.header: Hasty Pudding poet, then Benjamin West
narrative_blocks.body: He entered Harvard at seventeen, served the Hasty Pudding Club as vice-president and poet, and was asked to deliver a poem on the death of the general he was named for. In 1801 he entered the Royal Academy Schools under Benjamin West.

narrative_blocks.header: Rome, and a pupil called Morse
narrative_blocks.body: He worked through the Paris museums from 1803 and lived four years in Italy, meeting Washington Irving in Rome. Samuel Morse came to him as an art pupil and crossed to Europe with him in 1811, long before the telegraph.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave English the objective correlative
narrative_blocks.body: The Sylphs of the Seasons came out at London in 1813, the Italian romance Monaldi in 1841, and his Lectures on Art after his death. The Oxford dictionary credits him with the first use of the term objective correlative.

narrative_blocks.header: Boston’s Allston neighbourhood is his
narrative_blocks.body: He died with Belshazzar’s Feast unfinished, the canvas meant for his masterpiece. Longfellow said his memory perfumed the air like a quince in a drawer; the Allston neighbourhood is said to be the only American district named for a painter.

narrative_blocks.header: He married two women who were cousins
narrative_blocks.body: Anne Channing, sister of the Unitarian William Ellery Channing, married him in 1809 and died in February 1815. Fifteen years later he married Martha Remington Dana, a daughter of Chief Justice Francis Dana — and a cousin of his first wife.

narrative_blocks.header: His father died with a prophecy
narrative_blocks.body: Captain William Allston came home from Cowpens and died in 1781, thought poisoned by a servant. He asked for the child and said whoever lived to see him grown would see a great man; the widow then married Dr. Henry Collins Flagg.

narrative_blocks.header: At twenty he rebuilt Rochester's canal aqueduct
narrative_blocks.body: Barely twenty, Josiah took charge of tearing down Rochester’s leaking Erie Canal aqueduct and building its replacement across the Genesee, an 848-foot stone span finished in 1842. It never leaked in seventy-seven years; the city later ran its subway through the old canal bed, and Broad Street crosses the river on it still.

narrative_blocks.header: He raised the West's first engineer regiment
narrative_blocks.body: When the war exposed the Union’s near-total lack of engineers, Josiah proposed and then commanded the Engineer Regiment of the West, a thousand mechanics and artisans drawn from three states. His men cut a twelve-mile canal through the swamps that let Union gunboats slip behind the Confederate guns at Island Number Ten in 1862.

narrative_blocks.header: Grant wanted him gone; he resigned in protest
narrative_blocks.body: For all the praise his engineering won, Josiah made enemies — his own officers thought him tyrannical, and Grant, suspecting he had leaked to the Memphis press, wanted him gone. His nomination for brigadier general was tabled in the Senate, and in 1863, facing charges he called unjust, he resigned in protest.

narrative_blocks.header: He and a Hooker planted Rochester’s nurseries
narrative_blocks.body: In 1844 Josiah went into business with Horace Hooker, founding the Rochester Commercial Nursery on a stock of young fruit trees. The trade the two men helped start made Rochester the nursery and seed capital of the country by the century’s end.

narrative_blocks.header: His great suspension bridge fell in the night
narrative_blocks.body: In 1856 Josiah threw a suspension bridge 755 feet across the Genesee gorge near the Lower Falls, and his partner Horace Hooker pronounced it the safest bridge around. After a heavy snow the following spring it collapsed in the night, and five thousand people came the next day to view the ruins.

narrative_blocks.header: A celebrated engineer, with kin in his ranks
narrative_blocks.body: His engineers were widely praised through the war’s western campaigns, from Island Number Ten to the Siege of Corinth and Grant’s advance on Vicksburg. Among the officers Josiah led was his brother-in-law, Horace Hooker of Rochester.

narrative_blocks.header: His name became a law-book citation
narrative_blocks.body: A Rochester lawyer, Josiah reported the decisions of the federal Circuit and District courts for the Seventh Circuit, gathering them into an 1874 volume that attorneys came to cite simply as "Bissell's Reports." His name outlived him in the footnotes of the law.

narrative_blocks.header: He never worked anywhere but the family firm
narrative_blocks.body: After Cornell he went to the company his uncle Elon had founded at Niagara Falls, and he never worked anywhere else. He rose through sales to vice president, director, and a seat on the finance committee, and retired in 1962.

narrative_blocks.header: He finished the war before he finished college
narrative_blocks.body: He left the Hill School in 1916 and served as a lieutenant in the United States Army Air Corps during the World War. Only afterward did he go up to Ithaca, taking his Cornell degree in 1921.

narrative_blocks.header: A great thrill, he told his fraternity
narrative_blocks.body: He wrote back to his Cornell fraternity about a spring spent taking Grace and their two small boys, aged five and eight, through Italy, Switzerland, France, Belgium and Holland. “It was a great thrill,” he reported, and hoped to see the brothers at Ithaca soon. He was vice president in charge of sales at the time.

narrative_blocks.header: What the chemical man did after hours
narrative_blocks.body: Away from Niagara Falls he was a regional director of the Boy Scouts of America and sat on the board of the Boys Clubs of America. In Buffalo he gave the same attention to the Philharmonic and to the Albright-Knox gallery.

narrative_blocks.body: She belonged to the International Council of the Museum of Modern Art and to the American Federation of Arts, and to a string of other art organizations besides. Her death notice listed them before it listed anything else about her.

narrative_blocks.header: A college president married them at noon
narrative_blocks.body: She married Roger Wolcott Hooker at noon in the Salem Presbyterian Church, with Charles J. Smith, president of Roanoke College, officiating. Her sister Marian stood as maid of honor; the best man came down from Niagara Falls.

narrative_blocks.header: Two records disagree on where she was born
narrative_blocks.body: Her death notice said she was born and raised in Salem, Virginia; the cemetery record puts her birth in Missoula, Montana, in September 1908. Salem is where her father Henry Rhiel Garden settled the family, and where she was married.

narrative_blocks.header: He followed a Rockefeller out of Albany
narrative_blocks.body: Columbia Law put him into Nelson Rockefeller's service as deputy secretary to the governor, and he stayed with him to Washington as his assistant for Congressional affairs in the vice presidency. He served the Ford administration as an assistant transportation secretary, then went into corporate law as general counsel of Grand Met USA.

narrative_blocks.header: His last joke, a daughter on each side
narrative_blocks.body: A back operation left him paralyzed for the last seven years of his life, and his classmates remembered that he bore it with a sharp mind and the humor they had always known him for. Among his departing words, with his daughters sitting on either side of him: “I am in a pulchritude sandwich.”

narrative_blocks.header: A Conrad thesis and legendary paella
narrative_blocks.body: He majored in English at Princeton and wrote his thesis on Joseph Conrad, played two years of soccer, and held office in the eating clubs. A roommate remembered him at the center of the action ever after — the paella feasts built with volunteering sous-chefs, delicious and fun.

narrative_blocks.header: The lawyer who sat on dancers' boards
narrative_blocks.body: From Palisades, up the Hudson from the city, he gave his board service to dance and to art — the American Dance Festival, the Rockland Center for the Arts, and the Baryshnikov Arts Center.

narrative_blocks.header: A bookkeeper who cornered the world's oil
narrative_blocks.body: A Cleveland bookkeeper turned produce merchant, John never drilled for oil — when the 1859 Pennsylvania strike sent thousands chasing wells, he bet on the steadier business of refining it, founding Standard Oil in 1870. Within a decade it refined nine-tenths of America's oil, and by 1916 he was the country's first billionaire.

narrative_blocks.header: He swallowed his rivals one by one
narrative_blocks.body: He undercut competitors, wrung waste from every barrel, and bought out rivals by the dozen — in 1872 he absorbed nearly all of Cleveland's refineries in months. Standard, he said, was an angel of mercy pulling a drowning industry from the water; his rivals called it something else.

narrative_blocks.header: The Supreme Court broke up his empire
narrative_blocks.body: Ida Tarbell's exposé and a decade of antitrust fury ended in 1911, when the Supreme Court ordered Standard Oil broken into thirty-four companies — the seeds of Exxon, Mobil, and Chevron. The breakup only made him richer, as his shares in all thirty-four soared.

narrative_blocks.header: He turned charity into a science
narrative_blocks.body: He gave away some five hundred and forty million dollars and built giving into a system — foundations, matching grants, research institutes instead of scattered charity. He founded the University of Chicago and the Rockefeller Foundation, and funded the science that drove hookworm and yellow fever from the American South.

narrative_blocks.header: He rescued a school for Black women
narrative_blocks.body: In 1884 he paid off the debts of a struggling Atlanta seminary for freedwomen and kept giving; it took his wife's family name and became Spelman College. The Spelmans had been abolitionists who sheltered runaways on the Underground Railroad.

narrative_blocks.header: He believed his fortune was God's gift
narrative_blocks.body: For all his wealth John lived by his mother's thrift and his Baptist faith — tithing from his first clerk's wages, teaching Sunday school, handing out dimes to strangers. He believed the power to make money was a gift from God, to be used for his fellow man.

narrative_blocks.header: She paddled her own canoe
narrative_blocks.body: Valedictorian of her Cleveland high school at fourteen, Laura titled her graduating address "I Can Paddle My Own Canoe" and meant it — she became a teacher and, by twenty-two, an assistant principal. She believed women had every right to culture and independent thought.

narrative_blocks.header: She was raised to shelter runaway slaves
narrative_blocks.body: Laura grew up in an abolitionist household — her father hid runaways on the Underground Railroad — and she carried that conscience into her marriage. Standard Oil’s fortune, in her hands, flowed toward the education of Black Americans and women.

narrative_blocks.header: A great Black college carries her name
narrative_blocks.body: The Atlanta seminary for freedwomen that Laura and John rescued from debt took her family’s name and grew into Spelman College, today a leading historically Black institution. Her people, the Spelmans, had given their name first to abolition and then to the schooling it demanded.

narrative_blocks.header: The billionaire called her judgment better than his
narrative_blocks.body: Even as the family grew immensely rich, Laura kept her children to garden chores, music practice, and giving from their own earnings. John leaned on her counsel all their married life, saying her judgment was always better than his own.

narrative_blocks.header: A memorial in her name reshaped social science
narrative_blocks.body: After Laura died in 1915, John founded the Laura Spelman Rockefeller Memorial in her honor and poured tens of millions into it. It became a force in the young social sciences, funding child-development research at universities across the country.

narrative_blocks.header: The Senate's real boss for thirty years
narrative_blocks.body: For three decades Nelson Aldrich ruled the United States Senate as few ever have — chairman of the Finance Committee and one of the "Big Four" Republicans who decided what became law. The press called him the "General Manager of the Nation," and on tariffs and money his word was close to final.

narrative_blocks.header: A grocery clerk who came to rule Washington
narrative_blocks.body: Aldrich began as a clerk in a Providence wholesale grocery and never attended college, yet he climbed through Rhode Island's Republican machine to the Senate — and to a personal fortune built on streetcar and banking deals. Reformers charged that his power rested on a corrupt rural machine; a muckraker's exposé branded his state "Rhode Island: A State for Sale."

narrative_blocks.header: He laid the groundwork for the Federal Reserve
narrative_blocks.body: After the Panic of 1907 exposed how fragile American banking was, Aldrich chaired the National Monetary Commission and studied Europe's central banks for a solution. The plan he drafted became the foundation for the Federal Reserve System, created in 1913 — though its final form gave the president powers Aldrich himself opposed.

narrative_blocks.header: His scheme to block an income tax backfired
narrative_blocks.body: A champion of high tariffs, Aldrich tried to kill a proposed income tax by a clever gambit — offering a constitutional amendment he was certain the states would never ratify. To his dismay they did: the Sixteenth Amendment of 1913 gave the country the federal income tax it still pays.

narrative_blocks.header: Even Roosevelt called him the Senate's kingpin
narrative_blocks.body: Aldrich led the conservative, business-first wing of his party through the McKinley, Roosevelt, and Taft years, blocking or watering down the reforms progressives demanded. Theodore Roosevelt, who fought him constantly, still admitted that Aldrich was "the kingpin in my game" — the man a president had to reckon with.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter's marriage founded a dynasty
narrative_blocks.body: In 1901 Aldrich's daughter Abby married John D. Rockefeller Jr., joining the era's greatest political and industrial fortunes. Their son Nelson — named for his grandfather — became governor of New York and Vice President of the United States, and another son, David, one of the world's leading bankers.

narrative_blocks.header: An apothecary's ward who married a future power
narrative_blocks.body: Raised not by her farming parents but by a well-off aunt and her apothecary husband in Providence, Abby Chapman grew up in comfort and inherited a substantial estate of her own. When she married an ambitious young grocery clerk named Nelson Aldrich in 1866, her modest wealth and standing helped open the doors his talent would later batter down.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept a family through the Gilded Age
narrative_blocks.body: Across nearly twenty years Abby bore eleven children and ran the growing Aldrich households in Providence, Washington, and New York as her husband rose. Like many mothers of the era she knew deep loss — several of her children died young — yet she held the family together through decades of upheaval and ascent.

narrative_blocks.header: Her seaside estate hosted a dynasty's founding
narrative_blocks.body: The Aldriches' summer estate on Warwick Neck, overlooking Narragansett Bay, was where the Gilded Age's grandest match was sealed. There in 1901 Abby's daughter married John D. Rockefeller Jr., in a thousand-guest wedding that joined a senator's power to Standard Oil's fortune.

narrative_blocks.header: She was grandmother to a Vice President
narrative_blocks.body: Through her daughter Abby, she became grandmother to Nelson Rockefeller — named for her husband — who rose to be governor of New York and Vice President of the United States. She died in 1917 on Fifth Avenue, at the far end of a life that reached from a Connecticut farm town to the summit of American wealth and power.

narrative_blocks.header: From fashion model to shamanic counselor
narrative_blocks.body: Ordained a minister at the Sacred Stream and trained in depth hypnosis, Tracy works as a psychospiritual counselor and coach. She helps clients — many of them women — reach what she calls their deepest wisdom and clarity.

narrative_blocks.header: Her own hard road became her life's work
narrative_blocks.body: After years of infertility and loss on the way to her three children, Tracy turned the experience outward, guiding other women through the emotional gauntlet of trying to build a family. She led the yoga program at a New York fertility center and coached women toward what she called their silver linings.

narrative_blocks.header: She spent decades rebuilding homes for the needy
narrative_blocks.body: A Georgia-born English scholar, Chandler gave years to Rebuilding Together, the nonprofit that repairs homes for elderly, disabled, and low-income owners. She served as a volunteer leader and board member, a quiet counterpart to her husband's public career.

narrative_blocks.header: A quiet force across Washington's causes
narrative_blocks.body: Chandler served on the board of Planned Parenthood's Washington chapter, chaired a Girl Scout capital campaign, and rose to senior warden at St. Columba's Episcopal Church. Her volunteer work anchored the family through Paul's years in the public eye.

narrative_blocks.header: From Unadilla to Detroit, 1867
narrative_blocks.body: Addie Miller left Unadilla, in Otsego County, New York, to marry Dexter Ferry in October 1867. In Detroit the two of them belonged to the Woodward Avenue Congregational Church, and gave generously to its work.

narrative_blocks.header: She took Blanche to Rome in 1895
narrative_blocks.body: Touring Europe with her daughter Blanche in 1895, Addie was in Rome when Blanche ran into Elon Hooker again, two years after they had first met at Vassar. Blanche married him in Detroit in 1901.

narrative_blocks.header: She died back in Unadilla
narrative_blocks.body: Addie died at Unadilla, the town where she was born, on 2 November 1906, five days short of sixty-five, and was buried with the Ferrys at Woodmere in Detroit. Dexter died a year and eight days after her.

narrative_blocks.header: Father and son ran the hardware store
narrative_blocks.body: William Herbert Turnage went into business alongside his father, Bill, running the family hardware store in El Dorado, Arkansas. On his own he founded and operated Turnage Travel Service, turning a merchant's trade into a second career sending people out into the world.

narrative_blocks.header: Hamilton graduate who ran the Rome academy
narrative_blocks.body: After graduating from Hamilton College in 1864, Payson Miner went into the book and stationery trade with his brother Herbert, then into dry goods with their father as I. T. Miner & Sons. When the firm dissolved he served two years as principal of the Rome Free Academy before moving to Buffalo.

narrative_blocks.header: Found dead, no cause ever established
narrative_blocks.body: On a November morning in 1888, Payson was found dead on the parlor floor of his Buffalo home, a string drawn about his throat, hours after a quiet evening with visiting family. An autopsy revealed no poison and no marks, the doors and windows had been fastened from within, and no explanation was ever reached.

bio.bio_blurb: First Indian Affairs superintendent of Oregon

narrative_blocks.header: Oregon's first Indian Affairs superintendent
narrative_blocks.body: In 1850 Anson Dart was appointed the first superintendent of Indian Affairs for the Oregon Territory. Over two years he negotiated nineteen treaties with tribes from the Willamette Valley to the Rogue River, acquiring some six million acres for the government at roughly three cents an acre.

narrative_blocks.header: His fair treaties were tabled forever
narrative_blocks.body: Dart promised the tribes fair payment and the right to keep their own teachers and religious practices, defying orders to force American missionaries upon them. The Senate refused to ratify a single one of his treaties in 1852, and the broken promises helped ignite Oregon's Indian wars.

narrative_blocks.header: A Wisconsin pioneer before Oregon
narrative_blocks.body: Long before Oregon, Dart joined the frontier migration to the Wisconsin Territory around 1840, settling in Green Lake County at the outlet of Twin Lakes. There he and his sons built the area's first frame house.

narrative_blocks.header: He fired the agent who defended the tribes
narrative_blocks.body: In 1851 Dart dismissed his Astoria subagent, Robert Shortess, soon after Shortess opposed a white settler's claim on Chinook land. Critics then and since read the firing as Dart siding with settlers over the tribes he was meant to protect.

narrative_blocks.header: Lincoln refused to reappoint him
narrative_blocks.body: Dart resigned in December 1852 after the Senate tabled his treaties, and returned east. When his name came up again in 1861, President Lincoln declined to appoint him superintendent for Washington Territory, citing Oregon politicians' doubts about his character.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the daughter of Port Orford's founder
narrative_blocks.body: George, son of Indian-affairs superintendent Anson Dart, married Anna Tichenor in 1855. Her father, Captain William Tichenor, had founded Port Orford on the Oregon coast — the same shore Anson toured as superintendent.

people.research_notes: Death certificate 62361 (informant Frank Keene) names her parents as Anson and "Margaret Catlin Dart"; the mother is Elizabeth Catlin Dart (HD5201). Widowed; died of valvular heart disease at 1110 Buffalo St, Franklin.

narrative_blocks.header: A Portland pioneer when it was a hamlet
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth settled in Portland while it was still a small hamlet, married there in 1847, and later lived in the Milwaukie suburb. She was an aunt of the magazine cartoonist Harry Grant Dart.

narrative_blocks.header: A legislative page who rode with the cavalry
narrative_blocks.body: At nineteen Charles served as a page in the 1861 Wisconsin legislature, then enlisted that November in the 2nd Wisconsin Cavalry. After two years at the front he was detailed as chief clerk of the Madison draft rendezvous and then the adjutant-general's office in Washington.

narrative_blocks.header: Superior's attorney, legislator, and banker
narrative_blocks.body: A Columbia law graduate and one-time secretary to Caleb Cushing, Charles settled in the frontier city of Superior in 1884 as attorney for the Omaha Railroad. He helped organize the Bank of Commerce, served as its president, and represented his district in the state assembly.

narrative_blocks.header: Reared Presbyterian, he died a Christian Scientist
narrative_blocks.body: A Mason and the first eminent commander of Superior Commandery No. 25, Charles also belonged to the Grand Army of the Republic. Raised in the Presbyterian faith, in his later years he became a Christian Scientist.

narrative_blocks.header: He was lost in a shipwreck off California
narrative_blocks.body: Simeon died when his ship was wrecked near Point Reyes on the California coast. A squall crippled the vessel and it ran hard aground in fog; the captain and most of the crew were never found, and only two men survived.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father founded Port Orford, Oregon
narrative_blocks.body: Anna was a daughter of Captain William Tichenor, the sea captain who in 1851 landed nine men at Battle Rock and founded the town of Port Orford on the Oregon coast. His name still marks Tichenor's Humbug, a peak he mistook for the coastal range.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father knew Lincoln in Illinois
narrative_blocks.body: Before the gold rush drew him west, Captain Tichenor lived in Illinois, where he was master of a Masonic lodge and an acquaintance of Abraham Lincoln. Lincoln's petition to join the lodge went unfinished when Tichenor left for the California diggings.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran Franklin's gas works, then went blind
narrative_blocks.body: Edward came to Franklin in 1873 as superintendent of the gas company, when manufactured gas was a local industry. Struck blind about 1880, he passed his last decades living with his son.

narrative_blocks.header: His airship comic rivaled Little Nemo
narrative_blocks.body: In 1908 Dart drew The Explorigator, a fantastic airship crewed by children — Admiral Fudge, Detective Rubbersole, Nicholas Nohooks and the rest — conceived to rival Winsor McCay's Little Nemo. It ran for fourteen weeks and was celebrated for its imaginative, intricate visual invention.

narrative_blocks.header: From crayon ads to art editor
narrative_blocks.body: Dart's first jobs were brochures for the National Crayon Company and drawings for the Boston Herald, until the New York World sent him to Cuba as a sketch artist in the years before newspaper photography. He rose to become art editor of The World.

narrative_blocks.header: His cartoons imagined a futuristic world
narrative_blocks.body: A mainstay of Life and Judge into the late 1920s, Dart filled his pages with complicated perspectives, incredible detail, and futuristic speculation — flying machines and aerial cities decades ahead of their time.

LATERAL SET on both sides: they are contemporaries (b. 1868 and 1871) with no lineal relation, so the flight must go sideways rather than take direction from a generation gap.

narrative_blocks.body: Ernest served as a major in the 1st Army Cavalry through the Civil War. In his later years he made his home in Florence, Italy, where he died in 1890.

narrative_blocks.header: She pulled the invasives out of Fresh Pond
narrative_blocks.body: Pamela, a stubborn enemy of anything that did not belong in a landscape, started the Pamela Hart Landscaping Service in 1980 for organic gardens. With volunteers she ripped invasive plants out of what is now the Fresh Pond Native Garden in Cambridge.

narrative_blocks.header: French teacher turned landscape designer
narrative_blocks.body: Pamela took bachelor's and master's degrees in French, at Goucher and the Sorbonne, and taught it at Northeastern and other Boston colleges until she tired of teaching and earned a landscape-design degree at Radcliffe.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a Boston jazz bassist
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband, John Endicott Hart, played bass and piano with jazz groups in the clubs that replaced Scollay Square. Pamela, the eldest of five and an expert on New England wildflowers, spent every summer of her life at Canandaigua Lake.

sources.label: Pamela Hart obituary, February 2025

career.notes: Financial Q&A with Kenneth Hooker

cross_connections.display_label: collected Americana in Hartford and left Yale twelve thousand volumes

narrative_blocks.header: He started on the Courant's obituary desk
narrative_blocks.body: Kenneth and his wife Elaine were hired at the Hartford Courant in September 1969; he drew obituaries and envied her Wethersfield beat. He moved to courts, then ran the business pages, mentoring David Wessel, later of The Wall Street Journal.

narrative_blocks.header: A gas-station bookshop named for Liebling
narrative_blocks.body: In retirement Kenneth opened The Wayward Bookman in a former gas station in Wales, Massachusetts, naming it for A. J. Liebling's The Wayward Pressman. He collected the American humorists, and asked for gifts to the Mark Twain Foundation.

narrative_blocks.header: Pigs, chickens and German shepherds
narrative_blocks.body: Kenneth and Elaine moved to Southwick, Massachusetts, where they could afford land, and he fancied himself a gentleman farmer, with pigs, chickens and German shepherds. He was still driving a tractor in old age.

narrative_blocks.header: He built houses on the Canandaigua land
narrative_blocks.body: Kenneth, the only son among five children, grew up in Lewisburg, Pennsylvania, where his father taught at Bucknell, and spent every summer at the family land on Canandaigua Lake. He later built houses there.

narrative_blocks.header: English teacher at his children's school
narrative_blocks.body: Between newsrooms Kenneth taught English at his children's school and acted in community theater. He also collected knives.

argued in 1888 that a photograph beat a stuffed animal

narrative_blocks.header: He rode 2,000 miles for a book
narrative_blocks.body: In 1911 Chase rode horseback from the Mexican border to Oregon along the California coast, filling journals that became California Coast Trails. A reviewer said he wrote with a buoyant intensity that struck fire from the duller sensibilities of his readers.

narrative_blocks.header: He hoped the desert would stay unloved
narrative_blocks.body: In Our Araby (1920), one of the first travel books on Palm Springs, Chase prized the Coachella Valley precisely because so few wished to visit it. If too much peopled, he warned, its charm would be lost.

narrative_blocks.header: Like Muir, he fought to save the mountains
narrative_blocks.body: Chase campaigned to have the Santa Rosa and San Jacinto mountains set aside as a national park, echoing his better-known contemporary John Muir. His photographs and poetic prose were his argument for the unspoiled West.

narrative_blocks.header: His inheritance vanished the week he arrived
narrative_blocks.body: Landing in California in 1890, Chase put the inheritance from his publisher father into a bank that failed almost at once. Penniless, he lived frugally for years in the mountains near San Diego before tutoring and writing his way up.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a White sister at fifty-two
narrative_blocks.body: Come to Palm Springs in 1915 for its hot springs, Chase married Isabel White in 1917; her sisters Cornelia and Florilla had bought the town's original hotel. He lies beside Isabel at the foot of Mt. San Jacinto, his name also cut into his parents' stone in England.

narrative_blocks.header: She gave up driving when she married
narrative_blocks.body: Dorothy drove one of the first automobiles in West Bay City, Michigan — then gave it up after marrying, when it was thought improper for a woman to drive. She was known for immaculate dress: a Chanel suit, silk blouse, and pearls.

people.research_notes: Left a diamond ring with an emerald setting by the will of her grandmother, Eunice W. Emery of Bay City MI. Her mother, Harriet Godfrey (Emery) Handy, wife of Thomas L. Handy of West Bay City, was a genealogist and society member.

cross_connections.display_label: her aunt, paid her Katherine Gibbs tuition in 1941

narrative_blocks.header: A Katherine Gibbs girl who joined the WAVES
narrative_blocks.body: After Bradford Junior College and the Katherine Gibbs secretarial school in New York — her tuition paid by her aunt Mary Pierrepont White — Patricia enlisted in the WAVES in 1944 as a Yeoman third class in the Naval Reserve.

military_service.role: Adjutant; reported missing in Belgium, December 19, 1944

narrative_blocks.header: He went missing in the Ardennes
narrative_blocks.body: As adjutant of an armored field artillery unit, Lieutenant Godard was reported missing in Belgium on December 19, 1944, in the German counteroffensive. A Hamilton College man who had entered the service in 1941, he came through the war and lived until 1965.

people.relational_label_override: Mother-in-law of a Seventh Generation Hooker

narrative_blocks.header: She died abroad before the mansion was finished
narrative_blocks.body: Daughter of General Matthew Clarkson, Mary died at Funchal on the island of Madeira on Christmas Eve, 1838. She did not live to see the Rye mansion her husband was then building.

narrative_blocks.header: He was the nation's first Chief Justice
narrative_blocks.body: Appointed by Washington in 1789, Jay led a Supreme Court so new it decided only four cases in six years. He rode circuit across the states, carrying word of American neutrality.

narrative_blocks.header: He negotiated the peace that won independence
narrative_blocks.body: As a commissioner in Paris, Jay helped negotiate the 1783 Treaty of Paris that ended the Revolution and won recognition of American independence. John Adams judged him of more importance than any of the rest of us.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote five of the Federalist Papers
narrative_blocks.body: With Alexander Hamilton and James Madison, Jay co-authored the Federalist Papers under the shared name Publius, writing five of the eighty-five essays to win New York's ratification of the Constitution.

narrative_blocks.header: He freed New York's slaves but owned some
narrative_blocks.body: Founder and president of the New York Manumission Society, Jay signed the 1799 act for gradual abolition as governor. Yet the censuses record him owning slaves into the 1800s, freeing them only once he judged their labor repaid.

narrative_blocks.header: He could travel by his burning effigies
narrative_blocks.body: The deeply unpopular 1794 Jay Treaty with Britain made him one of the most reviled men in America. He joked that he could ride at night from Boston to Philadelphia by the light of his own burning effigies.

narrative_blocks.header: He fathered an abolitionist and a Recorder
narrative_blocks.body: His son William Jay became a noted abolitionist and jurist, while his eldest, Peter Augustus Jay, served as Recorder of New York City before raising the family mansion at Rye.

bio.bio_blurb: Revolutionary-era hostess; First Lady of New York

people.relational_label_override: Grandmother-in-law of a Seventh Generation Hooker

notable.notable_blurb: Revolutionary-era hostess; First Lady of New York

narrative_blocks.header: Paris mistook her for Marie Antoinette
narrative_blocks.body: In Revolutionary Paris, Sarah's beauty and grace once brought a theater audience to its feet in homage, mistaking the American for Marie Antoinette. She moved in the circles of Lafayette and Franklin as her husband negotiated the peace.

narrative_blocks.header: Her dinner table lobbied for the Constitution
narrative_blocks.body: As wife of the Secretary of Foreign Affairs she hosted the diplomatic corps in New York, and her celebrated 1787-88 guest lists doubled as instruments for winning ratification of the Constitution.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father was New Jersey's first governor
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah was the daughter of William Livingston, the first governor of New Jersey, a signer of the United States Constitution, and a Founding Father in his own right.

narrative_blocks.header: An Alsatian countess who married a Stuyvesant
narrative_blocks.body: Born in Strasbourg to Joseph Loewenguth and already the widow of a Dutch count, Mathilde married the land developer Rutherfurd Stuyvesant in London in 1902. She bore him two sons, Lewis and Alan.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed twice, she married a prince
narrative_blocks.body: After Rutherfurd died suddenly in Paris in 1909, Mathilde married Prince Alexandre de Caraman-Chimay, becoming a princess in her third marriage.

cross_connections.display_label: ran Grenfell's White Bay unit in Newfoundland from 1921 to 1925
nursed for the Labrador-Grenfell mission, reaching patients by dog sled

narrative_blocks.header: She served the Labrador coast with Grenfell
narrative_blocks.body: A Vassar graduate and daughter of the Brookline judge Philip Stanley Parker, Grace spent several years with Wilfred Grenfell's medical mission along the coasts of Newfoundland and Labrador before her marriage.

notable.notable_blurb: U.S. Ambassador to Chad

career.organization: U.S. State Department, Bureau of Intelligence and Research

career.role: Officer in Charge of Benelux Affairs

left the U.S. Embassy at Rabat in 1976, the year he arrived

narrative_blocks.header: A diplomat like his father before him
narrative_blocks.body: Peter followed his father, the ambassador Jay Pierrepont Moffat, into the Foreign Service and rose to ambassador himself.

narrative_blocks.header: He reopened America’s embassy in Chad
narrative_blocks.body: Moffat was the first ambassador to the newly reopened U.S. Embassy in N’Djamena, arriving as chargé d’affaires in 1982 and confirmed as ambassador in 1983. He served through the Chadian–Libyan conflict until 1985, closing out a Foreign Service career that had run from Kobe and Paris to Rabat.

narrative_blocks.header: Franklin and Jay both ran in his blood
narrative_blocks.body: Peter Moffat was a lineal descendant of two of the republic's founders — Benjamin Franklin and John Jay, the first Chief Justice. He carried the family's diplomatic vocation forward, fluent in French, German, and Russian across four decades of postings.

narrative_blocks.header: Third generation of a diplomatic dynasty
narrative_blocks.body: Moffat followed his father, ambassador to Canada, and his grandfather Joseph Grew, ambassador to Japan, into the Foreign Service. In 1953 he married Pamela Mary Dawson, daughter of the Folger Shakespeare Library's curator, and the two spent three decades posted across Japan, Europe, the Caribbean, and Africa.

narrative_blocks.header: In retirement, he loved the Times crossword
narrative_blocks.body: After retiring in 1997 from a last post as senior vice president of the National War College, Moffat split his time between New Hampshire and Washington. He filled his days with The New York Times crossword, tennis, hiking, and reading.

bio.bio_blurb: Foreign Service wife and peace activist

narrative_blocks.header: Daughter of the Folger’s Shakespeare curator
narrative_blocks.body: Pamela was the daughter of Giles Dawson, the rare-manuscripts curator and Shakespeare scholar at the Folger Shakespeare Library. She studied at Radcliffe before marrying Peter Moffat in 1953 and following him into a life abroad.

narrative_blocks.header: Arrested twice for protest in her seventies
narrative_blocks.body: Pamela spent three decades as a Foreign Service wife, posted from Japan to Chad, taking up the social duties of the role while joining local causes wherever she landed. Later, drawing on her father's fight to desegregate Washington's Columbia Heights, she turned to activism — and in her seventies was arrested twice at antiwar and antinuclear demonstrations.

narrative_blocks.header: Esquire, Holiday, and Horticulture answered to him
narrative_blocks.body: A Marine in the Second World War, Nutting rose through publishing to become publisher of Esquire, Holiday, and Horticulture magazines. He died in Brookline, Massachusetts, in 2004, at eighty-three.

narrative_blocks.header: Three New York firms before the war
narrative_blocks.body: He read law after Yale and practised in New York with Strong & Cadwalader, Lord Day & Lord, and Littlefield & Littlefield. He was a corporate and general lawyer for a dozen years.

narrative_blocks.header: He left the law to enlist
narrative_blocks.body: He gave up the practice for the army when the United States came into the war, served overseas, and came out a captain of field artillery.

narrative_blocks.header: He came back to broking, not the bar
narrative_blocks.body: The war ended his legal career. He went into broking instead and became a partner in F. S. Moseley & Co. at 120 Broadway.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a Russell of Middletown in 1905
narrative_blocks.body: Helen Pickering Russell married him on 25 May 1905 and their daughter Helen came in 1907. The marriage ended, she married Charles Francis Rogers in 1917, and she died at Acapulco in 1966.

bio.bio_blurb: U.S. Ambassador to Haiti and Peru

notable.notable_blurb: U.S. Ambassador to Haiti and Peru

career.notes: Thirty-one years of service

cross_connections.display_label: saw his daughter Emily become White's stepmother in 1920

narrative_blocks.header: He was born inside an American legation
narrative_blocks.body: John Campbell White was born at the American Legation in London, where his father, the diplomat Henry White, was posted. He followed him into the Foreign Service and gave it thirty-one years before retiring in 1945.

narrative_blocks.header: Minister to Haiti, then ambassador to Peru
narrative_blocks.body: White became U.S. Minister to Haiti in 1941, staying on as ambassador when the post was elevated in 1943, and was named ambassador to Peru in 1944. It capped three decades of representing the country across Europe and the Americas.

narrative_blocks.header: A Vanderbilt became his stepmother
narrative_blocks.body: After the death of White's mother, his father married Emily Vanderbilt Sloane, daughter of the railroad magnate William Henry Vanderbilt. The match tied the Whites to one of the great Gilded Age fortunes.

narrative_blocks.header: Daughter, wife, and niece of ambassadors
narrative_blocks.body: Margaret stood at the center of a diplomatic dynasty — daughter of Ambassador John Campbell White, niece of Ambassador Jay Pierrepont Moffat, and wife of Ambassador William Tapley Bennett Jr. A Foxcroft, Barnard, and Juilliard student, she married Bennett at Bernardsville, New Jersey, in 1945.

narrative_blocks.header: They dubbed her 'Maggie Wheatena from Argentina'
narrative_blocks.body: Margaret's diplomat father took the family from Riga to Buenos Aires, where she spent five years and learned to ride. Dropped into New York's Chapin School still full of Argentine schoolyards, she was tagged “Maggie Wheatena from Argentina” — a name she loathed, and her grandmother loathed more.

narrative_blocks.header: At drama school, even the math was Shakespeare
narrative_blocks.body: When Chapin couldn't hold her, Margaret landed at New York's King-Coit School, where the students lived, breathed, and acted Shakespeare. Even the arithmetic, she remembered, was taught in Shakespearean terms.

narrative_blocks.header: The unwritten craft of a diplomat's wife
narrative_blocks.body: Across postings in Austria, Italy, Portugal, Greece, and at NATO, Margaret ran the households, paid the calls, and received the wives of a swelling embassy — once greeting three or four callers a day in Santo Domingo. She thought her charmed run of assignments made her a poor example of the typical Foreign Service wife.

narrative_blocks.header: A college endowment now carries her name
narrative_blocks.body: In later years Margaret shared her Foreign Service life with students at Washington College, serving on its Board of Visitors and Governors. The college named its endowment for experiential learning in international studies — the Bennett Endowment for International Studies — in her honor.

bio.bio_blurb: U.S. Ambassador to NATO and the Dominican Republic

notable.notable_blurb: U.S. Ambassador to NATO and the Dominican Republic

career.role: U.S. Ambassador to the Dominican Republic

cross_connections.display_label: held Baghdad through two coups in those same years

narrative_blocks.header: The rookie ambassador who called in the Marines
narrative_blocks.body: Barely a year into his first ambassadorship, Bennett faced the Dominican Civil War of 1965. He advised President Johnson that the revolt had been seized by Communists and urged U.S. military intervention — a report that drew both praise and heavy criticism.

narrative_blocks.header: Relief from the tropics came as Portugal
narrative_blocks.body: Said to be seeking relief from the tropical heat of Santo Domingo, Bennett was moved to the embassy in Lisbon in 1966. From there he rose to represent the United States at the U.N. Security Council and, from 1977, at NATO in Brussels.

narrative_blocks.header: The longest-serving officer in the Foreign Service
narrative_blocks.body: Bennett retired in 1985 after more than forty years of diplomacy under nine presidents — by then the longest-serving officer in the American Foreign Service. He closed his career as Assistant Secretary of State for Legislative Affairs and was interred in Washington National Cathedral.

narrative_blocks.header: She found her heart's home at Yeamans Hall
narrative_blocks.body: A naval officer's daughter who grew up between strategic ports, Josephine claimed Ridgefield as her base but Yeamans Hall Club in South Carolina as her true home. After a brief first marriage, she wed Jordan Thurlow Jack and stayed married fifty-six years, remembered as the belle of any ball.

narrative_blocks.header: From Ford model to Hobe Sound designer
narrative_blocks.body: Molly Shriver began as a Ford Agency model and became an interior designer, co-founding the Hobe Sound shop Cloud 900. She lived to one hundred.

narrative_blocks.header: Widow of the first American killed in Vietnam
narrative_blocks.body: Nancy was first married to Lt. Col. A. Peter Dewey, the O.S.S. officer shot near Saigon in 1945 — often called the first American killed in Vietnam. After his death she married the financier John Pierrepont in 1950.

parents.mother_name: Marie Suzette de Marigny Hall Dewey

notable.notable_blurb: First American killed in Vietnam

education.school_name: University of Virginia School of Law

career.organization: Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs

cross_connections.display_label: was executed in one of those Japanese camps in 1943
was a St. Paul's master from 1893 to 1936, and died at his desk there

narrative_blocks.header: The first American killed in Vietnam
narrative_blocks.body: Heading a seven-man OSS team in Saigon in 1945, Dewey was shot at a Viet Minh roadblock — killed, his ambushers later said, in a case of mistaken identity for a Frenchman. He was the first American to die in Vietnam, and his body was never recovered.

narrative_blocks.header: He fought for Poland, France, and the OSS
narrative_blocks.body: Dewey enlisted in the Polish Military Ambulance Corps during the 1940 Battle of France, escaped through Spain, and later parachuted behind German lines in southern France as an OSS team leader. General Donovan pinned the Legion of Merit on him; France gave him the Legion of Honor.

narrative_blocks.header: He foresaw America's exit from Southeast Asia
narrative_blocks.body: Weeks before his death, Dewey warned that “Cochinchina is burning… and we are forced to get out of Southeast Asia” — a prophecy of the wars to come. He had just arranged the repatriation of 4,549 Allied prisoners from Japanese camps near Saigon.

narrative_blocks.header: His name is missing from the Vietnam Memorial
narrative_blocks.body: Because the Pentagon dates U.S. involvement in Vietnam to 1955, Dewey's name is absent from the Vietnam Veterans Memorial. He is remembered instead on the Tablets of the Missing in Manila, a cenotaph at Arlington, and an inscription in Washington National Cathedral.

narrative_blocks.header: He lost three children in eleven days
narrative_blocks.body: A Yale-trained minister, Edward married Amelia Wheeler in 1871. In January 1877, diphtheria took their three eldest — Edward Claudius, Agnes, and Ellen — within eleven days of one another.

bio.bio_blurb: Mount Holyoke graduate and school preceptress

narrative_blocks.header: From Mount Holyoke to a school preceptress
narrative_blocks.body: A graduate of Mount Holyoke in 1877, Anna Caroline served as preceptress of the Johnstown Union School before marrying the Rev. Dr. John Thomas Nichols in 1891. She followed him to pastorates across Washington State and New Jersey.

narrative_blocks.header: A beloved young pastor, gone at thirty
narrative_blocks.body: Thaddeus Howe Brown served as a Congregational pastor, a faithful and beloved shepherd to his people. He died at thirty, leaving his widow Lydia and their infant son Edward.

career.organization: Pataha, Washington; Seattle; Asbury Park, New Jersey

narrative_blocks.header: He built Congregational churches across the Northwest
narrative_blocks.body: After Yale Divinity, Nichols served Congregational pastorates across Washington State — Pataha and Seattle's Edgewater and Union churches — and led the Seattle Church Extension Society. From 1907 he was pastor at Asbury Park, New Jersey, and president of the Seattle Ministers' Association.

narrative_blocks.header: She built Straub Hospital's volunteer program
narrative_blocks.body: A registered nurse in Honolulu, Eleanor 'Sandy' Brown developed the volunteer program at Straub Hospital. Canadian-born, she lived to ninety-eight.

bio.bio_blurb: River Edge civic leader and tax collector

narrative_blocks.header: Seventeen years a councilman, thirteen a tax collector
narrative_blocks.body: Edwin Herrick spent his life in the civic affairs of River Edge, New Jersey — borough councilman for seventeen years, tax collector for thirteen, and director of civil defense for twenty-five. In 1961 he personally wrote to every delinquent property owner and collected the full year's taxes owed.

bio.bio_blurb: Sprinkler fitter and Korean War Marine

narrative_blocks.header: A Colgate soccer man and Korea Marine
narrative_blocks.body: Snowden 'Don' Herrick played four years of varsity soccer at Colgate and served as a Marine in the Korean War from 1951 to 1953. A lifelong River Edge man, he sat on the Board of Education, led a Cub Scout pack, and never lost his taste for a Sudoku.

bio.bio_blurb: Travel agent of New York and Sharon

narrative_blocks.header: She followed her father into the travel trade
narrative_blocks.body: Suzy Herrick studied at Dana Hall and Goucher, and at the Villa Mercedes in Florence. She followed her father into the travel business, working from Boston and New York to Greenwich and Newport.

bio.bio_blurb: Railroad engineer; lumber merchant; brevet colonel

cross_connections.display_label: was the only surgeon afloat off Fort Fisher as he stormed it

narrative_blocks.header: Quartermaster to brevet colonel in four years
narrative_blocks.body: He went in as first lieutenant and quartermaster of the Seventh Connecticut in September 1861, rose to major and assistant adjutant-general by 1863, and was brevetted lieutenant-colonel and then colonel for gallant service. He was adjutant-general of the Fort Fisher expedition and later of the Tenth Corps.

narrative_blocks.header: Fort Pulaski, Fort Wagner, Fort Fisher
narrative_blocks.body: He was at the sieges of Fort Pulaski and Fort Wagner, at Pocotaligo, James Island and Drury's Bluff, at the siege of Petersburg, and in the assault that took Fort Fisher in 1865. He was mustered out in May 1866.

narrative_blocks.header: He built a railroad, then sold lumber
narrative_blocks.body: He moved to Knoxville straight out of the army and was chief engineer of the Knoxville and Kentucky Railroad until 1869, then went into lumber as Burr and Terry on West Jackson Avenue. He retired in 1893 and turned to literary and scientific pursuits.

narrative_blocks.header: He chaired the board and ran the library
narrative_blocks.body: In Knoxville he was chairman of the board of trade, president and then treasurer of the Lawson-McGhee Library association, and a director of the East Tennessee National Bank. He belonged to the Order of Colonial Governors.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother took the fort he staffed
narrative_blocks.body: He was adjutant-general of the Fort Fisher expedition in January 1865, the assault that carried the works and took some two thousand prisoners. The general commanding it was his elder brother, Alfred Howe Terry.

parents.mother_name: Countess Sylvia Anita Gabriella Denise Irene Marie “Syvie” Széchenyi Szapáry

narrative_blocks.header: The last Vanderbilt to live in The Breakers
narrative_blocks.body: Gladys and her husband Paul lived on the third floor of The Breakers, the Newport palace her great-grandparents built. The Preservation Society kept them on after her mother died — it helped to tell visitors that the family was still upstairs — so she lived, as she put it, a guest in her own family home.

narrative_blocks.header: The girl who polished the brass before opening
narrative_blocks.body: As a teenager Gladys was all over The Breakers — minding the Children's Cottage gift shop, trailing the guides and the guards. Each morning before the doors opened to visitors, she polished the brass hinges on the great oak doors.

narrative_blocks.header: Her last stand was over a visitor center
narrative_blocks.body: When the Preservation Society moved to build a visitor center on The Breakers' lawn, Gladys fought it — in the newspapers, the boardrooms, and the courts — and lost. In 2017 fire codes ended the family's residency; "I'm waiting for them to throw my clothes out the window," she told a reporter.

career.notes: steam pumps

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote a Japanese phrasebook as a missionary
narrative_blocks.body: From 1889 to 1900 Anna Maria did private missionary work in Japan with her sister Fannie. Out of those years came her "Five Thousand Phrases (English-Japanese) for Common Use," printed in Tokyo in 1897 and reissued for years after.

narrative_blocks.header: Eleven years in Japan, beside her sister
narrative_blocks.body: Fannie left Brooklyn for Japan in 1889 and worked as a missionary there until 1900 — eleven years abroad with her sister Anna Maria. The two came home to Hartford together, and neither ever married.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Her husband's family pump works in Seneca Falls.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a pump magnate and moved upstate
narrative_blocks.body: Mary left Brooklyn to marry James Henry Gould and settle in Seneca Falls, where his family's pump works were known worldwide. Widowed at forty-two, she outlived him by more than twenty years.

burial.plot_notes: Cimetière Mont-Royal, Outremont, Montreal, Quebec, Canada

narrative_blocks.header: She mothered the world's first celebutante
narrative_blocks.body: By her first marriage Brenda was the mother of Brenda Frazier, the 1938 debutante so famous the press dubbed her the world's first "celebutante." The elder Brenda married three times; her last husband was the stockbroker Henry Pierrepont Perry.

notable.notable_blurb: Gilded Age socialite and philanthropist

cross_connections.display_label: was another of Mrs. Astor's fabled Four Hundred
kept the ballroom whose capacity gave the list its number

burial.plot_notes: Cypress Lawn Memorial Park, Colma, California

narrative_blocks.header: One of Mrs. Astor's Four Hundred
narrative_blocks.body: In 1892 Bertha and her widowed mother were named to Ward McAllister's "Four Hundred" — supposedly the number of people who could fit in Mrs. Astor's ballroom, and the roster of who mattered in Gilded Age New York. Three years later she married Pierre Lorillard Ronalds Jr. and moved to Paris.

narrative_blocks.header: From Paris society to an Oregon horse ranch
narrative_blocks.body: Widowed in 1928, Bertha left the Paris drawing rooms where she had lived for years and took up ranching in Oregon — breeding Tennessee walking horses, Arabians, and Shetland ponies on a spread that became the Metolius Meadows guest ranch. A quiet giver to charity, she spent her last decades in San Mateo, California.

narrative_blocks.header: Father to an aviator and a Thoroughbred breeder
narrative_blocks.body: Henry was a Wall Street stockbroker who kept a foot in Nassau. His marriage to Edith Lounsbery gave him two sons who each made a name — Richard, the young aviator killed at the controls in 1929, and William Haggin Perry, one of the great Thoroughbred breeders.

narrative_blocks.header: His third marriage tied him to Montreal society
narrative_blocks.body: Henry married three times. His last wife was Brenda Williams-Taylor, daughter of Sir Frederick Williams-Taylor of the Bank of Montreal; in 1942 the couple honeymooned at Murray Bay, feted by her titled parents.

cross_connections.display_label: flew aviation's earliest years and founded the Harmon Trophy

people.research_notes: Birth also given as Nov 23, 1906 (memorial text); FindAGrave gives Nov 26, 1906.

narrative_blocks.header: A rodeo rider who traded horses for airplanes
narrative_blocks.body: Fond of horses like his great-grandfather James Ben Ali Haggin, Richard rode rodeo at an Arizona ranch school before the flying bug took him. He learned to fly in Colorado Springs, built hours over Florida, and did experimental work for Fokker — all before he turned twenty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at the controls, saving his passengers
narrative_blocks.body: On a Sunday in May 1929 the rudder rod of Richard's plane snapped at 600 feet. He fought it down and cut the motor so it would not burn; his two passengers lived, but Richard — twenty-two, and already called a pioneer of commercial aviation — did not.

narrative_blocks.header: The schoolboy strongman none dared to fight
narrative_blocks.body: At St. George's, Richard was a genial rebel who threw himself at football, boxing, wrestling, and bodybuilding — and grew so strong that classmates learned to settle their quarrels with him some other way. He passed every subject but Ancient History, which beat him in his last year.

narrative_blocks.header: Great-grandson of a mining and racing tycoon
narrative_blocks.body: Richard's great-grandfather was James Ben Ali Haggin, who built a fifty-million-dollar fortune in Gold Rush mining and became one of America's great Thoroughbred breeders. Haggin died when Richard was eight, but the boy — a frequent visitor — inherited the family love of horses, and his brother William turned it into a champion racing stable.

narrative_blocks.header: His stepfather had ridden with the Rough Riders
narrative_blocks.body: After his parents divorced, Richard's mother married J. Lorimer Worden — one of Theodore Roosevelt's Rough Riders in the Spanish-American War, and, like Richard's own father, a stockbroker.

career.notes: Hasbrouck Heights, NJ

notable.notable_blurb: Thoroughbred owner and breeder

cross_connections.display_label: bred and raced champion Thoroughbreds in the mid-century era
bred Crème Fraiche, who won the Belmont Stakes in 1985

narrative_blocks.header: The mining heir who bred Belmont winners
narrative_blocks.body: William grew up between a Wall Street father and the vast California ranch of his great-grandfather James Ben Ali Haggin, a mining magnate and pioneering horseman. He turned that inheritance into one of America's great Thoroughbred stables, home to champions like Gamely, Lamb Chop, and the 1979 Belmont winner Coastal.

narrative_blocks.header: His only Triple Crown win upset Spectacular Bid
narrative_blocks.body: In 1979 Perry's homebred colt Coastal took the Belmont Stakes, upsetting the heavily favored Spectacular Bid by three lengths — his one victory in a Triple Crown race. The year after he died, he was inducted into Virginia's Thoroughbred Hall of Fame.

career.notes: Thoroughbred racing
hardware fixtures

narrative_blocks.header: He boasted of being Napoleon III's natural son
narrative_blocks.body: In 1896 Pierre and Bertha hosted the society arbiter Harry Lehr to lunch, where Pierre — to Lehr's irritation — claimed to be the natural son of Napoleon III. He was in fact the son of the sportsman Pierre Ronalds Sr. and the celebrated soprano Fanny Ronalds, and the couple lived for years in Paris.

narrative_blocks.header: The Arizona bride who watched the crash
narrative_blocks.body: Dorothy married Richard in Florence, Arizona, in 1926, when he was a rodeo rider turned pilot. Three years later she stood at a New Jersey airfield and watched his plane bank, dive, and go down; she outlived him by sixty-six years.

bio.bio_blurb: Seneca Falls pump manufacturer and banker

landmarks.landmark_blurb: The Seneca Falls pump works he led as president.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran Seneca Falls's world-famous pump works
narrative_blocks.body: James succeeded his father as president of the Gould Manufacturing Company — the Seneca Falls pump maker known around the world, with some five hundred hands. He also headed the Exchange National Bank, and when he died suddenly at fifty-two in 1896, the village draped itself in mourning.

narrative_blocks.header: His family's name still runs on pumps today
narrative_blocks.body: The pump works James led began in 1848 with his father Seabury's first iron-banded wooden pump, and stayed in Gould hands until 1964. It survives still as ITT Goulds Pumps — by the 1920s a household name, its Saturday Evening Post ads drawn by Norman Rockwell.

narrative_blocks.header: The foundry that cast bells and fire engines
narrative_blocks.body: Before it made pumps famous, the Gould foundry cast a little of everything — corn shellers, sad irons, sinks, tools, bells, even fire engines — pouring ten to fourteen tons of iron a day by 1860.

career.notes: Seneca Falls

narrative_blocks.header: The Social Register bride who married a bishop
narrative_blocks.body: Emily came of old Pierrepont wealth and figured in New York's Social Register when, in 1915, she married George Ashton Oldham at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine. Fourteen years later he became the third Episcopal Bishop of Albany.

burial.plot_notes: Cathedral of All Saints, Albany, New York

notable.notable_blurb: Third Episcopal Bishop of Albany

narrative_blocks.header: He took Albany's cathedra as the Crash hit
narrative_blocks.body: Oldham was installed as the third Episcopal Bishop of Albany in 1929 — 'a terribly unlucky year to begin any ministry,' with the Stock Market Crash only weeks away. He led the diocese through the Depression and the Second World War until he retired in 1950.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the catechism a generation learned
narrative_blocks.body: Oldham was the primary author of the catechism used across the American Episcopal Church for decades, until 1979. He also wrote The Fighting Church and preached widely on the church's duty to world peace.

narrative_blocks.header: His 'America First' sermon preached peace, not isolation
narrative_blocks.body: In a 1924 sermon at Washington National Cathedral titled 'America First,' Oldham meant not the isolationist slogan but a call for the nation to lead in 'things of the spirit' rather than tread again 'the old, worn, bloody pathway.' He sat on the executive committee of the World Council of Churches in 1944.

narrative_blocks.header: A jettisoned seaplane cargo cost him his cope
narrative_blocks.body: Flying home from a 1947 church conference in Australia, Oldham's seaplane had to dump its cargo and the passengers' luggage over the Pacific to stay aloft. Among the losses was the cope he had worn at his own consecration as a bishop.

narrative_blocks.header: He nearly became the church's presiding bishop
narrative_blocks.body: By 1937 Oldham was a serious candidate to be elected Presiding Bishop of the whole American Episcopal Church, and by the war's end he was counted among its foremost leaders. The deanery of Albany's Cathedral of All Saints still bears his name — Oldham House.

burial.plot_notes: Cathedral of All Saints, Albany, New York

narrative_blocks.header: She lost four children in a single year
narrative_blocks.body: Harriette Emma married Dr. Henry Sheldon and bore eight children in Brooklyn. In 1874 four of them died within months of one another — Evelyn, George, Emma, and Harry, none older than nine — and only two of the eight lived to grow up.

people.research_notes: Died suddenly of pneumonia; services at Green-Wood Cemetery.

narrative_blocks.header: She married her second cousin, a fellow Pierpont
narrative_blocks.body: Josephine married Dr. John Pierrepont Codrington Foster — her second cousin. Both were great-grandchildren of John Pierpont of New Haven: her grandfather Hezekiah Beers Pierrepont and his grandmother Mary Pierpont Foster were brother and sister.

notable.notable_blurb: Arizona prospector and lost-mine mythmaker

people.research_notes: Birth kept 1852 (FamilySearch); Arizona frontier sources give c.1836 (age 68 at 1904 death), inconsistent with being brother of Eugene b.1859.

narrative_blocks.header: He invented the Lost Dutchman Mine legend
narrative_blocks.body: After the old prospector Jacob Waltz died in 1891, Bicknell chased his story down — interviewing Waltz's caretaker and neighbors — and spun it into a San Francisco Chronicle article in 1895. His clues (Weaver's Needle, a five-mile circle, a stone house in a cave) became the foundation of America's most enduring treasure legend.

narrative_blocks.header: A millionaire who lived like a pauper
narrative_blocks.body: In 1899 Bicknell came into a fortune said to be two million dollars, with thousands of acres of New York timberland. Yet he lived frugally on the Arizona frontier — in privation most of his years — and cared little for money.

narrative_blocks.header: He hunted lost mines instead of writing
narrative_blocks.body: A newspaperman by trade, Bicknell preferred prospecting to prose, riding the Superstitions and Mazatzals after the Doc Thorne, Lost Soldier's, and Lost Frenchman mines. He found little gold, but he knew the Grand Canyon better than any writer of his day.

narrative_blocks.header: His clues outlived him by decades
narrative_blocks.body: Bicknell's Lost Dutchman clues drove treasure hunters for a century. In 1931 the searcher Adolph Ruth vanished in the Superstitions carrying a copy of Bicknell's 1895 article; his death made national headlines and revived the legend.

career.notes: Arizona Territory

bio.title: Dr.
bio.bio_blurb: New Haven physician and anatomy instructor

narrative_blocks.header: He taught anatomy to Yale's art students
narrative_blocks.body: After Yale Medical School, Foster built a large New Haven practice, much of it among the students. When Yale's Art School wanted anatomy taught for painting and sculpture, he gave the first course in 1877 and stayed on as its instructor.

narrative_blocks.header: He tried sugar planting before medicine
narrative_blocks.body: Before he was a doctor, Foster spent time as a sugar planter at Mandarin, Florida, near St. Augustine. He came home to New Haven, took his medical degree in 1875, and served for years as the city's Port Surgeon.

narrative_blocks.header: He married his second cousin, Josephine Bicknell
narrative_blocks.body: John married Josephine Bicknell, his second cousin. Both descended from John Pierpont of New Haven — John through his grandmother Mary Pierpont Foster, Josephine through her grandfather Hezekiah Beers Pierrepont, who were brother and sister.

career.notes: Port Surgeon
