bio.bio_blurb: New York lawyer, art collector, and WWI captain
bio.title: Capt.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: The bibliophile's club: he was a member of the Morgan Library.

military_service.notes: Captain in heavy combat in France; earlier a Squadron A cavalry trooper on the Mexican border, 1916.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty years at one New York law firm
narrative_blocks.body: A Yale and Harvard Law man, Allen practiced trusts and estates at Lord, Day & Lord in New York for nearly sixty years, rising to senior partner. He gave much of his energy back to the city that made him.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the checklist of Winslow Homer's art
narrative_blocks.body: A serious student of American art, Allen compiled 'A Checklist of Illustrations by Winslow Homer,' cataloguing the painter's magazine and book work. He served as president of New York's Art Commission and sat on its Landmarks Preservation Commission.

narrative_blocks.header: He led a machine-gun company in France
narrative_blocks.body: Allen served as a captain in the 305th Machine Gun Battalion of the 77th Division and saw heavy combat in France in the First World War. He had started as a Squadron A cavalry trooper, riding the Mexican border in 1916.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave decades to the city's poor children
narrative_blocks.body: For forty years Allen worked the charities of New York's children — the Sheltering Arms, the Kips Bay Boys Club — quietly serving underprivileged youth. He was a trustee of Berea College in Kentucky as well.

narrative_blocks.header: For thirteen years, secretary of the Grolier Club
narrative_blocks.body: Allen was a devoted bibliophile — a collector of prints, etchings, and rare books — and from 1935 to 1948 served as secretary of the Grolier Club, America's foremost society of book collectors. He belonged as well to the Century Association and the Morgan Library.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave his best collections to Yale
narrative_blocks.body: Allen gave away what he loved to gather: his Jongkind etchings went to Yale, and a Sadao Watanabe print, 'The Flight into Egypt,' to its art gallery. An honorary trustee of the Yale Library Associates, he was a benefactor to the end.

career.notes: trusts and estates, New York

landmarks.landmark_blurb: The Kenwood parish he led for twenty years; his ashes rest there.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty years rector of a Chicago parish
narrative_blocks.body: George Thomas led St. Paul's Episcopal Church in Chicago's Kenwood for twenty years, from 1915 until his death. He was remembered less as a preacher than as a pastor — finding jobs for single mothers and quietly paying tuition for fatherless boys.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept the church warm for Depression teens
narrative_blocks.body: As the Depression deepened, Thomas kept the heat on so his parish's teenagers had somewhere to go, grouped them, gave them tasks and purpose, and built friendships that lasted their lives. His funeral overflowed the church; hundreds stood outside in the February cold.

narrative_blocks.header: Fire took his church, but not his ashes
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas was cremated and his ashes interred beneath St. Paul's altar. When arsonists burned the church down in 1956, his urn was recovered from the ruins and reinterred in the rebuilt St. Paul & the Redeemer, where it rests still.

career.notes: Kenwood, Chicago

people.research_notes: English-born, of a family formerly of Kingston, Jamaica.

bio.bio_blurb: Editor of the Buffalo Commercial Advertiser

narrative_blocks.header: He edited a Buffalo paper for forty years
narrative_blocks.body: After the Civil War William settled in Buffalo and gave four decades to the Commercial Advertiser — associate editor, then editor-in-chief from 1878 until he stepped back in 1911. Before Buffalo he had briefly run a Lynchburg paper and read law in his father's New Haven office.

narrative_blocks.header: He paid the Navy through the Civil War
narrative_blocks.body: In 1862 William left a Connecticut staff post to serve as a Navy paymaster aboard the USS Memphis until the war's end. He belonged afterward to the Loyal Legion of Union officers, and later led the Yale Alumni Association of Buffalo.

notable.notable_blurb: Florida Superintendent of Public Instruction

narrative_blocks.header: He ran Florida's schools after Reconstruction
narrative_blocks.body: As Florida's Superintendent of Public Instruction from 1881 to 1884, Foster set out to professionalize a young school system — uniform teacher examinations, county teacher institutes, and normal schools to lift the standard of instruction. He pressed, too, for a state school for deaf and blind children, founded soon after.

narrative_blocks.header: A Yankee lawyer who judged in Florida
narrative_blocks.body: A Connecticut man and Yale graduate, Foster served as State's Attorney for Florida's Fourth Circuit and later as a circuit judge over Orange and Volusia counties. He spent his later years as counsel to the railroads of the Plant system.

narrative_blocks.header: He went south for his health and stayed
narrative_blocks.body: Failing health drove Foster out of Connecticut in 1866; he farmed at St. Augustine to recover and made Florida his home for the rest of his life. Illness dogged his career, forcing him from office more than once, and in 1899 he died at a New Haven hospital after the amputation of a leg.

narrative_blocks.header: Third of a line of New Haven lawyers
narrative_blocks.body: Foster came of three generations of New Haven lawyers — his grandfather a Yale man of 1802, his father Judge Eleazer Kingsbury Foster, State's Attorney and Speaker of the Connecticut House. He carried the family's law south to Florida, and named his son Eleazer Kingsbury the third.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father helped elect Thomas Jefferson
narrative_blocks.body: Stella was a daughter of Abraham Bishop, the New Haven firebrand who linked Jefferson's Republicans to their Connecticut rank and file. A fierce critic of Hamilton's Federalists, he helped carry the state for Jefferson's 'Revolution of 1800.'

naming_inspiration.description: Named for his grandfather, Pierrepont Beers Foster of New Haven.

narrative_blocks.header: She mothered abolitionists and Navy surgeons
narrative_blocks.body: Lucy married General John Minor of Fredericksburg and raised a houseful of children who left their mark. Her daughter Mary Berkeley became a noted Virginia abolitionist; two of her sons, Lewis Willis and James Monroe, served as Navy surgeons.

career.notes: F.R.G.S.

military_service.notes: Awarded the Distinguished Service Cross (D.S.C.), 1917.

narrative_blocks.header: He won the Distinguished Service Cross at sea
narrative_blocks.body: Alban went to sea young, trained on HMS Conway, and won the Distinguished Service Cross in the First World War. He rose to captain in the Royal Indian Navy.

narrative_blocks.header: No woman since has won her sailing title
narrative_blocks.body: Sharlie started racing her Atlantic-class sloop 'Carolina' at fourteen and won the class championship before she was twenty — no woman has taken the title since. She ski-bummed at Mad River Glen through slalom gates cut from saplings.

narrative_blocks.header: She called herself 'the soup lady'
narrative_blocks.body: For all her regattas, Charlotte wanted to be remembered for caring for people in need — a hospice volunteer and visiting-nurse board member. Her greatest joy, she said, was giving comfort where she could.

bio.display_name: Maria Ward Skelton Williams Sheerin Minor

people.research_notes: First married Charles Wilford Sheerin; after his death married Dr. John Minor in 1952.

narrative_blocks.header: She turned needlepoint designs into a shop
narrative_blocks.body: Ebbie was one of four women who founded Peacock Alley, a Grand Rapids needlepoint shop where her own designs became the heart of its stock. Trained in architecture and design at Michigan, she gave herself to the practical and domestic arts.

narrative_blocks.header: President of a dozen Grand Rapids causes
narrative_blocks.body: Ebbie led half of civic Grand Rapids — president of the Junior League, the Urban League, the historic-preservation council, and more. She sat on the board of the Kendall school of design her grandfather had founded, and helped it grow into a college.

narrative_blocks.header: A Capitol Hill family doctor of gentle repute
narrative_blocks.body: Maureen took her medical degree at George Washington and practiced as a family physician on Capitol Hill for years, sharing an office with Claudine Gay. Her patients remembered her gentle way and her compassion.

narrative_blocks.header: She presided over LA's first symphony orchestra
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Lyman Strong Mason presided over the original Los Angeles Symphony Orchestra and belonged to the Ebell Club, one of the city's leading women's cultural societies.

career.notes: Presided over the city's original symphony orchestra.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: The Roslyn business block her husband Frederick Hicks built, standing by the old grist mill.

narrative_blocks.header: From her deathbed she sent the suffrage vote
narrative_blocks.body: A daughter of suffragist Harriet Russell Strong, she was dying in 1918 when the Nineteenth Amendment came to a House vote. She urged her congressman husband, Frederick Hicks, to leave her bedside for the Capitol; he cast his vote and came back for her funeral.

people.research_notes: Appointed to the Nevada Militia in 1863 by Orion Clemens, brother of Mark Twain.

notable.notable_blurb: U.S. Congressman from New York; Alien Property Custodian

people.research_notes: Born Frederick Hicks Cocks in Westbury, N.Y.; took the name Frederick Cocks Hicks on adoption by relatives. Brother of Congressman William Willets Cocks. Quaker; lived on a 53-acre estate at Sands Point.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Between 1895 and 1905 he built three commercial stores on Old Northern Boulevard, beside the historic Roslyn Grist Mill.

narrative_blocks.header: He left his dying wife to vote suffrage
narrative_blocks.body: In 1918 he sat at the bedside of his dying wife -- a daughter of suffragist Harriet Russell Strong -- when a crucial House vote on the Nineteenth Amendment came due. At her urging he went to the Capitol, helped provide the winning margin, and returned home for her funeral.

narrative_blocks.header: Won by four votes after a year’s lawsuits
narrative_blocks.body: His 1914 election was among the closest and longest in House history. First called the winner by fifteen votes, he saw the lead whittled to four by lawsuits, was not certified until December 1915, and took his seat only when Congress reconvened in January 1916.

narrative_blocks.header: His Roslyn store row still stands today
narrative_blocks.body: Between 1895 and 1905 he put up three Queen Anne commercial buildings on Old Northern Boulevard, beside the old Roslyn Grist Mill. Sold as a single parcel ever since, the row still houses shops today.

narrative_blocks.header: He dropped dead at a magic show
narrative_blocks.body: In December 1925 the Alien Property Custodian went alone to Washington's Belasco Theatre to watch Thurston the magician. As the illusionist levitated a woman on stage, Hicks gasped, slumped in his aisle seat, and was carried out dead at 53 -- with few in the audience noticing.

career.notes: Began as a clerk in a leather firm; became a banking-house partner (later Hicks, Kip & Herrick), retiring in 1911 to enter politics.
Director of Floral Park Savings Bank, Glen Cove Insurance Co., Nassau County Trust Co., and other Long Island firms.
Republican; 64th-67th Congresses; House Committee on Naval Affairs; declined renomination in 1922 and a diplomatic post to Uruguay.
Managed President Coolidge's 1924 campaign from New York; special U.S. minister to Peru for the Ayacucho centennial.
Appointed by President Coolidge in April 1925; served until his sudden death that December.

California business executive; UCLA class of 1916; U.S. Navy ensign; attorney with California Delta Farms Inc.; father a native of Dumfries, Scotland. Married first (1923) Katharine Bixby of the Rancho Los Alamitos (Long Beach) family; married second (1984) Georgina Strong Hicks. His 1917 WWI draft card gives 1894, Los Angeles, and work as a salesman for Pacific Mutual Life Insurance Co.; family descendants still serve on the Rancho Los Alamitos Foundation board.

narrative_blocks.header: He married into the Rancho Los Alamitos dynasty
narrative_blocks.body: His first wife, Katharine Bixby, was a granddaughter of John William Bixby, who bought the historic Rancho Los Alamitos in Long Beach in 1881. Preston joined the Hotchkis-Bixby family that preserved the old adobe ranch and, in 1968, deeded its surviving acres to the city as a public museum.

people.research_notes: Mary S. Hedges, second wife of Rev. Amzi Francis (X01822). Born 1808; died 1897, age 88-89. Married Amzi after his first wife Eliza Talcott Francis (H01787) died in 1829. Mother of Henrietta E. Francis Talcott (U00038), the philanthropist who married James Talcott (H03207) in 1860. Widowed 1845 when Amzi died at Bridgehampton NY. Through her daughter Henrietta's marriage to James Talcott, Mary Hedges became step-grandmother to a Talcott line one generation removed from her own household. Birth place, death place, burial, and parentage not yet established. Source: FindAGrave memorial 34106648.
Assistant county treasurer; active in the development of telephone service in the Southland; secretary-treasurer of the Santa Monica Bay Telephone Company.

career.notes: Helped develop telephone service in the Southland.

bio.bio_blurb: Painter and former Viking Press publicity director

career.notes: New York.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at New Hope, her mother's town
narrative_blocks.body: Joan married Roger at St. Philip's Chapel in New Hope, Pennsylvania, on 18 January 1975, when he was Vice President Rockefeller's assistant for Congressional affairs; his brother Henry was best man. New Hope was where her mother grew up, the town of the Pennsylvania Impressionist painters.

narrative_blocks.header: Phi Beta Kappa, then Viking Press
narrative_blocks.body: Joan went from Milton Academy to Smith, class of 1965 and Phi Beta Kappa, and into publishing, where she was associate publicity director of Viking Press by the time she married. She paints in oil herself; her Still Life with Figs dates from 2024.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandfather painted her in a strawberry hat
narrative_blocks.body: In 1958 her grandfather, the Pennsylvania Impressionist John Folinsbee, painted Joan in a strawberry hat; the canvas hung in his shows at the Century Association and the Farnsworth Museum the next year. She is now a trustee of the John F. Folinsbee Art Trust, which keeps his catalogue.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father married her in his own chapel
narrative_blocks.body: She was a daughter of the Rev. William Montague Geer, long the vicar of St. Paul's Chapel at Broadway and Vesey Street. He was vicar emeritus when he performed her wedding there in 1927.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brother rode with Troop A
narrative_blocks.body: Alpheus Geer enlisted in Troop A Cavalry in its founding year of 1889 and rode with it against the Buffalo switchmen's strike in 1892. He went back in for the Mexican border and again for the World War, and made his living in silk.

people.research_notes: Daughter of the Rev. William Montague Geer, vicar and later vicar emeritus of St. Paul's Chapel, Trinity Parish, Broadway and Vesey Street, New York. Her brother was Alpheus Geer — Troop A Cavalry from its founding year 1889, field service in the Buffalo Switchmen's Strike of 1892, re-enlisted for the Mexican border in 1916 and for the World War in 1918; St. Stephen's College; career in silk manufacturing. narrative_blocks.header: The veil had dressed generations of brides
narrative_blocks.body: She married at All Saints Memorial in July 1951 in ivory satin trimmed with heirloom point lace, under a family veil of rosepoint and Brussels lace that several generations of brides before her had worn. Her sister Gertrude wore the same veil in the same church five years later.

narrative_blocks.header: Smith the month before her wedding
narrative_blocks.body: She left Brearley in 1947, Bradford Junior College in 1949, and Smith in June 1951, a month before she married. She had come out at the Cosmopolitan Club in December 1947.

Three children, none built: Edmund Hawley, Helen Talcott (m. Allie Roy Hart Jr.) and Suzanne Geer Melhado.

career.notes: Bond department.

narrative_blocks.header: He called it a royal flush
narrative_blocks.body: At Eaton Vance he started and led the high-yield investment group, having first seen the opening from the bond desk at John Hancock. When he retired in 1997 one of his funds ranked first over every time period, which he called a royal flush.

narrative_blocks.header: He stopped at every historical marker
narrative_blocks.body: Family road trips were punctuated by stops at each and every historical marker, and he read history for pleasure the rest of the time. He gave his conservation work to the Connecticut River Conservancy, the Trustees of Reservations, and Mass Audubon.

narrative_blocks.header: Three sisters, then three daughters
narrative_blocks.body: He grew up with Katharine, Suzanne and Gertrude and raised Julia, Barbara and Margaret. Those who knew him called him a champion of women.

narrative_blocks.header: Morgan, the family firm, then Hancock
narrative_blocks.body: After Army service in Germany he went to J.P. Morgan, then to Talcott National Corporation, the successor to the factoring house his great-grandfather had founded. From there he moved to John Hancock in Boston, where he first saw what high-yield could do.

Army service in Germany, then J.P. Morgan, Talcott National Corp., and John Hancock Boston, then Eaton Vance in the 1980s. Wife Jane McCurrach, 64 years; homes in Brookline MA, Lower Waterford VT, Martha's Vineyard. Union Boat Club president 1968-71. Retired 1997 for conservation work. Daughters Julia, Barbara '83, Margaret '86; eight grandchildren, two great-grandchildren. The J.P. Morgan and Talcott National career rows carry no start_year, so they render without a date suffix and sort last - the memorial gives no dates for them.

narrative_blocks.header: She understudied for Martha Graham
narrative_blocks.body: She began as a modern dancer in New York, understudying for the Martha Graham Dance Company and dancing with Pearl Lang's. In the 1970s she formed a company of her own and took her choreography around New York and New Jersey.

narrative_blocks.header: She performed her poems to classical music
narrative_blocks.body: After moving to Westerly in 1990 she founded Art Technology Inc. and performed her poetry to classical music with movement, at the public library and elsewhere. In 1998 she published Pieces of Me, poems on nature, creativity and spirituality.

narrative_blocks.header: She painted too, and showed it
narrative_blocks.body: She was a visual artist as well as a dancer and a poet, and hung her paintings in galleries at Westerly and Charlestown. Beach Street in Westerly was her address for most of her Rhode Island years.

narrative_blocks.header: The same veil, the same altar
narrative_blocks.body: She married John Richard Suydam Jr. at All Saints Memorial in September 1956, in a family gown of ivory satin and the heirloom rosepoint and Brussels veil her sister Katharine had worn there five years before. Her sister Suzanne was matron of honour and Katharine an attendant.

narrative_blocks.header: His crew twice won at Henley
narrative_blocks.body: He rowed on the Princeton lightweight crew that twice took the Thomas Challenge Cup at Henley. He reached Princeton in 1947 by way of Lawrenceville and a war, and belonged to the Charter Club.

narrative_blocks.header: Associate editor of the Yale Law Journal
narrative_blocks.body: He was associate editor of the Yale Law Journal and still a senior there when he married in July 1951, with Alexander Perry Morgan — a Princeton man a class ahead of him — standing as best man. The couple settled at New Haven for his last year of law school.

narrative_blocks.header: The Pacific came before Princeton
narrative_blocks.body: He served in the Pacific theatre in the Second World War as a lieutenant junior grade, between Lawrenceville and his Princeton class of 1947.

narrative_blocks.header: He worked for his wife's family firm
narrative_blocks.body: Between the United States Attorney's office in New York and the Ford Foundation he spent part of his career at the James Talcott Company, the factoring house his wife's great-grandfather had founded. He finished at the Small Business Administration and retired to New Mexico.

people.research_notes:

narrative_blocks.header: From steel to banking to his own shingle
narrative_blocks.body: He took an engineering degree at Yale in 1951 and went to the Allegheny Ludlum Steel Company at Albany, following the firm out to Ohio. In 1960 he changed trades altogether for Bankers Trust, and in 1982 changed again — up to Vermont, where he ran a General Business Services franchise for the next thirty years.

narrative_blocks.header: His workshop, and where not to step
narrative_blocks.body: He could make almost anything work better than it had, in some new and different way, and he kept his workshop in perfect order. Anyone who went in and put a thing back wrong found out quickly. He could still get a smile out of nearly everyone, and often an outright laugh.

narrative_blocks.header: A vicious slice and two holes in one
narrative_blocks.body: He carried a vicious slice around the golf course and still, twice in his life, put the ball in the hole from the tee. He fished a fly, loved the Adirondacks, paddled a canoe well and played a hard game of pool.

narrative_blocks.header: He sang in the Dorset choir for years
narrative_blocks.body: He was musical, sang, played the piano, and gave years to the choir at the Dorset Church. It was one of a long list of things he did for that town without being paid for any of them.

narrative_blocks.header: Treasurer of three Dorset institutions
narrative_blocks.body: He kept the books for Zion Episcopal Church, the Dorset Library and the Dorset Historical Society, all as a volunteer. He also sat on the boards of Habitat and the Vermont Community Loan Fund and on his church's investment committee.

narrative_blocks.header: She married in her mother's gown
narrative_blocks.body: She wore her mother's ivory satin wedding gown to Christ Church at Rye at the end of August 1942 — princess lace, rose point motifs, a cape of the same lace and a full skirt looped up into a court train. Her sister Hope was maid of honour and two more sisters, Joan and Anne, walked behind her. The reception was at Bramble Hill, her parents' house.

narrative_blocks.header: A dance at the Apawamis Club, 1936
narrative_blocks.body: Her parents brought her out at a dance at the Apawamis Club in September 1936, after Miss Hall's School at Pittsfield and before Vassar. Six years later she married a man still finishing medical school.

narrative_blocks.header: She died four days short of eighty-five
narrative_blocks.body: Born in New York in the May of 1918, she died at Newton, Massachusetts, on the ninth of May 2003. Her husband, the physician Thomas Clark Chalmers, had gone eight years before her.

narrative_blocks.header: She trained in occupational therapy at Columbia
narrative_blocks.body: After Concord Academy and Vassar she went to Columbia to study occupational therapy, and was still finishing when her engagement was announced. She married a doctor and they raised three children between Washington and Brookline.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived her husband by fourteen years
narrative_blocks.body: William died in 2004 after fifty-odd years of marriage, and she moved from Washington to Brookline. She died there in 2018 at ninety-four, leaving three children, eight grandchildren and seven great-grandchildren.

narrative_blocks.body: His own work was in arthritis and rheumatology, at Harvard, the Naval Medical Research Institute and Mass General. From 1963 he spent twenty-one years at the National Institutes of Health handing out the money that paid for research across the country.

narrative_blocks.body: He sang baritone at All Saints in Chevy Chase for thirty-three years. After retiring he gave his time to IONA Senior Services and sat on its board.

narrative_blocks.body: She married Lieutenant Francis Henry Curry of the Royal Air Service at the Presbyterian Church in Rye in July 1919, three months after his discharge. They sailed for Southampton within the week and went on to Buenos Aires, where he had a place with Standard Oil.

narrative_blocks.header: Her children were born in Buenos Aires
narrative_blocks.body: Three of the four came in Argentina and grew up crossing the Atlantic — the passenger manifests catch the family again and again, cabin class and first, with a governess in tow. The youngest was born in Surrey and died there at four.

narrative_blocks.header: He built a barn for his zebras
narrative_blocks.body: He imported Grevy's zebras and kept the only herd of Highland cattle in America, meaning to cross horse and zebra into a better farm animal. In 1907 he had the architect Frank A. Rooke put up a Zebra House at Rye, designed around what the animals needed.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote a book to answer the bigots
narrative_blocks.body: At a time when Chinese exclusion was law he compiled Who's Who of the Chinese in New York to set down what Chinese Americans had achieved. He had made his money importing Chinese tea when the war shut the German houses out of the American market.

narrative_blocks.header: He spent his fortune to save his bank
narrative_blocks.body: He had founded the Van Norden Trust Company in 1902 and was its president when the panic of 1907 came. He put a great part of his personal fortune into the bank to keep it standing, and sold control two years later.

narrative_blocks.header: City boys camped on John Jay's lawn
narrative_blocks.body: At Rye he kept hundreds of animals gathered from all over the world — zebras and zebus, deer and donkeys and prize-winning cattle dogs. He gave poor children of the city their summers there and let city boys camp on the grounds.

narrative_blocks.header: Two years in China, then a book
narrative_blocks.body: He travelled two years through China and Indochina before the First World War and sent back articles to the New York papers. He compiled a Chinese who's who for New York and in 1918 published a book on Chinese music and musical instruments.

people.research_notes: Banker; Columbia University. President of the Nineteenth Ward Bank and the Van Norden Safe Deposit Company. Son of Warner Van Norden (b. 2 July 1841, New York City), capitalist and director of the Van Norden Trust Co., Mercantile National Bank, Standard Milling Co., American Surety Co., Fifth Ave. Estates and D. Member of the American Bison Society, Bibliophile Society, New York Zoological Society, Geographical Society. Republican. Address 786 Fifth Avenue. Compiled 'Who's Who of the Chinese in New York'; with Grace founded the Van Norden Family Hospital for Men and the Grace Talcott Hospital for Women at Hepu, Guangxi. Made a fortune importing Chinese tea during the First World War when German firms were barred from the US market.

narrative_blocks.body: He went into the Army Air Force as a second lieutenant in 1943 and flew a good many missions in the Pacific, rising later to major in the reserves. The rest of his working life was investment banking, a Wyoming manufacturer, and Denver oil.

narrative_blocks.header: He finished up running a fishing camp
narrative_blocks.body: A lover of the outdoors, he settled at last in California and ran a fishing and skiing operation at June Lake in the Sierras. Strokes forced him to Atlanta, where he died in 1998.

narrative_blocks.header: He meant to be a doctor
narrative_blocks.body: His father was a physician at Potsdam and medicine was the plan. Both parents died while he was young, and a year running a Nebraska high school, with prayer meetings in neighbouring towns, turned him to the ministry.

narrative_blocks.header: He took a scattered few to six hundred
narrative_blocks.body: In twelve years at Spring Street he took the membership from a handful to six hundred and built the settlement house beside it, joining evangelism to social work as few had tried. His assistant later wrote his life to pay for the settlement.

narrative_blocks.header: The Triangle fire killed a bride he married
narrative_blocks.body: Daisy, forewoman on the ninth floor of the Asch Building, had married at Spring Street that January, her husband sailing for Switzerland a fortnight later. She burned in the Triangle fire that March, and Bates found her repeating 'My Father, oh, my Heavenly Father.'

narrative_blocks.header: His bachelor dinner was at the settlement house
narrative_blocks.body: He gave his bachelor dinner in June 1909 in the settlement house he had built; his bride's parents gave theirs at the Metropolitan Club. He married Edith Talcott at the Fifth Avenue Presbyterian Church that Tuesday.

narrative_blocks.header: Six men carried his stretcher through Cuzco
narrative_blocks.body: He sailed for South America with Edith in June 1913 to see the missions and to rest, having written that his strength had lasted just long enough for the last goodbye. They walked half a mile into Cuzco for want of carriages, and six men carried him on a stretcher that evening to a house where he never woke.

narrative_blocks.header: He prayed only to see his children grown
narrative_blocks.body: From Canada in January 1913 he wrote to his infant son Talcott that his daily prayer was to live to see the boy and his sister reach twenty-five. He had lost both his parents young and knew what that was.

people.research_notes: Son of Dr. Charles Carroll Bates and Charlotte Clark of Potsdam NY. Auburn high school 1890; principal of the high school at Elba, Nebraska for a year; Hamilton College 1895; Auburn Seminary 1898; ordained by the presbytery of Cayuga 24 Apr 1898. Assistant at the Church of the Sea and Land, then the Fourth Presbyterian Church under Dr. Wilbur Chapman; called to Spring Street Presbyterian Church in 1901 and stayed twelve years. Died at Cuzco, Peru while studying missionary work. S. Ralph Harlow — his assistant minister 1911-12 — wrote 'The Life of H. Roswell Bates' (1914), proceeds to the Spring Street Settlement House. The supplied photo filename reads 'Herbert R. Boswell'; treating it as a filename typo for Bates.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Bought it in 1928 and cut the ground floor into his surgery

narrative_blocks.header: The X-rays he pioneered burned his hands
narrative_blocks.body: He moved out of general practice into relieving pain by physical means and X-ray therapy and was early in both; through the 1920s he worked a Toepler-Holtz static machine on painful muscles, nerves and joints, and dismantled it when better methods came. The radiation burns on his hands stayed.

narrative_blocks.header: He survived three heart attacks and kept working
narrative_blocks.body: Typhoid, diphtheria, scarlet fever, polio that partly paralysed his eye muscles, Paget's disease of the spine and pelvis, three heart attacks, pneumonia, diabetes and arteries so blocked his feet had no pulse — he outlasted all of it across sixty years of practice. In his eighties the only complaint that troubled him was seeing double when he hit a tennis ball.

narrative_blocks.header: He dissected turtles to teach his daughters
narrative_blocks.body: On summers at Sheffield he carried his instruments everywhere, and a snapping turtle or a frog became an anatomy lesson on the spot. He played tennis until he was eighty-six and believed in relieving pain by physical means.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter became Kennedy's doctor
narrative_blocks.body: By his first wife, Janet Davidson, he had two daughters and raised them both to be physicians — no Talcott blood in either, since Edith was his second wife. One of them, Janet Travell, was the first woman appointed White House physician and treated President Kennedy's back.

people.research_notes: Williams College 1891; M.D. Albany College of Medicine 1898; practised in Manhattan sixty years. Specialist in electrotherapy and physiotherapy, a pioneer of manipulative medicine. Father, by his first wife Janet Davidson (d. 1928), of Dr. Janet Travell — the first woman appointed White House physician, personal physician to President Kennedy — and of Dr. Virginia T. Weeks, pediatrician. Edith was his second wife. Neither Janet Travell nor Virginia Weeks is built.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought the peak the county now owns
narrative_blocks.body: He and Peggy bought the core of Jacks Peak, the highest ground on the Monterey Peninsula, and sold it on to the Nature Conservancy, which sold it to Monterey County. The park opened in 1977 and holds one of only three native stands of Monterey pine left anywhere.

narrative_blocks.header: Lunch with King, the day classes were cancelled
narrative_blocks.body: Monterey Peninsula College cancelled classes on 24 March 1961 so its students could hear Martin Luther King Jr. on the moral and spiritual factors of integration, and King took lunch that day with Bates and his wife Peggy. That night he spoke on the power of nonviolence to nine hundred people in the college armory.

narrative_blocks.header: A veteran who sued to narrow veterans' relief
narrative_blocks.body: Bates, a veteran, joined a non-veteran taxpayer in suing California's State Board of Equalization over how assessors measured the property ceiling on the state's veterans' tax exemption. Counting property at full cash value rather than assessed value, as they asked, would have ended the exemption for nearly every veteran who owned a house.

narrative_blocks.header: He published twice in his stepsister's field
narrative_blocks.body: Bates published two papers on myofascial pain — the referred pain of skeletal muscle that his stepsister Janet Travell had defined and named. Their parents married in 1930, when he was eighteen and she was twenty-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: A healthy boy, then polio on day two
narrative_blocks.body: In the autumn of 1954 a twenty-year-old woman at term developed acute anterior poliomyelitis, and the question was whether the local hospital could take her at all. The boy was born healthy and came down with polio on his second day; the eleven other infants in the nursery were given gamma globulin, and Bates published the case in 1955.

narrative_blocks.header: She bought a mountain and gave it away
narrative_blocks.body: She and Talcott bought the core of Jacks Peak in the early 1960s and passed it to the Nature Conservancy, which passed it to the county; the park opened in 1977. Two years before she died she was still lobbying for the pines next door.

narrative_blocks.header: At thirty-two she won three school board seats
narrative_blocks.body: A newcomer to the peninsula, she stood for the Monterey elementary, high school and junior college boards at thirty-two and won all three. She chaired them from 1953 to 1957 and sat nine years on the state Board of Education after.

narrative_blocks.header: She talked its land out of Morse
narrative_blocks.body: Monterey Peninsula College was a set of grades bolted onto the high school until she built it out into a college. Then she talked S. F. B. Morse, who owned the peninsula, into giving it ground to stand on.

narrative_blocks.header: She recruited Black teachers to Seaside’s schools
narrative_blocks.body: She worked to bring Black teachers into the schools of Seaside, next to Monterey. When Martin Luther King Jr. spent 24 March 1961 at Monterey Peninsula College, classes cancelled so students could hear him, he lunched with her and Talcott.

narrative_blocks.header: Her parents fought her going to college
narrative_blocks.body: She took a B.A. at Barnard in 1940 and an M.A. in American history at Washington University, and was reading for a doctorate at Columbia under Henry Steele Commager when the war stopped her. Her family had resisted her going at all.

narrative_blocks.header: Four months to Kabul in a GMC Suburban
narrative_blocks.body: In 1972 she drove four months through Turkey, Iran, Afghanistan and Pakistan with her husband and their four sons in a GMC Suburban. She and Talcott were also among the first Americans into China after relations reopened.

parents.mother_research_notes: Mr. and Mrs. Arthur S. Johnson of Boston, per the 1947 engagement announcement of their granddaughter Joan.

narrative_blocks.header: She married into the factoring house at twenty-one
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Stoddard Johnson of Boston married James Talcott Jr. in the April of 1917, months before he enlisted in the Naval Reserve. She outlived him by four years and died at Rye in 1987, aged ninety-one.

narrative_blocks.header: His father managed the Titanic's line
narrative_blocks.body: Philip Eddowes Curry ran the White Star Line's Southampton office and in 1921 founded the Shipping Golfing Society there, giving it a silver cup and its first presidency. Francis went into shipping too, but on the other side of the Atlantic.

narrative_blocks.header: Three years in the Royal Air Service
narrative_blocks.body: He served three years as a lieutenant and was discharged only months before his wedding. His brother, a major with the D.S.M. for the American troop movement, stood as best man.

people.research_notes: Son of Philip Eddowes Curry (1861-1933) and Alice Maud Baker (m. 6 Dec 1888). His father was the White Star Line's manager at Southampton — the Titanic's line — and in 1921 founded the Southampton Shipping Golfing Society and was its first President; he is commemorated at St. Nicholas, North Stoneham. Francis served three years as a Lieutenant in the Royal Air Service and was discharged shortly before his 1919 marriage. His brother Major Philip Arthur Curry O.B.E. was best man and had the D.S.M. for work with the British Ministry of Shipping on the American troop movement. The couple lived in Buenos Aires (Standard Oil, then shipping), with returns to Thanet House, Bassett, and later Wimbledon and Kingston Hill. Neither his father nor his brother is built.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty-five missions over Europe
narrative_blocks.body: He left Princeton to fly a B-26 with the First Tactical Army Air Force and came back with the Croix de Guerre and an Air Medal with six oak leaf clusters. He was discharged in the October of 1945 and married the following week.

narrative_blocks.header: He entered Princeton a decade behind his brother
narrative_blocks.body: He came to Princeton from Solebury School ten years after his brother Talcott, and joined the Quadrangle Club. The war took him out in the middle of it; he came back afterward and took his degree in economics cum laude in 1948.

narrative_blocks.header: They scattered his ashes from a B-26
narrative_blocks.body: He died at Ponte Vedra Beach in the May of 1999. Over Memorial Day weekend his family took his ashes up in the same model of bomber he had flown across Europe and let them go.

narrative_blocks.header: He came into the family by adoption
narrative_blocks.body: Edith Talcott took him as her own and he carried the surname of her second husband, the physician John Willard Travell. His stepfather's obituary set it down plainly — Clark Travell of Wilton, who was adopted.

people.research_notes:
Adopted son of Edith Charlotte Talcott (T01467), who took the surname of her second husband Dr. John Willard Travell. The 1961 obituary of Dr. Travell lists 'three stepchildren, Dr. Talcott Bates... Clark Travell of Wilton, Conn. (who was adopted) and Mrs. Peggy Husband of Redding, Conn.' — stepchildren of John means children of Edith, which places Clark in the Talcott line by adoption. Per Sam (2026-07-25) adoption counts as blood in this tree, so he and his daughters are carried as descendants. Peggy Husband, the third child, is not built. Birth and death dates unknown.
[2026-07-25] BIRTH YEAR DERIVED, not sourced: Princeton class of 1945 (entering c.1941) implies a birth of c.1923; he was at Princeton when he enlisted and took his degree in 1948 after the war. Entered as 1923, year_only. TENSION WITH THE ADOPTION READING: the 1945 wedding notice calls him 'son of Dr. and Mrs. J. Willard Travell' and 'a grandson of the late Mr. and Mrs. James Talcott' — which confirms Edith as his mother — and the Princeton memorial calls him 'the younger brother of Talcott '34' (Talcott Bates, b. 1912). If he were Edith's biological son by Herbert Bates he could not be born later than 1913, since Bates died in July 1913. A c.1923 birth is therefore only consistent with an actual adoption, after Edith's 1930 marriage to John Willard Travell. Four daughters, divorced Joan Balch 1966; married Philippa Walter 1977 and divorced her after the 1995 reunion. Ashes scattered from a B-26 over Memorial Day weekend 1999.

narrative_blocks.body: She married Clark Travell at St. Matthew's in Bedford in the October of 1945, a week after his discharge. Neither of them had attendants and nobody came but family.

narrative_blocks.body: He came out of Yale in 1912 and joined Dartmouth in 1919, chairing the English department from 1936 to 1939. He retired as professor emeritus in 1959 and stayed in Hanover the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: He bused city children into Wellesley
narrative_blocks.body: He co-chaired the METCO programme that brought inner-city children out to the Wellesley schools, and gave the town meeting, the school board and the church the same attention. He coached the youth teams as well.

narrative_blocks.header: All but five of his platoon were hit
narrative_blocks.body: Joyce went from Yale in 1943 straight into the Marines, and was wounded on Sugarloaf Hill at Okinawa, a position that changed hands many times; all but five of his platoon were killed or wounded. He took a Purple Heart and a Presidential Unit Citation, and went in with the first landing at Yokosuka.

narrative_blocks.header: He made the books other people learned from
narrative_blocks.body: He edited textbooks and ran programmes for Scott, Foresman in Chicago and Boston, then went to Houghton Mifflin to build their economics and business lists. Bread Loaf had given him the English and his wife both.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept a hostel for the sick
narrative_blocks.body: Back in Hanover he led the Upper Valley Hostel, which housed people cheaply while they were treated at Dartmouth Hitchcock. He taught English as a second language, sang in the chorus and ran the historical society.

narrative_blocks.header: State junior tennis champion at Choate
narrative_blocks.body: At Choate he centred an undefeated hockey team and took seventeen tennis matches in a row, winning the New Hampshire junior singles title and a third ranking in New England. He played varsity hockey at Yale and reached the final of its tennis championship.

narrative_blocks.header: He met his wife at Bread Loaf
narrative_blocks.body: After the Marines he went to Middlebury's graduate school of English at Bread Loaf, where he met Barbara Boggs. They were married fifty-six years.

narrative_blocks.header: His father taught Dartmouth English forty years
narrative_blocks.body: Hewette Joyce senior came from New Brunswick and Yale to Dartmouth's English department in 1919, chaired it from 1936 to 1939, and retired emeritus in 1959. His son was born at Hanover in 1921 and died there in December 2012, at Kendal. Barbara had gone before him.

people.research_notes: Buried at Great Neck, Nassau County NY, 1929. No children by the marriage.

narrative_blocks.header: He ended segregation in the Canal Zone
narrative_blocks.body: Appointed governor of the Panama Canal Zone in 1960, William ordered the Zone desegregated and brought a halt, for a time, to the anti-American riots that had plagued it. He retired from the Army in 1962.

narrative_blocks.header: Bradley's engineer from Tunisia to Normandy
narrative_blocks.body: In the Second World War William was chief engineer of Omar Bradley's II Corps through Tunisia and Sicily, then of the First Army for the Normandy landings and the drive across Europe. He came home with the Distinguished Service Medal.

narrative_blocks.header: He planned a twelve-million-kilowatt dam
narrative_blocks.body: After ten years as senior engineering adviser to the Inter-American Development Bank, William went to Brazil in 1972 for the International Engineering Company as project manager for planning Itaipu, a twelve-million-kilowatt hydroelectric dam. He was sixty-five.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven years running the Mississippi
narrative_blocks.body: From 1950 to 1957 William was president of the Mississippi River Commission, where he made major general. The rest of the decade took him to logistics for Army installations and to the Far East Command and Eighth Army as an assistant chief of staff.

narrative_blocks.header: Second in his class at West Point
narrative_blocks.body: Born in Corsicana, Texas, and raised in Mississippi, William graduated second in the West Point class of 1930, took his commission in the Corps of Engineers and a civil engineering degree at Berkeley in 1933.

people.research_notes: Son of William Arnold Carter and Susan Young; born Texas, reared in Mississippi. West Point 1930; B.S. in civil engineering, University of California, 1933. Omar Bradley's chief engineer through the Tunisian and Sicilian campaigns; chief engineer of II Corps in the Mediterranean and of the First Army for Normandy and the European campaign. President of the Mississippi River Commission, where he made major general. Governor of the Canal Zone 1960-62. Afterwards principal engineer and then director of infrastructure and industrial projects at the Inter-American Development Bank; from 1972 project manager for the planning of the twelve-million-kilowatt Itaipu hydropower scheme in Brazil. DEATH PLACE CONFLICT: Wikipedia says Washington DC; the newspaper obituary and FamilySearch say Fairfax County (McLean), Virginia. Using McLean. His obituary names a surviving wife SARA, so Katharine (d. 1979) was an earlier wife; the later marriage is not built.

narrative_blocks.header: Three of six children died small
narrative_blocks.body: Anna Eliza died at nine, Mary Louisa in infancy and Horace Knevals at four. Amelia Leavitt, Sarah Wells and Charles Jenkins grew up, and were still at the New Haven homestead when their father died suddenly in 1871.

narrative_blocks.header: Her surname reached her twice
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother's second marriage, in the spring of 1841, made Dr. Elial Todd Foote her stepfather; Amelia was fourteen. She later married Elial's son Charles, so the Foote name came to her once through her mother and once through herself.

narrative_blocks.header: The pulpit her father left empty
narrative_blocks.body: Rev. Charles Jenkins of Portland died at the end of 1831, leaving her mother a widow with three children. Her brother Jonathan Leavitt Jenkins took a pulpit of his own, at Amherst and then Pittsfield.

people.research_notes: Daughter of Rev. Charles Jenkins and Amelia Stiles Leavitt (HD0856). Her Foote surname is her MARRIED name: she married Dr. Charles Cheney Foote (I02648), son of Dr. Elial Todd Foote by his first wife Anna Cheney. Her mother married Elial in 1841, which made Amelia his stepdaughter — so she married her own stepbrother by that second marriage. This supersedes the note of 2026-07-25 that treated her as a child of Elial, which the 1827 birth had made impossible.
Died at seven. Named for his father and his paternal grandfather Southworth Jenkins.
Named for his maternal grandfather Jonathan Leavitt. Stub — a clergyman like his father; no further detail entered.

RESTORED 2026-07-25 after being deleted the same day: her son Dr. Charles Cheney Foote turned out to be the husband of Amelia Leavitt Jenkins, which is where Amelia's Foote surname comes from — so Anna is load-bearing in the tree, not a placeholder.

bio.bio_blurb: First wife of Dr. Elial Todd Foote

narrative_blocks.header: She died at forty in Jamestown
narrative_blocks.body: She married Elial Todd Foote at Jamestown on the last day of 1817 and bore him five children there. She died in the town in the July of 1840, and he married again the following spring.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept the trade his father gave up
narrative_blocks.body: Elial Foote left medicine young for the courthouse and the land office. Charles took the degree and stayed with it, building one of the largest practices in New Haven and a name as one of the most popular physicians in the city.

narrative_blocks.header: Union College for arts, Jefferson for medicine
narrative_blocks.body: Jamestown Academy and Williston Seminary prepared him. He took his arts degree at Union College in New York and his medical degree at Jefferson Medical College in Philadelphia, then opened a practice in New Haven and gave it his whole attention.

narrative_blocks.header: He died suddenly at forty-six
narrative_blocks.body: He died without warning at his New Haven house on 9 November 1871, forty-six years old. His widow and their three surviving children stayed on at the homestead, and she outlived him by forty years.

narrative_blocks.header: The stepsister he grew up with, then married
narrative_blocks.body: Anna Foote died at Jamestown in 1840, and the next spring the widowed judge married the widow Amelia Jenkins, whose two children moved in. Charles was sixteen, young Amelia fourteen, and they were raised in one house from then on. Eleven years later they married.

people.research_notes: Son of Dr. Elial Todd Foote by his first wife Anna Cheney. Married Amelia Leavitt Jenkins — his father's stepdaughter after the 1841 remarriage — which is where her Foote surname comes from. From the family history Sam supplied 081226: second son of Hon. E. T. Foote, born Jamestown 5 September 1825; married at New Haven 22 April 1852 by Rev. Leonard Bacon. Six children — Anna Eliza died at 9, Mary Louisa in infancy, Horace Knevals at 4; Amelia Leavitt, Sarah Wells and Charles Jenkins grew up. Died suddenly at his residence 9 November 1871.

narrative_blocks.header: She died the day after her ninety-sixth birthday
narrative_blocks.body: Born in the February of 1859, she lived to see 1955. She died on the fifteenth, one day past her birthday, and was buried at Grove Street with her parents.

narrative_blocks.body: A New Haven physician, Yale 1883 and M.D. 1890, he bequeathed the gallery Samuel King's 1771 portrait of Elizabeth Hubbard Stiles. She was his great-great-grandmother, and the picture hangs where her husband's does.

narrative_blocks.body: Her books took the domestic arts to middle-class households that wanted a handsome room without the money for one. Redeeming Old Homes said as much in its subtitle — Country Homes for Modest Purses.

narrative_blocks.header: Her papers went to Winterthur
narrative_blocks.body: She took her degree at Barnard in 1905 and wrote on table settings, flower arrangement, landscaping and the saving of old houses. The Winterthur Museum keeps her papers.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote gardens for Vogue

In Vogue in 1921 she asked who, spending summer evenings on a veranda, does not know the strange unearthly beauty of the flowers at night.

narrative_blocks.body: He taught at the University of Pittsburgh and was acting dean of its law school from 1954 to 1957. His doctorate in law and judicial science came from Harvard; among the Allegheny County bar he was the authority on property law.

bio.bio_blurb: Lewiston lawyer; counsel to Bates College

narrative_blocks.header: He met his wife and firm at Yale
narrative_blocks.body: He took his bachelor's and his law degree at Yale, where he met Jane Skelton. They married in 1951 and moved to Lewiston, where he joined his father-in-law's firm, Skelton and Mahon — which carries his name today as Skelton, Taintor and Abbott.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-two years as the college's lawyer
narrative_blocks.body: As counsel to Bates he created the Bates-Morse Mountain Conservation Area, helped bring in the papers of Edmund Muskie, and settled the estate that paid for the college's skating rink. He left the board a trustee emeritus.

narrative_blocks.header: Remembered for bread and wooden bowls
narrative_blocks.body: He served in the Army in Panama and Puerto Rico before Yale, and afterward held directorships and trusteeships across an exhausting range of Lewiston-Auburn concerns. What people recalled was his unshakeable integrity, his home-baked bread, and the bowls he turned by hand.

education.notes: Psychology; Taylor Medal in German. Later a B.S. in nursing.

narrative_blocks.header: First woman to take the Taylor Medal
narrative_blocks.body: She left the University of Mississippi in 1944 with a degree in psychology and the Taylor Medal in German, the first woman ever awarded it. She went back later for a nursing degree, and later still for a doctorate in clinical psychology.

narrative_blocks.header: She buried three husbands
narrative_blocks.body: Charles Taintor, married in 1942, died in 1980; Alan Gresky, married in 1983, died six years later after a brief illness; Edwin Forrest, married in 1990, died in 2002 of wounds he had carried since the war. Forrest lies at Arlington.

narrative_blocks.header: They wrote his war down together
narrative_blocks.body: With her third husband she wrote A Rifleman Remembers, an account of his infantry service in the Second World War. Copies went out to veterans' hospitals across the Southeast, and the book sits in the World War II Institute archive at Florida State.

people.research_notes: Obituary gives birth as 19 April 1921; FamilySearch (3 sources) gives 19 April 1922. Entry follows 1922. Obituary also names her husband "Charles Wilson Taintor II, M.D." where this tree numbers him III (HD8160), and dates the marriage to June 1942 against the 27 May 1942 record already held.

narrative_blocks.header: Her family and the college grew up together
narrative_blocks.body: The Skeltons of Lewiston were bound up with Bates for generations, and her father's firm, Skelton and Mahon, was the town's law office. She met Frederick Taintor at Yale, married him in 1951, and brought him back to Lewiston, where he joined the firm and became the college's counsel.

bio.bio_blurb: Baltimore physician and writer on sex hygiene

career.notes: Nervous diseases; hypnotic suggestion.

narrative_blocks.header: He shipped out on a whaler mid-degree
narrative_blocks.body: He left medical school for a two-year whaling voyage, came back to study, then left again as second mate on a ship bound for Africa. He was in Iceland in 1880 and 1881, and took his M.D. at Vermont only in 1890, near thirty.

narrative_blocks.header: The Herald sent him after the Jeannette
narrative_blocks.body: He went north with the party searching for the Jeannette, the ship that had sailed from San Francisco in 1879 for the Pole; his own party was wrecked and badly used before it was over. The Herald sent him to Siberia in 1883 and afterward to the Soudan campaign.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the books doctors would not
narrative_blocks.body: Settled in Baltimore from 1891, he specialised in nervous disease and hypnotic suggestion and wrote for the public on subjects the profession would not touch. The Perverts came in 1892, Plain Facts on Sex Hygiene in 1910, Sex Structure of Society in 1914.

narrative_blocks.header: Readers liked him better than doctors
narrative_blocks.body: His notice in the medical press called him eccentric and irresponsible, a native ability wasted in a desultory, rambling life, and allowed that he was held in more esteem by the laity than by the profession. He had studied under Charcot in Paris and called on Albert Moll, and he ended at a house called Mossfell at Westboro.

people.research_notes: Death date conflict: FindAGrave gives 10 Mar 1918 at Boston; Kelly's medical biography and WikiTree give 11 Mar 1918 at Westborough. Entry follows 11 March, Westborough.

narrative_blocks.header: She died a week after bearing him
narrative_blocks.body: Bernard Shea Horne was born at Pittsburgh on 19 September 1867; she died on the twenty-sixth, seven days after. She was twenty-six, and lies at Allegheny Cemetery.

narrative_blocks.header: She met him while his father was President
narrative_blocks.body: She was in Washington as a senator's daughter when they met, and Abraham Lincoln was still alive. They married there in September 1868, three years after the assassination.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father sat in the Senate and Cabinet
narrative_blocks.body: James Harlan of Iowa went to the Senate as a Free Soiler in 1855 and stayed as a Republican through the war, leaving in 1865 to serve Andrew Johnson as Secretary of the Interior. He returned to the Senate two years later, and afterwards presided over the court that settled the Alabama claims.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived him by eleven years
narrative_blocks.body: She died at Washington in the spring of 1937 at ninety, and was buried beside him at Arlington. She had outlived her husband by eleven years and their only son by nearly half a century.

narrative_blocks.header: The pass he wrote was his last writing
narrative_blocks.body: On the afternoon of 14 April 1865 he wrote out a card admitting George Ashmun and a friend to the White House at nine the next morning. He was shot at Ford's Theatre that evening, and the appointment was never kept.

narrative_blocks.header: Less than a year of school, all told
narrative_blocks.body: His formal schooling came from itinerant teachers in Kentucky and Indiana and added up to under twelve months by the time he was fifteen. He read law on his own out of borrowed Blackstone and Chitty, and said later that he had studied with nobody.

narrative_blocks.header: Four sons, and only one grew up
narrative_blocks.body: Eddie died at three, probably of tuberculosis; Willie of a fever in the White House at eleven; Tad of edema at eighteen. Only Robert, born in 1843, lived to maturity.

narrative_blocks.header: The only president to hold a patent
narrative_blocks.body: In 1849 he patented a device for lifting riverboats over shoals — bellows fixed below the hull and inflated in shallow water. It was never built, and no other president has held a patent.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son had her committed to an asylum
narrative_blocks.body: In May 1875, alarmed at her spending and at her flight from a fire that was not there, Robert had her committed to a private asylum at Batavia. She smuggled letters out to the feminist lawyer Myra Bradwell and to a Chicago editor, and was released within four months. She and Robert did not reconcile until shortly before she died.

narrative_blocks.header: She chose Lincoln over Stephen Douglas
narrative_blocks.body: She came to Springfield at twenty-one, fluent in French and sharp about politics, and was courted by the rising Democrat Stephen A. Douglas among others. She married the circuit lawyer instead, in November 1842.

narrative_blocks.header: She buried three of her four sons
narrative_blocks.body: Eddie died of consumption in 1850, Willie of a fever in the White House in 1862, and Tad at eighteen in 1871. She was sitting beside her husband at Ford's Theatre when he was shot, and went with him across the street to the room where he died.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote letters home for wounded men
narrative_blocks.body: She went round the Washington hospitals with flowers and fruit and sat writing letters for soldiers to send their families. The headaches she had had all her life grew worse after a carriage accident during the war years.

narrative_blocks.header: She sat on the Consumers’ League executive
narrative_blocks.body: She served on the executive committee of the Consumers’ League of Ohio and on the Lake District committee of the Associated Charities. She put herself on record for woman suffrage.

narrative_blocks.header: Mittleberger’s, Rye Seminary, then kindergarten
narrative_blocks.body: She went to Miss Mittleberger’s School in Cleveland and finished at Rye Seminary in 1894, then took a year at the Cleveland Kindergarten Training School. She married at Dover Bay in 1899.

narrative_blocks.header: They summered where her grandmother began
narrative_blocks.body: The Bassetts kept a summer house at Cayuga in New York. Her grandmother Elizabeth Hutchinson Cowles had been born in that county.

career.notes: The post was abolished by Congress in 1885.

narrative_blocks.header: He spoke four languages like his own
narrative_blocks.body: A liberal college education at home was finished off by foreign travel and a course at the German universities, and he came away with German, French, Spanish and Italian, each as fluent as his native tongue. It was the languages that got him his posts.

narrative_blocks.header: John Hay was the first secretary above him
narrative_blocks.body: Appointed assistant secretary of the Paris legation in 1865 under Minister Bigelow, he served beneath Colonel John Hay — Lincoln's private secretary before the war and Secretary of State long after it. He rose through two more ministers to the consul generalship at Cairo.

narrative_blocks.header: Congress abolished the post under him
narrative_blocks.body: He held the consul generalship to Egypt with marked ability until Congress abolished the office in 1885. Two years later he died of apoplexy in Chicago without a moment's warning, leaving a boy of six in his grandparents' house.

people.research_notes: Death date: his obituary reads "Saturday, October 12, 1887," but 12 October 1887 was a Wednesday while 12 November was a Saturday, and the funeral is dated 15 November. Entry follows 12 Nov 1887. Birth: FindAGrave gives New York; the obituary names Madison NJ as his birthplace.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandfather raised him after Italy
narrative_blocks.body: His mother died at Florence when he was three and his father five years later, and he was brought up in Edwin Cowles's Cleveland house and sent to Princeton. His grandfather had founded and edited the Cleveland Leader.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty years selling America abroad
narrative_blocks.body: He spent more than twenty years travelling Europe and Asia for American firms looking to set up export arrangements, and retired in the early 1940s. He had served in the First World War and belonged to Princeton's American Legion post.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped found a constitutional society
narrative_blocks.body: In his last years he was a founder and vice-president of the Defenders of the American Constitution, one of the anti-communist organisations of the 1950s. He died at eighty and was buried in the family ground at Hopewell.

people.research_notes: Birth: FindAGrave gives 27 Mar 1881; a family account gives 27 May 1881. Death: FindAGrave gives 11 Feb 1962; the Trenton Times of 11 Feb reports him dying "yesterday," i.e. 10 Feb. Entry follows the FindAGrave dates.

death.cause: Fall from a train near Union Station

narrative_blocks.header: She fell from a train at Union Station
narrative_blocks.body: She and Eugene were coming back from visiting their son Livingston at Hopewell when she fell from the incoming train near Union Station and was killed. She had lived in Washington since her marriage, on New Hampshire Avenue.

narrative_blocks.header: Buried where Washington kept headquarters
narrative_blocks.body: The private service was held at the family's historic house at Hopewell, New Jersey, which had been George Washington's headquarters before the Battle of Monmouth. Her husband, her son-in-law and Eugene himself all lie in the same ground.

people.research_notes: Her age is given as 68 in both 1950 obituaries against a 20 Feb 1881 birth, which would make her 69. Married "about 1900" per the obituary; the family account dates the marriage 2 May 1903.

cross_connections.display_label: edited The Oregonian and saved Lake Oswego's Odd Fellows Hall

narrative_blocks.header: Born in Paris, died in Oregon at ninety-four
narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Paris in 1913 and wrote four books, and pieces for McCall's through the 1970s. She married the literary agent Alan Collins in 1950, buried him in 1968, and moved to Lake Oswego in 1984.

bio.bio_blurb: Shanghai journalist; captain, Frontier Force Regiment

death.cause: Executed as a prisoner of war

cross_connections.display_label: emptied the Japanese camps near Saigon two years too late for him
was lost in the next Asian war, and has no grave either

narrative_blocks.header: He escaped the Death Railway and was caught
narrative_blocks.body: An American working as a journalist in Shanghai, he took a captaincy in the 2/12th Frontier Force Regiment and was at Kota Bharu when the Japanese invaded. Taken at Johore Bahru in March 1942, he was worked on the Burma railway, broke out of Tha Makham camp with four others in January 1943, and was retaken on the Thai border.

narrative_blocks.header: Handed back, and bayoneted
narrative_blocks.body: The Thai police returned him to the Japanese, who tortured and executed him in February 1943. He was thirty, and has no grave; his name is on the Singapore Memorial at Kranji.

bio.bio_blurb: President of Curtis Brown literary agency

narrative_blocks.header: He took Churchill's sons across the Sahara
narrative_blocks.body: In 1961 the head of one of the world's oldest literary agencies organised an expedition across the Sahara, taking Randolph and Winston Churchill Jr. and a Smithsonian zoologist with him. He had come up through the Philadelphia Evening Ledger, the Ladies Home Journal and Doubleday.

people.research_notes: Birth date and year unrecorded; FindAGrave gives only New Orleans as her birthplace and January 1944 in New York County for her death. She is buried at Green-Wood, apart from the Cowles plot at Lake View.

narrative_blocks.header: The girl carried onto the moving train
narrative_blocks.body: She was the child her father took from her aunt and carried aboard a westbound Lake Shore train, with the sheriff following after. She was ten or so; she married Paul Hurst in 1915 and they are buried together at Marion on Buzzards Bay.

narrative_blocks.header: The last patroon's youngest daughter
narrative_blocks.body: Her father was the last American landlord to hold an estate under the old manorial system. She married John Schuyler Crosby in 1863, when he had just come home a colonel from the war.

narrative_blocks.header: She never made it back to Boston
narrative_blocks.body: She came up from Washington to summer at her son's place in West Manchester, fell ill at midsummer, and by winter was too weak to be moved. The doctor drove out to her nearly every day until she died there in December.

people.research_notes: Her obituary gives her age at death as seventy-four; a January 1838 birth against a December 1911 death makes her seventy-three. The same notice calls her a great-granddaughter of both Philip Schuyler and Alexander Hamilton - the Schuyler descent is right, through her grandmother Margarita "Peggy" Schuyler, but Hamilton married Peggy's sister Elizabeth and so was a great-granduncle by marriage, not an ancestor.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife's sister was Mrs. J. P. Morgan
narrative_blocks.body: A Boston investment banker of old New York stock, he married Henrietta Grew in 1895 and kept a Back Bay townhouse and a place on the North Shore. Her sister Jane was Mrs. J. P. Morgan Jr.; his sister Angelica had married John Brooks Henderson Jr., the Smithsonian regent. Their only son grew up with a Morgan for an uncle on one side and a Henderson on the other.

narrative_blocks.header: The son who would not be a banker
narrative_blocks.body: Harry was born in 1898 and raised between the Back Bay house and the North Shore, drove ambulances in France at nineteen, and took a desk at Morgan's Paris bank that he quit inside two years. He and his wife Caresse built the Black Sun Press instead, printing Joyce and Hemingway. In December 1929 he shot a mistress and then himself in a New York hotel, at thirty-one.

narrative_blocks.header: A mad and extravagant life, by cable
narrative_blocks.body: From Boston he managed the trust that paid for his son's life in Paris. In July 1929 Harry cabled him to sell more stock, adding: WE HAVE DECIDED TO LIVE A MAD AND EXTRAVAGANT LIFE. He sold it, and rebuked him for it.

narrative_blocks.header: A shell landed ten feet from his ambulance
narrative_blocks.body: At nineteen he drove for the American Field Service at Verdun, ferrying wounded from the front lines for three days without relief. On 22 November 1917 a shell destroyed Ambulance 741 around him and he walked away untouched; his best friend, following behind, took shrapnel in the chest. He said afterwards that was the night he stopped fearing death.

narrative_blocks.header: He married his godbrother's wife
narrative_blocks.body: J. P. Morgan Jr. stood godfather to both Harry Crosby and Richard Peabody, and it was Morgan who found Harry a desk at the family's Paris bank in 1922. By then Harry had taken Peabody's wife, Polly, who would become Caresse, and married her in New York that September. He quit the bank inside two years.

narrative_blocks.header: They renamed her to make a cross
narrative_blocks.body: He persuaded his wife Polly to change her name, insisting it begin with a C to go with Crosby and form a cross with his own. They settled on Caresse; the two names meet at right angles on the shared R.

narrative_blocks.header: Crane was a friend before an author
narrative_blocks.body: Hart Crane was a friend first and an author of the press after; the Black Sun was to bring out The Bridge with Walker Evans's photographs. Caresse remembered his Brooklyn rooms, the bridge cables drawn like netting across the window and the sailors lounging. Williams, Malcolm Cowley, Evans and cummings were the company that came with him.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave Cartier-Bresson his first camera
narrative_blocks.body: In 1929 he talked a commandant at Le Bourget into releasing the young Henri Cartier-Bresson, under house arrest for hunting without a licence, into his custody. They spent the days taking and printing pictures at his mill outside Paris, and he made the Frenchman a present of a camera.

narrative_blocks.header: He drew the ace of hearts
narrative_blocks.body: At Hart Crane's farewell party in Brooklyn on 7 December 1929, cummings held out a deck and Harry drew the ace of hearts, an unlucky card. Inwardly, Caresse wrote, all of us crossed ourselves. Three days later a borrowed studio door was broken open on him and Josephine Rotch, each shot once in the temple.

people.research_notes: The account of the godfathering is ambiguous about which Morgan: the Wikipedia sentence sits in a paragraph about J. P. Morgan Jr. and reads as him, while the family account calls the godfather "old JP," which would be Morgan Sr. Entry follows Morgan Jr.
people.relational_label_override: Nephew-in-law of Ninth and Tenth Generation Hookers

narrative_blocks.header: One sister married Morgan, she married Crosby
narrative_blocks.body: She was a Grew of Boston, and her sister Jane became Mrs. J. P. Morgan Jr. — which made the banker her brother-in-law and, to her son, Uncle Jack. She married Stephen Van Rensselaer Crosby in 1895; his sister Angelica had married John Brooks Henderson Jr. of the Smithsonian.

narrative_blocks.header: She put the poetry in him first
narrative_blocks.body: Religious and affectionate, a founder of the Garden Club of America, she gave her son a love of verse long before Paris and opium reached him. After his death she and his widow gathered the letters he had written home from the ambulance corps and printed them privately.

narrative_blocks.header: She sent him to the leading prep school
narrative_blocks.body: At fourteen his parents decided it was time for St. Mark's, and he went from there to the American Field Service and Harvard. She lived on at Manchester-by-the-Sea until 1957, twenty-eight years after burying him.

people.research_notes: Sister of Jane Norton Grew (X00362), who married J.P. Morgan Jr. Same parents, Henry Sturgis Grew and Jane Norton Wigglesworth; neither parent is built. Her son Harry was christened Henry Sturgis Crosby for that grandfather.

narrative_blocks.header: Two handkerchiefs and a pink ribbon
narrative_blocks.body: At nineteen, dressing for a ball, the whalebone corset cover poked out from under her sheer gown, so she called for two pocket handkerchiefs, some pink ribbon, a needle and thread. Girls mobbed her afterwards to ask how she moved so freely. She filed for a patent in February 1914 and the office granted her the Backless Brassiere that November.

narrative_blocks.header: She sold the patent; the corset firm profited
narrative_blocks.body: She opened a two-woman shop on Washington Street in Boston to make the wireless brassieres, but the orders never came and Harry, who disliked business, talked her into closing it. She sold the patent outright to a Bridgeport corset company, which made a fortune off it over the next thirty years. I can't say the brassiere will ever take as great a place in history as the steamboat, she wrote, but I did invent it.

narrative_blocks.header: Literary godmother to the Lost Generation
narrative_blocks.body: Time called her that, and Anais Nin called her a pollen carrier who mixed, stirred, brewed and concocted friendships. With Harry she founded the Black Sun Press, which printed early work by Joyce, Hemingway, D. H. Lawrence, Hart Crane and Kay Boyle. She kept it going for forty years after his death.

narrative_blocks.header: Camus reached English first in her folder
narrative_blocks.body: Portfolio: An Intercontinental Quarterly came out loose-leaf in a folder, printed on whatever paper she could get after the war, one issue out of Paris, one out of Rome, one out of Greece. Camus's Letter to a German Friend made its first English-language appearance in it, alongside Sartre, Picasso, Matisse, Gwendolyn Brooks and Bukowski.

narrative_blocks.header: A castle nobody could heat
narrative_blocks.body: She took the Castello di Rocca Sinibalda north of Rome in the 1950s, paid to electrify it and brought power to the village below, and filled it with artists and poetry seminars. The deed listed a hundred and eighty rooms; the villagers said three hundred and twenty. I wouldn't live here if you paid me, she told a reporter.

narrative_blocks.header: Greece called her dangerous and expelled her
narrative_blocks.body: After the war she founded Women Against War and Citizens of the World and tried to plant a world citizens' centre at Delphi. In October 1952 the police met her off the Corfu ferry, held her three days in a hotel, and told her she was considered dangerous to the economy and politics of Greece.
