bio.bio_blurb: Customs broker; Nevada City miner turned merchant

career.organization: United States Custom House, San Francisco

narrative_blocks.header: Mining, then groceries, then the Custom House
narrative_blocks.body: Born in New York City, he went out to Wisconsin as a young man and on to California in 1860, settling at Nevada City where he mined first and then kept a grocery and hardware store. In 1870 he moved to San Francisco and took an appointment in the customs service, rising to chief adjuster of duties.

narrative_blocks.header: He ended as president of the brokerage
narrative_blocks.body: He resigned from the customs service in 1887 to join John H. Boden and Company, custom house brokers, and was its president when he retired in 1913. He died three years later at the San Francisco house of his son-in-law Wilson Sigourney, one of two brothers who had married his daughters.

people.research_notes: His obituary says the funeral was held with interment at San Francisco; FindAGrave records the burial at Mountain View Cemetery, Oakland, where his son Charles II was laid beside him. Entry follows Mountain View. The obituary also names a surviving sister, Mrs. James A. Owen of North Yakima, Washington, not built.

narrative_blocks.header: Her sister married her husband's brother
narrative_blocks.body: She married Thaddeus Wellington Sigourney of Nevada City; her younger sister Elizabeth married his brother Wilson. Thaddeus shot himself in a woodshed behind their Oakland house in August 1910, leaving her a widow at forty-six with four children.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the Arizona copper post at forty-eight
narrative_blocks.body: Leavitt was a mining engineer, born at Nevada City in the California gold country. In 1916 he took a post with the United Verde Extension at Jerome, Arizona, and his wife and three children followed him out.

narrative_blocks.header: He married an Edelen and had three
narrative_blocks.body: He married Elizabeth Hamilton Edelen in 1902. Their three children — Charles, Susan and Elizabeth — reached Jerome a fortnight before the end, and Susan married nine years after her father was gone.

narrative_blocks.header: Ill on Wednesday, dead by Thursday night
narrative_blocks.body: He was taken suddenly ill on the Wednesday afternoon, carried to the company hospital on the Thursday morning, and dead that night. The post-mortem gave intestinal ulceration. He was forty-nine.

narrative_blocks.header: The Masons carried him home to Oakland
narrative_blocks.body: The funeral was at Christ Church in Jerome under Masonic auspices, and the order took the body across to Oakland to the family plot beside his father. His widow and the children settled in Los Angeles.

narrative_blocks.header: Both sisters married Sigourney brothers
narrative_blocks.body: She married Wilson Hill Sigourney; her elder sister Anne had already married his brother Thaddeus. Their father's obituary names his daughters simply as Mrs. Annie L. Sigourney and Mrs. Wilson H. Sigourney, and he died in Wilson's San Francisco house.

narrative_blocks.header: Three generations pulled back to New Jersey
narrative_blocks.body: His great-grandparents James and Eliza left the Cory homestead in the Westfields of New Jersey for the newly opening country in Ohio. His father Lewis took a Columbia law degree in 1883 and married Carrie Martin out of those same Westfields. Benjamin was born in Fresno and named for his doctor grandfather, and he went back east himself, to Princeton and then Harvard Law.

narrative_blocks.header: His namesake was San Jose's first doctor
narrative_blocks.body: Dr. Benjamin Cory crossed the plains at twenty-five and reached San Jose on the first of December 1847, the first American-trained physician to settle there. The pueblo held six or eight hundred people - Ohlone, Californios, Mexicans, trappers and traders - and he got there before the gold was found the following summer.

narrative_blocks.header: Good government came out of the office
narrative_blocks.body: The doctor was elected first assemblyman for the San Jose district, from Monterey to Martinez, and sat on the committees for public buildings and education. The legislators met in his office before the State House was ready, and it was said afterwards that more good government came out of Doctor Cory's office than out of both houses and the City Hall together.

narrative_blocks.header: A weaver's Great Bible went down the line
narrative_blocks.body: The family traced to John Cory, born in England in 1611, a weaver who settled at Southold on Long Island; his 1685 will left his son an iron kettle, the Great Bible, and half his weaving tackle. Corys were among the first to buy town rights in the Westfields, and gave the Presbyterian church there seven elders and three ministers.

people.research_notes: Son of Lewis Cory (LL.B. Columbia 1883) and Carrie Martin of Westfield NJ; grandson and namesake of Dr. Benjamin Cory, whose parents James and Eliza Cory left the Westfields for Ohio. None of those four is built. No evidence yet that he practised law, so no bio_blurb has been written from the Harvard degree alone.

bio.bio_blurb: Army colonel; chief of transportation in Korea

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the railroads of South Korea
narrative_blocks.body: As chief transportation officer under the occupation he headed an organisation of sixty thousand people, rebuilding and running more than two thousand miles of railroad, the merchant marine, and the port of Pusan. He was a principal delegate to the first American-Soviet conference on Korea.

narrative_blocks.header: Saipan with the Marines, then Okinawa
narrative_blocks.body: Commissioned out of the reserve corps at UCLA and called up in 1940, he went to the Pacific as a logistics officer attached to the 4th Marine Division for Saipan, and served with the Army's XXIV Corps at Okinawa.

narrative_blocks.header: He came back for Bloody and Heartbreak
narrative_blocks.body: In the Korean War he was a staff officer with the 2nd Infantry Division through the fighting for Bloody Ridge and Heartbreak Ridge in 1952. He took the Legion of Merit three times, and the Bronze Star with it.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-seven years, and he outlived her
narrative_blocks.body: He kept the house at Burke from 1950 and retired to it in 1965 after commanding the Gulf Terminal Command at New Orleans, having taught at the NATO Defense College in Paris along the way. Elizabeth died in 1992 after fifty-seven years; he followed four years later at Whiteoaks.

narrative_blocks.header: The family took the shot for a car
narrative_blocks.body: He came home in the early hours of a Saturday in August 1910, went into the woodshed behind the house on Piedmont Avenue and shot himself under the right ear. The household heard it and thought it an automobile; he was not found until seven that evening, when his son-in-law went out to the shed. He had been worried about money since losing a Modoc County ranch.

narrative_blocks.header: He married one Leavitt, his brother the other
narrative_blocks.body: He and his brother Wilson Hill Sigourney married the two Leavitt sisters, Anne and Elizabeth, daughters of the Nevada City merchant Charles Carroll Leavitt. He had been fifteen years a salesman for the Winedale Company of Oakland before taking the liquor trade.

Cross (1844-1876). Neither parent is built - they are non-notable non-descendants and do not meet the easter-egg bar.

narrative_blocks.header: His father-in-law died in his house
narrative_blocks.body: He married Elizabeth Charlotte Leavitt, whose sister Anne had married his brother Thaddeus. Charles Carroll Leavitt spent his last years with them and died at their San Francisco home in November 1916.

education.school_name: Columbia University School of Social Work

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Her parents bought it in 1931; she died there in 2019.
Summered at the Maryland plantation her grandparents restored.

trained in social work at Columbia, then moved west in 1956

narrative_blocks.header: First in the state to test for HIV
narrative_blocks.body: The Community Family Planning Council was the first provider in New York State to offer prenatal care, professional social work and HIV testing to women of every income. She was its director of social work.

narrative_blocks.header: Nearly every Olympics from 1960 to 2004
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband worked for the United Nations and cared about track and field, so they went to almost every Summer Games from 1960 to 2004. They lived in Taiwan for two years and went out to South Africa, his country, every other year.

narrative_blocks.header: Jan van Heerden came up for tennis
narrative_blocks.body: Jan van Heerden was asked up to Clove Brook Farm for a tennis weekend to make a fourth. She was finishing her masters at Columbia. They married that February and had fifty-three years.

narrative_blocks.header: Sidwell Friends for the war years
narrative_blocks.body: She spent sixth through eighth grade at Sidwell Friends while her mother was working in Washington. She came back to New York for Brearley, then took a degree in zoology at Cornell.

narrative_blocks.header: Clove Brook Farm, and the view she saved
narrative_blocks.body: Her parents bought Clove Brook Farm the year before she was born, and she counted it home all her life. She and her husband put a permanent conservation easement on it in 2001, and she died there with her dog on her lap.

narrative_blocks.header: Named for the deaf girl next door
narrative_blocks.body: Her father called her after Alice Cogswell, the deaf daughter of his Hartford neighbour Dr. Mason Fitch Cogswell: the child he had tried and failed to teach, and whose case sent him across the Atlantic for a method. By the time this Alice was born in 1833 the school that grew out of that failure was sixteen years old.

narrative_blocks.header: Her death in 1891 remade the family firm
narrative_blocks.body: She died in August 1891, two months before her daughter Annie married Philip Howard. That loss, together with the failing health of her son-in-law John Wattles, was what moved her husband to press Howard into The Sunday School Times, where he became publisher in 1893 and president of the company after Trumbull's death.

people.research_notes: One of eight children of Rev. Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet and Sophia Fowler Gallaudet; all eight are now built. RESOLVED 072626: Elizabeth Reynolds Budd was the wife of Alice's brother Rev. Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet (HD8242), married 15 July 1845, not a second wife of Henry Clay Trumbull. She is built as I02690.

notable.notable_blurb: Army chaplain, editor, and author

cross_connections.display_label: travelled Egypt and Judea with him in 1881

narrative_blocks.header: He preferred one soul to a thousand
narrative_blocks.body: Converted at twenty-one by a friend's letter, he resolved that nobody within reach of his influence should go without being asked the question directly, and he kept to it for half a century. Near the end he judged that he could see more result from his work with individuals than from all his preaching to thousands or his writing for hundreds of thousands.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-eight years editing one weekly paper
narrative_blocks.body: He moved his family to Philadelphia in 1875 to edit The Sunday School Times and held the chair until he died in 1903. He wrote thirty-eight books alongside it and was elected to the American Philosophical Society in 1884.

narrative_blocks.header: He was taken prisoner at Fort Wagner
narrative_blocks.body: Ordained in 1862, he went out as chaplain of the 10th Connecticut and was captured outside Charleston on 19 July 1863, the day after the assault on Fort Wagner. He was moved through a succession of Confederate prisons until his exchange that November, then rejoined the regiment and stayed with it until it mustered out in 1865.

narrative_blocks.header: His schooling stopped at fourteen
narrative_blocks.body: Poor health ended his formal education at fourteen and he never went to a college. Yale, Lafayette and New York University each gave him an honorary degree in the end, and Yale had him deliver the Beecher lectures in 1888.

narrative_blocks.header: He went to Egypt and found Kadesh Barnea
narrative_blocks.body: In 1881 he travelled through Egypt and Judea to see the biblical sites himself and identified what he took to be Kadesh Barnea, where the Israelites camped before entering Canaan. His companion on the journey was the Rev. Allen Dulles, whose sons would later run the State Department and the CIA.

narrative_blocks.header: He called friendship the master passion
narrative_blocks.body: His book of 1891 argued that friendship consists in being a friend rather than in having one, in giving affection unselfishly and without requiring its return. His son-in-law wrote that he was never a pastor but was constantly doing a shepherd's work, out on winter nights in the driving snow with his chaplain's hat pulled down over his eyes.

burial.plot_notes: Bronx, New York, 1941. Funeral at Chambers-Wylie Memorial Presbyterian Church, Philadelphia, 22 January 1941.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept his father's chair even longer
narrative_blocks.body: He edited The Sunday School Times from his father's death in 1903 until 1941, a decade longer than his father had. In 1907 he put the older man's method into a textbook of his own, Taking Men Alive, and wrote the introduction to the biography his brother-in-law Philip Howard made of him.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded a church that preached in signs
narrative_blocks.body: He was teaching at the New York Institution for the Deaf when he took orders, ordained deacon in 1850 and priest the year after. In October 1852 he founded St. Ann's Church for Deaf-Mutes, and by 1859 it had a church and rectory of its own on 18th Street near Fifth Avenue. One of his students there, Henry Winter Syle, became the first deaf man the Episcopal Church ordained, and the two are commemorated together on August 27, the day Gallaudet died.

narrative_blocks.header: He married into the world he served
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth Reynolds Budd, whom he married in July 1845, was deaf. She was a daughter of Dr. Bern W. Budd of New York, and they gave one of their sons his name.

narrative_blocks.header: Four cities copied St. Ann's
narrative_blocks.body: The Church Mission to Deaf-Mutes was incorporated in 1872 with him as its general manager, and churches on the St. Ann's model followed at Philadelphia, Baltimore, Albany and Boston. He was called the pioneer of church work among the deaf in this country.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded a home on the Hudson
narrative_blocks.body: In 1886 he opened the Gallaudet Home for Deaf-Mutes on a farm between New Hamburgh and Poughkeepsie, meant for the aged and the infirm among them. He had begun it in 1872 in a rented brownstone on East 13th Street, on the conviction that the old deaf were being left isolated in ordinary nursing homes among staff who could not talk to them. Its residents called themselves the Family, and were taken in without regard to religion.

narrative_blocks.header: He went to Milan and Brussels for it
narrative_blocks.body: He attended every convention of teachers of the deaf held in this country, and crossed for the congresses at Milan in 1880 and Brussels in 1883. In the summer of 1886 he went the other way, to California, on the same errand.

narrative_blocks.header: They died eight months apart, same address
narrative_blocks.body: He died at 112 West 78th Street in New York in August 1902, eighty years and not quite three months old, and was carried back to Hartford for burial. His wife died at that same address eight months later, and was buried beside him.

people.research_notes:
Per family genealogy transcript. Trinity College, Hartford, 1842. Taught at the New York Institution for Deaf Mutes 1843-1858; ordained deacon June 1850, priest 1851, Protestant Episcopal Church. Founded St. Ann's Church for Deaf-Mutes Oct 1852; church and rectory on 18th Street near Fifth Avenue secured 1859. Accepted the pastorate of the Sisterhood of the Good Shepherd Apr 1869 and the chaplaincy of the Midnight Mission Nov 1871 - both real posts, omitted from the NBs only for space. Church Mission to Deaf-Mutes incorporated Oct 1872, he general manager. Attended all US conventions of teachers of the deaf; Milan Sept 1880; Brussels 1883; California summer 1886. Founded the Gallaudet Home for Deaf-Mutes 1886, a farm on the Hudson between New Hamburgh and Poughkeepsie. Died 27 Aug 1902 at 112 West 78th Street NYC, aged 80y 2m 24d; buried Hartford.
FAMILY PATTERN worth an NB if Sam wants a seventh: his father founded the American School for the Deaf at Hartford, he founded the first church for the deaf, and his brother Edward Miner Gallaudet (HD8248) founded the college at Washington in 1864 - school, church and college across two generations.
NOT NOTABLE YET: he is a direct Thomas descendant and a plausible is_notable candidate, but that needs a primary_url and Sam's approval, so the flag is left false.
SOURCE ASTERISK: the transcript's two asterisk footnotes are page-bottom notes that OCR pulled inline at the wrong anchors - the Gallaudet College note has nothing to do with the Midnight Mission sentence it follows.
Married John Cumming Hunter 19 January 1854; widowed 1858; no children. Death 19 January 1865 per FamilySearch, 20 January 1865 per the family genealogy.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded the first college for deaf people
narrative_blocks.body: Congress let the Columbia Institution grant degrees in 1864 and Lincoln signed the bill: the first college in the world for deaf students. Grant signed the first three diplomas in 1869, and every Gallaudet diploma since has carried a sitting president's signature.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty years old, and handed a school
narrative_blocks.body: Amos Kendall gave two acres of his Washington ground in 1856 for a school for deaf and blind children and asked Gallaudet, not yet twenty, to come and run it. He went, and took his deaf mother with him to be its matron; he stayed fifty-three years.

narrative_blocks.header: Milan voted to ban signing in 1880
narrative_blocks.body: The international congress at Milan resolved that sign language be banned and speech alone used. He spent the rest of his career against that verdict, arguing it out with Alexander Graham Bell.

narrative_blocks.header: He quit the bank for its narrowing effect
narrative_blocks.body: His father died when he was fourteen and he went into a Hartford bank for three years. He left it because of what he called the narrowing effect of the work, and went to teach at the school his father had founded, taking a Trinity degree while he taught.

narrative_blocks.header: The board named his three unending fights
narrative_blocks.body: When he retired in 1910 a member of his board set down the three problems he had carried for half a century: the educational, the financial, and the social life of the place. The financial, he wrote, took Gallaudet's life's own blood.

narrative_blocks.header: The college carries his father's name, not his
narrative_blocks.body: In 1894 the college he had built was renamed Gallaudet after his father, though it was his own fifty-three years that made it. A bronze of him by Pietro Lazzari stands on the campus.

quotes.text: Deafness, though it be total and congenital, imposes no limits on the intellectual development of its subjects, save in the single direction of the appreciation of acoustic phenomena.

people.research_notes: From the family genealogy: educated Trinity College; began teaching 1856 at his father's institution in Hartford; went to Washington in 1857 at Amos Kendall's invitation accompanied by his mother, who helped organise the Columbia Institution. Visited the principal European institutions for the deaf in 1867 and published an elaborate report of his observations in 1868. Trinity LL.D. and Columbia Ph.D. both 1869. In 1881 he succeeded James A. Garfield as president of the Literary Society at Washington. President of the Convention of American Instructors of Deaf-mutes, Jacksonville, Illinois, 1883. In 1886 he went to England at the request of the British government to inform the Royal Commission on the education of the blind and deaf. The genealogy's death date of 23 Nov 1866 for him is a transcription error; he died 26 September 1917. It gives Jane Melissa Fessenden's birth as 19 October 1837 against FamilySearch's 16 October, and names her parents Edson and Lydia W. Fessenden.

narrative_blocks.header: In 1897 he edited Gray's Anatomy
narrative_blocks.body: He published his own Surgery Quiz Compends in 1892, and five years later took on the editorship of Gray's Anatomy, the standard anatomy of the English-speaking world. He had trained for that work at the College of Physicians and Surgeons and then in the hospitals of Vienna and Berlin.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-seven years teaching anatomy at one school
narrative_blocks.body: He arrived at the College of Physicians and Surgeons in 1887 as an assistant demonstrator of anatomy and was still on its faculty, by then associate professor, when he died in 1934. Alongside it he was a visiting surgeon at Bellevue from 1890 to 1909 and its consulting surgeon for the twenty-five years after.

narrative_blocks.header: Anatomists still say Gallaudet's fascia
narrative_blocks.body: The superficial investing fascia of the perineum is known as Gallaudet's fascia, named for him the way Denonvilliers' and Luschka's fasciae were named for the men who described them. It is the memorial an anatomist gets: a layer of the body that keeps the name in the textbooks.

bio.bio_blurb: British Army major-general; director of remounts

marriages.notes: Circa 1905 per source.

narrative_blocks.header: The whole army's horses were his problem
narrative_blocks.body: Appointed director of remounts at the War Office in September 1912, he held the post through the whole of the First World War and on to 1920, responsible for finding, buying and moving the horses the British Army still ran on. He had learned the trade in South Africa as an assistant inspector of remounts, where Kitchener described him in a despatch as perturbed by nothing.

narrative_blocks.header: His Staff College class produced Haig and Allenby
narrative_blocks.body: The 1896-97 class he entered at Camberley was the famous one, holding Douglas Haig and Edmund Allenby among a cohort that would command in South Africa and then in France. He came to it out of India, where he had served as a signalling officer on the Hazara and Chin Lushai expeditions.

narrative_blocks.header: The Japanese Army took to him immediately
narrative_blocks.body: In 1905 he spent a year attached to the Imperial Japanese Army in Manchuria. His obituarist put the success of the posting down to his immense size and genial nature, which made an excellent impression on the Allies and led them to hand him a great deal of valuable information for his reports.

narrative_blocks.header: He was broken by a fall in 1915
narrative_blocks.body: In 1915, in the middle of the work of supplying the army with horses, he was thrown from one and injured, and never fully recovered. He died fourteen years later after another fall, out walking at Saint-Briac on the Brittany coast.

burial.plot_notes: Collective grave 8.E.4. Royal Tank Regiment, R.A.C., service number 34569.

narrative_blocks.header: He took a tank regiment into North Africa
narrative_blocks.body: Commissioned into the Royal Tank Corps in February 1926, he served with armoured cars on the North-West Frontier until 1933, took an interpreter's course in Italy, and went on to staff duties in Egypt. He passed into the Staff College at Camberley in 1939 and in 1942 went to North Africa in command of a tank regiment, where he was killed on 23 April 1943, aged thirty-seven. He was mentioned in despatches.

narrative_blocks.header: He took a Kenyan battalion into Burma
narrative_blocks.body: He first saw action against the Italians in Somaliland, then in the autumn of 1944 commanded the 11th (Kenya) Battalion of the King's African Rifles through the Burma campaign. He came out of the war with a Distinguished Service Order.

narrative_blocks.header: Palestine, then Kenya, then the Territorials
narrative_blocks.body: In 1947 he commanded the 3rd Battalion of the Parachute Regiment in Palestine during the Emergency, and in August 1955 took the 70th East African Infantry Brigade through the Mau Mau uprising. He finished as Director-General of the Territorial Army and retired in 1966.

narrative_blocks.header: Father and son both reached major-general
narrative_blocks.body: His father Sir William Birkbeck was a major-general and the army's director of remounts through the First World War, and the son reached the same rank in the second half of the century. His elder brother Alexander, a lieutenant-colonel, was killed in Tunisia in 1943 and lies in the war cemetery at Medjez-el-Bab.

narrative_blocks.body: He was president of the Kips Bay Boys and Girls Club in New York from 1969 to 1981 and an honorary trustee afterwards. In 1998 the national organisation gave him an award for thirty-two years of it.

narrative_blocks.header: Paris first, then the analyst's desk
narrative_blocks.body: He served with the State Department at the American embassy in Paris before coming home to Wall Street, where he became a securities analyst and a partner at H.C. Wainwright. Harvard had come first, in 1950, after the Navy.

narrative_blocks.header: Crosswords, the piano, and the galleries
narrative_blocks.body: He was remembered for gentleness, a keen mind and a sense of humour, and for the crossword puzzles, fiction, piano playing and museum visits he shared with his family. He grew up at Southborough, where his grandfather had been headmaster of St. Mark's.

narrative_blocks.body: At the 1934 International Exhibition of Fine and Applied Arts by Deaf Artists, held at the Roerich Museum in New York, he refused a place in the North American section and was entered instead in the foreign one, which Paris had organised. His caricatures were the success of it, among them President Roosevelt, the exiled King Alfonso of Spain, and Mayor Fiorello La Guardia.

narrative_blocks.body: He was born in Puerto Rico and lost his hearing at seven to spinal meningitis, and learned to draw under Fernando Diaz Mackenna. He came to New York in 1927, worked as art director for the Spanish-language press, sold cartoons to the New York Times and the Saturday Evening Post, and placed high in chess tournaments on the side.

narrative_blocks.header: His father arrested his mother as a spy
narrative_blocks.body: Union major Joseph Clapp Willard took Antonia Ford of Fairfax into custody as a Confederate spy and sent her to the Old Capitol Prison, then fell in love with her while she was held and lobbied to get her out. He left the army and divorced his wife, she swore allegiance to the United States, and they married; of their three children only this one lived past infancy. She died on Valentine's Day 1871 of an illness she had contracted in the prison, days after her last child was born, and he never remarried.

narrative_blocks.header: Wilson sent him to Spain and he stayed
narrative_blocks.body: Appointed to Madrid in 1913, the first American ambassador there since the war with Spain, he presented his credentials that October and kept the post until July 1921, through administrations of both parties. He was on holiday in the United States when the world war broke out and sailed back aboard the USS Tennessee, leaving his daughter Belle behind with typhoid.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave Fairfax its town hall in 1900
narrative_blocks.body: Eight years in the Virginia House of Delegates and four as lieutenant governor were bracketed by service in the war with Spain as a captain of Virginia volunteers and by four years on the state corporation commission. His inheritance and his investments made him the wealthiest man in Virginia, and he built the colonnaded town office building at Fairfax and handed it over as a gift.

narrative_blocks.header: A shopping mall covers Layton Hall now
narrative_blocks.body: He lived on a Fairfax estate called Layton Hall. Part of its ground went to the county in 1954 for the school named after his widow, and in 1972 the rest was sold for development; a mall covers most of the ten acres.

narrative_blocks.header: He inherited the hotel that Washington ran on
narrative_blocks.body: His father and his uncle Henry had turned the old City Hotel on Pennsylvania Avenue into Willard's, two blocks from the White House and the room where the capital did much of its business. He took it over when his father died in 1897, and it is still called the residence of presidents.

narrative_blocks.header: Her last wish became a school
narrative_blocks.body: She asked that land from her estate be given for a school for children with disabilities. Her daughter carried it out within three years of her death, and Fairfax County put her name on the building: the first school the county ever built for special education.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the life of his father-in-law
narrative_blocks.body: He married Annie Trumbull in 1891, the year he left the University of Pennsylvania and joined The Sunday School Times, and fourteen years later published The Life Story of Henry Clay Trumbull, with an introduction by his brother-in-law Charles. He wrote fourteen books in all, most of them on church and mission work.

narrative_blocks.header: He came for a year and stayed fifty-five
narrative_blocks.body: Trumbull pressed him into the paper as a call from God, after his mother-in-law's death and John Wattles's collapse left it without a business head; he became publisher and then, on Trumbull's death in 1903, president of the company. He sat on the council of the China Inland Mission, was a trustee of the Belgian Gospel Mission, and took an honorary doctorate from Houghton College in 1937.

narrative_blocks.header: He signed his column a Philadelphia lawyer
narrative_blocks.body: His First Aid Law column ran daily on the editorial page of the Philadelphia Bulletin over the signature by a Philadelphia lawyer. Only a few editors and intimates knew who wrote it, and hundreds of readers wrote in to ask.

narrative_blocks.header: A dozen books, and four languages after
narrative_blocks.body: He wrote Wild Folk, Man and Beast, Lords of the Wild, Wild Honey and a life of Lincoln for children, mostly about animals and mostly for the young. They were translated into German, Norwegian, Hungarian and Finnish.

narrative_blocks.header: He walked with egg collectors, taking nothing
narrative_blocks.body: An associate of the American Ornithologists' Union from 1916, he published in The Auk and went out with oologists who emptied whole nests. Boxes of blown eggs left him cold, he wrote; he kept the days in the wilderness instead.

narrative_blocks.header: A burglar shot him at home in 1897
narrative_blocks.body: On 23 April 1897, living with his father at Stamford, Scoville was shot by a burglar in the house. He survived it.

narrative_blocks.header: Three bars, and the Supreme Court last
narrative_blocks.body: He took his Yale degree in 1893 and a law degree two years after, went to the New York bar in 1895, the Philadelphia bar in 1903 and the United States Supreme Court in 1910. The New York firm was Beecher & Scoville.

narrative_blocks.header: A cabin called Faraway in the Barrens
narrative_blocks.body: He kept a house at Cornwall in Connecticut, a peninsula on the coast of Maine, and a cabin in the New Jersey Pine Barrens that he called Faraway. He sat on the council of the Boy Scouts of America.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandfather was Henry Ward Beecher
narrative_blocks.body: His mother Harriet Eliza was the preacher's only surviving daughter, and his father the Rev. Samuel Scoville had held a Brooklyn pulpit of Beecher's. Two of his own sons were christened for the grandfather.

narrative_blocks.header: Committed to an asylum in 1943
narrative_blocks.body: Nine years into her marriage, in 1943, Emily was committed with schizophrenia and put through cold baths, fever lamps and electric shock. She was held in at least one of the asylums where her husband was performing lobotomies.

narrative_blocks.header: After the divorce, an apartment in New York
narrative_blocks.body: After the divorce Emily lived in a sleek modern apartment in New York, and came to a Sotheby's sale of American paintings to buy a watercolor. Her grandson Luke came to suspect she had been lobotomized; a niece who took tea with her there thought her hardly incapacitated.

narrative_blocks.header: She was married in Dorothy Cheney's garden
narrative_blocks.body: She married William Beecher Scoville on the last day of June 1934, in the garden of her aunt Dorothy Cheney's house at South Manchester. Warren Archibald came out from the South Congregational Church to perform it, and the bridegroom's sister Alice was maid of honour.

narrative_blocks.header: The Barrett name went to her eldest son
narrative_blocks.body: Her father was Henry Barrett Learned of South Manchester, and Barrett is the name she gave her first boy. He became Dr. Barrett Scoville, and was killed when his plane went down at Great Barrington in 1991.

narrative_blocks.header: She lived a hundred and one years
narrative_blocks.body: Born in Connecticut in 1908, she died at Cambridge in Massachusetts in 2010. She outlived her husband by twenty-six years and her eldest son by nineteen. Her grandchildren called her Bambam.

narrative_blocks.header: His sister argued the trial out with him
narrative_blocks.body: Alice sent him her research on their great-grandfather's adultery trial and he wrote back; the letters are in her papers at Yale. He was a Congregational minister, as Beecher had been, and as their grandfather Samuel Scoville had been before them.

people.research_notes: Given as Gordon in the family genealogy; Gurdon in FamilySearch, which matches the Trumbull family name and is used here.

narrative_blocks.header: He removed both hippocampi on a hunch
narrative_blocks.body: In 1953 Scoville offered Henry Molaison an experimental resection for epilepsy and, guessing the hippocampus was the seat of it, took out both. The seizures barely improved and Molaison could form no new memory again; Scoville called it a tragic mistake.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Henrys, and two bicycles
narrative_blocks.body: Molaison's seizures began after a bicycle knocked him down at eight. Scoville had lost his own younger brother Henry to a bicycle accident while he was away at college.

narrative_blocks.header: The mistake founded the science of memory
narrative_blocks.body: Penfield sent Brenda Milner from Montreal to study the case, and she found Molaison had lost the making of new memories while keeping the old ones and his skills. Scoville and Milner published him in 1957.

narrative_blocks.header: Wild Bill outran the troopers to work
narrative_blocks.body: He fled state police while speeding to the hospital, ruptured his spleen attempting a wheelie, and supervised his own disc operation through a rig of mirrors. Enzo Ferrari would not sell him a car, saying he would be dead within the year.

narrative_blocks.header: Three S's: simplification, speed and sterility
narrative_blocks.body: He founded Hartford Hospital's neurosurgery department in 1939 and led it twenty-nine years, opened Connecticut's first residency in the field and trained sixty-three surgeons. A retractor, a trephine and an aneurysm clip still carry his name.

narrative_blocks.header: One letter to seventeen societies
narrative_blocks.body: In 1955 he wrote to seventeen neurosurgical societies urging a congress that would seat every country, and the World Federation of Neurosurgical Societies grew out of it. Paul Bucy thought it his greatest work.

narrative_blocks.header: He operated on madness for his wife's sake
narrative_blocks.body: His wife Emily was committed with schizophrenia in 1943 and put through cold baths, fever lamps and electric shock. He performed more than six hundred lobotomies, and wrote to his son that twenty years of operating on mental illness had been for her sake.

narrative_blocks.header: She worked the Beecher trial for decades
narrative_blocks.body: Beecher's great-granddaughter spent years on the 1875 adultery trial, sifting the evidence and drafting a book about it. Her papers at Yale hold the research notes, her own verdict on him, and the letters in which she argued it out with her brother Gurdon.

narrative_blocks.header: She published under her married name
narrative_blocks.body: The Yale finding aid lists the work under Alice Scoville Barry. The same collection carries the Gallaudet papers on deaf education and the Trumbull family letters that came down the other sides of her family.

narrative_blocks.header: She was born the year her grandmother died
narrative_blocks.body: Harriet Eliza Beecher Scoville, the preacher's daughter, died in 1911, the year Alice was born. Alice lived to 2012 and a hundred and one, carrying the family's memory of the trial into the twenty-first century.

narrative_blocks.header: He regulated the drugs his father cut for
narrative_blocks.body: At the Food and Drug Administration he headed the division for neuropharmacological drug products and became an expert on epilepsy — the disease his father had operated on H.M. for in 1953. He taught psychiatry at Johns Hopkins from 1972.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote in defence of the slow way
narrative_blocks.body: Answering a pessimist in print, he held that toxicity testing and controlled trials are worth having before a compound goes out across the country. The agency had at times been unnecessarily rigid, he allowed, but it had helped bring orphan drugs like L-dopa and nitroprusside to market.

narrative_blocks.header: A captain at the 93rd Evacuation Hospital
narrative_blocks.body: He served in the Medical Corps in Vietnam from January 1967 to January 1969. He came home to nine years with the FDA and the National Institutes of Health, and in 1982 to Otsuka's office in Frankfurt.

narrative_blocks.header: A slalom champion who crossed the Atlantic alone
narrative_blocks.body: He had been Connecticut slalom skiing champion, and the achievement he was proudest of was a solo round-trip flight across the Atlantic in his Comanche.

narrative_blocks.header: His plane went down on takeoff
narrative_blocks.body: He had been visiting friends in the Berkshires when his single-engine plane crashed taking off from Great Barrington on 7 April 1991. He was fifty-five, and they held the service for him at Cornubia Hall in Cornwall.

narrative_blocks.header: Three Scoville households at the service
narrative_blocks.body: He left his mother Emily in New York, a sister at Cambridge and a brother out in Washington state, and his father's second family at Farmington — a stepbrother carrying his father's name, a stepsister, a stepmother. The memorial gifts went to the William Beecher Scoville Foundation.

narrative_blocks.header: She answered her son's book deal: “Oh, no”
narrative_blocks.body: Lisa knew her son Luke would be treading on the darkest parts of the family's history. When he called to say he had a book deal to write about his grandfather's most famous patient, her first words were “Oh, no.”

narrative_blocks.header: He named a later son for her father
narrative_blocks.body: She was a daughter of Edson Fessenden of Hartford, and married Edward Miner Gallaudet in 1858 at twenty. The son her husband had by his second wife was given her father's name: Edson Fessenden Gallaudet, who grew up to experiment with wing warping and build the first aircraft factory in America.

narrative_blocks.header: She buried her baby and died months later
narrative_blocks.body: Edward LeBaron, her third child, died in July 1865 at eight months old, and she died the following March at twenty-eight, leaving Katharine at four and Grace at two. Her own burial at Cedar Hill did not follow until November, eight months after the funeral at the Centre church.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed six months after the wedding
narrative_blocks.body: She married Francis Lockwood Kendall in May 1893 and he was dead by November of the same year. She waited fourteen years before marrying William Baxter Closson in 1907, and had no children by either man.

narrative_blocks.header: She christened a battleship and met her husband
narrative_blocks.body: In December 1901 she stood sponsor for the battleship Missouri, named for the state her father represented in the Senate, and Edson Gallaudet was among the guests. The Times called their engagement, announced a year later, the romance of the christening; they married at the Church of the Covenant in February 1903 with the President in a pew to the left of the sanctuary.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept her father's house from eighteen
narrative_blocks.body: Her Washington coming-out in the first days of 1894 was the occasion at which her mother took the cold that killed her within the week. She was eighteen, and from then until she married at twenty-seven she ran her father's household in Washington and in Missouri and was a recognised hostess of the Senate circle.

narrative_blocks.header: She strapped her skirts down to fly
narrative_blocks.body: By her family's account she held a pilot's licence of her own and was among the first women in the country to fly. She told afterwards of strapping her skirts down before going up, women not wearing trousers for any reason at all in 1910.

people.research_notes: Birth 23 August 1875 per FamilySearch; the Gallaudet family genealogy gives 3 August 1875, which is her death day and may be a transposition. Daughter of Gen. Francis Marion Cockrell and Anna Ewing.

Attorney. Died 8 June 1947 in New York, the same night as his wife Amelie Edgerton Marshall - he took his own life at their apartment and she followed within minutes. The press notice gives their ages as 36 and 32, which does not agree with the birth years on either grave.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale told him to drop the flying
narrative_blocks.body: As a Yale physics instructor he built and flew a large warping-wing glider model several years before the Wright brothers perfected that method of control; the kite he made in 1898 to test it is in the National Air and Space Museum. His superiors held that so questionable a field cast aspersions on the faculty, and he did not come back to aviation until 1910.

narrative_blocks.header: He put the propeller in the middle
narrative_blocks.body: His patented drive hung a four-bladed propeller on a ring amidships between wing and tail, leaving the crew the clear nose. The Navy bought the D-1 seaplane built around it in 1915, although his had been the highest of the fourteen bids.

narrative_blocks.header: He built America's first aircraft factory
narrative_blocks.body: The second of Edward Miner Gallaudet's children by his second marriage founded what is reckoned the first aircraft factory in America. His name came from Edson Fessenden of Hartford, the father of his father's first wife.

narrative_blocks.header: A hundred feet down at Hempstead Plains
narrative_blocks.body: In July 1912 his Bullet monoplane made an acute turn a hundred feet up, lost its momentum and buried its nose in the ground. He came out of it with a scalp wound, a cut chin and eye and a severed artery in his leg; it ended his flying and not one bit of his designing.

narrative_blocks.header: He took a pilot's licence in two countries
narrative_blocks.body: He qualified with the Aero Club of America on a Wright biplane at Garden City and took a French brevet on a Nieuport monoplane, both in 1911. He had come from electrical engineering: a Johns Hopkins doctorate, Westinghouse at Pittsburgh, and three years teaching physics at Yale.

narrative_blocks.header: The engineering firm became an aircraft works
narrative_blocks.body: He organised the Gallaudet Engineering Company at Norwich in 1908, and by 1917 it was the Gallaudet Aircraft Corporation, building at Norwich and East Greenwich in Rhode Island.

narrative_blocks.header: The year Yale had him coaching its crew
narrative_blocks.body: In 1899, while his superiors were pressing him to drop the glider work, he was head coach of the Yale crew. Alfred Cowles Jr., who had captained the champion boat of 1886, came back that year as his chief adviser.

On 18 September, a fortnight after Britain had declared war again, he inscribed a copy to his sister's four children, Amelie, John, Marion and Cruger Edgerton. Cruger was lost over Tokyo six years later.

narrative_blocks.header: Lost over Tokyo on the worst night
narrative_blocks.body: He lifted off from Tinian on the evening of 25 May 1945 to bomb the districts south of the Imperial Palace. Twenty-six Superfortresses went down that night, the heaviest single-day loss of B-29s of the war, and his was one of them; he and his whole crew were lost off the coast of Urayasu.

narrative_blocks.header: Five sports at Kent, then the Air Corps
narrative_blocks.body: He came to Kent in September 1932 out of Pine Orchard and played football, hockey, basketball, baseball and crew across five years. He was appointed an aviation cadet in 1941 while still an undergraduate, and had twenty-two missions out of the Marianas behind him before the last one.

narrative_blocks.header: The Branford marker is only a marker
narrative_blocks.body: Two of his crew stayed in the wreck and one body came ashore; no search was made at the time. The remains were recovered after the war and the whole crew buried together at Jefferson Barracks in Missouri, so the stone at Branford Center stands over nobody. He was promoted major after his death.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty Senate years, and no election before them
narrative_blocks.body: The Missouri legislature sent him to Washington in 1874 and he stayed five terms, chairing Claims, Engrossed Bills and finally Appropriations. It was the first elective office he ever held, and at the 1904 convention forty-two delegates voted to make him president.

narrative_blocks.header: He counted the cartridges off the dead
narrative_blocks.body: At Baker's Creek in May 1863 his Missouri brigade fired away the forty rounds in their boxes, then took what they could from their own fallen and stripped the enemy dead of cartridges, some men firing ninety rounds before the ammunition gave out. He lost six hundred of them that day, and wrote the report himself because his division commander was dead.

narrative_blocks.header: Wounded twice, captured at the very end
narrative_blocks.body: A shell took him in the hand during the siege of Vicksburg and he was hit again at Franklin in November 1864. He was commanding a division in the defence of Fort Blakeley in Alabama when it fell on 9 April 1865, the day Lee surrendered, and was paroled five weeks later.

narrative_blocks.header: Roosevelt came to his daughter's wedding
narrative_blocks.body: When Marion married Edson Gallaudet at the Church of the Covenant in February 1903 the President came, sat to the left of the sanctuary and went out directly behind the bridal party. At the breakfast he proposed the health of the bride's father, calling him a man he had admired since boyhood.

narrative_blocks.header: He commanded the Continental Army and mostly lost
narrative_blocks.body: Congress made him commander-in-chief in June 1775 and he held the Continental Army together for eight years, through Long Island, Brandywine and the Valley Forge winter. He understood he did not have to beat the British army, only avoid being destroyed by it.

narrative_blocks.header: He handed back his commission, then the presidency
narrative_blocks.body: In December 1783 he handed his commission to Congress at Annapolis and went home, and in 1796 he declined a third term and went home again. Both refusals became precedents the republic has kept.

narrative_blocks.header: He built America's first spy ring
narrative_blocks.body: In 1778 he set Major Benjamin Tallmadge to raise a network inside British-held New York, and the Culper Ring fed him intelligence for the rest of the war. It was the ring that saved a French force from a surprise British attack.

narrative_blocks.header: He freed his slaves only at the end
narrative_blocks.body: More than five hundred enslaved people lived and worked at Mount Vernon across his lifetime, and he stayed dependent on their labour to the last. He came slowly to oppose the institution and provided in his will for the emancipation of those he owned outright, which Martha carried out a year after his death.

narrative_blocks.body: Davenport gave him a Pioneer Day, with the school and every business shut for the afternoon, dinner in the public library, and the Methodist choir his wife had directed for years singing his favourite hymn. It ended with a parade of the children he had delivered.

narrative_blocks.body: He spent two years at the University of Nebraska as a member of the first class to enrol there, then took his medical degree at Jefferson in Philadelphia. His father had been a doctor in the Civil War before him.

narrative_blocks.header: Printer, then Speaker, then Chief Justice
narrative_blocks.body: He learned the printer's trade before he read law in Thomas Blair's office, and was admitted to the Pennsylvania bar in 1829. He was Speaker of the state House at twenty-eight, a congressman at thirty-eight, and Chief Justice of the Pennsylvania Supreme Court from 1866 to 1872.

narrative_blocks.header: He chaired the first party caucus in Congress
narrative_blocks.body: In the Thirty-first Congress he became the first recorded chairman of the House Democratic caucus, and the first official chairman of any party caucus in either chamber. He chaired the Judiciary Committee in the same term, and had sat in the Thirtieth alongside Abraham Lincoln.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife's brother followed him as Speaker
narrative_blocks.body: In 1828 Thompson married Mary Parker Snowden, five years his elder. Her younger brother, James Ross Snowden, also sat in the Pennsylvania House for Venango County, and was elected Speaker in 1842, seven years after Thompson held the chair.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother-in-law kept his court's records
narrative_blocks.body: In 1861 James Ross Snowden, just out as Director of the Mint, became prothonotary of the Pennsylvania Supreme Court, its chief clerk, while Thompson sat on its bench. Five years later Thompson became the court's Chief Justice.

narrative_blocks.header: An electoral vote for Van Buren, 1836
narrative_blocks.body: In 1836 Thompson was one of Pennsylvania's presidential electors and cast his vote for Martin Van Buren. The next year he sat in the state constitutional convention, and in 1838, at thirty-one, he became a district judge.

narrative_blocks.header: He refused promotion to stay with his men
narrative_blocks.body: Commended at Fredericksburg and appointed acting adjutant on the field, he declined to take the place permanently, preferring to remain with the men he had induced to enlist. He was in the Round House at Pittsburg in 1877 when the troops were driven out by the flames, and in personal command at Homestead in 1892.

people.research_notes: Major-General commanding the National Guard of Pennsylvania. Enlisted as a private in August 1862, mustered in as first sergeant of Company I, 142nd Pennsylvania Volunteers, a company he helped raise in Venango County; elected first lieutenant within weeks and promoted captain that autumn. Served with the 1st and 5th Corps at Fredericksburg, Chancellorsville and Gettysburg; commended at Fredericksburg and appointed acting adjutant on the field, which he declined in order to stay with the men he had enlisted. Afterwards captain of an infantry company, major and judge advocate on Gen. Hiudekoper's staff, and colonel of the Third Infantry, in which capacity he took part in the Pittsburg riots of 1877 and was in the Round House from which the troops were driven by the flames; his command drove the rioters from a Pittsburg battery they had seized. Brigadier-General commanding the First Brigade under Gov. Hartranft, recommissioned by Gov. Hoyt; on the death of Maj.-Gen. John F. Hartranft in 1889 given command of the National Guard and promoted major-general, in personal command at Homestead in 1892; reappointed July 1895. Studied law under C. Heydrick and admitted to the bar 30 April 1863. Assistant appraiser at Philadelphia from October 1885 under Cleveland; chief clerk of the United States Mint at Philadelphia from March 1894 under superintendent Dr. Eugene Townsend. He wrote the account of his great-grandfather Rev. Nathaniel Randolph Snowden in A Century of Pastors.

narrative_blocks.body: He bought Milton Point at Rye in 1864 and died seven years later. His son Col. J. Mayhew Wainwright, later Assistant Secretary of War and a four-term congressman, raised Wainwright House on the ground.

narrative_blocks.body: Martha Wainwright had been writing in secret and would not admit to it. The first thing she finished was The Lexie Song, a message to the new half-sister she had just acquired, and she kept it to herself for a while before playing it in public.

narrative_blocks.body: She is the one of the four children who did not go into music. She describes herself as a writer, a teacher and a reluctant scion of an American folk dynasty, who spends her days staving off existential dread by transmitting her vast knowledge of fractions to mostly-willing fourth graders.

people.research_notes: Only child of Loudon Wainwright III and Ritamarie Kelly, and the one of his four children who did not become a musician. BIRTH YEAR CONFLICT: Wikipedia says 1993; a Vanity Fair profile says Ritamarie Kelly gave birth to her in 1992; a 2017 radio interview calls her twenty-four. 1993 is kept and 1992 flagged. Her father deliberately stayed away for her first twelve months lest he grow attached, having seen her once at three weeks old, and wrote the song A Year about it - I touched your tiny perfect hand before I went uptown, I didn't pick you up because I'd have to put you down. Her half-sister Martha's very first song, written before she would admit to writing songs at all, was The Lexie Song, a message to the new baby. Her half-sister Lucy, about twelve, insisted on meeting her and went with their father to the apartment on the Upper West Side. In her own words she is a writer, teacher and reluctant scion of an American folk dynasty, published in Back of House, Rookie and the Claremont Colleges paper, known in her youth for drinking and for trying and failing to punch holes in walls, and now spending her days staving off existential dread by attempting to transmit her vast knowledge of fractions to mostly-willing fourth graders.

narrative_blocks.header: He was a poet for ten years first
narrative_blocks.body: Four books of poems and two novels came before a single record. He did not start a music career until he was thirty-two, and only then because the books were not selling and he was tired of the Montreal garment trade. Judy Collins recorded Suzanne that same year and made his name for him.

narrative_blocks.header: Hallelujah took twenty years to land
narrative_blocks.body: It came out on Various Positions in 1984, an album his American label declined to release, and did very little. A John Cale cover in 1991 gave Jeff Buckley the version everyone knows, and roughly two hundred artists have recorded it since. He spent years struggling with the words.

narrative_blocks.header: Ordained a Zen monk, still a Jew
narrative_blocks.body: He spent five years in seclusion at Mount Baldy from 1994 and was ordained a Rinzai monk in 1996 under the name Jikan, meaning silence, serving as his teacher's personal assistant. He saw no contradiction: in the Zen he practised there is no worship and no deity, so nothing in it argued with being a Jew. He kept the Sabbath on tour.

narrative_blocks.header: At seventy-three, back on the road
narrative_blocks.body: In 2005 he found that his manager had emptied his retirement accounts and sold his publishing, leaving almost nothing. He went back on the road in 2008 for the first time in fifteen years and stayed out until 2013, playing three-hour shows into his late seventies. He said it warmed some part of his heart that had taken on a chill.

narrative_blocks.header: His last letter to Marianne, three months early
narrative_blocks.body: Marianne Ihlen, whom he had lived with on Hydra through the sixties and written So Long Marianne for, was dying in 2016, and he wrote to tell her he was just a little behind her, close enough to take her hand, this old body having given up just as hers had. She died three months and nine days before he did.

people.research_notes: EASTER-EGG RATIONALE, a per-entry exception of the Commodore Vanderbilt kind: grandfather of a fifteenth-generation descendant, Viva Katherine Wainwright Cohen. The line runs only through his daughter Lorca; nobody above him is built and nobody should be. Leonard Norman Cohen, born 21 September 1934 at Westmount, Quebec, into an Orthodox Jewish family; his father died when he was nine. McGill, B.A. 1955; a term of law and a year at Columbia. Poet and novelist first - Let Us Compare Mythologies (1956), The Spice-Box of Earth (1961), The Favourite Game (1963), Flowers for Hitler (1964), Beautiful Losers (1966) - and no music career until he was thirty-two. Bought a house on Hydra in 1960 with money inherited from his grandmother and lived there with Marianne Ihlen for most of the sixties. Judy Collins recorded Suzanne in 1966 and made his name; John Hammond signed him to Columbia. Sang for Israeli soldiers in the Sinai during the Yom Kippur War of 1973. Five years' seclusion at Mount Baldy from 1994; ordained a Rinzai Zen monk in 1996 with the Dharma name Jikan, silence, and served as Joshu Sasaki Roshi's personal assistant, while insisting he remained a Jew. Companion of the Order of Canada, 2003; Prince of Asturias Award for literature and the Glenn Gould Prize, 2011. Died 7 November 2016 at Los Angeles after a fall, in his sleep, aged 82, leukemia contributing; buried by his own wish in a plain pine casket in the family plot at Shaar Hashomayim. Two children with Suzanne Elrod, whom he never married: Adam (1972) and Lorca (1974), the latter named for Federico Garcia Lorca. Three grandchildren, one of them Rufus Wainwright's daughter.

narrative_blocks.body: She worked as a photographer and videographer on her father's tours and shot the video for his song Because Of. narrative_blocks.header: Her father put Gould into railroads
narrative_blocks.body: Daniel Stratton Miller, a wholesale grocer, asked his son-in-law to help rescue his stake in the Rutland and Washington after the Panic of 1857. Gould bought the stock at ten cents on the dollar and came out owning the company. Every railroad he ever took began there.

narrative_blocks.header: Her daughter read law to hold Lyndhurst
narrative_blocks.body: Their eldest daughter Helen inherited the estate and read law so that she could manage her own money rather than have it managed for her. She turned the grounds into free sewing, cooking and carpentry schools for poor children and opened the greenhouse and the pool to the town six days a week. Her mother died three years before her father and saw none of it.

narrative_blocks.header: Why her daughter built the pool
narrative_blocks.body: In 1904 the General Slocum burned in the East River and hundreds of women and children drowned because they could not swim. Seven years later her daughter Helen put up a glass-roofed Roman bath at Lyndhurst and kept lifeguards on it full time. Girls, who at that time had little chance to learn, were taught to swim there.

narrative_blocks.header: The bowling alley was a point about women
narrative_blocks.body: Bowling was one of the few sports of the day in which women and men competed on the same terms, so her daughter Helen built an alley at Lyndhurst in 1894, regulation size and among the oldest anywhere still standing. She had been twenty-four when her father died and left her the estate and her younger brothers and sisters, and she bought the place outright in 1899.

narrative_blocks.header: Wounded soldiers convalesced on the lawn
narrative_blocks.body: During the Spanish-American War her daughter Helen worked in a New York hospital for wounded men and brought convalescents up to Lyndhurst to recover on the grounds. Her younger daughter Anna did the same for men coming home from the second war, and in 1961 gave the estate to the National Trust for Historic Preservation.

people.research_notes: Known as Ellie - kept as her chip name and out of the display name, at Sam's instruction. Born 20 September 1838 in New York City, third of the eight children of Daniel Stratton Miller, a wholesale grocer and merchant, and Ann Kip Bailey; baptized at the South Dutch Church on 31 October 1843. Married Jay Gould there on 22 January 1863; six children. The family was in New York in 1870 when he was president of the Erie Railroad and at Greenburgh, Westchester County, by 1880. Died 13 January 1889 aged fifty, after lingering several weeks at the point of death, and was buried at Woodlawn on the 16th; her will was probated on the 30th. A Louisiana paper reporting her death noted that her own mother was still living and over eighty. She is here as the grandmother-in-law of an eleventh-generation descendant, through her granddaughter Edith. HER FATHER IS WHY GOULD BECAME A RAILROAD MAN: Daniel Stratton Miller asked his son-in-law to help rescue his investment in the Rutland and Washington Railroad after the Panic of 1857, and Gould bought the stock at ten cents on the dollar and came out controlling the company. Six children: George Jay, Edwin, Helen, Howard, Anna and Frank Jay. Her daughter Helen (1868-1938) took Lyndhurst over when her father died, took a law degree so she could manage her own money, and ran free sewing, cooking and carpentry schools on the estate for poor children, opening the greenhouse and pool building to the town six days a week. She died at Lyndhurst in 1889, three years before her husband.

narrative_blocks.header: Knighted for shipping, married in an evening
narrative_blocks.body: He was made a Knight Commander of the British Empire in 1920 for voluntary service to the Ministry of Shipping, and sat on the board of Cunard. A widower, he met Edith Gould at Reno and married her at six that evening, hours after her divorce came through. He was seldom seen at East Hampton afterwards.

people.research_notes: Second husband of Edith Catherine Gould. Born 1879 at Cadder, Lanarkshire, son of Frederick H. Macneal - the family spelt it Macneal - and died at London in 1966. A widower when he met Edith at Reno; they married there at six in the evening on 25 January 1932, hours after her decree, having taken the licence at Minden fifty miles south. He was seldom seen at East Hampton. Here as the second husband of a descendant's former wife, which is thin; he is built because Sam asked for him.

Gilchrest is kept because it is what the family used; the school's spelling is probably the right one and this should be settled. Thirteen years a pupil at Nightingale, leaving in 1962 as president of the senior class. Returned to the school in the autumn of 1971 and stayed eighteen years, in turn alumnae affairs coordinator and secretary, history teacher, supervisor of Classes VII and VIII, director of admissions, and head of the middle school. Head of Greenwich Academy in Connecticut from 1988 to 2003. In 1994, with Patricia Young and Nancy Hoffmann and with Maxine K. Armstrong as founding board chair, she started REACH Prep at Greenwich Academy - she already knew Gary Simons's Prep for Prep at Trinity School in New York and called a meeting of trustees and parents to seed something like it. It began with highly motivated Black and Latina middle-school girls from the surrounding towns, opened to boys in 2000, and has placed more than three hundred and forty children in independent schools, with a twelve-year continuum of academic, family and college support behind each of them and a college completion rate around ninety per cent. narrative_blocks.body: Her mother knew Martha Dandridge before Martha was a Custis, and the two households kept it up afterward. Ann carried the friendship into her own marriage in 1782.

narrative_blocks.body: After her husband William died in 1803 she sold the Broadway townhouse to John Jacob Astor, who put the Astor House hotel up on the ground. She lived on until 1826 and lies at St. Paul's Chapel, a few blocks down the same street.

narrative_blocks.header: Lafayette came to Brooklyn to see her
narrative_blocks.body: On his 1824 tour Lafayette crossed to Brooklyn to call on her at her daughter's house. He stood a long while before the Stuart portrait of Washington and said only that yes, that was his noble friend.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father served on Admiral King's staff
narrative_blocks.body: Constantine Mittendorf came out of Yale and Columbia Law and spent the Second World War in Washington, in naval intelligence under Ernest King. King ran every American naval operation in both oceans.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother's third husband and the flying saucers
narrative_blocks.body: Widowed in 1960, her mother married twice more; the last was Serge Korff, a physicist who tracked cosmic rays by balloon. One of his 1947 flights, over New Jersey, Queens and Connecticut, set off a run of flying-saucer reports.

narrative_blocks.header: The sculptor in the family: Mary Callery
narrative_blocks.body: The modern art in her mother's houses came from Mary Callery, an abstract expressionist sculptor and her mother's aunt. Marcella carries the sculptor's family name as her own middle name.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother was a secretary in wartime Washington
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother met Constantine Mittendorf there. They married in 1942 at the Convent of the Sacred Heart, and moved in time into the East 95th Street town house he had grown up in.

narrative_blocks.header: The nursery school head friends called Mitten
narrative_blocks.body: She ran it through the years when getting a three-year-old into a Manhattan nursery school had become something parents competed for outright. A rival headmaster, mid-dispute, barked the nickname down the phone at her.

people.research_notes: Middle name set to Callery (the Callery line, via her mother) per Sam, 29 July 2026; the record previously held only the initial 'M.' FATHER — Constantine Joseph Mittendorf (d. 1960). Yale 1937; Columbia School of Law 1940. WWII service in Naval Intelligence, Washington DC, on the staff of Fleet Admiral Ernest J. King (COMINCH and Chief of Naval Operations, member of the Joint Chiefs). RANK DISCREPANCY, unresolved: maxfieldgenealogy.com/mittendorf0202.html gives Lieutenant, while his widow's obituary calls him 'a commander working in naval intelligence' — the NB avoids the rank for that reason. Later a New York attorney, PROBABLY a name partner at Casey, Lane & Mittendorf (Washington DC and New York), now Windels, Marx, Lane & Mittendorf — NOT CONFIRMED; the firm name is suggestive, not evidence, so it is deliberately absent from the NBs. Grew up in the East 95th Street town house, New York. MOTHER — Marcella Mittendorf, later Brett, later Baroness Korff. Obituary (screenshots supplied by Sam, 29 July 2026): worked as a secretary in Washington DC during the war, where she met Mittendorf; married 1942 at the Convent of the Sacred Heart, Manhattan; lived briefly in Washington and on East 82nd Street before the East 95th Street town house. Four children. Summers in Amagansett from 1953; after Mittendorf's death in 1960 she kept renting there, was briefly married to Philip Brett, then rented 'the Coop' on Beach Lane, Wainscott, for thirty years. In 1976 married Baron Serge A. Korff, the cosmic-ray physicist — one of his 1947 balloon assemblages crossed New Jersey, Queens and Connecticut and produced a run of flying-saucer reports. Inherited a modern-art collection from her aunt Mary Callery, the abstract expressionist sculptor. Her daughter Anne Mittendorf Ely (the subject's sister) is quoted saying she 'believed in education and was an animal lover' and kept a long succession of cats she called Everybody Good. SUBJECT'S OWN CAREER — head of the Park Avenue Christian Church Day School, New York. New York Times, 7 April 1996, Elisabeth Bumiller, 'Sifting Sandbox Aptitude Tests; Crayon-Chewing Time for Nursery School Directors': describes her school as a venerable East Side establishment, notes that she listed herself in the New York Independent Schools Directory as 'Marcella (Mrs. Stuyvesant) Wainwright' though friends called her Mitten, and records Irwin Shlachter, headmaster of Rodeph Sholom, barking 'Listen, Mitten' down the phone at her during a since-resolved dispute. AVAILABLE, NOT WRITTEN AS AN NB: the Amagansett summers from 1953 and the thirty years at the Coop in Wainscott (would be a sixth block, category family).

narrative_blocks.body: He is admitted in New York State and registered with the RAK Berlin as a foreign attorney, working on German-American inheritance law in both languages. narrative_blocks.body: When she fell ill her physician sent the family to Jacksonville for the winter, and that journey was her husband's first sight of the state. She died of the disease in 1881, and within four years he was building hotels in St. Augustine.

narrative_blocks.header: He came to her father's store at fourteen
narrative_blocks.body: Henry Flagler was sent out to Ohio at fourteen to clerk in the store her father kept at Republic. Nine years later he married the daughter of the house.

narrative_blocks.body: Flagler's mother was the widow of David Harkness, her father's brother, so the two families had been in and out of each other's houses long before the wedding. His half-brother Daniel Harkness was her first cousin.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the woman who had nursed her
narrative_blocks.body: Ida Alice Shourds had been her caregiver through the last illness, and became the second Mrs. Flagler two years after she died. That marriage ended when Ida Alice was declared insane and the Florida legislature was persuaded to make insanity grounds for divorce.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father's money went into the salt failure
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband borrowed from her father to keep a Saginaw salt company alive, and lost every dollar of it when the war killed the demand. He spent years paying it back and said afterwards that he would never again invest without investigating first.

narrative_blocks.header: She was buried twice
narrative_blocks.body: When she died in 1881 she was laid at Woodlawn in the Bronx. Once her husband had built the mausoleum beside the memorial church in St. Augustine, he had her brought south to lie with their daughter.

narrative_blocks.header: A hurricane letter paid his passage
narrative_blocks.body: Orphaned on Saint Croix and clerking for an import firm, he wrote a letter describing the hurricane that levelled Christiansted in 1772. It so impressed the island’s leading men that they raised a fund to send him to school in North America.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote fifty-one of the Federalist Papers
narrative_blocks.body: As the first Secretary of the Treasury he assumed the states’ war debts and built a national bank, a mint and a revenue service out of nothing. Of the eighty-five essays written to defend the Constitution, fifty-one were his.

narrative_blocks.header: Burr shot him at Weehawken in 1804
narrative_blocks.body: The rivalry ran from 1791, when Aaron Burr took the Senate seat of his father-in-law Philip Schuyler, to the pistols on the Jersey shore in July 1804. Hamilton was rowed back across the Hudson and died the next afternoon.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded the bank Wadsworth would run
narrative_blocks.body: He founded the Bank of New York in 1784, and Jeremiah Wadsworth of Hartford took it over as second president the year after. The two were allies in building the young country’s financial machinery.

narrative_blocks.header: Sappers cleared his path at Redoubt Ten
narrative_blocks.body: At Yorktown he took Redoubt Number Ten with bayonets alone, so that no musket flash would give the night attack away. The abatis in front of it had been cut open by Washington’s sappers, Sergeant Joseph Martin among them.

narrative_blocks.header: His heirs married into the House of Morgan
narrative_blocks.body: His great-grandson William Pierson Hamilton became a partner at J. P. Morgan and married the financier’s daughter in 1894. Their son Alexander Morgan Hamilton later led the society that rescued Hamilton Grange and gave it to the nation.

narrative_blocks.header: He tried to build the factory town himself
narrative_blocks.body: The Society for Establishing Useful Manufactures was his attempt to prove the Report on Manufactures on the ground: a company chartered in New Jersey to harness the Great Falls of the Passaic and spin cotton by water. The mills faltered within a few years, but the town it laid out kept the governor's name and is Paterson still.

notable.notable_blurb: Orphanage founder; keeper of the Hamilton papers

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-two years running the orphan asylum
narrative_blocks.body: Two years after the duel she helped found New York's first private orphanage, served as its second directress and then its first for twenty-seven years, and stayed with it until she left the city at ninety-one. More than seven hundred children passed through her care.

narrative_blocks.header: She spent fifty years gathering his papers
narrative_blocks.body: Widowed at forty-seven, she outlived him by half a century and gave it to reorganising every letter and paper he left, which her son John Church worked into a biography. In 1848 she persuaded Congress to buy and publish the writings.

narrative_blocks.header: She took in her husband's friend's orphan
narrative_blocks.body: In 1787 the Hamiltons took in two-year-old Frances Antill, whose mother had died and whose father, a colonel, died in Canada soon after. Her sister Angelica wrote admiringly of the generous action of taking the orphan under her protection.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son died on the same duelling ground
narrative_blocks.body: Philip, her eldest, was shot in a duel at Weehawken in November 1801 and died after fourteen hours with both parents beside him. Three years later his father was carried off the same field.

narrative_blocks.header: At ninety she raised money for a monument
narrative_blocks.body: Living on H Street near the White House with her widowed daughter, she joined Dolley Madison in raising funds for the Washington Monument. Presidents and generals called on her as a living link to the Revolution.

narrative_blocks.header: She wore his sonnet around her neck
narrative_blocks.body: The pieces of a poem he had written her during their courtship were sewn into a small package she kept at her throat. She was still describing him clearly in her nineties, after her short-term memory had gone.

narrative_blocks.header: She married him on his birthday
narrative_blocks.body: The wedding was at Lebanon on the twenty-sixth of March, 1767, the day Jonathan Trumbull turned twenty-seven. She was seventeen, the daughter of Ebenezer Backus of Norwich.

narrative_blocks.header: Her first child lived three weeks
narrative_blocks.body: A son, Jonathan, was born at the end of December 1767 and died in the middle of January. Four daughters followed — Faith, Mary, Harriet and Maria — and she outlived her husband by seventeen years.

narrative_blocks.header: Her daughters' letters home became a book
narrative_blocks.body: Maria and Harriet spent the winter of 1800 in New York, staying with Lady Kitty Duer while friends of their parents arranged lessons, plays and parties. The letters the girls sent back to Lebanon were published as A Season in New York, 1801, and are read now for what two teenage girls made of the city.

narrative_blocks.header: Maria died at twenty, a year after marrying
narrative_blocks.body: She married Henry Hudson of Hartford in 1804 and bore a son, Jonathan Trumbull Hudson. She died of complications of the birth in November 1805 and lies in the Center Church burial ground; a poet wrote that she moved "light as the gossamer, with fairy feet".

narrative_blocks.header: She buried two children on one day
narrative_blocks.body: Alfred was two and a half and Frances was six months, and both died on the fourth of August 1869. They lie together at Old Gray in Knoxville, where three of her five children are buried.

narrative_blocks.header: Of five children, two saw her out
narrative_blocks.body: She lost the two eldest as infants in 1869 and her daughter Clarissa at thirty-three in 1905. Only Harriet and Alfred were living when their father died the year after.

narrative_blocks.header: She married the man who taught the knife
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin Brabson Cates of Maryville married her at Knoxville in November 1896. He was professor of anatomy and clinical surgery at Tennessee Medical College, and he outlived her by thirty-eight years.
