narrative_blocks.header: Rodman to engineer of way in eight years
narrative_blocks.body: He went onto the Bridgeport improvement straight out of Sheffield as a rodman, and worked up through inspector, transitman and assistant engineer. By 1907 he ran the whole right of way, real estate and taxes department of the railroad.

narrative_blocks.header: A Terry at Yale in every generation
narrative_blocks.body: He took the civil engineering course at Sheffield with honors and rowed for the gymnastic team. The family, he told his class secretary, had been represented at Yale in every generation since the founding of the college.

narrative_blocks.header: Her cousin the judge gave her away
narrative_blocks.body: They married at noon in Christ Church, Hartford, in November 1908, and her cousin Judge Simeon E. Baldwin gave her away. They kept house afterwards at 30 Hillhouse Avenue in New Haven.

bio.bio_blurb: Author; first president of the Goodspeed Opera Foundation

narrative_blocks.header: She saved the Goodspeed Opera House
narrative_blocks.body: She was the driving force behind the restoration of the Goodspeed at East Haddam and became the first president of the foundation formed for it in 1959. She sat on its board until she died.

narrative_blocks.header: A Yale doctorate in 1907
narrative_blocks.body: She took her degree at Radcliffe and then a Ph.D. from Yale in 1907, when very few women held one. Her father Henry Campbell was an inventor and was already dead by her wedding.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote the book on Connecticut inns
narrative_blocks.body: In 1937, as a member of the Colonial Dames, she published Old Inns of Connecticut. She was a trustee of the Antiquarian and Landmark Association and kept at the East Haddam societies into her nineties.

narrative_blocks.header: She died at a hundred and one
narrative_blocks.body: She outlived her husband by fourteen years and reached a hundred and one at Hadlyme, where she had lived forty-five years. Her obituary recorded that she left no survivors.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty years of papers on the knife
narrative_blocks.body: He published on hernias, cancer and amputation from 1888 to 1939, in university bulletins and in the national journals of medicine and surgery. His own handwritten notes are bound in with the printed articles.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught the anatomy he operated on
narrative_blocks.body: At Tennessee Medical College in Knoxville he was Demonstrator of Anatomy and Operative Surgery, and then Professor of Anatomy and Clinical Surgery. He was one of the best-known doctors in the city.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote to the papers about everything
narrative_blocks.body: He sent letters to the editors of the Knoxville News Sentinel and the other local papers, most of them about his work or about the town. The papers wrote about him and his family in turn.

career.role: Lecturer on church polity and American church history

narrative_blocks.header: The Congregational Pope of New England
narrative_blocks.body: He took the First Church in New Haven in 1825 and held one of the most conspicuous pulpits in the region until 1866, without ever being dismissed from it. The name was what his denomination called him as his influence grew.

narrative_blocks.header: A sentence Lincoln borrowed
narrative_blocks.body: He wrote in Slavery Discussed that if the laws by which slavery exists are not wrong, nothing is wrong. Lincoln rephrased the sentence and it was quoted everywhere.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded a paper to fight slavery’s spread
narrative_blocks.body: He started The Independent in 1848 with Storrs, Leavitt, Thompson and Bowen, chiefly to oppose the extension of slavery, and edited it for fifteen years. He attacked the apologists for slavery and the Garrisonian radicals in the same breath.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded what became the Yale Review
narrative_blocks.body: He edited the Christian Spectator for twelve years from 1826, and in 1843 was one of the founders of the New Englander, the quarterly that in time became the Yale Review.

narrative_blocks.header: A Japanese girl in his household, 1872
narrative_blocks.body: The Iwakura Mission gave him charge of Yamakawa Sutematsu, twelve years old and sent from Japan to be educated. She grew up with his youngest daughter and became the first Japanese woman to take a college degree.

narrative_blocks.header: He put his sister’s accuser on trial
narrative_blocks.body: When Alexander MacWhorter dropped Delia Bacon and showed her letters round the divinity school, her brother charged him before a jury of twenty-three ministers with conduct dishonourable to the ministry. The vote acquitted him, twelve to eleven.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale still sings his commencement hymn
narrative_blocks.body: He wrote O God, beneath Thy guiding hand, our exiled fathers crossed the sea. Four of his six sons took Congregational pulpits, and his Genesis of the New England Churches came out in 1874.

narrative_blocks.header: The original mugwump of Connecticut
narrative_blocks.body: The Times gave him the name in 1884, when he left the Republicans over James Blaine and went across to Grover Cleveland. Party loyalty was near absolute then and independents were rare.

narrative_blocks.header: He resigned his pulpit without saying why
narrative_blocks.body: He gave up Dwight Place in March 1884 after a few members of one of the wealthiest congregations in New Haven complained of him, and the church wept as he read the letter. The Times reported later that Blaine's campaign had put the gossip about.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-five years teaching Europe at Berkeley
narrative_blocks.body: He came out to the First Congregational Church at Berkeley in 1887, took an instructorship in history the February after, and gave up the pulpit for it. From 1895 he held the chair of modern European history until he died.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale Banner, the Courant, the Morning News
narrative_blocks.body: He edited the Yale Banner and chaired the Courant board as an undergraduate, and wrote for the Atlantic and Scribner's. Afterwards he ran the New Haven Morning News for three years and was associate editor of the New Englander.

narrative_blocks.header: A year surveying railroad in Cattaraugus
narrative_blocks.body: Between college and the divinity school he spent a year surveying railroad line in western New York and a year travelling in Europe. He entered Yale Divinity in 1874 and took the degree in 1877.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave New Haven its centennial oration
narrative_blocks.body: On the Fourth of July 1884, months after the resignation, he delivered the oration for the hundredth anniversary of the city. It was printed the following year.

narrative_blocks.header: Five brothers took Yale degrees
narrative_blocks.body: Five of his brothers took bachelor's degrees at Yale, one a doctorate in medicine and one a master's, and four went into Congregational pulpits as their father had. He married at Terre Haute in 1880 and had no children.

bio.bio_blurb: Yale 1873; Colorado cattle and investment man

narrative_blocks.header: An after-dinner bicycle ride killed him
narrative_blocks.body: He rode out after dinner on the third of June 1901 and was seized by such pain that he had to dismount. A physician found him lying by the roadside and got him home, but he was dead before morning.

narrative_blocks.header: Bad health sent him to a Colorado ranch
narrative_blocks.body: He was reading medicine in New Haven when his health broke and he had to give it up. He travelled the West Indies and Europe, then went out to Greeley to work a ranch and camp in the mountains until he was well.

narrative_blocks.header: He organized a cattle company at twenty-nine
narrative_blocks.body: He went into stock raising in Wyoming in 1880 and helped organize the New England Live Stock Company the year after, becoming its secretary and treasurer in 1882. He moved down to Denver in 1892 and dealt in western investment securities.

narrative_blocks.header: The youngest of Leonard Bacon's sons
narrative_blocks.body: He was the last child of the New Haven pulpit and married Mary Prichard Woolsey, daughter of Yale's president. He left her a widow at forty-five with three children living.

narrative_blocks.header: Japanese Girls and Women, 1891
narrative_blocks.body: Japan had been closely studied, she wrote, and half its population left unnoticed. A Japanese Interior followed in 1893, made out of the letters she sent home from Tokyo.

narrative_blocks.header: She built Tsuda’s college for nothing
narrative_blocks.body: She went back to Japan in 1900 to help Tsuda Umeko start the Joshi Eigaku Juku, the first non-mission school in the country for the advanced education of women. She taught a heavy load and took no pay but her housing.

narrative_blocks.header: She named the hospital after her horse
narrative_blocks.body: The Hampton Training School for Nurses opened in 1891 and everyone called it Dixie, after the horse she carried patients in. She had raised the money after a student was refused nursing training because she was Black.

narrative_blocks.header: No colour line at the hospital door
narrative_blocks.body: She was proud that the hospital admitted patients without racial distinction. When donors later demanded segregated wards, she drafted the rule that made them pay every year to keep them.

narrative_blocks.header: A Japanese girl came to live with them
narrative_blocks.body: In 1872 the envoy Mori Arinori chose her father's New Haven house for one of the girls the Meiji government was sending abroad. Sutematsu Yamakawa was twelve and Alice fourteen, and they lived as sisters for ten years.

narrative_blocks.header: Harvard examined her; no college took her
narrative_blocks.body: Money kept her out of university, so she sat Harvard's examinations for women in philosophy and political economy and took a degree by them in 1881. Two years later she went to Hampton Institute to teach.

narrative_blocks.header: Two adopted daughters, and no marriage
narrative_blocks.body: She never married and adopted two Japanese girls — Watanabe Mitsu, Tsuda Umeko's niece, and Hitotsuyanagi Makiko, who married the architect of the Omi Brotherhood. Her aunt Delia Salter Bacon was the woman who first argued that Francis Bacon wrote Shakespeare.

narrative_blocks.header: Orphaned at two, in one year
narrative_blocks.body: His mother died in April 1806 and his father in September, leaving him two years old. His uncle Samuel William Johnson and his aunt Susan took him in at Stratford and raised him among their children.

narrative_blocks.header: He put Lucretius into blank verse
narrative_blocks.body: He read law at Litchfield in 1824 and never practised a day of it, farming and inventing instead. In 1872 he published his own translation of Lucretius, De Rerum Natura, in blank verse.

narrative_blocks.header: He built the only town clock in Owego
narrative_blocks.body: With John J. Speed of Ithaca he made the clock that went into the steeple of the First Baptist Church, the first the town had seen. He also took out a patent for a telegraph, noticed in the papers in 1849.

narrative_blocks.header: He sold the valley off in farm plots
narrative_blocks.body: The land his father left him in the Susquehanna Valley he cut into farms and sold to the first settlers. In 1837 he kept two hundred acres for himself at Meadow Bank, on the west bank of Owego Creek.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale in 1855, and tapped for Bones
narrative_blocks.body: He took his degree at Yale in 1855 and was taken into Skull and Bones, the senior society founded there in 1832. Yale added a master's in 1863 and a doctorate of humane letters in 1895.

narrative_blocks.header: Five years teaching midshipmen sums
narrative_blocks.body: From 1865 he was assistant professor of mathematics at the United States Naval Academy at Annapolis. His younger brother William Woolsey Johnson taught mathematics in the same place for forty years.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirteen years in the Trinity chair
narrative_blocks.body: Trinity College took him in 1883 and he held his professorship until 1896, when they made him emeritus. He kept the emeritus chair for another thirty-five years.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a fourth cousin in 1883
narrative_blocks.body: Ellen Frances Terry was his second wife. They were fourth cousins, both descended from Rev. James Pierpont of New Haven and his wife Mary Hooker, granddaughter of Thomas Hooker.

narrative_blocks.header: He outlived her by thirty-five years
narrative_blocks.body: She died suddenly at Hartford at the end of 1896, thirteen years into the marriage. He lived to ninety-four and died in the same city in 1931.

narrative_blocks.header: He proved the 15 puzzle impossible
narrative_blocks.body: In 1879 he showed by an odd-and-even permutation argument that the notorious puzzle could not be solved from every starting position. He wrote a second proof for people who were not mathematicians.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped found the New York Mathematical Society
narrative_blocks.body: He was one of its founders in 1888 and sat on the council after it became the American Mathematical Society in 1894. He pressed for its Bulletin and was among its first contributors.

narrative_blocks.header: He regretted that we counted our thumbs
narrative_blocks.body: Arguing for counting by eights, he wrote that our ancestors made the decimal system on their fingers, and that we must feel profound regret they perversely counted their thumbs as well. Nature, he said, had differentiated them sufficiently to have saved the race from the error.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years at Annapolis, and a Commodore
narrative_blocks.body: He taught midshipmen from 1881 until he retired in 1921, having been given commissioned rank by a special act of Congress in 1913. He left with the rank of Commodore.

narrative_blocks.header: A year at Cambridge with the whole family
narrative_blocks.body: He took the sabbatical year of 1886 and 1887 at the University of Cambridge and rented a house there for them all. He wrote his Treatise on Ordinary and Partial Differential Equations while he was in it.

cross_connections.display_label: co-invented the electric smelting furnace he later worked in

narrative_blocks.header: He patented ways to catch a boiling metal
narrative_blocks.body: A Trinity man of 1898, he worked in zinc smelting and the electric furnace, and took out patents for condensing volatile metals. The trade knew him for electro-metallurgy rather than for the family mathematics.

narrative_blocks.header: He lost his mother before he was four
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth McAlpine died at Owego in 1881 when he was three. He carried her surname as his middle name and passed it to his daughter.

naming_inspiration.note: Named for the brother who died at twenty-two months, three months before his birth

career.role: Professor of chemistry and natural philosophy

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote a book about the equator
narrative_blocks.body: He went to South America the year after he qualified and published Travels in the Equatorial Regions of South America in 1832, printed at Hartford in 1834. He was twenty-six when it came out.

narrative_blocks.header: He shipped his medicines from New York
narrative_blocks.body: Trying to set up a practice in Ecuador, he bought drugs in New York through an agent named Charles Swett and had them sent down to him. His father wrote out the political news from home for him.

narrative_blocks.header: Two wars, and the second killed him
narrative_blocks.body: He was a surgeon with the 1st Michigan Volunteers in the Mexican War of 1847, and came back in the Civil War as an acting assistant surgeon treating the wounded at Chicago. He died there in harness in December 1864.

narrative_blocks.header: He was named for the brother who died
narrative_blocks.body: The first Adrian Russell Terry died in June 1808 at twenty-two months. This one was born that September, three months later, and given the same name.

cross_connections.display_label: held the same acting assistant surgeon's post at Philadelphia

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at fifty-four, she lived to ninety-three
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband died on service at Chicago in 1864 and she outlived him by thirty-nine years. She had buried two of their four children before he died.

narrative_blocks.header: She died on her birthday
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Philadelphia on the twelfth of March 1850, she died at Baltimore on the twelfth of March 1916, sixty-six years to the day. She descended from John Leverett, governor of Massachusetts.

education.notes: Ph.D. on musical pitch among the ancient Greeks

narrative_blocks.header: His doctorate was on Greek musical pitch
narrative_blocks.body: He took his Ph.D. at Johns Hopkins in 1896 for a thesis on musical pitch and the measurement of intervals among the ancient Greeks. A friend congratulated him on being at once a musician, a mathematician and a Hellenist.

narrative_blocks.header: His father called him his mother's boy
narrative_blocks.body: Writing to a colleague, his father said he was glad the boy was his mother's, though he had mathematics enough in him to have written on the mathematical theory of music. The other son, he said, was more in his own line.

bio.bio_blurb: Last of the Navy's Corps of Professors

career.organization: Corps of Professors of Mathematics, U.S. Naval Academy

narrative_blocks.header: He was the last of the Corps
narrative_blocks.body: The Corps of Professors of Mathematics was set up in 1848 and abolished in 1929; his retirement in 1936 ended it formally. He lies at the Academy beside Paul Dashiell, another of them — neither had been a midshipman or served at sea.

narrative_blocks.header: He told Congress what teaching was worth
narrative_blocks.body: Testifying in 1929 that only six Corps professors were left and that he earned less than officers of his own rank, he was asked by the chairman whether he saw the difference between commanding a great warship and devoting one’s time to teaching. Congressman Woodruff answered for him: the government was big enough and just enough to be fair to those who ably serve it.

narrative_blocks.header: He was the engineer of the two sons
narrative_blocks.body: Where his brother went to Greek music, he went to steel. Johns Hopkins in 1892, the Stevens Institute in 1896, and from 1898 a steel inspector for the Navy; in 1910 he published a book on engineering descriptive geometry.

narrative_blocks.header: His father made the same case in 1907
narrative_blocks.body: William Woolsey Johnson wrote to Superintendent Sands that the Corps ought to have emeritus standing and part pay in retirement. Twenty-two years later his son was still asking Congress for it.

narrative_blocks.header: He buried his son at the Academy
narrative_blocks.body: His boy Webster was killed flying out of Norfolk in December 1940 and was carried to Annapolis for a military funeral. The captain and his wife travelled with the body.

narrative_blocks.header: She trained under Henri and Howard Pyle
narrative_blocks.body: She graduated from the Philadelphia School of Design for Women in 1894 and studied under Robert Henri, Howard Pyle, Charles Hawthorne and Clinedinst. Brigham Young showed her in 2005 among the women modernists Henri taught.

narrative_blocks.header: Her covers ran on the Saturday Evening Post
narrative_blocks.body: She supported herself by illustration before she married, and a Philadelphia paper said some of the prettiest covers for the magazines and the Saturday Evening Post were of her design.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandfather said after you, pilot
narrative_blocks.body: Her grandfather Craven went down with the Tecumseh at Mobile Bay in 1864, having let the pilot up the ladder ahead of him. A hundred and ten men died with the ship.

narrative_blocks.header: She ran the county war work for women
narrative_blocks.body: A suffragist, she was chairman of the women’s section of the Council of Defense for Anne Arundel County through the first war, and was decorated for it.

narrative_blocks.header: A dinner in 1935 saved colonial Annapolis
narrative_blocks.body: With fear and trembling she asked the president of St John’s College for help, and that December the governor and the superintendent of the Naval Academy dined at her house. They formed the Company for the Restoration of Colonial Annapolis.

narrative_blocks.header: Reynolds Tavern became the town library
narrative_blocks.body: The company got Reynolds Tavern for a library, stopped a street being widened, and pressed the Federated Garden Clubs to take on the Hammond-Harwood House. When it disbanded in 1954 its money went to the new Historic Annapolis.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son went into the water off Norfolk
narrative_blocks.body: Webb, the youngest and the family favorite, graduated from the Naval Academy in 1936 and was killed in December 1940 practicing landings on a carrier off Norfolk.

career.role: Ensign, USS Lexington and USS Yorktown

narrative_blocks.header: His crash fixed the Wildcat
narrative_blocks.body: He was flying an experimental F4F out of Norfolk in December 1940 when it came down in the rail yards beside the station, minutes after takeoff. The fault was thought to be a design defect, corrected because of the crash; the improved Wildcat became one of the Navy's great combat aircraft.

narrative_blocks.header: He was married three months before
narrative_blocks.body: He married Carey Shands at Norfolk in September 1940, sister of a lieutenant who became a rear admiral. She later married his own Academy classmate, Hollis Cooley.

narrative_blocks.header: His father and grandfather taught at Annapolis
narrative_blocks.body: Both were professors of mathematics at the Naval Academy, and he was born in the town. His classmates wrote that unlike the rest of them he came to the Academy with a naval background of several generations, so he should have known better.

narrative_blocks.header: Study hours seldom found him studious
narrative_blocks.body: He had an easy way with academics and the Lucky Bag said the study hours rarely caught him at work — but the Masqueraders and the Musical Show kept him hard at it. He was president of the Glee Club.

marriages.location: Church of the Good Shepherd, Meadowbrook

narrative_blocks.header: A Navy brother gave her away
narrative_blocks.body: Her father was dead, so her brother Lieut. Courtney Shands of the Navy escorted her up the aisle at the Church of the Good Shepherd in Meadowbrook. Fellow officers in full dress whites raised the arch of swords over the couple.

narrative_blocks.header: She died leaving two small boys
narrative_blocks.body: She married Charles Frederick Johnson in January 1872 and died at Owego in August 1881, at thirty-nine. Woolsey was not yet four and Jarvis was two months short of his first birthday.

narrative_blocks.header: He flew a Warhawk out of Thelepte
narrative_blocks.body: He was a second lieutenant with the 59th Fighter Squadron of the 33rd Fighter Group, flying Curtiss P-40s from the desert strip at Thelepte in Tunisia. He was killed in action on the second of February 1943, at twenty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: The second of the family to die flying
narrative_blocks.body: He carried the name of his great-uncle, the Annapolis mathematician, and was the second of the family to die in a wartime cockpit: his second cousin Webster went down in a Navy plane in 1940. He lies at Carthage, plot E, row 17.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Talbiya, Jerusalem — built by Hanna Ibrahim Bisharat in 1926.

narrative_blocks.header: She married out of Andover in 1947
narrative_blocks.body: She had taken her Vassar degree the year before and was living with her widowed mother at Andover when she became engaged to Maurice Bisharat, a young doctor interning in Hartford. He was the son of a Transjordan sheikh.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote to Vassar defending Jimmy Carter
narrative_blocks.body: In 2007, from Carmichael, California, she objected in the alumnae quarterly to the choice of commencement speaker and to that speaker's rudeness toward Carter over his book on Palestine. She had been married to a Palestinian for sixty years.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Talbiya, Jerusalem — built by Hanna Ibrahim Bisharat in 1926.

narrative_blocks.header: He was interning at St. Francis in 1947
narrative_blocks.body: He came out of the American University of Beirut in 1943 and was serving his internship at St. Francis Hospital in Hartford when he became engaged to Mary McAlpine Johnson. He practised medicine in California and died at Carmichael in 1998.

narrative_blocks.header: A boyhood in the fields of Talbiya
narrative_blocks.body: He was a boy in the new quarter when there was almost nothing else built near it, and he told his son afterwards about the fields and orchards around the house. He and his brothers walked up the road to the Catholic Terra Sancta College.

narrative_blocks.header: His father built the house for a caliph
narrative_blocks.body: Hanna Ibrahim Bisharat was a Christian, and he called the villa he raised in Talbiya in 1926 Villa Harun ar-Rashid, for the Abbasid caliph famous for eloquence and learning. Painted tiles carried the name above the second-floor balcony.

narrative_blocks.header: The RAF took the house on a lease
narrative_blocks.body: His parents' fortunes turned in the early thirties, so they let the villa to officers of the British Royal Air Force and moved to a smaller house nearby, meaning to come back. The frescoes were plastered over to suit the officers.

narrative_blocks.header: He was abroad when the house went
narrative_blocks.body: He and his brothers had come to the United States to study and their father had shifted his business to Cairo, so the family was outside Palestine on the fourteenth of May 1948. The British officers handed the keys to the Haganah.

narrative_blocks.header: His twin helped remake downtown Stamford
narrative_blocks.body: Victor Bisharat laid out the wall around their father's front yard in Talbiya as a boy and grew up to be the architect whose towers helped remake downtown Stamford, Connecticut. Maurice took medicine instead.

narrative_blocks.header: He found the name under the sandblasting
narrative_blocks.body: He went looking for the family house in 1977 with a photograph and a vague description, because every street in the quarter had been renamed. Resting in the shade he recognised a facade, and the tile above the balcony still read Villa Harun ar-Rashid.

narrative_blocks.header: Golda Meir lived in his grandfather's house
narrative_blocks.body: Hanna Ibrahim Bisharat built the villa in Talbiya in 1926 and named it for the Abbasid caliph. The family was outside Palestine in 1948 when the house was taken, and Meir occupied the upper flat in the 1960s.

narrative_blocks.header: Public defender first, then thirty years teaching
narrative_blocks.body: He took a Harvard doctorate in anthropology and Middle East studies in 1987 and spent four years as a San Francisco deputy public defender. He has taught law at Hastings since 1991 and wrote Palestinian Lawyers and Israeli Rule.

narrative_blocks.header: A Jerusalem father and a Hartford mother
narrative_blocks.body: Maurice Bisharat left Talbiya to study in the United States and married Mary McAlpine Johnson of Hartford in 1947. George was born in Topeka seven years later.

narrative_blocks.header: He died the day after his birthday
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Boston on the twentieth of March 1787 and died at New Haven on the twenty-first of March 1841, at fifty-four. He lies in Grove Street with the son who was killed at Big Bethel twenty years later.

narrative_blocks.header: He married his first wife's cousin
narrative_blocks.body: Julia Ann Rogers, daughter of Moses Rogers, married him at Stamford in 1808 and died in 1814. Two years after that he married Elizabeth Woolsey, who was Julia's cousin, and they had six children.

narrative_blocks.header: His father made the money in New York
narrative_blocks.body: Francis Bayard Winthrop the elder was born at New London and built a merchant business in New York that prospered through the Revolution. He married twice, as his son would.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: No. 23 Gramercy Park South, built 1847.

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband died in London
narrative_blocks.body: William Templeton Johnson died in the City of London in October 1868, five years after their daughter was born. She raised Oliver and Laura on Staten Island and was buried beside him at Green-Wood.

narrative_blocks.header: She put her dead brother into print
narrative_blocks.body: Theodore was living with the Johnsons at Elliottville when he enlisted in 1861, and was killed that June. With George William Curtis helping she saw his novel through the press, and later gathered his poems and his life into a book.

narrative_blocks.header: Three generations under one Staten Island roof
narrative_blocks.body: She and William moved out to Elliottville in 1850. Her mother followed in 1854 and her brother Theodore came the same year, so the house held her husband, her mother and the brother she would spend twenty years editing.

narrative_blocks.header: He took three medals out of Columbia
narrative_blocks.body: The class of 1832 gave him the Gold Medal for best general standing, the Bronze for the evidences of Christianity, and the Silver for Greek and Roman literature. He went into the law after it.

narrative_blocks.header: A new wife, then a new house
narrative_blocks.body: He married Laura Winthrop in 1846 and had a four-storey Greek Revival house finished at No. 23 the year after, on Samuel Ruggles's new square. Red brick trimmed in brownstone, plain enough outside and not plain within.

narrative_blocks.header: He died three thousand miles from home
narrative_blocks.body: He was fifty-four, and it happened in the City of London in October 1868. He was brought back across the Atlantic to Green-Wood.

narrative_blocks.header: The Johnsons came over with Gov. Winthrop
narrative_blocks.body: John and Margery Johnson landed in Massachusetts with John Winthrop's company, and their son Isaac was killed in 1675. Two centuries on, this William married a Winthrop.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother moved in the year after
narrative_blocks.body: His father, the reporter of the New York Supreme Court and of the Court of Chancery, died in 1848. Maria Templeton Johnson came to live with the family at Gramercy Park.

narrative_blocks.header: Suffragists met in his parlour in 1870
narrative_blocks.body: Norman Wiard built Union artillery in the house after him, and then Margaret E. Winchester ran it as a boarding house. In May 1870 she hosted the meeting there that formed the National Woman's Suffrage Association, with Elizabeth Cady Stanton in the chair.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: No. 23 Gramercy Park South, built 1847.

narrative_blocks.header: The only son of the Gramercy house
narrative_blocks.body: William and Laura Johnson had left No. 23 for Staten Island by the time he was born there in June 1851. He married Caroline Thomas of Baltimore in 1875 and was dead at thirty-nine.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: No. 23 Gramercy Park South, built 1847.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty years a widow
narrative_blocks.body: Oliver Johnson died on Staten Island in 1891, when she was thirty-eight and their youngest was twelve. She lived until 1951 and died in Pennsylvania at ninety-eight.

bio.bio_blurb: The Johnson money behind a diplomatic career

narrative_blocks.header: The Ames family was not rich, she was
narrative_blocks.body: Her grandson put it exactly that way in an oral history: the Ameses had no money and his mother did. She was the only daughter between the architect William Templeton Johnson and the second Oliver.

narrative_blocks.header: She followed the legations south
narrative_blocks.body: She married Ted Ames at the end of 1905 and went with him to Brazil, Argentina and Chile, where their eldest was born in a lumber town in 1907. The family came back and forth to Staten Island for twenty years.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave Balboa Park two of its museums
narrative_blocks.body: The Fine Arts Gallery rose at the head of the Plaza de Panama in 1926 and the Museum of Natural History six years after it, both his. The La Jolla library, the La Valencia, and the Trust & Savings tower on Broadway were his too.

narrative_blocks.header: His father died and he went roofing
narrative_blocks.body: Oliver Johnson died in 1891 and the boy was put to work roofing. That was where the architecture started; Columbia and the École des Beaux-Arts came a long time after.

narrative_blocks.header: He beat six architects to reach Seville
narrative_blocks.body: In 1929 he won a competition against six other men to design the American buildings at the Ibero-American Exposition in Seville. The same year San Diego opened his Serra Museum, got for him by his golfing partner George Marston.

narrative_blocks.header: A park historian called his facade a hodgepodge
narrative_blocks.body: He was told to work ready-made sculpture into the Natural History Museum — Egyptian cats, bison heads, bighorn sheep — and filled the gaps with griffins and sea horses. A historian of the park called the result a hodgepodge of inharmoniously related trivia.

narrative_blocks.header: He died in a house he drew himself
narrative_blocks.body: He was eighty, and the Mission Hills house was his own design. A San Diego paper called him a cultural leader in the city since 1913.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife founded the school he drew
narrative_blocks.body: Clara Sturges started the Francis W. Parker School in 1912 on the Chicago reformer's principles — the child at the centre, action before textbooks. He gave it a Spanish Mission quadrangle and open-air classrooms with sliding doors.

narrative_blocks.header: She lost two daughters in one summer
narrative_blocks.body: Nancy and Anna were both born in 1916 and both died in 1923. She lived another fifty-three years, to ninety-seven, and was buried at West Point beside the colonel.

narrative_blocks.header: His father's Spanish got him the post
narrative_blocks.body: Azel Ames had vaccinated Puerto Rico and come home with the language, and friends of his got the son into the diplomatic service. Ted took a minor secretaryship at Petrópolis, then Buenos Aires, and spoke excellent Spanish and passable Portuguese.

narrative_blocks.header: He was made to give up baseball
narrative_blocks.body: His father told him that if he became a successful baseball player his life would grow too expensive to pay for, and that he should play cricket instead. He played cricket at Harvard, and then at the Staten Island Cricket Club.

narrative_blocks.header: The cricket club was two hundred yards away
narrative_blocks.body: Katherine Johnson's family lived a couple of hundred yards from the Staten Island Cricket Club, where the north-shore British still played. They married at the end of 1905 and he took her to South America.

narrative_blocks.header: He sold technical books to Latin America
narrative_blocks.body: After the legations and the lumber company he traded under the name America South of Us, sending North American technical books south and bringing books about Latin America back. His son remembered him as tall, courtly and very good in clothes.

narrative_blocks.header: She founded a school and he drew it
narrative_blocks.body: In 1912 she started the Francis W. Parker School on the principles of the Chicago reformer it was named for: the child at the centre of learning, action before textbooks, citizenship as the point. All four of her children went through it.

narrative_blocks.header: She had known Coronado since it opened
narrative_blocks.body: Her family had been holidaying at the Hotel del Coronado since soon after 1888, so San Diego was no strange place when she and Templeton settled there in 1912. They came straight off a European tour and he opened his practice.

narrative_blocks.header: She cooked in the front trenches at dawn
narrative_blocks.body: She lived with two other women in the cellar of a bombed cottage near the Belgian border and set out at half past five every morning with soup and hot chocolate for men who had spent the night in the mud. She drove for the Red Cross the rest of the day, and the guns were two hundred yards ahead.

narrative_blocks.header: Belgium made her a Chevalier
narrative_blocks.body: The king gave her the Order of Leopold, the country's highest honour, and the British War Office gave her the 1914 Star. She was the first woman decorated as a Chevalier.

narrative_blocks.header: She went where the people she loved were
narrative_blocks.body: “I went to the war because those whom I loved were in the war,” she said. “I wished to go where they were.” She was a Coe College music major studying in France when it broke out.

narrative_blocks.header: A war novel was written about her
narrative_blocks.body: Arthur Gleason, a Collier's correspondent, made her the subject of Young Hilda at the Wars. Golden Lads was the joint account of what the two of them saw in Belgium.

narrative_blocks.header: A pianist running a naval hospital's mornings
narrative_blocks.body: She trained in music and went to work for the American Red Cross in San Diego, programming recreation and social hours for the patients at the naval hospital in Balboa Park. She married the architect in 1935.

narrative_blocks.header: Born in Paris during the training
narrative_blocks.body: William Johnson was three years into the École des Beaux-Arts when the boy arrived in Paris in May 1908, his father thirty and his mother twenty-nine. The family sailed for San Diego four years later.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a Colorado girl in 1933
narrative_blocks.body: Julia Ethel Porter came out of Delta, on the western slope, and they married on the second of February in the worst year of the Depression. They were together sixty-seven years, until he died.

narrative_blocks.header: His son was born in Honolulu in 1940
narrative_blocks.body: William Shepard Johnson arrived at Honolulu in May 1940, nineteen months before the harbour was bombed. Del and Julia both ended their lives back in Ramona, in the hills east of San Diego.

narrative_blocks.header: Del, and never Arthur
narrative_blocks.body: He carried his mother's family name, Delafield, as his middle one and went by the back half of it all his life. His brothers were Winthrop and Alan and his sister was Katharine.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Balboa Park, San Diego — designed by William Templeton Johnson, 1932.

narrative_blocks.header: He married out of his own class year
narrative_blocks.body: He and Barbara Hoel were both graduated from U.C.L.A. and married at St. Paul's Episcopal in 1939, with his brother Winthrop as best man and his brother Arthur among the ushers. His sister Katharine came west to be a bridesmaid.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at ninety-four in his own town
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Coronado in 1914 and died in San Diego in 2008. Of the four Johnson children he lived the longest by a good margin.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Balboa Park, San Diego — designed by William Templeton Johnson, 1932.
Lincoln Park, Chicago — namesake of the progressive school Clara Sturges Johnson founded in San Diego in 1912.

narrative_blocks.header: Kappa Kappa Gamma, U.C.L.A. 1938
narrative_blocks.body: She came out of Claremont, the daughter of Arthur Helmer Hoel, and took her degree at U.C.L.A. in the same class as the man she married. She was a Kappa Kappa Gamma; he was a Phi Gamma Delta.

narrative_blocks.header: Two students married mid-degree
narrative_blocks.body: She came up from Houston in September 1963 to marry Peter Moursund at the First Christian Church in Eugene, and both went straight back to the University of Oregon — she a junior in liberal arts, he a senior in history. Her grandparents came from Claremont for it.

narrative_blocks.header: He worked the other side of the case
narrative_blocks.body: He read history at the University of Oregon and spent his working life as a defense investigator, belonging to the state association of legal investigators. He gardened and worked wood, and volunteered with the Oregon State Police at Florence.

narrative_blocks.header: His father died when he was eight
narrative_blocks.body: Oliver Templeton Johnson died on Staten Island in January 1891, leaving him at eight with three older sisters and brothers. He married Mary Lea in 1909 and died in Manhattan in 1944.

narrative_blocks.header: Married in the Fort Myer chapel on Thanksgiving
narrative_blocks.body: She came down from Staten Island to marry a West Point lieutenant of the class of 1936 at four in the afternoon on Thanksgiving Day. The reception was at the Army-Navy Club and he took her to Fort Sill.

narrative_blocks.header: Winthrop on one side, Allerton on the other
narrative_blocks.body: The papers said she came down from Gov. Winthrop of Massachusetts on her father's side and from Lieut. Gov. Allerton on her mother's, and was a great-granddaughter of Don Alonzo Cushman. She was given out as a niece of the Eric Kings of Foxhall Village.

narrative_blocks.header: He grew up facing the Jefferson Davis casemate
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Fort Monroe in 1875, where his father commanded, and he and his twin sister Mabel lived in one of the paired quarters the post called the Tuilleries. It looked across at the casemate where Jefferson Davis had been held.

narrative_blocks.header: His headstone gives the wrong year
narrative_blocks.body: The stone at West Point says 1962. The academy's alumni records and the Pennsylvania record of burial both put his death on the twenty-sixth of September 1960.

narrative_blocks.header: He put Taps at the end of funerals
narrative_blocks.body: In 1862 he was credited with sounding the call over a burial in the field, and the custom stayed in the army afterwards. He commanded the horse artillery of the Army of the Potomac and Lincoln complimented him in person for Gettysburg.

narrative_blocks.header: Five brevets, a battlefield at a time
narrative_blocks.body: He was brevetted major for Gaines' Mill, lieutenant colonel for Antietam, brigadier general for the Po River, Spotsylvania and Petersburg, and colonel for Fort Stedman. He went from First Bull Run to Appomattox and was still a captain of regulars through most of it.

narrative_blocks.header: He met Lee at Harper's Ferry in 1859
narrative_blocks.body: He went out with the expedition sent to put down John Brown's raid, and found Robert E. Lee taking pains to call personally on every officer billeted about the place. Scrupulous in dress, he wrote, and with none of the airs of foppishness.

narrative_blocks.header: The army learned its guns from his book
narrative_blocks.body: His Manual of Heavy Artillery Service of 1880 was the army's guide for decades, and he wrote the standard account of the artillery service in the rebellion. Fort Tidball on Kodiak Island and a battery at Fort Randolph in Panama carry his name.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote down what Stonewall Jackson was like
narrative_blocks.body: He had been in Jackson's cadet company at West Point and remembered a shambling, blushing, squeaky-voiced student who walked through downpours without changing pace. His memoirs did the same for Burnside, Lee and Sherman.

narrative_blocks.header: He governed Alaska from a fort
narrative_blocks.body: He was the third commander of the Department of Alaska, the military government of the territory before there were governors, and lived up there six years. Afterwards he was aide-de-camp to Sherman for three.

narrative_blocks.body: Napoleon Dana was only three years older than the man who wanted his daughter and six years ahead of him at West Point, and twenty years older than she was. He gave way on Tidball's reputation and the plain affection between them.

narrative_blocks.header: He was given an empty museum
narrative_blocks.body: Paul Sachs put him into the Lyman Allyn at New London in 1930, while the building was still going up and the collection was empty. He filled it with drawings, prints and sculpture, and stayed twelve years.

narrative_blocks.header: He built two prefabs on museum ground
narrative_blocks.body: He saw General Houses at the Chicago fair in 1933 and put up a House of Steel and a Moto Home on the museum's land, believing the factory house was the future. The Winslow Ames House is on the National Register.

narrative_blocks.header: He registered as a conscientious objector
narrative_blocks.body: A pacifist, he spent the war in Civilian Public Service camps in Virginia and Ohio, then went to Paris for the Friends and ran the European Transport Unit, moving displaced people back to their farms.

narrative_blocks.header: He spent a year on Prince Albert's taste
narrative_blocks.body: After the war he studied Victorian art in England and Germany, which turned into Prince Albert and Victorian Taste in 1967. He also put Joseph Meder's great manual of drawing into English.

narrative_blocks.header: He took notes from a rented wheelchair
narrative_blocks.body: He and a friend hired self-propelled chairs at the Metropolitan so they could sit and sketch the paintings, and enjoyed the pity of passers-by. He would sometimes stand up suddenly to tease them.

narrative_blocks.header: Born in a Chilean lumber town
narrative_blocks.body: His father had left the legations for a lumber company on the Alto Paraná, and he arrived at Maullín in July 1907. He said he remembered nothing whatever of Chile.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a Johnson, as her mother was
narrative_blocks.body: Theodore Woolsey Johnson Jr. was her third cousin once removed: both lines run back to William Walton Woolsey and Elizabeth Dwight, hers through Laura Winthrop and his through Sara Woolsey. They had four children.

narrative_blocks.header: His name was given again two years on
narrative_blocks.body: He was born in 1816 and died in 1826, at ten. Two years later his parents had another son and called him Theodore Woolsey Winthrop as well; that one was killed at Big Bethel.

narrative_blocks.header: She carried her mother's name entire
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth Woolsey Winthrop the elder gave her every part of her own name. The daughter lived to 1907 and outlasted all five of her brothers and sisters.

notable.notable_blurb: Novelist; first Union officer killed, 1861

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Grove Street Cemetery, New Haven — the granite cross he asked his mother for.

military_service.unit: Seventh Regiment, New York State Militia
military_service.role: Killed at Big Bethel, believed the first Union officer killed in battle

naming_inspiration.description: Named for the brother who died in 1826, two years before he was born.

career.role: Major and aide-de-camp to Maj. Gen. Benjamin Butler
career.organization: Seventh Regiment, New York State Militia

cross_connections.display_label: appeared in the Atlantic's first number, as he did in its war ones
fell rallying a broken regiment too, fifteen months later
, a Dwight cousin, wrote Richard Carvel, which sold two million copies
was jailed in occupied Norfolk under Gen. Benjamin Butler
was a grandson of Gen. Benjamin Butler, the general he served

narrative_blocks.header: Gen. Butler credited him with the contraband idea
narrative_blocks.body: As aide-de-camp to Maj. Gen. Benjamin Butler, commander of the Union's Department of Virginia at Fort Monroe, Winthrop framed the policy that freed escaped slaves the moment they reached Union lines. Butler said afterwards the formulation was Winthrop's.

narrative_blocks.header: He shouted it from a fallen tree
narrative_blocks.body: The Union attack at Big Bethel had broken and he climbed onto a fallen trunk to turn the retreat — one more charge, boys, and the day is ours. A Minié ball took him through the heart.

narrative_blocks.header: Four men claimed to have killed him
narrative_blocks.body: Three soldiers of the 1st North Carolina and an enslaved man known in the records only as Sam, servant to one of their officers, each said the shot was his. Winthrop had spent his life against slavery.

narrative_blocks.header: He asked to die in his first battle
narrative_blocks.body: Ten years before Big Bethel he wrote that he did not want to waste his power in skirmishes. In the hour of deadly conflict may I nobly die, he wrote; in my first battle perish gloriously.

narrative_blocks.header: His novels all appeared after Big Bethel
narrative_blocks.body: Cecil Dreeme, John Brent, Edwin Brothertoft and The Canoe and the Saddle all appeared after Big Bethel. James Russell Lowell started the run at the Atlantic Monthly with his march-to-Washington piece, printed the month he was killed.

narrative_blocks.header: He refused to call it Mount Rainier
narrative_blocks.body: He guarded bullion for the Pacific Mail, caught smallpox on the northwest coast and rode three hundred miles over the shoulder of the mountain. Mountains should not be insulted by being named after undistinguished bipeds, he wrote; he used the name Tacoma.

narrative_blocks.header: A Washington town took his name
narrative_blocks.body: The Canoe and the Saddle, his account of riding through Washington Territory, sold so well after his death that the town of Winthrop, Washington, and the Winthrop Hotel in Tacoma were both named for him.

bio.title: Colonel
bio.bio_blurb: The nation's leading authority on military law

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the book on military law
narrative_blocks.body: He joined the artillery of the Seventh New York with his brother in 1861, Yale of '51 to Theodore's '48. He became the country's leading authority on military law.

narrative_blocks.header: He brought his brother's casket home
narrative_blocks.body: The Confederates gave Theodore's body back to him in a battlefield ceremony a week after Big Bethel. He carried it to New Haven, where a military procession and the students of Yale walked it to Grove Street.

notable.notable_blurb: Sanitarian who vaccinated Puerto Rico, 1899

cross_connections.display_label: drove malaria out of a North Carolina mill town with mosquito control
chaired international hygiene at the 1887 medical congress

narrative_blocks.header: He vaccinated an entire island
narrative_blocks.body: Sent to Puerto Rico as a major and brigadier surgeon of volunteers in 1899, he directed the programme that vaccinated the island's population against smallpox. His son got into the diplomatic service partly on the Spanish he brought home.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the drains for other men's cities
narrative_blocks.body: He gave up practice for public sanitation and was engaged to draw the health and drainage regulations of many large cities, sat on the Massachusetts State Drainage Commission, and went twice as the country's delegate to international sanitary conferences.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded a town's water and health board
narrative_blocks.body: At Wakefield, where he lived for years, he started both the water company and the board of health. In 1879 the town sent him to the legislature, where he was secretary of the committee on public health.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the log of the Mayflower
narrative_blocks.body: His books ran from The Mayflower and Its Log to Sex in Industry, Elementary Hygiene for the Tropics and The Family of John Philips. He was a genealogist as much as a physician.

narrative_blocks.header: His last years were spent as a patient
narrative_blocks.body: He was at Danvers State Hospital, then called the hospital for the insane, for a number of years before he died there in November 1908 at sixty-three.

narrative_blocks.header: She was his fraternity brother's sister
narrative_blocks.body: Winslow Ames met her through William Gerhard of Delta Psi and married her at St. Peter's in Philadelphia in June 1931. Their bookplate carried the Ames motto, fame is sweeter than the white rose.

military_service.unit: USS New York BB-34, USS Reid DD-292, USS Benjamin Franklin CV-13, USS Essex CV-9
military_service.role: Also served at the U.S. Naval Academy and the Bureau of Aeronautics, Washington

narrative_blocks.header: Told to sit down, he kept talking
narrative_blocks.body: He fought the city for public showers and restrooms at City Dock, and when a council member told him to sit down the room objected so loudly that he was allowed to finish. A Master Swimmer, he wanted the water open to everyone.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty years in the Naval Reserve
narrative_blocks.body: He was in from June 1925 to June 1955 and retired a commander. He served aboard the New York, the Reid, the Benjamin Franklin and the Essex, and ashore at the Naval Academy and the Bureau of Aeronautics.

narrative_blocks.header: The harbormaster's building took his name
narrative_blocks.body: Alderman Gil Cochran carried the resolution that put his name on the Annapolis harbormaster building, and a wooden plaque hung there for decades. The city gave it back to his daughter Alice, and it goes next to her grandson.

narrative_blocks.header: His first marriage ended before the war
narrative_blocks.body: Evangeline Stine married him in July 1925 and their daughter Derland came the following May, but by 1933 she had married Frank Jones. He afterwards married Millicent Ames, a third cousin once removed, and had four children with her.

career.organization: Saranac Lake Study and Craft Guild

education.school_name: Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts
Art Students League of New York
Eliot O’Hara watercolor school, Goose Rocks Beach, Maine

cross_connections.display_label: left the same Academy to teach crafts in Philadelphia
was grandson to the Trudeau whose sanatorium the Guild served

narrative_blocks.header: Three art schools in six years
narrative_blocks.body: She went from the Maryland Institute of Design to the Pennsylvania Academy and then the Art Students League, and in 1929 studied watercolor under Eliot O’Hara on a Maine beach.

narrative_blocks.header: She ran the metal shop at Saranac Lake
narrative_blocks.body: She had a one-man show at the Studio Guild in New York in 1940, and from 1942 to 1950 supervised the metal shop at the Saranac Lake Study and Craft Guild.

narrative_blocks.header: She married at twenty and went west
narrative_blocks.body: She married Henry Van Bergen Larom at Annapolis in April 1928, four months after turning twenty. Their second son was born in Wyoming in 1932, and she died at Albuquerque in 1971.

narrative_blocks.header: She married twice in eight years
narrative_blocks.body: She married Theodore Johnson in July 1925 and their daughter Derland was born the following May. By July 1933 she had married Frank Joseph Jones Jr., and she died at forty-three in 1950.

naming_inspiration.description: Named for his father's brother, LTJG Webster Cochran Johnson, killed in a Navy plane in December 1940, eleven years before this Webster was born.

career.organization: Darrow, Wilmington Friends, Mercersburg, Gilman, Park and Randolph-Macon

narrative_blocks.header: He taught the math and coached the team
narrative_blocks.body: He played varsity basketball at Lehigh and took a Maryland teaching certificate, then spent his career at Darrow, Wilmington Friends, Mercersburg, Gilman, Park and Randolph-Macon. He was assistant coach at Delaware, Johns Hopkins and Washington College.

narrative_blocks.header: He was named for the pilot uncle
narrative_blocks.body: His father's brother Webster Cochran Johnson went down in a Navy plane outside Norfolk in December 1940. This Webster was born eleven years later and given the name.

narrative_blocks.header: He sold houses in his own county
narrative_blocks.body: After the schools he became a realtor around Annapolis, where he had been born in 1951. He died suddenly at Front Royal in January 2016, four days short of sixty-five.

bio.bio_blurb: Wrote the Mountain Pony books for boys

notable.notable_blurb: Wrote the Mountain Pony books for boys

career.role: Founding dean and head of English

cross_connections.display_label: came to Saranac Lake for the cure in 1905 and died of it in 1909
grew up in the Riverside Drive house bought for a cure in 1910

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote six horse books for boys
narrative_blocks.body: The Mountain Pony series, set in the Wyoming Rockies, ran from 1946 to 1958 and was translated into French and other languages. Two of them took the Boys' Club of America award.

narrative_blocks.header: He came home sick and wrote a book
narrative_blocks.body: His first book was written at Saranac Lake after he went back there for his health. Before that he had been in a New York advertising agency, in motion pictures, and doing editorial work for the New Yorker.

narrative_blocks.header: No dean of his who never taught
narrative_blocks.body: Made founding dean of Rockland Community College in 1959, he said he meant to be a teaching educator and was rude in print about the sort who will not. He took the English department as well, and a Chancellor’s Award for teaching.

narrative_blocks.header: He waited until the end to write poems
narrative_blocks.body: Backtrail came out in 1974, the year before he died, and was the only poetry he ever wrote. One of them puts a boy awake on a Saranac Lake sleeping porch in 1910, listening to sleigh bells going toward a midnight hemorrhage.

narrative_blocks.header: A prize at Rockland still carries his name
narrative_blocks.body: The Henry V. Larom Award goes each year to a student story and a student poem at the college he founded. He had run its writers' conference guests from Van Wyck Brooks to Allan Nevins.

narrative_blocks.header: Born in Berlin during the study years
narrative_blocks.body: Her father was four years into an eight-year stay in Germany and Austria when she arrived at Berlin in December 1889. Her mother was Austrian.

naming_inspiration.description: Given both of her mother's names.

bio.title: Major
bio.bio_blurb: Civil War major of the Cheney silk family

cross_connections.display_label: , his first cousin, came home from Antietam with a shattered elbow

narrative_blocks.header: A major out of the silk mills
narrative_blocks.body: He came out of the Cheney silk-manufacturing family of Manchester and served as a major in the Civil War. He married a Cheney cousin of his own name and year of birth.

bio.bio_blurb: She mended the quarrel that made his career

narrative_blocks.header: She repaired the friendship he had wrecked
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband had fallen out badly with Robert Emerson, the man who first taught him photosynthesis, and she was the one who put it back together. They married at Cambridge in December 1938 and had fifty-four years.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father ran the first Lowell House
narrative_blocks.body: Julian Lowell Coolidge was the first master of Lowell House at Harvard, and the geometer who chaired the mathematics department. She went west with a botanist and died at San Mateo in 1992.

bio.bio_blurb: Photosynthesis pioneer; the French press bears his name

notable.notable_blurb: Photosynthesis pioneer; the French press bears his name

cross_connections.display_label: founded American plant ecology a generation before him
studies how plants move, as he studied how they eat
was a regular contributor to the Appalachian Mountain Club journal
was at Loomis with him, and graduated in the Class of 1925

narrative_blocks.header: The French press in every protein lab
narrative_blocks.body: Vannevar Bush, head of the Carnegie Institution, suggested forcing cells through a fixed hole; Stacy used an ammonia needle valve instead, driving chloroplasts through it with a piston so the shear at the valve tore them open. Labs still crack bacteria that way.

narrative_blocks.header: His name on the press was Bush's idea
narrative_blocks.body: When the American Instrument Company began making the press, Bush told Stacy to ask for his name on it and a free one for the lab. The name went on at once; the free press came twenty years later, and he drove it with an old car jack.

narrative_blocks.header: A year of Warburg saved his career
narrative_blocks.body: Barely on speaking terms with his Caltech chief, he was sent instead to Otto Warburg in Berlin, lived in the laboratory building and worked without distraction. He said he was grateful to Warburg for refusing to speak English, though he could do it better.

narrative_blocks.header: He failed his first year at Loomis
narrative_blocks.body: He repeated it, and the school later refused him permission to sit the Harvard entrance so as not to spoil its record. His mother put him through a year of Lowell High School and a summer course in botany got him in.

narrative_blocks.header: A mouse in the monochromator
narrative_blocks.body: When the readings came out wrong he found a mouse had moved into one of his big homemade monochromators. Afterwards he liked to blame an odd result on the mouse peering out the slit.

narrative_blocks.header: He climbed the Matterhorn in the twenties
narrative_blocks.body: He went up it before that was a common thing to do, helped build the Appalachian Mountain Club hut at Franconia Notch, and took Whitney, Shasta, Hood and Rainier. In 1934 he was with Norman Clyde's party that opened a new route on Shasta's Hotlum Glacier.

narrative_blocks.header: He grew penicillin from grapefruit rinds
narrative_blocks.body: To stay out of the draft he collected his Minnesota neighbours' rinds and grew penicillin on them for war use, and worked up a chlorophyll paint for camouflage. He mended his own trousers once with a stapler.

bio.title: Lieutenant Colonel
bio.bio_blurb: Antietam wound; treasurer of Cheney Brothers silk

landmarks.landmark_blurb: The Hartford silk mill, sold off the year before he died.

documents.blurb: His letter home from Boonsboro, two days after Antietam.

military_service.role: Wounded at the Lower Bridge, Antietam; discharged for disability

career.organization: New York, New Haven & Hartford Railroad

cross_connections.display_label: , his granddaughter, married into the Scoville and Beecher line
, his first cousin, left the same silk mills for the same war
was his niece, and married into the Chicago Tribune's Cowles family
was a private of his regiment, wounded with it at Antietam

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years treasurer of Cheney Brothers
narrative_blocks.body: He left Brown for the family silk house and after the war took the treasurership, holding it for life. The Manchester mills were the whole economy of the town.

narrative_blocks.header: He went to China to learn the trade
narrative_blocks.body: He spent two years in China and Japan before the war, settling the grading of raw silk and buying direct from the filatures. He had no liking for office, but let them run him for lieutenant governor in 1892.

narrative_blocks.header: A shot shattered his elbow at the bridge
narrative_blocks.body: He took his raw recruits to the Lower Bridge at Antietam on 17 September 1862 and was hit that afternoon. They dressed the arm in the Rohrbach parlour; he nearly lost it, and his life, and was discharged in December.

narrative_blocks.header: Hartford read that he had been killed
narrative_blocks.body: The Courant crowed that the rebel army had been captured or annihilated, and five days later the casualty lists carried his name among the dead. He was writing to his father from a Boonsboro hotel that the bullet through his arm was by no means dangerous.

narrative_blocks.header: His men did not know how to drill
narrative_blocks.body: The 16th Connecticut went to the front on 29 August 1862, a thousand men wholly ignorant of drill. He had never seen such waste of life, he said, and would not speak of the field hospital again.

narrative_blocks.header: His father's house was the first station
narrative_blocks.body: The Cheneys farmed at Mount Healthy north of Cincinnati, the first stop out of the city on the underground road. He was let into the secret at ten, and knew the knock on the window at night.

narrative_blocks.header: He told it to a club in 1901
narrative_blocks.body: Forty years on he read a paper to the Hartford Monday Evening Club on the black-curtained wagon that ran to Hamilton and the toll-keepers who saw nothing. Salmon P. Chase had been a visitor.

bio.bio_blurb: Hartford Art School founder; Horace Bushnell's daughter

landmarks.landmark_blurb: A founder, 1877

documents.blurb: Her side of the correspondence, gathered and printed in 1988.

cross_connections.display_label: was another of the school's five founders, and Mark Twain's wife
built the Wadsworth Atheneum, which housed her school from 1877
, her granddaughter, married Charles Hooker Talcott in 1937

narrative_blocks.header: She helped found Hartford's art school in 1877
narrative_blocks.body: In 1877 she and four other Hartford women — Harriet Beecher Stowe, Olivia Clemens, Elizabeth Colt and Susan Warner — opened the Hartford School for Decorative Arts. It met in the Wadsworth Atheneum, and is now the Hartford Art School of the University of Hartford.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father unpicked New England Calvinism
narrative_blocks.body: Horace Bushnell broke with the vengeful theology he was raised in and argued in Christian Nurture that a child should be brought up a Christian rather than converted into one. His paper of 1837 helped start a generation of colleges in the West.

narrative_blocks.header: She came to console them and he answered
narrative_blocks.body: The casualty lists after Antietam carried Frank Cheney among the dead. Mary Bushnell went to his parents' house to pay a call of condolence, and Frank opened the door to welcome her.

narrative_blocks.header: He could never overwhelm her
narrative_blocks.body: They married in November 1863, weeks after he came home wounded from Antietam. He wrote that some of her family thought him overbearing, but that she was the one person he could never overwhelm.

narrative_blocks.header: Her sister called him a thunder clap
narrative_blocks.body: Frank's letter pressing for an early wedding was a thunder clap, her sister wrote in 1863 — everyone gives up to him, everyone bows before him. You will never sip the nectar of existence, she warned; you will take it scalding hot.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandmother took him on trust
narrative_blocks.body: The old Boston grandmother wrote that she did not know Mr. Cheney, not even his personal appearance, but took him on trust in her granddaughter's judgment. Where there is a true and loyal spirit, she added, it will be carried into all the relations of life.

narrative_blocks.header: A perfect woman nobly planned
narrative_blocks.body: The Courant said in 1917 that she had her father's intellectual gifts and a home known far and wide for its hospitality. Edwin Parker reached for Wordsworth — a perfect woman nobly planned, to warn, to comfort and command. A friend of sixty years remembered a high, independent, fearless spirit.

people.relational_label_override: Mother-in-law & Grandmother-in-law of Hooker Descendants

bio.bio_blurb: Fifty-five years with Cheney Brothers silk

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-five years in the same house
narrative_blocks.body: He went from Yale in 1900 straight into Cheney Brothers and resigned as chairman of the board in June 1955, five months before he died. He was a director of the Pioneer Parachute Company in the same town.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought the war its scarce cloth
narrative_blocks.body: In the First World War he directed the Textile Alliance, the government agency that imported fabrics American industry could not get. Afterwards he ran the Textile Foundation, which paid the Alliance's earnings back into the trade.

narrative_blocks.header: He lost a daughter at twenty-seven
narrative_blocks.body: Hope was married from his drawing room at Manchester in January 1937 and dead before the end of 1940. He outlived her by fifteen years and his wife survived him by four.

people.relational_label_override: Father-in-law of a Tenth Generation Hooker

bio.bio_blurb: Of the Amory and Otis families of Boston

narrative_blocks.header: She brought Boston into the silk town
narrative_blocks.body: She was married from Chicago in June 1904 and belonged to the Amory and Otis families of Boston. Four of her five children outlived her; Hope did not.

people.relational_label_override: Mother-in-law of a Tenth Generation Hooker

narrative_blocks.header: She died at thirty-three
narrative_blocks.body: She married Charles Snowdon in 1947 and their son came three years later. She died in Kentucky in June 1955 and was buried at Brownsville, in the Pennsylvania county she came to.

narrative_blocks.header: He raced bikes up and down mountains
narrative_blocks.body: Road and mountain biking, skiing, golf and volleyball — he competed at all of them and drew other people into them. He died in Colorado at sixty-six.

narrative_blocks.header: She typed for a senator on the Hill
narrative_blocks.body: Out of the Masters School and a Pittsburgh secretarial course, one of her first jobs was secretary to Senator Gaylord Nelson, and she loved the work. Afterwards came Pressley Ridge, the Colonial Dames and the Garden Club of Allegheny County.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-nine years, and a daughter lost
narrative_blocks.body: She was married to David Smith for fifty-nine years. Their daughter Tina died in 1981; her grandsons called her Omah, and Alzheimer's took her at eighty.

bio.title: Admiral
bio.bio_blurb: CINCPAC in Vietnam; they called him Mr. Seapower

death.notes: On a military aircraft over the North Atlantic
death.city: At sea over the North Atlantic

notable.notable_blurb: CINCPAC in Vietnam; they called him Mr. Seapower

military_service.role: Silver Star and Bronze Star as a submarine commander; later CINCPAC

cross_connections.link_text: Rear Adm. Henry Sturgis Morgan Jr.
cross_connections.display_label: , his son-in-law, was a rear admiral too
was killed at Khe Sanh three months before he took the theatre
took his ship into the ironclad at Mobile Bay to shield Farragut
ran the Phnom Penh embassy in the theatre he commanded
built Henderson Field in 1942 on his father's orders

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-six hours down off Shanghai
narrative_blocks.body: In June 1943 the Gunnel sank two freighters off Tsushima and was hunted for a day and a half, most of it submerged, until the batteries failed and the air went foul. He surfaced at battle stations ready to fight and found the escorts gone.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave the orders over his son's prison
narrative_blocks.body: He commanded the whole Vietnam theatre from 1968 while his son was a prisoner in Hanoi, and the daily bombing orders named the city where the boy was held. Every Christmas he went up to the DMZ and stood alone looking north.

narrative_blocks.header: Nineteenth from the bottom of his class
narrative_blocks.body: He came out of Annapolis in 1931 ranked 423rd of 441, having spent his last year banished from the barracks to a receiving ship. He was rejected for flight school over a heart murmur and placed 28th of 29 at submarine school.

narrative_blocks.header: They called him Mr. Seapower
narrative_blocks.body: As chief legislative liaison he turned a Capitol Hill house into a room where senators, congressmen and admirals met, and he talked Congress into restoring the carrier money it had cut. Not everyone meant the nickname kindly.

narrative_blocks.header: He commanded everything, not just the Navy
narrative_blocks.body: Pacific Command answered for better than a million soldiers, sailors and airmen — the largest operational command in the American military. He held it four years, from 1968 until he retired in 1972.

narrative_blocks.header: Cambodia was the war he called his own
narrative_blocks.body: He pressed Nixon into the 1970 Cambodian incursion and took personal control of the arms going to Lon Nol, who recuperated at his Honolulu guesthouse after a stroke. Lon Nol sent him an elephant, too big for his plane, named Cincpachyderm.

narrative_blocks.header: Four stars, father and son
narrative_blocks.body: His father Slew McCain commanded the fast carriers and died four days after the Japanese surrender; they were the first father and son to hold four-star rank. He eloped to Tijuana in 1933 and was suspended five days for leaving his ship.

people.research_notes: [081226] Two blocks added on what CINCPAC actually meant, from the material Sam supplied. NOT WRITTEN, available for later: he was a domino-theory man famous inside the Pentagon for 'Chicom' briefings with red claws drawn out of China; he backed Vietnamization and was relatively optimistic in the 1969 National Security Study Memorandum 1 responses; he advocated Operation Lam Son 719 into Laos in 1971, which failed; he had a mild stroke around 1969 and was back in a month; Kissinger said 'we have to be careful about having McCain around the president too much, because he fires up the president'; he asked Nixon to extend his tour to see the war finish and was refused; Nixon said at his 1972 handover, 'in the story of the McCains we see the greatness of America'. His annual Christmas trip to the troops nearest the DMZ, where he stood alone and looked north toward his son, is written on the SON's card rather than here, so it is told once.

bio.bio_blurb: Her Capitol Hill parlour was her husband's ladder

narrative_blocks.header: She eloped to Tijuana at twenty
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother objected to her going about with a sailor, so she and the ensign crossed into Baja California and married in a bar in January 1933. Her father was a Los Angeles oil wildcatter who had retired to raise the children.

narrative_blocks.header: The house did the work of a campaign
narrative_blocks.body: Her Capitol Hill parlour drew Carl Vinson, Richard Russell and Everett Dirksen to breakfast, and Mountbatten and Clare Boothe Luce besides. His superiors thought her charm was half of why his career moved.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived two of her children
narrative_blocks.body: She was a hundred and eight when she died, two years and seven weeks after her son the senator and eleven months after her daughter Sandy. She had campaigned across the country for him at ninety-six.

people.relational_label_override: Sister-in-law & Grandmother-in-law of Hooker Descendants

cross_connections.display_label: , her brother-in-law, founded the Wadsworth Atheneum
, her elder sister, lived childless at Monte Video

narrative_blocks.header: She enrolled in his first class for ladies
narrative_blocks.body: In 1808 Silliman taught a course of popular chemistry for ladies and gentlemen in the Yale laboratory, the first of its kind. She was one of the women who signed up for it, and they married the following September.

narrative_blocks.header: Her uncle moved in with his paintings
narrative_blocks.body: John Trumbull the painter lived out his last years with them at Hillhouse Avenue and Trumbull Street. Through that arrangement Yale acquired his pictures and opened the Trumbull Gallery in 1832 — the first university art gallery in America.

narrative_blocks.header: Her granddaughters signed the register first
narrative_blocks.body: When the Yale School of the Fine Arts opened to both sexes in 1869, the first two names on the page were Alice and Susan Silliman, daughters of her son Benjamin. Her uncle's gallery had led directly to the school.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine children, four gone before three
narrative_blocks.body: She bore them between 1810 and 1826. Jonathan Trumbull died at five, Charles at three, Harriet inside her first year, Edward before he was two. The five who lived carried the family into American science.

narrative_blocks.header: Her sister's marriage built a museum
narrative_blocks.body: Faith married Daniel Wadsworth in 1794 and had no children, so what would have gone to a son went into the first public art gallery in America. Harriet's own share of the Trumbull inheritance went into laboratories.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote to her sister for five years
narrative_blocks.body: Eleven of her letters to Faith Wadsworth, written between 1827 and 1832, sit in the Wadsworth family papers at Yale. They lie beside fourteen of Daniel's to Faith and Faith's own two notebooks, kept from 1803 until she died.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the bank that became Citibank
narrative_blocks.body: Astor made him a director in 1837 and he took the presidency in 1855, holding it until he died. He insisted on heavy cash reserves so there was always ready money to lend, and the bank came through three national panics stronger each time.

narrative_blocks.header: He never once went to Cuba
narrative_blocks.body: He brokered for planters he never met, working through Henry Augustus Coit, who had the Spanish. The plantations that grew his sugar were worked by enslaved people, and Citi has since acknowledged that an early president's outside businesses profited from that labour; others have charged him with financing the illegal trade in people itself.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought the railroad at the bottom
narrative_blocks.body: The Panic of 1857 brought the Delaware, Lackawanna & Western to the edge of bankruptcy and he took control by buying up its outstanding shares. Within seven years they were worth dozens of times what he paid, and the line was among the country's first.

narrative_blocks.header: He signed the whitewash for Tweed
narrative_blocks.body: In 1871 he was one of three eminent businessmen asked to examine the books of the City of New York before an election. They reported Tweed's comptroller honest, and the press pilloried them as stooges of Tammany. Nast drew him into the cartoon.

narrative_blocks.header: A hospital for the men who dug coal
narrative_blocks.body: At the end of his life he gave to build a hospital at Scranton for the workers of his railroad and of the Lackawanna Iron & Coal Company. The Moses Taylor Hospital is still open.

narrative_blocks.header: He backed the cable across the Atlantic
narrative_blocks.body: He put money into Cyrus Field's telegraph company in 1854 and stayed with it through several failures. The line went through in 1866.
