narrative_blocks.header: She never cared for society
narrative_blocks.body: She was of a retiring disposition, religious and charitable, and a generation had gone by in which many who knew her husband and her children had forgotten there was a Mrs. Taylor at all.

narrative_blocks.header: She left the Episcopalians late in life
narrative_blocks.body: She was raised Low Church and went over to the Presbyterians in her last twenty years. She died a member of Dr. Hall's congregation.

narrative_blocks.header: She lived alone at 122 Fifth Avenue
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband's will left her the house and the place at Elberon for her lifetime. It was one of the last old houses on a street given over to shops and clubs, and she had her children and grandchildren there quietly. It came down soon after she died.

narrative_blocks.header: A tradesman's daughter, married very young
narrative_blocks.body: Her father was a New York tradesman named Wilson. She married Moses Taylor when she was a very young girl and he was still a self-made man in the making.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son-in-law went six weeks before her
narrative_blocks.body: Robert Winthrop died in November 1892 and she followed on the last day of the year. Four of his children were named in her notice: Albertina, Robert Dudley, Grenville Lindall and Frederic.

narrative_blocks.header: Her second son flew the mail
narrative_blocks.body: Kenneth Frick Lovejoy, whom they called Curley, was among the first air mail pilots, flying out of Bettis Field near Pittsburgh. He was born in 1896 and outlived her by six years.

narrative_blocks.header: Her eldest died at twenty-two
narrative_blocks.body: Francis Fleming Lovejoy was born in 1894 and gone by 1916. She and her husband and all three children lie together in the Allegheny burying ground.

narrative_blocks.header: Six months to make a carpenter
narrative_blocks.body: ARCH was the only programme in the District that put housing for the homeless and training for the unskilled in the same building. About two hundred and twenty-five people came through its classrooms and work sites, a third of them homeless, and half of those who started finished and held a job six months after.

narrative_blocks.header: He read law with his wife's father
narrative_blocks.body: Levi Lincoln Sr. took him as a reader and he was admitted in 1810. Seven years later he married Lincoln's daughter Rebecca, and afterwards practised alongside her brother William.

narrative_blocks.header: Six years prosecuting Worcester County
narrative_blocks.body: He was district attorney from 1818 to 1824, then sat for Worcester in the Massachusetts House and later in the Senate. He was a justice of the peace and the first president of the Worcester Mutual Fire Insurance Company.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped bring the railroad in
narrative_blocks.body: He built his practice with William Lincoln, his wife's youngest brother, and was one of the men instrumental in getting the line to Worcester. The Blackstone Canal had his money too.

narrative_blocks.header: Canal shares and eastern lands
narrative_blocks.body: He put money into the Blackstone Canal, held rented land at Columbia in Maine, and speculated in the Kennebeck Lumber Company. The Massachusetts General Hospital trustees wrote to him about the ground Isaiah Thomas had left them.

narrative_blocks.header: His son kept eleven diaries
narrative_blocks.body: Levi Lincoln Newton wrote them from 1837 to 1843, through Harvard's riots and its two-hundredth anniversary, abolition meetings, Wendell Phillips speeches, students taking exhilarating gas, and a meeting with Charles Dickens. He was dead at twenty-seven.

narrative_blocks.header: She founded a home for abandoned children
narrative_blocks.body: The Worcester Children's Friend Society was got up to find good homes for children abandoned outright, or whose parents had been disabled by what its charter called habitual, inveterate habits of intemperance. She was one of its founders.

narrative_blocks.header: She raised her sister's three daughters
narrative_blocks.body: Martha Lincoln Parker died at Shirley in 1822, at thirty-five, soon after her third girl was born. Her widower left the three of them to be brought up by Rebecca.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father was Jefferson's attorney general
narrative_blocks.body: Levi Lincoln argued the case that ended slavery in Massachusetts, served Jefferson as attorney general and briefly as acting Secretary of State, and finished as acting governor of the Commonwealth. She named her second son Levi for him, and her first Daniel, for her mother's father.

narrative_blocks.header: She died the day before her birthday
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Worcester on the eleventh of January 1792, she died there on the tenth of January 1855, one day short of sixty-three. Her father Levi Lincoln had taught her husband his law.

narrative_blocks.header: He went south for his health and died
narrative_blocks.body: The 1847 journey was meant to mend him. He wrote his mother and sister long descriptions of Richmond and of a slave auction, came home, and was dead in October at twenty-seven.

narrative_blocks.body: He was among the lawyers who carried the Quock Walker cases in 1781, and Commonwealth v. Jennison settled that slavery could not stand under the new state constitution. The court rested on the words all men are born free and equal; he had argued from natural law. Is it not a law of nature that all men are equal and free, he asked.

narrative_blocks.header: He answered every question but one
narrative_blocks.body: Jefferson had ordered him, as acting Secretary of State, not to deliver the commissions Adams left behind. Called to the stand in Marbury v. Madison he claimed privilege and the Fifth, took a day to think, then answered everything except what had become of them.

narrative_blocks.header: Jefferson's first attorney general
narrative_blocks.body: The post was part-time, so he kept to Worcester and served as the President's read on New England opinion and its patronage. In 1801 he founded the National Aegis to answer the Federalist papers, and his Letters to the People a year later flayed the clergy for preaching politics.

narrative_blocks.header: He proposed buying Louisiana sideways
narrative_blocks.body: To dodge the constitutional question he suggested the territory be taken in by enlarging the borders of a state that already existed. Jefferson and the rest of the cabinet said no and bought it anyway. He had already told them only Congress could declare a war on Tripoli.

narrative_blocks.header: He threw coins at a flock of geese
narrative_blocks.body: Nearly blind at the end, he mistook them for school children. He had gone out to his farms and his Merino sheep, and his sons remembered the old man sitting erect in his straight-backed chair by the library fire.

narrative_blocks.header: A blacksmith's apprentice who would not stay
narrative_blocks.body: His father put him to a Hingham smith and he would not have it, preferring to read; Harvard took him instead. When the news came from Lexington he marched with the militia to Cambridge and the lines around Boston.

narrative_blocks.body: Daniel Waldo Jr., who went as a delegate to the Hartford Convention, got up the Worcester Agricultural Society with her husband. Levi was its first president.

narrative_blocks.header: Congress cut a quarter of his draft
narrative_blocks.body: He wrote the Declaration in about seventeen days at Philadelphia in the summer of 1776 and then sat through the editing. The passage arraigning the king for the slave trade was among the parts struck out.

narrative_blocks.header: He doubled the country and doubted it
narrative_blocks.body: The Louisiana Purchase of 1803 took in more land than the United States already held, and he did not believe the Constitution gave him the power to do it. He did it anyway and left the question standing.

narrative_blocks.header: His epitaph leaves out the presidency
narrative_blocks.body: He wrote it himself and named three things: author of the Declaration of Independence, author of the Virginia statute for religious freedom, and father of the University of Virginia. Eight years in the President's house did not make the stone.

narrative_blocks.header: He died on the fiftieth Fourth of July
narrative_blocks.body: He went at Monticello on the fourth of July 1826, fifty years to the day after the Declaration. John Adams died the same afternoon at Quincy, not knowing it.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote it and did not live it
narrative_blocks.body: He held some six hundred people in bondage across his life and freed a handful, most of them Hemingses. The line about all men being created equal is in his own hand.

narrative_blocks.header: They set out for Monticello in a snowstorm
narrative_blocks.body: They were married on New Year's Day 1772 at The Forest, her father's Charles City plantation, and drove for the half-built house on the mountain through snow. She was a rich young widow of twenty-three; her first husband had died in an accident three years before.

narrative_blocks.header: Six children in ten years took her
narrative_blocks.body: Five daughters and a son came between 1772 and 1782, and only Patsy and Polly reached womanhood. She never recovered from the last birth and died in September 1782, leaving him prostrate for weeks.

narrative_blocks.header: He burned every letter she wrote him
narrative_blocks.body: After her death he destroyed their whole correspondence, and no likeness of her survives beyond a silhouette. The story that she made him promise never to remarry cannot be proved; he never did.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father married three times over
narrative_blocks.body: John Wayles came out of England to Virginia in the 1730s and buried three wives. Of his children by the first, Martha Eppes, only she lived to grow up.

narrative_blocks.header: He buried a wife and three children
narrative_blocks.body: Salome Sawtell died in 1818 at thirty-three, six days after her birthday; their daughter Salome had gone at birth in 1814 and Martha before she was two. He married Mary DeWolf the next year, and their only child lived two years.

narrative_blocks.header: He died in Omaha and came home
narrative_blocks.body: Eighty-seven years old and out in Nebraska when he went, in November 1897. They brought him back to the High Street ground at Greenfield where his father and grandfather lay.

narrative_blocks.body: He enlisted at twenty-two in September 1862 and went out a corporal in Company A. The regiment mustered out at Camp Miller in Greenfield the following August, and he went back to his trade.

narrative_blocks.header: He outlived her by fifty years
narrative_blocks.body: Anna Celestia died at Greenfield in 1876, at thirty-five, leaving him two small children. He went west, married again in time, and died at Denver in 1926 at eighty-six.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed by the war, married after it
narrative_blocks.body: Willard Powers married her in 1853 and was dead by 1865. She married Jonathan Henry Smead of Greenfield afterwards and had two sons by him, and she is buried at Greenfield though she died at New Bedford.

narrative_blocks.body: He went in on the ninth of September 1862 and mustered out at Camp Miller in Greenfield the following August. His name is on the framed company roster, written in by hand.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven generations on both sides
narrative_blocks.body: His father's people had been at Greenfield since the first settlement, seven generations back, and his mother's descended from the town's first settled minister. He kept to the North Parish Church as long as he stayed.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the chair works at Erving
narrative_blocks.body: The company centennial of 1926 has him managing the Erving plant of Heywood-Wakefield, chair manufacturers. By 1930 he was its treasurer, and the family lived at Orange.

narrative_blocks.body: The 1940 census has her at Natick keeping an architect's books while her husband billed for an optical firm. Ten years on she was registrar of a private school at Worcester, with two sons and a lodger in the house.

narrative_blocks.body: Born in Worcester County in 1946 and buried in the Red Butte ground under Aspen Mountain in December 1988. His brother Barry was four years older.

narrative_blocks.body: Orpah Gilman was her father's second wife and had been dead a year when he married her mother. The child born in 1824 carried the dead woman's name whole.

narrative_blocks.body: He went out on the nineteenth of April 1775 as a private in the company of his cousin Captain Agrippa Wells, and stayed in until after Bennington in August 1777. Afterwards he rose through the state militia to lieutenant-colonel in 1800.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixteen years the town's clerk
narrative_blocks.body: He kept Greenfield's books from 1793 to 1809 and was listed among its prominent men in 1801, his occupation given as farmer. He was one of the incorporators of the town's first water company, which supplied it until 1869.

narrative_blocks.header: The house at Wells and Main
narrative_blocks.body: He went out to Guilford in Vermont in 1788 and came back to Greenfield almost at once. The house on the corner afterwards belonged to his son Judge Daniel Wells and was still standing in good repair a century later.

narrative_blocks.body: Married at Colrain in 1808, he moved out to Byron in Genesee County and bought a half interest in a mill. He was a deacon first of the Congregational church and then the Presbyterian, and justice of the peace for years.

parents.father_research_notes: Rev. Samuel Taggart of Colrain, Presbyterian minister out of Londonderry in Ireland, fourteen years a member of Congress

narrative_blocks.header: Her father sat fourteen years in Congress
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel Taggart came out of Londonderry in Ireland to a Congregational pulpit at Colrain that he governed Presbyterian fashion, with elders. He represented western Massachusetts in Congress. She died at Byron when her younger son was fourteen.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty men selling books across the West
narrative_blocks.body: The American Tract Society sent him out in 1842 to build the colporteur system and he ran it twelve years, the reports calling his the best field in the country. Then sixteen churches organized in Iowa, and after that California.

narrative_blocks.header: He got Oakland its cemetery
narrative_blocks.body: Every burying ground in the town was encumbered one way or another, so he pushed a new one on the rule that all money from lots, once the land was paid for, went back into the grounds. Mountain View covers two hundred acres and he lies in it.

narrative_blocks.header: A church sold for taxes, and paid off
narrative_blocks.body: Ventura's Presbyterians had one active man, a few women, a debt and no building when he took them in 1870. On less than half his Oakland salary he had the debt clear in three years.

narrative_blocks.header: The railroad bought his land at ten times
narrative_blocks.body: He had three hundred acres bought cheap when land was cheap; the line went through it and the company paid many times what he gave. It kept him for the rest of his life, in a house he built across from the church.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a San Pablo landowner's daughter
narrative_blocks.body: Annie Nicholl came from San Pablo in Contra Costa County, daughter of John Nicholl, a prominent land-owner and farmer of the Santa Clara Valley. They married on the second of May 1889 and had an infant daughter soon after.

narrative_blocks.header: He came to Pittsburgh with a pine box
narrative_blocks.body: A boat to Erie, the canal to Beaver, another boat down. He landed on the nineteenth of November 1847 with everything he owned worth about twenty-five dollars, and went to the university his brother the minister had told him to attend.

narrative_blocks.header: The first American crucible-steel house
narrative_blocks.body: Hussey, Wells & Company turned from pork and bacon to steel in 1859, the first firm here given wholly to the higher grades. He managed it, went east to learn the trade, and sold out twenty-six years later.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought a paper, then ran it
narrative_blocks.body: He joined the purchase of the Philadelphia Press in 1877 expecting his partners to manage it. Two years convinced him otherwise and he took hold of it himself; it became one of the strongest papers in the country and the loudest for a protective tariff.

narrative_blocks.header: He married two sisters from Yeovil
narrative_blocks.body: Annie Glyde died at twenty-four in 1859 leaving him a daughter. Two years later he married her sister Mary. Both had come out of Yeovil in Somerset, daughters of the dry-goods man whose books he had once kept.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept the appointment and died that night
narrative_blocks.body: He had moved the annual meeting of the Forge and Iron Company up so he could get to Canada sooner and his son's cottage on Lake Muskoka. He went to the office that Monday, ate his dinner, sat on the porch, went up before nine and died in the chair.

narrative_blocks.header: Springs, spelter, and a thousand forge hands
narrative_blocks.body: From 1865 to 1884 Calvin held half of A. French & Co., makers of railway elliptic springs. In 1888 he took up spelter and founded the Illinois Zinc Company at Peru, Illinois, and his Pittsburgh Forge and Iron Company came to employ about a thousand men.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother died when she was four
narrative_blocks.body: Annie Glyde went in March 1859 and her father married her aunt Mary two years later. She married the Yale rowing man in 1881 and a Maine doctor thirty years after that, and lies at Hollywood.

narrative_blocks.header: He went to England for the stroke
narrative_blocks.body: Yale sent him over as a sophomore to study rowing at London, Cambridge and Oxford, and he brought the English orthodox style back with him. Coaching from 1872 to 1899 he was beaten four times in twenty-seven years.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried the man to the station first
narrative_blocks.body: Depew told it: a ruffian buried an axe in Cook's head, and Cook seized him, nearly knocked the life out of him, walked him to the police station a prisoner, and only then pulled the axe out and sent for a doctor.

narrative_blocks.header: The boathouse at Derby carried his name
narrative_blocks.body: Yale left New Haven harbour in 1924 for a house on the Housatonic designed by James Gamble Rogers and named for him. It stood seventy-five years.

narrative_blocks.header: Four years at stroke, and coach besides
narrative_blocks.body: Bob Cook came to Yale from Andover in 1871, and that autumn his scrub four won twice on New Haven Harbor while the varsity was not racing at all. He stroked and captained Yale for four years, choosing the crews and running practice well before he graduated in 1876.

narrative_blocks.header: He coached Yale by weekend train
narrative_blocks.body: After graduating, Bob Cook worked full-time in Philadelphia and came up to New Haven at weekends to coach. He was Yale's official coach from 1876 to 1898, twenty-two seasons of crews picked and trained on Saturdays and Sundays.

narrative_blocks.header: Six cups, dated 1873 to 1898
narrative_blocks.body: Shortly before he died, Bob Cook gave Yale the six crew and coaching cups he had kept. The first was dated 1873, the year of his first win; the last came from the freshman crew of 1898. In February 1923 they went into the trophy room at the Yale gymnasium.

narrative_blocks.header: Read law, then a term in Germany
narrative_blocks.body: Bob read law at Greensburg with A. M. Fulton and in Pittsburgh with John H. Bailey, and was admitted to the Pittsburgh bar in 1878. The year after his 1881 wedding he took a special course at a German university, and his daughter Elsa was born at Leipzig in February 1882.

narrative_blocks.header: The school made him permanent staff
narrative_blocks.body: He came in through Kid Reach and stayed eighteen years at Discovery Elementary in Gig Harbor. They ended by making him a member of the staff outright, which is not a thing schools do for volunteers.

narrative_blocks.header: Esparto to Mexico City and back
narrative_blocks.body: He grew up in the Capay Valley, went into the Navy for the Pacific, married Giorgina in 1965 and kept house with her in New Mexico and Mexico City. He retired out of the Grinnell Company there and they settled at Gig Harbor in 1992.

narrative_blocks.header: An electrician's mate in the Pacific
narrative_blocks.body: He went in as EM2 and served the war out in the Pacific theatre. Tahoma National has him in Section 28B, Site 2244.

career.role: Marine artist, studio gallery on the waterfront

cross_connections.display_label: has painted the Atlantic coast for fifty years

narrative_blocks.header: A book in a waterfront shop decided it
narrative_blocks.body: She had come to watercolour late, out of oils, and had not found her subject. Down at the San Francisco waterfront she picked up a book of Carl Evers's marine work, looked at it, and thought: this is it.

narrative_blocks.header: Her first commission was a disaster
narrative_blocks.body: The sails were going one way and the water the other. A marine painter has to know the technicalities of a boat and of water and weather, not only how to paint, and she went away and learned them.

narrative_blocks.header: The Navy, the port, two fire departments
narrative_blocks.body: From the studio gallery she opened on the San Francisco waterfront in 1980 came commissions for the United States Navy, the Port and the City of San Francisco, both the San Francisco and Oakland fire departments, Matson, Chevron and Foss Maritime.

narrative_blocks.header: They bought the house on a Tuesday
narrative_blocks.body: They had gone up to Bellingham so her husband could buy a tool and stopped at Gig Harbor on the way back to see where friends were moving. They arrived on a Sunday in September and signed for the land by Tuesday afternoon, knowing nobody.

narrative_blocks.header: Five of nine children became artists
narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Albuquerque into a family of nine and five of them went into art in one medium or another. Two are still painting. It is a hard profession, she says.

narrative_blocks.header: She found her own footprints in the paint
narrative_blocks.body: The studio had a sofa at one end and the easel at the other, and she walked between them all day looking at the work. Towards evening she looked down and saw where she had been.

narrative_blocks.header: She died in the year of the influenza
narrative_blocks.body: Born in California in 1891 and gone at twenty-seven in 1918. Her mother had died when she was eight and her brother was a year old.

bio.bio_blurb: Warren farmer on the Yale college lands

narrative_blocks.header: His second wife was his first cousin
narrative_blocks.body: Abigail died on the first of April 1792 and he married Eunice Newton that November. Her father John Newton and his mother Sibyl Newton were brother and sister, so the two of them stood in the same degree to old Rev. Roger Newton and to Mary Hooker.

narrative_blocks.header: He farmed land the State gave Yale
narrative_blocks.body: The house he was living in when the last child came stood on one of five three-hundred-acre tracts the colony deeded to Yale College in 1741. He moved the family afterwards to two hundred acres of wild and wooded ground in the West District, a mile and a half from Warren meeting-house.

people.research_notes: CONFLICTS (Ancestry vs the 1885 Morris memorial volume): memorial has John aged 32 and Amy aged 24 at Myron's birth in Nov. 1810, giving 1778 and 1786; Ancestry gives John 1784-1836 and calls the daughter ANNA, 1786-1842. Memorial has Garry aged 16 (b. ~1794); Ancestry 1795; an earlier FamilySearch list 1793. Using 1778 for John (memorial), 1786 for Amy, 1795 for Garry. Ancestry lists all six children under Newton John Morris without splitting them by mother; the split here follows the memorial's ages. NOTE: a birth of 1778 or 1784 for John predates the c.1785 marriage to Abigail.

military_service.unit: 2nd and 5th (Beekman) Regiments, Dutchess County militia; afterwards Capt. Benjamin Noxon's Company No. 9 of Light Infantry
military_service.role: Granted land bounty rights for his service; signed the Articles of Association

cross_connections.display_label: was his second cousin, born a year earlier in the same Milford

narrative_blocks.header: The new road ran through his land
narrative_blocks.body: He was overseer of the highways at Beekman in 1793 and told to work the new road, which had been dedicated the April before and cut across his own ground. A school stood near his house in 1795.

narrative_blocks.header: He came out of it a lieutenant
narrative_blocks.body: He served in the second regiment of Dutchess County militia and drew land bounty rights for the fifth, the Beekman regiment. Afterwards he was a lieutenant in Captain Benjamin Noxon's company of light infantry.

narrative_blocks.header: Fined for not turning up as a juror
narrative_blocks.body: Twenty shillings, at Dutchess County in June 1787, one of several who failed to appear. He had sued Joseph Balding three times in that same court in the years before.

narrative_blocks.header: He left Beekman and was not found again
narrative_blocks.body: He sold the last of the Beekman land in October 1799 and vanishes from the county records. He died at Ferrisburgh in Vermont in 1827 and lies in a burying ground that carries the family name.

narrative_blocks.header: The other Newton went east, he went west
narrative_blocks.body: He took his family to Ferrisburgh on the Champlain side of the Green Mountains. His second cousin David, born at Milford a year after him, crossed to Hartford on the Connecticut River side in 1777.

narrative_blocks.header: She married her first cousin
narrative_blocks.body: Newton John Morris was the son of her father's sister Sibyl. He had been a widower seven months when they married in November 1792, with three children already in the house.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived the whole family
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Milford in 1789, the last of her father's sixteen children, and dead there in 1881 at ninety-two. Her husband had been gone thirty-one years.

parents.father_research_notes: Lieut. Daniel Fenn (1743-1789)
parents.mother_research_notes: Sarah Miles Fenn (1757-1784), daughter of Samuel Miles and Phebe Platt; married 1772

narrative_blocks.header: Fenn and Miles on both sides
narrative_blocks.body: His father was Lieut. Daniel Fenn and his mother Sarah Miles, and he married a Newton whose own mother had been a Miles of Milford. The three families had been marrying each other in that town for five generations.

parents.father_research_notes: Samuel Hine IV (1743-1833)

narrative_blocks.header: Her surname is not recorded
narrative_blocks.body: She married Newton John Morris about 1785 and died on the first of April 1792, the year her last child was born. The genealogies give her only as Abigail.

bio.title: Reverend
bio.bio_blurb: West Hartford minister; Fellow of Yale

notable.notable_blurb: Congregational minister; Fellow of Yale College

cross_connections.display_label: sat beside him on the Yale Corporation for fourteen years

narrative_blocks.header: They called him Father Morris at school
narrative_blocks.body: He earned it at the village school in Warren for his steady habits and his way of staying at his lessons while the others played. He was a bashful boy, and set himself early to overcome it so that he might be of more use.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventy scholars and the patience of Job
narrative_blocks.body: He took a school at Union Vale in Dutchess County in the autumn of 1828, at seventeen, on condition that the wages went into the family purse. Fifty-four scholars by December and upwards of seventy by January. Teaching, he wrote his sisters, requires the patience of Job and the wisdom of Solomon.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried flour home to get a ride
narrative_blocks.body: The miller would lend him a horse and wagon if he took a load along, and he reckoned he might clear a little on the flour besides. My principal object, he wrote, is to get a ride home. He usually walked the distance, and his sisters teased him about the length of his legs.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-three years in one pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: Ordained at North Stonington in 1846 and installed at West Hartford in July 1852, he resigned in April 1875 and stayed on living among his people. Yale made him a Fellow of the Corporation in 1867 and he held it until he died.

narrative_blocks.header: Hooker blood down two lines
narrative_blocks.body: His mother's father and his father's mother were brother and sister, both of them great-great-grandchildren of Thomas Hooker through Mary Hooker's marriage to Rev. Roger Newton. He was, as the memorial put it, the inheritor by a double line of ministerial blood.

narrative_blocks.header: I hope nobody will ever eulogize me
narrative_blocks.body: He said it long before the end, out of a distrust of human praise. Four days' illness carried him off in July 1885, in his seventy-fifth year, and the church at West Hartford put out a memorial volume anyway.

parents.father_research_notes: Elisha Avery of Colchester, Connecticut
Samuel Whitman of West Hartford

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived him thirty-six years
narrative_blocks.body: The youngest daughter of Samuel Whitman of West Hartford, married there in 1855 and widowed in 1885. She died at Amesbury in Massachusetts in 1921, ninety-four years old.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: The mountain farm her husband held a share of

narrative_blocks.header: Born at Andover, buried at West Hartford
narrative_blocks.body: She came in April 1840 while her father was teaching at the Teachers' Academy in Andover, and married Francis Butler at West Hartford in September 1861, in the parish where her father had been installed nine years before.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived him by twenty-three years
narrative_blocks.body: He died at the hospital in Hartford at sixty-one, leaving her with three daughters and two sons all grown. She lived to eighty-two and lies beside him in the North Cemetery.

cross_connections.display_label: kept the records of his Yale class of 1882

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve pulpits in twenty years
narrative_blocks.body: Ordained deacon in 1889 and priest the year after, he took New Haven, Westminster in Maryland, Philadelphia, Boston, Amesbury, Brooklyn, Little Creek in Delaware, Niantic, Chester in Vermont and Albany, and came back to Amesbury as curate in 1912.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote on Ohio canals before ordination
narrative_blocks.body: Internal Improvements in Ohio, 1825-1850 came out in the Papers of the American Historical Association in 1889, the year he took deacon's orders. Trinity College at Toronto gave him a second master's in 1893.

narrative_blocks.header: He married at forty-four and had no children
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Josephine Burlingame had kept house with her elder sister Fannie and taught school at Amesbury until they married in October 1904. She outlived him six years and lies beside him.

parents.father_research_notes: Charles Austin Burlingame

narrative_blocks.header: She taught at Amesbury until she married
narrative_blocks.body: She kept house with her elder sister Fannie and taught in the town schools until 1904, when she married the curate at forty. There were no children.

parents.father_research_notes: Deacon George Butler of West Hartford, d. there 1877

landmarks.landmark_blurb: The mountain farm he held a share of

military_service.role: Enlisted with many others from West Hartford; served about a year

career.organization: Vermont Farm Machine Company, Bellows Falls

narrative_blocks.header: A year with the Twenty-second Connecticut
narrative_blocks.body: He went in with many others from West Hartford and served about twelve months. Afterwards, as a veteran, he took much interest in getting Memorial Day properly observed.

narrative_blocks.header: Farm machines, ice machines, furniture
narrative_blocks.body: He organized the Vermont Farm Machine Company at Bellows Falls in 1869 and was its treasurer, came back in 1872 to make ice-making machinery in New York, and in 1882 bought out the Cushman business and ran the Hartford Furniture Company on Asylum Street.

narrative_blocks.header: He went west for furniture and mined coal
narrative_blocks.body: He sold the Hartford business in 1890 and left for Denver meaning to set up in furniture there. He changed his plans, tried coal mining at Golden for a spell, and came back east.

narrative_blocks.header: He held a share of Talcott Mountain
narrative_blocks.body: At his death he was part owner of the McKee farm on the mountain and interested in other enterprises up there. The furniture store on Ford Street he had opened belonged to C. C. Fuller by then.

narrative_blocks.header: An obscure brain trouble
narrative_blocks.body: He had been failing for months and was taken to the hospital a few weeks before the end. His people had been in almost constant attendance and the death still surprised them; he went at one o'clock on a December afternoon, sixty-one years old.

narrative_blocks.header: He was born where his father built machines
narrative_blocks.body: Rockingham in Vermont, the town of Bellows Falls, where his father had gone the year before to organize the Vermont Farm Machine Company. The family came back to Connecticut when he was three, and he ended president of a Hartford furniture house.

parents.father_research_notes: Job Wiersma

narrative_blocks.header: Her ashes came north from Aiken
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Zwolle in the Netherlands and dead in South Carolina, she was carried up to New Boston in July 1989 and buried next to her husband's parents. The town's annual report for that year records it.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at Dayton at thirty-three
narrative_blocks.body: Born on Nantucket in 1909 and dead in Ohio in February 1943, leaving a wife and a daughter of six. They brought him home to New Boston.

narrative_blocks.header: A Pratt son who went by Platt
narrative_blocks.body: His parents were William Willard Pratt and Amy Morris, but the records carry him and his children as Platt. He kept it to the end of his life at Cortlandt Manor.

narrative_blocks.header: His father-in-law was buried from his house
narrative_blocks.body: Francis Butler's funeral was held at the Andrews house on Main Street in West Hartford in December 1899. He kept the cash at the Charter Oak National Bank in Hartford.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty years a widow
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband died at forty-five in January 1931 and she lived until the last day of 1981, ninety-three years old. They lie together at Fairview.

military_service.role: Distinguished Service Cross for extraordinary heroism near Soissons, 19 July 1918

narrative_blocks.header: He covered a battalion front alone
narrative_blocks.body: Near Soissons on the nineteenth of July 1918 he put his company across a battalion's frontage in a critical moment and directed it from the open, under fire. The citation calls it extraordinary heroism and gave him the Distinguished Service Cross.

narrative_blocks.header: Indianapolis, then home to West Hartford
narrative_blocks.body: He and Jeannette kept house in Indiana until 1930 and then came back to the town he was born in. Three children came of that marriage; he married again in 1954 and lived to eighty-five.

cross_connections.display_label: took her nursing degree at Yale in 1931, and nursed in New York

narrative_blocks.header: She took her nursing degree at thirty
narrative_blocks.body: Mount Holyoke in 1943, then the Yale School of Nursing seven years later, and a post on the staff of the Babies Hospital in New York. Her engagement notice ran that summer.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother announced it, her father gone
narrative_blocks.body: Mrs. George Morris Butler of West Hartford gave out the engagement in 1950; her husband had been dead seven years. The wedding was set for the early autumn and the groom was an assistant resident in surgery at New Haven.

parents.father_research_notes: Albert Martin Krementz of Maplewood, New Jersey
parents.mother_research_notes: Mrs. Albert Martin Krementz of Maplewood, New Jersey

education.school_name: University of Rochester School of Medicine

narrative_blocks.header: He was still a resident when they married
narrative_blocks.body: Wesleyan in 1939 and the Rochester medical school in 1943, and in 1950 he was an assistant resident in surgery at the New Haven Hospital. He came from Maplewood in New Jersey and they both ended in New Orleans.

narrative_blocks.header: Her notice counted the generations
narrative_blocks.body: It named her a ninth-generation descendant of Thomas Hooker, who founded Hartford, and a direct descendant of Elder William Brewster of the Mayflower. Her middle name had carried the first of those since birth.

parents.father_research_notes: Breckenridge Tomkins Clark Sr. of Evanston, Illinois

career.organization: Belmont Corporation, trading as Village Cabinets

narrative_blocks.header: He took two years off to write
narrative_blocks.body: Twenty-eight years as executive vice-president of Connecticut Plywood ended when the company was sold in 1985. He spent the next two years on one of his passions and came back in 1987 to found Belmont Corporation, which traded as Village Cabinets.

narrative_blocks.header: Fort Bliss and White Sands
narrative_blocks.body: Two years in the Army between Colby and his degree at Bryant, stationed in Texas and then at the proving ground in New Mexico.

career.organization: Belmont Corporation, trading as Village Cabinets

narrative_blocks.header: He started on the installing crew
narrative_blocks.body: He went in hanging cabinets for Village Cabinets in Bristol and became a designer, then ran the company his father had founded. At its height Belmont was among the largest custom cabinet makers in New England and employed better than seventy people.

narrative_blocks.header: Two months against a rare disorder
narrative_blocks.body: HLH, an immune disease that is nearly always fatal, took him in September 2019 at fifty-eight. He had been a champion lacrosse player at Alfred and was happiest, his notice said, anywhere there was water enough to float a boat.

narrative_blocks.header: A man named Ethel
narrative_blocks.body: The name went to a son of Josiah Hine in 1836, when it was still given to boys, and he passed it on to his own first-born as a middle name. Ralph Ethel Hine died at five.

military_service.unit: 518th Labor Supervision Company, United States Army
military_service.role: Sergeant

narrative_blocks.header: Sergeant, 518th Labor Supervision Co.
narrative_blocks.body: The stone at Arlington reads SGT 518 LABOR SUPERVISION CO USA. He registered in 1942 and served with a company that ran work details rather than rifles, and it is what put a San Francisco boy of 1899 into the national cemetery.

narrative_blocks.header: Named for his mother's father
narrative_blocks.body: Eli Hine of New Haven was his grandfather, and the name came down whole with Hotchkiss from his father's side. He gave his eldest son the Hine name in turn.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten weeks a widow
narrative_blocks.body: Thurlow died in August 1950 and she followed on the first of November, forty-six years married. They lie together at Middlebury.

narrative_blocks.header: Married on the first day of the century
narrative_blocks.body: The first of January 1900. He was nineteen and she twenty-two, and the marriage ran seventy-one years until he died at Mystic at ninety-one.

narrative_blocks.header: She and her brother died a week apart
narrative_blocks.body: She went at Derby on the sixth of August 1777 and Joseph at Milford on the thirteenth. She was forty-seven and he forty-four, and they were the two eldest of the four.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight children in thirteen years
narrative_blocks.body: Abigail Durand bore them at Milford between 1763 and 1776. He died the summer after the last, a week after his sister Phebe, and Abigail lived on forty-one years a widow.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-one years a widow
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph died in August 1777 leaving her eight children, the youngest a year old. She kept at Milford until 1818 and died there at eighty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: Adopted by Alvin and Sally Hine
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Middlebury in 1841 and taken into the Hine house as an adopted son. He died there in June 1855, at fourteen.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried the Hine name to New York
narrative_blocks.body: Born at New Haven in 1813, he married Nancy Emeline Riggs there in 1837 and went west into New York State. He died at Middleport in 1883 and was buried at Royalton Center in Niagara County.

CONFLICT: the earlier FamilySearch extract gave her death as 18 June 1834 at Milford — same day and month, ten years apart. 1824 taken here as the later and more specific source.

narrative_blocks.header: Nineteen days, and the name used again
narrative_blocks.body: She was born on the nineteenth of June 1772 and died on the eighth of July. Five years later her parents had another daughter and gave her the same name; that Charlotte lived to seventy.

cross_connections.display_label: married the other Fowler brother, and was his fourth cousin too

narrative_blocks.header: Both her weddings fell on 18 December
narrative_blocks.body: She married David Atwater on the eighteenth of December 1791 and Anthony Fowler on the eighteenth of December 1796, five years to the day. Seven children came of the second.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a fourth cousin in 1796
narrative_blocks.body: Both come down from the Rev. Roger Newton Sr. and Mary Hooker, Thomas Hooker's daughter — she through their son Samuel, he through their son Roger Jr. and again through their daughter Susannah. Five generations stand between each of them and that couple, which makes the bride and groom fourth cousins, and on his side twice over.

narrative_blocks.header: Two sisters, two different David Atwaters
narrative_blocks.body: Her sister Sarah married a David Atwater at Milford in December 1791. She married another in September 1798 — this one born 1776 to Deacon William Atwater and Mehitable Clarke, and married only the once. The two men were not the same.

narrative_blocks.header: Eleven children named for both families
narrative_blocks.body: Ephraim and Hannah Platt for his parents, Charles Pond and Martha Miles and Catharine Pond for hers, and Mary Prudden for the Milford founder's line. Eleven were born at Milford between 1801 and 1821.

notable.notable_blurb: 37th Governor of Connecticut

cross_connections.display_label: governed Connecticut too, and shares Pond's great-grandmother
was his great-grandmother, by her first marriage

narrative_blocks.header: He got the chair when Seymour quit
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas H. Seymour resigned the governorship on the thirteenth of October 1853 to go as minister to Russia, and Pond, his lieutenant governor, finished the term. He held it until the third of May 1854, did not stand in his own right, and never entered public life again.

narrative_blocks.header: Kansas-Nebraska fell in his seven months
narrative_blocks.body: The United States Senate passed the Kansas-Nebraska Bill while he sat, reopening the expansion of slavery that the Compromise of 1850 had quieted. It set Connecticut arguing, and he left office a few weeks after.

narrative_blocks.header: Admitted to the bar, he never practised
narrative_blocks.body: He read law two years with Roger Minott Sherman of Fairfield and was admitted in Fairfield County, and then his health failed. A long sea voyage suited him so well that he took another, and he followed the sea for years in his father's shipping trade, first as supercargo and then as captain.

narrative_blocks.header: Muscular, witty, and hard to argue with
narrative_blocks.body: At Yale he was known for unusual physical strength and an inexhaustible vein of wit. A man who knew him well said his talents were of the very first order, that no man was wiser in council, and none more devoted to the lasting interests of his country.

narrative_blocks.header: He outlived five of his seven children
narrative_blocks.body: His only son died at eighteen in 1828; two daughters went at eighteen and twenty in 1836 and 1837; Martha died in 1853 and Maria in 1855, and his wife Catharine in 1854. Only Charlotte and Susan were still living when he died at Milford in April 1861, two days past his eightieth birthday and in the month the guns opened on Fort Sumter. He is named on the town's Founding Fathers Memorial.

narrative_blocks.header: His great-grandmother made two governors
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah Newton of Milford married twice: Daniel Miles in 1707, and after his death Jonathan Ingersoll in 1712. Charles Hobby Pond comes down from the first marriage in three generations and Charles Roberts Ingersoll from the second in four, so the two men are half second cousins once removed. Two governors of Connecticut out of one woman's two husbands.

people.research_notes: Wikipedia and the National Governors Association call him the 37th Governor; Norton's Governors of Connecticut (1905) and one FindAGrave text call him the 20th. Sheriff dates given variously as 1819-1834 and 1820-1834. Memorialised on the Milford Founding Fathers Memorial - not yet built as a landmark.

cross_connections.display_label: was his elder brother, and married a third cousin of Martha's

narrative_blocks.header: He died in Montana, and came home
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Milford and raised at Orange, he died in December 1892 at Chouteau, Montana. His body was carried back to Connecticut and buried in the Orange Center ground with his people.

narrative_blocks.header: He died on his seventieth birthday
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Milford on the seventh of December 1813 and died on the seventh of December 1883, seventy years later to the day.

people.research_notes: Son of Deacon William Atwater (1745-1816) and Mehitable Clarke (1754-1784). DISTINCT from the David Atwater who married her sister Sarah Pond in 1791; that one is a separate record. Daughter Caroline is recorded b.1795, three years before this marriage — unreconciled in the source, not adjusted here.

Son of Ephraim Strong (1754-1843) and Hannah Platt (1760-1812); Hannah was daughter of Joseph Platt Jr. (1724-1806) and Hannah Buckingham (1726-1809). Sam flagged a possible cousin marriage through the Platt line — NOT confirmed: the tree's Platt records were cut back and Joseph Platt Jr. is not among those remaining, so the link cannot be tested here.

narrative_blocks.header: The governor's only son, dead at eighteen
narrative_blocks.body: He was a sophomore at Yale when he died at Milford in June 1828, and the American Sentinel gave him four lines. His stone calls him cheerful without levity, firm without austerity, and dignified without ostentation, crowned with the highest honours of his class.

narrative_blocks.header: Two husbands and a son inside six years
narrative_blocks.body: Robert Ramsey married her in 1848 and was dead by January 1849. She married Jonas Glenney in 1850; their son Charles was born in August 1851 and died at five months, Glenney died at Milwaukee in February 1852, and she followed in 1855 at thirty-four.

narrative_blocks.header: The family record came through her
narrative_blocks.body: What is known of her father's people — his parents Joseph Carder and Mary Dixon, his sister Mary Ann who married Thomas Seamans, his brother the doctor with the sawmills in Ontario — survives in her correspondence with Adam P. Carroll. She lived to 1948.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirteen years rector of this parish
narrative_blocks.body: His memorial says he was for thirteen years rector of this parish, and that full of labours he departed hence in peace, aged sixty-three. He had come down from Richfield in Otsego County, New York, and he died at Milford in 1866.

narrative_blocks.header: One share in three thousand three hundred sixty
narrative_blocks.body: From 1906 the Carder Letters went out to find the descendants of Hannah Carver Carder, who were to take shares in the estate of Henry Wood Lothrop, whose grandmother Eunice Carder Thornton was Hannah's sister. Each descendant's final share came to one part in three thousand three hundred and sixty.

people.research_notes: Son of Joseph Carder and Mary Dixon of Richfield, Otsego County, New York. SISTER: Mary Ann Carder, b. Otsego 31 Oct. 1806, m. Thomas Seamans 1823; their children Henry, George Dennison, William Lewis, Marietta, Eliza Jane, Sarah Ann and Adelia Marie Seamans. BROTHER: Dr. George Washington Carder, trained at the College of Physicians and Surgeons, Fairfield, Herkimer Co., NY, resident at Columbia NY, m. Caroline Dertick (daughter of Ira Dertick and Perris Loomis) 5 Oct. 1834 at Herkimer; a general merchant 1845-1861 and owner of several sawmills, two in the Hawtrey area of South Norwich, Ontario, where he lived in the 1870s (South of Sodom: A History of South Norwich); d. aged 72, a native of Richfield, buried with his father; their children James Monro, Dennison Delos, Francis Amenzo, Emily and Marshall Dixon Carder. Caroline was still living at the 1881 Canadian census, aged 72, widowed, with son Amenzo at Norwich, Oxford, Ontario. NO RECORDS BUILT for these siblings — they are collateral to the tree; say the word if they should have entries. Rector dates inferred from 'thirteen years' on the memorial and his 1866 death.

narrative_blocks.header: Second lieutenant, then hotel manager
narrative_blocks.body: He was a second lieutenant in the United States Army in the First World War and spent his working life managing hotels. He died at the Delaware Water Gap in 1964 and his ashes were carried back to Everett, Massachusetts.

narrative_blocks.header: He sent William James a reading list
narrative_blocks.body: James had offered him advice he did not ask for, and he answered with a list of what James ought to read instead. The letter survives folded into a copy of The Key at Harvard's Houghton Library.

narrative_blocks.header: He led New England's Theosophists
narrative_blocks.body: From 1890 he was president of one Theosophical society after another in New England, at a time when the movement was pulling in the same Boston circles that produced the new psychology. He had come to it as a Harvard lawyer, not a mystic by trade.

narrative_blocks.header: Harvard College 1879, Harvard Law 1882
narrative_blocks.body: He practised law in Boston for fifty years. Herndon and Bacon put his portrait and a biographical notice in Men of Progress in 1896, when he was thirty-nine.

narrative_blocks.header: Only Roosevelt should know it in full
narrative_blocks.body: He pressed for President Roosevelt to be told that agents of Great Britain and Japan were approaching a Mr. Wheaton about his war plan. His view was that only Roosevelt should have the secret entire.

people.research_notes: Son of David Ayers and Martha E. Huckins. Owned and signed a copy of A General Survey of Events, Sources, Persons and Movements in Continental Legal History (Boston: Little, Brown, 1912), Wigmore chair of the editorial committee. Biographical article and portrait in Richard Herndon and Edwin M. Bacon, Men of Progress (Boston, 1896), p.195. Theosophical presidencies dated 1890 to 189-, the end year illegible in the source.

education.school_name: New Hampton Literary and Theological Institution

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty years preaching to sailors
narrative_blocks.body: He left a paying business at his old pastor's urging, trained at New Hampton, and came to Boston as a preacher to seamen. He kept at it more than twenty years, and the memorial volume of the Baptist Bethel Society carries his name as the apostle to seamen.

narrative_blocks.header: The Soldier's Home was his idea
narrative_blocks.body: The Soldier's Home in the south part of Boston and the Mariner's Exchange, with its library and reading room, both began with him. He administered the temperance pledge to more than five thousand men, each with a New Testament, and put anti-swearing cards into circulation by the thousand.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the sailor home to his parlour
narrative_blocks.body: He would bring a man to his own house to talk and pray, then follow him to sea by letter, telling him to keep a journal if he could not write. One of the worst convicts at Charlestown prison, who had resisted everything else, gave way under him.

people.research_notes: Married first Emily, daughter of Isaac Smith, Esq., of Southington, Connecticut - no dates supplied, no record built. Career dates approximate from the memoir's 'over twenty years' in Boston.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten children born to a Prussian merchant
narrative_blocks.body: She married Theodore Vietor of Rinteln in 1829 and bore ten children, most of them at Brooklyn. He died at New York in 1867 and she outlived him by twenty-two years.

narrative_blocks.body: He went at South Yarmouth in February 1952 and his younger brother Edgar Victor at Carlisle that October. Francis Edward, the third of them, followed in 1954.

narrative_blocks.body: He married Jane Frothingham at the end of August 1937 and outlived her by twelve years, dying at Branford in Connecticut in 2012. He was buried at Marion on Buzzards Bay.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a fourth cousin in 1785
narrative_blocks.body: Both come down from the Rev. Roger Newton Sr. and Mary Hooker, Thomas Hooker's daughter, in five generations apiece — she through Ezekiel Newton and the Malletts, he through Fletcher Newton and the Fowlers. That makes them fourth cousins, married at Milford in 1785.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-nine years a widow at twenty-five
narrative_blocks.body: John Fowler died in 1790, five years after the wedding, and she was twenty-five. She lived on to 1829 with no second marriage on the record.

narrative_blocks.header: A Genevieve born at Geneva
narrative_blocks.body: She was born in the city her name comes from in December 1878 and married Edgar Frothingham at twenty-one. She died at Concord in Massachusetts in 1963 and lies with him in the Dublin ground.

people.research_notes: Son of Capt. Joseph Platt (1754-1833) and Mabel Clark (1754-1815); NOT built as records — collateral to the tree, say the word if they should have entries. NOT the Joseph Platt Jr. (1724-1806) named in William Strong's notes, a different and earlier man.

military_service.role: Served under Col. James Wadsworth

narrative_blocks.header: Lieutenant under Colonel Wadsworth
narrative_blocks.body: He served in 1775 and 1776 as a lieutenant of the Second Company, 1st Connecticut Regiment, under Col. James Wadsworth. The Daughters of the American Revolution carry him on that service.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-five pounds on the ministers' rate
narrative_blocks.body: In 1760 his estate was valued at forty-five pounds on the Tax List for Ministers' Rate at New Cheshire. The Ministers' Rate was the yearly tax that paid the parish minister's salary, and the figure beside a man's name is the assessed value of his rateable estate — land, livestock and trade — not the tax itself. It is the plainest measure of who was worth what in the parish.

narrative_blocks.header: He married her on her seventeenth birthday
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah Hull was born on the twenty-second of August 1738 and they were married on the twenty-second of August 1755 at Wallingford. Their first child came that November, and five more followed.

narrative_blocks.header: She died the year the last was born
narrative_blocks.body: Miriam arrived in April 1769 and Sarah died at Wallingford that November, at thirty-one. Joseph married Esther Sperry seven months later and had one more daughter by her.

narrative_blocks.header: The 1790 census left him with three women
narrative_blocks.body: At Cheshire in 1790 he was head of a family of himself and three females, all his sons grown and gone. A child of the house had also died in April 1771 without a name on the record.

people.research_notes: FIRST WIFE Sarah and their six children were named in Sam's 31 July batch but the paste collapsed — her surname, dates, her parents and all six children were lost and are NOT built. Esther Sperry is entered here as the second marriage, so a first marriage row is still missing. Death 28 Aug. 1797 at Cheshire and second marriage 13 June 1770 at Cheshire, from the printed genealogy (no. 32).

bio.bio_blurb: Cheshire soldier and father of twelve

military_service.role: Paid by the Selectmen of Cheshire for a horse and provisions to Danbury

narrative_blocks.header: A horse and provisions to Danbury
narrative_blocks.body: The Selectmen of Cheshire paid him as a Revolutionary soldier 'for a hors & provisions to danbery, No. 131, 01.00.0' — one pound for the lot. Danbury was the supply depot the British burned in April 1777.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-six pounds against his father's 124
narrative_blocks.body: In 1762 his estate was valued at thirty-six pounds on the Ministers' Rate at New Cheshire, against a hundred and twenty-four for his father and forty-five for his brother Joseph. The Ministers' Rate was the yearly tax that paid the parish minister's salary, and the figure beside a man's name is the assessed value of his rateable estate — land, livestock and trade — not the tax itself. It is the plainest measure of who was worth what in the parish.

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve children, and Chloe outlived him
narrative_blocks.body: They came between 1764 and 1783, the first nine at Wallingford and the last three at Cheshire. Two died as infants, and when the 1790 census was taken his widow Chloe was head of the family.

people.research_notes: Baptized 1 Dec. 1734 at Cheshire. DISCREPANCIES against the FamilySearch summary: it gives his BURIAL as 20 March 1779, nine years before his 14 March 1788 death — impossible, and the book records no burial date. It also dates Billious Ball to 2 May 1769; the book gives 2 Feb. 1771, which fits his April 1772 christening and leaves room after Silas in Sept. 1768.

narrative_blocks.header: Two brothers married two Hull sisters
narrative_blocks.body: He married Anna Hull at Wallingford in January 1765; his brother Joseph had married her sister Sarah there ten years before. Both were daughters of Samuel Hull and Sarah Hall, and both were dead before their husbands — Sarah in 1769, Anna in June 1776.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-two years before he married again
narrative_blocks.body: Anna died in 1776 leaving him five children, two of them infant sons who had not lived out their birth years. He did not marry Mary Bunnell until January 1798, at sixty.

people.research_notes: Birth corrected from 1735 to 4 Jan. 1738 on the printed genealogy. The Hull tie runs three ways: Joseph m. Sarah Hull 1755, Jared m. Anna Hull 1765, and Joseph's daughter Sarah m. Joel Hull of Wallingford in 1783. Whether Sarah and Anna were sisters is not stated in the book.
Christened 4 January 1730 at Cheshire, six weeks after his birth at Wallingford. Buried at HILLSIDE CEMETERY, NAUGATUCK (CEM1463) — not the Hillside at Cheshire (CEM007) where the Newtons lie.

narrative_blocks.header: Twin girls, and only one grew up
narrative_blocks.body: Esther and Eveline were both born in 1806. Esther died at sixteen in 1822; Eveline lived to 1882. Two of the eight carried names out of the family — Harry Sperry for his grandmother and Joel Newton for hers.

people.research_notes: Christened April 1735. Daughter of Daniel Sperry (1698-1768) and Abigail Ives (1704-1762) — NEITHER is in the tree, and the Sperrys already here are the unrelated Pierpont-side cluster. CORRECTED from the printed genealogy: born 8 Feb. 1734/5 (modern 1735) and died 8 APRIL 1797, not 1791 — she and Joseph died four months apart. Daughter of Daniel and Abigail (Ives) Sperry, neither of whom is in this tree.
Christened 29 December 1771 at Wallingford.

narrative_blocks.header: Eleven children, and three she outlived
narrative_blocks.body: They came between 1774 and 1798 at Cheshire. One son was born and died in 1785 without a name on the record, and Susanna died at fifteen in 1804.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the name north to Lake Ontario
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Wallingford in 1774 and married Lowley Hitchcock of New Haven in 1804, he went out to Sackets Harbor on Lake Ontario. Both of them died there and lie in the Lakeside ground, she fifteen years after him.

people.research_notes: UNRESOLVED: the marriage to Wooster Cooper is dated 25 Dec. 1822 but the daughter attached to them, Eunice Atwater Hall, is recorded born 1810 in Ohio and carries the surname Hall, not Cooper. Entered as supplied; the chronology does not work as it stands.

narrative_blocks.header: The family moved out to Canandaigua
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Wallingford in 1778 and married Ann Atwood about 1799; their children were born in Ontario County, New York. He came back east to die at Oxford in Connecticut in 1843, while Ann stayed and was buried at Canandaigua.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a second cousin in 1806
narrative_blocks.body: Her great-grandfather and his were the same man, Corporal Thomas Newton of Cheshire — she through his son Jared and the Hulls, he through his daughter Eunice and the Atwaters. That makes the bride and groom second cousins, married in September 1806.

people.research_notes: Christened 25 December 1749 at Cheshire.
Mrs. Leonard gives 3 Nov. 1756 instead, and suggests he is 'perhaps Capt. Joel Newton of Salisbury, VT'.

narrative_blocks.header: A tour at Horseneck in 1780
narrative_blocks.body: At eighteen he served a tour with the Connecticut militia at Horseneck, on the exposed western shore the British raided out of New York. He came home to Cheshire and died there in 1826.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at seventeen, dead at thirty-one
narrative_blocks.body: She married Joseph Newton on her seventeenth birthday in 1755 and bore six children in fourteen years. She died at Wallingford in November 1769, the year the last of them was born.

people.research_notes: Christened August 1738, Congregational church, Cheshire. Daughter of Samuel and Sarah (Hall) Hull of Wallingford; neither parent is in this tree. Sister of Anna Hull, who married Joseph's brother Jared in 1765. Full sibling list is on Anna's record.
Of Wallingford.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-four days, and the name reused
narrative_blocks.body: He was born on the twenty-ninth of October 1765 and died on the twenty-second of November. Four years later his parents had another son and called him Simeon as well.

narrative_blocks.header: Eleven years a widower, then Isabella
narrative_blocks.body: Lucinda Parker died in April 1808 leaving four children under twelve. He did not marry again until December 1819, when he took Isabella Pardee.

narrative_blocks.header: Both his children died in their twenties
narrative_blocks.body: Julia Ann went in 1823 at twenty-five and Sidney the year after at twenty. Their mother had died in January 1823 as well, and all of them lie in Grove Street.

burial.plot_notes: Braceville Center Cemetery, Trumbull County, Ohio

naming_inspiration.description: For his maternal grandmother Mary (Ball) Atwater, wife of Abraham Atwater of Wallingford.

narrative_blocks.header: His middle name came from his grandmother
narrative_blocks.body: His mother Chloe was the daughter of Abraham and Mary (Ball) Atwater, and the Ball came down to him as a given name. He is the only Billious Ball in the family.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at Newton Falls in Ohio
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Wallingford in 1771, he married Olive Peck in 1793 and took the family west to the Western Reserve. He died in 1831 at Newton Falls in Trumbull County and lies at Braceville Center.

people.research_notes: Christened 12 April 1772, Congregational, Cheshire. The FamilySearch summary dates his birth 2 May 1769; the printed genealogy gives 2 Feb. 1771, taken here.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the family into the Catskills
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Wallingford in 1776, he married Eunice Bushnell in January 1798 and went west into New York State. He died at Lexington in Greene County in 1854, at seventy-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-one years a widow
narrative_blocks.body: Nehemiah Bradley died at New Haven in February 1813, twelve years into the marriage. She lived on there until October 1854.

people.research_notes: Called Amos (Amasa) in the printed genealogy; removed to Illinois and married a Bushnell whose given name is not recorded.

narrative_blocks.header: Two daughters called Jane
narrative_blocks.body: Nine children came between 1806 and 1824. A Jane was born in 1812 and a Jane A. in 1820, and an Iraor in 1814 and an Ira in 1816 — the same names doubled twice over in one household.

narrative_blocks.header: Head of the family in the 1790 census
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas died in March 1788 and by the census of 1790 she was listed as head of the household at Cheshire. She kept it another thirty-three years and was buried in the old graveyard there.

people.research_notes: Daughter of Abraham and Mary (Ball) Atwater; her son Billious Ball Newton carries her mother's name.

narrative_blocks.body: Thelus Hull was the son of Jesse Hull, her mother Anna's brother. They married about 1787 and had seven children at Cheshire, and only the eldest, Philmona, left children of her own.

narrative_blocks.body: Her great-grandfather and his were the same man, Corporal Thomas Newton of Cheshire — she through his son Jared and the Hulls, he through his daughter Eunice and the Atwaters. That makes the bride and groom second cousins, married in September 1806.

narrative_blocks.header: Born in Ohio, dead in Ohio at ninety-four
narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Portage in 1810 and married Milton Spring in October 1834. She outlived him by sixteen years and died at Ottokee in Fulton County in 1904.

bio.bio_blurb: Pioneer who moved five times west

cross_connections.display_label: left New York by ox team for Illinois eight years before him

narrative_blocks.header: Five moves west in sixty-five years
narrative_blocks.body: Born near Canandaigua, he took the family to the Western Reserve in Portage County, Ohio in 1830, to Winnebago County, Illinois near Rockford in 1845, and to De Witt in Clinton County, Iowa in 1852. When Margaret died at Avoca in May 1875 the family went that same year to Milwaukie, Oregon.

narrative_blocks.header: The oldest man in the town
narrative_blocks.body: He died at Milwaukie in August 1894 aged eighty-eight years, one month and eight days, and the Oregon City Enterprise thought him perhaps the oldest man there. Of twelve children six were living, three in Oregon and three in Iowa. He was embalmed and carried back to Iowa to lie beside Margaret.

people.research_notes: Obituary, Oregon City Enterprise, 24 Aug. 1894. It gives his birth as 4 July 1806 and the marriage as 1825; FamilySearch gives 1805 and 5 Sept. 1829, taken here. Funeral at St. John's Episcopal church, Rev. Webb officiating; buried Graceland Cemetery, Avoca, Section 3, Row 18. TWELVE children are named in the obituary; only Charles Barlow is built here.

cross_connections.display_label: started overland the year before him, and rode the whole way

narrative_blocks.header: He crossed the plains with an ox team
narrative_blocks.body: Born in Ohio in 1832, he was drawn west by the California gold and the Willamette valley and reached the Oregon country in the spring of 1853, coming up from Iowa with a brother. For a few years he prospected, then laid down the pick and the sluice box and took up the plough.

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve children by two wives, six each
narrative_blocks.body: Luezia Jane Crow, of a family that came out of Missouri in 1847, bore him six and died in 1872. Two years later he married Lucinda Hicklin and had six more. Five of the first set and three of the second survived him.

narrative_blocks.header: Active in the grange to the end
narrative_blocks.body: He kept up in grange circles at Tigardville until he died in September 1913, at eighty-one. The notice of his death ran under the heading Grange Sidelights.

people.research_notes: Grange Sidelights obituary, Tigardville, Oregon, 1913. Only three of the twelve children are built here — Elmer Wayne, Bertha Violet and Lydia Jane, all by Lucinda.

narrative_blocks.header: She died at the fourth place they settled
narrative_blocks.body: Married in New York, she followed him to Ohio in 1830, to Illinois in 1845 and to Iowa in 1852. She died at Avoca in April 1875, and the family left for Oregon that same year without her.

people.research_notes: Stone reads 'Margaret M., Wife of Charles BUNNELL, Died April 29, 1875, Aged 64 Years'.

cross_connections.display_label: was found shot beside her dying son in Montreal in June 1901

narrative_blocks.header: Her son shot her while she slept
narrative_blocks.body: At about six on the morning of 11 June 1890, at the Bunnell farm east of Milwaukie, her son Daniel Harvey, thirty-five, her child by her first husband, shot her through the temple as she slept and then shot himself. She was sixty-four and died five minutes before him.

narrative_blocks.header: He sold the farm and wanted it back
narrative_blocks.body: Daniel had owned the thirty-five-acre place in his own name and sold it two months before. Afraid of ending up homeless and hungry, he tried again and again to buy it back, and told a neighbour something would happen.

narrative_blocks.header: The jury found temporary insanity
narrative_blocks.body: A coroner's jury sat that same day and found that Daniel had shot his mother in a fit of temporary insanity. Many in Milwaukie doubted it: he had bought the revolver new and had hinted for weeks at what he would do.

people.research_notes: Morning Oregonian, Portland, 12 June 1890, p.1. The coroner's jury of R. Scott, Henry Uartenstein, Bernhart Quant, John Klinkemann, Baptist Campbell and John Bernhard returned a verdict of temporary insanity. Her son-in-law Frank Wilson was among the witnesses. Bunnell was her second husband.
Of a pioneer family that came from Missouri in 1847; six children, five of whom survived their father. Dates beyond the 1872 death are not recorded.
Daughter of William C. and Hannah A. (Franklin) Hicklin; married in Clackamas County, Oregon in 1874.
Recorded as a child of Elmer Wayne Bunnell but carries the surname McDonald — stepson or adopted, not stated.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten children, and she died at thirty-four
narrative_blocks.body: They came between 1769 and 1785 at West Haven, two of them infants born about 1782 who did not see the spring of 1783. She was dead in May 1785, three months after the last was born, and Benajah lived on seventeen years.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine children, and two lost as infants
narrative_blocks.body: They married at Woodbridge in August 1779 and the children came for fourteen years. Mehetable died in the year she was born and a daughter lived one day in February 1793.

narrative_blocks.header: Six children, then dead at thirty
narrative_blocks.body: He married Anna Twiss, an Englishwoman out of Manchester, and they had six at New Haven between 1773 and 1781, the first two in the same year. He died there in July 1782, before the youngest was two.

narrative_blocks.header: The second Sarah Ann took the first's name
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah Ann was born in 1821 and died the next year; a second Sarah Ann came in 1823 and lived. Charles Allen had gone the same way in 1820, born and dead in one year.

people.research_notes: REJECTED AS A CONFLATION: FamilySearch also carries an 'Ezekiel M. Smith Jr.', born the same day at the same place, 1 Aug. 1781 Woodbridge, who died 25 July 1813 at Youngstown, Niagara Co., New York and married Rhoba Burlingame of Providence. That record gives his parents as Ezekiel Smith (1751-1828) and Anne Mowry, married 24 June 1772 at Smithfield, Providence Co., Rhode Island — a different family entirely, and Burlingame and Mowry are both Rhode Island names. Sam flagged it and it is not built here; this record is Anne Platt's son, who died at Wallingford in 1825.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the family to Michigan
narrative_blocks.body: Born at New York in 1787, he married Mary Ann Selleck in March 1813 and ended in Woodstock Township, Lenawee County, Michigan. Both of them died there, he in 1868 and she ten years after.

people.research_notes: Christened March 1741 at Wallingford.
NOT the Mary Frost already in this tree (HD0325), who was born at Milford, Massachusetts in April 1780 and died eleven days later.

Christened 14 November 1797 at Paris Hill, Oneida County, New York. Daughter of Peter Selleck Jr. (1756-1840) and Mary Lockwood (1763-1837) — NEITHER is in this tree, and the Sellecks and Lockwoods already here are the unrelated Norwalk and Stamford St. John cluster. Her son Alonzo Lockwood Smith carries her mother's maiden name.
Christened 4 August 1754 in Lancashire, England (a FamilySearch transcription gives 1954). Died in the United States, date unrecorded.
Titus is recorded born 1752, seven years before the marriage to Esther Benham is dated — unreconciled in the source, entered as supplied.
Daniel is recorded born 1765, a year before the marriage is dated, and George and Susannah are both given 1767 — twins or a source error. Entered as supplied.
Born at Huntington, Fairfield County, while his brother Jared Sr. was born at New Haven — two living sons of the same name is unusual and may indicate a source conflation, unresolved.

narrative_blocks.header: Two daughters past ninety, one past ninety-five
narrative_blocks.body: Ann was born in 1759 and died in 1856; Sarah was born in 1762 and lived to 1861, ninety-nine years. Both outlasted every brother.

people.research_notes: The printed genealogy gives his death as 14 Sept. 1811 at Washington; a FamilySearch extract gives 3 Sept. 1811, entered here. His wife Ann Smith was daughter of John and Elizabeth Smith. The Washington vital records also show an Ezekiel Newton, perhaps their son, who married Elizabeth Hurd 13 Feb. 1790 and had Wheeler b. 2 Aug. 1792, John b. 20 Oct. 1794 and Gary b. 16 Aug. 1797 — not built.
Christened 3 July 1800 at Fishkill, New York.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven months between their two deaths
narrative_blocks.body: Christopher Newton was lost at sea in February 1795. She died the following September, seven months after him.

people.research_notes: No children recorded. Marriage date estimated 1759-1785 in the source, not entered. Daughter of Samuel and Elizabeth (Downs) Terrill. The book gives her death as 'prob. 6 Sept. 179_'; the family notes read 1795, a FamilySearch extract reads 1790. 1795 taken.

narrative_blocks.header: Married on New Year's Day, eleven children
narrative_blocks.body: She and Philo Hodge were married on the first of January 1789 and had eleven between 1791 and 1815, nine of them daughters. Sarah and Susan were both born in 1806.

narrative_blocks.header: Two sons, named for two generals
narrative_blocks.body: Charles Kosciusco came in 1819 and Albert Lafayette in 1822, both named for foreign officers of the Revolution. Charles died at nineteen; Albert lived to ninety-seven.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: The library his son built carries his name.

narrative_blocks.header: Ninety-seven years in one town
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Roxbury in October 1822 and died there in March 1920, having outlived his wife by seventeen years and his brother by eighty-one.

narrative_blocks.header: A library carries his name at Roxbury
narrative_blocks.body: His son Charles left Roxbury the money for a library and museum in 1936 and asked that it carry his father's name. The Albert Lafayette Hodge Memorial Library and Museum opened in 1937, sixteen years after Albert's death.

people.research_notes: Daughter of Reuben Bunnell (1765-1853) and Sarah Sackett (1767-1851); neither is in this tree. POSSIBLE COUSIN MARRIAGE, NOT CONFIRMED: the tree already carries a Bunnell line out of Cheshire descended from Corporal Thomas Newton through Eunice Newton Atwater and Sarah Atwater Bunnell, and one of that family, Chester Bunnell, died at Oxford in New Haven County — the town where Ruth Ann was born. Her father Reuben (b.1765) is the right generation to be a brother of Abner Bunnel's children but no link is documented. Reuben Bunnell's own parents would settle it.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Her brother's bequest built it; her father's name is on it.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a Belgian doctor at thirty-three
narrative_blocks.body: Louis Jacques Pons had come from Liège, and they were married in December 1886. They ended their lives together at Milford and were carried back to Roxbury to be buried.

bio.bio_blurb: Roxbury bank president and library founder

landmarks.landmark_blurb: He left the town the money for it, and the endowment.

narrative_blocks.header: He left the town a library and museum
narrative_blocks.body: At his death in 1936 he gave Roxbury the money to build a library and museum and an equal sum to endow it. The stone building went up the year after and was named for his father, and his will required that it hold a museum room for Hodge family and Roxbury things.

narrative_blocks.header: From the lumber store to the bank
narrative_blocks.body: The 1910 census has him keeping a lumber and hardware store at fifty-four. By 1920 he was first vice president of the national bank and by 1930 its president, and single in all three counts.

narrative_blocks.header: His father lived with him at ninety-eight
narrative_blocks.body: The 1920 census lists Albert Hodge, widowed, aged ninety-eight, in his son's house at Roxbury. Charles was sixty-four and unmarried, and kept the household with one servant.

people.research_notes: 1910, 1920 and 1930 federal censuses, Roxbury, Litchfield Co. Bequest: fifteen thousand dollars to build and fifteen thousand to endow. Building completed 1937 by Clayton B. Squire. Career dates are inferred from the census years, not documented.

narrative_blocks.body: She was born in 1754 and died at three in 1757. Two years later her parents had another girl and called her Esther as well; that one lived to eighty-seven.

narrative_blocks.body: The Yale obituary of her husband says only that she died very suddenly, on the twenty-eighth of August 1805, in her forty-ninth year. He remarried seven months later.
