narrative_blocks.header: Father and son married mother and daughter
narrative_blocks.body: He married Irene Merwin on the first of January 1806. Ten weeks later, on the nineteenth of March, his father married Irene's widowed mother Lucy Pierce. Irene was dead by 1812 and he married again in 1814.

narrative_blocks.header: He fought the Boudinot wedding in 1826
narrative_blocks.body: As an agent of the Foreign Mission School at Cornwall, Daniel demanded that his wife's sister Harriet Gold be stopped from marrying the Cherokee student Elias Boudinot. Her father allowed it, and they married in March 1826.

narrative_blocks.header: Brigadier general of the state cavalry
narrative_blocks.body: He held the cavalry command in the Connecticut militia from 1817 to 1819, after reading at the Litchfield Law School in 1803. Local papers and diaries set him alongside Lyman Beecher.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-two years in the assembly
narrative_blocks.body: He sat as a state representative from 1816 to 1848 and served his town as its clerk. He died at Washington in November 1862, at eighty.

narrative_blocks.header: Three Connecticut men went to Baltimore
narrative_blocks.body: In December 1831 the National Republican Convention met at Baltimore to name candidates for President and Vice-President, about a hundred and forty men in all. Three came from Connecticut: Joseph Trumbull, John A. Rockwell and him.

narrative_blocks.header: Smallpox near Adam's Iron Works
narrative_blocks.body: In February 1831 the civil authority and selectmen of Washington met at Sheldon Camp's house as a board of health and chose him president. They found the smallpox prevalent in the northeast of the town, near Adam's Iron Works, and named seven men to a health committee to carry out their orders.

narrative_blocks.header: His son settled the estate he had judged
narrative_blocks.body: He sat as judge of the probate court for the district of Washington. Four days after he died the same court, under a new judge, made his son Thomas Franklin administrator of his estate and gave the creditors six months to come forward.

narrative_blocks.header: Justice, clerk, selectman and judge
narrative_blocks.body: He was justice of the peace thirty-four years, town clerk of Washington thirty-four, selectman twenty-nine, and ten years one of the judges of the county court for Litchfield. His obituary counts him an active member of the legislature in forty-four of its sessions.

narrative_blocks.header: Nothing was ever beyond his recollection
narrative_blocks.body: His obituary called an uncommonly powerful and retentive memory his most distinguished characteristic, and said it held to the end. No fact he had ever known, no person he had ever seen, no name that had been familiar to his ear seemed for a moment beyond the grasp of it.

narrative_blocks.header: A fever took him in a fortnight
narrative_blocks.body: At seventy-five he had lived a stranger to the attacks of disease and the common infirmities of old age. A fever then running through the town, which had already killed several men of worth there, took him two weeks after it reached him.

narrative_blocks.header: The party fell and took him with it
narrative_blocks.body: He was assistant judge of the county court from 1802, and when the old Federalist party collapsed in 1818 his public career closed with it. He had been on the bench sixteen years.

narrative_blocks.header: The General Assembly sent him to Bostwick
narrative_blocks.body: In November 1806 the assembly named him one of three commissioners on the insolvent estate of Joseph E. Bostwick of New Milford. They sat at Wells Beardsley's house in Washington on the third Monday of February to hear what the creditors claimed.

narrative_blocks.header: What his stone says he was
narrative_blocks.body: It reads: Integrity, Energy, and Ability marked his public condition. Sincerity, Benevolence, Piety adorned his private life. He was seventy-five.

narrative_blocks.header: A flood on the river broke him
narrative_blocks.body: He ran the Connecticut River Railroad out of Springfield until 1868, and a freshet on the river tore up his line. The severe pressure of the overwork it caused brought on a mental derangement he suffered at intervals for the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: He took one more road and lost it
narrative_blocks.body: When the Connecticut Western was building he was engaged as its chief engineer, and his mind broke down again under the pressure. For several years after he was from time to time an inmate of Dr. Buel's establishment.

narrative_blocks.header: Their old master in the practice of music
narrative_blocks.body: An old friend wrote that he had led a band of ten or fifteen of them when they were boys, and that they had never ceased to be grateful for the impulse his genial leadership gave them in the most social of the arts. The music probably sounded pleasanter at forty years' distance than it had at the time.

narrative_blocks.header: Modest in success, upright in adversity
narrative_blocks.body: He died suddenly at Spring Hill on a Sunday morning in May 1880, at sixty-one. His obituary said he had known how to face adversity with a fortitude that could hardly fail to bring tears to the eyes of old friends who remembered it.

narrative_blocks.header: His eldest son took over the Gunnery
narrative_blocks.body: He left a widow, two sons and a daughter — John Chapin, Anna Louisa and William Gold. The eldest, a Harvard graduate, had lately married a daughter of F. W. Gunn and was by then in charge of the noted Gunnery school at Washington, the town his father was carried home to on the Sunday train.

narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Towanda in Pennsylvania in January 1849, while his father was still shut out of Washington for his abolitionism. The family came home that summer, and he died in April 1865, the month the war ended.

narrative_blocks.header: Mistress and mother of the school since 1881
narrative_blocks.body: She was born and brought up in the Gunnery, taught in it for several years, and after her father's death in 1881 was its mistress and mother while her husband ran it. She had nine children in the same house.

narrative_blocks.header: She married her first cousin
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother Abigail and his father William Bartlett were sister and brother, so the bride and groom were first cousins. They married on the fourth of October 1876 — her father Frederick Gunn's sixtieth birthday, and the groom's own twenty-fourth.

narrative_blocks.header: She favoured woman suffrage
narrative_blocks.body: Who's Who of American Women lists her for the New Haven branch of the Women's Board of Foreign Missions, as regent of the Judea chapter of the D.A.R., and as a member of the League of Washington. It records plainly that she favours woman suffrage.

narrative_blocks.header: He is why Americans go to camp
narrative_blocks.body: In 1861 he marched his students thirty miles from Washington to Welch's Point at Milford and camped ten days, swimming, foraging and drilling for the war he knew was coming. The boys called it gypsying, and the American Camp Association dates organised camping in the United States from it.

narrative_blocks.header: The parson preached him out of town
narrative_blocks.body: Parson Gordon Hayes defended slavery from the pulpit at Washington and condemned the abolitionists, and parents began pulling their children out of Gunn's classroom until he could not earn a living. He went into exile at Towanda in Pennsylvania in 1847 and came home in 1849 to open his own school beside the same church.

narrative_blocks.header: Girls, and everybody else, from the start
narrative_blocks.body: He took girls into the school from its first year, then African American, Native American and international students, and from 1872 Chinese boys under the Hartford mission. Among his earliest pupils were the children of Harriet Beecher Stowe and Henry Ward Beecher.

narrative_blocks.header: He is in the first photograph of baseball
narrative_blocks.body: Seth Landon photographed a game in progress on the Washington green on the fourth of August 1869, at the first Gunnery alumni reunion, and Gunn is in it. It is the earliest known picture of baseball being played, and Ken Burns used it.

narrative_blocks.header: The first lending library was his parlour
narrative_blocks.body: He put Washington's first lending library in his own living room and auctioned the right to borrow to raise money for more books. The Gunn Memorial Library was dedicated in 1908, its facade of fieldstone hauled from nearby farms by his students.

narrative_blocks.header: His pupils put up the stone
narrative_blocks.body: He taught to the end and died at his home in Washington in August 1881, at sixty-four. The stone reads: erected to the founder of the Gunnery School by his pupils, 1847-1881.

people.research_notes: Eighth and youngest child of John Northrup Gunn (1772-1826), farmer and deputy sheriff, and Mary (Polly) Ford (1773-1827); orphaned at ten when both died in an epidemic, and raised by his eldest brother John. School at Cornwall 1829; studied with the Rev. Watson W. Andrews in the First Congregational meeting house at Washington 1831-33. Yale class of 1837, majored in botany. Classmates included Morrison R. Waite, later Chief Justice; William M. Evarts; Edwards Pierrepont; and Benjamin Silliman Jr., who wrote that 'his very distinctly pronounced individuality and his manliness are sharply defined in my memory'. Orville H. Platt said that twenty years later he would have been first in the university boat crew. Made his own hunting bow, 'a bow which none but he could fully draw'. Conductor on the Underground Railroad. Summer camps at Point Beautiful, Lake Waramaug, 1867-1879; A. S. Gregg Clarke of the class of 1889 revived them and founded the Keewaydin camps. Temperance man who held that his students had 'an inalienable right to their fun' and ran dances, debates and plays that became the town's Dramalites. Said one needed a 'boy-heart' to teach the young. NONE of his own family is built here.

narrative_blocks.body: Hunnewell Braman died at New Canaan on the twenty-fourth of July 1968 and she followed there on the twenty-third of August 1969, fifty-four years married. All four of their children were born at Washington.

narrative_blocks.header: Vassar, then nurse's training
narrative_blocks.body: Charlotte graduated from Vassar in 1915 and trained for two years as a nurse at Presbyterian Hospital in New York before she married Alfred at Washington on 26 June 1920.

narrative_blocks.header: Two cousin marriages, one generation apart
narrative_blocks.body: Charlotte's parents were first cousins. She in turn married a distant cousin, Alfred Raymond Bellinger, who like her descended from Thomas Hooker.

narrative_blocks.body: He sat in both the Connecticut house and senate and on the state constitutional committee, and belonged to the Council on Education and the American Academy of Political and Social Science. He was a Republican who joined the Progressive Party for a time and went back.

narrative_blocks.body: His mother was a daughter of Colonel Harvey Chapin and the sixth in descent from Deacon Samuel Chapin, who settled at Springfield in 1642. On the other side he came from the Rev. Daniel Brinsmade, Yale 1745, first minister of the Judea society at Washington.

narrative_blocks.body: He was county supervisor several years and went to the New York legislature in 1836 for three consecutive terms. He began a Whig, turned staunch Republican when the party was organised, and was a strong anti-slavery advocate and a Universalist.

narrative_blocks.header: They married on his birthday
narrative_blocks.body: Davis Hurd was born on the twelfth of April 1788 and married Amanda Turner on the twelfth of April 1812, his twenty-fourth. She bore eleven children, two of whom died as infants.

narrative_blocks.header: Hurd is a big man, meaning great
narrative_blocks.body: The family history says he was of perfect physique and magnificent stature, with a gentle manner firm at times almost to sternness, and that no one was ever turned away from his generous hearted philanthropy. The remark made of the name was that Hurd is a big man, meaning great.

narrative_blocks.header: He stayed on the land his sons left
narrative_blocks.body: He decided early to move toward the great unknown West and took up a tract near Middleport in New York that became his home and his son's. He loved the old place and remained quietly there, away from the busier life his boys longed to enter.

narrative_blocks.body: An Isaac was born in 1827 and another in 1835, and both are carried as living. Henry Freeman came the same year as the first Isaac, and the eight children ran from 1821 to 1845.

narrative_blocks.header: Ninety-nine years in the same town
narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Denmark in Lewis County in February 1856 and died there in August 1955, six months short of a hundred. Cassius had gone thirty-three years before her.

narrative_blocks.header: She married again at sixty-four
narrative_blocks.body: Reuben Pickett died at Fairport in July 1915 after five children. In February 1922 she married William Adam Kuder, and she died at Rochester in 1938.

people.research_notes: CONFIRMED by Sam: the five Pickett children are hers by the Rev. Reuben Willis Pickett, not her sister Lydia's. The earlier note in the batch reading 'lydia and reuben' was a slip, and the dates had already ruled Lydia out — she was born in 1867 and the eldest Pickett child in 1879. Reuben died in July 1915 and Linda married William Adam Kuder in February 1922.

narrative_blocks.header: She lived a hundred and one years
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Pulteney in Steuben County in November 1888, she married Harry Lawson in May 1910 and outlived him by twenty-two years. She died at Rochester in March 1990.

narrative_blocks.header: She married at forty, and had no children
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph Severance was fifty-nine and she was forty when they married in September 1839. They had no children, and he outlived her by nineteen months.

people.research_notes: Her gravestone at Greenfield gives the death as 25 March 1818; a FamilySearch extract gives 25 March 1813. Neither is resolved. A second Caroline was born in 1814.

narrative_blocks.header: Dead three weeks after her last child
narrative_blocks.body: Hannah Jane was born on the sixteenth of November 1840 and she died on the seventh of December, at thirty-five. Dr. Bates married her sister Harriet two and a half years later.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty years a widow, buried at Syracuse
narrative_blocks.body: Volney Cook died at Syracuse in April 1843, eleven years into the marriage and childless. She went home to Greenfield and died there in 1873, but was carried back to Syracuse to be buried.

bio.research_notes: Both daughters supplied 2026-08-01: Caroline Newton Elizabeth Bates (FamilySearch K6QN-2JH) and Elizabeth Cook Bates (G93N-G11).

narrative_blocks.header: She came into her sister's house
narrative_blocks.body: Hannah died in December 1840 leaving Dr. Stephen Bates with three young children. He married Harriet, her younger sister, in May 1843, and they had two more. Both sisters lie in the Village ground at Charlemont.

narrative_blocks.header: Both her girls were named for her sisters
narrative_blocks.body: Caroline Newton Elizabeth came in 1844 and Elizabeth Cook in 1847. Harriet had five sisters and two of them were Caroline — the first dead at ten in 1813, the second still living when the baby was named for them both. Elizabeth Cook carried the whole name of the sister widowed at Syracuse, married surname and all.

people.research_notes: Sam's batch records two children by Dr. Bates; neither is named in any source here.

narrative_blocks.header: Two daughters named Caroline
narrative_blocks.body: The first Caroline died as a child and the name was given again to a daughter born in 1814. Hannah was widowed at thirty-seven with seven children and kept on another thirty-one years, dying at Charlemont where two of her girls had married the same man.

people.research_notes: Christened 27 May 1781, nearly three years after birth. Stone: 'Mrs. Hannah Newton, Wife of the late Mr. Ozias Newton died March 16 A.D. 1846 Aged 67'.

bio.research_notes: Death year 1855 inferred from the burial record (Village Cemetery, Charlemont, 1855); FamilySearch MNF4-QGR records only 'Deceased'.

narrative_blocks.header: He married two Newton sisters
narrative_blocks.body: Hannah Newton bore him three children and died in December 1840. In May 1843 he married her younger sister Harriet and had two more, and all three of them lie at Charlemont.

people.research_notes: Married Delight Camp, daughter of Ebenezer Camp and a ward of his aunt Submit Newton Camp; Submit made her home with them after 1823. Delight is not built here.

narrative_blocks.header: The three-year-old who sat with her
narrative_blocks.body: Through the last two years of Abigail Fairchild Newton's life, when she lay a helpless invalid, her son Elisha's little boy was her comfort and company. She died in November 1825, when Israel was three. He kept to Durham the whole of his life and died there in 1900, at seventy-seven.

narrative_blocks.header: She married her first cousin at twenty-six
narrative_blocks.body: Abigail Maria Newton married Henry Ward of Middletown on the thirteenth of May 1852. His mother Parnell and her father Elisha were brother and sister, both children of Dea. Abner Newton, so bride and groom were first cousins.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-five years married in Middletown
narrative_blocks.body: He married Parnell Newton in 1814, when he was twenty-six and she was twenty-three, and they kept house on Main Street near Mill Bridge. He died at Middletown in November 1869 after fifty-five years of it, and she outlived him by eleven.

bio.research_notes: Son of Henry Ward (HD9360). Born 14 Jun 1850, two years before Henry's 13 May 1852 marriage to his cousin Abigail Maria Newton, so his mother is presumably an earlier wife not named in the sources supplied. Deliberately NOT attached to the 1852 marriage — flagged for Sam.

burial.plot_notes: Bloomfield, Hartford County, Connecticut; buried 14 May 1928

narrative_blocks.header: Eight children, and four small graves
narrative_blocks.body: They had eight children between 1898 and 1914 and buried four of them small. Herbert died the year he was born; 1912 took Henry Newton, born 1906, and the infant Charles; Edward died in 1921 at seven. Of the four who grew up, Helen Elizabeth married Glenn Racine Pierce in 1921 and had five children of her own.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave his children his siblings' names
narrative_blocks.body: He was the third of Joab and Harriet's four and the only one to leave descendants — Charles Walter died at one, Edward at a few months. His daughter born in 1901 was Helen Elizabeth for the sister ten years his senior, and a son born in 1914 was Edward for the brother he lost at three.

narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Chillicothe in Ohio in 1867 and married Robert Ward Loomis at East Hartford in October 1897. Their first child came the next year and was christened Herbert Dickinson Loomis, carrying her own family name. He died the year he was born.

narrative_blocks.header: She carried three of her aunts' names
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Charlemont in 1844, the elder of Dr. Bates's two daughters by Harriet. Caroline was for the aunt still living and the aunt who had died at ten, Newton was her mother's own name, and Elizabeth was for the aunt widowed at Syracuse.

narrative_blocks.header: Named for a widow, surname and all
narrative_blocks.body: Her aunt Elizabeth Newton married Volney Cook in 1832 and lost him at Syracuse in 1843, childless. Four years later this niece was christened Elizabeth Cook Bates, married name and all, and lived to 1906 — thirty-three years past the aunt she was named for.

narrative_blocks.header: Buried twelve miles from home
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Worthington in March 1768 and dead there in April 1821, at fifty-three. He was buried twelve miles off at Ware, and Susannah lived another thirty-four years without him.

narrative_blocks.header: Five years married, twenty-seven years alone
narrative_blocks.body: He married Sarah Waite in July 1838; she was twenty-three. She died in 1843 at twenty-eight, and he lived on until 1870 — twenty-seven years past her.

bio.research_notes: Surname spelled Peirce in the record (FamilySearch MN59-6TL); his brothers are recorded as Pierce.

naming_inspiration.description: Named for his grandfather, Rev. Roger Newton, D.D., of Greenfield.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept the old spelling of the name
narrative_blocks.body: Named in 1811 for his grandfather, Rev. Roger Newton, D.D., of Greenfield. The record spells his surname Peirce where his brothers John and William are Pierce.

narrative_blocks.header: Six children across twenty-three years
narrative_blocks.body: He married Adelaide Augusta Wheelwright of Cohasset in May 1864, when she was sixteen. Alice came in 1866 and Charlotte Augusta not until 1889, twenty-three years and five children later. He outlived his wife by two years and died in 1923, at eighty-three.

bio.photo_notes: Photographed with her husband, Clarence O. Green.

narrative_blocks.header: She died the day after her birthday
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Cohasset on the sixteenth of September 1871, she died at Whitman on the seventeenth of September 1957 — one day past her eighty-sixth birthday. She was buried three days later in Colebrook Cemetery there.

narrative_blocks.header: Two of her sons spell it Greene
narrative_blocks.body: She and Clarence O. Green had six children between 1890 and 1915. The four eldest are recorded Green and the two youngest Greene, and the second spelling is the one that carried on down to her grandchildren. Her firstborn, Minnie Adelaide, was named for her mother.

narrative_blocks.header: One hundred and one years
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Cohasset in 1873 and living until 1974 — a century and a year, and thirteen years longer than anyone else of the six. He was not the last of them to go, though: his youngest sister Charlotte Augusta, sixteen years behind him, outlived him by three.

bio.research_notes: Dates not supplied. Husband of Sarah Lurinda Pierce (HD9388).

narrative_blocks.header: Married at nineteen, a father at twenty-one
narrative_blocks.body: He married Josephine Madeline St Onge on the twenty-second of September 1915, three months before his twentieth birthday. Two children came to them in 1917, and the daughter was dead by the thirtieth of October. He lived on to ninety-four and died at Brockton in 1990.

narrative_blocks.header: Two years older than his nephews
narrative_blocks.body: He was born in 1915, fifteen years after the brother before him and the same year his eldest brother Irving married. Irving's first children came in 1917, so this youngest son of the house was an uncle at two.

bio.research_notes: Entered without a given name (FamilySearch LB97-LC5).

narrative_blocks.header: A niece was given her name entire
narrative_blocks.body: The eldest of Joab and Harriet's four, born in 1852, ten years ahead of her brother Robert. When his daughter was born in 1901 he called her Helen Elizabeth after this aunt, who lived on another fourteen years.

naming_inspiration.description: Given his mother's maiden surname; she was a Newton of Durham.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother's name became his middle one
narrative_blocks.body: The eldest of John and Parnell's four, born at Middletown in 1816 and dead there at seventy-seven. His mother was a Newton of Durham, daughter of Dea. Abner, and her maiden name came down to her first son as his middle.

narrative_blocks.header: At eighty-seven she still saw Aunt Mitty
narrative_blocks.body: Named for her aunt Content Newton, who never had children of her own. In old age she could still describe her great-aunt Submit Camp — hair cut short across the forehead, when every other woman in Durham bought a false front to wear under her cap once her own began to grey.

military_service.notes: Trained at the Training School for Chaplains, Camp Taylor; commissioned chaplain with the rank of first lieutenant; sailed for France June 1918. Killed instantly by a bursting shell at Xammes 29 Sept. 1918 and buried the next day at Bouillonville, Grave No. 40, on a hill south of the village with nearly sixty Americans of the Saint-Mihiel offensive. Reinterred New Florence, Missouri, 23 April 1922.

narrative_blocks.header: Pastor of Minneapolis, chaplain to the 354th
narrative_blocks.body: He left the First Church of Minneapolis for the front and died at Xammes in Lorraine in 1918, at thirty-seven. His body was brought back to Missouri and reinterred in the April of 1922.

narrative_blocks.header: Grave No. 40 on a hill above Bouillonville
narrative_blocks.body: A shell killed him instantly at Xammes on the twenty-ninth of September 1918 and he was buried the next day. Nearly sixty Americans of the Saint-Mihiel offensive lay on that hill, each grave marked by a wooden cross carrying the man's own identification tag.

narrative_blocks.header: He asked his church for leave to enlist
narrative_blocks.body: The First Church of Minneapolis released him for the length of the war so he could train at the chaplains' school at Camp Taylor. He was commissioned first lieutenant, sailed in June 1918, and was in the front line three months later.

narrative_blocks.header: Two years to study wherever he liked
narrative_blocks.body: The seminary gave him a two-year scholarship and the choice of spending it at home or abroad. He stayed, and put it into rural problems at Kansas State, Wisconsin and Amherst.

people.research_notes: Chaplain, 354th Infantry, 89th Division. Died at Xammes, France; body reinterred at New Florence, Missouri, 23 April 1922. From Sam's FamilySearch/FindAGrave extract, 1 Aug 2026. DATE CONFLICT: the FindAGrave field reads 29 Sept. 1918, the memorial text 29 August 1918; the structured field is taken. Memorial tribute by Rev. H. K. Painter, chairman of the Conference Committee on Necrology, quoted in Congregational Work of Minnesota, pp. 253-255; text supplied by Sam 1 Aug 2026. Career as given there: born Fort Madison, Iowa, 1881; graduated Yankton College, South Dakota, at twenty-six; a year teaching at Northland College, Wisconsin, supplying the church at Odana; three years at Chicago Theological Seminary while serving Jefferson Park Church as student pastor; then a two-year scholarship with the option of study at home or abroad, spent on rural problems at the State Agricultural College at Manhattan Kansas, Wisconsin University, and Amherst; taught a while at Chicago Seminary; called to the First Church of Minneapolis Sept. 1913. Granted leave of absence by the church for the period of the war. The grave marker at Bouillonville read: CHAPLAIN HARRY DEIMAN / 1st Lieut. 354th Inf. / Died Sept. 29, 1918 / Buried Sept. 30, 1918 / Grave No. 40. This settles the earlier 29 Aug./29 Sept. conflict in favour of 29 September. NOTABLE CANDIDATE, for Sam: the necrology states it is believed he was the only Congregational chaplain of the American forces killed in action in that war, and he held the pulpit of the oldest Congregational church in Minnesota. Not flagged is_notable — that needs an external URL and Sam's approval. The 'only' claim is hedged in the source and is deliberately NOT asserted in any block. President Ozora Davis of Chicago Seminary called him 'the most thorough scholar in recent years' there. Rev. Bacon of Park Avenue Church, Minneapolis, visited the grave and reported the wooden crosses, each carrying the dead man's identification tag. NB HEADERS REWRITTEN 2 Aug 2026 on Sam's instruction. The originals leaned on undefined referents — 'the committee that built it', 'fifteen days before', 'the whole way' — so a reader scanning the headers without expanding them learned nothing about the person. Schema §5 calls for a concrete anchor and says the header must never be obscure; the 29 July handoff records the same verdict. Rewritten to name a place, a number or a thing while still withholding the payoff.

Received into the West Hartford Congregational Church 20 Nov. 1831; a letter of dismission issued 14 May 1837 to 'Br. Calvin Newton and sister Newton, his wife' as they left for Iowa; he and his second wife received back by letter 2 Sept. 1848. About 1852 the family removed from Norwich to Pomfret, where he farmed. The 1850 Norwich census lists him at 42 with Mary H. 32, Reuben W. 14, Elizabeth 11 (born Iowa), George 4, and Maria one month old. Will dated 8 April 1871 left everything to his wife, the children unmentioned; Crosby Mill of Pomfret executor; proved 7 July 1875. The widow lived from at least 1880 with her daughter Lucy Ida. A DOUBLE MATCH WITH THE WHIPPLES, worth a CC if Joseph Whipple is ever built: Calvin married Sarepta Whipple, daughter of Samuel and Mary (Chaffee) Whipple, on 5 Oct. 1834 — eleven months after his sister Eunice (HD9511) married Joseph Whipple, son of the same couple. A brother and sister married a sister and brother. CC LABEL REWRITTEN 2 Aug 2026 on Sam's objection. The first version read 'Nelson Newton was the father of Edward Nelson Newton, who married Lucy Ida' — a statement about two other people that never said why Nelson belongs on this card. Calvin and Nelson are FIRST COUSINS whose children married each other; the label now says so. A CC that does not carry its own relevance is noise. Still unused from the chapter, if more is ever wanted here: the West Hartford church issued a letter of dismission on 14 May 1837 to 'Br. Calvin Newton and sister Newton, his wife' as they left for Iowa, and received him and his second wife back by letter 2 Sept. 1848 — the congregation formally let them go and formally took them back. About 1852 the family removed from Norwich to Pomfret. The Probate Clerk's note that the will's silence on the children 'probably means all property was held jointly' is the court's reading, not a fact, and is deliberately kept out of the block.

narrative_blocks.body: The wedding was in Lee County in the April of 1840. Within two years he had brought Harriet the twelve hundred miles back to Norwich, and every one of their six children was born on that Vermont ground, from 1842 to 1864.

narrative_blocks.header: His farm lay just north of cousin Nelson
narrative_blocks.body: The Norwich maps of 1859 and 1869 show a place carrying his initial a short way up the road from his cousin's. Truman's will of 1848 had given the largest legacies to Calvin, Joseph, Laura Ann and Sarah Lucinda, and Orson's part came to a twenty-fifth of Calvin's.

narrative_blocks.header: Three of his children died as babies
narrative_blocks.body: George Truman lived nine months and was gone in the September of 1857, Hattie a year and a fortnight, dying in the February of 1861. The second George, named for the first, was born in the April of 1864 and buried that October.

narrative_blocks.header: He made the journey to Iowa twice
narrative_blocks.body: The first time he went out, married and turned back for Vermont within two years. The second time he stayed, and he and Harriet both lie at Denmark in Lee County, where his brothers had settled.

bio.bio_blurb: Followed his brother to Iowa and stayed

narrative_blocks.header: Two brothers dismissed the same month
narrative_blocks.body: The West Hartford Congregational Church gave Daniel his letter of dismission and recommendation in the September of 1838, and gave Orson one in that same month. Calvin had gone out to Denmark in Lee County the year before, and Daniel followed him there.

narrative_blocks.header: He married in Vermont and never came back
narrative_blocks.body: The wedding was at Norwich in the July of 1837 and the first child arrived in Lee County thirteen months later. All five were born on that Iowa ground and he died on it at forty-five.

bio.bio_blurb: Norwich farmer; Millerite; put out of his church

burial.plot_notes: Denmark Cemetery, Denmark, Lee County, Iowa

narrative_blocks.header: Four were ever put out of that church
narrative_blocks.body: The West Hartford Congregational Church received him by profession in the March of 1835 and cut him and Lucy Anne off in the November of 1844. In the whole history of that congregation only the two of them and two others, Noah Dutton and Charles Thurston, were ever excommunicated.

narrative_blocks.header: They waited to go up in 1843
narrative_blocks.body: William Miller preached at Pomfret in the fall of 1842 and won converts across those towns, some of whom gave away everything they had against the end of the world. Enos and Lucy Anne turned Second Adventist the next year, and when the appointed time passed without them they renounced the church and turned to the world.

narrative_blocks.header: The census put him between Calvin and Rufus
narrative_blocks.body: At Norwich in 1850 he was thirty-three, a farmer with a hundred and ten acres improved and fifty more not, his wife and three small children in the house. He appears in no Norwich census after that one.

narrative_blocks.header: He died in Indiana and lies in Iowa
narrative_blocks.body: He and Lucy Anne both ended at Terre Haute, he in the May of 1888 and she two years later. Both were carried to Denmark in Lee County, where his brothers had settled.

narrative_blocks.header: All four children ended far from Norwich
narrative_blocks.body: Owen, Caroline and Flora all died in southern California, and Maria at Nanaimo on Vancouver Island. Every one of them had been born on the Norwich farm.

people.research_notes: From the printed Newton chapter 42 (Truman^6), page images read 1 Aug 2026. From Sam's FamilySearch extract, 1 Aug 2026. Received into the West Hartford Congregational Church by profession on 1 March 1835; he and Lucy Anne were excommunicated 2 November 1844, and with Noah Dutton and Charles Thurston were the only persons ever excommunicated from that church. He, Lucy Anne and Noah Dutton became Second Adventists in 1843 and, failing to go up at the time William Miller designated, renounced the church and turned to the world; Miller had preached at Pomfret in the fall of 1842 and converts across those towns gave away their property against the end. The 1850 Norwich census lists him between Calvin and Rufus Newton at thirty-three, a farmer, with Lucy A. thirty-one, Owen E. eight, Caroline F. six and Maria one, all born in Vermont; the agricultural schedule gives a hundred and ten acres improved and fifty unimproved. He does not appear in any later Norwich census. No canonical tag exists for Millerite or Second Adventist belief — proposed to Sam. narrative_blocks.body: She appears at Norwich in Vermont as Mary H. Newton, thirty-two, and again at Windham in Connecticut as Spencer, thirty-four, in her father's household.

narrative_blocks.header: He married Amos Wood's daughter and his farm
narrative_blocks.body: He came to Amos Wood's place in the spring of 1858 and married Frances that October. He worked the farm after Wood died in 1865 and owned it outright when Wood's widow died in 1890.

narrative_blocks.header: Married twice in three days, to one woman
narrative_blocks.body: He and Frances were married at Woodstock on the second of October 1858 and again at Pomfret on the fourth, by a different minister. He turned twenty-three the day after the second.

narrative_blocks.header: At six he rode home from Iowa
narrative_blocks.body: He was eighteen months old when his parents took him to Iowa and six when his father brought him and his little sister back, their mother dead. He could still tell much of the eight weeks on the road.

narrative_blocks.header: Four nephews carried him out
narrative_blocks.body: He was a deacon of the Pomfret Congregational Church for twenty-nine years. Elmer Newton, Coyt Dimick, John Doton and John Dana laid him at rest in the January of 1910.

people.research_notes: From the printed Newton chapter 56 (Calvin C.^7), page images read 1 Aug 2026. From Sam's FamilySearch/FindAGrave extract, 1 Aug 2026. A year old when the family went to Iowa in 1837 and six when his father brought him back in 1842. From the printed Newton chapter 72 (Reuben Whipple^8), read 1 Aug 2026. He went to work for Amos Wood in the spring of 1858 and married Wood's daughter that October; ran the farm after Wood died in 1865 and owned it after Wood's widow died in 1890. Deacon of the Pomfret Congregational Church 1881-1910 (Vail, History of Pomfret, 1930, v. 1 p. 233). No children. OBITUARY, from a Pomfret Historical Society scrapbook: he was eighteen months old when his parents went to Iowa and six when his father brought him and his little sister back, their mother dead, and he could tell much of the eight weeks on the road. In poor health his last six months; three weeks before the end he took the grip, which hastened troubles 'of a cancerous nature'. Funeral at his late home 7 Jan. 1910, Rev. Mr. Moe of Norwich officiating; he was laid at rest by four nephews — Elmer Newton, Coyt Dimick, John Doton and John Dana. The obituary names his three surviving sisters as Mrs. R. W. Newton of Hartford CT (Elizabeth Snow), Mrs. L. T. Wills of Sycamore Ill. (Maria Louisa) and Mrs. S. L. Dimick of West Hartford (Lucy Ida) — which also gives Lucy Ida's second husband's initials. MARRIAGE DATES: the Montpelier vital records show TWO ceremonies with Frances — Woodstock 2 Oct. 1858 by L. C. Dickerson and Pomfret 4 Oct. 1858 by Rev. Jonathan Clement — while the obituary gives 5 Oct., his own birthday. The second marriage, to Mary A. Keith, took place 7 June 1885 at Pomfret, Rev. Henry A. Van Dalsene officiating: her twenty-ninth birthday. NB HEADERS REWRITTEN 2 Aug 2026 on Sam's instruction. The originals leaned on undefined referents — 'the committee that built it', 'fifteen days before', 'the whole way' — so a reader scanning the headers without expanding them learned nothing about the person. Schema §5 calls for a concrete anchor and says the header must never be obscure; the 29 July handoff records the same verdict. Rewritten to name a place, a number or a thing while still withholding the payoff.

narrative_blocks.header: She and Roswell both died in 1924
narrative_blocks.body: They married in the February of 1862 and were still together sixty-two years later, when both died at Hartford. She had been born at Denmark in Iowa and carried back to Vermont at four.

narrative_blocks.body: He married Anna Crocker in the April of 1875 and died in the October of 1881, at twenty-nine. She outlived him by thirty-six years and lies beside him at Central Falls.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at thirty, and carrying a third son
narrative_blocks.body: Edward died in the May of 1886, leaving her a six-year-old boy, an elderly widowed mother and an unborn child. Jason had died of pneumonia ten months earlier; Elmer was born on the first of November.

narrative_blocks.header: The census called her the farmer, not him
narrative_blocks.body: In 1910 she was set down running a dairy farm on her own account, while Sheldon Dimick was a teamster driving oxen in the woods. She had held land in her own name since 1887.

narrative_blocks.header: She sold the farm but kept the graveyard
narrative_blocks.body: As administrator she deeded the whole Norwich place away in 1886, excepting a small burying ground and the right to keep it fenced. Rufus Newton, who cleared that farm, lies in it.

narrative_blocks.header: Her Bible history went into print in 1889
narrative_blocks.body: She wrote the family's history from David Newton down by hand and kept it inside the covers of her Bible. Tucker's History of the Town of Hartford drew on it when it was published in 1889.

narrative_blocks.header: She brought back the first radio in 1924
narrative_blocks.body: It was a two-tube Crosley carried home from Pawtucket, and that autumn's World Series was the first big thing heard on it. A hundred feet of aerial went up at her house and another at her son Erwin's.

narrative_blocks.header: She gave the red chair to a three-year-old
narrative_blocks.body: The chair had come out of Iowa on her father's wagon a decade before she was born. She passed it on to her great-grandson Ronald when he was about three.

people.research_notes: The family record-keeper. She wrote out 'The Newton Family' by hand and kept it within the covers of her Bible; that manuscript is the source of the sixteen-children passage quoted in her great-grandfather David's chapter, and she recited the covered-wagon and red-chair story. Her first husband was Edward N. Newton (chapter no. 70); Dimick was later. Neither husband is built at this level. From the printed Newton chapter 56 (Calvin C.^7), page images read 1 Aug 2026. From Sam's FamilySearch/FindAGrave extract, 1 Aug 2026. The chapter gives her death as 1943, FamilySearch 1945; FamilySearch taken per Sam's rule. Her maiden name and her first married name are both Newton, so display_name is set explicitly to 'Lucy Ida Newton Dimick' rather than assembled, which would double the surname. married_names keeps both. NB REMOVED 2 Aug 2026 on Sam's instruction: 'She married her own second cousin'. His point stands — this tree is substantially made of cousins, so the bare fact of a cousin marriage is not worth a block, and 'own' was straining for an astonishment the material does not carry. The cousin_marriage tag and the parent-to-parent CC hold the structure without it. A block here would need something the structure cannot show. From the printed Newton chapter 70 (Edward Nelson^8 and Lucy Ida^8), read 2 Aug 2026. Died in a private nursing home at Barnard, aged 89. MARRIAGE DATE — the one place FamilySearch is NOT taken. Sam's extract gives 16 March 1878; the chapter gives 16 March 1874 AND describes her as 'an 18-year-old bride'. Born 11 March 1856, she was eighteen in March 1874 and would have been twenty-two in 1878, so the source's own arithmetic rules the later year out. 1874 kept; she married five days after her eighteenth birthday. Detail not blocked, kept here: she was recalled as warm, bright-eyed, alert and religious, of slight build, rather short and somewhat stooped; she added a long hank of hair each morning — a 'rat' — to form a bun over thinning hair; she taught her grandchildren the card game Flinch; she kept a tallow candle mould and used it into the compiler's boyhood, electricity not reaching West Hartford until 1926; she made soap from lye and fat living alone; and she kept a small spinning wheel that had come down through the family. She lies in West Hartford Cemetery BETWEEN her two husbands under a stone reading 'L. Ida Newton, wife of Edward N. Newton and second wife of Sheldon L. Dimick'. She raised two sons by her first marriage, three stepchildren and the son of her second. Her grandmother Eunice (Wilson) Newton lived nearby until Lucy Ida was nearly fifteen, and several of David Newton's sixteen children were alive in her teens — one still living when she first married.

military_service.notes: Enlisted 14 Aug. 1863 as a substitute for Minor W. Allen of Hartford VT. Killed in action 5 May 1864 on the march toward the Wilderness.

narrative_blocks.header: He chose his guardian and enlisted that week
narrative_blocks.body: Committed to Calvin Newton in infancy and given the Newton name, he petitioned the court at eighteen to make the guardianship formal. Four days later he was mustered into Company G of the Third Vermont as a substitute for another man.

narrative_blocks.header: The Third headed the column that day
narrative_blocks.body: He was killed on the fifth of May 1864 on the march toward the Wilderness, which cost the regiment one man in three. Lucy Ida Newton remembered the day the report reached the house, and kept his wallet.

people.research_notes: NOT A BLOOD DESCENDANT and never legally adopted — classification is deliberately non-descendant. From the printed Newton chapter 56 (Calvin C.^7), page images read 1 Aug 2026. His own guardianship petition (Hartford District Probate, Woodstock VT, v. 26 p. 18) states he was born 16 Aug. 1845, the illegitimate son of Maria Carpenter, who had never married at the time; that the name George Newton was given him by Calvin Newton, a friend to whom he was committed in infancy and with whom he had since lived; and that his mother married some months later, leaving him with neither parent to act for him, so he chose Calvin as guardian. Calvin was appointed 10 Aug. 1863; George enlisted four days later, on the 14th, into Co. G, 3rd Vermont Volunteers, as a substitute for Minor W. Allen of Hartford. The chapter concludes the guardianship existed chiefly to let him enlist. Killed in action 5 May 1864 on the march toward the Wilderness, which the Third headed and on which it lost one in three of its rank and file (Vermont Revised Roster of Volunteers 1861-66, p. 94). The 1866 probate decree named his mother his sole heir. Aldrich's History of Windsor County and Lucy Ida Dimick both call him adopted; the chapter's verdict is that 'even though never legally adopted, George was considered and treated as a member of the Newton family'. BIRTH: the chapter's sworn petition gives 16 Aug. 1845, FamilySearch 1846; the petition is taken. FOR SAM: he sits in the marriage's children_ids so he renders as the household child he was, but carries no descent and no generation. PARENT LINK REPAIRED 1 Aug 2026 on Sam's catch: he sat in both parents' children_ids with an empty parents dict, so the link ran one way and his own card showed no parents. The household relationship is now bidirectional; the blood truth stays in classification, which carries no descent, and in the adopted tag — which is exactly what schema §6 defines it for: 'adopted child; not a blood descendant of the adopting parent(s)'.

narrative_blocks.header: His Newtons were Chittendens by blood
narrative_blocks.body: His grandmother was widowed young and then married a Roswell Newton, and her Chittenden sons took their stepfather's surname. So the Newton he carried was borrowed, and no blood tie stood between him and the Newton he married. A grandson was christened Roswell Allen Chittenden Newton in 1890.

The reason is that his Newton name is a STEP-NAME. Mrs. Leonard's 1915 Newton Genealogy, p. 774, records that his grandmother was first married to a Mr. Chittenden and, widowed, married Roswell Newton Sr.; her Chittenden sons took their stepfather's surname. They are not, and the reason is already on this record: his Newton name is a STEP-NAME taken from his grandmother's second husband, so no Newton in this tree is his blood relation and no Newton CC is valid for him. The Chittenden side was checked too: the file holds Huldah Newton Chittenden (HD0150, 1751-1794, of Middletown CT, who married Beriah Chittenden of Guilford and whose family went to Ohio). bio.bio_blurb: Hartford, CT banker; messenger to vice-president

career.organization: Mark Twain Library and Memorial Commission

narrative_blocks.header: He began at the bank as a messenger
narrative_blocks.body: He went into the Hartford Trust Company in 1881, at eighteen, carrying messages between desks. He was its vice-president from 1925 and president of the Industrial Bank of Hartford, and kept his house out at Andover while the office stayed on Main Street.

narrative_blocks.header: Treasurer of the Mark Twain memorial
narrative_blocks.body: He kept the accounts of the Mark Twain Library and Memorial Commission at Hartford. He sat as well with the Hartford chapter of the Archaeological Institute of America, the Connecticut Academy of Fine Arts, and the arts and crafts clubs of Hartford and Sarasota.

narrative_blocks.header: Clemens came back for his necktie
narrative_blocks.body: The family kept a story of Samuel Clemens, who lived next door in West Hartford, Connecticut, coming into the Newton kitchen almost every morning, and arriving one day without a tie. Scolded for it at home, he fetched the tie, walked back, and asked that it be laid on a chair and looked at for half an hour so his wife could be told he had been seen fully dressed.

narrative_blocks.header: Who's Who listed three of his four children
narrative_blocks.body: Nathaly, Kent and Sara were named in the 1938 entry. The first of them, Roswell Allen Chittenden, had been born in the March of 1890 and was dead by that August.

people.research_notes: Stub. From Sam's FamilySearch extract, 1 Aug 2026. From the printed Newton chapter 82 (Allen Herbert^9) and the Who's Who in New England entry of 1938 it quotes, read 2 Aug 2026. Son of Roswell Warner Newton, whose own ancestry the compiler could not trace, and Elizabeth Snow Newton, through whom the Hooker descent runs. Who's Who gives: banking; educated in the Hartford public schools; married Emily Katherine Case of Detroit in 1887; began as messenger at the Hartford Trust Company in 1881 and was its vice-president from 1925; president of the Industrial Bank of Hartford; treasurer of the Mark Twain Library and Memorial Commission; member of the Archaeological Institute of America (Hartford chapter), the Connecticut Academy of Fine Arts, the Sarasota Art Club and the Arts and Crafts club of Hartford; home at Andover, office at 750 Main Street, Hartford. The Industrial Bank presidency and the Commission treasurership carry no start year in the source; 1938, the year of the entry, is used so the rows render, and is a floor and not a date. THE CLEMENS ANECDOTE IS HEDGED IN THE SOURCE: Lucy Ida Newton Dimick told it of a Newton family living next door to Samuel Clemens in West Hartford, Connecticut, and the chapter says only 'perhaps that of the subject or of his parents'. It is placed here because Allen is the Newton with a documented Twain tie, but it is family lore and is written as such. No death date is recorded for him anywhere — FamilySearch has zero sources and says only Deceased. Flagged for Sam. PLACE DISAMBIGUATION 2 Aug 2026 on Sam's instruction: the tree holds a Hartford and a West Hartford in BOTH Connecticut and Vermont, and this session's Newton work sits almost entirely in the Vermont ones, so a bare 'Hartford' on this entry reads as Vermont to anyone coming down the branch. It is Connecticut throughout for Allen — birth, the Trust Company, the Industrial Bank, the Mark Twain commission, the office on Main Street — and the Clemens anecdote is set in West Hartford, CONNECTICUT, not the Vermont village of the same name that Erwin and Elmer lived in. The state is abbreviated, not spelled out, and appears only where a reader has no context for it: Allen's blurb, the Twain label ON ALLEN'S card, and the anecdote block. The label on TWAIN's card carries no state — that page is Connecticut end to end and spelling it out there is noise. Sam's rule, 2 Aug 2026.

narrative_blocks.header: The musician among the Hartford bankers
narrative_blocks.body: His brother Allen went from messenger to vice-president of the Hartford Trust Company and his brother Loomis into the Fidelity Trust in the same city. Clinton played for a living, and lived in that city too.

narrative_blocks.header: Born on the farm Rufus Newton cleared
narrative_blocks.body: His great-grandfather had taken that Norwich ground out of the woods three generations earlier, and Erwin was born on it in the January of 1880. His father died when he was six, and two years later his mother sold the homestead and moved the household two miles down the Podunk Road into West Hartford village. The house she bought stood near enough the Central Vermont tracks that a passing train could be felt through the parlor floor.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the stepsister he grew up beside
narrative_blocks.body: His mother married Sheldon Dimick in 1895, bringing the man's daughter Lydia Estelle into the house. Erwin and Lydia married eleven years later, in the February of 1906.

narrative_blocks.header: School ended in illness, engineering came by mail
narrative_blocks.body: He had gone from the village brick schoolhouse to Kimball Union Academy and then to the Moody School for Boys when sickness put him out of the classroom and into outdoor work. He finished courses in architecture and civil engineering by correspondence instead, and drew the plans himself for the large barn he raised for his brother Elmer in 1921.

narrative_blocks.header: He built wooden ships against the submarines
narrative_blocks.body: The same trade took him to the Navy Yard at Portsmouth during the war, where wooden hulls were going up to replace the tonnage German submarines were sinking. He carried the influenza home with him and it went through the whole family without killing anyone.

narrative_blocks.header: The flood took the bridge and the library
narrative_blocks.body: In the November of 1927 the White River carried off the covered single-arch bridge at West Hartford and the red-brick schoolhouse that held the village library, where he had learned to read and where he had been a trustee since 1925. He worked on the steel bridge put up in the old one's place and was in charge of the final stages of the job; the library was rebuilt with money sent up by the Connecticut town of the same name.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept the house alone for thirteen years
narrative_blocks.body: Lydia died in 1939 and the daughter who had been running the house married that fall, leaving Ruth, the eldest, home with him until her own death four years later. He stayed on alone and got his own meals until the illness of his last months.

people.research_notes: From Sam's FamilySearch/FindAGrave extract, 1 Aug 2026. From the printed Newton chapter 70 (Edward Nelson^8 and Lucy Ida^8), read 2 Aug 2026. Born 16 Jan. 1880 at Norwich. He married his stepsister Lydia Estelle Dimick in 1906; the chapter names them the compiler's parents. In 1921 he built a large new barn for his brother Elmer. From Sam's FamilySearch/FindAGrave extract, 2 Aug 2026. FamilySearch spells him Carleton and gives West Hartford as his birthplace; the chapter and FindAGrave both say Carlton and Norwich, and those are kept, two sources to one. From the printed Newton chapter 80 (Erwin Carlton^9), read 2 Aug 2026. Born on the farm his great-grandfather Rufus had cleared at Norwich; died in the Hitchcock Clinic at Hanover of complications from cancer of the pancreas within a few hours of admission, and was buried in the family lot just above the West Hartford church. Schooling: the West Hartford one-room brick school, Kimball Union Academy at Meriden and the Moody School for Boys at Northfield, left because of illness, then correspondence courses in architecture and civil engineering. Work: carpenter about Windsor and Woodstock; winters at Keene as a pattern maker for a foundry making water wheels; about five years on the International Paper maintenance crew at Wilder, rooming there in winter and mud time when the dirt highways were impassable; foreman at the Glens Falls mill in 1927; the West Hartford steel bridge in 1928; regularly employed except for seasonal layoffs until seventy-five. Offices: West Hartford Library trustee from 1925, Clerk of the West Hartford Congregational Church at his death and for many years before, and President of the West Hartford Cemetery Association — none of the three is wired as an institution record, as there is no INST id for them. Still unused: the 1930 Model A Tudor sedan, the family's first closed car and its first with a stick, and the group picnics of two or three cars; his growing enthusiasm for the fall foliage; the side curtains of cloth and isinglass and the cooling systems drained each night and refilled with hot water; the 1900 census counting him twice, as Irwin, a boarder in Sheldon Dimick's Hartford household, and as a twenty-year-old day laborer in a preacher's house at Sherburne; the houses on River Street at Woodstock in 1910, at Waterbury while he was on the Vermont State Hospital job, and the Sam Bruce house his mother bought in 1918, five hundred feet up the Tiger Town Road. The chapter's dollar figure for the steerage tickets is deliberately left out. FOUR NB-WORTHY SLICES ARE HELD BACK HERE ONLY because validate.py caps an entry at six blocks and two were already written: (1) the West Hartford house his mother bought stood so near the Central Vermont tracks that a passing train came up through the parlor floor; (2) illness took him out of the Moody School and he finished architecture and civil engineering by correspondence instead; (3) as a young man he and another crossed to Great Britain on cut-rate steerage tickets, disliked the class enough to pay up for the return, and he kept a piece of polished granite brought back from Scotland; (4) his black 1912 Model T had three doors and none for the driver, and he kept it running with his own ring and valve jobs and several replacement engine blocks until he traded it in 1924. Any of the four can be swapped in for an existing block on Sam's word. Career start years are read from the chapter, not stated by it: carpenter from the 1910 census return through the seventy-fifth year at which he stopped, the Navy Yard from the 1918 influenza he brought home, the Keene foundry from 'the early 1920s'. The International Paper maintenance crew at Wilder, about five years with much Sunday and holiday work and a winter room in the village when the dirt roads went to mud, has no year attached anywhere and so is left out of the career rows rather than guessed at. NARRATIVE BLOCKS REBUILT AS ONE UNIT 2 Aug 2026 on Sam's instruction — not appended to, re-authored end to end so the six blocks run as threads instead of six unrelated facts. The line now goes origin, household, the trade learned, the trade at war, the trade at its height against the 1927 flood, and the last years alone. NOTHING WAS DROPPED, only merged: the standalone barn block of 1 Aug is folded into the correspondence-schooling block, since drawing the plans and raising the barn is the payoff of learning engineering by mail and reads as duplication when split in two; the detail it carried — their mother deeded Elmer and Flossie a small lot in 1919, and the old horse barn was moved off the farmhouse shed and taken into the new one — is kept here. The standalone bridge block and the standalone library block are merged for the same reason: both turned on the same flood and each had to re-explain it. The trains through the parlor floor, previously banked, are now in the opening block.

bio.bio_blurb: Dairy farmer; fifteen cows milked by hand

narrative_blocks.header: He never owned a tractor or a car
narrative_blocks.body: He milked around fifteen cows by hand and put the milk through a DeLaval separator he cranked himself until his late years. Power for sawing wood and filling silo came from a one-cylinder Galloway engine bolted to a metal wagon, and he travelled behind a driving horse called Major.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother said his cows had no germs
narrative_blocks.body: He sold the milk fresh and unpasteurized to his brother Erwin's household and to the neighbors along the road. The cattle were unregistered, though every bull came from the Billings Farm at Woodstock, which bred registered Jerseys.

narrative_blocks.header: A hayrack tipped over under him in 1931
narrative_blocks.body: He was riding on it when it went, and the injuries put him in hospital. The land he farmed was hilly even where it was tillable, with slopes steep enough that the children of the village skied them.

narrative_blocks.header: Thrifty farmers, and he dressed the part
narrative_blocks.body: His blue denim overalls were faded and patched over and he and Flossie ran the place close, he on the cows and she on the books. He grew alfalfa, rotated his crops, and sat as a director of the Windsor County Farmers Exchange.

narrative_blocks.header: His second wife was his first wife's niece
narrative_blocks.body: Beatrice Lamphere was the daughter of Flossie's sister Cora and had been twenty years divorced when he married her in 1968, two years after Flossie died. She outlived him and was buried in her own family's lot in the same ground.

narrative_blocks.header: She would not give out a recipe
narrative_blocks.body: Asked how she made a thing, she answered with a pinch of this and a pinch of that. She cooked on a black wood-burning stove, and every late fall put down bacon, hams, salt pork and corned beef and canned the year's mincemeat.

narrative_blocks.header: Spring water ran through her refrigerator
narrative_blocks.body: A quarter-inch stream of cold spring water fell all day into a twenty-gallon crock in the cellar, and the milk and the other perishables stood in glass jars inside it. The overflow went to the sink and down the drain, and from late fall to early spring the meat kept frozen in the shed off the kitchen.

narrative_blocks.header: Rice on the platform for the eleven o'clock
narrative_blocks.body: They were married on a February morning at her father's house in front of the family alone. The village saw them off on the train under showers of rice for a few days with friends in Rhode Island.

narrative_blocks.header: The village children were always let in
narrative_blocks.body: She was known in West Hartford for her love of children, her own and everyone else's, and the house stayed open to them. She worked in the Ladies Aid Society, whose suppers raised the church's money and served as the village's social calendar.

narrative_blocks.header: Two days past her thirty-third anniversary
narrative_blocks.body: Her health had been failing since about 1930, and lateral sclerosis took her at home in the February of 1939. She and Erwin had married in that same month thirty-three years earlier, and the flowers sent to the funeral were counted a bed of them.

narrative_blocks.header: She stood easily under his raised arm
narrative_blocks.body: She was just over five feet and Erwin just under six in his stocking feet. At the wedding she weighed ninety-five pounds and wore a four-and-a-half shoe.

narrative_blocks.header: He took up the family history at sixty-five
narrative_blocks.body: Lucy Ida had put a history of the family into print in 1889, two generations before him. He retired from the government in the March of 1973 and turned to genealogical research in the fall of 1977, carrying the Newton line back to Roger and forward to his children.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-one years and eleven months of service
narrative_blocks.body: He entered on duty as an immigration clerk at Montreal in the May of 1931 and retired at Washington in the March of 1973. In between he was an immigrant inspector at Richford, a hearing examiner at Saint Albans, officer in charge at Houlton, and a special inquiry officer in a post later called administrative law judge.

narrative_blocks.header: Recruited out of a cornfield at seventeen
narrative_blocks.body: Officials of a commercial college at Northampton found him hoeing corn the summer he came out of high school as valedictorian, and signed him up for a course that led to federal clerkships. He passed the examination with a high mark and was told he could not be appointed at Washington, because Vermont's quota had never recovered from oversubscription under Coolidge.

narrative_blocks.header: At eleven he lit the village street lamps
narrative_blocks.body: The kerosene lanterns stood on wooden posts along the West Hartford streets, one of them in the middle of the covered bridge, and he went round them with a two-gallon can and a little blue ladder. Electricity reached the village in the January of 1925, and his pay for that year came to a small fraction of the year before.

narrative_blocks.header: He pulled the ferry across by hand
narrative_blocks.body: The flood of 1927 carried off the covered bridge and the house he had been born in, and the next summer he worked the temporary ferry that stood in its place. The river ran too low to push it over, so he hauled it across on a quarter-inch cable with autos and hay wagons aboard, and a pair of leather gloves lasted about three days.

narrative_blocks.header: Bertha was one of five in his division
narrative_blocks.body: Bertha Whitney came into the Newport office in the April of 1934 as one of thirty temporary clerks copying manifest books onto cards, and was among the few kept on. When he was put in charge of the statistical division that November she was one of five assigned to it, and she resigned in the March of 1936 to marry him.

people.research_notes: Stub. From Sam's FamilySearch/FindAGrave extract, 2 Aug 2026. From the printed Newton chapter 80 (Erwin Carlton^9), read 2 Aug 2026. He is the compiler of the printed Newton genealogy this branch is largely drawn from, and enters his own parents in it as number eighty. The chapter mentions a nephew, John Newton, who owns and has remodelled the Sam Bruce house on the Tiger Town Road; that nephew is not yet in the tree. The `author` tag is used for him and for Lucy Ida — flagged for Sam, as neither is an author in the literary sense. The family-history thread is wired here on Sam's instruction, 2 Aug 2026: Lucy Ida Newton Dimick, his paternal grandmother, is the documented family historian of the line (her Bible history in print in 1889, the burying ground held back from the farm sale) and he is the compiler who carried it to a full printed genealogy. Sam also asked for the same thread on his MOTHER, Lydia Estelle — NOT WRITTEN, because nothing in the five chapter pages read so far puts Lydia to any genealogical work; the only mother-and-son pair the sources support is Lucy Ida and Erwin, and Lucy Ida did the history. Flagged for Sam; his Robert Newton section may name her, and this should be revisited when that section is processed. His three blocks were likewise rebuilt as one unit rather than appended to, per Sam's standing instruction of 2 Aug 2026: the grandmother's history and his own genealogy were each re-explaining the other. When his own chapter is processed the set should be rebuilt again as a whole, not extended. From the printed Newton chapter 91 (Robert Sheldon^10), read 2 Aug 2026. BLOCKS REBUILT AS ONE UNIT on Sam's instruction, not appended to; the genealogy blocks were merged so the six run genealogy, career, how the career began, the two boyhood jobs, and the marriage. Career detail beyond the rows: promoted senior clerk 16 November 1934 in charge of the statistical division at Newport; the District Office moved from Montreal to Newport in February 1933 under political pressure and again to St. Albans by 1940; detailed to the Central Office at Philadelphia from September 1942 to March 1943 and to the Board of Immigration Appeals at Washington from June to September 1944; handled the Canadian Woodsmen Program, under which thousands of skilled Canadian woodsmen came temporarily into the northeastern woods; first place in the six-week Officers Training Course at Washington, 19 February 1960, covered by the INS Information Bulletin. Earlier work: getting in the cows for his uncle Elmer from the age of seven; two years at Bixby's General Store from 1925; pick and shovel on the West Hartford road after the 1927 flood; day labour on the Dimick or Stone Farm in the summer of 1929; waiting table and washing dishes at Bedford Lodge to earn his board at Northampton; cutting the family woodpile with his father, then an unemployed carpenter, in the winter of 1930-31, with bonfires at lunch time on the below-zero mornings; a temporary Veterans Administration clerkship at Newark and Millington processing World War I bonuses, 1 April to 11 May 1931. The ferry was built by Jack Howick, who had lived in western Canada. Travel: the Gaspe peninsula and Bonaventure Island from Houlton; Iran in November 1971; a twenty-one-day rail trip in 1979 to his brother Jason at Tucson and his sister Irene at Sun City; a month by Amtrak in 1983 that ended with Leila and Ernest driving them to Mount St. Helens, where they went up by helicopter to the crater. All dollar figures in the chapter are deliberately left out. CC LINK TEXT SHORTENED to first and last name, 2 Aug 2026 on Sam's note: the middle names read heavy in a cross-connection line. Applied to the Robert/Jason/Roger connections only, not swept across the tree. CC to Reuben Burnham Moffat added 2 Aug 2026 on Sam's suggestion. A sweep of the tree for other family genealogists turned up no closer match: Moffat is the only other person carried as a family's genealogist, and the two men did the same work for two different lines.

narrative_blocks.body: She came out of Hartford High School second in her class in the spring of 1931. Lydia's health had been failing since about 1930, and most of her time after that went to keeping her mother at home.

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband came to the funeral first
narrative_blocks.body: Ernest Dunbar came up from Sharon for Lydia's funeral in the February of 1939, one of the out-of-town mourners the village paper listed by name. They married that October at West Hartford, and her brother Jason gave the reception at Quechee.

narrative_blocks.header: She cared for her father at Woodstock
narrative_blocks.body: Erwin had kept the West Hartford house on his own since Ruth died in 1943, and got his own meals there. He came down to Leila at Woodstock for his last few months, and died in the Hanover hospital in the November of 1956.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-one hours from headache to death
narrative_blocks.body: She complained of headache and nausea at two in the morning on the twenty-ninth of March 1984 and was unconscious by three. She was moved to a second hospital at Seattle and died there at eleven that night, of meningitis.

narrative_blocks.body: He kept books for a gear-shaper works at Springfield and rose to the president's staff at Crompton and Knowles in Worcester, teaching business administration at Clark in the evenings. After two years managing a Vermont stock farm he finished as professor of business at Rhode Island Junior College.

narrative_blocks.body: Back injuries disabled him early in 1974 and he and Margaret left for Arizona that year for his health. They tried Las Cruces in 1979 to be near their son Richard, found the winters too severe, and went back to Tucson.

narrative_blocks.header: Born and died in the same village
narrative_blocks.body: He came into the world at West Hartford in the December of 1915 and went out of it there in the June of 2008, at ninety-two. Margaret had died in that village thirteen years before him.

narrative_blocks.header: Valedictorian in 1937, the fourth of them
narrative_blocks.body: Robert took the top of the Hartford High School class of 1929 and Jason of 1933, with Leila second in 1931, and Irene finished the set eight years after her eldest brother. She went on to a chemistry degree at Vermont in 1941 and into Phi Beta Kappa.

narrative_blocks.header: A chemistry degree, then hospital laboratories
narrative_blocks.body: She trained a year at the Worcester state hospital and was certified as a clinical laboratory technician. After a spell at Middletown in New York she went out to a Santa Barbara hospital in 1949, and stayed in California the rest of her life.

narrative_blocks.header: The children's birthplaces map his asthma
narrative_blocks.body: Raymond's allergies and asthma sent them from town to town looking for air that suited him, through Santa Barbara and Roseville, Renton and Seattle, Torrance, Joshua Tree, Redondo Beach and Yucca Valley. Paul was born at Santa Barbara, Robert at Roseville, Thomas at Renton and Susan at Seattle, in that order.

narrative_blocks.header: Born and died on the first of January
narrative_blocks.body: She came into the world at West Hartford on New Year's Day 1920 and went out of it at Hemet in California on the same day in 2005. She was buried at Redondo Beach, in the ground that already held both her husbands.

narrative_blocks.body: She came out of Brattleboro High School in 1931 in the Silver B honor society and took the second Austine Prize, standing second academically among ninety-four graduates. Three years later she went into the immigration service as a temporary clerk.

narrative_blocks.header: One of thirty, then one of five
narrative_blocks.body: She was hired at Newport in the April of 1934 with twenty-nine others to copy manifest books onto individual cards, and was among the few kept on for permanent work. That November she was one of five clerks assigned to the statistical division Robert had just been given charge of, and she resigned in 1936 to marry him.

narrative_blocks.header: Her Mayflower line runs through her mother
narrative_blocks.body: She researched and compiled the history of her parents' families and traced her mother's descent from the Pilgrims John Howland and Edward Fuller. That is the line her son Ronald would later serve as governor of the Vermont Mayflower Society.

narrative_blocks.header: Her parents kept the babies for months
narrative_blocks.body: Several hospital stays took her out of the house while the children were small, and Orlin and Ruth Whitney had Ronald and Sylvia at Brattleboro for long stretches. All three grandchildren went back there for their summers, right through their college years.

narrative_blocks.header: Neither Florida nor Vermont, so Washington
narrative_blocks.body: Many of their friends had retired to Florida and she did not want to go. He did not want to go back to Vermont winters, and they settled on staying where they already were.

narrative_blocks.body: He came out of Cornell in 1960, where he played clarinet in the Big Red marching band, and spent his working life analysing utility rates for the New York State Public Service Commission. He and Helen retired to Kennebunk in 1995.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty years on the Cornell hook and ladder
narrative_blocks.body: He was a volunteer fireman for three decades with that company and a commissioner of the fire district for twenty years. He was past master of the Social Friendship Lodge, and later gave his time to the Seashore Trolley Museum.

narrative_blocks.header: The three-year-old who was given the red chair
narrative_blocks.body: Lucy Ida Dimick put the little painted chair into his hands about 1940. It had come out of Iowa in 1842 on the wagon her father built.

narrative_blocks.header: Valedictorian at Ogdensburg in 1955
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Brattleboro in his grandparents' house, grew up at Saint Albans and went to Bellows Free Academy before the family moved across into New York. He took the top of his class at the Ogdensburg Free Academy in 1955.

narrative_blocks.body: He was in the intelligence branch of the Army from the March of 1963 to the January of 1965, and took a political science degree at Washington in 1971. He went from there to the Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms bureau as an investigator in its liquor excise division.

narrative_blocks.header: Co-valedictorian at a school one year old
narrative_blocks.body: Rouses Point High School was merged with Champlain that year to form Champlain Central, and she took the top of its first graduating class in 1957. The Latin teacher there had volunteered to carry her through a fourth year of the language on her own time.

narrative_blocks.header: She played oboe in four bands
narrative_blocks.body: Three high school bands and the Plattsburg community orchestra had her on the oboe, and she took two years of applied music at the Eastman school while she was at Rochester. The man she married was a French horn player in the West Point academy band.

narrative_blocks.header: Science teacher, social worker, then medic
narrative_blocks.body: She taught seventh-grade science at Highland Falls, supervised social work at Flagstaff, and settled at last into a primary classroom at Delanson. She joined the Duanesburg ambulance squad and was certified as an emergency medical technician in 1984.

narrative_blocks.header: They came east to look after the Whitneys
narrative_blocks.body: Late in 1967 she and Clinton left Arizona with an infant daughter, in part to be near Orlin and Ruth Whitney in their camp at Brookline. The grandparents died the next year and the family stayed on at the camp until 1970.

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband left in the February of 1972
narrative_blocks.body: Clinton was a talented musician and photographer who had built a studio into the Fireside Press and had no head for managing it. She carried the business on after he went, and took her divorce in the Windham County court in the August of 1973.

narrative_blocks.header: Her second husband was ill from the start
narrative_blocks.body: She married Gerald Curley at New Baltimore in the September of 1974, a widower with three teenagers at home. Doctors found bone cancer through his body shortly after, and he worked when he could as a chemical technician until he died in 1980.

bio.bio_blurb: Librarian who ran two libraries at Shiraz

career.role: Chief, army studies and military documents

career.location: Kirtland Air Force Base, New Mexico

cross_connections.display_label: was the Revolutionary soldier of her supplemental DAR line
descended from Roger Newton, and wrote the classic soldier's memoir
commanded a Confederate regiment and later ran San Antonio

narrative_blocks.header: She got her answer, and joined the DAR
narrative_blocks.body: In the summer of 1977 she told her parents they must have at least one Revolutionary War ancestor and set the two of them to finding out. She came into the Daughters of the American Revolution through her mother's line from the soldier Jehiel Isham, and filed supplemental applications on David Newton and Jeremiah Wilson.

narrative_blocks.header: She dropped out of high school for college
narrative_blocks.body: Summer courses at the University of Maine after her junior year led Orono to take her on that autumn as a regular student. Houlton High School counted her a drop-out and then handed her a diploma once her class had graduated.

narrative_blocks.header: Two library directorships at Shiraz
narrative_blocks.body: Pennsylvania sent her to Iran in 1970 under its contract with Pahlavi University, and she ran the medical school library for a year and the veterinary school library the next. Her parents flew out to her in 1971 and she drove them to Isfahan and Tehran.

narrative_blocks.header: Chief of the Air Force weapons library
narrative_blocks.body: She went into the federal civil service at Aberdeen in 1977, moved to the Army library at the Pentagon in 1979, and was made chief of army studies and military documents the following June. From 1982 she was at Kirtland with the Air Force Weapons Laboratory, and was made chief of its technical library branch in 1984.

narrative_blocks.header: Her kittens flew to Iran and back
narrative_blocks.body: She took two of them with her to Shiraz in 1970, and they came home ahead of her in 1972, to Kennedy and then to Albany. One of them, born in the March of 1968, was still with her at Albuquerque when the chapter was written.

narrative_blocks.header: Clarinet in three Maine all-state bands
narrative_blocks.body: She played in the Houlton high school band and the all-Aroostook county band as well, and earned the Curved Bar in the Girl Scouts there. She belonged to the Rainbow Girls, the Latin and French clubs, and the national honor society.
