narrative_blocks.header: He cut the laser rangefinder to four pounds
narrative_blocks.body: The prototype that measured distance for artillery fire weighed eighty pounds when he took it up, and he brought it down to a unit built into a field glass and run off a flashlight battery. One glass sighted the object and the other read the distance a second after the button, accurate to ten feet at four miles.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the manual for laser bombing
narrative_blocks.body: Called into the Army in 1963 and sent to Vietnam, he spent his second year at Fort Monmouth developing the laser as a range finder. He then developed and tested the pin-point helicopter bombing used late in that war, where the beam went down to the target and a nose camera locked on and followed it in.

narrative_blocks.header: Night glasses, and lasers for eye surgery
narrative_blocks.body: He worked on field glasses that gathered what light there was and amplified it electronically. He also worked with Johns Hopkins on the use of the laser for surgery on eyes, and moved out to the White Sands proving grounds in the December of 1977.

narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Worcester and travelled the world, near and far, but of everywhere she went it was New Mexico she claimed. She gardened, cooked and baked, painted and sculpted, took up foreign languages, led Girl Scouts and worked in 4H.

narrative_blocks.header: Machinist, then plant engineer at Randolph
narrative_blocks.body: He came out of the Worcester Boys Trade School in 1960 and worked as a machinist and toolmaker, then ran his own shop at Randolph. From 1968 to 1978 he was plant engineer of the furniture factory there, until a back condition disabled him as one had disabled his father.

narrative_blocks.header: He found the family history in a Bible
narrative_blocks.body: A written line back to David Newton was tucked inside the covers of his great-grandmother's Bible, and he sent a copy of it on to his uncle Robert for the genealogy. Lucy Ida had put a Bible history of the family into print herself in 1889.

narrative_blocks.header: A Morgan horse and a tandem bicycle
narrative_blocks.body: She quilted and sewed and gardened, rode her Morgan, and went out on the tandem with John. The two of them cruised around the world, drove across the country and camped all over New England.

narrative_blocks.body: The West Hartford library her husband's grandfather Erwin had been a trustee of in 1925 had her on its board of trustees seventy years later. She rarely missed a show at Northern Stage and kept up monthly lunches with the retired operating room nurses.

bio.bio_blurb: Psychologist who rediscovered the Old Connecticut Path

cross_connections.display_label: was his uncle, who compiled the Newton genealogy in 1984

narrative_blocks.header: He rediscovered the Old Connecticut Path
narrative_blocks.body: The trail his forebears walked west from Cambridge to Hartford — Thomas Hooker and his congregation in 1636, and Roger Newton on foot in 1640, the founders of the American Hooker and Newton lines — had all but vanished under four centuries of building. He spent ten years in the woods and along forgotten byways finding what was left of it, mapped a likely route across eastern Connecticut, and proposed a heritage trail from Thompson to Hartford.

narrative_blocks.header: It began as a family history project
narrative_blocks.body: He set out to find the road taken by Thomas Hooker and by Roger Newton, who married Hooker's daughter Mary and began the family in America. What he found he gave away, in talks to historical societies, in guided walks, in videos, and in a town-by-town guide he wrote himself.

narrative_blocks.header: He worked with autistic children first
narrative_blocks.body: He came out of Worcester State with a psychology degree in 1979 and went to work with autistic children. Two years later he took a master's and an advanced certificate in school psychology, and went into the Sutton schools as their psychologist.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten years editing the Academy's Annals

narrative_blocks.header: He was in the Ghost Army in Italy
narrative_blocks.body: He enlisted out of Hudson County early in 1942, a year into MIT, and served as a technician fifth grade in the 3133rd Signal Service Company. That was the unit that ran the tactical deception of the Italian campaign in 1944 and 1945.

narrative_blocks.header: Shorthand first, then back to MIT
narrative_blocks.body: The veterans' stipend that paid him weekly for a year went on secretarial school, so that he could take faster and fuller notes. He re-enrolled at MIT with what he had learned and graduated in the class of 1949.

narrative_blocks.header: He found the bad cylinder by cheekbone
narrative_blocks.body: He would rest a screwdriver handle against his face and its head against a running block, and name the cylinder that was misbehaving and why. He could sometimes do it down a telephone line from a stranded motorist's description.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-one years running the firm he founded
narrative_blocks.body: Dynamics Research Corporation was started in 1955 by him and others, working chiefly for the Defense Department, and he was its president and chairman until 1986. He came to it from a travelling salesman's job and an engineer's bench at Draper.

narrative_blocks.header: Blacksmithing, after his grandfather the farrier
narrative_blocks.body: He took the trade up late at a folk school in North Carolina, having wanted it since boyhood because his mother's father had kept a large farriery in Philadelphia. A 1953 Jaguar in the barn behind the Carlisle house was his other perpetual project.

Army serial number 11121677; enlisted from Hudson County, New Jersey, early in 1942 after a year at MIT, occupation before the war given as foreman. Grew up at Colonia, New Jersey; his father had served with the American Expeditionary Forces in France straight out of Cornell, and his Swiss-born grandfather had been a professor at Oberlin. Read A. Russell Bond's The Scientific American Boy at fourteen and took its lessons on self-reliance for life. Married Hope Ingersoll in 1959 and, after her death, Frances Garland in 1994, the two of them having known each other for years because their late spouses were cousins. Active in Republican politics; quoted at length before the Joint Economic Committee of Congress in 1985 on entrepreneurship. His Ghost Army service is documented on the Ghost Army Legacy Project roster. Career start years for Draper and the war are read from the narrative, not stated by it. narrative_blocks.header: Elected to the appellate bench in 1920
narrative_blocks.body: He was elected judge of the Court of Appeals for the eighth district of Ohio in November 1920, after thirty-five years at the Cleveland bar. He held the seat until he died two years later.

narrative_blocks.header: Six years as referee in bankruptcy
narrative_blocks.body: Judge Taylor appointed him in January 1910 and he served until January 1916. Lawyers and businessmen alike came to appreciate his fairness in the complicated matters that came before him.

narrative_blocks.header: He read law in his father's own firm
narrative_blocks.body: He studied with Burke, Ingersoll and Sanders, where his father was the middle name, and was admitted to the Ohio bar in 1885 and to the federal district court in 1887. He began practice at Cleveland the year he was admitted and never worked anywhere else.

narrative_blocks.header: He pitched for the college nine
narrative_blocks.body: He took a worthy part in college life and was pitcher on the old Western Reserve baseball team. Before that he had been on the football squad at East High School.

narrative_blocks.header: Golf, Dover Bay, and a hotel in winter
narrative_blocks.body: He kept a summer house at Dover Bay and was president of its country club in 1916 and 1917. In the winters he lived at a Cleveland hotel, and golf was his chief diversion.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a month before turning twenty-two
narrative_blocks.body: He married Della Bishop at Akron on the sixth of September 1881. Her grandfather Joseph Bishop was among the earliest pioneers of Hudson in Ohio. They had five children.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought the company he had joined
narrative_blocks.body: Out of the university he bought an interest in the Eynon company of Cleveland, makers of milling machinery. When Eynon died not long afterwards he took the controlling interest, and in 1889 incorporated the works under his own name.

narrative_blocks.header: He moved the whole plant to Rockford
narrative_blocks.body: In 1891 an offer took the works out of Cleveland to Rockford, which was then only beginning to be counted an industrial center. The initial plant was extended year on year until it employed six hundred people.

narrative_blocks.header: Milling machines for arsenals and navy yards
narrative_blocks.body: The company gave its whole attention to high-production milling and made nothing else. Its machines went to builders of automobiles, locomotives, ships and general machinery, and to governments for their arsenals and navy yards.

narrative_blocks.header: A park for the son killed in France
narrative_blocks.body: Clayton was killed flying in France on 26 April 1918, at twenty-one. He and Harriet gave Ingersoll Memorial Park to the Rockford park district in the boy's memory. Pneumonia killed him ten years later, in December 1928, at sixty-three.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty years on his church's board
narrative_blocks.body: He was a trustee and for many years president of the board of the Second Congregational church in Rockford. He and Harriet endowed a room at the Chicago Theological Seminary in honor of their pastor, John Gordon.

narrative_blocks.header: The Red Cross hospital on Russian Island
narrative_blocks.body: She was a physician at the American Red Cross hospital on Russian Island, off Vladivostok, after the war. She treated patients of nineteen different nationalities there, among them men out of the camps of the enemy.

narrative_blocks.header: She took a thousand Czechs home to Prague
narrative_blocks.body: When the maimed had partly recovered she went with one thousand and fifty crippled and invalid Czechs from the hospital to Prague. The route ran the long way round the world, by way of the United States.

narrative_blocks.header: The naval officers expected Bolsheviks
narrative_blocks.body: The officers in charge of the transport had been told they were taking on a great many Bolsheviks, she said afterwards. What they found were well-behaved, peaceful, singing groups of soldiers.

narrative_blocks.header: She ended at Asheville, where her sisters were
narrative_blocks.body: Two of her sisters had settled at Asheville and her mother died there in 1906, when she herself was still called Miss Louise Ingersoll of Cleveland at twenty-seven. She was buried at Riverside in the same city in 1962, at eighty-four.

narrative_blocks.header: A crash on route 47 near Forrest
narrative_blocks.body: The party was driving up to Rockford from Asheville when the chauffeur swung out to pass a truck, met a car coming the other way, and swerved. The car overturned twice and came to rest forty feet off the road. She died at the Fairbury hospital the next morning, at seventy.

narrative_blocks.header: Three of her four children died first
narrative_blocks.body: Clayton was killed in France in April 1918 and Helen in a Chicago automobile accident a few days before Christmas in 1922. Harold died in Colorado in 1934. Only Mildred was living when the crash near Forrest killed her mother.

narrative_blocks.header: She took her husband's seat at the hospital
narrative_blocks.body: After his death in 1928 she succeeded him as a director of Rockford hospital. She was a director of the local YWCA as well.

narrative_blocks.header: Choir, Sunday school, Mendelssohn club
narrative_blocks.body: She led the Sunday school at the Second Congregational church and sang in its choir. She was active in the Mendelssohn club and in the church's musical events for most of her forty-four years in Rockford.

narrative_blocks.header: Her sons kept the works in the family
narrative_blocks.body: She was the only one of Winthrop Ingersoll's four children still living when their mother died in 1935. Her husband had taken the head of the company in 1917 and her son Clayton held it until 1984.

narrative_blocks.header: Both dashes at the Chicago interscholastic
narrative_blocks.body: He ran for Lake Forest Academy and took both dash events at the interscholastic meet in Chicago in 1909. He had already been the star of the Rockford high school track team.

narrative_blocks.header: A lung ailment ended his freshman year
narrative_blocks.body: He went up to Dartmouth in 1911 and contracted a lung ailment there that forced him out of college. He had to live at high altitude for the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: He moved to Colorado Springs to get well
narrative_blocks.body: Pat, as his intimates called him, came back robust enough to serve a time as sheriff there, and he became a brilliant golfer. He was president of the Trans-Mississippi Golf Association and a director of the Western Golf Association, and he ran an automobile business in the city.

narrative_blocks.header: Secretary of the works his father built
narrative_blocks.body: He was named secretary of the Ingersoll Milling Machine Company after Winthrop Ingersoll's death in 1928. He could stay only a few weeks at a time in the Rockford climate, and the family lived at Broadmoor outside Colorado Springs.

narrative_blocks.header: A heart ailment at Pasadena, at forty-one
narrative_blocks.body: Ill health had forced him to the west coast the previous autumn. He died at Pasadena in March 1934 of what was believed to be a heart ailment. His sister Mildred had already left Rockford for California when word came that he was failing.

career.role: First lieutenant, Signal Corps aviation section

landmarks.landmark_blurb: The park west of Rockford was given in his memory, and carries his name.

narrative_blocks.header: First of the Rockford men to answer
narrative_blocks.body: He was at Cornell in the spring of 1917 when the country broke off relations with Germany, and he and some classmates volunteered at once for the naval reserve's launch branch. His name went on file as a pilot of one of the wasps, as the boats were to be called. He applied instead to the first officers' training camp and reached Fort Sheridan on 14 May 1917, one of the youngest of more than a dozen Rockford men.

narrative_blocks.header: Ground school in Toronto with the British
narrative_blocks.body: When the camp called for volunteers for the aviation section he took it and passed a perfect physical examination. He learned the ground work in a few weeks at Toronto, training with a squadron of the Royal Flying Corps. His cadet unit went on to Fort Worth in the fall and he was commissioned there in December.

narrative_blocks.header: He was engaged just before he sailed
narrative_blocks.body: The announcement of his engagement to Mary Katherine Nelson, from a house on the same avenue as his own, came just before he sailed from an eastern port in February 1918. On the eighth of April he spent a day in France with Wilbur McEachran, another Rockford flier, who wrote home that they had talked over old times.

narrative_blocks.header: He turned praise aside with banter
narrative_blocks.body: Casey to some and Pat to others, he had been popular since childhood. His officers knew him as a cool and determined pilot, but he made light of his own flying. He was a good golfer, an expert automobile driver and strong in the water.

narrative_blocks.header: An accident on the fifth field at Issoudun
narrative_blocks.body: His squadron was in advanced training at Issoudun, preparing to go up to the front, when his airplane came down on the fifth field on 26 April 1918. The telegram reached his father in Rockford four days later and gave no more than the fact. He was nine days short of twenty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: The gift and the body arrived together
narrative_blocks.body: His parents gave the Daisy Field tract west of Rockford to the park board, and on the morning the gift was announced his father received word that the body had reached Hoboken flag-draped with other American dead. He had lain two years in the army cemetery beside the field at Issoudun. The park was named for him and laid out with an eighteen-hole golf course designed by Thomas Bendelow of Chicago.

From Sam's extracts, 3 Aug 2026: FindAGrave, the Rockford Republic of 1 May 1918 and 26 October 1920, the Chicago and Rockford notices of Helen Crebs's death, December 1922, A History of Cleveland and its Environs by Avery, Bench and Bar of Northern Ohio by Neff, and The Waterways Journal's obituary of Albert Ingersoll, September 1953. He was a first lieutenant in the Signal Corps; the telegram to his father was signed McCain. The 1918 notice says he was twenty-two and born twenty-two years before, but the 5 May 1896 birth makes him twenty-one. Member of the Rockford Country Club and for several years active in the Wate-A-Wyle Club. Survived by his parents, his sisters Mildred Gaylord and Helen, and his brother Harold of Colorado Springs. The park is 135.24 acres, three miles west of the city, bought from the Plin Smith estate; the Ingersoll gift reimbursed the board and left enough for the landscaping, the links and the upkeep. Anderson Brothers graded the course. A memorial arch was planned over the entrance near the State road interurban crossing. The 1920 notice says interment would be in the West Side cemetery, where FindAGrave has him at Greenwood; they may be the same ground under two names.

narrative_blocks.header: Class secretary, then Smith and Wisconsin
narrative_blocks.body: She went through the Garrison and Walker grade schools and graduated from Rockford High School in June 1917, having served a year as class secretary. She went on to Smith College and to the University of Wisconsin, and belonged to Kappa Alpha Theta.

narrative_blocks.header: A truck hit the taxicab from the side
narrative_blocks.body: She and her husband were riding north in a cab near their home on North Paulina Street when a heavy truck struck it squarely in the side. The cab was shoved against the curb and her head was crushed between the wreckage and a telephone pole. She never came to, and died the next morning at the hospital in Evanston.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father was going to a funeral already
narrative_blocks.body: Winthrop Ingersoll was on his way to Cleveland to bury his brother, Judge Alvan Ingersoll, when word reached him that his daughter was dying. He turned around and was in Chicago by half past eight that night. Her mother and her sister Mildred had driven down from Rockford and were with her from four in the morning.

narrative_blocks.body: He came to the head of the Ingersoll Milling Machine Company in 1917, eleven years before his father-in-law Winthrop Ingersoll died. His second son Clayton succeeded him in 1958. The eldest boy was born at Minneapolis in 1916 and the family was at Rockford by 1919.

narrative_blocks.header: Cornell engineering, then the Navy
narrative_blocks.body: He went from Phillips Exeter to Cornell and took a bachelor of science in engineering in 1939. He enlisted of his own accord and served as a naval officer from 1942 to 1946.

narrative_blocks.header: He met Gini in New York in 1947
narrative_blocks.body: She had gone there to model and to study fashion design. They met that year and married at Rockford on the twenty-third of June 1950. She died in January 1999 and he outlived her by seven years.

narrative_blocks.header: He owned the works his grandfather built
narrative_blocks.body: He spent his working life as an officer and board member of Ingersoll and for many years managed the Ingersoll Foundation. He was still an owner of the milling machine company and of Ingersoll International until shortly before he died at eighty-nine.

narrative_blocks.header: He belonged to the Quiet Birdmen
narrative_blocks.body: The aviators' fraternity was one of his; the Rancheros Visitadores of Santa Barbara another. Ducks Unlimited and wildlife conservation held him the longest of any of it.

Also Junior Achievement, Rotary, the Rockford Country Club, the University Club of Chicago, the Navy Club and the Royal Poinciana Golf Club at Naples. narrative_blocks.body: She left Rockford for Chicago in 1944 and became a fashion model. In 1947 she went on to New York to take the work further and to study fashion design at the Traphagen and Parsons schools.

narrative_blocks.header: She owned a share of the machine works
narrative_blocks.body: She was an owner of the Ingersoll Milling Machine Company and of Ingersoll International. She sat on the board of the University of Wisconsin Madison Medical Center's department of ophthalmology and on the Rockford Women's Art Board.

narrative_blocks.header: He succeeded his father in 1958
narrative_blocks.body: His grandfather Winthrop Ingersoll founded the company in 1889 and his father took the head of it in 1917. He came to the chairmanship in 1958 and retired from Ingersoll International in 1984, by which time it employed more than two thousand people.

narrative_blocks.header: Nobody was laid off in 1982
narrative_blocks.body: When the downturn of that year had other manufacturers cutting their workforces, Ingersoll kept its people at work. Rockford's mayor called it a family decision that dug deeply into their own pockets and reserves.

narrative_blocks.header: There were no time clocks at Ingersoll
narrative_blocks.body: The same mayor, a Democrat who often clashed with him, remembered walking the plant floor beside him and the attention he paid every person there, knowing their names and taking pride in their work. There were no time clocks in the place; the men knew what they were to do and they were there.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped build the Rockford Institute
narrative_blocks.body: He held strong conservative views and played a large part in establishing and shaping the Rockford Institute, known internationally for advocating family-centered social and political values. He and his brother Edson carried the same ideals abroad through the Ingersoll Foundation, which awards the Ingersoll Prizes each year.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty years sailing on Lake Geneva
narrative_blocks.body: His daughter said he had been an avid sailor there for more than fifty years, and it was at the lake that he died, seventeen days short of seventy-nine. Conservation held him as well: Ducks Unlimited, and a wildlife research station in Canada.

narrative_blocks.header: He came back to Keith as a trustee
narrative_blocks.body: He was schooled at Keith and served it afterwards on the board. He was in early on the development and expansion of Rockford Memorial Hospital and was president of its board of trustees for many years.

narrative_blocks.body: A week before he died he sent a memo saying his condition was stable and that he was taking a leave of absence for cancer treatment. He wrote that he had devoted his life to Ingersoll, and that the policies and culture which had carried the company through the last century would see it through the next.

narrative_blocks.header: A field artillery captain in Germany
narrative_blocks.body: He entered Princeton from Exeter and belonged to Tiger Inn. He served as a captain of field artillery in the 131st Battalion of the 36th Division and saw combat in Germany. He came home and took his degree in English in 1947.

narrative_blocks.header: The last of the family in line
narrative_blocks.body: He joined the milling machine company after Princeton, third generation after his grandfather Winthrop Ingersoll and his father Robert Gaylord. When he died in 2000 at his retirement house in Scottsdale he was the last family member in line at Rockford's largest private industrial employer.

narrative_blocks.header: Bomb disposal in New Guinea and the Philippines
narrative_blocks.body: He was called up as an apprentice seaman in the summer of 1942 and commissioned an ensign in December. He disarmed bombs in New Guinea and Australia and was seconded to the Army for the campaign to retake the Philippines. He married Sally Ringe while back in the capital for bomb disposal training.

narrative_blocks.header: He flew his own plane to Olympia
narrative_blocks.body: He had earned a pilot's license in 1949 and was first known in the legislature for flying himself to the capital. He was re-elected three times from a rural district and by 1961 chaired the ways and means committee, the most powerful House Democrat after the speaker.

narrative_blocks.header: Folk music was offered as evidence
narrative_blocks.body: The case made against him in 1962 rested on his wife's Communist Party membership in the 1930s, on his son attending Reed College, and on her fondness for folk songs. A local editor called him a tool of a monstrous conspiracy, and he lost the primary three to one.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-three days in an Okanogan courtroom
narrative_blocks.body: He sued the newspaper and his accusers for libel and the trial ran forty-three days in the county courthouse. Kennedy was assassinated three weeks in. The jury found for him on five of nine claims in January 1964 and returned one of the largest libel awards the state had seen.

narrative_blocks.header: The Supreme Court took the verdict away
narrative_blocks.body: New York Times against Sullivan came down two months later and the judge set the award aside, holding that the falsehoods had not been shown to be malicious. He did not appeal or ask for a new trial. What he had wanted was the finding that the charges were false, and he had it.

narrative_blocks.header: The lie outlived him by six years
narrative_blocks.body: He never held office again, and cancer killed him in October 1979. Six years later a man who had heard at a Duck Club meeting that the Goldmarks were communists murdered his son Charles and Charles's wife and two boys. The defense argued at trial that the killer had confused the son for the father.

people.research_notes: From Sam's extracts, 3 Aug 2026: the Wikipedia articles on John Goldmark, Peter J. Goldmark and the murder of the Goldmark family, FindAGrave, and the Brooklyn Eagle obituary of Charles J. Goldmark. The only child of Charles Goldmark and Ruth Cornelia Ingersoll; his mother died six days after his birth and he was raised at Quaker boarding schools outside New York. First in his class at Haverford, law review at Harvard. Worked at the Office of Price Administration in 1941, where he met Sally Ringe. Bought a five-hundred-acre wheat and cattle ranch in Okanogan County in 1947, on the Colville reservation. Delegate for Adlai Stevenson in 1952 and 1960 and a keynote speaker for Kennedy in Seattle. A horse unseated him in 1966 and he nearly died of hypothermia before he was found, breaking his hip and having to learn to walk again; he and Sally then moved to Madrona in Seattle, where he practiced as a trial attorney. Lymph cancer was diagnosed in 1973. His chip name is John, which is what everyone called him. His great-uncle by marriage was Louis Brandeis.

bio.bio_blurb: New Deal worker; a library bears her name

narrative_blocks.header: A fire station made into a library
narrative_blocks.body: She worked to turn a former Seattle fire station into a branch of the public library. The Madrona branch carries her name.

narrative_blocks.header: She had joined the party in 1935
narrative_blocks.body: She paid dues and went to study groups from 1935, and said she resigned in 1943, the year after she married. Two federal agents questioned her in 1949 and a congressional committee subpoenaed her in 1956, and the family believed it was behind them.

narrative_blocks.header: She was awarded nothing
narrative_blocks.body: The jury found for her husband on five of nine claims and gave her no damages at all. A defense lawyer compared communism to a dog with rabies and asked how a communist could believe in God, and she left the courtroom in tears.

narrative_blocks.header: She died seven months before Christmas Eve
narrative_blocks.body: She died in May 1985, six years after her husband. That December her son Charles, his wife Annie and their two boys were killed at their house in Seattle by a man who believed the family were communists.

bio.bio_blurb: Seattle civil litigator and Democratic Party counsel

narrative_blocks.header: He left the firm with a K2 climber
narrative_blocks.body: He read law at Yale after Reed College and joined a large Seattle firm. In 1976 he left it with his friend Jim Wickwire, one of the first two Americans to reach the summit of K2, and the two started a firm of their own. He specialized in civil litigation.

narrative_blocks.header: He met her while stationed in Europe
narrative_blocks.body: He had joined an officers training program to become a military intelligence officer. In Europe he met Annie Carlsten, a French interpreter with a Swedish father and a French mother. They married and moved to Seattle and had two sons.

narrative_blocks.header: Counsel to the party, delegate for Hart
narrative_blocks.body: He was legal counsel to the Washington State Democratic Party. He went to the 1984 Democratic National Convention as a delegate for Gary Hart.

narrative_blocks.header: A stranger at the door on Christmas Eve
narrative_blocks.body: A stranger who believed the family were Communist officials talked his way into the house on Christmas Eve 1985 and attacked the four of them. Annie died that night and Colin four days later. Charles died on the ninth of January and Derek held on thirty-seven days.

narrative_blocks.header: His father's name was the one they meant
narrative_blocks.body: The killer had heard at a Duck Club meeting that the Goldmarks were communists, and his lawyers argued at trial that he had confused Charles for John, the legislator smeared twenty-three years earlier. No one in that house had ever been a communist.

narrative_blocks.header: The first memorial of its kind in Seattle
narrative_blocks.body: In 1992 an overlook above Lake Washington was named for the four of them, the first time private citizens murdered in the city were given a memorial. The plaque says they loved Seattle and its open spaces. The family foundation sends children to the island camp where the two boys had gone.

A founder of the Legal Foundation of Washington, which pays for the Goldmark Equal Access to Justice internships in his name. His old firm was Davis, Wright, Todd, Riese and Jones. The killer, David Lewis Rice, was convicted of aggravated murder on all four counts in June 1986 and sentenced to death; the conviction was overturned for incompetent defense and in 1998 he pleaded guilty in exchange for life without parole. The overlook is at Madrona Drive and Lake Washington Boulevard. Nothing of the manner of the attack has been written into the blocks beyond the fact of it. His birth is recorded only as January 1944; the month is kept in this note because the schema has no month-only precision value.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father Swedish, her mother French
narrative_blocks.body: She was working as an interpreter in Europe when she met Charles Goldmark, who was there as an intelligence officer. She went with him to Seattle and carried on translating after the move.

narrative_blocks.header: She died that night; the others later
narrative_blocks.body: A stranger who took the family for communists got into the house on Christmas Eve 1985. She was pronounced dead where she lay; her husband and both her sons died in hospital over the following five weeks.

narrative_blocks.body: He was twelve when a stranger attacked his family in their house on Christmas Eve 1985. He held on at the hospital longer than any of the four and died on the thirtieth of January. He and Colin had gone to the Bush School and to the camp on Orcas Island.

notable.notable_blurb: Washington lands commissioner with a molecular biology doctorate

cross_connections.display_label: ran Washington's largest timber company in the same forests
founded American plant ecology a lifetime before his own plant science

narrative_blocks.header: A doctorate in molecular biology, then the ranch
narrative_blocks.body: He took his bachelor's at Haverford in 1967 and a doctorate in molecular biology at Berkeley in 1971, then spent a research year at the Harvard medical school. He went home to the Double J Ranch in Okanogan County and has published on plant molecular genetics since, running a wheat breeding program.

narrative_blocks.header: He unseated the sitting commissioner in 2008
narrative_blocks.body: He ran for Congress in 2006 against Cathy McMorris and lost by thirteen points. Two years later he beat the incumbent Commissioner of Public Lands by thirty-one thousand votes, and he held the office from 2009 to 2017.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty years on wildland fire crews
narrative_blocks.body: He has volunteered as a wildland firefighter with the Okanogan county fire district for more than thirty years. Washington named him its Conservation Farmer of the Year in 1983.

narrative_blocks.header: He quit Agriculture inside six months
narrative_blocks.body: Governor Lowry made him director of the state Department of Agriculture in 1993 and he resigned before the year was out, saying he could not meet the demands of the job and the needs of his family at once. He said afterwards that his children were grown and he had hired help for the ranch.

narrative_blocks.header: Farmers and environmentalists at one table
narrative_blocks.body: In 1999 he co-founded a nonprofit called Farming and the Environment to bring the two sides together. He ranches on the principle that land is to be cared for rather than exploited.

people.research_notes: From Sam's extracts, 3 Aug 2026: the Wikipedia articles on John Goldmark, Peter J. bio.bio_blurb: Cowell and Hubbard secretary and treasurer

narrative_blocks.header: He helped renumber the streets of Cleveland
narrative_blocks.body: He was secretary and treasurer of the Cowell and Hubbard Company and among the best known retail men in the city. He sat on the Chamber of Commerce committee that established Cleveland's new street numbering system, the one that turned Case Street into East Fortieth.

narrative_blocks.header: Cancer of the stomach at fifty-two
narrative_blocks.body: He had been ailing more than a year when the trouble turned acute, and he went out to Saegertown in Pennsylvania. He was brought back to the hospital on the Saturday and died on the tenth of December 1906. He left a wife and six children, the youngest twelve.

narrative_blocks.header: A year of treatment in Winthrop House
narrative_blocks.body: Through 1654 and 1655 Amy lived as a member of the Winthrop family at New London, undergoing a long course of treatment by John Winthrop, Jr. Her husband was running the whole valley trade from Springfield at the time.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father governed the colony her husband left
narrative_blocks.body: Amy was the daughter of George Wyllys of Hartford, governor of Connecticut. Six years after her father-in-law pulled Springfield out of Connecticut and into Massachusetts, she married his son, on 30 October 1644.

cross_connections.display_label: was his great-grandfather, and the minister at Guilford, Connecticut

narrative_blocks.header: He followed his children west at sixty-two
narrative_blocks.body: Thirty-seven years of New York pulpits ended in 1895, when he moved to Palo Alto — a town that existed because Stanford did. His son ran its art department and his son-in-law kept its register.

narrative_blocks.header: He sent seven of eight children to college
narrative_blocks.body: The daughters went as well as the sons, in a household whose neighbors mostly did not send theirs. Only Gertrude took a kindergartner’s training instead.

narrative_blocks.header: His second book appeared the year he left
narrative_blocks.body: The Life of Society came out in 1885 and The Divine Indwelling in 1895, the year he closed his New York ministry. Two titles in thirty-seven years — one on how people live together, one on what lives within them.

narrative_blocks.header: He dropped dead on the ferry Berkeley
narrative_blocks.body: He died crossing San Francisco Bay on the ferry steamer Berkeley on 29 May 1902. Nine days later his son-in-law Herbert Nash, Stanford's first librarian, died at Pomona of Bright's disease.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a South Carolina pastor’s daughter
narrative_blocks.body: Martha Day Coit came from Cheraw, where her father was the Presbyterian church’s first pastor. Their eldest was born in 1860; within a year her brothers were in the Confederate army and he was preaching in New York.

narrative_blocks.header: The lake town where Bolton was born
narrative_blocks.body: The censuses of 1855 and 1860 put the family at Torrey, in Yates County on Seneca Lake. Its village of Dresden is where his son Bolton was born, a long way from the Sierra he would later map.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother is why this family is here
narrative_blocks.body: Harriet Henrietta Woodward was the daughter of Peter Woodward and Mary Fowler, and a great-granddaughter of the Hooker line. Every Stanford name in this house runs back through her to Rev. Amos Fowler’s pulpit at Guilford.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother went west; he stayed east
narrative_blocks.body: Edmund Woodward Brown took the New York pulpits and then Palo Alto. Horatio married Mary Jane McGinnes of Pennsylvania and raised seven children there, the youngest of them born at Williamsport in 1881.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brothers went south; she stayed north
narrative_blocks.body: She married a New York minister and bore her first child in 1860. By the next year her brothers were in Confederate uniform, and one of them would not come back.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brother was buried where the mortar fell
narrative_blocks.body: George Erasmus Coit, a lieutenant in the Palmetto Light Artillery, was killed by a mortar in Virginia in May 1863 at twenty-four. His brother William buried him on the field; his brother Julius went back afterward and brought him home to Cheraw.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brother rode home from Appomattox
narrative_blocks.body: William Henry Coit, Citadel-trained, raised a company of volunteers in 1861 and then commanded Coit’s Battery under Longstreet and Hood through Gettysburg. Paroled at Appomattox and allowed to keep his horse, he rode south and went into teaching.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father held the pulpit and the bank
narrative_blocks.body: John Caulkins Coit was the first pastor of the Presbyterian Church of Cheraw and president of the Merchants Bank there. He married Ellen Phoebe North in Orange County, North Carolina, in June 1834.

narrative_blocks.header: Her half-brother took the family to Texas
narrative_blocks.body: John Taylor Coit, a Princeton-trained lawyer, left Cheraw for north Dallas in 1858 and raised a cavalry company that became Company E of the 18th Texas. His is the earliest marked grave in Frankford Cemetery.

narrative_blocks.header: Her family names went into every child
narrative_blocks.body: Ellen Coit, Bolton Coit, Gertrude North — her children carry her father’s surname and her mother’s as middle names. A grandson born at Palo Alto in 1897 was christened David Coit Elliott.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed on a ferry crossing, she stayed west
narrative_blocks.body: Edmund died in 1902 on the bay steamer between San Francisco and Oakland, seven years after they came out. She remained in California until 1920 and lies beside him at Cypress Lawn in Colma.

William Henry Coit birth conflict: headstone 1834, the 1945 Coit family history 7 April 1835.

notable.notable_blurb: Memoirist; poet

cross_connections.display_label: wrote from an Amherst faculty house as she wrote from a Stanford one
sent the wire she assumed was her husband’s old joke

narrative_blocks.header: She kept cooking while he waved the telegram
narrative_blocks.body: Going to California had been the couple’s standing joke. When her husband came into the Ithaca kitchen in 1891 with Jordan’s wire in his hand, she assumed the joke had come round again and finished the dinner.

narrative_blocks.header: She thought the palms pretentious vegetables
narrative_blocks.body: California did not take at first — the yellow landscape got on her nerves, the brazen sunshine hurt her eyes, the mountains were bare. “I thought the palms pretentious vegetables,” she wrote.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote the early campus down as memoir
narrative_blocks.body: It Happened This Way: American Scene ran three hundred and thirty-two pages from the Stanford press. Her husband’s history of the university is the official account; hers is the kitchen, the yellow hills and the strangeness.

narrative_blocks.header: Her last book came out at ninety-three
narrative_blocks.body: The Winds: New Poems appeared in 1943 and The Leaves of Vallombrosa, twenty-five pages from a Palo Alto press, in 1954. She was born the December before Fort Sumter and died five days after her ninety-seventh birthday.

narrative_blocks.header: She and her husband both came from Cornell
narrative_blocks.body: Of the eight Brown children only one did not go through college. She took her degree at Cornell, where the English instructor she married was teaching, and both of them left it for Stanford in 1891.

narrative_blocks.header: Three of the eight landed on one campus
narrative_blocks.body: Her brother Bolton ran the art department and her sister Anna drew specimens for President Jordan. She and the registrar she married lived on the same campus, and their parents followed out from New York in 1895.

narrative_blocks.header: Jane Stanford and the nude models
narrative_blocks.body: He taught at Cornell before Stanford took him in 1891 to build a department of drawing and painting from nothing. He ran it eleven years and left over a dispute with Jane Stanford about using nude models in the classroom.

narrative_blocks.header: He put his own names on the Sierra
narrative_blocks.body: He worked the head-waters of the Kings River through 1895 and 1896, named Split Mountain and Arrow Peak, made the first ascent of the peak he called Mount Stanford, and finished by soloing Mount King, which had beaten him the year before. Most of his names are still on the maps, and the Climbers Guide calls that solo the first advanced aid-climbing in North America.

narrative_blocks.header: He picked the ground Byrdcliffe was built on
narrative_blocks.body: Ralph Radcliffe Whitehead sent him through the Catskills for three weeks to find a site for an arts colony, and Brown argued him out of a location further south and into Woodstock. He bought seven farms, laid the paths and plumbing, and was fired inside two years.

narrative_blocks.header: He signed prints he had only pulled
narrative_blocks.body: He held that the printer made a work as much as the artist did, and counter-signed every lithograph he pulled for someone else — Bellows, Sloan, Rockwell Kent. He made more than four hundred of his own.

narrative_blocks.header: They took a two-year-old into the High Sierra
narrative_blocks.body: In 1899 he and Lucy carried their daughter Eleanor back into the Kings River country, camping below Kearsarge Pass. The Sierra Club reckoned her the most youthful pioneer of the High Sierra.

narrative_blocks.header: He carved the boulder he lies under
narrative_blocks.body: He died at Woodstock in 1936, poor and alone, leaving books and articles on painting and lithography and twelve volumes of journals on his own printmaking. He had already chosen a boulder in his yard, carved it himself, and had it carried to the Artists Cemetery.

people.research_notes:
MADE NOTABLE 10 Aug 2026 on Sam's approval, with Wikipedia as the url. Painter, lithographer and
mountaineer; one of the founders of the Byrdcliffe Colony at Woodstock. BIRTH YEAR CONFLICT, unresolved: Wikipedia and the Crooked Lake Review give 27 Nov 1864, the
FindAGrave memorial 27 Nov 1865 (and calls him seventy at death, where Wikipedia says
seventy-one). 1864 kept, as the entry already carried it. NOT USED ON THE CARD: his sister was the scientific illustrator Anna B. Nash. His teaching stressed
rapid execution of natural subjects in the wilderness against the traditional method at the San
Francisco School of Design, and in 1898 he designed Stanford's new art studios with a continuous
eight-foot belt of glass and walls hung with the Paris avant-garde. His student Jennie V. Cannon
wrote several short lives of him. He exhibited one painting at the 1913 Armory Show. He later said
his break with Whitehead was less about budgets than about the "medieval" intentions Whitehead
harboured for the colony. Best-known lithographs: Moonlight Bathers (1915), Cloudy Dawn (1916),
Sifting Shadows (1916). SIERRA CCs 10 Aug 2026, on Sam's prompt ("marian osgood hooker? williamson next to whitney").
Dr. Marian Osgood Hooker (H04280) was the first woman to summit Mount Whitney, in 1903, with John
Muir's party; Lucy Fletcher Brown climbed Mount Williamson — the next great peak north of Whitney
— in the summer of 1896, and was with Bolton on two of his first ascents. Brown was a charter
member of the Sierra Club, which Muir founded, so all four connect through one range and one club
inside a decade. ID CORRECTION 10 Aug 2026. Everything on this card was first written to HD9890 by a build script
that hardcoded the id instead of reading it back from the live file — the exact failure schema
§D.1 names as the most expensive recurring defect. HD9890 is William Brown (1830-1900), Bolton's
uncle; he has been restored and every reference repointed here. Sam caught it by finding this
entry empty. REBUILT 10 Aug 2026 rather than added to, on Sam's instruction, once the Sierra Club material
arrived. Cornell first, then Stanford 1891 — eleven years, and the break was with JANE Stanford
specifically over nude models. THE 1895 AND 1896 SEASONS, from the Sierra Club account: 1895, Kings River Canyon, a failed
attempt on Mount King, then over to Simpson Meadow, up Mount Woodworth, up Cartridge Creek to the
head-waters of the South Fork, naming Split Mountain, Striped Mountain and Arrow Peak, back by
Paradise Valley. 1896 with Lucy: Kings River Canyon again, Mount Gardner with Joseph N. Le Conte,
Mount Brewer, over the Kings-Kern Divide and up Mount Williamson, the first ascent of Mount
Stanford which he named, and finally King, solo. 1899: back with their two-year-old daughter,
camped at Bullfrog Lake near Kearsarge Pass, naming The Fin. Flying Cloud Pass and Castilleja
Lake are the names of his that did not survive. NOT USED: his lithographs hang at the Library of Congress, the Brooklyn Museum, the Art Institute
of Chicago, Georgetown and Rochester, and he showed regularly at the Kleeman Galleries. He also
printed for George William Eggers and J.J. Lankes, and gave William J. Schwanekamp a lesson at
Woodstock on his way to visit Robert Frost. THE TALCOTT CC answers Sam's question about whether there was anything deeper than both being
painters. There is: they are the two American art colonies of the same moment. Talcott's first
summer at Florence Griswold's boarding house in Old Lyme was 1901; Brown founded Byrdcliffe at
Woodstock in 1902. Old Lyme and Woodstock are the two colonies that defined American landscape
painting in those years, and these two men are on the making end of each. CC TO NASH 10 Aug 2026, on Sam's framing — the two men's relationships with the same woman. Jane
Stanford ended Brown's eleven years at the university over his use of nude models. She also wrote
Herbert Nash into her holograph will of 1899 in her own hand, as "the devoted tutor and loving
friend of my dear son, also faithful Secretary of my dear husband". One man she remembered by
name; the other she removed. They were brothers-in-law: Nash married Brown's sister Anna in 1899,
the same year of that will. BOTH LABELS NOW NAME THE RELATIONSHIP, on Sam's instruction 10 Aug 2026 — they were carrying the
Jane Stanford contrast without saying that these two men were brothers-in-law. Nash married
Brown's sister Anna Louise in 1899, the same year Jane Stanford wrote Nash into her holograph

narrative_blocks.header: She drew fish, bones, fossils and flowers
narrative_blocks.body: She was the artist at the Hopkins Seaside Laboratory from 1893 to 1897 and came to California to do scientific drawing for David Starr Jordan in the early days of Stanford. She worked in the laboratories at Stanford, at Berkeley, in New York and in Washington, and was rated an expert.

narrative_blocks.header: She married the man who kept the books
narrative_blocks.body: About 1900 she married Herbert Nash, Stanford's first librarian, and lived on campus in the house he built for her. He was dead within three years, and the small trees she planted there grew into the park-like campus.

narrative_blocks.header: Two years abroad, then back to drawing
narrative_blocks.body: Widowed at thirty-five she went to Europe, studied art and kept a studio in Paris. She came home after two years of travel and took up scientific drawing again, and only late in life turned to oils and pastels of her own.

narrative_blocks.header: She came to a university her family ran
narrative_blocks.body: Her brother Bolton had built the art department and her sister Ellen's husband was the registrar, both there since the university opened in 1891. She arrived to draw for its president, and married its first librarian.

people.research_notes:
ENRICHED 10 Aug 2026 from two obituaries Sam supplied. She came to California to do scientific
drawing for PRESIDENT DAVID STARR JORDAN in the early days of Stanford, and was the artist at the
Hopkins Seaside Laboratory 1893-97. Syracuse art department, class of 1890. Married Herbert Nash
about 1900 and lived on campus in the house he built; the small trees she planted there became
part of the park-like campus. Widowed 1902, she went to Europe, kept a studio in Paris, came home
after two years and resumed drawing fish, bones, fossils and flowers in the laboratories of
Stanford, the University of California, New York and Washington — "she was rated an expert". Late
in life she painted in oil and pastel and had several modest exhibitions. Died at Santa Barbara,
an artist of Ojai. HER SIBLINGS, from the 1945 obituary, which is the best roster of that family anywhere in these
sources: "Rev. Harriett B. Coolidge (Mrs. Herbert Coolidge)" of Santa Barbara — HD9901 Harriet
Hamilton Brown, and note the title, a woman in orders; "Miss Zaidee Brown of New York City" —
HD9900; "Mrs. O. L. Elliott of Stanford university" — HD9895 Ellen; "Miss A. E. Brown, librarian
in Richmond" — HD9902 Agnes Bessie Brown, ANOTHER LIBRARIAN in a family that already has two;

those five is enriched yet; the obituary is the source when they are. Her birth year is given as 1866 in one notice and 1867 in the other; 1867 kept, as the entry had
it. DAVID STARR JORDAN is NOT an entry in this tree — he appears only inside narrative blocks on
Katharine Putnam Hooker, Marian Osgood Hooker and George Ellery Hale. With this family he would
now connect to five or six people; worth Sam's decision as an orbit easter egg. FOURTH BLOCK 10 Aug 2026, from the Hopkins Seaside account Sam supplied: "The family's affiliation
with Stanford University began in 1891 with the appointment of Orrin Leslie Elliott, her sister

I00592 Sherman Day Thacher, who homesteaded there in 1887 and founded the Thacher School in 1889,

career.role: Principal, then assistant superintendent of schools

narrative_blocks.header: He outlived every one of his seven siblings
narrative_blocks.body: Born the year Grant was elected, he died at Columbia, Missouri on 9 February 1969 at a hundred, the last of the eight by four years. Services and burial were at Waterloo, Iowa, where his daughter Margaret lived.

narrative_blocks.header: He was tracing this family until the end
narrative_blocks.body: He belonged to the Schuyler County Historical Society and kept up his study of local history and genealogy almost to the end of a hundred years. He had followed this family back to the early colonists of New York.

narrative_blocks.header: He rose to assistant superintendent in St. Louis
narrative_blocks.body: Ten years of teaching and running schools in New York State, and then Missouri — principal, then assistant superintendent of schools at St. Louis, where he stayed about thirty years. He retired in 1943, at seventy-five.

narrative_blocks.header: Cornell before any of them saw Stanford
narrative_blocks.body: He took his Bachelor of Letters there in 1890, and his sister Ellen took a Cornell degree too. Their brother Bolton taught art on that faculty and the English instructor Ellen married was on it as well — four of them through Ithaca before Stanford opened.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven went to college; she took the training
narrative_blocks.body: Of the eight Brown children, seven went through college — the daughters as well as the sons, in a household that made a point of it. She took a kindergartner’s training instead, and died at forty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: Her middle name is her grandmother’s maiden name
narrative_blocks.body: Ellen Phoebe North married the Presbyterian pastor of Cheraw, South Carolina, in 1834. Two generations later her name came north in a granddaughter’s, alongside the Coit her brother and sister carried.

narrative_blocks.header: Three sisters ended in one Santa Barbara plot
narrative_blocks.body: A stroke took her at Santa Barbara in November 1950, two weeks after it struck. Harriet had gone in 1949 and Agnes followed in 1965; all three sisters lie at Goleta Cemetery, a long way from Burdett.

narrative_blocks.header: She organized libraries in two states
narrative_blocks.body: She set up libraries in New York and Massachusetts, ran Long Beach’s for many years, and later held the same post at the State Teachers College at Upper Montclair. She worked on and off with H. W. Wilson, the library publishers.

narrative_blocks.header: She took a Stanford degree too
narrative_blocks.body: Four of the eight were tied to that campus: Bolton on its faculty, Anna drawing for its president, Ellen married to its registrar, and Zaidee a graduate. She is the only one of the four who went through it as a student.

narrative_blocks.body: She married Herbert Francis Coolidge in 1904 and by 1945 was living at Santa Barbara, styled Reverend Harriett Coolidge. Her father had been ordained Presbyterian in 1858; she took orders at a time when few women were given them.

narrative_blocks.header: Libraries, like the man her sister married
narrative_blocks.body: Of the eight she went into libraries, at Richmond, California, and was still there in 1945. Herbert Nash, who married her sister Anna, had been Stanford’s first librarian forty years before, and her nephew Coit ran the Richmond library after her.

people.research_notes: RICHMOND CORRECTED 11 Aug 2026 from Virginia to CALIFORNIA. The 1945 obituary of her sister Anna says only "librarian in Richmond"; the previous card guessed Virginia. Her nephew Coit Coolidge’s 1972 obituary calls him "former librarian for the city of Richmond" — Richmond, California — and Agnes died at Santa Barbara, so the family’s Richmond is the Bay Area one. Note that a different branch does reach Richmond, Virginia: William Wallace Merriman’s son Ted was living there in 2000.

narrative_blocks.header: A telegram from David Starr Jordan moved him
narrative_blocks.body: In 1891 Jordan, newly named president of a university that did not yet exist, wired the Cornell English instructor an invitation to join its pioneer personnel. The Elliotts left Ithaca that year and never came back.

narrative_blocks.header: He registered every Stanford student until 1925
narrative_blocks.body: He was registrar from the university’s inception through thirty-four years, and secretary to the president for a long stretch of them. Trained as a historian, he spent his working life keeping the record of an institution younger than he was.

narrative_blocks.header: He waited until retirement to write it down
narrative_blocks.body: Stanford University: The First Twenty-Five Years ran to six hundred and twenty-four pages when the university press published it in 1937, twelve years after he left the office. His preface calls the Jordan and Branner presidencies the heroic age.

narrative_blocks.header: He praised Jane Stanford and doubted her knowledge
narrative_blocks.body: Of the founder who had kept the university alive after her husband died, he commended her steadfastness, her courage and her devotion. He also wrote, more than once, that she spoke without adequate knowledge.

narrative_blocks.header: The Ross affair he wrote out in full
narrative_blocks.body: The dismissal of the economist Edward Ross and the liquor question were the two episodes a house historian might have walked around. He went at both, with frankness and at length, in a book the university’s own press printed.

narrative_blocks.header: The unpublished reminiscences went to the archive
narrative_blocks.body: He gave Stanford not only the history but its apparatus — source citations, copies of documents, reminiscences never printed, and the notecards George Crothers had used for his own book on the founding.

narrative_blocks.header: He married one of eight Brown children
narrative_blocks.body: Ellen Coit Brown was a Cornell graduate and a writer. Her brother Bolton founded Stanford’s art department the same year Elliott opened its register; her sister Anna married the man who was Leland Stanford’s private secretary and the first librarian.

Henry Taylor Blake (HD1568) is the closest shape in the tree: on New Haven’s park commission from 1889 and its president from 1898, he read the papers that became the history of the very ground he was administering. narrative_blocks.header: He trained at Camp MacArthur in Waco
narrative_blocks.body: He went to Stanford in the class of 1918, where his father was the registrar, and served as a private, attending officers training school at Camp MacArthur in Texas. He later clerked at the Federal Reserve Bank in Washington.

narrative_blocks.header: She climbed Mount Williamson in 1896
narrative_blocks.body: Lucy Fletcher was born at Paris and married Bolton Brown at Palo Alto in June 1896. That summer she climbed Mount Williamson, and she was with him on two of his first ascents in the Sierra.

narrative_blocks.header: Paris, because her father was studying there
narrative_blocks.body: William Baldwin Fletcher spent 1866 and 1867 in the hospitals of Glasgow, London and Paris, as ambitious American physicians of his generation did. Lucy was born at Paris in January 1867 and came home to Indianapolis an infant.

narrative_blocks.header: Lee reprieved her father from a firing squad
narrative_blocks.body: Captured near Big Springs, Virginia, he was put in solitary, wounded on the second of two escape attempts, and sentenced to be shot. Robert E. Lee reprieved him pending investigation; the Confederates then lost the paperwork and paroled him as an ordinary prisoner.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father burned the straitjackets in bonfires
narrative_blocks.body: Put in charge of the Indiana Hospital for the Insane in 1883, he burned more than five hundred straitjackets, covered cribs and restraint chairs. He ended the secret burials, brought in dental care, and hired the hospital’s first woman physician.

narrative_blocks.header: He named the abuses and lost the job
narrative_blocks.body: He was removed in 1887 after calling attention to political abuse in the state hospital system. The next year he opened Neuronhurst, a private sanatorium for mentally ill women, and hired Mary Spink, who went on to run it.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandfather’s diary fills nine volumes
narrative_blocks.body: Calvin Fletcher — lawyer, banker and state senator, and the man Fletcher Place in Indianapolis is named for — raised eleven children and kept a diary the Indiana Historical Society later published in nine volumes. He called this son Billy.

narrative_blocks.header: A Hoosier poet was his honorary pallbearer
narrative_blocks.body: James Whitcomb Riley wrote him into a poem called The Doctor, which keeps coming back to the line “Why not idealize the doctor some?” Riley was an honorary pallbearer when he was buried at Crown Hill in 1907.

HER FATHER 11 Aug 2026, from material Sam supplied on Dr. William Baldwin Fletcher (1837–1907). He is DELIBERATELY NOT AN ENTRY — the same treatment as Dane Coolidge: the material lands on his daughter’s card. Not used: Indiana Asbury (DePauw) before the College of Physicians and Surgeons, MD 1859; the Indianapolis City Dispensary he founded in 1870; professorships at the Indiana Medical College and the Central College of Physicians and Surgeons; election as Marion County’s state senator in 1882; Libby Prison, where he was put in charge of a hospital; the sanatorium’s rename to Neuronhurst after 1904; his decline after his wife’s death in 1904 and heart failure at his winter house in Orlando. The Indiana Medical History Museum now occupies the old hospital pathology building.
Her Paris birth and his 1866–67 European hospital year are the same fact seen twice — that is why she was born abroad.

narrative_blocks.header: He printed at the colony his father-in-law founded
narrative_blocks.body: He worked at Byrdcliffe as a lithographer through the 1930s and 1940s. That was the medium Bolton Brown had mastered, and the colony Bolton had picked the ground for, bought seven farms for, and been pushed out of within two years.

narrative_blocks.header: The prints outlasted everything else about him
narrative_blocks.body: He made only a handful of modernist lithographs, signing and dating each one in pencil, and died at fifty. The Good Earth, pulled in 1945, is the one that still surfaces; almost nothing else of his life was set down anywhere.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at Stanford the day they graduated
narrative_blocks.body: Jean married John B. De Nault, her high-school sweetheart, at Stanford on 8 June 1941, straight after their commencement. They were married seventy-five years. She died at a hundred and three.

narrative_blocks.header: He was never away from Stanford a day
narrative_blocks.body: He came out to San Francisco in 1881 and spent three years as private tutor to Leland Stanford Jr. When the boy died at Florence the Senator took him on as private secretary, and until Stanford died in 1893 Nash was not away from his side a day.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the dead boy his life
narrative_blocks.body: Leland Stanford Jr. died at Florence in 1884, fifteen years old. Nash compiled In Memoriam: Leland Stanford, Jr. and wrote the guide to the boy's own museum of antiquities, which was rebuilt inside the university museum when it opened in 1893.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept the books of the university
narrative_blocks.body: After the Senator died he stayed on as assistant to Mrs. Stanford, and in the mid-nineties became the first librarian of the university named for the boy he had tutored.

narrative_blocks.header: Both Stanfords remembered him in their wills
narrative_blocks.body: Leland Stanford's will left him a bequest as a mark of respect and esteem. Jane Stanford's, written in her own hand in 1899, called him the devoted tutor and loving friend of my dear son, also faithful Secretary of my dear husband.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine days after his wife’s father
narrative_blocks.body: He took leave from Stanford at Christmas 1901 and went south for his health — San Diego, Palm Springs, Pomona. He died there of Bright's disease on 7 June 1902, forty-two years old, his wife and her brother-in-law the registrar at the bedside.

people.research_notes:
BUILT 10 Aug 2026 from the San Francisco Call obituary, 7 June 1902, "STANFORD LOSES LIBRARIAN
NASH". Of English parentage, born at Nice. To San Francisco 1881; three years private tutor to
Leland Stanford Jr.; on the boy's death at Florence, private secretary to Senator Stanford until
the Senator's death in 1893, "never away from his employer's side a day"; then assistant to Mrs.
Stanford; librarian of the university from 1895. Died at the Hotel Keller, Pomona, of Bright's
disease, aged 42. O. L. Elliott, registrar of Stanford and his wife's brother-in-law, was with him
when he died. The same obituary reports that his wife's father, "Rev. E. Woodward Brown", had dropped dead on
the ferry steamer Berkeley at San Francisco a week earlier — that is HD9891, whose death this
tree already carried as 29 May 1902. Nine days between them. ENRICHED AND MADE NOTABLE 10 Aug 2026 on Sam's approval. THE TUTORING AND THE BOOK. Hired by Leland and Jane Stanford to tutor Leland Stanford Jr., a post
he held to the boy's death at Florence in 1884 aged fifteen. He compiled the laudatory In
Memoriam: Leland Stanford, Jr., which records the boy's travels and his interest in archaeology
and antiquities — Nash describes him spending hours in the Egyptian wing of the Louvre copying
hieroglyphics and sketching. He also wrote the short guide to the "Museum" the boy had made of his
own collections in the family's San Francisco mansion, which was recreated in the memorial rooms
of the University Museum when it opened in 1893. THE BEQUESTS, sums deliberately omitted from the blocks per the standing rule that money stays
out of user-facing prose. Leland Stanford's will: "to his private secretary, Herbert C. Nash, who
was also tutor to his son Leland, as a mark of respect and esteem." Jane Stanford's holograph will
of 1899: "I give and bequeath to Herbert C. Nash, the devoted tutor and loving friend of my dear
son, also faithful Secretary of my dear husband." DATE CONFLICT on the librarianship: the 1902 Call obituary says he became librarian in 1895, a
Stanford Archives note on the back of his photograph says 1896. The block says "the mid-nineties"
rather than choosing. The same archives note has him leaving on sick leave in 1901, which matches
the obituary's Christmas leave of absence. ALSO NOT USED: Bancroft's stenographers took a dictation from him on 14 September 1889 for a life
of Leland Stanford that was set in type and never published, after Stanford broke with Bancroft. JANE AND LELAND STANFORD ARE NOT ENTRIES in this tree. They appear only inside narrative blocks —
here, on HD9896 Bolton Coit Brown, and on H04268 Elizabeth 'Bessie' Augusta Hooker Lent, who wrote
Jane a condolence letter in 1884 over the death of the very boy Nash tutored. That last is now a
CC. With Nash, Bolton, Orrin Elliott, Anna Nash and David Starr Jordan, the Stanford cluster in
this tree is now large enough that the Stanfords themselves are worth Sam's decision. And see the CC to HD9896 Bolton Coit Brown, his wife's brother: Jane Stanford named Nash in her own
hand in the 1899 will and put Brown out of the university he had built a department for. TWO FIXES 10 Aug 2026 on Sam's read of the card. NB4's header was "Both Stanfords remembered him by name", which Sam rightly called a strange thing
to say — of course they knew his name. The point is the wills, and the header now says so. The Stoddard and Herrick labels were near-duplicates of one another, both ending "as Nash was
Stanford's" — the same fault Sam caught on James Pierpont's card, where two labels opened
identically. Each now carries what is distinctive about its own man: Stoddard as the first
American ever called librarian, Herrick as the man who proved the Perseids return. The parallel
with Nash is already the reason the CCs exist and does not need saying three times.

narrative_blocks.header: All four Huntington sisters went to Stanford
narrative_blocks.body: Katherine and her three sisters all went to Stanford, where she joined Chi Omega and was known as a pianist. Her eldest sister Frances taught English at Palo Alto High School for thirty-two years and never married.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Bronze Stars on the fleet oilers
narrative_blocks.body: He enlisted in the Navy in August 1942 and served to 1946, reaching full lieutenant as a supply officer on fleet oilers. He came out with battle ribbons for every major Navy operation and two Bronze Stars for bravery.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded an insurance company after retiring
narrative_blocks.body: He worked up through Farmers Insurance from accountant to treasurer and retired in 1965, then joined Lou Foster to found 20th Century Insurance and chaired it until 1998. He also bought enough of Liberty Bank to save its Boulder Creek branch.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran an eighth-scale steam railroad
narrative_blocks.body: He built and ran a one-eighth scale live steam railroad, swam with turtles off Mauna Kea, ran the Rogue River, and kept an almost perfect attendance record at Stanford home football games from the end of the war onward.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother turned out forty western novels
narrative_blocks.body: Dane Coolidge, his elder brother, took a Stanford degree in 1898, collected animal specimens for the British Museum and the Smithsonian, and wrote more than forty westerns. He married the Mills College sociologist Mary Roberts, and the two of them wrote The Navajo Indians.

narrative_blocks.header: His family counted a president as a cousin
narrative_blocks.body: The Coolidges came from Natick, Massachusetts, sons of Francis Coolidge and Sophia Whittemore, and reckoned Calvin Coolidge a cousin. Their father moved them to a farm at Riverside, California, and the boys grew up there.

narrative_blocks.body: He died at Chico in 1972 at sixty-six, a Rotarian and a member of Bidwell Memorial Presbyterian. Two sons had gone to Oakland and Salt Lake City; his son John and his daughter Elizabeth were both still at Richmond.

narrative_blocks.body: She came to Kalamazoo in the early 1930s for the children’s room of the public library, and after twelve years away returned as assistant librarian at Kalamazoo College. She finished at Milwood Junior High and teaching children’s literature at Western Michigan.

narrative_blocks.header: Phi Beta Kappa in library science
narrative_blocks.body: She took her bachelor’s in library science at Wisconsin and a master’s in literature at Columbia. Her aunt Agnes and her cousin Coit were running California libraries in the same years.

narrative_blocks.header: She was vice president of Cleveland’s League
narrative_blocks.body: The Merrimans lived at Cleveland from 1940 to 1952, where she served the Cleveland League of Women Voters as vice president. Her husband sold meat there, having run a Kalamazoo poultry market until 1939.

narrative_blocks.header: She talked about the family her father traced
narrative_blocks.body: Edmund Fowler Brown studied genealogy into his hundredth year and had followed this family back to the early colonists of New York. She was still telling people about it at ninety-one.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the Rolling Stone Poultry Market
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Kalamazoo and raised at Holyoke, Massachusetts, he came back after two years at Middlebury and kept the Rolling Stone Poultry Market until 1939. He sold meat at Cleveland afterward, then farm and orchard supplies across the Midwest.

notable.notable_blurb: Revolutionary governor of Connecticut

cross_connections.display_label: signed the charter for UConn, whose husky mascot carries his name
preached in the Western Reserve, where Trumbull County was carved

narrative_blocks.header: He succeeded himself as governor in 1776
narrative_blocks.body: Of the thirteen colonial governors he was the only one to take the Patriot side, and the only one to hold the office on both sides of independence. When Gage asked for his cooperation after Lexington and Concord he refused, telling him his troops would "disgrace even barbarians".

narrative_blocks.header: Washington called him Brother Jonathan
narrative_blocks.body: A merchant before he was a governor, he spent the war finding food, clothing, shoes and munitions for an army that had none, and sent cattle drives to Valley Forge — which is why Connecticut is the Provisions State. Washington named him "the first of the patriots". He left office in 1784 owing money he had run up supplying the war, and asked that his own unpaid army salary be divided among the soldiers instead.

narrative_blocks.header: A store on the green ran the war
narrative_blocks.body: The Council of Safety met more than a thousand times between 1775 and 1783, much of it in a gambrel-roofed store his father had built on the Lebanon green. Washington, Knox, Lafayette, Rochambeau, Jefferson, Franklin and Jay all passed through it, and a tunnel ran from it to his own house.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother drowned and he left the pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: He took his Harvard degree in 1727 and was licensed to preach at Colchester. In 1732 his older brother Joseph was lost at sea aboard a brigantine called the Lebanon, and Jonathan gave up the ministry for the family counting house — the trade that later fed an army. In 1736 he bought a girl named Flora from Eliphalet Adams of New London, a slave for life.

narrative_blocks.header: A college, a county, and a husky
narrative_blocks.body: Trumbull College at Yale, the town of Trumbull in Connecticut, and Trumbull County in Ohio, carved out of the Connecticut Western Reserve, all carry his name. So does Jonathan the Husky, the University of Connecticut's mascot.

He commissioned Nathan Hale a first lieutenant in July 1775. The family name was originally spelled Trumble.

narrative_blocks.header: She is remembered giving away her cloak
narrative_blocks.body: She gave up her scarlet cloak to be cut down for the army her husband spent the war clothing, and that is the act she is remembered by.

narrative_blocks.header: Her six children ran the Revolution between them
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph was the Continental Army's first commissary general and Jonathan Jr. was Washington's aide and later Speaker of the House. Mary married a signer of the Declaration, Faith married General Jedidiah Huntington, and John became the painter of the Revolution.

narrative_blocks.header: Marrying her made him almost nobility
narrative_blocks.body: A minister's daughter, she descended directly from John and Priscilla Alden of the Mayflower. In a colony that counted such things, the match lifted a Lebanon merchant into the first families of New England.

narrative_blocks.header: Secretary at twenty-one, president at twenty-nine
narrative_blocks.body: He went from Sheffield into his father's plant and learned every department of it before he was given anything. The company made him secretary in 1883 and president in 1891, the year his father died, and he ran it until his own death twenty-six years later.

narrative_blocks.header: He held five New Haven boards at once
narrative_blocks.body: Besides the boiler works he was president of the National Pipe Bending Company and vice president of the Yale Publishing Company. He was a director of the Merchants National Bank his father had once run, a trustee of the National Savings Bank, and a director of the New Haven Water Company.

narrative_blocks.header: He was his father's aide-de-camp
narrative_blocks.body: He took the Bachelor of Philosophy at Yale in 1881 and served as aide-de-camp on the governor's staff while his father held the office. He belonged to the Quinnipiac, the New Haven Country and Lawn clubs, and to the Yale and University clubs of New York.

narrative_blocks.header: He died on the golf course at fifty-four
narrative_blocks.body: Death came suddenly on 20 June 1917 while he was playing golf. He had run the largest boiler works in the city for twenty-six years and sat on the society committee of the Church of the Redeemer.

narrative_blocks.header: She married two men, both named Walter
narrative_blocks.body: Walter Pierpont Bigelow died in Manhattan in 1907 at forty, and she married the actor Walter Iles Percival afterward. She was a playwright and he was a tenor who produced plays; they lie together at Kensico.

narrative_blocks.header: He played Gratiano for David Belasco
narrative_blocks.body: A Philadelphia tenor who moved to New York, he sang in musical productions and took a lead in Belasco's Merchant of Venice on Broadway. He wrote and performed Will O' the Wisp, produced plays of his own, and belonged to the Lambs, the first theatrical club in America.

narrative_blocks.header: The actor kept championship cows
narrative_blocks.body: From 1908 he had a farm and estate at West Cheshire, Connecticut, where he bred prize cattle. For a time he opened the pond on the property to the public for swimming and picnicking.

narrative_blocks.header: He built the engine for a torpedo boat
narrative_blocks.body: Among his patents was the engine for the submarine torpedo boat Peacemaker, which he designed, patented and built himself. He had learned the machinist trade young, then moved to New Haven in 1853 to study surveying and civil engineering.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped build Minnesota's first railroad
narrative_blocks.body: He went west to work on the construction of the first railroad in Minnesota, then managed two large manufacturing works before coming home to New Haven. He belonged to a long list of engineering and trade societies.

narrative_blocks.header: He buried three wives and lived to ninety-six
narrative_blocks.body: Fanny Blake died in January 1855, thirteen days after their son was born; Julia Hinman died at Southbury in 1859, three years after the wedding; Maria Lindsley, who bore him five children, died in 1903. He outlived all three and reached December 1928.

Eli Whitney III (HD2082) built Whitneyville into a Civil War arsenal and sold Whitney Arms to Winchester in 1888 — New Haven's own war industry, in the same city and the same decades in which Bigelow designed, patented and built the engine for the submarine torpedo boat Peacemaker.
DID HE WORK FOR THE BIGELOW COMPANY? NOTHING SUPPLIED SAYS SO. Hobart bought the works in 1861 after being foreman at Ives & Smith; George was independently a machinist, surveyor and civil engineer, worked on the first railroad in Minnesota and managed two manufacturing works. ERASMUS DARWIN LEAVITT JR. narrative_blocks.body: He left the public schools at eighteen, declined the chance to go to college, and walked into the shoe house his father had founded on Chapel Street. It became Butler & Tyler of State Street, one of the oldest mercantile firms in New Haven, and he was in it until he died.
