narrative_blocks.header: One sentence turned Kennedy toward the blockade
narrative_blocks.body: With Bundy pressing for airstrikes on Cuba in October 1962, he told the room it was "a choice between limited action and unlimited action, and most of us think it is better to start with limited action." Kennedy took the blockade.

narrative_blocks.header: He killed the missile gap in one speech
narrative_blocks.body: In October 1961 he told the Business Council at Hot Springs that no sneak attack could disarm American forces. Business Week called it the most precisely confident statement of American strength in years, and the missile gap collapsed.

narrative_blocks.header: The Pentagon's longest deputy: 1,091 days
narrative_blocks.body: He was the tenth Deputy Secretary of Defense and served longer in the post than any of his nine predecessors. Robert McNamara treated him as an alter ego and habitually opened sentences with "Ros and I...".

narrative_blocks.header: A scholarship boy at Hotchkiss, then Cravath
narrative_blocks.body: He waited tables and cleaned rooms at Hotchkiss, and left with the class of 1924 alongside Paul Nitze and Charles Yost. From Yale and Yale Law he went to Cravath, Swaine & Moore, and was its presiding partner from 1966 to 1977.

narrative_blocks.header: Jackie Onassis's letters were stolen from Cravath
narrative_blocks.body: He escorted her often and always said they were only friends. Four of her letters were taken from his Cravath office and put up at auction, and he demanded their withdrawal. One read: "all you were and are and will ever be to me."

narrative_blocks.header: He built the DIA and the NRO
narrative_blocks.body: Reviewing the department's intelligence work in 1961, he signed the directive creating the Defense Intelligence Agency. That autumn he agreed with the CIA's Charles Cabell to stand up a National Reconnaissance Office over the satellites.

narrative_blocks.header: He signed off on Diem's removal
narrative_blocks.body: Kennedy gave him a Vietnam task force in 1961 whose report — more advisers, a stronger army — set policy there. Acting for McNamara in August 1963 he signed the cable endorsing Ngo Dinh Diem's removal; Diem was murdered that November.

narrative_blocks.body: He retired from the Foreign Service in 1981 after nearly twenty years as director of the Office of Foreign Commercial Services at the Department of Commerce. He died of emphysema at St. Augustine, Florida, at seventy-nine.

bio.bio_blurb: Rockefeller Foundation humanities officer; OSS captain

narrative_blocks.header: OSS captain, then CIA, then the humanities
narrative_blocks.body: He spent the war on the Board of Economic Warfare and then as an Army captain with the Office of Strategic Services in London and Germany, and was with the Central Intelligence Agency in Washington from 1947 to 1949. He left it for the Rockefeller Foundation and spent the next twenty-three years giving money away for philosophy, history and the arts, retiring in 1972 off the foundation's field staff in India.

narrative_blocks.header: His division took up the problem of meaning
narrative_blocks.body: In 1950 the Foundation's humanities officers overhauled their programme, and the first of the new headings was Language, Logic and Symbolism — the interplay of thought and language, with emphasis on the problem of meaning. He was the division's assistant director that year.

narrative_blocks.header: He found Wittgenstein in pyjamas in 1950
narrative_blocks.body: He was let in at six one evening to see Ludwig Wittgenstein, then sixty-one, too ill to leave his bed for more than a few hours a day and dressed in shabby clothes over his pyjamas. He wrote down an ascetic leanness in the face, skin remarkably fair, eyes that dominated and controlled your attention, a man speaking with great simplicity and compelling earnestness. Wittgenstein told him his thinking powers had failed, refused to say what he was working on, and was dead within the year.

narrative_blocks.header: Three brothers, three kinds of power
narrative_blocks.body: His elder brother Roswell was deputy secretary of defense under Kennedy and Johnson; his brother Donald ran American relief into wartime China and spent twenty years at Commerce. All three were sons of a Wall Street lawyer and a Mount Holyoke graduate who had herself been born to missionary parents at Osaka.

narrative_blocks.body: Swami Yogananda spoke at his Brookline church in the November of 1928. Leavitt wrote to thank him: the best of it, he said, was the background of fine understanding that made all feel in the same human brotherhood.

narrative_blocks.header: He would not have charity be condescension
narrative_blocks.body: At the Boston Seaman's Friend Society centennial in 1927 he described the old societies for the moral improvement of the poor, which had expected subservience in return. A finer democracy had come, he said, and no Christian now goes out to elevate his fellow man.

narrative_blocks.header: Bowdoin made him a doctor for wartime preaching
narrative_blocks.body: He held the State Street Congregational Church at Portland through the war and served in YMCA camps at home and abroad. Bowdoin gave him an honorary doctorate in 1918, citing an eloquent preacher of Christian duty.

narrative_blocks.body: His father gave him a saxophone at fourteen and he played it through Exeter and Yale. When he asked to sit in with the boys' band in the 1940s, the headmaster said well, if he wanted to do that kind of thing. So he did not.

narrative_blocks.header: He coached hockey before there was a rink
narrative_blocks.body: He had the varsity team from 1945 to 1950, when they played on Rabbit Pond and any other ice they could find. Most of the time, he said, went on shovelling snow or falling through it.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty-three years, and a chamber music series
narrative_blocks.body: He was married to Carol for sixty-three years; she loved classical music and he dragged her to smoky clubs to hear Ella Fitzgerald. Near eighty he took up the flute, and his teacher founded the Andover Chamber Music Series.

Obituary, 18 Aug 1920: 'Dr Wesselhoeft Dies at Sandwich — Cambridge Physician Well-Known Homeopath.' Died at his summer residence on Shawnee Hill, Sandwich. Son of Dr Robert Wesselhoeft, who brought the family to Boston in 1840 and founded the Water Cure at Brattleboro, Vermont. Harvard MD 1859; practised at Halifax, Nova Scotia, moving to Cambridge in 1873. Professor of clinical medicine at Boston University Medical School, emeritus from 1909. Visiting then consulting physician and trustee of the Massachusetts Homeopathic Hospital; active in the state and national homeopathic societies, working to reconcile the two schools of practice. MARRIAGE CONFLICT: FindAGrave dates his marriage to Mary A. Leavitt 7 Jun 1894, but the obituary says his first wife Mary Fraser of Halifax died in 1896. His seven children were all Mary Fraser's: Mrs Willard Reed, Mrs Ralph Hoffmann, Mary F. Wesselhoeft, Mrs Robert von Erdberg, Mrs Eleanor Hutchison, Robert Wesselhoeft of New York, Dr Conrad Wesselhoeft of Boston. SECOND OBITUARY TRANSCRIPT RESOLVES THE MARRIAGE CONFLICT: Mary Fraser died in 1886, not 1896, so the 1894 remarriage to Mary A. Leavitt stands. Parents Robert and Ferdinanda Emilia Wesselhoeft; paternal grandfather a publisher, maternal grandfather a clergyman. Uncle Dr William Wesselhoeft (1794-1858), who helped Constantine Hering found the nation's first homeopathic school at Allentown, Pennsylvania in 1835. Practised on Mt Auburn Street near Brattle Square, then the corner of Prescott and Harvard Streets, then Garden Street until he retired. Member of the American Institute of Homoeopathy, the Massachusetts and Boston Homoeopathic Medical Societies, corresponding member of the British and Mexican homoeopathic societies, the Massachusetts Reform Club and the Hughes Medical Club. BURIAL CONFLICT: the obituary says he was cremated and the remains buried in the family lot at Cambridge Cemetery; FindAGrave places him at Mount Auburn, which is what is recorded here.

narrative_blocks.header: A homeopath who called himself a mugwump
narrative_blocks.body: Walter held office in the state and national homeopathic societies and corresponded for the British and Mexican ones. On whether homeopathy beat regular medicine he called himself a mugwump, and pressed for understanding between the two.

narrative_blocks.header: Four duels, then Harvard Medical School
narrative_blocks.body: As a student in Germany Walter fought four duels, and his family brought him home to Boston, where he took his Harvard medical degree in 1859. Medicine was never his own choice, he wrote; he was simply destined for it.

narrative_blocks.header: Halifax never quite took to him
narrative_blocks.body: Walter practised at Halifax, Nova Scotia, from 1860. Society there welcomed him and the practice grew, but the other doctors never accepted an American, a Union man and a homeopath.

narrative_blocks.header: Turned away by the German army in 1870
narrative_blocks.body: In 1870 Walter went back to Germany to offer the German army his services as a surgeon. No place was open, so he spent two years in the clinics: Koelliker and von Recklinghausen at Würzburg, Simon and Becker at Heidelberg, Braun at Vienna.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty years a Cambridge physician, and a banquet
narrative_blocks.body: Walter practised in Cambridge from 1873, from Mount Auburn Street to Garden Street. In 1909 his colleagues gave him a dinner at the Hotel Somerset for fifty years of practice, and he went emeritus at Boston University.

narrative_blocks.header: The Wesselhoefts were homeopathy's Boston dynasty
narrative_blocks.body: Homeopathy's answer to the Warrens and Shattucks was the Wesselhoefts. Walter's father Robert founded the Brattleboro water cure, his uncle William helped found the Allentown school; Walter, a brother and two cousins were Harvard doctors.

narrative_blocks.header: William Dean Howells was his patient
narrative_blocks.body: William James and William Dean Howells were Walter's friends, Howells his patient for years. His daughter Amy saw callers lean toward him “as if they wanted to warm their old selves at anything so beautiful and sunshining as Father was.”

Paul attended the George Putnam Grammar School in Roxbury and the Boston Latin School. Pi Eta Society, Cercle Français, Mandolin Club; an accomplished pianist who travelled widely in Europe. Son of Elijah Gridley Strong and Sarah Ashley Partridge. Chronicled in John Sedgwick, From the River to the Sea: The Untold Story of the Railroad War that Made the West. Obituary, Los Angeles, 3 Aug 1914. Barstow, California was Waterman Junction until 15 Jan 1886.

bio.bio_blurb: Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe Railway president

narrative_blocks.header: Grow or Die: a war for the West
narrative_blocks.body: He took the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe presidency in July 1881 and ran it on Grow or Die, fighting Palmer's Denver and Rio Grande for the western passes. Eight thousand miles of track went down under him; by 1889 it was the largest railroad in North America.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother let him into the telegraph office
narrative_blocks.body: James, his older brother, ran the railway telegraph office and let him in to help. He left Bell's Business College for the station agent's job at Milton, Wisconsin in 1855, climbed through five railroads, and the Santa Fe made him vice-president a month after hiring him.

narrative_blocks.header: Three towns, a rail car, a comet chaser
narrative_blocks.body: Waterman Junction renamed itself Barstow in January 1886 for his middle name, where the Santa Fe put its shops; Strong City in Kansas and Stronghurst in Illinois carry the other half. A Santa Fe observation car took his name, and so did NASA's Stardust in 2004.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought a hill so Brownington could see
narrative_blocks.body: He came back to Brownington in his private car in 1889, the year he retired, bought Prospect Hill and put the first observatory on it, opening the view from Willoughby Gap to Jay Peak and the White Mountains. He gave the church its steeple for his grandparents.

narrative_blocks.header: The biggest man in railroading, then forgotten
narrative_blocks.body: He died at Los Angeles in August 1914, seventy-seven and twenty-five years off the railroad. The once most powerful man in American railroading has all but faded from memory — except in Orleans County, Vermont, where the family is still local history.

narrative_blocks.header: A sheriff's three sons, all of them somebody
narrative_blocks.body: His father Elijah Gridley Strong, Orleans County's high sheriff and a Vermont legislator, moved them to Beloit in 1851 for a temperance hotel. Brother Henry was five times mayor there; brother James became Carleton College's first president. All three schooled under Alexander Twilight.

narrative_blocks.body: Her parents, Holland and Marala Moore, were among the first white settlers at Beloit, and she was the first girl born to the New England company that founded the town. There were few whites anywhere in southern Wisconsin in 1838.

Born at Hammersmith Farm. BIRTH DATE CONFLICT, three readings: FindAGrave 28 Aug 1897 (used here), the Wikipedia infobox 29 Aug 1897, and Wikipedia's own opening line 15 Aug 1897. Son of Hugh Dudley Auchincloss (1858-1913) and Emma Brewster Jennings. Also studied at King's College, Cambridge. Clubs: University, New York Yacht, Grolier, Racquet and Tennis, Burning Tree, Metropolitan. Son of Hugh Dudley Auchincloss (1858-1913), merchant and financier, and Emma Brewster Jennings; maternal grandparents Oliver Burr Jennings and Esther Judson Goodsell. Elihu Senior Society at Yale. Navy service in the First World War interrupted his degree. In 1975 his Washington colleagues gave him a citation saying they had 'had their lives enriched by his high standards, a code of ethics and excellence.' THE AUCHINCLOSS LINE, from the material supplied 081226: great-grandfather Hugh Auchincloss (1780-1855), born at Paisley to a dry goods merchant, in New York from 1803, married Ann Stuart of Philadelphia, lived at 14 Gold Street and then at Pearl and Pine, president of the American Wholesale Dry Goods Association; his sons Hugh Jr. and John carried the business on as Auchincloss Brothers. The grandfather in between is not named in the material — born at New York, director of the Merchant's Bank, trustee of the Equitable Life Assurance Society, married Elizabeth Buck, six sons and two daughters, lived at 11 West 57th Street with a Newport cottage, died at Quebec leaving the oldest dry goods house in New York under continuous management. Father Hugh Dudley Auchincloss Sr. (1858-1913): born at Newport, Yale, cotton buying at Savannah, partner in Auchincloss Brothers from 1882 (US agents for J. & P. Coats of Paisley), later mining, manufacturing, transportation and banking — president of the Port Inglis Terminal Company, treasurer of the Dunnellon Phosphate Company, trustee of the Bowery Savings Bank. HAMMERSMITH FARM was built in 1887 for his uncle John Winthrop Auchincloss (1853-1938) and sold to his father in 1897; Emma Jennings had the Olmsted Brothers landscape it that year.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought his Exchange seat in 1931
narrative_blocks.body: He quit government service in 1931, bought a seat on the New York Stock Exchange and founded the Washington brokerage of Auchincloss, Parker & Redpath. It grew to sixteen offices along the East Coast before merging into Thomson & McKinnon in 1970.

narrative_blocks.header: A Republican who paid for Kennedy's campaign
narrative_blocks.body: He got Jacqueline Bouvier her first job, at the Washington Times-Herald, and gave her away at her wedding in 1953. A lifelong Republican donor, he gave to his Democratic stepson-in-law's campaign too, explaining that he wanted "to live in harmony with Mrs. Auchincloss and all the other members of the family."

narrative_blocks.header: Four generations of Scottish merchants before him
narrative_blocks.body: The Auchinclosses had been in New York since 1803, when his great-grandfather arrived from Scotland with cloth to sell. Ordered inland in the War of 1812 because he was a British subject, he put his stock on a wagon, traded on the road, and came home richer. Their firm bought Hammersmith Farm, the Newport estate where he grew up.

narrative_blocks.header: Three wives, and two of them famous mothers
narrative_blocks.body: His second wife was Nina Gore, mother of the writer Gore Vidal; his third was Janet Lee Bouvier, mother of Jacqueline and Lee. Five children came of the three marriages, and the novelist Louis Auchincloss was a cousin on his father's side.

narrative_blocks.header: Three hunter titles at the National Horse Show
narrative_blocks.body: She took the hunter championship at the National Horse Show three separate times. A 1932 portrait of her astride her horse Danseuse still hung over the fireplace of her Georgetown drawing room half a century later.

narrative_blocks.header: She claimed the Maryland Lees as kin
narrative_blocks.body: Her father James T. Lee was a New York lawyer and property developer, and both her parents were of Irish Catholic descent. She made varying claims about her ancestry all the same, among them that she came from the Maryland Lees.

narrative_blocks.header: Newport's oldest institutions took her on
narrative_blocks.body: She sat on the boards of the Newport Historical Society and the Redwood Library, and was honorary director of the Robert E. Lee Memorial Association at Stratford in Virginia.

narrative_blocks.header: Alzheimer's took her at Hammersmith Farm
narrative_blocks.body: She died at Hammersmith Farm on 22 July 1989 of complications of Alzheimer's disease, with both daughters at the bedside. It was six days before Jacqueline's sixtieth birthday.

narrative_blocks.header: Three marriages, and a bridesmaid who came back
narrative_blocks.body: She married Black Jack Bouvier in 1928, Hugh Auchincloss in 1942 and, at seventy-one, her childhood friend Bingham Morris. Morris's late wife Mary had been a bridesmaid at that first wedding, fifty-one years before.

people.research_notes: Known as Black Jack. Father of Jacqueline Bouvier Kennedy Onassis and Caroline Lee Bouvier Radziwill by this marriage. Eldest of five children of Major John Vernou Bouvier Jr. (1865-1948) and Maude Frances Sergeant (1870-1940). His sister Edith Ewing Bouvier Beale and her daughter Edith are not built as entries. Book and Snake and the Cloister Club at Yale; varsity tennis. Hereditary member of the Maryland Society of the Cincinnati, 1940. A 1920 engagement to Eleanor Carroll Daingerfield Carter of Baltimore was called off. Lived at 125 East 74th Street; never remarried.

cross_connections.display_label: met Joseph Bonaparte at the American minister's house in Paris

landmarks.landmark_blurb: His father's summer estate, where the Bouviers kept their horses

narrative_blocks.header: Black Jack was the tan, not the cards
narrative_blocks.body: The name came from an omnipresent dark tan and a flamboyant way of living. He went from Yale into his father and uncle's firm, Bouvier, Bouvier & Bouvier, in 1914, and the crash of 1929 hit him hard enough that he never fully recovered.

narrative_blocks.header: Wall Street to the Army Air Service
narrative_blocks.body: He joined the Navy in 1917, transferred to the Army and rose to major in the Army Air Service before his discharge in 1919. He went straight back to broking on a Wall Street that suited his tastes.

narrative_blocks.header: Too drunk to walk Jackie down the aisle
narrative_blocks.body: On the morning of his daughter's wedding to Senator Kennedy in September 1953 he began drinking at his hotel, and by the time he was due at the church he could not perform. He was kept from the ceremony and her stepfather Hugh Auchincloss gave her away.

narrative_blocks.header: Liver cancer, a coma, and St. Patrick's
narrative_blocks.body: Terminal liver cancer was found in the spring of 1957. He checked into Lenox Hill on 27 July, fell into a coma on 1 August and died two days later at sixty-six; his daughters arranged the funeral at St. Patrick's Cathedral.

narrative_blocks.header: A cabinetmaker's fortune, four generations on
narrative_blocks.body: His great-grandfather Michel Bouvier left France in 1815, made furniture in Philadelphia for Joseph Bonaparte and Stephen Girard, and turned the proceeds into real estate. The money came down to his father, who bought Lasata at East Hampton. His brother Bud drank himself to death at thirty-six.

people.research_notes: Raised by wealthy parents in Philadelphia. Son of John Boucher Morris of Baltimore and Violet Lee (nee Willing) Morris, who was born in Belgium and raised in Philadelphia; he described himself as half Irish. Iroquois and Hasty Pudding Clubs at Harvard. 'Booch' came from his father's middle name and his brother John Bucher Morris IV carried it too. BURIAL CONFLICT: FindAGrave gives Westbury Friends Cemetery (used here); FamilySearch gives Roslyn Cemetery, both in Nassau County. END OF MARRIAGE: Wikipedia says they separated in 1981 but remained married until her death; a local account says she divorced him in 1981.

narrative_blocks.header: Straw hats and overalls on a banker
narrative_blocks.body: An investment banker who went about in straw hats, overalls and T-shirts, and who had sailed round the world before he married again. Cleaned up he was six feet and good-looking, brown hair and brown eyes; everyone called him Booch, after his father's middle name.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty years between meeting her and marrying her
narrative_blocks.body: She was thirteen when they met, and they went about together while he was at St George's in Newport. Sixty years later, in October 1979, he married her at Newport with Jacqueline standing as her mother's witness — to the dismay of the rest of Janet's family.

narrative_blocks.header: A Republican who could not abide the Kennedys
narrative_blocks.body: He was a dyed-in-the-wool Republican who disliked the Kennedys and said so without much care for the company. It set him at odds with his new stepdaughter from the start.

narrative_blocks.header: His first wife was a bridesmaid at hers
narrative_blocks.body: He married Mary Rawlins in July 1934, in the depth of the Depression, and they had no children; she died in 1978. Mary had been a bridesmaid at Janet's first wedding, to Black Jack Bouvier, forty-four years before.

people.research_notes: A Russian noblewoman. Married Hugh D. Auchincloss Jr. 4 Jun 1925 in New York City; divorced 1932. Their son was Hugh Dudley 'Yusha' Auchincloss III (1927-2015), who is not built as an entry. DEATH DATE CONFLICT: FindAGrave 3 Jan 1990 (used here, 'aged 90'); FamilySearch 3 Jun 1990. MARRIAGE DATE CONFLICT: the 1932 New York Times report says 5 Jun 1925, Wikipedia says 4 Jun 1925. Her father's death: FindAGrave places him at Tsushima aboard the Alexander III, 27 May 1905; the Times obituary of 1932 says Port Arthur — Tsushima matches the date and the ship. Later married Elbridge Dexter Rand. Also recorded as Mata De Charpovitski in the 1928 wire story.

bio.bio_blurb: Russian and Far East relief worker

narrative_blocks.header: She worked for Russian and Far East relief
narrative_blocks.body: She came out of a Russian noble family that fled to the United States during the revolution, and took an active part in Russian and Far East relief. The papers of the day placed her in Washington, New York, Newport and Palm Beach.

narrative_blocks.header: She married in a Russian cathedral
narrative_blocks.body: She married Hugh D. Auchincloss Jr. in June 1925 at the Russian Cathedral on East Ninety-seventh Street, by the ritual of the Russian church. In 1932 she took a bungalow in Reno for the six weeks' residence a divorce required, and charged incompatibility.

narrative_blocks.header: A Sikorsky's propeller fractured her skull
narrative_blocks.body: On 15 July 1928 she stepped out of a Sikorsky at the Naval Air Station after a flight over Washington and was struck on the head by the propeller. Her skull was fractured and a transfusion was needed; for a time her life was despaired of.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father went down at Tsushima
narrative_blocks.body: Count Nicolas de Chrapovitsky of the Russian navy was lost on 27 May 1905 when the Alexander III went down at Tsushima, and his body was never recovered. She was five. Her mother later married Christopher Derfelden and brought her to New York.

Died of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. On Gallup's most-admired list twenty-seven times. [081226] Hickory Hill CC to Irene Alice Gerhardt Jackson added. narrative_blocks.header: She stopped presidents taking the furniture
narrative_blocks.body: Departing presidents had been carrying the furnishings off with them. She hired the first White House curator, founded its Historical Association and got a bill through Congress making the contents government property.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-six million watched her tour the house
narrative_blocks.body: On 14 February 1962 she walked American television through the restored house with Charles Collingwood of CBS. Fifty-six million watched, the film went to a hundred and six countries, and she won a special Emmy — the only First Lady ever to.

narrative_blocks.header: The pink suit she would not take off
narrative_blocks.body: She would not change out of the blood-stained Chanel suit, and stood in it beside Lyndon Johnson as he took the oath aboard Air Force One; she wanted them to see what they had done to Jack. It is sealed at the National Archives until 2103.

narrative_blocks.header: She talked Michael Jackson into Moonwalk
narrative_blocks.body: At Doubleday she persuaded Michael Jackson to write Moonwalk and wrote its foreword; it topped the bestseller list and sold a million. She had started at Viking in 1975.

narrative_blocks.header: She saved Grand Central from the wreckers
narrative_blocks.body: In the 1970s she led the campaign that saved Grand Central Terminal from demolition, and a plaque inside says so. She fought a Columbus Circle tower that would have shaded Central Park.

narrative_blocks.header: A one-day job at Vogue, then a newspaper
narrative_blocks.body: She beat several hundred women to a year at Vogue and quit after one day, on the managing editor's advice. She went home and became the Times-Herald's Inquiring Camera Girl, stopping strangers in the street for their pictures and opinions.

narrative_blocks.header: Marrying Onassis cost her the Secret Service
narrative_blocks.body: She married Aristotle Onassis on his island of Skorpios in October 1968, giving up the protection a president's widow is entitled to. The press took to calling her Jackie O.

narrative_blocks.header: She decorated for people never at home
narrative_blocks.body: She worked as an interior decorator in the manner of Lorenzo Mongiardino, who had done her London house and Turville Grange in Buckinghamshire — rooms Cecil Beaton and Horst photographed over and over. She once did a house, she said, for people who would not be there more than three days a year.

narrative_blocks.header: She hired the Maysles and got Grey Gardens
narrative_blocks.body: In 1972 she engaged Albert and David Maysles to film the Bouviers, and they began with her aunt and cousin, the two Edith Beales, in their decaying East Hampton house. Her project was shelved and she kept the footage; the brothers went back on their own money and made Grey Gardens.

narrative_blocks.header: Best-dressed lists kept her for sixty years
narrative_blocks.body: The society editors made her New York's leading debutante of 1950 and Life ran her full-page at Christmas. She entered the Vanity Fair International Best Dressed Hall of Fame in 1996, and the Guardian still had her among the fifty best-dressed over fifty in 2013.

narrative_blocks.header: Her Tracy Lord in Chicago was much criticised
narrative_blocks.body: She tried acting in the sixties — Tracy Lord in The Philadelphia Story at the Ivanhoe in Chicago in 1967, then a television Laura the year after. Both were heavily publicised and both were badly reviewed.

narrative_blocks.header: She introduced her sister to Onassis
narrative_blocks.body: She had grown close to Aristotle Onassis while Jackie was in the White House, and it was she who brought them together; asked later whether she had thought of marrying him herself, she said, "Who didn't?" When Jackie died in 1994 she left keepsakes to Lee's children and nothing to Lee.

narrative_blocks.header: He towed a burned man by his teeth
narrative_blocks.body: When a Japanese destroyer cut PT-109 in half off the Solomons in August 1943, he swam three miles to an island towing a badly burned crewman by a lifejacket strap held in his teeth. He carved a message into a coconut shell and handed it to islanders; the crew came off seven days later.

narrative_blocks.header: A mosquito that bit him took a risk
narrative_blocks.body: He had whooping cough, measles, chicken pox, scarlet fever at two, colitis, a ruptured spinal disc at Harvard, and Addison's disease found at thirty. The family joke was that a mosquito that bit him was almost sure to die of the blood.

narrative_blocks.header: Two books, one written from a hospital bed
narrative_blocks.body: His Harvard thesis on Britain's unreadiness for war became Why England Slept, a bestseller at twenty-three. Convalescing from spinal surgery in 1956 he wrote Profiles in Courage, on senators who risked their careers for their beliefs; it took the Pulitzer.

narrative_blocks.header: The second son, never meant to run
narrative_blocks.body: Joe Jr. was the one groomed for the presidency, and had announced as a boy that he would be the first Catholic to hold it. When his brother's plane blew up over Europe in 1944 the family turned to Jack, who had been thinking of teaching or writing.

narrative_blocks.header: Fourteen years in Congress first
narrative_blocks.body: He took a working-class Boston seat in 1947 and held it three terms, then beat Henry Cabot Lodge Jr. for the Senate in 1952 and was returned in 1958 by the largest margin in Massachusetts history. He called the Senate the most corrupting job in the world.

narrative_blocks.header: Ask not — and the thousand days after
narrative_blocks.body: The youngest man elected president, and the first Catholic. In a thousand days he faced down the missiles in Cuba, signed the first nuclear test-ban treaty, started the Peace Corps and set the country on course for the Moon. He was shot at Dallas in November 1963, forty-six years old.

narrative_blocks.header: A king thought he was a prince's son
narrative_blocks.body: He was born Anthony Kerslake and adopted as an infant by Cass Canfield, who ran Harper & Brothers for four decades and published John F. Kennedy's Profiles in Courage. By the memoirs of the Duchess of Westminster, Edward VIII believed him the natural son of his brother, the Duke of Kent.

narrative_blocks.header: A Marine at Iwo Jima, then Harvard
narrative_blocks.body: He left the Brooks School for the United States Marine Corps and was wounded at Iwo Jima. He came home to Harvard and took his degree in 1951.

narrative_blocks.header: Bag-carrier to two ambassadors, then Harper's
narrative_blocks.body: In London he was aide to Winthrop Aldrich and secretary to John Hay Whitney, successive American ambassadors to the Court of St James under Eisenhower. He stayed on as the London editorial representative of Harper & Row, where his father was the publisher.

narrative_blocks.header: The countess who married a duke after him
narrative_blocks.body: In June 1960 he married Laura Charteris, Countess of Dudley, twice divorced already and a sister of Ian Fleming's wife Ann. After his death she married the tenth Duke of Marlborough, her fourth husband.

narrative_blocks.header: A heart attack over the Atlantic at 43
narrative_blocks.body: He died on 20 December 1969 of a heart attack aboard a BOAC flight from New York to London. He was forty-three, and had been divorced from Lee Bouvier for eleven years.

narrative_blocks.header: Prince of a title Poland had abolished
narrative_blocks.body: The Radziwiłłs had been Princes of the Holy Roman Empire since the early sixteenth century, but the Polish republic abolished noble titles in 1921 and left the family pretenders to their own name. In Britain he was called Prince Radziwiłł regardless, though Debrett's held that a British subject needed the Queen's leave to use it.

narrative_blocks.header: From the Polish Red Cross to Olympic Airways
narrative_blocks.body: He was chargé d'affaires for the Polish government in exile at the League of Nations and a delegate of the Polish Red Cross, then a property dealer in London and a director of Olympic Airways.

narrative_blocks.header: St Anne's at Fawley Court, built for exiles
narrative_blocks.body: He helped organise the Sikorski Historical Institute in London and founded St Anne's Church at Fawley Court, beside the school the Marian Fathers ran near Henley-on-Thames for boys of Polish descent.

narrative_blocks.header: Sold out of Fawley Court, moved to Warsaw
narrative_blocks.body: He was buried in the crypt of St Anne's at Fawley Court in 1976. When that property was sold his remains were taken to Warsaw and laid in the Radziwiłł crypt at Cmentarz Wilanowski.

narrative_blocks.header: A mother lost in a Soviet labour camp
narrative_blocks.body: His parents were Prince Janusz Franciszek Radziwiłł and Princess Anna Lubomirska, and he was the youngest of three brothers. The war scattered them out of Poland and his mother died a prisoner in a Soviet camp.

burial.plot_notes: Radziwill family crypt; first interred at St Anne's, Fawley Court.

people.research_notes: Married the ballerina Nora Kaye in 1959; she died in 1987 and he was interred with her at Westwood Village Memorial Park. Stage debut 1942 as Third Witch in a touring Macbeth.

narrative_blocks.header: He directed Footloose and Steel Magnolias
narrative_blocks.body: He directed The Owl and the Pussycat, Play It Again Sam, The Goodbye Girl, California Suite, Footloose and Steel Magnolias. For The Turning Point in 1977 he was nominated for best picture and best director, and won the Golden Globe.

narrative_blocks.header: He choreographed Streisand onto Broadway
narrative_blocks.body: He came up a dancer and then a choreographer, working with Barbra Streisand, Stephen Sondheim, Richard Rodgers and Arthur Laurents. A Tree Grows in Brooklyn was his first Broadway show as choreographer in 1951, and Anyone Can Whistle brought a Tony nomination in 1964.

narrative_blocks.header: A postal clerk's son who quit school
narrative_blocks.body: His parents were Russian-Jewish immigrants in Brooklyn; his father was a postal clerk and his mother died when he was nine, after which the family went to Miami to run a luncheonette. He dropped out of high school and came back to New York to act.

narrative_blocks.header: A senator's daughter from Lawton, Oklahoma
narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Lawton in 1903 to the United States senator Thomas Pryor Gore and Nina Belle Kay. The Gores had come down from Maryland before the Revolution through the Carolinas into Mississippi, where they founded a farmers' party that spread across the South.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son wrote Ben-Hur and Myra Breckinridge
narrative_blocks.body: Her son by Eugene Vidal was the novelist and screenwriter Gore Vidal, who scripted Ben-Hur and Suddenly, Last Summer, wrote The City and the Pillar and Burr, and spent years in Italy acting for Fellini. He was born Eugene Luther Gore Vidal and kept only the part that came from her father.

narrative_blocks.header: Three husbands: Vidal, Auchincloss, Olds
narrative_blocks.body: She married the Roosevelt aviation appointee Eugene Vidal, then in 1935 the stockbroker Hugh D. Auchincloss Jr., and afterwards a third husband named Olds. The Auchincloss marriage ended in divorce in 1941 and had produced two children.

Born at Karatas, a suburb of Smyrna, to Socrates Onassis and Penelope Dologlou; sister Artemis and two half-sisters, Kalliroi and Merope. CITIZENSHIP: Argentine citizenship 1929 per Wikipedia, 1925 per another account; Greek consul general in Buenos Aires and trade negotiator from 1928. Left off the card for room: the 1954 US prosecution over the citizenship provisions of the shipping laws, the SS Arrow grounding and oil spill in Chedabucto Bay in 1970, Project Omega with the Greek junta, the Olympic Tower in Manhattan, and the yacht Christina O.

narrative_blocks.header: One tanker in 1938, seventeen in 1954
narrative_blocks.body: He had the 15,000-ton Ariston built in 1938, the largest tanker in the world and the model for every supertanker after it. In 1954 he ordered seventeen more, and when Suez closed his fleet carried oil the long way round the Cape.

narrative_blocks.header: A refugee passport and a night switchboard
narrative_blocks.body: The Great Fire of Smyrna in 1922 cost the family its property, his father his liberty, and three uncles and an aunt their lives. He reached Buenos Aires the next year at seventeen, on a Nansen passport, with four languages and a job on a night switchboard.

narrative_blocks.header: Peru sent bombers after his whaling fleet
narrative_blocks.body: From 1950 his factory ship Olympic Challenger worked the South American coast, taking whales of any size or season. In 1954 Peru sent warships and aircraft after them, bombed the water around the factory ship, and interned most of the fleet.

narrative_blocks.header: Monte Carlo was his, and then it wasn't
narrative_blocks.body: In 1953 he took control of the company that owned Monte Carlo's casino and a third of Monaco's land. Prince Rainier wanted hotels and tourists; in 1966 he created six hundred thousand new shares that cut Onassis below a third and out of the country.

narrative_blocks.header: The logo has six Olympic rings, not five
narrative_blocks.body: Granted the Greek air transport rights in 1956, he could not use the five Olympic rings in his logo and added a sixth. A director of the airline said he was married to the sea, but Olympic was his mistress.

narrative_blocks.header: A plane crash in 1973 finished him too
narrative_blocks.body: His son Alexander was killed in a plane crash in 1973 and he never recovered. Weakened by myasthenia gravis, he died in March 1975 of pneumonia after gall bladder surgery, and was buried on Skorpios beside Alexander and his sister Artemis.

narrative_blocks.body: He died at New Haven on 10 May 1821, a junior at Yale, eighteen years old. A sister published a memoir of him the next year, her name given on the title page only as 'a sister'; his father resigned both judgeships and never recovered.

narrative_blocks.header: New York's military censor in the Cuban war
narrative_blocks.body: In April 1898 the army took control of the cable and telephone systems running out of New York, and in June he was made United States Military Censor there. His work was to keep the correspondents' dispatches from the Cuban war out of print.

narrative_blocks.header: There are keener pleasures, he wrote
narrative_blocks.body: Writing in the Atlantic Monthly the next spring, he allowed that there are keener pleasures than editing the sensational, if not always truthful, narratives the correspondents sent from their perilous positions. He later helped Herbert Hoover with Belgian relief.

narrative_blocks.body: Samuel King painted her in 1771, the same year he painted her husband. The portrait came to the Yale University Art Gallery generations later as a bequest from Dr. Charles Jenkins Foote, a New Haven physician descended from her through four generations of women.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father cut lines from the wedding poem
narrative_blocks.body: She married Ezra Stiles at New Haven on 10 February 1757. Her husband's father wrote a poem for the occasion and sent it to her father, who thought three or four of its lines unfit for his daughter to see and advised that they be suppressed.

bio.bio_blurb: New Haven physician, judge and versifier

narrative_blocks.header: Eighty-three Yale students poisoned at breakfast
narrative_blocks.body: In April 1764 he wrote that eighty-three students had been seized with vomiting, thirst and spasms after breakfast, and that the physicians guessed arsenic in the cake. Suspicion fell on the Acadians living in New Haven, and no inquiry was ever made.

narrative_blocks.header: Commissary to the Crown Point expedition
narrative_blocks.body: He went into the French and Indian War as a major, serving as commissary for the Crown Point expedition from March 1755, and was made lieutenant-colonel of the Second Connecticut Militia in October 1757.

narrative_blocks.header: Drafted onto the Stamp Act committee
narrative_blocks.body: In May 1764 the Connecticut Assembly resolved to argue against a stamp duty in Parliament, and named him to the committee that was to collect the arguments. He protested that the talent did not lie that way, and wrote to his son-in-law for help.

narrative_blocks.header: A hymn for thirty loads of firewood
narrative_blocks.body: He was much addicted to poetical composition. When the people of New Haven carted about thirty loads of wood to Rev. Chauncey Whittelsey, he wrote them a Wood-Carting Hymn to be sung annually at the minister's fireside.

narrative_blocks.header: Physician, colonel and judge of probate
narrative_blocks.body: He came from Long Island to New Haven, practised medicine there, held a colonel's commission in the militia, sat for the town in the General Court, and was judge of the probate district from 1748 until he died. Yale gave him a master's degree in 1730.

narrative_blocks.header: His son Leverett led Connecticut's doctors
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth married Ezra Stiles in 1757. Her eldest brother, Col. Leverett Hubbard, took the Yale degree in 1744, commanded the second regiment of militia, and became first president of both the New Haven County and the Connecticut State medical societies.

people.research_notes: Born at Jamaica on Long Island. Honorary M.A., Yale, 1730. Letters to his son-in-law Ezra Stiles, 1757-1766, supplied 081226.

bio.bio_blurb: Mother of six, of New Haven

narrative_blocks.header: She died at forty-one; he married twice more
narrative_blocks.body: She died at New Haven in August 1744, in her forty-second year, and lies at Grove Street under a stone that names her the consort of Capt. John Hubbard. He married twice more, and outlived her by twenty-nine years.

narrative_blocks.header: Two sons of hers were named William Abdiel
narrative_blocks.body: She bore six children at New Haven. The fifth, William Abdiel, died small, and she gave the same name to the sixth four years later; her eldest, Leverett, became Connecticut's leading physician, and her daughter Elizabeth married Ezra Stiles.

people.research_notes: Gravestone at Grove Street: 'Here lies ye Body of Mrs Elizabeth Hubbard late Consort of Capt. John Hubbard died August ye 25th 1744 in ye 42 Year of her age.' Six children by him: Leverett (1725), John (1727), Daniel (1729), Elizabeth (1731), and two sons both called William Abdiel (1733, died young; 1737-1772).

narrative_blocks.header: Her father enlisted at fifteen
narrative_blocks.body: Calvin Munn went into the army in 1777 at fifteen and stayed to the end — the taking of Burgoyne, Rhode Island with Sullivan, the southern infantry with Lafayette, and Cornwallis's surrender at Yorktown. He drilled the recruits of the 4th Massachusetts, and kept an inn.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Put up by the men he worked with

narrative_blocks.header: Chairmaker, hatter, then the police beat
narrative_blocks.body: He made chairs, sold hats at Lowell, and served a short apprenticeship on the Eagle before going into the Boston Journal office in August 1848. He stayed nearly a quarter of a century, and was called the oldest reporter for the press in the city.

narrative_blocks.header: The night desk, then Young's Hotel
narrative_blocks.body: He left the Journal office near midnight and sat chatting with the officers and the other reporters. In the morning the chambermaid at Young's Hotel heard him say he would not get up yet awhile; a fellow reporter found him on the floor.

narrative_blocks.header: His colleagues paid for his headstone
narrative_blocks.body: He gave nearly thirty years to the Boston newspapers. The stone over him at Greenfield was put there by the men he worked with, and calls him a true friend and an honest man.

people.research_notes: Never married. His mother Nancy, then eighty-three and living at Roxbury, had asked to be told at once if he were taken ill; she was sent for, and the obituary says she 'held up bravely, but at his death her feelings overcame her'. A slight shock of apoplexy three months before, another at Christmas, and a fall on the ice ten days before the end. Funeral at the Berkeley Street church. His brother Thomas H. Leavitt was in Iowa at the time. Obituary read 081226 from the image supplied.

narrative_blocks.header: He wanted the country to burn peat
narrative_blocks.body: After the Civil War, with fuel scarce, he became the leading voice for peat. His Facts About Peat as an Article of Fuel, 1865, told businessmen where the peat under their towns lay and how to get it out; he revised it as the idea spread.

narrative_blocks.header: Coal and the railroads beat him
narrative_blocks.body: Cheap coal moved by rail answered the fuel question instead, and the peat movement died. When the coal strike of 1902 brought on a fuel panic he was almost the only man of the old movement still arguing, and brought out a new edition in 1904.

narrative_blocks.header: Selling the Nebraska prairie by rail
narrative_blocks.body: After the divorce he went west and became secretary of the land department of the Burlington and Missouri River Railroad, which was selling the Nebraska prairie. He married twice at Lincoln, and the Chautauqua circle there turned a meeting into a reception for his bride.

people.research_notes: SPOUSES SUPPLIED 081226, NOT BUILT — ask Sam: Mary Greenleaf Clement (1830-1912, m. 1857), Helen Agnes Roessig (1858-1884, m. 1881), Lura Eugenia Newhall (1842-1924, m. 1885). FROM THE NEWSPAPERS SUPPLIED, read 081226: the Burlington Hawkeye reported his 1881 marriage to Helen Roessig at her mother's house on South Hill, Burlington, Iowa, calling him secretary of the B & M land department and a resident of Lincoln. The Lincoln Daily News of 23 January 1886 described the Chautauqua Literary and Scientific Circle merging its meeting at the state house into a reception for the new Mrs. Leavitt, with 'The Chautauqua 20 Question Game' at the end. A later Lincoln notice records a farewell reception for the Leavitts at the First Congregational church, about a hundred members present, an etching presented, and Fred Shepherd speaking of the city's regret at losing them — they left that week for Boston. Full title of the 1865 book: 'Facts about peat as an article of fuel, with remarks upon its origin and composition; the various products obtained from it by distillation; the use of peat in the manufacture of gun-powder and paper, and for pavements, roofing tiles, and various articles for building and ornamental work'.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight years abroad, forty-three countries
narrative_blocks.body: She sailed from San Francisco in November 1884 almost penniless and did not see Boston again for eight years: a hundred thousand miles, forty-three countries, sixteen hundred meetings, interpreters in forty-seven languages.

narrative_blocks.header: A petition on a hundred rolls of canvas
narrative_blocks.body: She carried the Polyglot Petition round the world, asking every government to strip the drink and opium trades of legal protection. Signatures from six continents filled nearly a hundred rolls of canvas.

narrative_blocks.header: She ran her own school on Warren Avenue
narrative_blocks.body: She left the Boston grammar schools in 1867 for a school of her own and kept it fourteen years: sixty-five pupils, four languages and drawing, and herself teaching French, Latin and singing.

narrative_blocks.header: Eighty-six unions in countries she had never seen
narrative_blocks.body: She founded the WCTU in Honolulu with forty women in 1884, then in New Zealand, Australia, Japan, China, Burma, India, Ceylon, Madagascar and Natal: eighty-six unions and twenty-three men's societies.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven years without a face she knew
narrative_blocks.body: For seven of those years she met no one she had seen before. At the end she said the worth of it was not temperance but the fellowship it gave women in remote places.

narrative_blocks.header: The marriage ended after twenty-one years
narrative_blocks.body: She married Thomas Hooker Leavitt in 1857 and they had three daughters. He went out to Nebraska; they divorced in 1878, the year before she took the Boston union, and he married twice more.

narrative_blocks.header: A minister's house that kept no liquor
narrative_blocks.body: Her father, the Baptist minister Joshua Clement of Hopkinton, and her mother Eliza Harvey raised nine children in a house that kept no liquor and opposed slavery. She was the second.

people.research_notes: Daughter of the Baptist minister Rev. Joshua Clement and Eliza Harvey, second of nine children; her parents were teetotal and antislavery. Met Frances Willard in 1877, who described her as 'a notable New England type of calm, clear intellect, masterful will, true heart, and perfect self-control'. First superintendent of the National WCTU's Franchise Department, 1882. Spoke at the anti-lynching meeting at Chickering Hall, Boston, in 1899 alongside Julia Ward Howe. Fell out with the WCTU leadership at the end and resigned. Died at 18 Huntington Avenue, Boston. A reception for the new Mrs. Leavitt was reported in the Lincoln Daily News, 23 January 1886. Read 081226: the Lincoln Daily News reception notice says the Chautauqua circle 'vied to make the evening an enjoyable one' and that she 'gracefully acknowledged all congratulations and soon convinced all that Mr. L. had made a wise choice'. A later farewell reception at the First Congregational church marked the couple's departure for Boston.
Educated at her mother's Boston school; a translator and musician, and a graduate of the New England Conservatory of Music.

narrative_blocks.body: He was fifty-nine when the war began, too old to enlist, and served two years at the front with the United States Sanitary Commission instead — the civilian body that carried nursing, supplies and clean water to the Union camps.

narrative_blocks.body: No account of his working life survives, but the dates place him: born at Charlemont in 1834, his eldest son born in Iowa in 1861, himself dead at Minneapolis in 1909. His elder brother John had gone out to Waterloo, Iowa, as a banker in 1854.

narrative_blocks.body: He took his medical degree at Iowa in 1940, where his father chaired the School of Engineering, and spent the war as a major in a mobile army surgical hospital in the South Pacific. His orthopedic training came at Iowa and San Francisco after it.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-four years of Ventura County bones
narrative_blocks.body: He co-founded the Ventura Orthopaedic and Sports Medical Group and practised in the county for thirty-four years, a fellow of the American Academy of Orthopedic Surgeons.

narrative_blocks.header: The Ojai course record is still his
narrative_blocks.body: An avid fisherman, hunter and golfer, he played the Bing Crosby pro-am at Pebble Beach and was club champion many times over at Saticoy and at the Ojai Valley Inn, where the record of sixty-two on the original course is still his.

narrative_blocks.header: He romped with his girls a week before
narrative_blocks.body: He came home from a business trip on a Saturday evening in good spirits and romped with his two little girls in the yard. He fell ill the next evening, was rushed to hospital on the Monday for appendicitis, and died a week later at forty-three.

narrative_blocks.header: The foundry his father made, then land
narrative_blocks.body: He was schooled in Waterloo and went into his father's foundry and implement house, the leading firm of its kind in that part of the country. In his last years he turned to real estate and handled some of the largest deals in the city.

narrative_blocks.body: He was secretary of the American Peace Society for thirty-three years, to his death in 1870 — the whole middle of the century, with the Civil War inside it. He came to it after a decade of pulpits and lecture rooms.

narrative_blocks.body: He was ordained in 1827 and took the Congregational church at Lowell, and left it after two years. Every post he held afterwards was a teaching chair or a society desk.

notable.notable_blurb: Providence's leading still-life painter

narrative_blocks.header: The best still-life painter in Providence
narrative_blocks.body: He painted tabletop arrangements of fruit, flowers and dead game — well over a thousand canvases — for a middle class furnishing new houses. He first showed at the National Academy of Design in 1875 and came quickly into the front rank of New England painters.

narrative_blocks.header: He learned to draw in the Union navy
narrative_blocks.body: He enlisted at Boston at the outbreak of the war with his friend William Warren Flint of Walpole, and served in both branches of the Union service. He practised his drawing the whole time he was in.

narrative_blocks.header: He called painters dry goods merchants
narrative_blocks.body: Charles Walter Stetson despised the Fall River school and wrote so in his diary: 'Artists, they are not artists.' What stung was Leavitt's own line back to him — 'After all, Mr. Stetson, say what we may, we are only dry goods merchants in another line.'

narrative_blocks.header: He studied under a Group of 1855 man
narrative_blocks.body: Before that he was largely self-taught. His teacher was James Morgan Lewin, a Swansea landscape painter and one of the original Group of 1855 in Providence, and there is some evidence he also worked alongside Martin Johnson Heade.

narrative_blocks.header: His pictures hung in the Parker House
narrative_blocks.body: His still lifes decorated Boston's Parker House and the Narragansett Hotel in Providence, and he worked out of a studio in the Hoppin Homestead Building. Young painters came to him for tuition.

narrative_blocks.header: Three museums keep him, and almost nobody else
narrative_blocks.body: His work is at the Brandywine River Museum, the Cahoon Museum and the Cummer Museum, and Brandywine calls him Providence's most successful still-life painter of the nineteenth century. Outside of that he is largely forgotten.

cross_connections.display_label: deployed on the Forrestal to the Mediterranean in 1960

narrative_blocks.header: He refused to go home ahead of others
narrative_blocks.body: In mid-1968 the North Vietnamese offered to release him, because his father had just taken command of the whole theatre and it would have made a useful picture. He would not go before every man captured before him. The beatings started that August.

narrative_blocks.header: He signed, and said so ever after
narrative_blocks.body: After three days of beatings he signed an anti-American confession and carried the shame of it the rest of his life. He wrote that he had learned what everyone there learned — that every man has his breaking point, and he had reached his.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-five years, and two runs at it
narrative_blocks.body: He went to the House for Arizona in 1983 and to the Senate in 1987, and stayed until he died in office. He lost the 2000 nomination to George W. Bush and the 2008 election to Barack Obama.

narrative_blocks.header: He normalised relations with Vietnam in 1995
narrative_blocks.body: He sat on the Senate committee that investigated the POW and missing-in-action question, and helped bring the United States and Vietnam back to diplomatic relations in 1995. Some POW activists never forgave him for it.

narrative_blocks.header: A brain tumour, and then the deciding vote
narrative_blocks.body: Diagnosed with glioblastoma in 2017, he returned to the Senate floor and cast the deciding vote against the bill that would have partly repealed the Affordable Care Act. He died of the disease thirteen months later.

narrative_blocks.header: His father commanded that war
narrative_blocks.body: For four of his five and a half years in Hanoi his father was Commander-in-Chief, Pacific Command, directing every American force in the theatre. Each Christmas the admiral visited the troops nearest the DMZ and stood alone, looking north.

bio.bio_blurb: Reagan's White House Visitors Office director

narrative_blocks.header: She never told him about the crash
narrative_blocks.body: On Christmas Eve 1969 she was thrown from her car on an icy road near Gulph Mills and lay in the snow for hours. It cost her six months in hospital and twenty-three operations. Her husband was in Hanoi, and she kept it from him.

narrative_blocks.header: Her neighbours wore her husband's name
narrative_blocks.body: She raised three children at Orange Park in Florida through the five and a half years he was held, and worked in the prisoner-of-war movement. The people around her wore bracelets engraved with his name and the date he was taken.

narrative_blocks.header: She was four inches shorter when he returned
narrative_blocks.body: They were reunited in the March of 1973. She met him on crutches, four inches shorter than when he had left, and he was carrying his own injuries out of Hanoi.

narrative_blocks.header: She ran the White House visitors office
narrative_blocks.body: She came to the Reagans through Nancy Reagan's 1980 campaign and ran the visitors office from 1981 to 1987. She built the Easter Egg Roll into an extravaganza, with ten thousand signed eggs hidden for children to find.

narrative_blocks.header: A gentleman never would have called
narrative_blocks.body: An opponent of her former husband's rang her in 1982, looking for something damaging about the marriage. She would not discuss it, and told him a gentleman never would have called.

career.role: U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Agencies for Food and Agriculture

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-five medical missions in seven years
narrative_blocks.body: She founded the American Voluntary Medical Team in 1988 and led fifty-five missions over the next seven years — Kuwait five days after the Gulf War ended, Zaire for the Rwandan refugees, Bangladesh after the cyclone.

narrative_blocks.header: She told the reporters before they could
narrative_blocks.body: Two spinal operations left her on painkillers, and by the end she was taking twenty a day and having prescriptions written in her staff's names. Before prosecutors could make it public she gave the story to reporters herself.

narrative_blocks.header: She ran the world's food agency from 2023
narrative_blocks.body: She was ambassador to the United Nations food and agriculture agencies from 2021, then executive director of the World Food Programme from 2023 — years spent largely on Ukraine, and then on Gaza.

narrative_blocks.header: A Republican who endorsed the Democrat
narrative_blocks.body: She crossed party lines in 2020 to endorse Joe Biden for president. It was Biden who nominated her as an ambassador the year after.

narrative_blocks.header: She brought a baby back from Dhaka
narrative_blocks.body: At Mother Teresa's orphanage in Dhaka in 1991 she found two infants who needed treatment in America. She adopted one of them, Bridget, and arranged the other's adoption by a family friend.

career.organization: Martha Baird Rockefeller Fund for Music

narrative_blocks.header: She played at eight, and lost her mother
narrative_blocks.body: Her first public performance was in the June of 1903, playing In the Gypsies' Camp at the college where her mother taught piano and organ. Her mother was dead by the end of that year.

narrative_blocks.header: Albert Hall with Beecham, then the Boston Symphony
narrative_blocks.body: She took the New England Conservatory's piano prize in 1917 and studied in Berlin under Artur Schnabel. She made her London debut at the Royal Albert Hall with Sir Thomas Beecham, and played with the Boston Symphony under Koussevitzky.

narrative_blocks.header: The wedding present became a fund for musicians
narrative_blocks.body: Rockefeller gave her a trust on their wedding day in 1951, so that she might know the joy of giving. She turned it into the Martha Baird Rockefeller Fund for Music, which paid young soloists for twenty-five years.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father's bank failed and the family left
narrative_blocks.body: Her father opened the first bank in Madera, California, and lost it in a land scheme that became a statewide scandal. The family went south and then east, and she kept up the piano her mother had started her on.

narrative_blocks.header: Her third husband was her second husband's friend
narrative_blocks.body: Arthur Allen, the Providence lawyer she married in 1930, had been Rockefeller's classmate at Brown and his friend for half a century. She married Rockefeller in 1951, a year after Allen died, in the parlour of the Allen house.

notable.notable_blurb: Folger curator, paleographer, Shakespeare scholar

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-five years inside one library
narrative_blocks.body: He came to the Folger Shakespeare Library as a reference librarian in 1932 and was its curator of books and manuscripts from 1946 until he retired in 1967. His typed collation notes went into the backs of the books he catalogued.

narrative_blocks.header: His note on filthy scraps reunited a document
narrative_blocks.body: In 1966 he described a book stabbed and stitched into vellum leaves — both sheets, he wrote, filthy, tattered and torn. Because he set that down, a scholar could later match the two halves of one indenture, cut up to wrap two different books.

narrative_blocks.header: He claimed a seventh signature for Shakespeare
narrative_blocks.body: Six signatures of Shakespeare's are accepted as genuine. In the spring of 1992, at eighty-nine, he published an argument in Shakespeare Quarterly for a seventh.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the manual for reading old hands
narrative_blocks.body: With Laetitia Kennedy-Skipton he published Elizabethan Handwriting, 1500-1650 in 1966, a guide to reading the documents of the period. It taught the skill from fifty-four facsimiles.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventy-nine First Folios under one roof
narrative_blocks.body: In a paper of 1949 he set out what the library held: seventy-nine First Folios, a third of every copy then known to exist, besides six or seven thousand books printed in England before the Civil War.

narrative_blocks.header: He was still shelving books at ninety-one
narrative_blocks.body: From 1984 he volunteered as rare-book librarian at the Washington National Cathedral and kept at it until the May of 1994. He died that August, ninety-one years old.

narrative_blocks.header: His father catalogued birds; he catalogued books
narrative_blocks.body: He was a son of William Leon Dawson, the ornithologist, and Frances Etta Akerman. The father wrote the books about birds; the son spent his life on the books themselves.

notable.notable_blurb: Editor of Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine

narrative_blocks.header: He edited the book American medicine still opens
narrative_blocks.body: Harrison was founding editor-in-chief of Principles of Internal Medicine, published in 1950, and shaped its first five editions. It has been revised and reprinted ever since and translated into fourteen languages, and remains the best-selling internal medicine text in the world.

narrative_blocks.header: The patient is no collection of symptoms
narrative_blocks.body: The passage Harrison set at the front of the textbook told physicians that a patient is human, fearful and hopeful, and not a mere collection of symptoms and damaged organs. The true physician, he wrote, has a Shakespearean breadth of interest in the wise and the foolish, and cares for people.

narrative_blocks.header: He built four medical schools, one after another
narrative_blocks.body: Harrison was Vanderbilt's first chief resident in 1925 and stayed sixteen years, then went to Bowman Gray in North Carolina as founding chair of medicine and to Southwestern in Dallas as founding dean. At Alabama from 1950 he recruited from Harvard and the Mayo Clinic and carried a local school to international standing.

narrative_blocks.header: Osler wrote back that the boy should teach
narrative_blocks.body: His father Groce Harrison, himself a sixth-generation physician, had befriended William Osler at Baltimore and wrote to tell him of his son's birth in 1900. Osler answered that the boy should become a teacher of medicine, and that is what he became.

narrative_blocks.header: A heart book came before the famous one
narrative_blocks.body: Harrison's own field was the heart, and his 1935 Failure of the Circulation became a standard work long before the textbook that carried his name. He led the American Heart Association and the American Society for Clinical Investigation, and took the heart association's Gold Heart Award in 1963.

narrative_blocks.header: She is buried in her own church garden
narrative_blocks.body: Joan Cabaniss Harrison was a lifelong member of the Cathedral Church of the Advent in Birmingham, sat on its vestry, served in the St. Bridges Guild and kept a bible study at her house for years. She lies in the cathedral's Rector's Garden, where her husband was buried before her.

narrative_blocks.header: Four cities, four medical schools, one childhood
narrative_blocks.body: Betsy Harrison was born at Nashville in 1934 and grew up in Winston-Salem, Dallas and Birmingham in turn, each move following her father to another medical school. She met her husband at Vanderbilt, the school where her father had been the first chief resident.

narrative_blocks.header: She topped her firm selling Wilmington houses
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband's work took the family through a string of postings, including years in Germany. Living at Wilmington, Delaware, she built a real-estate career and became one of her firm's top agents, then retired in 1990 to Seabrook Island in South Carolina.

narrative_blocks.header: His stone gives a rank and a war
narrative_blocks.body: Kenneth Smith served in the United States Navy through the Second World War, rating engineman second class. The marker at Worcester County Memorial Park records the rate, the service and the war and nothing else of him.

narrative_blocks.header: Her church brought a family out of Laos
narrative_blocks.body: Through the outreach programme of the First Congregational Church of West Boylston, Dorothy Smith was central to sponsoring a Laotian family's passage to America. She worked the soup kitchen at the John Street Baptist Church on a standing basis.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-five years with the same Girl Scouts
narrative_blocks.body: She gave thirty-five years to the Montachusett Girl Scouts, and sat on a garden club, a college fund-raising committee and her town's bicentennial parade committee besides. Her family remembered her for a saying: we will be there in the finals.

narrative_blocks.header: She lost two sons in one year
narrative_blocks.body: Edward Devereux Burgwyn died in 1822 at three years old and William Bush at one, within months of each other. She bore a last daughter the following year, named Sarah Emily after herself, and died on 17 April 1823.

narrative_blocks.header: Her land brought two plantations to the marriage
narrative_blocks.body: Her marriage in 1806 opened tracts in Jones and Craven counties to her husband, among them the plantations Ravenswood and Alveston Hall. It was her side of the family that held the New Bern ground the household moved to in 1811.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brother died childless in 1839
narrative_blocks.body: Her half-brother George Pollock left no children, and his lands were divided among his heirs between 1840 and 1843. Her children took the Northampton estates only after the Devereux family fought them for it in court.

narrative_blocks.header: Forgers made him respell his own name
narrative_blocks.body: Finding that drafts were being forged on his accounts in foreign banks, Burgwyn altered the spelling from Burgwin to Burgwyn. His descendants have kept the change ever since.

narrative_blocks.header: Motherless at four, he was shipped to England
narrative_blocks.body: His mother died in 1787 and he and his sister were sent back to England to relatives, he to a Quaker kinsman at Plymouth and the schools of that town. He returned to North Carolina in 1801 and took up his father's import-export business.

narrative_blocks.header: He traded plantations, and the people on them
narrative_blocks.body: Burgwyn inherited the Hermitage and Castle Haynes in 1803 and ran ships in the European trade. Moving to New Bern in 1811, he exchanged both estates and the enslaved people held on them for his sister-in-law's land in Craven County.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped finish a university building
narrative_blocks.body: He subscribed toward completing the South Building at the University of North Carolina between 1809 and 1811, and led Christ Church at New Bern when it was rebuilt in 1824.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: He subscribed toward finishing it, 1809-1811.

narrative_blocks.header: Not one of the first five reached twenty
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah died at eighteen and Cameron at sixteen in the spring of 1845, three weeks apart. Anne Julia went at nineteen, Donald at eighteen, George Henry Edwards at nineteen. Only the last two, John Burgwyn and Kathrine Mary, grew up.

narrative_blocks.header: She married the rector of her father's church
narrative_blocks.body: John Fanning Burgwyn had led Christ Church at New Bern through its rebuilding in 1824. Fifteen years later his daughter married its rector, Cameron Farquhar McRae, in December 1839.

narrative_blocks.header: Her daughter came back to the same ground
narrative_blocks.body: She died at Philadelphia in June 1853 and was buried at Laurel Hill. Kathrine Mary, three years old that summer, was laid in the same cemetery sixty-five years later.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Her husband was its rector from 1838 to 1842.

narrative_blocks.header: Thornbury, on the Roanoke
narrative_blocks.body: He held Thornbury, the plantation on the Roanoke River in Northampton County, and his children grew up on it. His father had brought the family fortune out of the Cape Fear trade a generation earlier.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the place from Europe in 1851
narrative_blocks.body: A plantation account book survives from the year he spent abroad, together with the letters he sent his overseer from Europe. The estate was worked without him for a season and the correspondence is how it was done.

narrative_blocks.header: He married Boston and kept both houses
narrative_blocks.body: Anna Greenough came from Jamaica Plain, and the family went north to her people in the summers. Two of their sons were born there, on visits, rather than in the state they were raised in.

narrative_blocks.header: Two of his sons wore a colonel's stars
narrative_blocks.body: Harry was dead at Gettysburg at twenty-one, commanding a regiment. William came out of the same war a captain, put the uniform on twice more in peacetime, and lived to found banks in eight North Carolina towns.

narrative_blocks.header: One of the noted belles of the fifties
narrative_blocks.body: She came into Philadelphia society under Judge and Mrs Joseph Hopkinson, and Mrs James Rush chaperoned her to Saratoga, Newport and Boston with her father and uncle. Willis and Curtis were among the friends she named afterwards.

narrative_blocks.header: In Florence she knew the Brownings
narrative_blocks.body: She spent much of her later life in Europe, and living at Florence she became a friend of Mr and Mrs Browning, of Mrs Trollope and of Charles Lever. She kept the friendship of her friends' children after them, which was said to be a rare gift.

narrative_blocks.header: Her last twenty years, in her niece's house
narrative_blocks.body: She lived quietly in Philadelphia with Katherine McRae, her sister Julia's daughter, and died there in April 1905. The niece stayed on in the city and was buried at Laurel Hill thirteen years later.

narrative_blocks.header: She made an abolitionist of her husband
narrative_blocks.body: He said it himself: my wife made an out and out abolitionist of me, and she always preceded me in the adoption of the various causes I have advocated. They had met on a stagecoach to Greenfield in 1835 and married two years after.

narrative_blocks.header: Don't shilly-shally, Wendell, she told him
narrative_blocks.body: Massachusetts sent them both to the World's Anti-Slavery Convention in London in 1840, and the women delegates — Ann, Lucretia Mott and five others — were refused their seats on the ground of sex. Don't shilly-shally, Wendell, she said as he went in to argue their case. He lost, and the women watched from the gallery.

narrative_blocks.header: An invalid who ran the argument from bed
narrative_blocks.body: Ill from youth with something no source names, she kept to her room and often to her bed for most of her life, and lived secluded after they came home from Europe. She kept up her correspondence and her judgement, and he cared more for her approval than for the crowds.

narrative_blocks.header: They adopted an orphan and had no children
narrative_blocks.body: The Phillipses had no children of their own and took in an orphan, Phoebe Garnaut, in 1850. Ann had been orphaned young herself and raised by an aunt and uncle, the Chapmans, in a house of Garrison abolitionists.

narrative_blocks.header: He preached a God who loved you first
narrative_blocks.body: From his Brooklyn pulpit after 1847 he put God's love above sinfulness and doubted hell. He preached in slang, and filled three thousand seats a week.

narrative_blocks.header: Theodore Tilton sued him for adultery in 1875
narrative_blocks.body: Tilton was his protégé and edited the paper Beecher had made, and he charged the preacher with adultery with his wife Elizabeth, a member of Beecher's own congregation. The Brooklyn trial ran six months and drove Reconstruction off the front pages. The jury sat six days and could not agree.

narrative_blocks.header: Victoria Woodhull printed the charge first
narrative_blocks.body: Woodhull broke the story in her own weekly in 1872, to expose what she called the hypocrisy of a man who denounced free love in public. Plymouth Church and a council of Congregational ministers each cleared him; Elizabeth Tilton confessed in 1878.

narrative_blocks.header: Rifles to Kansas, nicknamed Beecher's Bibles
narrative_blocks.body: He sent Sharps rifles to Kansas, saying they would do more good than a hundred Bibles, and the press named the crates for him.

narrative_blocks.header: He auctioned a girl to buy her freedom
narrative_blocks.body: At a Sunday service in 1860 he auctioned an enslaved girl called Pinky, taking the collection until her price was met. Someone dropped a gold ring in the plate; he put it on her finger, and she brought it back sixty-seven years on.

narrative_blocks.header: Lincoln sent him to raise the Sumter flag
narrative_blocks.body: Lincoln sent him to Europe in 1863 to speak for the Union, and chose him to raise the flag again over Fort Sumter. But for Beecher, said Lincoln, there would have been no flag.

narrative_blocks.header: The dullest of the brilliant Beechers
narrative_blocks.body: Roxana Foote died when Henry was three and Lyman married Harriet Porter, whom the boy found severe. He stammered, was thought the dullest of thirteen children, and sat in the girls' corner in a dunce cap. At fourteen they sent him to Amherst.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote her Indiana years as a novel
narrative_blocks.body: Through a long illness she wrote up her first years as a minister's wife and published them in 1859 as From Dawn to Daylight, under the name A Minister's Wife. Indianapolis thought itself unkindly drawn, though she later called it the happiest home they ever knew.

narrative_blocks.header: Motherly Talks, and four more books after
narrative_blocks.body: Her Christian Union columns became Motherly Talks with Young Housekeepers, and Letters from Florida, All Around the House and Home followed. Whatever exceptional women managed, she held, the place of labour for a married woman was her own house.

narrative_blocks.header: They called her the ailing and wailing wife
narrative_blocks.body: Neither Indiana parish could pay well, and a minister's wife there got none of the standing she had known in New England. The congregations called her the boyish Beecher's ailing and wailing wife.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten years to the day after her husband
narrative_blocks.body: Henry Ward Beecher died on 8 March 1887 and Eunice died on 8 March 1897, at Stamford, ten years to the day. She had stood by him through the seven years of the Tilton scandal and outlived it by a decade.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten children, and four of them grew up
narrative_blocks.body: She bore ten children and buried six; Harriet, Henry, William and Herbert reached adulthood. She had been engaged to Beecher five years before he came east from Indiana to marry her in 1837.
