narrative_blocks.header: He held a Brooklyn pulpit of Beecher's
narrative_blocks.body: Scoville was pastor of the Congregational church at Norwich in New York, and at one time held a Brooklyn pulpit that carried Beecher's name. He married the preacher's only surviving daughter.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote his father-in-law's life with the son
narrative_blocks.body: With William Constantine Beecher, the preacher's second son, Scoville wrote A Biography of Rev. Henry Ward Beecher, published in 1888, the year after Beecher died.

cross_connections.display_label: wrote the first life of Poe as Scoville wrote his father-in-law's

narrative_blocks.header: Her father married her at the Beecher house
narrative_blocks.body: At the outbreak of the Civil War, with Henry Ward Beecher deep in his campaign against slavery, he married his only surviving daughter to the Rev. Samuel Scoville at the family home at Peekskill-on-Hudson.

narrative_blocks.header: She told a story like her father
narrative_blocks.body: Like him she had a keen sense of humour and was reckoned one of the most entertaining story-tellers anyone knew. At Norwich she was elected president of the Woman's Working Association of her husband's church.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven children, and four outlived her
narrative_blocks.body: She bore seven children, four of them living when she died at West Cornwall in 1911. She was laid beside her husband in the family plot on the Scoville farm.

narrative_blocks.header: The only daughter of ten who grew up
narrative_blocks.body: Ten children were born to Henry Ward and Eunice Beecher and four reached adulthood — Harriet Eliza and three brothers. Her sister Katharine Esther, born in 1846, was dead before she was two, and five more of the children died as infants.

notable.notable_blurb: Theologian; a founder of the College of California

narrative_blocks.header: He was offered the college presidency
narrative_blocks.body: The College of California offered him its presidency in 1856, and he would not leave his Hartford flock for it. He took the endowment appeal and the site search instead, unpaid.

narrative_blocks.header: The site can be chosen but once
narrative_blocks.body: He rode, coached and steamed round the bay hunting ground that would serve for ever, and settled on Napa. The trustees adopted it, then bought Berkeley a year later when an engineer found water could be got there. The college became the University of California in 1868.

narrative_blocks.header: His 1869 book called the vote unnatural
narrative_blocks.body: Women's Suffrage: The Reform Against Nature appeared the year the university opened to its first forty students. A claim by women to govern men, he wrote, was no less a revolt against nature than a claim to a beard.

narrative_blocks.header: Raise a Christian, do not convert one
narrative_blocks.body: Christian Nurture, in 1847, held that a child should grow up a Christian and never know himself otherwise. It was a blow at the revival meeting, and turned American religious thought toward the young.

narrative_blocks.header: No creed could match what it pointed at
narrative_blocks.body: Every noun outside mathematics is a worn-out image, he argued, so no creed can match the thing it points at — Munger called him theology's Copernicus. The view brought repeated attempts to try him for heresy, until in 1852 his own church withdrew from its consociation and left no body that could judge him.

narrative_blocks.header: He got America its first public park
narrative_blocks.body: He was the chief agent in procuring the first public park in the United States. Hartford named it Bushnell Park for him.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught a roommate to sharpen a razor
narrative_blocks.body: At Yale he roomed with Nathaniel Parker Willis, later a famous magazinist, who credited him with teaching him to sharpen a razor.

narrative_blocks.header: She lived a hundred years and three months
narrative_blocks.body: Born in Boston on New Year's Day 1805, she died at Hartford on the fourth of April 1905. She outlived her husband by twenty-nine years and saw the whole of the century between them.

narrative_blocks.header: She married the year he took the pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: Horace Bushnell was called to the North Church at Hartford in 1833 and married her the same year. A Boston Apthorp came to a Connecticut parsonage and stayed there through every heresy charge brought against him.

notable.notable_blurb: Oliver North's secretary in the Iran-Contra affair

narrative_blocks.header: She shredded until the machine jammed
narrative_blocks.body: On the day North was fired in November 1986 she destroyed so many documents that the office shredder jammed. She carried others out of the White House complex in her boots and her clothing and handed them to him.

narrative_blocks.header: Sometimes you have to go above the law
narrative_blocks.body: She testified for two days before Congress in June 1987 under a grant of immunity, and that line is what the country remembered. Her summary of the defence, Bob Woodward wrote, was simpler: we shred everything.

narrative_blocks.header: Two transposed digits lost the Sultan's money
narrative_blocks.body: Copying a Swiss account number for the Sultan of Brunei's contribution to the Contras, she reversed two digits and the money landed in a businessman's account instead. A Senate committee had to track it down.

narrative_blocks.header: She said the magazine offer was disgusting
narrative_blocks.body: Penthouse and Playboy both offered to pay her to pose after the hearings and she turned them down flat. For a season she was a tabloid property, with a red Fiero on FAWN plates and Farrah Fawcett ringing up to play her in a film.

narrative_blocks.header: Rob Lowe found her through the hearings
narrative_blocks.body: The actor saw her on television during the hearings, tracked her down, and took her to the American Film Institute ceremony in 1988. Before that she had spent a year with Arturo Cruz Jr., son of a Contra leader.

narrative_blocks.header: The Doors manager and the years after
narrative_blocks.body: In 1993 she married Danny Sugerman, who had managed The Doors, and moved to the Hollywood Hills. She was addicted to crack within a year and overdosed in 1994; she went into rehabilitation, and he died in 2005.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years on, she married her old boss
narrative_blocks.body: They met again at Betsy North's funeral and married quietly in Virginia in August 2025. Asked about it by a reporter, North answered with Rhett Butler's line and nothing else.

narrative_blocks.header: He answered the fan mail at twelve
narrative_blocks.body: A concert at thirteen made him a convert, and the Doors put him to work answering their post. When Jim Morrison died in July 1971 the band's manager left, and the job went to Sugerman at seventeen.

narrative_blocks.header: The book that brought the Doors back
narrative_blocks.body: No One Here Gets Out Alive, written with Jerry Hopkins in 1980, was the first full life of Morrison and it sold enormously. A band ten years dead had a second audience because of it.

narrative_blocks.header: His fanzine printed a teenage Cameron Crowe
narrative_blocks.body: In 1973 he started Heavy Metal Digest, a magazine for Morrison that lasted three issues and carried interviews with the Rolling Stones, Alice Cooper and Iggy Pop. One of its teenage contributors was Cameron Crowe.

narrative_blocks.header: He managed Iggy Pop and advised Oliver Stone
narrative_blocks.body: He took on Ray Manzarek's solo career and then Iggy Pop's, producing the song Repo Man. He was technical adviser on Oliver Stone's film of the band in 1991.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote his own excess down
narrative_blocks.body: Wonderland Avenue: Tales of Glamour and Excess, in 1989, set out his own years of addiction and his idolising of Morrison. Appetite for Destruction, on Guns N' Roses, followed in 1991.

narrative_blocks.header: He argued addiction was a medical problem
narrative_blocks.body: Methadone saved his life, he said, and he spent his last years arguing that addicts belonged with doctors rather than in jail. He worked with the Drug Policy Foundation, MusiCares and the Musicians Assistance Program.

narrative_blocks.header: Manzarek put him in the light with Morrison
narrative_blocks.body: He married Fawn Hall in 1993 and they stayed married until he died of lung cancer at fifty. His heart was in the heavens, said Ray Manzarek, and he is now in the light with the Buddha and Jim Morrison.

narrative_blocks.header: Burghley in 2007, Morven Park in 2011
narrative_blocks.body: She rode at the Burghley Horse Trials in England in 2007 and was still eventing four years later at the Morven Park trials in Virginia, on a horse called Jimminy Cricket.

narrative_blocks.header: She carries her grandmother's maiden name
narrative_blocks.body: Frances Lamkin Dornin married Jeb Stuart, and their daughter Elizabeth married Oliver North. The Dornin name dropped out as a surname for a generation and came back as a given one.

narrative_blocks.header: At twelve she was in a campaign ad
narrative_blocks.body: Her father put her in a television spot at the close of his 1994 Senate run. He had told a crowd that month that campaigning kept him from her school play — her Middleburg school had none until spring, and aides said he meant field hockey.

notable.notable_blurb: Episcopal rector in five states

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve months at West Point, then the church
narrative_blocks.body: He entered the military academy in 1827 and left within the year on his health, and he matriculated at the university in Chapel Hill without taking a degree. He served in the army, resigned to study for the ministry, and came out of the Virginia seminary in 1835.

narrative_blocks.header: A rector in five states in one lifetime
narrative_blocks.body: Ordained deacon in 1835 and priest the year after, he held Christ Church at New Bern, Emmanuel at Warrenton, St. John's at Jamaica Plain, two Philadelphia parishes, St. John's at Savannah and finally All Hallows in Maryland. He was a high church Anglican throughout.

narrative_blocks.header: He resigned his pulpit when the war came
narrative_blocks.body: At the outbreak of the war he gave up his Philadelphia parish and went home to North Carolina, where he served as chaplain of the fifteenth North Carolina infantry. He sat for Georgia at the general council of the Confederate Episcopal church.

narrative_blocks.header: The historian called him prominent, and left it
narrative_blocks.body: Kemp Battle, writing the history of the University of North Carolina, set him down simply as a prominent Episcopal minister in several states. He had never finished his degree there.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven by one wife, five by the next
narrative_blocks.body: Julia Theodosia Burgwyn bore him seven and died at Philadelphia in 1853. He married Susan Plummer in December 1861 and had five more, giving two of them the names of his first wife and himself.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: He was its rector from 1838 to 1842.

career.organization: All Hallows Church, Anne Arundel County

narrative_blocks.header: Two sons born in her Boston house
narrative_blocks.body: The Greenoughs were of Jamaica Plain, and the Burgwyns summered with them. Harry in 1841 and William in 1845 were both born in Massachusetts to a family whose land was four hundred miles south.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived her eldest son by twenty-four years
narrative_blocks.body: Harry, the eldest of her sons, was killed at Gettysburg in July 1863 and brought home to Raleigh four years later. She died at Henderson in 1887, in the town her second son had settled in, and was buried at Hollywood in Richmond.

narrative_blocks.header: Harry wrote home until the first of July
narrative_blocks.body: Letters ran between her and her sons through the whole of the war, hers going out and theirs coming back. Harry's stopped on the first day at Gettysburg; William's went on through two wounds and a prison camp.

bio.bio_blurb: Boston woman on a Carolina plantation

notable.notable_blurb: The Boy Colonel, killed at Gettysburg

narrative_blocks.header: Stonewall Jackson wrote him a reference
narrative_blocks.body: West Point never gave him the appointment he wanted, so he took a Chapel Hill degree and went to the Virginia Military Institute, where Professor T. J. Jackson taught him. He left in 1861 with Jackson's recommendation, a lieutenant colonel at nineteen.

narrative_blocks.header: I want no boy colonels in my brigade
narrative_blocks.body: When Zebulon Vance left the twenty-sixth North Carolina to be governor in 1862, the brigade commander objected to a twenty-year-old succeeding him. The regiment voted its confidence twice and D. H. Hill sustained the appointment.

narrative_blocks.header: Five hundred and eighty-eight of eight hundred
narrative_blocks.body: At Gettysburg on 1 July 1863 the regiment crossed Willoughby Run and went up McPherson's Ridge into the Iron Brigade. Twenty minutes cost five hundred and eighty-eight of eight hundred men, the heaviest single-day regimental loss on either side.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the colours and was shot through
narrative_blocks.body: The flag went down eleven times before he picked it up himself. A ball passed through both lungs as he turned to give an order, and he died about two hours later, twenty-one years old.

narrative_blocks.header: A private levelled a rifle for his watch
narrative_blocks.body: As they carried him off, a South Carolina lieutenant cut the watch from his neck and walked away with it. Private William Cheek cocked his rifle, made the man bring it back, and Burgwyn said he would never forget him.

narrative_blocks.header: Buried in a gun case, moved in 1867
narrative_blocks.body: They buried him north of the Chambersburg Pike in an empty gun case, under a walnut tree. His family took him up in 1867 and laid him in the family ground at Oakwood in Raleigh.

narrative_blocks.header: He guarded John Brown as a cadet
narrative_blocks.body: At the Institute he was one of the cadets detailed to stand over John Brown before the execution. He was born at Jamaica Plain because his parents were summering north, and he died unmarried.

notable.notable_blurb: Lawyer, soldier and banker

narrative_blocks.header: Drill master at sixteen, captain at eighteen
narrative_blocks.body: Illness took him out of Chapel Hill in 1861 and he went to the Hillsborough Military Academy, drilling recruits near Raleigh by that autumn. He was lieutenant of Company H of the thirty-fifth North Carolina, and had the company by 1863.

narrative_blocks.header: Shot at Cold Harbor, shot at Fort Harrison
narrative_blocks.body: A severe wound on 1 June 1864 kept him out until September, and on the thirtieth he was hit again at Fort Harrison. He was a prisoner at Fort Delaware until March 1865, paroled at last but never exchanged.

narrative_blocks.header: First honors, then a degree he never used
narrative_blocks.body: He went back as a sophomore, graduated in 1868 with first honors and gave the Latin salutatory. Harvard Law followed in 1870, and a Baltimore medical degree in 1876 he never sought a licence to use.

narrative_blocks.header: The first bank in the county, then more
narrative_blocks.body: He opened a private bank at Henderson in 1882, with no charter and no oversight beyond a sworn yearly statement to the tax lister. It became the Bank of Henderson in 1884 under him, and eight more followed, one of them in Florida.

narrative_blocks.header: He wired the town and piped its water
narrative_blocks.body: Henderson got its electric light, its water works and a tobacco factory from him. He was president of the Henderson Female College from 1886 and a university trustee from 1883.

narrative_blocks.header: He put the uniform back on twice
narrative_blocks.body: The Baltimore and Ohio riot of 1877 made him a lieutenant colonel of Maryland troops and then colonel of the fifth regiment. In 1898 he took the second North Carolina volunteers, though the Spanish war ended first.

narrative_blocks.header: Buried beside the brother dead at twenty-one
narrative_blocks.body: He married Margaret Carlisle Dunlop of Richmond in 1876 and they had no children. He died at a nephew's house there and was carried to the Confederate ground at Raleigh, where Harry had lain since 1867.

career.role: National bank examiner for the southern states

narrative_blocks.header: Seven years keeping his county's accounts
narrative_blocks.body: He was treasurer of Northampton County for more than seven years. The commissioners recorded absolute accuracy in his accounts, promptness in paying what the county owed, and above all politeness and kindness to everyone who came to him.

narrative_blocks.header: A loss difficult, if possible, to repair
narrative_blocks.body: The board wrote at his death that the people of the county, without regard to politics, race, craft or condition, had sustained a loss it would be difficult if possible to repair. He was forty-seven.

narrative_blocks.header: He read the lessons at Jackson
narrative_blocks.body: He was a lay reader in the Episcopal church at Jackson, where his own family was buried. The crowd that came to his funeral was remarked on as an immense concourse.

narrative_blocks.header: At twenty-five he won the cemetery design
narrative_blocks.body: In 1877 he entered the contest to design the westward expansion of Hollywood Cemetery and won it, young and untried. He worked with the fall of the ground rather than against it, and was buried in the result thirty-eight years later.

narrative_blocks.header: He strung Richmond's first telephone lines
narrative_blocks.body: In the autumn of 1878 he took the wires across rooftops and through trees from the penitentiary to the business district. Two years with the coast survey followed, in the Dismal Swamp.

narrative_blocks.header: He laid out Monument Avenue's first block
narrative_blocks.body: In 1887 he set the axial streets, the treed medians and the traffic circle, with Boston's Commonwealth Avenue behind the idea. He went to Paris to see Mercié's equestrian Lee before it was crated for Richmond.

narrative_blocks.header: His sketches moved a railway station downtown
narrative_blocks.body: The terminal was to go up north of the city until the chamber of commerce paid him for drawings of one downtown. Two railroads changed their minds, and Main Street Station is where his sketches put it.

narrative_blocks.header: A city hall built without a contractor
narrative_blocks.body: The council handed him and the city engineer the new city hall to build with day labour, bypassing the contractors. He came out of it interested in working men, and spent twenty years running the Virginia Mechanics' Institute.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote a novel about a Boston girl
narrative_blocks.body: The Huguenot Lovers, in 1889, sends a Boston woman south to have her ideas about the war rearranged and fall in love with a former Confederate officer. He had won Harvard prizes for Latin poetry, and followed it with a play.

narrative_blocks.header: Two brothers, and neither of them lucky
narrative_blocks.body: One brother was killed at Gettysburg and another shot and captured at Cold Harbor, in a family with as many New England ties as Carolina ones. He married Rosa Higginbotham in 1884.

set aside the ground for Green-Wood and gave the movement its model

bio.bio_blurb: Civil and hydraulic engineer of Richmond

narrative_blocks.header: The second daughter took the first one's name
narrative_blocks.body: Betty Gray Mason Long was born and died in 1911. The daughter born the next September was christened Betty Gray in her turn, and lived to eighty-three.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept the parish auxiliary's books
narrative_blocks.body: She kept the books of the Episcopal women's auxiliary in the town from 1915 to 1917, in the years her husband was chairing its board of commissioners.

narrative_blocks.header: She married into a town called deadly
narrative_blocks.body: She came from Jackson in 1886 and married the doctor in 1910, going to a mill village on the Roanoke that malaria had given a bad name. She outlived him by five years and lies beside him at Garysburg.

bio.bio_blurb: Doctor's wife and parish auxiliary secretary

notable.notable_blurb: Physician, legislator and hospital administrator

narrative_blocks.header: He drained the malaria out of the town
narrative_blocks.body: Roanoke Rapids was a cotton mill village people called a death trap, and malaria was why. He campaigned for mosquito control with the federal health service until the place was reckoned the healthiest town on the Roanoke.

narrative_blocks.header: A deduction from mill pay became Blue Cross
narrative_blocks.body: There was no hospital in the county and mill wages were small, so in 1912 he and two other doctors built one. His plan of taking a little from every worker's pay for medicine and a bed became the Hospital Savings Association, and then Blue Cross and Blue Shield.

narrative_blocks.header: The fightingest doctor in the Assembly
narrative_blocks.body: That was the press verdict on him after two sessions. He claimed the Halifax family that adopted the orphan John Paul Jones, and it was said that in a floor fight he never knew when he was licked.

narrative_blocks.header: He put health tests into state law
narrative_blocks.body: He carried premarital health examinations, blood tests for expectant mothers, and diphtheria immunisation for every child. He also got the money appropriated for a tuberculosis sanatorium in the east of the state.

narrative_blocks.header: One bill moved his own town's boundary
narrative_blocks.body: He fathered a measure to redraw the lines of Roanoke Rapids so that certain mills fell inside them and could be taxed. It became one of the most bitterly fought local bills in years, and split his own county's two House members.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventeen years mayor of the town
narrative_blocks.body: He chaired the board of commissioners from 1915, was mayor from 1922 to 1939, sat as a school trustee, and ran the town's bank. In Halifax County he was the political weather.

narrative_blocks.header: He died after a finance committee meeting
narrative_blocks.body: He married Maria Greenough Burgwyn in 1910 and they raised five children past infancy. He died at Raleigh on 3 February 1941, mid-term, coming out of a finance committee meeting.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote her father into the record
narrative_blocks.body: The account of Dr. Long in the Dictionary of North Carolina Biography carries her name at the foot of it. She was his second daughter, and the second to be called Betty Gray.

narrative_blocks.header: Five years Army, then a trading post
narrative_blocks.body: He organised a farm credit association in 1934 and was working for the state employment commission when the Army took him for five years, ending as a captain running transport for overseas trips. He came home to Jackson and opened a hardware and furniture store.

narrative_blocks.header: He got the ABC stores on the ballot
narrative_blocks.body: In 1965 he carried the petition to put liquor stores to a county vote, believing the revenue would help the place. He was made the first chairman of its board and built the system for nearly thirty years, retiring in 1995 at eighty-six.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave the churchyard its stone walls
narrative_blocks.body: He put the motion to establish a permanent cemetery fund at his church and gave the east and south stone walls himself. The centre flag pole at the county's veterans memorial was his too.

bio.bio_blurb: Northampton County businessman and ABC board chairman

narrative_blocks.header: A flight surgeon on the USS Leyte
narrative_blocks.body: He was a captain in the navy through the Korean War, flying as surgeon with the carrier's squadrons. He had taken his medical degree at Richmond in 1948, five years out of school.

narrative_blocks.header: Three hospitals and thirty-five years
narrative_blocks.body: He practised gynaecology at Petersburg from 1959, at Riverside in Newport News from 1965, and at the army community hospital at Fort Campbell from 1978 until 1994. He died in Tennessee that December.

narrative_blocks.header: He flew with the crew of Full House
narrative_blocks.body: He was a radar observer and gunner on a B-29 of the 393rd Bombardment Squadron, the 509th Composite Group, stationed on Tinian. His aircraft flew missions over Japan and had supporting roles in the two atomic missions of August 1945.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-five years in savings and loan
narrative_blocks.body: He read history at Virginia and came out in 1950, married that February, and spent most of his working life at Richmond Federal, where he was a senior vice president. At retirement in 1984 he started building houses in Hanover County.

narrative_blocks.header: He tied flies and taught boys to fish
narrative_blocks.body: He was a celebrated fly-tier and led the Federation of Fly Fishers, Trout Unlimited and the Virginia Anglers Club at various times. He co-founded Fly Fishers of Virginia and the state chapter of the Brotherhood of the Junglecock, which exists to put children on rivers.

cross_connections.display_label: readied the Hiroshima bomb his 509th Group carried from Tinian

bio.bio_blurb: Savings and loan officer; fly fisherman

narrative_blocks.header: The town gave her a day at 100
narrative_blocks.body: Jackson named the fifteenth of June Mary Virginia Burgwyn Day when she turned a hundred in 2012, for what she had done in the place. She died at home there the following March.

narrative_blocks.header: She started the Jackson Woman's Club
narrative_blocks.body: She was one of its charter members and the moving force behind getting it going. She served years on the vestry of the Episcopal Church of the Savior, where she was buried.

narrative_blocks.header: She taught James Taylor's brother
narrative_blocks.body: She took a primary education degree at Chapel Hill in 1957 and taught first grade there while her husband was in medical school. Her most famous first grader was Livingston Taylor.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty-three years, and everyone's Mimi
narrative_blocks.body: She met Ray Newsome in her last year at Chapel Hill, married him that same year, and they reached their sixty-third anniversary. Two sons, three grandchildren's weddings, three great grandchildren, and a long succession of Siamese cats.

narrative_blocks.header: She could explain how everyone was related
narrative_blocks.body: One of her favourite pastimes was setting out how the whole family connected, on the Barrow side and the Burgwyn side both. She kept up with aunts, uncles and cousins nobody else could have named.

education.school_name: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty-two years on the same Berlin farm
narrative_blocks.body: He was eight when his father brought the family up from Connecticut in 1814, and the Berlin place was his home for sixty-two years afterward. He was always a farmer, his neighbors said, and always an industrious one.

narrative_blocks.header: He worked until the day he was struck
narrative_blocks.body: Paralysis took him two weeks before he died, on a Monday he had hardly rested through. He had just finished four years as a deacon of the Congregational church, where the prayer meetings were what he liked best.

narrative_blocks.header: He outlived the son he moved in with
narrative_blocks.body: He married Betsey Maria Davis, daughter of the Congregational minister at Barnard, in January 1836, and Edwin Nelson was their only child. The parents came down to Montpelier to live in his house in 1877; Betsey died there in 1882 and Edwin in 1885.

bio.bio_blurb: Berlin, Vermont farmer and church deacon

narrative_blocks.header: Born at Farmington, baptized at Plymouth
narrative_blocks.body: His father had moved the family back to Farmington while his elder brother was still an infant, and he was born there. He was carried down to the Plymouth church for baptism, to the parish his mother had joined three years before.

narrative_blocks.header: His first marriage lasted seven weeks
narrative_blocks.body: He married Harriet Hamilton Washburn at Montpelier in October 1836 and she was dead by December. Mary Foster of Conway, New Hampshire, became his second wife and the mother of all nine of his children.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine children over twenty-four years
narrative_blocks.body: The first was born in 1846 and the last in 1870, and he farmed at Montpelier through all of it. He died at Berlin in 1883; Mary outlived him by eleven years, and four of the children had gone to Illinois, one to Colorado and one to Connecticut.

narrative_blocks.header: The doctor's mortar became a business
narrative_blocks.body: He was the youngest of Eleazer's sons and the one who went furthest from the Berlin farm. His grandfather Dr. Abijah Scovil had ground drugs by hand in a Connecticut kitchen; Amon manufactured patent medicines, and died at Cincinnati in March 1887.

narrative_blocks.header: In 1888 she was the last of six
narrative_blocks.body: Her brother Joseph died at Montpelier that autumn, and she was the only one of Eleazer and Abigail's six children still living. She had married John D. Goodwin and was at Fair Haven.

narrative_blocks.header: A Barnard minister's daughter on a farm
narrative_blocks.body: Her father was the Rev. Joel Davis, Congregational minister at Barnard, and she married Joseph Langdon Scovill in January 1836. Edwin Nelson was their only child, and she died in his Montpelier house on 23 May 1882.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Washburn weddings on the same day
narrative_blocks.body: She married James Bidwell Scovill at Montpelier on 17 October 1836. Ruth Emily Washburn married the Rev. John Harris Redington in the same town on the same day.

narrative_blocks.header: She was a wife for seven weeks
narrative_blocks.body: Harriet died at Montpelier on 9 December 1836, aged twenty-four. Her husband married again, and it is the second wife's children who carried the name on.

narrative_blocks.header: Her footstone names no parents
narrative_blocks.body: The Montpelier cemetery record gives her father and mother as Asahel and Polly Washburn, but no Washburn record lists a daughter Harriet, and Col. Asahel and his wife lie in a different Montpelier burying ground. Green Mount itself was not bought by the city until 1854, eighteen years after she was laid in it.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventeen years younger than her husband
narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Conway, New Hampshire, in September 1827, a daughter of Perley and Nancy Bean Foster. James Bidwell Scoville had buried his first wife seven weeks after that wedding, and married her eight years later.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine children over twenty-four years
narrative_blocks.body: The first came in 1846, when she was eighteen, and the last in 1870, when she was forty-two. She had been a member of the Congregational church since she was a child, and was active in its work for most of her life.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight of them came to her funeral
narrative_blocks.body: She died in April 1894 at her daughter's house on Ridgeland Avenue in Oak Park, where she had lived for four years. Eight of her children were there on the Monday, come in from Manchester, Marion, Denver and New Haven, and the body went back to Montpelier for burial on the Wednesday.

narrative_blocks.header: His parents came to live in his house
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph and Betsey left the Berlin farm in March 1877 and moved into his house at Montpelier. His mother died there in 1882 and he died in September 1885, three years before his father.

notable.notable_blurb: Rector of Trinity Church on the Green

narrative_blocks.header: He held one pulpit for fifty-five years
narrative_blocks.body: He came to Trinity Church on the New Haven Green as assistant minister in 1892, took the parish as acting rector in 1906 and as rector in 1908, and kept it until 1935. He was rector emeritus for the twelve years left to him.

narrative_blocks.header: He put steel inside Ithiel Town's church
narrative_blocks.body: The galleries were sagging under the weight of the crowds they drew. Between 1906 and 1912 the original wooden cluster columns came out for steel wrapped in limestone, and Harwood's stencilled ceiling went with them, replaced by gilt plaster groins.

narrative_blocks.header: The church turned a hundred under him
narrative_blocks.body: On 21 February 1916 Trinity kept the centenary of its consecration with communion at eight, historical addresses at half past ten, and a full choir at evening prayer. The dean of his own divinity school gave one of the addresses.

narrative_blocks.header: A Montpelier farmer's son, and a Pundit
narrative_blocks.body: He went through the Montpelier schools to the high school and on to Yale, where he took his degree in 1887 and belonged to the Pundits. Berkeley Divinity School at Middletown followed; he was ordained deacon in June 1889 and priest in July 1890.

narrative_blocks.header: London in 1908, the World Court in 1925
narrative_blocks.body: He was sent to the Pan-Anglican Congress in London the year he became rector, and to the General Convention as a clerical deputy in 1919. Trinity College gave him a doctorate of divinity that year, and he sat on the diocesan standing committee from 1927.

narrative_blocks.header: He married in the parish he was leaving
narrative_blocks.body: Lena May Isbell of Westville married him there on 1 June 1892, weeks before he moved to the Green. Their one child, Helen, went from Hillhouse High School to Wellesley and then to the Yale medical school.

narrative_blocks.header: She married the young rector of St. James'
narrative_blocks.body: Willis Bradley Isbell and Ida Nancy Hotchkiss of Westville were her parents, and Charles Otis Scoville had their village church for two years. They were married there on 1 June 1892, and he took the Trinity curacy in New Haven the same year.

narrative_blocks.header: She and her sister lie in one ground
narrative_blocks.body: Julia was at Ridgeland with her mother in 1894 and living at Chicago by 1917, as her sister Harriet was. She never married, died there in January 1945 at eighty-eight, and was buried beside Harriet at Forest Home in Forest Park.

narrative_blocks.header: Ridgeland in 1894, Chicago in 1917
narrative_blocks.body: She was at Ridgeland with her mother and her sisters when the family gathered in 1894, and in Chicago with Julia and Harry by 1917. She died in 1928, at sixty.

narrative_blocks.header: The youngest of nine, and a Chicago man
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Montpelier in 1870, twenty-four years behind the eldest of his mother's children. He was at Ridgeland with three of his sisters when she died in 1894, was in Chicago by 1917, and died in 1941.

narrative_blocks.header: Denver in 1894, Troy in 1917
narrative_blocks.body: He was living at Denver, Colorado, when his mother died in 1894, and had moved to Troy, New York, by 1917. Nothing else of him is recorded.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at forty, she lived to ninety-one
narrative_blocks.body: Porter Randell died in Ohio in April 1895, fourteen years after they married. She outlived him by fifty-one years and died at Chicago in February 1946.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother died in her Oak Park house
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Foster Scoville spent her last four years on Ridgeland Avenue with her and died there in April 1894. Eight of the nine children came to the funeral, and Harriet buried her husband eleven months after her mother.

notable.notable_blurb: Pathologist, and one of Yale medicine's first women

narrative_blocks.header: She was in the first class of women
narrative_blocks.body: Yale's medical school opened to women in 1916, and she took her M.D. in 1920 with the first class of them to graduate. Wellesley had given her a degree in 1915, and she did graduate work at Pennsylvania as well.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-six years a hospital pathologist
narrative_blocks.body: She was pathologist at the Pittsfield General Hospital in Massachusetts from 1929 until 1955. Washington had her next, on the staff of the National Academy of Sciences and the National Research Council, until she retired in 1958.

narrative_blocks.header: Three of them lie under one stone
narrative_blocks.body: She never married, and was buried at Grove Street in New Haven with her father and mother, whose names are cut on the same stone. She had outlived Charles by thirty years and Lena by twenty-seven.

narrative_blocks.header: The first child, dead within a year
narrative_blocks.body: She was born in May 1846, the eldest of the nine, and did not live to see two. She lies at Green Mount in Montpelier, where her mother was brought back from Illinois forty-seven years later.

narrative_blocks.header: She married for the first time at fifty-four
narrative_blocks.body: At her mother's funeral in 1894 she was living at Manchester, New Hampshire, and was still Miss Scoville at forty-five. She married Henry Wallace Brown on 5 May 1904, at fifty-four, and died at Bedford in 1909.

narrative_blocks.header: He died before his brother could reach him
narrative_blocks.body: He had left Ridgeland only a few months before for Ohio, where he was with a large picture-frame moulding house. Pneumonia struck him down and he was dead in a few days, before his brother could get there from Chicago, at about forty.

narrative_blocks.header: His business life began in Georgia
narrative_blocks.body: He spent his early years in trade in the South, principally in Georgia, and came north about 1828 to Geneva. He held the same homestead there for the last forty years of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: A positive man, in the best sense
narrative_blocks.body: He was vigorous in intellect and strong in will, scrupulously just in his own dealings and prompt to exact the same in return. He was known in Buffalo as well as in his own village, and remembered there as courteous and hospitable.

bio.bio_blurb: Southern trader who settled at Geneva

narrative_blocks.header: Sergeant of Company K, 4th Michigan Cavalry
narrative_blocks.body: He was born in Georgia while his father was trading there, and farmed at Hadley in Lapeer County for the rest of his life. He served through the Civil War in Company K of the 4th Michigan Cavalry, the regiment that ran down Jefferson Davis in Georgia in 1865.

military_service.role: Sergeant, Company K, 4th Michigan Cavalry

notable.notable_blurb: 38th mayor of Detroit; brewer and maltster

narrative_blocks.header: He bought Detroit a snake-infested island
narrative_blocks.body: His one term is remembered for a single act: he got the city to buy a swampy island in the Detroit River for a park. Belle Isle was laid out in the 1880s by Frederick Law Olmsted and is Detroit's park still.

narrative_blocks.header: The panic of 1877 took the fortune
narrative_blocks.body: He and N. G. Williams bought the Central brewery in 1864 and ran it as Langdon & Co.; he took it over alone in 1870, sold out and went into malting, and made a fortune. Most of it went in the depression of 1877, the year before he ran for mayor.

narrative_blocks.header: He won as a Democrat by fourteen hundred
narrative_blocks.body: Detroit had a hundred thousand people and a mayor-council government when he beat the Republican John Greusel, 6,905 votes to 5,480. William G. Thompson turned him out soundly in 1879 and he never ran for anything again.

narrative_blocks.header: Sent back to Farmington for his schooling
narrative_blocks.body: He was at boarding school in Batavia and then at an academy in Farmington, the town his family had left three generations earlier. At eighteen he clerked for a New York dry-goods house and farmed three years at Flint on his father's Michigan land.

narrative_blocks.header: Broke, he took a clerkship at City Hall
narrative_blocks.body: The setbacks that followed his term left him clerking for the city he had run. The custodian's post carried a pension, and his easy manner got him a name: in his later years Detroit called him Uncle George.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at a daughter's house in Geneva
narrative_blocks.body: Fannie Vallee died at Detroit in 1887, and two of their four daughters were already gone — Francesca at twenty-two and Kate at eleven. He went back to New York and died in June 1909 after a long illness, in the house of one of the two who outlived him.

narrative_blocks.header: He left Rolls-Royce for the Rome embassy
narrative_blocks.body: He was the Washington representative of Rolls-Royce until 1926, when he resigned to enter the commercial service of the United States. He was named commercial attaché at the American embassy in Rome and sailed for the post the Wednesday after his wedding.

narrative_blocks.header: Harvard 1917, then an officer in France
narrative_blocks.body: He graduated with the Harvard class of 1917 and went to France as an officer with the American Expeditionary Force. A Springfield man, son of William Charles Wholean, he kept the Racquet Club in Washington and the Harvard Club in New York.

military_service.role: Officer, American Expeditionary Force

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty years behind his father's counter
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph's father Reuben opened a dry-goods store in Hartford about 1817, and Joseph succeeded him and kept it more than fifty years. Under other hands it was still trading in 1901, as C. S. Hills & Co.

narrative_blocks.header: Vice-president of the Pratt Street Bank
narrative_blocks.body: For many years Joseph was vice-president of the Society for Savings, Hartford's Pratt Street Bank, which his father had served as treasurer. He watched the city grow more than sevenfold in his lifetime.

narrative_blocks.header: A Foot Guard officer to the end
narrative_blocks.body: As a young man Joseph was an officer of the First Company, Governor's Foot Guard, as his younger brother Charles was, and he kept his place in its Veteran Corps, and his enthusiasm for the company, until he died.

narrative_blocks.header: His stepson kept his books
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph married Mary Ann Mather of Westfield on New Year's Day 1835; their only son, Edward Mather Langdon, died at twelve. In 1874 he married the widow Nancy Hubbard Sheldon, whose son Charles kept his books for years.

narrative_blocks.header: A trolley car accident at eighty-three
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph died at Hartford on 3 June 1895, at eighty-three, from the effects of a trolley car accident.

cross_connections.display_label: was a major of the Foot Guard's Veteran Battalion by 1905

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-one years in dry goods
narrative_blocks.body: Charles went into dry goods at Hartford at twenty-three, joined a Boston commission house in 1851, and in 1855 founded the importing firm of Langdon Brothers in New York with his brother Reuben. He retired in 1893, fifty-one years on.

narrative_blocks.header: Thomson, Langdon & Company, 1858 to 1893
narrative_blocks.body: In 1858 Charles joined W. S. Thomson's New York house, which became Thomson, Langdon & Company. The two stayed close friends through twenty years as partners; in 1879 Charles bought Thomson out, and kept the firm's name.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Langdon brothers in the Foot Guard
narrative_blocks.body: Charles was made second lieutenant of the First Company, Governor's Foot Guard, in 1845, on Governor Isaac Toucey's commission. His elder brother Joseph, who kept their father's Hartford dry-goods store, was a Foot Guard officer too.

cross_connections.display_label: commanded Hartford's Governor's Foot Guard from 1802 to 1813

narrative_blocks.header: He carried Colonel House's papers to Paris
narrative_blocks.body: He entered the State Department in 1917 as assistant to its counselor, was secretary of the American War Mission to Paris and London, and secretary to his father-in-law Colonel House through the Peace Conference.

narrative_blocks.header: He hunted German money in American firms
narrative_blocks.body: He and his law partner David Hunter Miller were made special representatives of the State Department, to find financial activity in the United States that might be helping Germany. They practised as Miller and Auchincloss.

narrative_blocks.header: Receiver for Kreuger and the Insull wreckage
narrative_blocks.body: He was trustee or receiver through a run of large failures — Zimmerman & Forshay in 1923, the Eastern Insull units and the American Kreuger & Toll proceedings in 1932, Porto-Rican-American Tobacco in 1940.

narrative_blocks.header: Groton, Yale crew, and Scroll and Key
narrative_blocks.body: He came from Groton to Yale, rowed the freshman four and the university crew in his senior year, and took his degree in 1908. Harvard Law followed, and an LL.B. in 1911.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the Colonel's daughter in 1912
narrative_blocks.body: Janet House married him at Beverly, Massachusetts, on 14 September 1912, and the post as her father's secretary followed. He died of Hodgkin's disease in 1943 at fifty-six, leaving her, a daughter Louise, and a son named for the Colonel.

narrative_blocks.header: She was a suffragette before she married
narrative_blocks.body: Austin knew her as a young woman prominent in the suffrage movement. She left Texas for New York after marrying Gordon Auchincloss in 1912 and made her home there for the rest of her life.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-four years a widow at 950 Park
narrative_blocks.body: Gordon died of Hodgkin's disease in 1943, and she kept the apartment at 950 Park Avenue for the thirty-four years left to her. She died there on 16 January 1977, at eighty-nine.

narrative_blocks.header: She worked for the charity he had chaired
narrative_blocks.body: Gordon had been a director of the New York Association for the Blind from 1926 and ran its Lighthouse drive in 1939; she was still working for it decades after his death. Their son carried the Colonel's name on.

notable.notable_blurb: Woodrow Wilson's closest adviser

narrative_blocks.header: The colonelcy was a thank-you, not a rank
narrative_blocks.body: Governor James Hogg made him a lieutenant colonel on his military staff in July 1893, for running the campaign that saved him. No unit came with it and no duty; the papers shortened it to colonel and he answered to it for life.

narrative_blocks.header: He made four governors and held no office
narrative_blocks.body: Hogg in 1892, Culberson in 1894, Sayers in 1898 and Lanham in 1902 all reached the Texas governorship with him running it. He called his faction 'our crowd' and never stood for anything himself.

narrative_blocks.header: He refused the cabinet and took a bedroom
narrative_blocks.body: Wilson offered him any post but State, and he took none of them, saying he would serve wherever and whenever possible. He was given living quarters inside the White House instead.

narrative_blocks.header: He published a dictator novel anonymously
narrative_blocks.body: Philip Dru: Administrator came out in 1912 with no name on it — the hero wins a civil war, makes himself dictator, and reforms the country by decree. Wilson's Interior Secretary wrote that the President came to Philip Dru in the end.

narrative_blocks.header: Wilson never spoke to him again after Paris
narrative_blocks.body: Wilson decided at Paris that he had given away too much on the Council of Ten, sidelined him, and threw his son-in-law Gordon Auchincloss off the American commission for speaking slightingly of the President. They came home in 1919 and never spoke again.

narrative_blocks.header: Paderewski paid for his statue in Warsaw
narrative_blocks.body: Polish independence went into the Fourteen Points at his urging, and Poland has counted him a hero since. Paderewski financed a monument to him in 1932, in Skaryszewski Park in Warsaw.

narrative_blocks.header: His father ran cotton past the Union blockade
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas William House ran cotton through Matamoros past the Union blockade, trading it for equipment and ammunition. His son's diaries record a settled racism; as a boy he and his friends tormented freed slaves in the street.

narrative_blocks.header: She founded the San Francisco Ballet Guild
narrative_blocks.body: She was its founder and its first president, and a patron of the ballet for the rest of her life. Not long before she died she gave her collection of ballet books to the San Francisco Dance Archives.

narrative_blocks.header: The Prince of Wales praised her beauty
narrative_blocks.body: As a young woman she was a friend of the Prince of Wales, later Edward VIII, who called her the most beautiful girl in America. She sat on the board of the de Young Museum and handled the social arrangements in 1945 when the United Nations was founded in San Francisco.

narrative_blocks.header: Three husbands, and a ranch at Marbella
narrative_blocks.body: Charles William Dabney Jr. married her in 1925 and was dead by 1938; she was Mrs. Juilliard McDonald next, and last the wife of the artist James Bodrero. They divided their years between San Francisco and a ranch at Marbella in Spain.

narrative_blocks.header: Two cookbooks for multiple sclerosis research
narrative_blocks.body: Roxana wrote Golden Gate Gourmet, two volumes published in the 1950s and 1960s to raise money for multiple sclerosis research, the disease that had struck her husband in 1950. For thirty years she was vice president of the Northern California MS Society and president of its auxiliary.

narrative_blocks.header: One of Vogue's American Women in 1949
narrative_blocks.body: Vogue featured Roxana among its American Women in 1949. In the war she had served on the headquarters staff of the American Women's Voluntary Services, and she sat four years on the San Francisco Cotillion Committee.

narrative_blocks.header: From cattle ranches to Main Street Books
narrative_blocks.body: Roxana and her husband kept a house in San Francisco and ran cattle in Santa Barbara, where she had grown up, then in Sonoma County until 1959, raising quarter horses. From their ranch near St. Helena she became co-owner of Main Street Books.

narrative_blocks.header: President of the San Francisco Ballet Auxiliary
narrative_blocks.body: Roxana was president of the San Francisco Ballet Auxiliary for four years; her mother, Geraldine, had founded the San Francisco Ballet Guild. She also sat eight years on the Sarah Dix Hamlin School's board of trustees and six on St. Luke's Hospital Women's Board.

narrative_blocks.header: Married eight days past her seventeenth birthday
narrative_blocks.body: She married William Robertson, a young pilot of twenty-four, on 22 November 1943, eight days after she turned seventeen. The wedding filled San Francisco's society columns for days.

sources.label: Obituary, Roxana Robertson, Napa Valley Register, 6 Sep 1988

narrative_blocks.header: A combat pilot with the Flying Cross
narrative_blocks.body: William flew as a combat pilot in the Second World War and won the Distinguished Flying Cross and the Air Medal. By 1945 his father, a colonel recalled from retirement, was deputy chief of staff of the 21st Bomber Command on Saipan and Guam.

narrative_blocks.header: A wedding the society pages ran for days
narrative_blocks.body: He was a young pilot of twenty-four when he married Roxana Dabney on 22 November 1943, eight days after her seventeenth birthday. San Francisco's society columns ran the wedding for days.

narrative_blocks.header: Cattle in Santa Barbara, quarter horses in Sonoma
narrative_blocks.body: The Robertsons kept their house in San Francisco and ran cattle on a ranch in Santa Barbara, then on one in Sonoma County from 1945 to 1959, where they also raised quarter horses. In 1959 they bought a ranch near St. Helena.

narrative_blocks.header: Multiple sclerosis struck in 1950
narrative_blocks.body: In 1950, seven years after the wedding, William was stricken by multiple sclerosis. He lived with it twenty-six years and died at the Veterans Home in Yountville in May 1976, at fifty-six; Roxana spent thirty years raising money to fight the disease.

narrative_blocks.header: His father was among the Army's first pilots
narrative_blocks.body: His father, William Abbott Robertson Sr., left the cavalry for the Signal Corps Aviation School at San Diego in 1916, and in 1917 commanded the 1st Aero Squadron at Columbus, New Mexico. William was born in San Diego in 1919, while his father was flying out of Rockwell Field.

narrative_blocks.header: His father went missing in the Mexican desert
narrative_blocks.body: In 1917 his father, then a lieutenant, and Lt. Col. Harry Gore Bishop were lost in the desert of northern Mexico with no food or water. Cavalry, aviators and five civilian search parties went into the sand wastes after them, and both men came out alive.

narrative_blocks.header: Grandson of Ambassador Charlemagne Tower
narrative_blocks.body: His mother, Helen Tower Robertson, was born in Santa Barbara in 1894 and died there in 1964; she, William and Roxana all lie in Santa Barbara Cemetery. Her father was Charlemagne Tower, the American ambassador to Russia and to Germany.

narrative_blocks.header: She buried three of her five children
narrative_blocks.body: John died at thirty-seven in 1863, Sarah Cornelia at thirty-nine in 1871 and Abner at forty-one in 1876. She died at Middletown the following March, six years after her husband.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the paper's editorials from seventeen
narrative_blocks.body: From the age of seventeen he wrote for his father's Constitution, and for twenty years he prepared its leading editorial. He took his Wesleyan degree in 1847, taught in the high school, then read theology at Andover and New Haven.

narrative_blocks.header: Admitted to the bar, then back to divinity
narrative_blocks.body: Failing health turned him from theology to law; he read with Arthur B. Calef in Charles Whittlesey's office and was admitted in 1852. He returned to divinity, took the new Congregational church at Middle Haddam in 1856, and gave it up seven years later.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at thirty-seven, unmarried
narrative_blocks.body: The pulmonary trouble that had shown early killed him in August 1863. He never married, and his father outlived him by eight years.

narrative_blocks.header: She married her dead sister's husband
narrative_blocks.body: She lived at home until Sarah Cornelia's last illness, then went to Waterbury and took the place of mother to her sister's three children. Seven years after Sarah Cornelia died she married Edward Johnson herself.

narrative_blocks.header: Three children, and dead at thirty-nine
narrative_blocks.body: She married John Edward Johnson of Waterbury in October 1852 and lived at Beacon Falls and Waterbury. She died in March 1871 leaving Harriet, Edward Hall and Herbert Newton, and her sister came from Middletown to raise them.

narrative_blocks.header: He added a daily edition in 1872
narrative_blocks.body: His father died in 1871 and he became sole editor and proprietor of the Constitution. In July 1872 he began a daily edition and kept it running four years, and his last piece of writing was the editorial in the closing number explaining why it stopped.

narrative_blocks.header: He died of hard work, honorable but injudicious
narrative_blocks.body: A month confined to the house with no disease apparent ended in his death at forty-one, in spite of exceptional physical strength. That was the verdict on him: he died of hard work, mental and physical, honorable but injudicious.

narrative_blocks.header: The city trusted him with its money
narrative_blocks.body: He was a trustee of the Middletown Savings Bank and a director of the People's Fire Insurance Company, and sat on the common council and the board of education. He left his family one of the best houses in the city.

bio.bio_blurb: Editor and proprietor of the Constitution

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote for the paper her father founded
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband took over the Middletown Constitution and ran it for several years, and she gave him editorial help the family reckoned equal to her brother John's. She had read history closely since girlhood and shared his scholarly tastes.

narrative_blocks.header: Six children, and one who lived nine months
narrative_blocks.body: Anna Maria came in 1868, then the twins John Newton and Ward in December 1873. John died the next September; Sarah Newton, Caroline Sumner and Flora Adele followed.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father's works were the Russell mill
narrative_blocks.body: Daniel Harris was for years with the Russell Manufacturing Company at South Farms, and she was his and Hulda Coe's only child. She finished at Miss Robertson's Seminary for Young Ladies, was widowed at thirty-five, and outlived her husband by thirty-seven years.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a Berkeley Divinity man in 1899
narrative_blocks.body: Archibald Ravenscroft Balsley, an Episcopal clergyman out of the Berkeley Divinity School, married her in June 1899 and took her to Port Henry on Lake Champlain. Their son Kenneth came in 1901. She was a skilled musician and travelled a great deal.

narrative_blocks.header: He read law in his mother's cousin's office
narrative_blocks.body: He came to New Haven in 1894 and entered the office of Henry G. Newton as clerk and student. He took his Yale law degree in 1899, was admitted the same year, and the three of them formed Newton, Church & Hewitt.

narrative_blocks.header: Her forebear served in Talcott's regiment
narrative_blocks.body: Abraham Cruttenden came to Guilford from Cranbrook in 1639 in a party of four hundred and forty-eight, and his descendant of the same name fought in Colonel Talcott's regiment in the Revolution. Her father's grandfather Timothy Rossiter served in that war too.

narrative_blocks.header: A Rossiter did the colony's first autopsy
narrative_blocks.body: Dr. Bryan Rossiter of her family was the first physician in that part of the state to use anaesthetics in surgery, and the first to perform an autopsy in the Colony of Connecticut. The Rossiters had come with Edward Rossiter, a director of the Dorchester Colony, in June 1630.

narrative_blocks.header: First honors at sixteen, then Holyoke
narrative_blocks.body: She entered the Middletown High School at twelve and graduated at sixteen with first honours, going straight to Mount Holyoke and taking her degree there in June 1912. A summer at Harvard followed, and then the medical department of Johns Hopkins.

narrative_blocks.header: She died the year after Johns Hopkins
narrative_blocks.body: The medical course had barely begun when she died in 1913, at twenty-one. Her brother Roger Rossiter had gone two years before her, at seventeen.

narrative_blocks.header: Ward and Daisy adopted him at Durham
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Durham in January 1910 and taken into the Church household there. Ward had been born on a New Jersey farm and made his life in New Haven law; the boy grew up between the two.

narrative_blocks.header: His organ and piano were his pleasure
narrative_blocks.body: He was at the Middletown High School and had a natural talent for music, a very sweet voice as a boy and a correct ear. An accident ended his life at eighteen, and the piano his father gave the church carries his name.

narrative_blocks.header: She was organist of the First Church
narrative_blocks.body: Cleman Burr of Durham was her father and she came out of the Clinton High School. She played the organ at the First Church in Durham for several years before marrying Jonathan Edward Newton in May 1912.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept the professor's house for sixty years
narrative_blocks.body: She married William Seymour Tyler at Binghamton in September 1839 and went with him to Amherst, where he taught Greek for the rest of the century. Their four sons were raised in the pre-Revolutionary house on the hill that gave Tyler Place its name.

narrative_blocks.header: Her namesake became Smith's librarian
narrative_blocks.body: Amelia Whiting Tyler, named for her, was brought up in the house on the hill after her mother died. She went from it to Smith College, stayed on as the college librarian, and wrote the closing chapter of her grandfather's autobiography.

narrative_blocks.body: Samuel J. Tilden, governor of New York and the Democratic nominee for president in 1876, was his first cousin. Doubleday was dead by 1857, before any of that, having given his last years to unpaid missionary work in Brooklyn.

bio.title: Colonel

narrative_blocks.header: His hat business failed in 1876
narrative_blocks.body: He was a hatter in Brooklyn, and the business went under in 1876. His fourteen-year-old son left school for good and went out to work, and never went back to it.

notable.notable_blurb: Publisher; founder of Doubleday

narrative_blocks.header: Publishing was a rich man’s hobby before him
narrative_blocks.body: Before him the trade was a literary avocation for wealthy men. He built national advertising, collected sets, subscription packages, reprints and book clubs, and gave one reason for the 1927 Doran merger: to sell more books.

narrative_blocks.header: He left Scribner’s and borrowed on Carnegie’s name
narrative_blocks.body: Eighteen years at Scribner’s ended when Charles Scribner refused one book idea too many. Andrew Carnegie told him to walk into the best bank in New York and make them understand he was doing them a favour — and if they refused, to say that Carnegie would lend it.

narrative_blocks.header: Five houses turned down The Jungle
narrative_blocks.body: Upton Sinclair’s meatpacking exposé had been refused five times when it reached him, and the industry threatened to sue if he published. He advertised hard and fed excerpts to the papers; it sold a hundred thousand copies that year.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought a printing press at ten
narrative_blocks.body: He bought his own press with saved coins, then earned the cost back printing circulars for Brooklyn shopkeepers. When his father’s hat business failed in 1876 he left school for good and took a copy boy’s job at Scribner’s.

narrative_blocks.header: Kipling said he invented the edition
narrative_blocks.body: He proposed collecting Kipling’s scattered works into a uniform set, which meant prying the copyrights out of a dozen English houses. Kipling inscribed his copy to the man who invented the edition, and gave him the nickname Effendi from his initials.

narrative_blocks.header: He backed literary agents when rivals refused
narrative_blocks.body: He was among the first publishers to deal with agents rather than fight them, and pushed royalties up when Henry Holt held anything above a tenth to be immoral.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife died on Red Cross service
narrative_blocks.body: Neltje was serving as a Red Cross commissioner at Canton when she died there in February 1918. He married Florence Van Wyck before the year was out.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote about yawls, ranches and inventors
narrative_blocks.body: He published across four decades — A Gunner Aboard the Yankee, Cattle Ranch to College and A Year in a Yawl early on, then Photography is Fun, Long Island and Tree Neighbors in his last years.

narrative_blocks.header: His first book came out of the war
narrative_blocks.body: He served in the naval militia through the Spanish-American War, and the first book he published, in 1898, was A Gunner Aboard the Yankee. He joined his brother's firm afterwards.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote Marconi's story for boys
narrative_blocks.body: Stories of Inventors, in 1904, carried Guglielmo Marconi's wireless experiments and Alberto Santos-Dumont's airships to young readers, told as adventure rather than instruction.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran his brother's editorial department
narrative_blocks.body: For most of his working life he directed the editorial department at Doubleday, Page, having come in as its advertising manager in 1909. He died at Glen Cove, where he lived at a place called Meadow Springs.

served on the Yankee's sister ship Prairie and died homeward in 1898

narrative_blocks.header: Two cousins married on the same June day
narrative_blocks.body: Frank Nelson Doubleday married Neltje Blanchan on 9 June 1886. She married Starr Murphy on 9 June 1887 — the same date a year later, two first cousins out of the same family.

narrative_blocks.header: She brought Starr Murphy to Montclair
narrative_blocks.body: Her father John Mason Doubleday was a Montclair man, and it was after marrying her in 1887 that Murphy settled in the town. There he met Frederick Gates, who carried him into the Rockefeller work.

narrative_blocks.header: Rockefeller came into the family through her
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband became John D. Rockefeller's personal counsel in 1904. Four years later her first cousin Frank Nelson Doubleday began running Rockefeller's memoir in his own World's Work, having met him — by one account — through a cousin.

narrative_blocks.header: He vetted every large Rockefeller gift
narrative_blocks.body: For seventeen years he ran the searching examinations that came before any important Rockefeller donation. He was counsel to the Rockefeller Foundation and one of its founders, and a trustee of the General Education Board.

narrative_blocks.header: A Harvard gift got him the position
narrative_blocks.body: The first thing Rockefeller put to him was the legal side of a gift for new buildings at the Harvard Medical School. He handled it so well that he was asked to give up his own firm and move into the Standard Oil Building at 26 Broadway, which he did in 1904.

narrative_blocks.header: Summa cum laude at Columbia in 1883
narrative_blocks.body: Adelphi Academy in Brooklyn, then Amherst in 1881, then the Columbia law school, where he took his degree summa cum laude. He was admitted to the New York bar that May.

narrative_blocks.header: Montclair gave him a wife and a career
narrative_blocks.body: He settled at Montclair in 1887, the year he married Julia Brush Doubleday, and it was there he met Frederick T. Gates. Gates was the man who carried him into the Rockefeller work.

narrative_blocks.header: Two operations at Daytona, and no relief
narrative_blocks.body: An intestinal obstruction took him while he was Rockefeller's guest in Florida. Dr. Stuart McGuire of Richmond operated a second time on the Sunday, and he died at nine the next morning; the body went back to Montclair.

narrative_blocks.header: His name came from the Leech of Salem
narrative_blocks.body: The Starr came down through his mother's grandmother Harriette Starr from Dr. Comfort Starr, the physician they called the Leech of Salem. His father was the Rev. Elijah D. Murphy and his mother a daughter of the Rev. Simeon Smith Jocelyn of New Haven.

narrative_blocks.header: He retired after thirty-six years in oil
narrative_blocks.body: He was operational manager for a Columbia oil company office for thirty-six years and retired in 1956. He died at Aiken in South Carolina, where he had settled.

narrative_blocks.header: He was eighteen when America went to war
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Montclair in January 1899, he had just turned eighteen when the United States entered the First World War, and he served in it.

notable.notable_blurb: Amherst's Greek professor and its historian

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-six years at one college
narrative_blocks.body: He came to Amherst in 1829, graduated valedictorian in 1830, and never really left: tutor, then professor of Latin and Greek from 1836, then Williston professor of Greek from 1847 until 1893, then emeritus until he died.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the history of his own college
narrative_blocks.body: The History of Amherst College During Its First Half Century came out in 1873 and a second volume covering its first five presidents in 1895. He also edited Tacitus, Plato and Demosthenes for the schools, and wrote The Theology of the Greek Poets.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave Amherst a distinction it never had
narrative_blocks.body: In his history he claimed Amherst was the first American college to put its diplomas in Latin. Harvard was first, and the claim has been quietly corrected ever since.

narrative_blocks.header: Two houses on two campuses carry his name
narrative_blocks.body: He was one of the original trustees of Smith College, and Tyler House there is named for him; so is a dormitory at Amherst. He also presided over the trustees of Williston Academy and of Mount Holyoke Seminary.

narrative_blocks.header: A professor ordained at forty-nine
narrative_blocks.body: He read theology at Andover and under Dr. Skinner in New York before he ever took a chair, and was ordained a Congregational minister at North Amherst in October 1859. Harvard gave him a doctorate of divinity in 1857 and a doctorate of laws in 1886.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a Whiting of Binghamton
narrative_blocks.body: Amelia Ogden Whiting married him on 4 September 1839 and they raised four sons on the Amherst hill. He was the son of Joab and Nabby Seymour Tyler of Harford, Pennsylvania.

narrative_blocks.header: Hit in the chin, then in the knee
narrative_blocks.body: A shell caught him in the chin and neck at the Third Battle of Winchester on 19 September 1864, and a bullet took his knee at Petersburg on 25 March 1865. He fought in thirty engagements with the Sixth Corps of the Army of the Potomac.

narrative_blocks.header: Colonel on paper, never on the rolls
narrative_blocks.body: He went in as a first lieutenant of Company F, 37th Massachusetts, in August 1862, made captain in 1863 and major in March 1865. He was appointed lieutenant colonel that May and colonel in June, and was mustered into neither, having been honorably mustered out five days before the second commission.

narrative_blocks.header: His son finished the book from letters
narrative_blocks.body: He was near the end of a first draft of his war recollections when he died, and his son William edited it into Recollections of the Civil War, published in 1912 with the diary entries and the letters he had written from the seat of war. The chapters run from the Wilderness and Spotsylvania through Cold Harbor and Petersburg to Winchester.

narrative_blocks.header: He built Plainfield its public library
narrative_blocks.body: He was a founder and vice-president of the Plainfield Public Library board and one of the first trustees of Muhlenberg Hospital. He sat two terms on the common council and five years on the board of education, and left the library a bequest whose income was to buy books.

narrative_blocks.header: He died nine months after his wife
narrative_blocks.body: Eliza went in 1906 and he followed on 2 July 1907, unexpectedly, at a New York hospital after an operation he had been expected to survive. His library of rare books went with the house at 525 West Seventh Street in Plainfield.

narrative_blocks.header: First prize at the Philadelphia Centennial
narrative_blocks.body: The firm of Rioden & Tyler made turbine water wheels, and took the first prize for them at the Centennial Exhibition at Philadelphia in 1876. He kept the works from Mount Holly.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at forty-one, remarried at forty-four
narrative_blocks.body: Sallie Blakely Sherrerd of Scranton married him in September 1872 and died at Mount Holly ten years later, leaving a daughter of seven. He married Nellie Ramburger Bickings in October 1885.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught where his father was trustee
narrative_blocks.body: Amherst gave him his degree in 1865 and he began teaching at Knox College in Galesburg. He came back east to the chair of Greek and Latin at Smith College, where his father was one of the original trustees, and stayed there the rest of his working life.

narrative_blocks.header: He gathered the Greek lyric poets
narrative_blocks.body: Selections from the Greek Lyric Poets came out in 1879 with his historical introduction and notes. He wrote in the preface that American colleges studied Greek poetry while leaving out the very songs that had most to do with the common life of common people.

narrative_blocks.header: The largest stone in Knox County
narrative_blocks.body: His father found a great rock sitting on his desk at Galesburg and asked him what he was doing with it. Father, he said, this is the largest stone in Knox County, Illinois.

narrative_blocks.header: Valedictorian, then Göttingen and Leipzig
narrative_blocks.body: He was fitted at the Amherst high school and at Williston, took his degree in 1873 as valedictorian, and taught a year at Andover. Two years of theology at Union were followed by three in Germany, at Göttingen and then at Leipzig.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty years of biology at Amherst
narrative_blocks.body: He came back in 1879 as instructor in biology and held the chair from 1882 as Stone Professor, and Colgate gave him a doctorate in 1888. Men who had studied under him came back at Commencement for the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave the Morse lectures on evolution
narrative_blocks.body: Union Theological Seminary asked him for the Morse lectures in the spring of 1895 and he published them, enlarged, as The Whence and Whither of Man. Growth and Education followed in 1907 and Man in the Light of Evolution in 1908.

narrative_blocks.header: The brass kettle on his desk
narrative_blocks.body: A vast open brass kettle stood on the desk in his third-floor study and every letter he did not want to bother with went into it. Leave letters in that kettle for three months, he said, and most of them you need not answer.

narrative_blocks.header: He looked upon the work of the day
narrative_blocks.body: His wife Elizabeth kept a rose garden and competed at it with the president's wife next door; he did no gardening at all. Every evening he went out and, like the Lord, looked upon the work of the day.

narrative_blocks.header: A senator for a grandfather, Bradford behind him
narrative_blocks.body: Her grandfather was Elijah Boardman, United States senator from Connecticut, and she traced a lineal descent from Governor William Bradford of the Mayflower. Her grandmother was an own cousin of Jeremiah Mason, the constitutional lawyer and senator from New Hampshire.

narrative_blocks.header: Raised by an aunt at New Milford
narrative_blocks.body: Her father was the Rev. Dr. John Frederick Schroeder of Trinity parish, New York, and she was born in the city. After her mother died she lived at New Milford with her aunt Cornelia E. Boardman until she married Col. Tyler in 1869.

narrative_blocks.header: She died on a Sunday morning at home
narrative_blocks.body: Heart failure took her at Plainfield on 14 October 1906, and her husband followed nine months later. She belonged to the Mayflower societies of two states, the Society of Colonial Wars and the Daughters of the Revolution.

narrative_blocks.header: He put his father's war into print
narrative_blocks.body: His father died in 1907 with the manuscript unfinished. Chapter thirteen is where it stops as he wrote it; from there his son carried the story on out of the letters written on the march and on the battlefield, keeping the language, which is not always approved, for the sake of its freshness and vigor.

narrative_blocks.header: Autobiographies of the ranks are few
narrative_blocks.body: There are many histories of the war and autobiographies of great generals, he wrote, but autobiographies of the soldier in the camp and in the ranks are few. He verified each event he could and footnoted the authorities, and signed the preface at New York in April 1912.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped start the Columbia Law Review
narrative_blocks.body: Amherst in 1898, Columbia law in 1901, and one of the founders of the Columbia Law Review in the years it began. He practised in New York and lived his whole life at Plainfield.

narrative_blocks.header: Apples in Washington, wheat in Saskatchewan
narrative_blocks.body: Besides the law he raised apples in Washington state and held a wheat farm in Saskatchewan with a college friend, and he travelled widely. His wife did sculpture and pottery.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter was in Florence when he died
narrative_blocks.body: He died at his Plainfield home on the night of 21 March 1955, at seventy-nine. His wife was coming back from a visit to Italy; his sons John and David were at Edison Township and Worthington, and his daughter was living at Florence.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father talked the parks into being
narrative_blocks.body: Robert Sterling Yard was a reporter and editor at the Century and the New York Herald when Stephen Mather recruited him to argue for an independent parks agency, and paid his salary out of pocket to keep him at it. The writing and lecturing they did together helped carry the National Park Service into law.

narrative_blocks.header: He claimed kinship from the city streets
narrative_blocks.body: At the National Park Conference in 1915 he told the delegates: I, the treader of dusty city streets, boldly claim common kinship with you of the plains, the mountains, and the glaciers. He was no outdoorsman, and said so.

narrative_blocks.header: One of eight who began the Wilderness Society
narrative_blocks.body: He was a founding member of the Wilderness Society in 1935 and its first president from 1937 until his death eight years later. He had been the first executive secretary of the National Parks Association before that.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother died when she was seven
narrative_blocks.body: Sallie Sherrerd died at Mount Holly in September 1882 and the child went up to Amherst to her grandparents, and grew up in the house on the hill. Her father married again three years later.

narrative_blocks.header: She went from that house to Smith
narrative_blocks.body: Her grandfather was one of the original trustees of Smith College and its Tyler House carries his name. She took her degree there, stayed on as the college librarian, and held the post until she retired.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote the last chapter of his book
narrative_blocks.body: The closing chapter of her grandfather's autobiography, called Closing Days, is hers. She was buried at Wildwood in Amherst beside the grandparents who raised her, not at Hillside with her father.
