narrative_blocks.header: Galesburg to Northampton, and never back
narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Galesburg, in Knox County, Illinois, on 7 January 1843, and was in her twenties when a young Amherst graduate came out to teach at Knox College. She married Henry Mather Tyler, went east with him for good, and buried a ten-month-old daughter in Massachusetts before her last child was born at Northampton in 1879. She died at Northampton on 18 January 1918, still in the college town she had come east to.

narrative_blocks.header: He worked for Colonel House's Inquiry
narrative_blocks.body: The commission House assembled to prepare for a peace treaty needed someone on the Balkans and the Near East, because almost nobody in the country knew the region. He spent his last summers before the armistice gathering that material.

narrative_blocks.header: A war history written while the war ran
narrative_blocks.body: The Roots of the War came out from the Century Company in 1918, five hundred and fifty pages of non-technical European history from 1870 to 1914, written with the Minnesota historian William Stearns Davis and with William Anderson. He was working for the Inquiry when it appeared and was teaching at Minnesota himself the year after.

narrative_blocks.header: His book came out after he died
narrative_blocks.body: He was still holding it back at the end of his life, waiting for the German government to publish Die Grosse Politik so he could check what he had found elsewhere. The European Powers and the Near East, 1875-1908 was issued by the University of Minnesota in 1925, two years after his death at thirty-eight, with an editorial note signed by Guy Stanton Ford.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at thirty-one, she took a doctorate
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband died in 1923 and she went straight back for the degree, then taught in the Minnesota history department from 1927 until 1960, entering as an instructor and leaving as a full professor. She had come up from Knox College in Galesburg.

narrative_blocks.header: Freedom's Ferment sold a hundred thousand
narrative_blocks.body: The book came out in 1944 and was reprinted many times; the paperback sold a hundred thousand copies. She taught American colonial history and American social and intellectual history, and sat on the American Studies committee when the field was new.

narrative_blocks.header: She cleared the Amherst house in one summer
narrative_blocks.body: When her mother-in-law died in 1937 she emptied a house nobody had thrown anything away in since 1880, and sent the Tyler letters and her father-in-law's desk to Amherst College. What could not be given away burned in the driveway for seven days.

narrative_blocks.header: Old French at Columbia, then the Red Cross
narrative_blocks.body: She took her degree at Smith and a doctorate at Columbia in Old French, then went to France as a secretary for the American Red Cross. She caught influenza caring for refugees after the armistice and died at Sedan on 22 February 1919, three months into the peace, at thirty-one.

narrative_blocks.header: She learned to curtsey for the royal visits
narrative_blocks.body: She grew up in Vancouver at York House School for Girls, where the schooling included being prepared to curtsey to the British Royal Family. Summers were on Bainbridge Island, roller skating at the Grange, riding through the Douglas fir, and rolling logs in Puget Sound.

narrative_blocks.header: She resigned from the Junior League
narrative_blocks.body: She called herself nonclubby, and liked the Seattle Symphony because ours is a working board, we don't just sit there. She had quit the Junior League over it: my field is money-raising, and the League does not count the time I put in as volunteer service.

narrative_blocks.header: The poet talked to her like a teacher
narrative_blocks.body: Theodore Roethke was often a guest at her parents' place, and when they talked he would talk about poetry and the poets of his generation as a teacher would. He drowned in the pool there in 1963, and the family filled it in and made a rock garden of it.

narrative_blocks.header: A foundation for women wanting better work
narrative_blocks.body: She founded the Eulalie Bloedel Schneider Foundation to pay for job training in Seattle for low-income youth and for women trying to get better work. She sat on the boards of the Symphony and the Opera, and in 2012 endowed a fund for the Opera's artistic work.

narrative_blocks.header: The only calling she meant to excel at
narrative_blocks.body: Being a mother to her three children was, she said, her highest personal purpose, and homemaking is the only professional calling I care to excel at. She raised them abroad and kept them rooted by telephone.

narrative_blocks.header: She moved to a village three cows wide
narrative_blocks.body: After the divorce in 1964 she took her three children to Choulex, a farming village in the Canton of Geneva, and stayed in Switzerland fifty-two years. The village's main street was three cows wide.

narrative_blocks.header: You call that art? She loved the question
narrative_blocks.body: She grew up hearing you call that art, and came to love the question: first of all, it is rude, and rudeness is fascinating. Most of my art can slide both ways, she wrote, as art or thing, and sometimes my things can become art.

narrative_blocks.header: She gave twenty-four friends a shelf each
narrative_blocks.body: For an exhibition at her parents' gallery she invited twenty-four friends to show what they collected, one eight-foot shelf apiece: hair wreaths, folding chairs, chain-saw carvings, magician's stands, NASCAR memorabilia. Her own Space Needle tchotchkes and her grandmother's Staffordshire figurines went in beside her mother's Jeff Koons.

narrative_blocks.header: She wanted a fortress cut into the rock
narrative_blocks.body: For a weekend house in the San Juans she had the architect blast into a rocky outcropping rather than build on top of it. What I wanted was a fortress, she said; it was not going to be sitting on the rock, it was going to be in the rock.

narrative_blocks.header: He left Dia to run the family firm
narrative_blocks.body: He practised law, then ran the Dia Art Foundation in New York from 1985 to 1994, when his father and the family company's chairman asked him to take it over. The request came out of nowhere: literally a month before it came up, I don't think I'd given it any thought.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought them on faith they would grow
narrative_blocks.body: R. D. Merrill, his great-grandfather, bought Pacific Northwest timberland for descendants he would never meet. He recognised that it was a long-term investment, but he also recognised that families are long-term entities, he says. He bought these on faith that they would grow and become valuable for his descendants, and that's been true.

narrative_blocks.header: A man introducing Women take over
narrative_blocks.body: Introducing Elles, the Seattle Art Museum's show of women artists from the Centre Pompidou, he said he felt the irony of a man being the one to present a show marketed as Women take over. If a woman were in his shoes, he added, she would probably feel conflicted.

narrative_blocks.header: The third Wright to run that museum board
narrative_blocks.body: His father was president of the Seattle Art Museum's board from 1977, his mother from 1986, and he chaired it himself. The collection they built reached the museum in pieces across sixty years.

narrative_blocks.header: He photographs sunsets in broken mirrors
narrative_blocks.body: He embeds the strip of the frame, fragmented glass and silver leaf in layered and re-photographed images. The Broken Mirror / Evening Sky prints are sunsets reflected in shattered studio mirrors, and read like abstract stained glass.

narrative_blocks.header: One last project before dismantling the darkroom
narrative_blocks.body: In the fall of 2007 I had concluded that the alchemical magic of the silver-based medium was dying a slow death, he said, and decided to do one last project before dismantling my darkroom. He photographed silver leaf on glass, then dropped more leaf onto the wet print to adhere and tarnish in the picture plane.

narrative_blocks.header: A MoMA show in 1978 set him going
narrative_blocks.body: John Szarkowski's Mirrors and Windows at the Museum of Modern Art was formative when he was young, and he has been trying to make pictures with a mirror as the subject ever since. A photograph and a mirror are both silver-based picture planes.

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve feet of scattered dead flies
narrative_blocks.body: Fly Disaster Scroll is a twelve-foot scroll of silk and paper carrying his photographs of the scattered remains of flies, presented as continuous imagery the way a hand-painted Chinese or Japanese scroll is.

narrative_blocks.header: The third Weyerhaeuser to run the company
narrative_blocks.body: He was a grandson of Frederick Weyerhaeuser, who with fifteen partners bought fourteen hundred square miles of Washington forest from the Northern Pacific Railway in 1900, the largest private land deal in America to that time. He led the company himself, and his son followed him.

narrative_blocks.header: He registered as James Paul Jones
narrative_blocks.body: Told to book into Seattle's Ambassador Hotel under a false name and wait, he ran the personal advertisements the kidnappers dictated: we are ready, Percy Minnie. A note from his son came enclosed with the instructions, saying he was safe.

narrative_blocks.header: The first attempt failed over a missing note
narrative_blocks.body: He drove out with the money, found the second signal cloth on the dirt road but no note under it, and after hours of waiting drove back to the hotel. An anonymous caller told him next morning it was his last chance.

narrative_blocks.header: He walked away and left the money running
narrative_blocks.body: The next night he went from stake to stake following notes hidden in tin cans, until one told him to leave the car and walk back toward Seattle. A hundred yards on he heard a noise in the bushes; a man ran out, got into the car and drove off.

narrative_blocks.header: Summa cum laude at Smith in 1920
narrative_blocks.body: The daughter of a Seattle attorney, she went from Summit School to Broadway High School and took her degree summa cum laude from Smith College in 1920, and was elected to Phi Beta Kappa. She married a Weyerhaeuser the following year.

narrative_blocks.header: A trustee of Reed and the historical society
narrative_blocks.body: She was a past president of the Tacoma Junior League, a trustee of Reed College in Portland and a board member of the Washington State Historical Society. She belonged to the Sunset Club in Seattle, the Tacoma Garden Club and the Little Church on the Prairie.

narrative_blocks.header: Idaho first, then Tacoma for forty-six years
narrative_blocks.body: The first years of the marriage were at Coeur d'Alene and Lewiston, in Idaho, and she came to Tacoma about 1934. She died at Palm Springs after a long illness, leaving nineteen grandchildren and six great-grandchildren.

narrative_blocks.header: She left canvas for steel and stone
narrative_blocks.body: She began in the minimalist style and by the mid-1970s had largely left canvas for nontraditional supports, drawn to their texture and to what they let chance and process do. From the 1990s she worked on steel, painting it with Rust-Oleum bought at the hardware store.

narrative_blocks.header: The Art Students League under Edwin Dickinson
narrative_blocks.body: She left Annie Wright Seminary in Tacoma in 1953 for Sarah Lawrence, took her degree in 1957, and came to New York in 1959 to study at the Art Students League under the figurative painters Edwin Dickinson, Julien Levi and George Grosz.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-six contemporary women artists, 1971
narrative_blocks.body: Her work was in Twenty Six Contemporary Women Artists at the Aldrich in 1971 and in the same museum's 52 Artists: A Feminist Milestone in 2022. Her first solo shows were at the artist-run cooperative 55 Mercer.

narrative_blocks.header: Notes on Paint won a design award
narrative_blocks.body: She has published artist's books documenting her long-term and site-specific projects: Notes on Paint in 1990, which took an AIGA certificate of excellence and a Northwest Design Award, then Time and Materials, Oil and Water, and Public/Private.

narrative_blocks.header: She still works outdoors, in the weather
narrative_blocks.body: Her Pacific Northwest upbringing runs through the work and she has gone on making it outdoors through her career. Her paintings are in the Metropolitan, the Whitney, the Smithsonian American Art Museum and the Tacoma Art Museum.

narrative_blocks.header: She leaves work outside to fade
narrative_blocks.body: She has made site-specific interventions on fences and rock outcroppings and left them unprotected, so the weather takes them down over time. Eva Hesse's way with materials helped push her off canvas in the mid-1970s.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a painter and had two sons
narrative_blocks.body: She married the painter Robert Ryman in 1969 and they had two sons. David Zwirner has represented them both since 2021, two years after his death.

narrative_blocks.header: He guarded the pictures before he painted
narrative_blocks.body: He came to New York in 1952 to be a jazz saxophonist, having never taken an art class, and took a job as a guard at the Museum of Modern Art to leave his mind free. He stayed seven years, and standing in those rooms is what made him start painting in 1953.

narrative_blocks.header: He worked in white for sixty years
narrative_blocks.body: He insisted they were not white paintings: white was how he made other things visible. You can see the coffee very clearly if you spill it on a white shirt, he said, and on a dark shirt you don't see it as well. What painting is, is exactly what people see.

narrative_blocks.header: Coffee filter paper was one of his surfaces
narrative_blocks.body: He put paint on paper, canvas, linen, aluminium, vinyl, newsprint, fibreglass, steel, Plexiglass, tracing paper and coffee filter paper. He left the fasteners, screws, staples and masking tape visible, because a painting's relation to the wall was part of it.

narrative_blocks.header: His first Rothko was painted at the museum
narrative_blocks.body: Untitled, from 1958, was made while he was still a guard and took its cue from Mark Rothko. His first solo show was at the Bianchini Gallery in 1967 and his first museum show at the Guggenheim in 1972.

narrative_blocks.header: He hung two installations himself for decades
narrative_blocks.body: He chose and installed long-term presentations of his own work at the Hallen für neue Kunst in Schaffhausen, where they stood from 1983 to 2014, and at Dia:Beacon from 2003. Robert Storr's retrospective travelled from the Tate to Madrid, New York, San Francisco and Minneapolis.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a painter in 1969
narrative_blocks.body: Merrill Wagner was his second wife; they married in 1969 and had two sons. He died in New York in 2019.

notable.notable_blurb: Casualist sculptor of scrap wood and paint

narrative_blocks.header: He builds with studio sweepings and glue
narrative_blocks.body: He works in a Brooklyn studio from four-by-eight sheets and two-by-four boards, with gorilla glue, scrap metal, studio sweepings and every acrylic from matte to gloss, and leaves the rough edges showing. If a piece comes back from a show he takes it apart for the next: no work is finalised until it finds a new home.

narrative_blocks.header: The sides are the part he thinks about
narrative_blocks.body: The main thing about the edges and the sides, he said in 2009, is that I think about them. When the sides are accounted for, it makes the piece seem more like a thing or an independent entity as opposed to a picture of something.

narrative_blocks.header: Mute colour with a glow on the seams
narrative_blocks.body: He works mostly in white, silver and creamy orange, then puts small touches of bright colour on the edges and seams. The result throws a fluorescent glow back onto the gallery wall and onto the work itself.

narrative_blocks.header: A hundred small objects, casually made
narrative_blocks.body: Monkey Mind Symphony was more than a hundred small pieces, each made quickly and answered by the next, assembled into a show about the distractions of a day. A critic called him a maestro of the quotidian and the contingent.

narrative_blocks.header: Figurative sculpture until his first year
narrative_blocks.body: His early work was emotion-based figurative sculpture, and within a year at the School of Visual Arts he had gone abstract; by his second year he was making small collages, which is where the casual style started.

narrative_blocks.header: Red Brick was a stack of painted wood
narrative_blocks.body: For his 2010 show at DCKT Contemporary he made Red Brick, cut and painted wooden bricks stacked on one another in shades of red and pink. He has since done public commissions at Michigan State and under New York's Percent for Art.

notable.notable_blurb: Sculptor of the Park Avenue roses

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote plays for twelve years first
narrative_blocks.body: He took playwriting classes instead of college and spent twelve years on absurdist plays while working as a line cook. The Encounter, about two drunks who see something in the sky they cannot identify, opened in 1999.

narrative_blocks.header: He had been a sculptor writing plays
narrative_blocks.body: At thirty-two he began sculpting his own characters to see them properly: I took apart my bookshelves and my coat tree and built a hundred papier-mâché figures four feet tall. I realised I had been a sculptor trying to write plays.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-eight roses down Park Avenue
narrative_blocks.body: The Roses stood on the Park Avenue medians in 2011, up to twenty-five feet high, with aphids and beetles climbing the thorns. He meant a critique of what the street sells: a lot of people just saw pretty roses on a fancy street.

narrative_blocks.header: The city cut the litter from his design
narrative_blocks.body: His first drawings put a giant coffee cup, an empty Doritos bag and burnt matches among the flowers like dropped rubbish. The approval committee took them out for conflicting with the city's anti-trash campaign.

narrative_blocks.header: Five thousand nails on ninety thousand more
narrative_blocks.body: Bird went up in Flatiron Plaza in 2013, twelve feet and five tons of nails, standing on a nest of ninety thousand more.

narrative_blocks.header: Lincoln's cabin, in gold leaf
narrative_blocks.body: He rebuilt Abraham Lincoln's cabin at near life size and gilded it inside and out, inlaying the walls with shackles, arrowheads, bullets, phone cords, soda tabs and pills, and bricking the fireplace with iPads and iPhones. The Civil War, he said, was a major turning point in how this country did business.

narrative_blocks.header: He crawled on the Carl Andres
narrative_blocks.body: As a child he climbed over sculptures by Tom Doyle, Carl Andre and Sol LeWitt lying about his parents' Greenwich Village apartment. I grew up around people making art, not studying it.

narrative_blocks.header: Two husbands, and no children by either
narrative_blocks.body: Don Lee married her secretly at Riverside in April 1918, after a seven-month engagement and without telling even his intimate friends, and she was divorced from him by 1926. She married Ed Willis in 1936, was divorced about 1938, and had no children by either.

narrative_blocks.header: She met him in the museum library
narrative_blocks.body: She came out of Smith in 1958 into a job as a page in the Museum of Modern Art library, reshelving it after a fire and being farmed out to research for curators. Robert Ryman was a guard in the same building, and Sol LeWitt was working the night desk.

narrative_blocks.header: Six Years, and the dematerialised object
narrative_blocks.body: Six Years: The Dematerialization of the Art Object came out in 1973 and did more than any other book to fix what conceptual art had been. She has written thirty books since 1966 and curated some fifty exhibitions.

narrative_blocks.header: Her shows were named after city populations
narrative_blocks.body: The four numbers shows took their titles from the populations of the cities that held them, and their catalogues were sets of index cards. The first, 557,087, opened at the Seattle Art Museum in 1969, and the rest followed in Vancouver, Buenos Aires and Valencia.

narrative_blocks.header: Eccentric Abstraction put Hesse on the wall
narrative_blocks.body: She organised Eccentric Abstraction at the Fischbach Gallery in 1966 around Louise Bourgeois, Eva Hesse, Bruce Nauman, Keith Sonnier and others working in organic abstract form. Ten years later she wrote the book on Hesse, designed by Sol LeWitt.

narrative_blocks.header: Argentina in 1968 turned her political
narrative_blocks.body: She went to Buenos Aires as a juror in 1968 and came home into the anti-war movement and the Art Workers' Coalition. She co-founded Printed Matter, the Heresies collective, Political Art Documentation and Artists Call Against U.S. Intervention in Central America.

narrative_blocks.header: One son, and he became an artist too
narrative_blocks.body: She married Robert Ryman in 1960, when he was still an emerging painter, and they were divorced in 1966. Their son Ethan Ryman became an artist himself.

bio.bio_blurb: Critic of conceptual and feminist art

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote a column called With the Artists
narrative_blocks.body: Her first job out of the University of Washington was at the Seattle Times, writing for the society section and reviewing art in a weekly column called With the Artists. In 1963 she became the first director of the Northwest Craft Center, opened after the World's Fair.

narrative_blocks.header: When the Republicans were real republicans
narrative_blocks.body: She joined the local Eisenhower campaign in 1952 and went to Washington after the victory to work for the Republican National Committee. When the Republicans were real republicans, she said of it afterwards.

narrative_blocks.header: Clamming and crabbing at Kingston
narrative_blocks.body: She and Norman moved to Kingston to live in the great outdoors, where she grew vegetables and went regularly for clams and crab. She served two terms on the North Kitsap School Board, lobbying for school funding.

narrative_blocks.header: Third generation on Capitol Hill
narrative_blocks.body: She grew up on Capitol Hill with her brothers Richard and Daniel and spent the summers on Bainbridge Island. Her grandfather Daniel Kelleher founded what became Seattle First National Bank.

bio.bio_blurb: Seattle Times art critic and florist

narrative_blocks.header: He practised law until three months before
narrative_blocks.body: He took his degree at the University of Washington School of Law and practised with great passion until August 2012, three months before he died. He also worked to create alternative schools for marginalised young people.

narrative_blocks.header: Puget Sound, the San Juans, Desolation Sound
narrative_blocks.body: One of his greatest joys was navigating the waters around Puget Sound, the San Juan Islands and Desolation Sound, and his love of yachting was contagious enough to pull others out after him. His life was celebrated at the Seattle Yacht Club.

narrative_blocks.header: A lifelong student of history and politics
narrative_blocks.body: What he enjoyed most was a robust argument about a current or a historical question at a social gathering. He went to everything his children and grandchildren did, with great enthusiasm.

narrative_blocks.header: Her letter won an MGM contest
narrative_blocks.body: She came out of the American Airlines stewardess school in 1946, and in 1950 was one of a hundred and fifty stewardesses who wrote in to a Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer competition for the best account of life on a flight. Hers won, and was used in connection with Three Guys Named Mike.

narrative_blocks.header: A day at the studio with Lana Turner
narrative_blocks.body: The prize was a day at MGM. She went over the script with the producer Armand Deutsch and the writer Sydney Sheldon, and handed Lana Turner an American Airlines cap; Turner had been cast as the stewardess, but the part went to Jane Wyman.

narrative_blocks.header: The Campbells kept the men's store
narrative_blocks.body: She married Jack Campbell in July 1950, whose family owned Campbell's men's store at the corner of Third and Santa Monica Boulevard from the 1930s through the 1960s. They lived at Pacific Palisades.

narrative_blocks.header: He served with his brothers in the Navy
narrative_blocks.body: He grew up on the beach at Santa Monica with Joseph and Richard, went into the Navy at nineteen alongside them, and came home at twenty-three to the University of Southern California. He was blessed with super health, and swam off Malibu from the family beach house.

narrative_blocks.header: His father opened the men's store
narrative_blocks.body: Hansen Malin Campbell started Campbell's of Southern California, the first men's clothing store in the town, on the corner of Santa Monica Boulevard, and it stayed open fifty-six years. Jack married Dona Lee, who had been his childhood sweetheart.

bio.bio_blurb: Son of the Campbell's men's store

narrative_blocks.header: A musician of note, dead at thirty
narrative_blocks.body: He was an organist and composer of considerable note at Rochester. He married there in April 1845 and was dead ten months later, in the February after his thirtieth birthday.

narrative_blocks.header: An army invalid, and a train at last
narrative_blocks.body: He served in the Civil War and was carried afterwards on the rolls as an army invalid. He married Ellen Sherman in Oakland County in 1861 and, a widower, married again at Bloomington in 1902; he was killed by a train at seventy-nine.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother died the year he was born
narrative_blocks.body: Sally Ingersoll died at Auburn in 1835, the year of his birth and, it is thought, of its complications. His father remarried the following year and took the family to Michigan.

bio.bio_blurb: Civil War invalid, killed by a train

narrative_blocks.header: Smallpox took him, then the whole house
narrative_blocks.body: He was a baker, long resident at Lansing and well known there, and he died of smallpox at Detroit in the spring of 1903. His wife and children were all reported to be down with it as well.

narrative_blocks.header: Waterville, then the bar at Hampden
narrative_blocks.body: He took his degree at Waterville College in 1840, taught a year at the Wiscasset high school and then at Eastport and Bucksport, and came to the bar in 1843. He settled at Hampden, married a daughter of Elias Dudley there, and moved his law business to Yarmouth.

narrative_blocks.header: The cotton mill at the middle falls
narrative_blocks.body: He was for many years largely interested in the cotton manufacturing plant at the middle falls in Yarmouth, and in the granite quarries there. He sat on Bowdoin's board of overseers from 1857 and was a trustee of Yarmouth Academy.

notable.notable_blurb: Architect of Newport Beach and the Baja coast

narrative_blocks.header: A skin-diving holiday made him an architect
narrative_blocks.body: He was a draftsman in architects' offices until 1960, when he went to Puerto Vallarta on a skin-diving holiday and met a developer who invited him to design houses. He built sixteen of them on the Gold Coast.

narrative_blocks.header: He did not design rooms, he created spaces
narrative_blocks.body: Julius Shulman, the dean of architectural photographers, said that with the architecture of Edward Giddings there are no normal forms, and that he did not design rooms but created spaces. I reach to the deepest limits of my imagination, Giddings said, then bring the concept back into architectural reality.

narrative_blocks.header: Puebla tiles and eighteen-foot doors
narrative_blocks.body: The Newport Beach office he opened in 1965 built for Texas oilmen, investors and actors, David Janssen among them. His houses ran to hand-painted tiles from Puebla, rosewood lavatories from Puerto Vallarta, eighteen-foot Spanish entry doors and two-storey wine racks.

narrative_blocks.header: My clients set me right
narrative_blocks.body: My clients are knowledgeable people, he told the Times; if there is any flaw in the plans, they set me right.

narrative_blocks.header: Impressionist oils at Laguna and La Jolla
narrative_blocks.body: He had studied painting at the California School of Fine Arts in San Francisco and showed impressionist oils at the Laguna Beach and La Jolla museums and in galleries at San Bernardino and Santa Barbara. He met his first wife in those classes.

narrative_blocks.header: Two resorts on the Mexican coast
narrative_blocks.body: He designed and developed Club Cascadas de Baja at Cabo San Lucas and Ocho Cascadas at Puerto Vallarta. He died of a heart attack at the Cabo house in August 1993, and the family asked for memorial gifts to the Frank Lloyd Wright Foundation.

education.school_name: California School of Fine Arts, San Francisco

career.role: House architect on the Gold Coast

narrative_blocks.header: Lady Principal of Ingham University
narrative_blocks.body: Charlotte taught for seven years before her marriage, part of the time as Lady Principal of Ingham University at Le Roy, New York. From 1861 to 1865 she headed the Senior Department of the Brooklyn Heights Seminary.

narrative_blocks.header: Dark brown hair and hazel eyes
narrative_blocks.body: Charlotte had dark brown hair, dark hazel eyes and a somewhat dark complexion, and stood five feet four.

narrative_blocks.header: She married Benjamin at Brooklyn in 1865
narrative_blocks.body: Charlotte married Benjamin at Brooklyn in December 1865, taking on a widower with four children. Their daughter Bertha was born at Clinton in May 1867, the spring he gave up teaching for his books.

notable.notable_blurb: Founder of the Winter Park Bach Festival

narrative_blocks.header: She built a Bach festival out of nothing
narrative_blocks.body: She founded the Bach Festival at Winter Park in 1935 and, by sheer force of will, created the choir, the soloists, the musicians, the audience and the funds for it. It is Central Florida's oldest performing arts organisation and the third-oldest Bach festival still running in the country.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote to Schweitzer to get him down
narrative_blocks.body: She collected essays on Bach and translations of his texts for her own use, and corresponded with Albert Schweitzer, the theologian who had written the life of Bach, trying to bring him to Winter Park to lecture.

narrative_blocks.header: Her pupils paid for a MacDowell studio
narrative_blocks.body: Thirty-one of her music pupils at the Veltin School paid for a fieldstone studio named for her at the MacDowell Colony, built in 1915 and 1916, burned in 1976 and rebuilt that year from the same stones. She also kept a studio at Carnegie Hall and belonged to the Woman's Art Club of New York.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept her husband’s institute going
narrative_blocks.body: Charles Sprague Smith founded the People's Institute at Cooper Union and directed it until his death in 1910; she was a director of it herself. Rollins gave her an honorary degree in 1939.

narrative_blocks.header: She corrected the Times about her family
narrative_blocks.body: In June 1900 she wrote to the editor to say that an editorial on Jonathan Edwards had confused Aaron Burr the Vice President with his father, the Rev. Aaron Burr, who married Esther Edwards. She cited the page in the History of the Dwight Family and noted that the elder Burr was a man of irreproachable character.

narrative_blocks.header: Smith in 1891, then French at the Sorbonne
narrative_blocks.body: She took her degree at Smith in the class of 1891 and taught a year at Miss Nurse's School in Cincinnati before going to Paris to study French at the Sorbonne. She married Charles Buckingham Cole at Clinton in June 1896.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son ran Amherst when she died
narrative_blocks.body: She had lived forty-seven years at Upper Montclair when she died at Mountainside Hospital after a brief illness. Her son Charles was president of Amherst College by then, and her daughter Lois an editor in New York.

narrative_blocks.header: A heritage of sorrow into the house
narrative_blocks.body: The young life brought with it a heritage of sorrow into the Doctor's home: at its birth last November his young mother surrendered her life, and the Doctor bestowed upon the fateful little one an unusual amount of affection. He was a bright little fellow about eight months old.

notable.notable_blurb: Founder of New York's People's Institute

narrative_blocks.header: He built a forum at Cooper Union
narrative_blocks.body: He founded the People's Institute in 1897 and ran it from Cooper Union, presiding over a People's Forum that carried weight across the state. It ran social and civic clubs, a bureau of legislative information, and got a hundred thousand students and workers into theatres and concerts at cut rates.

narrative_blocks.header: His institute censored the movies
narrative_blocks.body: The People's Institute was responsible for and administered the Board of Censorship of Motion Pictures, the body that passed on American films before the studios wrote their own code.

narrative_blocks.header: Eleven years at Columbia, ended by illness
narrative_blocks.body: He came out of Amherst in 1874 and studied six more years in Europe before teaching Germanic languages at Columbia from 1880, then comparative literature and modern languages. Poor health ended the teaching in 1891.

narrative_blocks.header: She married again by contract, not away
narrative_blocks.body: She married Victor Starzenski in November 1915 and married him a second time by contract in 1916, because she wanted a form in which she was not given away. They lived at Schenectady, where he was an engineer at General Electric; by 1929 she was Hilda Sprague Smith again.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-one scrapbooks went to Berea
narrative_blocks.body: She kept her travels and the family's doings in thirty-one scrapbooks and journals, given to Berea College in 1942, the year she died of cancer at Winter Park. Her mother endowed a history book fund at Bryn Mawr in her memory.

notable.notable_blurb: The editor who got Gone With the Wind read

narrative_blocks.header: She was the first outsider to read it
narrative_blocks.body: She met Margaret Mitchell on a Macmillan posting to Atlanta and they became lifelong friends. When she heard there was a novel she asked to see it, was refused, kept asking, and in 1933 got the promise that she would read it first if it was finished.

narrative_blocks.header: She put her boss in front of Mitchell
narrative_blocks.body: She introduced Harold Latham, Macmillan's editor-in-chief, to Mitchell in 1935, and it was to Latham that the manuscript was finally handed. John and Lois were the only people she ever discussed it with in any detail, Mitchell said afterwards.

narrative_blocks.header: She turned down the name Scarlett
narrative_blocks.body: Mitchell wanted a better name than Pansy for her heroine and proposed Scarlett. Cole rejected it at first and then let it stand. She also edited the blurb and got the book into the Book of the Month Club.

narrative_blocks.header: Fought by my side with great gallantry
narrative_blocks.body: Mitchell inscribed the family copy: to Lois Cole, who fought by my side with great gallantry in the engagements of Dalton, Resaca, Peachtree Creek and the siege of Atlanta, and who managed to get me to press on time.

narrative_blocks.header: Like watching election returns
narrative_blocks.body: She wired Mitchell on release day that shipments to stores had passed fifty thousand copies, then tracked the reviews as they came in — a process she likened to watching election returns.

narrative_blocks.header: Six pen names, one shared with her husband
narrative_blocks.body: With her husband she wrote historical adventures for older children as Allan Dwight; Drums in the Forest of 1936 reached a twenty-second printing by 1970. Alone she published as Anne Elliot, Anne Lattin, Nancy Dudley, Lynn Avery and Caroline Arnett.

narrative_blocks.header: Mitchell introduced her to her husband
narrative_blocks.body: Peggy Mitchell brought her together with Turney Allan Taylor, a bachelor journalist and her own old deskmate at the Atlanta Journal. They married there in 1930.

narrative_blocks.header: I was always winning second prizes
narrative_blocks.body: He took second prizes in Latin and mathematics as a freshman, which he remembered with some sadness: I was always winning second prizes. By senior year he was editor-in-chief of the Amherst Student, and he graduated summa cum laude and Phi Beta Kappa.

narrative_blocks.header: An amateur wrote their physics text
narrative_blocks.body: In 1931 the college heads packed him off to Maine to write a text on physics and the modern world precisely because he was an amateur at it, guessing freshmen would understand it better from a nonscientist. He compressed a summer's reading into a hundred pages and thought the job a lot of fun.

narrative_blocks.header: He learned Spanish on the Yale commute
narrative_blocks.body: Accepting a visiting lectureship at Yale, he used the commute from Amherst to teach himself Spanish. Thirty years later Kennedy sent him to Santiago as ambassador.

narrative_blocks.header: A core curriculum instead of electives
narrative_blocks.body: As Amherst's twelfth president from 1946 he put freshmen and sophomores through a required core of English, European civilization, a foreign language and science instead of electives. It stood until 1966.

narrative_blocks.header: Colbert and a century of mercantilism
narrative_blocks.body: His subject was seventeenth-century France and mercantilism, above all foreign trade under Louis XIV. He published French Mercantilist Doctrines Before Colbert in 1931 and Colbert and a Century of French Mercantilism in 1939.

narrative_blocks.header: Not a garden you grow squash in
narrative_blocks.body: An inveterate gardener, his chief worry on becoming president was the new formal presidential garden. It's not the kind you grow squash in, he said; more suitable for lawn parties.

narrative_blocks.header: A heart attack on a Caribbean cruise
narrative_blocks.body: He was vice-president of the Rockefeller Foundation after Amherst and Chile, and a trustee of the Educational Testing Service, Williston Academy and the Fund for the Republic. He died at sea in February 1978 and was buried at Wildwood in Amherst.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept letters and diaries from age ten
narrative_blocks.body: She wrote letters and kept diaries from 1916, when she was ten, through 1949. Her husband had the whole run copied out in typescript and edited it himself.

narrative_blocks.header: Santiago, written up and set aside
narrative_blocks.body: She wrote a memoir of the years her husband was ambassador in Santiago and gathered her letters from them into a typescript in the late 1960s, meaning to see it published. She died at Pelham in February 1972, and he finished the editing without her.

narrative_blocks.header: Three scrapbooks for a Florida Bach festival
narrative_blocks.body: From 1948 to 1950 she kept the records of the Bach Festival Society of Winter Park, Florida, filling three scrapbooks with them.

narrative_blocks.header: Allan Dwight was two people
narrative_blocks.body: Allan Dwight was not a person: it was the name he and his wife Lois Dwight Cole signed their books with. Drums in the Forest of 1936 ran to a twenty-second printing by 1970, and Kentucky Cargo followed from Macmillan in 1939, illustrated by Harvé Stein.

narrative_blocks.header: Wine, Eisenhower, and long rifles
narrative_blocks.body: Under his own name he wrote What Everybody Wants to Know About Wine, What Eisenhower Thinks, and Morgan's Long Rifles for older boys. To the Walls of Cartagena, the last book he and his wife made together, came out from Colonial Williamsburg the year he died.

narrative_blocks.header: He covered the Russian front from a desk
narrative_blocks.body: He came to the Times Sunday department in 1942 after the Atlanta Constitution, the Atlanta Journal, the Encyclopaedia Britannica and the National Real Estate Journal. Through the war he wrote the weekly news summary and made the Russian front his specialty.

narrative_blocks.header: They both signed under the one name
narrative_blocks.body: They inscribed a presentation copy of Kentucky Cargo in October 1939 to a friend who had liked Timothy's Shoes: whose kind words about our books encouraged us to write this one. Both signatures stand above ALLAN DWIGHT in capitals.

cross_connections.display_label: wrote The Great Wine Rivers, and chose the wine for U.S. embassies

bio.bio_blurb: New York Times editor; half of Allan Dwight

career.role: Editor, Magazine and Week in Review

narrative_blocks.header: Atheneum, Farrar Straus, then Harper's
narrative_blocks.body: She worked in New York publishing after Bradford and Wheaton, briefly in motion pictures at Palomar Productions, then as an editorial assistant at Atheneum and at Farrar Straus and Giroux. She was managing editor of the Harper's Magazine Press.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote as Lisa Beaumont
narrative_blocks.body: She published two historical romance novels under the name Lisa Beaumont and was at work on others. She was also building a book out of the correspondence between her mother and Margaret Mitchell, a friendship that lasted a lifetime.

narrative_blocks.header: A fast skier and a ready laugh
narrative_blocks.body: She was an avid and fast skier, a spirited and vivacious conversationalist with many anecdotes, a superb cook and a traveller. Her special love was the family summer place in the wilderness on Cranberry Lake in the Adirondacks.

narrative_blocks.header: Swim club president in West Lafayette
narrative_blocks.body: After marrying she moved to West Lafayette, joined a women's company that put on plays for children, and was for many years president of the White Sharks age-group swim club. She sat on the boards of the county chamber music society and the Wabash Trust for Historic Preservation.

narrative_blocks.header: He was there when the quark model held
narrative_blocks.body: His first post was at Brookhaven, then the centre of American particle physics, and in 1964 he was on the team that found the Omega Minus — the experiment that confirmed the quark model and fed at least one Nobel Prize.

narrative_blocks.header: Top quark in 1995, Higgs in 2012
narrative_blocks.body: He was a founding member of the groups that built detectors at Fermilab and at CERN, and worked out ways of measuring particle energies still used everywhere. He was on the Fermilab team that found the top quark, and on the team that found the Higgs.

narrative_blocks.header: His doctoral adviser named nuclear fission
narrative_blocks.body: A top-ten finisher in the national Westinghouse science competition while still at school, he read physics at Harvard and took his doctorate at Cambridge as a Marshall Scholar. His adviser was Otto Frisch, who had coined the term nuclear fission.

narrative_blocks.header: He built a harpsichord and a bubble wand
narrative_blocks.body: For his sons and grandchildren he made a wand that blew bubbles twenty feet long and a dodecahedral Rubik's cube, and he built himself a harpsichord. He spoke French and German, collected African and Asian art, and skied until he was seventy-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: Love at first sight on the French Riviera
narrative_blocks.body: His first wife, the research scientist Barbara Green, died in 1963 leaving him a son. He met Linda Taylor while both were on holiday on the Riviera, and they married in 1970.

cross_connections.display_label: photographed sound at Brown a century before his particle detectors

narrative_blocks.header: His book on the Hidalgo revolt
narrative_blocks.body: Hugh's study of the Hidalgo revolt is counted among the major works on that period of Mexican history. He edited Dictatorship in Spanish America in 1965 and Caudillos: Dictators in Spanish America in 1992.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-three years at UConn
narrative_blocks.body: Hugh came to UConn in 1961 after four years at Ohio Wesleyan, and stayed thirty-three years as professor and associate dean. He founded its Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies, shared with Brown, Yale and UMass.

narrative_blocks.header: He organized Mansfield Center's historic district
narrative_blocks.body: Hugh organized the historic district at Mansfield Center, twice led the Joshua's Tract conservation trust, and was known for soccer games with every generation on the field.

narrative_blocks.header: He heard the electricity lectures at Yale
narrative_blocks.body: He went from Phillips Academy to Yale, where he took Silliman's and Jeremiah Day's lectures on electricity and painted miniatures to support himself. He graduated in 1810 with Phi Beta Kappa honours.

narrative_blocks.header: He painted Eli Whitney in 1822
narrative_blocks.body: His 1822 portrait of Eli Whitney went to Yale as a gift from George Hoadley two years after Hoadley's bank failed, and was entered as accession 1827.1 — among the very first works the Yale Art Gallery ever catalogued.

narrative_blocks.header: Eighty faces by lamplight in the Capitol
narrative_blocks.body: The House of Representatives, finished in 1822, put eighty individuals into a night session of Congress lit by lamps, to show that its dedication to democracy carried past daylight. Shown in New York in 1823, it drew no crowd.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded the National Academy of Design
narrative_blocks.body: He founded the National Academy of Design in 1826 and was its president to 1845 and again in 1861. In 1832 he became the first professor of painting and sculpture in the United States, at the University of the City of New York.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught the man who built Columbia Law
narrative_blocks.body: Theodore William Dwight studied natural science under him and under John William Draper before going on to organise Columbia Law School in 1858 and to found New York Law School in 1891.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave up the brush for the wire
narrative_blocks.body: He and Alfred Vail worked out the code in 1838, and he demonstrated the telegraph that January at New York University. Congress funded the line and he took the patent in 1844; on 11 May he sent the first message from Baltimore to Washington.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran for mayor on a nativist ticket
narrative_blocks.body: He stood for mayor of New York in 1836 on an anti-immigrant and anti-Catholic platform and took 1,496 votes. In the 1850s and 1860s he wrote arguing for the moral basis of slavery.

narrative_blocks.header: Hadley boy, West Point, three brevets
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Hadley, Mass., in 1814, grandson of a Revolutionary captain, he left West Point in 1837 twenty-ninth of fifty and took three brevets in Mexico, where the women called him the Handsome Captain. He resigned in 1853 to farm in Sonoma.

narrative_blocks.header: A Wenham Hooker, not a Hartford one
narrative_blocks.body: He does not descend from Thomas Hooker. His line runs back through five generations of Josephs to an emigrant at Wenham by 1689, probably out of southern England or Jersey. He had no children, so the line of Joseph Hookers ended with him.

narrative_blocks.header: Antietam, and he left with a foot wound
narrative_blocks.body: At Antietam his I Corps opened the bloodiest day of the war, driving into Stonewall Jackson's men until the two fought to a standstill. He left early with a foot wound, and said ever after the battle would have been decisive had he stayed.

narrative_blocks.header: Lee split a smaller army twice over
narrative_blocks.body: He took the Army of the Potomac in 1863, fed the men better, brought in corps badges and built its first intelligence bureau. At Chancellorsville a shell struck the column he leaned on; concussed, he held command and Lee routed him.

narrative_blocks.header: I will risk the dictatorship
narrative_blocks.body: Told that his new commander had said the country needed a dictator, Lincoln appointed him anyway and said so in writing: only those generals who gain success can set up dictators, and I will risk the dictatorship.

narrative_blocks.header: Lookout Mountain, and the credit went west
narrative_blocks.body: Sent to Chattanooga in November 1863 he helped break the siege and commanded at Lookout Mountain; Grant's report gave the credit to Sherman. Passed over for a Georgia command he resigned, and married Olivia Groesbeck at Cincinnati in 1865.

narrative_blocks.header: The nickname was a typesetter's mistake
narrative_blocks.body: A dispatch reading Fighting - Joe Hooker Attacks Rebels lost its dash in a New York composing room, and he was Fighting Joe for life. People will think I am a highwayman or a bandit, he said.

notable.notable_blurb: Massachusetts legislator, then college president

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the 1993 education reform act
narrative_blocks.body: Chairman of the legislature's education committee from 1990, he co-authored and carried the Massachusetts Education Reform Act of 1993. He was also chief sponsor of the gay rights bill filed every year since 1972, which passed at last in 1989 and made Massachusetts the second state to protect gay rights.

narrative_blocks.header: He lost to his cousin's husband
narrative_blocks.body: He was the Democratic nominee for governor of Massachusetts in 1994 and lost to the Republican incumbent, William Weld. Weld's wife Susan was his second cousin; both are great-grandchildren of Theodore Roosevelt.

narrative_blocks.header: He reopened a college that had closed
narrative_blocks.body: Antioch College had shut in 2008, and he was hired in 2011 to bring it back, recruiting faculty and students and restarting the cooperative education programme. He negotiated away Antioch University's claims on the college's campus and endowment, and accreditation came in 2016.

narrative_blocks.header: He closed schools and raised the bar
narrative_blocks.body: Appointed superintendent of Pittsburgh's public schools in 2005 on a performance-based contract, he closed under-used schools, opened accelerated learning academies and adopted a harder curriculum. The district met federal achievement standards for the first time under him.

narrative_blocks.header: He cut tuition by a third
narrative_blocks.body: At St. John's he told the board to take off its rose-coloured glasses, then centralised the two campuses under one presidency, cut tuition by a third and closed a structural deficit that ran to a fifth of the budget.

narrative_blocks.header: Our faculty do not profess
narrative_blocks.body: St. John's has tutors rather than professors, he said, because its faculty do not profess: a tutor opens the class with a question and keeps it moving, like the leader of a small jazz band. He asked that gifts marking his retirement go to raising tutors' pay.

narrative_blocks.header: She married first, her sister followed
narrative_blocks.body: She married John Lowe Boorum in April 1860, and fourteen months later her sister Amelia married his brother William. Both couples had eight children.

narrative_blocks.header: Her children carry the family names
narrative_blocks.body: Her eldest was Mary Edwards Boorum, for her grandmother Mary Ogden Edwards, and her second Caroline Mather Boorum, for her aunt Caroline Whiting Mather. She married William Burger Boorum in June 1861, fourteen months after her sister took his brother.

narrative_blocks.header: Her will paid six Brooklyn charities
narrative_blocks.body: She left bequests to the Institute of Arts and Sciences, the Children's Aid Society, the Association for Improving the Condition of the Poor, the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children, the Orphan Asylum Society and the Society for the Aid of Friendless Women and Children. Her house on Clinton Street and the bulk of the estate went to her sister, two nieces and a nephew.

narrative_blocks.header: He inherited his father-in-law's company
narrative_blocks.body: When William Burger Boorum died in 1901 he became president and treasurer of Boorum and Pease, the blank book manufacturers, having practised law and run other business interests until then. He was still at it days before his own death.

narrative_blocks.header: The Brooklyn Pool King, for a while
narrative_blocks.body: He went into business young and was known across the country for a time as the Brooklyn Pool King. He was called one of the most accomplished men at organisation in the country.

narrative_blocks.header: A widow sued her own trustee
narrative_blocks.body: Hannah Boorum, widow of his wife's brother Charles, made him trustee of her property before marrying an Englishman, to keep it beyond her new husband's creditors. She divorced the man in 1907, took the Boorum name back, and sued Jackson to recover it all.

narrative_blocks.header: Amherst 1889, then a Columbia law diploma
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Binghamton, he took his Amherst degree in 1889 and a law diploma from Columbia after it, and practised in New York. His younger brother Ernest followed him to Amherst and into the law, and died at twenty-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at 424 Clinton Avenue
narrative_blocks.body: He died suddenly after a short illness at his Brooklyn house in May 1919, in his fifty-second year, leaving no children. He had belonged to the Union League Club of Manhattan and before that the Oxford Club of Brooklyn.

notable.notable_blurb: Nature writer; Red Cross commissioner

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband’s house printed her bird books
narrative_blocks.body: She wrote as Neltje Blanchan, her own given names with the surname dropped, and eleven books followed — Bird Neighbors, Nature’s Garden, Birds Every Child Should Know. John Burroughs introduced the first of them in 1897.

narrative_blocks.header: She thought knowing birds would save them
narrative_blocks.body: She was no great authority and said so; her case was that a public taught to know birds would back the laws protecting them. She did not oppose hunting, only the kind that emptied the fields.

narrative_blocks.header: She went to China for the Red Cross
narrative_blocks.body: In 1917 she went out to the Philippines and China on special assignment as a Red Cross commissioner. She died suddenly at Canton in February 1918, aged fifty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: A Wyoming prize carries her pen name
narrative_blocks.body: The Wyoming Arts Council’s Blanchan award goes each year to a writer whose work is inspired by nature. Her granddaughter, named for her and born sixteen years after she died, endowed it.

narrative_blocks.header: A Chicago clothier’s daughter, schooled east
narrative_blocks.body: Her father Liverius De Graff kept a men’s clothing store in Chicago. She was sent east to St. John’s in New York and the Masters School at Dobbs Ferry.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept Conrad five weeks, then wrote it
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph Conrad stayed at Effendi Hill for five weeks from May 1923, and she looked after him each morning while her husband went to business. She set the visit down in Episodes in the Life of a Publisher's Wife, printed privately in 1937.

narrative_blocks.header: A stranger asked only to touch Conrad
narrative_blocks.body: He came off the ship so spent that he sat on a trunk on the pier, chin on his cane. A woman asked to speak to him, was refused, then asked if she might just touch him; she did, and turned away crying. He never felt it.

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband was offered Conrad in 1898
narrative_blocks.body: In 1898 William Heinemann told her husband there was a Polish sailor in London who wanted to write but could not afford to, and proposed they keep him between them. Effendi agreed; at year's end Conrad wrote that the book would not come.

narrative_blocks.header: Conrad showed her where he had stopped
narrative_blocks.body: The Rescue sat unfinished for twenty years. He showed her the page where he had broken off and made her promise never to tell, and she kept it so completely that she could no longer find the page herself.

narrative_blocks.header: Nineteen reporters came to tea for Conrad
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband brought every reporter out to the house at once to spare Conrad the pier. Asked for his philosophy of life, Conrad said that if he had not explained it in his books he must be very stupid.

narrative_blocks.header: Conrad asked leave to call her Florence
narrative_blocks.body: He went to her husband for leave first, then kissed her hand and said he knew people who called him Joseph but loved none as much as her. His published letters told his wife that Effendi had put him up to it.

notable.notable_blurb: Book publisher; Doubleday president

narrative_blocks.header: The publisher who did not read books
narrative_blocks.body: He liked to say that he did not read books, he sold them. He turned his father’s literary firm into a mass-market house, bought the Literary Guild, pushed cheap popular editions and expanded the business into Canada.

narrative_blocks.header: Kipling wrote the Just So Stories for him
narrative_blocks.body: Rudyard Kipling was his father’s friend and a fixture of the household — the Mill Neck estate was called Effendi Hill, the name Kipling had given his father. The boy asked the author for a book of animal stories, and the Just So Stories followed.

narrative_blocks.header: He built his own firm before his father’s
narrative_blocks.body: He set up in business for himself in 1910 and used the profits to publish under his own imprint. Only after serving in the First World War did he come into Doubleday, Page as a junior partner.

narrative_blocks.header: The boy found money in old magazines
narrative_blocks.body: Still a youth, he proposed selling the firm’s dated magazines at a discount rather than writing them off, turning dead stock into revenue.

narrative_blocks.header: He built Barberrys at Mill Neck
narrative_blocks.body: The house went up in 1916 to a design by Harrie Lindeberg, with grounds laid out over five years by Percival Gallagher and the Olmsted Brothers.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Lindeberg designed it; the Olmsted Brothers laid out the grounds

narrative_blocks.header: St. Luke's elected its first two women
narrative_blocks.body: In 1951 she became one of the first two women elected a trustee of St. Luke's Hospital, and she held the seat until she died. Her husband was vice-president of the same board.

narrative_blocks.header: She nursed at the hospital she later governed
narrative_blocks.body: Through the Second World War she served as a Red Cross nurse's aid at St. Luke's — the hospital whose board she joined six years afterwards, and where she died in 1964.

narrative_blocks.header: She founded a guild for embroiderers
narrative_blocks.body: She was a founder of the Embroiderers Guild of America. She also sat on the executive committee of the Planned Parenthood Federation and on the New York board of the English-Speaking Union.

narrative_blocks.header: Kipling engraved their bookplate
narrative_blocks.body: Rudyard Kipling, who had given her father the name Effendi, made a personal bookplate for her and her husband in the years after their 1915 wedding at Oyster Bay.

parents.father_research_notes: Adoptive father. Felix was the adopted son of Frank Nelson Doubleday and Neltje Blanchan; his biological parents are unrecorded.

narrative_blocks.header: The eldest Doubleday son was adopted
narrative_blocks.body: Frank Nelson Doubleday and Neltje Blanchan adopted him, and he was raised as the eldest of their children.

narrative_blocks.header: Kipling called him Jack and signed a book
narrative_blocks.body: In March 1899 Kipling inscribed a copy of The Second Jungle Book to him as Jack Doty, and wrote four lines of the Law of the Jungle on the facing page. He was eleven, and the author was his father’s closest friend among the writers.

narrative_blocks.header: He was at Leysin when his father died
narrative_blocks.body: His father's will left him a share as an adopted son, less what he owed the estate. He was at Leysin, high in the Swiss Alps, when it was proved in 1934, and he died at Lausanne seven years later.

narrative_blocks.header: He played the nationals once and lost
narrative_blocks.body: He entered the United States national championship in 1915 and went out in his only match, beaten in straight sets by William Marquitz. He turned out for doubles at Palm Beach too, partnered with Alex Standing of Scarsdale.

narrative_blocks.header: She was twenty-three at Compiègne
narrative_blocks.body: Her stone records her as First Lieutenant, Medical Corps, 3rd French Army, Compiègne, France, 1917. Few American women of twenty-three were doing that.

narrative_blocks.header: She published her forebears' Mexican War diaries
narrative_blocks.body: In 1936 she brought out the journals Major Philip Norbourne Barbour and his wife Martha kept through 1846 — his breaking off the day before he was killed at Monterey, hers written at Galveston waiting for a husband she would not see again.

narrative_blocks.header: She sued a Harvester heir over a promise
narrative_blocks.body: In 1933 she brought an action for breach of promise against Harold Fowler McCormick, the International Harvester heir, and it was settled. She then sued Max Fleischmann for slander over what he had said about her and the case on a California golf course.

narrative_blocks.header: Ascot, Monaco, and tigers in Bengal
narrative_blocks.body: Atlantic Between, in 1947, set down her own round — weekends at Ascot, dinners at Monaco, luncheons at Hyde Park and shooting in Bengal. It was not kindly received.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father rode with the Confederate cavalry
narrative_blocks.body: John J. Tanner enlisted as a private in 1862 and served as chief of escort to General George B. Hodge. Taken on a raid into Kentucky in 1864, he spent thirteen months in Camp Chase before the war ended.

narrative_blocks.header: She went back to Kentucky to be buried
narrative_blocks.body: She died at Groton in Connecticut in 1986 and was carried to Fernwood at Henderson in Kentucky, where her brother Brent had been brought sixty years before after dying in Paris.

narrative_blocks.header: Divorced in Reno, remarried that month
narrative_blocks.body: Her marriage to Nelson Doubleday ended in a Reno divorce in June 1931, and she married Richard Hoyt on the twenty-ninth of the same month, in her own apartment on Fifth Avenue. Hoyt died four years later.

narrative_blocks.header: Her last husband painted society and war
narrative_blocks.body: She married the painter John Lavalle, a great-grandson of Juan Lavalle, one of the founders of the Argentine Republic. He had flown bombers for the Royal Air Force in the First World War and was a camouflage artist for the Twelfth Air Force before the invasion of Sicily.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father made files and screws
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel Nicholson was president of the Nicholson File Company and the American Screw Company, and she grew up in Providence.

narrative_blocks.header: The firm’s authors were her friends
narrative_blocks.body: Daphne du Maurier, Noël Coward, Somerset Maugham, Edna Ferber and Ilka Chase were lifelong friends of hers rather than names on a list, and she kept up with them long after her husband died.

narrative_blocks.header: English writers sent her their children
narrative_blocks.body: She ran and maintained a house at Oyster Bay for the children of English authors, alongside her own.

narrative_blocks.header: She took a board seat and held it
narrative_blocks.body: After her husband died in 1949 she joined the Doubleday board of directors, and stayed on it until she moved to Honolulu in 1965.

narrative_blocks.header: Her papers went to Princeton
narrative_blocks.body: She left her Doubleday business and personal documents to the university — correspondence with the firm’s authors, family letters, and the records of the Doubleday estates.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father ran New Jersey’s utility
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas McCarter organized the Public Service Corporation of New Jersey and was its president for the first thirty-six years.

narrative_blocks.header: She came to Doubleday with two daughters
narrative_blocks.body: Her first marriage, to Atwood Violett of New Orleans, ended in divorce in 1931 after ten years, and her two daughters by him grew up alongside the Doubleday children.

notable.notable_blurb: Publisher; owner of the New York Mets

narrative_blocks.header: A classic last-place team, he called them
narrative_blocks.body: He put up most of the price when Doubleday bought the Mets in 1980, a record for a franchise then. The club he called a classic last-place team took the World Series six years later.

narrative_blocks.header: He sold the publishing house, kept the team
narrative_blocks.body: The firm had been in the family since his grandfather founded it, and by 1985 was barely earning. He sold the publishing house to Bertelsmann in 1986 but carved the Mets out of the deal and bought half the club himself.

narrative_blocks.header: The owner who never called the dugout
narrative_blocks.body: He hired Frank Cashen to run the club and left him alone, a deliberate contrast with George Steinbrenner across town. His rule was to get good people and stay out of their way; the dugout phone never rang with the owner on it.

narrative_blocks.header: On the CB radio he was Bookworm
narrative_blocks.body: He drove into Manhattan most days on CB radio with a group called the Cuckoo’s Nest Convoy; his handle was Bookworm. He shot pheasant in Somerset, sailed a yacht called Mandalay, and was not much of a reader.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped push out baseball’s commissioner
narrative_blocks.body: Bowie Kuhn wanted clubs in big markets to subsidize those in small ones. He shunned publicity as a rule, but took the lead in the campaign that removed Kuhn in 1984 and installed Peter Ueberroth.

narrative_blocks.header: The partnership ended in a lawsuit
narrative_blocks.body: Fred Wilpon went to federal court in 2002 to force him to accept a Mets valuation he thought too low, and the suit laid bare years of distrust. He sold his half, ending twenty-two years with the team.

narrative_blocks.header: His father died when he was fifteen
narrative_blocks.body: The stock his father left him came into his hands only in 1973, and not until his mother died in 1978 did he hold a controlling interest. He became president that May.

narrative_blocks.header: Her sister sold more dresses than juice
narrative_blocks.body: Her sister Lillian opened a juice stand in Palm Beach in 1958 and asked a dressmaker for something that would hide the stains. The printed shift that came back became Lilly Pulitzer, and Jacqueline Kennedy wore one on the cover of Life in 1962.

narrative_blocks.header: Her stepfather lost Secretariat on a coin toss
narrative_blocks.body: Ogden Phipps, who married her mother in 1937, bred Buckpasser, Personal Ensign and Easy Goer, all of them in the racing Hall of Fame. A coin toss with Penny Chenery settled which foal each would take, and the one he did not get was Secretariat.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother won the Grand National eight times
narrative_blocks.body: Lillian Bostwick Phipps raced steeplechasers while her husband bought flat runners, and took the American Grand National eight times between 1951 and 1987. Two of her horses, Oedipus and Neji, were voted champion six times between them and went into the racing Hall of Fame.

narrative_blocks.header: Standard Oil money came down her mother’s side
narrative_blocks.body: Her great-grandfather Jabez Bostwick was one of John D. Rockefeller’s founding partners in Standard Oil, and her mother grew up in a Fifth Avenue mansion. It was her grandfather Albert, a horseman and polo player, who turned the family toward racing.

narrative_blocks.header: Her aunt flew helicopters in 1942
narrative_blocks.body: Dorothy Bostwick, her mother’s only sister, became the first American woman to hold a helicopter pilot’s licence, in 1942. She lived to a hundred and two.

notable.notable_blurb: Abstract painter; rancher; philanthropist

narrative_blocks.header: She started drawing at thirty, alone in Wyoming
narrative_blocks.body: She had no training, and worked up to abstract canvases ten feet by thirty. Her work is held by the Smithsonian and the Yellowstone Art Museum, and Wyoming gave her its Governor’s Arts Award in 2005.

narrative_blocks.header: She bought the condemned inn in secret
narrative_blocks.body: The Sheridan Inn was closed and condemned when she bought it in 1967, and she kept her name off the sale for six months. She reopened the saloon, then the dining room, and ran it eighteen years.

narrative_blocks.header: She fought her own family for the company
narrative_blocks.body: Twice she moved to make Doubleday register with the S.E.C. and sell shares publicly. At the 1973 meeting her ex-husband chaired and her brother sat beside him, both voted against her, and she lost while abroad.

narrative_blocks.header: The poet Roethke slept in their bathtub
narrative_blocks.body: Theodore Roethke, whom her husband edited, slept in the bathtub of their New York apartment and once held a knife to her throat. Somerset Maugham gave her advice on marriage, and Daphne du Maurier made a pass at her mother.

narrative_blocks.header: Her ranch became a residency for strangers
narrative_blocks.body: In 2001 she created the Jentel Foundation, bringing artists and writers to her ranch at Banner eleven months a year. She left the ranch, studio and art collection to the University of Wyoming, its largest gift.

narrative_blocks.header: An award for the grandmother she never met
narrative_blocks.body: Leading the Wyoming Arts Council in the 1980s, she endowed a literary award for nature writing. It carries the pen name of her father’s mother, who died sixteen years before she was born.

narrative_blocks.header: Her memoir came out under her son’s imprint
narrative_blocks.body: North of Crazy appeared in 2016 from St. Martin’s Press, the house her son ran. She wrote about her father’s drinking, the abuse she suffered at nine, and her mother siding with her first husband over her own stock.
