career.organization: Lower Piney Creek ranch, Banner, Wyoming

notable.notable_blurb: Publisher; Doubleday president and chairman

narrative_blocks.header: Seven hundred books a year by 1979
narrative_blocks.body: By 1979 Doubleday was issuing seven hundred titles a year, with a dozen book clubs, twenty-six bookshops and four printing plants behind it. He had bought Dell and a textbook house to get there, and pushed the firm into radio and television.

narrative_blocks.header: The book publisher who bought a baseball team
narrative_blocks.body: As chairman he backed the purchase of the New York Mets in 1980, in partnership with his former brother-in-law Nelson Doubleday Jr. The club was still theirs when it took the 1986 World Series.

narrative_blocks.header: He edited Roethke, then the house published Jaws
narrative_blocks.body: He arrived as a copywriter straight out of the Navy and edited Theodore Roethke's poetry early on. Stephen King, Peter Benchley's Jaws, Alex Haley's Roots, Kurt Vonnegut and Gay Talese all came out of the house while he ran it.

narrative_blocks.header: Christmas Eve, singles only, no exceptions
narrative_blocks.body: His annual Christmas Eve party, given with the actress Joan Fontaine, admitted only unmarried guests, and the rule had no exceptions in it. A Salvation Army band played at midnight and the room sang carols.

narrative_blocks.header: A writers' fund he started in Rome
narrative_blocks.body: He became a trustee of the American Academy in Rome in 1980 and its president in 1988, and endowed a writer-in-residence fund there that still carries his name.

narrative_blocks.header: His ex-wife tried to take the firm public
narrative_blocks.body: In the summer of 1972 Neltje Doubleday led a minority of shareholders trying to force the family firm public, seven years after their divorce. Her mother and her brother sided with him, and it was defeated.

narrative_blocks.header: He brought Jackie Onassis to Doubleday
narrative_blocks.body: She had left Viking after it published a novel imagining an assassination plot against her former brother-in-law Edward Kennedy. He recruited her in 1978, and her authors there included Dorothy West and Michael Jackson.

cross_connections.display_label: came to Doubleday as an editor because he recruited her
was Alex Haley's agent while his house published Roots

bio.bio_blurb: Publisher; Doubleday chairman and chief executive

education.dates: one year; left to enlist in the Navy

narrative_blocks.header: She and Sargent bought an abbey in Tuscany
narrative_blocks.body: In the 2000s she and John Turner Sargent bought an abbey in the Val d’Orcia, between San Quirico and Montalcino, and turned the eleventh-century building into a house standing in twelve hectares of olives and vines. The garden was laid out by the designer Peter Curzon; she has since put the place up for sale.

notable.notable_blurb: Book publisher; Macmillan chief executive

narrative_blocks.header: The White House said stop; he published early
narrative_blocks.body: The president’s lawyers demanded that Henry Holt cease publication of Michael Wolff’s Fire and Fury; he moved the release forward a day instead. He told the staff no president would be allowed to achieve by intimidation what the Constitution kept him from winning in court.

narrative_blocks.header: Amazon pulled his buy buttons and lost
narrative_blocks.body: When Macmillan moved to set its own e-book prices in 2010, Amazon stripped the purchase buttons from every Macmillan title over a weekend, print and digital alike. It restored them and took the terms, conceding the publisher held a monopoly on its own books.

narrative_blocks.header: One e-book per library, however large
narrative_blocks.body: Macmillan capped each library system at a single digital copy of a new title for two months, on his argument that free lending was cannibalizing sales. The American Library Association called it unacceptable and petitioned against him until the policy was lifted during the pandemic.

narrative_blocks.header: Booksellers gave him an award, and themselves
narrative_blocks.body: The New Atlantic Independent Booksellers Association honoured him in 2012 for standing up to Amazon over e-book pricing, and in the same breath gave its Legacy Award to every one of its own member stores as well.

cross_connections.display_label: edited at Macmillan fifty years before he ran it

narrative_blocks.header: He nearly took the Picasso with him
narrative_blocks.body: A writer and painter from London, he married her after the Doubleday divorce and moved with her and her two young children to Wyoming. The marriage ran about six years, and by the end he had taken money from her and come close to taking a Picasso she loved.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran a textile house for thirty-three years
narrative_blocks.body: He joined J. H. Lane and Company in 1908 and was its president from 1929 until he retired in 1962. The firm sold textiles on commission and owned mills at Easthampton and at Montgomery, the latter making cotton cord for automobile tyres.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a Doubleday and joined the board
narrative_blocks.body: He married Dorothy Doubleday at Oyster Bay in May 1915, a daughter of Frank Nelson Doubleday and Neltje Blanchan, and served as a director of the publishing house himself.

narrative_blocks.header: He built housing on the Upper West Side
narrative_blocks.body: He was a founder of Morningside Heights, Inc., a nonprofit redevelopment corporation that put up housing in that part of New York.

narrative_blocks.header: A hospital library carries his name
narrative_blocks.body: He was a trustee of Woman's Hospital from 1943 and stayed on the board when it merged into St. Luke's. In 1960 he and his wife set up the Wivenhoe Fund for churches, hospitals, schools and medical research, and in 1965 the Babcock Library was dedicated in their honour.

narrative_blocks.header: She died on her seventy-ninth birthday
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Manhattan on 2 May 1922, she died at New Canaan on 2 May 2001, the same date exactly. Her daughter followed her before the year was out.

narrative_blocks.header: She married another Hooker descendant
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband Henry Waters Taft II came down from Thomas Hooker as she did, eleven generations on his side and eleven on hers — his through the Tafts, hers through the Doubledays. The two lines had run apart for centuries before the marriage joined them again.

narrative_blocks.header: Three surnames in thirty-five years
narrative_blocks.body: She became Dorothy Chapin Hobson in December 1966, carried Buckley after that, and was Dorothy Chapin Ermo from February 1977 until she died.

narrative_blocks.header: Her stone quotes the Little Prince
narrative_blocks.body: The inscription at Lakeview begins that in one of the stars she shall be living, and in one of them she shall be laughing.

bio.display_name: Dorothy Babcock Chapin Hobson Buckley Ermo

narrative_blocks.header: He married a Doubleday, then kept its books
narrative_blocks.body: He married Sylvia Babcock, a granddaughter of Frank Nelson Doubleday, in 1949, and was treasurer of the publishing company from 1953 to 1959.

narrative_blocks.header: He left the boardroom for a wilderness school
narrative_blocks.body: After eleven years as treasurer and vice president of Bristol-Myers he took over Outward Bound U.S.A., and in 1981 moved to Maine. He was a trustee of the Taft School and of the Conservation Foundation.

narrative_blocks.header: Rappelling the Tetons, sculling the open Atlantic
narrative_blocks.body: He rappelled in the High Tetons and sculled alone on the Atlantic, and served as an officer in two wars. On the students of Outward Bound he pressed Tennyson's line — to strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield.

cross_connections.display_label: was his wife's grandfather, and founded the house he kept books for

education.school_name: Harvard Graduate School of Business Administration

narrative_blocks.header: She worked the French Line before marrying
narrative_blocks.body: She was with the French Line for several years before her marriage in 1950. Later she sat on the board of the Bellevue Hospital schools of nursing, volunteered at North Shore Glen Cove Hospital, and was a trustee of the Village of Lattingtown.

narrative_blocks.header: Croquet was more than a lawn game
narrative_blocks.body: She played croquet in tournament after tournament — an addiction, her family called it, rather than a pastime.

narrative_blocks.header: She died five weeks before her brother-in-law
narrative_blocks.body: She died at Los Angeles on 27 December 1933 and Frank Nelson Doubleday at Coconut Grove thirty-four days later. The bequests his will had left her fell back into his estate.

narrative_blocks.header: Her first cross-country flight was a Condor
narrative_blocks.body: She flew down from New York to Bolling Field in February 1931 on one of Eastern Air Transport's Condors — her first cross-country flight, and she enjoyed it very much. Her husband, an Air Corps captain, met her at the field.

narrative_blocks.header: A Doubleday living on a bombardment base
narrative_blocks.body: Through the 1930s her address was March Field in California, the base where her husband flew, and she was named there among her uncle Frank Nelson Doubleday's heirs.

narrative_blocks.header: He radioed that he was turning east
narrative_blocks.body: Flying an attack monoplane from Albuquerque to Lowry Field through fog and sleet, he called the Trinidad airport to say he was fifteen miles west of it, hitting soup, and turning east. He and Corporal Maurice Melvin went down in a Kansas ravine that night.

narrative_blocks.header: The officers at Bolling Field called him Chief
narrative_blocks.body: He was a Native American, born at Petersburg in Virginia, and the nickname followed him through the service. He entered the Air Corps in the First World War, was commissioned first lieutenant in 1918 and made major in 1936.

narrative_blocks.header: Bolling Field, then a bombardment squadron
narrative_blocks.body: He served at Bolling Field outside Washington from 1926 to 1931, then sailed for California through the canal to join a bombardment squadron at March Field. He was stationed at Lowry Field in Denver when he died.

narrative_blocks.header: Now there are two aviators in the family
narrative_blocks.body: That was what he said when his wife stepped off the Condor at Bolling Field in 1931 after her first cross-country flight. He had gone out to meet her at the field.

narrative_blocks.header: Born in the Azores, died in Athens
narrative_blocks.body: She was born in the Azores in 1924 and died at Athens in 1972, while visiting her daughter there. She was buried at Columbia in South Carolina, where her parents had lived.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty years flying for the Air Force
narrative_blocks.body: He flew for thirty years in the United States Air Force and retired a colonel. Afterwards he was a partner in Miller and Miller, an executive search firm at Kirkland in Washington.

narrative_blocks.header: A car accident at Bountiful killed him
narrative_blocks.body: He died in January 1995 of complications from a car accident in Utah, in which his second wife Shirley was also hurt. He was seventy-four.

narrative_blocks.header: Born in Germany, raised by her grandmother
narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Hanover in 1909 while her father was at the Kaiser's artillery school. Her mother died when she was five, and she and her brother were brought up by their grandmother in Washington while their father remarried.

narrative_blocks.header: The velvet glove on a feared columnist
narrative_blocks.body: Through thirty-three years of marriage to Drew Pearson she was, her son said, the soft velvet glove of tact that soothed the people his column had offended.

narrative_blocks.header: Cissy Patterson fired her out of spite
narrative_blocks.body: She reviewed films for the Times-Herald until its owner, at odds with her husband over politics, threw his column out of the paper and fired her along with it.

narrative_blocks.header: She died at the bridge table
narrative_blocks.body: She collapsed at a friend's house on the Eastern Shore in March 1992 while playing bridge and feeding her poodle Scarlett. Her brother said that if she could have chosen her moment, that would have been it.

narrative_blocks.header: She was two when her mother died
narrative_blocks.body: Luvean Butler Moore died on R Street in Washington in March 1915, three months before her daughter's third birthday. Francesca was raised on the moves of her father, Col. Daniel Tyler Moore, who had founded the Army's artillery school.

narrative_blocks.header: Two marriages, forty years apart
narrative_blocks.body: She married Evan Jennings Kemp in Washington in May 1934 and was widowed in 1967, at fifty-five. Seven years later she married Charles William Bliss of Cleveland, and spent the rest of her life in Cleveland Heights.

narrative_blocks.header: She buried her son eight months before
narrative_blocks.body: Evan Jennings Kemp Jr. died in August 1997 and his mother the following April. She was laid beside her second husband at Lake View in Cleveland, where her daughter would join them in 2014.

narrative_blocks.header: His great-grandfather founded the Baltimore Sun
narrative_blocks.body: Arunah Shepherdson Abell started the Sun in 1837 and later the Philadelphia Public Ledger, and the family held an interest in the Sunpapers for generations. He was born in Baltimore on the strength of it.

narrative_blocks.header: He administered the oath to his son
narrative_blocks.body: He had been three years an assistant chief of protocol at the State Department when his son Tyler was named Chief of Protocol in 1968, and it fell to him to swear him in. The department called the ceremony unprecedented.

narrative_blocks.header: His son was taken back on Sark
narrative_blocks.body: In 1937 his former wife and her new husband Drew Pearson took the five-year-old boy back on Sark in the Channel Islands, saying he had carried the child abroad without her leave.

cross_connections.display_label: was fired by his family's Sun, and married Luvie after him

notable.notable_blurb: Washington Merry-Go-Round columnist

narrative_blocks.header: His column ran in six hundred newspapers
narrative_blocks.body: Washington Merry-Go-Round grew out of two anonymous books that cost him his job at the Baltimore Sun when he was found out. It ran from 1932 until his death in 1969, by then in some six hundred and fifty papers.

narrative_blocks.header: Sued for libel over a hundred times
narrative_blocks.body: He carried no libel insurance and would not let his syndicate pay judgments for him, and was sued more than a hundred and twenty times. He settled exactly once.

narrative_blocks.header: He broke the Patton slapping story
narrative_blocks.body: In 1943 he was first to report that Patton had struck a soldier under treatment for combat stress, which brought calls in Congress for the general's recall. The Secretary of War ordered a hunt for the leak.

narrative_blocks.header: He filled seven hundred boxcars for Europe
narrative_blocks.body: In 1947 he used the column and the radio to launch the Friendship Train, which crossed the country gathering food for France and Italy. France sent back a Merci train of forty-nine boxcars of gifts.

narrative_blocks.header: Two presidents called him a chronic liar
narrative_blocks.body: Roosevelt used the phrase at a press conference and Truman said he would have to add another liar's star to the man's crown. A senator once spent half an hour on the floor finding new ways to say it.

narrative_blocks.header: His stone calls him author, farmer, teacher
narrative_blocks.body: He lies on a rock above the Potomac at the Maryland farm that took the column's name, under a stone reading author, farmer, teacher, Washington Merry-Go-Round columnist, creator of Friendship Train. Her ashes were laid beside his.

cross_connections.display_label: won the Pulitzer for the war he was hunted for leaking
sued for libel and won where he was sued and never paid

notable.notable_blurb: State Department Chief of Protocol under Johnson

narrative_blocks.header: His father swore him in as ambassador
narrative_blocks.body: George Abell, three years an assistant chief of protocol, administered the oath to his son as the State Department's Chief of Protocol in 1968 while Bess held the Bible. The post carries the personal rank of ambassador.

narrative_blocks.header: Johnson's first sub-Cabinet appointment
narrative_blocks.body: He was Johnson's first sub-Cabinet pick, Assistant Postmaster General from December 1963, and came to the protocol post from private practice. He resigned the day Nixon took office.

narrative_blocks.header: They took him back on Sark
narrative_blocks.body: When he was five his mother and her new husband Drew Pearson took custody of him on Sark in the Channel Islands, saying his father had carried him overseas without her leave.

narrative_blocks.header: His stepfather's will made him the editor
narrative_blocks.body: Pearson left instructions that Tyler Abell should edit his diaries. He found twenty-four notebooks, published the first volume in 1974 and the second four decades later, and says he cut nothing for sensitivity.

narrative_blocks.header: He turned the farm into a horse community
narrative_blocks.body: With Bess he developed Merry-Go-Round Farm at Potomac, the Maryland place that had given the column its name, into a horse farm and a residential community.

cross_connections.display_label: ran the White House ceremony office forty years before him
held the same protocol office under Reagan, and held it longest

career.role: Chief of Protocol of the United States

notable.notable_blurb: White House social secretary

narrative_blocks.header: The Secret Service called her Iron Butterfly
narrative_blocks.body: She was Lady Bird Johnson's social secretary from 1963 to 1969, running the invitations, the seating and the entertaining for a family that entertained constantly. The handle was for the steel under the charm.

narrative_blocks.header: A thousand guests, arranged in a few hours
narrative_blocks.body: On 23 December 1963, the day the White House came out of mourning for Kennedy, Johnson decided to invite every member of Congress that night. She had the black crepe down, the decorations up and food for a thousand before they arrived.

narrative_blocks.header: Her counter-party opened the Gridiron Club
narrative_blocks.body: In 1974 she organised a Counter-Gridiron for the women journalists the Gridiron Club would not admit. It went so well that the club began taking women the following year.

narrative_blocks.header: She ran a train through the angry South
narrative_blocks.body: For the 1964 campaign she and Liz Carpenter organised the Lady Bird Special, a whistle-stop tour through Southern states where the Civil Rights Act had cost Johnson his support.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father governed Kentucky
narrative_blocks.body: Earle Clements was a congressman, governor of Kentucky and a United States senator, and her mother Sara was postmaster of their town. She grew up at Morganfield and took a political science degree at Kentucky.

cross_connections.display_label: ran a later First Lady's parties, for Nancy Reagan
presided over the Gridiron Club she later forced open

narrative_blocks.header: Her infant son died at Chicago in 1946
narrative_blocks.body: Her second marriage, to Joseph Martyn McMahon Jr. in November 1944, gave her a son who died at Chicago on 20 May 1946. He is the only child recorded from any of her three marriages.

narrative_blocks.header: Born the same day as her sister Mary
narrative_blocks.body: She and Mary Hoyt Cowles were both born at Chicago on 25 February 1923. Their father died at Denver four years later, and their mother remarried in 1929 and took them to Wisconsin.

narrative_blocks.header: A fighter pilot who kept on flying
narrative_blocks.body: Calvin flew fighters in the Second World War and retired from the Air Force Reserve a major. He kept flying all his life, as a corporate and instructor pilot, while serving as vice-president of Mace Laboratories in Neenah.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventy-one years married to Sarah
narrative_blocks.body: Calvin married Sarah Cowles on 3 March 1947, and they had been married seventy-one years when he died at ninety-four in May 2018. His memorial went to the EAA aviation museum at Oshkosh.

cross_connections.display_label: was her sister, and married her husband’s brother

narrative_blocks.header: A college library carries her name
narrative_blocks.body: Whitworth’s first real library was raised as a memorial to her after she died in 1938, paid for by her husband and her sons. Its president called it the very heart of the campus.

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband died before it opened
narrative_blocks.body: William H. Cowles died in 1946, two years before the building was finished, and their son carried the gift through in his place. President Frank F. Warren dedicated it on 10 November 1948.

narrative_blocks.header: The family kept paying for it for decades
narrative_blocks.body: They funded a new wing finished in 1969 and a third building opened in 1992, carrying the library from eight thousand square feet to better than fifty thousand. Her name is still on it.

narrative_blocks.header: She and her sister married two brothers
narrative_blocks.body: A daughter of the Manchester silk manufacturer Knight Dexter Cheney, she married William Hutchinson Cowles at South Manchester in February 1896. Her sister Elizabeth had married his brother Alfred seven years before.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Whitworth University, Spokane

narrative_blocks.header: Spokane to Vassar to a Santa Barbara porch
narrative_blocks.body: She took a Vassar degree in 1922 and married Buell Hammett at her parents’ Santa Barbara house in December 1930, the ceremony kept to immediate family at her own wish. He died in January 1945; she afterwards married John D. Graham and stayed in Santa Barbara until her death in 1975.

narrative_blocks.header: A carrier-salesman at sixteen
narrative_blocks.body: He entered the business in 1918 at sixteen, selling papers on a Spokane Daily Chronicle route his father owned. Home from Yale in 1924 he worked up through every department, and sat as a director of the Inland Empire Paper Company from 1927 until his death.

narrative_blocks.header: He held both papers and the radio too
narrative_blocks.body: President of the Spokane Chronicle Company from 1935 and of Cowles Publishing from 1946, he ran the city’s morning and evening dailies and the Northwest farm magazines. The company took radio station KHQ in 1946, and KHQ televised Spokane’s first commercial programme in 1952.

narrative_blocks.header: He crossed Castro over a free press
narrative_blocks.body: A director of the Inter American Press Association from 1950 and its president in 1959, he attacked Castro’s suppression of the press as Castro rose. Many Latin American publishers he had befriended were jailed by dictators for the same cause.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote discrimination into his deeds
narrative_blocks.body: In August 1953 he signed protective covenants on five South Hill subdivisions barring people of colour from the houses, some two hundred homes. He signed five years after the Supreme Court had ruled such covenants unenforceable, and the language sits on many deeds still.

narrative_blocks.header: A library for her, an auditorium for him
narrative_blocks.body: A Whitworth trustee from 1960 until his death, he and his family financed the library there for his mother and an auditorium for his father. The college gave him an honorary doctorate in 1954.

narrative_blocks.header: A museum for the brother the war took
narrative_blocks.body: He and his family funded the Cheney Cowles Memorial Museum at Spokane for his brother Cheney, killed on active duty with the Army Air Forces. He gave land at Diamond Lake for a Scout reservation besides.

narrative_blocks.header: Heart failure after a long illness
narrative_blocks.body: A long illness ended in heart failure at a Spokane hospital on 12 August 1971. He was sixty-nine.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Whitworth University, Spokane
Northwest Museum of Arts and Culture

narrative_blocks.header: A medium bomber came down near Mobile
narrative_blocks.body: The bomber he was in came down at Vinegar Bend, Alabama, fifty miles northeast of Mobile, on 12 May 1943, killing him and four other flyers. Barksdale Field announced the deaths; he was thirty-four.

narrative_blocks.header: He was managing editor, on leave for war
narrative_blocks.body: He was managing editor of the Spokane Daily Chronicle and on leave from that desk when he was killed. The paper was his family’s, and his brother was its general manager.

narrative_blocks.header: He left a daughter of two behind him
narrative_blocks.body: He married Sarah Elizabeth Ferris in 1939, and his daughter Phoebe was two years old when he died. A son, Frank Cheney Cowles, carried his name on in Spokane.

narrative_blocks.header: A Spokane museum was raised in his name
narrative_blocks.body: The Cheney Cowles Memorial Museum opened in 1960, funded by his family, and gave the Eastern Washington State Historical Society its first real exhibition hall. His widow later sat on that society’s board as its first vice president.

narrative_blocks.header: His stone gives his name and nothing else
narrative_blocks.body: The funeral was at the Cathedral of St. John the Evangelist on 19 May 1943, the interment private at Greenwood. The marker reads only MAJOR CHENEY COWLES, his two dates, and ARMY OF THE UNITED STATES.

burial.plot_notes: Stone reads MAJOR CHENEY COWLES 1908-1943 ARMY OF THE UNITED STATES

career.organization: McCutcheon, Olney, Mannon & Greene, San Francisco

narrative_blocks.header: An astrologer picked the opening minute
narrative_blocks.body: He was a founder of the Santa Barbara Museum of Art and its first president from 1938 to 1944, and he had an astrologer calculate the most propitious moment to unlock the doors. They opened at 11:43 on the morning of 5 June 1941, to fifteen hundred schoolchildren.

narrative_blocks.header: A gun duel on a Santa Barbara porch
narrative_blocks.body: In April 1942 he and Maj. William H. Wenstrom shot each other on the Wenstroms’ porch, over differences about the home guard unit he headed. Wenstrom and his wife were killed; Hammett was left with a shattered right leg and was cleared by a grand jury he testified before on a stretcher.

narrative_blocks.header: Harvard law, Oxford, then a sanitarium
narrative_blocks.body: He took an LL.B. at Harvard in 1921, read international law at Oxford, and practised with a San Francisco firm from 1922 to 1926. Ill health then held him at the Pottenger Sanitarium in Monrovia for four years.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother married the man who wrote Casey
narrative_blocks.body: His mother Rosalind Buel Hammett married Ernest Lawrence Thayer, who had written “Casey at the Bat,” and it was as Mrs. E. L. Thayer of Santa Barbara that she outlived her son. The younger of his two boys was named Lawrence Thayer Hammett for the stepfather.

narrative_blocks.header: Ill health took him at forty-nine
narrative_blocks.body: Three years after the duel, in January 1945, ill health brought him to take his own life at Santa Barbara. He was buried in the Santa Barbara Cemetery, where his widow joined him thirty years later.

bio.bio_blurb: Santa Barbara trust officer and museum trustee

career.organization: Hammett and Associates, real estate consulting

narrative_blocks.header: He left the banks for his own firm
narrative_blocks.body: He read business administration at Claremont Men’s College, then built a trust career at County National Bank in Santa Barbara, at Wells Fargo’s trust division, and at Title Insurance and Trust. He left to start his own real estate consulting firm, Hammett and Associates.

narrative_blocks.header: He joined his father’s museum board
narrative_blocks.body: He was a trustee of the Santa Barbara Museum of Art, the institution his father founded and first presided over, and of the Santa Barbara Historical Museum besides. Laguna Blanca, Friendship Manor, the University of Redlands and Trinity Lutheran had him on their boards too.

narrative_blocks.header: His children followed him to Claremont
narrative_blocks.body: He was a trustee of Claremont McKenna from 1996 to 2009 and endowed two scholarships and a faculty research fund there with his wife Astrid. His son Bob came up in the class of 1984 and his daughter Denise went to Scripps.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried his step-grandfather’s name
narrative_blocks.body: He was named for Ernest L. Thayer, who wrote “Casey at the Bat” and had married his grandmother Rosalind. He was ten years old when his father died at Santa Barbara in January 1945.

education.notes: Wharton School of Finance and Commerce
