Fifth Air Force, Pacific

narrative_blocks.header: He took up the big mountains at fifty
narrative_blocks.body: He began hiking in 1927 but made most of his climbs after he had passed fifty, and he climbed very fast. He went up better than a hundred and twenty peaks above fourteen thousand feet.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept pace with Lionel Terray at 55
narrative_blocks.body: In 1951, at fifty-five, he crossed all five summits of Mont Blanc in a single day beside the French guide Lionel Terray. That same summer he took all twenty-three Alpine peaks above fourteen thousand feet.

narrative_blocks.header: Two African summits in one day at 64
narrative_blocks.body: Between 1959 and 1960 he climbed all fifteen African peaks above sixteen thousand feet, taking Mount Kenya’s twin summits of Batian and Nelion in a single day.

narrative_blocks.header: He climbed Mount McKinley at sixty-five
narrative_blocks.body: In 1961 he went up Mount McKinley at sixty-five and left a journal of the ascent and a paper recommending the West Buttress route. His fellow Alpine Club members took it as proof they had years left in the hills.

narrative_blocks.header: He came home from France with the DSC
narrative_blocks.body: He served with the Army in France in the First World War and won the Distinguished Service Cross, the nation’s second-highest award for valour. In the Second he was a major with the Fifth Air Force in the Pacific.

narrative_blocks.header: Wharton, Wall Street, then the mountains
narrative_blocks.body: A Wharton man of 1918, he made his money as a Wall Street broker and afterwards ran a California real-estate business. The climbing came mostly once he had left the first behind.

narrative_blocks.header: New Year’s Eve meant Pikes Peak
narrative_blocks.body: He belonged to the AdAmAn Club of Colorado Springs and specially enjoyed its New Year’s Eve climb of Pikes Peak, where the members set off fireworks from the summit.

bio.bio_blurb: Popular historian and Hutton Settlement trustee

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-six years on one children’s board
narrative_blocks.body: She sat on the board of trustees of the Hutton Settlement, a home for underprivileged children, for fifty-six years. Its administrator said she had a soft spot for the underdog and was never averse to dirty-hands work in a good cause.

narrative_blocks.header: She married in her grandparents’ church
narrative_blocks.body: Her grandparents the Rev. Henry T. and Lucy Cowley came out in 1874 as missionaries to the Indians and founded Spokane’s first Protestant church five years later. She was married in it on 3 December 1930.

narrative_blocks.header: At eighty-five she won her Bloomsday class
narrative_blocks.body: She entered the Bloomsday road races year after year and finished first in her age division in 1988, at eighty-five. The YWCA honoured her that same year for thirty years of public service.

narrative_blocks.header: She gave tours in her mother’s clothes
narrative_blocks.body: She was a docent at the Campbell House and at the Cheney Cowles Museum, named for the brother-in-law the war had taken. She dressed in her mother’s clothing to give the tours, drawing on her own family’s pioneer history.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father chaired the Crescent
narrative_blocks.body: She was born in Spokane in 1902 to James L. and Agnes C. Paine, and her father was chairman of the board of the Crescent department store.

cross_connections.display_label: founded the Ojai school that took him, his father and his uncle
edited the Yale Daily News and read Harvard law fifty-six years first

career.organization: The Spokesman-Review and the Spokane Chronicle

narrative_blocks.header: He carried the papers before he ran them
narrative_blocks.body: He delivered the family papers on a Spokane route as a schoolboy, finished school in California, and came back to work most departments of the Spokesman-Review. He became its publisher in 1970, the third of his name to hold the title.

narrative_blocks.header: The owner turned up on Christmas evening
narrative_blocks.body: He had a habit of dropping in on the newspaper’s departments on holiday nights, bringing his family along at Christmas to introduce them. A pressman of twenty-two years said they came to expect it — he was just the owner.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale economics, a destroyer, Harvard law
narrative_blocks.body: He edited the Yale Daily News and took his degree in economics in 1953, then served three years in the Naval Reserve aboard a destroyer. He came out and took a law degree at Harvard in 1959.

narrative_blocks.header: He chaired the publishers, vice-chaired the AP
narrative_blocks.body: He was chairman of the American Newspaper Publishers Association and first vice chairman of the Associated Press, whose board he sat on from 1974 to 1983. He directed Landmark Communications, the Seattle Times Company and Allied Daily Newspapers besides.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale’s alumni voted him onto its board
narrative_blocks.body: Yale alumni elected him a fellow of the Yale Corporation for a six-year term, succeeding Gilbert Grosvenor of the National Geographic Society. He chaired KHQ and the Washington Roundtable in the same years.

narrative_blocks.header: He thought newspapers the most valuable trade
narrative_blocks.body: He called the newspaper business the most fascinating and socially valuable enterprise one could think of. Tom Foley, the Speaker of the House from his district, said his papers were fair to him even when they disagreed.

narrative_blocks.header: A heart attack out running, at sixty
narrative_blocks.body: He was stricken while jogging near his home in April 1992 and died soon after at Sacred Heart Medical Center. The Spokane Chronicle, the afternoon paper his grandfather bought in 1897, closed two months later.

notable.notable_blurb: Spokesman-Review publisher

military_service.notes: served aboard a destroyer

bio.bio_blurb: Inland Empire Paper chairman; Whitworth medallist

narrative_blocks.header: He held the company between two generations
narrative_blocks.body: When his brother William died suddenly in 1992, he took the family business and steadied it. He handed it on to his nephew Stacey and his niece Betsy, the fourth generation to run it.

narrative_blocks.header: He talked the railroads out of their land
narrative_blocks.body: His gift was negotiation, and it was he who persuaded the railroads to hand the city the ground for the 1974 World’s Fair. He worked those years alongside Tom Foley, Neil Fosseen and King Cole.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the paper mill on the river
narrative_blocks.body: He took the presidency of the Inland Empire Paper Company in 1962, with the company’s land and timber under him, and later chaired its board. He was vice president, chair and president of Cowles Publishing in turn, and sat on the Tribune Company board.

narrative_blocks.header: Whitworth gave them both its highest medal
narrative_blocks.body: Whitworth awarded him and his wife the George F. Whitworth Medal, given only rarely and hers posthumously. He had led the building of the campus music hall in the 1970s and endowed a chair in gifted education in her cause.

bio.bio_blurb: Actress, drama teacher, and land conservationist

education.school_name: London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art

narrative_blocks.header: She staged plays with her stuffed animals
narrative_blocks.body: From the start she put on plays and dramas with her friends and her stuffed animals. She took a drama degree at Whitworth in 1959 and a master’s from the Yale Drama School in 1965.

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband wrote her a one-woman show
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband the playwright Daniel A. Stein wrote her “An Independent Woman,” the abolitionist Anna Dickinson rebuilt out of her own lectures, and later “Just Between Us,” in which she carried more than fourteen characters. Critics set her beside the great monologuist Ruth Draper, whose sketches she performed.

narrative_blocks.header: Rep stages, then film and television
narrative_blocks.body: She played dozens of parts at the Long Wharf, Milwaukee and Louisville repertory theatres, from Maggie in “Cat on a Hot Tin Roof” to Annie in Ayckbourn’s “Table Manners.” Her screen work ran from a Jon Voight picture in 1973 to Marcus Welby and Law & Order.

narrative_blocks.header: She and Dan taught drama in Kentucky
narrative_blocks.body: The two of them taught drama classes at Northern Kentucky University through the late seventies and early eighties, while she went on acting.

narrative_blocks.header: Her apartment had a stage in it
narrative_blocks.body: She loved New York and kept a place there that held a small stage of its own. Her favourite spot was a primitive cabin on a lake her grandfather had once owned, where she lived without electricity.

narrative_blocks.header: She bought land to keep everyone off it
narrative_blocks.body: She took pride in widening her holdings around the lake and shielding the wild ground from development or any other human incursion. Her sister Agnes helped her raise a house built to look like a stone outcropping.

narrative_blocks.header: Christian Science, Hinduism, and the woods
narrative_blocks.body: She drew on Christian Science, Hinduism and Native American traditions, and took her solace from the land she spent her later years buying up and shielding.

bio.bio_blurb: Wellesley trustee and Spokane civic leader

cross_connections.display_label: sat on a Planned Parenthood board too, a generation ahead of her
built Mt. Hood Meadows as she was enlarging Mt. Spokane

narrative_blocks.header: A Wellesley editor who meant to profess
narrative_blocks.body: She was elected to Phi Beta Kappa and edited the Wellesley News in her graduating year of 1955, then took a master’s in history at Radcliffe intending to teach it. She married into newspapers instead and stayed in that world for life.

narrative_blocks.header: She married into two newspaper families
narrative_blocks.body: In 1959 she married William H. Cowles III and went out to Spokane, where his family owned the Spokesman-Review. Widowed in 1992, she married Arthur Ochs Sulzberger of the New York Times four years later, in her daughter’s Spokane house.

narrative_blocks.header: She argued a university into Spokane
narrative_blocks.body: She chaired the advisory board and the capital campaign for Washington State University’s Spokane branch, pressing to have a full campus seated in the city. She gave twelve years to the state’s Council for Postsecondary Education and was a trustee of Wellesley, Whitman and the Smithsonian.

narrative_blocks.header: Her two children took over the company
narrative_blocks.body: Her son Stacey succeeded his father as publisher of the Spokesman-Review and her daughter Betsy became chairwoman of the Cowles company. Stacey’s first real memory of her was a woman on the telephone, with a toy phone of his own for imitating her.

narrative_blocks.header: Family planning came down from her mother
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother was a public health nurse and an early advocate of family planning, and Cowles sat on the board of Planned Parenthood of the Inland Northwest. She wrote in 2004 that she was raised believing it immoral to bring unwanted children into the world.

narrative_blocks.header: A run at Mt. Spokane carries her name
narrative_blocks.body: She spent the 1990s on the development and expansion of the Mt. Spokane Ski Area, so that families of any means could ski there. One of its runs is called Allison's Way.

career.organization: Washington State Council for Postsecondary Education
career.notes: Twelve years on the council, three of them in the chair.
A state-funded technology assistance agency for the Inland Northwest.
Criminal defense for people who cannot pay for it.

career.organization: Planned Parenthood of the Inland Northwest

career.notes: Named to it after her first husband's death in 1992.

bio.bio_blurb: San Francisco arts patron and museum funder

narrative_blocks.header: A SFMOMA fund carries her name
narrative_blocks.body: She founded the Bay Area Contemporary Arts Exhibition Fund at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, which has underwritten exhibitions of California art for years. The Mills College Art Museum keeps a fund for special exhibitions in her name as well.

narrative_blocks.header: Her sister called her in on a house
narrative_blocks.body: When Peggy wanted a house at her lake made to look like a stone outcropping, it was Agnes she enlisted to help raise it.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Northwest Museum of Arts and Culture

narrative_blocks.header: Smith, where her mother had gone before
narrative_blocks.body: She went from Lewis and Clark High School to the Northampton School for Girls and then to Smith, taking her degree in 1937. Her mother and her aunt had gone there before her.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at twenty-eight by a bomber crash
narrative_blocks.body: She married Cheney Cowles in 1939 and lost him to a military airplane crash in 1943. She married twice more, E. L. Griffin of Tacoma in 1945 and Cecil R. Fuller in 1956.

narrative_blocks.header: She joined the board that kept his museum
narrative_blocks.body: She served the Eastern Washington State Historical Society as its first vice president, the society housed in the museum built in her first husband’s memory. She sat on the YWCA, St. George’s School and Joel E. Ferris Foundation boards besides.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father ran the bank’s eastern division
narrative_blocks.body: Her father Joel E. Ferris was executive vice president of the Seattle-First National Bank and managed its Spokane and Eastern Division. Her grandfather George H. Hughes had come out to Spokane from New York State in the early nineties.

narrative_blocks.header: A Gonzaga regent who backed Whitworth too
narrative_blocks.body: She was appointed to a three-year term on the Gonzaga University board of regents in 1972 and was active in support of Whitworth College. Whitworth was the school her first husband’s family had given its library.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Northwest Museum of Arts and Culture
Northwest Museum of Arts and Culture

cross_connections.display_label: won one of the paper's Pulitzers five years after he left the chair

military_service.notes: Pacific theatre

narrative_blocks.header: At thirty-seven, the youngest Times publisher
narrative_blocks.body: He took the paper in 1963 after his brother-in-law Orvil Dryfoos died having held it barely two years. He was thirty-seven, and his father and his grandfather Adolph Ochs had held the chair before him.

narrative_blocks.header: He read seven thousand pages, then printed them
narrative_blocks.body: He went through the Pentagon Papers himself before deciding to publish, and the Times ran the first of seven articles in June 1971. The Nixon administration demanded he stop; he refused, won in the Supreme Court, and the paper took a Pulitzer for it.

narrative_blocks.header: “My conclusion is simple. Nepotism works.”
narrative_blocks.body: A believer in family ownership, he liked to put the case in five words. His son took the publisher’s chair from him in 1992 and the family holds the controlling stake yet.

narrative_blocks.header: The armour that held him as a boy
narrative_blocks.body: He credited a boyhood fascination with the Metropolitan Museum’s arms and armour for a lifetime there, and he was its board chairman from 1987 to 1998. The museum named its arms and armour exhibition gallery for him in 2002.

narrative_blocks.header: He named a Wellesley pub for his wife
narrative_blocks.body: In 1996 he married Allison Stacey Cowles, four years after her first husband died, and they kept houses in New York and Spokane. He dedicated the Wellesley College pub — Punch’s Alley — in honour of her class of 1955.

narrative_blocks.header: A Marine in two wars before the newsroom
narrative_blocks.body: He enlisted in the Marine Corps in 1944 and served in the Pacific, then was recalled from the reserve for Korea. He reported on the Times city staff and out of its Paris, Rome and London bureaus before he ever ran it.

narrative_blocks.header: Fourth generation in the publisher’s chair
narrative_blocks.body: He joined the family company in 1989 and has been publisher of the Spokesman-Review since 1992, the fourth generation of Cowleses to hold the title. He is president of the print media division and of Cowles Company.

narrative_blocks.header: AP London, then KPMG in New York
narrative_blocks.body: Before he came home he was a newswriter in the Associated Press London bureau and a senior manager in business valuation and mergers at KPMG Peat Marwick in New York. He holds a Yale degree in economics and a Columbia business degree.

narrative_blocks.header: He backed Spokane’s first venture fund
narrative_blocks.body: He went on the board of Spokane Capital Management, the city’s first venture fund, in 1989 and has invested as an angel and venture capitalist since. He was founding chairman of the Downtown Spokane Partnership.

narrative_blocks.header: He agreed to give the paper away
narrative_blocks.body: The family agreed to transfer the Spokesman-Review to Comma Journalism Lab, a nonprofit, with matching funds from Cowles Company once Comma met its own fundraising goal. He sits meanwhile as a director of the Associated Press.

bio.bio_blurb: Cowles Company chairman; broadcasting and real estate

narrative_blocks.header: She took one station and made it nine
narrative_blocks.body: Joining the company in 1992, she carried its broadcast division from a single Spokane station to more than nine across Washington, Idaho and Montana. She is president of the broadcasting, insurance and real estate divisions.

narrative_blocks.header: She led the River Park Square rebuild
narrative_blocks.body: Her real-estate work included leading the redevelopment of River Park Square in downtown Spokane, along with acquisitions, technology centralisation and operational restructuring across the company.

narrative_blocks.header: Dartmouth, a law degree, a Seattle firm
narrative_blocks.body: She took her degree at Dartmouth and a law degree at George Washington University, then practised with Davis Wright Tremaine in Seattle before joining the family company.

narrative_blocks.header: She chaired the regents her mother had served
narrative_blocks.body: She is a past chair of the Board of Regents of Washington State University, where her mother had chaired the Spokane campus advisory board and its capital campaign. She has been a trustee of George Washington University and chaired Greater Spokane Incorporated.

bio.bio_blurb: Advocate for gifted education; Whitworth trustee

narrative_blocks.header: She gave her life to gifted children
narrative_blocks.body: She sat on the Washington State Advisory Committee for Gifted Education until 2009, and on the Spokane district’s gifted advisory committee and the Northwest Gifted Child Association besides. Whitworth gave her its Distinguished Community Service Award in 1985 for that work.

narrative_blocks.header: A trustee who chaired Whitworth’s academics
narrative_blocks.body: She was a Whitworth trustee from 1988 to 1995 and chaired its academic affairs and honorary degrees committees. Her passion shaped the university’s teacher preparation and certification programmes.

narrative_blocks.header: She taught school in California and Germany
narrative_blocks.body: She took a bachelor’s degree at UCLA in 1953 and a master’s in education at Stanford in 1961. She taught elementary school in California and in Germany before turning to a life of committees.

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve years on a Seattle science board
narrative_blocks.body: She gave twelve years to the board of the Pacific Science Center in Seattle and twelve more to Saint George’s School, and worked to bring a science centre to Spokane. She founded and led Spokane Business Assisting Scholastic Excellence.

bio.bio_blurb: Playwright; wrote his wife’s one-woman shows

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the shows his wife played alone
narrative_blocks.body: He wrote “An Independent Woman” for her, the abolitionist Anna Dickinson brought back through her own lectures, staged with the Actors Theater of Louisville. The two collaborated again on “Just Between Us,” in which she carried more than fourteen characters.

narrative_blocks.header: He put a forgotten woman back onstage
narrative_blocks.body: Critics said the Dickinson play asked why so remarkable a woman had been virtually erased from the history of the Civil War and of the American theatre. It ran in International Women’s Year.

narrative_blocks.header: An artist who married the publisher
narrative_blocks.body: She is an artist and a museum educator, and she married Charles Scribner on 4 August 1979. Their sons are Charles and Christopher Markoe Scribner.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father built Warner-Lambert’s legal side
narrative_blocks.body: Frank Markoe Jr. was general counsel to the Emerson Drug Company in Baltimore, oversaw its merger into Warner-Lambert, and rose there to executive vice-president and vice chairman of the board. He had flown with the Army Air Force from 1942 to 1945.

narrative_blocks.header: Carter sent her father to Radio Free Europe
narrative_blocks.body: President Carter appointed him to the Board of International Broadcasting, which oversaw Radio Free Europe and Radio Liberty, in 1977. He was president of the New Jersey Ballet in those same years.

narrative_blocks.header: He moved his two daughters to Far Hills
narrative_blocks.body: He brought her and her sister Andree to Far Hills as girls and went into New Jersey civic life and politics. In 1981 he began a second career running the New York Hospital-Cornell Medical Center.

notable.notable_blurb: Founder of Charles Scribner’s Sons, 1846

narrative_blocks.header: He invented a house that only published
narrative_blocks.body: In 1846 he joined Isaac Baker to found Baker and Scribner, unlike the printing shops and bookstores most publishers grew out of — theirs would exist purely to publish. That shaped a list confined largely to living authors.

narrative_blocks.header: The list began with Presbyterian theology
narrative_blocks.body: The firm’s early books were philosophical and theological, mostly Presbyterian. Only near the end of his life did it turn to reprints and translations of British and European literature.

narrative_blocks.header: His partner died and he took the name
narrative_blocks.body: Baker died in 1850 and he took control, renaming the firm Charles Scribner and then Charles Scribner and Company. In 1857 he set up Scribner and Welford with Charles Welford to import foreign books.

narrative_blocks.header: He got into magazines with Hours at Home
narrative_blocks.body: The company made its first venture into periodicals in 1865 with Hours at Home, a monthly. In 1870 it was folded into Scribner’s Monthly under the editorship of Josiah Holland.

narrative_blocks.header: Lawrenceville, a year at NYU, then Princeton
narrative_blocks.body: He was at Lawrenceville from 1834, spent a year at New York University, and graduated with Princeton’s class of 1840. He began to read law, but ill health sent him to Europe instead.

narrative_blocks.header: His eldest son ran the house eight years
narrative_blocks.body: John Blair Scribner left Princeton without a degree to work beside him, and took the presidency at his death in 1871. Pneumonia killed the son at twenty-eight, and his widow Lucy Skidmore went on to found Skidmore College.

narrative_blocks.header: Typhoid took him at Lucerne at fifty
narrative_blocks.body: He died of typhoid in August 1871 while travelling in Switzerland. He lies in the family plot at Woodlawn in the Bronx, where his wife had been laid two years before.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father was the magnate John Insley Blair
narrative_blocks.body: She was a daughter of John Insley Blair and Nancy Ann Locke Blair. Her brother DeWitt Clinton carried on their father’s business, and her nephew C. Ledyard Blair became a prominent investment banker.

narrative_blocks.header: Three of her sons ran the publishing house
narrative_blocks.body: She married Charles Scribner in 1846 and bore four children, three of whom would head the firm in turn — John Blair, Charles, and Arthur Hawley. She died at forty-one in 1869, two years before her husband.

narrative_blocks.header: Her eldest son’s last word to his brother
narrative_blocks.body: Her son John Blair Scribner died of pneumonia at twenty-eight, ten years after her. “Cheer up old fellow; you always look on the dark side; I shall soon be all right again,” he told his brother Charles from his bed.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother died six days after he came
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Rome on 9 April 1876 and his mother was dead by the fifteenth. He died himself at seventeen and was buried in the Davidson College ground in North Carolina.

military_service.notes: 316th Supply Company, Quartermaster Corps

narrative_blocks.header: She indexed the county’s lost cemeteries
narrative_blocks.body: She and a few friends spent years searching out and indexing burial sites across Baldwin County, and the work became a book of a hundred and three lost or found cemeteries. She was a charter member of Friends of Baldwin County Cemeteries.

narrative_blocks.header: She was born and died in one house
narrative_blocks.body: She was born, lived and died in the house her great-grandfather William McKinley built in the late 1850s. She said it gave her the love of history and of land that shaped the rest.

narrative_blocks.header: She ran adult education for the county
narrative_blocks.body: She took a degree in education at Georgia, taught at City Elementary in Milledgeville, then qualified in adult education and directed the county programme. She served a term as president of the statewide organisation.

narrative_blocks.header: All three of her sons made Eagle Scout
narrative_blocks.body: She was a den mother for her sons’ Cub packs and helped her husband run their Boy Scout troop. She was proudest that all three boys reached Eagle Scout.

narrative_blocks.header: She and her husband taught square dancing
narrative_blocks.body: The two of them were active in square dancing associations and taught its patterns and steps through Baldwin, Putnam and Washington counties.

narrative_blocks.header: Tampa-born, thirty years in Baldwin County
narrative_blocks.body: A native of Tampa, he spent his last thirty years in Baldwin County and retired from American Coach and from Stevens. He was active in the Boy Scouts and died at forty-nine after a short illness.

narrative_blocks.header: She died at twelve, four days before Christmas
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Winston-Salem while her father was a missionary in Carolina, she died at Maplewood in New Jersey on 21 December 1928. She was twelve years old.

military_service.notes: Medical Detachment, 813th Pioneer Infantry; from New York

bio.bio_blurb: Ziegfeld dancer, then an Army wife

cross_connections.display_label: had her father interned in Tokyo by that same morning’s attack
was sunk aboard the California in the harbor she rode past
danced the Follies a decade before her, trained by Ruth St. Denis

narrative_blocks.header: She danced for Ziegfeld with the Astaires
narrative_blocks.body: A member of the Albertina Rasch ballet, she danced in Ziegfeld’s Show Girl, in Sons of Guns, and in The Band Wagon with Fred and Adele Astaire. She played Honeymoon Lane for three years.

narrative_blocks.header: West Point ended her stage career
narrative_blocks.body: She spent her rare time off visiting the Military Academy, where she met James Maloney. They married in 1931 on his graduation, and the dancing stopped.

narrative_blocks.header: She watched the battleships burn from a bus
narrative_blocks.body: The family was in Army quarters at Schofield Barracks when the Japanese came on a Sunday morning in 1941, and her husband was ordered to the beaches. Evacuated to Honolulu, they camped a week in a high school, and the school bus took them along Pearl Harbor past the burning ships.

narrative_blocks.header: Vancouver, Schofield, Wyoming, Honduras, Boise
narrative_blocks.body: She kept house in Army quarters at Vancouver Barracks, Schofield and Fort Warren, bearing a son in Hawaii and another in Wyoming. Later postings took them to Germany, Ohio, Japan and Honduras, where her husband ran the military mission.

career.organization: United States Department of the Army

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years an Army entomologist
narrative_blocks.body: He read biology and chemistry at Florida and Brigham Young, then spent better than forty years as an entomologist for the Department of the Army, at Fitzsimons in Colorado and afterwards at Fort Lewis in Washington.

narrative_blocks.header: He was the family’s own genealogist
narrative_blocks.body: He collected coins and traced descent, and was known through the Latter-day Saint community for the quality of his genealogical research.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-three years a nurse in Aurora
narrative_blocks.body: She trained at Westminster College and St. Mark’s Hospital and nursed for twenty-three years while raising her family in Aurora. She married Frank Maloney in March 1972, and they were sealed in the Salt Lake Temple the year after.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept the books for three companies
narrative_blocks.body: A daughter of Loris and Lola Zinn of Tunnelton, she worked as an accounting clerk for Johns Hopkins and for Procter and Gamble, and retired from Montgomery Ward in Baltimore.

narrative_blocks.header: Dead at thirty, five years married
narrative_blocks.body: He practised at Plymouth in Michigan and married Helen Cowles there in January 1845. He was dead in September 1850, leaving her two boys of four and three.

narrative_blocks.header: He sold Missouri land and died in California
narrative_blocks.body: He spent his last years at West Plains in Missouri, dealing in real estate, and died at Los Angeles in April 1906.

narrative_blocks.header: His father died when he was four
narrative_blocks.body: Dr. Franklin Markham died in Michigan in September 1850, leaving two small boys. Their mother married Buel Goodsell Wheeler three years afterwards.

bio.bio_blurb: Lincoln's friend, present at Ford's Theatre

cross_connections.display_label: was his friend, and was shot at Ford’s Theatre in 1865

career.notes: Unable to serve himself

narrative_blocks.header: He was in the theatre with his wife
narrative_blocks.body: He was a friend of Abraham Lincoln, and on the night Booth shot the President he was sitting in Ford's Theatre with his wife and saw it happen.

narrative_blocks.header: Unfit to serve, he paid for a regiment
narrative_blocks.body: Poor health kept him out of the War of the Rebellion, so he raised and equipped a regiment at his own charge and it served with distinction. He died at ninety-one in a Medford hospital, living then with his granddaughter Edith at Union Park in Boston.

narrative_blocks.header: Three years married, dead at thirty
narrative_blocks.body: She married Edward A. Shedd at Chicago in October 1881 and was dead by July 1884, at thirty.

bio.bio_blurb: Concert pianist; Cleveland Institute piano chairman

cross_connections.display_label: was running Army intelligence when he joined its Japanese section
, his son-in-law, kept himself in liner notes before poetry

education.school_name: College of the City of New York

education.notes: now part of the Juilliard School

military_service.notes: linguist, Japanese

narrative_blocks.header: His first recital was Berlin, at nineteen
narrative_blocks.body: His German-born father taught him the piano before Zygmunt Stojowski took him on at the Institute of Musical Art. He gave his first concert at Berlin in 1913 and went on to tour Europe, Australia and the Far East.

narrative_blocks.header: He learned Japanese for Army intelligence
narrative_blocks.body: Commissioned in 1943, he worked in the Army’s Japanese intelligence department and mastered the language, retiring a major. He was the first American musician to play in Japan after the war, with the Nippon Symphony.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the social history of the piano
narrative_blocks.body: Men, Women, and Pianos came out from Simon and Schuster in 1954, eleven years after Humor in American Song. He was music critic of the Cleveland Press from 1938 to 1956 and wrote liner notes for Vladimir Horowitz.

narrative_blocks.header: He cut piano rolls a third man conducted
narrative_blocks.body: Through the twenties and thirties he played half of a duo with Wilfrid Pelletier, cutting AMPICO rolls of orchestral works arranged for two players. Arthur Bodanzky of the Metropolitan conducted those sessions.

narrative_blocks.header: He called Frank the evil of two Loessers
narrative_blocks.body: He was half-brother to Frank Loesser, who wrote Guys and Dolls and How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying. His recitals came paired with lectures that were known for their wit.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-three years at the same institute
narrative_blocks.body: He joined the piano faculty at Cleveland in 1926 and headed the department from 1953 until his death. Sergio Calligaris and Anton Kuerti came up through his studio.

narrative_blocks.header: A heart attack at the wheel outside
narrative_blocks.body: He had been rehearsing for a February concert when the dean, leaving the institute, saw him slumped in a parked car outside. He was pronounced dead at Mount Sinai that night, at seventy-four.

notable.notable_blurb: Concert pianist and musicologist

cross_connections.display_label: led the American PEN twice, sixty years before she did
dresses a New York dance company, and married a Hollander too

notable.notable_blurb: Historian of fashion, costume and art

narrative_blocks.header: Clothes reveal more than they hide
narrative_blocks.body: Seeing Through Clothes came out in 1978 and made a subject of how painting and photography mediate between the body and what we wear. Her thesis never moved: clothes reveal more than they conceal.

narrative_blocks.header: She sorted five centuries of painting by film
narrative_blocks.body: Moving Pictures divided European and American painting after 1500 into the cinematic and the non-cinematic, arguing that Vermeer and Bruegel had prefigured how movies work. Sex and Suits followed in 1994 on the man’s suit.

narrative_blocks.header: A Barnard degree, and no faculty post ever
narrative_blocks.body: She took her art history degree at Barnard in 1952 and never joined a university faculty, working the rest of her life as an independent scholar. She could date a painting by the way a fold of cloth was drawn.

narrative_blocks.header: She led PEN and wrote fashion for Slate
narrative_blocks.body: She reviewed for the New Republic and for the London and New York Reviews of Books, and was Slate’s fashion columnist in the late nineties. She was president of the PEN American Center in the 1990s.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother the sculptor taught her to sew
narrative_blocks.body: The only child of the pianist Arthur Loesser and Jean Bassett, a sculptor, she was taught by her mother to cut and make her own clothes. She married the poet John Hollander in 1953 and the philosopher Thomas Nagel in 1979.

narrative_blocks.header: She died with a book on Homer unfinished
narrative_blocks.body: Cancer took her at her Manhattan home in July 2014. She was at work on a book about costume in literature, from Homer to the present.

cross_connections.display_label: , his father-in-law, wrote liner notes for Horowitz too
first printed Emily Dickinson, in the century he later anthologised

notable.notable_blurb: Poet and critic; Yale Sterling Professor

narrative_blocks.header: Auden picked his first book at twenty-eight
narrative_blocks.body: A Crackling of Thorns took the Yale Series of Younger Poets in 1958, chosen by W. H. Auden. He went on to the Bollingen Prize in 1983 and a MacArthur fellowship in 1990.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirteen by thirteen by thirteen
narrative_blocks.body: Powers of Thirteen runs to a hundred and sixty-nine unrhymed stanzas of thirteen lines, each line of thirteen syllables. He said the constraint freed him rather than bound him, and conceived the whole as a perpetual calendar.

narrative_blocks.header: Ginsberg was his mentor at Columbia
narrative_blocks.body: He came out of the Bronx High School of Science to Columbia, read under Mark Van Doren and Lionel Trilling, and counted Allen Ginsberg his poetic mentor. Richard Howard, Jason Epstein and Robert Gottlieb were in the same rooms.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote liner notes to keep himself fed
narrative_blocks.body: Between his degrees he supported himself writing liner notes for classical records. Milton Babbitt and Elliott Carter later set his verse, and Philomel was written as a cantata text for Babbitt.

narrative_blocks.header: The Eagles set one of his poems
narrative_blocks.body: He let the band use An Old Fashioned Song, which became No More Walks in the Wood. He held that a poem had to satisfy the ear before anything else.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-five years a Sterling Professor
narrative_blocks.body: He taught at Connecticut College and at Hunter before Yale took him in 1977, where he ended as Sterling Professor Emeritus. Connecticut made him its poet laureate in his late seventies.

cross_connections.display_label: was a poet and an editor of The Paris Review in 1975

notable.notable_blurb: Poet and historian of Dutch Baroque art

narrative_blocks.header: Her first book took the Whitman Award
narrative_blocks.body: The Game of Statues won the Walt Whitman Award of the Academy of American Poets in 1989. Her poems have run in the Paris Review, Poetry, the Yale Review and the New Republic.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote on space in Dutch painting
narrative_blocks.body: An Entrance for the Eyes: Space and Meaning in Seventeenth Century Dutch Art came from the University of California Press in 2002. She has taught art history at Hofstra since 1995, and Baroque art is her field.

narrative_blocks.header: The poet’s daughter and the historian’s
narrative_blocks.body: Her father was the poet John Hollander and her mother the fashion historian Anne Hollander, and she took up both trades. She lives at Jackson Heights with her husband Jonathan Bumas.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote to the Times about Perelman
narrative_blocks.body: In 1986 he wrote to the New York Times arguing that Perelman had carried the comic essay to its limits and so helped end the form. He quoted John Hollander on Perelman, ten years before he married Hollander’s daughter.

narrative_blocks.header: He drew limericks for the telephone
narrative_blocks.body: He illustrated Phonethics: Twenty-Two Limericks for the Telephone, John Ciardi’s 1986 book from Palaemon Press, in an edition of seventy-five. When the press folded he illustrated George Garrett’s Poison Pen for its publisher.

narrative_blocks.header: He jacketed his wife’s stepfather’s essays
narrative_blocks.body: Among the book jackets he drew was one for Other Minds, the essays of the philosopher Thomas Nagel, who had married Anne Hollander. He works mostly in pastel, and belongs to the Pastel Society of America.

narrative_blocks.header: A Princeton prize for an unpublished novella
narrative_blocks.body: He took his degree at Princeton in 1978 and won the Shellabarger prize there for a novella, Toward the Gardens. Princeton and East Carolina both hold collections of his drawings.

bio.bio_blurb: Boston merchant; American Tract Society president

cross_connections.display_label: was the son of his Tract Society finance secretary
carried him, crying, from his bed to his mother when he was a baby
wrote eight tracts for the American Tract Society he headed

narrative_blocks.header: He whittled a fish fork from an oar
narrative_blocks.body: Wrecked on the ice in the Jupiter coming home from England in 1805, he passed three days and nights in an open boat with thirty-eight others. He cut a fork from an oar with his pocket knife and speared fish to keep them alive.

narrative_blocks.header: A silk handkerchief on an oar saved them
narrative_blocks.body: The ship went down with twenty-seven aboard. He waved his large handkerchief from an oar until a passing vessel saw it, and the boats were landed at Marblehead three weeks after.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years heading the Tract Society
narrative_blocks.body: He was president and treasurer of the American Tract Society for some forty years and an officer of the Foreign Missionary Society. In 1843 the government sent him to London for the international peace convention.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the anti-slavery side with his brothers
narrative_blocks.body: Like Arthur and Lewis he promoted the anti-slavery reform from a Boston counting house. He had made his money in trade and was known for the scale of his giving.

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve children by his first wife
narrative_blocks.body: He married Sarah Salisbury in 1805 and she bore him twelve children, two of whom died as infants. In September 1841 he married Hannah Pomeroy, the widow of Robert Burr Edwards.

narrative_blocks.header: The ballet staged Rubies to thank her
narrative_blocks.body: She was a founding board member of Pacific Northwest Ballet in 1974 and endowed the scholarship fund at its school. In 1988 the company staged Balanchine’s Rubies as a wedding-anniversary tribute to her and Sheffield.

narrative_blocks.header: She reported the war from the Chronicle
narrative_blocks.body: Out of Vassar in 1942 she went to work as a reporter for the San Francisco Chronicle through the war years, and moved to Seattle in 1946.

narrative_blocks.header: A car engine held her like the ballet
narrative_blocks.body: Her daughter said she would fasten on whatever caught her attention, a car engine or the ballet school, and be teaching it to someone five minutes later. She telephoned reporters and civic workers she did not know, to thank them for their work.

cross_connections.display_label: and Bagley carried the Seattle Rep as the Phelpses carried the ballet

bio.bio_blurb: Marine aviator and Seattle arts patron

education.notes: Left in 1941 to enter the service

career.notes: Began his career at the same firm and returned to run it.

narrative_blocks.header: Ninety-two missions in a photo-reconnaissance B-17
narrative_blocks.body: He left Yale in 1941 for the Marine Corps and flew ninety-two photo-reconnaissance missions over the South Pacific, coming home a major with the Distinguished Flying Cross and eleven air medals.

narrative_blocks.header: Without him there is no ballet company
narrative_blocks.body: He was president of the Seattle Opera board when it helped launch Pacific Northwest Ballet, then took the new company as its board president and in 1977 recruited Kent Stowell and Francia Russell to run it. Without him, Stowell said, there would not be a Pacific Northwest Ballet.

narrative_blocks.header: The building at Seattle Center is theirs
narrative_blocks.body: The headquarters and studios of Pacific Northwest Ballet are the Phelps Center, named for him and Patricia, who kept the company alive in its first seasons. Washington gave them its arts award in 1989 and Seattle Center its Legion of Honor.

narrative_blocks.header: He rose to run the firm he joined
narrative_blocks.body: He began at a Seattle mortgage house and came back years later as president of what by then was Seafirst Mortgage, sitting on the boards of eleven other banks and businesses before he retired in 1971.

narrative_blocks.header: At eighty he beat the Nawitti Bar
narrative_blocks.body: He took up sailboat racing late and raced with his second wife, Marda, from Victoria to Maui and around Vancouver Island. At eighty he rounded the Nawitti Bar, which had turned him back before, and won the Van Isle 360.

narrative_blocks.header: He water-skied to the party in a tuxedo
narrative_blocks.body: He arrived at a Lake Washington party for Seafair on water-skis in a tuxedo and top hat, crashed on the way in, and laughed.

notable.notable_blurb: Mortgage banker and Pacific Northwest Ballet president

cross_connections.display_label: guaranteed the Seattle Rep, whose theatre at Seattle Center is his
banked at Seattle First National and sat on the Intiman Theatre board

education.school_name: University of Puget Sound School of Law

narrative_blocks.header: The county had never had the job before
narrative_blocks.body: In 1975 she became the first Victim’s Assistance Officer King County ever appointed, and held the post three years. She had come to it by way of Spanish at Vassar and law school at Puget Sound.

narrative_blocks.header: She was a tenor bound for Lincoln Center
narrative_blocks.body: She began singing tenor with the Anna’s Bay Center for Music early in 2012, and that autumn the choir was invited to Lincoln Center to sing the Messiah in November. She died in October, weeks short of the trip.

narrative_blocks.header: She had the Storm Petrel built for her
narrative_blocks.body: In 2010 she commissioned Sam Devlin to build the Storm Petrel, a lobster-boat picnic cruiser for the Sound and the San Juans, and went on to take navigation courses and join the South Sound Sailing Society.

narrative_blocks.header: Public housing first, then English lessons
narrative_blocks.body: She spent years with the Market Foundation arguing for public housing and help for people who needed it, and later taught English as a second language at Casa Latina.

bio.bio_blurb: Dalmatian breeder and Woods Hole trustee

narrative_blocks.header: Her Dalmatian broke the record by twelve
narrative_blocks.body: She bred champion Dalmatians for seventy-five years under the Tioga Coach name, and in 1993 her KC took twenty all-breed Best in Show awards against a standing record of eight.

narrative_blocks.header: The boat and the kennel share a name
narrative_blocks.body: She and her third husband, Walter Smith, gave for years to the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, endowing a chair and its research vessel Tioga, and she was a life trustee at her death. Tioga was also what she called her kennel.

narrative_blocks.header: She raced the Bounding Clam as a girl
narrative_blocks.body: She sailed the Brutal Beast class at the Pleon Yacht Club off Marblehead Neck in a boat she called Bounding Clam, and in later years crossed to Nantucket and down the Maine coast in the sloop Elskov.

narrative_blocks.header: There were llamas and buffalo on the farm
narrative_blocks.body: At Sunswick in Hamilton she and Walter raised five children on a farm of dogs, horses, donkeys, llamas, pigs and buffalo. From 1983 they lived on Pine Cay in the Turks and Caicos, where she died at ninety-four.

narrative_blocks.header: From Dana Hall to a therapeutic riding farm
narrative_blocks.body: She rode at Dana Hall and kept horses at the Hamilton farm for the rest of her life, and her family asked that she be remembered at a therapeutic riding farm in North Andover.

narrative_blocks.header: She named the boat Beyond Hope
narrative_blocks.body: She kept a boat at Pine Cay for taking her eight grandchildren out to the reef, and she called it Beyond Hope.

narrative_blocks.header: A captain who died at forty-one
narrative_blocks.body: He served as a captain in the Confederate States Army and was dead at forty-one, at Hartford in October 1872. His widow Emily took the seven surviving children to Baltimore and stayed there thirty years.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried his father’s orders in Kentucky
narrative_blocks.body: He was aide-de-camp to his father when Leonidas Polk commanded at Columbus, Kentucky, and one of his orders survives, sending a cavalry captain to scout between Milburn and Lovelaceville.

narrative_blocks.header: A Hartford girl who stayed in Baltimore
narrative_blocks.body: She was the daughter of George Beach of Hartford and married Alexander Hamilton Polk there in June 1854. Widowed at forty-one, she kept a house on St. Paul Street in Baltimore for twenty-five years and died there of congestion of the lungs.

narrative_blocks.header: He married his brother’s widow in 1896
narrative_blocks.body: Francis Devereux Polk died at thirty-three in 1891, leaving Margaret Callaway with five children. Five years later Margaret married his younger brother Hamilton, and the two youngest boys grew up as his stepsons.

narrative_blocks.header: He practiced medicine in Baltimore
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Raleigh in 1863 and practiced as a physician at Baltimore, where his widowed mother had moved the family after his father died. He was dead at forty-three in 1906.

narrative_blocks.header: She married two Polk brothers in turn
narrative_blocks.body: She married Francis Devereux Polk at fifteen in November 1877 and bore him five children before he died in 1891. In 1896 she married his younger brother Hamilton, and outlived them both by nineteen years.

narrative_blocks.header: She sat for two Rockwell covers
narrative_blocks.body: Norman Rockwell painted her twice for the Saturday Evening Post, first as the girl in The Fortune Teller opposite Donald Gould, and months later in The Date opposite her husband Hugh Kilmer.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father was left the general’s binoculars
narrative_blocks.body: Her great-grandfather Leonidas Polk was killed at Pine Mountain while reconnoitering, and the glasses he was wearing were willed to her father, the general namesake.

narrative_blocks.header: She booked Fred Waring into a high school
narrative_blocks.body: Running ways and means for the New Rochelle hospital league from 1944, she brought Fred Waring and his sixty-eight Pennsylvanians to the high school for the winter concert. Paul Whiteman and his orchestra came the following year.

narrative_blocks.header: She got a wreath onto every hospital floor
narrative_blocks.body: She chaired the ward service of the New Rochelle League and collected the donations that put a Christmas tree and a wreath on every floor of the hospital, along with new electric units and decorations.

career.role: First vice president, ways and means

narrative_blocks.header: He founded the Storm Trysail Club
narrative_blocks.body: He was a founder and commodore of the Storm Trysail Club, which still runs its race around Block Island, and sailed eleven of the biennial ocean races from New England to Bermuda.

narrative_blocks.header: He filed the Bermuda race by radio
narrative_blocks.body: For the 1938 Bermuda race he covered the fleet for the New York Times, sending his dispatches by radio from a Coast Guard cutter.

sources.short: FamilySearch PWDP-FJX; New York Times, 25 Apr and 7 Jun 1959

narrative_blocks.header: She bought the magazine; he ran it
narrative_blocks.body: Anne Peretz supplied the money that bought The New Republic in 1974, and her husband edited it for the next thirty-eight years. The couple had earlier helped finance Ramparts, and withdrew that support when it turned critical of Israel.

narrative_blocks.header: They paid for Susan Sontag's treatment
narrative_blocks.body: In 1975 Susan Sontag had a stage-four diagnosis, no health insurance, and an experimental course of immunotherapy waiting in Paris. Her publisher Roger Straus and her editor Robert Silvers went round the rich; the Peretzes said yes, though they had never met her.

narrative_blocks.header: Four generations from a sewing machine
narrative_blocks.body: Her great-great-grandfather Edward Cabot Clark was Isaac Singer's partner, and built what the machines earned out into Manhattan real estate. By her generation the Clarks were reckoned as rich as the Fricks, and she turned the inheritance toward causes rather than leaving it still.

narrative_blocks.header: He called the marriage an arrival
narrative_blocks.body: Marty Peretz married her in 1967 and described the match as a social leap into ruling Protestant America — an escape for her, he wrote, and an arrival for him. She divorced him in 2009, citing repeated infidelities and his temper.

narrative_blocks.header: Marie Curie's daughter was her stepmother
narrative_blocks.body: Ève Curie married her father in 1954, nine years after her mother's death, and lived to 102. Anne's children counted Ève as a grandmother and theirs as a great-grandmother, and it was Anne who confirmed her death in 2007.

education.notes: Attended; a junior when she married in 1959.

notable.notable_blurb: Magazine publisher; New Republic editor-in-chief

cross_connections.display_label: founded The Nation and was accused of the same drift rightward
was a friend from his years after Brandeis whose politics he fought
was his New Republic managing editor, then executive editor

narrative_blocks.header: A liberal weekly that turned hawk
narrative_blocks.body: He ran The New Republic for thirty-six years and swung it toward neoconservative, pro-Israel positions abroad while it stayed liberal at home. Critics said he had made it a police dog patrolling the borders of respectable liberalism.

narrative_blocks.header: He promised three years and gave one
narrative_blocks.body: He bought the magazine in 1974 with Anne Labouisse's money and kept Gilbert Harrison, the editor he inherited, promising him three more years. Inside one, tired of his own pieces being turned down, he fired him, and most of the staff left.

narrative_blocks.header: He fired an editor to protect Al Gore
narrative_blocks.body: Al Gore had been his student at Harvard and stayed a friend. In 1997 Michael Kelly refused to run an unsigned editorial dismissing the fundraising allegations against the vice-president, and he fired Kelly by telephone days later.

narrative_blocks.header: Harvard called off the speech in his honor
narrative_blocks.body: In September 2010 he wrote that Muslim life was cheap and wondered in print whether Muslims deserved First Amendment protection. Harvard dropped him from the anniversary programme of the department where he taught, and he apologised twice.

narrative_blocks.header: The socialist crowd he never joined
narrative_blocks.body: The intellectuals he fell in with out of Brandeis were mostly Jewish and mostly socialist, Herbert Marcuse among them. His father was a fierce anti-communist and he never took the politics on — the magazine he bought went the other way.

narrative_blocks.header: A Yiddish chair carries the name twice
narrative_blocks.body: Harvard endowed the Martin Peretz Chair in Yiddish Literature in 1993, and Ruth Wisse holds it. He descends from I. L. Peretz, a founder of modern Yiddish literature, so the name sits at both ends of the chair.

notable.notable_blurb: Film and television director; bassist

cross_connections.display_label: directs documentaries and still releases his own albums
left Ratt the year Peretz left the Lemonheads

narrative_blocks.header: An Emmy for a wrestling comedy
narrative_blocks.body: Peretz won the Primetime Emmy for directing a comedy series for GLOW, Netflix's show about women's wrestling in the 1980s. He has also directed episodes of Girls, Orange Is the New Black, Divorce, Shrill and High Fidelity.

narrative_blocks.header: He quit the band right before it broke
narrative_blocks.body: He founded The Lemonheads in a Cambridge high school in 1986 with Evan Dando and Ben Deily, and left as bassist just before It's a Shame About Ray made them. He stayed on as the band's photographer and directed its videos.

narrative_blocks.header: A student film at fifteen, then no acting
narrative_blocks.body: Waiting tables at fifteen, he was talked into starring in two older waitresses' student film, and found the explicit scene it required so traumatic that he never acted again. Four days on the set decided him on directing instead.

narrative_blocks.header: The Grammy came from a music video
narrative_blocks.body: He won a Grammy for the Foo Fighters' Learn to Fly in 1999, one of a long run of videos reaching from the Breeders and Nada Surf to Selena Gomez. He also made MTV's Jimmy the Cab-Driver vignettes with two Harvard friends.

narrative_blocks.header: He filmed McEwan first, then Hornby
narrative_blocks.body: His feature debut in 1997 came from Ian McEwan's short story First Love, Last Rites. Twenty-one years later he adapted Nick Hornby's Juliet, Naked with Judd Apatow producing, and it premiered at Sundance.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote a comedy with his sister
narrative_blocks.body: Our Idiot Brother came out of a hard and sometimes comic stretch in the family: he wrote it with his sister Evgenia and her husband David Schisgall, and built it around a friend's brother who left prison for a monastery.

notable.notable_blurb: Journalist and screenwriter; documentary director

cross_connections.display_label: wrote Zodiac, and writes studio pictures as she does

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-five years on how the elite unravel
narrative_blocks.body: Peretz has been a contributing editor at Vanity Fair since 1999 and has written more than sixty features there, many of them on wealth and its institutions: Operation Varsity Blues, and Georgetown Prep after the Kavanaugh hearings. The same range took her to big-wave surfing and Deep Springs College.

narrative_blocks.header: She filmed her own reporting
narrative_blocks.body: Her Vanity Fair piece Scene Stealer investigated Elisabeth Finch, a Grey's Anatomy writer who had fabricated much of her own history. Peretz then directed Anatomy of Lies, the three-part Peacock series built from it.

narrative_blocks.header: She profiled her father's old student
narrative_blocks.body: Her political subjects have included Silvio Berlusconi, François Hollande, James Frey, Donna Tartt and Al Gore, who had been her father's student at Harvard and stayed his friend. Her piece on Bush in Texas, High Noon in Crawford, went into Best American Political Writing.

narrative_blocks.header: A prize for writing about the Taleses
narrative_blocks.body: Her 2017 profile of Nan and Gay Talese, The Lady and the Scamp, won a Silurian award. Her work has been collected in three anthologies.

narrative_blocks.header: Two films written for her brother to direct
narrative_blocks.body: She co-wrote Our Idiot Brother in 2011 with her brother Jesse and her husband David Schisgall, and wrote for Jesse again on Juliet, Naked, from the Nick Hornby novel.

career.organization: NYU Arthur L. Carter Journalism Institute

narrative_blocks.header: He learned the trade under Errol Morris
narrative_blocks.body: Schisgall worked as an associate of the documentary director Errol Morris on A Brief History of Time, Fast, Cheap and Out of Control and Mr. Death. He directed his own first film, The Lifestyle, in 1999.

narrative_blocks.header: The film advocates say started a movement
narrative_blocks.body: Very Young Girls, which he directed and produced in 2007, followed the commercial sexual exploitation of girls in New York City and the women working to get them out. Advocates in the field credit it with starting a movement, and it was nominated for best documentary at Warsaw.

narrative_blocks.header: He covered three wars for MTV
narrative_blocks.body: Between 2003 and 2004 he reported the second intifada, the war in Iraq and the Colombian civil war for True Life, putting foreign conflict in front of an audience of young Americans. The Iraq film won a Murrow award for best news documentary.

narrative_blocks.header: He filmed a reporter held by al-Qaeda
narrative_blocks.body: Theo Who Lived, in 2016, was built around the journalist Theo Padnos and the two years he spent as a captive of an al-Qaeda affiliate in Syria. Schisgall followed it in 2020 with The Oil War, on American military involvement in the Middle East.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote a comedy with his wife
narrative_blocks.body: Schisgall co-wrote Our Idiot Brother in 2011 with Evgenia Peretz and her brother Jesse, who directed it. He and Evgenia later made Anatomy of Lies for Peacock out of her Vanity Fair reporting.

cross_connections.display_label: ran the Metropolitan a generation before he was its vice-president
twice led the Modern, which he had chaired in the 1940s
wrote Percentage Baseball, and his slide rule is in the hall he made

military_service.role: Lieutenant-colonel, United States Army; awarded the Distinguished Service Medal.

narrative_blocks.header: He built baseball a hall in his village
narrative_blocks.body: Clark founded the National Baseball Hall of Fame at Cooperstown and paid for the building that opened in 1939. He chaired its board, as his son and granddaughter Jane Forbes Clark would after him.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought the Armory Show its costliest work
narrative_blocks.body: He helped organize the 1913 Armory Show and took home its costliest sculpture, Wilhelm Lehmbruck's Standing Woman, which he gave to New York's Museum of Modern Art. He was a founding trustee there in 1929 and chairman from 1939.

narrative_blocks.header: He fired the man who invented the museum
narrative_blocks.body: Alfred Barr had built the Modern from nothing since Abby Aldrich Rockefeller and two friends founded it in 1929, and defined what such a museum was for. Clark removed him in 1943, and it is what his chairmanship is remembered for.

narrative_blocks.header: One refusal ended a brotherhood
narrative_blocks.body: The trust paid only the four brothers and their natural children, and Stephen alone had any. When Sterling asked them to admit his wife's daughter he refused; Sterling pulled out his quarter, sold up in Cooperstown and never spoke to him again.

narrative_blocks.header: The Singer money reached him through a lawyer
narrative_blocks.body: His grandfather Edward Cabot Clark was Isaac Singer's lawyer and partner, and his father Alfred Corning Clark ran the company and put its earnings into Manhattan property. Stephen joined the Singer board the year he left law school, and built the Otesaga Hotel with his brother Edward.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought three Albany papers in the 1920s
narrative_blocks.body: Clark owned and published three newspapers in Albany through the 1920s, among them the Albany Evening Journal, which he bought from the Republican boss William Barnes Jr.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty paintings went to Yale
narrative_blocks.body: He collected Thomas Eakins in depth, some from the painter's widow, and left forty pictures to Yale including Van Gogh's Night Café. The Metropolitan took Renoir, Degas, Seurat and Cézanne.

sources.short: Wikipedia; FindAGrave; New York Red Book 1910

narrative_blocks.header: She married a childhood family friend
narrative_blocks.body: Susan Hun and Stephen Clark had known each other since childhood through their families, and married in February 1909. They were still on their honeymoon in Europe when his mother died that March.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father reported the courts for 32 years
narrative_blocks.body: Marcus Tullius Hun was New York's Supreme Court Reporter from 1874 until 1905, and has been called the most prolific of the state's nominative reporters. For a few years his Albany law firm included the young Learned Hand.

narrative_blocks.header: The middle name came from an adjutant-general
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother was Mary Keith Van Der Poel, daughter of Isaac Van Der Poel, once adjutant-general of New York. The Huns were one of Albany's old Dutch families, and her father ran the Albany Savings Bank at his death.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived three of her five children
narrative_blocks.body: Of the five children born between 1909 and 1917, one died in infancy, Elizabeth in 1945 and Robert in 1952. Susan survived Stephen by seven years and was buried beside him at Cooperstown.

notable.notable_blurb: Disability rights advocate; EEOC chairman

cross_connections.display_label: opened the first American school for the deaf in 1817
counseled disabled people as a peer consultant for Disability Advocates

narrative_blocks.header: The garage door that wrote a rule
narrative_blocks.body: The Securities and Exchange Commission told him he could use its garage entrance but must park elsewhere. In 1971 the door came down on his leg and broke it past walking; twenty-one years later he wrote the rule requiring employers to accommodate disabled workers, including letting them park in the company garage.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the seat Clarence Thomas left
narrative_blocks.body: Reagan named him to the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission in 1987 and Bush made him its chairman in 1990, succeeding Clarence Thomas. He had already done much of the behind-the-scenes drafting of the Americans with Disabilities Act, and shaped its final rules in 1992.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-nine firms turned him down
narrative_blocks.body: He finished in the top tenth of his class at the University of Virginia law school in 1964, and thirty-nine firms refused him. He went to the Internal Revenue Service because private practice would not hire a lawyer who lurched when he walked.

narrative_blocks.header: Twice he was told when he would die
narrative_blocks.body: At twelve he was told his muscle weakness was incurable and would kill him before fourteen. Still alive at fourteen, he was told it was a different disease and he would not reach twenty; the diagnosis that held came at twenty-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped build the wheelchair company
narrative_blocks.body: In 1979 he helped establish Invacare, which became the largest maker of wheelchairs in the world, and after leaving the commission in 1993 he founded Evan Kemp Associates to sell goods and services to disabled consumers.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a former urban guerrilla
narrative_blocks.body: Janine Bertram had served four years in prison for a California bank robbery and a bombing, and was an advocate for prison reform by the time they married.

career.organization: Internal Revenue Service, Office of the Chief Counsel

narrative_blocks.header: Her company cleaned cathedrals
narrative_blocks.body: Chessie and her husband Edgar Bleick ran K&E, a Cleveland firm making a specialty chemical used to clean cathedrals and other historic stone buildings. She had come to it from a first job as a librarian for General Electric.

narrative_blocks.header: She founded the friends of a park
narrative_blocks.body: She started Friends of Cain Park and was one of the founders of The Heights Fund, chaired the Junior League's house operations committee, and gave more than a decade to the Nearly New Shop, which paid for the Cleveland Sight Center.

narrative_blocks.header: She ran for council at fifty-five
narrative_blocks.body: After years of PTA presidencies at the Roxboro schools and a Kiwanian of the Year award, Chessie stood for Cleveland Heights city council in 1995.

narrative_blocks.header: She missed only the two poles
narrative_blocks.body: She travelled abroad steadily and got to every place she had meant to go except the Arctic and the Antarctic.

narrative_blocks.header: Her obituary named two fathers
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother's second marriage in 1974 gave her a Bliss household alongside her Kemp one, and when she died her death notice listed both Evan Jennings Kemp and Charles William Bliss among the fathers who had gone before her.

sources.short: Disability Rights Center; Mouth magazine; New York Times obituary of E. J. Kemp Jr., 1997

career.organization: American Association of People with Disabilities

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote the chairman his speeches
narrative_blocks.body: From 1988 to 1992 Bertram was assistant to Evan Kemp at the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, writing his speeches and reports through the drafting and passage of the Americans with Disabilities Act. He introduced President Bush at the signing in July 1990.

narrative_blocks.header: She now runs the center he once directed
narrative_blocks.body: The Disability Rights Center was founded in Washington in 1976 by Deborah Kaplan and Ralph Nader, and Kemp was its executive director from 1980 until the commission took him. Bertram is its president.

narrative_blocks.header: She took on Clint Eastwood over the act
narrative_blocks.body: Eastwood, whose Carmel hotel had been sued under the Americans with Disabilities Act, told a House subcommittee that its enforcement was a form of extortion. Bertram spoke against the bill he backed, and said afterwards that he was not used to being hissed at by a line of people with disabilities.

narrative_blocks.header: She collects the movement its own history
narrative_blocks.body: With the documentary photographer Tom Olin she compiles visual and oral histories of the disability rights movement for states and agencies, among them New Mexico, Pennsylvania, Maryland and the Federal Transit Administration.

narrative_blocks.header: She was nine when her father died
narrative_blocks.body: John Middleton Huger died in New Orleans in May 1912, two months after his daughter turned nine. She carried the Polk name of his mother, Elizabeth Devereux Polk, through the rest of her life.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at thirty-six, widowed at thirty-nine
narrative_blocks.body: Louise Huger left Hollins with the class of 1923 and did not marry until 1939, when she was thirty-six and John Andrew Beaver was fifty-five. He died in Manhattan three years later.

sources.short: The Blood-Horse obituary of J. Merrick Jones Jr., September 2001
The Blood-Horse obituary of J. Merrick Jones Jr., September 2001

narrative_blocks.header: Nancy Astor was her aunt
narrative_blocks.body: Virginia Brand was born at Eton in 1918 to Phyllis Langhorne, a Virginian whose sister became Viscountess Astor, and to Robert Brand of Lazard Brothers, who ran the British Food Mission to Washington through the Second World War.

narrative_blocks.header: The title lasted seventeen years
narrative_blocks.body: Her father was made Baron Brand of Eydon in 1946 for the Treasury work he had done in Washington. Her only brother, a lieutenant in the Coldstream Guards, had been killed in 1945, so the barony died with her father in 1963.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at twenty-one, widowed at twenty-nine
narrative_blocks.body: She married John Metcalfe Polk in December 1939 and lived in America until his death in 1948. She married Edward Ford the following year and spent the rest of her life in England.

narrative_blocks.header: Buried in the village of the title
narrative_blocks.body: She died in 1998 and was buried at Eydon in Northamptonshire, the village her father had taken into his title fifty-two years earlier.

narrative_blocks.header: The outstanding debutante of 1955
narrative_blocks.body: She came out in 1955 and was married that same season to Edward Beach Condon at the Foundry Methodist Church in Washington, with her sister Virginia among the bridesmaids.

narrative_blocks.header: Foxcroft, Switzerland, then a senator’s office
narrative_blocks.body: After Foxcroft she went to Clos des Abeilles in Switzerland, and came back to work on the Washington staff of Senator George Smathers of Florida.

narrative_blocks.header: Her second husband founded the AFI
narrative_blocks.body: In July 1965 she married George Stevens Jr., who two years later left the government to start the American Film Institute. Their sons were born in 1966 and 1968, and her daughter by Condon took the Stevens name.

narrative_blocks.header: The Kennedy Center from both sides
narrative_blocks.body: She stood between two builders of the same institution: her mother was a co-founder of the Friends of the Kennedy Center, and her husband ran the American Film Institute out of the building and made its Honors.

narrative_blocks.header: She sold pictures for Sotheby’s
narrative_blocks.body: A graduate of Briarcliff College, she worked in New York as an international representative for Sotheby's.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at her father’s house in King George
narrative_blocks.body: She married Massie Valentine of Richmond on 18 May in an Episcopal ceremony at her father's house at King George, a year after her mother died. She was forty-four, a first marriage behind her, and he was a widower of fifty-six.

narrative_blocks.header: The museum in Richmond carries the name
narrative_blocks.body: His father ran Valentine & Company, the Richmond patent-medicine house, and the Valentine Museum that the family gave the city. He took the University of Virginia degree and later presided over its board.

cross_connections.display_label: was her great-aunt and namesake, who married a Vanderbilt at Newport

narrative_blocks.header: Police held the crowds outside the church
narrative_blocks.body: She married John Jacob Astor in June 1934 at Trinity Church in Newport, and the streets round it filled so thickly that police were put on to hold the crowds back. His father had gone down with the Titanic twenty-two years before.

narrative_blocks.header: She came out in the last Newport season
narrative_blocks.body: Her debut was made in December 1933, among the last of the great interwar Newport years, in the same set as Doris Duke. After the Astor marriage the couple kept Chetwode at Newport, one of the most photographed houses of the day.

narrative_blocks.header: Divorced in 1943, remarried ten years on
narrative_blocks.body: The Astor marriage ended in 1943 after nine years, in one of the largest settlements of its time. She married Raymond Guest in April 1953, and that marriage ended in divorce as well.

narrative_blocks.header: Buried from the church where she had married
narrative_blocks.body: She died at her Newport house in September 1974, at fifty-eight. The funeral was held at Trinity Church, forty years after the wedding there, and she was buried at Island Cemetery in the town.

narrative_blocks.header: Napoleon’s sister is four generations back
narrative_blocks.body: The Murats descend from Joachim Murat, the cavalryman Napoleon made King of Naples, and from Caroline Bonaparte, the emperor's youngest sister, whose name came down to her. Her father was Prince Alexandre Murat and her mother Yvonne Gillois.

narrative_blocks.header: A Murat married in Caroline County
narrative_blocks.body: She married Raymond Guest on 24 June 1960 in Caroline County, Virginia, and spent the next thirty years between Paris and the horse farm at Powhatan. Two children came of it, Achille and Laetitia.

narrative_blocks.header: She died in Paris, and came back
narrative_blocks.body: Her last years were spent largely in France, and she died at the American Hospital in Paris in May 2012, at eighty-eight. She was brought back to King George County and buried beside her husband at Powhatan.
