bio.bio_blurb: Astor heir, yachtsman and town founder

narrative_blocks.header: Kept a junior partner all his life
narrative_blocks.body: He finished near the top of his class at Columbia and was then held as nothing more than a junior partner under his elder brother John Jacob, the father's favorite. The friendship soured, the politics diverged, and the quarrel passed down to their wives and sons.

narrative_blocks.header: Kept late at the club on purpose
narrative_blocks.body: He had no taste for the society his wife commanded, and she would have him held late at the club — coming home early he was apt to dismiss the orchestra and send the children to bed.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded a Florida town named for him
narrative_blocks.body: In 1874 he bought eighty thousand acres along the St Johns River and laid out a town he first called Manhattan, renamed Astor after him. He put up wharves, hotels, a school and a church, bought a railroad to reach it, and grew grapefruit there before Americans ate it.

narrative_blocks.header: His colt won the 1876 Kentucky Derby
narrative_blocks.body: His thoroughbred Vagrant took the Derby at Louisville in 1876. He kept the Ambassadress, then the largest private yacht in the world, and divided his time between her off Jacksonville and Ferncliff on the Hudson.

narrative_blocks.header: He paid to equip a Union regiment
narrative_blocks.body: He was for abolition before the war came, and when it did he found the money to equip an entire regiment for the Union army.

narrative_blocks.header: One of the fifty-two Patriarchs
narrative_blocks.body: For all his absence he was named among the fifty-two Patriarchs in 1889, the men who between them issued the invitations to the balls that decided who was in New York society.

narrative_blocks.header: One son and four daughters
narrative_blocks.body: The son, John Jacob Astor, went down with the Titanic twenty years after him. The daughters married Van Alen, Roosevelt, Drayton and Wilson, and it is through the third that this family reaches the Hookers.

people.relational_label_override: Grandmother-in-law of a Ninth Generation Hooker

cross_connections.display_label: was kept out of her opera house and built the Metropolitan Opera
was counted among the four hundred names on her list
made the same list in 1892, and later ranched horses in Oregon
made her four hundred, and won the first Westminster Best in Show
made the list in 1892 with her husband, Cleveland's Navy Secretary

narrative_blocks.header: She and McAllister drew up the Four Hundred
narrative_blocks.body: With Ward McAllister she settled which New York families counted, and the list they made — two hundred and thirteen names — became the first American social register. It is remembered as the Four Hundred.

narrative_blocks.header: Three generations from the dirty hands
narrative_blocks.body: Her rule was that a fortune must be three generations away from whoever had dirtied his hands making it. She stood just inside her own line: the Astor money came from her husband's grandfather and the beaver trade.

narrative_blocks.header: Eighteen boxes, and she held one
narrative_blocks.body: The Academy of Music had eighteen boxes and the Knickerbocker families passed them down among themselves; hers was one. Keeping the new fortunes out of them is what drove those men to build the Metropolitan Opera House and leave the Academy empty.

narrative_blocks.header: She called on the Vanderbilts at last
narrative_blocks.body: When Alva Vanderbilt got up a masquerade ball in 1883 and let it be known that no invitation could go to a family she had never called upon, the call was paid. The Vanderbilts were in, and her line moved to take them.

narrative_blocks.header: She received her guests beneath herself
narrative_blocks.body: The portrait painted of her in 1890 hung in the house where she stood to receive, so that callers met the woman and the picture at once. It hangs now in the Metropolitan Museum.

narrative_blocks.header: Four daughters married, and a son drowned
narrative_blocks.body: Her children married Van Alen, Roosevelt, Drayton and Wilson. The one son, John Jacob Astor, was lost with the Titanic sixteen years after she had seen the last of her daughters married.

narrative_blocks.header: A fall on the stairs ended it
narrative_blocks.body: She gave her last great party at the Fifth Avenue house in 1905, and days afterwards fell on the staircase and broke her hip at seventy-five. She spent her last three years in a wheelchair.

death.notes: Died at the American Hospital of Paris, Neuilly; buried beside George Haig at her own request.

narrative_blocks.header: A duel was called over her in Paris
narrative_blocks.body: In 1892 the papers had her spending too much time in London with another New Yorker, Hallett Alsop Borrowe, and her husband challenged him to a duel in Paris; friends stopped it. Her mother tried to mediate, and brought the pair to London to do it.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father cut her out the same year
narrative_blocks.body: William Astor died in 1892 and she found he had left her nothing, though he provided for her children. Her brother made it up to her at once out of his own pocket.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a Haig and lost the children
narrative_blocks.body: He filed first, she counter-sued, and the decree went to her in 1896 — though the children stayed with their father. That December she married George Ogilvy Haig of the whisky firm, whose brother would command the British armies in France.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty years in Paris after Brook Street
narrative_blocks.body: Haig died nine years into the marriage and she left Brook Street for Paris, where she stayed. She died there in 1920 with her sister beside her, eight years after the Titanic took her only brother.

narrative_blocks.header: The scandal of the generation was his
narrative_blocks.body: His challenge to Hallett Alsop Borrowe over his wife brought a proposed duel in Paris and a divorce four years later, and it was called the most conspicuous society scandal of the generation. He took the children.

narrative_blocks.header: He hired Mary Mallon to cook one summer
narrative_blocks.body: In 1902 he took a house at Dark Harbor in Maine and most of the household went down with typhoid. The cook was Mary Mallon, and the outbreak she left behind her that summer reached other families along the coast.

narrative_blocks.header: A swindler went about as him
narrative_blocks.body: In December 1903 a man named Carlisle was arrested for going round the country as J. Coleman Drayton and taking money from a woman in Minneapolis on the strength of the name.

narrative_blocks.header: A lawyer who all but retired at once
narrative_blocks.body: He read law in New York and was admitted to the bar after Princeton and eighteen months in Europe, then married and gave it up for travelling. He built the house in the Somerset Hills now called Stronghold, and died at Boxcroft in Newport.

people.relational_label_override: Uncle of the Husband of a Ninth Generation Hooker

birth.notes: Born at Ferncliff, the family estate.

cross_connections.display_label: spent his life arguing peat as fuel, and lost to oil
was one of four first-class women lost in the same sinking
went down with the Lusitania after giving his lifebelt away
designed the Astor Trust building, five years after he drowned
fought Cervera's fleet off Santiago as Schley's flag lieutenant

military_service.role: Lieutenant colonel of Volunteers on Gen. Shafter’s staff at Santiago, brevetted colonel; financed and equipped the Astor Battery.

narrative_blocks.header: He asked for the number of her boat
narrative_blocks.body: He put his wife into Lifeboat 4 and asked the second officer whether he might come, as she was in a delicate condition; he was told no man until the women were off. He asked for the boat's number so he could find her, kissed her, and said he would follow in another.

narrative_blocks.header: He built the Astoria against his cousin
narrative_blocks.body: In 1897 he put up the Astoria hotel alongside the Waldorf, which belonged to the cousin he was quarrelling with, and the two became one house under a joined name. He built the St Regis and the Knickerbocker after it.

narrative_blocks.header: He paid for a battery of artillery
narrative_blocks.body: He financed and equipped an artillery unit that went to the Philippines as the Astor Battery, served on Shafter's staff through the Santiago campaign, and lent the government his yacht. He was brevetted colonel and answered to the title afterwards.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote a novel set on Jupiter
narrative_blocks.body: A Journey in Other Worlds came out in 1894, imagining the year 2000 on Saturn and Jupiter. He also patented a bicycle brake, a machine for making gas out of peat, and a pneumatic road-improver.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-seven, and she was eighteen
narrative_blocks.body: He married Madeleine Force in his mother's ballroom at Beechwood in 1911, a year after his divorce and twenty-nine years her senior. Society was appalled, so they went to Egypt until the talk died down.

narrative_blocks.header: The son he never saw, born in August
narrative_blocks.body: His body was picked up a week after the sinking, identified by the initials on his collar. Four months later Madeleine bore the son who would be called the Titanic Baby.

people.relational_label_override: Cousin of the Husband of a Ninth Generation Hooker

birth.notes: Born at 840 Fifth Avenue.

narrative_blocks.header: Born four months after the sinking
narrative_blocks.body: Madeleine Astor was five months gone when her husband handed her into the boat, and she bore this son at the Fifth Avenue house in August. He grew up at Beechwood in Newport and went through life as the Titanic Baby.

narrative_blocks.header: His half-brother left him nothing at all
narrative_blocks.body: Vincent Astor had despised him from birth and doubted he was an Astor by blood, and left him out of the will entirely. He sued the widow, argued the will had been signed by a man not competent to sign it, and settled.

narrative_blocks.header: Jilted in January, engaged again by June
narrative_blocks.body: Eileen Gillespie broke off their wedding a fortnight before it, and he went to Shanghai to get over it. He came back in May and by the end of June had married her close friend, Tucky French, at Trinity Church in Newport.

narrative_blocks.header: Four wives, and the last one stayed
narrative_blocks.body: The marriage to Tucky ended in 1943, and two more followed it within eleven years, one of them lasting months. He married Sue Sandford in 1956 and stayed married to her until she died in 1985.

narrative_blocks.header: She went out through the promenade window
narrative_blocks.body: Five months pregnant, she had to be lifted through a window of the enclosed promenade into Lifeboat 4, which had been dropped to A deck to take more people. Waiting on the boat deck she had given her fur shawl to a third-class mother to wrap round her baby.

narrative_blocks.header: The priests would not marry them
narrative_blocks.body: She was eighteen and he was forty-seven and a year divorced, and Episcopal clergymen refused the ceremony one after another. A Congregational minister married them at Beechwood in September 1911, with his son standing as best man.

narrative_blocks.header: A luncheon for the men who came
narrative_blocks.body: At the end of May she came out of seclusion to give a luncheon at the Fifth Avenue house for Captain Rostron of the Carpathia and his ship's surgeon, hosting it with Marian Thayer, another of the widows.

narrative_blocks.header: She married again and lost the lot
narrative_blocks.body: The will gave her the income of a trust and the use of the houses only for as long as she stayed a widow. In 1916 she married William Dick, a banker she had known since childhood, and gave all of it up.

narrative_blocks.header: A Reno decree, then an Italian boxer
narrative_blocks.body: She divorced Dick at Reno in July 1933 and married Enzo Fiermonte, an Italian boxer of twenty-six, four months later. That ended in a Florida divorce in 1938 and she took the name Dick back.

narrative_blocks.header: One son drew birds for a living
narrative_blocks.body: John Henry Dick, born in 1919, became an ornithologist and bird painter whose illustrations went into the field guides. His elder brother William was born in 1917, and Jakey Astor was the eldest of the three.

cross_connections.display_label: was her husband’s younger brother, and married her sister Peggy

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at thirty-eight, remarried at forty-eight
narrative_blocks.body: She married Frank Lyon Polk in 1934 and bore Frank, Samuel and William over the next six years, and he died in 1952 at forty. In 1962 she married John Currie Wilmerding, buried her second husband three years after that, and lived on to eighty-nine.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father banked, and kept a camp
narrative_blocks.body: Louis Graveraet Kaufman ran the Chatham Phenix National Bank from Park Avenue and kept houses at Palm Beach and Short Hills, and a camp in the woods near Marquette in Michigan. She was buried at Marquette in the end.

narrative_blocks.header: Three husbands, the first a Biddle
narrative_blocks.body: She married George Drexel Biddle at St Thomas's in December 1926, in a wedding that went out on two thousand invitations. Frank Lyon Polk was the second, in 1938, and a Martin the third.

narrative_blocks.header: Calhoun hockey and the Banner board
narrative_blocks.body: He came to Yale from Groton and read American studies, played on the Calhoun College hockey team for two years and was voted the college's vice-president in his last. He sat on the Banner board for all four years.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventeen when his father died at forty
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Charlottesville in 1935 while his father was at law school there, and was the eldest of three boys. His father was dead by 1952, and he graduated from Yale six years later.

narrative_blocks.header: Named for the grandfather on the other side
narrative_blocks.body: The middle boy of the three carried his mother's maiden name, Salvage, where his brothers carried Polk ones. He was born in the city in 1938 and was fourteen when his father died.

narrative_blocks.header: The third boy took the surgeon’s name
narrative_blocks.body: William Mecklenburg Polk, his great-grandfather, was the Confederate general's son who became a New York gynecologist and the dean of Cornell's medical school. The name skipped two generations and landed on the youngest of the three brothers in 1940.

cross_connections.display_label: was flying in the era her book begins, and gave aviators their trophy

narrative_blocks.header: Four children’s books, then a flying life
narrative_blocks.body: She wrote four books for children, among them The Real Reason for Christmas and In the Beginning. Then she wrote her second husband's life as A Reckless Grace, an account of pilots and their planes from the Jennys to the jets.

narrative_blocks.header: She and her sister married brothers
narrative_blocks.body: She married James Potter Polk in 1933, and her elder sister Katharine married his elder brother Frank the year after, so the middle sister went first. Her second marriage was to the aviator Champe Taliaferro, whom she outlived.

narrative_blocks.header: Sunday school on Jupiter Island at ninety
narrative_blocks.body: She taught Sunday school at Christ Memorial Chapel and taught at the Hobe Sound Child Care Center on the Florida coast. She died on Jupiter Island in 2010, at ninety-five, and is buried at the chapel's memorial garden.

notable.notable_blurb: Founder of the American Film Institute

cross_connections.display_label: bought the Zapruder film for Life while he shot the world's mourning
co-founded the Kennedy Center's Friends before he made its Honors

bio.bio_blurb: Founder of the American Film Institute

military_service.role: Directed training films after college.

career.role: Director, Motion Picture and Television Service

narrative_blocks.header: He built the American Film Institute
narrative_blocks.body: At thirty-five he left the government to become the founding director of the American Film Institute, and ran it out of a suite in the Kennedy Center. In ten years it preserved some fourteen thousand films, and its conservatory turned out Lynch, Malick and Schrader.

narrative_blocks.header: He filmed Kennedy from the day after
narrative_blocks.body: On 23 November 1963 he proposed a film on the dead president, and camera crews were shooting in fourteen countries before the day was out. Congress had to pass a resolution before Americans were allowed to see it.

narrative_blocks.header: Murrow pulled him to Washington at thirty-one
narrative_blocks.body: Edward R. Murrow recruited him in 1962 to run the motion-picture service of the United States Information Agency, which turned out some three hundred short documentaries a year. One of them followed nine Black students into a white high school in Little Rock and won an Academy Award.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the Honors for thirty-six years
narrative_blocks.body: With Nick Vanoff he created the Kennedy Center Honors in 1978, and wrote and produced the broadcast every year until 2014. Most of his fourteen Emmys came out of that one night.

narrative_blocks.header: Thurgood Marshall, twice, for two actors
narrative_blocks.body: Separate but Equal put Sidney Poitier on television as Thurgood Marshall in 1991 and took the Emmy. Fifteen years later he wrote the stage play Thurgood, which James Earl Jones opened and Laurence Fishburne carried to Broadway.

narrative_blocks.header: A director’s son, first hired on Shane
narrative_blocks.body: He came into the business as a teenager, a production assistant on Shane, and later shot the Amsterdam locations for The Diary of Anne Frank. Both were his father's pictures, and George Stevens won directing Oscars for A Place in the Sun and Giant.

narrative_blocks.header: She took the name and the trade
narrative_blocks.body: She was six when her mother married George Stevens Jr., and she grew up under his name rather than Condon. She makes documentaries, the third generation of that family to work in film.

notable.notable_blurb: Producer and writer of the Kennedy Center Honors

cross_connections.display_label: won the same editorial-cartooning Pulitzer as Herblock, whom he filmed

bio.bio_blurb: Producer and writer of the Kennedy Center Honors

narrative_blocks.header: Seven Emmys, mostly from one night a year
narrative_blocks.body: He wrote and produced the Kennedy Center Honors from 2002, and the broadcast took Emmy nominations five years running from 2007 and won the last three of them. Seven Emmys came to him in all.

narrative_blocks.header: He filmed Fishburne as Thurgood Marshall
narrative_blocks.body: He directed and produced the HBO film of Thurgood, the one-man play his father had written, and took an NAACP award for the directing. He had been an associate producer on The Thin Red Line before that.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty Christmases and five AFI salutes
narrative_blocks.body: He produced the Christmas in Washington specials for more than twenty years and directed the last ten. He also staged the American Film Institute's salutes to Elizabeth Taylor, Jack Nicholson, Spielberg, Eastwood and Scorsese.

narrative_blocks.header: He put the inauguration on HBO
narrative_blocks.body: We Are One, the concert at the Lincoln Memorial for the 2009 inauguration, was his production. He made a documentary on the Washington Post cartoonist Herblock in 2013, and something over thirty primetime specials besides.

narrative_blocks.header: A Left Bank cinema turned him around
narrative_blocks.body: He went to Duke meaning to go into politics, then to Paris to chase a woman and write a novel, and neither came off. In a Left Bank cinema he watched The More the Merrier and found out what his grandfather had done.

narrative_blocks.header: He built an album for Bettye LaVette
narrative_blocks.body: He conceived and produced The British Rock Songbook for Bettye LaVette in 2010, and it took a Grammy nomination the year after. The Honors segments he built for Dylan, Springsteen, the Who and McCartney worked the same way.

narrative_blocks.header: Stomach cancer at forty-eight
narrative_blocks.body: He died in Los Angeles on 15 October 2015 of complications during treatment for stomach cancer, at forty-eight. His middle name was Murrow, for the newsman who had pulled his father out of Hollywood four years before he was born.

cross_connections.display_label: was her great-grandmother's sister, and married James Hooker in 1816
was her second cousin, and courted Edith Carow before Roosevelt did

narrative_blocks.header: Married in Lent, with no bridesmaids
narrative_blocks.body: She married Winthrop Rutherfurd at noon at Grace Church in February 1902, and because it was Lent there were no flowers, no bridesmaids and no reception. The papers called her very tall, blond and a great belle; he was forty, the most eligible bachelor in New York, and her fourth cousin once removed.

narrative_blocks.header: Dead at thirty-eight, six children behind her
narrative_blocks.body: Appendicitis took her in June 1917, suddenly, at thirty-eight, and left six children under fourteen. The governess hired to look after them was Lucy Mercer, who married their father three years later.

narrative_blocks.header: A Vice President’s fourth daughter
narrative_blocks.body: She was the fourth daughter of Levi Parsons Morton, Vice President under Benjamin Harrison and then Governor of New York, and of Anna Livingston Street. She was born at Newport and buried in the Rutherfurd plot at Tranquility.

narrative_blocks.header: Six children in eleven years
narrative_blocks.body: She bore six children between 1903 and 1913, five sons and a daughter. The eldest, Lewis Morton, died at sixteen on the eve of his father's second wedding; the daughter who carried her name died at thirty-nine.

notable.notable_blurb: Two-time Academy Award-winning film director

cross_connections.display_label: got into Paramount at fourteen pushing a mop, then shot its portraits
was general manager of Hal Roach Studios from 1919 into the 1950s

military_service.unit: Army Signal Corps — Special Coverage Unit (SPECOU), SHAEF
military_service.notes: Headed the film unit Eisenhower ordered him to raise; its footage is the only colour film of the war in Europe.

career.role: Director of photography and gag writer

narrative_blocks.header: He climbed the fence and claimed the job
narrative_blocks.body: There were no unions, so a cameraman who wanted an assistant had no way to find one. At seventeen he went over the fence at a studio that needed one and said he was an assistant cameraman. Two days later he was.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-five Laurel and Hardy shorts
narrative_blocks.body: He shot and wrote gags for thirty-five of their two-reelers at Hal Roach, and worked out that Stan Laurel's blue eyes would register on panchromatic stock when they vanished on orthochromatic. Comedy, he said, could be graceful and human.

narrative_blocks.header: Eisenhower gave him forty-five men
narrative_blocks.body: Ordered to London in 1943 to raise a film unit, he took Irwin Shaw, William Saroyan and Ivan Moffat among the forty-five. His own sixteen-millimetre camera shot the only colour film of the war in Europe.

narrative_blocks.header: He rode into Paris behind Leclerc
narrative_blocks.body: He got his unit in with the French armour rather than the American infantry behind it. The morning we came into Paris was the wildest thing I have ever seen, he wrote home — civilians cheering in the streets while the shooting went on around them.

narrative_blocks.header: Dachau, and the film shown at Nuremberg
narrative_blocks.body: He reached the camp two days after its liberation and stayed in Germany compiling the footage with Budd Schulberg for the prosecution. It was entered as evidence at Nuremberg and taken into the National Film Registry in 2008.

narrative_blocks.header: His fortieth birthday, in the Ardennes
narrative_blocks.body: The Germans counterattacked on 16 December 1944 and the Americans fell back. Two days later, turning forty, he wrote in his journal about the stunned look on the faces of the men.

narrative_blocks.header: After the war he was never hilarious again
narrative_blocks.body: The line is his own. The man who had made Swing Time and The More the Merrier came home to I Remember Mama, A Place in the Sun and The Diary of Anne Frank, and called Shane his war picture.

burial.plot_notes: Forest Lawn Memorial Park, Hollywood Hills, Los Angeles, California

notable.notable_blurb: Silent-film actress

cross_connections.display_label: cast the boy Charlie Chaplin as Billy the pageboy in Sherlock Holmes

narrative_blocks.header: She was in Dorothy Arzner's 1927 picture
narrative_blocks.body: She worked through the twenties in shorts and features under the name Yvonne Howell, among them Fashions for Women in 1927, directed by Dorothy Arzner — one of the very few women directing in Hollywood — and the Ken Maynard western Somewhere in Sonora the same year.

narrative_blocks.header: The giggle was meant to survive sound
narrative_blocks.body: When the talkies came she pinned her hopes on a distinctive giggle, and the papers ran it as news in the summer of 1929 — Giggles Win Role, Giggles Way Into Talkies. She made exactly one more picture after 1930, Working Girls in 1931.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother was billed as the girl Chaplin
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother was Alice Howell, a Keystone comedienne reviewers called the scream of the screen and the girl Charlie Chaplin; she appeared with Chaplin in Laughing Gas in 1914. In 1917 Howell became the third comedienne, after Mabel Normand and Marie Dressler, to be given her own production unit.

narrative_blocks.header: She was a nurse's aide in Army hospitals
narrative_blocks.body: Through the Second World War she worked as a nurse's aide in Army hospitals in California. Her husband was in Europe those years, filming the war for Eisenhower's Signal Corps unit.

narrative_blocks.header: Married in 1930, divorced after the war
narrative_blocks.body: She married George Stevens, then a cameraman, in 1930, and it was to her he wrote from Paris in the September of 1944. He came home from Europe a changed man by his own account, and the marriage ended in 1947.

narrative_blocks.header: She lived to a hundred and four
narrative_blocks.body: She outlived Stevens by thirty-five years and died at Los Angeles in 2010, a hundred and four years old. Their son George Jr. founded the American Film Institute.

bio.bio_blurb: Puritan missionary; translator of the Eliot Indian Bible

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Roxbury, MA

narrative_blocks.header: He was Thomas Hooker’s usher in Essex
narrative_blocks.body: He came out of Jesus College to assist Thomas Hooker at a private school at Little Baddow. When Hooker was driven to the Netherlands he sailed as chaplain on the Lyon and landed at Boston in November 1631.

narrative_blocks.header: The first Bible printed in the Americas
narrative_blocks.body: He put the whole Bible into Massachusett, and Samuel Green and Marmaduke Johnson set it at Cambridge in 1663 — the first complete Bible printed in the western hemisphere. The Nipmuc printer James Printer helped set the type.

narrative_blocks.header: A Pequot War captive taught him the words
narrative_blocks.body: Cockenoe, taken in the Pequot War of 1637 and made a servant, was the first he made use of to teach him words and to be his interpreter. Massachusett had no written alphabet until he made one for it.

narrative_blocks.header: His first sermon to them failed entirely
narrative_blocks.body: He preached to Cutshamekin's people at Dorchester Mills in 1646 and wrote that they gave no heed unto it, but were weary and despised what I said. That October he tried again in Waban's wigwam at Nonantum, which Newton's city seal shows.

narrative_blocks.header: The first book banned in North America
narrative_blocks.body: He wrote that Christ is the only right Heir of the Crown of England and called for an elected theocracy. When Charles II came in, the General Court made him retract, banned The Christian Commonwealth and burned every copy.

narrative_blocks.header: Fourteen praying towns, and then the war
narrative_blocks.body: He gathered Algonquian converts into fourteen planned towns, Natick the best recorded, and argued its boundary case against Dedham. King Philip's War broke all of them in 1675.

narrative_blocks.header: His school had to take Black pupils
narrative_blocks.body: He founded Roxbury Latin in 1645, and in 1689 gave seventy-five acres to a Jamaica Plain school on condition it take Black and Native students without prejudice. He died the next year at eighty-five, saying welcome joy.

burial.plot_notes: Eliot/Parish tomb, beside the Dudley tomb

people.relational_label_override: Wife of the Apostle to the Indians

narrative_blocks.header: The first marriage in the Roxbury book
narrative_blocks.body: Hers was the first entry in the Marages of the Inhabitants of Roxbury. The clerk wrote 4 September 1632, which cannot be right because she had not yet landed, and her husband put the wedding in October.

narrative_blocks.header: Member one hundred and forty-eight
narrative_blocks.body: She was admitted to the Boston church within weeks of arriving, as its hundred and forty-eighth member, and later to Roxbury's as its fiftieth. Six children came: Hannah, John, Joseph, Samuel, Aaron and Benjamin.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at thirty-one by a ship off Nicaragua
narrative_blocks.body: She married Lewis Ashmun of Northampton in 1846 and had two sons by him, Lewis and George. He died aboard the Decatur off Nicaragua in 1852, and in 1856 she married Jonathan Bird of Greenfield and went with him to New Jersey.

narrative_blocks.header: She died in Newark and came home
narrative_blocks.body: Greenfield had her at the start and at the end. She died at Newark in November 1896, at seventy-six, and was carried back to the Federal Street burying ground in the town she was born in.

notable.notable_blurb: Congressman; founder of Scudder & Carter

cross_connections.display_label: built the company he served as principal counsel

landmarks.landmark_blurb: 116 East 17th Street, New York City

military_service.role: Captain, Thirty-seventh Regiment, from 1862 to the end of the war.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded what became Carter Ledyard
narrative_blocks.body: Admitted to the bar in 1848, he founded Scudder & Carter in 1854 — now Carter Ledyard & Milburn — and was afterwards principal counsel to Standard Oil. The Times put him at the head of this city's bar for a third of a century.

narrative_blocks.header: One term, and he would not stand again
narrative_blocks.body: He went to the Forty-third Congress as a Republican in 1873 for New York's first district, and sat on the Committee on War Claims. He declined renomination and went back to his practice.

narrative_blocks.header: A captain of the National Guard
narrative_blocks.body: He was commissioned captain in the Thirty-seventh New York National Guard in 1862 and served to the end of the war. In 1865 he was advertising himself for a cook and a chambermaid sixty miles up the North River.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty years a trustee of his own college
narrative_blocks.body: He took his degree at Trinity College in Hartford in 1846 and sat on its board for twenty years and more. He gave the Town of Huntington the books its library began with.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at thirty-eight, remarried at forty
narrative_blocks.body: He married Louisa Henrietta Davies, daughter of the West Point professor Charles Davies, in 1853. She died at thirty in December 1864 while he was away with his regiment, and four-year-old Elizabeth soon after. Emma Willard of Troy followed in 1866.

narrative_blocks.header: Root and Evarts came to his funeral
narrative_blocks.body: He died at his house on East Twenty-second Street in February 1886, at sixty. Elihu Root, Senator Evarts, Joseph Choate and the mayor were at Calvary Church, and he went to the family ground at Northport.

narrative_blocks.header: A second Scudder in Congress
narrative_blocks.body: Townsend Scudder, his nephew, sat in the same House and later on the state supreme court, and lived to ninety-five. The line went back to Thomas Scudder, who came from Kent to Salem in 1630.

cross_connections.display_label: was a St. Paul's boy before he became the Navy's only World War I ace
staged the Seabiscuit–War Admiral match five years after St. Paul's
was a St. Paul's boy, and the first American killed in Vietnam

bio.bio_blurb: Master at St. Paul's School for forty-three years

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Memorial replica of his Shute Cottage
116 East 17th Street, New York City

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-three years a master at St. Paul’s
narrative_blocks.body: He had been a boy at St. Paul's himself and came back to teach there, and stayed forty-three years. He kept house at Shute Cottage, a pre-Revolutionary building the school's founder had bought in 1865.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-five years running the Halcyon boats
narrative_blocks.body: He was president of the Halcyon Boat Club for thirty-five years. Two days before he died he went down to Long Pond in the Halcyon barge and ran the boathouse through the annual race against the Shattucks.

narrative_blocks.header: The only president his society ever had
narrative_blocks.body: He founded the Concordian Literary Society and was the only president it had in forty years, and advised Horae, the school paper, besides.

narrative_blocks.header: Pince-nez, waxed moustache, the right attitude
narrative_blocks.body: A boy he had taught put him in a book the month he died: bifocal pince-nez, drooping waxed moustache, dressed to the height of fashion, at home at lawn parties, never letting a slight paunch become more than a slight paunch. Chanler Chapman meant it as an attack and it reads now as a portrait.

narrative_blocks.header: He revised a headmaster’s memorial
narrative_blocks.body: He read and corrected the manuscript and proof of Memories of a Great Schoolmaster in 1906, the life of Henry Augustus Coit, and was thanked in it by name. Coit had been rector when he was a boy there.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at his desk, mid-conversation
narrative_blocks.body: He was talking with friends in his study on the last night of May 1936 when he died at his desk. He had been ill a long time and had gone on regardless, the anniversary exercises that weekend included.

narrative_blocks.header: The school rebuilt his cottage for him
narrative_blocks.body: Four years after he died a memorial committee put up Scudder House at the school, a replica of the Shute Cottage he had lived in. It takes the school's visitors now.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: 116 East 17th Street, New York City
116 East 17th Street, New York City

narrative_blocks.header: A medical degree he never used
narrative_blocks.body: He came out of the College of Physicians and Surgeons a qualified doctor and never practised. He worked as a chemist instead, and wrote a long shelf of technical books.

narrative_blocks.header: Trinity, Columbia, and the Institute
narrative_blocks.body: He took a bachelor's at Trinity in 1892, a master's and a doctorate at Columbia by 1898, and studied at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology besides. The American Electrochemical Society and the Chemists' Club had him on their rolls.

narrative_blocks.header: Cyanide, at forty-six, in Boston
narrative_blocks.body: He died at Boston in February 1917, at forty-six, of cyanide poisoning. He never married, and was buried at Northport with his parents.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: 116 East 17th Street, New York City

education.school_name: New York School of Applied Design for Women

narrative_blocks.header: Applied design, then a doctor’s house
narrative_blocks.body: She went to the New York School of Applied Design for Women and married Dr. Edward Loughborough Keyes in November 1898. Six children followed between 1899 and 1913, and she died at Orlando in 1944.

narrative_blocks.header: One day in a Florida hospital
narrative_blocks.body: She stayed a New Yorker to the end but died at Orange General Hospital in Orlando in February 1944, a day after she went in, of double lobar pneumonia. She was seventy-two.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: 116 East 17th Street, New York City

career.role: Patent department, latterly in charge of patent work

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years at General Electric
narrative_blocks.body: He joined General Electric as a student engineer in 1902 and retired in July 1942, the month he died. He went from the railway engineering department into patents in 1907 and stayed there.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the foreign patents
narrative_blocks.body: He was assistant patent attorney in charge of foreign patents from 1911, and from 1919 had charge of all the patent work of International General Electric. Rensselaer had him lecturing on patents in his last eight years.

narrative_blocks.header: St. Paul’s, Yale, then Columbia
narrative_blocks.body: He went to St. Paul's at Concord, where his elder brother taught for forty-three years, then Yale in 1896 and Columbia for an electrical engineering degree and a master's by 1899.

narrative_blocks.header: He married at fifty-six, in Scarsdale
narrative_blocks.body: He married Alice Mabel Smith at Scarsdale in September 1931, when he was fifty-six. He was junior warden of St. George's at Schenectady, the church he lies at.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a sixth cousin
narrative_blocks.body: He and Alice Mabel Smith both descend from Samuel Hooker, the founder's son, and his wife Mary Willet — 7 generations up on either side to the same couple. They were sixth cousins, and married in 1931.

notable.notable_blurb: Urologist; consultant to the American Expeditionary Force

cross_connections.display_label: was dean of the medical school where he held the urology chair

military_service.role: Major to colonel; consultant in urology to the American Expeditionary Force. Officer of the Legion of Honour.

education.school_name: College of Physicians and Surgeons, Columbia

narrative_blocks.header: The first public campaign against VD
narrative_blocks.body: With Hugh Hampton Young he ran the army's campaign against venereal disease in the First World War, the first public campaign of its kind. Infection was reckoned to be costing more than seventy million soldier-days of leave.

narrative_blocks.header: The first specialist sent overseas
narrative_blocks.body: He went out a major of the Medical Corps and came home a colonel, consultant in urology to the American Expeditionary Force. France made him an Officer of the Legion of Honour.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-seven years in the Cornell chair
narrative_blocks.body: He held Cornell's chair of urology from 1910 to 1937 and taught there to the end of his life. Georgetown, the Polyclinic, Bellevue, St. Vincent's, Memorial and New York Hospital all had him at one time or another.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the decade’s standard textbook
narrative_blocks.body: Urology, in 1928, was the standard text of its day, and he had written Surgical Diseases of the Genito-Urinary Organs with his father in 1903. He wrote poetry and prose besides, and spoke Spanish and French.

narrative_blocks.header: Motes and atoms in the sunlight of science
narrative_blocks.body: He told the American Urological Association in 1916 that we are but motes and atoms in the bright sunlight of science, and may rejoice if for one instant we reflect a single ray of it into the surrounding ignorance. The path of progress, he added, is narrow but not straight.

narrative_blocks.header: President of four urological societies
narrative_blocks.body: He led the American Urological Association, the International Urological Society, the Clinical Urological Association and the American Association of Genito-Urinary Surgeons, and the American Social Hygiene Association besides. Its Snow medal was first given to him.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a sculptor at seventy-five
narrative_blocks.body: In 1948 he married Bessie Potter Vonnoh, the sculptor, who outlived him by a year. Emma Willard Scudder had been his wife for the forty-five before that.

cross_connections.display_label: was his Princeton roommate, and married his sister in 1926

bio.bio_blurb: St. Louis surgeon and cancer specialist

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty years cutting in St. Louis
narrative_blocks.body: He practised as a surgeon and cancer specialist in St. Louis for more than thirty years, and was president of the St. Louis Surgical Society. He was on the staff at Barnes, Jewish, St. Luke's and St. John's Mercy.

narrative_blocks.header: Baseball, hockey and soccer at Princeton
narrative_blocks.body: He came to Princeton out of Lawrenceville and played on all three teams. He was class president in his junior year and belonged to Cap and Gown.

narrative_blocks.header: Voted best all-around man in senior year
narrative_blocks.body: He was voted best all-around man by his class before he left Princeton, and the notice written when he died sixty-nine years later said it had been prophetic of the whole career.

narrative_blocks.header: The third Edward Keyes in medicine
narrative_blocks.body: He was the third Edward Keyes to practise medicine, and his son took the name and the Princeton class of 1951. He left four children, eleven grandchildren and nine great-grandchildren.

sources.short: New York Times, 3 February and 9 October 1926

narrative_blocks.header: Home from Oxford to marry
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth came home in 1926 from two years of study at Oxford, and on 9 October married Earnshaw Cook at her parents' house in Forest Hills. They were married sixty-one years.

sources.short: "Josephine Adrian, A.L. Keyes Engaged", New York Times, 15 July 1947

military_service.notes: General Mark Clark's headquarters, Italy and Austria

narrative_blocks.header: In Mark Clark's headquarters
narrative_blocks.body: Alexander took Phi Beta Kappa at Yale in 1933 and a Harvard law degree in 1936, served in the war as a lieutenant colonel in General Mark Clark's headquarters in Italy and Austria, and went on to the State Department.

cross_connections.display_label: founded the Farmington school she was sent to a century later

bio.bio_blurb: Founder of the first cancer information center

narrative_blocks.header: She built the first cancer information center
narrative_blocks.body: She took Dr. Carlos Perez's idea and made it: an empty room at Barnes in 1977 that she learned the field for herself and filled until it looked like a library. It is believed to be the first of its kind in the country.

narrative_blocks.header: Beijing, Thailand and Rio copied it
narrative_blocks.body: What she built became the model for cancer information centres across the country and well beyond it. For the first two years she volunteered almost full time, before there was any paid staff at all.

narrative_blocks.header: Diagnosed six years after founding it
narrative_blocks.body: Colon cancer was found in her in 1983, six years into the centre's life. Her son said it gave the work new meaning and made her the spokesperson for the people she had been counselling.

narrative_blocks.header: A red feather beat the horses
narrative_blocks.body: She was fifteen at a horse show in a Tyrolean felt hat with a red feather, and it took Frederick Hermann's attention off the horses. They married in 1949 and stayed married sixty-two years.

narrative_blocks.header: She thought of the stage, or the convent
narrative_blocks.body: As a child she considered the stage, the convent, or following four generations of physicians, her father among them. She went from Mary Institute to Miss Porter's at Farmington and then Pine Manor.

military_service.role: Navigation and intercept observer to 1956.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty years from assistant to president
narrative_blocks.body: He came to Emerson Electric in 1956 as assistant to the president and retired thirty years later as president of it. Sales grew more than two hundredfold between the two dates.

narrative_blocks.header: A navigation and intercept observer
narrative_blocks.body: He served in the Air Force as a navigation and intercept observer until 1956, and went from the separation straight into Emerson.

narrative_blocks.header: Biology at Princeton, and Cottage
narrative_blocks.body: He came out of St. Louis Country Day, read biology at Princeton and took his degree with honours in 1951, and belonged to Cottage.

narrative_blocks.header: He set up a bank with a classmate
narrative_blocks.body: After Emerson he founded the Fortune Group with a man from his own Princeton class, doing investment banking and business consulting.

narrative_blocks.header: She married the man who filmed the Arch
narrative_blocks.body: She married William Hoffman Otto in February 1954. He ran Laclede Gas's films about the city, one of them nominated for an Academy Award, and she outlived him by thirty-four years.

narrative_blocks.header: Shepley came down from her mother
narrative_blocks.body: The middle name was her mother's, Emily Catlin Shepley, and she gave the Keyes name on to her eldest son. Lawrence, Kathryn and Clay were the three.

cross_connections.display_label: founded the Farmington school she followed her sister to

narrative_blocks.header: Mary Institute, Farmington, Briarcliff
narrative_blocks.body: She went from Mary Institute to Miss Porter's at Farmington and then to Briarcliff, the second of the sisters sent to the Connecticut school.

narrative_blocks.header: The Junior League and a weekly shift
narrative_blocks.body: She sat on the board of the Junior League of St. Louis for years and worked a weekly shift at the Woman's Exchange.

narrative_blocks.header: Northeast Harbor, then Harbor Springs
narrative_blocks.body: She spent her childhood summers at Northeast Harbor in Maine, the coast her elder sister had been born on, and her later ones at Harbor Springs in Michigan.

military_service.role: Fourteenth Armored Division, France and Germany; Bronze Star.

narrative_blocks.header: A Bronze Star, then the engineering degree
narrative_blocks.body: He spent two years with the Fourteenth Armored Division in France and Germany and was cited for unusual versatility and tireless devotion to duty. Princeton gave him his engineering degree afterwards, in 1946.

narrative_blocks.header: He put the family tannery back up
narrative_blocks.body: He re-established Hermann Oak Leather and ran it as president, and the trade elected him head of its American association. His grandfather had founded the firm in 1881 to supply equestrian goods to settlers heading west.

narrative_blocks.header: The board that absorbed her centre
narrative_blocks.body: He was a trustee of Country Day and Mary Institute and sat on the boards of Barnard and the Siteman Cancer Center — Siteman being what his wife's information centre eventually became part of.

cross_connections.display_label: built America’s first covered tannery, four generations before his own

bio.bio_blurb: Fourth-generation head of Hermann Oak Leather

narrative_blocks.header: The fourth of his line at the tannery
narrative_blocks.body: He came back to Hermann Oak after Domino Sugar, a Darden degree and Scientific Atlanta, and was the fourth generation to run it. He put lean manufacturing into a vegetable tannery.

narrative_blocks.header: The trade called him the Professor
narrative_blocks.body: He became one of the world's foremost authorities on the intricacies of vegetable leather tanning, and the nickname stuck.

narrative_blocks.header: He met her coaching her hockey team
narrative_blocks.body: He was still at Country Day when he coached Robin Cornwell's women's ice hockey team, and they married in 1978. She died in 2016; he carried cancer himself, and took Celebrate Life for a motto.

narrative_blocks.header: Her hockey coach married her
narrative_blocks.body: She played women's ice hockey under a Country Day boy who was coaching the team, and married him in 1978. Two daughters and six grandchildren followed.

narrative_blocks.header: The Republican who nearly took Missouri
narrative_blocks.body: She was the daughter of Howard Elliott, the first Speaker of the Missouri House to come from the St. Louis area, who took the Republican nomination for governor in 1952 and lost. He chaired the commission whose 1949 report urged the state to open every public school and college to Black students.

narrative_blocks.header: May Queen at Mary Institute, 1956
narrative_blocks.body: She was crowned May Queen in her last year at Mary Institute, and went on to Centenary College and Washington University.

narrative_blocks.header: The Art Museum, the Exchange, the Zoo district
narrative_blocks.body: She sat on the boards of the St. Louis Art Museum and its Friends, presided over the Women's Exchange, chaired the History Museum's Thomas Jefferson Society and served on the Zoo Museum District commission.

narrative_blocks.header: A Keyes, and then a banker
narrative_blocks.body: She married Edward Lawrence Keyes in 1959 and afterwards Donald Brandin, chairman and chief executive of Boatmen's Bancshares. She outlived him by seventeen years.

narrative_blocks.header: Two widowhoods, and no Keyes children
narrative_blocks.body: She was widowed first by Jerome Combs and then by Edward Lawrence Keyes, whom she married in 1981 and stayed with thirty-two years. Her three children were Combs; none were Keyes.

career.role: Director of public relations and advertising

narrative_blocks.header: The Arch film went to the Academy Awards
narrative_blocks.body: He directed the gas company's sponsorship of films about St. Louis, and Monument to the Dream, on the building of the Gateway Arch, was nominated for an Academy Award. St. Louis, That Fabulous Summer covered the 1904 World's Fair.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-one years on one company’s face
narrative_blocks.body: He joined Laclede Gas in 1950, was made director of public relations and advertising five years later, and held the job for thirty-one years. The last campaign he ran was the one built around the character Ernest.

narrative_blocks.header: Musical Showcase, and a band in the parks
narrative_blocks.body: He put Laclede behind the city's music — the television programmes Musical Showcase and Sunday with Sorkin in the fifties, and the Laclede Concert Band playing the parks through the fifties and sixties.

military_service.role: Three years with the Counterintelligence Corps in Germany.

career.organization: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

narrative_blocks.header: President of the bank at forty-two
narrative_blocks.body: He joined First National in St. Louis in 1958 and was made president sixteen years later, the youngest man ever given the title there. He renamed it Centerre and built its tower at 800 Market Street, looking down on the old Busch Stadium.

narrative_blocks.header: The largest bank holding company in Missouri
narrative_blocks.body: By the early eighties the bank he ran was the biggest holding company in the state, with sixty offices at home and three abroad. He sat on the boards of AT&T, Dillard's, Steak n Shake and Pet, and directed the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifteen years growing an endowment
narrative_blocks.body: He retired from banking in 1989 and took the unpaid vice chairmanship of Washington University's trustees, holding it until 2004 and working with successive chancellors to build the endowment.

narrative_blocks.header: Counterintelligence in Germany
narrative_blocks.body: He spent three years with the Army's Counterintelligence Corps in Germany after Brown, and came home to the bank in 1958. Time named him one of two hundred young leaders in the country in 1974.

military_service.role: Consultant on the Manhattan Project at Oak Ridge; later industrial intelligence officer with the rank of colonel.
Enlisted 7 August 1918.

narrative_blocks.header: He set out to prove Cobb beat Ruth
narrative_blocks.body: He began with one question — whether Ty Cobb was the better hitter — and spent four years on the arithmetic. His scoring index put Cobb first and Ruth second, which no statistic had managed before.

narrative_blocks.header: Baseball Is Played All Wrong
narrative_blocks.body: Frank Deford came to interview him in the winter of 1964 and Sports Illustrated led its March issue with the result. Right now, Deford wrote, Earnshaw Cook knows more about baseball than anyone else in the world.

narrative_blocks.header: A slide rule, and the Hall took it
narrative_blocks.body: Percentage Baseball came out that summer, the first full-length book of its kind to reach a national audience, worked out on a slide rule and a mechanical calculator. Cooperstown asked for the rule; he called it his last testament to the greatest game of them all.

narrative_blocks.header: Two objects: score runs, and don’t make outs
narrative_blocks.body: The sacrifice bunt was usually a mistake, he found, and the best hitter should lead off. Walter Alston and Bill Veeck took him seriously and the rest of the game did not; it came round about thirty-five years later.

narrative_blocks.header: Oak Ridge, then a colonel’s commission
narrative_blocks.body: He consulted on the Manhattan Project at Oak Ridge and finished the war an Army industrial intelligence officer with the rank of colonel. Metallurgy had been his trade since 1922, at Bethlehem Steel and then American Brake Shoe.

narrative_blocks.header: Philip Roth wrote him into a novel
narrative_blocks.body: Roth based the boy-genius coach Isaac Ellis in The Great American Novel on him. Davey Johnson looked him up in Baltimore, played golf with him, and carried his ideas as far as a World Series with the Mets.

narrative_blocks.header: A duck-hunting book, and a cattle farm
narrative_blocks.body: He kept cattle on Kent Island in the fifties and wrote Hellica Snooze, on duck hunting, in 1957. His father had run Maryland's public schools for twenty years.

sources.short: "Josephine Adrian, A.L. Keyes Engaged", New York Times, 15 July 1947

narrative_blocks.header: A hundred and eight years
narrative_blocks.body: Born the year Edison filed for the phonograph, she died the year of the Iran-Contra hearings. She outlived her husband by forty-five years and was fifty-three when she married him.

narrative_blocks.header: Named for the aunt who went to Japan
narrative_blocks.body: Alice Mabel Bacon, her mother's youngest sister, carried the same two names and spent years teaching in Japan. The Bacons of New Haven were her mother's people, and Rev. Leonard Bacon her grandfather.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixth cousins, 234 years apart
narrative_blocks.body: Seven generations above both her and Hewlett Scudder stand Samuel Hooker, Thomas Hooker's son, and Mary Willet. Samuel died in 1697; the cousins married in 1931.

bio.bio_blurb: New York lawyer and field artillery major

military_service.role: Major; adjutant of the 52nd Field Artillery Brigade, then battalion commander of the 125th and 127th Field Artillery in France, 1918.
1st New York Field Artillery at Camp McAllen, Texas, 1916; promoted major on the border.

narrative_blocks.header: Squadron A to a field artillery brigade
narrative_blocks.body: He enlisted in Troop 4 of Squadron A cavalry in 1901, made sergeant by 1911, and took a commission in the field artillery in 1913. He went to the Mexican border as a major in 1916 and to France in 1918.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale in ninety-four, then the bar
narrative_blocks.body: He read for the law after Yale and practised in New York. His younger brother rode in Squadron A too, for a year at the start of the century.

narrative_blocks.header: Two years, then thirty-seven
narrative_blocks.body: She married a Colombian in 1943 and was divorced inside two years, then married Jacques Chabrier of Paris in 1948 and stayed married until his death in 1985. He adopted her daughter.

narrative_blocks.header: A dinner in the Public Library reading room
narrative_blocks.body: She ran Bryn Mawr's regional scholarship committee and in 1981 chaired a fundraising drive that opened with dinner in the reading room of the New York Public Library. Twenty-five summers went to a house the Chabriers inherited in the Loire.

narrative_blocks.header: Bible study where her forebear preached
narrative_blocks.body: She joined the Bible study at the First Congregational Church of Litchfield, where Leonard Bacon had held the pulpit in the nineteenth century. She was made a Eucharistic minister at St. Anthony's in 1995.

cross_connections.display_label: was her husband’s sister, and married her brother two years after

narrative_blocks.header: Two Agates and two Smiths, two weddings
narrative_blocks.body: She married Winthrop Davenport Smith in New York in January 1903, and two years later her brother Frederic married his sister Helen. Two Agates and two Smiths, in two weddings.

cross_connections.display_label: was her husband’s sister, and married her brother two years before

narrative_blocks.header: Two sisters past a hundred
narrative_blocks.body: She reached a hundred and her elder sister Alice reached a hundred and eight, both of them born to Katherine Bacon in the 1870s and 80s. Between them they covered a hundred and nine years of the family's history.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Agates married two Smiths
narrative_blocks.body: She married Frederic Joseph Agate at Norfolk in June 1905, two years after his sister Mary Virginia had married her brother Winthrop. The two households shared both sets of parents.

bio.bio_blurb: The first American to die in the line of duty in Iraq

military_service.role: Lieutenant commander; recalled 1940, posted Manila then Bahrain as naval observer.
Ensign in the Connecticut and the Michigan, lieutenant in the Ericsson and the Upshur; resigned November 1920.

narrative_blocks.header: Among the first Americans to die in Iraq
narrative_blocks.body: He talked his way onto an RAF flight to Basra on Friday the 13th of June 1941, carrying the cryptographic codes for his new post. The aircraft went into the desert and killed everyone aboard.

narrative_blocks.header: Sent to watch the U-boats from Bahrain
narrative_blocks.body: Recalled from civilian life in 1940, he went first to Manila and then to Bahrain as United States Naval Observer, to follow British anti-submarine work in the Indian Ocean and report on German submarines.

narrative_blocks.header: Buried at Basra by Assyrian buglers
narrative_blocks.body: British forces found the wreck on 4 July 1941 and buried him the next day in the Imperial War Graves cemetery at Basra, with an honour guard from HMS Seabelle and Taps sounded by buglers of the Assyrian Levies.

narrative_blocks.header: His class-supper speech was the Ladies
narrative_blocks.body: Annapolis in 1915 made him manager of the lacrosse team and leader of the glee club, and he was the only man to give a speech at the class supper. His subject was the ladies.

narrative_blocks.header: Ensign to lieutenant, then a broker’s desk
narrative_blocks.body: He served in the Connecticut and the Michigan as an ensign and the Ericsson and the Upshur as a lieutenant, and resigned in November 1920 for a brokerage in New York.

bio.bio_blurb: Neurosurgeon; editor of the Journal of Neurosurgery

military_service.role: Captain; chief neurosurgeon, Sixth General Hospital, North Africa. Earlier a volunteer year building the neurosurgical service at Birmingham under the air raids.

narrative_blocks.header: He edited the Journal of Neurosurgery
narrative_blocks.body: He ran it for 10 years and quadrupled its subscriptions, adding abstracts, key words and the Neurosurgical Forum. He valued the editorship above anything he did in an operating room.

narrative_blocks.header: Birmingham neurosurgery under the raids
narrative_blocks.body: Before America entered the war he volunteered a year in England and set up the neurosurgical service at Birmingham for the head and spine injuries the air raids were producing. He went to North Africa afterwards as chief neurosurgeon of the Sixth General Hospital.

narrative_blocks.header: She was casting as well as he was
narrative_blocks.body: He saw Katharine Agate on a river near Camp Blanding, fly-fishing as expertly as he did. Tuberculosis sent him home from North Africa, and they married at Denver in May 1944.

narrative_blocks.header: Paraplegic at T-2, and still working
narrative_blocks.body: Radiation for a lymphoma in 1950 left him paraplegic within a year. He wrote the standard paper on rehabilitating paraplegics out of it, and drove himself to Hanover through the snow from a wheelchair.

narrative_blocks.header: He took a two-year medical school to four
narrative_blocks.body: As associate dean at Dartmouth he raised the money, founded the Hitchcock Foundation and helped carry the medical school from two years to four. He was professor of anatomy there until 1971.

narrative_blocks.header: The World Court put him off the law
narrative_blocks.body: A summer observing at The Hague with Elihu Root convinced him the law was not for him. He went back to Hamilton for the pre-medical courses and taught English while he sat them.

bio.bio_blurb: President of the Omi Brotherhood academy

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Shiga Prefecture

narrative_blocks.header: She ran the Omi Brotherhood’s schools
narrative_blocks.body: She was president of the Omi Kyodaisha academy in Shiga, the chain of schools her husband's mission founded. She had been born a viscount's daughter, of the old lords of Komatsu in Iyo.

narrative_blocks.header: Adopted by an American in Connecticut
narrative_blocks.body: Alice Mabel Bacon adopted her, one of two Japanese girls she took as daughters and never bore. Bacon had come out from Connecticut to teach at the Peeresses' School, and adopted them both.

narrative_blocks.header: The other adopted daughter
narrative_blocks.body: She was Tsuda Umeko's niece, and the second of the two Japanese girls Alice Mabel Bacon adopted. Bacon never married and had no children of her own.

notable.notable_blurb: Architect of 1,600 Japanese buildings; founder of the Omi Brotherhood

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Shiga Prefecture

career.organization: Omi Mission, later the Omi Brotherhood

narrative_blocks.header: Sixteen hundred buildings, barely trained
narrative_blocks.body: He came to Japan in 1905 to teach English and turned to architecture with almost no formal training. His office grew past thirty staff and is credited with as many as 1,600 buildings across Japan and occupied Korea.

narrative_blocks.header: Sacked for filling his Bible class
narrative_blocks.body: The Shiga commercial school let him go in 1908 because a third of his pupils were coming to his Bible classes instead of the temples. He founded the Omi Mission ten years later and took architecture as the trade that paid for it.

narrative_blocks.header: Mentholatum paid for the mission
narrative_blocks.body: He set up the Omi Sales Company in 1920 to make an ointment called Mentholatum under licence, and it funded the mission. He also brought the first Hammond organs into Japan.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried the Emperor’s message to MacArthur
narrative_blocks.body: In September 1945 the former prime minister Konoe asked him to take a message to the occupation authorities on the Emperor's behalf, and he put forward the idea of renouncing divinity. He met the Emperor four times afterwards.

narrative_blocks.header: He became Japanese before Pearl Harbor
narrative_blocks.body: He was naturalised in 1941 and took the name Mereru Hitotsuyanagi, swearing allegiance to Japan weeks before the attack. The authorities suspected him anyway and shut most of his businesses down; Mentholatum survived because the army wanted it.

burial.plot_notes: Plot 52 Cedar Avenue East, beside Leonard Bacon

narrative_blocks.header: Nine children in eighteen years
narrative_blocks.body: She bore Leonard Bacon nine children between 1826 and 1843 — Rebecca, Benjamin Wisner, Leonard Woolsey, Francis, Theodore, George Blagden, James Hillhouse, Edward Woolsey and Lucy. Three of them were dead before she was.

narrative_blocks.header: The pulpit married again three years on
narrative_blocks.body: She died at forty-four in November 1844, and in 1847 her husband married Catherine Elizabeth Terry, who bore him five more. The two families lie in the same plot at Grove Street.

narrative_blocks.header: He married her in her own town
narrative_blocks.body: He was pastor at Terre Haute when he married her there in August 1880, and closed his work in the town nine months later. They had no children, and she died at Berkeley seven months before he did.

notable.notable_blurb: 2nd President of the United States

career.role: Vice President of the United States

narrative_blocks.header: He defended the Boston Massacre soldiers
narrative_blocks.body: In 1770 he took the defence of the eight redcoats who had fired into a Boston crowd, against the whole temper of the town, and six were acquitted outright. He counted it afterwards among the best services he ever did his country.

narrative_blocks.header: He signed the peace that ended the Revolution
narrative_blocks.body: Sent to Europe in 1778, he borrowed the money in Amsterdam that kept Congress solvent, then sat with Franklin and Jay at Paris to sign the treaty of 1783. He went on to St James's as the first American minister to the king he had helped rebel against.

narrative_blocks.header: The most insignificant office ever contrived
narrative_blocks.body: Eight years as Washington's vice president gave him a chair in the Senate, a record number of tie-breaking votes, and almost nothing else. He wrote to Abigail that it was the most insignificant office that ever the invention of man contrived.

narrative_blocks.header: Peace with France cost him the presidency
narrative_blocks.body: With his own Federalists demanding war after the XYZ insult, he built the Navy and then sent envoys to Paris and settled it. The party split, Jefferson beat him in 1800, and he asked to be remembered for the peace.

narrative_blocks.header: He signed the Alien and Sedition Acts
narrative_blocks.body: The same term produced the laws that jailed printers for criticising the government and stretched the wait for citizenship to fourteen years. He never repudiated them, and they outlived his presidency as the argument against it.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-four years and twelve hundred letters
narrative_blocks.body: He married Abigail Smith at Weymouth in October 1764. Through fifty-four years he wrote to her from Philadelphia, Amsterdam and Paris, put the business of government into the letters, and asked her judgement on it.

narrative_blocks.header: He died on the Fourth of July, 1826
narrative_blocks.body: Fifty years to the day after the Declaration, he died at Quincy at ninety. His last words were that Thomas Jefferson survives; Jefferson had gone at Monticello a few hours earlier.

career.organization: VX-5 Vampires, Naval Weapons Center China Lake

narrative_blocks.header: Drafted, and he chose to fly
narrative_blocks.body: A job was waiting at IBM after two summers there — a grey flannel suit, New York State, skiing close by — when the Vietnam draft took him. Allowed to pick a service, he volunteered for the Navy, learned to fly, and stayed twenty-eight years.

narrative_blocks.header: He had the Argonauts, then the Vampires
narrative_blocks.body: In August 1982 he took Attack Squadron 147, the first squadron in the Navy to fly the A-7 Corsair II. He was commanding VX-5 at China Lake by 1987, a captain in the desert testing what the fleet would later carry.

narrative_blocks.header: Tokyo alone at twelve, by train
narrative_blocks.body: Two years of his boyhood were spent in Japan, where he was let out on the trains into Tokyo by himself at twelve. He built model airplanes there and took trophies for aerobatics with them.

narrative_blocks.header: Named for an uncle he never met
narrative_blocks.body: The Eric he was named for was his father's brother, a Trinity freshman dead at nineteen two years before the wedding. He grew up on airfields because his father had flown B-24s across the Pacific.

military_service.notes: Drafted, volunteered for the Navy, and flew for twenty-eight years.

narrative_blocks.header: She died when the boy was eleven
narrative_blocks.body: Married at nineteen in 1881 to a schoolmaster ten years her senior, she was dead by about 1902, and George Kirchwey grew up after that in his father's college household at Brooklyn.

marriages.location: St. Philip's-in-the-Hills Episcopal Church, Tucson, Arizona

narrative_blocks.header: A Flint girl, and Michigan after
narrative_blocks.body: Howard Leslie Pettit's daughter, and a granddaughter of the Millers and of the George Anson Pettits of Flint, she took her degree at the University of Michigan before the Arizona wedding.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-two years, then a divorce
narrative_blocks.body: She married Samuel Neilson Hinckley Jr. at Tucson in 1949 and the couple went to Palo Alto. The marriage lasted until 1991, and he outlived it by seventeen years.

parents.father_research_notes: Charles Walker

narrative_blocks.header: A letter said she was recovering
narrative_blocks.body: Morse was in Washington painting Lafayette when a courier brought word that his wife was convalescent. He rode six days for New Haven and arrived to find she had died before the letter ever reached him.

narrative_blocks.header: Her death is why the telegraph exists
narrative_blocks.body: He gave the next forty-five years to sending word across distance faster than a horse could carry it, and to the code that bears his name. He did not marry again for twenty-three years.

narrative_blocks.header: She was nineteen when they married
narrative_blocks.body: Lucretia Pickering Walker married Morse at Concord, New Hampshire, in September 1818. She died at twenty-five, soon after the birth of a child, and he had her gravestone cut with a eulogy that runs to nine paragraphs.

education.school_name: New York School for the Deaf

narrative_blocks.header: She was deaf, and an early pupil
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah Griswold entered the New York School for the Deaf in 1833, one of its earliest students. She married Morse in 1848, when she was twenty-six and he was fifty-seven.

narrative_blocks.header: The Washington school began with her
narrative_blocks.body: She is said to have helped persuade Amos Kendall to found a school for the deaf at Washington — the institution that became Gallaudet University. Its elementary school still carries Kendall's name.

narrative_blocks.header: Born at a frontier fort, died in Berlin
narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Fort Brady, the post built at Sault Sainte Marie to watch the Canadian border. She died at her daughter's house in Berlin in 1901, having outlived Morse by twenty-nine years.

bio.extra_names: a.k.a. Abby Rockefeller Milton; known in the family as 'Babs'
bio.bio_blurb: Philanthropist; founder of the Greenacre Foundation

narrative_blocks.header: She built a waterfall on East 51st Street
narrative_blocks.body: In 1968 she created the Greenacre Foundation to run parks in New York for the public, and in 1971 gave it Greenacre Park — a vest-pocket lot on East 51st Street with a waterfall down one wall. She wanted New Yorkers to have 'some moments of serenity in this busy world,' and she served as the foundation's president herself.

narrative_blocks.header: Five brothers became public men; she did not
narrative_blocks.body: She was the eldest of the six Rockefeller children and the only daughter, and while John 3rd, Nelson, Laurance, Winthrop and David took governorships, foundations and public campaigns, she gave through boards and left almost no public trace of it. She sat on the board of the Rockefeller Brothers Fund from its founding in 1940 and was an honorary trustee of the Rockefeller Family Fund.

narrative_blocks.header: Memorial Sloan-Kettering gave her a medal in 1965
narrative_blocks.body: She was an advisory trustee of Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center in New York and, with her brother Laurance, one of its chief benefactors; the center gave her its Medal of Appreciation in 1965. Her giving also reached New York Hospital, the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the YWCA and the New York Zoological Society.

narrative_blocks.header: The family called her Babs for a reason
narrative_blocks.body: She was born Abigail Chapman Rockefeller and her mother was Abigail Greene Aldrich Rockefeller, so from childhood the household called her Babs and the confusion stopped there. The middle name was her mother's mother's: Abigail Pearce Truman Chapman, who married Senator Nelson Aldrich of Rhode Island.

narrative_blocks.header: A congressman called them the sure shot boys
narrative_blocks.body: Milton and a partner took control of the Equity Corporation — an investment trust that managed forty-four companies — with a small cash stake, shares in a dormant insurance company, and Equity's own money. In a single fortnight he was questioned by a House committee in Chicago and by the Securities and Exchange Commission in Washington, and Congressman Adolph Sabath's verdict was that the men were 'not speculators, they were sure shot boys.'

narrative_blocks.header: His wedding made front pages across the country
narrative_blocks.body: Fifty guests watched him marry Abby Rockefeller in her father's Manhattan house in May 1925, and twelve hundred came to the reception afterward, among them her grandfather John D. Rockefeller, Governor Alfred E. Smith of New York, and John W. Davis, the Democratic candidate for president the year before. The marriage ended in divorce in 1943, on her suit charging extreme cruelty, 'entirely mental in character.'

narrative_blocks.header: He carried Meriwether Lewis's name from his father
narrative_blocks.body: His middle name was Meriwether: through his father, David M. Milton Sr., he descended from Meriwether Lewis, who crossed the continent to the Pacific with William Clark. On his mother's side he was a grandson of Albert Fink, a prominent railroad builder of the later nineteenth century.

narrative_blocks.header: Endocrinology was suspect when he took it up
narrative_blocks.body: Pardee came home from the war to research neurology and endocrinology — the study of the body's internal secretions — at a time when the field was new and widely mistrusted. He ran the endocrine clinic at the Neurological Institute of New York, rose to chief of clinic and taught its postgraduate classes, and a generation of endocrinologists in American hospitals learned the subject from him.

narrative_blocks.header: A society he helped start later elected him
narrative_blocks.body: He was among the organizers of the Association for Research in Nervous and Mental Disease and became its vice president, was elected vice president of the American Neurological Association in 1942, and took the presidency of the New York Neurological Society in 1947. Columbia made him professor of neurology and executive officer of its neurology department.

narrative_blocks.header: His first wife's father helped found Shinnecock
narrative_blocks.body: In 1917 Pardee married Margaret E. Trevor, whose father Henry Graff Trevor was one of the founders of the Shinnecock Hills Golf Club on eastern Long Island. They had three children before the marriage ended in divorce.

narrative_blocks.header: Four Pardees before him had already been doctors
narrative_blocks.body: His father Ensign B. Pardee, his uncle and his grandfather were all physicians, and his great-uncle Charles Inslee Pardee had been dean of the New York Medical College. His brother Harold became a cardiologist and gave his name to Pardee's sign, a wave on the electrocardiogram that marks a damaged heart.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave thirty-two years to one trust company
narrative_blocks.body: Mauze joined the United States Trust Company in New York in 1941 and stayed until 1973, senior vice president for the last twelve years of it. He sat on the boards of the Freeport Sulphur Company and the Brooklyn Savings Bank besides, and ran the finance committee of New York Hospital.

narrative_blocks.header: The Pacific gave him a rank he kept
narrative_blocks.body: He served in the Pacific with the United States Naval Reserve through the Second World War and came out a commander. He held the reserve commission afterward, and the rank travelled with him into Manhattan banking and the University, River and Recess clubs.

narrative_blocks.header: He grew up moving from pulpit to pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: He was a preacher's son: his father, Joseph Layton Mauzé, took the First Presbyterian Church of St. Louis in 1902, the year before Jean was born there, and moved the family on to Huntington and then Kansas City. The father had come up through Augusta Military Academy and Hampden-Sydney to a doctorate at Union Theological Seminary in Richmond.

narrative_blocks.body: She married Irving Pardee in October 1917 and the marriage ended in divorce; he married Abby Rockefeller in 1946 and died three years later. She outlived him by forty-one years and his second wife by fourteen, reaching ninety-six.

narrative_blocks.header: William Brewster's line came down through her
narrative_blocks.body: She descended from William Brewster, the elder who sailed on the Mayflower in 1620 and led the church at Plymouth Colony, and passed that line to her children. Her father, Henry Graff Trevor, was one of the founders of the Shinnecock Hills Golf Club on eastern Long Island; her mother was Margaret Schieffelin.
