narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-two muscles, and where each one hurts
narrative_blocks.body: At a Staten Island tuberculosis hospital in the 1930s she kept meeting patients who complained more of shoulder and arm pain than of their lungs, and found tender spots that threw pain elsewhere in the body. She and Seymour Rinzler mapped the trigger points of thirty-two skeletal muscles and treated them with injected procaine.

narrative_blocks.header: A shoe lift and a rocking chair
narrative_blocks.body: Kennedy came to her on crutches in May 1955, two spinal operations having failed; she injected procaine into his lumbar muscles, found one leg shorter than the other and ordered a quarter-inch heel lift. She put him in a rocking chair too, and photographs of it in the Oval Office sent the maker's production up hundreds of per cent.

narrative_blocks.header: He refused to change doctors when elected
narrative_blocks.body: When Kennedy won in 1960 he would not change doctors, and she became the first woman ever appointed Physician to the President — and the first civilian in the post since Harding, over a military that had staffed it for forty years. She went on treating his father, his brother Robert and his niece Kathleen, and stayed for Lyndon Johnson after the assassination.

narrative_blocks.header: An ambulance surgeon with a lieutenant's rank
narrative_blocks.body: Through her internship at New York Hospital from 1927 she doubled as an ambulance surgeon on the city police force, ranked lieutenant, covering the waterfront, the West Side subway stations and Hell's Kitchen. She called it the most valuable part of her training.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father treated her pain with her method
narrative_blocks.body: Her father Willard Travell spent sixty years relieving pain by physical means, and she joined his West 16th Street offices in the 1930s. When her own shoulder began to hurt, he treated her with the injections she had just worked out.

narrative_blocks.body: A North Carolinian who had come north to Wall Street and played college sport, Powell met Janet Travell at a white-tie ball at the Hotel Astor in February 1927, and they married in June 1929. She said afterward that they had fallen in love on the dance floor that night and danced through life together ever since.

narrative_blocks.header: He moved into his father-in-law's house
narrative_blocks.body: After the wedding Powell moved into 9 West 16th Street with his wife and her widowed father, a brownstone across from the old New York Hospital with the family's medical practice on the ground floor. Their daughters Virginia and Janet were born there in 1933 and 1935.

narrative_blocks.header: He was the one his brothers followed
narrative_blocks.body: Named Nelson Aldrich for his mother's father, he was the second son of six and their leader, closest to Laurance. He and his brothers founded the Rockefeller Brothers Fund in 1940, and he put his divorce to them first in 1961.

narrative_blocks.header: He took Albany from Harriman and held it
narrative_blocks.body: He unseated Averell Harriman in 1958, held the governorship four terms, and served Gerald Ford as vice president. At the 1964 convention he was heckled sixteen minutes and would not leave the podium.

narrative_blocks.header: He asked his father for the UN's ground
narrative_blocks.body: Back from the Inter-American Congress in 1944, he persuaded John D. Rockefeller Jr. to give New York the land the United Nations headquarters stands on.

narrative_blocks.header: Venezuela made him a Latin America man
narrative_blocks.body: Five years with Creole Petroleum in Venezuela from 1935 left him fluent in Spanish and held by the hemisphere for life. Truman fired him from the Inter-American desk, and he kept a farm at Monte Sacro.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother founded the museum he later ran
narrative_blocks.body: His mother was among the founders of the Museum of Modern Art, which he served as trustee, treasurer and president; in 1954 he founded one of his own, the Museum of Primitive Art.

narrative_blocks.header: A divorce and a remarriage ended his run
narrative_blocks.body: Fire took the Governor's Mansion in March 1961, Tod waking him through the bedroom door; they were not seen together again. Five weeks after her divorce he married Happy, and eighteen Gallup points up on Goldwater became five behind.

narrative_blocks.header: His son went missing in New Guinea
narrative_blocks.body: Days after the separation was announced, his son Michael went missing from an expedition in New Guinea, collecting for the Museum of Primitive Art. He was twenty-three and did not come back.

narrative_blocks.header: She gave thirty-seven years to nursing schools
narrative_blocks.body: She began as a volunteer at the Bellevue Schools of Nursing in 1932, sat on the board for decades and served as its president, and stayed until the schools closed in 1969. The New York County Registered Nurses honoured her in 1959, the National League for Nursing in 1971, and Hunter College gave her an honorary doctorate in 1980.

narrative_blocks.header: She wanted a clean apron on the cook
narrative_blocks.body: Campaigning through western New York in 1958 she took a stool at a diner counter, and the cook asked what she would have. 'Well,' she said, 'the first thing I'll have is a clean apron on you, my man.' Asked by a reporter whether she had ever been to Albany, she said no — and had he?

narrative_blocks.header: She was First Lady and hated the spotlight
narrative_blocks.body: When her husband unseated Averell Harriman in 1958 she became First Lady of New York and went with him almost everywhere, while keeping the family's own affairs out of his politics. She held the post three years and never grew used to it.

narrative_blocks.header: Her family had held the ground since Penn
narrative_blocks.body: She was the second of eight children of Percy Hamilton Clark, a Philadelphia lawyer, and grew up at Bala-Cynwyd on land the family had held since it came from William Penn. Her mother's father, George B. Roberts, had been president of the Pennsylvania Railroad.

narrative_blocks.header: She gave up four children to marry him
narrative_blocks.body: She had volunteered in Rockefeller's 1958 campaign while living inside the Pocantico compound with her husband, a microbiologist at the Rockefeller Institute, and their four children. She divorced on 1 April 1963, signing custody of the children to their father, and married Rockefeller four Sundays later at his brother Laurance's cottage.

narrative_blocks.header: A senator denounced her from a school platform
narrative_blocks.body: Prescott Bush told a girls' school commencement that summer that a governor had persuaded a young mother to abandon her husband and four children. A table of Republican women rose and walked out of their own federation ballroom when she came in on Rockefeller's arm; she was thirty-six and he was fifty-five.

narrative_blocks.header: Albany for ten years, then Washington for three
narrative_blocks.body: She was First Lady of New York from 1963 until Rockefeller left Albany in 1973, and Second Lady of the United States while he served as Gerald Ford's vice president from 1974 to 1977. She had two sons with him, the first born during the 1964 California primary.

narrative_blocks.header: Three national parks came out of two families
narrative_blocks.body: As president of Jackson Hole Preserve he handed the federal government, in 1949, the valley land his father had quietly bought around the Tetons. He founded the American Conservation Association in 1958, had a hand in the Virgin Islands park on St. John, and in 1992 gave away his wife's family estate at Woodstock, which became a park in Vermont.

narrative_blocks.header: He called himself a gadgeteer and backed lasers
narrative_blocks.body: From the family office at Rockefeller Center he put risk capital into aviation, aerospace, electronics, lasers, data processing and nuclear power. From 1969 he did it through Venrock, the family's venture group, and ran Rockresorts, his own chain of conservation-minded hotels.

narrative_blocks.header: He and his sister backed the cancer centre
narrative_blocks.body: He joined Memorial Sloan-Kettering in 1947 and chaired it from 1960 to 1982 through a rebuilding of the whole institution, with his sister Babs an advisory trustee and, beside him, among its chief benefactors. The American Cancer Society gave him its Sloan Memorial Award in 1969, the year he also took the Medal of Freedom.

narrative_blocks.header: Philosophy at Princeton, then naval aeronautics
narrative_blocks.body: He took a philosophy degree at Princeton in 1932 and spent two years at Harvard Law without finishing. He served in the Navy's Bureau of Aeronautics from 1942 to 1945 and came out a lieutenant commander.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother married in his cottage at Pocantico
narrative_blocks.body: Of the five brothers Nelson was closest to him and put the divorce to him before anyone else; the remarriage to Happy in 1963 was held at Laurance's own cottage at Pocantico. He was a trustee of Babs's Greenacre Foundation too, and helped her build the park.

narrative_blocks.header: She flew fifty thousand miles for the YWCA
narrative_blocks.body: She joined the YWCA's national board in 1951 and chaired its international division from 1955 to 1973, taking the World Service Council for six of those years. She and Laurance flew more than fifty thousand miles on its business between them, and her mother had done the same work before her.

narrative_blocks.header: She gave away the Vermont estate she inherited
narrative_blocks.body: At forty-one she came into the Woodstock place her mother had from Frederick Billings — a mansion, a dairy farm and the ground around them. In 1992 she and Laurance handed it to the country as a national historical park, and Lady Bird Johnson dedicated the house.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brother had roomed with her husband's brother
narrative_blocks.body: Her older brother John had been Nelson Rockefeller's roommate at Dartmouth, and she met Laurance in 1927. They married at the Congregational church in Woodstock in August 1934 before three hundred guests, with the reception at The Hills above the village.

narrative_blocks.header: Her eldest daughter made a trade of disagreement
narrative_blocks.body: Her eldest, Laura, took degrees from Bryn Mawr, Harvard and Simmons and founded the Public Conversations Project, which put people on opposite sides of abortion and other quarrels in a room together to talk. Three more children followed her — Marion, Lucy and Laurance junior.

narrative_blocks.header: One Arkansan in nine called himself Republican
narrative_blocks.body: About one Arkansan in nine called himself a Republican in 1966, and his segregationist opponent called him a jet-set cowboy and a prissy sissy. He won.

narrative_blocks.header: The only Southern governor to mourn King publicly
narrative_blocks.body: He quietly finished the school integration that had convulsed Little Rock a decade earlier, and left Arkansas with the most integrated draft boards in the country. He was the only Southern governor to hold a public memorial for King.

narrative_blocks.header: He emptied death row on his way out
narrative_blocks.body: A lifelong opponent of capital punishment, he commuted the sentence of every man on Arkansas's death row as his last act in office. No other governor did the same for thirty-three years.

narrative_blocks.header: The party he beat reformed and produced Clinton
narrative_blocks.body: Losing to Dale Bumpers in 1970 was the price of having forced the Arkansas Democrats to reform themselves, and the reformers after Bumpers included Bill Clinton. The boy of twenty-one who unseated one of his legislators became Clinton's aide.

narrative_blocks.header: He enlisted as a private before Pearl Harbor
narrative_blocks.body: He signed on as a private in January 1941, while the country was neutral, and came out a lieutenant colonel of the 77th Infantry after Guam and Leyte. A kamikaze struck his troopship off Okinawa, and he took a Purple Heart and a Bronze Star.

narrative_blocks.header: He came for an army friend and stayed
narrative_blocks.body: He went to Arkansas in 1953 to see a friend from the war, was taken by the country, and bought Petit Jean Mountain. He built Winrock Farms there, and his ashes are buried on it.

narrative_blocks.header: Two brothers were nominated at the same convention
narrative_blocks.body: Nelson governed New York throughout his four years in Arkansas, and at the 1968 convention both their names went into nomination — eighteen Arkansas votes for him, two hundred and seventy-seven for Nelson. No two brothers had been nominated together before.

burial.plot_notes: Rockefeller Family Cemetery, Sleepy Hollow NY; ashes divided, the rest interred at Winrock Farms, Petit Jean, Arkansas

narrative_blocks.header: She was born Jievute Paulekiute at Noblestown
narrative_blocks.body: She was born in the Pennsylvania coal country in 1916, married Richard Sears and was Barbara Sears when she met Winthrop Rockefeller. They married in 1948 and divorced in 1954; their son Winthrop Paul became lieutenant governor of Arkansas.

narrative_blocks.header: Her first husband served at the Paris embassy
narrative_blocks.body: Richard Sears came out of St. Paul's and Harvard, served in the Navy through the war and went into the foreign service as a first secretary at the Paris embassy. He spent his last years painting in France and died at ninety-four.

narrative_blocks.header: She raised a whole state's money for art
narrative_blocks.body: In 1959 she and Winthrop led a fundraising campaign across Arkansas for what became the Arkansas Arts Center, and she was president of its board from 1960 to 1968. She oversaw the building, the opening, and the hiring of its first director.

narrative_blocks.header: She took mental illness onto daytime television
narrative_blocks.body: She was president of both the Arkansas and the National Associations for Mental Health and sat on the White House Commission on Mental Health under Johnson and Nixon. She had started in the late 1940s with teenage drug addicts and mentally ill children in New York.

narrative_blocks.header: She backed the King service at the capitol
narrative_blocks.body: After King was killed in 1968 she was an important backer of the memorial service on the Arkansas State Capitol steps, which drew thousands and took the heat out of a dangerous week. She sat on the national board of the Urban League.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandmother told her to give half
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother died when she was small and she was raised by her Seattle grandmother and namesake, wife of the shipbuilder David Skinner, who told her anyone who could should give half their free time to the community. She married four times, the last at her father's summer house at Hayden Lake in 1956.

narrative_blocks.header: His uncle chaired the bank he joined
narrative_blocks.body: A Chicago doctorate in economics and a year under Friedrich von Hayek stood behind him when he joined Chase National in 1946, where his mother's brother Winthrop Aldrich was chairman. He ran the bank himself through the 1970s and opened its first Moscow branch in 1973.

narrative_blocks.header: His Rolodex needed a room of its own
narrative_blocks.body: He kept a card index of some hundred and fifty thousand people he had met, and it filled a room beside his office. Foreign capitals received him with the honours given a head of state; he sat down with Khrushchev, Zhou Enlai, Sadat, Castro and Gorbachev.

narrative_blocks.header: He talked Carter into admitting the Shah
narrative_blocks.body: In 1979 he and Henry Kissinger persuaded President Carter to let the deposed Shah of Iran in for cancer treatment. Students in Tehran seized the American embassy in reply and held its staff for more than a year.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the minutes at the brothers' meetings
narrative_blocks.body: The five brothers met in Room 5600 above Rockefeller Center to settle what they held in common, and he kept the notes. Winthrop died in 1973, John in 1978, Nelson in 1979 and Laurance in 2004, leaving him sole head of the family.

narrative_blocks.header: He set up intelligence units in North Africa
narrative_blocks.body: He enlisted in 1942 and trained at Fort Ritchie among the linguists and refugees the army used for intelligence. Fluent in French, he built intelligence units in North Africa and France and spent seven months as an assistant attaché in Paris.

narrative_blocks.header: Accused of conspiracy, he pleaded guilty in print
narrative_blocks.body: He was the only one of the family to write an autobiography. In it he took up the charge that he conspired with others to build a more integrated world: if that is the charge, he wrote, I stand guilty, and I am proud of it.

narrative_blocks.header: She founded a trust that holds Maine's coast
narrative_blocks.body: She was sole founder of the Maine Coast Heritage Trust in 1970 and chaired it for years; it has since put some sixty-six thousand acres of Maine into conservation. Ten years later she was among the founders of the American Farmland Trust, and is reckoned its instigator.

narrative_blocks.header: At state dinners, and happier on a tractor
narrative_blocks.body: She began buying cattle in the mid-1970s on Bartlett Island in Maine, then at Pocantico, and in 1980 took four farms in Columbia County where she bred purebred Simmental. She had always loved the country and animals, she said, and read everything she could on farmland preservation until little by little she was trapped.

narrative_blocks.header: Two thousand Hudson acres, protected for good
narrative_blocks.body: In 1992 she and David put almost two thousand acres of their Hudson valley land under permanent protection with the American Farmland Trust and the county conservancy. Eight years after she died, her husband and daughter turned her Pocantico farming ground into a food and agriculture centre in her name.

narrative_blocks.header: Six books of wildflowers began as her idea
narrative_blocks.body: She sat on the board of the New York Botanical Garden and was a trustee of the Philharmonic from 1953 to 1970. The Garden's six books on American wildflowers were her idea and she raised the money for them; the two-acre rose garden it restored in 1988 carries her name.

narrative_blocks.header: Six children, and each took up a cause
narrative_blocks.body: She and David had six children between 1941 and 1952, who went into the family office, ecology, economics, global philanthropy, medicine and philanthropic advice. Abby, the eldest daughter, admired Fidel Castro and helped found the feminist group Cell 16.

narrative_blocks.header: The first spy chief who wasn't a soldier
narrative_blocks.body: Dulles ran the Central Intelligence Agency from 1953 to 1961, its first civilian director and still its longest-serving. He had helped write the 1947 law that created it.

narrative_blocks.header: Two governments fell in two years
narrative_blocks.body: The agency under Dulles put down Mohammad Mossadegh in Iran in 1953 and Jacobo Árbenz in Guatemala the year after. Both men had been elected.

narrative_blocks.header: Kennedy fired him; Johnson recalled him
narrative_blocks.body: The Bay of Pigs cost him the agency in 1961, and he called it the worst day of his life. Two years later Johnson seated him on the commission investigating Kennedy's assassination.

narrative_blocks.header: He was dressed for tennis when Lenin called
narrative_blocks.body: A man telephoned the Bern legation in April 1917 asking to see someone in authority, and Dulles, leaving for a tennis match, put him off. It was Lenin, who left for Russia the next morning.

narrative_blocks.header: The best spy of the war walked in
narrative_blocks.body: A German diplomat named Fritz Kolbe came to him in Bern and handed over more than two thousand documents out of the Foreign Office in Berlin. Dulles called him the best spy of the war.

narrative_blocks.header: He closed the Berlin office anyway
narrative_blocks.body: He came home from Germany in 1935 disturbed by what was being done to German Jews and pushed Sullivan & Cromwell to shut its Berlin office. His brother Foster, the firm's senior partner, objected; it closed.

narrative_blocks.header: His son came back from Korea wounded
narrative_blocks.body: Allen Macy Dulles was permanently disabled by his wounds and spent the rest of his life in and out of medical care. He outlived his father by fifty-one years.

narrative_blocks.header: Farmington first, then France
narrative_blocks.body: She was schooled at Miss Porter's at Farmington and came out into the Junior League. Then she and her sister Lisa went overseas to war work, and did not come home until 1919.

narrative_blocks.header: A seminary founder and a bank president
narrative_blocks.body: Her grandfathers were the Reverend R. K. Todd, who founded the Todd Seminary, and John S. Gilman, who ran the Second National Bank of Baltimore. Her father Henry Alfred Todd taught at Columbia.

narrative_blocks.header: She was married to him for forty-nine years
narrative_blocks.body: They married in 1920, the August after the engagement was announced, and she was widowed in January 1969. His sister Eleanor reckoned he had kept at least a hundred affairs, some of them while he ran the agency.

narrative_blocks.header: Three children, and one came home hurt
narrative_blocks.body: Their daughters were Clover and Joan. Their son Allen was wounded in Korea in his early twenties, and she had him in and out of medical care for the rest of her life.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived him by five years
narrative_blocks.body: Clover Dulles died at Washington in April 1974, having spent the last five years a widow. She was eighty.

narrative_blocks.header: He was a senator for four months
narrative_blocks.body: Dewey appointed him to Wagner's vacant New York seat in July 1949 and he lost the special election that November. It is the only elected office he ever sought.

narrative_blocks.header: The Shah went back on the throne
narrative_blocks.body: Dulles backed the plan to remove Mohammad Mossadegh, Iran's elected prime minister, and restore Mohammad Reza Pahlavi. The agency that carried it out was run by his younger brother.

narrative_blocks.header: Brinkmanship was his own word for it
narrative_blocks.body: He set out the doctrine in Life magazine: the ability to get to the verge without getting into the war is the necessary art. He built NATO, SEATO and ANZUS on the threat behind it.

narrative_blocks.header: He would not shake Zhou Enlai's hand
narrative_blocks.body: At Geneva in 1954 he forbade contact with the Chinese delegation and refused the handshake. He left before the conference could settle Vietnam, and it never did.

narrative_blocks.header: He had the Berlin mail signed Heil Hitler
narrative_blocks.body: As senior partner at Sullivan & Cromwell he required the firm's Berlin office to close its outgoing letters with the Nazi salute. The junior partners, led by his brother, forced him to cut the German business in 1935.

narrative_blocks.header: He opposed the bomb on Christian grounds
narrative_blocks.body: He wrote that if a professedly Christian nation felt free to use atomic energy that way, others would take the verdict, and the stage would be set for the sudden destruction of mankind.

narrative_blocks.header: A cardinal, a Brazilianist and a minister
narrative_blocks.body: John became a historian of Brazil at Texas and Lillias a Presbyterian minister. Avery turned Catholic, entered the Jesuits, and was the first American theologian made a cardinal.

narrative_blocks.body: Janet Avery was a granddaughter of Theodore M. Pomeroy of Auburn, congressman and briefly Speaker of the House of Representatives. She married Dulles at Auburn in June 1912.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived him by ten years
narrative_blocks.body: They were married forty-seven years and had three children. She was widowed in 1959 and died in 1969; they lie together at Arlington.

narrative_blocks.header: His men were first into Knoxville
narrative_blocks.body: He went in as a major of the 25th Indiana in 1861 and fought at Shiloh, then commanded mounted infantry under Ambrose Burnside; his troops were the first into Knoxville after the campaign that took it. He came out a colonel.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight months as Secretary of State
narrative_blocks.body: Harrison made John Secretary of State in June 1892, when Blaine resigned, and he held it eight months. He left in February 1893 to argue the Bering Sea case for the United States before the arbitration tribunal at Paris.

narrative_blocks.header: The Hawaiian treaty Cleveland withdrew
narrative_blocks.body: John quietly encouraged the Americans who deposed Queen Liliʻuokalani in January 1893, with sailors and Marines from the USS Boston ashore in Honolulu, and within weeks signed a treaty to annex her kingdom. Grover Cleveland withdrew it from the Senate on taking office.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the treaty that gave Japan Taiwan
narrative_blocks.body: Out of office he worked for the Chinese government and in 1895 drafted the Treaty of Shimonoseki, which ended the war with Japan, ceded Taiwan and recognised Korea's independence. He had earlier acted for China over the Rock Springs riot, in which twenty-eight Chinese labourers were killed in Wyoming.

narrative_blocks.header: Mexico, Russia and Spain before Washington
narrative_blocks.body: He was minister to Mexico for seven years from 1873, then to Russia, then to Spain, and is reckoned by some the first professional diplomat the country produced. He helped found the American Society of International Law and the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandson came to the honorary degree
narrative_blocks.body: Indiana gave him an honorary doctorate in 1905 and he took his seventeen-year-old grandson John Foster Dulles, then a Princeton freshman. Fifty years later Dulles came back to that university as Secretary of State, to mark the anniversary of his grandfather's graduation.

narrative_blocks.header: She led the DAR for one year only
narrative_blocks.body: She joined the Daughters of the American Revolution in 1891 as a charter member of its Washington chapter and was elected President General in 1895. She served a single year and refused a second so that her predecessor could return; Congress incorporated the society during her term.

narrative_blocks.header: Four states got their first chapters under her
narrative_blocks.body: Colorado, Louisiana, Texas and Washington were organised for the first time in her year, the office of Librarian General was created, and money was voted for the Prison Ship Martyrs Monument at Fort Greene. She pressed the marking of Revolutionary graves and began the society's history essay contest.

narrative_blocks.header: In St Petersburg she translated Russian fiction
narrative_blocks.body: Seven years in Mexico left her fluent and at home there; in Russia she spent part of her time putting Russian fiction into English, and in Spain she moved in the court of Alfonso XII. She came back, one writer said, more of an American than ever.

narrative_blocks.header: Two daughters, and both married the same office
narrative_blocks.body: Three daughters were born and two lived: Edith married the Presbyterian minister Allen Macy Dulles, and Eleanor married Robert Lansing. Lansing held the State Department under Wilson, as her husband had under Harrison and her grandson would under Eisenhower.

narrative_blocks.header: She entered Vienna in Hitler's requisitioned car
narrative_blocks.body: She drove into Vienna on 29 August 1945 in the back of Hitler's requisitioned touring car, in a convoy that also carried Mussolini's bulletproof limousine. She stayed four years as United States financial attaché and helped arrange the reform that took the Reichsmark out of Austria that October.

narrative_blocks.header: She got West Berlin a hall and library
narrative_blocks.body: From the State Department's Berlin desk after 1952 she brought public and private money into the divided city — a congress hall, and a library, a medical school and student housing for the Free University. West Berliners called her the Mother of Berlin; she had no authority to order any of it.

narrative_blocks.header: She took a Harvard doctorate on the franc
narrative_blocks.body: She had gone to France with the Presbyterian church to help war victims in the first war, then read economics at Bryn Mawr and took a Harvard doctorate in 1926 on inflation and the French franc. Roosevelt made her a director of the Social Security Board in 1936, and she was at Bretton Woods in 1944.

narrative_blocks.header: One brother ran State, the other the CIA
narrative_blocks.body: John Foster was Secretary of State and Allen ran the Central Intelligence Agency while she held a middle-level desk officer's post, blocked from more by her sex. She outlived them both, and their families came to her house at McLean for Christmas.

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband died before their son was born
narrative_blocks.body: She married David Blondheim in December 1932 against her family's wishes — a Johns Hopkins philologist of medieval Jewish texts, and an orthodox Jew marrying a Presbyterian minister's daughter. He took his own life fifteen months later, and their son was born after it.

narrative_blocks.header: First American to take the Volney prize
narrative_blocks.body: The Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres gave him its Volney prize in 1926 for a book on the Judeo-Romance dialects and the old Latin bible, and he was the first American to take it. He held the chair of Romance philology at Johns Hopkins and worked on the medieval French glosses in rabbinical texts.

narrative_blocks.header: He never saw the son who was born
narrative_blocks.body: He married Eleanor Dulles in December 1932, against her family's wishes. He killed himself at Baltimore fifteen months later, and their son was born after his death.

narrative_blocks.header: She edited every page Mark Twain published
narrative_blocks.body: Clemens left the day's pages by her bed, and she read them with the girls beside her, folding down the corner of any page she wanted rewritten. Susy and Clara complained that their mother cut the most delectable parts. He said he never wrote a serious word before he married her.

narrative_blocks.header: Mark Twain's copyrights were signed over to her
narrative_blocks.body: The Paige typesetter and his publishing house swallowed the family's money, and Clemens declared bankruptcy in 1894. Olivia was entered as a preferred creditor and his copyrights assigned to her, putting the family's income beyond the other creditors' reach. The Hartford deed was already in her name.

narrative_blocks.header: Helped found Hartford's art society in 1877
narrative_blocks.body: Three years into the Farmington Avenue house she helped found the Hartford Art Society, the drawing school that became the Hartford Art School, later part of the University of Hartford.

narrative_blocks.header: Julia Beecher and Isabella Hooker were her circle
narrative_blocks.body: She grew up in an Elmira house that was religious, reformist and abolitionist, and kept that company in Hartford. Isabella Beecher Hooker, who had known her since she was fourteen, was one of the women's-rights campaigners around her.

narrative_blocks.header: She turned Mark Twain down three times
narrative_blocks.body: Clemens proposed within days of reaching Elmira in August 1868; she refused, and offered to write as brother and sister instead. More than a hundred and eighty letters followed over seventeen months before she accepted him that November. Their first outing had been a Dickens reading.

narrative_blocks.header: Three daughters, and a son lost in infancy
narrative_blocks.body: Langdon, born premature in November 1870, died nineteen months later. Susy came in 1872, Clara in 1874 and Jean in 1880; when Susy died of meningitis at twenty-four, Olivia refused ever to enter the Hartford house again. She died of heart failure outside Florence in 1904, at fifty-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the Elmira pulpit an unbeliever
narrative_blocks.body: Beecher told Mark Twain plainly that he had come from Connecticut in 1854 a decided unbeliever, and had taken the pastorate meaning to compel himself into belief. Within two years, he said, he had managed it.

narrative_blocks.header: The crowds pushed him into the opera house
narrative_blocks.body: His services outgrew the church building, so he moved them to Elmira's opera house and, in fine weather, to Eldridge Park. The congregation voted almost unanimously to build what became Park Church.

narrative_blocks.header: As a chaplain he thought himself useless
narrative_blocks.body: He recruited across upstate New York and went to the field as chaplain of the 141st New York in 1862, writing that as a chaplain he was quite useless. Back in Elmira he was first to preach in the Confederate prison camp.

narrative_blocks.header: He started the library from his shelves
narrative_blocks.body: In 1876 Beecher opened Elmira's first free public library out of his pastor's study, stocking it from his own shelves. The new church was built with a hall for banquets and a room where the children could play.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept the city clock right himself
narrative_blocks.body: Through the 1880s Beecher set Elmira's public clock by taking noon sightings of the sun with his own transit. He rode an outsized tricycle about the town with tools, stopping to help neighbours with repairs.

narrative_blocks.header: He married Olivia's cousin four years later
narrative_blocks.body: Olivia Day died in 1853, two years after their marriage and while she was carrying their child. In 1857 he married her cousin and closest friend Julia Jones, a granddaughter of Noah Webster; they adopted three children and fostered many.

narrative_blocks.header: He was the Beecher who stayed conservative
narrative_blocks.body: Lyman Beecher was his father, Henry Ward Beecher and Harriet Beecher Stowe his half-siblings. Thomas opposed abolition as too radical before the war and rejected the women's rights movement they championed, which cost him his Brooklyn pulpit.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father was president of Yale
narrative_blocks.body: Olivia Day was a daughter of Jeremiah Day, who led Yale College for nearly thirty years, and of Olivia Jones. She married Thomas Beecher in Connecticut in 1851, when he was newly ordained.

narrative_blocks.header: She died carrying their child
narrative_blocks.body: She died at Williamsburg in Brooklyn in August 1853, twenty-six years old and expecting a child, two years into the marriage. Her husband was devastated by it.

narrative_blocks.header: Her cousin married him four years later
narrative_blocks.body: Julia Jones was her cousin and her closest friend. In 1857 Julia married Thomas Beecher and kept the Elmira parsonage for the next forty-three years.

narrative_blocks.header: She married her cousin's widower
narrative_blocks.body: Julia Jones was Olivia Day's cousin and closest friend. Four years after Olivia died she married Thomas Beecher at New Haven, in January 1857, and went with him to Elmira.

narrative_blocks.header: She was the suffragist in the marriage
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband set himself against the women's rights movement that his sister Isabella and his brother Henry Ward supported. Julia stood on the other side of the argument, inside his own house.

narrative_blocks.header: They adopted three and fostered many
narrative_blocks.body: The Beechers had no children of their own. They adopted three and took in many more across their years at Elmira, where she outlived him by five years.

narrative_blocks.header: Noah Webster was her grandfather
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother was Eliza Steele Webster, a daughter of the man whose American dictionary of 1828 settled how the country spelled. Julia was sixteen when he died at New Haven.

notable.notable_blurb: Yale Latin professor and administrator

narrative_blocks.header: Did a dean's work before Yale had deans
narrative_blocks.body: Timothy Dwight V said his influence with the faculty and the corporation equalled or surpassed that of any other officer of the college. He was reckoned one of the best disciplinarians Yale ever had and kept the devotion of the undergraduates anyway. He held the Latin chair from 1851 until his death.

narrative_blocks.header: Named his first son for James Luce Kingsley
narrative_blocks.body: James Kingsley Thacher was born in 1847 and named for the professor of Hebrew, Greek and Latin who had taught his father. When Kingsley died in 1852, Thacher wrote the discourse commemorating him. The son grew up to hold Yale's chair of physiology.

narrative_blocks.header: Taught the Crown Prince of Prussia in Berlin
narrative_blocks.body: A year's leave for study in Germany and Italy, granted in 1843, ran to two. In Berlin he worked under the Latinist Karl Zumpt and instructed the Crown Prince and his cousin Prince Frederick Charles. He was among the first American classicists to go abroad to advance his own scholarship.

narrative_blocks.header: Two wives, and nine children between them
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth Day died in 1858 leaving five sons, the eldest eleven. Two years later he married her cousin Elizabeth Baldwin Sherman, who raised those five and bore four more.

narrative_blocks.header: Two sons founded a New York law firm
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas Thacher, Yale 1871, was a founding partner of Simpson, Thacher and Bartlett, and his brother Alfred Beaumont practised there beside him. A third son, Sherman Day Thacher, went west for his health and built a school in the Ojai Valley instead.

narrative_blocks.header: A Yale president's daughter married a Yale tutor
narrative_blocks.body: She was born in New Haven in 1820 to Jeremiah Day, president of Yale, and Olivia Jones Day. She married Thomas Anthony Thacher at Norwich in 1846, four years into his assistant professorship.

narrative_blocks.header: She died at thirty-seven, leaving five sons
narrative_blocks.body: The boys were eleven, eight, six, four and two in May 1858. James Kingsley Thacher took Yale's chair of physiology, Thomas and Alfred Beaumont founded a New York law firm together, and John Seymour became a doctor. Her sister Livia had died five years before her, at twenty-six.

narrative_blocks.header: She raised five stepsons and bore four more
narrative_blocks.body: She married Thomas Anthony Thacher in 1860, two years after her cousin Elizabeth Day died and left five boys, the eldest eleven and the youngest two. Her own four followed: Sherman Day, William Larned, Elizabeth Baldwin and George.

narrative_blocks.header: She died at ninety-three in her son's valley
narrative_blocks.body: Sherman Day Thacher and his brother William built their school in the Ojai Valley in California, and she died there in 1917, three thousand miles from New Haven. She was carried back to Grove Street and buried beside both her husband and the wife who preceded her.

narrative_blocks.header: She married Providence out of Peace Dale
narrative_blocks.body: Margaret Hazard grew up at the Peace Dale mills and in 1908 married Robert Hale Ives Goddard Jr. of the Providence house of Brown & Ives. She is buried beside him at Swan Point, not with the Hazards in South Kingstown.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-two years with Planned Parenthood
narrative_blocks.body: Sturges worked with Planned Parenthood of Rhode Island from 1965, sat on the national federation's board from 1975 to 1980, and founded its alumni association in 1982. He was still an honorary board member in Rhode Island when he died.

narrative_blocks.header: Both his wives worked the same causes
narrative_blocks.body: Sandol Stoddard started hospital volunteering at eighteen and kept it up most of her life, working the Gallery Canteen in Providence through the war and volunteering for Planned Parenthood of Rhode Island. After she died in 1993 he married Barbara Tate, a nursing dean.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: South Kingstown, RI (1933)

narrative_blocks.header: She brought group therapy to married couples
narrative_blocks.body: Sturges took a master's in social work at Pennsylvania in 1955 and counselled at the Marriage Council of Philadelphia, then spent nineteen years at Family Service in West Chester. There she introduced a group therapy programme for couples.

narrative_blocks.header: She flew a plane and packed through Utah
narrative_blocks.body: In her early adulthood she took several horse pack trips through the slickrock country of Utah, and learned to pilot a plane.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote the poems, he drew the pictures
narrative_blocks.body: She and Robert Anthony published Water Over The Dam, her poems set against his artwork, and she followed it with Waves In The Making, her own poems and pictures together. She wrote two memoirs of her early years as well.

narrative_blocks.header: She took up trees and Modern Greek
narrative_blocks.body: Anthony and her husband Robert were lifelong members of Third Street Friends Meeting at Media, where they raised Hope, Caroline and Steve. She studied trees and Modern Greek in retirement, and lived past a hundred.

bio.bio_blurb: Co-founder of the New England Tap Company

narrative_blocks.header: He co-founded a Massachusetts tap works
narrative_blocks.body: Sturges was a co-founder of the New England Tap Company at Norwood, Massachusetts, which made industrial taps and threading tools. He kept Providence as home all his life and died there in 2001, stricken while walking near his house.

narrative_blocks.header: St. Paul's, Kent, then Yale in 1936
narrative_blocks.body: He went to St. Paul's School at Concord, New Hampshire, and to Kent School in Connecticut before taking his degree at Yale in 1936. John Williams Barclay, who married his sister Alice ten years later, was in the same Yale class.

narrative_blocks.header: He studied piano with Nadia Boulanger in Paris
narrative_blocks.body: Sturges was a prodigy, and went to Paris to work under Nadia Boulanger from 1932 to 1935 and again in 1938. At Harvard he studied with Walter Piston, taking his degree in 1940.

narrative_blocks.header: He debuted at Jordan Hall in 1952
narrative_blocks.body: He gave his first Boston recital at Jordan Hall in 1952 and a second there in 1954. He was a soloist with the Boston Civic Symphony, played chamber music in the Trio de Camera, and gave concerts at the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept two school choirs for eighteen years
narrative_blocks.body: Sturges directed the choir at the Buckingham School from 1950 to 1968 and at Concord Academy from 1960 to 1968. He taught for years on the Longy School faculty, which gave him its distinguished service award in 1988.

narrative_blocks.header: Musician in residence at Bread Loaf
narrative_blocks.body: His flair for lecturing on music took him to Middlebury College as musician in residence at the Bread Loaf Writers' Conference from 1952 to 1955.

narrative_blocks.header: He died twenty-three days after his wife
narrative_blocks.body: The Army posted him to Kansas City in the war, where he met Hedvig von Mayrhauser and married her after a courtship of six weeks. They had sixty-four years together, and he outlived her by twenty-three days.

narrative_blocks.header: Her family's name was on a department store
narrative_blocks.body: John Chess opened a dry goods shop at South Bend in 1832; his son-in-law Frederick Ellsworth took it over in 1871 and put the family name on it. Ellsworth's ran as one of the town's great stores until Wyman's bought it in 1957. Her father and brother carried both names.

narrative_blocks.header: A divorce, then a wedding at thirty-two
narrative_blocks.body: Her first marriage, to Daniel A. Davis, ended in divorce. In May 1946 she married John Pierrepont Sturges of Providence, and moved from Park Avenue to Rhode Island. She outlived him by seven years.

narrative_blocks.header: Four sons, and two of them went west
narrative_blocks.body: Her sons scattered from the Providence world she married into. Jock became a photographer whose work drew an FBI raid and a national argument; Peter left for northern California in 1974 and built a kayaking school on the Salmon River.

narrative_blocks.header: Farmington, Commonwealth Avenue and Manchester
narrative_blocks.body: She grew up between 90 Commonwealth Avenue in Boston and the family's place at Manchester, and was schooled at Miss Porter's in Farmington. Her sisters were Helene and Phyllis; her brother Frederick carried their mother's maiden name.

narrative_blocks.header: Maid of honour at a Treasury wedding
narrative_blocks.body: In March 1931 her sister Phyllis married Clarence Douglas Dillon at Emmanuel Church in Boston, with Alice as maid of honour and their sister Helene as matron. Dillon was then a Harvard senior who managed the football team. He became Secretary of the Treasury under Kennedy and Johnson.

cross_connections.display_label: spent two decades at Dillon Read, her brother-in-law's family firm

narrative_blocks.header: Four countries before she was sixteen
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Kiel in 1923, she grew up in Germany, the Netherlands, Austria and finally Italy, where she went to convent schools. The family emigrated to the United States in 1939 and settled in Kansas City, her mother's home town.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept the books for a refugee bakery
narrative_blocks.body: In 1949 she joined the board of the Window Shop, a Cambridge bakery and gift shop whose profits paid scholarships for refugees, and was its treasurer for many years.

narrative_blocks.header: They named a four-man scull after her
narrative_blocks.body: She became rental agent for the Cambridge Boat Club in 1982 and ran its operations until she retired at eighty, when the members held a ceremony and put her name on a four-man scull. She also handled the finances of the Cambridge Historical Society.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father ran a gyroscope works at Kiel
narrative_blocks.body: Kurt von Mayrhauser trained at the Technical Institute in Munich and became president of the Anschutz Gyroscope Company at Kiel. He came to Kansas City in 1913 to marry Miriam Lyon, retired in 1932 to the family estate in the South Tirol, and brought them all back to Missouri in 1939.

bio.bio_blurb: New Haven lawyer and Navy intelligence officer

narrative_blocks.header: Air combat intelligence on the carrier Hornet
narrative_blocks.body: He joined the Navy in 1941, served first in Washington, and in 1943 was assigned to the Hornet as air combat intelligence officer. He was aboard for every major Pacific engagement the carrier fought, and left the service a lieutenant commander in 1946.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote New Haven a strong-mayor charter
narrative_blocks.body: Barclay was secretary of the thirteen-member commission that drafted the city's strong-mayor charter in 1947. He was assistant corporation counsel from 1950 to 1953, and ran for state senator on the Republican ticket the same year he took that post.

narrative_blocks.header: Three Barclays served one rubber company
narrative_blocks.body: His father sat on the board of the Armstrong Rubber Company from 1931 to 1951 and his brother from 1952 to 1958. Barclay took it up in 1958 as general counsel and director and held it until 1983 — fifty-two unbroken years of Barclays.

narrative_blocks.header: He outlived Alice Sturges by forty-two years
narrative_blocks.body: Alice Knight Sturges of Providence died in 1962, at forty-two. He married twice more, and was buried at Grove Street in the city where he was born.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Fulbrights, in Geneva and above the Arctic
narrative_blocks.body: Her first Fulbright took her to the International Council of Nurses in Geneva in 1977, where she wrote The Nurses' Dilemma on ethics in nursing practice. The second, in 1983, sent her to the University of Tromso in Norway.

narrative_blocks.header: She edited Nursing Research, then deaned at URI
narrative_blocks.body: Tate directed research at the National League for Nursing and edited the journal Nursing Research before becoming dean of the College of Nursing at the University of Rhode Island, a post she left in 1984.

narrative_blocks.header: From hospital ward to doctorate in nineteen years
narrative_blocks.body: She qualified as a nurse at Mountainside Hospital in 1942, took a bachelor's at Elmira College in 1945, a master's at Columbia in 1951, and a doctorate in education there in 1961.

bio.bio_blurb: Art therapist and lifelong peace activist

narrative_blocks.header: He chained himself to a tree in 1989
narrative_blocks.body: Anthony fought the Blue Route expressway through Delaware County for twenty-five years, writing his own briefs and, in 1989, chaining himself to a tree in Smedley Park to stop the clearing. Seventeen acres of wetlands at the Tinicum refuge came out of that fight.

narrative_blocks.header: A conscientious objector who kept getting arrested
narrative_blocks.body: He refused to serve in the Second World War and became a Quaker in the 1940s. He was arrested in the 1950s for refusing to take part in civil defence drills, and again later over Vietnam, the Limerick nuclear plant and the Springfield Mall.

narrative_blocks.header: Drawing, he said, was acceptably antisocial
narrative_blocks.body: Anthony took a master of fine arts at the Pennsylvania Academy in 1951 and worked as an art therapist at the Devereux School and Eugenia Hospital until the late 1970s. Sketching, he told his family, was a socially acceptable way of being antisocial.

education.school_name: Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts

bio.bio_blurb: Bay Area ceramic sculptor and painter

narrative_blocks.header: She works clay the way others use paint
narrative_blocks.body: Steinman treats cracking, breaking, drooping and eroding as an impressionist treats brushstrokes, letting the clay's own behaviour accumulate into a figure. She says she is less interested in subject than in being led by the material.

narrative_blocks.header: She went to Warhol's Factory in the sixties
narrative_blocks.body: Trained on the east coast during the Pop Art years, Steinman visited Andy Warhol's Factory and made hard-edge pop paintings before she moved to California and took up clay.

narrative_blocks.header: Manuel Neri said the figures stood up
narrative_blocks.body: Her work follows the late east bay sculptor Stephen De Staebler. Manuel Neri was overheard saying it looked as though De Staebler's figures had got up and stood on their own.

narrative_blocks.header: Her animal jars answer Egyptian canopic ones
narrative_blocks.body: Steinman studied at the San Francisco Art Institute, exhibited alongside William Wiley and showed in New York. Her animal vessels take Egyptian canopic jars as their model, each abstract body topped with a specific creature's head.

ran her own studio too, working sculpture and painting together

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote a book about the League
narrative_blocks.body: Cashin's Sustaining the League of Women Voters in America argues that American civic associations have thinned out, and that the League — durable, nonpartisan and rooted in local chapters — is the model worth saving. She makes the case for giving such bodies a public boost.

narrative_blocks.header: She married at a New Mexico mission church
narrative_blocks.body: Maria Louisa Hoyt married Stephen Douglas Cashin in August 1986 at Holy Trinity in Arroyo Seco, New Mexico, with her sister Emily as maid of honour. She had taken her master's in public administration at New York University that June.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father taught international law at New Mexico
narrative_blocks.body: Edwin Chase Hoyt was professor emeritus of international law and American foreign policy at the University of New Mexico. Her mother, Mary Pierrepont Hazard of Providence, had followed him out to Albuquerque in 1959.

education.school_name: Albert Einstein College of Medicine, Yeshiva University

narrative_blocks.header: He has practised psychiatry in San Francisco
narrative_blocks.body: Ira Steinman took his medical degree at the Albert Einstein College of Medicine of Yeshiva University and has practised psychiatry in San Francisco for more than twenty years. He and Alice live at Mill Valley.

notable.notable_blurb: Photographer

narrative_blocks.header: He shoots families on an eight-by-ten camera
narrative_blocks.body: Sturges works chiefly with a large eight-by-ten view camera, photographing families and adolescents at naturist beaches in northern California and at Montalivet on the French Atlantic coast. He has returned to the same subjects for decades, following them from childhood into adulthood.

narrative_blocks.header: Four years a Navy Russian linguist
narrative_blocks.body: He served in the United States Navy from 1966 to 1970 as a Russian linguist, and taught photography at a services facility in Yokohama. He took a degree in perceptual psychology and photography at Marlboro College and a master's at the San Francisco Art Institute.

narrative_blocks.header: He worked seven years in Rhode Island
narrative_blocks.body: Before California he spent 1972 to 1978 in his family's home state — a commercial and marine photographer at Newport, then a printer working the negatives of Strand, Atget, Evans and Winogrand, then teaching at a Providence gallery.

narrative_blocks.header: A raid, a grand jury, a guilty plea
narrative_blocks.body: Agents raided his San Francisco studio in 1990 and seized his equipment; a grand jury declined to indict him, and later attempts to have two of his books classed as child pornography failed in Arkansas and Louisiana. In 2021 he pleaded guilty in Massachusetts to an unnatural and lascivious act with a child under sixteen, committed in the mid-1970s while he was a dorm head at the Northfield Mount Hermon School, and was sentenced to three years' probation.

bio.bio_blurb: Founder of the Otter Bar kayak school

narrative_blocks.header: He parked by the Salmon in 1974
narrative_blocks.body: Sturges squandered a small inheritance sailing in the Caribbean, fished a season with the Alaskan salmon fleet, and was driving a home-built camper through Mexico in 1972. Friends wrote in 1974 that they had found paradise in the mountains below Oregon; he stopped to look and never left.

narrative_blocks.header: Border guards planted a bag in his truck
narrative_blocks.body: He had grown his hair long as an experiment to see how he would be treated, and found out at the Mexican border in 1972 when guards shook him down and planted marijuana in the truck. He protested loudly enough that they sent him on. It made a socialist of him for a while.

narrative_blocks.header: A Karok elder taught him how to think
narrative_blocks.body: Living as a squatter off his camper, Sturges took a seventy-year-old Karok man, Johnny Bennett, as his mentor. Before that, he said, he had felt that if he touched something he would break it.

narrative_blocks.header: A Dufy paid the deposit on forty acres
narrative_blocks.body: Seasons with the Alaskan salmon fleet and the sale of a Raoul Dufy painting left him by a great-uncle produced the down payment on Jecker's forty acres, nearly a mile of Salmon River frontage. He cleared the old dump with a second-hand backhoe and built Otter Bar on it.

narrative_blocks.header: He met his wife at a two-room school
narrative_blocks.body: Kristy had dropped out and was teaching at the local two-room elementary school when they met in 1979. They built the lodge together and ran the kayak school for forty years.

narrative_blocks.header: A rapid is named for his torn tendon
narrative_blocks.body: Achilles Heel on the Salmon River was renamed after Sturges pitoned in the boulders at its entrance in the early 1980s and slid his heel under the footbrace, tearing his Achilles tendon. His paddling partner that day owned the company that made the footbrace.

narrative_blocks.header: Junior world freestyle champion at eighteen
narrative_blocks.body: Sturges won the junior world championship of freestyle kayaking at Graz in 2003 and went on to represent the United States at three more world championships. He is credited with inventing the Pistol Flip and the Hail Mary, a front flip off a waterfall.

narrative_blocks.header: First down the biggest rapids on earth
narrative_blocks.body: In 2011 he ran the Grand Inga rapids of the Congo with Steve Fisher, Tyler Bradt and Benny Marr, the first team to do it; seven people had died trying. He came home with malaria and a flesh-eating infection in his elbow.

narrative_blocks.header: His film about a dying river runner
narrative_blocks.body: Sturges founded River Roots in 2009 and has directed more than twenty documentaries. The River Runner, on Scott Lindgren's twenty-year attempt at the four rivers of Mount Kailash, took Banff's best mountain-sports film in 2021 and went to Netflix.

narrative_blocks.header: He calls his own music folk hop
narrative_blocks.body: Sturges records a mix of hip hop and folk-inflected rock on his own River Roots label, three albums so far. The songs draw on the mountains he grew up in, the friends he has lost on rivers, and the sport itself.

narrative_blocks.header: He brought a friend back in Veracruz
narrative_blocks.body: Filming on the Rio Tulija in Veracruz, Sturges helped rescue and resuscitate his teammate Gerd Serrasolses after a kayaking accident. The episode was later told in Jimmy Chin's Edge of the Unknown series.

narrative_blocks.header: He was in a boat at ten
narrative_blocks.body: Sturges grew up at Forks of Salmon, where his parents ran the Otter Bar kayaking school on the river outside the door. He was in a boat at ten and competing at thirteen.

bio.bio_blurb: Professor of American literature at Orono

narrative_blocks.body: Brogunier taught English at the University of Maine at Orono for thirty-six years and edited Paideuma, the Pound journal the National Poetry Foundation published there. Melville and Faulkner stayed his favourites.

narrative_blocks.header: A scholarship out of Hagerstown to Brown
narrative_blocks.body: He grew up in hardship at Hagerstown, Maryland, and won a scholarship to Brown, where he met Hope. His doctorate in modern American literature came from Minnesota in 1969.

narrative_blocks.header: Amnesty International, and a motorcycle commute
narrative_blocks.body: He belonged to Amnesty International all his life. He took his children backpacking and star-gazing, listened to the Rolling Stones, watched W.C. Fields, and rode a motorcycle to work.

narrative_blocks.body: He travelled to El Salvador in 1994 with his cousin Eli to observe the first election after the civil war; he was twenty-two. At home he gave years to the Peace and Justice Center in Bangor.

narrative_blocks.header: The cartoon that came before Homer Simpson
narrative_blocks.body: As a boy Brogunier and his Leighton Street friend Paul Tomlinson drew Jorgai Hoona, a cigar-smoking caricature his family reckoned the true forerunner of Homer Simpson. The drawing came early, and so did the imagination behind it.

narrative_blocks.header: Weights at the YMCA, then a skateboard
narrative_blocks.body: He spent his early teens tall and thin until he found Joe Weider's bodybuilding course and the weight room of the Hammond Street YMCA. Skateboarding followed, and a photo spread of his own, Skaters of the North East.

narrative_blocks.header: History and philosophy, and then a rig
narrative_blocks.body: Brogunier left Bangor High in 1990 and took a double degree in history and philosophy at Orono. He then drove over the road out of Columbus, Georgia, and lived by turns in Louisville, Portland and Minneapolis.

narrative_blocks.header: An impossible choice between clarity and care
narrative_blocks.body: A painful mental illness took hold in his last years, and the drugs that answered it cost him the intellectual clarity he prized above everything. He died at Bangor on 21 December 2008, at thirty-seven.

bio.bio_blurb: Brown & Ives partner and Goddard Park donor

narrative_blocks.header: He and his sister gave the estate away
narrative_blocks.body: In 1927 Goddard and his sister Madeleine, the Marquise d'Andigné, deeded their father's estate at Potowomut to Rhode Island. The terms bar admission fees, motor racing and political meetings on it for ever.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept the family in Brown & Ives
narrative_blocks.body: Goddard worked in Brown & Ives, the Providence investment house his great-grandfather Thomas Poynton Ives had founded with Nicholas Brown. He married Margaret Hazard of Peace Dale in 1908.

notable.notable_blurb: Burnside aide, Lonsdale mill president, and anti-corruption senator

narrative_blocks.header: He rode as Burnside's aide through the war
narrative_blocks.body: Goddard enlisted as a private in the First Rhode Island in April 1861, and came back in 1862 as aide-de-camp to General Ambrose Burnside. He was at Fredericksburg, Knoxville and Petersburg, and present when Lee surrendered.

narrative_blocks.header: Two brevets, for Knoxville and Fort Sedgwick
narrative_blocks.body: He was brevetted major for gallantry in the East Tennessee campaign and at the siege of Knoxville, and lieutenant colonel for Fort Stedman and the assault before Fort Sedgwick in Virginia. He resigned his commission in July 1865.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the Lonsdale mills and a railroad
narrative_blocks.body: Goddard was president of Goddard Brothers, the textile firm known as the Goddard Mills at Lonsdale, a long-serving director of the Rhode Island Hospital Trust, and held a controlling interest in the Providence and Worcester Railroad.

narrative_blocks.header: He led an anti-corruption party against Brayton
narrative_blocks.body: Goddard sat in the Rhode Island senate from 1907 as an independent, and led the Lincoln Party, a short-lived movement against the Republican boss Charles R. Brayton. He ran for the United States Senate that year and lost.

narrative_blocks.header: His children gave the estate to the state
narrative_blocks.body: Goddard planted thousands of pines, firs and spruce at The Oaks, his Potowomut estate. Eleven years after his death his son and daughter handed it to Rhode Island, on condition it stay forested and charge nobody admission.

narrative_blocks.header: He could have paid a substitute
narrative_blocks.body: Goddard enlisted as a private in April 1861 and fought at the first Bull Run before he was mustered out that August. Men of his standing routinely hired substitutes rather than serve. He volunteered again a year later.

narrative_blocks.header: The war he fought wrecked his own trade
narrative_blocks.body: His family's Lonsdale mills ran on Southern cotton, and the war he volunteered for destroyed that supply. He served four years against it anyway and came home to run the company.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty-nine years at one college
narrative_blocks.body: Day entered Yale in 1789 and was president from 1817 to 1846. He resigned at seventy-three, was at once elected to the corporation, and served on it until a month before he died.

narrative_blocks.header: He went to Bermuda expecting to die
narrative_blocks.body: Tuberculosis had followed him for years, and in 1801 a hemorrhage brought on by preaching sent him to Bermuda for nearly a year. He came home to his father's house with no expectation of recovery, and lived another sixty-six years.

narrative_blocks.header: He argued with a university, not a man
narrative_blocks.body: The Yale Report of 1828, written with Benjamin Silliman and James Kingsley, answered the non-classical course Jefferson had opened at the University of Virginia — though Jefferson had been dead two years by then. It held the old curriculum at Yale for another half century.

narrative_blocks.header: Outside Connecticut he was known for algebra
narrative_blocks.body: An Introduction to Algebra came out in 1814 and ran through many editions, followed by books on trigonometry, navigation and surveying. Beyond New Haven his name travelled on the textbooks rather than the presidency.

narrative_blocks.header: He outlived every one of those children
narrative_blocks.body: Mary died at six, an infant Jeremiah before her, Martha at twenty, Henry at twenty-three, Olivia at twenty-six and Elizabeth at thirty-eight. Their father lived to ninety-four.

narrative_blocks.header: He married twice and outlived both wives
narrative_blocks.body: Martha Sherman died in 1806, the year their son Sherman was born. Five years later Day married Olivia Jones at New Haven, and outlived her by seventeen years.

narrative_blocks.header: He followed Dwight twice, twenty years apart
narrative_blocks.body: Day took over the Greenfield Hill academy from Timothy Dwight in 1795, the year Dwight left it for the Yale presidency. Twenty-two years later he followed him into that office as well.

narrative_blocks.body: He owned and edited a newspaper at Brighton and later another at Lowell, running them for several years each. He gave up the press for real estate, first at Detroit and then at Buffalo, where the family was still living in 1923.

narrative_blocks.header: He farmed the place his parents bought
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Brighton in 1879 and farmed the old Lee homestead his parents had taken over the year before. He married Nellie May Lyon in 1903; their first child, Bernard, was born and died on the same March day in 1905.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father kept the hostelry at Wauconda
narrative_blocks.body: She grew up at Wauconda in Illinois, where her father ran an early-day hostelry, and was well known in the Barrington and Wauconda set before the turn of the century.

narrative_blocks.header: She brought a daughter to the marriage
narrative_blocks.body: Two children were born of her first marriage, to Charles Hendricks. Her daughter Olive Elizabeth, born in 1889, was adopted by Homer Drake after their marriage in 1896 and later married Nat Borquest.

cross_connections.display_label: , his second cousin once removed, mined at Premier in British Columbia

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-five days in the advanced line
narrative_blocks.body: Commissioned at Fort Sheridan and in England by January 1918, he was detailed to instruct troops in bomb throwing and spent forty-five days at the front before the Armistice. In one engagement he was the only officer left in the company; he came home in the summer without a wound.

narrative_blocks.header: Railroad office, then the College of Mines
narrative_blocks.body: He worked three years in a railroad office and then for a mining company before taking the course at the Michigan College of Mines, graduating in 1915. He spent the rest of his working life as a mining engineer for Cleveland Cliffs in the northern Michigan iron country.

narrative_blocks.header: He was expert before he reached dental college
narrative_blocks.body: He began helping his father in the surgery as a small boy and was expert in operative work by the time he entered the dental college at Ann Arbor. He took his degree in 1916 and went straight back to Marquette to practise in partnership with his father.

narrative_blocks.header: He left the family practice for oral surgery
narrative_blocks.body: He returned to Ann Arbor in 1919 for a post-graduate course and took a position at Cleveland in 1921 doing special work in oral surgery. He had enlisted in the Dental Reserves and served at one of the southern camps during the war.

cross_connections.display_label: , his first cousin, was at Varennes in the Argonne in October 1918

narrative_blocks.header: He carried despatches on the Rhine bridgehead
narrative_blocks.body: He had joined the National Guard shortly before it was sent to the Texas border, and asked to be transferred to Headquarters Company of the 107th Engineers, 32nd Division. He stayed with the Army of Occupation guarding the bridgehead on the east bank of the Rhine, carrying despatches.

narrative_blocks.header: He drew for a Kalamazoo architectural office
narrative_blocks.body: He worked as an architectural draftsman in the office of Billingham and Cobb at Kalamazoo, and went back to it when the war was over. He married Hazel Simmons of Scott's, Michigan, in December 1919.

narrative_blocks.header: She taught the kindergarten in her home town
narrative_blocks.body: She graduated from both the high school and the State Normal School at Marquette and taught kindergarten in the town where she was born. She was active in church work and in the Marquette chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution.

narrative_blocks.header: His father took a chemistry degree in 1900
narrative_blocks.body: He was the youngest of the four children of Edwin Wilson Oldham of Akron, who graduated from the Case School of Applied Science in 1900 with an engineering degree in chemistry and belonged to the American Chemical Society. The family moved from Canton to Akron when he was three.

narrative_blocks.header: She nursed at La Panne in 1914
narrative_blocks.body: Her 1914 passport application has her working for Dr. L. M. Moody in the hospital at La Panne, on the strip of Belgium the Germans never took. She had been widowed the year before, her second husband dying at Paris, and married Colonel Drake there in September 1918.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brother was Dallas's hot dog mayor
narrative_blocks.body: She was born in Colorado County, Texas, to Phocian Tate and Bettie Branch Carter, and lost her father young. Her brother John Waddy Tate served as mayor of Dallas from 1929 to 1931 and was known across the Southwest as the hot dog mayor.

cross_connections.display_label: , his first cousin, went to the Detroit Edison company

narrative_blocks.header: The Armistice caught him on the train
narrative_blocks.body: He finished at Crane Junior College in 1918, entered the Students' Army Training Corps at Northwestern and was chosen for the officers' camp at Fortress Monroe. He was on the train going there when the news of the Armistice came.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran electric light plants three states over
narrative_blocks.body: He finished his engineering course at Michigan and went into electric light plants, managing them in Ohio and Oklahoma before a transfer to Cairo, Illinois. He died in California at ninety-three.

narrative_blocks.header: Northwestern in 1922, then an artist wife
narrative_blocks.body: He came out of Winnetka High School and took a bachelor of science and an electrical engineering degree at Northwestern in 1922. In September 1924 he married Pauline Graf, an artist of Chicago.

narrative_blocks.header: She took the public school music course
narrative_blocks.body: She followed her brother through Winnetka High School and Northwestern, graduating in 1923 and taking the public school music course the year after. She played both piano and violin well, her mother having supervised the lessons herself.

narrative_blocks.header: The Oberlin strike over three cents an hour
narrative_blocks.body: She made the journey to Ohio in August 1843, to the one college that would take a woman, where Lucy Chadwick of Farmington was a year ahead of her. Paid three cents an hour for housework, half the men's rate, she resigned her teaching post in 1845 and demanded equal pay; the faculty gave way in three months.

narrative_blocks.header: She turned down the commencement essay
narrative_blocks.body: Chosen in 1847 to write one, she refused, because a faculty member and not she would have read it out to the hall. She took her degree that August, the first woman from Massachusetts to hold one.

narrative_blocks.header: A letter to the women meeting at Salem
narrative_blocks.body: Ohio's first women's rights convention sat at Salem in April 1850 under Betsey Mix Cowles. Massachusetts ought to have taken the lead and had not, Stone wrote to them; let her young sisters of the West set the example.

narrative_blocks.header: A city auctioned her furniture over a tax
narrative_blocks.body: She sent back the Orange tax bill unpaid: taxing a woman who could not vote broke the principle the country was built on. The city sold her goods that January, and the neighbours bought them and carried them home again, the baby's cradle among them.

narrative_blocks.header: She would not add Blackwell to her name
narrative_blocks.body: She married Henry Blackwell in 1855 and went on signing herself Lucy Stone, which is why women who kept their names were called Lucy Stoners. Registering for Boston's school-board vote in 1879, she was told to add Blackwell, and did not vote.

narrative_blocks.header: Letters to Isabella Hooker across the split
narrative_blocks.body: The movement broke in two in 1869, her American association against the rival National, and she and Isabella Beecher Hooker, who founded Connecticut's society that year, kept writing across the gap. Her last instruction, to her daughter Alice, was to make the world better.

cross_connections.display_label: called the convention that fused the Republican Party from his rooms
helped found Connecticut's Republican Party in the same years

narrative_blocks.header: In at the founding of the Republican Party
narrative_blocks.body: He came into the new party in its Cincinnati days, out of a literary club whose members included Salmon Chase and Rutherford Hayes. From 1858 he told audiences that giving women the vote was expedient for any party, whatever its principles.

narrative_blocks.header: The protest he read at his wedding
narrative_blocks.body: The paper he read out in 1855 renounced every legal advantage a husband held — his wife's person, the children, her earnings — and pledged that he would never use one of them. Other couples began reading it at their own weddings.

narrative_blocks.header: He grew beets to undercut Cuban sugar
narrative_blocks.body: His father had refined cane at Bristol and hated where the cane came from, experimenting with beets instead. The son patented a refining method and opened the Maine Sugar Beet Company in 1878, telegraphing home that slavery in Cuba was doomed.

narrative_blocks.header: He put the first thousand into the Journal
narrative_blocks.body: He gave the money that started the Woman's Journal in 1870, stayed its largest shareholder, edited it beside his wife from 1872 and alone for sixteen years after she died. It ran forty-seven years, and he never drew a salary from it.

narrative_blocks.header: Eleven states let women vote for president
narrative_blocks.body: He argued that a legislature could hand women the municipal and presidential vote by statute, without waiting on a constitutional amendment, and made that the American association's working strategy. Eleven states had presidential suffrage before the federal amendment passed.

narrative_blocks.header: Berea gave her a party at the Armory
narrative_blocks.body: When she turned a hundred the town of Berea gave her a public celebration at the Armory. She was born in Massachusetts in October 1792, a daughter of Joseph Brewer and Elizabeth Ingersoll of Tyringham, and died at Berea in 1893 in her hundred and first year.

narrative_blocks.header: Married a cousin, widowed for twenty years
narrative_blocks.body: She married Theodore Sedgwick Ingersoll in June 1812; the genealogy calls him her cousin, through her Ingersoll mother. She went west with him to Oberlin in 1833, bore seven children, and was carried back to the family plot there after him.

narrative_blocks.header: The first girl to live at Oberlin
narrative_blocks.body: She came out to the new colony with her father in 1833, at eighteen, and the Ingersoll genealogy records her as the first white girl to reside in Oberlin. She studied at the college, joined the Congregational church, and lived her last forty years at Berea.

narrative_blocks.header: He pulled teeth and wrote about it
narrative_blocks.body: Born on the Fourth of July in Massachusetts, he practised at Monroe, Michigan as a dental surgeon and wrote for the dental journals of his day. His boy Ernest spent his afternoons hunting the woods and fields around the town for curious specimens, and never stopped.

narrative_blocks.header: Three cousins took up the same trade
narrative_blocks.body: His first cousin Sarah Chadwick married a Drake, and three of her sons went into dentistry in the 1880s — Homer at Marquette and then Chicago, Elmer at Marquette, Rollin at Negaunee and later Ann Arbor. Sally Ingersoll Chadwick was grandmother to all three and aunt to him.

narrative_blocks.header: First scientists into the Mesa Verde canyons
narrative_blocks.body: As zoologist on the 1874 Hayden survey he rode with the photographer William Henry Jackson, and the two became the first trained scientists to describe the Mesa Verde cliff dwellings. His dispatches carried it east.

narrative_blocks.header: Agassiz died, and made him a journalist
narrative_blocks.body: He kept the college museum at Oberlin, then studied under Agassiz at Harvard. When Agassiz died in 1873 his sketch of the teacher went to the New York Tribune, which ran it and hired him.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-two months on the oyster coast
narrative_blocks.body: From 1879 he walked the shore from the Maritimes to Texas for the Fish Commission, interviewing tongers, planters and market men. His two monographs are the only full record of American shellfishing before 1900.

narrative_blocks.header: Roosevelt held him up against the fakers
narrative_blocks.body: Theodore Roosevelt, attacking the nature-fakers who embroidered the habits of wild animals, named him the writer whose accuracy was exemplary. They became friends, and in 1907 the President put him at the head of the Oyster Commission.

narrative_blocks.header: In the room when the Explorers Club began
narrative_blocks.body: A journalist called explorers together in New York in 1904 to bind them and press the work of exploration by every means in its power, and the club incorporated the next year. He was in at the start, served years as its secretary, and edited The Explorers Journal.

narrative_blocks.header: The notebook beat the box of dead birds
narrative_blocks.body: Lecturing to nature clubs about 1888, he told them a well-filled notebook was worth more than boxes of specimens, and a photograph more than a stuffed animal. Every person, he said, was a trustee of nature.

narrative_blocks.header: Half a million readers a week, for decades
narrative_blocks.body: From 1900 his weekly column in a Montreal paper reached half a million readers across Canada and the Caribbean. No guide to western birds existed, so he described nearly every Canadian bird himself; his daughter Helen drew the snakes.
