people.research_notes: Sources: Wikipedia; Clyde L. MacKenzie Jr., 'Biographic Memoir of Ernest Ingersoll', Marine Fisheries Review 53(3), 1991 (Sam, 7 Sep 2026). b. 13 Mar 1852 Monroe MI; d. 13 Nov 1946 in a Brattleboro VT nursing home after a four-year illness, aged 94; buried Caroline Church, Setauket NY. Oberlin 1867-1871 (curator of the college museum); Harvard Museum of Comparative Zoology student assistant, fall 1872 - spring 1874; summer 1873 with Agassiz at the Penikese Island seaside school. Hayden Survey zoologist 1874 (Photographic Division under William Henry Jackson); Mesa Verde. New York Tribune staff 1874. Forest and Stream natural history editor 1875-1877; second western trip 1877; Science News editorial staff 1878-79. Fish Commission / Census shellfishery agent 1 Oct 1879 - 1 Jul 1881. Manhattan Magazine editor 1883-84; Canadian Pacific guidebooks (called the first railroad press agent); lived Montreal 1887-88, New York from 1900. Rand McNally guidebooks 1890s-1905. Founder and first secretary, Linnaean Society of New York, 1878; elected fellow 1928. Authors Club secretary 1920-25; Barnard Club; Salmagundi Club 1916-37. Present at the founding of the Explorers Club 1905; director and secretary many years; editor of The Explorers Journal 1926-1931. Roosevelt named him an exemplar against the 'nature-fakers', lunched him at the White House, and appointed him head of the Oyster Commission 1907 (duties and length of service unrecorded). CHILDREN: Helen (b. 1874), who illustrated his books and part-wrote his 12-article series on eastern Canadian snakes, and Geoffrey (b. 1889); Helen was his only surviving child. NOT BUILT - each has a birth year and nothing else; awaiting Sam. CONFLICT: Wikipedia gives the wife as Mary Schofield (1853-1920); FindAGrave gives Mary Scofield Ingersoll, d. 24 Jan 1921. FindAGrave followed here. | The Explorers Club: called together in New York in 1904 at the request of the journalist Henry Collins Walsh, 'to unite explorers in the bonds of good fellowship and to promote the work of exploration by every means in its power'; incorporated 25 Oct 1905. Ingersoll is NOT on the published charter-member list (Brainard, Chapman, Cook, Parker, Saville, Walsh, Whitney, Dellenbaugh, Furness); the MacKenzie memoir says only that he 'was present at the founding' and was thereafter a director, secretary, and editor of The Explorers Journal 1926-1931. The Journal itself began Nov 1921. The club bought 46 East 70th Street - Stephen C. Clark's house - in 1965, nineteen years after Ingersoll died. Married three times: Mary Scofield (1873-1921), Frances Buchanan (1923-1929), Vera Edmondson (from 1930); all three children were Mary's. The New York Times wedding notices 24 Aug 1923 (Frances Buchanan, in her Carnegie Hall studio) and 17 Nov 1930 (Vera Edmondson Nelson, at the Marble Collegiate Church); the 1930 notice gives his age as seventy-eight and the couple's address as 88 Morningside Drive.

FindAGrave (Sam, 7 Sep 2026): b. 29 Dec 1853 Danbury, Fairfield County CT; d. 24 Jan 1921 aged 67; buried Caroline Church, Setauket NY; m. 1873 Ernest Ingersoll. CONFLICT: Wikipedia spells the name Schofield and dates her 1853-1920.

narrative_blocks.header: Four states in one life, always west
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Ogden in western New York in 1819, in the years his parents were moving the family from the Berkshires toward Ohio. His children were born at Sandusky, at Elyria and at Oberlin, and he died at Englewood on the south side of Chicago in 1887.

NOTE: his birth at Ogden NY places the family in western New York between Timothy's 1817 birth in Massachusetts and Theodore's 1833 arrival at Oberlin.

narrative_blocks.header: He was a broker and dealer in baskets
narrative_blocks.body: He left the Ohio colony for Jersey City and made his trade as a broker and dealer in baskets. He married Mary J. Frost of West Stockbridge, back in the Berkshires his father had come from, in August 1852; they had no children, and she died seven months before he did.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-eight years, then two years alone
narrative_blocks.body: He married Maria Porter at Olean in western New York in April 1850 and she died at Keokuk, Iowa in April 1888, after thirty-eight years. He waited two years and married Minnie Marsh Banks at Keokuk in June 1890, when he was sixty-six and she thirty-six.

narrative_blocks.header: Born at Ogden, dead on the Mississippi
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Ogden in Monroe County, New York in September 1823, one of three of Theodore Sedgwick Ingersoll's sons born there before the family went west to Oberlin. He died at Keokuk on the Iowa bank of the Mississippi in May 1897, at seventy-three.

narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Clyde in Wayne County, New York on 23 June 1842 and died on 23 June 1876, the same day of the year, at thirty-four. He left Caroline with two daughters, the younger not yet two.

narrative_blocks.header: Born at Oberlin, widowed in Los Angeles
narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Oberlin in 1852, in the colony her grandfather Theodore had helped settle, and married John Duffy Parle of New Brunswick in February 1874. He died at Los Angeles in July 1895; she was forty-two, and their youngest, Irene, was one.

narrative_blocks.header: Two of her five children died in 1918
narrative_blocks.body: LeRoy was forty and Alice thirty-five when both died in 1918, twenty-three years after their father. Their mother outlived them by eighteen years and died in 1936, at eighty-four.

narrative_blocks.header: Chicago, Iowa, Nebraska, then California
narrative_blocks.body: All five of her children were born along the way west — Edith at Chicago in 1875, LeRoy in Guthrie County, Iowa in 1878, then Alice, Edwin and Irene at Loup City in the Nebraska sandhills in 1883, 1886 and 1894. Her mother, Mary Kanady, died in Nebraska in 1895, the year John Duffy Parle died at Los Angeles.

narrative_blocks.header: A New Brunswick man dead at forty-five
narrative_blocks.body: He was born in New Brunswick in 1849 and married Ida Camelia Ingersoll, of the Oberlin family, in February 1874. He died at Los Angeles on the first of July 1895, at forty-five, with five children behind him, the youngest a year old.

narrative_blocks.header: Loup City to Los Angeles in a year
narrative_blocks.body: His youngest, Irene, was born at Loup City in Sherman County, Nebraska on 30 July 1894. He died at Los Angeles on 1 July 1895, so the family crossed from the Nebraska sandhills to southern California inside those twelve months.

narrative_blocks.body: He married Marion Seay of Hickman, Kentucky in March 1911, and their only child, Alice Warren, was born at Los Angeles in April 1916. He was dead before she was three; Marion outlived him by forty-one years and died at Los Angeles in 1960.

narrative_blocks.body: He married Erma Louise Simms of Lewistown, Illinois in January 1908, three weeks short of his twenty-second birthday. They had John Edwin and Winifred Louise; she outlived him by twenty-nine years and died at Newport Beach in 1980.

narrative_blocks.header: Born at Oberlin, buried out of Omaha
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Oberlin in February 1858, the last of William Brewer Ingersoll's four children and the only one born in the town his grandfather had helped settle. He married Gertrude Amanda Snyder in August 1881 and died at Omaha in 1931, at seventy-three.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Ingersoll households at Loup City
narrative_blocks.body: Three of his children were born at Loup City in Sherman County, Nebraska between 1883 and 1886 — the same town and the same years in which his sister Ida was bearing hers. Their mother, Mary Kanady Ingersoll, died in Nebraska in 1895.

narrative_blocks.header: He lost Benjamin the year his mother died
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin, his eldest, was born at Loup City about 1883 and died in 1895 at about twelve. Mary Kanady Ingersoll died that June; no cause is recorded for either.

people.research_notes: ORBIT FIGURE. Rev. Henry Cowles (1803-1881), listed by Oberlin College among the Oberlin Founders. b. 24 Apr 1803 Norfolk, Litchfield County CT, eldest son of Samuel Cowles (1771-1845) and Olive Phelps Cowles (1780-1864); ten siblings — Louisa (1802-88), John Phelps (1805-91), Maria Jane (1806-43), Eliza (1808-95), Roxana (1810-1904), Rachael (1812-58), James (1815-1904), Mary Ann (1817-74), Helen Keziah (1819-1903), Olivia W. (1822-93). NOT BUILT per Sam. Prepared under Rev. Ralph Emerson of Norfolk; Yale College 1822-1826; Yale Divinity 1826-28 under Nathaniel William Taylor, a follower of Timothy Dwight; licensed by the Litchfield North Association and ordained at Hartford 1 Jul 1828. To the Western Reserve Sept 1828 for the Connecticut Home Missionary Society: fourteen months Ashtabula, five months Sandusky, called to Austinburg 1830, installed 29 Jul 1831, there until Nov 1835 — the pulpit Rev. Giles Hooker Cowles (H00443) resigned in 1830 and beside which he died in Jul 1835. Oberlin: professor of Greek and Latin 1835; ecclesiastical history and pastoral theology 1837/38; Literature of the Old Testament 1840, REPLACING HIS BROTHER John Phelps Cowles; left the seminary 1848. Oberlin Evangelist part-time editor 1844-48, full-time 1848-1862 (suspended when Civil War subscriptions fell). Prudential Committee 1836-37, 1843-48, 1851-81; General Agent for the College 1860-63; trustee 1851-1881. D.D. Hillsdale 1863. Sixteen commentary volumes 1867-1881, copyrights deeded to the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions, the American Home Missionary Society and the American Missionary Association; also edited Finney's sermons as Gospel Themes (1876) and wrote Sin and Suffering in the Universe. OHIO ANTI-SLAVERY SOCIETY: formed 1835 with Theodore Dwight Weld, Asa Mahan and Charles Grandison Finney. His papers at Oberlin include the 'Catalog and Record of Colored Students in Oberlin' (1835-62) and a 'Memorandum on Business for Freedmen's Aid Society' (c.1864); correspondents include Finney, John Keep, Arthur and Lewis Tappan, Theodore Dwight Weld and Harriet Beecher Stowe. m1 30 Jul 1830 (FamilySearch: 27 Jul) Alice Welch (28 Apr 1804 - 14 Oct 1843), daughter of Dr. Benjamin Welch of Norfolk; she was Principal of Oberlin's Female Department 1836-1840, taking it over from Elihu Parsons Ingersoll (HD1696), who held it 1835-36. Six children: Helen Maria (1831-51), Henry Benjamin (b.1834), John Guiteau Welch (1836-1914, Oberlin 1856, chaplain of the 55th Ohio Volunteer Infantry), Sarah Florella (1838-1912), Mary Louisa (1839-59), Charles William (b.1842); only John Guiteau Welch and Sarah outlived him. Before her death Alice named four women for him to choose between, one of them Minerva Dayton (4 Apr 1800 Watertown CT - 29 Nov 1880 Oberlin), widow of Anson Penfield of Oberlin and already mother of eight; married 2 Mar 1844 at Colebrook CT. Sarah Cowles Little (1838-1912): Oberlin A.B. 1859, A.M. 1862; married the superintendent Mr. Little in Jul 1862; Superintendent of the Wisconsin State School for the Blind, Janesville, 1875-1891, thirty years connected with it, and a founder of the Janesville Public Library. Buried Westwood Cemetery, Oberlin, plot B-028-06B, with both wives. DEATH DATE: 6 September 1881 per the Biblical Cyclopedia, FamilySearch and the Oberlin archives; Wikipedia says 7 September. The 6th is used. UNRELIABLE SOURCE: a Zilpha Cowles Grant family narrative supplied by Sam gives his dates as 1803-1885, his Oberlin appointment as 1825, and his wife as 'Alice Walsh, daughter of Dr. Benjamin Walsh'; three of those are wrong and the whole passage should not be relied on. NO BLOOD OR MARRIAGE TIE FOUND to the Farmington/Bristol Cowleses of this tree; Henry was Norfolk CT stock. Wives, children, siblings and parents NOT BUILT — orbit entry, per Sam.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the pulpit Giles Cowles gave up
narrative_blocks.body: Sent to the Western Reserve in 1828 by the Connecticut Home Missionary Society, he served fourteen months at Ashtabula and five at Sandusky before Austinburg called him in 1830. Giles Hooker Cowles had resigned that pulpit in 1830 and died beside it in 1835.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept the register of Oberlin's Black students
narrative_blocks.body: Within months of reaching Oberlin in 1835 he joined Theodore Dwight Weld, Asa Mahan and Charles Grandison Finney to form the Ohio Anti-Slavery Society. His Catalog and Record of Colored Students in Oberlin, kept from 1835 to 1862, is among the earliest records of Black enrollment in America.

narrative_blocks.header: Languages, then the chair his brother held
narrative_blocks.body: He came in 1835 as professor of Greek and Latin, moved to ecclesiastical history in 1838, and in 1840 took the Old Testament chair from his brother, John Phelps Cowles. Oberlin counts him among its founders.

narrative_blocks.header: Fourteen years editing the Oberlin Evangelist
narrative_blocks.body: From 1848 he edited the Oberlin Evangelist full-time, and it carried Oberlin's abolitionism, revivalism and doctrine of sanctification through the northeast. Subscriptions fell away in the Civil War and the paper was suspended in 1862.

narrative_blocks.header: His dying wife picked four women for him
narrative_blocks.body: Alice Welch ran Oberlin's female department from 1836, taking it over from Elihu Parsons Ingersoll, and died in 1843 leaving six children. Before she died she named four women from whom he was to choose his next wife; in 1844 he married one of them, Minerva Dayton Penfield.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixteen volumes, and the profits given away
narrative_blocks.body: From 1867 he published sixteen volumes of commentary covering the whole of Scripture, deeding the copyrights to the missionary boards.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at his daughter's blind school
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah, one of two of his children to outlive him, ran the Wisconsin State School for the Blind at Janesville and founded its public library. He died at her house in September 1881.

narrative_blocks.header: The mill wage sent him to college
narrative_blocks.body: He left high school in 1928 meaning to skip college, because his parents were paying off the house they had built on Longwood Avenue. He took a job in a sash-and-door mill on Slauson Avenue and was made lay-out man, but the raise was so small that he took a second job nights in a gas station and entered Occidental in September 1929.

narrative_blocks.header: His geology cost him the job
narrative_blocks.body: His first work after graduating in 1933 was as a laborer at what was supposed to be a gold mine. On his day off he crawled into the rat hole and sampled the quartz vein himself; the recheck showed the first sample had been salted and the mine could not pay.

narrative_blocks.header: A roughneck weekdays, a footballer Sundays
narrative_blocks.body: A friend told him that if he came to Santa Barbara and played for the Athletic Club they would find him work in the oil fields north of town. He was a roughneck and well puller for the Honolulu Oil Company two and a half years before he made the engineering department.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-two moves in one married life
narrative_blocks.body: He met Bernice Bethell at Santa Barbara and married her at Los Angeles in March 1935. Her obituary counted twenty-two moves following his career — Bakersfield three separate times, Santa Barbara, Taft, Long Beach, Fresno, Los Angeles — and the fifteenth landed them at Sacramento in 1958.

narrative_blocks.header: He died the day after his birthday
narrative_blocks.body: He turned seventy-four on 2 March 1984 and died the next day at San Clemente. Bernice, married to him forty-nine years, lived another twenty-two.

narrative_blocks.body: She met and married Jack Parle while both were in college and raised two children while moving twenty-two times, following his career as a petroleum engineer with the oil companies. She went to Sun City from San Clemente in 1986, two years after he died.

narrative_blocks.header: Top five in a class of 108
narrative_blocks.body: He turned from engineering to dentistry at BYU, finished there in 1963, and was taken by the USC dental school on the strength of his post-mission grades. He came out in 1967 in the top five of a class of a hundred and eight and passed the state board that July.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years straightening teeth at Simi Valley
narrative_blocks.body: He took orthodontic training at USC from 1968 to 1970, bought a practice at Reseda, and in 1977 started his own at Simi Valley. He became a board-certified orthodontist, taught part-time in the USC graduate orthodontic program, and practised more than forty years.

narrative_blocks.header: Born on Easter Sunday, baptized at seventeen
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Los Angeles on Easter Sunday in April 1938 and was baptized into the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints in May 1955, while at John Burroughs High School in Burbank. He gave up a Naval ROTC scholarship at UCLA after a year, went to BYU, and served two years in the Great Lakes mission.

narrative_blocks.header: He married in the Idaho Falls Temple
narrative_blocks.body: Karen Ann Jones had been his sister Lora Lee's roommate at BYU. They agreed not to marry until he had a year of dental school behind him and she had her degree, saw each other three or four times in that year, and married in August 1964.

narrative_blocks.header: A high jumper with excellent penmanship
narrative_blocks.body: He lettered in track at UCLA specialising in the high jump, prospected uranium at Golden, Colorado one summer for the Union Pacific, and braked for the Southern Pacific in others. He drew, gardened, golfed and researched the family history.

narrative_blocks.header: She ran Oberlin's department for women
narrative_blocks.body: From 1836 to 1840 she was Principal of Oberlin's Female Department, taking it over from Elihu Parsons Ingersoll, who had held it through the college's first year. She had come out of Norfolk, Connecticut, a daughter of Dr. Benjamin Welch, and married Henry Cowles there in 1830.

narrative_blocks.header: She chose the four women he might marry
narrative_blocks.body: She died in October 1843 at thirty-nine, leaving six children, of whom four went before their father. Before her death she named four women from whom he was to choose his next wife, and within a year he had married one of them.

people.research_notes: ORBIT ENTRY, built at Sam's instruction 7 Sep 2026; children NOT built. Alice Welch (28 Apr 1804 Norfolk, Litchfield County CT - 14 Oct 1843), daughter of Dr. Benjamin Welch of Norfolk; first wife of Rev. Henry Cowles (X04037). Principal of Oberlin's Female Department 1836-1840, taking it over from Elihu Parsons Ingersoll (HD1696), who held it 1835-36. Six children: Helen Maria (1831-51), Henry Benjamin (b.1834), John Guiteau Welch (1836-1914, chaplain of the 55th Ohio Volunteer Infantry), Sarah Florella (1838-1912), Mary Louisa (1839-59), Charles William (b.1842); only John Guiteau Welch and Sarah outlived their father. Before her death she selected four women, one of them Minerva Dayton Penfield, for Henry Cowles to choose between as his next wife (Oberlin College Archives). CONFLICT on the marriage date: FamilySearch (Sam, 7 Sep 2026) gives 27 Jul 1830, the Yale obituary record and Wikipedia give 30 Jul 1830; the 27th is used. CONFLICT on the place of death: FamilySearch (Sam, 7 Sep 2026) gives Norfolk CT, but she is buried at Westwood Cemetery, Oberlin, with her husband and his second wife; both are recorded as given. A letter from her brother B. Welch with a chart of 'Diseases of Infants' and a commonplace book of 1837 survive in the Henry Cowles Papers at Oberlin.

narrative_blocks.header: A widow with eight, a widower with six
narrative_blocks.body: Anson Penfield of Oberlin died in 1838 and left her with eight children. She married Henry Cowles at Colebrook, Connecticut in March 1844, five months after his first wife died, having been one of the four women that wife had named for him.

narrative_blocks.header: Her daughter became a reformer and editor
narrative_blocks.body: Her daughter Josephine Penfield married and became Josephine Cushman Bateham, a social reformer, editor and writer. The census of 1880 still found her at Oberlin with Cowles and with another daughter, Mary Penfield; she died there that November.

narrative_blocks.header: Saffron, sage and sassafras were hers to define
narrative_blocks.body: For the 1920 Encyclopedia Americana she wrote the entries on beach plants, evergreens, ornamental plants, the forest trees of America and of the tropics, saffron, sage, sassafras and vallisneria. Another entry covered the plants that draw birds.

narrative_blocks.header: At twenty-two she kept the club's herbarium
narrative_blocks.body: In May 1896 Helen Ingersoll signed herself Curator of the Torrey Botanical Club, informing its secretary that Edward Berry had given the club fifty plant specimens gathered around Passaic, New Jersey. She was twenty-two, and the specimens went into the herbarium she kept.

narrative_blocks.header: She drew the snakes for her father's column
narrative_blocks.body: Helen illustrated a twelve-article review of eastern Canadian snakes that ran in her father's nature column in The Family Herald and Weekly Star, and wrote part of the text herself. She illustrated several of Ernest Ingersoll's books as well.

narrative_blocks.header: She was born into her father's Harvard years
narrative_blocks.body: Helen was born at Cambridge, Massachusetts on 15 January 1874, in the winter Louis Agassiz died and while her father was still a student assistant in Agassiz's Museum of Comparative Zoology at Harvard. The sketch Ernest Ingersoll wrote of his dead teacher went to the New York Tribune, which ran it and hired him, so the household she was born into changed trades in her first months.

narrative_blocks.header: The only one of three who grew up
narrative_blocks.body: Geoffrey Wiltshire Ingersoll was born and died in 1889, and the sister born at New Haven on 12 October 1890 died the same day, unnamed. Helen, fifteen years older than either, was the only one of Ernest Ingersoll's three children to reach adulthood.

Wikisource Author:Helen Ingersoll (1874-), 'United States naturalist, daughter of naturalist Ernest Ingersoll', listing ten signed entries in The Encyclopedia Americana (1920). Clyde L. MacKenzie Jr., 'Biographic Memoir of Ernest Ingersoll', Marine Fisheries Review 53(3), 1991: the twelve-article eastern Canadian snake series in his newspaper column was 'illustrated and partly written by Ingersoll's only surviving child, a daughter, Helen, who also illustrated some of his books'. TORREY ROLE NOW SOURCED (Sam's screenshot, 7 Sep 2026): Proceedings of the Torrey Botanical Club, 12 May 1896 - a communication read into the minutes reporting Edward Berry's gift of fifty plants from around Passaic NJ, signed 'HELEN INGERSOLL, Curator'. The Wikisource talk page's guess of 'librarian' was wrong; the title was Curator. Still UNVERIFIED from that talk page - middle initial M., possibly Marcy; 1930 census, age 55, occupation writer and botanist. Not written to the card. The same talk page gives her mother's birthplace as Massachusetts, which conflicts with Mary Scofield's recorded Danbury, Connecticut birth. FamilySearch M6KC-XMS (Sam, 7 Sep 2026), 9 sources: b. 15 Jan 1874 Cambridge, Middlesex County MA; d. 12 Jan 1958, three days short of eighty-four; no death place given. The Cambridge birth falls inside her father's 1872-1874 assistantship at the Harvard Museum of Comparative Zoology, and probably explains the Wikisource talk page's census claim that her mother was born in Massachusetts - Mary Scofield was born at Danbury CT. Agassiz died in 1873 (see HD10698 NB2) and Helen was born 15 Jan 1874, so the Tribune hiring that turned Ernest Ingersoll from museum work to journalism falls within weeks of her birth - cross-record arithmetic, not a sourced claim.

narrative_blocks.body: Frances Buchanan was sixty-seven and unmarried when she wed Ernest Ingersoll, a seventy-year-old widowed naturalist, on the morning of 23 August 1923 in her own studio at Carnegie Hall. Three people were present besides the couple - the minister and one attendant each - and the Ingersolls left afterward for the Lake Champlain country.

narrative_blocks.body: Vera Edmondson's women's page stories in The Philadelphia Inquirer during the First World War drew the notice of Mrs. Edward T. Stotesbury, a Philadelphia social leader then deep in war work. Stotesbury took her on as her public relations representative, a post she held for many years.

narrative_blocks.header: Both had buried a spouse before 1930
narrative_blocks.body: Vera Edmondson Nelson was a widow, and Ernest Ingersoll at seventy-eight had outlived two wives, when they married at the Marble Collegiate Church on 16 November 1930 before a few close friends. They settled at 88 Morningside Drive, and she outlived him by six years.

narrative_blocks.body: Vera Edmondson was born at Washington in 1884 to Rees Boyn Edmondson, who had served in his teens as a flag-bearer for Confederate troops. She took a Vassar degree and a reporter's desk on The San Francisco Chronicle, a continent from the city she was born in.

narrative_blocks.header: The Marines came before the badge
narrative_blocks.body: Cheever Newhall went to Vietnam as a Marine sergeant with the First Battalion, Third Marines, and came home to a police badge in Laconia and then thirty years with the New Hampshire State Police. He retired a sergeant, died at the state Veterans Home on Winter Street in Tilton, and was buried a week later at the veterans cemetery at Boscawen.

narrative_blocks.header: Troopers raised the money to fly him home
narrative_blocks.body: By 2015 Parkinson's disease and a hard recovery from knee surgery had left his wife Sandy unable to care for him in their Florida home. A retired executive major of the New Hampshire State Police opened a fund, and current and former officers across the Lakes Region paid for the flight that carried him back to New Hampshire.

narrative_blocks.header: He married four months after turning nineteen
narrative_blocks.body: Cheever Newhall married Sandra St. Lawrence on 22 March 1965, four months past his nineteenth birthday. They were still married fifty-five years later when he died at seventy-four.

narrative_blocks.header: He forgot a fish for every student's name
narrative_blocks.body: Jordan catalogued the fishes of North and Middle America in four government volumes and left at least nineteen hundred type specimens in the California Academy of Sciences alone. At Indiana he was best remembered for saying that every time he learned a student's name he forgot the name of a fish.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten minutes on a siding got him Stanford
narrative_blocks.body: In March 1891 the Stanfords' private railway car stopped on a Bloomington siding, and ten minutes of talk ended in the offer of a university that did not yet exist. Jordan turned to his wife Jessie, who told him to take it; he reached Palo Alto in June and opened that October with fifteen professors and four hundred students.

narrative_blocks.header: Stanford and Indiana took his name down
narrative_blocks.body: Jordan held that a race of men and a herd of cattle are governed by the same laws of selection. He chaired the American Breeders' Association's eugenics committee, was a vice-president of the first International Eugenics Congress in 1912 and sat on the founding board of the Human Betterment Foundation, which campaigned for compulsory sterilization; in October 2020 the trustees of both universities he had led voted to strip his name from their buildings.

narrative_blocks.header: He sailed to Hawaii to change the verdict
narrative_blocks.body: Jane Stanford died at Honolulu in February 1905 and a coroner's jury found strychnine. Jordan crossed to Hawaii, engaged a physician of his own and announced heart failure, a finding that matched none of the recorded symptoms and stood as the accepted account until scholars reopened the case in 2003.

people.research_notes: Admitted as a documented orbit figure, not as an honoree - he connects to at least six people already in the tree across two independent clusters: the Brown siblings inside Stanford at its founding (Anna Louise Brown Nash HD9897, who came west to draw for him; Ellen Coit Brown Elliott HD9895 and her husband the registrar Orrin Leslie Elliott I03224, whom he recruited from Cornell by telegram; Bolton Coit Brown HD9896, hired the same year to build the art department), and the West Adams salon in Los Angeles (Katharine Putnam Hooker X02255, Marian Osgood Hooker H04280, George Ellery Hale X02263). Herbert Charles Nash I03236 was his first librarian. SOURCES (Sam, 7 Sep 2026): Wikipedia; Sierra Club John Muir Exhibit biography; Katherine Montana, 'The Problematic Legacy of David Starr Jordan', California Academy of Sciences; FindAGrave; the San Francisco Examiner obituary of Jessie Knight Jordan, 25 Oct 1952; the funeral notice for Susan Bowen Jordan, Nov 1885. M.D. YEAR CONFLICT: the Sierra Club page gives Indiana Medical College M.D. 1874; Jordan's own autobiography, quoted on Wikipedia, says 'in the spring of 1875, I received the (scarcely earned) degree of Doctor of Medicine'. 1875 kept. MUIR, NOT BUILT AS A BLOCK: in 1878 he read Muir's 'The Humming Bird of the California Waterfalls' to his classes and later called it 'the finest bird biography in existence'; he met Muir in 1880 and they worked together to save the Calaveras Big Trees groves. He was a charter member of the Sierra Club in 1892 and one of its nine original directors. CHILDREN NOT BUILT (no Hooker tie, orbit line is terminal): by Susan Bowen - Edith Monica (1877-1965), Harold Bowen (1882-1959), Thora (1884-1886); by Jessie Knight - Knight Starr (1888-1947), Barbara (1891-1900), Eric Knight (1903-1926). BUTLER: the Mount Holyoke alumnae directory records that at Susan Bowen's marriage in 1875 her husband was dean of Butler University at Irvington, Indiana - not in the career array, because a fourth undated row would sort last and fall off the three-row card. Robert L. Herbert, 'The Two Careers of Henrietta Hooker (1851-1929): From Botany to Buff Orpingtons' (2019), Mount Holyoke archives, supplied by Sam 7 Sep 2026: in the summer of 1883 Henrietta Edgecomb Hooker 'at last went to Europe, joining her age peer David Starr Jordon (1851-1931), already an established ichthyologist who taught natural history at Indiana University (and who was married to Hooker's colleague Susan Bowen)'; and 'Jordan no longer partnered Hooker after 1884; he must have relinquished these travels when he became President of Indiana University in 1885.'

narrative_blocks.header: She went on his first fish-collecting trips
narrative_blocks.body: Susan Bowen took her Mount Holyoke degree in 1864 and taught natural history at the seminary until 1870, working in the botany rooms under Lydia Shattuck. She was at Agassiz's Penikese school the same summer as Jordan, six years her junior, and afterwards assisted him daily in his work, on his first collecting trips for fishes in Georgia and later in Europe.

narrative_blocks.header: She died five years before the Stanford offer
narrative_blocks.body: Susan Bowen Jordan died at Bloomington, Indiana in November 1885, at thirty-nine and after ten years of marriage, leaving Edith at eight, David Harold at three, and an infant daughter of three months who did not long outlive her. Her married life ran from Indianapolis to Irvington to Bloomington and no further; Jordan was president of Indiana University when she died, and the California university his name is attached to was still five years off.

people.research_notes: Funeral notice, Indiana paper, November 1885 (Sam, 7 Sep 2026): 'Mrs. Jordan's family live in Peru, Mass. She was a teacher of natural history in Mount Holyoke Semenary, and attended the Penikese School of Natural History with Dr. Jordan in 1872... Mrs. Jordan took an active interest in her husband's natural history work, and assisted him in it daily. She accompanied him in his first collecting trips for fishes in Georgia, and afterwards to Europe with parties of students and friends.' PENIKESE YEAR CONFLICT: the notice says 1872, but Agassiz's Penikese Island summer school opened in 1873; unresolved, both recorded. They married in the winter of 1875 - Wikipedia gives 10 Mar 1875 at Peru, Massachusetts, her home town - and lived two years at Indianapolis, then at Irvington. CHILD AGE CONFLICT: the notice leaves 'Edith, eight years old; David Harold, three years old, and an infant daughter of three months', which puts the baby's birth about August 1885; Wikipedia dates Thora 1884-1886. Not resolved. Burial per FindAGrave: Rose Hill Cemetery, Bloomington, Monroe County, Indiana, Spencer Addition, Lot 369. ONE HUNDRED YEAR BIOGRAPHICAL DIRECTORY OF MOUNT HOLYOKE COLLEGE 1837-1937, Bulletin Series 30 no.5 (Sam, 7 Sep 2026): 'Susan Bowen 1864 (Mrs David Starr Jordan), teacher 1868-1870 Mount Holyoke Seminary. Married 1875; husband was dean of Butler University Irvington IN. Died 1885 in Bloomington IN.' This fixes the death place and gives her own teaching years, and it settles the question directly: she never saw Stanford. Her whole married life was Indiana - Indianapolis, then Irvington, then Bloomington - and she died in November 1885, five years before the Stanford offer of March 1891 and six before the university opened. NOTE the directory has her teaching 1868-1870 while Henrietta Edgecomb Hooker (H04934) joined the Mount Holyoke faculty in 1873, so they did not overlap there, even though Robert Herbert's 2019 study calls Susan 'Hooker's colleague'. RESOLVED 7 Sep 2026 by the Mount Holyoke Alumnae Quarterly department history Sam supplied: 'Among those who worked with Miss Shattuck were Miss Harriet E. Sessions, Miss Susan Bowen (later the wife of Dr. David Starr Jordan), Miss Frances M. Hazen, and Miss Henrietta E. Hooker.' Both women are named on the same roll of Lydia Shattuck's botany staff, which is what Herbert meant by 'colleague'; the teaching years still do not overlap, so they were successive rather than simultaneous. Wikidata Q98115643 describes Susan Bowen as an American zoologist and university teacher, occupations collector, zoologist, university teacher.

narrative_blocks.header: She told him to take Stanford
narrative_blocks.body: When Senator Stanford's offer came on a Bloomington siding in March 1891, Jordan turned to his wife as he did in such crises, and she urged him to accept. She was twenty-four, with a small child and her own studies still under way.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept his room as he left it
narrative_blocks.body: After Jordan died in 1931 Jessie stayed on at Serra House on the western edge of the campus and kept the room where he had held his 'at home' meetings unchanged, his books and portraits still on the walls. She outlived her husband, all three of their children and every one of her brothers and sisters, and died at eighty-five.

people.research_notes: San Francisco Examiner, 25 Oct 1952, 'Private Rites Today For Mrs. David Jordan' (Sam, 7 Sep 2026): died early 24 Oct 1952 aged 85 at Palo Alto Hospital, in hospital since 25 Sep after a stroke; private service at the Roller and Hapgood mortuary followed by cremation at ALTA MESA CEMETERY (CEM1545, already in the tree); public memorial in Stanford Memorial Church. b. Jessie Knight 5 Nov 1866 Ware, Mass.; m. 10 Aug 1887 at Worcester, Mass., when Jordan was president of Indiana University. They met when she was a Cornell student and he an alumni representative of the board of trustees. 'A constant collaborator in her husband's distinguished career as university head, active scientist, writer and lecturer. She edited many of his books.' Credited with establishing the informal atmosphere that became a Stanford trademark, in days 'when a wife was supposed to be a shadow'. Member of more than twenty organizations, from the Society of Mayflower Descendants and the Children's Museum of Palo Alto to the National Council for Prevention of War and the California Roadside Council. Survived by two stepchildren of Jordan's first marriage, Mrs. Edith Jordan Gardner of Berkeley and Harold Owen Jordan of Talent, Oregon; grandchildren Mrs. Ruth Jordan Gates and Lee Knight Jordan; four great-grandchildren. None built - no Hooker tie.

burial.plot_notes: Cremated at Alta Mesa following the service, 25 October 1952.

narrative_blocks.header: She ran the Children's Bureau for four presidents
narrative_blocks.body: Eisenhower made her chief of the Children's Bureau in 1957 and she served through four administrations, heading the American mission to the board of what became UNICEF. When the bureau was abolished in 1967 Johnson made her deputy assistant secretary for family planning, and she left government in 1970 when that post went too.

narrative_blocks.header: She argued the children should stay home
narrative_blocks.body: When children with intellectual disabilities were still routinely sent to institutions, Oettinger held that most could be raised at home, and by the nineteen-sixties ninety-five per cent were. She pressed as hard on the parents, against those who blamed themselves and went from doctor to doctor looking for a cure.

narrative_blocks.header: Three newspaper articles saved the nursery schools
narrative_blocks.body: Federal money for Scranton's nursery schools came with a condition that the town match it, which a place still climbing out of the Depression could not do. Oettinger went to the Tribune; a series of illustrated articles ran, and after the third the Works Progress Administration carried the schools without a local share.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote the book on a taboo subject
narrative_blocks.body: Not My Daughter, written with Elizabeth Mooney in 1979, took on adolescent pregnancy when almost nobody would put it in print. Understanding of human sexuality, she said, could no longer be denied to adolescents on the false assumption that it encouraged promiscuity.

narrative_blocks.header: She dressed against the social-worker stereotype
narrative_blocks.body: Oettinger dressed well enough that papers covering her work kept describing her clothes, and a colleague called her one of the best-dressed women in social work. She told her students they would never get rich at it, but that the satisfaction came from helping humanity.

narrative_blocks.header: He sold furniture and interviewed Buster Keaton
narrative_blocks.body: Oettinger ran a furniture store in Scranton and sold articles to Vanity Fair, Smart Set and The New Yorker at the same time. His 1923 Picture-Play interview got Keaton to give away that the pancake hat and oversized collar were vaudeville stand-bys his father had rigged him out in, and that he had been taught never to crack a smile.

narrative_blocks.header: He took a finance degree into magazine work
narrative_blocks.body: Oettinger came out of the Wharton School at Pennsylvania and afterwards took English courses at Harvard. He finished as a publications specialist for the Pennsylvania health department and chief of publications at Boston University, and died of cancer at his Washington home at sixty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote for America from four foreign posts
narrative_blocks.body: Oettinger started at the Washington Post, publicised Huntley and Brinkley for NBC, and co-wrote Reluctant Regulators, a book on the Federal Communications Commission and its audience. He then spent his working life with the United States Information Agency in Washington, New Delhi, Vienna and Paris, and won its Leonard Marks Award for creativity in communication in 1986.

narrative_blocks.header: He died in Budapest after the river cruise
narrative_blocks.body: Oettinger retired to the North Carolina Triangle in 1995, presented 'Mal's Music' every month at the Forest at Duke and wrote for its magazine. He died on 28 June 2008 at Budapest, at the end of a Rhine and Danube river cruise with his second wife.

narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Gaines in Orleans County, New York, in 1812 and died at Cambridge in Furnas County, Nebraska, in 1890. He and Elsie Curtis had ten children, and the family scattered from Michigan to Kansas.

narrative_blocks.body: He married Sarah Huxford in November 1856 and they had a single child, Endora, born in 1859 and dead in October 1863. All three of them lie in Riverside Cemetery at Albion, Michigan.

narrative_blocks.header: Two brothers born in the same year
narrative_blocks.body: He and Ray Dean Barnes were both born in 1922, to Loren and Myrtle Barnes of Kansas. He died in 2006 and his brother followed the next year.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother was born the same year
narrative_blocks.body: He and Roy Lee Barnes were both born in 1922, to Loren and Myrtle Barnes of Kansas. Roy died in 2006 and he followed in 2007.

narrative_blocks.header: He moved freight for the Union Pacific
narrative_blocks.body: He was general freight agent of the Union Pacific Railroad at Omaha, where his only son was born in 1890. He had come out of New York state, died in 1917 at York Township in Illinois, and was buried back at Onarga.

burial.plot_notes: Onarga Cemetery, Iroquois County IL; buried 1 April 1917.

narrative_blocks.header: He managed the mills his father cut out
narrative_blocks.body: He was seventeen when his father took him into the Warren County woods to raise the first sawmill on the south branch of Tionesta Creek, and he grew up to manage the business. The mill was still standing sixty years later.

narrative_blocks.header: The Rouse fund arrived while he was commissioner
narrative_blocks.body: Warren County made him one of its commissioners, and the Rouse fund came to the county in his term; the measures he and his associates passed with it were still prized decades afterward. It was the only political office he ever held.

narrative_blocks.header: He paid for a church he never joined
narrative_blocks.body: He belonged to no denomination, but thought the town ought to have a church, so he got up the subscription list and headed it himself. The Methodist Episcopal society formed in his neighborhood.

narrative_blocks.header: They drilled for oil and struck gas instead
narrative_blocks.body: A Syracuse man contracted for ten acres of his land to drill for oil and found gas. Two New Yorkers then bought four acres, put up a long iron building, and made lamp-black out of it.

narrative_blocks.header: He drew his goods by team from Dunkirk
narrative_blocks.body: He opened a store opposite his house in 1850 and hauled its stock overland from Dunkirk, on Lake Erie. He kept it ten years, and later owned the tavern that had been the settlement's first.

narrative_blocks.header: He and Gilson built the town's first schoolhouse
narrative_blocks.body: About 1840 he and John Gilson put up a school-house in the Barnes neighborhood. His brother Leverett taught the second school ever kept in the township.

people.research_notes: BIRTHPLACE: FamilySearch gives Barnes, Sheffield Township PA, but the family did not reach Warren County until 1828; the Warren County history gives Yates County NY, which the chronology supports. DEATH DATE: the Warren County 'Brief Personals' gives 19 Jan 1875; FamilySearch gives 21 Jan 1875. MOTHER: the same sketch calls him a son of 'Timothy and Betsey Barnes', but Betsey Cole died in 1807 and he was born in 1817 — his mother was Almira, Betsey's sister.

narrative_blocks.header: He turned Mormon and married at Kirtland
narrative_blocks.body: He became a Mormon and married Letitia Force at Kirtland, Ohio, in September 1840 — the town the Latter-day Saints had built around their first temple. The next year he brought her east to Sheffield.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept the Barnes House for twelve years
narrative_blocks.body: He ran the tavern at Lower Sheffield until 1868 — the house John Gilson had built in 1839, the first in the settlement. The rest of his working life went in lumbering and farming.

narrative_blocks.header: He made the postmaster he replaced his deputy
narrative_blocks.body: He took the Sheffield post office in 1853, when James Osgood left it to become justice of the peace. After a few years he had Osgood appointed his own deputy and asked him to keep the office.

narrative_blocks.header: Four of his twelve children died small
narrative_blocks.body: Letitia bore twelve children between 1841 and 1865, and four of them — Almira, Mary, Sara and Anna — did not live. One of the eight who did was named Henderson Cole Barnes, for his mother's brother.

people.research_notes: Daughter of Zachariah Eddy of Warren.
Born and died 30 August 1847; given name never recorded. Sex recorded male.
NAME: the Warren County history calls him 'Timothy F. Barnes, late treasurer of Warren county'; FamilySearch gives Timothy Eddy Barnes. Middle name unresolved.

narrative_blocks.header: He was county treasurer and dead at thirty
narrative_blocks.body: He held the treasurership of Warren County, Pennsylvania, and died at Warren in September 1881, thirty years old. His father Erastus outlived him by thirteen years.

narrative_blocks.header: His widow outlived him by sixty-two years
narrative_blocks.body: He married Ada Almeda Houghton in December 1870, when both of them were twenty. She survived him until 1944 and died at Aberdeen, on the far side of the country in Washington State.

narrative_blocks.header: One son died at twenty; one went west
narrative_blocks.body: Hiram Erastus died at Barnes in March 1893, twenty years old. Percy Livingston lived to 1949, married four times, and died at Tacoma — in the same state his mother had gone to.

narrative_blocks.header: He married four times, from Warren to Tacoma
narrative_blocks.body: He married Isabelle McConnell in 1899, Sara Mefford in 1902, Hajnalka Pinter in 1919 and Elva Tanner in 1930. Born at Warren in Pennsylvania, he died at Tacoma in Washington — the state his mother Ada had moved to.

narrative_blocks.header: Rheumatic fever took him at twelve
narrative_blocks.body: He died at half past one on a Wednesday afternoon at the family home in Bath, after six weeks of rheumatic fever. He was in the seventh grade at the Bath public school and had lately become a Boy Scout.

narrative_blocks.header: His sister lay ill in the same house
narrative_blocks.body: Barbara Jean was shut in the house with scarlet fever at the same time, and was reported to be doing well on the day he died.

people.research_notes: Presumed lost with her husband when their Beechcraft Bonanza disappeared over Lake Erie, 4 Nov 1950; no wreckage found.

narrative_blocks.header: She met her husband at Oberlin College
narrative_blocks.body: She went from Haverling High School at Bath to Oberlin College in Ohio, where she met Stanley Dunbar. At Sharon she was known as a singer in church, as she had been at school in Bath.

narrative_blocks.header: The Beechcraft never reached Cleveland
narrative_blocks.body: On 4 November 1950 she and her husband flew out of Sharon, Pennsylvania, toward Cleveland for the Navy-Notre Dame game, another couple aboard with them. Radio contact broke at half past two, eighty-five miles out, after Stanley reported he believed the plane was in a spin.

narrative_blocks.header: Two air forces searched and found nothing
narrative_blocks.body: Aircraft of the United States Air Force, the Coast Guard and the Canadian Air Force combed a thousand-mile radius of Cleveland, Lake Erie included. The search was given up a week later and word sent to her mother at Bath.

narrative_blocks.header: She left three girls, the youngest one
narrative_blocks.body: The three daughters were five years old and younger, the last of them one. Stanley's mother and father were staying with them at Sharon while the search went on.

people.research_notes: Of Sharon, Pennsylvania. Lost with his wife and Mr. and Mrs. C. Richard Johnston when their Beechcraft Bonanza vanished between Youngstown and Cleveland, 4 Nov 1950. OBERLIN: inferred — the 1950 search story says Barbara 'attended Oberlin College in Oberlin, O., where she met her husband.' His own attendance is not stated outright.

narrative_blocks.header: He told the tower he was spinning
narrative_blocks.body: An experienced pilot, he flew his Beechcraft Bonanza out of Sharon on 4 November 1950 with his wife and another couple aboard, bound for the Navy-Notre Dame game at Cleveland. Eighty-five miles out he radioed the airport tower that he believed he was in a spin, and nothing more was heard.

narrative_blocks.header: Zero visibility, and the lake below
narrative_blocks.body: Visibility at Cleveland was zero and landing impossible; the plane was flying above the weather that had settled over the city. A week of searching by American and Canadian aircraft found nothing, and it is thought the plane went down in Lake Erie.

narrative_blocks.header: His parents kept the children at Sharon
narrative_blocks.body: He and Barbara left three daughters, the eldest five and the youngest one. His mother and father were staying with them at Sharon while the search went on.

narrative_blocks.header: Prattsburg raised him, Michigan buried him
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Prattsburg in Steuben County, New York, in 1823 and died at Oxford in Oakland County, Michigan, in 1900. He married Helen Wicks there in 1851 and Mary Ann Chamberlain twenty years later.

narrative_blocks.body: He was born at East Hartford in 1795 and removed to Berlin about 1819, the year he married Anna Hollister, and farmed there the rest of his life. He held various town offices and sat for Berlin in the legislature about 1833.

narrative_blocks.header: September 1848 took his wife and both children
narrative_blocks.body: Miranda died at Berlin on 17 September 1848; their son Orrin followed on the nineteenth and their daughter Helen on the twenty-first. Five days emptied the house.

narrative_blocks.header: He sat for Berlin in 1871 and 1875
narrative_blocks.body: He held various town offices, represented Berlin twice in the State Legislature, and was a director of the Berlin Savings Bank. He farmed the ground he was born on until 1883, then moved into Kensington village.

narrative_blocks.header: Three wives, and the second lived a year
narrative_blocks.body: Miranda Wilcox died in 1848, four years married. Mary Elizabeth Hooker died in December 1853, ten days after bearing Charles. He married Frances Elizabeth Miles in 1855, and she gave him four more children.

narrative_blocks.header: In a corporal, out an adjutant
narrative_blocks.body: He enlisted as a corporal in Company C of the 3rd Connecticut in April 1861 and was mustered out at Hartford that August, the regiment's three months served. He went back in that September with the 6th Connecticut and rose through first sergeant, second lieutenant and first lieutenant to adjutant by October 1864.

narrative_blocks.header: He sat for his portrait in the badge
narrative_blocks.body: Beers and Mansfield photographed him in uniform at their gallery on Chapel Street in New Haven, some time between 1861 and 1864, wearing the badge of the Tenth Corps. He was discharged in November 1864 and died six years later at thirty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: Her four sons ran the ironworks after her
narrative_blocks.body: She married Thomas Fitch Rowland at New Haven in 1855 and outlived only one of her five children's infancies — Caroline died at two. Thomas Jr. and Charles Bradley both spent their working lives at the Continental Iron Works their father founded.

people.research_notes: DISPUTED ANCESTRY: some sources make him a descendant of Henry Rowland (c.1625-1691) of Fairfield CT — Rowland DNA Group E — but the Rowland Genealogy project (newsletter #13, Dec 2023) lists his lineage among three Group E claims that are conflicting or unproven and calls for a Y-DNA test to settle it. NOT asserted on the card. The Gov. Thomas Fitch (1699-1774) descent is the one his given names carry. Vice-president and life member of the ASME; honorary member of the ASCE. NOT flagged is_notable — eminent, but an in-law; say the word. 1864: tried to sell the Continental Works and retire early; it did not come off. The company was liquidated in 1928 after his son retired. Listed on the Rowland Genealogy project Famous Rowlands page. New Haven Colony Historical Society MSS 57A (Farmington Canal Papers) holds his canal collection, including Frederick Bostwick's unpublished typescript history, written by his nephew and edited about 1907; the finding aid calls him a lineal descendant of Gov. Thomas Fitch and points to a separate George Rowland Papers, MSS 570, for his father. His obituary appeared in the Society of Gas Lighting proceedings, 1908.

narrative_blocks.header: Ericsson gave him the hull; 101 days later
narrative_blocks.body: The yard's first contract was a water pipeline across the Harlem River. Then John Ericsson handed it the hull of a new ironclad, on nothing but an outline and a section drawn to show the thing would float. The Monitor launched in 101 days.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven monitors, more than any other yard
narrative_blocks.body: The Monitor neutralised the Virginia at Hampton Roads that March, and the craze that followed sent his works seven monitors, more than any other firm, plus three turrets and a gunboat. A correspondent found his Passaic gouged and split open.

narrative_blocks.header: He was a miller's boy at thirteen
narrative_blocks.body: He went into his father's grist mill at thirteen, then fired the third passenger train sent over the New York and New Haven Railroad. In 1859 Samuel Sneden, asked for an iron ship he could not build, made him a partner; a year later it was his.

narrative_blocks.header: Gas mains, buoys, and welded torpedo casings
narrative_blocks.body: The postwar slump turned the works to gas holders, mains and whole gasworks, and made it a pioneer in welding — boiler furnaces, gas-illuminated buoys, wood-pulp digesters, and torpedo and depth-charge casings in the wars.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave his men Saturday afternoons off
narrative_blocks.body: He pioneered the Saturday half-holiday in New York and gave it to his own men without cutting their pay, and cleared the debt on the Ascension church in Kent Street.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty patents, and a prize still given
narrative_blocks.body: He filed more than fifty patents, one a wartime machine tool said to save the labour of seventy-five men. One of nine honorary members of the American Society of Civil Engineers, he endowed its Thomas Fitch Rowland Prize, awarded still.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother died when he was six
narrative_blocks.body: The only son among five children of George and Ruth Caroline Atwater Rowland, he lost his mother at six, his first child before her third birthday, and his son George five months before his own death. His father's money built the Farmington Canal.

education.notes: New Haven; left at thirteen for the mill

Rowland 1853-1926' and a 'Charles Bradley Rowland 1863-1926', which look like one man duplicated. EH birth kept. The Continental Iron Works company history (c. 1918) independently gives him 'born in Brooklyn in 1863' and a Columbia School of Mines degree in 1884, corroborating EH 5289 against the 'seventy-first year' of the 1926 obituary.

narrative_blocks.header: He went straight from the mines school
narrative_blocks.body: He graduated from the Columbia School of Mines in 1884 and entered the Continental Iron Works the same year, his father founder and president. He gave his whole career to it and was vice-president for his last twelve years.

narrative_blocks.header: The works ran day and night in 1917
narrative_blocks.body: During the First World War the Greenpoint yard worked around the clock making guncotton digesters in corrugated furnaces for ships. He was a vestryman of Christ Church in Greenwich, where he died in 1926.

narrative_blocks.header: Father and son died five months apart
narrative_blocks.body: He died at Larchmont on 7 July 1907, forty-one years old, and Thomas Fitch Rowland followed him on 13 December. He was buried in the Rowland plot at Evergreen in New Haven, where his mother had gone five years before.

narrative_blocks.body: He went into the Continental Iron Works the year he left Yale and stayed until it closed: secretary and treasurer from 1887, president from 1909, and the man whose retirement in 1927 ended the company. Its assets were liquidated the following year.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept the naval architects' school thirty years
narrative_blocks.body: He was a trustee of the Webb Institute of Naval Architecture from 1908 until his death, and belonged to the civil, mechanical and naval engineering societies alike. He was junior warden of Christ Church in Brooklyn from 1901.

narrative_blocks.header: The yard stopped building ships and welded
narrative_blocks.body: Under him the Continental Iron Works left shipbuilding for welded plate steel: corrugated boiler furnaces, welded drums for destroyer boilers, welded oil stills, and digesters for wood pulp and for the Government's explosive plants. The Greenpoint plant still ran two and a half blocks along the East River.

narrative_blocks.header: Roosevelt put him on the canal commission
narrative_blocks.body: He sat on the Isthmian Canal Commission that examined routes across Central America in 1902, and Roosevelt appointed him a member in 1904. Seth Low had recommended him; the president told James Dodge that Burr and Parsons were the men he wanted.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-two years teaching at three colleges
narrative_blocks.body: He taught mechanics at Rensselaer from 1876, engineering at Harvard in 1892, and civil engineering at Columbia from 1893 until 1916, ending as professor emeritus. Between the professorships he was general manager of the Phoenix Bridge Company.

narrative_blocks.header: Two tunnels and a bridge crossed his desk
narrative_blocks.body: As consulting engineer to the city he had a hand in the Holland and Lincoln Tunnels and the George Washington Bridge, and earlier in the University Heights and 145th Street bridges and the Harlem River Speedway.

narrative_blocks.header: He won the Potomac bridge competition in 1900
narrative_blocks.body: His design for a memorial bridge across the Potomac at Washington took first place in the national competition of 1900. He also sat on the boards that chose a deep-water harbour for southern California and planned the New York State Barge Canal.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the Rowland Prize in 1891
narrative_blocks.body: The American Society of Civil Engineers gave him its Thomas Fitch Rowland Prize in 1891, for the best paper on construction engineering. Rowland had endowed the prize seven years earlier.

narrative_blocks.header: He was widowed at forty-two
narrative_blocks.body: Caroline Kent Seelye died in 1894 after eighteen years, leaving him three children; he married Gertrude Gold Shipman in 1900. His son George was likewise widowed young and married again.

narrative_blocks.header: Five books, one on the isthmus
narrative_blocks.body: He published Stresses in Bridge and Roof Trusses in 1879 and The Elasticity and Resistance of the Materials of Engineering in 1883. Ancient and Modern Engineering and the Isthmian Canal came in 1902, the year he first sat on the commission.

narrative_blocks.body: He took first medals in the preparatory department but was compelled to leave college in 1872 when his eyesight failed. He read law for two years at Columbian University instead, and made patents his life's work.

narrative_blocks.header: Five years examining patents, then practising
narrative_blocks.body: He was an examiner in the United States Patent Office from 1875 to 1880, then resigned to take up the practice of patent law, which he continued for the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: His son found him dead in his bed
narrative_blocks.body: He went to a Board of Trade committee meeting on the Tuesday evening and retired at his usual hour. Ogle found him next morning at 2020 H Street, dead of apoplexy, after a day in apparently the best of health.

narrative_blocks.header: He led Washington's Board of Trade
narrative_blocks.body: Vice-president in 1913, he was elected president of the Washington Board of Trade the following autumn. The board postponed its twenty-fifth anniversary meeting when he died and sent its directors to the funeral.

narrative_blocks.header: Senior warden, and the diocese's treasurer
narrative_blocks.body: He was senior warden of St Michael and All Angels' Protestant Episcopal Church and treasurer of the Episcopal diocese of Washington. He was buried from that church.

narrative_blocks.header: First master of King Solomon Lodge
narrative_blocks.body: He was a charter member of King Solomon Lodge and its first master, and took the royal arch degree in Columbia Chapter in 1913. He was a vice-president of the Oldest Inhabitants' Association and presided at its New Year's gathering.

people.research_notes: Cadet application to West Point filed 8 Feb 1866 from Jefferson City, Cole County, Missouri, recommended by Hon. I. W. M. McClung. Wikipedia's infobox names his parents 'Jeremiah and Sarah'; the article body, the Holden genealogy and W. W. Campbell's National Academy memoir all give Edward and Sarah Frances (Singleton) Holden. His cousin by marriage George P. Bond directed the Harvard College Observatory, and a grandson of the same name patented the gauge used in modern fire extinguishers. Under him Lick gained the 33-inch correcting lens (1888), the Willard-Crocker telescope (1890), an electric plant given by Thomas Edison (1891), the D. O. Mills spectrograph (1894) and the Crossley reflector (1895), and sent five eclipse expeditions to California, French Guiana, Chile, Japan and India. Columbia gave him an LL.D. in 1887; Nicholas Murray Butler joined its faculty in 1885 and became its president in 1902. Two of Butler's letters to Holden survive in the family archive; their subject is not recorded in the finding aid.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the first mountaintop observatory
narrative_blocks.body: He came to the Naval Observatory in 1873, onto its 26-inch refractor under Simon Newcomb, who the next year named him to James Lick's trustees as the future director - twenty-seven, and barely a year an astronomer. He ran Washburn from 1881, took Lick in 1888, and founded the Astronomical Society of the Pacific.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the University of California at thirty-nine
narrative_blocks.body: The regents made him president of the University of California and Lick's director-designate on one day in October 1885. He was Berkeley's fifth president until the observatory opened in June 1888, and gave up Lick at the end of 1897 after his own staff turned on him.

narrative_blocks.header: Two craters carry his name, one on Mars
narrative_blocks.body: The asteroid 872 Holda and craters on the Moon and Mars carry his name; he found twenty-two NGC objects at Washburn. He entered the National Academy of Sciences in 1885, took five honorary degrees and helped found the Cosmos Club.

narrative_blocks.header: He ended as a librarian at West Point
narrative_blocks.body: He graduated third in the West Point class of 1870 and taught natural philosophy and military engineering there before resigning his commission in 1873. He came back in 1901 as the academy's librarian and held it until he died in 1914.

narrative_blocks.header: He and his wife lived thirty years apart
narrative_blocks.body: William Chauvenet taught him at Washington University and he lodged in the Chauvenet house; he married the daughter, Mary, in 1871. She left him in 1880 for her mother's house in St. Louis, and his 1914 obituary still called him survived by his widow.

narrative_blocks.header: He announced a third moon of Mars
narrative_blocks.body: On 28 August 1877, days after Asaph Hall found Deimos and Phobos, he announced a third moon of Mars; the observations proved badly wrong. He twice hunted the hypothetical planet Vulcan and found nothing.

narrative_blocks.header: Todd was with him at the Naval Observatory
narrative_blocks.body: David Peck Todd came into the Naval Observatory in 1875 and stayed to 1881, the years he was there. Both reached Mount Hamilton before the observatory existed: he in 1881 to set the meridian circle, Todd the next year for the transit of Venus.

career.role: Instructor in natural philosophy, then in military engineering

people.research_notes: FamilySearch gives her death as 11 Oct 1937 in Tuscany; Findagrave and the American consular death report of 7 Jan 1937 give 6 Jan 1937 at Florence, followed here. Her parents Professor William and Katherine (Hemple) Chauvenet are not built. Her 1937 New York Times obituary makes her resident at Florence since 1923 and names two survivors, Mrs. Mabel Randall-MacIver and Edward Chauvenet Holden - Mildred having died in 1932.

narrative_blocks.header: She went home to her mother in 1880
narrative_blocks.body: She separated from Edward Singleton Holden in 1880 and took Mabel, Mildred and Edward to her mother Catherine Chauvenet's house in St. Louis, where the three of them grew up. She lived at Florence from 1923 and died there in January 1937, ninety-two years old.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father founded the Naval Academy
narrative_blocks.body: William Chauvenet drew up the plans that became the United States Naval Academy, moved the school from Philadelphia to Annapolis and founded its mathematics department; he was afterwards chancellor of Washington University at St. Louis. Her mother was Catherine Hemple of Philadelphia, the city she was born in herself.

narrative_blocks.header: Her daughter said she never stopped loving him
narrative_blocks.body: She never ceased to love her husband, Mabel wrote, and the agony of it in her mother's heart left Mabel aghast. She kept the children and the St. Louis house for the rest of his life, and outlived him by twenty-three years.

cross_connections.display_label: chaired the rebuilding of France's villages as she rebuilt its music
founded the club she belonged to, and rebuilt France as she did

bio.bio_blurb: First president of the Fontainebleau School of Music

people.research_notes: Member of the Colony, Cosmopolitan and MacDowell clubs, New York. Her 1961 New York Times obituary names her only survivor as Mrs. Natalie Tuttle Martin, of the same address.

narrative_blocks.header: She was the music school's first president
narrative_blocks.body: She took her diploma cum laude from the Mary Institute at St. Louis in 1892 and studied piano at Vienna under Leschetizky and Carreno, then in New York under Stojowski. She helped found the American summer school for musicians at Fontainebleau after the war and was its first president.

narrative_blocks.header: Married twice in one day, at Florence
narrative_blocks.body: Widowed at twenty-six, she married Dr. George Montgomery Tuttle at Florence on 5 April 1906 - first in the Presbyterian church on the Lungarno Guicciardini, then before the lord mayor at the Palazzo Vecchio. Her five-year-old daughter Story attended her.

narrative_blocks.header: Her first husband died before the baby came
narrative_blocks.body: She married Dr. Thomas Story Kirkbride in December 1899 and he was dead at Philadelphia by 19 July 1900. Mabel Story Kirkbride was born there on 26 September, two months after her father.

narrative_blocks.header: A third husband at sixty-two
narrative_blocks.body: In 1936, twenty-four years after Tuttle died, she married David Randall-MacIver, who died at their Park Avenue apartment in 1945. She died there herself on a Monday night in May 1961, eighty-seven, with her daughter Natalie in the same rooms.

narrative_blocks.header: A neighbourhood house on a Maine island
narrative_blocks.body: She founded the Neighborhood House at Islesford on Little Cranberry Island, where the Tuttles summered, and was a trustee of the Music School Settlement in New York. She declared for woman suffrage, and was president of the Grace Church Trained Nurses' Club - the church where Natalie married in 1942.

narrative_blocks.header: France gave her the Legion of Honour
narrative_blocks.body: The Mayor of Rheims thanked her in 1919 for the work of the American Friends of Musicians in France, whose committee she chaired, in restoring the city's wrecked Conservatory, and in 1923 France made her a member of the Legion of Honour. In 1940 she took the chair of the American Association for Assistance to French Artists.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father wrote that he would not come
narrative_blocks.body: She set down eighty-eight typed pages on him - the brilliance that drew her, and that 'at the same time he deserted me and never asked me to be his all again'. When she asked him to visit he answered that he never wanted to see her mother again, and so could not come.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a painter and followed the colonies
narrative_blocks.body: She married Charles Rosen in New York in December 1904 and went with him to New Hope in Bucks County, where both their daughters were born. The family moved to Woodstock in 1920, and she died there in 1932, eighteen years before him.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept a hundred and twenty-eight letters
narrative_blocks.body: Her father wrote her from Mount Hamilton all through the 1890s, long letters, stern and proud of her by turns - 'you will make a mistake if you run counter to what I ask you, in this masterful fashion'. Her grandmother Catherine Chauvenet wrote her thirty-four of her own.

narrative_blocks.header: She was the go-between for the whole family
narrative_blocks.body: Her father asked after Mabel through her and sent letters on to Mabel through her, which is how the estrangement shows. He used her the same way to reach her brother Ned, whom he thought lazy and unmotivated.

narrative_blocks.header: She was told to join the Colonial Dames
narrative_blocks.body: Her father pressed her into the Massachusetts Society of Colonial Dames because 'membership in this society makes you at once accepted by the very people in America', and warned that Mabel was 'much too lax about this indispensable mark of good breeding'. He filed his own application to the California Sons of the American Revolution.

narrative_blocks.header: What he wrote her about most was money
narrative_blocks.body: He apologised for not providing better, and in February 1899 told her he had not been idle a moment but the pay waited on publication - he had not been given two good salaried places, would try for no more, and was 'tired of fighting slanders twenty years old'. In October 1901 a note said only that he had been appointed at West Point in charge of the library, and had accepted.

narrative_blocks.body: He married Emma Butterick Noyes of Brookline, Massachusetts, at Para in Brazil and made his life there. Their children were Edward Singleton and Faith, the second born at Brookline.

bio.bio_blurb: Gynecologist; twenty-eight years at Roosevelt Hospital

people.research_notes: Cremated; no burial recorded. His mother is Harriet Merriman in the Yale obituary record and the 1912 press, Harriet Merriam in the New York Times. The Yale record makes him professor of gynecology at Physicians and Surgeons from 1885 for eighteen years and at Bellevue 1885-1889; both 1912 newspapers give the chair as 1888-1893, followed here. Parents Rev. James Hawley Tuttle, D.D., and Harriet (Merriman) Tuttle, not built. His Yale obituary names William Tuttle as his earliest American ancestor and says the land Tuttle bought was afterwards sold to Yale; Wikipedia independently records that part of that William Tuttle's ground is now Yale campus, which is what fixes the shared descent with Elizabeth Tuttle. The 1883 Tuttle genealogy was compiled by George Frederick Tuttle (1823-1904), not built.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-eight years at the Roosevelt Hospital
narrative_blocks.body: He was attending gynecologist at the Roosevelt Hospital from 1884 until the day he died, and for part of that time president of its medical board. He had been physician in chief of the New York State Emigrant Hospital and attending physician at Bellevue, and held the chair of gynecology at the College of Physicians and Surgeons from 1888 to 1893.

narrative_blocks.header: Dresden, then Andover, then Yale
narrative_blocks.body: His father, the Rev. Dr. James Hawley Tuttle, had the Universalist pulpit at Rochester when he was born, and the family went on to Chicago and then Minneapolis. He studied a year at Dresden, prepared at Phillips Academy, Andover, took his Yale degree in 1877 and his medical degree from the College of Physicians and Surgeons in 1880.

narrative_blocks.header: Angina took him at fifty-six
narrative_blocks.body: He died early on 29 October 1912 at 38 West Fifty-second Street, of angina pectoris. He had married six years before at the Palazzo Vecchio in Florence and left one daughter, Natalie Chauvenet Tuttle.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale was built on his ancestor's land
narrative_blocks.body: His earliest American ancestor, William Tuttle, bought New Haven land that was afterwards sold to Yale College; South College, South Middle College and the Athenaeum were built on it. He took his own Yale degree in 1877.

narrative_blocks.header: He reorganised the immigrants' hospital
narrative_blocks.body: As physician-in-chief of the State Emigrant Hospital on Ward's Island he was instrumental in a thorough reorganisation of it. He then studied some months at Leipzig and served as a resident physician in the hospitals of Dresden and Prague, coming back to New York at the close of 1883 to practise.

narrative_blocks.header: Two voyages out to China and Japan
narrative_blocks.body: He travelled constantly, crossed to Europe many times and twice went out to China, Japan and the East. His last summers were spent at his house at Islesford on Mount Desert, the island where his wife founded the neighbourhood house.

notable.notable_blurb: Excavator of Great Zimbabwe, Abydos and Nubia

cross_connections.display_label: built the African section of the museum whose Egyptian one he had
was ordering the Athenian Agora while he read the Etruscans in Rome
had a painter brother, Sheldon, among the Monuments Men in Italy
tracked the Nazis' looted art across Germany as a Monuments Man

people.research_notes: The Penn Museum's Expedition article gives his death as 1947 aged 74; Wikipedia, Findagrave and the New York index to death certificates all give 30 April 1945 at 1075 Park Avenue, Manhattan, aged 71, followed here. An earlier FamilySearch paste placed the death at Rome, which is the memorial, not the death. The dynamiting of the German dig house at the Ramesseum belongs to Howard Carter, not to him.

military_service.role: Interpreter, Ferozepore Brigade headquarters in France, then Salonica
military_service.notes: Second lieutenant 1914, captain 1916, mentioned in despatches June 1918. War Office file WO 33/46265.

narrative_blocks.header: He proved Great Zimbabwe was African
narrative_blocks.body: He made the first detailed study of Great Zimbabwe in 1905 and 1906 and found nothing in it of non-African origin. Against the settled belief that Arab or Phoenician traders had raised the ruins, he argued in Mediaeval Rhodesia that they were purely African and fourteenth-century, and later archaeology bore him out.

narrative_blocks.header: A British captain, then an American citizen
narrative_blocks.body: He served the British through the first war and afterwards took American citizenship. In the second he stayed on in Italy and worked with the Allied Monuments, Fine Arts and Archives programme - the Monuments Men - to keep Italy's monuments from destruction.

narrative_blocks.header: He named the king of the Abydos temple
narrative_blocks.body: He went to Egypt in 1898 under Flinders Petrie and uncovered the mortuary temple of Senwosret III at Abydos; the credit for first identifying its royal owner is his. With Weigall and Currelly he mapped the complex Pennsylvania is still digging.

narrative_blocks.header: Pennsylvania's first professional Egyptologist
narrative_blocks.body: He took the Egyptian section of the University of Pennsylvania Museum in 1906 when Sara Yorke Stevenson resigned, and Eckley B. Coxe Jr.'s money let him begin the museum's own excavations. With Leonard Woolley he dug Areika, Karanog and Buhen in Nubia from 1907 to 1910.

narrative_blocks.header: He listed his languages to the War Office
narrative_blocks.body: In August 1914 he offered himself as 'as nearly absolute master of German as any Englishman ever is', good at French and Italian, strong in Spanish, and in perfect condition from a life outdoors. He interpreted in France, then at Salonica after a crash course in Greek, and came out a captain mentioned in despatches.

narrative_blocks.header: Randall was his stepfather's name
narrative_blocks.body: His father John MacIver died in 1875, when he was one, and his mother Eliza Mary Rutherford married Richard Randall, whose name the boy took. He took a first at Queen's College, Oxford in 1896 and was elected to the British Academy in 1938.

narrative_blocks.header: Born after her father died, dead at twenty-four
narrative_blocks.body: Her father died at Philadelphia on 19 July 1900 and she was born there on 26 September. At five she attended her mother at the Florence wedding, and she died in Italy in May 1925.

narrative_blocks.header: Her Bryn Mawr class made her a memorial
narrative_blocks.body: She went to Bryn Mawr, and the class of 1922 gave the college a memorial to her after she died in Italy at twenty-four. Thirty-three years later the president's office could find no photograph of it to send her mother.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten years at Fontainebleau under Casadesus
narrative_blocks.body: She studied ten years at the Fontainebleau School of Music, of which her mother was the first president, under Robert Casadesus and Isadore Philipp. She was a concert pianist and spent most of her life in Paris and Florence.

narrative_blocks.header: She hunted deer in the forest of Fontainebleau
narrative_blocks.body: For years before the war she rode with the club called La Chasse, hunting deer in the forest outside Paris. She came back to America with her mother when war broke out, and was a familiar figure on the bridle trails around Greenwich.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at Grace Church at thirty-three
narrative_blocks.body: She married Jean Martin, a French scientist who had lived in New York for eighteen years, at Grace Church on 20 June 1942. Her mother gave a small reception afterwards at 1075 Park Avenue, and the marriage was over by 1950.

cross_connections.display_label: founded Byrdcliffe at Woodstock long before he came to teach there
