grew up in Bucks County a painter's grandson, and quarried stone

narrative_blocks.header: He photographed dead miners at sixteen
narrative_blocks.body: He was born on a farm in Westmoreland County and at sixteen opened a photographic studio at West Newton in the western Pennsylvania coalfield, where most of his subjects were dead miners. He went to New York in 1898 meaning to be a newspaper illustrator and studied painting instead, under William Merritt Chase and Frank DuMond.

narrative_blocks.header: He threw away the style that made him
narrative_blocks.body: His large New Hope snowscapes brought the National Academy's Inness Gold Medal and Altman Prize in 1916, seven one-man shows and election to the Academy. Then he decided Impressionism belonged to the past, and by 1920 had gone over to a hard cubist-realist manner he kept for the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded a painting school at Woodstock
narrative_blocks.body: He came to Woodstock in 1918 to teach at the Art Students League summer school, ran it until 1921 and moved there for good in 1920, with George Bellows and Eugene Speicher for neighbours. In 1922 he started the Woodstock School of Painting with Henry Lee McFee and Andrew Dasburg, and by his death in 1950 he was the acknowledged dean of the colony.

narrative_blocks.header: He painted post offices for the government
narrative_blocks.body: Treasury commissions in the Depression put his murals in the post offices at Beacon and Poughkeepsie and at Palm Beach in Florida. The Beacon panels take in the Hudson Valley and New York City, and the Poughkeepsie panel of 1939 turns the town's history into cubes, cylinders and cones.

career.role: Instructor, then director of the summer school

narrative_blocks.header: Illness took her out of school for good
narrative_blocks.body: She went to the Holmquist School for Girls first as a day pupil and then as a boarder, and illness ended it before she could finish. She was nine when her father moved the family to Woodstock in 1920, and fourteen when they went on to Columbus, Ohio.

narrative_blocks.header: She worked for the Canine Catering Company
narrative_blocks.body: In the middle 1930s she went to Washington to live with her sister Katherine and took a job at the Canine Catering Company. In 1937 she married Richard Callaway Goff and kept house for him at Annapolis and at Woodstock until he died in 1970, and then lived with her daughters at Queenstown.

narrative_blocks.header: Six grandchildren, and five great-grandchildren
narrative_blocks.body: She lived with her two daughters at Queenstown after her husband died in 1970, and by the end there were six grandchildren and five great-grandchildren. Her ashes went back to the Artists Cemetery at Woodstock, where her father and mother already lay, and her funeral asked for gifts to the Southwest Indian Foundation and Heifer Project International in place of flowers.

bio.bio_blurb: Father of the United States Naval Academy

people.research_notes: Findagrave's biography makes him first commandant of the Naval Academy to 1859; the USNA mathematics department's own history makes him the first head of its Department of Mathematics, which is followed here. Parents Mary Kerr and William Marc Chauvenet, not built.

narrative_blocks.header: He drafted the school that became Annapolis
narrative_blocks.body: Hired in 1841 to teach midshipmen at the naval school in Philadelphia, he drew up the plans that became the United States Naval Academy in 1845, moved the school to Annapolis and headed its mathematics from the start. The reorganisation of 1850 made mathematics one of the six original departments.

narrative_blocks.header: An admiral called him the Academy's father
narrative_blocks.body: Admiral S. R. Franklin proclaimed him the Father of the Naval Academy in 1890, twenty years after his death. Chauvenet Hall, dedicated at Annapolis in 1969, holds the mathematics department he founded, and a Navy survey ship was named for him in 1970.

narrative_blocks.header: His trigonometry was taught across the country
narrative_blocks.body: He wrote the Treatise on Plane and Spherical Trigonometry and the Manual of Spherical and Practical Astronomy, and American colleges taught out of both. He was a founding member of the National Academy of Sciences and a president of the American Association for the Advancement of Science.

narrative_blocks.header: He left Annapolis for a St. Louis chair
narrative_blocks.body: He went to Washington University in St. Louis in 1859 to teach mathematics and astronomy and was its second chancellor from 1862 to 1869, giving it up when his health failed. He died at St. Paul in December 1870, fifty years old.

narrative_blocks.header: A prize for mathematical writing bears his name
narrative_blocks.body: The Mathematical Association of America created the Chauvenet Prize for mathematical exposition in 1925, and it is still awarded. Edward Singleton Holden lodged in his house as a student and married his daughter Mary in 1871.

career.role: Head of the Department of Mathematics

sources.short: NYT obituaries 30 Oct 1912 and 8 Jan 1937; Woman's Who's Who of America 1914; NAS Biographical Memoir by W. W. Campbell; Wikipedia; USNA Mathematics Department history; Findagrave

people.research_notes: Regis Chauvenet is described on this card rather than built as a person (Sam, 8 Sep 2026); his birth and death years were never supplied.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived him by thirty-eight years
narrative_blocks.body: She married William Chauvenet at Philadelphia in 1840 and outlived him by thirty-eight years. She died in the city she was born in, at eighty-nine, and every memorial that carries the Chauvenet name - the hall, the prize and the ship - came after her.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son ran the Colorado School of Mines
narrative_blocks.body: Her son Regis took his first degree at Washington University, where his father was chancellor, then a bachelor of science at Harvard, and went west as a mining engineer. He was professor of chemistry and metallurgy at the Colorado School of Mines and afterwards its president, wrote Chemical and Metallurgical Calculations, and presided over the Colorado Scientific Society in 1896.

narrative_blocks.header: She took the whole family into her house
narrative_blocks.body: She took her daughter Mary and the three grandchildren into her St. Louis house after the 1880 separation, ten years a widow herself. Thirty-four of the letters she wrote to Mildred survive.

bio.bio_blurb: Justice of the New York Supreme Court

people.research_notes: Elizabeth Page's typescript biography gives the senate as 1904-1908, the Appellate Division as 1913 and the referee appointment as 1929; Wikipedia and the 1931 New York Times obituary give 1905-1908, 1916 and 1930, followed here. Parents Charles Page and Angeline Rider, not built. He lived at 2,202 Loring Place in the Bronx; Yale holds the Page family papers, MS 772. Charles Evans Hughes, whom he put onto the gas inquiry and nominated for governor, is not in the tree - and is the same Chief Justice his great-granddaughter Jing befriended as a child on the Supreme Court terrace.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty years in New York's public affairs
narrative_blocks.body: He sat for the nineteenth district in the state senate from 1905 to 1908, went onto the Supreme Court of New York in 1910 and up to its Appellate Division, First Department, in 1916. He resigned the bench in 1923 for the firm of Ingraham, Page and Moran, and was made an official referee in the last year of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: His line came over with Winthrop's fleet
narrative_blocks.body: He came down from John Page of the Middle Temple, who reached Boston with Winthrop's company in 1630 and became a founder of Watertown, through four more Johns and a William who was a surgeon with a colonel's rank in the Revolution. His father died in his freshman year at Williams, and he left college to keep the family and read law at night.

narrative_blocks.header: He put Hughes onto the gas inquiry
narrative_blocks.body: He moved the resolution that set a committee on New York's gas and electric companies, sat on it, and it was by his doing that Charles Evans Hughes was engaged as its counsel. The report produced the eighty-cent gas bill, which he helped frame, and in 1908 he nominated Hughes for governor.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight hours a day for state work
narrative_blocks.body: He carried labour bills making eight hours a legal day's work on municipal and state jobs and for children, and cutting railroad men's hours to sixteen. He sponsored the mortgage tax bill and the measures that created the Public Service Commission.

narrative_blocks.header: He tried Harry Thaw over the Matteawan escape
narrative_blocks.body: In March 1915 he presided over the trial of Harry K. Thaw for conspiring to break out of the Matteawan State Hospital for the Criminally Insane. Thirteen years later he headed the lawyers' association committee that went after ambulance chasing.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife could not get to his bedside
narrative_blocks.body: He went to the Long Island Country Club at Eastport for the weekend, was stricken on the Saturday and died of pneumonia at Southampton Hospital. His daughter Marjorie and her husband were with him; Elizabeth had broken her hip the March before and could not leave the house.

bio.bio_blurb: Author of The Tree of Liberty; Grenfell volunteer and Quaker pacifist

people.research_notes: Her 1969 obituary gives her husband's death as 1959; FamilySearch gives 23 Aug 1960, followed here. She had no children; the obituary names a stepson, Burton Harris of Boulder, and two step-grandsons, Bert and Frank Harris, none built. A fourth book, Wilderness Adventure, and an unfinished book on the family background and youth of Thomas Jefferson are named there too. Findagrave gives her death as 12 Mar 1969 and styles her Elizabeth Merwin 'Bess' Page Harris; her Manchester obituary gives 11 March, followed here.

narrative_blocks.header: Four years running the White Bay unit
narrative_blocks.body: From 1921 to 1925 Bess ran the Grenfell mission's White Bay unit in Newfoundland, teaching hungry children and selling the fishermen's wives' handicrafts in America. She steered a small boat through fog to remote coves.

narrative_blocks.header: She drove the wagon trail in a Ford
narrative_blocks.body: At sixteen Bess read her great-uncle Henry Page's gold-rush letters of 1849. Working in a doctors' office at Basin, Wyoming, she made his story into Wagons West, following the covered-wagon route in her old Ford. Wild Horses and Gold followed, from a Basin old-timer's Yukon memories.

narrative_blocks.header: Jefferson against Hamilton, in a thousand pages
narrative_blocks.body: The Tree of Liberty runs three generations of one Virginia family through the clash between Jefferson's democracy and the aristocratic government Hamilton stood for. Henry Steele Commager reviewed it on the front page of The New York Times Book Review, and it was a best-seller through most of 1939.

narrative_blocks.header: Cary Grant played her hero
narrative_blocks.body: Columbia filmed The Tree of Liberty in 1940 as The Howards of Virginia, with Cary Grant and Martha Scott, and Bess wrote for the screen herself on The Dark Command. With the film money she bought annuities for three elderly relatives.

narrative_blocks.header: Her life of Jefferson was never finished
narrative_blocks.body: Bess spent her last years on Heritage and Challenge, a book on Thomas Jefferson's family and youth. She was still writing it when she died near Oaxaca in 1969, and her sister Marjorie could not find it a publisher.

narrative_blocks.header: In Europe for both world wars
narrative_blocks.body: Bess ran a Y.M.C.A. canteen near Bordeaux in the First World War and, as a Quaker, worked with refugees in Europe after the Second. In California she opposed the removal of Japanese Americans, and in 1968 she told the President she would not pay the Vietnam War tax.

narrative_blocks.header: A hundred and fifty letters, then a wedding
narrative_blocks.body: Bess met Dr. Herbert Taylor Harris at Basin, where he was married to her second cousin Caroline. After Caroline died in 1953 he wrote Bess nearly 150 letters, and they married in December 1954.

education.notes: On a scholarship in memory of its founder, her grandfather

narrative_blocks.header: A doctor in the Bighorn Basin
narrative_blocks.body: Bert practiced medicine at Basin, Wyoming, with Dr. Chester E. Harris, and from 1927 to 1931 Bess Page kept their office. She wrote Wagons West while she worked for them.

narrative_blocks.header: His son wrote John Colter's life
narrative_blocks.body: Bert's son Burton Harris wrote John Colter: His Years in the Rockies, published in 1952, a life of the Lewis and Clark man who went on to be the first white man known to see Yellowstone.

bio.bio_blurb: Career volunteer; force behind the Clayman Institute

people.research_notes: Her four children - Christopher 'Cricket', Timothy, Jennifer and the Rev. Holly Lyman Antolini - and her granddaughter, the radio producer Tina Antolini, are named in her obituary but not built. The Richard W. Lyman Graduate Residences and the Jing Lyman Commons opened at Stanford in 1997; the Stanford Alumni Association gave her the Degree of Uncommon Woman in 1991. She died at Channing House in Palo Alto after a two-and-a-half-year illness, and asked for gifts to Enterprise Community Partners or the Clayman Institute in place of flowers.

narrative_blocks.header: There would be no Clayman Institute without her
narrative_blocks.body: She was a key player in creating what is now the Michelle R. Clayman Institute for Gender Research at Stanford, founded in 1974, and told its founder which private supporters to ask. Myra Strober said flatly that without her there would be no institute.

narrative_blocks.header: A nonsense rhyme gave her the name Jing
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother, presented with her eight hours after the birth, said 'Ah, the Lady Jingly Jones', out of an Edward Lear rhyme, and could never afterwards explain why. She was Jingly as a child and shortened it herself; at eight, in Washington, she roller-skated on the marble terrace of the Supreme Court, which got her into trouble with the park police and into a friendship with Chief Justice Charles Evans Hughes.

narrative_blocks.header: She called herself a career volunteer
narrative_blocks.body: She defined it as a significant life work demanding focused energy, developing competence and ending in a recognisable sphere of influence, and said she had married a man who could support her habit because she never earned any money. She helped organise and sustain Midpeninsula Citizens for Fair Housing, the Stanford Midpeninsula Urban Coalition, Women and Philanthropy at Washington and the National Coalition for Women's Enterprise in New York.

narrative_blocks.header: She knitted through every meeting she sat in
narrative_blocks.body: Her knitting went everywhere, meetings and sports events alike - 'this is how I focus' - and produced masterful sweaters usually several sizes too large for whoever was to wear them. At her eightieth birthday party more than eighty guests came, each in a Jing-made sweater.

narrative_blocks.header: He saw her asleep in the Friends library
narrative_blocks.body: Richard Lyman noticed a gorgeous creature falling asleep in the Swarthmore Friends Library and asked a friend who she was. They married in 1947 on Great Spruce Head Island in Penobscot Bay, had four children, and she was first lady of Stanford from 1970 to 1980.

Wallace Sterling Professor of Humanities emeritus; fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and the Royal Historical Society, honorary fellow of the London School of Economics, member of the American Philosophical Society (1998); director of IBM and Chase Manhattan, of the Council on Foundations, and chairman of Independent Sector and of the Association of American Universities. NOTE: the Peter Goldmark who followed him at the Rockefeller Foundation is Peter C. Goldmark Jr. of the Port Authority, NOT Peter James Goldmark (HD9864) of Washington State - different men.

military_service.notes: Drafted 1943, served three years

narrative_blocks.header: Both his successors said he saved Stanford
narrative_blocks.body: He was provost from 1967 and president from September 1970 to 1980, through the most disruptive years an American campus had seen, and both the presidents who followed him said that Dick Lyman saved Stanford. He called in the sheriff to clear the Encina Hall occupation and told the Academic Council afterwards that no one was entitled to consider it a victory.

narrative_blocks.header: Rocks came through his children's windows
narrative_blocks.body: A bottle of red paint went through his kitchen window in April 1970, narrowly missing a security guard, and two large rocks were thrown through an upstairs window in the night, landing in the sewing room next to his sleeping daughter Holly. He took his wife and children to watch the police clear Encina, because Jing thought they should see for themselves.

narrative_blocks.header: The Economist tried to hire him away
narrative_blocks.body: He spent 1951 and 1952 at the London School of Economics on a Fulbright, researching a doctorate on Britain's first Labour government and publishing it in 1957. He wrote for The Economist while he was there and impressed its editor enough to be offered its Washington bureau, but he meant to be a historian.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the Rockefeller Foundation for eight years
narrative_blocks.body: He left Stanford in 1980 for the presidency of the Rockefeller Foundation and held it to 1988, then came back to found the university's institute for international studies and direct it until 1991. He chaired the Association of American Universities and the Commission on the Humanities, and France made him an officer of the Legion of Honour.

narrative_blocks.header: He read Larkin and identified with Eeyore
narrative_blocks.body: His daughter Holly said at his memorial that he held to fervent moderation and the priority of the rational over the emotional until things calmed down, and then laid the groundwork for the university that followed. She also said he loved the poetry of Philip Larkin and T. S. Eliot, and identified with Eeyore.

people.research_notes: Living; birth year not supplied. Her two daughters, Tina and Tessa, are named in the diocesan profile but not built. Her father's 2012 memorial address is hers.

narrative_blocks.header: The first woman to be St. James's rector
narrative_blocks.body: She was installed at St. James's in Cambridge on 21 September 2008, the first woman rector in that church's history, with the Bishop of Maine preaching in recognition of her twelve years in that diocese. She led the congregation through building a new parish house inside a condominium development.

narrative_blocks.header: She was nominated for bishop of Massachusetts
narrative_blocks.body: She was one of seven candidates for election as the sixteenth bishop of the Episcopal Diocese of Massachusetts, which went to Alan Gates. She had served as deputy and alternate to General Convention from both Maine and Virginia, sat two terms on Maine's Standing Committee, mentored seminarians and deacons in formation, and worked against racism.

narrative_blocks.header: She spoke for her father at his memorial
narrative_blocks.body: She said that something hopeful had held Richard Lyman, through affirmative action and Nixonian politics and the Vietnam protests, to fervent moderation and the priority of the rational over the emotional until things began to calm down. She was the one who told the room he loved Larkin and Eliot and identified with Eeyore.

narrative_blocks.header: Six parishes in twenty-six years of priesthood
narrative_blocks.body: She preached social justice in six parishes across Maine, Massachusetts and Virginia over twenty-six years, and founded an extra-faith contemplative environmental ministry, the small voice ministry at Pin Point Farm in Cushing, Maine. She took her first degree at Yale before the Church Divinity School of the Pacific.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a Harvard couple on Deer Isle
narrative_blocks.body: In September 1995 she performed the marriage of Cornelia Hughes Dayton and James Shilts Boster, both associate professors at Irvine, at the Pilgrim's Inn on Deer Isle in Maine. She likes to take credit for the marriages she has made.

narrative_blocks.body: She published an account in the Manchester Journal in February 1869, A Lost Family Found, of Cyrus Branch, the sexton of her church, who had got out of Virginia thirty-three years before and had not seen his family since. He had been chased by dogs and shot twice, and went armed with a loaded pistol until the Civil War, because the fugitive slave law reached even into Vermont.

narrative_blocks.body: She was preceptress of Oxford Academy in New York when she married Joseph Dresser Wickham in October 1834, and his daughter Emma was two, motherless since eight days after her birth. She found the child difficult - the pampered favourite, she said, of all her grandparents - and Emma named her own first daughter Elizabeth Merwin all the same.

bio.bio_blurb: 23rd Chief of Protocol of the United States

people.research_notes: Living. Daughter of Lebanese immigrants; valedictorian at Dobyns-Bennett High School, Kingsport, 1946. Chairman Emeritus of the Blair House Foundation; her Fleur Cowles correspondence is at the University of Texas at Austin and her Washington Opera collection at the Library of Congress. Oral history recorded by Charles Stuart Kennedy for ADST, November 2003. Author of Keeper of the Gate (Simon and Schuster, 1990). Nancy Reagan is credited with putting her name forward when Lee Annenberg resigned; Jackie Kennedy gave her the first interview of her marriage, which she said made her career. Her family came from Arsoun in Lebanon, the village that also produced Ralph Nader; she learned Arabic on two childhood years there and refused to speak it afterwards.

narrative_blocks.header: She held the protocol office longest
narrative_blocks.body: Reagan made her Chief of Protocol in April 1982 and she kept it to January 1989, longer than anyone before or since, running ten state visits a year. The call came from Mike Deaver while she was in Brazil for Town & Country; she had never asked for the job, or any job.

narrative_blocks.header: She was on a newspaper at sixteen
narrative_blocks.body: The daughter of Lebanese Druze immigrants at Kingsport in Tennessee, she wrote for the Kingsport Times from sixteen and went back every summer through school and Vassar, where her classmates named her Lucky for her luck at bridge and poker. She began on obituaries and moved to social copy - tea parties, brides' dresses - and never guessed she would end in the world of protocol.

narrative_blocks.header: He knew she was Druze by her head
narrative_blocks.body: Archie Roosevelt was the last of five State Department interviews on her list and she took him first, not knowing the CIA was interviewing her too. He told her he had seen at once she was neither Christian nor Moslem, and had worked out she must be Druze from the shape of her head. He drove her to Vassar next day and said they would marry; they did, three months later.

narrative_blocks.header: Six years to put Blair House right
narrative_blocks.body: She shut the President's guest house in 1982 and Reagan cut the ribbon in 1988 - four basements gutted into one kitchen, a wing added with a ballroom, the old press room turned into the table treaties are signed on. She raised the decorating money herself, and talked a Lebanese-American senator out of blocking the appropriation by asking why he would give a nice Lebanese girl such grief.

narrative_blocks.header: Mitterrand was late on purpose, exactly
narrative_blocks.body: Reagan had kept him waiting twenty minutes at the G-7, having stopped to see the widow of an embassy official who had been shot. She told the President to relax before that evening's dinner because Mitterrand would arrive exactly twenty minutes late, and he did. Diplomatic language, she said; the thing to do is ignore it.

career.role: Chief of Protocol of the United States

narrative_blocks.header: He catalogued American painters and their houses
narrative_blocks.body: He wrote for Harper's and The Century and published book after book on American art — American Painters, Hours with Art and Artists, Recent Ideals of American Art. Two more, Artistic Houses and Artistic Country-Seats, went room by room through the houses of the newly rich.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave the valedictory, then returned to teach
narrative_blocks.body: He entered the College of New Jersey in April 1860, near the close of freshman year, and graduated valedictorian of the class of 1863. Two years at Union Seminary followed, and then he returned to Princeton as tutor of Latin and, in 1866, of belles lettres.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught Oriental languages before writing on art
narrative_blocks.body: From 1867 to 1873 he was instructor in the Oriental languages at Union Theological Seminary in New York. He left that work for journalism and art criticism, and lived for years in London as the representative of the publishers D. Appleton & Company.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote his own classmates’ obituaries
narrative_blocks.body: Elected class secretary in the senior recitation room in March 1863, he kept the record of the class of sixty-three for forty years and printed its first volume in 1867. The long obituaries of seven classmates in the fortieth-year book were his, and the historian who followed him acknowledged the debt.

narrative_blocks.header: He got inside Tiffany’s own rooms in 1883
narrative_blocks.body: He put the hall of Louis Comfort Tiffany’s apartment on East Twenty-sixth Street, stained-glass window and all, into Artistic Houses in 1883. Tiffany and John La Farge were fighting in court that year over which of them had invented the glass.

narrative_blocks.header: He married into a Princeton president’s line
narrative_blocks.body: In April 1874 he married Sara Edwards Annin, whose great-great-grandfather Jonathan Edwards had died president of the college where he took his degree and taught. Her father had been shot in the New York draft riots eleven years before.

narrative_blocks.header: Three wars, and a colonel at the end
narrative_blocks.body: He served in the Spanish-American War, on the Mexican border, and in France, and was a colonel of infantry by the armistice. He was still at the Infantry School at Fort Benning in 1924, and died at Albany at fifty-four.

narrative_blocks.header: He walked forward under the guns at Grand-Pré
narrative_blocks.body: In the attack on Grand-Pré on 15 October 1918 he went forward through artillery and machine-gun fire and took personal command of his leading battalion, and the town was taken. He was given the Distinguished Service Cross for it, and for what he did three weeks later.

narrative_blocks.header: He went out to find the guns himself
narrative_blocks.body: When machine guns stopped his leading units before Oches on 4 November 1918, he crossed to the skirmish line himself to judge the strength of the enemy position. The guns he located were destroyed by American artillery, and he stayed with his forward elements through the advance to the Meuse.

military_service.notes: Distinguished Service Cross, awarded under the Act of Congress of 9 July 1918, for repeated acts of extraordinary heroism.
Service on the Mexican border.

narrative_blocks.header: Born and dead on the same date
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Montclair on 1 November 1877 and died on 1 November 1915, on his thirty-eighth birthday. His father had done the same thing, dying at Princeton on his own seventy-first.

narrative_blocks.header: He took his grandfather’s name to the bar
narrative_blocks.body: He went from Phillips Exeter into the law and became a partner in the New Rochelle firm of Albertson, Sheldon and Simmons. A heart attack killed him at Charlottesville, Virginia, at forty-seven.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine days short of his third birthday
narrative_blocks.body: He was nine days short of his third birthday when his mother, Leonora Wilson Sheldon, died in August 1904 and was buried at Princeton. She was twenty-seven, and he was her only child.

narrative_blocks.header: Her maiden name became her son’s first name
narrative_blocks.body: She was a Sheldon of the Princeton family, and when her son was born at Chicago in 1926 she gave him her maiden name for his given one. He signed it on half a century of American history books.

narrative_blocks.header: Both Sheldon sisters ended up in Chicago
narrative_blocks.body: She married Arthur Paul Meyer, a Chicago man, two days after Christmas in 1923 and had her son there in 1926. Her sister Katharine’s daughter was born in the same city the year after — two New Jersey girls raising children a thousand miles from Princeton.

narrative_blocks.header: A Chicago man who married into Princeton
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Chicago in May 1894 and married Hester Truslow Sheldon of New Jersey two days after Christmas in 1923. Their son Sheldon, born in Chicago three years later, took his mother’s surname for a first name and became Oxford’s great American-history editor.

narrative_blocks.header: He made Oxford an American history house
narrative_blocks.body: He joined Oxford University Press in 1956, when its American list had none of the standing of Harper or Knopf, and left it the dominant house in the field. Six of the books he edited won Pulitzer Prizes and seventeen won the Bancroft.

narrative_blocks.header: He hunted manuscripts on campus, not by mail
narrative_blocks.body: Other university press editors waited for manuscripts to arrive; he went onto campuses to ask young professors what they were working on and to tell them Oxford wanted it. Rival editors found he had reached every campus before them.

narrative_blocks.header: He built the black history shelf from nothing
narrative_blocks.body: He commissioned the books that founded whole fields — Lawrence Levine on black consciousness, Nathan Huggins on the Harlem Renaissance, Albert Raboteau on slave religion, Gerda Lerner on feminist consciousness. Each opened a subject the academy had thought unpublishable.

narrative_blocks.header: He argued jazz and baseball into Oxford
narrative_blocks.body: The dons of a press founded in 1478 took convincing that Basie and the Brooklyn Dodgers were fit subjects for it. He published Gunther Schuller’s Early Jazz, Alec Wilder’s American Popular Song and Harold Seymour’s history of baseball anyway, and Oxford took a prize for the jazz list in 1987.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave the Civil War its standard book
narrative_blocks.body: He brought out James McPherson’s Battle Cry of Freedom in 1988; it took the cover of the New York Times Book Review, won the Pulitzer, and became a national bestseller. It is still the one-volume history of the war people are sent to.

narrative_blocks.header: His authors wrote him his own book
narrative_blocks.body: In 2000 Oxford published American Places, essays by more than two dozen of his historians — a festschrift of a kind reserved for professors, never editors. He was still editing William Freehling and Ben Procter in the summer before he died.

narrative_blocks.body: Twenty-five years of strategic communications have carried her through Fountain House, the UN Development Programme and MedGlobal, through Dartmouth, John Jay College and Ascend Public Charter Schools, and through Deloitte and Chemonics. narrative_blocks.body: She works with the Chamberlain Network, Lawyers Defending American Democracy and the Unite for Veterans Coalition, on organizing locally and speaking nationally about American democracy. She lives in Washington.

narrative_blocks.header: He edited the overnight wire in New York
narrative_blocks.body: He was the overnight editor of the International News Service in New York through the 1950s, and afterwards public relations director of T. J. Ross. He died at forty-six, leaving a wife and three children at Katonah.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty years a studio member at McGuffey
narrative_blocks.body: She held a studio at the McGuffey Art Center in Charlottesville from 1978 to 1997, showing oils, collages and pastels in solo, duo and group exhibitions. Her work hung as well at the Babcock Fine Arts Center, the Staunton Fine Arts Gallery and the University of Virginia hospital.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept a Vinalhaven studio for thirty years
narrative_blocks.body: From 1970 she worked from a studio on Vinalhaven Island off the Maine coast, showing at Maine Coast Artists in Rockport, the Wingspread Gallery at Northeast Harbor, and galleries on Rockland, Vinalhaven and North Haven. She had come to Charlottesville from Katonah in 1977, and went north to Brunswick in 2002.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed by the Pacific, then divorced
narrative_blocks.body: She was widowed in 1943 when her first husband, Major Richard Mather Marshall Jr. of the Army Air Forces, was killed in the Pacific, and divorced in 1950 from the television executive James Otis Parsons Jr. William Annin Paddock was her third husband.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a Schieffelin at Mount Kisco
narrative_blocks.body: She was married in October 1984 at the Presbyterian Church of Mount Kisco to Andrew Lawrence Schieffelin, whose father had chaired the wine and spirit importers Schieffelin and Company. She had come through the Cisqua School, the Darrow School and Boston University.

narrative_blocks.header: His father chaired the family wine house
narrative_blocks.body: He was a son of William Jay Schieffelin III of Mount Kisco, who chaired Schieffelin and Company, the wine and spirit importers his family had run since Jacob Schieffelin founded the firm in New York in 1793. His grandfather had headed it for the forty years before that.

narrative_blocks.header: Jay on one side, Vanderbilt on the other
narrative_blocks.body: He came down from John Jay, the first Chief Justice, through his father’s line, and from Commodore Cornelius Vanderbilt through his great-grandmother Maria Louise Shepard. He went to the Bedford-Rippowam School and New England College, and was selling for the outfitter Eddie Bauer at Stamford when he married.

narrative_blocks.header: She went back to work as a programmer
narrative_blocks.body: She worked for IBM before marrying Robert Bradford Paddock of Katonah in 1955, and returned to the workforce in 1975 as a programmer and systems analyst with C-E Natco. She stayed fifteen years, and gave her own hours to the symphony, the ballet and the opera.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Wellesley women a generation apart
narrative_blocks.body: She took her Wellesley degree in 1954, forty-five years after her husband’s mother had taken hers at the same college and been elected Phi Beta Kappa there. Both of them then married Paddocks.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brother and sisters became the Carrs
narrative_blocks.body: She made What Katy Did out of her Cleveland childhood in 1872, turning her brother and sisters into the Carr children — Jane became Clover, Elizabeth and Theodora became Elsie and Johnnie, William became Phil. Katy Carr, tall and impulsive, was herself, and most of her shorter stories went first into the children’s magazine St. Nicholas.

narrative_blocks.header: Her pen name began as a family joke
narrative_blocks.body: She signed herself Susan Coolidge because her sister Jane had published stories as Margaret Coolidge, and she would be a sister of the famous Margaret. She kept the name for the next thirty-four years.

narrative_blocks.header: She nursed with Helen Hunt Jackson
narrative_blocks.body: Through the Civil War she worked at the Knight Hospital in New Haven, helping to organise its nursing service, alongside Helen Hunt Jackson. Jackson stayed her closest friend and pushed her into writing in earnest after her father died in 1870.

narrative_blocks.header: She edited Austen and Burney too
narrative_blocks.body: Between the Katy books she edited Mrs. Delany’s correspondence, Frances Burney’s diary and Jane Austen’s letters, translated Gautier, and published three volumes of her own verse. She read manuscripts for Roberts Brothers of Boston and appeared in their 1878 anthology A Masque of Poets, where every poem was printed unsigned.

narrative_blocks.header: She never married, and kept the Jungle
narrative_blocks.body: She never married. After her father’s death the family settled at Newport in a high-ceilinged, book-lined house they called the Jungle, and she lived there until she died in 1905. She lies in the Woolsey ground at Dosoris under one line: I shall be satisfied when I awake with Thy likeness.

narrative_blocks.header: She put real people into a children’s book
narrative_blocks.body: What Katy Did Next of 1886 walked Katy through Europe past real things — George Eliot climbing out of a cab in London, gowns ordered from Worth in Paris, books borrowed from an expatriate library in Florence. It is a girls’ novel and a record of Victorian travel at once.

narrative_blocks.header: She married Johns Hopkins’s first president
narrative_blocks.body: She was thirty-nine when she married Daniel Coit Gilman at Newport in June 1877, two years after he left the presidency of the University of California for the new Johns Hopkins. She was his second wife, and they had no children.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-six years of a university that didn't exist
narrative_blocks.body: Called to Baltimore in 1875, Gilman spent a year studying how universities were organised and choosing teachers before his inauguration in February 1876. He ran Johns Hopkins until 1901 and made the research doctorate the American standard.

narrative_blocks.header: Every medical school copied his entrance rule
narrative_blocks.body: Gilman opened the Johns Hopkins Hospital in 1889 and its medical school in 1893, and required a college degree of anyone who entered it. Every other American medical school followed.

narrative_blocks.header: California was told to copy no one
narrative_blocks.body: Inaugurated at the University of California in November 1872, Gilman told the state not to copy Berlin or New Haven but to build a university of the people. He put classroom buildings up at Berkeley and brought in the Toland medical school before the legislature wore him down.

narrative_blocks.header: A resignation letter blaming the climate
narrative_blocks.body: Gilman was the younger faculty's favourite for the Yale presidency, and the chair went to Noah Porter in 1871. His resignation the September after told Porter only that family and a change of climate had predisposed him to go.

narrative_blocks.header: A pamphlet that organised a scientific school
narrative_blocks.body: After two years among the technical schools of Europe, Gilman printed a private plan for organising Yale's school of science in 1856. He was the college librarian for nine years and took Sheffield's chair of physical and political geography in 1863.

narrative_blocks.header: Monroe, Dana, and the launching of a university
narrative_blocks.body: Gilman published a life of James Monroe in 1883, one of the Yale geologist James Dwight Dana, and a collection of his addresses as University Problems. The Launching of a University came out in 1906, four years after he took the new Carnegie Institution.

narrative_blocks.header: Four Yale years in his uncle's house
narrative_blocks.body: Gilman boarded through college with his uncle, the Latin professor James Luce Kingsley, instead of in college rooms. A cousin wrote fifty-six years later that he had been just like a son and brother to the household.

narrative_blocks.body: Woolsey reached Aiken from New Jersey about 1870 and joined the county's white residents in their campaign to take back the county government, staying active in it until they won in 1876. He lived there the next forty years and was counted a leader in the town's affairs.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at a Charleston hospital in 1910
narrative_blocks.body: Woolsey had been ill for months and went to the Riverside hospital at Charleston, where his family had good news of him on the Wednesday and word of his death on the Friday. He was carried north and buried in the Woolsey ground at Glen Cove two days later.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught English before he preached it
narrative_blocks.body: Before ordination Yardley was an instructor in English at Trinity College in Hartford, where he had been a student, and afterward at St. Stephen's College. He also served for years as secretary of the Catholic Club of Baltimore.

narrative_blocks.body: Isabel married Lieutenant Frank Marble of the Navy at her mother's house in Newport in August 1903, the Rev. E. J. Dennen of Trinity Church officiating before near relatives only. They went to Washington, where he had duty in the Bureau of Navigation.

narrative_blocks.body: Eva Thorne was the third of six children of William Henry Thorne and Eva Hart, who had married in Philadelphia in 1873, and a brother, Edmund, died before his second birthday. Her mother died in 1891, when Eva was thirteen.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived her husband by thirty-eight years
narrative_blocks.body: Eva married the Rev. Thomas Henry Yardley in 1905 and was widowed in 1933, when their three sons were twenty-seven, twenty-one and sixteen. She lived on at Chestnut Hill in Philadelphia and died in 1971, at ninety-three.

bio.bio_blurb: Episcopal priest and Rector of Chatham Hall

narrative_blocks.header: He ran a Virginia girls' school
narrative_blocks.body: William Woolsey Yardley taught English and the classics at day schools in New York and Pittsburgh, then took holy orders in his late thirties to qualify for the rectorship of Chatham Hall, a girls' school in southern Virginia. He held it from 1949 to 1973, and his son Jonathan grew up on that campus.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept Chatham Hall a school for girls
narrative_blocks.body: As boarding schools around him turned co-educational, Yardley held Chatham Hall to its founding purpose as a school for girls. In 1969 its first African American students enrolled.

narrative_blocks.header: The school keeps a day in his name
narrative_blocks.body: Chatham Hall marks Lee-Yardley Day every September for Yardley and the rector who chose him, Edmund Jennings Lee. He had started its first annual giving programme in 1956 and replaced the chapel's salvaged cinema organ with a baroque instrument built in Germany.

narrative_blocks.header: He owned one of three great Trollope collections
narrative_blocks.body: On a schoolmaster's pay Yardley assembled a house of fine American furniture and one of the three greatest collections of Trollope first editions in the country. The Redwood Library at Newport sold him what it called duplicates for as little as a dollar apiece.

narrative_blocks.header: He winked at God
narrative_blocks.body: William took holy orders in his late thirties more for the sake of the Chatham Hall job than from any true calling. His characteristic gesture was the wink: he winked at the world, and, his children knew, he winked at God.

narrative_blocks.header: He lies on Woolsey ground at Glen Cove
narrative_blocks.body: Yardley was buried in the Woolsey Cemetery at Glen Cove, the private burying ground of the Dosoris estate his grandmother's family had held since the 1720s. His great-great-grandfather John Mumford Woolsey lies there, and so does Sarah Chauncey Woolsey, his grandmother's sister. He was given the Woolsey name at birth and brought back to it at the end.

narrative_blocks.header: Two branches met again in his marriage
narrative_blocks.body: He came down from the Woolseys of New York through his grandmother Jane, and his wife Helen Gregory came down from the Ingersolls through hers. Two branches of one family had found each other again after nine generations.

narrative_blocks.header: Her sons carried the Ingersoll name
narrative_blocks.body: Helen and Alfred Gregory's first child, George Ingersoll Gregory, was born and died in 1910. Alfred Ingersoll Gregory lived to 2010, and Arthur Hawley Gregory took her father's first name and her uncle Robert's middle name: Robert Hawley Ingersoll, maker of the dollar watch.

narrative_blocks.header: She smuggled Lady Chatterley home from Mexico
narrative_blocks.body: Helen Gregory was in the first class to graduate from Bennington College, in 1936. As an undergraduate she came home from a trip to Mexico with a copy of Lady Chatterley's Lover, a novel then banned in the United States.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-four years as the rector's wife
narrative_blocks.body: From 1949 to 1973 Helen kept up the mandatory appearances, the student visits and the public composure that came with being the rector's wife at Chatham Hall, and raised four children. In later years she resented not having had more of a life of her own.

narrative_blocks.header: She read Jane Austen privately all her life
narrative_blocks.body: Helen Gregory Yardley took pleasure in Jane Austen throughout her adult life and kept the admiration to herself rather than to any society or circle. Her son Jonathan closed a column on Pride and Prejudice by saying the memory of that pleasure gave him the same.

narrative_blocks.header: We've all heard that one before
narrative_blocks.body: In retirement in Rhode Island, Helen grew impatient with her husband's rules for proper living and the rigid timetable he kept for comfort. Of yet another of his retold anecdotes, she said: "We've all heard that one before."

narrative_blocks.header: A son and a grandson with Pulitzers
narrative_blocks.body: Her son Jonathan won the 1981 Pulitzer Prize for criticism, and her grandson Jim won one in 2006 for reporting on the Chinese legal system, making them one of only two father-and-son pairs to have won.

narrative_blocks.header: He won the Pulitzer, then changed papers
narrative_blocks.body: Jonathan Yardley was book critic of the Washington Star when he won the 1981 Pulitzer Prize for criticism. He moved to the Washington Post the same year and reviewed books there for the next thirty-three years, retiring in December 2014.

narrative_blocks.header: He made careers and he ended them
narrative_blocks.body: Yardley championed Michael Chabon, Edward P. Jones, Anne Tyler and John Berendt early, and was as unsparing in the other direction: one book he called 'a genuinely, unrelievedly rotten book, one without a single redeeming virtue.' In 2003 he began Second Reading, a seven-year run of essays reconsidering neglected books.

narrative_blocks.header: He quoted Mao to Groton's graduates
narrative_blocks.body: Yardley finished at Groton in 1957 but could not afford to send his own children there. Invited back as its commencement speaker, he made a point of quoting Mao Tse-tung to the graduates.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote a whole book about his parents
narrative_blocks.body: When his mother died in 1986, Yardley found the letters, invitations and bills his parents had kept, and from them wrote Our Kind of People, published in 1989. His father William was an Episcopal minister and schoolmaster; his mother Helen brought the Ingersoll line into the family.

narrative_blocks.header: Father and son both won Pulitzers
narrative_blocks.body: Yardley and his son Jim, a New York Times foreign correspondent, are one of only two father-and-son pairs to have won Pulitzer Prizes. Jim's came in 2006 for reporting on the Chinese legal system, twenty-five years after his father's.

narrative_blocks.header: He drove the Mid-Atlantic to find his family
narrative_blocks.body: In States of Mind, published in 1993, Yardley drove the region he calls home and stopped in Philadelphia at the Church of St. James the Less to stand at his grandparents' graves. He went on to Yardley, Pennsylvania, where distant relatives still lived, and back to Chatham, Virginia, where he had learned his first lessons about race and regional identity.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-five years at one New York firm
narrative_blocks.body: Graham Sumner came out of Harvard Law in 1900 an editor of the Law Review, was admitted to the bar in 1901, and joined the New York firm that became Simpson Thacher and Bartlett. He practised there until the year he died, and sat as a special master of the U.S. District Court in 1934.

narrative_blocks.header: He edited two papers, at Yale and Harvard
narrative_blocks.body: At Yale he edited the Daily News in his senior year and was taken into Skull and Bones, graduating in 1897. He went on to Yale Law for a year and then to Harvard, taking his LL.B. cum laude in 1900.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran Englewood's schools and its war savings
narrative_blocks.body: Sumner sat on the Englewood board of education from 1913 to 1919 and was its president for four of those years. In the war he chaired the town's War Savings Campaign and served in the Englewood Home Guard.

narrative_blocks.header: He outlived his son by eleven months
narrative_blocks.body: His only recorded son, Graham Jr., died on 23 December 1945. Sumner died of cerebral thrombosis at Greenwich the following November and was buried at Alderbrook in Guilford.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Hooker lines met in his marriage
narrative_blocks.body: Graham Sumner came down from the Hookers through his mother, Jeannie Whittemore Elliott, who married the Yale sociologist William Graham Sumner. In 1903 at Newport he married Laura Woolsey Yardley, who came down through the Woolseys and the Dwights, so the descent ran into itself again.

narrative_blocks.header: Cuvier handed him the fossil fishes
narrative_blocks.body: Cuvier gave the young Swiss his own notes and drawings for a book on fossil fish, then died within months. Agassiz spent ten years on the five volumes of the Poissons fossiles and built a new classification out of scales and teeth.

narrative_blocks.header: He put an ice age over the north
narrative_blocks.body: In 1837 he told the Helvetic Society that glaciers had once flowed out of the Alps across Europe, Asia and North America and buried the northern hemisphere in ice. He built a hut on the Aar glacier and lived in it to watch the ice move.

narrative_blocks.header: He was the last to refuse Darwin outright
narrative_blocks.body: He founded Harvard’s Museum of Comparative Zoology in 1859, the year the Origin appeared, and argued against it for the rest of his life. A species, he said, was a thought of God, and after each extinction God made the world again.

narrative_blocks.header: He had two enslaved people photographed
narrative_blocks.body: In 1850 he commissioned daguerreotypes of Renty Taylor and his daughter Delia on a South Carolina plantation, to argue that Black people were a separate and lesser creation. They are the earliest known photographs of enslaved Americans.

narrative_blocks.header: His own descendants sided with Renty’s
narrative_blocks.body: The plates lay in a Peabody Museum attic until 1976. Tamara Lanier, who traces her descent from Renty, sued Harvard for them in 2019 with forty-three living Agassiz descendants backing her, and the case settled in 2025.

narrative_blocks.header: He opened a summer school on an island
narrative_blocks.body: In the summer of 1873 John Anderson gave him Penikese, a small island in Buzzards Bay off the Massachusetts coast below New Bedford, and endowed a school on it. Students there studied animals by direct observation, not out of books.

narrative_blocks.header: A boulder from the Aar over his grave
narrative_blocks.body: He died at Cambridge in December 1873, half a year after the first Penikese summer, and the school did not survive him by long. They set a boulder from the Aar moraine over him at Mount Auburn, under pines from his Swiss home.

narrative_blocks.header: A month spent reading Ulysses before he ruled
narrative_blocks.body: Customs had banned Ulysses on the ground that it might leave American readers with impure and lustful thoughts. Woolsey took almost a month to read the book and held on 6 December 1933 that it was not obscene in law and was a work of literary merit.

narrative_blocks.header: Random House printed his opinion in every copy
narrative_blocks.body: The case was a test engineered by Bennett Cerf, and when Random House began printing Ulysses it bound Woolsey's opinion into the front of every copy. The Second Circuit affirmed him two to one, and the opinion has been called the most widely distributed in judicial history.

narrative_blocks.header: Married Love and Contraception cleared customs too
narrative_blocks.body: Two years before Ulysses, Woolsey held that a physician's book on marital relations was not obscene, and then that Marie Stopes's book on birth control was neither obscene nor immoral and could not be seized.

narrative_blocks.header: Roosevelt's gold order fell on a signature
narrative_blocks.body: Woolsey struck down the executive order forbidding the hoarding of gold coin and bullion, on the ground that the President had signed it where the statute required the Secretary of the Treasury. The administration had to issue it again over Henry Morgenthau's name.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-two pages to clear Eugene O'Neill
narrative_blocks.body: A woman sued Eugene O'Neill and his publishers claiming Strange Interlude had been lifted from her privately printed novel. Woolsey found for O'Neill over forty-two printed pages, calling it a wholly preposterous claim, since no one may copyright words in the dictionary or ideas.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded the Columbia Law Review at twenty-four
narrative_blocks.body: Woolsey took his Yale degree in 1898 and his law degree at Columbia in 1901, and that same year founded the Columbia Law Review and served as its first secretary. Columbia gave him an LL.D. in 1929 and its law alumni made him their president in 1934.

narrative_blocks.header: He left Yale at seventeen for the Navy
narrative_blocks.body: Bacon quit Yale in 1861 and shipped as a captain's clerk, serving in the Caribbean and on the Mississippi aboard the Iroquois and Farragut's flagship Hartford. Dengue fever and failing eyesight did not stop him taking an infantry commission when he came ashore.

narrative_blocks.header: He led a Colored regiment into Richmond
narrative_blocks.body: Bacon took a captaincy in the 29th Connecticut Volunteers, a Colored regiment, saw hard fighting at Petersburg and led his men into Richmond on 3 April 1865. He was made major of the 117th United States Colored Infantry and served in the occupation of Texas.

narrative_blocks.header: His letters are franker than his sermons
narrative_blocks.body: Writing home to his half-sister Katherine through four years of war, Bacon set down what he thought of his black soldiers, of army mismanagement, and of orders sending them into Texas well hidden from their friends. An editor who printed the letters in 2009 called his view of them patronising at best.

narrative_blocks.header: He resigned his pulpit from a California holiday
narrative_blocks.body: Bacon had the Second Congregational Church at New London from 1877, and in 1885, away in California for his health, he abruptly resigned it to his congregation's surprise. Tuberculosis brought him back to California for good, and he died in Santa Clara County at forty-four.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandfather taught Yale medicine fifty years
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Elizabeth Staples was a granddaughter of Jonathan Knight, who became the first professor of anatomy and physiology when the Yale medical school was organised in 1813, moved to the chair of surgery, and lectured to students for more than fifty years. He resigned in May 1864 and died that August, and the government hospital at New Haven that took his name is now Yale-New Haven.

narrative_blocks.header: Leonard Bacon preached her grandfather's funeral
narrative_blocks.body: Leonard Bacon gave the funeral discourse for Jonathan Knight, and Bacon's son Francis, a physician, wrote the commemorative sketch. Five years later Mary married another of his sons, Edward Woolsey Bacon, and outlived him by seventeen years.

narrative_blocks.body: Martha Hooker married John L. Washburn of Duluth and was living at Concord and at Vinalhaven in Maine when he died. In January 1965 she married Edward H. deConingh of Shaker Heights in the chapel of the Arlington Street church in Boston, and went to live in Ohio.

narrative_blocks.header: Eleven years filling Duluth with parks
narrative_blocks.body: Paine ran Duluth's parks from 1926 to 1937 under Mayor Snively, with hundreds of WPA and CCC men to work with, and put in Leif Erikson Park, Chester Bowl, Chambers Grove, Memorial Park, Hartley Field, Wheeler Field and the Fond du Lac nursery. A city supervisor said later the volume of it would never be matched.

narrative_blocks.header: He opened Jay Cooke, then came back
narrative_blocks.body: Paine left the Forest Service in the West to become the first superintendent of Jay Cooke State Park in 1916, a year after it opened. He took leave to serve as a captain of engineers in the war, came back, and built Mission Creek Boulevard to link the park to Duluth's Skyline Parkway.

narrative_blocks.header: His plaque has spelled him wrong for decades
narrative_blocks.body: The marker put up for him at Oldenburg Point in Jay Cooke reads J. Rodney Paine, and the park has known about the wrong initial since at least 2012. That year Duluth named two thousand acres of forest above Fond du Lac the F. Rodney Paine Forest Preserve.

narrative_blocks.header: His father sat on the first park board
narrative_blocks.body: Frederic William Paine, a banker with a taste for land and giving it away, was a charter member of the Duluth park commission created the year his son was born. A city official said the son shared the passion but not the flash, and quietly left his mark.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped write the rules for pensions
narrative_blocks.body: Paine went from the Bureau of Labor Statistics into Hewitt Associates and became the firm's authority on benefits and pay. Hewitt was the only company asked onto the federal task force of 1964 to 1968 whose work became the pension act of 1974, and out of that came employee share plans and the 401(k).

narrative_blocks.header: Sinclair Lewis needed a chess opponent
narrative_blocks.body: The Nobel laureate spent a summer writing in Duluth and complained he could find nobody worth playing. Paine, then a boy known locally for his chess, spent the rest of that summer across the board from him.

narrative_blocks.header: Einstein asked him to tea over one article
narrative_blocks.body: Paine wrote a piece for the Princeton student paper on the futility and danger of the Cold War. Albert Einstein, then at the Institute, sent for him and gave him an afternoon of tea and talk about pacifism.

narrative_blocks.header: China, Hong Kong, then a Napa vineyard
narrative_blocks.body: In the early nineties Paine built a team to help the People's Republic privatise state industry, then another in 1994 to design Hong Kong's Mandatory Provident Fund before the handover. He retired from Hewitt, moved to Napa with his wife Teresa, and founded Vineyard 29, whose Cabernet reached cult status in ten years.

narrative_blocks.header: He left his hats at clients' offices
narrative_blocks.body: Hewitt gave up its rule that consultants wear hats to client meetings partly because Paine kept leaving his behind. He could turn almost any conversation to prime numbers, and could hang a row of spoons off his face in a good restaurant.

narrative_blocks.header: She fought for Duluth's wild parks
narrative_blocks.body: Anne was a persistent voice for the city's urban wilderness park system and helped lead the campaign that protected Brighton Beach. She was the fourth generation of her family to live in Duluth and the third to argue for its parks.

narrative_blocks.header: He photographed Booth and the woman on stage
narrative_blocks.body: For twenty years his gallery opposite the Metropolitan Hotel was the largest in New York, its painted sign calling it a Photographic Temple of Art. Sheridan and McClellan sat for him, and Tad Lincoln, and Laura Keene and John Wilkes Booth — who shared a stage at Ford's Theatre in April 1865.

narrative_blocks.header: He made the first life-sized portraits
narrative_blocks.body: In Paris in 1853 he used an enlarger of H. H. Snelling's to blow portraits up to life size, the first photographer anywhere to do it, and hired French artists to finish them in pastel. He brought half a dozen of those artists back to New York with him.

narrative_blocks.header: His first portrait was of a dead boy
narrative_blocks.body: The customs house at Angostura held his camera against a duty he would not pay. The chief merchant of the town, whose child had just died, paid it himself and asked Fredricks to take the picture; the town assembled to watch, and the first portrait he ever made was of the dead boy.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother's suicide note named him
narrative_blocks.body: George Fredericks took seventy grains of morphine in an office on the Bowery in July 1875, leaving a letter for the coroner that blamed his eldest brother — president and treasurer of the American Fire Detector Company — for a debt he would not pay. That brother was Charles, whose Broadway studio burned the same year.

narrative_blocks.header: He reached Paraguay driving a herd
narrative_blocks.body: His guides abandoned him on the Orinoco with his equipment, and he lay stranded twenty days before government men found him. He went back, crossed Brazil taking horses from villagers who had no cash, came into Paraguay driving a drove of them, and was given a jaguar at Buenos Aires.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother's firm took the name
narrative_blocks.body: He had set his brother Linson up in the photographic business on an agreement that the name would return when Linson withdrew, and in 1868 it reached a New York court. The advertisements began warning that no other photographer of the name worked in the city.

bio.bio_blurb: Brooklyn lawyer, and a photographer before that

career.notes: Living in Brooklyn and practising from a Chambers Street office by 1875.

narrative_blocks.header: He burst the door at 388 Bowery
narrative_blocks.body: Linson was at supper in Brooklyn when his brother's letter reached him, and he dropped everything and crossed the river. The door was locked and breaking it open was the work of a moment; inside, George lay on the floor with his head on a city directory and four chairs ranged in a row on either side of him.

narrative_blocks.header: A photographer who became a lawyer
narrative_blocks.body: Charles set him up in the photographic business on Broadway, and in 1868 he went to court to stop a former partner from trading as Fredericks and Company. By 1875 he was living in Brooklyn and practising law from an office at No. 7 Chambers Street.

narrative_blocks.header: He offered money and was always refused
narrative_blocks.body: Linson often pressed money on his brother George and George always turned it down, saying that Charles owed him and he wanted none from any other source. He was refusing it up to the week he died.

career.notes: He had read medicine in earlier years; the company office was where he died.

narrative_blocks.header: The letter was addressed to the coroner
narrative_blocks.body: "I do this thing with my eyes wide open and all my senses about me," he wrote on 21 July 1875, "simply to avoid starvation, which I believe is inevitable if I stay in the world." He had eaten one meal since Monday noon, and had taken seventy grains of morphine in pills he had made himself years before.

narrative_blocks.header: The debt he died over was his brother's
narrative_blocks.body: The note laid it on his eldest brother, who as president and treasurer of the American Fire Detector Company owed him money and did not wish to pay. The company itself owed George a sum that would have reached him within days; he owned some property and his credit was good wherever he was known.

narrative_blocks.header: Four chairs in a row on either side
narrative_blocks.body: Linson broke the locked door at 388 Bowery and found him on the floor with his head resting on a city directory and four chairs ranged in a row on each side of him. He was perfectly rational and began at once to talk about how soon he would die.

narrative_blocks.header: He had read medicine and knew the dose
narrative_blocks.body: He had studied medicine in earlier years and knew that poison on an empty stomach would do its work, so he stopped eating first. When his brother forced warm water, mustard and salt on him he drank it and remarked complacently that it would do no good.

narrative_blocks.header: He had tried once before and been stopped
narrative_blocks.body: Friends had interfered in time some years earlier. He was of a morbid disposition and constantly imagined that every kind of catastrophe would overtake him, and he left a wife and seven children.

burial.plot_notes: Cremated; ashes scattered from the air over California.

education.school_name: Air Force Aerospace Research Pilot School

military_service.notes: Twenty-six years. Two Distinguished Flying Crosses, the Legion of Merit, the Meritorious Service Medal and eight Air Medals.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the day after graduation
narrative_blocks.body: He met Theresa Varcolik in a Washington high school and won his West Point appointment from a District commissioner. They were married at the Holy Trinity Catholic Chapel the day after he graduated with the class of 1954.

narrative_blocks.header: B-47s first, then two tours in Vietnam
narrative_blocks.body: Pilot and navigator training put him on combat-ready Strategic Air Command B-47 crews through the Cold War. In Vietnam he was a forward air controller at Pleiku, an RF-4C reconnaissance pilot at Udorn and a war plans officer in Saigon.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Flying Crosses and eight Air Medals
narrative_blocks.body: He came out a colonel after twenty-six years, with two Distinguished Flying Crosses, the Legion of Merit, the Meritorious Service Medal and eight Air Medals. Most of the assignments between the combat tours were testing and evaluating advanced aerospace systems.

narrative_blocks.header: He died on a routine check flight
narrative_blocks.body: Out of the Air Force he kept flying as a test pilot, perfecting aerial refuelling for the Navy and validating weapons delivery systems. On 14 May 1993 he was the instructor pilot on a routine check flight over the Nevada desert when the aircraft came down.

narrative_blocks.header: His ashes fell from a skydivers' formation
narrative_blocks.body: They were scattered from the skies over California by a formation of his skydiving colleagues. His eldest son jumped with them.

narrative_blocks.header: Guys and Dolls got her a husband
narrative_blocks.body: She was teaching elementary school on the Marine Corps base at Quantico when a young Pentagon lawyer, hearing she had been in a production of Guys and Dolls there, asked her help blocking the choreography for a show he had been cast in. The collaboration ran to nearly sixty years of marriage.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifteen years on the school board
narrative_blocks.body: She took a master's at Fairfield University while raising three sons, ran for the Board of Education and stayed fifteen years, presiding as chairwoman through the consolidation of the town's two high schools into one. She had been president of the local League of Women Voters first.

narrative_blocks.header: Her first one-woman show came at seventy-two
narrative_blocks.body: She placed second at the Fairfield Sidewalk Art Show in the nineteen-seventies and painted watercolors from then on, through group trips to Provence and Italy. Her first one-woman show came at seventy-two, and glaucoma stopped the last painting at eighty-nine.

narrative_blocks.header: They called her Rocky
narrative_blocks.body: Family and close friends used the name for a determined, fighting spirit. She had a soft spot for poodles and left behind an extensive collection of poodle figurines.

career.notes: More than fifty years of practice in the town he settled in.

military_service.notes: Drafted after Yale Law School and sent to Officer Candidate School; served as a J.A.G. officer at the Pentagon.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty years of law in one town
narrative_blocks.body: Drafted out of Yale Law School in 1955, Fray went to Officer Candidate School and served as a Judge Advocate General officer at the Pentagon, where he met Claire Fredricks. He then practised in Fairfield for more than fifty years, and gave the Kiwanis Club there fifty as well.

narrative_blocks.header: He would break into a soft shoe
narrative_blocks.body: Fray danced, sang, acted and directed with the Nutmeg Music Theater, the Downtown Cabaret, the Patterson Follies and the Hoot Owls, and played trumpet in Bridgeport polka bands in the fifties. Tap was the great one: well into his eighties, wherever an audience could be found, he would break into a little soft shoe.

career.organization: Christ Our King School, Mount Pleasant, South Carolina

narrative_blocks.header: She went south as a Catholic missionary
narrative_blocks.body: Out of Trinity College she and some teacher friends moved to Charleston as Catholic missionaries to teach in the diocesan schools, and she took a post at Christ Our King in Mount Pleasant. She met Jack Santos there and married him in April 1963.

narrative_blocks.header: Six children over eighteen years
narrative_blocks.body: The first came in March 1964 and she gave up teaching for the house; six in all, and twelve grandchildren. She and Jack kept their fifty-first anniversary before he died in November 2014.

narrative_blocks.header: Her friends called her a steel magnolia
narrative_blocks.body: The name was for beauty on the outside and a steely resolve inside, and it held through the illness that killed her in March 2016. She never complained, and worried only that she was a burden to the people nursing her.

narrative_blocks.header: The first child, and dead before her brothers
narrative_blocks.body: Lavinia was born in April 1812, the year after her parents married, and was eleven years older than the twins who followed. She died in July 1851 at thirty-nine, forty-three years before the brother who became the best-known photographer in New York.

narrative_blocks.header: Ireland to New York to San Francisco
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth King was born in Ireland and was left a widow in July 1875 with seven children when her husband took morphine in an office on the Bowery. Inside five years she had the family across the continent in San Francisco, and she died there in January 1907.

people.research_notes: Born in Ireland. Widowed by her husband's suicide in July 1875 and in San Francisco with several of her children before 1880.

narrative_blocks.header: He went west after his father's death
narrative_blocks.body: George Fredricks Jr. was born and raised in New York City and came out to California with his mother and his brothers and sisters in the years after the suicide. He married Ines Booth at San Francisco in March 1889, lived at Oakland, and left no children.

Campbell farms in Carroll County. He was one of eleven children, and only two of his ten brothers and sisters were still alive when he died.

narrative_blocks.body: Emeline Purdy and Jacob James Haven Purdy were both grandchildren of Capt. Jacob Purdy of White Plains, she through Jacob Junior and he through Henry. They married in 1825 and had six children, and she died in November 1854 at forty-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: Her middle name came from her aunt

narrative_blocks.header: Grocer, then carpenter, then a cartman
narrative_blocks.body: Angevine kept a grocery at Reade and Church Street in 1795 and another on Pump Street two years later, worked there as a carpenter in 1798, and from 1799 until 1817 drove a cart — off Pump Street, then Grand Street, then the corner of Orchard and Broome. He was dead by about 1818, at forty-six.

narrative_blocks.header: The family farm became Cooper's home
narrative_blocks.body: His great-grandparents Lewis Angevine and Esther Sicard leased the Angevine Farm in Scarsdale Manor, and the family held it as tenants of the Heathcotes and the DeLanceys for more than a hundred years. It was afterwards known as the home of James Fenimore Cooper.

narrative_blocks.header: His widow outlived him by sixty-four years
narrative_blocks.body: Peter Angevine kept a grocery in New York and was dead by 1832, in his early thirties, leaving Catherine Beekman with a boy under two. She married a Tarrytown farmer, moved up to North Castle, and lived until 1896.

narrative_blocks.header: He buried two wives inside four years
narrative_blocks.body: John Angevine married Laury in 1820 and had three children by her before she died in 1833. He married Anna Pendleton the next year and she was dead by 1836, and his third wife Rebecca Farrington gave him a son in 1840; he outlived her too, and died at eighty-nine.

people.research_notes: Three marriages. Which wife bore which child is not stated; assigned here from arithmetic — John W., Susan E. and William James (1827-1832) to Laury, who died in 1833, and Charles Berrian (1840) to Rebecca Farrington. Anna Pendleton, married 1834 and dead by 1836, has no children recorded.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed young, and married a farmer next
narrative_blocks.body: Catherine Beekman came out of the Van Cortlandt and Livingston connection and was left a widow in her early twenties when the grocer Peter Angevine died. She married Horace Bartlett of Tarrytown, moved to a small farm at the corner of Banksville and Sniffen Roads in North Castle in the 1840s, and stayed there until about 1881.

people.research_notes: Daughter of Gerard Beekman V and Elizabeth Adams Beekman; granddaughter of Gerard G. Beekman IV and Cornelia Van Cortlandt Beekman. Descended from the Van Cortlandt, Van Schuyler and Livingston families and from the Scots houses of Fleming, Hamilton of Raploch and Weir of Blackwood in Lanarkshire. None of that ancestry built here — in-law line.

Second husband of Catherine Clinton Beekman (I03922) and stepfather of James Nickerson Angevine (HD11331). Theodore Brundage of Armonk noted in his diary that Bartlett died in Middle Patent and 'must be buried at Tarrytown with his wife'. Their son was George H. Bartlett, not built.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried a President to Washington's tomb
narrative_blocks.body: The Thomas Collyer put in below Mount Vernon on 27 April 1855 with President Pierce, his wife Jane and their party aboard, unannounced. Gedney was master and their guide, and cut a bouquet from Washington's own garden for Mrs. Pierce.

narrative_blocks.header: Daylong runs down the Potomac to the shrine
narrative_blocks.body: The Collyer ran from the capital to Mount Vernon and back inside a day, carrying tourists to the house, the tomb and the grounds. Those were the years the estate was visibly falling apart and its last Washington owner wanted a buyer.

narrative_blocks.header: A Union captain, and a government stone
narrative_blocks.body: He served as an officer through the Civil War and came out a captain, and the Union veteran registries carry his name. The marker over his grave at Carson City is the government headstone issued for Union dead.

narrative_blocks.header: He died in the Nevada desert at eighty
narrative_blocks.body: The Potomac steamboat master ended under a government headstone at Lone Mountain in Carson City, three thousand miles from the White Plains farmhouse his great-grandfather lent to Washington. He was eighty.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty odd, he answered across the water
narrative_blocks.body: Gedney took the tug Mary Lewis down the Potomac on 9 August 1873, dragging for the drowned of the burned steamer Wawaset. A passing boat hailed him for a count — twenty odd, he called back.

narrative_blocks.header: He numbered the graves of the unidentified
narrative_blocks.body: Gedney had the unrecognized dead buried in rough coffins along the King George shore, every grave numbered and the clothing described against it. Families who came later could find their own and take them home.

narrative_blocks.header: He had refitted the boat that burned
narrative_blocks.body: Gedney supervised the Wawaset's overhaul himself the winter before, widening the boiler opening by a foot and lining it with iron. Seven months later she burned off Chatterton's Landing with an excursion aboard.
