narrative_blocks.header: He arrived at five as somebody else's son
narrative_blocks.body: Abraham G. Crasto reached New York from Suriname in 1803, between five and six years old, with David G. Crasto and his wife Rachel, who raised him as their child. He was in fact David's nephew, adopted, and David concealed it.

narrative_blocks.header: A Westchester farm apprenticeship is how they met
narrative_blocks.body: Crasto was schooled in New York and then bound out to a farm in Westchester County until he turned twenty-one. Rebecca Lynch Purdy was a Westchester Purdy, and they married in the city on 9 July 1814, both of them seventeen.

narrative_blocks.header: He married her twice, in two faiths
narrative_blocks.body: The 1814 New York wedding was in a Christian church. On 2 April 1820 at Paramaribo the marriage was made again under Jewish law, he under his birth name Abraham de Mosseh Bueno de Mesquite — his Surinamese relatives held the church marriage invalid, the couple adulterers and the children illegitimate.

narrative_blocks.header: He changed religion to suit the country
narrative_blocks.body: Crasto could not practise Judaism and live easily in New York, and could not live as a Christian among his Jewish relatives at Paramaribo. He changed faith to suit whichever society he was standing in.

narrative_blocks.header: At forty-seven he learned he was no citizen
narrative_blocks.body: Because David Gabay Crasto was naturalised, everyone assumed the adopted son was too, and Crasto believed himself a citizen for forty-one years. The Native American party attacked him in handbills in 1844, the concealed adoption came out, and he filed his own papers that year.

narrative_blocks.header: His adoptive father was buried from his house
narrative_blocks.body: Crasto stayed close to his adoptive father all his life; David lived with him at various times, and when David died in 1849 the funeral was held in Crasto's house.

people.research_notes: FamilySearch KG8Y-64Y; Ralph Bennett, 'The Case of the Part-Time Jew', American Jewish Archives journal 46:1 (1994). Born Abraham de Mosseh Bueno de Mesquite; also recorded as Abraham George Crasto and Abraham Gabay Crasto. Adopted nephew of David Gabay Crasto and Rachel Gabay Crasto (d. New York March 1819). The surname Crasto/Crastow is a variant of the Spanish-Portuguese Castro; Gabay/Gabbai is Hebrew for treasurer or dues collector, and a Sephardic double surname marks a dynastic marriage between two houses. His father Moses Bueno de Mesquite (b. c.1770) was verger of the Sephardic synagogue in Surinam in the 1793-94 almanacs and a licensed ferry operator by 1825. The line runs back through plantation Pomibo to Benjamin Bueno de Mesquita (b. c.1600), who has the earliest grave, 1683, in the Chatham Square burial ground in New York.

burial.plot_notes: Sleepy Hollow Cemetery. Climb north from the Old Dutch Church burying ground to the Washington Irving plot; the Crasto plot lies to the west, with the Fanning plot between.

bio.title: Dr.

education.notes: Studied under Dr. James R. Wood of Bellevue.

military_service.notes: Contract surgeon at St. Aloysius before enlisting; brevet major 15 August 1865; mustered out 10 January 1866.

narrative_blocks.header: He went to war as an assistant surgeon
narrative_blocks.body: Williams was commissioned assistant surgeon in January 1864, served briefly aboard the wooden steamer Monticello, and was then put in charge of St. Aloysius Hospital in Washington. He was brevetted major in August 1865.

narrative_blocks.header: He signed his poems A.P. Williams
narrative_blocks.body: He wrote verse for adults and stories for children, publishing in The Manhattan alongside Julian Hawthorne, and gave readings around Bergen County in the early 1880s. St. Nicholas ran his 'The Big Black Dog and The Big Black Goat' in 1883.

narrative_blocks.header: Rutherford's other doctor-poet, a generation early
narrative_blocks.body: Williams was reading his poetry around Bergen County in the early 1880s, the same years William Carlos Williams was born in that town. No relation between the two doctor-poets has ever been found.

narrative_blocks.header: He planned the church he was warden of
narrative_blocks.body: Appointed in 1871 to the three-man committee planning Grace Episcopal Church at Rutherford, he was warden in 1872 and 1874 and held vestry meetings in his own house. The church went up in 1873.

narrative_blocks.header: A judge was told he was insane
narrative_blocks.body: Ill health, physical and mental, closed his Rutherford practice and sent him to live with his father-in-law in Manhattan. In 1890 the alienist Carlos F. MacDonald certified to a state judge that Williams was insane; he died of heart failure the following April.

narrative_blocks.header: His widow married the lay reader he hired
narrative_blocks.body: A month after Williams died his widow was granted his veteran's pension, and in July 1892 she married Nelson R. Boss — the young lay reader Williams himself, as vestryman, had agreed to take on at Grace.

people.research_notes: FamilySearch LW2D-Z3P; Rutherford History. His house and barn stood on six lots at the south-west corner of Montross and Donaldson avenues from 1870 until it was pulled down about 1943. Poems include 'Death, The Artist' and 'The Song of the Organ'.

narrative_blocks.header: He filled New York harbour with tall ships
narrative_blocks.body: Braynard and Nils Hansell conceived Operation Sail for the 1964 World's Fair, and he ran it three more times. On 4 July 1976 nearly three hundred ships from more than fifty countries came up the Hudson in an eighteen-mile parade, watched by about five million people.

narrative_blocks.header: He talked the Soviets into the Bicentennial
narrative_blocks.body: To get Russian ships to Op Sail 76 he sailed three days aboard the barque Kruzenshtern. Cornered with vodka he could not refuse, he asked the band director to whistle Shostakovich's Leningrad symphony with him, and the two whistled for over an hour.

narrative_blocks.header: A museum out of old waterfront blocks
narrative_blocks.body: Braynard and Peter and Norma Stanford formed the committee that created the South Street Seaport Museum in 1966, and he was its first programme director through the 1970s. From 1980 to 2000 he was curator at the Merchant Marine Academy's museum at Kings Point.

narrative_blocks.header: Six volumes on one ship, a million words
narrative_blocks.body: He wrote more than forty books, most illustrated with his own sketches, and the best known is a six-volume history of the liner Leviathan running to a million words and fifteen hundred illustrations. He called her scrapping in the 1930s a criminal act.

narrative_blocks.header: Asthma kept him home with the souvenirs
narrative_blocks.body: Childhood asthma kept Braynard indoors at Sea Cliff, and the souvenirs his travelling aunts and uncles brought back started the collection. At seven he sketched the Leviathan and spelled her name correctly before he could spell his own.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife died the night before his memorial
narrative_blocks.body: Braynard died on 10 December 2007 at ninety-one. Doris, his wife of fifty-eight years, had spent the weeks arranging his memorial service at Sea Cliff and died of a heart attack the night before it was held.

narrative_blocks.body: Noelle Braynard and Jonathan Hollander found a sixth-floor loft on Stone Street in 1976 and started Battery Dance there, in a financial district with no theatres. They stripped the walls to the brick and uncovered three windows the plaster had hidden.

narrative_blocks.header: He built a company where no theatres were
narrative_blocks.body: Hollander founded Battery Dance in Lower Manhattan in 1976, in a financial district with no performing arts at all. Having nowhere indoors to show the work, he took it into the bank plazas at lunchtime, and free public performance became the company's habit for good.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-five years of free dance downtown
narrative_blocks.body: Six years after the company he founded the Battery Dance Festival, now the longest-running free public dance festival in New York. It has introduced the city to more than five hundred companies.

narrative_blocks.header: A German president decorated him for it
narrative_blocks.body: In June 2018 the Federal Order of Merit was conferred on Hollander by President Frank-Walter Steinmeier for bringing young people together across borders through cultural exchange. He had been a Fulbright lecturer on dance in India in 1992 and a Fulbright Specialist in Malaysia in 2011.

narrative_blocks.header: Dancing to Connect went to seventy countries
narrative_blocks.body: The company's Dancing to Connect programme uses dance to build social cohesion and work at conflict, and has run in more than seventy countries on six continents. Hollander has made over a hundred and fifty works for it.

narrative_blocks.body: An artist all her life and well known around Rochester, she co-founded the Suburban Rochester Art Group and worked in oils and monoprint. Her snowy beach scene 'No Dogs Allowed' and the 1960s monoprint 'Earth Colors' still turn up at auction.

narrative_blocks.body: She hosted three Golden Apple Art Shows on the eighteen acres around her house in Wayne County, for the benefit of the Humane Society shelter, and used her painting to raise money for the hospital ship HOPE.

narrative_blocks.header: She painted as her mother had
narrative_blocks.body: Martha Braynard McFall worked in oils in the country outside Rochester, as her mother Martha Storey Braynard had done at Henrietta a generation before her. She died at eighty-nine in Walworth, in the house she shared with a niece and a nephew.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-nine volumes on the American West
narrative_blocks.body: Bancroft set out to write the history of the whole Pacific slope from Panama to Alaska and published thirty-nine volumes of it between 1874 and 1890 — five on the native races, seven on California alone.

narrative_blocks.header: His copies are all that survived 1906
narrative_blocks.body: Most Spanish and Mexican records of California burned in the fires after the 1906 earthquake. They survive at all only because Bancroft or his researchers had made verbatim copies and taken notes on their contents.

narrative_blocks.header: It was run like a literary factory
narrative_blocks.body: Scores of assistants copied archives, took oral histories and wrote whole sections, and Bancroft put his own name on the result. By any modern reckoning he was the editor and compiler of most of what he signed.

narrative_blocks.header: Berkeley bought the library and kept the name
narrative_blocks.body: The collection began in 1859 with fifty or seventy-five books cleared onto the shelves round his desk, and passed sixty thousand items. The University of California bought it in 1905 on the condition that it keep his name for good.

narrative_blocks.header: The Pioneers barred him for what he wrote
narrative_blocks.body: The Society of California Pioneers shut him out over what he had published about John Sutter, John C. Fremont and other heroes of the state's founding. Yale had given him an honorary master's in 1875 for the Native Races.

narrative_blocks.header: His first wife died at Alameda in 1869
narrative_blocks.body: Emily Ketchum married Bancroft in 1859 and died at Alameda ten years later, in childbirth with their second child. Her father, the historian of Buffalo, buried her at Forest Lawn.

notable.notable_blurb: Connecticut congressman and supreme court justice

narrative_blocks.header: He died on his father's old court
narrative_blocks.body: Seymour was appointed to the Connecticut Supreme Court in 1889 and sat on it until his death three years later. His father had been chief justice of the same court fifteen years before him.

narrative_blocks.header: A Democrat in a Republican decade
narrative_blocks.body: Seymour took Connecticut's fourth district for the Forty-eighth Congress and held it from March 1883 to March 1887. He had been in the state house in 1859 and 1870 and the state senate in 1876.

narrative_blocks.header: His father's cousin ran against Grant
narrative_blocks.body: Horatio Seymour of Utica governed New York twice and was the Democrat beaten by Ulysses Grant in 1868. He was first cousin to Edward's father, and a nephew of the Horatio Seymour who sat in the Senate for Vermont.

narrative_blocks.header: Brain fever took him at sixty
narrative_blocks.body: He died at his Litchfield house on 16 October 1892 of what the notices called acute brain fever, or cerebral meningitis. The seat went to Simeon Baldwin, and Seymour was buried in East Cemetery a few streets away.

narrative_blocks.header: A carpenter in the War of 1812
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin H. Tallmadge was born at Rhinebeck and worked as a carpenter in the Mohawk valley. He served as a soldier in the War of 1812, and married Mary Parker of Red Hook at Stamford in 1819, when he was thirty-three and she twenty-one.

narrative_blocks.header: He clerked for the spymaster, then went west
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel H. Tallmadge kept the store of his uncle, Colonel Benjamin Tallmadge, at Litchfield until 1818, then settled at Glens Falls, where he was justice of the peace for twenty years, county superintendent of schools and an elder of the Presbyterian church. He moved to Springfield, Ohio in 1848 and to Piqua in 1857, where he died.

narrative_blocks.header: Two children lost in ten weeks
narrative_blocks.body: Frederick S. died on 1 June 1829, three years old. A second son born that August was given the dead boy's name, and six days after that birth his sister Gloriana died too, fifteen months old.

narrative_blocks.body: Mary Ann Tisdale died at Adams in November 1833, thirty-eight years old, leaving William Tallmadge eight children, the youngest born that same year. He married Margaret Van Allen at Belleville the following September and moved the household to Watertown, where he bought a farm.

narrative_blocks.header: A carpenter who served in 1812
narrative_blocks.body: Tallmadge was born at Johnstown and worked as a carpenter. He served in the War of 1812 and married Mary Ann Tisdale at Cooperstown about 1818.

narrative_blocks.body: Betsy Brown died in September 1838 and John Tallmadge married Mary Conover on 6 December of the same year. Two more children followed, and Mary outlived Betsy by thirty-four years.

notable.notable_blurb: Antislavery congressman; NYU founder & president

narrative_blocks.header: Here will I hold my stand
narrative_blocks.body: On 13 February 1819 Tallmadge moved to bar slavery from Missouri and to free every child born there at twenty-five. Southern members threatened disunion, and he answered that if civil war must come, let it come.

narrative_blocks.header: The House passed it, the Senate killed it
narrative_blocks.body: Both of Tallmadge's amendments were adopted by the House and struck out by the Senate. A year later Congress settled on the Missouri Compromise instead, and he wrote to John Taylor that the bill was our child, and an ill fated offspring.

narrative_blocks.header: He had said it all at twenty
narrative_blocks.body: Tallmadge used his 1798 commencement oration at the College of Rhode Island to condemn the slave trade and call for universal emancipation, twenty years before Congress heard him. The college itself had been endowed by slave traders.

narrative_blocks.header: One term, and he would not stand again
narrative_blocks.body: He came to the House in a special election in June 1817, filling a seat left by a member-elect who died before taking it, and declined to run in 1818. He sat instead in the state assembly, then as lieutenant governor.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran New York University for sixteen years
narrative_blocks.body: Tallmadge helped found New York University and served as its president until 1846. He led the American Institute, a society for inventions and technical education, for twenty years after that.

narrative_blocks.header: He took cotton machinery to Russia
narrative_blocks.body: In 1836 Tallmadge went to Russia and helped introduce American mechanical inventions there, cotton-spinning machinery above all. His daughter Mary Rebecca, reckoned one of the handsomest women in the country, travelled with him.

narrative_blocks.body: Mary Rebecca Van Rensselaer died suddenly at Albany in August 1872, in the fifty-sixth year of her age. She was buried from Zion Church at Wappinger's Falls and carried on to the rural cemetery at Poughkeepsie, with carriages meeting the Hudson River Railroad two miles off at New Hamburg.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale 1826, then hotels and New York rents
narrative_blocks.body: Philip Stephen Van Rensselaer practised law and made his money in hotels and New York real estate. He lived for a time at New Hamburg in Dutchess county and spent a good deal of his life in Europe.

narrative_blocks.header: He inherited the Metropolitan Hotel block
narrative_blocks.body: Of the patroon's New York property the third son took the square that held the Metropolitan Hotel, which is how a landed man came to be a hotel owner. He was named for his uncle Philip, the old mayor of Albany.

narrative_blocks.header: His brothers split the rest of the manor
narrative_blocks.body: William P. took the west side of the Hudson and built near Greenbush, Cortlandt the clergyman had another share of the New York property, and Henry went out to the wild lands on the St. Lawrence and improved them himself.

narrative_blocks.header: A charming man, dead in an hour
narrative_blocks.body: One who knew him called him among the most excellent and charming men we ever had in our state. He died very suddenly at New York on 1 June 1871, in his sixty-fifth year.

cross_connections.display_label: , his grandfather, died in his Albany home five weeks before his birth

bio.bio_blurb: Lawyer, hotel owner, and New York landlord

people.research_notes: Son of General Stephen Van Rensselaer III (1764-1839), the last patroon of Rensselaerswyck and founder of the Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, and Cornelia Bell Paterson (1780-1844); neither is in the tree. Also recorded as Philip Schuyler Van Rensselaer Jr. Yale class of 1826. A Biographical Sketch of the Class of 1826, Yale College (1866), p.92, names his wife as 'Miss Louisa Talmadge' and says the class had failed to learn where he was living; she was Mary Rebecca. See also Genealogies of the State of New York vol.3 (1915), 1167-68, and the New York Herald, 2 September 1852. Martha J. Lamb, 'The Van Rensselaer Manor', Magazine of American History 11 (January 1884): the third son of the patroon, named for his uncle Philip S. Van Rensselaer, mayor of Albany; inherited the New York City square holding the Metropolitan Hotel; married 'the beautiful daughter of James Talmadge'. His brothers William P., Cortlandt and Henry took the other shares; none has an entry.
Recorded only as an infant daughter, born and died 1840.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten years of customs cases in New York
narrative_blocks.body: Van Rensselaer was made assistant United States district attorney in 1889 and kept the place through Democratic and Republican administrations alike, on the strength of his handling of customs cases. He had read law in the office of William Evarts after Harvard and a postgraduate year at Oxford.

narrative_blocks.header: A letter in high spirits, then appendicitis
narrative_blocks.body: He was on holiday in Boston when he died after an operation for appendicitis, fifty-seven years old. A colleague in the district attorney's office had a letter from him days before, saying he was in good health and high spirits.

narrative_blocks.header: He went to Paris on Garfield's money commission
narrative_blocks.body: In 1881 Van Rensselaer attended the International Monetary Conference at Paris with the commission President Garfield sent from this country. Two years later he took a seat on the New York board of aldermen.

career.organization: Eleventh Assembly District, New York City

narrative_blocks.header: Her father drowned in the Charleston hurricane
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas Norman Orton of Lewes, Delaware was a mariner, and the Great Hurricane took him at Charleston on 8 September 1854. Minnie was three, and her mother Sarah Penton was already dead.

narrative_blocks.header: Raised under three surnames, married under two
narrative_blocks.body: Her stepmother was widowed three times over, so the girl went by Orton and by Sackett as she grew up. At seventeen she married Ely Parker, General Grant's military secretary, and thirty years later she married James Tallmadge Van Rensselaer.

people.research_notes: Born Minnie Orton, December 1850 at Philadelphia, daughter of Capt. Thomas Norman Orton (Lewes, Delaware, 13 February 1827 - Charleston, South Carolina, 8 September 1854) and Sarah Ann Penton of Salem, New Jersey. Her stepmother Anna Sessilberg married in turn Thomas Orton, Gen. William H. Sackett and Amos Bissell, which is why Minnie was known as both Orton and Orton-Sackett; Minnie's death certificate names Anna as her mother and gives her maiden surname as Sackett. First husband, married 25 December 1867 at Washington: Gen. Ely Samuel Parker, Do-ne-ho-geh-weh (1828-1895), Seneca sachem and military secretary to General Grant, who is not in the tree; their daughter Maud Theresa Parker Bullard (1878-1956) is a step-relation and is not either. No children by the second marriage.

narrative_blocks.header: The church picked him out for the ministry
narrative_blocks.body: Two young men of Litchfield were chosen by their church to be trained for the ministry, and Stephen Mason was one of them. He went through Williams College and came out of Andover among its earliest graduates, and spent his first year as a missionary in Kentucky.

narrative_blocks.header: Nantucket air cost him his voice
narrative_blocks.body: After twelve years in the pulpit at Washington, Connecticut he preached five years on Nantucket, where his throat was so affected that he had to leave the island and never entirely recovered. He removed to Marshall, Michigan in 1837 and preached there while his health allowed.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-one years in his daughter's house
narrative_blocks.body: Illness kept Mason from the ministry for the last twenty years of his life, and he lived in his daughter's household for twenty-one of them. He died at his son-in-law's Marshall house of paralysis, three years after the first stroke, too blind by then to read.

narrative_blocks.header: Both his sons died before him
narrative_blocks.body: Mason outlived the two boys of his first marriage. Ebenezer Porter Mason died at twenty-one, already a brilliant astronomer whose memoir was written by Professor Olmsted of Yale, and David Burr Mason died three years after him at Marshall.

narrative_blocks.header: Temperance drove him off to Nantucket
narrative_blocks.body: Ministers and members drank moderately as a matter of course, and his stand against it made Washington untenable. He went to Nantucket in 1827, had a temperance address printed there, and built the church still in use.

He left money towards a Congregational house of worship at Marshall.

narrative_blocks.header: Orphaned of her mother at fifteen in Michigan
narrative_blocks.body: Her father took the family to Marshall when she was fourteen, and within two years her mother and her brother Ebenezer were both dead. She was sent east to her aunt Frances Marsh in Brooklyn and grew up in that house.

narrative_blocks.header: Her schooling at Northampton was unusual then
narrative_blocks.body: Her father settled at Goshen in Massachusetts expressly so that she could attend the school at Northampton nearby. She came out better educated than most women of her generation and read all her life.

narrative_blocks.header: An invalid from 1867, and her verses
narrative_blocks.body: From 1867 she was a confirmed invalid, and turned to reading, writing and handiwork. Those who kept her verses said they showed a gifted mind and a devout heart. She was timid, and preferred a few friends to company.

narrative_blocks.header: Pneumonia at fifty-one, after she had recovered
narrative_blocks.body: She had practically regained her health several years before the end. All seven of her children were born at Marshall, which was her home from her marriage in 1845 until she died there in 1875.

narrative_blocks.header: He sold the business, then died
narrative_blocks.body: Henry Curtis Haskell was the oldest insurance agent in Michigan and knew the end was near. On the Saturday he sold out his business, and by Monday he was dead at his house on North Kalamazoo Avenue, five months short of eighty-six.

narrative_blocks.header: Brought west to a Bellevue farm at seven
narrative_blocks.body: Haskell was born at Oakham in Massachusetts and brought west from New York State by his parents in 1827, to a farm in Bellevue township fourteen miles north of Marshall. He had been a Marshall man since 1836 and helped organise the old Coldwater and Marshall steam railroad.

people.research_notes: Obituary, The Evening Press, 18 December 1905. Clerk of the First Presbyterian church eighteen years and deacon and elder thirty-two. Second wife, married 8 January 1879 in Kalamazoo County (recorded as both Charleston and Galesburg): the widow Matilda Delaria Lamb Morse (1837-1903), who is not in the tree; no children by her. FamilySearch dates the first marriage 27 March 1845 and the family record 27 November 1845, Thanksgiving Day at Marshall.

narrative_blocks.header: His only child died at thirteen
narrative_blocks.body: Ethel Marguerite was born at Port Huron in 1881 and buried there in October 1894. He ran the copper mines at Port Huron and had married Nellie Wixom in June 1877; they had no others.

bio.bio_blurb: Superintendent of the Port Huron copper mines

narrative_blocks.header: Michigan in 1877, then Bellevue
narrative_blocks.body: Haskell took his medical degree at the University of Michigan in 1877 and trained further at the Bellevue Hospital Medical College in New York. By 1897 he was practising in the Michigan copper country and serving as president of the county board of education.

narrative_blocks.header: From the copper country to the orange groves
narrative_blocks.body: The family were still in Houghton County at the 1900 census and at 122 The Terrace in Redlands, California by 1902. Haskell died there in 1914, and Florence went back to Michigan and died at Calumet thirty years after him.

bio.bio_blurb: Physician and orange grower at Redlands

career.organization: Marquette County, Michigan, and Redlands, California

career.role: President of the board of education

people.research_notes: A Marshall notice: 'Dr. Henry Marsh Haskell, graduate of the U. of M. in 1877, former resident of this city and Mt. Pleasant, is dead in Redlands, Cal.' Both he and Florence are buried at Hillside Memorial Park, Original Block 3, Redlands. The family record gives William Lincoln Haskell's birth as 1863 where FamilySearch gives 1864.

narrative_blocks.header: Three of them followed her to Indiana
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Catharine Haskell married an Indiana man at Marshall in 1883 and went to Carroll County with him. Her sister Laura died at Delphi in 1924 and her brother Porter at Delphi in 1930, both of them unmarried and both a long way from the Michigan town they were born in.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a Delphi lawyer in 1883
narrative_blocks.body: Newberry Julius Howe practised at Delphi in Indiana and died there in May 1908, at fifty-two. She outlived him by twenty-eight years.

people.research_notes: FamilySearch KCX1-NPR gives her death as 19 May 1908, the day before her husband's, which looks like his record bleeding into hers; FindAGrave gives 9 December 1936 at Deer Creek and is followed here. Married by E. P. Johnson, pastor of the Marshall Presbyterian church.

narrative_blocks.header: Admiral Sims on his 1918 war poster
narrative_blocks.body: William's 1918 broadside poster put President Wilson between General Pershing and Admiral William Sims, above a soldier and a sailor with their sweethearts. An armed Uncle Sam strides the Atlantic with a German cowering under his cape.

narrative_blocks.header: He and Porter died on the same date
narrative_blocks.body: William Lincoln Haskell died at Los Angeles on 1 February 1955, ninety years old. His brother Porter had died on 1 February too, twenty-five years earlier and half a continent away at Delphi.

narrative_blocks.header: One other copy is known to exist
narrative_blocks.body: Charles Gustrine published the sheet at Chicago in 1918. The only other catalogued example is at the Pritzker Military Museum and Library in the same city.

narrative_blocks.header: She painted while he rode Baja
narrative_blocks.body: Joanne Crosby was an exhibiting watercolorist, and her daughter Ristin a painter of murals in Tijuana and Cabo San Lucas. Her husband's Baja expeditions, as he put it himself, left her to raise the family.

narrative_blocks.header: She painted the cover of his book
narrative_blocks.body: For Antigua California in 1994 Joanne Crosby made a watercolor facsimile of San José del Cabo after the drawings of Padre Ignacio Tirsch, and it went on the cover of her husband's book.

notable.notable_blurb: Historian and photographer

narrative_blocks.header: He quit chemistry and bought four mules
narrative_blocks.body: Crosby left the San Diego schools in 1963 after twelve years teaching chemistry. Commissioned to photograph the route of the 1769 Portolá expedition, he found the old road crossed the dirt track only three times in the whole peninsula, so he bought four mules and rode six hundred miles.

narrative_blocks.header: He put 180 rock-art sites on record
narrative_blocks.body: Ranchers along the way showed him painted caves, and at home he found that six or eight he had seen had never been published. He went back for fifteen months over several years, and his 1975 book brought a hundred and eighty new sites into the literature.

narrative_blocks.header: His caves became a World Heritage Site
narrative_blocks.body: Crosby's photographs and argument carried the Great Murals of the Sierra de San Francisco onto the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1993. He insisted they were far older than the thousand years archaeologists allowed, and a carbon-dating study in 2022 put the oldest at eleven thousand.

narrative_blocks.header: A missing page, and a midnight fax
narrative_blocks.body: Opening a box of newly printed Cave Paintings in 1997, Crosby found a page missing from every copy. He faxed his publisher that he would go on believing only his own twenty-five were flawed, adding that he also believed in campaign finance reform and the brotherhood of man.

narrative_blocks.header: Orchids, Bach, and a mule saddle
narrative_blocks.body: At home in La Jolla he grew hundreds of hybrid orchids and collected the church music of Bach for thirty years. He logged more than a thousand miles in the saddle across Baja, interviewing the ranch families of the mountains.

narrative_blocks.header: Eleven feet of negatives at UC San Diego
narrative_blocks.body: The Harry Crosby Collection at the University of California, San Diego holds his Baja negatives, his Tijuana pictures of 1964 and his study of peninsular ranch life from 1967 to 1997.

cross_connections.display_label: gathered the Berkeley library Crosby worked in for three years

career.notes: Memorial Junior High, Mission Bay High and La Jolla High.

people.research_notes: Wikipedia; Karen Kenyon, 'Tracking the Hispanic Roots of California', Los Angeles Times, 12 April 1987; Harry Crosby Collection, MSS 333, UC San Diego Library. Navy officer training during the Second World War. Accepted to medical school at the University of Southern California in 1947 and turned it down. Books: The King's Highway in Baja California (1974), The Cave Paintings of Baja California (1975), Last of the Californios (1981), Doomed to Fail (1989), Antigua California (1994), which won the Caroline Bancroft History Prize, Tijuana 1964 (2000), the novel Portrait of Paloma (2001), Gateway to Alta California (2003) and Californio Portraits (2015). His daughter Ristin, a painter who did the murals at the Agua Caliente track in Tijuana, is living and is not in the tree. Remembrance by his editor at Sunbelt Publications, 2024, which is the source of the 1997 fax and of his lecturing from memory at the Bancroft Library. An hour-long documentary about him by Isaac Artenstein aired on PBS.

notable.notable_blurb: Rock guitarist and songwriter; Ratt co-founder

narrative_blocks.header: Round and Round went triple platinum
narrative_blocks.body: Crosby was an original member of the San Diego band that became Ratt and co-wrote Round and Round, Wanted Man and Lay It Down. Out of the Cellar sold three million copies in 1984.

narrative_blocks.header: Six foot five, and called King
narrative_blocks.body: His solos were blues-based and owed everything to Hendrix, set against the faster playing of Warren DeMartini beside him, and the contrast gave Ratt a melodic edge.

narrative_blocks.header: Together at fifteen, and on the cover
narrative_blocks.body: Crosby and Tawny Kitaen moved in together at about fifteen and stayed six years. She is the woman on the covers of the 1983 Ratt EP and Out of the Cellar, and she appears in the video for Back for More.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a Playmate in 1987
narrative_blocks.body: Crosby married Laurie Ann Carr in 1987. Nikki Sixx was to have stood as best man and did not come, because there would be drink at the wedding and he was trying to get clean; the two did not speak for years afterwards.

narrative_blocks.header: He put his own story on the record
narrative_blocks.body: Crosby left the band in 1991 and said plainly what addiction had taken from him: his career and his fortune. In 2001 he told an interviewer he had been HIV-positive since 1994 and that his illness was terminal.

narrative_blocks.header: Little League and a red guitar
narrative_blocks.body: In his last years, ill and out of the public eye, Crosby coached Little League. He also worked on a limited run of replica Jackson King V guitars, copies of the red one he had played.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at forty-two, two years clean
narrative_blocks.body: Crosby had been clean for nearly two years at the start of 2002 when he moved in with an old friend he had used with. He died at Los Angeles on 6 June of complications from AIDS following a heroin overdose.

narrative_blocks.body: Carr studied commercial art in Texas and left it to model after a friend sent her pictures to Playboy. She was Playmate of the Month for December 1986 and the cover model for Slaughter's Stick It to Ya and Stick It Live.

narrative_blocks.body: She played a nurse in the horror comedy Mortuary Academy and guested on an episode of Full House before leaving the business. She works today as a chiropractor.

narrative_blocks.body: Carr married Robbin Crosby in 1987, three years after the cover of Out of the Cellar made the band. They divorced in 1991, the year he left Ratt, and had no children.

narrative_blocks.header: A hundred and fifty thousand copies
narrative_blocks.body: An address Marsh gave at Pomfret in 1829 was printed by the American Temperance Union as Putnam and the Wolf, and sold a hundred and fifty thousand copies before the Tract Society took it up and kept it in circulation for decades.

narrative_blocks.header: He never left the society he founded
narrative_blocks.body: Marsh helped form the Connecticut Temperance Society in 1829 and was its first secretary. He was soon pressed to take the secretaryship of the American Temperance Union, and held it from then until he died.

narrative_blocks.header: The last white wig in New England
narrative_blocks.body: Marsh was Yale 1804 and a Congregational minister like his father before him, the Rev. John Marsh of Wethersfield and a fellow of Yale for nineteen years. An annalist remembered the elder Marsh appearing at commencement in a venerable white wig, perhaps the last of the kind worn in New England.

people.research_notes: Pyne no.575; Yale obituary record of his son. Father of four; his own father was the Rev. John Marsh D.D. of Haverhill, Harvard 1761, pastor at Wethersfield and a fellow of Yale from 1801. Not flagged notable — an in-law; ask Sam.

narrative_blocks.header: Three generations of John Marsh in the pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: John Tallmadge Marsh was the third minister of his name in a row, after his father the temperance secretary and his grandfather the Wethersfield pastor. He went west and died at Scott Valley in California, a long way from Haddam where he was born.

narrative_blocks.header: Born in Bangor during her father's pastorate
narrative_blocks.body: Susan Huntoon was born at Bangor in 1832, where her father the Reverend Benjamin Huntoon had been installed over a new Unitarian church two years before. His health broke there, and he sailed south to Savannah to recover the winter after she was born.

narrative_blocks.header: She died six weeks after her son
narrative_blocks.body: Susan Marsh bore John Huntoon Marsh at Peoria on 4 May 1854 and was dead there on 15 June, twenty-one years old. Her husband took the boy back east and outlived her by thirty years.

people.research_notes: Her father, the Rev. Benjamin Huntoon (Salisbury, New Hampshire, 28 November 1792 - Canton, Massachusetts, 19 April 1864), Dartmouth 1817 and Andover 1819, was chaplain of the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts and pastor at Canton, Bangor, Milton and Cincinnati; he is not in the tree. His own grandfather Benjamin enlisted at sixteen for Louisbourg and fought under Stark at Bennington.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven years from Yale to the grave
narrative_blocks.body: John Smith Tallmadge took his Yale degree in 1818, read law, and married Ann Eliza Smith at Albany in 1823. He was dead at Lyons in October 1825, twenty-seven years old, leaving two sons who died young themselves.

notable.notable_blurb: Last patroon; RPI founder & lieutenant governor

narrative_blocks.header: They called him the Good Patroon
narrative_blocks.body: He took Rensselaerswyck on his twenty-first birthday and never sold it off, granting perpetual leases instead until he was landlord to eighty thousand tenants. He took grain and firewood for rent and let arrears run rather than evict, which is how he got the name.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded the school that became RPI
narrative_blocks.body: In 1824 he and Amos Eaton opened a school at Troy for the application of science to the common purposes of life. It became the Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute and still carries his name.

narrative_blocks.header: One vote decided the 1824 election
narrative_blocks.body: No candidate had a majority, so the House chose the president state by state. Van Rensselaer meant to vote for Crawford, changed his mind, and gave John Quincy Adams New York and with it the thirteen states he needed.

narrative_blocks.header: Queenston Heights finished him as a soldier
narrative_blocks.body: Given the Army of the Centre in 1812 partly to keep him out of a governor's race, he attacked across the Niagara in October with too few boats and too little ammunition. Militiamen refused to cross, the boatmen would not go back for the men stranded on the far bank, and he resigned.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-three years on the canal commission
narrative_blocks.body: He was among the first to argue for a waterway from the Hudson to the Great Lakes and sat on the Erie Canal Commission from 1816 until he died, fourteen of those years as its president.

narrative_blocks.header: His son preached to the enslaved in Virginia
narrative_blocks.body: Cortlandt Van Rensselaer, his son by Cornelia Paterson, went from Yale in 1827 to the seminaries at Prince Edward and Princeton, and spent 1833 to 1835 as a missionary among the enslaved people of Virginia.

narrative_blocks.header: His son's name reached a Yale first
narrative_blocks.body: John and Vashti Creed of New Haven named their son for Cortlandt Van Rensselaer, who was a friend of the Yale men who later admitted him to the medical school. Cortlandt Van Rensselaer Creed took his M.D. in 1857, the first African American to hold any degree from Yale.

people.research_notes: Built at Sam's instruction as an easter egg, September 2026; his wife Cornelia Bell Paterson (1780-1844) is not in the tree. His son Cortlandt Van Rensselaer (1808-1860), Presbyterian clergyman, Yale 1827, pastor at Burlington and at the Second Presbyterian Church in Washington, agent of Princeton Theological Seminary and secretary of the Presbyterian board of education, married Catherine Ledyard and had six children; he has no entry. A FamilySearch contributor calls Cortlandt a friend and classmate of Theodore Dwight Woolsey, Charles Hooker and Leonard Bacon — the three took their Yale degrees in 1820 and Cortlandt in 1827, so classmate is not supportable and only the friendship is carried here. Wikipedia. Eldest child of Stephen Van Rensselaer II and Catharina Livingston, daughter of the signer Philip Livingston; raised by his mother, his stepfather the Rev. Eilardus Westerlo and his uncle Abraham Ten Broeck after his father died when he was five. Harvard 1782, Phi Beta Kappa; honorary LL.D. from Yale 1822. Ranked the tenth richest American in the nation's history by the ratio of his fortune to contemporary output. Twelve children by two wives. His sons' attempt to collect the back rents after his death set off the Anti-Rent War and broke up the manor.

people.research_notes: Marker at Grove Street Cemetery, New Haven; Yale School of Public Health; Curtis Patton. Son of John W. Creed, a St. Croix immigrant, Yale steward and caterer, and Vashti Duplex Creed, the first Black schoolteacher in New Haven and daughter of Prince Duplex, a Revolutionary soldier freed by his service; none of them is in the tree. Married first Drucilla Wright, four sons; then Mary Paul of Brooklyn, six children. REGIMENT CONFLICT: the Grove Street marker says 1st Lieutenant and Surgeon, 31st U.S. Colored Infantry 1864; Yale gives the 31st USCT as the 30th Connecticut Volunteer Infantry; a third account says no military record under his name survives and he may have been a contract surgeon, and that he is not listed with that unit. The marker's reading is carried here pending Sam's decision. Named for Cortlandt Van Rensselaer (1808-1860), Presbyterian clergyman and son of Gen. Stephen Van Rensselaer III (X04064); the clergyman himself has no entry. His father John kept the rooms of the Calliopean Society and of Skull and Bones at Yale, catered the commencement dinners for years, and sold The Liberator; his mother Vashti taught at the school at the Temple Street Congregational Church, New Haven's first independent Black congregation. He took his M.D. the same year Richard Henry Greene, another Black New Havener, took his B.A. from Yale College; Greene is not in the tree. A second account gives the commission as the Thirtieth Connecticut Volunteers in January 1864, the state's second Black regiment, which was later folded into the 31st USCT — that reconciles the marker with the claim that no record survives under his name in the 31st.

narrative_blocks.header: The first Yale degree of any kind
narrative_blocks.body: Creed registered at Yale in 1854 and took his M.D. on 16 January 1857, the first African American to hold any degree from Yale. Yale College would not have him; the medical department, a separate body then, would.

narrative_blocks.header: The father Yale refused, then employed
narrative_blocks.body: John Creed came off St. Croix, applied to Yale College himself and was refused, then made his living there as caterer and custodian — keeping the rooms of the Calliopean Society and of Skull and Bones, which Alphonso Taft helped found. Twenty years on he asked again for his son, and a door opened.

narrative_blocks.header: Refused a commission, he wrote again
narrative_blocks.body: At the outbreak of the war Creed asked Governor Buckingham for a surgeon's commission and was turned down on account of his race. He got it in January 1864, in the Thirtieth Connecticut Volunteers, the second Black regiment the state raised.

narrative_blocks.header: His thesis was on the blood
narrative_blocks.body: On the Blood ran to the chemistry and physiology of blood in health and sickness. He wrote afterwards that for all the prejudice against colour in the country, he had never had other than the most polite treatment from his classmates.

narrative_blocks.header: The White House asked him about Garfield
narrative_blocks.body: Surgeons would not cut for the bullet in the wounded president until they could find it, and Creed was among the physicians the White House wrote to for suggestions. Garfield died of blood poisoning with the bullet still lost.

narrative_blocks.header: Arsenic, and two boys arrested
narrative_blocks.body: His forensic evidence helped settle the poisoning of a young New Haven woman, and two local boys were taken up for it. A novel of 2001, Arsenic Under the Elms, is built on the case.

narrative_blocks.header: He organised the Jubilee Meeting of 1862
narrative_blocks.body: Creed helped call the colored people of New Haven together in 1862 to mark the end of slavery in the District of Columbia, and afterwards organised a Freedmen's Aid Society in the city. His mother Vashti had been the town's first Black schoolteacher.

narrative_blocks.header: She turned the raiders back with a lie
narrative_blocks.body: Tories and Mohawks forced their way into the Schuyler house at Albany in August 1781 hunting her father. Peggy went down for the baby they had left behind and told the men he had gone to alarm the town; they ran, and one threw a tomahawk at her on the stairs.

narrative_blocks.header: Burgoyne burned her father's country house
narrative_blocks.body: British troops fired the Schuyler place at Saratoga after the battle there in October 1777, when Peggy was nineteen. Being General Schuyler's daughter in the Hudson valley meant the family was a standing target, and four years later the raiders came to the Albany house for him in person.

narrative_blocks.header: She was twenty-four and he was nineteen
narrative_blocks.body: Peggy Schuyler eloped with Stephen Van Rensselaer in June 1783, a distant cousin nearly six years younger, whose friends thought him far too young to marry. He came into Rensselaerswyck two years later.

narrative_blocks.header: Hamilton wrote the news to her sister
narrative_blocks.body: Her brother-in-law was in Albany on legal business as she failed, and he sat by her often and kept Eliza posted. On Saturday, my dear Eliza, your sister took leave of her sufferings and friends, he wrote in March 1801, to find repose and happiness in a better country.

narrative_blocks.header: Three children, and one grew up
narrative_blocks.body: Three were baptised at the Dutch church in Albany and only Stephen Van Rensselaer IV, born in 1789, reached manhood. He inherited the east side of the manor and sold his townships in the anti-rent troubles.

narrative_blocks.header: She buried two children in one year
narrative_blocks.body: Catherine Schuyler Van Rensselaer was born in 1784 and Stephanus in 1786, and both were dead in 1787. Only the third, Stephen Van Rensselaer IV, born in 1789, grew up; he inherited the east side of the manor and sold his townships in the anti-rent troubles.

people.research_notes: Wikipedia. Third daughter of Gen. Philip Schuyler and Catherine Van Rensselaer; sister of Angelica Schuyler Church, Elizabeth Schuyler Hamilton (X03825) and Philip Jeremiah Schuyler. Her parents are not in the tree, so she and Eliza are not linked as sisters structurally — building Philip Schuyler and Catherine Van Rensselaer would fix that. The tomahawk mark in the banister is family tradition, first printed in the 1830s, with no contemporary evidence in the Schuyler papers or the Loyalist records of the raid. Burr was a frequent visitor at the Schuyler mansion in Albany and read in Gen. Philip Schuyler's library there; in 1791 he took Schuyler's U.S. Senate seat from him. Her mother Catherine Van Rensselaer Schuyler ran the Schuyler household and the daughters' education through her husband's long absences and was painted by Thomas McIlworth in the 1760s; the Harvard digital-history essay on Peggy uses that portrait as the model for a daughter of whom no youthful likeness survives. Philip Schuyler advertised over nine thousand acres for lease or sale. Burgoyne burned the Saratoga estate after the battle in 1777. Her three children were Catherine Schuyler Van Rensselaer (1784-1787), Stephanus Van Rensselaer (1786-1787) and Gen. Stephen Van Rensselaer IV (1789-1868); none has an entry.

narrative_blocks.body: Cornelia Paterson was twenty-one and Stephen Van Rensselaer a widower of thirty-seven when they married at New Brunswick in May 1802. Nine children followed, among them Philip, who married Mary Rebecca Tallmadge, and Cortlandt, whose name reached New Haven.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the New Jersey Plan
narrative_blocks.body: At Philadelphia in 1787 Paterson put the small states' case: one chamber, every state equal. The Great Compromise kept his Senate and gave the large states the House, and he returned in September to sign.

narrative_blocks.header: Judicial review, eight years before Marbury
narrative_blocks.body: Riding circuit in 1795 he told a Pennsylvania court that the Constitution stood above any act of a legislature, holding the permanent will of the people. Marshall said the same in 1803 and got the credit.

narrative_blocks.header: Senator, governor and justice in four years
narrative_blocks.body: He was one of New Jersey's first two senators, then the first man ever to resign a Senate seat, leaving in 1790 to be governor. Washington put him on the Supreme Court in 1793.

narrative_blocks.header: He coined the word Cliosophic
narrative_blocks.body: Princeton suppressed its two student clubs in 1769, and Paterson, reading law in the town after his own graduation, helped talk President Witherspoon into allowing successors. He named one Cliosophic, praise of wisdom, and it still runs as the country's oldest debating union.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife died four days after their son
narrative_blocks.body: Their second daughter Frances died in June 1783, a year old. Cornelia Bell was carrying the third child, bore William Bell Paterson on 9 November, and was dead four days later at twenty-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: A coach accident three years in the killing
narrative_blocks.body: A circuit-riding coach turned over under him in 1803 and his health never came back. He set out for Ballston spa in 1806 and got as far as his daughter's house at Albany.

narrative_blocks.header: A city and a university carry his name
narrative_blocks.body: As governor in 1792 he chartered Hamilton's manufacturing society, and the town laid out at the Great Falls of the Passaic took his name. William Paterson University carries it too.

people.research_notes: Wikipedia; Federal Judicial Center; Leonard B. Rosenberg. Born at Antrim, brought to Delaware at two, raised at Princeton where his father kept a store opposite Nassau Hall. Read law with Richard Stockton. Second wife Euphemia White (1746-1832), married 1785; his other children Frances (1781-1783) and William Bell Paterson (1783-1832) have no entries. Declined the State Department in 1795. Buried in Section 14, Lot 1 at Albany Rural, the same lot as his son-in-law Stephen Van Rensselaer III. The Plain Dealing and Well Meaning Clubs of about 1765 were suppressed in March 1769; the American Whig Society followed on 24 June 1769 and the Cliosophic Society on 7 June 1770, both housed in Nassau Hall. Whig took its name from William Livingston's essays; Clio from Paterson's own commencement address. Madison was a Whig, Burr a Clio. The two merged in 1928 as the American Whig-Cliosophic Society.

narrative_blocks.header: Four days after her son was born
narrative_blocks.body: She lost her second daughter Frances in June 1783 and was carrying a third child at the time. William Bell Paterson was born on 9 November and his mother was dead on the thirteenth, twenty-eight years old.

people.research_notes: FindAGrave. Daughter of John Bell, a wealthy Somerset County landowner; married William Paterson in 1779. Three children: Cornelia Bell Van Rensselaer, Frances (1781-1783) and William Bell Paterson.

narrative_blocks.header: She was his second wife, and had six
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Adelina Paul came out of Albany County and married Cortlandt Creed after the death of his first wife Drucilla Wright. Six children were born to them, and the family moved between New Haven and Brooklyn as his practice did.

narrative_blocks.header: A daughter of her own name died first
narrative_blocks.body: A Mary Adelina Creed died suddenly at Brooklyn in December 1892, young, with her friends about her. The coroner's jury never called the man whose name was in every mouth, because he could not be found; he had left the country.

narrative_blocks.header: Three diseases named on her certificate
narrative_blocks.body: She outlived her husband by eight years and died in Kings County on 8 November 1908, at sixty-nine. The certificate gave chronic rheumatism, endocarditis and a carcinoma of the stomach.

people.research_notes: FindAGrave; New York death certificate. Daughter of Benjamin Paul and Eliza B. Hall; second wife of Cortlandt Van Rensselaer Creed, whose first wife was Drucilla Wright. Buried at Cypress Hills, Brooklyn. The Mary Adelina Creed whose death the Brooklyn Daily Eagle covered on 29 December 1892 as 'The Case of Miss Creed' cannot be this woman, who lived to 1908; on the name and the place she is almost certainly a daughter. The man the Eagle would not name was Henry F. Downing, a former U.S. consul at Loanda who fled to England, married there, and in 1897 became Paul Laurence Dunbar's manager in London — Dunbar complained to his mother that Downing kept most of a recital fee. None of them is in the tree.

marriages.officiant: Daniel Fawcett Tiemann, Mayor of New York

narrative_blocks.header: She married the brother first
narrative_blocks.body: John Hull Olmsted married her in 1851 and died of tuberculosis at Nice in 1857, leaving her with three children under six. His brother Frederick married her on 13 June 1859 and adopted all three.

narrative_blocks.header: The mayor of New York married them
narrative_blocks.body: Daniel Fawcett Tiemann, then mayor of the city whose park her husband was building, performed the ceremony himself.

narrative_blocks.header: Her first anniversary was her son's birthday
narrative_blocks.body: John Theodore was born on 13 June 1860, a year to the day after the wedding, and died in infancy. Marion followed in October 1861 and Frederick Law Jr. in July 1870, joining John Charles, Charlotte and Owen from her first marriage.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived him by eighteen years
narrative_blocks.body: She died at Brookline in April 1921 and was buried beside him in the family ground at Old North Cemetery in Hartford, the city he was born in.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter married an Ingersoll cousin
narrative_blocks.body: Born at St. Louis to Mary Jane Ingersoll and Jonathan Hall Drew, he married Mary Elizabeth McGrew in 1890. Their daughter Alice married Alanson Saunders Ingersoll in 1916, closing a branch of the family that had separated in Lee, Massachusetts.

narrative_blocks.header: She married the name back into the family
narrative_blocks.body: Her grandmother Mary Jane was born an Ingersoll at Lee, Massachusetts, and married a Drew. In 1916 at Newark, New Jersey, she married Alanson Saunders Ingersoll, her second cousin once removed, and the name came back.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Ingersoll brothers of Lee, then rejoined
narrative_blocks.body: Deacon David Ingersoll of Lee had two sons born in December 1801, William and Alvan Hyde. She comes down through William, her husband through Alvan Hyde, and the branches met again four generations later.

narrative_blocks.header: Six children, and the last four in Evanston
narrative_blocks.body: David was born at Montclair in 1917 and John at Newark in 1918, then the family settled at Evanston, where her parents lived. Robert Lyman, born there in 1925, lived eleven days; Mary Cornelia, William Jared and Alfred Drew reached their seventies and eighties.

bio.bio_blurb: Navy master chief and scout executive

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-seven years, two services, two wars
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Winona to Arthur H. and Evelyn L. Krings, he served in the Army and then the Navy across Korea and Vietnam, retiring as a master chief petty officer. The VFW post at Winona conducted the honors when he was buried there in 2010.

narrative_blocks.header: An Eagle Scout who never left scouting
narrative_blocks.body: Troop 6 at Winona made him an Eagle Scout and sent him to the 1950 National Jamboree at Valley Forge. He went professional in 1961 — Albert Lea, St. Paul, then Metairie — and was still running a Sea Scout ship in Florida the year he died.

career.notes: Army then Navy; 37 years across the Korean and Vietnam wars

career.location: Albert Lea MN, St. Paul MN, Metairie LA

burial.plot_notes: Section 1, Lot 162; moved from Woodland Cemetery 1 November 1870

narrative_blocks.header: Two Parsons brothers, two Ingersoll cousins
narrative_blocks.body: She married Charles Ashbel Parsons in 1881; eight years later his brother Edward married her second cousin Mary Augusta Ingersoll. The two women's fathers were first cousins, sons of the Ingersoll brothers of Lee.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at twenty-four, remarried at forty-one
narrative_blocks.body: Charles Parsons died at Brooklyn on the last day of 1885, four years into the marriage. In 1903 she married Timothy Dwight Merwin of New Milford, a Hooker descendant through the Merwins of Milford, and died in Los Angeles County in 1941.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty years in Pasadena after Cleveland
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Sandusky to the Rev. Edward Payson Ingersoll and Julia de Forest, she married Horace Arthur Fuller at Brooklyn in 1886 and kept house in Cleveland for most of their marriage. She outlived him by twenty-eight years, all but a few of them in Pasadena.

narrative_blocks.header: One daughter survived her, and six grandchildren
narrative_blocks.body: Marian died at Glendale in 1948, leaving Antoinette at Lake Arrowhead the only surviving daughter when she died in 1952. Six grandchildren and fifteen great-grandchildren outlived her, and she was carried back to Cleveland for burial.

cross_connections.display_label: was his brother, and married another Ingersoll cousin in 1889

narrative_blocks.header: He was a twin, and married twice
narrative_blocks.body: Born at New Milford in 1807 alongside his sister Marcia Harriet, he married Orria Gaylord in 1844 and had Joseph Butler and Timothy Dwight. After Orria died in 1865 he married Anna Amanda Carter of Ravenna, Ohio.

narrative_blocks.header: He came to the Ingersolls already a cousin
narrative_blocks.body: His great-grandparents Joseph Merwin and Phebe Platt married at Milford in 1766, which makes him a Hooker descendant in his own right. In 1903 he married Antoinette Ingersoll, the widow of Charles Ashbel Parsons.

narrative_blocks.header: He was in the counting room at eighteen
narrative_blocks.body: His father Samuel Augustus Fuller founded Condit, Fuller & Company and managed the Union Rolling Mill. He left high school at sixteen, took a year at Hudson and a year at Western Reserve, and went into his father's accounting department in January 1883.

narrative_blocks.header: At his father's death the mill became his
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel died in 1891; the son took the Union Rolling Mill's treasurership and general managership that year, and its presidency in 1911. Bourne-Fuller and the rolling mill were merged in January 1912, and he was elected president of the whole in 1914.

narrative_blocks.header: Three firms that became Republic Steel
narrative_blocks.body: The sales house, the rolling mill and the Upson Nut Company together made the largest independent steel group in Ohio. Six years after he died, Bourne-Fuller went in as one of the three constituents of the Republic Steel Corporation.

narrative_blocks.header: Cleveland clubs, and one in Pasadena
narrative_blocks.body: He sat on the Bratenahl village school board and directed Central National Bank, the American Box Company and the Sheriff Street Market. His clubs ran from the Union and the Tavern at Cleveland to Midwick at Pasadena, where he died in 1924.

narrative_blocks.header: Twin to the brother who kept New Milford
narrative_blocks.body: She and Marcus Elliott Merwin were born the same September day in 1807 to Deacon Joseph Merwin and Gratia Candee. He stayed in New Milford; she married the Rev. Maltby Gelston there in 1834 and went west to Ann Arbor.

narrative_blocks.header: She buried four of her eight children
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph Maltby died the day he was born in 1846, Gratia Mary at nineteen months, Adelaide at ten. Four were living when she died: Joseph Mills preaching at Pontiac, Henry Wisewell at Northfield, Antoinette married to a Harvey, and Sarah unmarried at Ann Arbor.

narrative_blocks.header: Her Ann Arbor house was a railroad station
narrative_blocks.body: In the abolition years the Gelston house was an important station on the Underground Railroad, kept busy moving fugitives north to Canada. She had come out from Connecticut with her family about 1863 and stayed until her death.

narrative_blocks.header: A stroke in November, and eight months dying
narrative_blocks.body: Paralysis took her in early November 1883 and she was nearly helpless from then on, through a second and a third stroke, until she died at a quarter past midnight on 19 July 1884. She was a fortnight short of seventy-seven.

narrative_blocks.header: A blacksmith with ten children at Lee
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Otis, he came to Lee about 1915 and shod horses there the rest of his life. Seven sons and three daughters survived him in 1932 — four still in Lee, one at Lenox, two at Springfield, and daughters at Lee, Great Barrington and Lowell.

narrative_blocks.header: She reached a hundred and three months
narrative_blocks.body: Born at South Lee in June 1914, she married Richard Reed in 1931 and worked years at the Eastover resort in Lenox. She outlived her husband by twenty-three years and her daughter Jean by four months, dying at Lenox in September 2014.

narrative_blocks.header: Mother, father and daughter in one year
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother Jean died in May 2014 and her father Richard in June; she followed in November, at fifty-eight, and was buried with them at Elmwood. She had lived at Egremont, and worked the Brooks pharmacy counter and Cumberland Farms for years.

narrative_blocks.header: Flora Gillett Merwin took her in
narrative_blocks.body: She was born a Wright in Mahoning County in 1882 and came into the family by adoption, Flora A. Gillett Merwin standing as her mother. She married Frederick Richard Brennan in Trumbull County in 1905 and raised three children in the Pennsylvania oil country.

narrative_blocks.header: He put Kant back into the argument
narrative_blocks.body: Modern logic, non-Euclidean geometry and relativity had left Kant's philosophy of mathematics for dead. Almost single-handedly he brought it back, showing what in Kant's account of intuition still bore on problems contemporary philosophers had run into.

narrative_blocks.header: Ask what structure a number sits in
narrative_blocks.body: Mathematical Thought and its Objects, in 2008, was his settled statement: there is no asking what a mathematical entity is, only what structure it plays a role in. Others defended structuralism too, but usually smuggled in a notion of entity; he did not.

narrative_blocks.header: He edited the papers Gödel never published
narrative_blocks.body: With Solomon Feferman and others he brought out Gödel's posthumous works, and wrote at length on Gödel, Frege, Quine and Brentano. In 2017 he gave the Gödel Lecture, on Gödel and the universe of sets.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the chair that had been Quine's
narrative_blocks.body: Quine and Burton Dreben supervised his Harvard doctorate in 1961. Twenty-four years at Columbia followed, then a return to Harvard in 1989 and, in 1991, the Edgar Pierce professorship that Quine had held before him.

narrative_blocks.header: He would stop mid-sentence and think
narrative_blocks.body: Lecturing or talking, he would break off in the middle of a sentence and weigh whether what he was about to say was exactly right — sometimes for a full minute or two — then pick the sentence up where he had left it.

narrative_blocks.header: A sociologist's son who took the logic
narrative_blocks.body: He grew up at Belmont in his father Talcott Parsons's Harvard atmosphere and read mathematics at the College. His own students — Higginbotham, Ludlow, Sher, Linnebo and others — went on to run the field he had opened.

narrative_blocks.header: Brazil, Bangkok, then Switzerland
narrative_blocks.body: Her parents took her to Brazil as a baby and she stayed until she was thirteen, but for a spell in Connecticut. A year in Bangkok followed, then four years at French-language boarding schools in Switzerland.

narrative_blocks.header: She went from Barnard to two Turkish villages
narrative_blocks.body: She graduated from Barnard in 1965 and went straight into the Peace Corps, posted to two villages in Turkey. Back in New York in 1967 she worked at Columbia's school of architecture and read philosophy at night.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirteen years in the soup kitchens
narrative_blocks.body: From about 1983 she worked with destitute mentally ill people through soup kitchens, first in New York and then in Boston, and kept at it until 1996. She took a divinity degree in 1987 and a social work degree two years later.

narrative_blocks.header: A garden the neighbours counted on
narrative_blocks.body: She kept a garden at Cambridge that her neighbours valued, went on studying ancient languages and religious texts, and was devoted to her cats and dogs. She died at a hospice in Wayland after a long illness.

narrative_blocks.header: His senior thesis and his last book agree
narrative_blocks.body: His Harvard thesis took the Society of Jesus and its Paris opponents in the 1550s. Three decades on he edited and translated Étienne Pasquier's The Jesuits' Catechism, and the texts from the expulsion of the Jesuits from France.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the counterfeiters into the state
narrative_blocks.body: Making Money in Sixteenth-Century France followed the royal Cour des Monnaies as it took hold of the coinage, and the forgers who worked the gap between a coin and its worth. The Renaissance Society of America gave it the Gordan Prize.

narrative_blocks.header: His first book asked where authority begins
narrative_blocks.body: The Church in the Republic took the fight over the liberties of the Gallican Church, one of the central arguments of early modern France, and used it to ask where authority inside any human institution comes from.

narrative_blocks.header: Harvard twice over in one generation
narrative_blocks.body: He took his degree at Harvard in 1990 and his sister Sylvia hers in 1992, at the college where their father taught philosophy. He went to Johns Hopkins for the doctorate and has taught at Duquesne since 2003.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a Merwin, as his grandmother was
narrative_blocks.body: Tryphena Merwin was his second cousin: his grandmother Susannah and her grandfather David were children of Joseph Merwin and Margaret Fowler of Milford. They married at New Milford in March 1825 and had nine children.

narrative_blocks.header: Her parents sent her to Miss Pierce's
narrative_blocks.body: Orange and Tryphena Merwin had her educated at the Litchfield Female Academy in 1816. Six years later she married the New Milford lawyer David Curtis Sanford, who would sit on the state's supreme court.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine days after her daughter was born
narrative_blocks.body: Caroline was born on 11 January 1824 and she died on the twentieth, at twenty-three. The child outlived her by thirteen months. Her husband married again in 1830 and served ten years as a judge.

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband's grandmother was born a Merwin
narrative_blocks.body: Marshall Stone Platt was her second cousin — his grandmother Susannah Merwin and her grandfather David Merwin were brother and sister, children of Joseph Merwin and Margaret Fowler. She married him in 1825, at eighteen.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten years on Connecticut's highest court
narrative_blocks.body: In 1854 the legislature he sat in elected David to the Superior and Supreme Courts, in the seat Judge Waite left on succeeding the late Chief Justice Samuel Church. David held that a court's duty is to declare the law, not to make it, and he died in office ten years on.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote Connecticut's temperance law himself
narrative_blocks.body: Sent to the state senate in 1854, he chaired the judiciary committee and drew the intemperance act of that session — framed to survive every constitutional objection. It stayed on the statute book largely unaltered long after him.

narrative_blocks.header: He learned law watching Litchfield's courts
narrative_blocks.body: At Litchfield David sat through every court he could, noticed for his good looks and polished manners and for the eager attention he paid judges and witnesses. Seth Beers, with whom he had studied, made him a partner and later left him the whole practice.

narrative_blocks.header: Norwalk, then home to New Milford for good
narrative_blocks.body: In 1832 David moved to Norwalk to fill the opening Judge Bissell left for the Supreme Court, and stood in the front rank of a strong Fairfield bar. His second wife, Amelia Seymour, died in July 1833, and that fall he went home to New Milford.

narrative_blocks.header: A storekeeper's son, reading law at nineteen
narrative_blocks.body: His father kept a store at what is now Bridgewater and had a common school education and a gift for mathematics, which he passed on. There was an academy term or two and nothing else; at nineteen he began reading law, and was at the bar by twenty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at twenty-five, a father at once
narrative_blocks.body: Caroline Merwin of New Milford, schooled at the Litchfield Female Academy, married him in September 1822. Their daughter Caroline was born on 11 January 1824; the mother died nine days later, and the child before her second birthday.

narrative_blocks.header: His deathbed words at New Milford
narrative_blocks.body: David was an Episcopal communicant from early life. Dying at New Milford in May 1864, he told his pastor the fear of death had passed, and said again and again, “How gently I am let down.”

narrative_blocks.header: Pacific, then Korea, then full honors
narrative_blocks.body: He served on ships in the Pacific through the Second World War and again in Korea, retiring a lieutenant commander. He died at ninety-eight, and in January 2020 a caisson drawn by seven white horses carried him through Arlington to a columbarium beside Carol.

career.notes: Pacific in the Second World War; served again in Korea

narrative_blocks.header: She put a lei on Admiral Halsey
narrative_blocks.body: She served in the Marine Corps through the war and stayed in the reserves after it. At the Naval Services reserve officers' convention in St. Louis in March 1947 she welcomed the guests, hanging a lei of ginger blossoms on Fleet Admiral Halsey with Navy Secretary Forrestal looking on.

career.role: Professor of History and Associate Dean

narrative_blocks.header: He kept the Great White Fleet notebook
narrative_blocks.body: His father Francis Decatur Roche sailed aboard the USS Minnesota on the 1907–09 cruise Theodore Roosevelt sent round the world — sixteen new battleships painted white and buff. He held on to the little notebook his father wrote in the whole way, and gave it to his son.

narrative_blocks.header: A medal from Yokohama, an inch across
narrative_blocks.body: Nobody aboard knew what to expect when the fleet came into Yokohama on 20 October 1908, with Japan militarised and the world uneasy about it. The Japanese threw parties for the crews and handed out a remembrance medal; that one came down to him too, an inch by three-quarters.

narrative_blocks.header: Born and dead the same April day
narrative_blocks.body: He was Henry Hulbert Ingersoll's first child, born at Kenton, Ohio, on 19 April 1865 and buried before the month was out. His cousin Edward Reed Ingersoll was born in the same town three months later, to his father's brother Ansel.

narrative_blocks.header: A River North gallery that booked bands
narrative_blocks.body: He opened the Byron Roche Gallery on North Franklin Street in Chicago in 1994 and ran it sixteen years, showing regional and national contemporary painters. Between exhibitions he put the city's singer-songwriters on in the same rooms.

narrative_blocks.header: Country, rocky, jazzy, bluesy, swingy folk
narrative_blocks.body: He picked up a guitar as a child and was performing around St. Louis at fifteen. Chicago took him in the mid-seventies for the clubs and the college circuit, and when asked what he plays he gives that string of adjectives, with classical overtones.

narrative_blocks.header: Four years, and the walk down the pier
narrative_blocks.body: He went to boot camp at San Diego in April 1968 and left the USS Ogden on 3 January 1972, saluting the officer of the deck and the flag for the last time. He calls it one of the happiest days of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: The YMCA sent the proofs to his mother
narrative_blocks.body: On his first liberty out of boot camp, nineteen and too young for the bars, he wandered San Diego in uniform and sat for the free photograph the YMCA offered graduates. He wanted only the free one; the studio posted the proofs to St. Louis and his parents bought the lot.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother died five days after his birth
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Manchester on 21 April 1829 and Frances Skinner Watson died on the twenty-sixth, at twenty. His father married her elder sister Susan two years later, and he grew up with half-brothers in the Champlain valley.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty years farming above the lake
narrative_blocks.body: He kept a farm at Port Kent for twenty years and retired from it about 1884. His last five years were spent in Brooklyn at his daughter's house on DeKalb Avenue, and he was carried back to Port Kent to be buried.

narrative_blocks.header: Elkanah Watson was his grandfather
narrative_blocks.body: His father's father was the merchant Elkanah Watson, who was in France during the Revolution and worked with Benjamin Franklin to press the French government for aid to the United States.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven children, and she outlived two brothers
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Kenmore, New York, to Josephine Lyman and the Harry Lewis of Buffalo, she raised seven children and died at Festus, Missouri, at eighty-seven. Fourteen grandchildren and eight great-grandchildren survived her, and a sister and a brother.

narrative_blocks.header: She loved the hymns best of all
narrative_blocks.body: First Baptist of Festus and Crystal City was her church, and she served in Christian Marriage Ministry and Friendship International. She was buried at the national cemetery at Jefferson Barracks.

narrative_blocks.header: Copley flew the first Stars and Stripes
narrative_blocks.body: Sitting to John Singleton Copley in London in 1782, he asked for a ship in the background bearing news of American independence home. Copley would not hoist the flag on her gaff while royalty walked his gallery — then on 5 December, after they had heard George III recognise the United States, he painted it in.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty thousand dollars sewn into his coat
narrative_blocks.body: At twenty, apprenticed to the Providence merchant John Brown, he carried his employer's money twelve hundred miles to Charleston with it stitched inside his clothes, and took seventy-seven days over it. He began the journal on that road and kept one for sixty years.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried Brown's dispatches to Franklin
narrative_blocks.body: Sent to France in the war with money and papers for Benjamin Franklin at Passy, he stayed a month in the old man's household, then opened a counting house at Nantes with François Cossoul. He was made a Freemason in France, and the partners sent George Washington an apron.

narrative_blocks.header: He proposed the Erie Canal in 1791
narrative_blocks.body: That December he told the New York legislature the state's own rivers could be strung together from the Hudson to the Great Lakes, and with Philip Schuyler built the first locks at Little Falls. DeWitt Clinton got the canal and the credit, and the two of them argued over it for years.

narrative_blocks.header: The first county fair, at Pittsfield in 1810
narrative_blocks.body: Retired to a Berkshire farm with imported Merino sheep, he staged a cattle show to shame his neighbours into better practice, and built it out with things for women and children to do. The Berkshire Agricultural Society followed, and the county fair became an American institution.

narrative_blocks.header: His son finished the memoirs he left
narrative_blocks.body: He began the autobiography in 1821 out of forty years of journals and died with it unfinished. Winslow Cossoul Watson completed and published it in 1856 as Men and Times of the Revolution, and named his own house the one his father built above Lake Champlain.

career.notes: Removed for advocating free schools, stage lines and turnpikes
