narrative_blocks.header: A mourning portrait with a tomb behind it
narrative_blocks.body: After her daughter Emily Watson Larned died, Elkanah paid Ezra Ames for a portrait of a daughter — a dark-dressed young woman with a monument behind her lettered E.W.L. Princeton holds the picture, and whether the sitter is Emily or her younger sister Mary in mourning has never been settled.

narrative_blocks.header: Indians in a canoe beside the monument
narrative_blocks.body: Ames put a canoe on the water to the left of the tomb. It was read as a sign of where Emily lay — buried in wilderness far west of the Albany she came from, a long way from her mother's house above Lake Champlain.

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband was a fourth cousin
narrative_blocks.body: Michael Peck descended from Rev. Roger Newton Sr. and Mary Hooker Newton through their son John Newton; she descended from the same couple through their son Roger Newton Jr. Five generations on, the two branches met at Milford on New Year's Day 1797.

narrative_blocks.header: Two founding lines met in her marriage
narrative_blocks.body: Her great-grandfather Robert Treat led the founders of Newark and governed Connecticut; her husband David Ingersoll came down from Thomas Hooker through the Newtons of Milford. They married there on 9 March 1768.

cross_connections.display_label: was her great-grandfather, and governed the colony from Milford

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband was a fourth cousin
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel Peck descended from Rev. Roger Newton Sr. and Mary Hooker Newton through their son John; she descended from the same couple through their son Samuel. The two Newton brothers' lines met again at Milford in January 1796 — and his brother Michael married her fourth cousin Mary Marshall the year after.

bio.bio_blurb: Wife of the Armour Brothers' banker

parents.mother_name: Juliana Ann Brooks Armour (1799–1879), m. 22 November 1825

narrative_blocks.header: The founder's older brother, not the founder
narrative_blocks.body: Philip Danforth Armour, three years younger, built Armour and Company at Chicago and ran it till he died. Andrew was one of five brothers in the same trade in different cities, and his city was Kansas City — the bank first, then the packing house.

narrative_blocks.header: He left the plough at forty-nine
narrative_blocks.body: Raised to the plough in Oneida, he had never been identified with large affairs when his brothers Philip and Simeon urged him west. He came to Kansas City in the spring of 1878 with much reluctance, and the open field stayed dearer to him than the street.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded a bank in a bank panic
narrative_blocks.body: Grain moved slowly that wet winter and cash ran out of the banks like water: the First National failed in January, the Mastin bank in August. Knowing nothing whatever of banking, he opened Armour Brothers' Bank in September, himself president.

narrative_blocks.header: Five brothers, five cities, one firm
narrative_blocks.body: Plankinton and Armour had packed at Kansas City since about 1870, and when Plankinton withdrew in 1885 the firm became Armour Brothers — Philip the founder, Simeon the eldest, Andrew, and Andrew's two sons. Herman held New York and the grain, Joseph Chicago.

narrative_blocks.header: The main line ended in his nephew's hands
narrative_blocks.body: Philip's heir apparent died at thirty-one and the company fell to the other son, J. Ogden Armour, who took it to the front of American business and lost it after the war. By the late twenties only one of Andrew's grandsons and one of Philip's sat on the board.

narrative_blocks.header: He died on a bench by the spring
narrative_blocks.body: At Excelsior Springs he drank at the Regent and said he felt better than he had in six months. His wife asked him not to walk on to the Siloam spring; he would not hear of it, and died on a bench beside it.

cross_connections.display_label: , his great-grandnephew, ranched cattle in Arizona and Florida

career.organization: Armour Brothers, later Armour and Company

burial.plot_notes: Armour family plot, on his son Kirkland's lot

bio.bio_blurb: Kansas City packer and cemetery president

narrative_blocks.header: He came west at sixteen to his uncle
narrative_blocks.body: He and his brother Charles left New York about 1870 for Kansas City and their uncle Simeon's packing house. When Plankinton withdrew in 1885 the two of them joined their father and uncles in Armour Brothers.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought the King of England's cattle
narrative_blocks.body: About 1900 he bought pedigreed Hereford stock out of the King of England's own herd and put it on the Armour farms in Missouri, helping fix the breed in American beef. His uncle Philip's company at Chicago was by then the largest meatpacker in the world.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave Elmwood a charter for 999 years
narrative_blocks.body: In 1896 he and a handful of other Kansas City men raised the money to buy Elmwood Cemetery outright and make it a not-for-profit, and took out a charter with the State of Missouri to protect it for nine hundred and ninety-nine years. He was its first president.

narrative_blocks.header: His widow answered with a chapel
narrative_blocks.body: The year after he died she paid for the Armour Chapel on the Elmwood grounds — gothic, native stone and carved timber, eighty-five seats, stained glass, oaken angels in the beams, a bell tower, working gargoyles to throw the rain off, and a marble columbarium underneath.

narrative_blocks.header: The homestead went to her outright
narrative_blocks.body: His will, filed at Kansas City a fortnight after he died, divided the estate share and share alike between his widow and three children, and gave her the house at Armour and Warwick boulevards without reservation. The executors were bonded to nothing, which made the estate impossible to value from outside.

career.organization: Armour Brothers, later Armour and Company

bio.bio_blurb: Kansas City packer and book collector

narrative_blocks.header: Thirteen when the packing house took him
narrative_blocks.body: He came out from Stockbridge about 1870, a boy of thirteen, to his uncle Simeon's packing house at Kansas City. He took a partner's share when the firm was remade as Armour Brothers in 1885.

narrative_blocks.header: The last Armour left at Kansas City
narrative_blocks.body: He was thirty-five when his father died and forty-four when his brother Kirkland followed. He stayed on another twenty-six years, into the era when the firm took the name Armour and Company.

narrative_blocks.header: A farmer's son with a coat of arms
narrative_blocks.body: He had an armorial bookplate engraved to paste into the books he collected. His father had come off an Oneida County farm at forty-nine.

narrative_blocks.header: A first edition of Burton's East African travels
narrative_blocks.body: He owned Richard Burton's First Footsteps in East Africa in the first edition of 1856, with four colour plates and two engraved maps. The explorer's own account of the journey, it was bound for him later in green morocco.

narrative_blocks.header: He sent Leigh Hunt to a London binder
narrative_blocks.body: His copy of Leigh Hunt's poems of 1832 went to William Worsfold, a third-generation London bookbinder, who covered it in crushed green morocco tooled with gilt ivy. The old cloth binding was kept and bound in at the back.

narrative_blocks.header: His first wife died four days past thirty-one
narrative_blocks.body: He married Sarah Annie Magie of Milwaukee in June 1885 and she died there in January 1889, four days after her thirty-first birthday. He married Rebecca Drummond Camp of Lyons four years later, and she outlived him by two years.

career.organization: Armour Brothers, later Armour and Company

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty years a deacon in one church
narrative_blocks.body: He kept the Congregational deaconship at Washington for sixty years and the Sunday-school superintendency for twenty in succession. In the days of the deacon's meetings he was the reading deacon, and he taught school and sat on the school board besides.

narrative_blocks.header: His widowed granddaughter came to keep him
narrative_blocks.body: He married Rebecca, daughter of Nehemiah Smith O'Dell, and their daughter Mary married Jerome Kinney. After Kinney died, Mary came back to her grandparents' house and cared for them; his wife died three years before he did, at eighty-seven.

career.notes: Sixty years a deacon; reading deacon at the deacon's meetings

narrative_blocks.header: She left New Milford at eight years old
narrative_blocks.body: She was born a mile west of New Milford village, eldest daughter of Nehemiah and Polly Morehouse O'Dell and granddaughter of Capt. William O'Dell, one of the first settlers there. At eight she came to Washington with her older brother William and was raised in her aunt Mrs. Nathaniel Galpin's house.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty years married, and eight months more
narrative_blocks.body: She joined the Congregational church in 1832 and married Stephen S. Baldwin on 9 April 1834. They kept their sixtieth anniversary that April at the Ford Homestead, where they had moved six years earlier to be near their granddaughter; the stroke came on 21 November and she died five weeks later.

narrative_blocks.header: A few weeks of suffering, and gone
narrative_blocks.body: She was the second of Stephen and Rebecca Baldwin's two daughters and lived only weeks. Her mother's obituary, fifty-two years later, still set her beside her surviving sister as one of the two children born to them.

parents.father_name: Capt. Wheeler of New Haven, master mariner

narrative_blocks.header: New Haven's past was her subject
narrative_blocks.body: Tall, courtly and proud, she had a great fondness for antiquity and antiquarian pursuits, and the men compiling the town's genealogies came to her for what she knew of New Haven and New-Haveners. She kept to Trinity Church and in later years worshipped with the Davenport Congregationalists.

narrative_blocks.header: Her closing years were clouded
narrative_blocks.body: Three or four times in her life she suffered a degree of insanity, and the last of it did not lift. She died at New Haven in January 1892, six years after her husband.

bio.bio_blurb: Shipmaster; died at sea off Hawaii

narrative_blocks.header: He rose to master of a vessel
narrative_blocks.body: Born at New Haven, he followed the sea out of his father's house and rose to master of a vessel. It carried him to the Sandwich Islands, where he married Kealohapauole Kamakaiwi in 1866 and had two daughters.

narrative_blocks.header: Only his companion came back
narrative_blocks.body: The two of them set out in a small boat and the other man returned alone, saying the voyage had run far beyond what they had provisioned for, that the supplies gave out, and that Glenney had died of starvation. He admitted he had been living on the body. Those who looked at the boat saw what appeared to be the marks of a desperate struggle.

, his granddaughter's husband, reached Hawaii as a ship's officer

narrative_blocks.header: Sailor, then naval officer, then soldier
narrative_blocks.body: He went all three ways in one life, at sea and then in uniform on land. He married and had a daughter, Flossie, who died young.

narrative_blocks.header: A photographer who began life again
narrative_blocks.body: He ran with one of the fire companies under the old regime and left the incorrect habits of his early years behind him, joining the Davenport Congregational church and the Sons of Temperance. He worked as a photographer at Waterbury, Milford and New Haven, and was reckoned a good artist and a genial friend.

career.organization: Waterbury, Milford and New Haven, Connecticut

narrative_blocks.header: Thirteen years postmistress at Heeia
narrative_blocks.body: She kept the Heeia post office on Oahu for the last thirteen years of her life and was ill more than a year before the end, dying at the Queen's hospital in August 1944 at sixty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-nine grandchildren, and eight children left
narrative_blocks.body: Of the seventeen she bore, eight were living when she died: Gertrude Lee, Adeline Todd, Margaret Tilton and Beatrice Stone, Grebell still unmarried, and Henry Jr., Smith and Coates. Twenty-nine grandchildren and six great-grandchildren survived her, all on Oahu.

parents.father_name: Frederick Emilius Adams, of the Honourable East India Company
parents.mother_name: Georgiana Augusta Cobb, youngest daughter of Capt. Smith Cobb RN

narrative_blocks.header: He came in with the Portuguese immigrants
narrative_blocks.body: Henry went to sea at fourteen and reached Honolulu in July 1883 as chief officer of the Hankow, bringing Portuguese immigrants from Madeira and the Azores. A year later he came back as purser of the City of Paris with more, and stayed.

narrative_blocks.header: They called him the Mayor of Kaneohe
narrative_blocks.body: Henry taught at the boys' industrial school in Palama, then at Kaneohe, where he settled. He was deputy tax assessor from 1896 and Koolaupoko magistrate from 1911, and at seventy-one lost the House nomination for the fifth district.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventeen children, and eight in infancy
narrative_blocks.body: He married Rebecca Kealohapau‘ole Kaleleiki in May 1897. Seventeen children were born to them: eight died as babies and one at nineteen, and eight grew up and had families of their own.

career.role: Registrar of births, deaths and marriages

steamers Hankow and City of Paris

notable.notable_blurb: The Mayor of Kaneohe

narrative_blocks.header: His sister's plane went down coming to him
narrative_blocks.body: He lay dying of pneumonia at the Molokai hospital on 3 January 1955 when the plane bringing his sister Beatrice to his bedside was forced down in the sea off the island and she was lost, at forty. He died at one the next morning, aged fifty-three, and they were buried from St. Andrew's together.

narrative_blocks.header: She was flying to her brother's bedside
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Kaneohe in 1914 and married to the highway engineer Edwin K. Stone in 1932, she was working for the Veterans Administration when the plane carrying her to her dying brother on Molokai came down in the water on 3 January 1955. Three of his children were aboard it with her.

parents.father_name: George Henry Bush (1807–1853), of Suffolk, to Hawaii from England in 1825

narrative_blocks.header: A printer's apprentice made royal governor
narrative_blocks.body: Son of a Suffolk man who came out in 1825 and a Hawaiian mother, he worked a whaling ship and learned the trade at the Hawaiian Gazette. Kalākaua made him Royal Governor of Kauaʻi in 1877, then put him in the Privy Council, the House of Nobles, and three times in the cabinet.

narrative_blocks.header: He sailed to build a Polynesian empire
narrative_blocks.body: Kalākaua sent him to Samoa in 1887 to bring Malietoa Laupepa into a Polynesian confederation, and the treaty was signed that March. His flagship was the Kaimiloa, a refitted British merchantman crewed by the reformatory school's boys' band, shadowed the whole time by a German warship that could have sunk her.

narrative_blocks.header: The empire of the calabash collapsed
narrative_blocks.body: While he was still at Apia the Honolulu Rifles forced Kalākaua to dismiss Gibson and sign away his powers, the Samoan expense given as the reason. His crew sold the ship's silver at Pago Pago for food and drink; Germany declared war on Laupepa the day after she sailed.

narrative_blocks.header: His paper was the loudest Hawaiian voice
narrative_blocks.body: Back home he founded Hui Kālaiʻāina in 1888 and from 1889 published Ka Leo o ka Lāhui — five thousand copies, the leading Hawaiian-language paper of the nineties. He was fined for contempt for writing that would bring the court into ridicule and bad odour.

narrative_blocks.header: His first wife was thrown at the Pali
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Ann Peters was reckoned one of the most beautiful women in the islands and had put a lei on the Duke of Edinburgh in 1869. Riding at the Pali in 1883 she was thrown, and died of a fractured skull. He married Mary Julia Glennie the year after.

cross_connections.display_label: governed Oʻahu and Maui for Kalākaua while he governed Kauaʻi

career.role: Publisher, Ka Leo o ka Lāhui and Ka Oiaio

notable.notable_blurb: Royal Governor of Kauaʻi; Hawaiian-language publisher

narrative_blocks.header: Nine children by the royal governor
narrative_blocks.body: She married John Edward Bush about 1862 and bore him nine — Mele, Henry Peters, Maria, Mary Ann, John Edward Jr., James Keiki, George Lihauanu, Molly and William. Her line runs on in Hawaii but not into this tree, which reaches Bush only through his second wife.

death.cause: Pneumonia; died at Shady Grove Adventist Hospital

narrative_blocks.header: She studied art in Paris and stayed
narrative_blocks.body: She trained as an artist in Paris and afterwards settled in Washington with the English painter Kingsley Utteridge. Two daughters followed, Judith in Washington and Helen in London.

narrative_blocks.header: No flowers, no service, give to the animals
narrative_blocks.body: She was a lifelong friend to animals, and asked that anything meant for flowers or a funeral go instead to the Humane Society's farm animal welfare work and to the Washington Humane Society. She died at ninety-six of pneumonia.

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband and a daughter went first
narrative_blocks.body: Cancer took her at Tacoma in July 2006, forty-eight years old, after a long fight. Her husband William and her daughter Malia had both gone before her; she left her mother Priscilla, her brothers Scott and George, her daughters Shannon and Hannah, and a granddaughter.

bio.display_name: Mary Ann Rita Kamahoahoa Peters Foster

bio.bio_blurb: Army platoon sergeant, Korea and Vietnam

narrative_blocks.header: Two wars, and the Purple Heart twice
narrative_blocks.body: He went in as a platoon sergeant and served through Korea and again in Vietnam. The oak leaf cluster on his Purple Heart means he was wounded a second time. He lies at the state veterans' cemetery at Kaneohe.

career.notes: Korea and Vietnam; Purple Heart with oak leaf cluster

narrative_blocks.header: She died on her twentieth birthday
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Honolulu on 5 March 1953 to Paul Glennie Will and Vesta Parker, she died on 5 March 1973 — the same day of the same month, twenty years to the day.

bio.bio_blurb: Kansas City widow who removed to Chicago

narrative_blocks.header: The north window is a memorial to her
narrative_blocks.body: She gave the Armour Memorial Chapel at Elmwood in 1902 as a memorial to Kirkland, and had George A. Mathews build it of native stone in the Gothic manner, with hand-carved oak and art glass. In the 1920s a three-panelled stained-glass window went into the north wall for her.

narrative_blocks.header: She followed the grandchild to Chicago
narrative_blocks.body: She stayed a widow at Kansas City until her elder son married Elsa Parker of Chicago and moved there, and the journeys back and forth to play with the baby and inspect each new tooth wore on her. She took a house on the South Side near the young couple's place on Prairie Avenue.

narrative_blocks.header: Her lace came out again forty-nine years on
narrative_blocks.body: A veil of antique Malines lace of hers was worn in 1970 by her great-granddaughter Diana Cochrane, married at St. James in New York. Annie had been dead forty-nine years by then.

narrative_blocks.header: He began at a bill clerk's desk
narrative_blocks.body: Named for his grandfather and sent to Phillips Academy, he took a bill clerk's desk in the Armour plant at Kansas City about 1900. He was in Chicago and a director of the company within a few years.

narrative_blocks.header: The last two Armours on the board
narrative_blocks.body: His cousin J. Ogden Armour overreached in the early 1920s, and the reversal cost the whole family its weight at Armour and Company. By the late twenties only he and his second cousin Lester were left on the board, and they resigned soon after.

narrative_blocks.header: Elawa spliced her name to his initials
narrative_blocks.body: In 1917 he bought a hundred and twenty-eight acres west of Lake Forest and called it Elawa — the first two letters of Elsa, the three initials of A. Watson Armour. He hired Alfred Hopkins, the leading designer of working estate farms, because he meant the place to work.

narrative_blocks.header: The Georgian house was never built
narrative_blocks.body: David Adler drew them a Georgian mansion, but the country went to war the year they bought the land and only the gatehouses were built. They lived in those for good, crossing the open air between the halves until Adler ran a tunnel underneath in 1936.

narrative_blocks.header: The next owners copied the naming trick
narrative_blocks.body: He died of a heart ailment in 1953 and the family sold Elawa the year after. Lelia and Wallace Carroll bought it and renamed it LeWa, on exactly his principle.

narrative_blocks.header: He died in the hospital he had run
narrative_blocks.body: He was a trustee of St. Luke's in Chicago from 1915 and its president from 1942 to 1951. He died there of a heart ailment in 1953, at seventy-one, after a month's illness.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried his grandchildren in a scooter sidecar
narrative_blocks.body: Always tinkering with some new gadget, he took the grandchildren around the farm in the sidecar of his little scooter. They came out for the tunnel, the picnics, and Billy the goat, who had acquired a taste for cigarettes.

was chief chemist at Wilson, the packing house across town

narrative_blocks.header: More of a dancing man than his relations
narrative_blocks.body: He was reckoned more of a dancing man than the rest of the Armours, whose early rising was proverbial in Chicago and who as a family kept out of society. He married Lacy Withers of Jackson County the following year.

narrative_blocks.header: He took a major's commission in his fifties
narrative_blocks.body: He served as a major in the United States Army in the Second World War, a man already in his fifties. He had been at Two Gables on South Green Bay Road in Lake Forest since at least 1920, when the telephone directory listed him there.

narrative_blocks.header: He died four days after Christmas
narrative_blocks.body: He and Lacy had one son, Laurance Hearne Armour Jr., born at Chicago in 1923. Laurance himself died at Chicago on the twenty-ninth of December 1952, and Lacy outlived him by twenty-seven years.

narrative_blocks.header: At nineteen she married into the Foreign Service
narrative_blocks.body: She married James Clement Dunn in 1914, when he was still an architect in Manhattan, and spent the next forty-two years moving with the Foreign Service — Madrid, Port-au-Prince, London, Rome, Paris, Rio. The Washington house they kept from 1927 to 1957 was the fixed point.

narrative_blocks.header: She was buried at Elmwood, not beside him
narrative_blocks.body: Dunn died in Florida in 1979 and was buried at Greenwich in Connecticut. She lived nine years more, and at ninety-three was taken to Elmwood at Kansas City, into the ground her father had chartered.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-five years on one hospital board
narrative_blocks.body: She sat on the woman's board of St. Luke's Hospital in Chicago for fifty-five years. The family's tie to the hospital had begun in 1914, when her husband was operated on there.

narrative_blocks.header: He left the packing house for fasteners
narrative_blocks.body: A fullback at Princeton who dropped out in junior year to travel, he put in a few years at Commonwealth Edison and ten at Armour and Company before joining Huck Manufacturing in 1946 and rising to its president. He grew up at Elawa Farm in Lake Forest and wintered at Hobe Sound.

narrative_blocks.header: How like an Armour to come so early
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at break of day, and one of his aunts said it: how like an Armour to come so early in the morning. The early rising of the Armour men was proverbial enough in Chicago society that a newspaper printed the line.

narrative_blocks.header: She modeled free and the professionals resented it
narrative_blocks.body: She modeled for years in the St. Luke's Hospital fashion show and for other causes, and never took a fee for it. Chicago's professional models were vexed enough at North Shore women working free that they complained in print, and named her.

narrative_blocks.header: Four generations of her family at one school
narrative_blocks.body: She went to Miss Porter's at Farmington as her mother and grandmother had, and sent her three daughters after her. Four generations of Armour women are cut into the school's bricks.

narrative_blocks.header: She married in a bower of yellow chrysanthemums
narrative_blocks.body: She married Washington Irving Osborne Jr. at St. Chrysostom's in Chicago in December 1931, the year after her debut. The church was crowded past its doors and banked with yellow chrysanthemums, December weddings being the fashion.

narrative_blocks.header: She died first after fifty-three years of marriage
narrative_blocks.body: She and Osborne were married fifty-three years and raised three daughters at Lake Forest — Adrienne, Gwendolyn and Karen. She died at Highland Park in August 1985; he lived on another seventeen years and was buried beside her.

cross_connections.display_label: founded the Farmington school four Armour generations attended

narrative_blocks.header: He advertised his terriers in the local paper
narrative_blocks.body: He grew up among the animals at Elawa and had charge of the family's pedigreed Irish terriers as a boy. At sixteen he was running their advertisement in the Lake Forester for weeks at a stretch.

narrative_blocks.header: He sold fasteners abroad for his brother's company
narrative_blocks.body: He followed his brother to St. Mark's and then Princeton, and after that to Huck Manufacturing, where he was director of overseas operations. The firm made metal fasteners for aircraft and railroads.

narrative_blocks.header: Polio closed his school and shut the farm
narrative_blocks.body: Infantile paralysis broke out at St. Mark's in late May 1936 and the boys were sent home, Charles and his cousin Philip among them. Elawa was quarantined a fortnight; his own case proved slight.

narrative_blocks.header: The village turned out to see his bride
narrative_blocks.body: He married Joan Monroe at the Church of the Holy Spirit in 1946, before generations of Armours; the little church filled and the lawn outside was dotted with passers-by come to look. The reception was in the garden at Whippoorwill, her family's farm off Mellody Road.

narrative_blocks.header: His son carried his great-grandfather's name
narrative_blocks.body: He and Joan had two children, Joan Elizabeth and Kirkland Brooks — the boy named for the Kansas City packer who was his great-grandfather. The marriage ended in 1960.

bio.bio_blurb: Chicago clothes collector and hospital volunteer

parents.father_name: Charles H. Schweppe, Chicago investment banker
parents.father_research_notes: Her mother was a daughter of John G. Shedd, chairman of Marshall Field & Company and donor of the Shedd Aquarium. Her brother was Dr. John Shedd Schweppe of Winnetka.

narrative_blocks.header: Her wardrobe went to the city's museum
narrative_blocks.body: Called the personification of glamour in the Chicago of her day, she gave the Chicago History Museum a great deal of what she had worn — Mainbocher, Dior, Adrian. Her grandfather John G. Shedd chaired Marshall Field & Company and gave the city its aquarium.

narrative_blocks.header: A chair of neurology answered her death
narrative_blocks.body: She led as a volunteer on the Medical Center's Woman's Board, and when she died at forty-eight her husband, the Armours and her friends endowed the Jean Schweppe Armour Chair of Neurology in her memory — the first endowed chair at any private hospital in the country.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father left a note on the dresser
narrative_blocks.body: Charles H. Schweppe, born at Alton and Harvard 1902, opened Lee Higginson's Chicago office in 1905 and rose to the corporation's presidency and the boards of Marshall Field and Fairbanks Morse. Four years after her mother died he was found shot in bed at Lake Forest, sixty years old, with an unaddressed note beside him: I've been awake all night. It is terrible.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandfather gave the house as a present
narrative_blocks.body: John G. Shedd had Frederick Wainwright Perkins build Mayflower Place on the Lake Forest bluff in 1917 and gave it to her parents as a wedding gift — ten bedrooms on five acres with a beach of its own. Her mother died in it in 1937 and her father in 1941, after which it stood empty near on fifty years and turned into a local legend.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the sleeping-car company from 1961
narrative_blocks.body: Out of Yale in 1926 he went into the family business, Cornell Paperboard Products in Wisconsin, and rose to its presidency. He joined the Pullman board in 1952, became president of the car company in 1961 and chairman in 1966.

narrative_blocks.header: He was known in the family as June
narrative_blocks.body: He was June to the Armours and to his own daughters, never Washington and never Irving. He had grown up at Evanston, at the Latin School and the township high school, and married Elsa Armour at twenty-seven.

narrative_blocks.header: He outlived his wife by seventeen years
narrative_blocks.body: He retired in 1974 to golf and bridge and gin rummy, and to board seats at Pabst, Baxter and Belden. Elsa died in 1985; he stayed on at Lake Forest and died at home there at ninety-seven.

narrative_blocks.header: Miss Porter's, Sarah Lawrence, then a classroom
narrative_blocks.body: She followed her mother and grandmother to Miss Porter's at Farmington, then took a degree in education and a teaching certificate at Sarah Lawrence. She taught elementary school at Del Rio in Texas while her husband was stationed there.

narrative_blocks.header: She stood for election to the library board
narrative_blocks.body: At Bloomington she was elected a trustee of the public library, and gave decades to Planned Parenthood, the county day care centre, the Girl Scouts and the hospital. She served on the vestry and the altar guild at St. Matthew's Episcopal.

narrative_blocks.header: Her eight grandchildren called her Shell
narrative_blocks.body: Her eight grandchildren called her Shell. She had figure-skated, fished and played tennis as a girl, and kept her summers at the family cottage at Charlevoix in Michigan.

education.notes: B.A. in education, with a teaching certificate.

narrative_blocks.header: He flew for the Air Force in Korea
narrative_blocks.body: He was an Air Force pilot in the Korean War and left the service a captain. He married Adrienne Osborne at Lake Forest in June 1954, while he was still stationed at Del Rio in Texas.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the radio company until 1988
narrative_blocks.body: He was chairman and before that president of Bloomington Broadcasting, and retired from it in 1988. He led or directed most of the rest of the town as well — the county historical society, Bloomington Unlimited, the association of commerce.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother’s brother was governor of Illinois
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Chicago to Ernest L. Ives and Elizabeth Stevenson, whose brother Adlai was governor of Illinois in the early 1950s. He spent his working life at Bloomington and carried a Paul Harris fellowship from its Rotary Club.

parents.father_name: Walter D. Monroe of Lake Forest

narrative_blocks.header: She rode before she was introduced
narrative_blocks.body: She was an accomplished horsewoman, schooled at Faulkner and at North Shore Country Day in Chicago, and came out in 1943. Her engagement to Charles Brooks Armour was announced from Lake Forest in May 1946.

narrative_blocks.header: Her second marriage lasted twice as long
narrative_blocks.body: The Armour marriage ended in 1960 after fourteen years. She married F. Lee H. Wendell, a Chicago management consultant, and was his wife for thirty-two years until he died at Lake Forest in 1994.

narrative_blocks.header: She married where Adrienne had three years before
narrative_blocks.body: She married Loomis Ives Lincoln at the Church of the Holy Spirit in 1957, three years after her sister Adrienne was married there. She had gone to Miss Porter's and then Vassar, and came out with Adrienne in 1951.

narrative_blocks.header: She married at St. Patrick's in 1966
narrative_blocks.body: She married John Edward McGovern Jr. at St. Patrick's Church in 1966, and the reception was at the Onwentsia Club. She had gone to Miss Porter's and then Briarcliff, and came out in 1958 with her cousin Laura Armour.

narrative_blocks.header: Princeton had him, then had his son
narrative_blocks.body: Princeton put him in the class of 1953 and took his son thirty-eight years later. He practised law at Chicago and retired a partner in Wildman, Harrold, Allen and Dixon, and taught the boy to hunt and fish at the family cabin in northern Wisconsin.

narrative_blocks.header: He followed Margot within the year
narrative_blocks.body: The only son of Laurance and Lacy Armour, he married Margot Boyd in 1954 and stayed her husband until she died on the eighteenth of February 2003. He died at home in Texas on the seventeenth of February the year after.

narrative_blocks.header: Coolidge pulled him home to run the ceremonies
narrative_blocks.body: He had been a third secretary at Madrid and chargé d'affaires at Port-au-Prince when Coolidge wanted someone to direct ceremonies at the White House. In February 1928 he became the first Chief of Protocol the United States ever had.

narrative_blocks.header: He ordered Bern to stop reporting the killings
narrative_blocks.body: In early 1943 he was part of the order sent to American diplomats in Switzerland telling them to stop forwarding reports of the mass murder of Europe's Jews. The Treasury found the cable a year later; a radio broadcast and a senator both named him for it.

narrative_blocks.header: He worked openly against the Italian Communists
narrative_blocks.body: Ambassador at Rome from 1947, he asked the prime minister outright to dissolve parliament and put the Communists out, and was credited with helping decide the 1948 election. Madrid and Rio followed, and in 1956 he was named one of the first American career ambassadors.

narrative_blocks.header: He practised as an architect before diplomacy
narrative_blocks.body: He was privately educated at Newark, read for a law degree, and worked as an architect in Manhattan before the navy sent him to Havana as an assistant attaché in 1917. Buildings interested him for the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: He married into the Kansas City packing family
narrative_blocks.body: He married Mary Augusta Armour in 1914 and they had two daughters, Marianna and Cynthia. They kept a house in Washington for thirty years, retired to Rome in 1956, and came back to New York in 1977.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a Belgian count at twenty
narrative_blocks.body: Her engagement to Count Guy de Baillet Latour of Brussels was announced from Paris in the autumn of 1935, when her father was chief of protocol and special assistant to the secretary of state. They married that April and had a daughter, Anne, at Brussels the following February.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at twenty-five on a Scottish island
narrative_blocks.body: Guy died on Arran in the Firth of Clyde on the first of September 1941, when she was twenty-five and their daughter four. She married Maximilian Gevers three years later.

bio.bio_blurb: Foreign Service officer and army colonel

narrative_blocks.header: He went to Moscow on a hunch
narrative_blocks.body: He arrived in the Soviet Union with no Russian and no post, on the guess that an American embassy was about to open there. It did, and he became personal secretary to the first ambassador, William Bullitt.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught Soviet cavalrymen to play polo
narrative_blocks.body: A West Point graduate who had played the game there, he got up a team of Russian cavalrymen so that the Americans and Soviets could have what one witness called a hard-fought, clean, friendly match. He had nine languages besides English before he was done.

narrative_blocks.header: He started the Russian service, then ran VOA
narrative_blocks.body: He established the Voice of America's Russian service in February 1947 and was made director of the whole operation the year after. He had been chargé d'affaires at Kabul in 1942, and in the OSS at Belgrade and in Austria before that.

narrative_blocks.header: Hoover and McCarthy forced him out in 1953
narrative_blocks.body: He complained publicly that the FBI's slow security clearances were starving his staff, and Hoover investigated him for years without persuading anyone he was a risk. In March 1953 he was made to resign anyway, to buy Senate confirmation for his brother-in-law Charles Bohlen as ambassador to Moscow.

narrative_blocks.header: He preferred Majorca to Siberia or Dachau
narrative_blocks.body: He went to Majorca to live beyond the reach of Senate subpoenas, and wrote in his diary that under Stalin you went to Siberia and under Hitler to Dachau, but under McCarthy to Majorca — which counts as progress. He wrote nine books, and hunting pieces for Sports Illustrated.

narrative_blocks.header: Her marriage joined stockyard to packing house
narrative_blocks.body: She married Frederick Henry Prince IV at St. James in New York in 1970. His great-grandfather and namesake chaired Chicago's Union Stock Yard and sat on the Armour board; hers, Kirkland Brooks Armour, ran the Armour house at Kansas City.

narrative_blocks.header: Four cousins under nine attended her
narrative_blocks.body: Her attendants were four young cousins, none of them older than eight, and her half-brother James Dunn Thayer was an usher. She wore a veil of antique Malines lace that had been her great-grandmother Annie Armour's.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandparents gave the dance in Washington
narrative_blocks.body: She came out in 1962 at a dance the Dunns gave for her in Washington, and again at the Washington Debutante Ball. She had gone to Madeira and then to Vassar.

narrative_blocks.header: Georgetown gave her its garden party
narrative_blocks.body: Tudor Place, the 1815 house on five and a half acres in Georgetown, made her an honorary trustee and honoured her at its garden party in May 2023. Recovering from surgery, she sent her daughter Daisy to take the award for her.

narrative_blocks.header: She modelled Pucci in the sixties
narrative_blocks.body: Before marrying she modelled briefly in the 1960s, in Pucci. The photograph of her from those years hangs in her daughter's bathroom in New York, among the women of the family Daisy says advise her before she goes out.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped stop Disney building on a battlefield
narrative_blocks.body: He backed the grassroots campaign that killed Disney's America, a theme park planned beside Virginia's Civil War battlefields. The fight it started put smart growth on the map around Washington and has since protected over 350,000 acres.

narrative_blocks.header: A tenth of an island kept open
narrative_blocks.body: His support revived the Aquidneck Land Trust in Rhode Island, which has since conserved 2,500 acres of open space — a tenth of the whole island. He was a trustee of the Prince Charitable Trusts for forty years.

narrative_blocks.header: He worried about who looks after the rescuers
narrative_blocks.body: One strand of his giving went to the morale of hospital staff and other caregivers, and he helped establish a protocol for the people who attend disasters involving children — the group most likely to be damaged by the work.

narrative_blocks.header: The first court tennis court in seventy-four years
narrative_blocks.body: He founded Prince's Court at McLean in Virginia, the first court tennis court built in the United States in seventy-four years, and it carries his name. He rode with the Orange County Hunt, skied in winter and windsurfed in summer.

narrative_blocks.header: Two of the first thirty-seven flew for France
narrative_blocks.body: His grandfather Frederick Prince Jr. and his great-uncle Norman Prince were among the original thirty-seven of the Lafayette Escadrille, the American volunteer pilots whose exploits helped turn American opinion toward entering the war.

narrative_blocks.header: His namesake bought Armour and Company
narrative_blocks.body: Frederick Henry Prince, his great-grandfather and namesake, took a New York Stock Exchange seat at twenty-five, merged the Chicago yards into the Union Stock Yard and Transit Company, and in the early 1920s bought Armour and Company.

narrative_blocks.header: She died at thirty-four with three small children
narrative_blocks.body: She married Moses Parmelee at Bethlehem in December 1795 and died in August 1803, leaving Herman at seven, Almira at five and Catherina at two. Her husband outlived her by thirty-nine years.

narrative_blocks.header: She followed him west and came back alone
narrative_blocks.body: She married Eleazer Crane in 1798 and moved with him from Woodbury to Colebrook in New Hampshire, back to Bethlehem in 1807, and finally to Beloit in Wisconsin where their son Robert had already settled. Ten years after Eleazer died there she came back to Connecticut, and stayed among her children until her death.

narrative_blocks.header: She helped found a church in a kitchen
narrative_blocks.body: She was one of twenty-four who organized the First Congregational Church of Beloit in Caleb Blodgett's kitchen on the thirtieth of December 1838, with her sister Hannah and her two eldest children beside her. They had all come out from Colebrook in New Hampshire.

bio.bio_blurb: Charter member of Beloit's first church

narrative_blocks.header: Eight of the twenty-four were her family
narrative_blocks.body: When the First Congregational Church of Beloit was organized in a kitchen in December 1838 she joined with her husband, her son Alfred and his wife, her sister Nancy Crane, Nancy's two eldest children, and her son-in-law. A third of the founding congregation was one household out of Colebrook.

bio.bio_blurb: Public affairs executive and political operative

narrative_blocks.header: He was a Speaker's aide for seven years
narrative_blocks.body: He was press secretary to J. Dennis Hastert of Illinois, Speaker of the United States House, and spent more than seven years at the top of the Speaker's operation. He also ran Keep Our Majority, the political action committee that tied the Speaker's national strategy to congressional candidates.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran Mark Kirk's first campaign in 2000
narrative_blocks.body: He managed Mark Kirk's first run in Illinois's tenth district, and had directed communications for Peter Fitzgerald's Senate race two years before that. He had been press secretary to the Illinois Republican Party from 1994, and went to every Republican convention from 1996 on.

narrative_blocks.header: He left the campaigns for public affairs
narrative_blocks.body: He spent seven years at Resolute Consulting in Chicago, running its corporate, financial and legal communications practice as executive vice-president. In 2017 he became a principal at the Thurston Group, a private-equity firm.

narrative_blocks.header: He joined the board of the family farm
narrative_blocks.body: He sat on the Elawa Farm Foundation board, the body that keeps the Lake Forest farm his great-grandparents built in 1917. He served the Boys and Girls Clubs of Chicago too, and was vice-president of the Art Institute's auxiliary board.

narrative_blocks.header: He was better dressed than everyone else
narrative_blocks.body: His friends called him Johnny Mac. He read history for pleasure and argued for it, played a fierce hand of bridge, kept up an interest in architecture and art history, and was an unabashed preppy who turned out better than anyone in the room.

narrative_blocks.header: He took his boy to the ballpark
narrative_blocks.body: He took his elder boy Caldwell to his first Cubs game in the spring before he died, from the third-base line where he always sat. He had learned to hunt and fish from his father at the family cabin in northern Wisconsin.

narrative_blocks.header: She was named for her father
narrative_blocks.body: Wentworth Caldwell Jr. of Nashville gave her his name, and she grew up at Cliff Lawn, the Hill family house his family had held for three generations. She married at St. George's in Nashville in 2011, having given up event planning there three years before.

narrative_blocks.header: He built a saw mill in New Hampshire
narrative_blocks.body: He put up a saw mill at Colebrook in New Hampshire, went back to Bethlehem in 1807, and returned north again before following his son to Wisconsin in 1836. He died at Beloit three years after he got there.

narrative_blocks.header: She was one of the twenty-four
narrative_blocks.body: She came out from Colebrook with her mother and brother and was among the charter members who organised the Beloit church in Caleb Blodgett's kitchen in December 1838. She was thirty-four then, and died at thirty-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: He walked the last of it from Detroit
narrative_blocks.body: He was one of fourteen men who formed the New England Emigrating Company at Colebrook in October 1836 to plant a New England village in the west. He came by steamer from Buffalo to Detroit with Otis Bicknell and set out on foot, finishing a half-built house at Ann Arbor when his money ran out, and reached the Turtle on the ninth of March 1837.

narrative_blocks.header: He went to Wisconsin ahead of his parents
narrative_blocks.body: He had made a home at Beloit before his mother and father followed out in 1836, and his father died there three years after arriving. Robert stayed on, and lies at Oakwood with two of his three wives.

narrative_blocks.header: Three wives, and a daughter taken in
narrative_blocks.body: He married Almira Bicknell of Vermont in 1835 and buried her at Beloit in 1854. Jane French of Colebrook, the New Hampshire town his family had settled, followed and died in 1868; with his third wife he took in a daughter, Jessie, in 1870.

cross_connections.display_label: held Beloit's first religious service in a shanty he had built

narrative_blocks.header: Two of Thomas Hooker's daughters, rejoined
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband came down from Thomas Hooker's daughter Mary, through the Newtons and the Pruddens; she came down from his daughter Sarah, through the Wilsons, the Lows and the Bicknells. The two lines parted at Hooker's own children and met again when they married in 1835.

narrative_blocks.header: He married at fifty-three, she at forty-one
narrative_blocks.body: Gurdon Huntington was born at Norwich in 1768 and carried the title of doctor. He married Mary Strong Prudden in November 1821 and died at Cairo in New York in 1847, twenty-six years later.

narrative_blocks.header: Three separate lines back to Thomas Hooker
narrative_blocks.body: His father came down from Hooker's daughter Mary by the Newtons and Pruddens; his mother carried two more, from Sarah and again from Mary, because his ancestor Elizabeth Wilson Low had a Hooker descendant for each parent.

narrative_blocks.header: Boston's first minister is in the same line
narrative_blocks.body: John Wilson, who gathered the First Church at Boston in 1630 and kept it until he died, stands eight generations above him on his mother's side. The Hooker descent comes down that same line.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a Rawson, then wrote the Rawsons
narrative_blocks.body: Crane married Salona Aldrich Rawson in 1859 and afterwards produced the revised memoir of Edward Rawson, secretary of the Massachusetts Bay colony from 1650 to 1686, carrying his descendants down nine generations.

narrative_blocks.header: The yard burned and he never rebuilt
narrative_blocks.body: He came to Worcester in 1867 and set up as a lumber dealer with John French, bought French out, and ran the yard alone until it burned to the ground on 8 July 1900. He was sixty-four, and he left the trade instead of starting again.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave the rest to records
narrative_blocks.body: After the fire Crane took up genealogical and historical research for good. He had helped found the Worcester Society of Antiquity, served several years as its president, and kept its library for fifteen.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty books carry his name
narrative_blocks.body: The Crane genealogy came out in 1895, tracing the descendants of Henry Crane of Wethersfield. He also wrote on Colonel Timothy Bigelow's Revolutionary regiment and edited the 1907 Historic Homes and Institutions of Worcester County.

narrative_blocks.header: California first, then the Isthmus home
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Colebrook in New Hampshire and raised from a year old at Beloit in Wisconsin, he went out to California and came back east across the Isthmus of Panama. By 1862 he was keeping books for a Boston lumber dealer.

narrative_blocks.header: Three Williams between her and the secretary
narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Mendon in Worcester County to George Rawson and Lois Aldrich, and her descent runs back through Simon, Edward, and three Williams to Edward Rawson, secretary of the Massachusetts Bay Colony. Her line came through his son William; the Hooker Rawsons came through his son Grindal.

narrative_blocks.header: They named him for the preacher outright
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth Wilson Low was Thomas Hooker's great-granddaughter, and she and Samuel Low put the name on their son outright. He married Elizabeth Kinnicutt, and the two of them died in the same year.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a Rawson of Mendon in 1842
narrative_blocks.body: He was practising at Potosi when he married Abigail Rawson of Mendon in Massachusetts, at Beloit in October 1842. Seventeen years later his nephew Ellery, who carried the Bicknell name, married Salona Rawson of that same town.

narrative_blocks.header: Husband and both daughters gone by 1879
narrative_blocks.body: John Buffington died at Warren in September 1877, and their younger girl Alice the same year, at three. Florence followed in 1879, ten years old. Hannah lived on at Barrington another forty-four years.

narrative_blocks.header: She was born under Zachary Taylor
narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Barrington in 1849 and died there a hundred and one years later. Of the seven children in that house only her youngest sister Ruth outlived her, and by four years.

narrative_blocks.header: The church was organized in a kitchen
narrative_blocks.body: On the thirtieth of December 1838 the First Congregational Church of Beloit was organized in the large kitchen at the east end of Caleb Blodgett's house. He stood first on the list of twenty-four charter members, and eight of the twenty-four were his own family, all lately of Colebrook in New Hampshire.

cross_connections.display_label: held the Beloit pulpit for nineteen years in the church he founded

narrative_blocks.header: She died in New Mexico, not Wisconsin
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband died at Beloit in 1860 and she outlived him by twenty-four years. She died at Las Vegas in New Mexico in 1884, where her eldest son Edward had taken a ranch.

narrative_blocks.header: He arrived with four oxen and four barrels
narrative_blocks.body: The colony was short of food in the summer of 1837 when he came up with a four-ox team and four barrels of flour, which the county history says relieved them from severe distress. He was also one of the fourteen of the New England Emigrating Company, and read the sermon at the settlement's second Sunday gathering.

narrative_blocks.header: He stepped down between platform and train
narrative_blocks.body: At Delavan in December 1868 he went to board a freight and stepped off the platform to the ground instead of onto the car. The train moved as he did, the caboose steps caught him against the platform and rolled him a rod along it, and he was dead before anyone reached him.

narrative_blocks.header: She married the man who named the town
narrative_blocks.body: Her father's household came out from Colebrook to Beloit, and she married Lucius George Fisher there in June 1842. He had helped name the place, was six years its county sheriff, and would be an inaugural trustee of its college.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother and father both buried her
narrative_blocks.body: She died in March 1850 at thirty-six, leaving a boy of six and a girl of two. Her mother lived four years longer and her father six, so both of them outlived her.

narrative_blocks.header: A hundred days at Memphis, then home
narrative_blocks.body: He enlisted as a private in Company B of the 40th Wisconsin in May 1864 and was mustered out at Milwaukee four months later. He married Etta Webber in 1906, when he was sixty-three, and lies at Oakwood.

narrative_blocks.header: Four children, none of them reached eighteen
narrative_blocks.body: James died at two in 1874, Caroline at two in 1878, Helen at nine in 1884, and Elizabeth at seventeen in 1890. She was widowed in 1901, married William Dixon Spalding in 1908, and lived to eighty-one.

narrative_blocks.header: He asked for a plain funeral
narrative_blocks.body: He headed J. N. Bates and Company until he retired in 1895, and kept his summers at a model farm in the Vermont town he was born in. His Brooklyn funeral was held at his own house on Remsen Street, plain at his request, with three hymns and eight of his friends carrying him.

narrative_blocks.header: He held the first service in a shanty
narrative_blocks.body: On Sunday the thirteenth of August 1837, four days after he reached the place, he led a prayer meeting in a twelve-by-sixteen shanty Robert Crane had put up east of what is now State Street. It was the first public religious service held at Beloit; Ira Hersey led the singing and offered the first prayer.

narrative_blocks.header: He was one of the college's founders
narrative_blocks.body: He was among the founders of Beloit College, whose first organising convention met in August 1844 in the church he had helped charter. Professor Joseph Emerson, naming the men who formed the college though none of them had been to one, listed him with Dexter Clary, Alfred Field and Lucius Fisher.

narrative_blocks.header: He was among the oldest settlers left
narrative_blocks.body: He died at Beloit on the fifth of November 1860, fifty-seven years old and one of the oldest settlers the town had left. He was remembered for keeping his heart and hand open to the afflicted and the oppressed, as far as his influence could reach.

narrative_blocks.header: Two presidents made him surveyor general
narrative_blocks.body: Harrison appointed him surveyor general of New Mexico and McKinley reappointed him. He had been a Beloit city surveyor, a civil engineer, a principal of two academies, and for seven years the editor of the Western Magazine.

narrative_blocks.header: He outlived his wife and his only son
narrative_blocks.body: Edward Brinsmead Hobart died at three. Marian Cunningham, the Beloit seminary teacher he married in 1859, died at Santa Fe about 1908, and he followed in 1912 with his brother Horace beside him.

narrative_blocks.header: His hundred days ran into Forrest at Memphis
narrative_blocks.body: He enlisted from Appleton in May 1864 as first lieutenant of Company E, and the regiment went down to Memphis on train-guard and garrison duty. It supported a battery engaged during Forrest's raid that August, and followed the enemy two miles after the skirmish.

narrative_blocks.header: He called on friends with his own apples
narrative_blocks.body: He kept a ranch on the Rio Grande at Hobart and was postmaster there while living at Santa Fe, where he was adjutant of the Grand Army post. He took delight in calling on his friends and handing them choice apples and other fruit out of his own orchard.

narrative_blocks.header: He signed for a Santa Fe Indian school
narrative_blocks.body: As surveyor general he put his name beside the acting governor's on a petition urging Congress to equip the new Indian school at Santa Fe, the town having given more than a hundred acres of land for it. The Territory counted twenty thousand Indians at the time.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded the Railway Age in 1876
narrative_blocks.body: He and a partner started the Railway Age in June 1876, and he carried most of its editorial work himself until he stepped back in January 1898. The Railroad Gazette bought it out in 1908 and took its name over its own; the magazine still publishes under the title he gave it.

narrative_blocks.header: He was hit while quartermaster of the battalion
narrative_blocks.body: He enlisted in the First Wisconsin Cavalry in 1861, the year after he took his Beloit degree, and was serving as battalion quartermaster when he was seriously wounded and mustered out in 1862. Beloit gave him a master's degree the year after that.

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve years and five Chicago papers
narrative_blocks.body: Between the war and the Railway Age he reported for the Chicago Tribune, ran the city desk at the Evening Post, managed the Evening Mail, held the American Press Association's western office and owned half of the Jacksonville Daily Journal.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran Hyde Park before Chicago took it
narrative_blocks.body: He was president of the board of trustees of the Village of Hyde Park from 1879 to 1882, before it was absorbed into the city. He spent his last twenty-nine years at Evanston.

narrative_blocks.header: He was the church's first baptism
narrative_blocks.body: His parents had him christened in November 1839 in the Beloit congregation they had helped charter, the first baptism it performed. He died Deacon Emeritus of the First Congregational Church of Evanston, eighty-nine years later.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father was Wisconsin's treasurer four times
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel D. Hastings was state treasurer of Wisconsin for four terms and one of the early men of Madison, working for abolition and for prohibition. She married at Madison in December 1872 and died at Chicago in 1914.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-three years in the same partnership
narrative_blocks.body: He was a partner in Hobart and Oates, general agents at Chicago for the Northwestern Mutual Life Insurance Company, from 1911 until 1944. He lived on Prospect Avenue at Winnetka and died at Billings Memorial hospital five years after retiring.

narrative_blocks.header: A chemical engineer who photographed industry
narrative_blocks.body: He took a Harvard degree in 1931 and worked for the Dewey and Almy Chemical Company at Cambridge, where he lived from 1942 until he died. He was a vestryman and senior warden of Christ Church there, an industrial photographer besides, and a member of the Harvard Musical Association.

narrative_blocks.header: He was born into the Chicago Fairbanks
narrative_blocks.body: His mother Janet Ayer Fairbank wrote a Chicago trilogy and sat on the Democratic National Committee, and his sister Janet sang with the Chicago Opera. He left all of it for a chemical company at Cambridge and stayed forty-four years.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded an anti-slavery society at twenty-two
narrative_blocks.body: He started the Union Anti-slavery Society at Philadelphia in 1838 and helped organise the Liberty Party in Pennsylvania before he was thirty. He went out to the Wisconsin Territory in 1846 and settled at Geneva.

narrative_blocks.header: His resolutions forced both parties to answer
narrative_blocks.body: Elected to the Wisconsin Assembly as a Free Soiler in 1849, he put up a series of bills demanding no new slave states, no slavery in any federal territory, and the repeal of every law favouring slave labour. The votes they forced convinced the Free Soilers that merging with either old party was not worth pursuing.

narrative_blocks.header: He held the state's money through the war
narrative_blocks.body: He was state treasurer of Wisconsin from 1858 to 1866, eight years covering the whole of the Civil War, under four governors. He had come in as a Free Soiler and returned to the Assembly in 1857 as a Republican.

narrative_blocks.header: He took prohibition to three other countries
narrative_blocks.body: He was grand chief templar of the international Good Templars and spoke for prohibition across the United States and in England, Australia and New Zealand. He stood as the Prohibition candidate for governor of Wisconsin in 1884 and lost.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at his daughter's house in Evanston
narrative_blocks.body: He kept his Wisconsin residence to the end but died in 1903 at Emma's house in Evanston, in his eighty-seventh year. He was a founding member of the Wisconsin Academy of Sciences, Arts and Letters and for a time its treasurer.

narrative_blocks.header: He spoke the name the town settled on
narrative_blocks.body: He bought land in the Wisconsin town of New Albany and was in the room when it was renamed. Wanting something that sounded like Detroit, he said Balloit, then Beloit, and the meeting took the second.

narrative_blocks.header: Six years sheriff of Rock County
narrative_blocks.body: He was appointed sheriff in 1839 and held it six years, having been a schoolteacher and a sheriff's deputy before the Panic of 1837 cost him his travelling sales job and sent him west.

narrative_blocks.header: Lincoln made him postmaster, Johnson unmade him
narrative_blocks.body: Lincoln appointed him postmaster of Beloit in 1861 and he held the office until Andrew Johnson removed him in 1867. He had sat a term in the Wisconsin Assembly from 1856 and declined to stand again, wanting his business back.

narrative_blocks.header: He was an inaugural trustee of the college
narrative_blocks.body: He was among the original founders of Beloit College and one of its first trustees. Joseph Emerson later named him with Dexter Clary, Alfred Field and Horace Hobart as the men who made the college without having been to one themselves.

narrative_blocks.header: He buried his first wife at thirty-six
narrative_blocks.body: He married Caroline Amelia Field at Beloit in June 1842 and she died in March 1850, thirty-six years old, leaving a son and a daughter. He married Rachel Colton the next year and had three more daughters.

, a fellow founder of Beloit College, died in the town in 1893

notable.notable_blurb: Rock County sheriff; Beloit postmaster and legislator

bio.bio_blurb: Chicago paper manufacturer and real-estate investor

narrative_blocks.header: Gold fever took him west with oxen
narrative_blocks.body: He was about to enter Beloit College when the gold rush caught him, and he talked his father into letting him go west with a wagon and a team of oxen. He came back east to clerk in a New York hardware store in 1861.

narrative_blocks.header: A hundred days, then the navy
narrative_blocks.body: He mustered with the 84th New York Infantry National Guard in 1863 and was discharged when its hundred days were up. He signed on with the navy and did administrative work aboard the steamer Wyandack until the war ended.

narrative_blocks.header: He began as a porter in the mill
narrative_blocks.body: He joined the Rock River Paper Company as a porter and was running its whole paper-bag operation within five years. In the 1870s he incorporated the Union Bag and Paper Company and grew it by swallowing other Midwestern makers.

narrative_blocks.header: Burnham built him eighteen storeys on Dearborn
narrative_blocks.body: He commissioned Daniel Burnham to design the Fisher Building at 343 South Dearborn, eighteen storeys of orange terra cotta and glass, among the tallest in the world when it went up in 1896. He also bought the Greek statuary from the 1893 world's fair and gave it to Beloit College.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought the costliest house in Chicago
narrative_blocks.body: In 1900 he bought Samuel Nickerson's Italianate mansion on East Erie Street, reported the most expensive residence in the city when it was built, and had George Washington Maher turn its sculpture gallery into a trophy room. He died in it in 1916.
