kept a Chicago mansion on Prairie Avenue among the Armours and Fields

notable.notable_blurb: Chicago paper manufacturer and real-estate investor

narrative_blocks.header: Three sons gone in a single year
narrative_blocks.body: Henry was six, Philip four and Lucius two when all three of them died in 1880. Three more children came after, and she lived to seventy-eight at Richmond in Illinois.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father organised Beloit's Presbyterian church
narrative_blocks.body: Rev. Alfred Eddy came out from Bellona in New York and gathered a Presbyterian congregation at Beloit in 1849, staying six years. She was born at Bellona about the time he left it, and married into the family that had chartered the Congregational church there eleven years before.

narrative_blocks.header: She died at a German spa at sixty-one
narrative_blocks.body: She and Lucius Fisher were at the baths in Baden when she died suddenly in August 1910. He brought her body home by ship and buried her at Graceland, and outlived her by six years.

narrative_blocks.header: He owned the building his father put up
narrative_blocks.body: He was one of the owners of the Fisher Building at Van Buren and Dearborn and president of the Wheeler-Fisher Paper Company. Yale had him in the class of 1897.

narrative_blocks.header: He died in a hotel apartment at forty-six
narrative_blocks.body: He had been ill for some time and had recently had an operation when he died in his rooms at the Congress hotel in December 1918. He kept up various clubs and took an interest in yachting.

narrative_blocks.header: The Foster name came down from her marriage
narrative_blocks.body: She married Alexis Caldwell Foster at Chicago in October 1897, the Tribune carrying the announcement that week, and became Alice Eddy Fisher Foster. The surname came down from that marriage, four generations, to Jodie Foster.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Fisher sisters married two Dixons
narrative_blocks.body: She married William Warren Dixon at Chicago in June 1910 and had two sons by him. Her younger sister Katharine married Homer Dixon, and it was Katharine who kept the Erie Street house after their father died in it.

narrative_blocks.header: He was born at Batticaloa in Ceylon
narrative_blocks.body: He was born on the east coast of Ceylon in 1842 and married Annah Fisher at Chicago in 1871. He died at Richmond in Illinois at ninety-three, having outlived three of his seven children by fifty-six years.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at thirty-one, remarried at thirty-five
narrative_blocks.body: Charles McConnell died at Chicago in 1903, three years after she married him. She married Thane Blackman at Richmond in 1907, had two daughters by him, and outlived him by six years.

narrative_blocks.header: A Nashville boy who ran a Denver bank
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Nashville and spent most of his life in Denver, where he was president of the Bankers Trust Company. He married Alice Fisher in 1897 and died at Bronxville in New York in 1945.

bio.bio_blurb: Denver investment banker; Navy chief quartermaster

narrative_blocks.header: He chased submarines thirty miles offshore
narrative_blocks.body: He left Yale in 1918 for the Naval Reserve Force and served aboard the submarine chasers 64 and 166 on patrol duty thirty miles off the American coast. He went in a seaman second class and came out a chief quartermaster.

narrative_blocks.header: Two months at Annapolis, then Yale
narrative_blocks.body: He prepared at Salisbury and at Hotchkiss, spent two months at the Naval Academy, and came to Yale for the class of 1921. He commanded a section of the Yale Naval Training Unit before leaving college altogether.

narrative_blocks.header: His friends called him Lush
narrative_blocks.body: He married Constance Robertson at Atlantic City in April 1919 and their daughter Alice Courtnay was born at Denver the next summer. He went into investment banking there and died at Gloucester in Massachusetts at seventy-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: Once is enough for Constance, they said
narrative_blocks.body: She was a Denver debutante and a noted dancer when she married Lucius Foster secretly in 1918, while he was a Yale student newly enlisted in the navy. She divorced him in April 1928, taking the children, and married a Chicago clubman a month later.

narrative_blocks.header: Her second wedding was in her own rooms
narrative_blocks.body: It was made at her apartment on North State Street in Chicago's gold coast, as quietly as the first had been. That marriage lasted months; she married again in 1929 and was living as Mrs Gerst by the time she died at Beverly Hills.

narrative_blocks.header: Her will left everything to her grandchildren
narrative_blocks.body: She left a short will naming only her grandchildren, Michael and Ming Toy and any others she might have. Louis Gerst, who claimed sixteen years as her husband, contested it and lost; her son administered the estate.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father practised law in Denver
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel R. Robertson was born at Jackson in Tennessee and brought the family out to Colorado while she was small, practising law at Denver the rest of his life. She was born at Paris in Tennessee and grew up a Denver debutante.

narrative_blocks.header: She died of pneumonia at thirty-eight
narrative_blocks.body: She went to school at Denver and in California and finished at the Spence School in New York, then married Alexander von Schoeler at Bad Arolsen in Germany in 1928. She was back in Denver under her own name when she died at Mercy Hospital in 1945, leaving a son.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived her husband by seventeen years
narrative_blocks.body: She married Paul Wolf in December 1934 and their son Bruce was born in Utah ten years later. She died at Littleton in 2005 at ninety-seven, and lies with her husband at Fort Logan.

narrative_blocks.header: He spent two years contesting her will
narrative_blocks.body: Connie Foster left a short will in 1950 naming only her grandchildren. He contested it as her husband of sixteen years, and the handwriting expert he called testified that the signature was hers after all, though made by a nervous hand. He lost on appeal in 1957.

narrative_blocks.header: He married her in 1940 and outlived her
narrative_blocks.body: He was born in New York in 1894 and married Connie Foster in 1940, when she had two marriages behind her. She died at Beverly Hills in 1955 and he four years after her, and was buried at Montefiore in Queens.

bio.display_name: Lt. Col. Lucius Fisher Foster III

narrative_blocks.header: He left the war a lieutenant colonel
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Denver in 1922 and served through the Second World War, leaving the service a lieutenant colonel. Afterwards he developed real estate at Los Angeles, and died at North Hollywood at ninety-four.

narrative_blocks.header: A judge called him charming and dangerous
narrative_blocks.body: At eighty-nine he was convicted on twenty-one counts of grand theft, taking money from poor and elderly people for houses of cargo containers. Nothing was built. The judge called him charming and dangerous, and gave him five years.

narrative_blocks.header: He married across the border in Tijuana
narrative_blocks.body: He married Evelyn Almond in Mexico in 1954 and they had four children — Lucinda, Constance, Lucius the fourth and Alicia — before it ended. He was his mother's only surviving child, and administered her estate through a long contest.

narrative_blocks.header: His youngest daughter never knew him
narrative_blocks.body: The marriage was over before Jodie was born, three years after the divorce, and she grew up with no relationship with him at all. The three older children were small when he went, and he took no part in the house that raised them.

bio.bio_blurb: Big-band singer, publicist and talent manager

narrative_blocks.header: She was given away days after birth
narrative_blocks.body: She was born in the Bronx in 1928 to Josie Almond and taken from her within days, to be raised by Josie's cousin John Clinton Almond and his wife Lucy. The 1930 census lists her as their adopted daughter.

narrative_blocks.header: She met him at a fencing match
narrative_blocks.body: She took her big-band singing from Rockford to California in the forties and met Lieutenant Colonel Lucius Foster at a fencing match. She was then a Hollywood publicist for Arthur Jacobs, whose clients ran to Grace Kelly.

narrative_blocks.header: Divorced, she managed her children
narrative_blocks.body: Left with four children, she turned what she knew of the business to managing her son Buddy's acting, and then her youngest daughter's — from a Coppertone advertisement at three to a second Oscar in 1991. She died at home in 2019.

narrative_blocks.header: Rockford in 1945, Tijuana in 1954
narrative_blocks.body: She married Raymond Mazur at Rockford at seventeen and Lucius Foster in Mexico nine years later, and both marriages ended. Her youngest was born three years after the second divorce and never knew her father.

narrative_blocks.header: Josephine Hill shared the house for thirty years
narrative_blocks.body: After the divorce she raised the four children at Los Angeles with Josephine Dominguez Hill, who lived with the family until her death in 1984. Jodie's name is said to have come from hers; she went by Jo D.

narrative_blocks.header: The whole household lived on one child
narrative_blocks.body: There was no other income: the three-year-old from the Coppertone advertisement was carrying her mother and three older children. She warned the girl the career would be over at eighteen, and set out to make it last longer.

narrative_blocks.header: Corkscrew hair and well-placed four-letter words
narrative_blocks.body: Five feet tall, her children said, and nobody could beat her style. The daughter who was angry with her at thirty came to say she had wanted her respected and never objectified, and given a long career instead of a short one.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty-five missions, one of them D-Day
narrative_blocks.body: Mazur enlisted in the Army Air Corps at the start of the war and flew B-26 medium bombers with the 394th Bomb Group. He counted sixty-five combat missions over Europe, one of them over Normandy on June 6, 1944.

narrative_blocks.header: Bradley engineering, then Rexham and Florida
narrative_blocks.body: Mazur came home a first lieutenant with the Air Medal, four oak leaf clusters and three battle stars. He took an engineering degree at Bradley and worked as an engineer until Rexham moved him to Sarasota in 1977.

narrative_blocks.header: She played the girl at the ambulance
narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Los Angeles in October 1954, the eldest of Brandy Foster's four children, and went into acting. Her screen credit is Weekend at Bernie's, where she is the girl at the ambulance.

narrative_blocks.header: The eldest of the four Foster children
narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Los Angeles in 1954, four years before Buddy and eight before Jodie, and was the first of the four. She married Michael Duffy and the marriage ended in divorce.

narrative_blocks.header: She hosted a children's show in Des Moines
narrative_blocks.body: She studied theatre at Drake University and was the hostess of The Floppy Show on WHO television at Des Moines. She has acted in Chicago Story, Chicago Med and Moon Garden, and has tap-danced since she was five.

narrative_blocks.header: She doubled for her sister on Taxi Driver
narrative_blocks.body: The Board of Education would not license Jodie for the suggestive scenes without a double, so their mother put Connie in, being a similar size and over eighteen. She said later that it was like Halloween, and that they were only dressed up.

narrative_blocks.header: Four children, one notice for their mother
narrative_blocks.body: She and her three siblings put their names to a single notice when their mother died in 2019 at ninety. They called her a champion and a fighter, full of fire and love, and said nobody could beat her style.

bio.bio_blurb: Child actor, later a building contractor

narrative_blocks.header: He was Mike Jones on Mayberry R.F.D.
narrative_blocks.body: He began acting at eight and played Mike Jones, Ken Berry's son, through three seasons of Mayberry R.F.D. from 1968. He guested on Hondo, Land of the Giants, Dragnet and The Six Million Dollar Man.

narrative_blocks.header: He was the boy who asked the owl
narrative_blocks.body: He spoke the child's line in the 1969 Tootsie Pop advertisement, asking how many licks it takes to reach the centre. The credit has often gone to another child actor instead.

narrative_blocks.header: He left acting at twenty-three for building
narrative_blocks.body: His last screen appearance was a small part in Foxes in 1980, a film his sister starred in; the adult roles had not come as the child ones did. He settled at Duluth in Minnesota as a building contractor.

narrative_blocks.header: He took his sister to the audition
narrative_blocks.body: He was up for a Coppertone commercial when he brought his four-year-old sister along to the casting call. She charmed the agents and got the job, and it was the beginning of her career.

narrative_blocks.header: His book cost him his sister
narrative_blocks.body: Foster Child, published in 1997, set down the family's story and his mother's relationship with Josephine Hill. His sister replied in a rare public statement calling him a distant acquaintance. All four signed their mother's notice in 2019.

narrative_blocks.header: Her siblings gave her the name Jodie
narrative_blocks.body: She was born Alicia Christian Foster at Los Angeles in November 1962, and her three older brothers and sisters called her Jodie. She was three when she was noticed at one of Buddy's auditions and put into a Coppertone advertisement.

narrative_blocks.header: Her sister stood in for her at twelve
narrative_blocks.body: She played Iris in Martin Scorsese's Taxi Driver, and the Board of Education would license her only if a double took the suggestive scenes. Her older sister Connie, a similar size and over eighteen, did them.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote her Yale thesis on Toni Morrison
narrative_blocks.body: She read African-American literature at Yale and wrote on Toni Morrison under Henry Louis Gates, graduating magna cum laude in 1985. She had learned to read at three and gave the French valedictory at the Lycee Francais in 1980.

narrative_blocks.header: A man shot a president to reach her
narrative_blocks.body: John Hinckley, fixed on her part in Taxi Driver, moved to New Haven during her freshman year and then shot President Reagan to draw her attention. The judge held that she had been unwittingly ensnared, and her videotaped testimony was played at his trial.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Best Actress Oscars before thirty
narrative_blocks.body: The Accused brought her the first in 1988 and The Silence of the Lambs the second in 1991. She has directed four features since Little Man Tate, taken an Emmy for True Detective, and had an asteroid named after her.

narrative_blocks.header: Love and work equals art, she told them
narrative_blocks.body: She hid her acting from her sons while they were small and only understood later why: she wanted them to know her as their mother and not as a persona. Taking her first Emmy for True Detective she handed them the formula instead, that love and work equals art.

notable.notable_blurb: Actor and director; two Academy Awards

narrative_blocks.header: The cadets called him Rosy
narrative_blocks.body: He came to West Point from Colorado Springs on the second district's appointment and rose to regimental sergeant major. He sang in the choir all four years and composed the Hundredth Night show in three of them; whenever somebody wanted the piano made to talk, Rosy was sent for.

narrative_blocks.header: She photographed the ground under Malibu
narrative_blocks.body: Everybody Knows This Is Nowhere, made between 2008 and 2012, records the shifting terrain beneath the Malibu beach houses she grew up in. It opened in Beverly Hills and travelled to Cascais, where Time Out named it one of the ten best exhibitions in Lisbon that year.

narrative_blocks.header: She quit acting because it faced outward
narrative_blocks.body: She took some twenty television parts across the nineties, from Melrose Place to Tomorrow Never Dies, and stopped in 1998. Actors have to be front and centre all the time and that was not her, she said, so she picked up a camera and made a living shooting head shots.

narrative_blocks.header: Ithaka took its name from a Cavafy poem
narrative_blocks.body: She shot the series in the temperate rain forest of North America and showed it first in London, and The New Yorker put it in Passport to the Arts in 2008. Barclays Capital took her on for international sponsorship the same year.

narrative_blocks.header: Acting was in the family before her
narrative_blocks.body: Her father is the actor David Hedison, and acting, she said, was in her blood before it was ever her job. She married Jodie Foster in April 2014, after a year together.

notable.notable_blurb: Fine art photographer and director

narrative_blocks.header: He thought his mother was a construction worker
narrative_blocks.body: He was four, and the sets he visited were full of men in tool belts, so he decided that was what she did. She had kept her work from both boys on purpose, wanting them to know her as someone who went away to a job she loved.

narrative_blocks.header: He went to Yale, as his mother had
narrative_blocks.body: He acted and worked crew on a run of Yale theatre productions and took his degree there, at the college she had gone to. He is an actor now and at work on his first independent film; from the Golden Globes stage she called him her actor son.

narrative_blocks.header: He called himself a theater geek
narrative_blocks.body: He put himself down as a theater geek who loves to write and improvise, and added that he hoped he was funny. He worked Yale productions as actor and as crew for four years running.

narrative_blocks.header: He wore his mother's hat to the taping
narrative_blocks.body: He turned up in the Tonight Show audience in a red hat, a denim jacket and green trousers, and waved when Fallon went looking for him. The hat was hers, she said from the couch.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother calls him her scientist son
narrative_blocks.body: He took his chemistry degree at Princeton and went into science rather than the family trade. His mother has said she does not understand a word of what he tells her, and that she waited many years before showing him The Silence of the Lambs, because he was a sensitive child.

narrative_blocks.header: Two mothers raised him in Los Angeles
narrative_blocks.body: He grew up at Los Angeles with his brother Charlie and two mothers, Jodie Foster and her partner Cydney Bernard, who separated when he was seven. His mother has said she set out to give her sons the routine, stable life she had missed herself.

narrative_blocks.header: She met Jodie Foster on the Sommersby set
narrative_blocks.body: She was working as production coordinator on Sommersby in 1993 when the two met, and the relationship lasted fifteen years. They raised two sons at Malibu and separated in 2008, remaining close and co-parenting the boys.

narrative_blocks.header: Foster broke a forty-year silence to name her
narrative_blocks.body: She had been with Foster fourteen years when Foster, who had never once discussed her private life in public, stood up at a Women in Entertainment breakfast and thanked her beautiful Cydney, who sticks with her through all the rotten and the bliss. At the Golden Globes six years later Foster called her a heroic co-parent and a righteous soul sister.

narrative_blocks.header: She and her husband died the same summer
narrative_blocks.body: She married William Smith in January 1799 at sixteen. She died at Fayetteville on 8 July 1801 at nineteen, and he followed her on 6 September, two months later.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at eighteen to a man of thirty-four
narrative_blocks.body: Hugh Campbell married her at Fayetteville in February 1809. He was sixteen years her senior, and died there on the day after his fiftieth birthday.

narrative_blocks.header: A daughter born and dead the same day
narrative_blocks.body: Her second child was born and died on 24 June 1821 at Fayetteville. Campbell was dead three years later, leaving her a widow at thirty-four with one surviving daughter.

narrative_blocks.header: The firm was C. & P. Mallett
narrative_blocks.body: He traded at Fayetteville in partnership with his brother Charles Peter. A lingering illness took him in April 1830, in his thirty-fifth year, and the notice said he went in charity with all men.

narrative_blocks.header: Two wives in fourteen years, both gone first
narrative_blocks.body: Margaret Isabella Gibbs married him in 1816 and died in 1824 at twenty-six, leaving two daughters. Ellenor de Berniere married him in 1827 and was dead the year after. He outlived them both by two years.

narrative_blocks.header: Six months as Secretary of the Navy
narrative_blocks.body: Harrison made him Secretary of the Navy in March 1841 and Tyler kept him on when Harrison died a month later. He stood up the Home Squadron and pressed for steam, then resigned in September with most of the cabinet over Tyler's bank vetoes.

narrative_blocks.header: The Senate would not vote on his seat
narrative_blocks.body: Fillmore nominated him to the Supreme Court in January 1853 to succeed John McKinley. The Senate voted to postpone rather than decide, and the president withdrew the nomination three days later.

narrative_blocks.header: He left Yale when the money ran out
narrative_blocks.body: He was at Yale in 1810 and 1811 and left without a degree for want of funds. He read law instead, was admitted at nineteen, and was on the bench of the state superior court at twenty-five.

narrative_blocks.header: A Unionist who then backed the Confederacy
narrative_blocks.body: He sat in the 1861 convention as a Unionist and supported the war effort once the state had gone. He enslaved twenty people. Four of his sons enlisted, and all four came home.

narrative_blocks.header: Two destroyers and a Liberty ship
narrative_blocks.body: USS George E. Badger and USS Badger carried his name to sea, and a Liberty ship built at Wilmington carried it through the second war. He was a cousin of three Badger admirals.

took the same Navy portfolio as its forty-fourth secretary

education.notes: Left for want of funds; read law instead.

notable.notable_blurb: 12th U.S. Secretary of the Navy

narrative_blocks.header: Nineteen, and the fourth wife of a sixty-year-old
narrative_blocks.body: She married Gen. William Williams of Montmorenci in 1826, a man three times widowed and thirty-six years her senior. He died six years later and left her a share of six thousand acres; she married Judge Badger three years after that.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a Hessian and went to Tennessee
narrative_blocks.body: Johannes Heinrich Christian Weber was born at Marburg in Hesse and went by Henry in America. They married in 1852 and raised two sons in Tennessee. She died at Birmingham at eighty-three; both lie at Mount Olivet in Nashville.

narrative_blocks.header: His second wife was his second cousin
narrative_blocks.body: Maria Hill died in 1902 after forty-one years, and two years later he married Caroline Green Mallett. Both were great-grandchildren of Col. Peter Mallett by different sons. He was sixty-four and she fifty-six.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a cousin at fifty-six
narrative_blocks.body: Edward Joseph Hale had been a widower two years when they married in December 1904. Their common great-grandfather was Col. Peter Mallett — hers through Charles Peter, his through Caroline Mary — which made them second cousins.

narrative_blocks.header: A caucus made him a colonel
narrative_blocks.body: Nobody in Davie County had heard of any promotion until the Southern Citizen announced it, and a correspondent wrote in to say the party caucus had done it. He left no military record of any kind.

narrative_blocks.header: The knife fight at Mocksville
narrative_blocks.body: One paper had him stabbed two or three times by a man named Wilson who had run out of argument. A witness wrote that Pearson forced himself into the conversation, struck first with a stick, then called on the bystanders for help.

narrative_blocks.header: West Point for a year, then the law
narrative_blocks.body: He was at the United States Military Academy in 1822 and 1823 and did not stay. He practised law, worked for railroads and canals, found partners for mill owners, and joined the superior court in 1838.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a governor's sister
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth Ellis was the sister of John W. Ellis, who took North Carolina out of the Union in 1861 and had read law under Giles's own brother, the chief justice. Giles died of a heart condition at forty-one.

narrative_blocks.header: He lies in his wife's family ground
narrative_blocks.body: Annabella Beatty died at thirty-three in 1844 and he followed at forty in 1849. Both are in the Beatty burial ground in Bladen County, with the daughter they lost at four.

narrative_blocks.header: She died weeks after her daughter was born
narrative_blocks.body: She married the Reverend Charles Everest at Hamden in 1842 and bore a daughter in June 1843. She died that same month at twenty-three, and the child followed in October at four months. Both lie at Cedar Hill in Hartford.

bio.bio_blurb: Hymn writer, abolitionist poet, and Hamden rector

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote a hymn at nineteen
narrative_blocks.body: Take Up Thy Cross came out of a verse in Matthew while he was still at Washington College, and first saw print in 1833 over the signature Omega. Anglicans, Baptists, Catholics, Lutherans, Methodists and Presbyterians all sing it.

narrative_blocks.header: Hymns Ancient and Modern rewrote him
narrative_blocks.body: The 1861 British collection took his five stanzas, altered the text and added a doxology, and that is broadly the form sung now. Only one other American was in it, George Washington Doane. Bach harmonised one of its tunes.

narrative_blocks.header: The Rectory School had ponies and drill
narrative_blocks.body: The rectory salary was thin, so in 1843 he opened the Rectory School, taking boys as boarders and teaching them military tactics and horsemanship, with ponies in a barn behind the church. Fires closed it in 1873.

narrative_blocks.header: The church and the barn both moved
narrative_blocks.body: Grace Church was carried straight across Dixwell Avenue in 1966, and the school barn went to Town Center Park in 2001. Both are still standing, neither where he left it.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote for the abolitionists’ annual
narrative_blocks.body: Stanzas to the Abolitionists of America went into the Liberty Bell, the gift-book the movement sold to fund itself. He edited Poets of Connecticut in 1843, which carried work by William and George Burleigh.

cross_connections.display_label: , her father-in-law, was shot dead at the Georgetown post office

narrative_blocks.header: A year old when his mother died
narrative_blocks.body: Georgia Beal Sneed died in Milam County in December 1884 and lies in the Sneed ground at Crossroads. He was raised in his father's house at Georgetown with an older half-brother, John Beal.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-nine in the year of the killings
narrative_blocks.body: In March 1912 a tenant shot his father dead at the Georgetown post office. His half-brother stood trial twice for murder that same year and walked free both times, and seven men died before it was over.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought the Calvert house the year after
narrative_blocks.body: He and Cara Carleton Weber took the grand Victorian at Calvert in 1913, and she raised its thirty-one live oaks from acorns gathered off the ground at Texas A&M. The house still stands.

narrative_blocks.header: He left a son of fourteen
narrative_blocks.body: He died at Calvert in December 1934, at fifty-one. The boy spent his summers cowhanding on his uncle's Panhandle ranch, and went on to the deanship at Duke and thirty-five years on the Ninth Circuit.

bio.bio_blurb: Ninth Circuit judge and Duke law dean

narrative_blocks.header: He put Kenneth Starr on Whitewater
narrative_blocks.body: He sat on the three-judge panel overseeing the independent counsels, and in August 1994 it removed Robert Fiske from the Whitewater inquiry and named Kenneth Starr in his place. Starr had been his student.

narrative_blocks.header: Nixon made him deputy attorney general
narrative_blocks.body: He was dean at Duke when the nomination came in January 1973, and held the department's second post six months — long enough to preside over the seventy-one-day standoff at Wounded Knee. Nixon then sent him to the Ninth Circuit.

narrative_blocks.header: Four law schools before the bench
narrative_blocks.body: Ten years on the faculty at Texas, five at Cornell, nine at Stanford, then the deanship at Duke. He took a doctorate in juridical science at Harvard in 1958 and spent a year teaching in London and Ghana.

narrative_blocks.header: He made the team missing a vertebra
narrative_blocks.body: He was born a vertebra short, head listing to one side and lungs weak, and was told to avoid exertion. He made himself a winning high school football player anyway, and spent his summers cowhanding on the family ranch.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter called him her true north
narrative_blocks.body: Carly Fiorina, who ran Hewlett-Packard and later stood for president, said he had given her a strong internal compass. She was the middle child, and went by her middle name, Carleton.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-four years with a painter
narrative_blocks.body: He met Madelon Juergens while stationed with the Army in Texas and married her in 1944. She painted portraits and abstracts; a Stanford yearbook said she painted and played tennis. She died in 1998.

narrative_blocks.header: A staff sergeant in the Army Air Corps
narrative_blocks.body: He served from 1942 to 1946, between the business degree at Southwestern and the law degree at Texas. He took the LL.B. in 1947 with the Order of the Coif.

education.school_name: University of Texas School of Law

notable.notable_blurb: Ninth Circuit judge and Duke law dean

narrative_blocks.header: She painted portraits and abstractions
narrative_blocks.body: Painting was her work, in portraits and in abstraction both. In the Stanford yearbook that announced the family's year abroad she got a single line, as a woman who paints and plays tennis.

narrative_blocks.header: She ran away from Ohio and enlisted
narrative_blocks.body: She left home in Toledo for the Women's Army Corps and was posted to Sheppard Field in Texas, where she met an Army Air Forces man named Joseph Sneed. They married at New York in March 1944 and had fifty-four years.

narrative_blocks.header: Six cities and two continents in one marriage
narrative_blocks.body: His teaching carried them from Austin to Ithaca, Palo Alto, Durham, Washington and San Francisco, and for a year to London and Ghana. She raised three children through the moving, and the middle one came out of it a pianist.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty years a trial lawyer in Austin
narrative_blocks.body: He read law at Texas after taking his degree there and spent two decades in civil litigation at Austin. He was killed in a car accident near Navasota in July 2012, at fifty-five, and lies in the Sneed burial ground at Crossroads.

education.school_name: University of Texas School of Law

bio.bio_blurb: First woman to lead a Fortune 20 company

narrative_blocks.header: First woman to run a Fortune 20 firm
narrative_blocks.body: Hewlett-Packard made her chief executive in July 1999. She had come up through AT&T, where she was its first woman officer, and then Lucent, and Fortune had already called her the most powerful woman in American business.

narrative_blocks.header: She won the Compaq fight by 51.4 percent
narrative_blocks.body: The founder's son Walter Hewlett turned against the merger and ran a proxy fight to stop it. She carried the shareholders by a hair, made HP the largest seller of personal computers in the world, and cut thirty thousand American jobs.

narrative_blocks.header: She sent the NSA trucks of servers
narrative_blocks.body: Weeks after the September 11 attacks the director of the National Security Agency telephoned her for computing power. She turned HP trucks around in Tennessee and sent them to Fort Meade under escort, not knowing what they were for.

narrative_blocks.header: Her running-mate candidacy lasted six days
narrative_blocks.body: Ted Cruz named her for vice-president on 27 April 2016 and suspended his campaign six days later, the shortest such candidacy in modern American history. A faithless elector in Texas voted for her anyway.

narrative_blocks.header: Every Sneed generation has carried Carleton
narrative_blocks.body: She was born Cara Carleton Sneed at Austin and has always gone by the middle name. It has come down the family every generation since the Civil War — her great-grandmother was Cara Carleton Weber, her aunt Cara Carleton Sneed.

narrative_blocks.header: Five high schools, one of them in Ghana
narrative_blocks.body: She was a Brownie who never made Girl Scout because the family moved too often, and went through five high schools, one in Ghana and one in London, before finishing at Durham. She had meant to be a concert pianist.

narrative_blocks.header: She left law school after one semester
narrative_blocks.body: She quit UCLA law, took a receptionist's desk at a Los Angeles property firm for six months, and worked up to broker. She had spent her college summers typing for a temp agency.

cross_connections.display_label: was a national account executive at AT&T as she rose there

education.notes: B.A. in philosophy and medieval history.

notable.notable_blurb: First woman to lead a Fortune 20 company

bio.bio_blurb: Novelist and historian of the Sneed-Boyce feud

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote the feud twice, fact and fiction
narrative_blocks.body: Because This Is Texas set out the Sneed-Boyce killings from the archives and the private letters. Before We Turn to Dust went back to the same events as a novel, to get inside Lena, Beal and Al Boyce the younger.

narrative_blocks.header: The Boyces helped her write it
narrative_blocks.body: She worked with the family her great-uncle's shotgun had widowed, and they gave her documents and their own account of it. Telling every side, she has said, moves people from judgment toward empathy. The two families are on terms again.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-five years between article and novel
narrative_blocks.body: The Panhandle-Plains Historical Review printed her account in 1999. Blue Handle brought out the novel in December 2024 and republished the history the following June, and the Texas Authors Institute gave her its grand prize.

narrative_blocks.header: Poet first, then IT, then tutoring
narrative_blocks.body: She read English at Berkeley for a bachelor's and a master's, raised a son, ran the IT systems of a San Francisco law firm, and taught writing and Spanish for a second career. She had begun as a poet.

narrative_blocks.header: Born in Texas and never got over it
narrative_blocks.body: A childhood spent moving landed her in California. She and her husband now keep one foot in Berkeley and one in Milam County, where the family buries its dead.

cross_connections.display_label: , her great-uncle, killed two men and was acquitted twice

education.notes: B.A. and M.A. in English literature.

narrative_blocks.header: All-State stage band four years running
narrative_blocks.body: She took up the tenor saxophone in a fifth-grade junior band at DeKalb and never put it down, winning district and region honours three years and the All-State stage band all four. Her class voted her band captain and wittiest.

narrative_blocks.header: Married on a Maui beach at Easter
narrative_blocks.body: She met Harold Pantusa in the autumn of 1986 and married him on Easter Sunday 1987 in a chapel on the beach at Makena. They lived in Virginia and Connecticut and came back to Dallas in 1997, and had thirty-one years together.

narrative_blocks.header: He brought two daughters to the marriage
narrative_blocks.body: His girls Tracy and Lori were small when he met Cara Sneed, who has written that she loved the children before she loved him. They married in 1985; she had been a manager at AT&T and wanting a family.

narrative_blocks.header: Two police officers in the living room
narrative_blocks.body: He had asked the paramedics he once volunteered with in New Jersey to look in on Lori, three thousand miles away. The police came to the house instead, and stood on the carpet, and said she was dead. She was thirty-four.

narrative_blocks.header: Lori was best at whatever she took up
narrative_blocks.body: She read at Fairleigh Dickinson while living at home, went into pharmaceutical sales and was good at it, and was abusing prescription drugs the whole while. Three stays in rehab did not hold, and her body gave out.

narrative_blocks.header: He shot an unarmed banker in a lobby
narrative_blocks.body: Albert Boyce Sr. had come to Fort Worth to get the kidnapping charge against his son dropped. Sneed put five bullets into him in the lobby of the Metropolitan Hotel in January 1912, saying the old man had helped break up his home.

narrative_blocks.header: He waited two weeks in a rented cottage
narrative_blocks.body: He took a room opposite the Polk Street Methodist Church at Amarillo and waited for Al Boyce Jr. to pass without his brother. Three blasts of a twelve-gauge, and he walked to the courthouse and handed the sheriff his gun.

narrative_blocks.header: Georgia O’Keeffe watched him surrender
narrative_blocks.body: A young schoolteacher was in the crowd that saw him give himself up to the Potter County sheriff in September 1912. She was Georgia O'Keeffe, then teaching in Amarillo.

narrative_blocks.header: Because this is Texas
narrative_blocks.body: Two juries called the killings justifiable homicide. Asked why, the foreman said a man in Texas has the right and the obligation to safeguard the honour of his home, even if he must kill the person responsible.

narrative_blocks.header: He had her committed for moral insanity
narrative_blocks.body: Lena told him in October 1911 that she loved Al Boyce and wanted a divorce, and he put her in the Arlington Heights Sanitarium at Fort Worth. Boyce got her out inside the month and they ran for Canada.

narrative_blocks.header: Leavenworth, then a gunfight with a grocer
narrative_blocks.body: A federal court sent him down two years in 1922 for bribing a juror. Out again, he shot the Paducah grocer who had killed his son-in-law five times; the man lived, shot back, and both were acquitted.

narrative_blocks.header: They stayed married another forty-eight years
narrative_blocks.body: Lena came back and never left again. They made money in the East Texas oilfield, lived thirty years in Dallas, and lie side by side at Hillcrest — he of bone cancer in 1960, she of heart failure in 1966.

narrative_blocks.header: She was committed for asking a divorce
narrative_blocks.body: She told Beal Sneed in October 1911 that she loved Al Boyce, and he had her put in a Fort Worth sanitarium on a finding of moral insanity. Boyce got her out inside a month and they went to Winnipeg.

narrative_blocks.header: All three of them were at Southwestern
narrative_blocks.body: She, her husband and Al Boyce grew up around Georgetown, where their families had helped found Southwestern University. All three were students there, and the two men had competed for her.

narrative_blocks.header: She went back, and stayed fifty years
narrative_blocks.body: Her father took her to New Mexico after the arrest in Canada, and she returned to Beal. Her lover and his father were both dead inside the year. She outlived Beal by six and lies beside him.

people.relational_label_override: Wife of the Half-brother-in-law of a Tenth Generation Hooker

bio.bio_blurb: Georgetown cattleman killed in the feud year

narrative_blocks.header: He was shot fetching his mail
narrative_blocks.body: R. O. Hilliard, a tenant on a Sneed farm, shot him dead as he stepped into the Georgetown post office in March 1912, then turned the gun on himself. The note he left his wife blamed mistreatment at the elder Sneed's hands.

narrative_blocks.header: The papers called it a Kentucky feud
narrative_blocks.body: It fell two months after his son Beal shot Albert Boyce Sr. at Fort Worth, and the press read the killings as one blood feud. Authentic reports, one paper insisted, said this one had no connection with the other.

narrative_blocks.header: His son took it for Boyce work anyway
narrative_blocks.body: Beal believed the Boyces had reached his father. Six months later he lay in wait at Amarillo and killed Albert Boyce Jr. Seven men died inside the year, four of them in the mob outside the Fort Worth courthouse.

narrative_blocks.header: He built the Georgetown ranch in 1879
narrative_blocks.body: The cattle operation he founded carried the family for generations. His sons ran steers on Panhandle range he had bought into, and after he died Joe Jr. added cows and calves and never sold a foot of land.

narrative_blocks.header: Beal sold his Panhandle share to him
narrative_blocks.body: Beal and Joe Jr. rode out to look at the old LX range in Moore County with an uncle who liked it until a two-day dust storm changed his mind. The brothers bought it anyway, and Beal sold his part to his father.

Mother-in-law of a Tenth Generation Hooker

narrative_blocks.header: She died at twenty-eight, before any of it
narrative_blocks.body: Harold was a year old when she died in Milam County in December 1884, and she lies in the Sneed burial ground at Crossroads. The killings that made the family name were twenty-eight years off.

marriages.spouse_notes: Father of Benjamin Frank Davis Sr. No union with the mother; the assault is recorded in the narrative blocks.

narrative_blocks.header: Four children with a Black neighbour
narrative_blocks.body: Mollie Spencer lived near him in Marengo County and they had as many as four children together at a time when interracial sex was a crime across the South. He sold her two hundred acres, which suggests more than a passing tie.

narrative_blocks.header: His name stayed off their records
narrative_blocks.body: None of the children took his surname; they were entered as Spencers and Davises, and the connection survived only as a story one of them told her niece about a white father. DNA proved it in 2023, ninety-four years after he died.

narrative_blocks.header: Through him the line reaches the Mayflower
narrative_blocks.body: Through him, and only through him, William Brewster — born in England about 1570, the elder aboard the Mayflower — is Angela Davis's tenth great-grandfather. Told so on camera, she said her ancestors did not come here on the Mayflower.

marriages.spouse_notes: Mother of Benjamin Frank Davis Sr. No union with the father; the assault is recorded in the narrative blocks.

narrative_blocks.header: The two hundred acres were in her name
narrative_blocks.body: Murphy Jones sold her two hundred acres of Marengo County at a time when a Black woman holding land outright in Alabama was rare. She had as many as four children by him, and every one was entered under her husband's surname.

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband had left long before
narrative_blocks.body: Edward Davis was gone years before Frank was born, but the marriage was never undone and his name went on the children anyway. That is how Angela Davis came to carry the surname of a man she was not descended from.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father took his old owner to court
narrative_blocks.body: Isom Spencer was freed at the end of the war and found the man who had held him was keeping his nephews. He brought the case through the Freedmen's Bureau and won; the boys were turned over to their family.

narrative_blocks.header: The first of her line born free
narrative_blocks.body: Isom Spencer, born into slavery about 1830, and Mary Knox had her in Marengo County on 8 August 1869 — four years after the surrender. Everyone above her in the line had been somebody's property.

narrative_blocks.header: One of her daughters kept the story alive
narrative_blocks.body: The children knew their father was a white man nearby, and a daughter passed that on to Angela Davis years later. It was the only record of him until a DNA test in 2023 put a name to it.

narrative_blocks.header: She finished a long way from Marengo County
narrative_blocks.body: She died in Los Angeles on 28 September 1955, eighty-six years old. Her life ran from an Alabama county four years out of slavery to postwar California, and her granddaughter Angela was eleven when it ended.

people.relational_label_override: Mother of a Tenth Generation Hooker

narrative_blocks.header: Edward Davis was not his father
narrative_blocks.body: He carried his mother Mollie Spencer’s married surname, and Edward Davis had left her long before he was born. A DNA test eighty years on named the white neighbour Murphy Jones, who had sold Mollie two hundred acres of land.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandfather sued to get the boys back
narrative_blocks.body: Isom Spencer was freed at the end of the war, but his former owner held on to his nephews. Spencer took the man to court over it and won — the boys were turned over to their family.

narrative_blocks.header: He and Sallye both got death threats
narrative_blocks.body: He and Sallye worked in the NAACP through the Birmingham years, which in that city meant death threats at home. Their children grew up on Dynamite Hill and were sent north to school to get them away from the bombs.

bio.bio_blurb: Teacher and Southern Negro Youth Congress organizer

narrative_blocks.header: She organised for the Youth Congress
narrative_blocks.body: She was a national officer of the Southern Negro Youth Congress, the left-wing organisation building alliances among Black Southerners, and a schoolteacher in Birmingham. Her daughter grew up among the organisers who came through the house.

narrative_blocks.header: She worked for the Scottsboro Boys
narrative_blocks.body: In the 1930s she joined the campaign for the nine Alabama teenagers accused of rape on a freight train, working beside communists at a time when that was itself a charge. Her politics were Black and white together against racism.

narrative_blocks.header: She never learned her parents’ names
narrative_blocks.body: She grew up in a foster home and went to her grave in 2007 without a name for either parent. Sixteen years later her daughter learned on television that her father had been John Austin Darden, a white Alabama lawyer and legislator.

narrative_blocks.header: She took the microphone in Oakland
narrative_blocks.body: On 13 July 1972, with her daughter facing the gas chamber, she stood at a Free Angela rally in Oakland and spoke to hundreds. The schoolteacher who had spent twenty years in front of children handled a microphone the same way.

narrative_blocks.header: Their marches were attacked
narrative_blocks.body: She and Frank Davis were both in the NAACP and both got death threats for it. She walked her children into civil-rights marches that segregationists broke up, which is how Angela first understood the fight as Black against white.

narrative_blocks.header: Teaching was the method, not the job
narrative_blocks.body: She taught elementary school in Birmingham and ran the house on the same principle — reading, argument and the political news were ordinary evening fare. Four children came out of that kitchen into law, scholarship, sport and the stage.

narrative_blocks.header: Third woman on the FBI most-wanted list
narrative_blocks.body: Guns she had bought were used in the Marin County courthouse takeover of August 1970, in which four died. Hoover put her on the Ten Most Wanted; she was held sixteen months and acquitted of every charge by an all-white jury in 1972.

narrative_blocks.header: UCLA fired her twice in one year
narrative_blocks.body: She was in the Communist Party and running political education for the Los Angeles Black Panthers when the Regents dismissed her in 1969, Reagan urging them on. A judge ruled it illegal; they fired her again in 1970 over four speeches.

narrative_blocks.header: She grew up on Dynamite Hill
narrative_blocks.body: Her Birmingham street was bombed through the fifties to drive middle-class Black families out. She knew the four girls killed in the 1963 church bombing, and heard of it while studying in France.

narrative_blocks.header: She picketed segregation as a Girl Scout
narrative_blocks.body: She marched against segregation in Birmingham while in the Girl Scouts, and went north in her junior year on a Quaker programme that placed Black Southern students in integrated schools.

narrative_blocks.header: Marcuse showed her it could be both
narrative_blocks.body: She met him at a rally during the Cuban missile crisis and became his student. He taught her, she said, that it was possible to be an academic, an activist, a scholar and a revolutionary all at once.

narrative_blocks.header: She founded Critical Resistance in 1997
narrative_blocks.body: She has argued for forty years that the American prison system is a new form of slavery, and co-founded the organisation working to abolish it. Are Prisons Obsolete? came out in 2003.

narrative_blocks.header: The Mayflower turned up on television
narrative_blocks.body: Henry Louis Gates told her on Finding Your Roots in 2023 that she descends from William Brewster, who came over on the Mayflower. Her grandfather was a Jones of Fayetteville.

education.notes: B.A., magna cum laude; Phi Beta Kappa.

bio.bio_blurb: NFL cornerback, then a Cleveland businessman

narrative_blocks.header: Seven straight games with an interception
narrative_blocks.body: He started at cornerback in 1968, led the Browns with eight interceptions and the league in interception return yards, and was named All-Pro. The record for seven consecutive games with a pick is still his.

narrative_blocks.header: He led the league in punt returns
narrative_blocks.body: Drafted 439th and last-round in 1967, he was moved off receiver because Warfield, Collins and McNeil already had the job. He averaged 12.7 yards a punt return that first year, better than all but three Browns ever.

narrative_blocks.header: He finished high school at fifteen
narrative_blocks.body: The family sent its children away from the night riders' bombs on Dynamite Hill. He took his diploma at Fair Lawn in New Jersey at fifteen, waited out a Maine prep school until he was old enough for college, and went undefeated at Defiance.

narrative_blocks.header: One of the first Black-owned cable companies
narrative_blocks.body: He sold for Xerox after football, then co-founded Telecable Broadcasting of America at Cleveland in 1982, among the first Black-owned and operated cable television firms in the country. A Tulsa radio station and a Xerox dealership followed.

narrative_blocks.header: A torn knee cost him eighteen months
narrative_blocks.body: The anterior cruciate went in 1969 and kept him out through half of 1970. He came back for three more seasons at Cleveland and three at Detroit, ten years in all, and has lived in Cleveland since 1967.

cross_connections.display_label: played fullback for the Steelers his Browns had to beat
ran the league he had played in, a generation after him
ran Ohio's largest broadcaster the year Davis founded Telecable

notable.notable_blurb: NFL cornerback, then a Cleveland businessman

narrative_blocks.header: He taught a course about his sister
narrative_blocks.body: He was a sophomore at Defiance College in Ohio when Angela was arrested, and in January 1971 a sociology professor asked him to teach a month-long course on her case in the black studies programme. He spoke for her across the Midwest.

narrative_blocks.header: He sat on the panel thirty-three years later
narrative_blocks.body: In 2005 Harvard Law brought the trial lawyers back together and put him and Ben on the stage with them. Both brothers said the same thing about those months: the case had pulled the family in tighter than it had ever been.

bio.bio_blurb: Civil rights lawyer; restorative justice founder

narrative_blocks.header: She led the campaign to free her sister
narrative_blocks.body: She dropped her philosophy doctorate at San Diego and spoke coast to coast and across Europe — sixty thousand in France, twenty thousand in Rome — through the sixteen months Angela was held. She began it five months pregnant.

narrative_blocks.header: Arrested at her sister's trial
narrative_blocks.body: She and sixteen others were arrested outside the Santa Clara County courthouse in January 1972 for defying the rules on demonstrating during pre-trial motions. A photographer caught her fist up as they loaded her on the sheriff's bus.

narrative_blocks.header: She came north on a Quaker scholarship
narrative_blocks.body: She went to high school at Glen Ridge in New Jersey on the same Quaker programme that took her sister to Greenwich Village, read at Swarthmore, then followed Angela to San Diego to study under Marcuse.

narrative_blocks.header: Her sister’s lawyers decided her career
narrative_blocks.body: Angela's defence attorneys made her want the work. She practised civil rights law from the late seventies into the middle nineties, then stopped, saying the hyperaggressive stance the job demanded had put her out of balance.

narrative_blocks.header: She studied with a Zulu healer
narrative_blocks.body: She took a doctorate in Indigenous knowledge at the California Institute of Integral Studies and apprenticed to African healers, one of them a Zulu in South Africa. She came home and founded Restorative Justice for Oakland Youth.

narrative_blocks.header: She wants a truth and reconciliation process
narrative_blocks.body: She argues the American racial wound needs what South Africa attempted — testimony heard nationally, and circles at local level between the people harmed and the people who did the harm.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother’s friend lost a daughter that day
narrative_blocks.body: She heard of the 16th Street bombing when her mother told her a close friend had driven down to collect her girl from church and found no Carole, and no body. Two of the four dead were her friends.

cross_connections.display_label: taught her at San Diego and employed her in his department

narrative_blocks.header: He baked the wedding cake himself
narrative_blocks.body: Two Congregational ministers married him to Angela Davis at her parents' Birmingham house in July 1980; both were thirty-six. A pianist played the Lohengrin march, and the white-and-yellow cake was the groom's work.

narrative_blocks.header: Lancaster, Cuba, and a dormitory search
narrative_blocks.body: He and Fania organised the Black community at Lancaster while he was at Franklin and Marshall. The two were in Cuba when Angela was captured, and by then he was serving one to two years for a concealed weapon and the makings of explosives.

narrative_blocks.header: A roadside stop became eighteen felony counts
narrative_blocks.body: Deputies stopped Fania hitch-hiking on Highway 101 at Del Mar in November 1969 and asked her name. He walked up, said she was his wife and it was a family matter. By the end of the night the two of them faced eighteen felony counts.

narrative_blocks.header: The judge found the deputies were the aggressors
narrative_blocks.body: Judge Staniforth threw out all eighteen counts in December 1970, holding the officers had acted outside their authority. The state appealed and lost in August 1971; the court noted nobody had thought to ask Fania whether she needed help.

narrative_blocks.header: She put her childhood on a stage
narrative_blocks.body: Her play Angela's Mixtape is about growing up in this family — the aunt on the posters, the mother practising law, the grandmother who taught school. She wrote herself into it as the girl trying to work out what any of it meant.

narrative_blocks.header: Born while her aunt awaited trial
narrative_blocks.body: She was born while her aunt sat in jail awaiting trial and her mother Fania was crossing the country and Cuba to campaign for her release. The family met her between hearings.

narrative_blocks.header: The first name she never uses
narrative_blocks.body: She was christened Angela Eisa Davis for the aunt who was in a cell the season she arrived, and has gone by the middle name ever since. She was still at Harvard when she first put the family on a stage.

narrative_blocks.header: He invented a course for one undergraduate
narrative_blocks.body: Angela Davis walked into his Brandeis lecture hall as a first-year and told him she wanted philosophy. He built an independent tutorial for her alone, then sent her to Frankfurt to read with Adorno and Horkheimer.

narrative_blocks.header: He was first through the chancellor’s door
narrative_blocks.body: She left Frankfurt mid-doctorate to follow him to San Diego, finished a dissertation on Kant under him, and occupied the chancellor's office beside him for Lumumba-Zapata College. By her account he went in first, then paid for the door.

narrative_blocks.header: He spoke beside her at the Berkeley rally
narrative_blocks.body: The Regents moved against her for belonging to the Communist Party, and in 1969 he took the platform with her at Berkeley. He and his wife Inge kept up public support through her imprisonment and celebrated the 1972 acquittal.

narrative_blocks.header: The New Left’s philosopher worked for the OSS
narrative_blocks.body: From 1941 he analysed Germany for the Office of Strategic Services, the agency the CIA grew out of, and stayed in government intelligence until 1950. His wife Sophie Wertheim, a mathematician, was working for US Naval Intelligence.

narrative_blocks.header: He argued comfort was the better cage
narrative_blocks.body: One-Dimensional Man held that an affluent society disarms its critics by satisfying them, flattening the space in which an alternative can even be imagined. It made him the philosopher the students of 1968 actually read.

narrative_blocks.header: A book against capitalism that never names Marx
narrative_blocks.body: Eros and Civilization built its case on Freud instead — that the drives capitalism cannot satisfy are the measure of what it costs. Marx does not appear once in it.

narrative_blocks.header: He minded horses, then read Heidegger
narrative_blocks.body: Drafted in 1916 at eighteen, he spent the war minding the infantry's horses and came out of it a politics man, briefly joining the Spartacist rising. He went back to Freiburg in 1928 to write his habilitation under Martin Heidegger.
