narrative_blocks.header: She edits the magazine of the One Percent
narrative_blocks.body: She took over Avenue in 2012, the free monthly left in the lobbies of the best buildings on both sides of the park. It is not a scandal sheet, she says: to be in it you must have done something, usually philanthropic.

narrative_blocks.header: Vanity Fair, London, then back downtown
narrative_blocks.body: She wrote for Vanity Fair and ES in London, where she and Hugh Chisholm lived eight years before returning in 2009. They settled on lower Fifth Avenue, looking onto the arch in Washington Square, the Village she had wanted since Barnard.

narrative_blocks.header: The other Daisy Prince gets her mail
narrative_blocks.body: She is regularly mistaken for the Broadway producer Hal Prince's daughter, who has the same name and the same city. The two began receiving each other's post, so she rang her up — and then interviewed her for the magazine.

narrative_blocks.header: A hurricane, a newborn and a borrowed pram
narrative_blocks.body: She brought her first son to Newport four days old, and Hurricane Irene arrived soon after. The clubs shut, so ten were fed at home; her mother had brought down from the attic the Silver Cross pram Daisy was wheeled in.

narrative_blocks.header: He invests only in what interests him
narrative_blocks.body: He founded O Street Capital in Washington and runs it on a simple rule: he backs what he is already interested in. The portfolio runs through film, music, gaming, technology and controlled botanicals.

narrative_blocks.header: He built a studio on a Salvadoran beach
narrative_blocks.body: He began as a DJ and music producer, playing venues around the world, and built Hazmat Studios at Mizata on the Pacific coast of El Salvador. Musicians from every genre have recorded there beside the ocean.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the white supremacist part on purpose
narrative_blocks.body: In the short film Perception he plays a white supremacist — a part he chose in order to put the harder side of the immigration argument on screen. It won him Best Supporting Actor at the Omaha Latino Film Festival.

narrative_blocks.header: He played the lawyer who argued for Roe
narrative_blocks.body: He was an executive producer on Roe v. Wade and appeared in it as Cyril Means, the attorney who built the pro-choice case. His other pictures include The Preppie Connection and the thriller Synchronic.

narrative_blocks.header: A relative’s illness put him into marijuana
narrative_blocks.body: After someone in the family was helped by medicinal marijuana he launched Ocean State Controlled Botanicals, the largest medical marijuana production facility in Rhode Island.

narrative_blocks.header: His great-grandfather edited the 11th Britannica
narrative_blocks.body: The eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, published 1910–11 and still the one collectors argue is the best, was edited by a Hugh Chisholm before him. A set stands on the shelves of the Greenwich Village flat he and Daisy keep.

narrative_blocks.header: The causes she and Octavius carry together
narrative_blocks.body: They give to the Preservation Society of Newport County, the Surfrider Foundation, Cubs Charities and the Shirley Ryan AbilityLab, and to the Foundation to Be Named Later, which runs the Hot Stove Cool Music benefit.

bio.title: Reverend
bio.bio_blurb: Old Light pastor of New Haven's Center Church

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-five years in one New Haven pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: Ordained over New Haven's First Church in 1716, he held it until he died in 1761 and was buried in the crypt beneath it. He had taken the pulpit his wife's father left.

narrative_blocks.header: A Yale tutor at twenty-two
narrative_blocks.body: He took his Yale degree in 1709 and was made a tutor within a year of it, holding the post five years before New Haven called him.

narrative_blocks.header: A council refused to give him a colleague
narrative_blocks.body: The Great Awakening split his congregation, and by the 1750s he needed help. A council met and declared against ordaining Chauncey Whittlesey, or any other candidate; the next day it installed him anyway.

narrative_blocks.header: Son of one Yale founder, son-in-law to another
narrative_blocks.body: His father, Rev. James Noyes of Stonington, was among the ten ministers who founded the Collegiate School in 1701. So was James Pierpont, whose daughter he married and whose New Haven pulpit he took.

narrative_blocks.header: His son married a Mayflower descendant
narrative_blocks.body: John Noyes took his Yale degree in 1756 and married Mary Fish of Stonington, whose mother was a great-granddaughter of John Alden. He was dead at thirty-two, leaving three sons.

cross_connections.display_label: , his father-in-law, left him the pulpit and now shares his crypt
was installed beside him after a council refused to do it
called him to Wallingford in 1729 over two cases of scandal

burial.plot_notes: Buried in the crypt beneath Center Church.

people.relational_label_override: Husband of Stepdaughter of Third Generation Hooker

narrative_blocks.header: Three generations went to sea
narrative_blocks.body: His father John was a ships captain at Middletown, he commanded ships himself, and his son Reuben worked as a ships carpenter. Of the three, only he is confirmed to have died at sea, in 1803.

narrative_blocks.header: Three brothers, three bibles, three canes
narrative_blocks.body: Family tradition held that three Barnes brothers left England on the Speedwell, each carrying a bible and a cane. The Middletown line in fact traces to Shamgar Barnes, who came to the town about 1707.

narrative_blocks.header: He built ships instead of sailing
narrative_blocks.body: His father captained vessels and his grandfather was a sea carpenter, and both died at sea. He worked as a ship's carpenter at Middletown and died there in his bed in 1844.

narrative_blocks.header: Born the year of the wedding
narrative_blocks.body: His parents married at Middletown in August 1790 and he was born that year, their only child. He was thirteen when his father was lost.

narrative_blocks.header: Her daguerreotype survived in the family
narrative_blocks.body: A daguerreotype of her was kept and passed down by her granddaughter Nellie Ham, who wrote the account that preserves most of what is known of the family.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine children in twenty-four years
narrative_blocks.body: She married Reuben Barnes of Middletown and bore nine children between 1814 and 1838. She died at Wallingford in April 1860.

narrative_blocks.header: The first machine-made wallpaper
narrative_blocks.body: He built the first wallpaper in America produced by machinery, at a factory in Brooklyn where his brother Asa worked for him. He opened and sold others at New Brunswick, Lynn, Chelsea and Roxbury.

narrative_blocks.header: Chestnuts bought his first trousers
narrative_blocks.body: He left school at about ten and kept himself after that. He remembered to the end of his life the first dollar he earned, gathering and selling a bushel of chestnuts, and the colour of the trousers he bought with it.

narrative_blocks.header: He died with a picture unfinished
narrative_blocks.body: He never took a lesson, and learned to mix colours in the paint factories. At his death he left a painting of the house where his daughter was born, worked up entirely from memory.

narrative_blocks.header: Gold fell through the cabin floor
narrative_blocks.body: He carried gold east to west and his children lost the coins in the cracks of a Kansas log cabin, so the floor had to come up. In one storm the men went out and held the logs against the house.

narrative_blocks.header: He answered an advertisement
narrative_blocks.body: A mother in New York City advertised for a home for her twelve-year-old. He took Ann Eliza in at New Brunswick because she had brown hair and eyes like his children.

narrative_blocks.header: He fished the Adirondacks
narrative_blocks.body: He and Chloe went north to fish the Adirondacks and the White Mountains. He could answer almost anything asked of him and kept the memory to his death at eighty-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: A pioneer of carriage making
narrative_blocks.body: He was one of the pioneers of carriage manufacturing in the country, first with the L. F. Gladding company at a time when it was a prominent firm, and later in partnership with Alvah Bristol.

narrative_blocks.header: Pneumonia came through his partner
narrative_blocks.body: Alvah Bristol, eighty-five and his partner of years, fell seriously ill with pneumonia. It carried Ransom off first, at his Plainville home on a Monday night in December 1902, aged eighty-six.

narrative_blocks.header: Four daughters and no sons
narrative_blocks.body: He left four daughters: Mrs Erskine Andrews and Mrs H. D. Stanley of Bridgeport, Mrs S. F. Guernsey of Southington, and Antoinette, unmarried and living at Plainville.

narrative_blocks.header: Gladding took him in as partner in 1852
narrative_blocks.body: Lewis Gladding expanded into two buildings across from the post office and took him and Horace Johnson as partners. The firm carried Gladding's name until 1875, when it became the Plainville Carriage Company.

cross_connections.display_label: built New Haven’s great carriage works while he built Plainville’s
, his nephew, carried the name out to Oklahoma

narrative_blocks.header: A hunting party shot out his eye
narrative_blocks.body: He wintered in the Carolinas hunting and fishing, always with men around him, and one of them shot him in the eye by accident. He wore a glass one after that.

narrative_blocks.header: Tall and stately, like a lord
narrative_blocks.body: He lived at New Brunswick in New Jersey and grew wealthy. His niece wrote that he was so tall and stately he looked like a lord.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a Gould Andrews
narrative_blocks.body: She stayed in Connecticut and married Gould Andrews. The family did not think he was any relation to the Andrews her sister Frances married.

bio.bio_blurb: Papermaker; Free State legislator and cavalry captain

narrative_blocks.header: He arrived a Democrat, turned Free State
narrative_blocks.body: He sold up in New Brunswick in 1858 and settled Mt Pleasant township in Atchison County, his wife and children following the next April. He changed parties soon after landing and became a known champion of a free Kansas.

narrative_blocks.header: Twice sent to the Kansas legislature
narrative_blocks.body: Atchison County elected him to represent it in the state legislature on two separate occasions. He held no other office and was said to have wanted none.

narrative_blocks.header: The Price Raid made him a captain
narrative_blocks.body: He organized Company A of the Twelfth Kansas Cavalry and led it as captain, and helped raise a company for the Thirteenth Kansas Infantry. His bravery in the defence against the Price Raid is what fixed the title to his name.

narrative_blocks.header: His letters west pulled his brother
narrative_blocks.body: His accounts of Kansas were glowing enough that Reuben Curtis Barnes packed up and followed him to Atchison County. The brother who had worked for him in the wallpaper factory became his neighbour.

narrative_blocks.header: From New Haven back to Kansas
narrative_blocks.body: She married an Andrews and lived at New Haven, and in the 1870s travelled out to Atchison to see the family. One of her daughters married a Bishop who sat as a judge of the common pleas court.

narrative_blocks.header: She died at twenty-three
narrative_blocks.body: She married and lived at New Brunswick in New Jersey, and left a daughter, Isabel Stevens, remembered in the family as very beautiful.

narrative_blocks.header: He worked the Meriden silver works
narrative_blocks.body: He spent his working life at the silver works in Meriden, Connecticut. The family believed he left no children.

narrative_blocks.header: Her slipper caught the runaway
narrative_blocks.body: When her daughter Francina slipped away at Chelsea to show a neighbour boy the shipyards, she was paddled with Chloe's slipper on her return.

narrative_blocks.header: Her sister came west to nurse them
narrative_blocks.body: Through the hardships of the Civil War years at Atchison her sister Sarah Beach, unmarried and a nurse, came out from the east to be with them.

narrative_blocks.header: Adopted from a newspaper advertisement
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother advertised in New York City for a home for her. Reuben Curtis Barnes took her at twelve because she had brown hair and eyes like his children, and she was the only one of the household not born to him.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived the family she made
narrative_blocks.body: She married Benjamin Kelly at Chelsea and had two children, George and Carrie. She was ill most of her life and kept a nurse, and every one of them died before she did.

people.research_notes: Adopted daughter, born New York City; taken in about 1849 aged twelve.

narrative_blocks.header: He guarded the Lincoln conspirators
narrative_blocks.body: He enlisted in the Civil War and was out again before he turned twenty-one, having served four years — three in the regular army and one in the Hancock Corps, stationed at Washington. He helped guard the prison holding the conspirators.

cross_connections.display_label: prosecuted a conspirator out of the prison he had guarded

narrative_blocks.header: A tomato was thought to be poison
narrative_blocks.body: A boarder in the Lynn house walked in the garden carrying her and gave her a tomato to play with. They were called love-apples then and held to be poisonous, and she ate part of it before anyone could stop her.

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve years old on the Atchison boat
narrative_blocks.body: She rode the steamboat up from St Louis at twelve and made friends with the captain's daughter, the same age, and the two of them ate at the captain's table.

narrative_blocks.header: Scarlet fever took her sister
narrative_blocks.body: She and her younger sister Susan both took scarlet fever. Susan died of it at four; Francina lived to eighty-one.

narrative_blocks.header: Scarlet fever took her at four
narrative_blocks.body: She caught scarlet fever along with her elder sister Francina, who recovered. Susan did not.

narrative_blocks.header: Her will bought pink Westerly granite
narrative_blocks.body: She left about eight thousand dollars. Two thousand went into trust for her sister Antoinette, and a thousand more to a monument of pink Westerly granite and the care of the plot at Mountain Grove.

narrative_blocks.header: Three months ill at her daughter’s house
narrative_blocks.body: She died at 195 Barnum Avenue in Bridgeport, the home of her daughter Mrs A. J. Smith, after three months of illness. Judge William Comley was among the bearers.

naming_inspiration.description: Named for his father’s elder brother Ransom Barnes, the Plainville carriage manufacturer.

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve years old on the road to Kansas
narrative_blocks.body: His father went out to Atchison County in 1858 and sold New Jersey behind him; Harriet brought the children on in April 1859. Ransom was the eldest of eleven and twelve years old.

narrative_blocks.header: A Missouri farm swap brought her to him
narrative_blocks.body: Aramenta's father Richmond Dolton, a Union man in a Southern-sympathising Missouri town, traded his farm for one in Kansas rather than quarrel with his neighbours. His daughter met the New Jersey settler there.

narrative_blocks.header: Kansas to Guthrie to Pocasset
narrative_blocks.body: He married Aramenta Dalton in 1869, and the family left Kansas for Guthrie in 1893, the Dutton community near Verden in 1901, and Pocasset by 1910. All their children reached adulthood.

narrative_blocks.header: He lost Hattie at twenty-nine
narrative_blocks.body: Hattie died in 1901, the first of his children to go. Ten years later Pearl's husband, a railroad policeman, was killed on duty, and Pearl followed him, leaving a small son named Joseph McDonald.

narrative_blocks.header: Friendship Cemetery, twenty-seven years first
narrative_blocks.body: He died in 1912 and was buried at Friendship Cemetery near Dutton. Minty kept the place and was laid beside him in February 1939.

cross_connections.display_label: , his grandson, carries his name in the middle
, his uncle, made carriages at Plainville

narrative_blocks.header: New Brunswick to the Colorado mountains
narrative_blocks.body: Born in New Jersey the year before the family sold up for Kansas, he went further west still. He died at Glenwood Springs in 1910; his wife outlived him twenty years and died at Salida.

people.research_notes: Bought the 207-acre home farm in Mt Pleasant township from his father and the heirs. Children named in the county history but undated, so not built: Fannie, Herbert, Bertha (Pease), Leola (Saggs), Ernest L., Dora (Lee), Cora.

bio.bio_blurb: Pioneer settler of the Dutton community

narrative_blocks.header: Richmond Dalton’s daughter, out of Illinois
narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Galesburg in Illinois to Richmond Dalton and Priscilla Hahn, and married Ransom Barnes in Kansas in 1869. Two brothers, Will and Edd, were still living at Enid and Chapman when she died.

narrative_blocks.header: Her granddaughters came to live with her
narrative_blocks.body: When Hattie died in 1901 her two girls, Estella and Gladys Beasore, came to Dutton and stayed for a time with their grandparents. Minty was fifty.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven children, twenty-five grandchildren
narrative_blocks.body: Her obituary counted seven surviving children, twenty-five grandchildren and fifteen great-grandchildren, scattered from Los Angeles to Black Rock in Arkansas. The eldest was Mrs Effie Henson of McLoud.

narrative_blocks.header: A lingering illness, and a Sunday morning
narrative_blocks.body: She died at nine on a Sunday morning in February 1939, eighty-seven years old, and lay at the Hansen Funeral Home in Verden until Tuesday. Rev. J. E. Frohock read the service at the Dutton Church.

narrative_blocks.header: Buried beside him after twenty-seven years
narrative_blocks.body: She was laid at Friendship Cemetery beside the husband she had outlived since 1912. She had come to the community in 1901 from Guthrie, and to Guthrie from Kansas eight years before that.

bio.bio_blurb: Oklahoma farm wife & mother of eight

narrative_blocks.header: Born within a year of the wedding
narrative_blocks.body: Ransom Barnes and Aramenta Dalton married in Kansas in 1869, and she arrived in February 1870, the first of their eleven. She was the one the family called levelheaded.

narrative_blocks.header: The land run failed and they stayed put
narrative_blocks.body: Albert Henson came back from the Cherokee Strip without a claim, and they settled Lincoln County east of Oklahoma City instead. The children came there, the youngest in 1904.

narrative_blocks.header: She saw her children schooled past her husband
narrative_blocks.body: Albert had almost no formal education and made it the household's rule. The youngest walked half a mile to a room of fifty children, then went to Iowa State and into government science.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother’s obituary named her first
narrative_blocks.body: When Aramenta died in 1939 the paper listed seven surviving children, and Mrs Effie Henson of McLoud headed them. Effie outlived her by nineteen years and was buried at New Salem in Lincoln County.

bio.display_name: Jennie Anne Marcia Jane Dyer Barnes

narrative_blocks.header: He married at Shanghai in 1926
narrative_blocks.body: He and Virginia Bier of Wheeling were married at Shanghai on 17 September 1926. Their daughter Phyliss was born in Massachusetts two years later.

narrative_blocks.header: Dead at thirty with three under eight
narrative_blocks.body: He married Maria Bigelow in 1894 and died in July 1902, leaving a boy of seven and twin girls of two. She never remarried and outlived him by fifty-one years.

narrative_blocks.header: He buried a son at six
narrative_blocks.body: John Sherman Guernsey, born in 1918, died in 1924. Jane came in 1920 and Fenn in 1925, the last carrying the Fenn name the family had used for four generations.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the Cherokee Strip and got nothing
narrative_blocks.body: He drove a mule-drawn buckboard into the Oklahoma countryside for the Cherokee Strip land run and failed to stake a claim. He and Effie settled in Lincoln County, east of Oklahoma City, instead.

narrative_blocks.header: No schooling, and every child sent to it
narrative_blocks.body: He had little formal education himself and made it the household's priority. His youngest, Paul, walked half a mile to a one-room school of fifty children and finished high school at nineteen.

naming_inspiration.description: Named for his mother Effie’s father, Ransom Aaron Barnes of New Jersey and Kansas.

narrative_blocks.header: He went to the Delta to breed crops
narrative_blocks.body: He took a government post at the Delta Branch Experiment Station at Stoneville in 1931 and brought Betty south with him. He finished his career at the Beltsville Agricultural Research Center in Maryland.

narrative_blocks.header: His thesis was on hybridising soybeans
narrative_blocks.body: He left an Oklahoma one-room school of fifty children and two teachers for Iowa State, judged farm crops on the team that placed third nationally in 1927, and took his degree in July 1928.

narrative_blocks.header: He noticed her legs outside the campus restaurant
narrative_blocks.body: She was Elizabeth Brown, twenty-one, secretary to the dean of Maryland's College of Agriculture. He courted her for two years of weekend tennis parties at the Browns' before she married him.

narrative_blocks.header: He married his late wife’s sister
narrative_blocks.body: Betty Brown died at Albuquerque in 1972. He later married her sister Barbara, called Bobby, and lived out his life at Ahoskie in North Carolina, where the third Brown sister had settled.

cross_connections.display_label: , his grandfather, is the Ransom in his name

narrative_blocks.header: Secretary to the dean of agriculture
narrative_blocks.body: At twenty-one she worked for Harry Patterson, dean of Maryland's College of Agriculture. A graduate student eating his lunch watched her walk to the campus restaurant and set about getting introduced.

narrative_blocks.header: His hands came down her side
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother Sarah could paint, draw, sew, carve and handle tools, and had been accepted to art school before her father's death ended it. Two generations on, her son sketched, carved and sewed the first Muppets.

narrative_blocks.header: The house shook when the trains went by
narrative_blocks.body: The Browns lived by the railroad tracks at Hyattsville, in a place the family called perfectly awful, until they moved to Marion Street in 1923. She and her sister Attie paid into the mortgage out of secretary wages.

narrative_blocks.header: Hot and cold baths for whooping cough
narrative_blocks.body: Her father took up Christian Science and the three girls were raised in it, moderately: prayer and homeopathy for an illness, but a doctor called when her sister broke a leg in a car crash.

narrative_blocks.header: A Washington girl who sounded like Memphis
narrative_blocks.body: She was born in the District and raised in Maryland, but Southern Railway moved the family to Memphis and New Orleans long enough for the accent and the manners to stick.

narrative_blocks.header: Uncle Fritz taught all three to play
narrative_blocks.body: Fritz Hinrichs taught the sisters tennis and dancing, and the Browns' weekend tennis parties kept the family in the Washington Post society pages. Paul Henson courted her across two years of them.

narrative_blocks.header: Two years in Albuquerque, then gone
narrative_blocks.body: She had lived in Albuquerque only two years when she died at sixty-four. Her obituary named one surviving son, James M. Henson of New York, two sisters and five grandchildren.

narrative_blocks.header: A car crash at twenty-three
narrative_blocks.body: He died on 15 April 1956 at Pensacola and was buried at Arlington. His brother Jim was nineteen, and his wife Jane later traced the sweet melancholy in Jim's work to that spring.

narrative_blocks.header: The first Kermit was blue
narrative_blocks.body: He cut it from an old felt coat of his mother's, with a halved table tennis ball for eyes, while he was sitting with his dying grandfather. Soft materials let a puppet carry an expression that carved wood could not.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother died in a 1956 crash
narrative_blocks.body: Paul was twenty-three and a Navy ensign; Jim was nineteen. Jane Henson traced both the sweet melancholy in his work and the relentless drive behind it to that loss.

narrative_blocks.header: He used the four sides of the screen
narrative_blocks.body: An Ernie Kovacs admirer, he stopped pointing a camera at a puppet theatre and let the lens and the edges of the home television set become the frame. His puppets were born in and made for the television generation.

narrative_blocks.header: Sesame Street took him full-time in 1969
narrative_blocks.body: Joan Ganz Cooney's team asked him to work full-time on a children's programme for public television. He performed Ernie, Guy Smiley and Kermit as a roving reporter; PBS called him the spark that ignited the service.

narrative_blocks.header: America said Muppets were for children
narrative_blocks.body: The networks turned down a weekly Muppet series, certain the audience was juvenile. He took it to Lew Grade instead and shot The Muppet Show at Elstree in Hertfordshire, syndicated worldwide.

narrative_blocks.header: A sore throat killed him in three days
narrative_blocks.body: He mentioned a sore throat on 4 May 1990 and would not break his schedule for a hospital. Streptococcal toxic shock took him on 16 May at fifty-three; his doctor said hours earlier might have saved him.

narrative_blocks.header: No black at the funeral
narrative_blocks.body: He left instructions that no one wear black. Big Bird sang 'Bein' Green' from the stage of the Cathedral of St John the Divine, and the Dirty Dozen Brass Band closed with 'When the Saints Go Marching In'.

notable.notable_blurb: Puppeteer; creator of the Muppets

narrative_blocks.header: He bought a schoolhouse at sixteen
narrative_blocks.body: He and his friend John Kahn bought an old school house at Saugerties in New York, and Kahn taught him home building, furniture design and sculpture. He spent his life on buildings there, each one treated as an art project.

narrative_blocks.header: He was Sweetums for eleven years
narrative_blocks.body: He performed Sweetums from 1992 to 2003 and worked as a full-body performer inside other creatures, among them the Coca-Cola polar bear. After his father died in 1990 he became a shareholder and sat on the board.

narrative_blocks.header: He left trade not long after marrying her
narrative_blocks.body: Mary was a daughter of Israel W. Munroe, the Boston merchant, and Priscilla Burbank. She married Faxon in November 1852, when he was twenty-nine and already rich; within a few years he had quit business for the temperance war.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Her husband's gift of the old South Commons

narrative_blocks.header: He buried two sons before either turned two
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin Munroe died at a year old in 1867 and Warren Munroe within the year of his birth in 1870. The two daughters, Lucretia and Ellen, both lived into their seventies.

narrative_blocks.header: Her daughter lived a single day
narrative_blocks.body: Abbie married Charles Allen Howland in December 1860. Their daughter was born and died on April 23, 1864. Abbie herself was dead fifteen months later, at twenty-six.

naming_inspiration.note: The Torrey surname, carried as a given name

narrative_blocks.header: She carried a surname four generations gone
narrative_blocks.body: The Munroes had not been Torreys since 1801, when Hannah Torrey married Nehemiah Burbank. Two generations later a granddaughter was christened Hannah Torrey Munroe. She died at twenty-one.

cross_connections.display_label: , her fourth great-grandfather, gave her the surname she carried

narrative_blocks.header: He speculated in whiskey and rum
narrative_blocks.body: Apprenticed to a shoemaker in 1843, Faxon kept a grocery and an auction room before his firm turned wholesaler, speculating in staples — whiskey and rum among them. The profits went into land, and he became the largest landlord in Quincy.

narrative_blocks.header: Quincy called him the millionaire policeman
narrative_blocks.body: Faxon got Quincy to raise a special police force for the liquor laws, had himself made its enforcer and refused the pay. "It is not for office or honor that I take so active a part in politics," he said, "but to do my political duty."

narrative_blocks.header: He bought a tavern to shut it down
narrative_blocks.body: The Hancock Tavern sold strong drink, so Faxon bought the building and closed it. Daniel Webster had waited there for the Marshfield mail coach, and the regulars said he gave some of his best orations to that room.

narrative_blocks.header: He spoke forty times at one town meeting
narrative_blocks.body: Quincy sat through forty speeches from Faxon in one town meeting, and the next year the voters abolished town meeting for a council. He sat in the legislature in 1864 and 1871, a Republican who refused to run as a partisan.

narrative_blocks.header: He paid for the Reform Club a hall
narrative_blocks.body: Faxon led the Reform Club movement in Massachusetts and covered most of the cost of building and fitting out Faxon Hall in Quincy as its headquarters. He argued for Black rights and for women's rights from the same platform.

narrative_blocks.header: His book of liquor laws did not sell
narrative_blocks.body: In 1883 Faxon published Quincy Under the Ban of Prohibition, collecting every law against gaming, Sabbath-breaking and drunkenness. Four years earlier he had hosted and paid for a Boston meeting open only to temperance Republicans.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave Quincy the park named for him
narrative_blocks.body: The ground was the town's South Commons until 1818, and his father Job Faxon bought much of it. Faxon gave thirty-seven acres to the city in 1885 and his son added twenty more in 1935. He also paid for every Quincy Sunday school Christmas.

cross_connections.display_label: , his brother-in-law, chaired the Academy boarding in a Faxon building
carried the same Massachusetts temperance cause around the world

notable.notable_blurb: Quincy's temperance millionaire

landmarks.landmark_blurb: He gave the city the first thirty-seven acres in 1885

bio.bio_blurb: President of the Mount Wollaston Bank

narrative_blocks.header: The trust company owned the middle of Quincy
narrative_blocks.body: Faxon was president of the Mount Wollaston Bank. By the 1920s the Faxon Trust Company was the largest property owner in the city, holding a good share of the retail blocks and a great deal of the housing.

narrative_blocks.header: His buildings turned up at a flea market
narrative_blocks.body: Arnold Almquist Jr. bought two boxes of black-and-white construction photographs at a New Hampshire flea market, recognised the Faxon name and gave them to the Thomas Crane Public Library. Most were shot by the H. A. Frink Company.

narrative_blocks.header: He built a house and gave it away
narrative_blocks.body: Faxon put up a house on Dixwell Avenue in 1932 and handed it to the United First Parish Church two years later. It served as the parsonage for more than sixty years.

narrative_blocks.header: He finished his father's park in 1935
narrative_blocks.body: Henry Hardwick Faxon gave Quincy thirty-seven acres in 1885. His son added twenty more in 1935, and sat on the church music committee at the 250th anniversary while his father sat on finance.

cross_connections.display_label: , his uncle by marriage, held the Mount Wollaston presidency first

landmarks.landmark_blurb: He added twenty acres to his father’s gift in 1935

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote the family down herself
narrative_blocks.body: Bessie Faxon published Family, Then and Now, an account of the Quincy generations she had married into — Faxons who had been buying Braintree land since Thomas Faxon came over from England in 1647.

narrative_blocks.header: He served in both world wars
narrative_blocks.body: Faxon went to the first war as a young man and to the second as a major, operating in North Africa and then in Italy. He came home to the Cushing V.A. Hospital at Framingham.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught surgery at three medical schools
narrative_blocks.body: Faxon held a professorship of surgery at Tufts and sat on the faculties of Harvard and Boston University as well, while running the surgical service at the Boston V.A. until he retired in 1966.

narrative_blocks.header: He was named for the tavern-buyer
narrative_blocks.body: The surgeon took his name from his grandfather, the Quincy millionaire who bought the Hancock Tavern in order to close it. Two generations on, the name belonged to a man who ran a hospital surgical service.

narrative_blocks.header: The freshman eleven elected him captain
narrative_blocks.body: Faxon came to Harvard from Milton Academy, where he had played football three seasons and captained two of them. In October 1917 the class of 1921 made him captain. He was eighteen, six foot one, and played left tackle.

narrative_blocks.header: He practised law for sixty-seven years
narrative_blocks.body: Bannister was senior partner of Bannister, Still, Holloway and Krause in New York and chairman of the board of the G. R. Kinney Company. He was still working when he died at ninety-two.

narrative_blocks.header: Schooled in England, France and Germany
narrative_blocks.body: Bannister was educated across three European countries before he entered Harvard with the class of 1909. He took his degree from Harvard Law School in 1911 and was admitted the same year.

narrative_blocks.header: Squirrel Island was the home she claimed
narrative_blocks.body: Ruth summered on Squirrel Island in Maine every year of her life and called it home rather than Montclair. In 2001 she moved to Boothbay Harbor on the mainland to be nearer to it.

narrative_blocks.header: She ran a power boat called Tabasco
narrative_blocks.body: Ruth sailed, and spent long hours besides in a power boat she named Tabasco. On the island she served for years on the Squirrel Island Association and the Chapel Committee.

narrative_blocks.header: Colby Junior College, then a medical office
narrative_blocks.body: Ruth went through the Montclair schools and on to Colby Junior College in New Hampshire, then worked as a medical secretary in Montclair. She never married.

narrative_blocks.header: He was wearing a wounded man’s vest
narrative_blocks.body: Wales had left the steel vest his father gave him back in Washington. A brother officer, already hit, pressed his own on him before Wales went forward at Antietam on September 17, 1862.

narrative_blocks.header: He forgot he had the armor on
narrative_blocks.body: A bullet struck just below the heart and knocked him down. He walked back, told General Ferrero "I am hit, sir," and sat to check the damage — and only on reaching for his cartridge-box belt realised what he had on.

narrative_blocks.header: It struck the weakest spot on the plate
narrative_blocks.body: It landed where four plates met, held to each other by rivets alone. The dent cut through vest, shirt and undershirt into the flesh; for a fortnight Wales could not draw a long breath.

narrative_blocks.header: Brave men wore it and kept quiet
narrative_blocks.body: Officers thought it wrong to be better protected than their men. "Two of as brave officers as I ever knew wore it," Wales wrote — his colonel, and his major, killed when a bullet grazed the bottom edge of the vest and went through him.

narrative_blocks.header: He came out of hospital to fight
narrative_blocks.body: Wales had been sick in the days before Antietam. He rejoined the 35th Massachusetts carrying an Enfield rifle and saying he wanted to get a lick at the rebs. He was nineteen.

narrative_blocks.header: Taken prisoner, exchanged, made major
narrative_blocks.body: Confederates captured Wales near White Sulphur Springs in November 1862. He was paroled and back on duty by February, commissioned major that April, and brevetted twice in 1865 for commanding the regiment at the siege of Knoxville.

narrative_blocks.header: The vest came from the Arctic boot man
narrative_blocks.body: His father Thomas Crane Wales built a Boston fortune in rubber boots, having patented a lined waterproof winter boot he called the Arctic. It was that father who handed his son a steel vest on the way to the war.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father was sixty-three at her birth
narrative_blocks.body: Col. Nathaniel Wales buried his first wife in 1901, married Ellen Lunt Munroe in 1904, and had this one daughter in 1906. Jerry outlived him by eighty-nine years and died at a hundred and six.

narrative_blocks.header: Six-oar in the Yale eight at Paris
narrative_blocks.body: Kingsbury rowed the six seat when Yale beat the Navy crew that had won in 1920, then went to Paris and won the Olympic eights on the Seine in July 1924.

narrative_blocks.header: Benjamin Spock was in the same boat
narrative_blocks.body: The crew that won at Paris carried J. Stillman Rockefeller at four, who later ran what became Citibank and lived to a hundred and two, and at seven Benjamin Spock, who got aboard as a last-minute substitute.

narrative_blocks.header: He rowed against Cambridge for Oxford
narrative_blocks.body: Kingsbury went from Yale to The Queen's College, Oxford, and took the six seat again for the Oxford crew in the 79th Boat Race in 1927.

narrative_blocks.header: Engineering first, then a life in schools
narrative_blocks.body: Kingsbury tried civil engineering and left it. He spent the rest of his working life as a teacher, a rowing coach and finally a headmaster.

narrative_blocks.header: Adopted, and given his grandfather’s name
narrative_blocks.body: Ox and Jerry Kingsbury adopted a boy in 1940 and named him for her father, the Antietam colonel. He is buried on the same Maine island she is.

narrative_blocks.header: A former Presiding Bishop blessed it
narrative_blocks.body: Nat married Sylvia Macy Thorndike at Emmanuel Episcopal Church in Boston on December 30, 1964. Henry Knox Sherrill, lately head of the Episcopal Church in America, gave the benediction, and Sylvia wore the veil of Nat's grandmother.

narrative_blocks.header: He was on active duty at Newport
narrative_blocks.body: Nat came out of the Brooks School at North Andover and took his Yale degree in 1963. He married the next year as a lieutenant junior grade in the Naval Reserve, stationed at Newport.

narrative_blocks.header: The family summered out in Penobscot Bay
narrative_blocks.body: Ox and Jerry Kingsbury kept houses at North Andover and on North Haven in Maine. Both Jerry and Nat were buried out in that bay rather than on the mainland.

narrative_blocks.header: She came out in Boston in 1962
narrative_blocks.body: Sylvia Thorndike was presented at the Boston Cotillion and the Salem Debutante Assembly in 1962, while still at Stephens College. Her mother, Lucy Saltonstall Rantoul Thorndike, had died before the wedding two years later.

bio.bio_blurb: President of Quincy Mutual Fire Insurance

narrative_blocks.header: He learned bookbinding and sold insurance
narrative_blocks.body: Howland picked up his father's bookbinder's trade while still at school, then clerked in the Registry of Deeds. His father had gone over to insurance by then, and one of the companies he represented was the Quincy Mutual.

narrative_blocks.header: Secretary for twenty-four years, then president
narrative_blocks.body: Howland adjusted losses in his first year at Quincy Mutual and rose to adjuster, then assistant secretary. He was installed as secretary on April 14, 1861, kept it twenty-four years, and was made president and treasurer in 1884.

narrative_blocks.header: He chaired half the boards in Quincy
narrative_blocks.body: Howland ran the Mount Wollaston National Bank from 1893, was a trustee of the Quincy Savings Bank, directed the Hingham Cordage and Lawrence Duck companies, and was treasurer of the Citizens' Gas Light Company he had helped found.

narrative_blocks.header: His first wife died at twenty-six
narrative_blocks.body: Abbie Flint Munroe married Howland in December 1860. Their daughter was born and died on one day in April 1864, and Abbie was dead by July 1866. He married Helen M. Moore of Duxbury in 1871.

narrative_blocks.header: He came down from a Mayflower signer
narrative_blocks.body: Howland stood in the seventh generation from John Howland, whose name is the thirteenth of the forty-one on the compact signed in the Mayflower's cabin on November 21, 1620.

narrative_blocks.header: Both her husbands descended from Thomas Hooker
narrative_blocks.body: Robert Thaxter Bicknell and Dr. Joseph Hawley Dorr were both born in 1807 and both came down from Sarah Hooker Wilson — Bicknell six generations through the Torreys, Dorr five through the Rawsons. She married them eighteen years apart.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at twenty-eight with four children
narrative_blocks.body: Bicknell died at Philadelphia in May 1839; the youngest of the four was two. Marinda married Dorr in January 1847, and they had no children of their own. She outlived him by thirty-four years.

narrative_blocks.header: The Utica teachers’ special left the rails
narrative_blocks.body: An excursion train carrying Utica's schoolteachers ran onto defective track near Martins Creek and derailed. Eleven were lost. Bicknell, the road’s tourist agent, was one of four Pennsylvania men who died alongside seven teachers.

narrative_blocks.header: Passengers climbed out through the windows
narrative_blocks.body: Those who could pulled themselves up the sides of the cars to reach the windows. One woman ran an eighth of a mile across a ploughed field. Fifty of the teachers were hurt, and the investigation laid the wreck to the track.

narrative_blocks.header: The third Robert Thaxter Bicknell running
narrative_blocks.body: His great-grandfather carried the name to Philadelphia and died there in 1839, his father was born with it in 1863, and he got it in 1905. Thaxter came out of the Weymouth Bicknells, three generations before any of them.

narrative_blocks.header: One headstone, front and back
narrative_blocks.body: Bicknell served as a sergeant first class through the second war and again in Korea. He and Maxine lie together at Golden Gate National Cemetery under a single stone — his name on the front, hers on the back.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a Bicknell widow with four children
narrative_blocks.body: Robert Thaxter Bicknell died at Philadelphia in 1839 leaving Marinda with four children under nine. Dorr married her, raised them, and died himself in 1855. Her stone calls her widow of one man and relict of the other.

narrative_blocks.header: Hawley came down from a Roxbury grandmother
narrative_blocks.body: The name reached him through his great-grandfather Rev. Joseph Dorr of Mendon, whose mother was Elizabeth Hawley. His stepson Charles Peter Bicknell passed the whole of it to a son in 1857.

narrative_blocks.header: Eleven children on the Canadian side
narrative_blocks.body: Levi was born at Cornwall in Upper Canada, married Ann Maria Putnam there at nineteen, and they raised eleven children in Ontario. His grandfather Jonathan had never left Abington.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven of their eleven got classical names
narrative_blocks.body: Nehemiah and Hannah named the first two for themselves, then reached for Rome and Greece: Venilia, Rectus, Vesta, Dares, Solon, Orestes and Lysander. The fashion was new in the young republic and they took it further than most.

narrative_blocks.header: She bore eleven over twenty-five years
narrative_blocks.body: Hannah Shaw married Nehemiah Richards at Abington in 1782 and had children from 1783 to 1808. She buried Vesta at three and outlived her husband by ten years, dying at Cummington at eighty-five.

narrative_blocks.header: His family Bible ended up in Iowa
narrative_blocks.body: Dares Richards kept the births, marriages and deaths in the family register of his Bible. The pages are now held by the C. G. Brisee Genealogy Library at Irwin, Iowa, four generations and fourteen hundred miles from Cummington.

narrative_blocks.header: She married on Christmas Day at sixteen
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah Nash was born at Abington in March 1719 and married James Torrey on December 25, 1735. She bore ten children in twenty-one years and was widowed at thirty-seven.

narrative_blocks.header: He was thirty-five and she eighteen
narrative_blocks.body: Micajah Torrey married Lucy Lothrop of Norwich in June 1784. Their first daughter, Wealthy, was born that same year in Bozrah, and the family stayed in Connecticut.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight children, all born at Exeter
narrative_blocks.body: Lucinda Hyde came up from Connecticut as a child and married John Sutherland at Otsego in 1824. Every one of their eight was born at Exeter. She buried John at seven in 1841 and named the next son John W. four years later.

naming_inspiration.note: Wealthy Torrey

narrative_blocks.header: He clubbed his musket at Bunker Hill
narrative_blocks.body: John Torrey fought on Bunker Hill and, when the ammunition ran out, turned his gun around and used the butt of it like the men beside him. Abigail drew a widow's pension on that service after he died.

narrative_blocks.header: No stone marks the orchard grave
narrative_blocks.body: John, Abigail and their son William were buried in an orchard on a farm two miles south of Stafford village in Genesee County. The family Bible kept the record; the ground never got a marker.

bio.bio_blurb: Lebanon man who went to New Lebanon

narrative_blocks.header: He named a son John Independence
narrative_blocks.body: Jesse left Lebanon in Connecticut for New Lebanon in New York and died there in 1840. Jerusha Davidson gave him five children and Azuba West two more, the elder of whom he called John Independence Torrey.

naming_inspiration.note: William Torrey

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve children, three wives, one letter
narrative_blocks.body: Asenath, Asa and Alonzo came from Sally Annis; Aurelia, Albert and Almon from Amanda Judd; Amanda, Andre, Alfred, Allen, Alvin and Adora from Melissa Cooley. Jesse buried two wives and never once broke the pattern.

narrative_blocks.header: He piped on Boston Common for a crowd
narrative_blocks.body: As a young man Jesse played the bagpipe, and he would set up on Boston Common until a crowd had gathered around him. Then he sold them his merchandise.

narrative_blocks.header: They blazed a road to two cabins
narrative_blocks.body: Jesse, his sons and two neighbours cut a path through the woods from the Thread flouring mills, marking the trees as they went, and reached the Torrey settlement on October 19, 1833. Flint had two log houses then. He was past fifty.

narrative_blocks.header: A Methodist, an abolitionist, a teetotaller
narrative_blocks.body: Jesse gave eighty acres apiece to Asa and Alonzo and took the rest of the section himself. He was an anti-slavery man before it was safe to be one in that county, and he and four of his sons built the old Torrey church.

narrative_blocks.header: The township school stood on his land
narrative_blocks.body: Flint Township raised its first schoolhouse in 1878 on the bank of Swartz Creek, on ground belonging to Jesse Torrey. The Torreys had taken four hundred acres of section twenty-four and were only the second family in the township.

cross_connections.display_label: came out of Connecticut to Michigan too, and raised eight there

narrative_blocks.header: His cabin had two roofs, not one
narrative_blocks.body: Asa's log house had a single shake roof and a floor of split basswood. Alonzo built his with two roofs of white ash shingles, and when it was done he went back to Shelby in New York and fetched a wife to live in it.

narrative_blocks.header: He could bind two bundles in the air
narrative_blocks.body: Alonzo could bind a bundle of wheat, throw it up, and bind a second before the first came down. He and Asa had built threshing machines together at Middleport before either of them went west.

narrative_blocks.header: He invited his sixth cousin, the president
narrative_blocks.body: Both men came down from William Torrey of Weymouth, dead in 1690 — the judge through his son Micajah, Taft through his son Angel, seven generations each. For the thirteenth reunion he wrote and asked him. Taft thanked him and declined.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife was elected to run the reunions
narrative_blocks.body: In 1910 Mrs. J. M. Torrey was voted president of the Torrey family reunions. The judge had spent years getting relatives to Flint for them, and told the Flint Journal how his grandfather had reached the place in 1833.

narrative_blocks.header: She opened her house when school burned
narrative_blocks.body: The log schoolhouse in the Torrey settlement burned down, so Lydia took the scholars into her own rooms and taught them there for three months, then four months more once the frame school was up. She and Alonzo had no children.

narrative_blocks.header: Children left her door with red apples
narrative_blocks.body: Lydia LeValley came out from Shelby in 1836 with a good education and a cheerful temper, and the settlement remembered her sending its children home with a basket of apples and an instruction to be good.

narrative_blocks.header: Ontario to Buffalo, a hundred and four years
narrative_blocks.body: Jared King was born at Brussels in Ontario in October 1867, married Ina Torrey at Flint in 1904, and died at Buffalo in April 1972. He outlived her by twenty-four years.

narrative_blocks.header: She came from New York and stayed
narrative_blocks.body: Ermina Culver came to Flint from New York as a young woman and spent thirty years there. She died of dropsy in October 1907 at a house on Walker street, leaving a daughter in the city and a sister at Bloomingdale.

narrative_blocks.header: She buried two sons in the same year
narrative_blocks.body: Kenneth Pound died at Grand Blanc in August 1916, eighteen years old; Hugh Max died the same year at four. Lottie had eight children between 1898 and 1912 and lost four of them.

narrative_blocks.header: Killed two days before the armistice
narrative_blocks.body: Bernhardt was a rifleman with G Company, 3rd Battalion, 1st Marines. An explosive device killed him in North Korea on July 25, 1953. The armistice was signed on the twenty-seventh.

narrative_blocks.header: He married on his twenty-first birthday
narrative_blocks.body: Ralph Bernhardt was born on April 30, 1928 and married Janet Kathryn Moher on April 30, 1949. He was dead in Korea four years later, and Janet afterwards married his older brother Raymond.

narrative_blocks.header: At sixteen he canvassed the whole town
narrative_blocks.body: Through the winter of 1803 Jesse Torrey went door to door in New Lebanon with a plan for a free lending library open to every youth between twelve and twenty-one, girls as well as boys. By spring it was running out of his own house.

narrative_blocks.header: He met a coffle on a Washington street
narrative_blocks.body: On December 4, 1815 a boy called out that the Georgia men were going by with a drove chained two and two. Torrey followed and asked a driver where they were bound — Georgia, and had they not enough such people yet? Not quite enough.

narrative_blocks.header: A woman jumped from an F Street garret
narrative_blocks.body: A woman leapt from the third storey of an F Street tavern rather than be carried to Georgia. Torrey got the landlord's leave to see her: both arms broken, her back shattered. They had taken her and two children and left the husband unsold.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave Congress the kidnappers by name
narrative_blocks.body: Torrey swore a statement to John Randolph's committee on the slave traffic in April 1816, naming William Thompson, Bennett Smith and James D. Bennett, and the free people of Delaware and Maryland they had seized and sold south.

narrative_blocks.header: He interviewed free Black families at home
narrative_blocks.body: Torrey went into the houses of free Black Washingtonians and found them living in fear of being seized and sold. What he collected became A Portraiture of Domestic Slavery in 1817, and an expanded American Slave Trade in London after.

narrative_blocks.header: Two presidents heard him out and declined
narrative_blocks.body: A visit to the Madisons turned into an argument over slavery; Torrey wrote to apologise and was told they had taken no notice. At Monticello in 1815 he asked Jefferson to back a science of living bodies. Jefferson declined.

narrative_blocks.header: Tax the liquor, he said, and buy books
narrative_blocks.body: Torrey proposed funding free public libraries out of a tax on spirits. A Pleasing Companion for Little Girls and Boys ran to twenty-five editions and his Moral Instructor to ten, and in 1829 he patented a bookbinding machine.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a girl from his uncle’s settlement
narrative_blocks.body: Nancy Dow was born at Bethany in Genesee County, where his uncle John Torrey had taken the family after the Revolution. She married Royal in 1814, bore eight children, and died at Angels Camp in the California gold country at eighty-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: From Montezuma to the California legislature
narrative_blocks.body: Mark Sibley Torrey went west with the family and sat in the California State Legislature in 1885. His will, proved in 1898, named his brothers George and Frank, his sister Harriet Wood and a niece.

bio.bio_blurb: Governor, senator, and Central Pacific president

narrative_blocks.header: He served the baby under a silver cover
narrative_blocks.body: Eighteen childless years ended in May 1868. At a Sacramento dinner for close friends Stanford rose to introduce someone, a covered platter was set in the middle of the table, and the lid came off on the baby lying in blossoms.

narrative_blocks.header: Jane saw him kneel for the first time
narrative_blocks.body: Jane had fallen off the veranda into a flowering bush in her last trimester, and the birth was not expected to go well. She said afterwards it was the first time she had ever seen her husband kneel to pray.

narrative_blocks.header: Four hundred feet of track to the stables
narrative_blocks.body: Stanford bought the Palo Alto land in 1876 to give his son the country boyhood he had had in New York. The boy got a pony, a shooting range, a creek to fish, and a working train that ran from the house down to the stables.

narrative_blocks.header: He drove the last spike at Promontory
narrative_blocks.body: Stanford and three other Sacramento merchants incorporated the Central Pacific in June 1861 and he was elected its president. On May 10, 1869 he swung at the ceremonial spike joining his track to the Union Pacific at Promontory.

narrative_blocks.header: He warned against the men he was hiring
narrative_blocks.body: In a message to the legislature in January 1862 Stanford called Chinese immigration the dregs of Asia and urged that it be checked. His own Central Pacific was importing Chinese labourers to build the road, and it cost him support.

narrative_blocks.header: The children of California, he told her
narrative_blocks.body: That is what he said to Jane after Florence. They signed the Founding Grant the following year for a university named after the boy, open to women and to men and tied to no church, and its first student was Herbert Hoover.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten more years was all he asked for
narrative_blocks.body: Stanford was dying of locomotor ataxia and only learned it near the end. Help me to last ten years more to carry out my plans, he told a physician. He went to bed at Palo Alto in June 1893 and was found dead at midnight, his face at rest.

narrative_blocks.header: Albany thought she had been deserted
narrative_blocks.body: Leland sailed for California in 1852 and Jane stayed in Albany to nurse her dying father. They were apart three years and the town talked. Forty years on, after he died, she burned every letter they had exchanged rather than have them read.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept the university on her housekeeping
narrative_blocks.body: When Leland died in 1893 the estate froze and the federal government sued it for Central Pacific debt. Jane paid the university out of the allowance meant for running her household until probate cleared five years later.

narrative_blocks.header: She sold her jewels to buy books
narrative_blocks.body: Having failed to sell them in London at the Diamond Jubilee, Jane gave the trustees leave in February 1905 to sell her jewels and put the proceeds into a fund for the library. Books are still bought from it.

narrative_blocks.header: She capped the women at five hundred
narrative_blocks.body: Women had risen from a quarter of the students to two in five by 1899. Jane amended the Founding Grant to cap them at five hundred, fearing that a school full of women would keep men away and make a poor memorial to her son.

narrative_blocks.header: She died believing she had been poisoned
narrative_blocks.body: In January 1905 a glass of water at her San Francisco house was found to hold strychnine. She left for Hawaii and died at Honolulu six weeks later. Traces turned up in her bicarbonate and in her stomach; the cause was never settled.

narrative_blocks.header: She made the president let a professor go
narrative_blocks.body: Jane wanted Edward Ross out of the sociology chair for his pro-labour and anti-Japanese politics, and David Starr Jordan dismissed him in 1900. The fight over who may tell a professor what to think helped bring American tenure into being.

narrative_blocks.header: A watch from Leland, New Year's Day 1868
narrative_blocks.body: Leland bought a gold Patek Philippe in San Francisco in October 1867 and gave it to Jane on New Year's Day, engraved J. Lathrop Stanford from Leland. Their only child, Leland Jr., was born that May.
