narrative_blocks.header: At nine he made them change his name
narrative_blocks.body: He had been christened Leland DeWitt for his father's younger brother. At nine he found out he was not legally a junior, said he wanted his father's name exactly, and got it.

narrative_blocks.header: His tutor remembered the pony and the dogs
narrative_blocks.body: Herbert Nash wrote that the boy rode the farm with the dogs barking at his heels, spent whole days in the fields among the labourers, and thought a picnic in the redwoods the best thing there was. He did not prefer his grammar to his gun.

narrative_blocks.header: He was building a museum of his own
narrative_blocks.body: He filled a room on the third floor of the San Francisco house with what he brought home, bought coins and Egyptian bronzes on a strict allowance, and handed the fakes back to the dealers. Nash wrote the guide to it after he died.

narrative_blocks.header: He sat in his mother’s darkened room
narrative_blocks.body: Jane's headaches kept her in the dark for days at a stretch, and the boy would come in from sightseeing and tell her everything he had seen. In Rome he climbed the Holy Stairs on his knees, saying a prayer for her on every step.

narrative_blocks.header: At fifteen he was worried about them both
narrative_blocks.body: Writing to an aunt from the Germanic in June 1883: Papa has not improved as much as we hoped for, and Mama has only been to the table twice. His father was nearly sixty and his mother fifty-four. He was dead before either of them.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote to Wilsie down the block
narrative_blocks.body: A handicapped boy on Nob Hill got letters in careful schoolboy cursive — snowballing in the Sierras till their fingers went numb, and later an apology from a moving train because the car was going much faster now, so excuse the shakeness.

narrative_blocks.header: Florence, and a year later the Grant
narrative_blocks.body: Typhoid took him at Athens in the snow and he was carried on to Naples, Rome and Florence, where straw was spread in the street to quiet it. A year later his parents signed the Grant. The seal still reads Leland Stanford Junior University.

cross_connections.display_label: tutored him three years and wrote his life after Florence

narrative_blocks.header: His first wife died at twenty-five
narrative_blocks.body: Merritt married Mary Ann Todd in May 1821. She died in March 1828, twenty-five years old, and he married Grace Fitch that September. He stayed in North Haven the whole of his ninety-two years.

narrative_blocks.header: His second family went into the Hoadleys
narrative_blocks.body: Matilda Barnes died in November 1847, a year after the wedding. Fitch married again, and the daughter of that marriage, Mary Bentley Fitch, married Lemuel Goodrich Hoadley in 1878 — which is why the Hoadley genealogy carries him.

narrative_blocks.header: Four years old in the August of 1884
narrative_blocks.body: Myra McQueen was born at New Haven in April 1880 and buried there the same year she died, 15 August 1884. Her brother Arthur, six years older, lived to seventy-nine.

narrative_blocks.header: He was postmaster of Guilford in 1911
narrative_blocks.body: His brother-in-law's obituary that December names L. O. — Rhoda's brother — as the sitting postmaster of Guilford. He was sixty-seven, and outlived his sister by twelve years.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept the store until he was eighty-five
narrative_blocks.body: Cruttenden ran the general store at East River for many years and gave it up only a year before he died, at eighty-six, of heart trouble. He was senior deacon of the Third Congregational Church at Guilford.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty-two years, and no death in the house
narrative_blocks.body: He married Rhoda Chittenden of North Guilford in May 1849. When he died in December 1911 the papers noted that in sixty-two years of married life his was the first death to occur in the family. Three sons survived him.

narrative_blocks.header: The name lost a letter in one generation
narrative_blocks.body: His grandfather and father spelled it Cruttenden. Robert Elton was registered a Crittenden, and so was one of his daughters — the other kept the older spelling.

narrative_blocks.header: Both sisters ended in the same Florida town
narrative_blocks.body: Ethel was widowed at twenty-six when John Rapsey died in 1932, and married Elmer Shields the next year. She died at Belleview in Florida in 2001; Ruth had died in the same town four years before.

naming_inspiration.description: Named for her paternal grandmother Hannah Pierpont Brockett of North Haven.

cross_connections.display_label: , her grandmother, was the Hannah she was named for
was the father of the man his daughter Mary married in 1896

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband was her father's second cousin
narrative_blocks.body: Alice May Stiles and Ernest Stiles Vinton both descended from Capt. Isaac Clark Stiles of North Haven, she through his son Isaac and he through his son Zophar. They married about 1915.

narrative_blocks.header: She married at about thirty-seven
narrative_blocks.body: Alice was born in March 1878 and married about 1915; Ernest was six years the elder. Neither had married before, and no children are recorded.

bio.bio_blurb: Forest geneticist; N.C. State faculty senate chairman

narrative_blocks.header: Nineteen years in the Forest Service first
narrative_blocks.body: He joined the U.S. Forest Service as a junior forester in Michigan in 1935 and worked forest genetics in Connecticut and then California. He did not take a full professorship until 1963, at fifty-one.

narrative_blocks.header: He studied how wind bends a growing pine
narrative_blocks.body: Duffield's two standing questions were the wind-induced movement of conifer stems and what it does to their growth, and stock-scion relationships in conifers. He had fifty-six papers in print.

narrative_blocks.header: The senate he chaired wrote to the governor
narrative_blocks.body: Six days after Martin Luther King was killed, the North Carolina State faculty senate passed a resolution backing the governor in the cause of social and economic justice. Duffield, its chairman, sent it to Raleigh.

narrative_blocks.header: He came home comparing Yugoslavs to Calhoun
narrative_blocks.body: After nine months lecturing at Ljubljana as a Fulbright professor, he told reporters that some Yugoslavs were every bit as strong for states rights as anyone in American politics, and named Calhoun and Byrd.

narrative_blocks.header: He thought wilderness an illusion
narrative_blocks.body: Duffield held that the public had learned to look at forests and forgotten that houses and paper come out of them. There was no wilderness left, he said, and no area of complete solitude.

narrative_blocks.header: Second lieutenant to major in four years
narrative_blocks.body: He left forest genetics for the Army in 1942 and served in North Africa and Italy with a quartermaster truck regiment, rising from second lieutenant to major before his discharge in 1946.

cross_connections.display_label: had the region replanting seedlings before he came to breed them

notable.notable_blurb: Forest geneticist; N.C. State faculty senate chairman

military_service.notes: North Africa and Italy, 1942-1946.

narrative_blocks.header: She went to Ljubljana with him at fifty-three
narrative_blocks.body: Marjorie Duffield went to Yugoslavia with her husband for the nine months of his 1968 Fulbright year. She was fifty-three; their three children were grown, two of them students at Washington.

narrative_blocks.header: They were married sixty-six years
narrative_blocks.body: Marjorie Olney of Bonanza, Oregon married John Warren Duffield in January 1939. She died in February 2005 and he followed her seventeen months later.

narrative_blocks.header: He was adopted twelve years after Eva
narrative_blocks.body: Dorr and Emma Torrey of Flint had a daughter, Eva May, born in 1880. Ellis came to them by adoption twelve years later, and was raised as their son.

narrative_blocks.header: Two deaths brought him the family firm
narrative_blocks.body: His brother Edward had been trained to take their father's place and was killed on a railway in 1913. When George was killed in a car in 1927, months after their father died, Frank took the directorship.

narrative_blocks.header: He began in electricity, not natural history
narrative_blocks.body: Out of Princeton he did graduate work in electricity, tested for General Electric at Schenectady, supervised installations in Canada for two years, and spent a year with a Georgia power company.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave the firm to a university
narrative_blocks.body: At his suggestion the University of Rochester took over Ward's Natural Science Establishment in 1928 and ran it as a non-profit until 1940, when it was sold back to the family.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty years a volunteer fireman
narrative_blocks.body: Albert Seymour, called Bubs, volunteered with the Brighton Fire Department for more than thirty years and belonged to the Vanderbilt Marsh Club. He gardened, fished and hunted.

narrative_blocks.header: He outlived Abigail by thirteen years
narrative_blocks.body: Abigail Adams Seymour died in 2006, and his brother Morton before her. He kept to the Canandaigua Lake place until his own death in May 2019.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father ran to Bunker Hill at fourteen
narrative_blocks.body: John Corbett ran from Milford to the Continental Army at fourteen and fought at Bunker Hill. Taken prisoner with Jonathan Stearns, he got away, was lost in the woods for days, and killed an animal and ate it raw before he turned for home.

narrative_blocks.header: She married the bass-viol player at nineteen
narrative_blocks.body: Lovice Corbett married Thomas Whittemore at Milford in September 1821, three months after his ordination. She was nineteen, they had eight children, and she outlived him by twenty-one years.

narrative_blocks.header: The town took the name of his works
narrative_blocks.body: He began making axes at South Canton on the Farmington River in 1826, and the place was renamed Collinsville for him. Water power turned the grindstones, and his axes left Connecticut already sharp enough to use out of the box.

narrative_blocks.header: He hired Root, and the axes got faster
narrative_blocks.body: About 1827 his craftsman Charles Morgan mapped every step of making an axe and gave each step to a separate man. In 1832 Collins took on Elisha K. Root, twenty-four years old, who remade both the quality and the speed of the work.

narrative_blocks.header: A quarter of a million axes a year
narrative_blocks.body: By 1835 the works were turning out a quarter of a million axes a year, most of them sold to cotton plantations on the expanding frontier of slavery. The machetes went to Central and South America, and the name was known there for a century.

narrative_blocks.header: The grindstones and the cleared acres
narrative_blocks.body: Silicosis was common among the men at the Connecticut grindstones. In western Tennessee an enslaved man with a sharp axe could clear about four acres of forest in a year, and one county there had cleared sixty-five thousand by 1860.

narrative_blocks.header: Rather not make a cent, he said
narrative_blocks.body: He would rather not make one cent, he said, than have men go away worse than they came. He cut working hours where he could, built a library, a school and a chapel, and paid for many of the houses that still make up Collinsville.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought the burying ground for one man
narrative_blocks.body: In 1832 an employee named Franklin Gordon died with nowhere in the village to be put, so Collins bought the land. It became the Collinsville Cemetery, and he lies in it himself at Row B Lower.

narrative_blocks.header: Grindstones turn up all over Canton
narrative_blocks.body: The stones started near six feet across and weighing a ton, and were thrown out at about a foot. Workers carried them home for foundations, walkways and garden steps, and a bench at his own grave is cut from one of them.

cross_connections.display_label: wrote the standard history of American machine tools, and it runs through his axe shop

bio.bio_blurb: Founder of the Collins Company axe works

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived him by eighteen years
narrative_blocks.body: She was born the same year as her husband and survived him by eighteen. She died in May 1889 at eighty-six or eighty-seven, and was buried beside him in the ground he had bought for the village.

narrative_blocks.header: He left Princeton for the flying boats
narrative_blocks.body: He read engineering at Princeton and went out at the end of his junior year for aeronautical engineering at New York University and flight training. It put him on the Pan American Clippers as a flight engineer.

narrative_blocks.header: A commission in Naval Air Transport
narrative_blocks.body: The war found him already flying the Atlantic for Pan American, out to Africa, to Ireland and to France. He took a commission in the Naval Air Transport Service and went on flying.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-three years at Curtiss-Wright
narrative_blocks.body: He worked at Republic and at Fairchild, then went to Curtiss-Wright, where he spent twenty-three years as chief dynamics engineer. He finished at the FAA Technical Center, trying new navigational aids and cockpit instruments.

narrative_blocks.header: Prices second only to Brewster’s
narrative_blocks.body: He succeeded his father in the spring and axle works, enlarged it into carriage building, and in 1862 began making light carriages of a superior character. Only the Brewsters of New York commanded higher prices.

narrative_blocks.header: His partner was his wife’s brother
narrative_blocks.body: He married Mary A. Tuttle, a daughter of Abiud Tuttle, in April 1850. Her brother Milo D. Tuttle was his partner for the length of the business, and Brockett & Tuttle kept repositories through the North and West.

narrative_blocks.header: He preferred home to public affairs
narrative_blocks.body: He was a selectman of Hamden, a New Haven county commissioner and a director of the county bank, but of a retiring disposition, preferring the quiet of home to the strife of public affairs. He never took a conspicuous part in them.

narrative_blocks.header: Failing health sent him out to Milford
narrative_blocks.body: Three years before the end his health gave way and he moved to Milford, where he lived in comparative retirement. He died there on the last day of October 1880, a member of Calvary Church, and the Iowa papers carried the news.

cross_connections.display_label: ran Henry Hooker & Co., the other great New Haven carriage house

career.organization: Brockett & Tuttle, carriage manufacturers, New Haven

narrative_blocks.header: Philadelphia knew him for eyes first
narrative_blocks.body: Conrad Berens was a well-known ophthalmologist of Philadelphia, living at Bala, and he married Mary Elizabeth Brockett of Mount Carmel in October 1885. The son who carried his name took the same specialty to New York.

notable.notable_blurb: One of the world’s leading ophthalmologists

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty years at the Eye and Ear
narrative_blocks.body: He came to the New York Eye and Ear Infirmary as a house-surgeon in 1913 and never left it, ending as its advisory attending surgeon and consulting pathologist. He was also for years the ophthalmic surgeon at Sing Sing Prison.

narrative_blocks.header: Sterile gloves and the first orthoptic course
narrative_blocks.body: His clinic became one of the most progressive in New York: general medical surveys, bacteriological tests before operating, sterile gloves in the theatre, sutures to close surgical wounds, and the first course in orthoptic training.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped build aviation medicine
narrative_blocks.body: He went to France in the First World War with the Army Medical Corps and served there with Colonel Wilmer. He was one of the founders of the Research Laboratories for Aviation, which grew into the Army’s School of Aviation Medicine.

narrative_blocks.header: Almost single-handed, a research association
narrative_blocks.body: He organized the Association for Research in Ophthalmology very nearly by himself and lived to see it among the largest of its kind anywhere. With Harry Gradle and Moacyr Alvaro he founded the Pan-American Association of Ophthalmology.

narrative_blocks.header: His textbook went round the world
narrative_blocks.body: The Eye and its Diseases, which he edited, came out in 1936, again in 1949 and in Spanish in 1954, and ophthalmologists everywhere used it. He was joint author of six other textbooks and wrote papers past counting.

narrative_blocks.header: The Seeing Eye and the blind
narrative_blocks.body: He sat on the boards of The Seeing Eye, the New York Association for the Blind and the National Society for the Prevention of Blindness, and was vice-president of the international association of the same name.

narrative_blocks.header: Two marriages, and Center Island at the end
narrative_blocks.body: He married Katharine Simpson in 1916; their son Richard was born that September and she died in November at twenty-three. He married Katherine Andrea Parker in 1923, and died at his house on Center Island in March 1963.

cross_connections.display_label: was the Infirmary’s ear surgeon through the years he came up in eyes
lost her sight to retinitis pigmentosa and still trekked the Himalayas

bio.title: Dr.
bio.bio_blurb: One of the world’s leading ophthalmologists

career.organization: New York University Postgraduate Medical School
New York Eye and Ear Infirmary

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty years of school concerts at Haverford
narrative_blocks.body: For more than twenty years she taught elementary music and directed the choruses of the Haverford School District, at Brookline, Coopertown and Lynnewood. The concerts her children gave every year were what she was known for.

narrative_blocks.header: She never lost the Southern accent
narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Lenoir in North Carolina to Hazel Evans and Francis Mooney, and kept the soft accent all her life in Pennsylvania. She played the piano to an appreciative audience well into her later years, and told a story well.

bio.bio_blurb: Haverford elementary music teacher and choral director

career.role: Elementary music teacher and choral director

narrative_blocks.header: Glee club, song book, Wolf’s Head
narrative_blocks.body: He sang in the Yale Glee Club four years and led it as a senior, co-edited the Yale Song Book, played in the university orchestra and was financial editor of the Courant. Wolf’s Head took him in his last year.

narrative_blocks.header: Law first, then medicine, then Vienna
narrative_blocks.body: He took his degree in 1883, spent a year in the Yale law school, then the medical school and an M.D. in 1886. A second degree followed at New York Medical College in 1887, and he studied at Vienna in 1891 and 1892.

narrative_blocks.header: New Haven, Tacoma, then Los Angeles
narrative_blocks.body: He practised at New Haven in 1888 and went out to Tacoma the next year. In 1897 he moved to Los Angeles and set up as an oculist and aurist, and kept at it until he retired in 1924.

narrative_blocks.header: He examined eyes for the draft board
narrative_blocks.body: In the First World War he was oculist to Local Draft Board No. 17 at Los Angeles. He sat on the city civil service commission, presided over the Children’s Home Society of California, and led the Yale Club of Southern California.

narrative_blocks.header: Coronary occlusion at eighty-nine
narrative_blocks.body: He married Elizabeth Brockett at New Haven in August 1889 and she died in 1934. He died at Pasadena in October 1944 of coronary occlusion, and his ashes were put with hers at Hollywood.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave his body to the university
narrative_blocks.body: Sanford was born at Tacoma in 1894 while his father was practising there, took his Yale degree in 1917 and died at Los Angeles at fifty-five. He left no grave: his body was donated to medical science.

narrative_blocks.header: His stone carries three wars
narrative_blocks.body: Sanford junior was born at Los Angeles in 1923 and went into the Air Force as a young man. The marker over him names the Second World War, Korea and Vietnam, and gives his rank as major.

bio.title: Maj.
bio.bio_blurb: Air Force major of three wars

narrative_blocks.header: He signed the Emancipator ad in 1838
narrative_blocks.body: In February 1838 sixteen Avon men put their names to a full-page notice in the anti-slavery Emancipator, calling a convention at Hartford for the end of that month. Kellogg was one of the sixteen.

narrative_blocks.header: One of the six old-line abolitionists
narrative_blocks.body: Writing to W. H. Siebert in 1896, Oliver Gabriel named the six old-line abolitionists of Avon and put Kellogg among them. Fugitives bound for Canada stopped in the town overnight and were given food, clothing and shelter.

narrative_blocks.header: He voted for Birney in 1840
narrative_blocks.body: He cast his vote for James G. Birney, the Liberty Party candidate, when the strongest faith dared not hope for the victories that came in his own lifetime. He was an anti-slavery man when abolitionist was an insult.

narrative_blocks.header: Harness maker, postmaster, judge of probate
narrative_blocks.body: He learned the harness trade at Hartford as an apprentice of Thomas Smith and Company, then kept a store at Avon. He was postmaster twenty-five years, town clerk, justice of the peace, and judge of the Avon district probate court.

narrative_blocks.header: A ragged man at the fire, 1829
narrative_blocks.body: On a cold January night in 1829 his father the pastor was being read to when a ragged black man came in, and they kept him till morning. We have the pleasure of entertaining black as well as white, the old man wrote.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughter married Yung Wing
narrative_blocks.body: Of his seven children, Mary married Yung Wing of the Yale class of 1854. Two of their sons, Morrison and Bartlett Yung, followed their father to Yale, in 1898 and 1902.

bio.bio_blurb: Avon harness maker, postmaster and abolitionist

people.relational_label_override: Father of the Husband of a Ninth Generation Hooker

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve Mayflower passengers behind her
narrative_blocks.body: Mary was a daughter of the Rev. John Bartlett, pastor at Bloomfield and West Avon. She was reckoned to descend from twelve of the Mayflower passengers, among them the Aldens, the Brewsters and the Howlands.

people.relational_label_override: Mother of the Husband of a Ninth Generation Hooker

narrative_blocks.header: Husband and wife died on the same date
narrative_blocks.body: She married Charles Augustus Paul Des Granges of Königsberg in May 1883 and went to live in Rome. He died there on the twenty-second of January 1911; she died in the same city on the twenty-second of January, thirty years later.

narrative_blocks.header: A passport from the embassy at Rome
narrative_blocks.body: In January 1915 she applied at the American embassy in Rome to stay six months at the Palazzo Altieri, giving New Haven as her permanent home. The form noted that she had married a German citizen.

narrative_blocks.header: A Yale degree he could never use
narrative_blocks.body: He graduated from Yale in 1872 and ill health kept him from any profession or business afterwards. He lived his last years with his sister at Sakonnet Point in Rhode Island, and died there at forty-one.

bio.bio_blurb: Yale 1872; kept from work by ill health

narrative_blocks.header: He left home for a drug counter
narrative_blocks.body: Out of the village school and the Kensington Academy, he went to New Haven before he was twenty and took an apprenticeship behind a drug counter. It was his business for the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: The shop became a wholesale house
narrative_blocks.body: He was in the firm of Cowles and Olmstead from 1845, and in 1849 he and Charles L. Leete opened a store of their own. It grew into a wholesale house well enough known through the state.

narrative_blocks.header: A quiet man, never much in politics
narrative_blocks.body: He kept to his business and his family and stayed out of public life. He joined the Kensington Congregational Church in 1838 and later the College Street church at New Haven, and died on Christmas Day 1871 at forty-eight.

career.organization: Cowles & Leete, wholesale druggists, New Haven

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived every one of them
narrative_blocks.body: Eliza was born at Kensington in 1795, joined the church in 1821 and never married. She was ninety-four when she died in May 1890, having outlived both her brothers, both her sisters, and her brother Luman by sixty-seven years.

narrative_blocks.header: A year and seventeen days
narrative_blocks.body: Linus Cowles married her at Southington in May 1827, two years after his first wife died. She was dead by the end of the next May, thirty-one years old and childless, and that November he married a third time.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine children, and four buried young
narrative_blocks.body: He married Roxanna Munson at Berlin in May 1841 and they had nine children over twenty-two years. Jane died at two and Albert at two, Albro at ten and Edward at sixteen. Five of the nine came through.

narrative_blocks.header: Kensington to Creola in Alabama
narrative_blocks.body: He married Susan Jennet Howd of Branford in April 1833, and the two of them went south. Both died at Creola in Mobile County, Alabama — she in December 1870, he five and a half years after her.

narrative_blocks.header: He married two Gorton sisters in turn
narrative_blocks.body: He went out to Marion in Ohio and married Olive Marietta Gorton there in November 1838. She died at twenty-one in February 1841, and thirteen months later he married her younger sister Susan Elizabeth. He was dead at thirty-seven.

narrative_blocks.header: The firm was G. and N. A. Cowles
narrative_blocks.body: Nelson went into the insurance business at New Britain with his father, and the two of them traded under both their initials. He was fifty-five when he died at Kensington in June 1900, a few months before the century turned.

career.organization: G. and N. A. Cowles, New Britain

narrative_blocks.header: One of the largest stove houses in Hartford
narrative_blocks.body: He built up one of the largest stove and plumbing establishments in Hartford, out of nothing, in about nine years. He was thirty-two when typhoid fever killed him there in December 1881, and the estate was probated three days later.

narrative_blocks.header: His widow married again and went to Woodbury
narrative_blocks.body: He married Ada Frances Harding of Bristol in June 1876, a daughter of Daniel Strong Harding and Charlotte Olive Matthews of Hartford. She was twenty-four when he died, remarried afterwards, and lived out her life at Woodbury.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept to New Britain
narrative_blocks.body: George Burnham married Minnie Boehm of New Britain and the two of them stayed in the town. Their only son Graydon was born there in 1892 and went out to Plattsburg when the war came.

narrative_blocks.header: She died unmarried at twenty-five
narrative_blocks.body: Mary was the youngest of the five and the last born at Kensington. She died in July 1881, twenty-five years old and unmarried, five months before her brother John Norton was carried off by typhoid at Hartford.

narrative_blocks.header: He married Mrs. Rosabelle Starrett
narrative_blocks.body: Herbert kept books at Hartford and moved to Lowell about 1910. On New Year’s Day 1903 he married Rosabelle Jacques of Athol, already a widow under the name Starrett, and a daughter of John Baptist Jacques and Lydia Angie Hathaway of Barre.

bio.bio_blurb: Hartford bookkeeper who removed to Lowell

narrative_blocks.header: Five months from induction to discharge
narrative_blocks.body: He was inducted at Plattsburg on 21 July 1918 and served as a private in the 134th Depot Brigade until September, then went to the field artillery officers’ training school at Camp Taylor in Kentucky. He was discharged that December.

narrative_blocks.header: An RN at Plattsburgh for many years
narrative_blocks.body: Nancy was born at AuSable Forks in 1931 and married Michael Petrashune at St. Matthew’s in Black Brook in 1955. She nursed at the CVPH Medical Center for many years, and died at ninety-two in February 2024.

narrative_blocks.header: He went down the mine at sixteen
narrative_blocks.body: He was sixteen when he went to work for Republic Steel at the Lyon Mountain mines, to help support the family. He ran a machine there until the mines closed, and ran heavy machines for construction outfits after that until he retired.

narrative_blocks.header: The North Country knew him for the cooking
narrative_blocks.body: Big Mike was known across the North Country for beef barbeques, clam bakes and pig roasts. He belonged to Operating Engineers Local 106 and to two hunting clubs, and what he liked best was the company around the fire.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine children of Stanislaus and Sofia
narrative_blocks.body: He was a son of Stanislaus and Sofia Kviecin Petrashune of Lyon Mountain, one of nine. Three brothers went before him. He married Nancy Cowles at St. Matthew’s in Black Brook in 1955 and died at home on Route 374 at seventy-nine.

bio.bio_blurb: Lyon Mountain miner and North Country cook

narrative_blocks.header: The Clarkes were at Cranford in 1894
narrative_blocks.body: Caroline married Charles H. Clarke and the two of them were living at Cranford in New Jersey in 1894, with a son William and a daughter Minerva. She died at Huntington in Massachusetts in 1917.

narrative_blocks.header: She was Daughter of the Revolution 43452
narrative_blocks.body: Emma took her national number in the Daughters of the American Revolution and was living at Westville in 1894 with her husband Robert Veitch and their two boys, Robert and Willard.

narrative_blocks.header: The Judds were at Greenwich in 1894
narrative_blocks.body: Edward married a Greenwich woman and settled there. The Cowles genealogy calls her Ella Mead and gives three boys — Chandler, Roger and an Edward born in 1891; the Greenwich records give her as Mary Ellen Knapp.

narrative_blocks.header: Robert Veitch & Son, seeds and flowers
narrative_blocks.body: He came out of Temple in Midlothian and built the New Haven seed and flower house that carried his name and his son’s. The firm was trading under both of them by 1894, when the family was living at Westville.

bio.bio_blurb: Seed merchant and florist of New Haven

career.organization: Robert Veitch & Son, seed merchants and florists, New Haven

narrative_blocks.header: From the post office to a Kensington store
narrative_blocks.body: He was assistant postmaster at New Britain, and by 1894 held a position in a store at Kensington. He was back in New Britain by 1914. In July 1879 he married Jennie Henry, who had come down from Claremont in New Hampshire.

narrative_blocks.header: Frank was born and died in April 1888
narrative_blocks.body: Leon Seward came first, in May 1880 at Kensington. The second boy, Frank Weiant, was born in April 1888 and died the same month. Leon married Grace Stoddard of New Britain and gave them three grandsons.

narrative_blocks.header: Farmer, merchant, marketman
narrative_blocks.body: He farmed at Kensington and kept a market there, a Republican and a Congregationalist all his life. He was born in July 1868 and died at New Britain in February 1958, in his ninetieth year.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife was a Cowles four times back
narrative_blocks.body: Alice Cornelia Upson was a great-great-granddaughter of Samuel Upson and Ruth Cowles, so the two were cousins before the wedding. Her mother Mary Wilcox Hart came down the same line he did, and at the same remove.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Revolutionary soldiers behind her
narrative_blocks.body: Her descent carried Samuel Upson, a captain of the fifteenth Connecticut militia, and Samuel Hart, who served as a fifer at sixteen. Both are entered in the lineage book of the Daughters of the American Revolution.

narrative_blocks.header: Secretary at the board, and at the club
narrative_blocks.body: Virginia was born at Berlin and lived most of her life at New Britain, where she was secretary to the Board of Education for a number of years. She was an active member of the town and secretary of the New Britain Women’s Club.

bio.bio_blurb: Secretary to the New Britain school board

narrative_blocks.header: She and Jack founded the travel firm
narrative_blocks.body: Betsy and Jack Perkins married in 1962 and raised their family in New Britain, where she was born. In 1985 the two of them founded the Perkins Travel Corporation, which handles business, vacation and group travel at home and abroad.

narrative_blocks.header: Alberta, Bridgeport, then Dwight Place
narrative_blocks.body: He took his degree at Trinity in 1915 and read at the Hartford Theological Seminary and a year at Atlanta. In 1920 he was doing pastoral work in Alberta, and by September 1922 he was assistant pastor at Dwight Place in New Haven.

career.organization: Dwight Place Congregational Church, New Haven

narrative_blocks.header: He could still name the 1949 class
narrative_blocks.body: His first post was at the Morgan School in Clinton, where he met and married Shirley Niles. Into his late nineties he could still recite the names of every pupil in his 1949 history class.

narrative_blocks.header: MacArthur watched him teach the GED class
narrative_blocks.body: He went into the army and served in the Korean War, working on telephone poles and teaching the high-school equivalency class to GIs. General MacArthur came through and watched him teach one day.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-four years of history at Newtown
narrative_blocks.body: He chaired the history department at Newtown High School and took lay minister training at Yale Divinity School while he taught. He retired from the classroom in 1984 and went straight back to Yale as a student.

narrative_blocks.header: Ordained at sixty, and a hundred pulpits
narrative_blocks.body: He took his divinity degree and was ordained in the United Church of Christ, serving at Tolland and, with his second wife Jean, at East Hartford and Stafford Springs. As pulpit supply he preached in over a hundred churches.

narrative_blocks.header: He outlived Shirley, Lynne and Michelle
narrative_blocks.body: His first wife went before him, and so did their daughter Lynne, and Lynne’s daughter Michelle, and his brother William. He died in his sleep in February 2024 at ninety-five, leaving Jean and eight grandchildren.

bio.title: Rev.
bio.bio_blurb: Newtown history teacher turned UCC minister

career.organization: United Church of Christ, Tolland and East Hartford

narrative_blocks.header: His carrier went down at Leyte Gulf
narrative_blocks.body: He came out of the Naval Academy and spent the war in Argentina and Brazil and then aboard an aircraft carrier that was sunk in the battle of Leyte Gulf. He died of pneumonia and emphysema at Sarasota at sixty-three.

narrative_blocks.header: His sister was Martha Gellhorn
narrative_blocks.body: He was a son of Dr. George Gellhorn of St. Louis. His sister was the war correspondent Martha Gellhorn, of London and Naivasha; his brothers were Alfred, dean of the Pennsylvania medical school, and Walter, professor of law at Columbia.

bio.bio_blurb: Naval Academy man who financed development abroad

career.organization: Agency for International Development, Brazil and Panama

narrative_blocks.header: She met her husband at Black Mountain
narrative_blocks.body: She went from Friends Seminary in New York to Black Mountain College in Asheville, and married David Resnik there on 22 November 1947. The two of them were part of the community of artists and thinkers the place is remembered for.

narrative_blocks.header: A few strokes and it was the animal
narrative_blocks.body: She drew and sketched all her life, and what people remembered was how few strokes it took her to catch the particular person or animal in front of her. She read to the smallest visitors at the Stockbridge library for years.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-one years in one town
narrative_blocks.body: Mexico and Taos came before New York, and the family reached Stockbridge in 1957. She stayed fifty-one years and died there in July 2008 at eighty-one, having buried her daughter Katharine in 1978 and her son Christopher in 1988.

bio.bio_blurb: President of C. Cowles & Company, New Haven

narrative_blocks.header: His uncle founded it, his father ran it
narrative_blocks.body: C. Cowles and Company was founded in 1838 by Chandler Cowles, his father’s half-brother. Ruel Pardee came in at the organising of 1855 and rose to president, and Louis followed him through secretary and treasurer to the chair.

narrative_blocks.header: The firm outlived all three of them
narrative_blocks.body: Chandler founded it, his father took it through the war years, and he had it himself from about 1910 until he died in 1932. C. Cowles and Company is trading still, out of North Haven now instead of Water Street.

narrative_blocks.header: Her people were New Haven Bradleys
narrative_blocks.body: He married Mary Booth Bradley in 1890 and they had no children. She was a daughter of Charles Atwater Bradley and Jane Maria Fowler, married at New Haven in 1861, and a granddaughter of Harvey Bradley and Maria Atwater.

cross_connections.display_label: was his father’s half-brother, and founded the firm in 1838

bio.bio_blurb: Third president of C. Cowles & Company

notable.notable_blurb: Composer; professor of music at Florida State

narrative_blocks.header: College choir, Apollo Glee Club, Pundits
narrative_blocks.body: He came to Yale out of Hillhouse High and Hopkins Grammar, sang in the college choir and the Apollo Glee Club, held the Lockwood music scholarship and belonged to the Pundits. He took a B.A. and a B.Mus. in 1906.

narrative_blocks.header: Paris, then thirty years at Tallahassee
narrative_blocks.body: He went on from Yale to the Schola Cantorum at Paris. In 1930 he came to the Florida State College for Women, which became Florida State University in his time there, and taught music, conducted and composed for twenty years.

narrative_blocks.header: Back to John Cowles of Farmington, 1638
narrative_blocks.body: His obituary traced him to John Cowles of Farmington, who came over in 1638. He died at Tallahassee in December 1959, leaving Elfrida, his sons Chandler in New York and Leonard at the consulate in Naples, and six grandchildren.

narrative_blocks.header: He called out the Harvard Glee Club
narrative_blocks.body: When Harvard withdrew from the intercollegiate glee club contest in 1926 because it disliked the chosen song, he wrote to the Times from New Haven. After two straight defeats, he said, it would have been more sportsmanlike to play the game.

narrative_blocks.header: The song was his old teacher’s
narrative_blocks.body: The piece Harvard objected to was The Silver Lamp in the West, by the late Professor Parker of Yale — Horatio Parker, who had taught him and Charles Ives both. He signed the letter with all three of his names.

narrative_blocks.header: Town children played in his college orchestra
narrative_blocks.body: The orchestra he conducted at Tallahassee took in high-school players from the town, one of whom went on to an international career as a singer and actress. Dean Ella Scoble Opperman had built the music school he joined.

cross_connections.display_label: , his grandson, took his degree from Florida State as well
led Yale's Apollo Glee Club as a junior in 1911

bio.bio_blurb: Composer; professor of music at Florida State

career.organization: Florida State College for Women, later Florida State University

cross_connections.display_label: drafted the statute of the Free Territory of Trieste in 1946

narrative_blocks.header: Atlanta, then a childhood in Havana
narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Atlanta in 1920, the youngest of five, and spent her girlhood in Havana. She married Leonard Ruel Cowles at St. John’s in Tallahassee in 1946 and they had fifty years together.

narrative_blocks.header: Haifa, Naples, Trieste, then home
narrative_blocks.body: As a Foreign Service officer’s wife she kept house at Haifa in Israel and at Naples and Trieste in Italy. She came back to Tallahassee in 1968 and stayed, and kept her summers in Vermont, where they are both buried.

notable.notable_blurb: Broadway producer who was sunk at Pearl Harbor

narrative_blocks.header: His ship went down at Pearl Harbor
narrative_blocks.body: He went from Yale into the Navy, and was a lieutenant aboard the U.S.S. California when she was torpedoed and sunk at Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941. It is the thing he is still named for, eighty years on.

narrative_blocks.header: Eleven New York productions in fourteen years
narrative_blocks.body: He acted on Broadway in Call Me Mister and The Cradle Will Rock, then produced: Menotti’s Telephone and Medium in 1947, The Consul, Billy Budd, The Saint of Bleecker Street, Transposed Heads and Caligula by 1960.

narrative_blocks.header: Balanchine was a friend for life
narrative_blocks.body: He co-produced Menotti’s Telephone and Medium with Efrem Zimbalist Jr. and worked on that 1947 production with George Balanchine, who stayed a friend the rest of his life. In 1955 he ran the American Shakespeare Festival.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Emmy nominations for one documentary
narrative_blocks.body: He wrote and produced I, Leonardo: A Journey of the Mind for CBS in 1983, and was nominated for an Emmy in both capacities for it. He had been general manager of NBC Opera since 1956.

narrative_blocks.header: Four wives, and a pianist at the end
narrative_blocks.body: Katharine Drexel Henry married him at St. Vincent Ferrer in June 1941 and gave him Christopher and Matthew. Then the actress Lenore Lonergan, then the NBC producer Adrienne Zuckert, and last the Bulgarian pianist Pavlina Dokovska.

married his son Matthew, and took two Tonys of her own on Broadway
rode a bus past the burning ships his own was among
, a Honolulu fire chief, fought the fires on the ships that morning

bio.bio_blurb: Broadway producer who was sunk at Pearl Harbor

narrative_blocks.header: She married him six months before the sinking
narrative_blocks.body: Katherine Drexel Henry married Chandler Cowles at St. Vincent Ferrer in New York in June 1941. By December he was in the water at Pearl Harbor. They had Christopher and Matthew, and divorced in 1949.

narrative_blocks.header: Buried in the town her son made home
narrative_blocks.body: In 1960 she married Geoffrey Hellman of The New Yorker, and died in 1980 at sixty. She was buried at Evergreen in Bethlehem, the Connecticut town where her son Matthew taught catechism and where he was laid on Carmel Hill in 2014.

narrative_blocks.header: Dinah Lord, at eleven, to Hepburn’s Tracy
narrative_blocks.body: She was eleven when she played Dinah Lord, younger sister to Katharine Hepburn’s Tracy, in the 1939 Broadway run of The Philadelphia Story. Brooks Atkinson found in her a stout sort of humor that suited her groaning little figure.

narrative_blocks.header: Third generation of a theatrical tribe
narrative_blocks.body: Her grandfather Lester Lonergan came out of Ireland to act, and her father and her brother acted after him. She and her brother went to the Professional Children’s School, and she debuted at six in Mother Lode with Melvyn Douglas.

narrative_blocks.header: Fluffy Adams, and the hoarse voice
narrative_blocks.body: She played juveniles and was known for the hoarseness of her voice: Fluffy Adams in Junior Miss by Chodorov and Fields, a part in Norman Krasna’s Dear Ruth, Crime Marches On, Fields Beyond, and the film Tom, Dick and Harry.

narrative_blocks.header: Cancer took her at Stuart at fifty-nine
narrative_blocks.body: She married Chandler Cowles in 1951 and they divorced three years later. She died of cancer at her home in Stuart, Florida, in August 1987, survived by her husband Richard Bertram and her son John Holtzman.

cross_connections.display_label: was the model for Tracy Lord, whose little sister she played in 1939

bio.bio_blurb: Stage and film actress of the forties

notable.notable_blurb: Actor and playwright; Billy Clyde Tuggle

narrative_blocks.header: The title role in Malcolm at twenty-one
narrative_blocks.body: In 1966 he played the title part in Edward Albee’s stage adaptation of James Purdy’s Malcolm, at the Shubert. Two years later he was on with Al Pacino and John Cazale in Israel Horovitz’s The Indian Wants the Bronx.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the villain he played
narrative_blocks.body: Billy Clyde Tuggle on All My Children was a part he created and wrote himself, and he played it from 1984 to 1990. It brought him three daytime Emmy nominations, and it is the role most people knew him by.

narrative_blocks.header: Pacino debuted in his first film too
narrative_blocks.body: His first picture was the 1969 comedy drama Me, Natalie, in which he played Harvey Belman and Al Pacino also made his debut. Four decades later he took a supporting part in Scorsese’s Shutter Island.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught catechism at Bethlehem
narrative_blocks.body: He was a devout Catholic and taught religious education at the Church of the Nativity in Bethlehem, Connecticut. He rode motorcycles, and died there of congestive heart failure in May 2014, and lies on Carmel Hill.

narrative_blocks.header: The black sheep of Cowles and Drexel
narrative_blocks.body: A profile of his wife called him the black sheep of a family with ties to Cowles publishing and Drexel banking. He married the actress Christine Baranski in 1983 and they had two daughters, Isabel and Lily.

cross_connections.display_label: was in Me Natalie too, and on All My Children after it

narrative_blocks.header: She played Billy Clyde Tuggle’s wife
narrative_blocks.body: Her part on All My Children was Estelle LaTour Tuggle, married on the serial to its famous villain Billy Clyde — a character Matthew Cowles created and wrote for himself. She and Cowles were married from 1980 until 1982.

bio.bio_blurb: Actress; Estelle LaTour on All My Children

notable.notable_blurb: Two-time Tony winner and Emmy-winning actress

narrative_blocks.header: Cheektowaga, the Felician Sisters, Juilliard
narrative_blocks.body: She was raised in the Polish quarter of Cheektowaga outside Buffalo, a newspaper editor’s daughter whose grandparents were said to have been Polish theatrical actors. She went to the Felician Sisters’ Villa Maria Academy, then to Juilliard.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Tonys, and the hundredth Simon award
narrative_blocks.body: She won the Tony for featured actress in 1984 as Charlotte in Stoppard’s The Real Thing, and again in 1989 for Neil Simon’s Rumors. Accepting the second, she said she was the hundredth person ever to win an award for a Simon production.

narrative_blocks.header: Married, delivered, and won a Tony
narrative_blocks.body: She married Matthew Cowles in October 1983, had Isabel, and took the Tony and the Drama Desk for The Real Thing inside the same twelve months. When they met, she said, he was leaving for the jungle on a Harley-Davidson.

narrative_blocks.header: Jeremy Irons twice, and both times an affair
narrative_blocks.body: Her first Tony came for playing a woman having an affair with a character of Jeremy Irons’s, in a play that won him one too. Five years later she did it again in Reversal of Fortune, and that time he took the Oscar.

narrative_blocks.header: Maryann first, then Diane Lockhart
narrative_blocks.body: Maryann Thorpe on Cybill brought the Emmy for supporting actress in 1995, after eighteen years of New York theatre. From 2009 she played Diane Lockhart through a hundred and fifty-six episodes of The Good Wife and then led The Good Fight.

narrative_blocks.header: She read for Princess Leia in 1977
narrative_blocks.body: She auditioned for Princess Leia in the first Star Wars picture; the part went to Carrie Fisher. Terrence McNally later wrote Lips Together, Teeth Apart for her, and she was in the first workshops of Sondheim’s Sunday in the Park.

narrative_blocks.header: Great clothes and funny lines
narrative_blocks.body: She put the length of her career down to never having carried the mantle of beauty. I was never beautiful so I am not unbeautiful, she said; I may not have been a leading lady, but I had great clothes and funny lines.

cross_connections.display_label: was the serious actress she named — beauty combined with intelligence
was her father-in-law, and produced Menotti’s operas on Broadway
, her husband's grandmother, came of the Drexels her Gilded Age show depicts
guested on The Good Wife in its last season

bio.bio_blurb: Two-time Tony winner and Emmy-winning actress

career.organization: The Good Wife and The Good Fight

narrative_blocks.header: Penn, then the Brooklyn district attorney
narrative_blocks.body: She taught inner-city students to grow vegetables and cooked in a locavore kitchen at Houston under Monica Pope. A Pennsylvania degree in 2006 led into environmental journalism, then law school, the bar, and the Brooklyn district attorney.

narrative_blocks.header: No publisher would take the novel
narrative_blocks.body: When no traditional publisher would buy the novel she had written, she opened a site of her own and called it The Noble Try, and has run reflective essays there since. Her writing mentor is Davyne Verstandig.

narrative_blocks.header: The verdict at twenty-one: middle-aged housewife
narrative_blocks.body: She had acted as a child in British television, in Lovejoy opposite Ian McShane and in The Brittas Empire, and at twenty-one gave a year to a conservatory. Its head told her she would do her best work as a middle-aged housewife.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son played her sister in the woods
narrative_blocks.body: In July 2022 Lily shot a scene for her own film in the Connecticut woods where the two of them grew up, and six-year-old Augie played his aunt in the flashbacks. Watching him, Isabel felt what she named as jealousy and then as grief.

narrative_blocks.header: She books the work under another name
narrative_blocks.body: She woke the next morning having become the type she was promised, enrolled in a class, and took the first job in an empty Long Island office park. She has played the busy upscale mother in commercials since, under a false name.

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve days a month, and the driver knew
narrative_blocks.body: Until Cybill took Christine Baranski to Los Angeles, her parents had commuted into New York by car or on her father’s motorcycle. Home then came to about twelve days a month, and the family driver said her mother wept on every leaving.

notable.notable_blurb: Actress; Isobel Evans in Roswell, New Mexico

narrative_blocks.header: Religious studies, then Los Angeles
narrative_blocks.body: She grew up in rural Connecticut and read religious studies at Princeton, doing fieldwork on religion in Mozambique. Then she went west and took work as personal assistant to Jonah Hill while he was making True Story.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-two episodes as Isobel Evans
narrative_blocks.body: Her first part was in Enchantments in 2015 and a recurring one in the satire BrainDead the year after. From 2019 to 2022 she played Isobel Evans in the CW’s Roswell, New Mexico, in fifty-two episodes.

narrative_blocks.header: Helen Park, in two Call of Duty games
narrative_blocks.body: She voiced and performed Helen Park in Call of Duty: Black Ops Cold War in 2020 and again in Black Ops 6 four years later, and the character carried over into Call of Duty: Mobile. She was Zendara in Immortals of Aveum.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father died the year before she started
narrative_blocks.body: Matthew Cowles died at Bethlehem in May 2014, the year before her first part. She had grown up in that corner of rural Connecticut with an older sister, Isabel, who went into the law.

cross_connections.display_label: was her grandfather, and produced on Broadway for fourteen years

bio.bio_blurb: Actress; Isobel Evans in Roswell, New Mexico
New Yorker staff writer for nearly fifty years

notable.notable_blurb: New Yorker staff writer for nearly fifty years

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty years of Talk of the Town
narrative_blocks.body: Thornton Wilder’s word got him onto the Herald Tribune book pages out of Yale, and by 1929 he was reporting Talk of the Town. He stayed nearly fifty years, leaving twice for about a year — long enough, he said, to realise he was foolish.

narrative_blocks.header: He made the city’s institutions his beat
narrative_blocks.body: He wrote The New Yorker’s pieces on the Bronx Zoo, the Metropolitan Museum, the Modern, the Public Library, the Morgan Library, the United Nations and the Stock Exchange. Robert Moses, the parks commissioner, sent him story ideas.

narrative_blocks.header: A footman with a perfume burner
narrative_blocks.body: His humour ran to old wealth gone to seed: before every party of Mrs. de Peyster’s a footman goes through the house with a perfume burner, sneezing like a fool. He wrote the Smithsonian’s book and the Natural History Museum’s.

narrative_blocks.header: His butterflies were of museum quality
narrative_blocks.body: He chased and collected butterflies seriously enough that the collection was called museum quality. He belonged to the Racquet, the Century, the Coffee House and the Grolier, and was active in the New-York Historical Society.

narrative_blocks.header: He anathematised a colleague at the Grolier
narrative_blocks.body: He was a Harold Ross loyalist and fought anyone who called the founder irascible. From the Grolier Club floor he anathematised Brendan Gill’s Here at The New Yorker, and the two men stopped speaking.

narrative_blocks.header: Reno, hours after the first wife’s divorce
narrative_blocks.body: He married the harpist Daphne Bayne at Reno in 1941, hours after her divorce came through, and they had the sitar player Daisy Paradis. That ended about 1958, and in 1960 he married Katherine Henry; their daughter was Katharine.

cross_connections.display_label: chartered in his parlour the museum whose history he later wrote
was hired as a checker in 1929 and ran the checking department until 1974

narrative_blocks.header: He played his aunt in her own film
narrative_blocks.body: In July 2022, at six, he stood in for Lily Cowles in the flashbacks of a picture she had been ten years making, shot in the Connecticut woods where she and his mother grew up.

bio.bio_blurb: Son of the general who governed Puerto Rico

narrative_blocks.header: His father held the Medal of Honor
narrative_blocks.body: Guy Vernor Henry rose to major-general, took the Medal of Honor, and was military governor of Puerto Rico before his death in 1899. His brother Guy Henry Jr. carried the name on in the army after him.

narrative_blocks.header: The two families had crossed once already
narrative_blocks.body: His father’s first wife was a sister of the Lucy Wharton who married Joseph William Drexel. A generation later he married that Drexel’s youngest daughter, Josephine, in May 1915.

bio.bio_blurb: Youngest of the four Joseph Drexel children

cross_connections.display_label: , who married her grandson, stars in a drama that puts the Drexels on screen

narrative_blocks.header: An Emmet first, then a Henry
narrative_blocks.body: She married Dr. John Duncan Emmet in 1904, a great-grandson of the physician Thomas Addis Emmet, and they divorced ten years later. In 1915 she married Seton Henry, and the Cowles line runs from that second marriage.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father quit rather than fight Morgan
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph William Drexel was a partner in Drexel, Morgan and Company beside his brother Anthony. In 1876, worn down by battling the brusque J. Pierpont Morgan, he walked out of the firm and gave his life to giving the money away.

narrative_blocks.header: A farm for men out of work
narrative_blocks.body: He ran two hundred acres outside New York where men without work were housed, fed and taught farming until they found a job. In Maryland he laid out Klej Grange and sold the lots to the poor at cost, and bought Michigan land to do the same.

narrative_blocks.header: Grant finished the memoirs in his cottage
narrative_blocks.body: In 1881 he bought Mount McGregor above Saratoga Springs, put a hotel on the summit and ran a narrow-gauge railway up to it. In 1885 he lent his summer cottage to Ulysses Grant, who wrote there for six weeks and died in it.

narrative_blocks.header: Six thousand scores became a library
narrative_blocks.body: He collected music until he had more than six thousand items, and at his death the Drexel Collection went to the Lenox Library. It is the foundation of the New York Public Library’s music division to this day.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandfather painted Bolívar first
narrative_blocks.body: Francis Martin Drexel left Dornbirn to dodge Napoleon’s conscription and painted portraits through Peru and Chile, Bolívar among them, before founding Drexel and Company at Philadelphia in 1837. Anthony, her uncle, founded the university.

narrative_blocks.header: Two of her sisters married two Dahlgrens
narrative_blocks.body: Lucy married Eric Dahlgren and Elizabeth married his brother John Vinton, both sons of the admiral. Elizabeth buried him, then married Harry Lehr, then Lord Decies, and spent her last years known as Lady Decies.

notable.notable_blurb: Government chemist of the 1907 whiskey study

bio.bio_blurb: Government chemist of the 1907 whiskey study
bio.photo_notes: The Times-Democrat, 15 June 1913 — captioned "Head of Uncle Sam's food inspection factory."

career.role: Chief chemist, then director of research

career.organization: Bureau of Chemistry, Department of Agriculture

cross_connections.display_label: published The Jungle, which forced the law he then enforced
sat on Armour’s board while he ran the laboratory at Wilson
was the USDA research service's Scientist of the Year in 1985

narrative_blocks.header: Eight years on what wood does to whiskey
narrative_blocks.body: Recruited from graduate work at Berkeley, he joined the Internal Revenue chemists about 1900 and went onto the whiskey maturation study Charles Crampton had begun in 1898. The last year went on 31 barrels of rye and bourbon.

narrative_blocks.header: The paper the whole industry rests on
narrative_blocks.body: By 1906 he was head chemist and had to compile the data. Every year of the bonded period a seal was broken and a quart drawn off; in 1906 all eight years of samples went under complete examination at once, and the paper followed in 1907.

narrative_blocks.header: He crossed over to Harvey Wiley
narrative_blocks.body: The year the paper appeared he left Internal Revenue for a better-paying post under Harvey Wiley at the Bureau of Chemistry, the man who had just got the Pure Food and Drug Act signed. He stayed eleven years.

narrative_blocks.header: He went to the meatpackers after Sinclair
narrative_blocks.body: In 1918, twelve years after The Jungle, he left government for Wilson and Company of Chicago, a young packer trying to prove the quality of its goods. He was chief chemist, then director of research, until he died in 1949.

narrative_blocks.header: Red peppers, olive oil, Cuban pineapples
narrative_blocks.body: The bureau put him on everything edible: olive oil and its substitutes, the varieties of red pepper, Cuban fruit and canned pineapple, Concord grape juice, American beers and ales, and potato culls as a source of industrial alcohol.

narrative_blocks.header: Head of Uncle Sam’s food inspection factory
narrative_blocks.body: That was the caption under his photograph in 1913, the year the papers took to selling the government chemists to the public as tasters — men who could tell one product from another by smell and by tongue alone.

bio.bio_blurb: Director of the Smithsonian's national art collection

career.organization: National Collection of Fine Arts, Smithsonian

career.role: Assistant curator, Division of Graphic Arts

cross_connections.display_label: ran the Philadelphia museum as he ran the Smithsonian’s
built her museum for the American art the Met refused
