summered at Newport with Malbone, then took him to England
was chief curator of the National Gallery of Art from 1970 to 1983

narrative_blocks.header: He went in a preparator and left director
narrative_blocks.body: He joined the Smithsonian’s Division of Graphic Arts in 1912 to prepare other men’s work, and climbed it rung by rung — aide, assistant curator, curator — to acting director of the National Collection of Fine Arts, and director in 1946.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-six presidents and governors in miniature
narrative_blocks.body: He was a nationally known painter of miniatures, among them twenty-six miniature portraits of American presidents and governors. He founded the Miniature Painters, Sculptors and Gravers Society of Washington and served as its president.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the life of Malbone
narrative_blocks.body: Edward Greene Malbone was the finest American miniaturist and had been dead a century and a half. Tolman spent years on him, and The Life and Work of Edward Greene Malbone came from the New-York Historical Society after his own death.

narrative_blocks.header: How Prints Are Made toured for twenty years
narrative_blocks.body: From 1923 to 1946 he put on a monthly show of living artists at the Smithsonian, and built a travelling exhibition called How Prints Are Made that circulated the country for two decades.

narrative_blocks.header: He photographed the institution’s own people
narrative_blocks.body: He turned a camera on Smithsonian staff, the buildings and grounds, the exhibitions and Washington streets through the thirties and forties. Some of the men and women in those scrapbooks have still never been identified.

narrative_blocks.header: California art schools, then a patent
narrative_blocks.body: He came up through Pomona prep, the Mark Hopkins Institute at San Francisco, the Los Angeles School of Art and Design and Berkeley, then the Corcoran. In 1909 he patented a carrier for wet canvases.

bio.bio_blurb: Nurse, then a Dade County forensic investigator

narrative_blocks.header: She read the dead for Dade County
narrative_blocks.body: She nursed at New Haven, went south to Florida in 1953, and worked as a forensic investigator in the Dade County medical examiner’s office until she retired in 1966. Then she moved up to Inverness and joined the First Christian Church.

narrative_blocks.header: She asked for no service at all
narrative_blocks.body: She outlived her husband by fifty years and buried two of her daughters, Bonnie and Sheri, before her own death at Inverness in 2015. A very private woman, she asked to be remembered as she was in life, with no repose and no service.

career.organization: Dill & Dill Insurance Agency, Fort Wayne

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-two years selling insurance at Fort Wayne
narrative_blocks.body: He came out of Pierceton and took his degree at Indiana in 1932, then spent thirty-two years at Fort Wayne with the Dill and Dill agency. He was a deacon of Plymouth Congregational Church and a Mason of Summit City Lodge 170.

narrative_blocks.header: He died in the evening at fifty-eight
narrative_blocks.body: A Royal Order of Jesters man, a Shriner on the Mizpah directors’ staff, he belonged to the Orchard Ridge club and the St. Joe Athletic Club. He died at Parkview Memorial Hospital in May 1968, leaving Helen and two daughters.

bio.bio_blurb: Air Force captain, then a Charlotte builder

military_service.notes: Flew a B-57 bomber.

narrative_blocks.header: He flew a B-57 over Vietnam
narrative_blocks.body: He came out of Syracuse and served as a captain in the Air Force through the Vietnam War, flying a B-57 bomber. It is the thing his family put first when they came to write him down.

narrative_blocks.header: Maryland to Charlotte, and seventeen years of it
narrative_blocks.body: He moved down from Maryland in 1984 to work for Tomlinson Engineering, then spent seventeen years in management at Warco Construction, building the city through the years it boomed.

narrative_blocks.header: One of the first kidneys at Carolinas
narrative_blocks.body: Around 1987 he took one of the first kidney transplants done at Carolinas Medical Center, and it gave him twenty-five more years and let him meet his grandsons. His family stayed grateful to the strangers who had decided to donate.

cross_connections.display_label: was held back with dyslexia and became the father of software quality

narrative_blocks.header: Three master’s degrees, and one classroom
narrative_blocks.body: She taught elementary school for Hastings Schools in Michigan and took three master’s degrees from three different institutions along the way, which is a fair measure of how she felt about learning.

narrative_blocks.header: She helped start a school for dyslexia
narrative_blocks.body: She worked with students who had dyslexia, sat on the Hastings Literacy Council, and joined with others to found a school in New York built specifically for dyslexic children and the resources they needed.

narrative_blocks.header: Syracuse, the same school as her brother
narrative_blocks.body: She met Charles J. Semerad Jr. at Syracuse, where her brother Jim also took his degree, and they married at Rochester in August 1958. She outlived him, and outlived her sister and her brother both.

notable.notable_blurb: Washington painter of portrait miniatures

cross_connections.display_label: painted miniatures too, three of them firsts at the 1896 Salon

narrative_blocks.header: She married her drawing teacher
narrative_blocks.body: She came up from Salisbury in North Carolina to study at the Corcoran School of Art, where Ruel Pardee Tolman was one of her instructors. They married in 1914, and about 1926 she took up the miniatures he was known for.

narrative_blocks.header: Bertha Jaques, in watercolour on ivory
narrative_blocks.body: Her 1936 miniature of the etcher Bertha Jaques reached the Smithsonian in 1941 as a bequest from the sitter herself. Her portrait of Elizabeth Wickersham hangs in the Philadelphia Museum of Art.

narrative_blocks.header: Three societies, and the 1935 independent
narrative_blocks.body: She showed with the Miniature Painters, Gravers and Sculptors Society, the Washington Water Color Club and the Arts Club, and hung at the Corcoran and the Pennsylvania Academy. She was in the 1935 Greater Washington Independent.

narrative_blocks.header: He publicised the Ten Most Wanted
narrative_blocks.body: He took his law degree at George Washington in 1941 and was made a special agent of the Bureau that year. He rose to inspector on the public-relations side, and the publicity around the Ten Most Wanted Fugitives Program was his to handle.

narrative_blocks.header: Washington, then Orlando, then back
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Washington and grew up at Orlando in Florida, returning to the city as a student. A stroke preceded the pneumonia that killed him at the Washington Hospital Center in May 1990, at seventy-six.

bio.bio_blurb: Daughter of Chief Justice Francis Dana

narrative_blocks.header: Her father signed the Articles of Confederation
narrative_blocks.body: Francis Dana took his Harvard degree in 1762, led the Sons of Liberty, sat in the Continental Congress and signed the Articles of Confederation in 1778. He was a judge of the Massachusetts supreme court and founded the American Academy.

narrative_blocks.header: He joined her father’s academy first
narrative_blocks.body: Washington Allston was made a Fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 1826, four years before he married the daughter of the man who founded it. She was also a cousin of his first wife.

naming_inspiration.description: Named for her mother, Katherine Stickney Cowles.

cross_connections.display_label: bred Standardbreds at Walnut Hall while he foaled Thoroughbreds
, his grandfather, taught music at Florida State, his own college

narrative_blocks.header: He studied where his grandfather taught
narrative_blocks.body: His first degree came from Florida State University — the college where his grandfather Walter Ruel Cowles, the man he is named for, had been professor of music and conducted the orchestra. Then the veterinary school at Auburn.

narrative_blocks.header: He arrived as another man’s farm vet
narrative_blocks.body: He reached central Kentucky in 1980 as resident veterinarian to Spendthrift Farm, then opened a practice of his own. In 1984 he bought seventy-five acres at Winchester, called it Hidden Creek, and began raising thoroughbreds himself.

narrative_blocks.header: The farm outgrew itself twice over
narrative_blocks.body: Hidden Creek filled to capacity, so in 1996 the family bought a hundred and fifty acres on Russell Cave Road outside Lexington and named it Gunston Hall. They added as much again at Iron Works Pike in 2004, and eighty acres for foaling in 2

narrative_blocks.header: Three hundred acres and twenty broodmares
narrative_blocks.body: He oversees the ground and all the veterinary work on it, keeps a band of twenty broodmares, and runs a small racing stable mostly on the east coast. The farm boards, breeds, foals and prepares horses for the sales ring.

narrative_blocks.header: He handed the farm down in 2016
narrative_blocks.body: In late 2016 he and Lisa gave the farm over to Larmon and Cristina, meaning it to last past them. His other son Joe had bought his first horse at eighteen, in partnership with his parents.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought his first horse at eighteen
narrative_blocks.body: He bought it in partnership with his parents, and has handled nearly all the buying and selling for the family racing and breeding operation since. T/C Stable has run Trout River Red, Big Lou, Genuine True, Wadena and Minister Lady.

narrative_blocks.header: A lawyer who spends his time on horses
narrative_blocks.body: He grew up at Lexington, read at Centre College and took his law degree at Capital University in 2002. He works as a national business executive for Humana, and gives most of the rest of his time to bloodstock.

narrative_blocks.header: She collects debts for horse farms
narrative_blocks.body: Her practice runs to commercial litigation and creditors’ rights, and into equine law, where she acts for horsemen, farms and veterinarians on collections and contracts. She spoke to the Kentucky Horse Council on the legal side of the busin

narrative_blocks.header: Nashville to Lexington for a degree
narrative_blocks.body: She was raised at Nashville and came to Lexington for her undergraduate degree, which is where she met Joe Cowles. She is admitted in Kentucky and in both federal districts of the state.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the degrees and chose the horses
narrative_blocks.body: He read accounting and finance at Kentucky and went to the farm full time in the autumn of 2004 instead. He tries to lay eyes on every horse on the place each day, and attends the foalings himself.

narrative_blocks.header: She came for an internship and stayed
narrative_blocks.body: She had spent three years in the equine hospital at the Gávea racetrack in Rio before coming to Kentucky in 2010 to intern for Dr. Cowles. She took her Kentucky veterinary licence in 2018, and in her free time she runs.

naming_inspiration.description: The third to carry the name of Walter Ruel Cowles, professor of music at Florida State.

bio.title: Capt.
bio.bio_blurb: Dead of smallpox in the year he married

narrative_blocks.header: The smallpox took him inside the year
narrative_blocks.body: He married Abigail in 1773 and was dead before it was out. His stone at New Haven reads that he fell a victim by the small pox on the twenty-ninth day of April, and he was twenty-four.

military_service.unit: Company D, 4th Georgia Infantry Regiment, Confederate States Army
military_service.notes: Mustered First Corporal 26 April 1861; First Sergeant 28 April 1862; Junior 2nd Lieutenant 15 July 1862; First Lieutenant 1863. Captured at Spotsylvania 12 May 1864 commanding the regiment’s sharpshooters; paroled at Charleston in December.

cross_connections.display_label: captained the 14th Connecticut across the field at Sharpsburg

narrative_blocks.header: A Berlin boy in the 4th Georgia
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Berlin in Connecticut and mustered into Company D of the 4th Georgia as a first corporal in April 1861. He rose to first sergeant, then junior second lieutenant, then first lieutenant by 1863.

narrative_blocks.header: Commended at Sharpsburg by his brigadier
narrative_blocks.body: The official records place him on the field at Sharpsburg, where his brigade commander commended his conduct. It was the bloodiest single day of the war, and men from his native state were in the lines opposite.

narrative_blocks.header: Taken at Spotsylvania with the sharpshooters
narrative_blocks.body: He was commanding the regiment’s sharpshooters on the twelfth of May 1864 when he was captured at Spotsylvania Court House. He was held until December and paroled at Charleston.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-five years with one company
narrative_blocks.body: He went to the Southern Express Company of Atlanta after the war and stayed with it the rest of his working life, retiring as its superintendent. He died at Atlanta in 1911 and lies at Westview.

narrative_blocks.header: Born and dead on the same date
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Pepperell on the twenty-third of February 1833 and died at Pepperell on the twenty-third of February 1902, sixty-nine years to the day. His elder sister Sarah Elisabeth had died there at four.

bio.bio_blurb: Killed in Tunisia with the 45th Division

military_service.unit: 157th Infantry Regiment, 45th Infantry Division, United States Army
military_service.notes: Service number 31062544, entered from Massachusetts. Purple Heart with Oak Leaf Cluster. Killed 14 November 1943.

cross_connections.display_label: was killed in North Africa too, and lies in the same ground

narrative_blocks.header: A private of the 157th, dead at twenty-seven
narrative_blocks.body: He went out with the 157th Infantry of the 45th Division and was killed on the fourteenth of November 1943. He lies at Carthage in the North Africa American Cemetery, plot B, row 18, and holds the Purple Heart with an oak leaf cluster.

bio.bio_blurb: Navy man, then thirty-six years an engineer

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-six years at the Navy laboratory
narrative_blocks.body: He served in the Navy, took his degree at Florida State, and spent thirty-six years as an electronics engineer at the Naval Coastal Systems Laboratory. He was a deacon of St. Andrews Baptist for more than fifty years.

bio.bio_blurb: Panama City photographer and tuba player

narrative_blocks.header: From bass guitar to church tuba
narrative_blocks.body: He played bass guitar in his church youth group and marched with the Bay High Million Dollar Band, class of 1971. He ran Chip Lloyd Photography in Panama City all his working life, and latterly played tuba in his church orchestra.

narrative_blocks.header: A band of his own at eleven
narrative_blocks.body: He took up the guitar at seven and his first solo was Do Lord. At eleven he started a band with friends he kept for life, and in his teens founded Authorized Personnel, which toured the region and drew a following.

narrative_blocks.header: Music missions out of Budapest and Zagreb
narrative_blocks.body: He met Evelyne in the Netherlands on a music missions tour and married her in 1988. They worked out of the Netherlands, Budapest and Zagreb with the band Morgan and the Tramps, and he cut albums for musicians in Albania and Kosovo.

narrative_blocks.header: Counselling military families on five stations
narrative_blocks.body: From 2012 he counselled military families under contract in Spain, Germany, the Netherlands, England and Japan, meeting his four daughters in Europe when he could. A cardiac arrest killed him at Sasebo, four months short of fifty-four.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-five years over the same ledgers
narrative_blocks.body: She left Tubman High in 1931 for Queens College at Charlotte, came home, and kept the books at the Hollingsworth Candy Company for thirty-five years before she retired. She lived her whole life in Augusta and died there at a hundred and two

narrative_blocks.header: She was the family memory
narrative_blocks.body: Her recall was the primary source on Augusta and on all her kin. She traced the family to Jamestown in the early sixteen-hundreds and, she maintained, back to Charlemagne, and liked to tell of the ancestor naturalised at Augusta in 1802.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifteen lineage societies, and offices in most
narrative_blocks.body: She helped found the Augusta junior chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution in 1939 and was its first treasurer, a member seventy-five years. She led the Colonial Dames of the Seventeenth Century chapter and served the Colonial

narrative_blocks.header: She welcomed new citizens with her own story
narrative_blocks.body: At naturalisation ceremonies in the federal court house at Augusta she told the story of her own ancestor, naturalised in that city in 1802. She travelled widely, to Europe and to the world fairs at Chicago and New York.

bio.title: Col.
bio.bio_blurb: Tanner; deputy sheriff; temperance society president

narrative_blocks.header: Hemlock bark turned him back from New York
narrative_blocks.body: A tanner, he had arranged to begin the world in western New York when the tanning properties of hemlock bark were discovered. Connecticut forests were full of it, so in 1802 he moved from Berlin to Winsted instead.

narrative_blocks.header: The sheriff wanted deputies who looked the part
narrative_blocks.body: He served several years as a deputy under Sheriff Landon, who picked his staff for bearing as much as ability — able men, but portly and fine-looking ones, to sustain the dignity of the county magistracy.

narrative_blocks.header: He closed his public life with temperance
narrative_blocks.body: The presidency of the Litchfield County Temperance Society was the last office he held, and he filled it with punctuality and ardent zeal for seven or eight years.

narrative_blocks.header: At ninety he still remembered everyone
narrative_blocks.body: He read widely and kept up with current events to the end, and at ninety could summon an acquaintance or an event of his youth as readily as a young man. Winsted called him the chronicler and patriarch of the village.

narrative_blocks.header: Two daughters named Harriet, neither of whom lived
narrative_blocks.body: Elisabeth died thirteen days short of her sixth birthday, and Harriet the same year, 1804. A daughter born in 1813 was given the lost Harriet’s name, and she was gone by 1816.

narrative_blocks.header: She and Amos died the same day
narrative_blocks.body: Esther Hinsdale and Amos Hills married in Connecticut about 1799, raised five children, and moved north to Cabot, Vermont. Both of them died there on 4 July 1852, in their mid-seventies.

bio.bio_blurb: Fire insurance agent; Winsted Savings Bank president

narrative_blocks.header: Fire insurance made him at thirty-one
narrative_blocks.body: In 1848 he took the agency for this part of Connecticut for a number of leading fire insurance companies and built it into one of the largest and most lucrative in the state. He retired from it in 1871.

narrative_blocks.header: The panic of 1837 cost him his place
narrative_blocks.body: He had gone to Hartford at sixteen to clerk in a mercantile house; the crash of 1837 put him out of work. The store he opened back in Winsted failed, so he entered the Foundry and Machine Company and learned the machinist’s trade.

narrative_blocks.header: Deacon since the church’s founding in 1854
narrative_blocks.body: He was an original member of Winsted’s Second Congregational Church and became a deacon when it organized in January 1854, serving as its clerk and treasurer as well and keeping a statistical record the town thought invaluable.

narrative_blocks.header: Selectman through the war years
narrative_blocks.body: He was one of Winsted’s selectmen during the Civil War, and townsmen long remembered how faithfully he served their interests. Assessor, water commissioner, borough clerk and treasurer followed — offices he never sought.

narrative_blocks.header: Elijah Burritt taught him at New Britain
narrative_blocks.body: He went from the common schools to New Britain High School, where the principal was Elijah Burritt, brother of the self-taught Connecticut blacksmith Elihu Burritt.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventh in descent from a Dedham founder
narrative_blocks.body: He stood seventh in descent from Robert Hinsdale, one of the founders of the church at Dedham, Massachusetts, in 1638.

narrative_blocks.header: The same fourth of July took them both
narrative_blocks.body: Amos and his wife Esther Hinsdale both died at Cabot, Vermont, on 4 July 1852. He was seventy-five and she about seventy-three, and they had been married some fifty-three years.

bio.bio_blurb: Paso Robles parks director; college football official

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty years of Paso Robles parks
narrative_blocks.body: The city made him its director of parks and recreation in 1972 and he stayed nearly thirty years, starting T-ball, youth soccer, co-ed softball and senior programs, and building Pioneer and Larry Moore parks.

narrative_blocks.header: He worked the first USFL title game
narrative_blocks.body: A friend got him officiating six-man football at Shandon and Templeton in 1961. By 1978 he was working Division I, and in 1983 the new United States Football League sent him to its championship at Mile High Stadium.

narrative_blocks.header: The Air Force sent him to Greenland
narrative_blocks.body: After a year at Antelope Valley Junior College he enlisted, and the tour took him to Cheyenne, Fort Worth, Sondrestrom in Greenland and Panama City in Florida before he came home.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten years of highway work, then Interstate 5
narrative_blocks.body: He worked a decade in his father-in-law’s highway construction business, then left for a Bakersfield company engaged on the building of Interstate 5.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty acres from the Chandler Ranch
narrative_blocks.body: His hardest piece of work was Centennial Park, and raising the money the state grant required to finish it. He later dealt with the Chandler Ranch family for the forty acres that became Barney Schwartz Park.

narrative_blocks.header: Rotary, the fire house, and troubled kids
narrative_blocks.body: He gave thirty years to Rotary and served a term as its president, volunteered ten years with the Paso Robles fire department, and sat on the youth guidance council that worked with young people in trouble.

bio.title: Dr.
bio.bio_blurb: Hartford homeopathic physician; Isle of Pines planter

cross_connections.display_label: turned to him at Hartford when Dr. Taft died, and kept no other
opened the 1864 reorganization of the Connecticut homeopathic society
, a Union private turned homeopath, survived a shipwreck at ten

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-three years of Hartford practice
narrative_blocks.body: He took his degree from the New York Homeopathic Medical College in 1867, practiced a year at Danbury and three more at Southington, and moved to Hartford in May 1871. He stayed thirty-three years.

narrative_blocks.header: Twain’s wife would accept no other doctor
narrative_blocks.body: He took on the Clemens household after Cincinnatus Taft died and left it unsettled about physicians. Mark Twain wrote that Livy was thoroughly satisfied with him and would want no substitute nor accept of any.

narrative_blocks.header: He meant to be a musician
narrative_blocks.body: He left the high school at Collinsville with no thought of medicine, giving his attention to musical study. The war ended that: waiting for orders near New London, he was offered a hospital steward’s place at Fort Trumbull.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept the commission Grant signed
narrative_blocks.body: Three years as a hospital steward in the regular army’s medical department had him often doing an assistant surgeon’s work. The commission, over the signature of Ulysses S. Grant, he kept as a souvenir of it.

narrative_blocks.header: Ill health sent him to a fruit plantation
narrative_blocks.body: Poor health drove him out of Connecticut for a milder climate. He bought land on the Isle of Pines in the West Indies, and in 1904 took over the management of a large fruit plantation with his sons to help him.

narrative_blocks.header: Treasurer, then vice-president, then president
narrative_blocks.body: He rose through every chair of the Connecticut Homeopathic Medical Society, and in 1901 was president of the alumni association of the New York Homeopathic Medical College and Hospital.

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve Mayflower passengers behind his mother
narrative_blocks.body: His mother Mary Bartlett was a daughter of the Rev. John Bartlett and descended from twelve of the Mayflower pilgrims, among them John Alden, Elder Brewster and John Howland.

people.relational_label_override: Brother-in-law of a Ninth Generation Hooker
Sister-in-law of a Ninth Generation Hooker

bio.bio_blurb: Teacher to the Chinese Educational Mission

narrative_blocks.header: The Mission boys brought her to Yung Wing
narrative_blocks.body: When the Chinese Educational Mission distributed its students among New England homes, she took charge of the education of several of them and grew deeply interested in the work. That was how she came to know the man who began it.

narrative_blocks.header: Chinese officials at an Avon wedding
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph Twichell, a warm friend to them both, married them at Avon on 24 February 1875. Chinese officials attended, and the Hartford paper called the occasion one of peculiar interest.

narrative_blocks.header: Washington, while home stayed in Hartford
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband was much aided in the educational work by her, and she kept her interest in it after the commission was withdrawn. When he was called to the Chinese legation she lived much of the time in Washington.

narrative_blocks.header: Two years of consumption, then Bright’s disease
narrative_blocks.body: She had been failing with consumption for two years or more when an acute attack of Bright’s disease killed her at thirty-four. She left two boys, ten and seven, and was buried at Cedar Hill.

people.relational_label_override: Sister-in-law of a Ninth Generation Hooker

notable.notable_blurb: First Chinese graduate of an American university

education.notes: Surveying; abandoned on his return to China

cross_connections.display_label: took the mission's Chinese boys into his Gunnery school from 1872
took Yale's first medical degree by a Black man three years later

narrative_blocks.header: The first Chinese man to finish Yale
narrative_blocks.body: He came by way of a mission school at Macao and Monson Academy, and took his degree at Yale in 1854 — the first Chinese student recorded to have graduated from an American college. He was librarian of Brothers in Unity.

narrative_blocks.header: A hundred and twenty boys to New England
narrative_blocks.body: He argued the Qing government into sending its young men to study science and engineering in America. From 1872 the Chinese Educational Mission placed a hundred and twenty boys in New England households; it was recalled in 1881.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty years a citizen, then not one
narrative_blocks.body: He was naturalized in 1852. Half a century on, the State Department wrote that the Chinese Exclusion Act had voided it and he could not return. Friends slipped him in anyway, in time to watch his son Bartlett graduate from Yale.

narrative_blocks.header: A price on his head after the coup
narrative_blocks.body: He had followed the Guangxu Emperor, whom he called the great pioneer of reform in China. When the Empress Dowager Cixi crushed the Hundred Days’ Reform in 1898 and the reformers were beheaded, a bounty was posted and he fled Shanghai.

narrative_blocks.header: Sent to Peru to see the labor camps
narrative_blocks.body: In 1874 he and the Hartford pastor Joseph Twichell traveled to Peru to look into the conditions of the Chinese laborers there. They found brutality that had already driven the men to strikes and brought violent suppression.

narrative_blocks.header: He came home unable to speak Chinese
narrative_blocks.body: After 154 days at sea a pilot boarded off Hong Kong and the captain asked him to interpret. He could not summon the Chinese for rocks and shoals. Being a Chinese, he wrote, yet not able to speak the language.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother asked what the degree paid
narrative_blocks.body: He had been gone ten years when he reached Macao, and she asked how much money the Yale parchment conferred. Knowledge is power, he told her, and power is greater than riches — and no other mother in China had such a son.

people.relational_label_override: Brother-in-law of a Ninth Generation Hooker

notable.notable_blurb: Fourth mayor of Brooklyn; New York state senator

career.organization: Smith & Bulkley, ferry and railroad concerns

cross_connections.display_label: laid out Green-Wood, and merged the ferries he came to head
, his granddaughter, drew the most used tarot deck in the world

narrative_blocks.header: The first Brooklyn mayor the people chose
narrative_blocks.body: The Board of Aldermen made him mayor in 1839; the next year the voters did it themselves, and he was the first man in Brooklyn to hold the office by their choice. A Democrat turned him out in 1842.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the ferries to Manhattan
narrative_blocks.body: After office he went in with William Bulkley, taking the presidency of Smith & Bulkley with the Catherine and Gouverneur Street crossings. He was the head and front of the Union Ferry Company, and a Brooklyn City Railroad director.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded the ground he is buried in
narrative_blocks.body: He was among the founders of Green-Wood Cemetery, and of the Brooklyn City Hospital. Green-Wood took him in February 1877, and his wife three months after him.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty years on the school board
narrative_blocks.body: He sat on the Brooklyn Board of Education for thirty years, and always took the part of public schooling. The state senate of 1856 was the last elective office he filled.

narrative_blocks.header: Six months in Brooklyn before a client
narrative_blocks.body: A farmer’s son from Hanover, he worked his way through Dartmouth, read law, and reached Brooklyn in 1827. Six months passed before a client came; he filled them making friends, and led the choir at the First Presbyterian.

narrative_blocks.header: He took in three Trumbull orphans
narrative_blocks.body: When Asaph Trumbull died in 1842 his three children — Charles Henry, Sarah and Mary Louise — came under Smith’s guardianship. They were not adopted, and kept their father’s name.

narrative_blocks.header: His granddaughter drew the tarot
narrative_blocks.body: Pamela Colman Smith, daughter of his son Charles, painted the eighty designs for Arthur Waite’s 1909 tarot pack. It is still the most widely used deck in the world.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty-three years in the one church
narrative_blocks.body: He joined Brooklyn’s First Church as a young man and stayed a member sixty-three years. The year after he died the congregation raised the Bryan Hooker Smith Memorial Building, holding the church house office and the minister’s study.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the ferry partner’s daughter
narrative_blocks.body: His father Cyrus Porter Smith ran the Catherine and Gouverneur Street crossings as Smith & Bulkley. In 1854 he married Elizabeth Conkling Bulkley, and their eldest son was christened William Bulkley Smith for the partner.

bio.bio_blurb: Shipping merchant; bank cashier; paint and lead partner

death.notes: At sea aboard the steamer Ville de Paris, returning from Europe

career.organization: F. W. Devoe & Co., paint merchants, Fulton Street
E. D. Hurlbut & Co., shipping merchants, South Street

narrative_blocks.header: Scarlet fever took him between Brest and home
narrative_blocks.body: He went ashore at Brest for a stroll, seemingly well, and complained of illness on re-embarking. Scarlet fever set in on the Sunday and killed him on the Tuesday, at sea aboard the Ville de Paris.

narrative_blocks.header: Shipping, then paint, then a bank
narrative_blocks.body: Home from his first Europe, he went into E. D. Hurlbut & Co., shipping merchants of South Street. The firm failed; he turned to paint and lead with James A. H. Bell, then took a cashier’s desk at the Importers and Traders Bank.

narrative_blocks.header: The bank desk broke his health
narrative_blocks.body: The confinement of the cashier’s work told on him and he resigned, going in with F. W. Devoe & Co. of Fulton Street. He was a partner there when he died, at thirty-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: He was coming home from his second Europe
narrative_blocks.body: He sailed on 2 June 1869 with his wife, fifteen years after his first crossing in company with his elder brother. He left four sons and a daughter; Ellen Maria outlived him by fifteen years.

narrative_blocks.header: The Ausable runs through her window
narrative_blocks.body: She and Willis Lord Ogden summered in the Adirondacks, and the small river in the Tiffany window raised to them at Brooklyn’s First Church is the Ausable. It is reckoned the finest glass in that sanctuary.

narrative_blocks.header: The two ferry houses married each other
narrative_blocks.body: Her family and her husband’s ran the East River crossings together as Smith & Bulkley — the Catherine and Gouverneur Street lines that fed the Union Ferry monopoly. Their eldest son was named William Bulkley Smith for the partner.

narrative_blocks.header: A Tiffany window holds their river
narrative_blocks.body: The fifth window in the sanctuary of Brooklyn’s First Church, The River of Life, came from Louis Comfort Tiffany’s studio and memorialises him and his wife. The water in it is the Ausable, in the Adirondacks where they summered.

cross_connections.display_label: , her three-times-great-grandfather, died a colonel mid-Revolution

narrative_blocks.header: Her leg was buried a sea away
narrative_blocks.body: She died at Kingston in July 1896 and was buried in Jamaica. Her amputated leg had been shipped to Brooklyn and put, that November, in an unmarked plot at Green-Wood — nowhere near the family graves.

notable.notable_blurb: Illustrator of the Rider–Waite tarot deck

cross_connections.display_label: collected her gouaches, and they hang in his castle still
, her grandfather, was mayor of Brooklyn before she was born
worked the same four trades, and published a novel at seventeen
published the Panchatantra jackal fables in English eighty years on
had a one-man show from Alfred Stieglitz in 1938

narrative_blocks.header: She painted eighty cards in six months
narrative_blocks.body: Waite commissioned a tarot pack from her in 1909 for a token fee, and she painted eighty designs between April and October. Rider published them, and the deck is still the most widely used in the world.

narrative_blocks.header: Stieglitz hung her before any other painter
narrative_blocks.body: In 1907 Alfred Stieglitz gave her a show at his Little Galleries of the Photo-Secession — the first work by anyone but a photographer to hang there. Thirty-three drawings sold, and he showed her twice more.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote down the Anansi stories
narrative_blocks.body: Part of her childhood was spent in Jamaica, where she learned the folk tales in Patois. Annancy Stories came out in 1899 and Chim-Chim in 1905, both written and illustrated by her.

narrative_blocks.header: Her press published women, then folded
narrative_blocks.body: She founded The Green Sheaf in 1903 and hand-painted the art in every copy; it lasted thirteen issues. The Green Sheaf Press followed in 1904 and printed mostly women writers before the money ran out.

narrative_blocks.header: She went to jail for the vote
narrative_blocks.body: She drew posters and cartoons for London’s Suffrage Atelier, a collective of professional illustrators working for women’s suffrage. She joined the protests too, and was jailed at least once.

narrative_blocks.header: She painted what the music looked like
narrative_blocks.body: She had synaesthesia, and painted the visions that came while she listened — Beethoven, Bach, Chopin, Debussy. She called them music pictures, and they are what Stieglitz wanted on his walls.

narrative_blocks.header: The certificate called her a spinster
narrative_blocks.body: She died at Bude in September 1951 with nothing. Her possessions were auctioned to pay her debts and her grave was never marked. The occupation entered on her certificate was Spinster of Independent Means.

narrative_blocks.header: He left the law for a classroom
narrative_blocks.body: He came first in the Ohio bar in 1948 and practised three years with Calfee, Fogg, McChord and Halter before quitting to teach at University School. He taught twenty-three years, and his favourite subject was the Constitution.

narrative_blocks.header: Every promotion, he asked to go back
narrative_blocks.body: The school kept handing him administration — college counselling, alumni secretary, head of the Lower School, assistant headmaster. After each stint he asked to be returned to the classroom.

narrative_blocks.header: He retired and learned the piano
narrative_blocks.body: At sixty he took piano lessons and started acting at the Chagrin Valley Little Theater. With George Spencer orchestrating he wrote seven musicals; five were staged at Chagrin Valley and one at Ashtabula.

narrative_blocks.header: Reminiscing in Tin Pan Alley
narrative_blocks.body: He carried a one-man programme of that name to nursing homes, churches and parlours, singing from the twenties through the fifties with patter on Duke Ellington, Count Basie and the Broadway houses.

narrative_blocks.header: A blow at eight kept him ashore
narrative_blocks.body: The Navy discharged him before Pearl Harbor on account of a head injury he had taken at the age of eight. He went to Dartmouth instead, and in his last year took the prize for the most improved grades since freshman year.

narrative_blocks.header: Alzheimer’s took him at Fairmount
narrative_blocks.body: He was an elder at Fairmount Presbyterian in Cleveland Heights for most of his life and died at its health centre in April 2005, after a long bout with Alzheimer’s. University School keeps a faculty fund in his name.

narrative_blocks.header: Vietnam, then thirty years of mail
narrative_blocks.body: He served in the Vietnam war and kept his American Legion membership after it. More than thirty years of his working life went to the Post Office, and he was a steady guitar player.

narrative_blocks.header: The All Cleveland girls’ hockey team
narrative_blocks.body: She played field hockey at Laurel School and again at Smith, and while still in high school was picked for the All Cleveland girls’ team. Tennis and golf came later; her knitting went everywhere, stop lights included.

narrative_blocks.header: She was treasurer of everything
narrative_blocks.body: Strong in mathematics and with money, she kept the books and raised funds for Project Friendship, Laurel School, the Junior League and Breckenridge Village. Project Friendship became Big Brothers Big Sisters of Cleveland.

narrative_blocks.header: Three years away, for his law degree
narrative_blocks.body: She married Jack in September 1943, and they lived about Cleveland all their lives but for the three years he spent at law school in Los Angeles. She outlived him by fourteen years.

narrative_blocks.header: Three names on one yield curve
narrative_blocks.body: With John Cox and Stephen Ross he set out a theory of the term structure of interest rates in 1985. The Cox–Ingersoll–Ross model carries the three names still and is standard equipment for pricing bonds.

narrative_blocks.header: He read physics before he read finance
narrative_blocks.body: His bachelor’s degree from MIT in 1971 was in physics, taken Phi Beta Kappa. The master’s and the doctorate that followed were from the Sloan School, and Robert Merton supervised the thesis.

narrative_blocks.header: Named Financial Engineer of the Year
narrative_blocks.body: The International Association of Financial Engineers gave him the title in 2002, the same year Risk magazine put him in its hall of fame. He was a founding committee member of the Society for Financial Studies.

narrative_blocks.header: Tell me the price of tomatoes
narrative_blocks.body: He put the logic of derivative pricing in a line: tell me the price of tomatoes, and I’ll tell you the price of ketchup. He did little consulting — having the time to think, he said, mattered more than the money.

narrative_blocks.header: How we ruined the world with derivatives
narrative_blocks.body: He liked to open a course by promising to teach how he and his colleagues ruined the world with derivatives. After 2008 he put it another way: the trouble is that we model a horse race as though it were roulette.

narrative_blocks.header: Students just call it The Ingersoll
narrative_blocks.body: Theory of Financial Decision Making appeared in 1987 and is still set in doctoral courses, where students use no title but call it The Ingersoll. He retired in 2018 after thirty-five years at Yale, meaning to revise it.

narrative_blocks.header: He took VPI to a conference title
narrative_blocks.body: In 1916 he coached the Virginia Agricultural and Mechanical College — Virginia Tech now — to seven wins and two losses, and to first place in the South Atlantic conference, unbeaten inside it.

narrative_blocks.header: Head coach the year after he stopped playing
narrative_blocks.body: He played quarterback at Dartmouth from 1907 to 1910 and had Colgate’s head coaching job the next season, at twenty-two. That year went three and five; his whole record came to ten and eight.

narrative_blocks.header: Three of the name, two of them Jack
narrative_blocks.body: He was the second Jonathan Edwards Ingersoll of three. His nephew, born in 1918, was called Jack as well and went to Dartmouth as well; that nephew’s son is the economist of the yield-curve model.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the Chicago Renaissance
narrative_blocks.body: The Chicago Renaissance in American Letters came out in 1956 and his Chicago’s Public Wits in 1983. Between them he covered the city’s literary flowering and the comic newspaper tradition that ran beside it.

narrative_blocks.header: Oberlin, Ohio State, then Duke
narrative_blocks.body: He took his first degree at Oberlin and his doctorate at Ohio State, taught at Michigan State and Minnesota, and joined the Duke English department in 1963 to teach American poetry.

narrative_blocks.header: A Fulbright year in Copenhagen
narrative_blocks.body: A Fulbright carried him to the University of Copenhagen in 1970, and he was a visiting professor at Irvine. His last book, in 1986, was on the writing of William Carlos Williams.

narrative_blocks.header: Oberlin, then a parish schoolroom
narrative_blocks.body: She went from Chagrin Falls High School to Oberlin, as her brother Bernard did, and taught the lower grades at St. Joan of Arc in Chagrin Falls. She outlived two husbands and was ninety-three at her death.

narrative_blocks.header: Almost forty years in the same gym
narrative_blocks.body: He taught physical education at University School for close to forty years, coaching middle school and varsity soccer, swimming and track. In all that time his soccer teams had one losing season.

narrative_blocks.header: A million pennies to show a million
narrative_blocks.body: To teach the boys what a million looked like he ran a million-penny drive, and the money went to a scholarship. He brought movement exploration into the school’s curriculum and wrote parents a booklet on throwing and catching.

narrative_blocks.header: He followed his father-in-law into teaching
narrative_blocks.body: He married Kim Ingersoll and went after her father Jack, class of 1936, into the University School faculty. In later years he taught physical education there alongside his own son Bill.

narrative_blocks.header: Lincoln, and the question of the day
narrative_blocks.body: He was a student of Abraham Lincoln and liked telling the primary boys about him. His lunch table waited on his question of the day, and he gave historic tours for the Chagrin Falls Historical Society.

bio.bio_blurb: Second First Lady of the United States

cross_connections.display_label: was sent a birthday poem by her son John Quincy Adams in 1846
, her great-great-granddaughter, married into the Perkins family

narrative_blocks.header: Remember the ladies, she wrote in 1776
narrative_blocks.body: In March 1776 she asked John and the Congress to remember the ladies and not put unlimited power into the hands of husbands, or the ladies would foment a rebellion. He wrote back about the despotism of the petticoat.

narrative_blocks.header: Her opponents called her Mrs. President
narrative_blocks.body: She held a dinner every week, appeared in public constantly, and knew the business of her husband's administration before the public did. Opponents took to calling her Mrs. President. She backed the Alien and Sedition Acts.

narrative_blocks.header: She ran the farm and bought the debt
narrative_blocks.body: With John at Philadelphia and then in Europe she ran Braintree and the money alone. Through her uncle Cotton Tufts she put the family savings into war debt, and federal payment at face value carried the Adamses for the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: She taught a free black boy to read
narrative_blocks.body: A free black youth came to her Philadelphia door in 1791 asking to be taught his letters. She placed him in an evening school over a neighbour objecting, and answered that she had not thought it a disgrace to teach him in her parlour.

narrative_blocks.header: No schooling, and the best read of them
narrative_blocks.body: Sickness and her sex kept her out of school; her mother taught her to read and cipher. She read her way through her father, grandfather and uncle libraries in English and French, and was the most erudite woman ever to be first lady.

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve hundred letters, and hers the better
narrative_blocks.body: Twelve hundred letters between her and John survive, written across his years at Philadelphia and in Europe. They argue government and politics as equals, and the self-taught wife is the more vivid writer of the two.

narrative_blocks.header: She told him it would not be long
narrative_blocks.body: Typhoid took her at Quincy on 28 October 1818, a fortnight short of seventy-four. Her last words were do not grieve, my dearest friend, I am ready to go — and John, it will not be long. He followed on 4 July 1826.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought the room where Hartford dealt
narrative_blocks.body: A farmer at West Springfield until his own father died, he came to Hartford on the first day of 1817 and bought the Exchange Coffee House, where the town settled its business. He took the City Hotel in 1829 and retired in 1835.

narrative_blocks.header: Aetna's first policy covered his own house
narrative_blocks.body: He was among the founders of the Aetna Fire Insurance Company in 1819 and a director of it to his death — and the first policy the company ever wrote was the one he took out on his own property.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought out the partners who hesitated
narrative_blocks.body: The Great Fire of New York in 1835 burned out Wall Street houses Aetna had insured. He took over the stakes of investors who balked at paying, the claims were met at once, and the firm's premiums tripled on the reputation it made.

narrative_blocks.header: He undid his son's first partnership
narrative_blocks.body: Junius took a partnership with the Boston banker Alfred Welles against his advice, and inside a year he had to settle the debts and dissolve it. He put the boy into Morgan Ketchum at New York, then bought him into Howe Mather at Hartford.

narrative_blocks.header: The house of Morgan started at his inn
narrative_blocks.body: He left farming for a tavern, a stagecoach line and a hotel, and put the profits into banks, canals, railroads and steamship lines. What he left in 1847 set Junius up in London, and his grandson was J. Pierpont Morgan.

narrative_blocks.header: Pierpont was born in his Asylum Street house
narrative_blocks.body: He settled the family on Asylum Street, and there on 17 April 1837 his son Junius and Juliet Pierpont had the boy they called Pip — John Pierpont Morgan. The house is gone; a photograph of it as a boarding house survives.

narrative_blocks.header: His daughters married Hartford families
narrative_blocks.body: Mary and Lucy both married into leading Hartford houses, Lucy into the Goodwins. The Morgans were Trinity Episcopal, where the Goodwins were a first family, and Junius kept a dry goods store on Main Street before banking took him to Boston.

bio.bio_blurb: Director of the Hartford Orphan Asylum

landmarks.landmark_blurb: The Asylum Street house she kept; her grandson was born in it in 1837.

narrative_blocks.header: Sally ran the orphan asylum at Hartford
narrative_blocks.body: She was known as Sally, and she was director of the Hartford Orphan Asylum in the years her husband kept the coffee house where the town did its business and sat on the board of the insurance company he had helped found.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at twenty, three children by six
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah Spencer married Joseph Morgan of West Springfield at Middletown on 20 September 1807. She was twenty and he twenty-seven. Mary came in 1808, Lucy in 1811 and Junius in 1813.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother's people held a Scituate pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: The Eells came down her mother’s side. Rev. Nathaniel Eells kept the Scituate parish forty-seven years, rode to his parishioners doors to ask after their health, and prepared Thomas Clap, later president of Yale, for Harvard.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived Joseph by twelve years
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph died at Hartford in July 1847 and she lived on there to August 1859. Both lie at Cedar Hill. By then Junius was a partner in London, and her grandson Pierpont was twenty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: He took Connecticut deeds in New York
narrative_blocks.body: Union College sent him to the law, and from 1844 to 1850 he was Connecticut’s commissioner of deeds in New York — the officer who made a Connecticut conveyance good across the line. He rose from that to the Superior Court bench.

narrative_blocks.header: The second Edward Elias, and a third bachelor
narrative_blocks.body: He was named for the brother who had died at five in 1808, two years before he was born. Like James and Henry Booth he never married, and like them he was buried at Rhinebeck. He was fifty-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: Her four sisters were her bridesmaids
narrative_blocks.body: She married the Rev. William Henry Morrison, rector of the Church of the Ascension at Rhinecliff, in June 1894. Louise, Florence, Clara and Mabel stood up with her and their brother Henry ushered. Her daughter Dorothy came the next June.

narrative_blocks.header: She did not reach fourteen
narrative_blocks.body: She was born at New York in June 1895, the only child of the Rhinecliff rector and Catherine Esselstyn, a year after their wedding. She died at Rhinebeck in October 1908, at thirteen.

narrative_blocks.header: He laid out downtown Jersey City
narrative_blocks.body: With his cousin Richard Varick and Justice Jacob Radcliff he bought up Paulus Hook, and in 1804 the three formed the Associates of the Jersey Company. The streets and squares they drew are still the plan of downtown Jersey City.

narrative_blocks.header: He freed Hannah in 1811
narrative_blocks.body: On the third of July 1811 he set his hand and seal to a deed manumitting Hannah, a woman of about thirty-three whom he had bought from Isaac Clason — freeing her fully, freely and absolutely, without claim upon her ever after.

narrative_blocks.header: Washington slept in his grandfather's house
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Preakness in his grandfather Col. Theunis Dey’s house, which Washington took as headquarters through part of 1780. That house stands in New Jersey farm country, not on the Paulus Hook flats he laid out later.

narrative_blocks.header: Dey Street was cut through family ground
narrative_blocks.body: The Manhattan land was older still. Dirck Dey came out of the Holland navy in 1638 and took ground in the lower city; the street driven through it carries the name yet. Eight generations alternated Dirck or Richard with Theunis or Anthony.

narrative_blocks.header: Lafayette and Hamilton came to that house
narrative_blocks.body: The room kept as Washington’s office at Preakness saw Anthony Wayne, Nathanael Greene, Alexander Hamilton, Henry Knox and the Marquis de Lafayette. The house stands, and the family name is on it still.

narrative_blocks.body: She married Joseph Howland Bill of Norwich in 1838, at seventeen, and bore ten. Two girls christened Lillian died as infants, and two boys were both Edward Woolsey. Widowed in 1865, she died at West Chester in 1889.

narrative_blocks.body: The eldest Dey son went south and died of yellow fever at New Orleans in September 1847, at twenty-four. His brother James and five sisters all outlived him, four of them into the twentieth century.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded the magazine Frontiers
narrative_blocks.body: John founded Frontiers, the natural history magazine of the Academy of Natural Sciences in Philadelphia, and was its editor. He also wrote for Scientific Monthly and the Philadelphia Evening Bulletin.

narrative_blocks.header: A column called Along the Mall
narrative_blocks.body: After the war John created the Department of Public Interest at Columbia Presbyterian Medical Center, and from 1951 worked in marketing and then as a shopping-center consultant. His How to Promote Your Shopping Center was among Library Journal's top fifty business books of 1973, and he wrote the monthly column Along the Mall for Chain Store Age.

narrative_blocks.header: A Silver Star in the South Pacific
narrative_blocks.body: John was awarded the Silver Star and several Navy commendations for his service in the South Pacific in the Second World War, and retired from the Naval Reserve a commander in January 1954.

narrative_blocks.header: A garden at the Marine Museum
narrative_blocks.body: At Amagansett John founded the Friends of the East Hampton Town Marine Museum, raised its funds and organized its children's safari, and the museum named its new garden for him. He was a director of the East Hampton Historical Society.

narrative_blocks.header: Stories of the war, not yet a book
narrative_blocks.body: John was gathering his short stories about the war into a book in his last months. One of them, “A Year and a Day,” ends: “A man is often hard put to explain himself to himself . . . you can only trust that business inside yourself — intuition.”

narrative_blocks.header: The son lived twenty months
narrative_blocks.body: He married Eleanor Verlenden Dick of Darby, and their son Thomas was born at Philadelphia in May 1943 and buried in Chester County before his second birthday. The three of them lie together at Chester Springs.

narrative_blocks.header: Funny, four Pynes and a Maine churchyard
narrative_blocks.body: She married Herbert Rivington Pyne Jr. in February 1948 and had Lydia, James, Joseph and Blair. The family called her Funny. She died at Waldoboro in Maine in 2006 and lies there, and her son James was brought back to the same ground.

narrative_blocks.body: Margaret married Preston Lea Spruance at Annapolis on 25 June 1932, and they had four children. In April 1961 she married John Herbert Fulweiler, whose first wife, Susan Candler Kennedy, had married Preston Spruance six years before.

Carrier Division 2 aboard USS Enterprise; Guadalcanal; Leyte Gulf; present at the surrender aboard USS Missouri.
