narrative_blocks.header: The admiral who ran the Pacific war
narrative_blocks.body: He commanded the South Pacific from October 1942 and the Third Fleet from 1944 — the naval war against Japan from Guadalcanal up to Tokyo Bay. The press called him Bull. Hit hard, hit fast, hit often, he said, and the Navy repeated it.

narrative_blocks.header: He escorted convoys before he ever flew
narrative_blocks.body: His first war was the other one. He took the destroyer USS Shaw across the Atlantic in 1918 through water the German U-boats patrolled, shepherding convoys, and came out of it with the Navy Cross. He was thirty-five.

narrative_blocks.header: He learned to fly at fifty-two
narrative_blocks.body: Offered the Saratoga in 1934 on condition he qualify as an air observer, he enrolled in the full twelve-week pilot course instead and took his wings in May 1935 — the oldest man ever to earn them in the United States Navy.

narrative_blocks.header: He was at sea when Pearl Harbor burned
narrative_blocks.body: His task force, built round the carrier Enterprise, was two hundred miles out when the Japanese struck on 7 December 1941. For weeks after, it was very nearly the only operational battle group left in the Pacific.

narrative_blocks.header: He turned north and left the strait open
narrative_blocks.body: At Leyte Gulf in October 1944 he took the whole Third Fleet after Ozawa’s carriers and sank all four. San Bernardino Strait was left unguarded, and Kurita came through it onto the escort carriers off Samar.

narrative_blocks.header: A typhoon cost him three destroyers
narrative_blocks.body: In December 1944 he held formation against a Pacific storm on a forecast that proved wrong. Typhoon Cobra took three destroyers, eight hundred and two men and a hundred and forty-six aircraft. A court of inquiry found an error of judgement.

narrative_blocks.header: He stood on the Missouri for the surrender
narrative_blocks.body: Japan signed on the deck of his flagship on 2 September 1945. He took the oath as Fleet Admiral that December, the fourth and still the last naval officer to hold the rank, and lies at Arlington beside his parents.

parents.father_research_notes: Frank Louis Grandy of Norfolk, Virginia

people.research_notes: MARRIAGE DATE, TWO SOURCES: FamilySearch has John Herbert Fulweiler marrying Margaret Bradford Halsey on 12 April 1961, and her gravestone reads 'Margaret Bradford Halsey Spruance-Fulweiler … (m. 1961)', so the Fulweiler marriage is on the stone. His own obituary lists Susan Chandler Kennedy (1938), Maude Lennox (1959) and Virginia Hohensee Beadle (1977) and omits her. Both Maude and Virginia are built. Worth a marriage record naming the groom if one turns up; nothing here is in question beyond the ordering of his wives. Margaret's first husband was Preston Lea Spruance (daughter Margaret Grandy "Poppy" Spruance, 1935-2000, not in the tree).

bio.bio_blurb: Wife of Fleet Admiral William F. Halsey Jr.

narrative_blocks.header: She learned he was flying by letter
narrative_blocks.body: She married him at Norfolk on the first of December 1909. He had her blessing to train as an air observer in 1934; she found out from a letter that he had switched to pilot. What is the old fool doing now, she said.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried the name to the Pacific coast
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Brooklyn in October 1887 and named for his grandfather, he ended ninety-seven years away at Carmel-by-the-Sea in California, with Phyllis Burn of Ontario. The Brooklyn Smiths lie at Green-Wood; these two do not.

people.research_notes: Parents, research only per Sam: Hugh Lenox Hodge Dick (1883-1940) and Rebecca Lewis Verlenden Dick (1885-1941).
Second wife per his obituary, m. 10 Oct 1959 at Lyme, New London County, Connecticut.
Third wife per his obituary, m. 8 Oct 1977 at East Hampton, Suffolk County, New York.

career.organization: New York & New Jersey Fire Proofing Company, Keyport

narrative_blocks.header: Scutari is Shkodra, in the Albanian north
narrative_blocks.body: Shkodra, or Scutari to the consulates, was the chief town of Gheg Albania under Ottoman rule, and Britain had kept a vice-consul there since Edward Lear's day. He took the post in 1901 and acted a while as charge d'affaires at Cetinje.

narrative_blocks.header: Fourteen months married, and dead at Menton
narrative_blocks.body: He married Dorothy Christine Richards on 30 October 1901, in the middle of the Albanian posting. He was dead on the French Riviera at Menton on 6 January 1903, at thirty, and she had been his wife for fourteen months.

bio.bio_blurb: Victoria Cross general of the Madras Engineers

narrative_blocks.header: He shouted, and the matchlock turned on him
narrative_blocks.body: At Mundisore in November 1857 he saw an Afghan mercenary levelling a matchlock at Lieutenant George Dew, who was riding past unaware of him. He shouted and rode at the man, who turned and fired into his ribs, close to the heart.

narrative_blocks.header: The ball came out just before the gangrene
narrative_blocks.body: Surgeons argued over the wound while his condition worsened. A military surgeon, William Mackenzie, finally cut the ball out of his ribs in time to stop the gangrene setting in. He was back in the field by the new year.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-odd crosses on a foggy day at Windsor
narrative_blocks.body: Queen Victoria pinned the Victoria Cross on him in the quadrangle at Windsor on 4 January 1860, with more than twenty others of the Mutiny. He thought little of the parade: they advanced on her, he wrote, in slovenly style.

narrative_blocks.header: Mandalay in a month, and no command after
narrative_blocks.body: He took the Burma Field Force out in October 1885 and held Mandalay by 29 November, which brought him a knighthood. The rising that followed went badly with the men he had, and he was never offered a senior command again.

narrative_blocks.header: Eighty-three old soldiers out of the workhouse
narrative_blocks.body: He sat on the committee for the Albert Hall commemoration of the Mutiny's fiftieth anniversary in 1907 and led the fundraising for its survivors. It took eighty-three of them out of workhouses and lifted 243 off the Poor Law.

narrative_blocks.header: His Victoria Cross was called a fake
narrative_blocks.body: In the 1980s the National Army Museum suggested the cross his family had lent it was a copy. A study of the metal in 2020 found it an unusually close match to other crosses struck the same year. It is displayed at Chatham.

education.school_name: Leland Powers School of Radio and Theatre

parents.father_research_notes: Reed Lewis of Waterford and Northumberland, Saratoga County, New York

narrative_blocks.header: She was twenty-seven, and the baby followed
narrative_blocks.body: A daughter of Reed Lewis of Waterford in Saratoga County, she married Elijah Cowles in the April of 1845. She died at Farmington in the September of 1848, and her infant son Gad died within days of her.

bio.bio_blurb: Farmington town officer and company treasurer

narrative_blocks.header: Register of voters, constable, notary, treasurer
narrative_blocks.body: He held the small offices of Farmington for thirty years — register of voters from 1876, constable from 1878, notary public from 1893 — and was bookkeeper and then treasurer of the Upson and Hart Company at Unionville.

narrative_blocks.header: He left Farmington at fifty-seven
narrative_blocks.body: After more than fifty years in the town he was giving a New York City address by 1903 and living in Brooklyn by 1907, probably until he died. He was buried back at Farmington all the same.

career.organization: Upson and Hart Company, Unionville, Connecticut

narrative_blocks.header: Five years of Shakespeare before the camera
narrative_blocks.body: Out of Yale he went on the stage and spent five years in the Shakespearean repertory company of Augustin Daly, the New York theatre manager. He did not make a film until 1914, when he was thirty-six.

narrative_blocks.header: The Lost World, Lord Jim, and Buster Keaton
narrative_blocks.body: He turned up across the silent landmarks: the dinosaurs of The Lost World and Keaton's Seven Chances, both 1925, Lord Jim the same year, then The Scarlet Letter and Lon Chaney's London After Midnight.

narrative_blocks.header: A mean looker, but a perfect gent
narrative_blocks.body: He was cast for a hard face and spent the silent years playing heavies, henchmen and hard cases. A New York paper ran his picture in March 1924 under exactly that line, thinking the contrast worth printing.

narrative_blocks.header: He was still working the year he died
narrative_blocks.body: From 1914 to 1943 he worked steadily as a character actor, billed variously as Jules Cowles, J. D. Cowles and Julius D. Cowles. His last pictures reached the screen the year he died at Hollywood, at sixty-five.

narrative_blocks.header: His great-uncle held the name sixty-seven years
narrative_blocks.body: He was born in 1877 and given the name of his grandfather's brother, Julius Deming Cowles of Farmington, who was then sixty-seven and lived another seventeen years. Hollywood shortened it to Jules.

cross_connections.display_label: acted in Augustin Daly's company before she married a Gould

notable.notable_blurb: Silent-era film character actor

education.notes: Economics, magna cum laude; Phi Beta Kappa.

bio.bio_blurb: Manila shipping clerk; Red Cross official

narrative_blocks.header: He went out to Manila at sixteen
narrative_blocks.body: At sixteen he sailed for the Philippines and went into the old Boston shipping houses of Russell, Sturgis & Co. and Peel, Hubbell & Co. He did not come home to the United States until 1882, seventeen years later.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the Red Cross in Puerto Rico
narrative_blocks.body: In the First World War he took charge of Red Cross work in Puerto Rico. He was near seventy, and had been out of the tropics for more than thirty years by then.

narrative_blocks.header: Two sons, born when he was past sixty
narrative_blocks.body: George Austen Jr. was born at Charlottesville in 1908 and became a doctor at Chestnut Hill in Massachusetts; David Edward followed thirteen months later. He kept the house on Rugby Road and thirty years in Albemarle County.

career.organization: Russell, Sturgis & Co. and Peel, Hubbell & Co., Manila

narrative_blocks.header: She married a man thirty years older
narrative_blocks.body: She was twenty-eight and George Austen fifty-eight when they married in October 1907. Their two sons were born at Charlottesville in the next two years, and she outlived him by almost eleven.

narrative_blocks.header: Garden clubs in two states, and Monday Club
narrative_blocks.body: She kept houses at Brandon in Vermont and at Charlottesville, and worked in the garden clubs of both towns. At Brandon she belonged to the Monday Club as well.

narrative_blocks.header: She went back to Vermont at the end
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Alburgh on Lake Champlain in 1878, she was living at Brandon again after George died at Charlottesville in 1938. She died in a Boston hospital in January 1949 after a long illness, leaving six grandchildren.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father sat for Alburgh in the legislature
narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Alburgh on 18 November 1878 to Hardy L. Reynolds, born 1855 and dead in 1927, and Anna Gallagher, married the year before. Her father sat for the town in the Vermont legislature; she took her grandmother Julia Landon's name.

narrative_blocks.header: He went inside for Kairos and Cursillo
narrative_blocks.body: He worked the Kairos and Cursillo prison ministries in Texas and in California, going into the prisons to run them. He retired from Con-Agra and came back to Texas in 1992 to be near the family.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-one years married, then ten alone
narrative_blocks.body: He married Betty Gaines at the Robert Carr Chapel in Fort Worth in April 1957, and they had fifty-one years. She died in 2008 and he lived another ten, dying at Arlington at ninety-two.

career.organization: Kairos and Cursillo prison ministries, Texas and California

narrative_blocks.header: He came off the Tuscania off Islay
narrative_blocks.body: A corporal with the 20th Engineers, he sailed from Hoboken in January 1918 and was aboard when the submarine UB-77 put a torpedo into the troopship Tuscania off Islay on 5 February. She sank in about four hours; 210 did not come off.

cross_connections.display_label: bought French timber for the army as a major of the forestry engineers

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-two years at the ballistics lab
narrative_blocks.body: Willis served in the Army, then spent thirty-two years of civil service as an engineer at the Ballistic Research Laboratory at Aberdeen Proving Ground, from 1954 until he retired in 1986.

narrative_blocks.header: The lab that ordered the ENIAC
narrative_blocks.body: The laboratory Willis joined had commissioned the ENIAC, the first electronic general-purpose computer, to work out artillery firing tables, and when he arrived it was running the same work on the ORDVAC, built for it at the University of Illinois.

narrative_blocks.header: King Sized Numbers Just For Laughs
narrative_blocks.body: At Willis's laboratory the ORDVAC and its successor, BRLESC, wrote the hexadecimal digits ten to fifteen not as A to F but as K, S, N, J, F, L: King Sized Numbers Just For Laughs.

cross_connections.display_label: designed the arithmetic of the ORDVAC built for his Aberdeen lab

career.organization: Ballistics Research Laboratory, Aberdeen Proving Ground

sources.label: Wikipedia, ORDVAC; Wikipedia, Ballistic Research Laboratory

narrative_blocks.header: A nurse who retired into a travel agency
narrative_blocks.body: She took her registered nurse's diploma at the Episcopal Hospital School of Nursing in Philadelphia, worked hospitals in Harford and Baltimore counties and taught nursing at Harford Community College. In retirement she sold travel.

education.school_name: Episcopal Hospital School of Nursing, Philadelphia

narrative_blocks.header: He was the one who went to Victoria
narrative_blocks.body: The youngest of the four, born at San Antonio in 1888, he was living at Victoria on the coastal plain by the time his mother died. He outlasted all three of the others, dying in 1961.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at thirty-five by a Virginia field
narrative_blocks.body: Felix Todd died in the crash near Saxe in June 1943, when she was thirty-five. She outlived him by fifteen years, and was buried beside him at Fort Sam Houston.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at the base dispensary at forty-seven
narrative_blocks.body: He was a civilian inspector for the Air Force. On 1 March 1960 a heart attack took him at forty-seven, and he was pronounced dead at the USAF dispensary at Kelly Air Force Base in his own city.

career.organization: United States Air Force, Kelly Air Force Base

narrative_blocks.header: Three mayors of San Antonio behind her
narrative_blocks.body: She descended from John W. Smith, the city's first mayor under the Republic of Texas, and from her great-grandfather Samuel C. Bell, another mayor. Col. Samuel Galitzin Newton, a third, was her great-great-grandfather.

narrative_blocks.header: A Canary Island family founded her city
narrative_blocks.body: She was reckoned a descendant of Maria de Jesus Curbelo, of one of the Canary Island families brought out to found San Fernando de Bexar in 1731. John W. Smith, who took thirty-two men from Gonzales into the Alamo, was also of her line.

cross_connections.display_label: was custodian of the Alamo before her 1907 marriage

narrative_blocks.header: Insurance for years, then Del Rio and horses
narrative_blocks.body: She worked in insurance for many years before keeping house, and lived her whole life at Del Rio. She kept horses and dogs and was remembered for a contagious smile and a vivacious laugh.

narrative_blocks.header: He was both a reverend and a doctor
narrative_blocks.body: He carried the Reverend in front of his name and the M.D. behind it. He was named for his grandfather Henry Martyn Newton, who had been born out in the Cherokee Nation.

narrative_blocks.header: She died on her ninety-first birthday
narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Wichita in Texas on 29 December 1924 and died on 29 December 2015, ninety-one years to the day.

bio.notes: Name unknown

narrative_blocks.header: Buried under a coconut palm off Mazatlan
narrative_blocks.body: He died of a ruptured appendix aboard the USS California in Mazatlan harbour in July 1914, at thirty-two. They buried him on Isla de Venados among the coconut palms, and his people later brought him home to Marfa.

narrative_blocks.header: She came from Alameda to a river ranch
narrative_blocks.body: She married at the end of 1916 and came out from Alameda in California to live at La Sauceda, down towards the Rio Grande. She remembered the neighbours and the river guards calling in through those first years.

narrative_blocks.header: She taught at Brownsville for many years
narrative_blocks.body: She took her degree from the University of Texas in 1916, the year she married, and taught school at Brownsville long after. She belonged to the Daughters of the American Revolution, the Art League and the Self Culture Club.

bio.bio_blurb: Field artillery colonel and family genealogist

narrative_blocks.header: He took the 325th to the Elbe
narrative_blocks.body: He organised and commanded the 325th Field Artillery Battalion of the 84th Division, the Railsplitters, through the Rhineland, the Ardennes and central Europe. Their war ended on the west bank of the Elbe.

narrative_blocks.header: His father died at sea; he was four
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Devisadero in El Salvador to a mining engineer, he was four when his father died aboard ship off Mazatlan. His mother took him home to Marfa, where Judge and Mrs. W. W. Bogel raised him and he worked as a ranch hand.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the day after he graduated
narrative_blocks.body: He tried plebe years at both the Naval Academy and Texas A&M before joining the West Point class of 1934. He graduated on 12 June and married Charlotte Nanson at West Point on the 13th.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote his family's genealogy at eighty
narrative_blocks.body: After years of research on both sides of the Atlantic he published The Genealogy of the Hubbard and Bogel Families of Presidio County, Texas, in 1990. He died the February after it came out.

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve granite benches on Trophy Point
narrative_blocks.body: He chaired the committee that chose his class's fiftieth reunion gift to West Point - twelve granite benches on Trophy Point, presented to the Superintendent in June 1984.

narrative_blocks.header: A floral Railsplitter patch at his burial
narrative_blocks.body: He died of pulmonary fibrosis a little after noon in February 1991 and was buried two days later at Fort Bliss, the ceremony carrying a large floral patch of his old division. He was moved to West Point afterwards.

cross_connections.display_label: was his first cousin, and took the Bogel stories down in 1953
took up genealogy at sixty-five and traced the Newton line to Roger

narrative_blocks.header: A distinguished graduate in the war year
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Fort Sam Houston, raised at Marfa and Brownsville, and took chemical engineering at Texas A&M in the class of 1943 as a distinguished graduate. He married Anne Rootes the same year.

bio.bio_blurb: Family chronicler of the Marfa Bogels

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote the stories down in 1953
narrative_blocks.body: In 1953 her father sat and told her the Bogel ranch country whole - the burro milk, the cave at La Tinaja, the cattlemen who roped the tent - and she set it on paper. Much of what the family knows of Marfa comes down through her.

cross_connections.display_label: was her first cousin, and put the Hubbard and Bogel families in print

narrative_blocks.header: West Point, twenty-four years behind his father
narrative_blocks.body: He took the class of 1958 at West Point, twenty-four years behind his father's class of 1934, made colonel as his father had, and served in Vietnam. They lie in the same post cemetery.

narrative_blocks.header: She died on the day he had died
narrative_blocks.body: Craig Chamberlain died at Albuquerque on 10 April 2012, after forty-five years of marriage. She died at Albuquerque on 10 April 2025, thirteen years later to the day, and was buried beside him at Santa Fe.

narrative_blocks.header: Four tours in Vietnam with Special Forces
narrative_blocks.body: He gave thirty years to the Army, most of them in Special Forces, and served four tours in Vietnam. He came home with the Distinguished Service Cross, a Purple Heart, and the Bronze Star with V.

narrative_blocks.header: Weddings, buryings and everything between
narrative_blocks.body: He piped with the Ballut Abyad Shrine band around Albuquerque, and said of it that he played for weddings, buryings and everything in between.

narrative_blocks.header: He rode to Fort Huachuca to inspect it
narrative_blocks.body: A Norwich man of 1909 and a career ordnance officer, he commanded the arsenal at Fort Sam Houston. He made the inspection at Fort Huachuca on horseback, which his grandson was still telling fifty years later.

cross_connections.display_label: , his grandson, was stationed at Fort Huachuca two generations later

narrative_blocks.header: An ordnance officer's daughter in the Philippines
narrative_blocks.body: Her father's postings carried the family around the country and out to the Philippines in the 1930s. She married Charles Baker at San Antonio in June 1942, and the two of them lie in the same national cemetery as her parents.

narrative_blocks.header: She was Doady Collins, then Doady Ireland
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Davenport in Iowa, she followed her veterinarian husband around army posts and Germany and raised two sons who both took commissions. After he died in 1974 she went to Boca Raton and married again.

narrative_blocks.header: Three wars, then agriculture at Holland High
narrative_blocks.body: He served the Army through the Second World War, Korea and Vietnam and was a lieutenant colonel of the Texas National Guard. He then taught vocational agriculture at Holland High School until he retired in 1975.

narrative_blocks.header: An Army veterinarian through three wars
narrative_blocks.body: He took his degree in veterinary medicine at Ohio State in 1942 and a regular commission in the Veterinary Corps, serving the Second World War, Korea and Vietnam. After twenty-four years he inspected meat for North Carolina.

narrative_blocks.header: He was posted where his grandfather had ridden
narrative_blocks.body: Trained as a chemical officer, he was stationed at Fort Huachuca - the post his grandfather Everett Collins had once ridden to on horseback to inspect. Vietnam followed, with the 1st Air Cavalry Division.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote up the world's mines for Interior
narrative_blocks.body: After a geology master's he went to the Bureau of Mines and then the Geological Survey, covering South America and later Australia and Oceania, and wrote chapters of the Minerals Yearbook.

cross_connections.display_label: , his grandfather, rode horseback to inspect Fort Huachuca

education.school_name: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

bio.display_name: Lt. Col. Felix Alexander Todd Jr.

narrative_blocks.header: He trained the Army's infantry officers
narrative_blocks.body: Born in Muskogee County in Oklahoma in 1905, he went into the infantry and commanded battalions of the First and then the Second Student Training regiment at Fort Benning, the school that turned out the Army's infantry officers.

narrative_blocks.header: Six died when the transport hit a rise
narrative_blocks.body: He was on the operations staff of the Army War College by 1943, flying back to Washington from Benning on 30 June, when the transport dropped a flare, tried a field near Saxe in Virginia, hit a rise and burned.

bio.bio_blurb: Bristol-born wife of a Sherborn doctor

parents.father_research_notes: Angel Torrey (1657-1728)

narrative_blocks.header: Her father was named Angell
narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Bristol to Angell Torrey of Weymouth, who removed to Mendon and then to Rhode Island, and his wife Hannah Williams. Her grandfather was Capt. William Torrey of Weymouth; these are not the Torreys already in this tree.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brother’s line reached the White House
narrative_blocks.body: Her brother William, born at Bristol in 1700, was great-great-grandfather to Louise Torrey, who married Judge Alphonso Taft in 1853. Their son William Howard Taft became president and then chief justice.

cross_connections.display_label: , her brother William's great-great-granddaughter, bore President Taft

narrative_blocks.header: He carried the Sherborn family to Dublin
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Sherborn in 1766 to Benjamin Learned and Elizabeth Wilson, he farmed at Dublin in New Hampshire, married Hannah Wight there in 1797 and had eight children by her. He died of dysentery at eighty-nine.

bio.bio_blurb: Dublin farmer on the Old Troy Road

narrative_blocks.header: He married two Darracott sisters
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah Jane Darracott married him in 1854 and bore nine children before she died of diabetes in May 1878. He married her sister Bessie Maria that same year, buried her in 1880, and lived on another thirty-four years.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine children on the Old Troy Road farm
narrative_blocks.body: The Allison farm stood off the Old Troy Road, and the nine children Sarah Jane bore him were raised on it. The seventh was Henry, who left the farm for a store, a camera and the legislature.

bio.bio_blurb: Dublin storekeeper, photographer and town historian

narrative_blocks.header: Dublin’s storekeeper, photographer and postmaster
narrative_blocks.body: He joined his father-in-law's store opposite the Dublin town hall in 1891 and owned it from 1901 for twenty-five years, running the post office out of it from 1914 to 1922 and broking summer rentals on the side.

narrative_blocks.header: He found Mark Twain a Dublin house
narrative_blocks.body: As a rental broker he placed Mark Twain at Lone Tree Hill for the summer of 1905 and the Upton house the next year. Twain sent him a complete set of his works for what he had done to make the stay comfortable.

narrative_blocks.header: Glass plates let Thayer paint an empty room
narrative_blocks.body: His photographs of Dublin, mostly on glass plates around 1900, are the main record of how the town looked. Some were of Abbott Thayer's models, made so the painter could work with the sitter absent.

narrative_blocks.header: A Bull Mooser the Treasury Secretary fought
narrative_blocks.body: He ran for the legislature in 1913 as a Progressive Republican. Treasury Secretary Franklin MacVeagh, who summered in Dublin, missed the vice-president's funeral to campaign against him, and he won two to one.

narrative_blocks.header: At eighty-three he wrote the town’s only history
narrative_blocks.body: Dublin Days Old and New, published privately in 1952, set down what he had seen in a long life there. It remains the only published source for the town's history after 1916.

narrative_blocks.header: His signature cast in bronze on his stone
narrative_blocks.body: He was called New Hampshire's outstanding calligrapher, taught handwriting in the 1890s and was still lettering citations in his nineties. He had his own signature, flourishes and all, cast for his headstone.

narrative_blocks.header: The last Allison in Dublin died in 1994
narrative_blocks.body: His great-grandfather Andrew came to Dublin from Londonderry in 1783, and he was cemetery superintendent for his own last fifteen years, keeping the records in his hand. When his son Elliott died none were left.

cross_connections.display_label: rented two Dublin houses through him, and paid in a set of his works

bio.bio_blurb: Nantucket Coffin who married a Pinkham

narrative_blocks.header: Her daughter married a Coffin cousin
narrative_blocks.body: She married Capt. John Pinkham in May 1757 and had two children by him. Her daughter Susanna married James Josiah Coffin, carrying the line straight back into the family she had married out of.

bio.bio_blurb: Nantucket woman of the Coffin double descent

narrative_blocks.header: She married a fourth cousin, both Coffins
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband James Josiah Coffin came down from Tristram Coffin by the son Peter and the grandson Jethro, who built the oldest house on the island. She came down from the same Tristram by the son James.

narrative_blocks.header: Five of her seven died inside six years
narrative_blocks.body: Josiah died in 1819 at twenty-six, George and Charles both in 1821, William in 1822 and Susan in 1825: five of her seven children inside six years. Lucy, who lived until 1864, was the one who outlived her.

bio.bio_blurb: Nantucket Coffin of two Tristram lines

narrative_blocks.header: He descended from Tristram twice over
narrative_blocks.body: His father's line ran back to Tristram Coffin through Jethro, who built the oldest house on the island. His mother's ran back to the same Tristram through the son John. His wife Susanna made a third line to him.

cross_connections.display_label: , her great-grandfather Josiah's sister, was born on Sunset Hill

bio.bio_blurb: Staten Island engineer and Seventh Regiment man

narrative_blocks.header: Boston trust company, then New York engineering
narrative_blocks.body: Out of the Roxbury Latin School he went into the Old Colony Trust Company at Boston. He moved to New York in 1907, spent a few months with the Trust Company of America, and then joined the Industrial Engineering Company.

narrative_blocks.header: Years in Company K of the Seventh
narrative_blocks.body: He served many years with Company K of the Seventh Regiment, New York National Guard. He lived on Staten Island, took a hand in its civic affairs and was fond of outdoor sport.

career.organization: Industrial Engineering Company of New York

bio.bio_blurb: Staten Island girl of the Delafield line

narrative_blocks.header: She married at Christ Church, New Brighton
narrative_blocks.body: She married Thomas McMahon Rianhard Jr. of Waterbury on 19 April 1936, the Rev. Charles W. Forster officiating at New Brighton. She had been schooled at Dongan Hall and he at Gilman and Yale.

narrative_blocks.header: She spent the war in Bermuda
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Wigglesworth served there in Army engineers intelligence, while her brother Thomas was with the Army Air Corps in England. She married Richard McAdoo in 1948.

narrative_blocks.header: Beaver Country Day, then St. Timothy's
narrative_blocks.body: She left the Maryland school in 1939 and did civilian work for the Army Intelligence Corps, first in New York and then Bermuda. After the war she lived in New York City and studied music.

narrative_blocks.header: She chaired the Kodály board at Cambridge
narrative_blocks.body: Mary McAdoo worked for Cambridge Hospice after the move in 1968 and chaired the board of the Kodály Musical Training Institute. She belonged to the Women's Study Club and led the Nucleus Club of Boston.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty-seven years married, and five grandchildren
narrative_blocks.body: She married Richard McAdoo on 26 June 1948 and they went first to Cold Spring Harbor. Nora and Lucas Neustadt, Rémy and Cassia Denton and Sarah Winship came of their three daughters.

military_service.notes: Engineers intelligence, stationed in Bermuda.

bio.bio_blurb: Dye chemist, spring maker, shoe-machinery executive

parents.father_research_notes: Henry D. Hyde

narrative_blocks.header: He sold springs to Ford, and to Henry
narrative_blocks.body: His Hyde Engineering Company made springs for the Model T and sold ten thousand sets about New England. He fitted fourteen cars belonging to Ford executives, Henry Ford's among them, and turned down a royalty from Chevrolet.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty chemists, and a case put to Congress
narrative_blocks.body: He built a staff of forty chemists in the war, making dyestuffs for textile mills — colours hard enough that his firm was first in the country to manage some. As a governor of the Dyes Institute he pressed Congress to protect the trade.

narrative_blocks.header: An usher in 1914, a husband in 1942
narrative_blocks.body: He was one of the ushers when his Harvard classmate Edward Wigglesworth married Sarah Rackemann at Milton in June 1914. Wigglesworth died in 1945; Hyde had married his widow three years before that.

cross_connections.display_label: took him to Europe in 1908 and made him an usher in 1914
made the first wagon springs in America, ninety years before his
came into United Shoe Machinery as a chemist after him

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-one years at Harper, then Houghton Mifflin
narrative_blocks.body: He went into publishing in 1946 and edited at Harper & Brothers in New York until 1967. Cambridge and Houghton Mifflin followed, where he was editor-in-chief and retired vice-president and general manager in 1982.

narrative_blocks.header: He finished Harvard early to enlist
narrative_blocks.body: He took the class of 1942 ahead of time and went into the army, fighting through Europe with the 989th Field Artillery. He was discharged a captain in 1945.

narrative_blocks.header: He took up sculpture after he retired
narrative_blocks.body: Richard McAdoo studied for years with Joseph Wheelwright, having first driven the country with Mary by camper. Weekends and summers went to their 1770 farmhouse at Temple.

narrative_blocks.header: The fund they left the town of Temple
narrative_blocks.body: He and Mary set up the Temple 250th Anniversary Fund, which gives grants to public projects there. He worked for land conservation and the Monadnock Conservancy, and sat on the board of Monadnock Music.

narrative_blocks.header: Two speakers aimed across the fields
narrative_blocks.body: The Temple house was where they kept open door. At night he and Mary sent music out of two large speakers from the porch, across the fields and into the woods.

narrative_blocks.body: Princeton in 1943 and Harvard Medical School in 1946, then two years as a navy medical officer in Argentina and Newfoundland. In 1967 the Air Force sent him to Vietnam to try to raise the survival rate of men evacuated by helicopter.

narrative_blocks.header: A wool merchant in the family firm
narrative_blocks.body: Whitney Wright took his Harvard degree in 1939 and spent four years in the Army, coming out a lieutenant. He went into wool at Wright Brothers in Boston as a partner, and lived on Gloucester Street.

narrative_blocks.body: He left a gathering at Kennebunkport with Zachary Wells in the small hours of 20 December 2012 and was not seen again. Two life jackets and their clothes came ashore on Goat Island on Christmas Eve.

narrative_blocks.header: He returned to the boat school for design
narrative_blocks.body: He took the marine systems programme at The Landing School in Arundel in 2011 and came back to study yacht design. He grew up in Barnstable, a sailor and a waterman who lived for the water, with a dog named Scupper.

narrative_blocks.body: She came from Northumberland in Saratoga County, a daughter of Reed Lewis, and married James Cowles at Farmington in the February of 1838, joining the church there the same year. She died at Richmond but lies at Farmington.

bio.bio_blurb: Farmington girl who married into Richmond

narrative_blocks.header: She married a Georgia planter from Virginia
narrative_blocks.body: Felix Wyatt of Richmond was born in Virginia in 1829 and was planting in Georgia when they married at Farmington in the October of 1867. She was twenty-one. She died at Richmond in 1924, having long outlived him.

bio.bio_blurb: The Father of the Parcel Post

narrative_blocks.header: The Father of the Parcel Post
narrative_blocks.body: He gave a quarter of a century to postal reform, ran the Postal Progress League as its secretary and treasurer, and wrote A General Freight and Passenger Post, which Putnams put through three editions.

narrative_blocks.header: Two paper mills came down on him
narrative_blocks.body: In the spring of 1888, he wrote, he found himself under the ruins of two New England paper mills that had failed largely through railway freight discrimination. He had inherited an ample fortune and spent much of it on the cause.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran for Congress on his own platform
narrative_blocks.body: He stood as an independent in 1896 for free trade, sound money, an end to railroad monopoly and public ownership of public works. He was not elected.

narrative_blocks.header: Admitted to the bar, and never practised
narrative_blocks.body: Russell's Military School at New Haven, then Yale for a B.A. in 1866 and, twenty years later, its law school and an LL.B. in 1888. He took the Connecticut bar that year and never practised, turning to economics instead.

narrative_blocks.header: He credited his daughters’ art to their mother
narrative_blocks.body: He wrote in 1896 that whatever talents his daughters showed as artists came from their mother's line, and that Edith and Mildred had just divided the Ethel Walker prize at the Yale Art School. All four became known artists.

narrative_blocks.header: He broke up the Farmington house in 1902
narrative_blocks.body: The house he kept at Farmington was one of the landmark colonial houses of the state. He gave it up in 1902 and lived afterwards in New York City, Washington and Richmond, where he died in 1922.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded two postal leagues
narrative_blocks.body: He set up the Postal Congress League of Massachusetts in 1902 and the World Postal League in 1914, and put out a seven-page tract calling the post office the simplest mechanism ever devised for human advancement.

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband credited the daughters to her
narrative_blocks.body: James Lewis Cowles wrote in 1896 that whatever talents his daughters showed as artists came from their mother's line. She was a daughter of the Rev. James Lancaster Gwaltney of Sussex County and Martha Vaughan of Suffolk.

narrative_blocks.header: Murals and windows, always with her twin
narrative_blocks.body: She and Genevieve trained together and took the same commissions: mural decorations for Christ Church in New Haven and Grace Church in New York, and the windows of Grace Church's Honor Room.

narrative_blocks.header: She drew for Scribner’s and McClure’s
narrative_blocks.body: She illustrated Hawthorne's House of the Seven Gables and drew for Scribner's and McClure's in pencil and ink wash on board. She exhibited at the Paris Exposition of 1900 and at St. Louis in 1904. One of her Scribner's drawings is now in Princeton's Graphic Arts Collection.

narrative_blocks.header: A club where women hired their own models
narrative_blocks.body: She was an early member of the Art Workers' Club for Women, founded in 1898, which kept a brownstone on West Fifty-eighth Street with meeting rooms, a restaurant and a boarding house. Members hired models without a fee.

narrative_blocks.header: She died at thirty-four in New York
narrative_blocks.body: She died in New York in the May of 1905, thirty-four years old, and was buried at Riverside in Farmington. Genevieve outlived her by forty-five years and kept working.

narrative_blocks.header: She painted dazzle on wartime ships
narrative_blocks.body: In the First World War Genevieve trained under William Andrew Mackay as a camoufleur for the U.S. Shipping Board, one of very few women in the work, painting ships in the dazzle patterns that hid a vessel's shape and heading from U-boat periscopes.

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve thousand ships, nine lost
narrative_blocks.body: Writing in the Hartford Courant in 1932, Genevieve explained how dazzle worked: a U-boat commander had seven seconds between waves to read a ship's angles, and the black blots made him misjudge them. Of twelve thousand ships camouflaged by Americans, she wrote, only nine were lost.

narrative_blocks.header: Convicts as models for a prison chapel
narrative_blocks.body: After Maude's death Genevieve proposed a religious mural for the chapel of the State Prison at Wethersfield, with the prisoners as her models, and the work made her a lifelong advocate of prison reform. In 1932 she likened dazzle paint to the prejudice that hides a prisoner's real character.

narrative_blocks.header: Her Scribner’s drawings are at Princeton
narrative_blocks.body: Two of her illustrations for Scribner's Magazine, pencil and ink wash on board from about 1897, sit in Princeton's graphic arts collection. She designed the Grace Church Honor Room windows and painted church murals besides.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived her twin by forty-five years
narrative_blocks.body: The two had trained together and shared every commission: illustration, mural painting, stained glass. Maude died in 1905 at thirty-four; Genevieve worked on to 1950 and was buried beside her at Farmington.

narrative_blocks.body: The Farmington girl who took prizes at the Yale Art School ended her life as a religious at Florence under the name Mother Francesca Chiara. She died there in the May of 1958, six days short of eighty-four.

narrative_blocks.header: She split the Yale prize with her sister
narrative_blocks.body: She and Mildred divided the Ethel Walker prize at the Yale Art School in the spring of 1896. Their father wrote that year that he thought the two younger girls would prove as able as their elder sisters.

narrative_blocks.body: Redbank: Life on a Southern Plantation came out in 1893 as number eleven of the Arena Library Series, three hundred and seventy pages of it. She was seventeen, and her mother's people were Virginians.

narrative_blocks.header: Painter, illustrator, craftsworker, writer
narrative_blocks.body: She worked in four trades at once, and in the spring of 1896 she and Edith divided the Ethel Walker prize at the Yale Art School. She was the youngest of the four sisters, all of them known as artists.

narrative_blocks.header: The first chair of its kind in America
narrative_blocks.body: Yale made him professor of agricultural chemistry in 1846, a professorship newly created. With Benjamin Silliman Jr. he set up the department of philosophy and the arts, which grew into the Sheffield Scientific School.

narrative_blocks.header: He went to Edinburgh to learn the oat
narrative_blocks.body: He studied under James Johnston at Edinburgh from 1844, and his study of the oat was read at the British Association in June 1845. He went on round the continental laboratories, to Giessen and to Mulder at Utrecht.

narrative_blocks.header: The boy who would not study
narrative_blocks.body: Theodore Dwight ran through every branch of learning with him without success until he mentioned mineralogy. The boy had been buying minerals for two years and had tried three times to arrange them by colour.

narrative_blocks.header: He got a town to protect its birds
narrative_blocks.body: He gave his first public lecture to a local lyceum on the subject of birds, and defended them so well that the town meeting passed a law for their protection the next time it sat.

narrative_blocks.header: Elements of Scientific Agriculture, 1850
narrative_blocks.body: He wrote it for farmers, and papers besides on the chemistry of crops. His pupil Samuel William Johnson became one of the country's foremost men in scientific agriculture after him.

narrative_blocks.header: Measles at Washington, then a rapid decline
narrative_blocks.body: Winter journeys twice weekly to lecture in a neighbouring state broke his health in the spring. Florida gave his friends hope, but measles caught him at Washington on the way home and he died at his father's house.

narrative_blocks.header: A small statue of him in the Capitol
narrative_blocks.body: He is one of very few scientists on the Edmond Amateis bronze doors at Washington. The Italian villa Henry Austin built him on Hillhouse Avenue in 1849 is Yale's Steinbach Hall now, bought by the college in 1923.

narrative_blocks.body: He took his degree at the Albany Law School in 1872, began practice in the city in 1873 and gave it up in 1877. Eight years in Europe followed, and his son was born in London in the middle of them.

narrative_blocks.header: He reported on wood carving at Paris
narrative_blocks.body: He was an honorary member of the World's Exposition Commission at Paris in 1878 and wrote a report on the wood carving shown there. In 1893 he was commissioner for New York's Third Judicial District at Chicago.

narrative_blocks.header: Vice-president, then president of the club
narrative_blocks.body: He was vice-president of the Fort Orange Club at Albany from 1902 and its president from 1904 to 1906. He lived at 300 State Street and was buried at Albany Rural, where his wife had gone before him.

bio.bio_blurb: Coxsackie lawyer’s daughter of the De Witt line

narrative_blocks.header: Her father was Clinton De Witt of Coxsackie
narrative_blocks.body: Clinton De Witt was a lawyer and orator who died at New York in 1845, the year she was born. Her mother was Elsie, a daughter of Abraham Van Dyck of Coxsackie, and her brother Abraham Van Dyck De Witt practised law at Albany.

bio.bio_blurb: Acorn Club and Colonial Dames of Philadelphia

narrative_blocks.header: Acorn Club and Colonial Dames
narrative_blocks.body: She belonged to the Acorn Club and to the Colonial Dames of America. She had left Albany for Philadelphia on her marriage in 1904, and went back to Albany to be buried.

narrative_blocks.header: She died where her daughter worked
narrative_blocks.body: She died in the February of 1955, seventy-eight years old, in the Woman's Medical College Hospital, where Mary was on the staff. Her sister Katharine, by then Mrs. Gerald Holsman, outlived her.

narrative_blocks.body: She served as a navy physician through the war, in charge of the women's branch of the hospital at the Marine depot at Parris Island. She was still a lieutenant when her father died in the September of 1944.

narrative_blocks.header: Bryn Mawr, then Penn medicine at twenty-four
narrative_blocks.body: She took her Bryn Mawr degree in 1928 and her medical degree at Pennsylvania in 1932. She taught at Albany Medical College from 1938 and at the Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania from 1946.

narrative_blocks.header: She led the Philadelphia obstetrical society
narrative_blocks.body: She was president of the Obstetrical Society of Philadelphia from 1961 to 1962, and published on ovarian pathology, the menopause and the influence of ovarian hormones through the journals of her field.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother died in her own hospital
narrative_blocks.body: Elsie Norton Pettit died in 1955 at the Woman's Medical College Hospital, where her daughter was on the staff. Mary was then living at Pembroke Road in Bryn Mawr, the college she had gone to.

narrative_blocks.body: The Markoe family papers went to the Historical Society of Pennsylvania in 1966 and her great-grandfather John Pitkin Norton's to Yale in 1969. Drexel gives a fellowship in her name to junior medical faculty.

narrative_blocks.body: She went from the Agnes Irwin School to dramatic schools in New York, played the road company of the Theatre Guild's Strange Interlude, and was afterwards with the Moscow Art Players.

narrative_blocks.header: A Red Cross captain at Wilton
narrative_blocks.body: She was a captain of the Red Cross Motor Corps at Wilton in Connecticut through the Second World War. She kept a dress shop with her mother after it, and died at forty-eight, unmarried.

narrative_blocks.header: He matched Arabic place-names to Hebrew ones
narrative_blocks.body: Travelling Palestine in 1838 with Eli Smith, whose Arabic was fluent where his own was not, he recovered Anathoth from Anath, Bethel from Beitin, Ramah from er-Ram. The Royal Geographical Society gave him its Gold Medal in 1842.

narrative_blocks.header: He called himself a geographer, not a digger
narrative_blocks.body: The only excavating of his life was clearing debris from the Tomb of the Kings outside Jerusalem. He described terrain and identified sites; the arch he recognised on the Temple Mount's south-west flank has carried his name since.

narrative_blocks.header: His first printing of five thousand sold out
narrative_blocks.body: Biblical Researches in Palestine ran to three volumes in 1841. Catholic Austria banned it for unseating pilgrimage sites and John Henry Newman attacked it in print; Protestant America bought it faster than it could read it.

narrative_blocks.header: Union's professor was also its first librarian
narrative_blocks.body: He held the chair of biblical literature at Union Theological Seminary from 1837 until his death, and was the first librarian of what is now the Burke, 1841 to 1850. His Greek lexicon of 1836 was by then the American standard.

narrative_blocks.header: Seth Norton was his uncle and his professor
narrative_blocks.body: Raised on a Southington farm, he taught school at East Haven and Farmington in 1810 and 1811 to earn college money, then went to Hamilton in Clinton, New York, where his mother Elizabeth Norton's brother Seth held a chair.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote his own father's memoir
narrative_blocks.body: The 1859 memoir of the Rev. William Robinson of Southington, printed as manuscript for private distribution, is his: a son's account of a father, and the source for nearly all that is known of him.

narrative_blocks.header: Buried twice, the second time in October
narrative_blocks.body: He died at Manhattan in the January of 1863 and was laid first in the New York Marble Cemetery on Second Avenue. He was moved out to Green-Wood in Brooklyn that October.

notable.notable_blurb: German translator; Goethe praised her Serbian songs

narrative_blocks.header: Goethe championed her Serbian folk songs
narrative_blocks.body: Grief at a sister's death in 1823 sent her into Serbian, and she wrote to Goethe about the project despite an almost overpowering timidity. He praised her Volkslieder der Serben of 1826 above Jakob Grimm's stricter literal versions.

narrative_blocks.header: Talvj was an acrostic of her own name
narrative_blocks.body: Therese Albertine Louise von Jacob signed herself by her initials from Psyche in 1825 onward. Her Walter Scott translations had gone out as Ernst Berthold, and a set of literary criticisms simply as ein Frauenzimmer.

narrative_blocks.header: Shut out of school, she read the library
narrative_blocks.body: Her father Ludwig von Jakob's chairs took the family to Kharkiv in 1806 and St Petersburg in 1811, and at neither place was she given lessons. She had the university library instead and read enormously in history.

narrative_blocks.header: She reached America and took up its languages
narrative_blocks.body: Landing in 1830 for her husband's Andover chair, she began on Native American languages and put John Pickering's survey of them into German in 1834. Her history of the Slavic tongues came out the same year.

narrative_blocks.header: She proved Ossian a forgery in 1840
narrative_blocks.body: Die Unaechtheit der Lieder Ossian's argued that James Macpherson wrote the Gaelic epics he claimed to have discovered. She published it at Leipzig from Germany, where she sat out her husband's Palestine years.

narrative_blocks.header: Bryant and Olmsted came to her house
narrative_blocks.body: George Bancroft, William Cullen Bryant, Bayard Taylor and Frederick Law Olmsted were among the literary men at the Robinsons' New York house, and from 1846 she counted Washington Irving a friend.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived him by seven years in Hamburg
narrative_blocks.body: Edward Robinson died in 1863 and she went back to Germany, to the Hamburg where their son Edward was American consul, and died there in April 1870. Her daughter put three of her tales into English.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a graduate of her father's college
narrative_blocks.body: Edward Robinson took his degree in 1816 from the Hamilton her father had founded in 1793 as the Hamilton-Oneida Academy. The marriage put the college's founder and one of its graduates into one family.

narrative_blocks.header: She was four when her mother died
narrative_blocks.body: Jerusha Bingham died at Stockbridge in 1788, where the household had moved once the war reached the Mohawk Valley. Eliza was four, and her father was two hundred miles west among the Oneida.

narrative_blocks.header: She died at Duxbury at thirty-five
narrative_blocks.body: Her death came on 5 July 1819 at Duxbury on the Massachusetts coast. Her husband married again at Halle nine years afterward and did not bring that household to America until 1830.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brother was president of Harvard
narrative_blocks.body: John Thornton Kirkland, fourteen years her senior, held the Harvard presidency from 1810 to 1828. He was one of eleven Kirkland children, most of them raised between the Oneida mission and Stockbridge.

narrative_blocks.header: Traders broke his rum ban with free casks
narrative_blocks.body: In the autumn of 1766 he put the question to the Oneida and gave them six days; they voted unanimously to banish rum and held to it three months. Traders whose business had collapsed then brought in eighty casks free of charge.

narrative_blocks.header: His academy took Oneida and white boys
narrative_blocks.body: He opened the Hamilton-Oneida Academy at Clinton in 1793 and it took both, naming it for Alexander Hamilton, who sat on its first board of trustees. It was chartered as Hamilton College in 1812, four years after he died.

narrative_blocks.header: Two of the Six Nations followed him
narrative_blocks.body: Four of the Six Nations went with the British; he argued the Oneida and Tuscarora onto the American side, and was chaplain at Fort Schuyler from October 1779 to November 1783, going with Sullivan into the Iroquois towns.

narrative_blocks.header: Famine had him eeling for his own food
narrative_blocks.body: Famines ran through the summers of 1765, 1766 and 1767 until he released his assistants and kept only David Fowler and his wife. He wrote that week to week he went eeling with the Oneida at Oneida Lake for his subsistence.

narrative_blocks.header: He took land from the people he served
narrative_blocks.body: He helped New York negotiate its land purchases from the Oneida and secured large parcels for himself and his friends. His assistant James Dean stood at every cession the state took between 1785 and 1818.

narrative_blocks.header: He had word lists for two hundred languages
narrative_blocks.body: The Italian traveller Paolo Andreani came in 1790 and found he had collected basic vocabularies of more than two hundred languages. Andreani watched him hold Sunday service in Oneida, with the psalms translated.

narrative_blocks.header: His school burned and closed inside a year
narrative_blocks.body: The first class at the Hamilton-Oneida Academy was four Oneida children and twenty-five white ones. The main building burned three months in, the school shut after a year, and the rebuilt one took two Oneida in a decade.

narrative_blocks.header: War moved her household two hundred miles
narrative_blocks.body: Mohawk Valley war scares moved her back to Stockbridge in Massachusetts by 1774, and her husband carried two households from then on. She died there in 1788, twenty years before he did.

narrative_blocks.header: She put her mother's tales into English
narrative_blocks.body: Three of Talvj's German tales reached American readers in her translations: Heloise, or the Unrevealed Secret in 1850, Life's Discipline the year after, and The Exiles in 1853, reissued as Woodhill in 1856.

narrative_blocks.header: The 1874 tales carry her life of Talvj
narrative_blocks.body: The two volumes of Gesammelte Novellen that came out at Leipzig in 1874 carry her biography of her mother. It is the account of Talvj that later writers have worked from.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father took the family to Regent's Park
narrative_blocks.body: Henry La Tourette de Groot, a New York importer with heavy English interests, moved them to London in 1831 and kept a Regent's Park mansion with coaches and liveried servants. He died there in 1835, when she was six.

narrative_blocks.header: Brooklyn to Mendham in a single month
narrative_blocks.body: She was married out of Brooklyn on 1 July 1852. Within the month she had moved to Mendham in New Jersey, where her husband took his first pastorate, and she had four years of it before New York.

narrative_blocks.header: One son wrote music, the other built libraries
narrative_blocks.body: Frank Seymour Hastings banked, raced yachts, composed and took photographs. Thomas Hastings built the New York Public Library at Fifth Avenue and Forty-second Street in partnership with John Carrere.

narrative_blocks.header: An importer's fortune paid for an architect
narrative_blocks.body: The money her father made importing, and left at his death in 1835, is what schooled her second son. Thomas went from it into the partnership that took the Fifth Avenue commission.

narrative_blocks.header: Her sons' cousin painted and collected at Nice
narrative_blocks.body: Adelaide Milton de Groot, cousin to Frank and Thomas, was a painter and collector who went out to Nice in 1891 and stayed in Europe forty years. Back in New York from 1933, she took up the family's genealogy.

narrative_blocks.header: Hyde Park to Asheville, and twenty-one years
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Hyde Park on the Hudson, she came south about 1947, three years a widow, and had twenty-one years of Asheville. She died there in March 1968 after a long illness, a member of St George Episcopal.

narrative_blocks.body: His dry goods store and auction house stood on Main Street in Hartford, and the money went into real estate and bank directorships. He helped found the Pearl Street Congregational Church, a deacon like his father before him.

narrative_blocks.header: He married again at fifty-eight
narrative_blocks.body: Lavinia Benton had given him three children before 1850. He married Louise Robinson on 2 September 1869, when he was fifty-eight and she forty-three, and they lie in one plot at Spring Grove.

narrative_blocks.body: The ground his mill worked became Bushnell Park, and in 1899 his son John J. Corning set a fountain there for him: twenty-eight feet of bronze and granite under a hart, Hartford's own emblem.

narrative_blocks.header: On Colonel Webb's rolls he is Solomon Coles
narrative_blocks.body: He wrote the name that way himself in early life, the way Farmington said it, and strangers wrote it that way after him. It is under Coles that his Continental service stands on Samuel B. Webb's rolls.

narrative_blocks.header: Princeton, Yale and Harvard inside four years
narrative_blocks.body: He was at Princeton through 1775 and 1776, was admitted to the Yale sophomore class on 25 June 1778, and left it for Harvard on 1 April 1779. Ezra Stiles set the departure down in his Literary Diary.

narrative_blocks.header: Witherspoon asked the students to drill
narrative_blocks.body: At eighteen he joined a company Princeton's president John Witherspoon asked the students to raise under Henry Livingston. After Trenton and Princeton part of it went to Washington and wintered with him at Morristown.

narrative_blocks.header: He saw Kingston burn and Burgoyne surrender
narrative_blocks.body: As lieutenant under Capt. John P. Wyllys he was at Danbury in April 1777, at New Brunswick in May, at Fort Montgomery when the British took it, at Esopus when it burned, and at Burgoyne's surrender in October.

narrative_blocks.header: Ensign at seventeen, major general at forty-nine
narrative_blocks.body: Ensign of the Farmington 2d Company in December 1775, he came back to the militia after the war and went up it: captain of cavalry in 1790, colonel commandant in 1799, brigadier in 1801, major general of the 1st Division in 1807.

narrative_blocks.header: He joined the society against bondage in 1791
narrative_blocks.body: He was a member of the Connecticut Society for the Promotion of Freedom and for the Relief of Persons unlawfully holden in Bondage. He had joined the Society of the Cincinnati four years before, on the Fourth of July.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought into a million acres of Ohio
narrative_blocks.body: In 1795 he was one of forty-nine men who took the Western Reserve off Connecticut and formed the Connecticut Land Company. Part of what he held lay in Ashtabula County, and two of his sons were living on it when he died.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight children in twenty-three years
narrative_blocks.body: Isaac and Mary Smith Gleason of Farmington were her parents. She married in 1779 and bore eight children before she died in February 1803, the last of them Sarah, still an infant when she went.

people.research_notes: Cowles gen. gives 'age 46' at death, implying c.1815; FamilySearch's 22 Feb 1808 birth is taken over it.

narrative_blocks.header: A druggist and postmaster who never married
narrative_blocks.body: He kept a druggist's shop in Farmington as his father had and was the town's postmaster from 1872 to 1879. He never married, and died that December within days of his sixty-ninth birthday.

people.research_notes: Death date contested: Cowles gen. prints 17 Dec 1887, the same calendar day as his birth; FamilySearch has 7 Dec 1887.

cross_connections.display_label: took his Sheffield degree two years later and built bridges

narrative_blocks.header: Fourteen cities for iron and steel
narrative_blocks.body: He designed and contracted structural iron and steel for bridges and buildings, and the work moved him through Baltimore, Savannah, Atlanta, Youngstown, Cleveland, Pittsburgh, Pottsville and Chicago, several of them twice.

narrative_blocks.header: He married his mother's first cousin
narrative_blocks.body: Hattie Alford and his mother Harriet Beadle were both granddaughters of Orator Blakeslee of Wallingford. That made his wife his first cousin once removed, though she was ten years the younger.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale's Sheffield school at nineteen
narrative_blocks.body: He took a B.Ph. with the Sheffield Scientific School class of 1878 after the Wallingford schools. Who's Who in Engineering carried him in 1922, the year he died at Oak Park.

career.organization: structural iron and steel, bridges and buildings

bio.bio_blurb: First National Bank of Wallingford president

narrative_blocks.header: Teller in 1897, president in 1926
narrative_blocks.body: Eight years bookkeeping at the Farmers and Mechanics in Hartford took him away; he came back as teller, made assistant cashier in 1912 and cashier a year later. The board elected him president two days after Christmas 1926.

narrative_blocks.header: Treasurer of nearly everything in town
narrative_blocks.body: At nineteen he was secretary-treasurer of the lawn tennis club, and the pattern held: town treasurer, the Pilgrim Club, the Fourth of July committee, Rotary president, the YMCA state board, Boy Scout gift drives.

narrative_blocks.header: He crossed the street to the Episcopalians
narrative_blocks.body: Sunday school superintendent at the First Congregational in 1896 and a deacon there in 1932, by 1944 he was a delegate for St Paul's Episcopal, a hundred and fifty yards down the street, and a vestryman the year after.

narrative_blocks.header: He left school at fourteen for the bank
narrative_blocks.body: In 1887 he took a clerk's job at the First National Bank of Wallingford, where his father Robert sat on the board. He was its president by 1926 and marked seventy years in banking in 1957.

people.research_notes: VA Master Index 1917-1940: military date 7 Jun 1919, residence Oak Park, Illinois.

narrative_blocks.header: Copy desk, then the library association
narrative_blocks.body: She sub-edited at the Chicago Daily News, moved to the American Library Association, and closed out her working life running the bookstore at Hinsdale Central High School.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty-four years married to Bill Campbell
narrative_blocks.body: They married in 1947 and were still married when he died in December 2011. She followed him five years later at Naperville, ninety years old, having outlived him alone in the house.

bio.bio_blurb: Public educator; Fulbright teacher in Berlin

parents.father_research_notes: Martin Campbell of Cherokee, Iowa

narrative_blocks.header: Two degrees at Iowa, a doctorate at Illinois
narrative_blocks.body: He took his bachelor's and master's at the University of Iowa and a doctorate in education at Illinois, and spent his working life in public schools.

narrative_blocks.header: A year teaching in Berlin on a Fulbright
narrative_blocks.body: He went out to Berlin as a Fulbright exchange teacher and spent another year at Northwestern as a John Hay Fellow. Both were leave from the public-school classrooms he worked in otherwise.

narrative_blocks.header: He enlisted at eighteen at Camp Dodge
narrative_blocks.body: A private in the Air Corps reserve, he enlisted on 27 May 1944 at Camp Dodge in Iowa with four years of high school behind him. He was living at Cherokee, where he had been born that March.

narrative_blocks.header: His whole war was six weeks at Yale
narrative_blocks.body: He enrolled at New Haven on 11 September 1918 as a seaman second class and served at Yale from 1 October to 11 November, the day the guns stopped. He was on inactive duty by 21 December.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught microbiology at Yale
narrative_blocks.body: His father's 1963 death notice names him professor of microbiology at the Yale School of Medicine. He had come back to New Haven after the war and stayed in Connecticut the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: Four men, one name, four generations
narrative_blocks.body: His father Fred was born in 1872, he in 1903, his son Ted in 1932 and his grandson Rick after that. Frederic Morgan Cowles four times over, and each of them went by something else at home.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale in 1926, married at Montclair in 1928
narrative_blocks.body: He took his Yale degree in 1926 and married Dorothy Curtis Smith of Montclair, New Jersey, on 15 September 1928. He lived to ninety-seven and died at West Hartford in 2001.

narrative_blocks.header: He made the firm its research department
narrative_blocks.body: Forty years with Putnam and Co. of Hartford, 1926 to his retirement as managing partner in 1966, and the statistics and research department there was his doing. The firm merged into Advest soon after.

narrative_blocks.header: Cabinetmaking, and his son after him
narrative_blocks.body: He kept a summer place at Canton for more than seventy years and liked cabinetmaking and outdoor construction projects. Ted took up both and was remembered for them in his own turn.

career.organization: St. James Episcopal Men's Club, West Hartford

narrative_blocks.header: He catalogued the Walters' painted enamels
narrative_blocks.body: Curator at the Walters Art Gallery in Baltimore from 1953 to 1965, he brought out the Catalogue of the Painted Enamels of the Renaissance in 1967 — four hundred pages on Limoges work.

narrative_blocks.header: Montreal held him for twenty-eight years
narrative_blocks.body: He came to Canada in 1965 as titular professor at the Universite de Montreal, was naturalised in 1973, and stayed on emeritus there until he died in 1993.

narrative_blocks.header: The Sorbonne, then the school at Rome
narrative_blocks.body: He took his master's at the Sorbonne in 1935, was agrege of the Ecole Normale Superieure in 1936 and a member of the Ecole Francaise de Rome in 1938. He flew with the French Air Force in between.

narrative_blocks.header: He reported the Marshall Plan, then left it
narrative_blocks.body: He covered American foreign policy on the Marshall Plan in 1947 and 1948 before going back to art history. The Legion of Honour and a Killam fellowship followed, and the Kress chair at the National Gallery in 1983.

narrative_blocks.header: Covid took him in May 2020 at eighty-seven
narrative_blocks.body: He died on 7 May 2020 of complications from Covid-19, having grown up in West Hartford, gone through Loomis in 1951 and Middlebury in 1958, and served three years in the Marine Corps.

narrative_blocks.header: Investments at Travelers, syrup on the side
narrative_blocks.body: He worked in the investment department at Travelers and gave his time to the Canton Land Conservation Trust, the Avon-Canton Rotary, the Connecticut maple syrup producers and the Appalachian Mountain trails committee.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty years in one Simsbury church
narrative_blocks.body: He and Janet von Wettberg raised their family at Simsbury, where he belonged to St Alban's for over fifty years and where he is buried in its memorial gardens.

parents.father_research_notes: Eduard Feltberg von Wettberg Jr.

narrative_blocks.header: She and Ted both finished Middlebury in 1958
narrative_blocks.body: She took her B.A. at Middlebury in 1958 and a master's in teaching at Radcliffe the year after, having grown up at Wilmington in Delaware. Ted was in the same Middlebury class, and they married in 1960.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-four years counselling at Region 7
narrative_blocks.body: She was a guidance counselor at Northwest Regional School Number 7 for twenty-four years, tutored English as a second language, and mentored a Hartford girl through Covenant to Care for Children.

narrative_blocks.header: Four months after her husband, in her sleep
narrative_blocks.body: Ted died of Covid in May 2020 and she died on 25 September that year at eighty-four, in her sleep. Both had been at St Alban's in Simsbury for over fifty years.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded the Knights of Pythias in 1864
narrative_blocks.body: Five government clerks organised Washington Lodge No. 1 on 19 February 1864. Its precepts were toleration in religion, obedience to law and loyalty to government, and politics were barred from its portals.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the ritual in a Michigan schoolhouse
narrative_blocks.body: The ritual turns on the friendship of Damon and Pythias, and he had written it before the order existed, while teaching at the Eagle Harbor schoolhouse on Lake Superior in the winter of 1858.

narrative_blocks.header: He was christened for his grandfather Dwight
narrative_blocks.body: He was named Henry Edwin Dwight at birth, for his mother's father, and carried it until he was ten. The name was changed then to Justus Henry, for his own father.

narrative_blocks.header: A volunteer nurse, then a hospital steward
narrative_blocks.body: He nursed at Cuyler General Hospital in Germantown from January 1863 and was a hospital steward at Washington from that July. His chief steward Robert Allen Champion told him to found the order.

narrative_blocks.header: Treasury, a news company, then the War Department
narrative_blocks.body: He clerked in the Treasury from 1865 to 1869, went to the Independent News Company of Boston and New York until 1873, and was a War Department clerk from 1874 until he died.

narrative_blocks.header: The order put a statue over his grave
narrative_blocks.body: His wife died in 1887 and he in 1889 at Lima in Ohio, fifty years old. The Knights named him founder that year and raised a monument with his likeness over the Utica grave in 1892.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-five years in one Dalton pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: He came to the Dalton Congregational church in 1883 and stayed until he died in 1918. He was dean of the Protestant ministers of Berkshire county and three years president of its Congregational club.

narrative_blocks.header: He rebuilt the town's schools himself
narrative_blocks.body: He reorganised Dalton's school system and was its superintendent of schools from 1884 to 1888, sitting on the school board ever after. Wesleyan gave him a doctorate in 1902.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a Rathbone at fifty-two
narrative_blocks.body: Anna S. Kane of Williamstown married him in 1882 and died in 1899 leaving four children. He married Sarah Dwight Rathbone in 1903, and a paralytic shock took him at Dalton in 1918.

narrative_blocks.header: From Pasadena to the national board
narrative_blocks.body: Lucy was a board member and past president of Planned Parenthood of Pasadena and was later elected to the organization's national board. Her love of music, her family said, was rivaled only by her passion for family planning.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventy-one years on the Coleman board
narrative_blocks.body: A pianist with degrees from Mount Holyoke and the Yale School of Music, where she met Henry Clifford, Lucy joined the board of Pasadena's Coleman Chamber Music Association in 1937 and was still an honorary member when she died in 2008, two days after her ninety-ninth birthday.

narrative_blocks.header: Sermons and Gilbert and Sullivan
narrative_blocks.body: Lucy grew up at Dalton, Massachusetts, listening to her father's sermons and to her family's renditions of Gilbert and Sullivan, and settled in Pasadena with Henry after their wedding in 1933.

cross_connections.display_label: wrote the thirty-nine volumes that are No. 3 of the Zamorano 80
wrote The Mountains of California, No. 56 of the Zamorano 80

narrative_blocks.header: Eighty books to own early California
narrative_blocks.body: In 1945 the Zamorano Club of Los Angeles, named for California's first printer, published a list of the eighty most important books on the state's early history, from Spanish voyage narratives to Dana, Twain and Muir. Owning every one in first edition became the great test of a Californiana collector.

narrative_blocks.header: He was the third ever to finish
narrative_blocks.body: Henry began collecting stamps as a boy and spent thirty-five years on the Zamorano 80 before he found the last of the eighty in 1988. Only Thomas Streeter and Frederick Beinecke had done it before him, and only one collector has done it since.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale holds the only other set
narrative_blocks.body: Frederick Beinecke gave his complete set at once to Yale's Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, still the only institution with all eighty in first edition. By the time Henry finished, his and Yale's were the only two complete sets in existence.

narrative_blocks.header: A book thief cased his house
narrative_blocks.body: The rarest of the eighty is Yellow Bird's 1854 Life and Adventures of Joaquín Murieta, known in only two first editions. Henry bought the second from a collector in Maine, and the book thief Stephen Blumberg and his accomplices planned a burglary of his house to get it.

narrative_blocks.header: The set went under the hammer in 1995
narrative_blocks.body: Henry's collection was sold at auction in 1995, the year after his death, and his Murieta went to Daniel Volkmann, the fourth and last collector to complete the list.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother proved theorems, he bought books
narrative_blocks.body: Alfred Hoblitzelle Clifford, two years his elder, was the mathematician of the family: Hermann Weyl's assistant at Princeton, later head of mathematics at Tulane, and the founder of Semigroup Forum.

narrative_blocks.header: The brothers died fourteen months apart
narrative_blocks.body: Alfred had a stroke at New Orleans in December 1992 and died that month. Henry died at Pasadena in February 1994, eighty-four years old.

narrative_blocks.body: Her class notes record twin girls born to her on 10 July 1912, Clara Tuttle and Fannie Scudder Heck. She was an assistant librarian at Virginia, where her father held the biology chair, and she married a professor there.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at forty-two, dead at forty-five
narrative_blocks.body: Influenza killed William Heck in January 1919 and she followed him in January 1922, leaving Clara and her twin orphaned at nine. Her father Albert Tuttle, retired from the biology chair, outlived her by five years.

narrative_blocks.header: He measured how much school tires a child
narrative_blocks.body: 'A Study of Mental Fatigue in Relation to the Daily School Program' and 'Mental Discipline and Educational Values' came out of the Curry chair. A third book was finished and unpublished when he died.

narrative_blocks.header: From the General Education Board to Virginia
narrative_blocks.body: He took a master's at Wake Forest and a doctorate at Columbia, then served as assistant secretary of the General Education Board in New York until Virginia made him professor of education in 1905.

narrative_blocks.header: Two weeks of influenza ended him at thirty-nine
narrative_blocks.body: Pneumonia followed the influenza and he died in the university hospital on 4 January 1919, fourteen years into the chair. The funeral left the East Lawn house at four and his body went to Raleigh by evening train.

narrative_blocks.header: Born at Raleigh to Jonathan M. Heck
narrative_blocks.body: His father was Jonathan M. Heck of Raleigh and his mother a Callendine. He married Anna Seeley Tuttle, daughter of the Virginia biologist Albert Tuttle, in 1912, and left her twin girls of six when he died.

people.research_notes: Son of Col. Jonathan McGee Heck, a Confederate officer of West Virginia who became an industrialist and developer, a shareholder of the Oakwood Cemetery association at Raleigh and grand marshal of the 1892 centennial parade there. His father is not built.

narrative_blocks.header: She married at Landstuhl in occupied Germany
narrative_blocks.body: The wedding was on 14 August 1953, when she was forty-one and James Hampton, born in Harlan County, was twenty-eight. Both ended in Kentucky, he at Frankfort in 1977 and she at Wilmore twenty-two years later.

narrative_blocks.header: Orphaned at nine, one of July 1912 twins
narrative_blocks.body: She and her sister were born the same July day in Albemarle County while their father held the Curry chair of education at Virginia. He died of influenza in 1919 and their mother followed him in 1922.

narrative_blocks.header: Harlan County to Landstuhl and back again
narrative_blocks.body: He was born in Harlan County in 1925 and married Clara Heck at Landstuhl in August 1953. They came back to Kentucky, where he died at Frankfort in 1977, aged fifty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: Berkeley from 1936, and she never left
narrative_blocks.body: She married Pembroke Gochnauer there the year he settled in the city, and raised Pembroke Jr., William Tuttle and John Marshall, all three still living in Berkeley when their father died.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived her husband by thirty-eight years
narrative_blocks.body: Pembroke Gochnauer died at Berkeley in 1967, two years after leaving his San Francisco firm. She lived on in the city until 2005 and died at ninety-three, having lost both parents before she was ten.
