narrative_blocks.header: Two wartime boards and one law firm
narrative_blocks.body: He read law at Virginia and practised with Angell, Adams and Holmes at San Francisco until January 1966. He sat on the War Labor Board through the second war and the Wage Stabilization Board through Korea.

narrative_blocks.header: California in 1923, Berkeley in 1936
narrative_blocks.body: He came west from Loudoun County at twenty-two and settled at Berkeley in the year he married Fannie Heck. Their three sons were all living in the city when he died in 1967.

narrative_blocks.header: One son and four daughters at Montreal
narrative_blocks.body: She married George Stephen Cantlie and bore him five children, among them Giana and the Celia of the pressed-flower letters. His attestation papers name her next of kin at 502 Sherbrooke Street West.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father was seigneur of Bic
narrative_blocks.body: William Darling Campbell was Queen's Notary and seigneur du Bic on the lower St Lawrence. She was born in 1872 and died in 1923, at fifty-one, while her husband still had a third of a life to run.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son was a stockbroker and a colonel
narrative_blocks.body: Stephen Douglas Cantlie, born at Montreal in 1903, went through the Royal Military College and into a broker's office before he commanded his father's battalion. He died in the city in August 1967.

bio.bio_blurb: Queen's Notary and seigneur du Bic

bio.bio_blurb: Chicago lawyer; part owner of the White Sox

narrative_blocks.header: He part-owned the White Sox and the Bulls
narrative_blocks.body: Counsel at Schiff, Hardin and Waite from before the war until his death, he acted for the White Sox, the Bulls, the Cubs, the Bears, Merrill Lynch and Pepsi, and was vice-president of the White Sox.

narrative_blocks.header: Three years a destroyer officer, then law school
narrative_blocks.body: Princeton in 1940, where he managed the soccer team, then Northwestern law, interrupted by the navy. He made partner at Schiff Hardin in 1952 and stayed with the firm the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: He buried Patricia at forty-five
narrative_blocks.body: She died at Highland Park in May 1964, at forty-one, and lies at Memorial Park in Skokie where he joined her thirty years later. He married Eleanor Fuelner afterwards and lived to 1994.

narrative_blocks.header: His father chaired a Chicago investment bank
narrative_blocks.body: Newton Phillips Frye of Glencoe led the Central Republic Company from 1931, as president and then chairman, and governed the Investment Bankers Association. He died at Evanston in 1957, at sixty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: Hamden to Ohio, and her daughter to Illinois
narrative_blocks.body: She married James Caul in Connecticut in 1839 and died at Geneva Township in Ashtabula County sixty-five years later. Their eldest, Marian, was born at Heyworth in Illinois in 1840 and died in the same town.

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve children at North Haven in twenty years
narrative_blocks.body: Twins came in November 1892, Joseph and Josephine, and Joseph was dead within the year. Hattie May lived four months in 1899 and Rob Roy no longer in 1910. The other nine grew up.

narrative_blocks.header: She led Vermont's home demonstration work
narrative_blocks.body: A pioneer of the state extension service, she was Home Demonstration leader for the St Albans area for many years, and served the Franklin County Farm Bureau and the Vermont Republican Women's Club.

narrative_blocks.header: Phi Beta Kappa at the University of Vermont
narrative_blocks.body: Born at New Haven in 1877, she took her degree at Vermont with Phi Beta Kappa honours and married Hezekiah Kibbe Brooks of the Maquam Road in 1922, when both of them were forty-four.

narrative_blocks.header: She married her dead sister's husband
narrative_blocks.body: Hetty Ann married William Henry Tracy in December 1824 and died at Guayama in June 1840. Frances Cornelia married the same man in September 1841 and outlived him by twenty-six years.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-five years U.S. Consul at Guayama
narrative_blocks.body: He came out to St. Thomas from Norwich, reached Puerto Rico in 1822 and took his naturalisation papers in 1830. He held the consulate at Guayama until he died, and the harbour colours flew at half mast for him.

narrative_blocks.header: He married two Coit sisters in turn
narrative_blocks.body: Hetty Ann married him in December 1824 and died at Guayama in 1840. He married her younger sister Frances Cornelia in September 1841. A Puerto Rican historian records that he had no children by either.

narrative_blocks.header: Apoplexy took him with the sale unfinished
narrative_blocks.body: He was arranging to sell Hacienda La Concordia to Eduardo Lind when he died suddenly in April 1852. His widow, his only heir, completed the sale four months later as his will directed. He lies at Green-Wood.

narrative_blocks.header: Dead at twenty-one with three businesses
narrative_blocks.body: He held a large sugar and coffee plantation on St. Lucia, a mercantile house and a shipping business. He died in 1819, when his son Joseph William was five months old.

bio.bio_blurb: Pine Bluff judge, colonel and mayor

cross_connections.display_label: was his great-aunt, and married into the Lillingtons who raised him
, his great-grandfather, died among the Lillingtons who raised him

narrative_blocks.header: Pine Bluff had eight log houses in 1837
narrative_blocks.body: He landed there in 1837 at eighteen, read law in James Yell's office and was admitted in 1840. He was state attorney for the second judicial district from 1844 and judge of the county court.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the Silver Wave on the Arkansas
narrative_blocks.body: Hindman ordered him to seize the supply boat in April 1861. The two of them raised the Second Arkansas Infantry, and he went from lieutenant-colonel to colonel of it inside the year.

narrative_blocks.header: He built Confederate factories in east Texas
narrative_blocks.body: Taken off the line, he put up works at Mound Prairie in Anderson County making cotton, wool, shoes, clothing and army supplies, and surrendered to General Herron at Shreveport in 1865.

narrative_blocks.header: The mill burned uninsured, rebuilt in ten weeks
narrative_blocks.body: Fire took the planing mill, the sash and door factory and the lumber on 24 August 1873. The new works started on the first of November. He also held the patent on his improved jack screw cotton press.

narrative_blocks.header: Orphaned at three, raised by a Coit cousin
narrative_blocks.body: His father died at twenty-one when he was five months old, and his mother on reaching New York, where she lies in Trinity churchyard. He spoke only French, and was given to Sarah Ann Lillington of Wilmington.

narrative_blocks.header: Du Bocage was built on a Carolina plan
narrative_blocks.body: The house he finished at Pine Bluff in 1866 was patterned on Gen. Lillington's place in North Carolina, where he had been raised. He was elected mayor of the town in 1888, at sixty-nine.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave up medicine after reading too much
narrative_blocks.body: He studied it for a year in Chicot County from 1836, then fell ill and convinced himself he had contracted every disease in the medical journals. He went to Pine Bluff and read law instead.

military_service.notes: Raised the regiment with Thomas Hindman; surrendered to Gen. Herron at Shreveport in 1865.

notable.notable_blurb: Pine Bluff judge, Confederate colonel, and mayor

people.primary_url_label: Find a Grave — Judge Joseph William Bocage

narrative_blocks.header: The Yankees took the house and the piano
narrative_blocks.body: A Union commander occupied the Bocage home at the end of the war and put the family down the street. On summer evenings they sat on that porch and heard someone else playing her piano.

narrative_blocks.header: She built the Arkansas Collection from nothing
narrative_blocks.body: Librarian at Forrest City from 1931 to 1958, she took it from five hundred volumes to twelve thousand and gathered thirteen hundred separate Arkansas items. She would say only that it was better not to ask.

narrative_blocks.header: Forrest City called her the birthday lady
narrative_blocks.body: For fifty years she sent cards to local citizens, college students and former residents on their birthdays. She married Dr. Feaster Proctor in 1909 and outlived him by eighteen years.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandfather was rector of Yale
narrative_blocks.body: Thomas Clap led the college for twenty-six years, and her father Timothy Pitkin was Farmington's minister. Her brother Timothy sat fourteen years in Congress and wrote the first statistical view of American commerce.

cross_connections.display_label: drew for the Yale papers too, and made a career of cartooning

narrative_blocks.header: He started on the Seagram with Philip Johnson
narrative_blocks.body: His first work was with Philip Johnson on the Seagram. In 1968 the Architectural Record gave him an award of excellence for a Baltimore house, one of the twenty best designed in America that year.

narrative_blocks.header: A handwritten island newspaper, eleven issues
narrative_blocks.body: Between fourteen and sixteen he edited and illustrated Vado Journalen for the people of the family's summer island, from 1942 to 1945. It is held in the Swedish Literature Society archives at Helsinki.

narrative_blocks.header: He drew cartoons for the Burlington Free Press
narrative_blocks.body: He took first place in the New England Press Association's cartoon contest in 1982. A governor's wife told him he could be hilariously funny and never nasty.

narrative_blocks.header: Named for a pastor and a mill owner
narrative_blocks.body: His grandfather Johannes Ilmanen was Lutheran pastor at Ilmajoki and sat for the clergy in the Diet of Finland; his grandfather Willem Stork owned the family textile mills at Hengelo in Holland.

cross_connections.display_label: held the same Institute for Advanced Study membership in 1955
carried Vienna's mathematics back to Yale; he stayed in Zurich instead
was on the faculty of the Institute for Advanced Study when he was a member in 1991

narrative_blocks.header: He proved the Riemannian Penrose inequality
narrative_blocks.body: With Gerhard Huisken he showed that the inverse mean curvature flow exists for all time, and used it to settle a 1973 conjecture of general relativity - the fifteenth problem on Yau's list.

narrative_blocks.header: His multiplicity-one conjecture was proved in 2023
narrative_blocks.body: He made it in a 1995 preprint about mean curvature flow in three-dimensional space. Bamler and Kleiner proved it thirty years on, and he lived to see it, as he did the other conjecture settled that year.

narrative_blocks.header: He died weeks before his retirement
narrative_blocks.body: ETH Zurich had him from 1999 and his emeritus date was set for the end of December 2025. He died unexpectedly on the twenty-second, at sixty-four, and his family put his unpublished lecture notes on arXiv.

notable.notable_blurb: Mathematician; proved the Riemannian Penrose inequality

narrative_blocks.header: Adopted as an infant, a worker in glass
narrative_blocks.body: She made stained glass and came back to live beside her mother's Baltimore land, saying the move put a face on the neighbourhood's fear of what might be built there. Her brother had to agree to anything done with it.

bio.bio_blurb: Eagle Squadron pilot; Fresno helicopter operator

cross_connections.display_label: won the George Medal in the same air force the same year

narrative_blocks.header: One of sixteen Americans flying for the RAF
narrative_blocks.body: He learned to fly at the Curtiss-Wright institute in Glendale in 1940 and went to the Eagle Squadrons in 1941, before his own country was in the war. He came back to the US Navy, and polio ended his flying service.

narrative_blocks.header: He married another Grumman test pilot
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth Hooker was flying for the same company at Bethpage when they married in New York in 1944. They ran a charter service on Long Island after the war, and he flew two years for the Brooklyn Dodgers.

narrative_blocks.header: He opened the Bay Area's first self-serve pumps
narrative_blocks.body: The Grings moved to California in 1948 and he set the station up at El Cerrito. He founded the Hokys drive-ins, with branches at Walnut Creek, Emeryville and Richmond, and then General Helicopter at Fresno.

narrative_blocks.header: Four days missing at nine thousand feet
narrative_blocks.body: He went up into the Sierras to salvage parts from downed helicopters and did not come back. An Army machine from Fort Ord found the wreck upside down in timber above deep snow near McClure Meadow.

burial.plot_notes: Ocean View Triangle, Lot 091, Quadrant NW 1

education.school_name: Curtiss-Wright Technical Institute of Aeronautics, Glendale

military_service.branch: Royal Air Force, later United States Navy
military_service.notes: One of sixteen American pilots who went to fly for the RAF before US entry; transferred to the Navy as a fighter pilot and was medically discharged after contracting polio.

narrative_blocks.header: Pineapple on Oahu, ranches on Molokai and Maui
narrative_blocks.body: His father was a Bay Area and Hawaii industrialist who held a principal stake in the San Francisco Seals. The son kept a Honolulu car dealership before the plantation and the ranches, and retired a stockbroker.

narrative_blocks.header: A heart attack at Montecito at fifty-six
narrative_blocks.body: He was schooled in the east and at Yale, came from Honolulu to Santa Barbara in 1958, and died at home on a Sunday in September 1972. He was buried at Holy Cross in Colma.

cross_connections.display_label: took over a family newspaper in the same years he came up in one

narrative_blocks.header: Associate publisher of the News-Press
narrative_blocks.body: He learned the paper from the bottom up as a schoolboy on his holidays, took Cornell in 1932 as his grandfather had, and went into its affairs at once. His father Thomas M. Storke ran it.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandfather was Santa Barbara's first mayor
narrative_blocks.body: Charles Albert Storke volunteered at sixteen into the 36th Wisconsin, came through the Wilderness, and was one of thirty-nine of his company left after Cold Harbor. He founded the Los Angeles Herald in 1873.

narrative_blocks.header: Eighth generation of his family in Santa Barbara
narrative_blocks.body: He was great-grandson to T. Wallace More, whose brother owned Santa Rosa Island and ran sheep on it. He helped form that island's chapter of the Santa Cruz Island Foundation in 1993.

narrative_blocks.header: He married Elizabeth at seventy-seven
narrative_blocks.body: Barbara Sellar Bullard, who had borne him five children, died in 1984. He and Elizabeth Hooker married in 1988, and he died at Santa Barbara ten years after that, at eighty-seven.

narrative_blocks.header: He chaired two funds listed since 1929
narrative_blocks.body: Ober joined The Adams Express Company in 1980 as a research analyst, went onto the portfolio team in 1986, and was elected chairman of Adams Express and Petroleum & Resources in 1991. He retired in 2013.

narrative_blocks.header: Princeton engineering, then test pilot school
narrative_blocks.body: He took the degree in 1968 and spent three years as a test project engineer at the U.S. Naval Air Test Center, graduating from the Naval Test Pilot School. Commercial lending in Baltimore came after that.

builds abstractions from slow repeated lines and Eastern thought

narrative_blocks.header: He paints with a car pinstriping tool
narrative_blocks.body: Kenneth Ober found the Beugler tool in 2007. It was made for striping automobiles, draws very fine lines of any length, and he builds whole fields out of thousands of them in many colours.

narrative_blocks.header: Jung's mandalas turned his work over
narrative_blocks.body: He had gone from fine art at Maryland into Buddhist philosophy and a year at Naropa in Boulder. Chicago in 1995, and Jung's writing on mandalas, moved him to weaving layers of text and graphic together.

narrative_blocks.header: He left Maryland to paint on his own
narrative_blocks.body: A schoolteacher who had started several artistic careers pushed him into diverse media first. He withdrew from College Park in 1993, and took his degree at Otis College of Art and Design in 2001.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten to fifteen art festivals a year
narrative_blocks.body: He began showing outdoors in 2012 and was doing that many by 2015. The Arizona circuit led him to Bisbee, an eclectic early-twentieth-century mining town in the southern mountains, and he moved there in 2020.

education.school_name: Geisel School of Medicine at Dartmouth

Robert Wood Johnson Clinical Scholars Program

career.role: Professor of Medicine, Emeritus; Senior Research Scientist
Director, Ambulatory Component of the Internal Medicine Clerkship

career.organization: Yale School of Medicine, Section of General Internal Medicine

cross_connections.display_label: showed what makes the first minutes of a stroke irreversible
worked on preventing stroke from the neurology side, decades earlier
has studied insulin resistance and heart disease at Harvard

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the trial on insulin resistance
narrative_blocks.body: Kernan was principal investigator for Insulin Resistance Intervention after Stroke, which gave pioglitazone to patients who had had a stroke but were not diabetic. It was the largest prevention trial the NINDS had funded, and it worked.

narrative_blocks.header: He led stroke trials without being a neurologist
narrative_blocks.body: He built an international career in stroke research out of general internal medicine. Prevention trials in the field had a long history of failure, and his was one of the few that came out positive.

narrative_blocks.header: He built a clerkship out of the clinic
narrative_blocks.body: He founded the ambulatory half of Yale's internal medicine clerkship, one of the first required ambulatory postings in any American core medicine clerkship, and ran it for nearly twenty-five years.

narrative_blocks.header: The clerkship directors elected him president
narrative_blocks.body: Clerkship Directors in Internal Medicine, the national body, chose him on the strength of what he had built at Yale. He later helped marry the clerkship to psychiatry's.

narrative_blocks.header: The trial lost its neurologist in year two
narrative_blocks.body: Lawrence Brass had joined the Yale faculty when Kernan did, and the two had worked on stroke together since 1988. Brass died of lung cancer at forty-nine in 2006, and Karen Furie took the neurology over.

narrative_blocks.header: A colleague said Alvan would be surprised
narrative_blocks.body: Alvan Feinstein had been his fellowship mentor, and nobody, himself included, had assumed research would be his career. When the NIH grant came, Kernan's answer was that Alvan was a smart man.

narrative_blocks.header: He came back to Yale and stayed
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Milton in Massachusetts, he read at Harvard, took his medicine at Dartmouth and his residency at Johns Hopkins, then came to Yale in 1987 as a Robert Wood Johnson fellow and never left.

people.research_notes: Son of Beatrice Houghton Hooker & Louis Reed Huppman. b. Nov 29 1951. Living; minimal detail.

narrative_blocks.header: He could not place all his grandmother's shots
narrative_blocks.body: Tim Kernan showed her turn-of-the-century albums at the Wakefield Estate in March 2014 and asked the room for help. He and his wife Susan had not worked out where some of the Milton pictures were taken.

narrative_blocks.header: The oldest Farmington families were hers
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Norton was born at Avon in 1827 to George Norton and Elizabeth Frisbie, and her father's line ran back to the first settlers of Farmington. She married Ebenezer Curtiss in October 1846.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived him by thirteen years
narrative_blocks.body: Widowed in 1890, she went to live with their son Charles at Simsbury. She had been a Congregationalist there for many years, and was in excellent health still in her seventies.

narrative_blocks.header: He drove western cattle back to Connecticut
narrative_blocks.body: Ebenezer Curtiss farmed in early manhood, then settled at Weatogue and went into cattle. He bought his stock in the west and had it driven east.

narrative_blocks.header: Simsbury sent him to the legislature
narrative_blocks.body: He was a prominent Democrat in his corner of Hartford County and represented the town in the Connecticut State Legislature. He belonged to St. Mark's Lodge at Simsbury.

narrative_blocks.header: Born near the Canton line, buried at Simsbury
narrative_blocks.body: He was born in the Bushy Hill District in 1822, and spent part of his boyhood at Southwick in Massachusetts where his parents lived a while. He died at Simsbury in 1890 and was buried there.

cross_connections.display_label: ran Stanley Rule & Level, one of the New Britain hardware firms

education.school_name: District schools of Weatogue and Meadow Plain

narrative_blocks.header: He came home to Simsbury in 1879
narrative_blocks.body: Before that he clerked in a Simsbury general store, sold shelf hardware across New York State for Humason & Beckly, ran a livery at Oneonta and kept books for a Westfield grocer. Ensign, Bickford took him on after.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought the house with seven elms
narrative_blocks.body: The Averett Wilcox homestead at Simsbury took its name from the trees across its front. Curtiss moved into The Seven Elms on 10 April 1889, and the county reckoned it the best appointed residence in the town.

narrative_blocks.header: A Democrat who would not stand for office
narrative_blocks.body: He voted the state and national tickets without fail, and in town matters picked the best men regardless of party. He declined every time he was asked to be a candidate himself.

narrative_blocks.header: One of the best stables in the county
narrative_blocks.body: Curtiss was an enthusiastic horseman and was reckoned an excellent judge of the animal. He kept his horses at Simsbury, and belonged to St. Mark's Lodge there as his father had.

narrative_blocks.header: He could name every district teacher
narrative_blocks.body: He began at Weatogue under Ellen Marks, moved to the Meadow Plain school in 1859 for Lucy Alford, Addie Allen and Minnie Case, and finished with a single winter at Guilford Institute.

narrative_blocks.header: Nobody wrote down where she came from
narrative_blocks.body: Mercy Thompson was born in 1791 and married Hooker Dorchester about 1814. The Hounsfield deeds make John Thompson her father, and Lucy Phelps and Lucretia Potter her sisters.

narrative_blocks.header: Three children, and dead at thirty-four
narrative_blocks.body: Delia Ann came in 1815, Henry Cowles in 1818 and Alfred in 1820. Mercy Dorchester died in the spring of 1825, and Hooker had married Maria Van Schaick before the year was out.

narrative_blocks.header: Two censuses, and then dead at twenty-four
narrative_blocks.body: Delia Dorchester was counted at Richmond in 1790 and at Westmoreland in 1800. She died in May 1810, the year the family moved to Jefferson County, one of only two of Anna's nine to reach twenty.

narrative_blocks.header: A hundred and one years old
narrative_blocks.body: Delia Ann Dorchester was born at Hounsfield on 8 June 1815 and lived until 1916. She was five when the census counted her and twenty when she chose her own guardian, and she outlived the century.

narrative_blocks.header: A neighbour called her amiable in 1833
narrative_blocks.body: Nancy Phelps wrote that spring that Delia Ann, Henry and Alfred were in good health and as amiable children as their best friends could wish. Their mother had been dead eight years.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifteen at his father's death in 1835
narrative_blocks.body: Alfred Dorchester was born in 1820, the last of Mercy Thompson's three. He and his brother and sister petitioned the Jefferson surrogate that April for Thompson Phelps to be their guardian.

narrative_blocks.header: Two wives, and six children between them
narrative_blocks.body: Susan Grow bore Clarissa, Hooker Grove and William Hardy before she died at thirty-one in 1852. Chloe Baker came in 1857 and gave him Edwin, Dillie and Sarah. He died at Brownville in 1888.

narrative_blocks.header: Stepdaughter to the first governor of Iowa
narrative_blocks.body: Ansel Briggs took office in 1846, and Illinois Carpenter was his stepdaughter. She married A. J. Dorchester in 1860, bore eight children in twenty-one years and died at Bellevue in July 1890, forty-nine.

narrative_blocks.header: She took four years off her age
narrative_blocks.body: Georgia Dorchester married Frank S. Fanning before a justice of the peace at Savannah in Illinois in February 1904. The licence gives her as thirty-six; she was born in 1864 and was forty.

narrative_blocks.header: The statue on the family lot is him
narrative_blocks.body: Andrew Jackson Dorchester Jr. was two and a half when he died in May 1872, the first death in the family and his father's only son. The Bellevue monument carries a reclining boy with his dog.

narrative_blocks.header: She died on her nineteenth birthday
narrative_blocks.body: Mabel Dorchester was born on 6 April 1874 and died on 6 April 1893, the same day of the same month. Her small stone at Bellevue stands beside her brother's.

narrative_blocks.header: Denver, after a visit to California
narrative_blocks.body: Carrie Rentz left Bellevue High School with the class of 1900 and made her home at Denver with William Rentz. She had six children, buried him in 1944, and was stricken soon after coming home in 1946.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine children, and Michigan at the end
narrative_blocks.body: Martha Dorchester married Nathaniel Perkins at the close of 1848 and bore nine between 1850 and 1868. The family left Brownville for Richland Township in Saginaw County after the war.

narrative_blocks.header: A widow's pension, and eighty-seven years
narrative_blocks.body: Nathaniel Perkins served in the Tenth New York Heavy Artillery from 1862 and went into the Navy in 1864. He died in 1907, she filed for the widow's pension that December, and she lived to 1913.

narrative_blocks.header: A son born before the marriage
narrative_blocks.body: Franklin Benjamin appears in the 1850 and 1855 censuses under that name and not Witt, so Eli Witt was not his father. From 1855 on he is in the Witt household under the Witt surname.

narrative_blocks.header: Typhoid pneumonia took her at forty-two
narrative_blocks.body: Caroline Warner was living at Lyme when she died on 10 January 1875. The state mortality schedule set down the cause. She and Ely Warner had two daughters, Anna and Kate.

cross_connections.display_label: served in the same Tenth New York Heavy Artillery from 1862

military_service.unit: Co. I, 10th New York Heavy Artillery
military_service.notes: Enlisted at Brownville 7 Aug 1862 aged eighteen; corporal Sept 1862, sergeant Dec 1862, quartermaster-sergeant Sept 1864; mustered out at Petersburg 23 June 1865. Broadbent Post, G.A.R., Dexter.

narrative_blocks.header: Private at eighteen, sergeant by December
narrative_blocks.body: He enlisted at Brownville on 7 August 1862 into the Black River Artillery, which became the Tenth New York. Corporal that September and sergeant by Christmas, he mustered out at Petersburg in June 1865.

narrative_blocks.header: His age was set down to the day
narrative_blocks.body: He was in poor health two or three years and kept his bed the last month, dying at Limerick in May 1902. The count given was fifty-eight years, seven months and eighteen days.

narrative_blocks.header: Four daughters left, and one buried
narrative_blocks.body: Elsie died in 1880, the year after she and Alice were born. Nellie, Lydia, Carrie and Alice all outlived their father, and Vernelia Allen outlived him by sixteen years.

narrative_blocks.header: Pearl died at thirty-one, the children small
narrative_blocks.body: Pearl Flint bore Paul in 1900, Mildred in 1903 and Clifford in 1906, and died in May 1909. Thomas Dorchester was left with a nine-year-old, a six-year-old and a boy of three.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixteen years a widow at Dexter
narrative_blocks.body: Vernelia Allen married Henry Cowles Dorchester and bore him five daughters, one of whom died in infancy. He went in 1902 and she in 1918, and they lie in the Dexter burying ground.

narrative_blocks.header: Mrs Gale of Pamelia, and ten children
narrative_blocks.body: Nellie Dorchester married George Gale of Brownville and was named that way in her father's notice of 1902, the eldest of his four surviving daughters. Ten children came of the marriage.

cross_connections.display_label: put a boy on a Saranac Lake sleeping porch in 1910 into a poem

bio.bio_blurb: Methodist church organist at Saranac Lake

narrative_blocks.header: She knew at school whom she would marry
narrative_blocks.body: Kitty Ober met Jack Peightal at school and married him in September 1948, the year she took her Syracuse degree in art and industrial engineering. They had fifty-one years less ten.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-five years at the church organ
narrative_blocks.body: She played every Sunday at the First United Methodist Church in Saranac Lake. She was a teacher's assistant, a quilter and a gardener, and volunteered at the Free Library and Pine Ridge Cemetery.

narrative_blocks.header: The house her grandfather bought for the cure
narrative_blocks.body: Fred Everett took the Riverside Drive house in 1910 so Nellie could cure for tuberculosis with her five children near her. Kitty was raised in it and raised her own three daughters there.

military_service.notes: Infantryman; afterwards appointed to West Point, discharged on a shoulder injury.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-two years of Saranac Lake mathematics
narrative_blocks.body: He chaired the department and coached football in the fifties and sixties and skiing in the seventies, retiring in 1984. Students remembered the Dixieland banjo and what he knew about the Civil War.

narrative_blocks.header: West Point took him, then discharged him
narrative_blocks.body: He served as an army infantryman in the war and won an appointment to the military academy afterwards, but a shoulder injury ended it. He took his degree at Albany State instead.

narrative_blocks.header: She covered federal courts for Reuters
narrative_blocks.body: Maisie McAdoo reported and edited business and the federal courts for Reuters and Knight-Ridder Financial News. Before that she was a reporter and researcher for the New York City teachers union.

narrative_blocks.header: She teaches newswriting at Brooklyn College
narrative_blocks.body: She keeps the discipline of journalism and holds to an interest in education and labour. She writes fiction as well as non-fiction, and lives between Brooklyn and the northern Catskills.

career.role: Reporter and editor, business and the federal courts

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-five years of drawing Truckee
narrative_blocks.body: Pamela McAdoo works in drawing, painting, printmaking and book arts, and came to the Sierra from the farmland outside New York City she was raised on. Music, dance and architecture are hers too.

narrative_blocks.header: She puts overheard words into the drawings
narrative_blocks.body: In The Moment takes after Paul Madonna, whose synthesis of text and reportage illustration she admired. She sets down conversations overheard, or the thought that arrives while she is drawing.

cross_connections.display_label: wrote the poems of Heaven is in Truckee, in 2021

narrative_blocks.header: Steamboat captain, then lumber at Bellevue
narrative_blocks.body: Hooker Grove Dorchester came to Bellevue in 1870 and ran a small steamer between there and Galena. He went into produce, then into lumber with his uncle A. J. Dorchester, then into Dorchester and Hughey.

narrative_blocks.header: Several terms mayor of Bellevue
narrative_blocks.body: He held various offices of trust across nearly half a century in the town. He moved to California about 1923 and died at Glendale, and Josie Warren, whom he married in 1873, followed in 1939.

narrative_blocks.header: His son wired the news back to Bellevue
narrative_blocks.body: He died at Glendale on a Sunday and was buried there two days later, Fred sending the word from California to the paper at home. He had been in poor health for some time.

cross_connections.display_label: enlisted in that same Tenth New York Artillery at eighteen

military_service.notes: Enlisted 1862; transferred to the United States Navy in 1864. Invalid pension certificate 23037.

narrative_blocks.header: Two months short of eighty-eight
narrative_blocks.body: Josephine Warren was born at Bellevue on 18 February 1852, daughter of Captain W. A. Warren. A second stroke took her at Los Angeles that December, and she was cremated at Forest Lawn.

narrative_blocks.header: Bellevue until 1923, then California
narrative_blocks.body: She was active in social affairs and church work in the town where she and Hooker Grove Dorchester made their home from 1873. Her ashes were placed beside his.

burial.plot_notes: Cremated at Forest Lawn; ashes placed beside her husband

narrative_blocks.header: He carried the President's wireless in 1905
narrative_blocks.body: Fred Dorchester was with the DeForest company aboard the West Virginia when she took Roosevelt from New Orleans to Annapolis. Four ships ran in column above eighteen knots, which had not been done before.

narrative_blocks.header: Colón next, to test a high-power station
narrative_blocks.body: He wrote home that the cruise was the finest experience he had ever had, and then left for Panama to be gone the winter. He settled afterwards at Escondido in California.

parents.father_research_notes: Charles (Karel) van Baerle, 1715-1771. Dutch line; not built.

narrative_blocks.header: She bought four hundred Manhattan acres
narrative_blocks.body: Frederica van Baerle took the Bloomingdale land off James McEvers in 1792, in what was then open country above the city. She died the next year, and the farm passed to her husband.

narrative_blocks.header: Mother to a congressman's wife
narrative_blocks.body: Her daughter Margaret married Ralph Isaacs Ingersoll of Connecticut in 1814. He went to Congress and afterwards to St Petersburg as American minister to the Russian Empire.

narrative_blocks.header: Charles van Baerle's daughter, a baron's wife
narrative_blocks.body: She was born in 1755 to Charles van Baerle and Geertruid van Grunningen, and became the second wife of Jan Cornelis van den Heuvel after his first wife died in 1771.

marriages.notes: First husband a Gresham; the marriage ended in divorce

narrative_blocks.header: She made a life out of colour
narrative_blocks.body: She took an M.F.A. at Virginia Commonwealth and painted for sixty years, taught by Theresa Pollak, Adele Clark, the Campbells and a dozen more. Late on it was Ikebana, and the Richmond society's motto, Friendship through Flowers.

narrative_blocks.header: An artist married a microbiologist in 1981
narrative_blocks.body: Her first marriage, to a Gresham, ended in divorce and left her two daughters. In February 1981 she married Dr. Stephen Scott Morse, then teaching microbiology at Rutgers, at St. Paul's Episcopal in Richmond.

narrative_blocks.header: She walked to the market until the end
narrative_blocks.body: She lived alone in her own house and garden in Richmond and was still walking to the farmers market three weeks before she died, at ninety-one. Summers she went to Woods Hole with the family.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandfather ran Wilson's currency
narrative_blocks.body: John Skelton Williams was Comptroller of the Currency from 1914 to 1921 and president of the Seaboard railway before that; her grandmother was Lila Lefebvre Isaacs. Her brother was the third John Skelton Williams.

narrative_blocks.header: He joined two fields that ignored each other
narrative_blocks.body: Environmental Pollution and Mental Health came out in 1973, co-authored, at a time when neither discipline admitted the other existed. What he was describing turned into a field of its own.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped invent community-based conservation
narrative_blocks.body: As a senior scientist at the World Conservation Union he worked on the idea that the people who live in a place should run its conservation. He consulted for the World Bank, the Population Reference Bureau and the World Wildlife Fund.

narrative_blocks.header: He counted houses for the Carter administration
narrative_blocks.body: He taught social research at the New School and at Connecticut before co-founding MetroStudy in Washington, which did demographic work on urban housing, much of it for federal agencies in the late 1970s.

narrative_blocks.header: Poetry and technology, rivers and cities
narrative_blocks.body: He was a soft-spoken Virginian and a fierce environmentalist, at home in a city and happiest outdoors. He paddled for years with the Washington Canoe Club on multi-day river trips and sat on the board of American Rivers.

narrative_blocks.header: The third of the name, and the last
narrative_blocks.body: His grandfather John Skelton Williams drew the Federal Reserve districts and was Wilson's Comptroller of the Currency; his father sold life insurance in Richmond. He was born at Richmond and died at Silver Spring at eighty-eight.

parents.father_research_notes: Of New London; son of Frank L. McGuire. Her maternal grandmother was Mrs. James T. Connolly of Newburyport.

made marine watercolour her subject on the other coast

narrative_blocks.header: Words turned into an alphabet of her own
narrative_blocks.body: She read creative writing, languages and playwriting at Connecticut College and drew all over her notebooks, until the words themselves became calligraphic marks. That invented alphabet stayed in the work.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty years painting the same ocean
narrative_blocks.body: The Atlantic was there from the time they were born, she said — New London, then Newburyport. She painted the Maine coast in 1986 and 1987, and from 1990 worked out of a sailboat at Chester in Nova Scotia.

narrative_blocks.header: Look at Art, written over and over
narrative_blocks.body: Her studio was in lower Manhattan, not far from the towers. After September 2001 she wrote plain words in rows across the paper — breakfast, lunch, dinner, silence — as a ritual. It could only transform it.

narrative_blocks.header: Used tea bags on a linen canvas
narrative_blocks.body: Tea, made in London in 1974, gives each spent bag its own volume and horizon line. She had an Islington studio there and bought the largest canvases that would fit inside a taxi.

narrative_blocks.header: Married the day they both graduated
narrative_blocks.body: She met Anthony Enders in 1961 at a Labor Day party his aunt gave at Waterford. They married in June 1962, the day she took her Connecticut College degree and he took his from the Harvard business school.

narrative_blocks.header: A master's at forty-eight, then the shows
narrative_blocks.body: New York University gave it to her in 1987, and she joined the board of Artists Space that year alongside Cindy Sherman and Elizabeth Murray. The one-person exhibitions followed from 1992.

narrative_blocks.header: Whitney, Brooklyn, Boston, Detroit
narrative_blocks.body: Her work hangs in those and in the Wadsworth Atheneum, the Addison, Smith, Colby, the Tang and the Art Gallery of Nova Scotia. The Lyman Allyn gave her a retrospective in 2009.

narrative_blocks.header: An Oscar-nominated short
narrative_blocks.body: Camilla starred in Speed for Thespians, nominated for the Academy Award for best live-action short film in 2001, and has played in New York and regional theater and on Law & Order.

narrative_blocks.header: "The fastest woman alive"
narrative_blocks.body: Jim Bernfield cast Camilla as a superhero, "the fastest woman alive," in his student film Alphamale Takes on the World!. Their first coffee after the shoot lasted six hours, and they married in Manhattan in October 2003.

sources.short: "Camilla Enders, James Bernfield", New York Times, 12 October 2003

career.organization: New York and regional theater; Law & Order

narrative_blocks.header: He helped build the first SERF magnetometers
narrative_blocks.body: In Michael Romalis's group at Princeton, Thomas helped develop the first SERF magnetometers, which read faint magnetic fields from the spins of electrons in potassium vapour, and for his dissertation built a co-magnetometer to test fundamental physics.

narrative_blocks.header: Twinleaf, named for a wildflower
narrative_blocks.body: In 2007 Thomas and Jill founded Twinleaf to sell those magnetometers, among the most sensitive made. They named it for the twinleaf, a rare spring wildflower of the eastern woods; his parents had spent eight seasons counting wild orchids.

narrative_blocks.header: Two astrophysicists met at Princeton
narrative_blocks.body: He was reading for a doctorate in astrophysical sciences there and Jill Foley had taken hers. They married at the Quaker meeting house at Crosswicks in New Jersey in October 2005.

narrative_blocks.header: President of Twinleaf
narrative_blocks.body: Jill is president of Twinleaf, the magnetometer company she and her husband founded at Princeton in 2007. Her own Princeton doctorate was on neutral-beam diagnostics of hot, magnetised plasmas.

narrative_blocks.header: Research physicist at Nova Photonics
narrative_blocks.body: She took her doctorate in astrophysical sciences at Princeton and went to the alternative-energy company there. Massachusetts had given her the first degree, and she goes by Jill.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father ran three Albany companies
narrative_blocks.body: Delphine Pumpelly was born at Owego in 1833 to Harmon Pumpelly, president of the Albany Savings Bank, the Albany Insurance Company and its gaslight company. She married John Meredith Read at Albany the day after her twenty-sixth birthday.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed in Paris, and she stayed
narrative_blocks.body: Delphine was widowed at Paris in December 1896 and stayed on in the city, dying five and a half years later at No. 128 Rue La Boetie, off the Champs-Élysées. She was buried beside her husband at Saint-Germain-en-Laye.

narrative_blocks.header: Her children ran from 1803 to 1823
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth Barnard married John Bradford Ripley out of Hartford, and their children ran from Henrietta in 1803 to Edwin in 1823. She outlived her husband by eighteen years, dying at Blandford in 1870 at eighty-seven.

narrative_blocks.header: The first woman in Marion County to fly
narrative_blocks.body: Barbara Lindner grew up in Ocala, the daughter of Dr. Eaton George Lindner, and was the first woman in Marion County to hold a pilot licence. She left the town when she married Ben Wood.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote the travelling down afterwards
narrative_blocks.body: Barbara followed her husband through the Foreign Service postings and lived most of her life outside America. She wrote about the people she met along the way, and kept up an interest in astrology.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote the book that made de Wolfe
narrative_blocks.body: Wood ghosted The House in Good Taste for Elsie de Wolfe in 1913, and de Wolfe's Ladies Home Journal pieces besides. The book is why most people know de Wolfe as a decorator at all.

narrative_blocks.header: Wanamaker put her over Belmaison
narrative_blocks.body: Wood ran Belmaison, the decorating division inside the John Wanamaker store in New York, before opening Ruby Ross Wood, Inc. in the 1920s. Alfred Vanderbilt, Rodman Wanamaker and Brooke Astor were clients.

narrative_blocks.header: Her drawing room was vermilion throughout
narrative_blocks.body: Walls, ceiling, rug, curtains, lampshades and upholstery in Wood's Manhattan drawing room were all the one molten vermilion. She was a chain-smoker with a sharp tongue who called herself a working girl.

narrative_blocks.header: She started out writing, not decorating
narrative_blocks.body: Wood wrote fiction, poetry and design pieces for The Delineator under its editor Theodore Dreiser, using her first married name. Her architecture series became a book, The Honest House, in 1914.

narrative_blocks.header: A hundred and sixty-six words in the Times
narrative_blocks.body: Wood died of lung cancer in February 1950 and the New York Times printed a hundred and sixty-six words. Elsie de Wolfe died five months later and got column inches and a photograph.

narrative_blocks.header: Billy Baldwin kept her rule
narrative_blocks.body: Wood hired Billy Baldwin in the 1930s, and the man who became the dean of American decorating called her the finest who ever lived. He kept her rule: 'The final judgement is not the logic of the mind, but the logic of the eye.'

cross_connections.display_label: co-owned Villa Trianon with Elsie de Wolfe, whose book Wood ghosted

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Little Ipswich, Syosset

narrative_blocks.header: Doris Lessing introduced his first book
narrative_blocks.body: Wood's first Kalila and Dimna volume came out from Knopf in 1980 with an introduction by the novelist Doris Lessing, who went on to write one for all seven English editions.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote it in a Fife fishing cottage
narrative_blocks.body: Wood wrote that first book in a fisherman's cottage at Anstruther in Fife. Then he went back to London and set up Frame Up Ltd, importing ready-made German picture frames into Britain.

narrative_blocks.header: Mornings teaching, afternoons on book two
narrative_blocks.body: Wood spent his mornings at Emerson House in London teaching dyslexic children to read and type off colour-coded screens, and wrote his second volume in the afternoons. His two favourite ambigrams are dollop and swims.

narrative_blocks.header: He called the fables the first remix culture
narrative_blocks.body: Lecturing at Fez in 2011, Wood argued that the Jataka tales, Aesop and the Panchatantra are among the oldest examples of what Lawrence Lessig calls remix culture. No original Sanskrit or Greek text survives.

narrative_blocks.header: Edinburgh saw it as a one-man play
narrative_blocks.body: Stuart Cox of Theatr Taliesin Wales made the first volume into a play, A Word in the Stargazer's Eye, with Nigel Watson alone on the stage. It opened at the Edinburgh Festival in 1984.

narrative_blocks.header: A diplomat's son, and Saigon at sixteen
narrative_blocks.body: Wood was born in Texas in 1943 and moved with his father's postings through Belgium, the Philippines, Virginia and Florida, reaching Vietnam in 1959. He left Harvard in 1964 for London and photojournalism.

narrative_blocks.header: His consulting room was in the house
narrative_blocks.body: Butler practised medicine at Hartford and kept his consulting room in the Main Street house. He owned a grist mill, a saw mill and a paper mill besides, and bought the ground the house stands on in 1782.

narrative_blocks.header: He built the oldest house on Main Street
narrative_blocks.body: Butler put up a twin-chimney house at 396 Main Street in 1782, onto a blacksmith's shop of about 1740 that became its kitchen. It is the only eighteenth-century house left on Hartford's Main Street.

narrative_blocks.header: His patients paid him in clapboards
narrative_blocks.body: Butler's account book shows customers settling their debts on the new house by working it off: clapboarding the west end, working on the chimney, putting in three cellar windows, whitewashing rooms and buttery.

narrative_blocks.header: A falling beech turned up his rubbish heap
narrative_blocks.body: A windstorm in August 1979 toppled a copper beech twenty feet behind the kitchen, and its root mat came up full of the household's leavings. Fifteen thousand artifacts were recovered, and the ceramics dated to about 1790.

narrative_blocks.header: He and Sarah died six days apart
narrative_blocks.body: Butler died on 18 January 1812 and Sarah Sheldon followed on the twenty-fourth. Their son John bought the house out from his sisters two years later, and it stayed in the family for another century and a half.

narrative_blocks.header: His ledger names the women in the mill
narrative_blocks.body: Butler took over his father's paper mills and kept the books himself. Mill Ledger C, running from 1818 to 1826, records what he paid the men and the women who worked in them.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought the house off his sisters
narrative_blocks.body: Butler took full rights to the Main Street house from his sisters in 1814, two years after both their parents died in the same week.

narrative_blocks.header: He married at fifty-six and refitted the house
narrative_blocks.body: Butler was fifty-six when he married Eliza Lydia Royce in May 1837. The kitchen and back room were made over that year, and she furnished the parlour with a sofa, card table and rocking chair from Isaac Wright's factory.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at twenty-one just starting out
narrative_blocks.body: Butler died at New York on 11 November 1806, in his twenty-second year. He had only just started in business, and was remembered at Hartford as a young man of amiable life and excellent character.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived her husband by six days
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah Sheldon married Dr. Daniel Butler and bore eleven children in the Main Street house between 1780 and 1798. She survived him by six days, dying on 24 January 1812, and lies with him at Old North.

narrative_blocks.header: The mills came to Butler through her
narrative_blocks.body: The paper, grist and saw mills Dr. Daniel Butler owned had belonged to Sarah's first husband, and came to Butler with the marriage. Their son John took them on after him and kept the ledgers himself.

narrative_blocks.header: She came to the Butlers a widow
narrative_blocks.body: Eliza Lydia Royce was already widowed from a Shelden when she married John Butler in 1837, and brought a daughter, Mary Sheldon, into the Main Street house. Mary kept her own room there and helped run the household.

narrative_blocks.header: The garden came too late for her
narrative_blocks.body: Jacob Weidenmann laid out the formal garden behind the Main Street house in 1865. It was her daughter Mary Sheldon who brought him to it, seven years after Eliza herself had died.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: 396 Main Street, Hartford

narrative_blocks.header: Born, married and died in one house
narrative_blocks.body: Eliza was born at 396 Main Street in 1840, married John James McCook in the same house in 1866, and died in it in 1917 at seventy-seven. Her grandfather Dr. Daniel Butler had built it.

narrative_blocks.header: Her middle name was her great-grandmother's
narrative_blocks.body: Eliza carried the Sheldon of Sarah Sheldon, who had married Dr. Daniel Butler and borne eleven children in that house. Eliza bore eight of her own in it.

narrative_blocks.header: He proposed on her mother's parlour sofa
narrative_blocks.body: The sofa Eliza Lydia Royce bought from Isaac Wright's factory in 1837 was still in the south parlour when John James McCook proposed on it in 1866. It has never left the house.

narrative_blocks.header: A Weidenmann garden behind the house
narrative_blocks.body: Jacob Weidenmann laid out a formal garden behind 396 Main Street in 1865, an oasis in an industrialising Hartford. Eliza and her half-sister Mary Sheldon had just come back from three years in Europe.

narrative_blocks.header: He counted Hartford's tramps himself
narrative_blocks.body: McCook's studies of vagrancy, drink and the tramp were among the first American attempts to put numbers to them. He wrote on prison reform, public education, homelessness, voter fraud and disabled veterans.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty years of modern languages at Trinity
narrative_blocks.body: McCook took his Trinity degree in 1863 and came back in 1883 as professor of modern languages, staying more than thirty years and chairing the board of fellows. The college endowed a chair in his name.

narrative_blocks.header: Rector at East Hartford for fifty years
narrative_blocks.body: McCook was rector of St. John's Episcopal Church in East Hartford for half a century, after pastorates at Detroit.

narrative_blocks.header: One of the Fighting McCooks
narrative_blocks.body: McCook was born at New Lisbon in Ohio into the family Ohio called the Fighting McCooks, which sent fifteen men to the Union army. He came east to Trinity and never went back.

narrative_blocks.header: He married her in her own birthplace
narrative_blocks.body: McCook married Eliza Sheldon Butler at 396 Main Street in June 1866 and moved into it. They kept their golden wedding there in 1916, and he outlived her by ten years.

narrative_blocks.header: He was a lieutenant at eighteen
narrative_blocks.body: McCook went out at eighteen as a lieutenant in the 1st Virginia volunteers, a regiment raised almost wholly in Ohio. He resigned in the autumn of 1862 and went back to take his Trinity degree.

narrative_blocks.body: McCook went out as a first lieutenant and assistant surgeon with the 1st Connecticut in 1898, the year of the Spanish-American War. He practised medicine at Hartford the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: One of fifty women sent out in 1898
narrative_blocks.body: Eliza went to China under the United Thank Offering of 1898, one of fifty women the Women's Auxiliary sent to the mission fields that year. She was at Hankow from 1899 and married Roots there in 1902.

narrative_blocks.header: She sent her sketchbook home to Hartford
narrative_blocks.body: Eliza drew what she saw in China and filled a sketchbook she sent back to her family at Hartford. Her mother had recorded her own life the same way, and the drawings are still in the Main Street house.

narrative_blocks.header: She died of tuberculosis at Kuling
narrative_blocks.body: Eliza went out to the American Church Mission at Hankow and spent her life in China. She died of tuberculosis in the hills at Kuling in 1934 and lies in the foreign cemetery there, with a cenotaph on Mackinac Island.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave Lucky Luciano thirty to fifty years
narrative_blocks.body: McCook sat twenty-four years on the New York Supreme Court. He presided over the special grand jury that indicted Charles Luciano and over the trials that followed, and sentenced Luciano to thirty to fifty years.

narrative_blocks.header: He crossed the fire three times to telephone
narrative_blocks.body: Sent to reconnoitre the line near Lion-devant-Dun in November 1918, McCook crossed artillery and machine-gun fire twice to telephone his report and was hit on the third crossing, his leg broken.

narrative_blocks.header: He went to a third war at sixty-nine
narrative_blocks.body: McCook went to Puerto Rico a corporal of infantry in 1898 and was a major in the Meuse-Argonne in 1918. At sixty-nine he took a colonelcy in the Judge Advocate's department for the second war.

narrative_blocks.header: His son died in the Pacific in 1944
narrative_blocks.body: McCook had left the bench for the Judge Advocate's staff and was sitting on a court-martial at Cincinnati when word came that his son Daniel, a captain with the 27th Division, had died in the Pacific.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Democratic governors picked him
narrative_blocks.body: McCook was a staunch Republican, and Franklin Roosevelt still put him over the Ewald-Healy job-buying inquiry in 1930, which led on to the Seabury investigation. Herbert Lehman gave him the rackets inquiry in 1935.

narrative_blocks.header: He pestered Stimson from Pearl Harbor on
narrative_blocks.body: McCook had been at Henry Stimson since 7 December 1941 for a commission. The Secretary of War gave him one in 1943, a month before McCook would have hit the bench's mandatory retirement at seventy.

narrative_blocks.body: Frances worked through probate, birth, death and marriage records in the library to build the family tree back to the men who left Massachusetts to found Hartford in 1637. She was the last of them to live in the house.

narrative_blocks.header: Dewey named him on the first list
narrative_blocks.body: McCook left Wall Street in 1938 when Thomas Dewey, then district attorney, named him in the first round of appointments to his office. He stayed until he went into the army.

narrative_blocks.header: He died seven months after his wedding
narrative_blocks.body: McCook married Cornelia Sloane at Princeton in September 1943 and was dead by the following April, serving with the 27th Division in the Pacific. He was thirty-four.

narrative_blocks.header: Four generations of the family in uniform
narrative_blocks.body: His father was wounded in the Argonne, and his grandfather and great-grandfather were officers in Union armies. McCook entered as a captain on the general staff of the 27th Division in 1940.

military_service.notes: Died on service in the Pacific, 11 April 1944.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the Election Frauds Bureau
narrative_blocks.body: McCook was made special assistant attorney general over New York's Election Frauds Bureau in 1950, directing a staff of volunteer lawyers through that autumn's elections.

narrative_blocks.header: A Farmington girl and a Harvard law student
narrative_blocks.body: McCook was still at Harvard Law when his engagement to Anne Whaples of Farmington was announced at the end of 1935. They married in the June of 1937.

cross_connections.display_label: wrote on voter fraud two generations before his grandson prosecuted it

career.role: Special Assistant Attorney General, Election Frauds Bureau
career.organization: New York State Department of Law

narrative_blocks.header: Vassar in 1942, then the OSS
narrative_blocks.body: Cornelia Sloane came out of Vassar in 1942 and was working for the Office of Strategic Services in Washington when her engagement was announced the next year.

narrative_blocks.header: They called him the Red Bishop
narrative_blocks.body: Roots kept open house at Hankow for journalists and politicians of every stripe, Edgar Snow and Agnes Smedley and Zhou Enlai among them, and was called the Red Bishop for it. He was on good terms with Chiang Kai-shek as well.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-two years on the Yangtze
narrative_blocks.body: Roots went out in 1896 to teach English at the Boone School in Wuchang and stayed forty-two years. He chaired the China Continuation Committee from 1913, the first body that tried to unite the Christian forces of China.

narrative_blocks.header: He presented China's bishops to George V
narrative_blocks.body: As Primate of the Chinese Episcopal Church, Roots led its House of Bishops from 1926 and took them to London for the Lambeth conference of 1930, where he presented them to King George V.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped launch the Oxford Group in China
narrative_blocks.body: Roots met Frank Buchman, founder of the Oxford Group, at Kuling in 1917 and helped him hold its first international gathering there the year after. He left China in 1938 to lead the movement, by then renamed Moral Re-Armament.

narrative_blocks.header: Chiang sent a plane for his wife's funeral
narrative_blocks.body: When Eliza died at Kuling in 1934, Roots and his sons were crossing Siberia from Europe. Chiang Kai-shek sent his private plane to Peking for the last leg, and Madame Chiang came to the funeral.

narrative_blocks.header: Fort Roots was named for his uncle
narrative_blocks.body: Roots was the son of a Little Rock banker and the namesake of his uncle, Colonel Logan H. Roots, for whom Fort Roots in Arkansas is named.

cross_connections.display_label: got sober through the movement Roots helped Buchman launch

notable.notable_blurb: Episcopal Bishop of Hankow

narrative_blocks.header: Zhou Enlai invited her back in 1972
narrative_blocks.body: When Washington and Peking resumed relations in 1972, Zhou Enlai asked Frances and Richard Hadden to come as his personal guests and play a duet recital. It was the first by an American musician there since 1949.

narrative_blocks.header: She built a suite from a stone-carriers' chant
narrative_blocks.body: Frances was born at Kuling on Lu Shan and grew up hearing the chant the stone carriers sang on the mountain. She made it the theme of her Lu Shan Suite in 1966 and played it on that 1972 tour.

narrative_blocks.header: Two composers married at Caux
narrative_blocks.body: Frances and Richard Hadden wrote the music for the wartime revues You Can Defend America and Pull Together Canada. They married in 1947 at Caux sur Montreux, the Swiss centre of her father's Moral Re-Armament movement.

narrative_blocks.header: She made a book of her parents' letters
narrative_blocks.body: Frances drew From China with Love out of the letters her parents wrote each other across thirty-four years in China. It is a portrait of a marriage as much as of a mission.

narrative_blocks.header: Nineteen years nursing in China
narrative_blocks.body: Mamie-Lou took her degree at Wooster in 1926, trained at Johns Hopkins, and went out to China as a nurse for the Episcopal Board of Missions. She served nineteen years, married there, and raised her family there.

narrative_blocks.header: They had both grown up in China
narrative_blocks.body: Libby was the son of missionaries who founded Nanchang Hospital, and went back to Japan at the end of the war as an army translator. He married Loretta Roots in 1967, who had grown up in China too.

military_service.notes: Translator and intelligence officer in Japan.

narrative_blocks.header: Ordained a deacon at St. Peter's
narrative_blocks.body: Libby was ordained deacon in the Roman Catholic Church at the Basilica of St. Peter in October 2004, and priest at Gaylord the following July. On Mackinac Island he had worked at his aunt's inn and taught at the public school.

parents.father_research_notes: George E. Hadden of Metuchen, New Jersey

parents.mother_research_notes: Mrs. Heywood H. Whaples of Farmington

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandfather sailed with Farragut
narrative_blocks.body: Anne Whaples grew up at Farmington and went to Miss Hall's School at Pittsfield. Her grandfather ended a Hartford bank president, having gone to sea in his youth aboard Farragut's flagship Hartford.

bio.bio_blurb: Physician and volunteer Union surgeon; head of the Tribe of John of the Fighting McCooks

narrative_blocks.header: He followed his brother Daniel into Ohio
narrative_blocks.body: He took his medicine at Jefferson College in his native Canonsburg and read further at Cincinnati. His brother Daniel, a lawyer, had gone out to eastern Ohio in 1826; he followed, practising at New Lisbon and then Steubenville.

narrative_blocks.header: A lifelong Democrat who joined the Republicans
narrative_blocks.body: He was a Democrat the whole of his life until the war came, when he went over to the Union Republicans and put the whole weight of his influence behind the government. He was fifty-five that year, and his five sons were going out.

narrative_blocks.header: Past fifty, he went out as a surgeon
narrative_blocks.body: He was fifty-five when the war began and served as a volunteer surgeon. Fifteen McCooks of the two families went in, all commissioned but his nephew Charles, who refused a commission and died of his wounds from Bull Run.

narrative_blocks.header: The Fighting McCooks were two families
narrative_blocks.body: The Ohio papers wrote of one family; there were two. His brother Daniel and eight of Daniel’s sons were the Tribe of Dan, and he and his own five the Tribe of John — Edward, Anson, Henry, Roderick and John.

narrative_blocks.header: The children were all baptised in one day
narrative_blocks.body: He and his wife did not join the Presbyterian church at New Lisbon until the last of their children had been born. All of them were baptised together, on one Sabbath, by Dr. A. O. Patterson.

narrative_blocks.header: He and Daniel each ran a Sunday school
narrative_blocks.body: He was superintendent for years of the Sunday school at the First Church in Steubenville. His brother Daniel had organised the first Sunday school at the Presbyterian church in Carrollton and run it himself.

narrative_blocks.header: He died at his son's headquarters
narrative_blocks.body: He died just after the war closed, on a visit to the Washington headquarters of his son, General Anson George McCook, and was brought home to Steubenville and buried beside his wife, who had gone seven months before.

cross_connections.display_label: organised the War Democrats in 1864, the move he had already made

military_service.notes: Volunteer surgeon.

narrative_blocks.header: She taught her sons to read aloud
narrative_blocks.body: Catharine taught her five sons declamation and composition before the neighbourhood schools offered either. She could give Scott's Marmion and the Lady of the Lake from memory, and Burns, and she sang.

narrative_blocks.header: She died seven months before him
narrative_blocks.body: Catharine died in Ohio on 11 March 1865 and her husband on 11 October, seven months to the day. They lie together at Steubenville.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son went back to her Hartford
narrative_blocks.body: Catharine was born in Hartford of an old New England family and raised her five sons in Ohio. The youngest, John, took his degree at Trinity, married a Butler of Hartford and was rector at East Hartford for fifty years.

bio.title: Maj. Gen.
bio.bio_blurb: Cavalry general who governed Colorado Territory and Florida; member of the Fighting McCooks

people.relational_label_override: Brother-in-law of an Eighth Generation Hooker

narrative_blocks.header: He rode ahead of Sherman as a diversion
narrative_blocks.body: His hardest service was a feint: he took his cavalry through the Confederate lines before Sherman turned for the sea, did great damage, took more prisoners than he could hold, and came back out in front of Hood's whole army.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the surrender of Florida
narrative_blocks.body: He was sent to Tallahassee in May 1865 to receive the surrender of the Confederate forces in Florida, and stayed on as the state’s military governor until June. He was brevetted major-general for the war’s work.

narrative_blocks.header: A secret errand bought him a commission
narrative_blocks.body: He was a lawyer in Washington in the anxious months before the war, mixed up with the Kansas Legion, and did something for the government daring enough that they made him a lieutenant of cavalry in the regular army for it.

narrative_blocks.header: Grant made him governor of Colorado twice
narrative_blocks.body: He was appointed governor of Colorado Territory twice, both times by President Grant, and held it on and off from 1869 to 1875. In between he had resigned his regular commission to go out as minister to the Sandwich Islands.

narrative_blocks.header: He was a Pike’s Peak lawyer first
narrative_blocks.body: He went out to practise law and was among the earliest settlers of the Pike’s Peak country, which then belonged to Kansas. He sat for that district in the Kansas legislature before the Territory was divided.

narrative_blocks.header: Four years from the ranks to a division
narrative_blocks.body: He went in with the Second Indiana cavalry in 1861, was a colonel by 1862 after his advance at Chattanooga, and in April 1864 had the First Cavalry Division. Perryville, Chickamauga, Atlanta, Alabama, Franklin and Nashville.

narrative_blocks.header: Minister to the Hawaiian Kingdom
narrative_blocks.body: President Andrew Johnson sent Edward to Honolulu as minister resident. He presented his credentials in July 1866 and gave up the post in December 1868, while John Owen Dominis was governor of Oahu for Kamehameha V.

military_service.unit: Second Indiana Cavalry; First Cavalry Division
military_service.notes: Perryville, Chickamauga, the Atlanta campaign, Alabama, Franklin and Nashville; received the Confederate surrender of Florida at Tallahassee, May 1865.

cross_connections.display_label: had a Confederate corps at Perryville and Chickamauga, facing him
was governor of Oahu while he was the American minister there

sources.short: U.S. Department of State, Chiefs of Mission by Country, 1778-2005: Hawaii

bio.title: Gen.
bio.bio_blurb: Congressman and Secretary of the United States Senate; member of the Fighting McCooks

people.relational_label_override: Brother-in-law of an Eighth Generation Hooker

career.role: Secretary of the United States Senate

narrative_blocks.header: The first company out of eastern Ohio
narrative_blocks.body: He raised a company of volunteers as soon as the war opened and was elected its captain. Company H of the Second Ohio was the first to go into the service from eastern Ohio, and it was at the first Bull Run inside three months.

narrative_blocks.header: He read law in Edwin Stanton’s office
narrative_blocks.body: He came home from California in 1859 and went into the law office of Stanton & McCook at Steubenville. The senior partner left it two years later to become Lincoln’s secretary of war.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten years keeping the Senate’s records
narrative_blocks.body: He sat three terms in Congress for New York’s eighth district, lost the renomination in 1882, and the Republican caucus made him Secretary of the United States Senate instead. He held that desk from 1883 to 1893.

narrative_blocks.header: He rose as the men above him fell
narrative_blocks.body: He went in a captain and was brevetted brigadier-general by President Johnson in 1866, promoted along the way through the deaths and resignations of his seniors. He commanded a brigade at Peach Tree Creek, outside Atlanta.

narrative_blocks.header: New York’s cash box, then its law books
narrative_blocks.body: Mayor Strong made him City Chamberlain of New York in 1895, the officer who holds the city’s cash. He left in 1898 and was president of the New York Law Publishing Company until he died.

narrative_blocks.header: Overland to the California gold at nineteen
narrative_blocks.body: He was schooled at New Lisbon and went overland to California in 1854 to mine. Five years of it were enough; he came home to Ohio, read law, and was admitted to the bar just before the war.

narrative_blocks.header: His father died at his headquarters
narrative_blocks.body: His father came to Washington in October 1865 to visit him at his headquarters and died there, seven months after his mother. Both were taken home to Steubenville.

military_service.unit: Second Ohio Infantry; One hundred and ninety-fourth Ohio
military_service.notes: Captain of Company H, the first out of eastern Ohio; first Bull Run, Perryville, Stone River, Lookout Mountain, Missionary Ridge, Resaca, Peach Tree Creek.

cross_connections.display_label: had a division at the first Bull Run, where he had a company

bio.title: Rev.
bio.bio_blurb: Presbyterian pastor, naturalist and novelist; member of the Fighting McCooks

people.relational_label_override: Brother-in-law of an Eighth Generation Hooker

narrative_blocks.header: The ants and the spiders made his name
narrative_blocks.body: He wrote up the agricultural ant of Texas, then Tenants of an Old Farm and Nature’s Craftsmen, and was an officer of the American Entomological Society. The naturalists of Europe knew his name better than his congregation did.

narrative_blocks.header: He went back to war at sixty-one
narrative_blocks.body: Thirty-six years after he resigned his first chaplaincy he took another, with the Second Pennsylvania in the Spanish-American War. He was sixty-one, and a Philadelphia pastor of nearly thirty years’ standing.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote a novel about the Whiskey Rebellion
narrative_blocks.body: The Latimers is set in the western Pennsylvania rising of 1794, the country his father came out of. He took its title from the family his uncle Daniel had married into at Washington, a few miles from Canonsburg.

narrative_blocks.header: A summer trip west turned into a war
narrative_blocks.body: He was a seminary student when the war opened, and had arranged to spend the vacation out west. He got as far as Clinton, Illinois, stayed to raise troops, and after Bull Run enlisted there as a private soldier.

narrative_blocks.header: He went home to be ordained a chaplain
narrative_blocks.body: The Forty-first Illinois took him in as a first lieutenant and then wanted him as its chaplain, which meant going back to Ohio to be ordained by the Presbytery of Steubenville before he could hold the post.

narrative_blocks.header: He judged he was worth more at home
narrative_blocks.body: He resigned the chaplaincy inside a year, meaning to take some other place in the army, and then decided he could do the government more good in a pulpit. He went back to his church at Clinton.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years in one Philadelphia pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: He was a home missionary and then a pastor in St. Louis before Philadelphia called him in 1869. He stayed, and the church he kept there was counted one of the first in the East.

cross_connections.display_label: was publishing on Canadian moths in the same years as his ants

military_service.notes: Enlisted a private after first Bull Run.
1898, at sixty-one.

bio.bio_blurb: Commander in the United States Navy; member of the Fighting McCooks
bio.photo_notes: Cloudinary; supplied by Sam. In uniform.

narrative_blocks.header: A navy officer took a regiment’s surrender
narrative_blocks.body: At New Berne in March 1862 he took a battery of naval howitzers off his ship and fought it ashore, and took the surrender of a Confederate infantry regiment — probably the only such surrender of the war. The reports commended him by name.

narrative_blocks.header: Fort Fisher took his health from him
narrative_blocks.body: He was executive officer of the monitor Canonicus from 1863, and went in against Fort Fisher twice, in December and again in January. The iron heat of the monitors did for his health and he never got it back.

narrative_blocks.header: He watched Charleston handed over
narrative_blocks.body: On 18 February 1865 he was there when the mayor of Charleston gave the city up to General Schimmelfennig. He had spent the previous two years on the James and in the North Carolina sounds.

narrative_blocks.header: A midshipman at fifteen, hunting slavers
narrative_blocks.body: He was appointed midshipman in September 1854, before he was sixteen, and took his Annapolis degree in 1859. His first two years at sea were off the African coast, chasing slave ships; he brought one home with a prize crew.

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve years abroad, then his own river
narrative_blocks.body: He had command of warships on the West India and Asiatic stations from 1866 to 1878. Failing, he took the Ohio river lighthouses in 1880 — the river his family had lived along since 1826, and where he now lies.

narrative_blocks.header: A buggy threw him at forty-six
narrative_blocks.body: He was retired in February 1885 and took a farm at Vineland in New Jersey to get his strength back. He was thrown from his buggy onto his head within the year and died of the injury.

narrative_blocks.header: Two destroyers have carried his name
narrative_blocks.body: The navy has named two ships USS McCook for him. The second was a Gleaves-class destroyer of the later war, converted to a minesweeper and photographed off Philadelphia in July 1945.

military_service.unit: USS Minnesota, USS Stars and Stripes, USS Canonicus
military_service.notes: Midshipman 21 Sept 1854; lieutenant 31 Aug 1861; lieutenant-commander 25 Dec 1865; commander 25 Sept 1873. Africa patrol 1859-61; New Berne; both battles of Fort Fisher as executive officer of the Canonicus; present at the surrender of Charleston. Retired 23 Feb 1885.
