narrative_blocks.header: Her son married her brother’s daughter
narrative_blocks.body: Her only son, Walter, married Julia Terry in 1876 — the daughter of her brother Henry Dwight Terry, the general. She had been dead two years by then, and the two young people were first cousins.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father owned the town before it existed
narrative_blocks.body: Christian Clemens bought a distillery on the Clinton River in 1800, the first building on the site, and five hundred acres round it the year after. The village was platted there in 1818 and named for him. She was born in it in 1822.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father spent that war in a dungeon
narrative_blocks.body: When the British took Detroit in 1812 they shut Christian Clemens in a dungeon and held him for much of the war. He was not harmed, and walked back to his house on the Clinton River when it was over.

narrative_blocks.header: A Mennonite farmer’s son out of Pennsylvania
narrative_blocks.body: Her father was born at Horsham in Pennsylvania in 1768, one of thirteen children of a Mennonite farmer who paid the fines rather than fight in the Revolution. He came west to Detroit at twenty-seven, to make leather.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave the county its courthouse ground
narrative_blocks.body: He got Mount Clemens made the county seat when Macomb County was organised in 1818, handed over the land for the courthouse and paid toward putting it up. He gave ground for churches and for a burying place as well.

narrative_blocks.header: She was the last of four sisters
narrative_blocks.body: Her mother, Elizabeth Talmadge Allen, was a Detroit physician’s widow with two children of her own when she married. The four daughters who grew were Harriet, Ann, Elizabeth Keturah, and Louisa last.

narrative_blocks.header: She is buried in her father’s town
narrative_blocks.body: She died in Macomb County on 7 May 1890 at sixty-eight, and lies at Clinton Grove on the ground her father spent his life settling — beside her husband, carried back from Washington twenty-one years before her.

burial.plot_notes: Clinton Grove Cemetery, Clinton Township, Macomb County

sources.label: Find a Grave and FamilySearch both give her birth as 1822 (aged 67-68 at death); the Macomb County account of Christian Clemens gives her as Louise Marion, 1818-1890

narrative_blocks.header: She was born in her grandfather’s town
narrative_blocks.body: Mount Clemens was laid out on land her mother’s father had bought and was named for him. She was born there in the spring of 1859, the second of Henry Dwight Terry’s three children.

narrative_blocks.header: She was seventeen when she married
narrative_blocks.body: She married Walter Taylor Dwight at Detroit in November 1876, three months short of eighteen. He was her first cousin — his mother and her father were sister and brother — and they went to live in Chicago.

narrative_blocks.header: Two of her three children died small
narrative_blocks.body: Amasa was ten when he died in 1890 and Dorothy five in 1892. She lived twenty-four years after Dorothy, and left one surviving child, Marion.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father died when she was ten
narrative_blocks.body: The general came home from the war sick and died in Washington in 1869, of Bright’s disease. She was ten. Her mother took the family from Michigan to Chicago and lived until 1890.

sources.label: Find a Grave and WikiTree both give birth April 1859 (aged 57 at death, which agrees); FamilySearch gave 1 May 1855, retained here

narrative_blocks.header: He married his first cousin at twenty-one
narrative_blocks.body: He married Julia Terry at Detroit in November 1876. Her father was his mother’s brother, so the two were first cousins; he was twenty-one and she seventeen. They settled in Chicago, where he sold real estate.

narrative_blocks.header: He buried two of his three children
narrative_blocks.body: Amasa died at ten in June 1890 and Dorothy at five in December 1892, inside thirty months of each other. Only Marion grew up, and every descendant of the marriage comes down through her.

narrative_blocks.header: Ninety-four years, Detroit to New Jersey
narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Detroit six years before the Civil War and died in New Jersey in 1950. Julia had been dead thirty-four years by then, and the two children he had buried sixty.

narrative_blocks.header: His uncle was also his father-in-law
narrative_blocks.body: Henry Dwight Terry was his mother’s brother, which made him an uncle, and Julia’s father, which made him a father-in-law. The general had been dead seven years when the wedding took place.

sources.label: FamilySearch indexes this child as "Clembers D Dwight"; Find a Grave and WikiTree both name him Amasa, for his grandfather Amasa Fiske Dwight

narrative_blocks.header: The only one of three who grew up
narrative_blocks.body: Her brother Amasa died at ten and her sister Dorothy at five, both before she was ten herself. She was the one who lived, and every descendant of Walter and Julia Dwight comes through her.

narrative_blocks.header: She went by her middle name, Roby
narrative_blocks.body: Born Marion Roby at Evanston in 1883, she was Roby all her life and gave the name on to her daughter Roberta. The two women are muddled in the indexes to this day.

narrative_blocks.header: Evanston in 1904, then east for good
narrative_blocks.body: She married Laurence Colin Ward at Evanston in September 1904, at twenty-one. He took her back to his own Newark, and she kept house there and raised three children, and died in New Jersey at fifty-eight.

sources.label: Find a Grave and WikiTree both give her as Marion Roby "Roby" Dwight Ward and say she went by Roby; FamilySearch indexes her as Roberta Marion Dwight

narrative_blocks.header: He began and ended selling motor cars
narrative_blocks.body: He was selling automobiles in Newark when they were still a novelty, went off to the Willow Company and into the battery trade, and came back at the end to sell cars again. Fifty years, and the same work at both ends.

narrative_blocks.header: He went to Illinois for a wife
narrative_blocks.body: He was the youngest son of Elias Sayre Ward of Newark, and in September 1904 he married Marion Dwight at Evanston, outside Chicago, and brought her home to New Jersey. Three of their children grew up.

narrative_blocks.header: They died six months apart at ninety-one
narrative_blocks.body: He and Margaret were born six months apart in 1905 and married in 1934. He died at Hightstown in May 1997 and she in November, both ninety-one, and they lie together at Mount Pleasant in Newark.

narrative_blocks.header: A passport in his freshman spring
narrative_blocks.body: He entered Princeton in 1924 and took out a passport that May, at eighteen. He was at the American Telephone and Telegraph Company by 1930, and spent the rest of his working life a treasurer and an investment man.

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived him by six months
narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Newark in December 1905 and married Robertson Ward in 1934. He died at Hightstown in the May of 1997 and she in the November, both of them ninety-one, sixty-three years married.

narrative_blocks.header: Princeton in winter, Hyannis Port in summer
narrative_blocks.body: When his son married in 1967 the Times gave the parents’ address as Princeton, New Jersey, and Hyannis Port, Massachusetts. He had been born at Newark and married Elizabeth Campbell there in February 1936.

narrative_blocks.header: They went south and both died in Florida
narrative_blocks.body: He died at Vero Beach in June 1995, at eighty-six, and Elizabeth in Indian River County three years after him. She was carried back to Mount Pleasant at Newark, where his parents lie; his own grave is not recorded.

narrative_blocks.header: Five generations later, back to Hartford
narrative_blocks.body: His great-great-grandfather Henry Dwight Terry was born at Hartford in 1812 and left it for Michigan. The family went on to Chicago and then Newark — and he came back to Hartford, for Trinity.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at the Church of the Epiphany
narrative_blocks.body: He married Anne Pendleton of Westport, Connecticut, in New York in May 1967. She had come from the Mary A. Burnham School and North Carolina, he from Deerfield and Trinity. He died at Boston in 1991.

narrative_blocks.header: The first of four in three years
narrative_blocks.body: Baptised at New Haven on the last day of October 1778, she died at twenty-three in February 1802 — the first of four the family buried inside three years, before her mother, her sister Mary and her father.

sources.label: Whittlesey genealogy: Baptised at New Haven 30 Oct 1778

narrative_blocks.header: Killed cutting wood at the door
narrative_blocks.body: He was sixteen and cutting wood at the door of the house when he was killed. The family genealogy gives the manner of it in nine words and nothing else. He was the eldest son and carried his father’s name.

sources.label: Whittlesey genealogy: Killed while cutting wood at the door, aged sixteen

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandmother took her and kept her
narrative_blocks.body: She was the third child, and her mother’s mother carried her off to Middletown and kept her there so long that five more were born at New Haven whom she could not say she had ever seen, though it was the next town.

narrative_blocks.header: She married five weeks after her father died
narrative_blocks.body: She married James Casey at Middletown on 16 January 1805. Her father had been dead thirty-eight days. The genealogy dates his death by her wedding, which is the only fixed point it has for him.

cross_connections.display_label: , her grandmother, took her to Middletown and kept her there

sources.label: Whittlesey genealogy: Married at Middletown 16 Jan 1805 to James Casey

narrative_blocks.header: Two wives, and New York at the end
narrative_blocks.body: He married Mary Larkin McIntire in August 1804, seven weeks after his sister Mary died, and Mary Herbert of Monmouth in New Jersey five years after that. He died at New York city in 1830, at forty-seven.

sources.label: Whittlesey genealogy: Married Mary Larkin McIntire 1804, then Mary Herbert of Monmouth NJ 1809

narrative_blocks.header: Nineteen, and a young woman
narrative_blocks.body: She died on 8 July 1804, a year and a week after her mother. The genealogy gives no cause and calls her only “a young woman.” She lies at Middletown with both her parents.

sources.label: Whittlesey genealogy: Died 8 July 1804, “a young woman”

narrative_blocks.header: He married out of Watertown, then again
narrative_blocks.body: He married Sarah Blackman at Watertown in Massachusetts in January 1811, at twenty-four, and Betsey Ann Slawson after her. He was the sixth of the nine and lived to 1851, longer than four of them.

sources.label: Whittlesey genealogy: Married Sarah Blackman of Watertown 1811, then Betsey Ann Slawson

narrative_blocks.header: Yellow fever, in the South, unmarried
narrative_blocks.body: He went south to settle and yellow fever took him there. The genealogy gives neither the year nor the place, only that he was unmarried when it happened and had gone to make a life.

sources.label: Whittlesey genealogy: Died of yellow fever, unmarried, in the South where he had gone to settle

narrative_blocks.body: He married Catharine Rice of Kensington, in Kensington, in October 1819 at twenty-nine. He lived to 1860 and to seventy, which two of his eight brothers and sisters also managed and five did not.

narrative_blocks.body: He captained the Phillips Academy team, played until he was fifty-eight, coached and refereed Rochester youth hockey, and in 2015 endowed the women’s coaching position at RIT. A knee injury at Yale had ended him as a player there.

narrative_blocks.body: He was born at Roxbury in Connecticut and made his life at Malone in northern New York, where the book gives him as farmer and attorney together. He died there at seventy, five days before his wife’s sixty-seventh year began.

narrative_blocks.header: She died eight days after her father
narrative_blocks.body: Chauncey Whittlesey died on 19 February 1836 and his daughter Mary on the 27th, eight days later. She was fifteen. Her mother buried a husband and a child inside nine days and lived another thirty-three years.

narrative_blocks.header: He took his degree into the cholera year
narrative_blocks.body: He had his medical degree from New York University in 1845 and was assistant physician at Randall’s Island by 1848. In 1849 he went to the Centre Street cholera hospital, and from July that year ran the Nursery Hospital on Randall’s Island.

narrative_blocks.header: A man with a bright future, they wrote
narrative_blocks.body: The family book gives him more space than any of his brothers and sisters and ends on a phrase it uses for nobody else — a man with a bright future, esteemed by every one. He died at forty-seven.

narrative_blocks.body: He entered the Naval Academy in 1878 and came out in 1882, and went straight to the Hartford — Farragut’s old flagship — as a midshipman on the Atlantic and Pacific stations.

narrative_blocks.header: Ensign on the Tallapoosa the year she sank
narrative_blocks.body: He was promoted ensign in 1884 aboard the Tallapoosa, which went down off Martha’s Vineyard that same year after a collision in the night. He was at sea again on the Ranger in the Pacific before the year was out.

narrative_blocks.header: Two turns ashore in naval intelligence
narrative_blocks.body: He was at the hydrographic office in Washington from 1887, the Monocacy on the Asiatic station from 1889, and the Office of Naval Intelligence from 1892. Lieutenant in 1894, the Puritan in 1897, Ordnance in 1898.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the modern life of Woodrow Wilson
narrative_blocks.body: Woodrow Wilson, World Statesman came out in 1987 and The Presidency of Woodrow Wilson in 1992, with a reference volume co-written with Eric Cheezum after that. He was interviewed for the 1997 film Woodrow Wilson: Reluctant Warrior.

narrative_blocks.header: Then he took on Hoover, Bryan and Byrnes
narrative_blocks.body: Hoover, Conservation, and Consumerism appeared in 2000 and the first volume of a life of Herbert Hoover in 2010. He had begun in 1982 with William Jennings Bryan, Missionary Isolationist and an edition of James F. Byrnes's Cold War papers.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-nine years in one department
narrative_blocks.body: He came to Columbia in 1967 and taught American diplomatic history, general American history and Canadian history at the University of South Carolina until he retired in June 2006. The university keeps him on as emeritus.

narrative_blocks.header: The fifth generation of them teaches now
narrative_blocks.body: His great-grandfather Asahel Kendrick held Rochester's Greek chair and his grandfather Ryland took it after him; his father Alling taught at RIT until 1956; his uncle Nathaniel was dean at Bowdoin. His own son is a dean at St. Jude.

narrative_blocks.header: He would not let Princeton erase Wilson
narrative_blocks.body: Wilson segregated the federal workforce, and Princeton debated stripping his name from its buildings. Clements wrote for the university's own site: “Since we cannot eradicate the past, the question is what use we should make of it.”

narrative_blocks.header: She fought to keep her sons' school open
narrative_blocks.body: When white flight through Columbia brought proposals to close Satchel Ford, where her two boys went, she fought them and the school stayed. She worked for the Democratic party in South Carolina for years, always behind the scenes.

narrative_blocks.header: She taught piano and sang in the chorus
narrative_blocks.body: A Berkeley graduate, she taught piano for many years in Columbia and sang with the Columbia Choral Society. She travelled whenever the chance came — Europe, Asia, Africa — and went with her husband on sabbaticals in Taiwan and Canada.

narrative_blocks.header: California to Columbia, by way of 1967
narrative_blocks.body: She was the youngest daughter of Albin Theorin and Anna Wilson Spongberg of Oakland. She married Kendrick Clements in 1964 and moved to Columbia in 1967, when he joined the history department at the University of South Carolina.

naming_inspiration.description: The Kendrick name descends from his great-great-grandfather Asahel Clark Kendrick through four generations; whether he was named for the man or for the line is not established.

cross_connections.display_label: , his great-great-grandfather, gave him the Kendrick and taught Greek

narrative_blocks.header: He studies where blood first comes from
narrative_blocks.body: Blood stem cells are made once, in the wall of an embryo's dorsal aorta, out of cells that were otherwise going to be plain vessel. He works on what tells them to become blood instead, and calls the place it happens the specification niche.

narrative_blocks.header: His leukemia patients are zebrafish
narrative_blocks.body: He builds zebrafish that develop B-cell leukemia, so a driving oncogene and a lost tumour suppressor can be watched working in a living animal. The same line of work asks how a cancer takes over the ordinary programs that make blood.

narrative_blocks.header: Hematology at St. Jude, and its graduate school
narrative_blocks.body: He is an associate member in the Department of Hematology at St. Jude Children's Research Hospital in Memphis, and associate dean of the PhD program at the St. Jude Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences.

narrative_blocks.header: He went to Williams, as his father did
narrative_blocks.body: Kendrick Clements took his degree at Williams College before Berkeley and a life of Woodrow Wilson; his son took his at Williams before Seattle and a life of blood. The Kendrick in the middle of his name reaches back four generations.

narrative_blocks.header: Five generations of them have taught
narrative_blocks.body: Asahel Kendrick took Rochester's Greek chair in 1850 and his son Ryland took it after him. Alling Clements taught at RIT until 1956, Kendrick Clements history until 2006, and the St. Jude PhD program is this one's. No break since 1831.

narrative_blocks.header: He started pumping gas and ended up chairman
narrative_blocks.body: He took a job at a Socony filling station the year he left Harvard, was managing it in 1934 and selling for the company by 1936. Vice-president for foreign trade in 1951, president in 1955, and chairman of Mobil by 1961.

narrative_blocks.header: He chaired the New York Fed
narrative_blocks.body: He sat as a director of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York from 1961 and chaired it from 1969 to 1971, the years after he left Mobil. He had chaired the Business Council in 1967 and 1968.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandfather's house was his school
narrative_blocks.body: The main building of the Noble and Greenough School at Dedham had been built as the residence of Albert W. Nickerson, his grandfather. He left it with the class of 1929 and took a science degree at Harvard in 1933.

narrative_blocks.header: He placed men for the war, in 1943
narrative_blocks.body: He ran the placement bureau of the War Manpower Commission in 1943, finding workers for the industries the war depended on. He was thirty-two, and eleven years into the oil company he would end up running.

narrative_blocks.header: Rockefeller, the Symphony, the Museum
narrative_blocks.body: He was a trustee of Rockefeller University, of the Boston Symphony Orchestra and of the American Museum of Natural History, sat on Harvard's Board of Overseers from 1959 to 1965, and took the American Petroleum Institute gold medal in 1973.

narrative_blocks.header: He married in a Greenwich garden in 1936
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth Perkins married him at her parents' place at Greenwich on 13 June 1936 and they had four children. He died at Cambridge in 1994, at eighty-three, having outrun the filling station by sixty-one years.

narrative_blocks.body: He worked at building quantitative reasoning programmes into Groton, Carleton College and Yale. He sat on the boards of Carleton, the Walker Art Center, the Minneapolis Symphony, the Commonfund, PIMCO and SEI.

narrative_blocks.header: Silver Lining, kept at Baddeck
narrative_blocks.body: He skied hard enough to serve on the United States Ski Patrol at Stevens Pass while he was in the Navy, and sailed a boat named Silver Lining out of Baddeck in Nova Scotia for years afterward.

narrative_blocks.header: He left his brain to the research
narrative_blocks.body: Henry lived with Parkinson's disease for many years, and gave his brain to the MIND programme at the Massachusetts General Hospital so that the disease could be studied. He died at Manchester in June 2021.

narrative_blocks.header: Louisa was his eighth cousin once removed
narrative_blocks.body: Henry and Louisa both descended from Rev. Samuel Hooker of Farmington. Henry's line ran through Samuel's daughter Mary, wife of Rev. James Pierpont, and Louisa's through Samuel's son James.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty years married, and a Rockefeller by marriage
narrative_blocks.body: Louisa Perkins married him in 1961 and was still his wife sixty years later. His grandfather Henry Homes Porter of Chicago had married a Prentice whose brother married Alta Rockefeller, John D. Rockefeller's eldest daughter.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the plan that saved the Pinelands
narrative_blocks.body: Governor Byrne made him the first chairman of the New Jersey Pinelands Commission in 1979 and he held it nine years, carrying through a regional land use plan for 1.1 million acres — a fifth of the state, and still the national model.

narrative_blocks.header: A Pine Barrens preserve carries his name
narrative_blocks.body: In 2003 the New Jersey Conservation Foundation named its newly bought 9,400 acres in the heart of the Pine Barrens the Franklin Parker Preserve. He had co-founded that foundation and been its second president forty years earlier.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years a lawyer, then a second career
narrative_blocks.body: Exeter, Yale in 1945 and the Virginia law school in 1950, then Davis Polk and afterwards a partnership at Patterson Belknap. He left the practice at sixty-five to run the Trust for Public Land's New Jersey office.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped save the Great Swamp
narrative_blocks.body: He was one of the leaders of the fight that kept the Great Swamp out of an airport in the early 1960s, and sat as a trustee of the Natural Resources Defense Council for more than thirty years afterward.

narrative_blocks.header: Commissioned at Yale, recalled for Korea
narrative_blocks.body: Yale commissioned him into the Navy on graduation and he served until August 1946, then was called back to active duty during the Korean War. He was married in 1955, between the uniform and the conservation work.

narrative_blocks.header: He was born on what became Earth Day
narrative_blocks.body: His birthday was 22 April, which forty-five years later became Earth Day, and he began his conservation career in the decade after the first one. He left a wife of fifty-three years, six children and fifteen grandchildren.

narrative_blocks.body: She volunteered as an archivist at the Metropolitan Museum of Art and was a trustee of the Union Theological Seminary, a New Yorker by birth who lived there until nearly the end. She belonged to the Colony Club.

narrative_blocks.header: She lies in the Havemeyer tomb at Green-Wood
narrative_blocks.body: Horace Havemeyer's daughter went back to the family vault at Green-Wood in Brooklyn, plot 8174. She died at Needham in October 1998, having asked that gifts go to the whaling museum at New Bedford.

narrative_blocks.body: He was a lieutenant junior grade in the naval reserve when he married Mildred Duer Baxter of Rye at St. Andrew's Dune Church in July 1961, his brother Thomas standing as best man. St. Paul's and Yale were behind him.

narrative_blocks.header: Topsfield, and a Boston investment house
narrative_blocks.body: He settled his family at Topsfield in Massachusetts and was a vice-president of Reynders Gray, investment bankers in Boston. His father chaired Citicorp's executive committee and his own son went to sea instead.

narrative_blocks.body: Four generations of his family ran banks; he took Hampshire College and then the helm of the Harvey Gamage, a schooner out of Gloucester. He married Alden Landry Jones at her parents' house in Boston in January 1994.

notable.notable_blurb: Editor of the American National Biography

military_service.notes: Swimming instructor

narrative_blocks.header: Seventeen thousand American lives, in one work
narrative_blocks.body: He campaigned through the 1980s for a new biographical record of the country and got it in 1999: the American National Biography, 17,500 essays under his general editorship. The Times of London compared it to the Moon landing.

narrative_blocks.header: He let Lodge's grandson argue in the footnotes
narrative_blocks.body: His 1953 life of Henry Cabot Lodge was the first scholarly one, and he invited the senator's grandson, Ambassador Henry Cabot Lodge Jr., to write footnotes disagreeing with him. They were printed in the book.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years at Columbia, and a textbook
narrative_blocks.body: Brooklyn College in 1941, a Columbia doctorate in 1948, twelve years at Michigan State and then Columbia from 1959 until he retired in 1990, chairing the department part of the seventies. His American Nation reached a thirteenth edition.

narrative_blocks.header: He was the historian behind Schoolhouse Rock
narrative_blocks.body: Among the television work he consulted on in the sixties and seventies were the Schoolhouse Rock shorts, which taught a generation of American children their grammar, their arithmetic and their Constitution three minutes at a time.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught swimming in the Merchant Marine
narrative_blocks.body: His war was spent as an instructor in the United States Merchant Marine, teaching men to swim. He was twenty-one when he took his first degree and twenty-eight when he took his doctorate, with the war in between.

narrative_blocks.header: Six marathons in his sixties
narrative_blocks.body: He took up distance running in his late fifties and ran six marathons in the decade after, mostly at New York but one at Paris. He loved Mozart, and collected Dubuffet, Rouault, Robert Indiana, Calder and Léger.

narrative_blocks.header: He viewed adverbs with contempt
narrative_blocks.body: He cut so much from other people's prose that he called himself an environmentalist, and he had no patience with the praise that collects around a dead subject. “Don't put labels on people,” he said. “Tell the reader what they did.”

narrative_blocks.header: She was an accomplished cellist
narrative_blocks.body: She played the cello well, and she and Mitchell Gratwick shared music and a bond over history, English history in particular. When she died he founded a fund at Milton Academy in her name that has paid for a concert a year since.

narrative_blocks.header: The Forum printed her poems
narrative_blocks.body: Several of her poems appeared in the Forum Magazine while she was still in her twenties. She was at school in Switzerland through 1924 and 1925 and at Radcliffe after that, and came out in the season of 1925 and 1926.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at Jackson's Hole at twenty
narrative_blocks.body: Mitchell Gratwick was a master at Milton Academy, the school her father had been a trustee of since 1903. They married at Moose in Wyoming in June 1927, and he left Harvard the year after to take the Nichols School at Buffalo.

narrative_blocks.header: A Boston banker's daughter and his niece
narrative_blocks.body: John Forbes Perkins, her father, was a Boston banker and a judge; Thomas Nelson Perkins, her uncle, was the American representative on the Reparations Commission. She kept house at 909 Memorial Drive in Cambridge before Buffalo.

narrative_blocks.header: Dead at twenty-two, and no cause given
narrative_blocks.body: She died late on a Sunday afternoon in a Buffalo hospital, six weeks past her twenty-second birthday and not three years married. Nothing that survives of her says what killed her; she had been living in the town less than two years.

bio.bio_blurb: Headmaster of the Horace Mann School

education.school_name: Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine

cross_connections.display_label: was dean of freshmen at Williams, then ran Advanced Placement

narrative_blocks.header: Eighteen years headmaster at Horace Mann
narrative_blocks.body: He ran the Horace Mann country day school for boys at Riverdale from 1950 until he retired in 1968. Call it a college preparatory school if you will, he said, but more accurately it is a school to train boys for living.

narrative_blocks.header: He made the boys learn to survive outdoors
narrative_blocks.body: He built a nature programme and a summer laboratory of outdoor living and survival technique, because too many boys panicked when they fell back on themselves. He added Russian, navigation, communications and meteorology as electives too.

narrative_blocks.header: He took a medical degree between headmasterships
narrative_blocks.body: He took his medical degree at Johns Hopkins in 1936 and was five years in medicine, then put it aside in 1941 for the headmastership of Hackley at Tarrytown. In 1950 he was asked to succeed Charles Tillinghast at Horace Mann.

narrative_blocks.header: Football, hockey, track and a boxing title
narrative_blocks.body: At Harvard he made the varsity in three sports and was a champion boxer, and stayed on afterwards as assistant dean of freshmen. He had grown up on a farm in the Genesee Valley.

narrative_blocks.header: He outlived his first wife by fifty-two years
narrative_blocks.body: Katharine Perkins died at Buffalo in 1930, three years married. He founded the concert fund at Milton Academy in her name that year, married Barbara Burnett afterwards, and had five children and eleven grandchildren by her.

narrative_blocks.header: National president of the Headmasters Association
narrative_blocks.body: While he ran Horace Mann he was also national president of the Headmasters Association. He had left an assistant deanship of freshmen at Harvard in 1928 to take the Nichols School at Buffalo, and never went back to university work.

narrative_blocks.header: A nature centre had him to the end
narrative_blocks.body: Nature interested him all his life — it is why he built the survival laboratory into Horace Mann — and when he moved near Philadelphia he worked as a volunteer at the Schuylkill Valley Nature Center until shortly before he died.

narrative_blocks.header: Geology at Princeton, then forty years of stone
narrative_blocks.body: He read geology at Princeton and put in two years with the Army artillery, then spent his working life in mining and quarrying. Luck Stone took him on in 1972 and he retired in 1995 as its senior vice-president of operations.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandfather painted Pennsylvania
narrative_blocks.body: William Langson Lathrop, the Pennsylvania impressionist landscape painter, was his mother's father, and his own father Rolf Bauhan was a noted architect at Princeton. He grew up on the family farm in Bucks County.

narrative_blocks.header: He tutored refugees and painted landscapes
narrative_blocks.body: Retirement went to Commonwealth Catholic Charities, where he tutored refugees, and to history, the farm and garden, hunting, fishing, golf, and the landscape painting his grandfather had made a living at.

narrative_blocks.header: Stone, hounds and a family service board
narrative_blocks.body: He was active in the National Stone Association, sat on the board of Goochland Family Services, and belonged to the Deep Run Hunt Club. He died at his Goochland County farm in June 2014 after a long illness.

narrative_blocks.header: Nearly fifty years married to Polly
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Laughlin Perkins — Polly to him — married him in September 1964 and survived him by a few months short of their fiftieth year. Hobey, Johnny and Annie were their three, and five granddaughters came after.

narrative_blocks.header: An ambassador's grandson married a Morgan's
narrative_blocks.body: She married Walter Hines Page 2d at St. John's, Cold Spring Harbor, in January 1942. She was J. P. Morgan's granddaughter; he was grandson to the Walter Hines Page who was ambassador to the Court of St. James through the First World War.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-six years, and three weeks apart
narrative_blocks.body: They married in January 1942 and she died at Cold Spring Harbor in December 1998; Walter followed twenty-four days later. Jane, Walter and Mark were their three, and eight grandchildren came after them.

naming_inspiration.description: Named for his father's father, Walter Hines Page (1855-1918), United States ambassador to Great Britain through the First World War.

narrative_blocks.header: An ensign seven weeks after Pearl Harbor
narrative_blocks.body: Milton Academy and Harvard in 1937, then the naval reserve. He was an ensign on active duty when he married Jane Norton Nichols at Cold Spring Harbor in January 1942, seven weeks after the attack on Pearl Harbor.

narrative_blocks.header: He carried the ambassador's whole name
narrative_blocks.body: Walter Hines Page, his grandfather, was Wilson's ambassador to Great Britain from 1913 and so openly pro-British that Washington discounted him. He sold Britain the American munitions and food that kept it in the war before America entered.

narrative_blocks.header: The grandfather founded a press and a university
narrative_blocks.body: Before the embassy the elder Page edited the Atlantic Monthly, made Doubleday, Page & Company into one of the great publishing houses, and petitioned the North Carolina legislature in 1885 for the college that became its state university.

narrative_blocks.header: He outlived his wife by twenty-four days
narrative_blocks.body: Jane died at Cold Spring Harbor on 15 December 1998 after fifty-six years of marriage, and he followed on 8 January. They left three children — Jane, Walter and Mark — and eight grandchildren.

narrative_blocks.body: She and George Nichols were both physicians and married in June 1944, she twenty-three and he twenty-one. She practised on Long Island and ended her life at a retirement community in Cockeysville, Maryland, at eighty-six.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father came out of Rimersburg
narrative_blocks.body: James Leslie Pinks was a New York lawyer on Park Avenue who had come from Rimersburg in Pennsylvania by way of a state normal school, Indiana University and the Columbia law school. He died in 1947, three years after her wedding.

naming_inspiration.description: Named for his mother's uncle, the physician Caspar Wistar.

cross_connections.display_label: took his New Testament from him at Princeton in 1879

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty years teaching the New Testament
narrative_blocks.body: He took the Princeton Seminary chair in 1861, left vacant by the death of Addison Alexander who had tutored him as a boy, and held it until he died. For a time his father and his brother taught beside him, three Hodges on one faculty.

narrative_blocks.header: He filled sixteen volumes and published none
narrative_blocks.body: Sixteen thick volumes of manuscript lecture notes survive on the canon, the life of Christ and the apostolic church. He wrote almost nothing for the press, and a colleague guessed his father's reputation had set the bar too high.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother was Franklin's great-granddaughter
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah Bache Hodge descended from Benjamin Franklin, and Charles Hodge his father was the seminary's great systematic theologian. He grew up in the Hodge House on the campus, among the students.

narrative_blocks.header: He would never let you know he cared
narrative_blocks.body: He kept to himself so completely that some thought him cold. His brother said of him that Wistar will never let you know that he cares for you, but if you were in trouble he would do more for you than anybody in Princeton.

narrative_blocks.header: Consumption took two wives in five years
narrative_blocks.body: His first wife, his stepmother's daughter, died of consumption after a few years. Harriet Terry Post married him in June 1863 and was dead of the same disease by April, ten months on. He married a third time in 1869 and that one lasted.

narrative_blocks.body: She came into the world at Honolulu in November 1866, nine months after her parents married and while Hawaii was still a kingdom under Kamehameha V. She lived to eighty-eight and married twice.

narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Hartford in November 1869, two years before the Chicago fire, and died at San Francisco in June 1971. Her mother had gone out to California before her and died there in 1922; she stayed on another forty-nine years.

narrative_blocks.header: Nellie Terry, of Jacksonville
narrative_blocks.body: She married Dr. Percy St. John Stollenwerck at Jacksonville in 1893 and kept house there while he built a large practice; his obituary calls her Nellie. Her brother Charles came down to Jacksonville himself and died there.

narrative_blocks.body: Marion Louise Stuart married him at Detroit in 1903, and she was Gen. David Stuart's granddaughter — thirty-four years after the general's daughter Marion married his uncle, Cmdr. Edward A. Terry. Two Marion Stuarts, two Terrys.

narrative_blocks.header: Three wives, and a daughter by the second
narrative_blocks.body: The Detroit marriage ended; Gladis Kruger Combs married him in May 1920 and Barbara came the year after. Mildred Pellens was the third. He had gone from Hartford to Jacksonville in Florida, and died there in 1945.

narrative_blocks.body: Analysis of Parergasia came out under her name with Thomas A. C. Rennie — parergasia being the term psychiatry then used for schizophrenia. She published it as Gladys C. Terry, keeping the name after the marriage had ended.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a Terry, then a Cushing
narrative_blocks.body: Dr. Charles Edward Terry married her in May 1920 and Barbara was born the year after. That ended, and in September 1939 she married Thurber Wesson Cushing in the 1681 meeting house at Hingham, the oldest still standing in America.

narrative_blocks.header: The second son to carry the name
narrative_blocks.body: His parents named a son Obed in 1736 and buried him at thirteen months. He was born three years later and given the same name, and he was the one who lived, to seventy-two, long enough to see grandchildren on the island.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-six years with Priscilla, then Abial
narrative_blocks.body: He married Priscilla Russell at Nantucket in February 1760, when he was twenty, and she bore him three children before she died in 1786. Two years later he married Abial Gardner, and that second marriage gave him none.

narrative_blocks.header: A Gardner again, four generations on
narrative_blocks.body: His second wife was a Gardner, as his great-grandmother had been. Mary Gardner, daughter of the half-share man John Gardner, married Jethro Coffin in 1686, and the house they built still stands as the oldest on Nantucket.

narrative_blocks.header: He saw the sleeping cars dying and turned
narrative_blocks.body: The house had washed for the Wagner Palace Car Company since 1888 and followed the sleeping cars to Chicago when Pullman bought Wagner. He judged after the war that the trade was finished, and turned the firm to other men's linen.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventy-three years on one company's board
narrative_blocks.body: He joined his father on the Morgan Services board in 1931 and succeeded him as president in 1941. The laundrymen made him their man of the year in 1969. He gave up the chair in 2001 and was still a director when he died at ninety-four.

narrative_blocks.header: He took the world instead of college
narrative_blocks.body: He finished at the Raymond Riordan School in Highland, New York, and did not go on to college. He travelled around the world instead and was gone close to two years, coming home in 1930 to start work at the Chicago headquarters.

narrative_blocks.header: Deaf since his forties, and reading history
narrative_blocks.body: He had been almost deaf since his forties and led, his daughter said, a very active interior life. He read history tremendously — a wealth of knowledge and quite a scholar of it, back through his own line to the Mayflower.

narrative_blocks.header: A Thatcher first, then a Coldren
narrative_blocks.body: He married Virginia Thatcher in 1938, of the River Forest family Thatcher Woods is named for. She died in 1977; two years later he married Loise Coldren, and they had a last quarter-century together in Los Angeles.

narrative_blocks.body: He married Carol Pearl Brain in 1934; she had been born in Salt Lake City. Their two boys were raised at Wilmette on the North Shore but driven out to Utah to their grandparents every year, and the family became a Latter-day Saint one.

narrative_blocks.header: Out of the family firm, with both sons
narrative_blocks.body: In 1982 he and both his sons broke away from the company his father and brother had run and renamed their share of it Morgan Systems. He had spent his whole working life in linen, and he died at Chesterfield, Missouri, in 1994.

narrative_blocks.body: Her aunt and uncle of 47 East Elm Street announced her engagement, her own father being in New York. He was the Lake Shore Drive Morgans' son. They married that June and went to Cincinnati, where he was in business.

narrative_blocks.body: For twenty years she lived outside Gold Hill above Boulder and owned and ran its trading post. She came down to Palisade in 1985 and to Clifton in 1987, and died there at sixty-nine after a long illness, a retired shopkeeper.

narrative_blocks.body: She was active in American Indian affairs and supported a string of American Indian charities. When she died her family asked that the money go to the Little Bighorn College library fund at Crow Agency in Montana.

narrative_blocks.body: She was born at Salt Lake City and in 1934 married into a Chicago linen dynasty that traced itself to the Mayflower. Her sons were driven back to Utah every summer; the younger served a mission and was married in the Logan temple.

narrative_blocks.body: Edward Brain was fifty-four and Mary Ann Johnson twenty-four when their son Ebenezer James Brain was born at Salt Lake City in 1875. He married Irene Fanny Hayes there in 1901, had four children, and stayed in Utah about forty years.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten children, born in four states
narrative_blocks.body: The children arrived wherever the linen plants sent him: Deborah at Dayton, Stephen at Indianapolis, Blair at Jamestown in New York, Ryan and Douglas back at Indianapolis, and the last five at St. Louis, ending with twins.

narrative_blocks.header: Two years in the Northwestern States Mission
narrative_blocks.body: He served a mission for the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints from 1961 to 1963 and then went to Brigham Young. A cousin introduced him to his wife's best friend, Carolyn Maw; they married in the Logan temple in 1964.

narrative_blocks.header: He managed the plants, then split the company
narrative_blocks.body: He entered the family business at Dayton in 1965, took the Indianapolis plant in 1971 and the St. Louis plant in 1974. In 1982 he, his father and his brother went independent as Morgan Systems, and they sold it in 2003.

narrative_blocks.header: The employment centre and the eye van
narrative_blocks.body: After the sale he volunteered full time for seven years at the Latter-day Saint employment centre in St. Louis, and drove the UMSL Mobile Eye Van, which brought sight tests to inner-city children. He also served as a bishopric counsellor.

narrative_blocks.header: He called himself a man of the cloth
narrative_blocks.body: He took the chairmanship of Morgan Linen Service at Menands in 1981 and held it thirty-nine years, until he died. He liked to call himself a man of the cloth, and was known on every level of the plant, which is the harder thing.

narrative_blocks.header: Chicago, Utah, then upstate New York
narrative_blocks.body: He grew up on the North Shore and went out to Weber State at Ogden for a finance degree; he met Susan Price there and married her in 1970. They left Salt Lake City for New York in 1981, and he ran the Albany plant from then on.

narrative_blocks.header: The Bears and the Cubs, blessed at dinner
narrative_blocks.body: Tabor Academy gave him a lifelong love of open water, and the Country Club of Troy gave him the golf. He stayed a Chicago fan to the end: the Bears and the Cubs were named in the family's dinner prayers.

narrative_blocks.header: He saw his mother and two aunts out
narrative_blocks.body: He supported his mother and two aunts through their last days, and gave himself to Community Hospice besides. He was buried from a funeral home on Hoosick Street in Troy, a mile or two from the plant he had chaired for thirty-nine years.

narrative_blocks.header: Leicester Cathedral came to her for Richard III
narrative_blocks.body: When Leicester Cathedral built a new altar for the reinterment of King Richard III, it went looking for someone who could make the linens for it and found a woman in upstate New York, working from her own house.

narrative_blocks.header: She taught a lost craft across the diocese
narrative_blocks.body: From 1985 she was Altar Guild Directress for the Diocese of Albany, and set herself to reclaim the making of altar vestments and linen. She learned the crafts first, then drove the diocese teaching parish women, and wrote the books down.

narrative_blocks.header: She sold church linen out of her house
narrative_blocks.body: In 1997 she started Church Linens online and ran it from home for twenty-seven years, to the week she died, supplying fabric, patterns and instruction to altar guilds and liturgical seamstresses. She also made stoles for military priests.

narrative_blocks.header: Dobermans, canaries, monarch butterflies
narrative_blocks.body: She wove baskets and spun her own wool, gardened, and raised monarch butterflies in order to let them go. Dobermans, cats and canaries at home; snakes and whales and wild birds beyond it. Animals were where she found her solace.

narrative_blocks.body: He joined Morgan Services in 1974 and ran it from that year, succeeding his wife's father. He turned the old wisdom round from customer first to Morgan employee first, and the trade gave him its lifetime award in 2013.

narrative_blocks.header: The only man to chair both trade bodies
narrative_blocks.body: He chaired the Textile Rental Services Association from 1983 and the Uniform and Textile Service Association from 2002, the only person ever elected to the top of both. The two organisations blended in 2008.

parents.father_research_notes: A geologist who worked for Central Mining in South Africa and kept a nursery; died before his son's 1960s marriage.

narrative_blocks.header: His first break was McCartney's garden
narrative_blocks.body: Out of the Architectural Association, the job that made him was a glass geodesic dome for Paul McCartney's garden in St John's Wood. He designed a London nightclub with George Harrison as well, and kept a share in it.

narrative_blocks.header: He took Worth Avenue back to 1925
narrative_blocks.body: His firm became the official architect of Palm Beach and returned Worth Avenue to the year it was laid out, coconut palms and all, adding the clock tower so the avenue could be picked out from the ocean road. It finished a week early.

narrative_blocks.header: He built the world's finest croquet ground
narrative_blocks.body: When Chuck Steuber bought a failed nursery to give American croquet a home, he asked Bridges to design it and to supervise the building. Its twelve fast lawns are the best anywhere, and the Hall of Fame took him in 2017.

narrative_blocks.header: A plane flew into his town hall
narrative_blocks.body: He chaired Delray Beach's planning board and sat six years on the Ocean Ridge council, two of them as mayor. A twin-engine aeroplane crashed into the Ocean Ridge town hall he had designed, before the building was finished in 2008.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother found tsavorite, and died for it
narrative_blocks.body: His younger brother Campbell was the gemologist credited with finding tsavorite in the 1960s, and was killed by a mob in Kenya in 2009 over what was taken to be mining rights. The two had meant to write a book together.

narrative_blocks.body: Given up at birth in Salt Lake City to a private adoption, she went looking in her thirties for medical reasons and found the woman who bore her. They came to know and love each other, and she nursed her through the cancer that killed her.

narrative_blocks.header: She drove through a town and stayed
narrative_blocks.body: Driving across the country after college to see family at Cheyenne, she went through Torrington and decided on the spot that it was where she would live. She stayed forty years, and raised other people's children though she had none.

narrative_blocks.header: Betty Crocker Homemaker of Tomorrow
narrative_blocks.body: At Rowland Hall she won a national contest as a Betty Crocker Homemaker of Tomorrow for cooking, sewing and merchandising. She did blackwork and bargello and cross stitch, and taught needlework at Eastern Wyoming College.

narrative_blocks.header: Fan fiction, M*A*S*H, and the Redskins
narrative_blocks.body: She was a master of trivia, loved British history and irises and rocks, and wrote fan fiction to fill out the story lines of the shows she watched, gathering her own readers online. From Wyoming she stayed loyal to Washington's team.

narrative_blocks.header: Four generations of East Hampton summers
narrative_blocks.body: His father's people had been East Hampton residents four generations deep. He coached tennis at the Green Hollow club through school and ran the Sandy Hollow camp at Southampton, and married at Saint Luke's there.

narrative_blocks.body: She married at the Maidstone Club in East Hampton in January 2016, in the same room her brother had held his wedding reception. Rabbi Susan Talve officiated and an Episcopal priest took part beside her.

narrative_blocks.body: Nina Walker Wainwright, who ran the Colony Club and was one of a dozen docents at the Metropolitan, was her father's mother. The girl was christened with both her names, and the Walker in them goes back to the man who ran Macy's.

narrative_blocks.header: Caltech, the Navy, then Venezuela
narrative_blocks.body: Richard took his B.S. at the California Institute of Technology in 1943 and served as a lieutenant in the Naval Reserve. He married Doris Dow of Aberdeen, Scotland, in November 1944, and took her to Venezuela in 1947.

narrative_blocks.header: The Dreamers sang on Hornell radio
narrative_blocks.body: Lois sang in the Dreamers, a trio with Norma Jacox and Miriam Tooke, for eight years through Alfred-Almond Central School and Alfred University. They sang for local organizations and on WWHG, the Hornell radio station.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten years in Peru, then Caracas
narrative_blocks.body: Lois married George Tappan, Alfred class of 1950, and followed him abroad: ten years in Peru, then Caracas, where she was living when the Dreamers met again at Alfred in 1958, and Tripoli, Libya, by 1970.

narrative_blocks.header: A missionary childhood in Shanghai
narrative_blocks.body: Lois lived with her missionary parents in Shanghai for several years before the family moved to Alfred when she was eleven or twelve.

narrative_blocks.header: Back to Shanghai with her husband
narrative_blocks.body: Marion took her Alfred degree in 1956 and settled in Paris with her husband Jean Attali, an endocrinologist. He lectures in Shanghai, and several times a year she goes with him, back to the city she lived in as a girl.

narrative_blocks.header: President of the boards her father sat on
narrative_blocks.body: Mimi was president of the Junior League of Rochester, the Rochester Friendly Home, Hillside Children's Center and Allendale Columbia School, the last two boards her father had sat on. She won the Phoenix Award and the B. Forman Flair Award.

narrative_blocks.header: A solo sail every morning on Canandaigua
narrative_blocks.body: Mimi and Terry reached all seven continents together. At Canandaigua Lake she took a solo sail every morning she could.

narrative_blocks.header: A Kodak man and a Key Largo commodore
narrative_blocks.body: Terry worked for Eastman Kodak until he retired in 1991, and served in the Coast Guard Reserve. Like his father-in-law, Bob Gordon, he was a commodore of the Key Largo Anglers Club, and he captained every boat he sailed.

education.school_name: Syracuse University School of Business Administration

narrative_blocks.header: She built the garden at Nunnally House
narrative_blocks.body: Lucia and her husband Mike built the Gumaer Gardens behind Nunnally House in Brunswick, Georgia, where cancer patients stay free. Dedicated in October 2017, the garden has a dry stream shaped as a cancer ribbon.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years of wills and trusts
narrative_blocks.body: Mike joined the Rochester firm of Nixon, Hargrave, Devans & Doyle out of Cornell Law in 1958, made partner in 1964, and practised tax, estate and trust law until he retired as a senior partner.

narrative_blocks.header: Life trustee of the University of Rochester
narrative_blocks.body: Mike became a trustee of the University of Rochester in 1972 and a life trustee in 2000, and chaired the Eastman School of Music.

narrative_blocks.header: Every summer of his life on Nantucket
narrative_blocks.body: Friends took Mike to Nantucket in his senior year at Harvard, and he spent every summer there for the rest of his life. He was commodore of the Nantucket Yacht Club from 1991 to 1993.

narrative_blocks.header: An environmental and construction lawyer
narrative_blocks.body: John took his law degree at Indiana in 1965 and practised environmental and construction law: general counsel of the Potlatch Corporation, managing partner at Gaston Snow & Ely Bartlett, and special counsel at Tobin & Tobin from 1989.

narrative_blocks.header: Dominoes at the Pacific-Union Club
narrative_blocks.body: John loved bridge, golf and riding, and kept a usual seat at the games table of the Pacific-Union Club in San Francisco, where his wit and his dominoes were well known.

narrative_blocks.header: A Marine who studied the weather
narrative_blocks.body: Before the law, John served in the Marine Corps, graduated with honors in meteorology from the U.S. Naval Aerology School, and took his electrical engineering degree at Purdue in 1958.

military_service.notes: Marine Corps veteran by 1957.

narrative_blocks.header: A factory built on a workman's inventions
narrative_blocks.body: William built his Rochester tobacco works around a handful of small devices invented by one of his employees. It grew into one of the world's largest tobacco companies, and the cigarette division alone made 750 million cigarettes a year.

narrative_blocks.header: A 21-foot Mercury on the smokestack
narrative_blocks.body: In 1881 William had his brother-in-law, J. Guernsey Mitchell, make a 21-foot bronze Mercury for the smokestack of his new factory on Court Street. Mercury outlived the building, which came down in 1951.

narrative_blocks.header: Kimball Castle at Troup and Clarissa
narrative_blocks.body: William built Kimball Castle on the hill at Troup and Clarissa Streets in Rochester's Third Ward. It held an art gallery, an orchid house, a pipe organ in its own music gallery, and the world's finest collection of pepper boxes.

narrative_blocks.header: Orchids, and a house by Tiffany
narrative_blocks.body: William bought lot after lot at Mrs. Mary J. Morgan's sale of rare orchids in New York in 1885. His Rochester house was one of only two in America known to have been designed by Tiffany.

narrative_blocks.body: Laura married William Kimball on 11 August 1880, a month before her thirty-eighth birthday, and had their daughter Cecelia in October 1882, at forty.

narrative_blocks.body: Austin graduated from the Naval Academy in 1925 and served in the North Atlantic and the Pacific in the Second World War, taking command of the escort carrier Shipley Bay just before Okinawa. In Korea he commanded the carrier Essex.

narrative_blocks.body: Christian was three when his father, president of the Hecker Insurance Company, built the family house at 1763 Iroquois in Detroit, designed by MacFarlane, Maul and Lentz. His grandfather was Colonel Frank J. Hecker.

narrative_blocks.body: Pat graduated from the Ethel Walker School in Simsbury at sixteen and took an associate degree at Bradford Junior College at eighteen. In 1991, in her fifties, she took a degree in Biblical Studies at Miami Christian College.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty years running the company office
narrative_blocks.body: When her husband Tom started the Crompton Construction Company in 1984, Pat became its office administrator and ran it for more than twenty years.

narrative_blocks.header: A Marine Corps wife from 1959
narrative_blocks.body: Pat married Tom Crompton in 1956, and when he was commissioned out of the Naval Academy in 1959 she became a Marine Corps wife, with postings to Quantico, Jacksonville and Key West.

narrative_blocks.body: James was the Fairport agent of the George Urban Company, Buffalo millers, until ill health made him retire. He served in the Fairport Fire Department, and was a grandson of James Gordon, an early Fairport landowner.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at Rome in November 1934
narrative_blocks.body: Cynthia married Richard Alhart at Rome in November 1934, and they set up at the Coolidge Apartments on East Avenue. She was active in the Daughters of the American Revolution and the Rochester Colony of New England Women.

narrative_blocks.header: In Monroe High's first graduating class
narrative_blocks.body: Richard was in the first graduating class of Monroe High School in Rochester, and co-owned the Alhart Electric Company. He belonged to the Power Squadron for fifty years, and he and Cynthia traveled widely.

narrative_blocks.body: Warren loved music and played the organ for many Masonic lodges, among them ERAC Lodge 163 and Unity Lodge 479. He was given a Masonic funeral in May 2005.

narrative_blocks.body: Betty is the Stout family's genealogist. She has traced the line back through James Stout, born at Gravesend on Long Island in 1648, to Jean de Trou, born at Lille in 1540.

narrative_blocks.body: Joel took his degree at Sheffield in 1897 and his M.D. at Johns Hopkins in 1901, and stayed on there as an intern and instructor in anatomy. He was a surgical house officer at the Massachusetts General Hospital from 1903 to 1905.

narrative_blocks.header: A New England surgeon who went to Tucson
narrative_blocks.body: Joel practised surgery at Springfield and taught it at Yale, then moved west to Tucson, where he was on the staff of the Southern Methodist Hospital and Sanatorium and sat in the AMA's House of Delegates in 1917.

narrative_blocks.body: In June 1918 Joel was ordered as a captain of the Medical Reserve Corps to the base hospital at Fort Des Moines, Iowa.

narrative_blocks.header: Shot down near Hannover on his ninth mission
narrative_blocks.body: Stephen flew B-17s as a pilot in the 331st Squadron of the 94th Bomb Group. On 11 January 1944, on his ninth mission, bound for the aircraft factories at Braunschweig, his bomber was shot down by a German fighter near Hannover.

narrative_blocks.header: His parachute had not opened
narrative_blocks.body: The other nine men of his crew came down alive and were taken prisoner. Stephen's body was seen near the plane; his parachute had not opened. He lies in the Ardennes American Cemetery in Belgium.

narrative_blocks.header: From Scovill to the Air Forces
narrative_blocks.body: Stephen went from the Taft School and Lehigh to the training room of the Scovill Manufacturing Company in Waterbury, and entered the service in June 1942. His mother received his Air Medal for him at Bradley Field.

military_service.notes: Pilot of B-17F 42-29961 (MACR 1882), shot down by an enemy fighter on the 11 January 1944 mission to Braunschweig and crashed near Hannover; the other nine of the crew became prisoners. Entered service June 1942; overseas from October 1943; eight missions before 11 January. Purple Heart; Air Medal.

narrative_blocks.body: Martha was born at 32 Franklin Street in Medford, lived her whole life in that house, and died there in November 1928, at eighty. She belonged to the First Universalist Church of Medford Center and the Woman's Relief Corps.

narrative_blocks.header: The dean of Alaska architecture
narrative_blocks.body: Ed designed the Captain Cook Hotel, the Egan Convention Center, much of Providence Hospital and the first master plan for the University of Alaska Anchorage. By the early 1980s his firm was the largest in Alaska.

narrative_blocks.header: A job notice on an MIT bulletin board
narrative_blocks.body: Ed was doing graduate work at MIT when he saw a notice for a job with the Alaska Territorial Housing Authority. He took it, moved his family to Anchorage, and soon opened a practice of his own there.

narrative_blocks.header: A year in Helsinki studying Aalto
narrative_blocks.body: In 1963 Ed took his family to Helsinki for a year to study northern design, above all the work of Alvar Aalto and Ralph Erskine. In 1979 he became Alaska's first Fellow of the American Institute of Architects.

narrative_blocks.header: Married in Ketchikan in 1944
narrative_blocks.body: Ed was stationed at Ketchikan with the Coast Guard when he met Kit Carson, who had come north for a summer visit. They married there in 1944 and were together sixty-five years.

narrative_blocks.header: The Stormbird and the Inside Passage
narrative_blocks.body: Ed sailed all his life, and for years took his children and grandchildren up and down the Inside Passage in his sailboat, the Stormbird. At Sitka he took up watercolors, and painted almost to the end.

narrative_blocks.header: She put the bike trail under C Street
narrative_blocks.body: When the city planned to run C Street across the Chester Creek greenbelt, Kit organized citizens, won the case in court and got the road raised over the creek. The trail and the underpass are still there.

narrative_blocks.header: Preserving a city only fifty years old
narrative_blocks.body: In 1970, saving the historic buildings of a town barely fifty years old was a radical idea. Kit saved the Oscar Anderson House, helped found the Urban Design Commission, and chaired the Historic Preservation Commission for ten years.

narrative_blocks.header: She came north to Ketchikan in 1943
narrative_blocks.body: At a childhood friend's urging, Kit took a job at the Tongass Trading Co. in Ketchikan in 1943. There she met Ed, a Coast Guard lieutenant, and married him within the year.

narrative_blocks.header: Eliza Doolittle and Lady Bracknell
narrative_blocks.body: Kit studied drama at Illinois Wesleyan and acted and directed all her life, in college and in Anchorage. She drove her six children to school teaching them poetry and Broadway songs.

narrative_blocks.header: Get Mears!
narrative_blocks.body: In 2001 Kit published Get Mears!, a biography of Col. Frederick Mears, who built the Alaska Railroad and laid out the townsite that became Anchorage. She never took a salary for her civic work.

narrative_blocks.header: A large collection of her art
narrative_blocks.body: Katie studied fine arts at the California College of Arts and Crafts, and went on making art and writing all her life. A long illness began in her college years; she lived with it in Seattle, then at home in Anchorage.

narrative_blocks.header: Clayton found his way back to her
narrative_blocks.body: Katie's greatest love was her son, Clayton Olander. He found his way back to her about 2015, eight years before she died, and brought his wife Hannah and four grandchildren into her life.

narrative_blocks.header: Friends at Walmart and in the park
narrative_blocks.body: Katie made friends easily and laughed quickly, with workers at Walmart and strangers in the park alike. She was witty, unconventional, mischievous and tender.

narrative_blocks.header: Anchorage, then Finland, then Switzerland
narrative_blocks.body: Katie went to school in Anchorage until her junior year, when the family moved to Finland for her father's year in Helsinki. She graduated from an academy in Switzerland.

narrative_blocks.header: A seat on the commission his mother chaired
narrative_blocks.body: In 2009 the mayor named John to the Anchorage Historic Preservation Commission, which his mother, Kit, had helped create and chaired for ten years. He had sat on the Urban Design Commission she helped found, too.

narrative_blocks.header: Saving the Fourth Avenue Theatre
narrative_blocks.body: In 1989 John prepared the original application to put Anchorage's Fourth Avenue Theatre on the National Register, and designed a remodel that kept its walls and its sloped floors.

narrative_blocks.header: Building against permafrost and snowdrift
narrative_blocks.body: Designing clinics in the Bering Strait villages taught John to build against severe cold, drifting snow and permafrost. He co-wrote the cold-climate section of Architectural Graphic Standards.

narrative_blocks.header: A fine arts building on his father's campus
narrative_blocks.body: John was project architect on the University of Alaska Anchorage's Fine Arts building in the 1980s, on the campus whose first master plan his father had drawn.

narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth took over the Taos Community Foundation at the end of 2001 and led it for more than thirteen years, making most of its grants in Taos and Colfax County and a few as far off as Nepal.

narrative_blocks.header: She came to Taos in 1973, mid-college
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth first came to Taos in 1973, partway through college, and lived around Taos, Santa Fe and Crestone. She made her living in business, from Native American crafts to small-business consulting.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventy-one miles of old irrigation ditch
narrative_blocks.body: Harriet co-founded the High Line Canal Conservancy in 2014 and led it for eleven years, turning Denver's 71-mile nineteenth-century irrigation canal into a greenway through more than fifteen communities.

narrative_blocks.header: She went into labor on the canal
narrative_blocks.body: Harriet walked the canal almost daily with her three children, hunting frogs, salamanders and snakes in its dry bed. One day, out walking it, she went into labor with her daughter.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-five miles kept open for good
narrative_blocks.body: In June 2024 Denver Water put forty-five miles of the canal under a conservation easement the conservancy manages, keeping it public open space. For the tenth anniversary Harriet walked all 71 miles.

narrative_blocks.header: A downhill ski racer from Anchorage
narrative_blocks.body: Harriet grew up racing downhill skis in Anchorage, where her mother, Kit, fought to keep the Chester Creek greenbelt whole and to run its trail under C Street.

narrative_blocks.body: Mike studied natural resource and environmental law at the University of Denver, then built a small Denver firm that invests in, brokers and develops urban infill projects.

narrative_blocks.body: Mike married Harriet Crittenden, a downhill ski racer from Alaska two classes behind him at Colorado College. They raised three children in Denver. He has climbed thirty-three of Colorado's fourteeners.

narrative_blocks.body: Ben took his architecture degree at Yale in 1935, then taught mathematics, mechanical drawing and blacksmithing at the Newton School in Windham, Vermont, and practised as an architect in Manchester.

narrative_blocks.header: Married by the bride's father in 1937
narrative_blocks.body: Ben married Caroline Neill on 10 July 1937 at St. Mary's in South Manchester, where her father was rector and performed the ceremony; his brother Albert was best man. They were married sixty-three years.

narrative_blocks.header: Apples, raspberries and blueberries
narrative_blocks.body: Ben loved forestry and working his own land in Vermont, where he grew apples, raspberries and blueberries. The family kept a summer cottage on Columbia Lake for many years.

narrative_blocks.body: In 1951 Abe and Eva bought the 600-acre Plantation Ranch near Stewarts Point, logged over, and in 1952 opened the Plantation Farm Camp to fifty boys and girls. They ran it until they moved to Sea Ranch in 1986.

narrative_blocks.header: Tree Farmers of the West, 1974
narrative_blocks.body: Abe and Eva studied forestry, mended the ranch's land and water against erosion, and worked it as a tree farm. In 1974 they were named Tree Farmers of the West.

narrative_blocks.body: Abe married Eva Smith in 1938, the year they both graduated from Pomona College. His brother Ed finished at Pomona that same year.

narrative_blocks.body: Eunice lived in Wethersfield for sixty years, sang in the choir at Center Church in Hartford for as long, and loved best her summers with the family at Columbia Lake.

narrative_blocks.body: Lyman spent his career as a poultry geneticist, known to his colleagues simply as Critt, and in 1985 was named the USDA Agricultural Research Service's Scientist of the Year.

narrative_blocks.header: He met Margaret at the NIH
narrative_blocks.body: Lyman met Margaret Lambert Hillhouse while they both worked at the National Institutes of Health, and married her in Washington on 13 June 1959. In retirement he sorted generations of family pictures to share.

narrative_blocks.header: A biostatistician at the NIH
narrative_blocks.body: Margaret took her master's in biostatistics at Minnesota in 1956 and went to the National Institutes of Health in Bethesda, where she met Lyman. From 1976 to 1984 she was a biostatistician for Michigan's health department.

narrative_blocks.header: Partners in science, sailing and camping
narrative_blocks.body: Margaret and Lyman began with a shared love of science and math, sailing and camping, and passed gardening, travel and reading on to their daughters and grandchildren. They were married fifty-three years.

narrative_blocks.body: John was a trustee of Center Church's Warburton Trust Fund, worked with Center City Churches, and gave his time to caring for Hartford's homeless.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty years of Newar women's stories
narrative_blocks.body: For more than thirty years Ellen has recorded the oral histories of older Newar women in the Kathmandu Valley: goddess possession, healing, and tending the land. Her Columbia thesis was runner-up for the 2017 Brodsky award.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine years old in Kathmandu
narrative_blocks.body: Ellen first saw the Kathmandu Valley in 1970, at nine, when her father was posted there. He went back as ambassador from 1981 to 1984, while she was in college, and so did she.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father in his morning coat
narrative_blocks.body: Each year at the Living Goddess's festival Ellen watched her father squeeze into a morning coat that no longer fit him, to attend the girl Kumari with the other diplomats.

narrative_blocks.header: His five thousand books went home to Nepal
narrative_blocks.body: After her husband Ted died in 2020, Ellen sent his library of more than five thousand books on Nepal from New Mexico and New York to Bhaktapur, where it opened as the Ted Riccardi Memorial Reading Room.

narrative_blocks.header: He tasted the artifacts on television
narrative_blocks.body: From 1949 to 1964 Carl was a panelist on What in the World?, the Penn Museum's television quiz, known for his irreverent remarks and for now and then tasting an artifact to identify it.

narrative_blocks.header: Hotu man in an Iranian cave
narrative_blocks.body: In 1949 Carl made the first serious search for fossil man in Iran, and in 1951 he excavated Hotu man from a neolithic cave in the northeast. The next year he won the Viking Medal for physical anthropology.

narrative_blocks.header: Measuring the mountain men of Albania
narrative_blocks.body: In 1929 and 1930 Carl measured 1,067 men from ten regions of northern Albania. Boston's Albanian community helped him finish in 1946 and 1947, and The Mountains of Giants followed in 1950, as the field fell out of favour.

narrative_blocks.header: Behind the lines in North Africa
narrative_blocks.body: In the Second World War Carl served the Office of Strategic Services in North Africa and the Middle East, and was awarded the Legion of Merit in 1945.

narrative_blocks.header: The Story of Man and The Seven Caves
narrative_blocks.body: Carl wrote novels as well as monographs. Readers knew him best for The Story of Man in 1954 and The Seven Caves in 1957, his account of digging for early man in the Middle East.

narrative_blocks.header: A theory of race long since rejected
narrative_blocks.body: Carl rose to president of the American Association of Physical Anthropologists, but is remembered above all for his theory that the human races evolved in parallel, scientific racism disputed even in his lifetime.

narrative_blocks.header: A son who played bridge for money
narrative_blocks.body: Carl's younger son, Charles, born in 1931, won bridge's Vanderbilt Cup in 1961 and finished second to Italy's Blue Team in the 1962 Bermuda Bowl. He made his modest living at the tables of the money clubs.

narrative_blocks.body: Michael spent thirty-five years at the National Cancer Institute working out how chromosomes exchange DNA during meiosis, using budding yeast. Errors in that exchange are a leading cause of infertility and birth defects.

narrative_blocks.header: The National Academy, the year he retired
narrative_blocks.body: Michael was elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 2016 and to the National Academy of Sciences in 2022, the year he retired from government service. He stayed on at the NIH as a volunteer researcher.

narrative_blocks.header: He dug in the Kathmandu Valley
narrative_blocks.body: With Mohan Khanal, Ted ran some of the only archaeological digs ever allowed in the Kathmandu Valley, at Dumakhal in 1984-85 and 1988-89, and published them in the Harvard Oriental Series in 2007.

narrative_blocks.header: Sherlock Holmes goes to India
narrative_blocks.body: After Columbia, Ted wrote two books of new Sherlock Holmes stories, The Oriental Casebook of Sherlock Holmes in 2003 and Between the Thames and the Tiber in 2011, drawing on India, Europe and music.

narrative_blocks.header: A prodigy in his father's band
narrative_blocks.body: Ted grew up in a Philadelphia family of musicians. His father, a cellist and bass player, found he had perfect pitch, and by his early teens Ted was playing piano in his father's bands on nights and weekends.

narrative_blocks.header: He met Ellen in Nepal
narrative_blocks.body: Ted met Ellen Coon in Nepal in the 1980s and married her in 1995. They lived for long stretches in Kathmandu, where she documented Newar religious practice, and he wrote on with Parkinson's for twenty years.

narrative_blocks.header: A medal from the King of Nepal

narrative_blocks.body: Harriet joined the Kamehameha president's office in 1954, typed and edited Harold Kent's Charles Reed Bishop, Man of Hawaii, and ran alumni affairs for a quarter century. In 1995 the schools gave her the Order of Ke Ali'i Pauahi.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight years old on Duval Street
narrative_blocks.body: Christie was eight and dressed for church when a stray bomb hit the back of the family house on Duval Street on 7 December 1941. Her mother carried her and her little sister Elizabeth over the garden wall.

narrative_blocks.header: Paired by height in dance class
narrative_blocks.body: At five foot eight Christie was the tallest woman in her University of Hawaii dance class, so she was paired with the tallest man, a six-foot-four basketball player named Lawrence Keolanui. They married in December 1953.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-five years an Army wife
narrative_blocks.body: Christie followed Larry through twenty-five years in the Army, from second lieutenant to lieutenant colonel: West Germany, Panama and eight states, and home in Hawaii while he served two tours in Vietnam.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote Aloha ʻOe
narrative_blocks.body: Lydia found her gift for composition at school and wrote more than 150 songs in her life. The most famous, Aloha ʻOe, began as a love song.

narrative_blocks.header: The only queen Hawaii ever had
narrative_blocks.body: Lydia became heir in 1877, taking the name Liliʻuokalani, and came to the throne on her brother Kalākaua's death in January 1891: Hawaii's only queen regnant, and its last sovereign.

narrative_blocks.header: She yielded under protest
narrative_blocks.body: In January 1893, with troops from the USS Boston ashore, she gave up her authority 'to avoid any collision of armed forces,' signing that she yielded under protest to superior force.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight months in her own palace
narrative_blocks.body: Arrested in 1895, the queen was held in ʻIolani Palace and made to sign an abdication to save her loyalists from execution. After eight months she went home under house arrest, and was freed in 1896.

narrative_blocks.header: She married the boy from the fence
narrative_blocks.body: Lydia married John Owen Dominis in 1862, the schoolmate who had climbed the Royal School fence to see the royal children. He died seven months after she became queen.

narrative_blocks.header: Her niece may have stopped Major André
narrative_blocks.body: Peggy's niece Cornelia Van Cortlandt Beekman refused to hand Lt. John Webb's uniform to a man who had no written order. Major André was in that man's house; in the uniform, it was said, he might have slipped through the lines.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son's will renamed a Rutherfurd
narrative_blocks.body: Peggy's son Peter Gerard died childless in 1847 and left the family fortune on condition that a young kinsman take the name: Stuyvesant Rutherfurd, at six, became Rutherfurd Stuyvesant.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father studied under Solomon Stoddard
narrative_blocks.body: Peggy's father, Gilbert Livingston, a younger son of the first lord of the Manor, was sent to Northampton to study under the Rev. Solomon Stoddard. He chose trade instead, and later sat for the Manor in the Assembly.

narrative_blocks.header: A Livingston and a Beekman
narrative_blocks.body: Peggy was a granddaughter of Robert Livingston, first lord of Livingston Manor. Her great-grandfather Wilhelmus Beekman sailed to New Amsterdam with the first Peter Stuyvesant, and her sister Joanna married Pierre Van Cortlandt.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine children and thirteen years a widow
narrative_blocks.body: Peggy Livingston married Peter Stuyvesant in October 1764 and had nine children with him. She outlived him by thirteen years and died in 1818.
