narrative_blocks.body: Mary, third daughter of Andrew Buchanan of Baltimore, married Senator Nathan Sanford in 1828, twenty-three years her senior. She outlived him by forty-one years and died at Poughkeepsie in 1879.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the college president's sister

narrative_blocks.header: The Lost Order was on his paper
narrative_blocks.body: Robert E. Lee's Special Order 191, found in an envelope with two cigars in a field near Frederick, Maryland, in September 1862 and carried to McClellan before Antietam, was written on paper embossed 'Platner & Porter, Congress', from Samuel's mill.

narrative_blocks.header: Whitman's notebooks, Twain's letters
narrative_blocks.body: The Platner & Porter mill made fine writing and book papers and sold to the U.S. government. Walt Whitman's handmade notebooks in the Library of Congress are on it, and so is some of Mark Twain's correspondence, and a letter of Jefferson Davis's.

narrative_blocks.header: A mill village with some taste
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel came from Lee, Massachusetts, and in 1848 he and William Platner bought the Stone & Carrington mill at Unionville and soon built a second. Their mill and tenements were models of neatness and good taste, a local historian wrote, and gave the village a tone it had lacked.

narrative_blocks.header: Connecticut sent him to Chicago in 1860
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel went to Chicago in May 1860 as one of Connecticut's delegates to the Republican National Convention, the one that met in the Wigwam and nominated Abraham Lincoln on the third ballot.

narrative_blocks.header: He voted for the Fifteenth Amendment
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel backed Unionville's abolitionist causes, and in 1869, sitting for Farmington in the Connecticut legislature, he voted to ratify the Fifteenth Amendment and its guarantee of the vote to formerly enslaved men. He later served as state bank commissioner.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Hulbert wives, both young
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel lost his first wife, Maria Hulbert, in 1855, when she was twenty-seven. In 1857 he married Esther Hulbert, ten years younger and like Maria from Lee, Massachusetts; Esther died at Syracuse thirteen months later, at twenty.

narrative_blocks.header: A third marriage, and six more children
narrative_blocks.body: Samuel was thirty-nine when he married Frances Ann Smith, eighteen, a first cousin of J. Pierpont Morgan, in February 1861. They had six children and lost two as babies, Kate in 1867 and Frances Morgan in 1874.

narrative_blocks.body: Mary's first husband, Aaron Lyon, died in 1858, and their only child, Charles, died at twenty-one in 1878. The next year, at fifty-eight, she married Charles Fuller of Sturbridge, then sixty-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: A Yale lawyer who died at thirty-four
narrative_blocks.body: Aaron graduated from Yale in 1849, read law at the Yale Law School, and settled at Sturbridge in 1851. He married Mary Porter there the next year and practised until he died in August 1858, leaving a son not two.

narrative_blocks.body: Mary married William Dold in Rockbridge County in September 1850, and named their sons for her father, Edwin Porter, and for her sister Mehetable's husband, Rev. George Dod Armstrong.

narrative_blocks.header: The brother who stayed in Hadley
narrative_blocks.body: James lived all his life at Hadley. In 1829 his brother Jeremiah wrote him from Troy, urging him to travel to New York and "leave aside your foolish excuses," and offered to pay part of the way.

narrative_blocks.header: "The first church ever formed in Chicago"
narrative_blocks.body: Jeremiah came to Fort Dearborn in May 1833 with the troops from Fort Brady and on 26 June organized the First Presbyterian Church, twenty-six members in the fort's carpenter shop, six weeks before Chicago was a town.

narrative_blocks.header: The little girl on the boat
narrative_blocks.body: On the voyage to Fort Dearborn Jeremiah was cheered by Major Fowle's daughter, a year and a half old. Forty years later a Boston woman asked if he remembered the little girl on board; she was Mrs. Henry Durant, founding Wellesley.

narrative_blocks.header: Ninety miles by canoe to his first mission
narrative_blocks.body: Jeremiah reached Fort Brady in the autumn of 1831 after weeks of travel, the last ninety miles by canoe with two French boatmen in bitter cold. The church of five he founded there grew to thirty-three.

narrative_blocks.header: Chicago's first crusade against gambling
narrative_blocks.body: Jeremiah led Chicago's first campaign against gambling, and his session called members to account for drink and dancing. In late 1835 he gave the city up and took a church at Peoria.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped bury Vicksburg's dead
narrative_blocks.body: Jeremiah entered Vicksburg on 6 July 1863, two days after its surrender, and helped bury the dead found in its hospitals, then served the town's Presbyterian church through the winter.

narrative_blocks.header: A chaplain from Memphis to Cheyenne
narrative_blocks.body: Jeremiah was a chaplain with the 1st Illinois Light Artillery at Fort Pickering in Memphis, served the troops on the Rio Grande from 1865, and was post chaplain at Fort Brown, Fort Sill and Fort D. A. Russell until 1882.

narrative_blocks.header: In the wake of Sherman's march
narrative_blocks.body: In 1864 Jeremiah, Eliza and Mary Bickerdyke toured the tent hospitals at Little Rock and cared for the wounded left in Sherman's wake.

narrative_blocks.header: Chicago's first public school
narrative_blocks.body: In 1833 Eliza opened Chicago's first public school in a log house by Fort Dearborn: twenty-five pupils, no desks, some paddling across the Chicago River by canoe. A Chicago school has carried her name since 1937.

narrative_blocks.header: A church belfry on the Underground Railroad
narrative_blocks.body: At Green Bay the Porters' house was the last stop before Canada. When a fugitive and his three small children came in the night, Eliza hid them in the church belfry for four days, until a boat could carry them to a steamer.

narrative_blocks.header: A Sanitary Commission director in 1861
narrative_blocks.body: In October 1861 Eliza took charge of the Chicago Sanitary Commission's office. She nursed at Cairo during Shiloh, carried the wounded to Mound City, and brought volunteer nurses to the tent hospitals at Savannah, Tennessee.

narrative_blocks.header: Mother Bickerdyke's little brown bird
narrative_blocks.body: In 1864 Eliza nursed the wounded from Lookout Mountain and Missionary Ridge beside Mary Bickerdyke, who called her her “little brown bird.” At Resaca that May her son James was in the thick of the fight.

narrative_blocks.header: She wrote to Lincoln for the sick
narrative_blocks.body: In 1863 Eliza asked Lincoln to furlough sick and wounded veterans as he did the men who reenlisted, warning that keeping the sick in Southern hospitals was hurting the Union's recruiting more than anything else.

narrative_blocks.header: Schools for freed children
narrative_blocks.body: Eliza opened a school for Black children at Memphis in 1862, helped found one for freed slaves at Shiloh, and after the war ran a Sunday school and a kindergarten for freed children at Austin, Texas.

narrative_blocks.header: A school at every post
narrative_blocks.body: Eliza opened a school wherever Jeremiah was sent: she reopened the Rio Grande Seminary at Brownsville in 1868 and taught the garrison children at Fort Sill and Fort D. A. Russell.

career.organization: Mackinac Island, St. Ignace and Fort Dearborn schools

narrative_blocks.header: Missionary doctor at Tianjin
narrative_blocks.body: Henry went to China in 1872 as a doctor and minister for the American Board and stayed thirty-four years, at Tianjin and in Shandong, where he founded Williams Hospital. In the Boxer Rebellion he led the mission headquarters at Tianjin.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the Beloit president's daughter
narrative_blocks.body: Henry married Elizabeth Colton Chapin at Beloit College in April 1879; her father, Aaron Lucius Chapin, had helped found the college. Their three sons were born in China.

narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth's aunt Ellen Chapin had married William Porter, Beloit's Latin professor, in 1854. Twenty-five years later Elizabeth married his cousin Henry Dwight Porter at the college her father had helped found.

narrative_blocks.header: San Diego's first free-standing public sculpture
narrative_blocks.body: In 1926 Tank made La Jolla's tribute to Ellen Browning Scripps: a bronze girl kneeling over a pool before a carved limestone bench, San Diego's first free-standing public sculpture. It was stolen in 1995 and never found.

narrative_blocks.header: He worked in Gutzon Borglum's studio
narrative_blocks.body: After Pomona and the Art Students League, Tank worked in Gutzon Borglum's Connecticut studio and helped him on Virginia's war memorial around 1919. In 1929 he founded the Contemporary Artists of San Diego and was its first president.

narrative_blocks.header: Carl Akeley asked him to Africa
narrative_blocks.body: Carl Akeley invited Tank to go with him to Africa, most likely to model animals for the Natural History Museum. With only one foot, Tank decided he could not stand the journey.

narrative_blocks.header: Ping An Shan, the Hill of Peace
narrative_blocks.body: In 1905 the Porters bought the Roach house at La Mesa with ten acres of citrus and named it Ping An Shan, the Hill of Peace. Tank hung rings from his bedroom ceiling there to keep strong through his years in bed.

narrative_blocks.header: A football injury cost him a foot
narrative_blocks.body: At about fourteen a football bruise turned into bone tuberculosis; Tank lost a foot, later a kidney, and spent five years in bed. He enrolled at Pomona in 1910 and graduated in 1914.

narrative_blocks.header: Bronze sprinkler heads from his foundry
narrative_blocks.body: In the Depression Tank turned his La Mesa foundry to bronze sprinkler heads, invented a rotating lawn sprinkler, and ran the Browning Manufacturing Company until 1956. He sat on La Mesa's planning commission for thirteen years.

narrative_blocks.header: Out of China ahead of the Boxers
narrative_blocks.body: Tank was born at Tianjin, the son of missionary parents, and the family fled China at the Boxer Rebellion. In 1899 he entered the academy at Beloit, which his grandfather Aaron Lucius Chapin had helped found.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-five years at the San Diego Zoo
narrative_blocks.body: Anne worked for more than twenty-five years in administration at the San Diego Zoo, a job she loved. After she retired she travelled far and wide, China and Cuba among the places.

narrative_blocks.header: Parasailing, and a mule to the cave paintings
narrative_blocks.body: Anne climbed trees, parasailed, kayaked and rode a mule to see cave paintings. She sang in community choirs and played the piano for services at the Summit Unitarian Universalist Fellowship.

narrative_blocks.header: The cheerleader and the football player
narrative_blocks.body: The only child of the La Mesa artists James and Lenore Porter, Anne met her husband Gene at Grossmont High School, where he played football and she was a cheerleader. After college they married and followed his Marine Corps postings.

narrative_blocks.body: Edward died at Racine in 1876, at thirty-nine. Six years later his widow, Julia, founded Chicago's first children's hospital in memory of their son Maurice, who had died at thirteen.

narrative_blocks.header: Treasurer of Hopkins Academy, like his grandfather
narrative_blocks.body: William was treasurer of Hopkins Academy for fifty-one years and gave it up the day before he died. His grandfather, Dr. William Porter, had been treasurer when it was incorporated, and the office came down from father to son.

narrative_blocks.header: From Hadley's store to Springfield shoes
narrative_blocks.body: William ran Hadley's country store for fifteen years, then moved to Springfield in 1880 and bought into L. Z. Cutler's wholesale shoe firm, Cutler & Porter, where he stayed until 1912.

career.organization: Second National Bank and Union Trust Company, Springfield

narrative_blocks.header: Chicago's first children's hospital
narrative_blocks.body: After her son Maurice died of rheumatic fever at thirteen, Julia opened the Maurice Porter Memorial Hospital, an eight-bed cottage in Lincoln Park, in 1882, free to children “without restriction as to race, color, creed, or ability to pay.”

narrative_blocks.header: It became Lurie Children's
narrative_blocks.body: Julia ran the hospital's affairs and money herself, with nine women she invited onto its board of managers. In 1904 she agreed to rename it Children's Memorial; it is now the Ann & Robert H. Lurie Children's Hospital of Chicago.

narrative_blocks.header: Her land became part of the Loop
narrative_blocks.body: Julia inherited land that later became part of the Chicago Loop, the root of the Porter family's wealth, and after Edward's death she gave herself to philanthropy. Her son built her a house at Winnetka in 1897.

career.organization: Maurice Porter Memorial Hospital, later Children's Memorial, Chicago

narrative_blocks.header: A hospital in his name
narrative_blocks.body: Maurice died of rheumatic fever, a disease of the heart, at Chicago on 26 March 1881, at thirteen. The next year his mother opened the Maurice Porter Memorial Hospital, the city's first hospital for children, in his memory.

narrative_blocks.header: He built two houses on the Winnetka bluff
narrative_blocks.body: In 1897 James bought land on the bluff above Lake Michigan at Winnetka and built a Tudor house at 1077 Sheridan Road for his mother, Julia, and a Georgian one at 1085 for his own family of five children.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought an island in Maine
narrative_blocks.body: In 1912 James bought Great Spruce Head Island, a mile of Penobscot Bay with nobody on it, and designed a fourteen-bedroom house there. The family summered on it for the rest of their lives.

narrative_blocks.header: Biology, architecture, and the Loop land
narrative_blocks.body: James took a Harvard master's in biology and studied architecture at Columbia, but spent most of his life managing the Chicago real estate his mother had inherited, which became his.

career.organization: Winnetka and Great Spruce Head Island

narrative_blocks.header: A poet with liberal causes
narrative_blocks.body: Ruth, a Bryn Mawr graduate from a literary New England family, wrote poetry and backed liberal social causes, and raised her five children at Winnetka and on Great Spruce Head Island.

sources.short: FamilySearch: maternal grandparents Alexander Wadsworth (1806-1898) and Mary Elizabeth Hubbard Fairfield (1807-1881)

narrative_blocks.header: The eldest Porter, to a hundred and one
narrative_blocks.body: Nancy was the eldest of James and Ruth Porter's five children and lived to be a hundred and one. Her daughter Lucy died at four, in 1930.

narrative_blocks.header: He made color photography an art
narrative_blocks.body: Eliot's birds were the first color photographs ever shown at the Museum of Modern Art, in 1943, and his Intimate Landscapes of 1979 was the Metropolitan Museum's first one-man show of color photography.

narrative_blocks.header: Stieglitz talked him out of medicine
narrative_blocks.body: Fairfield introduced his brother to Alfred Stieglitz around 1930, and in 1938 Stieglitz showed Eliot's work at An American Place. The next year Eliot gave up teaching biochemistry at Harvard to photograph full time.

narrative_blocks.header: Thoreau and the Sierra Club, 1962
narrative_blocks.body: For twenty years Eliot looked for a publisher for his color photographs set beside lines of Thoreau. The Sierra Club brought out In Wildness Is the Preservation of the World in 1962, and he sat on its board from 1965 to 1971.

narrative_blocks.header: The canyon under Lake Powell
narrative_blocks.body: Eliot's The Place No One Knew recorded Glen Canyon before the Lake Powell reservoir drowned it. "My pictures are a form of editorial comment," he said; "they show the way I feel."

narrative_blocks.header: Kodachrome and fast birds
narrative_blocks.body: When a publisher turned down his bird book because black and white could not tell the species apart, Eliot used his chemical training to master the new Kodachrome and dye transfer printing.

narrative_blocks.header: Buried on the family island
narrative_blocks.body: Eliot died at Santa Fe in 1990 and was buried on Great Spruce Head Island in Maine, where he had photographed its birds as a boy. His archive of more than 9,000 prints went to the Amon Carter Museum.

narrative_blocks.header: "There is my own spirit"
narrative_blocks.body: After the 1938 show Stieglitz wrote Eliot that some of his photographs were the first to make him feel "there is my own spirit." In 1939 Beaumont Newhall chose his work for Sixty Photographs, which opened MoMA's photography gallery.

narrative_blocks.header: A realist among the Abstract Expressionists
narrative_blocks.body: Fairfield kept painting landscapes, interiors and portraits of his family and friends in the years Abstract Expressionism ruled New York, and was criticized and revered for it. He left about 250 works to the Parrish Art Museum.

narrative_blocks.header: Vuillard at the Art Institute, 1938
narrative_blocks.body: Fairfield found how he wanted to paint at a Vuillard and Bonnard show at the Art Institute of Chicago in 1938. His career began only after the war, when writing for Art News led to his first exhibitions.

narrative_blocks.header: Elaine de Kooning got him to ArtNews
narrative_blocks.body: On Elaine de Kooning's recommendation Fairfield became an associate editor at ArtNews, and the reviews he wrote there brought him exhibitions and, at last, recognition. He reviewed for The Nation and Art in America too.

narrative_blocks.header: He painted the New York School poets
narrative_blocks.body: Fairfield's sitters included the poets John Ashbery, Frank O'Hara and James Schuyler; his portrait of Elaine de Kooning hangs in the Metropolitan Museum.

narrative_blocks.header: Summers on Great Spruce Head Island
narrative_blocks.body: Fairfield's father bought Great Spruce Head Island in Maine in 1912 and built the family house there. Fairfield summered on the island from the age of six, and it is the subject of many of his paintings.

narrative_blocks.header: His book on Thomas Eakins
narrative_blocks.body: Braziller published Fairfield's book on Thomas Eakins in 1959, a critical study of a painter he thought held back by an over-strict conscience.

narrative_blocks.header: He met Trotsky at twenty
narrative_blocks.body: On a 1927 walking tour Fairfield joined a group of Americans bound for Moscow and met Leon Trotsky, whom he found charming. Back in Winnetka in 1936 he went door to door raising money for Trotsky's defense.

narrative_blocks.header: A finalist at eighty-three
narrative_blocks.body: Anne wrote poems from childhood but published little until after Fairfield died in 1975. Her first collection, An Altogether Different Language, gathered sixty years of work and was a National Book Award finalist in 1994, when she was eighty-three.

narrative_blocks.header: Her great-uncle wrote her poems down
narrative_blocks.body: Before Anne could write or spell, her great-uncle Laurence Minot wrote her poems down and illustrated them. Her first book, published when she was eighty-three, is dedicated in part to him.

narrative_blocks.header: A little girl with a big white nose
narrative_blocks.body: Anne met Fairfield Porter at sixteen, through her sister's college roommate, and powdered her nose for it with the only thing at hand, talcum. He remembered her afterwards as a little girl with a big white nose; they married in 1932.

narrative_blocks.header: Dorothy Day answered her letter
narrative_blocks.body: Anne tried, for the sake of her atheist in-laws, to be an atheist herself; it didn't work. She wrote to Dorothy Day, who answered with the name of a priest, and at forty-three Anne became a Catholic. Her mother cried.

narrative_blocks.header: James Schuyler stayed eleven years
narrative_blocks.body: The big Southampton house, bought in 1949, took in painters and poets: James Schuyler came after a breakdown and stayed eleven years, and John Ashbery and Frank O'Hara came and went. Anne often posed for Fairfield's paintings.

narrative_blocks.header: The servants with no last names
narrative_blocks.body: Anne grew up in a Boston town house run by Irish servants in black who, as far as the children knew, had no last names. As a teenager it began to trouble her, and in old age she was a secular Franciscan, working among the poor.

narrative_blocks.header: She married a distant cousin
narrative_blocks.body: Anne and Fairfield Porter, married in 1932, were distant cousins: both came down from Rev. James Pierpont of New Haven and his wife Mary Hooker, Thomas Hooker's granddaughter.

narrative_blocks.header: A Paris scholarship with André Lhote
narrative_blocks.body: Aline won a scholarship in 1928 to study painting with André Lhote in Paris, and stayed two years. Her mother was a painter and her father an architect.

narrative_blocks.header: Betty Parsons gave her a show, 1979
narrative_blocks.body: In 1979 Betty Parsons gave Aline a one-woman show in New York. She was known too for her boxes, built from objects gathered on Great Spruce Head Island and at home in Tesuque.

narrative_blocks.header: She pointed Eliot toward Thoreau
narrative_blocks.body: Aline told Eliot that his photographs of nature made her think of Thoreau. The pairing became In Wildness Is the Preservation of the World, the Sierra Club's first book of color photographs, in 1962.

narrative_blocks.header: Georgia O'Keeffe, and a pink floor
narrative_blocks.body: Georgia O'Keeffe was Aline's close friend, and Agnes Martin hung one of her paintings where she could see it every day. One small room in her Tesuque house had a floor painted shocking pink.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brother introduced her to Eliot
narrative_blocks.body: Aline's brother, the artist and inventor Peter Kilham, introduced her to Eliot in Cambridge. They married in 1936, and on Peter's advice moved to Santa Fe in 1938.

narrative_blocks.header: A reporter in Portland and St. Louis
narrative_blocks.body: After Harvard and the Korean War, Eliot Jr. reported for the Portland Press Herald and then the St. Louis Post-Dispatch, and he and Jane raised their five children in St. Louis.

narrative_blocks.header: Dogs, underdogs and nature
narrative_blocks.body: His family remembered Eliot Jr. as a self-taught man and a champion of dogs, underdogs and nature.

narrative_blocks.body: Charles went from the Belmont Hill School and Harvard into three years with the Marine Corps, then to the National Shawmut Bank of Boston. In November 1965 he married Kent Pendleton Perley of Pittsburgh.

military_service.notes: Three years

narrative_blocks.header: Sputnik went up, and he chose China
narrative_blocks.body: Jonathan took his Harvard degree in astronomy in 1960, just after Sputnik, and gave it up for Chinese history: a Colorado master's, a Berkeley doctorate in 1971, and forty-two years teaching at the University of New Mexico.

narrative_blocks.header: Chair, senate president, program director
narrative_blocks.body: Across forty-two years at New Mexico Jonathan chaired the history department, presided over the Faculty Senate and directed Asian Studies. His course on Imperial China was the core of his research on the social history of Chinese science.

narrative_blocks.header: All Under Heaven, with his father
narrative_blocks.body: Jonathan arranged two long trips through China with his father in 1980 and 1981, and they made All Under Heaven: The Chinese World together, Eliot's photographs and Jonathan's text.

narrative_blocks.header: Two years in Taiwan
narrative_blocks.body: For his Berkeley doctorate Jonathan spent 1967 to 1969 in Taiwan, in Chinese language study and research.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty years of recommendation letters
narrative_blocks.body: For more than sixty years Jonathan wrote letters for New Mexico students bound for the military, diplomatic and intelligence services, many of them the first in their families to finish college.

narrative_blocks.header: An authority on Macau
narrative_blocks.body: Jonathan spoke Portuguese and was a noted authority on Macau, the subject of much of his four books and seventeen articles on China.

narrative_blocks.header: Out West like colts, 1946
narrative_blocks.body: The Porters drove west to Tesuque in July 1946. At the New Mexico line, his father wrote, the boys ran about "like colts first out to pasture"; Jonathan lived in Santa Fe country for the rest of his life.

career.role: Chair, History Department; President, Faculty Senate

narrative_blocks.body: Jane was Keeper of the Portsmouth Athenaeum from 1986 to 2000 and oversaw its purchase of the Peirce Building in 1995. The Athenaeum has her bronze bust, made by Sumner Winebaum in 2003.

narrative_blocks.body: Jane's Friendly Edifices: Piscataqua Lighthouses and Other Aids to Navigation came out in 2006. At St. Louis she had co-written a guide to the architecture of Compton Heights.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the West's great dam years
narrative_blocks.body: Michael was Commissioner of the Bureau of Reclamation from 1945 to 1953, its busiest years of dam building: Grand Coulee and Shasta were dedicated and Hungry Horse built while he held the post.

narrative_blocks.header: Harold Ickes's right hand
narrative_blocks.body: A Chicago newspaperman who became Washington bureau chief of the International News Service, Michael joined Harold Ickes at Interior in 1933 as aide and press man, and was First Assistant Secretary by 1943.

narrative_blocks.header: Housing Comes of Age, in 1938
narrative_blocks.body: In 1938, still Ickes's aide, Michael published Housing Comes of Age, an account of the Public Works Administration's housing program.

narrative_blocks.header: He dedicated the Adams Tunnel and Hungry Horse
narrative_blocks.body: As commissioner Michael stood with Oscar Chapman at the dedication of the Alva B. Adams Tunnel under the Continental Divide in Colorado, and toured the Hungry Horse Dam site in Montana while it rose. He left the bureau in 1953, soon after Eisenhower took office.

narrative_blocks.header: Brother-in-law to two Porters
narrative_blocks.body: Michael married Nancy Foster Porter in 1924, and through her was brother-in-law to the photographer Eliot Porter and the painter Fairfield Porter. He died at Washington in August 1970.

narrative_blocks.body: Edward was Class Orator of Yale's class of 1913, won the DeForest Prize medal and was elected to Phi Beta Kappa. He spent most of his working life selling investments in New York.

narrative_blocks.header: 6,600 hours in 86 aircraft
narrative_blocks.body: Ed enlisted in the Navy after Pearl Harbor and flew 6,600 hours in 86 aircraft, from Cubs to F-4Bs. He flew Demons with VF-124, directed the test pilot school at Patuxent River and commanded Attack Squadron 45.

narrative_blocks.header: His last command was on Kauai
narrative_blocks.body: Ed's last billet was command of the Pacific Missile Range Facility at Barking Sands on Kauai. He retired to Westlake Village in 1975 after thirty-two years in the Navy.

narrative_blocks.header: They met in the third grade
narrative_blocks.body: Ed met Barbara Hale in the third grade at Ware, and there was never anyone else for either of them. They married in April 1945 and were together until her death in 2007.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father brought back the bicycle
narrative_blocks.body: Geraldine's father, Leon Southmayd, ran the Cycle Trades of America and spent the 1920s and 1930s bringing cycling back into fashion, with bicycle trains and riding clothes designed for women. He died in 1937, when she was twenty.

narrative_blocks.body: Barbara was named the outstanding athlete of the Ware High School class of 1940, in basketball and tennis, and worked at the Ware Trust Company until she married Ed in 1945.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty years of Navy moves
narrative_blocks.body: Barbara followed Ed's Navy career to Florida, Michigan, Rhode Island, Virginia, California, Hawaii and Japan before they settled at Westlake Village in 1975.

narrative_blocks.header: From architecture to open textbooks
narrative_blocks.body: Domi practised and taught architecture and lighting design in New York for twenty years, then founded Open Assembly to bring free course materials to community colleges. She later ran academic technology at Columbia.

narrative_blocks.header: A Waterford family since 1904
narrative_blocks.body: Domi's family has lived in Waterford since 1904, and in 2024 she joined the board of the Waterford Land Trust, where she treats each preserve as a cultural landscape of the town's history.

narrative_blocks.header: The Long Telegram and the X article
narrative_blocks.body: From Moscow in February 1946 George sent the Long Telegram, and in 1947 he published The Sources of Soviet Conduct as "X"; together they gave America its policy of containing the Soviet Union.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped draft the Marshall Plan
narrative_blocks.body: As the State Department's first Director of Policy Planning under George Marshall, George played a central part in drafting the Marshall Plan that rebuilt Western Europe.

narrative_blocks.header: A letter from Roosevelt won the Azores
narrative_blocks.body: In charge at Lisbon in 1943, George went to President Roosevelt himself for a letter to Salazar, and won Portugal's consent to American forces in the Azores.

narrative_blocks.header: Ambassador at Moscow and Belgrade
narrative_blocks.body: Truman sent George to Moscow as ambassador in 1952, and Kennedy sent him to Belgrade in 1961, where he worked to keep Yugoslavia independent of the Soviet bloc.

narrative_blocks.header: Half a century at the Institute
narrative_blocks.body: George joined the Institute for Advanced Study at Princeton in 1956 and worked there until he died in 2005, at a hundred and one, writing the history of Russian-American relations.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Pulitzers and the Medal of Freedom
narrative_blocks.body: George won the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Award for Russia Leaves the War, a second Pulitzer for his Memoirs, 1925 to 1950, and the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1989.

narrative_blocks.header: His son married an Enders
narrative_blocks.body: In April 1982 George's son Christopher married Domitilla Enders, daughter of the diplomat Thomas O. Enders, at Niantic in Connecticut.

narrative_blocks.header: Easels side by side in Prospect Park
narrative_blocks.body: Jane and her husband, John Lloyd, began painting around 2006 and spent weekends at their easels in Prospect Park and on the Brooklyn Heights Promenade, painting streets, gardens and waterfront in oils. They married in 2010.

narrative_blocks.header: Manhattan as a still life
narrative_blocks.body: Jane painted for color and movement. In the Heights, she said, a canopy of trees made "an effect of soft lighting" on the earth colors of the buildings, and from a Promenade bench downtown Manhattan became a "still life" in shifting light.

narrative_blocks.header: A melon, a jar, a pot of marigolds
narrative_blocks.body: At a 2012 show with her husband at the TAI Group, Jane's still lifes stood out: a large melon and jar in a cool, limited palette, and marigolds on a windowsill with the city beyond. Her color owed most to Matisse and Jane Freilicher.

narrative_blocks.header: A textile designer by trade
narrative_blocks.body: Jane studied at the Rhode Island School of Design and works in textile design. Since 2016 she has tutored woven design, surface design and CAD software at the Fashion Institute of Technology in New York.

narrative_blocks.header: The Sparrow missile and China Lake
narrative_blocks.body: Tom, an electrical engineer, was credited with inventing the Sparrow missile and directed the Navy's weapons laboratory at China Lake before he went to the Air Force.

narrative_blocks.header: A washer the size of a silver dollar
narrative_blocks.body: Before a House subcommittee on Pentagon buying, Tom held up a flat washer that had cost nearly 350 times what it did once others could bid. A man who objected to such prices, he said, had been blackballed and now owned a lawn care service.

narrative_blocks.header: A briefing the military did not enjoy
narrative_blocks.body: Tom's unofficial briefing took military audiences through weapons innovations since the Civil War and had them vote on each. The pattern agitated them: most advances that mattered had been forced on the military from outside.

narrative_blocks.header: Some programs were too dumb to admit to
narrative_blocks.body: Tom worked beside A. Ernest Fitzgerald in the Air Force's financial management office until he retired in 1991. Some secret programs, he said, were just "something so dumb you don't want anyone to know about it."

narrative_blocks.header: The memo on the retiring colonel
narrative_blocks.body: In a 1983 memo Tom explained why officers in charge of buying rarely fought over cost: forced out at forty-three with a mortgage and children at college, an officer who made a fuss knew "no nice man will come to see him when he retires."

narrative_blocks.header: He grew up a congressman's son in Elkhorn
narrative_blocks.body: Tom was four when his mother, Marian, died in 1930, and the next year his father went to Congress. He grew up in Elkhorn with his father and his stepmother, Gehrta, and the family moved to Madison in 1942.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-three years at the mining journal
narrative_blocks.body: In 1867 Rossiter took over the American Journal of Mining, soon the Engineering and Mining Journal, and edited it for twenty-three years. He turned it against crooked mining companies, and it stood above every other paper in the trade.

narrative_blocks.header: The Grand Old Man of the Institute
narrative_blocks.body: Rossiter helped found the American Institute of Mining Engineers, was its president from 1872 to 1875 and its secretary from 1884 to 1911, and edited forty volumes of its Transactions. Members called him the Grand Old Man of the Institute.

narrative_blocks.header: He defined the lode for the Supreme Court
narrative_blocks.body: Rossiter's definitions of the lode and the law of the apex shaped mining lawsuits, and the Supreme Court heard him on mining law. In his late fifties he read law, was admitted to the bar in 1898, and taught mining law at Columbia.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight reports on the mining West
narrative_blocks.body: As US Commissioner of Mining Statistics from 1868 to 1875 Rossiter crossed the Far West and wrote eight reports to Congress on its mines. In 1871 his party of six became the first recorded visitors to what is now Yellowstone.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty years at Plymouth Church
narrative_blocks.body: Rossiter led the Sunday school at Henry Ward Beecher's Plymouth Church in Brooklyn for fifty years. His best-known lines, "death is only a horizon, and a horizon is nothing save the limit of our sight," adapt a prayer of William Penn's.

narrative_blocks.header: From Frémont's staff to the Rising Sun
narrative_blocks.body: Rossiter served as a captain on John C. Frémont's staff in the Valley of Virginia and was commended for gallant conduct. In 1911 Japan made him a Chevalier of the Order of the Rising Sun for years of help to its mining engineers.

narrative_blocks.header: A Sierra peak named for him
narrative_blocks.body: The Whitney Survey named Raymond Peak, 10,014 feet in the Sierra Nevada, for Rossiter in 1865. Raymond Lake, Raymond Canyon Creek and Raymond Meadows below it take their names from the peak.

narrative_blocks.body: Louisa marked a yarn's twist with a \ or a /, matching the slant of the thread, in her 1945 report on the Dura-Europos textiles, a series her brother Alfred helped edit. The notation became known as the slash system.

narrative_blocks.header: Eighteen years at the Textile Museum

narrative_blocks.header: His copper lamps sold around the world
narrative_blocks.body: Larry taught himself metalsmithing and founded the Washington Copper Works, where for more than forty years he and a few craftspeople made copper lamps and lanterns of his own design. They sold all over the world.

narrative_blocks.header: No novocaine, even for a root canal
narrative_blocks.body: Larry refused every anesthetic, even novocaine for a root canal, worried it might dull his readiness to stand up to bullies and tyrants. He tried to live by asking what a good person would do.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught himself everything

narrative_blocks.header: Marches, solar power and the voting machines
narrative_blocks.body: Larry helped organize Vietnam War and civil rights marches and brought speakers to Washington and the Gunnery. He gardened organically, tried solar power early, and for years assembled the town's lever voting machines.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty-six years in one house
narrative_blocks.body: Born in Paris, Larry came to the Gunnery as a teenager, met Liz there, and fell for a strange old house in Washington. He lived in it for sixty-six years and raised their four children there.

narrative_blocks.header: Her wagon journal of 1810
narrative_blocks.body: In 1810, at nineteen, Margaret rode by wagon from New Haven to her cousins at Warren, Ohio, and kept a journal of the trip for her cousin Elizabeth Woolsey. Yale published it in 1912 as A Journey to Ohio in 1810.

narrative_blocks.header: Raised by her grandmother Dwight
narrative_blocks.body: Margaret's father died when she was five, and her grandmother Mary Edwards Dwight took her in at Northampton and raised her as her own. When her grandmother died in 1807 she went to her aunt Elizabeth Woolsey's family in New Haven.

narrative_blocks.header: Married a year after she reached Ohio
narrative_blocks.body: Margaret married William Bell Jr., an Irish-born merchant, on 17 December 1811, a year after she reached Ohio, and they settled at Pittsburgh. She died there in October 1834, a month after her thirteenth child was born.

narrative_blocks.header: Sheets too dirty to sleep in
narrative_blocks.body: On the road west Margaret and her companions had to share one room with no curtain or screen, "and our sheets there were so dirty I felt afraid to sleep in them."

narrative_blocks.header: Her great-grandson was Winston Churchill
narrative_blocks.body: Through her daughter Margaret DeWitt Bell Blaine, Margaret was the great-grandmother of the American novelist Winston Churchill.

narrative_blocks.header: Books and flowers outside Brooklyn

narrative_blocks.header: He built St. Charles College
narrative_blocks.body: When his mother offered money for a Protestant school at St. Charles, George built the house himself in 1834 and made her gift its endowment. St. Charles College opened in 1835, and his will left it a further endowment the county matched.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother milked a hundred cows
narrative_blocks.body: George's widowed mother began with two milk cows and built a dairy of a hundred. In 1815 she brought her sons west to St. Charles, where they peddled goods on their backs before opening stores at St. Charles, Troy and St. Louis.

narrative_blocks.header: A wholesale grocer who became a banker
narrative_blocks.body: George was a large wholesale grocer at St. Louis and a wealthy banker there. His first wife, Frances Euphrasia Morrison, whom he married in 1826, left him five children; Sarah Ann Bell was his second.

narrative_blocks.header: Married by a judge, not a priest
narrative_blocks.body: George's first wife, Frances Morrison, was Catholic, but he refused a priest, and Judge Benjamin Emmons married them in 1826. When her mother wanted a second ceremony, George told her that if she wanted her daughter back she could take her.

narrative_blocks.header: Enslaved women sewed for the stores
narrative_blocks.body: George's mother kept enslaved women at St. Charles sewing coarse shirts for her sons' stores, and the 1850 census lists George himself as a slaveholder at St. Louis.

narrative_blocks.body: In March 1896 the family's summer house above Clear Lake burned, and their youngest, John Pierre, died in it at five. Mary built St. John's Episcopal Church at Lakeport in his memory.

narrative_blocks.header: He started the Bureau of Reclamation
narrative_blocks.body: As Secretary of the Interior under McKinley and Theodore Roosevelt from 1899 to 1907, Ethan set up the Reclamation Service in 1902, prosecuted western land frauds and reorganized Indian affairs.

narrative_blocks.header: The first American ambassador to Russia
narrative_blocks.body: McKinley sent Ethan to Russia as minister in 1897, and when the mission became an embassy in 1898 he was the first American ambassador accredited to the Tsar's court.

narrative_blocks.header: A fortune made in Hong Kong
narrative_blocks.body: Ethan ran the Hong Kong office of Olyphant & Co., became a partner in 1866 and retired in 1872 with a fortune. He married Margaret Dwight Collier at St. Louis in 1869, and their daughter Sarah was born at Hong Kong.

narrative_blocks.header: His fraud cases cost him friends
narrative_blocks.body: Ethan's charges of land fraud against Republican congressmen did not endear him to the party, and he was never one of Roosevelt's tennis cabinet. He resigned in March 1907.

narrative_blocks.header: Named for his great-grandfather Ethan Allen
narrative_blocks.body: Ethan was named for his great-grandfather Ethan Allen, the Revolutionary hero, and was a nephew of Major General Ethan Allen Hitchcock. His father sat on Alabama's Supreme Court.

narrative_blocks.header: Richard Carvel sold two million copies
narrative_blocks.body: Winston's Richard Carvel (1899) sold some two million copies in a nation of 76 million and made him rich. The Crisis, The Crossing, Coniston, Mr. Crewe's Career and The Inside of the Cup each topped the best-seller list.

narrative_blocks.header: The other Winston Churchill changed his name
narrative_blocks.body: In the 1890s the American Winston Churchill was the better known of the two. The young British Churchill wrote to him about the confusion and agreed to sign himself Winston Spencer Churchill, later Winston S. Churchill.

narrative_blocks.header: Woodrow Wilson summered in his house
narrative_blocks.body: In 1899 Winston built Harlakenden House at Cornish, New Hampshire, named for his wife Mabel, and from 1913 to 1915 leased it to Woodrow Wilson as a summer home. It burned in 1923.

narrative_blocks.header: The Progressive candidate for governor
narrative_blocks.body: Winston sat in the New Hampshire legislature in 1903 and 1905 and ran for governor as the Progressive candidate in 1912. In 1919 he stopped writing and withdrew from public life.

narrative_blocks.header: He started the Naval Academy crew
narrative_blocks.body: At the Naval Academy Winston organized the first eight-oared crew and captained it for two years. He graduated in 1894 and soon left the Navy to write.

narrative_blocks.header: A pedigree the Times took apart
narrative_blocks.body: In 1912 a published pedigree traced Winston back through Plymouth to the Dorset Churchills and the Duke of Marlborough's line. The genealogist Wharton Dickinson showed in the New York Times that the dates could not work.

narrative_blocks.header: Treasurer of the national suffrage association
narrative_blocks.body: Mabel was treasurer of the Cornish Equal Suffrage League and of the National American Woman Suffrage Association, vice-president of New Hampshire's, and in 1915 one of three finalists for the national presidency.

narrative_blocks.header: The railroad, the mills and the liquor men
narrative_blocks.body: Mabel blamed the railroad, the Amoskeag mills and the liquor interests for defeating woman suffrage in New Hampshire in 1912. She wanted bills against child labor in the mills and for a nine-hour day for women.

narrative_blocks.header: Maxfield Parrish's Cleopatra
narrative_blocks.body: Mabel's fortune let Winston write full time, and their Cornish house was named Harlakenden for her. She was Maxfield Parrish's model for his 1917 painting Cleopatra.

narrative_blocks.header: A mother and a suffragist too
narrative_blocks.body: Could a mother be a suffragist and still look after her children? "I think a woman can look out for her children a great deal better," Mabel told a reporter in 1912, "if she takes an interest in public affairs."

narrative_blocks.header: He desegregated the dormitories
narrative_blocks.body: Ethan became the first alumnus to serve as chancellor of Washington University in 1954 and soon desegregated its dormitories. By 1961 the streetcar college for local students had become a national university.

narrative_blocks.header: He stood by William Masters
narrative_blocks.body: In the McCarthy years Ethan defended the gynecologist William Masters and his research on sexual function, and in 1959 the American Association of University Professors gave him its Alexander Meiklejohn Award for Academic Freedom.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped write Missouri's constitution
narrative_blocks.body: As a delegate-at-large to the 1943-44 convention Ethan chaired its committee on taxation and helped write Missouri's present constitution. In 1964 he was the Republican candidate for governor and lost to Warren Hearnes.

narrative_blocks.header: The Second Century Campaign
narrative_blocks.body: Ethan's Second Century Campaign, begun in 1955, was the second largest of its day for an American university. It built Olin Library, Urbauer and Busch halls, Steinberg Hall and the South 40 dormitories.

narrative_blocks.body: Sophie helped lead the campaign to save Sheridan's old WYO movie theater from demolition and turn it into an arts center, then ran it as executive director for ten years. She won the Wyoming Governor's Arts Award.

narrative_blocks.header: Miss Adelaide and Dolly
narrative_blocks.body: Sophie once hoped to be the next Debbie Reynolds. In Sheridan she starred for the Carriage House Theater, happiest as Miss Adelaide in Guys and Dolls and as Dolly in Hello, Dolly!

narrative_blocks.header: She met Jack at Eatons Ranch
narrative_blocks.body: Sophie's family were regular guests at Eatons Ranch in Wyoming, where she met Jack Pelissier, a wrangler, in 1957. They married at St. Louis on 10 November 1962 and settled at Big Horn.

narrative_blocks.header: He turned a dude ranch into a community
narrative_blocks.body: Jack's proudest deal was turning the Fordyce family's TP Dude Ranch in the Big Horn Mountains into a homeowners' association in 1972. The TP Association still thrives.

narrative_blocks.header: An FBI childhood, then Eatons Ranch
narrative_blocks.body: Jack's father was an FBI field agent, and the family moved from city to city before settling near Sheridan in the early 1950s. Jack wrangled summers at Eatons Ranch, where he met Sophie Shepley in 1957.

narrative_blocks.header: Century 21 in Sheridan
narrative_blocks.body: Jack sold insurance and ranch real estate as a partner in Galey-Pelissier and then BHJ, and owned Century 21 BHJ Realty from 1995 to 2005. After he retired he still went to the office every day.

narrative_blocks.header: Really, really, really pretty
narrative_blocks.body: Jack first saw Sophie in the summer of 1957, a high school junior from St. Louis, while he was wrangling at Eatons' Ranch. "I thought she was really, really, really pretty," he said, and they had fifty years together.

narrative_blocks.header: A letter home from boarding school
narrative_blocks.body: In May 1967, at seventeen, Michael wrote home from his New England boarding school to tell his family he was gay. His father wrote back three days later affirming his love and support, though he worried for his son's happiness.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-five years of New York publicity
narrative_blocks.body: Michael spent forty-five years in New York in public relations, representing nearly every corner of entertainment, then retired home to St. Louis. He wrote a book about his life, and his papers are at the Missouri Historical Society.

narrative_blocks.header: "Think of me as Mike Shepley"
narrative_blocks.body: The letter is now in the Missouri History Museum's Gateway to Pride exhibition. "Please don't think of me as 'Homosexual'," it ends, "think of me as Mike Shepley."

narrative_blocks.body: At thirty-seven Lela was one of the youngest women senior vice presidents at her Wall Street bank. In 1990 she married Rob Gamble, her old summer-camp sweetheart, and moved to his Algonquin Park cabin with no road, water or power.

narrative_blocks.header: She co-founded a Montessori school
narrative_blocks.body: When their son Ethan neared school age, Lela and two other mothers opened Muskoka Montessori in Ontario. She was its principal for thirteen years.

narrative_blocks.header: Water for parched earth
narrative_blocks.body: Lela took up Nichiren Buddhism with the SGI in 1989 and has practised it ever since. A year after Rob died in 2017 she moved home to St. Louis, where she tells its story as "water on parched earth."

narrative_blocks.body: Virginia builds her abstractions slowly, from rhythmic, repeated marks in gouache, pencil and ink on watercolor paper, in earth and skin tones. She took her MFA in painting at John F. Kennedy University in 2001.

narrative_blocks.header: Painting from the unconscious
narrative_blocks.body: Virginia works from psychic automatism and Eastern philosophy, using line and biomorphic forms to explore unity and duality. She paints on a farm in North Carolina, and her work has been shown in California and North Carolina galleries.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote straight to the President
narrative_blocks.body: In 1901, with his superiors ignoring him, William wrote directly to Theodore Roosevelt that the Navy's gunnery was dangerously poor. Roosevelt made him Inspector of Target Practice, and his continuous-aim firing spread through the fleet.

narrative_blocks.header: He crossed to England as S. W. Davidson
narrative_blocks.body: In April 1917 William sailed for Liverpool under the name S. W. Davidson, sent to consult the British before America was at war. War was declared while he was at sea, and his ship struck a mine two days later.

narrative_blocks.header: Convoys cut the losses to under one percent
narrative_blocks.body: In London Admiral Jellicoe showed William how fast the U-boats were sinking shipping. His convoys, escorted by American destroyers out of Queenstown, cut losses from 20 percent to under one, and no American troopship was lost.

narrative_blocks.header: A Pulitzer Prize for an admiral
narrative_blocks.body: William's account of the naval war, The Victory at Sea, won the 1921 Pulitzer Prize for History. He may be the only career naval officer ever to win a Pulitzer.

narrative_blocks.header: First captain of the Nevada
narrative_blocks.body: William commanded the battleship Minnesota and the Atlantic destroyer flotilla, where he worked out new destroyer tactics. In 1916 he became the first captain of the Nevada, then the Navy's largest and most powerful battleship.

narrative_blocks.header: He refused the Distinguished Service Medal
narrative_blocks.body: After the war William publicly attacked the Navy Department's conduct of it, and he declined the Distinguished Service Medal because he objected to its going to undeserving officers. He served twice as president of the Naval War College.

narrative_blocks.header: Four ships carried his name
narrative_blocks.body: Two destroyers named Sims, the transport Admiral W. S. Sims and a frigate all bore his name. He married Anne Hitchcock, daughter of the Interior Secretary, in 1905, and they had five children.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote his father-in-law's biography
narrative_blocks.body: Elting married Admiral Sims's daughter Anne in 1935, and in 1942, months after Pearl Harbor, published Admiral Sims and the Modern American Navy. It became the standard biography and won the Dunning Prize.

narrative_blocks.header: They were holding the horses
narrative_blocks.body: Elting's best-known story is of an artillery crew in which two men stood rigidly at attention through every shot. An old colonel finally worked it out: they were holding the horses, long after the guns stopped needing any.

narrative_blocks.header: He edited Theodore Roosevelt's letters
narrative_blocks.body: From 1948 Elting directed the Theodore Roosevelt Research Project and edited the eight volumes of The Letters of Theodore Roosevelt, published from 1951 to 1954. His life of Henry L. Stimson won the Parkman Prize.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded MIT's STS program
narrative_blocks.body: Elting taught at MIT from 1946, left in 1966 to be master of Yale's Timothy Dwight College, and came back in 1972 to plan the program that became Science, Technology and Society.

narrative_blocks.header: Great-nephew of a bridge builder
narrative_blocks.body: Elting was a great-nephew of the bridge engineer George S. Morison, who argued for the Panama route for the canal, and spent much of his boyhood in the house his great-uncle built facing Mount Monadnock.

narrative_blocks.body: During and after the Second World War William worked in the political intelligence and historical sections of the US Naval Headquarters in London, where his father had commanded in the First.

narrative_blocks.header: Argentina for the CIA
narrative_blocks.body: William joined the Central Intelligence Agency in 1949, served in Argentina until 1952 and then at headquarters until he retired in 1972.

narrative_blocks.header: A wit and a chess player
narrative_blocks.body: William played at the Arlington Chess Club and was known at Wake Robin as a wit and a strong player. In 1996 he was to be honored as a founder of the Ethan Allen Homestead.

narrative_blocks.header: Diabetes research at the University of Vermont
narrative_blocks.body: Ethan taught at the University of Vermont College of Medicine, researching metabolism and diabetes, and lived in South Burlington from 1950 to 1993. In 1990 UVM gave him and Dorothea honorary doctorates for their diabetes work.

narrative_blocks.header: He inherited Ethan Allen's 1784 book
narrative_blocks.body: Ethan inherited an original 1784 copy of Ethan Allen's Reason the Only Oracle of Man, printed at Bennington. His grandfather Ethan Allen Hitchcock wrote in it, "This is a work of my grandfather"; Allen was really his great-grandfather.

narrative_blocks.header: He read Ethan Allen beside Einstein
narrative_blocks.body: Ethan, a scientist and a Unitarian, read it for Allen's astronomy. "It's interesting to see how he jibes with Einstein and Schweitzer," he said in 2000. "He was really a transcendentalist."

narrative_blocks.header: Embezzlers, thieves and Republicans
narrative_blocks.body: Ethan reckoned the most of his DNA that could have come from Allen, his great-great-great-grandfather, was a thirty-second, and that a family tree read upside down "must hold a lot of ancestors who were embezzlers, thieves and Republicans."

narrative_blocks.header: Born when the Admiral was fifty-seven
narrative_blocks.body: Ethan was born at Newport in April 1916, the last of five children, when his father was fifty-seven and his mother forty-one. His father died in 1936 while Ethan was in college, and he married Dorothea Merriman as a medical student in 1939.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty years living with diabetes
narrative_blocks.body: Dorothea lived with diabetes for fifty years and made it her work. As a Radcliffe Bunting Fellow in 1974–75 she began her pioneering work in diabetes patient education, and she helped draw up the national standards for such programmes.

narrative_blocks.header: She spoke on diabetes in twenty-two states
narrative_blocks.body: Dorothea helped found the Vermont chapter of the American Diabetes Association, sat on its national board and the NIH's National Diabetes Advisory Board, and spoke on living with diabetes in twenty-two states.

narrative_blocks.header: A founder of the Vermont Youth Orchestra
narrative_blocks.body: In 1957 Dorothea was a founder of the Friends of Music for Youth and the Vermont Youth Orchestra, and late in life she worked to endow its Elley Long Music Center. Memorial gifts at her death went to the orchestra.

narrative_blocks.header: She taught fine arts in Florence
narrative_blocks.body: After Radcliffe, Dorothea taught fine arts in Florence in 1938–39, and in 1939 married Ethan Sims, then a medical student. They were married sixty-one years.

narrative_blocks.header: Honorary doctorates for husband and wife
narrative_blocks.body: The University of Vermont gave Dorothea and Ethan honorary doctorates of science together in 1990 for their work as teachers, caregivers and authors on diabetes. The American Diabetes Association gave her its Charles Best Medal in 1985.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father held Harvard's Gurney chair
narrative_blocks.body: Dorothea was the daughter of Roger B. Merriman, Gurney Professor of History at Harvard, and grew up in Cambridge.

narrative_blocks.header: Two prizes for safer medical devices
narrative_blocks.body: Nat won the Laufman-Greatbatch Prize of the Association for the Advancement of Medical Instrumentation in 2006 for the smart pump, and MGH's Nathaniel Bowditch Prize in 2017. He holds the Newbower/Eitan Endowed Chair at MGH.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped found pediatric endocrinology
narrative_blocks.body: Allan worked out much of what is known of acid-base balance, fluid and electrolyte metabolism and intravenous therapy in children, and he and his students, searching for the body's metabolic controls, helped found pediatric endocrinology.

narrative_blocks.header: He worked out the lifeboat ration
narrative_blocks.body: In his life raft studies during the Second World War, Allan showed that carbohydrate prevents ketosis and limits fluid loss in castaways, and so gave lifeboat rations an objective basis.

narrative_blocks.header: One of the first health maintenance plans
narrative_blocks.body: Allan was chief of pediatrics at Massachusetts General and professor of pediatrics at Harvard Medical School, and helped organize White Cross, one of the first health maintenance organizations in the country.

narrative_blocks.header: The AMA questioned his patriotism
narrative_blocks.body: Allan wanted group practice paid by capitation, not fee for service, and it set him against the American Medical Association. His patriotism was questioned and Harvard and the MGH were pressed to fire him; both kept him.

narrative_blocks.header: The Howland Award, 1969
narrative_blocks.body: The American Pediatric Society gave Allan the Howland Award in 1969, the highest honour in academic pediatrics.

narrative_blocks.body: Susan's mother was a pilot and one of the Ninety-Nines, and Earhart was her childhood hero. She spent years on East to the Dawn, much of it in Earhart's papers at the Schlesinger Library, and went to Trepassey and Harbour Grace.

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband named the book
narrative_blocks.body: Susan meant to call it Amelia Earhart, An Extraordinary Woman; her husband Allan suggested East to the Dawn, since Earhart's great flights, and her last, all flew into the sunrise.

narrative_blocks.header: Roosevelt and Stalin, and Yalta
narrative_blocks.body: Susan edited the complete Roosevelt–Stalin correspondence in 2006 and wrote Roosevelt and Stalin: Portrait of a Partnership in 2015. She went to Yalta for the conference's seventy-fifth anniversary.

narrative_blocks.header: Her Earhart book became a film
narrative_blocks.body: East to the Dawn was one of two books behind the 2009 film Amelia, with Hilary Swank as Earhart, and the director Mira Nair asked Susan to check the script for accuracy.

narrative_blocks.header: "The only one which re-creates" her
narrative_blocks.body: Gore Vidal, whose father had loved Earhart, said Susan's was the only book of the dozen he had read that re-created "that singular woman."

narrative_blocks.header: He let The Masses go through the mail
narrative_blocks.body: In 1917 Learned ruled that the Post Office could not bar The Masses under the Espionage Act unless its words urged readers to break the law. He was overturned, but in 1969 the Supreme Court in effect made his test law.

narrative_blocks.header: The most quoted judge below the Supreme Court
narrative_blocks.body: Learned sat on the federal bench for fifty-two years, and led the Second Circuit from 1939 to 1951, when it was reckoned one of the finest appeals courts in the country's history. No lower-court judge has been quoted more.

narrative_blocks.header: Twice passed over for the Supreme Court
narrative_blocks.body: Holmes wanted Learned on the Supreme Court by 1923 and Frankfurter lobbied hard for him, but Hoover passed him over in 1930 and Roosevelt in 1942. "It was the importance, the power, the trappings," he said later, "that really drew me on."

narrative_blocks.header: His daughters posed for Maxfield Parrish
narrative_blocks.body: From 1910 the Hands summered at Cornish, New Hampshire, and in 1919 bought a house there they called Low Court. Maxfield Parrish lived in nearby Plainfield, and the Hand girls posed for some of his paintings.

narrative_blocks.header: "I was never any good as a lawyer"
narrative_blocks.body: Learned admitted he had no success at all in practice, in Albany or on Wall Street, and at thirty-five set out to become a judge instead. Taft appointed him in 1909, at thirty-seven, one of the youngest federal judges ever named.

narrative_blocks.header: Named for two Billings Peck Learneds
narrative_blocks.body: His mother's family, the Learneds, used surnames as given names, and Learned was named for her father and her brother, both Billings Peck Learned. He dropped Billings as pompous in 1899 and went by B.

narrative_blocks.header: The spirit of liberty
narrative_blocks.body: In Central Park in May 1944, before new citizens and a vast crowd, Learned said: "The spirit of liberty is the spirit which is not too sure that it is right." The speech made a folk hero of him.

narrative_blocks.header: His father jumped from the Kenilworth Inn
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph's father, a Pittsburgh lawyer and state senator, built the Kenilworth Inn at Asheville in 1889 beside Vanderbilt's rising Biltmore. When it burned in 1909 he escaped by jumping from a third-floor window.

narrative_blocks.header: A coal town named Gazzam
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph's father was an incorporator of the Beech Creek Railroad, William H. Vanderbilt's line carrying Clearfield coal into the New York Central, and the company town at its terminus was named Gazzam.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother worked for suffrage war relief
narrative_blocks.body: Joseph's mother, Nellie Mae Reed Andrews Gazzam, married his father in 1893, two years before Joseph was born. She was active in the temperance movement and became a leader of suffrage war relief work.

narrative_blocks.header: Two years at the Pasteur Institute
narrative_blocks.body: After training in immunology, Phil worked two years at the Pasteur Institute in Paris, and he and Betsy toured France in a dilapidated Citroën convertible. Then came decades of laboratory research at the NIH.

narrative_blocks.header: From the laboratory to psychiatry
narrative_blocks.body: Phil did research at the NIH, the Centers for Disease Control and Brown, then took a second residency, in psychiatry, at Brown and spent the rest of his career seeing patients at Providence clinics.

narrative_blocks.header: A sailboat before a house
narrative_blocks.body: Phil and Betsy liked to say they owned a sailboat before they ever thought of buying a house. They sailed the Chesapeake and the New England coast, and spent summers at Kennebunk, where his family had deep roots.

narrative_blocks.header: He painted the sea
narrative_blocks.body: Phil painted all his adult life, the sea above all, and tried ceramics and printmaking too. At the Providence Art Club he was known for taking several classes at once.

narrative_blocks.body: Larry went from Bowdoin and a Cornell MBA to Paine Webber, managed Hornblower and Weeks at Springfield from 1964, and ended working with his son J at Dwight Investment Counsel. He loved history and economic cycles.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-five years on Kennebunk's budget committee
narrative_blocks.body: Larry was a Longmeadow selectman in the 1970s, then sat thirty-five years on Kennebunk's Town Budget Committee and eight on the Finance Authority of Maine, and was vice chairman of the Maine Municipal Bond Bank.

narrative_blocks.header: Outdoor hockey and the Meddiebempsters
narrative_blocks.body: At Bowdoin Larry played defense, outdoors, on the first team to win the small New England college hockey championship, and sang with the Meddiebempsters. On a Glee Club visit to Pine Manor he met Rae on a blind date.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept a record of coastal storms
narrative_blocks.body: Larry photographed the storms that came ashore at Kennebunk and kept journals of them, and was known in town as a local expert on the coast's weather.

narrative_blocks.header: His first hole in one, in 2016
narrative_blocks.body: In 2016, soon after Rae died, Larry made his first hole in one, at Dunegrass in Scarborough. His only regret was that he could not tell her when he got home.

narrative_blocks.header: The first pediatric endocrine clinic, 1935
narrative_blocks.body: In 1935 Lawson opened the world's first pediatric endocrine clinic, at the Harriet Lane Home in Baltimore. In 1946 he gave up twenty-five years of private practice to do nothing but research and teach the subject.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the field's standard text
narrative_blocks.body: Lawson's Diagnosis and Treatment of Endocrine Disorders in Childhood and Adolescence became the authoritative text worldwide, and his 1940–41 studies of cholesterol in hypothyroid children are still counted classic.

narrative_blocks.header: Surgery for intersex newborns
narrative_blocks.body: With John Money, Lawson pioneered surgery on newborns with visibly intersex anatomy. At the time, intersex anatomy was understood almost entirely as a birth defect rather than as a natural variation.

narrative_blocks.header: His trainees named their society for him
narrative_blocks.body: In 1972 the doctors Lawson had trained founded the Lawson Wilkins Pediatric Endocrine Society. It kept his name until 2010, its annual Lawson Wilkins Lecture still does, and Johns Hopkins has a chair in his honor.

narrative_blocks.header: A Baltimore doctor's son, and a soldier
narrative_blocks.body: Lawson's father George was a Baltimore physician. Lawson took his Hopkins medical degree in 1918, served in the First World War, trained in pediatrics at Yale, and came home to practise in the city he was born in.

narrative_blocks.header: He founded the Bank of the Ohio Valley
narrative_blocks.body: W.W. founded the Bank of the Ohio Valley, a forerunner of Fifth Third Bank, and was president of the Cincinnati Gas, Light and Coke Company. At his death he was among the wealthiest men in Cincinnati.

narrative_blocks.header: Six years at Mazatlán
narrative_blocks.body: Before Cincinnati, W.W. spent six years trading at Mazatlán, on Mexico's Pacific coast, from 1837 to 1843. The next spring he married Sarah Van Beuren at Zanesville, and by 1846 he was a Cincinnati merchant.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten children at Woodburn
narrative_blocks.body: W.W. and Sarah had ten children between 1845 and 1865 at Woodburn, their place outside Cincinnati. Three died as small children, and Robert eight weeks after his wedding.

narrative_blocks.body: William clerked for federal judge Martin Pence in 1969 and practised law at Hilo until 1982, when he was appointed a District and Family Court judge there. He sat twenty-five years across the Island of Hawaii.

narrative_blocks.header: The Hawaiian hawk, photo book of the year
narrative_blocks.body: William's 2015 book ‘Io Lani: The Hawaiian Hawk was named photo book of the year by the Hawaii Book Publishers Association. Three of his standing-stone images hung in the 2007 Artists of Hawaii show.

narrative_blocks.header: Sent home from the 1968 draft
narrative_blocks.body: At the San Francisco induction center in 1968 an Army medic looked at William's freshly repaired forearm and sent him home. He later made a poem of that morning, Inductees.

narrative_blocks.header: Basho, Frost, and the right word

narrative_blocks.header: Bird catchers, and a princess
narrative_blocks.body: William's mother's forebears were kia manu, Native Hawaiian bird catchers and feather workers on the Hamakua coast, and his great-grandmother's sister was Princess Ka‘iulani, heir to the throne in 1893.

narrative_blocks.header: The judge who said I hear you
narrative_blocks.body: When William retired from the Hilo courtroom, the clerk who introduced him at his luncheon called him “the judge who said I hear you.”

narrative_blocks.header: A Dartmouth history he never saw printed
narrative_blocks.body: Frederick gathered the papers of Dartmouth's founding and first forty years for a history of the college and Hanover. He died in 1890; his brother-in-law John King Lord saw it into print in 1891, and the college reprinted it in 1928.

narrative_blocks.header: Dartmouth's treasurer and the county judge
narrative_blocks.body: Frederick came home to Hanover in 1874 and was elected treasurer of Dartmouth College. In 1876 he was made probate judge for Grafton County as well, and he held both posts until he died in 1890, at forty-nine.

narrative_blocks.header: A Treasury clerk through the Civil War
narrative_blocks.body: Frederick taught chemistry briefly at Dartmouth and school at Chattanooga, then read law in Hanover. In 1861 he went to the Treasury in Washington, moved to the Secretary's office in 1864, and took his law degree there in 1867.

narrative_blocks.header: Auditor of the ground he lies in
narrative_blocks.body: The Dartmouth Cemetery Association held its annual meetings in Frederick's Hanover law office in the 1880s. He was its auditor, and with the treasurer was charged with investing its permanent fund. He was buried there in 1890.

narrative_blocks.header: Johnnie K., the Latin teacher
narrative_blocks.body: Generations of Dartmouth men knew John as Johnnie K. He taught Latin there from 1869 to 1916, as Daniel Webster Professor from 1892, tolerated no idleness, and showed many a student that the old writers had grandeur after all.

narrative_blocks.header: Acting president, and nearly president
narrative_blocks.body: John was acting president of Dartmouth in the troubled year between Presidents Bartlett and Tucker, 1892 to 1893, then presided over the faculty until 1909, when he came close to being elected president himself.

narrative_blocks.header: He finished his brother-in-law's history
narrative_blocks.body: When Frederick Chase died in 1890, John took over his papers and saw Chase's Dartmouth history into print in 1891. His own second volume, covering 1815 to 1909, came out in 1913, and a history of the town of Hanover followed.

narrative_blocks.header: Foster father to the Chase children
narrative_blocks.body: When his brother-in-law Frederick Chase died in 1890, John took a father's place with Frederick's five children. It was John who told his nephew Stephen, a world-record hurdler, to skip the 1896 Olympics and finish college.

narrative_blocks.header: The hospital, the schools, and Lord Hall
narrative_blocks.body: John chaired the trustees of the Mary Hitchcock Memorial Hospital and wrote its first twenty-five years, sat on Hanover's school board, and from 1917 was a life trustee of Dartmouth. The college named Lord Hall for him in 1929.

narrative_blocks.header: His last afternoon on a mountain brook
narrative_blocks.body: John loved above all to fish mountain streams. In June 1926, days after his last Commencement, he spent the afternoon on a brook in the Sandwich range, came home to Wonalancet exhausted, and died, at seventy-seven.

narrative_blocks.header: A Vermont boyhood, then the president's house
narrative_blocks.body: John's father, a Cincinnati minister, died of cholera when John was eight months old, and he grew up at his mother's family home in Hardwick, Vermont. At Dartmouth from 1864 he lived much in his grandfather President Nathan Lord's house.

narrative_blocks.header: Hurdler Steve, after a fall
narrative_blocks.body: Stephen went at his first hurdle in the Dartmouth gym, hit it and fell headlong, and was joshed as Hurdler Steve, so he swore to be one. Running for the New York Athletic Club in 1894, he won the national title in a world-record 15.6.

narrative_blocks.header: He talked the starter out of a penalty
narrative_blocks.body: When England's Godfrey Shaw broke twice at the start of their heralded 1895 race, Stephen persuaded the starter to reset Shaw on the line rather than set him back six feet. He won in 15.4 seconds, then beat Shaw again the next week.

narrative_blocks.header: His uncle kept him home from Athens
narrative_blocks.body: Stephen was nominated for the American hurdles team at the 1896 Olympics, but it sailed before his commencement, and his uncle John King Lord insisted the diploma came first. He stayed, and sometimes regretted it.

narrative_blocks.header: Four decades of citrus at Dunedin
narrative_blocks.body: From 1922 until a few years before he died, Stephen ran a large citrus grove at Dunedin, Florida, and was president of the Pinellas growers' cooperative. At Danville, Vermont, he bred prize gladiolus, a grand champion among them.

narrative_blocks.header: Knox football, leather, and the wartime meat count
narrative_blocks.body: Stephen coached Knox College football for a season, 2–6–1, ran the Passumpsic Fiber Leather Company in Vermont from 1897, added the Hanover experiment farm in 1907, and in 1917 headed livestock statistics for the Food Administration.

narrative_blocks.header: Dartmouth's oldest alumnus at ninety-four
narrative_blocks.body: Stephen was Dartmouth's oldest living alumnus when he died in 1968, the son of its treasurer and grandson of its mathematics professor. His grandson Fred, class of 1953, was the fifth straight generation to graduate there.

narrative_blocks.header: The captain who made athletics respectable
narrative_blocks.body: As captain, Stephen brought in Elmer Carleton as trainer and helped build the hurdles for Dartmouth's new field in 1896. Years later a professor said, “It was Steve Chase who made athletics respectable at Dartmouth.”

narrative_blocks.body: Maxey reported for the Norristown Times Herald, the Inquirer and the Evening Ledger. In the war he did public relations for Curtiss-Wright in Alaska, then spent its last two years as the War Production Board's information director.

narrative_blocks.header: The Appalachian Trail, after retirement
narrative_blocks.body: Retired, Maxey joined the Philadelphia Trail Club and walked the Appalachian Trail from North Carolina to Maine, then led the club's walking trips to England, Wales, Scotland, Austria, Switzerland, Denmark, Norway and the Caribbean.

narrative_blocks.header: Scholar-athlete at Lawrenceville and Princeton
narrative_blocks.body: Maxey won Lawrenceville's 1925 prize for the best scholar among its all-round athletes, then played varsity football at Princeton, was treasurer of Tower Club, and graduated Phi Beta Kappa in 1929.

narrative_blocks.header: Maple Run, given to Stowe for good
narrative_blocks.body: Fred retired to Stowe, Vermont, in 1996 to be near his sons. He bought a mountain tract there called Maple Run and handed it to the Stowe Land Trust to hold in perpetuity.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-seven years of Florida family law
narrative_blocks.body: After Dartmouth in 1953 Fred served as a Marine Corps first lieutenant, then spent a summer sponge diving at Tarpon Springs with his brother John. He took his law degree at Florida and practised family law at New Port Richey until 1996.

narrative_blocks.header: An energy audit for every church
narrative_blocks.body: In 2010 Fred brought the Rev. Canon Sally Bingham to keynote his diocese's Episcopal convention, which resolved that every church have an energy audit within two years. In 2011 he brought Dartmouth's Big Green Bus to his Lake Forest church.

narrative_blocks.body: Fred was born at Hanover in March 1931 and named class baby of his father's Dartmouth class of 1930, and of Smith's class of 1930 too. At eight he left Jackson Heights for Dunedin, Florida, to live with his father and grandfather Stephen.

narrative_blocks.header: A cleaner for biopsy forceps
narrative_blocks.body: John spent most of his career at Honeywell building guidance systems for aerospace, but was proudest of what he did after retiring: he invented a device to clean biopsy forceps, cutting waste while keeping surgical hygiene.

narrative_blocks.header: 188 letters to the editor on drug laws
narrative_blocks.body: In retirement John campaigned to decriminalize drug use, which he saw as a cause of unjust and racially unequal imprisonment. 188 of his letters to the editor ran in newspapers, and he went to public hearings.

narrative_blocks.header: Florida's first catamaran, out of Popular Science
narrative_blocks.body: As a boy John built three sailboats and a rowboat. One, a catamaran designed from a Popular Science article, is believed to be the first of its kind in Florida. Later he built solar water heaters for the Florida sun.

narrative_blocks.header: Raised by an uncle, then a grandfather
narrative_blocks.body: At eight months John was sent to live with his uncle Stephen Chase Jr., who adopted him, and at twelve he went to his grandfather Stephen on the Dunedin waterfront. He lived the rest of his life in Pinellas County.

narrative_blocks.body: Stephen's lifelong subject was the Galois theory of rings and fields, with a Hopf algebra, group scheme or groupoid in the classical group's place. His 1965 memoir with Harrison and Rosenberg set out the theory for commutative rings.

narrative_blocks.header: Hopf algebras meet Galois, 1969
