narrative_blocks.header: He patented a working human jaw
narrative_blocks.body: Frederic taught anatomy at the Dartmouth Medical School from 1911 to 1947, to some six hundred students. He studied the jaw joint and chewing, built models that moved like the real thing, and patented one of the human jaw.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven years a doctor at Iowa City
narrative_blocks.body: After his Dartmouth M.D. in 1903 Frederic practised general medicine at Iowa City, assisting in surgery and anesthesia at the state university and teaching anatomy there until 1911.

narrative_blocks.header: The YMCA's medical chief in Paris
narrative_blocks.body: In 1918 and 1919 Frederic went to France as a civilian with the American Expeditionary Force, directing the medical department of the YMCA in Paris.

narrative_blocks.header: Hanover's first school nurse
narrative_blocks.body: Frederic sat on Hanover's school board from 1920 to 1927, served as school physician, and in 1928 founded the town schools' first school-nurse program. He was a trustee of the Howe Library for thirty-five years.

narrative_blocks.header: Dartmouth's Lords, nearly unbroken since 1821
narrative_blocks.body: With Frederic on the medical faculty, a Lord served Dartmouth almost without a break from 1821, when his great-grandfather Nathan Lord became a trustee. His son Frederic Mather Lord graduated in 1936.

narrative_blocks.header: Every Smith student on campus
narrative_blocks.body: As Smith's warden from 1922 to 1944, Laura made every student live on campus, having missed dormitory life herself as an undergraduate. In 1936 Smith named a new dormitory the Laura Scales House; Gloria Steinem later lived there.

narrative_blocks.header: Dartmouth's third woman doctor of letters
narrative_blocks.body: Smith gave Laura an honorary doctorate in 1931, and in 1939 she became only the third woman to receive an honorary Dartmouth doctorate. Her 1922 book Boys of the Ages came out from Ginn & Company, where her brother Arthur worked.

narrative_blocks.header: Boston's art museum, then Carnegie Tech
narrative_blocks.body: Widowed after four years of marriage, Laura joined the educational staff of Boston's Museum of Fine Arts in 1913, became a museum instructor, and left in 1920 to be dean of women at the Carnegie Institute of Technology.

narrative_blocks.header: Her Chase cousins stood up at her wedding
narrative_blocks.body: Laura married Robert Leighton Scales in the Dartmouth College Church in October 1908. Her cousin Mary Chase Lane was matron of honor, and her cousin Frederick Chase and Ernest M. Hopkins, later Dartmouth's president, were ushers.

narrative_blocks.header: A hundred and ten years of reading
narrative_blocks.body: Laura lived 110 years and 211 days, one of the oldest people in the world when she died at Northampton in 1990, and read almost to the end. Education, she said, was “the backbone of living. It makes the world interesting.”

narrative_blocks.header: The father of modern testing
narrative_blocks.body: Fred's 1951 Princeton dissertation began item response theory, which rates each test question by its difficulty. His methods at Educational Testing Service came to shape how the SAT, GRE, GMAT, LSAT and TOEFL are scored.

narrative_blocks.header: Lord's paradox
narrative_blocks.body: In a two-page note of 1967 Fred showed two correct analyses of the same dining-hall weight data reaching opposite answers about the diet. Lord's paradox is still argued over in statistics and causal inference.

narrative_blocks.header: Adaptive testing, before the computers
narrative_blocks.body: In three papers of 1971 Fred worked out how a test could choose each next question to fit the person taking it, harder after a right answer and easier after a wrong one, a decade before computers could deliver it.

narrative_blocks.header: A basement explosion, then a try at novels
narrative_blocks.body: As a boy Fred set off an explosion in the family basement with a chemistry experiment. After Dartmouth he drifted to the Midwest to try writing novels, until the University of Minnesota turned him to test theory.

narrative_blocks.header: A Life Master at the bridge table
narrative_blocks.body: Fred reached Life Master in contract bridge and grew orchids. In 1985 a bus struck the car he was riding in South Africa, and he came out of a coma after twenty-one days. He died at Naples in 2000.

narrative_blocks.header: He died carrying the colors at Chantilly
narrative_blocks.body: At Chantilly in September 1862, after five color bearers of his old 79th New York had fallen, Isaac seized the flag and was shot dead leading the charge. Lincoln, who was weighing him for command, had him made major general after his death.

narrative_blocks.header: Washington Territory's first governor
narrative_blocks.body: Appointed by President Pierce in 1853, Isaac governed the new territory until 1857, pressing its tribes into the treaties of Medicine Creek, Point Elliott and others, then served four years as its delegate to Congress.

narrative_blocks.header: He pardoned himself for contempt
narrative_blocks.body: In the Yakama War of 1856 Isaac declared martial law to try settlers he suspected of aiding the tribes. When Judge Edward Lander resisted, Isaac had him arrested, was convicted of contempt, and pardoned himself.

narrative_blocks.header: Surveying a railroad route to Puget Sound
narrative_blocks.body: On his way west in 1853 Isaac led the northernmost Pacific Railroad survey, from St. Paul to Puget Sound, with George McClellan as his second-in-command. Congress published his report in two volumes.

narrative_blocks.header: First in his West Point class
narrative_blocks.body: Isaac stood five foot three and graduated first in West Point's class of 1839. He was breveted twice for gallantry in the Mexican War, at Churubusco and Chapultepec, and badly wounded in the fighting for Mexico City.

narrative_blocks.header: A county, a lake and two forts
narrative_blocks.body: Stevens County and Lake Stevens in Washington, Stevensville in Montana and Army forts in Oregon and Washington, D.C., carry his name. Historians still divide over him; in 1962 he entered the Hall of Great Westerners.

narrative_blocks.header: His son climbed Mount Rainier first
narrative_blocks.body: His son Hazard, wounded beside him at Chantilly, won the Medal of Honor and made the first documented ascent of Mount Rainier. His daughter Kate christened Lake Washington's first floating bridge in 1940.

narrative_blocks.header: Geneticists on a Berkshire dairy farm
narrative_blocks.body: In 1910 Ezra and Alta bought 1,400 acres near Williamstown, Massachusetts, and Ezra made Mount Hope Farm one of the outstanding experimental farms in the country, with geneticists on staff breeding better dairy cattle and poultry. Massachusetts gave the farm a gold medal for agricultural research in 1924.

narrative_blocks.header: From the Commerce Clause to Hunger and History
narrative_blocks.body: Ezra wrote first as a lawyer, The Commerce Clause of the Federal Constitution in 1897 and Federal Power over Carriers and Corporations in 1910, then as a farmer: Breeding Profitable Dairy Cattle, Farming for Famine, and Hunger and History in 1939.

narrative_blocks.header: Counsel to Illinois Steel
narrative_blocks.body: After Amherst in 1885 and the Harvard Law School, Ezra was admitted to the Illinois bar in 1886 and became general counsel to the Illinois Steel Company and the Lake Shore and Erie Railroad. From 1900 to 1924 he practised in New York with Murray, Prentice and Aldrich.

narrative_blocks.header: Decorated by Italy and Bulgaria
narrative_blocks.body: Italy made Ezra a Commander of the Order of the Crown in 1924, and Bulgaria gave him its Order of Civil Merit, both for his work in international agriculture.

narrative_blocks.header: Job Swift's clock at Mount Hope
narrative_blocks.body: At Mount Hope Ezra kept the tall clock that had belonged to his great-great-grandparents, Rev. Job Swift and Mary Ann Sedgwick.

narrative_blocks.header: A Chicago lawyer who married a Rockefeller
narrative_blocks.body: Ezra, a Chicago lawyer, married Alta Rockefeller, John D. Rockefeller's daughter, on 17 January 1901. Her father gave them a house at 5 West 53rd Street as a wedding present.

narrative_blocks.body: Pierrepont went from Amherst to the Chicago Medical College, then took the post of surgeon at the hospital of the Minnesota iron mines at Soudan, meaning to follow it with a year of study in Europe. He died of typhoid fever there on 4 January 1890, at twenty-four.

narrative_blocks.header: The Nyack Plan went nationwide
narrative_blocks.body: Sartell started the Nyack Plan, a nonsectarian back-to-church movement holding that a church deserved the same community support as any lay organization. Hundreds of towns as far west as California copied it, Julius Rosenwald sat on its national board, and his own church gained 171 members. In Nyack he also founded the Good Government Club, which drew in most of the leading citizens of Rockland County.

narrative_blocks.header: Four days short of his cathedral book
narrative_blocks.body: A tourist near the towers of Amiens asked Sartell whether there was anything to see inside, and he spent his last eleven years answering in The Heritage of the Cathedral, published in 1936, and The Voices of the Cathedral, on their glass and carving. A fluent linguist, he knew nearly every great church from Arabia to Scotland at first hand. He died of a heart attack in his New York library in October 1937 while revising the second, telling his family he needed four more days.

narrative_blocks.header: Britain asked for him; Washington said no
narrative_blocks.body: Sartell spoke for the National Security League and the Red Cross in 1917, and was one of five speakers the British government asked for to lift British morale, then one of eleven with ex-President William H. Taft. The American government refused to let either commission sail.

narrative_blocks.header: A folding organ, carried ward to ward
narrative_blocks.body: In June 1918 Sartell went to France as a Red Cross chaplain, at Base Hospital 101 in St. Nazaire and then Evacuation Hospital 13, behind the lines in the Meuse-Argonne. His Nyack congregation sent a collapsible organ, which he carried from ward to ward, and two communion sets.

narrative_blocks.header: France's influenza cost him his pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: Sartell caught an undiagnosed influenza in France and was invalided home in January 1919. It dogged him the rest of his life and made him resign in 1923, closing nineteen years at Nyack, the longest pastorate in the church's history, in which the congregation paid off its new brick church.

narrative_blocks.header: Married on his twenty-ninth birthday
narrative_blocks.body: Sartell married Lydia Beekman Vanderpoel of Kinderhook on 30 September 1896, his twenty-ninth birthday, and they kept their fortieth anniversary the year before he died.

narrative_blocks.header: “Why not?” in Ward 19A
narrative_blocks.body: A soldier in Ward 19A asked him, “I don't suppose it would be possible for me to have communion would it, Padre?” Sartell answered, “Why not?” and told the story in Padre: A Red Cross Chaplain in France.

narrative_blocks.header: Cleveland's Little Italy took her name
narrative_blocks.body: Around 1900 Alta founded Alta House, a settlement house in Cleveland's Little Italy that still carries her name. Settlement houses, hospitals and museums shared in her money for the rest of her life.

narrative_blocks.header: Married on her parents' staircase
narrative_blocks.body: Alta married Ezra Parmalee Prentice on 17 January 1901 on the staircase landing of her parents' house at 4 West 54th Street. A church wedding had been planned, but her nephew John Rockefeller McCormick had just died of scarlet fever.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventy-two rooms in the Berkshires
narrative_blocks.body: Elm Tree House, the Prentices' seventy-two-room summer house at Mount Hope Farm near Williamstown, was finished in 1928, and the estate was reckoned the most valuable in the Berkshire Hills. Williams College owns the house now.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brownstone became part of MoMA
narrative_blocks.body: Alta died in 1962 at ninety-one, the last surviving child of John D. Rockefeller. She left her Manhattan brownstone to her neighbour the Museum of Modern Art, which pulled it down for a new wing, and her Berkshire estate to Lenox Hill Hospital.

narrative_blocks.header: A Chicago lawyer who bred dairy cattle
narrative_blocks.body: John practised law in Chicago from 1931, ten years with Sibley, McPherson, Austin and Burgess on LaSalle Street and again after the war. Dairy cattle were a family interest from his father's Mount Hope Farm in Williamstown, and he was secretary of the Chicago Farmers in 1935 and 1936 and for several years president of the American Dairy Cattle Club.

narrative_blocks.header: He led the American Breeders Service
narrative_blocks.body: John was a pioneer of artificial insemination in dairy breeding, and headed the American Breeders Service until he retired in 1967, by which time it had become part of W. R. Grace. The Holstein-Friesian World counted him a major influence on the dairy cattle industry.

narrative_blocks.header: Re-enlisted a private, came home a major
narrative_blocks.body: John had resigned as a captain of the 124th Field Artillery in 1936, and in March 1941, aged thirty-eight, he re-enlisted in it as a private at Camp Forrest. He was a captain again by 1942, served on the staff of the Seventh Infantry Division in the central Pacific, and finished the war a major with the 124th in New Guinea and the Philippines.

narrative_blocks.header: Skull and Bones and Phi Beta Kappa
narrative_blocks.body: At sixteen John won the prize for the best Yale entrance examination, and went on to take the Berkeley Premium in Latin, a Ten Eyck speaking prize and a scholarship earned answering telephones at New Haven Hospital. He was elected to Phi Beta Kappa and Sigma Xi as a junior, tapped for Skull and Bones in 1927, and ran on the cross-country squad.

narrative_blocks.header: He married his law firm's receptionist
narrative_blocks.body: In August 1941, a new lieutenant at Camp Forrest, John married Abra Cantrell of Freeport, Illinois, the receptionist at his Chicago law firm, at Monteagle, Tennessee.

narrative_blocks.header: Four Boston years to earn Yale back
narrative_blocks.body: Suspended from Yale in 1920 for poor scholarship and cut off by his parents over debts, John went to work for Chase, Parker & Co., wholesale hardware and iron merchants in Boston. He paid his way back to New Haven in 1924 and graduated with honors four years later.

Eastern Mandates (captain, 7th Infantry Division staff), New Guinea, Southern Philippines, Luzon (captain and major, 124th Field Artillery Battalion). Stationed in Japan after the war.

narrative_blocks.body: Madeline graduated from the Yale University School of Nursing in 1931 and nursed at New Haven Hospital before taking her Vassar B.A. In New York she was nurse to the psychiatrist Dr. Smiley Blanton from 1932 to 1934, and worked at Mid-Town Hospital in 1936 and 1937.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at home, by her uncle
narrative_blocks.body: Madeline married the inventor Benjamin Davis Gilbert on 16 October 1937 in the hall of Elm Tree House at Mount Hope Farm, and her uncle Rev. Sartell Prentice married them, under a special dispensation from Governor Charles Hurley. The veil she wore had been her mother's at the 1901 Rockefeller wedding.

narrative_blocks.header: He built La Coquille Club on the ocean
narrative_blocks.body: Around 1955 Spelman founded the La Coquille Club, a private oceanfront club at Manalapan, south of Palm Beach, in Mid-century Modern buildings by Byron F. Simonson. Whitneys, Fords and Vanderbilts swam there; he sold it in 1972, and The Ritz-Carlton stands on the ground now.

narrative_blocks.header: Prenalta, named for his mother
narrative_blocks.body: Spelman started at Humble Oil in Houston and moved to Standard Oil at Louisville, Kentucky, in 1937, then explored for oil and gas through his own Prenalta Corporation, named for his mother Alta, and Bluewater Oil and Gas in Canada. In his last years he turned to investment management and charities.

narrative_blocks.header: A major Y in track at Yale
narrative_blocks.body: Spelman came to Yale from the Taft School and won his major Y in track and a minor Y in cross-country, the squad his brother John had run on. He was elected to the Elihu senior society and graduated in 1934.

narrative_blocks.header: Beef cattle at Lyndonville, Vermont
narrative_blocks.body: Spelman kept a farm at Lyndonville, Vermont, where he raised beef cattle in the 1940s. Cattle ran in the family: his father bred dairy stock with geneticists at Mount Hope Farm, and his brother John headed the American Breeders Service.

narrative_blocks.header: A Palm Beach fixture who went west
narrative_blocks.body: Spelman was a presence in Palm Beach society, where he and Lola Pierce Noyes lived on North Lake Way after their 1953 marriage, and in 1959 he left New York for California. He died at Montecito in 2000, one of the last surviving grandchildren of John D. Rockefeller.

narrative_blocks.header: Time's publisher through the war
narrative_blocks.body: Perry joined Time Inc. in 1929 as business manager of the new Fortune, became circulation director of Time, and published Time magazine from 1941 to 1945. He was a vice-president of the company from 1939 until he retired in 1965.

narrative_blocks.header: He published Architectural Forum
narrative_blocks.body: Later Perry published Time Inc.'s Architectural Forum and House & Home, and became an authority on property tax. The Chicago architect Bertrand Goldberg wrote to him often, in 1966 about building adult education into high-rise communities like Marina City.

narrative_blocks.header: Four newspapers before Time Inc.
narrative_blocks.body: Perry came to Time Inc. from newspapers: reporter on the New York Herald Tribune, editor and general manager of the Camden Post-Telegram, managing editor of the New Bedford Times and news editor of the Philadelphia Record.

narrative_blocks.header: Married on his parents' anniversary
narrative_blocks.body: Perry married Mildred Belcher at Brooklyn on 30 September 1922, his parents' twenty-sixth wedding anniversary and his father's fifty-fifth birthday. Perry took a Reno divorce on 28 October 1944, and four days later, on 1 November, he married Janet McNeir Pflieger at Warrenton, Virginia.

narrative_blocks.body: Janet's son by her first husband, Jean Paul Pflieger, was John Ely “Jack” Pflieger, born in 1931, who went through the Hill School and Yale and followed his stepfather Perry Prentice into publishing. Jack spent twenty-five years with Time Inc. in New York before becoming its lobbyist in Washington.

narrative_blocks.header: Jack's Washington, from Wolf Trap to Harvard
narrative_blocks.body: In Washington Jack directed special projects for Sports Illustrated, sat on the Wolf Trap board and chaired the policy advisory board of Harvard's Joint Center for Housing Studies. He died there in January 2018, after a stroke on New Year's Day.

narrative_blocks.header: A Greenwich wedding, a Palm Beach divorce
narrative_blocks.body: Jack's first marriage, to Natasha Magee Boissevain, born at Nice, was at Greenwich on 24 November 1951, and it ended in divorce at Palm Beach in 1953. He was survived by his second wife, Donna, and two sons.

narrative_blocks.header: From Ipswich in 1643 and Biggar, Scotland
narrative_blocks.body: Ben descended from Humphrey Gilbert, who settled at Ipswich, Massachusetts, in 1643, and on his mother's side from Robert Biggar of Biggar, Scotland, who came to Canada in 1799. He gave his elder son the name Humphrey.

narrative_blocks.header: He produced To Leslie through Alzheimer's
narrative_blocks.body: Diagnosed with Alzheimer's in 2012, John spent his last four years producing films with his childhood friend Ward Cleary and Ward's daughter Ceci, and finished two features, 40-Love and To Leslie. The work held back the worst of the disease.

narrative_blocks.header: Live radio and comedy in Santa Rosa
narrative_blocks.body: In 1987 John opened Studio KAFE in Santa Rosa with John and Rande Duran, a restaurant with a live radio station where diners could go on the air. Co-hosting its comedy nights led him to acting, and he took 81 television, film and video credits.

narrative_blocks.header: A company named for three neighbours
narrative_blocks.body: John's first company, Automatic Board Meeting, was named because its three principals lived next door to one another. It made greeting cards for Jostens, then children's quilts and pillows, some licensed from Holly Hobbie.

narrative_blocks.header: Signalman, model, private eye, bartender
narrative_blocks.body: John served two years as a signalman on the destroyer USS Gearing in the Caribbean and Mediterranean. Back in New York he worked as a model, a private detective and a bartender.

narrative_blocks.header: The Scottish Dutchman, seventeen caps
narrative_blocks.body: Frans won seventeen caps for Scotland as a lock from 1959, scored a try against Wales in 1962 and helped win in Cardiff for the first time in thirty-five years. He disliked being called the Scottish Dutchman, and retired at twenty-six for business.

narrative_blocks.header: Three cocoa boats out of Bordeaux
narrative_blocks.body: In 1940 Frans's Dutch father drove the family down the Belgian coast ahead of the Germans and waited two weeks at Bordeaux, where three cocoa boats were leaving for Britain. The captain took the children and then their parents; the other two boats were torpedoed.

narrative_blocks.header: Pamela told him to get a proper job
narrative_blocks.body: Pamela had no love for the rugby crowd, and with Helena on the way Frans turned down a tour of South Africa. He worked for Courtaulds, then built a printing company at Brentford into a listed business.

narrative_blocks.header: Too Dutch for the Cameron Highlanders
narrative_blocks.body: When Frans applied to do his National Service with the Cameron Highlanders, the colonel wrote back that he was “obviously a thoroughly good chap” but that this was a Scottish regiment. He went into the Argylls instead.

narrative_blocks.header: “A big lump o' potted meat”
narrative_blocks.body: The night before Scotland played France at Colombes in 1963, the prop Hugh McLeod told Frans he was “jist a big lump o' potted meat.” Scotland won 11–6, and Frans said of McLeod, “You know, I'd follow him anywhere.”

narrative_blocks.header: Her name is on Chicago's maternity hospital
narrative_blocks.body: Abra's gifts are behind the Prentice Women's Hospital and the Prentice Pavilion, one of the largest birthing centers in the Midwest, on Northwestern's medical campus in Chicago. She sat on the Taft School board for more than thirty years, and on the Lincoln Park Zoo’s.

narrative_blocks.header: The renegade who worked for a living
narrative_blocks.body: Abra joined the Chicago Sun-Times part-time in 1962, the year she finished Bradford Junior College, and became a general assignment reporter; she called herself “the renegade of the family” for working. She married a fellow reporter there, Jon Anderson, in 1968.

narrative_blocks.header: “Jon & Abra” and The Chicagoan
narrative_blocks.body: In the early 1970s Abra and her first husband, the writer Jon Anderson, were Chicago's golden couple, with a Daily News gossip column called Jon & Abra. In 1973 she underwrote The Chicagoan, the magazine he ran; they divorced in 1976.

narrative_blocks.header: Applause in the pews, then Sinatra
narrative_blocks.body: When Abra married James Wilkin at St. Chrysostom's in 1986, given away by her uncle Spelman Prentice, the guests broke into applause. The next evening the couple went to Frank Sinatra's opening at the restored Chicago Theatre, and Abra, a Sinatra fan, cried through the concert.

narrative_blocks.header: A Mafia death threat from Montreal
narrative_blocks.body: As TIME's Montreal bureau chief from 1960, Jon drew a Mafia death threat for his coverage of the city's crime. TIME moved him to Chicago in 1963, where he worked the murder of eight student nurses.

narrative_blocks.header: Leonard Cohen's teacher taught him to write tight
narrative_blocks.body: Jon was born on St. Urbain Street, in Montreal's immigrant quarter, and at Westmount High School shared an English teacher with Leonard Cohen, who taught them both to “write tight.” He took a law degree at McGill before choosing journalism.

narrative_blocks.header: City Watch, and The Chicagoan
narrative_blocks.body: Jon ran The Chicagoan, the magazine Abra underwrote from 1973, and wrote the Tribune's City Watch column, collected as City Watch: Discovering the Uncommon Chicago. At fifty-five he took a master's in nonfiction writing at Iowa.

narrative_blocks.body: In 2012 Ashley wrote in Redbook about the manic depression that nearly took her from her three children, and the electroshock therapy that brought her back. She signed it with her own name, to take the stigma off the illness.

narrative_blocks.header: First president of the ski areas' association
narrative_blocks.body: Dave was elected the first president of the National Ski Areas Association in 1962, when new ski areas were opening everywhere with no national standards for lifts, trails or safety. He won the Sherman Adams Award in 1976 and entered the U.S. National Ski Hall of Fame in 1997.

narrative_blocks.header: The Blizzard, 10th Mountain Division
narrative_blocks.body: In the Second World War Dave served with the 10th Mountain Division in northern Italy, earning a Bronze Star, and was chief editorial writer of the division's newspaper, The Blizzard. Veterans of the division went on to found, run or teach at sixty-two American ski resorts.

narrative_blocks.header: The first overnight ski camp for juniors
narrative_blocks.body: Dave and Hooker started the Otis Ridge Junior Ski Camp in the Berkshires, the first overnight camp for young skiers, with sixteen instructors, four dormitories and beds for a hundred. Dave ran the Otis Ridge Ski Area beside it.

narrative_blocks.header: The first cabin at Mad River Glen
narrative_blocks.body: About 1950 Dave and Hooker built the first cabin at the base of Mad River Glen, while the area's founder, Roland Palmedo, was still sleeping in a rehabilitated tool shed.

narrative_blocks.header: Ski fiction for the Saturday Evening Post
narrative_blocks.body: Dave took up skiing at Yale, then wrote ski fiction for the Saturday Evening Post and in 1940 edited SKI Magazine.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten years certifying ski teachers
narrative_blocks.body: From 1958 to 1968 Dave sat on Roland Palmedo's committee certifying professional ski teachers for the U.S. Eastern Amateur Ski Association. “We could always count on his advice and encouragement,” said the ski-school founders Paula and Paul Valar.

narrative_blocks.header: News editor of the Oregon Journal
narrative_blocks.body: Charlie went to Portland in 1962 as a copy editor on the Oregon Journal and was its news editor from 1977. When the Journal merged with The Oregonian in 1982 he became deputy news editor of the combined paper, and retired in 1986.

narrative_blocks.header: An internship program in his name
narrative_blocks.body: In his memory the family endowed the Charles Snowden Program for Excellence in Journalism at the University of Oregon, which has placed Oregon college students in newsrooms since 1998. It has funded more than four hundred internships, and its interns have gone on to the Associated Press, CNN and NPR.

narrative_blocks.header: He saved Lake Oswego's Odd Fellows Hall
narrative_blocks.body: In retirement Charlie bought the Lake Oswego Odd Fellows Hall and saved it from demolition, and it is now on the National Register of Historic Places. He and his wife Juliana also bought and remodeled older houses.

narrative_blocks.header: The Coral Sea's paper at eighteen
narrative_blocks.body: Charlie began in journalism as an eighteen-year-old Navy seaman, editing the ship's newspaper aboard the USS Coral Sea. Back in Philadelphia he reported for the Conshohocken Recorder and the Norristown Times Herald before moving to the Allentown Morning Call in 1961.

narrative_blocks.header: Lost aboard the Manley in March 1918
narrative_blocks.body: Richard was executive officer of the destroyer Manley when she collided with a British ship in the convoy she was escorting on 19 March 1918, and her own depth charges exploded. He was twenty-nine.

narrative_blocks.header: A destroyer carried his name
narrative_blocks.body: The destroyer Elliot was launched at Philadelphia on 4 July 1918, named for him, and his widow Joan sponsored her. She served into the Second World War, sweeping mines off Attu in 1943.

narrative_blocks.header: He went into the flooded engine room
narrative_blocks.body: Aboard the destroyer Aylwin, after a boiler exploded, Richard went into the flooded engine room to rescue the men trapped there, and was distinguished for exceptional bravery.

narrative_blocks.header: Crew and French at Annapolis
narrative_blocks.body: Richard rowed four years on the Naval Academy crew and sang in the choir, graduating in 1909, and spoke French with a Parisian accent. His classmates wrote that he would rather row twelve miles than go to a dance.

narrative_blocks.header: Married thirteen months before he died
narrative_blocks.body: Richard married Joan Hooker Packard at St. Mark's Church, Philadelphia, on 10 February 1917. He died aboard the Manley thirteen months later, and was buried from the Church of the Redeemer at Bryn Mawr.

narrative_blocks.header: Head of checking at a four-year-old magazine
narrative_blocks.body: Freddie was hired as a checker in 1929, when The New Yorker was four, and ran checking for his last twenty-five years. Its library grew from an 1898 Baedeker, a Spalding's Baseball Guide and a Webster's into a walled reference room.

narrative_blocks.header: A gentleman-scholar on deadline
narrative_blocks.body: Brendan Gill called Freddie a gentleman-scholar who, instead of poring over folios in some dim library, worked hard in a midtown office under constant deadlines. He was stocky, with straight dark hair and a close-cropped mustache.

narrative_blocks.header: Funny, cranky pieces about the city
narrative_blocks.body: Freddie wrote funny, cranky pieces about what befell him trudging around the city, or more likely in his imagination, and contributed fiction and Talk of the Town pieces. Nobody called him anything but Freddie.

narrative_blocks.header: Spot drawings in pen and watercolor
narrative_blocks.body: Freddie made small pen-and-ink and watercolor sketches, and dozens ran in the magazine as spots, the last in the issue of November 4, 1974. Twenty-three of them turned up decades later in a tattered New Yorker envelope.

narrative_blocks.header: Late afternoons at the Cortile
narrative_blocks.body: In the late afternoons Freddie was a regular at the Cortile, near the magazine's West 43rd Street offices, where the art editor James Geraghty held court among artists and the critic John McCarten.

narrative_blocks.header: He proposed within a year
narrative_blocks.body: Freddie proposed to Eleanor Gould a year after she joined the magazine, and they married on December 7, 1946. Both fluent in French, they spent summers in France, Scotland and Ireland, and went to Morocco several times.

narrative_blocks.header: Ninety-nine years between them
narrative_blocks.body: Freddie died in November 1974, two years before he meant to retire, and William Shawn handed Eleanor his last paycheck. His forty-five years and her fifty-four at The New Yorker added up to ninety-nine.

narrative_blocks.header: Following nitrogen from land to sea
narrative_blocks.body: Wally is a professor at Boston University, where in 2008 she founded a laboratory that studies how carbon, nitrogen, silica and oxygen cycle through coastal waters, salt marshes and oyster farms. Her work follows nitrogen across the land-sea boundary and asks how climate change and human activity reshape it.

narrative_blocks.header: A Sloan Fellow and a Metcalf Cup winner
narrative_blocks.body: Wally took her master's and doctorate in oceanography at the University of Rhode Island, in 2003 and 2007, and was named a Sloan Fellow in 2012. Boston University gave her the Metcalf Cup and Prize for teaching in 2019, and in 2024 she won a Simons Foundation Pivot Fellowship.

narrative_blocks.header: An advocate for mothers in science
narrative_blocks.body: Wally speaks up for women and parents in science, especially mothers, and works toward a scientific community where people thrive rather than simply survive.

narrative_blocks.header: He blazed the Shenipsit Trail
narrative_blocks.body: From 1946 Morgan laid out Connecticut's Shenipsit Trail for the Forest and Park Association, winning landowners' permission, painting its first light-blue blazes and drawing its first maps. By 1947 it was established.

narrative_blocks.header: A measuring wheel in the Adirondacks
narrative_blocks.body: A president of the Adirondack Mountain Club, Morgan measured the high-peak trails with a wheel, rain or shine, and rewrote its Guidebook to the Adirondack Mountains. At home he was chief timer of Manchester's Thanksgiving road race.

narrative_blocks.header: An engineer at Pratt and Whitney
narrative_blocks.body: Morgan graduated from Yale's Sheffield Scientific School in 1924, worked as an engineer at Pratt and Whitney in East Hartford, and from 1955 taught mechanical engineering at Rensselaer's new graduate center.

narrative_blocks.body: Bill loved swing bands, Lake Champlain, red wine and chocolate. His favorite sayings were “I've been a very lucky guy” and, after a glass of pinot noir, “I ain't mad at nobody!”

bio.bio_blurb: Tax lawyer; Marine Corps Scholarship Foundation counsel

military_service.notes: Active duty in the Mediterranean; reserve until 1 July 1984

narrative_blocks.header: Counsel to the Marines' scholarship fund
narrative_blocks.body: Morgan was pro bono general counsel to the Marine Corps Scholarship Foundation for decades and planned its Chicago dinner from 2001 to 2014. In 2001 he won its largest gift yet by talking to the stranger in the next airline seat.

narrative_blocks.header: Twice before the Tax Court
narrative_blocks.body: After Michigan Law in 1964 Morgan spent a decade in the IRS regional counsel's office in Chicago, arguing and winning twice before the Tax Court, and from 1978 practiced tax law as Porter & Porter.

narrative_blocks.header: An honorary Marine Raider
narrative_blocks.body: Morgan went from Yale ROTC into the Marines and retired from the reserve a lieutenant colonel. Made an honorary Marine Raider, he paid to build a school in the Solomon Islands and visited it unannounced in 2022.

narrative_blocks.header: A touchdown against Harvard
narrative_blocks.body: Morgan made the Yale varsity as a small, fast back, and scored his only touchdown in the Harvard game with his parents watching from the stands. At Yale he also patented a collapsible airship.

narrative_blocks.header: Libraries for villages in Siberia
narrative_blocks.body: Morgan visited eighty-three countries, Russia twelve times, and sent school libraries to villages from Papua New Guinea to Siberia. He curled four times a week and was president of the Chicago Curling Club.

narrative_blocks.header: Named for Lewis Henry Morgan
narrative_blocks.body: Morgan was named for his great-great-uncle Lewis Henry Morgan, the anthropologist of the Iroquois.

bio.bio_blurb: Author of The Wayfarers; Harcourt Brace editor

narrative_blocks.header: A best-seller at twenty-four
narrative_blocks.body: Dan's first novel, The Running of the Deer, came out in 1937, when he was twenty-four, and was a best-seller about two middle-class families on Long Island, where he had grown up the son of English-born parents.

narrative_blocks.header: The best novel of 1945
narrative_blocks.body: A few years on a Michigan newspaper gave Dan the setting for The Wayfarers, which Orville Prescott of The New York Times picked as the best novel of 1945. It was a Literary Guild selection, and Eleanor Roosevelt praised it in her column.

narrative_blocks.header: He edited The Pawnbroker
narrative_blocks.body: Dan joined Harcourt Brace in 1953 and rose to senior editor, working with Eudora Welty, James Gould Cozzens and Wendell Berry. He brought in Edward Lewis Wallant and edited his 1961 novel The Pawnbroker.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten months beside Lake Atitlán
narrative_blocks.body: Dan lived ten months among artists at Panajachel, beside Lake Atitlán in Guatemala, and came home in May 1948. The lake became the setting of The Dry Season, his 1950 novel.

narrative_blocks.header: One of the ablest novelists
narrative_blocks.body: After The Dry Season, Orville Prescott called Dan "one of the ablest of contemporary American novelists," who had "not yet received the critical recognition that is his due."

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-six years running The New Yorker
narrative_blocks.body: Dorothy was executive editor of The New Yorker for twenty-six years and hosted its podcast The Political Scene from 2007 to 2022, after fifteen years at The New Republic and two editing national affairs at Newsweek.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandmother's letters from Colorado
narrative_blocks.body: Dorothy found her grandmother Dorothy Woodruff's 1916 letters from the Colorado mountains, told the story in The New Yorker in 2009, and expanded it into Nothing Daunted, a New York Times best-seller.

narrative_blocks.header: Three friends in Auburn
narrative_blocks.body: Her book The Agitators follows three friends and neighbors in Auburn, New York, Harriet Tubman, Frances Seward and Martha Coffin Wright, through the Civil War years, in the town where her grandmother grew up.

narrative_blocks.header: Phi Beta Kappa at William Smith
narrative_blocks.body: Dorothy graduated magna cum laude from William Smith in 1976, was a Nieman Fellow at Harvard in 1988 and a MacDowell fellow in 2018, and has honorary doctorates from Hobart and William Smith and from Iona.

narrative_blocks.header: He picked Miami for the lab
narrative_blocks.body: Stew chose Miami from more than a hundred sites for a new federal ocean laboratory, for its hurricane research. When a budget cut stopped the building, he won Miami's leaders over, and the lab opened in 1973 with Stew as its first director.

narrative_blocks.header: Flying transports over the Coral Sea
narrative_blocks.body: Stew left Princeton after Pearl Harbor to fly transports over New Guinea and the Philippines, and came home loving the sea. He finished his geology degree in 1948 and took a doctorate in oceanography at Scripps.

narrative_blocks.header: Chief oceanographer in 1957
narrative_blocks.body: Stew dived as a geologist mapping the sea floor off California before he became chief oceanographer of the U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey in 1957, sailing to the Caribbean, the South China Sea and three oceans.

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve books, some of them funny
narrative_blocks.body: Stew wrote more than 120 scientific papers and twelve books, from The Global Sea and Deep Challenge, which explained oceanography to general readers, to Id of the Squid and No Dinosaurs in the Ark.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a distant cousin in 1959
narrative_blocks.body: Stew married Elsie Cunningham in 1959, a distant cousin; both came down from the Rev. Samuel Hooker. Elsie died in 1988, and his second wife, Louise Conant Thompson, died four weeks before him in 2000.

narrative_blocks.header: He looked with his heart
narrative_blocks.body: Late in life, when he could barely see, Stew still told his old secretary she looked as beautiful as ever. "He always looked at people with his heart, not with his eyes," she said.

bio.bio_blurb: Village trustee and Wells College slide curator

narrative_blocks.header: A class of three at Cayuga Academy
narrative_blocks.body: Ann grew up on the Auburn Theological Seminary campus, where her grandfather was president, and graduated in a class of three from Cayuga Academy in Aurora. Too young for college, she spent two years at the Baldwin School.

narrative_blocks.header: Married by her father, given away by Stew
narrative_blocks.body: Ann married Charles Burch, a Cornell botany student, at the Aurora Presbyterian Church in November 1946. Her father performed the ceremony, and her brother Stew gave her away.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty years at the Aurora Free Library
narrative_blocks.body: Back in Aurora from 1967, Ann was a village trustee and an election official, curated slides for the Wells College art department, and volunteered at the Aurora Free Library for more than thirty years.

narrative_blocks.header: A hundredth birthday at Friends Meeting
narrative_blocks.body: Ann celebrated her 100th birthday in June 2024 at the Poplar Ridge Friends Meeting, a month before she died. She had gone to Ireland at 88 to look into her Scotch-Irish roots, and turned 90 in Norway.

narrative_blocks.header: The golf writer in Maryland
narrative_blocks.body: For his last twenty years at The Baltimore Sun John covered golf, from the U.S. Open and the Masters to Maryland amateur events. The PGA named him Golf Writer of the Year in 1991 and 1995, and gave him its Keeper of the Game Award in 2009.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty more years after he retired
narrative_blocks.body: John retired from The Sun in 1999 and covered Maryland golf for twenty more years for the state's golf associations. He stayed until the last player was off the course, then drove home to write against his deadline.

narrative_blocks.header: A record for scorecards received
narrative_blocks.body: John sat at the scoring table of hundreds of tournaments, and the Mid-Atlantic Golf Association's former president said he held the record for most scorecards received. The association put him in its Hall of Fame in 2011.

narrative_blocks.header: Nicklaus at Baltusrol, Tiger at nineteen
narrative_blocks.body: John's 1981 story on Jack Nicklaus at Baltusrol won the Golf Writers Association's feature prize. In 1995 he watched Tiger Woods, nineteen, win the U.S. Amateur at Newport with an 8-iron on the 36th hole.

narrative_blocks.header: Five Olympics and two World Series
narrative_blocks.body: John covered the 1960 Rome Olympics for the Yonkers papers, then the 1968, 1972, 1976 and 1984 Games for The Sun, along with the Colts, Maryland basketball and the Orioles' 1970 and 1983 World Series.

narrative_blocks.header: AstroTurf at the Calvert Street desk
narrative_blocks.body: John shared a desk in The Sun's Calvert Street newsroom with Jimmy Jackson for more than twenty years. They argued over whose media guide was whose, and Jackson called him AstroTurf for his crew cut.

narrative_blocks.header: Three letters at Colorado College
narrative_blocks.body: John lettered in basketball, baseball and football at Colorado College, which put him in its Athletic Hall of Fame in 2001, and then served four years as a Coast Guard quartermaster.

narrative_blocks.body: Eleanor applied to The New Yorker by pointing out two errors in a new issue, and William Shawn hired her on October 3, 1945, her twenty-eighth birthday.

narrative_blocks.header: Inside every sentence for fifty-four years
narrative_blocks.body: For fifty-four years Eleanor read nearly every nonfiction piece in galley proof, from E. B. White and John McPhee to Pauline Kael and Ved Mehta. The title of grammarian was coined for her.

narrative_blocks.header: Four errors in a three-word sentence
narrative_blocks.body: Her marked galleys, called Gould-proofs, carried notes like "How so?" and "NOT Grammar!" She was said to have found four errors in a sentence of three words.

narrative_blocks.header: She helped revise The Elements of Style
narrative_blocks.body: E. B. White wrote to Eleanor with grammar questions and had her help revise The Elements of Style, which acknowledged her from its second edition on.

narrative_blocks.header: Deaf, and still at her desk
narrative_blocks.body: Eleanor woke one morning totally deaf and lost the concerts and ballet she loved. She kept working by written note and fax until a stroke in 1999.

narrative_blocks.header: Mrs. Packard only outside the office
narrative_blocks.body: Eleanor married Freddie Packard, head of the magazine's fact-checking department, on December 7, 1946, and stayed Miss Gould at the office. They were both fluent in French and spent summers in France, Scotland and Ireland.

narrative_blocks.header: "She has been inside my sentences"
narrative_blocks.body: David Remnick, the magazine's editor, called her the one indispensable person at The New Yorker: "she has been inside my sentences."

narrative_blocks.body: Susan travelled with her mother to remote places, and when Eleanor was in her late seventies, after reading Apsley Cherry-Garrard's The Worst Journey in the World, the two of them set off for the Antarctic.

narrative_blocks.header: Two years at her mother's college
narrative_blocks.body: Susan spent two years at Oberlin, her mother's college, in the class of 1969, then came home to New York and graduated from New York University.

narrative_blocks.header: Destroyers in two oceans
narrative_blocks.body: Gerry left Westtown School for the Navy in 1942 and served on destroyers in the South Atlantic and the Pacific until 1946. He was called back for the Korean War.

narrative_blocks.header: Tanker crew on his vacations
narrative_blocks.body: While he studied at Penn and then taught at The Haverford School, Gerry spent his vacations sailing with the Sun Oil Company's tanker fleet.

narrative_blocks.header: From the classroom to paper sales
narrative_blocks.body: Gerry taught at Haverford and at Penn, set up an educational development program at Westtown School, then spent twenty years as sales manager for a paper company in Downingtown.

narrative_blocks.header: Sheep for the show ring
narrative_blocks.body: On their hobby farm Gerry and Rita raised sheep for market and the show ring, along with three children, many dogs and a cat, and for several years he ran the sheep exhibit at the Kimberton Fair.

narrative_blocks.header: A crabbing shanty on Jenkins Creek
narrative_blocks.body: Late in life Gerry bought a crabbing shanty on Jenkins Creek below Crisfield, Maryland, and fixed it up. He fished and crabbed there for a decade and started an oyster farm that still flourishes.

narrative_blocks.header: A Quaker who went to war
narrative_blocks.body: Gerry's families became Quakers in 1657. He set the peace testimony aside to serve in the war, but stayed an active member of Downingtown Friends Meeting and helped care for the old Caln Meetinghouse.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty-two years with Rita
narrative_blocks.body: Gerry met Rita Rhein at Penn, married her in 1954, and was her husband for sixty-two years.

bio.bio_blurb: Chief engineer, New York City Telephone Company

narrative_blocks.header: Chief engineer of the telephone company
narrative_blocks.body: Leonard was chief engineer of the New York City Telephone Company and consulting engineer to the Empire City Subway Company and several like it. In 1893 the Times called his business career unusually brilliant.

narrative_blocks.header: Beckwithshaw above the Stockbridge Bowl
narrative_blocks.body: In 1892 Leonard and Margaretta built Beckwithshaw, a thirty-one-room house above the Stockbridge Bowl. He called himself its architect, though H. Neill Wilson drew it, and bought 1,800 acres around Curtisville with its old pulp mill, meaning to revive the village.

narrative_blocks.header: The breakdown at the World's Fair
narrative_blocks.body: In October 1893 Leonard broke down at the World's Fair in Chicago. For two years friends had heard stranger plans, an airship to fly to Brazil and a railway lifted by balloons, and that fall a sheriff's jury found him insane.

narrative_blocks.header: His brother Arthur vanished
narrative_blocks.body: Leonard's older brother Arthur, an artist, fell ill too. He escaped one asylum and was found two years later living wild in Cuba, escaped another in 1895 and was never seen again, and a court declared him dead in 1903.

narrative_blocks.header: His sister's suit, and his death
narrative_blocks.body: In August 1895, with Leonard in a Massachusetts asylum, his sister Helen Leigh charged that he had failed to account for money he held for Arthur. He died at Bronxville that November, at fifty-one.

narrative_blocks.header: The house where Tanglewood began
narrative_blocks.body: Beckwithshaw stayed on the market for years until Sam Hill bought it in 1905. As Dan Hanna's Bonnie Brier it later held the first concerts of the Berkshire Symphonic Festival, the beginning of Tanglewood.

bio.bio_blurb: Orientalist; Princeton professor of Semitic languages

narrative_blocks.header: Iron rungs up the Precipice
narrative_blocks.body: As chairman of the Bar Harbor path committee, Rudolf drove the Precipice and the Beehive straight up the cliffs on iron rungs and ladders, paying part of the cost himself. Hikers flocked to them; others grumbled that the crowds drove off the nesting eagles.

narrative_blocks.header: The Titanic bride who never was
narrative_blocks.body: Bar Harbor told it that Rudolf built his big house above the Schooner Head cliffs for a bride who went down with the Titanic, giving her lifeboat place to an older woman. Edith Evans did die that way, but she was his friend, and Rudolf was a widower building for five children.

narrative_blocks.header: He did not fall from his own trail
narrative_blocks.body: Guides still say Rudolf died on the Precipice. He did not. In October 1916 he was scouting a new route off the Orange & Black Path with three of his children when the rock gave way under his brother-in-law Edward Beckwith, who fell twenty feet and was four hours being brought down.

narrative_blocks.header: The first modern map of Petra
narrative_blocks.body: In 1897 and 1898 Rudolf and Alfred von Domaszewski rode into Arabia twice to survey the old Roman province, and came back with the first modern map of Petra, the rock-cut Nabatean capital. It won him the Drexel Medal, which had gone before him to Flinders Petrie.

narrative_blocks.header: A widower who brought the children home
narrative_blocks.body: Rudolf taught at Heidelberg for fifteen years and married Marguerite Beckwith at Lenox in 1894. When she died at Bonn in 1907 he gave up Germany, brought their five children to Princeton to grow up American, and took them to Bar Harbor every summer from 1909.

narrative_blocks.header: An astronomer's son, not a German
narrative_blocks.body: Rudolf was born at Ann Arbor, where his father ran the university's observatory and his mother was the president's daughter, and he held the highest degrees Strasbourg could give. The Bar Harbor paper called him German-born when he died, and had to correct itself a week later.

narrative_blocks.header: Eric in the fall, Rudolf in the spring
narrative_blocks.body: In the fall of 1916 his eldest son, Eric, set off for his first term at Princeton, caught infantile paralysis in New York and was dead in two days, before Rudolf could reach him. The next April pneumonia took Rudolf in two days as well, and he was buried beside Eric at Princeton.

narrative_blocks.header: A chemist from Washington, Connecticut
narrative_blocks.body: Marguerite grew up in Washington, Connecticut, went to Westover School and took a chemistry degree at Connecticut College in 1952. She stayed close to the college all her life, as her class's vice president and its gift officer.

narrative_blocks.header: Her great-grandmother's Brussels lace
narrative_blocks.body: Marguerite married John O'Connell in Washington's First Congregational Church in November 1952, three months after her father's death, and her uncle gave her away. She wore the Brussels lace veil her mother and great-grandmother had worn.

narrative_blocks.header: Laid beside him at Arlington
narrative_blocks.body: John was executive officer of the Coast Guard cutter Cowslip when they married and made his career in the service, retiring a captain. When Marguerite died in 2014 she was buried in his grave at Arlington the next July.

narrative_blocks.header: A Paul Revere cann from a lost wedding
narrative_blocks.body: Marguerite inherited a silver quart cann Paul Revere made in 1768 for Edmund Quincy to give his fiancée, Rebecca Lloyd; Quincy died at sea before the wedding. The cann came down six generations of her family to her.

narrative_blocks.header: Granddaughter of the man who built the Precipice
narrative_blocks.body: Marguerite never knew her grandfather Rudolf Brünnow, who mapped Petra and cut the Precipice Trail up the cliffs at Acadia; he died fourteen years before she was born.

narrative_blocks.header: A partner when women partners were rare
narrative_blocks.body: Emily taught at Nightingale-Bamford, the Spence School and the American School in Japan, then went into finance and worked her way up to partner at Adams & Peck, when a woman partner in a brokerage was still a rarity.

narrative_blocks.header: She could change a head gasket
narrative_blocks.body: Emily learned to sail on Cape Cod in boats her family built themselves, crossed the Atlantic five, seven or nine times depending on who told it, and could navigate, steer or change a diesel head gasket better than most men.

narrative_blocks.header: Rear Commodore of the Ocean Cruising Club
narrative_blocks.body: Emily joined the Ocean Cruising Club in 1976 after sailing from the Virgin Islands to Oyster Bay, served as its Rear Commodore for the American northeast, and in 1991 was made an honorary life member for seeing it through hard years.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight months aboard Blithe Spirit
narrative_blocks.body: In 1990 Emily and Forbes sailed their Swan 43, Blithe Spirit, from Darien to Cork and on through France, Spain, Portugal and Madeira, then back across to Barbados and the Caribbean, eight months in all.

narrative_blocks.header: Tap dancing and the Bedford prison
narrative_blocks.body: While she cared for Forbes at Pound Ridge, Emily took up tap dancing, trained a puppy to guide the blind, worked in a thrift shop, and taught library skills to the women at the Bedford prison.

narrative_blocks.header: She meant to become a clown
narrative_blocks.body: Told in 1997 that she had stage four cancer, Emily met two years of it with courage and cheer. Her last ambition was to become a hospital clown, having seen what clowns did for sick children. She died in October 1999.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-four years to say so
narrative_blocks.body: Adele and Bill Nevins were classmates at the Polytechnic School in Pasadena, each quietly taken with the other and neither saying a word. Planning their fortieth reunion in 2006, he took her fly-fishing and stood behind her to teach the cast.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at sixty
narrative_blocks.body: They married in May 2008 at his mother's house in Pasadena, when Adele was sixty. She had turned down a proposal in her twenties: the women in her family lived into their nineties, she said, and seventy years of marriage was too long.

narrative_blocks.header: A New York paralegal
narrative_blocks.body: Adele graduated from New York University and worked as a paralegal at the New York law firm Dreyer & Traub until she retired.

narrative_blocks.header: Old Silver Nails
narrative_blocks.body: Leading an attack on Spanish-held Saint Martin in 1644, Peter was wounded in the right leg, which had to come off. He stumped about thereafter on a wooden leg studded with silver nails, and took his survival as a sign God had work for him.

narrative_blocks.header: I shall govern you as a father
narrative_blocks.body: Peter reached New Amsterdam in May 1647 to find a colony wrecked by his predecessor's wars, with only 250 to 300 men left able to bear arms. "I shall govern you as a father his children," he told them, and set the Nine Men to advise him.

narrative_blocks.header: Fire buckets and a wall on Wall Street
narrative_blocks.body: Peter banned wooden chimneys, taxed every household a beaver skin to buy 250 leather fire buckets from Holland and set a night fire watch, America's first volunteer fire company. His town built the wall on Wall Street and the canal that became Broad Street.

narrative_blocks.header: He fought Lutherans, Jews and Quakers
narrative_blocks.body: Peter refused the Lutherans a church, tried to keep Jewish refugees from Brazil out of the colony, calling them a deceitful race, and in 1657 had the young Quaker Robert Hodgson publicly tortured. His own company overruled him on the Lutherans and the Jews.

narrative_blocks.header: He deepened the colony's slavery
narrative_blocks.body: Under Peter New Netherland leaned harder on slave labor, and the company told him to use enslaved workers where it could not send tradesmen. He himself owned two, bought with the farm he took from the company in 1651.

narrative_blocks.header: His settlers would not fight
narrative_blocks.body: When four English ships came in 1664, the settlers of New Amsterdam refused to fight, and Peter had to give the colony up. In the Articles of Capitulation he won its people their civil rights and their freedom of worship.

narrative_blocks.header: A pear tree on Third Avenue
narrative_blocks.body: Peter spent his last years on his farm, the Bouwerie, which gave the Bowery its name. A pear tree he was said to have brought from Holland in 1647 stood at Thirteenth Street and Third Avenue until a storm took it in 1867, bearing fruit almost to the last.

narrative_blocks.header: She nursed the one-legged soldier
narrative_blocks.body: Judith Bayard was in her mid-thirties and unmarried when Peter Stuyvesant came home to Holland without his right leg, lost to a Spanish cannonball at Saint Martin. He recovered in the house of his sister Anna, who had married Judith's brother, and Judith nursed him.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brother bet he would never ask
narrative_blocks.body: When Peter told Judith's brother he meant to propose, the brother scoffed that he would never find the nerve, and wagered a good quantity of French wine on it. Peter asked, and Judith said yes.

narrative_blocks.header: A friend's poem nearly spoiled it
narrative_blocks.body: Peter's friend John Farret, who traded poems with him, answered the engagement with verses declaring that the god of fertility had died in him and the marriage would never be consummated. Peter was furious, and accused Farret of trying to make him lose the bet.

narrative_blocks.header: Four months pregnant on Manhattan
narrative_blocks.body: Judith and Peter married in 1645 and sailed for New Amsterdam, which he had been sent to govern. When they stepped ashore in May 1647, Peter stood on a new wooden leg and Judith was four months pregnant with the first of their two sons.

narrative_blocks.header: Fourteen years a widow in Manhattan
narrative_blocks.body: Judith, born in Breda in 1608, stayed on in Manhattan after the English took the colony, and outlived Peter by nearly fourteen years. She died in March 1686, at seventy-seven, and was laid in the Stuyvesant vault, where St. Mark's in-the-Bowery now stands.

narrative_blocks.header: The only one of three who lived
narrative_blocks.body: Daisy was the only one of her parents' three children to grow up; her brother Harry died at eight, and another child in infancy. In January 1924 her own son, Nelson Porter Beardsley, died in Manhattan at eight, a week short of his ninth birthday.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father enlisted before sixteen
narrative_blocks.body: Daisy's father, Oliver Nelson Koen, joined Company B of the Sixth West Virginia Infantry in 1861, before his sixteenth birthday, and served the Union three years. He came home to Mannington and kept store there for the next nineteen.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandfather's store was Koon's Corner
narrative_blocks.body: Daisy's grandfather Samuel Koen farmed and kept a general store on his own land outside Mannington, West Virginia, and the store named the place: Koon's Corner, from the old spelling. The center of Mannington was built on that land.

narrative_blocks.header: A hotel, a Colorado ranch, then oil
narrative_blocks.body: Her father kept the Commercial Hotel at Mannington fourteen years, went west to irrigate thirty-five hundred acres near Lamar, Colorado, then came home and reopened as the Koen Hotel. The oil boom struck soon after, and he was among the first to put money into the wells.

narrative_blocks.header: A Yale man from Auburn
narrative_blocks.body: Daisy married Glover Beardsley of Auburn, New York, a Yale graduate, at Germantown in Philadelphia on 29 December 1910. By 1923 he was managing the Otis Elevator Company's New York City zone, and they were raising their daughter Annette in Manhattan.

narrative_blocks.header: Ninety-two, and home to Woodlawn
narrative_blocks.body: Daisy outlived Glover by eleven years and died at Jacksonville, Florida, in October 1972, at ninety-two. She was laid at Woodlawn in the Bronx, in the mausoleum that carries both family names, Beardsley and Koen.

narrative_blocks.header: A photographer on the reservations
narrative_blocks.body: Annette was a photographer, and she spent many summers on Montana's Indian reservations with her camera. Her work drew her son Glover west: the summer before college he went to work on the Pine Ridge Reservation, the start of his road to the ministry.

narrative_blocks.header: Announced in the Ritz Crystal Garden
narrative_blocks.body: Her parents announced Annette's engagement to Charles Wagner of Dayton at a large dinner dance in the Crystal Garden of the Ritz-Carlton in December 1937. They married the next June at Christ Methodist Episcopal Church on Park Avenue.

narrative_blocks.header: Colonel of the Knickerbocker Greys
narrative_blocks.body: Nelson came up through the Browning School in Manhattan and rose to colonel of the Knickerbocker Greys, the city's old cadet corps for boys, before going south to the University of Virginia.

narrative_blocks.header: Cars in Jacksonville, and the sea
narrative_blocks.body: From Virginia Nelson moved to Jacksonville and made his passion for automobiles his life's work. Away from the cars he was on the water, a master of boating and fishing, and he was a champion skeet shot.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty-two, after a brief illness
narrative_blocks.body: Nelson died at Baptist Memorial Hospital in Jacksonville on 14 October 2003, at sixty-two, after a brief illness with advanced mesothelioma. He left his wife Paula, his brother Glover in Bozeman and his sister Mary-Anne in Madison.

narrative_blocks.header: The Rolling Stones from the pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: On his twenty-fifth Palm Sunday at Pilgrim, with children parading in costume and waving palms, Glover opened with the Rolling Stones, 'You can't always get what you want,' and preached past the parade to the honest, embarrassing reality of the cross.

narrative_blocks.header: Pine Ridge, the summer before college
narrative_blocks.body: Glover's mother, the photographer Annette Beardsley Wagner, spent summers on Montana's Indian reservations, and before college he went to work for an Episcopal priest on the Pine Ridge Reservation. He saw people who were very poor, he said, with a tremendous peace and joy in their faith.

narrative_blocks.header: Milton sent him to the Bible
narrative_blocks.body: Glover read English literature at Lawrence University in Appleton, Wisconsin, and found that everything from Shakespeare to Milton was grounded in the Bible. That was when he really began reading it, and he went on to Union Theological Seminary in New York.

narrative_blocks.header: His anniversary is Palm Sunday
narrative_blocks.body: Glover came to Pilgrim Congregational in Bozeman on 23 March 1979, after churches at Absarokee, in New Hampshire and at Billings. The congregation keeps his anniversary not on the date but on the day he arrived, Palm Sunday.

narrative_blocks.header: An open and affirming church
narrative_blocks.body: In 2011, under Glover, Pilgrim adopted a mission statement welcoming gay and lesbian members and became an open and affirming congregation. It was the church he had served for thirty-two years.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-two apartments for Bozeman
narrative_blocks.body: Glover chaired Interfaith Housing, the coalition of Bozeman churches that built a twenty-two-unit apartment house for low-income families, and sat on the board of the Intermountain Children's Home.

narrative_blocks.header: Grief is a deeper wisdom
narrative_blocks.body: In an essay for his church Glover took up the farmer and palliative counselor Stephen Jenkinson's charge that we suffer from 'grief illiteracy,' and asked whether a death could feed tomorrow, as Jesus', Gandhi's, Lincoln's and King's had.

narrative_blocks.header: From Japan, across Siberia
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth was living in Italy in 1909 and in Japan in 1910 and 1911, and from Japan she applied for a passport to travel overland across Siberia and Russia. She was an unmarried woman of forty-three from Unionville, Connecticut.

narrative_blocks.header: Blue eyes and a decided chin
narrative_blocks.body: Her passport described her at forty-three: five feet one and a half, blue eyes, a high forehead, a straight nose, a small mouth, light brown hair, a fair complexion, an oval face, and a decided chin.

narrative_blocks.header: An Atlantic crossing nearly every year
narrative_blocks.body: Through the 1920s Elizabeth crossed to Europe almost every year, coming home from Cherbourg, Boulogne or Rotterdam on the Veendam, the Volendam and the Rotterdam. In 1923 she came in twice, from Jamaica in April and from France in November.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventy-one, with a lodger
narrative_blocks.body: The 1940 census found Elizabeth at seventy-one in West Hartford, never married, with a traveling salesman lodging in her house. She had had a single year of high school, and had lived in Italy and Japan.

narrative_blocks.header: Home to Hillside at eighty-five
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth died in April 1954, at eighty-five, and was buried at Hillside Cemetery in Unionville, the town she was born in, where her father had lain since 1907.

narrative_blocks.header: His uncle's name, in full
narrative_blocks.body: James carried the whole name of his mother's brother, 1st Lt. James Quincy Porter, who was killed in France in July 1944, six years before James was born. His mother, Mary Ellen, had lost her brother at twenty-four.

narrative_blocks.header: Director of the Army's ammunition center
narrative_blocks.body: A veteran himself, James rose to direct the U.S. Army Defense Ammunition Center as a civilian, and the Department of the Army gave him its Meritorious Civilian Service Award. The Joint Logistics Commanders and the Association of the U.S. Army honored him too.

narrative_blocks.header: Springfield, then Ada
narrative_blocks.body: James graduated from Southwest Missouri State University in 1972, in the Ozarks country his Porter grandparents had settled, and later took a master's degree at East Central University in Ada, Oklahoma.

narrative_blocks.header: Home to West Plains at fifty-six
narrative_blocks.body: James died at Broken Arrow, Oklahoma, in February 2007, at fifty-six. He had already lost a son, Patrick, and was brought home to Oak Lawn Cemetery at West Plains, where his mother was buried five years later.

narrative_blocks.header: Ready for college at sixteen
narrative_blocks.body: Franklin was ready to enter college as a sophomore at sixteen, but his parents in Dalton could not afford it, and he spent some years in business and teaching before he turned to the law.

narrative_blocks.header: He read law with his future father-in-law
narrative_blocks.body: In 1842 Franklin entered William Porter's law office at Lee as a student. He graduated from Harvard Law School in 1844, was made Porter's partner the moment he was admitted in 1845, and that September married Porter's daughter Mary.

narrative_blocks.header: A Hartford practice, and a law book
narrative_blocks.body: About 1860 Franklin moved to Hartford and practiced with Ezra Hall, and in 1865 he sat in the Connecticut House. In 1869 he published American Commercial Law, a guide with practical forms for every state in the Union.

narrative_blocks.header: The house Harriet Beecher Stowe bought
narrative_blocks.body: Franklin built a house at 73 Forest Street in 1871, on the Nook Farm land he and Mary owned, and sold it two years later to Harriet Beecher Stowe, who lived in it until her death in 1896.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught radio to the Navy
narrative_blocks.body: Otis joined the Naval Reserve in 1940, trained at Annapolis, and spent most of the war teaching, at the Radio Material School in Washington and then at the Navy's school at Bowdoin College. He went to sea in the Atlantic only that last winter, and came out a lieutenant commander.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at Bowdoin, and twice related
narrative_blocks.body: Otis met Louise Gross of Brunswick while he was stationed there, and married her at Bowdoin College in June 1944. His sister Abby married Louise's brother William.

narrative_blocks.header: Lexington, La Jolla, then Mere Point
narrative_blocks.body: After the war Otis went to the Harvard Business School and began assisting its dean, and he and Louise raised three sons at Lexington, with three years at La Jolla. In 1981 they retired to Mere Point at Brunswick, next to the cottage Louise had summered in as a girl.

narrative_blocks.body: Henry took his Harvard A.B. in 1941, trained with the Naval Reserve at Newport, and served as an ensign and then a lieutenant aboard the carriers Yorktown and Ticonderoga. Discharged in December 1946, he went to Harvard Medical School.

narrative_blocks.header: A thoracic surgeon on a motorcycle
narrative_blocks.body: Henry, a thoracic surgeon who rode motorcycles, practiced in Fairfield County and served as an assistant medical examiner there. His five children and his second wife Joan's four made nine; he died at Ridgefield in 2004, at eighty-four.

narrative_blocks.header: Four children and five made nine
narrative_blocks.body: Joan married Henry Minot, the much-loved motorcycle-riding thoracic surgeon, who had five children to her four. So now there were nine, as her family put it.

narrative_blocks.header: An advice column in New York
narrative_blocks.body: Joan went to school in Westport, graduated from the University of Michigan, and in her early twenties lived in New York, answering readers' questions in a magazine's advice column.

narrative_blocks.header: Pools that blended into the land
narrative_blocks.body: For a few years Joan ran a landscaping business with Bill Rodier of Rodier Flowers, designing custom in-ground pools to blend into the land around them. She belonged to two Ridgefield garden clubs and was sometimes president of both.

narrative_blocks.header: Uptick, forty-five years
narrative_blocks.body: Joan kept a bridge club going for sixty years and a women's investment group, Uptick, for forty-five, and did her own investing until her eyesight failed.

narrative_blocks.header: Croquet and bread at Meadow Ridge
narrative_blocks.body: After fifty-five years in Ridgefield Joan moved to Meadow Ridge in Redding, where she played in croquet tournaments, joined the opera club and kept the store's accounts, stocking it with bread. She died there in July 2020, at ninety-four.

narrative_blocks.header: Oscar Hammerstein's stepson
narrative_blocks.body: Joan's first husband, Henry S. Jacobson, was the son of Dorothy Blanchard Hammerstein and the stepson of Oscar Hammerstein II, and Oscar's shows and music ran through their lives. They moved to Ridgefield in 1953 and parted after twenty-three years.

narrative_blocks.header: Bowdoin's first co-ed
narrative_blocks.body: Louise grew up at 11 Boody Street in Brunswick, in a family that was a mainstay of Bowdoin College and set out from there on expeditions to the Bay of Fundy, Panama and Ecuador. Auditing a Bowdoin course, she liked to call herself the college's first co-ed.

narrative_blocks.header: Biology at Smith, genetics at Columbia
narrative_blocks.body: Louise majored in biology at Smith, graduating in 1942, took a year of genetics at Columbia, and in the last years of the war taught biology and chemistry at Chatham Hall in Virginia.

narrative_blocks.header: Five solo shows after ninety
narrative_blocks.body: Louise never settled into one art form, and the Maine mid-coast was her favorite subject; her political cartoons ran in the town paper. She had five solo shows with the Casco Bay Art League after her ninetieth birthday.

narrative_blocks.header: Home to Mere Point
narrative_blocks.body: Louise and Otis retired in 1981 to Mere Point, next to the cottage she had summered in as a girl. After his death she married Vernon Westcott in 1997, and when he died she came back to Mere Point, where she died in 2020 at ninety-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: Her Christmas cards went early
narrative_blocks.body: Louise was an extrovert and a tireless correspondent with friends around the world. She mailed her 2019 Christmas cards early, 'just in case,' and died the following April.

narrative_blocks.header: Watching Boston's City Hall
narrative_blocks.body: Laurence studied at the Harvard Law School and went into the trust side of his father's office, but gave much of himself to the Good Government Association, Boston's league for municipal reform: chairman of its municipal statistics from 1897, and of its executive committee from 1903.

narrative_blocks.header: His orphaned niece's home
narrative_blocks.body: When his brother William died in 1900, three years after William's wife, their daughter Katharine made her home with Laurence. In 1904 he walked her up the aisle at King's Chapel and gave the wedding breakfast at his house on Commonwealth Avenue.

narrative_blocks.header: Given away by her uncle at King's Chapel
narrative_blocks.body: Katharine lost both parents by 1900 and made her home with her uncle Laurence Minot, who gave her away at King's Chapel at noon on 22 November 1904. She married Henry Morse Channing of Brookline, a Harvard man of 1902, with B. J. Lang at the organ.

narrative_blocks.header: A poet and two scholars' wives
narrative_blocks.body: Her daughter Anne married the painter Fairfield Porter and became a poet in her own right. Her daughter Katherine married the political scientist Pendleton Herring, and Barbara the geophysicist Francis Birch.

narrative_blocks.header: A miler and a violinist
narrative_blocks.body: William was one of the best intercollegiate milers of his day and captained the Harvard track team before taking his degree in 1907. He was also a cultivated musician and a fine violinist.

narrative_blocks.header: He succeeded his uncle Laurence
narrative_blocks.body: After two years at the Harvard Law School William joined the family office under his uncle Laurence Minot, and when Laurence died in 1921 he took over its large practice in trusteeships and real estate. In 1934 he formed Minot, Williams and Bangs.

narrative_blocks.header: Housing for wartime Savannah
narrative_blocks.body: In the First World War William directed building, housing and town site facilities at Savannah, Georgia, and afterwards directed real estate organizations across the country and was president of Minot, Kendall & Co., the investment bankers.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at thirty-three
narrative_blocks.body: William's first wife, Lucy Woodworth, the daughter of a Brookline tea merchant, died in 1919, and their first child, Lucy, had lived only four months. In 1922 he married Elizabeth Chapman of Brewster.

narrative_blocks.header: A year in Germany, and a sister's letters
narrative_blocks.body: Before Harvard, Hal was sent to live and study in Germany for a year, and his sister Barbara, fourteen, wrote him nearly every week from 1897 to 1898, once in verse: 'There was a youth named Hal Channing, who after much fussing and planning, sailed across the blue sea.'

narrative_blocks.header: He wanted to come home for the war
narrative_blocks.body: When war with Spain broke out in 1898, Hal was ashamed to be abroad and wanted to come home and enlist. His father, the psychiatrist Dr. Walter Channing, told him to wait; there were men enough.

narrative_blocks.header: Channing and Frothingham
narrative_blocks.body: Hal took his Harvard degree in 1902 and his law degree in 1904, the year he married Katharine Minot at King's Chapel. He practiced in Boston, in the family firm of Channing and Frothingham and with Channing, Rice & Tudor.

narrative_blocks.header: Counsel to the War Industries Board
narrative_blocks.body: In 1918 Hal was chief of the legal section of the War Industries Board, the agency that ran American industry for the war. Twenty years before, his father had kept him from enlisting for the war with Spain.

narrative_blocks.header: 273 acres by Little Pond for Audubon
narrative_blocks.body: In 1963, the year before he died, Hal gave the Massachusetts Audubon Society 273 acres adjoining Little Pond. He was vice-president of the Trustees of Reservations and belonged to the Massachusetts Forest and Park Association and the state and national Audubon societies.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty years at the Channing Sanitarium
narrative_blocks.body: From 1921 to 1951 Hal was president and a director of the Channing Sanitarium, the private hospital that carried the family name; his father, Dr. Walter Channing, was a psychiatrist. He also sat on the boards of the Winsor School and Garland Junior College.

narrative_blocks.header: Married again at eighty-three
narrative_blocks.body: His wife Katharine died in 1961. In January 1964, at eighty-three, Hal married Katherine Barbour Hartt in New York, and he died that October at his home on South Street.
