narrative_blocks.header: He took Little Boy to Tinian
narrative_blocks.body: Francis headed the engineering of the Little Boy bomb at Los Alamos, oversaw its manufacture, and went with it to Tinian to supervise its assembly and loading into the Enola Gay. The Navy gave Commander Birch the Legion of Merit.

narrative_blocks.header: The double plug
narrative_blocks.body: Francis devised the double plug that let the bomb be armed only after the Enola Gay was airborne, so that a crash on takeoff from Tinian would not set off a nuclear explosion.

narrative_blocks.header: What the Earth is made of
narrative_blocks.body: In 1952 Francis showed that the Earth's mantle is chiefly silicate minerals and its core crystalline and molten iron, conclusions still accepted. The Birch-Murnaghan equation of 1947 and Birch's law of 1961 carry his name.

narrative_blocks.header: Certain means dubious
narrative_blocks.body: His 1952 paper warned unwary readers that language changes under high pressure: certain means dubious, undoubtedly means perhaps, positive proof means vague suggestion, and pure iron an uncertain mixture of all the elements.

narrative_blocks.header: A telephone engineer turned physicist
narrative_blocks.body: Francis took an electrical engineering degree at Harvard in 1924 and worked for the New York Telephone Company, then studied magnetism at Strasbourg under Pierre Weiss. Back at Harvard he took his doctorate under Percy Bridgman.

narrative_blocks.header: A geophysicist by Depression chance
narrative_blocks.body: In 1932 Harvard offered Francis a research post in geophysics, though he knew little of rocks; with jobs scarce in the Depression he took it. He stayed his whole career, Sturgis Hooper Professor of Geology from 1949.

narrative_blocks.header: The National Medal of Science
narrative_blocks.body: President Johnson gave Francis the National Medal of Science in 1967, the Royal Astronomical Society its Gold Medal in 1973, and he led the Geological Society of America in 1964.

narrative_blocks.header: The blueprint for the Pentagon and CIA
narrative_blocks.body: Pendleton's 1941 book The Impact of War was among the first to speak of national security. In 1945 he worked for Ferdinand Eberstadt on the report that became the National Security Act of 1947, which created the Defense Department, the National Security Council and the CIA.

narrative_blocks.header: Wilson's inauguration at nine
narrative_blocks.body: At nine Pendleton went to Woodrow Wilson's inauguration in 1913, and it set him on the road to political science. He took an English degree at Johns Hopkins in 1925 and a doctorate in political science three years later.

narrative_blocks.header: Pressure groups before Congress
narrative_blocks.body: His dissertation, published in 1929 as Group Representation Before Congress, became one of the founding studies of pressure groups and how they work on government.

narrative_blocks.header: Harvard's school of public administration
narrative_blocks.body: Pendleton taught government at Harvard from 1928 and from 1936 was secretary of its new Graduate School of Public Administration, shaping what it taught. In 1946 he headed the secretariat of the United Nations Atomic Energy Commission.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty years running the SSRC
narrative_blocks.body: From 1948 to 1968 Pendleton ran the Social Science Research Council, which grew fourfold under him and drew the leading scholars of the day onto its committees. He was president of the American Political Science Association in 1952.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty years for Woodrow Wilson
narrative_blocks.body: From 1962 Pendleton led the Woodrow Wilson Foundation for nearly thirty years. He pressed the Johnson administration and Congress to create the Woodrow Wilson International Center for Scholars, and helped bring out Wilson's papers.

narrative_blocks.header: A hundred at the Windrows
narrative_blocks.body: Pendleton married Katherine Sedgwick Channing in 1933; she died in 1969, and two years later he married Virginia Staman Wood. He died at the Windrows in Plainsboro, New Jersey, in August 2004, at a hundred.

narrative_blocks.header: A Flaubert encyclopedia
narrative_blocks.body: Laurence taught French and comparative literature at Michigan State from 1963, a full professor from 1973, and published a dozen books, among them A Gustave Flaubert Encyclopedia and a study of Madame Bovary.

narrative_blocks.header: An elegy for his father
narrative_blocks.body: Laurence wrote an elegy for his father, Fairfield Porter, in 1978, and in 2020 gave away his papers about him, among them a copy of Rudy Burckhardt's 1953 film A Day in the Life of a Cleaning Woman, starring his parents.

narrative_blocks.header: Senegal, Canada and France
narrative_blocks.body: His teaching reached past France into African and Canadian studies. A U.S. Information Agency grant took him to Senegal in 1991, and Michigan State gave him its Distinguished Faculty Award in 1995.

narrative_blocks.header: Three Harvard degrees
narrative_blocks.body: Laurence took three Harvard degrees, an A.B. cum laude in 1957, an A.M. in 1959 and a doctorate in 1965, with six years in the Army Reserve's Corps of Engineers along the way.

narrative_blocks.header: A Boston Marathon runner
narrative_blocks.body: A professor of French who ran competitively, Laurence entered the Boston Marathon, and backpacked, played tennis and made music besides.

narrative_blocks.header: A whirlwind wartime romance
narrative_blocks.body: Alice met Ted Deppe, a B-24 pilot in training, while she was visiting her college roommate at Montgomery, and married him at Boise in September 1944 on his birthday. The marriage lasted sixty-four years.

narrative_blocks.header: The same cove every summer
narrative_blocks.body: Alice was an expert sailor. She summered at Bourne's Point in Wareham, at the cove she had come back to nearly every summer since she was a child, and took long trips across Buzzards Bay to the Islands.

narrative_blocks.header: Social work, and the League of Women Voters
narrative_blocks.body: Alice took her degree in social work at Wisconsin in 1946 and worked two years for the Dane County pension department. At Bloomington she was president of the League of Women Voters and a member for fifty years.

military_service.notes: Served stateside July 1945 to December 1946.

narrative_blocks.header: Three Genres, never out of print
narrative_blocks.body: Stephen's textbook Three Genres, on writing poetry, fiction and drama, came out in 1965 and never went out of print. At his death it had been used to teach writing in all fifty states, and a ninth edition, written with Diane Thiel, was due that spring.

narrative_blocks.header: Maine after the bomb
narrative_blocks.body: His first novel, Chill of Dusk, published by Doubleday in 1964, is set in a small Maine community decades after a nuclear war, beset by barbarians and sun worshippers. Surviving the Flood, in 1981, told Noah's story as his youngest son Ham saw it.

narrative_blocks.header: A peace candidate for Congress
narrative_blocks.body: In 1966 Stephen ran for Congress in Connecticut's 6th District as a third-party candidate against the Vietnam War and took 5,731 votes. He counseled students applying as conscientious objectors, and a short film, One Man Can Make a Difference, was made about him.

narrative_blocks.header: Stories in the Atlantic and the Paris Review
narrative_blocks.body: Stephen's stories ran in the Atlantic, Harper's, Playboy and the Paris Review, one was chosen for the O. Henry Prize Stories, and he won two National Endowment for the Arts fellowships. The Sewanee Review's editor called him one of the finest short story writers of his generation.

narrative_blocks.header: Founding chair at Riverside
narrative_blocks.body: After teaching at Bowdoin and at Trinity College in Hartford, Stephen went west as the first chair of the new Department of Creative Writing at the University of California, Riverside, which became the only undergraduate creative writing major in the UC system. He retired in 1995.

narrative_blocks.header: A world federalist at twenty
narrative_blocks.body: After Brooks School Stephen served stateside in the Air Rescue Service from 1945 to 1946, then worked full time as a volunteer for the Student Federalists, the campus movement for world government. He took his Harvard degree in 1951 and a Johns Hopkins master's in 1955.

narrative_blocks.header: A saltwater farmhouse at Harpswell
narrative_blocks.body: Stephen and his wife Ginny, a Riverside printmaker whose work sometimes went on his covers, spent their summers at Harpswell, Maine, in an 1800 saltwater farmhouse that found its way into his fiction and into her paintings.

narrative_blocks.header: Inside LEGO's turnaround
narrative_blocks.body: As IMD's LEGO Professor of Innovation from 2002 to 2010, Dave was given rare access to the company's management through its turnaround, and told the story in Brick by Brick: How LEGO Rewrote the Rules of Innovation and Conquered the Global Toy Industry, in 2013.

narrative_blocks.header: Computer engineering, like his father
narrative_blocks.body: After two years at Wesleyan, Dave took his computer engineering degree in 1982 at Illinois, where his father James had designed the arithmetic of the ILLIAC computers. MIT's Sloan School gave him his doctorate in 1990.

narrative_blocks.header: McKinsey, Sweden and software
narrative_blocks.body: Before teaching, Dave spent five years at McKinsey in the United States and Sweden, ran the consulting firm ATG, and held executive posts at software companies, including a year as chief executive of Tradeffect.

narrative_blocks.header: Enterprise architecture as strategy
narrative_blocks.body: Dave is known as much for enterprise architecture as for innovation: with Jeanne Ross and Peter Weill he wrote Enterprise Architecture as Strategy in 2006, and on his own The Power of Little Ideas.

narrative_blocks.header: Innovation Navigation on Sirius XM
narrative_blocks.body: At Wharton Dave hosted Innovation Navigation, a weekly live show on Sirius XM's Wharton Business Radio, unscripted conversations with executives, faculty and thought leaders about how companies innovate.

narrative_blocks.header: Wharton, then MIT Sloan
narrative_blocks.body: From 2011 to 2017 Dave was a Professor of Practice at Wharton, and he now teaches product development and digital product management at the MIT Sloan School, where he took his doctorate.

narrative_blocks.header: An afternoon in the library
narrative_blocks.body: At Biogen and then Pfizer, Phoebe helped build biomedical text-mining, automated tools that let researchers read the whole literature before repeating old work. She summed it up for them: a week in the lab will save you an afternoon in the library.

narrative_blocks.header: Proteins, from Toronto to Chicago
narrative_blocks.body: After Miami University Phoebe did research at Toronto's Hospital for Sick Children, then took a doctorate in molecular biology at Chicago in 1997, with work on how cells break down their own proteins.

narrative_blocks.header: Boston to Montreal and back by bike
narrative_blocks.body: In 2001 Phoebe rode the 750-mile Boston-Montréal-Boston and she ran several full marathons; her daily commute included eleven miles on a folding bicycle.

narrative_blocks.header: Telluride to Moab
narrative_blocks.body: Her last vacation was a seven-day mountain-bike ride from Telluride to Moab. Winter weekends went to skiing at Killington, and summers to West Beach at Beverly Farms.

narrative_blocks.header: A keynote she never gave
narrative_blocks.body: The week she died Phoebe was due in Tokyo to give the keynote at the Languages in Biology and Medicine Symposium. She died unexpectedly near her home in Beverly in December 2013, at forty-seven.

narrative_blocks.header: A promise of college to every student
narrative_blocks.body: At E City, the after-school entrepreneurship program he founded in Cleveland in 2002, John told every student the same thing: if you stay here, you will get into a four-year college. That's my promise to you.

narrative_blocks.header: Software he sold to Xerox
narrative_blocks.body: John founded the Bradley Company, a software firm in Warrensville Heights, in 1983 and sold it to Xerox in 1998, then turned to teaching inner-city Cleveland teenagers to start businesses of their own.

narrative_blocks.header: Street smarts, put to work
narrative_blocks.body: E City rested on his belief that inner-city kids with mental toughness, street smarts and creativity could turn them to business: each student got a small grant to buy goods and resell them, then pitched a plan to a panel of judges.

narrative_blocks.header: E Prep, eleven months a year
narrative_blocks.body: In August 2006 John opened E Prep, a charter school for 125 sixth-graders in uniform, in class from 7:30 to 5:30 eleven months a year. On the first day, he said, he would shake each child's hand and tell them they were going to college.

bio.title: T/5
bio.bio_blurb: Cavalry reconnaissance soldier killed in action

military_service.notes: Service number 36458387. Enlisted at Kalamazoo 25 March 1943; overseas October 1943. Died of wounds in Belgium 31 December 1944. Purple Heart. Buried Netherlands American Cemetery, Margraten, Plot E, Row 3, Grave 14.

narrative_blocks.header: Money for his brother's schooling
narrative_blocks.body: In the battle that killed him, Robert handed one of his buddies a sum of money with instructions to send it to his younger brother Jerry, so that Jerry could go to Culver too. He died of his wounds in Belgium on the last day of 1944, at twenty.

narrative_blocks.header: Varsity three times over at Culver
narrative_blocks.body: At Culver Military Academy Robert was a member of the Troop and played varsity baseball, tennis and basketball, and his letters were full of the place. He enlisted at Kalamazoo in March 1943 and was overseas that October.

narrative_blocks.header: A grave the Dutch adopted
narrative_blocks.body: Robert served as a technician fifth grade in the 78th Division's cavalry reconnaissance troop. He lies at the Netherlands American Cemetery at Margraten, where Dutch families have adopted every grave since 1945.

military_service.unit: U.S. Army Air Forces, B-24 pilot
military_service.notes: Enlisted at Chicago 25 February 1943; trained at Miami Beach; commissioned at Stewart Field; flew B-24 combat missions from Italy over Germany and Austria (22 per the Minot genealogy, 27 per his obituary); Air Medal; discharged 5 October 1945.

career.role: Professor, and for twenty-one years chairman, Department of Parks and Recreation

narrative_blocks.header: An NCAA champion turned away
narrative_blocks.body: Ted played on Wisconsin's 1941 NCAA championship basketball team, and in February 1943 a basketball injury got him turned down when he tried to enlist. He went to another recruiting center and was taken.

narrative_blocks.header: A B-24 pilot who had never flown
narrative_blocks.body: Ted had never been in a plane, but he became a B-24 pilot. Learning the bomber at Montgomery, he met Alice Minot, who was visiting her college roommate; they married at Boise on 2 September 1944, his birthday, and he went to Italy to fly missions over Germany and Austria.

narrative_blocks.header: A year or two that lasted thirty-four
narrative_blocks.body: Ted came to Indiana University for his doctorate in recreation and was asked to stay on for a year or two; he stayed from 1953 to 1987, chairing the Department of Parks and Recreation for twenty-one years, and co-wrote Recreation in American Life.

narrative_blocks.header: A recreation curriculum for New Zealand
narrative_blocks.body: A Fulbright took Ted to Lincoln College in New Zealand for six months, where he helped set up its recreation curriculum. Before Indiana he had been the first superintendent of recreation at Superior, Wisconsin.

narrative_blocks.header: A thousand miles around Ireland at nineteen
narrative_blocks.body: In 1970, at nineteen, Ted walked a thousand-mile circle around Ireland, a six-month hike set up as an independent study with a poetry professor at Earlham College. Ireland felt like his second home from then on.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty years a nurse
narrative_blocks.body: Poetry paid nothing, so Ted became a registered nurse and spent twenty years in coronary care units and psychiatric hospitals; his first two books came out while he was still nursing. Nursing, he said, requires an active attention, just as poetry does.

narrative_blocks.header: The dream that made him write
narrative_blocks.body: One night Ted dreamed he was dying of a heart attack and leaving his children only his poems, then realized the poems were terrible and ran to destroy them. Waking, he decided to start writing good ones, and wrote at least two hours a day.

narrative_blocks.header: The southernmost house in Ireland
narrative_blocks.body: At fifty, worn down by hospital staffing cuts, Ted and Annie sold their house and rented the southernmost house in Ireland, on the sea cliffs of Cape Clear Island, for a year. He was offered a teaching post and they stayed; Cape Clear became the title of his 2002 collection.

narrative_blocks.header: Orpheus on the Red Line
narrative_blocks.body: Ted's collections run from Children of the Air in 1990 through The Wanderer King, Cape Clear and Orpheus on the Red Line to Liminal Blue in 2017. He won a Pushcart Prize and two National Endowment for the Arts fellowships.

narrative_blocks.header: Director of Stonecoast in Ireland
narrative_blocks.body: From 2006 Ted directed the Stonecoast MFA's residencies in Ireland, holding workshops in the living room of a bed-and-breakfast by the sea, and he taught in Lancaster University's distance MA. He had been writer in residence at Phillips Academy and at the James Merrill House.

narrative_blocks.header: Alive and well, despite the notice
narrative_blocks.body: In 2018 the Berea College magazine printed Ted's death notice by mistake. He wrote in as Bob, the name his nursing classmates of 1978 knew him by, to say he was alive and well, with six books of poetry and his hospital poems in four nursing anthologies.

narrative_blocks.body: Jack won the Indiana state title in the 100-yard backstroke in 1970 and 1971, setting a state meet record as a junior and lowering it as a senior, and Bloomington High won the team title both years. He swam in the Olympic trials in 1972.

narrative_blocks.header: Chateaubriand against the Iraq war
narrative_blocks.body: Reid's tastes ran from jazz to Neapolitan song and art song, and from the classics through eighteenth-century letters to Wallace Stevens and R. Crumb. To protest the invasion of Iraq, he read Chateaubriand in French for a year.

narrative_blocks.header: In University Hall in 1969
narrative_blocks.body: At Harvard, where he took his degree in philosophy in 1972, Reid was part of the SDS takeover of University Hall in the spring strike of 1969.

narrative_blocks.header: A nurse in mental health
narrative_blocks.body: Reid took nursing degrees at Texas in 1977 and Hunter in 1984 and made his career in Austin from 1987 as a clinical nurse specialist in mental health: director of nursing at Seton Shoal Creek Hospital, then psychiatric emergency services, then private practice until 2023.

narrative_blocks.header: His father's Harpswell
narrative_blocks.body: Reid spent as much time as he could at the family's summer place at Harpswell, Maine, taming the vegetation and swimming and kayaking in the cold water. He died at Austin in April 2024 of injuries from a road accident, at seventy-three.

narrative_blocks.header: She seemed to be sitting in the sky
narrative_blocks.body: In her poem The Bullig Path, Annie sits in the rock chair on the Cape Clear cliffs watching for whales while Ted and their daughter hike down to the sea arch. Climbing back, Ted tells her she seemed to be sitting in the sky, and the line became the title of her first book, in 2003.

narrative_blocks.header: A novel that became poems
narrative_blocks.body: Annie met Ted in the poetry workshop at Earlham College. On Cape Clear Island in 2000 she meant to write a novel and wrote much of Sitting in the Sky instead; Wren Cantata followed in 2009 and Night Collage in 2021.

narrative_blocks.header: Connecticut, then Connemara
narrative_blocks.body: After many years in Connecticut, Annie and Ted moved to Ireland in 2000 and settled on the Connemara coast, where they run the Stonecoast MFA's Irish residencies. Her grandparents' Irish birth gave them both Irish passports.

narrative_blocks.header: He took over his father's papers in 1982
narrative_blocks.body: In 1982 Ralph took over Ingersoll Publications, the group of small Northeast dailies and weeklies his father had begun in 1957, and ran it from Lakeville, Connecticut. The company made its name buying struggling papers and restoring them to financial health.

narrative_blocks.header: One of the country's largest newspaper groups
narrative_blocks.body: Under Ralph the company grew through the 1980s into one of the largest newspaper groups in the United States, at its height 41 dailies and 200 weeklies, the New Haven Register among them. He also sat on the board of United Press International.

narrative_blocks.header: He took on St. Louis from Illinois
narrative_blocks.body: Ralph moved on St. Louis from the Illinois side: the Suburban Journals weeklies in 1984, the 150-year-old Alton Telegraph in 1985, and in 1989 a new daily tabloid of his own, the St. Louis Sun.

narrative_blocks.header: Built on junk bonds, sold in 1990
narrative_blocks.body: The expansion was financed with junk bonds arranged through Michael Milken of Drexel Burnham Lambert. When that market collapsed, Ralph sold his American papers to his partner, E. M. Warburg, Pincus & Co., in 1990, and ran the group's papers in England and Ireland until 1994.

narrative_blocks.header: He started in a one-room workshop
narrative_blocks.body: Ian founded his furniture shop in 1975 in a one-room workshop at West Cornwall, in the Litchfield County hills where his father lived. It grew into a guild of craftsmen, but each piece is still made by hand by one person, and ships as far as Europe and Japan.

narrative_blocks.header: Eighty-five percent of a design is history
narrative_blocks.body: His shop works to a rule: eighty-five percent of a design is grounded in history and fifteen percent is intuition. It builds in any style or period, or to its own designs, and to take an intelligent step forward, it holds, you have to know everything that came before.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother died giving birth to him
narrative_blocks.body: Ian's mother, Elaine, died giving birth to him in 1948, the year PM folded, leaving his father, Ralph Ingersoll, with two babies and no income.

narrative_blocks.header: Seventeen years at Grace Baptist
narrative_blocks.body: Martin came to Washington about 1946 as pastor of Grace Baptist Church and stayed until 1963, then led Allentown Baptist Church in Fort Washington, Maryland, until 1968. He held master's and doctor's degrees in theology from Eastern Baptist Theological Seminary.

narrative_blocks.header: A gospel tent on Summer Street
narrative_blocks.body: As pastor of First Baptist Church at Doylestown, Pennsylvania, Martin opened a month of nightly meetings for a Young People's Crusade for Christ in a gospel tent on Summer Street in Passaic, New Jersey, preaching Sundays at half past three and again at nine.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a Bangall girl in 1918
narrative_blocks.body: Martin married Effie Knickerbocker of Bangall, New York, in June 1918, and they were together fifty-six years, until her death in 1974. Their son Herbert followed him into the Baptist ministry, and Herbert's son Paul did too.

notable.notable_blurb: U.S. Open polo champion; killed in action, 1945

narrative_blocks.header: Eight goals at twenty-one, two over his father
narrative_blocks.body: Charles won the 1941 U.S. Open at Meadow Brook with John and Michael Phipps and Alan Corey, and the National 20-goal the same season, at twenty-one and rated eight goals. His father, Skiddy, had won the Open four times between 1912 and 1920 on a rating of six.

narrative_blocks.header: Hockey, baseball, hunt races, and a voice
narrative_blocks.body: At St. Paul's School Charles took his letters twice in baseball and twice in hockey, and after it he rode in the hunt races and trained as an architect. The thing people remembered first, though, was his singing voice.

narrative_blocks.header: Married seven weeks after Pearl Harbor
narrative_blocks.body: Charles married Sara Clucas on January 24, 1942, in the private chapel at Hamilton Farms, the Cutting estate at Gladstone, New Jersey, with his brother Skiddy as best man and sixteen ushers, H. Clay Frick among them. Within weeks he had enlisted in the Army.

narrative_blocks.header: A Teller mine, four weeks before V-E Day
narrative_blocks.body: Charles went overseas early in 1945 as executive officer of D Troop, 93rd Cavalry Reconnaissance Squadron, 13th Armored Division. On April 10, south of Hennef, his jeep ran over a Teller mine. He was twenty-five, and the war in Europe had twenty-eight days left.

narrative_blocks.header: Letters to a daughter he never met
narrative_blocks.body: Charles wrote home through his last winter to Sara, who was carrying their second child. Frederica was born seven weeks after the mine, read those letters for hours as a girl of eight, and took his voice to the Metropolitan Opera; in 1998 she premiered Elegies, a song cycle made from them.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed before her daughter came
narrative_blocks.body: Sara grew up at Far Hills, New Jersey, and married Charles von Stade in January 1942. She was carrying their second child when he was killed in Germany in April 1945; Frederica, born seven weeks later, became a Metropolitan Opera star.

narrative_blocks.header: A secretary at the CIA
narrative_blocks.body: After the war Sara married Horace Fuller, a State Department official, and lived for a time in Greece and Italy. When that marriage ended she worked in Washington as a secretary for the CIA, before moving to Oldwick, New Jersey.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifteen years in County Kildare
narrative_blocks.body: After years at Oldwick, New Jersey, Sara moved to County Kildare in Ireland, to Ballytore, about 1968. She died in February 1983 at Nassau Hospital in Mineola, Long Island, at sixty-four.

notable.notable_blurb: Metropolitan Opera mezzo-soprano

narrative_blocks.header: Salesgirl at Tiffany's, then Mannes
narrative_blocks.body: After a year in Paris Frederica sold stationery at Tiffany's in New York and sang in nightclubs and summer stock. In 1966 she walked into the Mannes School of Music for a part-time course in sight-reading and was talked into its full degree instead.

narrative_blocks.header: Rudolf Bing signed her from an audition
narrative_blocks.body: A semifinalist in the Met's 1969 auditions, Frederica was called out of a rehearsal room to sing privately for Sir Rudolf Bing, and left with a three-year contract. She made her debut on January 10, 1970, as the Third Boy in The Magic Flute, then sang eighteen pages and maids.

narrative_blocks.header: Cherubino, from Santa Fe to Vienna
narrative_blocks.body: Cherubino in The Marriage of Figaro became Frederica's calling card: Santa Fe in 1971, then Paris and Glyndebourne in 1973, Salzburg in 1974 and Vienna in 1977, with Rosina at Covent Garden and La Scala between. Her range ran all the way to Magnolia in Show Boat.

narrative_blocks.header: The Met mounted Mélisande for her
narrative_blocks.body: For Frederica's twenty-fifth season the Metropolitan Opera staged a new Pelléas et Mélisande in 1995, and for her thirtieth a new Merry Widow in 2000. She made more than a hundred recordings and was nominated nine times for a Grammy.

narrative_blocks.header: She sang for four presidents
narrative_blocks.body: Frederica sang at the White House for Presidents Nixon, Carter, Reagan and George H. W. Bush, starred in the gala for the 1992 Winter Olympics, and sang in Leonard Slatkin's televised concert for the dead of September 11.

narrative_blocks.header: A song cycle from her father's letters
narrative_blocks.body: For years Frederica wanted a song cycle made from the letters her father wrote home in 1945. Kim Vaeth turned them into poems, Richard Danielpour set them as Elegies, and in January 1998 she sang the premiere at Jacksonville, with Thomas Hampson singing her father.

narrative_blocks.header: Born seven weeks after the mine
narrative_blocks.body: Frederica was born in New Jersey seven weeks after her father, Charles von Stade, was killed in Germany, and read his wartime letters for hours as a girl: "There was a kind of glamor about my having an absentee father who was a war hero."

narrative_blocks.header: Maria Callas picked him for Juilliard
narrative_blocks.body: As a student Peter worked through the Goldovsky opera workshops in Denver and Wheeling and at Hunter College, and Maria Callas chose him for the Juilliard Opera Center.

narrative_blocks.header: He inherited his teacher's studio
narrative_blocks.body: When their teacher Sebastian Engelberg fell ill, Peter took over Frederica von Stade's lessons, from 1975 to 1985, and after Engelberg died in 1979 Mannes asked him to fill the vacancy; he stayed on its faculty more than a decade.

narrative_blocks.header: Master classes in ten countries
narrative_blocks.body: Peter has taught master classes for singers and instrumentalists in ten countries, from the Vienna University of Music to the Teatro Colón, where he presided over the judges for the Richard Wagner Foundation. In 2007 he published The Telling of Our Truths.

narrative_blocks.header: A divorce taught in law schools
narrative_blocks.body: Peter met Frederica at Mannes in 1967, married her in 1973 and had two daughters with her before they divorced in 1990. Their case, Elkus v. Elkus, decided in 1991, turned on whether her career and earnings were marital property, and first-year law students still read it.

narrative_blocks.header: Immanuel House, for Hartford's elderly poor
narrative_blocks.body: As minister of Immanuel Congregational Church, Robert was the moving force behind Immanuel House, a large Hartford apartment complex for low-income elderly people. His daughter Edith spent her last years living in it.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-four years at Immanuel
narrative_blocks.body: Robert was minister of the First Congregational Church of Litchfield for seven years from 1949, then came to Immanuel in Hartford in 1956 and stayed until 1980. He led the Greater Hartford Council of Churches and sat on the board of the Connecticut Prison Association.

narrative_blocks.header: Five years in Army intelligence
narrative_blocks.body: Robert left a Harvard teaching fellowship for the Army in 1941 and spent five years in intelligence, as a captain in the War Department's Intelligence Division in Washington and then with G-2 at Frankfurt. He came out with the Bronze Star.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the life of Horace Bushnell
narrative_blocks.body: Robert wrote Of Singular Genius, Of Singular Grace, a life of Horace Bushnell, Hartford's great nineteenth-century pastor, and several widely used hymn texts, the craft his father Deane had championed at the Hymn Society. He called his memoir My Moment in History.

narrative_blocks.header: Nephew of the Dulles brothers
narrative_blocks.body: Robert's mother, Margaret Dulles Edwards, was a sister of John Foster Dulles, Eisenhower's Secretary of State, of Allen Dulles of the CIA, and of the diplomat Eleanor Dulles.

narrative_blocks.header: Ordained when few women were
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah was ordained in April 1951 by the Connecticut Conference of Congregational Christian Churches, in the Litchfield church where her husband Robert was minister, at a time when few women served in the ministry. She went on to interim pulpits across northwest Connecticut.

narrative_blocks.header: First woman on Union Seminary's board
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah took her divinity degree at Union Theological Seminary in 1950, and in 1962 she became the first woman on its board, where she sat until 1977.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-five years of New Testament Greek
narrative_blocks.body: With a Hartford Seminary doctorate in 1974, Sarah taught the New Testament there as an adjunct professor for twenty-five years, a teacher of its Greek and a scholar of the Gospel of John. With Robert Berkey she wrote Christological Perspectives and Christology in Dialogue.

narrative_blocks.header: Uppsala for the Hartford Times
narrative_blocks.body: In 1968 Sarah covered the World Council of Churches assembly at Uppsala, in Sweden, as press representative for the Hartford Times. At home she led an ecumenical women's study group that all Hartford knew as the Bible Ladies.

narrative_blocks.header: Married by the groom's father
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah married Robert Lansing Edwards on September 6, 1947, in the Randolph Community Church in New Hampshire, near her family's summer place, Sugar Plum Farm; his father, Deane Edwards, performed the ceremony. They were married fifty-eight years.

narrative_blocks.header: The house her father built for the elderly

narrative_blocks.header: He presided over the Woodmere Art Museum
narrative_blocks.body: Charles spent many years on the board of the Woodmere Art Museum in Chestnut Hill and served as its president. He was also co-vice chair of the Morris Arboretum of the University of Pennsylvania and a trustee of the Morris Animal Refuge.

narrative_blocks.header: He ate the soup from Warhol's signed can
narrative_blocks.body: At Penn, where he led Zeta Psi, Charles played bass in a band called the Magic Mushrooms, which played a concert at an Andy Warhol party. Hungry one day, he opened the Campbell's soup can Warhol had signed and ate the soup.

narrative_blocks.header: Wissahickon skater, Millbrook class president
narrative_blocks.body: As a boy Charles competed as a skater with his sister Trish at the Wissahickon Skating Club. At Millbrook School in New York he was president of both his class and the student council, graduating in 1965.

narrative_blocks.header: He rode his motorcycle to Maine
narrative_blocks.body: Charles rode his motorcycle between Philadelphia and his house at Northeast Harbor, Maine, and toured Italy on one. He changed his own brake pads and bled the lines himself, and taught his son Andrew to do the same.

narrative_blocks.header: He lost his mother at seventeen
narrative_blocks.body: Charles lost his mother, Alice, at seventeen and was a father at twenty-two, when his daughter Anna was born. Over a year of evenings he built a model railroad across the basement with his son Andrew.

narrative_blocks.header: Born and died at Chestnut Hill Hospital
narrative_blocks.body: Charles was born at Chestnut Hill Hospital in Philadelphia on 15 November 1946, and died there after a short illness on 15 January 2025, seventy-eight years later.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote the book on his grandfather's patient
narrative_blocks.body: Luke's 2016 bestseller Patient H.M. retold the case of Henry Molaison, the man his grandfather's operation left unable to form new memories. It won the PEN/E.O. Wilson Literary Science Writing Award and the Los Angeles Times Book Prize.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandmother had been in the asylum
narrative_blocks.body: Luke grew up hearing only that his grandmother Emily had once had a breakdown. Researching the book, he found she had been committed to an asylum where his grandfather was performing lobotomies, and letters suggesting the surgeon hoped to cure her.

narrative_blocks.header: MIT disputed his account of Henry Molaison
narrative_blocks.body: For decades a small group of MIT scientists had controlled both access to Henry Molaison and the telling of his story. Patient H.M. challenged their account of gentle, ethical research, MIT publicly criticized the book, and Luke answered each point.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran a marathon in Antarctica on assignment
narrative_blocks.body: On assignment Luke has run a marathon in Antarctica, tracked a bull elephant across northern Kenya and walked three hundred and forty miles of the Mexican border. His article Tonight on Dateline This Man Will Die was the basis for the film Primetime.

narrative_blocks.header: He was nine when his grandfather died
narrative_blocks.body: Luke was nine when his grandfather died in 1984, and knew him as a dashing surgeon and world traveller with a rotating fleet of sports cars.

narrative_blocks.header: His verdict on mid-century psychosurgery
narrative_blocks.body: Luke wrote of the era his grandfather worked in: “By the middle of the twentieth century, the breaking of human brains was intentional, premeditated, clinical.”

narrative_blocks.header: She married the stonemason in 1818
narrative_blocks.body: Janet McPhee, from Glengarry in Upper Canada, married John Redpath at Montreal on 19 December 1818, two years after he had walked in from Quebec City.

narrative_blocks.header: She died the year John James was born
narrative_blocks.body: Janet died at Montreal on 26 July 1834, the year her youngest, John James, was born, and was buried at Mount Royal. Her husband married again the next year.

narrative_blocks.header: Her daughter Elizabeth married John Dougall
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth, Janet's eldest, married John Dougall, the editor of the Montreal Witness, and her father gave the couple the old Desrivières house on his Mount Royal estate.

narrative_blocks.header: Her daughter Helen married the refinery's manager
narrative_blocks.body: Helen married George Alexander Drummond, a young Edinburgh chemist at her father's refinery, in 1857. He became Sir George, a senator and president of the Bank of Montreal, and one of the sugar ships carried her name.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son Peter built McGill's Redpath Museum
narrative_blocks.body: Peter, Janet's eldest son, born in 1821, founded McGill's Redpath Museum in 1880, retired that year to the Manor House at Chislehurst in Kent, and gave the university its Redpath Library in 1893.

narrative_blocks.header: Drummond Street was named for her
narrative_blocks.body: In May 1842 Jane's husband gave the city the land for a street and named it Drummond Street for her, not for General Gordon Drummond, as is often supposed.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father trained John Redpath
narrative_blocks.body: Jane was the daughter of George Drummond, the Edinburgh stonemason and building contractor under whom John Redpath learned his trade before he left for Canada in 1816.

narrative_blocks.header: Mistress of Terrace Bank until 1907
narrative_blocks.body: Widowed in 1869, Jane stayed on at Terrace Bank under her husband's will for thirty-eight more years. Her nephew, the architect Andrew Thomas Taylor, lived with her there from 1883 to 1890. She died in the house in 1907.

narrative_blocks.header: Married in 1835, a month short of twenty
narrative_blocks.body: Jane married John Redpath on 11 September 1835, a month short of her twentieth birthday. He was a widower with seven children by Janet McPhee, and Jane bore him ten more.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son George married Alice Mills
narrative_blocks.body: Jane's son George Drummond Redpath married Alice Stiles Mills, the late mayor's youngest daughter, at Shanklin, in England, in May 1867. Alice died two years later, and George died at Colorado Springs in 1877, at thirty-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: Her brother married her stepdaughter
narrative_blocks.body: In 1857 Jane's younger brother, George Alexander Drummond, a chemist at the Redpath refinery, married her stepdaughter Helen. He became Sir George, a senator and president of the Bank of Montreal.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven Sisters, seven women presidents
narrative_blocks.body: Bryn Mawr named Pat its sixth president in March 1978, while she was away on sabbatical in California, and her inauguration marked the first time all of the Seven Sisters colleges were headed by women.

narrative_blocks.header: Nineteen years at the head of Bryn Mawr
narrative_blocks.body: Pat took office in a time of double-digit inflation and in nineteen years led two capital campaigns, balanced the budget, brought in long-term planning and built two new libraries. Bryn Mawr and Haverford opened majors to each other's students as she began.

narrative_blocks.header: From philosophy fellow to dean
narrative_blocks.body: Pat taught philosophy at the University of Delaware, then came to Bryn Mawr in 1961 as an assistant and fellow in the department. She took her doctorate there in 1969, and the next year was made dean of the undergraduate college.

narrative_blocks.header: The Mellon Foundation, then Franklin’s society
narrative_blocks.body: After Bryn Mawr Pat spent ten years as a vice president of the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation, and in 2007 became executive officer of the American Philosophical Society, the country's oldest learned society, which had elected her in 1983.

narrative_blocks.header: Zestful delight in the human comedy
narrative_blocks.body: At her retirement Hanna Holborn Gray, chairing the trustees, praised Pat's unwavering dedication to rigorous standards of intelligent thinking and constructive debate, joined to her humor and zestful delight in the variety and range of the human comedy.

narrative_blocks.header: Granddaughter of Johnson & Johnson's builder

narrative_blocks.body: Howard's parents were first cousins, Howard Melville Hanna Jr. and Jean Claire Hanna, playmates since childhood. narrative_blocks.header: Married eleven months
narrative_blocks.body: Howard married Pamela Humphrey in September 1935. He died at Bratenahl the following August, at twenty-seven, and she was a widow at twenty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: His father and hers ran the same company
narrative_blocks.body: His father became the first president of the M. A. Hanna Company when it incorporated in 1922, and its chairman in 1929, the year he organized the National Steel Company. That same year George Humphrey, the father of the girl Howard would marry, became its president.

narrative_blocks.header: Grandson of Mark Hanna’s brother
narrative_blocks.body: His grandfather Howard Melville Hanna was the younger brother of Senator Mark Hanna and a schoolmate and lifelong friend of John D. Rockefeller. In 1896 he bought Pebble Hill Plantation at Thomasville, where the family wintered.

narrative_blocks.header: She grew up at The Wings on Dosoris
narrative_blocks.body: Louise grew up at 12 East 53rd Street and at The Wings, her father's house on Dosoris Island at Glen Cove, which James Gamble Rogers remodeled in 1913. She married David Ingalls in 1922, and their children were Edith, Louise and David.

narrative_blocks.header: Dosoris, from the Woolseys to the Morgans
narrative_blocks.body: Dosoris had been the Woolsey family's estate since the 1740s and then Charles Dana's arboretum; in 1905 Paul Dana sold her father its fifteen acres with the old house. After her mother died in 1947, Junius Spencer Morgan III, who owned the rest of the island, bought The Wings too.

narrative_blocks.header: Her grandfather was Henry Flagler's half-brother
narrative_blocks.body: Her grandfather Daniel Harkness was a half-brother of both Henry Flagler and Stephen Harkness, who backed Rockefeller's refinery, and her grandmother Isabella was the sister of Flagler's first wife, Mary. Stephen's son Lamon, her father's cousin, built Walnut Hall.

narrative_blocks.header: A curatorship at the Cleveland Museum of Art
narrative_blocks.body: Edith became a noted Cleveland art collector, and in 2003 the Ingalls Foundation endowed the Paul J. and Edith Ingalls Vignos Curator of European Painting and Sculpture at the Cleveland Museum of Art, in her and her husband's names.

narrative_blocks.header: Sarah Lawrence named a program for her
narrative_blocks.body: Edith went to Laurel School and Westover and graduated from Sarah Lawrence College in 1945, the year she received a Meritorious Achievement Award for her war service. In 1998 Sarah Lawrence created the Edith I. Vignos Faculty Outreach Program, which sends its faculty to give seminars in cities across the country and abroad.

narrative_blocks.header: Regent of Washington's sister's house
narrative_blocks.body: Edith was a regent, and by 1986 president of the board of regents, of Kenmore in Fredericksburg, Virginia, the house of George Washington's sister Betty and her husband Fielding Lewis.

narrative_blocks.header: Trustee from Laurel to the frontier nurses
narrative_blocks.body: Edith was a trustee of Laurel School for almost twenty years and of the Visiting Nurse Association of Cleveland, the Great Lakes Shakespeare Festival and the Frontier Nursing Service of Kentucky, and sat on the board of the Cleveland Botanical Garden.

narrative_blocks.header: Bonefish in the Yucatán, Luders races in Maine
narrative_blocks.body: Edith gardened at Hunting Valley and at Milestone, the family plantation at Thomasville, Georgia, fished for bonefish in the Yucatán, and summered at Northeast Harbor, Maine, where she raced in the Luders class. In 1996 she travelled to India.

cross_connections.display_label: rode as a Frontier Nursing Service courier in the Kentucky hills

bio.bio_blurb: President, Cleveland Museum of Natural History

narrative_blocks.header: Navy pilot, aircraft builder, museum president
narrative_blocks.body: David Jr. flew Navy fighters from 1956 to 1960, helped found Grumman American Aviation in 1969, and led the Cleveland Museum of Natural History's board from 1979 until his death, raising the money for a new wing. He was mayor of Hunting Valley for two terms.

narrative_blocks.header: The museum's highest honor, in 1992
narrative_blocks.body: Made a life trustee in 1988, David received the Harold Terry Clark medal, the Natural History Museum's highest honor, in 1992, a year before he died at fifty-eight. He also led the Cleveland Eye Bank, as his father had led the Central Eyebank.

education.school_name: Western Reserve University School of Medicine

career.role: Physician, then director of the Division of Rheumatic Disease
Founder, rheumatology division and Muscle Disease Clinic

narrative_blocks.header: He kept Duchenne boys walking
narrative_blocks.body: Paul specialized in muscular dystrophy and helped discover the gene behind Duchenne muscular dystrophy. With braces, orthotics, surgery and physical therapy he kept children with the disease walking for several years longer than before, and he devised the Vignos scale to rate a patient's muscle function.

narrative_blocks.header: One of the first rheumatology divisions
narrative_blocks.body: Paul spent his career at University Hospitals of Cleveland, from 1949 until he retired in 1995. In 1963 he founded and led one of the nation's first rheumatology divisions, along with its Muscle Disease Clinic and a laboratory for research in muscle metabolism.

narrative_blocks.header: 108 papers, as far away as Australia
narrative_blocks.body: Paul presented 108 papers, some as far away as Australia, and published 68 more, ten book chapters and a book on physical therapy for patients with muscle disease. He showed that too much steroid treatment could backfire, and the University of Marseille gave him its medal.

narrative_blocks.header: Canton, Notre Dame, and the new Air Force
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Canton, where his father was an engineer, Paul graduated from Notre Dame in 1941 and took his medical degree at Western Reserve in 1944. After the war he served two years in the medical corps of the new U.S. Air Force, then trained at Presbyterian Hospital in New York.

narrative_blocks.header: A curator and a chair in his name
narrative_blocks.body: In 2003 the Ingalls Foundation endowed the Paul J. and Edith Ingalls Vignos Jr. Curator of European Painting and Sculpture at the Cleveland Museum of Art, and in 2006 a rheumatology chair in his name at University Hospitals. He was a trustee for life of the museum and the Cleveland Orchestra.

narrative_blocks.header: Defending Cleveland to Leon Uris
narrative_blocks.body: Paul and Edith liked to hunt, and he liked to praise Cleveland. One night at dinner he defended the city with passion to Leon Uris, the author of Exodus.

narrative_blocks.header: His secretary for fifty years
narrative_blocks.body: Rita Waldhelm was Paul's hospital and private secretary for fifty years. The children just loved seeing him, she said, because he had so much compassion.

narrative_blocks.header: The only man out of the Baltic
narrative_blocks.body: Willard, a navigator with the 95th Bomb Group, had already won the Distinguished Flying Cross for removing a bullet from a fellow officer's leg during a bombing run. On 13 June 1943, after a raid on Kiel, his Flying Fortress went down in the Baltic; all twelve men got out, and he alone lived, treading water for hours until the Germans picked him up.

narrative_blocks.header: The tunnels behind The Great Escape
narrative_blocks.body: Willard spent two years as a prisoner of war, tried several escapes and helped other prisoners get out, and his work directing the digging of escape tunnels was an inspiration for the film The Great Escape. Near the end of the war he and Cyrus Eaton Jr., son of the Cleveland industrialist, broke out and reached the American lines.

narrative_blocks.header: He quit Clevite to run for mayor
narrative_blocks.body: In 1962 Willard resigned as vice president of Clevite, gave up his corporate board seats and moved from his Hunting Valley estate into Cleveland to run for mayor as a Republican against Ralph Locher. His was the most energetic Republican campaign in years, but the city's Democrats held.

narrative_blocks.header: Graphite Bronze to University Circle
narrative_blocks.body: After the war Willard was an assistant law director for Cleveland and practised with Jones, Day, Cockley and Reavis, then went into industry in 1952 and became president of Cleveland Graphite Bronze. After the mayoral race he founded and led University Circle Research Center, which built research facilities by Case Western Reserve.

narrative_blocks.header: She founded the TinkerBell School
narrative_blocks.body: Jammy started the TinkerBell School, a preschool in New Canaan that ran for more than ten years, then taught and coached field hockey at the New Canaan Country Day School until she retired in 1979.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-seven years with High Hopes
narrative_blocks.body: After moving to Lyme in 1980 Jane was a volunteer and board member of the Lyme Land Conservation Trust and of High Hopes Therapeutic Riding, where she served for twenty-seven years.

narrative_blocks.header: A pilot’s licence, like her husband
narrative_blocks.body: Jane and her husband Cottie were both licensed private pilots. Her father, David Ingalls, had been the only Navy flying ace of the First World War.

narrative_blocks.body: Born in London in 1930 and raised partly at Bratenahl, Ohio, Wanda married two officers of the Black Watch: Major Ronald Maxwell in 1950, who died in 1960, and Lt. Col. Denys Rowan-Hamilton in 1961. She died at Killyleagh Castle in County Down in 2022, an MBE.

narrative_blocks.header: From Rhodesia and Korea to Damascus
narrative_blocks.body: Denys was aide-de-camp to the Governor of Southern Rhodesia in 1947, when he was made MVO, and a major with the 29th Brigade in Korea in 1953. He commanded a Black Watch battalion from 1960 and was defence attaché at Damascus and Beirut until 1967.

narrative_blocks.header: High Sheriff of County Down, 1975
narrative_blocks.body: Retired from the Black Watch in 1967, Denys settled with Wanda at Killyleagh in County Down, served as a deputy lieutenant and was High Sheriff of the county in 1975. He died there in May 2018, at ninety-seven.

bio.bio_blurb: Olympic silver medallist in the British eight

death.notes: At home

narrative_blocks.header: Olympic silver in the Montreal eight
narrative_blocks.body: David rowed in the British eight that took silver at the 1974 World Championships in Lucerne and again at the 1976 Olympics in Montreal. Four years earlier, at Munich, he and Mike Hart had finished eighth in the coxed pair.

narrative_blocks.header: Two Boat Races won, one of them stroked
narrative_blocks.body: At Jesus College, Cambridge, David rowed in the Blue Boat that beat Oxford by ten lengths in 1971, and stroked the 1972 crew to a nine-and-a-half-length win. That summer his coxed pair set a national championship record.

narrative_blocks.header: Silver for Eton at seventeen
narrative_blocks.body: At Eton David rowed in the eight that took silver at the 1968 FISA World Youth Championships in Amsterdam, then won the Visitors' Challenge Cup at Henley in 1969 and a second junior silver at Naples.

narrative_blocks.header: The most talented natural oar
narrative_blocks.body: His Cambridge coach, Donald Legget, put him at two in his all-time university eight, and called him “possibly the most talented natural oar I have ever coached.”

narrative_blocks.header: The cottage on Lake Muskoka
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin kept a summer cottage on Lake Muskoka in Ontario. In the summer of 1909 his father moved the Forge and Iron Company's annual meeting forward to get up there sooner, and died at home in Pittsburgh before he could go.

bio.display_name: Elsa Wells Cook Greenfield Tracy Kenyon

narrative_blocks.header: Three husbands in thirteen years
narrative_blocks.body: Elsa married Charles Edward Greenfield of San Francisco in 1904, the Marine officer James Kennard Tracy in 1915, and the playwright and screenwriter Charles Kenyon in 1917. She died in San Francisco in October 1924, at forty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: A society wedding, and an unhappy marriage
narrative_blocks.body: Dorothy met Harry Grant in Europe and married him in 1910 at what he later cursed as a society wedding. Her family wanted him to be a gentleman of leisure; he would not be one, and the marriage was unhappy. She died at Los Angeles in 1923, at thirty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: From Yale to the wholesale grocery trade
narrative_blocks.body: Chauncey Milton Griggs was born in St. Paul in February 1860 and went east to Yale, class of 1883. He came home a wholesale and manufacturing grocer, in the city where his father had founded Griggs, Cooper and Company the year before, the largest wholesale grocery house in the Northwest.

narrative_blocks.header: He married a Pittsburgh steel man’s daughter
narrative_blocks.body: In October 1885 Chauncey married Mary Chaffey Wells, daughter of the Pittsburgh crucible-steel man Calvin Wells. They had eight children in sixteen years and named the first Calvin Wells Griggs; their daughter Katherine lived only from 1890 to 1893.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother founded the Tacoma Art League
narrative_blocks.body: His mother, Martha Ann Gallup of Ledyard, Connecticut, had presided over St. Paul's Protestant Orphan Asylum. In Tacoma after 1890 she helped found the Tacoma Art League and the Aloha Club, and was State Regent of the Washington Daughters of the American Revolution from 1896 to 1899.

narrative_blocks.header: His father sawed a million feet a day
narrative_blocks.body: In 1888 his father, Col. Chauncey Wright Griggs of the Third Minnesota, took Minnesota lumbering to Tacoma and founded the St. Paul and Tacoma Lumber Company on Northern Pacific timber. Its mill stood on pilings over the tideflats, the first bandsaw mill on the Pacific coast.

cross_connections.display_label: was treasurer of the Tacoma lumber company Colonel Griggs founded

narrative_blocks.header: A second marriage, to a Maya archaeologist
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth raised four sons with Henry Gilman Nichols in Greenwich and Lincoln, and was widowed in 1962. In 1968 she married Ledyard Smith, the Harvard archaeologist of the Maya, in the year Guatemala gave him the Order of the Quetzal. She died at Rockport, Maine, in 1991.

residence.notes: 1989; summers at Cable, Wisconsin

narrative_blocks.header: A twin from Evanston, married twice
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Allen Brown was born at Evanston in March 1921, a twin of Beatrice Marie Brown. Her first marriage, to William Thomas Ingram II in 1943, ended in divorce in 1946, and the next year she married Charles Griggs.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixteen army years, from Greece to England
narrative_blocks.body: Nancy married Lt. William Daugherty in 1950 and spent the next sixteen years following the army: first to Greece, then Germany, a run of American posts and finally England. The family came home to Tacoma for good in 1966.

bio.title: Dr.
bio.bio_blurb: Founder of Virginia Mason's pulmonary department

narrative_blocks.header: He built Virginia Mason’s lung department
narrative_blocks.body: Dr. Edward Morgan came to Virginia Mason in Seattle in 1950, straight from a pulmonary fellowship at the Mayo Clinic, and set up its department of pulmonary medicine. He ran it until 1982, and a chair in pulmonary and critical care medicine there now carries his name.

narrative_blocks.header: Late to every dinner, and hunting in wingtips
narrative_blocks.body: Colleagues who asked him to dinner learned he would be late, because he would still be with his patients. Tate Mason, who headed urology at Virginia Mason, found him dapper and at ease in any crowd, and once saw him out hunting in a pair of freshly shined business shoes.

narrative_blocks.header: First in his class four years running
narrative_blocks.body: At Northwestern's medical school he stood at the top of his class all four years and took his degree in 1943. The Army sent him to Fort Lewis, where he met Mary Griggs of Tacoma; they married in 1944 and were together fifty-two years.

cross_connections.display_label: was a regional regent of the American College of Chest Physicians

narrative_blocks.header: He helped put Northwest into 747s
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin was instrumental in Northwest's purchase of the Boeing 747 and the McDonnell Douglas DC-10, the wide-bodied long-range jets that carried the airline into new markets across Asia. He worked closely on the route development behind that expansion.

narrative_blocks.header: One airline, from Yale to retirement
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin joined Northwest Orient out of Yale in 1950, served two years in the Army, and never worked anywhere else. He was assistant to the president by 1961 and vice-president for operations in 1964, and retired in 1989 as executive vice-president over more than 10,000 employees.

narrative_blocks.header: The executive who loaded the baggage
narrative_blocks.body: During one of Northwest's labour disputes in the 1960s he went out and loaded baggage himself. He also won awards for noise abatement, working with the pilots on take-off and landing procedures that spared the neighbourhoods under the flight paths.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten years on Madeline Island, then the sea
narrative_blocks.body: After his wife Mimi died in 1996, Benjamin lived year-round on Madeline Island for more than a decade, and sat twenty-five years on the board of its ferry line. He died at Denver in 2013, and after a service at Carmel he was buried at sea.

cross_connections.display_label: chaired Pan Am as it pushed its routes across the Pacific to Asia

narrative_blocks.header: Her rector called her Mrs. St. Paul’s
narrative_blocks.body: Julie ran nearly everything at St. Paul’s Episcopal Church in Burlingame, from the rummage sale to the Daughters of the King study group, and her rector called her Mrs. St. Paul’s. Elsewhere she often held the president’s chair, from the Florence Crittenton Home to the San Francisco Symphony League.

narrative_blocks.header: Born into 471 Beacon Street
narrative_blocks.body: Henry was born in April 1894 into 471 Beacon Street in the Back Bay, which his father, the attorney Henry Gilman Nichols, had bought the summer before. His father died in May 1900, and that September his mother, Elsie Quincy Nichols, took Henry and his sisters Frances and Elsie to Europe.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Childhood home, 1894-1900

bio.bio_blurb: President of the Fiduciary Trust Company

narrative_blocks.header: Japan between Exeter and Harvard
narrative_blocks.body: Gimmy left Phillips Exeter in 1946 for two years in Japan as an Army technician fifth grade, then went on to Harvard and graduated in 1952. He finished his career at the Fiduciary Trust Company in Boston, president from 1982 until he retired in 1993.

narrative_blocks.header: Founder of the Gin and Tonic Golf Tournament
narrative_blocks.body: Summers meant the whole Nichols clan on North Haven, Maine, sailing and picnicking, and Gimmy was a founding member of the island's Gin and Tonic Golf Tournament. Most mornings he made a routine inspection of J.O. Brown's Boatyard.

narrative_blocks.header: His neighbours called him Our Own Milt
narrative_blocks.body: Milt spent more than thirty years in St. Paul as a commercial real estate broker and developer. Family and neighbours had the use of his inventiveness and his handiwork, which earned him the nickname Our Own Milt, and his happiest place was his workshop.

career.role: Commercial real estate broker and developer

narrative_blocks.header: From a North Haven dig to the Dordogne
narrative_blocks.body: Volunteering at the dig at Turner Hill Farm on North Haven sent Ellen back to college in the 1970s for a degree in archaeology, and she spent several years working at Abri Pataud, the Late Stone Age rock shelter in the Dordogne.

narrative_blocks.header: Among the first hospice volunteers
narrative_blocks.body: Ellen was among the first volunteers for the new Hospice of the North Shore in the 1980s, and later sat on its board and served a term as its president. She spent many years on the board of Gould Farm at Monterey, Massachusetts, for its work in mental health.

narrative_blocks.header: Radcliffe, cut short by mononucleosis
narrative_blocks.body: Born in New York in 1926 to Keyo Tetsuka and Clement Royal Ford, Ellen went from the Chapin School and St. Timothy's to Radcliffe, class of 1948, until mononucleosis ended it in her sophomore year. A first marriage, to C. Ernest Swigert of Portland, Oregon, lasted a couple of years.

cross_connections.display_label: was the Maya archaeologist her mother-in-law married in 1968
excavated prehistoric sites in the Dordogne in the summer of 1923

narrative_blocks.header: The first Maya dig dated by its pottery
narrative_blocks.body: At Uaxactun in the Petén, first under Oliver Ricketson and then as field director, Ledyard Smith ran the first Maya excavation to join large-scale digging to pottery analysis, tying buildings and ceramics to Initial Series dates. It also opened the first Preclassic levels in the Maya lowlands.

narrative_blocks.header: The Carnegie’s last dig, at Mayapan
narrative_blocks.body: From 1950 Ledyard worked at Mayapan in Yucatán, the last project of the Carnegie Institution's archaeology division, mapping the city with Karl Ruppert. When the division closed in 1958 he moved to Harvard's Peabody Museum as an assistant curator.

narrative_blocks.header: Guatemala gave him the Order of the Quetzal
narrative_blocks.body: For the Peabody he dug Altar de Sacrificios with Gordon Willey from 1958 to 1963, then Seibal until 1969. In 1968 Guatemala gave him the Order of the Quetzal for his service to the country's culture and heritage.

narrative_blocks.header: Two brothers who both dug the Maya
narrative_blocks.body: Ledyard went to school at Lausanne and then St. Paul's before Harvard, class of 1925, and joined the Carnegie archaeologists in 1927. His brother Robert Eliot Smith became a Maya archaeologist as well; their grandfather Augustus L. Smith had been mayor of Appleton, Wisconsin.

found some of the oldest pottery in the Americas, on the Amazon

narrative_blocks.header: Aerobatics in his seventies
narrative_blocks.body: Chauncey ran Griggs Contracting for more than forty years, but his life turned on the garage, where he customised cars, boats and airplanes. He was an early adopter of fixed-wing sails for ice boating and land-sailing, building his own boat and wings, and in his seventies he took up aerobatic flying.

cross_connections.display_label: built his own ice boat and a Coot amphibian, and learned to fly

narrative_blocks.header: A child psychologist at Children’s Hospital
narrative_blocks.body: Ethel graduated from Summit School and studied at Smith and the University of Minnesota, then worked for many years as a child psychologist at Children's Hospital. After retiring she stayed with a sand-play therapy group.

bio.title: Lt. Col.
bio.bio_blurb: Commandant of the Portsmouth Naval Prison

narrative_blocks.header: Commandant of the Portsmouth Naval Prison
narrative_blocks.body: James Kennard Tracy joined the Marine Corps in 1900 and rose to lieutenant colonel. He was commandant of the Portsmouth Naval Prison when he died in the Naval Hospital there in May 1929.

narrative_blocks.header: He commanded the Alcatraz of the East
narrative_blocks.body: Tracy's command was the Portsmouth Naval Prison at Kittery on the Piscataqua, a castle of reinforced concrete built from 1905 to 1908 on the model of Alcatraz, with the tidal currents to deter escape. A decade before him, Thomas Mott Osborne had run it as an experiment in prison reform.

narrative_blocks.header: The island once held Admiral Cervera
narrative_blocks.body: Before the prison, the site had been Fort Sullivan in the Revolution, and in the summer of 1898 its stockade, Camp Long, held 1,612 Spanish prisoners of war, Admiral Pascual Cervera among them. The prison took the camp's place in 1908.

cross_connections.display_label: commanded the Portsmouth Navy Yard, where his prison stood, in 1929
helped defeat Admiral Cervera's fleet off Santiago in July 1898

narrative_blocks.header: Screenplays for more than 110 films
narrative_blocks.body: Charles Kenyon wrote or co-wrote more than 110 screenplays between 1915 and 1946, from Tom Mix Westerns to The Iron Horse in 1924, Show Boat in 1929, A Midsummer Night's Dream in 1935 and The Petrified Forest in 1936.

narrative_blocks.header: Kindling, a play before it was a film
narrative_blocks.body: Before the pictures, Charles was a playwright. His play Kindling was celebrated in his native San Francisco in 1912, and in 1915 it became one of his first two screen credits.

cross_connections.display_label: played himself in his 1937 screenplay One Hundred Men and a Girl
sang Magnolia in Show Boat, the story he adapted for film in 1929

notable.notable_blurb: Screenwriter of more than 110 films

bio.display_name: Dorothy Carter Stevenson Clark Walling Pansini

narrative_blocks.header: Three husbands, and a death in Rome
narrative_blocks.body: Dorothy married David Lewis Clark II in 1934, then in 1939 the Paramount portrait photographer Bill Walling, with whom she had a son and a daughter, and afterwards a man named Pansini. She died in Rome about November 1962, at fifty.

narrative_blocks.header: A mop, a debt, and Cecil B. DeMille
narrative_blocks.body: Bill's father had once worked for Cecil B. DeMille in San Francisco and taken a gun and a watch in lieu of pay. At fourteen Bill walked into Famous Players-Lasky, reminded DeMille of the debt, and was paid with a job: seven days a week mopping the floors where the wet film hung to dry.

narrative_blocks.header: Gallery No. 2 at Paramount
narrative_blocks.body: Bill worked up to assistant cameraman on the Fox Sunshine Comedies and acted in silent pictures as Richard Walling. In the 1930s he had Paramount's portrait gallery No. 2, shooting the young players and difficult ones like W. C. Fields, and he retired from Universal around 1970.

narrative_blocks.header: Found by his father’s whistle in 1906
narrative_blocks.body: Bill was two when the 1906 earthquake caught him and his mother in San Francisco. His father hurried in from the ranch on Atlas Peak and, kept out of the Marina refugee camp, whistled the tune he used to call his wife until she heard it. Bill's own book ends on hearing that whistling again.

narrative_blocks.header: He designed the Walling loom
narrative_blocks.body: In North Hollywood Bill and his fourth wife, Marie, designed the first Walling weaving loom. He patented it and sold it to Groff in the early 1970s, and it lives on as the Oregon Trail loom.

narrative_blocks.header: His father played leads for Belasco
narrative_blocks.body: His father, Will R. Walling, was a matinee idol with the Yorkville stock company in New York and leading man of the Belasco Stock Company in Portland. In pictures he played in The Village Blacksmith in 1922, a Tom Mix train-robbery Western and a John Wayne range feud.

cross_connections.display_label: talked his way into a studio as an assistant cameraman at seventeen

narrative_blocks.header: He gave the Milwaukee Journal to its staff
narrative_blocks.body: When Lucius Nieman died in 1935, Harry Grant was offered backing to take control of the Milwaukee Journal and chose instead to put its stock in its employees' hands. His plan began in 1937 with a quarter of the shares; by his death the staff owned three quarters, and later nine-tenths.

narrative_blocks.header: Rayon, then advertising, then the Journal
narrative_blocks.body: He sold advertising for N. W. Ayer, went to London for the Rubberset Brush Company, and in 1910 was made manager of what became the American Viscose Company, set up to make rayon in America. Lucius Nieman hired him as the Journal's advertising manager in 1916, and within three years he was its publisher.

narrative_blocks.header: McCarthy called it the Daily Worker
narrative_blocks.body: In McCarthy's home state the Journal attacked the senator so fiercely that he called it the Milwaukee edition of the Daily Worker. Colonel McCormick of the Chicago Tribune called it a wood pussy, and one Milwaukeean paid his newsboy to tear out the editorial page.

narrative_blocks.header: Running the Journal from a fishing boat
narrative_blocks.body: In his seventies Harry spent half of each year at Miami Beach, running the Journal from his house on Biscayne Bay and from his 71-foot cruiser High Tide, where he read the airmailed paper for two hours a day between turns at the fishing line.

narrative_blocks.header: Harvard twice, and never a degree
narrative_blocks.body: Harry was fifteen when his father, a horse dealer, took his own life, and he left school to support the family. He saved, studied at night, reached Harvard as a special student in 1903, ran out of money, sold roofing, went back in 1905, and gave up after his sophomore year.

narrative_blocks.header: Freedom, freedom, freedom
narrative_blocks.body: “The Journal must be our Fair Lady,” he said. “We must have freedom, freedom, freedom — not to be willful, or bigoted, or swell-headed — but so that the Journal can act entirely as it thinks best for the community.”

cross_connections.display_label: , his wife's grandfather, owned and ran the Philadelphia Press
ran the independent Springfield Republican and sat on the AP board
held the Harvard fellowship named for Lucius Nieman, who hired him
ran against Joseph McCarthy for the Senate in Wisconsin in 1952

notable.notable_blurb: Publisher of the Milwaukee Journal

narrative_blocks.header: She held the last tenth of the Journal
narrative_blocks.body: By 1980 the employees of the Milwaukee Journal owned nine-tenths of the company her father had put in their hands, and Barbara held the rest. A scholarship for journalism students at the University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee carries her name and her husband's.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped found Swiss Colony cheese
narrative_blocks.body: Shortly before he joined the Journal, Don Abert helped found the Swiss Colony Company, which sold gift packages of cheese by mail. It grew into the largest mail-order house for cheese and gourmet food in the world.

narrative_blocks.header: From the promotion department to chairman
narrative_blocks.body: Don came to the Journal Company in 1928, fresh from the University of Wisconsin, in the promotion department. He was publisher of the Milwaukee Journal by 1968, chairman of the company from 1977, and retired in 1982.

narrative_blocks.header: President of the symphony that went major league
narrative_blocks.body: In 1968, while publisher of the Journal, Don was president of the Milwaukee Symphony as it took on Kenneth Schermerhorn as music director, the man credited with making it a major orchestra. Its principal bass chair carries Don's name.

narrative_blocks.header: A fantasy novel from his daughters’ dreams
narrative_blocks.body: Pratt turned the dreamwork sessions he held with his daughters Juliette and Paola into Raising Sleeping Stones, a middle-grade fantasy about two sisters learning the ancient art of DreamKeeping. Published under the name P.H.T. Bennet, it won a Newbury Comics Award in 2013.

narrative_blocks.header: Hired in Paris to rebuild an office
narrative_blocks.body: After Yale he went to Paris with no plan and little money, and an acoustic architecture firm hired him to turn its raw space into a two-storey office. He stayed five years and began teaching business English to French executives, the work that later led him into coaching them.

narrative_blocks.header: Coaching leaders on how people learn
narrative_blocks.body: Pratt taught at Berklee College of Music and trained other educators, then became vice-president of learning and development at AceUp, building group coaching programmes with researchers such as John Medina, Daniel Pink and Dan Coyle.

career.role: Assistant professor, Liberal Arts and Sciences

narrative_blocks.header: Forty years at McKay, summers at Beaumaris
narrative_blocks.body: Rowland came to Princeton from Choate and the Babson Institute, graduated in 1930, and married Elizabeth Dewey Wells that June. He spent nearly forty years with the McKay Company, retiring a vice-president in 1968, and every summer took the family to Beaumaris on Lake Muskoka.

narrative_blocks.header: He followed his father into the House
narrative_blocks.body: His father, William Stiles Bennet, had sat in the House for New York from 1905 to 1911. Augustus followed him there thirty-four years later, after twenty-one years as the federal referee in bankruptcy at Newburgh.

narrative_blocks.header: One term in Congress, and no second
narrative_blocks.body: Elected from New York's 29th district in 1944, Augustus served the single term from 1945 to 1947. In 1946 his own party would not renominate him, and Katharine St. George took the seat.

narrative_blocks.header: Amherst, the Flying Corps, then Columbia Law
narrative_blocks.body: He graduated from Amherst in 1918 and went straight into the Naval Reserve Flying Corps as a chief quartermaster until January 1919, then took his law degree at Columbia in 1921 and opened a practice at Newburgh.

narrative_blocks.body: Lisa took her medical degree at Brown, trained in internal medicine and endocrinology at the University of Minnesota, and spent a further year on diabetes at UC San Diego. narrative_blocks.header: The Met Opera’s first woman president
narrative_blocks.body: Louise was the first woman to serve as president of the Metropolitan Opera Association. Her mother, Peg Allen Ireland, had been the first woman to head Ohio's department of health, education and welfare.

narrative_blocks.header: First woman on Florida’s wildlife commission
narrative_blocks.body: After Bud died Louise moved to Leon County, and in 1984 became the first woman on the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, serving until 1999. She put most of the 13,000-acre Woodfield Springs Plantation under a Tall Timbers conservation easement.

narrative_blocks.header: Couriers on horseback for the frontier nurses
narrative_blocks.body: In their twenties Louise and her sister Kate rode as volunteer couriers for the Frontier Nursing Service in Kentucky, guiding health officials on horseback into the back country.

narrative_blocks.header: A Hanna on her father’s side
narrative_blocks.body: Louise's father, Robert Livingston Ireland Jr., was a son of Kate Hanna, whose uncle was Senator Mark Hanna. The Humphrey she married was running the company Mark Hanna had founded, and his sister's first husband had been Kate Hanna's nephew.

bio.bio_blurb: Arts patron and opera company chairman

narrative_blocks.header: She led Toronto’s opera and its art gallery
narrative_blocks.body: Margo was president of the Art Gallery of Ontario, president and chairman of the Canadian Opera Company and president of the Toronto Arts Council, and helped found The Country Day School in Ontario. For the Metropolitan Opera she chaired the Great Lakes region.

narrative_blocks.header: Margo Bindhardt Day, three weeks before
narrative_blocks.body: Back in the Red Hills she chaired the Florida Arts Council and Tallahassee's Seven Days of Opening Nights. On 1 May 2009 she helped break ground for the Arts Exchange, and Florida's capital proclaimed Margo Bindhardt Day; she died on 20 May.

narrative_blocks.header: Five minutes ahead of her twin
narrative_blocks.body: Margo was born at Chagrin Falls on 19 March 1942, five minutes before her twin brother George. Her mother became the first woman president of the Metropolitan Opera Association, and her grandfather George Humphrey was Eisenhower's Treasury Secretary.

bio.bio_blurb: Industrialist and University Hospitals vice chairman

narrative_blocks.header: Captain of Yale football, and the Mallory Prize
narrative_blocks.body: George captained Yale's freshman and varsity football teams and won the Mallory Prize, given to the undergraduate who best represents American sportsmanship and the Yale tradition. He graduated in 1964, took a Michigan law degree and left the Marines a captain in 1970.

narrative_blocks.header: Harmonica with Charlie McCoy at sixty
narrative_blocks.body: George taught himself the harmonica in his late forties, and at his sixtieth birthday at the Union Club of Cleveland he played The Orange Blossom Special with his idol, the country harmonica star Charlie McCoy.

narrative_blocks.header: University Hospitals’ first Lifetime Director
narrative_blocks.body: George joined the University Hospitals board in 1980, was vice chairman from 1988 to 2004 and led its 1991 capital campaign, the most successful in the hospital's history to that time. When he retired in 2006 it named him its first Lifetime Director.

narrative_blocks.header: Five years in London for Hanna
narrative_blocks.body: George worked for Hanna Mining, five of those years in London as its European representative, until 1984. He then recruited executives for Russell Reynolds, chaired Philips Container from 1987 to 1994 and was president of the plastics maker Extrudex until 2006.
