narrative_blocks.header: A Belmont winner, bred with his aunt
narrative_blocks.body: With his aunt Pamela Firman, Watts bred Crème Fraiche, winner of the 1985 Belmont Stakes, and with William S. Farish he bred Sacahuista, champion three-year-old filly of 1987. His wife Sally had bred the 1980 Kentucky Derby winner, Genuine Risk.

narrative_blocks.header: The World Series, then Keeneland
narrative_blocks.body: A partner in the St. Louis Cardinals, Watts watched them win the World Series in October 2011, and the next day became leading owner of the fall meeting at Keeneland, which had given him its Mark of Distinction in 1999.

narrative_blocks.header: Fillies kept, colts sold, at Shawnee Farm
narrative_blocks.body: At his 1,000-acre Shawnee Farm near Harrodsburg, Kentucky, Watts keeps some sixty broodmares, sells his colts and races his fillies before they go back to the breeding shed. His daughter Vicki Oliver and her husband Phil train many of them.

narrative_blocks.header: Plastics machinery out of Pittsburgh
narrative_blocks.body: After Yale and Harvard Business School, Watts made his business life in Pittsburgh as president of GWH Holdings and chairman of the plastics-machinery makers IPEG and Conair. He has sat on the boards of Churchill Downs and Keeneland and served as a steward of The Jockey Club.

narrative_blocks.header: A Silver Star and three Purple Hearts
narrative_blocks.body: After Yale, Watts spent three and a half years in the Marines, a first lieutenant commanding an infantry company, and came home with the Silver Star, the Bronze Star, the Navy Commendation Medal and three Purple Hearts. Harvard Business School followed, from 1970 to 1972.

narrative_blocks.header: Summers at his aunt’s Shawnee Farm
narrative_blocks.body: Through his Yale summers Watts worked at Shawnee Farm, the Harrodsburg place of his aunt Pansy Poe, and after Harvard he went back and bought it when she died in 1979. In 2017, as chairman of Churchill Downs, he was the Thoroughbred Club of America's Honor Guest.

bio.bio_blurb: Canadian show jumper and real estate executive

narrative_blocks.header: Team gold at the 1970 World Championships
narrative_blocks.body: Moffat found horses young at Don-Alda Farms and rode twenty years for the Canadian Equestrian Team, taking team bronze at the 1967 Pan American Games and team gold at the 1970 World Championships in France. He chaired Canada's jumping team at the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics and was twice named to the Jump Canada Hall of Fame.

narrative_blocks.header: The observatory his grandmother gave
narrative_blocks.body: His grandfather David A. Dunlap wanted a great observatory for the University of Toronto, and in 1930 his widow Jessie gave the land and money for the David Dunlap Observatory at Richmond Hill. When light pollution closed in, Moffat and the other heirs agreed in 2008 to sell the land, and the proceeds endowed the Dunlap Institute for Astronomy and Astrophysics.

narrative_blocks.header: Land for Canada's Wonderland
narrative_blocks.body: In 1972 Moffat founded Moffat Dunlap Real Estate, dealing in country and equestrian property around Toronto. He bought the land for Canada's Wonderland, sold Eaton Hall to Seneca College, and advised the Koffler family when they gave Jokers Hill to the University of Toronto.

narrative_blocks.header: President of the Royal Winter Fair
narrative_blocks.body: Moffat was a director, horse show chairman and president of the Royal Agricultural Winter Fair, and in 1971 co-founded The Country Day School at King City, which all four of his children attended. Toronto made him an honorary doctor of laws in 2011.

narrative_blocks.header: Moscow for the 1972 Summit Series
narrative_blocks.body: A Maple Leafs fan, Moffat went to Moscow for the 1972 Summit Series, belonged to the Toronto Club for fifty-eight years and was president of the Nicholson's Island Club on Georgian Bay. His friend of more than seventy years was the rider Jim Elder.

narrative_blocks.header: Show rider at eight, trainer by 1999
narrative_blocks.body: Vicki began show riding at eight and kept at it through Wittenberg University, then rode exercise at the major tracks and learned the trade in veterinarians' practices, racing offices and the barns of leading trainers. She and Phil founded Oliver Racing Stable in 1999.

narrative_blocks.header: Training her father’s homebreds
narrative_blocks.body: Oliver Racing trains many of her father Watts Humphrey's Shawnee Farm runners, and its Grade 1 winners include Last Full Measure and Personal Diary. The stable keeps under fifty horses and has never had a positive drug test.

narrative_blocks.header: From Lester Piggott’s yard to Santa Anita
narrative_blocks.body: Phil grew up at Chipping Norton and was riding at three; before he left for America at eighteen he worked for the champions Stan Miller and Lester Piggott. At Santa Anita he started as assistant to Ian Jory, helping bring on Video Ranger and Best Pal.

narrative_blocks.header: He met Vicki in Elliott Walden’s barn
narrative_blocks.body: Phil assisted Bruce Headley with the champion Bertrando, then Elliott Walden with Menifee, Victory Gallop and Distorted Humor, and in Walden's barn he met Vicki Humphrey. In 1999 they set up Oliver Racing Stable together.

narrative_blocks.header: Grade 1 winners, winters at Payson Park
narrative_blocks.body: Phil trained Grade 1 and graded stakes winners including Last Full Measure, Autonomy, Closing Range and First Lieutenant, wintering the stable at Payson Park in Florida and summering at Keeneland. He died at Indiantown in February 2024, at fifty-three.

bio.bio_blurb: First governor of the New York Fed

narrative_blocks.header: He built the New York Fed
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin left the presidency of Bankers Trust in October 1914 to become the first governor of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, and led it for fourteen years. A biographer called him the de facto leader of the whole Federal Reserve System.

narrative_blocks.header: The world’s most exclusive club
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin made the buying and selling of government securities the Fed's working tool, and in July 1927 he met the heads of the Bank of England, the Reichsbank and the Bank of France near New York, a gathering the press called the world's most exclusive club.

narrative_blocks.header: Fired for his handwriting
narrative_blocks.body: Family money ran short when he finished at Montclair High School, so instead of Princeton he went to Wall Street at eighteen, and his first employer fired him for poor penmanship. By 1914 he was president of Bankers Trust.

narrative_blocks.header: Running the bank from sanatoriums
narrative_blocks.body: From 1916 he fought tuberculosis of the throat and lungs, running the bank from Western holidays and European resorts. After an operation for diverticulitis in October 1928 a hemorrhage killed him at fifty-five, and President Coolidge sent his condolences.

narrative_blocks.header: At Jekyll Island in 1910
narrative_blocks.body: In November 1910 Benjamin was one of the handful of bankers Senator Nelson Aldrich brought to the Jekyll Island Club to draw up the Aldrich Plan. The Federal Reserve Act of 1913 was built on its outline.

narrative_blocks.header: A railroad superintendent’s son
narrative_blocks.body: His father, Benjamin Strong, was superintendent of the Dutchess and Columbia Railroad at Fishkill, and his elder brother Oliver Smith Strong became professor of neurology at the College of Physicians and Surgeons. His first wife died in 1905; in 1907 he married Katherine Converse.

bio.bio_blurb: Assistant Secretary of War for Air, museum president

narrative_blocks.header: He founded the First Yale Unit
narrative_blocks.body: At Yale in 1916 Trubee gathered a dozen classmates to learn to fly at their own expense, training that summer off Peacock Point in flying boats his father helped buy. The Navy took the First Yale Unit into its Reserve as the nucleus of naval aviation, and Trubee was given the Navy Cross for organizing it.

narrative_blocks.header: Assistant Secretary of War for Air
narrative_blocks.body: Trubee held the new post of Assistant Secretary of War for Air from 1926 to 1933, under Coolidge and Hoover, through the Army air arm's years of rapid growth. In 1932 he ran for lieutenant governor of New York on Wild Bill Donovan's ticket and lost in a landslide.

narrative_blocks.header: Chosen at twenty-nine to fight crime
narrative_blocks.body: Trubee sat in the New York Assembly for Nassau County from 1922. In 1925 Judge Elbert Gary's committee passed over its famous members and made the twenty-nine-year-old assemblyman chairman of the National Crime Commission, and Time put him on its cover.

narrative_blocks.header: Eighteen years at the Museum of Natural History
narrative_blocks.body: Trubee was president of the American Museum of Natural History from 1933 to 1951, carried it through repeated money crises and helped bring about the Hayden Planetarium. In 1933 he and Dorothy went to Africa with Martin and Osa Johnson for the elephants that stand in Akeley Hall.

narrative_blocks.header: A general, then the CIA’s personnel chief
narrative_blocks.body: Back in uniform from 1941, Trubee planned the Army's demobilization on the Air Staff and left a brigadier general with the Distinguished Service Medal. In 1951 and 1952 he organized the new CIA's personnel system under Walter Bedell Smith.

narrative_blocks.header: He broke his back on his wings test
narrative_blocks.body: Flying his test for Navy wings over Huntington Bay on 28 July 1917, Trubee spiralled into the sea and broke his back. Lamed for life, he taught himself to walk without crutches and then without a cane, and became a keen yachtsman.

narrative_blocks.header: He married the headmaster’s daughter
narrative_blocks.body: A Groton boy, class of 1914, Trubee married Dorothy Peabody, daughter of his old headmaster, in 1920. After his father died they built a house on the Peacock Point estate to keep his widowed mother company.

narrative_blocks.header: Daughter of Groton’s original headmaster
narrative_blocks.body: Dorothy was born at Groton in 1899, a daughter of the Rev. Endicott Peabody, who founded the Groton School and ran it from 1884 to 1940. He taught Franklin Roosevelt there and married him to Eleanor.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father’s church in Tombstone
narrative_blocks.body: Before Groton, her father had spent 1882 in the Arizona Territory, where he organized St. Paul's Episcopal Church in Tombstone, the oldest Protestant church in the state.

narrative_blocks.header: Her nephew, the governor
narrative_blocks.body: Dorothy's brother Malcolm Peabody became Episcopal bishop of Central New York, and his son Endicott, her nephew, won the Silver Star in the Navy and was governor of Massachusetts from 1963 to 1965. Malcolm's daughter Marietta Tree, her niece, represented the United States on the UN Human Rights Commission.

narrative_blocks.header: A securities lawyer who flew
narrative_blocks.body: Cottie flew as an Army Air Force pilot in the Second World War and kept a private pilot's license, as his wife Jane did. Flying ran in both families: his father Trubee founded the First Yale Unit, and Jane's father, David Ingalls, was the Navy's only ace of the First World War.

narrative_blocks.header: Captain of Yale's 1947 football team
narrative_blocks.body: Cottie came to Yale from Groton after the war, captained the 1947 football team and was tapped for Skull and Bones in the same years as George H. W. Bush. He took his degree in 1948, married Jane Ingalls that year, and finished law school at the University of Virginia in 1951.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale's fund-raiser, 1971 to 1976
narrative_blocks.body: From 1971 to 1976 Cottie was Yale's director of institutional development and capital support, running a campaign that beat its goal. The rest of his working life he practised securities law with Winthrop, Stimson, Putnam & Roberts, as a partner from 1959 to 1980 and of counsel after.

narrative_blocks.header: Trustee of his grandfather's school
narrative_blocks.body: Cottie sat on the board of the American Museum of Natural History, which his father had run for eighteen years, and was a trustee of Groton, the school his grandfather founded. He also led the National Parks and Recreation Association and sat on the boards of Union Theological Seminary and Mystic Seaport.

narrative_blocks.header: He ran the Red Cross through the war
narrative_blocks.body: Woodrow Wilson made Henry chairman of the American Red Cross War Council in 1917, and he ran it without salary through the war, raising hospitals, ambulances and relief across Europe. He was given the Distinguished Service Medal for it.

narrative_blocks.header: Founder of the League of Red Cross Societies
narrative_blocks.body: After the war Henry pressed for a permanent alliance of the national Red Cross societies, and in 1919 founded the League of Red Cross Societies, now the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, as its first chairman.

narrative_blocks.header: From a Bridgeport bank to Morgan’s partnership
narrative_blocks.body: Raised in modest circumstances at Troy, Pennsylvania, Henry started in banking at Bridgeport, ran the Liberty National Bank in New York, helped organize Bankers Trust in 1903, and in 1909 became a partner of J. P. Morgan & Co.

narrative_blocks.header: At Jekyll Island in 1910
narrative_blocks.body: In November 1910 Henry was one of the bankers Senator Nelson Aldrich gathered at Jekyll Island, Georgia, to draw up the proposals on which the Federal Reserve Act of 1913 was built. He died at Peacock Point in 1922, at fifty-four.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave quietly, and left nothing to charity
narrative_blocks.body: Henry's will left nothing to charity. His lawyers explained that he had given quietly and generously while he lived, and some gifts so quietly that his own partners at J. P. Morgan & Co. learned of them only after he died.

narrative_blocks.header: Amiable but ineffective Geneva gentlemen
narrative_blocks.body: Henry wanted his new League to take over from the International Committee of the Red Cross, which he called a committee of “amiable but somewhat ineffective Geneva gentlemen.” The rivalry between the two bodies outlasted him by years.

narrative_blocks.header: She equipped the First Yale Unit
narrative_blocks.body: In 1916 Kate helped organize and equip the First Yale Aviation Unit, the Yale students, her son Trubee among them, who trained at Peacock Point and grew into the nucleus of American naval aviation.

narrative_blocks.header: Nassau County’s Red Cross, 1917 to 1944
narrative_blocks.body: In 1917 she founded the Nassau County chapter of the American Red Cross at Mineola and chaired it until 1944, the year the National Institute of Social Sciences gave her its gold medal.

narrative_blocks.header: An electric car in wartime
narrative_blocks.body: When gasoline was rationed in the Second World War, Kate drove a 1922 Detroit Electric about the grounds of Peacock Point, a battery car good for twenty miles an hour.

narrative_blocks.header: A Bridgeport merchant’s daughter
narrative_blocks.body: Kate was born at Bridgeport in 1871, a daughter of Frederick Trubee, partner in the wholesale house of David Trubee & Co. and a trustee of the Bridgeport Savings Bank. He was buried at Bridgeport in 1912 and later moved to Locust Valley.

narrative_blocks.header: Oxford and Cambridge men for Yale
narrative_blocks.body: In 1923, the year after Henry died, Kate set up a fund to bring six students a year from Oxford and Cambridge to Harvard, Yale and Princeton.

narrative_blocks.header: A queen at tea, and five thousand guests
narrative_blocks.body: In October 1919 Queen Elisabeth of the Belgians was guest of honour at a Red Cross tea at Peacock Point, with General Pershing among the company, and in July 1931 five thousand came to a party for the county Safety Council. Kate opened the grounds to the YWCA and the Frontier Nursing Service too.

bio.bio_blurb: Founding headmaster of the Groton School

narrative_blocks.header: He founded Groton and ran it 56 years
narrative_blocks.body: Peabody opened Groton in 1884 with twenty-seven boys and two other masters, Sherrard Billings and Amory Gardner, on land the Lawrence family gave on condition that he build a chapel. He ran it for fifty-six years, until 1940, pressing the sons of the rich toward public service.

narrative_blocks.header: He married Franklin to Eleanor
narrative_blocks.body: His most famous pupil was Franklin Roosevelt, whose marriage to Eleanor he performed in 1905 and who had him preach at his inauguration. Roosevelt said that next to his father and mother no one had meant more to him, and quoted him in his fourth inaugural, two months after Peabody died.

narrative_blocks.header: A church in Tombstone, 1882
narrative_blocks.body: Peabody reached Tombstone in January 1882, three months after the gunfight at the O.K. Corral, and by June had built St. Paul's Episcopal Church, the oldest Protestant church building in Arizona; the Earp family gave its altar rail. Homesick, he left that July.

narrative_blocks.header: The White House, and then Sing Sing
narrative_blocks.body: By 1938 one of Peabody's old boys was in the White House and another in Sing Sing. Richard Whitney, star athlete and prefect, had led Wall Street's fight against the New Deal, then confessed to embezzling trust funds. The rector visited him in prison and stayed loyal to the end.

narrative_blocks.header: He expelled six seniors for a drink
narrative_blocks.body: In the fall of 1927, at seventy, Peabody learned that some seniors had taken a drink or two in graduates' rooms after the Harvard-Yale game, and expelled six of them. Parents and alumni protested loudly, and one old boy called him the Vicar of Bray. He did not relent.

narrative_blocks.header: He married his first cousin Fanny
narrative_blocks.body: Peabody was desperately in love with his first cousin Fanny Peabody, daughter of his father's brother Francis, and by 1883 had nearly given up hope. Their engagement was announced in October 1884, the month he ushered at his cousin Alice Lee's wedding to Theodore Roosevelt; they married in 1885 and had a son and five daughters.

narrative_blocks.header: A Hoover voter who toasted Roosevelt
narrative_blocks.body: Peabody voted for Herbert Hoover in 1932, then came round to the New Deal and stood by his old pupil against the alumni who hated him. At an alumni dinner in his honor at the Union Club in New York, he closed by calling Franklin Roosevelt a gallant and courageous gentleman he was happy to count as his friend, and the room went silent.

narrative_blocks.header: Child protection at MGH Chelsea
narrative_blocks.body: Betsy volunteered at the Charles Street Jail before taking her social-work master's at Boston College, then worked in child protection at the MGH Chelsea Health Center. On Cape Cod she kept a private therapy practice and consulted for Cape Cod Academy.

narrative_blocks.header: A master’s degree with four teenagers
narrative_blocks.body: Betsy finished college and graduate school while raising four teenagers, shared her husband Jack's work for civil rights in his parishes, could feed fifteen parishioners on a weeknight, and once painted a four-bedroom house inside and out by herself.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father died when she was two
narrative_blocks.body: Betsy's father, George Phillips Reynolds, died in 1939, when she was two, and her mother married the Rev. George Krumbhaar in 1942. Through both parents she descended from Thomas Hooker.

narrative_blocks.header: Rector in Somerville, Westwood and Winchester
narrative_blocks.body: Ordained an Episcopal priest in 1952, after a Master of Divinity at the Episcopal Theological School, Jack was rector in Somerville, Westwood and Winchester and taught preaching at the seminary as adjunct professor of homiletics. Retired, he kept filling pulpits as interim rector from Dedham to Woods Hole.

narrative_blocks.header: Civil rights, and women at the altar
narrative_blocks.body: Jack campaigned for civil rights from his parishes, with his wife Betsy beside him, and for the ordination of women as Episcopal priests, which the church did not approve until 1976.

narrative_blocks.header: Longest-active member of the Cruising Club
narrative_blocks.body: Ted learned to sail on Vinalhaven, at the summer house his grandfather Dr. Edward Reynolds built there in 1900, and cruised the Maine coast all his life, starting with his honeymoon. At his death he was the longest-active member of the Cruising Club of America.

narrative_blocks.header: Seabees in the Philippines, then Harvard crew
narrative_blocks.body: Out of Milton Academy in 1944, Ted enlisted in the Navy and served two years with a construction battalion in the Philippines. At Harvard he rowed on the first freshman crew and then three years on the varsity, graduating in 1950, and took his business degree in 1953.

narrative_blocks.header: From Pratt & Whitney to John Wiley
narrative_blocks.body: Ted's first job was with Canadian Pratt & Whitney Aircraft outside Montreal, where he and Joan lived seven years and had three of their sons. From Concord he held executive posts at the Mitre Corporation and Houghton Mifflin, and finished at John Wiley & Sons in New York.

narrative_blocks.header: Four sons who took up building
narrative_blocks.body: Wherever the family lived, Ted did the repairs and upkeep himself, usually with one of his young sons watching closely. Two of the four went into architecture, one became a building contractor, and the fourth took up woodworking.

narrative_blocks.header: Carmen and Herbert died the same day
narrative_blocks.body: Carmen and her husband Herbert Goldings both went from Radcliffe and Harvard to Harvard Medical School and practiced medicine and psychiatry around Boston. Married in 1955, they died together at their home in Needham on 23 November 2009, she eighty-one, he eighty.

narrative_blocks.header: Japanese on Kwajalein and Okinawa
narrative_blocks.body: Tim served in the Navy as a Japanese language officer in the Pacific until the war ended, going ashore with Army troops on Kwajalein and on Okinawa.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-two years of law in Milwaukee
narrative_blocks.body: After Harvard Law School in 1948, Tim joined Quarles & Brady in Milwaukee, became a partner, and practiced there until he retired in 1990. He died at home at nearly ninety-four, of old age, as he had wanted.

narrative_blocks.header: Herbert and Carmen died the same day
narrative_blocks.body: Herbert and his wife Carmen Reynolds, both Harvard Medical School graduates, practiced medicine and psychiatry around Boston. Married in 1955, they died together at their home in Needham on 23 November 2009, he eighty, she eighty-one.

bio.title: Dr.
bio.bio_blurb: Director of the Advanced Placement Program

narrative_blocks.header: From 93 high schools to over 8,000
narrative_blocks.body: Harlan ran the College Board's Advanced Placement Program from 1965 to 1989, for twenty-three of those years almost single-handedly. It grew from 93 high schools to more than 8,000, and from 34,000 students to about 315,000.

narrative_blocks.header: He built Harvard's advanced standing office
narrative_blocks.body: In 1954 Harvard began giving credit for college-level work done in high school, and Harlan, still a graduate student, was handed the job of making it work. When he left its Office of Advanced Standing in 1957, the first year's 39 students had become 174.

narrative_blocks.header: Ford money for the International Baccalaureate
narrative_blocks.body: In the mid-1960s Harlan sat on the first council of what became the International Baccalaureate. He helped win it its first big grant, from the Ford Foundation, and its diploma's recognition at Harvard and Princeton.

narrative_blocks.header: German at Williams, and dean of freshmen
narrative_blocks.body: Harlan left Harvard in 1957 for Williams College, where he taught German, chaired the German-Russian department and was dean of freshmen. He also translated a History of the Weimar Republic.

narrative_blocks.header: Drafted out of Harvard in 1943
narrative_blocks.body: The Army Air Forces took Harlan out of Harvard in 1943. He came back after the war, spent time in Alsace on a scholarship, and graduated summa cum laude in 1948.

narrative_blocks.header: Senior tutor at Kirkland House
narrative_blocks.body: Harlan married Dorothea Reynolds, a Radcliffe graduate, in 1950, the year he became an assistant dean at Harvard. They lived in Kirkland House, where he was senior tutor, and had four children.

narrative_blocks.header: Two chose IB, two chose AP
narrative_blocks.body: Harlan, a big man with a dry wit, gave each of his four teenagers the facts about the two programs he had championed and let them choose. Two picked the International Baccalaureate and two Advanced Placement, and in each case, he said, they chose right.

narrative_blocks.header: Westover and Sarah Lawrence, like her mother
narrative_blocks.body: Caren went to Westover and Sarah Lawrence, as her mother Edith had, and was studying for a master's in art history at Hunter College when she married Sheldon Sturges at Gates Mills in July 1970.

narrative_blocks.header: He fell from his own harbor patrol
narrative_blocks.body: An efficiency expert with offices at Rockefeller Plaza, Morgan organized a civilian defense patrol in 1942 to watch Port Jefferson harbor for U-boats. Taking his turn one February night aboard a 35-foot yawl, he slipped on the icy deck into the Sound; his son-in-law Michael Hare pulled him out, but he died the next day of shock and exposure.

narrative_blocks.header: Five generations of Meigs doctors
narrative_blocks.body: Edward took his Princeton degree in 1900 and his Penn medical degree in 1904, a physician like his great-grandfather, grandfather and father before him and his son after. He never needed to earn a living, and gave his whole energy to scientific research for the delight and service of it.

narrative_blocks.header: He wrote of his father's passion for truth
narrative_blocks.body: In a memoir of his father, Edward described a man with a passion for truth, whose mind had a peculiar exactness and never fooled itself into thinking it understood a matter before grasping it. His obituarist in 1940 turned the same words back on Edward.

narrative_blocks.header: Drink bred a false sense of cheerfulness
narrative_blocks.body: Edward disapproved of drinking because it encouraged a false sense of cheerfulness. His daughter Mary remembered a gentle, patient man prone to disabling depression, who yielded to his wife's forceful wishes and suffered all his life from believing in the honesty of others.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept Edward waiting nearly a decade
narrative_blocks.body: Margaret put off accepting Edward's proposal for nearly ten years. A month before their 1910 wedding she wrote to him that all his talk of getting to know each other made her feel like a specimen under a microscope, and she hated it.

narrative_blocks.header: Votes for women, but no college
narrative_blocks.body: In 1906 Margaret argued in public that women, being morally superior, ought to have the vote. She saw no reason for a woman to go to college, though, and scoffed at Bryn Mawr as pointless beside learning to run a household staff; her daughter Mary went anyway.

narrative_blocks.header: Roosevelt Democrats in Washington society
narrative_blocks.body: Margaret and Edward were renegades in their set as supporters of Franklin Roosevelt, and she later called Senator Joe McCarthy a demagogue. She took pride in her Quaker grandmother's work on the Underground Railroad.

narrative_blocks.header: His mother made him take up boxing
narrative_blocks.body: When Margaret decided Arthur was spending too much time with girls, she insisted he take up the manly art of boxing, and his father reluctantly went along.

bio.bio_blurb: Painter and author of Lily Briscoe: A Self-Portrait

narrative_blocks.header: She came out in print at sixty-four
narrative_blocks.body: Mary was sixty-four when Lily Briscoe: A Self-Portrait appeared in 1981, telling for the first time that she was a lesbian. She had held back, she wrote, because she could not bear being squeezed into corners and reduced to clichés. The Medusa Head, The Box Closet and The Time Being followed.

narrative_blocks.header: A landscape painter in Wellfleet
narrative_blocks.body: After Bryn Mawr, the Art Students League and two years as a WAVE in the Navy, Mary settled in Wellfleet on Cape Cod. She became known there as a landscape painter, played with the Provincetown Symphony, and fell in with Edmund Wilson and Mary McCarthy.

narrative_blocks.header: Barbara Deming, the first love of her life
narrative_blocks.body: Mary met the writer and pacifist Barbara Deming in 1954, when both were thirty-seven, and they were together for more than a decade; the friendship that followed she called permanent and unshakeable. She helped run the Money for Women Fund that Deming founded in 1975, and left it an annuity that paid out until 2017.

narrative_blocks.header: Three women under one roof for six years
narrative_blocks.body: In 1963 Edmund Wilson, researching his book on Canadian culture, introduced Mary to the Quebec novelist Marie-Claire Blais, twenty-two years her junior. Mary, Blais and Deming lived together for six years, and in 1975 Mary moved to Quebec to be with Blais, her partner for the rest of her life.

narrative_blocks.header: The Company of Strangers made her famous
narrative_blocks.body: In 1990 Mary played herself in Cynthia Scott's National Film Board film The Company of Strangers, about eight older women stranded in the countryside, and spoke on camera about being gay. People stopped her in the street afterward, and her book on the filming won the Quebec Writers' Federation Award in 1992.

narrative_blocks.header: Mary McCarthy put her in a novel
narrative_blocks.body: In A Charmed Life, her 1955 novel of a Cape Cod artists' colony, Mary McCarthy drew Mary as Dolly Lamb, a tiresome painter whose pictures were cramped with preciosity and mannerism.

narrative_blocks.header: She kept writing after the strokes
narrative_blocks.body: After her first stroke in 1999 Mary taught herself to sketch left-handed and kept writing, and she was discussing her next book with her publisher hours before she died. Those last pieces became Beyond Recall in 2005, a Lambda Literary Award finalist that closes with a poem called On Death.

narrative_blocks.header: Her sister married a ski trooper in 1942
narrative_blocks.body: In November 1942 Camilla was the only attendant when her sister, Mary Maynard Riggs, married Lt. Charles Crane Bradley at the Church of the Ascension in New York. The couple left for Camp Hale, Colorado, where he was posted to the 87th ski mountaineer troops.

bio.title: Dr.
bio.bio_blurb: Editor, Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery

narrative_blocks.header: Two decades at the orthopaedic journal
narrative_blocks.body: Thornie succeeded Dr. William Rogers as editor of The Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery in 1958 and held the chair until 1978. He took it to eight issues a year, launched Orthopaedic Transactions in 1977, and built an annual bibliography of the field with the National Library of Medicine.

narrative_blocks.header: Authors brought the ingredients, he made the cake
narrative_blocks.body: Each edited manuscript went back to its author with a long list of Thornie's questions, and some authors bristled; none could say the published paper was not better. He carried the work everywhere in a large, tattered brown briefcase, bulging with manuscripts.

narrative_blocks.header: A Marine battalion surgeon in the Pacific
narrative_blocks.body: Thornie finished Harvard College in 1936 and Harvard Medical School in 1940, then went to the Pacific in the Second World War as a battalion surgeon with the Marines. He came home to an orthopaedic residency at Massachusetts General and Boston Children's, and practised at Mass General from 1948.

narrative_blocks.header: Not a pillar but the foundation
narrative_blocks.body: On many Sundays Thornie went home from First Parish in Milton after the service, changed his clothes, and came back to work on the church for the rest of the day. He chaired its Parish Committee and sat for years on Buildings and Grounds; his minister called him not a pillar of the church but its foundation.

narrative_blocks.header: In due time, I will dance
narrative_blocks.body: Near the end, a caregiver asked Thornie whether she could help him move about his room. Not now, he told her, and then, after a moment, that in due time he would dance.

career.organization: The Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery

narrative_blocks.header: The Peak, Land Hope and a Newport summer
narrative_blocks.body: Haddie was forty-one and Arthur fifty-three when they married in September 1935, and they honeymooned in Bermuda. They kept two estates, The Peak in Radnor and Land Hope at Unionville, where his steeplechasers ran, and in the summer of 1941 leased Whetstone in Newport.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father gave Penn its red and blue
narrative_blocks.body: In 1874 her father, H. Laussat Geyelin, became the first man to run for Penn in intercollegiate track. Lining up for the 100-yard sprint at Saratoga, he was asked his school's colors. Penn had none, so he answered red and blue, and the university has worn them ever since.

narrative_blocks.header: The Father of Penn Athletics
narrative_blocks.body: Her father was the first Penn athlete to letter in three sports, track, rowing and football, and played on the university's first football team. He helped found the Athletic Association and chaired the Athletic Council, and died in 1921 known as the Father of Penn Athletics; his name is on a plaque outside Franklin Field.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Their estate in Radnor

bio.bio_blurb: Lesbian feminist writer and nonviolent activist

narrative_blocks.header: Jailed again and again for nonviolence
narrative_blocks.body: Reading Gandhi on a trip to India, then a visit to Cuba in 1960, turned Barbara to nonviolent struggle. She went to Hanoi during the Vietnam War, was jailed many times for peaceful protest and wrote Prison Notes in 1966, and in 1968 pledged to refuse the taxes that paid for the war.

narrative_blocks.header: She founded Money for Women in 1975
narrative_blocks.body: In 1975 Barbara founded the Money for Women Fund for feminist writers and visual artists, and ran it with help from Mary Meigs. Renamed for her after her death, it is the oldest ongoing feminist granting agency in the United States and Canada, and more than 750 women have had its grants.

narrative_blocks.header: Capote praised it; every publisher said no
narrative_blocks.body: Running Away from Myself, her study of 1940s movies, was praised by her New City neighbour Truman Capote and turned down by every publisher she tried; it came out only in 1969. She placed film criticism in Partisan Review, Vogue and The Nation, and said later she was almost killed as a writer in the forties and fifties.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten years and more with Mary Meigs
narrative_blocks.body: Barbara met the painter Mary Meigs in 1954, when both were thirty-seven, and they settled together in Wellfleet on Cape Cod. For six of those years the Quebec novelist Marie-Claire Blais lived with them, and after the three parted Barbara and Mary stayed close friends until Barbara died in 1984.

narrative_blocks.header: She fell for Norma Millay at sixteen
narrative_blocks.body: Barbara was sixteen when she fell in love with Norma Millay, Edna St. Vincent Millay's sister and a woman her mother's age, at New City. She wrote then that she was a lesbian and must face it, and a few years later that it was the devil who said this was the devil.

narrative_blocks.header: Illness holds me by the ankle
narrative_blocks.body: On 2 September 1971, driving to a conference in Georgia, Barbara was nearly killed in a car crash; she spent four months in hospital, and for a time her sight was in danger. The fragility never left her, and in 1977 she and the painter Jane Verlaine moved to Sugarloaf Key.

narrative_blocks.header: I want you to know I die happily
narrative_blocks.body: Told in June 1984 that her cancer could not be cured, Barbara went home to Sugarloaf Key to spend her last days among friends. Her last note told them how much she had loved her life and them, and that she died happily. She slipped into a coma on July 31 and died two days later.

bio.bio_blurb: Quebec novelist and playwright; Prix Médicis winner

narrative_blocks.header: Left school at fifteen, published at twenty
narrative_blocks.body: The eldest of five in working-class Limoilou, Marie-Claire left school at fifteen to work in shops and factories, writing in every free hour. A night course at Université Laval caught the eye of Jeanne Lapointe and Father Georges-Henri Lévesque, and in 1959, at twenty, she published La Belle Bête.

narrative_blocks.header: A Prix Médicis for Emmanuel
narrative_blocks.body: A Season in the Life of Emmanuel won the Prix Médicis in Paris in 1966, and Claude Weisz's film of it took a prize at Cannes. The Manuscripts of Pauline Archange, Deaf to the City and Soifs each won the Governor General's Award, and she was made a Companion of the Order of Canada in 1972.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten novels without a paragraph break
narrative_blocks.body: From 1995 to 2018 she wrote Soifs, ten novels with no chapters and no paragraph breaks, set in an island town modeled on Key West, where she kept her home in a circle that included John Hersey and James Merrill. Its hundred-odd drag queens, painters, writers and barflies all gather in the last book.

narrative_blocks.header: Edmund Wilson found her in her twenties
narrative_blocks.body: Marie-Claire was still in her twenties when Edmund Wilson, researching Oh, Canada, championed her novels and in 1963 introduced her to the painter Mary Meigs. She lived with Mary and Barbara Deming for six years, then with Mary in Brittany and from 1975 in Quebec, off and on for three decades.

narrative_blocks.header: The smiles of the angels at Chartres
narrative_blocks.body: At Mary's memorial in Montreal in 2002, Marie-Claire said they would miss her exquisite presence, her humour, her nobility and her lucidity, and would go on feeling the irony of her smile, a compassionate irony like the smiles of the sculpted angels at Chartres.

narrative_blocks.header: Chief librarian at Balboa, Panama
narrative_blocks.body: Carol finished her career as chief librarian of the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute at Balboa, Panama, retiring in 1984. Before that she had worked at the Library of Congress, the CIA and the U.S. Information Agency, and as social science bibliographer at the University of Massachusetts.

narrative_blocks.header: A doctorate in anthropology at fifty-six
narrative_blocks.body: Carol took a Vassar degree in art history in 1938, then went back to school two decades later: library science and anthropology master's degrees from Catholic University in 1960 and 1963, and a doctorate from the University of Massachusetts in 1973, at fifty-six. From 1965 to 1976 she taught pre-Columbian and American Indian art at six colleges, Harvard and Tufts among them.

narrative_blocks.header: A Cluett of Cluett Peabody
narrative_blocks.body: Rick's grandfather Albert E. Cluett spent many years with the family's Troy clothing concern, Cluett Peabody & Co., and his father was an assistant vice president of Manufacturers Hanover Trust. Rick went through the Berkshire School and Hobart College to Berkeley Divinity School, and in 1969 was on leave from it to work for Head Start.

bio.bio_blurb: Argentine general; president for three days in 1943

narrative_blocks.header: President for three days in June 1943
narrative_blocks.body: On 4 June 1943 Arturo, commanding the cavalry at Campo de Mayo, led ten thousand troops into Buenos Aires and overthrew President Ramón Castillo, ending the Infamous Decade. He declared himself president that day, ahead of Pedro Pablo Ramírez. Three days later he was gone, the shortest mandate of any Argentine president who was not merely acting.

narrative_blocks.header: He left the Casa Rosada in a jeep
narrative_blocks.body: Arturo's cabinet choices alienated the officers of the GOU, and he wanted Argentina in the war on the Allied side while most of them wanted neutrality. Col. Elbio Anaya came to his office and told him he was ruling by a misunderstanding; Arturo resigned, refused a military escort and drove away in a jeep, never having taken the oath of office.

narrative_blocks.header: The coup he thought was his own
narrative_blocks.body: The officers' lodge that planned the coup, the GOU, did not include Arturo, and he did not know it existed. When an emissary offered him the government, he assumed the man was joining a rising Arturo had been preparing on his own account.

narrative_blocks.header: A cavalryman on the Chaco frontier
narrative_blocks.body: Arturo graduated from the Military College in 1905 and taught there, led cavalry campaigns against the Chaco peoples in the 1920s, served as military attaché in Bolivia and directed the Cavalry School. He later wrote a book on Argentina and Bolivia in the wars of independence.

narrative_blocks.header: Ambassador, then prisoner twice
narrative_blocks.body: After his fall Arturo went to Brazil as ambassador until 1944. He was arrested and tried in 1945 for opposing President Edelmiro Farrell, and jailed again in 1951 for backing General Benjamín Menéndez's failed rising against Perón; a heart attack killed him in Buenos Aires the next year.

narrative_blocks.header: A Massachusetts doctor's great-grandson
narrative_blocks.body: Arturo was born in Santiago del Estero in 1884 into a San Juan family of American origin: his great-grandfather Amán Rawson had come from Montague, Massachusetts, to Buenos Aires as a young surgeon in 1818. He married Delia Sixta Borda in 1916, and they had four children.

narrative_blocks.header: A match made through Henry James
narrative_blocks.body: Henry James introduced John La Farge to his friend Thomas Sergeant Perry at Newport, and in October 1860 John married Thomas's sister Margaret, granddaughter of Commodore Oliver Hazard Perry. She bore eight children, seven of whom grew up, and outlived John by fifteen years.

narrative_blocks.header: Benjamin Franklin was her great-great-grandfather
narrative_blocks.body: Through her mother, Frances Sergeant, Margaret was a great-granddaughter of Sarah Franklin Bache, Benjamin Franklin's daughter. The family line ran back further still, to Governor Thomas Prence and Elder William Brewster of the Mayflower.

narrative_blocks.header: Her aunt Clover married Henry Adams
narrative_blocks.body: Mabel was an artist and writer, the daughter of Edward William Hooper, treasurer of Harvard. Her aunt Clover Hooper had married Henry Adams, who took her father-in-law John La Farge to Japan, and Mabel gave the name Henry Adams to her third son.

narrative_blocks.header: Whistler began a portrait of her sister
narrative_blocks.body: Their father, a collector of Whistler's paintings, commissioned the painter in 1890 to paint Mabel's red-haired older sister Ellen, a portrait never finished. Mabel became a writer and an artist whose work is in the Smithsonian American Art Museum.

bio.bio_blurb: Healthcare executive and Pasadena city councilman

narrative_blocks.header: He counted Pasadena's oaks his best work
narrative_blocks.body: Sidney joined the Pasadena City Council in 1997 to deal with the utility debt left by power deregulation, and chaired the city's Deregulation Committee in 2001. Asked what he was proudest of after twelve years, he named the 2004 tree protection ordinance, which shielded oaks and other species on public and private land.

narrative_blocks.header: From the Marines to hospital operations
narrative_blocks.body: Raised partly on his family's cattle ranch at Carbondale, Colorado, Sidney took a Harvard degree in American government in 1954 and served three years with the Marines in Korea and Japan. He went into pharmaceutical marketing research at SK&F in 1957, moved the family to Pasadena in 1969, and retired from Tenet Healthcare in 1994 as executive vice president.

narrative_blocks.header: He watched his successor debate first
narrative_blocks.body: In 2008 Sidney decided against a fourth term and recruited Terry Tornek to run for his seat, but would not endorse him until he had watched Tornek's first debate at Pasadena City College. He died in March 2014 after a fall from his bicycle on California Boulevard, not far from home.

education.school_name: Haas School of Business, UC Berkeley

bio.bio_blurb: Aviator; founder of the Sonoma Flight Academy

narrative_blocks.header: He taught Sonoma County to fly
narrative_blocks.body: Aviation was Harry's life: he worked for Cessna and for the Smithsonian's Air and Space Museum in the East, then founded the Sonoma Flight Academy, which trained many of the county's pilots. He presided over the board of the Sonoma Skypark airport and started Falcon Flight Aviation.

narrative_blocks.header: A banker who went back to teach reading
narrative_blocks.body: Peter spent his career at the Philadelphia National Bank, later First Union, and on retiring in 1998 became a reading teacher for adults at the Center for Literacy in Philadelphia. He died at home of pancreatic cancer in October 2001, at sixty-one.

narrative_blocks.header: The granite arches of Saint John the Divine
narrative_blocks.body: As president of the Mohegan Granite Quarrying Company in Westchester, Evelyn built the elevated portion of the New York subway and the great granite arches of the Cathedral of Saint John the Divine. He died suddenly at Peekskill in December 1910, at sixty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight years scouting New York's aqueduct
narrative_blocks.body: From 1885 to 1893 Evelyn ran the reconnaissance for the New York Aqueduct Commission, then spent three years building dams and reservoirs on the Croton watershed. In 1892 he published a history of the New York water supply in Engineering News.

narrative_blocks.header: Born at Fort Leavenworth on Christmas Day
narrative_blocks.body: Evelyn was born at Fort Leavenworth on Christmas Day 1848 and went from the Sheffield Scientific School to the railroads: the Northern Pacific from 1870, the Spring Valley Water Works in San Francisco, and five years as a contracting engineer on the Canadian Pacific in British Columbia.

career.organization: Spring Valley Water Works, San Francisco

narrative_blocks.header: Her father was captured at Occoquan
narrative_blocks.body: Helen's father, Vincent Shepard Caleb, enlisted in 1861 as a private in Company D of the 2nd Pennsylvania Cavalry, was captured with twenty-two comrades at Occoquan, Virginia, in December 1862, and was held fourteen days at Richmond. His name is on the Pennsylvania Monument at Gettysburg, and he later made steel in Chicago.

narrative_blocks.header: Last resident of the HemisFair grounds
narrative_blocks.body: Florence lived in the house she was born in, built at 434 South Alamo Street in 1866 as a wedding present to her parents, until she turned one hundred. When the land was taken for HemisFair, the city let her stay until that birthday, the last person living on the fair site, and she died at one hundred and two.

narrative_blocks.header: Custodian of the Alamo
narrative_blocks.body: Before her marriage Florence was custodian of the Alamo, and after studying art in New York she illustrated In the Shadow of the Alamo, written by her friend Clara Driscoll. At forty, in 1907, she married Colonel Harris Lee Roberts and went with him to Manila.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father reached Texas by sea, 1850
narrative_blocks.body: Florence's father, Robert Eagar, sailed from New York to Texas in 1850 on the W. H. Wharton and clerked for Vance Brothers in San Antonio. After the Civil War he joined the citizens working to bring the railroad to the city.

narrative_blocks.header: From Hamilton to Brooklyn
narrative_blocks.body: Edward took Saint Thomas Church at Hamilton, New York, in July 1847, a year after its church was built, and stayed about a year. In October 1857 he became rector of Emmanuel Church in Brooklyn, a new brownstone Gothic church for seven hundred on Smith and President Streets, and served until 1860.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: His father's house at Skaneateles.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-seven years in his grandfather's house
narrative_blocks.body: Richard came to Middletown about 1875 and moved into his grandfather Edward Russell's Greek Revival house on High Street, next door to the Samuel Russell House. He lived there until his death in 1932, fifty-seven years later.

narrative_blocks.header: He built the house later called Roosevelt Hall
narrative_blocks.body: Retired from building a flour mill and the Varick Canal at Oswego, Richard bought 220 acres at Skaneateles in 1838 and laid the first stone of a twenty-five-room Greek Revival mansion in May 1839. His family called it Lake Home and held that he designed it himself; he died there in June 1848, three days before his grandson Richard was born.

narrative_blocks.header: A wedding ball at the new house
narrative_blocks.body: The house was finished by August 1840, when Richard's daughter Emeline married Captain James Hughes Stokes of the U.S. Army at Saint James' Church in Skaneateles, and the evening ended with a ball at the DeZeng house.

narrative_blocks.header: Son of a Hessian baron
narrative_blocks.body: Richard's father, Frederick Augustus, Baron de Zeng, had been a major among the Hessian officers in the British army before settling at Red Hook, New York, where he married Mary Lawrence.

narrative_blocks.header: His nephew taught Eli Lilly to coat pills
narrative_blocks.body: Richard's sister Sarah married Richard Lawrence, and their son Henry Lawrence ran a drugstore in Lafayette, Indiana, where he took on the young Eli Lilly as an apprentice. He taught Lilly to dip pills in molten gelatin from a French journal's method, and Eli Lilly and Company later marked his grave.

narrative_blocks.header: Her cousin married her widower
narrative_blocks.body: Ruama died of inflammation of the bowel on 11 December 1847, at twenty-five, leaving a five-year-old daughter, Olive. John Rockwell later married her first cousin Mary Ingham, and Olive and her half-sister Mary stayed close all their lives.

narrative_blocks.header: From Coventry to Holland to Boston
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth Wooley, born at Coventry in 1603, married John Davenport, a Coventry mayor's son, and followed him into exile in Holland, where their son John was born at The Hague in 1635. Two years later she crossed with him to Boston and went on to found New Haven.

narrative_blocks.header: Six years a widow in Boston
narrative_blocks.body: In 1668 Elizabeth went back to Boston with her husband when he took the First Church pulpit, and he died there two years later. She outlived him by six years, died on 15 September 1676, and was buried in King's Chapel Burying Ground.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at forty with ten children
narrative_blocks.body: Alma married Frederick Russell Stewart in April 1908, at eighteen, and bore ten children in under twenty years. When Frederick died in October 1929 she was forty, and Kathleen, the youngest, had been born the year before; Alma lived on for nearly fifty-two years.

career.organization: Detroit, Arlington, Lansing and Grand Rapids

narrative_blocks.header: He nearly walked past the door
narrative_blocks.body: On Christmas Day 1942 Quentin, an Army MP at Long Beach, walked past the Los Angeles house where he was expected for dinner, argued with himself at the corner, and went back to ring the bell. Mary King answered. Sent out together for cream cheese, they found every store shut and talked like old friends.

narrative_blocks.header: The Pacific Ocean was in the wrong place
narrative_blocks.body: Every Michigan schoolboy knew the Pacific lay to the west, so Quentin hitchhiked from Long Beach to Los Angeles believing he was heading east. Going back, he rode on contentedly until the driver mentioned they were nearly at Santa Monica, twenty miles up the coast.

narrative_blocks.header: A bad eye sent him to the 773rd
narrative_blocks.body: Drafted in September 1942, Quentin was classed limited service for amblyopia in his left eye and posted to the 773rd Military Police Battalion, in which every man had some physical disability. It guarded the Long Beach airport, where Douglas was building B-17s.

narrative_blocks.header: Asked to Christmas dinner, then to cook it
narrative_blocks.body: Mary was working long hours at Douglas Aircraft's El Segundo plant to pay for her mother's cancer operations when her mother's cousin Bessie Morris asked them both for Christmas 1942. A day or two before, Bessie went off to a Christmas program instead and asked Mary to cook the dinner.

narrative_blocks.header: She met Fremont at Gene Stratton-Porter's home
narrative_blocks.body: Betty came to Indiana from Georgia in 1992 and was working at the Gene Stratton-Porter historic site at Rome City when she met Fremont Stewart. They married on 29 July 1994, the day before her sixty-fifth birthday, and travelled America and Europe together.

narrative_blocks.header: A school that stayed open all summer
narrative_blocks.body: Betty grew up at Stubbs, Texas, where the school stayed open through the summer so that pupils could borrow its books. It made her a reader for the rest of her life, and in her sixties she went to see the places she had only read about.

narrative_blocks.header: Noah always called her Becca
narrative_blocks.body: Rebecca was the daughter of William Greenleaf, sheriff of Suffolk County, and Noah's diary followed their courtship through the spring of 1787. They married on 26 October 1789, when she was twenty-three, and he called her Becca all his life.

narrative_blocks.header: A ring holding both their hair
narrative_blocks.body: Rebecca and Noah spent their first Thanksgiving as a married couple at his birthplace in West Hartford in 1789. A ring of theirs survives with hair believed to be both of theirs set in the centre, and their two names engraved on the back.

narrative_blocks.header: Eight children in eighteen years
narrative_blocks.body: Rebecca bore eight children between 1790 and 1808. Henry Bradford died as a baby, and Mary, who had married Horatio Southgate, died in 1819. Rebecca outlived Noah by four years and was buried with him at Grove Street in New Haven.

narrative_blocks.header: Barbara Walters's successor at twenty-five
narrative_blocks.body: Jane had been at Chicago's WMAQ-TV only ten months, the city's first woman co-anchor of a major evening newscast, when NBC chose her in 1976 to replace Barbara Walters on Today. She was twenty-five, and co-hosted the show for thirteen years, with Tom Brokaw and then Bryant Gumbel.

narrative_blocks.header: A teacher called her Margaret all year
narrative_blocks.body: Jane was so shy as a little girl that she let her second-grade teacher call her Margaret all year rather than say she went by her middle name. By high school at Warren Central in Indianapolis she was the state's top girl in extemporaneous speaking.

narrative_blocks.header: Twins born in front of the Today audience
narrative_blocks.body: Jane married Garry Trudeau on 14 June 1980. In 1983 she gave birth to twins after a very public pregnancy on Today, and became a model for working mothers; they had three children in all, and in 1989 she left Today hoping for more time with them.

narrative_blocks.header: Four thousand letters when she left Today
narrative_blocks.body: In 1989 NBC gave Deborah Norville a bigger part on Today, and Jane asked to leave and was at first refused. When she went that December the show lost a tenth of its audience within weeks, and more than four thousand letters of support reached her.

narrative_blocks.header: She made her bipolar disorder public
narrative_blocks.body: In her 2004 memoir Skywriting Jane made public her diagnosis of bipolar disorder, calling it the easiest decision she ever made. She has spoken for mental health ever since, and says she takes her medication every day, with no holidays.

narrative_blocks.header: Sunday Morning, forty years after Today
narrative_blocks.body: On 9 October 2016, nearly forty years to the day after her first Today broadcast, Jane succeeded Charles Osgood as host of CBS Sunday Morning, at sixty-five. The show had taken her on two years earlier after viewers wrote in about a profile of her.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father helped build the Monitor
narrative_blocks.body: Adra was the daughter of Isaac Vergilius Holmes, superintendent of construction on the Monitor at New York's Novelty Iron Works in the Civil War. He went on to build the Eclipse windmill works at Beloit, Wisconsin, which became the great Fairbanks-Morse plant.

cross_connections.display_label: built the Monitor's hull while her father worked on the ironclad

narrative_blocks.header: A railroad builder's daughter
narrative_blocks.body: Ethel was born at St. Joseph, Missouri, in 1873, where her father, John Fiske Barnard, an engineer trained at Rensselaer who had built railways in Canada, was superintendent of the Kansas City, St. Joseph & Council Bluffs. From 1886 he was president of the Ohio & Mississippi.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty-one years to the day after Adra
narrative_blocks.body: Ethel married George Bushnell in 1902, when she was twenty-eight and he forty-nine, and outlived him by thirty-three years. She died on 27 June 1957, sixty-one years to the day after his first wife, Adra, and was buried beside him at San Gabriel.

narrative_blocks.header: An Army daughter who married two officers
narrative_blocks.body: Mary, born at Beloit, Wisconsin, in 1882 to an Army surgeon, married Capt. Albert Brookes, a West Point man, in 1903; he died at Santa Fe ten years later. In 1919 she married Eugene Ferry Smith, five years her junior, just home from the Air Service in England.

narrative_blocks.header: Died in office as New Mexico's adjutant general
narrative_blocks.body: Albert graduated from West Point in 1895, retired from the Army as a captain, and in 1910 became Adjutant General of New Mexico. He died in office at Santa Fe in November 1913, at forty-three, of pneumonia after gallstone surgery, and lies in the national cemetery there.

narrative_blocks.header: He commanded the Americans at Shotwick
narrative_blocks.body: Commissioned a first lieutenant in the aviation section in November 1917, Eugene crossed to England in July 1918 and commanded the American detachments at Shotwick from August until after the Armistice. He came home on the Mauretania in December and was discharged at Camp Kearny on New Year's Eve.

military_service.branch: Aviation Section, Signal Officers Reserve Corps

narrative_blocks.header: He died reading at home
narrative_blocks.body: Charles went from the Montreal High School to Hopkins Grammar School in New Haven and on to Yale, then came home to the family drug house as a junior partner. He later formed Lyman, Knox and Company, and died of heart failure while reading at his Mackay Street home in November 1909.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty-six years with Lymans
narrative_blocks.body: Arthur joined Lyman, Sons and Company in 1880, at seventeen, became vice-president in 1904, president when it incorporated as Lymans Limited in 1910, and chairman in 1935. He married Ethel Paul of Toronto in 1926, at sixty-three, and died at his Côte des Neiges home in 1946.

cross_connections.display_label: , his grandfather, built the family drug house in Montreal and Toronto

narrative_blocks.header: A hundred and eleven years old
narrative_blocks.body: Ethel was born at Toronto in 1880, taught school across Canada all her working life, and married Arthur Lyman in 1926, at forty-six. She lived alone in her Westmount apartment until 1987, kept her 109th birthday at Pierrefonds Manor, and died in December 1991, at a hundred and eleven.

military_service.branch: 15th Field Regiment, Royal Canadian Artillery, Canadian Active Service Force

death.notes: Died a day old; buried south of St. Clair, Michigan

narrative_blocks.header: The third John Simpson in a row
narrative_blocks.body: The family numbered its Johns, and John was the third. His father, John 2, had come from Scotland at about twenty with his parents and seven brothers and sisters, six weeks from Dumfries on the schooner Thomson's Packet, landing at Philadelphia on 13 July 1818.

narrative_blocks.header: Freight wagons to Fort Snelling
narrative_blocks.body: In the winters of 1854 and 1855, when the Cook County farm lay idle, John hauled supplies by wagon from Chicago to Fort Snelling, some 650 miles there and back. On those trips he saw the Minnesota land he moved his family to in 1856.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife's uncle took his daguerreotype
narrative_blocks.body: John's likeness survives in a daguerreotype made by William Ward Snell, the brother of Sarah's mother, Martha, who took pictures of the family.

narrative_blocks.header: Dead at fifty-nine on the Waterford farm
narrative_blocks.body: John registered for the Civil War draft at Waterford in 1863, at thirty-eight. He died there of a gallstone obstruction on 19 May 1885, at fifty-nine, and was buried at Red Rose Cemetery, where Sarah joined him fourteen years later.

birth.notes: born after 1871

narrative_blocks.header: Fifteen when he enlisted in 1861
narrative_blocks.body: Kirkland was fifteen when he joined Company F of the 7th Connecticut Infantry at New Haven in 1861, and he served until the regiment was mustered out in July 1865. He moved to New London, Ohio, in 1871, commanded its Grand Army post for years, and died there in 1935, at eighty-nine, one of Huron County's last Union veterans.

narrative_blocks.header: She dedicated Dr. A. J. Chandler Park
narrative_blocks.body: Rosa, of an old Southern family, married Chandler at Denver in 1941, bringing two children, Barbara and Stephen, from an earlier marriage. They lived in his bungalow on the San Marcos grounds until his death in 1950. She came back in the 1970s to dedicate the town's central park as Dr. A. J. Chandler Park, and in 1987 for the city's seventy-fifth anniversary.

people.relational_label_override: Third Wife of the First Husband of a Ninth Generation Hooker

narrative_blocks.header: Brakeman at sixteen, station master by 1914
narrative_blocks.body: Burnside went railroading at sixteen as a brakeman, following his father, James, a station agent, and was agent himself at Orleans and Ryegate. In 1914 he moved to Bradford as the Boston & Maine's station master, and he retired in 1955, half a century after he started.

narrative_blocks.header: He bought a Michigan governor's house
narrative_blocks.body: In 1934 Burnside bought the Queen Anne house at Bradford built in 1891 for Albert Colburn of the Wait's River Paper Company. The seller was Albert E. Sleeper, Michigan's twenty-ninth governor, a Bradford Academy graduate. Vermont marked it the Hooker Family House in 2017.

narrative_blocks.header: Delivered by her grandfather, the doctor
narrative_blocks.body: Phoebe was born at South Ryegate on 20 April 1914, delivered by her grandfather Dr. George W. Darling, the only child of Burnside and Grace Hooker. She lived in Bradford all her life, for many years in her house on North Main Street.

narrative_blocks.header: On the commission that zoned Bradford
narrative_blocks.body: Phoebe graduated from Bradford Academy with high honors in 1932 and from the University of Vermont, where she studied elementary education. She was named to the original planning commission that drew up Bradford's zoning by-laws, and was long active in the Eastern Star and the DAR.

bio.bio_blurb: Collector of Chinese and Korean art

narrative_blocks.header: A Korean collection unmatched even in Korea
narrative_blocks.body: Over thirty-seven years Charles built one of the foremost private collections of Chinese ceramics, mostly of the Tang and Song dynasties. His Korean pieces were thought so complete that they might not be matched even in Korea itself.

narrative_blocks.header: He left it all to Boston
narrative_blocks.body: Charles bequeathed his Chinese and Korean ceramics, sculpture, bronzes, paintings and prints to the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, which catalogued them in two volumes from 1964. For more than twenty years he sat on the Fogg Museum's visiting committee at Harvard, and kept a house at Cambridge for the work.

narrative_blocks.header: He died on his way to Europe
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Kenosha, Wisconsin, the son of Col. James J. Hoyt, Charles was schooled at Lawrenceville and travelled widely, above all in East Asia. He sold his early Japanese prints in 1920, and died in a New York hotel in March 1949, at fifty-nine, on his way to Europe.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale's surgeon for twenty-six years
narrative_blocks.body: William opened an eye practice at New Haven in 1876 and three years later became Yale's professor of ophthalmology and otology. In 1881 he took the chair of surgery and held it until 1907, pressing from the first for the union of the medical school with New Haven Hospital.

narrative_blocks.header: His rounds by horse and buggy at ninety
narrative_blocks.body: For half a century beside his Yale teaching William kept a general practice in New Haven, and he went on making his calls by horse and buggy until he retired in 1927, past ninety. Yale made him a Doctor of Laws at its last commencement before his death.

narrative_blocks.header: Carbolic spray to the X-ray
narrative_blocks.body: William's case reports trace surgery's revolution as it happened: operations under Lister's carbolic spray, then asepsis, intestinal anastomosis, appendicitis and peritonitis, the first uses of the X-ray, and early surgery on the gall bladder.

narrative_blocks.header: The eye surgeon who studied cows
narrative_blocks.body: In 1864 William was a charter member of both the New York and the American Ophthalmological Societies, and he died the last survivor of the national society's founders. In the same years he operated on Blackwell's Island and wrote an authoritative report on infectious abortion in cows.

narrative_blocks.header: Four years under Waldeyer in Germany
narrative_blocks.body: In 1870 William gave up his New York practice and went to Germany, studying for some four years under Stricker and Waldeyer and following Waldeyer to Strasbourg at the close of the Franco-Prussian War. He came home grounded in pathology.

narrative_blocks.header: Gruff, and no patience for bunk
narrative_blocks.body: Usually gruff and, when the occasion demanded, brutal, William neither tolerated bunk nor bent on ethics, and held his students to a rigorous standard. He presided over the city, county and state medical societies and the American Surgical Association, and in 1922 Yale received an anonymous gift for a professorship in his name.

narrative_blocks.header: Raised a Quaker on a Pennsylvania farm
narrative_blocks.body: Born to Quaker parents at Friendsville, Pennsylvania, in 1836, William grew up on a farm and did not settle on medicine until he was twenty-one. He graduated from the College of Physicians and Surgeons in New York in 1861 and served with the Union forces in the Civil War.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father garrisoned Fort Delaware in 1861
narrative_blocks.body: Helen's father, a son of Joseph Ashmead Clay, enlisted at Philadelphia in April 1861 as a private in the Commonwealth Independent Company of Heavy Artillery, which garrisoned Fort Delaware until August, and served again in 1862 as a corporal in Robertson's Independent Battery.

narrative_blocks.header: President of Alcoa Inter-America
narrative_blocks.body: John spent most of his working life selling for Alcoa abroad, living with his family in Puerto Rico, Venezuela, Peru and Jamaica, and in 1968 he was made president of Alcoa Inter-America and moved the family to Miami.

narrative_blocks.header: A carrier's catapult officer
narrative_blocks.body: After Shady Side Academy John took a degree in aeronautical engineering at Rensselaer in 1947 and served with the Navy on an aircraft carrier as its catapult and arresting gear officer.

narrative_blocks.header: One putter for a whole golf career
narrative_blocks.body: John played his whole golf career with one custom Ben Sayers roll-in putter, whatever his children did to upgrade him. At Lake Wylie, South Carolina, from 1977 he sang in the River Hills church choir and drove for the local ambulance squad.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-one years racing, then teaching it
narrative_blocks.body: Tony's real passion was racing cars, which he called the most fun one could have with his clothes on. He retired with a division championship after twenty-one years and stayed on the track as a racing instructor.

narrative_blocks.header: The firm his grandfather founded in 1915
narrative_blocks.body: Tony was an investment counselor with Clifford Associates, the firm his grandfather founded in 1915. He loved fixing and building just about anything for family and neighbors, guided visitors as a docent at the USS Hornet Museum, and belonged to E Clampus Vitus.

narrative_blocks.header: A window for her at Grace Chapel
narrative_blocks.body: Helen lost her mother to cholera in 1852 and her father, Harper Gillingham of New Orleans, in 1861, and married George Coppell there in March 1862. She died in New York in February 1894, and the next year a memorial window to her was placed in Grace Chapel.

narrative_blocks.header: Three Eby children buried in 1864
narrative_blocks.body: In 1864 Emily Bartlett Eby lost three of her children, William Leroy, Charles Newton and baby Lenora, and Peter Eby died the following June. Of their five children, only Arabella, called Belle, outlived Emily.

narrative_blocks.header: Quartermaster to North Carolina's troops
narrative_blocks.body: At forty-two John Devereux took a major's commission as chief quartermaster of North Carolina's Confederate troops, supplying them in large part through the state's blockade-running ships.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped surrender Raleigh to Sherman
narrative_blocks.body: In April 1865, with William T. Sherman's army closing on Raleigh, Major John Devereux was one of the delegation sent out to surrender the city.

narrative_blocks.header: Winters at Runroi, summers at Wills Forest
narrative_blocks.body: In 1846 John Devereux bought Runroi, the family plantation in Bertie County, from his father. He and Margaret built a Greek Revival house at Wills Forest in Raleigh, on land she had inherited, and summered there.

narrative_blocks.header: Wills Forest was named for a shipwreck survivor
narrative_blocks.body: Wills Forest is said to take its name from Will, one of two men who survived a slave-ship wreck off North Carolina around 1760. Margaret's great-grandfather Joel Lane would not hold Will and Mark as slaves and built them a cabin.

narrative_blocks.header: Died the same day as his cousin Michael
narrative_blocks.body: Kenneth, a student at West Middle School, died on 19 November 1994 from injuries in an automobile accident, nine months after his father, James Edward Johnson, died at forty-one. His double first cousin, Michael Gene Johnson, died of accident injuries the same day.

narrative_blocks.header: Her son died at sixteen, her nephew too
narrative_blocks.body: Linda's son, Michael Gene Johnson, a sixteen-year-old sophomore at South Side High School, died on 19 November 1994 from injuries in an automobile accident. Her sister Glenda's son, Kenneth Joe Johnson, thirteen, died of accident injuries the same day.

narrative_blocks.header: Killed in a car accident at forty-three
narrative_blocks.body: Linda died at Jackson-Madison County Hospital on 10 January 1997, at forty-three, from injuries in an automobile accident, two years after her son Michael.

narrative_blocks.header: Plantation Sketches, written for her grandchildren
narrative_blocks.body: Margaret Lane Mordecai married John Devereux in 1842 and lived between Raleigh and the family plantations in Bertie County. Past sixty-five she wrote down stories of those years for her grandchildren, published in 1906 as Plantation Sketches, a memoir told from inside a slaveholding family.

narrative_blocks.header: The Federals buried her silver deeper
narrative_blocks.body: When Sherman's army reached Raleigh in April 1865, Federal troops camped in the grove at Wills Forest. The family silver lay buried in the branch below the house, and soldiers digging a watering place for their horses threw sand on the box and buried it deeper.

narrative_blocks.header: Daddy Will's spring at Wills Forest
narrative_blocks.body: Margaret's mother, Nancy Lane Mordecai, built the house at Wills Forest. The woods were named for Will, a survivor of a wrecked slave ship whom Joel Lane settled there, and the spring below was still Daddy Will's spring when Margaret and her half-sister Ellen were children.

narrative_blocks.header: Born six weeks after her father died
narrative_blocks.body: Margaret was born in October 1824, about six weeks after her father died at Sweet Springs in Virginia. He had kept the Jewish faith all his life; in 1833 her mother and three of the children were baptized at Christ Church in Raleigh.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father cut the candle in two
narrative_blocks.body: Her father, Moses Mordecai, was a short, blunt circuit lawyer. At a Virginia inn in 1822, finding one candle lit, he told the waiter: “in Carolina when we have two candles we light them both—and when we have but one, we cut it in two and light both pieces.”

narrative_blocks.header: Barrett School trustee for thirty years
narrative_blocks.body: Emma Batchelder served as a trustee of the Barrett School for more than thirty years. Born in Yerington in 1880, she lived there all her eighty-four years and was buried in the family plot at Yerington Cemetery.

narrative_blocks.header: He gave the land for the community hall
narrative_blocks.body: George Batchelder donated the land on which a large community hall was built near his Mason Valley home. When he died in September 1931, his funeral was held in that hall, which he had helped to build.

narrative_blocks.header: From a Quebec log cabin to Mason Valley
narrative_blocks.body: Born in a log cabin near Crampton Village, Quebec, in 1856, George Batchelder worked three years in a Vermont cheese factory, reached Reno in September 1876, mined at Ione for two years, and settled in Mason Valley in 1878.

narrative_blocks.header: A fall while picking peaches
narrative_blocks.body: In September 1931, at seventy-five, George Batchelder fell from a ladder while picking peaches at his home five miles south of Yerington. He broke his back on the Saturday and died the following Monday.

narrative_blocks.header: He built his own engine for fun
narrative_blocks.body: Lorain Forbush ran Forbush Salvage and Repair all his adult life, fixing farm and construction machines and, for many years, cars. He collected and rebuilt old engines, and designed and built one of his own for the fun of it.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty years of Part Art
narrative_blocks.body: For his last three decades Lorain Forbush made what he called Part Art. He rarely entered it in competitions, but when he did, it won awards.

narrative_blocks.header: To Peru after Smith
narrative_blocks.body: After graduating from Smith College with a degree in English, Peggy went to Peru with the Experiment in International Living.

narrative_blocks.header: Two sisters, two naval aviators
narrative_blocks.body: Peggy married Jack Chilton, a naval aviator, in Jackson, Mississippi, in October 1942. Six years later her younger sister Lavinia married another, Carl Holmquist.

narrative_blocks.header: From Macy's buyer to social worker
narrative_blocks.body: Peggy worked for a time as a buyer for Macy's in New York, and later as a social worker for San Diego County. She lived in Coronado for fifty-three years, from 1961 until her death at ninety-five.

narrative_blocks.header: She bought 140 acres of drained swamp
narrative_blocks.body: In 1989, the year after her husband died and while she was being treated for metastatic breast cancer, Lavinia bought Betts Meadows: 140 acres of drained swampland fifty miles north of Spokane, on the south slope of Chewelah Peak.

narrative_blocks.header: A logging sale stopped on Chewelah Peak
narrative_blocks.body: With her son Gunnar, Lavinia spent years restoring the wetland, and fought beside The Lands Council to stop a logging sale and protect the 5,000 unroaded acres of national forest that make up the whole watershed of Betts Meadows.

narrative_blocks.header: Four children through Navy postings
narrative_blocks.body: Lavinia, a twin, married Carl Holmquist, a naval aviator, in March 1948. They raised Kurt, Derek, Kristen and Gunnar through postings from Port Washington, New York, to Point Mugu, and two of the boys went to Annapolis.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty years with advanced cancer
narrative_blocks.body: Lavinia lived more than twenty years with advanced breast cancer, and wondered whether the meadows had bought her the extra time. "The land had its own way," she would say, "and it brought us along with it."

narrative_blocks.header: Hellcats off the Yorktown
narrative_blocks.body: Jack Chilton won his Navy wings in 1941 and flew F6F Hellcats with Fighting Squadron 1 off USS Yorktown, and was listed as wounded. The men of that squadron stayed with him for the rest of his life.

narrative_blocks.header: Test-flying DC-6s for the Navy
narrative_blocks.body: Called back for the Korean War, Jack served as the Navy's engineering and inspection officer at Douglas Aircraft in Santa Monica, test-flying DC-6s. He had trained as an electrical engineer at Mississippi State, class of 1937.

narrative_blocks.header: Swing guitar in Coronado
narrative_blocks.body: A jazz musician since his college days, Jack played guitar with the Coronado Swing Band in retirement, and played tennis regularly into his early nineties.

death.notes: Cremated; ashes scattered at sea
