quotes.text: With our present system, too much money is spent on paper studies that are largely worthless.

military_service.notes: Gunnery officer in seven campaigns: Guadalcanal, New Georgia, Gilberts, Marshalls, Marianas, Aleutians, Indian Ocean. Commendation from Adm. Halsey. Naval aviator 1945.

career.organization: Naval Training Device Center, Port Washington

narrative_blocks.header: Chief of Naval Research at fifty
narrative_blocks.body: On 1 June 1970, after eleven months as deputy, Rear Adm. Carl Holmquist was installed as Chief of Naval Research, the head of the Navy's science program, in a change-of-command ceremony at the Naval Research Laboratory.

narrative_blocks.header: Seven Pacific campaigns on one destroyer
narrative_blocks.body: Carl graduated from Annapolis in June 1942 with the accelerated Class of 1943 and joined the destroyer USS Dunlap as gunnery officer. He fought in seven campaigns, from Guadalcanal to the Indian Ocean, and found Vella Gulf the toughest.

narrative_blocks.header: Six years before the Navy let him fly
narrative_blocks.body: Carl joined the Navy wanting to fly, but was told he needed five or six years of regular service first. Home in Salt Lake City after two and a half years in the Pacific, with a commendation from Admiral Halsey, he left for flight school.

narrative_blocks.header: A Caltech doctorate in aeronautics
narrative_blocks.body: After the Naval Postgraduate School, Carl earned a Ph.D. in aeronautics at Caltech in 1953. He became chief engineer of flight test at the Naval Air Test Center, and experimental officer at the Naval Weapons Center at China Lake.

narrative_blocks.header: The missile center at Point Mugu, 1964
narrative_blocks.body: In 1964 Captain Holmquist, forty-four, left the Naval Training Device Center at Port Washington, New York, to command the Naval Missile Center at Point Mugu, California, and moved there with Lavinia and their four children.

narrative_blocks.header: Prize articles for the Naval Institute
narrative_blocks.body: Carl wrote steadily for the Naval Institute's Proceedings and Naval Review, and won its Award of Merit. On fighter design in May 1970 he warned that "too much money is spent on paper studies that are largely worthless."

death.cause: A-6E Intruder lost on a night training flight

cross_connections.display_label: flew the A-6 Intruder with its first fleet squadron in 1963
was shot down over Vietnam in 1972 and has never been found

military_service.notes: A-6E BuNo. 161673 lost 1 April 1985 northwest of Santiago, Panama; wreck located 2019.

narrative_blocks.header: Lost over the Panama jungle, 1985
narrative_blocks.body: On the night of 1 April 1985, Derek was flying an A-6E Intruder from USS Nimitz on a low-level training run when it vanished on a jungle mountainside northwest of Santiago, Panama. His navigator, Lt. Glenn Ziegler, was lost with him.

narrative_blocks.header: A hunter found the wreck in 2019
narrative_blocks.body: In May 2019, thirty-four years on, a villager out hunting photographed wreckage in the mountains that matched Derek's A-6. The Secretary of Defense ordered the two fliers recovered, but weather and the pandemic stalled the work.

narrative_blocks.header: Annapolis, thirty-one years after his father
narrative_blocks.body: Derek graduated from the Naval Academy in 1973, thirty-one years after his father, Carl Holmquist, and played rugby there. Classmates found him hard to get to know, and well worth the effort.

narrative_blocks.header: Shelly in Buried Child, spring 1984
narrative_blocks.body: In May 1984 Amanda played Shelly, the girlfriend in a black leather miniskirt thrown into a chaotic farm family, in Ohio University Theater's production of Sam Shepard's Buried Child. Three months later she was dead, at twenty-one.

narrative_blocks.header: A theater scholarship in her name
narrative_blocks.body: Ohio University's School of Theater awards the Amanda Talcott Garry Memorial Scholarship to its full-time juniors and seniors.

narrative_blocks.header: A duet with a bullfrog
narrative_blocks.body: Painting by the lake in Prospect Park, John once heard a man playing the saxophone and a bullfrog answering back. "A duet between a man and bullfrog," he said. "You can't make this stuff up."

narrative_blocks.header: Painting to escape the screen
narrative_blocks.body: A freelance graphic designer, John painted outdoors on weekends because at work he stared at a screen five inches from his face. Painting outside, he said, was a way to remember "a three-dimensional world around me."

narrative_blocks.header: Four or five days on each building
narrative_blocks.body: John paints city architecture outdoors, and in the four or five days a painting takes he often learns the building's history and meets its neighbors. He and Jane paint almost entirely in Brooklyn, and their work can be hard to tell apart.

career.organization: St. Mark's Episcopal Church, New Canaan

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-eight years at St. Mark's
narrative_blocks.body: Robert Neide was rector of St. Mark's Episcopal Church in New Canaan, Connecticut, for twenty-eight years, until apoplexy killed him in March 1918 at fifty-eight. He was buried in the Thompson mausoleum in Erie.

narrative_blocks.header: A clergyman's son, one of nine
narrative_blocks.body: Robert was one of nine children of Rev. George Little Neide, an Episcopal priest and sometime poet who was chaplain to the Bishop of Albany and a friend of Peter Cooper. His brother George also became a priest, in Memphis.

narrative_blocks.header: A homeopath in the Army medical corps
narrative_blocks.body: John Ireland studied medicine at the University of Michigan and graduated from Hahnemann College in Philadelphia at twenty-two. In the World War he held a captain's commission in the medical corps at Camp Oglethorpe, Georgia.

narrative_blocks.header: From runner to president of the bank
narrative_blocks.body: Horace went to work in 1911 as a runner for the Bridgeport Trust Company, the bank his father had helped found. He was its secretary by 1914, a director by 1917, and in 1929, when it merged with the City National Bank, president of the new Bridgeport-City Trust.

narrative_blocks.header: He helped found Bridgeport's Morris Plan Bank
narrative_blocks.body: Taken with the Morris Plan banks' success at lending small sums on personal credit, Horace helped establish the Morris Plan Bank of Bridgeport in 1915. He was its president from 1921 and its chairman from 1933 until the trust company bought it in 1944.

narrative_blocks.header: Branches in Fairfield and on the East Side
narrative_blocks.body: In 1920 Horace organized the Fairfield Trust Company and ran it until it became the Fairfield branch of his bank in 1937. In 1934 he opened an East Side office at East Main and Arctic streets, and its new building, designed under his direction, was going up when he died.

narrative_blocks.header: Captain of ordnance in the First World War
narrative_blocks.body: Horace served eighteen months with the Army Ordnance Department in the First World War and was commissioned captain before his discharge. In the Second he was active in civilian defense.

narrative_blocks.header: His first two children died in 1916
narrative_blocks.body: Horace married Marjorie DeForest Pierce in 1913. Their first two children, Bradford and Prudence, both died in 1916; Horace and Delight survived him, and Horace followed him into the Bridgeport-City Trust as a vice president.

military_service.notes: Eighteen months; commissioned captain before his discharge.

narrative_blocks.header: Two spells at the Litchfield Female Academy
narrative_blocks.body: Amelia studied at the Litchfield Female Academy from 1821 to 1824 and again in 1827, as her mother, Salima Storrs Seymour, had before her. Her diploma survives in the academy's collection at the Litchfield Historical Society.

narrative_blocks.header: She married the widower David Curtis Sanford
narrative_blocks.body: Amelia, a daughter of Ozias Seymour of Litchfield, married David Curtis Sanford, then a Litchfield lawyer, on 25 May 1830. She died on 15 July 1833, at twenty-four, three years into the marriage.

narrative_blocks.header: Killed at Wyse Fork in March 1865
narrative_blocks.body: Elias was one of thirteen men of the 15th Connecticut killed at Wyse Fork, near Kinston, on 8 March 1865, the day the regiment was captured. In the whole war it lost twenty-six men in action and nearly eight times as many to disease.

narrative_blocks.header: Company H of the 15th Connecticut
narrative_blocks.body: Elias enlisted in Company H of the 15th Connecticut in August 1862, two months before his third son was born, and fought at Fredericksburg that December. The regiment then spent more than a year at New Bern.

narrative_blocks.header: Clara brought him home from the field
narrative_blocks.body: Elias was buried on the field where he fell. When the war was over his widow, Elvira Clarissa, recovered his remains and brought them home to Connecticut.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirteen years at Rochester
narrative_blocks.body: Elias worked at Rochester, New York, from 1840 until the summer of 1853, when the family came back to Connecticut; his son Edgar was born there in 1851. His first wife, Mary Bigalow, died in October 1848, a year after their marriage.

narrative_blocks.header: Andrew on the muster roll, Andrews at home
narrative_blocks.body: Early records call Elias Andrew and later ones Andrews, the form his widow and sons kept. The clerks wrote down what they heard.

cross_connections.display_label: led Company K of his regiment at Fredericksburg in December 1862

military_service.notes: Enlisted Aug 1862. Fredericksburg, Dec 1862; more than a year at New Bern. Killed 8 Mar 1865 at Wyse Fork near Kinston NC, one of thirteen of the regiment killed that day; regiment captured. Buried on the field; remains recovered and removed to Connecticut by his widow after the war.

narrative_blocks.header: He died nine days after his degree
narrative_blocks.body: Simon, the eldest of Thaddeus's children, was prepared for college at the Woodstock Academy and was thought a young man of promise. He died at Thompson on 21 September 1810, in his twenty-third year, nine days after receiving his degree.

narrative_blocks.header: He kept his father's farm at Thompson
narrative_blocks.body: Noadiah farmed at Thompson all his life on the land he inherited from his father, and never married. Some of his papers are among the Larned family papers at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania.

narrative_blocks.header: Six when her mother died
narrative_blocks.body: Nabby was six when her mother, Abigail Russell, died in March 1797, and her aunt Esther became her stepmother when her father remarried. In 1813 Jacob Dresser wrote to Thaddeus and Esther asking for her hand.

narrative_blocks.header: Away at a Hartford seminary at fifteen
narrative_blocks.body: In the summer of 1805 Nabby was at a female seminary in Hartford, lodging with Thomas Bull, kin of her uncle Simon's wife. Her father's letter that July, written in haying season, closed: “Your Mama wishes you to be particularly careful of your ankle & inform whether it still remains lame.”

death.city: At sea near Rio de Janeiro

bio.bio_blurb: Army major, entrepreneur, ranked tennis player

narrative_blocks.header: A funeral train out of Grand Central
narrative_blocks.body: Charles had belonged to New York's Church of the Heavenly Rest for ten years. When he died by his own hand at his wife's family homestead in New Haven in January 1906, scores of friends heaped his coffin with flowers, and a special train carried the mourners from Grand Central to Woodlawn.

narrative_blocks.header: Charter member of the Hartford Hearing League
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah was a charter member of the Hartford Hearing League and in time its president. She belonged to St. John's Episcopal Church in East Hartford for more than fifty years.

narrative_blocks.header: Married to Hartford's first radiologist
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah married Dr. Robert Sythoff Starr, who became Hartford's first radiologist, and they raised two sons and a daughter. Widowed in 1952, she lived on at South Windsor for sixteen years and died in November 1968, at eighty-nine.

narrative_blocks.header: Hartford's first radiologist
narrative_blocks.body: Robert took his M.D. at Columbia in 1901 and joined his father in practice at Hartford. Dr. Pierre Sythoff Starr had been an assistant surgeon with the 39th Ohio Volunteers in the Civil War, and Robert became the city's first radiologist.

narrative_blocks.header: A middle name from The Hague
narrative_blocks.body: Robert's middle name came from his grandmother Catherine Sythoff, whose parents lived at The Hague. On the Starr side he went back to Dr. Comfort Starr, who came over from Kent in 1637, and through two Starr wives to Elder William Brewster and John Alden.

cross_connections.display_label: descended from Dr. Comfort Starr, the Leech of Salem

bio.title: Rev.
bio.bio_blurb: Free Will Baptist minister and convention president

narrative_blocks.header: He presided over the Free Will Baptists
narrative_blocks.body: Egbert taught school in Rusk County, Texas, and became a Free Will Baptist minister about 1905. In 1915, at Stratford, Oklahoma, he was elected president of the Southwestern Convention, the Free Will Baptists of Missouri, Oklahoma and Texas who had stayed out of the 1911 merger with the Northern Baptists.

education.dates: B.S., M.S., social work and counseling

narrative_blocks.header: The 173rd Airborne, then forty years in oil
narrative_blocks.body: Daniel served in Vietnam with the Army's 173rd Airborne and came home to finish a chemical engineering degree at Texas A&M. He spent more than forty years in the oil and gas industry before he retired.

military_service.notes: U.S. Army; honorably discharged.

narrative_blocks.header: A cabinetmaker who turned country preacher
narrative_blocks.body: Lyndon learned the cabinetmaker's trade in the Farnham household at Hardwick, and in March 1820 married Anna Farnham. He went into the ministry and preached in turn at Moretown, Duxbury, Fayston, Warren and Coventry, and at Franklin from 1845 to 1861.

narrative_blocks.header: Six sons in the Union army
narrative_blocks.body: Six of Lyndon's sons served in the Union army in the Civil War, twelve years of service among them.

narrative_blocks.header: Everyone home for the Fourth of July
narrative_blocks.body: On 4 July 1879 the whole family met at Franklin: Lyndon, Anna, their eight sons and three daughters, and all their families. Six days later Lyndon died there, at eighty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: An encyclopedia of religious knowledge
narrative_blocks.body: The Rev. W. C. Smith of St. Albans said of him: "Lyndon S. French is an encyclopedia of religious knowledge, and a system of unimpeachable theology."

narrative_blocks.header: Pitcher for the Tecumsehs
narrative_blocks.body: Harry pitched for the Tecumsehs, one of the best semi-professional baseball clubs around Fall River in the late 1880s and early 1890s, with Charles "Chuck" Holland catching. He had been a frail boy, and trained himself into one of the leading gymnasts on the bars and rings in YMCA circles.

narrative_blocks.header: From mill clerk to the Herald to auditor
narrative_blocks.body: Out of Fall River High School, Harry kept books at the Barnaby Manufacturing Company under Stephen B. Ashley, and when the Barnaby mills closed he reported for the Fall River Herald. He went on to audit the accounts of many corporations, and drew and painted in watercolor besides.

narrative_blocks.header: Chief boatswain's mate of the Prairie
narrative_blocks.body: Lynward was a Fall River man in the Massachusetts Naval Militia, and in May 1898 he sailed from New York as chief boatswain's mate of the Prairie, a Morgan liner bought for the war and manned mostly by militiamen from Fall River and New Bedford.

narrative_blocks.header: Coaling eighteen hours at Tompkinsville
narrative_blocks.body: In late June Lynward and his shipmates coaled the Prairie at Tompkinsville for the run south, working from five in the morning through Sunday night, nearly eighteen hours at a stretch. At midnight they dropped asleep on deck amid the coal dust, too tired to reach their hammocks.

narrative_blocks.header: Two hours of gunfire off Mariel
narrative_blocks.body: Lynward was aboard on 5 July 1898 when the Prairie ran twenty-five miles in little over an hour to the blockade-runner Alfonso XII, aground off Mariel, and set her burning with her six-inch guns. One shot sank a Spanish gunboat that came out of the harbor.

narrative_blocks.header: A week on the hawsers at Ponce
narrative_blocks.body: Off Ponce in August the Prairie spent a week hauling the transport Massachusetts, full of cavalry, off a sand bar, her hawsers snapping like twine, and the next week freed the Manitoba from the same bar. Nearly a quarter of the crew went on the sick list, Lynward among the worst.

narrative_blocks.header: Buried with the Marines at Guantánamo
narrative_blocks.body: Lynward was put aboard the St. Paul to be sent home and died on the way on 9 August 1898, at twenty-seven. He was buried with the Marines who fell at Camp McCalla, Guantánamo, and brought home to Oak Grove in Fall River in 1899.

narrative_blocks.header: His shipmates' album of the cruise
narrative_blocks.body: The Fall River men who had served with Lynward paid for an album of photographs of the Prairie's cruise in his memory, and his sister Sarah Hathaway French gave it to the Fall River Historical Society in 1946.

cross_connections.display_label: was a naval militia gunner on the Prairie's sister ship Yankee
landed at Ponce on 2 August 1898 and went home with fever

notable.notable_blurb: Chief boatswain's mate of the USS Prairie, 1898

military_service.notes: Fell ill off Puerto Rico in August 1898; died aboard the St. Paul on the way home; buried at Camp McCalla, Guantánamo, and reinterred at Fall River in 1899.

narrative_blocks.header: Vassar chemistry, three years at Yale Medical
narrative_blocks.body: Barbara Ann took a degree in chemistry at Vassar and spent three years at Yale Medical School, and worked for a time in research for Dr. Janet Travell, later President Kennedy's physician.

narrative_blocks.header: She learned to sail at Warwick Woods
narrative_blocks.body: Barbara Ann learned to sail at Warwick Woods Camp in Wisconsin and sailed all her life, and she saw to it that her husband and their eight children learned too. A canoe and a sailboat were about the only possessions she cared for.

cross_connections.display_label: employed her in research, then became President Kennedy's physician

narrative_blocks.header: Stamford's first thoracic surgeon
narrative_blocks.body: After Fordham, Yale Medical School, an internship at McGill and a residency at the Overholt Clinic in Brookline, Frank came to Stamford as its first thoracic surgeon. He practised cardiovascular surgery there for twenty-eight years and was chief of surgery at both Stamford Hospital and St. Joseph's.

narrative_blocks.header: Law school at fifty-eight
narrative_blocks.body: At fifty-eight Frank started law school at Quinnipiac, took his J.D. at sixty-two, and practised as a legal medical consultant, still answering his colleagues' and friends' medical questions.

narrative_blocks.header: A teenager in the wartime Merchant Marine
narrative_blocks.body: Born in 1927, Frank served in the Merchant Marine in the Second World War while still in his teens.

narrative_blocks.header: The Red Cross, the TB association, Yale
narrative_blocks.body: Frank presided over Stamford's Tuberculosis and Health Association and the New Canaan Red Cross, sat on Stamford Hospital's ethics committee, and in later years chaired the Yale Medical School alumni association.

cross_connections.display_label: was secretary of the Maritime Commission that manned the wartime fleet
served in the wartime Merchant Marine and co-created Yang–Mills theory

bio.title: Rev.
bio.bio_blurb: Senior minister of Wayzata Community Church

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty years at Wayzata Community Church
narrative_blocks.body: Harold was senior minister of the Wayzata Community Church from 1957 until he retired in 1977, and greatly enlarged both its membership and its buildings. His warmth toward everyone made him known as the Hugging Pastor.

narrative_blocks.header: Farmington, then the legislature's chaplain
narrative_blocks.body: Before Wayzata, Harold served the First Church of Christ, Congregational, in Farmington, Connecticut, from 1938 to 1957, and for several years was chaplain to the Connecticut General Assembly in Hartford.

narrative_blocks.header: Ten years of interim pulpits
narrative_blocks.body: Harold sat on the United Church of Christ's Board for World Ministries from 1964 to 1972, and for ten years after he retired served one Twin Cities church after another as interim minister.

cross_connections.display_label: held the Farmington pulpit thirty-six years, from 1661

narrative_blocks.header: From Winnetka to Village of Golf
narrative_blocks.body: Rebecca graduated from Vassar in 1927, and her daughter Patricia followed her there. In 1955 she and Carleton left Winnetka for Florida, where she was a founding member of the Country Club of Florida at Village of Golf and of Quail Ridge at Boynton Beach.

bio.bio_blurb: Show-jumping owner and Hall of Fame inductee

narrative_blocks.header: A junior horse show at thirteen
narrative_blocks.body: Fran grew up showing and hunting horses around Chicago, and as a girl co-produced one of the first all-junior horse shows, which earned her a certificate of honor from the Chicago Sun in 1946. She went on to win many year-end Amateur Owner Hunter awards.

narrative_blocks.header: Starman, silver at Seoul
narrative_blocks.body: Fran's Westphalian stallion Starman carried Anne Kursinski to team silver at the 1988 Olympic Games in Seoul and a tie for fourth individually, and won the Grand Prix of Aachen in 1991. He went into the Show Jumping Hall of Fame in 2012, five years before she did.

narrative_blocks.header: Livius and Eros, horses held in shares
narrative_blocks.body: Fran owned Livius, one of the first syndicate-owned show jumpers, who won individual and team gold at the 1983 Pan American Games. Eros, an Australian Thoroughbred she also syndicated, won the Pulsar Grand Prix of Mexico and team silver at the 1996 Atlanta Olympics.

narrative_blocks.header: A World Cup qualifier at Flintridge
narrative_blocks.body: In California Fran rode at the Flintridge Riding Club with her daughter Francie, served as its president and helped create the Grand Prix of Flintridge, one of the first FEI World Cup qualifiers in the West. She was a founding member of the American Grand Prix Association.

narrative_blocks.header: Forty-five years in the Gold Medal Club
narrative_blocks.body: Fran was the first donor to reach thirty-five consecutive years in the USET Gold Medal Club and carried the run to forty-five, and she was a trustee of the USET and its Foundation for fifty years. The Show Jumping Hall of Fame inducted her in 2017.

cross_connections.display_label: rode twenty years for Canada's show-jumping team, gold in 1970
founded the Association of American Horse Shows in 1917

bio.bio_blurb: Co-founder of the Golden Apple Foundation

narrative_blocks.header: The Oscars night that began Golden Apple
narrative_blocks.body: Watching the Oscars at home one night, Pat and her husband Mike wondered why the country made so much of its actors and so little of its best teachers. In 1985 they founded the Golden Apple Foundation, which gives Chicago's finest teachers an awards night of their own on public television.

narrative_blocks.header: Vassar, then publishing in Manhattan
narrative_blocks.body: Pat grew up in Winnetka, the middle of Carleton and Rebecca Blunt's three daughters, went to Vassar as her mother had, and worked in publishing in Manhattan before she married Mike Koldyke in 1960.

narrative_blocks.header: Against handguns, for city schools
narrative_blocks.body: From Kenilworth, where she and Mike raised four children, Pat worked for the Illinois Coalition for Handgun Control, the Chicago Council on Foreign Relations and the Academy for Urban School Leadership.

bio.bio_blurb: Navy attack pilot and Rocketdyne engineer

narrative_blocks.header: 152 carrier landings in the Mediterranean
narrative_blocks.body: Bill flew with Attack Squadron 45 as flight officer and assistant special weapons officer, logging more than 750 hours and 152 carrier landings in the Mediterranean, two hundred of those hours at a hundred feet or so. His squadron's move to Florida in the Cuban missile crisis was called off.

narrative_blocks.header: Rocket engine tests, then insurance
narrative_blocks.body: Out of the Navy, Bill engineered material-handling equipment and rocket engine tests at Rocketdyne, then turned to financial planning and underwriting with Connecticut General Life. He never quite retired, consulting from a home office for many years.

cross_connections.display_label: made 659 carrier landings in thirty-one years of Navy flying

bio.bio_blurb: Show jumper; Medal and Maclay Finals winner
Founder of Frontenac and the Golden Apple Foundation

narrative_blocks.header: The venture capitalist behind Frontenac
narrative_blocks.body: Mike founded Frontenac, a Chicago private equity firm, sat on the board of Northwestern University and chaired Chicago's public television station.

narrative_blocks.header: Teachers' own Oscars
narrative_blocks.body: In 1985 Mike and Pat founded Golden Apple, which honors ten Chicago teachers a year in a prime-time broadcast on public television, with a cash prize, a computer and a tuition-free term at Northwestern.

narrative_blocks.header: A residency for city teachers
narrative_blocks.body: In 2001 Mike started the Academy for Urban School Leadership, which trains mid-career recruits for a year beside practicing teachers, on the model of a medical residency. Within a few years it ran eleven Chicago schools and kept ninety-five per cent of its teachers.

narrative_blocks.header: Brainstorm, after Desert Storm
narrative_blocks.body: At the 1991 Golden Apple awards Mike asked whether the will that had won Desert Storm could be turned to a campaign he called brainstorm, an energy surcharge to pay teachers what they were worth. "Shouldn't a Golden Apple teacher with 20 years experience make as much as a beginning lawyer in Chicago or Los Angeles?"

cross_connections.display_label: , his father-in-law, was a life trustee of Northwestern University

narrative_blocks.header: A Wolfeboro doctor's daughter
narrative_blocks.body: Susan was born at Wolfeboro, New Hampshire, in August 1839, the eldest of the four children of the town's physician, Dr. Jeremiah Hall, and his wife Annette. Her mother died in 1865, the year Susan married Ainsworth Blunt and went with him to Cleveland, Tennessee.

narrative_blocks.header: Railroad builder and Dalton storekeeper
narrative_blocks.body: Benjamin came south from Vermont to help build the Western and Atlantic Railroad at Cross Plains, Georgia, married Martha Blunt there in September 1842, and went into the mercantile business with her father on the corner of Thornton Avenue and Morris Street in Dalton.

cross_connections.display_label: , his father-in-law, was his partner in a Dalton store

bio.bio_blurb: Eighth Air Force pilot and executive recruiter

narrative_blocks.header: Nineteen missions as lead pilot
narrative_blocks.body: Charles flew with the 34th Bomb Group of the Eighth Air Force out of Mendlesham in East Anglia: twenty-seven combat missions over Europe, nineteen of them as lead pilot, and two mercy missions. He came home with the Distinguished Flying Cross and the Air Medal with four oak leaf clusters.

narrative_blocks.header: Yale after the war, then executive search
narrative_blocks.body: Charles finished Yale in 1947, with a major Y, and became a management consultant in New York, rising to partner and senior director of the executive search firm Spencer Stuart.

narrative_blocks.header: Ethics at Oxford in retirement
narrative_blocks.body: In 1988 Charles retired to study ethics at Oxford, and the next year he founded the Alling Institute of Ethics. In Maine he sat on several boards, among them Maine Businesses for Social Responsibility.

narrative_blocks.header: A book written with his daughter
narrative_blocks.body: Charles was chairman emeritus of the Foundation for Leadership and Ethics in New York, with which his institute was affiliated, and Defense Secretary William Cohen named him to the Board of Visitors of the Air University at Maxwell Air Force Base. With his daughter Elizabeth Alling Hildt he wrote A Mighty Fortress.

cross_connections.display_label: estimated the German fighters waiting for each Eighth Air Force raid
flew in the war, then was tapped for Skull and Bones a year after him

awards: Air Medal with four oak leaf clusters
military_service.notes: 27 combat missions, 19 as lead pilot, and two mercy missions, from Mendlesham.

narrative_blocks.header: A book written with her father
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth wrote A Mighty Fortress with her father, Charles Booth Alling Jr.

bio.bio_blurb: Biospherian, marine biologist and expedition leader

narrative_blocks.header: Two years sealed inside Biosphere 2
narrative_blocks.body: On 26 September 1991 Abigail was one of the eight biospherians who went through the airlock of Biosphere 2 and stayed sealed inside its 3.15 acres for two years, recycling their own air, water, food and wastes. She wrote Life Under Glass with Mark Nelson and Sally Silverstone while still inside.

narrative_blocks.header: A million-gallon coral reef under glass
narrative_blocks.body: From 1986 to 1994 Abigail was director of marine ecological systems at Biosphere 2, where she built and ran a million-gallon mangrove marsh and coral reef, the largest artificial marine ecosystem ever made.

narrative_blocks.header: Two captive dolphins set free
narrative_blocks.body: In the 1980s Abigail spent five years in Sri Lanka setting up a marine mammal sanctuary with the WWF and the United Nations, and she was the marine biologist who supervised the first successful release of two captive bottlenose dolphins back to the wild.

narrative_blocks.header: Six weeks among the humpbacks
narrative_blocks.body: As expedition chief of the research ship Heraclitus on its circumnavigation of South America, Abigail spent six weeks off the Antarctic Peninsula studying the population genetics of humpback whales with the National Cancer Research Institute.

narrative_blocks.header: A sailing ship for the coral reefs
narrative_blocks.body: In 1991, while still inside Biosphere 2, Abigail co-founded the Biosphere Foundation with her fellow biospherian Mark Van Thillo, and as its president she runs coral reef, sea turtle and marine mammal programs from its 113-foot sailing ship Mir in the waters off Bali.

narrative_blocks.header: The next Cousteau, said James Cameron
narrative_blocks.body: The filmmaker James Cameron said of Abigail and Mark Van Thillo: "These are the people who are the next Cousteau."

cross_connections.display_label: was in the room when the Explorers Club began in 1904
was chief oceanographer of the Coast and Geodetic Survey in 1957

notable.notable_blurb: Biospherian, marine biologist and expedition leader

narrative_blocks.header: Married in a prison camp in 1863
narrative_blocks.body: Mary married Capt. Lovell M. Brooks of the 128th Ohio on 27 August 1863 at the Johnson's Island prison camp on Lake Erie, where her father was the regiment's surgeon. Brooks died of typhoid fourteen months later, and in 1866 she married Benjamin Warner Wells.

narrative_blocks.header: Married at the prison camp on Lake Erie
narrative_blocks.body: Lovell was captain and assistant quartermaster of the 128th Ohio, and on 27 August 1863 the chaplain Robert McCune married him to Mary Woodbridge at the Johnson's Island prison camp, where her father was the regiment's surgeon. Fourteen months later he died of typhoid fever at Rock Island, Illinois.

bio.title: Cmdr.
bio.bio_blurb: Navy commander; Schley's flag lieutenant at Santiago

narrative_blocks.header: Schley's flag lieutenant off Santiago
narrative_blocks.body: Ben was Rear Admiral Schley's flag lieutenant on the armored cruiser Brooklyn in 1898, and distinguished himself in the battle with Admiral Cervera's fleet off Santiago.

narrative_blocks.header: From Annapolis to the Monadnock
narrative_blocks.body: Appointed to the Naval Academy from Illinois in 1883, Ben graduated in 1887, took his ensign's commission in 1889, served on the monitor Monadnock in 1895 and 1896, and was made a lieutenant in March 1897.

narrative_blocks.header: He met his wife at Ponce
narrative_blocks.body: At Ponce in Porto Rico in 1898 Ben met Julia Rommell, a Boston nurse working in the field hospital through the worst of the fever season, and they married at the Church of St. John the Evangelist in Boston in January 1899.

narrative_blocks.header: Retired, then recalled in 1917
narrative_blocks.body: Ben retired a commander in 1906 and spent much of his time in New York, until the Navy recalled him to the office of the Judge Advocate General. He died of heart trouble at Washington in June 1917 and was buried at Arlington.

narrative_blocks.header: She taught French at Oberlin
narrative_blocks.body: Isabella, a linguist who had studied at Northwestern, taught French at Oberlin College as a substitute whenever her health allowed. Severe asthma wore her heart down, and she died at Campton, New Hampshire, in July 1925, when her son Charles was twelve.

narrative_blocks.header: A nurse in the fever hospital at Ponce
narrative_blocks.body: Julia went out to Porto Rico in 1898 as a nurse with the Episcopal Sisterhood of St. Margaret, under Sister Frances, and worked in the field hospital at Ponce through the worst of the fever season. There she met Lt. Benjamin W. Wells, the admiral's flag lieutenant, and married him in Boston the next January.

narrative_blocks.header: West in a prairie schooner
narrative_blocks.body: Charles was carried from Vermont to Nebraska in a prairie schooner as a child of two or three in the early 1870s. He went to the University of Nebraska, then to Williams, class of 1898, and spent his working life publishing college and school textbooks with Ginn & Company.

cross_connections.display_label: sold textbooks for Ginn & Company from 1926 to 1958

bio.title: Lt.
bio.bio_blurb: Monuments Man and National Gallery chief curator

narrative_blocks.header: A Monuments Man in Germany
narrative_blocks.body: A Navy gunnery officer through most of the war, Charles joined the Monuments, Fine Arts and Archives section in April 1945. Working under James Rorimer he helped locate 1,036 repositories of looted art in southwest Germany alone, and France made him a chevalier of the Legion of Honor in 1948.

narrative_blocks.header: He signed the Wiesbaden Manifesto
narrative_blocks.body: In November 1945 Charles refused an order to ship German-owned paintings from Wiesbaden to the United States, and signed the Monuments Men's manifesto against it. When a colonel reminded him he had a wife and two children to think of, he walked out of the room; his wife said it was the act he was proudest of.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifteen cases of crown jewels
narrative_blocks.body: Charles talked a castle caretaker into showing where the Bavarian royal crown jewels were hidden, deep in a tower behind a wall of pantry shelves lined with jars. Behind the shelves was a secret room holding fifteen cases of them.

narrative_blocks.header: Alaska roads before the museums
narrative_blocks.body: Charles meant to be a scientist until a Williams course with Karl Weston turned him to art. After graduating in 1935 he spent two years in Alaska building roads and bridges, teaching music and coaching basketball, then took his M.A. at Oberlin and his M.F.A. at Princeton under Erwin Panofsky.

narrative_blocks.header: A conservation laboratory at Oberlin
narrative_blocks.body: As director of Oberlin's Allen Memorial Art Museum from 1949, Charles founded the Intermuseum Conservation Laboratory in 1952, the country's first regional non-profit center for conserving art. He ran the Baltimore Museum of Art from 1962 and as president of the American Association of Museums began its accreditation of museums.

narrative_blocks.header: Chief curator through the East Building
narrative_blocks.body: In 1942 Charles had helped move the National Gallery's most important pictures to safety at the Biltmore estate. He came back in 1970 as its assistant director and chief curator, and saw the East Building through its construction before he retired in 1983 to teach and curate at Williams and Smith.

narrative_blocks.header: The Burghers of Calais in the woods
narrative_blocks.body: Walking through the forest below a castle near Neuschwanstein, Charles saw what he took for woodsmen standing close together, dejected and not moving. It was a cast of Rodin's bronze of the six citizens who offered their lives to save Calais in 1347, left in the snow because it was too heavy to haul up the mountain. "Then in a flash I realized I had stumbled on The Burghers of Calais," he said, "just sitting in the woods!"

bio.bio_blurb: First woman vice president of Amtrak

narrative_blocks.header: The first woman vice president at Amtrak
narrative_blocks.body: Rima was the first woman to hold a vice presidency at Amtrak, as vice president of passenger services, after Washington years as assistant director of the American Civil Liberties Union and executive director of the Democratic National Committee's Democratic Advisory Council.

narrative_blocks.header: Every performance at the Kennedy Center
narrative_blocks.body: Rima was the first director of government affairs at the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, a job she loved because she could attend every performance. Later she and Sandy Spence formed Parkhurst-Spence Consultants, and she worked with former Senator Birch Bayh at his law firm.

narrative_blocks.header: A green scooter into her nineties
narrative_blocks.body: Retired to Easton, Maryland, Rima sat on the boards of the Academy Art Museum, the Chesapeake Chamber Music Society and the Talbot Arts Council, and spent years as a court-appointed advocate for children. She rode her green Metropolitan scooter around town into her nineties, and to every offer of help said, "I can do it myself."

career.role: Professor of the History of Art

narrative_blocks.header: A poet and editor at The Paris Review
narrative_blocks.body: Nancy went to the Brearley School and Syracuse University, and by 1975 she was a poet and one of the editors of The Paris Review in New York. She also represented the Livingstone-Learmonth Gallery, and married Gifford Whitney there that October; her first marriage had ended in divorce.

narrative_blocks.header: She posed with the Beatles in 1964
narrative_blocks.body: Walter got Nancy and her younger sister Kathy tickets to The Ed Sullivan Show in February 1964, and at the rehearsals on 8 February the Beatles put their arms around the two girls for a photograph. Two months earlier, on 10 December 1963, Walter had put a CBS report on the Beatles on the Evening News.

narrative_blocks.header: She answered for her father's will
narrative_blocks.body: Walter's 2005 will divided his estate among Nancy, her sister Kathy, her brother Chip and two CBS aides, and left out Joanna Simon, his companion in his last four years. Nancy said her father had been generous to Joanna in life but, out of respect for her mother Betsy, never meant to marry her or leave her his estate.

cross_connections.display_label: is a poet whose work has run in The Paris Review

narrative_blocks.header: Boat lessons for Harry's sake
narrative_blocks.body: Settling Gifford's estate in March 2005, Francine met Fernando Banhara at Consolidated Yachts on City Island, where Gifford had kept his boats and dirt bikes. Fernando taught her basic boating so she could take her son Harry out on Long Island Sound as his father had, and they married in April 2007.

narrative_blocks.header: Trusted above every politician in 1972
narrative_blocks.body: Walter anchored the CBS Evening News from 1962 to 1981, signing off each night with "And that's the way it is." In a 1972 Oliver Quayle poll of public trust he scored 73 percent, ahead of Nixon, McGovern, Muskie and Edward Kennedy, and CBS began calling him the most trusted man in America.

narrative_blocks.header: Johnson watched him call Vietnam a stalemate
narrative_blocks.body: Back from Vietnam after the Tet Offensive, Walter told viewers in February 1968 that it seemed "more certain than ever" the war would end in a stalemate. Lyndon Johnson reportedly said, "If I've lost Cronkite, I've lost middle America," and five weeks later announced he would not run again.

narrative_blocks.header: He fired a machine gun over Germany
narrative_blocks.body: Walter was one of eight reporters the Army Air Forces flew on B-17 raids over Germany, the Writing 69th, and on one mission he fired a machine gun at a German fighter. In 1944 he rode a glider into Holland with the 101st Airborne, then covered the Bulge and, after the war, the Nuremberg trials.

narrative_blocks.header: From Mercury to John Glenn again in 1998
narrative_blocks.body: Walter covered the space program from Project Mercury through the Moon landings, and he was the only person outside NASA given its Ambassador of Exploration award. In 1998, seventeen years after leaving the anchor desk, he was back on the air for CNN when John Glenn returned to space.

narrative_blocks.header: Fired over a fire that never happened
narrative_blocks.body: At KCMO radio in Kansas City, on the air as Walter Wilcox, Walter refused to broadcast a fire the program director's wife had phoned in until someone checked it. The program director read the bulletin himself; there was no fire, and Walter was the one fired.

narrative_blocks.header: He called Kennedy's retake lousy sportsmanship
narrative_blocks.body: In 1960 Senator John F. Kennedy fumbled a filmed CBS interview at his Georgetown house and asked to do it over. Walter climbed the stairs, told him CBS would say on air that he had asked for a retake, and called it "the lousiest bit of sportsmanship I ever saw"; Kennedy said, "Let it run!"

narrative_blocks.header: His yacht honored a Dutch bride of 1642
narrative_blocks.body: When CBS judged auto racing too dangerous for its anchor, Walter took up sailing, and from 1974 he summered at Edgartown on Martha's Vineyard. He named his Sparkman & Stephens yacht Wyntje, for the woman who married his first Dutch forebear in New Netherland in 1642.

narrative_blocks.header: Sixty-five years from a Kansas City station
narrative_blocks.body: Betsy Maxwell met Walter in 1936 at KCMO radio in Kansas City, where he was calling the sports. They married in 1940 and were together sixty-five years, until her death in 2005, and their daughter Nancy said her death devastated him.

bio.bio_blurb: Writer and photographer of expatriate Europe

narrative_blocks.header: A Rome studio for American expatriates
narrative_blocks.body: Richard moved to Europe in 1960, and his photography studio in Rome became a social and intellectual centre for the Americans living there. Other artists photographed and sculpted him in turn, and he had a cameo in the film of Tender Is the Night.

narrative_blocks.header: From Venice, Frail Barrier to twelve stories
narrative_blocks.body: Richard wrote and photographed Venice, Frail Barrier, and followed it with Caravansary, Goodbye Europe and Lost in the City of Light. His last book, Certain Restrictions May Apply, gathered twelve stories set in the places he had lived, and for four years he taught writing at Marymount College.

narrative_blocks.header: A singer at the Ruban Bleu
narrative_blocks.body: As a teenager Richard sang and played the piano, first in American cities, then in Paris, and at last at the Ruban Bleu, the Manhattan supper club.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-nine years with Miles Morgan
narrative_blocks.body: Richard and Miles Morgan were partners for fifty-nine years, from about 1954 until Richard's death in December 2013, and Richard spent his last years between Manhattan, La Colle-sur-Loup in Provence and Venice. Miles's niece Quincy, who called him her uncle, still recommends his stories.

bio.bio_blurb: Nine-goal polo player and Hall of Famer

narrative_blocks.header: Overtime winner at the 1976 Gould World Cup
narrative_blocks.body: Taught the game by his father Les, Red reached a nine-goal rating at his peak and played in many of the biggest matches of the 1970s. In 1976 he scored the overtime winner in the first Gould World Cup at Oak Brook, a professional all-star match with seven future Hall of Famers on the field.

narrative_blocks.header: Camacho Cups and the Cup of the Americas
narrative_blocks.body: Red won the Camacho Cup for the United States in 1974 and 1975 and the Coronation Cup in 1974, and he played against Argentina in the Cup of the Americas in 1979 and 1980. At home he won the USPA Gold Cup in 1977 and again in 1995 with Kerry Packer's Ellerston White, three Silver Cups, and the 1979 World Cup.

narrative_blocks.header: Into the Polo Hall of Fame in 1999
narrative_blocks.body: Red served the United States Polo Association as a governor and as chairman of its handicap committee, and on 26 February 1999 he was inducted into the Museum of Polo and Hall of Fame at Lake Worth. He was known as a team player with a keen eye for horses.

narrative_blocks.header: From Belmont Park to Wall Street
narrative_blocks.body: At fifteen Louise climbed the fence at Belmont Park to talk a trainer into a job hot-walking thoroughbreds, among them Secretariat, Ruffian and Hoist the Flag. When her father died suddenly in 1981 she went to work for two brokers at Thomson McKinnon to keep her family, joined Bear, Stearns in 1985, and later ranked among the country's top women advisers at JPMorgan.

narrative_blocks.header: A daughter of the Swamp tanner
narrative_blocks.body: Anna was a daughter of Jacob Lorillard, a younger son of the founder of Lorillard Tobacco, who made his own fortune as a leather merchant with a tannery in the Swamp, later made tobacco with his brothers, and became president of the Mechanics' Bank. Six of his ten children grew up and married, among them the wives of Lewis Gouverneur Morris and Daniel Edgar.

narrative_blocks.header: A widow for nearly thirty-four years
narrative_blocks.body: Anna married George Cammann in 1833 and was widowed in February 1863, when he died at fifty-eight. She lived on until December 1896, dying in New York at eighty-seven, and was buried beside him at Trinity Church Cemetery.

artworks.artwork_blurb: National Museum of Amer. History, DC

death.note: after September 1808

narrative_blocks.header: Sister of Brigham Young's mother
narrative_blocks.body: Betsey was a daughter of Phineas Howe and Susannah Goddard of Hopkinton; her sisters Abigail and Rhoda became the mothers of Brigham Young and Willard Richards. She died in March 1821, leaving seven children, the youngest not yet four. Her stone at Holliston reads: "The righteous have peace in their death."

narrative_blocks.header: A widower and his seven children
narrative_blocks.body: Judith married the widower John Haven at Holliston in February 1823, when she was twenty-four and he forty-eight, and raised his children alongside their own daughters, Maria and Eliza. She was baptized with him in 1838, came west in 1848, and outlived him by thirty-eight years.

narrative_blocks.header: Known in Salt Lake as Mother Haven
narrative_blocks.body: Known in Salt Lake City as Mother Haven, Judith stayed strong and healthy into her nineties until a fall broke her hip in 1891. She died at the home of her son-in-law, Bishop R. T. Burton, on the morning of 25 August, her last words "I am going home."

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty years in the Charlton pulpit
narrative_blocks.body: John trained for the Congregational ministry at Amherst College and the seminary at East Windsor, Connecticut, and took his first pulpit at York, Maine. He served ten years at Stoneham, Massachusetts, and then thirty as pastor of the Congregational church at Charlton, where he died in September 1892 at eighty-three.

narrative_blocks.header: A minister baptized with his father
narrative_blocks.body: On 30 June 1838, while serving as a Congregational minister, John was baptized into the Latter-day Saints on the same day as his father. He kept his Massachusetts pulpits for the rest of his life, and nothing he left says what the baptism meant to him.

narrative_blocks.header: Three marriages in eight years
narrative_blocks.body: John's first wife, Nancy Read, died in August 1838, two years after their wedding and a year after their son John Edward was born, and his second, Martha Curtis Morrison, died in 1842. In 1844 he married Martha McMillan Chadbourne, who lived until 1900.

narrative_blocks.header: A hymnbook from the Holliston church
narrative_blocks.body: A copy of the 1830 Musical Monitor in the collection of the Daughters of Utah Pioneers carries a note that John and his brother Jesse both sang from it in the Holliston Congregational church.

education.school_name: Theological Institute of Connecticut, East Windsor

narrative_blocks.header: Seminaries at Bradford and Amherst
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth worked her way through the seminaries at Bradford and Amherst and taught school for years before and after her marriage. At Nauvoo her pupils included the children of Joseph Smith and of his brother Hyrum.

narrative_blocks.header: Baptized by her cousin Willard Richards
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth was baptized at Holliston in the fall of 1837 by her cousin Willard Richards, over her deacon father's objection. The next fall she set out with her eight-year-old niece for Far West, Missouri, fifteen hundred miles away.

narrative_blocks.header: She met Israel Barlow at Quincy
narrative_blocks.body: At Quincy, Illinois, Elizabeth met Israel Barlow, and they married there on 23 February 1840 and later worked on the Nauvoo temple. Crossing the plains with her father in Brigham Young's company of 1848, she gave birth to a son on the way.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifteen years leading Bountiful's Relief Society
narrative_blocks.body: Elizabeth was present when the first Relief Society was organized at Nauvoo on 17 March 1842, and later led the first one at Bountiful for more than fifteen years. During the move south in 1858 she drove a team to Payson and back.

narrative_blocks.header: Twins while Israel was in England
narrative_blocks.body: A few months after Israel left on his mission to England in 1853, Elizabeth gave birth to twin boys at Bountiful; one, Willard, died as an infant. She died at Bountiful on Christmas Day 1892, three days short of eighty-one, leaving forty-nine grandchildren and nineteen great-grandchildren.

bio.bio_blurb: First LDS mission president in South Africa

narrative_blocks.header: A church founded on the Lion's Head
narrative_blocks.body: Jesse landed at Cape Town with William Walker and Leonard Smith in April 1853, and on 23 May the three climbed the Lion's Head and organized the church in the Cape of Good Hope, with Jesse as its president. Mobs broke up their early meetings, but when he left in December 1855, 176 people had been baptized in the colony.

narrative_blocks.header: Home in 1856 to a son of three
narrative_blocks.body: In May 1856 Jesse and Edward Martin brought more than eight hundred emigrants from Liverpool to Boston on the Horizon. He led a handcart group for three hundred miles before it merged with Martin's company, crossed the plains with the Hodgetts wagons, and reached Salt Lake on 15 December, meeting his three-year-old son for the first time.

narrative_blocks.header: Facing Johnston's Army in 1857
narrative_blocks.body: In 1857 President Buchanan sent about 2,500 troops under Albert Sidney Johnston to replace Brigham Young as governor, and Jesse was a leader in the militia raised to keep them out. No battle was fought, and the troops entered peacefully in 1858 under a pardon for the settlers.

narrative_blocks.header: Probate judge of Morgan County
narrative_blocks.body: After two years as chaplain of the territorial legislature, Jesse moved to a farm in Morgan County in 1862. When Brigham Young asked whether he would take another mission to Africa, he said he would rather not but would go if told; he was made circuit judge instead, and was probate judge from 1869 to 1878.

narrative_blocks.header: A temperance society at sixteen
narrative_blocks.body: Jesse joined Holliston's Congregational church at thirteen, where his father was a deacon, and at sixteen helped start a temperance society and a singing school, which his neighbors mocked. Opposition, he wrote later, "instead of discouraging me, made me more zealous."

narrative_blocks.header: He called on Solomon Spaulding's widow
narrative_blocks.body: When Holliston's Congregational minister published what he called an affidavit from Solomon Spaulding's widow, naming her husband's manuscript as the source of the Book of Mormon, Jesse went to see her at Monson. She denied the story, and his father John published her denial.

narrative_blocks.header: Martha, Abigail and Sarah
narrative_blocks.body: Jesse married Martha Hall in 1842 and Abigail Cram in 1850, a week after reaching Salt Lake City, and in 1857 Sarah Taylor, who had crossed the plains with him; they divorced in 1860. Abigail's son Jesse Cram Haven died in 1879 at twenty-five, and Jesse died at Enterprise in December 1905, at ninety-one.

bio.bio_blurb: Member of the 14th Quorum of Seventy
Zion's Camp veteran and Bountiful nurseryman

narrative_blocks.header: With Zion's Camp in 1834
narrative_blocks.body: Baptized by Brigham Young in 1832, Israel marched with Zion's Camp from Ohio to Missouri and in 1835 was ordained to the original First Quorum of Seventy. In 1839 he led Joseph Smith to the land at Commerce, Illinois, that became Nauvoo.

narrative_blocks.header: A nurseryman at Bountiful
narrative_blocks.body: After presiding over the Birmingham conference in England, Israel brought a company of emigrants home on the Samuel Curling in 1855. At Bountiful he was known as a nurseryman, raising berries, sugarcane and vegetables in the dark loam of the northwest part of town.

cross_connections.display_label: came to Bountiful in 1854 and kept a diary of the Utah War

narrative_blocks.header: From York, Maine, to Auckland
narrative_blocks.body: John Edward was born at York, Maine, where his father was pastor, and lost his mother when he was a year old. He settled in New Zealand, married Elizabeth Mahony of County Cork at Auckland in 1871, and died there in December 1908.

landmarks.landmark_blurb: Rufus Sibley's Rochester store

narrative_blocks.header: Sibley's, Rochester's store for a century
narrative_blocks.body: Rufus met Alexander Lindsay and John Curr while keeping books for a Boston dry-goods store, and in 1868 the three opened the Boston Store in Rochester. As Sibley, Lindsay & Curr, known to the city simply as Sibley's, it lasted more than a century, and Rufus was its president until 1924.

narrative_blocks.header: A twelve-story store at Main and St. Paul
narrative_blocks.body: In 1893 Rufus moved the store into the new twelve-story Granite Building at the corner of Main and St. Paul streets, replacing the old corner store. A Rochester neighbor wrote that he was "all engaged over building the new Store."

narrative_blocks.header: Prize Jerseys on 700 acres at Moose Hill
narrative_blocks.body: From about 1887 Rufus bred Jersey cattle at Moose Hill in Spencer, Massachusetts, the town where he was born. The farm grew past seven hundred acres, and its herd of more than 150 won medals for milk from the American Jersey Cattle Club, which he served as president.

narrative_blocks.header: Six times a deputy to the Episcopal convention
narrative_blocks.body: An Episcopalian, Rufus was six times a deputy to the church's General Convention. In Rochester he presided over the University of Rochester's trustees and the Chamber of Commerce, and chaired the board of the City Hospital.

narrative_blocks.header: A distant cousin of the Western Union Sibleys
narrative_blocks.body: Rochester had two Sibley families, and Rufus's line met that of Hiram Sibley, the Western Union founder, only five generations back. Rufus and his second wife, Elizabeth Conkey, moved in the same circles as Hiram's family all the same.

narrative_blocks.header: Martha Haven, married by her father in 1870
narrative_blocks.body: Rufus married Martha Haven at Charlton on 11 October 1870, with her father, the Rev. John Haven, performing the ceremony. Two of their three children died young, Martha died in 1883, and in 1885 Rufus married Elizabeth Conkey of Rochester.

narrative_blocks.header: He enlisted at forty in 1917
narrative_blocks.body: Edward enlisted in the Army when the United States entered the First World War, though he was forty, and rose to captain with several commendations. He served more than a year overseas and was badly hurt in an automobile accident in France.

narrative_blocks.header: A physician who taught at Penn
narrative_blocks.body: After St. Paul's School, the University of Virginia and the University of Pennsylvania's medical school, Edward practised in Philadelphia and taught at the Penn medical school. He retired about 1934, lived at Hyannis Port, and spent his last decade at Palm Beach, where he died in July 1954.

narrative_blocks.header: A camp in their daughter's memory
narrative_blocks.body: Edward married Margaret Morris of Philadelphia in 1911. Their only child, Margaret, died in 1920 at eight, and in her memory they established a camp for underprivileged children near Philadelphia.
