narrative_blocks.header: Buried at night among walnut trees
narrative_blocks.body: Lucinda died at half past six on the morning of Sunday, 14 May 1854, near Salt Creek in Kansas, at twenty-four, and Newton buried her that night beside the road in a cluster of walnut trees. She had told him that if she had consumption she did not want to linger, as many did.

narrative_blocks.header: A grass-covered mound by Salt Creek School
narrative_blocks.body: Unable to find Salt Creek on a 1988 map, two of Newton's great-granddaughters, Inez Barker and Julia Brough, found it on 1850s maps at the Daughters of Utah Pioneers museum. Julia's husband, LeGrande Brough, followed Newton's description to the remains of a walnut grove near Salt Creek School and found a grass-covered mound at its centre.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father would not bid Newton goodbye
narrative_blocks.body: Lucinda joined the church on 21 July 1853, and on 3 April 1854 she, Newton and their daughter Clara left North Haven for Utah. Her father, Samuel Mix, would not speak to Newton or bid him goodbye; she already had consumption, and her mother said she would not live three months.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-three Saints on the Keystone State
narrative_blocks.body: The family travelled with fifty-three Saints through New York and Philadelphia to Pittsburgh, where on 7 April they boarded the Keystone State for Cincinnati, Lucinda homesick and seasick. From St. Louis they went up to Fort Leavenworth on the Sam Cloon, with Lucinda and Clara both sick on the way.

narrative_blocks.header: Buried at night on Grasshopper Creek
narrative_blocks.body: Clara fell very sick on the trail on 18 June 1854, and Orson Pratt laid hands on her and blessed her. She died early on the evening of 23 June, forty days after her mother, and Newton had a coffin made and buried her that night in a cove on Grasshopper Creek.

narrative_blocks.header: A machinist's daughter from New Haven
narrative_blocks.body: Emily's father, Amos Pease Stone, was a gunsmith and machinist who built a steam engine and ship-block machinery at New Haven for George W. Staples of New York. Her parents joined the Latter-day Saints there in December 1844, and her mother, Amelia Bishop, died before the family could go west.

narrative_blocks.header: A bride at sixteen in Salt Lake City
narrative_blocks.body: Emily reached Utah in September 1850, at eleven, with the Joseph Young company, and married Newton Tuttle at Salt Lake City on 7 April 1855, at sixteen. She raised eleven children at East Bountiful and died there in December 1927, at eighty-eight.

narrative_blocks.header: Four acres, and horses named Nibs and Navrix
narrative_blocks.body: When Edgar married in 1887, his father gave him four acres in Bountiful and built a two-room brick house with a lean-to. The barn stood at the foot of a small hill, with cows, pigs and two horses, Nibs, a black, and Navrix, a white.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty pounds of flour on his shoulder
narrative_blocks.body: Asked to come back to the temple next day to finish the Tuttle family sealings, Edgar said he had to work, and was promised his family would never want for bread. Years later, with no flour in the house, his wife Cynthia told their daughter Lydia he would find work that day, and he came home with fifty pounds on his shoulder.

narrative_blocks.header: From the brickyard to the Mercur mines
narrative_blocks.body: When the Bountiful brickyard closed in 1901, Edgar went to the mines as a mucker and became a miner. In 1906 he moved the family to the Johannesberg quarter of Mercur, joining two three-room houses into one for his nine children.

narrative_blocks.header: He died tending the chapel furnace
narrative_blocks.body: In 1911 the family moved to Pleasant Green, across from the ward chapel, where Edgar became custodian and built a bakery with an inheritance, worked by his son Newton, who had learned the trade at Mercur. He died there on 20 March 1912, at forty-nine, while tending the chapel furnace during a ward dance.

narrative_blocks.header: Twins born the night of the loose hogs
narrative_blocks.body: In June 1895, pregnant and alone at their log cabin at Mendon while Edgar was in the canyon for logs, Cynthia was kicked trying to catch loose hogs, and twins were born that night. The boy, Amos, lived long enough to be blessed and named, and his sister Annie lived. Cynthia recovered slowly, and the family sold the farm and went back to Bountiful, the payments going to her doctors.

narrative_blocks.header: He married two Gorham sisters
narrative_blocks.body: In 1850 John, a New Haven merchant, lived in his father-in-law Elah Gorham's house with his wife, Almira, and her sister Harriet. Almira died in March 1854, at twenty-five, and that August John married Harriet, with whom he had three children.

narrative_blocks.header: Omaha winters, Connecticut summers
narrative_blocks.body: Jean and her husband, Dr. James Foote, lived at Omaha for more than twenty-five years and spent their summers on the east coast. She fell ill in 1919 and died that December at her sister Florence Bradbury's home in Naugatuck.

bio.title: Dr.
bio.bio_blurb: Teachers College historian of women's education

narrative_blocks.header: Her doctorate under John Dewey
narrative_blocks.body: Willystine trained at the Welch Normal Training School in New Haven and went on to Teachers College, Columbia, where she wrote her master's thesis on Rousseau in 1906. Her doctorate, The Conflict of Naturalism and Humanism, was written under John Dewey and published in 1910.

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty-one years at Teachers College
narrative_blocks.body: Willystine taught the history and philosophy of education at Teachers College for thirty-one years. She founded the Women's Faculty Club at Columbia and was its first president, and sat on the board of the journal Social Frontier.

narrative_blocks.header: Books on the family and women's schooling
narrative_blocks.body: Her books moved from philosophy to the family and to women: A History of the Family as a Social and Educational Institution in 1915, The Education of Women in 1923, and Pioneers of Women's Education in the United States in 1931, on Emma Willard, Catharine Beecher and Mary Lyon.

narrative_blocks.header: Injustices in the marriage relation
narrative_blocks.body: In 1929 Willystine pointed out that outside women's colleges such as Wellesley, academic posts were all but closed to women. Her History of Marriage and the Family of 1935 set out, in her words, to reveal existing injustices and evils in the marriage relation.

narrative_blocks.header: An award in her name since 1981
narrative_blocks.body: Since 1981 the American Educational Research Association's group on women and education has given a yearly Willystine Goodsell Award to an educator who advances the education of women and girls.

cross_connections.display_label: opened her 1931 book Pioneers of Women's Education
was Columbia's president through her years at Teachers College
turned the Albany normal school into a four-year college for teachers

notable.notable_blurb: Teachers College historian of women's education

bio.title: Dr.
bio.bio_blurb: Creighton professor of physiology and pathology

narrative_blocks.header: Telling animals from humans by the femur
narrative_blocks.body: James taught physiology and pathology at Creighton's medical college in Omaha for thirty years. His long study of bone showed that lower animals and humans could be told apart by the cross-section of the femur, and the Smithsonian published his Comparative Histology of Femur and his work on the circulatory system of bone.

narrative_blocks.header: Buried beside Jean at Naugatuck
narrative_blocks.body: James married Jean Goodsell in Chicago in 1894, and they lived in Omaha for more than twenty-five years. She died at her sister's home in Naugatuck in December 1919, and after three years of paralysis from a stroke he died at Omaha in 1925 and was buried beside her.

narrative_blocks.header: Headmaster at Oyster Bay until 1967
narrative_blocks.body: Langdon was headmaster of the East Woods School at Oyster Bay, on Long Island, until 1967, and taught history and Latin. He worked with the Educational Testing Service and the independent schools' association, and consulted after retiring.

narrative_blocks.header: Assistant head at Eaglebrook, then Fay
narrative_blocks.body: Out of Princeton in 1930, where he was in Cannon Club, Langdon went into schoolmastering, as assistant headmaster at Eaglebrook in Deerfield and then at the Fay School in Southborough, before East Woods.

narrative_blocks.header: Ship models and Essex history
narrative_blocks.body: Retired to River Road in Essex, Langdon presided over the Essex Historical Society, wrote articles on the town's history, sat as a trustee of the Connecticut River Foundation and built ship models. Judith was married at the house in 1968.

narrative_blocks.header: Anna Roosevelt remembered his school
narrative_blocks.body: Anna Roosevelt, the archaeologist, was a pupil at East Woods under him, and credited his Latin with leading her into the classics. She remembered him as “calm, humane, and always alert intellectually.”

cross_connections.display_label: studied Latin under him at East Woods, and took it into archaeology

bio.bio_blurb: Mountaineer, Red Cross social worker and watercolorist

narrative_blocks.header: The only woman on the Grand Teton, 1938
narrative_blocks.body: In 1938 Peg climbed the Grand Teton as the only woman in a party of eight. Sixty-one years later she went back to Wyoming to raft the Snake River with her children and grandchildren.

narrative_blocks.header: In Guam harbor the day Japan surrendered
narrative_blocks.body: Trained at Smith and the New York School of Social Work, Peg served in the war as a Red Cross medical social worker aboard a Navy hospital ship, which lay in Guam harbor the day Japan surrendered.

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-five years on the Elisabeth Morrow board
narrative_blocks.body: Peg sat on the board of the Elisabeth Morrow School in Englewood for twenty-five years and was for a time its librarian, building up the shelves by asking every child to give the school a book.

narrative_blocks.header: Swimming in the rain at Edgartown
narrative_blocks.body: Peg first came to Martha's Vineyard in 1917, bought a house at Edgartown in 1963, and spent part of every year there for almost forty years, sailing, gardening and swimming in the rain, often alone in the water.

narrative_blocks.header: Pastries past Emily Post's house
narrative_blocks.body: In her college summers on the Vineyard, Peg and her friends sneaked bakery goods past Emily Post's house, against Mrs. Post's ruling that ladies do not carry packages.

narrative_blocks.header: She voted on her last day, at ninety-two
narrative_blocks.body: On 12 April 2002, at ninety-two, Peg voted, drove to the library and the post office, talked with friends and worked on a paper about medieval tapestries. She died in her sleep that night.

narrative_blocks.header: Her first gallery show at eighty-six
narrative_blocks.body: Peg took watercolor classes from Maine to Florida and at eighty-six held her first professional show, at the Sculpin Gallery in Edgartown. She sold most of the paintings, she said, because “I'm small and I'm cheap.”

cross_connections.display_label: worked for the Red Cross on Guadalcanal, Guam and Okinawa
sailed out of Edgartown every summer from 1974

education.school_name: New York School of Social Work

career.organization: American Red Cross, Navy hospital ship, Pacific

education.school_name: College of Physicians and Surgeons, Columbia University

narrative_blocks.header: Downhill skiing at forty-five
narrative_blocks.body: Alison met Tom Eckels at a Quaker Friends meeting and married him in 1982. At forty-five, at his urging, she took up downhill skiing, and the two of them volunteered for their children's middle-school ski program.

narrative_blocks.header: Keeping KRAB's transmitter on the air
narrative_blocks.body: Tom left a theology doctorate at Chicago unfinished, moved to Seattle in 1976 and kept the transmitter running at KRAB radio. He spent the rest of his career with Hatfield and Dawson, designing radio systems for public projects.

narrative_blocks.header: Driving toward St. Helens as it erupted
narrative_blocks.body: With the geology students he shared a Seattle house with, Tom hopped freight trains to backpack in Glacier, spent two summers at Copper Lake below Vesper Peak, and drove as close as they could get to Mount St. Helens as it erupted.

cross_connections.display_label: lost 68,000 acres of timber to the 1980 St. Helens eruption

narrative_blocks.header: Aerodynamics at Lockheed's Skunk Works
narrative_blocks.body: David spent his career as an aerodynamic engineer with the Skunk Works at Lockheed Martin, working on many of its most advanced projects.

narrative_blocks.header: A C-130 commander in the Vietnam War
narrative_blocks.body: David went from Newtown to the Air Force Academy, graduated in 1963, and served four years as an Air Force captain, commanding a C-130 in support of combat operations in Vietnam.

narrative_blocks.header: He taught others to fly gliders
narrative_blocks.body: In his spare time David taught others to fly, as an instructor in small aircraft and gliders. His memorial service was held at the Air Force Academy in July 2019.

cross_connections.display_label: was a pilot and flight instructor, kept out of the war by polio

military_service.notes: C-130 commander supporting combat operations in Vietnam

narrative_blocks.header: He found American Mensa with 121 members
narrative_blocks.body: On a 1961 visit to England John became intrigued by Mensa, and he found its new American chapter with 121 members. He became its first selection officer; by 1967 it had 12,000 members, and by his death in 1993, fifty-five thousand.

narrative_blocks.header: Press, radio and television in one week, 1961
narrative_blocks.body: When Victor Serebriakoff came from London in November 1961, two days by prop plane through Reykjavik and Gander, John met him and had him interviewed by newspapers, radio and television all week.

narrative_blocks.header: First chairman of American Mensa, 1961 to 1966
narrative_blocks.body: John chaired American Mensa from 1961 to 1966; Victor Serebriakoff, who had rebuilt Mensa in England, called him its most effective builder in North America. Critics who called him an autocrat eventually pushed him out.

narrative_blocks.header: He had just sold his publicity firm
narrative_blocks.body: John had just sold his interest in a successful publicity company at a fashionable Manhattan address when he joined Mensa in 1961, and with no need to earn a living he took on the unpaid work of building it in America.

narrative_blocks.header: Metallography at Stevens, sculpture at the League
narrative_blocks.body: A New Rochelle native, John went to Cooper Union, studied metallography at the Stevens Institute of Technology and sculpture at the Art Students League, and spent most of his working life in advertising and public relations.

narrative_blocks.header: Consulting at Basking Ridge until 1991
narrative_blocks.body: In 1977 John joined Science Management Corporation at Basking Ridge, New Jersey, and retired as a vice-president in 1991, the year after American Mensa gave him its Lifetime Membership Award. He died in July 1993, at sixty-four.

narrative_blocks.header: One more lady to interview, 1961
narrative_blocks.body: Margot Seitelman ran American Mensa's office from her Brooklyn home from 1961 to 1990. She got the job because, on Serebriakoff's last day in New York, John phoned: “Don't decide yet. I have one more lady I'd like you to talk to.”

cross_connections.display_label: helped make the Army Alpha intelligence test, taken by two million men
was one of the founders of modern public relations

notable.notable_blurb: First chairman of American Mensa

career.organization: Codella Duffus, Baker, Inc., New York

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty-three years a widow
narrative_blocks.body: Florence married Job Clark Crane of Elizabeth in March 1876. He died in November 1890, with their four children still young, the eldest thirteen, and she outlived him by fifty-three years, to 1943.

bio.title: Dr.
bio.bio_blurb: Elizabeth physician and Civil War surgeon

narrative_blocks.header: Clara Barton's friend at Sandy Hook
narrative_blocks.body: Near the end of the war John was made a surgeon in the regular army, and at the hospital at Sandy Hook he became a close friend of Clara Barton. Governor Reuben Fenton of New York made him a brevet major.

narrative_blocks.header: Medical student, then Sickles's 71st New York
narrative_blocks.body: John was studying medicine at Washington Medical College and the St. Louis Homeopathic College when the war began. He enlisted in the 1st New York Mounted Rifles and was moved to the 71st New York Volunteers under Gen. Daniel Sickles.

narrative_blocks.header: Doctor in Elizabeth from 1867
narrative_blocks.body: John settled at Elizabeth, New Jersey, in 1867 and practised medicine there for many years. He married Gertrude Langdon there in September 1870, and died at Elizabeth in January 1929, at ninety-two.

cross_connections.display_label: was on Daniel Sickles's staff at Gettysburg

military_service.unit: 1st New York Mounted Rifles; 71st New York Volunteers
military_service.notes: Later surgeon in the regular army; brevet major by Gov. Reuben Fenton

narrative_blocks.header: Schoolcraft's legends, retold for children
narrative_blocks.body: William retold Henry Schoolcraft's Native American legends as American Indian Fairy Tales and put La Fontaine into Fables in Rhyme for Little Folks, the children's books he is remembered for.

narrative_blocks.header: He adapted Molnár's The Devil for George Arliss
narrative_blocks.body: Night editor of the St. Louis Republic in his newspaper years, William later adapted Ferenc Molnár's play The Devil for the actor George Arliss.

narrative_blocks.header: His grandfather gave Fort Larned its name
narrative_blocks.body: William's grandfather, Col. Benjamin Franklin Larned, was Paymaster General of the Army from 1854 until he died in 1862, and Fort Larned in Kansas, and the town beside it, were named for him. His father was a deputy paymaster general.

cross_connections.display_label: toured in George Arliss's Merchant of Venice for Winthrop Ames
wrote Star, the Story of an Indian Pony, for young readers
retold Kalila and Dimna, the Indian fables La Fontaine drew on

career.organization: American Indian Fairy Tales; Fables in Rhyme for Little Folks

narrative_blocks.header: Seventeen days short of a hundred and one
narrative_blocks.body: Elsie was born at Elizabeth, New Jersey, on 23 April 1877 and died at Highland Park, Illinois, on 6 April 1978, seventeen days short of her hundred-and-first birthday.

narrative_blocks.header: His slides are in the Metropolitan
narrative_blocks.body: Frank became an outstanding photographer, and his slides went into the collections of the Metropolitan Museum and the National Gallery. He was also archivist of Chicago's University Club.

narrative_blocks.header: Fire control in the war, retired a commander
narrative_blocks.body: A Dartmouth physics man who took his electrical engineering at MIT in 1931, Frank worked for Commonwealth Edison, General Cable and the Joslyn Manufacturing Company, and in the war on fire control, retiring a commander.

cross_connections.display_label: helped find the land for Forest Home, where he is buried

military_service.notes: Fire control

bio.bio_blurb: Jazz drummer, banker and Jazz Institute president

narrative_blocks.header: He helped start the Chicago Jazz Festival
narrative_blocks.body: In 1979 Charlie helped found the Chicago Jazz Festival and raised its first money from the City Arts Program and the musicians' union. He was president of the Jazz Institute of Chicago from 1980 to 1982 and from 1999 until he died.

narrative_blocks.header: Banker by day, drummer at the Plugged Nickel
narrative_blocks.body: Charlie studied jazz drums with Joe Porcaro while at Trinity College in Hartford, then went into banking at Chicago's National Boulevard Bank. At night he played the London House, Basin Street, the Plugged Nickel and the Hideaway.

narrative_blocks.header: His papers are at the University of Chicago
narrative_blocks.body: Six boxes of his papers on Chicago jazz and the Jazz Institute are in the University of Chicago Library's special collections. In retirement he led a band of his own, the Weeks Hornblowers.

cross_connections.display_label: argued jazz onto Oxford University Press's list

narrative_blocks.header: His mother wrote the governor
narrative_blocks.body: Tom Waxter was passed over for the Baltimore City Circuit Court four times, once by Governor William Donald Schaefer and three times by Parris Glendening. In 1996, at 62, he got the seat after his 92-year-old mother wrote to Glendening.

narrative_blocks.header: He stood for gay rights at City Hall
narrative_blocks.body: Tom held Baltimore's 5th District council seat as a Democrat from 1975 to 1987 and defended gay rights at City Hall. In 1983 the district was redrawn so most of his voters were Black or Jewish, and he won it again.

narrative_blocks.header: A social worker's degree before the law
narrative_blocks.body: Tom's father, Thomas J. S. Waxter Sr., was Maryland's director of public welfare, and a state children's center bears his name. Tom took a master's in social work at Penn in 1959 and sat on Baltimore's Welfare Commission from 1963 to 1966.

education.school_name: University of Maryland School of Law

bio.bio_blurb: Corporate lawyer and Conservation Law Foundation director

narrative_blocks.header: A corporate lawyer on the CLF board
narrative_blocks.body: David practised as a corporate lawyer, spent his free time on New England's waters, and for many years sat on the board of the Conservation Law Foundation. His son Bill and daughter Nancy both took up the foundation's work.

narrative_blocks.header: His father taught law at Harvard
narrative_blocks.body: David's father, David Farquhar Cavers, was Harvard Law School's first associate dean and its Fessenden Professor of Law, a leading scholar of the conflict of laws, and at Duke had founded the journal Law and Contemporary Problems.

narrative_blocks.header: Heaven is in Truckee, 2021
narrative_blocks.body: Nancy's chapbook Heaven is in Truckee came out from the Orchard Street Press in 2021, after she was a finalist in its 2020 Quiet Diamonds contest. It follows Tape Recorder On, Memory in Salt and Levee Town, and the collaborative Silk.

narrative_blocks.header: The cello and the written word
narrative_blocks.body: Nancy plays the cello and works across music, visual art and writing. In Sebastopol she supports a homeless shelter for women, counseling for teenagers and art-making in groups.

cross_connections.display_label: has spent twenty-five years drawing Truckee

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty years financing wind and solar
narrative_blocks.body: Bill spent thirty years financing large solar, wind and other clean-energy projects and retired in 2017. He took a nonprofit-management course at UConn, then joined the Conservation Law Foundation and set up its Connecticut office.

narrative_blocks.header: Executive director of Bedford Audubon, 2021
narrative_blocks.body: In September 2021 Bill became executive director of Bedford Audubon. He sits on two committees of the Long Island Sound Study and on Darien's Coastal Commission, and has sailed the New England coast all his life.

narrative_blocks.header: He followed his father onto the CLF
narrative_blocks.body: Bill's father, David Cavers, a corporate lawyer, sat on the Conservation Law Foundation's board for many years. Bill and his sister Nancy carried it on, Bill as a senior fellow in 2020 and on its first Connecticut state advisory board.

cross_connections.display_label: brought 180 groups together for Audubon's Long Island Sound alliance

career.organization: Connecticut State Advisory Board, Conservation Law Foundation

bio.bio_blurb: Founder of Make: magazine and Maker Faire

narrative_blocks.header: He started Maker Faire in 2006
narrative_blocks.body: Dale founded Make: magazine in 2005, giving the name makers to people who build things with their hands, and started Maker Faire in the Bay Area in 2006. It spread to nearly two hundred places in forty countries.

narrative_blocks.header: O'Reilly, and the first web portal
narrative_blocks.body: A co-founder of O'Reilly Media and the first editor of its computing books, Dale wrote sed & awk and in 1993 launched the Global Network Navigator, the first web portal and the first site paid for by advertising.

narrative_blocks.header: Introduced by Obama at the White House
narrative_blocks.body: The White House named Dale a Champion of Change in 2011, and at its 2014 Maker Faire President Obama introduced him as an American innovator. He wrote Free to Make with Adriane Conrad.

cross_connections.display_label: wrote Brick by Brick, the story of LEGO's turnaround, in 2013
patented routing between IPv4 and IPv6 at Google
wrote Born Digital in 2008, on the first generation to grow up online

narrative_blocks.header: A master's in botany at twenty
narrative_blocks.body: Fern took a master's degree in botany at the University of Minnesota in 1926, the year she turned twenty. In thirty years at Summit she belonged to the Summit Association of Scientists and the College Club.

bio.notes: Name unknown

narrative_blocks.header: From Cranbrook to the printmaking press
narrative_blocks.body: Julia went from Milton Academy to Williams College, class of 1980, and took a Master of Fine Arts at the Cranbrook Academy of Art. She paints and makes prints, and in 2026 showed in Making An Impression at the Rocky Neck Art Colony.

narrative_blocks.header: A LEED Silver house in Newton
narrative_blocks.body: In 2009 the house Julia and her husband James built in Newton Centre earned a LEED Silver certificate, the second custom home in Newton to win one. Julia designed the railing for its loft bedroom.

narrative_blocks.header: She drew holiday stamps for the Post Office
narrative_blocks.body: Before printmaking, Julia illustrated for newspapers, magazines and advertising agencies, among them holiday stamps for the U.S. Postal Service. Scolded for doodling in school, she still fills a sketchbook about every six months.

narrative_blocks.header: Her students print with a steamroller
narrative_blocks.body: Julia teaches a class in carving large relief prints at the Mosesian Center for the Arts in Watertown. It ends at the town's community arts fair, where she and her students print their linoleum blocks under a steamroller.

narrative_blocks.header: Escher, she says, was the gateway drug
narrative_blocks.body: Julia paints on linoleum before she carves it with Japanese tools; On the Night You Were Born, made at a California residency, prints from three 24-inch panels. She says M. C. Escher was her gateway drug to art.

cross_connections.display_label: was a painter, printmaker and illustrator for Cricket Magazine

career.organization: Newspapers, magazines and the U.S. Postal Service
Mosesian Center for the Arts, Watertown

narrative_blocks.header: Four hundred papers on diabetes
narrative_blocks.body: James has spent more than twenty years on the causes and prevention of type 2 diabetes and heart disease, and has written more than four hundred papers. In 2009 the American Diabetes Association gave him its Kelly West Award.

narrative_blocks.header: A Mass General internist for thirty years
narrative_blocks.body: Alongside the research James has practiced primary care internal medicine at Massachusetts General Hospital for more than thirty years, and has mentored some fifty young clinical investigators.

cross_connections.display_label: ran Yale's trial treating insulin resistance after stroke

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-five years a school chaplain
narrative_blocks.body: After Harvard Divinity School, Barbara spent twenty-five years as chaplain, pastor and teacher at Episcopal boarding schools with many students from abroad, teaching philosophy and world religions. She works in French and some Arabic.

career.role: Assistant to the director of development

narrative_blocks.header: Twenty-one years building New Profit
narrative_blocks.body: Douglas joined New Profit, the Boston venture philanthropy, in 2005, when it had ten staff and six grantees. When he retired as chief operating officer at the end of 2025, its staff was six times larger and it backed nearly a hundred.

narrative_blocks.header: Board chair at Equal Opportunity Schools
narrative_blocks.body: Doug joined the board of Equal Opportunity Schools, which works to bring overlooked students into advanced courses, in July 2020. He became its treasurer in 2022 and its board chair in October 2025.

narrative_blocks.header: He launched zapdata.com from iMarket
narrative_blocks.body: Before New Profit, Doug was president of iMarket, a business-data company, and launched its internet spinoff, zapdata.com. He went on to run the prospecting solutions unit at Dun & Bradstreet as a vice president.

career.role: Chief Operating Officer and Managing Partner

narrative_blocks.header: She outlived all five of her children
narrative_blocks.body: Maria bore five children at Montpelier and buried every one: a daughter who lived a day, Maria Eliza at two, Cadwell Jay at fifteen, Cornelia at twenty-eight and William Williams at forty-eight. She died there in 1886, at eighty-two.

narrative_blocks.header: From Montpelier to the Canadian line
narrative_blocks.body: Julia Ann married the Montpelier merchant Levi Spalding in 1833 and followed his trade to Rock Island, just over the line in Canada, and in 1845 to Derby Line, Vermont. She bore ten children and died at Derby Line in 1854, at forty-five.

narrative_blocks.header: A divorce, then a Chicago merchant
narrative_blocks.body: Eliza Ann married Joseph Hutchins of Montpelier, whose sister Mary was the wife of her uncle Aaron Decius Hooker Cadwell, and bore their son James in 1835. She divorced Joseph and married John Palmer, a merchant at Chicago.

bio.notes: Name unknown
Name unknown

bio.bio_blurb: Bridge engineer, New Hampshire's first highway engineer

narrative_blocks.header: New Hampshire's first highway engineer
narrative_blocks.body: When New Hampshire formed its State Highway Department in 1905, John was put in charge of its roads and bridges as state engineer. In 1903 he had been secretary of the Good Roads League under the former governor Frank W. Rollins.

narrative_blocks.header: The arch above Quechee Gorge
narrative_blocks.body: John designed the steel deck arch that carried the Woodstock Railway across Vermont's Quechee Gorge in 1911, 160 feet above the Ottauquechee. When the line folded in 1933 it was decked over for US Route 4, and it still carries the road.

narrative_blocks.header: Deaf from scarlet fever, an engineer anyway
narrative_blocks.body: Scarlet fever in childhood left John with poor eyesight and almost no hearing. He qualified as an engineer all the same, in 1885, the year he married Carrie Dow of Concord.

narrative_blocks.header: A bridge book for town selectmen
narrative_blocks.body: In 1918 John and his son Edward published a handbook on short-span bridges for road agents, town clerks and selectmen, with designs strong enough for twelve- and fifteen-ton motor trucks and road rollers.

cross_connections.display_label: wrote Stresses in Bridge and Roof Trusses for engineers in 1879
became New York City's chief engineer of bridges in 1906
spent thirty-one years as an Oregon state highway engineer

career.organization: John W. Storrs and Son, Concord

narrative_blocks.header: He and his father wrote the bridge handbook
narrative_blocks.body: In 1918 Edward and his father, John W. Storrs, published a handbook on short-span bridges for New England towns from their firm in Concord. Both belonged to the Boston Society of Civil Engineers.

narrative_blocks.header: Eye trouble ended Dartmouth in a year
narrative_blocks.body: Edward entered Dartmouth with the class of 1908 and left during his freshman year because of eye trouble. He learned bridge work instead at the American Bridge Company in Elmira, New York.

narrative_blocks.header: Bridges for the towns, stoves on the side
narrative_blocks.body: Edward joined his father in Storrs and Storrs, consulting bridge engineers to many New Hampshire towns, and held an interest in the Ford Foundry Company of Concord, which made Dartmouth ranges, stoves and sinks.

career.organization: American Bridge Company, Elmira, New York

narrative_blocks.header: Drowned in the Winooski at six
narrative_blocks.body: Charles was born in Vermont in 1803, the son of Polly Cadwell and her first husband, Charles Plum. In 1809, at about six, he drowned in the Winooski River.

bio.notes: Name unknown

bio.bio_blurb: Derby Line merchant and bank president

narrative_blocks.header: A bank president on the Canadian line
narrative_blocks.body: Levi kept businesses on both sides of the border, at Derby Line and at Stanstead in Lower Canada, and for many years was president of the First National Bank of Derby Line. He is buried there beside Julia Ann.

narrative_blocks.header: His father came to Sharon at eleven
narrative_blocks.body: Levi's father, Deacon Reuben Spalding, born at Tyringham in 1758, came to Sharon, Vermont, in 1769 at eleven, when the town had seven families. He served as a Revolutionary sergeant and lived on that farm until he died in 1849.

narrative_blocks.header: One of twelve, unbroken until 1847
narrative_blocks.body: Levi was one of Reuben and Jerusha Spalding's twelve children, a family that stayed unbroken until his brother Dr. Jason Spalding died in 1847. The whole family gathered at the Sharon farm, and their father spoke over the casket.

cross_connections.display_label: , his grandson, was named Levi Spalding for him

career.organization: First National Bank of Derby Line
Derby Line, Vermont, and Stanstead, Lower Canada

bio.title: Lt.
bio.bio_blurb: Union lieutenant killed at Port Hudson

death.cause: Killed at the battle of Port Hudson

narrative_blocks.header: He said he would lead the charge
narrative_blocks.body: The night before the charge of 14 June 1863 at Port Hudson, Stephen told a friend he would be at the head of his regiment, and Captain Barstow that he would not spend another night with him. He fell to a minié ball in the head.

narrative_blocks.header: On the road to Washington in six hours
narrative_blocks.body: A University of Vermont graduate reading law in New York, Stephen was on his way to Washington with the 7th New York less than six hours after the attack on Fort Sumter, and served out its three months.

narrative_blocks.header: He resigned one commission for his brother
narrative_blocks.body: Stephen raised another New York regiment and was made its second lieutenant, but resigned when his eldest brother fell dangerously ill and went home to read law at Derby. In December 1861 he joined Company B, 8th Vermont.

narrative_blocks.header: Killed in the second assault
narrative_blocks.body: Stephen was adjutant of the 8th Vermont in the second assault on the Port Hudson works, on 14 June 1863, the 24th day of the siege and eleven days short of his twenty-third birthday. His body was recovered and sent home to Vermont.

narrative_blocks.header: In command of Company B at New Orleans
narrative_blocks.body: When the 8th Vermont reached New Orleans, Company B's captain was put on detached service and Stephen took the company. In the spring of 1863 he was made adjutant of the regiment, still leading his company in action.

cross_connections.display_label: shelled Port Hudson from the sloop Richmond during the 1863 siege

career.role: Adjutant, commanding Company B in action

military_service.notes: Enlisted 13 April 1861 with the 7th New York (the Spalding Memorial calls it the 7th New York Battery) and went to Washington. Recruited for the Butler Brigade, then first lieutenant of Company B, 8th Vermont, 19 December 1861, commanding the company at New Orleans while its captain was detached. Adjutant of the regiment from spring 1863. Killed in the second assault on Port Hudson, 14 June 1863.

narrative_blocks.header: Two widowed sisters at Derby
narrative_blocks.body: Clara married Charles O. Brigham, a lawyer and Civil War major, in February 1867; they had no children. Widowed in 1890, she shared a house at Derby with her widowed sister Sarah, and died there in 1914.

narrative_blocks.header: She saw her sister shot
narrative_blocks.body: Clara was in the next room of the Derby Line Hotel on 31 August 1876 when Edwin Hayden shot her husband, then her sister Gertrude, who died six days later.

narrative_blocks.header: Captain, then major, of Connecticut artillery
narrative_blocks.body: Charles was born at Fitchburg, Massachusetts, and served in the Civil War with the 1st Connecticut Heavy Artillery, as a captain and later a major. He practised law afterwards and died at Derby, Vermont, in 1890.

narrative_blocks.header: Shot through the lung for his sister-in-law
narrative_blocks.body: On 31 August 1876 Charles barred Edwin Hayden from his wife's sister Gertrude at the Derby Line Hotel, and Hayden shot him through the lung before killing her. Charles recovered and testified at the trial.

cross_connections.display_label: , his wife's sister, was killed by her husband at the Derby Line Hotel
shot him through the lung at the Derby Line Hotel in 1876

military_service.notes: Captain, later major.

narrative_blocks.header: Chicago, then a widow's last years
narrative_blocks.body: Sarah married William S. Hall in June 1865 and lived with him for a time in Chicago. Widowed in 1894 and childless, she was living with her sister Clara at Derby by 1900. She took her own life at Newton, Massachusetts, in 1903.

narrative_blocks.header: Fifty years in Dorchester
narrative_blocks.body: Juliet grew up in Cambridge and moved to Dorchester when she married Lyman Spalding in 1878. She was a charter member of the Dorchester Women's Club and attended the First Parish Church there until her death in 1934.

bio.bio_blurb: Belle of Derby Line, killed by her husband

death.cause: Shot by her husband, Edwin C. Hayden, at the Derby Line Hotel

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband came to the hotel armed
narrative_blocks.body: In August 1876 Gertrude went to stay with her sister Clara and Clara's husband, Charles Brigham, at the Derby Line Hotel. On 31 August her husband, Edwin Hayden, came with a borrowed revolver to see her. Brigham refused him.

narrative_blocks.header: Her husband shot her: “Oh, Edwin”
narrative_blocks.body: Her husband, Edwin Hayden, shot Brigham through the lung, walked into the next room and shot Gertrude in the head. She turned, crying “Oh, Edwin,” and he shot her again in the back. She died on 6 September 1876, at twenty-three.

narrative_blocks.header: The belle of Derby Line
narrative_blocks.body: The acknowledged belle of Derby Line, Gertrude married Edwin Hayden at Boston in 1871 over her family's objections, just after coming into an inheritance. Her money set him up in a Boston corset factory, which burned in the fire of 1872.

narrative_blocks.header: She left her husband in 1875
narrative_blocks.body: Her money went next into a hotel her husband, Edwin Hayden, kept at Stanstead, and was spent there. In 1875, after years of his beatings, Gertrude left Edwin for a sister at Allston, near Boston, and would not go back while he drank.

narrative_blocks.header: What she said before she died
narrative_blocks.body: Before she died Gertrude said her husband, Edwin Hayden, had often knocked her down, and had once forced her to sign over bonds by threatening to shoot her.

cross_connections.display_label: , her brother-in-law, was shot trying to keep her husband away

bio.bio_blurb: Murderer of his wife, hanged in 1881

death.cause: Hanged at the Vermont State Prison for the murder of his wife

narrative_blocks.header: He shot and killed his wife, Gertrude
narrative_blocks.body: On 31 August 1876 Edwin shot and killed his wife, Gertrude Spalding Hayden, at the Derby Line Hotel, where she had taken refuge with her sister. That morning he had borrowed a revolver at a store, saying a dog had bitten him.

narrative_blocks.header: He shot her brother-in-law first
narrative_blocks.body: When Charles Brigham refused to let him see Gertrude, Edwin shot him through the lung, walked into the next room and shot his wife in the head and, as she turned, in the back. Brigham and others pinned him down.

narrative_blocks.header: Hanged for murdering his wife
narrative_blocks.body: Convicted in September 1877 of the first-degree murder of his wife, Edwin spent more than three years in the state prison at Windsor and was hanged there on 25 February 1881. On the scaffold he denied ever abusing her.

narrative_blocks.header: His last plea failed at Montpelier
narrative_blocks.body: A legislative committee sent new evidence to the judges, and Governor Farnham reprieved him to February. On 16 February 1881 the court ruled he had been as sane as ever men are in committing such crimes.

narrative_blocks.header: A paymaster's clerk in 1864
narrative_blocks.body: Born at Cincinnati, Edwin was raised partly by his grandfather Russel Perry at Montpelier and went to Barre Academy. In 1864 he joined the Union army as an assistant paymaster, under his guardian, General Pitkin.

narrative_blocks.header: Corsets in Boston, a hotel at Stanstead
narrative_blocks.body: After clerking for Jordan, Marsh and travelling for Champney Brothers, Edwin started a Boston corset factory with his wife's money; it burned in the 1872 fire. He then kept the Studdert Hotel at Stanstead, Quebec.

cross_connections.display_label: took his bullet in the lung and testified against him
heard his last plea at Montpelier in February 1881 and refused it

narrative_blocks.header: The Silurian Spring and the Casino
narrative_blocks.body: In the 1890s Lee ran the Silurian Spring and the Casino at Waukesha, and in 1901 he built a house on Hartwell Avenue there. He was an editor at Chicago when he died in 1945, and lies at Rosehill beside his parents.

cross_connections.display_label: , his grandfather, gave him the name Levi Spalding

career.organization: Silurian Spring and the Casino, Waukesha

narrative_blocks.header: A state oil inspector and a Mason
narrative_blocks.body: Arthur was born in Kansas City and moved to Waukesha as a boy. He worked as a deputy oil inspector for the state at Madison until 1957, and belonged to the Masonic lodge and the Wisconsin Consistory.

narrative_blocks.header: Her father edited the Waukesha Freeman
narrative_blocks.body: Margaret was the daughter of T. W. Haight, once editor of the Waukesha Freeman, and lived most of her life in Waukesha. She died at Madison in 1957, at sixty-nine, and was buried at Prairie Home.

cross_connections.display_label: , her granddaughter, was named Margaret for her

bio.title: Dr.
bio.bio_blurb: Milwaukee surgeon, St. Mary's chief of staff

narrative_blocks.header: Front-line surgery with Patton's army
narrative_blocks.body: From 1943 to 1945 David operated with the 4th Surgical Auxiliary, attached to Patton's Third Army, on soldiers too critically wounded to be carried back to a hospital.

narrative_blocks.header: He brought open-heart surgery to St. Mary's
narrative_blocks.body: David joined the staff of St. Mary's Hospital in Milwaukee in 1947, was its chief of surgery from 1960 and its chief of staff from 1966 to 1970, when he led the push to begin open-heart surgery there.

narrative_blocks.header: One of Wisconsin's first HMOs
narrative_blocks.body: Worried by rising costs, David worked with American Motors and St. Mary's in 1972 to organize the physicians who founded Northpoint, one of the earliest health maintenance organizations in Wisconsin.

cross_connections.display_label: helped organize White Cross, one of the first HMOs in the country

bio.title: Dr.
bio.bio_blurb: Arizona radiologist and digital angiography pioneer

narrative_blocks.header: The first digital subtraction angiography
narrative_blocks.body: Terry led a series of NIH-funded projects at the University of Arizona that built the first digital subtraction angiography system, then the first digital display console and the first mini PACS, taking radiology from film to digital.

narrative_blocks.header: Twelve years chairing Arizona radiology
narrative_blocks.body: Terry came to Tucson in 1974 after a cardiovascular radiology fellowship under Kurt Amplatz in Minnesota. He made full professor in 1982, ran the diagnostic division seven years, and chaired the department from 1993 for twelve.

narrative_blocks.header: The physician's physician
narrative_blocks.body: Terry taught generations of radiologists and cardiologists the reading of cardiac angiograms, led the Eastern Radiological Society and the chairs of academic radiology, and worked in Arizona's cardiothoracic imaging until 2020.

education.notes: Residency and cardiovascular radiology fellowship under Kurt Amplatz

career.organization: University of Arizona College of Medicine
University of Arizona Department of Medical Imaging
University of Arizona Department of Medical Imaging
Society of Chairs of Academic Radiology Departments

narrative_blocks.header: From nursing to native landscapes
narrative_blocks.body: After a nursing degree at Vanderbilt, years in Perth and Cambridge, and a decade at McDonough District Hospital in Macomb, Margaret took a master's in landscape architecture and opened Western Illinois Land Design, working in native plants.

narrative_blocks.header: Restoring the Illinois River lakes
narrative_blocks.body: Retired, Margaret restores land west of Macomb, sits on the Macomb Tree Board, works for a local foods co-op, and joins the Emiquon Corps of Discovery in The Nature Conservancy's restoration of Thompson and Flag lakes.

cross_connections.display_label: , her grandmother, gave her the name Margaret

narrative_blocks.header: From Alaska to Oregon
narrative_blocks.body: Betsy graduated from Whitefish Bay High School in 1964, became a nurse, and lived in Alaska, Florida, Colorado and Wisconsin before settling in Oregon, where she has since retired.

narrative_blocks.header: Nine months old
narrative_blocks.body: Robby was born at Boston on 10 October 1881 and died there on 9 August 1882. He is buried at Cedar Grove in Dorchester, where both his parents were later buried too.

narrative_blocks.header: Colonial Dames president in Oklahoma
narrative_blocks.body: Raised and schooled in Dorchester and Boston, Ethel came to Oklahoma City in 1925 with her husband. She was a president of the Colonial Dames there and active in the Art League, the Rose Society and St. Paul's Episcopal Church.

bio.title: Col.
bio.bio_blurb: Cavalry colonel and Princeton military professor

narrative_blocks.header: After Pancho Villa with Pershing
narrative_blocks.body: John went to the Philippines with the 7th Cavalry in 1906, and in 1916 rode with Pershing's squadron into Mexico after Pancho Villa.

narrative_blocks.header: Princeton, then a Yale law degree
narrative_blocks.body: John taught military science and tactics at Princeton and retired from the Army in 1919. He then took a Yale law degree in 1923 and a doctorate in 1924, and came to Oklahoma City that year.

narrative_blocks.header: Broadlawns, northwest of Norman
narrative_blocks.body: John practised law briefly in Oklahoma City and in the Second World War headed its retired officers' bureau. From 1933 he and Ethel lived at Broadlawns, a country house northwest of Norman, where Ethel died in 1947.

education.school_name: United States Military Academy, West Point

career.role: Professor of military science and tactics

military_service.notes: Philippines 1906; with Pershing after Pancho Villa 1916; retired 1919.

narrative_blocks.header: His father gave Atlanta its zoo
narrative_blocks.body: John's father, George Valentine Gress, an Atlanta lumberman and Union veteran of the 56th Pennsylvania, bought a bankrupt circus south of Atlanta in 1887 and gave its animals to the city. They became the start of Zoo Atlanta.

narrative_blocks.header: His father gave the Cyclorama painting
narrative_blocks.body: George Valentine Gress also gave Atlanta the great painting of the Battle of Atlanta, shown for decades in the Cyclorama at the zoo and now at the Atlanta History Center. He sat in the Georgia House in 1901.

narrative_blocks.header: He died about to preach
narrative_blocks.body: On Sunday 4 July 1937 Boudinot was getting ready to preach at Mount Baker Presbyterian in Seattle when he collapsed in the church study and died, at fifty-nine.

narrative_blocks.header: First pastor of Rose City Park
narrative_blocks.body: After Williams College and Princeton Seminary, Boudinot preached at Wilmington and Philadelphia, then in 1910 became the first minister of Portland's new Rose City Park Presbyterian church and later ran the church's Oregon home missions.

narrative_blocks.header: Three of their four children died as babies
narrative_blocks.body: Boudinot and Mayannah lost three of their four children as infants: Amelia in 1905, Ross in 1908 and a son named Boudinot in 1910. Only Tyler, born at Philadelphia in 1906, grew up.

career.organization: Oysterville and Ocean Park church, Washington
Rose City Park Presbyterian Church, Portland
Presbyterian churches at Wilmington, Delaware, and Philadelphia

narrative_blocks.header: Named for his grandfather Tyler Woodward
narrative_blocks.body: Tyler was named for his mother's father, Tyler Woodward, a Portland pioneer who left a trust for his education when he died in 1914; Tyler was seven. By 1926 he also held the cane his grandfather L.B. cut at Mount Vernon.

narrative_blocks.header: His wife died the day their daughter arrived
narrative_blocks.body: Tyler married Mary Lois Bridwell at Walla Walla in May 1937. She died there on 21 April 1939, the day their daughter Mary Lois was born. In 1942 he married Emma Jane Johnson of Pendleton.

narrative_blocks.header: A boy magician in the margins
narrative_blocks.body: In his 1914 eighth-grade geography book, kept at the family's beach house, West Dunes, Tyler filled nine pages with drawings, among them a playbill for Seeley in his new and startling feat of magic, conjuring eggs from a top hat.

narrative_blocks.header: Engineer in charge on the Mount Hood Loop
narrative_blocks.body: When the state built the Mount Hood Loop Highway, Carrol was the highway department's engineer in charge.

narrative_blocks.header: Three years on an engineering job in China
narrative_blocks.body: After Williams College and Stanford, Carrol spent three years on an engineering job in China.

cross_connections.display_label: was New Hampshire's first state highway engineer

career.organization: U.S. Army engineer corps, World War I

bio.title: Dr.
bio.bio_blurb: Physician at St. Luke's Hospital, New York

narrative_blocks.header: Dead of heart failure at twenty-five
narrative_blocks.body: Lamar, a doctor on the staff of St. Luke's Hospital in New York City, died suddenly of heart failure on the morning of 14 June 1907. His parents in Portland learned of it from a message that evening.

career.organization: St. Luke's Hospital, New York City

narrative_blocks.header: Her father left a trust for her son
narrative_blocks.body: Mayannah's father, Tyler Woodward, a Vermont-born Portland pioneer, died in 1914 and left her a lot on First Street and a trust for the education of her son, Tyler, then seven.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother was born on Ross Island
narrative_blocks.body: Mayannah's mother, Mary Jane Ross Woodward, was born on Ross Island in the Willamette in 1852, a daughter of the pioneers Sherry and Rebecca Ross, and took a degree at Ohio Wesleyan before marrying Tyler Woodward in 1872.

narrative_blocks.header: Her mother died the day she was born
narrative_blocks.body: Mary Lois was born at Walla Walla on 21 April 1939, and her mother, Mary Lois Bridwell Seeley, died the same day, at twenty-six. She married Robert Bedeau in 1960 and raised two daughters at Indianapolis.

bio.extra_names: Sarah Hubbell

narrative_blocks.header: Lost his eldest son at thirty
narrative_blocks.body: Zalmon's eldest son, George, died at New Haven in August 1854 at thirty, leaving a wife, a baby daughter and a son born the next spring.

narrative_blocks.header: Lost two children, his mother and his wife
narrative_blocks.body: William buried two of his children in 1851, Charles Carroll and Amanda Jane, and his mother, Eunice Hooker Hubbell, died that December. In September 1852 his wife, Sarah Ann Sharp Hubbell, died at Birmingham at thirty-one.

bio.extra_names: George Hubbel

narrative_blocks.header: Dead at thirty, a son on the way
narrative_blocks.body: George died at New Haven on 23 August 1854, seventeen days after his thirtieth birthday. His wife, Elizabeth Maria Opdyke Hubbell, was carrying their son George L., born the next March.

narrative_blocks.header: Born seven months after his father died
narrative_blocks.body: George L. Hubbell was born on 29 March 1855, seven months after his father, George, died at thirty. His parents' first son, also George, had died as a baby, and his mother died in 1857, when he was two.

bio.extra_names: Helen Mary Gilkey
Martha Graham

narrative_blocks.header: Thirty years a widow, mother of eleven
narrative_blocks.body: Eunice had eleven children between 1899 and 1924. Her husband, William Robert Bradford, died at Pinson, Tennessee, in May 1928, and she lived thirty more years.

narrative_blocks.header: Widowed at twenty-six with a baby son
narrative_blocks.body: Jennie married William Hitchcock on 24 May 1877. Their son, Orrin Beardsley Hitchcock, was born at New Haven on 6 June 1879, and William died on 16 September 1880, when Orrin was fifteen months old.

narrative_blocks.header: Died the same day as his cousin Kenneth
narrative_blocks.body: Michael, a sophomore at South Side High School, died on 19 November 1994 from injuries in an automobile accident. His double first cousin, Kenneth Joe Johnson, thirteen, died of accident injuries the same day.

narrative_blocks.body: Stan carried the name of his uncle, 2nd Lt. Stanley Warren Johnson, a P-38 pilot and wingman to Medal of Honor ace Dick Bong, who was last seen over Rabaul on 7 November 1943 diving out of a fight with four Japanese Zeroes on his tail.

narrative_blocks.body: Marjorie married John Boyd at State College, Pennsylvania, on 15 March 1941. He was killed in action at sea on 12 October 1943.

Significance: Famous gathering place beneath the elm where John Hooker, his son Roger, and grandson Roger hosted the 'sages of the town' on summer evenings. A regional landmark known throughout Connecticut.
Destruction: Felled when the estate passed to William Gay, who had the tree cut down to make a straight path from the front door to the street. The house was also rebuilt and modernized until 'scarcely a feature of its Hooker character remained.'
Last occupant: Major Roger Hooker, who died without issue in 1830
Not to confuse with: The Hooker Oak of Chico, California — named after botanist Sir Joseph Dalton Hooker; The Sarah Whitman Hooker House liberty tree in West Hartford, Connecticut
Associated family: Hooker
Source: Edward Hooker 1909 — Entry 30 narrative

Spelling note: Early Hartford settlers spelled the name 'Standley' with a 'd'. The Stanley family history assumes this was a mistake and attempts to trace the family to the English Stanley family. Edward Hooker notes Sir John Standley was an officer in Cromwell's army — possibly the correct origin.
One of the oldest houses in Farmington. A well-preserved saltbox with post-medieval construction features. Connected to the Standley/Stanley family of Farmington — the same family as Abigail Standley (I00031), wife of John Hooker (H00030).
Designations: National Historic Landmark (1960); National Register of Historic Places (1966)

Source: National Register of Historic Places
Built ca. 1720 on property acquired by Capt. John Stanley (X00035) and bequeathed to his son Deacon John Stanley (X00055), who commissioned the house 1709-1719 but sold it before occupying it. NHL designation 1960. NRHP 1966. Museum since 1935. Oldest 18th-century structure in Farmington. Solomon Whitman (son of Rev. Samuel Whitman, who succeeded H00007 Samuel Hooker as Farmington minister) added the lean-to that created the famous saltbox silhouette ca. 1750.

Warren 1887 (Stanley book) confirms Daniel Hooker 'inherited the farm of Thomas Hooker of West Hartford.' Exact location within West Hartford not yet researched.
Significance: Farm originally belonging to Rev. Thomas Hooker (H00001) in West Hartford. Inherited by his grandson Dr. Daniel Hooker (H00036), who deeded it to his sons in 1728. The Hooker family's tangible land connection to the Hartford founding generation.
Not to confuse with: The Sarah Whitman Hooker House in West Hartford — a different property with a different history; The Hooker Elm site in Farmington (LM001) — that was John Hooker's house, not Thomas Hooker's farm

Significance: During the American Revolutionary War, this house was owned by Thomas Hart Hooker, a descendant of Rev. Thomas Hooker (H00001), and his wife Sarah Whitman Hooker. The Hookers held as captives Andrew and Philip Skene — Loyalists captured after Americans took Fort Ticonderoga. The house was built c.1720 by John Seymour in one of the first settled areas of Hartford's West Parish. Currently owned by the Town of West Hartford.

Open question: Thomas Hart Hooker EH entry number [research_needed] Wikipedia identifies him as 'a descendant of Thomas Hooker, founder of Hartford.' Which branch? The 'Hart' middle name suggests Hart-Hooker family connection. Could be a descendant of the Hooker-Hart marriages documented in H00099/H00100/H00101 or H00098.

Significance: Built c. 1725 for Dr. Daniel Hooker (H00036), grandson of Rev. Thomas Hooker (H00001) and first tutor of Yale College. One of the oldest surviving brick structures in Connecticut and the oldest surviving two-chimney house in Wethersfield. Originally one story with gambrel roof; raised to two full stories in early 19th century. Daniel sold the property to Caleb Griswold in 1733; remained in Griswold family until 1848. Preservation easement donated by Lee Kuckro to Preservation Connecticut.
Construction notes: Brick construction was rare in 18th-century Connecticut. Clay deposits in the Connecticut River Valley were used for local brick production. House lacks the Georgian center hallway typical of later two-chimney houses — considered transitional. Enlarged in 1825 by Timothy Griswold.

Significance: Built 1686 as a wedding gift for Jethro Coffin (X00015) and Mary Gardner (X00016). Believed to be the oldest residence on Nantucket still on its original site. Designated National Historic Landmark 1968. Struck by lightning 1987; restored. Now owned and operated by the Nantucket Historical Association. Jethro Coffin was the father of Margaret Coffin (I00015) who married into the Hooker tree.
GPS note: 41°17′15″N 70°6′25″W per Wikipedia
Home of Major Benjamin Tallmadge, Washington's spymaster and Culper Ring leader. Also associated with his merchant partnership with Oliver Wolcott Jr. and his presidency of Phoenix Branch Bank.

Home of Captain Jacob Purdy, husband of Abigail Smith Purdy (H00331, EH 331). General Washington used it as his headquarters during the Battle of White Plains (October 28, 1776) and again for two months in 1778. One of White Plains' most famous historic sites.

Home of Major Roger Hooker (H00306, 1751-1830) — Continental Army officer, Society of the Cincinnati member, Sheriff of Hartford County, Justice of the Peace until age 70. Roger Hooker "is the Roger Hooker referred to in the account of the Hooker House and the Hooker Elm" (EH). In 1776, he and his brother Elnathan purchased 40 acres at Congee (with dwelling house and barn) from Tunxis men Cornelius Indian and Elijah Wampey for £150. Source: deed at NativeNortheastPortal; Hurlburt, Farmington Town Clerks and Their Times.

Built 1804 by Capt. John Hurlbut — who in Nov. 1796 sailed as first mate on the ship Neptune, Daniel Green master from New York, on a voyage around the globe. "This cruise is said to have been the first in which the globe was circumnavigated by an American vessel." (Hon. S.W. Adams, Hartford CT.) Capt. Hurlbut died of smallpox in New York City in 1808, just four years after building this house. Federal style brick house; later owner in the 1850s added Italianate features (projecting cornice with brackets, entry portico, side veranda, belvedere tower). Jane Robbins Dunham left the property to the Wethersfield Historical Society. Now a historic house museum. The Hurlbut-Hooker connection: Capt. Hurlbut's daughter Anne Wright Hurlbut (X00422) married Henry Wadsworth Terry (HD1345), great-great-grandson of Thomas Hooker, and their daughter was Rose Terry Cooke (HD1353), noted American realist author. Source: Posted May 23, 2007 (Federal Style, Houses, Italianate, Wethersfield)

On the night of October 31, 1687, Joseph Wadsworth (uncle of Rev. Daniel Wadsworth, who was father of Col. Jeremiah Wadsworth X00417) seized the Charter of Connecticut given by King Charles II and hid it in a hollow oak tree in Hartford — aided by Lt.-Col. John Talcott (T00035, great-great-grandfather of Abigail Talcott, mother of Col. Jeremiah Wadsworth). This act of defiance preserved Connecticut's self-governance against Governor Andros. The tree blew down in a storm August 21, 1856. The wood was used to make numerous commemorative objects including a chair still in the CT State Library. HOOKER-TALCOTT-WADSWORTH CONVERGENCE: Both the man who hid the Charter (Wadsworth) and the man who helped him (Talcott) were ancestors of Col. Jeremiah Wadsworth — who 93 years later hosted Washington and Rochambeau at the Hartford Conference of 1780. Source: Talcott Pedigree, entry on Lt.-Col. John Talcott; Wikipedia: Charter Oak
Current site: The original tree is gone (fell 1856). Charter Oak Place marks the site in Hartford. Memorial plaque and museum pieces at CT State Library. The Charter itself is at the CT State Library.

Built ca. 1772 by James Hooker (H00348, b. Aug 15, 1742 Hartford CT; d. Dec 10, 1805 Windsor CT). Great-great-grandson of Rev. Thomas Hooker. Son of Nathaniel Hooker 2d (H00115) and Eunice Talcott (I00054, daughter of Gov. Joseph Talcott). REVOLUTIONARY WAR: Merchant partner in "Hooker and Chaffee" — the firm helped supply American soldiers during the Revolution. Commissioned as CAPTAIN in the Continental Army. House built several years after death of first wife Hannah Allin; he remarried 1777 to Dolly Goodwin; after her death 1784 married Mary Chaffee — daughter of neighbor Dr. Hezekiah Chaffee and sister of his business partner John Chaffee. ARCHITECTURE: Original Federal style; Greek Revival exterior elements added ca. 1840s (entablature below roof, corner pilasters). Interior gutted for Chaffee School classrooms. Part of PALISADO AVENUE HISTORIC DISTRICT, National Register of Historic Places. Rev. William Russell Jr. (H00358) is buried at Palisado Cemetery, Windsor — the same historic district. NOTE: The Chaffee connection links to the family network — Mary Chaffee's father lived next door; her brother was James's business partner. TALCOTT CONNECTION: James's mother Eunice Talcott was daughter of Gov. Joseph Talcott — the same governor whose other children married into the Russell-Pierpont-Hooker lines. Source: Palisado Avenue Historic District description; OpenCRS / preservationist records. LOOMIS CHAFFEE NOTE: The Chaffee School that later used this house was founded in 1874 by John Hubbard Chaffee — a different branch of the Chaffee family from Dr. Hezekiah Chaffee's line. The school name coincidence reflects the prevalence of the Chaffee family in the Windsor area, but the Loomis Chaffee founders are not direct descendants of James Hooker's business partner John Chaffee.
Current site: Became part of Chaffee School; interior significantly altered. Exterior retains ca. 1840s Greek Revival elements over original 1772 structure.
National Register district: Palisado Avenue Historic District

Built 1826-1828 for Samuel Russell (HD, 1789-1862), founder of Russell & Company. Greek Revival mansion, Middletown CT. Architect: Ithiel Town — the same architect used for the Wadsworth Atheneum (founded by Daniel Wadsworth HD1330, also a Hooker descendant). Samuel Russell had personal contact with the firm of Town and Davis during construction; his brother Edward supervised the building. The house is on the same High Street as Edward A. Russell House (LM017). Russell & Company records note correspondence with Ithiel Town 1827-1830 during construction. Now known as "Russell House" on the Honors College at Wesleyan University campus. DICKENS LEGEND: "High Street is the most beautiful street I have seen in America." Lucy Colton Wells (1942 article) recalled her mother saying Dickens spoke these words "at a dinner party in the Samuel Russell House." Dickens visited Connecticut in 1867 — five years after Samuel Russell's death, but the house was still in the family. NOTE: The same quote is attributed to Dickens about 50 other streets he visited, and some Middletown sources say it was Mark Twain or William Dean Howells. Yale makes the same claim about Hillhouse Avenue. (Source: Wesleyan University Archives; Suzy Taraba, Wesleyan magazine.) Regardless, High Street was genuinely beautiful: "three-story Corinthian columns and legendary rose gardens" on the Russell house in 1867.
Current site: Wesleyan University Honors College.

[Stage 6Y-268]: NRHP listed Oct 6, 1970 (#70000688). Designated National Historic Landmark Aug 7, 2001. Owned by Wesleyan University since 1937; currently houses the Department of Philosophy. Architectural detail (per Wikipedia): Greek temple form, six full-height Corinthian columns, low flushboarded pediment, brick masonry walls covered with stucco scribed to resemble ashlar, brownstone foundation. Talbot Hamlin placed the design 'in the richest Greek vein'; Roger Hale Newton called it 'indicative of the hand of Town in its undeniable sophistication.' Per Wikipedia: built 1828 while Russell himself was in Canton — friend Samuel D. Hubbard worked with Russell's wife to supervise construction; Russell returned to Middletown in 1831. Two-story north wing added c.1855, attributed to Alexander Jackson Davis (Town's former partner). Around the same time rear portico enclosed and a double iron stair added connecting first floor to garden.

hooker_connections.role: Builder/owner; 8th-gen Hooker descendant via Pierpont line

landmarks.notes:
Built 1841-1842 for Edward Augustus Russell (HD1374, 1797-1874), China trade merchant and Mayor of Middletown 1859-1861. Site occupies the original NOADIAH RUSSELL HOMELOT dating to the seventeenth century — Rev. Noadiah Russell (d. 1713) was a founding trustee of Yale College 1701 and Edward Augustus Russell's great-great-grandfather, anchoring the entire Russell-Pierpont-Hooker line. Last Greek Revival house built on Middletown's most prestigious street (High Street between Church and Washington Streets was the city's premier nineteenth-century residential corridor). Attribution to Town and Davis is speculative but plausible: Edward had personal contact with the firm while supervising construction of his brother Samuel W. Russell's 1828 Greek Revival house next door (LM016 — now Wesleyan Honors College). Stylistic affinity to the DeRham Brevoort House (Davis, NYC) and 'Highwood' (Town and Davis for Henry Whitney, New Haven, 1835-36) supports the attribution. Structural system: load-bearing masonry, flat roof, brick and flushboarding walls, brownstone foundation. Edward's grand-nephew Richard L. deZeng (1847-1932) occupied the house until his death; Wesleyan purchased it from the Russell estate in 1934 and sold it to the Alpha Sigma Delta (later Kappa Nu Kappa) fraternity alumni association. The fraternity altered the building substantially — cornice lowered to the second floor with third-floor windows added above; window cornices removed; south facade reworked; upper floors divided into three-room suites. The first floor remains largely unaltered. Currently owned by Wesleyan University and used for lectures, concerts, and special events.

[Stage 6Y-270 fraternity update]: Wesleyan University Archives (Middletown Connecticut manuscripts 1000-171, Richard L. de Zeng correspondence and bills 1872-1873, Box 1) describes the property as 'the house on High Street later occupied by the Epsilon Gamma Chapter of the Sigma Nu Fraternity.' Chain of fraternity occupancy after the 1934 Wesleyan sale appears to be: Alpha Sigma Delta (1934) → Kappa Nu Kappa (renaming?) → Sigma Nu Epsilon Gamma Chapter. The same archives note Richard L. de Zeng's late bills and father-to-son business correspondence from the 1872-1873 period when he still owned the house.

Built 1901-1902 for Thomas Macdonough Russell Sr. (HD, 1874-1936), chairman of Russell Manufacturing Company and mayor of Middletown. Colonial Revival style. "A descendant of Samuel Russell, whose famous 1828 Greek Revival House (LM016) is across the street." (historicbuildingsct.com) Russell donated the Russell & Company records to the Library of Congress in 1931 while living at this address. The three Russell houses on High Street (LM016, LM017, LM018) represent three generations of the Hooker-Russell family's presence on the same block. Now: Wesleyan University Center for African American Studies. Source: https://historicbuildingsct.com/the-thomas-macdonough-russell-house-1902/
Current site: Wesleyan University Center for African American Studies.

landmarks.primary_name: Pierpont Homestead and Store, 29 State Street (1785)
landmarks.notes: Georgian Colonial built 1785 by Stephen Jacobs (cabinetmaker, early North Haven settler). Purchased ca.1809 by Daniel Pierpont Esq. (H00877, EH 877), also a cabinetmaker. "The house does not presently face State Street" — the road originally curved to a ford across the river. Daniel built a rear addition 1846. Son Rufus Pierpont purchased half and started a store next door; store remained in business for the next 100 years. "The Pierpont Homestead and Store were the center of life at the Pines Bridge in North Haven." Now a North Haven local historic district. Source: North Haven historical notes (Pierpont genealogy).

landmarks.primary_name: John Pierpont House, Elm Street New Haven (1767)
landmarks.notes: 149 Elm Street, New Haven CT — the OLDEST SURVIVING BUILDING in New Haven. Built 1767 by John Pierpont (H00388, gen 5 Hooker descendant) for himself and his new wife Sarah Beers. The land was deeded to his grandfather Rev. James Pierpont (X00126, Yale co-founder) by the Town of New Haven on September 25, 1685 — "the only conveyance that intervenes between its present owners and the aboriginal Indians from whom it was purchased more than 250 years ago." (EH 1909) In 1779 during the Revolution, British troops pillaged the house and used it as a hospital. John Pierpont died here 1805; his wife Sarah Beers Pierpont outlived him by 30 years (d. 1835 age 90). Inherited by daughter Mary Pierpont Foster (H00981); her children owned it until 1900 — more than 130 years after it was built. Sold 1900 to Anson Phelps Stokes (Secretary of Yale), who added rear wings and hosted the first Yale missionary board meeting here; Yale in China was established in this house. Yale acquired 1921; served as Faculty Club, later Office of Undergraduate Admissions. Now: Yale University Visitor Center (front) and Henry Koerner Center for Emeritus Faculty (back). Restored 2002. Georgian style. (NHBA Yale record; Yale Visitor Center)

Two-story brick Gothic Revival villa designed by Alexander Jackson Davis for Edwards Pierrepont (1817-1892), built 1867 in Garrison, Putnam County NY. Features: four-story flat-roofed tower (added later from southeast corner); pointed arch porch openings with wooden polygonal columns; diamond-pane windows; circular windows in gable peaks; three-part pointed arch windows on gable ends. Two-story frame carriage house north of main house. 15.8 acres total. ALTERATIONS: A.J. Davis proposed additions; in 1912-1913, "Mrs. L. Beckwith, daughter of Edwards Pierrepont" (i.e. Margaretta Pierrepont Beckwith) commissioned Cross & Cross Architects of New York for further alterations including brickwork around veranda, three-story northeast wing, kitchen repositioned from basement, and servant quarters. DESCENT: Estate descended to Margaretta Pierrepont Beckwith, then to her children (Edward Pierrepont Beckwith and Sidney Forbes Beckwith), who lived there until 1968. Present owners acquired 1969; carriage house sold separately 1970. NRHP significance: "associations with a master architect and a person significant in the political history of the United States." Listed National Register of Historic Places Nov 23, 1982, NRHP #82001247. Part of Hudson Highlands Multiple Property Submission. Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurst-Pierrepont_Estate
Area: 15.8 acres
Source: NRHP nomination form #82001247 (1982)

location.address: 15 Perry Ave., Warsaw, Wyoming County, New York

landmarks.notes:
Two-story wood-frame dwelling built 1824, expanded c.1843. Federal style cornice. Home of Seth M. Gates from c.1843 until his death 1877. UNDERGROUND RAILROAD STATION: For 15+ years, Gates concealed escaped enslaved people in the cellar and attic. Due to his antislavery stance, a Southern planter offered $500 for his apprehension. From 1893-1924 housed the Society of Village Works (local charitable organization). 1924 sold to local DAR chapter; 1977 transferred to Warsaw Historical Society for $1.00. Listed on the National Register of Historic Places 1992. Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seth_M._Gates_House
Source: Wikipedia

landmarks.primary_name: 1 Pierrepont Place, Brooklyn Heights (Pierrepont Family Mansion)
landmarks.notes: Four-story brick mansion on Brooklyn Heights, built c.1858. Home of Henry Evelyn Pierrepont (HD1533) × Anna Maria Jay (X00496) and their family. Anna Jay Pierrepont (HD1627) was born here January 1, 1861 and died here November 17, 1940 — "the last of her generation in one of New York's oldest families." (NYT 1940) Her NYT obituary describes the house as "crowded with antiques and historical letters." THE WASHINGTON PORTRAIT: "In the front parlor is an original Gilbert Stuart full-length portrait of George Washington, who made his headquarters on the Pierrepont property during the Long Island campaign." The portrait hung here until at least 1940, then was donated to the Brooklyn Museum. Pierrepont Place and Pierrepont Street in Brooklyn Heights are named for the family. (NYT obituary Nov 19, 1940; Wikipedia on Henry Evelyn Pierrepont)

landmarks.primary_name: Pierrepont Manor House and Land Office (c.1823)
landmarks.notes: William Constable Pierrepont (HD1534) arrived at Bear Creek (now Pierrepont Manor) in 1820 to manage the family's ~1,000,000 acres of land. He first lived in the Land Office while building the Pierrepont Manor house (completed c.1823). Both buildings still exist and are on the National Register of Historic Places. The Pierrepont Manor Cemetery, directly across the road from the Manor House, holds William C. Pierrepont, his wife Cornelia Butler, and their sons. William C. Pierrepont's 29 volumes of diaries (1823-1885) are at Cornell University Library (Collection #1094) — day-to-day weather records and land sale details. The hamlet was renamed Pierrepont Manor in his honor. (Cornell University Library Collection 1094; FamilySearch)

Greek Revival mansion built 1836 by Peter Augustus Jay (X00907) on his father Chief Justice John Jay's Rye estate. Peter Augustus inherited the land in 1822 (deeding from his father confirmed 1822; household expenses managed from 1814). Peter Augustus contracted with builder Edwin Bishop in 1836 to replace the failing farmhouse — reusing structural elements from "The Locusts" where his father grew up. The property was a National Historic Landmark as of November 2008 — the first NHL structure in Westchester County and oldest NHL in New York State to be fitted with a geothermal heating/cooling system. Now operated by the Jay Heritage Center as an educational center for American history. The JHC holds the Constable-Pierrepont family artifacts donated in 2019 including the Gilbert Stuart Washington portrait engraving and Stuart's original receipted bill. (Jay Heritage Center; Wikipedia on Peter Augustus Jay)

Construction history: Peter Augustus Jay contracted with builder Edwin Bishop in fall 1836 to replace the failing farmhouse "The Locusts" (named by James Fenimore Cooper, who used the Jay household for his 1821 novel The Spy). The Greek Revival mansion was completed in 1838. Mary Rutherfurd Clarkson Jay died on the island of Funchal in Madeira on Christmas Eve 1838 — before she could enjoy the home she had helped plan. The porch facing Long Island Sound was built the exact same length as the porch of the original farmhouse where John Jay celebrated the end of the Revolutionary War. The mansion dates to 1836 (contracted) / 1838 (completed) — prior entry said 1836.
Notable lessees 1891-1904: Junius Spencer Morgan II (numbering uncertain — our JSON has HD1238 as JSM III, b.1867), James Talcott (H03207, gen 8 Talcott line), and Mr. and Mrs. David Percy Morgan (Edith Parsons Morgan, daughter of neighbor John E. Parsons).
John Jay history: Peter Jay (father of Chief Justice John Jay) acquired 250 acres in Rye on March 26, 1745. John Jay used the estate as a refuge throughout his life. James Fenimore Cooper visited and drew characters from the Jay household. Caesar Valentine, enslaved by Peter Jay and manumitted 1824, remained on the property under a lifetime stipend in Peter Augustus Jay's will; died 1847.

landmarks.primary_name: Walter E. Hope Mansion, 43 East 70th Street
landmarks.notes:
Residence of Walter E. Hope (Assistant Secretary of the Treasury under President Hoover, 1929-1931) and his wife Florence, with daughters Helen Talcott Hope (TD0056) and Marian T. Hope. 
WALTER E. HOPE: Appointed by President Hoover Mar 4, 1929. Oversaw Bureau of Internal Revenue, Bureau of Engraving and Printing, Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, Bureau of the Mint, and Secret Service. Also chaired National Republican Finance Committee. Resigned Mar 1, 1931. Continued as political advisor — President Hoover walked from the Waldorf-Astoria to Hope's home for breakfast Mar 1933. 
HELEN TALCOTT HOPE (TD0056): Vassar College; debutante tea dance at Colony Club Nov 28, 1930; afternoon reception at mansion Dec 12 (debutante season). MARRIED Mar 18, 1938: David Edward Austen, Madison Avenue Presbyterian Church. NYT: "Helen numbers among her ancestors two early Governors of Connecticut, John Talcott and Thomas Hooker." 
MARIAN T. HOPE: Married Apr 14, 1944 at the mansion; reception at Colony Club.
