FLORENCE HOPE: Active in People's Chorus of New York; Carnegie Hall Christmas festivals. Reception for La Traviata benefit for Vassar College Fund. Reception for opera stars Elisabeth Rethberg, Lauritz Melchior, Lawrence Tibbett, Ludwig Hoffman of the Met (1935). 
(Dayton in Manhattan blog, Dec 2015; NYT archives)

The street (Percival Avenue) bears the family name. Near a pond that turned several mills.
Significance: Built by Dr. James Percival Jr. (X01934), prominent Kensington physician. James Gates Percival (X01936) grew up here; it is where he completed his first book of poems (published New Haven 1821), and where his alleged suicide attempt occurred in summer 1820. The house sits on the street now bearing the family name, southwest of Kensington Congregational Church. Ward's 1866 biography describes it: 'a plain wooden building, bordering close upon the street, with a long sloping roof in the rear — a style of dwelling which our ancestors brought from England.'
Associated family: Percival / Hart
Source: Ward, Life and Letters of James Gates Percival (1866)

Blue porch ceiling is a landmark feature. The stone store built by Timothy on the adjacent lot was destroyed by fire Jul 21, 1864. The school was founded by Sarah Porter (X01980), sister of Rev. Noah Porter III (X01979, Yale president 1871-1886), son of Rev. Noah Porter Jr. (X01977) who preached the funeral of Horace Cowles (H00697) and hosted the first ABCFM meeting 1810.
Significance: Built by Major Timothy Cowles (H00698) in 1815 as his home — the first house south of the Congregational Church on the same side of Main Street. Now owned by Miss Porter's School, affectionately called 'Tim-Co' by students. The blue-painted porch ceiling follows a 200-year-old New England tradition. The adjacent stone store built by Timothy was destroyed by fire on July 21, 1864.
Associated family: Cowles
Source: Cowles Genealogy #643

Part of the Farmington National Historic District. Listed in the NPS Amistad itinerary as one of the houses that sheltered the three Mende girls during their 1841 stay. The Cowles family took in the girl believed to be Kagne, who attended school five hours each morning with the other Mende and shared in domestic activities of the Cowles household. Built 1815 by Major Timothy Cowles (H00698).

Queen Anne style. William Gay purchased lot 1871 from heirs after Timothy's stone store burned 1864. William Gay may be ancestral to the compiler — flagged for research.
Significance: Built 1875 as the Parsonage of the First Congregational Church. The site was previously occupied by the stone store built by Maj. Timothy Cowles (H00698), which was destroyed by fire on July 21, 1864. William Gay, a merchant with several Farmington real estate parcels, bought the lot in 1871 and sold it to the First Ecclesiastical Society, who built the Queen Anne parsonage. NOTE: William Gay connection — potentially ancestral to the compiler; needs research.
Associated family: Cowles
Source: Farmington, Village of Beautiful Homes

Built 1769 for Samuel Smith. Later home of Horace Cowles (H00697, 1782-1841) and wife Mary Ann Steele Smith Cowles (X01969). Underground Railroad station — Horace and Mary Ann hid fugitive slaves here. One of three Mende girls from the Amistad (believed to be Teme/Tamie) stayed with the Cowles family during the Mende's 8-month stay in Farmington after the trial. After Horace's death the property passed to son Samuel Smith Cowles (HD2873), who continued Underground Railroad work and edited the Charter Oak anti-slavery paper. Daughter Mary Ann Cowles (HD2878) is documented as having refused entry to a slave catcher while left in charge as a young girl.

landmarks.secondary_name: 27 Main Street, Farmington CT — Amistad Itinerary
landmarks.notes: National Park Service Amistad itinerary entry. Horace Cowles (H00697) was a founding member of the Hartford County Anti-Slavery Society and the Connecticut Anti-Slavery Society, and an Underground Railroad stationmaster. The Mende girl Teme (or Tamie) from the Amistad lived with the Cowles family. After Horace became ill and died, son Samuel Smith Cowles (HD2873) inherited and continued the Underground Railroad work, editing the Charter Oak anti-slavery paper.

landmarks.secondary_name: Built 1774 by Capt. Elijah Wadsworth; later birthplace of Harriet Beecher Stowe
landmarks.notes: Built 1774 by Capt. Elijah Wadsworth (TD0059), then unmarried. In 1810, Wadsworth sold the house to Rev. Lyman Beecher (1775-1863), minister of Litchfield's First Congregational Church. In 1811, Harriet Beecher Stowe — author of Uncle Tom's Cabin — was born here. The family lived here until 1826. Harriet recalled it as 'a wide, roomy, windy edifice that seemed to have been built by a succession of afterthoughts.' She left at age 13 (1824) to attend the Hartford Female Seminary. In 1872 the house was moved by oxen to a new location, later converted to a sanitarium and dormitory for Forman School (est. 1930). Fell into obscurity until 1996 when Forman School offered it for sale at $50,000. CT Historical Commission placed it on the state's Register of Historic Places. Declined by Litchfield Historical Society ('not much left of it from the Beecher era'). Sold for $1. Deconstructed by Chandler Saint and Stephen Solley for a proposed museum — project collapsed in 2001 after local opposition. Deconstructed house placed in secret storage. Acquired by art dealer Art Pappas; listed on eBay 2016 at $14.5M, dropped to $400K. As of 2026, reportedly still in storage — listed on Craigslist for $150,000. Harriet Beecher Stowe's memoir of her childhood in this house appears in 'Poganuc People.' Source: https://americanaristocracy.com/houses/beecher-house

Built c.1800 by Jesse Hart (H00587), cabinet-maker, tavern-keeper and postmaster. Brick house with chimneys at each of its four corners, with corresponding fireplaces inside. In 1813 Hart purchased the tavern at Boston Corners. The house was later owned by Leon LeClair. (Historic Buildings of Connecticut; History of Berlin, Catharine Melinda North, 1916)

Built 1874 for Mark Twain (Samuel Clemens). Part of the Nook Farm community on the western edge of Hartford. Twain's neighbors included John Hooker (H01626) and Isabella Beecher Hooker (I00170), who had established the community, and Harriet Beecher Stowe (X02034). Twain lived here 1874-1891. Now the Mark Twain House & Museum.

24-room fieldstone castle built 1914-1919 by William Hooker Gillette (H02979). Features 47 unique door locks, secret passages, trap doors, and a miniature railway. Purchased by CT 1943 for $29,000. 184 acres. Added to National Register of Historic Places 1986.
Birthplace of Peter Rawson Taft (1785). Added to National Register of Historic Places Oct 7, 1983.

landmarks.secondary_name: Historic Richmond Hill Estate, French Broad River, Asheville NC

dates.status: destroyed by arson 2009; site continues as OM Sanctuary retreat

landmarks.notes: Queen Anne mansion built 1889 by Congressman/Ambassador Richmond Pearson. Named for combination of builder (Richmond Pearson) and designer (James G. Hill). 25 rooms; running water; 10 fireplaces; pulley baggage elevator. Social/political center for years. Moved 600 feet and restored in 1989 as inn. Restaurant named 'Gabrielle's' after his wife. Destroyed by arson March 19, 2009 during foreclosure proceedings. No criminal arrests. Federal jury ruled insurance fraud (civil). Site now OM Sanctuary retreat (54 acres).
Completed 1906 as J.P. Morgan's private library. Made public 1924 by HD1172. Henry Sturgis Morgan (HD1175): trustee, president, chairman. National Historic Landmark.

Built 1888 for Sen. John Brooks Henderson (I00287) and Mary Foote Henderson (HD3149). 30-room castle, 58-foot tower, Seneca sandstone, Richardsonian Romanesque style. Architect: Eugene C. Gardner (Massachusetts). Later additions by T.F. Schneider (1892, 1897) and Totten & Rodgers (1902). Interior: Moorish entrance hall modeled on the Alhambra; octagonal art gallery/ballroom; oak-panelled dining room. Mary Henderson purchased 200+ paintings by artist Lucien Whiting Powell (built him a studio at the castle). 1906: temperance members emptied and smashed husband's 40-year wine collection on the front lawn. After Mary's death (1931), furnishings auctioned 1935. Failed to sell. 1937: converted to 16 apartments ('Castle H Tennis and Swimming Club'). 1941: purchased by Eugene Meyer for $150,000 solely to demolish it. Demolished 1949. Battlemented walls along Florida Ave remain.
London estate in Roehampton associated with HD1171. Formerly connected to the court of Napoleon III.

landmarks.secondary_name: Thomas Barney House; Mix House; Austin Williams House
landmarks.notes: Rev. Samuel Hooker (H00028), father of Giles and Samuel, lived in the Mix House — located just south of the old burying ground on Main Street, Farmington, directly opposite the Giles Hooker house on the George Cowles place. In EH's time (1909) a flat stone in the sidewalk just below the brow of the hill still covered the old well of the Giles Hooker house. The house was later owned by Austin Williams. Contains an 1½-story English barn contributing to the Farmington Village National and Local Historic District.

landmarks.secondary_name: Enders estate, Avon CT (1931-1994). Original house demolished c.1998. Enders Reserve (2.65 acres) preserved by Avon Land Trust.
landmarks.architect: Talcott & Talcott (Seth Talcott TD0061 and Charles Hooker Talcott T01460)
landmarks.style: International style; ceramic hollow tile walls
landmarks.notes: 57-acre farm built 1932-1933 by Talcott & Talcott (brothers Seth and Charles Hooker Talcott) for Alice Talcott Enders (TD0064) and Ostrom Enders (I00181). International style with ceramic hollow tile walls — "expensive to design and build and acceptable to only the most advanced tastes." Original house demolished c.1998; greenhouse and mature white oak still survive. Alice and Ostrom named the farm "Northington" after a historic name for the Avon area. Cheviot sheep, hay fields, large vegetable garden, cutting garden. 1950s: 120-sq-ft sunken greenhouse added by Alice for rare geraniums. Three ponds dug for wildfowl; Enders bred Nene geese with Smithsonian Sec. S. Dillon Ripley — sent hatchlings to Hawaii. Waterfowl given to National Zoo (DC) and Bronx Zoo (NY). The Waterville Beagles — competitive show beagles, New England field trials 1937-1941. Map "The Waterville Beagles" (March 20, 1939) at Connecticut Historical Society. Three-room library addition housed 6,000 ornithological books donated to Watkinson Library at Trinity College 1982. Enders Reserve (2.65 acres, 125 Cider Brook Road) donated to Avon Land Trust 1995. SOURCES: Smithsonian Archives of American Gardens AAG.GCA File CT705; Avon Land Trust Fall Newsletter 2022. BIBLIOGRAPHY: "A Long, Low House for the Country," Art Decoration Magazine, 1934-1935. "House of Ostrom Enders," Architectural Record 77, March 1935. Connecticut Historical Commission Architectural survey, 1997. Photos at Connecticut Historical Society (Garden Club of Hartford). GUID: https://n2t.net/ark:/65665/kb60743533a-fc0c-40cf-b814-c972fd74b5eb

landmarks.secondary_name: Donated by Phineas Talcott Jr.; became a public park 1895

location.address: Elm Street / Prospect Street / Park Street

landmarks.notes: Donated to the town of Vernon by or in memory of T01062 Phineas Talcott Jr., who used the land across from his home at 68-70 Prospect Street as a cow pasture. Named Talcott Park in 1895, 32 years after his death. The park association planted elm trees; after the Hurricane of 1938 toppled them, maples were planted in their place. Originally featured a fountain and bandstand. Talcott's house on Prospect Avenue later became the Union Church parsonage; housed the Vernon Historical Society until 1980. Image: Talcott Park, 1870 — Tankerhoosen Valley History.

landmarks.secondary_name: Donated to Northern Connecticut Land Trust by John G. Talcott Jr., 2010

location.address: Between Interstate 84 and Hop River State Park, Vernon CT

landmarks.notes: 20-acre parcel on the Tankerhoosen River, Vernon CT. Contains waterfalls and striking rock formations. Donated to Northern Connecticut Land Trust (NCLT) by John G. Talcott Jr. in December 2010. Historically significant: Peter Dobson, constructing a cotton mill near the gorge in the early 1820s, observed glacially abraded boulders and published the first American paper on glacial theory (American Journal of Science, July 1826). Used for hiking, fishing, and bird watching. Family parcels along Rail-To-Trail and Elm Hill remain in Talcott family ownership. SOURCE: Northern Connecticut Land Trust; Journal Inquirer Dec 28, 2010.

landmarks.secondary_name: Gothic Revival mansion, 1 Hillside Place New Britain CT (1859-1860)
landmarks.notes: Gothic Revival mansion built 1859-1860 for Timothy Wadsworth Stanley, successful businessman and Connecticut state legislator. Originally surrounded by a four-acre estate. Grounds designed by landscape architect Jacob Weidenmann — the same Weidenmann who completed the Olmsted/Vaux plan for the Hartford Retreat grounds (INST079) in the same era, working with T01062 Phineas Talcott Jr.'s institution. SOURCE: Historic Buildings of Connecticut.

landmarks.secondary_name: Now site of British Embassy, Washington DC

location.historical_access: Originally accessed from Georgetown via Parrott's Lane (now Lovers Lane).

landmarks.style: Devonshire cottage — clay, straw, and pebbles construction with walls four feet thick
landmarks.notes:
Built circa 1830 by Robert Barnard (1786-1852) on 24 acres in Georgetown DC. A Devonshire cottage of clay, straw, and pebbles with walls four feet thick. Named after the Norfolk boarding school operated by Rev. Michael Maurice near Lowestoft, where Robert had been educated as a boy after his mother's death in 1790. Robert's first son Samuel Maurice was named jointly for his father and this teacher.

Owners and inhabitants: Robert and Sophia Cropley Barnard (1830-1852); after Robert's death, the estate passed through inheritance to multiple children. 1863 sale advertisement listed 24 acres. Eventually inherited by R.S.T. Cissel by 1881. Theodosia Talcott (I00265, daughter of Robert and Sophia) lived at Normanstone with her widowed mother and unmarried sisters from 1867 (after Charles Talcott's death in Mexico) until 1899 (her remarriage to Hambleton).

Lucia Beverly Talcott (T01872) married Herman Hollerith (I00272) at Normanstone in 1890. The newlyweds lived there, and again during a period of financial hardship in 1895-1896. Theodosia Talcott's professional income at the Patent Office reportedly kept the family solvent during Hollerith's down periods (per Geoffrey D. Austrian, 'Herman Hollerith: Forgotten Giant of Information Processing,' Columbia University Press, 1982).

1886: Sold by Dr. R.S.T. Cissell of New York to a Philadelphia investor; transferred to a syndicate including Isaac N. Jackson and Richard H. Goldsborough. R.H. Goldsboro testified buying for $60,000 and selling for $125,000 (Star, Aug 5, 1891).

1925: British Office of Works bought the embassy site from Harry Wardman, Thomas Bones, and James Hobbs.

1930: British Ambassador's residence completed, designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens. The original Normanstone cottage was demolished. The British government acquired adjacent lots between 1941 and 1953.

1960: Modernist embassy office building completed northwest of the residence.

Quote: 'Through Lover's Lane we went to Normanstone, the home of the two Misses Barnard and their sister, Mrs. Talcott. It was a quaint little house, which stood just about where the British Embassy now is. The name is commemorated by Normanstone Drive.' (Grace Dunlop Peter, 'Portrait of Old George Town')

landmarks.secondary_name: Hollerith family estate, Mathews County VA

location.address: Off New Point Comfort Highway, near Mathews
location.features: Private peninsula between Tabb's Creek and the East River, near Mobjack Bay (Chesapeake Bay tributary). Roughly one mile of water frontage.

landmarks.style: Coastal Virginia retreat — main 'Summer House' (6,066 sq ft) and 'Winter House' (2,508 sq ft, ~1940). Combined 12 bedrooms, 5 full baths, 2 half-baths, long screened porches.
landmarks.notes:
Purchased 1916 by Herman Hollerith (I00272) — inventor of the punched-card tabulating machine and founder of the company that became IBM. Named 'Brighton.' Hollerith also acquired the adjacent Mobjack Farm to run a Guernsey cow dairy operation. The 61-acre property has been kept in the Hollerith family ever since 1916 — across more than a century — though as of 2024 it is being marketed for sale.

The main 'Summer House' (6,066 sq ft) was built in the early 1900s after the 1916 purchase to accommodate Herman and Lucia Hollerith's family of six children. Around 1940, with grandchildren growing up, Herman built a second home — the 2,508 sq ft 'Winter House.' Together the two dwellings include 12 bedrooms, 5 full baths, 2 half-baths, spacious living and dining areas, large kitchens with butler's pantries, a library, a private office, and long screened porches stretching the entire length of both houses.

Lucia Beverly Talcott Hollerith (T01872) summered at Brighton with her three daughters after Herman's 1929 death; she died at Brighton on August 4, 1944.

landmarks.name: Edward Hooker House (1811)
landmarks.notes:
1811 Federal-style house built for Edward Hooker (H00630) on High Street in Farmington CT. Edward operated his 'Old Red College' preparatory school in his PARENTS' old farmhouse (a separate building, a former Cheever-descendant home) — NOT in this 1811 house. He closed the school in 1816 when the town opened its own academy in the village center.

Edward Hooker's daughter Elisabeth Daggett Hooker (H01625) married Francis Gillette (later a U.S. Senator) — a notable marital tie between the Hooker and Gillette families.

After Edward's death in 1846, this house was inherited by his son John Hooker (H01626), the Hartford lawyer married to Isabella Beecher Hooker (I00170). John and Isabella lived in Farmington until the early 1850s, when they moved to Hartford and helped establish the Nook Farm neighborhood with the Gillettes. The Farmington house remained in the Hooker family until sold in 1864.

Tied to abolitionist history: John Hooker rented an office at Deming's Store on Mill Lane Farmington — directly next door to a room used by the Africans from the Amistad during their stay in Farmington. The Mendi captives also attended school in an upper room of what became the Farmington post office building.

landmarks.name: Hooker Hall (1937)
landmarks.notes: Three-story Mediterranean-Revival dormitory at Rollins College, Winter Park FL, named in honor of Dr. Edward Payson Hooker (H02539, 1834-1904) — Middlebury graduate/professor/trustee, Congregational missionary pioneer in Florida, and first president of Rollins College (1885-1892). Construction cost ~$60,000; architects Kiehnel and Elliott designed the building to match the typical Mediterranean campus architecture. Metal windows alternate with rugged concrete structure to give an aura of serenity. After 1937 completion, the 7,310-sq-ft dormitory housed Theta Kappa Nu fraternity (1937-1939), then Lambda Chi Alpha, and today Chi Psi. The 1979 renovation added a wing including student rooms, lounge, and library.

landmarks.name: Nook Farm
landmarks.address: Forest Street + Hawthorn Street + Farmington Avenue intersection
landmarks.notes: Reformist literary community founded 1853 in Hartford CT when John Hooker (H01626) and his brother-in-law Sen. Francis Gillette (I00173) jointly purchased 140 acres on Farmington Avenue. They sold lots to family and kindred-spirit reformers, building a community that included Harriet Beecher Stowe, Mark Twain, Charles Dudley Warner, the Hooker family, the Gillette family, and Isabella Beecher Hooker. Mark Twain moved in 1874 — a decade after Stowe arrived. The Hookers raised three children at the corner of Forest and Hawthorn streets. Surviving houses include the Mark Twain House and the Harriet Beecher Stowe Center — both museums today. Katharine Seymour Day (HD3004), John and Isabella's granddaughter, spent her life preserving the community.

landmarks.name: Hooker Auditorium
landmarks.description: Theater building at Mount Holyoke College, named for Prof. Henrietta Edgecomb Hooker (1851-1929), the college's longtime professor of botany.

landmarks.name: Sierra Bonita Ranch

location.address: Sulphur Springs Valley, ~27 miles north of Willcox
location.region_notes: Sulphur Springs Valley between Galiuro and Pinaleño Mountains; part of Coronado National Forest region

landmarks.description: Founded 1872 by Col. Henry Clay Hooker on the ruins of an early-1800s Spanish hacienda destroyed by Apache raids. Sierra Bonita ('beautiful mountains') was the first permanent American cattle ranch in the Arizona Territory and became its largest, peaking at ~800 square miles (30 by 27 miles) and 30,000 head of cattle. The original adobe headquarters — a fortress 80 by 100 feet, U-shaped around a central patio, with 20-inch-thick walls 16 feet high, no exterior windows or doors, and gunports in the parapets — survives substantially intact and is shaded today by giant cottonwoods. The ranch was watered by five springs, several cienegas, seasonal creeks, and an underground river just below the surface tapped by wells. At 4,000 ft elevation it escaped extremes of heat and cold — an ideal breeding range. Hooker introduced the first graded Hereford stock to Arizona in the 1880s, transforming the territory's beef industry. The ranch survived the catastrophic 1891 Arizona drought (which killed over half of the territory's 1.5 million cattle) thanks to fenced pastures, controlled grazing, and engineered ditches from the mountains to ranch reservoirs. After Hooker's death in 1907, Sierra Bonita passed in succession to son Edwin R. Hooker (H04271, 1907-1931), Harry E. Hooker (until 1952), Mrs. Harry Hooker (Jacqueline Hooker Hughes), Charles Hooker Davis (5th gen), and as of 2012 Jesse Hooker Davis (6th gen). Today the ranch is ~45,000 acres (about one-fifth its peak size) and continues to raise Hereford bloodlines tracing to Hooker's original 1880s Oregon imports — Arizona's oldest ranch under continuous single-family ownership.

sources.short: National Park Service / National Historic Landmark designation 1964
Lynn R. Bailey, Henry Clay Hooker and the Sierra Bonita
NHL nomination form (Sulphur Spring Valley historical sources)

landmarks.research_notes: First permanent American cattle ranch in Arizona Territory. Stocked initially with 1,000 Texas Longhorns + Mexican corrientes in 1872; transitioned to Durham shorthorns; Hereford imports 1880s. Hooker's pragmatic Apache diplomacy (Cochise red blanket; nickname 'Captu'/Capto') reduced raid losses. Ranch was social center of southeastern Arizona — Hooker hosted politicians, military officers, scientists, artists, writers; guests required to wear coats at dinner (extra coats available). Augustus Thomas's play 'Arizona' was set at Sierra Bonita with characters Canby and Bonita based on the Hooker family. Wyatt Earp's Vendetta Ride posse sheltered here March 27, 1882. Billy the Kid (William H. Bonney) employed briefly 1877 before his first killing in nearby Bonita. Six generations of continuous family ownership: Henry Clay → Edwin R. → Harry E. → Mrs. Harry Hooker → Charles Hooker Davis → Jesse Hooker Davis (current).

landmarks.name: Hooker Telescope (100-inch reflector, Mount Wilson Observatory)

location.region_notes: San Gabriel Mountains, ~10 miles NE of Pasadena CA

founded.founder: John Daggett Hooker (H02709) — initial donor; George Ellery Hale — director; Carnegie Institute — additional underwriter

landmarks.description: The 100-inch (2.5 m) Hooker reflecting telescope at Mount Wilson Observatory above Pasadena, California — operational from November 2, 1917 first light. The largest telescope in the world from 1917 until the 200-inch Hale Telescope at Palomar saw first light in January 1949. Initial donor was John Daggett Hooker (H02709), the Hinsdale-NH-born iron-pipe and oil magnate of Los Angeles whose $45,000 pledge funded the casting and grinding of the giant mirror at the Saint-Gobain factory in France in 1908 (polishing took nine years). Hooker died in May 1911, six years before first light, with $10,000 of his pledge unpaid; the Carnegie Institute filled the gap, and the project was completed under astronomer George Ellery Hale's direction. The dome was designed by D. H. Burnham & Co. of Chicago, fabricated by the Morava Construction Company, pre-assembled in a Chicago lot, then disassembled and hauled up the Mount Wilson toll road by mule and truck. Edwin Hubble used the Hooker through the 1920s to make the two foundational discoveries of modern cosmology: in 1923 he proved that Andromeda is a separate galaxy outside the Milky Way (using a Cepheid variable measurement), and in 1929 he and Milton Humason established that distant galaxies recede at velocities proportional to their distance — Hubble's Law and the expanding universe. Subsequent discoveries included Fritz Zwicky's 1930s evidence for dark matter, Seth Nicholson's 1938 discovery of two Jupiter satellites, Walter Baade's 1940s stellar populations distinguishing two types of Cepheid variables (which doubled the calculated size of the universe), and 1963 detection of water vapor on Mars. The telescope was decommissioned in 1985, restarted in 1992 with adaptive optics, equipped with the UnISIS laser guide star system in 1997, and converted in 2014 into the world's largest telescope dedicated to public observing — regular public sessions began with the 2015 season. Designated an International Historic Mechanical Engineering Landmark in 1981. Resolving power 0.05 arcsecond.

sources.short: Helen Wright, 'Explorer of the Universe: A Biography of George Ellery Hale' (1966)
Kevin Starr, 'The Dream Endures: California Enters the 1940s' (1997)
West Adams Heritage Association — John Daggett Hooker biography

landmarks.image_caption: 100-inch Hooker Telescope at Mount Wilson Observatory; Cloudinary copy
landmarks.research_notes: ARGUABLY THE MOST CONSEQUENTIAL TELESCOPE IN THE HISTORY OF ASTRONOMY. Edwin Hubble's 1923 measurement of a Cepheid variable in Andromeda using the Hooker established that the Milky Way is one galaxy among many; his 1929 redshift-distance relation established the expansion of the universe. These discoveries — made on a Hooker-funded instrument — are the empirical foundation of modern Big Bang cosmology. Per West Adams Heritage Association source: there was an estrangement between Hooker and Hale starting in 1909 (over both glass-quality concerns and Hooker's jealousy of Hale's friendship with his wife Katharine) that lasted until Hooker's 1911 death. Hooker died with the rift unresolved and the final $10,000 installment unpaid; Carnegie made up the difference but the telescope was named for Hooker anyway. 1981 designated International Historic Mechanical Engineering Landmark by ASME. Three Hooker brothers (sons of Henry Sr H01393): Henry Clay (Sierra Bonita LM054), Charles Gay (SF hardware), John Daggett (this telescope) — the single most consequential family productions in the post-Civil-War American West. Albert A. Michelson developed a 6-meter optical astronomical interferometer attached to the Hooker in 1919 — first instrument ever to measure the precise diameter of a star (Betelgeuse). Henry Norris Russell developed his star classification system based on Hooker observations.

discoveries.description: Conclusively proved the Andromeda nebula to be external to the Milky Way galaxy — first measurement of a Cepheid variable in M31, establishing the existence of other galaxies. Foundation of extragalactic astronomy.
Confirmed that the Universe is expanding (Hubble's Law), measured its expansion rate, and measured the size of the known Universe. Foundation of modern Big Bang cosmology.
First evidence for dark matter — observed that galaxy clusters contain far more mass than visible from luminous matter alone.
Discovered two satellites of Jupiter, then designated #10 (Lysithea) and #11 (Carme).
Distinguished stellar populations and discovered two different types of Cepheid variable stars, doubling the size of the known universe previously calculated by Hubble.
Detection of water vapor in the atmosphere of Mars.

construction.first_donation: $45,000 from John Daggett Hooker (H02709) for purchase + grinding of the mirror
construction.hooker_unpaid: $10,000 final installment defaulted at death; made up by Carnegie Institute
construction.dome_designed: D. H. Burnham & Company of Chicago
construction.dome_fabricated: Morava Construction Company of Chicago (founded by Bohemian-born engineer Wensel Morava); 100-foot steel hemisphere pre-assembled in vacant Chicago lot for testing then disassembled and shipped to CA
construction.transport: Mule-and-truck haul up primitive Mount Wilson toll road; Mack Truck photo 1917

operational_eras.notes: Until Caltech-Carnegie 200-inch Hale Telescope at Palomar saw first light January 1949
1995 visible-light adaptive optics; 1997 UnISIS laser guide star adaptive optics
World's largest telescope dedicated to public use; regularly scheduled public observing began 2015 season

landmarks.primary_name: Hooker Telescope (100-inch reflector, Mount Wilson Observatory)

landmarks.name: John Bowman House (1824)
landmarks.address: West side of Lake Road, Village of Clarkson NY (first house entering village from south)
landmarks.notes: Large brick house in interesting row of old brick houses on west side of Lake Road in Clarkson NY (when Clarkson was first called Murray). Built 1824 for Hon. John Bowman — lawyer, prominent in politics, represented Monroe County at 1822 State convention, member of NY Assembly 1823, NY State Senator 1824-1826, later county judge. The 'Some Old Houses of Monroe County' survey believed Lemuel Haskell (mason, came to Clarkson 1819) built this and the row of brick houses, with his younger brother. Property lineage: Bowman family (1824 to ~1875) → Clark Allen (~1875-1893, 18 years) → Fred H. Gordon (Fred Hooker Gordon Sr, HD3266 — his Whitehall Farms holdings in Clarkson; he was 'present owner' per the historical survey). The house comes with the Perry and Reid farms attached. Connection to the Hooker line: Fred Hooker Gordon Sr (Ida May Hooker's son) was the documented owner. Possible relevance to Whitehall Farms — same property or adjacent.

landmarks.name: Hooker Lent Building
landmarks.address: 503 Market Street, San Francisco CA (Cunard Building — also referenced as 'Hooker Lent Building' in 1916 SF Commercial Club records and Risdon Iron Works 4th Floor lease records)
landmarks.notes: Office building at 503 Market Street San Francisco housing the Hooker & Lent real estate firm. Variously referenced as the 'Cunard Building' (per Burlingame Country Club roster: 'HOOKER. ROBERT G.. Cunard Bldg.. 503 Market St.') and as the 'Hooker Lent Building' (Risdon Iron Works occupied the 4th Floor of the 'Hooker Lent Bldg' per period business records). Whether the firm OWNED the building (and renamed it after themselves) or merely occupied a major office in the Cunard Building is unclear — both names appear in period sources. The building was a center of SF real estate + industrial business in the early 20th century, with Hooker & Lent (real estate + insurance + rent collection) and Risdon Iron Works (industrial machinery) among its tenants. EARLIER FIRM ADDRESS: 14 Post Street, SF (period unspecified — the Hooker & Lent partnership's first office before moving to 503 Market). RESEARCH FLAG: Confirm whether the building was owned by the firm; investigate post-1932 building history; verify Cunard ↔ Hooker Lent name relationship.

landmarks.name: Chelmsford Estate
landmarks.notes: 10-acre estate in Greenwich CT, named after Thomas Hooker's English parish where he served as Anglican lecturer in the 1620s. Created in the early 1900s by Elon Huntington Hooker (H03434) for his wife Blanche Ferry Hooker (X02319) — herself a competent plantswoman. The Hooker family raised their four daughters at Chelmsford: Barbara (H04639), Adelaide (H04640), Helen (H04641), and Blanchette (HD3284 — who later became Mrs. John D. Rockefeller III). It was at Chelmsford in March 1933 that Helen first met Irish revolutionary Ernie O'Malley at a Sunday lunch (their 1935 marriage and Burrishoole Lodge years followed). It was also at Chelmsford that Helen and Richard Roelofs Jr. married Aug 15, 1956. Designed variously by Warren Manning (master plan, 1910), Charles Gillette (landscape architect 1910-1942), Bryant Fleming (1920-1925), and Phillip Watson (1998) — all earlier designers had worked in the offices of Frederick Law Olmsted. Features: swale, half-mile of shaded walking trails, perennial beds, root cellar, knot garden, 100-foot-long folly of rose-clad stone arches, dogwood grove, riverbank fern garden. Currently owned by Garden Conservancy Board Member Alease Fisher Tallman + her husband Paul. Selected for inclusion in the Smithsonian's Archives of American Gardens (2024+) for preservation of its early 20th-century landscape design. Garden Conservancy Open Day annually (typically June). Reference URL: https://www.gardenconservancy.org/garden-directory/open-days/chelmsford-84346906-f779-45a4-8b86-d27bb9564ee4

landmarks.name: Rockefeller Guest House
landmarks.notes: Modernist guest house at 242 East 52nd Street in Manhattan's Turtle Bay neighborhood, commissioned by Blanchette Ferry Hooker Rockefeller (HD3284) in 1948 from architect Philip Johnson — one of the first residential buildings in NYC to reflect the influence of the Modern movement. Construction completed 1950 on a 25-by-100-foot lot purchased June 1948 by the Empire Mortgage Company (Rockefeller family agent). The lot sat about halfway between Blanchette's One Beekman Place residence and MoMA, where Johnson was the unofficial architect for decades. Blanchette built the house as a standalone structure for displaying her growing modern art collection and entertaining friends — her mother-in-law Abby Aldrich Rockefeller had earlier built a similar private salon at 10 West 54th Street. The Rockefellers donated the house to MoMA in 1955; it was designated a NYC landmark in 2000. Modernist style; reference Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockefeller_Guest_House

landmarks.name: Lake Whitney
landmarks.address: Mill River dam, Whitney Avenue, Hamden CT
landmarks.primary_url_label: Eli Whitney Museum — Mill River, Lake Whitney and waterworks
landmarks.notes: 120-acre reservoir created 1860-1861 by Eli Whitney III (HD2082) by raising the Mill River dam significantly above the low dam his father had installed in 1798. The expansion served two purposes: replacing waterwheels with more efficient hydraulic turbines for the Whitney Armory, and creating the first public water supply for the city of New Haven (founding the New Haven Water Company). The Lake Whitney Dam is a Class C high-hazard structure, originally built with stone and concrete, and remains core infrastructure of the South Central Connecticut Regional Water Authority (SCCRWA) today. The reservoir's creation flooded upstream waterpower sites and prevented further industrial development on the Mill River, leaving the Whitney Armory as southern Hamden's only major industrial site for the rest of the 19th century. Adjacent to the Eli Whitney Museum and Workshop (INST108) which preserves the original 18th-century armory site. A 2.7-mile trail from the museum connects to East Rock Park.

Limestone-faced Regency Revival mansion built 1928-1929 for Walter Ewing Hope (X02362) and Florence Hazen Talcott Hope (TD0055), designed by Mott B. Schmidt. Their daughter Helen Talcott Hope (TD0056) made her debut here in 1930 and married David Edward Austen at Madison Avenue Presbyterian Church in 1938 with the reception following at the house. Older daughter Marian Talcott Hope (TD0105) married in the mansion in 1944. After Walter's death in 1948 Florence sold to banker and philanthropist Maurice Wertheim, who filled it with a notable modern French painting collection bequeathed at his wife's 1974 death to Harvard's Fogg Art Museum. Today the house is owned by Qatar's Permanent Mission to the United Nations. SOURCE: Daytonian in Manhattan, December 2015. HISTORICAL PARALLEL: Maurice Wertheim, who bought the mansion in 1948-49, was the brother-in-law of Henry Morgenthau Jr. (his first wife Alma's brother) — Morgenthau served as FDR's Treasury Secretary 1934-1945, exactly bracketing Hope's 1929-1931 Hoover-era tenure as Asst Treasury Secretary. The mansion thus changed hands between Treasury-connected families of opposing parties.

landmarks.name: Edward Dewey House
landmarks.address: Originally 120 State Street, then 128 State Street, then 144 State Street
landmarks.notes: Brick Queen Anne house designed in 1889 by Montpelier architect and mayor George Guernsey for Edward Dewey (TD0140), son of National Life Insurance Company founder Julius Yemans Dewey. Edward built it on the site of the family's earlier home; the old house was moved down the street to 144 State Street where it stood until demolition 1969. Edward's 1889 house was itself moved to 128 State Street in 1948 to make way for the Vermont State Office Building (Burlington architect William Freeman, Art Deco/Modernist). The office building's frieze between fourth and fifth floors bears Vermont's county names; the front doors carry a bas relief of Ceres, looking across the street at the Ceres statue atop the Vermont State House. Image source: Paul Carnahan, Vermont Historical Society, Digital Vermont collection.

landmarks.name: North-Evans Chateau
landmarks.notes: North-Evans Chateau, the Austin home of Ira Hobart Evans (TD0163) — Civil War Medal of Honor recipient, Texas House Speaker, and Austin civic and business leader. Now the location of the Austin Woman's Club. Designated an Austin Historic Landmark. Evans's home was the meeting place for the Texas State Historical Association during his life.

landmarks.name: Evans Industrial Building
landmarks.notes: Evans Industrial Building, constructed 1912 at Tillotson College (now Huston-Tillotson University, INST116) Austin TX. Built with a $10,000 donation from Ira Hobart Evans (TD0163), the Civil War Medal of Honor recipient and longtime college trustee — for the training of Black students in construction skills. Refurbished 1984. Designated a Texas Historical Site. Named for Evans.

landmarks.name: Porter Perrin Farm
landmarks.address: Intersection of Scott Hill Road and Airport Road (south end of Knapp Airport)
landmarks.notes: Porter Perrin Farm, built 1815 by Porter Perrin (T01395, the first male child born in Berlin VT). Located at the intersection of Scott Hill Road and Airport Road, on land that was part of his father Zachariah Perrin's 1300-acre East Road School District farmstead. Possibly the oldest original Berlin house with little modification still standing. Occupied by Perrin descendants until 1920, after which the property was purchased by the Dodge family. The farm is the subject of an 1874 dairy-farm diary kept by a descendant Porter Perrin (born November 1, 1858, twin brother of Elisha; great-great-grandson of Zachariah; son of Vermont state legislator Justus Newton Perrin) — transcribed and published by vermonthistoryexplorer.org. Diary documents 36 head of cattle (some Jerseys), 612 maple trees tapped in 1874, 20 cents/week paid to Porter for chores, and his father's October-November legislative service. Genealogical gap: the connecting two generations between Porter Perrin (T01395, 1790-1871) and the 1858 diary-Porter (including likely father Justus Newton Perrin) are not yet built in this database. Pilot103: The 1874 diarist is now identified as Porter Elisha Perrin (TD0204, 1858-1946), twin of Elisha Newton Perrin (TD0203), son of Justus Newton Perrin (TD0200) and Mary Wild Perrin (X02410). The connecting generation gap between Porter Perrin (T01395, 1790-1871) and the diarist is now closed: T01395 → TD0200 Justus Newton → TD0204 Porter Elisha.

landmarks.name: Zachariah Perrin Farmstead
landmarks.address: Southeast corner of East Road and Scott Hill Road
landmarks.notes: Zachariah Perrin Farmstead, established 1789 by Zachariah Perrin Esq. (X01832) after his ox-sled migration from Hebron CT. Located at the southeast corner of East Road and Scott Hill Road, Berlin, Washington County, Vermont. Original log cabin (built summer 1788) was a few hundred yards south of this intersection on the east side of East Road; its roof had collapsed under three to four feet of snow when the family arrived in March 1789. Zachariah subsequently built permanent farm buildings near the corner, and the house — although greatly altered — is still standing. The farmstead originally encompassed approximately 1300 acres in the East Road School District, much of which has continued to be owned by Perrin descendants into the modern era. Distinct from the Porter Perrin Farm (LM065) at Scott Hill Road and Airport Road, built 1815 by Zachariah's son on the same family land.

landmarks.name: E.A. Werner Home, Washington Street, Atlanta
landmarks.notes: Home of Edward Alphonso Werner Sr (I00425), pioneer Atlanta citizen and Georgia Railroad agent. Built 1870s on Washington Street near Mitchell. Werner arrived in Atlanta 1845; 'first man to record a legal paper on the books of the city.' He 'saw Atlanta build up from a little village.' Torn down 1912. Photo shows the home plus a group photo of Georgia Railroad Freight Depot employees including E.A. Werner (6th from left).
landmarks.primary_name: E.A. Werner Home, Washington Street, Atlanta

landmarks.name: Eliphalet Austin House
landmarks.architectural_style: Italianate (1860s remodel by grandson Louis B. Austin)
landmarks.notes: Brick residence built by Judge Eliphalet Austin Sr (X02782, founder of Austinburg Township) c.1811-1815. Heavily remodelled in Italianate style by his grandson Louis B. Austin during the 1860s — no extant US building is known to have used the Italianate style before 1844, dating the remodel features. Listed on the National Register of Historic Places February 24, 1975 (reference 75001313). One of three NRHP-listed properties in Austinburg Township along with the Congregational Church of Austinburg and the L.W. Peck House in Eagleville. Located at 1879 State Route 45.

Founded 1884 as the University YMCA at UC Berkeley. The original 1892 Romanesque Revival building stood on the bank of Strawberry Creek (where Haas Pavilion is today) and was donated by Ann Jane Waters Stiles (X02814) in memorial to her late husband Anson Gale Stiles (X02813) — the building took his name. Moved to a small Victorian where Lower Sproul Plaza now sits in 1932; moved to current Bancroft Way location in 1951; eventually separated its activities from the Y. For 140 years a steady force for racial justice and educational equity in California — hosted Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X in the 1950s-60s, principled stand against Japanese American internment in 1940s, fought 1930s housing discrimination in Berkeley. Anson Gale Stiles's grandson Anson Stiles Blake (HD4106) chaired the building's YMCA board for fifty years, named 'Grand old man of Stiles Hall' by the California State Legislature.

Sugar storage, refining, and museum complex on Toronto's waterfront. Opened 1958. The Toronto facility is the modern continuation of Canada Sugar Refining Company founded by John Redpath Sr. (X02825) in Montreal in 1854. Complex includes Building 1 (eight floors, refining), chimney stack, and Building 2 (five floors, museum). Sugar cane sourced from the Caribbean and Brazil and delivered via Saint Lawrence Seaway. Redpath Sugar Museum opened 1979; affiliated with Canadian Museums Association, Canadian Heritage Information Network, and Virtual Museum of Canada. North-facing wall of Raw Sugar Shed features a whale mural by artist Wyland. The red illuminated 'Redpath Sugar' sign was taken down 2006 when Tate & Lyle owned the company; Redpath is now owned by American Sugar Refining. In May 2019 Toronto's poet laureate Albert Moritz composed a new poem reusing four lines from a poem John Redpath had composed in 1858, to commemorate the 60th anniversary of the Toronto refinery opening. The poem stirred controversy and Redpath Sugar declined to have Moritz read it at the celebration ceremony because it touched on the sugar industry's early reliance on slave labour.

landmarks.secondary_name: The Lost Hamersley Mansion, No. 1030 Fifth Avenue
landmarks.notes: Fifth Avenue mansion of J. Hooker Hamersley (H03408). Site of Margaret Willing Chisolm Hamersley's death on January 5, 1904. Their son Louis Gordon Hamersley (H04621), the famous 'seven million dollar baby,' grew up here. Photo: https://res.cloudinary.com/dc5clrqtw/image/upload/v1779029502/hamersley_house_zgdo4o.jpg

landmarks.name: Hooker Homestead
landmarks.notes: Settled by Rev. Bunker Gay when he came to Hinsdale in 1763 to take the pulpit of the new Congregational church; sometimes called 'the Gay place' in early sources. The farm passed to his daughter Abigail when she married Seth Hooker in 1789, and from that point the property is documented as 'the Hooker place' in town records and the Gazetteer of Cheshire County. Four generations of Hookers lived there: Seth and Abigail; their son Henry (who died there at ninety-three); Henry's eleven children with Mary Daggett (six of whom left for California, Arizona, and Brooklyn). A child's side chair carried from the homestead to San Francisco by Charles Gay Hooker in 1851 returned east after his 1905 death and is now in the New Hampshire Historical Society collection (object 1960.062). The Hooker Cemetery (CEM454) sits on the property's edge.

landmarks.name: Worthington Hooker School
landmarks.address: 180 Canner Street (lower school, K-2) and 691 Whitney Avenue (middle school, 3-8)
landmarks.notes: Public elementary and middle school in the East Rock neighborhood of New Haven, Connecticut, part of the New Haven Public Schools district. Named after Dr. Worthington Hooker (1806-1867), Yale Professor of Theory and Practice of Medicine 1852-1867 and author of Physician and Patient (1849). The original 180 Canner Street building, erected 1900, now houses kindergarten through grade 2 and is a contributing property in the Whitney Avenue Historic District listed on the National Register of Historic Places. The middle school building for grades 3-8 was completed in 2009 at a cost of $36.5 million on Whitney Avenue after the Connecticut Supreme Court unanimously upheld the city's zoning authority against a neighborhood lawsuit (August 2007). Officially dedicated 21 December 2009. NCES School ID 090279000588; current principal Margaret Mary Gethings; enrollment 444 (2016-2017); school colors green and white; mascot Lion. Reports the highest achievement of New Haven's K-8 public schools. Hooker connections: named for H01407 Dr. Worthington Hooker himself, with H01407's two wives (X00159 Mary Ingersoll, X00160 Henrietta Edwards) and four children (HD3048 Worthington Jr., HD3049 Elizabeth Martin, HD04869 Edward I., HD04870 Edward Ingersoll) linked as the immediate family. Whitney Avenue Historic District (containing the 180 Canner Street building) was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1989. The school earned National Blue Ribbon School designation in 2015 for outstanding academic performance and STEM equity programs. The institution follows the Comer School Development Program for culturally responsive teaching — a program developed at the Yale Child Study Center, fittingly continuing Hooker's intellectual lineage at Yale.

5,205-acre New York State park along the western shore of the Hudson River. Established by 1909 NYS legislation principally organized by Dr. Edward Lasell Partridge (X00643, husband of HD2001 Gertrude Edwards Dwight Partridge, great-granddaughter of Pope Dwight). The 1910 Harriman bequest of 100,000 acres created adjoining Harriman State Park. Both parks placed under Palisades Interstate Park Commission on which Partridge served four 5-year terms 1913-1930. During his tenure Bear Mountain was extended by ~50,000 acres and Storm King Highway was constructed.

1,439-acre Hamden CT state park whose two miles of traprock mountaintop resemble the profile of a large sleeping man — with distinct 'head,' 'chin,' 'chest,' 'hip,' 'knee,' and 'feet' outcrops visible across central Connecticut. According to Native American legend (Quinnipiac), the Giant was formed when the spirit Hobbomock grew angry and stamped his foot, diverting the Connecticut River away from the Quinnipiac people; as punishment Keitan, a good spirit, cast a spell on Hobbomock sentencing him to eternal sleep underneath the traprock where he lies to this day. The mountain was once the site of a quarry whose continuous blasting threatened to alter the Giant's shape, which spurred the preservation movement. Acquisition for public use was begun by the Sleeping Giant Park Association — organized 1924 by Mount Carmel residents including the artist Bancel La Farge (X02844). La Farge served as the association's Vice President from its 1924 founding until 1934, then as President 1934-1938. The state acquired the property as a State Park in 1933. La Farge's 'Edgehill' home was at the foot of the Giant.

landmarks.name: La Paix
landmarks.address: York Road near Sheppard Station, Towson MD
landmarks.photo_notes: Sam-supplied photo of La Paix porch (group photo at Maryland Historical Society), Cloudinary hosted.
landmarks.notes:
La Paix was the summer home of Lawrence Turnbull, designed by architect John Appleton Wilson and built in 1885 on York Road near Sheppard Station in Towson MD. Inherited by his son Bayard Turnbull (I01138) who lived there with his wife Margaret Carroll Jones Turnbull (TD0242).

F. SCOTT + ZELDA FITZGERALD: 1932-1933 the Fitzgeralds rented a cottage on the La Paix estate, where Zelda was being treated at the nearby Sheppard Pratt Hospital for schizophrenia and F. Scott was working on 'Tender Is the Night.' Andrew Turnbull (TD0244, Bayard + Margaret's son, then age 11-12) befriended F. Scott Fitzgerald during their stay, beginning a relationship that would result in Andrew's 1962 definitive Fitzgerald biography and his 1956 New Yorker essays on Fitzgerald at La Paix.

GRAEME TURNBULL LECTURES: Margaret organized at La Paix the Graeme Turnbull lecture series (named for Bayard's brother who died young), bringing T.S. Eliot, W.H. Auden, Robert Frost, Archibald MacLeish, and Marianne Moore to the estate to lecture.

DEMOLITION: Razed in 1962 to make way for St. Joseph Hospital. The site is now part of the hospital campus.

Hooker-tree connections (this stage 2; will grow):
- I01138 Bayard Turnbull (inherited from father Lawrence)
- TD0242 Margaret Carroll Jones Turnbull (resident; lecture series organizer)
Future (Stage 6Y-205):
- TD0243 Frances Litchfield Turnbull Kidder (grew up here)
- TD0244 Andrew Winchester Turnbull (grew up here; befriended Fitzgerald age 11)
- TD0245 Eleanor Sterett Turnbull Pope (grew up here)

Dedicated October 31, 1930, Boxford MA. Lewis Kennedy Morse (I01204) — Boston attorney and Wellesley College treasurer — arranged to donate land adjacent to the new Aaron Wood School as a playground, but died March 8, 1930 before it was completed. His widow Ednah Rich Morse carried out his wishes, donating the land and arranging for a stone marker. Local volunteers Jim Rix, Raymond Perley and Leo Richardson gave their services. The land now forms part of Cole School grounds. Source: Boxford Historic Document Center, Martha Clark, Oct 17, 2015. HD4949 Anna Hooker Morse Haynes was Lewis's daughter.

landmarks.name: Jonathan Newton Harris House
landmarks.photo_notes: Italian Villa-style residence. Now New London United Methodist Church. Cloudinary. Superseded photo: https://res.cloudinary.com/dc5clrqtw/image/upload/v1779561952/harrishouse_y5dcjh.jpg
landmarks.nrhp: April 27, 1982 — Reference #82004375 (Criterion B: significant person; Criterion C: architecture)
landmarks.description: Italian Villa-style residence built 1860 for Jonathan Newton Harris, New London mayor and merchant. Designed by architect Leopold Eidlitz. National Register of Historic Places (1982). Later used as Williams Memorial Institute classrooms (1917) and now the New London United Methodist Church. Harris also built the Harris Building (1885) on State Street, a Romanesque Revival commercial block, also designed by Eidlitz. Both buildings associated with his philanthropic and commercial legacy.

landmarks.name: Pierrepont Manor
landmarks.notes: The hamlet of Pierrepont Manor in the Town of Ellisburg, Jefferson County NY was named for William Constable Pierrepont (HD1534), who came in 1822 from his father Hezekiah Beers Pierrepont's Brooklyn family to manage the family's Northern New York landholdings. The three-story 26-room frame Manor House was built in 1826 on 7.17 acres — an impressive structure with tall pillars in front and a beautiful colonial doorway with leaded glass transome and sidelights. In his day the house was heated with Franklin stoves, and one bedroom was known as the 'Bishop's room' for the Episcopal bishop who always slept there when in Pierrepont Manor. Across the street William Constable Pierrepont built Zion Episcopal Church in 1836, adjacent to a cemetery where he is buried under a huge flat slab of gray granite. The two-room Land Office on the property — where William stored cash in a vault — is now the public library. On Dec 1, 1899 Pierrepont's executors sold the manor to William M. McConnell; from him to son Ralph B. McConnell; then on April 18, 1935 to Guy E. Mendell, Albany insurance agent and wife (the present owners as of the photo article). In William Constable Pierrepont's day the manor house was peopled with 35 persons including servants. Population of the Pierrepont Manor hamlet at 2020 census: 212. ZIP code 13674. GNIS feature ID 960363.

Built c.1769 by Elijah Hooker (H00267); modernized in the mid-19th century by his grandson Henry Hooker (H01452), the carriage manufacturer, who died here in 1873 and for whom the house is named. NRHP-listed 1978. In Kensington, town of Berlin.

Brownstone obelisk on the grounds of Kensington Congregational Church, Berlin CT. Dedicated July 28 1863 after Rev. Elias Brewster Hillard learned of six Kensington war dead; designed by sculptor Nelson Augustus Moore; cut from Portland brownstone. The first Civil War monument in Connecticut and among the first in the United States; a period cannon was added at the 1913 semi-centennial. NRHP-listed 2013. Frank Allyn Cole (HD5647) is named on it; his father Ira (H01453) and brother Edward (HD5649) helped raise it.

landmarks.name: Magoun-Whitney House
landmarks.notes: Mid-18th-century house in East Medford, Massachusetts, on land once owned by shipbuilder Thatcher Magoun. In 1868 Jophanus H. Whitney and his father-in-law Ebenezer S. Flanders bought the Franklin Street lot from the Magoun heirs for $2,400; the house was later moved and is now addressed 7-9 Vine Street. Documented in the Medford Historical Commission survey (MDF.A, 2017/2021).

landmarks.name: Hugh White Homestead
landmarks.notes: Built in 1830 by Joshua Clark of Cohoes for Congressman Hugh White, of brick and timber prepared at Chittenango and shipped down the Erie Canal — a house of the Federal-to-Greek-Revival transition on Saratoga Avenue. Marked for demolition in 1964, it was bought by a group of Waterford residents and moved to its present site, becoming the Waterford Historical Museum and Cultural Center.

landmarks.name: 65 Marlborough Street
landmarks.notes: Built in 1876 by the masons I. & H. M. Harmon as the home and medical office of Dr. Francis Minot. His daughter Julia lived there and, after marrying the attorney Felix Rackemann in 1886, raised her young family in the house. Later residents included the shipping merchant and botanist Francis Blackwell Forbes and the attorney Philip Dexter, whose interiors were designed by Ogden Codman Jr.

landmarks.name: George R. Minot House
landmarks.notes: National Historic Landmark (designated 1976), a Colonial Revival brick house in Brookline. Home of Nobel laureate Dr. George R. Minot while he carried out his pernicious-anemia research.

location.notes: Built on Main Street, Springfield, between 1722 and 1733 by David Ingersoll. Bought in 1743 by Josiah Dwight, who added the Connecticut River Valley broken-scroll doorway, window pediments and gambrel roof in the 1750s. A rooming house by the later 1800s; moved to Howard Street in 1884 and to Historic Deerfield in 1950.

landmarks.notes: Built about 1754 on Main Street, Springfield, for Josiah Dwight; inherited by his son Thomas. Long the last colonial building in Springfield, it was moved to Historic Deerfield in 1950 by Henry and Helen Flynt; its scroll-pediment doorway is now at the Winterthur Museum. An earlier owner was George J. Seuss, grandfather of Dr. Seuss.

Colonial Revival estate house built in 1892 for Stephen Olney Metcalf by the Boston firm Andrews, Jaques & Rantoul. Metcalf bequeathed it to the Rhode Island School of Design, and it has served as the RISD President’s House since 1953.

landmarks.blurb: A Downing Gothic Revival cottage built 1858-59 of brick McKinley kilned himself, named for his first wife Patience Barrow; it served as a Federal headquarters during Sherman's March to the Sea.

landmarks.notes: Ten-acre Kensington estate of Anson Stiles Blake, grandson of UC trustee Anson Gale Stiles. Blake House (1924) served as the University of California presidential residence 1967-2008; the garden is now the UC Berkeley landscape-architecture teaching laboratory.
Built 1784 in the Kensington parish of Berlin; birthplace in 1795 of the poet and naturalist James Gates Percival, son of Dr. James Percival.
Brick house built 1824 by Frederick Wadsworth in Edinburg Township; listed on the National Register of Historic Places May 29, 1975.

landmarks.primary_name: Bayard Wootten Birthplace (NC Highway Marker C-70)
landmarks.notes: North Carolina state highway historical marker honoring photographer Bayard Wootten, at her birthplace on East Front Street, New Bern; cast 1992.
San Francisco Landmark No. 216. One of the oldest surviving Italianate houses in the city, built by city engineer Milo Hoadley near the western edge of his Hoadley Tract.
Home of Declaration signer William Floyd; now part of Fire Island National Seashore (National Park Service).

Where Washington bade farewell to his officers in 1783; acquired in 1904 for the Sons of the Revolution chiefly with funds willed by Frederick Samuel Tallmadge, whose memorial tablet is affixed to the building.
Brick firehouse built in 1871 on land donated to the village by William Curtis Noyes; later Citizens Hose Company No. 1, now owned by the Village of Castleton-on-Hudson.
Colonial house built by Gen. Elijah Wadsworth in 1799, later home of Treasury Secretary Oliver Wolcott Jr.; since 1966 the home of the Oliver Wolcott Library.

Built 1901 with funds from John Arent Vanderpoel to house Litchfield's free library and the Litchfield Historical Society, founded 1856; named for his grandmother Julia Tallmadge Noyes and enlarged 1906-07. The library moved to its own building in the 1960s and the Historical Society took the whole, enlarging it again in 1989-90.
Greystone country house built for financier John Bond Trevor; since 1924 part of the Hudson River Museum in Yonkers.
Neo-Federal townhouse Emily Trevor built on Carnegie Hill, a block from her brother John's mansion.
Restrained limestone townhouse on Carnegie Hill, diagonally opposite the Andrew Carnegie mansion.
Upper West Side rowhouse long home to the Fisher family, where the mountaineer grew up.
Four-story brick Troy townhouse of Judge John Paine Cushman, a founder of the city's private Washington Park.
The Big River redwood sawmill Williams helped establish in 1852-53; its site is now part of Mendocino Headlands State Park.
Monument to the Army of the Potomac's Artillery Reserve, commanded at Gettysburg by Brig. Gen. Robert Ogden Tyler.

50-room Georgian Revival estate in Villanova/Radnor, designed by Horace Trumbauer, completed 1912 for Col. Robert Leaming Montgomery. The Main Line social world it hosted inspired The Philadelphia Story.

landmarks.primary_name: George F. Tyler Mansion (Indian Council Rock)
landmarks.notes: Sixty-room brownstone country house ('Indian Council Rock'), designed by Charles Willing and built 1930-31 — the largest residence ever built in Bucks County. Added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1987; estate land now divided between Tyler State Park and Bucks County Community College (Tyler Hall).

42-acre Gilded Age estate built for William L. Elkins; Horace Trumbauer designed Elstowe Manor (1898) and Chelten House (1896, for son George W. Elkins). Later a Dominican retreat house; now an events venue.

Greek Revival house built 1852 for abolitionist trustee Jabez Burrell; bought by Henry Churchill King, who enlarged it as the Oberlin presidential residence. Now Oberlin Conservatory's Community Music School; NRHP-listed and a city landmark.
Miami University's main library, named for Edgar Weld King, its longest-serving director (1922-1956). Georgian-style building; south wing opened 1966, completed 1973.

Built soon after the Revolution by Gen. Selah Hart; never out of family possession as of 1900; his brigadier general’s commission signed by Gov. Trumbull hung on its wall (Connecticut Magazine, 1900).

Built 1740 for Deacon John Hart, across Main Street from First Congregational Church; preserved by Annie Burr Lewis (1947 American Scenic and Historic Preservation Society award) and deeded to Miss Porter’s School in 1954.

Federal-style house of Asahel Hart (1764-1821), tailor, son of Capt. Samuel Hart — identified by death year against the house history (Rev. Asahel Hart d. 1775 predates construction). Inherited by son Freedom Hart, who made combs from Berlin turtle shells (not in tree).

Home of Rev. John Rutgers Marshall, Sarah (Bryan) Marshall — a Hooker descendant — their nine children, and three enslaved people, 1771-1786. Site of the secret March 25, 1783 meeting that elected Samuel Seabury first American bishop. Restored 1923 under Henry Watson Kent of the Metropolitan Museum; opened as one of the nation’s earliest historic house museums, 1925. NRHP ref. 71000902, listed March 11, 1971; contributing property, Woodbury Historic District No. 1. Built 1746 per NRHP (museum says c. 1740 — variant noted). Georgian style, 2 acres. Landmark qualifies per compiler condition: the Marshall household was a Hooker-descendant household through Sarah Bryan Marshall (H-line via Bryan-Newton).

Built c. 1763 on what was then the Bream Cove waterfront (Cove Street, now Coit Street); the cove was later silted and filled. Home of the Revolutionary captain William Coit of the shipbuilding Coit family.

dates.status: NPS Network to Freedom, designated July 16, 2004; now part of the Academy at Charlemont campus

landmarks.notes: Safe house 1838-1844 for Basil and Louisa Dorsey and their children, Freedom Seekers from Liberty, Maryland. The 2004 marker notes the home was shared with Roger and Chloe Maxwell Leavitt, parents of Roger Hooker.

One of only two urban houses by H. H. Richardson still standing largely in original form (the other: Glessner House, Chicago). Brownstone facade with gargoyles, Gothic pinnacle bearing carved boars’ heads and the likenesses of Mr. and Mrs. Sard. Critiqued by Hitchcock (1936); reassessed by Sinclair.
Federal-style brick house, NHL 1965; now Middlebury College Admissions Office.

40-acre lake formed by the Cassin Lake Dam, built 1907 by William Cassin to irrigate his land. Now protected by conservation easement along the Howard W. Peak Greenway Trail; NRHP-eligible. Town of Cassin named for the family.

Federal-style residence built 1848 by Ainsworth Blunt; the second-oldest house and first two-story house in Dalton. Hosted Confederate Gen. Joseph E. Johnston 1863–64, then served as a Union field hospital. Family-occupied until 1978; NRHP-listed 1981; now a museum of the Whitfield-Murray Historical Society.

landmarks.name: Paul Revere House
landmarks.description: Built c.1680; home of Paul Revere 1770-1800. Saved from demolition in 1902 by his great-grandson John Phillips Reynolds Jr., restored, and opened in 1908 as one of the first historic house museums in America.

landmarks.name: 79 Marlborough Street
landmarks.description: Back Bay home of John Phillips Reynolds Jr. and Lucretia Munroe Reynolds from 1907 to 1922. Earlier occupants included author Richard Henry Dana Jr.
landmarks.notes: Bought 1 April 1907 from the trustees under John L. Gardner's will; the Reynoldses had lived at 279 Marlborough before. Transferred to Bessie F. Hanington in January 1908 for Lucretia's sole use. Both children lived here; the family also kept Wharf House at North Haven, Maine. Sold July 1922 to Paul Barron Watson.

landmarks.name: 89 Marlborough Street
landmarks.description: Home and medical office of neurologist Dr. William Norton Bullard and his wife Mary Robbins Reynolds from 1886/1900 until about 1928. Built ca.1867 for attorney William Everett.

landmarks.notes: Historic 1851 adobe in Monterey’s Old Town National Historic Landmark district. In the mid-20th century, architect Will Shaw and his wife Mary Morse Shaw added architectural flair to the building. Recognized under the Mills Act.
14.6-acre Chicago park in Portage Park, named c.1950 for Robert J. Dunham (1876-1948), first president of the Chicago Park District.
Pollinator-friendly native-plant garden at the Belvedere-Tiburon Library honoring artist and gardener I’lee Hooker (d. 2019), spearheaded by her husband Anthony Hooker.

landmarks.primary_name: Community Hospital of the Monterey Peninsula
landmarks.notes: Designed by Edward Durell Stone on Del Monte Forest land donated by S. F. B. Morse; Maurine Church Coburn shaped its healing-arts environment and endowed its programs.

The 100-inch Hooker Telescope at Mount Wilson, funded by John Daggett Hooker and built under George Ellery Hale, was the largest telescope in the world from 1917 to 1949. Edwin Hubble used it here to establish that the universe is expanding.

landmarks.primary_name: Tapping Reeve House and Litchfield Law School
landmarks.notes: Home of Tapping Reeve and site of the Litchfield Law School (1784–1833), the first law school in the United States.

Built 1884 in the Nook Farm district as a stylistic rival to the adjacent Mark Twain House; bought by Day in 1940 to protect the Stowe House, now the administrative center and library of the Harriet Beecher Stowe Center.

landmarks.primary_name: Dr. William Hooker Smith Historical Marker

landmarks.notes: The town of Porter, Maine — first called Portersfield Plantation, incorporated 1807 — took its name from its principal proprietor, Dr. Aaron Porter, father of Harriet Porter Beecher. The Old Porter Meetinghouse was begun in 1818 and not fully finished until 1824, serving both as the Freewill Baptist meetinghouse (its congregation, under Rev. Jeremiah Bullock, locally called the Bullockites) and as the town's meeting hall. A plain vernacular structure — single large chamber, gallery on three sides, original plaster with visible trowel marks, original box pews, replica pulpit — it survives as a rare intact early New England meetinghouse.

Standardbred breeding farm founded by Lamon V. Harkness in 1892, grown from 400 to 5,000 acres. Its 1897 'Big Barn' survives; part of the land became the Kentucky Horse Park. Still held by Harkness descendants.
Rev. Benjamin Woolsey's estate at Musketa Cove (now Glen Cove), Long Island, named 'Dosoris' — from dos uxoris, 'wife's dowry.' The Woolsey-Dwight family seat; the house was later demolished.
Greek Revival mansion (1833, Isaiah Rogers) built for Margaret Perkins Forbes by her China-trade sons; National Historic Landmark; museum since 1964.
The Rice family home on Back Bay; later owned by Gillette razor inventor William E. Nickerson.
America's oldest stone house (1639) and Connecticut's first state museum; Rev. John Hart's chair is on display there.
Built by David Hidden in 1838 for the widowed Mary Hooker Cornelius, who wrote her cookbook here before selling in 1852.

landmarks.primary_name: Green's Farms Church (West Parish of Fairfield)
landmarks.notes: Founded 1711 by the Bankside Farmers (incl. Francis Andrews, a co-founder of Hartford with Thomas Hooker). Edward William Hooker pastored here 1821-29; daughters Mary Lanman and Faith Huntington were born in the parsonage.
Queen Anne residence built 1880; his surviving New Britain home.

landmarks.primary_name: William H. & William S. Edwards House (Bellefleur)
landmarks.notes: Italianate residence built 1871; NRHP-listed 1990.
Harlem public school named for the abolitionist.
Built 1892, Pierce & Bickford, Richardsonian Romanesque; NRHP 1979; Tiffany Last Supper mosaic.
Federal-style residence built 1833–34; NRHP; the Park family's home for 64 years.
Florida botanical garden named for the naturalist.
landmarks.description: Forty-eight-acre Florida garden grown from the horticultural and orchid collections of naturalist Theodore L. Mead.

dates.notes: Sedgwick home from 1824; school founded c.1828; razed 1903

landmarks.notes: Lenox home of Charles and Elizabeth Sedgwick and the site of Elizabeth's School for Young Ladies — students included Jenny Jerome (Churchill's mother), Ellen Emerson, and Mary Fillmore — and a literary salon drawing Catharine Maria Sedgwick, Fanny Kemble, Emerson, and Henry Ward Beecher. Demolished 1903; Spring Lawn now stands on the site.
Prairie School house designed by Frank Lloyd Wright 1902-03 for Francis and Mary Little; part of the West Bluff Historic District, Peoria.

hooker_connections: Built and lived in by Deacon Edward Lucas Hart and his Hooker-descended wife Nancy Champion Hooker (H01623)
landmarks.notes: Built 1847 by Deacon Edward Lucas Hart, with a school-house on the premises. Acquired 1892 by Amasa A. Redfield, NYC lawyer; held by his son Robert Latimer Redfield, 1902-1925.

landmarks.primary_name: Janet Annenberg Hooker Hall of Geology, Gems, and Minerals

location.notes: National Museum of Natural History, Smithsonian Institution

hooker_connections: Endowed by Janet Annenberg Hooker; named for her married Hooker name. Houses the Hope Diamond and the Hooker Emerald and Yellow Diamonds.
landmarks.notes: Janet Annenberg Hooker gave $5 million of the $10 million cost; the Hope Diamond is on permanent display.
1803 brick house Solomon Cowles built for his son Gen. George Cowles as a wedding gift; Julius Deming Cowles later lived out his life here. NRHP-listed 1982.
Chicago's first steel-framed home; the 1894 Prairie Avenue mansion of William H. Reid and his wife Caroline Whittlesey. NRHP-listed.

Built 1845 as the District No. 2 (Palmer) Schoolhouse, the last survivor of five one-room schools in Boxford. Anna Hooker Morse Haynes, a former pupil, gave it to the town's children in 1931. The adjacent Lewis Morse playground is gone; the schoolhouse alone remains, on the National Register and under restoration by the Friends of the Little Red Schoolhouse.

Greek Revival/Federal farmhouse built by Pierpont Edwards Johnson, grandson of William Samuel Johnson. Sold 1844 to José DeRivera, believed one of Connecticut's first Puerto Rican immigrants, who anglicized his name to 'Revere.' Demolished after arson; the Jettie Tisdale School now stands on the site.
Built 1807; the oldest remaining home in Warren, Ohio. Moved from its original location and now operated as a museum.

Italianate brick plantation house built by John and Frances Louisa (Bristol) Murdoch on a ~1,100-acre cotton plantation worked by enslaved African Americans. After emancipation, Ben Coleman, formerly enslaved there, managed the plantation from 1864 into the 1920s and is buried on the property. Listed on the National Register; now a bed-and-breakfast bordered by the Canemount Wildlife Management Area.

Gothic Revival mansion built in 1871 for the railroad builder Henry Farnam and his wife Ann Sophia Whitman, designed by Russell Sturgis. Remodeled in Colonial Revival style in 1934 and given to Yale; since 1937 it has served as the official residence of the presidents of Yale University.

Summer estate built around 1900 by Dr. Gorham Bacon overlooking Mill Pond at Yarmouth Port on Cape Cod. It later became the locally famous Cummaquid Inn; the historic building was destroyed by fire in 2024.

Built about 1769 by Elijah Hooker in the Kensington section of Berlin, Connecticut, and much altered in the mid-19th century by his grandson Major Henry Hooker — a new bracketed roof with dormer gable, a new entry portico, and the old center chimney removed for a central hall rising three stories. Listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
