Guilford, CT.
McLean, VA (1870s). Sold to John F. Kennedy in 1955.
LaGrange, NY (1838). The Hart family homestead, held by the family for generations.
Rubicon Bay, Lake Tahoe. The Pennoyer family summer house, bought 1936.
Kensington, CT. Built by Matthew Hart Jr. on Glen Street; later the Sheldon Moore place.
Stamford, CT. John Adams Morgan's private island off the Connecticut coast.
Brooklyn, Connecticut. Colonel Daniel Putnam's farm.
Macalester College, Saint Paul, Minnesota
Grave and memorial of Revolutionary general Baron von Steuben, Oneida County, New York.
The first hotel in Palm Springs, built by Welwood Murray; bought by the White sisters in 1913-14.
1893 bungalow built of salvaged Palmdale Railroad ties; Cornelia White's home, now at the Village Green Heritage Center.
Grew from the Palm Springs Desert Museum; Cornelia White deeded land that seeded it.
Gothic Revival family memorial by Richard Upjohn at Green-Wood Cemetery, atop a man-made hillock.
Brooklyn Heights waterfront warehouses tied to the Pierrepont shipping and development interests.
East River distillery Pierrepont bought from Philip Livingston, producing the popular Anchor Gin.
The Pierrepont family mansion on Pierrepont Place, Brooklyn Heights.
The Lea and Anne Luquer house at 321 West 80th Street, Manhattan.

landmarks.primary_name: Seth Low Pierrepont State Park Reserve
St. Ann & the Holy Trinity Church

landmarks.notes: Funded by Henrietta Talcott (opened 1921) as a memorial to her husband James; a Gothic redesign by architect Wilfred E. Anthony that won a Fifth Avenue Association silver medal. Now the Swedish Seamen's Church (Church of Sweden).
The building Henrietta Talcott funded for the New York Bible Society; the Church of Sweden's Swedish Seamen's Church has occupied it since 1978.
Women's dormitory at Oberlin College (1887), funded by James Talcott's philanthropy.
Greenhouse in the Mount Holyoke College botanic garden, funded by James Talcott's philanthropy.
The Wall of Faces Memorial

A room on the second floor of the Loring Hall Annex at the American School of Classical Studies at Athens, named in memory of Lucy Talcott in February 2024, the gift of William T. (Rob) Loomis, President of the School's Trustees. Talcott was Secretary of the Agora Excavations 1931-1958.

Gallaudet University, Washington, D.C. Built 1858 by Amos Kendall as the Primary Department Building, school and dormitory for the elementary-age children; enlarged in 1862 and 1866, and later housed female college students once Gallaudet admitted women. Condemned as a fire risk and demolished in 1916, replaced by the present Fowler Hall on the same site. Named for Sophia Fowler Gallaudet. [080926] built_year (1858) removed from the record so the card row does not print two different years - the name already carries (1862) and the 1858 construction is stated above; the landmark subtitle is composed as 'City, ST (built_year)' by resolveLandmarks.

Artificial island in Biscayne Bay carrying a 110-foot obelisk to Flagler, with four allegorical figures at its base facing the cardinal directions. Commissioned in 1920 by Miami Beach co-founder Carl G. Fisher, seven years after Flagler's death; deeded to the City of Miami Beach in 1939. Sculptor H. P. Peterson. Long in disrepair from marine exposure, fire and vandalism. Also known as Flagler Memorial Island.
Private liberal arts college founded 1968 on the grounds of Flagler's Ponce de Leon Hotel (opened 1888, architects Carrere and Hastings), now a National Historic Landmark and the campus centerpiece.

Steam yacht built 1897 for E. C. Benedict, taken into the Navy as USS Oneida (SP-432) in the First World War. NOT the earlier Oneida: Jennie Louise Flagler died aboard an Oneida in 1889 and Grover Cleveland's secret 1893 cancer surgery was performed on one, both before this hull existed. Benedict owned several in succession and reused the name.
Founded 1895; the Fifth Avenue main branch designed by Carrere and Hastings.

The only house Alexander Hamilton ever owned, built 1802 to his own design with James McComb Jr. and named for his father's home in Scotland; he had two years in it before the duel. Elizabeth stayed until 1833. Moved twice — by St. Luke's Episcopal Church in 1889 to save it from the advancing street grid, then in 2008 to St. Nicholas Park, the southeast corner of Hamilton's original 32 acres. Reopened by the National Park Service on Constitution Day 2011 after a five-year restoration returned the piazzas and the front entrances. The only national memorial in the United States dedicated to Hamilton.
Two thousand square feet; the stable from the Wadsworth property at Hartford.

Genesee Valley homestead of 1788. NOTE: built by the GENESEO Wadsworths (James and William, of Durham, Connecticut), a different branch from Jeremiah's Hartford line though both descend from William Wadsworth the Hartford founder. Jeremiah's own Genesee link is the Treaty of Big Tree, 1797, where Washington sent him as Treaty Commissioner and which opened these lands. Attached on Sam's instruction; the house was not his.
Olmsted and Vaux's Greensward plan of 1858, substantially complete by 1876.

Brick Federal house built 1804 for Capt. John Hurlbut of the Neptune; Italianate cornice, portico, veranda and belvedere added by a later owner in the 1850s. Jane Robbins Dunham left it to the Wethersfield Historical Society and it is a museum.

350-ton New Haven merchant ship, the largest built in that port; first Connecticut vessel to circumnavigate, 1797-1800, under Capt. Daniel Greene with John Hurlbut as first mate. Attached to Ann alone — she has no brother in the tree; Sam asked for 'Ann and her brother' and the ship is her FATHER's.

Talbiya, Jerusalem. Built 1926 by Hanna Ibrahim Bisharat and named for the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid; leased to British RAF officers in the 1930s, taken in 1948 and vested under the Absentee Property Law, and occupied in the 1960s by Golda Meir.

Balboa Park, San Diego. Reinforced concrete, fire- and earthquake-proof, funded largely by Ellen Browning Scripps; designed by William Templeton Johnson with the entrance on the second floor above a grand staircase.

Lincoln Park, Chicago. Progressive school on the Dewey and Col. Francis Wayland Parker philosophy. NOTE: the school Clara Sturges Johnson founded in 1912 is the SAN DIEGO Francis Parker School, a separate institution sharing the same namesake; this record is the Chicago school Sam supplied.

No. 23 Gramercy Park South. Greek Revival, four storeys over a brownstone English basement, built 1847 for William Templeton Johnson on Samuel Ruggles's new square. Later home to the inventor Norman Wiard, to the suffragist Margaret E. Winchester (who hosted the 1870 meeting that formed the National Woman's Suffrage Association), and to Frederick Samuel Tallmadge, who willed it to the Sons of the Revolution as a museum.

Grove Street Cemetery. He had told his mother that when he died she should put a granite cross over his grave; Upjohn designed it, cut with the endless cord for eternity and carrying no inscription but his name and the date and place of his death.

World War I steamboat. Wooden-hulled twin-screw motor boat, 59 ft 8 in, built 1917 at Morris Heights, New York by the Gas Engine & Power Co. and Charles L. Seabury Co. to Theodore Partridge's own design; taken on free lease 25 September 1917, commissioned 18 October, served the Second Naval District, and returned to him 25 November 1918.

Hartford, Connecticut (1907). Built 1854 at Market and Morgan Streets because South Manchester had too few tenements and the Irish contract weavers preferred the city. Sold to the New York, New Haven & Hartford in 1907 and the work moved to Manchester in 1908; the building stood over a century and came down for the interstates.

Watch Hill, Rhode Island. The summer colony's golf and social club, where Florence Talcott Hope attended the fancy dress ball in a costume made of lobster shells; the Hopes summered at Ridgecrest on Ridge Road.

No. 3 Sutton Place, New York. Mott B. Schmidt combined Nos. 3 and 5 into one four-storey neo-Georgian house with a roof garden, completed 1922, modelled on the 1765 Samuel Powel House and the Benjamin Wister Morris House in Philadelphia and built with bricks salvaged from the buildings it replaced. Sold in 1952 to Arthur Amory Houghton Jr., who gave it to the United Nations Association in 1972; it has been the residence of the UN Secretary-General since 1973.

Hartford, Connecticut (1844). He had wanted to give the city a gallery of fine arts and was talked into something wider: the gallery shared the building with the Connecticut Historical Society, a natural history society and the forerunner of the Hartford Public Library. The oldest public art museum in the country.

Back Bay, Boston. The Tylers married in February 1880 and were living here at the 1880 census, probably their first house together, while he was Massachusetts general agent for the Connecticut Mutual. They had moved on to 120 Marlborough by the following winter season.
Street Hall, home of the Yale School of the Fine Arts, open to both sexes from its founding.
Systematic collecting at Yale began in 1802 with Silliman's appointment; the mineral cabinet he built drew O. C. Marsh, whose uncle George Peabody founded the museum.

24 Hillhouse Avenue, New Haven. Benjamin Silliman bought the corner house at Hillhouse and Trumbull in 1807 and owned the odd triangle next door, marsh left over where the Farmington Canal crossed. When the railroad bought the canal and asked to throw its fill on the lot, he sold it to the Danas; the bank was raised four feet and the house went up in 1848-49 to a Henry Austin design. National Historic Landmark 1965. The Dana family deeded it to Yale in January 1962.
13,061 feet on the eastern boundary of Yosemite, the second highest peak in the park; Dana Meadows and the Dana Glacier lie at its foot.

Built 1905 as a summer house on the site of the 1858 stone villa The Elms, whose Victorian features Winthrop had stripped out. Carrere & Hastings designed the replacement to a classical symmetrical order. He directed the grounds himself: massed shrubs, ornamental ponds, decorative outbuildings, tailored hedges and no flowers. Bought by the Bondys after his death in 1943 for the Windsor Mountain School; now owned by Boston University.

Built 1853, over two hundred and fifty feet, paddle-wheel driven, with marble, velvet and gold below decks. Left New York on 21 May 1853 and made England in eleven days, then St. Petersburg, Denmark, France, Malta and Constantinople. From 1854 she carried passengers and mail.
Worcester. Named for Levi Lincoln Jr., the son who governed Massachusetts nine years and was the city's first mayor. The family's Worcester tract is now the Lincoln Estate-Elm Park Historic District.
Francis George Butler was part owner of the McKee farm on Talcott Mountain at his death in 1899 and was interested in other enterprises on the mountain.

Roxbury, CT. Charles Watson Hodge left the town money at his death in 1936 to build a library and museum and to endow it. The stone building was completed in 1937 by Clayton B. Squire and named the Albert Lafayette Hodge Memorial Library and Museum for his father, and his will required a museum room for Hodge family and Roxbury artifacts. A north wing was added in 1967. In 1988 Mabel and Sandford Sturdevant Smith gave 3.45 acres on South Street in memory of Mabel's parents, and the Minor Memorial Library completed there in 1994 — named for her mother, a descendant of Captain John Minor who explored Roxbury in 1673 — replaced the Hodge building at three times its size.

Washington, CT. Opened in 1850 as the Gunnery in Frederick and Abigail Gunn's own house on the Washington green, a few doors from the Congregational church whose minister had driven him out of town for abolitionism three years earlier. Girls were admitted from the first year, and African American, Native American and international students after; the children of Harriet Beecher Stowe and Henry Ward Beecher were among the earliest pupils. Gunn's 1861 march to Milford with his students is dated by the American Camp Association as the beginning of organised camping in the United States. He was headmaster until his death in 1881, when the school passed to his son-in-law John Chapin Brinsmade. Renamed the Frederick Gunn School.

Given to the Rockford park board in October 1920 by Winthrop and Harriet Ingersoll in memory of their son Clayton, killed flying in France on 26 April 1918. The Daisy Field tract, 135.24 acres three miles west of the city, bought from the Plin Smith estate; the gift reimbursed the board and left enough for the landscaping, an eighteen-hole course laid out by the Chicago architect Thomas Bendelow, and the upkeep. Named at the time Lieut. Clayton C. Ingersoll Memorial Park, with a memorial arch planned over the entrance near the State road interurban crossing. It carries the name Ingersoll Centennial Park today.
Gathered 1637, the year after the founding of Springfield.

location.address: Corner of Fort and Main Streets

landmarks.notes: The first brick house in the Connecticut Valley, begun by John Pynchon on his return from England in 1657; in January 1659 he ordered fifty thousand bricks burned at Northampton and wanted them delivered by that December. Garrisoned as a fort during King Philip's War in 1675, when much of Springfield was burned, and known in that role as the Pynchon Fort. Stood at the corner of Fort and Main Streets, Springfield; known from an 1830s illustration. LM374, briefly recorded separately as "Pynchon Fort", was merged here 10 Aug 2026 on Sam's instruction — one building, two names. The street address never renders on the card.

Stanford University, built on the Stanfords' Palo Alto stock farm and still called the Farm. Opened 1891 — the year Orrin Leslie Elliott became its first registrar, Bolton Coit Brown its first art department head, and the year Herbert Charles Nash was its first librarian.

Founded by Ralph Radcliffe Whitehead, Bolton Coit Brown and Hervey White. Brown chose the site after three weeks walking the Catskills, bought the seven farms and laid out the paths, and was pushed out within two years.
13,538-ft peak in the Sierra Nevada named for him. He named a great deal of that country himself; this is the one that was named back.

Centred on Florence Griswold's boarding house. Henry Ward Ranger meant it as an American Barbizon; Childe Hassam's arrival in 1903 turned it Impressionist. From 1902 it held an annual summer exhibition in the town library — a first for an American art colony — and in 1921 the Lyme Art Gallery became the first gallery financed by a summer colony.

Built c.1732 by his father as the Captain Joseph Trumbull Store; used from 1775 to 1783 as the seat of Connecticut's Council of Safety. Called the Pentagon of the Revolution. Owned by the Sons of the American Revolution.

landmarks.name: Leavitt-Riedler Pumping Engine
landmarks.description: The 1894 Leavitt-Riedler pumping engine at the Chestnut Hill High Service Pumping Station, Boston — the only one of Erasmus Darwin Leavitt Jr.'s roughly eighty engines to survive. Idle since 1928; an ASME historic mechanical engineering landmark, now the Metropolitan Waterworks Museum.

landmarks.notes: McLean, VA (1919). The Auchincloss house on the Potomac Palisades, sold in 1961.
East Hampton, NY (1917). The Bouvier summer place on Further Lane; the name means 'place of peace'.
Newport, RI (1887). The Auchincloss farm above Narragansett Bay, and the setting for the 1953 Kennedy wedding reception.

Charlemont, MA. Built as a tavern by Consider Scott about 1818 of bricks made in the town, the town poor house 1824-29, then Roger Hooker and Keziah Leavitt's home from 1835. Underground Railroad safe house; now part of the Academy at Charlemont and on the NPS Network to Freedom.
Charlemont, MA. The second of the two Charlemont houses on the NPS National Underground Railroad Network to Freedom.
Greenfield, MA (1797). Designed by Asher Benjamin; now the Leavitt-Hovey House and long the Greenfield Public Library.
Yale University (1961). Eero Saarinen's rubble-masonry college, built with no right angles in the living areas, named for Yale's seventh president.
Yale University (1961). Saarinen's twin to Ezra Stiles, sharing a kitchen with it; two of its rooms had eleven walls apiece.
Greenfield, MA. Erected by his associates on the Boston newspapers.
Deerfield, MA. The Tennessee-marble shaft subscribed by his former pupils at Deerfield Academy, 1875.

Lenox, MA (1818). The white Carpenter Gothic church at 33 Church Street, consecrated 7 September 1818; the congregation moved to a new stone church in 1888 and the old building still stands, without its spire.
The Wall of Faces Memorial
Cambridge (Newtowne), MA

Hartford, Connecticut. The first publicly funded park in the United States, carried by a city vote in 1853 and laid out on the land bought the following year; renamed for Bushnell, who had pressed for it from the 1830s, after his death. The Soldiers and Sailors Memorial Arch stands at its edge.
Chester, New Hampshire, opened 1965 as White Pines College and renamed Chester College of New England in 2001; it closed in 2012.
Chapel Hill, North Carolina. Begun in 1798 and left a shell for years; Burgwyn was among those who subscribed between 1809 and 1811 to finish it, and it was completed in 1814.

New Bern, North Carolina. Craven Parish dates from 1715 and the first building from about 1750; the brick Gothic Revival church consecrated in 1824 burned in 1871 and was rebuilt inside its own surviving walls, consecrated again in 1875. A five-piece communion service given by George II in 1752 is still in use.

Ithiel Town's Gothic Revival church on the New Haven Green, consecrated 21 February 1816 and one of the earliest Gothic Revival churches in the country. Rebuilt internally 1906-1912 under Charles Otis Scoville, when steel columns in limestone surrounds replaced Town's wooden clusters and gilt plaster groins replaced Edwin Harwood's stencilled nave ceiling. Scoville held the parish 1892-1935.

Bronze tablet at Wigglesworth Hall, Harvard Yard, set in 1938. It records that the College was placed at Newtowne — now Cambridge — in consideration of the ministry of the Rev. Thomas Shepard, quoting Cotton Mather. Wigglesworth Hall, the freshman group on the Massachusetts Avenue side of the Yard behind Widener, was named in 1931 for the two Edward Wigglesworths, Hollis Professors of Divinity, who lived on the site for nearly seventy years.

Col. Mason Whiting Tyler was a co-founder and vice-president of the library board and left it a bequest whose income was to buy books; the board chose United States history and Americana, and much of it is still on the shelves.

Named for William Seymour Tyler, one of the original trustees of Smith College. A dormitory at Amherst carries his name as well. His granddaughter and namesake Amelia Whiting Tyler went from his house to Smith and became the college librarian.
Gardens, pools, lawns and arbors made by Prentice and Virginia Bloedel around their Bainbridge Island residence; open to the public. His ashes were scattered here.
Six hundred and five feet, built by Pentagram Corporation for the 1962 World’s Fair. Bagley Wright was its first president.
The Seattle Repertory Theatre’s 842-seat house, named for its founding president.
Two-storey Georgian Revival, 1908-1909, by Charles Adams Platt with Carl F. Gould as local associate; garden by Lord and Schryver. Passed to the two Merrill daughters.
Hearing research centre at the University of Washington School of Medicine, named for Virginia Merrill Bloedel; endowed with the proceeds of her husband's rare-book library, auctioned in 1996.
The Wagner estate garden at Lakewood, Washington; open to the public.
Founding board member from 1999, chairman from 2004; his memorial was held here.

location.address: Above the Hollywood sign, Griffith Park

landmarks.notes: Named for Don Lee. The Don Lee television transmitter stood on the summit; transmissions ceased in October 1951.

location.address: Lincoln Log Cabin State Historic Site

landmarks.notes: Don Lee's Cadillac showroom on Van Ness; KFRC broadcast from its top floor.
Willis Polk & Co., Beaux Arts. Showrooms and garage on the first floor, garages on the second, repair and body shop on the third, upholstery and top-making on the fourth.

landmarks.name: Sheridan Inn
landmarks.notes: National Historic Landmark, designated 1964; NRHP 1966. Buffalo Bill Cody operated the hotel 1894-96 and auditioned Wild West Show riders from its porch. Closed and condemned by 1967, when Neltje Doubleday Kings bought it and reopened the saloon, dining room and Ladies Parlor; she ran it eighteen years. Owned by the Sheridan Heritage Center from 1990.

landmarks.name: Barberrys
landmarks.notes: Nelson Doubleday estate at Mill Neck, designed c.1916 by Harrie T. Lindeberg with landscaping by the Olmsted Brothers. His father’s Effendi Hill stood nearby; the 1914 fire and the rebuilding on old foundations belong to that house, not this one.

landmarks.name: Effendi Hill
landmarks.notes: Designed c.1914 by Kirby, Petit & Green for Frank Nelson Doubleday on the site of a prior residence of 1904 — a Georgian Revival brick mansion in the Tidewater Virginia manner, loosely after Westover. His daughter lived at Pepperidge Point and his son at Barberrys, both in Mill Neck. Sold after his death in 1934 to the admiralty lawyer Cletus Keating, who renamed it Holly Hill; in 1950 the top two storeys of the main block were taken off, leaving a formal ranch house.

Built by Richard Rose Goetchius, builder and architect, for his wife Mary A. Bennett; originally at 11th Street and 2nd Avenue. Passed to their daughter Mary and her husband Guy Cummins McKinley, then to their daughter Mary and her husband Samuel Marshall Wellborn, then in 1955 to Samuel Marshall Wellborn Jr., who gave it to the Historic Columbus Foundation. Moved to lower Broadway and restored in 1969.

landmarks.primary_name: Shenandoah River “Andy” Guest Jr. State Park
landmarks.notes: Named in his honour in 1995, on the south fork of the Shenandoah in Warren County.
Roxbury’s town centre from 1630, named for him; NRHP 1973 and the nucleus of Roxbury Heritage State Park.

Sloop of war of 566 tons, built 1838-39 at the New York Navy Yard and named for Commodore Stephen Decatur. Twice with the African Squadron against the slave trade; landed men at Tuxpan and Tabasco in the Mexican war; fought at the Battle of Seattle in January 1856; evacuated Americans caught in William Walker’s Nicaragua expedition in 1857; fitted as a floating battery off San Francisco in 1863 and sold at Mare Island in 1865.
Built 1940 by the Willard Scudder Memorial Committee at St. Paul’s School as a replica of Shute Cottage, the pre-Revolutionary house he lived in; now a guest house for the school’s visitors.
Four-storey brownstone off Irving Place. Home of both Scudder families until the move to East 22nd Street in 1882; afterwards let as a boarding house and sold by the estate to W. S. Patten in 1895.
Stands on ground she gave.
In the town where he built and where the Omi Brotherhood still is.

John Jacob Astor built the white frame country seat on thirteen acres of the old Waldron farm above the East River, and left it to his grandson Charles Astor Bristed for life. Pulled down in 1869 as the city reached it.

location.address: West shore of Lake Mahkeenac (Stockbridge Bowl), off Route 183

landmarks.notes: The Pines, a farmhouse of Juliette Starr and Richard Perkins Dana, was sold to Charles Astor Bristed in 1864 and burned in 1885. The Colonial Revival house that replaced it was built for his son by the Pittsfield architect H. Neill Wilson, who also designed Shadowbrook next door. Still in family hands.

landmarks.name: Jacks Peak Park
landmarks.notes: 525-acre Monterey County park around Jacks Peak, 1,068 ft, the highest point on the Monterey Peninsula; holds one of only three remaining native stands of Monterey pine. The Bateses bought the first 55 acres and sold them to the Nature Conservancy, which sold to the county; the county added the rest from Del Monte Properties in 1971 and the park opened in January 1977.

landmarks.name: Robert Kelly House
landmarks.notes: Greek Revival brownstone built 1840, in the Prentice family for 85 years before Dr. J. Willard Travell bought it in June 1928. He took off the stoop, moved the entrance to basement level and turned it into a doctor's office; both his daughters practised there. Upper floors were cut into apartments in 1939. Senator Kennedy came here for treatment on 26 May 1955.

landmarks.name: Greenacre Park
landmarks.notes: 6,360 sq ft vest-pocket park, a 1971 gift of Abby Rockefeller Mauze to the Greenacre Foundation she created in 1968. Designed by Hideo Sasaki, former chair of landscape architecture at Harvard, with architect Harmon Goldstone; assembled from three lots that had held a store, a garage and part of a synagogue. A 25-ft waterfall, a trellis with heat lamps, honey locusts, azaleas; about 700 visitors a day. Studied in William H. Whyte's The Social Life of Small Urban Spaces (1980). Listed on the National Register of Historic Places 2018.

Founded 1877 as the Hartford School for Decorative Arts by five Hartford women — Harriet Beecher Stowe, Olivia Langdon Clemens, Elizabeth Colt, Mary Bushnell Cheney and Susan Warner. Housed for a time at the Wadsworth Atheneum, the nation's oldest public art museum, built by Daniel Wadsworth (HD1330). Merged with Hillyer College and the Hartt College of Music in 1957 to form the University of Hartford; now at 200 Bloomfield Avenue, West Hartford.

Built 1922 on College Hill for Elizabeth Hazard Sturges, opposite the John Brown House of 1788. Designed by William T. Aldrich — MIT and the Ecole des Beaux-Arts, son of Senator Nelson W. Aldrich and brother of Abby Aldrich Rockefeller — in a restrained Georgian/Adam Revival of warm brick with a flat roof and a lateral stair hall. Walled garden by Beatrix Farrand. Given to Brown University in 1947 in memory of Elizabeth's father Rowland Gibson Hazard; the official residence of Brown's president since 1949, Henry Wriston being the first to live there.

Built 1933 as the summer residence of Rush and Elizabeth Hazard Sturges on a 200-acre South County estate. Thomas Pym Cope of Philadelphia designed the rough stone manor in the Norman Romanesque manner; he was recruited through family ties, his sister Anne having married Elizabeth's brother Thomas Pierrepont Hazard, and the commission led on to his rebuilding of the Dunes Club after the 1938 hurricane. Formal gardens by Beatrix Farrand, a founding member and the only woman among the American Society of Landscape Architects in 1899. The Sturgeses retired here in 1942. A portion was sold in 1959 to the Sisters of the Cross and Passion, who opened the Prout School in 1966 and used the residence as offices; the house stood empty from 2012 until it was bought and restored in December 2020, reopening as the Shepherd's Run winery, inn and event venue on thirty-six acres.

Class IV rapid on the Salmon River below Forks of Salmon, California. Known as Screaming Left Turn until the early 1980s, when Peter Sturges — founder of the Otter Bar kayak school upstream — pitoned in the boulder entry, slid his heel under the footbrace of a Perception Mirage and tore his Achilles tendon. His paddling partner that day was Don Banducci, who owned Yakima, the company that made the footbrace. Technical granite entry, then a hidden vertical drop and hole against the river-right wall. Commercial rafters sometimes call it Cataract.

landmarks.primary_url_label: Santa Barbara Museum of Natural History
landmarks.notes: Founded 1916 by William Leon Dawson as the Museum of Comparative Oology, to hold his own egg collection, in two small buildings on his Mission Canyon property. Rowland Gibson Hazard joined the board in 1917 and died in January 1918; his sister Caroline Hazard took his seat and in 1922 gave family land for new buildings, which his widow Mary Pierrepont Bushnell Hazard paid for and which were dedicated to his memory. Dawson resigned in 1923 and the museum was renamed the Santa Barbara Museum of Natural History. Now over three and a half million specimens on seventeen acres of oak woodland along Mission Creek, with the Gladwin Planetarium.

Newbury, Massachusetts, settled 1635. The monument names the town's first settlers, Anthony Morse among them — a Marlborough shoemaker who came from Southampton on the James with his brother William, reached Boston 3 June 1635, and was admitted freeman 25 May 1636.
The cliff dwellings of southwest Colorado, which Ernest Ingersoll and the photographer William Henry Jackson were the first trained scientists to see and describe, on the Hayden survey of 1874.

The Explorers Club's first regular meeting place, in the Studio Building at 23 West 67th Street. The club moved to 544 Cathedral Parkway in 1928 and bought Stephen C. Clark's house at 46 East 70th Street (LM422) in 1965. Ingersoll used the 67th Street rooms; the Clarks are attached to this record at Sam's instruction (7 Sep 2026) though their tie is to the 70th Street house.
Episcopal parish at Brockton, Massachusetts. Rev. George Alexander Strong was its rector; in Lent 1897 he began holding services in Whitman that became All Saints' Mission under St. Paul's auspices.
University of California, San Jose. Edward Singleton Holden was its first director, 1888-1897.
United States Naval Academy, Maryland. Dedicated 1969; home of the mathematics department William Chauvenet founded.

Manchester, Vermont, established 1828 on the legacy of Joseph Burr - Vermont's first privately endowed academy, built 1831 in square-cut local limestone after a firing of bricks failed. Josiah Burton's 1853 bequest endowed a joint institution for girls, making the renamed Burr and Burton the first coeducational secondary school in Vermont.

location.address: 60 Park Avenue, White Plains, New York

landmarks.notes:
Built about 1721 by Samuel Horton, an early settler who held it until after 1730, when Samuel Purdy bought the house and 132 acres. Title moved back and forth between Samuel and his son Jacob before settling on Jacob about 1785 — two of Samuel's five sons had gone Loyalist and fled to Canada. Jacob held it until his death in 1822 and the family kept it until it was sold to Samuel Mott in 1869.
Washington's headquarters: source-documented 23 July to 16 September 1778; the city's own account gives 21 July. Historians also believe the house served as headquarters in the days around the Battle of White Plains, 23-28 October 1776, but that use is not documented.
By the 1960s the house was a multi-family dwelling and slated for demolition by the Urban Renewal Agency. The Battle of White Plains Monument Committee bought it in 1963 and repaired the beams and shingles; in 1973 it was moved from Spring Street to the top of Purdy Hill on Park Avenue, on part of the original 132-acre farm, and deeded to the City of White Plains. A further renovation about 1980 used professional craftsmen alongside local teenagers in an apprentice program.
Listed on the National Register of Historic Places 31 August 1979 (ref. 79001651). Now the headquarters of the White Plains Historical Society, which holds a Washington's Birthday event in February and a Battle of White Plains commemoration in October. The surrounding 1.37-acre Jacob Purdy Park was developed by the city to receive the house.

location.address: 585 and 587 Broadway, opposite the Metropolitan Hotel

landmarks.notes: Charles DeForest Fredricks contracted for 585 and 587 Broadway, opposite the Metropolitan Hotel, and opened for himself in 1855. From 1854 the painted sign called it a Photographic Temple of Art and it carried the name more than thirty years — for twenty of them the largest and most stylish photographic gallery in New York. Fire destroyed the Broadway studio in 1875 and he moved to 770 Broadway, the former George Phillips Parker mansion at Ninth Street, where his brother's firm Fredericks & O'Neil had been a tenant since 1876. He took the whole building in 1885 and had Jonathan B. Franklin raise it to four storeys with a mansard and a cast-iron storefront whose banner read 'Photographic Portrait & Art Gallery'. The block was cleared about 1902 for the Wanamaker Annex.

Founded out of a committee formed in 1966 by Peter and Norma Stanford with Frank Braynard, who was its first programme director. Occupies 18th- and 19th-century buildings and three piers across seven blocks of Lower Manhattan.
Bancroft's private collection, bought by the University of California in 1905 on the condition that it keep his name. Photographed at 1538 Valencia Street, San Francisco, about 1890.

Plot B, Magnolia Avenue East, in the Creed family ground. The inscription lists him as 1st Lieutenant and Surgeon of the 31st U.S. Colored Infantry 1864, first African American graduate of Yale, first to earn an M.D. from an Ivy League medical school, one of nine African American physicians to serve in the Union Army, physician at the Knight U.S. Army General Hospital, member of the Connecticut Medical Society and the Colored Freedmen's Aid Society, and an expert consultant on President Garfield's assassination.

Ashlar granite, built 1828 to a Sheldon & Merritt design under Charles Watson's supervision; centrepiece of a five-thousand-acre property above Lake Champlain. Later the residence of Winslow C. Watson.

Founded 1863 by Samuel Strong Clarke in a small frame building at 14 South Adams; a four-storey store in 1910, an eight-storey store dedicated in 1923. Closed 1951; the building became the Citizens Building and was demolished in 1980.

Built 1917 at 405 N Mayflower Road as 'Mayflower Place', designed by Frederick Wainwright Perkins — a wedding gift from John G. Shedd to his daughter Laura and Charles Hodgdon Schweppe. Ten bedrooms on five acres above Lake Michigan. Laura died there in 1937 and Charles in 1941; the house then stood empty for nearly fifty years and became Lake Forest folklore.

landmarks.name: Fisher Building
landmarks.notes: Downtown Chicago Loop, 343 South Dearborn Street.

landmarks.name: Nickerson House
landmarks.notes: North Side, Chicago; 40 East Erie Street.

landmarks.name: William Coit House
landmarks.notes: 92 Washington Street, at Coit Street; bell-cast gambrel roof. Waterfront on Bream Cove when built. Survived Arnold’s raid of 1781.

landmarks.name: Richmond Hill Inn
landmarks.notes: Victorian manor built for the Pearsons; a museum in the 1950s, moved by the Preservation Society of Asheville, later an inn. Burned 18-19 March 2009.

landmarks.name: The Sneed House
landmarks.notes: Grand Victorian bought by Harold Marvin and Cara Carleton Weber Sneed in 1913; the thirty-one live oaks were grown from acorns she gathered at Texas A&M. Now the Pin Oak Bed & Breakfast.

landmarks.name: Highlands Inn Renovation
landmarks.notes: Arts and Crafts inn opened 28 July 1917; sold to investors 1981. Will Shaw’s renovation took first place in the historical renovation category of the ASID Project Design Award in 1984 and an AIA Top Honor Award; completed May 1985.

landmarks.name: Cal Poly School of Architecture
landmarks.notes: Home of the College of Architecture and Environmental Design, whose building Will Shaw designed. Over 1,900 students across five departments; DesignIntelligence rated its undergraduate architecture programme first in the nation in 2014. About one American architect in twenty, and one Californian in five, trained here.

landmarks.name: St. Anne's Tolling Bell
landmarks.notes: Given to St. Anne's Church in 1865 by George Wells, president of the Farmers National Bank and the largest property owner about Annapolis. It hangs in the church tower.

landmarks.name: Clover Dairy Farm
landmarks.primary_url_label: Thorpe, North Haven in the Nineteenth Century
landmarks.notes: 225 acres in North Haven, once part of Rev. James Pierpont’s holdings. Passed to Lieut. Joseph Pierpont, then Giles Pierpont, then Capt. Giles Pierpont Jr., whose son Edwards Pierrepont was born there. Named Clover Dairy Farm by D. W. Patten.

landmarks.name: Faxon Park (1885)
landmarks.primary_url_label: North and South Rivers Watershed Association
landmarks.notes: Once the town's South Commons, sold into private hands in 1818 and bought in large part by Job Faxon. His son Henry H. Faxon gave 37 acres to the city in 1885; Henry M. Faxon added 20 more in 1935. Now holds a softball field, basketball and disc golf courses, a soccer field, a playground and a picnic pavilion. The land lies in the country of the Neponset band of the Massachusett.

landmarks.name: Headstone (1871)
landmarks.notes: Collinsville Cemetery. A bench at the grave is cut from one of the works’ ax grinding stones.

landmarks.name: Collins and Company Works
landmarks.notes: Axe and edge-tool works on the Farmington River, founded 1826.

landmarks.name: Roosevelt Birthplace
landmarks.notes: 28 East 20th Street. Bought by the Roosevelts in 1854, demolished 1916, rebuilt as a replica 1923.

landmarks.name: Bulloch Hall
landmarks.notes: Greek Revival mansion finished 1839 for Major James Stephens Bulloch; Mittie married Theodore Roosevelt Sr. in its dining room in 1853.

landmarks.name: Reid House (1894)
landmarks.notes: Prairie Avenue. Beers, Clay & Dutton, completed 1894; the only house on the street never converted from a single-family home.

landmarks.name: Mount Agassiz
landmarks.notes: A peak of the Palisades in the Sierra Nevada, named for him.

landmarks.name: C. Cowles & Co.
landmarks.notes: 83 Water Street at Chestnut. Founded 1838 as Conwell and Cowles; C. Cowles & Company since 1855.

landmarks.name: Burgoyne’s Cannon
landmarks.notes: A gun surrendered with Burgoyne’s army in 1777, now permanently in the park’s collection. Jabez Cowles marched with Capt. Ichabod Norton to Albany in January 1778 to bring the captured artillery back to Farmington. Col. Noadiah Hooker commanded a Connecticut regiment in the Saratoga campaign that took them.

landmarks.name: Gunston Hall Farm
landmarks.notes: Family-run thoroughbred farm on Russell Cave Road: boarding, breeding, foaling, lay-ups, sales preparation and bloodstock.

landmarks.name: Worthington Meeting House
landmarks.notes: Built 1774 for the Worthington Ecclesiastical Society from timbers of the 1738 meeting house; church to 1850, then town hall, school and Berlin’s first library.

landmarks.name: USS Charles F. Adams
landmarks.notes: Lead ship of the Charles F. Adams class of guided-missile destroyers, named for the 44th Secretary of the Navy.

landmarks.name: Weetamoe
landmarks.notes: Designed by Clinton Hoadley Crane, built in Tobin bronze by the Herreshoff yard and launched 10 May 1930 for a syndicate headed by Junius Spencer Morgan III. Beaten by Enterprise in the 1930 defender trials; scrapped 1937.

landmarks.name: JP Morgan birthplace
landmarks.notes: Joseph Morgan III's Hartford house, where his grandson John Pierpont Morgan was born 17 April 1837. Demolished; known from a photograph taken after it became a boarding house.

landmarks.name: Dey Mansion
landmarks.notes: Col. Theunis Dey’s house at Preakness, now Wayne, Passaic County, New Jersey. Washington’s military headquarters through part of 1780; Anthony Theunis Dey was born in it. Washington received Anthony Wayne, Nathanael Greene, Alexander Hamilton, Henry Knox and the Marquis de Lafayette in the room kept as his office.
Built 1848-49 by Henry Austin as an Italian villa; bought by Yale in 1923 and now Steinbach Hall.

landmarks.address: South-west flank of the Temple Mount
landmarks.notes: Springing stones of a staircase that led up to the Temple Mount; Robinson recognised them in 1838 and they have carried his name since.

J. Massey Rhind, dedicated 1899; twenty-eight feet of bronze and granite, four Saukiog braves at the lower basin, four Oneida maidens at the pedestal, a hart above. Given by John J. Corning for his father.

Bought from Stephen Wilkinson, a Revolutionary veteran, in 1814 and named by Benedict Brooks. A station on the Covington Connection under his son Hugh. Five generations of Brookses lived there; the dinner bell still hangs in the belfry over the garage.
Stone pyramid in Concord Cemetery, Ink, Arkansas.
Fort Parker Memorial Park, near the site of the 19 May 1836 raid.
Raised by the Knights of Pythias in 1892 over his grave, with a statue of his likeness.
Stephen Mason raised the edifice now in use during his pastorate of 1827-1832; his wife Phebe and daughter Laura were on the island with him.
Recreation centre founded about 1916 by Donald Russell Hooker and Edith Houghton Hooker.

Built 1885 as Nowood, the Lenox cottage of Robert Spencer. Bought in 1911 by Edwards and Emily Meredith Read Spencer, who doubled its size and renamed it Shipton Court. Sold in 1951 to Larry and Sophie Howitt, who renamed it Seven Hills and opened it as an inn for Tanglewood.

Twenty-nine-acre estate on the Syosset-Woodbury Road, designed by William Adams Delano for Chalmers Wood Jr. and his second wife, the decorator Ruby Ross Wood. House and outbuildings were levelled in the early 1990s and the land became the Pironi Estates development.

Built in 1782 at 396 Main Street for Dr. Daniel Butler, who kept his consulting room in it. The only eighteenth-century house left on Hartford's Main Street. Jacob Weidenmann laid out the garden in 1865. Four generations lived in it for 189 years; listed on the National Register in 1971 and run as a museum by Connecticut Landmarks.
Gleaves-class destroyer, the second navy ship named for Cdr. Roderick Sheldon McCook.
Destroyer No. 25, laid down at Newport News in 1909 and commissioned in 1910, the first of two navy ships named for Cdr. Edward A. Terry.

landmarks.photo_notes: The dome in the garden at 7 Cavendish Avenue
landmarks.notes: Paul McCartney asked Robert Fraser for a folly; Fraser put him on to an English architect, and the result was the glass geodesic dome McCartney called his meditation platform. Digby Bridges names it as his first break in the business. The Beatles' Mad Day Out photo session of 28 July 1968 ended inside it, with Martha the sheepdog. No build date is recorded; the dome was standing by 28 July 1968. RENDER NOTE: the card's landmark subtitle is built from the registry location and nothing else, so the descriptive place sits in location.city on purpose.

landmarks.photo_notes: The Kimball Tobacco Factory on Court Street, Rochester
Interior looking southeast, St. Mary's Episcopal Church, 4502 Cassin Drive, Anchorage (HABS AK-2-ANCH-19)
The John R. Stuyvesant stable, 231 East 9th Street, Manhattan
landmarks.notes: Two-story brick stable at 231 East 9th Street, standing by the 1850s.
Stuyvesant family chapel from about 1660; the present church, sold to the Episcopal Church by Peter Stuyvesant in 1793 for one dollar, consecrated 1799. The Stuyvesant vault lies within its walls.
Georgian mansion near what became 8th Street, between First and Second Avenues; pulled down after Nicholas William Stuyvesant's death in 1833.

A marble block topped by a slender five-and-a-half-foot stone, beside his father's marker at Farmington; inscribed with Robert's words, 'I shall go into battle trusting in God that he will do by me what is best for us.'
Eliza Chappell Elementary School, 2135 West Foster Avenue, Chicago, named 20 October 1937 for Eliza Emily Chappell Porter, who opened Chicago's first public school in 1833.

The Maurice Porter Memorial Hospital, an eight-bed cottage at Halsted Street and Belden Avenue opened by Julia Foster Porter in May 1882; renamed Children's Memorial Hospital in 1904, now Ann & Robert H. Lurie Children's Hospital of Chicago.
Sierra Nevada Range, CA

Dwight's Rural High School, opened 1858 by Rev. Benjamin Woodbridge Dwight as a boarding school: four structures joined into one, with verandas, towers and balconies on the north, east and south, facing Elm Street. Leased 1863; burned 1865.
Built in 1935 with its sister house, King, and named for Laura Woolsey Lord Scales of the class of 1901, Smith's first dean of students, who held the post for twenty-two years.

Private oceanfront club at Manalapan, south of Palm Beach, founded by Spelman Prentice with developer Robert Bissett; architect Byron F. Simonson. Sold 1972; original buildings razed in the mid-1980s; the club reopened inside The Ritz-Carlton Palm Beach in 1991.
Home of Isaac Ingalls Stevens, first governor of Washington Territory, and his family in Olympia; the site on the Capitol Grounds now holds the World War II monument.
DD-146, launched by William Cramp & Sons, Philadelphia, 4 July 1918; sponsored by Mrs. R. M. Elliot; named for Lt. Cmdr. Richard McCall Elliot Jr.

Paper mill, Unionville, CT. Bought by Samuel Quincy Porter and William Platner (Stone & Carrington mill) 1848; Platner & Porter Manufacturing Co. from 1860; fine writing and book papers; sold late 1870s, later part of American Writing Paper Co.; torn down 1933. Union School stands on the site.
Built 1871 for Franklin Chamberlin and Mary Weld Porter Chamberlin on former Nook Farm land; sold 1873 to Harriet Beecher Stowe and Calvin Stowe, her home until her death in 1896.

Museum in Norwalk, CT. Second Empire country house built 1864-68 at "Elm Park" for the railroad and banking magnate LeGrand Lockwood (a distant cousin of the Norwalk Lockwoods), designed by Detlef Lienau, interiors by Herter Brothers and Leon Marcotte. Lost to foreclosure 1874; bought 1876 by Charles Drelincourt Mathews; Norwalk bought it 1941; saved from demolition, restored by the Junior League, National Historic Landmark 1971. Its 2026 America 250 exhibition features Capt. Eliphalet Lockwood.

landmarks.description: 105 N Broad, Youngstown. Irving and Rebecca Sanzenbacher Callahan bought the house from the Newton estate and the property became known as the Callahan farm; Callahan Rd., Neff Dr. and S. Hillside were later laid out on the land.

Brownstone town house of 1883 from the office of H. H. Richardson, one of only two of his urban houses standing largely as built; carved likenesses of Mr. and Mrs. Sard on the entry pinnacle.
Los Angeles club of bibliophiles founded in 1928 and named for Agustín Vicente Zamorano, the first printer in California; publisher of The Zamorano 80 (1945).
Second Empire mansion at 40 Fifth Avenue, home of the Henry Rutgers Remsen family from 1871; leased by George Coppell from 1895 until his death there in 1901; demolished 1928.

landmarks.notes: Mordecai House, Raleigh, NC: the Henry Lane house of about 1785, enlarged in 1825-26 by William Nichols for Moses Mordecai's widow; bought by the city in 1967 and opened as Mordecai Historic Park in 1972.

open_research_threads.thread: Why did Milford congregation accept Roger Newton Sr. — an outsider from Hartford network — as Prudden's successor?
open_research_threads.notes: Milford was founded by Prudden's tight Hertfordshire company (Platt, Fowler, Tapp, Buckingham, Welch). Roger Newton Sr. was a Hartford/Farmington man — Hooker's student and son-in-law, not from the Milford founding cohort. Yet he was ordained second pastor Aug 22, 1660, four years after Prudden's death (1656). Newton had joined the Milford church July 29, 1660 — only a month before ordination, suggesting a quick installation. Possible explanations: Newton had been in Milford in some capacity during the 1656-1660 interregnum; the Hooker reputation carried decisive weight; factional dynamics within the Milford church after Prudden's death; or Newton had family/social ties to Milford families not yet traced. The Milford families were also more relaxed about church membership than New Haven — Prudden's founding design was deliberately more inclusive than Davenport's.
open_research_threads.action: Check Milford church records 1656-1660 for Newton's presence; look for any pre-ordination connection to Milford founding families

open_research_threads.thread: Confirm whether Prudden line in I00084 connects back to Rev. Peter Prudden as first minister of Milford
open_research_threads.resolution: Confirmed via Families of Early Milford. Chain: Rev. Peter Prudden (X00104) → Samuel Prudden (X00103, bpt Feb 18, 1643/4) → John Prudden (X00101, b. Mar 20, 1680) → John Prudden (I00084, bpt Jun 10, 1711) → married Hannah Newton (H00153), great-great-granddaughter of Thomas Hooker. Also: Benjamin Fenn's son James Fenn married Joanna Prudden (Samuel's daughter).

open_research_threads.thread: Mary Newton Johnson — birth listed as St Martin in the Fields, Westminster, England 1740
open_research_threads.notes: Mary, daughter of H00059 John Newton Jr. and Martha Smith, has an online birth record giving "St Martin in the Fields, Westminster, Middlesex, England" and "May 11, 1740." Her parents are documented Connecticut residents throughout this period. This is almost certainly a data error — possibly a transcription confusing another Mary Newton, or a record from an English Newton family. Ignore unless corroborating evidence found.
open_research_threads.action: Disregard unless confirmed by primary source. Treat as transcription error.

open_research_threads.thread: President William Howard Taft connection through Edmund Rawson (H00078)
open_research_threads.notes: H00078 Dea. Edmund Rawson is documented as an ancestor of President William Howard Taft (27th President, 1909-1913). The connection runs through the Rawson line in Uxbridge, Massachusetts. Likely through Edmund's son Edmund Jr. (H00201) — need to trace the path to the Taft family. Alfons Taft (father of William Howard Taft) was from Vermont; his mother was Sylvia Howard. The Howard/Hayward name on Edmund Rawson's wife Elizabeth Hayward is suggestive. UPDATE: Aaron Taft (b.1722 Mendon) married Rhoda Rawson — likely H00215 daughter of H00080 John Rawson. Their son Peter Rawson Taft (b.1784) → Alphonso Taft → President William Howard Taft. The "Rawson" middle name on Peter Rawson Taft is the marker. Confirm via Taft family genealogy: Aaron Taft's wife's parentage.
open_research_threads.action: Trace Taft genealogy backward from William Howard Taft to confirm Rawson connection and identify which child of H00078 is the common ancestor
open_research_threads.resolution: CONFIRMED via Vital Records of Uxbridge MA. Aaron Taft Jr. (b. May 28, 1743, s. of Peter and Elisabeth) married Rhoda Rawson (b. Oct 4, 1749, d. of Abner and Mary) June 1, 1769. Rhoda is daughter of H00202 Abner Rawson (s. of H00078 Edmund Rawson). Their son Peter Rawson Taft (b. Apr 14, 1785) → Alphonso Taft → President William Howard Taft. H00215 Rhoda Rawson (d. of John Rawson H00080) was NOT the Taft wife — corrected.

compiler.talcott_line_note: John Talcott (T00001) is the second primary ancestor of the compiler, through the maternal line. The Talcott tree is toggled separately from the Hooker tree in the visualization. Intersection entries (people who descend from both Thomas Hooker and John Talcott) get H prefix and family_lines: ['hooker','talcott'].

notable_stories.title: Rev. Roger Newton harbored regicide fugitives Goffe and Whalley in his Milford home
notable_stories.summary: Roger Newton sheltered the English regicides William Goffe and Edward Whalley — men who had signed the death warrant of King Charles I — when they were hunted fugitives in New England. Gov. William Leete did the same in Guilford. The I00003 entry has the full anecdote keyed "jonah_story".

notable_stories.title: Two men in our tree both connected to the Phantom Ship — the lost New Haven vessel of 1647
notable_stories.summary: Thomas Gregson (father of X00084 Phebe Gregson Whiting) died aboard the New Haven vessel that vanished at sea in 1647. Richard Miles helped build that same ship. Both men are now in our tree through separate lineages — Gregson through the Whiting-Ingersoll chain, Miles through the Newton-Miles chain. The ghostly apparition of the ship reportedly appeared over New Haven harbor months after its disappearance.

notable_stories.title: "Newton as steel inflexible from right / In Faith in Law in Equity in Fight"
notable_stories.summary: The gravestone epitaph of Col. Roger Newton at Milford Cemetery includes a verse rarely matched in colonial New England. He commanded CT troops at the Siege of Louisbourg and was Chief Judge for 34 years. Full text in H00044 anecdotes.

notable_stories.title: The Connecticut Stamp Master forced to shout "Liberty and Property" three times by 500 horsemen
notable_stories.summary: Jared Ingersoll Sr., appointed Connecticut Stamp Master in 1765, was intercepted on the road to Hartford by 500 men on horseback with three trumpeters. They took him to Wethersfield and compelled his resignation. He then had to shout "Liberty and Property" three times and throw his hat in the air. His son Jared Jr. went on to sign the U.S. Constitution.

notable_stories.title: A Natick sachem plotted to kill Governors Haynes, Hopkins, and William Whiting — foiled by a friendly Indian
notable_stories.summary: In 1646, Sequasson, Sachem of the Naticks, organized a plot to assassinate Major William Whiting and Governors Haynes and Hopkins, apparently in revenge for their protection of Uncas. A friendly Indian disclosed the plot. Whiting died the following year, the same year as Thomas Hooker. Full anecdote in X00085.

notable_stories.title: Rev. Jonathan Ingersoll freed his enslaved man Cyphax one year before his own death
notable_stories.summary: In 1777, Rev. Jonathan Ingersoll petitioned the Ridgefield selectmen to free Cyphax, his 20-year-old enslaved man — one of the few documented manumissions in 18th-century Ridgefield. Ingersoll died the following year. Full anecdote in HD0115.

notable_stories.title: French and Indian War chaplain wrote that God showed "distinguishing mercy" to CT troops at the Fort Ticonderoga slaughter
notable_stories.summary: Rev. Jonathan Ingersoll served as chaplain at Abercromby's catastrophic 1758 assault on Fort Carillon (Ticonderoga). British regulars were mowed down; the CT companies escaped with few deaths. Ingersoll wrote to a colleague about God's "distinguishing mercy." Full anecdote in HD0115.

notable_stories.title: "Thus we have to this day our dead Hooker, yet living in his worthy son Samuel Hooker"
notable_stories.summary: Cotton Mather wrote in Magnalia Christi Americana that Rev. Samuel Hooker carried his father's legacy as minister at Farmington for 36 years — "measured against his father for his entire ministry." Full anecdote in H00007.

notable_stories.title: The 1658 wedding of Rev. Samuel Hooker concluded with "Samuel and Mary did then brew a great bowl of punch"
notable_stories.summary: One of the few personal moments recorded from Samuel Hooker's otherwise public-facing life — a wedding celebration detail preserved in the Willet family tradition for generations. Full anecdote in H00007.

notable_stories.title: Rev. Samuel Shepard and wife Dorothy died 55 days apart in 1668, leaving an 8-month-old infant
notable_stories.summary: Dorothy died February 12, 1668; Samuel died April 7 — almost certainly an epidemic moving through Rowley. Father's will written three days before his death. Infant son Samuel left to Flint grandparents. Full anecdote in H00008.

notable_stories.title: Alice Newton's bequest funded a Yale ministry position decades after her death
notable_stories.summary: Alice Newton left a bequest that funded a ministry position at Yale years later — one of the more remarkable long-term philanthropic threads in the Newton family. See H00018 yale_bequest field.

notable_stories.title: Jonah Newton and wife Phebe Platt died three days apart in April 1756
notable_stories.summary: Jonah Newton died April 29, 1756; his wife Phebe Platt died April 26 — three days earlier. Their son Jonah Jr. was about 11. EH records both dates without comment. Full anecdote in H00132.

notable_stories.title: Mary Standley had been betrothed to Roger Hooker — who died. She married his brother Nathaniel instead, seven months later
notable_stories.summary: Mary Standley was betrothed to Roger Hooker, who died April 29, 1698. Seven months later, December 28, she married his brother Nathaniel. Full anecdote in H00033.

notable_stories.title: The Hooker Elm of Farmington — John Hooker's famous tree, destroyed but once a landmark
notable_stories.summary: John Hooker and the elm tree associated with him on Main Street Farmington. See LM001 in the landmarks array and H00030 anecdotes.
notable_stories.one_line: Three Hooker generations gathered under it. The next owner cut it down to straighten a path.

sections.header: The elm his father gave him
sections.body: When John Hooker married in the 1680s, his father Rev. Samuel Hooker gave him a site on the west side of Farmington's main street, north of the Meeting House. He built his house under the branches of a great elm — and the tree became famous through all the region for the hospitality and company that gathered beneath it on summer evenings, while the long pipes of the town's sages sent up fragrant smoke.

sections.header: Three generations of Hookers and their elm
sections.body: The estate passed to Roger Hooker — "a thorough gentleman of the old school" — who kept the hospitality and the elm. Then to another Roger, described as "a polished gentleman, a patriotic soldier, a delightful conversationalist, and a brilliant wit." Major Roger Hooker was the last Hooker occupant of the place, dying without issue in 1830.

sections.header: The axe
sections.body: When the property passed into other hands, a remarkable thing happened. The new owners decided the famous Hooker Elm interfered with making a straight path from the front door to the street. EH, writing in 1909, could barely contain his contempt: "as if to obliterate all memories and lingering Hooker associations... an axe was laid at the roots and the famous 'Hooker Elm'... was laid low in the dust. Peace to its ashes."

notable_stories.title: Two men in the Newton-Leete circle sheltered regicide fugitives Goffe and Whalley — Roger Newton in Milford, Gov. Leete in Guilford
notable_stories.summary: William Goffe and Edward Whalley (who signed King Charles I's death warrant) were hunted across New England. Roger Newton, Gov. William Leete, and Roger Hooker all sheltered them at different times. The network of protection spans our tree's key families.
notable_stories.research_notes: H00032 Roger Hooker (b.1668, d.1698) is listed in person_ids but was too young to personally shelter the regicides (died 1675-1679). Possibly should be H00007 (his father Rev. Samuel Hooker of Farmington) who was active during this period. Verify before publishing.

notable_stories.title: From Hartford founder Major William Whiting (1605–1647) to Constitution signer Jared Ingersoll Jr. (1749–1822) — five generations in our tree
notable_stories.summary: X00085 Major William Whiting → X00083 Rev. John Whiting → X00081 Col. Joseph Whiting → I00078 Hannah Whiting → H00146 Jared Ingersoll Sr. → HD0120 Jared Ingersoll Jr. (signer). Both the Hartford founding and the Constitutional founding are threaded through the same family chain.

notable_stories.title: Burwell Newton was born without a roof to his mouth — and spelled his principal crop "ri"
notable_stories.summary: Burwell Newton had a cleft palate from birth. When schoolchildren laughed at his speech, he refused to attend. He taught himself to read and write, kept careful accounts, but spelled phonetically. His account book from 1762 was preserved and published. His impediment also made Revolutionary War service dangerous — he risked being shot for failing to give the countersign intelligibly. Full anecdote in H00149.

notable_stories.title: Capt. Isaac Newton was at West Point when Benedict Arnold fled — and saw Washington aboard the Vulture
notable_stories.summary: Capt. Isaac Newton was present at Fort Edward when Burgoyne surrendered, at West Point when Benedict Arnold's treachery was discovered, and on board the Vulture where he saw General Washington. He received his Captain's commission July 1, 1781, the same day he took command of 113 men at West Point. Full anecdote in HD0154.

notable_stories.title: A hill near the Newton homestead was named after an enslaved woman — her name survived; her master's did not
notable_stories.summary: The schoolhouse hill near the Durham Newton home was called Phillida — named, by tradition, after a slave woman purchased to care for an invalid master, who sold the land for the money that bought her. The slave's name survived through the centuries on the landscape; the master's name was forgotten entirely. The story appears in the context of Rev. Roger Newton's early education at that schoolhouse. Full anecdote in H00151.

notable_stories.title: Alice Newton's dying wish for a minister in the family was fulfilled — 50 years later, by a great-grandnephew she never met
notable_stories.summary: Alice Newton, youngest daughter of Rev. Roger Newton, died childless after 1740 and left a conditional Yale bequest hoping her little grand-nephew Roger would become a minister like his great-great-grandfather. Roger Newton graduated Yale 1758, was ordained at Greenfield 1761, and served 55 years. Full anecdote in H00151.

notable_stories.title: The Prudden, Willett, and Hooker families formed a triangle: Prudden's widow married Willett, whose daughter married Hooker
notable_stories.summary: Rev. Peter Prudden was the first minister of Milford. After his death, his widow Joanna Prudden married Thomas Willett (first Mayor of New York) on September 20, 1671. Willett's daughter Mary Willet married Rev. Samuel Hooker in 1658 — before the Prudden-Willett marriage. When Hannah Newton Prudden married John Prudden, she entered a family directly connected to both the founding minister of Milford and the first Mayor of New York, and thus back to the Hooker tree through H00007's wife.

notable_stories.title: "All gracious Heaven is this the end of man / A dreadful thought / A melancholy plan" — gravestone of Capt. John Fowler, age 39
notable_stories.summary: Capt. John Fowler, son of Ensign John and Mary (Newton) Fowler, died August 17, 1787 at 39. His gravestone in Milford Cemetery carries this verse. He was a Revolutionary War lieutenant and sea captain. Full anecdote in HD0175.

notable_stories.title: "All gracious Heaven is this the end of man / A dreadful thought / A melancholy plan"
notable_stories.summary: The gravestone of Capt. John Fowler at Milford Cemetery — a sea captain and Revolutionary War lieutenant who died at 39. His mother Mary Newton Fowler had died of smallpox thirteen years earlier. Full anecdote in HD0175.

notable_stories.title: Two Platt sisters married two Newton first cousins — Hannah Platt to Fletcher Newton, Phebe Platt to Samuel Newton
notable_stories.summary: Hannah Platt and Phebe Platt were daughters of Joseph Platt. Hannah married Lieut. Fletcher Newton; Phebe married Samuel Newton. Fletcher and Samuel were first cousins — both grandsons of Rev. Roger Newton. The two Platt-Newton households lived near each other in Milford.

notable_stories.title: "In memory of Mary...who died Nov. 1, A.D. 1753, aged ten years and ten days"
notable_stories.summary: Mary Bryan, daughter of Yale-graduate Joseph Bryan Jr. and Mehitable Clark, was baptized November 1749 and died November 1, 1753 — ten years and ten days old. Her gravestone stands in the Episcopal Burying Ground in Stratford, Connecticut. Her father Joseph Bryan Jr. had himself died young, at age 29, two years before her. Her grandfather Joseph Bryan and great-grandmother Mary Newton Hooker both outlived both of them.

notable_stories.title: William Pantry's home lot was between Thomas Hooker's and James Olmstead's — and he walked to Hartford with John Talcott
notable_stories.summary: Before the Hartford migration, William Pantry lived in Cambridge with his home lot recorded in the 1635 land survey as sitting between Rev. Thomas Hooker's and James Olmstead's. He was in the Adventurers Party with John Talcott in October 1635 — both men arrived in Hartford before Hooker's party. Pantry's daughter Mary later married Richard Bryan of Milford, whose son Joseph Bryan married Mary Newton, granddaughter of Thomas Hooker. Hooker's neighbor in Cambridge became the great-grandfather-in-law of Hooker's own granddaughter.

notable_stories.title: Joanna Fenn Stone died at 24; her husband John Stone remarried within eight months
notable_stories.summary: Joanna Fenn Stone died May 19, 1741, age 24, and is buried at Milford Cemetery. Eight months later, on January 14, 1742, her husband John Stone (H00160) married Susannah Mansfield. The speed of remarriage was common in colonial New England — a widower with a household to run could not remain unmarried long. Joanna was likely of the Fenn family of Milford (the same family as Martha Fenn Newton and Susanna Fenn Hooker), though this is unconfirmed.

notable_stories.title: Susannah Fowler, 15, drowned in Long Island Sound on December 13, 1727
notable_stories.summary: Susannah Fowler, eldest daughter of John Fowler Sr. and Susannah Burwell Newton, drowned in Long Island Sound on December 13, 1727, fifteen years old. EH's entry for H00162 notes simply "d. Sept. 18, 1727" — the Fowler genealogy gives the drowning and corrects the date to December 13. Her mother Susannah Burwell died seventeen years later.

notable_stories.title: William Fowler built a mill in 1645 near New Haven — on the site later occupied by Eli Whitney's cotton gin factory
notable_stories.summary: One of the Seven Pillars of the Milford church, William Fowler built a mill about two miles from New Haven in 1645 — the town bought it from him in 1659 for £100. The mill stood on the site later occupied by the establishment for manufacture of firearms erected by Eli Whitney, inventor of the cotton gin. His wife Mary Tapp's sister Jane married Governor Robert Treat, making Fowler the Governor's brother-in-law. His granddaughter Susannah Burwell married John Fowler's son, completing a circle back to the Fowler family.

notable_stories.title: Two daughters of Thomas Welch — one married Samuel Newton, one married John Fowler — linking the Newton and Fowler families as in-laws
notable_stories.summary: Thomas Welch, one of the Seven Pillars of the Milford church, had at least two daughters. One became the second wife of Samuel Newton (H00011), mother of HD0007 Abner Newton (Durham branch). Another married John Fowler, whose son John Fowler Sr. married Susannah Burwell (H00053), a Hooker descendant. Their children (H00162-165) are first cousins of HD0007 Abner Newton. Two founding Milford families woven together through Thomas Welch's daughters.

notable_stories.title: Mary Welch Burwell Tibbals — born 1814, died 1902, buried Milford Cemetery. The first descendant in this tree to live into the 20th century.
notable_stories.summary: Mary Welch Burwell Tibbals lived from January 12, 1814 to June 21, 1902 — seven generations from Thomas Hooker, spanning from the early republic to the first years of the 20th century. Her gravestone at Milford Cemetery reads: "IN MEMORY OF / MARY BURWELL / WIFE OF / JOHN TIBBALS / 1814-1902." She died in the same town — Milford — where her ancestor Susannah Newton was born in 1654.

notable_stories.title: Rev. Peter Prudden founded Milford in 1639. Rev. Thomas Hooker founded Hartford. Four generations later their great-great-grandchildren married each other.
notable_stories.summary: Rev. Peter Prudden and Rev. Thomas Hooker were the two great Puritan ministers of early Connecticut — Hooker at Hartford, Prudden at Milford. When Prudden died in 1656, Hooker's son-in-law Roger Newton Sr. took over the Milford pulpit. Three generations later, Hannah Newton — great-great-granddaughter of Thomas Hooker — married John Prudden, great-great-grandson of Peter Prudden. The two founding families, separated by the ministerial succession of 1660, rejoined through marriage in 1706.

notable_stories.title: Joanna Fenn united three of Milford's founding families in one marriage — granddaughter of Benjamin Fenn and of Rev. Peter Prudden, marrying into the Newton-Hooker line
notable_stories.summary: When Joanna Fenn married John Stone in 1740, three founding Milford families converged. Her grandfather Benjamin Fenn was one of Milford's original free planters, magistrate, assistant governor, and Commissioner of United Colonies. Her other grandfather was Samuel Prudden, son of Rev. Peter Prudden, first minister of Milford. Her husband John Stone was grandson of Susannah Newton — daughter of Rev. Roger Newton Sr., who succeeded Prudden as Milford's minister, and whose wife was Mary Hooker, daughter of Thomas Hooker. Fenn, Prudden, Newton, Hooker — all in one Milford household, 1740.

notable_stories.title: Lewis Mallett — grandson of a Huguenot refugee who fled religious persecution in France — married Eunice Newton, great-granddaughter of Thomas Hooker
notable_stories.summary: John Mallett the Huguenot fled France during religious persecution, came to New Rochelle ca.1695 with other French Protestant refugees, and built a prosperous life in Connecticut. His son Lewis was taken by his uncle Dr. Lewis Lyon of Milford as a child and became his heir. Lewis Mallett then married Eunice Newton — great-granddaughter of the Puritan minister Thomas Hooker — uniting the French Huguenot refugee line with the English Puritan founding line. Lewis served as Captain in the Revolutionary War. The Mallett genealogy published 1896 traces this Huguenot family from 1694 to 1894.

notable_stories.title: Rev. Christopher Newton — grandson of the man who succeeded Peter Prudden — converted from Congregationalism to Episcopalianism in 1753
notable_stories.summary: Christopher Newton's grandfather Roger Newton Sr. had succeeded Rev. Peter Prudden as the Congregationalist minister of Milford in 1660. Christopher studied theology, was licensed to preach as a Congregationalist — and then in April 1753 conformed to the Episcopal Church, the Anglican communion that the Puritan founders of Connecticut had explicitly rejected. He preached at several Connecticut towns before settling at Ripton (later Huntington). His will names his children and a granddaughter, but not his conversion. He is the only Newton in the tree to leave the Congregationalist fold.

notable_stories.title: Martha Smith Newton died July 10, 1750 — the same day her last child Martha was baptized
notable_stories.summary: Martha Smith Newton's gravestone at Milford Cemetery reads: "Here lyes ye body of Mrs. Martha Newton wife to Mr John Newton who Died July 10 AD 1750 in ye 37th year of her age." She had married John Newton in 1733 and bore six children in twelve years. Her daughter Martha was baptized on the day she died — whether Martha was born that day or whether the baptism was rushed is unknown. John Newton lived another 31 years as a widower, dying in 1781 at 84.

notable_stories.title: David Newton — great-great-grandson of Thomas Hooker — moved to Vermont in 1777, had 16 children who all lived, and fought in the Revolutionary War
notable_stories.summary: David Newton (great-great-great-grandson of Thomas Hooker) moved his family from Connecticut to Hartford, Vermont in 1777. He served in the Vermont Militia during the Royalton Alarm of 1780. He and wife Mary Hazen had 16 children, all of whom survived — an extraordinary rate for the era. His descendants scattered across Vermont, Ohio, Illinois, and California over the next generation. He died in Hartford, Vermont in 1839, 86 years and thousands of miles from Milford, Connecticut where his great-great-grandfather Thomas Hooker's daughter Mary was born.

notable_stories.title: Zachariah Pond was killed by an accidental gunshot in a shop near his house in Milford, April 1782
notable_stories.summary: Lucy Newton (daughter of Ezekiel Newton and Mary Collins) married Zachariah Pond of Milford. In April 1782, Zachariah was killed by an accidental gunshot in a shop near his house — leaving Lucy with at least four children. She remarried within the year to widower William Clark, a Revolutionary War officer, and had two more children. William Clark died in 1792, leaving Lucy a widow again. She lived until December 1821.

notable_stories.title: "Come Lord Jesus, come quickly" — the last words of Rev. Grindal Rawson, as recorded by his wife Susanna Wilson in her letter to Cotton Mather
notable_stories.summary: Rev. Grindal Rawson died February 6, 1714 at Mendon, Massachusetts, after 35 years of ministry. His wife Susanna Wilson (daughter of Rev. John Wilson Jr. and Sarah Newton, granddaughter of Thomas Hooker) wrote his biography in a letter to Cotton Mather, preserved in Mather's records. She described his deathbed: the morning of his death he asked his physician "Dear Brother, is there no comfortable prospect of Death?" He called his children to be patient and let the Lord's work be carried on. "The last word he ever said was Come Lord Jesus, come quickly!" Susanna Wilson was literate, theologically serious, and wrote this account herself — one of the most personal primary documents in the entire Hooker tree.

notable_stories.title: Rev. Grindal Rawson married his second cousin Susanna Wilson — his paternal grandmother and her paternal grandfather were siblings
notable_stories.summary: When Grindal Rawson married Susanna Wilson in 1682, they were second cousins. His paternal grandmother and her paternal grandfather were siblings. Susanna Wilson was herself the daughter of Rev. John Wilson Jr. and Sarah Newton — Thomas Hooker's granddaughter. The marriage concentrated Hooker-line ancestry in their children, including H00077 Susannah Rawson Reynolds and H00079 Wilson Rawson.

notable_stories.title: Thomas Hooker's 7th-generation descendant fought for the Confederacy and later served in Congress — dual Hooker descent, born in Mississippi
notable_stories.summary: James Grafton Spencer was born in Port Gibson, Mississippi in 1844 — seven generations from Thomas Hooker, the Puritan founder of Hartford, Connecticut. His ancestor Sarah Wilson had dual Hooker descent: father from Wilson-Hooker line, mother from Newton-Hooker line. Spencer enlisted in the Confederate Army in 1863, was captured at Blakely, Alabama in 1865, and imprisoned at Ship Island. After the war he returned to Port Gibson, practiced law, and was elected as a Democrat to the 54th Congress (1895-1897). The distance between Thomas Hooker founding Hartford in 1636 and his descendant serving the Confederacy in Mississippi 1863 is 227 years and an entire continent of migration.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Amán Rawson

notable_stories.title: A Massachusetts Navy surgeon arrived in newly independent Argentina in 1818 — and founded a city
notable_stories.summary: Dr. Haman Rawson — 6th-generation descendant of Thomas Hooker — received his medical degree in 1814, served as a U.S. Navy surgeon, and arrived in Buenos Aires in 1818. He settled in San Juan Province, converted to Catholicism to marry, founded the city of Caucete in 1822, served as provincial deputy, chief physician, and emergency chairman of government. In his last days he smuggled copies of Sarmiento's "Facundo" — a pamphlet against dictator Juan Manuel de Rosas — by hiding them in medicine drawers marked with a warning about venereal disease remedies. He died in San Juan in 1847. His son Guillermo Rawson became one of Argentina's most prominent physicians and ministers of state.
notable_stories.one_line: His father fought in the Revolution. He emigrated to Argentina the year after independence. His sons became its interior minister and founding painter.

sections.header: Private Edmund Rawson fought in the Revolution
sections.body: Edmund Rawson of Massachusetts (HD0275) served as a private in the American Revolution. His son Haman — born 1792 in Montague — received a medical degree in 1814 and joined the U.S. Navy as a surgeon.

sections.header: 1818: he arrived in Buenos Aires
sections.body: In 1818, two years after Argentina declared independence, the 26-year-old Navy surgeon sailed to Buenos Aires. He spent time in Mendoza before settling in San Juan in 1819, where he married, converted to Catholicism, opened a pharmacy, built an imposing mansion, and never left.

sections.header: His sons became Argentina's interior minister and founding painter
sections.body: Guillermo Rawson (gen 7 from Thomas Hooker) became Argentina's Interior Minister in 1862, negotiating the Welsh settlement of Patagonia. The capital of Chubut Province bears his name. His brother Benjamín Franklin Rawson became the country's first major portrait painter.

notable_stories.title: Dea. Edmund Rawson of Uxbridge is documented as an ancestor of President William Howard Taft — the Hooker-to-White-House connection through the Rawson line
notable_stories.summary: Deacon Edmund Rawson (H00078) — son of Rev. Grindal Rawson and Susanna Wilson, grandson of Thomas Hooker — is an ancestor of William Howard Taft, 27th President of the United States (1909-1913) and later Chief Justice of the Supreme Court. The exact path from H00078 to Taft is flagged as open research (likely through Edmund's son Edmund Jr. and the Howard/Hayward family). If confirmed, this is the first documented President in the Hooker descendant tree.

notable_stories.title: In 1749, Edward Rawson named his firstborn son "Hooker" — 100 years after Thomas Hooker's death and four generations removed
notable_stories.summary: Thomas Hooker died in Hartford in 1647. A century later, in 1749, his great-great-great-grandson Deacon Edward Rawson named his firstborn son "Hooker Rawson." This was not an accident — four generations of family tradition had kept the Hooker name alive through Wilson Rawson, Susanna Wilson, Sarah Hooker. The name was a deliberate act of ancestral memory in a generation that could only have known Thomas Hooker as history, not lived experience. Hooker Rawson's mother Mary Morse was herself a granddaughter of Susannah Rawson Reynolds — another Hooker descendant — making him Hooker-descended through both parents.

notable_stories.title: Dea. Edward Rawson married the granddaughter of his own aunt — a first-cousin-once-removed match documented by Edward Hooker himself
notable_stories.summary: When Edward Rawson (H00208) married Mary Morse in 1748, he married the granddaughter of his aunt Susannah Rawson Reynolds (H00077). Mary's mother was Mary Reynolds (daughter of Susannah), who had first married Samuel Morse, the physician, and after his death in 1743 remarried Edward Rawson. EH notes the connection explicitly: "Gr. dau. of his Aunt Reynolds, of Bristol, R.I." The Rawson-Reynolds family network was tightly woven — even their marriages stayed within the extended family.

notable_stories.title: Capt. Paul Rawson — master of a Nantucket vessel — was lost at sea with all his crew in 1772
notable_stories.summary: Paul Rawson was born in Mendon, Massachusetts in 1725, son of Wilson Rawson and Margaret Arthur of Nantucket. He married Phebe Gardner — daughter of Capt. Abel Gardner of Nantucket — and settled on that island as a ship captain. In 1772, he was lost at sea with his entire crew. His wife Phebe survived him by 21 years, dying in 1793 aged 63. They had six children: Wilson, Phebe, Margaret, Abel, Deborah, and Stephen.

notable_stories.title: Two cousins in the same Rawson generation were both named "Hooker Rawson" — one died at age 2, the other survived
