notable_stories.summary: In the same generation of Thomas Hooker's great-great-grandchildren, two different Rawson families independently chose the name "Hooker." HD0289 Hooker Rawson was born Dec 3, 1738 in Uxbridge to John Rawson (H00080) — and died June 5, 1741 at age 2. HD0282 Hooker Rawson was born Apr 21, 1749 in Mendon to Edward Rawson (H00208) — and survived. The name was passed down across multiple Rawson branches, each independently commemorating their Hooker ancestry a full century after Thomas Hooker's death.

notable_stories.title: Rev. Joseph Dorr succeeded his future father-in-law Rev. Grindal Rawson as pastor of Mendon — then married Rawson's daughter and held the pulpit for 52 years
notable_stories.summary: Rev. Grindal Rawson (I00005) — son of Susanna Wilson and grandson of Thomas Hooker — was pastor of Mendon for 35 years until his death in 1714/15. Rev. Joseph Dorr settled as his successor in 1715. Nine years later, Dorr married Rawson's daughter Mary (H00081). Dorr then served the same Mendon congregation for 52 years, dying in 1768 "highly respected and very much beloved." The Mendon pulpit stayed within the extended Hooker family for nearly 90 years.

notable_stories.title: Katherine Taft Stetson and her husband Capt. Samuel Stetson died three days apart in July 1804 — he reportedly died while her funeral was being held
notable_stories.summary: Katherine Taft (HD0314) — great-great-granddaughter of Thomas Hooker — died July 18, 1804 in Boston aged 40. Her husband Capt. Samuel Stetson died July 21, 1804, aged 37. The family tradition recorded in the Descendants of Cornet Robert Stetson states that Samuel died while Katherine's funeral was being held, though the FindAGrave record gives separate dates three days apart. Both are buried at the Old Burying Place in Watertown, Massachusetts. Their shared stone reads: "Sacred to the Memory of CAPT. SAMUEL STETSON of Boston, who died July 21, 1804 Æt. 37. Also to that of CATHARINE, his wife. She died the 18th of the same month, Æ. 38."

notable_stories.title: Rev. Ezekiel Emerson's son died while hunting near Moosehead Lake, Maine — deep in the wilderness his father had ministered
notable_stories.summary: Rev. Ezekiel Emerson (I00113) had been the first settled minister of Georgetown, Maine, the earliest town east of the Kennebec River, and had moved his family to Norridgewock during the Revolutionary War. His son Ezekiel Jr. (HD0317) died in 1809 in the wilderness near Moosehead Lake — one of the remotest places in New England — while hunting. He had married a widow named Mary Blethen Fish in 1786 in Georgetown. His brother Luther moved to Ohio. The family scattered across the Maine frontier and beyond.

notable_stories.title: Elias Frost named all four of his children with "Dorr" as a middle name — commemorating his grandmother Mary Rawson Dorr three generations on
notable_stories.summary: Elias Frost (HD0326) was the son of Susannah Dorr Frost (H00221) and Rev. Amariah Frost. When he had children in New Hampshire in the 1810s-1820s, he gave each one "Dorr" as a middle name: Edwin Dorr Frost, Mary Dorr Frost, Susan Jane Dorr Frost, George Dorr Frost. The Dorr name honored his grandmother Mary Rawson Dorr (H00081), Thomas Hooker's great-granddaughter. Mary Dorr Frost (HD0328) lived 1819-1916, spanning 96 years from the Monroe administration to the First World War — carrying the Hooker-Rawson-Dorr name into the 20th century.

notable_stories.title: President William Howard Taft was a 7th-generation descendant of Rev. Thomas Hooker — through the Rawson family of Mendon and Uxbridge, Massachusetts
notable_stories.summary: Confirmed via Uxbridge vital records. The chain runs: Thomas Hooker (Hartford, 1636) → Sarah Hooker Wilson (H00006) → Susanna Wilson Rawson (H00026, wife of Rev. Grindal Rawson) → Edmund Rawson (H00078, Deacon of Mendon) → Abner Rawson (H00202) × Mary Allen → Rhoda Rawson Taft (HD0339, b. Oct 4, 1749 Uxbridge) × Aaron Taft Jr. (I00117, b. May 28, 1743) → Peter Rawson Taft (HD0336, b. Apr 14, 1785 Uxbridge) → Alphonso Taft (HD0337, Secretary of War, Attorney General) → William Howard Taft (HD0338, 27th President 1909-1913, Chief Justice 1921-1930). The middle name "Peter Rawson Taft" explicitly marks the Rawson ancestry. Taft is the only person to serve as both President and Chief Justice of the United States. Primary source: Vital Records of Uxbridge MA — marriage "Rhoda and Aaron Taft Jr., June 1, 1769" and birth "Rhoda, d. of Abner and Mary, Oct. 4, 1749."

notable_stories.title: Rachel Rawson Wood lived to approximately 100; her husband Samuel Wood to 94 — the longest-lived couple in the Hooker tree
notable_stories.summary: Rachel Rawson (H00082) — daughter of Rev. Grindal Rawson and Susanna Wilson, granddaughter of Thomas Hooker — died in 1802 at approximately age 100. Her husband Samuel Wood died in 1790 at approximately age 94. They married around 1717 and had one child, Priscilla Wood Davis. Rachel outlived her husband by about 12 years and outlived most of her grandchildren. At her death in 1802, she would have been born when Thomas Hooker's daughter Sarah was still a living memory in Mendon.

notable_stories.title: Samuel Hooker, age 99, fell back in his chair and died on hearing that his brother Giles had just died at age 97 — two brothers, 196 years of life between them
notable_stories.summary: Samuel Hooker (H00086) was born April 6, 1688 in Farmington, Connecticut. His younger brother Giles Hooker (H00087) died in March 1787 at age 97. On hearing the news, Samuel — age 99 — fell back in his chair and expired, March 1, 1787. Together the two brothers accumulated 196 years of life. Samuel had outlived his first wife Mercy Leete by 36 years, his second wife Mary Elliott Pierson by 16 years, and had watched his youngest children grow old. He was born in the reign of King James II and died in the first term of George Washington. His grandfather Thomas Hooker had founded Hartford 151 years before Samuel's death.

notable_stories.title: In June 1741, John Rawson lost his youngest son, then his wife two days later, then two more children in the same week — a probable epidemic
notable_stories.summary: In spring and summer 1741, John Rawson's household was struck by what appears to have been an epidemic. Hooker Rawson (HD0289) died June 5. His mother Mercy Hayward Rawson (I00110) died June 7 — two days later. Jonah Rawson (HD0288) and Molly Rawson (HD0291) both died June 12. Four deaths in the same household within six weeks. John Rawson was widowed at approximately age 46 with surviving children ranging from infant to age 21. The cause is unrecorded, but the clustering strongly suggests an infectious illness — epidemic dysentery, typhoid, and diphtheria were common killers in New England summers.

notable_stories.title: William Hooker married four times, had five children — only one survived past childhood, and he died unmarried at 27
notable_stories.summary: William Hooker (H00089) was born in Farmington in 1695 and lived to 87. His first wife Lydia Woodward died in 1723, likely in childbirth, leaving infant Roger. His second wife Anna Steele died December 12, 1727 — ten days after giving birth to Richard. Richard survived his mother by 46 days, then died January 27, 1728. His third wife Abigail Phelps bore Anne (1732) and William (1734), both dead by 1735. His fourth wife Esther (surname unknown) outlived three predecessors and died in 1780. Of five children across three marriages, only Roger survived past infancy — and he died unmarried in 1750 at 27, leaving no descendants. William Hooker's entire branch of the Hooker family ended with him, despite his own survival to age 87.

notable_stories.title: Esther Hooker married Rev. Isaac Stiles — whose first wife was a daughter of Rev. Edward Taylor, the greatest Puritan poet in American literature, and whose son Ezra Stiles became President of Yale
notable_stories.summary: Rev. Isaac Stiles's first wife Keziah Taylor was the daughter of Rev. Edward Taylor (1642-1729), physician and poet of Westfield, Massachusetts — now recognized as the greatest Puritan poet in American literature. Keziah died in childbirth in 1727, leaving infant Ezra Stiles. Isaac then married Esther Hooker — Thomas Hooker's great-granddaughter. Ezra Stiles grew up with Esther as his stepmother, went to Yale, and became its 7th President (1778-1795), corresponding with Washington, Franklin, and Jefferson. The Hooker-Stiles household in North Haven connected the founding Puritan minister of Hartford to the intellectual leadership of Revolutionary-era New England.

notable_stories.title: Thomas Hooker's great-granddaughter Esther Hooker raised Ezra Stiles — who became President of Yale and one of the most important intellectuals of the American Founding
notable_stories.summary: When Keziah Taylor died in childbirth on December 4, 1727, her infant son Ezra Stiles was left motherless. Less than a year later, Rev. Isaac Stiles married Esther Hooker (H00092) — Thomas Hooker's great-granddaughter. Esther raised Ezra alongside her own ten children in the Stiles household in North Haven. Ezra Stiles went on to become the 7th President of Yale College (1778-1795), one of the most learned men in Revolutionary America, corresponding with Washington, Jefferson, and Franklin. His mother Keziah's father was Rev. Edward Taylor — the greatest Puritan poet in American literature, whose verse was kept secret until 1937. The chain: Thomas Hooker founded Hartford → his great-granddaughter Esther raised the stepson of the greatest Puritan poet's daughter → that stepson led Yale through the American Revolution.

notable_stories.title: "The Great Red Dragon" — Capt. William Coit, great-grandson of Thomas Hooker, raced to Bunker Hill at midnight, commanded the first Continental Navy vessels, and claimed to be the first American to turn the British flag upside down
notable_stories.summary: News of Lexington reached New London the night of April 20, 1775. A few hours later, Capt. William Coit — Yale 1761, selectman, Thomas Hooker's great-grandson — was on the road with his company, marching through the night. They reached Cambridge by April 23. He marched to Bunker Hill while the battle was in progress, covering the retreat of the provincials. In October 1775, Gen. Washington commissioned him to command the schooner "Harrison," one of the first two armed vessels of what would become the Continental Navy. He intercepted two British supply ships and made the prisoners land on Plymouth Rock and cheer for American arms. He claimed to be "the first man in the States who turned his majesty's bunting upside down." Known for wearing a scarlet cloak, he was called "The Great Red Dragon." In 1781, Benedict Arnold captured him when he burned New London. He died in 1802 in North Carolina, buried in an unmarked grave near Gen. Lillington.

notable_stories.title: Ann Coit died on March 30, 1792 — her 22nd birthday and the day fixed for her marriage to the eldest son of Bishop Seabury
notable_stories.summary: Ann Coit (HD0351) was the daughter of Capt. William Coit "The Great Red Dragon" and Sarah Prentiss. She was born March 30, 1770. Her marriage to the eldest son of Bishop Samuel Seabury — first Episcopal Bishop of America — was planned for March 30, 1792, her 22nd birthday. She died that day. Her tomb was inscribed: "A Mournful Birth Day to her friends."

notable_stories.title: The same Huguenot refugee family — the Malletts of New Rochelle — married into the Hooker tree in two separate generations, once through Lewis Mallett and once through his nephew Peter Mallett
notable_stories.summary: John Mallett the Huguenot fled France after the revocation of the Edict of Nantes, settled at New Rochelle ca.1695, and founded a Connecticut dynasty. His son Lewis Mallett (I00096) was taken by his uncle Dr. Lewis Lyon of Milford and married Eunice Newton (H00168) — Thomas Hooker's great-great-granddaughter — in generation 4. His grandson Peter Mallett (X00115), born New Rochelle 1744, moved to North Carolina and married "Pretty Sally" Sarah Mumford (HD0357) — Thomas Hooker's great-great-great-granddaughter — in generation 5. The same Huguenot family, two generations, two different Hooker branches.

notable_stories.title: Susannah Hooker died at 19, one month after her daughter was born — her only child, who was given the same name and also died young
notable_stories.summary: Susannah Hooker (H00094) was born in 1690, the posthumous daughter of William Hooker. She married Nathan Selleck in August 1708 at age 18. On September 3, 1709 her daughter Susannah was born. On October 5, 1709 — one month later — Susannah Hooker died at age 19, almost certainly of childbed fever or complications. Her daughter Susannah Selleck grew up without her mother, married Capt. Joseph St. John of Norwalk, and died herself at 40 in 1749. Her gravestone bore a remarkable epitaph: "She that lies at rest within this tomb / Had Rachel's face and Leah's fruitful womb, / Abigail's wisdom, Lydia's faithful heart / With Martha's care — we hope Mary's better part."

notable_stories.title: "Hooker St. John" — a fifth-generation descendant named explicitly for Thomas Hooker, died unmarried in 1782 having never reproduced
notable_stories.summary: Hooker St. John (HD0367) was born in Norwalk ca.1742, the great-great-great-grandson of Thomas Hooker through Susannah Hooker. His parents named him "Hooker" as an explicit tribute to the founding ancestor — continuing the pattern seen in the Rawson family with two "Hooker Rawson" children. He served the town of Norwalk as Commissioner, Selectman, and Lister, but died unmarried in 1782 at approximately age 40. His brother William St. John was a Loyalist who sent an enslaved man to fight in the Revolution in his stead. The Hooker name ended with him in this branch.

notable_stories.title: In September 1750, Hezekiah Hooker lost daughter Eunice, then son Jesse and daughter Abigail — all within a single week — and possibly his wife on the same day
notable_stories.summary: Eunice Hooker (H00261) died September 17, 1750, age 15. One week later, on September 24, 1750, her brother Jesse (H00260, age 18) and sister Abigail (H00257, age 25) both died — on the same day. If the alternate death date for their mother Abigail Curtis Hooker (I00130) is correct — September 24, 1750 — she died that same day too. Hezekiah Hooker survived, dying suddenly in Woodbury in February 1756. The cause is unrecorded, but three deaths in one week in one household in late summer strongly suggests epidemic disease — most likely dysentery, typhoid, or diphtheria.

notable_stories.title: Rev. John Hooker of Northampton died of smallpox in 1777 — nine months later his daughter Sarah married Caleb Strong, the Founding Father who had joined his congregation five years earlier
notable_stories.summary: Rev. John Hooker (H00264) was pastor of the Congregational church in Northampton, Massachusetts. Caleb Strong joined his congregation in 1772. Rev. Hooker died of smallpox February 6, 1777. On November 29, 1777, Strong married his pastor's daughter Sarah Hooker (H00525). Strong went on to be a delegate to the 1787 Philadelphia Convention, a member of the inaugural U.S. Senate, co-drafter of the Judiciary Act of 1789, and 6th and 10th Governor of Massachusetts. He was the only delegate to the Philadelphia Convention who was also a direct descendant of Thomas Hooker — through his wife. Sarah's gravestone notes she was "daughter of the Rev John Hooker."

notable_stories.title: When Clarissa Strong (Thomas Hooker's 6th-generation descendant) married Timothy Dwight Jr., two lines of descent from Thomas Hooker converged — the Dwights descended from Hooker through the Edwards-Pierpont line
notable_stories.summary: Two separate lines of descent from Thomas Hooker (H00001) converged in one New Haven household. Line 1 (Clarissa's): Thomas Hooker → John Hooker II → John Hooker III → Rev. John Hooker of Northampton → Sarah Hooker Strong → Clarissa Strong. Line 2 (Timothy's): Thomas Hooker → Samuel Hooker → Mary Hooker Pierpont → Sarah Pierpont Edwards → Jonathan Edwards → Mary Edwards Dwight → Rev. Timothy Dwight Sr. (8th President of Yale) → Timothy Dwight Jr. The same Puritan minister who founded Hartford in 1636 thus appears in the ancestry of both husband and wife at this 1809 New Haven wedding, through entirely separate lines maintained across seven and eight generations.

notable_stories.title: Thomas Hooker's great-granddaughter Abigail Hooker has a 7th-generation descendant who became a Union Brigadier General in the Civil War — wounded at Williamsburg, commanded Johnson's Island Prison Camp
notable_stories.summary: Chain: Abigail Hooker (H00099) × Nathaniel Hart → Sarah Hart Marsh (H00268) × Dr. Jonathan Marsh → Abigail Marsh Ripley (HD0379) × Maj. John Ripley (Rev. War) → Julia Ripley Terry (HD0382) × Henry Terry → Brig. Gen. Henry Dwight Terry (HD0383). Terry organized the 5th Michigan Infantry in 1861, was wounded at Williamsburg in 1862, suffered heavy losses at Seven Pines, and commanded Johnson's Island Prison Camp in 1864. Two generations of the family served in American wars — Maj. John Ripley in the Revolution, his granddaughter's son in the Civil War.

notable_stories.title: Lois Hart died October 11, 1736; her father Matthew Hart died October 30 — nineteen days later; and her brother Matthew was born posthumously in January 1737
notable_stories.summary: In the autumn of 1736, Sarah Hooker Hart lost her daughter Lois (H00284, age 6) on October 11, then her husband Matthew Hart (I00030) on October 30. Sarah was pregnant — her son Matthew (H00286) was born January 23, 1737, posthumously. Widowed with a newborn and grieving a daughter, she later remarried Huit Strong in 1739 and ultimately died in Durham, New York in 1775 at age 73 — having survived two husbands and outlived most of her children.

notable_stories.title: Capt. Joseph Hooker became so corpulent in old age that the militia would march around his house to salute him where he sat in his big chair by the door, smoking his pipe
notable_stories.summary: Joseph Hooker (H00102) was an enthusiastic militia captain in his younger days. In later years he became excessively corpulent — so much so that for several years before his death he was unable to attend to any active business. On fine days a large chair was placed in the front yard near the door, and he sat there smoking his pipe and visiting with passersby. When the local militia paraded or when there was any military assemblage at Farmington, it was customary for them to march around by Capt. Hooker's house and salute him as he sat in the big chair by the door. He died December 19, 1764 and is buried in Memento Mori Cemetery, Farmington.

notable_stories.title: Joseph Hooker married Sarah Lewis in 1735 — uniting two of Hartford's founding families, three generations after their ancestors arrived together in 1636
notable_stories.summary: William Lewis the Hartford Founder (b. 1594) was part of the "Adventurers Party" that preceded Rev. Thomas Hooker's party to Connecticut in October 1635. Lewis was among the first settlers of Hartford and later Farmington. His granddaughter Sarah Lewis (I00132) married Joseph Hooker (H00102) in January 1735 — great-grandson of Rev. Thomas Hooker. Both families are buried in the same Memento Mori Cemetery in Farmington, where the oldest gravestone belongs to Stephen Hart (1689) and where Samuel Hooker (Thomas Hooker's son) also rests.

notable_stories.title: In September 1736 Ruth Hooker Strong lost three children within ten days — Lois and Ruth both on September 6, Elnathan nine days later on September 15
notable_stories.summary: Lois Strong (H00294, age 3) and Ruth Strong (H00295, age 1) both died on September 6, 1736. Elnathan Strong (H00293, age 5) died September 15, 1736 — nine days later. Three children under six years old, dead within ten days. Ruth Hooker and her husband Capt. Asahel Strong then named their next three children Lois No. 2 (b.1737), Ruth No. 2 (b.1739), and Elnathan No. 2 (b.1742) — all replacement names for the three who died. This triple replacement naming is the most systematic instance of the pattern in the entire Hooker tree.

notable_stories.title: Solomon Whitman celebrated his 90th birthday by making a pair of shoes, served as Town Clerk at 92, and died at 93 from over-fatigue settling a fence dispute between two brothers
notable_stories.summary: Solomon Whitman (I00134) was Ruth Hooker's second husband — she was 64, he was 62 when they married in 1772. Ruth died in 1777 and Solomon remarried again. He had learned shoemaking as a young man but rarely practiced it. On his 90th birthday he made a pair of shoes. He served as Town Clerk of Farmington at age 92 — having also been Justice of the Peace (1751), Deputy to the General Assembly (1751), and the first Judge appointed to the Farmington Probate Court. "Though not a college graduate, he was well educated and deeply interested in all literary matters." He died at age 93 from over-fatigue after personally settling a fence boundary dispute between two quarreling brothers.

notable_stories.title: Roger Hooker — favorite son of John Hooker, who traveled with his father on official business — was the best-informed grandson of Rev. Thomas Hooker on the family's English origins
notable_stories.summary: Roger Hooker (H00104) was the favorite son of Hon. John Hooker (H00030), the prominent Farmington magistrate who held the family homestead. He accompanied his father on official journeys around the Colony, brought his wife to his father's house and continued living there. EH writes: "He undoubtedly received from his father full information about the origin of the family and the English connections, and his father was unquestionably the best informed upon the subject of all the grandsons of Rev. Thomas Hooker." This makes Roger Hooker — who died in 1774, 35 years before EH published — the likely source, through oral tradition, of whatever English origin information EH had access to. Roger is also the direct ancestor of the compiler through the Talcott line.

notable_stories.title: Rev. John Hart — Yale's first-ever B.A. graduate and second tutor — married Mary Hooker, great-granddaughter of Thomas Hooker; his predecessor as Yale's first tutor was her uncle Daniel Hooker
notable_stories.summary: John Hart (Yale 1703) was the first student to receive a Bachelor's degree from Yale College. He graduated alone at Saybrook on September 15, 1703; his original diploma is preserved at Yale. On the same day he was appointed the second tutor of Yale — succeeding Daniel Hooker, son of Rev. Samuel Hooker (H00007) of Farmington, who had been Yale's first tutor in 1702. Daniel Hooker was the brother of Mary Hooker Pierpont (H00010), wife of Rev. James Pierpont, Yale's founding patron. In 1720, John Hart married Mary Hooker (H00105) — granddaughter of Rev. Samuel Hooker and great-granddaughter of Rev. Thomas Hooker, the founder of Hartford. The Hooker family thus appears at both the founding and early teaching of Yale.
notable_stories.research_notes: NOTE: Daniel Hooker (H00036) was the first TUTOR — he resigned in favor of Hart. EH calls Daniel "the first B.A. of Yale" and Hart "nominally the second, but really the first actual student." Both H00036 and I00137 are now in person_ids.

notable_stories.title: Eight generations from Thomas Hooker to Frances Foote Godkin, wife of E.L. Godkin — founder and first editor of The Nation magazine (1865)
notable_stories.summary: The chain: Rev. Thomas Hooker (H00001, Hartford 1636) → Samuel Hooker (H00007) → Judge James Hooker (H00031, Guilford) → Mary Hooker Hart (H00105) → Sarah Hart Hill (H00315) → Hon. Henry Hill (HD0398) → Catherine Hill Elliott (HD0402) → Elizabeth Elliott Foote (HD0403) → Frances Foote Godkin (HD0404). Frances married Edwin Lawrence Godkin (1831-1902) in 1859. Godkin had come to America in 1856 as a war correspondent, and in 1865 founded The Nation — one of the most influential intellectual journals in American history, still published today. Frances died in 1875; Godkin died in 1902. The Puritan founder of Hartford cast a long shadow.

notable_stories.title: Sarah Hooker Bartlett named her son "Hooker" for her ancestor — and her will bequeathed an enslaved man named Peleg alongside her estate
notable_stories.summary: Sarah Hooker (H00107) — granddaughter of Thomas Hooker — married Capt. John Bartlett of Guilford. She named her second son "Hooker Bartlett" (H00319), a deliberate tribute to the founding ancestor. Her husband Capt. John Bartlett's estate inventory listed an enslaved woman "Rose" (£90) and an enslaved man "Jethro" (£210). Sarah's own will bequeathed an enslaved man named Peleg to her daughter Anna Ruggles, with provision that if unsold at Anna's death, he should pass to grandson Nathaniel Ruggles Jr. The probate inventory values Peleg at £65. The Hooker name carried forward as a symbol of founding heritage in the same household that held enslaved people as property — a stark conjunction of the period.

notable_stories.title: Thomas Hooker's great-granddaughter Abigail Smith married the man whose house George Washington used as his headquarters during the Battle of White Plains — twice
notable_stories.summary: Abigail Smith (H00331) was the daughter of Mehitable Hooker (H00109) and Rev. Dr. John Smith — Thomas Hooker's great-granddaughter. She married Capt. Jacob G. Purdy, whose family owned the Purdy House in White Plains. Gen. George Washington used the house as his headquarters during the Battle of White Plains in October 1776, and again for two months in 1778. The Jacob Purdy House is now listed on the National Register of Historic Places (1979) and serves as headquarters of the White Plains Historical Society. Abigail lived to age 93.

notable_stories.title: Rev. John Smith walked with Jonathan Edwards along the Hudson — and seven years after his death the Battle of White Plains was fought in front of his church, destroying it
notable_stories.summary: Rev. Dr. John Smith (I00140) — husband of Mehitable Hooker, Yale 1727 — practiced medicine and ministry simultaneously at White Plains for nearly 30 years. On one occasion, walking along the Hudson with Rev. Jonathan Edwards (who had married Sarah Pierpont, great-great-granddaughter of Thomas Hooker through a different line), Smith said: "To be separated from my endeared friends and companions are the most bitter trials of my life." Smith died February 26, 1771. Seven years later, in October 1776, the Battle of White Plains was fought in front of his White Plains church — the building was destroyed. He was buried in the churchyard; a later church was extended over his grave.

notable_stories.title: Maj. Benjamin Tallmadge Jr. — Washington's spymaster, handler of the Culper Ring, interrogator of John André — was Thomas Hooker's 5th-generation descendant through Mehitable Hooker Smith
notable_stories.summary: Chain: Thomas Hooker → Samuel Hooker → James Hooker → Mehitable Hooker (H00109) × Rev. Dr. John Smith → Susannah Smith (H00323) × Rev. Benjamin Tallmadge Sr. → Maj. Benjamin Tallmadge Jr. (H00757). Tallmadge organized and ran the Culper Spy Ring — the most effective intelligence network of the American Revolution. He personally interrogated Maj. John André, the British officer who had negotiated with Benedict Arnold for the surrender of West Point. When André asked Tallmadge how he would be treated, Tallmadge — whose classmate Nathan Hale had been executed by the British — replied: "Yes, precisely similar, and similar shall be your fate." André was hanged October 2, 1780 at Tappan NY. See also: major_andre_execution_three_hooker_family_connections.
notable_stories.one_line: Washington's spymaster — the man who ran the Culper Ring, interrogated Major André, and told him "similar shall be your fate" — was a direct descendant of Thomas Hooker.

notable_stories.title: Dr. William Hooker Smith recorded his wife's death in his Oxford Bible: "My wife, Sarah, died on Friday, the 12th of June, 1778, about nine o'clock at night" — two weeks before the Battle of Wyoming
notable_stories.summary: Dr. William Hooker Smith (H00320) kept a family record in his Oxford Bible (printed 1772). His entry for his wife Sarah Brown's death reads: "My wife, Sarah, died on Friday, the 12th of June, 1778, about nine o'clock at night, was buried the 14th, following, on my own land at Jacob's Plains." The Battle of Wyoming — one of the bloodiest frontier massacres of the Revolution — occurred on July 3, 1778, three weeks later. Dr. Smith served as surgeon at Forty Fort during that campaign. He had just buried his wife on his own land when the battle he was treating survivors of arrived. Congress passed a special act in 1836 — 58 years after the battle — authorizing $2,400 to his heirs for his war services.

notable_stories.title: Thomas Hooker's 6th-generation descendant founded the first permanent school for deaf students in North America — the American School for the Deaf, Hartford, 1817
notable_stories.summary: Chain: Thomas Hooker (Hartford, 1636) → Samuel Hooker (H00007) → Nathaniel Hooker (H00033) → Alice Hooker Howard (H00111) → Alice Howard Hopkins (H00340) → Jennett Hopkins Gallaudet (HD0405) → Rev. Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet (HD0411, 1787-1851). Gallaudet co-founded (with Laurent Clerc and Mason Cogswell) the American School for the Deaf in Hartford on April 15, 1817. He married former student Sophia Fowler, born deaf, known as the Mother of the American Deaf. Their son Edward Miner Gallaudet founded what became Gallaudet University in Washington DC. The school opened in Hartford — the same city Thomas Hooker founded 181 years earlier.

notable_stories.title: Hon. Daniel Edwards — Judge of Connecticut's Supreme Court and husband of Sarah Hooker — had four enslaved people baptized at First Church Hartford in 1760: Jethro, Dick, Mina, and Betty
notable_stories.summary: Hon. Daniel Edwards (I00053) — Yale 1720, Judge of the Supreme Court of Connecticut — married Sarah Hooker (H00112) in 1728. He held four enslaved persons: Jethro, Dick, Mina, and Betty. "He was such a good churchman that he saw to it that his Negro slaves, Jethro, Dick, Mina and Betty were baptized in the First Church in 1760." He died in 1765. His only surviving child Sarah had died the year before, and his wife Sarah Hooker survived him by ten years, dying in 1775. Daniel Edwards was a half-brother of Rev. Timothy Edwards, father of the theologian Jonathan Edwards.

notable_stories.title: Rev. Nathaniel Hooker's family record — preserved in his will — noted both Thomas Hooker's burial place and his connection to the Hooker family of Exeter, Devonshire: a key source for EH's since-disproven Devon origin theory
notable_stories.summary: Rev. Nathaniel Hooker (H00346, Yale 1755, minister West Hartford) kept a family record that EH cites in entry 346. This record "makes allusion distinctly to Rev. Thomas Hooker's connection with the Hooker family of Exeter Devonshire, England" — the source for EH's Devon origin theory, later superseded by Hutchinson's 1917 evidence placing Hooker's birth at Birstall, Leicestershire. Nathaniel also noted Hooker's burial place as "near where the old prison stood, it being the first burial ground of the town, though not long improved for that purpose." Nathaniel died June 9, 1770 age 32; in his will he directed his only surviving daughter Ruth to be sent to Boston for a better education — "on her return Ruth became a famous belle."

notable_stories.title: The three eldest sons of Thomas Hooker's great-grandson all married sisters — daughters of a family that descended from William Hyde, who came to America with Thomas Hooker himself
notable_stories.summary: James Pierpont II (H00116) — great-grandson of Thomas Hooker through Mary Hooker Pierpont — had three sons whose marriages created a remarkable convergence. Evelyn (H00351), Robert (H00352), and James III (H00353) all married daughters of Charles Collins of Litchfield, Connecticut. The Collins sisters were granddaughters of Rev. Timothy Collins (4th settled minister of Litchfield), who married Elizabeth Hyde — great-granddaughter of William Hyde, one of the original proprietors of Norwich, who came to America with Rev. Thomas Hooker. Rev. Timothy Collins's mother was Anna Leete, granddaughter of Gov. William Leete (whose daughter Mary Leete married Judge James Hooker, already in this tree). Three brothers married three sisters whose lineage traced directly back to two of the founding families of Connecticut — the Hydes and the Leetes — both connected to Thomas Hooker himself.

notable_stories.title: William Huntington Russell, co-founder of Yale's Skull and Bones (1832), was a 6th-generation descendant of Thomas Hooker through Mary Pierpont Russell
notable_stories.summary: Chain: Thomas Hooker → Samuel Hooker (H00007) → Mary Hooker Pierpont (H00034) → Mary Pierpont Russell (H00118) → Noadiah Russell (H00360) → Matthew Russell → Matthew Talcott Russell → William Huntington Russell (1809-1885). Russell co-founded Skull and Bones at Yale in 1832 with Alphonso Taft — whose mother Rhoda Rawson was herself a Hooker descendant (through H00202 Abner Rawson). Two co-founders of Skull and Bones were independently descended from Thomas Hooker. Russell described himself as "a descendant of several old New England families, including those of Pierpont, Hooker, Willett, Bingham, and Russell." His ancestor Rev. Noadiah Russell was a founding trustee of Yale College in 1701.

notable_stories.title: Samuel Russell (1789-1862) — founder of Russell & Company, largest American trading house in China, who dealt in opium — was Thomas Hooker's 6th-generation descendant
notable_stories.summary: Chain: Thomas Hooker → Samuel Hooker → Mary Hooker Pierpont (H00034) → Mary Pierpont Russell (H00118) → Samuel Russell (H00359) → John Russell → Samuel Russell (1789-1862). Samuel Russell founded Russell & Company in Canton, China in 1823 — the largest and most important American trading house in China from 1842 to 1891. The firm dealt extensively in opium, described as "an extremely profitable activity." Samuel Russell was second cousin of William Huntington Russell, co-founder of Skull and Bones. Both were descended from Thomas Hooker through the Pierpont-Russell line.

notable_stories.title: Rev. William Russell's aunt married Mary Pierpont's uncle — making their own marriage a second Hamlin-Hooker union in the same generation
notable_stories.summary: EH explicitly notes the double connection: Rev. William Russell's mother was Mary Hamlin. Mary Hamlin's sister Mehitable Hamlin married Samuel Hooker Jr. (H00028) — a brother of Mary Hooker Pierpont (H00034), who was Mary Pierpont's mother. Two Hamlin sisters (Mary and Mehitable) married into the Hooker family. Then one of those Hamlins' son (Rev. William Russell) married a Hooker granddaughter (Mary Pierpont). The Russell-Hooker connection thus ran through two independent family ties before Rev. William and Mary Pierpont ever wed.

notable_stories.title: Two children of Mary Hooker married two siblings of the Russell family — whose father, like their grandfather, was a founding trustee of Yale College
notable_stories.summary: Joseph Pierpont (HD0416) married Hannah Russell (I00145), while his sister Mary Pierpont (H00118) married Hannah's brother Rev. William Russell (I00144). Both the Pierponts and the Russells were children of Yale's founding trustees: Rev. James Pierpont (Yale founding trustee 1701-1714, married Mary Hooker) and Rev. Noadiah Russell of Middletown (also a founding trustee 1701). The two clerical families who built Yale together also intermarried across two sibling pairs simultaneously. Hannah Russell's gravestone in North Haven reads: "Relict of Samuel, she was formerly wife of Joseph Pierpont, and daughter of Rev. Noadiah Russell, age 86 yrs."

notable_stories.title: In seven months of 1758, Sarah Pierpont Edwards lost her husband Jonathan Edwards (March), son-in-law Aaron Burr Sr. (September 1757), daughter Esther (April), and then died herself (October) while collecting her orphaned grandchildren
notable_stories.summary: Aaron Burr Sr. died September 1757. Jonathan Edwards died March 22, 1758 — 34 days after becoming Princeton president, from complications of a smallpox inoculation. Esther Edwards Burr died April 7, 1758 — fifteen days later. Sarah Pierpont Edwards traveled to Philadelphia to collect the orphaned children of Esther and Aaron. She died October 2, 1758 — days after arriving. Four deaths in seven months. The orphaned children of Esther and Aaron Burr Sr. included Aaron Burr Jr. — the future 3rd Vice President of the United States — who was then only two years old.

notable_stories.title: Timothy Edwards — son of Jonathan Edwards and Sarah Pierpont, great-great-grandson of Thomas Hooker — named a son "Edward Hooker Edwards," explicitly carrying the Hooker name into the 5th generation of the Edwards family
notable_stories.summary: Timothy Edwards (H00381, b.1738) was the son of Jonathan Edwards and Sarah Pierpont, granddaughter of Rev. James Pierpont and Mary Hooker, great-granddaughter of Rev. Samuel Hooker, great-great-granddaughter of Thomas Hooker. Timothy named his son "Edward Hooker Edwards" (b.1763) — deliberately embedding the Hooker founding name as a middle name. This is now the 5th generation to carry a deliberate Hooker tribute name in this line. Timothy was a Princeton graduate, merchant, and judge at Stockbridge, Massachusetts. His son William Edwards (b.1770) later revolutionized American tanning technology.

notable_stories.title: J.P. Morgan's middle name "Pierpont" derives from this family — Thomas Hooker's great-great-great-grandson John Pierpont is J.P. Morgan's great-grandfather
notable_stories.summary: Chain from Thomas Hooker to J.P. Morgan: Thomas Hooker (H00001) → Samuel Hooker (H00007) → Mary Hooker Pierpont (H00034) × Rev. James Pierpont (Yale founding trustee) → Hezekiah Pierpont (HD0419) → John Pierpont (H00388, 1740-1805) → James Pierpont → John Pierpont the poet (1785-1866, abolitionist minister, author of "Jingle Bells") → Juliet Pierpont × Junius Spencer Morgan → John Pierpont Morgan (J.P. Morgan, 1837-1913). J.P. Morgan's middle name "Pierpont" explicitly honors this New Haven clerical family. The Pierpont who wrote "Jingle Bells" and the Pierpont who co-founded Yale are the same family tree. Note: the Morgan family line descends from James Morgan of New London CT — entirely separate from Theophilus Morgan who married Hezekiah's widow.

notable_stories.title: Hannah Hooker named both her first and second son "Hooker Norton" — and three generations later her great-grandson Hooker Bartlett carried the name to Wisconsin, serving in the War of 1812
notable_stories.summary: Hannah Hooker (H00126) and Reuben Norton named their first son "Hooker Norton" (H00399, b.1741) — he died at 20 months. They named the next son "Hooker Norton No. 2" (H00401, b.1744). Their daughter Azubah Norton (H00405) had a son named "Hooker Bartlett" (HD0436, b.ca.1788), carrying the tribute name into the fourth generation. Hooker Bartlett served as a Private in the War of 1812, Vermont Militia. He removed to Wisconsin, and the 1850 census records him as "Hawker Bartlett" — a clerk's phonetic rendering of the name "Hooker." His daughter Miranda Emily Bartlett Adams lived to age 96 (1817-1914), spanning the entire 19th century from the War of 1812 to the eve of World War I.

notable_stories.title: Rev. Samuel Hooker — Thomas Hooker's son and Farmington's minister — formed the prosecutorial tribunal in the Hartford witch trials of the 1660s, which EH's 1909 genealogy does not mention
notable_stories.summary: The Hartford witch trials of the 1660s predate Salem by nearly thirty years. Connecticut was New England's most aggressive witch prosecutor — every person indicted in the colony's early years was convicted and hanged. Rev. Samuel Hooker of Farmington (H00007) formed a prosecutorial tribunal with Rev. Samuel Stone (Hartford) and Rev. Joseph Haynes (Wethersfield). The tribunal gathered evidence, recorded testimony, and interrogated witnesses. Rebecca Greensmith broke under interrogation — "felt as if her flesh had been pulled from her bones" — and confessed, implicating her husband Nathaniel. Both were hanged. Governor John Winthrop Jr. intervened gradually, and Connecticut became the colony that ended witch executions three decades before Salem began. Edward Hooker's 1909 genealogy makes no mention of this history. The prosecutorial role of ministers in these trials is documented by Connecticut State Historian Walter Woodward (UConn), whose Prospero's America won the Homer Babbidge Prize.

notable_stories.title: The first documented California death in the Hooker family tree: Roxanna Leete Goodwin, great-great-great-granddaughter of Thomas Hooker, died in Sacramento in 1875 — also a direct descendant of Governor William Leete of Connecticut
notable_stories.summary: Chain: Thomas Hooker → Samuel Hooker → Samuel Jr. → Elizabeth Hooker Gilbert (H00224) → Esther Gilbert Hubbard (H00416) → Elizabeth Hubbard Leete (HD0437) → Roxanna Leete Goodwin (HD0438, b.1806 Vermont, d.1875 Sacramento CA). Roxanna was also a direct descendant of Governor William Leete of Connecticut Colony (1676-1683) — the same Leete family as Mercy Leete Hooker (I00119) who married into the Hooker line. Her migration path: Peru NY → Winnebago IL (1848) → Bremer County Iowa (1856) → Sacramento CA. Two of Connecticut's founding families, converging again in Sacramento 239 years after Thomas Hooker founded Hartford. Her son Lyman Loomis Goodwin (HD0502) died April 1, 1913 in Kalama, Washington — extending the family migration to the Pacific Northwest. Her daughter Martha Goodwin van Gorder (HD0503) died 1920 in Iowa. The family trail: New Haven Colony → Braintree MA → Vermont → New York → Illinois → Iowa → Sacramento CA / Kalama WA.

notable_stories.title: Yale 1766 graduate William St. John — Loyalist — sent his jointly-owned enslaved man Dover to fight in the Continental Army to exempt himself from service, paying his brother in Dover's labor
notable_stories.summary: William St. John (HD0368, Yale 1766) was a Loyalist during the Revolution. On June 3, 1777, he and his brother Stephen executed a written agreement: William received half-ownership of Dover — "now inlisted into the Continental Service" — from Stephen, "to exempt me from all actual service," with William obligated to repay sixty dollars on demand. Dover, an enslaved man whose full name and fate are unrecorded, fought in the Continental Army while his owner avoided service. William's Loyalist sympathies meant he was effectively paying an enslaved man's freedom as the price of his own exemption. The note documenting this transaction was preserved in Norwalk for over a century.

notable_stories.title: Thomas Hooker's 6th-generation descendant Katherine Marsh Haven launched a chain that reached Fresno and Glendale, California by 1892 — through the Haven, Eames, and Hunting families
notable_stories.summary: Chain: Thomas Hooker → Sarah Newton Wilson → Sarah Wilson Marsh (H00060) → Alexander Marsh No.2 (H00187) → Katherine Marsh Haven (HD0462) → Anna Haven Leland (HD0468) → Mary Cutler Eames Hunting (HD0477) → William Henry Hunting (HD0484, d. Fresno CA 1892) and Juliet Hunting Morse (HD0483) → Mary Alice Morse Latshaw (HD0485, buried Glendale CA 1931). The migration path: Braintree MA → Holliston MA → Hopkinton MA → Ohio → Kansas → California. Note: the Morse family Sam Hooker (the project's creator) descends from through his father's mother Nancy Morse is a separate Morse family (Attleboro/NH line), not the George Henry Morse in this chain.

notable_stories.title: Enos Hine — 7th-generation Hooker descendant — died during an expedition to southern Texas, the first documented Texas death in the family tree
notable_stories.summary: Enos Hine (HD0489, b.1800) was the son of Eli Hine (HD0230) and Hannah Bronson, great-great-great-great-grandson of Thomas Hooker through Susannah Burwell → Susannah Newton → Mary Hooker → Thomas Hooker. He died during an expedition to southern Texas — date and exact circumstances unrecorded. His brother Alvin Hine married Sally Pierce, daughter of Rachel St. John — another connection to the St. John family already in the tree through H00094 Susannah Hooker Selleck.

notable_stories.title: Sarah Marsh Hall's widower John Hall married Susannah Boylston as his third wife — making him the stepfather of President John Adams
notable_stories.summary: Sarah Marsh (H00185), daughter of Sarah Wilson Marsh (H00060) and granddaughter of Thomas Hooker, married John Hall of Braintree in 1748. She died in 1765. Three years later, her widower John Hall married Susannah Boylston (Oct 17, 1766) — who was the mother of John Adams, 2nd President of the United States. Sarah Marsh had no children by John Hall; it is his third marriage that created the Adams connection. The Hooker-Adams link is tangential but documents the tight social network of founding Massachusetts families in the same generation.

notable_stories.title: The first sleigh bells ever manufactured in New Britain were made in 1800 in a house then occupied by the family of Elihu Burritt — by Joseph Shipman, husband of Mary Lee, great-granddaughter of Mercy Hooker
notable_stories.summary: In spring 1800, Joseph Shipman and his fellow apprentice James North Jr. set up the first sleigh-bell manufacturing operation in New Britain, Connecticut, working in the north room of the Sugden house — then occupied by the family of Elihu Burritt. Burritt (the "Learned Blacksmith" of New Britain) is himself a Hooker descendant through the Hart family, and appears elsewhere in the tree. Shipman started with $50 borrowed from Dr. Smalley, transported his goods to Boston on horseback, and grew into a major manufacturer — until the business revulsion of 1837 wiped out his works on Stanley Street. His wife Mary Lee Shipman was the granddaughter of Abigail Goodrich Lee (H00422), great-great-granddaughter of Thomas Hooker.

notable_stories.title: Chandler Cowles — great-great-grandson of Thomas Hooker — founded C. Cowles & Co in New Haven in 1816; the company is still in business in 2025, over 200 years later
notable_stories.summary: Chandler Cowles (HD0522, b.1816) was the son of Luman Cowles and Eunecia Pardee, grandson of Jabez Cowles (H00435, Revolutionary War soldier), great-grandson of Esther Hooker Cowles (H00230, died age 26), and great-great-great-grandson of Thomas Hooker. He founded C. Cowles & Co in New Haven, Connecticut, manufacturing carriage trimmings and lanterns. He died in 1865 age 48. His nephew Ruel Pardee Cowles (HD0518), a Civil War quartermaster, later became president of the company. As of 2025, the company has evolved and continues to operate — a 200-year-old enterprise tracing back to Thomas Hooker's Kensington descendants. Website: https://www.ccowles.com — currently based in North Haven, Connecticut.

notable_stories.title: After Luman Cowles died at 33, his widow Eunecia Pardee married his brother Linus Cowles — a levirate remarriage that kept the Cowles farm and children together
notable_stories.summary: Eunecia Pardee married Luman Cowles (HD0511) on January 1, 1812. Luman died January 24, 1823, age 33, leaving two young children. Five years later, on November 23, 1828, Eunecia married Luman's brother Linus Cowles (HD0510), who was already widowed after his first wife Ruth Cowles died in 1825. Eunecia and Linus then had three more children together — including Chandler Cowles (founder of C. Cowles & Co) and Ruel Pardee Cowles (Civil War quartermaster). The two brothers were both Esther Hooker's grandsons. Eunecia outlived both husbands, dying in 1869 age 74.

notable_stories.title: Hooker Dorchester — named for his Hooker ancestry — died in 1835 at age 46 from an accidental self-inflicted gunshot in Hounsfield, New York
notable_stories.summary: Hooker Dorchester (HD0525, b.1788) was the only child of Anna Cowles Dorchester (H00441) and Dea. Alexander Dorchester — named "Hooker" honoring his maternal Hooker ancestry. His father Alexander had served in both the Revolutionary War and the War of 1812. Hooker married Maria Van Schaick in 1825 and had at least two children. He died April 6, 1835 in Hounsfield, Jefferson County, New York, from an accidental self-inflicted gunshot wound at age 46. He was buried in Muscalunge Cemetery, Hounsfield.

notable_stories.title: Ebenezer Hooker Mix — named for his Hooker ancestry — began as supercargo on East India trade ships, rose to captain them, and retired as "one of the notable characters" of Farmington
notable_stories.summary: Ebenezer Hooker Mix (HD0523, b.1776) was the son of Judge John Mix and Martha Cowles Mix (H00437), grandson of Martha Hooker Cowles and Ezekiel Cowles. EH describes him as "one of the quaint sailor characters of Farmington. In his younger days he had been supercargo of ships in East India trade and subsequently he commanded ships in that trade. As his years increased and he retired from business became one of the notable characters of the town." His middle name "Hooker" was a deliberate tribute to his maternal Hooker ancestry.

notable_stories.title: Laura Hooker Thompson — named "Hooker" by her Cowles mother — married John Newton and moved to Ohio, potentially linking the Hooker and Newton founding families a generation after their 1636 Hartford connection
notable_stories.summary: Laura Hooker Thompson (HD0532, b.1789) carried the Hooker name as a middle name through her mother Pamelia Cowles (H00442), granddaughter of Martha Hooker Cowles. She married John Newton of Goshen CT in 1810 and removed with him to Richfield, Ohio. Her husband John Newton was the son of Isaac Newton and Rebecca Minot of Goshen CT. The Goshen Newton family may descend from the same Newton line as Roger Newton who married Mary Hooker (H00003) in Hartford c.1650 — if so, this marriage would be a convergence of the Hooker and Newton founding families across eight generations. Verification required.

notable_stories.title: Sarah Hooker married Hooker Gilbert in 1807 — her father and his mother were siblings, uniting two branches of Samuel Hooker Jr.'s family in a first-cousin-once-removed marriage
notable_stories.summary: Samuel Hooker Jr. (H00086) of Kensington had two children who each named a child for the Hooker family: Samuel (H00228) named daughter Sarah, and Elizabeth (H00224) named son Hooker Gilbert (H00420). In 1807, Sarah Hooker (H00432) married Hooker Gilbert (H00420) as his second wife. EH notes for Sarah's entry simply: "(For record look under her husband's name)" — a dry acknowledgment of the double-branch connection. The marriage united two grandchildren of Samuel Hooker Jr. in the same generation.

notable_stories.title: Austin Jay Knickerbocker — Duke University graduate and professional baseball player, generation 10 from Thomas Hooker — served in WWII and died in Dutchess County, New York in 1997
notable_stories.summary: Chain: Thomas Hooker → Samuel → Samuel Jr. (H00086) → Samuel (H00228) → Ann Hooker Stanley (H00429) → Amelia Stanley Hooker (HD0539) → William Hooker (H02791) → Janette Hooker Knickerbocker (H04402) → Jay Knickerbocker (HD0544) → Austin Jay Knickerbocker (HD0548). Austin attended Duke University, became a professional baseball player, served in World War II, married Helen Gertrude Germond in 1941, and died February 18, 1997 in Clinton Corners, Dutchess County, New York. Ten generations from the founding of Hartford to a professional ballplayer in Dutchess County.

notable_stories.title: Henry Dykeman — Thomas Hooker's 9th-generation descendant — drove a Model A camper to California and back in 1924 and founded a four-generation vegetable farm in Pawling still operating in 2021
notable_stories.summary: Henry Dykeman (HD0550, b.1900) was the son of Effie Keziah Hooker Dykeman (H04404) and Peter Dykeman, 9th-generation descendant of Thomas Hooker. In 1924, the first year of their marriage, Henry and Velma Ellis converted a Model A Ford into a camper and drove to California and back — reaching the Pacific coast that Thomas Hooker's congregation had set in motion when it walked from Cambridge to Hartford in 1636. Henry founded the Dykeman Family Farm in Pawling, a four-generation vegetable farm still operating in 2021. He was married 60 years. A stained glass window in the Pawling Baptist Church bears the names of his parents Effie and Peter Dykeman.

notable_stories.title: Ezra Stiles — Yale president 1778-1795 — was raised from infancy by his stepmother Esther Hooker Stiles, Thomas Hooker's great-granddaughter; his half-siblings were Hooker descendants
notable_stories.summary: Rev. Isaac Stiles (I00126, Yale 1722) had Ezra Stiles (b.1727) by his first wife. He married Esther Hooker (H00092) in October 1728, when Ezra was approximately one year old. Esther Hooker Stiles — great-granddaughter of Thomas Hooker — raised Ezra from infancy as his stepmother and lived until 1779, when Ezra was 52 years old and already a prominent minister and Yale president. Ezra is NOT a Hooker descendant by blood, but he grew up in the household of one and knew the Hooker legacy intimately. His half-siblings through Esther Hooker — Isaac Stiles Jr. (H00238) and siblings — were Thomas Hooker's great-great-grandchildren. Ruth Stiles (H00246, daughter of Esther Hooker Stiles) was described in sources as "niece of Ezra Stiles, President of Yale College" — confirming that contemporaries recognized the family connection. The North Haven genealogical record of Mabel Clark Stiles confirms the same. Two of Yale's greatest 18th-century presidents had deep Hooker connections: Ezra Stiles (raised by Hooker's great-granddaughter) and Timothy Dwight (married granddaughter of Sarah Pierpont Edwards, HD0379).

notable_stories.title: Lyman Ezra Munson — Thomas Hooker's great-great-great-great-grandson — was appointed by President Lincoln in 1865 as the first judge to the Supreme Court of the Territory of Montana
notable_stories.summary: Chain: Thomas Hooker → Samuel → Samuel → Esther Hooker Stiles (H00092) → Kesia Stiles Munson (H00239) → Job Lucianus Munson (H00455) → Ebenezer Beach Munson (HD0564) → Jeremiah Munson (HD0567) → Lyman Ezra Munson (HD0570, b.1822 Great Barrington MA). Yale Law School 1851. Appointed by Abraham Lincoln in 1865 as the first judge to the Supreme Court of the Territory of Montana. Served as Chief Justice for three years. Died Feb 13, 1908 New Haven. Buried Grove Street Cemetery. His daughter Mary Munson married Thomas Hubbard Russell — son of William Huntington Russell (Skull and Bones co-founder) — creating a second Hooker-Russell connection entirely separate from the Pierpont-Russell descent already documented.

notable_stories.title: William Huntington Russell — Yale co-founder of Skull and Bones — connected to Thomas Hooker's descendants TWICE: by his own Pierpont-Russell descent, and by his son's marriage to Mary Munson of the Stiles-Munson Hooker line
notable_stories.summary: William Huntington Russell (1809-1885) co-founded Skull and Bones at Yale in 1832 with Alphonso Taft. He was himself a Hooker descendant through the Pierpont-Russell line (documented in the existing Skull and Bones story). Now a second connection: his son Thomas Hubbard Russell (b.1851 New Haven) married Mary Munson (HD0571), daughter of Lyman Ezra Munson — Lincoln's first Montana judge — who was Hooker's great-great-great-great-grandson through Kesia Stiles Munson (H00239). The Russell family's connection to Thomas Hooker runs through two entirely separate branches of the Hooker family tree, uniting in the same New Haven household two centuries after Hartford was founded. Note also: "Mary Talcott Russell" (HD0572, granddaughter) — the name "Talcott" appearing in the Russell family again.

notable_stories.title: Henry Herbert Lyman — Thomas Hooker's great-great-great-great-grandson — perished with his wife on the Empress of Ireland in 1914 on their delayed honeymoon; he bequeathed his life's work to McGill University, founding the Lyman Entomological Museum
notable_stories.summary: Chain: Thomas Hooker → Samuel → Samuel → Esther Hooker Stiles (H00092) → Ashbell Stiles (H00241) → Hannah Stiles Lyman (H00463) → Henry Lyman (HD0583) → Henry Herbert Lyman (HD0587). Henry Herbert Lyman (b.1854 Montreal) spent years as a partner in the family pharmaceutical company while pursuing entomology as his life's passion. He spent decades caring for his ailing mother, delaying marriage until age 57. He married Florence Holwell Kirkby ca.1912. On May 28, 1914, they boarded the Empress of Ireland for their delayed honeymoon voyage. On May 29, 1914, the ship sank in the St. Lawrence River — 1,012 people died, more than the Titanic in proportion. Neither Henry nor Florence's body was recovered. In his will, he bequeathed his lepidoptera collection of ~20,000 specimens and $40,000 to McGill University — founding the Lyman Entomological Museum, still operating today. He had published over 60 papers on North American Lepidoptera. The Lyman Museum at McGill is the living legacy of Thomas Hooker's descendant. The Lyman collection now numbers nearly 3 MILLION specimens — the 2nd largest insect collection in Canada and one of the largest in North America. It holds the world's best collection of grasshoppers and crickets. The collection includes approximately 100 type specimens and a BEETLE COLLECTED BY CHARLES DARWIN IN THE 1830s. Museum URL: https://www.mcgill.ca/historicalcollections/departmental/lyman

notable_stories.title: John Easton Mills — mayor of Montreal, husband of Hooker descendant Hannah Lyman — was elected mayor in 1846 and died of typhus in 1847 while personally nursing Irish famine immigrants in the Pointe-St-Charles immigrant sheds
notable_stories.summary: Hannah Lyman (HD0581), daughter of Hannah Stiles Lyman (H00463) and Elisha Lyman, married John Easton Mills in Montreal in 1826. Mills was a prominent Montreal merchant who was elected mayor of Montreal in 1846. In 1847, at the height of the Irish famine migration, thousands of infected immigrants were held in sheds at Pointe-St-Charles. Mayor Mills went personally to care for the sick and contracted typhus. He died November 12, 1847, in office, aged 51. Their daughter Ada Maria Mills (HD0585) married into the Redpath sugar family; Ada and her youngest son Clifford died of gunshot wounds together June 13, 1901, in their Sherbrooke Street home, leaving an estate of ~$5M in today's value. Their daughter Alice Stiles Mills (HD0586) bore the name "Stiles" as a middle name — a tribute to the Stiles/Hooker ancestry running back to Esther Hooker of North Haven. The Redpath Mansion murders remain unsolved. Police were not called; the family convened a private coroner's inquest and buried both bodies within 48 hours. Speculation has persisted into the 2020s — murder-suicide, or possibly a third party. The case is included in "Great Unsolved Mysteries in Canadian History" (interactive series) and has been covered by multiple podcasts including Stuff You Missed in History Class. The Redpath Mansion was demolished by Montreal in 2014. Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1901_Redpath_Mansion_murders

notable_stories.title: The name "Esther Hooker" traveled from Thomas Hooker's granddaughter to her children's names across five generations: Esther Hooker Stiles (1702) → Esther Hooker Stiles (1760) → Alice STILES Mills (1845)
notable_stories.summary: Thomas Hooker's granddaughter Esther Hooker (H00092, b.1702) married Rev. Isaac Stiles. Her son Ashbell Stiles (H00241) named his firstborn daughter "Esther Hooker Stiles" (H00460, b.1760) — preserving the full two-name tribute. Three generations later, Ashbell's great-granddaughter in the Montreal Lyman family was named "Alice STILES Mills" (HD0586, b.1845) — Stiles as a middle name honoring the same ancestry, now in a Canadian family 200 years after Thomas Hooker arrived in Hartford.

notable_stories.title: Lemuel Bradley — described by EH as "an offensive Tory" — fled to Nova Scotia in 1783 with three children, leaving his eldest son and possibly his wife behind, and was never heard from again
notable_stories.summary: Esther Stiles Bradley (H00244), daughter of Esther Hooker Stiles (H00092) and granddaughter of Thomas Hooker, married Lemuel Bradley. EH's description is unusually pointed: Bradley "was a Tory in the Revolutionary War, and appearances seem to indicate that he was an offensive one." In 1783 — the year the Loyalist evacuation of New York brought thousands to Nova Scotia — Bradley took his three youngest children (Esther Stiles, Leverett, Hamlin) to Nova Scotia, leaving eldest son Chauncey behind. He may also have left his wife Esther, or she may have already died. No record of Bradley exists after 1783. His son Leverett eventually settled in Saint John, New Brunswick, where he married Mary Coy — a woman who became a published author of her spiritual memoir (1849, Boston) and a figure of the Second Great Awakening. The Hooker line continued in New Brunswick through an irony: the descendant of Hartford's founding Puritan minister arrived in Canada as the child of a man who opposed the Revolution.

notable_stories.title: Buckingham St. John — Yale College tutor and Thomas Hooker's great-great-grandson — drowned sailing from New Haven to Norwalk in 1771 at age 25; a formal elegy was published mourning his death
notable_stories.summary: Buckingham St. John (H00482) was the son of Susannah Selleck St. John (H00253), great-great-grandson of Thomas Hooker. He was serving as a Tutor at Yale College when he drowned May 4, 1771, sailing home to Norwalk from New Haven, age approximately 25. A formal elegy was published in his memory, written in the graveyard elegiac tradition: "The world now yields to night's returning sway; / The deeper glooms lead on the solemn hour..." The poem imagines his shade rising from the sea to warn a friend: "I once was St. John! from the bounds / Of unknown realms beneath the dreary wave..." His brother Hooker St. John (HD0367) had already died unmarried. His brother William St. John (HD0368, Yale 1766) sent the enslaved man Dover to fight in the Continental Army in his stead. Three brothers: one drowned as a Yale tutor, one died a Loyalist, one evaded service through an enslaved man's body.

notable_stories.title: Elizabeth Stone married Thomas Hooker's great-great-grandson Hezekiah Hooker; her sister Anna Stone married David Field — grandfather of Cyrus W. Field, who laid the first transatlantic telegraph cable in 1858
notable_stories.summary: EH notes explicitly: "Anna Stone, sister of Elizabeth who married Hezekiah Hooker, married David Field, grandfather of Cyrus W. Field, of telegraphic memory." Cyrus West Field (1819-1892) organized and financed the first successful transatlantic telegraph cable, completed August 1858 — connecting North America to Europe for the first time by wire. The connection is by marriage of siblings, not by descent: Elizabeth Stone became a Hooker; her sister Anna Stone became a Field. Hezekiah Hooker's children and Cyrus Field's father were first cousins by marriage. The two Stone sisters from Woodbury, Connecticut thus linked the founding family of Hartford to the family that wired the Atlantic.

notable_stories.title: The name "Hooker" traveled as a given name through four consecutive Fuller generations — Martin Hooker Fuller, John Hooker Fuller, Ralph Martin Hooker Fuller — from Hampton NY to Olympia, Washington, by 1971
notable_stories.summary: Samuel Hooker (H00494) of Hampton NY named his daughter Laura Hooker. Her son was Martin HOOKER Fuller (HD0591, b.1829) — Hooker as middle name. His son was John HOOKER Fuller (HD0594, b.1856 Poultney VT) — Hooker as middle name. His son was Ralph Martin HOOKER Fuller (HD0595, b.1881 St. Paul MN, d.1971 Olympia WA) — Hooker as middle name, fourth consecutive generation. The Fuller family preserved the Hooker name across four generations, migrating from Hampton NY through Vermont, Minnesota, and finally Washington State, where Thomas Hooker's great-great-great-great-great-grandson died in Olympia in 1971 — 335 years after Hooker walked to Hartford.

notable_stories.title: Josiah Hooker died July 24, 1776 in the aftermath of the Battle of Quebec, where Gen. Richard Montgomery was killed — the first major American assault of the Revolution
notable_stories.summary: Josiah Hooker (H00492, b.1758 Woodbury CT), son of James Hooker (H00255), served in the Continental Army and died July 24, 1776. EH: "died in the army at the defeat of Gen. Montgomery." The Battle of Quebec took place December 31, 1775 — General Richard Montgomery was killed in the assault. The American forces suffered significant casualties and prisoners. Josiah likely died of wounds or illness in the months following the battle. He was about 17 years old. His parents removed to Poultney, Vermont in 1779, three years after his death. His father honored him by naming a later son "Josiah No.2" (H00498, b.1777).

notable_stories.title: Mary Hooker — born 1777 in Woodbury, died Gorham NY ca.1876 — was among the longest-lived descendants of Thomas Hooker, reaching approximately 99 years of age
notable_stories.summary: Mary Hooker (H00507), daughter of William Hooker (H00259) and Mary Moseley, was born February 3, 1777. EH gives her death at "Gorham, N.Y. 1876" — Gorham, Ontario County, New York, on the Canandaigua Lake. She married first C.S. Fessenden of Genoa NY, then Edward D. Lake (previously widowed, b. ca.1775 Stratford CT). If she died in 1876, she was approximately 99 years old. Her second husband Edward D. Lake died March 27, 1864 aged about 89. Both reached near-century lifespans. Compare her father's mother Abigail Curtis Hooker — the Hezekiah,4 branch had notably long-lived family members.

notable_stories.title: Harriet Hooker Ingersoll — named for her Hooker ancestry — died at 27 in Michigan; her daughter Frances Harriet Mead reached Portland, Oregon, completing a journey from Hartford to the Pacific coast across seven generations
notable_stories.summary: Clarissa Hooker Ingersoll (H00512) moved to Augusta, Illinois and named her daughter "Harriet Hooker Ingersoll" (HD0602) — preserving the Hooker name into generation 6. Harriet Hooker died in Michigan in 1844 at age 27, leaving three young children. Her daughter Frances Harriet Mead (HD0604, b.1842 Farmington MI) married Eliphalet Pratt Hawley and died August 24, 1917 in Portland, Oregon — the first documented Oregon death in this Hooker line. Seven generations: Thomas Hooker (Hartford 1636) → William → Hezekiah → William → Clarissa → Harriet Hooker → Frances → Portland, Oregon 1917.

notable_stories.title: Bryan Hooker — Thomas Hooker's great-great-great-grandson — established one of Connecticut's first woolen manufacturies, served in the state legislature, and was a delegate to the 1818 Hartford convention that wrote Connecticut's first constitution
notable_stories.summary: Bryan Hooker (H00515, b.1764 Woodbury CT) was the son of Asahel Hooker (H00262) and great-great-great-grandson of Thomas Hooker. He established one of the first woolen manufacturies in Connecticut — his fulling mill, the "old yellow shop" on East and South Streets in Bristol, operated until it was destroyed by fire in 1903. Town Clerk 1806 and 1811-1820; State Representative 1812-1817; appointed July 4, 1818 as a delegate to the Hartford convention that framed Connecticut's first written Constitution of Civil Government. Deacon of the Congregational Church; noted for private charity and poor relief. Thomas Hooker founded Connecticut's first civil government in 1638; his great-great-great-grandson helped write its first formal constitution 180 years later.

notable_stories.title: George Ashmun — Thomas Hooker's great-great-great-grandson — presided over the 1860 Republican National Convention in Chicago that nominated Abraham Lincoln for President
notable_stories.summary: Chain: Thomas Hooker (H00001) → John Hooker (H00030) → John Hooker (H00102) → Rev. John Hooker (H00264) → Lucy Hooker Ashmun (H00532) → George Ashmun (HD0613). George Ashmun (b.1804, Yale 1823) was a Whig Congressman from Massachusetts 1845-1851, Speaker of the Massachusetts House, and a co-founder of the Republican Party with newspaper publisher Samuel Bowles. He presided over the Republican National Convention in Chicago in 1860 that nominated Abraham Lincoln for President of the United States. Thomas Hooker helped write the Fundamental Orders of Connecticut in 1638 — considered the first written constitution in the Western world. 222 years later, his great-great-great-grandson called the convention to order that elected the president who preserved the union those principles had founded. Note: George's brother John Hooker Ashmun was Royal Professor of Law at Harvard, first buried on Harvard Hill, and died at 32 still teaching despite terminal illness.

notable_stories.title: Two branches of the Jonathan Edwards–Thomas Hooker family network converge in Springfield: Worthington Hooker married Henrietta Edwards (great-granddaughter of Jonathan Edwards), while his brother Richard married Aurelia Dwight (granddaughter of Yale president Timothy Dwight who married Mary Edwards)
notable_stories.summary: In the Springfield MA branch of Judge John Hooker's family, the Edwards line crossed the Hooker line twice in the same generation. H01407 Worthington Hooker married Henrietta Edwards in 1855 — her great-grandfather was Jonathan Edwards, the Great Awakening preacher whose wife Sarah Pierpont (HD0418) was already a Hooker descendant through the Pierpont branch. H01408 Richard Hooker married Aurelia Dwight — whose grandfather was Rev. Timothy Dwight (Yale president 1795-1817), who had married Mary Edwards (H00379), daughter of Jonathan Edwards. Thomas Hooker's Northampton descendants thus married into the Edwards family through two different siblings in the same decade, long after Hooker and Edwards were the two most prominent ministers of New England Puritanism — the 1637 Antinomian Crisis that shaped both families.

notable_stories.title: Polly Hooker — daughter of Elijah Hooker of Kensington — was killed by lightning on May 31, 1821, age 30
notable_stories.summary: Polly Hooker (H00545, b.1791 Kensington CT) was the eleventh child of Elijah Hooker (H00267) and Susannah Judd Seymour Hooker. EH records simply: killed by lightning, May 31, 1821, Kensington, CT. She was 30 years old, unmarried, with no children. Her father Elijah died two years later in September 1823, as did her brother Anson (October 1823) — three deaths in the family within two years.

notable_stories.title: Hart Lee Marsh — named "Hart" to honor the Hart family ancestry of his great-grandmother Sarah Hart Hooker — carried the name from Norwich CT to Chautauqua County NY, where his wife Badorah founded a pioneer homestead still remembered in 1891
notable_stories.summary: Sarah Hart (H00268), daughter of Nathaniel Hart and Abigail Hooker (H00099), married Dr. Jonathan Marsh. Their son Joseph Marsh (HD0380) married Eunice Huxley. Their son was named "Hart Lee Marsh" (HD0649) — Hart honoring the maternal Hart ancestry, Lee possibly honoring the Lee family (Sarah's sister married Samuel Lee). Hart Lee removed to Chautauqua County, New York. His wife Badorah Marble Marsh was described in her 1891 obituary as: "one of the pioneers of Parkertown... settled and cleared the farm adjoining the old high bridge... consistent member of the church 65 years... always ready to lend a helping hand." She was survived by 33 great-grandchildren and 1 great-great-grandchild.

notable_stories.title: EH erroneously attributed Submit Hurlbut (b.1746) to Mehitable Hooker — corrected: Submit was daughter of Abigail Hart (H00269), resolving a confusion noted by EH himself in 1909
notable_stories.summary: EH 1909 entry 226 lists "Submit, b. Kensington, Sept. 5, 1746" as daughter of Mehitable Hooker and James Hurlbut. EH 269 then notes there is "considerable confusion in the record" and omits children. The Hurlbut Family Genealogy (1888, entry 118) definitively states: James Hurlbut married (1) Abigail Hart, sister of Gen. Selah Hart of Kensington. Submit (#321) is listed as their child, born Sept 5, 1746. The Farmington VR confirms the birth: "Sumbitt, d. Jeames, b. Sept. 5, 1746" but does not name the mother — consistent with Abigail Hart, NOT Mehitable Hooker. EH's error was attributing Submit to the wrong Hooker descendant. This research thread, opened when we found the Hurlbut genealogy entry in an earlier session, is now resolved.

notable_stories.title: Agathus Hart Hurlbut — named "Hart" for his grandmother Abigail Hart — was born June 28, 1776 while his father was away with the Continental Army; his mother died when he was two months old
notable_stories.summary: Raphael Hurlbut (HD0676) was away with the Continental Army in the summer of 1776. His wife Sarah Hubbard died in Wallingford CT when son Agathus Hart was about 2 months old. Agathus was named "Hart" honoring his paternal grandmother Abigail Hart Hurlbut (H00269), sister of Gen. Selah Hart of Kensington. Raphael continued with the army for years after Sarah's death — the Hurlbut genealogy notes he served "mostly in the capacity of teamster, or had charge of transportation trains; he was called Captain." He eventually removed to Springfield, Portage County, Ohio ca.1812, where he died in 1822.

notable_stories.title: Jessie Willcox Smith — celebrated illustrator of Good Housekeeping and Little Women — was Thomas Hooker's great-great-great-great-granddaughter through the Hart family of Berlin, Connecticut
notable_stories.summary: Chain: Thomas Hooker (H00001) → Samuel Hooker (H00007) → Samuel Hooker (H00028) → Mary Hooker Hart (H00100) → Capt. Samuel Hart (H00281) → Capt. Samuel Hart of Kensington (HD0056) → Jesse Hart (HD0715) → Harriet Hart Willcox (HD0726) → Katherine DeWitt Willcox Smith (HD0731) → Jessie Willcox Smith (HD0735). Jessie Willcox Smith (1863-1935) studied under Thomas Eakins at PAFA and Howard Pyle at Drexel. She illustrated 60+ books including Little Women, A Child's Garden of Verses, and Evangeline. She created all Good Housekeeping covers from December 1917 to 1933. Widely regarded as "one of the greatest pure illustrators" of the early 20th century. She lived in an artistic household in Villanova PA with Elizabeth Shippen Green and Violet Oakley, known as "The Red Rose Girls." She never married and had no children. Her mother Katherine was described as "a woman of remarkable beauty of person and character" in the History of Berlin, Connecticut (1916) — the same town her Hooker ancestors had helped found.

notable_stories.title: Sage Hurlburt — Thomas Hooker's great-great-great-great-great-grandchild — was killed when his carriage struck a train in Ohio in 1912, his wife injured beside him
notable_stories.summary: Chain: Thomas Hooker (H00001) → Hannah Hooker Hart (H00099) → Hannah Hart Stanley (H00272) → Seth Stanley (H00553) × Ann Hooker Stanley (H00429) → Nancy Stanley Hurlbut (HD0538) → Samuel Stanley Hurlbut (HD0747) → Stanley Sage "Sage" Hurlburt (HD0750). Note: Seth Stanley married Ann Hooker — herself a Hooker descendant through Samuel Hooker (H00228). So Sage Hurlburt carried Hooker blood through two converging lines. Sage was a leading merchant, postmaster, and township trustee in Freedom Township, Ohio. He died March 1, 1912 when his carriage collided with a train near Ravenna. His wife Josephine's first husband had also died young — she had married Sage after relocating from Michigan. She was injured in the same accident but survived.

notable_stories.title: Seth Stanley — son of Hannah Hart Hooker — married Ann Hooker, daughter of Samuel Hooker, making their children doubly descended from Thomas Hooker
notable_stories.summary: Seth Stanley (H00553) was the son of Hannah Hart (H00272, Hooker descendant) and Thomas Stanley. Ann Hooker (H00429) was the daughter of Samuel Hooker (H00228) and Sarah Norton — a direct Hooker descendant. Seth and Ann were both great-great-grandchildren of Thomas Hooker through different lines. Their children — Amanda, Lydia H., Samuel, Seth, Nancy, and Amelia — were doubly descended from Thomas Hooker: once through the Hart-Stanley maternal line, once through the Hooker paternal line. Nancy Stanley then married Sylvester Hurlbut and moved to Ohio, further carrying both Hooker lines westward.

notable_stories.title: In 1777, Gen. Selah Hart sat in a British prison while his enslaved man Pharaoh fought for American freedom at Germantown — yet Hart later claimed all of Pharaoh's army wages as the price of his freedom
notable_stories.summary: Selah Hart (H00273), son of Nathaniel Hart and Abigail Hooker (H00099), owned at least two enslaved men: Jack and Pharaoh. Hart was captured at the Battle of Long Island Aug 27, 1776 and held ~2 years. During that imprisonment, Pharaoh was fighting for the Continental Army at Germantown (1777) and Monmouth (1778), having been allowed to enlist on the condition that he pay Hart a portion of his wages for his freedom. At the end of Pharaoh's service, Hart claimed all wages — not just a portion — citing the economic hardship of his imprisonment and lost farm labor. Pharaoh had no legal recourse. Jack, by contrast, was freed at 21 without payment, having been given "living, clothing, and education better than the average white lads." Hart was also a delegate to the 1788 CT Constitutional Convention, magistrate, constable, deacon, and "Patron Saint of Connecticut." Both Pharaoh and Selah Hart received Revolutionary War pensions 35 years later. Source: Christopher Menapace, Digital Farmington Project; Slavery in Berlin — Forgotten No Longer (Berlin Peck Library, 2022).

notable_stories.title: In December 1721 and January 1722, two Lee sisters married two Langdon brothers within three weeks — a Farmington family celebration whose grandchildren would marry into the Hooker tree through two separate lines a generation later
notable_stories.summary:
Stephen Lee of Farmington had two daughters born two years apart: Elizabeth (b. Jul 12, 1694) and Sarah (b. Nov 8, 1696). On December 28, 1721, Elizabeth Lee married Samuel Langdon. On January 18, 1722 — three weeks later — Sarah Lee married John Langdon. Two brothers, two sisters, one winter. This was almost certainly a family occasion — a double celebration in the tight-knit Farmington community where families had known each other for generations. 

A generation later, their granddaughters separately married into the Hooker tree: Elizabeth × Samuel → Susannah Langdon → married Ashbel Hooker (H00266); Sarah × John → Martha Langdon → married Samuel Goodrich → daughter Rhoda Goodrich → married Selah Stanley (H00555), son of Hannah Hart Hooker (H00272). 

The two granddaughters were first cousins. Neither marriage was arranged — they were simply the natural consequence of a community where the same families had intermarried for three generations. The Kensington kinship network was not a web of calculation; it was the residue of people living, marrying, and dying in the same few square miles for a hundred years.

notable_stories.title: Cyprian Hart — son of Nathaniel Hart No. 2 of Kensington — was adopted at age four by his childless uncle General Selah Hart and made his heir; his widow and General Hart's widow kept the Kensington homestead together for thirty-eight years
