notable_stories.summary: General Selah Hart (H00273) of Kensington, Connecticut — captured by the British at the retreat from New York in September 1776, later commander of Connecticut Militia, the orator 'too full for utterance' when Washington breakfasted in Berlin in 1789 — had only one natural child, Mary (H00556), who died young. When his brother Nathaniel Hart No. 2 (H00274) died at Kensington on October 13, 1773, Selah adopted his orphaned four-year-old nephew Cyprian Hart (H00562), son of Nathaniel and Martha Norton, and raised him at the General Hart homestead as his heir. Cyprian married Lucy Hooker (H00537) of the same Kensington parish on December 24, 1795 — they were second cousins through their shared great-grandfather Hon. John Hooker — and had six children. Cyprian died on March 1, 1806 aged thirty-seven, predeceasing his adoptive uncle Selah by fourteen weeks (Selah died June 10, 1806). Per Edward Hooker's 1909 genealogy: 'his widow and the widow of his uncle Gen. Selah Hart occupied the General Hart house and property together as long as they lived.' Ruth Cole Hart, Selah's second wife, lived in the house until her death January 15, 1844 at the age of one hundred and one years, two months, and sixteen days — thirty-eight years a widow. Lucy Hooker Hart lived another seven years alone, dying July 8, 1851 at seventy-nine. The General Hart homestead descended through Cyprian's daughter Abigail Hart (H01446), who married Oliver Moore on March 25, 1829; the Hart Genealogy locates the family farm: 'where the late Oliver Moore lived.' Three generations of property descent — General Selah Hart → adopted nephew Cyprian → daughter Abigail Moore — ended Hart family ownership of the house Selah had built before the Revolution.

notable_stories.title: Gideon Cole — husband of Chloe Beckley, great-great-granddaughter of Thomas Hooker — was offered the land on which Rochester, New York was later built, but refused to settle in a swamp and chose the hills of Steuben County instead
notable_stories.summary: Ensign Gideon Cole (b. May 15, 1751 Farmington CT; d. Sep 2, 1826 Prattsburg NY) served under Lt. Col. Marinus Willett's Regiment of Levies in the Revolutionary War. He married Chloe Beckley (HD0756) on Sep 25, 1777 — his third cousin once removed, daughter of Anna Hart Hooker (H00277). The couple removed to Prattsburgh, Steuben County, NY ca.1795. Per family tradition: "he was offered the tract of land on which the city of Rochester was later located, but he refused to settle in a swamp and preferred the Hills of Steuben." Rochester is now the third-largest city in New York state.

notable_stories.title: Anna Celia Babcock Adams — Thomas Hooker's great-great-great-great-great-great-granddaughter — ran Head Start programs at Cabrini-Green in Chicago and at the US Capitol as part of President Johnson's War on Poverty
notable_stories.summary: Chain: Thomas Hooker (H00001) → Mary Hooker Hart (H00100) → Lt. Samuel Hart (I00029) → Anna Hart Hollister (H00277) → Chloe Beckley Cole (HD0756) → Emily Cole Parmalee (HD0760) → Elizabeth Elvira Parmalee Waldo (HD0762) → Theron Linsley Waldo (HD0764) → Florence Waldo Babcock (HD0765) → Anna Celia Babcock Adams (HD0773). Generation 10 from Thomas Hooker. Anna Celia Babcock (1926-2017) graduated Cornell age 19 on wartime accelerated program. Earned Masters at Northwestern. Ran Head Start near US Capitol for Dept. of Labor during Johnson's War on Poverty. Executive Director, Lutheran Welfare Service Head Start, Chicago — regularly visited Cabrini-Green Center during the era of gang-related sniper fire. "Never met a child she did not like." Died Sep 4, 2017 Evanston IL age 90. Thomas Hooker arrived in Hartford in 1636 to build a godly community. 381 years later, his direct descendant was still building communities for children at the margins of American life.

notable_stories.title: Mary Hart — great-granddaughter of Thomas Hooker — married Dr. Joseph Welles of Wethersfield, almost certainly a descendant of Gov. Thomas Welles, who arrived in Hartford the same year as Thomas Hooker
notable_stories.summary:
Thomas Hooker led his congregation from Newtown (Cambridge) to Hartford in 1636. Thomas Welles arrived in Hartford the same year, 1636, settling first in Hartford before removing to Wethersfield. They were fellow founders of the Connecticut colony. Welles served as Treasurer, Secretary, Deputy Governor, and Governor (1655, 1658); he and Hooker were among the most prominent men in early Connecticut. 

When Mary Hart (H00279) — great-granddaughter of Thomas Hooker through Samuel Hooker (H00028) and Mary Hooker Hart (H00100) — married Dr. Joseph Welles of Wethersfield on January 17, 1754, she united two of the founding families of Hartford Colony in the third generation of American-born descendants. 

The specific Welles genealogy line for Dr. Joseph has not yet been confirmed in the published Welles genealogy; the Wethersfield geography and generation strongly suggest descent from Gov. Thomas Welles. The Welles Family Association (wellesfamily.org) published a three-volume genealogy (completed 2015, Barbara Jean Mathews CG FASG) that may confirm the line. Contact WFA when project launches.

notable_stories.title: Simeon Lincoln — husband of Huldah Porter, great-great-granddaughter of Thomas Hooker — was lost at sea near Surinam in January 1821 when the sloop Alexander sank, killing 14 others; the death notice was published by his own son, Simeon Lincoln Jr.
notable_stories.summary: Simeon Lincoln (b. ca.1756 CT; d. Jan 1821) married Huldah Porter (H00578) ca.1780. He is described as "of Berlin, CT, aged 65." In January 1821, the sloop Alexander sank near Surinam (West Indies). Simeon Lincoln drowned with 14 others. The obituary notice was published in a New York newspaper by his son, Simeon Lincoln Jr., who was the editor of the newspaper where the notice appeared. Huldah Porter had died 1812, nine years before her husband. The death notice reads: "Lost by the shipwreck of the sloop Alexander near Surinam in January last, Mr Simeon Lincoln, of Berlin, (Ct.) aged 65. Fourteen others were lost at the same time."

notable_stories.title: Dr. Thomas Goodrich Lee — Hooker descendant — was the first physician to introduce religious exercises among patients at McLean Asylum and died at age 28 "in the midst of a bright career of usefulness"
notable_stories.summary: Thomas Goodrich Lee (HD0786, b. Sep 1, 1808 Berlin CT; d. Oct 29, 1836 Worcester MA) was son of Thomas Lee and Electa Riley Lee (HD0778), great-great-great-granddaughter of Thomas Hooker through Huldah Hart Porter (H00280). Yale Medical College 1830. Assistant physician at the Retreat for the Insane, Hartford 1830-34. Superintendent of McLean Asylum, Charlestown MA 1834-36. The Hartford Courant Nov 1836: "Dr. Lee was the first to introduce religious exercises among the insane and the experiment was attended with the happiest results." "He was cut off in the midst of a bright career of usefulness, but not until he had matured the plan which has done so much for the sons and daughters of affliction." He died at age 28 while visiting Massachusetts Hospital in Worcester. His widow Susan Clark married Rev. Joseph S. Gallagher of Bloomfield NJ. Thomas Hooker himself preached extensively on the relationship between spiritual healing and the soul's distress — his descendant Thomas Goodrich Lee found a way to bring that connection into the first modern institutions for mental illness.

notable_stories.title: Frances Livingston Hart — great-great-granddaughter of Thomas Hooker — married Rev. Clement Moore Butler, Chaplain of the US Senate, who delivered the funeral addresses for both John C. Calhoun and Henry Clay
notable_stories.summary: Chain: Thomas Hooker (H00001) → Sarah Hooker Hart (H00101) → Matthew Hart Jr. (H00286) → Seth Hart M.A. (H00608) → William Henry Hart (HD0793) → Frances Livingston Hart Butler (HD0794). Frances Hart married Rev. Clement Moore Butler in Washington DC in 1836. Butler served as 36th Chaplain of the United States Senate 1850-1853. On April 1, 1850, he delivered the funeral address for Senator John C. Calhoun. On July 1, 1852, he delivered the funeral address for Senator Henry Clay. He later served as chaplain in Rome (1861-64) and professor of ecclesiastical history in Philadelphia until 1884. The ordination scandal: Bishop Onderdonk, who ordained Butler in 1837, was subsequently suspended for alleged improper advances toward Mrs. Butler in a carriage the evening before the ordination. Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clement_Moore_Butler

notable_stories.title: Matthew Hart Jr. (son of Matthew Hart, Hooker descendant) married Urania Hooker Hart (daughter of Ashbel Hooker) — uniting two separate Hooker descendant lines through the tight Kensington kinship network
notable_stories.summary: Matthew Hart Jr. (H00607) descended from Thomas Hooker through Samuel Hooker → Samuel Hooker → Sarah Hooker Hart → Matthew Hart → Matthew Hart Jr. Urania Hooker Hart (H00534) descended directly through Thomas Hooker → John Hooker → John Hooker Jr. → Ashbel Hooker → Urania. Their daughter Ruth Hart Bly (HD0626) carried both Hooker descent lines.

notable_stories.title: Col. Noadiah Hooker and Rebecca Griswold lost twin sons within days of their birth in 1766, then their daughter Lucy died on her 17th birthday in New Haven
notable_stories.summary: Among the eleven children of Col. Noadiah Hooker (H00288) and Rebecca Griswold: Sarah (EH 620) died October 19, 1765 — 4 days after birth. In October 1766, twins John and Joseph were born on the same day (Oct 24) and died within a day of each other — Joseph Oct 25, John Oct 26. Three infant deaths in the first two years of marriage. Then Lucy (EH 624) was born January 16, 1771, and died January 16, 1788 — exactly on her 17th birthday — in New Haven CT. Col. Noadiah Hooker was raising the first troops at Farmington for the Revolution during these years, commanding 100+ men to Boston. The public hero and the private grief ran in parallel.

notable_stories.title: Col. Noadiah Hooker died in Farmington on June 3, 1823; his daughter Sally died in St. Armand, Canada 33 days later on July 6 — father and daughter unknowingly dying within a month of each other across the border
notable_stories.summary: Col. Noadiah Hooker (H00288), the Revolutionary War hero who marched 100+ men to Boston before any other Connecticut troops, died at Farmington CT on June 3, 1823, age 85. His daughter Sally (HD0390) had married George Koch Cook, a prominent citizen of St. Armand, Quebec, in 1810. She died at St. Armand on July 6, 1823 — 33 days after her father. Whether she knew of her father's death before she died is unknown. Communication between Farmington CT and St. Armand Quebec in 1823 would have taken days to weeks by post.

notable_stories.title: Joseph Hooker Jr. — son of the Farmington Hookers — remained neutral in the Revolution through his Loyalist wife's influence, was ostracized by his hometown afterward, and rebuilt his reputation from scratch in New York
notable_stories.summary: EH's portrait of Joseph Hooker Jr. (H00292) is one of the most psychologically acute in the entire book. He was a Lieutenant in the Militia before marriage; he married into the Ingersoll family, "strong loyalists, though never of a tricky, untrustworthy kind." Through Mary's influence he stayed neutral. After the war: "the confidence of the town was entirely withheld from him... honors and important trusts were heaped upon his brother and cousins who had taken an active part in the war." His brother was Col. Noadiah Hooker (H00288) — the man who marched 100+ troops to Boston before any other Connecticut company. "Sensitive under this very natural want of confidence he removed to New York." In Litchfield, Herkimer County, he built a reputation for "strict and unswerving integrity, and strong loyalty to the new born nation." He died there June 1799. His wife Mary Ingersoll outlived him until 1805.

sources.label: St. Paul's Episcopal Church Medina OH

sources.short: Church Life magazine, Diocese of Ohio, Summer 2018

notable_stories.title: Sally Pomeroy — great-great-granddaughter of Thomas Hooker — married Rev. Roger Searle, who organized the first Episcopal parish in Ohio and preached the first religious service in Medina County on March 11, 1817
notable_stories.summary: Sally Pomeroy (H00655) married Rev. Roger Searle Aug 7, 1800. Searle (b.1775 CT; d.1826 Ashtabula OH) came to Ohio as a missionary and organized St. Peter's Parish, Ashtabula — the first Episcopal parish in Ohio — on February 19, 1817. On March 11, 1817, he preached the first religious service in Medina County at the Hamilton cabin, organizing St. Paul's Church of Medina. He also organized Trinity Cleveland, St. Mark's Columbia, St. James' Boardman, and St. Luke's Ravenna. Thomas Hooker himself arrived in Hartford as a minister to found a godly community. His great-great-great-granddaughter's husband became the founding minister of the Episcopal Church in Ohio.
notable_stories.one_line: A Connecticut Hooker descendant's husband became the founding minister of the Episcopal Church in Ohio — and their son practiced law there for 43 years.

sections.header: March 11, 1817 — first religious service in Medina County
sections.body: Rev. Roger Searle of Connecticut rode into Medina Township on March 11, 1817, and met with settlers at the home of Zenas Hamilton. He organized St. Paul's Episcopal Church and shortly after, congregants cleared land near Weymouth and built a log church — which also served as a school and meeting house for other denominations.

sections.header: He attended the 1817 General Convention representing Ohio
sections.body: Already a clerical deputy from the Diocese of Connecticut, Searle was appointed by Ohio's fledgling church to represent their interests before the General Convention in New York, given $60 for expenses. He arrived with a letter from Col. James Kilbourn describing 'the religious situation in Ohio.' The Convention placed Ohio provisionally under the Bishop of Pennsylvania and enabled the election of Ohio's first bishop.

sections.header: Seven parishes, one missionary, one decade
sections.body: Searle organized seven Episcopal parishes in Ohio: St. Peter's Ashtabula (the first, Feb 19, 1817), St. Paul's Medina, Trinity Cleveland, St. Mark's Columbia, St. James' Boardman, and St. Luke's Ravenna. He died in Ashtabula in 1826 at 51. Thomas Hooker arrived in Hartford as a minister to found a godly community. His great-great-great-granddaughter's husband became the founding minister of the Episcopal Church in Ohio.

notable_stories.title: Frances Johnston married William Allee on December 5, 1876 — just 15 months after he had buried her sister Adelaide, his previous wife, who died two days before her 36th birthday
notable_stories.summary: Adelaide Sophronia Johnston Allee (HD0837) died September 8, 1875 in Paola, Kansas, two days before her 36th birthday, leaving infant son Victor Burnette Allee. William Allee had previously been widowed twice (Polly Beckwith, Samantha Beckwith). On December 5, 1876 — 15 months after Adelaide's death — he married Adelaide's sister Frances Ellen Gertrude Johnston (HD0838). Frances and Adelaide were daughters of Nancy Sarah Marie Searle Johnston (HD0834), daughter of Rev. Roger Searle and Sally Pomeroy (H00655). Frances lived until 1937 — a descendant of the founding Hooker family who outlived the century she was born in.

sources.short: Orderly Book of Capt. Ichabod Norton, Col. Mott's Regiment, 1776
sources.notes: Original MS owned by Charles Mulford Robinson, Rochester NY, 1909

notable_stories.title: In 1777 at Peekskill, Capt. Ichabod Norton — husband of Ruth Strong, daughter of Ruth Hooker — served under Colonel Noadiah Hooker, a direct Hooker descendant: two branches of the Hooker family tree converging on the same battlefield
notable_stories.summary: Col. Ichabod Norton served in the Revolutionary War under Col. Mott's Regiment in 1776 (Northern Campaign: Skeensborough, Fort Ann, Ticonderoga, Mt. Independence VT). In 1777 he served at Peekskill under Colonel Hooker — documented in his own Orderly Book. That Colonel Hooker was Col. Noadiah Hooker (H00288), Thomas Hooker's great-great-grandson, the man who marched 100+ men to Boston before any other Connecticut company. Norton's wife Ruth Strong (H00297) was Thomas Hooker's great-great-granddaughter through the Strong line. Norton was promoted to Major for his service. His Orderly Book manuscript was held in 1909 by his descendant Charles Mulford Robinson of Rochester NY, through the line of his eldest daughter Elizabeth Norton Robinson.

notable_stories.title: Rev. Cyprian Strong — great-great-great-grandson of Thomas Hooker — married Sarah Bull, granddaughter of Capt. Thomas Bull who had followed Thomas Hooker to Hartford in 1636
notable_stories.summary: Capt. Thomas Bull sailed to New England on the "Hopewell" in September 1635 and removed to Hartford with Rev. Thomas Hooker on May 31, 1636. He served under Capt. John Mason in the Pequot War of 1637. His granddaughter Sarah Bull married Rev. Cyprian Strong (H00299) on November 9, 1768 — Thomas Hooker's great-great-great-grandson. Two of the founding families of Hartford Colony united in marriage 132 years after they arrived together.

notable_stories.title: Siblings Cyprian Strong and Elizabeth Strong — both great-great-great-grandchildren of Thomas Hooker — married siblings Martin Bull and Sarah Bull on the same day in 1768
notable_stories.summary: On November 9, 1768 in Farmington, Connecticut: Rev. Cyprian Strong (H00299) married Sarah Bull, AND Elizabeth Strong (H00300) married Deacon Martin Bull — Sarah's brother, on the same day. Cyprian and Elizabeth were brother and sister, children of Capt. Asahel Strong Jr. and Ruth Hooker Strong (H00103). Martin and Sarah were brother and sister, children of Jonathan and Abigail Bull of Farmington. EH explicitly notes the connection: Martin Bull was "brother of Sarah Bull, who m. her brother Cyprian Strong." The Bull family had arrived in Hartford with Thomas Hooker in 1636 — Capt. Thomas Bull was a Hartford founder. Three generations later, two Bull siblings married two Hooker-descendant siblings in a double wedding.

notable_stories.title: Rev. Samuel Hooker preached his Farmington sermon while eight armed guards stacked muskets inside the church door — news had just arrived that Hezekiah Willet, brother of his wife, had been killed by Native Americans at Swansea
notable_stories.summary: Julius Gay's Historical Pamphlets on Farmington (1890-1911) describes the scene in Samuel Hooker's church: guards with muskets march in, stack arms within reach, and take assigned seats. "Why this armed invasion of the house of God? Simply because the noble savage is on the war path." Hezekiah Willet — brother of Samuel's wife Mary Willet Hooker — had just been killed at Swansea. Johanna Smith of Farmington had been killed at Hatfield; Roger Orvis wounded. The passage describes Samuel Hooker "fresh from the honors of Harvard" turning the hourglass and ascending the lofty pulpit. He had previously declined a call from Springfield, and was installed as successor to his brother-in-law Rev. Roger Newton (I00003). Source: Gay pamphlet, archive.org/details/historicalpamphl00gayj

notable_stories.title: John Hooker Esq. — Thomas Hooker's grandson — fined Captain Hawley for disturbing church worship during Farmington's singing controversy, setting off a petition to the General Assembly full of "humor and learned puns"
notable_stories.summary: The Farmington singing controversy of the 1720s pitted the "Old Way" of psalm-singing against the "New Way" introduced by Boston ministers. Deacon Hart set a new tune ("Bella tune"); Capt. Joseph Hawley, used to the old Cambridge Short Tune, sang over him, causing "unhappy discord." John Hooker, Esq. (H00030) — Thomas Hooker's grandson and town magistrate — promptly fined Hawley for a breach of the Sabbath. Hawley, a member of the General Assembly, appealed to that body with a petition described as "full of humor and learned puns" explaining he had not known "helium tune from pax tune." The controversy lasted until just before the Revolutionary War. Asahel Strong Sr. (father of Capt. Asahel Strong Jr., I00055) was separately presented to court for erecting an effigy of Capt. Hawley at the Farmington parade ground in a "clandestine manner." Source: Julius Gay, Historical Pamphlets, Farmington 1890-1911.

notable_stories.title: Henrietta Swan Leavitt — great-great-great-great-granddaughter of Thomas Hooker — discovered the period-luminosity relationship for Cepheid variable stars, providing the "cosmic yardstick" that enabled Edwin Hubble to prove the universe is expanding
notable_stories.summary: Chain: Thomas Hooker (H00001) → Samuel Hooker → Roger Hooker (EH line) → Sarah Hooker (H00302) → Roger Hooker Leavitt (H00685? No — through Roswell) → Roswell Leavitt → Erasmus Darwin Leavitt → George Roswell Leavitt (HD0881) → Henrietta Swan Leavitt (HD0886). Generation 8 from Thomas Hooker. Henrietta Swan Leavitt (1868-1921) worked at Harvard College Observatory, earning $0.30/hour cataloging photographic plates. In 1908 she noted, and in 1912 confirmed, that Cepheid variable stars with greater luminosity have longer periods — a precise, predictable relationship. This "period-luminosity relationship" became the fundamental cosmic yardstick for measuring distances across the universe. Edwin Hubble used her work to determine that galaxies exist far beyond the Milky Way and that the universe is expanding — the foundation of modern cosmology. Gösta Mittag-Leffler attempted to nominate her for the 1926 Nobel Prize in Physics, only to learn she had died of cancer in 1921. The Nobel Prize cannot be awarded posthumously. Asteroid 5383 Leavitt and a lunar crater bear her name. "A straight line can readily be drawn among each of the two series of points... showing that there is a simple relation between the brightness of the variables and their periods." — Henrietta Swan Leavitt, 1912.

notable_stories.title: Rev. Jonathan Leavitt — husband of Sarah Hooker — was dismissed from one church for dragging a runaway enslaved woman home by rope, and from another for Loyalist sympathies, then sued his parishioners for back wages and won £700
notable_stories.summary:
Rev. Jonathan Leavitt (Yale 1758) married Sarah Hooker (H00302) in 1761. 

PORTRAIT IN WORDS: Leavitt "wore a large, full-powdered wig, and when he entered the meeting-house, the whole congregation rose to do obeisance to the man in black, who, in his turn, always responded with a full bow." His wife Sarah followed in "full suit of brocade lutestring, without any bonnet, holding a fan to shade the sun from her face, as was the fashion 'down country'." 

HIS SERMONS: A colleague recorded: "His sermons are not fresh and beautiful by the imagination, not ardent and overflowing with love, but didactic, dry, and clean, and very long. His services were delivered in a dull monotony, and his prayers were incredibly long, in public and in family devotions." Another noted he "would do more execution with one nod of his wig, than you or I could in talking half an hour." 

AT WALPOLE NH: "Having dragged home a negro slave, a woman, who had run away, by a rope attached to his saddle" — Col. Bellows declared he would "unsettle" him. Dismissed ca.1764. 

AT CHARLEMONT MA: Loyalist sympathies caused congregation to hold back pay. Town voted to shut the church; constable barred him. Leavitt moved to the schoolhouse and preached another decade. Finally turned out 1785; sued his parishioners; won approximately £700. 

DESPITE ALL THIS: His descendants included Underground Railroad operators, an abolitionist editor, the astronomer who enabled Hubble to prove the universe is expanding, and a US Ambassador to Iraq. 

OLIVER ELLSWORTH CONNECTION: His sister Jemima Leavitt married Capt. David Ellsworth — making Jonathan the uncle of Chief Justice Oliver Ellsworth, Founding Father and first Chief Justice of the US Supreme Court.

sources.short: NPS Underground Railroad Network to Freedom

notable_stories.title: Roger Hooker Leavitt and his brother Hart — grandsons of Sarah Hooker — operated Underground Railroad stations in Charlemont, Massachusetts, sheltering fugitive slave Basil Dorsey for five years; Roger's home is on the National Park Service Underground Railroad Network to Freedom
notable_stories.summary: Roger Hooker Leavitt (H00685) remained on the old Heath homestead and then purchased a brick mansion in Charlemont on the Deerfield River. His son Col. Roger Hooker Leavitt Jr. (HD0880) sheltered Basil Dorsey, who escaped Frederick County, Maryland in 1836. "It was always understood that a resting place was at Mr. Blake's and Mr. Leavitt's." Dorsey remained with the Leavitt family 5+ years. Hart Leavitt's adjoining farm also sheltered escaped slaves. Their brother Rev. Joshua Leavitt (abolitionist editor) coordinated from New York. The home of Col. Roger Hooker Leavitt is now part of the Academy at Charlemont campus and is listed on the National Park Service's National Underground Railroad Network to Freedom. Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Hooker_Leavitt A Thomas Hooker descendant whose grandfather preached in a Connecticut Congregational church in 1636 — four generations later, his descendants hid escaped enslaved people in the hills of western Massachusetts.

sources.short: Emerson Davis, Biographical Sketches of Congregational Pastors

notable_stories.title: Sarah Hooker Leavitt — great-great-granddaughter of Thomas Hooker — died suddenly in 1791 after her daughter Clarissa gave her the wrong medicine; Clarissa herself died unmarried seven years later
notable_stories.summary: Sarah Hooker (H00302) died October 11, 1791 at Heath, Massachusetts age 49. Per her husband's biography (Emerson Davis, Biographical Sketches of Congregational Pastors, vol.5 p.238): "She died suddenly as a consequence of taking wrong medicine." Per FindAGrave biography: the wrong medicine was given by her daughter Clarissa. Connecticut Courant obituary (Nov 7, 1791): describes her as "virtuous and amiable." Clarissa Leavitt (HD0856) — the only daughter, born 1762 — died January 11, 1798, unmarried, six years after her mother's death. Sarah had 12 children. She is buried at South Cemetery, Heath MA. Her gravestone reads: "Here lies the body of Sarah Leavitt, consort of the Rev'd J Leavitt, who died Oct 11 1791 in the 49 year of her age."

sources.short: Vietnam Veterans Memorial Wall of Faces

notable_stories.title: Gridley Barstow Strong — generation 10 from Thomas Hooker, son of the US Ambassador to Iraq — was killed by artillery fire in Vietnam on April 21, 1968 at age 21, during the Battle of Khe Sanh
notable_stories.summary: Chain: Thomas Hooker → Samuel → John → Roger → Sarah Hooker (H00302) → Roswell Leavitt → Erasmus Darwin Leavitt → George Roswell Leavitt → Martha Almira Leavitt Strong → Robert Campbell Strong (US Ambassador to Iraq) → Gridley Barstow Strong. Ten generations from Thomas Hooker's 1636 arrival in Hartford to a Marine rifleman killed in Quang Tri Province, Vietnam in 1968. The same generation as his great-aunt Henrietta Swan Leavitt's discovery — Gridley was born 47 years after Henrietta died. His father Robert C. Strong had just completed his posting as US Ambassador to Iraq the year before Gridley deployed. Vietnam Veterans Memorial Wall of Faces: https://www.vvmf.org/Wall-of-Faces/50331/GRIDLEY-B-STRONG/

sources.notes: Leavitt-Riedler Pumping Engine, ASME Historic Mechanical Engineering Landmark, 1894

notable_stories.title: Erasmus Darwin Leavitt Jr. — great-great-great-great-great-grandson of Thomas Hooker — was a founding member of the American Society of Mechanical Engineers, designed the steam engine for the USS Hartford, and served in the Civil War Navy
notable_stories.summary: Erasmus Darwin Leavitt Jr. (HD0880, 1836-1916) was born in Lowell, Massachusetts. He trained at Corliss & Nightingale in Providence RI before becoming assistant foreman for Harrison Loring in Boston. CIVIL WAR: Served aboard the USS Sagamore (Navy); later instructor in steam engineering at the United States Naval Academy. After the war he became a consulting engineer and one of the most prominent mechanical engineers in America. He was a FOUNDING MEMBER of the American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME). His 1894 Leavitt-Riedler Pumping Engine at Boston's Chestnut Hill High Service Pumping Station is designated an ASME Historic Mechanical Engineering Landmark. Patents: steam pumping engines, hoisting engines, steam cylinders. Member, American Academy of Arts and Sciences. He was the grandfather of Henrietta Swan Leavitt (HD0886) — the astronomer who provided the cosmic yardstick for the universe. WikiTree photo: https://www.wikitree.com/photo.php/a/a2/Leavitt-1291.jpg

sources.short: History and Proceedings of the Pocumtuck Valley Memorial Association, Volume 5
William Hooker Leavitt, A Sketch of the Life and Character of Rev. Jonathan Leavitt (1904)
sources.notes: Written by John's brother; published two years before John's death.

notable_stories.title: John Hooker Leavitt — generation 7 from Thomas Hooker, son of Underground Railroad operator Roger Hooker Leavitt — founded a bank in Waterloo, Iowa, served in the Iowa State Senate, and was an early benefactor of Talladega College, Alabama's oldest historically Black college
notable_stories.summary: John Hooker Leavitt (HD0870, Oct 11, 1831 – 1906) was born at the old parsonage in Heath, Massachusetts — the home his grandfather Rev. Jonathan Leavitt had retired to after his turbulent ministerial career. His father Col. Roger Hooker Leavitt was an Underground Railroad operator; his uncle was abolitionist editor Rev. Joshua Leavitt. In 1854, age 23, he struck west to Iowa, first contracting with John Roebling (builder of the Brooklyn Bridge) to survey land. In 1856 he founded a private bank in Waterloo; over 50 years this became Leavitt & Johnson National Bank with $200,000 capital. "For fifty years President Leavitt was during business hours almost constantly to be found at his desk carefully superintending the trusts committed to his care." Iowa State Senate 1871. Early benefactor of Talladega College, Alabama's oldest historically Black college — continuing the family's abolitionist tradition three generations on. Member Congregational Church of Waterloo for 50 years. His brother William Hooker Leavitt co-authored a book about their controversial grandfather Rev. Jonathan Leavitt: "A Sketch of the Life and Character of Rev. Jonathan Leavitt, the first Minister of Charlemont, Mass." (1904). Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hooker_Leavitt Pocumtuck Valley Memorial Association history: https://books.google.com/books?id=194WAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA159

sources.short: Foote Family Genealogy, Abram W. Foote

notable_stories.title: Amelia Stiles Leavitt — granddaughter of Sarah Hooker, great-great-great-granddaughter of Thomas Hooker — married Dr. Elial Todd Foote: the first physician of Jamestown NY, its county judge for 20 years, founder of Chautauqua County Bank, abolitionist, and one of the organizers of the Republican Party in 1856
notable_stories.summary: Amelia Stiles Leavitt (HD0856) was daughter of Judge Jonathan Leavitt (H00684) and Emilia Stiles (daughter of Yale President Ezra Stiles). She married Dr. Elial Todd Foote on April 27, 1841 in Greenfield MA. Foote's biography reads like a founding of a city: arrived Jamestown NY 1815 as its first physician; purchased Holland Land Company tract on which most of Jamestown was built; served as county judge 1824-1843 (20 years, reappointed by successive governors); founded Chautauqua County Bank in 1831 when the nearest bank was 90 miles away in Buffalo; Canal Committee during Erie Canal construction 1819-20; three terms in NY State Assembly; anti-slavery activist; helped organize the Republican Party in New Haven in 1856. His antislavery papers are preserved at the Chautauqua County Historical Society. "He was a fine looking man, of large frame and a rather broad face." — Judge Holden. Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elial_T._Foote Source: Foote Family Genealogy, Abram W. Foote, Vol.1 pp.292-293 (1907).

notable_stories.title: Prof. Worthington Hooker — Yale professor, grandson of Judge John Hooker Springfield — married Henrietta Whitney Edwards, great-granddaughter of Jonathan Edwards, uniting the two greatest names of New England Puritanism
notable_stories.summary: Worthington Hooker (H01407) was son of Judge John Hooker of Springfield MA (H00527) and grandson of John Hooker of Northampton. Yale graduate and later professor. On Jan 31, 1855 he married Henrietta Whitney Edwards — great-granddaughter of Jonathan Edwards through: Jonathan Edwards → Pierpont Edwards → Henry Waggaman Edwards → Henrietta. His brother Richard Hooker (H01408) also married into the Edwards-Dwight circle: Aurelia Dwight, granddaughter of Yale President Timothy Dwight (himself Jonathan Edwards's grandson through another line). The Hooker and Edwards families — the two intellectual giants of New England Puritanism — converged in the Springfield/New Haven circle of the mid-19th century.

notable_stories.title: Elizabeth Dwight Hooker — granddaughter of Judge John Hooker of Springfield — married Frederic Adolphus Packard, who edited 2,000 American Sunday School Union publications, projected the first children's newspaper in the United States, and declined the presidency of Girard College
notable_stories.summary: Frederic Adolphus Packard (Harvard 1814) married Elizabeth Dwight Hooker (H01403) on May 16, 1822 in Springfield MA. He edited the Hampden Federalist in Springfield for 10 years and served in the Massachusetts legislature 1828-29. In 1829 he became editor of American Sunday School Union publications — 2,000 total, more than 40 written or compiled by himself. He projected the Youth's Penny Gazette (later Child's World) — the first child's newspaper in the United States. In July 1849 he was elected president of Girard College — and declined. He edited 11 volumes of the Philadelphia Journal of Prison Discipline. His son Lewis Richard Packard became a Yale professor; his son Thomas Hooker Packard carried the Hooker name forward.

sources.short: Letter from Emma Willard to genealogist compiler, July 1862
sources.notes: Quoted in Hurlbut Family Genealogy 1888, entry 118

notable_stories.title: Dr. James Hurlbut — "one of the fathers of medicine in Connecticut," dark-eyed and well-proportioned — died in rags from cancer of the leg and was buried without a monument in Wethersfield, his grave unmarked for decades
notable_stories.summary: Dr. James Hurlbut (I00153, b.1717 Kensington CT; d. Apr 11, 1794 Wethersfield CT age 77) was "one of the fathers of medicine in Connecticut." "He was a tall and well-proportioned man, and his eyes were dark and piercing." "In early life Dr. Hurlbut possessed considerable property, but careless in his pecuniary affairs, rarely keeping any account of his services, embarrassments ensued, and in age his dress was rags." He was a leading man in Farmington and a church member "in close communion" — then "became hopelessly intemperate, and his name was erased in the list of membership." After his first wife Abigail Hart died in 1789, he moved to Wethersfield where he had formerly practiced extensively and "received much public sympathy and aid in his fallen estate." His second marriage to Ann Hollister Booth was disastrous — "not many days had gone by before high words had passed between them; without doubt the union was of short duration." He died of "protracted illness, generally said to be cancer of the leg" at a friend's house in Wethersfield. "He was buried in the grave yard of Wethersfield, near the north wall of the church, but there has been no monument to mark the spot where he was laid." Emma Willard (of Troy NY, founder of the Troy Female Seminary) wrote in 1862: "Dr. James Hurlbut of Berlin CT was dead before I can remember, but he was my mother's physician during the early part of her life... he must have been a remarkable man, since he impressed himself so vividly upon the generation who came after him." His son Raphael (HD0676) served seven years in the Revolution and died in Ohio. His son Agathus Hart Hurlbut (HD0689) was born while Raphael was at war and his mother died two months after his birth.

notable_stories.title: George Edward Murrell — born in Bedford County, Virginia weeks after Appomattox, son of Mary Ann Hart (Hooker descendant) — served in the Virginia House of Delegates 1899-1904 and chaired its Committee on Retrenchment and the Economy
notable_stories.summary:
Mary Ann Hart (HD0795) married John William Murrell of Lynchburg, Virginia in 1843. The family was in Campbell and Bedford Counties, Virginia throughout the Civil War. John William Murrell (b.1822) was 39-43 during the war years in Confederate Virginia. 8 children, including William Hart Murrell (1848-1888, named "Hart"). 

George Edward Murrell was born July 5, 1865 in Bedford, Virginia — weeks after the Confederate surrender at Appomattox Court House (April 9, 1865, in adjacent Appomattox County). He was born into post-war Virginia and became a Democratic politician: Virginia House of Delegates, Bedford County, 1899-1904. He chaired the Committee on Retrenchment and the Economy. 

His daughter Mary Hart Murrell (b.1890) carried the "Hart" name into the 20th century — she married William Francis Douville in Washington DC on June 17, 1919. 

Research note: John William Murrell Confederate service — check Virginia Civil War records for Bedford/Campbell County units.

notable_stories.title: Sarah Marsh Hall — great-great-granddaughter of Thomas Hooker — died in 1765; her widower John Hall then married Susannah Boylston, the mother of President John Adams
notable_stories.summary: Sarah Marsh Hall (H00185, b.1704 d.1765) was daughter of John Marsh (H00184) and granddaughter of Sarah Wilson (H00060), who was great-granddaughter of Thomas Hooker. She married Lt. John Hall on June 15, 1748 as his second wife. After Sarah died in 1765, John Hall married Susannah Boylston on October 17, 1766 — Susannah Boylston was the mother of John Adams, 2nd President of the United States. The Hooker tree and the Adams family thus share a stepfather connection three generations from Thomas Hooker. John Hall died ca.1780. Source: History of Braintree, Mass.; online vital records.

notable_stories.title: Capt. John Fowler — great-great-great-grandson of Thomas Hooker, Revolutionary War lieutenant and sea captain — died at 39; his Milford gravestone reads: "All gracious Heaven is this the end of man / A dreadful thought A melancholy plan"
notable_stories.summary: Capt. John Fowler (HD0175, b.1748 Milford; d. Aug 17, 1787 age 39) was son of Lt. John Fowler (H00164) and Mary Newton Fowler (H00155), who was daughter of Lieut. Fletcher Newton (H00047). He served in 1775 as Lieutenant in Capt. Samuel Peck's Company, Connecticut Militia. He worked as a sea captain. He married Mary Ann Harpin on Oct 22, 1767 — she descended from Dr. John Harpin of Rochefort, France, who came to America ca.1690. He died August 17, 1787 at only 39 years old. Three sons survived: John (1769-1790), Anthony William Harpin Fowler (1775-1863), and Mark Fowler (1782-1815). His gravestone in Milford Cemetery: "All gracious Heaven is this the end of man / A dreadful thought A melancholy plan."

notable_stories.title: Susannah Fowler — great-great-granddaughter of Thomas Hooker — drowned in Long Island Sound in 1727 at age 14
notable_stories.summary: Susannah Fowler (H00162, b. Dec 8, 1712) was the eldest child of Lt. John Fowler (I00091) and Susannah Burwell Fowler (H00053). She drowned in Long Island Sound on September 18, 1727, age 14. She was the first of the eleven children of H00053 to die, and her death came just three years after the family settled in Milford.

sources.notes: History of the Fowler family, Milford CT

notable_stories.title: The Fowler family of Milford — whose line married into Thomas Hooker's descendants — were among the "Seven Pillars" of the Milford Congregational Church (1639) and magistrates of the New Haven Colony, with a marriage connection to Governor Robert Treat
notable_stories.summary: William Fowler (great-great-grandfather of Lt. John Fowler, H00164) was: One of the "Seven Pillars" of the Milford Congregational Church, formed Aug 22, 1639 (alongside Rev. Peter Prudden, Edmund Tapp, Thomas Buckingham, Thomas Welch, Zachariah Whitman, John Astwood). Magistrate of the Colony of New Haven, elected Oct 26, 1643. Built a mill near New Haven (1645) — later purchased by the town and eventually the site of Eli Whitney's firearms factory (inventor of the cotton gin). William Fowler's wife was Mary Tapp, sister of Jane Tapp — who was the wife of Governor Robert Treat. TREAT CONNECTION: The Treat family appears in the Hooker tree through Lt. John Fowler's own grandfather's will, which mentions "my honorable uncle, Robert Treat, Esq., the Governor." Thus the Fowlers of Milford were connected by marriage to the Treats, who are a recurring cross-connection in the broader Hooker network. When Susannah Burwell (H00053, great-great-granddaughter of Thomas Hooker) married into this Fowler family in 1712, she joined one of the founding families of the New Haven Colony.

sources.short: Online vital records and genealogy databases

notable_stories.title: Bryan Hooker — great-great-great-great-grandson of Thomas Hooker — established one of the first woolen manufacturies in Connecticut and was a delegate to the 1818 Hartford convention that framed the Connecticut Constitution
notable_stories.summary: Bryan Hooker (H00515, 1764-1826) was son of Asahel Hooker of Bristol CT (H00262), manufacturer and farmer. Bryan's fulling mill — "the old yellow shop, near the bridge on the corner of East and South Streets" in Bristol — was one of the first woolen manufacturies in CT. (The mill was destroyed by fire in 1903.) He served as Town Clerk of Bristol 1806 and 1811-1820, and represented the town in the CT General Assembly in 1812, 1813, 1814, and 1817. On July 4, 1818, he was appointed delegate to the Hartford convention to frame a new Constitution of Civil Government for Connecticut — a document ending the colonial-era Fundamental Orders. "He voted on the conservative side often and was chairman of many important committees." He was a deacon of the Congregational Church for many years, "frequently serving on the Board of the poor relief." WikiTree photo: https://www.wikitree.com/photo.php/9/9c/Hooker-2191.png

sources.short: Note in possession of Horace Gibbs, 19 Arch St., Norwalk CT (1904)
sources.notes: Norwalk, Conn., June 3, 1777 receipt, William St. John

notable_stories.title: William St. John — Yale 1766, reported Loyalist, great-great-great-grandson of Thomas Hooker — paid his brother $60 for half-ownership of an enslaved man named Dover who was "enlisted into the Continental Service" in William's place
notable_stories.summary: June 3, 1777: William St. John (HD0368) signed a receipt acknowledging receipt from his brother Stephen of "the one half of his Negro boy named Dover, now enlisted into the Continental Service, for the one half of which boy I am obliged to pay sixty dollars on demand, to exempt me from all actual service." Dover — an enslaved man — served in the Continental Army in William's stead. William was a reported Loyalist. His brother Stephen (HD0365) also enslaved people: his 1786 inventory listed an enslaved man named Peter and an enslaved woman named Phyllis. Their father Capt. Joseph St. John (husband of Susannah Selleck, H00253) had enslaved Jenny, London, and Peter at his death in 1756. Slavery runs through three consecutive generations of this Hooker descendant family, and an enslaved man served in the Revolution in the place of a Hooker descendant who was himself a Loyalist.

Jane Gordon, "For a Former Slave, a Scholarly Tribute," Oct 9, 2005
Summons for Thomas Hart Hooker to appear before CT General Assembly

notable_stories.title: Thomas Hart Hooker — great-great-grandson of Rev. Thomas Hooker — freed his enslaved man Bristow by Deed of Manumission on May 9, 1775, just before enlisting; Bristow had PAID £60 for his own freedom, equivalent to 400 days of labor
notable_stories.summary: In April/May 1775, Thomas Hart Hooker (H00303) prepared to enlist in the Revolutionary army. Family tradition says he declared he "would not own property in a human being while he, himself, was fighting for freedom." The manumission document (held at Connecticut Historical Society) tells a more nuanced story: Bristow, an African man aged 44, PAID £60 for his freedom — the equivalent of 400 eight-hour days of labor (~$25,000 in 2004 dollars). Deed text: "I Thomas Hart Hooker... do by these presents fully freely and absolutely release manumit and set at full Liberty a Certain Negro man Named Bristow... that he may go & come when & wherever he pleases without any Hindrance or molestation." Witnesses: Salomon Whitman, Mary Root. Signed May 9, 1775. Bristow subsequently worked for Thomas's brother Roger Hooker, and in his 1791 will bequeathed "all my estate both real and personal unto Thomas Hart Hooker and Abigail Hooker, children of Thomas Hart Hooker late of Hartford" — an act of profound loyalty to the children of his former enslaver. Bristow Middle School in West Hartford was named for him in 2005 — believed to be the first CT school named after a formerly enslaved person. The homestead (later owned by abolitionist Samuel Deming, who sheltered Amistad survivors 1841) is on the Connecticut Freedom Trail. Sarah Whitman Hooker held British POW Col. Phillip Skene and his son at the homestead 1775-76, dispersing a mob planning to tar and feather them.

notable_stories.title: Maj. Roger Hooker — great-great-great-grandson of Thomas Hooker, half-brother of Thomas Hart Hooker who died in the same war — rose from private to Major in the Continental Line, fitted out fire ships at New York in 1776, and personally carried news of Burgoyne's surrender to the British commander under a flag of truce
notable_stories.summary: Roger Hooker Jr. (H00306) made 11 voyages to the West Indies before the Revolution, then at the Lexington alarm enrolled in his cousin Capt. Noadiah Hooker's company — 111 men, "the first men from Farmington for the war, and the first from Connecticut to reach the army collecting before Boston." He rose through every rank: sergeant → ensign → second lieutenant (when Washington took command) → eventually Major of the Continental Line. In 1776 he fitted out fire ships at New York "with which Gen. Washington endeavored to destroy the British ships." As brigade major he managed correspondence for the generals. He was "sent with the flag of truce to communicate to the British general commanding New York, information of the surrender of Gen. Burgoyne" — one of the war's most consequential communications. "Throughout the war held in high esteem by Gen. Washington, and was frequently entrusted with responsible and important duties." Member, Society of the Cincinnati. After the war: Sheriff of Hartford County, Justice of the Peace to age 70, Farmington selectman. His half-brother Thomas Hart Hooker (H00303) died of pleurisy at Roxbury in the same war.

notable_stories.title: "From these two sons, John and Samuel, are descended all of the name of TALCOTT in America" — every American Talcott descends from John Talcott, Hartford founder, through his two surviving sons
notable_stories.summary: The Talcott Pedigree (1876) states explicitly: "From these two sons, John and Samuel, are descended all of the name of TALCOTT in America." Capt. Samuel Talcott (T00036) graduated Harvard 1658 — "the scholar of the family." His father John Talcott (T00011) bequeathed him all books except the "Martyr Book." Samuel's wife Hannah Holyoke was granddaughter of Hon. William Pynchon, one of the original patentees of the Massachusetts Bay Colony Charter (1629) and founder of Springfield MA. Mary Pynchon's gravestone in Springfield bears an inscription still standing in 1876: "She that lies here was, while she stood, A very glory of Womanhood; Even here was sown most precious dust, Which surely will rise with the just." Samuel's son Deacon Benjamin (T00135) built the Glastonbury homestead in 1699 on land that was "still owned by his descendants" at the Pedigree's publication in 1876 — over 230 years of continuous family ownership. The compiler (Samuel Talcott Hooker) descends from this line through T01389.

notable_stories.title: A single piece of Connecticut land — purchased from Samuel Sherman and Richard Gildersleeve in 1643 — passed through four generations of Talcotts and was still owned by the family in 1876: 233 years of continuous ownership
notable_stories.summary: The land chain begins with John Talcott (T00011), Hartford founder, who in 1643 purchased a lot from Samuel Sherman and Richard Gildersleeve in Glastonbury — "44 rods wide, running back from the river three miles to the great wilderness." John Talcott's will bequeathed this lot to his son Capt. Samuel Talcott (T00036), "the scholar of the family." Capt. Samuel's will (1691) bequeathed the Glastonbury land to son Benjamin (T00135). Deacon Benjamin Talcott built a house on the lot in 1699 (moved in Nov 22, 1699) — "a large wooden building on the Main street" fortified against Indian attacks, "bearing the marks of the bullets, until it was taken down, soon after the year 1854." Benjamin's will (1727) divided the home lot between sons Samuel (south half, T00458) and Elizur (north half with buildings). The Talcott Pedigree (1876) records: "This farm and buildings thereon are now owned and occupied (1876) by Jared G. Talcott, one of his descendants, having been in the family over 200 years." That is 233 years of continuous Talcott ownership from the 1643 purchase to the 1876 publication. The compiler (Samuel Talcott Hooker) descends through the south half of this lot via T00458 → T01001 → T01389.

notable_stories.title: On May 25, 1738, Governor Joseph Talcott's wife Eunice died suddenly at noon — and he returned to preside over the upper house of the General Assembly that same afternoon, "not suffering his private grief to interfere with his official duty"
notable_stories.summary: Governor Joseph Talcott (T00045), grandson of Hartford founder John Talcott (T00011), was the first Governor of Connecticut born within its limits (served 1724-1741, 17 years). On Thursday May 25, 1738, his wife Eunice died suddenly about noon. The Deputy Governor was absent at the Commissioner's Court at Norwich, and public business was pressing. "Gov. Talcott did not suffer his private grief to interfere with his official duty, but returned and presided in the upper house in the afternoon." The General Assembly appointed a joint committee to confer on what to offer the Governor "on the sudden and painful event," and the Speaker, Clerk and Capt. Samuel Willard were appointed to draw an address of condolence. His daughter Eunice married Capt. Nathaniel Hooker of Hartford — connecting the two founding families (Talcott and Hooker) in yet another generation.

notable_stories.title: Betsey Mix Cowles — great-great-great-great-granddaughter of Thomas Hooker — was one of the pioneer students at Oberlin College and an abolitionist associated with William Lloyd Garrison
notable_stories.summary: Betsey Mix Cowles (H01148, 1810-1876) was the daughter of Rev. Giles Hooker Cowles (H00443) and granddaughter of Martha Hooker Cowles (H00232). "After the death of her father in 1835 she went to Oberlin College to prepare herself for the battle of life; she was one of the pioneer students and her name occurs in the triennial catalogue as a member of the third class graduated from the ladies' course." "She afterwards taught school with great success; she was an advocate of woman's rights and abolition of slavery, and she was associated with Wm. Lloyd Garrison and other noted abolitionists in the anti-slavery agitation." She died unmarried in Austinburg, Ohio, Jul 25, 1876. Her father Rev. Giles Hooker Cowles built the first church with a steeple in Ohio and had studied theology with Dr. Jonathan Edwards the Younger in New Haven.

notable_stories.title: Charles Olcott — Yale-educated great-great-great-great-grandchild of Thomas Hooker — was Medina Ohio's pioneer lawyer, leading abolitionist whose book was read in Congress, and the man who patented the iron ship in 1835
notable_stories.summary: Charles Olcott (1793-1857) was the son of Cynthia Hooker (H00310) and Rev. Allen Olcott, and thus a great-great-great-great-grandchild of Rev. Thomas Hooker. He graduated Yale College 1816 and arrived in Medina, Ohio ca.1820-21 as one of its first lawyers. He served as county prosecutor 1825-1833 while building his reputation as an abolitionist. His book "A Blow at Slavery" became "famous among North American abolitionists and was often cited in newspapers and abolitionist journals." His 1838 lectures on slavery and abolition "were read aloud in Congress as evidence in support of his position." Medina was Underground Railroad station #27. He mentored Joel Tiffany, who became both an abolitionist legal theorist and the inventor of the refrigerator railroad car. On July 13, 1835, Olcott patented the iron (metallic) ship — "constructing ships and all other kinds of sea vessels and watercraft wholly of iron." The Naval Board called it "entirely impractical." The Navy built iron ships shortly after. Olcott, a small-town lawyer of limited means, never received compensation. He died unmarried in Medina in 1857. His sister Betsey Mix — wait, that's Betsey Mix Cowles (H01148), a parallel Hooker abolitionist. Two Hooker descendants active in abolition in the same generation. Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wIEun5SX-m0

sources.short: Online historical sources re: Leete's Island raid 1781

notable_stories.title: Ebenezer Hart — great-great-grandchild of Thomas Hooker — was killed defending Guilford against a British/Loyalist raid at Leete's Island on June 18, 1781
notable_stories.summary: Ebenezer Hart (H00712, b. Oct 3, 1757) was a son of Thomas Hart (H00312) and Concurrence Bartlett. On June 18, 1781, three British vessels landed 150 men — many of them Loyalists — at Leete's Island, Guilford CT. They were not detected until close enough to torch two houses. The militia arrived and drove the invaders back to their boats. Two Guilford defenders were killed in the skirmish — Ebenezer was one of them, both men in their 20s. He was 23 years old. Never married.

notable_stories.title: The 1767 estate inventory of Hooker Bartlett — a man named for the Hartford founding family — lists fractional ownership of two enslaved men: "2/3 of Jethro" and "2/3 of Peleg"
notable_stories.summary: Hooker Bartlett (H00319, 1725-1767) was named for his Hooker ancestry and lived his whole life in Guilford, Connecticut. When he died at age 42, his estate inventory recorded: "2/3 of [slave] Jethro" worth £26:13:4, and "2/3 of [slave] Peleg" worth £43:6:8. The fractional ownership notation (2/3) indicates these men were jointly owned with another party, likely a family member or neighbor. Peleg was valued higher than Jethro. We know their names — Jethro and Peleg — but nothing else about them. Connecticut did not abolish slavery until 1784, seventeen years after this inventory was taken. The names Jethro and Peleg are both Old Testament names, common for enslaved people in colonial Connecticut. This entry is part of a broader pattern across the Hooker-Hart-Bartlett extended family in Guilford — the same community that also produced Thomas Hart Hooker's 1775 manumission of Bristow. The same enslaved man Peleg appears in a connected thread: Sarah Hooker Bartlett's will bequeathed Peleg to her grandson Nathaniel Ruggles Jr. (H00726) — son of Annie Bartlett Ruggles (H00317) and Dr. Nathaniel Ruggles (X00282). The name 'Peleg' thus traces through two generations of Guilford wills across the same extended family.

notable_stories.title: Dr. William Hooker Smith — surgeon in the Continental Army — was living in Wyoming Valley when the "Wyoming Massacre" of July 3, 1778 killed ~300 Patriots; his wife Sarah died ten days later and he recorded the moment in his family Bible
notable_stories.summary: Dr. William Hooker Smith (H00320) was named "William Hooker" for his Hooker ancestry and became a surgeon in the Revolutionary Army (3rd Co, 1st CT Regt / 10th Continental Regt). He had removed to Wyoming Valley (Luzerne County, Pennsylvania) where he practiced medicine. On July 3, 1778, a combined British Loyalist and Haudenosaunee force attacked the settlement. Fort Wintermoot and Fort Jenkins surrendered July 1; on July 3, ~300 Patriot militia and 60 Continentals sallied from Forty Fort and were killed — the "Wyoming Massacre." Lieutenant Colonel Nathan Denison surrendered on July 4. Dr. Smith's wife Sarah (Brown) Smith died on June 12, 1778 — the month after the battle. In his family Bible (printed Oxford 1772), he wrote: "My wife, Sarah, died on Friday, the 12th of June, 1778, about nine o'clock at night, was buried the 14th, following, on my own land at Jacob's Plains." He remarried in November 1779 and lived until 1815, dying at Tunkhannock, Wyoming County PA at age 90. His descendant Charles Ryan, ten generations removed from Thomas Hooker, served on D-Day and at the Battle of the Bulge in WWII.

notable_stories.title: Charles Ryan — a 10th-generation descendant of Rev. Thomas Hooker through the William Hooker Smith line — fought on D-Day, at the Battle of the Bulge, and helped liberate a concentration camp in WWII
notable_stories.summary: Charles Ryan (b. ca.1916; d. ca.2011) descended from Thomas Hooker through a chain of ten generations: Thomas Hooker → Samuel → James → Mehitable (Hooker) Smith → William Hooker Smith (surgeon, Wyoming Valley) → James Smith → Hooker Smith (b.1785, named for the ancestor) → Anson Smith → Etta Deborah Smith Ryant → Fred Smith Ryant → Charles Ryan. He served in World War II: D-Day, Normandy, June 6, 1944; Battle of the Bulge; helped liberate a concentration camp; was reportedly 12 miles from Moscow when the war ended (likely a town named Moscow/Moskau in Germany, not Russia). He died ca.2011 at approximately age 95. Family record provided by a descendant. The naming tradition persisted through the line: "William Hooker" Smith → "Hooker" Smith — the Hooker name carried three generations from Thomas Hooker into 19th-century rural New York.

notable_stories.title: Major Benjamin Tallmadge — great-great-great-grandchild of Thomas Hooker, classmate of Nathan Hale — was Washington's spymaster, ran the Culper Ring that helped expose Benedict Arnold, and married the daughter of a Signer of the Declaration of Independence
notable_stories.summary: Benjamin Tallmadge Jr. (H00757, 1754-1835) was the son of Susannah Smith Tallmadge (H00323) and grandson of Mehitable Hooker Smith (H00109). He graduated Yale 1773, where Nathan Hale was his classmate and close friend. After Lexington and Bunker Hill, he entered the army. Washington appointed him director of military intelligence. He assembled the Culper Ring — Abraham Woodhull and Robert Townsend as primary agents, operating alias "John Bolton." The Culper Ring revealed Benedict Arnold's betrayal: Tallmadge suspected André and Arnold, and though he could not stop Arnold's escape, André was placed in Tallmadge's custody and executed. Fort St. George raid (Nov 21-22, 1780): 80 men, whaleboats across Long Island Sound, captured and burned the fort, destroyed 300 tons of British hay at Coram, zero American casualties. Washington wrote him a personal letter of thanks. He married Mary Floyd, daughter of Gen. William Floyd, Signer of the Declaration of Independence — his father Rev. Tallmadge officiated. Society of the Cincinnati founding member. U.S. Congressman (Federalist) 1801-1817. The town of Tallmadge, Ohio; Tallmadge Hall at Fort Huachuca (Army Intelligence headquarters); Talmadge, Maine; and the AMC series Turn: Washington's Spies all bear his name or story. His brother William (H00756) was taken prisoner at Long Island on the SAME DAY Benjamin was engaged there, and died in a British prison that same year.
notable_stories.one_line: A direct Thomas Hooker descendant ran Washington's spy network, married a Declaration of Independence signer's daughter, and had his town and an Army Intelligence building named after him.

notable_stories.title: Elder William Goodwin married Thomas Hooker's widow in 1669-70; 187 years later, Goodwin's descendant Mordecai married a descendant of Thomas Hooker himself — the two Hartford founding families converging twice, across two centuries and four states
notable_stories.summary:
Elder William Goodwin (ca.1591-1674) was one of the original Hartford founders — he arrived in Cambridge, Massachusetts aboard the ship Lyon in 1632, was a member of the Adventurers Party that scouted Hartford in October 1635, and was among the sixteen founders living in Hartford before Hooker's party arrived in 1636. He was a church sidesman in Braintree, Essex, England, then Elder in Cambridge. After the death of his first wife Elizabeth White, Elder Goodwin married SUSANNAH GARBRAND — the widow of Rev. Thomas Hooker — before January 1669-70 in Farmington CT. Susannah Garbrand had been Hooker's wife since England; she outlived him until 1676. The marriage united the two founding families at the root. 
Goodwin's son William Jr. (b.1629 Braintree) began a line that moved from Connecticut to Pennsylvania: William Jr. → Nathaniel → Hezekiah → John Pantry Goodwin → Elijah Goodwin (b.1763) → Daniel Goodwin (b.1801) → Mordecai Goodwin (b.1835, Huntington, Luzerne County, Pennsylvania). 
In January 1857, Mordecai Goodwin married Catherine Elsie Kline (HD1021) — a descendant of Thomas Hooker himself through the line: Thomas Hooker → Samuel → James → Mehitable (Hooker) Smith → William Hooker Smith → Mary Smith Baker → Thomas Baker → Eltruda Baker Kline → Catherine Kline. 
The families first united in Farmington, Connecticut in 1669-70 when the Hartford founder married Hooker's widow. They united again in Columbia County, Pennsylvania in 1857 — 187 years later, and more than 1,000 miles from Hartford — when their respective descendants married each other, with neither likely knowing the full historical weight of the connection.

notable_stories.title: Two Purdy brothers fought on opposite sides of the Revolution — Capt. Jacob Purdy (Patriot, Washington's HQ) and Gabriel Purdy (Loyalist, DeLancey's Corps) — and their grandchildren married each other in Nova Scotia
notable_stories.summary: Capt. Jacob G. Purdy and Gabriel T. Purdy were brothers, sons of Samuel Purdy Jr. of Westchester County, New York. When the Revolution came, the family was torn apart. Jacob joined the Westchester Militia in 1775, became a Captain, and his house became General Washington's headquarters during the Battle of White Plains (October 28, 1776) and again for two months in 1778. Gabriel — at age 21 — joined the British Army, fought at White Plains on the opposite side, was promoted to Sergeant in DeLancey's Corps of West Chester Refugees and Light Infantry. After the war, Gabriel was expelled from New York as a Loyalist. He left for Nova Scotia on June 15, 1783 and never returned. He ultimately married five times, had 17 children, 170 grandchildren, and 52 great-grandchildren by the time of his death in 1841. But the families did not stay apart. Jacob's daughter Abigail Smith Purdy (H00331) and Capt. Jacob Purdy (X00121) raised their daughter Sarah (H00779) in White Plains. In January 1811, Sarah married Jacob Griffin Purdy — the son of Gabriel's son, raised in Nova Scotia. The Patriot's granddaughter married the Loyalist's grandson. They moved to Nova Scotia, completing the family's journey from New York to Canada. Their great-grandchild Douglas Black Weldon (b.1895) was born in Moncton, New Brunswick — a direct descendant of Thomas Hooker living in Maritime Canada.

notable_stories.title: Brock Purdy — starting quarterback for the San Francisco 49ers — is a likely descendant of Rev. Thomas Hooker through the Mehitable Smith Purdy line, 10 generations removed
notable_stories.summary: Brock Purdy (b. Dec 27, 1999) is the starting quarterback of the San Francisco 49ers, selected last overall ("Mr. Irrelevant") in the 2022 NFL Draft. The documented chain from Thomas Hooker runs: Thomas Hooker¹ → Samuel Hooker² → Hon. James Hooker³ → Mehitable Hooker Smith⁴ (H00109) → Mehitable Smith Purdy⁵ (H00330) → Nathaniel Purdy⁶ → Thomas Purdy⁷ → Theodore James Purdy⁸ → George Anthony Purdy⁹ → Wilber Charles Purdy¹⁰ → [gap to confirm] → Brock Purdy. The gap between Wilber Charles Purdy (d.1951) and Brock Purdy's father Randy Purdy needs documentation before this can be stated definitively. The same Mehitable Smith Purdy line also connects to Major Benjamin Tallmadge — Washington's spymaster and Culper Ring leader — through the same generation. CONTEXT: The Purdy family was deeply split by the Revolution — Brock Purdy's direct ancestors include both a Patriot whose house was Washington's headquarters and a Loyalist who was expelled to Nova Scotia.

notable_stories.title: Gen. Selah Hart freed his enslaved men and allowed Pharaoh to earn his freedom fighting at Germantown and Monmouth — both received federal pensions 35 years later; Hart was also the orator "too full for utterance" when Washington breakfasted in Berlin in 1789
notable_stories.summary: General Selah Hart (H00273, 1732-1806) was the only Revolutionary War General from Berlin CT, son of Abigail Hooker (H00099). He freed his enslaved man Jack when Jack turned 21. He allowed enslaved Pharaoh to enlist for 3 years on condition Pharaoh's wages would buy his freedom. Pharaoh fought at Germantown (1777) and Monmouth (1778). "Thirty-five years later, both men received pension from the federal government. Pharaoh was living in New Jersey in 1818." Hart had been captured Sep 15, 1776 during Washington's retreat from NYC — held prisoner nearly 2 years while his wife did not know if he was alive. Nov 10, 1789: President Washington breakfasted in Berlin. Selah Hart was the veteran orator who greeted him. Having taken several drinks, he stood up, bowed, and said: "General, I am too full for utterance!" Washington wrote in his diary: "Breakfasted at Worthington in the Township of Berlin." His wife Ruth Cole (1743-1844) outlived him by 38 years, dying at approximately age 101.

notable_stories.title: Emma Hart Willard's father Capt. Samuel Hart was wounded at the Battle of Saratoga in 1777 — one of the decisive battles of the Revolution — and encouraged all 17 of his children to read and think for themselves
notable_stories.summary: Capt. Samuel Hart (H00583, 1738-1813) was born in Berlin CT, youngest son of Samuel Hart and Mary Hooker. He fought in the French and Indian War (1757, Fort William Henry alarm) and the Revolutionary War, where he was wounded at the Battle of Saratoga on September 19, 1777, serving under Gen. Wolcott's detachment. He also commanded a Berlin militia company that turned out for the New Haven Alarm in 1779 when British General Tryon invaded Connecticut. He was First Clerk and Treasurer of Berlin Congregational Church. "A great thinker but could not speak in public without having his ideas written out." He became a Universalist. He encouraged all 17 of his children to read and think, and notably supported his daughter Emma's education. Emma Hart Willard (H00597, 1787-1870) went on to found the Troy Female Seminary (1821), the first institution of higher education for women in the United States. Her sister Almira Hart Lincoln Phelps (H00598) also became a pioneering educator. Samuel Hart's father was Samuel Hart Sr. (EH 281), son of Mary Hooker (H00099) — connecting Emma Hart Willard directly to Thomas Hooker through four generations.

sources.short: Hart Family Genealogy, Hart Book entry #1765

notable_stories.title: Joseph Hart — husband of Thomas Hooker's great-great-great-granddaughter Eunice Ellery — built a West India trading empire in Hartford, "connected by marriage and business with the most noted families in Hartford," then became embarrassed, left the country, and was lost overboard at sea about 1810
notable_stories.summary: Joseph Hart (X00315, b.1755 Saybrook CT) married Eunice Ellery Hart (H00792), granddaughter of Eunice Hooker Ellery (H00347) and great-great-great-great-grandchild of Rev. Thomas Hooker. Joseph was son of Rev. William Hart of Saybrook and a merchant. From the Hart Book (#1765): he "was engaged in the mercantile business at Hartford from 1785 to 1800, and probably later, first in company with his brother, General William Hart, and subsequently by himself, and was much engaged in the West India trade. His store was located near the river, and he appears to have been in the wholesale business." "He became connected, by marriage and business, with the most noted families in Hartford, but for some cause became embarrassed, left the country, and was lost overboard at sea about 1810." His wife Eunice died in 1813, three years after his disappearance, age 51. Of their seven children, at least four died before age 35. Henry F. Hart, the youngest, was also "supposed to have been lost at sea." Two generations of sea losses in the same family.

notable_stories.title: Justice Frank Arthur Hooker — stonemason who taught himself law, Michigan Supreme Court Chief Justice for 18 years, explicitly self-identified as "a descendant in the eighth generation of Rev. Thomas Hooker"
notable_stories.summary: Frank Arthur Hooker (HD, 1844-1911) was born in Hartford CT, the son of James Sedgwick Hooker (a contractor who lost his fortune in 1856 and moved to Ohio), grandson of Dr. Nathaniel Hooker (EH 804, Sackett's Harbor merchant), and great-grandson of Horace Hooker (H00350, partner in Hooker & Chaffee). His lineage: Thomas Hooker¹ → Samuel² → Nathaniel³ → Nathaniel⁴ → Horace⁵ → Nathaniel⁶ → James Sedgwick⁷ → Frank Arthur⁸. He apprenticed as a stonemason at 16, taught himself higher mathematics, history, and Latin from an older sister educated in New England, and graduated from the University of Michigan Law Department in 1865. He practiced law in Charlotte, Michigan, served as Eaton County schools superintendent, prosecuting attorney for two terms, circuit judge from 1878, and was elected to the Michigan Supreme Court in 1893, serving as Chief Justice in 1893, 1902, and 1903. Over 18 years he authored approximately 1,700 opinions across 73 volumes of the Michigan Reports. His judicial philosophy — "shortest cut, based upon reason, common sense and the experience of centuries" — was explicitly connected to his Hooker ancestry and the founding Hartford tradition of consent-based governance. He died of heart failure at the New York Central railroad station in Auburn NY on July 10, 1911, while en route to an American Bar Association conference in Chicago.

notable_stories.title: Evelyn Pierpont — Thomas Hooker's great-great-grandchild and Yale graduate reduced to working at Yale for wages — was the rightful heir to the Duke of Kingston title refused by Parliament because he was American; his children were killed in a duel, died at sea off Norway, and died on a Navy sloop
notable_stories.summary: Evelyn Pierpont (H00351, 1755-1808) was the son of James Pierpont II (H00116, gen:3) and great-great-great-grandchild of Thomas Hooker through Mary Hooker Pierpont. His father named him "Evelyn" — the Pierpont genealogy notes — "in a sycophantic nod to his English relations." Those English relations were the Dukes of Kingston, and Evelyn was the legitimate heir to the titles, honors, and estates of that peerage, "his line of descent and hereditary right having been fully established, but being an American the English Parliament refused to recognize the family." He served as 2nd Lieutenant in the defense of New Haven during Tryon's 1779 invasion. After the Revolution he farmed at Litchfield, became financially reduced, and found employment at Yale — where he was a graduate — and worked there until he died in 1808. The Duke's title that Parliament denied him descended in irony: his oldest son Evelyn Jr. (EH 812), who would have inherited first, died at sea off the coast of Norway during the War of 1812, unmarried. His son James (EH 814) was killed in a duel in New Orleans in 1823, age 27. His son Lorenzo (EH 818) died as a U.S. Navy officer aboard USS Sloop Cyane during the Florida War (Second Seminole War). Three sons lost to war, the sea, and a dueling pistol.
