notable_stories.title: Anne Eliza Isham — 8th-generation Hooker descendant, daughter of Robert Todd Lincoln's law partner — boarded the Titanic at Cherbourg and was one of only four first-class women to die in the disaster; her body was never identified
notable_stories.summary: Anne Eliza Isham (HD, 1862-1912) was the daughter of Edward Swift Isham (HD) and granddaughter of Vermont Supreme Court Justice Pierrepont Isham (HD). Her lineage: Thomas Hooker → Samuel → Mary Hooker Pierpont → James Pierpont II → Robert Pierpont → Anna Pierpont Isham → Pierrepont Isham → Edward Swift Isham → Anne. Her father Edward had founded the Chicago law firm Isham, Lincoln & Beale in partnership with ROBERT TODD LINCOLN, son of President Abraham Lincoln, in 1872. Anne had lived abroad for nine years, mostly in Paris with her sister Frances (Mrs. Harry Shelton). She boarded the Titanic at Cherbourg on April 10, 1912 — first-class cabin C-49, next to Col. Archibald Gracie who did not remember ever seeing her. Arthur Larned Ryerson, a partner in her father's firm, was also on board. On April 15, 1912, the Titanic sank. Anne Eliza Isham was one of only four first-class women who died — the others being Countess of Rothes, Mrs. Allison, and one other. Her body, if recovered, was never positively identified. A memorial was erected at Dellwood Cemetery, Manchester, Vermont.

sources.short: Keefer, The Town of Morris, 1937, Morris CT Library

notable_stories.title: Three Pierpont brothers, snowbound for weeks at the Collins house in Litchfield County, each married a Collins daughter — a storm that produced the ancestry of J. Pierpont Morgan and poet John Pierpont
notable_stories.summary: The story, preserved in the Morris, Connecticut library (Keefer, The Town of Morris, 1937), records that three Pierpont brothers traveling from New Haven through Litchfield County stopped overnight at the home of Rev. Timothy Collins's son in South Farms. "A great storm, long remembered for one of the severest ever known, overtook them, and they were snowbound for weeks." "This was Cupid's opportunity, and the three young men married three daughters of the family." Robert Pierpont (H00352) married Lois Collins; his brother Evelyn (H00351) married Rhoda Collins; their brother James married a third Collins daughter. Their descendants included "John Pierpont, the poet; J. Pierpont Morgan, the financier; and James Pierpont, professor in Yale University and becoming famous for his contributions to Mathematical science." (Keefer.) This family was noted for intelligence, the Collins family for physical vigor, and "their descendants, numbering not a few, have been forceful leaders in society." NOTE: J. Pierpont Morgan (1837-1913), the financier, is not a direct descendant through the Hooker line — his descent runs through a different Pierpont branch. This story explains the naming pattern: J.P. MORGAN's middle name "Pierpont" honors the same Pierpont family ancestry.
notable_stories.one_line: A blizzard stranded three brothers at a farmhouse for weeks — and all three married daughters of the family.

sources.short: Obituary, George Frederick Humbert Jr., 2006; online vital records

notable_stories.title: Dr. George Humbert Jr. — 9th-generation Hooker descendant through the Sperry-Pierpont line — was a NASA flight surgeon who developed life support systems for the moon landing and monitored the astronauts during the first moon walk in 1969
notable_stories.summary: Dr. George Frederick Humbert Jr. (1932-2006) traced his Hooker ancestry through: Thomas Hooker → Samuel → Mary Hooker Pierpont → James Pierpont II → Robert Pierpont → Laura Pierpont Sperry → Anson Sperry Jr. → Edwin Anson Sperry → Frances Bradley Sperry Humbert → George Frederick Humbert Jr. A Navy flight surgeon who earned his wings and flew at Mach 2, he joined NASA's Johnson Space Center in 1966. His chief contributions included developing life support systems for the Apollo moon landing and monitoring the astronauts during the first moon walk on July 20, 1969. He left NASA in 1973 and practiced family medicine in California until retiring to Pahrump, Nevada. He built his own house by hand, walked the Grand Canyon rim to rim, and reportedly cared for a neighbor's pet tigers and lions.

notable_stories.title: J.P. Morgan — the greatest financier of the Gilded Age — was a 7th-generation descendant of Rev. Thomas Hooker; his middle name "Pierpont" explicitly honored that ancestry through his mother Juliet Pierpont, daughter of the abolitionist poet Rev. John Pierpont
notable_stories.summary: John Pierpont Morgan (1837-1913) traced his Hooker ancestry through: Thomas Hooker¹ → Samuel² → Mary Hooker Pierpont³ → James Pierpont II⁴ → James Pierpont III (EH 353)⁵ → Rev. John Pierpont⁶ → Juliet Pierpont Morgan⁷ → John Pierpont Morgan (J.P. Morgan). His middle name "Pierpont" was given explicitly to honor his mother's Pierpont ancestry and, through it, his descent from James Pierpont, one of the founders of Yale College. His mother Juliet was the daughter of Rev. John Pierpont (1785-1866) — Yale 1804, abolitionist, temperance reformer, poet ("Airs of Palestine"), 25-year pastor of Hollis-Street Unitarian Church, Boston, and author of "The National Reader." The same Rev. John Pierpont's other son James Lord Pierpont (1822-1893) composed "Jingle Bells" in 1857. J.P. Morgan formed U.S. Steel, General Electric, and International Harvester; controlled 21 railroads; was described as "America's greatest banker." Remarkably, the Morgan line became largely childless by the 3rd generation — J.P. Morgan's four children produced few grandchildren who survived, and many of those had no children themselves. His daughter Anne Tracy Morgan never married; she became the first woman honored with a marble plaque at the Hôtel des Invalides in Paris. His granddaughter Dr. Mabel Satterlee Ingalls (1901-1993) was the last surviving grandchild. His great-grandson Henry Sturgis Morgan Jr. married Jean Alexandra McCain, sister of Senator John McCain.

sources.short: UU World, Unitarian Universalist Assoc., Winter 2014

notable_stories.title: James Lord Pierpont — son of Boston's abolitionist Unitarian minister Rev. John Pierpont — composed "Jingle Bells" (1857), served the Confederate Army, and died in Florida; his brother's daughter became the mother of J.P. Morgan
notable_stories.summary: James Lord Pierpont (HD, 1822-1893) was a 6th-generation descendant of Rev. Thomas Hooker and the son of Rev. John Pierpont — Boston's most prominent abolitionist Unitarian minister. "A rebellious musician with a bad reputation" (UU World, 2014). He left his wife and children twice: first for the California Gold Rush, then permanently for Savannah, Georgia. In 1857 he composed "The One Horse Open Sleigh" for a Thanksgiving Sunday school program in Boston — later renamed "Jingle Bells," now one of the most performed songs in history. "Although it is strongly associated with Christmas, this story of a wintertime sleigh ride contains not a single holiday reference." The song was inspired by one-horse sleigh races on the road between Medford and Malden, MA. In sharp contrast to his abolitionist father, James served the Confederate cause and composed Confederate songs ("Strike for the South," "Our Battle Flag"). His daughter Lillie Pierpont (1853-1939) became the first woman in Florida appointed as a federal Indian Agent for the Bureau of Indian Affairs. His brother's daughter Juliet Pierpont married Junius Spencer Morgan I, making James Lord Pierpont uncle of J.P. Morgan.

sources.short: Medal of Honor citation, U.S. Army

notable_stories.title: Pierpont Morgan Hamilton — great-great-great-grandson of Thomas Hooker AND great-great-great-grandson of Alexander Hamilton — won the Medal of Honor at Operation Torch in 1942
notable_stories.summary: Lt. Col. Pierpont Morgan Hamilton (1898-1982) was the son of William Pierson Hamilton and Juliet Pierpont Morgan (HD), daughter of J.P. Morgan. William Pierson Hamilton was the great-great-grandson of Alexander Hamilton. Pierpont Morgan Hamilton therefore descended from BOTH Thomas Hooker (through his mother) AND Alexander Hamilton (through his father). At Port Lyautey, French Morocco, November 8, 1942 — Operation Torch — he volunteered to accompany Col. Demas Craw on a mission to the French commander to bring about a cease-fire. Their truck was hit by machine-gun fire at point-blank range; Col. Craw was killed instantly. Hamilton was captured immediately after but completed the mission. Medal of Honor citation: "For conspicuous gallantry and intrepidity in action above and beyond the call of duty." Also awarded: Legion of Merit, Army Commendation Ribbon (3 oak leaf clusters), Order of the British Empire, Portuguese Order of Marito Christo.

sources.short: Obituary, John Pierpont Woods, Harpswell ME, May 2012

notable_stories.title: John Pierpont Woods — DFC naval aviator, Connecticut legislator, and airline pilot — retired at 62, bought a blue school bus, drove to Costa Rica with his dog, came back, and set world age-group swimming records in his 90s
notable_stories.summary: John Pierpont Woods (1918-2012) was the son of NYC Police Commissioner Arthur Hale Woods and Helen Morgan Hamilton Burgess, great-great-granddaughter of J.P. Morgan and great-great-great-great-grandchild of Rev. Thomas Hooker. Brooks School (5th class); Harvard; Distinguished Flying Cross in WWII Naval Air Force. Flew for American Airlines. CT General Assembly representative. Director of Operations and Air Traffic Control, National Business Aircraft Association. On retirement in 1980: loaded all possessions and his dog into a blue school bus and drove to Costa Rica, where he lived for seven years. Returned to Harpswell, Maine. Became an avid marathon runner, then master swimmer — set world age-group swimming records into his 90s. Spoke Spanish, French, German, and Chinese fluently. Played guitar. Mentored young athletes. Neighbor Dick Parks visited every day. Died at home May 23, 2012, age 94. Survived by four daughters, seven grandchildren, two great-grandchildren.

notable_stories.title: Leonard Pierpont of Illinois — great-great-great-grandchild of Rev. Thomas Hooker — lost three sons in the Civil War: one died of wounds in Texas, one died as a prisoner of war in Virginia, one was killed on the last day of fighting
notable_stories.summary: Leonard Pierpont (1819-1874) was the son of James Pierpont III (H00353, EH 353) and his second wife Lucy Strong — a half-sibling to the Rev. John Pierpont branch. He removed from Connecticut to Illinois before the war. Three of his eight children died in the Civil War: LEONARD JR. (1842-1865): Company K, 76th IL Infantry; campaigned in 8 states including Vicksburg; only off duty 2 weeks in 35 months; died of wounds Galveston TX, Jul 17, 1865 — 4 days before his regiment started home. Kept a diary titled "While in the Servis." WALTER (1843-1864): 1st CT Cavalry; wounded and captured at Ashland VA Jun 1, 1864; died the next day. "Fell mortally wounded in the fury of a charge" (Croffut, 1869). EDWARD SHERMAN (1844-1865): 8th IL Volunteer Infantry; killed at Fort Blakeley, Mobile Harbor AL, April 9, 1865 — the last major engagement of the western theater, fought the same day Lee surrendered at Appomattox. A fourth son James Morris Pierpont (1839-1868) served as captain in the 11th CT Infantry and died in 1868, his health destroyed by the war. So of Leonard's sons who served, FOUR were casualties — three killed or died of wounds, one dead of ruined health.

sources.short: Online vital records; Wikipedia: James Pierpont (mathematician)

notable_stories.title: James Pelham Pierpont — great-great-great-grandchild of Rev. Thomas Hooker, son of a New Haven horse-railroad president — became one of Yale's leading mathematicians, earning his PhD in Vienna and pioneering real analysis and non-Euclidean geometry
notable_stories.summary: James Pelham Pierpont (1866-1938) was the son of Cornelius Pierpont, president of the Dixwell Avenue Horse Railroad in New Haven. He studied mechanical engineering at Worcester Polytechnic, then turned to pure mathematics. After Worcester he went to Europe — Berlin, then Vienna — and earned his PhD at the University of Vienna in 1894 under Leopold Gegenbauer and Gustav Ritter von Escherich. Thesis: "Zur Geschichte der Gleichung fünften Grades bis zum Jahre 1858." Returned to New Haven; appointed lecturer at Yale 1894; professor 1898. Early work in Galois theory; after 1900, real and complex analysis (introduced a Lebesgue-style integral definition in his textbooks, later critiqued by Maurice Fréchet); in the 1920s, non-Euclidean geometry. Died San Mateo CA 1938. His niece Marion Pierpont Snow (sister's daughter) lived to age 106 in the same family.

sources.short: Online vital records; Snow & Pierpont family genealogy records

notable_stories.title: Marion Pierpont Snow — great-great-great-great-grandchild of Rev. Thomas Hooker — lived to age 106; her father invented the "universal food chopper," selling millions and making the family wealthy
notable_stories.summary: Marion Pierpont Snow (1893-1999) was the daughter of Sila Harrison Pierpont Snow and Levi Tracy Snow — an inventor and manufacturer who made his fortune with the "universal food chopper," a kitchen device that sold millions of copies. Levi traced his Snow ancestry to Constance Hopkins, a Mayflower passenger, via Nicholas Snow who married her in 1627. Marion married Clarence Lynwood Sibley (Yale) before 1917 in New Haven. She died October 6, 1999 in New Haven, aged 106. Her uncle was Prof. James Pelham Pierpont, the Yale mathematician. Her mother Sila died young at 50, in 1913, before seeing her daughter reach such an age. Marion's brother Pierpont Melvin Snow died at age 9 in 1909; another brother Cornelius Pierpont Snow died in infancy in 1893. Marion outlived them all by decades.

sources.short: Honeoye NY newspaper obituary, Jan 1906 (text preserved in document)

notable_stories.title: David A. Pierpont and his wife Sarah both died on January 6, 1906 — within hours of each other after 63 years of marriage, fulfilling a wish they had often expressed together
notable_stories.summary: David A. Pierpont (1815-1906) was the son of David Pierpont (H00833) of Allen's Hill, NY. He married Sarah Elizabeth Phillips in 1843 and they had been married 63 years. Per the Honeoye NY newspaper obituary: "Saturday afternoon, Jan. 6, Sarah Elizabeth Pierpont passed away, aged 83 years and six months. In a few hours her husband, David A. Pierpont, aged 90 years, joined her. Mr. and Mrs. Pierpont had often expressed a hope that they might die together." David had served as town supervisor of Richmond seven terms, was deeply interested in politics, and at one time came within a few votes of being elected senator. "They are survived by a son, David O., a daughter, Mrs. Carrie Green, and a grandson, Pierpont Green." "It will be hard to fill their places."

sources.short: Diary of Edward Austin Pierpont (text preserved in document)

notable_stories.title: On Election Day 1864, Edward Austin Pierpont wrote in his diary: "Went to Litchfield to vote for the last president of the United States I expect" — he was wrong; Lincoln won, and the Union survived
notable_stories.summary: Edward Austin Pierpont (ca.1828-1894) kept a diary his entire life — mostly weather and farming. Two entries stand out. June 14, 1862 (son Frederick born near midnight): "Hoed corn. Uncle George helped us. Had a son born tonight about 5 minutes to 12. Delia and the babe are smart. Clear and cool." November 8, 1864 (Presidential Election Day): "Foggy and wet. Presidential election. Went to Litchfield to vote for the last president of the United States I expect." He was voting during the darkest period of the Civil War, uncertain whether the United States would survive as a republic. Lincoln won the election and was inaugurated for a second term in March 1865. Lee surrendered six weeks later. The Union survived. Edward Austin served in the 6th CT Infantry during the war. His house stood on Wilson Rd., Litchfield until it was burned by the fire department in the 1970s after vandals made it uninhabitable.

notable_stories.title: Two sons of David Pierrepont (EH 354) became Vermont Supreme Court figures: Robert Pierpoint served as Lt. Governor 1848-1850 and learned law from Governor Richard Skinner — who had married into another Hooker-descendant Pierpont family; his brother John served as Chief Justice 1865-1882
notable_stories.summary: Robert Pierpoint (H00834, 1791-1864) and his brother John D. Pierpoint (H00840, 1805-1882) were sons of David Pierrepont (H00354, EH 354) — great-great-grandchildren of Rev. Thomas Hooker. Robert studied law at age 16 with Governor Richard Skinner of Vermont. Governor Skinner had married Frances Pierpont (H00820), daughter of Robert Pierpont (H00352, EH 352) — a different branch of the same Pierpont-Hooker family. So the young Robert Pierpoint learned law from a man who had married his own cousin. Robert rose to 16th Lieutenant Governor of Vermont (1848-1850) and Circuit Court Judge (1850-1856). His brother John graduated Litchfield Law School, served as associate justice (1857-1865) and then Chief Justice of the Vermont Supreme Court (1865-1882). Their sister Laura (H00841) moved to Michigan. "Hon. John Pierpont of Litchfield, a nephew of the poet, was chief justice of Vermont from 1865 to his death 1882." (Connecticut Quarterly, 1903-4.)

sources.short: Online vital records — Pierpont, Russell, Talcott genealogies

notable_stories.title: Mary Pierpont Russell (EH 118) was the daughter of Yale's co-founder, the granddaughter of Hartford's founder, and married the son of another Yale founding trustee — concentrating three of colonial New England's most important founding families in one woman
notable_stories.summary: Mary Pierpont Russell (H00118, gen 3) was: (1) The granddaughter of Rev. Thomas Hooker, who founded Hartford CT in 1636. (2) The daughter of Rev. James Pierpont Sr. (X00126), one of ten founding trustees of Yale College in 1701. (3) The wife of Rev. William Russell (I00144), whose father Rev. Noadiah Russell was also a founding trustee of Yale in the same 1701 charter as her father. The 1701 Yale founding was not a large event — roughly ten men gathered to give books and establish what became Yale. Two of those ten men were the fathers of a married couple. Through Mary Pierpont Russell's daughter Mary Russell Talcott (H00356), the family also merges with the Talcott family (Gov. Joseph Talcott) — whose other child Eunice Talcott married into the Hooker surname line directly (H00115). Four of colonial Connecticut's founding dynasties — Hooker, Pierpont, Russell, Talcott — converge in the single generation of Mary Pierpont Russell's children. ADDITIONAL LAYER: Rev. James Pierpont Sr.'s first wife was Abigail Davenport — daughter of Rev. John Davenport, founder of New Haven. She died six weeks after the wedding from a cold. So the man who founded Yale was first married to the founder of New Haven's granddaughter, then ultimately married the founder of Hartford's granddaughter. Both of New England's foundational figures — Hooker and Davenport — are grandparents-in-law of Yale's founder.

notable_stories.title: Sarah Pierpont — granddaughter of Rev. Thomas Hooker and daughter of Yale's co-founder — married Jonathan Edwards, the Great Awakening's most famous theologian; their granddaughter's son Aaron Burr killed Alexander Hamilton in 1804
notable_stories.summary: Sarah Pierpont Edwards (HD0418, 1710-1758) was the granddaughter of Rev. Thomas Hooker through the line: Thomas Hooker → Samuel Hooker → Mary Hooker Pierpont (H00034) → Sarah. She was also the daughter of Rev. James Pierpont Sr., co-founder of Yale College 1701. She married Jonathan Edwards (1703-1758) on July 20, 1727 — the most influential theologian of the Great Awakening, author of "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God" (1741), and later president of Princeton. Their daughter Esther Edwards Burr (1732-1758) married Rev. Aaron Burr Sr., president of the College of New Jersey (Princeton). Their son Aaron Burr (1756-1836) served as 3rd Vice President of the United States under Thomas Jefferson, and on July 11, 1804 shot and killed Alexander Hamilton in a duel at Weehawken, New Jersey. Thomas Hooker → Samuel → Mary Hooker Pierpont → Sarah Pierpont Edwards → Esther Edwards Burr → Aaron Burr, VP and Hamilton's killer. Five generations. NOTE: Alexander Hamilton's daughter-in-law Juliet Pierpont Morgan Hamilton (HD1173) was ALSO a Hooker descendant — through a different Pierpont branch (H00353). Hooker blood on both sides of America's most famous duel.

sources.short: National Inventors Hall of Fame, inducted 2016
National Women's Hall of Fame, inducted 2001

notable_stories.title: Harriet Williams Russell Strong — 7th-generation descendant of Rev. Thomas Hooker — was a self-taught inventor whose dam patents laid the technical foundation for the Hoover Dam; she is in both the National Women's Hall of Fame and the National Inventors Hall of Fame
notable_stories.summary: Harriet Williams Russell Strong (1844-1926) descended from Thomas Hooker through: Hooker → Samuel → Mary Hooker Pierpont → Mary Pierpont Russell (H00118) → Rev. William Russell Jr. (H00358) → Col. Samuel Andrews Russell (H00844) → Henry Pierpont Russell → Harriet. Her middle name "Russell" and her father's middle name "Pierpont" both preserved the founding family heritage. Widowed at 39 with four daughters and a bankrupt California ranch, she taught herself agriculture, patented dam construction innovations in 1887 and 1894, became the largest commercial walnut grower in the United States, and traveled with Susan B. Anthony promoting women's suffrage. In 1918 she appeared before Congress urging the Colorado River dam system she had designed — "It was thought of by a woman," Congress replied, and rejected it. Congress later approved the Hoover Dam in 1928; it was completed 1935. The All-American Canal — the world's largest irrigation canal — based on her methods, began construction 1942. Her daughters were named Harriet Russell, Nelle de Luce, Mary Lyman, and Georgiana Pierrepont — the last explicitly preserving the Pierpont ancestry.

notable_stories.title: Col. Jeremiah Wadsworth — raised by the uncle who had married his future wife's own sister — became commissary general for both the American and French armies, hosted Washington and Rochambeau at his Hartford table, and served three terms in Congress
notable_stories.summary:
Col. Jeremiah Wadsworth (1743-1804) was the son of Abigail Talcott (T00068), daughter of Governor Joseph Talcott of Connecticut. After his father's early death, he was placed by his mother with his uncle Matthew Talcott of Middletown, in whose vessels he sailed before the mast to improve his health. Matthew Talcott had married Mary Russell (H00356) — and when Jeremiah grew up he married Mary's own sister MEHITABLE RUSSELL (H00362), another granddaughter of Thomas Hooker through the Pierpont line. During the Revolution, Wadsworth served as commissary for American troops from 1775, and when Rochambeau arrived with the French army, he personally assumed responsibility for supplying all provisions for the French — a role so demanding and so well performed that the French government paid his accounts "freely and liberally" in Paris in 1783. Washington's diary records his Hartford mansion as a gathering place. Washington was at Wadsworth's table with Rochambeau when Arnold's treason was discovered at West Point. A French traveler wrote of Wadsworth in 1788: "universally known for the service he rendered the American and French armies." He served in the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Congress, was a friend of the Constitution, and received honorary degrees from Dartmouth and Yale in 1796. His son Daniel Wadsworth (1771-1848) founded the Wadsworth Atheneum in Hartford — the oldest continuously operating public art museum in the United States. His daughter Catherine (1774-1841) married Nathaniel Terry, Mayor of Hartford 1824-1831 and U.S. Congressman.
PRIMARY SOURCES: The Hartford Conference at Wadsworth's home is documented in the Washington Papers: Founders Archives https://founders.archives.gov/documents/Washington/03-28-02-0173-0001 Hans Axel von Fersen's description of Washington comes from a letter to his father written from Newport, Oct 16, 1780. The French commissary details for the 1781 march are documented at: NPS Washington-Rochambeau Revolutionary Route, https://www.nps.gov/waro/learn/historyculture/washington-rochambeau-revolutionary-route.htm

notable_stories.title: Three children of Governor Joseph Talcott of Connecticut each connected to the Hooker family by a different route in the same generation — one directly into the Hooker surname line, two through the Russell-Pierpont branch
notable_stories.summary: Governor Joseph Talcott (T00045, 1669-1741) served as Governor of Connecticut for 17 years — longer than any predecessor except Gov. Winthrop, and the first Governor born within Connecticut's limits. Three of his children created distinct connections to the descendants of Rev. Thomas Hooker: (1) EUNICE TALCOTT (I00054) married Nathaniel Hooker 2d (H00115) — directly into the Hooker surname line. (2) MATTHEW TALCOTT (T00070/X00127) married Mary Russell (H00356) — Hooker descendent through the Pierpont branch. Mary Russell was the daughter of Mary Pierpont Russell (H00118), daughter of Rev. James Pierpont (Yale co-founder) and Mary Hooker. (3) ABIGAIL TALCOTT (T00068) married Rev. Daniel Wadsworth; their son Col. Jeremiah Wadsworth was raised by his uncle Matthew Talcott, then married Mehitable Russell (H00362) — Mary Russell's own sister. Mehitable was another granddaughter of Thomas Hooker through the Pierpont line. So the same Governor's three children each married into the Hooker family: one through the direct Hooker line, two through different branches of the same Pierpont-Russell-Hooker complex. This is the genealogical basis for "Talcott" being preserved as a family name by descendants of Thomas Hooker.

notable_stories.title: Lucy Munson Russell married Henry Hill, appointed U.S. Consul to Brazil by Thomas Jefferson — and several of their children were born in Bahia, Brazil, including a daughter whose grandson invented the modern industrial loom
notable_stories.summary: Lucy Munson Russell Hill (HD1323, 1785-1860) was the daughter of Col. Samuel Andrews Russell and granddaughter of Rev. William Russell Jr. (H00358) — herself a 6th-generation descendant of Rev. Thomas Hooker. She married Henry Hill (1778-1841), who was appointed U.S. Consul to Salvador (Bahia), Brazil by President Thomas Jefferson in 1808. The appointment letter was signed by Secretary of State James Madison. Henry Hill served until ca.1821 and the family lived in Brazil for many years. Several of their 11 children were born in Bahia: Maria Louisa (1808), Lucea Munson (1811), Harriet Ann (1814), Henry Marcus (1816), Charlotte Henrietta (1824), Sophia Joanna (1826). Sophia Joanna Hill was born in Brazil; her great-granddaughter Annie Jacobs Bullard married Washington Irving Bullard, who published "Brazil: The Promising Land" — a book about the very country where her grandmother was born. Bullard also invented the modern loom, promoted women's rights, and traveled the world. Charlotte Henrietta Hill Jacobs's granddaughter Annie Bullard's husband received a letter of consular appointment at Bahia signed by James Madison — as had Lucy's own husband Henry Hill more than a century earlier.

National Register of Historic Places, listed 1970

notable_stories.title: Daniel Wadsworth — 5th-generation Hooker descendant through the Russell-Pierpont line — founded the Wadsworth Atheneum in Hartford in 1844, the oldest continuously operating public art museum in the United States, in the city his ancestor founded in 1636
notable_stories.summary: Daniel Wadsworth (HD1330, 1771-1848) was the son of Col. Jeremiah Wadsworth and Mehitable Russell (H00362), making him a 5th-generation descendant of Rev. Thomas Hooker. His father had been commissary general for both the American and French armies; his mother was granddaughter of Rev. James Pierpont (Yale co-founder) and Mary Hooker. He married Faith Trumbull, daughter of Jonathan Trumbull Jr. (Speaker of the House, Governor of Connecticut). No children of his own. In 1841, at age 70, he donated land on Main Street Hartford and announced plans to build "a Gallery of Fine Arts." The Wadsworth Atheneum opened in 1844. He assembled the collection from the defunct American Academy of Fine Arts in New York, purchased major landscapes from Thomas Cole, and housed the Connecticut Historical Society alongside the gallery. The Gothic Revival building, designed by Ithiel Town and Alexander Jackson Davis, still stands as one of Hartford's landmarks. A direct descendant of Hartford's founder created Hartford's greatest cultural institution — 208 years after Thomas Hooker led his congregation through the wilderness to found the city. The Wadsworth Atheneum is STILL ACTIVE — 75,000 sq ft of exhibition space, National Register of Historic Places (listed 1970), noted for European Baroque, Hudson River School landscapes, French and American Impressionist paintings, and early American furniture. The largest art museum in Connecticut, located at 600 Main Street, Hartford.

notable_stories.title: On September 20, 1780, George Washington and French General Rochambeau held their Allied strategy conference inside the Hartford home of Col. Jeremiah Wadsworth — husband of a granddaughter of Rev. Thomas Hooker — and it was there that news of Benedict Arnold's treason arrived
notable_stories.summary: Col. Jeremiah Wadsworth (X00417) was married to Mehitable Russell (H00362), granddaughter of Rev. Thomas Hooker through the Pierpont-Russell line. Wadsworth served as commissary general for both the American and French armies, and his Hartford home was the site of the critical Allied strategy conference of September 20-22, 1780. Washington brought Hamilton, Henry Knox, Lafayette, Lt. Col. Gouvion, and 40 horses. Rochambeau came from Newport with Admiral Ternay. Lafayette served as interpreter — Washington spoke no French. Hans Axel von Fersen (Rochambeau's aide-de-camp) described Washington from this meeting: "His noble and majestic, but at the same time gentle and honest face agrees perfectly with his moral qualities; he has the air of a hero; he is very cold, speaks little, but is polite and civil." The conference ended abruptly when news arrived of Rodney's British fleet and Arnold's betrayal at West Point. Washington departed Hartford September 23 and learned of the treason en route to his army. Rochambeau's chief commissary Blanchard wrote: "They returned enchanted... an easy and noble bearing, extensive and correct views, the art of making himself beloved." For the 1781 Yorktown campaign, Wadsworth orchestrated the entire French army's march logistics: 855 horses, 600+ oxen, 239 American wagon conductors, 15 (mostly female) cooks, bread ovens built along the route. Wadsworth's management made the Yorktown campaign operationally possible. A Hooker descendant's husband was the linchpin of the Franco-American military alliance.

notable_stories.title: Rose Terry Cooke (1827-1892) — one of the first American realist writers, a regular contributor to The Atlantic Monthly — was a 7th-generation descendant of Rev. Thomas Hooker through the Wadsworth-Russell-Pierpont line
notable_stories.summary: Rose Terry Cooke (1827-1892) descended from Thomas Hooker through: Hooker → Samuel → Mary Hooker Pierpont → Mary Pierpont Russell (H00118) → Mehitable Russell Wadsworth (H00362) → Catherine Wadsworth Terry (HD1331) → Henry Wadsworth Terry (HD1345) → Rose Terry Cooke. Her grandmother Catherine Wadsworth was the daughter of Col. Jeremiah Wadsworth — who hosted Washington and Rochambeau at the Hartford Conference of 1780. Her grandfather Daniel Wadsworth founded the Wadsworth Atheneum. Rose Terry Cooke published extensively in The Atlantic Monthly, Putnam's, and Harper's. She is credited as one of the founders of American literary realism, known for unflinching portrayals of rural New England life. She married Rollin Hillyer Cooke in 1873 at age 46 — he was 17 years her junior and later became a genealogist (an ironic postscript given her descent from several of New England's great founding families). Her connection is confirmed by the Hurlbut genealogy book, entry 1014: "Ann (or Nancy), she m. Henry (son of Gen. Nath. Terry); their dau. Rose Terry Cooke is the well-known authoress."

notable_stories.title: Gen. Alfred Howe Terry — 6th-generation Hooker descendant through the Wadsworth-Russell line — captured Fort Fisher (the last Confederate port) in January 1865 and commanded the expedition that found Custer's Last Stand
notable_stories.summary: Gen. Alfred Howe Terry (1827-1890) descended from Thomas Hooker through: Hooker → Samuel → Mary Hooker Pierpont → Mary Pierpont Russell (H00118) → Mehitable Russell Wadsworth (H00362) → Catherine Wadsworth Terry (HD1331) → Alfred Terry Sr. (HD1347) → Alfred Howe Terry. SOURCE CONFLICT RESOLVED: The Talcott Pedigree called him Jeremiah Wadsworth's "grandson by one of his sons" but the line runs through Jeremiah's daughter Catherine — making him a great-grandson. Alfred Terry Sr. confirmed this connection by naming his own children "Harriet Wadsworth Terry" and "Jeremiah Wadsworth Terry." A lawyer with no military training who became one of the Civil War's most capable generals. Fort Fisher, January 15, 1865: his coordinated assault captured the last major Confederate port, taking 2,000+ prisoners and 167 cannon. Congress voted its thanks; Yale gave him an honorary degree. In 1876, his were the orders Custer carried up the Rosebud — and it was Terry's column that arrived after the massacre to find the dead. Two generations of the Wadsworth-Hooker line at America's pivotal military moments: Jeremiah Wadsworth provisioned the French army's march to Yorktown in 1781; Alfred Howe Terry closed the Confederacy's last supply line 84 years later.

sources.short: Talcott Pedigree, entry on Lt.-Col. John Talcott and entry 68

notable_stories.title: On October 31, 1687, Joseph Wadsworth — uncle of Rev. Daniel Wadsworth, father of Col. Jeremiah Wadsworth who married Hooker descendant Mehitable Russell — hid Connecticut's Charter in the Charter Oak, aided by Lt.-Col. John Talcott, ancestor of Jeremiah's own mother Abigail Talcott
notable_stories.summary: The night of October 31, 1687: Governor Andros arrived in Hartford to seize the Connecticut Charter granted by King Charles II. Joseph Wadsworth, aided by Lt.-Col. John Talcott (T00035), seized the charter and hid it in a hollow oak tree — preserving Connecticut's self-governance. HOOKER CONNECTION: Joseph Wadsworth was the uncle of Rev. Daniel Wadsworth (X00418) — who married Abigail Talcott (T00068), daughter of Gov. Joseph Talcott, and fathered Col. Jeremiah Wadsworth (X00417). Lt.-Col. John Talcott (T00035) was the grandfather of Gov. Joseph Talcott — great-great-grandfather of Abigail Talcott, mother of Jeremiah Wadsworth. So both men who saved the Charter were direct ancestors of Col. Jeremiah Wadsworth, who 93 years later hosted Washington and Rochambeau at the Hartford Conference of 1780 while married to Hooker descendant Mehitable Russell (H00362). Three generations of Wadsworths and Talcotts at Connecticut's defining moments: Charter Oak 1687 → Yale founding 1701 → Hartford Conference 1780.

notable_stories.title: Edward Hooker's 1909 genealogy explicitly notes that Jeremiah Wadsworth and his wife Mehitable Russell were already distant cousins twice over — through both the Standley bloodline and the Hooker bloodline — before they ever married
notable_stories.summary: EH entry 62 contains an unusual editorial note documenting a double cousinship between Jeremiah Wadsworth and his wife Mehitable Russell: (1) STANDLEY BLOOD: Jeremiah descended from Elizabeth Standley of Farmington, sister of Abigail Standley who married John Hooker (H00030). "Therefore a degree of relationship existed through the Standley blood between this branch of the Wadsworth family and descendants from John Hooker, Esq., of Farmington." (2) HOOKER BLOOD: Mehitable herself descended from Thomas Hooker through the Pierpont-Russell line. "The cousinship also existed through Hooker blood between these Hooker descendants and Mehitable Russell, wife of Col. Wadsworth." NOTE: It was previously supposed that Gen. Joseph "Fighting Joe" Hooker also descended from this Farmington Hooker line, but Isaac P. Gragg's 1900 genealogical study definitively established that Fighting Joe's line was a separate Massachusetts Joseph Hooker family, with no demonstrated connection to the Connecticut Hooker families.

sources.short: Gragg, Isaac Paul. "Homes of the Massachusetts Ancestors of Major General Joseph Hooker." Boston, 1900.
sources.notes: Full text freely available as PDF and EPUB via Google Books. OCLC 1336192741.

notable_stories.title: Gen. Joseph "Fighting Joe" Hooker was NOT a descendant of Rev. Thomas Hooker — a 1900 genealogical study definitively separated his Massachusetts Joseph Hooker line from the Connecticut Hooker family, correcting a widespread family tradition
notable_stories.summary: Isaac P. Gragg (Brevet Captain US Vols), 1900 genealogical study, Boston MA: "Until recently it was the supposition that the General's ancestors were of the Connecticut Hookers... this was not surprising as persons of that name moved from Connecticut up the valley and settled in the region where the Town of Hadley is located and where the General was born." Gragg establishes five generations of Joseph Hooker, all named Joseph: Joseph 1 (emigrant, Westford MA 1736) → Joseph 2 (d. 1777) → Joseph 3 (Captain, Greenwich/Enfield CT) → Joseph 4 (moved Hadley MA 1806) → Gen. Joseph Hooker (b. Hadley 1814). The emigrant came probably from southern England or Isle of Jersey. "Among all the other Hooker families of New England as far as research has developed, there has not been another Hooker by the name of Joseph" — meaning this is a distinct and traceable line with no overlap with the Thomas Hooker / Samuel Hooker Connecticut line. The family tradition of Connecticut Hooker ancestry (represented by newspaper clippings preserved in the inherited EH 1909 copy) reflected the pre-1900 assumption. It was a reasonable mistake: Joseph Hooker 4 moved from Enfield CT (adjacent to the Connecticut Hooker territory) to Hadley MA in 1806, which made the Connecticut connection seem plausible. The family is NOT wrong to feel kinship with Fighting Joe Hooker — the Hooker name, the New England Puritan heritage, the same regional world. But the genealogical line is separate.

sources.short: Talcott Pedigree, entry on Jerusha Talcott and Dr. Daniel Lathrop

notable_stories.title: Jerusha Talcott — daughter of Governor Joseph Talcott and sister of the Talcott women who married into the Hooker family — raised the poet Lydia Huntley Sigourney, "the Sweet Singer of Hartford," after all three of her own sons died in infancy
notable_stories.summary: Jerusha Talcott (T00072, 1717-1805) was the daughter of Gov. Joseph Talcott (T00045) and sister of: Eunice Talcott (I00054, who married Nathaniel Hooker 2d), Matthew Talcott (who married Mary Russell, Hooker descendant), and Abigail Talcott (T00068, whose son Jeremiah Wadsworth married Mehitable Russell). She married Dr. Daniel Lathrop of Norwich (Yale 1733) in 1744. All three sons died before the eldest reached age 4. "Three precious sons cut down like flowers of the field, almost at a single sweep of the scythe." "Madam Lathrop" then raised the childhood of LYDIA HUNTLEY SIGOURNEY (b. Sept 1, 1791 Norwich; m. Charles Sigourney of Hartford 1819) — the most celebrated female poet of 19th-century America, known as "the Sweet Singer of Hartford." Sigourney "repaid her tenderness with filial veneration and has embalmed her memory in hallowed verse." Mrs. Sigourney's own Hartford literary career flourished in the same city where the Hooker-Talcott-Wadsworth network had long been centered. Source: Talcott Pedigree.

sources.short: NOTE: Edward Hooker 1909 deliberately omitted this line

notable_stories.title: Samuel Russell — 5th-generation Hooker descendant, grandson of EH 359 — founded Russell & Company, the largest American opium trading house in China (1819-1891), whose partners included Warren Delano Jr., the maternal grandfather of President Franklin D. Roosevelt
notable_stories.summary: Samuel Russell (1789-1862) was the son of Capt. John Russell (H00850, EH entry skipped) and grandson of Capt. Samuel Russell (H00359). He was a 5th-generation descendant of Rev. Thomas Hooker through the Russell-Pierpont line. EDWARD HOOKER DID NOT INCLUDE HIM IN EH 1909 — EH gives no starred entry for John Russell (EH 850) and no mention of Samuel Russell or Russell & Company. Given that Russell & Company's primary business was opium trafficking — illegal in China, addicting millions — EH's omission was almost certainly deliberate. The Russell Book (Sebastian V. Talcott, 1883) similarly omits this line. RUSSELL & COMPANY: Founded Canton (Guangzhou) 1819. By 1831 was smuggling ~3,500 chests of Indian opium per month into China — roughly 20% of China's total annual opium imports. By early 1840s the largest American trading house in China. Closed 1891 as Shewan & Company. WARREN DELANO JR. was a partner and head partner from the 1830s-1840s. He was the maternal grandfather of President Franklin Delano Roosevelt (through his daughter Sara Ann Delano who married James Roosevelt I). THE IRONY: The Hooker family tree includes Joshua Leavitt (abolitionist newspaper editor), Roger Hooker Leavitt and Hart Leavitt (Underground Railroad operators), and Samuel Russell (largest American opium trafficker into China) — all within the same family, within two generations of each other. Edward Hooker chose which stories to tell. This project does not have to make the same choice. TWO HOOKER-DESIGNED GREEK REVIVAL LANDMARKS: Samuel Russell commissioned Ithiel Town for his mansion (1828, LM016); Edward Augustus Russell likely used the same firm for his house (1842, LM017). Both sit on High Street, Middletown CT — the original Noadiah Russell homelot — the same Noadiah Russell who was Yale's founding trustee in 1701.

sources.short: "Barons of Middletown and the Decline of the Northeastern Anglo-Protestant Elite," Wesleyan journal

notable_stories.title: Samuel Wadsworth Russell — the China opium trader — returned to Middletown in 1831 and in 1834 co-founded Russell Manufacturing Company, which became Middletown's largest employer; the Russell family thereafter dominated Middletown civic life for a century, with their descendants serving as mayors and their Greek Revival mansions now forming the core of Wesleyan University's High Street campus
notable_stories.summary: Samuel Wadsworth Russell (HD1371, 1789-1862) returned from Canton to Middletown in 1831 and in 1834 co-founded Russell Manufacturing Company with Samuel D. Hubbard — a textile firm (elastic webbing) that became Middletown's largest manufacturer. The Russell family then dominated Middletown civic and social life for a century. Descendants served as mayors (Edward Augustus Russell 1859-1861, Thomas Macdonough Russell Sr.), held Connecticut legislative seats, directed railroads and banks. THREE CONSECUTIVE RUSSELL LANDMARKS on High Street, Middletown: Samuel Russell House (LM016, 1828, now Wesleyan Honors College), Edward Augustus Russell House (LM017, 1842, Wesleyan campus), Thomas Macdonough Russell House (LM018, 1902, Wesleyan Center for African American Studies). The Wesleyan connection: "the Russells... did not depart then. On the contrary, T. Macdonough Russell, Elijah Kent Hubbard and Governor Frank Weeks remained in the city for many more years." (Barons of Middletown, Wesleyan journal) Katherine Fearing Hubbard (daughter of Russell Manufacturing president Elijah Kent Hubbard) married Clarence Wadsworth — whose family founded Hartford's Wadsworth Atheneum. The Hooker → Russell → Pierpont line thus reconnected to the Wadsworth family through the Russell Manufacturing Company in the 20th century. Dean Acheson (Secretary of State under Truman) grew up in Middletown and recalled "the last of the barons still lived there — the Russells, the Hubbards, the Alsops, Governor Weeks." T.M. Russell donated the Russell & Company Canton opium records to the Library of Congress in 1931. NOTE: The Russells did NOT found Wesleyan University. Wesleyan was founded by Methodists in 1831. The Russell connection is that Wesleyan eventually acquired their High Street mansions.

sources.short: Wesleyan University Archives; Wesleyan magazine, Suzy Taraba "Historical Row"

notable_stories.title: High Street in Middletown — where the Hooker-Russell family built three consecutive Greek Revival mansions — was claimed by family legend to be the street where Charles Dickens declared "the most beautiful street I have seen in America," with the dinner party held at the Samuel Russell House
notable_stories.summary: Lucy Colton Wells wrote in 1942 that her mother heard Charles Dickens say "High Street is the most beautiful street I have seen in America" "at a dinner party in the Samuel Russell House." Dickens visited Connecticut in 1867, five years after Samuel Wadsworth Russell's death, but the house was still in the family. The Russell House (1828) had "three-story Corinthian columns and legendary rose gardens." Next door: the Edward Augustus Russell House (1842). Decades later: the Thomas Macdonough Russell House (1902). All three now belong to Wesleyan University. "A century later, all of the buildings that comprised this section of 'the most beautiful street in America' belonged to Wesleyan." (Wesleyan archivist.) CAVEAT: Dickens made the same compliment about approximately 50 other streets. Yale claims it for Hillhouse Avenue. Some Middletown sources say it was Mark Twain or William Dean Howells. The story is a legend but a well-documented one. Source: Wesleyan University Archives; Suzy Taraba, Wesleyan magazine.

sources.short: Yale Biographical Sketches (Dexter), Matthew Talcott Russell entry
New Haven Daily Morning Journal and Courier, Apr 21, 1888 (sea chest letter)

notable_stories.title: William Huntington Russell — 6th-generation Hooker descendant, named for his ancestor Matthew Talcott who funded his father's education — co-founded Skull and Bones at Yale in 1832, the same year his second cousin's Russell & Company was smuggling opium into China
notable_stories.summary: William Huntington Russell (1809-1885) descended from Rev. Thomas Hooker through: Hooker → Samuel → Mary Hooker Pierpont → Mary Pierpont Russell (H00118) → Noadiah Russell (H00360) → Matthew Talcott Russell (H00856) → William Huntington Russell. His father Matthew Talcott Russell was NAMED for Col. Matthew Talcott of Middletown (who had married Mary Russell, Noadiah's sister, and funded Matthew's education), and studied law with Oliver Ellsworth (future Chief Justice of the United States). William Huntington Russell co-founded Skull and Bones at Yale University in 1832 with Alphonso Taft (father of President William Howard Taft). He was the SECOND COUSIN of Samuel Wadsworth Russell (HD1371), founder of Russell & Company — the largest American opium trading house in China. Skull and Bones was founded the same year Russell & Company was smuggling ~3,500 chests of Indian opium per month into China. Yale historians have documented this connection. His family's sea chest, brought from England in 1638-39 by immigrant ancestor William Russell, is now at the New Haven Museum (LM019). The provenance letter accompanying the chest traces the exact Hooker descent chain from 1638 to 1888 in one document.

sources.short: New Haven Daily Morning Journal and Courier, Apr 21, 1888
New Haven Museum (formerly New Haven Colony Historical Society)

notable_stories.title: A sea chest brought from England in 1638 by William Russell — ancestor of the Thomas Hooker line — was preserved for 250 years in the same family before being donated to the New Haven Colony Historical Society in 1888, with a letter documenting the exact descent from 1638 to the Skull and Bones co-founder
notable_stories.summary: William Russell arrived in New Haven in spring 1638-39 with Rev. Henry Whitfield, George Fenwick, and William Leet — part of Davenport and Eaton's company. He signed the founding covenant June 4, 1641. His sea chest (broad on bottom, narrow on top — the colonial ship chest design) was preserved in the family for 250 years. Esther Russell (H00857, daughter of Noadiah Russell H00360) "took the chest when she married Thaddeus Larned." George Larned married Harriet Russell; their son George Huntington Larned loaned it to the New Haven Colony Historical Society on April 19, 1888. The accompanying letter by George H. Larned documents the provenance chain: William Russell → Noadiah Russell → William Russell → Noadiah Russell (H00360) → Matthew Talcott Russell (H00856) → William Huntington Russell → Talcott Huntington Russell (living in New Haven, 1888). Now at the New Haven Museum, 114 Whitney Avenue, New Haven CT. Source: New Haven Daily Morning Journal and Courier, April 21, 1888.

notable_stories.title: The Governor who founded UConn: Hobart Baldwin Bigelow, a 7th-generation Thomas Hooker descendant, signed the legislation creating Storrs Agricultural School in 1881
notable_stories.summary:
In 1881, brothers Charles and Augustus Storrs donated 170 acres of farmland, a former orphanage, six thousand dollars, and a few barns to the state of Connecticut. On September 28 of that year, three faculty members welcomed 13 students to the new Storrs Agricultural School. The governor who signed the legislation accepting that gift was Hobart Baldwin Bigelow (HD1438, 1834-1891) — the 50th Governor of Connecticut, a New Haven Republican who served 1881-1883. 

What no Bigelow biography has documented: he was a 7th-generation descendant of Thomas Hooker, through a line that runs: Thomas Hooker → Samuel Hooker → Mary Hooker Pierpont (H00034) → Mary Pierpont Russell (H00118) → Lt. Joseph Pierpont → Joseph Pierpont (H00873, Yale 1751) → Belinda Pierpont Bigelow (HD1437) → Gov. Hobart Baldwin Bigelow. 

The school he founded outlasted the name three times: Storrs Agricultural College (1893), Connecticut Agricultural College (1899), Connecticut State College (1933), and finally the University of Connecticut (1939). Women were admitted in 1893, the same year it became Connecticut's land-grant college. Today UConn is one of the top-ranked public universities in the United States. 

Bigelow also required fire escapes for workplaces employing 12 or more people and reformed Connecticut's election procedures during his single term. He had previously served as Mayor of New Haven (1879-1881). He died in 1891, 50 years before the school he founded took its current name. 

Thomas Hooker founded Hartford in 1636. His 7th-generation descendant founded Connecticut's flagship state university 245 years later. 

(UConn official history; Wikipedia on Hobart Baldwin Bigelow; EH 1909)

sources.short: Thorpe, North Haven in the Nineteenth Century (1901), p.133

notable_stories.title: Edwards Pierrepont — born Munson Edwards Pierpont in North Haven CT — was U.S. Attorney General (1875-76), U.S. Minister to Great Britain, prosecuted the John Surratt Lincoln assassination trial, and helped bring down Boss Tweed's Tammany Hall; his biographies acknowledge descent from Yale co-founder Rev. James Pierpont but never trace it back to Rev. Thomas Hooker
notable_stories.summary: Edwards Pierrepont (1817-1892) was one of the most prominent American lawyers and public officials of the Grant era. Born Munson Edwards Pierpont in North Haven CT, he changed his name at Yale, adding an extra "r" to reclaim the original French spelling. His accomplishments include: prosecuted the 1867 Surratt trial (hung jury); helped shut down Boss Tweed's Tammany Hall on the Committee of Seventy 1871; as U.S. Attorney General obtained 110 Whiskey Ring convictions; as U.S. Minister to Great Britain introduced Grant to Queen Victoria; commissioned a Saint-Gaudens marble bust now in the Smithsonian. His country estate in Garrison NY (Alexander Jackson Davis, 1867) is on the National Register of Historic Places as the Hurst-Pierrepont Estate. HOOKER CHAIN (6 generations): Thomas Hooker → Samuel Hooker → Mary Hooker Pierpont → Mary Pierpont Russell → Lt. Joseph Pierpont → Giles Pierpont (H00372, 1741-1832) → Capt. Giles Pierpont Jr. (1783-1842) → Edwards Pierrepont. All published biographies acknowledge the James Pierpont / Yale connection and stop there — the Hooker connection is entirely undocumented. PARALLEL: Governor Bigelow (HD1438) is a cousin-line descendant through the Joseph Pierpont branch (H00366), while Edwards Pierrepont comes through the Giles Pierpont branch (H00372) — both brothers, both lines undocumented.

notable_stories.title: Lyman Brockett (great-grandson of Thomas Hooker through Hannah Pierpont) had three sons die violent maritime deaths: Miles killed by a shark in the West Indies, Loyal died of yellow fever at sea as a ship officer, and Lyman Goodsell died in the East Indies as a ship officer
notable_stories.summary: Lyman Brockett (great-grandson of Thomas Hooker through Hannah Pierpont) had three sons die violent maritime deaths: Miles killed by a shark in the West Indies, Loyal died of yellow fever at sea as a ship officer, and Lyman Goodsell died in the East Indies as a ship officer

notable_stories.title: Mary Pierpont's surname became a given name carried for five generations: PIERPONT Brockett (Baptist minister, 6,300 sermons), his son Linus PIERPONT Brockett (50 books, Civil War historian), and grandson George PIERPONT Brockett — while another son Edward Judson Brockett compiled the very genealogy used as a source for this project
notable_stories.summary: The Pierpont surname as a given name ran through five generations from Mary Pierpont (H00371): Joseph Brockett (her son) named his son Rev. PIERPONT Brockett (1787-1868), who in 41 years preached 6,300 sermons across 12 Connecticut churches. His son Linus PIERPONT Brockett M.D. (1820-1893) wrote ~50 books including "Woman's Work in the Civil War" (1867) and 2,000+ articles for Appleton's Cyclopedia. His brother Edward Judson Brockett (1833-1919) compiled the Brockett Genealogy — itself a primary source for this project — and explicitly stated Mary was "a grand-daughter of Rev. Thomas Hooker." Edward's son was named George PIERPONT Brockett — the name reaching 1864, 91 years after Mary Pierpont's death in 1773.

Churchwell, Mary Jo. Palm Springs: The Landscape, the History, the Lore (Ironwood Editions, 2001)

notable_stories.title: Dr. Florilla Mansfield White and Cornelia Butler White — Thomas Hooker descendants through the Brooklyn Pierrepont branch — arrived in Palm Springs CA in 1913 when there were 15 buildings in the entire village; Cornelia's gift of property became the founding site of the Palm Springs Art Museum
notable_stories.summary: From Hartford Puritan to Palm Springs pioneer in eight generations. Florilla (M.D.) and Cornelia White (adventurer, builder, naturalist) were great-great-great-granddaughters of Hezekiah Pierpont (HD0419) — brother of Lt. Joseph Pierpont, the North Haven patriarch. They escaped the Mexican Revolution in 1913 on a hand car over burning railroad ties. Neither wore skirts. Florilla served as Palm Springs village health officer in WWI and organized the volunteer nurses for the 1918 flu epidemic. Cornelia deeded her property to what became the Palm Springs Art Museum in 1947; the main-floor gallery is dedicated to her. Both buried at Welwood Murray Cemetery, Palm Springs.

notable_stories.title: Among the 31 co-founders of the American Geographical Society in 1851, at least two — Joshua Leavitt (abolitionist editor) and Henry Evelyn Pierrepont (Brooklyn's "first citizen") — were Thomas Hooker descendants through completely separate genealogical lines, neither aware of the shared ancestry

Decorative Arts Trust 7th Annual Emerging Scholars Colloquium (Jan 22, 2023)
Connecticut Historical Society, Hartford CT — apron in collection

notable_stories.title: A 1730s silk embroidery apron at the Connecticut Historical Society — made of Chinese silk, French metallic thread, and European-dyed embroidery silk — threads together three generations of "Mary" in the direct Hooker-Pierpont-Russell-Talcott line
notable_stories.summary: The Connecticut Historical Society holds a silk embroidered apron from the 1730s associated with three successive "Mary" generations: Mary Hooker Pierpont (H00034, 1673-1740, granddaughter of Thomas Hooker), her daughter Mary Pierpont Russell (H00118, 1702-1740), and her granddaughter Mary Russell Talcott (b.1720, m. Matthew Talcott 1740, d.1799). Research by Olivia R. Scott (Master's thesis, Decorative Arts Trust grant) found: the silk is Chinese (not English) — identified by temple holes from the loom, high luster, and dimensions matching Chinese looms of 28-34 inches vs. English looms of 19-22.5 inches. Three types of metallic thread (filet, bullion, phrased/frisé), all likely French. Eight colors of European-dyed embroidery silk. Motifs: Tree of Life, carnations, tulips, acanthus leaf, Persian vase — hybrid English/Orientalist decorative vocabulary. Scott argues Mary Russell Talcott (the third generation, b.1720) is the most likely embroiderer — she would have attended finishing school in Boston in the 1730s, fitting the apron's date. Scott also notes Mary Russell Talcott died in 1799 without heirs, ending the direct maternal line. RESONANCE WITH THIS PROJECT: The Chinese silk connection is striking given that this same Russell family network later produced Samuel Wadsworth Russell and Russell & Company — the largest American trading house in Canton, importers of Chinese goods including silk. Presented: Decorative Arts Trust 7th Annual Emerging Scholars Colloquium, Park Avenue Armory, NYC, January 22, 2023. Video: youtube search "Genealogical Threads Unraveling the History of the Hooker-Pierpont-Russell-Talcott Family Apron Olivia R. Scott" VIDEO: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EJmuT2fz65g (Decorative Arts Trust, 19 min, Jan 22 2023, Park Avenue Armory NYC)

notable_stories.title: Three Hooker-descended Leavitt brothers ran an Underground Railroad network in Massachusetts — their grandfather had been dismissed from his church for allegedly dragging an enslaved woman home by rope.
notable_stories.summary: Rev. Roger Leavitt (H00685) and sons Joshua (HD0867), Roger Hooker (HD0868), and Hart (HD0869) present one of the starkest moral arcs in the Hooker network. Their grandfather Rev. Jonathan Leavitt (X00153) allegedly dragged an enslaved woman home by rope tied to his saddle, and was later dismissed for Loyalist sympathies. Two generations later his grandsons operated one of Massachusetts's most active Underground Railroad stations. Basil Dorsey escaped from Frederick County MD unassisted 1836 and lived with the Leavitt family — moving between Roger Hooker's home, Hart's adjoining farm, and the patriarch Roger's house — for over five years. Joshua in NYC coordinated from afar as editor of The Emancipator (INST015): "I feel for Mr. Dorsey in his bereavement and trust that you will do all that Christian benevolence requires." Roger Hooker's home and Hart's farm are both on the NPS Underground Railroad Network to Freedom. The brothers' correspondence (1812-1871) is at the Library of Congress Manuscript Division.

notable_stories.title: The gin distiller's great-great-grandson and the founding of AA
notable_stories.summary: Five generations from Brooklyn gin distiller Hezekiah Beers Pierrepont (H00976) to Rowland Hazard III (HD1578) — "Rowland H." in the AA Big Book — who consulted Carl Jung in 1926, arranged Ebby Thacher's release from an asylum in 1934, and set in motion the chain of events that led Bill Wilson to found Alcoholics Anonymous.

sources.note: Rowland Hazard III; AA Big Book p.26; RI Historical Society MSS 483

notable_stories.title: Drowned near Beaufort helping freedmen
notable_stories.summary: James Pierrepont Blake (HD1575, b.1839) drowned near Beaufort, South Carolina in 1865 while trying to assist newly freed enslaved people in the immediate aftermath of the Civil War. He was 25-26 years old and unmarried. His brother Edward Foster Blake (HD1574) had been killed at Cedar Mountain three years earlier. Two brothers, two deaths in service.

notable_stories.title: Killed at Cedar Mountain, August 9, 1862
notable_stories.summary: Edward Foster Blake (HD1574), son of inventor Eli Whitney Blake and Eliza Maria O'Brien Blake (HD1556), was killed at the Battle of Cedar Mountain on August 9, 1862 in Culpeper County, Virginia. He was approximately 24 years old. His middle name "Foster" honored his mother's Foster half-siblings.

notable_stories.title: Portrait by Jarvis, New Haven Museum
notable_stories.summary: Mary Pierpont Foster (H00981, b.1778), great-granddaughter of Rev. James Pierpont and granddaughter of John Pierpont (H00388), had her portrait painted as a watercolor miniature by John Wesley Jarvis c.1815. The work is held at the New Haven Museum, catalog #NPG 1977.338B. She is depicted as a young married woman, the wife of lawyer Eleazer Foster.

notable_stories.title: National Inventors Hall of Fame: Eli Whitney Blake (married into family)
notable_stories.summary: Eli Whitney Blake (X00503, b.1795), nephew of cotton-gin inventor Eli Whitney, married Eliza Maria O'Brien Blake (HD1556), granddaughter of John Pierpont (H00388) and 6th-generation Thomas Hooker descendant. Blake invented the Blake Stone Crusher (1857), the first practical stone-crushing machine in the world, which revolutionized road-building and was inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame. Five of their 12 sons graduated Yale.

sources.note: Eli Whitney Blake; National Inventors Hall of Fame

notable_stories.title: U.S. Ambassador to Canada, died at post 1943
notable_stories.summary: Jay Pierrepont Moffat (HD1639, b.1896), 9th-generation Thomas Hooker descendant, was U.S. Ambassador to Canada from 1940 to 1943 — the first year of American involvement in WWII. He died in Ottawa of surgical complications on January 25, 1943 at age 47, while still serving. His wife Lilla Cabot Grew was the daughter of Ambassador Joseph Grew, who was interned in Japan following Pearl Harbor. His father-in-law donated Moffat's diplomatic papers to Harvard. He was also a lineal descendant of John Jay, first Chief Justice of the United States.

sources.note: Jay Pierrepont Moffat; Harvard University Library

notable_stories.title: Two brothers killed in World War II
notable_stories.summary: Rowland Gibson Hazard IV (HD1581, b.1917) died April 29, 1944 as a Captain in the U.S. Army. His brother Peter Hamilton Hazard (HD1582, b.1918) died March 27, 1945 at Okinawa. Both were sons of Rowland Hazard III — "Rowland H." of the AA founding chain — and 10th-generation descendants of Rev. Thomas Hooker.

notable_stories.title: The Attorney General's wife: Saturday Night Massacre, gen 10
notable_stories.summary: Anne Frances Hazard Richardson (HD1587, b.1929), 10th-generation descendant of Rev. Thomas Hooker, married Elliot Lee Richardson — the U.S. Attorney General who on October 20, 1973 resigned rather than obey President Nixon's order to fire Watergate special prosecutor Archibald Cox. His resignation (and Deputy AG Ruckelshaus's simultaneous resignation) precipitated the constitutional crisis that ended with Nixon's resignation. Richardson told Anne in advance; she supported the decision without hesitation: "There was never any doubt about Elliot's resignation." He held four Cabinet positions — one of only two people in U.S. history to do so. Anne spent the rest of her life in civic leadership, building Reading Is Fundamental from 3 million to 3.7 million children served.

sources.note: Anne Francis Hazard Richardson obituary, Jul 28, 1999 (Bart Barnes)
MSS 483 sg 9 Thomas P. Hazard and Anne F. Cope Hazard Papers

notable_stories.title: Died on his favorite ski run, Feb 19, 2025
notable_stories.summary: Peter Rowland Hazard (HD1653, b.1964), 11th-generation descendant of Rev. Thomas Hooker, died February 19, 2025 in Telluride, Colorado from cardiac arrest at the bottom of his favorite ski run, "Kant-Make-Em." He had been skiing with close friends that day, "laughing on the lift and charging down the hill in his inimitable style." He was 22-year resident of Telluride, known for his work in the bike and ski industries, his carpentry, and his management of Valentine Farm. His grandfather Rowland Hazard III (HD1578) was "Rowland H." in the AA Big Book — the man whose consultation with Carl Jung set in motion the founding of Alcoholics Anonymous. Four generations from that pivotal moment.

sources.note: Peter Rowland Hazard, Telluride Daily Planet, March 2025

notable_stories.title: In the party that captured John Wilkes Booth
notable_stories.summary: Egbert Ingersoll (HD1701, b.1823) — 7th-generation descendant of Rev. Thomas Hooker and great-great-grandchild of Sarah Edwards Parsons (daughter of Rev. Jonathan Edwards) — was a Civil War government detective who was part of the party that captured John Wilkes Booth at the Garrett farm, Virginia, April 26, 1865. He lived to nearly 100 and was among the earliest pioneer residents of Lansing, Michigan.

sources.note: Lansing newspaper obituary 1923: "government detective during the Civil War and one of the party that captured John Wilkes Booth"

notable_stories.title: The Dollar Watch founders: Thomas Hooker's great-great-great-great-grandchildren
notable_stories.summary: Robert Hawley Ingersoll (HD1714) and Charles Henry Ingersoll (HD1715) co-founded the Ingersoll Watch Company in 1892 and introduced the $1 "Yankee" watch in 1896 — the first mass-produced dollar watch — selling 50M+ watches before bankruptcy in 1921. Their company's assets became the Waterbury Clock Company, the predecessor of Timex. They were 8th-generation descendants of Rev. Thomas Hooker and great-great-great-grandchildren of Sarah Edwards, daughter of Rev. Jonathan Edwards.

sources.note: Robert H. Ingersoll; Charles Henry Ingersoll

notable_stories.title: Provisional Governor of Alabama — slaveholder — 7th-generation Hooker descendant
notable_stories.summary: Lewis Eliphalet Parsons (HD1672, 1817-1895) was appointed by President Andrew Johnson as the 19th (Provisional) Governor of Alabama June-December 1865. He owned 16 enslaved people per the 1860 slave schedule. He was a 7th-generation descendant of Rev. Thomas Hooker and a Confederate officer. His first cousin once removed Fanny Parsons Gates (HD1673) was married to Seth M. Gates — an antislavery U.S. Congressman whose house was a station on the Underground Railroad. The same EH 376 descent line produced both.

sources.note: U.S. Federal Slave Schedule 1860, Talladega County AL

notable_stories.title: Underground Railroad station owner married into the Hooker line
notable_stories.summary: Seth Merrill Gates (X00541), antislavery U.S. Congressman 1839-1843, married Fanny Jennette Parsons (HD1673) — 7th-generation Hooker descendant, great-granddaughter of Sarah Edwards (daughter of Rev. Jonathan Edwards). His Warsaw NY home (1824) concealed fugitives in the cellar and attic for 15+ years. A Southern planter offered $500 for his capture. His house is on the National Register of Historic Places (1992).

sources.note: Seth M. Gates; Seth M. Gates House

notable_stories.title: President of Rutgers and Amherst — shaper of Indian policy
notable_stories.summary: Merrill Edwards Gates (HD1687, 1848-1922) — son of Seth Gates (Underground Railroad) and Fanny Parsons (7th-gen Hooker descendant) — served as president of Rutgers College (1882-1891) and Amherst College (1890-1899), and as Secretary of the U.S. Board of Indian Commissioners (1884-1900). An 8th-generation Thomas Hooker descendant and great-great-great-great-grandchild of Rev. Jonathan Edwards.

notable_stories.title: Cast the first iron ploughs in Canada — died at 38 in Chippewa Ontario
notable_stories.summary: Erastus Parsons (HD1671, 1789-1827) moved to Canada in 1824 and cast the first iron ploughs in Canada before dying at Chippewa, Ontario at age 38. He was a 6th-generation Hooker descendant, grandson of Sarah Edwards and great-grandson of Rev. Jonathan Edwards.

notable_stories.title: First white child born in Lenox, Massachusetts
notable_stories.summary: Rhoda Hinsdale (X00537, b. Nov 28, 1751) is said to have been the first white child born in Lenox, Massachusetts. She married Elihu Parsons Jr. (H00903), grandson of Sarah Edwards and great-grandson of Rev. Jonathan Edwards. A silver spoon marked "R.H." that belonged to her descended through five generations to her great-granddaughter, eventually held by Hon. Sanford C. Hinsdale of Denver.

notable_stories.title: The astronomer who connected Maxwell to Michelson — 8th-gen Hooker descendant
notable_stories.summary: David Peck Todd (HD1758, 1855-1939), 8th-generation descendant of Rev. Thomas Hooker, received a letter from James Clerk Maxwell on March 19, 1879, asking about Jupiter satellite eclipse data to detect Earth's motion through the ether. The letter caught the attention of Todd's colleague Albert Michelson, influencing Michelson's famous speed-of-light experiments. Todd also produced the first known photographs of the 1882 transit of Venus, led 11+ global eclipse expeditions, established Standard Time in Peru (1907), and had a crater on Mars's moon Phobos named after him. His mental deterioration forced his institutionalization in 1922; his wife Mabel Loomis Todd edited Emily Dickinson's posthumous poetry.

notable_stories.title: First woman to earn a Harvard PhD in geology — buried at Arlington National Cemetery
notable_stories.summary: Millicent Todd Bingham (HD1759, 1880-1968) was the first woman to earn a doctorate in geology and geography from Harvard (1923). She then abandoned her geography career at her dying mother's request to publish 600+ unpublished Emily Dickinson poems. She established the Todd Wildlife Sanctuary on Hog Island Maine (donated to Audubon Society) and the Mabel Loomis Todd Forest at Amherst College. She is buried at Arlington National Cemetery next to her husband Walter Van Dyke Bingham, WWI/WWII Army psychologist who developed the intelligence tests that classified millions of military recruits. She was a 9th-generation descendant of Rev. Thomas Hooker.

notable_stories.title: HM3 Robert Louis Tracy — killed in Vietnam, 11th-generation Hooker descendant
notable_stories.summary: Robert Louis Tracy (HD1788, 1947-1968) was a Hospital Corpsman Third Class serving with the Navy and Marines (1st Reconnaissance Battalion) who died in Quang Nam province, Vietnam, on January 18, 1968, age 21. He was an 11th-generation descendant of Rev. Thomas Hooker and a great-great-great-great-great-great-great-great-grandchild of Sarah Edwards Parsons (daughter of Rev. Jonathan Edwards). He is buried next to his mother Gertrude at Lower Brandywine Presbyterian Church Cemetery, Delaware. Second Vietnam War death in the Hooker tree.

sources.note: HM3 Robert Louis Tracy; WikiTree Tracy-2380

notable_stories.title: Emily Dickinson's first editor married into the Hooker-Edwards line
notable_stories.summary: Mabel Loomis Todd (X00568, 1856-1932) — first editor of Emily Dickinson's poetry, first Western woman to climb Mt. Fuji, traveler to 30+ countries — married David Peck Todd (HD1758), 8th-generation Hooker descendant and great-great-great-great-great-grandchild of Sarah Edwards. She had a 13-year affair with Emily Dickinson's brother Austin Dickinson. Emily Dickinson herself was deeply rooted in the Connecticut River Valley that Thomas Hooker founded. Her daughter Millicent Todd Bingham became the first woman to earn a Harvard PhD in geology.

notable_stories.title: Cigar box manufacturer refused to make ammunition boxes — "did not wish to be connected with killing"
notable_stories.summary: Henry H. Sheip (X00576, 1850-1916), founder of the Henry H. Sheip Co. of Philadelphia (cigar box manufacturer), was married to Mary Ella Bower Tracy (HD1779), 8th-generation Hooker descendant. When WWI began and Sheip was urged to convert his factories to gun stocks and ammunition boxes, he declined, explaining that "in his old age he did not wish even indirectly to be connected with the killing of his fellow men." He also had a large plant in Tampa FL with orange groves.

notable_stories.title: Mount Lee above the Hollywood sign — named for a 9th-generation Hooker descendant
notable_stories.summary: Donald Musgrave Lee (HD1828, 1880-1934), 9th-generation descendant of Rev. Thomas Hooker, was the exclusive West Coast Cadillac distributor and pioneering broadcaster who launched the 12-station Don Lee Network (CBS affiliated 1929-1936). In 1931 he received the first LA television license for station W6XAO, which became KCBS-TV — the CBS West Coast flagship still broadcasting today. The ridge above the Hollywood sign where Lee established his transmitter is still called "Mount Lee" — a permanent mark on the Los Angeles skyline. He also launched Harley Earl's career, who went on to head GM's styling department and design the Corvette.

notable_stories.title: Bought a Rothko for $1,000 — shaped Pacific Northwest art for 60 years
notable_stories.summary: Virginia Prentice Bloedel Wright (HD1836, 1929-2020), 11th-generation Hooker descendant, purchased Mark Rothko No. 10 for $1,000 at the Sidney Janis Gallery in New York. She went on to serve as president of the Seattle Art Museum (1986-1992), grow its endowment to $100M+, found the Washington Art Consortium (7 museums), and donate 200+ works to SAM. The Virginia Wright Fund placed major sculptures including a Barnett Newman across Washington State. "You can't tell the story of Seattle's art world without telling the story of Jinny Wright" (SAM).

notable_stories.title: The Weyerhaeuser kidnapping of 1935 — the victim's wife was a 10th-generation Hooker descendant
notable_stories.summary: George Hunt Walker Weyerhaeuser Sr. (X00597) was kidnapped off a Tacoma street at age 8 in 1935. His family paid $200,000 in unmarked bills; he was released after 8 days. He later advocated for the release of one of his kidnappers and offered him a job. He went on to serve as CEO of Weyerhaeuser Company (1966-1991) and hold boards at Boeing, Safeco, the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, Rand Corporation, and Chevron. His wife Wendy Wagner Weyerhaeuser (HD1838) was a 11th-generation descendant of Rev. Thomas Hooker through the Sally Ingersoll → Chadwick → Lee → Merrill → Wagner line.

notable_stories.title: The Ingersoll genealogy was compiled by a Hooker descendant
notable_stories.summary: Lillian Drake Avery (HD1819, 1856-1930), 8th-generation Hooker descendant, compiled "A Genealogy of the Ingersoll Family in America 1629-1925" (1926, New York). She was the daughter of Francis Marion Drake and Sarah Elizabeth Chadwick — granddaughter of Sally Ingersoll (HD1693) and David Ingersoll (X00543). The Ingersoll genealogy she compiled is one of the key sources for this very database, making a Hooker descendant an essential authority on the Ingersoll family history.

sources.note: "Ingersolls in America" compiled by Lillian Drake Avery, Pontiac MI

notable_stories.title: Founder of Mt. Hood Meadows ski resort — 10th-generation Hooker descendant
notable_stories.summary: Franklin Griffith Drake (HD1844, 1928-2021), 10th-generation descendant of Rev. Thomas Hooker, won the 1966 U.S. Forest Service competitive bid to develop Mt. Hood Meadows on the southeast face of Mt. Hood. He also built major Portland landmarks (Fremont Bridge approaches, Rose Garden Arena/Moda Center) and BART underground stations in San Francisco. Remained CEO of Mt. Hood Meadows until 2006; died age 93 in 2021.

sources.note: Oregon Live / River View Cemetery, Portland OR, 2021

notable_stories.title: Talcott Parsons: Harvard's foremost sociologist was named for his Talcott ancestry — and theorized that Hooker's Puritanism made America
notable_stories.summary: Talcott Parsons (HD1861, 1902-1979) was a 9th-generation descendant of Rev. Thomas Hooker and simultaneously descended from the Talcott founding family of Hartford. His name "Talcott" honored his great-grandmother Catharine L. Talcott (T01488), great-great-great-great-granddaughter of John Talcott, Hartford founder. As Harvard's most influential sociologist (1930-1973), Parsons argued that Calvinist-Puritan values — the very tradition of Thomas Hooker's Connecticut — became institutionalized as the foundational American value system. A Hooker-Talcott descendant became the 20th century's leading theorist of how the Hooker-Talcott Puritan founding shaped all of American civilization.
notable_stories.generation_span: 7 generations (gen 6 Alvan Hyde Ingersoll to gen 9 Talcott Parsons)

notable_stories.title: Disbarred for refusing the KKK oath — then appointed to the Tennessee Supreme Court
notable_stories.summary: Judge Henry Hulbert Ingersoll (HD1867, 1844-1915), 7th-generation descendant of Rev. Thomas Hooker, was disbarred from 1870 to 1875 for refusing to take the "Ku Klux Oath" required of lawyers in Reconstruction-era Tennessee. After reinstatement, he rose to the Tennessee Supreme Court (1879), became Dean of the University of Tennessee Law School (1891-1914), and Vice President of the American Bar Association (1907-1912). Yale class of 1863; Civil War veteran; Grand Master of Tennessee Freemasons. Author of The Handbook of the Law of Public Corporations.

notable_stories.title: First professor of sacred music in any American college — 1835 Oberlin
notable_stories.summary: Rev. Elihu Parsons Ingersoll (HD1696, 1804-1887), 6th-generation Hooker descendant and youngest son of David and Sarah (Parsons) Ingersoll, was appointed in November 1835 as the first Professor of Sacred Music at Oberlin College — the inaugural such chair in any American college. He was a Yale graduate (class of 1832) and Congregational minister. He also served as a Kansas pioneer, county surveyor, and opponent of pro-slavery forces during Bleeding Kansas. Named for his maternal grandfather Elihu Parsons Sr. (X00536), a Revolutionary War patriot.

notable_stories.title: Corporal Henry I. Ingersoll — killed in France, buried at the Somme American Cemetery
notable_stories.summary: Corporal Henry I. Ingersoll (HD1875, 1893-1918), 9th-generation Hooker descendant, was killed in action at Beauvoir-Wavans, Pas-de-Calais, France on September 15, 1918. He is buried at the Somme American Cemetery and Memorial, Bony, Aisne, France. His grandfather was Judge Henry Hulbert Ingersoll, who had been disbarred for refusing the KKK oath in Reconstruction Tennessee. Third generation to serve in wartime in this branch.

notable_stories.title: The marriage that joined Hartford's two founding families — Hooker and Talcott
notable_stories.summary: When George Lyman Ingersoll (HD1846), 7th-generation Hooker descendant, married Catharine L. Talcott (T01488) on January 12, 1855 in Lanesboro MA, it joined two blood lines from Hartford's founding generation: Rev. Thomas Hooker (founder of Hartford, 1636) and John Talcott (one of Hartford's original proprietors). Catharine was a great-great-great-great-granddaughter of John Talcott.
