The Edwards legacy (revival, moral urgency, covenant responsibility) ran through the Leavitts, the Dwights, and the Gates line. The tree also contains the failures and contradictions: slaveholders, men who benefited from slave labor, and the cotton gin that made it all worse. The full picture is more honest than a simple heroic narrative. 

(EH 1909; DAB; Wikipedia; Still, The Underground Railroad 1872; William H. Edwards, Timothy and Rhoda Ogden Edwards and Their Descendants 1903)

notable_stories.title: Elias Cornelius — ABCFM Secretary and missionary to the Creek and Cherokee — married Mary Ann Hooker, a double Hooker descendant whose two grandfathers were both Thomas Hooker descendants born within two years of each other
notable_stories.summary:
Elias Cornelius (1794-1832) was Secretary of Domestic Correspondence for the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions (ABCFM) from 1819 until his death at age 37 — one of the most active Protestant missionaries to Native Americans in the early 19th century. In the spring of 1817 he conducted an extensive tour to the Creek and Cherokee nations, distributing religious literature, preaching, and assessing sites for permanent stations. He extended the journey to New Orleans by April 1818. His fieldwork directly shaped ABCFM strategy for the southeastern tribes during a period of intense cultural pressure and forced migration. 

He married Mary Ann Hooker (H01355, b.1796 Goshen CT) — a double Hooker descendant in one of the most concentrated examples of converging Hooker lineage in the tree. Her two grandfathers: Asahel Hooker Sr. (H00262, b. 1736) — Hooker surname line; Timothy Edwards (H00381, b. 1738) — Pierpont-Edwards line. Two Hooker descendants born within two years of each other, whose grandchildren converged in Mary Ann. Her father Rev. Asahel Hooker Jr. (H00514) was himself a double Hooker descendant by marriage (see the double convergence story). 

The naming consequence: Rev. Edward William Hooker (H01354), Mary Ann's brother, named his own son "Elias Cornelius Hooker" (HD2244, 1832-1873) for his brother-in-law who died that same year. 

(Wikipedia on Elias Cornelius; Dictionary of American Biography; EH 1909 #1355)

notable_stories.title: Mary Hooker Cornelius (1821-1914) — daughter of the Cherokee missionary, granddaughter of the double Hooker convergence — published "The Young Housekeeper's Friend" (1859)
notable_stories.summary:
Mary Hooker Cornelius (b. Jul 3, 1821 Salem MA; d. 1914 Newton Center MA, age ~93) published "The Young Housekeeper's Friend" in 1859 under the pen name "Mrs. Cornelius," with a revised edition in 1888 (Riverside Press, Houghton). The book became a widely-used domestic manual for young married women in middle-class New England households, covering cooking, household management, and healthful food at moderate expense. 

She was the daughter of Rev. Elias Cornelius (1794-1832) — the ABCFM missionary who visited the Cherokee and Creek nations (1817-1818) and wrote the first published account by a white person of the Etowah Indian Mounds — and Mary Ann Hooker (H01355), herself a double Hooker descendant whose two grandfathers (Asahel Hooker Sr. b.1736 and Timothy Edwards b.1738) were both Thomas Hooker descendants born within two years of each other. 

Mary Hooker Cornelius apparently never married (listed as "single" in the 1904 Cornelius genealogy). She lived 93 years — born in the early republic, alive to see the First World War. Her brother Thomas Hooker Cornelius died in San Francisco in 1853; her father died when she was 10. 

(Library of Congress; Cornelius genealogy book 1904; archive.org)

notable_stories.title: The missionary who married a Hooker descendant selected a Cherokee boy for school in 1818 — that boy's son fought for the Confederacy; the decision contributed to the Trail of Tears
notable_stories.summary:
In 1818, Elias Cornelius (X00724) — about to marry Mary Ann Hooker (H01355) — selected a Cherokee adolescent named Gallegina Watie for the ABCFM's Foreign Mission School in Cornwall, Connecticut. The boy adopted the name Elias Boudinot, became editor of the Cherokee Phoenix (first Native American newspaper, 1828), and named his own son "Elias Cornelius Boudinot" in honor of the missionary who had chosen him. 

Boudinot and his faction signed the Treaty of New Echota in 1835, ceding the Cherokee homeland. The treaty facilitated the Trail of Tears (1838-1839), in which approximately 4,000 Cherokee died during forced relocation. Boudinot was assassinated on June 22, 1839, by tribal opponents who viewed him as a traitor. 

His son Elias Cornelius Boudinot (1835-1890) — the one named for Cornelius — became a Confederate colonel (2nd Cherokee Mounted Rifles), the first Native American admitted to practice before the US Supreme Court, and a railroad lobbyist whom historian Richard White called "among the great scoundrels of the Gilded Age." 

A single selection decision in 1818 by the man who married into the Hooker family tree rippled through four decades of Cherokee history. 

(Wikipedia on Elias Cornelius; Wikipedia on Elias Cornelius Boudinot; Wikipedia on Elias Boudinot; Wikipedia on Trail of Tears)

notable_stories.title: Princeton's second president Aaron Burr Sr. — husband of Esther Edwards Burr, father of VP Aaron Burr Jr. — purchased an enslaved man in 1756
notable_stories.summary:
Aaron Burr Sr. (X00613, 1716-1757) — second president of Princeton (then the College of New Jersey, 1748-1757) and husband of Esther Edwards Burr (H00378, daughter of Rev. Jonathan Edwards) — purchased an enslaved man named Caesar on September 2, 1756, while serving as Princeton's president and residing in Nassau Hall, the building he had led the college into. 

He died the following year, September 24, 1757, at age 41 — one year after moving into Nassau Hall. His wife Esther died six months later at age 26. Their son Aaron Burr Jr. (H00913) was left orphaned at 18 months and went on to become the third Vice President of the United States, kill Alexander Hamilton in a duel (1804), and in 1785 introduce a bill in the New York legislature to abolish slavery — which failed by one vote. 

The Princeton & Slavery Project documents Burr Sr.'s slave purchase; Burr Jr.'s failed abolition bill is a documented story elsewhere in this tree. The moral arc from father's slave purchase (1756) to son's failed abolition bill (1785) runs across 29 years and three deaths. 

(Princeton & Slavery Project; Wikipedia on Aaron Burr Sr.; EH 1909; https://slavery.princeton.edu)

notable_stories.title: Alla Mary Edwards married her first cousin Edwin Tyler — both 6th-generation Hooker descendants through Timothy Edwards
notable_stories.summary: Edwin Tyler (HD2278) married Alla Mary Edwards on Sep 4, 1821 in Brooklyn CT. Alla Mary was the daughter of Richard Edwards (H00939). Edwin's mother was Sarah Edwards Tyler (H00936) — the sister of Richard Edwards. Both Richard and Sarah were children of Timothy Edwards (H00381). A first-cousin marriage within the Hooker tree: two 6th-generation descendants through the same grandfather. (FindAGrave; William H. Edwards 1903)

sources.short: William H. Edwards, Timothy and Rhoda Ogden Edwards 1903

notable_stories.title: Joan Prout and Wenda Prout — living 11th-generation Hooker descendants and potential project collaborators
notable_stories.summary:
Joan Prout (b. Jan 1951) and Wenda Prout are living 11th-generation descendants of Thomas Hooker: Thomas → Samuel → Mary Hooker Pierpont → Sarah Pierpont Edwards → Timothy Edwards → Richard Edwards → Timothy R. Edwards → Samuel Hall Edwards → Mary Emma Edwards Allen → Harriet Marshall Allen Prout → Lewis Austin Prout → Joan/Wenda. 

Their genealogy research began at Trinity Cemetery, Portland CT, June 2016 — 7 generations of ancestors in the same cemetery, less than a mile from their father's birthplace. Joan is active on WikiTree (Prout-286); Wenda is Prout-287. Both are potential project contacts. (WikiTree profiles; Joan's online genealogy biography)

notable_stories.title: Dozens of families honor "Edwards" in their names across generations without knowing the chain runs through Sarah Pierpont Edwards all the way back to Thomas Hooker, founder of Hartford
notable_stories.summary:
One of the most consistent patterns in the Hooker tree is the naming echo: families who knew they were descended from Jonathan Edwards — and honored that heritage in the names of their children — but stopped the chain there, not knowing that their Edwards ancestor's wife was Sarah Pierpont, daughter of Rev. James Pierpont of Yale, whose mother was Mary Hooker, daughter of Samuel Hooker, son of Thomas Hooker, founder of Hartford. 

The pattern is visible across multiple branches: 

**The Annin family (gen 7-9):** Sarah Edwards Annin (HD2263, gen 7) had a son named William EDWARDS Annin (1857-1903). His children included Susannah EDWARDS Annin (1887-1984, lived to 97), and William EDWARDS Annin Jr. and III. Four consecutive generations carrying "Edwards" as a first or middle name — the heritage explicitly honored. Almost certainly none of them knew the chain went back to Thomas Hooker. 

**The Forbes line:** A Yale obituary for William Jehiel Forbes (1856-1921) explicitly notes that his mother "Hannah Edwards Forbes was the daughter of Timothy and Sarah (Haigh) Edwards, and a great-granddaughter of Jonathan Edwards (BA 1720)" — stopping exactly there, at Jonathan Edwards, without going one generation further to Sarah Pierpont Edwards and from there to Thomas Hooker. 

**The Prout line:** Lewis Austin Prout's WikiTree profile (Prout-286, active 2024) documents his Mayflower descent (through Edward Doty) in detail but does not mention Thomas Hooker at all, despite the complete chain existing through Samuel Hall Edwards → Timothy R. Edwards → Richard Edwards → Timothy Edwards → Sarah Pierpont Edwards → Mary Hooker Pierpont → Samuel Hooker → Thomas Hooker. 

**The UConn connection:** No biography of Governor Hobart Baldwin Bigelow (who signed the legislation founding the Storrs Agricultural School in 1881) mentions his Hooker connection, despite the direct Pierpont line. Wikipedia traces him to Rev. James Pierpont (Yale founder) but stops there. 

**Why it stops:** For branches that run through Sarah Pierpont Edwards, Jonathan Edwards is the gravitational name — the theologian, the revivalist, the Princeton president. He absorbs the full attention of genealogists. Thomas Hooker, two generations earlier on the female line through Mary Hooker Pierpont, was simply invisible behind that famous name. 

This visualization makes the full chain visible for the first time for many of these families.

sources.short: Yale obituary for William Jehiel Forbes (class of 1877)

notable_stories.title: Henry Davis Minot (1859-1890) — Hooker descendant, Theodore Roosevelt's Harvard classmate, ornithologist — died at 31; Minot, North Dakota named for him
notable_stories.summary:
Henry Davis Minot (HD2336, 1859-1890) was an 8th-generation descendant of Thomas Hooker through the Rhoda Edwards Dwight → Elizabeth Buckminster Dwight Sedgwick → Katharine Maria Sedgwick Minot line. At Harvard he was a classmate and close friend of Theodore Roosevelt — both were keen ornithologists. He published "The Land Birds and Game Birds of New England" at age 17 in 1877. He left Harvard as a sophomore to pursue railroad investments, eventually directing Jim Hill's Great Northern Railway. In 1886 when the railroad stopped for winter in a Dakota tent city, the place was named Minot for him — it grew into Minot, North Dakota, the "Magic City." Minot Air Force Base carries his name indirectly. He died at 31 in a train crash near New Florence, Pennsylvania, November 14, 1890. 

His memoir notes the family as "fifth generation from Jonathan Edwards" — another example of the Edwards connection documented and the Hooker connection invisible. (Wikipedia on Henry Minot; Wikipedia on Minot ND)

notable_stories.title: C.D. Jackson — Time-Life publisher, Eisenhower advisor, buyer of the Zapruder film — married a 9th-generation Hooker descendant through the Bristed-Astor-Sedgwick line
notable_stories.summary:
C.D. Jackson (1902-1964) married Katherine Elizabeth Bristed, whose grandmother was Grace Ashburner Sedgwick Bristed (HD2330) — daughter of Elizabeth Buckminster Dwight Sedgwick (HD2283) and granddaughter of Rhoda Edwards Dwight (H00945). Making Katherine Bristed Jackson a 9th-generation Hooker descendant. 

C.D. Jackson was publisher of Time-Life, psychological warfare advisor to President Eisenhower, and the man who purchased the Zapruder film for Time-Life in the days after President Kennedy's assassination in November 1963. Time-Life's purchase and long suppression of public access to the film became a central element of JFK assassination discourse. He and his wife Grace are buried in the Sedgwick family's famous "pie" — the circular family plot at Stockbridge Cemetery. 

Grace's father was Charles Henry Maine Astor Bristed Jr. (1869-1936), grandson of John Jacob Astor through the fur-trading fortune. His grandfather Charles Astor Bristed Sr. made the earliest known use of the term "conspiracy theory" in a letter to the New York Times on January 11, 1863. 

(Wikipedia on C.D. Jackson; Wikipedia on Charles Astor Bristed; FindAGrave)

notable_stories.title: Dr. Francis Minot Rackemann (1887-1973) — 9th-generation Hooker descendant, founder of the first US allergy clinic at Massachusetts General Hospital 1923
notable_stories.summary:
Francis Minot Rackemann (HD2362) was born in 1887 to Felix Rackemann (HD2361) and Julia Minot Rackemann. His father Felix was the son of Elizabeth Dwight Sedgwick Rackemann (HD2331) and Friedrich Rackemann of Bremen — making him a 9th-generation Hooker descendant through the Rhoda Edwards line. 

He graduated cum laude from Harvard Medical School in 1912 and founded the Allergy Clinic at Massachusetts General Hospital in 1923 — the first clinic of its kind in the United States. His landmark 1918 paper categorized asthma as extrinsic (allergic) or intrinsic, a classification still in use today. He was the first president of the American Association of Allergy in 1934. 

His dictum: "There is always something that can be done to help the asthmatic." 

Curious footnote: his son Francis Minot Rackemann Jr. worked at Time magazine in New York — the same publication whose publisher C.D. Jackson (who married a Hooker descendant, HD2342) had purchased the Zapruder film just a decade earlier.

sources.short: American Academy of Arts and Sciences biography

notable_stories.title: Samuel Gelston Dwight (1815-1880) — great-nephew of Yale president Timothy Dwight IV and 7th-generation Hooker descendant — settled in Hawaii, married a Hawaiian woman, and founded a Dwight family line that endures there today
notable_stories.summary:
The Hooker connection to Hawaii runs through one of the most unexpected chains in the tree. Samuel Gelston Dwight (HD2376, 1815-1880) was the son of James Adams Dwight (HD2375, died Sacramento 1850 of scrofula during the Gold Rush), grandson of Jonathan Edwards Dwight (H00917), and great-great-nephew of Yale president Timothy Dwight IV (H00914) — making him a 7th-generation descendant of Thomas Hooker through the Mary Edwards Dwight line. 

Samuel went to Hawaii during the missionary era and married Anna Haaheo Mahoe, a Hawaiian woman. Their children carried the double heritage: Samuel Castle Dwight (1856-1930, born on Maui, named for ABCFM lay agent Samuel Northrup Castle of Castle & Cooke), Juliette Cooke Dwight (1857-1917, named for ABCFM missionary Juliette Cooke), and Charles Bishop Dwight (1859-1904, born on Molokai, named for Hawaii businessman Charles Reed Bishop who married into Hawaiian royalty). Every child's middle name honors a different pillar of the ABCFM missionary network. 

Charles Bishop Dwight's son Charles Bishop Dwight Jr. (1895-1949) had a son Charles Bishop Dwight III (1926-2013), an Ashford & Wriston attorney in Honolulu — a 10th-generation Hooker descendant who spent his entire life in the Hawaiian Islands. 

The Hawaii connection begins with Timothy Dwight IV himself: he co-founded the ABCFM in 1810, the organization that launched the first Christian mission to Hawaii in 1819, and whose missionaries permeated the islands' New England settler community — the same community Samuel Gelston Dwight joined a generation later. The "Dwight" in missionary Dwight Baldwin's name was almost certainly chosen in honor of President Timothy Dwight IV.

sources.short: FindAGrave entries for Hawaii Dwight family

notable_stories.title: Theodore Dwight Sr. (1764-1846) — Hooker descendant, Hartford Convention Secretary, first US newspaper on a steam press, early Jefferson-Hemings whistleblower, and one-time law partner of Aaron Burr
notable_stories.summary:
Theodore Dwight Sr. (H00920), 5th-generation Hooker descendant and younger brother of Yale president Timothy Dwight IV, packed several historic firsts into one career. 

**The Aaron Burr partnership:** Early in his career he had a brief law partnership with his cousin Aaron Burr Jr. (H00913) in New York — but their fierce political differences (Dwight was a Federalist, Burr a Republican) ended the partnership quickly. He later became the first to publicly call Burr a villain in print. 

**The Hartford Convention:** As Secretary of the 1814-1815 Hartford Convention, Dwight was at the center of New England Federalists' ill-fated attempt to challenge Madison's War of 1812. The convention's resolutions arrived in Washington just as news broke of the Treaty of Ghent and Andrew Jackson's victory at New Orleans — destroying the Federalist Party's credibility overnight. 

**The steam press:** His New York Daily Advertiser (founded 1817) became in 1825 the first American newspaper printed on a steam-powered cylinder press — capable of 2,000 issues per hour. Destroyed in the Great Fire of December 1835. 

**The Jefferson-Hemings disclosure:** His 1839 book "The Character of Thomas Jefferson as Exhibited in His Own Writings" argued Jefferson's duplicity and referenced his relationship with Sally Hemings — among the earliest public treatments of this subject in American publishing. 

**The abolitionist oration:** He delivered "An Oration Before the Connecticut Society for the Promotion of Freedom" — arguing enslaved people had a natural-law right not just to freedom but to reparations, having never consented to the social contract.

sources.short: Dwight, The Character of Thomas Jefferson (1839)

notable_stories.title: Theodore Dwight Jr. (1796-1866) — Hooker descendant who helped preserve the only Arabic slave autobiography in America, founded the American Ethnological Society, and died jumping off a moving train
notable_stories.summary:
Theodore Dwight Jr. (HD2050), Yale class of 1814 and nephew of President Timothy Dwight IV, led an unusual intellectual life. 

**Omar ibn Said:** Working with the enslaved West African scholar Omar ibn Said, Dwight persuaded him to write his autobiography in Arabic in 1831 — the only known extant slave autobiography written in Arabic in America. Dwight's intent was explicitly abolitionist: he wanted the document to undermine pro-slavery arguments by demonstrating Africa's deep literary and monotheistic culture. Omar, a Muslim, had been captured and enslaved in North Carolina around 1807. 

**American Ethnological Society:** Dwight founded this institution (INST033) to advance the study of human cultures — a pioneer in what would become anthropology. 

**The Northern Traveller (1825):** He compiled the second tourist guidebook ever published in the United States, regularly updated through 1841. 

**His death:** On October 16, 1866, at age 70, he accompanied his daughter to board a train at Jersey City. He jumped from the car while it was in motion, sustained severe injuries, and died the next day at his Brooklyn home.

notable_stories.title: The Connecticut River Gods — the 18th-century gentry network of the Connecticut Valley that Thomas Hooker's descendants helped constitute
notable_stories.summary:
Eighteenth-century western Massachusetts was controlled by a tight kinship network contemporaries called the "River Gods" — seven intermarried lineages (Ashley, Dwight, Partridge, Porter, Pynchon, Stoddard, and Williams) that monopolized pulpits, courts, military commissions, and land grants through royal patronage. 

The Hooker tree runs through the center of this network. Mary Hooker (H00034), daughter of Rev. Samuel Hooker (H00007, Thomas Hooker's son), married Rev. James Pierpont of Yale — and their daughter Sarah Pierpont married Rev. Jonathan Edwards, whose daughter Mary Edwards Dwight (H00379) married Major Timothy Dwight III (X00635), a core River God. Their son Timothy Dwight IV (H00914) became Yale's president. 

The River Gods were also connected to the Stoddard family — Rev. Solomon Stoddard (1643-1729), Jonathan Edwards's grandfather, was the dominant Puritan minister of the Valley for decades. Jonathan Edwards himself (X00128) was therefore embedded in the River God network by both blood (through Stoddard) and marriage (through Sarah Pierpont). 

The River Gods' power collapsed after the American Revolution — their Federalist politics, loyalist tendencies (Major Dwight's Natchez colony), and ecclesiastical establishment all became liabilities. But their descendants — the Dwights, the Porters, the Woolseys, the Storers — populated the leadership of Yale, Hamilton College, Columbia Law, and the emerging ABCFM missionary network for another century.

notable_stories.title: Sereno Edwards Dwight (1786-1850) — Chaplain of the US Senate, President of Hamilton College, editor of the definitive Jonathan Edwards biography — whose career was destroyed by accidental mercury poisoning
notable_stories.summary:
Sereno Edwards Dwight (HD1970) was the son of Yale president Timothy Dwight IV (H00914) and a 6th-generation Hooker descendant. Named "Sereno Edwards" to honor both an uncle and his great-grandfather Jonathan Edwards, he achieved remarkable institutional prominence before mercury poisoning ended his career. 

**Chaplain of the United States Senate:** Served Dec 16, 1816 – Dec 19, 1817. 

**Park Street Church, Boston:** Ordained at Park Street Church Sep 3, 1817 — the same church that became a major center of antebellum reform. Strongly influenced hymnwriter Ray Palmer there. 

**Jonathan Edwards biography:** His Life and Works of Jonathan Edwards (10 volumes, 1830) — as great-grandson of Edwards — remains a primary source. 

**3rd President of Hamilton College (1833-1835)** — Clinton, NY. The same campus where Elliott Anthony (X00639) later taught Grover Cleveland. 

**Mercury poisoning:** Accidental exposure during his Boston years permanently damaged his capacity for sustained work. His life after 1839 was described as "solitary and comparatively uninfluential." He died in New Haven in 1850, his early promise unfulfilled.

notable_stories.title: The missionary named "Dwight" — Dwight Baldwin (1798-1886), Yale 1821, ABCFM missionary to Maui, whose first name almost certainly honors the Yale president who co-founded the ABCFM
notable_stories.summary:
Dwight Baldwin (X00776, 1798-1886) was an ABCFM missionary physician on Maui for over three decades — patriarch of a family that co-founded Alexander & Baldwin, one of Hawaii's "Big Five" corporations. 

His first name is not a surname but a given name — almost certainly chosen in honor of Timothy Dwight IV (H00914), the Yale president who co-founded the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions (ABCFM) in 1810. Baldwin entered Yale in 1817 (the year of Dwight's death), graduated under Dwight's successor President Jeremiah Day, and sailed with the ABCFM's Fourth Company in 1830. 

This naming pattern was common: missionary families frequently honored prominent clergymen by giving their children those clergymen's surnames as given names. The ABCFM was Dwight's most visible institutional legacy. 

Not a Hooker descendant by blood, but a living monument to Timothy Dwight IV's influence — embedded in the same Hawaii in which his colleague's great-nephew Samuel Gelston Dwight (HD2376) was simultaneously founding a Hawaiian Hooker-descendant line.

notable_stories.title: From Amelia Dwight Flint to the Met Museum president to the 'glamour deb' who died in a Newport plane crash — a Hooker descendant thread through Gilded Age and Depression-era New York
notable_stories.summary:
Amelia Dwight Flint (HD2286, triplet daughter of Rhoda Edwards Dwight) married Dr. Joseph Henshaw Flint. Their daughter Mary Dwight Flint (HD2357) married New York merchant Daniel Gorham Bacon. Their son Dr. Gorham Bacon (HD2406, Harvard MD 1879) married twice — his second wife Margaret Butterfield subsequently married William Sloane Coffin Sr. (1879-1933), Yale class of 1900 and president of the Metropolitan Museum of Art's Board of Trustees from 1931 until his death in 1933. Their son William Sloane Coffin Jr. (1924-2006) became one of the most prominent social justice activists of the 20th century — Yale chaplain 1958-1975, Freedom Rider, leading Vietnam War opponent, senior minister of Riverside Church. 

Gorham's brother Robert Ogden Bacon (HD2416) had a son nicknamed "Bunty" (Robert Ogden Bacon II, 1912-1972) who briefly married Eleanor Jane "Cookie" Young (1918-1941) — "one of the glamour debs of the Depression era," daughter of financier Robert Ralph Young and Anita O'Keeffe Young (sister of artist Georgia O'Keeffe). Cookie died at 23 in a plane crash off Newport on July 1, 1941, with Greek shipping heir Nicholas Embiricos. Her father later died by suicide in Palm Beach. 

The thread runs: Thomas Hooker → Samuel Hooker → Mary Hooker Pierpont → Sarah Pierpont Edwards → Mary Edwards Dwight → Josiah Dwight → Rhoda Edwards Dwight → Amelia Dwight Flint → Mary Dwight Flint Bacon → Dr. Gorham Bacon → Margaret Butterfield → William Sloane Coffin Sr. → William Sloane Coffin Jr.

William Sloane Coffin Jr. was a CIA officer, Yale chaplain, Freedom Rider, and the leading religious voice against the Vietnam War. His son David Coffin (b. ~1955, Gloucester MA, davidcoffin.com) is a folk and maritime musician with a YouTube audience in the millions — and one of his ancestors was Tristram Coffin (1605-1681), who bought Nantucket Island in 1659 for thirty pounds and two beaver hats. Tristram Coffin is also the ancestor of Jethro Coffin (X00015) in this tree. David Coffin is the strongest living outreach candidate in this line.

sources.short: Wikipedia on William Sloane Coffin Sr.
Wikipedia on William Sloane Coffin Jr.

notable_stories.title: Rev. William Sloane Coffin Jr. — CIA officer, Skull and Bones member, Freedom Rider, Yale chaplain — orbit connection to the Hooker tree through his father's marriage to a Hooker descendant's widow
notable_stories.summary:
William Sloane Coffin Jr. (1924-2006) is one of the most remarkable orbit connections in the Hooker tree — connected not by blood but by his father's marriage to Margaret Butterfield, who had previously been married to Dr. Gorham Bacon (HD2413), great-great-great-granddaughter of Amelia Dwight (HD2286), daughter of Rhoda Edwards Dwight (H00945). 

**The biography reads like a novel:** He studied piano in Paris under Nadia Boulanger at age 15. He applied to the OSS as a spy in 1943 but was rejected for lacking "sufficiently Gallic features." He served as a CIA case officer in West Germany from 1950-1953. He was inducted into Skull and Bones at Yale by his friend George H.W. Bush. He became Yale chaplain in 1958 and organized Freedom Riders — "busloads of students" — to challenge segregation in the South. He was indicted with Dr. Benjamin Spock in 1968 for conspiracy to counsel draft resistance; the conviction was overturned. Garry Trudeau immortalized him as "Rev. Scot Sloan" in Doonesbury. His first wife Eva was a daughter of pianist Arthur Rubinstein. His son Alexander died in a car accident at 24; the sermon Coffin preached afterward became his most requested. 

**His son David Coffin** (b. ~1955, Gloucester MA, davidcoffin.com) is a folk and maritime musician — YouTube audience of millions for his sea shanties. He is the living end of this chain and a strong outreach candidate. 

**Tristram Coffin thread:** Both David Coffin and Jethro Coffin (X00015, already in this tree) descend from Tristram Coffin (1605-1681), who bought Nantucket Island in 1659 for thirty pounds and two beaver hats. Priscilla Rawson Coffin (H00205, gen 4 Hooker descendant) is from the same Nantucket Coffin family — creating a distant echo between three separate points where the Coffin family touches the Hooker tree.

sources.short: Wikipedia on William Sloane Coffin Jr.

notable_stories.title: Tad Coffin's 1976 Olympic gold — Violet Bodman's OSS and Time-Life career — and how two Hooker orbit threads converge in one Vermont family
notable_stories.summary:
Edmund "Ned" Coffin (X00795) and Violet Bodman (X00796) connect to the Hooker tree through Gorham Bacon (HD2413), whose second wife Catherine/Margaret Butterfield subsequently married William Sloane Coffin Sr. (X00792), making Ned Coffin Catherine's step-son-in-law's step-son. 

Son **Tad Coffin won the gold medal** in equestrian three-day event, 1976 Montreal Olympics. 

Violet Bodman worked for the OSS in London, then Time magazine in Cairo, then Life magazine in New York — the same Time-Life empire whose publisher C.D. Jackson (X00748) married Hooker descendant Katherine Elizabeth Bristed Jackson (HD2342) and purchased the Zapruder film in November 1963. Two separate Hooker orbit threads converged at the same publishing house. 

Ned and his brother Rev. William Sloane Coffin Jr. (X00794) — Yale chaplain, Freedom Rider, Doonesbury's "Rev. Scot Sloan" — spent their final years as neighbors on the Strafford Common in Vermont. Ned introduced Bill to his third wife Randy Wilson, who moved across the street.

sources.short: Violet Bodman Coffin obituary, The Oregonian 2008

notable_stories.title: Two printing revolutions in one Hooker orbit — Theodore Dwight Sr.'s 1825 steam-press newspaper and the Hoe rotary press dynasty that married into his descendant's family
notable_stories.summary:
The Hooker tree touches two of the most significant revolutions in printing history, separated by one generation. 

**1825 — The steam press:** Theodore Dwight Sr. (H00920), 5th-generation Hooker descendant, founded the New York Daily Advertiser in 1817. In 1825 it became the first American newspaper printed on a steam-powered cylinder press, capable of 2,000 issues per hour. 

**1843-1871 — The rotary press:** Richard March Hoe (1812-1886) invented the rotary printing press in 1843 and the "Hoe web perfecting press" in 1871 — which used a continuous 5-mile roll of paper, printed both sides at 800 feet/minute, and delivered 18,000 completely printed and folded newspapers per hour. First used by the New York Tribune. Hoe Avenue in the Bronx is named for him. 

**The connection:** Hoe's grandson Richard March Hoe Harper Sr. (X00797) married Mabel Simpkins Bacon Harper (HD2426, 1882-1961) — daughter of Dr. Gorham Bacon (HD2413), great-great-granddaughter of Amelia Dwight (HD2286), and 9th-generation Hooker descendant. Their son Gorham Bacon Harper Sr. (HD2427, 1907-1963) carried both the "Gorham Bacon" and "Hoe" heritage into the 20th century — named for his maternal grandfather the Harvard-trained surgeon, while inheriting the printing dynasty lineage through his father. 

Theodore Dwight Sr.'s steam press and Richard March Hoe's rotary press were the two most transformative innovations in American newspaper printing in the 19th century. Both touch the Hooker tree.

sources.short: FindAGrave — Harper family, Woodside Cemetery Yarmouth Port MA

notable_stories.title: A polite professional letter, 1838 — Dr. Samuel Bayard Woodward invites Rev. Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet to preach at the Worcester Insane Asylum, unaware both men connected through Thomas Hooker
notable_stories.summary:
On February 16, 1838, Dr. Samuel Bayard Woodward (X00804) wrote to Rev. Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet (HD0411) a brief, warm, practical letter. The letter survives at Pabook Libraries. 

Woodward was first superintendent of the Worcester State Hospital (the first public asylum for the mentally ill in America) and would become founding president of the organization that later became the American Psychiatric Association. Gallaudet had founded the American School for the Deaf in Hartford in 1817. Both were prominent Hartford-area Congregationalist reformers in the same professional milieu of institutional care for the marginalized. 

The letter's substance is entirely practical. Woodward invites Gallaudet to preach on a specific Sabbath and pivots to the real point: would Gallaudet consider the full-time chaplaincy position? He pitches the congregation honestly — "We have 210 patients, 150 of whom attend our chapel...a snug congregation of 200" — and sweetens a role he frankly admits offers "no great encouragements" by noting Gallaudet could continue his writing ("book making") as profitably in Worcester as in Hartford. He offers to cover travel and put Gallaudet up at the American Temperance House. 

The letter is collegial and courteous — no theology, no debate, no mention of shared ancestry or personal connection beyond professional esteem. "My Dear Sir" was the conventional salutation among men of their standing. The article's author frames it as a window into how these two great reform institutions — the first asylum and the first school for the deaf — circled each other in the same New England reform community, their founders corresponding as peers. 

What neither man knew: they were connected through Thomas Hooker. Gallaudet (HD0411, gen 6) descends through the Hopkins line. Woodward's wife Maria Porter (HD2442, gen 6) descends through Susannah Edwards (H00382) → Eleazer Porter III (HD2432) → Maria Porter → Thomas Hooker. The small professional letter crossed a genealogical bridge neither writer could see.

sources.short: Letter from S.B. Woodward to T.H. Gallaudet, Feb 16, 1838 (Pabook Libraries)

notable_stories.title: Susannah Edwards (1740-1803) — daughter of Jonathan Edwards, sister of Timothy Edwards — whose son Jonathan Edwards Porter married his first cousin Fidelia Dwight, creating a double convergence of the Hooker-Edwards line
notable_stories.summary:
Susannah Edwards (H00382, 1740-1803) was the daughter of Rev. Jonathan Edwards and Sarah Pierpont Edwards (HD0418) — and the sister of Timothy Edwards (H00381), patriarch of the large Edwards-Hooker descendant network. She married Eleazer Porter Jr. (Yale 1748, judge and landowner of Hadley MA) on September 17, 1760. 

Her son Jonathan Edwards Porter (X00660, c.1765-1821) later married Fidelia Dwight (H00922) — his first cousin, since Fidelia was the daughter of Major Timothy Dwight III, who had married Mary Edwards Dwight (H00379), another daughter of Jonathan Edwards. 

This marriage was therefore a DOUBLE HOOKER CONVERGENCE in two ways: (1) Jonathan Edwards Porter was himself a Hooker descendant through Susannah Edwards; (2) his wife Fidelia Dwight was a Hooker descendant through Mary Edwards Dwight — and both spouses were grandchildren of Jonathan Edwards. 

Susannah's other children include Eleazer Porter III (HD2432), whose daughter Maria Porter married Dr. Samuel Bayard Woodward (first president of the American Psychiatric Association) — and through whose family the 1838 Woodward-Gallaudet letter passes. 

Her naming choice is visible across generations: Pierpont Porter (1775-?) was named for the Pierpont ancestry. Theodore Woolsey Porter (HD2053, Yale 1819) was named for his first cousin Theodore Dwight Woolsey. The Edwards-Porter network was densely intermarried and named accordingly.

sources.short: Eleazer Porter family papers, Yale Archives
FindAGrave and FamilySearch for Porter family

notable_stories.title: Mehetable Hughes Porter Armstrong (1821-1855) — 7th-generation Hooker descendant who died in the Norfolk Yellow Fever epidemic of 1855, along with three of her children, at age 34
notable_stories.summary:
Mehetable Hughes Porter Armstrong (HD2450) was the daughter of Edwin Porter (HD2449) and Mary Wyllis Porter, a granddaughter of Eleazer Porter III (HD2432), great-granddaughter of Susannah Edwards (H00382), and 7th-generation descendant of Thomas Hooker. 

She married Rev. George Dod Armstrong (X00805), professor of chemistry at Washington College (now Washington & Lee), later pastor of First Presbyterian Church, Norfolk VA. Armstrong was also a vocal defender of slavery — his 1857 publication "The Christian Doctrine of Slavery" laid out a Biblical defense of the institution. 

In the summer of 1855, the yellow fever epidemic devastated Norfolk and Portsmouth, killing roughly 3,000 of 23,000 residents. Rev. Armstrong stayed to minister to his congregation. He paid a severe price: his wife Mehetable died September 27, 1855 at age 34; their 12-year-old daughter Mary died late in September; two other children, Cornelia and Grace, survived (Grace appears in this tree as the ancestor of Valerie Dornin, a living contact on WikiTree Dornin-11). 

Armstrong published "The Summer of the Pestilence" in 1856 — one of the most vivid first-hand accounts of a 19th-century epidemic. A church was named Armstrong Memorial Church in his honor. He remarried in 1857 and continued his ministry until 1891.

notable_stories.title: Judge Douglas Woodruff Hillman (1922-2007) — U.S. District Judge nominated by President Carter, WWII B-24 bomber pilot who flew over Ploiești — 10th-generation Hooker descendant
notable_stories.summary:
Douglas Woodruff Hillman (HD2499, 1922-2007) was the son of Dorothy Woodruff Hillman (HD2496), daughter of Caroline Porter Beardsley Woodruff (HD2488), daughter of Anna Phillips Porter Beardsley (HD2437), daughter of William Porter (HD2433), son of Susannah Edwards (H00382), daughter of Jonathan Edwards and Sarah Pierpont — a 10th-generation Hooker descendant. 

**WWII:** He flew B-24 Liberator heavy bombers with the Fifteenth Air Force from bases in Italy, including missions over the Ploiești oil refineries in Romania — among the most dangerous air missions of the war due to intense anti-aircraft defenses. His father had died when he was 8; his mother Dorothy served as executive secretary of the Grand Rapids American Red Cross through the Depression. 

**Judicial career:** Nominated by President Jimmy Carter in 1979; confirmed by the Senate and seated as a U.S. District Judge for the Western District of Michigan. Chief Judge 1986-1991. Oversaw decades-long Berry v. School District of Benton Harbor desegregation litigation; finally declared the district unitary in 2002. Also shaped Native American gaming law. Retired 2002 after 23 years on the bench. 

His son Clayton Douglas "Clay" Hillman (1956-1996) died at 40, described as "painfully handsome...one of the most gracious people that ever lived." 

Two Yale connections in the family: his grandfather John Hermon Woodruff (Yale 1863) founded Auburn Button Works; his uncle Douglas Woodruff (Yale 1905) succeeded as its president.

notable_stories.title: Four generations of Yale men in Auburn, New York — the Beardsley-Woodruff family that gave the city its button industry and a federal judge
notable_stories.summary:
The Anna Phillips Porter Beardsley family (HD2437, 7th-generation Hooker descendant through Susannah Edwards) produced one of Auburn, New York's most accomplished extended networks — distinguished by a remarkable Yale thread. 

**The Yale men:** Nelson Beardsley (uncle of Anna's husband; not in the tree), Yale 1827, law partner of William H. Seward, bank president for 50 years, $7M fortune. Porter Beardsley (HD2492, grandson of Anna), Yale 1886, Phillips Academy Andover 1882, Auburn lawyer and park commissioner. John Hermon Woodruff (X00821, son-in-law of Anna), Yale 1863 (Scroll and Key, "Spoon Man" — the highest senior honor), who founded Auburn Button Works in 1876 and pioneered the composition button industry. Douglas Woodruff (HD2498, great-grandson of Anna), Yale 1905, who succeeded his father as president of Auburn Button Works. 

**Auburn Button Works** grew from a factory in the post office on Exchange Street to a multi-plant operation manufacturing pearl buttons, typewriter keys, rifle butt plates, and 78-rpm records — becoming Auburn Plastics in 1957. 

**The judge:** Dorothy Woodruff Hillman (HD2500, great-great-granddaughter of Anna) raised her son Douglas Woodruff Hillman (HD2502) as a widow after her husband's early death in 1930, serving as executive secretary of the Grand Rapids American Red Cross. He flew B-24 bombers over Ploiești in WWII, then became a U.S. District Judge nominated by President Carter — overseeing the Benton Harbor desegregation case for decades. 

All of it traces back to Anna Phillips Porter Beardsley (HD2437) — granddaughter of Susannah Edwards (H00382), daughter of Jonathan Edwards.

sources.short: History of Cayuga County, New York

notable_stories.title: James Powers Flint (Princeton 1883) — prospected for oil with Doheny and for gold with Death Valley Scotty — grandson of Nelson Beardsley, uncle of the Hooker descendants in Auburn NY
notable_stories.summary:
James Powers Flint (X00836, 1861-1936) is one of the more remarkable figures in the extended Hooker orbit — connected through his grandfather Nelson Beardsley (not in the tree), who was the uncle of Alonzo Glover Beardsley Sr., husband of Hooker descendant Anna Phillips Porter Beardsley (HD2437). 

Flint was Princeton class of 1883 and president of his class. He bought 200,000 acres of prime Montana sheep land, then lost every acre in the Panic of 1893. He moved to Southern California and prospected for oil with Edward Doheny — who went on to become the central figure in the Teapot Dome scandal, one of the biggest political corruption cases of the early 20th century. He then prospected for gold and silver in the Panamint Mountains with Death Valley Scotty — the legendary desert con man and self-promoter who built a castle in the Mojave. 

His wife Mary Caroline Moore was appointed by the Governor of California to select the site for Pacific Colony, an institution for developmentally disabled children — the original buildings later became Mount San Antonio College (Mt. SAC). 

The family that includes the B-24 pilot who became a federal judge, the Yale man who pioneered the button industry, and the man who helped build the first American school for the deaf also, at two degrees of orbit, contains this gold-rush adventurer.

sources.short: Flint Family History of the Adventuresome Seven

notable_stories.title: Julia Edwards Porter (1896-1998) — named for Jonathan Edwards, lived to 102 years old — 9th-generation Hooker descendant through the Moses Porter pioneer line
notable_stories.summary:
Julia Edwards Porter (HD2546, 1896-1998) was the eldest daughter of Edgar Lovejoy Porter (HD2545) and Lily Field Brewer. She is a 9th-generation descendant of Thomas Hooker through: Susannah Edwards (H00382, gen 4) → Col. Moses Porter (HD2434, gen 5) → Benjamin Porter (HD2524, gen 6) → George Ives Porter (HD2541, gen 7) → Edgar Lovejoy Porter (HD2545, gen 8) → Julia Edwards Porter (gen 9). 

Her name honors the Edwards heritage directly: "Julia Edwards" echoes Julia Ann Porter (daughter of Jonathan Edwards Porter X00660 and Fidelia Dwight H00922, the famous double-convergence couple who were both grandchildren of Jonathan Edwards). 

If the 1998 death year is correct, Julia Edwards Porter lived to approximately 102 years old — born in the same year as Oliver Stanley Powell, one year before the Mexican-American War Treaty was signed. 

She was orphaned at ~24 when her father died in 1920, and subsequently raised her youngest adopted brother Arthur Field Porter.

notable_stories.title: Rev. Moses Porter Snell (1839-1909) — led the 39th U.S. Colored Troops, ran the Freedmen's Bureau, and was licensed at Talcott Street Church Hartford — 7th-generation Hooker descendant named for his grandfather
notable_stories.summary:
Moses Porter Snell (HD2558, 1839-1909) carries one of the most remarkable biographies in the Moses Porter branch. He is named for his grandfather Col. Moses Porter (HD2434) — who was himself named for his father Moses Porter (HD2434), who was the son of Susannah Edwards (H00382). The "Moses Porter" name runs three generations deep. 

In the Civil War, he enlisted as a private in the 36th Massachusetts Volunteers, then transferred to become First Lieutenant and Brevet Captain of the 39th U.S. Colored Troops — one of the regiments of Black Union soldiers. In 1865, he served as aid-de-camp to General Duncan at Newbern, NC, then as Superintendent of the Freedmen's Bureau in Washington DC. 

After the war, he graduated from Amherst College (1868) and Hartford Theological Seminary. He was licensed at Talcott Street Church, Hartford — the historic Black Congregational congregation founded in 1833, the oldest African American congregation in Hartford, on the street that bears the name of Sam Talcott's ancestral family. 

His son Major Charles Livingston Snell (HD2559) is buried at Arlington National Cemetery. His granddaughter Elizabeth Rittenhouse Snell (HD2561) married Lt. Gen. Charles Harold Hayes USMC, who landed at Guadalcanal with aviation supplies and got Henderson Field operational in 4 days under daily Japanese air raids — earning the Navy Distinguished Service Medal.

notable_stories.title: Two 9th-generation Hooker descendants born in the same year 1908 who lived to 104 and 89: Carolyn Snell Purchase and Joseph Wickham Roe
notable_stories.summary:
The Moses Porter branch (HD2434, gen 5) produced two 9th-generation Hooker descendants who stand out for longevity and distinction. 

**Carolyn Esther Snell Purchase (HD2563, 1908-2012)** lived to 104 — born the same year as Douglas Woodruff Hillman (another gen 9 descendant from the Susannah Edwards line). Granddaughter of Rev. Moses Porter Snell (Civil War officer, Freedmen's Bureau superintendent, Hartford minister). Teacher, pastor's wife, lifelong Presbyterian. "Went home to be with the Lord on Friday, November 9, 2012." 

**Joseph Wickham Roe (HD2557, 1871-1960)** is the great-grandson of Amy Porter Wickham (HD2554), whose mother died giving birth to her. Yale Sheffield Scientific School 1895; Professor of Industrial Engineering at NYU; President of the Society of Industrial Engineers; WWI Army major; WWII Navy consultant. Author of "English and American Tool Builders" (1916) — a foundational text in the history of machine tools and manufacturing. Roe family papers at Yale: MS 774. 

User note: Joseph Wickham Roe's work on machine tools connects to the broader theme of Hooker descendants in weapons and industrial manufacturing — a thread worth surfacing in the visualization.

sources.short: Quarryville Presbyterian obituary for Carolyn Purchase 2012
Yale Library MS 774 — Roe family papers

notable_stories.title: The "immoral book" was a midwifery textbook: Jonathan Edwards dismissed from Northampton 1750 after 23 years — and exiled to Stockbridge where he wrote his greatest works
notable_stories.summary:
The dismissal of Jonathan Edwards from the Northampton parish in 1750 — the most consequential event in his life — had a tragicomic proximate cause. He had read names from the pulpit of young people reading "immoral books," implicating the best families in the congregation without, apparently, distinguishing accurately between the guilty and innocent. The book was a midwifery textbook. The resulting upheaval damaged his standing irreparably. Combined with his insistence on "Strict Communion" (no sacrament without demonstrated conversion — reversing the "Half-Way Covenant" his grandfather Solomon Stoddard had established) the parish turned against him. His own relatives — the Williamses and Hawleys — led the opposition. A council of churches met for months; he was dismissed Jun 22, 1750. His Farewell Sermon was Jul 1st. He left £2,000 in debt, refused pastoral calls from Virginia and Scotland. 

He went to Stockbridge — 12 white families, 250+ Housatonnuck Indians, preaching through an interpreter. In this exile he wrote his masterworks: "The Freedom of the Will," "The Nature of True Virtue," "The Doctrine of Original Sin." The dismissal that humiliated him produced the philosophy that outlasted the parish. 

For descendants tracing their lineage through Sarah Edwards, Timothy Edwards, Esther Edwards Burr, Susannah Edwards Porter, and the other eight surviving children: these years in Stockbridge (1751-1758) are where the family's intellectual inheritance was written — in a mission town on the frontier, through an interpreter, by a man who had just lost everything he had built over 23 years.

sources.short: The Record LXXI — Jonathan Edwards genealogical articles

notable_stories.title: The marble in the US Capitol came from the quarry of a Hooker descendant's husband — and he cut down all his apple trees because people kept getting drunk on his cider
notable_stories.summary:
Sarah Parsons (H00907, 1760-1837), daughter of Sarah Edwards (H00376) and granddaughter of Rev. Jonathan Edwards, married Deacon David Ingersoll II in Stockbridge, Massachusetts in 1781. 

David Ingersoll owned a farm near the Lee Congregational Church — of which he was one of the founders — and on that farm was a marble quarry. "Much of the marble in the Capitol in Washington came from this quarry." 

Deacon Ingersoll's other notable decision: finding that so many people were getting drunk on his cider, he cut down all his apple trees except those needed to supply fruit for his own family. 

Thirteen children — all thirteen grew to maturity, married, and mostly had large families. Over 2,000 descendants have been recorded. At age 75, before railroads reached the West, Deacon Ingersoll made a journey to Ohio and Michigan to visit his children. "It was in the days of rugged constitutions, and such a one had David Ingersoll." 

The chain to Thomas Hooker: Thomas Hooker → Mary Hooker Pierpont → James Pierpont → Sarah Pierpont Edwards → Rev. Jonathan Edwards → Sarah Edwards Parsons → Sarah Parsons Ingersoll (H00907) → 2,000+ descendants whose ancestor's marble is in the seat of American government.

sources.short: The Record LXXI — Edwards genealogical articles
Avery, Genealogy of the Ingersoll Family in America (1926)
Descendants of William Smith of Glastonbury CT (archive.org)

notable_stories.title: Rhoda Hinsdale — first white child born in Lenox, baptized by Jonathan Edwards, married his grandson Elihu Parsons Jr. — her ancestor killed in the Deerfield Massacre
notable_stories.summary:
Elihu Parsons Jr. (H00903, 1753-1804), son of Sarah Edwards (H00376) and grandson of Jonathan Edwards, married Rhoda Hinsdale in Stockbridge, Massachusetts. 

Rhoda Hinsdale was born Nov 28, 1751 in Lenox — the first white child born in that town. She was baptized by Rev. Jonathan Edwards A.M. himself (her future father-in-law's grandfather). 

Her father Jonathan Hinsdale was one of the first settlers of Lenox. The family descended from Robert Hinsdale (ca. 1617-1675), who came from England to Dedham, Massachusetts Bay Colony about 1632 — and was killed by the Indians in the Deerfield Massacre. 

The arc: from the Deerfield Massacre to the first child born in Lenox to the baptismal hands of Jonathan Edwards to the grandchild of Sarah Pierpont — three generations compressing the entire arc of the New England frontier.

sources.short: The Record LXXI — Edwards genealogical articles
History of Western Massachusetts, J.G. Holland

notable_stories.title: Erastus Dwight (1756-1821): the forgotten Loyalist brother of Yale's president — thrown in prison, shot in the face by a guard, lived as a recluse for 44 years
notable_stories.summary:
Of the thirteen children of Major Timothy Dwight IV and Mary Edwards Dwight, the most obscured is Erastus (H00916, 1756-1821). His older brother Timothy would become the 8th President of Yale. Erastus entered Yale College in 1776, left in his sophomore year, and chose the Loyalist side in the Revolution — following his father's politics rather than his mother's Edwards-lineage defiance. For this he was thrown in prison. While imprisoned, a guard shot him in the face. "This experience unbalanced his mind, and for forty-four years he lived as a recluse." He never married. He lived until 1821 — 44 years of withdrawal from the world, sharing the Northampton home with his mother and bachelor brother Cecil. 

The contrast within the family is stark: Timothy, the great Yale president and "Pope of Connecticut," preached and published and presided; Erastus, shot in the face for his politics, disappeared from public life. Except for the source noting he was "confined to prison" and shot, essentially nothing else is known of his interior life.

sources.short: The Record LXXI — Edwards genealogical articles

notable_stories.title: Madam Dwight "believed in the Divine Right of the Edwards dynasty" — and refused to sit in the meetinghouse when a Hooker succeeded her father
notable_stories.summary:
Mary Edwards Dwight (H00379, 1734-1807) was described as believing in "the Divine Right of the Edwards dynasty." When the Rev. John Hooker — "a distant cousin" of the Rev. Thomas Hooker, founder of Hartford — succeeded her father Jonathan Edwards as pastor of the Northampton congregation after his dismissal in 1750, she refused to sit in the meetinghouse auditorium under his ministry. She had her own chair placed in the vestibule, below the belfry, opposite the pulpit. On communion Sabbaths she rode 12 miles on a pillion behind her son Cecil to take communion at a different church. 

The irony is layered: Mary's own Hooker lineage runs through her mother Sarah Pierpont (granddaughter of Rev. Samuel Hooker, great-granddaughter of Rev. Thomas Hooker). She carried Hooker blood through her mother's line while refusing to sit under a Hooker minister. 

Her Tory husband had fled to Natchez and died there. Her grain fields were burned by Patriot rabble. She was deserted with 10 children under 21. The news of her husband's death did not reach her for a full year. She endured 31 years of widowhood, operated her farms with her sons, used snuff, and owned slaves. The source calls her "very opinionated and self-willed" and "of uncommon beauty and intelligence." She was the only Edwards child who stayed in Northampton.

sources.short: The Record LXXI — Edwards genealogical articles

notable_stories.title: Judge Jahleel Woodbridge: Revolutionary War captain at Ticonderoga, trusted with Stockbridge Indian wages, kidnapped in Shays' Rebellion — and negotiated his own release
notable_stories.summary:
Jahleel Woodbridge (X00690, 1738-1796), husband of Lucy Edwards (H00380, daughter of Rev. Jonathan Edwards), was among the most politically significant figures in Revolutionary-era Berkshire County. 

MILITARY CAREER: Listed as member of the Stockbridge company, Berkshire County Militia, 1764. Commissioned First Lieutenant 1771. Commissioned Captain 1777, commanding the Stockbridge company for the rest of the war. In 1777 he commanded the company on its march from Stockbridge to Ticonderoga on the evacuation of the fort. 

PROVINCIAL CONGRESS (1775): Member of the Third Provincial Congress at Watertown. On July 5, 1775, Congress resolved that wages of the Stockbridge Indians serving in the Continental Army be paid to Woodbridge and his brother-in-law Timothy Edwards — because the Indians themselves petitioned Congress to protect them from alcohol, "being sensible of their want of prudence in disposing of their money." 

SHAYS' REBELLION (1787): As judge of the Court of Common Pleas, Woodbridge was a named target of the insurrectionists. In January 1787, rebels broke into his home at Stockbridge in the dead of night, pillaged the house, and marched him to Great Barrington as a prisoner. A rescue party set out from Stockbridge. Meanwhile, Woodbridge negotiated his own release, and met the volunteers halfway between the two towns. Edward Bellamy used these events in "The Duke of Stockbridge" (1900).

sources.short: The Record LXXI — Edwards genealogical articles
Autobiography of a Blind Minister (Timothy Woodbridge)
Edward Bellamy, The Duke of Stockbridge (1900)

notable_stories.title: Rev. Timothy Woodbridge (1784-1862): went blind at 17 at Williams College, became a minister and founder of two academies — with Mark Hopkins as his amanuensis
notable_stories.summary:
Timothy Woodbridge XI (H00935, 1784-1862) was the youngest child of Jahleel Woodbridge and Lucy Edwards. At age 17, while at Williams College, he became totally blind — an affliction that lasted until his death 61 years later. 

Rather than withdraw from public life (as his Loyalist uncle Erastus Dwight had done after being shot in the face), Timothy studied law in his brother's office with others reading aloud for him, then abandoned law for the ministry. He preached for decades in Columbia County, New York. 

Among his amanuenses: MARK HOPKINS — the famous president of Williams College — his own nephew. And CHARLES EDWARDS LESTER — his nephew by marriage, who would go on to author 29 books and serve as a diplomat. 

He founded the Green River Academy and the Spencertown Academy, both celebrated institutions. He received a D.D. from Williams College in 1846. 

Contrast with his uncle Erastus Dwight (H00916): both men were catastrophically injured young — Erastus shot in the face, retreated into 44 years of reclusion; Timothy blinded at 17, built two academies and preached for four decades.

sources.short: The Record LXXI — Edwards genealogical articles
Autobiography of a Blind Minister (Timothy Woodbridge XI)

notable_stories.title: Shipwreck off Cape Hatteras to the Nobel Peace Prize: Eunice Edwards' line through a Confederate bishop-general to Henry Labouisse accepting the 1965 Nobel for UNICEF, married to Marie Curie's daughter
notable_stories.summary:
Eunice Edwards (H00383, 1743-1822), fifth child of Jonathan Edwards, married Thomas Pollock III of North Carolina in 1764. Their granddaughter Frances Pollock married John Devereux — a Catholic-trained Irish sailor shipwrecked off Cape Hatteras, who arrived in New Bern penniless and became one of the wealthiest merchants in North Carolina. 

Frances Ann Devereux (HD2594, gen 6) married Leonidas Polk — West Point classmate of Jefferson Davis, Episcopal Bishop of Louisiana, founder of the University of the South (Sewanee), Confederate Major General. Polk was killed June 14, 1864 at Pine Mountain, Georgia by an artillery shell that "nearly cut him in two." Three books were found in his coat pocket. 

Elizabeth Devereux Polk Huger (HD2600, gen 7) → Frances Devereux Huger Labouisse (HD2603, gen 8) → Henry Richardson Labouisse Jr. (HD2606, gen 9): Princeton, Harvard Law, Marshall Plan implementor in France, U.S. Ambassador to France and Greece, Director of UNICEF 1965-1979. In 1954 he married Ève Curie (1904-2007) — younger daughter of Pierre and Marie Curie. In 1965, he accepted the Nobel Peace Prize on behalf of UNICEF, completing the Curie family chain of five Nobel Prize recipients. Ève: "There were five Nobel Prizes in my family... only I was not successful." 

9 generations. Thomas Hooker → Marie Curie's son-in-law, via a Cape Hatteras shipwreck and a Confederate general killed at Pine Mountain.

sources.short: Wikipedia on Henry Richardson Labouisse Jr.

notable_stories.one_line: A Thomas Hooker descendant shipwrecked off Cape Hatteras in 1804 began a chain that ends with the Nobel Peace Prize — and a marriage to Marie Curie's daughter.

notable_stories.title: Leonidas Polk: Episcopal Bishop, Confederate General, West Point classmate of Jefferson Davis — killed at Pine Mountain 1864 with three books in his coat pocket
notable_stories.summary:
Leonidas Polk (X00867, 1806-1864), husband of Frances Ann Devereux (HD2594), granddaughter of Eunice Edwards (H00383). At West Point his best friend was Jefferson Davis (future Confederate President). After graduating, resigned his commission for the Episcopal seminary; rose to Bishop of Louisiana; one of the wealthiest slaveholding bishops in the country; owned Leighton Plantation (worked by enslaved people from wife's NC plantations); founded University of the South (Sewanee TN) 1857. 

When the Civil War began, Davis commissioned him Major General despite no battlefield experience. His invasion of neutral Kentucky is called by historians "one of the greatest blunders of the war" — it locked Kentucky into the Union. 

June 14, 1864, Pine Mountain, Georgia: Sherman spotted a cluster of generals — Polk, Johnston, Hardee — and ordered artillery. The third shell struck Polk and "nearly cut him in two." In his coat pocket: three copies of "Balm for the Weary and Wounded," inscribed to Johnston, Hardee, and Hood, dated June 12 — two days earlier. Military historian Woodworth: "one of the worst shots fired for the Union cause during the entire war" — Polk's incompetence made him more valuable alive. Fort Polk, Louisiana carried his name until renamed Fort Johnson in 2023.
notable_stories.one_line: A Thomas Hooker descendant's son-in-law was West Point classmate of Jefferson Davis, Episcopal Bishop of Louisiana, Confederate Major General, and was killed at Pine Mountain with three books in his coat pocket.

notable_stories.title: Lillie Devereux Blake (suffragist) and Catherine Ann Devereux Edmondston (Civil War diarist) — two notable women from Eunice Edwards' line
notable_stories.summary:
The Eunice Edwards (H00383) branch produced two remarkable 19th-century women. 

Lillie Devereux Blake (HD2595, 1833-1913), daughter of George Pollock Devereux (HD2593), was a prominent suffragist, novelist, and women's rights advocate — a leading figure in the New York suffrage movement. 

Catherine Ann Devereux Edmondston (HD2607, 1823-1875), daughter of Thomas Pollock Devereux (HD2592), kept a Civil War diary published posthumously as "Journal of a Secesh Lady: The Diary of Catherine Ann Devereux Edmondston, 1860-1866" — a primary source for Civil War-era North Carolina planter society. 

Both were 7th-generation Hooker descendants.

sources.short: Journal of a Secesh Lady (NC Archives 1979)

notable_stories.one_line: Two Hooker descendants through the same Eunice Edwards line fought on opposite sides of the Civil War: one wrote the most vivid Confederate diarist account of Sherman's march, the other led the suffragist fight for women's rights.

notable_stories.title: Jonathan Edwards Jr. — his father owned slaves, he wrote antislavery articles as "Antidoulios" in 1773 and preached the first major New England antislavery sermon in 1791
notable_stories.summary:
Jonathan Edwards Jr. (H00384, 1745-1801) is one of the most remarkable figures in the Hooker-Edwards tree — not for following in his famous father's footsteps, but for explicitly departing from them on the most consequential moral question of his era. 

Jonathan Edwards Sr. (X00128) owned at least four slaves during his lifetime, including two he likely brought to serve him during his 35-day presidency at Princeton. His son considered this a direct contradiction of Christianity. 

In 1773, while serving as pastor of the White Haven Church near Yale, Edwards Jr. published a series of antislavery articles in the Connecticut Journal under the pseudonym "Antidoulios" — Greek for "against slavery." He was 28 years old. He applied the Golden Rule to slavery with moral precision: "Should we be willing that the Africans or any other nation should purchase us, our wives and children, transport us into Africa and there sell us into perpetual and absolute slavery?" 

In 1791 he delivered his most powerful antislavery sermon from his New Haven pulpit. Princeton calls him "one of the few abolitionists Princeton ever produced." A eulogist in Savannah wrote: "That all men are born equally free was his firm belief, and by this maxim of eternal justice he regulated his practice." 

He was also a pioneering linguist: he grew up in Stockbridge MA speaking Mohican better than English, and in 1788 published a landmark study of the Mahican language. George Washington thanked him for a copy; James Madison sent one to Thomas Jefferson. 

His grandson Tryon Edwards (gen 6) compiled and published his complete works in 1842.

Coda: His daughter Maria Edwards (HD2624, gen 5) married a slave trader; her son John Samuel de Montmollin II (HD2643, gen 6) organized the illegal slave ship Wanderer in 1858 — which returned from the Congo River with 400 African captives, deposited on his own plantation. The ship's log survives at Emory University and died in a boiler explosion near the very island where his captives had been held.

sources.short: Princeton & Slavery Project: Jonathan Edwards Jr.
Archive.org: Observations on the Language of the Muhhekaneew Indians

notable_stories.one_line: Jonathan Edwards Jr. — whose own father owned slaves — became one of America's first abolitionists, writing as "Antidoulios" in 1773; his grandson organized the illegal slave ship Wanderer in 1858.

notable_stories.title: Six brothers all graduated from Yale: Jonathan Walter Edwards' sons, including Tryon Edwards, whose "Dictionary of Thoughts" is still in print, and Eugene Edwards, who kept the 1740 family portraits for 80 years
notable_stories.summary:
Jonathan Walter Edwards (HD2619, 1772-1831), son of Jonathan Edwards Jr. (H00384) and lawyer in Hartford CT, had 10 children — six sons, all of whom graduated from Yale College (classes 1819, 1820, 1828×2, 1832, 1839). This was itself remarkable; the obituary noted it explicitly. 

The most notable son was Tryon Edwards (gen 6, 1809-1894), theologian and author of "A Dictionary of Thoughts" — a compendium of quotations still referenced today. He edited and published the complete works of his grandfather Jonathan Edwards Jr. (1842) and great-grandfather's "Charity and Its Fruits." 

The youngest son, Eugene Edwards (gen 6, 1819-1899), was the last of the six Yale-graduate brothers to die. He was the family's keeper of the 1740 portraits of Jonathan Edwards and Sarah Pierpont — painted in Boston by Joseph Badger, shipped to Scotland, held by Scottish admirers for decades, returned to Jonathan Edwards Jr. after the Revolution. Eugene received them from his sisters Catherine Agnes and Sarah Pierpont Edwards, both of whom died unmarried. His son Eugene Phelps Edwards (gen 7, 1862-1938) inherited the portraits and bequeathed them to Yale University in 1939. They now hang in the dining hall of Jonathan Edwards College.

sources.short: The Record LXXI — Edwards genealogical articles

notable_stories.one_line: Six brothers of the same Thomas Hooker descent all graduated Yale; the youngest compiled "A Dictionary of Thoughts" still in print today and preserved the family's 1740 portrait commission at Yale, where it hangs in a residential college named for his ancestor.

notable_stories.title: Jonathan Edwards Jr. was America's leading abolitionist minister — his grandson organized the illegal slave ship Wanderer in 1858 and died in a boiler explosion near the island where his captives were held
notable_stories.summary:
The moral arc of the Edwards-Hooker tree reaches its most shattering moment in the life of John Samuel de Montmollin II (HD2643, 1808-1859). 

His maternal grandfather was Jonathan Edwards Jr. (H00384) — who wrote antislavery articles as "Antidoulios" in 1773, preached the first major New England antislavery sermon in 1791, and was called by Princeton "one of the few abolitionists Princeton ever produced." His great-grandfather Jonathan Edwards Sr. (X00128) had owned at least four slaves. 

Montmollin was a slave trader, city marshal, and banker in Savannah, Georgia. He built the Montmollin Warehouse (still standing) in 1856-1858 — the third floor was a slave pen. He wrote to slave dealer Ziba B. Oakes requesting "four Black Boys ages 18 to 21, large-size ones preferred, field hands preferred, 'buy them as cheap as possible.'" The letter survives in the Boston Public Library Anti-Slavery Collection, donated by James Redpath via William Lloyd Garrison — the nation's leading abolitionist. 

According to his daughter-in-law (interviewed 1931), Montmollin organized the Wanderer — one of the last illegal slave ships to transport captives from Africa to the United States — in 1858. 

On June 9, 1859, a boiler exploded on the Savannah River steamboat "John G. Lawton." Montmollin was killed. His body was found "embedded in the marsh, head downwards, to the hips, some seventy to eighty yards" from the explosion. He died "within a short distance of the spot where his Wanderer captives had been incarcerated" on an island in the Savannah River. In April 1859 — two months before his death — a federal grand jury DECLINED TO INDICT Montmollin for "holding African negroes" at his plantation. He died without legal accountability. His widow later sold 81 enslaved people for $88,000 in April 1863. That same year, his 9-year-old daughter "Tattie" died. 

His will had specified: excellent education for his children, Christian conduct, no liquor or tobacco, and that they "learn foreign languages fluently, especially French and Spanish." 

His son Louis Henri de Montmollin (gen 7) became an alderman of Savannah and a prominent member of the Savannah bar. His eldest son John Samuel III was being schooled in Switzerland when the boiler explosion killed his father; he returned immediately to Savannah. 

THE BUILDING BECOMES A SCHOOL: The Montmollin Warehouse at 23 Barnard Street, City Market, Savannah — whose third floor had been a slave pen, and which after Montmollin's death was used by Alexander Bryan to continue holding and selling enslaved people — was confiscated by the U.S. government when General Sherman captured Savannah on December 21, 1864. Savannah's African-American community formed the Savannah Educational Association (SEA) and established Bryan School in the building. On January 10, 1865 — five and a half years after Montmollin's body was found embedded in the marsh of the Savannah River — hundreds of Black children marched from First African Baptist Church (the oldest Black Baptist church in America, founded 1788) to his former slave pen for the school's opening day. In July 1865 the children publicly showcased their knowledge of grammar, history, geography, arithmetic. The American Missionary Association absorbed the SEA in 1867 and founded Beach Institute, which consolidated several schools including Bryan School. The historical marker at 23 Barnard Street was erected by the Georgia Historical Society and the Mayor and Aldermen of the City of Savannah. 

The chain: Thomas Hooker → Samuel Hooker → Mary Hooker Pierpont → James Pierpont → Sarah Pierpont Edwards → Jonathan Edwards Jr. (abolitionist) → Maria Edwards → John Samuel de Montmollin II (organized the Wanderer).

One additional thread: John Samuel III named his son "Aaron Burr de Montmollin" (b. 1871) — keeping alive the name of Vice President Aaron Burr (H00913), who was the first cousin of Maria Edwards, raised alongside her by Timothy Edwards II, and who lodged at the de Montmollin home in Savannah in 1802 and 1807. The family carried that name into the eighth generation.

sources.short: Boston Public Library Anti-Slavery Collection (Ziba Oakes letter)

notable_stories.one_line: The grandson of America's first abolitionist minister organized the illegal slave ship Wanderer in 1858, depositing 400 Africans on his Georgia plantation — and was killed in a boiler explosion near the island where his captives had been held.

notable_stories.title: Thomas Hooker → Pierpont Edwards (1st CT Grand Mason, Jefferson's judge) → Sally Edwards → Judge Bristol → Caroline Bristol → married Yale mineralogist Edward Salisbury Dana, whose brother's family endowed New Haven's arts
notable_stories.summary:
Pierpont Edwards (H00386, 1750-1826), youngest son of Jonathan Edwards, Princeton 1768: Revolutionary War officer, Speaker of the Connecticut House, first Grand Master of Masons in Connecticut, framer of Connecticut's 1818 Constitution, federal judge appointed by Thomas Jefferson. His daughter Sarah "Sally" Edwards (HD2096) married Judge William Bristol — who succeeded Pierpont Edwards in the U.S. District Court seat. 
Two more generations of Yale lawyers followed. Their son William Brooks Bristol (HD2655, Yale 1827) practiced law in New Haven. His daughter Caroline "Carrie" Bristol (HD2668, gen 7) married Edward Salisbury Dana (X00898) — Yale mineralogist and physicist, member of Scroll and Key, editor of the American Journal of Science for 51 years, and son of JAMES DWIGHT DANA — the pre-eminent American geologist of his era, Copley Medal winner 1877, Silliman Professor at Yale, whose System of Mineralogy and Manual of Mineralogy defined two fields for generations. Both Danas have portraits at the Yale Art Gallery. 
Edward Salisbury Dana's brother, ARNOLD GUYOT DANA (1862-1947), retired to New Haven in 1922 and spent the rest of his life compiling ~150 scrapbook volumes titled "New Haven Old & New" — covering every street, institution, and building in the city. The collection is "the most unique piece of material" in the New Haven Museum's Whitney Library (librarian Ed Surato). Arnold also compiled 102 volumes on "Yale: Old and New." He was still working on the project when he died at 85. 
Arnold's grandson JAMES DANA ENGLISH (1932-2021) — Yale 1954 — spent a decade indexing the entire scrapbook collection at the New Haven Museum. In February 2022, his estate gave $35 million to New Haven nonprofits — the largest gift ever received by the Community Foundation for Greater New Haven — distributed among the New Haven Symphony Orchestra (40%), New Haven Museum (40%), Neighborhood Music School (10%), and Clifford Beers Community Care Center (10%). 
The English brothers (James and Richard) were "descended from two Connecticut Governors" — James Edward English (Governor 1867-1869, 1883-1885) on the English patrilineal side, and Jonathan Trumbull Jr. (Governor 1797-1809) through the Silliman/Trumbull maternal line (hence Katharine's middle name "Trumbull"). 
The Bristol family papers — covering the same family — are preserved at Yale as MS 101. 
The chain: Thomas Hooker → Samuel Hooker → Mary Hooker Pierpont → James Pierpont → Sarah Pierpont Edwards → Pierpont Edwards → Sarah Edwards Bristol → William Brooks Bristol → Caroline Bristol Dana → [married Edward Salisbury Dana, whose brother Arnold Guyot Dana → Katharine Trumbull Dana → James Dana English, $35M benefactor of New Haven].

Coda: When John Wolcott Bristol (HD2667, Yale 1877) served as senior counsel for Yale University, a member of his law firm was "Thomas Hooker, Jr., '03" (Yale 1903) — almost certainly a descendant of the same Thomas Hooker who founded Hartford in 1636. In the same firm: J. Dwight Dana ('11), Bristol's own nephew James Dwight Dana II (HD2670). Three family lines converging in one New Haven law office, 270 years after Thomas Hooker's death.

sources.short: Wikipedia on Pierpont Edwards; Wikipedia on Edward Salisbury Dana
Community Foundation for Greater New Haven, June 2022 press release

notable_stories.one_line: Thomas Hooker's great-great-great-granddaughter married the judge who took her father's federal court seat; her great-granddaughter married Yale's leading mineralogist, whose brother's family gave $35 million to New Haven nonprofits in 2022.

notable_stories.title: Eugene Stuart Bristol served as a Union officer in the 29th Connecticut Colored Troops — grandson of the first Grand Master of Connecticut Masons, great-great-grandson of Jonathan Edwards
notable_stories.summary:
Eugene Stuart Bristol (HD2660, 1843-1910) enlisted in the Union Army in December 1863 and was mustered into the 29th Regiment of Connecticut Volunteers (Colored) — one of the 175 United States Colored Troops regiments. He served as a Second Lieutenant, later promoted to First Lieutenant, in the Army of the James. He was wounded at the Battle of Chaffin's Farm (September 29, 1864) in the Siege of Richmond/Petersburg and mustered out October 24, 1865. 
Eugene was the son of William Brooks Bristol (HD2655, Yale 1825), grandson of Judge William Bristol (X00895) × Sarah "Sally" Edwards (HD2096), great-grandson of Pierpont Edwards (H00386) — the first Grand Master of Masons in Connecticut — and great-great-grandson of Jonathan Edwards the theologian. 
He graduated Yale Sheffield Scientific School in 1868, became a manufacturer and banker in New Haven, and married Julia Silliman Gilman in 1903 with no issue. He died in New Haven in 1910. 
The Bristol family produced no fewer than five Yale graduates across three generations: William Bristol (1798), William Brooks (1825), Albert G. (1827), Louis H. (1859), Eugene S. (1868S), John Wolcott (1877).

Eugene's 3rd cousin, John Samuel de Montmollin III (HD2644, b. 1844), enlisted in the Confederate Army on May 11, 1861. His father had organized the illegal slave ship Wanderer in 1858. Eugene was leading Black Union troops at Chaffin's Farm in 1864; his cousin's specific regiment is unknown.

sources.short: U.S. Civil War records; FindAGrave memorial for Eugene Stuart Bristol

notable_stories.one_line: A great-grandson of the first Grand Master of Connecticut Masons served as an officer in a United States Colored Troops regiment — wounded at Chaffin's Farm in 1864, while his third cousin fought for the Confederacy.

notable_stories.title: Hooker against Hooker? — 3rd cousins, both 7th-generation descendants of Thomas Hooker, born one year apart, on opposite sides of the Civil War: Eugene Bristol commanded Black Union troops; John de Montmollin III fought for the Confederacy, son of the man who organized the Wanderer slave ship
notable_stories.summary:
On September 29, 1864, Eugene Stuart Bristol (HD2660, b. 1843) — First Lieutenant, 29th Connecticut Volunteers (Colored) — was wounded in action at the Battle of Chaffin's Farm, Virginia, fighting in the Army of the James. The 29th Connecticut Colored was one of 175 United States Colored Troops regiments; fourteen Black soldiers earned the Medal of Honor at New Market Heights that same day. 
Somewhere in the Confederate lines defending Richmond was a cohort of soldiers that may have included his 3rd cousin, John Samuel de Montmollin III (HD2644, b. 1844) — who had enlisted in the Confederate Army on May 11, 1861, at age 17. JSM III's specific regiment and battles are undocumented. Whether he stood in the Confederate trenches opposite Eugene Bristol at Chaffin's Farm cannot be confirmed. But both men were fighting in Virginia in the fall of 1864. 
The two men shared the same great-great-great-grandparents: Thomas Hooker (gen 1), founder of Hartford. Their great-great-grandparents were brothers: Jonathan Edwards Jr. (H00384) and Pierpont Edwards (H00386) — both sons of the theologian Jonathan Edwards and Sarah Pierpont Edwards, granddaughter of Yale's founder James Pierpont. 
The irony runs deeper: 
Eugene Bristol's line: Pierpont Edwards → Sally Edwards → William Brooks Bristol → Eugene. Pierpont Edwards was the first Grand Master of Masons in Connecticut, a federal judge appointed by Thomas Jefferson. 
JSM III's line: Jonathan Edwards Jr. → Maria Edwards → John Samuel de Montmollin II → JSM III. Jonathan Edwards Jr. had written the first major American antislavery sermon in 1791.
