artworks.title: Charity
artworks.medium: Silk embroidered picture on silk ground
artworks.location: Textile Collection, National Museum of American History, Smithsonian Institution, Washington DC
artworks.notes: Accession TE*E388172, Image No. 81-5200. Based on a mezzotint engraving by P. Stampa. Stitched by Rachel Breck in 1810 at age 18 while attending the Misses Patten's School in Hartford, Connecticut — a girls' academy whose curriculum included Latin, Greek, English, French, mercantile arithmetic, bookkeeping, geography, astronomy, natural philosophy, drawing, painting, embroidery, filigree, and ornamental work. Two inscriptions on the backboard: in ink, 'Worked by Rachel Breck Hooker in 1810 in the 18th year of her age'; the liner backed with grey rag paper inscribed 'Wrought by Mrs. Rachel Breck Hooker in 1810, the 18th year of her age.' A penciled amendment to '1803 in her 11th year' is contradicted by the documentary inscriptions and by Rachel's actual age. The piece is nearly identical to one embroidered by Sarah Marshall (now in the DAR Museum) which carries Misses Patten's School provenance — strongly suggesting Rachel stitched hers at the same Hartford academy. Donated to the United States National Museum (now NMAH) in 1951 by collectors Dr. and Mrs. Arthur Greenwood. Her earlier sampler (made probably at Northampton or Deerfield Academy 1806-1810) was purchased separately by collector Richard Wormser (1898-1975) and later acquired by the NMAH, reuniting the two pieces in the same collection — the Textile Collection's first paired example of a girl's earlier sampler and her later, more technically advanced silk embroidered picture.

artworks.title: Portrait of Samuel Huntington
artworks.medium: Oil on canvas (copied from family ivory miniature)
artworks.notes:
Left-facing portrait of Samuel Huntington, third Governor of Ohio 1808-1810. Huntington shown wearing a dark jacket with four gold buttons, gold vest, white shirt; dark hair pulled back. Copied from an ivory miniature in the family's possession.

Provenance: In 1867 the Ohio General Assembly passed a joint resolution directing the Secretary of State to procure portraits of all Ohio governors, state and territorial. William Henry Smith, Ohio's sixteenth Secretary of State, corresponded with families and traveled the country to meet them. Ohio's Executive Documents and Annual Reports for 1872 list a payment of January 3, 1871 to 'Miss C.L. Ransom for painting portrait of Gov. Huntington $100.00.' The Capitol Square Review and Advisory Board took over the care of the Statehouse and its collections in 1988.

artworks.title: Judge Joel Jones and George Stroud
artworks.artist_research_notes: Auguste Edouart (1789-1861) — French-born silhouette artist who worked extensively in the United States during the 1840s. Created over 3,800 American silhouettes of prominent figures including presidents, judges, and clergy. Not built as separate tree entry (no Hooker-tree connection beyond having silhouetted TD0239).
artworks.medium: Ink wash, chalk, and cut paper on paper
artworks.current_location: Smithsonian Institution, National Portrait Gallery, Washington D.C.
artworks.credit_line: Gift of Robert L. McNeil Jr.
artworks.photo_notes: Sam-supplied photo of the silhouette, Cloudinary hosted.
artworks.notes:
Silhouette portrait of Judge Joel Jones (TD0239, left, with top hat) facing George Stroud (right) — both men's names written above the figures. Some additional writing on the bottom of the image. Created 1842 — the year Joel was 47, serving as Presiding Judge of the Philadelphia District Court (had been Associate Judge since 1835).

Auguste Edouart was a French-born silhouette artist who emigrated to the US in 1839 and worked extensively in major American cities through the 1840s, creating over 3,800 American silhouettes including presidents (Van Buren, Tyler, Polk, Pierce, Adams) and many other prominent figures. His silhouettes are considered among the finest of the genre and survive in major American museums.

George Stroud was a Philadelphia judicial colleague of Joel Jones's. Not currently built in tree.

Held at the Smithsonian Institution, National Portrait Gallery, Washington D.C. — Object ID JJGS1884; gift of Robert L. McNeil Jr. Smithsonian + National Portrait Gallery not built as separate INSTs (single Hooker-tree connection).

artworks.title: Elizabeth Sparhawk-Jones
artworks.artist_research_notes: Alice Kent Stoddard (1885-1976) — American painter, exact contemporary of her sitter (both b. 1885). PAFA-trained portraitist + landscape painter; studied under Cecilia Beaux and William Merritt Chase. Best known for society portraits and Monhegan Island ME landscapes. Not built as separate tree entry (no Hooker-tree connection beyond having painted TD0241).
artworks.current_location: Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts, Philadelphia (INST141)
artworks.photo_notes: Sam-supplied photo of the portrait, Cloudinary hosted.
artworks.notes:
Three-quarter-length oil portrait of Elizabeth Sparhawk-Jones (TD0241, 1885-1968) by her exact contemporary and fellow PAFA-trained painter Alice Kent Stoddard (1885-1976). Both women studied at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts under Cecilia Beaux and William Merritt Chase.

The portrait was painted c.1910 — the year of Elizabeth's father's death and the inflection point in her early career, immediately before her mental breakdown. Acquired by the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts in 1911 (accession 1911.4) through the Henry D. Gilpin Fund.

Now part of PAFA's permanent collection (INST141 in this tree).

artworks.title: Pipe Tomahawk (Chickasaw)
artworks.collection: Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian (NMAI)
artworks.notes: Pre-1838 Chickasaw pipe tomahawk with documented provenance chain: originally owned by Chief Kemp (Chickasaw) → his son also called Kemp → purchased after the younger Kemp's death by Judge Brooks of Pontotoc, Mississippi → given by Judge Brooks to Reverend Edward Fontaine of Pontotoc Mississippi in 1838 → acquired at an unknown date by Dr. Joseph L. Jones (1833-1896) of New Orleans, Louisiana (Confederate surgeon, Tulane medical professor, husband of Hooker descendant Susan Polk) → purchased by George Heye from Jones's widow Susan Polk Jones (HD2599) in 1906 → now in the collection of the Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian (NMAI accession 7662). Place of creation likely Mississippi (inferred). One of the better-documented Native American ethnographic objects with a continuous 19th-century provenance chain through a Hooker-descendant family.

Dunbar (1862-1927) in the Corcoran building, took about five weeks in clay, was cast in plaster in three sections to make a hollow mould, and the bronze was cast in Philadelphia and taken to Norwich. The figure represents grief. THIS SETTLES AN OPEN QUESTION: when the statue was stolen in February 2010, a local historian speculated it might be an Augustus Saint-Gaudens worth several hundred thousand dollars. The newspaper account from the time of casting names Dunbar, so the Saint-Gaudens attribution is wrong. Known locally as the Blue Lady of Yantic Cemetery; recovered after the theft and restored by the city.

battles.notes: July 1 - November 18, 1916. One of the largest battles of WWI. Lt-Col George Stephen Cantlie D.S.O., commanding the 42nd Battalion CEF (Royal Highlanders of Canada / Black Watch), wrote his 'Dear Wee Celia' letters with pressed flowers from bivouac fields during this period to his infant daughter Celia in Montreal. Ten of these letters form the basis of the Canadian War Museum's touring 'War Flowers' exhibition.

battles.name: Rabaul Fighter Sweep — VMF-214 Black Sheep
battles.location: Rabaul, East New Britain, Papua New Guinea
battles.notes: January 3, 1944. Eight VMF-214 'Black Sheep' aircraft under Pappy Boyington joined a 46-plane sweep of Rabaul. Boyington's Corsair was shot down and he was captured; Capt. George Malcolm Ashmun (HD4955) was also shot down and killed. Both Boyington and Ashmun scored aerial victories before being lost. Ashmun's first and only kill came in this engagement.

battles.name: Battle of Anzio
battles.notes: Allied amphibious landing, January-June 1944. Joseph Commodore Thomas was captured here and held as a POW for the remainder of the war.

battles.name: Italian Campaign — Minturno and the Gustav Line
Bombing of Tokyo, 25-26 May 1945
battles.notes: Night incendiary raid on the districts south of the Imperial Palace by the Twentieth Air Force out of the Marianas. Twenty-six B-29s were lost, the heaviest single-day Superfortress loss of the war. Cruger Gallaudet Edgerton, pilot and flight commander of the 389th Bomb Squadron, 504th Bomb Group, went down with his whole crew off Nekozane, Urayasu. No other person in this tree is documented in the Tokyo air campaign - checked 2026-07-27.

battles.name: Siege of Fort Meigs
battles.notes: May 1–9, 1813. Elisha Whittlesey (X01997) was taken severely ill at Fort Meigs during the siege. Nursed by Rev. Joseph Badger; given up to die by all but Dr. Stonard of the Virginia line. Recovered and returned to Canfield March 1813.

battles.name: Whittlesey's Ride — Maumee Rapids to Chillicothe
battles.location: Maumee Rapids to Chillicothe, Ohio (180 miles)
battles.notes: Feb 1813 — SOLO RIDE. Maj. Whittlesey rode alone from Maumee Rapids to Chillicothe, 180 miles in three days and nights, carrying dispatches to the Ohio legislature following Winchester's defeat. First 15 miles at night through the frozen 'black swamp': large irregular ice cakes on mud, trail obscured, moving at night to avoid Indian scouts. 'Before daylight fifteen miles had been passed, over ground that would generally be considered impassable.' (Whittlesey Genealogy #310 — no companions mentioned)

wars.name: King William's War

wars.notes: First of six colonial wars fought between New France and New England. North American theater of the Nine Years' War (1688-1697). Ended by the 1697 Peace of Ryswick — boundaries unchanged. Caused partly by unmet terms of the First Indian War (1675-1678). Distinguished from the French and Indian War (1754-1763).

battles.name: King William's War — New England frontier campaigns
battles.notes: Dunstable MA was a frontier settlement under constant threat. Rev. Grindal Rawson served as fleet chaplain in Canada expedition, appointed July 31, 1690 by vote of both houses. Rev. documents.property: Approximately three-quarters of an acre at Indian Neck, Farmington CT. Bounded east by Captain William Wadsworth, west and south by William Hooker's own land, north by heirs of Sergeant Samuel Judd and Jonathan Root.
documents.notable_quote: I, Sue Squa, hath hereunto set my hand and seal.
documents.description: Land transfer deed from a Native American widow to William Hooker of Farmington. Sue signed with her mark. John Hooker (H00030) served simultaneously as witness, certifying official (Assistant), and Registrar — concentrating legal authority over the transaction in a single Hooker. The deed records one of the final transfers of Native land in the Farmington township.
documents.editorial_notes: A focal document for the "literal advantage" research lens — whose perspective is encoded in historical records. The deed is in Sue's name and uses the language of her free will, but she signed with a mark and the certifying official was the grantee's first cousin. See userMemories note on the 1733 Sue Squa deed.

documents.title: Letter from Dr. Samuel Bayard Woodward to Rev. Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet, 1838
documents.recipient: Rev. Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet (HD0411), Hartford CT
documents.description: A brief professional letter from Dr. Samuel Bayard Woodward — first superintendent of Worcester State Hospital (first public asylum for the mentally ill in America) and future founding president of the American Psychiatric Association — inviting Gallaudet to preach and explore a chaplaincy position. Woodward pitches the congregation honestly: "We have 210 patients, 150 of whom attend our chapel." He offers to cover travel and host Gallaudet at the American Temperance House. No theology, no mention of shared ancestry. Neither man knew they were both Hooker descendants.
documents.notable_quote: We have 210 patients, 150 of whom attend our chapel — a snug congregation of 200.
documents.editorial_notes: What neither man knew: both were descendants of Thomas Hooker. Gallaudet (HD0411, gen 6) descends through the Hopkins line. Woodward's wife Maria Porter (HD2442, gen 6) descends through Susannah Edwards (H00382) → Eleazer Porter III → Maria Porter. The small professional letter crossed a genealogical bridge neither writer could see. Drawn from notable_story key: woodward_gallaudet_1838_letter_two_hooker_descendants_asylum_school_deaf

documents.title: Poem to Almira, June 2, 1855
documents.recipient: Almira Hart Phelps (H00598) — inscribed in a copy of Hollister's History of Connecticut
documents.repository: Amherst College Archives — Emma Hart Willard Papers
documents.description: Written by Emma Hart Willard in a copy of Hollister's History of Connecticut sent to her youngest surviving sister Almira (H00598). One of Emma's last personal poems — she died April 15, 1870 age 83. The poem names their father Samuel Hart and their mother, and ends with the awareness that Almira will be 'a sole surviving one.' The lines 'FATHER! I see thee! calm-with dignity / That speaks of high communings' are the most direct portrait of Capt. Samuel Hart's character in the record.
documents.notable_quote: Sister! we boast an honored ancestry / Of parents nobly virtuous, reared in thee, / CONNECTICUT! whose earliest sires were ours.

documents.title: Letter to James Gates Percival, March 19, 1832

She writes: 'I should like much to meet you' and asks if he will be in New York, adding: 'I would rather found it on kindred of soul than anything else.' documents.title: Holograph order, Col. Elizur Talcott to Capt. Benjamin Wright, June 12, 1776
documents.recipient: Capt. Benjamin Wright, Fourth Company, Sixth Regiment of the Colony of Connecticut
documents.repository: Between the Covers — Rare Books (Inventory item 415963)
documents.repository_notes: Approximately 9 inch x 8 inch handwritten document on laid paper, signed by Col. Tallcott. Slightly irregular margins, small tears and folds, else near fine. On verso: note dated June 19, 1776 from Capt. Wright in Wethersfield reporting Solomon Buckley chosen Lieutenant; choice ratified and signed by Titus Hosmer for Lower House and George Wyllys for Upper House.
documents.description:
Col. Elizur Talcott orders Captain Wright to call legal warning of all officers and soldiers and others entitled to vote in the choice of commissioned officers, to elect a Lieutenant after the previous Lieutenant's resignation request. Signed at Glastonbury CT.

Historical context: 'Interesting primary source documentation of the widespread practice of electing officers; presumably in late June the Colonies were anxious to have their militias fully staffed with officers' (Between the Covers description).

Notable signers on the verso: Captain Benjamin Wright later served as lieutenant directly under George Washington; his son (also Benjamin Wright) is considered the Father of American Civil Engineering and was Chief Engineer of the building of the Erie Canal. Titus Hosmer was a Connecticut delegate to the Continental Congress and signed the Articles of Confederation. George Wyllys served as Connecticut Secretary of State (a Wyllys family member held the role for 96 consecutive years).
documents.notable_quote: Your Lieutenant having made application to me to be dismist from his said office....[I] therefore... order and direct you to cause Legal Warning to be given to all the officers and soldiers belong to s[ai]d and all others allowed to vote in the choice of Commission officers to meet... lead them to choice of a Lieutn. and such other officers as shall be found... Given under my hand in Glastonbury, [Connecticut] the 12th Day of June A.D. 1776.

documents.title: Herman Hollerith Papers
author_names: Herman Hollerith Sr. + multiple Talcott family correspondents
documents.repository_notes: Six series: Personal Correspondence, Business Correspondence, Special Correspondence, Miscellany, Addition I, Addition II. Documents are physical-only at the Library of Congress — finding aid online but the documents themselves require in-person visit.
documents.description:
The papers of Herman Hollerith (1860-1929) span 1850-1982, with the bulk of material between 1910 and 1927. The collection focuses on Hollerith's tabulating-machine work, business operations of the Tabulating Machine Company, the 1911 merger into Computing-Tabulating-Recording (CTR), and later association with International Business Machines (IBM, named 1924). Includes correspondence, scrapbooks of newspaper clippings on tabulating machines and census-taking, patent files, blueprints, and one Hollerith machine punch plate.

TALCOTT FAMILY CORRESPONDENCE (Addition II — major genealogical interest for this project):
  - Letters 1865-1866 chronicling Charles G. Talcott Sr.'s (T01839) employment as civil engineer building the Vera Cruz to Mexico City railway under Maximilian.
  - 360+ letters (1868-1889) between Theodosia Talcott (the Hollerith matriarch / Hollerith mother-in-law, our I00265) and her eldest son Charles G. Talcott Jr. (T01869) — covering his Brattleboro VT boarding school, USNA Annapolis years, and naval tours of duty as assistant engineer in Argentina, Brazil, China, Italy, Japan, Korea, and Uruguay. His letters contain detailed drawings of ports of call.
  - Theodosia's October 3, 1877 letter describing the fire which nearly destroyed the U.S. Patent Office where she was one of the first female clerks (this is how Hollerith met her — he was an assistant Patent examiner there).
  - Theodosia's September 15, 1890 letter to her son Harry (T01870) describing the wedding of her daughter Lucia (T01872) to Hollerith.
  - Letter from Nellie Keohan to Lucia B. Hollerith (T01872) recounting the 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire.

BIOGRAPHIES IN ADDITION II: Drafts and published material by Geoffrey D. Austrian (Hollerith's major biographer) and Virginia Hollerith (the inventor's daughter). Hollerith's 1884 diary. IBM's 1929 announcement of his death.

documents.title: Susan & Horace Hooker Civil War Correspondence
documents.location: Rochester, New York / Union Army theaters of operation
documents.summary: Hundreds of letters exchanged between Susan Pamelia Huntington Hooker and her husband Horace B. Hooker during his Union Army service in the Civil War. The collection documents the daily life of a Union soldier and a 19th-century woman during wartime, and shows how a young Rochester family communicated and remained close through years of separation. A distinctive feature: throughout Horace's letters, every instance of 'darling,' 'I love you,' and similar declarations of affection has been deliberately scribbled over with blue crayon or pencil — by whom, when, and to what end remains unknown. Whether the marks were meant to highlight or to obscure these intimate sentiments is one of the collection's open questions. The collection also includes creative writing pieces and artwork from the Huntington-Hooker children. Held by the Department of Rare Books, Special Collections and Preservation at the University of Rochester, as part of the Helen Hooker O'Malley papers.
documents.notes: Source: Rochester Library exhibit on the Helen Hooker O'Malley papers — Susan Pamelia Huntington Hooker and Horace B. Hooker were her paternal grandparents (their son Elon Huntington Hooker H03434 was Helen's father, and Helen H04641 was a major dance figure married to Irish Republican general Ernie O'Malley). The Rochester URL hosts photographs of selected letters and the children's sketches; users can read the originals online.

documents.title: Mott Titus to Dr. William Hooker, July 18, 1838
documents.recipient: Dr. William Hooker (H01429), physician and NY State Legislator, South Dover, Dutchess County, New York
documents.repository_notes: Letter transcribed in full at Spared & Shared 3. Author biographical detail: Mott Titus (1802-1861), son of Samuel Jackson Titus and Ruth Amelia Titus, originally of Dover NY where he was politically active; widower of Maria Dean (1806-1836). At time of writing he had migrated to Bloomingburgh Ohio with five children, settling on a farm near the East Fork of the Little Miami River two miles from Batavia in Clermont County. He was an active Democrat in Ohio and in 1840 wrote newspaper articles attacking William Henry Harrison's Whig candidacy.
documents.description: A diaspora letter — the kind of document that held antebellum social networks together as New Yorkers pushed westward and their credit and correspondence stretched behind them. Mott Titus, formerly of the Dover Dutchess County community where Dr. Hooker practiced medicine, had migrated to Clermont County Ohio with fifteen dependents in October 1837. The letter has two practical purposes: first, a neighbor near Batavia is 'hard pressed' for $3,000 and 10% interest is the going rate, but 'there is no money to be let here' — so Titus writes East to the one prosperous contact he trusts, specifying 'I shall write to no one but you.' Second, Titus is recruiting Dr. Hooker to Ohio outright, closing with the warning that the state is filling up fast and he should come soon. The canal infrastructure passage — 450 miles operating, 300 under contract for 1839, four additional company-aided projects underway — documents the specific moment when Ohio's transportation revolution made the frontier feel like an investment rather than a gamble. The Ohio River within ten miles, macadamized turnpikes being built, land at $8-30 an acre: these are the pull forces Titus is cataloguing for a physician who might plausibly transplant a practice. The political section registers Democratic anguish at the 1838 Whig sweep of New York — Titus's former political home — with a sharp observation that voters 'change their opinions and say it is the effect of principle' but really act on self-interest. Both men are implicitly Democrats. The letter also carries a rueful self-portrait of Titus as a procrastinator who quotes Shakespeare on the subject ('Tomorrow and tomorrow and tomorrow') before finally sitting down to write. The full transcription is preserved at Spared & Shared 3.
documents.notable_quote: With an inexhaustible supply of the most valuable mineral products — such as Iron, Coal, and Salt — and with the capacity to support from the productions of her own soil a more dense population than any other state, I think there is little hazard in saying that Ohio possesses more of the self creating and self sustaining elements of future greatness than any other territory of equal extent on the face of the globe.

documents.title: Diary of Samuel Cowles, Cleveland 1849-1850
documents.summary: Approximately 50 pages, leather-backed boards (rebacked), in clear hand with a few lines in Pitman's shorthand. Bookseller's label to front pastedown: M. C. Younglove, Cleveland. Daily entries July 1849 through July 1850 by Hon. Samuel Cowles (HD3710), documenting his Cleveland legal practice (criminal defense, real estate, civil matters; clients accused of rape, arson, insanity); the 1849 cholera epidemic which Cowles himself contracted and survived; his service as secretary-treasurer of Cataract Fire Company No. V; eyewitness accounts of steamboat fires (including a man encountered in the streets crazy with grief over losing his wife and children the day before); an hour-by-hour record of President Zachary Taylor's death; joining a posse to recapture 1850 jail escapees; meeting Henry Clay; LocoFoco/Whig/Free-Soil disputes; his partner's marriage and his own son's birth; and his self-recorded depression — 'Business stagnated, and the door of the poor house opens in the distance.' Important primary source for early Cleveland history.
documents.notes: Diary covering Samuel Cowles' last full year in Cleveland before the 1852 California migration with childhood friend Edwin P. Mastick. The diary is preserved with bookseller M. C. Younglove of Cleveland; viewable via Carpe Librum Books listing.

documents.repository: Mark Twain Project, University of California
documents.notes: Buffalo, 25 January 1871. Olivia writes to her girlhood friend Alice Hooker Day five months after the death of her father Jervis Langdon, calling him her backbone; she writes in pencil from a room in the Buffalo General Hospital, where she brings the infant Langdon each day to a wet nurse. She mourns Emma Nye, who had died in the Clemens home. Clemens adds a postscript apologising to Alice's mother, Isabella Beecher Hooker, for a curt telegram.

documents.title: Deed from Wawowos of the Tunxis to Samuel Hooker Jr., 1711
documents.grantor: Wawowos, Tunxis Indian of Farmington CT (signed with his mark)
documents.grantee: Samuel Hooker Jr. of Farmington CT
documents.witness_notes: Acknowledged before William Wadsworth, Justice of the Peace, 22 July 1726 — fifteen years after the deed was dated.
documents.property: One acre and thirty rod of meadow at Indian Neck, Farmington CT, in the grindlet or hollow running through the neck; bounded north on Hooker's land and Capt. John Hart's, south on land Hooker bought of Searion, east on Capt. John Hart's, west on William Lewis.
documents.description: Sale of Tunxis meadow at Indian Neck to a Hooker, endorsed "Samuel Hooker's Indian deed." One of the transfers that emptied the Farmington township of Tunxis land — the same ninety acres at Indian Neck that Hon. John Hooker told the General Court in 1738 had always belonged to the tribe.
documents.editorial_notes: Grantee read as Samuel Hooker II (H00028), the Farmington merchant. "Jr." in 1711 is ambiguous — his son Samuel Hooker III (H00086) was 23 that year and could equally be meant. NEEDS SAM'S CALL.

documents.title: Letter from Jesse Torrey to Thomas Jefferson
documents.notes: Charlottesville, 15 August 1815. Torrey presents himself as "an enthusiastic Student of Physiology and Philosophy" and argues that the laws Newton, Franklin, Priestley and Davy found in inanimate matter must govern living bodies too. Jefferson received him and declined to collaborate.

documents.title: Testimony on the traffic in kidnapped people
documents.notes: Sworn before John Randolph of Roanoke, chairman of the House committee investigating traffickers in slaves and kidnappers, 29 April 1816. Torrey describes the coffle of 4 December 1815, the woman who leapt from the F Street tavern on the 20th, the marshal turned away at the door with a habeas corpus writ, and names the men working the trade in Delaware, Maryland and the Carolinas.
